## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**A Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library, entire, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the times of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all extant monuments of Catholic tradition through the first twelve centuries of the Church, very carefully corrected by comparison with the most accurate editions and with certain manuscripts; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the completion of the most extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with special analytical indexes following each volume or each author of some importance; arranged with chapters properly set within the text itself, and with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject matter; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal but possessing some authority with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched by two general indexes: one, namely, of subjects, by consulting which whatever each of the Fathers wrote on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other, of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented upon each passage of each biblical book, and in what places in their works. A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others if one considers: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the completeness of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and number of works reprinted, the extremely convenient form of the volumes and its consistent uniformity throughout the work, the low price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time brought together in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.**

**Second Series, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Clergy Library, or Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. The Patrology has been published in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. — The 260 volumes of the Latin edition are sold for 1,300 francs; the 1,300 [sic] volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for 800 francs. — The wholly Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are supplied in it only in Latin translation.**

## Within the Years of the Lord 1182–1190: John Beleth, Parisian theologian

[Col. 0009]

## Historical and Literary Notice

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, IV, 56)

John Beleth—Pitseus calls him Bilethus—whose being English or French Pitseus doubts. Certainly, he was head of the theological school at Paris, as Henry of Ghent testifies in chapter 18 of *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*. Afterwards he flourished in the church of Amiens in Gaul, according to Alberic’s *Chronicle* under the year 1182, p. 363. He wrote the *Rationale of Divine Matters*, or *Summary on the Divine Offices*, published at Antwerp in 1553 under the supervision of Cornelius Laurimannus; at Dillingen; and again at Antwerp in 1570, in octavo; together with Durand’s *Rationale*, at Venice in 1572 and 1581, in quarto; and at Lyons in 1565, 1583, 1592, and 1612, in octavo. Moreover, Trithemius, chapter 415, mentions various sermons of his. Pitseus also mentions a *Jewel of the Soul*, on the authority of Henry of Ghent already cited; but in Henry’s catalogue there is not a word—*οὐδὲ γρῦ* (“not even a murmur”)—about it.

[Col. 0009]

# Rationale of the Divine Offices

By John Beleth, Parisian theologian. A work written nearly four hundred years ago, now at last brought to light through the labour of Cornelius Laurimannus. (Lyons, 1672, quarto, at the end of Durand’s *Rationale*.)

## Preface of Cornelius Laurimannus of Utrecht to the Reader

Devout reader, I was not unaware, when I proposed that this book *On Ecclesiastical Offices* should first be printed, that I would almost kindle countless fires against myself. For even then, with eyes, as it were, wide open, I sufficiently foresaw that this modest labour of ours would encounter various censures. And indeed, not without reason. For, to pass over those who, however devoutly enough they think concerning matters of this kind—that is, matters belonging to the Church—cannot nevertheless restrain themselves from somehow applying their censorious rod to the labours of others: certainly I dare promise myself no safety from the bites of those who daily devise innumerable inventions of new doctrines.

These are the people who are not ashamed to call themselves Evangelicals and Paulines, although nothing is less characteristic of them than carrying out what is commanded in the Gospel and judging rightly the things handed down by Paul, who was not without reason called the chosen vessel. That this is very true has for many years now been abundantly shown by various writers, no less devout than learned. Human audacity—indeed, lest I say folly—has reached such a point; that thoughtless and headlong desire of certain people has fallen to such a point, that they do not fear, with a certain obstinacy, to take upon themselves what is most remote from them.

Therefore, I know well that I shall not be safe from their poisonous attacks; for they will never approve what we have done in this matter. For by what reasoning could they approve things which they see to conflict with their foolish and harmful teachings? What we here establish by sound and evident arguments, they utterly reject. And what, indeed, do they reject if they have invented for themselves a new Church and, in it, established new ceremonies—if the gods please! [Col. 0011]

But, by the immortal God, what kind of madness could be more evident than to wish to be wiser than the apostles, who received this present Church of ours from Christ and handed it down to us, as it were, from hand to hand? These people, then, will have much to say against me; they will make many cavils at the work we publish, lest there be someone who might plainly convict their absurdities. Indeed, it is chiefly for this purpose that we bring this author to light: that it may at last become clear how ridiculously they laugh at the things done in our Church.

First they will cry out that he is ancient, almost consumed already by moths and cockroaches, and therefore blinded in darkness so that he cannot behold the light. Yet we have made every effort to rescue him from moths of this sort; and we have done it so thoroughly that he may now readily recognize the light. In that light, unless my judgment deceives me, he will conduct himself so successfully and prosperously that heretics will receive from him no slight wound, one which no medicine, however effective, will be able adequately to heal.

Not that there are not many others capable of doing the same, or even more; but we are firmly convinced that, when he is joined to the other defenders of our Church, we shall make a much stronger and easier assault upon the line of heretics, should they form one, so that they will be compelled either to cast down the spear or yield the field to us. Indeed, I earnestly wish that many more such opponents of heretics might arise daily—men who would not shrink from fighting them with comparable strength, but would undertake to strike at their empty subtleties with the strongest arguments, like spears grasped in the hand.

For, if I possess any judgment at all—and I know how slight it is—I do not think it possible by any other means suitably to check the obstinate perversity of these innovators, unless with one united charge we pierce them, as though with swords, with the testimonies of sacred writings, so that, once they have turned their backs, they may thereafter dare not renew any novelty. In this matter we shall readily have God, best and greatest, as our helper, provided only that we enter the battle and do not shrink from joining hands in open combat with these most ruinous citizens of the Christian commonwealth. For God will never permit the Church, of which He is the head, to suffer any injury. Although I do not deny that, since the Church was founded, there have always been many and diverse heretics, we firmly believe that this happened in order that Christ might thereby rouse our indolence.

But what shall we now say? Are we not all so sunk in idle luxury and so asleep that we allow our most holy Church—which we ought uniquely to defend—to be torn, seized, shredded, and trampled by sailors, craftsmen, fullers, cobblers, buffoons, barbers, bird-catchers, fishermen, fishmongers, cooks, tailors, charioteers, and porters—in the market-place, at crossroads and brothels, at drinking parties, in workshops and barbers’ shops, publicly and privately—so that now, if it is lawful to say it, a thousand heresies are born within her? For scarcely anyone exists who has not devised some new opinion about her. But where am I being carried?

Certainly, devout reader, I can truly say this: no sufficiently bitter exclamation can be found that is fitting for this matter. Therefore, to return to ourselves, we are in no doubt that whatever we have accomplished in publishing this work will not be approved by heretics and innovators of that sort. But what is that to us, if we do not please those for whom our Church is hateful, though we render her, as is right, every honour as to a mother? To speak frankly, I pay no attention to them. I care nothing, I say, if they reject us, provided we are received by our own—that is, by those who think truly and devoutly concerning the Church, the sole bride of Christ and our mother.

For our hearts are not so hard that we would not prefer, if it were possible, praise from a single one of these persons to that of ten such wicked heretics and corrupters of the Church. Let those rage, then, for all I care, to whom, as we have said, our Church is distasteful—though I would not venture to say whether anything ought to be dearer, purer, and holier than she. For we must admit anything whatsoever rather than despise here what Christ, the source of our whole salvation, left us as the best pledge He possessed when He departed hence to the Father.

What, I ask, should we despise? Rather, let us not be so thoughtless as even to suspect anything sinister concerning her whom Christ, already fastened to the wood of the cross, took as His bride and most beloved wife. I judge this to be she of whom that delicate boy Solomon sang mystically in this manner: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song of Songs 4). She must be exceedingly beautiful in whom not even one spot is found, and who is endowed with every grace of beauty so that you can never discover anything lacking which belongs to such perfection.

Such is the Church, and she is so adorned with the virtues of her bridegroom that those who defile her and foully pollute her with their own filth ought rather to atone with death than that we should admit any excuse here. I am by no means unaware that the serpent Leviathan zealously works through his agents and raises such clouds and storms on every side in order that he may one day engulf this little vessel—the sole vessel, as it were, of our salvation—in tempests and finally sink and destroy it completely. Yet he labours in vain in all this; and, since he does not cease to fight against God in this matter, he is certainly, as the saying goes, kicking against the goad.

From what we have said, therefore, you may easily gather, even if I now say no more, how necessary it was for this work on ecclesiastical offices to be brought into public view. For if the Church ought to be as dear to us as Christ Himself requires; if she undoubtedly bestows innumerable benefits upon all Christians; if she freely receives us when we come, weary from the road and burdened with the heavy loads of our sins; if in her, after the harmful heat of a burning mind and the hopeless misery of a wasted life, we receive gentle consolation, refreshing coolness, and the delightful whispering of breezes; if, finally, we betake ourselves to her as to a most pleasant retreat, distinguished by clear springs and emerald banks, where, having laid aside the burden of sin, we are restored by food and drink so sweet and health-giving that whatever is troublesome may easily be shaken off there—then surely we cannot altogether neglect her laws, rites, and ceremonies.

Indeed, in this matter I shall readily have all pastors and priests especially well-disposed toward me, for their chief duty is so to instruct the people and flock committed to them in ceremonies of this kind that they may have no further uncertainty about them. For, if we do not wish to be ignorant of what is known even to the bleary-eyed and barbers, surely from this ignorance proceeds the whole flood of disturbances in the Christian commonwealth. And alas! How many pastors and priests are found in our time who are not merely ignorant of these matters, but are even unwilling and ashamed to learn them!

But I beg such persons to remember what Ezekiel says to them: “They profaned me among my people for a handful of barley and a fragment of bread, so that they might kill souls that should not die and preserve alive souls that should not live, lying to my people who believe lies” (Ezek. 13). Therefore the Lord God says: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who have not strengthened what was weak or healed what was sick” (Ezek. 34). What, I ask you, is this, in brief, when they are more concerned with the delicacies of food by which they may stuff their bellies than with how they may cure the errors of the people? For they are understood to do this only when they do not expound to the people the word of God and the things that belong to the salvation of souls, although God has appointed them physicians of souls and shepherds of such a kind as feed the Lord’s flock according to God’s intention—that is, as Jerome wished, with knowledge and understanding.

Indeed, I think it altogether impossible for anyone to teach another things of which he himself is inexperienced and ignorant. These men, then, will kindly receive our modest endeavour if they plainly understand that it is for their advantage. [Col. 0013] “They profaned me among my people,” says the prophet, when they strive rather to know what a fortunate cast, a cultic rite, or a throw of Venus may portend, and to judge whether wine is stronger, than to learn those disciplines which they may faithfully impart to God’s people with the greatest benefit to souls.

But woe to such people! For just as Joseph told his brothers that he would by no means admit them to his presence unless they also brought their brother with them (Gen. 43), so too Christ, the true Joseph—of whom the former expressed only a shadow—will demand from His brothers, namely priests and pastors of the most holy Church, the blood, that is, the soul, of their least brother, and will require it from their hands. If they cannot bring him, good God, how badly it will go with them! I judge no one, nor do I strike at any particular person; but “if anything—lest anything,” as the comic poet says. For, to omit other considerations, it is exceedingly disgraceful to be ignorant of the matters with which we are occupied every day.

This work, then, must be of the greatest concern to those to whose fidelity the helm of the Church has been entrusted. For here, besides the method of lawfully reading and singing the divine office, and the rites and ceremonies of the Church, they will find a truly luminous explanation of certain more obscure places of sacred Scripture, confirmed by substantial testimonies of the ancient orthodox. Moreover, I readily believe that many will accuse us of negligence and inconsistency, as though we had considered too little what becomes us: we who long ago gave ourselves the name of jurists and have hitherto served in that camp, now meddle with matters belonging to theologians.

I admit that I am acting outside my profession; and if this is to sin, I admit that as well. Yet in my judgment every profession is silent in matters concerning the common good. Certainly, the office of every person is to benefit as many as possible and harm no one. Nor am I someone who attributes so much to my own judgment that I alone conceived the whole plan of bringing this work to light. For when it first came into my hands, I immediately shared it with certain friends. Their judgment and more-than-ordinary learning were so well known to me that I did not hesitate to undertake whatever they finally persuaded me to do, even at perpetual risk to my name.

They not only urged me to publish it, but also by honourable admonitions roused me, sometimes yawning and drowsy as I was, so that it has resulted also from this that the work could not come forth more polished. We have therefore taken pains that this author—who for nearly four hundred years lay hidden, rough, uncultivated, meagre, and squalid, among the foulest papers, almost wholly gnawed away by mice—might at last come into the hands of learned men somewhat cleaner, more adorned, and more polished, with those errors removed which could have caused disgust to the reader.

You, reader, will say more truly how great were the labours this cost me when you have carefully examined every part by attentive reading. For that ancient manuscript codex was written in characters so close and compressed that it was extremely difficult for me to read; so much so that, very often, if I wished to elicit some meaning, I truly had to guess. Yet I am not unaware how odious—indeed, dangerous—guesswork is in matters of this kind.

Meanwhile, grant me pardon if words occur from time to time that are less than classical Latin, but such as ought not to have been changed. For I would have you consider here what you would willingly do elsewhere: namely, that every discipline has its own particular modes of expression. No one even moderately learned fails readily to know that the Church too has not only its own vocabulary, but also very many turns of phrase wholly unheard of among the authors of the Latin language. Yet they are of such a sort that, if I had wished to change them here, I could not; and if I could, I would not have wished to do so, lest what commonly happens to many should happen to me, who, while trying to make a matter clear, utterly distort it.

Nor should anyone be offended if he finds here at times explanations that are diffuse and, as they may seem, trivial, since in some matters this author sought not so much explanations that were true as ones that were pious and commonly familiar—for example, those concerning the disappearance of the star seen by the Magi, why a Mass for the dead is celebrated on the second feria, and other similar matters. I wished to warn you of this as well.

Therefore, finally, devout reader, I ask only this: receive with equanimity whatever labour and diligence you judge to be present here, and kindly embrace the readiness alone by which we have not allowed anyone to be deprived of this work any longer. For we confidently hope that, if it is not useful, it will at least be less burdensome to those accustomed to devote themselves especially to sacred learning and piety; so that henceforth they may learn thereby to love, honour, and observe the Church more zealously, and so in due time may be able to reach that eternal Church of which this present Church of ours is only a certain outline. That Christ may bring this about, we pray again and again, Him whom we especially desire to be honoured in this edition.

## Life of John Beleth, from John Trithemius

John Beleth, once a distinguished theologian of the Parisian school, learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in secular philosophy, ready in intellect and scholastic in speech, not undistinguished among the doctors of his age, conveyed his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity through writing and disputation. For he wrote a work not without usefulness, *On the Divine Offices*, and also various sermons. He is said to have written many other things as well, but they have not come to my knowledge.

# Rationale of the Divine Offices

## Preface and Brief Division of the Whole Work

[Col. 0013A]

In the primitive Church it was forbidden for anyone to speak unless there were someone to interpret. For what, I ask, would speaking profit if it were not understood? [Col. 0014A] Certainly nothing. Hence there grew up in certain regions of the Church that commendable custom that, after the Gospel had been read literally, it was immediately explained to the common people in the vernacular.

But what shall we say about our own times, when scarcely—indeed, hardly even scarcely—is there anyone [Col. 0015A] who understands what he has read or heard, or who adequately notices what he has seen or done? Thus we may truly say what the prophet once lamented: “The priest perishes like one of the people.” It would seem, therefore, better to keep silence than to chant, to be wholly silent rather than to dance, if we have fallen into this misfortune of the times.

Yet, lest at any time the mouths of those singing to You, Lord God, be shamefully closed, we shall apply a threefold remedy to avoid this harm, if we speak as briefly as possible: first of ecclesiastical institutions; then of expositions of the divine words; and finally of the calculation of days. The first may belong to those who are only beginning; the second [Col. 0015B] to those who already feel some progress; and the third, finally, to those who have attained a certain perfection. Let us therefore speak of these matters briefly and concisely in what follows, so that through us some provision may be made for the ignorance of those who truly do not know how they ought to think about these things.

## Chapter I. On Things Especially Consecrated to God

Although God created this entire universe from nothing chiefly for our benefit, and therefore is deservedly called the Lord of all things, according to the saying, “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Ps. 23 [24]); nevertheless, from that universe He retained certain things especially [Col. 0015C] for Himself. For just as it may be divided into four parts, so from each part He claimed something as His own: from places, places worthy of reverence; from times, feast days; from things, tithes, firstfruits, offerings, and whatever other things are customarily given; and finally from persons, those whom He holds as consecrated to Himself, such as ministers of the altar, monks, and nuns.

Of all these, namely places, times, things, persons, and their various offices, we shall speak in order below. And first, of places.

## Chapter II. On Place

Of venerable places, then, some are dedicated to prayer and others assigned to human need. The places [Col. 0015D] assigned to human need are these: a *xenodochium* (hostel for strangers), *nosocomium* (hospital for the sick), *gerotocomium* (home for the aged), *orphanotrophium* (orphanage), *prototrophium* [uncertain; perhaps an institution for foundlings], and *brephotrophium* (home for infants). Thus the Fathers and religious emperors established certain places to which pilgrims, orphans, old persons, veterans, the sick, the weak, and the wounded might resort.

But among places dedicated to prayer, some are sacred, some holy, and some religious. Sacred places are those duly consecrated to God and, as it were, sanctified by a bishop. They are called by various names, especially these: church, sanctuary, holy place, chapel, temple, oratory, tabernacle of God, monastery, cenobium, *κυριακή* (*kyriakē*, “the Lord’s [house]”), house of prayer, basilica, chapel.

But it must not be overlooked that *oratory* is sometimes used for the church [Col. 0016A] itself; and indeed any other place appointed for prayer is called an oratory, such as monks have established for themselves in their monasteries. Holy places, however, are places of immunity surrounding monasteries, secured under the threat of a specified penalty. Such may be seen in our Paris, as a kind of cloister in which stand the dwellings of the canons. For whoever is guilty of any crime, if he flees there as to an asylum, is granted very great security. Thus the walls and gates of a city, and theatres as well, were decreed by laws to be holy.

Finally, a religious place is said to be one in which an intact human body, or even merely a head, has been buried. For a mutilated body, unless the head also is present, cannot make a place religious. [Col. 0016B] Therefore, since we have so far spoken of places, one thing should be added: let us briefly explain how a church ought to be built. Once the site of the foundation has been prepared, the bishop must first sprinkle it with lustral water, which is called blessed water; and then he himself must lay the first foundation-stone, which ought to bear a cross impressed upon it, or another priest commissioned by him must lay it if he cannot be present. It is also altogether necessary that it be built facing east—that is, toward the equinoctial sunrise—and not toward the summer solstice, as some both wish and do.

## Chapter III. On Times

[Col. 0016C]

Having thus briefly explained these things concerning places, we must speak of times. Here we understand “times” as days: some of which are feast days, some solemn days, and others *profesti* (non-festal days). They are called *profesti* because they are supported by no spiritual celebration. Yet the Jews call their days one way, the pagans and their philosophers another, and Christians finally another.

The Hebrews call the first day Sabbath, which is especially esteemed among them. All the rest are named from it. Thus they call the day after the Sabbath the first, or second, of the Sabbath; the following day the second of the Sabbath; and so on through the seventh day, which they call either the seventh of the Sabbath or the Sabbath of Sabbaths.

Among the pagans, both the common people and philosophers used the same names [Col. 0016D], although their rationale differed. Both called the first day the day of the Sun; the second, of the Moon; the third, of Mars; the fourth, of Mercury; the fifth, of Jupiter; the sixth, of Venus; and the seventh, of Saturn. The common people gave them these names because they believed the sun, Mars, Mercury, and the others to be gods; philosophers, however, for this reason: that the nature of human life is governed by the movements of these planets. Accordingly, sacred Scripture by no means accepts these names, though they are commonly used everywhere.

Finally, Christians name the days very differently from these, namely by proper appellations. They did not reject the Jews’ Sabbath so completely as not gladly to retain it with them, partly because of the authority of the Hebrew language [Col. 0017A], and partly because of the meaning of the interpretation. But the following day they call the Lord’s Day, both because of Christ’s resurrection and because of the sending of the Holy Spirit from heaven, or because John the Evangelist named it so in his Apocalypse. For he says there: “I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s Day” (Rev. 1).

The day immediately after the Lord’s Day they call the second feria, and likewise the other days up to the Sabbath. They are called *feriae* from *feriari*, “to be at leisure,” not because we must be at leisure and abstain from the necessary works of life, but because throughout the whole course of our lives we ought to be free from vices.

Feast days, moreover, are solemn days, accepted, as it were, by prescription and institution in order that they alone might be observed. For *solemne* derives either from *sol* (“sun”) or from *solitum* (“customary”). [Col. 0017B] Hence the Church calls those feasts *solemnia* which have been established by fixed observance. From this also comes *solemnity*, which may be fourfold: namely, that of festivals, stations, litanies, and fasts.

## Chapter IV. On the Solemnity of Festivals

First, therefore, we must deal with the solemnity of festivals, which is commonly expressed by several names: *festivitas* (“festival”), *festum* (“feast”), *celebritas* (“celebration”), *exitus* (“departure”), *transitus* (“passage”), *obitus* (“death/departure”), *assumptio* (“assumption”), *depositio* (“laying down”), *dormitio* (“falling asleep”), *passio* (“passion”), *dedicatio* (“dedication”), *nativitas* (“birth”), *natalis*, *natale*, and *natalitium* (“birthday,” or birthday feast”).

A *festivitas* is so called as if it were the holy birth-feast of some saint. *Nativitas*, properly speaking, [Col. 0017C] is the feast of that birth which is in the flesh and in the world; thus only the birth of Christ, the Blessed Mary, and John the Baptist is called a *nativitas*, because the Church celebrates only their births. *Natalis*, *natale*, and *natalitium* refer to the departure of saints from this world, because as they die to this age and world, so then they are born into heaven. The three terms, however, are used interchangeably.

The feast concerning the death of the blessed is also called a *transitus* (“passage”), because their souls, leaving their bodies, must pass through various places unknown to them: namely, if it may be said, through the aerial, ethereal, and crystalline heavens, until they reach the empyrean heaven. It is called an *obitus* (“going to meet”), as though angels then come to meet the souls, as is recorded of St Martin. It is called a *passio* (“suffering”) [Col. 0017D] because then the body especially suffered when the soul departed from it. Consequently, the death of every person can be called a passion, since that departure of the soul and separation from the body takes place only with great pain.

For it is not without reason that St Jerome, in the *Lives of the Fathers*, tells of a certain holy man who asked the Lord to show him how a soul leaves the body without pain or distress. One day, when this man happened to be returning from his little hut, he saw beside the road a poor man lying wretchedly prostrate before him and already at the point of death. Several angels, as he clearly saw, stood near him, awaiting his soul in order to carry it to the heights. But after they had waited there [Col. 0018A] a long time, a voice sent from heaven was immediately heard addressing the angels: “Why, then, do you delay?” They replied that the Lord had commanded them to draw out the man’s soul without the body’s anguish, which they certainly could not do. Not without reason, therefore, may everyone’s death be called a passion.

The *Assumption*, properly speaking, is the passage of the Blessed Mary; and the *Deposition* is that of St John the Evangelist, who entered the tomb alive and, as it were, laid himself down in it. Finally, the death of saints is also called *dormitio* (“sleep”), because for them it is like most desired rest. For just as we generally rise from sleep stronger and more whole, so saints too will rise without difficulty in glorified bodies, as though awakened from sleep. Hence the Lord’s statement [Col. 0018B] concerning Lazarus: “Lazarus our friend sleeps” (John 11).

## Chapter V. On Feasts
Some feasts are general, others particular. General feasts are those celebrated universally by all, such as the feasts of the Trinity, the Blessed Mary, the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, Pentecost, the Holy Cross, the apostles, the evangelists, St John the Baptist and Evangelist, Lawrence, Nicholas, Sylvester, Martin, and so forth. Particular feasts are those observed only in one province, such as the feast of Blessed Hilary, which is kept only in Aquitaine. Or again, those held in a single diocese, village, or parish are called particular feasts. It should meanwhile be noted in passing that, in celebrating feasts, a certain dignity and order must be observed. The feasts of the Trinity are to be celebrated with more dignified observance; then the feasts of the Blessed Mary, especially that of the Assumption; and finally the feasts of the Holy Cross, of which there are two. Concerning the others, one who understands can easily judge. It should be known that there are as many feasts of the Blessed Mary as feasts of the Trinity. What the reasons for feasts are, and why some are celebrated not at their proper time but at another, will be explained more conveniently in what follows.

## CHAPTER VI. On Stations

It would not be inappropriate to speak now of the litanies, were we not to discuss them somewhat more suitably [Col. 0018D] when we treat of feasts according to the variety of seasons. It is therefore worthwhile to set them aside for the present and speak now of stations, in which six points must be considered. First, what a station is and why it is so called; second, whence it took its beginning; third, how many kinds there are; fourth, why this sort of solemn observance of stations was instituted; fifth, how they ought to be carried out; and lastly, what difference there is between stations, processions, and litanies.

A station, as the term is used here, is a procession made to another church in order that thanks may be rendered to God. It is called a station because we give thanks to God standing, not with bent knees as in litanies; nor do we use voices of supplication in them, but sing praise to God. Stations nevertheless seem to have come down to us from the Old Law. For then the Jewish people, and also many pagans, assembled at Jerusalem on the greatest solemnities, such as Easter and Pentecost, in order to worship in the Temple, offer gifts there, and finally give thanks to God for innumerable benefits. From this custom comes the practice still observed by our Church: that all alike should assemble from towns, villages, and other suburban places at the episcopal church in Easter Week and at Pentecost.

There are likewise other stations which derive their origin from the Romans, who engaged in such observances very frequently. Whenever at various times they perceived themselves to be besieged on every side by enemies, or graver dangers to be threatening them, they implored the intercessions of the saints, that whatever danger there was might at last cease. Having done this, they assembled in procession at the church of the saint through whose patronage they had been delivered, so that they might render God worthy thanks for so great a benefit. Thus a station was held at St Paul’s on the day when the Lord, through the invocation of his help, had delivered them; and similarly for the others.

There are two kinds of stations. Some are general and others particular. General stations are those customarily held at the principal church during the two weeks just mentioned; particular ones are held in various churches for the reason just given. Sometimes stations are also held merely for veneration, with no other cause intervening: for example, when on a saint’s feast a procession goes from the principal church to another church. Again, stations are sometimes said to take place when, for the same reason of veneration, we proceed to different altars on feast days. From what we have said, I think it is sufficiently clear what the institution of stations is.

Yet this must be added: just as the Romans decreed that stations should be held annually in their city in order to avert dangers, so also in other cities they instituted their own stations for a similar reason. We need not be overly concerned about the vestments to be used at stations, since they ought to be such as may be worn daily in choir, always observing that they are especially appropriate to the season in which the stations occur. Here there is no fasting, as in litanies. [Col. 0019D] Here, as has been said, knees are not bent; rather, songs of rejoicing are sung—namely responsories, as we call them, and antiphons, or something similar. It sometimes happens that, while stations are being performed, Mass is celebrated in the church to which the procession goes, and sometimes it is not. However this may be, when the station prayer has been completed, one always returns to the place from which one set out.

The difference between stations, litanies, and processions is this: stations are held for the causes stated above and in the manner explained; litanies, which signify supplications and petitions, are held to avert dangers and escape every misfortune, but not without fasting and humble clothing or mournful dress, with voices fashioned as supplication. Hence litanies are indeed called supplications. But all this will become clearer when we treat of it more fully a little later.

## CHAPTER VII. On Processions

Finally, there are two processions. One is that which we observe each year on Palm Branches—that is what we call the Sunday immediately preceding Easter. This represents the procession offered to the Lord by the crowds of Jews and by children with palm branches, when he came to Jerusalem riding upon an ass. The other is that which we celebrate on Sundays in memory of the procession which the disciples offered Christ on the day of the Ascension itself, after they went together with him to [Col. 0020B] the Mount of Olives, whence he was taken up while they watched. Not that this happened on a Sunday, but the procession and the whole celebration of that day were transferred to Sunday, so that it might be observed both together and more solemnly when the people especially flock to church.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Fasting

We must now consider what fasting is, whence it is named, the authority and praise, or commendation, of fasting, and its manifold distinction. The first concerns definition; the second, interpretation or origin; the third, confirmation; the fourth, love; and the fifth, finally, knowledge.

Fasting is the common satisfaction of all the members: that is, the members should make satisfaction for the sins which they have committed. Thus, if the appetite has sinned, let it fast and make satisfaction. Let the one who alone bears guilt alone bear punishment. Likewise with the eye. Hence Jeremiah: “My eye has ravaged my soul” (Lam. III). And: “Through the windows of my eyes death entered into my soul” (Jer. IX). Thus Augustine says: “Nothing is more wicked than the eye.”

Fasting may be said to derive its name from the *jejunum*, a certain intestine which, as anatomists say, is found completely empty in a dead human being. For we likewise, when fasting, ought to be wholly empty of vices, both in soul and body. Thus Augustine more fully defines fasting in his commentary on John: “It is a great and general fast to abstain from iniquities and carnal pleasures.” For this fast is perfect and complete in every respect. It is not unlike what Paul says: “Let us live soberly, piously, and justly in this age” (Tit. II).

For, he says, living soberly plainly pertains to ourselves; living piously, to the Lord; living justly, to our neighbour. Hence piety is worship rendered to God, opposed, as it were, by impiety or idolatry. Many err concerning this word *piety*, agreeing with the common usage that calls pious a person who willingly shares something from his goods with the poor, and impious one who takes to himself what belongs to the poor. But, lest we wander too long by means of a certain analogy, we shall briefly describe the vices related to impiety and the virtues which seem plainly to correspond to the name of piety.

There is a great difference between a disgraceful act, a crime, and impiety. A disgraceful act concerns ourselves; a crime is committed against one’s neighbour; impiety, against God. Likewise, a great distinction is made between mercy, clemency, and piety. For just as mercy is chiefly concerned with nature, so we say that clemency concerns justice, and piety God. For example, it is mercy when someone sees a man justly condemned being led to punishment and, moved and affected by a natural inclination, frees him from punishment. Likewise it is called mercy when we restore to a poor person what has been stolen from him. Clemency, however, is when we see someone punished unjustly and expose ourselves to dangers in order to rescue him by force. Piety, finally, is worshipping God, and doing so from pure love; the Greeks call this *latreia* (λατρεία, “service” or “worship”) or *theosebeia* (Θεοσέβεια, “reverence for God”), while we may rightly call it the worship of God.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Authority of Fasting

The authority of fasting is threefold. It has authority partly from the antiquity of time, partly from the character of the place, and partly, finally, from the institution and majesty of the commandments. From the antiquity of time, because it began immediately after the creation of the world, in humanity’s very creation, when it was said: “You shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (Gen. II). From the character of the place, because it was instituted in Paradise. From its teacher, because it was ordained not by a human being but by God.

Again, fasting is commended by times and persons. By times, indeed, because fasting was always observed in the time before the Law, in the time under the Law, and in the time of grace: before the Law by Moses, under the Law by Elijah, and in the time of grace by Christ. Its commendation is full of examples. Eve, so long as she abstained, remained an incorrupt virgin and remained in Paradise. But once she violated the commandment of fasting, she immediately experienced the corruption of the flesh, was subjected to her husband, and shortly afterwards was shamefully cast out of Paradise. In the same way Adam, as soon as he broke the fast, was cast down from the delights of Paradise into this misery of mortality (Gen. III).

Moses spoke with God after fasting. Elijah likewise, after fasting, was carried into heaven in a fiery chariot (IV Kings II). Jerusalem, in the time of King Hezekiah and Isaiah, was delivered from Sennacherib when one hundred and eighty-five thousand were slain from heaven in a single night; and, lest they should stink among the burned bodies, Sennacherib alone fled with only ten men to Nineveh, where sixty days later he was killed by his own sons (II Chron. XXXII). Likewise, when Jonah proclaimed God’s wrath, the Ninevites, undertaking a penitential fast in sackcloth and ashes, obtained pardon (Jonah III). Joshua son of Nun likewise, by fasting—while he continued it through an entire day at Gibeon—restrained the course of the sun and moon and conquered his enemies. Thus fasting is commended by these persons; and by its place, because it was born in Paradise. The distinction of fasting follows.

## CHAPTER X. On the Distinction of Fasting

Fasting may first be divided thus: one kind is of the flesh, another of the mind. It is a fast of the flesh when someone abstains from food; of the mind, when someone fasts from vices. A fast of the flesh may also be said to occur when someone fasts because of excessive corpulence, lest the body become too fat. But this has no virtue at all; it should rather be called a regime of slimming. In the same manner we wish the mind’s fasting to oppose luxury, lest it likewise grow excessively fat and indulge itself in many things.

Second, fasting is distinguished in this way also: one kind is of institution, another of devotion, another of equality, and another [Col. 0022B] of dispensation. The fast of institution is Lent, instituted long ago by the holy Fathers. For just as under the Old Law the holy Fathers were accustomed to render to God tithes and first-fruits of all their possessions, so we too ought to offer him tithes and first-fruits, not only from our possessions—namely crops and other things we own—but also from ourselves: by fasting, that is, bodily from food and mentally from vices. For, as we have just said, fasting is alike of flesh and mind. We offer God first-fruits and tithes from ourselves when we do good works.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Institution of Lent and the Other Forms of Fasting

[Col. 0022C] Lent was instituted as a tithe of the days. But why it is named from the number forty rather than another number has an evident explanation: in a year we can plainly find forty days as a tithe. Just as the Levites, from the tithes offered them, rendered a tenth part to the high priest, so we give a tithe to Christ, the true high priest, from the thirty-six days which are a tenth of three hundred and forty days, and from the six hours and a quarter which are beyond the three hundred and forty days. Since, therefore, there are in total forty-one days and a quarter, from forty we have four as a tithe; when these are counted with the other thirty-six, they make forty. One day and a quarter still remains, namely thirty hours, a tenth part of which is three hours; for these we fast on Easter Saturday until night.

There are, however, three hundred and forty-six days in a year, a tenth part of which is thirty-six days, together with the tenth of a quarter, on account of which Augustine wished the Mass of that day to be celebrated by night on the vigil of Easter. Hence, on that day, we read in the prayer which we call the collect: “O God, who hast made this most holy night …” Lent is therefore called, as it were, “four with the tithe.” Four days, which come from the tithe, are added to thirty-six days. The first is of sanctification—that is, purification, if one may so speak—because then a person is cleansed and washed both in soul and body. The other three [Col. 0023A] are of first-fruits.

The first of the forty days is the Wednesday of Lent. The other three, as has been said, are of first-fruits. It should certainly not be unknown that three fast-days are observed in each season; they are called first-fruits because this arrangement has been made concerning them. Accordingly, the fast of dispensation is that which is said to occur on the vigils of great solemnities. Our forebears used to keep vigil on the night immediately preceding a feast; hence they called the days immediately preceding feasts “vigils.” Young men and women, singers and players, assembled at these vigils, as still happens in many regions, such as Poitou, especially at the feasts of church patrons. But because many inconveniences arose from this, fasts were instituted to take the place of vigils, so that excessive feasting and the drunkenness which frequently occurred might thereby be removed.

We have received that this was so arranged by the Church. Yet if someone were both to fast and keep vigil, he would certainly not do badly. Nothing prevents the doubling of a good thing. This arrangement is called a dispensation, as though it were, so to speak, a weighing-out among different things. For this fast was introduced as compensation for vigils, which were abolished so that those frequent feasts and drunkenness might no longer occur. Sometimes, however, a dispensation is a just relaxation, made for a due reason by the person concerned, of canonical strictness—as also in this instance. For they saw that fasting was better than keeping vigil.

The fast of devotion is when someone fasts voluntarily, as on the vigil of Blessed Martin and Blessed Nicholas. The fast of equality is when we fast on the vigil of St James, Bartholomew, and the other apostles, for whom fasting has not been instituted. Yet we do so because all the apostles are equal in merits and rewards. For those whose merits are equal must plainly have equal souls in heaven.

For this reason the Church judged it fitting that all alike should have fasts. Of the apostles, however, only six have a fast of institution; and since four of these are fasted jointly, there are only four apostolic fasts in all. Peter and Paul have one jointly, because they suffered on the same day. So too Simon and Jude, who thus make two fasts together; Matthew has the third, and Andrew the fourth.

Why we fast for these but not for the others is readily explained. The Holy Church decreed that this should be done on their vigils so that, just as they suffered for Christ’s name, we too might in some degree suffer with them if we wish to live blessedly with them. It would have instituted the same practice for the other apostles also, had something else not prevented it. These impediments are as follows. The feast of Philip and James falls on the Kalends of May, always between Easter and Pentecost; since that is a season of gladness and joy, one must not fast. The fasts which occur on the days of the Litanies or Rogations do not conflict with this, since they are held for another necessity, as will appear more clearly in what follows. For some also fast then in expectation of the Holy Spirit.

James the son of Zebedee was beheaded by Herod during the days of unleavened bread; consequently he has neither a fast nor can his feast be celebrated then. For his feast, observed on the seventh day before the Kalends of August, is held not in remembrance of his Passion or death, but of his translation. At that time a church was first dedicated to him in Spain, as will be shown more fully where we discuss his feast. There is another impediment to fasting for Bartholomew, whose feast falls on the eighth day before the Kalends of September. For he is said to have been flayed on one day and to have died on the next, although this is not at all found in his *Legend* or *Life*. If this were so, it would be necessary for his vigil to be kept on the second day before the feast, contrary to the rule of the other festal fasts.

There is no need to fast for Blessed Thomas because his feast falls in the Advent of the Lord, during which we ought to observe what is virtually a continuous fast. Barnabas has no fast because he is not among the number of the apostles. Indeed, he is called an apostle only because, as Paul’s companion, he was sent out to preach like the others. Hence: “Set apart Barnabas and Paul” (Acts XIII). No fast was instituted for Matthias because his feast more commonly falls in Lent, [Col. 0024C] when fasting occurs anyway; or because he was not one of the original apostles, but after Christ’s Passion was chosen by the others to replace Judas (Acts I). Of him it is said: “Let another take his episcopate” (Ps. CVIII). Finally, the feast of Blessed John the Evangelist is always celebrated on the third day after Christ’s Nativity, when fasting is not permitted because of the feast days.

Nevertheless, nothing prevents the fasts of all the apostles from being observed. Whoever fasts does very well, just as those who honour Blessed James fast on his vigil, the seventh day before the Kalends of August. But this kind of fasting is called a fast of equality, because it is undertaken according to merit, not institution.

Again, one kind of fasting is of inspiration, another of prudence. A fast of inspiration is such as that of Blessed Nicholas, who, still an infant in his cradle, abstained from his mother’s breasts twice a week and sucked only once on Wednesdays and Fridays. A fast of prudence is when we fast because of an impending storm, danger from enemies, or some similar misfortune.

Further, one fast is reasonable and another unreasonable. A reasonable fast is one which reason itself readily accepts: when we take food and drink moderately, lest the body thereby be weakened. Hence the Apostle says: “Let your service be reasonable” (Rom. XII); “not in feasting and drunkenness,” and so forth (Rom. XIII). An unreasonable fast is when someone wishes to fast for two or three continuous days, or even a whole week. God does not approve such fasting: he wishes fasting to compel vices to die, not nature to be destroyed. Thus it is quite plain that the fast which some prolong from the Lord’s Supper until Easter may be forbidden.

There are also other forms of fasting, which we shall touch upon with the same brevity. One is of quality, another of quantity, another of number, another of utmost strictness, another of alternation, so to speak, and another of xerophagy. We call a fast of quality one in which we impose upon ourselves abstinence from meat for the future; of quantity, one in which someone restricts food to a fixed measure and has, as though weighed out, exactly how much he will eat each day. A fast of number is when someone resolves that thereafter he will take food only once each day, or twice, because those who do it more frequently debase and cast themselves down so that there is plainly no difference between them and brute animals. For just as animals are chiefly born for feeding, so they fill their bellies more than once each day. To refresh oneself twice is human; once, they say, angelic. Therefore those who have resolved to eat only once each day with the angels are thought to practise this kind of fasting.

This is more tolerable; stricter is that called a fast of utmost strictness, such as is observed by those who eat roots and herbs, like John the Baptist in the desert and Mary of Egypt in the wilderness. She crossed the Jordan with only two loaves and lived an austere and solitary life for five years. A fast is said to be one of alternation when someone fasts alternately: that is, if he abstains on one day, he eats the next. Xerophagy is a fast in which someone eats dry food. For *xerophagy* derives from Greek *xēros* (ξηρός, “dry”) and *phagō* (φάγω, “I eat”), as though we said “dry eating”; it may consist of apples, pears, chestnuts, plums, and other things of that sort. Some, however, think that dry eating means raw or cooked legumes, provided that they are eaten without broth.

Lastly, there is a fast of vanity or pretence, as among hypocrites who fast because of feigned holiness so that all may admire them; a fast of necessity, as among beggars; and a fast of virtue, as among those who impose true abstinence upon their bodies, abstain in soul from fault, kindly distribute to the needy the food that they deprive their own bellies of, and wish others who are hungry to be satisfied from their own provisions. So much, then, concerning fasting and its manifold distinctions.

## CHAPTER XII. On Persons

After speaking thus far of times spiritually consecrated to God, the subject itself requires that we speak in the same manner next of persons devoted to the divine offices, that is, ecclesiastical persons. For a fuller explanation of this matter, it must first be known that there are three sects most approved among humankind: one of the gentiles or pagans, another of the Hebrews, and [Col. 0026A] a third of Christians. The first is of error, the second of truth, the third of salvation. In the first we suffer shipwreck; in the second we are indeed rescued from danger; but in the third we are saved. The first again cuts us off and separates us from God; the second enlightens us; the third wholly saves and delivers us.

But pagan custom has been converted into Christian rite—a change, by God Most Good and Great, truly most beautiful. For Christian persons, both secular and ecclesiastical, have been derived from the other two sects, namely the Hebrew and the pagan. For just as among us there are two kinds of persons—lay or popular persons (*laikos*, λαικός, means “the people”), and ecclesiastical persons—so there were among pagans and Hebrews, from whom ours took their beginning.

Among the pagans, secular persons were these: the monarch, namely the Roman emperor; patricians, who were also called senators and at whose discretion all things were ordered; kings, dukes, governors, prefects, tribunes of the people, military tribunes, praetors, centurions, decurions, commanders of four, tribunes, quaestors, aediles, and palace doorkeepers. In the ritual of temples there were chief flamines, flamines, and priests of both sexes. For among them, no differently from among us now, there were religious communities of women and men. Among poets there were judges of songs, comic poets, tragedians, historiographers.

Among the Hebrews likewise there was the same diversity of persons. Some were secular and others continually devoted to divine worship in temples. The persons in temples were these: the high priest, lesser priests, Levites, Nethinim, trimmers of lamps, exorcists, gatekeepers or temple-keepers, and singers. Among secular persons, Moses was first the leader of the people for governing; under him, according to the counsel of his father-in-law Jethro, he appointed these: chiliarchs, hecatontarchs, pentacontarchs or pentecosiarchs, and decarchs—that is, commanders of thousands, hundreds or centurions, fifties, and tens. For *chilia* (χιλία) denotes the number thousand, and *archōn* (ἄρχων) “ruler”; hence a *chiliarch* (χιλίαρχος) is one who presides over a thousand. Likewise *hekaton* (ἑκατόν) means a hundred; hence a hecatontarch is one whom a hundred obey, and a pentacontarch one whom fifty obey, for *pentēkonta* (πεντήκοντα) means fifty. Those who have ten under their authority are rightly called decarchs from *deka* (δέκα), “ten,” because they are over groups of ten.

Among Christians likewise, persons are partly popular and partly clerical. The popular persons are not different from those we say existed among pagans, although clerical persons are not everywhere the same. Clerical persons administer the Church and are called *apo tou klērou* (ἀπὸ τοῦ κλήρου), “from the lot,” as though chosen by lot. For in the Old Testament priests were chosen by lot. Likewise, pagans chose one of their children for clerical office by lot. They may nevertheless be called clerical because they receive the Lord’s inheritance, namely tithes and offerings. For *klēros* (κλῆρος) among the Greeks means not only what we call a lot, but also an inheritance. It is equivocal among them: by one word it signifies both things.

Clerical persons are divided into monks—said to be those living alone, from *monos* (μόνος), “alone,” and *echō* (ἔχω), “I have,” because they ought to live by themselves apart from others—and ecclesiastics. What diversity there is among monks is, I think, sufficiently well known. For the whole matter must be taken from the variety of orders, some of which they call white or clothed in white, others black.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Ecclesiastical Persons

There are two kinds of ecclesiastical persons. Some are persons of dignity, others of order. Persons of dignity are the pope, patriarch, cardinal, primate, archbishop or metropolitan—the two terms having the same meaning—bishop, archdeacon, and archpriest. In choir there are the dean, subdean, cantor, subcantor, treasurer, and scholaster. Persons of order are priest, deacon, subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, reader, and doorkeeper. There are seven grades in the order, signifying the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, through whose gift they carry out the duties of those orders.

But since we have undertaken to treat of ecclesiastical persons according to our own time, let us see how persons have been transferred from the ancient custom of both pagans and Jews to the worship of the present Church, both in order and dignity. First, in respect of order: in the Old Testament there were priests, such as the sons of Aaron, who offered sacrifices for the people. [Col. 0027C] There were also certain teachers among the people, such as Nicodemus. In their place our priests have succeeded: they offer to God for us the sacrifice of the altar and are obliged to teach God’s word to the people committed to them. They are called *sacerdotes*, as though “givers of sacred things,” and presbyters, as though elders—not indeed in age, but in learning and morals.

The order of deacons—that is, ministers, for that is all the term means—takes the place of the Levites. For just as under the Old Law the Levites assisted the priests of the Old Testament in sacrifices, so these assist the priests of the New Testament in the sacrament of the altar. Subdeacons have been put in place of the Nethinim, who were so called because they served in humility. For just as they administered sacred things under the Levites, so subdeacons do under deacons; hence they are called subdeacons.

In the Temple there were trimmers of lamps, who both lit and extinguished candles. In our Church these are those whom we call acolytes and candle-bearers, who carry and prepare wax candles and the censer. In the time of the Old Law exorcists—that is, adjurers—drove demons from people by Solomon’s teaching. We similarly have exorcists, who exorcise those who are to become catechumens, namely when by adjuration they expel demons from them. There were singers in the Temple; among us there are readers or anagnosts. In our Church doorkeepers fulfil the office of the Temple’s gatekeepers. For the gatekeepers’ duty was to close and open the Temple, admit the clean, and exclude the unclean. The duty of doorkeepers [Col. 0028A] is to introduce into the church catechumens who are to be baptized and penitents already reconciled by bishops.

## CHAPTER XIV. How Persons of Dignity Passed from the Ancients to Us

We must now see how persons of dignity came to our Church from the ancients. The lord pope—that is, “Father of fathers” or “guardian of fathers”—holds the place of the high priest who existed under the Law, just as the Roman emperor does that of the monarch. Senatorial power and the dignity of patricians, which perhaps were observed among the Jews, still remain in our Church in the three patriarchs: those of Antioch, Alexandria, and Constantinople. Primates, who preside or may preside over three archbishops, represent the king, whose authority extends to three duchies. Metropolitans or archbishops are compared to dukes, who preside over several counts; for archbishops too are said to preside over several bishops. Bishops resemble counts. Co-bishops, whose dignity has now been abolished, are equated with prefects. Abbots imitate military tribunes; chancellors, praetors; archdeacons, centurions; deans, decurions. Archpriests take the place of advocates; presbyters, of aediles; deacons, of commanders of four; subdeacons, of tribunes. Finally, exorcists represent quaestors; doorkeepers, palace doorkeepers; readers, reciters of poems; acolytes, writers of poems.

## CHAPTER XV. On Things Especially Owed to God

[Col. 0028C]

Let us now undertake the fourth matter we proposed: briefly to explain what things are spiritually owed to God, though they are sufficiently clear in themselves. They are tithes, first-fruits, vows, sacrifices, offerings, and gifts. First-fruits had their beginning with the first human beings. For we read that Cain and Abel offered God first-fruits from the produce of their labours: Abel, lambs; Cain, sheaves of grain. One of them, however, because he offered all that was best both justly and with a cheerful countenance, richly earned God’s favour, and his flock abounded in offspring of the greatest fertility; for this reason, innocent and prefiguring Christ, he became the first martyr. The other, because he did not render first-fruits rightly, giving all that was worst, displeased God and became the first to incur the sin of parricide or homicide, because he did not obtain the expected return from his labour (Gen. IV).

In the same way, we have learned from God’s command that the people of Israel gave God first-fruits from all their labour. Therefore reason itself requires that we Christians do likewise. What is to be given, and in what manner, the example of Abel and Cain teaches us abundantly enough.

Indeed, we cannot fail to remember that we have received all things from God, and that whatever we possess has proceeded from him; for that very reason it is fitting that we offer him firstfruits and in some manner render thanks for benefits received. [Col. 0029A] But if it is asked to whom the firstfruits should be given, and in what amount, we readily answer that they should be bestowed upon priests. This, however, is not to be understood as though they must necessarily be given to these alone and not also to others. For we may, if we wish, give to hermits, to those who lie hidden and enclosed in remote places, and to other religious persons. Nor is there any fixed and determined amount in these matters: one may give as much as seems proper, and no more, provided that it proceeds from charitable affection.

In the Old Law it was commanded that they should give tithes from all their goods, because God claimed for himself a tenth from all things, which he assigned to the tribe of Levi for the performance of its office. Thus we too ought likewise to act. But if tithes are unjustly possessed by laymen, [Col. 0029B] we are nonetheless bound to pay them. Nor is it lawful to wink at them or to dispense with them, but they must render them for so long as God has not corrected their unjust possession into something better. Therefore, if anyone has presumed to withhold a tithe, he has certainly become a transgressor and violator of the divine commandment, and has sinned mortally. Moreover, whoever does this should know that he not only withholds the tenth, but also undoubtedly possesses unjustly the other nine parts. So serious a thing is it not to render what belongs to God!

## CHAPTER XVI. On vows and sacrifices

We owe our vows to God. Hence: “Make vows and fulfill them,” etc. (Ps. 75). But some vows are of necessity, others of free will. Necessary vows are those joined to faith, such as those which we make in baptism, when we vow that we shall observe Christ’s faith and wholly renounce the works of Satan. By a vow of necessity we are likewise bound to observe the Ten Commandments. Such vows cannot at all be altered, but must be observed perpetually.

Among voluntary vows, some are made with discretion and some without discretion. Vows of children are indiscreet, while they are not yet their own masters but are under their parents. Such vows may lawfully be omitted, if that seems expedient, or if the parents, under whose authority they are placed, choose to oppose them. Thus women’s vows are called indiscreet when they are under the authority of their husbands. [Col. 0029D] For example: if a girl not yet marriageable and not yet arrived at the years of puberty had vowed perpetual chastity, and shortly afterwards her parents wished to compel her to contract marriage, she could indeed marry and would not be bound to fulfill her vow.

Likewise, if a man’s wife, without her husband’s knowledge, had made a vow of a journey to Jerusalem, her husband could, if he wished, recall her, because she is under his authority. But in that case the wife could not recall her husband, unless he had vowed chastity. For this is permitted to neither of them except insofar as both consent to it. One therefore cannot, and ought not, vow chastity without the other, since each is bound to render the marital due to the other.

Yet indiscretion in vows is understood not only in persons of this kind. Sometimes even among more mature persons, and those entirely free, vows are made indiscreetly which deserve punishment rather than fulfillment. [Col. 0030A] Such would be the case if someone vowed to do what he could not possibly accomplish, or what would so weaken his nature that there would be danger of his succumbing under the burden and being deemed his own killer. Certainly, whatever vows we make with deliberation and sound judgment must be kept perpetually and altered at no time.

Whereas many kinds of sacrifice were offered under the Old Law, as is found in Leviticus, in the Church of Christians or believers only one sacrifice is celebrated: namely, that of the body and blood of the Lord. Since we shall speak of this more fully in what follows, when we treat the office of the Mass, let us for the moment pass it over.

## CHAPTER XVII. On offerings and donations

Now concerning offerings. Just as under the Old Law the people gathered at Jerusalem for certain great solemnities—namely, the feasts of Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles—in order to pray in the Temple, where all were also bound by obligation to make an offering, so all Christians, by the institution of the holy Fathers, are bound to offer according to the measure of their means at the four principal solemnities: the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, Pentecost, and the feast of All Saints, so that priests may thereby have their sustenance. Moreover, they ought to offer in order that [Col. 0030C] the paschal wax candle may be bought and that both oil and wax for lighting the church may be procured. At other times no one is to be compelled to make offerings. If they are made, however, they are voluntary, as are those customarily given after confessions. But the sale of burial places in certain churches, and the exaction of gifts for the ringing of bells, is as though the sacraments of the Church were being sold.

## CHAPTER XVIII. What the office is, and how many kinds there are

Since, then, we have so far explained, as was proposed, the places, times, persons, and things spiritually dedicated to God, it follows that we must now speak of the fifth and final item in the proposition: ecclesiastical offices. First we must see what an office is; second, why it is so called; third, how it should be treated. An office is, as Isidore defines it, the proper or fitting action of each person according to the laws and customs of the city or the institutions of his profession. Monks have different offices, canons different ones, solitaries and hermits others, and so with the rest.

But, as Jerome says in the book *On Duties*, *officium* [duty] is so called as though from *efficium* [performance]. For it is fitting that each person perform his own duty. Here we must treat offices partly in general and partly in particular. There are certain general and uniform offices observed throughout the year, such as [Col. 0031A] the prayers of the hours, Vespers, Compline, and certain Masses and Matins. There are also certain special offices, differing according to the variety of seasons and the distinction of solemnities. They vary by season because some are celebrated in the Easter season, others in Lent, others in summer, and still others in Advent; and by the interval or distinction of solemnities, because one manner is used at this solemnity and another at another. For at Easter itself only three lessons are recited, but at the Nativity nine.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the general office

First we must speak of the general office, and in this order: first, let us consider what should be sung and chanted; next, by whom the ecclesiastical office was instituted; third, to what end it contributes, why and when it was ordained; and finally, by whom it was canonized and confirmed.

First, then, we say generally that nothing should be sung, chanted, or even read that has not been approved by the supreme pontiff. In the primitive Church different persons sang different things, each according to his own inclination, provided that what he sang pertained to divine praise. Yet for the most part they observed the offices established from the beginning—by Christ, such as the Lord’s Prayer, or by the Apostles, such as the Creed.

Later the Church was, as it were, torn apart through various heresies and schisms. When the Emperor Theodosius, who in his own time extirpated all heresies, saw this, he instructed Pope Damasus to summon to him some wise Catholic who might order the ecclesiastical office. Damasus therefore commanded Jerome, a man most skilled in three languages and at that time suited to the task, to reduce certain ecclesiastical offices to a fixed order. At that time Jerome lived at Bethlehem with Paula, Eustochium, and other religious virgins, after he had previously lived at Rome under the seven apostolic men.

Accordingly, as regards the psalms, he arranged which should be sung on which days. He also put the Gospels, Epistles, and other offices into a certain order, so that it might once for all be established what should be sung on each day. For he composed almost all the chants, except those which other doctors of the Church added later. [Col. 0031D] When Jerome had completed this work, he sent it to Rome, where it was approved by Pope Damasus and canonized in a general council. Finally, Pope Damasus gave the work such authority that thereafter it would always be observed in all churches as it had been ordered therein. Thus it has now been shown by whom ecclesiastical offices were instituted, for what reason, when, to what end, and who canonized them.

## CHAPTER XX. On the office itself

With these points considered, it is worthwhile to pursue the office itself, beginning with the night office. [Col. 0032A] For this order is fitting and appropriate, lest we proceed from light toward darkness, but rather emerge from darkness into light.

It must therefore be known that in the time of the primitive Church it was customary to rise three times during the night to celebrate the divine office: first, about the first sleep, in consideration of the time when ordinary people were accustomed to give themselves to rest; second, about midnight; and third, a little before daybreak. The order was that, when the nocturns had ended and the lessons with their responsories had been read, before daylight, as dawn appeared, they would sing *Te Deum laudamus* to the ringing of bells, and then the morning praises.

At the first nocturn only the ministers of the Church rose, who, having gone to bed earlier, had already slept. But since we frequently use the term *nocturna*, it will be useful to explain what it signifies. Thus *nocturna nocturnae* is understood as the hour, and *nocturna nocturnorum* as the offices themselves. Or the *nocturna nocturnae* are called the psalms said on Sundays before the lessons are recited. Likewise those said on weekdays—for instance, on Monday, “The Lord is my light” (Ps. 26)—and so with the rest. The *nocturnae nocturnarum* are the times at which the psalms are sung. The *nocturni nocturnorum* are called the nine psalms and nine lessons with their responses.

Let us now continue. At solemnities, ministers and married persons alike—men as well as women—rose for the second [Col. 0032C] nocturn. Finally, all rose together for the third nocturn. But afterwards, as charity toward God grew cold and that fervor of divine worship in people cooled, so that both the ministers of the Church and the rest had become too sluggish to rise for the night office at those appointed hours, it was decided that at least all should rise at midnight, in accordance with the Prophet’s saying, “At midnight I rose,” etc. (Ps. 123), and then immediately complete the whole night office. This is still observed by many religious communities.

But this institution too shortly fell into disuse, when people gave themselves more to banquets and luxury than to God’s service. [Col. 0032D] Therefore it was again otherwise established: all should rise at the time of the last nocturn, about the dawn. But now the state of divine worship has sunk so low that boys rise earlier than ministers of the Church, and sparrows sing before priests. So completely has that love of God grown cold in people.

In remembrance of that first highly praiseworthy custom, the Church still celebrates the night office in summer at the time of the first nocturn, which we call Vigils—though sometimes somewhat earlier. This is done for two reasons: to commend the ancients, and to exhort us ourselves, so that we may know how sober they were in the night offices in winter, whom the shortness of summer nights did not in the least delay although [Col. 0033A] they rose three times every night. Yet how many of us can now cheerfully rise for that office when the sun is already shining? We seem to be Penelope’s suitors, born to sleep through the middle of the day. But why do I speak of the night office? How many are there who properly attend even to the day office? Certainly, if one may speak as the facts are, very few.

But lest anyone doubt on which feasts that ancient custom is observed, it should be known that it is observed at the three Vigils: of John the Baptist, of Peter and Paul, and of the Assumption of Blessed Mary. For these are the principal solemnities which we have in summer.

## CHAPTER XXI. Why they rose three times at night

[Col. 0033B] The following reason may be given why they rose three times during the night: our forefathers were moved to it by a certain analogy. Just as those whose city is besieged by enemies can readily defend themselves from attack by day, when they combine their common forces, but cannot do so by night, they therefore usually divide the night into three watches. During the first sleep all keep watch, because that time is most dangerous; shortly afterwards only those remain at the walls who were first assigned to watch, until cockcrow; then those rise whose duty it is to keep the second watch and stay awake until the cock crows; and finally the third guards rise, until it is day.

Thus the holy Fathers adopted a similar custom of taking watches in turn for guarding the most holy Church, which is the one city of all believers. The devil attacks it daily and seeks in every way to overthrow it once for all, especially at night, when he chiefly lies in wait for us. Night is suited to shameful sins—thievery, adulteries, and many others—because people hope to remain concealed and feel less shame. Hence: “He who does evil hates the light” (John 3). For as light is open, it leaves nothing covered; but night, being dark, does not know how to blush. Therefore we must keep more careful watch at night against the hidden enemy’s snares, lest we be driven by them to shameful acts.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the representation of the three times

[Col. 0033D] It should also be noted that in these offices of the three nocturns we represent three times: the time before the Law, the time under the Law, and the time of grace. Each of these varies through three divisions.

The first division of the time before the Law was from Adam to Noah; the second, from Noah to Abraham; the third, from Abraham to Moses. The time under the Law had these divisions: from Moses to David; from David to the Babylonian captivity; and from the captivity to Christ. Finally, the first division of the time of grace was the time of apostolic and evangelical preaching; the second, the time of assault, which [Col. 0034A] produced all heresies; the third, the time of peace, when every heresy was wholly extinguished.

When these divisions are counted together, we find nine varieties of times, which we find not obscurely in the number of psalms sung in the night office. On feast days we employ nine psalms, nine lessons, nine responses, and nine verses. In each nocturn there are three psalms, three lessons, three responses, and three verses. Yet it should be understood that the set of nine psalms, the set of nine lessons, and the set of nine responses with as many verses are taken as one and the same thing with respect to the figure of the world.

In the varieties of times just enumerated, the holy Fathers kept watch most excellently, diligently applying themselves to good works. In order that we too may in some manner be made like them through their merits, we express this in the night office by the number nine of psalms, lessons, and so forth, to God’s praise, mutually rousing one another against the devil’s snares.
