Therefore in the three nocturns we say nine psalms and lessons with the rest, that we may chiefly please the Trinity and be able to be joined to the nine orders of angels.

Nor is it without reason that we chiefly do these things at night, since this present city of ours—the Church—is, as it were, a shadow of that heavenly Church which we shall attain by divine grace. This office of the three nocturns is celebrated especially on Sundays, at the solemnity of the Trinity, and on saints’ feasts, because we firmly believe [Col. 0034C] that they have already attained the joys of the Lord’s resurrection, which Sunday signifies. For the same reason, on their feasts we offer nine psalms with as many lessons and responsories, in order to show that they have been joined to the nine orders of angels.

On the nights of days that are not solemn, however, twelve psalms—what ordinary people call a *dieta*—are sung with six antiphons, and three lessons and as many responses are recited, because twelve hours are assigned to the day and as many to the night. Thus we offer God one psalm for each hour of the night, that by God’s countless mercy we may be freed from the night of error and from the blindness of our mind, into which the devil cast us through the sin of the first parent. The six antiphons signify the six works of mercy; if we observe these rightly, we shall without doubt come from the darkness of this night to the true light, that is, Christ.

Moreover, we join two psalms here in order to show through them that our praises and works are of no value without charity, which consists in love of God and neighbor, between whom there is no middle term. But we conclude the two psalms thus joined with one *Gloria*, because our praises are then acceptable to God when we persevere in charity. Finally, the three lessons denote the three ages: childhood, youth, and old age. In these we are bound, by keeping the best watch, to praise the Lord lest we be deceived by the devil.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the arrangement of St Benedict

[Col. 0035A] Blessed Benedict arranged the night office quite differently, not because he disagreed with the Church’s earlier institution, but for another reason, as we shall immediately say. Nor was he contradicted in anything; whatever he did was approved and confirmed by Blessed Gregory. Since this most holy man was truly regarded as enlightened by the Holy Spirit, it was believed that he would not have arranged the office otherwise unless he had received it from the same Spirit.

Blessed Benedict, then, aspiring to the summit of a more perfect life, ordained that six psalms should be sung in the first nocturn, together with four lessons and four responsories, and the same number in the second, [Col. 0035B] thereby plainly indicating to us the twofold life, contemplative and active. For the number six of the psalms signifies the active life, in which it is fitting to practice the six works of mercy if we wish happily to attain the perfection of the contemplative life. This latter is expressed here by four lessons just as it is through the four Evangelists.

In the third nocturn, moreover, he ordained that three canticles be sung in praise of the Trinity, from whom we certainly believe and hope that every perfection of life is given to us. These canticles end with *Alleluia*, the song of heavenly joy, so that it may be clearly indicated that the Trinity is worthy of heavenly praise and that human praise is not sufficient fully and perfectly to praise it.

The four Gospel lessons which follow signify that those who praise God ought, through the teaching of the four Gospels, to be adorned with four virtues; and the four responsories accordingly signify the zeal of those who praise. But lest, while doing this, they ascribe all this good to themselves, and rather that they may attribute everything to divine praise and recognize themselves as God’s servants in all things, *Te Deum laudamus* is suitably added. Afterwards the Gospel is read, which signifies the number ten—that is, eternal life—which will be worthily rendered to those who praise. By the hymn which follows, namely, *Te decet laus*, etc., is denoted the joy which the saints will have after their labor as the recompense of the denarius. But since the office of monks seems to have nothing to do with us, it is enough to have said this much about it; let us pursue our subject.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the ringing of bells and the beginning of the morning time

When the ministers of the Church rise for the night office, just as guards in a camp awaken one another with trumpets, so they first ring the bells as a sign to the faithful that they should keep vigil through the night, fortify themselves against the devil who lies in wait, and exalt their Creator with praises. Through him they most certainly hope to be delivered from the darkness of sins and the wickedness of demons.

How bells should be rung on great solemnities, Sundays, lesser feasts, and other ordinary days will more suitably be said elsewhere. While the bells are ringing, the church [Col. 0036A] is opened. As soon as the ministers of the Church have entered, they ought before all else to go to the altars of the saints and there, prostrate and in a low voice, implore them, that by their aid they may be able, through vigilant watchfulness, to guard both themselves and their flock from the prince of darkness and to persevere forever in divine praises.

But since we have mentioned bells, it will readily be granted us if we uncover, as it were by stripping off the bark, whatever mystery lies hidden here. The bell signifies preachers, who likewise exhort us to divine prayers. The beam extending above the bell’s crown signifies the Lord’s cross; and the clapper—thus they call that hanging piece of iron, which the Greeks more correctly call *rhopalon* (ῥόπαλον), “club” or “striker,” by whose blow the bell gives its sound—signifies the preacher’s mind. [Col. 0036B] For just as a bell cannot be struck except by means of a clapper, so a preacher who lacks a mind is useless.

Furthermore, the cord hanging from the bell signifies sacred Scripture, because, just as a cord is chiefly made from three strands, Scripture is said to be threefold: historical, allegorical, and ethical. That the bell is raised and lowered indicates to us that sacred Scripture sometimes speaks loftily and sometimes humbly. Let us now return from the digression we began.

Once the bells have been rung, the weekly officiant (*hebdomadarius*, as we call the one whose duty it is to conduct the office in choir throughout the whole week) begins in a loud voice: “Lord, you will open my lips” (Ps. 50), that is, “Open”—the future being used in place of the imperative. “Lord,” I say, “open, and my mouth shall declare your praise” (ibid.). But had he not had his mouth open before, when he was praying? He had indeed; but this is a manner of speaking. For a person is not said to have had his mouth open while praying in a low voice; rather, he is said to open it when his voice first begins to be heard clearly. Or he had not yet opened his mouth for praising the Lord, although he had opened it for prayer.

Or again, this touches upon the religious practice of priests in the primitive Church: when they went to bed, they fortified themselves with the sign of the cross, suppressing their voices until morning, and only then burst forth in voices of praise to God. But because a person has from God the ability to praise him, he asks God himself that his mouth be opened, saying: [Col. 0036D] “Lord, you will open my lips.”

Yet because the devil always hates God’s praise, and attacks a person most fiercely when he promises to praise the Lord, the one who praises God implores divine help lest he be overcome by the devil, whom it is not easy to resist. He says: “God, attend to my aid” (Ps. 69). Hence even now it is customary to make the sign of the cross at that point. Then, relying on divine help—which is always at hand when we invoke it—he happily begins the promised praise not only of the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit individually, but of the whole Trinity, saying: “Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.”

Having thus begun the praise of God, the cantor, who is as it were the herald of the Church or its representative, exhorts the others—still continuing their prayers before the altar—to praise the Lord, saying: “Come, let us exult in the Lord,” etc. (Ps. 94). This psalm also contains certain reasons why the Lord should be exulted in.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the hymn and the things done up to the third nocturn

When the exhortation is finished—which is called the *invitatory* because it invites the others to God’s praise—the praise itself follows, namely the hymn. It is sung standing, in order that by the uprightness of our bodies we may show how we ought to raise our hearts on high in praising the Lord.

For unless the mind accords with the tongue, it is certain that a voice, however loud, does not please God. The antiphon which follows, and which is sung in sweet modulation, signifies the devotion of mind which we have in praising the Lord. It is first begun, however, and then sung in full after the psalm, which is modestly sung with it, because we rightly modulate our praise when, having begun it from good devotion of mind, we complete it with like devotion. Antiphons are, as it were, songs inserted among divine praises for the refreshment of the spirits.

The versicle sung afterwards signifies that we then turn from the office of psalms to the office of lessons. It is sung by boys, so that we may understand that our service pleases God only if we perform it with innocence. Afterwards the Lord’s Prayer is said, which enjoys the highest privilege of authority among prayers. [Col. 0037C] It is said so that through it the temptations of the devil may be restrained. For when the devil perceives that we wish to read the lessons, in which are related victories won against him by the saints, or matters chiefly read for instruction in morals and formation in virtues, then he attacks us more fiercely. Therefore, lest we be defeated by his attack, we apply ourselves more to prayer than to the voice.

The final part of the prayer is recited aloud, namely: “And lead us not into temptation,” in order that it may be clear for what purpose that prayer is said: namely, lest the reader perform the reading for vainglorious self-exaltation and so be seduced by the devil, and lest the minds of the hearers be deprived, through his phantasmal temptations, of the understanding and profit of the lesson.

Then the reader approaches the book and, before beginning to read, asks the priest for a blessing as permission to read, saying: “Command, lord, a blessing.” By this it is implied that no one ought to read in church unless he has asked leave, has been commanded, or has previously been granted permission to do so.

But it should be observed that the reader here says *domne*, not *Domine*, because he speaks to a human being, who, as he is half-full and imperfect in comparison with our Lord, is addressed with a contracted word. At the end of the lesson, however, he says *Domine* in full, in this manner: “But you, O Lord.” This is particularly observed by monks when they say *domnus abbas*, “lord abbot,” not *dominus abbas*. Hence too servants attending their masters, when they offer them cups, [Col. 0038A] ought not bend both knees but only one, namely the left, by which side is signified bodily servitude, owed to human beings alone and not spiritual servitude. Nor should one bow to a secular prince face-on, but with the head bent toward the left ear.

When the lesson is concluded, the reader adds: “But you, O Lord,” not *domne*, since he addresses a perfect Lord, wholly one worthy of the perfect and full term. Nor does this belong to the lesson or continue the lesson just read. Rather, having finished the lesson, the reader turns his speech to the Lord and excuses himself, saying: “You, O Lord, have mercy upon us.” The meaning of these words is this: “Lord, perhaps I sinned while reading, by modulating my pronunciation from desire of human praise; and perhaps the hearers also sinned because they attended to various thoughts and did not give the lesson its due hearing. But you, O Lord, have mercy upon us.”

But the general response of all, “Thanks be to God,” belongs to the lesson and is the voice of the Church rendering thanks to God. It is as if they said: “God has fed us with words of salvation, which are food for the soul; for this benefit we in turn give thanks to God.”

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the third nocturn

In the third nocturn lessons are likewise recited, but from a homily on the Gospel. The reason is that the third nocturn signifies the time of grace, as stated above, in which Gospel matters were treated.

It should meanwhile be noted that there was a time when the truth of the Trinity was especially attacked by heretics. But after the heresy had been refuted and expelled, and the people restored to knowledge of the truth, the holy Fathers ordained that the ninth lesson, with its responsory, should be read concerning the Trinity. [Col. 0038C] This was observed for some time but was afterwards neglected. For when it was no longer necessary for the Church to read a lesson on the Trinity, since all Christians already believed rightly, it omitted the lesson but retained its responsory. Hence on Sundays in summer we always sing a new responsory concerning the Trinity.

Strictly speaking, however, it is not then called a responsory, since it does not answer the lesson which precedes it. Responsories ought always to answer the lessons to which they are appended; hence they receive their name. So too they are called verses, as though, when these have ended, the responsories turn—that is, return and are sung again, or at least some portion of them. Thus is resolved the musical question concerning the verses of the second tone, which end in C although the second tone always ends in D. We say that here there is no ending, but rather in the repetition of the responsory.

Yet it may be said that it is called a common responsory, not because it answers the lesson just preceding, but because it answers that lesson on the Trinity which used to be read. When the nocturns have been completed, the church lights are lit, the bells are rung, and *Te Deum laudamus* is sung aloud. This signifies the joy and gladness of the woman who, having lit a lamp, found the drachma she had lost. [Col. 0039A] The fact that the end of this canticle—namely, “Day by day”—and the verses which follow are sung somewhat more loudly signifies the congratulations of the neighbors, who rejoiced with the woman over the recovered drachma. The ringing likewise represents their summoning together.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the day office

After the night office, we must treat the day office, which is divided into seven parts: morning praises, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline. The Mass belongs to the office of Terce or None, for Mass is regularly celebrated at these two hours.

That we perform the day office divided into seven hours comes from the Prophet, who says: “Seven times in the day I have given praise to you” (Ps. 123). But why, pray, seven times? Because, since the night office signifies the time of mercy, when the human race, besieged by the devil, was miserably held in bondage, it fittingly follows that the day office signifies the time of our redemption, or our deliverance accomplished through Christ, the sun of righteousness. By the brightness of his divinity he illumined our darkness and drew us out of the devil’s servitude. Therefore we also sing praises to God seven times in the day, because through so great a benefit we have received the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit.

Since we come from the darkness of sins by the way of penitence to the liberty of life, it arose that on non-festal days, or ferias, the penitential psalm was sung at morning praises: “Have mercy upon me, O God” (Ps. 50). [Col. 0039C] On feast days, except during Lent: “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with majesty” (Ps. 92). Of this psalm, as of the others, we shall speak later.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Why we praise the Lord seven times in the day
There is also another reason why we should praise the Lord seven times a day: each day represents the lifetime of each individual. Not that every person possesses it, but that he would possess it if he did not sin. This life has seven stages: that of the infant, child, adolescent, young man, mature man, old man, and decrepit man. Infancy is represented by Matins; childhood by Prime; [Col. 0039D] adolescence by Terce; youth by Sext; mature age by None; old age by Vespers; and decrepitude and the end of human life by Compline. In all these ages, indeed, we are obliged to praise the Creator. That we can praise the Lord even in the time of our infancy is plainly demonstrated by the example of St Nicholas, who, through the power of abstinence, did not suck his mother’s breast on Wednesdays and Fridays. The other ages are sufficiently evident.

There are likewise very many reasons why we especially praise the Lord at the times of these hours. When the reddening dawn of day appears, we sing Matins, which are called “morning” (*matutinae*) from *mane*, “good,” since light is good and nothing seems better than light. [Col. 0040A] Morning, therefore, is good, since at that time light is restored to us. They are called “praises” because this office chiefly sounds forth divine praise, which we give him because he has led us from the darkness of error to the light of truth. We therefore sing praises to God at this time because at such an hour he created the world and the angels, who, as soon as they were created, joyfully acclaimed their Creator with sweet song and melody. At the same time he safely led the people of Israel through the Red Sea and drowned the Egyptians. Again, at this same hour Christ rose victorious from death.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the other six hours

There follows an account of the other six hours, under which another six are likewise included. Thus twelve hours are assigned to the day [Col. 0040B] and as many to the night. Under Prime we include two hours, namely the first itself and the second; under Terce, three—the third, fourth, and fifth; likewise under Sext, three—the sixth, seventh, and eighth; under None, two—the ninth and tenth; Vespers represents the eleventh; Compline, the twelfth.

But someone may ask why the daytime office is celebrated at these particular hours—at the first rather than the second, the third rather than the fourth or fifth, the sixth rather than the seventh or eighth, and the ninth rather than the tenth. Because these hours are distinguished by certain notable privileges. At the first hour Christ was handed over to Pilate by the Jews; and, rising from death, he appeared at the first hour to Mary Magdalene. At the first hour [Col. 0040C] he was seen on the shore by the seven disciples who were fishing, to whom he said: “Children, have you anything to eat?” (John 21). At the third hour he was crucified by the tongues of the Jews and scourged; and at the same hour, on the day of Pentecost itself, the Holy Spirit was given to the disciples. At the sixth hour Christ was fastened with nails to the wood of the cross for us; and at the same hour, on the day of the Ascension itself, he reclined at table with the disciples. At the ninth hour, crying out, he gave up his spirit; and when pierced with a lance, he brought forth for us from the side of his body two sacraments: namely, the water of baptism and the blood of our redemption and salvation. In the evening he was taken down from the cross; at that same hour, in the Last Supper, he supped with his disciples and gave them the sacrament of his body and blood, which, when departing from this world, he left us as a most saving testament. Again, at the same hour he was recognized in the breaking of bread by his two disciples journeying to Emmaus.

Finally, at Compline he prayed to the Father for his disciples; and at that same hour he was laid in the tomb.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the psalms sung at these hours

I think it sufficiently well known which psalms and canticles ought to be used at these hours. But since these belong to another treatment, and we have undertaken at present to discuss the general office, let us set down briefly the points to be taught here. It should therefore be known generally that six psalms are always sung in Matins [Col. 0041A] and likewise in the other hours. By them are designated the six works of mercy, to which labourers in the Lord’s vineyard must necessarily devote themselves. If we perform them devoutly and with a pure body, we shall undoubtedly be freed from the devil’s servitude and come to the freedom of life; and as the reward for most faithful labour we shall receive the divine denarius, that is, eternal life.

Here it should certainly be observed that at Matins we join two psalms—namely, “O God, my God, from the dawn I watch for you” (Ps. 62) and “May God have mercy upon us” (Ps. 66)—and conclude them with only one *Gloria*. But why this is done may be explained as follows: one of these signifies love of God, the other love of neighbour; and these two loves are so joined to one another [Col. 0041B] that neither can be understood without the other in Christian perfection.

But we do not add *Gloria Patri* to the hymn of the three boys, namely, “Bless, all things,” etc. (Dan. 3), because they were cast into the fiery furnace on account of such a confession of faith. By this deed the Trinity was especially dishonoured. Or it is because the final verse of that hymn has the same meaning as *Gloria Patri*, lest anything superfluous be found in the Holy Scriptures.

At Matins, moreover, we do not sing a jubilus except in the final antiphon alone. For, since by the Lord’s praises we understand the resurrection, in which he lacked absolutely nothing, having already attained blessedness and immortality, there is surely no need here of a jubilus, which signifies desire for some thing. [Col. 0041C] Nor is it used at Compline, which signifies the eighth, that is, the resurrection. This is not because jubilation will cease after the resurrection—indeed, we shall more truly sing jubilation to our Creator with the angels themselves—but because it will then lose its meaning, whereby it is called the desire for some thing. For then we shall desire nothing, as the Lord says: “On that day you will ask me nothing” (John 16).

When the psalms have thus been said with the antiphon, the priest reads the lesson, which we call by another name the “chapter” (*capitulum*), because it is taken from the beginning of that day’s epistle. It is read without “Bid, lord, give a blessing” (*Jube, domne, benedicere*) and without the priestly blessing, because it belongs properly to the prelates of the Church and to priests always to read it; they do not ask permission to read, since they ought to grant it to others. [Col. 0041D] Nor should anyone object: if, in the nocturnal office—as commonly happens—a priest reads the lesson, is it also necessary for him to ask permission and say, “Bid, lord, give a blessing,” since it belongs to him to give blessing and permission? For we say that if a priest reads the lesson in this manner, he is acting outside his office, since it belongs to the reader. But if the reader is not present, then it is readily permitted that either a priest, or a cleric of priestly rank, or even someone of a lower order, as one about to read, should say, “Bid, lord,” and receive the blessing from the priest.

When the chapter has been completed, he does not add, “But you, O Lord” (*Tu autem, Domine*), because reason requires a priest to be perfect and not easily to yield to the devil’s suggestions. Therefore the priest, in the person of the Lord, admonishes us in understanding through the chapter [Col. 0042A] and exhorts us orally to persevere in faith and continually to apply ourselves to works of mercy.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the hymn and the other following parts

Then the hymn is sung, by which is expressed the joy that we have on account of the liberty attained. But because Christ acquired this joy for us, lest we seem ungrateful for the benefit received, when the hymn is ended we break forth in his praise; and because he has freed us, we render him thanks by singing aloud: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel” (Luke 1). And why, pray? Because he visited us when we were in misery and “made redemption for his people” (ibid.).

When this canticle [Col. 0042B] with its antiphon has been completed—the antiphon signifying the love which we have in praising the Lord—the priest says to the people: “The Lord be with you.” This was indeed taken from the book of Ruth; for there Boaz and Obed are said to have greeted their reapers thus (Ruth 2). And immediately the people answer: “And with your spirit.” This is taken from Paul’s Epistles (Gal. 6; Phil. 4). It is as though the priest said: “May our praise be acceptable to God; may he receive it favourably and reward us with the prize of life.” When the people answer, “And with your spirit,” it is as if they said: “You will pour out prayers to the Lord for us; but since God approves and hears only those prayers which proceed from a good disposition, may he himself—without whom there is no good—be with your spirit.”

Then the priest, as though distrustful of his own goodness, says to the people: “Let us pray.” [Col. 0042C] This is said for the sake of humility and avoiding arrogance, as though he said: “Pray with me, that we may more swiftly obtain what we ask.” He then says the prayer, and when it has been said the choir responds: “Amen,” as though saying: “May it happen to us as you prayed”; or, “May your prayer be successfully accomplished.” *Amen* was taken from the Apocalypse of John (Rev. 1, 5, 7, etc.).

And in the same manner the priest again greets the people and repeats what he said before: “The Lord be with you,” as though saying: “If you have obtained God’s grace, persevere in it.” The people again answer: “And with your spirit,” as though promising: “You have prayed for us, and we in turn pray for you.” Then the boys sing: “Let us bless the Lord.” [Col. 0042D] This we have received from the third psalm. The choir in turn answers them: “Thanks be to God,” which we ascribe to the Apostle (Rom. 6). By this is signified that, until the end of life, we ought to serve God in innocence and bless him, rendering thanks for his benefits.

Lastly follow the suffrages of the saints. For as long as we live, we stand as it were on slippery ground and fragile ice, and day by day struggle most fiercely with demons, so that we cannot fail to need the saints’ intercessions. After the suffrages, “Let us bless the Lord” is repeated, not by the boys but by the priest—as also at Compline and, in some churches, on major solemnities by the senior clergy. By this is signified that in eternal blessedness [Col. 0043A] we shall be perfect praisers with the Lord. For in this life we cannot be perfect.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the office of the altar

Let us now speak of the office of the altar. First we must explain the vestments of priests and their meanings; then what the office of the Mass, the introit, and tropes are called. The remaining matters we shall briefly touch upon in their order, as in a summary. For the matter is difficult and easily exceeds the powers of our intellect.

The priest, then, as an advocate and a combatant about to fight with the ancient enemy, is clothed in sacred vestments as in armour. He puts on sandals as greaves, so that no stain or particle of dust may cling even to his affections. He covers his head with the amice as with a helmet; with the alb he covers his whole body as with a breastplate; he takes the girdle as a bow and the subgirdle as a quiver. [Col. 0043B] The subgirdle is something on the stole which is bound with the girdle. When he places the stole around his neck, he brandishes it as a spear against the enemy who resists him. He uses the maniple as a club; he is protected by the chasuble as by a shield; his hand is armed with the book as with a sword. Thus equipped, he finally renounces the devil’s dominion through confession.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the priest’s confession before Mass

Before singing Mass, the priest ought to pronounce the confession. For, as Solomon says, “A wise man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech” (Prov. 18). He ought to confess sins generally and not exceed due measure. Thus fortified for battle against “the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6), he proceeds to the altar to appease the judge’s wrath toward those subject to him; and on weekdays the people, as though about to pray for their own champion, prostrate themselves upon the ground.

But when he sings the prayers and recites the remaining parts, he fights, as it were, against the devil with all his strength. When he folds the chasuble upon his shoulder, he prepares it like a sword against the enemy, so that, when the Gospel is read, the devil is as it were struck by a sword. At the end the peace is given, announcing rest to the people after the enemy has been conquered and overthrown. Then permission to depart having been given, the people thank God, and each returns to his own affairs.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the office of the Mass

[Col. 0043D]

The office of the Mass, or “Mass,” is called everything said from beginning to end, namely from the introit to “Go, the dismissal is made” (*Ite, missa est*), whose sense and meaning is this: “Go to Christ and follow him, because the victim has been sent for you to appease the Lord.” Sometimes, however, more narrowly and in a special sense, the first part sung, namely the introit, is called the office of the Mass. It is so called because an angel is sent there.

The Mass is divided altogether into four parts: supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings. For every Mass consists of supplication, petition, and thanksgiving. The first part extends to the offertory; [Col. 0044A] the second to the end of the Lord’s Prayer, when “Amen” is answered; the third to Communion; the fourth to the end. The first part belongs to catechumens, or neophytes, which is nearly the same thing, since a catechumen is called one newly instructed, whether baptized or not yet baptized; and a neophyte likewise, one newly instructed, whether baptized or not. They are not permitted to remain longer or take part further, any more than Jews or pagans, because they are not yet members of the Church. For this reason the deacon must say aloud from the pulpit: “Let the catechumens go out.”

Hence this part is called *missa*, from sending out, because they are then sent out. This originated from what is said of the Lord: “But Jesus did not entrust himself to them, knowing what was in man” (John 2). [Col. 0044B] For by catechumens are signified those of whom this was said. Thus the entire office from the introit to “Go, the dismissal is made” is called Mass, although we also sometimes call “Mass” those words by which the body of the Lord is consecrated.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the introit, tropes, and the languages in which Mass may be celebrated

The introit is so called because, when the priest is about to begin Mass, he must first enter the altar area, like a bishop who on feast days is sometimes clothed in God’s armour outside the choir. For while the introit is sung, he enters the altar. Therefore it is customarily sung twice on weekdays, but three times on solemnities. Tropes are sometimes inserted. A trope is called by the Greeks a “turning” (*conversio*) for us, because certain turns are customarily made there.

It should be observed here that Mass is celebrated in three languages—Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—because the title of Christ while he hung upon the cross was written in Greek, Hebrew, and Latin. Hence something from each of these three languages is added in every Mass. From Hebrew, because it is the most excellent language, come: *Alleluia*, *Amen*, *Sabaoth*, and *Hosanna*. [Col. 0044C] Since *Alleluia* is interpreted in many different ways, which we have adequately discussed elsewhere, we now wish to pass them over. Yet according to Jerome’s interpretation, which is the best of all, it means “Praise the Invisible One.” What *Amen* means is well known. *Sabaoth* means “of hosts” or “of armies,” “powers,” and “victories.” Finally, *Hosanna* means, “Save, I pray.” And where, pray? “In the highest.” *Hosi* means “I pray”; *anna* means “save.” Thus *Hosanna*, as it were *Hosianna*, is formed from a corrupted and an uncorrupted expression.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On *Kyrie eleison*, etc.

There follows *Kyrie eleison*, and *Christe eleison*, etc. It is sung in Greek in order to show that the Church began first in Greece and was afterwards brought thence to Rome, from which point the remaining parts are Latin. It is sung three times in succession for the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and this is done in three sets so that it is said nine times altogether, on account of the nine orders of angels with whom we ask to be associated. In some churches [Col. 0045A] *ἠμᾶς* (*hēmas*, “us”) is added, as though they said: “O Lord, have mercy upon us.”

On solemn days there follows the hymn from the Gospel, or evangelical hymn: “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2), which formerly alone was said at Mass. St Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, added the rest—namely, “We praise you,” and the other words which follow—and ordained that these too should be sung at Mass. It is, however, customary only when the feast of apostles, martyrs, confessors, or of those in whose honour a church has been dedicated is celebrated, whatever that church may be.

When it is ended, the priest greets the people, saying, “The Lord be with you.” This greeting is taken from the Old Testament, namely, as has been said, from the book of Ruth (Ruth 2), and belongs to lesser priests. There is another greeting, namely, [Col. 0045B] “Peace be with you,” which, as it is taken from the Gospel (John 20), belongs only to bishops and those above them. This expressly indicates that the New Testament is more worthy than the Old Testament. The people’s response, “And with your spirit,” is taken from the Apostle’s Epistle to Titus (Titus 3).

Finally, when he says, “Let us pray,” he gathers the universal Church to himself, as though he were a *syndicus*, speaking in the person of many. For this is what *syndicus* signifies. Long-established antiquity confirms our saying “Let us pray.” For the ancients, after first saying “Let us pray,” immediately added the prayer together in common; having omitted that practice, we have retained only the words “Let us pray.”

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the prayer, and how often the priest turns in Mass

[Col. 0045C]

The prayer, or collect, immediately follows—although “collect” properly denotes the prayer made in a procession, when the people and all the clergy proceed from one church to another. Then the priest or bishop, once the whole multitude had assembled, customarily used over the people a prayer properly called a collect. But now that prayer has been omitted and we have retained only, as stated, “Let us pray.”

It should incidentally be noted that in every Mass the priest turns five times and greets the people seven times. First, at the very beginning; second, at the Gospel, which ought to be read not at the altar but on a lectern or some reading stand facing north, [Col. 0045D] with the chasuble folded on the shoulder, because he then performs the deacon’s office; third, when he returns to the right-hand corner of the altar, whence he came, after the creed has been said, if there is a solemnity—for then he turns toward the people; fourth, after the offertory, when he says, “For ever and ever,” and then, “The Lord be with you,” although he does not turn around. For, as is said, “No one who has put his hand to the plough should look back” (Luke 9). Fifth, when he says, “The peace of the Lord be always with you,” and he does not turn then either; sixth, after Communion; and finally, at the end.

As for the prayer, it should be known that now one, now three, now five, now seven may be read, but no more. One is used because there is one Epistle and one Gospel, or because of the unity of God. Three are used because of the Trinity; for God delights in an odd number, or because the Lord prayed three times during the Passion. Five may be read because of the fivefold Passion of Christ or his five wounds. Seven, however, are used because the Lord’s Prayer contains seven petitions, or because of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit enumerated in Isaiah (Isa. 11). [Col. 0046A] No one ought to exceed the number seven.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the epistle, gradual, Alleluia, and prose

[Col. 0046B] Then the epistle is read. It is a message sent from one absent person to another absent person, and is so called from the Greek verb *ἐπιστέλλειν* (*epistellein*), meaning “to send.” Such are the letters of Peter, Paul, James, and John sent to various persons, which are for the most part read in this place. But if it happens—and it often does—that something from the Apocalypse or the Prophets is read here, it is nevertheless called an epistle, for the reason that the Gospel is then, in a certain sense, sent forth.

One must take the greatest care that no one presume to read the epistle unless he is a subdeacon, deacon, or priest. It is better for a priest to read it, even if he is singing Mass, than for an acolyte to do so. After the epistle a responsory with its verse is sung, or, as it is called, the gradual. It is called a gradual [Col. 0046C] because it is customarily sung by the junior clergy on the steps before the altar, or by the senior clergy, even on weekdays; but on solemnities it is sung at a higher place, that is, from the pulpit, even by boys. Or it is so called because it is sung step by step, or because we must proceed from step to step—that is, ascend “from virtue to virtue.”

It is also called a responsory because it responds to the verse, which is likewise named from turning, either because we turn toward the east, or because after the verse there is a return to the response or to another office, as at Matins. Afterwards follows *Alleluia*, whose interpretation according to Jerome was explained above. At its end we “pneumatize,” that is, we sing a jubilus, prolonging the ending and adding to it, as it were, a tail. There is indeed a difference between *neuma, neumatis* and *pneuma, pneumatis*. *Neuma* is feminine: it means a jubilus, as at the end of antiphons; *pneuma* is neuter: it means the Holy Spirit. Then the verse is said, from which likewise a return is made to *Alleluia*. There follows the sequence, which we call prose.

It is reported that Notger [Note: [Col. 0045D] This bishop was bishop of Liège, about the year 850.], abbot at Saint Gall and a Teuton by nationality, was the first to compose sequences, and that their subsequent singing in church was instituted by Pope Nicholas. After him Hermannus Contractus, the inventor of the astrolabe, is said to have made these two: “Almighty King, on this present day,” and “May the grace of the Holy Spirit be with us,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the Gospel

[Col. 0047A]

When the sequence has ended, the Gospel is read. It has a threefold beginning: either through “The beginning of the holy Gospel,” as at the beginning of the four Gospels; or through “At that time”; or through another designation of royal or some other great authority, such as “It was in the days of Herod” (Luke 1), and “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar” (Luke 3).

“Gospel” is called from *εὖ* (*eu*), “well,” and *ἄγγελος* (*angelos*), “messenger,” as though it were called “good and joyful news.” Thus a Gospel is sometimes said to be according to history, sometimes according to allegory, sometimes according to person, sometimes according to part, and sometimes [Col. 0047B] according to the whole.

According to history, for example: “Mary Magdalene and Mary of James and Salome,” etc. (Mark 16), and also that which is sung on the Nativity of the Lord at the second Mass concerning the shepherds. According to allegory is the passage customarily read at the Assumption of Blessed Mary concerning Mary Magdalene and her sister Martha: “Jesus entered into a certain village,” etc. (Luke 10). Since Mary Magdalene signifies the contemplative life and Martha, who was serving, the active life, this Gospel teaches that in the Blessed Virgin Mary there was the perfection of both lives, contemplative and active.

A Gospel is sung according to person, as on the feast of St Thomas the Apostle, where it is said: “Thomas, one of the twelve,” etc. (John 20). According to part, as on the feast of the Holy Cross: then that Gospel concerning Nicodemus is recited because of its final portion, which is: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3). [Col. 0047C] In these words Christ indicated his Passion and the lifting up of his body on the cross. Therefore the Gospel containing this portion is read on the feast of the Holy Cross. Finally, according to the whole, there is that short passage observed at the Circumcision of the Lord: “After eight days were completed” (Luke 2).

It should therefore be observed that on weekdays only one wax candle precedes the deacon when he approaches to read the Gospel. Nor without reason: by it is signified Christ’s first coming, which was humble and hidden and was preceded by only one forerunner, namely John the Baptist, who was the lamp of the Word. On feast days, however, two wax candles precede him, because at the second coming, which will be solemn and manifest, two forerunners are to be sent beforehand, namely Elijah and Enoch. Or this is also because the Lord sent his disciples out two by two before his face to preach.

It should likewise be carefully noted that, as soon as the Gospel begins, all the people—clerics and laypersons alike, both he who proclaims it and he who hears it—ought to make the sign of the cross on the forehead, mouth, and breast. [Col. 0048A] On the forehead, because it is the seat of shame and modesty; hence we call shameless people “barefaced,” as it were, without a forehead. By placing the sign of the cross on our forehead, therefore, we plainly show that we are not ashamed to believe in the Crucified One and to acknowledge as our God and Lord him whom Jews and pagans reproach to us. Thus, by Hercules, the Apostle says: “But we preach Christ crucified: to the Jews a stumbling block, and to the Gentiles foolishness” (1 Cor. 1).

On the mouth, moreover, this is done to signify that we boldly preach the Lord’s cross. Finally, on the breast, it is done to show plainly that we are prepared to suffer openly for Christ’s name. Again, by marking mouth and breast with the cross, we expressly signify that we boldly confess with the mouth and believe with the heart that Christ crucified, whose book is being read, is our God and Lord.

The priest or deacon who is about to read the Gospel signs himself on mouth, forehead, and breast, as though saying: “I am not ashamed of the Lord’s cross, but I preach it with my mouth and believe it with my heart.” He also marks the book with the cross, as though saying: “This is the book of the Crucified One.”

One might ask here how the sign of the cross ought to be made: from right to left or from left to right. Some hold that the cross should be made from left to right, and take authority from such a verse as: “He went forth from the Father,” etc. (John 16). The Son came from the Father into the world, and therefore we begin the cross at the upper part, by which [Col. 0048C] the Father is signified. But because he came from there into the world without any interval—the world being understood through the left side—after descending from the upper part, we immediately proceed from left to right; for afterwards he ascended to the part signified by the right hand. Others think that it should be made from right to left, because Christ, coming from the right to the left—that is, from the Father—drove back the devil by the cross, the devil being signified by the left.

When the title of the Gospel has been spoken, everyone answers: “Glory to you, O Lord.” For when the Gospel is set forth to be read, in which the glory is treated partly of God and partly of ourselves—namely, inasmuch as Christ conquered the devil and redeemed us, and as victor ascended to the Father’s glory—the hearers of the Gospel rejoice and say and cry out in praise of their Creator: “Glory to you, O Lord,” as though saying: “May your glory, preached to us in this Gospel, remain with us forever without end and always increase and grow.”

When the Gospel has been read, each person ought to say, “Amen.” Or, as others wish, once the Gospel has been recited we ought immediately to say, “Thanks be to God,” just as after every reading or chapter. But it is better that “Amen” be said and that we fortify ourselves with the cross against the devil, lest he snatch the Lord’s words from our breast.

It is also wholly necessary that, while the Gospel is read, coverings be removed from the head. For the Gospel’s preaching removed all the veils of the law and enabled men, who previously saw the Lord as it were in an enigma and through a lattice, now to see and understand truth itself through open knowledge of the law. [Col. 0049A] Men, therefore, should hear the Gospel with uncovered head, so that their five senses may be more fit for hearing. Hence clerics should not wear long hair but should be closely tonsured, that they may hear more rightly and perfectly. Yet they wear a crown in order to show that there is no intermediary between them and the Lord. Clerics, then, ought not to have long hair, if the length of hair signifies the multitude of sins.

Women, however, ought to hear the Gospel with their heads covered and veiled, even if they are virgins, because of the forbidden fruit. If it happens that a virgin’s head is uncovered or that she has no veil, it is necessary for her mother or any other woman to place a cloth or something similar upon her head. Likewise, until the Gospel has been proclaimed, we ought to stand erect, or with bowed head, provided that we do not sit unless necessity compels. Under the law it was prescribed that, while they ate the Paschal lamb, they should hold staffs in their hands (Exod. 12); but while the deacon reads the Gospel, we set down our staffs, because, when Christ preaches, the observances of the law are laid aside.

## CHAPTER XL. What the creed is, when it is to be sung, and how many there are

Immediately after the Gospel, the creed of faith ought to be added, namely: “I believe in one God, the Father,” etc., if there is a solemnity. Yet it is not used at every solemnity, but only on the feasts of those who are mentioned in the creed: the feast of the Trinity; the Nativity, Circumcision, Epiphany, Easter, Ascension, Pentecost; the feast of All Saints; the Transfiguration of the Lord; Blessed Mary; all the Apostles; the Holy Cross; and every Sunday. It ought not to be said on other solemnities.

Nor is it customarily sung on the solemnity of the angels, because they do not believe, but already know, since they possess full and perfect knowledge. Nor is it customarily sung at the solemnity of the two Evangelists who were not apostles, namely Luke and Mark. Some say that the creed should be said on the feast of St John [Col. 0049D] the Baptist because Christ’s birth was then commemorated. But by the same reasoning Blessed Mary is mentioned every day, and therefore it would have to be sung every day. Some also think that it ought to be sung on the feasts of those who composed it, and in support of this they adduce what is found in John’s Gospel: namely, that the apostles’ faith increased daily because of the miracles performed (John 2), although elsewhere authority states that faith has no merit when human reason supplies proof by experience.

When the creed has been pronounced, the sign of the cross ought to be made at its end, because it is evangelical speech just like the Gospel itself, except that it is an abbreviated speech. Hence it has been said of it: “The Lord will make an abbreviated word upon the earth” (Rom. [Col. 0050A] 9); and thus: “An abbreviated word will come upon the children of God” (Isa. 10). Likewise, the sign of the cross ought to be made at all evangelical words, such as at the end of the Lord’s Prayer, the *Gloria in excelsis*, the *Benedictus*, the *Magnificat*, and the *Nunc dimittis*. All these, like the Gospel, ought to be heard standing.

It should be noted that there are four creeds. The least is that which everyone commonly says in daily prayer and which the apostles composed together. The second is that recited at Prime: “Whoever wishes to be saved”; it was composed by Athanasius, patriarch of Alexandria, against the Arian heretics, although many wrongly suppose him to have been Anastasius. The third was issued by the Synod of Constantinople, namely that which is customarily sung in Mass to this day. The fourth came forth from the Council of Nicaea. St Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, wrote a book *On Synods*, in which he also composed it; it ought to be read at every synod, either in full or at least in some portion. From this it is plainly apparent how mistaken those are who read another lesson there.

## CHAPTER XLI. On the offertory
After the Creed has been said, the Offertory, or “offering,” as some call it, is sung. It is called Offertory from offering, because then we make offerings. But it must here be considered that there are altogether three things which we ought to offer: first, ourselves; then those things [Col. 0050C] necessary for the sacrifice—namely bread, wine, and water, and whatever else is suitable for sacrifice. Incidentally, we may say here that this bread is, as it were, named from the Greek word πᾶν, παντός, meaning “all” or “the whole.” For both here and in the world to come this bread is our whole life. Wine, moreover, may in much the same way be derived from the vine, to which the Lord compares himself in the Gospel, saying: “I am the true vine” (John 15). Nor, finally, do I think it unknown that water is said to be named from equality, because through this sacrament we both certainly believe and hope that we shall be made equal to the angels, although water sometimes signifies the people. Hence: “Many waters, many peoples” (Rev. 17). For neither could there be blood without the salvation of the people, nor the people’s salvation without blood.

The water is then blessed when it is mixed with the wine, but by no means the wine, since it awaits its own special blessing. In certain churches, on great solemnities, precious ecclesiastical vessels are offered and placed upon the altar or in suitable places. Third and last follow the manual offerings of the laity. Clerics do not make offerings, except at the funerals of the dead and at the first celebration of a priest. For it would seem inhumane if those were obliged to offer who live from the offerings of others. At the Offertory the priest is in no way permitted to hold in his hand a pyx or anything of that kind, so as to avoid every suspicion of avarice.

## CHAPTER XLII. On the sacrifice

[Col. 0051A]

“Sacrifice” is so called, as it were, because something is made sacred by it. Here it should be known that in former times sacrifice in the primitive Church was celebrated by the apostles and apostolic men with wooden vessels and common garments. For then, as the saying goes, there were wooden chalices and golden priests. Now the reverse is true. A little later, however, Pope Severinus ordained that it be done with glass vessels. But because these were fragile, Pope Urban wished sacrifice to be offered in silver or gold vessels, or, on account of poverty, even in pewter ones, provided that they do not readily rust.

According to the Hebrews, *hostia* is named from *ostium*, “door,” because it was offered at the door of the tabernacle. According to the pagans, however, it is derived from *hostis*, “enemy.” For, as he says, “from conquered enemies the victim has its name.” It was also called *victima* from conquering; and *immolatio*, because there Christ is sacramentally immolated—he who in truth was once immolated on the cross for our sins. It is called *immolatio* from *mola*, the meal with which, in sacrifices, a kind of grain called *far* or *ador* used to be ground. Hence:

> “… and cakes of spelt meal upon the grass.”  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid*, VII.109)

For it was placed between the horns of the altar—or of the animal—after a hole had there been made with a knife. But the *mola* on an altar is called the middle part beneath which relics are sealed, upon which a cross is impressed at the dedication of a church, and where [Col. 0051C] the body of Christ is consecrated.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the second part of the Mass

Now the second part of the Mass immediately follows, the part properly called “Mass,” which, as we have said, belongs to prayer. For the first part, discussed thus far, is called the part of supplication. Thus this part of the Mass—if by “Mass” we mean the entire office from the Introit to *Ite, missa est*—is, when the term is taken strictly, called Mass in the proper sense. It has four divisions. The first is called the Secret; the second, the Preface; the third, the Canon; the fourth, the Lord’s Prayer with its Preface.

This part extends to the end of the Lord’s Prayer: “But deliver us from evil. Amen,” which must be spoken silently by the priest. Here it must be considered that as many collects, in the same order and concerning the same matters, ought to be said in the Secret after Communion as preceded in the supplicatory part before the Epistle at the beginning of Mass—neither more nor fewer—always observing that the number does not exceed seven. Great care must likewise be taken that, if a collect for the dead is inserted, it be said not last but next-to-last or third from last. For the end ought to return to its own beginning. Finally, it should generally be known that in a Mass for the dead no prayer for the living ought to be inserted, except this common one: “O God, who rulest alike over the living and the dead.”

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the Secret

[Col. 0052A]

It is called the Secret because it is pronounced secretly, although formerly it was said aloud, so that all the laity could readily retain it. It happened, therefore, that at one time shepherds placed bread upon a certain stone; and while they spoke the words of this Secret, it was changed into flesh and perhaps, if I may so speak, transubstantiated into Christ’s body. A most severe vengeance was divinely inflicted upon them: every one of them, without exception, was struck down by a heavenly judgment sent from above. From this occurrence it was decreed that thereafter it should be said quietly and softly. Or it is said secretly and, as it were, in silence lest it become cheapened—just as sacred Scripture is said to be obscure for the same reason; [Col. 0052B] or finally, lest it become known to the laity. Thus there is a threefold reason for the silence.

When the priest says, “Pray, brethren,” he immediately begins to pray; and we likewise, upon hearing this, ought to pray quietly and sing two psalms, namely, “May the Lord hear thee” and the one following it. But when he meanwhile says, “Pray, brethren,” it is as though he were quietly saying, “The Lord be with you,” when he turns himself toward the people. Therefore let us remember that the priest turns toward the people five times in saying, “The Lord be with you,” on account of the five appearances on the very day of Easter. And because one appearance was not manifest—when, as most think, he appeared to Blessed Mary Magdalene—he says “The Lord be with you” secretly and, as it were, in silence at the point where he openly says, “Pray, brethren.”

“Throughout all ages of ages,” that is, through ages succeeding one another. Or “ages” is said by antonomasia, as “Song of Songs.” It has been asked why the prayers following the offerings are said secretly. We answer that this is done because, after the raising of Lazarus, the Jews immediately wished to kill Jesus; he hid himself in the city of Ephraim, in a wilderness (John 11), and entirely ceased and kept silent from preaching and working miracles until the Sabbath before Palm Sunday, when he came to the house of Simon the leper and preached openly (Matt. 26). This is expressly indicated by that exultant raising of the priest’s voice when he says, “Throughout all ages of ages.” [Col. 0052D] To this “Amen” is added, so that we may clearly affirm what has been said by the priest, because through Christ the age was created. For Amen is a name of God. Hence in the Apocalypse: “I am Amen, the faithful witness” (Rev. 3).

There follows, moreover, “The Lord be with you,” and then, “Lift up your hearts,” which we ought to have lifted up to the Lord in heaven, not fixed upon earthly things, so that we do not seek Esau’s blessing, which, being transitory and weak, is entirely located in earthly things. The bishop’s sandals clearly signify precisely the same thing. Since they are open above, they admonish us always to have our hearts raised toward the Lord; and since they are solid below, they teach us to have our minds altogether dull toward earthly things, as though we ought not to seek the blessing that is earthly, but Jacob’s blessing, which is in heaven.

Afterwards follows: “Let us give thanks to the Lord our God,” because for all the benefits that he has graciously bestowed upon us, we rightly ought to render him thanks. There is found there a certain figure [Note: [Col. 0053D] Perhaps a figure of this sort was depicted in books of the ancients.] resembling our delta—that is, a D closed on every side—which in its preceding portion encloses our V, open at the top; across their middle portion a little transverse stroke is drawn, joining the two parts in the form of a cross. This was not done without reason. By the circularly closed delta the divine nature is represented, which has neither beginning nor end. By the V is expressed Christ’s human nature, which had its beginning in the Virgin but will lack an end. The little stroke in the middle joining the two parts, however, is the cross through which human things are joined to divine things.

## CHAPTER XLV. On the Preface

The Preface is called, as it were, a preliminary utterance, which is preparation for the ministry. For the nine orders of angels are noted there, whom we certainly believe to be present. The Majesty mentioned here is also called, as it were, “greater standing” or “greater power.”

It should be known that there are in all ten Prefaces in the Mass: the first, of the Trinity [Note: [Col. 0054D] An eleventh may be that common one of the Holy Trinity.]; the second, of the Nativity; the third, of the Epiphany; the fourth, of Lent or fasting; the fifth, of the Lord’s Cross; the sixth, of the Resurrection; the seventh, of the Ascension; [Col. 0053C] the eighth, of the coming of the Holy Spirit; the ninth, of the Apostles; and the tenth and final one, of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

Afterward, “Holy, holy, holy” is sung three times, taken from the Old Testament. For Isaiah says that he saw the Lord upon a high throne and the Seraphim crying, “Holy, holy, holy” (Isa. 6). But what follows—“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!”—is taken from the Gospel (Matt. 21), and when it is sung, the sign of the cross ought to be made. Finally, we sing the songs of the angels here because through this sacrifice we do not doubt that earthly things are joined to heavenly, and therefore we cry with them that we may be saved in the highest.

## CHAPTER XLVI. On the Canon

[Col. 0053D]

Next follows the Canon, for this is what it is called by the Greeks; for us it is the Rule, because by it the consecration of this sacrament is regularly effected. It is also called the Action, because then our cause is transacted with God. For this reason we pray standing on feasts, but prostrate on ordinary days or fast days.

It is said silently for three reasons. First, because God attends not to the cry of the mouth but of the heart; hence he said even to Moses, “Why do you cry to me?” (Exod. 14), though Moses himself was silent. Nevertheless we utter words, lest we be thought wholly ignorant of what we ask, or what we ought to ask. Second, the Canon ought to be said softly lest, if it had to be uttered aloud, we should grow weary through prolonged shouting. Or third, for this reason: lest the words of so great a mystery become cheapened through daily use and be pronounced indiscriminately everywhere in inappropriate places, and thus finally be extinguished and perish, as was related shortly before concerning the shepherds. For it has been forbidden by decree, under anathema, that anyone except one wearing sacred vestments, from a book consecrated upon the altar, should utter these words.

The priest therefore says: “Thee, therefore, most merciful Father,” etc. He addresses the Lord as present. He begins with the letter tau, T, made in the form of a cross. For through Christ’s passion all these things were completed upon the cross and have their efficacy. Hence it is certainly proper that an image of the Crucified One be painted there. [Col. 0054B] Then follow many things, such as the names of apostles, martyrs, bishops, and virgins, all of whom exposed themselves to sacrifice for Christ our Lord. Certain other matters follow as well, which we are not permitted to explain except perhaps to priests alone; and therefore we shall be silent concerning them. Yet we shall add this one point: no one is permitted here either to subtract or to add anything, except at times the name of those for whom the sacrifice is specially or individually offered.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On the Lord’s Prayer

We must now speak of the Lord’s Prayer, in which seven petitions are contained. What is prefaced is, as it were, a winning of goodwill. The first three concern the future life; the four following concern the present. The middle one, however, as some hold, may be taken in common, so that it is referred to both lives: namely, that which we call “our daily bread,” which the Greeks call ἐπιούσιον, the Hebrews *segola*, and we call either “superessential,” “excellent,” or even “household” bread.

But it should be observed that when the priest says, “Let us pray. By the commandments,” etc., we ought to pray prostrate until the end of the Lord’s Prayer, if the days are ordinary days. If it is a feast, however, or the Paschal day, we must pray not prostrate but standing, and answer: “But deliver us from evil. Amen.” The reason why the priest says this Lord’s Prayer not quietly or in silence [Col. 0054D] is that it is drawn from the Gospel.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On peace

Afterward the priest says: “The peace of the Lord be always with you,” which belongs to the third part of the Mass. Yet it should be noted that here the priest ought silently to say a certain prayer which in the Ambrosian Church is pronounced openly. Having received the kiss of peace from the Eucharist itself, as some think—or, according to others, from the tomb and the altar themselves—he imparts it to the deacon or subdeacon, so that through them it may descend to the others. But care must be taken that men do not pass it to women, lest perhaps some thought of wantonness [Col. 0055A] or carnality secretly enter the mind.

“Agnus Dei” is sung three times. This is the true Lamb, declared and prefigured in the Paschal lamb, concerning whom the Gospel says: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). It is sung three times so that his threefold body may be understood: namely, that which is glorified in heaven; the mystical body, which still walks on earth; and that which rests in tombs until the final examination of judgment. Twice it is said with “Have mercy upon us”; the third time with “Grant us peace.” At the Lord’s Supper, however, it ought to be said three times with “Have mercy upon us.” But neither of these is added in a Mass for the dead; rather, it is said three times with “Grant them rest.” It must everywhere be observed that it is said not continuously but at intervals and separately, with a prayer inserted.

ἁγνός in Greek means “pure” and “pious,” because by piety alone, as a pure victim, he redeemed us. Or it may be from *agnoscendo*, “recognizing,” because, just as a lamb recognizes its mother by bleating alone, so Christ in his passion recognized his mother and commended Virgin to virgin. This, too, may explain why the *Agnus Dei* is sung three times: because Christ, hanging on the cross, recognized his Father by obeying him unto death; fixed upon that same cross, he recognized his mother and commended her to a virgin; and finally there also recognized the human race by redeeming it.

That “Have mercy upon us” is repeated twice here and altered the third time into “Grant us peace” is entirely drawn from the Old Testament, where, when they cried to the Lord, they were accustomed to say: [Col. 0055C] “Spare, O Lord, spare thy people” (Joel 2), and to add the third time: “Do not give thy inheritance to reproach” (ibid.). Therefore, when we say, “Lamb of God, who takest away sins,” we expressly imitate John the Baptist, who said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1).

Certainly it should not be unknown that in the primitive Church those who attended the Canon of the Mass were accustomed to communicate every day. But later, as the multitude of believers increased, it was ordained that communion should be received only on Sundays. When this too shortly afterward could not be observed, it fell into disuse, and a third institution followed: that at least three times yearly—at Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost—all Christians should receive the Eucharist. A threefold remedy was nevertheless devised: namely, that the kiss of peace should be given every day, and on Sundays the *eulogia*, that is, blessed and consecrated bread—something which could not be observed in Lent and appointed periods of abstinence without violating the fast. Therefore at that time this ordinance was promulgated: that at the end of Mass a collect should be said over the people, with the words, “Bow your heads to God,” when a lesser priest celebrates. But if it is a bishop, he will say: “Humble yourselves for the blessing.”

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the final part of the Mass

The final part of the Mass now follows, called the thanksgiving, and it begins with Communion. It is called Communion, as it were, participation, which we sing for this reason: that through it we may become sharers with the saints in divine grace. [Col. 0056A] It is also called Completion, because through it the Mass, so to speak, is completed.

The Mass ends in three ways. First, on solemnities, by “*Ite, missa est*”—“Go, the dismissal is made”—which is, as it were, permission to depart, and is taken from Exodus (Exod. 12), not according to the words but according to the sense and meaning of the event, when the Israelite people departed from Egypt with Pharaoh’s permission. Or likewise when, Cyrus permitting, it returned from Babylonian captivity to its own land, giving thanks to God. So too, having received the final blessing, we ought to return to the heavenly homeland, where we shall always live happily in thanksgiving.

“*Ite, missa est*” is said whenever *Te Deum laudamus*, *Gloria in excelsis*, and Alleluia are sung. When “*Ite, missa est*” has been pronounced, we ought to answer “Thanks be to God,” the utterance of one rejoicing. Second, on ordinary days, “Let us bless the Lord” is said, taken from the Apostle (Eph. 1). Third and finally, in a Mass for the dead, “May they rest in peace,” which arose from common custom alone.

When, then, “*Ite, missa est*” is said, the priest must turn his face toward the people; but when “Let us bless the Lord” or “May they rest in peace” is said, he faces east. These three must be uttered only by the priest or deacon. But at the first Mass of the Nativity of the Lord, “*Ite, missa est*” ought not to be said, lest the people seem to have permission to return home.

## CHAPTER L. At what hours Mass is to be celebrated

[Col. 0056C]

Mass may regularly be celebrated only at three hours: the third, sixth, and ninth. At the third, because then Christ was crucified by the tongues of the Jews, as they urgently cried, “Crucify, crucify him” (John 19), and endured mockery, curses, reproaches, blows, scourges, the spittle of his taunters, and the crown of thorns. At the sixth, because then he was led to the cross and had to endure the most cruel nails and draughts tinged with gall, so that he might at last be sacrificed for us. At the ninth, finally, because then he breathed out his soul and commended his spirit to the Father.

Yet it may be that Mass is celebrated before Prime in commemoration of the Lord’s resurrection; this is what vicars do. And it may be celebrated after Prime but before Terce in commemoration of the fact that between Prime and Terce Christ was handed over to Pontius Pilate, while the Jews shouted, “Crucify him,” and he himself was silent. Thus Mass is sung on feast days at the third hour; on ordinary days at the sixth; and at the ninth in Lent and on other fast days. Not, however, on all such days: for on the Ember Saturdays of fasting Mass may and ought to be celebrated very late on account of holy orders, a practice which also pertains to the following Sunday. On the Saturday of Easter and of Pentecost it is sung late because of the consecration of the wax candle, which we call the Paschal candle. This may readily be perceived or inferred from the words “This is the night,” and from this prayer: “O God, who hast made this most holy night,” etc.

On the very day of the Lord’s Nativity the first Mass is sung at night. It may nevertheless lawfully be sung very early in the morning, but only after Prime and Terce have first been completed. Thus the day sacred to the Lord’s Nativity is excepted from those hours, since Prime is sung at night. Nor is this without reason, as we shall say later. The Saturday of Easter and Pentecost are also excepted, because at that time we expressly say: “This is the night,” and “O God, who hast made this most holy night.” Finally, fast days are excepted on account of holy orders.

## CHAPTER LI. What Masses ought to be celebrated on which days

We must now say what Masses ought to be celebrated on which days. There was once a time when the Sunday office had not yet been arranged and diverse heresies were everywhere springing up. It therefore came about that, lest the divine office perish, on the first weekday a Mass of the Trinity was sung; on the second, of Charity; on the third, of Wisdom; on the fourth, of the Holy Spirit; on the fifth, of the Angels; on the sixth, of the Cross; and on the seventh, of the Blessed Virgin Mary. But afterward it was decreed that, when the cause ceased, that too should cease which had been done under the pressure of necessity.

Accordingly, once the Sunday office had been arranged, it was established that the first weekday should have its own special office of the Trinity, and the second of the Angels, because then they were created in gratuitous goods and light was divided from darkness—that is, good angels from evil. For at that time the evil fell and the good were confirmed; but on the first weekday angels were created and [Col. 0057C] established in natural goods. For another reason, however, a Mass for the dead is sung, namely, that we may provide them with the aid of angels. A Mass for the dead is likewise celebrated on that day because, as most say, those in purgatory receive refreshment on the first weekday and immediately return on the following day to their usual punishments and labour; thus, on the day when some aid is afforded to their labours, Mass is sung for them.

On the third weekday the Introit of the Sunday Mass ought to be repeated. Moreover, it was also instituted that the fourth weekday be a fast; and therefore the Sunday Mass was then sung. On the fifth weekday likewise the office of Sunday should be said, namely the Introit, Epistle, and Gospel, because Thursday is especially akin to Sunday. For on such a day a procession used to be made in memory of the Lord’s Ascension; later, as stated above, it was transferred to Sunday.

On the sixth weekday the Cross is observed, and on the seventh the Blessed Virgin Mary. We have received that this was not established without cause, for it has a miraculous origin. Once, in a certain church at Constantinople, there was an image of the Blessed Virgin before which hung a curtain covering it entirely. It happened that every Friday, at Vespers, this curtain fell away from the image without anyone moving it and, by a divine miracle, was as if carried into heaven, so that the image could then be seen fully and perfectly by all; afterward, when Vespers on Saturday were completed, it descended again to the same image and remained there until the following Friday. [Col. 0058A] Since this miracle was seen repeatedly, it was decreed that the Blessed Mary should always be sung of in church on that day.

There may, however, be another reason why an office of Blessed Mary is sung on Saturday. Since she is for us the gate of the heavenly kingdom, aptly signified by Sunday, we solemnize her on the day immediately preceding Sunday. Let this be enough concerning the explanation of the office of the Mass, provided that we understand that no one ought to celebrate two Masses on one and the same day, whether with one sacrifice or with two, but one with sacrifice and another dry Mass. Therefore we shall bring this matter to an end [Note: [Col. 0057D] On Consecration, distinction I, chapter “Three.”] if I briefly resolve two further questions.

One is whether, if a priest eats before Vespers and afterward cannot sleep, he ought or can celebrate Mass on the following day. We answer plainly that he ought not. The other is whether he can celebrate a second Mass if, in the preceding one, while washing his hands, he tasted a little water. Certainly, this too must be known to be forbidden. Now, then, to other matters.

## CHAPTER LII. On Vespers

At Vespers we sing five psalms, because we are imperfect, on account of the five senses: namely, so that what has been committed through the five bodily senses may be wholly forgiven through the singing of five psalms. It should therefore be noted that for the same reason we strike our breast with five fingers as we sing five psalms. Monks, however, insofar as they show themselves more perfect, say only four. For whatever is square remains always the same, firm and solid, whichever way it is turned. In the same manner, one who has made progress remains always the same and immovable in whatever place or at whatever time.

When the psalms are finished, there follows a short reading, without “Command, lord” and without “But thou, O Lord”; this is the chapter. Then comes the responsory, or a verse in its place, with hymns and an antiphon, and thereafter the *Magnificat*. Often, however, the hymn of Blessed Mary, namely the *Magnificat*, is used in place of the hymn, so that no other hymn is sung in addition. Finally follows the collect, [Col. 0058D] which we have called the prayer. Since up to now we have used customary and ecclesiastical expressions, we wish henceforth, as those handing down ecclesiastical offices, to employ ecclesiastical terminology.

It should therefore be known that the short reading ought to be sung from the same day and feast. For example: if one item is from the preceding Sunday, the rest likewise; if one is from the following Sunday, the rest likewise. It should further be observed that, when there is a solemnity of nine lessons, all the Vespers of that feast ought to be celebrated, as on the feast of Blessed Stephen and of Saint John the Evangelist. After Vespers, a collect of the saint whose feast follows must be said, or an antiphon with the *Magnificat*. Yet one exception exists: the feast of Saint Sylvester. Although it has nine lessons, its Vespers belong to the following feast.

## CHAPTER LIII. How many psalms are sung at Compline

Four psalms are sung at Compline, to signify perfection. For, since we have in some manner shown that the sins which we committed through the five bodily senses, those most destructive attendants, have now been forgiven through the preceding five psalms, there is another reason: the devil always lies in ambush for our heel, so that afterwards we ought neither to speak with others nor say anything except prayers. Monks carefully observe this, and do not drink afterward. For the devil thinks he has conquered if he conquers at that moment.

[Col. 0059B] Therefore, to run briefly through what seems to remain here: after the psalms follows the chapter and verse, then the hymn; when it is finished, the antiphon and *Nunc dimittis*. Afterwards the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed of our faith are recited; after we have added the collect to these, “Let us bless” must immediately follow. It is altogether fitting that this be sung by a boy at Vespers, so that by this we may show ourselves to be children in rendering praises to God.

## CHAPTER LIV. How prayers ought to be concluded

In order to have clear and full knowledge of how the prayers we call collects [Col. 0059C] ought to be concluded, one must first know that in them speech is sometimes directed to the Father, sometimes to the Son, sometimes to the Holy Spirit, and sometimes also to the whole Trinity. When it is directed to the Father, it must again be considered whether the address to him includes mention of the Son or the Holy Spirit, or not. And if, in a prayer directed to the Father, mention is made of the Son, it matters greatly whether this is made before the final clause or in the ending itself. We say this because according to these differences the conclusion of the prayer is different.

If the speech is directed wholly to the Father without mention of the Son and Holy Spirit, it will end thus: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, thy Son, who liveth and reigneth in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.” If mention of the Holy Spirit occurs there, you will say: “In the unity of the same Holy Spirit, God,” with the rest remaining unchanged. If mention of the Son is made before the final clause, it will say: “Through the same Lord,” etc., as above. If, on the other hand, mention is made in the ending itself, we say only: “Who liveth and reigneth with thee,” etc., as may be seen in this collect of Blessed Stephen:

> Almighty and everlasting God, who didst consecrate the first-fruits of the martyrs in the blood of blessed Stephen the levite: grant, we beseech thee, that he may be for us a perpetual intercessor, who prayed even for his persecutors to our Lord Jesus Christ, who liveth and reigneth with thee in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.
