If the prayer is addressed to the Son, as in this: “Stir up thy power, O Lord, and come,” and in others of the Advent of the Lord, it will end thus: “Who livest and reignest with God the Father,” etc. If it is addressed to the Holy Spirit, we shall say: “Who with the Father and the Son livest and reignest, one God,” etc.; and to the Trinity thus: “Who livest and reignest in perfect Trinity,” etc.

But in exorcisms, and those rites performed for making children catechumens, consecrating fonts, blessing water, and many other things of that kind, it will properly be said thus: “Through him who is to come to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.” This is done because no utterance frightens the devil as much as this: “who is to come,” etc.; so much so that as soon as he hears these words he is compelled to flee. Above all else, he fears the judgment by fire, being certain that after the day of judgment he will be punished by eternal fire. For the same reason Lord Gilbert wished prayers in the office of the dead to end in a similar manner. But our common Collectary contradicts him, maintaining that one ought to say: “Through our Lord,” etc.

## CHAPTER LV. On the varieties of offices

It has now been said thus far concerning ecclesiastical offices in general. It remains to undertake a fuller explanation of them throughout the entire course of the year. For the offices themselves vary according to the variety of seasons. But I think it worthwhile, before coming to the exposition itself, first to set forth a division of the four seasons.

Therefore, just as our solar year proceeds principally through the succession of four seasons—winter, in which seeds are sown; spring, in which the seeds come forth; summer, in which they whiten for harvest and are cut by the sickle; autumn, in which the grains are separated from one another by winnowing and stored in barns, while the chaff is burned—so too the great year of the present life, lasting from the beginning until the end of the world, is measured by the variety of four seasons.

There was a time of estrangement in the human race, namely from Adam to Moses, in which human beings turned aside from divine worship to idolatry. For then man abandoned the Lord his Creator and said to stones and the works of his own hands: “You are my God.” [Col. 0060D] This period suitably corresponds to night and winter. For just as night or winter has no light except contingently and accidentally, as from fire or a candle, so that age was wholly one of blindness and ignorance.

There was likewise a second period, of recall: from Moses until Christ’s birth. In it people were taught by the laws and prophets concerning Christ’s coming, the avoidance of sin, and the love of the one God. Then God said to Israel: “Hear, Israel: thy God is one God; thou shalt worship him alone and serve him alone” (Deut. 2, 6).

The third period was one of return, reconciliation, or justification, from the Lord’s birth until his ascension, through which grace and the preaching of the Gospel came to humankind. [Col. 0061A] The fourth and final period is that of pilgrimage, which began at the Lord’s ascension and will endure until the end of judgment, when there will be the consummation of the world.

These same periods are customarily called by other names. The period of estrangement is called the time of guilt and punishment. For through estrangement humanity became subject to guilt, and through guilt to punishment. The period of recall is called the time of teaching and prophecy: teaching because of the Decalogue, through which God taught the human race, saying, “Hear, Israel: thy God is one God”; prophecy because then we received this saving prophecy: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive” (Isa. 7). The period of reconciliation is accordingly called the time of joy and gladness; and finally, the period of pilgrimage, the time of mourning and struggle. [Col. 0061B] Hence it is surely necessary that we fight against our flesh, the world, and the powers of the air—especially against the flesh, since it has much familiarity with us, and no plague is more cruel than to have an enemy within one’s household.

Moreover, these times may be considered according to the principal divisions of the day: night, which corresponds to the time of deviation; morning, to the time of recall; noon, to the time of reconciliation or return; and evening, to the time of pilgrimage. Consider now the fitting epithet of each: night is dark, and those who wandered from the worship of the true God were blind. This fourfold division of times may also be elegantly discerned in the human being. Before baptism a person is born [Col. 0061C] and becomes a child of wrath; in baptism that person is reborn and becomes a child of grace; thereafter that person acts rightly and becomes an offspring of righteousness, loving God above all and the neighbour with a certain fervour of charity; finally, passing through death into eternal life, that person will reign together with Christ, having become an heir of eternity and glory.

Winter, spring, summer, and autumn may likewise be understood in each of the foregoing divisions. The same times are also signified by Christ’s four principal acts: namely, his birth, passion, resurrection, and coming for judgment, together with all their concomitants; so completely do these correspond to the human race. Christ’s life, therefore, is our teaching; Christ’s action is our reading; indeed, Christ’s entire manner of life is our instruction. I said “together with their concomitants,” because circumcision, manifestation, baptism, and purification belong to the birth; fasting and temptation are referred to the passion; ascension into heaven and the sending of the Holy Spirit belong to the resurrection; finally, transfiguration and the working of miracles belong to the coming for judgment. For he was more efficacious and had greater power after the transfiguration than before it, because then at last he showed us what we are to become. The passion is compared to winter, the birth to spring, the resurrection to summer, and judgment to autumn, when that Ancient of Days will sit, holding the winnowing-fan in his hand, and will thoroughly cleanse the threshing-floor, etc. (Matt. III).

Likewise, Christ’s birth is compared and corresponds to the time of recall [Col. 0062A], because the prophets foretold it in many ways; the passion, to the time of deviation; the resurrection, to the time of return, because of joy; and the coming for judgment, to the time of pilgrimage, because such a time will endure until the final day of judgment. Hence the Prophet: “I am wretched and a pilgrim, as were all my fathers” (Ps. XXXVIII).

Considering, then, these times of that great year, the Church transformed them into the service of God, laudably employing a varied order of offices every year according to their character and diversity. Yet, though the Church does this, she preferred to begin from the time of recall rather than from the time of deviation. Therefore she begins: “To thee have I lifted up my soul” (Ps. XXIV), “looking from afar,” etc.; since even now we see, as it were, through a mirror and lattice-work. And this continues until the Nativity [Col. 0062B] of the Lord. Throughout the whole season of Advent until Christmas, therefore, the Church recalls the time of recall, which came about through the Law and the prophets, applying a poultice to the wound. Thus she then reads Isaiah, who, seeing the incurable wound, said: “The whole head is sick, and the whole heart sorrowful,” etc. (Isa. I); and again, “there is no poultice to apply,” etc. A *malagma* is a kind of plaster, called an *epithema*.

Then the gradual begins: “To thee have I lifted up,” as though saying: “In the time of deviation, people lifted up their hands and hearts to the work of their own hands, and gave service to stone and wood; but thou art my God, and I have lifted up my soul to thee, my God,” etc. Thus she rightly begins the offices of her warfare from the time of recall rather than from the time of deviation, lest she seem to begin from error. She observes the matter itself well, therefore, though she does not follow the order—a thing the Evangelists also frequently do. Hence, if someone seeks sound health and wishes to be cured as well as possible, it was altogether necessary that he should begin with physicians.

## CHAPTER LVI. On the Remaining Times

In the season of Septuagesima, from the Sunday commonly called “They surrounded me” until the octave of Easter, the Church recalls the time of deviation. Hence at that time the book of Genesis is read through Kings, where the transgression of the first parents and of many others is treated, all of whom were submerged by the cataclysm or flood. During this time, therefore, the Church prays briefly [Col. 0062D], bends the knee, and fasts.

In Eastertide—that is, Easter, or rather from the octave of Easter to the octave of Pentecost—she recalls the time of joy and reconciliation, since the Apocalypse is read then, where the new city Jerusalem is mentioned, together with the Catholic Epistles and the Acts of the Apostles. Accordingly, the Church imposes little upon herself: she does not fast, she refrains from genuflection, she uses white vestments, and is content with three psalms and three readings, with three responsories and an equal number of verses.

From the octave of Pentecost until the coming of the Lord, she recalls the time of pilgrimage. In this time we have continual conflict and struggle against the three most hostile enemies, as was said: namely, the world, the flesh [Col. 0063A], and the devil. The world is a sophistical enemy; the flesh, a domestic enemy; the devil, an ancient enemy. Yet none of these enemies is more effective in harming us than our familiar enemy, namely the flesh, which we cherish with clothing and restore with food, and to which, as to a beast of burden, three things are due: food, lest it fail; a burden, that it may be tamed; and a rod, that it may walk not crookedly but straight.

To signify such combat, the Church then reads the book of Kings, which treats of battle. And because wisdom is especially needed in battle, the book of Solomon follows. But because in combat we should have nothing so much as patience, the book of Job is most fittingly appended. Then follows the book of Tobit, because of the particular mercy which we seek in this conflict. After this we also append the books of Judith, Ruth, and Esther, because of fortitude, justice, and temperance. Yet, since the struggle is still frequent, the book of Maccabees is necessarily joined to them, for in it there is continual conflict against pride. For once all other vices have been overcome, pride still remains to be conquered.

Someone may now ask under which of those times the period from Christmas to Septuagesima is contained. We may readily meet this question, for we have learned that some have answered it not inelegantly. One part of it, from Christmas until [Col. 0063C] the octave of Epiphany, is contained under the time of return, which, as stated, is a time of joy. Hence in certain churches white vestments are used throughout this period, as in Eastertide; neither fasting nor genuflection occurs then. The other part, from the octave of Epiphany to Septuagesima, is included under the time of pilgrimage; and the twelve Epistles of Paul are read, where his labour in struggle and conflict is treated.

Yet although Isaiah is customarily read even on the very day of the Lord’s Nativity, do not suppose that this day belongs to the time of recall. This is done for another reason: before the Gospel at Matins and before the Epistle at Mass, so that it may be placed beneath, as it were, as the base of a column, and Christ’s birth may be attested by both Testaments.

## CHAPTER LVII. Who Ordered the Ecclesiastical Offices for Certain Days

[Col. 0063D]

These ecclesiastical offices, as has been said, were instituted by Blessed Jerome at the request of Pope Damasus, as were also all the other readings from the Old and New Testament in the Church. Gregory, however, added certain chants; Gelasius, certain hymns; and others added other things. In the time of the Emperor Theodosius, psalmody was performed without order; he asked Pope Damasus to arrange the ecclesiastical office wisely. Damasus accomplished this diligently, as we said above.

In the aforesaid times there are certain doubled days, namely when feasts occur together. In these one must observe the maxim commonly used in moral philosophy: “Yield to the greater, and make place for the better.” That is, the more excellent office is to be celebrated [Col. 0064A], while only a commemoration of the lesser is made on that day, its proper office being reserved for the following day—as in certain churches with Peter and Paul when they fall on Sundays. For Peter is first celebrated because he was prince of the Apostles; Paul on the following day. The same occurs with certain other feasts falling on Sundays: the Sunday is to remain free, and the feast is then performed during the week.

We see that the same was done in the Old Testament. When Solomon dedicated the Temple on the twelfth day of the month, on which the Feast of Tabernacles occurred, he celebrated the dedication of the Temple for seven consecutive days and postponed the Feast of Tabernacles until after the dedication. Thus, among the above-mentioned times, there are certain principal Sundays before which other feasts yield, except Easter and Pentecost, which are far superior to all others because of the Resurrection and the sending of the Holy Spirit.

Some of these Sundays are more eminent and solemn, and their offices are consequently changed: such are the Sunday at the beginning of Advent, Septuagesima, and the Sunday in the octave of Easter. Others are not so eminent, such as the two called by their common names “Laetare Jerusalem” and Palm Sunday. If the feast of the Annunciation falls on Palm Sunday, or on the very day of the Resurrection, it is passed over altogether; the entire mystery of the Annunciation is performed on the Saturday preceding the Sunday [Col. 0064B] called Palm Sunday. For this Saturday readily yields its right to the greater feast.

In the same manner, if the feast of a dedication occurs during the Lord’s Passion, its mystery is by every right celebrated in the following week; likewise, if the same feast falls on the Ascension. It must necessarily be deferred to another time.

## CHAPTER LVIII. How Ecclesiastical Offices Should Be Performed, and What Their Books Are

In order, then, to begin with Advent and proceed to discuss ecclesiastical offices throughout the cycle of the entire year, two things in general must be diligently avoided: namely, that they be performed compulsorily or without discretion. They should not be compulsory, according to the Prophet who says: “I will sacrifice to thee willingly,” etc. (Ps. LIII). Thus Obal, who is also called Bezeleel, is said to have built the Temple for the Lord willingly. Although some think that Obal and Bezeleel were two persons, both are forbidden to be voluntary in an indiscreet manner, because the beast which chews the cud but does not divide the hoof is unclean. The division of the hoof is understood as discretion. Therefore the Lord loves one who makes voluntary and discriminating sacrifices.

For this reason the holy fathers established how we should serve God with discretion. They appointed readings at each hour: for example, at Matins and at Mass they instituted Epistles and Gospels; at the other hours, short readings called chapters. But since the ecclesiastical office is almost wholly occupied with reading and chant, it is worthwhile to know that there are five books of readings in the Church and three books of chants: namely [Col. 0065A] the Gradual, the Antiphonary, and the Troper.

The Antiphonary takes its name from the more important element, namely the antiphons, although the same book contains responsories and verses. For it is read in the Tripartite History that Ignatius, Patriarch of Antioch, heard angels singing antiphons on a mountain; afterward he instituted the singing of certain antiphons in the Church and the chanting of psalms according to antiphons. Hence antiphons are so called in relation to psalmody, just as a responsory is in relation to a history. Since psalms and antiphons had previously been sung confusedly and as if in a dance, the fathers ordained that the choir should sit separately and sing alternately: that one part of the choir should sing one verse of a psalm, and the other another.

The Antiphonary therefore begins thus: “Looking from afar.” Yet this is not Gregorian—that is, not composed by Gregory—but was merely added by another monk; for this reason it should not properly precede what Gregory composed. Nevertheless, custom has established that it be said by the whole Church. Things which have become established through long usage are certainly not easily corrected or changed. The rest, however, is by St. Gregory.

## CHAPTER LIX. On the Remaining Books

The second book is the Gradual, so called from the steps, because on feast days one ought to ascend the steps and sing there at the ambo. It is called an *ambo* from *ambio, ambis*, “I go around,” because that place is surrounded by steps; or from *ambo, ambae, ambo*, “both,” because there are, indeed [Col. 0065C], two ways there—that is, at the pulpit situated before the place where the Gospel is read. Thus there must be two sets of steps: one on the left, for ascent; the other on the right, for descent, according to: “They returned into their own country by another way” (Matt. II). On weekdays it is sung in the middle of the choir before the steps of the altar. This book begins: “To thee have I lifted up.”

The third book is called the Troper, from the Greek word τρόπος (*tropos*), “turning.” For from the end we return to the beginning of the chant. Thus a belt is called a *trope*, because it turns from one side to the other, passing around as far as the navel. The Troper is the book containing the chants customarily sung with the entrance of the Mass, especially by monks: namely tropes, sequences, *Kyrie eleison*, and neumes. They are called tropes because first a verse is sung, then *eleison*; then again a verse, and afterward *eleison*.

It should also be noted here, as we said once before, that *neuma*, feminine and without a *p*, means a jubilant melody. But the Holy Spirit is called in Greek *pneuma, pneumatis*; in Hebrew *Ruath*; and in Latin *spiritus*. Thus in the prose: “The holy *Pneuma* will descend upon thee.” Finally, the Troper has no fixed beginning, because its contents are sung at will. No one is bound to say this rather than that *Kyrie eleison* on a particular feast. By contrast, the Antiphonary has a fixed beginning, namely “Looking from afar,” just as the Gradual begins “To thee have I lifted up.” For the Church begins with Advent.

## CHAPTER LX. On the Five Books of Readings

[Col. 0066A]

Let us now consider the five books of readings. The first is the Bible-library (*bibliotheca*), from βίβλιος (*biblios*), “book,” and θήκη (*thēkē*), “repository.” For it contains the whole of both Testaments. Hence, by excellence, as though it were the worthier and greater, it alone of all books retained the name of its material. For all books were made from *biblos*; hence booksellers are called *bibliopolae*. Or, more correctly, this book is called a *bibliotheca* because, like a library, it embraces many and various books.

The second book is the Passionary, of which there are several. The third is the Legendary. The fourth, the Homiliary. The fifth, finally, is the Sermologus, or book of sermons [Col. 0066B]. Let us return, then, to the first and examine each somewhat more carefully.

The word *bibliotheca* is ambiguous and homonymous, or, as people now say, equivocal. By one name it signifies both the place in which books are stored—that is, a bookcase—and a great volume formed by binding together all the books of the New and Old Testament. It contains twenty-two volumes of the Old Testament and eight of the New: the four Evangelists, the Epistles of Paul, the Apocalypse, the Catholic Epistles, and the Acts of the Apostles.

The volumes of the Old Testament are the five books of Moses, namely the Pentateuch, properly called among the Jews *Thoral*, that is, “Law,” or “books of the Law.” They swear upon these, as we do upon the Gospels, as holier in the New Testament. Other books are enumerated in this manner: Joshua, Judges—of which Ruth is the final pericope or section—Samuel, and Malachim. These two volumes are counted as one, namely Kings, although it has four divisions or distinctions. Afterward four others follow in one volume: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and David. The twelve Minor Prophets are included in one volume because of their extreme brevity.

The following nine are counted as Hagiographa, though they are authentic: the book of Psalms, the book of Job, the three books of Solomon—namely Parables, or, if you prefer, Proverbs; Ecclesiastes; and the Song of Songs—the book of Chronicles, Judith, and [Col. 0066D] Esther. Finally, four books are enumerated as apocryphal: Tobit, Maccabees, Philo’s book, whose opening is “Love righteousness,” and that of Jesus son of Sirach, which begins: “All wisdom is from the Lord,” etc., and is also called Ecclesiasticus. Some do not receive these four, but the Church approves them because they generally have the character of Solomon’s books, even though she does not know their authors with certainty and truth.

We believe that Ezra composed two other books; he restored the whole library of the Old Testament after it had been burned by the Babylonians. We read our Bible-library, namely the Old and New Testament, at different times according to the various histories in each month, so that the whole may finally be completed with the cycle of the entire year. Hence I do not fail to know that the arrangement should first be assigned and explained at the Advent [Col. 0067A] of the Lord; but the explanation will appear easier and clearer if the arrangement begins with another season.

## CHAPTER LXI. What Should Be Read in Septuagesima

In Septuagesima, therefore, we read the whole Pentateuch as far as these days extend, namely the fifteen days before Easter. Thus four histories in all are sung: [three] from Genesis, and the fourth from Exodus. The first book of Moses is Genesis, which treats of the origin of the world; the second is Exodus, treating the departure of the Israelite people from Egypt; the third is Leviticus; the fourth, Numbers; the fifth, Deuteronomy—that is, “the second law”—which offers, as it were, a recapitulation of the Law.

During those fifteen days until Easter, Jeremiah and the book of Baruch his scribe are read, as some testify, under one volume. Jeremiah’s *Threni*, or Lamentations, are recited during the three days before Easter which we call Tenebrae. They are called *Threni* because Paschasius expounds them in three ways: historically, allegorically, and tropologically. Or from Mount Threnarus, where the lamentations of souls were first heard. Or they are called *Threni* because after every third verse there is a letter of the alphabet. For that work is written with a fourfold alphabet: that is, the entire alphabet is repeated in it four times. Or finally—and this I think truer—these readings are called *Threni* because they contain lamentations [Col. 0067C]. Among the Greeks θρῆνος (*thrēnos*) means “lament.” Thus the history narrated during those fifteen days is taken partly from Jeremiah and partly from the Lord’s Passion in the Gospel. Let us now pass to the octave of Pentecost, in order to pursue in similar fashion the order of the Old Testament.

## CHAPTER LXII. What Should Be Read from the Octave of Pentecost Until Christmas

From then until the Kalends of August, Samuel, Malachim—that is, the book of Kings—and Chronicles are read, together with the history “God of all.” Yet on the octave of Pentecost it is customary to sing and read of the Trinity. Although Pope Alexander, when asked whether this should be done, said that he knew no particular day either for the Trinity or for the Unity, we believe that its office was instituted chiefly because of heretics.

Here we should remember, until the Kalends of August, what we instructed shortly before concerning precautions. If a feast falls on Sunday, we shall safely change the history. Likewise, if the Kalends of August fall on Monday, Tuesday, or Wednesday, we may freely change the history on the preceding Sunday. But if they fall on Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, we may do the same on the following Sunday. This is our general rule. Finally, if the Kalends of a month fall on a weekday, we change the history on the Sunday nearest the Kalends, whether it precedes or follows them.

From the Kalends of August [Col. 0068A] until September, the three books of Solomon and the two apocryphal Wisdom books are read, so that the middle part of the Song of Songs is reserved until the Nativity of Blessed Mary in September, and the other part is read at her Assumption. For the discourses found there, such as “You compel me, O Paula and Eustochium,” and “It is an approved custom,” etc., should rather be read in the dining-room or refectory.

Then the history “In the beginning God” (Gen. I), “before the earth,” etc., is sung; this pertains to creation. For that other “in the beginning,” which belongs to Sexagesima, concerns creation. Accordingly, from the Kalends of September Job is read for fifteen days; and for another fifteen days Tobit, Ezra, Judith, and Esther, with the history “I ask thee, Lord.” In October the book of Maccabees is read, with the histories: “O Adonai, Lord God,” and “May the Lord open.” In November, Ezekiel, Daniel, and the twelve prophets are read, with the history “I saw the Lord.” Finally, in December Isaiah is read entire until the Nativity of the Lord, except that the reader should pass over what is read on Christmas itself—“The people of the Gentiles,” “Comfort ye,” “Arise”—and what is recited at Epiphany, namely “Arise, be enlightened, O Jerusalem.” For these concern Christ already born; the other passages read in Advent concern Christ yet to be born. Therefore those passages must be omitted until Christmas, because new things should then be heard.

Yet during the Ember fasts of Advent and on the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, nothing from Isaiah is read, because they have their own readings and offices. Hence other fasts are accustomed to borrow offices from these, as more solemn fasts [Col. 0068C].

The reason why these have such offices and not the others is that formerly the Roman pontiff was accustomed to confer orders during these fasts. But if the feast of Thomas falls within these fasts, the Church says the readings of the saint rather than those of the fast. For this custom has become established. The Roman Church, however, does not observe this: it recites six readings of the fast and the last three from the homily on the Gospel of the feast itself.

In Advent there are sometimes three histories, sometimes four if Advent has four weeks, which rarely occurs. This is enough concerning the Old Testament; now let us consider the New. From the octave of Easter until Pentecost, John’s Apocalypse is read for three weeks and the Catholic Epistles for the following two, until the Ascension; they number seven. The first is James the Less’s; the next three are the Evangelist John’s; the fifth and sixth are Peter’s, prince of the Apostles; and the seventh is Thaddaeus’s, who is also called Jude, brother of Simon. From the Lord’s Ascension until Pentecost, the Acts of the Apostles are read: “First indeed,” etc. The history is “Worthy art thou, Lord,” for all the foregoing matters.

From the octave of Epiphany until Septuagesima, the fourteen Epistles of Paul are read, both those sent to four persons and those sent to ten churches—for example, to Titus and to the Corinthians. The Gospels and Psalms will be discussed in their proper place. Thus we have the Church’s arrangement of both Testaments [Col. 0069A].

Meanwhile, it should be noted in passing that readings end in four ways: with “But thou, O Lord”; “Thus says the Lord: Turn to me and you shall be saved”; in Jeremiah’s Lamentations, with “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, return to the Lord thy God”; and finally, in readings for the dead, with “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord.” The use of the last in the Church, however, is very rare. But we say not what is done, but what ought to be done.

The Homiliary, which we said was the fourth book, is read at the Nativity and on the feasts of those who have their own Gospels, such as the feast of Blessed Thomas, Easter, Pentecost with its weekdays, and also on Sundays. The eight days of Easter are counted with Septuagesima, because it is the seventh week from Quadragesima, through which the same thing is signified as through Septuagesima: in its seventh decade the children of Israel received leave to return and were already, as it were, free. Thus songs of joy are raised on those days. On the Saturday in White, the *Alleluia* is doubled because Septuagesima ends. This signifies that, once the course of this present life has been completed, we shall receive a double garment when we have reached our Jerusalem. This Saturday is called “in White” because those baptized on Easter Saturday then laid aside the white garments which they had received on the eighth day.

The Passionaries are read on the days of martyrs. But some of these, as Gelasius testifies, are apocryphal: for example, those concerning Blessed Gregory, the martyrs Quiricus and Julitta, and all writings of that kind said to have been composed by heretics. Because of their ill repute, they are prohibited by the Church. Why they have been canonized will be stated in its proper place. Nor are all homilies approved: some are Origen’s, who lapsed into heresy. Yet certain of his homilies, corrected by Jerome, are read, though the author’s name is suppressed because of the disgrace of heresy. Similarly Solomon’s name is omitted in readings because of the stigma of idolatry, and Moses’ because of the hesitation he displayed at the Waters of Contradiction, when he provoked the Lord. For one does not say, “A reading from the book of Genesis of Moses the lawgiver,” as one says, “A reading from the book of the Apocalypse of John the Apostle” [Col. 0069D].

Some nevertheless think that this should be said at the beginning of homilies: “A homily of Origen, corrected by Jerome”; and afterwards, as it were, “A homily of the same author.” Those who have left Homilies to posterity are chiefly Augustine, Gregory, Bede, and Origen.

In short, Passions should be read on martyrs’ feasts; Lives on feasts of those who have proper Gospels, such as Blessed Thomas’s. The last three readings ought to be from homilies, and the others from Passions. The Legendary is the book which relates the lives and deaths of confessors, such as Hilary, Martin, and others whom the holy Church has confirmed. On their feasts this book must necessarily be read. Finally, the book of sermons, also called the Sermologus [Col. 0070A], should be read from Christmas until the octave of Epiphany; Pope Leo and many others composed these sermons. The same book is read on the Purification of Blessed Mary the Virgin and, besides other feasts, also on All Saints’ Day.

Gregory and Bede composed the principal homilies. Bede, however, composed none except those which Augustine had previously issued; for he added only this of his own: he clothed them, as it were, in his own words, so that where Augustine’s text contains only the words of disputation, Bede’s contains the words of a sermon and reading.

## CHAPTER LXIII. On the Books of Chants

Let us now return to the books of chants, and do so according to the days of Advent [Col. 0070B]. The first responsory is followed by three verses. If we survey the entire year, we shall plainly find that this happens nowhere else. It is done because of the three ages of the ancient Fathers awaiting Christ’s coming. The first was from Adam until Noah, namely until the Flood; the second until Moses; the third until Christ.

The threefold repetition in the same responsory—first from a higher pitch, second from one less remote, and third again from one less remote and lower—has this reason: in this manner we show that the Fathers of the first age were farther from Christ’s advent than were those of the second or third, and again that those of the second were farther away than those of the third. So also there are three ages of the newer Fathers awaiting Christ’s coming. The first was that of the primitive Church, of Jews converted to the faith; the second is now present, when the admission of the Gentiles or heathen has taken place; but the third will be when all Israel is saved. Thus the first are, or rather were, more remote than the last, so that this allegory may be adapted to both advents.

Finally, “Glory be to the Father” is joined with three verses, because all our desire and service must be directed to the triune Lord. No part is repeated here, but the entire responsory, because after this all the times of the present life will be brought to completion. Then God will be all in all (1 Cor. XV): that is, the completion and sufficiency of all things [Col. 0070D].

Let us now consider the character of the office, and the reverence, continence, and abstinence appropriate to the season. Its character concerns what ought to be retained or omitted. We have already taught in some measure what should be retained or observed; and we add that, at the end of Advent, seven antiphons of the second tone should be sung, each in order on its own day until Christmas. They are all in the second tone either because they signify the twofold love—of God and of neighbour—or because of Christ’s two natures. There are seven because of the sevenfold Spirit, by whom those awaiting Christ were enlightened. It should be known, however, that two other antiphons have been added to these seven antiphons concerning the Sacrament: one for Blessed Thomas, the other for Blessed Mary the Virgin [Col. 0071A].

## CHAPTER LXIV. What Must Be Omitted in Advent

In Advent, as in Septuagesima, certain songs of joy must be omitted: such as *Te Deum laudamus*, *Gloria in excelsis*, and *Ite, missa est*. Yet because this season is partly one of joy, *Alleluia* is not suppressed as it is in Septuagesima, which is wholly a season of mourning. Thus we may observe that these three follow one another, but not invariably.

Certain churches, on the feast of the Chair of Blessed Peter, say *Te Deum laudamus* even when that feast falls in Lent, though the other praises are silent, because this chant is customarily used for installing persons in their sees. For Peter was established in the chair of Antioch on that day. Again, *Gloria in excelsis* and *Ite, missa est* are said on the solemn day of the Supper if a bishop is present and celebrates the office of the three Oils; but *Te Deum laudamus* is not said, because one rises for Tenebrae. For this same reason, *Gloria Patri* is omitted from psalms and responsories on those days, because the Trinity was then greatly dishonoured, especially during that three-day period.

Likewise, at the first Mass of the Lord’s Nativity, *Gloria in excelsis* is sung, but *Ite, missa est* is not said until the third Mass has been completed. Otherwise the people would depart and not hear Matins. Hence some priests reserve the collect, or final prayer, of the first Mass until Matins are sung, and afterward say it and conclude the Mass with *Benedicamus Domino*. Then the second Mass begins and ends in like fashion; or, in certain churches, it ends with “Behold, they are completed,” so that the people are not given leave to depart but know that they must still hear the third Mass. At its end *Ite, missa est* is pronounced. This acclamation pertains to the Resurrection, just as *Gloria in excelsis* pertains to the Nativity.

This, then, is why both are omitted in Advent: both are then eagerly awaited. But *Te Deum laudamus* is silent either so that it may be resumed with greater fervour on the feast day itself, or because the one whom we await is not yet present, whereas we customarily use this chant for those who are present. Thus, instead of “The Lord hath reigned” (Ps. XCVI), “Have mercy on me, O God” (Ps. L) is said, together with the canticles of Anna, Moses, Habakkuk, and the others used there, such as: “I said” (Isa. XXXVIII), and “Hear, O heavens” (Deut. XXXII), which are said each week. The Hours of the Blessed Virgin are omitted because the entire office of that season is directed to her praise.

Hence it must also be observed that, on feasts of nine lessons occurring in Advent, the solemn Mass should be celebrated at Terce, with the *Gloria in excelsis* and *Ite, missa est*. Therefore, in most churches they remove their black copes for that Mass, as in the Paschal season, and knees should not then be bent. Once the Mass is finished, the copes are resumed; and, after Sext and None have been sung, the Mass of the fast begins. [Col. 0072A] At such a Mass, and throughout fasting seasons, the deacon ought to pronounce *Flectamus genua* (“Let us bend the knee”), except on the weekdays immediately following Pentecost. On these, out of reverence for the feast, the songs of joy—namely *Alleluia*, *Te Deum laudamus*, and *Ite, missa est*—are not suppressed.

Accordingly, no commemoration of any saint ought to be made here, whether the saint preceded Christ’s Advent—for all those of that time descended into hell, and therefore the Church does not celebrate solemnities for them—or followed Christ’s Advent, since a commemoration ought to be made for each of them on his own day. “Behold, the Lord will come,” etc. (Isa. LXVI), is the antiphon sung after *Benedicamus Domino*, and the following prayer follows: “Cleanse, we beseech thee, O Lord, our consciences by visiting them, [Col. 0072B] that our Lord Jesus Christ, when he comes with all his saints, may find in us a dwelling prepared for himself, who with thee,” etc. In the antiphon occur the words “all his saints with him,” and in the prayer, “with all his saints,” so that it is unnecessary on that account to make a separate commemoration of particular saints.

But we must understand this prayer as referring to the second Advent, which occurs in the human mind, when it is read: “That the coming Lord Jesus Christ may find in us a dwelling prepared for himself.” Yet then “with all his saints” should not be added. For if that is added, it will seem already to refer to the third Advent. Christ’s Advent is threefold: in the flesh; in the mind, which occurs daily in human souls [Col. 0072C] through the Holy Spirit; and, thirdly, in majesty, which will occur on the day of judgment. Of the second Advent, which takes place in the human mind, Solomon says: “Lord, send thy wisdom, that it may be with me and labour with me” (Wis. IX).

There is also another explanation of the following text, namely that it signifies for us two Advents: “Stir up, O Lord, thy power, and come, that from the imminent dangers of our sins,” etc. It refers to the first Advent when it says, “May we deserve to be delivered by thy protection”; but to the second when we read, “May we be saved by thy deliverance.”

## CHAPTER LXV. On the seasons in which marriages ought not to be celebrated

Marriages ought not to be celebrated in Advent, [Col. 0072D] nor in Septuagesima, since such seasons are especially devoted to prayer, and at that time everyone ought rather to abstain from the marriage-bed than to join it. The same must be done on sacred solemnities and their weekdays, as at Easter and Pentecost. Indeed, continence ought especially to be observed also on Sundays and feasts of the Apostles. For solemnities were instituted so that prayer might be pursued more freely. Yet country people, on the contrary, prefer to gather on those days in order to devote themselves to drinking. But in all these matters the priest must be cautious. For it often happens that a dumb beast instructs a divine animal—that is, a layman instructs a cleric.

In general, it must be observed that, whenever one abstains from marriage, one should abstain [Col. 0073A] from a spouse’s embrace, except when, through the weakness of incontinence, the husband demands the marital due from his wife, or she from her husband. For it must be rendered to one who asks, since, as the Apostle says, “the husband has no authority over his own body, but the wife does” (I Cor. VII), and conversely.

For these reasons, marriages should likewise not be celebrated during the three weeks preceding the feast of St John the Baptist. Yet in certain churches this has long since fallen into disuse. Nevertheless, there was a reason why the Church had established that Lent should be kept before the feast of St John, as before Christmas. But because of human frailty, those two Lents were reduced to one; and it was then divided into three weeks preceding Christmas and three preceding [Col. 0073B] the feast of St John. Since, therefore, these times are chiefly dedicated to prayer—which we undertake in order to attain heaven, though we cannot do so without two other things, namely fasting and almsgiving, which readily bear a person to heaven—fasting was ordained so that what remains to us through fasting may be distributed to the poor. Thus the bridegroom too ought to abstain from his wife’s bed, that he may devote himself to prayer more freely and conveniently.

And so marriages are not contracted from the first Sunday of Advent until Epiphany; nor would they be contracted until the octave of Epiphany, unless the Lord had honoured marriage both by his presence and by a miracle. Furthermore, in Advent any verse may be said, [Col. 0073C] provided it concerns the Advent, such as: “The Lord shall go forth from his holy place in his majesty, and shall come to judge” (Isa. XXVI); and, “Come, O Lord, to deliver us” (Isa. XXXVI). This may be said of any Advent. For the Advent in the flesh delivered our souls from the slavery of the devil; the Advent in the mind delivers souls from sin; and finally the Advent in majesty delivers bodies.

Finally, it should be noted in passing that the feast of St Lucy has attached to it, in Italian, *charthar* [reading uncertain], because at that time meat is especially customarily laid aside, just as the second Sunday of Septuagesima is commonly called *carnisprivium* (“the taking away of meat”).

## CHAPTER LXVI. On the feasts and fasts of Advent

Next let us consider the matters [Col. 0073D] pertaining to Advent, namely its feasts and fasts. First, it should be understood that, if the feast of St Andrew falls on the first Sunday, it must be transferred to Monday. We wish the same to be observed for every feast of Apostles or martyrs which falls on the privileged Sundays that we shall mention shortly. Likewise, if such a feast falls on Sunday and has a vigil, its office shall be celebrated on Monday, and there shall be a fast on Saturday, provided that the vigil is *inofficiata*, that is, has its own proper office.

Likewise, if on any other privileged Sunday there falls the feast of an Apostle, or especially of some martyr, or of another saint having a proper office, it remains to be seen whether the following week is *inofficiata*—that is, whether every day [Col. 0074A] of that week has its own proper office. If it does not, we shall set aside the office of that Sunday and celebrate in its place the feast of the guest, that is, the saint arriving upon the Sunday. But if it does, the Sunday office remaining in place, the feast shall be transferred to Monday. Thus Sunday sometimes yields to the feast and sometimes does not. Why? Because in the latter case the office is renewed.

Accordingly, the Ember fasts must be observed in the third week of Advent. Advent ought to contain twenty-one days, that is, three complete weeks, apart from the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord. Since Advent always begins on Sunday, if the Nativity of the Lord likewise falls on Sunday, it is necessary that Advent [Col. 0074B] extend through four weeks. Otherwise the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity and the Ember fasts would coincide, though each has its own particular office and belongs to a different season. For the vigil belongs to the season of joy, since it is not of Advent but of the Nativity; consequently Advent would not have twenty-one days, with the vigil excepted, as we say.

But if the Nativity of the Lord falls on Monday, or thereafter up to Sunday, then in addition to the twenty-one days we shall readily have a day on which to observe the vigil, because on the Sunday itself, which has no proper office, the vigil will be celebrated and *Alleluia* sung on account of Sunday. Yet the fast will be observed on the preceding Saturday, [Col. 0074C] both for the Ember fast and for the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity.

As regards fasts generally, it should be understood that, although the spring fasts were first instituted in the first week of spring, the summer fasts in the second week of June, the autumn fasts in the third week of September, and the winter fasts in the fourth week of December, all that was abolished on account of the many confusions arising from it; and it was regularly determined at what time each was to be observed. Of the winter fasts it has already been said that they are always held in the third week of Advent. But concerning the others, it should regularly be understood that the spring fasts always begin in the first week of Lent; the summer fasts, always in the week of Pentecost; while the autumn fasts retain the old institution, since they always occur in the third week of September. [Col. 0074D]

Meanwhile, great care must be taken not to err in reckoning these weeks. For if the Kalends of that month—that is, if the month itself—begins on the first, second, third, or even fourth weekday, then that week of the month is counted, and the fasts are held in the third week from it. But if the month begins on the fifth, sixth, or seventh weekday, we shall begin to count the three weeks from the following Sunday, and the fasts shall likewise occur in the third. Thus the preceding days are wholly useless for the reckoning of weeks. We therefore have this rule: from that Sunday which is nearer to the Kalends of September—that is, which is always immediately before or after the first day of the month—the first week must be counted, whether it follows or precedes them.

## CHAPTER LXVII. On anniversaries of the dead and vigils of saints

[Col. 0075A]

Concerning anniversaries of the dead, we say that, if they fall on Sunday or on any other celebrated solemnity, they should not be moved and deferred to the following day, as we said concerning saints’ feasts; rather, they should be observed on the preceding day, so that relief may sooner be brought to the punishments which the dead endure in purgatorial fire. For as saints have no need of our assistance and benefit, so it is altogether necessary for the other dead.

A Mass for the dead may be celebrated at any time when the corpse is present, except on Good Friday. For then the Body of Christ should not be offered, nor Mass sung; but on the following day, Saturday, Mass may be sung for the deceased and the body buried. [Col. 0075B] The same must be done on Easter Day itself. For if anyone dies then, Mass must be celebrated on the following day, with the body kept above ground in the meantime. For burial ought not take place without Mass.

Concerning saints’ vigils generally, we say that if they have a proper collect at Mass, it ought to be said at Vespers. If Sunday falls on the vigil, we shall say Vespers of Sunday and afterwards those of the saint; or, with the *Magnificat*, we shall recite only the collect, as the Church of Mainz and the monks do; or, with a single antiphon, we shall say the prayer or collect of the feast if it has no proper and special vigil, adding at the end: *Benedicamus Domino*.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. On the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity

[Col. 0075C]

Next comes the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, which has its own Mass and proper collect, and this likewise ought to be said at Vespers, as is also observed in other vigils. But if the contrary is the case—that is, if the vigil has no particular office—the collect of the following feast ought to be said at Vespers.

On the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity these Psalms are sung: “Praise the Lord, ye children” (Ps. CXII); “Praise the Lord, all ye nations” (Ps. CXVI); “Praise the Lord, O my soul” (Ps. CXLV); “Praise the Lord, for he is good” (Ps. CXLVI); and “Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem” (Ps. CXLVII). But at Compline the hymn *Veni, Redemptor gentium* (“Come, Redeemer of the nations”) ought to be sung.

## CHAPTER LXIX. On the Nativity of the Lord

[Col. 0075D]

Let us now treat of the very day of the Nativity, on which it is customary before the first Nocturns to place three cloths upon the altar, as a representation of three periods, and to remove one at each Nocturn. The first was black, for the time before the Law; the second whitish, for the time of revelation; and the third red, for the time of grace—because of the beloved bridegroom, “white and ruddy.” Elsewhere you may readily find how the ancients customarily rose at intervals and at different times for the Nocturns: namely at cockcrow, at midnight, and before dawn.

After the third Nocturn the church lights are kindled; and, after the Gospel, “The book of the generation” (Matt. [Col. 0076A] I), has been recited, *Te Deum laudamus* is sung, to mark the rejoicing that occurred at finding the drachma which the woman had lost. To find it she lit a lamp and overturned the whole house; that is, the triumphant Church is wholly drawn forth from hell through Christ.

Four Gospels are read that day: one from Matthew, the second and third from Luke, and the fourth from John, so that four witnesses may bear witness to Christ’s Nativity. Yet two—or at most three—would suffice, since “every word stands in the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Deut. XVII). Why Isaiah is read in the first Nocturn has been shown above.

But here we must carefully observe that the writings of three men are used more frequently in the Church at this time than those of others: first, the prophet David, who was a murderer, traitor, and adulterer; secondly, the Apostle Matthew, who was also called a publican and was infamous by that very name; and finally, the Apostle Paul, who persecuted the Church. [Col. 0076B] This institution was not without purpose: it was meant to prevent other persons, however sinful on account of their preceding deeds, from despairing that almsgiving or prayers are displeasing to God; rather, if they repent, they may know assuredly that they can readily obtain forgiveness, however entangled in grievous guilt they may be.

After *Te Deum laudamus*, the priest, having now come out of the vestry, ought to say *Confiteor*, and the first Mass should begin. In it Christ’s eternal generation, obscure and unknown, is treated; for this reason it ought also to be sung at night. Once it is finished, Lauds are said and concluded with the same prayer as the Mass, in order to indicate that it and the Mass signify precisely the same office.

At dawn the second Mass begins at once, in which the fulfilment or accomplishment of the promises concerning Christ’s birth is treated. Therefore we begin it thus: *Lux fulgebit* (“Light shall shine”), since it begins with the dawning day and the appearance of morning. But some half-educated grammarian may say here: “Then it ought to read *lux fulgens*, ‘shining light.’” This is not true, because then the sky is red. Rather, as we have said, it must be understood of the fulfilment of the promises—as though we said: “Light shall shine when Christ has come,” [Col. 0076C] he who is the true and eternal light, and when all that has long been said about his Advent will be fulfilled. Accordingly this Mass, as has also been said above, ends thus: “Behold, all things are fulfilled,” etc.

The first Mass therefore concerns the eternal generation from the Father without a mother; the second, the temporal generation from a mother without a father; but the third is, as it were, compounded and joined together, for it presents both. For what is said at its beginning, “A child is born unto us” (Isa. IX), concerns the temporal generation; but John’s Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word” (John I), concerns the eternal. Yet the final part of that Gospel, namely “The Word was made flesh,” etc., must be referred to the temporal birth.

This double nativity is spoken of in order that we may understand clearly that Christ’s earthly nativity undoubtedly conferred upon us a heavenly nativity. Hence it is said on the feast of St Stephen: “Yesterday Christ was born on earth, that Stephen might be born in heaven today.” Finally, the *neumae* performed at Mass represent joy. They are customarily made rather on *e*, as in *Kyrie*, or on *a*, as in *alleluia*, than on the other vowels, so that by these we may signify the spiritual joy restored to us at the Virgin’s childbirth, when the word *Eva* was transformed as the angel greeted her saying, “Ave, Maria” (Luke I). [Col. 0076D]

For the meaning of that name, namely *Eva*, endured until the angel’s salutation. Infants express this meaning—the sorrow of Adam and Eve—when they are born: if a girl is born, she utters, as the common people suppose, *e*; if a male, *a*. Those *neumae*, then, represent the grief which Adam’s and Eve’s transgression brought upon us. But joy was wholly restored in the Blessed Virgin, to whom was said not *Eva* but *Ave*.

## CHAPTER LXX. On the feasts following the Nativity

Next, in fitting order, we must treat of the feasts immediately following Christ’s Nativity. The Vespers of the Nativity should first be celebrated in full; afterward the deacons assemble, as it were in festal dancing, and sing the *Magnificat* with the antiphon of St Stephen, while the priest recites the collect. The deacons celebrate the Nocturns and the whole office of the following day, because Stephen was a deacon; [Col. 0077C] and they give the blessings at the lessons. Yet the Mass of that day is to be celebrated by the weekly officiant, that is, the one whose turn it then is to perform it.

Likewise, the priests shall perform the whole office on the day of St John, because he was a priest; and the boys on the feast of the Innocents, because the Innocents were slain for Christ. But it should not be unknown that the passion of blessed Stephen took place in August, on the day on which his discovery is celebrated; whereas his discovery occurred on the day after the Lord’s Nativity. Yet because the feast of a Passion is worthier and more eminent than that of a discovery, it was transferred to the season of the Lord’s Nativity. Or perhaps this was because a basilica was dedicated to him on this same day.

There may, however, be another reason: after the Lord’s Passion, Stephen was the first to suffer martyrdom for Christ, which is called being born in heaven; Christ’s birth in the flesh conferred such a nativity upon us. It was therefore fitting that the Nativity of St Stephen should be joined to Christ’s Nativity, to indicate thereby that one nativity follows from the other. Hence it is also read in his Life: “Yesterday Christ was born on earth, that Stephen might be born in heaven today.”

Nearly the same judgment should be made concerning the feast of St John the Evangelist: although the day on which, after celebrating the sacred rites, he laid himself down in the grave was the Nativity of St John the Baptist, yet this feast yielded to that of the Baptist, of whom the Lord had said: “Among those born of women none greater has arisen,” etc. (Luke 7). His feast was transferred to the third day [Col. 0078A] after the Lord’s Nativity, so that the bridegroom, who is ruddy and white, might have all his companions. Or this may also be because a basilica was dedicated to him on that day, or finally because he was exiled on that day; for he was Patriarch of Ephesus. Then he wrote the Gospel of which Bede says: “Had he thundered a little more deeply, the whole world could scarcely have contained it.” Thus Jerome also calls him “the voice of an eagle.”

For a similar reason, the Innocents did not suffer immediately on the fourth day after the Nativity, but on the fourth day when the year had come round. For since Herod had been accused by his sons, he had to go to Rome and defend his case before Caesar Augustus; and as soon as he had won the case and returned, he committed that monstrous crime, killing all the boys two years old and under (Matt. II). He believed that the child born—whom the stars served—would become great, and he feared that he would lose his kingdom through him. This is read more fully in Matthew.

On the feast of the Innocents the songs of joy are entirely suppressed, because they descended into hell. But if their feast falls on Sunday, none is suppressed, because of the day of Resurrection. Nor are any songs of joy suppressed in their octave, so that we may signify the joy which they will receive in the octave—that is, at the Resurrection.

## CHAPTER LXXI. On the Circumcision

At the Circumcision, two things coincidentally occur: those of the woman giving birth [Col. 0078C] and of the birth itself, on account of the octaves. Hence, on that day we ought to celebrate two Masses: the first of the Blessed Virgin, namely *Vultum tuum* (“Thy countenance”); the other of the Octaves, namely *Puer natus est nobis* (“A child is born unto us”). On that day Luke’s Gospel is said: “When eight days were fulfilled” (Luke II), etc.

There are others who think that three feasts coincide here: that of the Blessed Virgin, that of the octaves, and that of the Circumcision. For even if he had not then been circumcised, the octaves would nevertheless have been kept. But since we have now mentioned the octaves, it will not be unsuitable to discuss them somewhat more fully.

Some octaves are of institution, such as those belonging to feasts that have vigils; some are of devotion, such as may be observed in honour of any saint; and some are of veneration, as are said to belong to God alone. Thus the octaves of the Nativity, Easter, and Pentecost are octaves of reverence for Christ. There are also octaves of signification, such as those of the Innocents, through which our Resurrection is signified; [Col. 0078D] hence songs of joy or praise are sung then. For although they descended into hell, they will nevertheless rise with us in glory. Yet octaves of signification may likewise be said to belong to any other saints.

Meanwhile, the whole period extending to the Purification treats of the Saviour’s infancy; hence commemorations of other saints ought not to be made during it—especially of the Holy Cross—in accordance with the common saying: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk” (Exod. XXXIV).

## CHAPTER LXXII. On the feast of subdeacons

[Col. 0079A]

The feast of the subdeacons, which we call the Feast of Fools, is observed by some at the Circumcision, but by others at Epiphany or its octave. [Note: [Col. 0079D] See Pope Innocent III, constitution 79.] Four festive revelries take place in the Church after the Lord’s Nativity: those of the levites, the priests, the boys—that is, those lower in age and rank—and the subdeacons, whose order is uncertain. Thus it happens that they are sometimes numbered among the sacred orders and sometimes not; this is expressly apparent from the fact that they have no fixed time and that their office is celebrated in a confused manner.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. On Epiphany

[Col. 0079B]

After this follows the day of manifestations, or epiphanies, several of which are reported to have occurred on the same calendar day, though in different years. One occurred through the star on the thirteenth day after Christ’s birth. This is properly called *Epiphany*, from the Greek verb ἐπιφαίνομαι, “I appear.” Another occurred through the voice of the Father, on the same day in the thirtieth year, and is called *Theophany*, θεοφανία, from Θεός, “God.” The third was called *Bethany*, a name formed from Hebrew and Greek, namely from *beth*, “house”; it likewise occurred in another year on the same day. For he appeared in a house by changing water into wine. These three epiphanies are recounted in the Gospel as having occurred on the same day.

Bede, in his Commentary on Luke, added a fourth, occurring on the same day when the year had come round: namely, the feeding with loaves. It is called *phagiphania*, from Greek φάγω, “I eat.” By all these things Christ was manifested to be God. Thus four feasts occur on one day.

If someone asks how the kings could have come so quickly, since the star was first seen by them on the very day of Christ’s birth, so that it would have been difficult to travel overland to Jerusalem from foreign lands in thirteen days, we may answer in two ways: either, as most maintain, the star appeared to them before the Nativity; or, as others think, they came on dromedaries. A dromedary is an animal somewhat smaller in stature than a camel, but much swifter in running. For it can cover in one day as much distance [Col. 0079D] as a horse in three days.

If someone further asks where that star disappeared, we shall again answer in two ways: either it fell, as some hold, into a well, where it may still readily be seen, but only by virgins; or, as others think, it was dissolved into its former matter.

On the feast of Epiphany itself we do not say *Venite* (“Come”) at the first Nocturn, for two reasons: because the kings came to adore Christ without being invited; and lest we seem to imitate Herod. For he summoned all the wise men of his kingdom to counsel, not in order to adore Christ, as he falsely said, but rather [Col. 0080A] in order to destroy him. For the same reason, three days before Easter we do not give the kiss of peace, in order to show ourselves unlike Judas the betrayer.

At the second Nocturn, however, at the sixth antiphon we sing: *Venite, exsultemus* (“Come, let us rejoice”; Ps. XCIV), because in the sixth age of the world the Gentiles came to faith in Christ. The first of these were the three kings who set out from their kingdoms to adore Christ. At the third Nocturn, finally, we sing the antiphon: *Fluminis impetus laetificat civitatem Dei* (“The rush of the river makes glad the city of God”; Ps. XLV), and the psalm *Deus noster refugium* (“God is our refuge”; ibid.), in reverse psalm order. This occurs at no other time in the entire year except the feast of All Saints; but why it is done then will be said elsewhere.

It is at the third Nocturn because in the third time—that is, the time [Col. 0080B] of grace—the rush of the river, namely Baptism, gladdens the city of God, namely the holy Church militant, cleansing it and purging it from every stain, so that it may happily attain the seventh age of those at rest, where it will then be gladdened more fully and abundantly. And since God’s city will receive, as it were, its full state in the seventh age of those at rest, when it is freed from every penalty and enjoys the most welcome sight of its Creator, this antiphon is sung in the seventh place.

At the third Nocturn we frequently sing *Alleluia*, in order to show that joy came in the third time through Baptism. Matins ought therefore to begin as follows: *Domine, labia mea aperies* (“O Lord, thou wilt open my lips”; Ps. L). Then follows the hymn, if it is a monastic church. If not, by way of example there follow: *Afferte Domino, filii* (“Bring unto the Lord, ye sons”; Ps. XXVIII), and *Deus noster refugium* (“God is our refuge”; Ps. XLV). Finally, to proceed to the remaining points, we may readily suppose that the kings did not come alone but brought with them a great retinue of princes.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. On the Gospels of the Manifestation

There are three Gospels for this feast: one concerning Baptism, namely, “It came to pass, when he was baptized” (Luke III); the second concerning the Magi, namely, “When Jesus had been born” (Matt. II); and the third concerning the wedding feast (John II), which is read on the following Sunday.

Moreover, we must not overlook that two Gospels concerning Christ’s generation are read at night: one at the Nativity and the other at Epiphany. For both generations of Christ occurred at night—that is, they were obscure and could not be apprehended by the understanding of the first Fathers. One generation takes place by descending, the other by ascending, because the one is carnal and the other spiritual. In the one, “begot” is used (*genuit*, Matt. I), to express the succession of carnal and temporal generation; in the other, “who was” (*qui fuit*, Luke III) is used, so that the adoption of spiritual generation may be bestowed. The first ended in the Virgin’s childbirth; the second began through Baptism.

Between the octave of Epiphany and Septuagesima, some read responsories “of the Psalms,” so called because they ought to answer and correspond to the lessons, although the Psalms ought not to be read except during the three days before Easter. [Col. 0081A]

## CHAPTER LXXV. On saints’ feasts

Let us now briefly pass to the feasts immediately following. Concerning blessed Agnes, whose Life Ambrose is said to have composed, it is enough to know only that she has no octave of institution. Otherwise, she does have an octave for another reason of signification. Her solemnity began to be celebrated because of a certain miracle which befell her parents on the eighth day while they were lamenting at her tomb.

On the feast of St Paul certain verses with antiphons are sung, as is also done on the feasts of St Lawrence [Col. 0081B] and St Stephen. For Paul laboured more than all in exhorting and preaching; Lawrence suffered more grievously than the rest; and Stephen was the first martyr for Christ’s faith. The same ought also to be done for Blessed Mary, because she was privileged in virginity, since she both was and was called the Virgin of virgins.

## CHAPTER LXXVI. On the Sunday after the octave of Epiphany

On the Sunday after the octave of Epiphany is sung: “Let all the earth adore thee” (Ps. LXV). The explanation given for this is as follows. Since Augustus ruled over the whole world for the glory of the Roman Empire, he issued and proclaimed an edict that every year someone should come to Rome from each city of the world, bringing with him as much earth as he could grasp in the hollow of his fist. [Col. 0081C] This was done so that it might thereby be certainly and clearly established that all were subject to the Roman Empire.

Afterwards, when a kind of little mound had been made from that earth, a church was founded upon it by the Romans after their conversion to the faith, in honour of God, on that Sunday. Christians gathered for its dedication from different regions. Therefore, because that mound on which this church was erected had been formed from earth from every land, the office “Let all the earth adore thee,” etc., is sung at its dedications on that day.

## CHAPTER LXXVII. On Septuagesima, Sexagesima, Quinquagesima, and Lent

[Col. 0081D]

Having spoken of the period lying between the Lord’s Nativity and Septuagesima, the order of our subject requires that we next speak of Septuagesima itself and its meaning, of Sexagesima, Quinquagesima, and Lent, in this order especially: first, what they signify; secondly, where they begin and end; thirdly, their institution; and fourthly, their offices.

Septuagesima, then, represents the time of wandering astray, or of punishment and guilt. Thus, on its very first Sunday the history of Genesis begins to be read, and it is read until the Sunday preceding the Sunday called Palm Sunday, where the wandering and error of the first parents are treated. Here we also lay aside *Alleluia*. Some do this on Saturday before Sext, some before None, some at Vespers, some at night for the Nocturns, and finally some on Sunday itself at Prime. [Col. 0082A] This diversity arose from different ways of beginning the day.

For some peoples begin the day at noon and end it at noon on the following day; others begin it at None and end it at the next None; others again begin it at Vespers and carry it through to the following Vespers, which is the better practice; while others finally begin it at midnight and end it at the following midnight, as is still observed according to Roman decrees. For if one person has made an agreement with another for a specified day, he is not considered to have broken the agreement before the following midnight if he fulfils it then.

There are some churches which lay aside *Alleluia* with great festal rejoicing. Septuagesima begins on the Sunday on which *Circumdederunt me* (“They surrounded me”; Ps. XVII) is sung, and ends on Saturday in Albis, that is, the Saturday after Easter.

Moreover, that we may dispatch everything at once, Sexagesima begins on the Sunday following *Circumderunt me* and ends on the Wednesday after Easter. Quinquagesima likewise begins on the third Sunday after *Circumdederunt me* and ends on Easter Day itself. Quadragesima, however, begins on the Sunday on which the Church sings *Invocavit me*, and we end it at the Lord’s Supper. Septuagesima is so called because it contains seven times ten days. Yet this seventy-day period, which the present Church observes, signifies for us those seventy years during which Israel was in Babylonian servitude. For just as they laid aside their instruments, saying, “How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?” (Ps. 136), so we too lay aside songs of praise. But afterward, when Cyrus gave them permission in the sixtieth year to return, they began to rejoice; likewise, on Easter Saturday we resume and sing *Alleluia*, thereby indicating the joy which they experienced because permission to return had been granted them.

But just as, while preparing for their return, they labored greatly in gathering their little bundles, so we too immediately add the tract after the *Alleluia*: “Praise the Lord” [Col. 0082D], by which we signify labor. Again, just as they returned joyfully but were nevertheless wearied by the labor of the journey, so throughout the whole Easter week we sing the gradual with *Alleluia*. By the gradual we express labor; by *Alleluia*, joy. Further, just as they received complete joy upon entering their homeland, so on the Saturday on which Septuagesima ends we sing *Alleluia* to the Lord.

Indeed, both our Septuagesima of days and their Septuagesima of years are, as it were, a certain history in which the exile of the whole human race from Adam to the end of the world is figuratively represented. This exile is enacted through the cycle of seven days and enclosed within seven thousand years, so that by seventy days or seventy years we may understand seventy hundreds of years [Col. 0083A]. For from the beginning until the Ascension we reckon seven thousand years. Thereafter, whatever time follows until the end of the world is comprehended within the seventh millennium, whose end God alone knows.

Therefore, just as the children of Israel were freed from Babylonian captivity in the seventieth year through Cyrus, so we have been redeemed through Christ, in the seventh age of the world or in the seventh millennium, from the bondage of the devil; the robe of innocence has been restored to us through baptismal remission. Hence, on Easter Saturday we sing one *Alleluia*, already rejoicing in the hope of eternal rest and of the recovery of our homeland. Israel labored in preparing to return and in returning; likewise we must labor in the present Church in satisfaction for the ten commandments of the Law [Col. 0083B]. But when the time of our exile has ended and we arrive in our homeland, we shall be adorned with a twofold robe—when body and soul alike are glorified. This is signified by the two *Alleluia*s sung toward the end of Septuagesima.

Note in passing, therefore, that Septuagesima begins in sorrow and ends in joy, like the so-called penitential psalms. Septuagesima, moreover, means six times ten and signifies the time of the Church’s widowhood and her grief at the Bridegroom’s absence. For although Christ is present to us according to his divinity, as in the saying, “I am with you unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28), nevertheless, insofar as he is human, he is in heaven and sits at the Father’s right hand—that is, he is equal to the Father [Col. 0083C]. Hence he himself says, “For I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20), that is, “I am not yet equal to him, as you suppose.”

Yet six works of mercy are here given to the bride as remedy and consolation: feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, visiting the sick, clothing the naked, receiving the poor and the stranger in hospitality; and from Tobit a seventh is added, namely, burying the dead (Tob. 1). These are given to the bride so that she may exercise herself in them and, through their observance together with that of the Decalogue, merit to have her Bridegroom’s door opened to her and to enjoy his most sweet embrace.

Thus Quinquagesima is called, as it were, five times ten, and signifies a time of remission, just as the fiftieth year in the Old Law was called the year of remission. Hence in this season Psalm 50 is especially sung, namely, “Have mercy upon me, O God,” the psalm of penitence and remission. Therefore we fast at this time in order to obtain forgiveness of sins.

Finally, Quadragesima is chiefly commended by the place of its institution, as has been said; by three periods; and by the persons who fasted in them. By its institution, because it was instituted in Paradise, when God forbade Adam to eat the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; by the periods and persons, because in the time before the Law Moses fasted, in the time of the Law Elijah fasted, and in the time of grace Christ fasted.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. On the institution of the aforesaid seasons

[Col. 0084A]

Having seen what the foregoing things signify, let us next discuss their institutions, first of Quadragesima. First, then, it must be considered why it is called Quadragesima, when it ought rather to be called “a tenth,” since it is a tenth of the days. But this arose from the custom of pagans or gentiles. For just as the Hebrews gave a tenth part of all their goods, so the gentiles gave a fortieth, and called such revenues a *quadragesima* or a tithe. Accordingly, after the analogy of the royal treasury, toll, or Roman tax levy, we call the tenth of the days which we pay to God a *quadragesima*.

Although it has only thirty-six days for the tenth, and Quadragesima begins, as stated, on the Sunday on which *Invocavit me* is sung, nevertheless, because Christ fasted forty days and we ought to be his imitators, four days were added so that we too might fast forty days. We also fast forty days so that we may not pass beyond the forty days from Easter until the Ascension, which we are to spend in joy, without being able to follow Christ our Head into heaven.

The same should be understood concerning Quinquagesima. Since clerics considered that they preceded the people in rank, they judged it fitting that they should also precede them in holiness. Therefore they added two days and begin fasting on the Sunday before *Invocavit me*. Thus Quinquagesima was instituted [Col. 0084C]. Or again, we spend fifty days in penitence so that, after completing the fifty days of joy after Easter, we may be found worthy on Pentecost itself to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit.

The institution of Septuagesima arose in this way. Pope Miltiades and St Sylvester ordained that food might also be eaten twice on Saturday, lest nature be weakened by the abstinence and bodily affliction endured on Friday—which was always fasted, and still ought to be fasted by all. Therefore, to compensate for the Saturdays of that period, they added one week, and thus Sexagesima was instituted, extending only to the Wednesday after Easter.

Septuagesima likewise has another origin. For, because of reverence for Ascension Day, on which our nature ascended to heaven, exalted even above the angelic choirs, the holy Fathers decreed that Thursday should always be celebrated as a feast day. But because on that day we attend more effectively to our own affairs, it came about that we do not observe that day solemnly according to the ancient custom. Therefore, to make up for these days, they again added one week to Sexagesima, beginning to fast from *Circumdederunt me*. Thus Septuagesima was instituted, extending, as stated, to the Saturday after Easter.

## CHAPTER LXXIX. On the office of these seasons

Having briefly considered these matters, we must consider generally the offices of these seasons [Col. 0085A]. It should be known that some things are entirely omitted at this time, some are altered, and some are substituted for others.

Three songs of praise are omitted: *Alleluia*, *Gloria in excelsis*, and *Te Deum laudamus*. An exception is made, however, on the Chair of St Peter, when we sing *Te Deum laudamus*, since that hymn belongs especially to the enthronement of those installed in office, and therefore we sing it. Likewise, on the day of the Supper—another exception—we say *Gloria in excelsis* and *Ite, missa est*; and similarly on Easter Saturday, *Gloria in excelsis Deo*, but not *Ite, missa est* or *Te Deum laudamus*.

From Septuagesima until Easter we do not utter *Alleluia*, but employ certain phrases in its place. At the beginnings of the canonical hours, we say, “Praise to you, Lord, King of eternal glory”; and in antiphons and responsories we say “For ever” in place of *Alleluia*. At Mass, in place of *Alleluia* with its verse, we sing the tract, as we call it.

Although the phrase “Praise to you, Lord,” etc., seems equivalent in force to *Alleluia*, a great distinction is nevertheless made between them: *Alleluia* is an angelic word, whereas the other is human; and the former has greater authority because of the dignity of the Hebrew tongue, while the latter has less because of the deficiency and poverty of Latin. In these matters generally, it must be observed that the two phrases “Let us bend the knee” and “Bow your heads” accompany one another, and neither should be said on Sunday.

## CHAPTER LXXX. On the alteration of the offices

[Col. 0085C]

The offices are altered in this way: the psalm “The Lord reigns” (Ps. 92), a psalm of joy customarily sung first at Lauds, is not sung in this season; instead, “Have mercy upon me, O God” (Ps. 50), a penitential psalm, is sung. Yet the former is sung at Prime on Sundays, to signify that nothing in the psalter should be omitted, but that the entire psalter should at least be read through in the week—something the ancients used to do in one day.

At Prime, for the same reason, “Give thanks to the Lord” (Ps. 135) is also sung, indicating that children ought to be instructed so that on Palm Sunday they may know how to sing praises to the Lord. For this psalm pertains especially to that day, chiefly because of this verse: “O Lord, save me,” etc. (ibid.).
