At this time we must all lay aside splendid and ornate garments and take up garments of humility. During Quadragesima, flesh-meat must likewise be laid aside and omitted, both solid and liquid. There are two kinds of liquid flesh-meat: one is made liquid by art, as fat rendered by frying; the other naturally so, such as cheese and eggs. Jerome says against Jovinian: “Egg and cheese are nothing other than liquid flesh.” But it is asked why fish may be eaten at this time, whereas flesh-meat may not; why, in any fast, fish and flesh-meat are not alike forbidden to us and to all religious persons.

The reason may be this [Col. 0086A]: God did not curse the waters. For he knew that through the waters of baptism there would be a cleansing from sins; thus this element is deservedly most excellent. This is easily observed, because it washes away filth, and before the world’s creation the Spirit of the Lord was accustomed to move over the waters, as Scripture relates (Gen. 1). But God cursed the earth in the work of man; hence no kind of flesh that lives upon the earth—whether quadrupeds or birds—may be eaten in fasts. For although some birds live in the air and some in the waters, whether born in them or outside them, they are nevertheless said chiefly to dwell upon earth and to belong to the nature of earth.

Therefore, since certain fish have the form of a fish in one part and the form of a quadruped in another—for example, the porpoise, dogfish, and wolf-fish—they may seem able to be eaten in fasts insofar as they are fish, but not insofar as they are otherwise [Col. 0086B].

## CHAPTER LXXXI. On the feasts occurring at the beginning of Septuagesima, and first on the Purification of Blessed Mary

We must now speak of the two feasts which sometimes fall to be celebrated at the beginning of Septuagesima: namely, the feast of Blessed Mary and that of St Blaise. The feast of Blessed Mary has three names. It is called either the Purification of Blessed Mary, Candlemas, or the *Hypantē* of the Lord.

It is called the Purification of Blessed Mary because, on that day, the fortieth after the Nativity of the Lord, the Virgin Mary came to the Temple according to the custom of the Law in order to be purified [Col. 0086C]—not because she was unclean, but because of childbirth, after the manner of other women. For she was not subject to the law which thus commands: “If a woman, having received seed, bears a male child, she shall be unclean from entering the Temple for thirty-three days” (Lev. 12), and for seven days excluded from human society. But the Blessed Virgin Mary had not given birth from received seed—according to the phrase “not from a man’s seed,” etc.—yet she wished to observe the custom of the Law, because Christ came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it (Matt. 5).

Why it is called Candlemas has no other authority, but rather derives from the ancient custom of pagans or gentiles. In ancient Rome it was customary around this time, at the beginning of February, to purify the city by walking around it in processions, each person carrying a burning candle; and this was called the *amburbale* [city-circling rite]. Thus, what was done by pagans for undiscriminating purposes around the beginning of February is now done by Christians on the feast of Blessed Mary for her praise and veneration [Col. 0086D].

Or we carry candles in order thereby to imitate the holy virgins, of whom the Blessed Virgin Mary is the head: namely, that with the lamp of chastity kindled within us, we may deserve with her to enter the temple of glory to meet the true Bridegroom. Or it is also called Candlemas because of the multitude of candles and the meaning contained in them. In a candle are wax, fire, and wood. The wax denotes Christ’s flesh and virginity; the fire, the Holy Spirit; the wood, divinity hidden in flesh [Col. 0087A].

This feast is called the *Hypantē* of the Lord because Simeon and Anna the prophetess came to meet Christ when he was brought by his parents into the Temple to be presented. For *hypantē* means an offering or presentation.

## CHAPTER LXXXII. On the feast of St Blaise

The other feast of this season is that of Blaise. He was a most holy physician who, for a long time, lived in hiding upon a certain rock and healed the people who came to him. In the same way, if they brought him their sick animals, he immediately cured them. At last, after he had become bishop of the city of Sebaste, he was seized and imprisoned [Col. 0087B]. For a long time, a certain pious woman brought him food and a candle in prison.

When he foresaw that the day of his death was at hand, he told this woman that, so long as she lived, she should offer a candle every year on the day of his death in his memory; God would protect her from illnesses and preserve her in great prosperity. This indeed came to pass. Many people therefore did likewise when they happened to fall ill, and recovered health. From this arose the widespread custom that, if anyone suffers from his teeth or any other part of the body, or if one’s animals fall sick, candles should be offered in his honor.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. On the Chair of St Peter

[Col. 0087C]

At this time the Chair of St Peter is likewise customarily celebrated—both that which was at Rome and that which was later than the one at Antioch.

> [Note: [Col. 0087] Durandus transferred all these matters into his *Rationale*, as he himself acknowledges.]

But the chair which was at Antioch is certainly more solemn than the other, as the collect of this day, which concerns the enthronement at Antioch, sufficiently attests; and it is called the feast of the banquets of Blessed Peter. For the ancient pagans used every year, on a certain day in February, to set meals beside the tombs of their parents. At night demons consumed these meals, while souls were believed—no less falsely than absurdly—to be refreshed by them. For they thought that such feasts were consumed by souls wandering about the tombs.

This custom and the error of such false belief could scarcely be uprooted by Christians [Col. 0087D]. When holy men perceived this and wished utterly to extinguish the custom, they instituted the feast of the Chair of St Peter, both that at Rome and that at Antioch, on that very day on which those abominable pagan practices took place. In this way, the feast of that insignificant custom might be wholly eradicated by this solemn feast. Hence, from those banquets, this feast was also called the feast of the banquets of Blessed Peter.

Let us understand in passing that the ancients used to say that souls were *animae* while they were still established in human bodies; that they were called *manes* when they were among the dead below; *spiritus* when they had ascended to heaven; and *umbrae* when burial was still recent or when they wandered about the tombs [Col. 0088A].

## CHAPTER LXXXIV. On feasts generally celebrated during Septuagesima

That we may at once dispose of all the great solemnities celebrated within Septuagesima—whether during Passiontide itself or before it—such as the three aforesaid feasts of Blessed Agatha, St Matthias, the Annunciation of the Lord, St Gregory, and, should it occur, the feast of the church’s patron, its anniversary, or someone’s annual baptismal Easter, we say generally that songs of praise—namely, *Te Deum laudamus*, *Gloria in excelsis*, *Ite, missa est*, and other chants which would be sung if they occurred in other seasons—ought to be sung at them, except *Alleluia* [Col. 0088B]. For feasts of this kind seem generally to belong to the Easter season.

If it is objected that at the Annunciation of the Lord, *Gloria in excelsis*, which is a chant proper to the Nativity of the Lord, and *Ite, missa est*, which is proper to the Resurrection, and *Te Deum laudamus*, which signifies the joy of the found drachma, ought not to be sung, since those events had not yet occurred at the Annunciation of the Lord, we answer briefly: even though the Nativity of the Lord, the Passion, and the finding of the drachma had not yet actually occurred, they were nevertheless already certainly hoped for. For this feast is, as it were, the fountain and beginning of Christ’s feasts.

An annual Easter is called the occasion when someone celebrates each year the day on which he received baptism. The office of Easter for that very day ought to be sung in full, except *Alleluia* if it occurs during Quadragesima [Col. 0088C]. Meanwhile, be certain that the Churches of Lyons and Milan, where Ambrose held the archiepiscopate, celebrate no solemnity during Passiontide, but make only a commemoration.

## CHAPTER LXXXV. On the office of Quadragesima and the writing of the laity

Since the office of Quadragesima has thus far been treated generally, we must now discuss its office according to the season. From the Sunday which we call *Isti sunt dies* until Easter, the verse “Glory be to the Father,” which pertains to the praise of the Trinity, is entirely omitted from the offices [Col. 0088D], because on that Sunday the Passion of Christ begins to be celebrated, in which the whole Trinity seems, as it were, to have been dishonored by the Jews.

For the same reason, that verse is never sung in the song of the three children, namely *Benedicite*, because God was then greatly dishonored when the three children, who worshipped him especially and vehemently detested idols, were cast into the fiery furnace. Most especially, however, that same verse is omitted during the three days before Easter, because then the Trinity suffered the greatest dishonor. For besides the fact that the death of Christ is first dealt with here, he is now scourged, now vilely spat upon, struck with blows, and finally crucified. Hence Isaiah says: “We saw him as having neither form nor beauty” (Isa. 53).

The openings of the Hours and the titles of the lessons are likewise entirely suppressed then—namely, “O God, come to my assistance,” and “A reading from the book,” etc.—because Christ our Head is taken away from us as to the presence of his flesh [Col. 0089A]. Blessings are neither requested for nor given before the lessons, because Christ the Shepherd, who blesses his flock, is no longer present. Or the blessing is neither requested nor is “But you, O Lord” said because, in these days, the apostles were neither sent out to preach nor returned from it. Therefore, to signify this, we say neither “Command, Lord” nor “But you.”

It should also be considered that two prefaces are recited in Quadragesima: one of fasting and the other of the Passion. The preface of fasting is sung from the first fast until Palm Sunday. The preface of the Passion begins to be sung from that day until Easter. Yet someone may perhaps think it absurd that such a preface should be sung on Sunday, since Sunday is not a fast-day. But one may say that, even if there is no numerical fast on that day, there is a qualitative fast—that is, from fleshly food—as on other days.

But since what we have said seems chiefly to concern clerics, a few things must now be said concerning the writing of the laity, which consists principally in two things: pictures and ornaments [Col. 0089C]. For, as Gregory says, what writing is to a cleric, painting is to a layperson. Some pictures, therefore, are above the church, such as a cock or eagles; others are outside the church, such as an ox and lion on the façade of the doors; others are inside the church, such as icons, statues, figures, and various other kinds of images painted on vestments, walls, or glass.

All these matters will be discussed later in their proper place. One point, however, must be observed: the image of our Savior is more fittingly and appropriately depicted in church in these three ways—namely, seated upon a throne, hanging upon the cross’s gibbet, or resting in his mother’s lap.

Ornaments, however, consist in three things: the furnishing of the church, the choir, and the altar [Col. 0089D]. The furnishing of the church consists in curtains, hangings, cloths, silks, purples, and the like. The furnishing of the choir consists in backcloths, as they are called, tapestries, and floor-coverings. Finally, the furnishing of the altar consists in veils, crosses, reliquaries, textile coverings, and phylacteries. There is also the adornment of persons who either sing in the choir or serve at the altar.

Concerning these and similar matters, we say that everything pertaining to ornament ought during Quadragesima to be hidden, removed, or covered. Nor should the cross be carried in church at that time except covered. Two veils, however, are retained: one is placed around the choir; the other hangs between the altar and the choir, so that the things within the Holy of Holies may not be seen. This signifies that the understanding of the divine Scriptures has not yet been opened to the minds of unbelievers [Col. 0090A].

These two veils are folded up on Sundays, because those days belong to the Easter season. At the first Tenebrae, namely on the Wednesday before Easter, when the Lord’s death is treated, they are wholly renewed, because at his death the veil of the Temple was torn, so that what had lain hidden within the Holy of Holies was then first made manifest to all.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI. How bells are to be rung in Quadragesima

Let us also explain briefly how ringing is to be done in church. To make this clearer, it should first be known that there are six kinds of instruments by which ringing is done [Col. 0090B]: the *tintinnabulum*, the *cymbalum*, the *nola*, the *nolula*, the *campana*, and the *signa*. The *tintinnabulum* is rung in the dining hall and refectory; the *cymbalum* in the choir; the *nola* in the monastery; the *nolula* in the clock; the *campana* in towers. Jerome, writing to Eustochium, calls its diminutive a *campanula* in a monastery: “How long will the little bell be rung in the cloister?” The *signa* may be understood as instruments rung to signify something.

Generally, then, it must be known that throughout Quadragesima on weekdays we ought neither to ring fully (*compulsare*) nor to strike down [the bells] (*depulsare*)—for it may be permitted here to use common and customary terms—but to ring simply (*simpulsare*), that is, simply to ring for the Hours or Matins.

In well-ordered churches, at Prime two bells are rung: one to summon, the other to begin. At Terce, three are rung according to the number of Hours sung under it: one for changing, another for gathering, and the third for beginning [Col. 0090C]. The same is done at Sext and None; and in the same order the same bells are rung simply for Matins. At Mass and Vespers, however, two bells are rung. In smaller churches, only simple ringing is to be used. But on Sundays and solemnities, bells are rung fully as in other seasons. We shall speak more fully of these matters below.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII. Why we do not fast at the time when Christ fasted

It is commonly asked: since in this Quadragesima we imitate Christ’s fast, why do we not also fast at the time when Christ is said to have fasted? For Scripture relates that he began to fast immediately when he had been baptized. Yet there is a fourfold reason why we continue our Easter fast.

The first is that, if we wish to rise again with him, we must also suffer with him what he himself suffered for us. The second is that thereby we may imitate the children of Israel, who first departed from Egypt at that time and afterward departed at the same time from Babylonian bondage. This can readily be proved from the fact that both the former and the latter had celebrated Passover immediately before departing.

The third is this: since the ardor of lust is ordinarily more apt to inflame us in springtime, we fast especially then in order to restrain the heat of the body [Col. 0091A]. The fourth is that immediately after the fast we ought to receive Christ’s body, so that we may mystically receive the Paschal sacraments. This is as when the children of Israel, before eating the lamb, afflicted themselves and ate wild lettuces. Thus we too must first afflict ourselves through penitence, that we may be found worthy to eat the Lamb of life.

Meanwhile note that, if two offices coincide in Quadragesima—days which we call doubles—it is necessary for the office of the feast to be sung at Terce without genuflection, and the office of the true fast at None, not without bending the knee.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII. On privileged days

[Col. 0091B]

After this, it must be set forth which days are, as it were, privileged, especially within this season. There are four privileged Wednesdays, four Saturdays, three Sundays, one Thursday, one Friday, and one entire week.

The Wednesdays are these: first, that on which we begin to fast in Quadragesima; the second, in the following week; the third, in the week after *Laetare Jerusalem*; the fourth, in the final week.

The four Saturdays are these: the Saturday of the first week, when ordinations are celebrated; that of the fourth week; that of the fifth week; and the Saturday in the vigil of Easter [Col. 0091C].

The three Sundays are: *Invocavit me*, *Laetare Jerusalem*, and Palm Sunday. The Thursday is in *Parasceve*, and the seventh privileged observance is the final week of Quadragesima. It is called the greater week because it has a greater and more extended office; or it is also called burdensome because then we ought especially to punish our bodies and vices. Let us therefore proceed in order through the privileges of these days.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX. On the first Wednesday

The first Wednesday is distinguished by four privileges. The first is that we then begin to fast. We do this because, as is read, Christ began his fast on Wednesday; that this is true will become sufficiently clear to anyone who investigates carefully [Col. 0091D]. For he was born on a Sunday, so that whoever carefully calculates the years from then until his thirtieth, according to the rules of computation, will readily find that he was baptized on Tuesday and began his fast when he entered the desert on the following day.

The second privilege of that day is that confessions are heard in church and penances imposed on those confessing. The third is that ashes are placed on heads as a sign of humility. The fourth, finally, is that on that day there is such a procession as does not occur at any other time throughout the year. For penitents are then expelled from the church with procession and cross, in order that on the day of the Supper they may be received back into it [Col. 0092A]. Penitents are expelled and driven from church then in order to represent the exile of Adam and Eve because of their eating of the fruit.

## CHAPTER XC. On the second and third Wednesdays

The following Wednesday is privileged because those who are to be ordained on the following Saturday are questioned and examined from the sacred writings, and tested as to whether they are sufficiently fit to receive orders. Hence two lessons are read at Mass: one in the natural or nocturnal voice—that is, grave and subdued—and the other in the ordinary voice. The first signifies the Old Testament; the latter the New, in order to declare thereby that those about to receive orders ought to be learned in both Testaments.

We have, moreover, the following as a general rule: whenever two lessons are read at Mass on Wednesday, ordinations may be celebrated on the following Saturday. The third Wednesday, however, has its privilege in that on this day the instruction and examination take place in church of those who are to be baptized on the Saturday before Easter [Col. 0092B].

This instruction is performed in the following way. Those who wish to be baptized assemble at the church doors, women on the left and men on the right; and they are asked by the deacon or priest whether they wish to be baptized, or he asks the sponsors the same question. But the exorcist must first ask whether they renounce Satan and all his pomps, so that a child, if an adult, may answer that he renounces them; if not an adult, the sponsor answers for him.

No one may be admitted as a sponsor unless he knows the Lord’s Prayer and is acquainted at least with the lesser creed, since he is bound to teach his spiritual children. Nor should one ignorant of these be considered a Christian or admitted to give any testimony according to the decrees. The priest must therefore by all means inquire into this of the sponsors. Otherwise, if they do not know them, they ought not to be accepted, unless perhaps they promise to learn them as quickly as possible.

> [Note: [Col. 0091D] 2, question 7, *Non potest*, and what follows.]

Then the acolyte writes down the names of those wishing to be baptized; hence he is also called the notary, because he writes the names of those to be baptized. After they have been sufficiently instructed in the faith by the priest and the exorcists have performed adjurations over them, they are led into the church by the doorkeeper and placed in the nave: the men on the right and the women on the left [Col. 0092D].

Two persons, however—a male and a female—are led within the Holy of Holies, signifying that some of those to be baptized will be saved. Then, finally, the Lord’s Prayer and the lesser creed are read in Greek and Latin because of the dignity of those languages. For they are more worthy than the others: Greek because of wisdom, Latin because of Roman power. Afterward four lessons and the beginnings of the four Gospels are recited; finally Mass begins. When the offertory has been sung, the archdeacon or deacon ascends the pulpit and cries aloud: “If anyone here is a catechumen, let him go out.”

For these signify, as explained above, those of whom it was said: “But Jesus did not entrust himself to them; for he knew what was in man” (John 2). Thus all the catechumens then go outside, since this is done in the same manner concerning them seven times before they are baptized [Col. 0093A].

## CHAPTER XCI. On the fourth Wednesday

That Wednesday which follows the Sunday *Laetare Jerusalem* is privileged because two lessons are then read, since ordinations are celebrated on the following Saturday. Likewise, the Wednesday of the final week—namely, the one before the Supper—has a privilege because two lessons are again read then. This is because on that day Christ was sold for thirty denarii, just as Joseph was sold for thirty pieces of silver. “For the servant is not greater than his lord, nor the disciple than his master” (Matt. 10).

From this Wednesday arose the practice that we ought always to fast and abstain from fleshly things every Wednesday. Consequently, after Friday this day is always enjoined upon penitents as a day of abstinence [Col. 0093B].

## CHAPTER XCII. On privileged Saturdays
The Saturday of the first and of the fourth week enjoy privilege because ordinations are celebrated on them. [Col. 0093C] Yet you should know that minor orders may be conferred on all feasts of the apostles and on Sundays; major orders, however, only on the six Saturdays. On the first of these, several readings are read, among which is one during whose chanting no one ought to sit. This is the hymn of the three youths, which they sang when they had already been placed in the furnace for their faith in the Trinity. One ought not, therefore, to bend the knee during this hymn, because they refused to bend theirs before Nebuchadnezzar’s statue, as many other princes had done.

Likewise, on Good Friday we do not bend the knee at the prayer offered for the Jews, on account of the mockery of those who, while deriding Christ, said: “Prophesy [Col. 0093D] to us, Christ: who is it that struck you?” (Matt. 26). On the Saturday before *Laetare Jerusalem*, the epistle of Susanna is recited. For at that time the station is held at Rome in the monastery of the blessed virgin Susanna. Thus also, because of a certain resemblance, the Gospel concerns the woman caught in adultery, whom the Lord set free (John 8). Behold how Gospel and Epistle agree, as many others agree as well.

The Saturday before Palm Sunday receives its privilege from the fact that at that time the lord pope distributes alms—that is, performs his *mandatum*, which he ought to perform on the very day of the Supper. But because he could not do so then, owing to the lengthy office of that day, he suitably performs it on this Saturday. Or it seems especially to possess this privilege [Col. 0094A] because on that day the Lord dined in the house of Simon the leper, with Martha serving, and Mary washed his feet with her tears, dried them with her own hair, and poured ointment upon his head (Luke 7).

Yet let us remember that, among all God’s commandments, this alone is called *the commandment* (*mandatum*) by antonomasia: that which Christ commanded to be observed and obeyed with greater solemnity, when he washed his disciples’ feet, saying: “If I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13). And he did so with a certain threat, as he threatens Peter: “Unless,” he says, “I wash your feet, you will have no share with me” (ibid.). Therefore, because of such a command, that Saturday is free from office. From this arose the authoritative rule that, if anyone is [Col. 0094B] so entangled and burdened with affairs that he can scarcely devote himself both to prayer and almsgiving, he should at least exchange almsgiving for prayer, and conversely.

Finally, the Saturday before Easter is privileged because ordinations are then celebrated, catechumens are baptized, and the Paschal wax candle is consecrated. Yet the same Mass must serve both the day and the ordinations, and several readings are then recited.

## CHAPTER XCIII. On privileged Sundays

We next consider Sundays. The first Sunday of Lent is privileged because Lent itself begins from it. Lent [Col. 0094C] represents the time during which the children of Israel stayed and lingered in the wilderness. For as they stayed there through forty-two encampments, fed with manna, so we too, from this Sunday until Easter, for forty-two days abstain from bodily pleasures, are refreshed by the word of life, and devote ourselves to prayer, so that through Christ we may be brought into the land of the living, just as they were brought in through Jesus son of Nave—that is, Joshua—into the land of promise.

Three things are to be noted concerning the Israelite people: their sojourning in Egypt, when Jacob and his sons went down into Egypt; their captivity, which befell them in Babylon; and of these two we make remembrance. The third was their dispersion, and it still continues throughout [Col. 0094D] the whole world. We do not mention it, because they will never be recalled from that dispersion, which took place under Titus and Vespasian. Hence it was said: “I shall deliver them into a hand from which they will not be able to rise” (Lam. 1).

The Sunday *Laetare Jerusalem*, which is the seventh from the first Sunday of Septuagesima, is marked by privilege because it represents for us the freedom of return granted to the children of Israel in Babylon in the sixtieth year, although they fully obtained it in the seventieth. Accordingly, the whole office of that day concerns joy: partly that we may express their joy, and partly our own, which, after the seven ages have ended, we shall possess when freed from the world’s exile and admitted into the heavenly paradise, which is truly our homeland.

## CHAPTER XCIV. On Palm Sunday

[Col. 0095A]

Palm Sunday merited its privilege for three reasons. First, because on that very day the children of Israel entered the land of promise and crossed the Jordan dry-shod. For it happened that, in that year, there were as many days until Easter as there are from this Sunday. Second, because on this day Jesus, coming from Bethany into Jerusalem, was received with the highest honour; and on the same day he most powerfully drove those selling from the Temple—the third reason for this day’s privilege.

This day is called by three names. It is called Palm Sunday because on that day palm branches are carried in processions, signifying [Col. 0095B] those which the children of Israel placed in the road when Christ was coming. Or we carry them as a figure of the branches and flowers of virtues which we ought to bear whenever we go to Christ. When we do not have palms, we carry laurel or boxwood, whose perpetual greenness signifies the virtues; or flowers also, which for a similar reason signify virtue.

Therefore, on this day we make a great and notable procession, to signify that the Lord will come to us and lead us to the eternal tabernacles. After the procession we ought to come before the crucifix and say, “Blessed”; nor for that reason should the other procession be omitted, but it should take place before terce.

Incidentally, consider that Lot’s wife was changed and transformed into an image of salt because she looked back, so that she might season and instruct us not to go backward. For, as Scripture says, no one who has put his hand to the plough ought to look back (Luke 9).

## CHAPTER XCV. On Thursday

Thursday, called the Supper of the Lord, is distinguished by four privileges. The first concerns penitents now returning to the Church. For then the Church receives back penitents whom it had expelled on the first day of the fast. Penitents are received into the Church and separated from evil penitents especially on Thursday, because God made birds from the waters on the fifth day. For this reason [Col. 0095D] also, by the fact that he let some fall back into the water, we signify evil persons delighting themselves in carnal things; and by the fact that he raised some into the air, we understand the good, those delighted by heavenly things.

The second privilege is that the New Testament then began, and the Old was ended. The third privilege of this day is the consecration of oil. There are, indeed, especially three kinds of sacred anointing in the Church of God: chrism, the oil of the sick, and the oil with which the baptized are anointed. Chrism is made from the purest balsam and the purest oil. Oil easily surpasses other liquids in brightness, and balsam in fragrance.

That oil is brighter than another liquid can be shown as follows. A sailor sometimes casts an anchor into the sea; and if it happens [Col. 0096A] to catch on a rock so that it cannot be drawn out, the sailor descends there with his mouth full of oil, for this purpose: if, owing to turbid and dark water, he cannot see the rock to which the anchor clings, he pours out the oil. When this is done, so great a brightness arises there, and the waters become transparent through the poured-out oil, that the sailor can easily see the rock.

Chrism originated in the Old Testament, when the Lord commanded Moses to make chrism with which he should anoint the tabernacle at its dedication and the ark of the covenant. Aaron and the priests, and likewise kings, were also anointed with it. Moses, however, is not read to have been anointed, except with spiritual anointing, as Christ also was. Nevertheless, Christ wished us to be anointed with material anointing, so that through the material we might attain the spiritual.

Everyone is anointed twice with chrism on the crown of the head by an ordinary priest, and on the forehead by a bishop. The reason for the twofold anointing is that after the Resurrection the Holy Spirit was given twice: first when Christ breathed upon the disciples, saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 21); and again when that same Spirit was sent to them from heaven in tongues of fire.

When, therefore, someone is anointed with such holy oil, it must be done upon the shoulders and especially upon the breast. Upon the shoulders, so that he may not expend his labour fruitlessly on vain things, but may be strong to bear faithfully the burden of the law; upon the breast, that he may receive understanding of God’s commandments.

Accordingly, the sick and infirm are anointed with the oil called the oil [Col. 0096C] of the sick. Of this anointing blessed James says in his Epistle: “If anyone is sick, let him summon the priests, and let them pray over him and anoint him with holy oil; and his infirmity will be relieved, if it is expedient and beneficial for him; and his sins will be forgiven” (James 5)—namely venial sins, or [his sins will be forgiven] if he is not in mortal sin. Such anointing may, however, be administered by one priest; but this should not be done if several can be present.

Finally, the fourth privilege of this day is the *mandatum*. There is a difference between this *mandatum* and that performed on the preceding Saturday. The former is performed by prelates and great men of the Church, and represents what Christ did; this, however, every priest ought to perform in this manner. First, they should feed the poor; afterwards they should eat a little, though no more than is customary. Then they ought to rise from the table and wash the poor persons’ feet. Once this is done, they may return to the table and eat again. This does not break the fast but interrupts it. For no one ought to eat twice on that day, lest the fast be broken, both with respect to the one hour and to the whole week—although in many places this is nevertheless done.

This day is more solemn than every other solemnity, except the solemnities of the Trinity; so much so that those who can wear solemn vestments ought to do so, just as on other solemnities. Therefore, on this day all songs of joy are sung as on other solemnities, [Col. 0097A] except *Alleluia*. Nor is “Grant us peace” said, because on the following night Judas betrayed Christ with a kiss.

Observe here that the time of restoration began from the hour at which Adam was expelled from paradise, and still continues, enduring until the death of every individual. From this it is evident that to restore is greater than to create. Thus it has also been said that it is more arduous and greater to make a godly person out of an ungodly one than to create heaven and earth, and that it was greater to raise Paul in mind than Lazarus in body.

Observe also that the Nativity of the Lord is the feast of the Father, since through him the Father became known to the world. Yet, because it is the feast of the Father, it is also the feast of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. For in the term “Word” the Father of the Word is understood. [Col. 0097B] Or it is so for the other reason that the Son made the Father manifest to all. Easter, however, is the feast of the Son, because then he rose from the dead and appeared as true God. Pentecost is the feast of the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, each of these solemnities is called a feast of the whole Trinity. For the works of the Trinity are undivided, although some seem more proper to one than to another.

## CHAPTER XCVI. On the privileged Friday

Next, Friday, which is also called *Parasceve*, enjoys privilege because Christ suffered on this day. Therefore all other Fridays receive their privilege from this Friday, just as all other Sundays receive theirs from the following Sunday. *Parasceve* [Col. 0097C] means “preparation,” because the Jews then customarily prepared the foods that they ate on the Sabbath, since they were forbidden to prepare anything on the Sabbath.

On the very day of Parasceve we eat only one dish, because on that day Christ acquired only one for himself—namely, the thief. Hence he said: “I am alone until I pass over” (Ps. 130). But it is asked why we observe this day with mourning, sadness, and abstinence, when we are accustomed to celebrate the sufferings of saints joyfully. We reply that this is because the saints ascended to heaven immediately after suffering martyrdom, whereas Christ descended into hell. But when he had broken the infernal regions, brought the souls of the saints out from there, and rose on the third day, then we rejoice especially. Hence also we do not celebrate the passions of the holy Fathers who descended into hell.

Some also ask here why, since Christ was honourably received when riding upon a she-ass, and appears dishonoured on the cross, we worship the cross rather than the she-ass. This can easily be resolved: the honour he received on the she-ass was earthly, and earthly things are not to be cared for; hence nothing need be cared for concerning the she-ass. But through the cross the wall of sins set between us and the Lord was broken and destroyed, for Christ made satisfaction for us. Consequently, no one newly baptized, even an adult, however great the sins he may have committed, [Col. 0098A] is held by any of them, either as to penalty or as to guilt; nevertheless, he must have contrition. Therefore, just as David’s sword, by which he slew Goliath, was preserved for a long time and held in honour, so too is the cross of the Lord, which is in some manner prefigured by that sword.

Finally, let us consider that the office of this day lacks its head, because Christ our head was then taken from us. It lacks the invitatory, so that we may not imitate that perverse imitation which the Jews made when they took counsel how they might catch Jesus in speech and hand him over to death. Hence also we do not give anyone the kiss of peace, because of Judas’s kiss; nor do we greet anyone, because Judas betrayed Christ with a kind of greeting, saying: “Hail, Rabbi” (Mark 14).

Judas gave those who seized Christ signs so that they should not seize James in his place, for James was very like him and was therefore even called the Lord’s brother. Note, then, that Judas said: “Hold him” (ibid.), as if he said: “Bind him tightly and hold him, because otherwise he may easily escape your hands.” For Judas believed him strong because of what he himself had seen when Christ drove the sellers and buyers out of the Temple. Moreover, he had seen how Christ had escaped the hands of those who wished to seize him; hence it is said: “And passing through their midst, he went away” (Luke 4).

The reason Judas sold and betrayed Christ was this: he had recently conceived hatred toward Jesus because of the ointment which Magdalene poured upon [Col. 0098C] his head. Judas was in charge of the Lord’s money-bags. Since it was an ancient custom that one performing such an office should receive as his pay a tenth of what was put into his masters’ purses, Judas reckoned that the ointment poured out by blessed Mary Magdalene was worth three hundred denarii. Hence he said: “Why this waste? For this could have been [sold],” etc. (Matt. 26). He therefore began to consider how he might recover from Christ what he had lost through the ointment; and since one tenth of three hundred denarii is thirty denarii, he sold and betrayed him for that sum.

The office of the dead also ought not to have an invitatory unless the body is present; nor should “Grant us peace” be said in [Col. 0098D] the Mass, nor “Glory be to the Father” throughout the office, because it follows and imitates the obsequies of its Saviour.

There are therefore six privileges of this day: Christ’s sacrifice; the despoiling of hell; the trampling down of death; the redemption of humankind; the opening of paradise; and the disclosure of the Scriptures. It should be observed here that by his Passion Christ redeemed not only those who were then in the limbo of hell, the place called Abraham’s bosom, but also all future people who were to end their lives by a holy death. Yet he did not draw out every person who was in hell. Hence the prophet Hosea: “O death, I shall be your death; I shall be your bite, O hell” (Hos. 13).

Today the Scriptures were made manifest because the Scriptures of the Old [Col. 0099A] Testament, formerly obscure, are today explained. Hence the Lord says: “It is finished” (John 19), as if to say: “All things hitherto written about me are now fulfilled”—a stumbling-block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles.

The cross of the Lord was prefigured in many ways in the Old Testament. The angel striking Egypt was told: “Whatever house you enter, kill in it all the firstborn, both little ones and old people, both men and women. But where *Tau* is written, do not enter” (Ezek. 9). *Tau* is the sign of the cross, so that all are condemned unless they are saved through the sign of the cross.

Likewise Moses raised up the bronze serpent in the wilderness, and all who looked at it were immediately healed from the bites of serpents (Num. [Col. 0099B] 22). The bronze serpent has the likeness of a serpent, yet is not a true serpent. Similarly, Christ had the likeness of sinful flesh, but not flesh truly sinful, since he never sinned.

Likewise Daniel was told by the angel: “There shall be two weeks, and after seventy-seven Christ our leader shall be slain” (Dan. 9). Thus Moses says plainly: “By day and by night our life shall hang, and you shall see and not know” (Deut. 28). It is indeed true that he hung by night, because darkness came from the sixth hour, etc. (Matt. 27); and that he hung by day is certain.

Jeremiah likewise says: “Setting the daughter of the quiver in my loins” (Lam. 3). “The daughter of the quiver,” that is, the lance. Likewise: “I shall gather all nations, and *Tau*, T, shall be a sign to them” (Isa. 66), which is the cross of the Lord. Again: “Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall” (4 Kings 20). And David: “Let these things be written for another generation, and the people who shall be created will praise the Lord” (Ps. 101)—that is, the new people, namely the Gentiles.

And elsewhere another says: “I planted my chosen vineyard, and it was turned into bitterness” (Jer. 2). And why, pray? Because “they gave gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68). Likewise David says elsewhere: “They divided my garments among themselves, and cast lots upon my clothing” (Ps. 21). Although this may seem to have been said of the Lord’s seamless tunic, in the same place he says more expressly: “They counted all my bones” (ibid.), because [Col. 0099D] they stretched him so far upon the cross that all his bones could easily have been counted. Finally Isaiah also says: “His dominion shall be upon his shoulder” (Isa. 9). For Christ bore the cross in which he triumphed; thus it is commonly said that the Cyrenian carried the cross, but not as Man and God did.

## CHAPTER XCVII. Why Christ’s body is not consecrated on Parasceve, and on the order of its office

The body of Christ is not consecrated on this day for four reasons. First, because on this day Christ was truly sacrificed for us; and when the reality comes, the figure should cease and give place to it. Second, because on such a day the Bridegroom of the Church was in fact taken away: for he descended into hell. [Col. 0100A] Third, because at that time the veil of the Temple was torn and the horns of the altar were set crosswise, so that there would have been nowhere for us to consecrate Christ’s body. Fourth, because Moses said in Exodus: “Another will fight for you, and you will be silent” (Exod. 14): the other is Christ.

It remains to examine the order of the office of this day. First, two readings from the Old Testament are read, one from the Book of Kings and the other from the Prophets, namely Hosea, and this without titles. Then two tracts, as they are called, are sung: one of four verses, the other of more verses; after the latter the Passion is read, likewise without a title. When this has been completed, prayers are made for every rank of the Church: that is, for Gentiles or pagans, Jews, heretics, and schismatics. Then the cross is brought forth, and with it we proceed three times on bended knee, singing three times in Greek, *ἅγιος* (*hagios*, “holy”), and in Latin, “Holy God,” etc., with three verses. Afterwards the Lord’s body, which had been reserved on the very day of the Supper, is placed upon the altar; and after the Lord’s Prayer is sung with the prefatory introduction—namely, “Let us pray, instructed by saving precepts,” etc.—Communion is received. Then the psalms of Vespers are sung with the prayer “Look upon us, O Lord.” Thus at last the office ends.

## CHAPTER XCVIII. Why the office of this day is so appointed

Having thus set these matters forth historically, let us now see what they signify. The fact that two readings are read declares that Christ suffered chiefly for two peoples, namely the Hebrew and the Gentile. One of them is taken from the Law, namely Leviticus; the other from the Prophets, namely Hosea, because Christ’s Passion was both prefigured beforehand by the Law, foretold by the Prophets, and revealed to us under a certain veil by the patriarchs.

For Abraham secretly sacrificed the flesh of Christ when he sacrificed the ram; so too Abel when he offered the lamb as a victim. These were figures of Christ, hidden as if under a veil, so that they could not have been understood unless explained. Moreover, he was likened in the Prophets; hence the Lord says: “As Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so shall the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth” (Matt. 12).

The readings and the Passion are recited [Col. 0100D] without title because Christ, our head, is taken away from us. By the tract of four verses we understand that humanity was redeemed by Christ’s Passion, since humanity is composed of four elements. Hence Christ was crucified neither in heaven nor on earth, but in the middle—that is, in the air. For he made peace between heavenly and earthly things, and also reconciled peace among earthly things themselves, after enmities and hostilities had existed between one person and another; though they had been greater between angel and human being. Christ himself made peace in all things through the cross, joining what was separated and divided, and making one from two. For he is the cornerstone.

Or the four verses of the tract signify the four [Col. 0101A] parts of the cross, which resembles the final letter of the Hebrew alphabet, namely *Tau*, which, when interpreted, means “sign.” All the books of the Old Law signified the Lord’s cross.

Therefore on this day four verses must be said in one tract, to declare the four parts of the cross, just as five are said on Wednesday because Christ shed his blood five times: first at circumcision; second in prayer; third in scourging; fourth in crucifixion; fifth when he was pierced by the lance.

The longer tract represents David’s great battle against Goliath. For Christ, our David, today defeated the great Goliath—that is, the devil. Certain churches sing the tract, namely, “He who dwells,” etc. (Ps. 90 [printed “XCX”]), because Christ was first secretly tempted by the devil, as by some dragon lurking beneath a rock; but afterward in the Passion he was fiercely assailed as by a strong lion. This is readily expressed by the verse: “You shall walk upon the asp and basilisk, and shall trample down the lion and the dragon” (ibid.).

The Passion is read because Christ was truly suffering then. When the place is reached, “They divided my garments among themselves, and cast lots for my clothing” (Matt. 27), two subdeacons remove two cloths, or two other pieces of linen, placed upon the altar. This represents the history: the four soldiers who crucified Christ made garments for themselves from his two articles of clothing. Or rather, the removal of the cloths signifies the flight of the apostles, who were as it were Christ’s garments. Peter denied him at the voice of one servant-girl, and John fled naked. The third cloth, left upon the altar, signifies that the Lord’s seamless garment was not torn or divided, but came by lot to one person. For the unity of the Church cannot, nor ever could, be torn by heretics and schismatics, since there is no wisdom against the Lord.

When Christ suffered upon the cross and was afflicted by the greatest anguish of soul, he prayed at length, chanting ten psalms, namely from “My God, my God, look upon me” (Ps. 21) to “In you, O Lord, I have hoped” (Ps. 30), until he came to this verse: “Into your hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit” (ibid.), by which he gave up [Col. 0101D] the spirit. Therefore we too, after reciting the Passion which expresses Christ’s anguish and grief, pray, however uncommon and unusual this custom of prayer may be. For it has long been received usage that on other days prayers are said before the Gospel. But on this day the order is reversed, as was said by us at the beginning, where it was shown that certain offices are altered in Lent.

Christ prayed for three groups: for himself, saying, “Father, glorify your Son” (John 17); for his own, saying, “Father, I pray for those whom you have given me” (ibid.); and also for those who would believe in him, saying, “Father, I pray not only for them, but for all who will believe in me” (ibid.).

[Col. 0102A] From this it appears to follow that we ought not to pray for those whom we know will not be saved, such as those who remained in hell and Judas, who despaired. So we likewise pray partly for ourselves and partly for every rank of the Church: namely, for neophytes, Gentiles, Jews, heretics, and schismatics, that God may pour his grace into them and convert them to the Catholic faith. We do bend the knee for the others, but not for the Jews, because they bent the knee in mockery of Christ.

Incidentally, note that what is read before the genuflection is not a prayer but an exhortation, such as “Let us pray,” and as it were an indication of those for whom we are about to pray. What is said afterwards, however, is the prayer. Again note that there were three mockeries which the Jews performed toward Christ with bent knees. The first was when his face was veiled in the high priest’s court; the second was in the praetorium. For after Pilate handed him over to the Jews to crucify him, the soldiers, plaiting a crown of thorns, mocked him with bended knees. Although this was not done by the Jews, it is nevertheless attributed to them because they furnished the cause. The third mockery was when passers-by said to him as he already hung upon the cross: “Ha! You who destroy,” etc. (Matt. 27).

Against these three mockeries, before the unveiling of the cross we offer three acts of adoration, saying *Agios* three times, etc., as though honouring three times him who was mocked for our sake; and this in two languages, because the third is still silent. Hence we should note that, although there are many kinds of languages, three are especially principal: Latin, because of the nobility and dominion of the Roman Empire; Greek, because of wisdom; and Hebrew, because it is the mother of the other languages. The Lord’s title on the cross was written in these three languages. Therefore, apart from other languages, these three alone are used in Mass, when we sing in Greek *Kyrie eleison*, “Lord, have mercy”; in Hebrew *Alleluia*, “Praise the Lord”; and so forth in Latin.

Against the three accusations made by the Jews against Christ, we utter three defenses in the person of the Saviour, namely, “My people,” in which Christ reproaches them with his benefits: deliverance from Egypt, guidance in the wilderness, and introduction into the excellent land. It is as though Christ says: “You accuse me [Col. 0102D] of having forbidden tribute to be paid; rather, you ought to give thanks because I freed you from Egyptian slavery. You accuse me of having made myself king; rather, it would be better to give thanks because I fed you splendidly and regularly in the wilderness. Finally, you accuse me of having said that I am the Son of God; rather, show a sign of gratitude because I gave you a land flowing with milk and honey.”

After these things have been said, the cross is brought forward uncovered and bare, to signify that all things formerly obscure were then made manifest. The cross is greeted with these words, “Behold the wood,” etc., because through the cross salvation is renewed and restored to all. Afterwards it is adored—that is, kissed reverently. God alone is to be adored, and other things are to be venerated for his sake. The cross is therefore adored in order to show that we ought humbly to do what they did proudly.

Once the cross has been kissed, the Lord’s body is placed on the altar, and then the priest, with the prefatory introduction, namely, “Let us pray, instructed,” etc., which blessed Gregory added, sings the Lord’s Prayer. This represents the ancient custom of the apostles, which they employed in celebrating Masses. For of old the apostles uttered only the words spoken by the Lord: “This is my body,” etc. (Matt. 26), and “This is the blood of the new testament,” etc. (ibid.); later the apostolic fathers themselves added the Lord’s Prayer. This is the custom of the apostles represented here, in the manner in which it was anciently celebrated; but Pope Gelasius, Gregory, [Col. 0103B] and Celestine later added many things, as stated above.

After Communion, Vespers are immediately sung with the prayer, and both Mass and Vespers conclude with one collect. Once this has been done, the crucifix should be restored to its place, before which the choir must chant psalms, and likewise the bishop, or his vicar in his place, for as long as until the hour at which Christ rose. Then he ought to celebrate the mystery of the Resurrection. For first comes labour, second crying out, and third being heard; hence the Psalmist says: “To the Lord, when I was troubled, I cried, and he heard me” (Ps. 119). Therefore we too ought to be his imitators.

## CHAPTER XCIX. On the two parts of the sacrament

[Col. 0103C]

We must now say why one part of the sacrament, namely the body under the species of bread, is reserved on the day of the Supper, while the other part, namely the blood under the species of wine, is not reserved. There are two reasons why the body is reserved. The first is lest someone perhaps depart this life without viaticum, which might happen if it were not reserved; and this was instituted by Pope Innocent. The second is that during those three days all religious persons who have need should most especially communicate. Therefore this sacrament must be reserved, because it ought not to be consecrated on that day, as shown above.

There are three reasons why the sacrament of wine is not kept. [Col. 0103D] First, because, since wine is liquid, it could not be kept as well without easily being spilled through some negligence. Second, because God has approved two rites of sacrifice in their respective times: that of the old Law in its time, and the new rite in this time. Bread and wine signify these two rites, although both things belong to the new sacrament: bread signifies the new, and wine the old. Nor should it seem strange if the old sacrifice is signified by a thing of the new sacrament, since the converse is also found, namely that a thing of the Old Testament declares the new.

For on the Wednesdays of the weeks when ordinations are celebrated, two readings from the Old Testament are recited. One, which is rendered in the nocturnal tone, signifies the Old Testament; the other, rendered in the [Col. 0104A] common tone, the New. Therefore, from the fact that wine is not reserved, it is shown that the old sacrifice ought to cease. The third reason why it is not reserved is that Christ said at the Supper: “Amen I say to you, that from now on I shall not drink of this fruit of the vine until I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father” (Matt. 26).

If anyone should ask whether the wine which is consumed in Communion on that day is consecrated through contact with the Lord’s body: although the writings of many seem to assert this, we, following truth more closely and what the holy Fathers have handed down, say that the wine is not at all consecrated by that contact, but sanctified. For there is a difference between “consecrated” and “sanctified.” “Consecrated” [Col. 0104B] is said of that which, in consecration, is—so to speak—transubstantiated. “Sanctified,” however, is that which is made holy through the force of words without any transubstantiation, such as lustral water, which we therefore call blessed. Again, that is called sanctified which, through contact with a sanctified thing, is made more fit to be treated reverently.

But if it were said that wine or water were consecrated by contact alone, great disorder and confusion of things would certainly follow. For then the chalice could not be washed; and it would follow that six hundred loaves could be consecrated, without words, by contact with one host. And if some single drop of lustral or blessed water were poured into a pond or a well supplied by pools, [Col. 0104C] that water would remain blessed forever; and countless other inconveniences of this kind would arise. I pass over also the fact that, if wine were consecrated by contact with the Lord’s body, this would be contrary to the decree which forbids consecration on that day.

The question raised here—why Christ first gave his disciples his mystical body before offering it in truth—has been sufficiently discussed elsewhere. We must therefore observe here, and repeat, what we said a little earlier: in accordance with the threefold crucifixion of Christ which actually occurred on this day, Masses are to be celebrated throughout the year at three hours, namely the third, sixth, and ninth. For at the third hour he was crucified by the tongues of the Jews crying, “Away, away, crucify him” (John [Col. 0104D] 19). At the sixth hour he was placed upon the cross, and at the ninth he expired. Therefore these hours were canonically appointed for the celebration of Masses, which mystically represent Christ’s immolation.

On feast days, when one must abstain from sexual indulgence, Mass ought to be celebrated at the third hour; on ordinary non-fasting days, at the sixth; and on fast days, at the ninth. If it is done otherwise, it is certainly neither canonical nor regular—except, meanwhile, at those times when Mass must be celebrated at night, as at the Nativity of the Lord and on the Saturday of Easter. For the Mass then celebrated belongs not to Saturday, but to the day of the Resurrection. Hence even now at Rome and throughout the archdiocese of Ravenna, under which the Church of Bologna is included, Mass is not celebrated then until night. That this should be done is sufficiently shown [Col. 0105A] by the prayer then said: “O God, who this most sacred night,” and by that which is sung in the blessing of the candle called the paschal candle: “This is the night.” Likewise, whenever ordinations are performed, Mass must be celebrated at night, because the office of the major orders pertains to the Lord’s Day. But since it ought to begin from the fast, we begin it on Saturday after Vespers and prolong it until night.

## CHAPTER C. On the Office of Tenebrae

We must now consider why we celebrate, for three successive nights, the office called Tenebrae; how the signal for that office should be made; why and how many candles are lit, [Col. 0105B] how they are extinguished; and finally the character of the office itself.

When Christ was placed upon the cross, there was darkness for three hours, from the sixth to the ninth, inclusive, while the sun suffered an eclipse—not a natural one, but a miraculous eclipse—although unbelievers falsely alleged that it had occurred according to nature. Therefore, in remembrance of that great miracle, we represent those hours during these three nights.

For the office of Tenebrae, bells are not rung, but wooden boards are struck. Bells, as has been said, signify preachers. Therefore the bells are not rung, because the preachers—that is, the Lord’s disciples—not only failed to proclaim his name, but denied it, as Peter did, and fled. For it is written: “I shall strike [Col. 0105C] the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered” (Matt. 26). Therefore the Lord, seeing that they were ready for flight, said: “Whom do you seek?” (John 18), as though to say: “If you seek me, let these go” (ibid.).

Yet a great sound is made from wood. The wooden board signifies Christ, who cried out, preached, and prayed upon the wood, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23). Thus wood is struck because Christ alone was then the preacher.

## CHAPTER CI. On the Number of Candles

We must now speak of the candles. Here there is diversity in number. Some light seventy-two; some twenty-four; some [Col. 0105D] fifteen; some twelve; some nine; and some seven. Yet all do this with mystical meaning.

The seventy-two candles signify the seventy-two disciples, whose preaching or proclamation was extinguished in Christ’s death; or they signify, by synecdoche, that the Lord rested seventy-two hours in the tomb, as he is said to have lain hidden for three days and three nights in the heart of the earth; or they signify the seventy-two nations and the seventy-two kinds of languages.

The twenty-four candles, first lit and then extinguished, signify the verse, “Glory be to the Father and to the Son,” etc., which is customarily sung twenty-four times in the nocturns of feasts but is entirely omitted in this office, because [Col. 0106A] the praise of the Trinity, to which that verse belongs, appeared to be extinguished in Christ’s death.

The fifteen candles signify the twelve apostles and the three Marys, all of whom then fell silent in the praise of God. Yet while the apostles fled, the three Marys, since they were less afraid, remained about him insofar as they could. Hence we read: “When my flesh was consumed, my bone clung to my skin, and only my lips were left around my teeth” (Job 19): that is, the women, who are like a certain thin skin.

The twelve candles represent the twelve apostles. The nine, however, signify the human race, which because of its sin was removed from fellowship with the nine orders of angels and excluded from the true light. By the seven candles is shown the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0106B] which was almost extinguished in the disciples’ hearts.

Whatever number of candles there may be, all must be extinguished with a waxen hand. By the waxen hand is understood that hand which Belshazzar, king of the Assyrians, saw writing on the wall these words: *Mane, Thecel, Phares* [*Mene, Tekel, Peres*], which Daniel thus interpreted: *Mane*, “he has numbered”; *Thecel*, “he has weighed”; and *Phares*, “he has divided” (Dan. 5). The meaning is this: The Lord says, “I have numbered the time of your kingdom and your good and evil deeds; I have weighed them and found more evil than good; therefore your kingdom shall be divided among the Persians and Medes.” This indeed came about through Cyrus and Darius.

Therefore, just as that kingdom was extinguished because of the king’s evil works and divided [Col. 0106C] forever, so too the kingdom of the Jews, because of the sin committed in Christ’s death, was divided and thereafter utterly destroyed. Or, better still, the waxen hand represents the hand of Judas, which was waxen—that is, pliable toward evil—through which Christ, our king and the true lamp, was betrayed and extinguished, as far as Judas was concerned. Thus the waxen hand signifies the hand of him of whom Christ said: “He who has touched his hand with me,” etc. (Matt. 26). For as this hand extinguishes the light, so that hand extinguished the true light, as far as it lay in its power.

Sometimes, however, more candles are lit without a fixed number, and no number is observed, so that any woman or man may light one there for himself or herself. These candles signify the prophets and other holy Fathers [Col. 0106D] who announced Christ, the light of the world, as one who was to come; who proclaimed and preached words of salvation to others; and who, afflicted by various punishments, died and were extinguished.

Nor are all the candles extinguished at once, but successively—now this one, now that one—because the disciples did not all depart from him at the same time, but little by little: when one had gone away, another also went. Yet one candle, placed in their midst, is not extinguished, but is hidden and concealed; afterward it is brought forth openly, and by its light all the lights of the church are lit again. This is Christ, who, although he appeared to be extinguished according to the body, nevertheless lived according to his divinity, which was hidden from them. Soon afterward, rising with most brilliant light, he manifested himself to his disciples, when [Col. 0107A] by his illumination he rekindled in their minds the charity that had almost been extinguished.

Let us now proceed to the office itself, which speaks throughout of Christ’s Passion. The first verse, with which the night office otherwise customarily begins—namely, “Lord, thou wilt open my lips” (Ps. 50)—is omitted, because Christ our head has been taken away from us. So too we do not say, “O God, come to my assistance,” because, our shepherd having been struck, we his sheep have no one from whom to ask aid.

The Invitatory is likewise not used, lest we somehow imitate by it that wicked counsel of the Jews formed against Jesus; rather, by the silence of the Invitatory we detest it. Nor is a blessing either requested or given before the lessons, because the shepherd who blesses his flock is no longer present. Or because by “Bid, lord” (*Jube, domne*) are signified those who go out to preach, and by “But thou” (*Tu autem*) those who have performed the office of preaching [Col. 0107B] and returned from it. But neither these nor those were then present, since they had fled.

The lessons, therefore, should be read mournfully, especially those which we call the *Threni* of Jeremiah, who bewailed that holy king Josiah. The Church then likewise laments the Passion and death of the Lord. But because we lost him through our sins, if we wish to recover him, we are admonished at the end of the lessons by the verse, “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, return to the Lord thy God,” to turn to repentance.

The *Threni* of Jeremiah—that is, “lamentations,” if we translate word for word—are so called from Mount Trenarus, where the laments of souls punished there are often heard. They may, however, be called *Threni* because after every third verse there follows a letter of the Hebrew alphabet, which is set forth in full, in order, four times in these lamentations. We read Jeremiah’s Lamentations because, just as he mourned Josiah’s death and the future destruction of his people, so we mourn Christ’s death.

## CHAPTER CII. An Explanation of the Three Further Things Observed in This Office

There remain three matters to investigate: first, why, in this night office, the antiphon sung with the *Benedictus* [Col. 0107D] and the entire psalm are sung in so loud and almost terrible a voice; next, why certain tropes are sung mournfully at the end of this office; and finally, why on these three nights the night office itself is sung loudly, almost terribly and audibly, while the day office is sung quietly and with the voice entirely subdued.

The antiphon at the *Benedictus*, and the psalm itself, being sung in a raised and almost dreadful voice after the candles are extinguished, signify the tumult of the band which Judas brought with him, armed with swords and clubs, when he was to betray Christ.

The nocturnal office of Tenebrae signifies the prophecy of the prophets, while the daytime office signifies the preaching or proclamation of the apostles. Therefore the night office is sung aloud because the prophets openly foretold what was to happen to [Col. 0108A] Christ and announced without any fear what the Holy Spirit dictated to them. But the daytime office is sung in a subdued voice, because the apostles either were altogether silent or preached and proclaimed secretly.

The band contained fifty soldiers, who were sent with Judas in so great a number to seize Christ because the Jews feared that the people, who gladly listened to him, would, if they learned of this betrayal, intervene to free him. Or perhaps because they thought him very strong, indeed such a man that a few would not suffice to capture him. For they had seen, on the preceding Sunday, that he alone had powerfully driven all the sellers and buyers from the temple with a whip made of cords, and vigorously overturned the money-changers’ tables. In that action, moreover, they had seen a certain brilliance, as though rays of fire issued from his face.

Now the tropes—that is, those verses which during these three nights are sung mournfully at the end of the office with *Kyrie eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”) and *Domine, miserere* (“Lord, have mercy”)—signify the laments and grief of the women who, because of kinship, had followed Jesus from Galilee. Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary of James, and Salome, weeping near the tomb (Matt. 27). When the tropes have been sung, in certain churches they prostrate themselves upon the ground and say, “Have mercy on me, O God” (Ps. 50), and the collect, namely: “Look down, we beseech thee, O Lord, upon this family,” etc.

## CHAPTER CIII. On the Cleansing of the Pavement

[Col. 0108C]

After this we must say why, on Thursday, the pavement of the church is cleaned and the altars are stripped; and then why, on that same day, the altars themselves are washed with wine and water, and scrubbed, as it were, with rough branches, especially of yew or boxwood.

To understand the first point readily, we must know that there is a bodily Church and a spiritual Church. The bodily Church is the building in which the divine office is performed; the spiritual Church is, as it were, an assembly of the faithful. For just as the bodily church is constructed from stones gathered from various places, so the spiritual Church is gathered from different people. Thus the Church itself has been called an assembly, although that name belongs more properly and truly to the spiritual Church [Col. 0108D] than to the bodily one. For people are assembled, not stones. Yet it often happens that the name of the thing signified is attributed to the sign.

In the spiritual Church, Christ’s poor are the pavement—that is, the poor in spirit, who humble themselves in all things and are therefore especially likened to pavement because of their humility. We should note in passing that there are three kinds of poverty. The first is called poverty of necessity, found among the needy; the second, poverty of pretence, found among hypocrites; and the third is called spiritual poverty, which exists among the good. The first poverty is tolerable, the second detestable, and the third praiseworthy; so that good is to be done to all of them for the Lord’s sake. In the case of the first poverty, indeed, no regard should be had to fortune; [Col. 0109A] nor, in the case of the second, to its cause; but rather to human nature. Therefore he cleans the pavement of the church who, for the Lord’s sake, washes the feet of the poor and performs the other works of mercy.

## CHAPTER CIV. On the Stripping of the Altar

Next comes the stripping of the altar, the more worthy part of the church, so much so that, if an altar is removed and the whole church is rebuilt, the church must be consecrated again. Conversely, even if the church is removed—that is, some part or parts of it—while the altar remains unmoved, the church is not consecrated again, but cleansed by another sanctification.

For the altar signifies Christ. God commanded in the Law: “You shall make me an altar of earth” (Exod. 20). The altar of earth is Christ [Col. 0109B] born of the Virgin. Hence it is said: “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Ps. 84). This is the earth which gave its fruit: a sublime fruit, namely Christ, exalted above the choirs of angels in heaven.

The stripping of the altar, therefore, shows that Christ appeared stripped and despoiled in his Passion of those signs by which he had formerly appeared glorious when working miracles, as when he alone drove the sellers and buyers from the temple, rays of splendor issuing from his face. He who had formerly appeared so powerful and glorious now appeared weak and despised in the Passion. Hence Isaiah says: “We saw him as having neither form nor beauty” (Isa. 53); and Hilary says: “Before the Passion he appeared God and man; in the Passion, wholly man; after the Passion, wholly God.”

[Col. 0109C] Or again, the stripping of the altar represents Christ’s literal and true stripping, when the soldiers despoiled him, divided some of his garments, and assigned others away by lot. Or we may say that Christ’s garment was the apostles, with whom Christ was adorned as with certain garments and through whom his name was magnified. The altar is therefore stripped because Christ was abandoned when his disciples fled and his name fell silent.

Accordingly, the wine and water with which the altar is washed signify the blood of our redemption and the water of regeneration that flowed from Christ’s side when his side was opened by the lance. The altar is thus washed because Christ’s body, the true altar, is believed to have been sprinkled with blood and water on [Col. 0109D] the cross. The rough branches with which the altar is scrubbed signify the crown of thorns with which Christ was crowned; or the bitter scourges, the welts from blows, and the severe pains which he endured in death.

The branches are therefore bristly, like the yew branches with which the pavement is cleaned, because we ought to be cleansed from vices and provide alms for the poor, so that they may receive us into eternal dwellings. For theirs is the kingdom of heaven—this being understood of the poor of good will, or of spirit.

## CHAPTER CV. On Saturday

Having thus dealt with Friday, we must proceed to Saturday. In due order, we must first speak of the name of the day itself and then of its office. This Saturday is properly called Holy Saturday, *kat’ antonomasian* (by antonomasia). *Sabbath* means “rest,” because, at the creation of the world, which God completed in six days, he rested from work on the seventh day. Therefore God commanded in the Law that this day be observed free from all servile work, so that it was held holy under the Old Law.

But this Sabbath is so called *kat’ exochēn*, that is, “pre-eminently,” [Col. 0110A] because it signifies Christ’s rest from the work of re-creation in the seventh age. For just as God, having completed the work of creating the world on the sixth day, rested on the seventh, so also, in the sixth age, having completed the work of re-creation—namely his birth, Passion, and all the other things foretold of him—he rested in the seventh age, which, in the opinion of some, began with his Passion. Others, however, say that it began with Abel’s death. For when Christ’s soul had put off mortality and every capacity of the body for suffering, he rested, as it were, in repose.

## CHAPTER CVI. On the Office of Saturday

We must now consider the office of this day. At the beginning of the office, every fire in the church must be extinguished; afterward another is struck from flint or steel. This should be done from a vine branch, because Christ said of himself: “I am the true vine” (John 15). The fire must then be blessed with the cross and lustral water. When this has been done, the candle called the paschal candle [Col. 0110C] is blessed and lighted, together with two other smaller candles lit from it. One stands on one side and the other on the other side, while the largest candle is set between them.

The two smaller candles signify the saints of the Old and New Testaments, all of whom, both the former and the latter, were enlightened through Christ. Or the two candles signify the teaching of the apostles and prophets, who agree and concur with Christ in doctrine.

Finally, in certain churches twenty-four lessons are read. At Rome it is customary for twelve to be recited in Greek and the same number in Latin. In some churches only twelve are read, and in others only seven. Those, however, who read twenty-four recite twelve in Greek because of the authority of the Seventy Translators, whose authority once flourished greatly in Greece and also in that part of Italy formerly called Greater Greece. But twelve are said in Latin because of the authority of Jerome’s translation. In the smallest churches there are only six, owing to the number six, which is in some way perfect. Those who retain twelve do so because of the number of the apostles.

When the lessons have been read, they go in procession with the litany to the font, where the water is blessed and consecrated. But when the baptism of those to be baptized has been completed, they return in the same manner with the litany. When it is finished, we begin the Mass itself with *Kyrie eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”). In that Mass the Introit, Gradual, Offertory, and Communion are omitted, contrary to the usual practice. Likewise, the *Agnus Dei* (“Lamb of God”) is said by some but not by others. Once the host has been received, Vespers are immediately sung, and these have only two psalms, namely, “Praise the Lord, all nations,” etc. (Ps. 116), together with the *Magnificat* (Luke 1). Thus, with one prayer added, the whole office of that day is completed.

## CHAPTER CVII. Why All These Things Are Done

Having briefly and, as it were, historically described these matters, let us set out the reasons why all these things are done and consider in order what they signify.

The fire in the church before the new fire is struck denotes the Old Law. Therefore, the extinguishing of the old fire signifies that all the legal observances of the Old Testament were fulfilled by Christ’s Passion and must thereafter cease. The stone from which the fire is struck is Christ, the solid and firm rock on which the Church is built, and from whom the fire of the Holy Spirit proceeds.

Sometimes, however, fire is produced from crystal. For if crystal is placed beneath the opening of a flask full of water in the sunlight, fire is immediately struck from the crystal, provided that tinder, customarily placed there for fire, is added. Crystal signifies Christ’s pure and transparent flesh, which was without stain.

The paschal candle, renewed and illuminated, signifies that Christ, rising from the dead, appeared in glorious flesh as true God. Thus the lighted candle represents Christ illuminated by the splendor of divinity. [Col. 0111C] That the two smaller candles and the other lights of the church are lit from the fire of the greatest candle shows not only that the prophets and apostles, signified by the two smaller candles as said shortly before, were illuminated by the fire of the Holy Spirit, but also that all the faithful of the Church are enlightened by that same fire.

In the same way, the fullness of divinity in Christ is shown by the fact that some light the candle at the beginning of the blessing, although it seems certainly better and more fitting that it should first be lit when the blessing reaches the subject of fire. A cross made of incense is impressed upon the candle, signifying, namely, a holocaust—that is, something wholly offered and wholly burned, received without fire. In the Old [Col. 0111D] Testament they customarily performed two sacrifices: the morning sacrifice, which was wholly burned and called a holocaust. The cross made of incense denotes the evening sacrifice of the Law, which prefigured Christ’s immolation upon the altar of the cross, performed at the very evening of the world, and fulfilled in his Passion.

## CHAPTER CVIII. What Is Signified by the Paschal Candle

The year from the Incarnation of the Lord is marked upon the paschal candle.
