For Christ is the ancient and great year, full of days, if we begin our reckoning from the conception, when Blessed Mary said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke 1). For the moment she spoke these words, Christ was a human being, and she herself was full of the Holy Spirit.

Christ is therefore called a year because, just as in the year of days there is fullness of fruits, so in Christ there both was and now is the fullness and abundance of every good thing. Christ has his months and his days: the twelve apostles are the twelve months, while all other Christians and faithful persons are the days, whose hours are the newly baptized.

The indiction, or the *aera*, and the epact are likewise inscribed on the paschal candle, because the actions of all persons and the succession of times are rightly ordered by God’s disposition. An indiction was formerly called a period of fifteen years, consisting of three five-year periods, during which, after the world had been conquered, tribute was paid to the Romans from the whole world. In the first five-year period gold was paid; in the second, silver; in the third, iron for making weapons and bronze for adorning the city. Thus each five-year period in that fifteen-year span was likewise called an indiction. When the fifteen years had ended, the assessment of tribute returned as before; and because it was assessed in this manner over three *lustra*—five-year periods—it was so named.

This tribute was also called *aera* [Col. 0112B], “accounts,” because in the same manner every year the whole world had undertaken to pay to the Roman state whatever sort of bronze or money it owed. Indictions therefore existed first, and afterward the *aerae*, so called from *aes, aeris*, “bronze.” Finally, the name *epact* was added, signifying “addition,” from the Greek verb ἐπάγω, “to bring on; add.”

## CHAPTER CIX. On Consecrating or Blessing the Candle

The candle must be blessed and consecrated by a deacon, not by a priest or bishop, even if they are present, however much greater their order and dignity may be. This signifies that Christ, rising from the dead, first offered and showed himself to women, through whom—since they belonged to the weaker sex—he announced the glory of his Resurrection to his disciples.

Nor did the Lord do this without purpose. For just as the beginning of death entered the world through a woman, so it was necessary that the beginning of our restoration and salvation should be announced to the world through a woman. Hence we should briefly consider that women enjoy three privileges: first, that woman was formed and created in paradise; [Col. 0112D] second, that Christ was born from a woman; and third, that, after rising from the dead, he first appeared to a woman (John 20).

## CHAPTER CX. Why the Titles Are Here Omitted, and On Baptism

The titles of the lessons are not sung beforehand for two reasons. The first is that Christ our head has not yet been restored to us. The second is that those who are to be baptized, to whom the whole office of that day pertains, are still held immersed in the deepest depths of ignorance of the Scriptures. Therefore, since they do not understand the Scriptures, it is not fitting to name their authors.

For the same reason lessons are then recited from the Old Testament, the knowledge of which is perfectly revealed only to those reborn in the Spirit. [Col. 0113A] When the lessons have been completed, in some large churches the litany is sung according to the number of religious persons who assemble there. In some churches, however, it is said three times, to represent faith in the Trinity.

That the litany is sung while going to the font and while returning declares that the saints pray for those to be baptized: that they may receive the sacrament of baptism in true faith and, once baptized, may thereafter be strengthened in the truth of faith and in the sacrament.

Let us know, then, that in baptism in the time of the apostles nothing at all was said except this: “I baptize you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” But Blessed Clement, from the teaching of Blessed Peter, added the anointing with chrism and oil. Later Leo and Damasus, supreme pontiffs, and blessed Ambrose added the remaining rites; formerly they baptized [Col. 0113B] in rivers and ponds.

That the priest gently breathes into the water signifies that a faithful person can easily drive away the devil. He breathes there, therefore, so that the devil may be expelled from it; for the devil can be repelled by a light breath by one who trusts in the Lord.

The candle is placed in the water because contact with Christ’s body sanctified the waters in baptism and conferred upon them the power of regeneration. The candle, set upon a column and lit, represents the pillar of fire which went before the children of Israel by night when, leaving Egypt, they entered the Red Sea, in which baptism was prefigured, that they might come through the wilderness into the promised land. When extinguished, it shows the pillar of cloud which likewise went before them by day.

For the pillar provided three things: it protected them from the sun and from enemies, [Col. 0113C] and at night gave them light. In the same way Christ, going before the baptized, overshadows them against the incitements of vices, protects them from enemies—that is, demons and worldly desires—and gives light through charity. Hence it is said: “A fire consuming the vices within us.”

Accordingly, the pouring of chrism into the water signifies that heavenly things are joined to earthly by faith in baptism. For this reason too, we say, the priest changes his voice, sometimes using a loud voice and sometimes a subdued one. This indicates to us that lower things—that is, earthly things—are joined to heavenly things through baptism.

Once the water has been consecrated, those to be baptized come, or are brought by their sponsors, and are baptized; but first they are questioned concerning the faith. Then they are anointed with oil on the breast and shoulders: on the breast, that they may be capable of understanding God’s commandments; on the shoulders, that they may be strong to bear the yoke and burden of the Law. Then they are immersed three times, because they are baptized in faith in the Trinity.

The first immersion must be made with the face turned toward the water and the head toward the east; the second with the head turned north; and the third with the head turned south. At the first, the priest must say, “In the name of the Father,” immersing the child in the water with his face turned east; then wash him a little and say, “and of the Son,” immersing him toward the left side; then wash him a little again and say, “and of the Holy Spirit,” immersing him toward the right side. Finally, he must lift [Col. 0114A] him up and entrust him to the sponsors, who must receive the child from the priest’s hand; hence they are called *susceptores*, “receivers” or sponsors. The priest must not leave the child in the water, but hand him over to the sponsors.

The baptized person is then anointed on the crown of the head, signifying that the Holy Spirit is given to him. The Holy Spirit, however, was given twice: first, while Christ was still dwelling on earth, when he breathed upon his reclining disciples and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive,” etc. (John 20); second, from heaven. Therefore every person is twice anointed with chrism: first at baptism, on the crown of the head; afterward at confirmation by the bishop, on the forehead.

For the Holy Spirit is given to us twice: in baptism, for cleansing and the bestowal of virtues; in confirmation, for strengthening. Once the baptized person has been anointed with chrism, a *chrismale* is placed on his head—a round sort of cap signifying the crown of life—or he is clothed in a white garment made, in the manner of a hooded cowl, from the whitest cloth with a red thread woven over it. The white garment signifies the robe of innocence restored to us in baptism.

It should be noted that they ought to wear such a white garment for seven full days and not be confirmed until those seven days have been entirely completed, because of the sevenfold Spirit given in baptism. But the red border sewn and woven onto this garment signifies Christ’s Passion, through which the sacrament of baptism is fulfilled. Or the red border represents the cord which Rahab let down from the window at Jericho because of the lodging she had provided to the scouts sent by Joshua; by that sign her house was saved with all her family (Josh. 2).

Moreover, observe again what was said above: no one ought to be accepted as a sponsor unless he knows the Lord’s Prayer and the twelve articles of his faith. For all sponsors are bound to teach these two things to their godchildren, since they are, as it were, sureties for their faith. Therefore they must watch over them as diligently as possible, lest they ever fall away from faith and righteousness; for on the Day of Judgment they will answer for all the grievous acts which these persons have committed. [Col. 0114D] The priest likewise is the father and sponsor of those whom he baptizes, so that he too is obliged to instruct them. But because, owing to their number, he could not attend to everyone, all this care is entrusted to the sponsors. The priest is also said to be the spiritual father of those to whom he preaches the word of life and whose confessions he hears. Hence he is said to sin more grievously if he lies with a woman of his own parish than with a woman from another, since such a woman is called his spiritual daughter.

Among some persons a question commonly arises about the number of sponsors, and how many must necessarily be present to receive a child from the sacred font. We do not say that one could easily suffice. But since every matter is established by the testimony of two or three witnesses [Col. 0115A] (Deut. XIX), at least three are therefore necessarily required: one of whom must be a man and two women; nor should there be more, lest carnal intercourse be impeded through spiritual relationship.

There are four classes of persons whom the Church does not admit as sponsors: abbots, monks, abbesses, together with their nuns, form one class. Unbelievers belong to another; and those not yet confirmed belong to the third. For these should not truly be called believers, and therefore cannot be genuine witnesses in this matter. The final class comprises a husband together with his wife, unless both have previously made a vow of chastity. For if both were permitted to receive the same child from the font, they would thereby become each other’s spiritual parents, [Col. 0115B] and thereafter could not lawfully know one another carnally, as is forbidden in the decrees. [Note: [Col. 0115] 30, question 4. This appears to be *Extra, De cognatione spirituali*, chapters II and IV.]

It is also especially fitting that persons should receive from the font a child to whom they are related by kinship. For the love of charity ought, insofar as possible, to be extended through baptism. Thus, although pagans or gentiles customarily built their temples around springs and always kept water readily available there, by whose sprinkling they believed themselves purified—so that they called these springs *delubra*, from *diluere*, “to wash away,” and thus approached baptism naturally—nevertheless we did not derive baptism from their custom. We have it principally from three things found in the [Col. 0115C] Old Testament: namely, the cataclysm, that is, the Flood; the Red Sea; and the Jordan, which presented to us, as it were, a figure of baptism.

But someone may ask whether it is also permitted to baptize someone in boiled water, as in beer or mead, wine, oil, or some other liquid. In truth, this is permitted in no substance other than pure water alone, whether it be melted from snow and ice, sea-water, or river-water. But it must be noted that baptism ought not to be celebrated except on Holy Saturday at Easter and at Pentecost. It may, however, be performed because of necessity, which is threefold.

The first is necessity of protection: if a king wished to besiege a city, then its children may lawfully be baptized, lest they happen to die in some danger [Col. 0115D] before being baptized. The second is sickness—understood here broadly as any infirmity of nature which may quickly prove fatal, so that we know neither the day nor the hour. Baptism is therefore frequently performed without solemnity and out of season, that is, at a time neither suitable nor fitting. The third is necessity caused by persecution from the gentiles. The Greeks, however, used to celebrate baptism at Epiphany, because the Lord was baptized then; and thus they baptized on three successive days.

Meanwhile, let us consider that there are four kinds of holy water: the water in which the ordeal of purification is performed; water consecrated at the dedication of a church; water with which we are sprinkled on Sundays; and baptismal water, with which we formerly used to be sprinkled before being anointed with chrism—a practice still observed in certain places. But afterwards it was forbidden, lest some foolish and inexperienced person think that by sprinkling himself with this water he was cleansed anew from sins, when it is perfectly evident that no one can be baptized twice.

Baptism is therefore celebrated on these two Saturdays because, on the first, we are redeemed through Christ’s Passion; on the other, because on Pentecost itself the Holy Spirit is given to us, through whom remission of sins has been effected.

## CHAPTER CXI. On the remainder of the office on the Easter Vigil.

Let us now return to our subject. When baptism has been celebrated, [Col. 0116B] one returns to the choir with the litany; and when it has been sung, the sacred rite, or Mass itself, is begun without an introit, at *Kyrie eleison*. The introit is omitted because our head, Christ, has not yet been restored to us. It begins with *Kyrie eleison* in order to represent the ancient custom of beginning Masses which prevailed before Pope Celestine.

The *Gloria in excelsis* is sung because the angels rejoice in heaven over those reborn in baptism and over the neophytes; they sang this hymn when the Lord had just been born. Paul’s Epistle, however, must be read in an ordinary tone and voice, because it signifies the teaching of the apostles, which must be preached and explained to those recently baptized. But the preceding lessons [Col. 0116C] are recited in the nocturnal tone because they signify the prophets.

The gradual is not sung because the baptized have as yet performed no works and made no advance in virtues. The *Alleluia*, an altogether angelic utterance, is especially sung because the angels rejoice that the baptized have been delivered from the devil’s slavery and converted to the faith. But because they must still labor as long as they remain in this life, the tract, namely, “Praise the Lord, all nations,” is immediately added. The offertory is further omitted, in order thereby expressly to indicate that the women came silently to the tomb. For the three Marys stood by the sepulchre in silence and with subdued voices (Matt. XXVII).

Nor ought we to give the peace at this Mass, because Christ, who is our peace, [Col. 0116D] has not yet risen. But the *Agnus Dei* is said three times, with “Have mercy upon us.” What is now sung concerning the resurrection, however, should be understood as done for the sake of those reborn—that is, those who have just been baptized. The communion is also silent, because the baptized have not yet communicated; for they ought to communicate on Easter Day itself.

After communion, immediately before the collect or prayer, Vespers are sung with a single psalm of two verses, namely, “Praise the Lord, all nations,” and with the hymn, namely, the *Magnificat*; both are said without *Gloria Patri*. Vespers are shorter so that the neophytes, still unaccustomed to divine worship, may not [Col. 0117A] be wearied by the length of the office. *Gloria Patri* is not said because the Son, who is the third person in the Trinity, has not yet been restored to us. Vespers are also sung before the prayer of the Mass so that, once Mass is ended, the people may not seem free to depart, as though they had nothing further to await. Or indeed the whole office is concluded with one prayer because the entire sacrament of baptism is consummated in Christ’s Passion.

## CHAPTER CXII. On the time of return.

Thus far we have spoken of the two periods of recall and departure. There now follows the time of return itself, not in the chronological [Col. 0117B] order of the seasons but according to the logic of the offices. This time is called Eastertide, and signifies that time which will come after the Day of Judgment. For then, by God’s mercy, we shall return to the homeland of life which we lost through Adam.

Yet it should be understood that the first week of this season is common both to this period and to the preceding one. For it belongs wholly to Septuagesima, as was said above. Hence the tract sung on Easter Saturday and the gradual sung throughout that whole week signify labor. Those two are sung in relation to Lent; the *Alleluia* and the other songs of joy, in relation to the time of return. This week is called Easter week, [Col. 0117C] so named from Easter, the first day of this season.

## CHAPTER CXIII. On the office of this season.

In order, therefore, to set forth suitably the office of this season and to begin with its first day, we must first consider the name itself, its rationale and cause, and then the office of the day itself. This day is called Easter, or the Resurrection of the Lord. *Pascha* is a Greek word and means to us “passing over,” not “suffering,” as most suppose. In Hebrew it is called *phase*.

Yet we call this day by its Greek, not its Hebrew, name, although the Hebrew language is more dignified, so that we may not seem to Judaize—not only in other things, but not even in its name. For the same reason, Easter and Pentecost, which the Jews themselves celebrate, are not marked on a fixed day in our calendars, nor do we ever celebrate them at the time when they do, lest we imitate them in anything, or again follow certain heretics who said that the Gospel could not suffice for salvation without legal ceremonies.

We call this day by a Greek rather than a Latin term because Greek formerly possessed such authority among the Romans that they called their feast-days and offices by Greek names: *Pascha*, *Pentecost*, ὑπαντὴ (*hypantē*, “meeting”), *Epiphany*, *Apostle*, *Bishop*, *Archbishop*, and so forth. Or, according to Augustine, it may be said that this name *Pascha* was fashioned by divine appointment from the Greek verb τοῦ πάσχειν (*tou paschein*), [Col. 0118A] “to suffer,” and from the Hebrew name *Phase*, which, rendered in Latin, means “passing over.” For the two names πάσχειν (*paschein*) and *Phase* rightly meet in the name *Pascha*, both in meaning and in sound.

They agree in meaning because there was a passing-over in Christ’s Passion. Through the Passion Christ passed from death to life and, in his resurrection, made a way for us believers so that we too might pass from death to life. Thus this name rightly bears the meaning of both names; and it also artfully contains in its very sense the Latin meaning of that word, so that from two languages a third—Latin—is produced. Easter is, indeed, the day of the resurrection itself. But Eastertide is called the period from Palm Sunday [Col. 0118B] to the octave of Easter, though Palm Sunday is called a lesser Easter because the lamb was then brought in which was to be sacrificed on Friday. Properly speaking, Easter was the day on which the lamb was sacrificed.

We must now speak of the reason for the name. This season is called Easter according to history, tropology, allegory, and anagogy. According to history, because when Easter was first celebrated, the people of Israel passed through the Red Sea as they came out of Egypt; or because when the destroying angel passed through Egypt and killed the firstborn of all Egypt, from man to beast (Ps. CXXXIV), he passed over those houses on whose doorposts he found the blood [Col. 0118C] of the lamb in the form of the letter T.

According to allegory, because at this season the Church passes through baptism from unbelief to faith. Allegory is called “other-speaking,” or rather inversion, when we show one thing in the words and another in the meaning. According to tropology, because at this season through confession we pass from vices to virtues; and it is called tropology as though it were a turning of speech toward morals. Finally, according to anagogy, because Christ has now passed from mortality to immortality, and has caused us, just as he has already risen, to pass in the last and universal resurrection from this world’s misery to eternal blessedness. For those who were in hell also then passed over, [Col. 0118D] namely from hell to the gate of paradise.

*Anagogy* is named from ἀνὰ (*ana*), “upward,” and γωγὴ (*gōgē*), “leading”: that is, an upward leading. For by God’s will we shall pass from mortality to immortality; and this passing is subtle and lofty. Thus in the name Jerusalem these four senses can be found: history, as concerning the city to which guests and pilgrims travel; allegory, as it is the Church militant; tropology, as it is any faithful soul; and finally anagogy, as it is the heavenly Jerusalem. Understand, however, Christ’s passing anagogically, not allegorically, in the matters mentioned above—namely Easter and the rest.

Concerning the office of this first week generally, we say that at night office only three psalms with three antiphons, likewise three lessons with three [Col. 0119A] responsories, are to be said, and these only from homilies. In certain churches, moreover, *Gloria Patri* is attached to each responsory. In very many churches it is also done that, after the final responsory has been sung, they go with lighted wax candles and a solemn procession from the choir to a certain place where an imitation tomb has been prepared. Some persons, representing the women and the disciples John and Peter, enter it; one returns sooner than the other, as John ran more quickly than Peter. Other persons represent angels, who declare that Christ has risen from the dead.

When this has been done, these persons return to the choir and report what they have seen and heard. Then, on hearing of Christ’s resurrection, the choir breaks forth in a loud voice: [Col. 0119B] “We praise thee, O God.” At Prime, however, some say throughout this week the psalm, “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good” (Ps. CV), which deals especially with Christ’s resurrection.

The creed of Athanasius, “Whosoever will,” etc., is not sung during all this season, because it relates chiefly to faith. But this season signifies the eighth age, where there will not be faith but reality, not figure but truth. In certain churches, however, the practice is somewhat different, as in our church at Paris. Observe, nevertheless, that although “I believe in one God” is likewise a creed of faith, it is nevertheless read at Mass, and this is done for the instruction of the neophytes in the articles of faith. The other creed, called the lesser creed, is entirely omitted at Prime [Col. 0119C] because of its significance. For when that which is perfect has come, that which is partial will be abolished (1 Cor. XIII). Further observe that this solemnity is so great that, by antonomasia and excellence, it is called the Solemnity of solemnities.

## CHAPTER CXIV. Matters to be observed at this season.

Before proceeding with the rest, we must briefly discuss certain matters which require consideration at this point: the adornment of the church; reconciliation with one’s neighbor; the manner of greeting; reverence for this season; the table of the body; and finally a certain December liberty.

As we have said, one church is material and another spiritual. [Col. 0119D] The material church is that made of wood, cement, stone, rock, and other building materials; the spiritual church is ourselves. Both must be cleansed at about this season; both must be adorned and polished. For at this time we must go to the baths, not for pleasure, but to signify that through the outward washing of the body we ought to understand that an inward cleansing of the soul must take place.

This season also requires us to shave our beards and the tonsures and crowns which we wear upon the top of the head, and to cut our hair. The cutting of hair and beard—which arise from the superfluous humors of the stomach, just as nails from the superfluous humors of the heart—signifies that we ought to cut away vices and sins which are superfluous to us. [Col. 0120A] We must cut the hair beyond the ears so that we may have the five bodily senses unencumbered and ready to serve God. We shave the crown of the head in order to show thereby that nothing stands between us and the Lord.

Therefore we ought here to put on clean and festive clothing, especially white garments, having laid aside black and penitential ones. For this season signifies that second resurrection in which we shall be clothed bodily with the robe of salvation or glorification, and in mind with the robe of righteousness; or it does so on account of those reborn, who are then clothed in white garments; or finally, because the angels appeared in white garments at the Lord’s resurrection.

## CHAPTER CXV. On the adornment of the material church.

[Col. 0120B] The cleansing of the material church has been discussed above. Let us now explain its adornment, which is threefold: in decorating the walls, the choir, and the altar. Curtains, hangings, and silk cloths are to be suspended on the walls. In the choir there should be back-cloths, carpets, and seats for the clergy. Carpets are coverings decorated with various colors, spread especially beneath bishops’ feet, signifying that they ought utterly to tread worldly things underfoot.

There must likewise be a veil, removed from before the crucifix; behind it a cloth is placed, signifying that the things hidden before Christ’s Passion are now revealed. In certain places a cross is raised on high with banners, signifying Christ’s victory. The altar [Col. 0120C] is also adorned with its ornaments: crosses arranged in order, caskets, Gospel texts [the source's reading is uncertain], and reliquaries.

There is, however, a distinction between *phylacterium* and *phylacteria*. A *phylacterium* is a little written sheet on which the ten commandments of the Law were inscribed, such sheets as the Pharisees used to wear before their eyes as a sign of religion. Hence in the Gospel: “For they enlarge their phylacteries and make their fringes broad” (Matt. XXIII). This *phylacterium* is named from φυλάσσω (*phylassō*), “I guard,” and *thoral*, meaning “law.” But a *phylacteria* is a small vessel of silver, gold, or even crystal, in which the ashes and relics of saints are placed.

There are three reasons why the Church’s treasury is displayed openly on great feasts. [Col. 0120D] First, for the sake of prudent safeguarding, so that it may be seen how careful its guardian has been in preserving what he was obliged to preserve. Secondly, for reverence toward the solemnity; and finally, in remembrance of the offering—that offerings may be made in memory of those who formerly gave such goods to the Church.

Before the altar there ought to hang some beautiful covering, namely a cloth or something similar, or a panel of gold if one is available. Before this ornament, in certain great churches, it is customary to place veils of three colors: one red, another off-white, and a third black. These three signify three periods. At Easter, when the first lesson and its responsory have ended, the black veil, signifying the time before the Law, is removed. After [Col. 0121A] the second lesson and responsory have been completed, the white veil, expressing the time under the Law, is removed. Finally, after the third lesson and responsory have ended, the red veil is taken down, signifying the age of grace, in which through Christ’s Passion access to the Holy of Holies—that is, eternal glory—stands open to us.

## CHAPTER CXVI. On reconciliation with one’s neighbor.

There follows reconciliation with one’s neighbor. Since on that day we must all communicate, if we are at variance with anyone, we must necessarily be reconciled with that person. Otherwise, certainly, we would receive judgment upon ourselves; this may elegantly be proved from the lesser case, according to that Gospel saying: “If you offer your gift,” etc. [Col. 0121B] (Matt. V).

Hence, on Sundays, after he has finished preaching, the priest is obliged to explain the Lord’s Prayer and the articles of faith to the people in the vernacular. For this reason too, the Lord’s Prayer is sung aloud at Mass, so that everyone may learn it and thereby be exhorted to reconciliation with one’s neighbor. Throughout this Easter week it would be proper, unless a different custom now prevailed, to greet everyone thus: “The Lord has risen” (Matt. XXVIII); and the person so greeted should answer, “Thanks be to God,” while they exchange kisses as a sign of love and charity.

## CHAPTER CXVII. On reverence for this season.

[Col. 0121C] Let us now also say a few words on reverence for this season. This season is to be revered and observed so greatly that we ought to close all workshops, workrooms, and places of business, whether of women or men, and put no wares on sale except those without which supper could not be prepared. Furthermore, throughout this whole week we ought to release quarries and other kinds of prisons, and restore prisoners to the common air, so that they may share our joy with us.

*Latomiae* are stone-quarries, where stones are cut and to which persons condemned to labor in mines used to be sentenced. Yet the word may be used for any prison, either because at Rome a *latomia* of this kind was a prison near [Col. 0121D] the Tullianum, or because in the language of Syracuse *latomia* meant “prison.”

We ought certainly at this season to relax all the severity of servitude toward male and female slaves and all who are bound to our service, as also toward our herdsmen, whether they tend horses, pigs, cattle, sheep, or goats, so that all may freely and safely gather to hear the divine office and communicate. It is likewise inhumane at this time to exact debts from debtors; whence it is said that pastures are then common.

## CHAPTER CXVIII. On the table of the body.

On Easter Day [Col. 0122A] we ought to eat nothing which has not been blessed by a priest. Hence in some regions there is still an accepted custom for people to carry to church, in a large vessel, all the dishes they wish to eat that day. In its courtyard and porch, the priest, wearing sacred vestments, blesses them with the cross and with lustral water, which we call blessed water. Afterwards the priest takes some of each item for his own needs.

Indeed, no one ought on any day either to eat or drink anything that has not first been blessed. Thus Blessed Jerome recounts of a certain nun in the book which he entitled *Lives of the Fathers*: “For when she happened to go into her garden and ate lettuces without a blessing, she unwittingly swallowed with them the devil that had hidden itself beneath them; and it tormented her cruelly for a long time.” [Col. 0122B]

On this day every person ought especially to practise three things: mercy, generosity, and sobriety. Mercy: that one should receive the needy and wandering into one’s house, perform works of mercy for them, and send something, as is commanded in the Law, to those who have cooked or prepared nothing for themselves. Generosity must especially be practised at this time, so that whoever has abundance may share something with neighbors and friends. Sobriety is required because on that day we ought to eat more temperately, so that each person may be sparing toward himself but generous toward others. Let each therefore observe mercy toward the poor, generosity toward friends, and sobriety toward himself.

## CHAPTER CXIX. On a small breakfast.

[Col. 0122C]

We must now explain a certain small breakfast which ought to take place before the great Easter meal, after communion. For it has been ordained in certain churches—and it ought everywhere to be done—that on that day bread and wine should be kept in the church; and when people have communicated, each person should immediately receive a morsel of bread before departing, and a little wine, lest some part of the sacrament should remain in the mouth and be easily expelled by spitting. This could readily happen if food were not eaten immediately.

This praiseworthy custom is approved by all, and took its origin from the institution of Saint Benedict. For that most holy man ordained for the same reason that those who must serve the other brethren at their meal after communion should first eat something. This meal is commonly called the mixed meal (*prandium mistum*). Religious persons ought to communicate every day, and should at least eat an apple, some spice, or something similar, [Col. 0122D] which checks nausea.

For the same consideration, the Church ordained that Mass should be celebrated at three fixed hours according to the character of the days: at the third hour on feast days, the sixth on ordinary days, and the ninth on fast days, so that after Mass is ended and communion completed, the meal may immediately follow and those who have communicated may not incur the danger mentioned above. I have said these three hours because, when Mass has been celebrated at them, one may dine according to the character of the day, but not before.

But if it should happen, whether on this day or any other, that any part of the sacrament falls from the chalice, it must be understood that if it is of the body, it ought to be consumed. But if it is of the blood and falls upon a cloth, all of it should, insofar as possible, be licked up; and if that cloth must be washed, it should be washed in the piscina. If it falls upon stone or wood, however, the place must be scraped away completely; what is scraped off must be burned, and the ashes deposited beneath the altar. The same is to be done if anything similar occurs through nausea. [Col. 0123A]

Let us observe here, therefore, that something is washed principally for two reasons: for reverence toward the sacrament, as when the priest washes his hands when he touches the sacrament; and because of uncleanness, so that what is unclean may be made clean. Also observe that at a certain council of Poitiers it was decreed that no one should ever communicate or celebrate Mass without a light.

Accordingly, together with what we have just said, let us observe that neither layman nor priest ought, after communion and before eating, to spit in a place where the spittle can easily be trampled underfoot. Care must also be taken not to spit into an unclean or impure place.

As to the question raised here—how the canon should be said, quickly or slowly?—we reply that the words ought to be pronounced quickly, but distinctly. And why, pray, quickly? So that flies arriving may not carry off the sweetness of the ointment. This is also evident from the Old Testament [Col. 0123B] in Exodus, where it says: “You shall eat in haste” (Exod. XII). For this saying concerns the sacrifice of the lamb.

## CHAPTER CXX. On a certain December liberty.

It remains to discuss what was proposed last in the foregoing division: namely, a certain December liberty, observed in some places at this season. There are certain churches in which it is customary for even bishops and archbishops to play with their subjects in monasteries, even lowering themselves to play ball. This liberty is called December liberty because among the pagans it was formerly customary, in this [Col. 0123D] month, for male and female slaves and herdsmen to be granted a kind of liberty and to become equal in condition with their masters, celebrating common feasts after the gathering of the harvest.

Although great churches, such as that of Reims, observe this custom of playing, it nevertheless seems more praiseworthy not to play.

It should also be noted that in many regions, on the second day after Easter, women beat their husbands, and men in turn beat them on the third day, just as slaves were permitted in December to accuse their masters without punishment. They do this in order to show that they ought mutually to correct one another, lest at that season either spouse demand the marital debt from the other.

Hence it should be understood that at the Council of Elvira, under Pope Sylvester, [Col. 0124A] the following was decreed: husband and wife, when they were to communicate, were to abstain from embraces for three days before communion, and afterwards likewise for at least three days, or for five or seven, on account of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

This decree was taken from the Book of Kings, from the place where David, fleeing from Saul, is said to have come to Nob, to the priest Abimelech, and asked him for food. Since the priest had nothing to give him except the bread of the Presence, which only priests—and even they only when clean—were permitted to eat, David nevertheless asked that it be given to him. “Are your young men clean?” he said. David replied, “If you ask concerning women, we have abstained since yesterday and the day before” (1 Sam. XXI).

Other manuscripts read thus: [Col. 0124B] “If your young men are clean, especially from women, let them eat.” As though he said: necessity has no law. Yet if they are unclean from intercourse, I shall not give it to them even in necessity. And David says to him: “Since yesterday and the day before we have kept ourselves continent, and the vessels of the young men are holy”—that is, the bodies in which souls are contained, or the young men themselves. “The way indeed is defiled, but today it shall be sanctified in the vessels” (*ibid.*). As though he meant: perhaps on the journey we have contracted some uncleanness, but bodily purity is enough to cleanse it.

Nor do I say that, if a husband demands the marital debt from his wife, she should not render it to him; rather, she ought gently to admonish him not to demand it. But if he persists and yields to no admonition, she should pay it, lest he who demands it should perhaps sin more grievously on that account, as is reported to have happened not long ago among certain Germans.

For in Germany, when a husband and wife, living chastely throughout the whole of Lent, had slept separately, it happened that on Easter night, when they rose for Matins, the woman demanded the marital debt. Her husband diligently corrected her; but when his good admonitions achieved nothing, he promised to do what she requested as soon as he returned, and thus went to Matins. She, however, remained at home as though mad and went to a certain young man, her husband’s brother, sleeping in the same house, asking him to know her carnally. Because of the reverence and holiness of the time, and because of the incest which she shamelessly requested, he refused utterly to comply and went back to sleep. Then the woman, [Col. 0124D] burning more fiercely because of the rejection she had suffered, killed the sleeping young man. When the husband returned home, she related the entire matter in order, saying: “You are the author of this evil; you compelled me to do these things.” Accordingly, both performed long and severe penance, but were not therefore separated.

Therefore, in this respect it must be understood that a husband is set over his wife in all things and has every authority over her, except concerning the genitals, in which both have equal dominion and authority. Hence it is said: “The husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does; nor does the wife have authority over her own body, but the husband does” (1 Cor. VII)—that is, concerning the genitals; for Augustine so interprets it.

This also explains why priests do not have wives. For if [Col. 0125A] they had them, whenever they demanded the marital debt from their wives, they would be bound to render it, and thus could not minister at the altar during the following three days. It should further be understood that the three days following Easter are to be kept wholly as holidays; but on the fourth day men may perform agricultural labor, while women must abstain from spinning. For the tasks connected with cultivating fields are more necessary than those others. Hence Gregory says: “It is better to dig and plough on the Lord’s Day than to lead dances.”

From this, we say, it follows that each of these days has its own proper offices and proper responsories, while other days do not, except by a kind of adaptation. In this week, moreover, nothing is to be read from the Old Testament, but each day has its own offices. Nor is “Whosoever will” to be sung, because this season signifies that future time which we believe will come after the resurrection, when all faith and all hope will utterly be destroyed.

After the office this verse is said: “Lord, thou hast searched me and known me” (Ps. CXXXVIII); and some omit “my sitting down” (*ibid.*). Yet both may be said, signifying Christ’s twofold birth. Prime may be sung in two ways: more briefly or more fully. More fully, when it is called full Prime, and it is performed with a litany and prayers. More briefly, when it is called less full, and is performed either with prayers only and without a litany, or without litany and without prayers. This is the form which we sing on these days [Col. 0125C] without prayers, and altogether more briefly than at other times.

Great care is likewise needed in admitting persons to communion: the priest should first hear the confession of those who are about to communicate; and if anyone bears hatred toward his brother or has committed some grave offence, he must first be warned not to communicate before being reconciled with his brother. But if such a person heedlessly presents himself with the others, communion is not to be denied him; nor should one do as certain people do, who keep both consecrated and unconsecrated hosts, so that, should some approach who harbour fraternal hatred or some grave sin, they may communicate from the unconsecrated ones. Yet it is quite evident that such people sin grievously. For they deceive them [Col. 0125D]; although others who receive are no less—indeed, more—at fault, since they are guilty knowingly and willingly. For they think that they receive the true Body, and do not dread receiving it unworthily. Therefore the priest ought to have consecrated bread, so that, should such persons approach, they too may communicate from that bread.

There are four ways of communicating in the Church: by receiving the Body of the Lord; by giving the kiss of peace; by receiving a blessing; or, at the end of Mass, when it is said, “Humble yourselves for the blessing.” This was instituted so that, if anyone does not communicate in one way, he may at least do so in another. In the primitive Church it was commanded that the Body of the Lord be received daily; later, as the number of believers increased, that it be received every Sunday. Hence even now in Greece one who has not communicated for three Sundays is placed under anathema [Col. 0126A]. At present, however, we are bound on three solemnities: namely Easter, Pentecost, and Christmas.

That first solemnity is called Pascha, “the lamb” and “the passing-over”; and at that season one ought to greet others in this way: “The Lord has risen.” Likewise, on that day a sermon should be preached to the people at the beginning of Mass, or after the Gospel; and those at variance should be urged toward concord. For this reason, it is thought, the Lord’s Prayer is first said in a low voice and then pronounced aloud and distinctly at Mass: so that even by this means those who are in fraternal hatred may be exhorted, and discordant persons stirred toward concord before they communicate. Nor can Christ’s Body ever be received more unworthily than in such a condition.

## CHAPTER CXXI. Explanation of certain observances, both at this season and elsewhere

Why bishops and other churchmen may play during these Easter weekdays has now been explained. But let us next explain some other matters done both here and elsewhere. We shall begin with this: among some people, immersions in water are performed at this season, lest, because they kept vigil throughout the whole of Lent, they should wish to sleep during these holy days.

At this time we also put on white garments: both because the children who have been regenerated wear them, and because on that day angels were seen in white. For the reasons stated above, *Whosoever will* is omitted [Col. 0126C], and *I believe in one God* is sung.

Observe here in passing that, if wine in the chalice should freeze, the priest ought to breathe upon it for a while, until the ice melts. If it cannot be thawed in that way, it must be placed by the fire. But if anything should accidentally fall into the chalice—whether a fly or a spider, or indeed whatever it may be—the priest must swallow all of it.

Accordingly, the following Saturday is called “in White,” from an ancient custom: on that day they wholly put off black garments and put on white ones. Some, however, do this on Easter Saturday. Immediately on the following Sunday nine lessons are to be sung; hence they also have the history, namely, “Worthy art thou, O Lord.” Thus it is done at Rome.

During these days knees are not to be bent [Col. 0126D], but prayer is to be made standing upright; for, as Ambrose says near the end of his commentary on Luke, the women came to the tomb and did not bend their knees, but looked straight into the sepulchre.

Meanwhile note that on the feast of the Annunciation of Blessed Mary the sequence—which, as we have said, was also called a prose—is not to be sung, even out of devotion; nor is it ever sung unless *Alleluia* is sung. For the custom was that after *Alleluia* a *neuma* should be sung. The *neuma* was the chant which followed *Alleluia*. Later, however, a certain pope instituted that a sequence should be sung in place of the *neuma*; and it seems to have been called thus because it follows the *Alleluia*.

Nevertheless, it is permitted at this season for someone to bend the knee, provided that he does it not openly but secretly; and anyone who wishes may also fast. “For,” as Jerome says, “would that we could fast at all times!” Meat is forbidden in fasting, as are eggs, cheese, and milk; for Jerome himself thinks that all these are liquid meats [Col. 0127A]. Blessed Benedict, however, allowed eggs, milk, and cheeses to be eaten, so that, although they are in some respects incentives to lust, they may nevertheless be eaten for a greater crown and victory. Fish are permitted to those who fast; but, as Jerome says, only “a few little fishes,” by which it is readily understood that they ought to be both small and few.

This season is called Quinquagesima because it represents the time of jubilee, when liberty will be complete and our inheritance restored to us. Therefore we also sing *Alleluia*. Yet we do not bend the knee, but pray standing, except in the litanies.

[Col. 0127B] Finally, let us observe that the Passover of the Jews was a figure of our Pascha, and that our Pascha in turn signifies the future Passover, which will be at the end of the world. To make this clear, one must know that there are two works of God: the work of creation and the work of re-creation. The work of creation was in the beginning, when God created the world and everything contained in it. The work of re-creation occurs daily; but God will exercise it especially on the Day of Judgment, when all things shall be renewed. Our Pascha corresponds and agrees with the time of each work.

It corresponds with the time of creation because then the angels praised the Lord; whence it is said in Job: “Where wast thou when the morning stars praised me, and all the sons of God rejoiced before me?” (Job 38). So too, reborn in our Pascha [Col. 0127C], we sing *Alleluia* in praise of the Lord.

By the same reasoning, our Pascha directly represents the time of re-creation. For the three days preceding Pascha signify the time of Antichrist, to whom three kings will give their hands, and to whom seven kingdoms will afterwards subject themselves through them, while ten kingdoms will serve his rule. For just as, among us, at that time—that is, on the very day of the Supper—penitents are received into the church, and on the same day the feet, which are the extremities of Christ’s Body, are washed, so at the end of time the Jews will be cleansed by the water of baptism. See: “The remnant of Israel shall be saved” (Romans 9).

On the day of the Preparation, the Passion is read, just as then the Church will persecute most severely. For Satan will then be loosed [Col. 0127D], having been kept bound in hell since the Passion of the Lord. And just as cymbals are not struck on this day, so preachers, or proclaimers, will then fall silent. Therefore in Tenebrae the *Benedictus* is sung in a loud voice, because at that time, after Antichrist has been slain, many will rejoice. Thus the fire which now appears in the darkness to be wholly extinguished and is afterwards brought forth signifies that, at that time, in those persons in whom the fire of the Holy Spirit appears to have been extinguished, it will shine forth again.

Thus children are baptized on Saturday, and then the Jews will be baptized. On the very day of the Resurrection we sing in the person of Christ, “I have risen, and am still with thee” (Psalm 138); but then we shall say this same thing in our own person, when, rising again, we pass from this mortality to immortality. Therefore [Col. 0128A] during the octave of Easter nine lessons from the Apocalypse ought to be said, as is shown by the responsory, “Worthy art thou, O Lord” (Revelation 4). For it is called a responsory because, as has often already been said, it must answer the lesson which preceded it.

Nor should anyone object that in every season the Sunday responsory is said of the Trinity, though no lesson concerning it is read. For in the primitive Church it was instituted that every Sunday both the ninth lesson and the responsory should be said of the Trinity. But because that lesson fell out of use, only the responsory remained.

Throughout Eastertide we ought neither to bend the knee nor be obliged to fast. Yet, as we have said, this is permitted out of piety and devotion. For this Easter season signifies the eighth age, in which there shall be perfect joy for all the saints. Hence we do not fast here, nor bend the knee, but pray standing and eat more delicately and more sumptuously—except during the two litanies, of which we must now speak.

## CHAPTER CXXII. On the litanies

First, then, we must consider what a litany is; second, since there are two litanies, why one is called the greater and the other the lesser; third, why they were instituted; fourth, how one should fast and dress during them; and fifth and last, what the people ought to sing in a litany.

*Litany* is interpreted in Latin as “supplication” or “petition.” It is called a supplication because we then beseech God to defend us from sudden death and every adversity [Col. 0128C]. It is called a petition because we ask the saints to intercede for us with the Lord.

There are two litanies, the greater and the lesser. The greater is held on the feast of Blessed Mark the Evangelist. It is called the greater both because of the authority of its institution—Pope Gregory the First of that name, also called Gregory the Great, instituted it—and because of the authority of its place. For it was instituted at Rome, and it was decreed by public ordinance that it should be celebrated everywhere. The other litany is called the lesser because it was instituted by one of lesser rank, namely Blessed Mamertus, a bishop, and at Vienne. This one is celebrated only in the Church on this side of the Alps.

Paul the monk of Monte Cassino, historian of the Lombards, gives the following reason why the earlier litany was instituted. “For,” he says, “in the time of Pope Pelagius there was so great a flood of waters throughout all Italy that the water rose as high as the upper windows of the church of Blessed Zeno at Verona, yet by a miracle the water did not enter the church. From this inundation a multitude of serpents was carried through the Tiber into the fields, among them a huge dragon; and all entered the sea through the two mouths of the Tiber. From the poisonous breath of these serpents, and especially of that dragon, the air was corrupted and infected, so much so that a most grievous plague of the groin arose from it, by which people died everywhere. Then Pope Pelagius proclaimed a fast and ordered a procession to be held; and this was done. But in the procession itself he died, together with seventy others. In his [Col. 0129A] place Gregory the Great was appointed, and he commanded that such a litany be observed throughout the world.”

Concerning the second litany, which is celebrated for three days, Gregory, bishop of Tours, says “that in the time of Blessed Mamertus, at Vienne and around Vienne, earthquakes occurred frequently, and so great that even very large houses and many churches collapsed and fell. This disturbance lasted for a whole year. Likewise, on Easter Saturday, while Mamertus himself was celebrating the divine office, fire sent down from heaven burned the palace of the city. Moreover, beasts such as wolves and boars came out of the woods into the city and devoured people. Because of these calamities Blessed Mamertus proclaimed a three-day fast, after the example [Col. 0129B] of the Ninevites, and ordered them to make a procession, so that, as those people escaped the destruction of their city by a three-day fast, so these might be delivered from adversities of this kind. And so it was done.”

That Gregory, whom we mentioned shortly before, is said to have been exceedingly small in stature. When he happened to come to Rome, everyone despised him; and the pope himself was astonished that so tiny a man had been made a bishop. To him he answered courteously: “It is God himself who made us, and not we ourselves” (Psalm 84).

Blessed Hilary said something similar to a man who called him a Gaul: “I was not born a cock, but am from Gaul; and you are a lion, but not from the tribe of Judah”—for that was his name.

## CHAPTER CXXIII. On the institution and manner of the litanies

[Col. 0129C]

Blessed Mamertus therefore instituted that every year this litany should be celebrated for three consecutive days in the Church on this side of the Alps; and this was canonically established at Rome. Pope Liberius also instituted that, in the face of famine, plague, disaster, and similar threatening adversities, we should always perform litanies, so that by supplications, prayers, and fasts we might avoid them.

These processions are called litanies, by a Greek term on account of the authority of the Greek language, as are Pascha and Pentecost. In these litanies one must fast with Lenten food and wear penitential garments. [Col. 0129D] For everyone on that day, including male and female servants, ought entirely to abstain from worldly work and attend the procession for as long as it is celebrated, so that, just as all have sinned, so all may also plead for pardon.

In such processions people proceed in great churches in seven ranks; hence they are called sevenfold. In the first rank are clerics; in the second monks and canons; in the third nuns; in the fourth boys; in the fifth elderly laypeople; in the sixth widows; and in the seventh married persons. But what we cannot supply in the number of persons, we make up in the number of litanies. For we ought to say the litany seven times.

Here we may observe in passing that Rupert, abbot of Deutz, said that the last litany had begun many years [Col. 0130A] before the first. We chiefly perform these litanies at this season because wars especially tend to arise then, and the fruits of the earth, still tender or in blossom, may be damaged by the harm of mists or in many other ways. Therefore, that God may avert all these things, we institute litanies, joining the last one to the Ascension, so that through fasting and prayers we may deserve to follow Christ and ascend to heaven.

The dragon carried during those three days, with an inflated and lengthy tail, proceeds before the cross and banners on the first two days, and on the last follows behind. It signifies the devil, who in three periods—before the Law, under the Law, and in the time of grace, indicated by these three days—deceived, or seeks to deceive, humankind.

In the first two periods he was, as it were, lord [Col. 0130B] of the world; hence Christ calls him “the prince of this world” (John 14). But in the time of grace he was conquered through Christ, and no longer dares reign as openly as before. Instead, by suggestions he secretly seduces those whom he sees sluggish and lax in good works and not following the way of life; just as in the wilderness enemies coming from behind killed the weak and infirm, and those who remained at the rear, as though straying. Hence he goes before on the first two days and follows on the last.

He is both dragon and lion. He is now a dragon because he deceives people not so openly but secretly. He will be a lion in the time of Antichrist, because then he will rage openly against the name of Christ. He was a dragon when, upon the pinnacle of the Temple, where he had formerly seduced many by vainglory, he sought secretly to deceive Christ and tempted him, saying: “If thou art the Son of God, cast thyself down” (Matthew 4). And, as though Christ could safely do this, he added: “For he hath commanded his angels,” etc. (Psalm 89). For he understood the Scriptures well; but he suppressed what was to his own harm: namely, “Thou shalt walk upon the asp and the basilisk,” etc.

But he was a lion in the Passion of the Lord, when he contrived even to have him crucified. John says of him in the Apocalypse: “Behold a great red dragon, having seven heads and ten horns, and on his heads seven diadems; and his tail drew after it a third part of the stars” (Revelation 12). The stars here signify people, who are divided into three classes: the perfect, the imperfect, and the reprobate. Therefore the devil draws after himself the third part of the stars, namely the reprobate; for these [Col. 0130D] are his tail.

Elsewhere Christ calls him Satan: “I saw Satan fall from heaven like lightning” (Luke 10); and he says to Peter: “Go behind me, Satan” (Mark 10). This should not be understood as though he calls Peter the devil, but “adversary,” which is the meaning of *Satan*. For this is the sense and force of the passage: “Go behind me, Satan”—that is, follow me by imitating my Passion; do not disturb my Passion.

Or rather, as Blessed Hilary says, Christ saw the demon whispering in Peter’s ear in order to hinder his Passion, and said to him: “Satan, Satan,” as though to say, “You labour vainly and to no purpose.” Then, turning to Peter, he said: “Go behind me,” that is, follow me by imitating my Passion.

## CHAPTER CXXIV. On the feast of the Apostles Philip and James

[Col. 0131A]

We must now speak of certain solemnities celebrated at this season in the churches: namely, the feast of Saints Philip and James, and of all the apostles—for so it stands in the great and complete calendars—the Finding of the Holy Cross, the feast of John before the Latin Gate, of Blessed Mary at the Martyrs, and the commemoration of Saint Michael.

This season, as was stated before, signifies the eighth age, in which the good that shall belong to each person in differing degrees of glory shall also be the good of all. For each person will rejoice in another’s good just as in his own; the good of all will belong to each individual. Therefore, since this season is especially suited to solemnities, and since [Col. 0131B] in the primitive Church the apostles did not have individual solemnities, it was appointed that on the Kalends of May a solemnity should be celebrated in honour of all the apostles.

On this day also is the feast of Philip and James, because perhaps they suffered on that day. This James was called the Less, not on account of age, but of vocation, as happens among monks: one who became a monk earlier, even if he is a boy, nevertheless precedes a person of whatever age who entered the monastery later. He was also called the Lord’s brother, either because, as is said, he resembled him in face, or because he was the son of Alphaeus, brother of Joseph, the husband of Blessed Mary, and of Mary his sister. Those who were thus related through blood on both sides were called brothers among the Jews. Jesus, however, was thought to be Joseph’s son.

This James is said to have celebrated Mass at Jerusalem first after Christ’s Passion, while Peter did so at Antioch. This same James was made bishop of Jerusalem; and, because he preached and publicly confessed the name of Christ, he was thrown down by the Jews from the pinnacle of the Temple and killed with a fuller’s club. The other James was called the Greater, both in vocation and dignity, because he was more intimate with Christ. For Christ called him to the secret acts of his work: when he was transfigured, for example, and when he raised a dead person in the house.

## CHAPTER CXXV. On the Finding of the Holy Cross

When the Cross of the Lord was found by Helena, mother of Constantine, through Judas, as the history relates, its feast was first celebrated at Jerusalem [Col. 0131D]. But Eusebius, the thirtieth pope from Blessed Peter, afterwards commanded that it be celebrated throughout the world.

That Judas through whom the Cross was found is said later to have been converted at the end, to have changed his name to Quiriacus, and finally to have been made bishop of Jerusalem. When the devil was awaiting another friend of his, he is reported to have said of him: “Through Judas Christ was handed over to death, and through this Judas the dead Christ was exalted; but shortly my friend Julian will be king, and he will avenge me splendidly upon him.” This indeed came about, as is said, when Julian killed him.

They relate that this Julian was a monk and a great dissembler in religion [Col. 0132A], so much so that a certain woman entrusted three jars laden with gold to his keeping. The gold was covered with ashes at the mouths of the jars, so that it might not readily be discovered; and yet she did not confess that there was gold in them, since she believed the man to be holy. But after he had found and stolen it, he filled the jars with ashes and returned the deposit to the woman when she demanded it. When shortly afterwards the woman sought her gold and could not find it, she could not prove that he had it, because she had no witnesses concerning the gold. For the other monks, in whose presence she had delivered the jars, had seen nothing in them except ashes. Thus he obtained the gold.

After fleeing to Rome and holding the consulship for a considerable period, he became emperor. Since from childhood he was skilled in the magical art and greatly loved it, he gathered many teachers about him. One day, when his teacher was absent and he was alone at home, he began to read invocations of demons. A great multitude of demons came before him, all black as Ethiopians. Then, terrified, he made the sign of the cross, and they all immediately disappeared. When Julian recounted this to his teacher, who asked what he had seen, the teacher told him that the demons hated that sign above all else. Therefore, after being elected emperor, still remembering this incident, he became an apostate because he wished to practise magic. He destroyed signs of the cross everywhere and persecuted Christians as far as he could, believing that the demons could not otherwise obey him. [Col. 0132C] Therefore he also killed Judas, now called Quiriacus, through whom the Cross had been found.

We further read that a soldier, likewise called Quiriacus, killed this Julian. For when Julian was leading his army through Ephesus against other pagans who had risen against him and the Romans, he saw there a certain abbey and ordered its inhabitants to prepare meals for him. But they flatly refused, both because he was an apostate and because they were poor. Enraged at this, he sent word again that, before the year ended, he would destroy the place, kill them, and bring it about that crops should grow there.

On hearing this [Col. 0132D], the monks were afraid; but their abbot, a most holy man, strengthened them in the Lord and so fortified them by his encouragement that they were now prepared for martyrdom. One night, while the abbot persisted in prayer, Blessed Mary appeared to him opening the monastery. She came to the tomb of a certain soldier, called Quiriacus, who had died fewer than seven days before and had been buried there; she ordered him to rise from it, arm himself, and avenge her upon Julian.

Then he rose, put on his armour, which was still hanging in the church, mounted his horse, which was still in the stable, in the abbot’s sight, and made for Julian’s borders. The next day the abbot recounted in order to his monks all that he had seen. They opened the soldier’s tomb to test the matter and found neither the body [Col. 0133A], nor the horse, nor the armour.

On the third day, as Julian fought his enemies, he was killed by the aforesaid soldier. On the following night the soldier, in the abbot’s sight, returned to his tomb and put the horse and armour back in their places.

After this Julian came Cyprian, a man given to gluttony and lust. When he wished to incite the blessed virgin Justina to his own lust, he sent a demon that presided over such uncleanness; but it was repelled by the sign of the cross. He sent another, stronger demon, which likewise confessed that it had been overcome by the sign of the cross; and thus Cyprian was converted to the faith. Such is the power of Christ’s cross, through which he restored us, wholly undeserving as we were, to eternal blessedness.

## CHAPTER CXXVI. On Saint John the Evangelist before the Latin Gate

[Col. 0133B]

Nero had killed Peter and Paul. After his death Vespasian succeeded him, then Titus, and afterwards Domitian. Under him the blessed John the Evangelist went to Rome to preach the word of God there. Domitian had him placed in a vat full of boiling oil before the Latin Gate, as it was called. But Blessed John suffered no injury there, divine grace protecting him. Yet, so far as his own part was concerned, he was a martyr. Therefore his feast is observed, just as though he had undergone martyrdom there. Domitian then banished him to the island of Patmos. At length he was recalled by the emperor Nerva.

Let us note here that only three apostles were alive at Rome: Peter, Paul, and John; and likewise three evangelists: John, Mark, and Luke [Col. 0133C]. Further, let us observe that Christ’s apostles or disciples did not suffer because they preached Christ, but because they deified him and declared him to be God without Roman authorization, which the Romans had forbidden.

## CHAPTER CXXVII. On the feast of Blessed Mary at the Martyrs

Since individual Roman idols could not each have a temple at Rome, the Romans made one temple for all idols, called the Pantheon. Pope Boniface IV commanded Phocas, emperor at Constantinople, to give this temple to the Church of Christ, and, after casting out the idols [Col. 0133D] and all their filth, dedicated it in honour of Blessed Mary and all martyrs—for feasts were not yet celebrated for confessors. He established that the feast of martyrs should be celebrated every year on that day, just as the feast of the apostles was celebrated on the Kalends of May.

But because in that month provisions are not as abundant as in others—for food commonly becomes scarce then—and because the people flocking to those solemnities could sometimes not properly devote themselves to the celebration owing to a lack of food, Gregory the Lesser, the fourth of that name, transferred these two feasts and appointed them to be held on the Kalends of November, when there is a greater abundance of things. He also ordered its office as a general feast, not only of the apostles and martyrs, but also of the Trinity, all angels and archangels, patriarchs, prophets, and all other saints [Col. 0134A], both male and female.

## CHAPTER CXXVIII. Why we do not celebrate the feasts of the saints who rose with Christ

It is asked why at this season we do not celebrate the feasts of the saints who rose with Christ or ascended to heaven with him. For we ought to rejoice and keep solemnity over their glorification, as we do for other saints, since we are certain that they ascended. But the reason is this.

We do not keep solemnity for their death, because they descended into hell; but for their glorification in the soul we ought to celebrate a feast either at Easter or at least at the Lord’s Ascension. Yet we cannot do so because of the authority and magnitude of the offices of those days [Col. 0134B]. Their festival would be overshadowed by the dignity of the greater solemnity. It is as if one of a king’s retainers came with the king: because of the king’s presence, one would not attend to him as carefully as one would if he came alone.

It was therefore established that their feasts should be celebrated at other times of year, on the days upon which churches were dedicated to them: thus the feast of Blessed John the Baptist is kept near the end of August, although he died around Easter; and, for the same reason, the feast of Blessed James of Compostela is observed in July. The feast of Blessed Peter in Chains will be discussed elsewhere.

Observe, therefore, that the feasts of Old Testament saints—Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, David, Daniel, and others—are honoured in Greece and at Venice [Col. 0134C], and that they have churches there.

## CHAPTER CXXIX. On Saint Michael

Concerning the feast of Saint Michael, we say that at this time barbarians entered Apulia and cruelly ravaged it. Therefore the Christians invoked the aid of Saint Michael during the said three-day fast. When they had assembled and drawn up their battle-line, leading their army against the enemy, Saint Michael appeared to them as though offering them assistance; then the enemies turned in flight. Because they gained victory through Blessed Michael, it was established that his feast should always be celebrated on that day.

## CHAPTER CXXX. On the variations of this season

[Col. 0134D]

Having spoken of the feasts, we must consider certain variations of this season. These three weeks are, as it were, designated by their own special names. The first is Easter week; the second is “in White”; the third is the week of expectation, namely that after the Lord’s Ascension.

The first is called sanctified, because persons sanctified through baptism wear throughout that week the garment in which they received baptism, signifying the first robe. The second week is called “in White,” because then, on the second Saturday, those who have been baptized put off their baptismal garments and put on white garments. Or because those who have been baptized are then customarily confirmed by bishops and put on other white garments until the following Saturday. Or indeed it is called “in White” [Col. 0135A] because it signifies eternal life, in which we shall be clothed with both robes.

The third is finally called, as we said, the week of expectation, because it represents that time in which the apostles awaited the coming of the Holy Spirit. Hence let us observe that some customarily fast from the Ascension until Pentecost, because the apostles are said to have fasted at that time. But Master Gilbert thinks one should not fast, since it belongs to the Easter season.

Another variation is to be noted here. Easter week extends only to Saturday in White, and thus Easter has only six days for its octave. The week in White begins on Saturday in White and ends on the following Saturday, thus lasting eight days. The octave of the Ascension ought to end on the fifth feria before Pentecost. Although the two days remaining beyond the octave can readily take their Mass office from Sunday, they would not have an invitatory or responsories at Nocturns unless they drew them from the Ascension of the Lord. Thus those ten days are counted as one octave. Nor is this strange, since the whole Easter season is regarded as one octave, just as is the period from the Nativity of the Lord until the octave of Epiphany.

## CHAPTER CXXXI. On Pentecost

Having briefly explained these matters concerning the Easter season, we must next treat of the Lord’s Pentecost. The people of Israel principally observe four solemnities: Pascha, because then the Lord delivered them from Egyptian slavery and from the stroke of the angel, when they had sprinkled the doorposts with the blood of an unspotted lamb. For there was no Egyptian house in which no dead person was found. But there was none in the houses of the Hebrews [Col. 0135C].

They further celebrate Pentecost because then they received the Law; and in September the Feast of Tabernacles (*Scenopegia*), which means “the pitching of tents.” Finally, in winter they celebrate *Encaenia*, that is, the dedication of the Temple.

We, however, observe only two of these: Pascha and Pentecost, but for a reason different from theirs. They celebrate Pascha because they were then delivered from Egyptian slavery; we celebrate Pascha because we were then redeemed through Christ. They celebrate Pentecost because they then received the Law; we do so because then we receive the Holy Spirit.

They received the Law written outwardly on tablets of stone: on tablets of stone, to signify their hardness; written outwardly, because the letter did not attain spiritual understanding. But the Holy Spirit was given to the seventy-two disciples, with the finger of God inwardly dictating spiritual understanding in their hearts.

Yet observe that Pentecost is one thing and Quinquagesima another; and that “fiftieth” is understood in several ways. There is a fiftieth of days, years, psalms, persons, and denarii. Again, this fiftieth of days is threefold. One runs from the Sunday commonly called *Esto mihi* to Easter; another from Easter to Pentecost; and the third from Saturday in White to the Saturday after Pentecost [Col. 0136A]. The first is one of penitence and affliction; the second, of joy and exultation; the third, as it were, of figure, for it prefigures the eighth age, in which we shall be clothed with both robes.

Hence we sing those two Alleluias of Quinquagesima: the first signifies the robe of the body, the second that of the soul. Likewise, there are three fiftieths of psalms. The first is from *Blessed is the man* to *Have mercy on me*; the second from *Have mercy on me* to *Lord, hear*; and the third from *Lord, hear* to *Let every spirit praise the Lord*.

These fiftieths signify the days of the Flood. For the inundation of waters lasted so many days, namely one hundred and fifty days [Col. 0136B]. We sing the three fiftieths of psalms so that God may defend us from such a flood and from every evil.

The fiftieth of years was the jubilee. Of the fiftieth of persons, Genesis tells us where Abraham asks the Lord in this manner: “If,” he says, “seventy righteous persons are found in the city, wilt thou spare them?” (Genesis 18). “Yes,” God answered; and afterwards likewise concerning sixty and fifty, down to ten (ibid.). Of the fiftieth of denarii, the Gospel tells us where two debtors are discussed, one owing one hundred denarii and the other fifty. But let what has been said about these suffice.

Pentecost is therefore called from πεντήκοντα, “fifty,” because this day is fifty days distant from the Lord’s resurrection. [Col. 0136C] Hence πεντεκοστός is called in Latin *quinquagesimus*, “fiftieth.” For just as the people of Israel, on the fiftieth day after the Passover which they celebrated at Rameses, came to the mountain of God, Horeb or Sinai—for these are the same—and then received the Law (Exod. XX), so on the fiftieth day after the Lord’s Passion the Holy Spirit was given in fiery tongues to the disciples awaiting his coming in the upper chamber. He was given in tongues, certainly, so that they might be eloquent in every kind of language and speech (Acts II); and in fiery tongues so that they might be inflamed with the love of charity.

The Holy Spirit was therefore given to the disciples; his grace is sevenfold, because the Jews especially observe the number seven in all things, and this not without the appearance of a figure. For they [Col. 0136D] observe the seventh day, namely the Sabbath; the seventh week, namely Pentecost; the seventh month, namely September, which is held especially solemn among them; and the seventh year, inasmuch as slaves were set free by the Jews if they wished. But if anyone did not wish to be freed, but to remain in the service of his master, he was led to the doorposts of the tabernacle or temple, and his ears were pierced with an awl. This was a sign of servitude, so that he might not thereafter be freed, should he perhaps later wish to be released from slavery. Likewise, in that year whatever the earth freely produced was common property, for it was not cultivated that year.

By the same reasoning, we celebrate baptism on the seventh day, namely the Sabbath. For Sabbath signifies rest, and through baptism we “keep Sabbath,” [Col. 0137A] that is, we rest; because when a person is baptized, his soul has repose, resting in the unity of faith after being cleansed from vices by the Spirit. It should therefore be known that baptism is regularly celebrated on only two Sabbaths: the Sabbath of Easter and that of Pentecost. On the Easter Sabbath, indeed, because in Christ’s Passion we are all baptized—that is, redeemed; but on the Sabbath of Pentecost because then we are cleansed and sanctified through the Holy Spirit. The office of this Sabbath must now be discussed.

## CHAPTER CXXXII. On the Office of the Sabbath of Pentecost

The office of this day differs in no respect from the office of the [Col. 0137B] Sabbath of Easter, except that there the first reading is about Adam, that is, about the creation of the world; here, however, the first is about Abraham. A canticle is appended to this reading about Abraham, but not, certainly, to the one about Adam. These two readings signify those two fathers, one of whom was the father of error and falling away, namely Adam; the other the father of faith and restoration, namely Abraham.

We do not append a canticle to the reading about Adam because he did not sing well for us, since he transgressed God’s command. Hence we do not respond to him, as to one singing badly to us. That he sang badly is evident from the words said to him: “Cursed is the earth in your work” (Gen. III). We append a canticle to the reading about Abraham, as to one who sang well for us; thus it was said to him: [Col. 0137C] “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII).
