On this day the titles are omitted, on account of the little children who do not yet know the authors of the New and Old Testaments. The Mass on this Sabbath begins, as on the Sabbath of Easter, namely with *Kyrie eleison*—“Lord, have mercy.” Accordingly, *Gloria in excelsis* is sung both on this Sabbath and on that one, and also on Maundy Thursday, but only in the church where chrism is consecrated. It ought not to be sung elsewhere.

Finally, at Vespers these Psalms are said: “Praise the Lord, children” (Ps. CXII); “Praise the Lord, all nations” (Ps. CXVI); “Praise the Lord, O my soul” (Ps. CXLV); “Praise the Lord, for he is good” (Ps. CXLVI); and “Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem” (Ps. CXLVII).

## CHAPTER CXXXIII. On the Fasts of the Four Seasons

[Col. 0137D]

We must now speak of the fasts of firstfruits, which customarily occur in the week of Pentecost. We must consider first their origin; second, their institution; third, their name and its rationale; then their office; and finally the orders celebrated in them. The origin of these fasts is taken from the Old Testament. For just as that people gave God firstfruits from all their possessions, so we ought to give firstfruits from our times—and not only from our times, but from everything that we possess. We proceed now to their institution.

## CHAPTER CXXXIV. On the Institution of the Fasts of the Four Seasons

[Col. 0138A]

In the primitive Church it was ordained that these fasts should take place three times a year. But Pope Calixtus ordained [Note: [Col. 0137D] Distinction 66.] that they should take place four times, deriving his reasoning from the Old Testament. For the Jews fasted four times in the year: before Passover; before Pentecost; before the Feast of Tabernacles (*Scenopegia*), that is, before the making of tabernacles in September; and before the Dedication (*Encaenia*) in December.

Moreover, if they occurred three times, and fasting took place for three days on each occasion, then, with the year divided into three parts, there would always remain certain days from which we did not offer firstfruits. There are again many other reasons why they are held four times in the year. One is that the constitution of human nature contains four [Col. 0138B] qualities: we are hot, cold, moist, and dry. From these qualities each person seeks pleasures of sinning. Therefore, that we may restrain these four qualities from the desire to sin, we fast four times a year.

Or this reason may also be given. A human being consists of soul and body. The body consists of four elements; but the soul has chiefly three capacities: to reason, to become angry, and to desire. Therefore, that these may be moderated in us, we fast three days four times a year, so that the number four refers to the body and the number three to the soul.

Again, the year is divided into four seasons, each of which has three months. Therefore we fast three days four times a year, one day for each month. There is yet another reason [Col. 0138C] why we fast four times, namely on account of the four seasons of the year. In winter we entrust seeds to the earth; in spring trees blossom and vines put forth shoots; in summer we reap certain crops; and in autumn grapes are gathered.

Again, we fast four times because, just as the ancients also fasted the fortieth day four times in the year, so we fast three days in these seasons. These are called the fasts of the Four Seasons, or the fasts of firstfruits, or double fasts, because they occur on the three days on which we customarily fast in one week. They were instituted, as has been said, by Pope Calixtus.

The first fasts of this kind occur in March, namely in the first week of Lent, so that vices may wither in us; for they cannot be entirely extinguished. The second occur in summer, namely [Col. 0138D] in the week of Pentecost, so that, since the Holy Spirit then came, we too may be fervent in spirit. The third fasts occur before the feast of Saint Michael, in the third week of September, because, just as the fruits of trees are then gathered, we too ought to render to God the fruits of good works. Finally, the fourth occur in the week before the Nativity of the Lord, namely in December, because, as plants then die, so we must die to the world and be reborn to God.

On the Wednesday of these fasts two readings should be said: one from the Old Testament in the nocturnal tone or voice, the other from the New in the common tone and voice, [Col. 0139A] signifying that those to be ordained on the following Sabbath ought to be learned in both Testaments. The episcopal mitre indicates the same thing by its two horns. [Note: [Col. 0139D] 23, question I, chapter *Episcopus*.] For a bishop ought not to be ignorant of either Testament, so that, as with a double horn, he may strike the enemies of the faith and heretics.

On the Friday of the fast, only one reading should be said, because the author of the Old and New Testaments is one and the same God, and one Gospel has been made from the Old and New Testaments. On Saturday four readings are recited before the orders are celebrated. The first concerns the people; the second, the leaders of the Church; the third, the ministers; the fourth, all religious persons.

The reading from Daniel concerning the three youths follows because those to be ordained ought to be tested in faith, as they were. These men must be examined especially in three respects: in regard to birth, namely whether they were begotten in lawful marriage; in regard to learning; and in regard to life and good conduct. Let us therefore note here that the archpriest ought first to present those to be ordained to the archdeacon; hence he is also called a vicar here, because in this matter he fulfills the role of the priests. It would be their duty to do this.

The office of the archdeacon is to examine and investigate them in life, birth, and honorable conduct, and then to hand them over to the schoolmaster, whose task is to test them in learning. Thus, after careful examination, they should be handed over to the bishop. After the reading from Daniel, the chant *Benedicite*—“Bless”—is appended. But why knees are not bent at the reading [Col. 0139C] from Daniel has been said above. Then the Epistle of Paul is read, at which we do not bend the knee because it belongs to the New Testament. A tract is then appended to it in a solemn chant, because those ordained ought to be sober and steadfast, lest they be carried away by a light gust of pride.

Incidentally, it should be observed that no one is permitted to be ordained twice on the same day. But if necessary, a person may be ordained deacon on Saturday and priest on the following Sunday; afterward, in the octave of Pentecost, he may be consecrated bishop.

## CHAPTER CXXXV. On the Time of Pilgrimage and the Feasts Contained in It

From this Sabbath begins the time of pilgrimage, [Col. 0139D] because we are on the journey by which we come to our homeland; but before we reach it, we have enemies and adversaries—namely our flesh, the world, and the devil. At this time we read the Book of Kings, in which wars and victories are set before us, so that we too may fight bravely against our enemies and, having gained victory, may at last be crowned in heaven.

Let us also note in passing that writers call the Jews principally by three names. First, they are called *recutiti*, “the recut,” whence Isaiah says: “Recut Sabbaths,” that is, Jewish Sabbaths, because they have the skin of their private parts cut away. They are also called Palestinians, whence Ovid:

> “The seventh land cultivated by the Palestinian man.”  
> (*Ovid, Art of Love*, I.415)

[Col. 0140A] And they are called Jews by the common name derived from Judah, son of Jacob, who was one of the twelve patriarchs. Although there were twelve tribes descended from Jacob’s twelve sons, they were called Jews from Judah because Jacob prophesied concerning the kingdom of Judah in this manner: “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until he comes who was promised” (Gen. XLIX). Our Lord Jesus Christ came from the tribe of Judah.

Further, let us note that some octaves are octaves of devotion, such as those of Saint Nicholas and Saint Mary Magdalene. They have no octaves [in themselves], but because they are patrons of certain churches, octaves are kept for them. Some octaves are of veneration, as at the great solemnities; and some of signification, such as those of Peter and Paul, which signify the second robe that they will possess, namely the glorification of the body.

Paul the historian, a deacon of the Roman curia and monk of Monte Cassino, was once consecrating the Paschal candle when his throat became hoarse, although he had formerly possessed a sufficiently strong voice. Therefore, that his voice might be restored, he composed in honor of Saint John the hymn “*Ut queant laxis*,” etc.; at its beginning he asks for restoration of his voice, just as Zechariah’s was restored through the merit of Saint John. We shall speak of this, if first we briefly explain the feast of Gervasius and Protasius.

Here we say only this: in their office is sung, “The Lord shall speak peace to his people” (Ps. LXXXIV). This is indeed said at that time not without cause, because at their feast concord was restored between the Lombards and the Roman Empire. History fully recounts the rest concerning them.

## CHAPTER CXXXVI. On the Nativity of Saint John

Let us now consider the Nativity of Saint John himself, and first why his nativity is celebrated when he was conceived in sins. For no conception occurring in the embrace of male and female can be without sin. Some are without father and mother, as Adam; others are from a father without a mother, as Eve; others are from father and mother, which is most common, as Abel; and finally others are from a mother without a father, such as Christ. Hence it is said in his person: [Col. 0140D] “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. XXI), that is, born according to the law of worms, not of human beings.

But let it be observed here that a human being is first, so to speak, sown; afterward he is conceived in the womb, and there flesh is formed. Yet after forty-six days, according to theologians—who are more to be believed than physicians—the soul is created and infused into the body. Therefore this nativity is celebrated as the second, when he first comes forth into the light. The first is when the soul itself is infused into the body; the second, when he comes into the light. Thus, in respect to the second, he was conceived without sin. For he was sanctified in the womb, as Jeremiah was, in whose prophecy it is thus contained: “Before you came forth [Col. 0141A] from the womb I sanctified you,” etc. (Jer. I). This perhaps was said in prefiguration of him.

But God knows what sort of sanctification is meant there. Some think it was said of original sanctification, and endeavor to prove it thus: the Holy Spirit filled the child, and consequently, from this filling of the Holy Spirit, the mother too was filled. Yet if she were in original sin, she would certainly also be in mortal sin. Therefore neither the child nor his mother would have been filled with the Holy Spirit. Nor does it matter that very many wicked persons prophesied, such as Caiaphas and Balaam, and that even the ass spoke.

Yet it seems to the contrary that his original sin was not remitted. For John said to Christ: “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me to be baptized?” (Matt. III). From this it is understood that he wished to be cleansed from original sin. But it must plainly be understood that he said this in the person of the Church; this interpretation is also widely current in the gloss.

## CHAPTER CXXXVII. On the Vigil of Saint John

The feast of Saint John has a vigil; that is, the day preceding that feast is called the vigil, or, in its place, a fast, which was instituted in lieu of vigils. For it was the custom among the ancients that at feasts men should gather at church with their wives and daughters, and there keep watch with lamps and candles. But because at these vigils it frequently happened that girls were violated and malicious people had an opportunity conveniently to carry out their crimes, the vigils were changed into fasts. Hence even now the old name has been retained: it is called a vigil.

The Nativity of John is celebrated both for its historical account—for the Gospel says, “And many shall rejoice at his birth” (Luke I), which Christians and pagans observe—and for allegory and mystery. For John signifies the dawning of grace. Thus we solemnize it more for the mystery than for the person himself. We believe that he was sanctified in the womb, as Jeremiah was; hence Jeremiah is read on that day. But by what kind of sanctification is neither entirely clear nor stated in Scripture. Nevertheless, most affirm that he was cleansed from every sin.

The Savior brought us the dawning of grace. John preceded him in announcement, birth, preaching, Passion, and descent to hell. His office consists partly of the Old Testament and partly of the New, because he was the end of the Old and the beginning of the New. For he was like a cornerstone, joining the New and Old Testaments. The fact that we fast at this feast arises wholly from a certain sympathy and compassion: we sympathize with him because he fasted in the wilderness and lived there a very harsh life.

At this time, moreover, it is customary from an ancient practice to burn the bones of dead animals. This has the following origin. There are animals which we call dragons, whence the Psalm says: “Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons” (Ps. CXLVIII)—not *thracones*, as some read erroneously, that is, “passages of the earth.” [Col. 0142A] These animals, I say, fly in the air, swim in water, and walk on land. But when they are aroused to lust in the air—which often happens—they frequently discharge their semen into wells or into river waters, from which a deadly year follows.

Against this, therefore, this remedy was devised: a pyre should be built from bones, so that its smoke might drive away such animals. Since this was especially done at this time, the practice is still observed by all. There is another reason why animal bones are burned: the bones of Saint John were burned by pagans in the city of Sebaste.

It is also customary on this vigil to carry burning torches, because John was a burning lamp and prepared the ways [Col. 0142B] of the Lord. They think that the turning of a wheel likewise has this origin: at that time the sun descends to the circle beyond which it cannot proceed, and from which it is compelled gradually to descend; just as popular report concerning Blessed John reached its height when he was thought to be Christ, and afterward declined and diminished, as he himself bears witness about himself: “I must decrease, but he must increase” (John III).

Some think this was said because at that time the days begin to diminish and decrease, while at Christ’s Nativity they increase. But since sometimes days decrease before the feast of Saint John and increase before the Nativity of the Lord, this must be understood of their conception in their mothers’ wombs, when each was conceived. John was conceived during diminishing days, namely in September, and Jesus during increasing days, namely in April.

Accordingly, the office of the Mass of this day takes partly from the Old and partly from the New Testament, since it contains some things from the New Testament and some from the Old. For “the law and the prophets were until John” (Matt. XI), so that he was placed, as it were, between the Old and New Testaments. Christ, however, was afterwards circumcised.

On the same day John the Evangelist went down into a grave; but because his feast could not be fully venerated owing to the Nativity of Blessed John the Baptist, it was transferred to the Nativity of the Lord. Since there also, because of the feast of Saint Stephen, it could not have a vigil, we say that [Col. 0142D] on this day a double Mass is sung: one for the vigil of the Evangelist, namely, “The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree”; the other for the vigil of the Baptist. Yet we may say that the vigil of John the Baptist has a complete and full office. It would follow, indeed, that on that day the vigil of Saint John the Evangelist would not be celebrated.

## CHAPTER CXXXVIII. On the Feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul

Thus far we have dealt with the Nativity of Saint John and its vigil. There follows the feast of the two apostles, Peter and Paul. There is a great controversy concerning them: whether they suffered on the same day. Henry the Solitary seems to maintain that they suffered on the same day, though in different years. But Pope Pelagius, and other holy Fathers who wrote about them [Col. 0143A] in the Decretals, hold that they suffered on the same day and at the same hour under that most wicked emperor Nero. Otherwise, the accounts handed down concerning them would be false.

They suffered, however, in different places and by different punishments. Peter was fastened to a cross, while Paul was beheaded, a penalty thought more honorable, for he was a Roman citizen, as is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles. Afterwards their bodies were laid in the same place and in the same tomb, where they remained together for a long time. But when the Roman emperor had been converted to the Christian faith and Christian religion was growing ever more, a separate church was built for each apostle. When they wished to separate the bodies, however, they were uncertain which bones belonged to Peter and which to Paul. After they prayed and completed a fast, a heavenly answer was given: the larger bones were those of the preacher, the smaller those of the fisherman. Thus the bones were indeed separated from one another and placed in their respective churches.

Although their feasts fall to be celebrated on the same day, Blessed Gregory ordained that Peter’s feast alone should be celebrated on that day, because he was greater in holiness and held the primacy at Rome; the feast of Paul, however, should be observed on the following day. Yet on Peter’s day, the prayer in the Mass—or, as it is called, the collect—is shared by both. Therefore the Mass may begin either with Saint Peter, or with this introit: “This place is fearful” (Gen. XXVIII), because Peter’s church was dedicated on that day.

A question is raised here whether Linus was pope, and likewise whether Cletus was. The answer is both yes and no: they were Peter’s disciples and filled his role only in matters belonging to the active life—one within the walls, the other outside them. But Peter devoted himself to prayer; hence even now at Rome, besides the pope, there is another bishop. It should further be considered that Paul is sometimes found to be lesser than Peter, sometimes greater, and sometimes their equals are asserted. This controversy may be resolved as follows: Paul was lesser than Peter in dignity, since Peter was prince of the apostles; but he was greater in preaching and equal in holiness of life.

Their feast, therefore, has three principal features: fasting, [Col. 0143D] octaves, and solemnity. There is fasting because, if we desire to reign with them, we must also suffer with them. At the solemnity we rejoice because of their glorification. In the octave, finally, we rejoice in their future blessedness in body and soul, of which we are certain.

## CHAPTER CXXXIX. On the Division of the Apostles

Writers of great authority disagree concerning the feast of the division of the apostles. Some maintain that this division should be understood as that which occurred at Jerusalem after twelve years, when the apostles were apportioned and separated to preach to the Gentiles. Others think this feast should be understood of the division of Peter and Paul—that [Col. 0144A] mentioned above. They judge that it was performed on this day, which certainly may well have happened.

On this day is said the great sequence of the apostles, which begins: “The heavens declare,” and the Gospel of the Ascension, though not in full, beginning there: “And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken” (Mark XVI). To prove the latter part, some here mention two disciples of Peter. When they had been sent to preach and had journeyed for about twenty days, one of them died and the other returned to Peter. They say that this man was Blessed Maternus. Peter gave him his staff and sent him back, commanding him to go to the body of his companion and touch it with the staff. When he had done this, the other, who had already been dead for forty days, immediately revived at the touch of the staff. Thus was truly fulfilled what the Lord had said: “You shall do greater things than these” (John XIV). For the Lord raised Lazarus when he had been dead four days, which was indeed exceedingly great; but greater still was the revival, at Peter’s staff, of the man who had already been dead forty days.

## CHAPTER CXL. On the Feast of Saint James

This is the feast of James the Greater, brother of John the Evangelist and son of Zebedee. His body rests at Compostela, which is part of Spain. For he was sent to preach the word of God to the Spaniards. But because of the malice and hardness of their rulers, he could convert no one except a single person to the faith of Christ. When the holy man saw this, he returned to Jerusalem to see whether those whom he had left there were still sufficiently established in Christ’s faith. He found many wandering from it, indeed nearly abandoning it altogether, because of Hermogenes and Philetus, who by magical arts performed apparent miracles and miserably deceived people.

The apostle confronted these magicians, converted them to the faith, and restored the people to God’s worship. Then, when he was being led to Herod, he healed a certain paralytic on the way, converted to the faith the man who was leading him, and baptized him. At last he was beheaded by Herod himself.

Then those magicians, now become his disciples, [Col. 0144D] embarked with the body in a ship along with three other disciples; and they entrusted themselves to the sea without a helmsman, so that divine providence might grant him a place of burial. At length the ship reached Spain, in the kingdom of Lupa. At that time there was a certain queen in Spain of this name, whose life and character fully suited her name. Some of the disciples therefore went out to that queen and spoke to her thus: “The Lord Jesus Christ has sent you the body of his disciple, so that you may receive dead the one whom you refused while living.” They related to her the entire miracle, explaining how they had arrived there.

When Lupa heard this, she sent them to a certain most cruel man, who cast them into prison. But as he was dining, an angel of the Lord led them out of prison. Leaving the city like pilgrims, in the sight of the people and with no one hindering them, they returned to their companions.

After dinner, that tyrant ordered the captives brought before him. But those sent to the prison found it open and the captives absent, and reported this to their master. Angered, he immediately commanded his servants to pursue them. But when these had learned from the townspeople that two such men had been seen here and there and had crossed the city bridge, they rushed toward them with violence. The bridge broke, and they were drowned in the water.

As soon as the ruler heard this, fearing for himself and his followers, he was moved to repentance. He sent others to beg those holy men to return to him safely, promising to do whatever pleased them. They returned and converted the people of the city to the faith of Christ. Queen Lupa was deeply grieved by this. When the disciples returned to her, she did not dare harm them openly; concealing deceit beneath her words, she said: [Col. 0145B] “Take the oxen I have, yoke them to a cart, and take away the body of your lord wherever you please.”

But she said this with a thoroughly malicious intention. For she knew that the oxen were unbroken and that they could not be yoked or harnessed to a wagon; or at least that, if this could be done, they would run now here, now there, scatter and kill the disciples, and cause the body itself to fall. But there is no wisdom against the Lord. For after the disciples made the sign of the cross, the oxen immediately became gentle as lambs and did not fear human handling.

The apostles then placed the body on a great stone, which made itself fit to the body as though it had been fashioned for this by human workmanship, and provided the body with a tomb. Having together placed it and the body upon the wagon, the oxen brought the wagon straight to Lupa’s palace without any driver, and did not stop until they came to the middle of the palace itself. Astonished by this event and terrified by so great a miracle, the queen was converted to the faith. From her palace she dedicated a church to the saint, consecrated all the ornaments which she possessed there for the service of the church, and finally died a most blessed death.

The feast of Blessed James is observed on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, [Col. 0145D] not because he died then—for he suffered around Passover, as is clear in the Epistle for this day: “King Herod sent,” etc. (Acts XII)—but because his church at Compostela was dedicated on this day. Nor does this feast have an instituted fast, for the reason explained above.

## CHAPTER CXLI. On the Feast of Peter in Chains

Theosebia, wife of Emperor Theodosius, while travelling through Alexandria to Jerusalem, encountered people of that region who at that time observed a feast in honor of Caesar Augustus, commemorating his triumph [Col. 0146A] over Cleopatra and Mark Antony. Seeing this, Theosebia was deeply distressed that so great an honor was offered to a pagan and condemned man.

When she reached Jerusalem, chains by which Peter had been bound under Herod were given to her through someone’s generosity. Eventually, on returning to Rome, she consulted the supreme pontiff about what she had seen in Alexandria, and showed him the chains which she had received as a gift in Jerusalem. The pope also ordered brought the chains in which Peter had been bound under Nero. As soon as they touched the others, they were joined and intertwined as though they had always been the same chains.

When Theosebia saw this, she ordered, on the pontiff’s advice, a church built in honor of Blessed Peter and placed those chains within it. Its dedication was held on the Kalends of August. The pontiff ordained that what the undiscerning and foolish will of human beings had hitherto done for the Roman ruler should henceforth always be done throughout the whole world by Christian devotion for Peter, prince of the apostles. In this way Peter’s solemnity extinguished Augustus’s solemnity.

## CHAPTER CXLII. On the Feast of the Maccabees

It should be observed that these Maccabees are not those among whom Judas Maccabaeus was one, but those who were the sons of Felicitas, as some hold. Others affirm that Felicitas was the mother of another seven brothers who suffered for Christ’s name and whose names the Church does not know. Blessed Gregory calls this Felicitas more than a martyr because she suffered seven times in her seven sons, and finally an eighth time in her own body.

Certainly, that Felicitas whose children these are, whose feast is here in question, endured a double martyrdom: she saw her sons suffer different torments, and afterward suffered martyrdom herself. For she had seven sons, although some think that these were not they. Both the Eastern and Western Church commemorate their feast, although they celebrate the feasts of many saints and have no feast for any saint of the Old Testament except these, if they are indeed such.

Yet both Churches venerate them because they suffered for the observance of the Law, when they refused to eat swine’s flesh. There is another reason, namely that they were seven in number. But the number seven, as it is full and perfect beyond other numbers, expresses the number of the whole. Therefore in these seven are signified all martyrs, of both the Old and New Testaments. They are set before the martyrs of the New Testament as an example, so that, just as they suffered for their Law, we too may not shrink, if necessary, from incurring the peril of death for ours. Thus this feast is celebrated more for the sake of those signified than of those who signify them.

## CHAPTER CXLIII. On the Finding of Saint Stephen

We must next speak of the feast of Blessed Stephen [Note: [Col. 0145D] This feast was instituted by Callixtus III; thus it is necessary to say [Col. 0146D] that this chapter is not by this [Col. 0147D] author, but was added later by some writer. Yet, since all the copies which I have used agree consistently in including it, we do not think it should rashly be omitted here.], namely [Col. 0147A] of his finding.

Yet it should be considered that his finding was performed on the day on which his Passion is celebrated, and conversely. This change was made for two reasons. The first is that Christ was born on earth so that human beings might be born in heaven. Since Blessed Stephen was the protomartyr, and the martyrdom of the saints is their birth in heaven, the birth of Stephen the protomartyr is rightly observed after the Nativity of the Lord. Hence the common saying: “Yesterday Christ was born on earth; today Stephen will be born in heaven.”

The second reason is that, when a very great multitude of people had assembled for his finding and saw the very many miracles God performed at the finding, they annually celebrated that day with greater veneration than [Col. 0147B] even the day of his Passion. The holy Fathers therefore decreed that the feast of the Passion should be transferred to this day of the finding, and conversely the feast of the finding to the feast of the Passion, because this is more worthy, so that they might therefore celebrate that day annually with greater veneration; and the people observed in August, with more fervent devotion, the day which follows the Nativity of the Lord.

Let us note here incidentally that, if the feast of a martyr and that of a confessor coincide, and the confessor is more illustrious and has a full office, his collect or prayer should be given precedence, and the other should be mentioned or commemorated only in the second [prayer].

## CHAPTER CXLIV. On the Feast of Blessed Sixtus and the Transfiguration of the Lord
[Col. 0147C] After these matters, we should in due order speak of the feast of Blessed Sixtus; but since his Passion is sufficiently plain and known to all, let us proceed to other things. On this same day the feast of the Transfiguration of the Lord is observed—not because the Transfiguration occurred on that day, but because at that time it was first revealed and made public by those who had been with him on the mountain. For the Lord had commanded them to tell no one until he had risen from the dead (Matt. 17). They, however, kept silent until this day. Indeed, it is certainly established that this Transfiguration took place near the end of winter and about the beginning of spring, when the Gospel concerning it is read.

Let us also note that on this day Christ’s blood is consecrated from new wine, if it can be found, or from a little juice pressed into the chalice from a ripe grape; [Col. 0147D] and that clusters of grapes are blessed, from which people then receive communion. The reason for this is as follows: on the day of the Supper the Lord Jesus said to the apostles and the others dining with him: “Amen, I say to you, henceforth I shall not drink of this fruit of the vine until I drink it new in the kingdom of my Father” (Matt. 26). Since, therefore, he then said “new,” and the Transfiguration of the Lord pertains to the form which he acquired after the Resurrection, new wine is sought for this feast.

## CHAPTER 145. On Saint Lawrence

We must now speak briefly concerning the feast of Blessed Lawrence. [Col. 0148A] Blessed Sixtus, whom we mentioned shortly before, travelled to Spain and brought back with him to Rome two young men, namely Lawrence and Vincent, his kinsman. One of them, Lawrence, remained with him at Rome and endured most grievous torments, as his history relates at sufficient length. His kinsman Vincent returned to Spain and there ended his life in a glorious martyrdom.

This feast has three principal features of the sort usually possessed by great solemnities: a fast, the solemnity of the day itself, and an octave. This saint has privilege especially in three respects. First, in regard to fasting: alone among the martyrs, he has an established fast. Secondly, in regard to octaves: among martyrs only he [Col. 0148B] and Blessed Stephen have octaves; while Blessed Martin has them among confessors, as will be said later when we treat his feast. His final privilege consists in the repetition of antiphons, as Blessed Paul has it. Paul has it because of the supreme penalty of martyrdom; Lawrence, because of the excellence of his preaching.

There are three privileges in the most holy Church: baptism, preaching, and martyrdom; but Lawrence holds the privilege of martyrdom. For although many others endured torments equally grievous—such as Blessed Vincent and George, and perhaps even greater and more numerous ones—the Church does not observe all the things related of their torments. Or he enjoys this privilege above others because of the dignity of the place: he suffered at Rome.

## CHAPTER 146. On the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary

We must next treat of the Assumption of Blessed Mary. First, however, one must know that the passing of saints is called by many names. It is called departure, passage, death, birthday, birth, nativity, natal feast, sleep, deposition—as in the case of John the Evangelist—Passion, and Assumption. But this last name is used, as though by antonomasia, only of Blessed Mary.

We know with certainty that Blessed Mary, with respect to her soul, was assumed; but whether her body too was afterward assumed is certainly uncertain. Nevertheless, we devoutly believe that she was assumed whole: first in soul and then in body. Yet a most devout woman called Elisabeth, who is still alive and dwells in the borders of Saxony, says that it was revealed to her that the body was assumed about forty days after the Assumption of the soul. [Col. 0148D] She composed a small work on this matter, but it has not been approved by the Roman Church.

Why, then, is the Gospel concerning Blessed Mary Magdalene and Martha sung on that day? For a clearer explanation, it must be known that a Gospel is sometimes read in church for as many reasons as we explained sufficiently above. At times a Gospel is read because of the matter it itself contains, as on Trinity; at other times because of one part of the matter, as the *Book of the Generation* (Matt. 1), which is recited because Christ is mentioned in its final verse. Sometimes it is read because of the whole, as is certainly the Gospel customarily said at the Circumcision: “After the eight days were completed,” etc. (Luke 2). Sometimes it is read because of the time, as on the first day of Lent; sometimes because of a fast; and sometimes because of litanies, as is the Gospel that mentions the egg, fish, and bread.

Sometimes, finally, it is read because of the place, as that read at Septuagesima: “A man went out to sow his seed,” etc. (Matt. 13). This man is said to be Blessed Paul, who sowed the seed, that is, the word of God. Therefore on that day the collect of Saint Paul is recited, at the end of which occurs: “Doctor of the Gentiles,” etc. For on that day the Lord Pope celebrates Mass in the church of Blessed Paul. [Col. 0149B] Lastly, a Gospel is sometimes used according to its history, as at the Circumcision, and sometimes according to its allegory, as is the Gospel read at the Assumption of the Virgin Mary concerning Mary Magdalene and Martha.

Therefore, the reading here of such a Gospel indicates that both ways of life, contemplative and active, were present in the one Virgin Mary. She herself was Magdalene—that is, one engaged in the contemplative life. She herself was Martha—that is, one wholly occupied with the active life [Col. 0149C] as well. This can clearly be shown from many passages. That she diligently engaged in contemplation is sufficiently declared by these words: “But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2).

This feast has an established fast and an octave, unlike the other feasts of Mary; nor is any of her feasts greater or more celebrated. The same judgment must be made of every other saint: that saint’s passing is more solemn than any other feast of the same saint. The feast of John the Baptist is excepted, since his Nativity is far greater than his Passion, because of what it signifies and announces.

Let us note here that there are five authentic and approved feasts of the Virgin Mary. The first [Col. 0149D] is the Nativity. Some have at times celebrated the feast of the Conception [Note: [Col. 0149D] See the Council of Basel, etc., *Firmissime*, on Consecration, distinction 4.], and perhaps still celebrate it; but it is not authentic or approved. Indeed, it seems rather that it should be prohibited. For she was conceived in sin [Note: [Col. 0149D] A phrase unworthy of Christian speech, though not heretical; for the dogma of the Immaculate Conception, which from the beginning has flourished and been cherished in the heart of the Church, had not yet come forth—indeed, alas, it had not yet come forth even in our own times! Although the fifth century has now been running since the most holy Synod of Basel defined “that doctrine, as pious and consonant with ecclesiastical worship, the Catholic faith, right reason, and Sacred Scripture, to be held and embraced by all”; nevertheless, what can scarcely be confessed without tears may, I say, nevertheless be done without injury to one’s name for orthodoxy: one may dishonour the Mother of the Lord and malign her most holy Conception. But the day made by the Lord is at hand, the day longed for by the prayers of all Catholics: namely, 8 December of this year (1854), on which Christ will rescue his beloved Mother from a deceitful tongue. For on that day Pope Pius IX, whom God chose according to his heart, will rise up and utter from the chair of Peter a good word, and, amid the applause and rejoicing of the whole world, will number the Immaculate Conception of Blessed Mary among the dogmas of faith. (PATROLOGY EDITION.)].

The second is that of the woman giving birth—that is, at the Nativity of the Lord. But because the feast of the Son is then also observed, and it requires a full office, we observe no solemnity of hers until the octave. Then all the responsories concerning Blessed Mary are sung with the first Mass of that day, whose introit is: “Your countenance.” The second Mass is of the Child. The third feast of Mary is the Purification; the fourth, Mary at the Martyrs, which is now called the feast of All Saints. Finally, the fifth is the Assumption, for whose sake we give all this account.

Moreover, it is worthwhile to observe that there are in all four Gospels concerning Blessed Mary. One is “Gabriel was sent” (Luke 1), although it is used only in Advent [Col. 0150B] and at her Annunciation; another is “A certain woman, raising her voice”; a third, “Mary arose in those days and went into the hill country with haste” (Luke 11; Luke 1), etc.; and finally a fourth, “There stood by the cross” (John 19). These latter three are such that, whenever a particular Mass of her is celebrated, they may be sung or read.

Meanwhile, let us remember that the feast of the Annunciation belongs not so much to Mary as to the Lord—indeed, rather to him than to her—as is shown by the fact that the same preface is used at the Nativity of the Lord and at his Annunciation. Therefore, at this feast of the Assumption, the psalms and other things that are customarily used in general on the day of a church’s Dedication are sung specifically concerning Blessed Mary. [Col. 0150C] For just as the Church is mother of all saints and bears the name of virginity—namely, virginity of mind and faith, which is preferred to bodily virginity—and is called the bride of Christ, whence: “I have espoused you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 9), so Blessed Mary is called both Virgin and the holiest of saints.

Lessons are read from the *Song of Love*: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1). From it the responsories and antiphons are also taken. One should also observe carefully that at this time the books of Solomon ought to be read: first Proverbs, from the beginning of August; then Ecclesiastes; and finally the *Song of Love*, half of which is read at this feast until the octave, while the other half is reserved until the Nativity of Blessed Mary. [Col. 0150D] Fourth is read Ecclesiasticus; fifth, the book of Sirach; and sixth, finally, the book of Philo—namely Wisdom—which was called Solomon’s because it contains Solomon’s sayings, and Philo’s because he collected them into a book.

It is not fitting, however, that this sermon of Jerome be read in church on the very day of the Assumption, but rather in chapter, for which indeed it seems properly to have been composed. Finally, then, observe here what was said shortly before: namely, that virginity of mind excels bodily integrity. That this is true may readily be seen from the words of Blessed Mary. For she says: “He has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1). She does not say “virginity,” but “humility”—that is, faith and purity of mind. And let these remarks concerning the feast of the Assumption suffice.

## CHAPTER 147. On the Beheading of Saint John

To take up now the Beheading of the Baptist, one must know above all that he was beheaded at the Paschal season; his body was buried by his disciples at Sebaste, but not his head. What was later done with his head, and how it came into Aquitaine, will be said elsewhere. The question arises: since the trunk was buried in one place and the head in another, in which of those places is John said to be buried? But a solution to this controversy can be drawn from what has been said above.

Let us proceed. In the place where the body lay, God daily worked many and very great miracles, so that a great multitude of Christians flocked there. When the pagans saw this, they were greatly distressed; and since Julian the Apostate, the greatest persecutor of the Church, was emperor at that time, they destroyed the mausoleum of Saint John, to the dishonour of Christians, [Col. 0151C] and scattered his bones through the fields. But when Christians went there nonetheless and the miracles did not cease, the pagans again gathered the bones and burned them. Yet the finger with which he had pointed out the Lord coming to the Jordan, saying, “Behold the Lamb of God,” could not be burned. Many Christians, however, who were present among the pagans while the bones were being gathered, preserved what they could.

For this reason Lord Gilbert thought that this feast should rather be called that of the Gathering than of the Beheading. Some think that Blessed Thecla brought from the lands beyond the sea to Mauretania the finger of Saint John which could not be burned, and there built a church in honour of Blessed John; it was dedicated on this day. Therefore the pontiff decreed [Col. 0151D] that throughout the Christian world this day should be sacred to Blessed John, according to which this feast seems to be called that of the Dedication.

We pass over the feast of Bartholomew, because his history supplies more than sufficiently what should here be said. Yet he preached the word of God in India, where on the first day he was flayed, on the second beheaded, and was translated to Benevento.

## CHAPTER 148. On the Feast of Saint Augustine

Regarding the feast of Augustine, this alone seems worthy of inquiry: since several feasts coincide on the same day, such as those of Augustine, Hermes, and Julian, we should consider whose office ought rather to be celebrated on that day. The following answer may be given on this question, and on others like it. [Col. 0152A] If all were martyrs, the office of him who was more renowned among them would be celebrated. But if one were a confessor and another a martyr, or if several were martyrs, and the confessor were more renowned than the martyr or possessed some privilege, as Blessed Martin does, and his office were established generally in the Church of God, the office should certainly be of the confessor, while mention or commemoration is to be made of the martyr. If not, the martyr’s feast is to be celebrated.

## CHAPTER 149. On the Nativity of Blessed Mary

Next follows the Nativity of Blessed Mary. This feast was not formerly observed. But at some time a certain devout man, praying at night, heard angels singing in [Col. 0152B] heaven. The same thing happened for several years on the same night. Therefore he asked the Lord to reveal what this might mean. He was told that the angels rejoiced and kept, as it were, a solemn feast in heaven because Blessed Virgin had been born on such a night.

Accordingly, he reported what he had heard to the pope. When the pope learned that he was a holy man of great authority, he believed him to speak the truth and instituted the celebration of this feast throughout the Christian world. It has neither an established fast nor an established octave. Nevertheless, it may have them as a matter of devotion.

At this feast the Gospel is read: “The book of the generation” (Matt. 1), where Christ’s genealogy is treated. But one may ask why Joseph rather than Blessed Mary is counted in the genealogy, since Christ is not Joseph’s son. In the Old Testament, however, reckoning is customarily made through men rather than women; nor does it matter much through whom the reckoning is here made, since Joseph and Blessed Mary had the same lineage. And Christ preferred to be called the son of a craftsman rather than that his mother should be crushed with stones. In truth he was the son of a craftsman: not that Nazarene’s craftsman, but the Craftsman who made the dawn and the sun.

## CHAPTER 150. On Saints Sophia, Felix, and Audactus

Sophia was a holy woman who had three daughters: Faith, Hope, and Charity. All of them suffered martyrdom with their mother. But concerning Blessed Felix and Audactus, it should be known that, as Blessed Felix [Col. 0152D] was being led to martyrdom for Christ’s name, a certain man suddenly stepped forward into their midst and said, “I too am a Christian.” The executioners answered him: “Then you too shall come.” Since his name was unknown, he was called Audactus, as though he had boldly associated himself with Blessed Felix.

## CHAPTER 151. On the Exaltation of the Holy Cross

The holy cross was exalted, and its feast instituted, at the time when Heraclius defeated Cosroes, king of the Persians. After destroying Jerusalem and taking the Lord’s cross from it, this Cosroes built a house in the likeness of heaven and made himself a seat in it. He placed a piece of wood on his right in the place of the Son, a cock on his left in the place of the Holy Spirit, and, standing in the middle, wished himself to be called God and Lord.

When Heraclius, emperor of the Romans, heard this, he moved his army against him beside that Danube which is among the Persians—not this Danube which rises in Swabia. For perhaps we may say that the other came from these regions to those and was named after this one, just as the Trojans are said to have done. [Col. 0153A] After defeating Cosroes’ son in single combat, Heraclius took the Lord’s cross and wished to restore it to its place. But when he approached Jerusalem, the city gates closed of themselves, so that he could not enter. As he marvelled greatly at this, a voice was heard from heaven, saying that the King of kings had not entered Jerusalem in such finery, but humbly and seated upon an ass.

Immediately recognizing his own pride, he leapt down from his horse, humbled himself greatly, and the gates opened for him of their own accord. He entered the city barefoot. At his entrance many persons suffering from various kinds of illnesses were healed through the cross.

They relate that Adam sent his son Seth into Paradise; an angel gave him a branch there, which he brought back to his father. Adam, at once recognizing the mystery of that tree, planted it in the earth, and it grew into a great tree. Later, when trees were brought from various parts of the world for the construction of the Temple, this tree was brought too but discarded as useless. Thus it was later placed over certain pits of the city, so that people could conveniently cross by it. When the queen of Sheba saw it, she refused to cross over it and instead adored it. Later it was thrown into the Sheep Pool, which dried up at the time of Christ’s Passion; then the wood appeared, and since they found no other, they fastened the Lord to it.

The feast of the Finding is greater than that of the Exaltation, because it was instituted by Eusebius, who on that day caused the people to assemble to adore the cross. He was the thirtieth Roman pontiff.

## CHAPTER 152. On Blessed Maurice and His Companions

Next we must consider the feast of Blessed Maurice and the Theban Legion. There are many Thebes. One is in Egypt, founded by Busiris, king of Egypt, and otherwise called Heliopolis. Maurice was born there, and hence they are called Thebans. Another is in Boeotia, founded by Cadmus, son of Agenor, [Col. 0153D] from which the Thebans derive their name. A third is in Judaea, from which the Thebites are named. Those, however, who died with Maurice were from Egyptian Thebes.

When the Gauls led out their army against the Romans, the commander of Egypt assembled an army in which was Blessed Maurice. He commanded a legion of six thousand, six hundred, and sixty-six men. But when they were already in the army, the tyrant wished to compel them to worship idols. When they refused, he took a tenth part and killed them. Seeing this, Maurice addressed his companions, begging them to act manfully and stand firm. Strengthened by him in this way, they suffered martyrdom. But they had been baptized before they came to Rome.

## CHAPTER 153. On Saint Matthew

[Col. 0154A]

Of Blessed Matthew we say only this: he was a Levite and therefore more learned in the Law. Hence he made arguments of profound significance against his opponents. He was a Hebrew, and therefore wrote the Gospel in Hebrew for the Hebrews. Note in passing that we say “Hebrews” when speaking of the language, and “Jews” when speaking of rite or people.

Afterward his book was translated into Greek, and then from Greek into Latin. He preached under Gaius Caligula, so called because when he was born on campaign he was covered in soldiers’ boots (*caligae*). John wrote under Nerva; Mark, under Nero. But at what time Luke wrote is uncertain. [Col. 0154B] The name *Matthaeus*, as Bede says, is written in its proper orthography with a double *t*.

## CHAPTER 154. On the Feast of the Angels, or of Michael

The feast of the angels observed at this time is that of a Dedication, when basilicas were dedicated to them, because it is called the feast of all angels. The account of the flight of the barbarians and the bull is treated between Easter and the feast of the Ascension, when the feast of angels is discussed.

Accordingly, concerning the names of angels, we say that they neither gave names to themselves nor were names given to them by God, but by human beings; by whom, however, we do not know. Yet at the feast of Saint Michael, although all the angels are concerned, Michael is named because he presides over Paradise and has been appointed chief for receiving souls. [Col. 0154C] Since he appeared on Mount Gargano and chose for himself a lofty place, a basilica is nearly everywhere established for him in an elevated location. But churches are dedicated in low places to saints, as human and earthly beings.

Some say that there are in each order of angels as many legions as there are units in a legion—namely, six thousand, six hundred, and sixty-six. It is certain, however, that there are more legions than orders; hence the Lord says to Peter: “Do you not know that, if I ask my Father, he will send me more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matt. 26).

Haymo, third bishop of Halberstadt, says that if anyone could see spiritual creatures, he would see them bubbling in the air like the tiniest motes in the brightness of the sun. The Emperor Constantine also, when he was travelling to the lands beyond the sea, met Eusebius, a most holy man, and said to him: “Holy man, ask of me how your Church may be enriched.” He replied that his Church abounded sufficiently in riches, but asked that the names of saints, the times of their Passions, the rulers under whom they suffered, and the manner in which they suffered be investigated in all regions of the world, and reported to him. When this had been done, Eusebius relates that on every day of the year feasts of more than five thousand saints coincide. Hence Gregory is reported to have said: “The whole world is full of saints.”

Some wish Michael’s battle against the dragon to be understood allegorically: namely, Michael means Christ. Others, however, say it must be understood historically, [Col. 0155A] because the devil was cast down through the ministry of Michael and his angels. For this reason he is also so portrayed in church, for the sake of lay people. Moreover, one may ask whether Michael is the name of one angel or of several. Some say it belongs to one. Others think that whenever one of the angels is sent to do some great and wonderful deed, he is called Michael. It is certain, however, that Michael was sent into Egypt, inflicted the celebrated and famous plagues, and divided the Red Sea.

## CHAPTER 155. On Saint Remigius

Saint Remigius is called the pontiff of the Gauls because [Col. 0155B] he was the first to anoint the king of the Gauls. Consequently he is held in such honour and veneration in France that his feast eclipses that of Blessed Michael.

## CHAPTER 156. On Saint Luke

Luke was Syrian by nationality and an Antiochene by birthplace. He preached in Bithynia and there happily ended his life by a natural death, without martyrdom. He lived eighty years and left two volumes to posterity: the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles. He was a disciple of Paul, from whom he learned what he taught, as Mark learned from Peter. Yet in the prologue to the Gospel it is found that he learned from certain persons who had been with the Lord from the beginning. From this it might appear [Col. 0155C] that he did not learn from Paul, since Paul had not been with the Lord from the beginning. But he learned some things from Paul and some from others, although he was chiefly taught by Paul.

## CHAPTER 157. On Simon and Jude

James, Simon, Jude (who was also Thaddaeus), Joseph Barsabbas (also surnamed Justus, lest he be thought to have been rejected from the apostleship because of injustice)—these were brothers. The casting of lots took place between Joseph Barsabbas and Matthias. That James was called the Lord’s brother was because all kinsmen are called brothers in the Hebrew idiom, or because he was exceedingly like him. Joseph is called the Lord’s kinsman either because he was his putative father, or because he was related on his mother’s side, namely through Blessed Mary.

Simon is said to have been crucified. But first he preached in Egypt; afterward he came to Jerusalem and there, after Blessed James the Less, called the Lord’s brother, was made bishop. He lived one hundred and twenty years; before his death he raised thirty dead persons—the son of his host, drowned by the waves, and the others for his sake. He died at the age of one hundred and twenty in Bosporus, not in Pastophorium, as some think. Pastophorium, according to some, is a portico of the Temple in which the Temple guards lay. Jude preached among the Persians and Medes and died there among the Armenians.

## CHAPTER 158. On the Feast of All Saints

[Col. 0156A]

After treating these matters concerning the saints thus far, it is plainly necessary to come to that greatest and general feast, namely All Saints. Why it was instituted, and why it is observed especially at this time, has, I think, been sufficiently shown above. Yet a few things remain to be said concerning it: namely, its fast and the order of its office.

This feast has an established fast. No one should eat before evening, and the fast ought not to be changed, as some do because of the feast of Saint Quintin. For he says: “Do you think that saints delight in foods, who earned life by fasts?” Since this is the feast [Col. 0156B] of All Saints, its office is varied in accordance with the variety of saints. The first antiphon, first lesson, and first responsory are sung of the Trinity, whose feast is Trinity. Secondly, those of Blessed Mary are sung; thirdly, of the angels; fourthly, of the prophets; fifthly, of the apostles; sixthly, of the martyrs; seventhly, of the confessors; eighthly, of the virgins; ninthly, of All Saints.

Authority is observed in the lessons of these offices. The most eminent person in the church, if a bishop is present, shall recite the lesson of the Trinity; otherwise the dean, or at least a priest. Then the readers descend in rank down to the boys. One of the boys reads the eighth lesson. The ninth lesson, however, belongs to a more important reader.

## CHAPTER 159. On the Office of the Dead and the Manner of Burial

We must now treat of the office of the dead: first, the place where they should be buried; second, those who are to be buried and the manner and rationale of burial; third, who discovered it and why; and finally, the office itself. I do not think it worthwhile to repeat the division concerning places made at the beginning; for that, we now refer the reader back.

But we should know only this here: according to Roman laws and institutions, a place is called religious in which the body of some person, or merely the head, is buried. I say “the head” because no one can have two burials: where the head is, there [Col. 0156D] that person’s burial is said to be. Thus, whether a Christian, a pagan, or even an unbaptized infant is buried in any place, that place according to Roman institutions will be called religious. Christians, however, do not judge that place religious where a Jew, pagan, or unbaptized infant is buried, but only where a Christian is buried—so much so that, if an excommunicated person is buried there, he is removed and cast out beyond the cemetery.

This place is called by various names, such as *coemeterium* and *polyandrium*. The grave itself is likewise called: mausoleum, dormitory, monument, ergastulum, sarcophagus, pyramid, and tomb. *Coemeterium* is derived from the Greek word κοιμάω, “I put to sleep,” as though the dead sleep there; hence it is also called a dormitory. A *polyandrium* is the place where there are many public graves.

A mausoleum is so called from the tomb of Mausolus, which his wife Artemisia built with works so outstanding that it is counted among the seven wonders of the world. It rises to a height of twenty-five cubits and is encircled by thirty-six columns. Therefore, from this tomb all costly graves have been called mausoleums. A monument is named from *monere*, “to remind,” because those who are in monuments and graves remind us passers-by that they too once lived and were mortal like ourselves, so that we may remember that we are ashes and shall return to ashes, dust and shall return to dust.

A tomb (*tumulus*) is so called as though from swelling earth—that is, a hill—because earth is customarily heaped up there. *Ergastulum* is named by antiphrasis from ἐργάζομαι, “I work,” as though bodies in graves do not labour at all but rest, they who die in the Lord. Likewise *sarcophagus* is named from σάρξ, σαρκός, “flesh,” and φάγω, “I eat,” as though flesh is consumed and eaten there. A pyramid is also such a tomb because it resembles a flame, narrowing from a broad base to a point. It is the tallest kind of burial.

At Rome one may see such a structure, in which the ashes of Julius Caesar were placed; it is called Saint Peter’s Needle, and it remains uncertain whether it consists of one stone or of several. Caesar built a similar pyramid at Tours, beside the bank of the Loire, and enclosed in it the ashes of a certain friend of his who had been killed.

[Col. 0157C] Let us now speak next of those who are to be buried: first, in what places they ought to be buried and whether the place benefits them at all. Some indeed believe that a place does not benefit the dead, and they seek to confirm this by observing that Lucifer was cast from heaven and Adam expelled from Paradise—places which are excellent, yet gave them no benefit. Likewise, Joab was killed in the tabernacle, while Job triumphed on the dung-heap.

A place may, however, harm someone, if one is buried in a church without being worthy. Certainly no body should be buried in a church unless it is the body of holy Fathers, who are called patrons, that is, defenders. By their merits they defend the entire land. [Col. 0157D] Others, however, should be buried around the church. Some say that a space of thirty feet around a church ought to be consecrated for that purpose. Others think that the bishop’s circuit alone, when he dedicates the church, is sufficient.

Formerly, among the ancients, people were accustomed to bury their dead in their own houses. But because of the stench of corpses, they decreed that burials should occur outside the city and made a certain common place, as it were, holy for this purpose. Nobles, however, were buried on mountains, whether in their midst or at their foot.

Accordingly, if someone is killed in a siege or some disturbance and cannot have a cemetery, let him be buried where possible. If someone dies at sea and land is nearby, they should sail there and bury him there. But if they are far from land and see an island in the middle [Col. 0158A] of the sea, they should turn their sails there and bury him on the island. If they see no land at all, a small wooden structure should be made for him, if timber can be had, and he should be cast into the sea. This should also be done if he is rich. But he should be cast out with his treasure, if he has any, so that those who find him may know from the treasure that he was noble—or at least may commit him to the earth out of love for the treasure.

But note that whenever a Christian is buried, a cross ought to be placed at his head, wherever the burial occurs, to signify that he was Christian. It is also done because the devil greatly fears this sign and dreads approaching a place marked by the cross.

The question must next be considered: whence did the cemetery take its beginning? Namely, from Abraham. For he bought from Ephron the Hittite a field in which was a double cave, where he himself was buried with Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, Adam, and Eve. He bought it for this purpose: that it might serve as a burial-place for himself and his people (Gen. 23). It was called a double cave because two persons, husband and wife, were buried there next to one another. Or because there were two caves, and men were buried in one and women in the other; or again because, for each person buried, the cave was made twofold in the form of a chair. For they were buried as though seated; and the upper part of the cave, which received the trunk from the nostrils downward, was called one cave, while the part containing the feet, legs, and thighs was called the other cave.

Here it is fitting to observe that in the first age only two sacraments are read to have been instituted, namely offering and repentance; but in the second age the worship of God was enlarged. For Noah made an ark, and enclosed in it many animals to sacrifice to God. In the fourth age, however, divine worship was increased still more. For then the Law was given, and many kinds of sacrifices were offered to the Lord. Thus in the fifth age it was increased still further. For then the Temple was made, and divine worship truly received excellent growth. Finally, in the sixth age Christ came, who offered himself to God as a pleasing and sufficient victim for all.

Moreover, in the cemetery of Christians no one but a Christian ought to be buried—yet not every Christian. For no one killed in his wrongdoing ought to be buried in the cemetery; for example, a robber if he is killed while committing robbery. Understand “wrongdoing” here to mean mortal sin, as when someone is killed in adultery or in the games of the heathen. But if he dies suddenly in customary games, as in a ball game, he may be buried in the cemetery, but without psalms and without funeral rites. Further, if someone, returning from a brothel or another place where he has fornicated, is killed on the road, or dies by some other accident without confession, then, if lawful witnesses can prove that he committed fornication and did not afterwards confess, he ought not to be buried in the cemetery. If it cannot be proved, burial is permitted. A robber is to be buried in the place where he is hanged, unless he has first made satisfaction; but if he has made satisfaction, he is to be buried in the cemetery.

If a woman dies in childbirth, she certainly ought not to be committed to burial in the church, but outside it. Funeral rites are therefore to be sung for her, and afterwards she is to be buried in the cemetery; but the child is to be cut from her womb and buried outside the cemetery. The dead ought to be buried in this manner: clothed in winding-sheets, with hose around their shins and shoes on their feet, signifying that they are thus prepared for judgment. Moreover, they are to be laid with their heads toward the west and their feet toward the east. Clerics, if they are ordained, are to be buried in the vestments in which they were ordained; if they do not have orders, they are to be treated in the manner of laymen, and are to be shorn and shaved. The bodies of all must be washed, signifying that if the soul has been cleansed from guilt through confession, then both—the soul and the body—will possess everlasting glorification on the day of judgment.

But if someone dies in a joust without repentance—that is, when he does not seek a priest—he is to be buried like an ass; and likewise if he dies on a riverbank. But if he sails for sport or to conduct his own business and perishes, he may be buried in the cemetery. For the Church does not openly judge such persons. If someone dies suddenly, not through any manifest cause but by the hidden judgment of God, let him be buried honorably. For the righteous person, whatever cause of death he may have, will be saved. Finally, those who lay hands upon themselves and voluntarily procure death ought not to have burial in the cemetery.

Here it is usually asked whether, after the day of judgment, human beings will be naked or clothed. It seems indeed that they will be clothed, since angels are accustomed always to appear clothed, and Christ too was seen clothed after the resurrection and was clothed also at the Transfiguration. Hence: “His garments appeared white as snow” (Matt. 2 [probably 17]). On the other hand, it seems that they will be naked, from the authority which says that we shall then be in the form in which Adam was before sin, and indeed in a better one; but at that time he was naked; therefore we too shall likewise be naked. Yet let us presume nothing by speaking about clothing or bodily appearance, except this one thing: that there will be neither deformity nor infirmity there.

## CHAPTER 160. On the institution of the office.

There follows discussion of the office: first, by whom it was instituted; second, by whom it was performed; third, from whom it took its beginning; fourth, concerning the manner of celebration. The Office of the Dead was first instituted by the apostles; but from the beginning, as Isidore testifies in the book *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, it was performed and, for the most part, arranged. Hence blessed Augustine commends it in a certain book which he calls the *Enchiridion*, saying that it was second among ecclesiastical offices after the apostles.

This office took its beginning from the Old Law. For it is read that, when Jacob had died, Joseph and his other brothers, as he had commanded them, brought him with many Egyptians to Hebron; but first they mourned him in Egypt for thirty days, and afterwards for seven days at the threshing-floor of Atad (Gen. 50). Further, it is read that, after Moses died, the Israelite people mourned him for thirty days (Deut. 34), as they also report was done for Aaron and Miriam. But observe that, when Joshua died—the one who had led them into the promised land—the people are not read to have mourned him, though the contrary is nevertheless believed. History is silent about Joshua because he prefigured Christ, and his death prefigured Christ’s death: that is, the death of him who, redeeming us from death, led us back to the homeland of life, where there is neither mourning nor pain. Therefore history is silent concerning his death because of the figure, just as elsewhere it is silent concerning the father of Melchizedek, who prefigured Christ, because he is not read to have had a father, just as Christ had no human father.

Concerning Moses, although he is believed to have been better than Joshua, and concerning the others who died in the wilderness, the people are said to have wept, because the wilderness sometimes signifies estrangement from God. Therefore those who are estranged from God through their sins ought to be mourned. On this matter Solomon says: “The mourning for your wise son who has died lasts seven days; the mourning for your foolish son is eternal” (Prov. 10), since he will be punished eternally. Thus: “A wise son makes his father glad, but a foolish son is the sorrow of his mother” (Ecclus. 23).

Thus the seven-day and thirty-day mourning of the dead took its origin from the Old Testament: just as Jacob’s sons mourned seven days, so the office sometimes observes thirty days for its dead. Meanwhile, let us note that the dead are assisted in four ways: by prayer, by the almsgiving of friends, by the fasting of relatives, and by the celebration of Masses. Therefore we perform the office for our dead for seven days, so that they may more quickly attain the Sabbath of souls. Or certainly because of the sevenfold nature of soul and body. For the soul has especially three capacities: reason, desire, and anger; but the body consists of four elements. Therefore, that the sins which a person has committed through these seven may be wiped away, we observe a sevenfold rite for the dead.

Three times ten makes thirty. By three we understand the Trinity; by ten, the Decalogue. Therefore we perform the thirty-day observance for the dead so that whatever they have sinned in observing the Ten Commandments may be forgiven them by God’s mercy. Some, however, do this for three days, so that Christ’s three-day burial may be represented thereby, and so that what the living person sinned in thought, word, and deed may be forgiven when he is dead. But though many perform an office for nine days, doing so with the intention that through such an office their dead may be freed from punishments and joined to the nine orders of angels, it is nevertheless not approved, but is altogether forbidden, because it seems to have been taken from the heathen, who on the ninth day deposited the ashes and tombs of their dead. For just as we do not imitate the Jews in celebrating Passover, so it is plainly forbidden to imitate the heathen in this office.

There are, moreover, some who perform a fifty-day observance, and others a forty-day one; but both appear to do enough with prayer. Those who perform a fifty-day observance seem to take their occasion from Abraham, who, when the Lord intended to overthrow Sodom, asked whether, if there were fifty righteous persons in it, he would spare them. For the number fifty is also perfect, and signifies the year of jubilee—that is, the eighth age—in which there will be remission and full liberty. Therefore, so that the souls of the dead may obtain full freedom and forgiveness of their sins, some celebrate the office for them for fifty days. Others perform a forty-day observance so that those who have departed and transgressed in the Ten Commandments and in the teaching of the four Evangelists may be forgiven.

## CHAPTER 161. On the celebration of the Office of the Dead.

Let us now consider the celebration of this office itself. First, so that we may know what ought to be omitted; and second, what ought to be said. For the Office of the Dead imitates Christ’s three-day burial and follows its traces in every respect. Therefore, as during those three days, so in this office we suppress all songs of joy. Hence at Matins, or the Vigils of the Dead, “O Lord, open thou my lips” is not said; nor is “O God, come to my assistance” said at the beginnings of the hours; nor “Come, let us rejoice” (Ps. 94); nor “Glory be to the Father” at the responsory or at the end of the psalms. Similarly, at the readings we neither ask nor give blessings, nor do we ever say “But thou, O Lord” or “Thanks be to God”—not even at Mass.

Another reason may be given why these things are omitted in the Office of the Dead. When we celebrate the funeral rites of the dead, we come to mourn and shed tears, not to keep a festival. For this reason we suppress songs of joy. For “Come, let us rejoice” and “O Lord, open thou my lips” do not suit this office, but rather seem contrary to it.

The Office of the Dead begins at Vespers, which we begin in this manner: “I will please the Lord” (Ps. 114). When these are concluded, Compline follows, and afterwards the Vigils, of which there are three kinds. In some churches nine readings from Job are read; in others, the same number, but from the Book of Wisdom. These begin thus: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” (Eccles. 7). Again, there are other churches in which likewise nine readings are recited, but from a certain sermon of blessed Augustine, which he composed concerning the dead and ended thus: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Rev. 14). Some say this at the end of the readings in place of “But thou, O Lord,” just as at Advent, Christmas, and Epiphany readings from Isaiah are ended in this manner: “Turn to me and you shall be saved”; and the Lamentations of Jeremiah at Tenebrae in this manner: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, turn to the Lord your God.” But on other days they end thus: “But thou, O Lord,” and so forth. Thus there are four ways of ending readings.

Accordingly, incense ought not to be offered at the Mass, although this usage has become customary in our time. For in the Old Law it was forbidden that oil of gladness or sweet incense should be offered for sin; where sin is, there is darkness, and there ought to be neither joy nor sweetness, but mourning and contrition of heart. Therefore the funeral rites which we perform because of the sins of the dead are celebrated.

Observe, meanwhile, that in the Law of Moses the Lord forbade anyone to burn fragrant *thimyama*—that is, sweet-smelling incense—as a sacrifice for his own use, so that he might enjoy its fragrance; if anyone did so, he would perish from his people. Therefore it is customary in the Church for blessed and consecrated incense to be offered at the altar; but when the censer descends either to clerics or to laypeople, other incense, without blessing, is then used and offered to people.

It is commonly asked here why the peace is not given at the Mass for the dead; and indeed a threefold reason is assigned. The first is that this office, as has been said, signifies Christ’s three-day burial, when peace is not given because of Judas’s kiss. The second is that we do not communicate with the dead, because they make no reply to us. Hence also the body or corpse ought not to be in the church while the Mass of the day is celebrated; indeed, if it is present, it should be removed from there while Mass for the dead is sung. The third reason is that, just as one loaf is made from many grains gathered together, and wine is pressed from many clusters, so from many faithful persons—some good and some evil—one Church is constituted. Since, therefore, when a person has died it is unknown whether he belongs to the fellowship of the Church and has peace with his Creator, we do not give the peace at Mass. Nor do we say “Let us bless the Lord,” nor “Thanks be to God,” nor offer any praises, because there is no cause for giving thanks, since their rest does not yet appear.

Further, it should be observed that the Office of the Dead ends at the ninth hour and does not have second Vespers, signifying that this office will have an end, since the souls of those to be saved, freed from every punishment, will enjoy everlasting joy—namely, the saints, concerning whose glorification in the soul the Church is certain. They have first and second Vespers if nine readings are sung in their office: first Vespers because of the glorification of the soul, and second Vespers because of the glorification of the body which they will have and which will never have an end. But if only three readings are sung, they have first Vespers alone.

Now it must be said how the body is to be buried, how it is to be entombed and carried to the church, by whom, and when. Therefore, when someone appears already to be at the point of death, he ought to be placed on the ground upon ashes or straw, signifying that he is ashes and will return to ashes. Blessed Martin is read to have done this, to offer an example of himself to others. The Passion of the Lord, or some part of it, ought further to be recited before the dying person if he is literate and learned, so that he may be moved to greater contrition. Likewise, a cross ought to be placed before his feet, so that in dying he may look upon it and thereby be more deeply contrite. He ought to lie straight, with his face turned upward, so as to look at heaven.

Before he breathes his last, it is necessary that bells be rung, so that the people, hearing them, may pray for him. For women, they are rung twice, because woman introduced estrangement: she was the first cause by which man was estranged from God. Therefore the second day did not receive a blessing. But for a man they are rung three times, because in him appeared a certain image of the Trinity in humankind. First Adam was formed from earth; then woman from Adam; and afterwards, from both, a human being was created; thus from this there arose a kind of Trinity. Finally, for an ecclesiastic they ought to be rung as many times as he has orders, so that the people may know for whom they are to pray. By the same rule they must be rung when he is carried to the church, and again when he is carried from it to the grave.
