Before the body is buried and the cloth lifted, the priest or his vicar ought to come there with lustral, or blessed, water, pouring out prayers to the Lord for him, invoking the saints, and asking them to receive his soul and convey it to the place of joy. For there are certain souls that are perfect, which, as soon as they depart from their bodies, fly up to heaven. There are others altogether evil, which immediately fall into hell.

But besides these there are other intermediate souls, for whom such a commendation is made, and this only because of uncertainty. Therefore, after the body has been washed and veiled, it ought to be carried to the church, and then Mass ought to be sung. Here, indeed, observe that in some churches a candle is given to each person in choir in one hand, and in the other something to offer; and thus, when the Gospel has been read, these things are offered to the priest for the dead, and then this verse is customarily sung: “offerings and prayers.” After Mass has been celebrated, the priest chants before the corpse; and if there are several priests, all ought to have stoles and say prayers with him. When the chanting office has been completed, it is carried to the grave with such psalms as “On departing,” “Give thanks,” and others that have been instituted especially for this purpose.

It ought to be carried by persons of the same rank: if he is a deacon, by deacons; if a priest, by priests, if they are available there. But if not, this is not required, since necessity is not subject to law. Thus a cleric is carried by clerics, a Catholic by Catholics. If he belongs to a fraternity—so called, and often formed among people—he ought to be carried by them. But women are not permitted to carry anyone’s corpses, lest their bodies be seen naked, which might perhaps sometimes happen; just as they are not permitted to give the peace, to avoid wantonness.

Then he is placed in the grave, and blessed water and coals with incense are put there. Blessed water is used so that demons may not approach the body, for water of this kind drives and repels them. For devils often rage upon the bodies of the dead, and what they could not do during life they do at least after death. Incense is used to remove the stench of the body; and coals signify that the ground may no longer be returned to common use. For charcoal remains under the earth longer than anything else that may be left there as a testimony. Ivy or laurel, which forever retain the greenness of their leaves, are placed in the sarcophagus near the bodies, to declare that those who die do not cease to live in that state: although they die in body, they nevertheless live in soul. Cypress, however, had another significance at funerals. For just as it, when cut down, does not become green again but dies entirely, so a person, once he has died, does not live again. Let what has been said about the dead suffice; let us now discuss the feast of the Four Crowned Ones.

## CHAPTER 162. On the feast of the Four Crowned Ones.

There were nine, but four of them are called the Crowned Ones because their names were unknown to people. They were stonecutters who had come to build Diocletian’s temple, which was at Rome. But when he learned that they were Christians, they were crowned with martyrdom; and because their names were unknown, they were called the Crowned Ones.

## CHAPTER 163. On the solemnity of blessed Martin.

It should be known concerning blessed Martin that he was called equal and peer to the apostles because he raised certain dead persons, as many suppose, although he and many other martyrs and confessors did the same. Rather, he was so called because of a certain miracle that occurred while he was bishop at Tours. During the winter months a poor man, half-naked, met him and begged for clothing. Martin immediately summoned the archdeacon and ordered that the shivering man be clothed. When the archdeacon delayed doing this, the poor man burst into the sacristy which Martin had entered, complaining that the cleric had disregarded him and lamenting his cold. On hearing this, Martin at once secretly took off his own tunic and gave it to his petitioner. Before he celebrated, he asked the archdeacon for the tunic which he had ordered him to buy for the poor man, and secretly put on that cheap, rough, short garment. Thus he prepared himself for the solemn celebration of Mass.

But when he stood before the altar, as is customary at the Preface, and raised his hands to the Lord, so that his arms could easily be seen because the sleeves were wide and short, golden bracelets immediately covered them decently, and a fiery globe was seen above his head. This clearly showed that the Holy Spirit had descended upon him for confirmation and strength, as upon the apostles on the very day of Pentecost. Therefore he was not without reason called equal to the apostles. He was born in Pannonia, which is near Austria; blessed Jerome was also from there. He further performed many signs and countless miracles, which Sulpicius and Fortunatus recorded, since they loved him greatly.

With regard to the office, it should be observed that he alone among confessors has octaves established for him, just as blessed Lawrence has a vigil, because on the day of his passion he said what the Church repeats on his feast: “You have tested me by fire” (Ps. 16), and so forth. But Martin, in the agony of death, said to the demon standing by: “You will find nothing in me, bloody beast.” See how excellently their merits correspond. Therefore Lawrence, as one who surpassed the other martyrs by far, has a vigil; and this confessor, likewise more excellent than the others, alone has octaves.

## CHAPTER 164. On the feast of the apostles Andrew and Thomas.

It is worth knowing that Andrew was dark in complexion, with a long beard and of medium stature. We say this so that it may be known how he ought to be painted in the Church; and the same should be done with all the apostles and other saints. Otherwise we should be lying in the writing of the laity—that is, in paintings. He preached in Achaia, Athens, and the surrounding regions. He possessed very outstanding merit; nor was it without reason that blessed Gregory was so devoted to him that he made his office the first and founded a monastery for him, where he too was a monk.

He raised forty dead people at once, something that is not read of any other. The son of his host, sailing with thirty-nine companions, was drowned when the ship was wrecked. When his father was lamenting miserably upon the shore, Andrew, moved by compassion, poured out prayers to the Lord, and all were restored to life. At length the proconsul Aegeas summoned Andrew to himself in order that he might sacrifice to idols. When Andrew refused and rejected this, as is read in his life, they fastened him to a cross, despite the outcry and opposition of the people. He therefore hung alive for two entire days upon the cross, laid crosswise, as some think. Nevertheless, he continued to preach and proclaim the word of God. At last he happily passed to heaven.

He has no instituted vigil because his feast occurs during the season of fasting; therefore it was unnecessary for a vigil to be instituted for him. As for blessed Thomas, I have nothing here that needs to be said, since his life can be known fully enough from the history written about him. Yet I thought it should be added that he does not have the instituted fast, for the same reason for which we said that Andrew does not have one. Here the Gospel is read: “Thomas, one of the twelve” (John 20). Why this is done is sufficiently clear from what has been said above.

## Conclusion of the whole work.

Thus, in two ways, according to the slender measure of our ability, we have explained ecclesiastical offices and the matters that seemed to pertain to them: first generally, and then specifically, treating each in the order shown to us by the course of the year. We have also reserved the feasts of the saints for their proper place—that is, for the day on which they are customarily celebrated—so that, on the day on which we say each feast is observed, an explanation of that feast itself might be found there. No one, however, should suppose that we could have treated these matters so absolutely that nothing whatever might be lacking in them, since the divine offices are of such a kind that they cannot be fully and adequately explained in many volumes.

# A.D. 1177–1180 . . . HUGH ETHERIANUS

## NOTICE

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, III, 292.)

Hugh Eterianus, Etherianus, Aetherianus, Heterianus—incorrectly Eretrianus—a Tuscan [Note: He is celebrated among Florentine writers by Julius Niger, p. 522.], in the year 1177 sent to Pope Alexander III, to his brother Leo the Tuscan, and to Caciareda [Note: In Trithemius, ch. 398, *De S. E.*; to Cardinal Ardoinus.] from Constantinople, where he was living at the court of Manuel Comnenus, three books: *On the Heresies Which the Greeks Cast upon the Latins*, or *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, against Greek Errors*. Among the letters of Alexander III is the forty-ninth, in which he thanks Hugh.

Those three books, written in Latin, were published at Basel in 1543, and thence in Bigne’s *Bibliotheca Patrum* in 1589, and in the Paris, Cologne, and Lyons editions that followed it, vol. XXII, p. 1198. They were appended to another book by the same Hugh, *On the Soul Now Released from the Body*, or *On the Immortality of Souls and Their Return from the Lower Regions*, addressed to the clergy of Pisa. This had first been published at Cologne in 1540, in octavo; it was afterwards reprinted also in the *Orthodoxographa*, Basel, 1569, folio, and was separately printed in German at Hamburg in 1579, quarto.

A letter of this Hugh to Aimery, patriarch of Antioch, by which he sends him the book *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, is found in Edmond Martène, *Anecdotorum*, vol. I, p. 479, together with Aimery’s letter, p. 480, in which he thanks Hugh and praises the book sent to him in both Greek and Latin. Moreover, Allatius notes in *On the Agreement of the Two Churches*, p. 654, that Hugh’s book was translated by Greeks into Greek, not without elegance. Other writings of his are read in the anonymous treatise against the Greeks, published in Latin by Stevartius and apparently compiled from the writings of several authors; it was reprinted afterwards in Basnage’s new edition of Canisius, vol. IV, p. 29 ff., and in the Lyons *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. XXVII, p. 590. See, if you wish, the *Bibliotheca Graeca*, vol. X, pp. 443 and 423. Besides these, Trithemius, ch. 398, testifies that this Hugh wrote a book *On the Immortal God*.

# HUGH ETHERIANUS’S BOOK *ON THE SOUL NOW RELEASED FROM THE BODY, OR ON THE RETURN OF SOULS FROM THE LOWER REGIONS*, ADDRESSED TO THE CLERGY OF PISA.

(From the Lyons *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. XXII, p. 1176.)

## LETTER OF THE CLERGY OF PISA TO HUGH.

To the most distinguished and prudent HUGH, finely equipped in both the Greek and Latin languages, the whole clergy of Pisa: greeting and the attainment of desired happiness.

The fame of your prudence and marvelous learning, like a ray of the sun, is spreading day by day more and more over almost the whole world; believe us, this is as welcome to us as can possibly be. For who would not grow rich in delight at such advancement and grace, with the pleasure of his whole body and soul? The excellent fruit of a noble garden so fills all nostrils and senses with its sweet fragrance that no mind fails to aspire to it. You are the pillar of this people. Therefore, in fairness, provide for your city, in whose honorable duties you hold no insignificant place. Since you have done this diligently until now, you deserve high praise from us and a fitting expression of gratitude.

Moreover, it is our common desire that, out of your abundant learning, you should write something in which your judgment may appear concerning the acts performed for the life and souls of deceased Christians. We would embrace such a work with no less eagerness than if it were by blessed Augustine. For there are among us some who, in their despair, say that neither prayers nor even sacrifices benefit the faithful dead. Since these same persons also fall into doubt concerning the resurrection, we hope and desire that you will not omit that subject in the work you compose.

Farewell, most excellent sir in every respect.

## HUGH’S REPLY.

To the reverend clergy of the city of Pisa, HUGH Etherianus: may you abound in a spirit of uprightness, and always embrace in your hearts him who is.

Seeds are entrusted in steadfast faith to fertile clods of earth. For when they have sprung up, they endure more properly the cold of the north wind, the violence of the east wind, and the intemperance of the south wind. Admiring me as fortunate in talent and eloquent, you asked me, as one skilled in singing, to fashion, out of lyric metres (*μελικοῖς*), some most effective harmony, by which the rancid and biting phlegm might fall from the nostrils and the swollen tonsils from the constricted throats of those who doubt the resurrection. You ask likewise that, by blessed discourse, the corrupt morals of those who deny that the saving sacrifice and other offerings benefit the dead may be corrected.

Certainly, it is easier to command such a task than to carry it out, because it requires a mind fully present, polished arguments, clear distinctions of clauses, and complete diligence through repeated nocturnal labors. Receive, therefore, what I have produced under God’s guidance; consult the most renowned Albert and his illustrious colleagues, since I have submitted this to your prudent judgment. For, as I hope, it will give delight to the ears, be honey-sweet to the mouth, reform those infirm through a fault of mind, and, if they deign to read, hear, and understand it, will open heaven to them after Satan’s snares have been impeded.

Farewell in him, without whose favor nothing anywhere can have strength.

## CHAPTER ONE.

“Love is strong as death” (Cant. 8), and is the pledge of purified goodwill, preserved without admixture. Therefore, prompted by your friendly request, which ought not to be rejected, and by the exhortation and assistance of my beloved brother Leo, the eminent interpreter of the imperial court, while I seek those things in which I am wholly inferior, my body has been almost separated from my soul.

For in many books, both Greek and Latin, I searched after the manner of bees and found a honeycomb prepared, which ought to distil through your mouths. I am still uncertain and await the judgment of your examination to assure me: examine what I send for reading, and, upon examination, approve and confirm it, if it deserves approval. I do not doubt that this will occur, since these are not my own teachings, but now the senses, now the words, of the saints—Gregory, John Chrysostom, Ambrose, Gregory of Nyssa, Jerome, Basil, Augustine, John Damascene, Hippolytus the martyr, Nilus the martyr, Anastasius, Cyril, and others whose names will identify them, as you are now about to hear.

Therefore, I ask you, lay up in your hearts what the aforesaid God-loving company declares concerning the human soul, concerning repentance and confession, concerning death, resurrection, and judgment. Likewise, with vigilant mind observe how firmly it maintains that acts performed devoutly for the faithful dead—especially the offering of the saving sacrifice—provide them with a most effective remedy. This writing may perhaps seem full of fear and horror to some; yet to those who have faith it will instil overflowing consolation, even though it touches each subject only in passing. Finally, by its very nature it requires modulation, deserves to be heard, must be understood, and should be kept more firmly in the seats of memory.

## CHAPTER II.

I begin my discourse from the familiar observation of bodily health and the common frailty of nature, because nothing in human beings retains a lasting stability (1 Chron. 29). Indeed, human life and glory are compared to an evening shadow and withered grass (Isa. 40). But what is thinner than a shadow? What is more languid than grass? Yet our hunger, sicknesses, infirmities, and the dangers that suddenly befall us—on land and sea—and death emerging unexpectedly from ambush, are certainly more frail than these. For what is easier than for a human being to die? Wretched man swells with pride and, because he has not yet died, rushes forth with beastly violence. Therefore the Prophet says: “Surely man passes by as an image; he heaps up treasure and does not know for whom he will gather it” (Ps. 38). Every living human being is vanity (Ecclesiastes throughout), because, compared with that blessedness, this life is vanity. And the rich are compared to a vanishing vapor: in vain he builds and vainly piles up riches, since they differ in nothing from a painted image (Jas. 4).

They certainly fade, like an image, through the aging of time; yet nonetheless they strive, contend, quarrel, and endure labors, sweat, and afflictions in order to acquire riches, not knowing who will be their heir after them. This disturbance is vain, because they are troubled by vain desires, by food and clothing. It is not without reason that, among all vices, the Prophet selected avarice, since covetousness is the root of all evils and the tinder of every vice (1 Tim. 6). Hear Solomon: “Vanity of vanities,” he says, “and all is vanity and affliction of spirit” (Eccles. 1, 11). For what is more vain than man, when the earth, which was made for human beings, remains, while man himself, lord of the earth, is suddenly dissolved into dust? (Gen. 3). A living human being is vanity; a dead one is vanity of vanities. Yet heaven and earth, and all that is in them, are good, because “God saw all that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Gen. 1); but in comparison with the Lord they are reckoned as nothing.

It is as the light of a lamp when the blazing orb of the sun swiftly bursts forth from Ocean. Invisible things, in relation to God, are called vanity; visible things, vanity of vanities. Wretched man is disturbed in pursuit of the most fitting prey: an unmade statue, an animated idol, a daily shadow, a runaway servant, an animal capable of suffering and dissolution, changeable and shifting—now for the better, now for the worse. For this reason, from the beginning he preferred the creature to its Creator. For it is written: “When he was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48).

[Col. 0170B] To this day we are subjected to many evils because we cherish the ancient disgrace and reckon the inestimable splendor of glory as nothing. Certainly, the rational image and the first likeness ought to be recovered; but alas, while we are detained among these visible things, we are stripped away from intelligible realities. We dishonor our image, which is according to the likeness of God, bearing the image of the earthly man and living according to the flesh; but whoever bears the heavenly image embraces virtues (1 Cor. 15). Man was indeed made in the image of God (Gen. 1), because the nameless and unknown, intelligible and immortal substance of the soul exists as an image and typological likeness of the nameless, unknown, and immortal God.

For from the origin of the world no human being has known the substance of the rational soul. Though one, it constitutes and governs the fourfold nature of the body; and this is after the image of God, who governs this entire fourfold and four-bounded creation, and likewise that which is above. And just as we do not know God’s place or where he dwells, but only believe that he is everywhere, so too we do not know the soul’s place, but only know that it is throughout the whole body and acts within it. Moreover, in this also the living being exists after God’s likeness. For just as God is none of the things that are, but is distinct from all, so the rational soul is distinct from every creature.

Furthermore—and more wonderfully—it exists in another respect after the likeness of God, because the human mind cannot comprehend the account of God’s substance, nor can it discover the essence of the human soul: whence or how it came to be present. Therefore those who have imagined that they comprehend it have been swallowed up in the blind abyss of darkness and departed from truth. Some have asserted that it is sent from heaven and infused into bodies; others that it comes by propagation; others that it is produced from male and female intercourse, as a spark is struck from iron and stone dashed together. Others have declared it consubstantial with angels. Although their error was manifold, the one truth that they omitted sufficiently confounds them.

But, as has been understood above, it was made in the image of God. This is shown most clearly by the fact that it is neither visible nor comprehensible as spirit or form, in quality, subsistence, or beauty; yet it possesses inestimable beauty and comeliness. For this reason the heavenly spirits seem to have a certain envy, beholding its most excellent beauty, especially in this: that it alone among other creatures is read to have been made according to the likeness of God (Gen. 1), and indeed is so. For every incomprehensibility, difficulty, and uncertainty indicates nothing else than that it was truly created in God’s image. Thus, because we do not know all that belongs to it, we apprehend its essence and presence only from the actions it performs in the body; just as God’s essence too is apprehended only from what he does and works in his creatures.

[Col. 0171B] Finally, the discordant company of pagan philosophers asserts that the rational soul is threefold: one part of the soul is appetitive, another rational, and another irascible. They say that through desire it is stirred toward love of God; through reason it receives knowledge and wisdom from God himself; and through anger it repels and rejects spiritual wickedness. In this threefold division, moreover, the image of God may again be described. For he administers and governs in three ways all the parts of the universe—that is, things heavenly, earthly, and infernal (Phil. 2)—namely by creative power, wise providence, and merciful expulsion of vices (Wis. 14). For everything that he does, he accomplishes according to one of these three modes: by creating, by foreknowing, or by chastising.

The appetitive faculty of the soul is therefore in some manner likened to God’s creative activity, since desire brings the one who desires into action; the rational faculty imitates God’s foreknowledge; but the irascible faculty appears to belong to the Holy Spirit, according to the saying: “By the Spirit of God he casts out demons” (Matt. 12), and: “When the Paraclete comes, he will convict the world concerning sin,” etc. (John 16). From the appetitive faculty arise the rational and irascible faculties. For before a child can speak, it desires the breast and seeks sleep; likewise reason precedes the irascible faculty. For before virtue can discern, it does not become angry; nevertheless the three appetencies are present together.

Therefore, whoever delights to know how he has been formed after the image of his Creator should investigate these things, search them out, and reflect on them: let him inquire into the constitution of his own nature; let him learn in detail and with subtlety all that belongs to the rational soul—what its parts are, what are the parts of its parts, what its modes are, what its additions and distinctions are, what in the soul is uniform and what lacks form, and how, although it is one, it is considered in three respects.

Yet the soul must in no way be thought to be distinguished by persons, since it cannot be called any one of its own parts. It is one in substance, but it is not one in the contemplation of its parts; for it has desire, reason, and anger. If you separate from the soul its desire for good, it ceases to be a soul; if you separate reason, you render it irrational; if you remove mind, it will certainly be dead and not life-giving. [Col. 0172A] It is evident, therefore, that in the soul there are three things according to reason, but one according to nature and substance; and these are incomprehensible and indivisible, for the soul is always one.

If you attend to these things, you will never be cast into uncertainty about the Trinity; rather, through the principles of nature you will investigate what is above nature. Nor will you say, “If God is Trinity, he is not unity; and if he is one, he is not three.” For he made your soul in the likeness of his Trinity so that you might not fall into the vertigo of such inquiries. For the soul is invisible; it remains invisibly in the body and invisibly departs from the body. Unless the soul were present to the body, it would neither give life to the body within nor feel from without what pricks it.

But because much uncertainty concerning the soul exists among the ancients, it seemed fitting, after setting aside the various opinions, to make known to those wishing to hear what the choir of saints has set forth on this matter. Of all things that exist, some are known by sense and others conceived by intellect. Things presented to the senses are abundantly made known by the senses themselves. By direct contact, without any interval, they form in us an impression of the object placed before us. But things apprehended by intellect are perceived not through themselves, but only through their effects. Since the soul is unknown in itself, it is recognized and demonstrated in the body only through its effects. Let the attentive listener observe how this occurs.

When our body moves, it must be moved either inwardly or outwardly. But our body does not receive motion outwardly, except perhaps in collisions or dispersions, like inanimate bodies. Therefore, receiving motion only inwardly, it moves, yet not merely by nature. For if our body moved only according to nature—as fire, which never ceases from motion so long as it remains outside its proper region—it would move either only upward or only downward. But since it moves upward and downward, forward and backward, to the right and to the left, by the soul that supplies life, nearly in the manner in which instruments are moved by an artisan, it is beyond doubt that it is moved. Therefore it is clearly evident that the soul is in the body.

When the soul is separated from it, the body remains ineffective, as sight itself shows you—just like the tools of any craftsman if they are abandoned by the one who directs them. And since this kind of soul remains one and the same, now just, then unjust; now diligent, then vicious; foolish today and wise tomorrow, it is proved beyond doubt to be a substance. For it is proper to substance to be capable of justice and injustice, virtue and wickedness, and other opposites. Therefore the soul is in the body. When it is seized by violently assailing sensations, it serves in subjection and relinquishes authority together with its sovereignty; it becomes deranged, as though made sick by frequent passions. Hence, not using fitting motion, it is cast headlong through the various defects of nature, and goodness and nobility are immediately darkened within it.

[Col. 0173A] The truth that the soul is a substance is also shown in another way. That the soul is something which exists is made evident by justice, wisdom, and its actions; since these cannot exist by themselves, they must have a subject. Yet the soul is none of those things which do not admit the definition of substance. It is not quantity, for all things to which the definition of quantity belongs can be measures of small or large things. But the soul is not the measure of any things, nor does it increase or diminish, as will be clear. Nor is the soul a mixture, contrary to the assertion of certain physicians, because if every body constituted from elements possesses a mixture, every body would have to possess life; if this were granted, the other kind of body—that is, the inanimate—would be destroyed.

Nor is the soul a quality. For qualities are inseparable, because they cannot exist without a subject. But when the rational soul leaves the body, it remains with itself and exists by itself. Since, then, the soul is neither quantity nor quality—the things it most seemed likely to be—it is evident that it is not an accident but a substance. But whether the soul is a corporeal or incorporeal substance must be considered briefly.

There were philosophers who asserted that the soul is a body. The Stoics maintained that the soul is a hot and fiery breath. Critias called it blood, Democritus fire, and many others fashioned similar theories, saying that we are like our parents not only in body but also in soul, for example in habits and passions belonging to bodily nature. Ammonius, Plotinus, and Mimmius reject their opinions by arguments and reasons. “Every animate body,” they say, “is wholly changeable, dissoluble, and divisible without limit. Every such body, however subtle, being unable to escape division, needs something to contain and govern it, lest the condition it has received waste away.” From this they infer that that which contains an animate body is indivisible and incorporeal.

Again, every composite body is moved either from within or from without. That which is moved from within is animate; that which is moved from without is inanimate. But neither of these can be predicated of the soul. For the soul is neither animate nor inanimate. Again, every animate body needs bodily nourishment, but the soul needs no bodily food. Therefore the soul in no respect admits the definition of an animate body. In this it is plainly shown that the opinion of those who believed the soul to come by propagation is false, since it is alien to generation. Everything that comes to be through generation is corruptible; but the human soul is incorruptible and immortal, and therefore does not come by propagation.

By contrast, the souls of irrational animals, which arise naturally by propagation, do not escape death’s destruction, and they prevail in the likenesses proper to their species. Hares are similarly timid, wolves cunning, pigs filthy; the race of apes everywhere has a propensity for imitation. But in human beings the ways of human actions are not thus uniform. What is called rational is plainly something free and self-governing.

[Col. 0174A] Therefore individual human beings do not possess one and the same disposition, skill, work, and result. But among the varieties of other animals, each nature has the same motion and impulse, the same cunning and dullness. The acts of rational beings are not identical in all by necessity. For the Creator implanted in the bodies of irrational animals a fitting soul, so that in their actions they might have, by their constitution, no more than their inborn simplicity displays. Every irrational animal is indeed moved by a natural impulse toward that use of activity which it received from the beginning, and only toward things not opposed by its bodily form.

Yet the first Creator did not leave them without assistance, since he endowed each with a certain natural sensation rather than rational prudence; to some he granted cunning, as an image of skill and a shadow of the rational soul, so that by these they might avoid present snares and foresee future ones. That they do not do these things through reason is evident from the fact that every animal of a given species does them similarly, differing in action only according to more and less. The entire species is moved by the same impulse and marked by a comparable variety of actions. This occurs through the soul, beyond doubt; for it is that by whose presence animate things endure and by whose absence they fail.

To those who say that the soul has three dimensions because it entirely occupies a body extended in three distances, I think it must be answered that the soul in no way has three dimensions, though it gives life to the whole body—just as unity does not have three dimensions because a human being is called one. Therefore the soul is not a body. Those also erred who said that it is blood or water itself, since many animals are found that are nourished neither by drink nor irrigated by blood.

Chrysippus, however, used this argument to prove that the soul is a body: “Death is the separation of the soul from the body. But nothing incorporeal is separated from a body, for what is incorporeal is not fitted to a body. The soul is fitted to the body and separated from the body. Therefore the soul is not an incorporeal substance.” Nevertheless, the soul does not touch the body. Properly speaking, touching means having only extremities together. A body cannot fail to lie next to a body in its entirety. For no body occupies another’s place unless what is contained gives way to the one occupying it. But if the soul lay next to any body, it would by no means animate the whole living being. Since the whole living being is animate, the soul neither lies next to the body nor can be a body.

Again they say: “Nothing incorporeal suffers with a body. But the soul suffers with a wounded and sick body, and likewise the body suffers with the soul. For when the soul is confused, the body blushes and suffers. Therefore the soul is a body.” This is wholly remote from truth. For, in processes of generation and corruption, qualities suffer and change together with the body, though they are not bodies. Since the soul is not a body, as has been shown, nor any accident, it is evident that it is an incorporeal, intelligible, and immortal substance. For it is not subject to corruption in every way. It lives not because of the body; rather, it gives life to the body. Nevertheless, it has certain faculties which it cannot exercise apart from the body, such as the appetitive and nutritive faculties. But it exercises the intelligible faculty continually.

Would you know that the human soul is a rational and immortal spirit? Hear what Moses, the friend of God, says: “God formed man from the mud of the earth, breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul” (Gen. 2). Yet one must in no way believe that this breath was some flowing emission of spirit made from God’s mouth. Since the divine is incorporeal, it is simple and without all composition. Rather, the soul is from God in the sense that he made and created it. For God’s breathing is nothing other than making a soul.

This accords with what Isaiah says: “For a spirit goes forth from me, and I have made every breath; and because of a small sin,” he says, “I grieved him and struck him” (Isa. 54). What does he mean by “breath” except the soul, which was struck and grieved because of sin? Thus the soul is from God in such a way that it is neither God’s substance nor a body, but spirit: not begotten from God’s substance, nor proceeding from God’s substance, but made by God, as it is written: “He who fashioned their hearts individually, who understands all their works” (Ps. 32).

For the soul is not given by parents, as that wise man also affirms: “Let the dust return to the earth whence it was, and let the spirit return to the Lord who gave it” (Eccles. 12). By this testimony we are sufficiently taught that God made the soul of the first human being from nothing, not from some already created creature, as he made the body from earth. Therefore when it returns, it has nowhere to return except to the Author who created it. Hear Job saying: “Remember, I pray, that you made me like clay; you granted me life and mercy, and your visitation preserved my spirit” (Job 10). After the body’s creation comes the wondrous infusion that gives life.

[Col. 0175D] From this source comes bodily lowliness; from that, ineffable dignity: dignity belongs to the spirit, while usefulness comes through the flesh, which calls the Judge to mercy. “Remember, I pray”: by these words I have shown the union of marriage, the propagation of children, and one marriage-bed transformed into countless forms; I have shown that the soul is created by God and set over the government of the body, and is rational and immortal. For unless the soul’s immortality is believed without doubt, faith and the place of virtue perish among human beings. How could virtue exist in those for whom the soul is destroyed and nothing whatever remains beyond?

The rational soul, moreover, is beyond doubt incorruptible by a certain singular nature of its own, existing by itself amid bodily grossness. For just as, by knowing this whole world through the reception of the senses and through our actions concerned with the senses, we are raised to things above sense, with the eye serving us as interpreter of the almighty Wisdom that governs all things through itself, so too, by looking upon our own world, we have no small occasions for conjecturing about hidden and manifest things. Most hidden is that which exists by itself and is conceived by intellect alone; for, being invisible, it escapes the investigation of the senses.

Although the rational soul is incorporeal and without matter, it infers certain hidden things through bodily instruments; moreover, it teaches what the ear hears and the eye sees. Hence a physician, touching a sick person’s arteries with his fingers, as it were hears through the pulse crying out the patient’s nature and interpreting the causes of illness. For, with the pulse secretly indicating them, the physician perceives the causes of sickness and, from the intensity of fevers, how many days the patient must remain delirious.

What then? Does not the inhabitant who governs and sustains the house disclose and reveal these things? What hand, or any other part of the body, could itself have taught the physician, unless intellect through touch had opened knowledge of hidden diseases? It is not far from the truth what certain philosophers say: “The mind of each person is the person himself.” For it is the mind that remembers, hears, and understands.

[Col. 0176C] How is it that, by observing the sun—that most brilliant body—the geometer declares not that it is only as large as it appears to most people, but that by the magnitude of its circle it exceeds the whole circumference of the earth by many times? How does he establish that the moon shines with borrowed light? Clearly such things do not belong to the capacity of an elemental body. Why should I mention other geometrical investigations, which by sensible figures raise us to things surpassing every sense? The rational soul, utterly different from bodily nature, perceives and comprehends these things and all like them. For no body constituted from the elements, considered as such, can be capable of this sort of power or understanding. This is known to be the distinctive and proper characteristic of incorporeal substances.

Therefore, because the rational soul is incorporeal, it can cleave to God as being like him. For every nature is in some way attractive to what resembles it; from this it is plainly understood that the human spirit is drawn by God. What belongs to God must return to God. Thus, if the soul has not rendered itself superfluous to itself through ever-heavier stains, it hastens joyfully and swiftly toward the one drawing it. But if it is weighed down by the mass of sin, iniquity presses upon it and the cord drawing it is broken; made wretched and unlike God, it is left on earth, bereft of God’s help.

I think it is now clear to us that, because of likeness, the soul embraces the paths of virtue. For if it possessed no likeness to God, it would never transcend the boundaries of its nature, leave earthly things, and seek things above. Just as animals lacking reason do not desire to speak in human fashion, but use the voice associated with them and natural to them, and do not regard it as a loss to live without reason and obey only the belly, so the soul, if it lacked the higher nature, would never be kindled with desire for virtue.

When this soul begins to exist, it receives, according to the will of its Creator, freedom of choice and the power to do what it wills. How this occurs is plainly indicated to anyone by the bodily eye. Sight belongs to it by nature; not seeing results from its will or from an intervening affection. In the same way, the soul, released from necessity, is left to its own choice, that it may embrace what seems better to it—either good by its own will or evil through the snares of the domestic enemy, who harms and blinds the closed eye, as the destroyer of human life and most cunning ambusher (Gen. 2).

Thus it is blinded when wickedness intervenes; and because it did not approve having God in its knowledge, it is given over to a reprobate mind (Rom. 1). It voluntarily closed its eyes and refused to see the sun; by its own most manifest fault it falls into the pit. For it withdrew its eyes not merely from sunlight, but from the sun’s light. Therefore, just as by faith we understand that the ages were framed by the word—that is, the command—of God, so that visible things came to be from invisible things, so by faith we must understand that, when the body has already been formed, the soul is placed in it by God, so that from the invisible soul arise many of the actions that we see in our bodies (ibid.).

If these actions are not perfect from the beginning, no one should wonder because they are hindered by the body’s neediness and deficiency. Thus the senses, which are familiar to the body, emerge immediately after birth; afterwards the faculty of reason appropriate to them dawns when the body has reached puberty. But perhaps someone who thinks himself wise seems to oppose this view, asserting that human souls are placed in some region until, after bodies have been perfected, they are sent into them to give them life. “I received a good soul,” he says, “and, being still better, I came into an undefiled body” (Wis. 8).

Does this not appear to you to establish that souls come from above into bodies, and that in that region of souls some are good and others not good; that by a certain lot they go forth, and one or another is allotted to particular human beings, so that perhaps they are thought to enter bodies according to the merits of their souls? This plainly conflicts with the Apostle’s statement: “For when they had not yet been born, nor had done anything good or evil” (Rom. 9), God’s foreknowledge might be fulfilled according to grace, not according to a debt of merits. It was said to Rebecca, “The elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. 25), because foreknowledge rejected one and chose the other.

But what the Wise Man says does not contradict the position stated. For he says: “I was an intelligent child and received a good soul” (Wis. 8:19), through the abundance of wisdom given to me. “When I was newly brought forth, I had no understanding; I desired, and understanding was given to me. I invoked, [Col. 0178A] and the spirit of wisdom came upon me.” And when, through given wisdom, I was very good, I came through the progress of age to the body’s undefilement, and knew that I could not otherwise be continent unless God gave it. It is clear that Solomon’s spirit received wisdom from the heavenly Craftsman, obtained it by prayers, and found goodness by grace; but, deprived in the growth of his age of the grace he had received, he defiled his body in many ways.

You have heard the testimonies of Moses, David, Job, and Isaiah concerning the human spirit. All the prophets likewise, taught by the heavenly Craftsman, sang in harmony with these things, so that no one may suppose that Greeks received one substance, Latins another, Egyptians another, Persians, Massagetae, and Sauromatae another. For the writer of Genesis taught that God made one human being in the beginning and formed woman from his rib (Gen. 1–2); from their union he filled the world with human beings. He willed the human race to arise from one pair, so that no one might dare suppose that human beings possess different natures.

He formed woman from a rib, first, so that he might establish her neither as man’s slave nor as his mistress, and secondly so that one nature might not be thought to belong to the man and another to the woman. He imposed the same laws upon both. Although their bodily forms differed in appearance, they were equal in rational soul. Both were equally rational and equally capable both of choosing and of doubting. To each punishment was promised for wrongdoing, and to each rewards for virtue (Gen. 1).

Human laws indeed punish offenders, but God threatens sinners with unquenchable fire—and rightly so. For since a human being is rational and has free choice, he can restrain the impulse of passions; voluntarily he becomes a transgressor of laws, and voluntarily, often abandoning vice, he advances along the way of virtues. If man sinned by necessity, God would never have given laws of punishments through Moses. Nor would those who received rule have assigned people to most grievous tortures if human beings were compelled to sin by necessity of fate or nature.

Therefore the Physician of souls set life and death under human choice. Hence he does not compel the unwilling to receive healing, for he created rational nature as sovereign and self-governing. By instructions and laws he prohibits evils and exhorts toward better things; but he compels no unwilling person, otherwise he would have made law equal to nature. Therefore he cries through the prophet: “If you are willing and hear me, you shall eat the good things of the earth.” And again: “Learn to do good” (Isa. 1). And David: “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. 33), with many similar passages. But I ask you, listener, do not take it amiss if I again connect my argument concerning the rational soul, in order to remove every uncertainty.

## Chapter III

In matters that are hidden, assertions of this kind are certainly very useful. Come then: the human spirit has discovered arts that confer countless benefits upon human life and are worthy of much praise. Whatever is truly praiseworthy has been discovered and elaborated by reason. Do you not observe that a merchant vessel, although it lacks no equipment, seeks only the depths of the sea when it is deprived of the guidance of the helmsman’s reason? Do you not see that we are insufficient for knowledge of things through exercise of the senses alone? For the senses are dulled in distinguishing things equal in shape and alike in color because they do not possess reason.

Since the senses are irrational and convey to us a false appearance of things, we must consider whether the things imagined can truly be comprehended or not. If they can be comprehended, it is beyond doubt that there is another faculty, far superior to the senses, which accomplishes this without deception. Therefore, if things falsely represented by the senses are opened to our knowledge, it is undoubtedly the mind that comprehends and judges all of them by reason. This is the soul’s power; this is the soul’s eye; this is the capacity for understanding. It is not generated from external things; rather, existing in itself, it orders external things, describes particulars, and then brings them to completion.

The greatest and most excellent dignity of the soul is to do everything with reason; in this the mind is most plainly distinct from the senses. Yet certain goods belong to human beings through the soul: to be chaste, just, sober, and whatever is akin to these. Bodily affections are not ordinarily manifested apart from them. The soul has reserved certain things for itself, in whose exercise it needs no bodily instrument. Of this kind are reason, memory, and contemplation of things that truly exist.

Since it is clearer than light that the human soul is rational, and enough has been said distinctively about it, it is fitting to discuss its union with the body. Therefore we must not pass over what the Hebrews have handed down concerning Adam’s immortality. They say that man was from the first origin neither mortal nor immortal, but was created with a nature between the two, so that he might be subject to bodily passions through the body’s passions. But if he set before himself the goods of the soul, he would be established as heir of immortal life.

For they say: if God had made him mortal from the beginning, he would not afterward have condemned him to death as guilty. It is not just to condemn one who is mortal to death. But if he had made him immortal, he would not have constituted him as needing food, for nothing immortal needs bodily food. Nor would God have repented so suddenly as immediately to punish the one whom he had made immortal.

Angels, certainly, although they sinned, nevertheless did not depart from their original nature, undergoing for sin a punishment other than death. Yet many teachers reject this opinion, maintaining that, though Adam was made mortal, he could nevertheless have become immortal by progress in virtue, because immortality lay within his power. He was forbidden to taste of the tree, lest he should know his own nature before attaining the summit of perfection; for this was in no way advantageous. Therefore God did not wish him to know his own nature before perfection [Col. 0180A], lest, observing that he stood in need of many things, he should pursue bodily uses while neglecting care of the soul. Among the precious trees of Paradise was that one whose taste simultaneously bestowed knowledge of good and evil; Adam, though forbidden, tasted of it. In tasting it he violated obedience; he came to know himself; he fell from perfection and, having become needy of bodily uses, immediately resorted to clothing. For it is written: “The eyes of both were opened; and when they knew that they were naked, they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths” (Gen. III). Their eyes were opened to mutual desire, to sin, and to the punishment of the flesh conceived in death itself. They had not been made with their eyes shut, wandering blind and groping through the paradise of delight, so as unknowingly to touch even the forbidden tree or, groping, ignorantly pluck the prohibited fruits. [Col. 0180B] Therefore their eyes were opened to behold and know something which they had not previously perceived.

There can be no doubt whatever that Adam was placed in a bodily Paradise, watered by four rivers and adorned with trees of most precious shoots and fruits. His Creator gave this Paradise to Adam to cultivate and work, as it is written: “that he might work it and keep it” (Gen. II). He was to work for its delight and keep it lest he suffer expulsion. The rivers which flowed out, and their names, are well known throughout the world: namely Gihon, Pishon, Tigris, and Euphrates. To explain the interpretations and figurative meanings of these names is not the concern of the present [Col. 0180C] time. God had also placed in the midst of Paradise the tree for discerning between good and evil. Nor should allegory compel us to say that it was not a tree and that something else is signified by the name “tree.” For although it is written that wisdom is “a tree of life to those who embrace her” (Prov. III), and although eternal Jerusalem is said to be in heaven, it has nevertheless also been founded and signified as a city on earth.

Adam became guilty of the command and subjected his body to the necessity of death, because previously he had not possessed the necessity of dying. For before he was cast down, this alone remained: that he should be changed and, made spiritual, receive full immortality, where he would have no need of corruptible food. But since enough has been said concerning the body of the first man [Col. 0180D], we must speak briefly of those matters which have been decided from it; and this is not irrelevant, for thus it will become clear whether the points previously touched upon concerning the condition of the soul stand supported by truth.

## Chapter IV

Accordingly, very many have sought to establish by numerous arguments that the soul, like the body, comes into being by division from a propagated stock. They bring forward Paul’s testimony to support their opinions. “You hear,” they say, “Paul declaring: ‘Thus through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin death; and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned’” (Rom. V). And again: “As through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one man many are made [Col. 0181A] righteous” (Rom. V).

They therefore say: “If sin or sinner can be understood only according to the flesh, we are not compelled by these words to believe that the soul comes from parents. But if, although through the enticements of the flesh, no one sins except the soul, how should we understand the statement, ‘in whom all sinned’? How were they made sinners through his disobedience, if they were in him only according to the flesh and not also according to the soul? For we must beware lest either God appear to be the author of sin, if He gives a soul to flesh in which it must sin, or lest a soul be possible apart from Christ’s grace—a soul for whose liberation from sin Christ’s grace is not necessary because it did not sin in Adam. But if we sinned in Adam only according to the flesh [Col. 0181B] and not according to the soul, then in the baptism of infants only the bond of the flesh, not that of the soul, is loosed. And if by this sacrament provision is made only for their bodies and not also for their souls, the dead too ought to be baptized. But the Church abhors this, administering it only to the living. Therefore it remains that every infant has existence from the first parent Adam both according to body and according to soul, and for that reason Christ’s grace is necessary to all. For that age has itself done nothing either good or evil; hence the soul there is most innocent if it has not been propagated from Adam. How then can it go thence into condemnation if it departs from the body without baptism?”

It is written: “The flesh desires against [Col. 0181C] the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. V). But the flesh seems unable to desire anything without the soul; and thus the cause of fleshly desire is not in the soul alone, but much less in the flesh alone. For it arises from both: from the soul, because no pleasure is felt without it; and from the flesh, because fleshly pleasure is not accomplished without the flesh. Therefore the flesh that desires and the spirit are, beyond doubt, fleshly pleasure which the spirit has from the flesh and against the flesh, opposed to the pleasure which the spirit has alone. For the spirit alone seems to have that desire which is not mixed with the pleasure of the flesh or longing for fleshly things: “The soul longs and fails for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. LXXXIII). It alone likewise possesses that of which it is said: “You have desired [Col. 0181D] wisdom: keep the commandments, and the Lord will give it to you” (Ecclus. LI).

The following answer removes this objection. Defect—that is, corruption and weakness—remains in the flesh before its union with the soul, and from this decay the soul is stained. It is as if a vessel had been impregnated with a foul odour: whatever liquid it receives, it infects by its own corruption. For even if there is no guilt in the flesh before the infusion of the soul, because it lacks reason, it nevertheless possesses a condition of mortality together with passibility. Therefore it is said to have sin in the flesh, because the cause of sin is from the flesh, not from the soul: the flesh which comes by propagation is the origin of sin. For the flesh of the first man, weakened and softened through transgression, put on mortality.

Hence [Col. 0182A] the soul of each individual is afflicted by weakness and mortality; in a shadowy and dark place, it is struck by the ignorance of blindness—not by will, not by necessity, but by association alone. It grows sick and is weakened. For if the soul were corrupted by will, this would be called not original but actual sin. Again, if it fell by necessity into the abyss of sin, such a defect would no longer be imputable to it. For what happens by necessity is not excluded from forgiveness. From this it is clear how the Apostle’s statement is to be understood: “Through the disobedience of one, many were made sinners” (Rom. V). Once one had sinned and been cast down into death, there is nothing incongruous in those who come from him becoming such. But what consequence is there in another being made [Col. 0182B] a sinner through his disobedience? If one was not made a sinner by will, how is one worthy of punishment? Therefore he calls sinners persons liable to punishments and condemned to death. Thus, merely through union with a weakened mass, the soul has drawn a pestilential and calamitous condition, which, unless aided by grace, neither attains knowledge of truth nor can resist fleshly desire.

This is why children contract original sin from fathers to whom it has been remitted through the sacrament of faith. For though it has been remitted as guilt, it remains as punishment and besieges the human race. Original sin is the tinder of actual sin: concupiscence, the weakness of nature which stirs evil desires. The sin of the first man indeed proceeded from will; but in his descendants it is not present by will, but, as has been said, by association. [Col. 0182C] Nor should you wonder that children derive original sin from parents cleansed of that sin through baptism, because chaff remains in the pure grain of seed.

Likewise, a father does not generate his son inasmuch as he is baptized, but inasmuch as he himself was carnally generated. The soul of the son, therefore, is born neither by division nor propagation from the father, nor in any other way. For no rational creature can be another’s matter: always abiding in its own simplicity, it is, plainly, an incorporeal substance, removed from every movement of the body. It does not increase, diminish, come to birth, or decay so as to cease to be [Col. 0182D]. Such a substance cannot be propagated. If it passed over, it would pass over wholly; for it is one thing and utterly indivisible, and cannot be essentially divided into many, so as to pass wholly and entire to the son while remaining wholly and entire in the father.

Finally, authority tells you: “Let the dust return to the earth from which it was taken, and let the spirit return to the Lord who gave it” (Ecclus. XII). In this it is plain that the soul is not derived from soul, but flesh is materially propagated from flesh. For as the first man’s body was formed from mud, into which the Maker breathed a soul, so all Adam’s children receive from him the first matter of their bodies and, beyond doubt, receive their souls from the Creator. Hear David saying: “He who formed their hearts one by one, who understands all their works” (Ps. XXXII). For one spirit is not begotten from another spirit as one body is generated from another body; rather, that wondrous Maker daily creates new souls from nothing.

Hear also Moses’ testimony on this matter. [Col. 0183A] He says: “If two men quarrel and strike a pregnant woman, and her child comes out not yet formed, he shall suffer loss according to what the woman’s husband imposes. But if the fetus has been formed, he shall give life for life, eye for eye, and so forth” (Exod. XXI). Behold, the lawgiver here openly shows that flesh is propagated from flesh, but soul is not generated from soul. For if the father had sown the soul in the flesh, it would have been just for the assailant to be subject to the same punishment in the case of an unformed and a formed miscarriage. But since money is paid in the unformed miscarriage and a soul is rendered in the formed one, it is plain that one [Col. 0183B] had a soul and the other did not. The order which existed in the first man is certainly preserved perpetually and without change in his descendants.

First, that earth-born man received his form from mud; afterwards he became a living soul. Likewise, in the womb the human race is first formed, and, when its limbs have been formed, the Author of life immediately infuses the rational spirit. Every person must indeed beware of adhering to that text: “All go to one place. All were made from the earth, and all return to the earth. And who knows whether the spirit of the children of men ascends upward, and whether the spirit of the beast itself descends downward into the earth?” (Ecclus. III).

It is not surprising if, in this life, there is no distinction between the just and the wicked, but they are tossed about by uncertain outcomes. [Col. 0183C]

For but they are tossed about by uncertain outcomes. For between beast and human being there is no manifest difference as regards the lowliness of the body. The condition of birth is the same, and the lot of death one. Together we come into the light, and together we are dissolved into dust. Yet we must not suppose that Solomon thought the soul perishes together with the body, or that human beings and beasts have one receptacle. Rather, he spoke in this way because before Christ’s coming all descended into hell. Hence Jacob says that he will descend into hell (Gen. XXVII), and Job complains that the pious are held in hell (Job VII, XIV, XVII). And indeed, before that flaming sword was removed from the gates of Paradise, heaven was shut, and an equal lowliness of the spirit of beast and human being confined them both (Gen. III). [Col. 0183D] Even though one is dissolved and the other preserved, there was not much difference between perishing with the body and being held in the darkness of hell.

Therefore, he says, God willed this alone to distinguish human beings from beasts: we speak, while they are mute. We utter speech by will, and in speech differ from beasts; yet in bodily frailty we are cattle. As a beast dies, so a human being dies, and all have one breath—this air. The fate of human beings is the fate of beasts: as is the death of this one, so is the death of that one, and there is one spirit in all according to the nature of the body. We breathe the same air; we undergo a similar death; through hunger, thirst, and other sufferings, we are joined to beasts. Therefore, under the figure of the living creature, he declared the fate of human beings and beasts to be the same. For he knew [Col. 0184A] that the spirit of beasts perishes with their bodies, while the rational spirit—that is, the human spirit—hastens to things above. For after much else he explains himself, saying: “Let the dust return to the earth from which it was taken, and let the spirit return to God who made it” (Eccl. XII).

Hear David also: “Your hands made me and formed me” (Ps. CXVIII). He uses a great opening of commendation when he says that he is God’s work according to both his natures, so that he might more readily incline his Maker’s favour toward himself and demonstrate the great prerogative of the human being. But “made” he referred to the soul, while “formed” he referred to the body. For of other works it is written: “He spoke, and they were made” (Gen. I); but He fashioned the human being with His hands [Col. 0184B], conforming him to the Son and to the Paraclete Spirit. Therefore, in the human body there is a soul: an immortal substance, participant in reason, a queen suited to the body.

## Chapter V

But who can explain how the soul dwells with the body? Such a person must be said to possess the spirit of the gods. Things which unite to become one do not remain what they previously were, as we see in the mixtures of elements with one another. Yet the soul is joined to the body while remaining in itself without confusion; and without corruption it enters into the part of the living creature. What then are we to say? The soul is certainly not in the body as a crowd is in a marketplace. Nor does it lie alongside the body as [Col. 0184C] one pebble adheres to another. Nor is it mixed with the body as water with wine. For in these cases separation can take place, both in actuality and in thought, without corruption; but soul and body cannot be separated from one another without the pitiable corruption of one of them.

Since, then, it is neither united, nor contiguous, nor mixed, for what reason is the living creature called one? Because of this, certain philosophers denied that the living creature consists of soul and body, declaring that the soul uses the body as the body employs clothing. They did not consider that the one who puts on clothing cannot become one with the garment. The soul grants life to the body, admitting no substantial union in the connection it enters with the body; and that it is joined to the body is shown by fellow-feeling. For the whole living creature suffers sympathetically with itself in a uniform manner, as one being.

That the soul remains unconfused in the body is evident [Col. 0184D] from the fact that in dreams it is in some manner separated from the body. For often, while a human being sleeps, the soul foresees future things and approaches intelligible realities. While awake, moreover, using no bodily instrument, it handles and contemplates the things that truly are, and, as though seated in its watchtower, so far as possible separates itself from the body. Indeed, while in the body, it passes beyond all corruptible things by contemplating them without the body, remaining incorruptible, unconfused, and unchangeable. For just as the sun’s radiance changes the air itself into light, makes everything transparent by its presence, and diffusely imparts its own light to it without confusion and at the same time in unity, so the rational soul, united to the body, remains in every respect [Col. 0185A] without confusion.

There is, however, a difference. Since the sun is a body, it is circumscribed by place and cannot accompany its rays everywhere; remaining in heaven, it extends the brilliance of its light to things absent. But the soul is incorporeal and is not circumscribed by place; the whole body is illuminated by the light of its presence, and no part of the body in which the soul is not present is illuminated. For it is not contained under the body; rather, it directs, supports, and governs the body, since it is not in it as in a bag or some vessel, but as the sun’s light is in the air. For the soul changes the body, yet does not cease to be what it is—unlike food, which changes the body and, changed in turn by the body, ceases to be what it was.

## Chapter VI

[Col. 0185B]

Concerning the relation by which the soul is held in the body, certain philosophers have held an opinion beyond the common one. They say that the soul is held in the body as a woman, companion of sobriety and honour, is bound by love and affection to her husband: not locally, not bodily, but according to relation. For, being altogether indivisible and devoid of bulk and size, it can certainly receive no surrounding boundary of circumscription. For how, I ask, can that which has no parts be circumscribed by place, when place seems to subsist through bulk? For place is the boundary of that which contains, by which what is contained is circumscribed.

But if someone insists that the soul [Col. 0185C] is in Paradise or hell, in Rome or Jerusalem, they reply that it performs acts there. Such names indeed signify places; but, as has already been said, the soul is understood according to relation, not according to place—unless perhaps accidentally, because that which contains the soul is in a place. Thus the soul is said improperly to be here or there because its action appears in this or that place; “place” must be understood in the sense of relation or action. It is therefore apparent how indivisible the soul is and that it is not circumscribed by place, because it is like God, whose workmanship it is. Solomon bears witness to this: “God created man imperishable, and made him in the image of His own likeness” (Wis. II).

Therefore [Col. 0185D], when separated from the body, the soul will return to Him. If a soul separated from the body did not live, the holy apostles and martyrs of Christ would not have despised this present life, nor would they have surrendered their souls through the death of the flesh unless they knew that a more certain life of souls would follow. Because they believed this, they shine forth in daily miracles. For by the presence of the bodies of saints the sick are freed, lepers cleansed, and dead people raised. Consider and be astonished: the mausoleums of kings and rulers of the world—the great Pompey, Germanicus Caesar, Augustus, wicked Nero, and others—are little known among the Gentiles and less honoured. But the tombs of the apostles are adored by the rulers of the world and held in great veneration. It is therefore manifest that souls live after death and, after their venerable departure, confer great honours upon the bodies which they formerly inhabited. And when they depart wondrously from their bodies, they are often seen by holy men. [Col. 0186A]

## Chapter VII

A man of venerable life, Benedict, saw the soul of his sister Scholastica leaving the body and penetrating heaven. Likewise, a certain man, a solitary of great holiness, on the island called Lipari, saw King Theodoric on the same day on which he had died in Italy. When Theodoric was being led, set apart between Pope John and the patrician Symmachus, with hands bound and barefoot, he was cast into Vulcan’s cauldron, which was near the man of God.

It is therefore evident how immortal and separable from the body you are, O human being. The image fashioned by the Craftsman ought to make you precious and glorious. The work of the Craftsman and remembrance of your origin ought to admonish you. Do you wish to hear about the dignity and excellence with which human beings are endowed? I shall state it briefly.

## Chapter VIII

[Col. 0186B]

The human being was wonderfully made: not only for beauty, surely, but also so that in perception through touch he might surpass other animals. He is not wrapped in thick hide, like oxen and other creatures clothed with dense skins; nor covered with hair, like sheep, goats, hares, and foxes; nor enclosed by scales, like the serpent and the greater kinds of fish; nor feathered like birds. Thus he needed clothing, because he was covered with smooth skin so that he might perceive keenly [Col. 0186C] and without hindrance. Skill in medicine and the benefit of healing were granted him, lest the continuity of his constitution should be dissolved through an imbalance of qualities. Food and drink were given to restore what is evacuated and evaporated.

Why say more? The Craftsman made all these lower things for the human being and subjected them to his service, as his bearing and countenance plainly show. Bird, land animal, and aquatic animal render service to the human being. They feed, clothe, offer healing, provide delight, and sometimes even inspire wonder. Therefore it is clear that they were made for the human being alone. For things made for another come into being to supply some deficiency—of food, clothing, healing, or something similar. But [Col. 0186D] neither an angel nor any heavenly creature has need of such things. We must therefore seek the rational creature for whose sake all these things were created. But none is found other than the human being; it follows that they were created for the human being.

Because of the greatness of the dignity possessed by humanity, the human being has been called the lesser world. Not only lower things, but even higher ones render continual service to him. Behold the splendid and visible mass of the firmament, with its host, continually turning above his head lest attendance upon humanity be lacking. God Himself, who surpasses every creature, became human for humanity’s sake. Who could set forth the magnitude of the dignity of this living creature made in God’s image? He crosses the sea; by observing heaven he traces the movements, [Col. 0187A] risings, and settings of the stars, considering their sizes and distances; he lays claim to what sea, air, and earth possess. He scorns huge whales and most savage beasts; he perfects every path of learning; and by letters he speaks, whenever he wishes, with persons absent. He presides over all things, possesses all things, and enjoys all things assigned to his own service. He debates with angels and God; commands nature; rules demons; investigates the nature of things that truly exist; and becomes God’s house and temple if he does not forget the authority granted him.

## Chapter IX

Among the other things humanity has received, these two are worthy of admiration: first, that if one repents, one receives forgiveness; second, that this mortal body, when it rises, shall become immortal [Col. 0187B] (I Cor. XV). The devil’s sin certainly has no pardon, because he fell not by suggestion but by his own pride. But the human being, because he fell not by himself but through another, can rise through Jesus Christ.

Yet after death confession is feeble, when the assault of every malicious spirit is most violent; for they strive to cast down not only the sinner but even the righteous into hell’s depths. The apostle Jude bears witness: “When Michael the archangel, disputing with the devil, contended concerning the body of Moses, he did not dare to bring a judgment of blasphemy, but said: ‘May the Lord rebuke you’” (Jude, sole chapter). Wishing to make manifest the devil’s tyranny over the human race, God permitted the devil to meet Moses’ body while it was being buried, so that we might learn that Satan, with his company and apostate host [Col. 0187C], restrains spirits from passing to places of rest and blessedness.

No Christian ought in any way to doubt that angels receive souls as they depart from the prisons of their bodies. For when they leave the mass of the body, good angels and the envious host of demons immediately meet them; with subtle inquiry they examine the qualities of their deeds and contend with one another as to which party may rightfully claim them. Michael’s contention with the devil concerning Moses’ body shows you this. Yet the good angel uttered no abuse against him, leaving judgment of that dispute to the Lord of all. Therefore, while we enjoy life, by good works we ought to obtain angelic defenses against the bands of demons.

[Col. 0187D] Who, stained by the filth of sins, would not fear the presence of demons murmuring against him, snarling and maliciously dragging him through the air with utmost cruelty? After they have carried out their exactions and administrations in the air, they proceed to hell and to abominable dwellings there. For just as blessedness gladdens the elect, so it must be believed that from the day of their departure fire burns up the reprobate.

Hear what Dionysius the Areopagite says concerning those who die: “When they arrive,” he says, “at the final road of this life, they behold more clearly, now stripped bare by its nearness, the incorruption to which they are going; for the nearer the night of this age approaches its end, the more fully the day of judgment shines forth.” These are filled with delight, since they no longer fear [Col. 0188A] that they can turn toward worse things; they are certain that they shall hold what they possess in unchangeable permanence. But those full of disgraceful deeds, who at some time received a taste of sacred instruction but turned toward corrupting desires and then melt away in deadly pleasures from their inward passions—these praise the life from which they foolishly fell, and unwillingly depart from it with great fear, because they embrace no good hope in their hearts.

Here one must repent; here one must confess sins, lest at the time of departure any one of the faithful be found guilty of timidity (*timiditatis*). The mystery of death is terrifying, when that dreadful host seeks the soul. It inspires fears, changes its forms, reproaches sins, draws the departing soul to itself, and threatens grievous things, so that before torment such distress may itself suffice for punishment. Then indeed the wretched person shudders as though he had tasted deadly poison. [Col. 0188B] The calamity of unstable dread grows heavy; he is stunned by atrocious deeds; the vigour of his senses is numbed; the thoughtless endurance of pains withers away; he is afflicted with fierce sharpness and utterly fails beneath inescapable disgrace. Do you not know how, on the last day, shameful deeds torment the soul and press the heart downward?

Hence many are seized by terrors, seeing dreadful faces whose sight they can no longer endure. Suddenly raising their heads, they support themselves on an elbow and shake the very bed [Col. 0188C] with great force; with wandering eyes they look here and there, while inwardly the soul is sent forth, unwilling to be separated from the body. For if we fear when we see terrifying human beings, what shall we not suffer when we behold close at hand death-bringing angels and unyielding powers? Hear what is said to you: “Do not delay from day to day, lest you fall,” I say, “without expecting the day when opportunities for living will abandon you and failure and inconsolable tribulation will come upon you—when physicians yield, household members flee; when difficulty of breathing becomes thick and dry, as fever kindles and ravages you; when you sigh from the depths of your heart and find no helper; you will deceive [or: seek?] the frail and weak, but there will be no one to hear you.” [Note: Col. 0187D: The passage is corrupt.]

For everything [Col. 0188D] then said by you will be despised as delirium, insanity, or madness. Let no one therefore deceive you with frivolous and empty words. Sudden destruction and the whirlwind of storms shall come upon you. A merciless angel will come, dragging and drawing away by violence your soul bound by sins, often turning back toward what is here and grieving voicelessly, its instrument of lament and sorrow cut off. Oh, how often you will tear yourself! Oh, how often you will sigh in vain, repenting of what you wickedly willed and did! How often you will speak in the sorrow of your heart: “Woe is me, because I cannot cast off this heavy burden of sin! Woe is me, because the stains cannot be washed away! O evil counsels! O foul unions! Because I had the practice of sinning for a [Col. 0189A] time, I shall be tormented eternally. Because of the pleasure and burning of the flesh, I am handed over to fire. God’s judgment is just: I was called and did not listen; they admonished me, and I mocked.”

You will cry out these and such things if you are snatched away before repentance. Have mercy upon yourself here. Impress upon your mind the last day of departure: anguish, suffocation, the hour when the spirit is seized, God’s pressing sentence, hastening angels, and the soul tossed amid these things—darkened, trembling greatly, doubting uselessly, repenting when repentance is of no avail. You have heard God saying: “I gave her time to repent, and she was unwilling to repent” (Job XXIV). There is no reason for you to doubt with cause; there is no reason for you to despair without cause.
