Arm yourself with these examples for confession; arm yourself with them for repentance. [Col. 0189B] For God delays punishment in order to find repentance; using the intervals granted to those who delay, He prolongs patience, lest judgment seize what mercy possessed. God does not await former evils or count past errors; He praises what has been corrected. You have the promise of Him who urges you to repentance: if you do not repent, He will impute it. “And I gave her time,” He says, “to repent, and she was unwilling to repent.” Similarly, there is added that prophetic saying: “And I said, after you had committed all these acts of fornication, ‘Return to me’; and afterward she would not return to me” (Jer. III).

Therefore, if, surrounded by the enormity of your crimes, you plunge yourself into the whirlpool of despair, hope of the promised restoration is immediately taken from you. The swallowing abyss of wicked deeds will carry you off into the precipice [Col. 0189C]; your eyes are closed by the night of sin, lest they see the gleaming ray of true light. Deceiving angels will lead you about here and there; every crime will become pleasant, and complete license to sin will wholly please you. The devil will hold you enslaved under the appearance of freedom, so that you may be free to sin but not to live. The author of crimes holds you captive; he has put the fetters of lust upon your feet and surrounded you on every side with an armed guard. He has given you a law, so that you may judge lawful everything that is not lawful; and he has plunged you alive into the pit of eternal death.

Confess, I beg you, all things by which you remember yourself guilty; confess, and anticipate the face of God by the duty of satisfaction. Humble your heart before Him; bow your neck in His sight; bend your knees; and, striking your face, prostrate yourself upon the earth. The heavenly physician will immediately receive your groaning [Col. 0189D], He who is accustomed to give believing penitents the support of protection. For it is written: “You have mercy on all, Lord, because You can do all things, and You overlook human punishment for the sake of repentance” (Wis. II). For the power is yours whenever you will it. “Return to me,” He says, “and I will return to you” (Zech. I). This is the indignation which He threatens from mercy; this is the wrath which brings mercy.

Blessed is the person who acknowledges that his Lord calls him, who does not prolong the time of conversion through pleasures, who lies prostrate in weeping so that he may be raised in joy, who sows in tears that he may reap in gladness. Do not delay in turning to the Lord, lest His anger destroy you at the time of vengeance; “for mercy and wrath are from Him” (Ecclus. V). Let us not give our bodies to the dominion of crimes, but obey [Col. 0190A] the Apostle who says: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey it” (Rom. III). Thus, since sin cannot be absent, it at least must not reign—that is, license to sin must not be made unrestrained, without regard for escape.

How do you suppose that time remains to you, when an unexpected and unending departure comes upon us and the courses of our lives are uncertain because death is uncertain? (Isa. XXXVIII). Hear Scripture saying: “While living and healthy, you will confess and praise the Lord; go to the portion of the holy age, with those living and making confession” (Ecclus. XVII). For the person who is allowed to repent possesses a sure gift of pardon.

It is written of penitents that God gave them the way of righteousness, strengthened the failing to endure, and appointed for them a portion of truth. Therefore [Col. 0190B] in the Gospel he warns you, saying: “When you are going with your adversary to the ruler on the way, make every effort to be released from him, lest perhaps he drag you before the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer cast you into prison. I tell you, you shall not leave there until you have paid even the last farthing” (Matt. XV). But he will never pay it, because there will be no other judgment. Therefore his torment will never be discharged. Great is the mystery of repentance. Hear how highly Christ values repentance. Luke says: “There were present at that very time some reporting to him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. And Jesus answered them: ‘Do you suppose that these Galileans were sinners above all the Galileans, because they suffered such things? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, [Col. 0190C] you will all perish likewise’” (Luke XIII).

Concerning Judas the Galilean we read in the Acts of the Apostles. Being an interpreter of the law, he said that no human being, not even Caesar himself, ought to be designated by the title “Lord,” and that no sacrifice should be offered other than that which Moses had commanded (Acts V). Therefore Pilate mingled the blood of Judas and his disciples with the sacrifices offered for Caesar. But the Jews attributed this to the sins of Judas and his companions. The Saviour, however, does not deny that Judas and his companions were wicked; but he does not affirm that they suffered because they were more criminal than others. Therefore he says, “Unless you repent, you will all perish likewise.” The faithful ought to be instructed by such cases, not exalted by them. For if, while we sail safely in harbour, [Col. 0190D] others succumb to storms, we are not therefore righteous.

Indeed, we are then taught by their fate to amend ourselves without delay for the better, lest we perish as they were destroyed by Titus and Vespasian, and are tormented endlessly in hell because they did not repent. The parable which he next adds concerning the fig tree also pertains to repentance: its master had waited three years for fruit. Each one of us is called a fig tree, planted in the vineyard and regenerated by the water of baptism in the Church. The steward of the vineyard is the angel given us for protection; when we are afflicted by more grievous dangers, he intercedes with the Lord for us: “Lord,” he says, “leave it alone; it will repent even this year.” Here he shows you the trench into which dung must be cast. The sinner is dug about when [Col. 0191A] he shakes the dust from his soul by worldly occupations and, becoming lighter, is disturbed toward good fruits. Dung is cast around it when, in place of precious and soft clothing, cheap and rough clothing is put on for the sake of fruit; when, in place of the glory and display of this world, one embraces the rule of monastic life or of any holy way of life.

If after the space of three years you bear no fruit, you will be cut out of the vineyard as idle, useless, and merely occupying the ground. For one who sees you persisting in sins through adolescence, youth, and old age, and knows the circumstances, is scandalized and becomes worse. Therefore such a person is rightly to be cut down, since, shameful in his barrenness, he grievously hinders his neighbour from bearing fruit. One cannot bear fruit whom the pleasure of joys is accustomed to dissolve. Everything gathered by desire of the flesh is cut down by the heel of its end. Certainly the soul will remain deformed if it is not at least covered by the veils of repentance and the garments of confession. You hasten to hide bodily ugliness, yet do not strive to remove the stains of the soul by repentance? If you do not erase these by repenting, and by confessing do not turn away God’s face from your sins, then in hell they will be known against your will and made manifest to all.

## Chapter X

All the dead in turn know one another and are known (Luke XVI). Abraham teaches you this; Lazarus suggests it; that rich man affirms it. For [Col. 0191C] if Abraham had not known Lazarus, he would never have spoken to the rich man placed in torments about his former affliction, saying that he had received evil things in his lifetime. And if the wicked did not know the wicked, the rich man in torments would never have remembered his absent brothers. For how could he be unable to recognize those present when he took care even to plead on behalf of those absent, remembering them? Thus the good know the wicked, and the wicked know the good. The rich man is known by Abraham, to whom it was said, “You received good things in your lifetime”; and the chosen Lazarus is known by the reprobate rich man, who earnestly begs that he be sent, saying: “Send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am grievously tormented in this flame” (ibid.).

In this knowledge [Col. 0191D] the fullness of recompense for both parties is increased at length: the righteous rejoice more because they behold rejoicing with them those whom they loved; while the wicked, tormented together with those whom in this world they loved while despising God, are consumed not only by their own punishment but by theirs as well. Something still more wonderful occurs among the elect: they not only recognize those whom they knew in this world, but recognize as though already seen and known good persons whom they have never seen.

It appears, moreover, that the dead are touched by grief concerning what happens after death to their own people. For that rich man of whom we are now speaking, while he suffered torments in the lower world, lifted up his eyes to Abraham and said among other things: “I have five brothers, lest they too come into this place of torments” (ibid.). The dead, therefore, have concern for the living, whom they know to be alive, because they do not see them in places of punishment. But the rich man, though separated from his brothers and not in the repose of the blessed, recognized Abraham and Lazarus from afar.

## Chapter XI

The chasm between the rich man and Lazarus signified the difference and distance separating the righteous from sinners. As their wills had been different, so too were their dwelling places. Some suppose hell to be a region of darkness and shadows beneath the earth. Hence the Psalmist says: “You rescued my soul from the lowest hell” (Ps. LXXXV). Thus the lower hell is rightly understood to be beneath the earth, while the upper hell is above it; and each is divided into many different places.

[Col. 0192B] John in the Apocalypse seems to confirm this opinion. He says that the book sealed with seven seals was opened by the Lion of the tribe of Judah. “No one was found worthy to open it in heaven,” because an angel cannot; “no one on earth,” because a living human being in the body cannot; “no one beneath the earth,” or in hell, because neither the spirit of a devil nor of a human being can (Rev. V–VI). Certainly none besides our Saviour was found who could interpret the wings of the silvered dove and the hind parts of her back with the pallor of gold—that is, both Testaments.

Others called it *infernum* (“the lower world,” hell) from the soul’s disappearance from view. So long as the soul is in the body, it is seen through its own actions; but when it has departed from the body, it is in every way unknown to us [Col. 0192C] (Ps. LXVII). Consider the miserable rich man, despairing of himself and pouring out prayers for others. Behold: in torments he did not lose his memory, because he urgently demanded that Lazarus, whom he had despised, be sent to his brothers, so that they might see him whom they had seen dripping with discharge, gaping with ulcers, and exhausted by poverty, now healed and possessing most ample honour. “It cannot be,” says the rich man, “but if someone goes from the dead, they will believe.” “They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them” (Luke XVI), replies the patriarch.

If a return from hell conferred faith, the Saviour would often have granted this to humankind. O rich man, you joined in contradiction with those who said, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” (Isa. XXII). “Who has returned from hell, that we should believe him?” O fool: if your father had risen, would you have believed one who was to die again—you who did not place faith in Scripture when it instructed you? Let your brothers therefore search the Scriptures and give them their faith. For the devil too could make the dead appear to rise by phantasy; he could lead the foolish in heart away from the path of truth and disseminate doctrines of error and wickedness concerning the things in hell. Sacred Scripture instructs us so that we may not be deceived by his craft or his cunning. It is the lamp by whose light a thief appears and is found. It is therefore to be believed; nor should it be demanded that the dead rise as if to proclaim what is done in hell. And since that miserable rich man is tormented in flame, a few words must now be said about the fire of hell.

## Chapter XII

[Col. 0193A]

There is one fire of Gehenna in hell, but it does not torment all sinners in one manner. For there each suffers punishment as much as his guilt requires. Just as one sun here does not equally warm every body, so there one fire burns souls differently according to the character of their crimes. Nor should it be doubted that that fire is bodily in nature, since spirits are certainly tormented in it. It is so stubborn in its burning that, if the sea flowed into it, it would feel no less heat.

Likewise, unbearable cold is said to exist in the lower world. For it is written: “They shall pass from snowy waters to excessive heat” (Job XXIV). This cold is considered so effective in freezing that by its contact it would transform mountains of fire into ice. Hence arise weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. XII). There are worms there which never die; avenging cares, viperish envy, and pallid decay provide them with food. There is there a pool, dreadful by the multitude of demons, armed with iron chains for binding; and there are many other forms, terrible beyond belief [Col. 0193B] (Isa. LXVI). There is certainly a river there called in Greek ἀχέρων (*Acheron*), muddy and filthy, dreadful in its vast abyss, exhaling a cloud of intolerable stench.

But why do I attempt to enumerate Tartarean hardships and horrors? They are more numerous than language can express or human understanding explain or comprehend. Fear the Judge, therefore, friends; dread the punishments and torments of hell. For if here the darkness of vices is loved, there the light will not be seen through the darkness of hiding places. If here we are not scourged for our sins, there we shall diligently be beaten with iron hammers. Hear what David says: “They are not in the labours of men, nor shall they be scourged with men” (Ps. XXVII). Because they are not scourged with the saints, eternal punishment is prepared for them: “Therefore pride has held them; they are covered with their iniquity and impiety” (Ps. LXXII). Pride holds them fast, lest they escape; iniquity covers them, lest they come to their senses. They are miserable because they are thought happy, and they proceed to fulfil their heart’s desire, constrained not by necessity but by appetite. They reject the measure of humanity, unaware that their pride will be cut down like a spider’s web.

[Col. 0193D] Cast away, O hearer, every perverse habit, mindful of punishment and infernal fire. Do you not know that you may be taken unexpectedly and torn suddenly from here; that the day of death, coming like a thief by night, will creep upon you and hurl you headlong, prone to vices? Set before your eyes the mass of all the harshest punishments of insatiable hell; prudently keep in mind the condition of death; fear the tumults, afflictions, and cruelties of demons, so that impious Tartarus may not consume you in time, hell may not press upon you, and that dreadful pit may not open its mouth against you. In it is perpetual heat, which exists without wood and is never quenched. The fire of hell is not kindled by humankind; it is not fed with wood and remains forever unquenchable. It needs no kindling [Col. 0194A] and always possesses excessive heat.

The flame of Gehenna gives light only for punishment. Into it the miserable and criminal soul is cast, that it may see those for love of whom it sinned and feel an increase of condemnation, because it loved them in error against the command of its Creator. The miserable spirit is tormented by bodily fire because, while here, it committed crimes as it served the body. He rolls in the lake of burning, bodily fire, prepared for the devil’s angels, so that he may be bound with his leader under the same sentence of condemnation; and what is written may be fulfilled: “The vengeance of the flesh of the wicked is fire and worms” (Ecclus. VII). For both fire and worm will be the punishment of the flesh.

Souls burn in hell; yet that fire in which they see themselves to be is wholly unlike our fire. For this fire burns what it touches not through sight, hearing, or understanding, but through touch alone. Yet the rich man was held in hell when he cried out to Abraham as though entreating him: “Send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger” (Luke XVI). Observe that the soul of Lazarus is represented as having fingers, and that of the rich man a tongue. For every rational soul expresses a likeness of the human body, possessing, as some have thought, an image like the reflection returned in a mirror. Therefore through such an image Lazarus and the rich man are recognized, see, and are seen in this world, in hell, and in paradise. Though incorporeal, it is thought to be a body. It seems to be somewhere, yet is contained by no spatial boundaries. Although it lacks the instruments of the senses, it has intellect and memory; it is affected by joy [Col. 0194C] and sorrow, fades through fear, and receives strength through hope. Remove sensation and understanding from human souls, and no punishment of fear would remain for them in the lower world.

But when the miserable spirit is assigned to punishment, it is afflicted, grieves, is tortured, cries out and shouts, complaining of the injuries of demons, of lost freedom, and of the leisure it yielded to pleasures. Therefore, O hearer, I beg you, lend your ears: know that it is not I speaking, but the spirit itself, without lie or any deceit, relating the miseries it suffers in hell; imagine it pleading for itself.

## Chapter XIII

O friends, pain sharper than pain itself—the pain which the company of transgressors inflicts upon me to torment me—compels me to cry out [Col. 0194D] and to make known to you, at the beginning of your mercy, the wrongs that I suffer. This enemy with whom I now lodge promised light and covered me with palpable darkness. The apostate too, who threatens more severe punishments, wrapped in bitterness, wished to take from me the remedy of repentance. He praised evils, doubled my guilt, and, by offering an occasion for sinning, taught an excuse for crime. The winding serpent, which sometimes lies deep in the abyss, confined me in its snares, soothed me with flattery, and ensnared me with false hope.

Alas for me! Now I burn; now I am gripped by anguish. Surrounded by miseries, I have lost my great refuge. What remedy can I obtain to lessen my pain? The demons malign me, rage, and gnash against me; they reveal their malice [Col. 0195A], now pouring forth the poison they had concealed and openly forcing it upon me against my will. They now show in the face the crime that had lain hidden in the depths of the heart; they entangle knots of wrongdoing, adding crime to crime, and hurl me, grieving, into danger. And because they had summoned me by deceit, I have become openly hateful to them. Every day they devise destructions against me and seek matter for accusation, without rest. They rage, persecuting me with clamour; they rush violently upon me with shouts. They wish to cast me into the snows’ cold, winter’s chill, the storm of terror, and Gehenna’s heat, so that in dying I may live and while living may melt away.

The executioners of my substance strive to remove me from every remedy. Therefore they bind me with fetters, tighten chains upon me, and exercise against me manifold kinds of cruelty. Therefore tears have failed me through the abundance of grief; blood flows in place of tears. Moreover, chaos and destruction open their mouth to swallow me. What, then, shall I do? The fall of my fortune is pitiable indeed; but the whole host of demons, being without mercy, cannot be moved to pity. Yet you, in whom is my hope, who remain alive and are my brothers in Christ, now live far from me and therefore think that you can bring no help to me or to those who are here torn apart by similar savagery. But have mercy on me, I beseech you. You can, I know, assist us wretches in this most harsh prison. For the hand of the Lord [Col. 0195C] is not shortened, nor his mercy, so that he cannot deliver (Isa. LIX). Behold, the Psalmist David says: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures for ever” (Ps. CXVII).

Before I departed from you, before I left the body, before I was consigned to winding serpents, I received the pledge of the holy Church. And although until the day of my departure, until the hour of death, I embraced harmful deeds, defiling lust, and wicked crimes, nevertheless in my final hour I broke and humbled my heart; I ate the gift of our redemption, namely the body of the Saviour, in the full sacrament of faith. If I had kept silent when I was allowed to speak, Tartarus would rightly now suffocate me and all like me. But I confessed Christ, uncovered my crimes, and shed tears—as do all who beseech pardon with me. Therefore I ought to be saved with those who are with me. Justice plainly seems to require that, if final silence is a cause of destruction, final confession likewise be a cause of salvation.

The Lord speaks to the prophet: “You, son of man, say to the children of my people: The righteousness of the righteous shall not deliver him on whatever day he sins; nor shall wickedness harm the wicked person on whatever day he turns from his wickedness; and the righteous shall not be able to live by his righteousness on whatever day he sins” (Ezek. XXXIII). To one doing evil it was said, “You shall die”; to one doing good it was said, “You shall live”; and, “Where I find you, there I shall judge you.” Each person is found in repentance, faith, and confession.

Paul, aware of God’s secrets, says: “For if you confess with your mouth [Col. 0196A] the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you shall be saved” (Rom. X). Therefore what I held in my heart I confessed with my mouth. For I believed that the Son of Man came to seek and save what had perished and to snatch captives from Satan’s jaws. The final confession of one thief and the obstinate mind of the other thief have certainly brought me to this confidence. The one, because he does not believe, is devoured by Gehenna’s fire. The other, although likewise stained with bloody robberies and always a standard-bearer of devilish savagery, though he had never remembered God, had kept none of the commandments of the law, and his whole hope had been despair—yet because he came to his senses while placed in punishment, he found the Lord’s great and surpassing remedy and, where he hung, recognized him as the future Judge. And [Col. 0196B] because he disclosed to him the crimes of his conscience, he entered paradise with him that same day. He believed and obtained pardon; sprinkled with that most sacred blood, he was made higher than the angels. Therefore in the twinkling of an eye he entered paradise with the Saviour himself.

Although I did not bodily behold the body which hung upon the altar of the cross, nor touch that blood—in the appearance, I mean, of blood—yet spiritually, believing, I drank the one and ate the other in the same manner. Let my departure from hell therefore be slower, because I am the most wicked of robbers and was not crucified with Christ as he was. Yet, because I confessed my crimes and execrated my drunken deeds, the perpetuity of torment ought to be cut short by the remedy of healing.

Have mercy also on my companions, O Christian men. Your aid is now needed, that you may offer for us the Paschal victim, namely the saving Lamb who takes away the sins of the world. Thus—yes, truly thus—you can draw us from the abyss of hell. Pray to God for us, pour out prayers before him, and give alms to the needy. By these riches, petitions, and gifts, hell’s abyss restores its captives, releases them, and permits them to depart into life. But I know that many are corrupted by empty opinions, thinking that prayer should not be made for the dead because neither Christ nor the successors of his apostles have made this known in writing. They do not know that there are many highly necessary practices observed by the holy Church whose tradition is not found in Scripture. Nevertheless [Col. 0196D] they pertain to the worship of God and possess the greatest force; if they are despised, they will wound the faith which shone forth through the Gospel. But for brevity’s sake I wish to mention a few things out of many.

## Chapter XIV

No Scripture of the New Testament prescribes that the foreheads of believers, who hope to obtain everlasting salvation, should be signed in the name of Christ Jesus with the sign of the Lord’s cross. Likewise, what Scripture has shown that those engaged in prayer should turn their faces toward the east? Again, the mystical words by which the grace of the Holy Spirit is invoked to sanctify the bread of life are found in no sequence of the New Testament. The blessing of baptismal water, the threefold immersion of the baptized person in water [Col. 0197A], and the blessing of chrism are observed in the Church without the writings of Christ and the apostles. Christ did not wish his Church to be bound only by written traditions. For it was not expedient for their teaching to be publicly committed to writing concerning matters which the uninitiated may not know.

But, passing over these things, because perhaps some of you do not know why the Church fixes its gaze toward the east when it prays, I shall explain briefly. Every Christian, then, when engaged in prayer, turns his face toward the east. Why? That by praying he may seek again the ancient homeland which he lost; that by sincere petitions he may regain paradise, from which he was expelled and which God planted in the east; that he may behold the face of Christ hanging on the cross turned toward the west. For Christ, crucified, looked toward the western quarter to which he was turned.

Therefore on the first day of the Sabbath each believer performs his prayers standing in the courts of the Lord’s house, that, rising with Christ, he may seek the things above, as the excellent teacher exhorts. The manner of prayer, performed without alternation of bending on the Lord’s days, signifies the future resurrection. For that day is an image of the age to come, in which the knees of those praying are not bent. Hence Moses calls it not “the first” but “one”: “And it was evening and morning, one day” (Gen. I). As though repeatedly brought back in a cycle, it is the same one and also the eighth, which will have no change: nothing declining after this time has run its course, since it will be without evening, without succession, without old age.

On other days, however [Col. 0197C], when the knees touch the ground, the fall of humankind through sin and its expulsion from paradise are signified. But when the face is again raised on high, it is plainly shown that the exile is recalled to heaven through the mercy of the Redeemer. It is clear, therefore, I think, how many things there are in the Church, full of power, abounding in holiness, strengthening faith, and directing human actions toward what is better, which were not committed to pages by the first Shepherd.

But he himself handed them down to be held in his hidden judgment and did not permit them to be clothed in pages and ink through the apostles who were his vicars. We must certainly adhere to apostolic commands, even when unwritten. Hear Paul saying: “I praise you in all things, because you remember me [Col. 0197D] and hold the traditions as I handed them down to you, whether by word or by letter”—that is, whether orally or in writing (II Thess. II). One of those traditions which the Apostle delivered in writing is prayer for the departed. Not Paul alone, but the entire choir of apostles established such a tradition from the beginning of the Church. Nor indeed does a tradition, continually flowing through the use of time from long custom, fail to adhere deeply to the Church of God. Therefore, just as the Church itself observes many sacraments without a written declaration, so from the beginning it has continually poured forth holy and devout prayers to the Lord for departed believers, though it has no support for this in the writing of the new law.

You know, surely, that where no written proof is found, the established credibility of witnesses excludes every ambiguity: “By the mouth [Col. 0198A] of two or three witnesses,” says the Almighty, “every word shall stand” (II Cor. XIII). Receive, then, the proof of witnesses who do not know how to deceive. Herman, bishop of Capua, found Paschasius the deacon, who had long ago passed from this world and whom that wicked troop of demons, when it could, brought here, in the baths at Puteoli. He obtained pardon through the bishop’s prayer; and so the act for which he was held did not condemn him after the rebuke of confession. For though defeated by the unanimous judgment of all, he nevertheless persisted in his own opinion until the day of his death, loving and preferring Laurentius, whom the Church had refused, by the judgment of the bishops, to set over him. He had been assigned to a penal place because in the party of Laurentius he had taken a position against Symmachus.

Will not your prayers for me, then—for me who repented—be able to erase the written bond of condemnation? The gracious Lord will grant to your prayer and almsgiving the one whom he had assigned to the pools and sulphurs of burning Gehenna.

## Chapter XV

Judas Maccabaeus was a righteous man and God’s friend. This man, who had very often obtained the Lord’s mercy by many and great prayers, lifted up in hope toward higher things, understood in devout devotion that sacrifice should also be offered for the dead (II Macc. XII)—indeed, for those who had transgressed the commandments of the law and had obeyed idols captured from Timothy and Sosipater. For when Judas, moved by piety, was committing them to their ancestral burials, [Col. 0198C] he found under the garments of the slain votive offerings to idols, from which the law forbade the Jews. It was therefore made manifest to all that they had fallen for this reason; accordingly they blessed the righteous judgment of the Lord, who had made hidden things manifest. Then, turning to prayer, they asked the Lord that the sin which had been committed might be blotted out.

For this reason Judas collected silver and ordered it to be offered at Jerusalem for the aforesaid offence, mindful of the saying: “A most pure vessel shall come forth” (Prov. XXV). He did not suppose that those who had violated the law would suffer eternal punishment. He did not fear the surface of the letter, but, grasping by understanding the mercy of God the Creator, he gathered silver of great weight for offering, that he might rescue those who had been condemned from eternal fires. Then he addressed the people when he appeared inclined toward mercy for his brothers, when their hearts were moved for their brothers’ offence. He made a collection of silver, but did not choose an arbitrary number. For he took only twelve thousand, that by the twelve the faith of the holy Trinity, which was to be preached through the four parts of the world, might be indicated; and by the thousand its integrity and perfection might be commended.

A drachma was a silver denarius bearing the royal image. By the offering of this denarius, Maccabaeus resolved to redeem from the capital sentence those who had been created in the image of the highest King. If prayer should not be made for the dead, the man of God would never have judged that such a thing should be done [Col. 0199A]. If he had known that he would offend God, he would never have made a collection of drachmas for transgressors of the law. How could the friend of God have sent an offering to Jerusalem for the dead and not have been heard?

Finally, sacred Scripture would not have preserved to the present day the memory of this man as God’s friend if, by such an offering, he had presumed something against the Lord. I know that Scripture says: “You shall render to each according to his works”; “what a man sows, that shall he reap”; and, “Who shall confess to you in hell?” (I Cor. III; Gal. V). But this pronouncement will be fulfilled at the second coming of the Redeemer, at that terrible judgment and the consummation of the world. Then undoubtedly all worldly time will pass away; then every prayer will be ineffective. For where then will the poor be? Where the solemnities of Masses? Where psalmody? Where acts of charity? When the marketplace has been dissolved, it is pointless to return to buying and selling.

Therefore I beg you, friends, before that hour make my burdens lighter, because I have not covered my sin with the darkness of denial. Pour out prayers before the merciful and compassionate Lord. He will certainly hear your cry for me and for others who have not yet passed into everlasting punishments. When we were among you in the world, we prayed that we might somehow merit to be aided by your services. We are not burned in that flame in which the rich man is tormented. The great chasm has not yet been placed before us; return has not yet been blocked. Give aid and offer for us the sacrifice of redemption. For by such suffrages [Col. 0199C] our punishments are lessened and melt away, a place of rest is opened, and the true light of the divine face, which had been hidden from us, shines upon us for a little while.

Terrible are the threats of almighty God, but his ineffable mercy conquers them. For this reason his saving descent illuminated these Tartarean caverns. For this reason he brought back from the lower world many who believed in him: kings and prophets, rulers and judges, and a numerous people from among the Hebrews.

Therefore I think that he wished all those to share in the booty and the spoil—those who believed that he was man and true God, born of a virgin, and had received with an impartial mind the miracles which he performed above nature: miracles involving the dead, blind, mute, deaf, leprous, dropsical, withered, and demon-possessed persons; [Col. 0199D] his walking on the sea, multiplication of loaves and fishes, and changing water into wine. Before he rose, he wounded this hell for their sake.

The merciful God indeed wishes you who live to bear the burdens of us who are dead, provided that before—or even while—we were called, we received the pledge of the Church; provided that we gave faith to those sacraments with a full heart; and provided that we spiritually ate the flesh and blood of Jesus Christ not in outward appearance but by faith, not through external sight but through inward affection. In the fullness of his mercy God wishes you to direct your attention to helping us and your neighbour. “Those who are well have no need of a physician.” Why would he, through the unbloody sacrifice, have given occasion for remembrance [Col. 0200A] to be made for us who have gone before you? Why would the holy Church, apostolic and catholic throughout the ends of the earth, celebrate commemorations of all the dead on the thirtieth and anniversary days in its writings and observances? For if the Redeemer of humankind regarded such service as impious, abominable, frivolous, or useless, how could so many holy Fathers have died up to this point without any one of them receiving a revelation that such errors should be removed from God’s Church? Nor would the successors of the apostles have thought that prayers for those who sleep should always be offered in the sacred rites, in the mysteries themselves, in this manner: “To those who have no place of refreshment, light, and peace, let whoever is able give help.”

Do you not know what Gregory’s *Dialogues* relate—Gregory to whom the highest angels ministered during the solemnities of sacrifices? Once, as he walked across a stone bridge which the emperor Trajan had built, he delayed his journey a little and deliberately poured forth a fervent prayer to the Lord for the remission of Trajan’s sins. Immediately a voice came to him from heaven, saying: “I have heard your prayer and will grant pardon to Trajan; but henceforth refrain from praying for the impious.” Do not, I beg you, say in your hearts that this is false or fabricated. Inquire, if you please, among the Greeks: the whole Greek Church certainly testifies to this. And although Trajan had shed the blood of many martyrs, yet Tartarus, otherwise more inexorable, was compelled by the holy man’s prayer to give him back.

But that great Athanasius, in the discourse which he wrote concerning those who sleep, speaks thus: “Prayer for departed believers must not be omitted, wherever death may have overtaken them. The saving sacrifice is to be offered; oil is to be offered; candles, as though for burial, are to be offered, calling Christ the Lord to help. These,” he says, “are acceptable to God and bring abundant recompense from him. Oil and the candle emit the fragrance of an odour. But the unbloody sacrifice obtains propitiation. The giving of alms produces an accumulation of recompense.”

Such should be the intention of one making an offering for those who sleep as is that of parents who have a tender and weak child: when he is ill, they offer sacrifice, oil, and candles in the church. [Col. 0200D] But the child neither touches nor offers anything, being wholly ignorant of the sacrifice, just as of the renunciations and professions made at baptismal regeneration.

But the faith of those who promise and offer undoubtedly makes these things highly effective for those on whose behalf they are done. Such practices the Apostles, taught by the Holy Spirit, established. Such practices the successors of the Apostles confirmed in the Spirit of God. Such practices the teachers of the Church afterward approved by teaching. Hence they gain ground and spread from the rising of the sun to its setting, from north to south, to the glory and praise of the King of all ages. God indeed accepts the sacrifice of the altar, the sacrifice of praise, because He thirsts for the salvation of humankind. Did God prepare rewards for labours or crowns for angels? Did He descend to earth for angels, assume flesh, become human, and overcome suffering and death? Will He say to angels: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you” (Matt. 25:24)? No faith underlies this assertion; rather, as He suffered for humanity, so He prepared all things for humanity. Hating its death, He loves its life.

For who ever prepared a great banquet, invited friends, furnished tables with dishes, set out the food, and then forbade the guests to eat? Yet I, indeed, and those with me, through negligence, sloth, and uncleanness, have become unworthy and are barred from the door of the banqueters. Therefore comply with our request; make good what is lacking, but send on to us what we omitted. [Col. 0201B] Supply on our behalf what we ought to have done, and reconcile for us wretches the Redeemer whom we offended.

Yet no uncertainty should afflict anyone concerning the case of the needy and poor, lest they fail to attain salvation merely because they leave no survivor to invite a priest to offer sacrifice, to distribute alms, or to devote himself to prayers. Do you suppose that God is unjust—merciful to one who has an intercessor, yet without mercy toward one who has none? Far be it! God is certainly just: He counts those without benefactors together with those who have them, for the merciful God accepts on behalf of all those who merited in life to be capable of receiving help the benefits which each person performs for his own dead. Therefore [Col. 0201C] you should strive all the more that sacrifice be offered, prayers be urgently made, and almsgiving increase; for what you regard as exceptional, the kindly Judge accepts as common.

Likewise, the souls of the righteous, who dwell in the starry abodes, although they pray for all, pour out their prayers to the common Lord more eagerly for those who lack the service of the living and particular acts of devotion. For they do not need to beseech the Judge on their own behalf. In heaven, where they are, there is the highest good and no evil; but in the lower hell there is no good, but the greatest evil. With us, however, there is evil indeed, yet we are not tormented to the utmost. Therefore we can be helped by your benefactions; by them [Col. 0201D] our guilt may be expiated, so that we either suffer a more tolerable condemnation now or obtain complete remission.

Bestir yourselves to render services for Christians who have died. Even if these avail little for those whose left-hand scale has touched the earth, they are nevertheless remedies and consolations for those who perform them. All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. The Judge always relaxes something of the punishment due to evil. If He marked iniquity, who could endure the Judge? If, amid the waves of inward and outward calamity, He crushed us as much as He could, God would forget to show mercy and would restrain His mercies in wrath. Therefore He does not inflict upon the wretched penalties proportionate to the weight of their crimes. Every human life is surrounded by sins; every conscience is accused by its own thoughts. [Col. 0202A] Yet propitiation does not cease, because in judging all things He is not merely a Judge who observes iniquities, but merciful.

Do you wish to hear how much the Paschal sacrifice benefits us? Bishop Felix obtained pardon through sacrifice for a man whom he had found, long after his death, serving him amid vapours. Likewise blessed Pope Gregory ordered the saving sacrifice to be offered for thirty consecutive days for a certain monk of his who was being tormented in this fire. And it came to pass that, when the thirtieth offering had been completed, the monk received communion and at the same time escaped punishment.

Can you bear to hear how much alms bestowed for the dead benefit us? Near Alexandria there was a bishop of most venerable life who had in his neighbourhood a philosopher named Evagrius. Although he was a pagan, he was nevertheless the bishop’s friend, because he had once been his pupil in a school of philosophers. Desiring to bring him to the Christian faith, the bishop frequently preached to him words of salvation. But since the philosopher was not at all persuaded by them, he is reported to have said to the bishop:

“My lord, among all things this displeases me: that you Christians dream that the world will end, that there will be a resurrection of bodies, that rewards will be rendered according to works; and further assert that whoever has mercy on the poor lends to the Lord, and that one who, in Christ’s name, assists Christian poor people for the souls of your dead will receive a hundredfold. Since all these things are far [Col. 0202C] from the truth, I count them among amusements and fables.”

But when the bishop affirmed by many arguments that there was nothing false in Christian doctrines, the philosopher departed; and not long afterward he believed the bishop’s preaching and was baptized.

At last, when he was about to settle his affairs, he summoned the bishop and said to him: “Take sixty pounds of gold, to distribute among the poor as you have said, giving me a written bond that I shall receive from Christ the Judge, in that age of which you speak so much, one hundred for one.” When the bishop had done this without hesitation, he received the money in the manner he had foretold to the philosopher, intending to distribute it to the poor. Finally, when the philosopher was dying, he ordered his sons to bury the bishop’s written acknowledgment in his hand. After these things had been done, on the third day the philosopher appeared to the bishop in a dream and said:

“Go to my tomb, bishop, and receive your written bond; for I have received the entire debt. You are no longer bound to me in any way, since I have long since certainly received a hundredfold from Christ. Indeed, lest any doubt trouble you, I have signed it with my own hand.”

The bishop was astonished, being wholly ignorant of what had happened. Therefore at dawn he ordered the philosopher’s sons to be summoned. When he learned from them that what he had seen in the dream was true, he convened the clergy of the city and went to the tomb. When it was opened, they saw the philosopher sitting upright and extending his hand with the document. One of the bishop’s clergy, attempting to take it, could not pull it from [Col. 0203A] his hand, for he was holding it out to the bishop. When the bishop received the document, the philosopher lay back down; and the bishop read it aloud before everyone.

The wording of the document, which the philosopher himself had issued a little earlier, was as follows:

> Evagrius the philosopher sends greetings in the Lord to the most holy bishop.  
>   
> I have learned, Father, that you do not know that I have received back a hundredfold, as you promised me, all the money which I gave you while still living in the body. Therefore you are under no obligation to me on account of any debt.

When these words were heard, all who stood by were astonished. But the bishop’s bond was preserved by a careful order. From this, friends, it is clear what the offering of the most sacred Body, prayer, and almsgiving confer upon us: without doubt they transform the lead of perversity into the silver of sincerity.

## CHAPTER XVI

Finally, Joseph and Nicodemus teach that you ought not omit the duty of the last rites. Bearing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds, they embalmed the Lord’s body and thereby obtained the highest praise and glory.

## CHAPTER XVII

Likewise, the holy women prepared many costly perfumes in order to perform the same duty. Therefore they deserved to see the Saviour himself. And with what praise they are daily extolled throughout the whole world is beyond doubt. If Christ our Master had refused that tombs, funeral arrangements, and services be rendered to the dead, He would never have displayed [Col. 0203C] His own body to the whole world as an example. Behold, Joseph and Nicodemus spent much money in order to protect that holy body from worms. Certainly, whoever is able ought to expend an abundance of wealth in honourably burying a friend’s body, but especially in delivering the soul from the jaws of demons.

And, praying for us, secure us by your benefactions; bring help to us poor people. Above all, strive more earnestly toward that remedy which is greatest before every other: namely, that the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world may be sacrificed more frequently in remembrance of the dead.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Having addressed you with such discourse, the rational spirit, believing that it has persuaded you, asks at once for your assistance [Col. 0203D] and favour—which you will doubtless give, you who live by faith. We, who were long ago of the same condition as you, shall soon have you here as companions. But because the discourse has now proceeded rather far, it remains that, with minds warmed and hearing renewed, we explain the few matters still to be said concerning funeral lamentations, the coming of Antichrist, the Lord’s final day, His resurrection, and judgment.

## CHAPTER XIX

The conflict of human necessities moves me to recall for my friends certain causes of our common calamity. But much more does the depth of the divine plan make me soar away, when I consider how God forms infants in the womb, fits together their limbs, joins nerves and arteries, and assigns fitting functions to every particle of the human body. He gives life to clay and joins spirit to dust; He transforms food into flesh, wine into blood, phlegm into bones. In the womb, like a good painter, He outlines images; distinguishes colours and qualities; and fixes the limits of life that He determined before the foundations of the visible fabric of the world.

This depth of counsel skillfully puts the soul into the body and, I think, more wonderfully separates it from the body. For what human being lives and shall not see death? We are mortal, earthly, and destined to return to dust. From this sorrow is born; from this fear arises; and from this groans resound. For one who yesterday shone in a garment woven with gold, elevated in a semicircular tribunal, lifted up in pride, splendidly surrounded on every side by a crowd of attendants, today is carried lifeless and even stinking upon a bier to the tomb. He is buried pitiably, attended by a great procession and multitude of friends, honoured with laments and chants, celebrated with funeral rites. Yet shortly afterward even these things, along with the memory of his name, will be lost. No one’s friendship extends any further than the grave. Thus one who swelled with pride yesterday today gasps under sickness; one who shortly before was feared is today seen as foul-smelling; beautiful yesterday, loathsome today; yesterday in his house, today in his tomb.

Where is the rich man? Where is pride? Where are the officials who threw everything into confusion? Where are acts of violence, power, vast possessions, wars, marshaling of standards? All are [Col. 0204C] dust, all ashes, all embers, passing more swiftly even than shadows. Where have all these gone? Has greatness of glory vanished? Where are the foremost persons? Where is the daughter and the sweet son? Where is the brazen wife? Where the friend? Where the enemy? All have failed; and one died only a little while ago. Another perished for his country; a storm at sea overwhelmed this man; another was killed by the bites of wild beasts. Truly this shadowy existence differs in nothing from spring flowers. For like them, a human being melts away and withers.

Hence it is abundantly apparent that the structure of our body differs in no respect from that of beasts of burden. Go a little ahead; hurry on; run before us; inspect the tombs of the dead, and you will not refuse to see a sad and wholly unpleasant spectacle. Apply yourself carefully, and restore in your mind the disfigured condition of the dead. Look upon the dust of dissolution and endure the calamity of our pride. Endure being filled with an overpowering, intolerable smell. These things are yours, not another’s. Bear bravely the breath evaporating from putrefaction and the vapour exhaled from decay. Endure seeing heaps of worms. If you please, examine more closely; distinguish, if you are able. Fit bone to bone again; and, if you wish, join every part you see dissolved to its corresponding part. Consider, if you can, whose this is and whose that is; who this man is and who that; whether he lived as an old man or a youth, fortunate or crushed by misfortunes, long-lived or quickly dead, glorious or obscure. Ponder these things; look around: by how much grief and sadness will you be tormented? You will say: “Where has the form and beauty of these people gone?” [Col. 0205A] How ungrateful, displeasing, foul, and death-bringing is this sight—alas for this lot! The flesh has dissolved, the entrails burst, the parts of the creaturely structure and fabric have been scattered, beauty has been destroyed.

Certainly each of us will be laid in coffins in like manner, will rot, and then, consumed by the same greediness of worms, will be dissolved. Do you understand, human being, what is being said? Look around at the tombs; see the bones of the human frame; then return to yourself, weep with yourself, groan, sigh from the depths, and consider the human calamity—what end it has received. From the appearance or opposition of these bones you cannot declare who was king, rich, poor, noble, obscure, free, soldier, ruler, righteous, condemned, wise, foolish, eloquent, barbarian; which woman conceived or gave birth; who was father or son.

Why say more? The best thing perceived by our senses among us, seeing the bones, undergoes equal corruption; yet all human care strives to cling to life. For this reason the construction of houses and buildings was devised, that cold and heat might not destroy our bodies. What else is agriculture but a kind of preparation for living? Concern to preserve life is exercised only by fear of death. Medicine likewise is held in honour among human beings for the same reason, for by a certain art it seems to resist the punishment of death. Breastplates, shields, helmets, spears, greaves, military equipment, circuits of walls, gates with iron bars, and the fortifications of ramparts—why else were these devised except because of fear of death?

Since death, so dreadful through its bitter hatred, oppresses life, how could a survivor fail to be touched by pity for the dead? Is it not worthy of sorrow when we see one who was alive a little before suddenly made mute and motionless, the instruments of nature extinguished, neither sight nor any other sense functioning? Whether you apply fire or iron to him, pierce his body with a sword, throw him to birds that feed on flesh, or cast him into mud—the one lying there is affected in the same way by all these things. Once these transformations have occurred, the vital principle, whatever its nature, vanishes [Col. 0205D] and departs in the twinkling of an eye, like a lamp that has been burning is extinguished: its flame neither remaining in the wick nor passing elsewhere, but withdrawing into complete disappearance.

How can anyone bear such a weight of sorrow without pain? We hear of the soul’s departure and see the body left behind; yet we do not know what the spirit that gave it life is by nature or where it has gone. Neither air nor water nor anything else displays that power which animated the body. When it has departed, what remains lies dead and exposed to envious corruption. Who, then, even if made of iron, can restrain tears when such a loss comes upon him? Hence hair is torn, eyes drip, and the breast resounds under the blows of clasped hands.

## CHAPTER XX

[Col. 0206A]

Nevertheless, the wretched person vainly afflicts himself with lamentations, weeping and wasting away for the dead. It is vain to mourn those who dwell in tombs, dissolved and already returned—or shortly to return—to their own dust. How long shall there be mourning and crying, tumult and noise, griefs, blasphemies, and self-laceration even at the graves? After the burial has been attended to, faces are slashed, and lamentation occurs in marketplace and home. What are you doing, human being? You see the dead man sleeping and burst into reproaches. You mourn a son who died first as though you were not going to die. You have his end before your eyes, yet do not await your own.

Think with yourself who you are; since you are mortal, the one you begot was like you. Since you had his beginning, you ought to have expected [Col. 0206B] his end. Do not be distressed when you see a young person summoned away and passing to a better state. You yourself will shortly follow and accompany the one you mourn; no human being can escape that end. This is not a removal from better things to worse, but from corruptible things to incorruptible, from visible things to invisible, for which we are destined.

Do not, therefore, exceed measure in weeping. In accordance with what our Lord and Saviour says, “Blessed are those who mourn” (Matt. 5:5), this is not on account of funerals but on account of their sins. But I know what you say: “I am human; I cannot help being sad.” You are not forbidden to weep or grieve; nature constrains and impels you to this. It demands habitual, daily companionship and conversation. You are not forbidden to be saddened, as Christ taught you, for He wept over Lazarus. You too may weep, but with propriety and with fear of God.

But if a singularly sinful person has died, one who gravely offended God, it is lawful only to weep—although this brings him no benefit. Yet give whatever consolation you can through alms and offerings: this is to assist him. One should rejoice because his wickedness has been cut off. Conversely, if he was righteous, one should rejoice, for he has reached the haven he desired, removed from the uncertainty of this course. If he was young, one ought to be glad, because he has been snatched from the snares of the world. If old, there is no cause for grief: having attained what seemed most desirable to all, [Col. 0206D] he has departed satisfied.

Be sad, if you greatly wish, but do not go beyond measure. For death comes naturally: humanity entered the world in order to leave it. Human life upon earth is a pilgrimage. When one has walked far, one must return. Each day leads to the same end. Do you not know that one who is excessively troubled demands something greater than nature itself? A human being is born mortal. If nature has completed its course, why are you sad? No one grieves at being nourished by food and drink; no one desires to live without them. Yet you seek to be free of death, contrary to nature—the laws of nature alone [give otherwise]. Death certainly belongs among the things that happen once to a human being. Accept what nature has given in common to all. Let not doubled grief wrap biting cares around your heart. The blows are gentle; therefore let your griefs be becoming.

With a sound and upright mind, every fortune is despised, and however great it may be, the burden of trial is made light. This anxiety of grief has appeared to you so that you may emerge unharmed from frequent storms and the varied waves of the world. The Wise Man urges this upon you: “Join yourself to the Lord, and endure, that your life may increase at its end” (Ecclus. 2). How many things are there that cannot be healed without a wound! These pains are thought harmful, but if you bear them, they will afford you remedies. In burning by fire and cutting by iron, a remedy is expected. A biting aid is sometimes the source of cures. The heavenly physician comes to heal you; do not make what is spiritual into something merely animal. Is it good to be reproved by the Lord? It ought to be pleasant to be chastened by the Lord.

And indeed, for those who receive affliction painfully and beyond measure, terrible is what is said: “Let the wicked depart from me. For I do not wish to know their ways, because their lamp is extinguished and they shall have groaning in their life. For they shall be like chaff driven by the wind and like dust raised by storms.”

Christ is the one way that brings believers to the heavenly palace. Whoever grieves for the dead immoderately will not walk by that way. His fall will come quickly; he will be vexed by sickness because he has driven away the physician standing by. One must weep; one must grieve. We entered the world weeping, so that with tears we might drain [Col. 0207C] the first portion of sorrows. Hear what the Wise Man says: “I too, when born, received the common air; I fell upon the earth fashioned in like manner; I uttered my first cry, weeping like all others; I was wrapped in swaddling clothes and brought up amid great cares. For no king had any other beginning of birth. Therefore all have one entrance and a like departure” (Wis. 7).

Therefore it is necessary that one who comes should pass on. Why, then, are you consumed by grief? The time of mortal life is certainly very narrow. A person is born and at once is overwhelmed by death. Conquer by patiently bearing the burden laid upon you. Any burden hurts more severely if it is carried unwillingly. It is not in human power not to die, because it was not within human choice to be born. Prosperous events are rare in this world, while turbulent ones are most numerous. Trials should be welcome, so that the virtue dwelling within may be tested. When winds cease, the skill of the helmsman is neither tested nor known. It befits Christ’s servants to be tested by calamities and to grow amid pressures and straits like a kindled fire. Through such exercises and contests virtue grows and expands, and reaches the harbour of desired blessedness.

Hear Paul saying: “Whenever I am weak, then I am more truly proved; and I delight in my weaknesses” (2 Cor. 12). Frequent experience of labours makes the body very strong; idleness and sloth make virtue weak and lax.

## CHAPTER XXI

Hear, women, whose companion is grief, who practise bitterer mourning, because you imitate the footsteps of those who have no faith. Many of them, for their dead, cut their faces, tear their flesh, and pull out their hair. Tell me, woman: why do you mourn if you believe that he will rise? Believe me: he sleeps. Creeping sleep has closed his eyes.

“But,” you say, “perhaps it is because of the intimacy, assistance, and care of affairs which he provided, and because of many other things that he managed.” Yet when you lose a child, he was encumbered by the weaknesses of infancy, wholly incapable and useless for every task. Why do you weep? What do you seek?

“He was,” you say, “of good character, and therefore I expected fruit from him; he was begotten of me. For this reason I lament a husband taken away, mourn for a son; for these things I weep and tear myself—not as an unbeliever that they will not rise again, but because I am deprived of great hope and bereft of comfort. [Col. 0208B] My head has been taken from me; I have lost the master of my household. He who shared in everything, whose presence refreshed me, who comforted me, is dead. This is what I mourn. I know that he will rise again, but I cannot patiently endure the separation that intervenes. Great confusion of affairs surrounds me. I am exposed to every injury. A female dependent who formerly respected me now despises me. Whoever suffered some harm at his hands now insults me and shows his anger against me. These are the things that do not permit me to bear what has happened more evenly. By these and similar things the mind is provoked, the spirit grows bitter, and the whole bodily frame melts away. What remedy can be offered for this pain? What discourse will soothe grief and expel it from her mind?”

## CHAPTER XXII

[Col. 0208C]

First, then, she must be reproved, because these are not causes of grief and irrational suffering. For if you mourned for these reasons, you would have to mourn the one who died forever. But before a year passes, you forget him as though he had not existed—especially if you wish to marry a second time. Yet the present discourse does not address such a woman, but one who keeps the marriage-bed of her husband undefiled. Why do you mourn a child? Why lament a husband? You mourn the former because he did not produce the fruit you expected; the latter because you expected greater fruit from him. What great unbelief and faithlessness it is to suppose that a husband or son establishes you in security, and not God! How do you not see that you embitter yourself?

Therefore God removes such persons from the midst, so that you may not remain so strongly bound to them that you turn your hope away from Him. For God is jealous and wishes to be loved by us above all, because He Himself loves us greatly. He knows that the habit of those who love immoderately is very jealous: they would rather give up their life than displease those whom they love. For these reasons He cuts short the days allotted to them. In ancient times there were neither widows nor orphaned children. Therefore He allowed Abraham and Isaac to live for a long time, because while they lived they set God above their own will. For He said to Abraham, “Sacrifice,” and he sacrificed. Likewise Sarah grew old because she obeyed God more than herself; yet neither because of son nor husband did she embitter God.

But now, because you women are inclined in this direction, you set your husbands above God; [Col. 0209A] therefore He, inviting you to desire Himself, draws you away from them. Do not love your husband more than God, and someday you will not feel widowhood. Do you wish to hear how God ought to be loved? Do not first love father or mother and afterward God; do not be held in love for son or daughter more than in the love of God. Christ says, “He who loves father or mother above me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10). Love your husband as flesh; love God also, but love Him not as flesh and blood, but as spirit (1 Cor. 6). “For he who cleaves to God is one spirit” (Matt. 22). You ought to love God in the first place with all your heart, all your mind, and all your strength; but your neighbour as yourself. You must not love your neighbour with all your heart, mind, and strength. Again He says, “Love your enemies” (Matt. 22); He did not add “with all your heart,” nor “love your enemies as yourselves,” but only, “Love your enemies.” It is enough for them that we love them and do not hate them. Therefore God must be loved above all (Matt. 5).

If you love God more, do not weep. For He who is loved more is immortal and does not allow you to experience the pain of one less loved. Therefore blessed Job was not at all tortured in mind when he heard of the sudden death of his children (Job 1). What do you say, woman? A husband and son used to support you, and God will not help you? Who gave him to you? Was it not He who also created you? Was it not He who brought you from non-being into being, breathed a soul into you, bestowed understanding, implanted a mind, and did not spare His only-begotten Son for you? Will He forget you, while a servant remembers? These words are full of the most burning indignation.

If your husband has benefited you, he has returned a benefit received. But we have nothing of this kind to say about God. “For who has first given to Him, and it shall be repaid to him?” Since He has no need of our goods, by goodness alone He bestows benefits on the human race: He promised you a kingdom, gave you incorruptible life, granted adoption as children, and made you co-heir with His only-begotten Son. Yet after such benefits you remember rather your child or husband! What did both give you? Pains, labours, insults, reproaches, rebukes, manifold troubles. But God made His sun rise upon you; He gave late and early rain, and refreshes you with this year’s [Col. 0209D] bread, wine, and oil.

O what greatness! Therefore He takes your husband from you so that you may seek the Master. But when your husband departs, you cling to him and forsake God, saying: “He clothed me in garments woven with gold; he adorned my breast with necklaces; with shining rings and ornamental bracelets he made me like the eastern star.” Certainly, if you endure, you will be adorned with a far more fitting ornament. Does not sobriety make you admirable to all? This King possesses precious garments, woven with varied patterns, with which the soul is clothed so that it may not become contemptible prey for demons. Then you will rule over the household servants, if perhaps you possessed them. Then incorporeal virtues, principalities, and powers will serve you.

But you are anxious about who will feed little children and orphans. The Father of orphans and Judge of widows will provide sustenance [Col. 0210A] for survivors and for those afflicted on either side. The Lord and Saviour Himself says: “Is not the soul more than food, and the body more than clothing?” (Matt. 6). You have God as Father, and do you fear hunger? That certain people proceed magnificently even amid the greatest throngs of people is of no benefit here. If you wish, you may serve in heaven and be numbered in that army. Those chosen there are not carried on horses but borne in clouds. They have not mortal scouts, but angels themselves; they attend not a mortal king but an immortal one. Look up to heaven and see how much more splendid the royal court is. If that higher royal court differs so greatly from this lower one that, compared with it, this appears muddy, what blessedness will not befit anyone who has attained it?

[Col. 0210B] Therefore, if the resurrection and renewal of our bodies are held in most certain hope, no place remains for complaint. Indeed, that you may be sustained by such hope: our flesh, which the Son of God assumed, He did not hide in the earth but carried into heaven; He reclaimed His deposit, and took back what He had laid down by His power. He Himself rose, prepared the way, opened the gates; therefore we too shall rise.

## CHAPTER XXIII
Since we have reached the point at which we must discuss the resurrection, which Antichrist and the day of the Lord will precede, having first touched on those matters concerning the coming of Antichrist and the day of the Lord which I judged worthy of mention, my discourse will here labour to establish that each person ought to have as great certainty of the resurrection’s arising as he has of death. [Col. 0210C] The prophet Daniel declares the coming of Antichrist and the universal resurrection of all the dead, not obscurely but openly. For among other things he prophesies this concerning Antichrist:

“And he shall rule over the treasures of gold and silver, and over all the precious things of Egypt; he shall also pass through Libya and Ethiopia. And a report concerning him shall spread from the east and from the north; and he shall come in great strength, to crush and kill many, and shall pitch his tent before the Lord, between the two seas upon the renowned and holy mountain; and he shall come even to its summit, and no one shall help him” (Dan. XI).

Porphyry falsely alleges that Antiochus did all these things. For Antiochus held Libya and Antippia. But Antichrist, [Col. 0210D] after conquering Libya and Ethiopia, will hear that wars are rising against him from the regions of the north and east. Coming with a great multitude, he will kill many and pitch his tent at Appadano, situated not far from Jerusalem, near Nicopolis, formerly called Emmaus, where the mountainous regions of the province of Judaea begin to rise. Then, advancing further, he will ascend as far as the Mount of Olives and there pitch his tents between two seas: one of these is called the Dead Sea in the east, and the other the Great Sea, on whose shore lie the Palestinian cities Caesarea, Joppa, and Ascalon. Then he will come to the summit of that province, to the crest of the Mount of Olives, which was called renowned and holy because from it our Lord and Saviour [Col. 0211A] ascended to the Father. Yet no one will be able to help Antichrist when the Lord rages against him. For that impious one will perish where our Saviour and Lord ascended into heaven.

The same prophet subsequently says: “At that time Michael shall arise, the great prince who stands for the sons of his people.” For, as this prophet indicates, the care of the Jews has been entrusted to Michael the archangel, so that he may turn those who oppose them to confusion and flight. Therefore, while Antichrist oppresses the Jews, Michael will meet him in opposition, as will Elijah, who will come to announce the coming of the Saviour, so that believers may obtain the reward of salvation.

Then, recounting the abundance of evils which he will bring to completion, he adds: “And there shall be tribulation such as has not been from the time when nations began to exist until that time” [Col. 0211B] (Dan. XII). For in the time of Antichrist there will be tribulation such as neither was before nor will be afterward. When Antichrist has been overthrown and extinguished by the breath of the Saviour, the people written in God’s book will be saved. He calls God’s foreknowledge “the book,” as though saying: Those found worthy, as predestined by God, will obey Elijah’s preaching. According to the diversity of merits, some will rise to eternal life, but others to everlasting reproach. Clearly, the prophet proclaims the common resurrection of all (Dan. XII).

Some teachers infer from this passage that, at the resurrection, those who have instructed others will have the likeness of heaven and will be compared to the brightness of the stars (Apoc. [Col. 0211C] XII). For it is not enough to know wisdom unless you also instruct others. Silent teaching does not build up another and therefore cannot receive a reward. For to whom was a reward ever given for idleness? They therefore hold that a holy and learned man will differ from a holy and simple man as heaven differs from the stars.

The Apostle speaks thus concerning Antichrist: “Unless the falling-away comes first and the man of sin, the son of perdition, is revealed—the one who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshipped” (II Thess. II), “so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God” (Matth. XXIV).

In this passage the Apostle makes Antichrist’s ways clear, reveals great mysteries, and reveals Antichrist himself. He calls him “the falling-away” and “the man of sin,” because he will give many over [Col. 0211D] to apostasy and destruction from the faith, even casting scandal upon the elect themselves, if that were possible; and because he will commit innumerable crimes through which he will cast his followers into ruin. Antichrist is called the son of perdition because through him perdition will come into the world. He is a man, not God; wholly a servant of sin and the devil, not by nature but by imitation; a man, not an angel, who will oppose Christ and his members, and therefore is to be called Antichrist.

“He will exalt himself above everything called God or worshipped” (II Thess. II), whether by false or true opinion, wholly taking the devil into himself together with his deeds. Yet he will show no reverence to idols. For he will not be an idolater, but in every respect contrary to our God. He will smash all the gods of the nations as mute images. [Col. 0212A] He will render worship to no image whatsoever, because he will command that he alone be adored as God. He will sit in God’s temple, in the Church, showing himself as though he were God. Rightly has he been called “the falling-away.” For when he comes, most people will revel in pleasures; children will plot against their fathers; a wife will threaten her husband’s life; deceit and fraud will be prized. The criminal love of possession will rule human hearts.

Antichrist himself, in order to satisfy that utterly evil generation, will dig up and expose riches, the incentives of evil. Hence wars will arise, weapons will clash, piety will be overcome, brotherly love will be absent, and whatever passion persuades each person will be counted reason. Masters will be inhuman to slaves, nor will slaves submit to their masters. No one will reverence old age; [Col. 0212B] no one will pity the beauty of the young; God’s temples will be despised. The overthrow of churches will occur everywhere. Sacred Scriptures—or even trivial tales—will be scorned. The ears of the accomplices of that falling-away will obey curses, blasphemies, lies, and provocation; they will delight in shameless songs and abominable sounds; they will accuse one another, incite lawsuits, bring false charges, and pour forth everything unworthy of a Christian.

They will rush headlong into every form of wantonness and, unrestrained, roll in every whirlpool of lust; they will eagerly pursue obscene and foul desires. Those called Christians will openly practise sorceries and incantations. False apostles and false prophets will [Col. 0212C] rise against one another, lying; they will become greedy, perjured, slanderous wolves. Christ’s priests will embrace lies; monks will cleave to the things of this world. The rich will be merciless; rulers will not pity the poor. Unjust judges, eagerly serving bribery, will shut the sacred and utterly necessary house of justice against the just; they will not observe the tests of the laws, but, blinded by gifts, will pursue injustice.

But why do I enumerate the detestable crimes of our people? The elements of the world will abandon their appointed laws. Earthquakes will occur throughout all cities; throughout all regions there will be most severe famine. There will be mournful thunders and dreadful flashes of lightning, setting houses and country dwellings ablaze. The entire earth will be scattered by conflicts of winds. Knotty oaks [Col. 0212D] will be overthrown; the sky will resound and fires will leap from the clouds. The seas will be shaken from their deepest beds by the force of winds. The earth will be battered by the magnitude of hail; there will be the grievous affliction of a most severe winter, intolerable harshness of frost, and immoderate heat. Sudden lightnings and unexpected conflagrations will arise. And, to say it simply, weeping and mourning without hope of consolation will invade every living soul. For where iniquity has abounded, the love of many grows cold.

Therefore, since in the time of Antichrist concord will suffer so great a disaster, while discord overflows, that plague is rightly called “the falling-away” (Gen. XLVII). He is to be born from the tribe of Dan, as Jacob prophesied: “Dan,” he says, “is a serpent in the way and a horned serpent (*cerastes*) in the path, biting the horse’s hoof, so that its rider falls [Col. 0213A] backward” (Dan. XII). The *cerastes* is said to be a horned serpent, by which Antichrist is fittingly signified: he will arm himself against the life of the faithful with the bite of poisonous preaching. The horse signifies this world, and the horse’s hoof, the end of the world. Antichrist will bite the horse’s hoof because he will harass its last days by striking; and he will fall backward because, full of iniquity and malice, he will suddenly fall from divine power out of this life, to be dragged away to eternal punishments. The Apostle plainly indicates this when he says: “Then that wicked one shall be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth” (II Thess. II).

Antichrist will come, but he is not to be feared, because the Lord Jesus will kill him by the power of the Holy Spirit, who is called the Spirit of Christ’s mouth because he proceeds from him. In the time of Antichrist the Roman kingdom [Col. 0213B] will be removed, as the holy doctors affirm. For just as the kingdom of the Medes was destroyed by the Babylonians, that of the Persians was demolished by the Macedonians, and the Romans took dominion from the Macedonians, so the Roman empire will experience its downfall through Antichrist. Antichrist himself, however, will be destroyed by Christ the Lord, our liberator.

The coming of that Antichrist will indeed be according to Satan’s working, with every power and with lying signs and wonders, and with every seduction of iniquity. Some will perish through these because they did not receive the love of truth so as to be saved. Thus the pestilential Antichrist will perish by Christ’s arm, as you see small creatures when a great fire comes upon them—and deservedly so. For his activity will be in falsehood, [Col. 0213C] not in truth. By magical art and illusion he will deceive people, as Simon Magus is believed to have done, appearing to do what he did not do.
