Satan, then unleashed, will enable Antichrist to do many strange and unprecedented things, teaching every path of error, every fabrication, and everything opposed to God. Hence by threats, flatteries, and every means he will seduce those given over to animal passions, who did not receive Christ, in whom all promises have been fulfilled. It is certainly just that those who did not receive truth should find perdition.

Therefore everything Antichrist will do will either be phantasmal illusions, full of every kind of falsehood, or mockeries producing false delusions for those who are perishing. This one, as Daniel [Col. 0213D] says, “will speak words against the Most High and crush the saints of the Most High, striving to change times and laws.” For Antichrist will rage against the saints for three years and six months. After overcoming them, he will rise in pride in order to change God’s laws and ceremonies. But when the period of three years, with the addition of half a year, has been completed, he will preside over judgment, “so that his power may be taken away and he may be crushed and perish unto the end.”

“Why,” you ask, “has God permitted this to happen? What is this dispensation? What benefit is there? What fruit? What confidence can there be in his coming, when he is to come for the destruction of our generation?” Blessed Paul says that his coming is most useful for those who perish, because if Antichrist had not come to them, they might allege a cause for unjust condemnation (II Thess. II). What [Col. 0214A] benefit, then, is there in this? Because those same persons who perish will in some manner be tested. For whether Antichrist came or did not come, they would never have believed Christ. Antichrist will therefore come so that faithless unbelievers may be convicted, lest they say: “Christ indeed called himself God; but we learned from the Law that there is one God, from whom are all things; therefore we did not believe.” Antichrist will invalidate their excuse. For when he comes, prescribing nothing sound and doing nothing whole, he will stop the mouths of his disciples with lying illusions and fabricated wonders.

For if you did not believe Christ, you ought by no reasoning to have believed Antichrist. Behold, Christ said that he had been sent by the Father; Antichrist asserted the contrary. Therefore Christ said to the Jews: “I came in the name of my Father, and you did not receive me; if another comes in his own name, you will receive him” (John V). I know that you will say: “He performed astonishing signs before our eyes, shone forth with miracles, and displayed wonders” (Acts X). Yet Christ performed many great works, and all the prophets bear witness to his goodness, just as, conversely, they render detestable testimony concerning Antichrist: for they have called him the son of perdition, acting according to Satan’s operation, and “the falling-away.”

## CHAPTER XXIV

Antichrist will indeed come to inflict manifold persecution upon Christians. But do not be shaken by fear, because the efficacy of his malice will nest in those who perish. For Elijah will then come to strengthen [Col. 0214C] believers, as it is written in the Gospel: “Elijah is coming, and he will restore all things” (Luke I). For he will restore the Hebrews then found to have almost fallen away from their ancestral lot, and will recall to their memory the prophecy of the Gospel.

He will say: “Hear the Saviour saying: ‘If anyone says to you, “Here is Christ,” or “Behold, there,” do not believe it. For false Christs and false prophets will arise and will give signs and wonders, to deceive, if possible, even the elect’” (Matt. XXIV). Take heed. Behold, he has foretold all these things to you, so that you may not be deceived. For “as lightning comes out of the east and flashes as far as the west, so shall the coming of the Son of Man be.” Therefore he needs no herald, since he will certainly be manifest to all, like lightning [Col. 0214D] which suddenly appears to everyone. For when he comes to judge, Christ will not travel from place to place, but in the twinkling of an eye he will be present everywhere.

“And as, where the corpse is, there the eagles gather,” so, wherever Christ is in the clouds, the saints will swiftly come. And immediately after the tribulation of those days, when the brightness of the true light comes, sun and moon will appear darkened by the splendour of the incoming light. The powers of heaven too will be astonished, sensing the world’s renewal and that all human beings from Adam until that time must render account to that great Judge. Then Antichrist’s people will be afraid; those fallen from the faith will tremble; then the wretched Pharisees will shudder. When they asked Christ when God’s kingdom would come, he answered: “The kingdom of God does not come with observation. [Col. 0215A] Behold, the kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII).

God’s kingdom is not of this world, as you suppose, nor is it observable in that manner. For it has no fixed time; God’s kingdom is always present to one who is willing. Leave the things of the world, not by change of place but in mind; not by departure but by progress. And God will reign in you. This answer, indeed, he gave to the Pharisees; but to the disciples he said:

## CHAPTER XXV

“Days will come when you will desire to see one day of the Son of Man, and you will not see it” (Luke XVII). Beware lest you be deceived. For at the judgment I shall not be confined to a place or hide in concealment, but, like lightning, I shall flash from one end of the earth to the other. Meanwhile I await the precious fruit of the earth, the early and [Col. 0215B] latter rain of youth and old age.

Peter prophesies concerning that day of the Lord: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief, in which the heavens will pass away with a great rushing sound, while the elements will be dissolved by heat; and the earth, and the things that are in it, will be burned up” (II Pet. III). By “night” he signified the Lord’s coming as uncertain, and by “a thief” as unexpected. For night removes things from human use. David also wrote concerning the passing of the heavens: “In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They themselves shall perish and be changed” (Ps. CI).

Unless the heavens were the works of God’s hands, they could not be changed or undergo alteration. If heaven had not been made, it would be without end and unchangeable. But since God is the maker of the heavens, he can change them when he wishes, because he established them when they did not exist. [Col. 0215C] There is only one thing that cannot be changed and always remains the same: namely God, in the ocean of whose substance nothing is remote, nothing is stretched forth, nothing future, nothing past; with whom one day is as a thousand years and a thousand years as one day (Ps. LXXXIX). Therefore human deeds and thoughts cannot be hidden from such a judge: in a moment he will examine every individual, rendering to each according to what he has done. Rightly, therefore, heaven will pass away, since God alone remains the same, whose years do not fail.

For this reason the same Apostle writes: “We await new heavens and a new earth, according to God’s promises, in which righteousness dwells” (II Pet. III). John likewise confirms this in the Apocalypse, saying: “I saw a new heaven and a new earth. For the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea is no more” (Apoc. XXI). The same prophet Isaiah agrees: “For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered” (Isa. LXV). And again: “For as the new heavens and the new earth which I make remain before me, says the Lord, so shall your name and seed remain” (Isa. LXVI).

Humanity will indeed be renewed in the resurrection, and the heavens, seas, and earth will also be renewed. For all these things had been subjected to vanity—that is, to corruption—on account of humankind. Since man put on a mortal and passible body, he incurred so great a curse and brought forth thorns and thistles. But when this mortal body is made immortal and free from the bondage [Col. 0216A] of corruption, it is fitting that creation, which has been our companion in affliction, should recover the strength of its former incorruption. Just as, when heaven and earth are renewed, the sea will no longer exist, because the succession of changes, generation, and corruption will be wholly given over to destruction.

It is therefore not doubtful that the day and the Lord of judgment will come. Behold, the prophet Zechariah is the author of the same teaching: “The Lord my God will come, and all the saints with him. And on that day there shall not be light, but cold and frost. And there shall be one day, known to the Lord, neither day nor night; and at evening time there shall be light, and waters shall go forth from Jerusalem to both seas” (Zech. III). The prophet, revealing the end of the present age, announces to the world Christ’s coming from heaven to judge. “The Lord,” he says, “will come in the glory [Col. 0216B] of God and the Father, with his holy angels and with his prophets and apostles.”

David likewise sings the same: “For the Lord will not cast off his people” (Ps. XCIII), until righteousness is converted into judgment. He calls the Saviour “righteousness,” who after the resurrection ascended into heaven and will return at the last day for judgment, together with all who are upright in heart. Now day and night are distinguished from one another by the succession of times; but after all sinners have drawn to themselves their cold and frost, there will be one perpetual day, no longer alternating between light and darkness, day and night. The Lord himself will be the light of all, of whom Isaiah says: “You shall no longer have the sun for the light of day, nor shall the rising [Col. 0216C] of the moon illuminate you by night; but there shall be eternal light, and your God shall be your glory” (Isa. LX).

But those whom cold has killed will be in darkness, while those who followed the apostles and prophets will walk in light. Then, at the time of night, through Christ there will be day. For beneath heaven he will shine, darkness having been entirely abolished, so that henceforth it will no longer offend the heavens of the saints. That day is known to God alone, the Most High. Of that day Christ our Saviour says: “No one knows that day, neither angel in heaven nor the Son, but the Father alone” (Zech. XIV). Yet insofar as he is human, the Son is said to be ignorant; insofar as he is God, nothing can be hidden from him.

From that day Christ will be everlasting light to the saints, as John says: “And the city will have no need of the light of the sun, because [Col. 0216D] God Almighty will be its light” (Apoc. XXI). From that day also, according to Zechariah’s prophecy, living waters will go forth from Jerusalem. Half of them will go to the eastern sea, commonly called the Dead Sea (Zech. XIV), because nothing can live in its waters; the other half to the western sea, which leads toward Egypt. “In summer and in winter it shall be,” he says, so that they are neither bound fast by winter frost nor dried by summer’s excessive heat.

For after the day of judgment, the Saviour will pour out from the heavenly Jerusalem living water—his Spirit—upon his saints, but no longer as a pledge. For in the temple wholly at peace, the Spirit will no longer be in us by measure; rather, we shall be abundantly watered by his fullness. He is rightly said to come from the heavenly Jerusalem, [Col. 0217A] because Holy Scripture plainly declares that the God of all dwells in heaven and, though existing in heaven, fills the whole world.

Because Sacred Scripture customarily compares the Holy Spirit to waters, the giver of that same Spirit testifies, saying: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, ‘Rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.’” The Evangelist interpreted this by saying: “Now he said this concerning the Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive” (John VII). It should be noted that he distributes the grace of the Spirit in the same measure to those from Israel and to those from the Gentiles who have believed. This is signified by the life-giving water, one half of which will flow to the eastern sea and the other half to the western sea. He called the first sea Israel, [Col. 0217B] and the western sea the Gentiles, who believed after Israel.

The prophet did not mean that the Holy Spirit is divided, or that he is found without fullness in either people, when he declared that one half went here and the remaining part there. Rather, it must be confessed that grace is distributed equally to both. For “half and half” signifies an equalizing grace. The pouring out of those waters will therefore occur in winter and summer—that is, at every time—so that people may come from east and west to recline with Abraham and Isaac, when the voice of the turtledove is heard in the land, when winter has passed, when the necessary spring arrives, when flowers appear upon the earth, so that we may celebrate Passover and Pentecost, in which we pass from earthly things to heavenly and [Col. 0217C] offer all our fruits to God.

Then the Lord will be king over all the earth, when we say: “The Lord has reigned; let the earth rejoice,” and “Say among the nations, ‘The Lord has reigned and has set right the world, which shall not be moved’” (Ps. XCVI); when he removes every error, so that the world may thereafter experience no alteration. He will judge in righteousness, so that the world coming under judgment may receive a reward according to the merit of holiness. He will judge in truth so that he may grant perfection of knowledge to the peoples among whom God’s miracles had a place, when that which is partial has ceased. He will judge the world, not a part, but the whole, because he did not purchase only a part: he gave the price for the whole. Therefore equity and truth will be in that judgment. What could be more equitable [Col. 0217D] than to place the elect at the right hand and the reprobate at the left?

In the present life all are mingled, and the good are not distinguished from the evil. But then he will separate the righteous from sinners, removing them from their conflicts in order to make them secure in safety. For this reason he calls the latter goats and the former sheep. Goats, as you know, are barren and naturally unfruitful; but a rational creature becomes barren by free choice, and for this there is no excuse. Sheep, however, yield abundantly: milk, offspring, wool, and meat. Likewise, when sheep find pasture, they feed abundantly and store it within themselves, so that in a time of hunger they may bring it from stomach to palate and have it again as food by chewing the cud. Imitate these, since the one who loves God is called by their name.

Now the kingdom of God must be seized; now the heavenly food must be tasted beforehand [Col. 0218A] and preserved in the belly of the heart, so that at the time of resurrection all the members may be protected and cherished at his revelation. Now one must live by the Spirit; now one must renounce the deeds of the left, so that a place may be found at the right, where the Son of God, consubstantial with the Father, has determined to sit. Moreover, those who will be at the right, though they will share the resurrection with all, will nevertheless obtain something outstanding beyond others. For they will be irradiated by God with mighty splendour, so that they seem to shine like the morning star upon the world, taking wings like eagles.

Indeed, if the souls of eagles, while their bodies are vigorous, raise them into the air, it is much easier to believe that human spirits, after the resurrection, will carry their bodies [Col. 0218B] above the stars. The saints are called eagles because they will fly upward to meet Christ. And just as eagles gaze upon the sun itself without being dazzled, so the righteous, stripped of the bondage of corruption, will behold the rays of the true light—Christ himself—coming in the clouds, as is read in the Apocalypse: “Behold, he will come with clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him. And all the tribes of the earth will mourn themselves” (Apoc. I).

For just as he ascended in a cloud, so he will come in a cloud. That cloud will be refreshment to the saints but terror to the impious, as in the wilderness the cloud refreshed the Hebrews and tormented the Egyptians. Likewise the fire that will go before the Judge will illuminate the good and set his enemies ablaze round about. Those who mourn over him, when [Col. 0218C] they see the eternal fire prepared for them and behold the glory from which they are excluded, will be tortured with intolerable distress and pain.

The prophet Daniel likewise prophesies concerning that coming: “I looked,” he says, “in the vision of the night, and behold, one like a Son of Man was coming with the clouds of heaven; and he came even to the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him; and he gave him a power that shall not be taken away, and a kingdom that shall not be corrupted” (John VII). For once the Roman empire has been destroyed and Antichrist has died, there will no longer be an earthly empire, but the commonwealth of the saints and the coming of the triumphant Son of God. Christ’s kingdom and power will be everlasting. The devil’s power, however, is incomplete and will have an end. For he often wishes to harm but cannot; he has done only as much as he received power to do. [Col. 0218D] His strength and power will be made void on the day of judgment, and he will be assigned with his followers to eternal torments.

Dreading this day, the prophet cries: “Why should I fear in the evil day? The iniquity of my heel shall surround me.” He calls it an evil day: a day of disasters, plagues, and punishments. Such will it be for sinners at that terrible judgment. That day of calamity is called simply “the day,” because everything that was hidden will be uncovered and made manifest in it. That day of wrath is also called evil because it will be full of cause for condemnation for the wicked. On that day the wretch will fear whose heel the cruel tyrant wounded by watching him and, by pleasant suggestion, [Col. 0219A] cast down into the judgment of lust.

The devil is quite certainly said to lie in wait for the heel of human beings, because he especially watches the end of mortal life—otherwise so full of misery—in order to suffocate the spirit and deceive it before departure, so that after death he may drag it, by the inextricable snare of his pestilential malice, to endless punishment. The heel sometimes signifies deception, as in: “He lifted his heel against me.” Such a thing is sin: it entices, ensnares, and deceives. Therefore there is only one thing a human being ought to fear in the day: not poverty, not illness, not low birth, but only the stain of crime and the wickedness of life, lest it seize you in the evil day. That day is the end of the human day and the beginning of the Lord’s day. [Col. 0219B] Therefore it is exceedingly fearful.

For in his own day a human being did whatever he wished. But in the Lord’s day action is taken away, the result remains, and every power of choice is extinguished. He will stand for judgment before the utterly pure gaze of angels, where the secrets of conscience will be wholly opened. Each person will reveal himself and confess whatever he has done, without alleging external witnesses; the deeds he performed will stand openly present and bear testimony that cannot be contradicted. It is therefore clear that there will be a judgment and a resurrection of bodies.

## CHAPTER XXVI
Let the sect of the Sadducees perish, then—the men who said that there would be no resurrection of bodies. To them the Savior [Col. 0219C] and our teacher gave this answer: “You are in error, knowing neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. Have you not read, concerning the resurrection of the dead, what was said to you by God: ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matt. 22; Mark 12).

He plainly teaches here that the resurrection of bodies will truly occur, though not such a resurrection as the Sadducees imagined. For they thought that after the resurrection marriage, childbirth, and sexual union would be restored, and that people would again bring their lives to an end by death. Thus it is said to them: “You are in error, and do not understand the Scriptures.” If you knew the Scriptures, you would surely know that God is not the God of the dead, but the God of the living. And if the power of God had been so known to you, you would certainly believe that all things are possible to God, and that by resurrection he will make human beings very like angels. [Col. 0219D]

“I am,” he says, “the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” He is not the God of the dead and of those who are not, but of those who endure and exist. If Abraham and the others had passed into nothing, God would by no means have said, “I am the God of Abraham,” but rather, “I was.” Although Abraham and the others are dead, they yet live in the hope of resurrection.

Paul too, following the Master, says: “This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.” And again: “It is sown in corruption; it shall rise in incorruption. An animal body is sown”—that is, a fleshy and passible body—“a spiritual body shall rise” (1 Cor. 13): unchangeable, impassible, and subtle; such as was the body of the Lord Savior [Col. 0220A] after the resurrection. It entered to the disciples while the doors were shut, needing neither food nor sleep nor anything of that kind.

But someone says: “How shall the dead rise?” O folly! O unbelief! He who by his will changed dust into a body—will he not unite scattered bones? And if you still doubt, let your own work produce faith in you. “What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies. And when you sow, you do not sow the body that is to be, but a bare grain—for example, of wheat or of some other kind.” For you do not sow the plant, or the stalk, or the many coverings of grains contained in the husk, although the seeds rise along with them. But God gives the grain a body with husk and ear, as he wills.

Therefore, just as the seed rises clothed, with much increase and beauty, so the dead person can by God’s power live and rise with a glorified body. [Col. 0220B] God gives each seed its own body, the body it ought naturally to have. He does not give the same body to every grain, but to each its own: to wheat, that of wheat; to barley, that of barley. Consider seeds buried in furrows as though in graves: who gives them roots, provides stalks, leaves, and ears? Is it not the maker and creator of all things? So believe that there will be a resurrection of the dead.

Thus the Apostle says: “For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus” (1 Thess. 4:13). Christ indeed rose from the dead, the first fruits of those who sleep, [Col. 0220C] so that we may believe that by that same power and strength by which he himself rose, he must raise us on the last day. For Christ’s resurrection is the written pledge of the universal resurrection of all. If the resurrection of the dead were not to occur, neither would Christ have risen. Indeed, he rose in order to be found the first fruits of those who sleep. If Christ had not risen, apostolic preaching would be empty; and without doubt our faith too would be empty.

If Christ has not risen, how did the apostles perform signs in his name? And if they did not perform signs, how did a people of Gentiles believe fishermen and unlearned men? But if Christ could not raise himself from death, neither did he bear the sins of the world, nor despoil hell, nor destroy death, nor [Col. 0220D] open paradise; and thus all who have slept in Christ have perished. As all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ. Through Christ’s resurrection all shall rise, because he alone was found without sin. But each shall rise in his own order: Christ the first fruits; then those who belong to Christ, who believed at his coming.

The faithful will rise first on that day, when Christ descends from heaven for judgment, with the voice of the archangel and with the trumpet of God. Those who shine in the merit of righteousness, raised up by the good of mercy, will be caught up into the clouds to meet Christ in the air. But the impious and sinners will await the Judge upon the earth, as defendants, as condemned persons, as those assigned to sulphurous fires. He will descend with trumpet and the voice of the archangel because, throughout the world, he will summon as soldiers to battle those scattered in the dust of the earth, [Col. 0221A] and invite them to the solemnity of eternal glory.

Even those then alive he will, with the swiftest snatching away, change into death and then from death into life. The Greeks, however, think that those who will then be found alive will not die, but will merely be changed from mortality to immortality. They support this by the testimony of Paul’s Epistle to the Corinthians: “We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all sleep” (1 Cor. 15:51), that is, die. But the Latin text has: “We shall not all be changed,” which Ambrose explains as change into the glory of blessedness.

Therefore one should not expect a resurrection of souls, but of the bodies which they themselves inhabited. For if death is nothing else than the separation [Col. 0221B] of soul from body, resurrection will surely be the joining together of both, and the restoration of what has been dissolved and torn apart in every way. Thus the very body that had been scattered and dispersed will be re-formed in a moment.

If the dead do not rise, brute animals would be far superior to us, since they live without sorrow and other painful affections. If immortality is hoped for in vain, then human beings and all else are governed not by divine providence but by chance. Do we not see very many righteous persons in need, hemmed in by distress, possessing no consolation, while sinners and wicked people are wealthy, powerful, and overflowing with delights? Who of sound mind would not suppose this to be the work of just judgment and wise providence?

There will therefore be a resurrection of the dead, because God is just and will render to each according to his deserts. What good did John the Baptist and James, the Lord’s brother—to say nothing of others whose virtue was greatest—have in this age? With what delights did wicked Nero and most evil Herod abound? What sort of God’s justice would this be considered, if a fitting reward were not rendered to both these and those? Yet it cannot be rendered unless the body is restored to the soul. Certainly it is fair that souls which contended for virtue or vice in bodies should receive crowns or torments in those same bodies. [Col. 0221C]

Moreover, an end to such succession and change must be awaited not merely by faith but by a certain necessity. Human nature will not forever flow in and flow out, propagating itself in a straight downward line through those succeeding one another, without an end being found to the succession of children. For every nature of the higher beings, allotted a number within eternity, abides in its own fullness. But human nature is like the higher beings. It is fitting, therefore, that when propagation has been abandoned, it should at some time attain the end of completion. Surely, if it were always engaged in propagation, it would always be deficient, never attaining stability, never finding perfection—things that are of the highest excellence in natures.

Furthermore, if the number of created souls had always to be increased, there would never be a final number for that creation. But if there is no final number, God does not know how many souls he will create. How abominable it plainly is to think this! Human life, therefore, will reach its fullness; its radical stock will wholly stand firm. [Col. 0221D] This is nature’s advancement, when the resurrection of bodies supervenes.

But when nature has necessarily embraced its final limit, another state of life will succeed this life, separate from the life that consists in generation and corruption. Once generation ceases, there will be nothing to be dissolved, since one thing’s generation is another’s corruption. At some time, therefore, the increase in the number of created souls will come to an end. Corruption will altogether cease, and there will follow the hoped-for blessedness of an indissoluble and endless life.

Finally, the prophet Ezekiel speaks of the resurrection of the dead: “Dry bones, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God to these bones: Behold, I will bring spirit into you, and you shall live. And I will cause flesh to grow over you, and will stretch skin over you, and will give you spirit, and you shall live; and you shall know that I am the Lord” (Ezek. 37). Behold, here the prophet openly declares that the resurrection of bodies will occur.

“But,” you say, “a man perished when his ship was wrecked in mid-ocean, and a multitude of fish devoured him. These fish, when caught, were consumed for human use; yet perhaps those who fed upon them were torn apart by wild beasts. The beasts in turn, struck down by hunters’ skill, satisfy the human appetite. By what means, I ask, will that shipwrecked man—who through such varied transformations became nourishment to many living creatures—rise on that dreadful day?”

Why do you say this, man, weaving webs of madness and proposing these matters as though doubtful? Who is he who gathers dust from the ground? Tell me: suppose that he did not fall into the sea, was not devoured by fish, nor the fish by other fish, and these afterward by countless human beings, and so on; but, after the funeral rite had been performed, the dead man was placed in a mausoleum, and neither worms nor anything else caused any harm. How will what is altogether subject to complete dissolution rise? How will ashes and dust gather themselves again? From where will the remaining flower of the body come? Certainly, the resurrection of a body devoured so many times is no more difficult than that of one which has undergone no such alteration.

Why do you marvel, why do you doubt concerning the resurrection? Do you not know that every bodily life comes from corruption? Absolutely every one. All seeds rise into life in the manner described. [Col. 0222A] Do you not see how great a stem the fig has, how great a trunk, how many branches, leaves, and roots sunk deep? All this great visible thing arose, as it were, from a millet grain, after that grain had first rotted. For unless it first decays and is dissolved, none of the things mentioned results.

Likewise the vine, so beautiful, spreading its offspring widely and pleasing to look upon, is born from a lowly berry. That grain is changed not only into wood and vine-shoots, but also into wine and clusters. Let whoever can explain by what means that tiny thing is changed into so great and varied a reality. But no explanation is available.

Consider human seed, which is nearer to you: after conception, by what means is it changed into eyes? How into ears, how [Col. 0223A] into hands, how into the heart? How is it marked out and fitted together in such diverse ways?

Are there not innumerable differences in the body: of shapes, sizes, qualities, positions, powers, and orders? There are also different members: nerves, veins, flesh, arteries, joints, and many other things, whose consideration belongs to physicians—things which constitute our nature from a tiny seed. Does this not seem to you much more open to doubt than that other matter: how what is moist and soft is condensed into bone, which is hard and cold; how into flesh; how into nerve, which is tender and cold? From where are all these things? Explain, if you can.

Do you not doubt such things, though you observe every day resurrection and death in the stages of life? How has youth passed away? From where [Col. 0223B] has old age come? How can one who has grown old not make himself young again? Yet he begets a little child: what he cannot provide for himself, he provides for another without difficulty. This may be seen in trees and animals as well. Yet, according to human reasoning, what one provides for another one ought first to possess oneself.

But where God is the craftsman and creator, every human invention and dispute ceases. Since human understanding is thus dulled over the vine, the fig, and other such things, why do you undertake the business of disputation concerning works that belong to God alone? But you say that what comes to be is the power not of the berry but of the earth. Yet, to speak more truly, what comes to be belongs neither to earth nor seed, but to the Lord of seedtime and soil. Therefore he caused such things to spring up both with seed and without seed. In one case he displayed power; in the other, might, when he said, “Let the earth bring forth green grass.” But by the other work of power he instructs us toward labor and love of cultivation. [Col. 0223C]

These things have been said so that we may in no way doubt the resurrection of our bodies. For there will be a re-forming of bodies not only from earth, but also from the most hidden bosom of the other elements, into which the fallen corpses withdrew: they will be given back and restored in a moment of time. This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Those who are in the tombs shall hear the voice of the Son of God; and those who have done good shall go forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5).

He certainly raised Lazarus and other dead persons in order to create faith in that resurrection which death does not follow. [Col. 0223D] For which is easier: to make something out of what does not exist, or to raise again what has been dissolved? Christ says: “The men of Nineveh shall rise in judgment with this generation and shall condemn it,” etc. (Matt. 12). Isaiah also says: “The dead shall rise, and those who were in the tombs shall rise through the Word made flesh, the Son of Man” (Isa. 65). He himself, certainly, in the form of his humanity, will raise bodies. After the Gospel has first been preached throughout the whole world, he will appear in that same form to all at the judgment; and he will utter the voice by which the dead shall rise and go forth from the tombs.

The angels will bear before him the sign of the cross, as Matthew says: “Then shall appear the sign [Col. 0224A] of the Son of Man.” It should be noted that not Christ alone will judge, but the saints will judge the nations with him. For he himself said to his apostles: “You also shall sit upon twelve seats,” that is, you shall share in the perfection of those judging—namely, of those who, leaving all things, followed Christ (Matt. 19).

Then both good and evil will see the glorified form of Christ which he has as man; but it will appear terrible to the impious and gentle and merciful to the righteous (Matt. 24). Then that great Satan, who had come forth from his confinement for three years and six months to deceive the nations, will lose the power of deceiving and harming, being bound again in the hiding places of his malice and distress.

The Gospel sequence sets forth for us the order of that dreadful judgment: “He will send his angels with a trumpet, and they will gather the elect from the four winds.” And again: “The angels will go out and separate the wicked from among the righteous, and cast them into the furnace of fire.” And likewise: “He will send his angels, who will gather out of his kingdom all scandals, and cast the wicked into the furnace of fire” (Matt. 24). [Col. 0224B]

When the Lord comes for judgment, a fiery river will precede him with great force, like a sea full of winds and boiling; by it the face of the world will burn, and heaven and earth—not in substance, but in form—will perish, and then the sea also. The ether will be dissolved; the stars will fall; the sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon likewise; heaven will be rolled up like a book. Nevertheless, as certain saints maintain, at the judgment the fire will rise only as high as the waters rose in the flood [Col. 0224C]. But that fire will be destruction for the wicked who are found; it will inflict no injury upon the good.

## CHAPTER XXVII

When this purification of the world by fire has been completed, that great voice will be heard by which the dead are restored to life; and at the same time, through the ministry of angels, the threshing-floor will be winnowed and the grain separated from the chaff. For the good will be gathered by angelic ministry from the four quarters of the world, and immediately likewise caught up to meet Christ in the air, while the wicked remain clinging to the earth which they loved. Then those proclamations to the good will be set forth: “I was hungry, and you gave me food”; and those reproaches to the wicked: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food.” [Col. 0224D]

Then indeed the sentence will be pronounced: “Come, blessed ones” (Matt. 25); come, prophets and patriarchs, who were exiles for my name, who obeyed me before I appeared in the flesh, longing for my coming. Come, apostles, who passed through various tribulations with me. Come, martyrs, who did not blush for me before kings and governors, and endured sufferings and torments for my sake. Come, priests, who continually offered my body and blood without stain. Come, saints, who sanctified my name in mountains, caves, and caverns of the earth. Come, you who sold what you possessed and distributed it to the poor. Come, you who believed my words and meditated day and night upon my law, desiring to please me. [Col. 0225A]

Behold, my kingdom is prepared for you. Behold, my paradise is open; crowns of immortality are prepared. Whose mouth can describe those good things which no eyes have seen, no ear heard, and which have not entered into the human heart, which God has prepared for those who love him? Since, therefore, you have known joy without succession, a kingdom without change, delights of good things knowing no end, know also that dreadful voice which the just Judge, in anger and wrath, will pronounce against those on the left: “Depart from me, cursed ones, into eternal fire” (ibid.), which you have prepared for yourselves.

I planted, and another will possess. I brought you forth from the womb, and you despised me. I fed and nourished you, and you would not serve me. I devoted the fullness of earth [Col. 0225B] and sea to your use, and you cast my commands behind your back and provoked me to anger by unspeakable crimes. Go, accursed ones; I do not know you. You have obtained another lord: be with him in the gloom of darkness, where the worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished. I was hungry, I thirsted, I was naked, and you did not look upon me.

The spectacle of life is dissolved; error and illusion have passed away. You forgot me, to whom every knee bends. I am merciful, but I am also a just Judge to all, rendering according to merits, giving each one according to his own work. To all who have fought well, the crown of glory is offered. I would have mercy, but I do not find oil in your vessels. I would have mercy, but while you lived in the world, you did not show mercy. I am moved by mercy, but because your lamps are dark, depart from me. For judgment without mercy comes upon him who has not shown mercy. Go into eternal fire, because the righteous shall go into eternal life.

Behold, I have driven away the clouds of sufferings; and, removing every pain and sorrow far from them, I illuminate them all without end by the splendor of my countenance. [Col. 0225C]

Therefore, O friends, let us despise this present age and place the remembrance of the dreadful judgment in the treasury of our hearts. While it is permitted, let us wipe away the stains of sins by tears of repentance and the efficacy of confession. Let us not cease to weary the merciful Judge with prayers for our dead. Nor in service to the departed should we be bronze, which merely sounds and does not shine, but silver, which gives pleasure both by its brightness and by its ringing, by which it is distinguished.

The mercy of our Redeemer is abundant. Accordingly, through the sacrament of the Lord’s body, prayers, and the benefit of almsgiving, he releases those bound in hell, brings them out, and opens for them the entrances of the heavenly kingdom. For the sacrifice is not offered for the life of the departed in vain; alms are not carelessly poured into the bosom of the poor; prayers are not fruitlessly poured out before God. Indeed, many long ago escaped the torments of hell through such things, as was set forth above; but remedies are bestowed upon those asleep especially through the offering of the unspotted sacrifice. [Col. 0226A]

For when the sacrifice is in the hands, angels and archangels stand by, and even the Son of God himself. Therefore it is a great honor, in the presence of the Lord, to deem those who have died worthy of remembrance, when that dreadful mystery is commemorated: how God gave himself for the world. In this miracle Christ is fittingly and opportunely invoked, that he may grant pardon to those who have departed.

Just as, when the triumph of an imperial victory is celebrated, those who shared in the victory are praised, and those held in chains are also released at that time—yet not everyone obtains remission merely by taking advantage of that interval—so this is the time for suffrages. “As often as you eat this bread,” he says, “you will proclaim the Lord’s death.” Therefore let us not approach casually, nor suppose that these things occur in any ordinary way: it is the Lord whose flesh is touched by hands. Hence this is a most fitting time for obtaining forgiveness for the sins of the dead. [Col. 0226B]

Knowing these things, let us do what we can: let us provide remedies for those who have departed this life; prayers instead of tears, alms instead of mourning, and, instead of adornment of the tomb, offer the living sacrifice, so that they and we may become sharers in inward joy and life without end.

[Col. 0227]

# Three Books of Hugh Eterianus on the Heresies Which the Greeks Direct Against the Latins, or That the Holy Spirit Proceeds from Both, Namely from the Father and the Son: Against the Greeks

*(Bibliotheca Patrum Lugdunensis, vol. XXII, p. 1198.)*

## Letter of Hugh Eterianus to Pope Alexander III

*He prays that the dedication of his book may receive a favorable welcome.*

To ALEXANDER, pontiff of the first see, truly worthy, his most loving father and lord of the ends of the earth, HUGH ETERIANUS offers service with all devotion.

The completed work I have undertaken concerning the immortal God, destined to bring Greece to judgment, flees charges directed against it and foreign inhumanity, so that it may at last be freed from fear. And since it is now unwilling to remain hidden, fearing to be wounded by the swords of combatants, it flies to the most exalted and most approved authority of the Roman height, to beg the clemency of your supreme pontificate that, according to law and right, it may be guarded from its adversaries. These indeed rage violently in offended fury and, envying our trophies, do not honor even the image of our triumphs. But by public decrees and elaborated discourses they strive to destroy them; and with every effort they contend that they may use the narrow limits of the world.

Yet a concern clings to my mind: that the unevenness of my discourse may seem to grow only in its belly, having almost no solid nourishment, like a cucumber. Perhaps the exposition will be deemed thin and headlong, and the conclusions wandering and diffuse in your sight, before which nothing commonplace can appear worthy. Surely, in your judgment, the disciplines of propriety and beauty—disciplines worth the effort of learning—may be thought to fall somewhat short and, through poverty of expression, to lack persuasive splendor. For whom would not the greatness of your wisdom, the refined gravity of your character, and the sharpness of your true judgment terrify? These, indeed, are what philosophers called the highest, indeed the only, goods.

Yet I am not abandoned by hope. I believe that one who has already produced some works ought to be received throughout all the regions of Hesperia: one who, according to the rite of the Latin Church, has set himself against martial men and refuted them as adversaries. I speak of one who freely offers at the Apostolic feet not gold, silver, or precious stones, as most do, but that which surpasses every metal and every stone and can calm the deadly controversy of the Greeks.

Moreover, your singular and most excellent virtue lessens my fear; for, without the introduction of acquaintance by custom, it has won for me your favor, as though sprinkled with the famous stream of Pactolus. Therefore I hope that, by the judgment of your pontificate, after the Medusa’s head has been cut off, any faults removed, and the work rescued from age and oblivion, it will be entrusted to public memorials; so that descendants may gather fruit from it, while the favor of so great a pontiff protects it and preserves it for the use of generations to come.

## Reply of Pope Alexander

[Col. 0227]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Master HUGH, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0229] Recognizing the great labor which you have undertaken in composing the book that you sent us through our beloved Master Caciareda, and considering also the fruit which we hope will accrue from it to the Church of God, we have received the book itself with grateful and joyful hand. For this we render most abundant thanksgivings to your devoted solicitude and generosity. We desire and intend that you, whom until now we have held dear through the reports of our people returning from the regions of Constantinople, should henceforth be loved more fervently, held much dearer, and embraced more sincerely.

We ask and earnestly admonish your prudence that, just as you composed the aforesaid book for God and from devotion to the Church, so also you should, by loving admonitions, urge and by exhortation induce our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious and glorious emperor of Constantinople, to render devotion and reverence to the most holy Roman Church and to its unity; so that, as it ought to be, there may be one fold and one shepherd.

Given at Troy, on the Ides of November.

## Hugh’s Letter to Aimery, Patriarch of Antioch

*He sends him his book on the procession of the Holy Spirit. (About the year 1170.)*

*(D. Martène, Thesaurus Anecdotorum, I, 479, from Clairvaux.)*

[Col. 0229]

[Col. 0229A] To AIMERIC, his most loving lord, by God’s nod and providence most reverend in every respect patriarch of Antioch of the holy apostolic see, HUGH ETERIANUS offers the service of a faithful friend and embraces in spirit him who alone is without change.

The bodies of flower-gathering bees put on tardy wings; and, once they have put them on, sometimes intending to sit at Thyestes’ table and drink the waters of Phlegethon, they flit to foreign nations. They do not understand speech and do all things without command; they seek among individual flowers, but do not take from all; nor do they inflict harm upon any flower. They go out empty and return laden.

The maker of the heavens and of the vast structure beneath them, and the keeper of the archives of unshaken providence, carried me—bearing the likeness of those honey-bearing little creatures—across the Hebrus, Xanthus, and Simoeis, as far as the mouths of the Pontic sea. [Col. 0229B] There, in leafy groves, seeking a hundred mouths and a hundred voices through branching paths, I traced out, as I think, what is truly useful to very many people.

Moreover, the sun, moon, and firmament itself do not run with their utmost swiftness for their own sake alone, but for the preservation of the universe of things. [Col. 0230A] I gathered Cecropian thyme and the galactite stone, which promotes the abundance of nursing breasts; with these, cunning interpretation sought to mix the galbanum-like fragrance of talkative Greece, and wished to send them to silent, watery fish. But the imperial voice of the most learned and intelligent emperor Manuel scattered the poisonous plan and venomous envy, openly declaring that life—than which nothing is better—could by no means be taken from my offspring.

And because this has been drawn from among Greek springs while I dwell at Constantinople in the knowledge of heavenly things, it is entrusted to your learned investigation, unless for the attainment of a third defense, which must be burned by no fire and must not be abandoned through the peril of ending. You will learn its purpose from its title and by repeated reading. Therefore, lest the language of the letter, more prolix than is expedient, delay cultivation longer and deny the harvest, receive with gracious mind the book published by me in both languages, now to be offered through the hand of the most glorious prince Raynald to your profound investigation; and, if you believe the title, give your ears to its volumes—you who have never known how to be satiated by hearing good things. [Col. 0230B]

## Aimery’s Reply to Hugh

*He praises Hugh’s book on the procession of the Holy Spirit, requests other books from him, and sends him a silver cup.*

*(Martène, ibid.)*

[Col. 0229]

[Col. 0229B] AIMERIC, by the grace of God patriarch of Antioch of the holy and apostolic see, to Master HUGH ETERIANUS, [Col. 0230B] beloved son in Christ, greeting and patriarchal blessing.

[Col. 0231A] Since the splendor of your learning now shines serenely upon almost the whole world, we rightly judge that we should rejoice above other Latins. For the nearer we are to the Greeks, the more secure we are made under the protection of your polished learning. Therefore we receive with great gladness of heart the books on the procession of the Holy Spirit which you sent, written both in Greek and in Latin. As soon as we could devote the care of our study to reading them, we greatly admired your genius, eloquence, and manner of expression.

Accordingly, we prefer you to the ancient philosophers of the Gentiles and, unless the majesty of your love is offended by this, compare you with the great teachers of the Church. We have often wished that you would come to us, [Col. 0231B] and we still persist in this same intention; but just as we rejoice at your coming, so it is good for us that you remained where you are. You do not live for yourself alone, but for us and for the universal Church; and on behalf of all Latin Christendom you have placed yourself as a most powerful bulwark. Thus, as we have said, we ought rightly to rejoice, since we have such a mediator, against whom neither learned Greece can stand nor objections fabricated out of sophisms can prevail.

Finally, there are three matters for which we address our request to your love, trusting that you will take pains so that we and all Latin Christendom may benefit, and that this itself may be a monument to the praise of your renown more enduring than bronze. First, we ask for a treatise of St. John Chrysostom on the Epistles of Paul, from which certain persons, attributing very much to themselves rather than to its author, have furtively removed portions. If your labor should sweat over this matter, their presumption would deserve laughter, the theft would be exposed, and the fraudulent claim would yield to greater authority.

Second, we ask for the chronicles held among . . . . from the time when their emperors were divided from the Roman Empire down to our own times. Third, we ask for the proceedings of the Council of Nicaea, which we have heard are in the possession of the lord emperor. If it pleased your love, we would receive these three things as a great gift. [Col. 0232A] We would also repay your labor with double expenses and, for so great a work completed through our prayers, offer you fitting thanksgivings. Nor should we be silent about the past time, in which we know that you have labored effectively for the common good. [Col. 0232B]

We send you one silver cup, from which we wish you to drink both for our love and in our honor. We would have sent you some other things as well, but our messengers unexpectedly set out on their journey so that, in the short time available, we could not prepare them according to our wish.

## Hugh’s Preface

[Col. 0231]

[Col. 0231C] Once Moses, descending into Egypt after converse with God, when he was thought to possess every branch of learning and held the rod of God in his hand, wished to take with him his foreign wife together with the two pledges of his offspring. Under the figure of this narrative, therefore, when one enters, by whatever necessity, into a controversy of theology, one must take up the subtlety of pagan philosophers’ arguments as though taking up shield and sword for battle. One must arrange inductions and syllogisms if one wishes to offer a demonstration worthy of belief concerning the most difficult and primary philosophy.

Nevertheless, the spurious offspring of this subtlety must be cut away by the delimitation proper to their nature, by which alien things are recognized. This is suitably done if Zipporah—that is, “keenness of beauty”—shows Gershom, indeed, to be a stranger to the world, and shows Eliezer—that is, “God my helper”—to have God as his helper. [Col. 0231D]

Eager to advance along this path, and compelled to speak of that philosophy which is believed to be above every philosophy, I have adopted for the course of the present disputation certain arguments from Attic learning, cutting away their harmful, impure, and alien contamination, because they are very necessary. For I suppose that such foreign materials will greatly assist and make clear what must be said, if they are easy, commonplace, and few.

Physicians report that if a large quantity of pepper is taken, it affects the bladder and stirs up bile; but when its quantity is moderated by smallness, it loosens the bowels and becomes a health-giving medicine. [Col. 0232C] Yet when I undertake to taste the beginning of supreme philosophy, I seem like an aquatic tortoise wishing to swim across seas: thought is besieged by stupor, the mind wastes away, and the tongue is delayed as though it had tasted the Egyptian palm, which among the Greeks is called *adiperos* [reading uncertain]. The understanding as a whole simply falters, as though it had encountered the most overwhelming of sensible things.

Moreover, the relation of fire or iron to diamond is feeble: the diamond overcomes iron, stubbornly resistant to engraving, and therefore has not yet been found conquerable by fire [Col. 0232D]. Yet I judge that it is incomparably harder and more difficult to write concerning the divine, which transcends not only sense but every intellect. And therefore I wished to linger about these recesses, like an unwar-like soldier trembling at the prospect of battle; and, lest I should seem lucid in a meagre style, to avoid the difficulty, magnitude, and fragrance of so great a matter, as Libyan serpents avoid rue (*piganum*). But while I was at Constantinople, I was summoned for consultation by the great and most august Emperor Manuel, as to whether the Latins possessed any authorities of the saints [Col. 0233A] asserting that the Holy Spirit is from the Son. When I came before him, after unraveling on either side the many-guaranteed knots of the questions, I finally gave that great emperor an answer suited to imperial majesty: firm in authority, weighty in dignity, and close to the best arguments. I brought forward Basil, Athanasius, and Cyril—great lamps of faith, each in his own right—asserting procession from the Son. And because I then perceived the serenity of the empire to be intent upon the sacredness of the divine disputation, to examine closely the covering of words, and to be equal to resolving the most weighty labyrinths of controversy, a strong desire entered me to treat this most lofty matter more carefully. To this was added the repeated and frequent urging of Hugh of Ostia [Col. 0233B] and Bernard of Porto, great bishops, as also of John, the venerable cardinal of Saints John and Paul. Nevertheless, many things drew me to write on these matters: the controversy boiling between Greeks and Latins. The Greek is indeed a vehement defender of the proposition that the Spirit [Col. 0234A] proceeds from the Father alone; the Latin, however, professes that the same Spirit proceeds equally from Father and Son. Therefore, although I am not sufficient to unfold fully the beauty of the truth in so great a matter—for not everything that is kindled bursts forth into flame—yet, with God’s help, I shall first set forth the purpose of the Latin assertion. Then I shall attempt, according to my ability, to repel and refute, by arguments, examples, and authorities, the Greek contentions together with their accusations against the Latins.

But the case will be given support from its consequences, from such common conceptions as may be discovered, and from Scripture inspired by God. Finally, I shall add demonstrative syllogisms from the testimonies of the holy shepherds of the Church, sought for a long time at Constantinople [Col. 0234B], which most strongly give assent and support to the Latin doctrine and confirm the tenor of its faith. For by their induction, I think, it may be considered more easily and directly to which side truth favors peace.

# BOOK I

[Col. 0233]

# CHAPTER I

[Col. 0233B]

[Col. 0233C]

> **Note:** [Col. 0233D] Although Hugh was orthodox and learned, these following three books should be read cautiously and with judgment; for in certain places he seems to depart from the theologians’ proper and exact norm of speech, especially in that he very often calls the Father the cause of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

The blessed and immortal Trinity, which became plainly known to the apostles through Jesus Christ, so far as was possible, the philosophers of the nations proclaimed while concealing it under exceedingly dark riddles. For the philosopher Plato wrote such things concerning the Trinity to Dionysius:

> **Note:** [Col. 0223D] In the second letter to Dionysius I would read as follows: “I must speak to you now in certain riddles, lest—if these tablets sent by sea or land should happen to be intercepted—the reader understand it. The matter is this: Around the King of all are all things, and for his sake are all things; and he is the cause of all good things. Around the second are second things, and around the third, third things.”

“Therefore I must speak to you in riddles, so that if this tablet should suffer some mishap in the folds of sea or land, the reader may not understand. For it stands thus concerning the King of all: all things are around him, and all things are for his sake, and he is the cause of all good things; the second is around second things, and the third around third things.”

The Greek reads:

> **Φραστέον δή σοι δι’ αἰνιγμῶν, ἵν’ αὕτη ἡ δέλτος ἢ πόντου, ἢ γῆς ἐν πτυχαῖς πάθῃ, ὁ ἀναγνοὺς μὴ γνῷ. Ὧδε γὰρ ἔσχει περὶ τὸν πάντων βασιλέα. Πάντα ἐστὶ, καὶ ἐκείνου ἕνεκα πάντα, καὶ ἐκεῖνο αἴτιον ἁπάντων τῶν καλῶν· δεύτερον δὲ περὶ τὰ δεύτερα, καὶ τρίτον περὶ τὰ τρίτα.**
>
> “I must speak to you in riddles, lest, if this tablet should meet with some fate in the folds of sea or land, its reader understand. For this is how it stands concerning the King of all: all things are around him, and all things are for his sake; and he is the cause of all good things. The second is around second things, and the third around third things.”

Which, rendered into Latin speech, reads thus: “It must be spoken to you through riddles, lest the book, whether in tablets of sea or land, should suffer, and the reader understand not. For it is so concerning the King of all: he is all things, and all things are for him; and he himself is the cause [Col. 0233D] of all good things; the second, around second things; and the third, around third things.”

Plotinus likewise set forth similar statements. “There are,” he says, “three things beyond time and eternal: the Good, Intellect, and the Soul of the universe.” Among us these are the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, whom the philosophers called the soul of the world. But Timaeus of Locri seems to have been ignorant of the Trinity, as though professing a solitary God: “There is one unbegotten [Col. 0234B] principle of all things. For if it were begotten, it would not be a principle without beginning, but that from which it proceeded would be so.” [Col. 0234C] Here he makes no mention of the Son or Spirit. This principle is regarded not only as the exalted God, invisible and incorporeal, but by Christians as the Father, existing alone without cause and without beginning. From him the Son is generated immediately and directly, in accordance with the fruitful power of the begetter. With the Son as intermediary, the Spirit proceeds from the same Father, from his inexhaustible and boundless cause. Therefore the Son is from a cause, and the Holy Spirit is from a cause.

For the clarification of what is to be said, the difference among things proceeding from causes—an obscure matter, loving a misty volume—must here be distinguished briefly. Some things flow forth and remain, as a ray and light from the sun, and fragrance from musk and balsam. Others flow forth altogether and do not remain [Col. 0234D], as a spark struck from stone, and lightning from clouds. Others remain together and are not separated from that in which they are: hearing, smell, taste, touch, and also sight, according to Aristotle. None of these admits number together with its principle, nor is marked by any personal distinction in itself, being inseparable from its cause. Therefore that which, in proceeding, does not remain with its cause is incapable of union with it, as the example of the spark and lightning shows.

Every sort of procession completely separates effects from their causes and carries them farther from those causes. But things that proceed and at the same time remain always touch their causes and adhere to them more closely, because they behold their principle at close range. This is the mode of proceeding that seems least alien to the Son and Holy Spirit: the Father, because of the fruitful power he possesses, multiplying himself from his own substance, produces without change or alteration the person of the Son by generation and the person of the Spirit by procession. For the Father is neither changed into them nor diminished; and rightly so, since neither the Son [Col. 0235B] nor the Holy Spirit is derived from him by any division. They are equally and indivisibly one cause of all visible and invisible things, just as they are one God.

These three persons are one—not by participation in unity. Since they are one before all ages, they do not become one, because that which exists does not become what it already exists as. If the divine were made, it would either have begun to be made with time or through the beginning of time, and would have had something before itself. But if it neither began nor had anything before itself, it is clear that it always was and always will be. Hence nothing is prior to God, who is truly one—as is said—not united, not finite, and not distinct from one. Since he is infinite, eternal, and simple, nothing can accrue to him, nor can anything belonging to his essence perish, nor can what is not come to be.

The Father, then, is the immediate begetter of the Son, who is equal to the powerful begetter and possesses equal power. Likewise, according to the Latin assertion, the Father emits the Spirit from himself. For they say that although Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one—one unity, one substance, one principle—the Father is nevertheless called the cause or principle of the Son by paternal authority, that is, insofar as he gives being and begets; and he is called the cause or principle of the Holy Spirit insofar as he gives being and emits him. In this they judge that the Father differs not at all from the Son; and thus, according to them, the Son is from the Father, while the Holy Spirit proceeds from Father and Son.

For they say [Col. 0235D]: “If the Spirit had his procession from only one of the two, he would not belong equally and without distinction to both, but especially to the one from whom he proceeded. But the Spirit belongs equally and without distinction to both: he is not less the Son’s and more the Father’s. Therefore the Spirit does not have his procession from only one of the two.”

Again they say: “Everything that proceeds from something, through however many things it advances, is joined to as many and receives as many common relations, as appears in logic. For the most general genus is said to be without a principle, without a cause, and the cause of all things under it, though it is not the only existing thing and principle. For subordinate causes of species also exist; yet only the nearest substance is the cause and principle, while of an animate body not only the most general but also the subordinate genus is a principle and cause.” Things belonging to a similar order do not reject this condition. Likewise, in natural things matter is understood to be without principle and without cause. Form too, together with matter, is a cause and principle of material things.

But the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son; therefore the Holy Spirit is joined to the Son, receiving something from him as he advances and proceeds through him. The similarity between the two compels us to confess the same thing. For the Spirit is like the Son insofar as he is from a cause, from his immediate principle: as he communicates immediately with that principle, so he proceeds from it without intermediary and through it is joined to the Father [Col. 0236B]. Whatever in its procession receives an intermediary receives through that intermediary something for union and communion with its, so to speak, primary cause. Hence no one ought to doubt that the Spirit’s communion with the Father is referred through the Son. Thus it is evident that the Word of God the Father is in no way external to such fellowship.

The Spirit remains in the Father and remains also in the Son; he proceeds from the Father and proceeds also from the Son. For what proceeds again from one in whom it remains is not wholly inseparable, having once acquired division, but is entirely distinct from him. Yet the Spirit has an explicitly personal communion with the Son, and, flowing from him, remains in him. Certainly, if he only remained and did not proceed, he would not be personally distinct from his principle, nor would he be understood as another person. Therefore the Spirit both remains in and proceeds from the Son. For just as every sort of distinction destroys identity and communion, so every sort of remaining together and union removes the distinction of persons. From this it seems plainly evident that the Spirit, remaining in the Son as belonging properly to him, proceeds and goes forth from him as from the Father.

# CHAPTER II

But the Greek theologians strive by every means to destroy this with the objection that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone. They all agree in this opinion, although no holy Father has clearly asserted [Col. 0236D] that the Spirit does not proceed from the Son. What, then, is the method of knowing that he does not proceed from the Son? How can Theodoret—the inventor and herald of this negation—appear competent by promulgating what has nowhere been written? How can anyone dare to establish this, when none of the holy Fathers has asserted it, when it has been revealed to no one? Yet those whom the modern age has produced proclaim in their books, as though they were the strictest guardians of justice, that the Spirit does not proceed from the Son. They also bring forward very many apparent refutations to demonstrate this position.

# CHAPTER III

For the bishop of Nicomedia frames and entwines this syllogism [Col. 0237A] in this manner: “If the Holy Spirit proceeds from Father and Son, then what proceeds from certain things has the principles from which it proceeds. Therefore the Holy Spirit has two principles.”

Nicholas, bishop of Methone, frames a refutation in nearly the same sense: “If the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son, then there will indeed be a unity from duality and two principles of one thing. For the Holy Spirit is one, as the Father is one and the Son is one; but Father and Son are not one, but two, although they are one in nature. For one is one person and the other another, although they are not one thing and another thing. Yet the principles of all things are first in God and are distributed by him to all things. Therefore every unity discerned in things will arise from duality, and duality will be the principle of unity”—which is absurd and contrary to the common conception according to which the one and unity are prior to duality and every number, because unity is the principle of duality and of every number. And very many others infer the same thing as though from truths suddenly familiar, though by no means plausibly.

# CHAPTER IV

For it is not possible to syllogize falsely from truths. Everything demonstrated from truths is true; but although this antecedent is true, the assumption and conclusion are full of falsehood. The conclusion does not follow with syllogistic necessity, since what is shown by the propositions does not follow from them. For the statement laid down in the assumption—I mean, “what proceeds from certain things has the principles from which it proceeds”—is both curtailed [Col. 0237C] and indeterminate. It may be referred to the ten categories, so that what is said means: “What proceeds from certain substances, or qualities, or quantities,” and similarly with each of the other categories. Or it may again be understood to mean that what proceeds from certain principles or causes has the causes and principles from which it proceeds.

But Aristotle reduces such indeterminacy to a determinate form in the *Analytics*, saying: “The things from which a demonstration proceeds ought to be of the same kind. Where their genus is different—as arithmetic and geometry—it is not fitting to adapt an arithmetical demonstration to attributes of magnitudes, unless the magnitudes are numbers. For the extremes and middle terms must be of the same genus [Col. 0237D]. Therefore it is not possible, by geometry, to show that there is one science of contraries. Hence it is clear,” he says, “that one cannot demonstrate each thing simply, but from the principles of each thing.” By “principles in each genus” I mean those things whose existence it is not fitting to demonstrate.

Alexander, commenting on the same chapter, says: “He no longer takes the premise generally, but adds: ‘If he speaks of numbers, [he speaks of] numbers.’ For he says: ‘If equal numbers are taken from equal numbers.’ By adding the genus, he makes what is common proper. Likewise, if magnitudes are taken from magnitudes, and similarly in other cases.” For this is the principal proposition: “In demonstrations, all terms must be of the same genus [Col. 0238A].” One must not pass from one genus to another in the things demonstrated.

Therefore, since the discussion concerns divine persons, the major premise that is introduced—“what proceeds from certain things has the principles from which it proceeds”—can have no meaning except: “What proceeds from certain divine persons has the principles from which it proceeds.” This is plainly false. For Father and Son, from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds, are not simply two things. They are not properly two things, but one; not two substances, but one; not two principles, but one; not two gods, lords, or holy beings, but one God, one Lord, one Holy One. Hence it is clear that Father and Son are called two only in a qualified respect: namely, two persons, two hypostases. Therefore, since these two persons are not two principles, nor simply two things, it is evident that whatever proceeds from them does not proceed from two principles, even if it be posited and granted that the Spirit proceeds from both. And therefore it is impossible to infer that Father and Son are two principles.

The introduction of examples will also certainly show this argument to be false, if in this matter it is permitted to use comparisons for dispersing the darkness of obscurities, clarifying truth, destroying paralogisms, and aiding and refreshing readers—as painters use many-colored streaks to decorate and beautify paintings. Indeed, there seems to be a certain necessity of using comparisons, both so that veils may be torn by varied diversity and the fruit of public good may appear, and so that discourse—fond of the luxuriance of a flowering field and impatient of sameness—may not grow sluggish. Behold: the same substance may be called seed, fruit, and food: seed with reference to the earth that bears it; fruit with reference to the harvest that has passed; food insofar as it is transformed into the substance of the body. Yet I do not think it can rightly be inferred that, if food proceeds from seed and fruit, it therefore proceeds from two principles.

> **Note:** [Col. 0237D] Observe these examples, and beware of Sabellius.

For seed and fruit are not two except in conception. So too ascent and descent: namely, the route from Thebes to Athens and from Athens to Thebes. The stretch of road in both is one; it is downward upward, and upward downward [Col. 0238D], but the conception differs. For the person beginning here it is an ascent, while for the person beginning there it is a descent. Thus Father and Son are both one principle of the Holy Spirit. Yet it does not follow that the Father is the Son, or the Son the Father, or that both are two principles. For neither does the fact that the length of the route from Athens to Thebes is one, and likewise from Thebes to Athens, make ascent descent, or conversely; nor do ascent and descent become two roads or two journeys. Rather, there is one road and one journey.

But perhaps, as has been said, support from comparisons should not be supplied for this matter. For Gregory the Theologian seems to forbid this in his discourse on the Spirit, saying: “One must not compare the divine nature with any of the things below. Even if some small likeness is found, what is greater escapes it. Leaving myself below, I conceived a vein, a spring, and a river as an illustration. For perhaps one would make this the Father, that the Son, and the other likewise the Spirit. For these are neither separated in time nor divided from one another by continuity, and they seem in some manner to be divided by three properties. But I feared, first, that I might accept a certain flow in the Godhead, which has no stability [Col. 0239A]. Second, I feared lest by this likeness one thing in number should be introduced; for vein, spring, and river are one thing in number, transformed in different ways.

“Again I considered the sun, ray, and light; but here too there is fear: first, lest some composition be understood in the nature that has no composition, as of the sun and the things in the sun. Second, lest we make the Father substance and the Son and Spirit other powers of God, inhering but not subsisting. For the ray and brightness are not another sun, but certain emanations and substantial qualities of the sun; and through the comparison we would attribute to God both being and not-being. Therefore, if the likeness is preserved in the Trinity, the Father alone will be called substance, while the Son and Spirit will be qualities or properties of the Father.”

So much for that. But the man who calls Father and Son a duality because the Spirit proceeds from both, and who denies the Son the principle of emission, thinks that the Father alone should be called the principle of the Spirit. Hence, if the Son emits the Spirit while not being a principle of emitting him, that is absurd. Still more absurd is it if the principle of one should be understood in the other and not each one’s own proper emission. But if such a principle is recognized equally in Father and Son, he again says that the absurd consequence follows: namely, that duality precedes unity and is its principle [Col. 0239C].

# CHAPTER V

This man seems not to attend to what must especially be considered in the Trinity: namely, that unity is attributed only to nature, while duality is attributed to any two persons. Therefore it is not true that, if the Spirit proceeds from Son and Father, unity proceeds from duality [Col. 0239D]. For nature, which is understood as unity, is in no way asserted to proceed from anything; nor is the Spirit, understood personally, ever called unity, unless perhaps the term be used improperly.

Again, when he says that the principles of things are in God, the name “God” there does not signify the person of Father or Son, but substance and nature, or, to speak simply, the Trinity. The name “duality,” however, applies only to persons. But the term “principle,” when it is said that Father and Son are one principle of the Holy Spirit, does not signify a single personal property, but one common to Father and Son: simple, not twofold. This appears true from what is considered concerning the persons of Father and Son. For although the Father is and is called an unbegotten [Col. 0240A] principle, and the Son a begotten principle; although the Father is an unbegotten cause and the Son a begotten cause; nevertheless they are by no means regarded by anyone as two causes or two principles, but as one. Therefore, if the unbegotten and the begotten are truly one principle, they are not distinct principles of the Spirit.

Thus it can be clear from what has been said that neither the Father, insofar as he is Father, is properly called one or unity, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit; rather, each is “one, one, one,” not three nor two. Therefore Son and Father are not properly called a duality, since they are not two, as has been shown. For the fact that Father and Son are called two in a qualified respect does not make them simply two. Nor does unity arise from duality. Duality may in some manner be referred to persons, but unity, as has been shown, pertains to nature [Col. 0240B].

# CHAPTER VI

[lacuna] It must be feared lest, when disputing about divine things, we be compared to fire and snow, one of which—as the philosopher says—burns without knowing why, while the other cools without observing the cause. There is no doubt that God alone possesses perfect knowledge and that what has been said belongs to him alone: the wise person ought not to be commanded, but to command, as knowing the first things and the last. God’s knowledge is not only cognizant of all things but effective of every good thing; but human knowledge is in some persons merely superficial, and perfective in none, because it belongs to contemplation, not action.
