Before it reaches the sum [Col. 0240C] of the matter, it fails away; before it unfolds it, it gives out; and it suffers miscarriage before it gives birth.

Nevertheless, the most beneficial knowledge of God abundantly supplies human beings with the nourishment of instruction and study, distributing according to the worthiness of those receiving, without respect of persons. God’s goodness and power extend to everything capable of receiving them; they extend, I say, through the Son, whom the Father alone generates. Therefore he belongs to the Father alone and is so called; and they extend through the Spirit also, who does not belong to the Father alone and is not emitted by the Father alone. This is what he seeks entirely to demonstrate.

For no incorporeal thing which comes from one without a principle through an intermediary is devoid of a relation to that intermediary—or to intermediaries, if there are several intermediaries through one intermediary. For everything proceeding in this way derives something from each intermediary and, together with the one without beginning, is a principle of what proceeds from itself [Col. 0240D], as is clear from logical methods. But in the Holy Trinity the Son is intermediate between Father and Spirit. Therefore the Son together with the Father is the principle of the Holy Spirit. For the three divine persons always have the same order, since they have no relation to all other things and are unmixed.

Therefore, since every division is absent from the blessed Trinity—in which there is no falling away, no inequality, no disparity—the Spirit must be joined to the Father through the one intermediary, namely the Son. Otherwise the continuity of the three persons would not be preserved according to personal procession. But where continuity is absent, division intervenes. If division is granted in the Trinity, then the Spirit, who is a person, is wholly separated from the Son [Col. 0241A]. For if the Spirit is joined to the Father alone, he is foreign to the Son and belongs in no way to his property—just as one who dwells in a building does not thereby belong to the building. But the chain of continuity must extend as far as the Spirit.

For if the Spirit is the Son’s and the Son does not emit him, the Son appears thereby powerless and unlike the Father, who emits the same Spirit. Indeed, the Spirit too would be weak if, being the Son’s and in the Son, he could not proceed from him. Therefore the Spirit proceeds from the Son and does not, in his procession from the Son, depart more from the Father than he does from the Son, since he exists through both. For both are his cause of existence, enduring without defect and without diminution.

The Spirit of the Father, who is proper to the Son and fills all things, is sufficient for Father and Son; for if Phoebus’ light is sufficient for the sun and its ray, much more is the Spirit sufficient for Father and Son. Therefore this Spirit does not seek change, since he is in the best condition; nor passage elsewhere, since he finds all things in himself; nor does he demand increase, since he is supreme perfection and all things are perfect in him. He has nothing added to him, but eternally possesses all things, as the Spirit of Father and Son, emanating equally from both. What flow forth from him are called his operations or graces; by their warmth we are made alive and ripened though very bitter. When made alive and ripened, we become sweet.

God the Father gives life, as the Apostle says: “I charge you in the sight of God, who gives life to all things” [Col. 0241C] (1 Tim. 6). The Son also gives life: “My sheep,” he says, “hear my voice, and I give them eternal life” (John 10). The Spirit also gives life, as it is written: “The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6). The Apostle testifies that he is the Son’s: “May the peace of Christ, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts” (Phil. 4). The peace of Christ surpassing all understanding should be understood as nothing other than his Spirit; whoever obtains it will be filled with every good thing and every abundance of delights.

Therefore the Son, while remaining Son, possesses the Spirit of the Father, just as he possesses all things proper to the begetter. But it is proper to the one who begot to emit the Spirit. Therefore the Word of God, who is Son by nature and not by appointment, likewise emits the Spirit of the begetter. But if this is not so, he does not possess at all what is proper to the one who begot him. Yet no one should suppose that the Son’s being able to beget is included here among what is proper to the Father, because I have said that the Son possesses everything proper to the Father. Every individual may indeed receive what is proper to its species, but it will never itself be the species [Col. 0241D].

Those who say these things do not honor the Son as they honor the Father, asserting that the Son would be the Father if everything which the Father has were also possessed by the Son. It is clear, however, that the Son possesses the Spirit in himself just as the Father does, because the Father did not first generate him and then give him the Spirit—as any other giver gives something to a person who has long existed. Rather, just as giving him life meant generating him living, so giving him the Spirit meant generating him as possessing the Spirit [Col. 0242A]. If this were not so, the Son was first generated and afterward, in time, received the Spirit.

Therefore, just as there are the terms “life” and “living,” “judge” and “truth,” so there are “giver” and “emitter” of the Spirit. For although the Son disavows his own will, even though the Father’s will is clearly his, when he says, “I do not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 5), nowhere is he found to have said anything similar concerning the Spirit. Nowhere is it written that he said, “The Spirit of the Father is not mine, nor does he proceed from me.” It is thus entirely clear that the Spirit belongs equally to him and to the Father.

There should therefore be no doubt that the Spirit is the Son’s and is from him. Nor should one infer from this that he has two principles or two causes. The metropolitan of Nicomedia does not syllogize correctly when he says: “If the Father is the cause of the Spirit’s emission, and the Son also is a cause because the Spirit proceeds from him as from the Father, then there are again two causes, just as there are two principles.” Perhaps the falsity of this paralogism’s conclusion will be clear from the following. Every created thing composed of elements has some cause: the Father, in order that it may exist; and the Son, because all things were made through him. It cannot be denied that both are causes. Therefore there are two causes and two principles of every such creature. But that this conclusion does not follow was shown above, where it was stated that Father and Son are called two in a qualified sense and not simply; and therefore Father and Son are one operator.

For we hear the Savior say through John [Col. 0242C]: “My Father works until now, and I work.” They are not two workers but one, just as they are one God and one Creator. Were all things made through the Son apart from the Father? Far from it. For it is written: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” And again: “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created; he set a commandment, and it shall not pass away” (Gen. 1). This is the greatest power. For just as speaking and commanding are easy for anyone, so for God it was more ready—and much more easily accomplished—to make things that did not exist and to preserve things made. “The sea is his, and he made it.” The same is written concerning the Son: “In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands” [Col. 0242D] (Heb. 1). It does not say, “Through you the heavens were made and the earth founded,” but, “You made the earth, and heaven is your work.” Behold, it is clear that Father and Son create: they are not two creators, two principles, or two causes, but one cause.

Therefore, since Father and Son are not two principles or two causes of creatures, much less will they be reckoned two causes or two principles of the Holy Spirit, who differs from them by reason of his procession and belongs equally to each. It should also be observed that “cause,” “principle,” “begotten,” “proceeding,” and similar terms are not features of nature or substance, but are reverent and careful inquiries concerning persons and certain most sacred marks. This is clearer from the first creation of living creatures. For the first living creatures were made and created by command [Col. 0243A], not by generation. They did not proceed from like things, since no such things previously existed. Thus, although unbegotten, they can nevertheless, like those derived from them, rightly be called begotten only in a qualified sense. Hence unbegottenness and begottenness are not offspring of animal nature, because they are not present alike in all animals as properties belonging substantially to animals by birth, and because both are never found in the same animal—namely, begotten and unbegotten.

Therefore, since Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one cause and one principle of every creature, alike and unlike, much more, in their own proper order, Father and Son—being immediate, proper, and unique causes of the same Spirit—are without doubt one cause or one principle [Col. 0243B]. Moreover, the Father alone is the cause of the Son. If the Son stood apart from the Father in emitting the Spirit, he would not be equal to the Father in possessing the same Spirit by an undifferentiated relation. But the Spirit is possessed equally and without distinction by both; therefore the same Spirit is emitted equally and without distinction by both. Otherwise the Father would not be so much similar according to the image as differently endowed, if the emission of the Spirit were foreign to him—which is absurd. For like things are joined by likeness, not by unlikeness. As unlikeness separates all things and makes them distant, so likeness—whether substantial or non-substantial—joins and unites them. Therefore the Spirit is joined to the Son because he is like him, as his image; and this image indicates communion, union, and likeness [Col. 0243C].

Moreover, from the harmony and likeness which the Spirit has with the Son, He has received this same name, being called Paraclete. “I will ask the Father,” He says, “and He will give you another Paraclete” (John 14). For the Father is not called Paraclete, but the Spirit and the Son are; and this name appears at least to be common to them equivocally. John the theologian, not unaware of this community, wrote in his First Epistle (ch. 2): “If anyone has sinned, we have a Paraclete with the Father, Jesus Christ.” Yet in the same manner we have the Spirit as Paraclete, interceding with the Father for us, as does the Son—although these statements [Col. 0243D] may seem to have been expressed in human fashion and according to the economy. For they have nothing added or superimposed, since, in that they are God, they eternally possess the principles of all things. Therefore the Spirit is like the Son, and the Son like the Father—but not in the manner imagined by certain heretics.

For some, holding a perverse doctrine, supposed that Father and Son were alike in species but unlike in substance; and therefore they made the Son of God composite from opposites, namely likeness and unlikeness. With them dwell not only the ruin of impiety, but detestable absurdities follow them. For if He were composed of like and unlike, He would not be simple, nor wholly light, wholly truth, and wholly God by nature; and something would be understood as prior and more ancient than Him. For the conjunction of simple things produces composites, which are prior to the things constituted from them and older by nature. But the Son is from the substance of the Father: simple from the simple, like from the like, and equal from the equal. Yet the Son is in the Father, and there is nothing in the Father Himself prior to Him or apart from Him. Therefore the very emission of the Spirit is not without the Son.

## CHAPTER VII

But Nicetas of Byzantium, the philosopher, strives to prove by adducing absurd consequences that the Spirit does not proceed from the Son, and that there is something in and from the Father without the Son. For he maintains that the Spirit proceeds from the Father while the Word in no way shares in this. [Col. 0244B] “If,” he says, “as some acknowledge, the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, since it is most plainly and truly known to us from theological teaching that the Spirit proceeding from the Father is given through the Son, rests in the Son, and is also united with the Father; but, according to them, also proceeds from the Son, then it is surely necessary that, in the manifestation and distribution of the Spirit from Him, the Son should be given by the Son. But if this is so, He will be the Son’s son and will therefore be called a grandson. And again, according to their nonsense concerning the grandson, a great-grandson will appear; and he in turn will need another; and this will continue to infinity. Therefore, according to their vanity, the Spirit does not proceed from the Son as from the Father. From this it is plainly apparent that the Spirit is from the Father alone, as the Church throughout the whole world has rightly taught from long ago until the present day.” [Col. 0244C] But that this too is not correctly said can easily be seen.

## CHAPTER VIII

First, because the argument has not been syllogistically constructed. For the major proposition, which says, “Whatever emits the Spirit has a Son,” ought to be universal, but it is taken as particular. For the proposition which is the basis of the inferred conclusion and which ought rightly to complete such a syllogism is this: “Everything that emits the Spirit has a Son.” This is indemonstrable and impossible, because it is neither a self-evident principle nor receives its credibility from any such principle.

The emission of the Spirit does not make one Father or Son, since the Spirit’s procession from the Father is not generation, [Col. 0244D] by which alone the Son differs from the Father. For in the emission of the Spirit and in all other respects, the Father appears to communicate with the Son and, together with Him, to emit the Spirit from His own substance. But substance itself neither emits, nor generates, nor is generated. Whatever belongs to the divine substance according to nature belongs to every Person. Thus, if substance were generative, both the Son and the Spirit would surely generate—nothing could be further from the truth. Hence it is clear that the Father generates the Son from His substance not insofar as He is substance, but insofar as He is Father, and according to this relation. If He did not generate from His own substance, He would not at all be called Father according to nature; yet in generating from His substance He makes no separation.

For that substance is not a body; rather, as light does not acquire its radiance from without but pours it forth from its own substance, so the Father does not have the Son from without, but begets Him from His own substance while remaining undivided. [Col. 0245A] Therefore He is truly Father, “from whom all fatherhood is named.” Accordingly, the Persons must not be believed or conceived as existing without substance, as though the individual character of Persons could be understood without any substance. For the singular character of the Persons is observed, through distinctive properties, in relation to one and the same substance. Substance is not naturally fitted to produce such a character; whereas the emission of the Spirit is neither a distinctive property nor an individual character.

That this is manifest is clear from the fact that emitting the Spirit is not the distinctive mark of the one Person of the Father. For the Father emits the Spirit not insofar as He is Father, but insofar as He is cause or principle.

> **[Note: Col. 0245D]** Hugh, when dealing with the Greeks, sometimes—and indeed rather often in this work—employs their manner of speaking, for whom “cause” and “principle” are altogether the same. But the Latin Fathers rightly recognize “principle” in the Trinity *ad intra*, while they do not similarly affirm “cause.” They call the Father and the Son the principle of the Holy Spirit, not His cause, for the excellent reasons collected by St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, I, q. 33, art. 1.

This can be seen as follows. If the Spirit does not proceed from the Father as begotten, the Father does not emit the Spirit as begetter. For if the Father emitted the Spirit insofar as He is begetter, the Spirit would proceed from the Father as begotten. But the Spirit is not from the Father as begotten, since the Father is believed to have not two sons but one only. It is therefore clear that the Father does not emit the Spirit as begetter.

Further: since the Father is emitter of the Spirit, He emits Him either in that by which He differs from the Son, or according to that in which He does not differ. But He does not emit Him in that by which He differs. For the Father does not emit the Spirit in that alone in which He differs from the Son. [Col. 0245C] Likewise, John’s Gospel—and Chrysostom also—seems to confirm what has been said. Where the Savior says, “My Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father” (John 5), Chrysostom says: “Shall we then call Him the Father Himself? Far from it! For this reason He said ‘the Son,’ that we may honor the Son remaining Son as we honor the Father. But whoever calls Him the Father has not honored the Son as Father, but has confused everything.” And shortly afterwards: “Whatever the Father is, that is the Son, begotten and remaining in the being of Son.”

According to this holy man’s understanding, I say: the Father emits the Spirit; therefore so does the Son. Whoever removes this from the Son does not honor Him [Col. 0245D] as the Father. Hence it is plainly understood that the Father emits the Spirit not in that by which He differs from the Son, but in that which He communicates.

But here one must consider that, although the Father differs from the Son and from the Spirit, and conversely, they nevertheless have very few differences from one another, because the abundance of what they share according to nature is exceedingly great. Therefore, in my judgment, it cannot be inferred that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three gods, because what is considered in relation to nature is exceedingly extensive, whereas what pertains to the properties is very limited. In created things, especially animals, the opposite is apparent. For animals differ in movement, appetite, actions, wills, time, place, and many other respects.

Hence the following argument is not rejected: Socrates is a man, Peter is a man, and John is a man; but John is not Peter, nor Peter Socrates; therefore they are three men. But in the divine Persons there are three immutable properties: fatherhood, sonship, and procession. By these alone the three Persons—namely Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are distinguished. These properties are not observed now in these Persons, now in others; nor at one time in more and at another in fewer; but always in the same Persons. These Persons neither receive increase, so as to become four, [Col. 0246B] nor diminution, so as to be reduced to two, since they are equally one God without change.

For if several men who are one in species are one [thing], much more fittingly are three Persons proclaimed one God by pure faith and undefiled religion. One must not ask how they are three, since they are utterly and completely inseparable; for persons weak in faith are harmed in such inquiries, as the Apostle says. For it is a sickness of the soul to inquire maliciously and idly concerning God. Rather, one who approaches God must believe the things declared and made manifest by the saints, and not investigate by arguments what they are not.

Now, just as all the faithful believe that God the Father has one only Son, so all the sincerity and devotion of the Latins believes that the Holy Spirit is eternally, inseparably, and in like manner proper to Father and Son, and proceeds from both. Yet the bishop of Nicomedia, crying out in opposition, seems to carry the argument toward an impossibility. He says: “If the Father emits the Spirit, and the Son, who is begotten from the Father, also emits Him, then this is proper to the Father as bestowed from a cause; consequently it will also belong properly to the Son. Thus the Son will have, in place of one, two proper attributes mutually contrary: passivity and activity—namely, being generated and emitting. For although the Father is said to beget the Son and to send the Spirit, this is not a diversity of properties, but rather a difference in some manner of possessing what is from Him.”

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0246D]

This is certainly ignorance of refutation—that is, when an *epicheiresis* (ἐπισχείρησις), an argument, is constructed not from the given premises by syllogistic necessity. For emitting the Spirit is not proper to the Father alone, as can be demonstrated by many direct arguments and by arguments from impossibility.

And even if it were granted to be proper to the Son, it still would not follow that the Son has, in place of one, two mutually contrary proper attributes—passivity and activity. For the Son of God suffers nothing when He is generated or born; [Col. 0247A] since to suffer is to be subjected to passion, and this necessarily belongs wholly to time. But God is not subjected to passion, nor is He born or begotten from the Father in time. For the Father begot the Son before all ages and times.

Finally, even among created things not every action entails passion; for example, actions considered complete in themselves, such as governing, running, breathing, and the like, as some say. Much less does any action give rise to passion in God. For the divine, being simply good, cannot be altered; and what cannot be altered is destroyed by the conjunction of anything else conceived as added to it. What is divine is impassible. The Son of God suffers nothing insofar as He is born from the Father.

Moreover, it has already been shown that generation and emitting the Spirit are diverse properties. The former is distinctive of a Person; the latter is not. If, however, while the Father is simple and indivisible, what is called generating stood in the same relation to Him as what is called emitting, then what is called foreknowing would stand in the same relation as making, so that no composition would be understood in the divine even here. But if this were so, He who foreknows evils would also make them—not merely in the manner in which the divine foreknows, but altogether in the manner in which He makes. Therefore generating is not the same as emitting, just as generating is not the same as communicating. For the Father alone generates, but He does not alone create; yet this does not introduce a privation of simplicity into God.

Further, if generating and emitting are the same, the emitter will be the generator and what is emitted will be begotten. But nothing of this sort exists between the Father and the Son. Rather, the Father always and the Son always emit the Spirit: not as something diffused in emitting, not dissolved into air, nor driven by any need. For He is a sanctifying power subsisting in Himself, susceptible neither of virtue nor vice, neither of change nor alteration. When He is sent and proceeds from the Father and the Son, being sent and proceeding does not mean a passage from place to place. How else has He filled the whole world—heaven, earth, sea, and the rational beings in them? Everywhere the Spirit remains in them and contains them, being the Spirit of the Lord, that is, of the Son, and being sent and emitted by Him as by the Father. This, I think, is established by the unavoidable necessity presupposed in the argument. [Col. 0247D]

## CHAPTER X

Everything sent or given by the Son, if it is not from the substance of the sending or giving Word Himself, is either His work, possession, creation, or something else separable from Him. For the Son either does not send the Spirit at all, or sends Him from without, or sends Him inwardly from His own substance. The Savior plainly contradicts anyone who denies that He sends Him. But who could maintain that He sends from external things, when the Spirit searches the depths of the Son?

Moreover, everything which He sends or brings forth from without is later than Him and, according to its first origin, is from nothing—for example the heavenly host, heaven, stars, and the world together with its primordial matter. [Col. 0248A] Therefore, if the Son sends the Spirit from without, the Spirit is either one of the things mentioned or something else separable from Him. It remains, then, that the Son sends the Spirit inwardly from His own substance. But if He sends Him inwardly and not from His own substance, He has Him as an adventitious participation and addition—just as odor and many other things belong to the substances from which they proceed by participation.

But the Son, insofar as He is from God, is in no way sent by the Spirit. For the same thing can be a cause of one thing and caused by another; but nothing can be both cause and caused in relation to the same thing. The Father is indeed cause of the Son and Spirit,

> **[Note: Col. 0247]** Read cautiously, and return to the note on chapter 8. You must do this in many similar passages that occur throughout the work.

but it must not be denied that the Son is cause of the Spirit: He sends Him as being His substantially, having nothing adventitious, nothing added, nothing by participation, but according to nature. [Col. 0248B] For as the Father has and sends Him simply, so also does the Son. Therefore, existing from the substance of each, He is sent and comes forth from both alike; since to have existence from someone is nothing other than to proceed from Him from whom one has being.

Further, if the Person of the Holy Spirit is sent and given inseparably by the Son, the Spirit must be inseparably from the Son. For if He is not inseparably from the Son, then, since He is sent and given by Him, He is separably from Him in some other manner. But He who is sent and given without division and inseparably by another is in some manner from that other.

Further, if certain things sent separably flow from the causes from which they are sent, much more should He who is sent inseparably by someone be judged to be from the sender. How production from a cause occurs in both ways is clear: a trunk is produced separately from a root; teeth from the brain; horns and hoofs from flesh; and veins from the substance of the heart. But a ray is sent inseparably from the sun, and radiance from fire. All these proceed from what sends them. Therefore the Holy Spirit, who is sent and given inseparably by the Son, flows from Him and has existence from Him.

But the bishop of Methone does not agree with this, constructing his syllogism in this way: “If the Spirit is one and perfect because He is God, and God is one and perfect because He is good—for everything that is not perfect—indeed, that is not a good of this kind—is from one perfect principal cause, namely the Father—then each thing is from one perfect principal cause. But if He is not from one and that one alone, but also from the Son, then He is not the same one. For how can that which is from not one sole and principal cause be one cause? For the Father and Son are two, and neither of them is perfect insofar as they need one another for production. Therefore the Spirit Himself is not perfect. For how can He be, since He is from imperfect beings? Nothing [Col. 0249A] perfect comes from imperfect beings; indeed, a diarchy expels monarchy from the one Deity.”

## CHAPTER XI

But according to this reasoning, neither is the Father perfect, since He is not from one; for the Father is from none. Similarly, heaven and the stars are not at all perfect, since they have not received existence from one Person alone, although three Persons equally bestowed upon them the foundation of being—though some regard the Father as the principal cause, the Son as the creative cause, and the Holy Spirit as the perfecting cause.

Their reasoning is likewise this: if the Spirit is not from the Father alone but also from the Son, He is therefore not the same one. One must ask in what sense “one” is said. For “one” is used in many ways in divine Scripture and likewise among philosophers: by genus, species, and number. What is one in genus is several in species; what is one in species is several in number, since one species is predicated of many numerically distinct things.

A thing is one in number in many ways: either as continuous, as when I call one body one by the continuity of the whole—though it is many in its parts and one as a whole—or as what cannot by nature be divided, such as a point and a unit; or things having the same definition though their names differ, such as a tunic and a garment. Yet a point and a unit, although they cannot be divided, are nevertheless called respectively beginning and end, earlier and later.

Indeed, in divine Scripture “one” is customarily understood of a multitude, and also of that which is one by nature and by number. Of a multitude it is said: “The whole earth was of one speech and one language” (Gen. 11); and Luke gives a similar statement in Acts: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul.” Likewise, concerning numerical unity, it says: “One is your master, Christ” (Acts 4). [Col. 0249C]

Again, divine Scripture has another sense of “one”: what is one in substance and nature but not in properties, as are the three divine Persons, which are properly called three properties. Yet neither the nature nor the substance is three. For the divine is one, simple, indivisible, and unique. The saints affirm that we confess the distinction of Persons from the properties by the intellect alone. We do not believe in three Persons as three countable things—one, one, and one—but only in the distinction of properties. Nor are they believed to be three different things, although there are in act three Persons according to three properties. These do not introduce a cutting or division of things, but distinguish what is proper from what is common. For a person, being a singular, manifests in itself and marks the concurrence of distinctive properties, considered according to the account derived from the properties; as an individual it separates from, and indicates, what is common.

For this reason the elders give the following definition of person: they say that person is a substance differing in number from substances of the same nature by its properties. The whole and complete sense of this definition seems to be this: a person is a rational substance that can be understood as singular through [Col. 0250A] its own properties: the Father through generation, the Son through birth, and the Holy Spirit through procession; and through similar things which can be joined singularly to each Person. Their substance and nature, however, are simple and uniform. The three Persons are one in nature and of the same substance, being, so to speak, simple.

For composites are not said to be one in nature, even if they are one in number. Thus the world, composed of different natures, is not considered one in nature but one in number. For this reason Scripture properly uses the plural number only of the Persons in God, as in: “Let us make man” (Gen. 1), and, “Come, let us descend and confuse their languages” (Gen. 11). This signifies not merely one simple and uncompounded manner, but one nature and a distinction of Persons. For the divine is one in nature, but not in Persons.

How, then, is “one” to be understood in the foregoing conclusion, which says: “If the Spirit is not from the Father alone but from the Son, He is therefore not the same one”? If it says that the Spirit is not the same one as the Father and Son, the absurdity is manifest, because they are the same one in substance and nature. But if it means that the Spirit is not one Person because He proceeds from two Persons, this too is wholly remote from the truth. For a third light proceeds from two lights without any diminution of the two; again, action proceeds from substance and power; a river flows from a vein and a spring; the Spirit is sent from Father and Son; and the world was created by Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Hence it is clear to all that the stated inference and conclusion are false—namely, that a diarchy expels monarchy from the Deity. [Col. 0250C] For it is plainly apparent from what has preceded that the Father and Son are called neither two principles nor two causes; nor, although the Father is without principle, is He called monarch. For monarchy belongs to nature, not to Person. Therefore the alleged absurdity—that the Spirit proceeds not from the Father alone but from the Son—does not follow.

## CHAPTER XII

Yet Nicetas presses the contrary argument, saying: “If all who rightly reflect on divine doctrines hold as certain, unambiguous, and unquestionable that whatever is seen or shared in the life-originating and all-creating Trinity in a similar manner is either predicated of all three or said singularly of one Person; but the emission, spoken of in the life-originating Trinity according to the same procession, is not common in the same manner, then it will be entirely of one alone. If so, will they confess it to belong to the Father alone, or also to the Son? If to the Father, then, however unwillingly, they will disavow their own opinion. But if to the Son—alas, what impiety!—they take it from the Father and assign it to the Son. They must then concede that the proper attributes of the Persons are exchanged and succeed one another. Indeed, there will be complete confusion and disorder in the Deity, which sets other things in order; and not only this, but the Holy Trinity ceases to be what it is when the properties yield place and succeed one another in turn. All this is full of impiety. Therefore the Spirit does not proceed from the Son as from the Father, as some maintain.”

This argument might perhaps have been necessary if the points alleged by the opponents had been granted and established. But they have neither been granted nor established by the opponents; nor are they self-evident, as is clear from what follows. It is evident that whatever are properties of nature are common to the Persons of the same substance: such as being eternal, immortal, and unchangeable in oneself. For beings unchangeable by participation, such as holy angels, have a limit and an end. But there is no end to the greatness of God. “Where shall I go from Your Spirit?” The divine is everywhere and in all things, and the three Persons are in all things, mutually consubstantial, receiving the same account of substance.

But the Son is from the Father, and the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son; and therefore the properties by which Father and Son are distinguished do not succeed one another. Nor are sonship or fatherhood empty or merely consequent names, understood as a bare name attached to a bare substantive. The Greeks mockingly assert to the Latins: “If the Spirit proceeds from the Son, the Father has fallen away from His property; it is certain that He is not consubstantial with Him.” But, if the Persons are consubstantial, they are in no way able to exchange their properties. For how can what is singular possess another’s property? Hence a character—that is, a property distinctive of a Person—and every singular property adheres immovably when considered in relation to each divine Person. Yet not every property is either of one Person alone or of all three, as what follows will show.

The divine substance is indeed indivisible, yet each of the Persons possesses it most fully and without diminution. What absurdity, then, can there be if, while the Persons remain wholly inseparable, some property belongs in common to the Son and Father? Not every property describes a Person. That is, just as certain properties are held to separate a nature from the rest, so some properties in things of different substances distinguish their natures. In consubstantial things—that is, things of the same nature—they appear to distinguish Persons, as laughability and neighing in a human being and a horse. Since these are properties of different natures, within the same species neither divides a substance; rather, with number added, it merely provides an indication for separating persons. Right and left, however, and the like [Col. 0252A] neither divide substance nor define persons.

Similarly, the divine Persons have certain properties which do neither. But they have others which distinguish one Person from another, and these alone are three: fatherhood, sonship, and procession. For the property called being cause, or being the principle of some Person, is not distinctive; nor are certain others, such as being unbegotten, being without cause, being without principle, emitting, being without a father, not being the Holy Spirit, not being processible, having the Holy Spirit, and sending the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Father communicates most of these to the Son. Likewise, the Son has certain properties that are not distinctive, and He communicates some to the Spirit: such as not being causative, not being without principle, not being Father, and other things of this sort. In the same way the Spirit has some properties which the Father communicates: for example, not being the Son, not being begotten, differing from the Son, and other such things, which are not hypostatic or personal properties.

> **[Note: Col. 0251D]** Personal properties are called “hypostatic” in Greek: those which distinguish the individual hypostases, that is, Persons. Other properties do not distinguish individual Persons, but are common to two Persons—Father and Son—or to the Son, Father, and Spirit; and he says that these are considered in relation to substance, not as properties proper to the individuals. God is not thereby composite or deprived of simplicity if He has several qualities called properties; nor is the divine nature composite because it exists in three Persons. The soul also suffers with the body’s affections. Argyrophylus’s translation reads: “To reason, to love, or to hate are not affections of the soul, but of that which has it, insofar as it has it,” *On the Soul*, book I, ch. 4.

All these are considered in relation to substance and do not belong to an individual Person. Therefore there are properties which are not distinctive of Persons. But one property in the divine Trinity distinguishes one Person unfailingly, without diminution and without change: fatherhood the Father, and sonship the Son. For if all other things belonging to the Father are set aside—being unbegotten, being principle, emitting the Spirit—and only this one remains, namely being Father, the Son will always be spoken of in relation to Him, and conversely the Father in relation to the Son. [Col. 0252C] For the Son is called the Son of the Father, and the Father the Father of the Son; the Son is not spoken of in relation to “the unbegotten.” For where there is no Father, there is no Son.

If one property distinguishes one hypostasis unfailingly and without any diminution—while each of the three has several properties—there will be properties which do not distinguish Persons. Consequently, having properties is not the same as being distinguished by them. For each animal has several properties, none of which distinguishes it. It is clear, therefore, I think, that no absurdity follows if the Father and the two Persons who are with Him possess properties of this kind, since a differing relation does not introduce composition, as is plainly apparent in points and units.

For if three units are set in order, the middle is regarded as second in relation to the first, and the third, however, as first; yet the same first and second unit do not receive composition. For it is impossible for passion to belong to units, since they are indivisible: they neither become lesser nor greater than one another, nor increase, nor suffer contraries. Perhaps, in relation to the first, one may be understood as right, [Col. 0253A] and in relation to the second as left; yet, though it is the same thing that is right and left, it does not thereby lose its proper simplicity. Neither, therefore, will the divine nature be called composite because it has power and action and exists in three Persons. In every way the divine nature is simple; yet it is wholly the Father’s, wholly the Son’s, wholly the Holy Spirit’s.

Why then should it seem incredible to anyone, while the one Deity remains in three Persons, that one property belongs to and is spoken of two inseparable Persons? Further, from affections of the soul, as some suppose, certain traces remain in the body, and from bodily affections others remain in the soul; physiognomists infer the soul’s dispositions from the form of the body. Since certain traces from bodily passions adhere to the soul—for plainly the soul suffers with one in pain and is afflicted with one wounded—the soul suffers not only in old age but also in drunkenness and illnesses, and because of the body’s intemperance is hindered from its activities. When it recovers from such a fall, the soul shines forth again; yet no other sense is born in it, since after drunkenness it remembers former things.

But Aristotle referred all these and similar matters to the composite in *On the Soul*, saying: “To perceive, to love, or to hate are not affections of mind, but of that which possesses it insofar as it possesses it.” Though he judged that the soul does not move, he did not thereby abolish every communion of body and soul through mutual passive motion. There is no doubt that the body has acquired certain singular properties, such as being red, black, white, divisible, having parts situated here and there, and the like. But the rational soul can understand without the body, though it is in the body; when it wills to understand one thing, it understands; it needs none of the things external to it; and the more lofty things it receives in itself, the more easily it governs the lower. It knows and contemplates itself. Hence it is shown to be separable and immortal; and both body and soul have certain common properties: being in the whole, constituting an animal, being able to be separated from one another, and to be joined again.

Yet even if today the soul rejected all communion with the body, once every doubt has been removed, after the resurrection it will obtain some fellowship of relation with it. For the Apostle says: [Col. 0253D] “This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.” Again: “A natural body is sown; a spiritual body shall rise” (1 Cor. 15)—not because it will be changed into spirit, but because it will have more things in common with its rational spirit.

The subtlety, lightness, inviolable brightness, and glory of immortality and incorruption belonging to the desired body of Jesus our Savior and of His Mother, blessed above all women, appear to resolve exactly every knot of doubt in this matter. These qualities must unquestionably belong equally to body and spirit. Therefore, since soul and body, though very different from one another, share certain things besides the singular properties which they possess, there is surely nothing absurd if Father and Son—undivided in will, not separated by intervals, inseparable, incapable of division—share certain non-substantial properties and together are one cause and one principle of the Holy Spirit. For we perceptibly observe two lights from one light to be one cause and one principle.

## CHAPTER XIII
But the adversary does not yet cease to repeat his objections. “If,” he says, “the Son and the Father are one cause of the Spirit, then such a cause is one either numerically or specifically. If the cause of the Holy Spirit is one numerically, and the Father with the Son is one numerically identical cause of the Holy Spirit, why are the Father and the Son not two persons? Again,” he says, “every cause that is numerically one either derives from some principle or has no principle. For to have a principle and to lack a principle do not seem possible for one and the same thing numerically. But the cause mentioned has no principle insofar as the Son is called [Col. 0254B] such; hence the Son and the Father are not one numerically identical cause of the Holy Spirit, nor are the Father and the Son one proximate cause of the Spirit specifically. For things which have their being from one thing, not numerically but specifically, likewise have that one thing? Surely those which are compared with one thing specifically have it in like manner as one. But if this is so, that which has its being from a cause that is specifically, rather than numerically, one, will not be numerically one. Moreover, a cause one according to number is necessarily one numerically; that which is one specifically belongs to many. Thus the syllable *ba*, which has one thing according to species, is found as a part of many and different words; if it had one thing numerically, it would be numerically distinct and a part of only one word.”

But whoever says this does not reason correctly, since it is truly said that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, yet these three are neither the begotten God nor the unbegotten God. Why, then, are they not one God? “I say,” replies the Greek, “that God there is not one numerically but according to nature or species. For when we say, ‘The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God,’ we understand nothing else than that the Father, Son, [Col. 0254D] and Spirit are of such a substance, through which the Father is God—not God the Father—and the Son is God—not God the Son; for insofar as the Father is God, or insofar as the Son is God, no personal properties are admitted in their being God.”

This objection, I think, may be resolved both by many other arguments and by those set out below. The division of a cause said to be one either numerically or specifically is customarily applied to material or formal cause and the other causes which follow. But neither the Father alone nor the Father with the Son is the material or formal cause of the Holy Spirit. Nor indeed is either an efficient or final cause, as may be made clearer through an exposition and division of the fourfold kinds of causes spoken of by the earliest philosophers.

For [Col. 0255A] of these, one is efficient, another material, another formal, another final. Again, some are intrinsic, as material and formal causes; others are understood as external, as efficient and final causes. An efficient cause is external because it belongs to will: for we arrange things to be done according to will, and things capable of local motion are moved according to will. But neither is the Father outside the Son, nor is the Son a thing made.

A material cause is inherent in a thing, as a foundation in a house, bronze in a statue, and an element in syllables. Bronze can indeed exist without the statue; but it is impossible that the Spirit should exist without the Son and the Father. A formal cause likewise designates things; for things are marked out according to species—not that which exceeds genus by differences, but that which is divided—unlike matter. But the Father is not the species of the Son or of the Holy Spirit. Rather, the Son would be the species of the Father, if this could be said; for he revealed the Father’s name to humankind. A final cause is that for the sake of which things to be made come into actuality, as medicine exists for health. It is a final cause because of which other things exist, while it itself is the cause of nothing; it is considered outside the thing and is absent from it. But the Father always is and is never separated from the Spirit. Therefore the Father is not the final cause of the Spirit.

It is thus evident that, according to none of the stated modes, is the Father the cause of the Son or of the Holy Spirit; for that mode by which the Father is deemed Father and cause of the Son, and by which the Father and the Son are one cause and one principle of the Holy Spirit, is unspeakable and ineffable. It is clear that what has been said does not apply to the divine persons on account of the causes already mentioned. Therefore each, being always existent, brings into presence things which do not exist. For just as the Father, so too the Son and the Holy Spirit can never be inferior to anything, each being desirable in itself, free in itself, good in itself.

Since, therefore, it has been shown that cause is not a personal property, it is manifest and evident that no incongruity follows if the Father and the Son are believed to be one cause and one principle of the Holy Spirit. Thus plainly false is the position of the bishop of Nicomedia, or of others, who say: “What is not proper to one is common to three. Therefore, if the cause of the Spirit’s emission belongs not only to the Father but also to the Son, it must also belong to the Spirit; and thus the Spirit will be both sender and sent.” This is full of falsehood.

For it is common to the Father and the Son not to proceed from another, not to be another’s spirit, and not to be the Holy Spirit—just as, in the category of substance, “not to be” is common to every substance, both primary and secondary. And, as Porphyry says, it is common to a property and an inseparable accident that they never subsist apart from those things in which they are considered. To omit the negations of this sort, I say that having relation to one another is common to the Father and the Son. For every relation, although it is considered with reference to several things, is nevertheless distinguished as one relational property. Hence it is again clear that two possess one property, which, though it seems to be spoken of in the plural, uses the plural number not because of itself but because of its participants; for through the things that have a relation, the relation itself is more readily made manifest.

It is also common to the Father and Son to have the character of looking toward one another, and likewise equally to differ from one another relationally. And who can deny that it is common to the Father and Son, among things which are relative, to be spoken of reciprocally? For as the Father is called Father of the Son, so the Son is called Son of the Father. The predication is balanced from one to the other, and this is called conversion, because as this is predicated of that, so that is predicated conversely of this. Likewise the definition of relative things—namely, things whose very being consists somehow in standing in relation to another—is predicated of the Father and Son as relative beings, but not at all of the Spirit.

Since these things, I think, suffice against the objection advanced, the matter itself requires us to proceed to the remaining contradictions.

## CHAPTER XIV

Behold what the bishop of Methone proposes: “If the procession of the Spirit from the Father is perfect—and it is perfect because the Spirit is God from God the perfect Father—what, I ask, does that procession from the Son contribute to it? If it too contributes something, the former is not perfect. For how is it perfect if it lacks as much as the latter contributes? But if the procession of the Spirit from the Son is identical with the procession from the Father, and nothing further can be found or said for declaring the Spirit’s perfection, then that which is from the Son becomes altogether superfluous; and superfluous and vain is that which introduces something superfluous into a Trinity already complete and perfect.”

Such reasoning does not, in my judgment, suffice to remove the procession of the Spirit from the Son. Indeed, since every soul subject to passions is unable to conceive anything great and noble, especially concerning divine things while it suffers darkness, those who thus wage war do not inflict dreadful wounds. Certainly ignorance in this place is wiser than such cavilling. These and very many similar objections are thrown at the Latins as though at children fearing shipwreck from every wind.

May not one similarly ask: “The Son is perfect from the Father; he is perfect because God is perfect, from God the perfect Father. For God alone truly seems perfect: he alone being perfect, beyond whom nothing is supreme and who needs nothing; while all other things only seem and are called perfect improperly, whether according to quantity, quality, or metaphorically—as a perfect calumniator, a perfect thief, a perfect destruction. For to perfect a thing is said to be to reduce it to nothing. If therefore God is perfect, and the Son is from God the perfect Father, what, I ask, does the Spirit contribute to this perfection? If he contributes something, neither the Father nor the Son is perfect. For how is one perfect if he needs as much as the Spirit gives? But if the one God—the Father and Son—is perfect, and nothing further can be found or said to manifest the Father’s perfection, then the Spirit becomes superfluous,” which it is impious to think.

For just as the universe appears to belong to the Father and the Son, so also does it belong to the Holy Spirit. Whom the Father and the Son call, the Son and the Spirit call. Those whom the Father sanctifies, the Spirit also sanctifies, although it was said of the Spirit: “He will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak” (John 16). This chiefly demonstrates the truth of community of the same nature, and not any inferiority.

For every rational being who is born, possessing a will of its own, speaks from itself when it wishes—not from weakness or by chance; but the Spirit of God does not do so. Whatever the Spirit wills is God’s will, and whatever God wills is the will of the Holy Spirit. The prophets and other human beings, however, do not will whatever God wills. Peter denied his Master; Aaron murmured against Moses; Jeremiah rejected prophecy. But the Spirit is not so. For he does not at one time will what belongs to God the Father and at another what belongs to himself, because he does not have another will within himself; nor does the Son, since the will and perfection of the three persons are one and the same.

Accordingly, the perfect procession of the Spirit from the Father ought not to exclude that which is said to be from the Son, just as the perfection of the Son from the Father does not exclude the perfection of the Holy Spirit from the same Father. Hence it is plain that the Spirit has both perfection and being from both. For if the Spirit’s procession were separately and independently from the Father, with the Son in no way participating, the dignity of the Begotten would be diminished. For if the Spirit proceeded from the Father alone, the Father alone would send and bestow him. This becomes clear thus: if the Son, because he is begotten by the Father alone, is given and sent by the Father alone, then by the same reasoning, if the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, the Father alone bestows and sends him. But to send and give the Spirit belongs to the dignity of the Son. Therefore, if the Father sends the Spirit separately and independently, the Son’s dignity is diminished—an impious and wicked thought. Therefore the Spirit’s procession is from both.

Moreover, as shown above, the Father and the Son have nothing in common insofar as the one is Father and the other Son; personally they are altogether divided from one another, after the likeness of the individuals of any species understood under a substance. But the Spirit is, as it were, a quality of the Father and the Son, as the great Cyril seems plainly to affirm in his seventh discourse to Hermias, saying: “Christ never wrought signs and wonders through Paul by the power of the Holy Spirit; the Holy Spirit is a certain natural and living activity and, so to speak, a quality of the Son’s divinity. But if this is so, how can that which is naturally in God and from God be a thing made?” And again the same author says: “He is like a sort of vapor and a quality of the very substance of the Father; and this quality is holy indeed, yet such a quality is not an accident, but rather one of the persons of the Holy Trinity and true God.”

The theologian John seems to bear witness to the same thing when he says: “God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4). When this love for one’s neighbour is fervent and unfailing, it is the Spirit in us, who makes us remain in God and God in us; and this is known especially through works. Just as one perceives that the soul, which no one sees, is present and exists in us through actions and motions, so God’s love in us is known through certain motions and actions which the given Spirit produces, as it is written: “Because he has given us of his Spirit” (1 John 3), who, being pure, bestows pure and immaculate gifts.

The Holy Spirit is such a gift; he is called love, through which the Father loves the Son and the Son loves the Father. This love is equally shared by the Father and the Son, for the one who is loved ought to return an equal affection to the lover; since sincere and certain love consists wholly in mutual and equal love. Otherwise love would be blameworthy: it would return unequal affection to one who loves and would respond differently to the lover and the beloved.

Therefore this love, which ineffably joins the Father to the Son and the Son to the Father, is the union which draws us to the love of God and the Son to the love of the Father. For love is not idle in God, by which the three persons are mutually joined. Hence one must not suppose that God is called love only on account of human beings. Before all ages he exists as love, which is the Holy Spirit, as the evangelist Paul testifies, saying: “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us” (Romans 5), an overflowing and rich gift, as Chrysostom declares.

“For he gave the greatest gift, not heaven, earth, and sea, but that which was more honourable than all these: that which made angels out of human beings, and prepared them as sons of God and brothers of Christ.” And shortly afterward, in the Epistle to the Romans: “He did not honour us after an interval and gradually, but suddenly poured out the fountain of good things, and this before the contests. Therefore, though you may not be very worthy, do not despair, having love as a great advocate before the Judge.”

What does he call the fountain of all gifts and good things, the greatest of all? Surely God the Holy Spirit, whom the evangelist called love when he said, “God is love.” Jerome also says of this in the fourteenth Psalm: “The Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but the love which the Father has for the Son and the Son for the Father.” Augustine likewise says in the sixth book *On the Trinity*: “In all things the Son is equal to the Father and is of one and the same substance.” Therefore the Holy Spirit also stands in the same unity and equality of substance; whether he is the unity of both, or holiness, or love, it is clear that he is not one of the two, but that by which both are joined, by which the Begotten is loved by the Begetter and loves his Begetter.

Since therefore the Spirit is the love of the Father as he is also the love of the Son, and as he proceeds from the Father so he proceeds from the Son, it is clear from what has been said that, if he is not the Spirit of the Son and does not proceed from him, the same Spirit cannot be the Spirit of the Father or proceed from him. For it was shown above that the Spirit’s procession from the Father and from the Son is one and the same, and that it is common to the two—the Father and the Son—to emit the Spirit from themselves. It was also shown that together with the property of emitting, the Father and Son have several other common properties which do not belong to the Spirit. It was further said that the Father emits the Spirit not insofar as he is Father, but insofar as he is principle and cause; nor are they therefore confused into one person, even if the Spirit comes forth from both by one undifferentiated procession.

Nor is indivisibility and simplicity destroyed, nor does the monstrosity of a semi-Arian or the error of a semi-Sabellian arise, as though the Father did not retain his own property but communicated some of it to the Son. Likewise, the Son is not marked by the filial property alone in such a way that the Father assumes some of it. For not everything belonging to the Father and Son is also common to the Spirit, nor conversely. Therefore he is not correct who says: “Whatever the Son has, the Spirit also has, except being begotten.” For if the Son has the power of emission, the Spirit will also have it—which is far from the truth. The Son, having the same Spirit, sends him; but the Spirit is not properly said to send a spirit, nor himself.

## CHAPTER XV

This new philosopher of Byzantium does not agree with these and similar arguments. For he says: “If the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, as certain persons assert and say, the Spirit’s procession from the Father and Son must either be simultaneous, timeless, and eternal, or according to before and after. If according to before and after, wherever this is assigned to either of the two, the blasphemy is evident. For the Spirit will be prior and posterior to himself, eternal and temporal, recent and ancient, under time and before times, since the procession of the Spirit and his existence will not be simultaneous—which is full of impiety. But if he proceeds from both, namely from the Father and the Son, simultaneously, outside time, and eternally—the position on which those who fight on the other side rely as on a bulwark—it must be asked of them whether they mean simultaneous, timeless, and eternal procession, and in what manner. For if they say that he proceeds principally from both, the blasphemy is manifest. For in the superessential, supernatural, and life-originating Trinity there will be two principal, unoriginate, and uncaused persons; consequently, two causes, two principles, and two beings having neither cause nor principle. Thus things belonging to the Christian religion will be transferred into a plurality of two, and no slight injury will be inflicted upon the life-originating and superessential Trinity. But if not principally, though simultaneously and eternally, but more nearly and more remotely, or primarily and secondarily, then impiety is also brought forth. First, the Son will be more a cause of the Spirit and the Father less so; for the proximate cause is more a cause, as common notions and the discourse of truth declare. But in the unchangeable and immutable divinity, and in the divine hypostases, no ‘less’ can be found, because all things common to the divine persons subsist equally and in the same glory.”

This philosopher devises and sharpens these and other arguments, but they inflict no wounds upon the opponents. The Latins do not assert in God “before and after” in time, nor “principally and secondarily,” and rightly so. For the divine is above number and temporal sequence; where communion is one and the same, no deficient number is admitted, and concord is united into oneness.

Therefore, removing the claim that the Spirit proceeds principally from either, they affirm that he comes forth equally from both. For they say: “If there is in the Holy Trinity no priority in time, nature, honour, or power, none of the three persons proceeds from another principally; indeed, what proceeds from no one in a posterior manner does not seem to proceed from anyone principally.” Therefore, from the most exceptional mode of causality and the ineffable order by which the Spirit is accounted third and the Son second from the Father, nothing of this sort can be inferred. For if, because the Father has the Spirit from no one but the Son has him from the Father, the Spirit belongs principally to the Father, then for the same reason whatever the Son has will belong principally to the Father. If this is so, the Father alone lives principally, reigns principally, judges principally, and indeed is principally a person. If these things are granted, they seem to make the Apostle guilty of falsehood when he says: “He did not consider it robbery for the Son to be equal to God the Father” (Philippians 2). And how will this stand: “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14), together with many other passages that could be added?

As for the ensuing claim—namely, that the proximate cause is more a cause and the remote cause less—this is sufficiently answered, I think, by observing that such a statement has place in natural, logical, and similar matters, in which the same cause is not everywhere both proximate and remote. But in the divine persons it has no place, both for many other reasons which it is better now to pass over, and because the Father and Son are held to be altogether the same cause, proximate and mediate.

Moreover, the Father is not prior to the Son in time, nature, or any other respect, so that the Spirit should proceed principally from the Father and secondarily from the Son—or in no manner, as the Greeks most improbably assert. For as the Father and Son are together by nature before all ages and of the same honour, so whatever the Father can do the Son can also do; and nothing can be excluded from the power of the Father and the Son.

The Father cannot sin; the Son cannot sin, because sinning is not something that exists, but only a privation of good and a weakness, as the Apostle says: “Christ died for us when we were weak” (Romans 5); and David: “Their weaknesses were multiplied” (Psalm 15). Therefore it is not possible for God to sin, just as God cannot make what has happened not to have happened. For God is truthful, but making what has happened not to have happened is a lie. It would sooner be easy for him to differ from himself, repent, and abandon his own nature—that is, to say that he can cease to be God—which is altogether ridiculous and useless.

Therefore, as Aristotle says: “There is no power concerning the past, but only concerning the present or the future. For it is in no way possible for past time to exist now; nor was it true in the past to say that the portion of time which has passed now exists. If past time cannot return to the present or future, none of the things now existing or to exist can have existence in past time. But to whatever all aptitude for existing is removed, no power can truly be attributed. Therefore there is no possibility concerning the past, but only concerning the present or future.”

Accordingly, all the past is necessary, not possible or contingent. The Father and Son can equally do all things, but they will the better things. If someone says, “The Son cannot do everything the Father can do, nor conversely, because the Father, being Father, cannot be Son, nor can the Son be Father,” the answer is that these and similar things are rather negations; negations are infinite and have neither nature nor subsistence, and therefore are not powers. Hence it is evident that to be the Son is not within any power of the Father, since it would destroy both terms.

Again, if someone says that to be able to beget differs from to be able to be begotten, and that the Father alone can do the former while the Son alone can do the latter—so that the Father and Son appear to have powers differing from one another—the answer is that the power in the Father whereby he can beget is the same power as that in the Son whereby he can be begotten, although they shine forth in different properties. Thus there is one power of human learning, according to which both an orator and a philosopher are capable; nevertheless, one is called an orator with respect to rhetoric and another a musician with respect to music.

By distinctions of this kind, the powers and properties of the three persons are shown to be like a balance-scale. But if, as the Greeks maintain, the Father alone can emit the Spirit, the distinctions suffer deficiency; the equality of the persons’ powers and properties seems to perish. This may be shown as follows: the Father alone can do two greatest things uniquely in the Trinity—namely, beget the Son and emit the Spirit. That these are different is clear from the contradiction that follows: insofar as he can beget, he can have the Son; but insofar as he can emit, he cannot have the Son. Therefore he can beget in one respect and emit in another.

But whoever alone can uniquely do two greatest things in the Trinity can uniquely do more things than one who alone can uniquely do one thing of the same kind there, as the Son can only be begotten. If the Son can uniquely do only this one thing in the Trinity, he is not thereby equal to the Father, who uniquely can do two greatest things in the Trinity. For if he is equal to the Father in the Trinity, he can uniquely do as many things in the Trinity as the Father. But neither the Son nor the Spirit can uniquely do two things in the Trinity. Therefore the Father alone can uniquely do more things in the Trinity than the Son alone or the Spirit alone.

But perhaps someone will object: “Such a conclusion does not follow from the foregoing, because ‘can,’ referred to in the plural, is applied only to properties. Thus, as a person understood singly is said according to substance but, when brought into plurality, indicates not substances but properties, so this may be seen from the consequence of propositions: if there is one person with one substance, then two persons as antecedent will not imply two substances or anything of that kind. In this manner,” they say, “‘can,’ understood singly, is said substantively, because the three persons are one. In whatever two can do, each of the three can do as much alone; but ‘can’ in the plural, when spoken within the Trinity, indicates properties alone. Therefore the true sense of the conclusion stated above—‘the Father alone can uniquely do more things in the Trinity than the Son alone or the Spirit alone’—is this: the Father alone can have more individual properties than the Son alone or the Spirit alone.”

## CHAPTER XVI
Yet I seem to see that such an answer obstructs rather than resolves the matter. For whether one says that the Father has two properties or two powers, while the Son has only one, one introduces inequality either of properties or of power—both of which I judge detestable. Certainly, just as the power of the Three is one and the same, according to which the Father can do one thing singly, the Son another, and the Spirit another, so the number of properties belonging to each person is kept altogether the same, lest any inequality appear. Since God does or possesses nothing whatever in vain, I do not think it should be admitted that the Father has more properties than the Son. For if the begetter exceeds the Son in some property, either he can do something according to it, or he cannot. If he can, there is not complete equality between Father and Son in their individual power. Nor is the conclusion drawn to be censured: if he cannot, it is in vain. Therefore, since no property of the divine persons can possibly be possessed apart from a title of power, it is beyond doubt that, if one exceeds another in any property, it also exceeds the other in an individual power corresponding to it.

But it must be observed that such a combination has no place wherever properties can be causes of weakness or incapacity, or wherever one property can be equivalent to several greater ones; [Col. 0263A] otherwise a creature would surpass its Creator in power, and any servant would often surpass his Lord. Further, if the Spirit, according to His own individual property of proceeding, can do as much as the Father can according to each of His two individual properties, the Spirit’s power is stronger than either power of the Father. Again, if the power belonging to the Spirit’s own individual property cannot do as much as both paternal properties alike, then the Father can do more things individually in the Trinity, as the foregoing shows, than the Son or the Spirit.

The cause and origin of such and similar inconveniences is the Father’s relation to the Spirit, a relation excluded from the Son. And since impossibilities follow from such a doctrine, it remains that the Father alone can individually beget, the Son alone be begotten, and the Holy Spirit alone be sent forth. Nor should the personal existence of this Spirit, because He is thought to proceed from two, be made double. As is evident in mathematics: a point placed upon a point without interval does not make a pair, nor does it become anything other than it was before. Likewise, if a line is placed upon a line, it does not form a surface, nor does it increase or pass into another kind of figure. The same is held of a surface and of the pattern of letters.

But since the Spirit proceeds from the whole being of Him who begets and of Him who is begotten, every excess, avenue, and individual inequality among persons possessing their individual properties is excluded. Therefore, according to the doctrine of the Latins, no combination may be asserted of the Three by which one of them has more properties than another, or can do more than another individually. For whatever is introduced in this way is ἀνακόλουθον, that is, consequent, as the foregoing has shown. Thus every inequality is excluded, including that supposed to exist in the Spirit in relation either to the Father or to the Son: because the Father can do something individually and something with the Son; the Son likewise something individually and something with the Spirit; and the Spirit something individually and something with the Father, although perhaps no term expressing this has yet been found.

Certainly, what is signified by these expressions—“to be immediately joined to the Son,” “to be cause,” or “causative”—belongs in the Trinity only to the Father and the Spirit together; likewise ἀπάτωρ, “fatherless,” is predicated of both alone. Again, to differ from the Son, to be excluded from the Son, to be another person than the Son, and to have another distinguishing property belong to both in such a way that each belongs only to the two; and their equivalents are likewise found in the Son in relation to the other of the two. Moreover, there are other things common to Father and Son, Son and Spirit, Spirit and Father, which have no relation to the individual persons: for example, being two persons, having two distinguishing properties, and being able to do certain things individually in the Trinity, together with any similar things that may be conceived.

Accordingly, if the Father and Son can do two individual things in the Trinity, while the Spirit can do one, no inequality or disparity follows, for the Spirit has that same thing together with the Father. And it should be noted that, just as one thing is common to sensible objects and another peculiar to them—the common feature being that they are perceptible by sense, while the peculiar feature is that they are perceived by color through sight or by sound through hearing—so it is common to the three persons to be marked by a personal property. But it is common to two to send forth; to two, to be causative; and to two, to be immediately joined to the Son. When all these are referred to the individual persons, it is proper to one to beget, to another to be begotten, and to the third to proceed.

If anyone presses the point that being from the Father is different from being from the Son, he nevertheless does not establish that the procession from one is different from the procession from the other—just as it is one thing to be sworn to the king and another to be sworn to the royal heir, yet the oath by which one is bound to each is one and the same. Thus it is clear from what has been said that in the Trinity nothing prior or posterior, principal or secondary, is to be asserted from the fact that the Spirit proceeds from the Son; nor should that which is not be inferred from Augustine’s statement: “Is not God the Father said to be He from whom the Word is begotten and from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds principally?” Nor from Jerome’s statement: “We believe in the Holy Spirit, who proceeds properly from the Father.”

Augustine immediately explains the sense in which this was said: “I added ‘principally,’ because the Holy Spirit is also found to proceed from the Son; but the Father gave this also to Him by begetting Him: that the Holy Spirit should proceed from Him.” Thus “principally” and “properly” were used improperly, in the sense that the Father has this from Himself and not from another, whereas the Son has it from the Father: namely, that He exists and proceeds from Him, just as the Holy Spirit exists and proceeds from the Father. These facts make absolutely no difference in procession, as may clearly be understood from grammatical practice. For example, a verb receives no tense from anyone, while a participle receives its tense from the verb; yet each possesses tense in the same manner, and tense belongs equally to both. For in every way the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son just as from the Father.

This is again confirmed by what follows. If, as the Greeks confess, the Father alone sends forth the Holy Spirit, then the Holy Spirit belongs to the Father alone. For just as the Father is not Father except of the Son begotten from Him, and the Son is not Son except of the Father who begets Him, so it is evident that the Spirit is the Spirit of no one except of the Father who sends Him forth. Therefore, if He is the Spirit of the Son, it plainly appears that He is also sent forth by Him.

Again, it is proper to the Father to beget, to the Son to be begotten, and to the Holy Spirit to proceed. But the Father is Father of the Son alone, and the Son is Son of the Father alone, because He is begotten by Him alone. Therefore the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father alone, if He proceeds from Him alone; for if He does not proceed from the Son, He is not the Spirit of the Son. Moreover, the Father is Father only of Him whom He begot, because the Son is Son only of Him by whom He is begotten. Hence it is evident that, if the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son, He is not the Son’s Spirit. But this is impossible. Therefore that which follows from it is impossible—namely, that the Spirit does not proceed from the Son.

Again, the Spirit is the Son’s Spirit, not as one acted upon (ἐνεργούμενος), nor by grace, but by nature, just as He is the Father’s Spirit because He manifestly proceeds from Him.
