If to be Father of someone by nature is the same as to beget him, and likewise to be Son of someone by nature is the same as to be begotten by him, it is evident that to be Spirit of someone by nature is the same as to be sent forth by him. Therefore, since the Spirit is the Son’s by nature, He is also sent forth by Him. And that the Son has the Spirit by nature—that is, not by grace nor as one acted upon—may plainly be inferred from the fact that the divine nature, or any of the divine persons, has nothing accidental, corruptible, or divisible.

## CHAPTER XVII

[Col. 0265B]

Moreover, I cannot pass over in silence that most weighty objection, trumpeted far and wide and filling Latin ears, although I consider it utterly unlawful to devise trifles concerning the divine, or to advance fabrications of this sort. Behold, the bishop of Nicomedia cries out with others: “If the Son is from the Father, and the Spirit from the Father and the Son, then the Spirit is surely the Father’s grandson; for among us a grandson is immediately derived from one through whom he is derived, by a middle term, from his grandfather.”

What should be said or answered to this? It does not follow even in natural things. A first bird lays an egg; from the bird and the egg a sparrow comes forth; therefore the bird that has come forth will be judged the granddaughter of the bird. Much less does such a refutation have any place in divine matters, where there is neither bodily generation nor passibility. Everything subject to such generations must be divisible; and everything divisible is passible.

I am astonished at such arguments, especially because not only that bishop but all who have written against the Latins on this question have employed the same paralogism as the most ancient heretics, and arguments that have application nowhere except in natural matters. In this matter, those who raise these objections contend only according to appearance and not according to truth; and by arguing so they advance no inconvenience against those who embrace the truth directly opposed to them. This is plainly beyond doubt from what has been said.

For if the begetter, precisely as Father, has a relation and reference to the Spirit, then, because the relation of begetter is identical, it necessarily follows that the Spirit is begotten and is the Son. Thus either the persons are confused, or the Spirit is fabricated as the Son’s brother—which likewise confuses the persons.

Therefore the begetter is not cause of the Spirit in being begetter, but in being cause and principle, as has been repeatedly emphasized. Hence the Spirit is neither alien from the Son nor to be judged without relation to Him. Nor does this entail the supposed inconvenience: if the Son does not send forth the Spirit in being Son, neither is the Father cause of the Spirit in being Father—contrary to what Nicetas tries to prove syllogistically. For he says:

> “If the Son is not cause of the Spirit in being Son, it follows that He is so according to some other relation. If so, the Son will be Son as existing from a cause, but Himself cause as sender forth of the Spirit; and from this inconveniences arise on both sides.”

For either the Son possessed being sender forth of the Spirit without existing from a cause, or He possessed it as existing from a cause, namely the Father. But if He possessed it without existing from a cause, then again in the supernatural and superessential Trinity there will be two principles without principle, namely Father and Son—and thus two principles and two causes. But if the Son, existing from a cause, is sender forth of the Spirit, then He received this entirely from the Father. For He is said to have from the Father both that He is Son and everything whatever that He has. But if He has this from the Father, what is this disinheritance and loss of filial existence: that the Son should not, precisely as Son, beget a Son and be deemed Father, while the Father, precisely as sender forth, shows the Son again to be sender forth of the Spirit?

For if the Son’s generation from the Father is unimpaired, how will the Son be shown to be sender forth of the Spirit? It would be necessary to find no deficiency in the divine nature: it begets the Son, and some supposed grandson is here fashioned, while the Son, as Son from the Father, is also shown to be sender forth of the Spirit. But if this is so, a heap of impiety and a deep pit emerge. Therefore the Spirit does not proceed from the Son as from the Father.

Such arguments, by which this prudent man attempts to remove from the Son the causality of procession, seem rather those of an ignorant man than of a diligent one. He asks what disinheritance and loss there is to the Son if, in being Son, He is not Father—though this should not have been asked, and still less inferred. This may be seen from many other examples: for instance, if the Father, in being maker, shows the Son to be maker. “All things were made through Him” (John 1). Must the Son necessarily be Father in order to show that, in being maker, He is begetter? Yet no deficiency is found in the divine nature.

The fallacy becomes entirely plain if an example is taken from our own affairs. If a father, in being foolish, shows his son to be foolish, there is clearly no necessity to infer the generation of a foolish son, lest the father’s foolishness suffer loss. I think an error in this form of expression is concealed because the same thing is not explained by the same interpretation. For this inference concerns substantial things, not properties. This may be seen when the hiding places are opened, if for a brief while one sets aside divine religion and turns one’s mind to the propagation of the human race. Does not the son of any human being, although he possesses all that is substantial to his father, sometimes retain a very small share of those things that are not such?

If the generation of the Son and the sending forth of the Spirit belonged substantially to the Father, the Son would necessarily have acquired the very same things—and indeed the Holy Spirit also, and this to infinity. But the Father begets the Son or sends forth the Spirit not in being substance, nor in that whereby He differs as God from the Son or Spirit, for these Three are one and the same God. Rather, He differs from the Son in that He begets; and from the Spirit alone in that He sends forth. Thus it is evident that such an inference has place only regarding substantial things.

For it is indisputable that personal or hypostatic properties are unchangeable, and that their interchange would produce such confusion and indistinction of the persons—persons known as different only when all other considerations are excluded. But being cause, or, so to speak, causative, and sending and being sent, together with many other things, are not hypostatic or personal properties. Therefore there is no confusion of persons when it is said: “The Son and the Father are one cause of the Holy Spirit.”

For nature is, as it were, one substantial reality; properties, however, are marks and differences of indivisible persons, and are not themselves the marks of persons. In created things, on the other hand, it happens that there is some difference within the same nature, that natures are separable, and that they often do not have the same properties.

The Son alone is from the Father as offspring, according to: “I came forth from the Father” (John 16), and: “From the womb before the morning star I begot you” (Psalm 109 [CIX]). This does not mean that God has a womb, but that lawful offspring are more commonly accustomed to be brought forth from the wombs of those who conceive. Therefore the expression means nothing else than to establish that the Only-begotten is the Father’s legitimate offspring. Consequently the Spirit is proper to the Son, as He is to the Father, since among all that belongs to the Father there is nothing alien to the Son. “All mine are yours, and yours are mine” (John 17).

How, then, would anyone dare to attribute the Spirit’s causality to the Father alone? He faces danger at the very threshold by separating the Spirit from the Son when he says that the Spirit is not from the Son, from whom He has existence as from the Father, as has been shown. The Spirit is certainly poured forth by the Son; but He is not the Son’s possession: He is the gift of Father and Son, not a creature. He teaches without being taught by another, because, being God, He knows all things and possesses all things.

We, however, though made gods through Him, are products; and what is made is not of the maker’s substance, as what is begotten is of the begetter’s substance. Therefore the Son is begotten from the Father’s substance and is the figure of the Father’s substance, because He alone exists from Him by birth. But the Spirit is from the substance of the Father and Son by procession.

If the Spirit has existence from the Father’s substance but not from the Son’s substance, whose Spirit He is by nature, then the Father is separable from the Son; the person of each is not of one and inseparable substance. But the Father is not separable from the Son, since they have the same knowledge, the same substance, and the same life. For things not of the same substance are not comprehended by one knowledge, nor can they give life in the same way. Therefore, since the Spirit is substantially from both, He has existence from each equally and in the same manner.

Thus He says: “As the Father knows me, and I know the Father,” that is, I know Him as perfectly as He knows me; thence I know all things, because “the Father is in me, and I in the Father” (John 10). Therefore, if the Spirit is the Father’s by nature, He is the Son’s also, if He is the Father’s and Son’s substantially. For the Father loves the Son, shows Him all things, and gives Him whatever He Himself has. Yet the Son is the Father’s wisdom, and the Father neither knows nor possesses anything without the Son.

From this it is clear that the Spirit, by whom the Father loves the Son and whom He gives Him without measure, belongs equally to both. In loving the Son, the Father exists in the Son and the Son in the Father—not as something contained within a container, but as those for whom being one, the same, and equal is identical. Therefore He says: “If you knew me, you would surely know my Father also” (John 8). This inference must certainly be charged with falsehood if the Spirit does not proceed from the Son. For if the Father has some property that is not the Son’s, perfect knowledge of the Father is by no means obtained through knowledge of the Son.

Perhaps this will be clearer in the following way. Knowledge of no one discovers in the Son that which does not belong to Him; but sending forth the Holy Spirit belongs to the Father alone. Therefore knowledge of no one discovers in the Son the sending forth of the Holy Spirit, which is the Father’s proper attribute. Thus it is not true that, if the Son is known, the Father is known also. We must avoid the things from which inconveniences arise and hold to the rule of truth: “If you knew me, you would surely know my Father also.” Since this is true, it is evident that the Spirit comes forth from the Son as from the Father.

The persons are not separated or distant from one another, but mutually exist in one another without confusion. Therefore we are called three human beings, since we are three persons distant in place and in many other respects, and are not properly one. But in the Holy Trinity there is one God, not three gods, because of the persons’ identical substance and their unconfused mutual indwelling. They differ not in power, are not extended through time, and are not divided by spaces; for there is nothing between Father and Son such that the Father’s existence is earlier than the Son’s. Therefore, since the Son’s communion with the Father is eternal and equal in all things, the Holy Spirit’s communion with the Son is eternal also; from the Son He differs in nothing except procession, just as He differs from the Father.

## CHAPTER XVIII

But Nicholas, bishop of Methone, still brings forward his novelties of expression as though they were Latin opinions, pronouncing them insultingly; and, like a good athlete in contests, or like an eagle in the clouds urging its young to fly, he rises and swells in speech in order to catch positions that he has not yet understood. For he says:

> “If, because the Father and Son are one, and are altogether one in nature, it must therefore be granted that the Spirit proceeds from the Son as from the Father—this being the novelty sought by Latin doctrine—then it must also be granted that the Son is necessarily begotten from the Spirit as from the Father, because Father and Spirit are one in nature.”

But if this is not so, the Spirit is endangered, since He is not one in nature with the Father; and Macedonius is once again plainly vindicated. Yet this man comes nowhere near the truth. For the Latins do not say that the Spirit is from the Son because Father and Son are one God, nor are they compelled to say this by any argument. Rather, they confess that the Spirit proceeds from both because He belongs equally to the Son and the Father—not as made, not as born, not as a possession, but as belonging to both alike; not as a human act or work, but somewhat as radiant light belongs to the sun.

Moreover, it is evident from this too that the Spirit is the Son’s and is from the Son: the Son is Himself the figure of the Father’s person and, so to speak, an equal measure of the greatness and balance of that same person. Since the figure of the Father’s person is equal, and the person is equal to its figure, and since the Spirit is declared to proceed from the Father’s person, it is necessary that, since the same Spirit belongs to the Son, who is in every way equal to the Father, He should also be declared to proceed from the Son. Therefore, if the Spirit proceeds from the Father, He proceeds from the Son—or else the Son is not the equal and balanced figure of the Father’s person.

Again: the figure is equal to the greatness and person of the Father. But the Spirit is declared to proceed from that greatness and person. Therefore the same will be declared to proceed from the figure also. Thus the Son sends forth the Spirit as does the Father.

Someone may object: “The Spirit is equal to the Father’s person; but the Father’s person is declared to have the Son. Therefore the same will be predicated of the Spirit, and the Son will be the son of the Holy Spirit.” But I say that this is not an equivalent comparison, because it has never been granted that the Son belongs equally to the Father and the Spirit, whereas all confess that the Spirit belongs equally to the Son and the Father.

Therefore, in matters from which nothing unworthy or improper follows for the divine persons, we call the Father cause and the Son co-cause; and no injury is done thereby to the Son, Father, or Holy Spirit. For in embassies and gifts of the Spirit, the Son is always the Father’s partner. But to call the Spirit Father, or to call the Son the Spirit’s son, is execrable and profane.

Nor does the proposition which says that sending forth is common to Father and Son destroy the property by which the paternal person is fitted to be distinguished, and which the Father alone possesses. This is fatherhood alone, according to which, as is clear from the foregoing, He is not seen to be sender forth, but Father alone. Every property customarily preserves the source of its name in all things denominated from it, as heat does in what is hot and coldness in what is cold. No property causes the individual thing under consideration to be denominated twice from one source. But fatherhood is one property, existing only in the Father. Therefore the Father is called Father only according to fatherhood, and not sender forth.

The philosophers say that three things are required for what is denominated from something: the thing from which it is denominated; the name; and, further, a distinctive termination belonging to that thing alone. If any of these three is lacking, denomination is prevented. It is clear, therefore, that “sender forth” is denominated neither from fatherhood nor from sonship. Hence it is apparent that the begetter begets according to one property and sends forth the Spirit according to another.

And it must be observed that the Spirit proceeds from the Son as from the Father not because of equality of honor between Father and Son. For if the Spirit emanated from both because of equality of honor, it would seem to follow that, because of equality of honor, the Son is from the Spirit as He is from the Father. This is asserted by the bishop of Methone, who will be found, against his will, to be right in what he says:

> “When two of equal honor proceed from the Father, if one confers upon the other the benefit of existence, the other ought to render an equal return to preserve their equality of honor. If he does not return it, where is the observance of immutable order? If he cannot, he is weak; if he will not, he is envious.”

Ah, a good Spirit—upright and principal, consubstantial in nature and of the same power with the Son and Father. This man, and everyone wishing to understand, will find what has been said true. For the Spirit, being equal to the Son, renders grace as God to God. The return which the Father receives by the Spirit’s proceeding from Him, the Spirit makes to the Son by proceeding from Him: for both are called, and are, senders forth.

From what has been said, I think, the objection of the bishop of Nicomedia will also be resolved. It says:

> “In whatever the Son shares with the Father, He does not share more or less. Therefore, if He shares in causality, He must share equally. But if He shares equally, then He must be begetter just as He is sender forth, since both are referred to the notion of cause. But if this is not so, by what reasoning will He have half and not the whole cause? For what is partial is imperfect, and nothing concerning the Lord is imperfect.”

I marvel at this man, first because he makes, as it were, a mixture of substantial matters and properties. For cause is neither among substantial matters nor a hypostatic or personal property, as was said earlier. Second, he draws a conclusion as though from a univocal term. But “cause” is not univocal here, nor even properly equivocal, as some suppose. They say it is not equivocal because it shows a community of causes, according to which they have in common some relation to things of which they are causes. Yet in equivocal things no community of realities is considered according to the equivocal name. Causes do, however, equally have this in common: they are prior to those of which they are causes, either in power or in act. Therefore the word is not homonymous.

That it is not univocal is clear. A univocal term has an indifferent relation to the thing, so that one and the same definition belongs to all things contained under its univocal designation. But here the rationale belonging to the Father is not the same as that belonging to the sender forth. For the Father is called begetter for one reason and sender forth for another, as has already been shown. Those who propose such arguments say that the name “cause” is, as it were, from one to one.

Finally, what truth can support the inference: “If the Son shares causality with the Father, He shares in every causality”; or again, “if in some causality, then in every”—for this seems to be the sense of the proposition set forth above? In neither case does the consequent follow from the antecedent. For an indefinite statement customarily entails a particular, not a universal.

Nevertheless, the proposition that the Son shares equally with the Father in whatever He shares is not to be denied. Since He shares with the Father in sending forth the Spirit, He does not share with Him in begetting. The Father alone begets, but the Father alone does not send forth the Spirit.

Therefore the fallacy in question, and the particular communion of the Son and Holy Spirit, may be recognized by a similar example: “In whatever the Spirit shares with the Son, He shares equally, not according to more or less. Therefore, if He shares with Him in paternal consolation, He must share altogether equally. If so, He will be Word just as He is Paraclete, since both are referred to the notion of consolation. But if not, by what reasoning will He have half and not the whole cause of paternal consolation? For what is divided is imperfect.”

The Spirit and Son also have other things in common. Certainly Scripture expresses a communion not merely of the Three as Trinity, but also of two alone—namely, Son and Spirit. Moses conveys unity figuratively while intimating the Trinity: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, God is one” (Deuteronomy 6). In this He teaches unity and in some manner manifests the Trinity. For by saying “Lord” once and “God” twice, he sets forth the number of the Trinity; by adding “is one,” he gives believers a fitting doctrine of one God. For the holy Trinity has one substance, power, and will.

The same is confessed by the host of heavenly powers chanting a hymn to God: when they say “holy” three times and “Lord” once, in the one expression they show the number of the properties, and in the other they recall the unity of nature. From this it is again most evident that there are three divine persons of one substance.

But the Savior confesses in the Gospel the indivisible and inseparable character of the Holy Trinity, saying to the devil: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him alone shall you serve” (Matthew 4). And elsewhere: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart” (Matthew 22). Do you suppose that because He did not say, “the Lord your God and His Son,” we ought not to love—or rather, love together with the Father—the Son and the Holy Spirit of both? This indeed is the Spirit who alone is divine. Certainly no creature is called a divine spirit or a spirit of sanctification.

But Paul plainly shows that the name “divine” in itself belongs only to the three persons, when he calls the Athenians superstitious on account of their images, as Luke reports in Acts in these words: “Since we are God’s offspring, we ought not to think that the divine is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by human art and thought” (Acts 17).

But concerning the Son and Spirit, the prophet says—as some maintain, speaking in the person of Christ—that He shows that the Father sent Himself and the Spirit: “The Lord has sent me, and His Spirit.” Solomon also testifies concerning the sending of the Spirit in the Book of Wisdom:

> “We scarcely apprehend the things upon earth, and discover with labor the things before our eyes; but who has searched out the things in heaven? And who has known your mind, unless you gave wisdom and sent your Holy Spirit from the heights?” (Wisdom 9)

Therefore the Savior declares in the Gospel: “If you love me, keep my commandments; and I will ask the Father, and He will send you another Paraclete” (John 14). He says “another Paraclete,” that is, another like me. And again: “I have spoken these things to you; but the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name”—that is, in my power and through me—“will teach you all things” (John 15).

It is therefore evident from what has been said that the Son and Spirit have something in common besides the Father: namely, being Paraclete, existing from the Father—something that none of the created beings can possess—and making known to human beings the Father’s name and will, as those who know it well and perfectly, which belongs to no creature. Therefore it is not improper that the Son is one cause and one principle with the Father of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XIX
But it must be observed with great care that “principle” or “cause,” as is clear from what has gone before, when referred to the Spirit, are rightly understood to belong, not singly to the Father alone nor singly to the Son alone. They are properly attributed to both, without peril to the soundness of faith. But when God from God, light from light, principle from principle is said, [Col. 0272C] the Son is understood in each clause; just as, when it is said that the unbegotten is the principle or cause of the Son, the Father is understood in both expressions. For, I think, it makes no difference to say: “The unbegotten is the principle or cause of the begotten”; “The unbegotten is prior to the begotten”; “The Father is the principle of the Son”; and “The Father is the cause of existence to the Word.” For in such expressions “principle” or “cause,” delimited by any other property, produces an understanding of the Father alone.

Therefore, according to the rule of the dialecticians, of things which are simultaneous by nature neither is the cause of the other’s being. For it is not the Father, but the reality which the Father is, that is the cause of the Son’s being; and likewise it is not the Son, but the reality which the Son is, that is the cause of the Father’s being. For the Father comes to be Father [Col. 0272D] when the Son has come to be. They therefore say: since the Father is not prior to the Son in time, while the cause of anything is prior in actuality or potentiality to that of which it is the cause, it is quite evident that neither confers the cause of existence upon the other.

This opinion does not share the truth concerning the first and heavenly Father; for the Father is the cause of the Son. Yet it does not appear that the reality which is simply Father is the cause of the Son’s existence. Indeed, when the Lord calls the unbegotten the principle of the begotten, and the begetter the cause of the Word, not the substance which is simply Father, but the Father seems to be understood in each case. [Col. 0273A] Likewise, when it is said, God from God, light from light, principle from principle, not the substance which the Son is, but simply the Son is conceived from the utterance of the individual nominatives; as though in each clause this were expressed: the Son exists from the Father, and the holy Fathers write “God indeed from God,” “light from light,” and “principle from principle.” According to this account, “cause” is most correctly proclaimed in the sermon on the Nativity of the Son himself, namely: “Christ is born—glorify him.” Gregory, great in theology, bearing witness to the doctrine of the Latins, declares in these words:

> “The Word of God was before the ages—invisible, incomprehensible, incorporeal; principle from principle, light from light, the fountain of life and immortality.”

Certainly, if that Word is in no way cause and principle of the Paraclete, he alone is vainly called principle from principle. For the Spirit too is God from God, light from light, and, with the Father and that same Word, [Col. 0273B] principle and cause of every creature from principle. Yet divine Scripture does not much employ such expressions as “God of God,” “cause of cause,” “light of light,” or “principle of principle.” Therefore the Father alone is cause or principle of the Son, because he alone begets; and for this reason the only-begotten Word of God is said to be of the Father alone, because he alone is begotten from him. But the Holy Spirit is not said to be of either one alone, but equally of both. From this it again [Col. 0274A] appears that God the Father and the Son confer the cause of existence upon the Holy Spirit, and that the Father’s distinctive property is not impeded if the Son, together with his begetter, emits the Spirit.

## CHAPTER XX

Therefore let no one, torn apart by errors, grind his teeth; let no one, borne on the Stygian oar [*scalmo* for *calmo*] of faith’s ruin, be carried irretrievably down to Tartarus; let no one shut out from himself the sight of the whole true sun; let no one, set against truth with a crooked balance, pervert the interpretation of the sayings cited. Rather, let him have more deeply fixed in his mind that God, the ruler of simplicity, excludes his only-begotten Son from the emission of the Spirit, although the Son has need of nothing and can never [Col. 0274B] be inferior to anything.

And since much still remains for the resolution of all the questions, and since the pen of my beloved brother Leo—the keenness of my intellect and the incentive of this undertaking—cannot continue its accustomed service of writing, both because it is occupied with interpreting imperial letters and because he recently crossed the Hellespont to the Asiatic region with the most august prince Manuel, I am compelled here to pause for breath and to bring this section briefly to a close.

## PREFACE TO THE SECOND BOOK. TO LEO THE TUSCAN

[Col. 0273]

Your return, my brother Leo the Tuscan, has exhausted the breathless fuel of my heart’s surging waves and greatly strengthened its zeal for investigating the generation of the eternal persons. For when the prudence displayed by the nobility of your mind proves itself as though steeped in heavenly liquid, and foretells a secure ability to observe the contests of others, it gives great help to a brother’s anxiety. And when it declares that the examination of the most weighty judges need no longer be feared, if I should expound what I have conceived concerning matters great, exalted, splendid in majesty, and best by nature, it makes light the burden which seemed inexplicable—the eminence of supreme authority and lofty dignity.

For this reason, since your departure, the keen edge of my mind, as though pricked by blows, has been constrained night and day; it supposes itself to roam through airy breadths by means of inanimate thought, and to touch something of lyrical sweetness. I do not doubt that this will happen if, through the facility of understanding, setting aside the rich vein of elaborate speech, the bombast of eloquence, and the many figures which a brilliant discourse commonly demands, I try, as far as I can, to unfold the conceived argument by completed reasonings.

For the approaches are difficult, and many are the doors which both exclude what seeks admission and open themselves only with difficulty, scarcely making room for an intention that knocks. Therefore, since Fortune exercises her envy in such matters, a thousand bolts stand before every entrance, to be broken by a rich array of plausible and necessary arguments. What mind, not moderately stirred, does not seek to come to the milk-pail and investigate more carefully who pours in blood and who the sweetness of milk?

That neither we nor others may regret the purpose and its execution, there is need not of the anointing of wrestlers in the palaestra, but of the oil of gladness—that is, of God’s inspiration and breathing—he who governs this whole fabric, the flashing globes of the flaming spheres, and contains in the ether the whole heavenly love of immeasurable light. Therefore I invoke this supreme Creator of things, that he may come to one who hungers with loaves and grant the abundant completion of the work begun. For without him hope is deprived of attaining its end; the impulse to speak is vain; usefulness is useless; and error is destructive.

Certainly, the investigation of such great matters, the labour overflowing into unwearied life, and the commendable earnestness of your contemplative diligence, brother, do not come from human counsel. But, breathed upon by that same Spirit of whom the discourse is undertaken, you urge the steel of this enterprise as the Cyclopes of Etna do, and assign skill to the sevenfold pipe in words more lofty and resonant, as though you had found in your brother the treasure of that philosophy.

Since, then, I see you exceedingly desirous both of the threshold of this formidable disputation and of its completion, I shall try to shorten the long windings chosen by gravity, and direct the course of the discourse begun amid citron-wood or cypress-panelled ceilings. In this purpose that Gospel saying gives much confidence: “Where the body was, there the eagles shall be gathered” (Matt. XXIV), and the flock of other birds feeding upon the flesh of such a body. For where the truth of the Christian faith is, the testimonies of the saints abound; and the ointment, namely the Holy Spirit, by dispersing the darkness of falsehood, descends upon Aaron’s beard—that is, upon those who cultivate such truth and plough furrows with the ploughshare of rectitude.

Yet contradiction never leaves such persons, just as storms do not leave the ocean, because attachment to one’s native soil is obstinate and the ancestral garment cannot easily be stripped away. You certainly know to the letter how the host of adversaries will confront the discourse undertaken. If it remains uncorrected, it will be deprived, like a pruned vine, of the delight and sweetness of its fruits. For a crafty race of men, which cannot exist without the bitterness of gall, despising the stability of antiquity, most often embraces untimely arguments more for their emptiness than for their truth. Indeed, some things are burned by the same flame, others are scarcely warmed, some become white like silver, and others black like bronze.

To this end the most circumspect caution of divine discourse allows none of its own content to be violated; excluding the necessity of harm, it forbids one to set foot hastily upon a most difficult matter. For whether viewed near at hand or from afar, it bars the one desiring to unravel it by unexpected recesses, as though he were a troublesome intruder hunting the understanding of most splendid brightness.

Finally, domestic exercise in refuting calumny does not seem weak, nor the daily concern of the Greeks, perhaps concealed by a veil, whose arguments are so firm that they think the walls of our common refuge will be melted by their assaults. Therefore they burn with the fiercest disputes, armed with intent to injure more than a hawk is armed with claws. Hence, I think, it has come about up to the present that their accusation, softened by no contests—indeed, that evil has spread more widely than was supposed—has violated the rule of Catholic faith and brotherly justice. Therefore, the greater the danger, the more watchfully must we labour in this discourse which you request, employing the same former kind of argument, as the subject requires.

And since a pen, unless moved by the hand of a scribe, naturally accomplishes nothing by itself, come, my brother, half of myself: as you have already committed and praised what has been given to the pages, undertake, with God as guide, the matters to be spoken. For what follows will mutually embrace what precedes, and, in seeking the reward of public benefit, will be fitted both to firmness of thought and to elegance of words.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0275]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0275A]

Concerning God the Father, and the Son and Spirit proceeding differently from his substance, whereas there ought to be one confession among Christians, alas, there is a variety of opinion, as there is among philosophers concerning the generation of the world. Some of them maintained that this world is eternal and unbegotten, saying: “This world neither any god nor any human being made, but it always was.” Others said that it is generated solely because it is perceptible, not because it began at some point in time. For what is thus generated necessarily precedes time, although it received existence under some time, as Aristotle says: “He indeed calls the world ungenerated in this respect, that time did not precede it”; but generated again [Col. 0275B] in that it received its existence from a divine cause, as the same writer says in the book *On the Heavens*: “The heaven is moved by that which is unmoved, and nothing comes to be better than it.” And again, near the beginning of the *Metaphysics*: “God appears to be some principle of all causes.”

For it is impossible that the first cause should be generated. For just as every effect is made by some efficient cause, so everything that is begotten is begotten by some begetter. Therefore, according to Aristotle, “God is the first cause of all invisible and visible things; this God is one and simple, than whom nothing simpler can be conceived.” All things participate in him, and nothing which does not participate in him exists. God is participated in not sensibly, nor is he spatially contained by those who participate in him; rather, without relation, he is wholly present in the participation of each individual and is wholly received by all. Certain saints demonstrated this by a comparison, saying: Just as all who are present—young men, children, women, old people, and even irrational creatures—participate according to their own capacity in the voice of one possessing a loud and piercing voice, while the voice in which they participate remains in itself unparticipated; so God, according to substance, is neither participated in nor known. Yet he is said to be participated in inasmuch as all things are from him as efficient cause and all things are contained in him in their being, as the great Dionysius testifies.

“God,” he says, “is participated in wholly by each and in no part by anyone, as the centre in the middle of a circle is participated in by all the lines surrounding the circle; just as the impressions of a seal participate in the archetypal seal—wholly and identically in each impression, but in none according to any part.”

Therefore, although God is participated in by many, he is one—not as the principle of numbers, but as received by all and having nothing after himself which can be communicated to him. Hence this world, which while it comes to be receives existence from the divine cause, does not subsist from itself and is not properly one, since it is divisible and subjects part to part. But what is properly indivisible must be without separation and be joined wholly to its own whole. What truly exists through itself and has no principle is indivisible; but every divisible thing has separation and derives its being from without.

But God alone, since he has nothing from without, is truly indivisible and one, as he himself teaches Moses: “For I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Jer. XI); and, commanding that worship not be divided, he says: “You shall have no other gods besides me” (Exod. XX). Then, plainly showing that none of the things which can be seen is fittingly attributed to him, he says: “You shall not make for yourself a graven image, nor any likeness of the things which are in heaven above, and which are on earth below, and which are in the waters beneath the earth” (ibid.). “You heard a voice; [Col. 0276C] you saw no form. You shall make no figure, because the Lord your God is one.” He is not divisible, nor does he derive his being from without; indivisibly he knows divisible things, things in time without time, and mutable things without change.

And although God is indivisible, as has been shown, he is nevertheless divided into the Trinity, which is indissoluble and indivisible, not compounded of parts, nor existing in a subject, so that, by bearing a subject in act or potentiality, it should cease to exist by difference from that subject. Rather, it is everlasting eternity, possessing all its being gathered together at once, not diffused or unfolded through the extension of time. This Trinity contains all things at once, provides for all things at once, and alone measures all things at once, while itself measured by no one. For time measures temporal things part by part. But it measures all things together, as though adapted to measured things. It certainly differs entirely from things which come to be, and from all things which are to be; for it neither was nor will be, but, since this is its proper mode, is wholly present at once. No part of it subsists while another part will already subsist or does not yet exist.

It is infinite and has neither before nor after; it is without matter, beyond every simplicity, beyond every limit, beyond every intellect, and beyond the comprehension of every rational creature, as the great Dionysius writes:

> “It is not permitted to praise the thearchic superessentiality, which is above all beings, as mind or substance; for it exists before all things and contains all things in itself, is received by all as superessential and supergood, and is the principle originating above, so that nothing which may be said of it can be said properly.”

From this, I think, it follows that many err in their division of it. Of them one must fear that, while they try to maintain that they are suffocated by the best ointment, like Ericius, they are deadened by the fragrance of life—a thing divine Scripture has in no way produced. One of these is Nicetas of Byzantium, the philosopher, who, inventing vain charges against his neighbour, frames his arguments in this manner.

## CHAPTER II

“If,” he says, “the Spirit proceeds from the Son as from the Father, then he proceeds either by the same procession or by a different one. If by a different one, that procession will be either prior to the paternal procession or inferior to it. If it is superior, then the Son will altogether be better than the Father. For those whose natural emission is superior are themselves altogether better. But if it is inferior, the Spirit will be inferior and superior to himself, since by a different procession he has existence; and the Son will not be consubstantial with God the Father. For those whose natural emissions are inferior have inferior natures as well. But if it is equal, it will be the same as the paternal procession. [Col. 0277D] If it is the same, I ask whether it completes the Spirit’s existence in actuality or not. If it does not complete it, it is superfluous; but nothing concerning God is superfluous. If it completes it in operation, the emission from the Father is imperfect, and therefore the Son supplements it. If the paternal emission of the Spirit is perfect—how could it not be, when it produces perfect existence for the Spirit?—then that which is from the Son is again superfluous. For it contributes nothing to the completion of the Spirit, since that which is from the Son is the same as the paternal emission, also because of the simplicity of the Spirit’s existence.”

What shall I answer to this? I confidently confess that it is equal—indeed, rather, the same. But the question which follows, “Does it complete the Spirit’s existence or not?” indicates two things to me: first, that the emission from the Father is needy, which is in no way to be accepted; second, that the Spirit’s emission from the Father is full, as is that from the Son—a confession which is pious. Therefore, the conclusion, “If it does not complete, then it is superfluous,” does not follow. For what consequence can there be in saying that, if the paternal emission is not needy, that which is from the Son is superfluous? Nor does this conclusion follow: “If it contributes—that is, completes in actuality—the Father’s emission is imperfect.” For neither the Father nor the Son emits the Spirit in part; each emits him wholly and perfectly, equally.

For the Son alone exists from the Father without an intermediary; therefore he emits the Spirit perfectly, as does the Father. Existing in the Father, he does not have his being as Son from elsewhere; and the Father is in him, because he has nothing unlike the Father. For the Son is the image of the Father, and the Father is known in him as in an image. The true Word of God is a seal representing the Father in himself; therefore he emits the Spirit perfectly, just as the Father does. Do we not call God the Father perfect, and the Son likewise perfect and in the same way? Yet neither is needy.

A similar question may be asked concerning this, with a few additions. The Saviour says in the Gospel: “No one knows who the Son is except the Father, nor who the Father is except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. XI). And rightly, he says, because “I am of the same nature and substance as he is; and just as no one knows him, so no one knows me except the Father alone. And this is greater than all things which I possess: to know the Father and to subsist with him in the same substance and nature.”

Why, then, does the Son know the Father, and the Father the Son? The Father certainly reveals himself, and the Son reveals himself as well. The Father reveals himself, as the Saviour testifies in answering Peter: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVI). The Son also revealed the Father and himself, yet not as he himself knows himself, but insofar as one worthy of revelation can know. For he appeared to Ezekiel, from the loins upward, in the appearance of electrum (Ezek. VIII); to Daniel as the Ancient of Days (Dan. VII); and to Isaiah veiled by the Seraphim (Isa. VI). Likewise he reveals the Father himself: “For I am in the Father, and the Father in me; and he who sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV). Thus both Father and Son revealed themselves to Peter.

Come then: was the revelation the same or different? One must confess it altogether the same. But if it is the same, one must ask whether the Father’s revelation completes in actuality the Son’s knowledge, or not. If it completes in actuality and operation, the Son’s revelation is superfluous; but God does nothing in vain. If it completes in actuality and operation, the Father’s revelation will be imperfect and the Son will therefore supplement it. But if the Father’s revelation is perfect, the Son’s is again superfluous. This plainly does not follow, since neither deficiency nor separation nor division can appear or exist in the divine persons.

Therefore they reveal equally, but not according to the measure in which they themselves know, but according to the capacity of those to whom the revelation is made. The Father and Son know one another, not by revelation, but by nature. Rational creatures, however, receive knowledge and revelation by grace. For by removing the veil laid over our heart, each reveals himself to us in the Father. No one knows the divine Trinity, because it is set beyond every understanding; therefore it alone is known by itself alone, as the Evangelist proclaims: “No one has ever seen God” (John I).

Certainly, unless someone has the same knowledge of God—which has happened to no one and never will—he cannot know him as he truly knows himself. This may be made clear from the following: all knowledge embraces the comprehension of the truth of things either through sense, intellect, likeness, or imagination.

Again:

> “There are five things through which the soul receives knowledge: art, prudence, discipline, wisdom, and mind. But through none of these can anyone receive perfect knowledge of God, especially because there is no accident either in God or concerning God. For the fewer accidents there are in anything, the more difficult it is to know, and the greater diligence it requires. Since, therefore, there is no accident in God, and like is known by like, his substance cannot be known.”

Again:

> “There is no knowledge of infinite things; for unless knowledge comprehends what is knowable, it does not know it at all. But God is infinite; therefore he cannot be comprehended by any of the aforementioned modes. He surpasses in his purity every likeness of bodies and incorporeal things. He may be believed, but cannot at all be comprehended; he is approached only by mind and faith, without which the mind cannot see intelligible things. For creatures are not such as their maker, as Parmenides says; nor are they as great as he is.”

Therefore, since the Father and Son reveal equally, know one another by nature, and equally and perfectly emit the Spirit, it is evident that the emission from neither is imperfect, needy, or superabundant.

## CHAPTER III

But, that the discourse may return to the same point, the bishop of Methone again begins weaving paralogisms. For he does not reason either simply or in response to his opponent in this manner:

> “If the Son, consubstantial with the Father who is without beginning and cause, is in turn a principle, there are two different principles in the Trinity: one in that he is without principle and established in the primacy of dignity; the other in that he is at once intermediate and initiating, and initiated by the difference of relative relations.”

Many answers to this objection may be given in reply, as is evident from what was set forth in the first book. For if Father and Son are not said to be two simply, but in a certain respect, and neither is separated from the other, much less will they be proclaimed two principles or two causes, since both together are the cause and principle of the Holy Spirit. Is not the Word of God, the Father’s Word, God with God? And God indeed begotten from unbegotten God, yet not two gods, begotten and unbegotten, but one and the same God. Thus there is one principle and one cause of the Holy Spirit: the Father, who is without beginning, and the Son, who is called principle and head, as Hilary says: “For the Son is the head of all things, but God is the head of the Son.”

Now the number two, where similar names used in counting intend to show some plurality of things, does so even if it does not state their mode of existence. For such terms reveal neither continuity nor distinction nor the difference of things divided, but only some diversity. But no such diversity exists between Father and Son in their conferring being upon the Spirit: each is one principle and one cause of the Spirit.

We must also heed Gregory the Theologian, who philosophizes in this way concerning the one without beginning, the one who is principle, and the one with the principle: “He who is without beginning, he who is principle, and he who is with the principle, are one God.” To be without beginning is not the nature of the one who has no beginning, or of the unbegotten. For it is not some thing, but the assertion that it is this: it is the position of an existing thing, not the destruction of what does not exist. Nor is the one who is principle divided, insofar as he is principle, from the one who is without beginning. For principle is not his nature, just as being without beginning is not the other’s nature. These things concern nature, but they are not nature. Thus he who is with the one who has no principle and with the one who is principle is nothing other than they are.

The name of the one without beginning is Father; of the one who is principle, Son; and of the one with the principle, Holy Spirit. The one nature of the three is God; the Father is harmony, from whom and to whom the things which follow in order are referred, not in order to collide but to be joined. Behold: this holy man plainly calls the Son “principle” and counts the Holy Spirit from him, because the Son is immediately the principle of the Spirit. For all three persons equally are principle of all creatures; from this it is clear that the Son is principle of the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, both what belongs to the Son and what belongs to the Spirit are referred to the Father, who alone is without beginning and without cause. But the Son, begotten from the Father, is the principle of the Holy Spirit, as can be demonstrated by the following syllogism.

Whatever is a principle in the holy Trinity is the principle of something in it; otherwise the holy man would have called the Son “principle” merely for nothing, although all three persons are equally judged the principle of all created things. But the Son is a principle in the holy Trinity; therefore the Son is the principle of something in it. Yet the Son is not the principle of the Father. Therefore he must be the principle of the Holy Spirit.

It is evident, then, from what has been said that “principle” does not divide the persons, since in Scripture the Father is called both principle and ἄναρχος (*anarchos*, “without beginning”). But although the Son is not called ἄναρχος, for he is from the Father, he is nevertheless called principle—perfect from a perfect Father—not as day comes from dawn, since what is perfect does not come from what is imperfect. For things brought into being proceed from imperfection: such is the nature of things, that they advance in an order given by Providence.

But the order observed in the divine persons, although its nature is unspeakable and ineffable, nevertheless plainly intimates this to those who think piously concerning the Trinity: that what is called first is the cause of that which is announced as nearest from it. Thus the Father, who is without beginning and cause, is first; nearest to him, without an intermediary, is the Son, who beyond all doubt, according to the account given, is principle of the Spirit. For the Spirit is not his own cause. Although the Spirit through himself fills the individual things that have him in themselves, he does not proceed from himself. For if he emitted himself, he would exist before he was emitted, and would emit himself when he did not exist. Therefore either the stated order is rendered void, or the Son must be understood as the Spirit’s cause according to the transmitted enumeration.

From this it is evident that false is the person who says:

> “Everything predicated of the life-originating and all-creating Trinity is found either to be said commonly, in the same way and univocally, of the three persons, or singularly of one. But since the mission of the Spirit is equally from the Father and Son, it is neither common to all three nor singularly of one.”

But the bishop of Nicomedia, pouring out arguments to the contrary, strives thus:

“Whatever God is, he is properly that, and does not admit its opposite: thus the Father is properly Father because he is not Son, and the Son is properly Son because he is not Father. But nature is not proper, because it belongs to both. Since these matters stand thus, the Son, being from the cause—that is, from the Father—is not himself a cause. For to be both cause and from a cause, in respect of nature which admits no division, is impossible, as reason has demonstrated.”

I say that this is not a syllogism, nor does any doctrine of the Latins admit an absurdity from it, since this statement touches truth only with respect to hypostatic and personal properties. But “principle” and “causative” are not such properties. Therefore the proposition, “Whatever God is, he is properly that,” is not true of these. For “principle” and “being from a cause” are not included under it. Gregory of Nyssa makes this clear in the third homily on the *Our Father*, saying:

> “The distinctive property of the Father is not to be from a cause; but this is not distinctive in the Son or Spirit. For the Son came forth from the Father, as Scripture says, and the Spirit proceeds from God and the Father. But just as being without cause belongs to the Father alone and cannot belong to the Son or Spirit, so conversely being from a cause is distinctive of the Son and Spirit and has no place in the Father’s nature, since it is common to Son and Spirit.”

And below:

> “But although the Son is from God, he is not the Spirit, nor is he called so, because this relational consequence is not reversible, so that the statement can be converted by reciprocal resolution and we may call the Spirit Christ just as we call Christ’s Spirit.”

This property plainly and without confusion distinguishes one from the other. Behold: a pure man rests upon pure doctrine, a good man upon good doctrine, and an upright man upon upright doctrine. Therefore whoever dares to assert that being from a cause is not proper to Son and Spirit, and likewise that the Spirit is not of the Son just as he is of the Father, plainly contradicts this great man.

From this it can also be evident that being a cause is not proper to the Father, because neither is being from a cause proper to the Son, as has been shown. For what is relative does not have as its proper attribute another relative; nor does what is relative have a relative as a proper attribute. For example, “double” is said in relation to “half,” and “exceeding” in relation to “excess”; but exceeding is not proper to double, nor is excess proper to half. Likewise, Father is said in relation to Son, and cause in relation to what is caused. But being from a cause is not proper to the Son, because it belongs also to the Spirit; nor is being a cause proper to the Father.

And because the Spirit is of the Son and of the Father, some have called him, as it were, the concord of both. Others assert that he is called concord because he is the cause of concord in our souls, which he makes harmonious and brings together into one. For so long as the Spirit is present, they say, no joining which even a needle’s cut could divide is severed. Therefore the Spirit was given in order to unite nations divided by language; and it is his equal care that the soul should agree with the body simply and uniformly.

But the bishop of Methone, crying out against the foregoing arguments, is not brought to shame:

> “If the Father,” he says, “is the cause of those who are from him, inasmuch as he is greater not by reason of nature but by reason of person, and the account of the paternal person does not belong to the Son, by what account is the Son, as Son, cause of the one Spirit in the Trinity? By reason of nature? Nature, then, is greater, and the battle against the Spirit (*πνευματομαχία*, *pneumatomachia*) is manifest. Or by reason of person? Then the Son will be fitted to the account of the Father’s person—the very Son whom Sabellius notoriously asserted to be Father—and in no respect is the Son cause of the Spirit. For if the Son is cause of the Spirit’s person by the same account by which the Father is cause of those who are from him, these two absurdities follow in the same respect: namely, that the Son is called Father of the paternal hypostasis, although the one is cause of two and the other of one; and that he completes the Father’s person in actuality, as though it were diminished before its completion. Nor should this be passed over without refutation.”

## CHAPTER IV
Accordingly, I say that the distinction which signifies that the Spirit proceeds from the Son, whether by reason of nature or by reason of person, has been made inadequately. For since they possess the same nature, neither is from the other according to substance—for how can nature beget itself? Nor likewise is this so by reason of person. For just as the Father is not, insofar as He is Father, the sender, so also the Son is not, insofar as He is Son, the cause and principle of the Spirit. Therefore, the Spirit has being from the nature of the Father and the Son, and from the person which is Father and that which is Son; yet not insofar as the one is Father and the other Son, but insofar as they bestow existence upon Him. Nor are there two principles, because in the emission of the Spirit they do not admit number. For number belongs not to what is one and altogether the same, but to that which has this and that. Hence, when one asks how many persons there are in the Father and Son, the answer is two. But when the ineffable and inexpressible cause of the Holy Spirit is carefully investigated, Father and Son are called not two causes of the Spirit, but one, according to the aforesaid manner of concord.

For this reason, one ought not to use a term signifying different principles or causes of the Holy Spirit. For if the Son of God and man is one person, and if the divine and human nature is one Christ, it ought not to seem incredible that two persons are one cause of the Holy Spirit. For among grammarians one cause signifies both substance and quality, and there is one signification of the name; according to their opinion, almost every name signifies substance and quality. Yet the fact that it signifies these does not mean that it signifies two things, nor is any name called equivocal; nor are substance and quality, [Col. 0283B] which are one signification of the name, confused.

It is therefore clear that the Son does not complete the person of the Father as though it suffered some deficiency; nor is anyone compelled to say that the Son Himself is a part of the Father’s person because the Spirit proceeds from Him. For how, if the Son is numbered with the Father on the same basis as the Spirit, would the Son be found to be a portion of the Father’s person in both respects? Certainly, if Lot’s daughter is cause of a son in the same respect as his parent, and is a cause together with that parent, she is by no means forced into the composition of the father’s person.

Further: if the Spirit had no relation to the Son, and were neither sent by Him nor proceeded from the Father through Him, He would not even be one of three persons sharing a divine property; rather, He would exist after the Son and would be His product, as Eunomius said. Therefore the Spirit has a relation to the Son, just as He has a relation to the Father, while differing equally from both. For the three divine persons differ in no way according to nature; but according to their personal properties they not only differ, but also agree.

Therefore the Son, like the Father, gives, sends, and emits the Spirit. For the Spirit overflows to us from the Son Himself, as He Himself testifies: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink, he who believes in me” (John 7), “as Scripture says: ‘Rivers of living water shall flow from his belly’” (ibid.). The Evangelist explains this by adding: “Now He said this concerning the Spirit, whom those believing in Him were to receive” (ibid.). The Spirit and His grace are called living water because He is active: if He finds a fitting dwelling-place, He does not leave it nor become emptied; and His grace does not flow forth from the belly of believers except through Him.

Thus, sent and given by Christ, He filled the flaming hearts of the disciples. From this it is clear that He had the Spirit more abundantly than they did, and in another manner, though the apostles, like ourselves, were passible. Although they worked great things by power, and gave the Holy Spirit to believers through prayer and often without prayer, merely by invoking the Lord’s name, they accomplished nothing of themselves in such matters. Rather, the Son gives the Spirit by His own power and from Himself; therefore the Spirit proceeds from the Son. [Col. 0284A] But Nicetas argues against this opinion, employing arguments of the following length.

## Chapter V

“Every image,” he says, “has a dissimilar relation to that of which it is said to be an image, except that which is called natural.”

Now man is the image of God, and was made according to God’s image. Since man is twofold, he bears, by analogy, a twofold likeness to the life-originating Trinity. In one way, because the first man is unbegotten: for he is a creature formed; Seth, however, is begotten, for he is offspring; while Eve is neither of these, because she is a division. In another way, because our mind is generative without passion and without flux, producing in us speech (*oratio*); for speech/reason (*ratio*) is the offspring of the mind. But spirit, though distinct from mind and speech in us, proceeds together with speech.

Therefore, what is considered in man according to the image of God, with respect to the difference of hypostatic properties—according to which, by analogy, it reflects a likeness to the Holy Trinity—is incommunicable to the remaining persons included within the range of the stated image, namely, the likeness. Indeed, one cannot imagine that the property of the first man could at any time come to Seth as something common; nor that Eve’s property could belong to either progenitor or offspring; nor again that Adam or Eve could possess the capacity to be born which belongs to the offspring.

If you examine the things within us, you will see the same. For you will not find in speech the property of mind by which it produces speech; nor in mind the property of speech as begotten; nor in spirit the property of spirit. But if, in things which have a fainter, imaginable likeness by analogy, there is found an incommunicable difference of properties, much more will this be so in that which is beyond sense and understanding. In the wholly unchangeable and immutable Trinity, who could find an incommunicable existence of personal properties?

For if that which appears less likely to belong will belong, then that which appears more likely to belong will also belong. Now it seems far less likely that in a flowing, created, changeable nature there should be no movement or change of the properties of persons by which it represents, by analogy, a likeness of the image. Much more, then, will this belong to the nature which is unchangeable, immutable, and always the same. If this is true, as has been shown, the emission of the Spirit is not common to Father and Son, as those who say so teach in a detestable and utterly impious manner.

What seems true to each person is not true, as Protagoras thought—for example, that the sun is one foot wide, though it is shown to be one hundred and seventy times larger than the earth. This philosopher almost certainly errs when he asserts that God the Father and the first man are similarly called “unbegotten.” In this he seems to stray little less than the heretic Eunomius, who attempted by arguments of this kind to demonstrate that “unbegotten” belongs to the divine substance alone.

[Col. 0285A] He said: “That which is called unbegotten cannot be understood as a privation; for it belongs among things that are privations according to nature, and are therefore subsequent to relations. But in God none preceded whose privation ‘unbegotten’ might signify.”

Likewise: “That which is divine is not in part begotten and in part unbegotten.” For it is indivisible, and there is nothing diverse in it; it is simple, one, and solely unbegotten. Therefore the substance itself is unbegotten, and is not to be divided so that one part may be pronounced unbegotten and another begotten.

First, then, it must be said that such statements do not introduce composition; next, that “unbegotten” does not indicate privation in God. Further, perhaps he was led astray by the addition or subtraction of one letter, namely *nu* (ν). For *agenēton* (ἀγένητον), written in Greek with one ν, means “uncreated”; and this name, if so understood, belongs not only to the divine nature but to all three persons, since nature together with the persons is uncaused. But when *agennēton* (ἀγέννητον) is written with two νν, it properly belongs to the Father alone—not to the Son, not to the Spirit, nor to any creature—indicating that He has no principle and no cause through Himself.

Therefore, if the divine substance is called *agenēton*, it must be understood as “uncreated,” with one ν; because, when two νν are written, the Father alone is meant, just as by “begotten” the Son is understood. But the Holy Spirit is neither *gennētos* (“begotten”) nor *agennētos* (“unbegotten”), although He is called “not begotten,” just as He is not called unbelieving or impious, although He does not believe, nor does He worship or venerate anyone, being God.

“Unbegottenness,” and similar terms said of God, show no likeness of the Creator to created things. For every likeness concerns form and existence; but the first man, in being unbegotten, had no likeness to the life-originating Trinity, because unbegottenness does not belong to nature or existence. For if unbegottenness belonged to nature, then, since all animals came forth unbegotten in the beginning, all would surely be of the same nature. Adam did not beget insofar as he was unbegotten, nor did Seth beget insofar as he was begotten.

[Col. 0285D] Therefore, God is called unbegotten because no cause preceded Him; but Adam, because he had God as his efficient cause, namely his former, is called unbegotten in another respect: because he was not from propagation, nor confined by the narrowness of a womb. It is clear that Adam’s being called unbegotten is not according to the likeness or image of God. For if Adam were called made in God’s image on that account, irrational creatures too—an utterance not to be permitted—would likewise be declared made in God’s image.

It must further be understood that “unbegotten” has different senses among philosophers. It is called unbegotten in one sense when something now exists which did not exist before, apart from extension and change of time; as some say concerning touching and moving. In another sense, when something can come to be and not come to be, as a house, which, while it is being made, does not yet exist. In another sense, when it is altogether impossible for something at one time to be and at another not to be, as God the Father, who is neither begotten nor receives a beginning from anything. Being eternal and unchanging, He has never come into contact with the cause of any beginning; for this reason He is properly called unbegotten.

A principle is also named as a proceeding cause, because it grants existence, makes, and brings to completion. But the subtlety of heretics called “begotten” the contrary of this, because the Word of God has generation, using an argument of this kind: if He has a principle in order to be, He was not before He was begotten, and there was a time when He was not. Yet the Word of God is not shown to exist as things born under time. This name in no way circumscribes the nature of the Word; for He is from the substance of the Father, as light and offspring, and thus exists eternally with Him.

But Adam’s unbegottenness was not a signifying property of his person, nor Eve’s division, nor Seth’s birthability. For every signifying property is considered in relation to the thing which it signifies. Adam’s unbegottenness, however, is not considered in relation to the thing signified, but externally; and similarly Eve’s division: for first a rib was cut off, and afterwards Eve was formed. But it should be noted that “begotten” appears to be a signifying property of the Son, and of Him alone, which no other son has ever possessed or will possess. For if the birth of all sons were personally a signifying property, they would all have the same character of person; nor would human beings differ numerically, whereas a signifying property is the cause of their difference, since it is impossible, in the things set before us, to find the same thing in another.

For things having the same property do not differ numerically, as “sword,” “blade,” and “weapon.” These remarks concerning “unbegotten” show that it is not a personal property and does not signify substance, since it comes from outside. Therefore one may briefly reply to the objections: it does not follow, if Adam, Eve, and Seth do not share the three aforesaid properties, that they share no others.

For behold, soul and body share neither incorporeality nor corporeality; nevertheless, as explained above, they have certain other common properties. In the same way Father and Son differ by the difference between unbegotten and begotten, but agree in cause and principle. Concerning speech, spirit, and mind, I say that the resemblance is weak and wholly unsuitable to the proposition, whether *logos* (λόγος) is understood as reason or as spoken discourse. For the mind does not generate reason; rather, reason seems in its own fashion to have its constitution from the mind.

Thus the comparison must be understood only of speech uttered with the voice, which, like spirit, is administered through bodily instruments; both are diffused and dissipated in the air. But in the Holy Trinity the Begotten and the Emitted are so without body, without passion, and without change. The Son proceeds from the Father alone; the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son, without passion, separation, or division. Among humans it is not so. For spirit is found without speech, as in groans and non-signifying sounds; speech without mind, as in drunkards, demoniacs, and many others; and mind alone without speech, without senses, indeed even without imagination, acts when it turns toward itself, embraces understanding of incorporeal things, contemplates the divine, and meditates uncertainly upon knowledge of universals that do not subsist.

For such a community subsists when the things participating in it undoubtedly exist. Things of one species have the same nature and participate in the same thing; and to contemplate this in itself belongs to mind alone. But speech and spirit are always exercised through the body. It is therefore clear that arguments of this sort and similar ones must be rejected, because they provide no trustworthy ground for drawing an incongruous conclusion. Nor do they establish that any property of the divine nature may be predicated of one person only of the divine majesty, or, conversely, that a property of any one of the persons may be predicated of the divine nature.

Therefore the proposition rests entirely upon truth: the emission of the Spirit is common to Father and Son. The bishop of Nicomedia does not agree. He says: “If the Son is from a cause, as from the Father, and is in turn a cause, as emitter of the Spirit, then the same thing is divided, since it is both cause and from a cause. But that which is divine is simple and is not divided. Therefore, if it is from a cause, it is not from a cause; for what God has, He has inseparably and not accidentally.”

Just as the finite cannot be equal to the infinite, so neither can that which is material be equal to that which is without matter. This argument, however, has no material relevant to the cause and is not suitably fitted. Unless “cause” is understood as that from which something is first made and into which it is finally dissolved—such as prime matter, which, in whatever things it is found, preserves its substance, and from which the elements are first made. Aristotle proves these elements to be simple by their motions, for each naturally has one motion and one matter. For matter numerically one is actually receptive of one form; this is clearer in composite things. One piece of wood cannot simultaneously be a bench, a table, and a wall, although one species numerically can produce many things, just as an art and any artisan produce many and different things.

But if the elements, though composed of matter and form and though causes of composite bodies, do not lose their simplicity, much more does the Son of God, though He is a cause and from a cause, remain in His simplicity.

Further: “Action, as third, proceeds from substance; power, counted as an effect of substance, and springing from it without intermediary, is second. Therefore substance, from which power proceeds, is prior in dignity to power.” From this it can be made sufficiently clear [Col. 0288A] that, just as substance is the cause of power and power of action, while remaining simple and indivisible, so the Father is the cause of the Son and the Son the cause of the Spirit, while remaining simple and indivisible.

It should be known, however, that some, distinguishing action, say that it is considered in two ways even in relation to Father, Son, and Spirit. One action they call attendant and not proceeding externally, according to which the Begetter and the Begotten alike and in the same manner emit the Spirit. The other they attribute to nature, which accompanies the three persons equally; according to this, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit create and make from nothing things alien to those persons. Therefore, if power proceeds from substance and action from power, power is not thereby twofold or composite. Much more, then, from the Father, who is power without beginning, proceeds power—namely the Son—from whom, as from the Father, the outflow of the Holy Spirit flows.

Again: “A paralogism by ‘another thing’ may deceive: the mind is uniform; the mind knows itself; therefore that which is uniform knows itself.” The mind, then, is twofold: known and knowing; understood and understanding; acting and acted upon. Therefore Plato said: “The soul is always moved—that is, it always knows itself.” Given this, let whoever wishes infer that the mind is superior and more honourable than itself, since that which acts is more honourable than that which is acted upon.

Such and similar inferences sometimes attain truth in things having matter and composition, and completing their operations under time; but in things without matter the truth escapes the conclusion.

Further: “The Son is sent and sends, yet is not thereby twofold.” From this, I suppose, another paralogism of the same bishop is refuted, which says: “If the Son has being from the Father alone, but the Spirit from Father and Son, then the Spirit has a twofold principle of being.” But how can what admits no composition be twofold? Such arguments certainly ought to be avoided. For if the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son in such a way that He has a twofold principle of being, the Father will likewise be found to possess a duality by the same reasoning, since He alone begets the Son but does not alone send and give the Spirit.

Yet such relations do not introduce duality. For “cause” and “causative,” so to speak, do not signify a substance, quantity, or quality, but signify relation. Hence it is clear that none of such relational names produces duality by being what it is. If names signifying substances, quantities, or qualities do not introduce duality when predicated of God, much less will names signifying relations do so.

For the Lord is called door, way, bread, truth, vine, light, and life. Though He is one and simple substance, He is thus named because of certain properties discerned in His works. Again, the Father is called *anarchos* (ἄναρχος), “without beginning”; *anaitios* (ἀναίτιος), “without cause”; unbegotten; begetter; and the like. Yet He is one, simple, and indivisible in subject—not only the Father Himself, but also the Son and the Holy Spirit: indeed, the whole Trinity is very often named from things that do not inhere in it.

For because it cannot be seen by man, it is called invisible and imperceptible; because it surpasses every understanding, inaccessible and infinite; because it is above corruption and death, incorruptible and immortal; without beginning and without rest—as though an infinite and boundless sea of substance, limited in persons but slipping away before it can be grasped and fleeing before it can be understood. These names derive not from what belongs to it in itself, but from things around it. We know from the Father—but rather, we perfectly believe—that the Father begets the Son and together with the Son emits the Spirit. Those who deny this do not judge rightly.

For the Spirit proceeding from the Father either touches the Son or does not touch Him. If He does not touch Him, there is nothing joining and uniting the Spirit to the Son, since the person does not include any property of the Spirit from the Son and has no personal community with Him.

If this is so, He is not the Son’s Spirit. For if the Spirit receives no marks or determinations of His being from the Son, He is neither the Son’s Spirit nor His image; and these are surely the Spirit’s marks and determinations.
