But if He receives these from the Son, He is always emitted from the Son as from the Father. For Father and Son are always emitter and creator; yet though they always emit, they do not always create, because of the weakness of the things created, which cannot be equal to the Trinity that is without beginning.

Therefore those who say that it is impossible for the Holy Spirit to be shared by Father and Son in the same respect do not judge piously or truly. They arrange words not to establish faith but, if possible, to ensnare. “Just as,” they say, “in those things in which the Father communicates with the Spirit, He cannot in any way be distinguished or separated from the Son, so in those things in which He has distinction in relation to the Spirit, it is impossible for Him to communicate with the Son in that respect.”

But this is wholly remote from truth. From what has gone before it is clear that the Father communicates certain things to the Son which He does not communicate to the Spirit, and certain things to the Spirit which He does not communicate to the Son. Whatever He communicates to both belongs to nature, insofar as it belongs according to nature. Hence it never occurs that, in that in which one of the three is personally separated from another, He is in that same respect joined to that other in the same manner. For it is altogether impossible and inconsistent that a genuine contradiction should declare in the Trinity the same thing personally distinct and joined in the same respect—not to mention asserting this of any beings, much less of the persons of the divine majesty.

Nor does it follow, if the emission of the Spirit is common to Father and Son, that the emission of the Spirit is the nature of both, and that nature and person are the same.

## Chapter VI

But Nicetas continues to extend his argument. He says: “If everything said of each person of the divine majesty is not predicated of it more and less, and if cause and principle are predicated of the person of the Father, then the Father will not be more cause insofar as He is begetter of the Son than insofar as He is emitter of the Spirit. Yet He does not impart to the Son the property, namely fatherhood, by which He is begetter of the Son, so that the Son Himself may appear Father and there may not be one God called Father in the Trinity.”

Therefore, insofar as He is emitter and cause, He does not give the emission of the Spirit to the Son, so that God the Father may not appear more or less cause of the Son than of the Spirit. To one who still more shamelessly persists in arguing the contrary, we say: what deprivation is it that, though God and Father is cause and principle of Son and Spirit, He attributes emission to the Son but not fatherhood? But if nothing said of any person of the divine majesty is said according to more and less—since there is no new division in the omnipotent and superessential Trinity—it is certainly clear that God the Father alone is cause of the Spirit insofar as He is emitter, just as He alone is begetter of the Son.

Opinion is more readily deceived than sense, for two reasons: either because sense deals with manifest and certain things, while opinion deals with hidden things; or because sense is almost immediately applied to things, whereas opinion proceeds through intermediaries. Things concerning God are hidden and uncertain to us; from these a mind that presumes too much is deceived.

Certainly it is in every respect inconsequential to say: the Father does not grant the Son that the Son Himself may be Father; He does not give Him fatherhood; He does not grant Him the emission of the Spirit—just as the Father does not grant the Spirit that He may be born, nor grant Him that He may be glorified together with the Father, receive from the Son, and announce to us.

Further, he looks far from the truth: “If the Father alone is cause of the Son, but is not alone cause of the Holy Spirit, then the Father is more cause of the Son than of the Spirit. For the most general genus, substance, is cause and principle only of its proximate genus, but not only of the most specific species.” Yet I do not think that a genus or cause is called more so of higher things than of lower, or said to contain higher things more than lower. For relations, whether mediate or immediate, proximate or remote, can sometimes make things different, but do not bring increase or diminution, intensity or remission.

Therefore the falsity of such a construction is exposed even in the Trinity: if the Father alone is cause of the Son but is not alone cause of the sending of the Holy Spirit, then He is more cause of one than the other. No rightly believing person accepts this. Consequently it is superfluous to ask why the Father gave emission without granting fatherhood, since faith in no way admits two Fathers or two Sons in the Trinity.

Such questions are unsuitable in formulation, just as is this one: since the soul is cause and principle of imagination and gives it the imagining of whatever things, why has it not bestowed on it opinion? For we can imagine whatever we wish: a man not merely three cubits but twenty or a thousand cubits high. We can also imagine a goat-stag and a hippocentaur, although we cannot form opinions about whatever we wish. For we can say that twice two is eight, but we cannot believe it, because opinion follows belief, as the philosopher says: “One who holds an opinion cannot fail to believe what seems true to him.” Yet the soul is not more cause of imagination than of opinion.

Therefore, just as one must not inquire how God begot, so one must not investigate how two are cause of one. For if one asks “how” in God, one will also ask “where,” as concerning place, and “when,” as concerning time, and likewise the other categories.

But if it is inconvenient and absurd not to believe the holy Fathers, and instead to oppose their writings with uncircumcised heart, saying, “Who was Ambrose? Who was Augustine, that they assert the Spirit proceeds from the Son?”—they certainly taught this as instructed by the Spirit, as did very many others. And surely the same Spirit taught that the Father is not the Son, but the power of the Mighty One, the wisdom of the Wise One, the proper character of hypostasis and substance. This is the Spirit whom the Lord of all calls the Spirit of truth: the image of the Son, and the finger, as Spirit of His mouth; Lord together with the Father and Son, and Creator.

And if the Apostle refers all creation to the person of the Father, saying, “One God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we in Him,” he likewise says: “One Lord, the Son, through whom are all things, and we through Him” (Eph. 4). There are not three creators, but one. For no one would dare assert that the three cooperate with angels in creation; nor should anyone understand one person when the Creator is called one—just as neither are the words spoken in the prophets said in one person: “I overthrew them,” He says, “as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah”; and elsewhere, “I will save them in the Lord their God” (Jer. 50). The Apostle uses the same figure of speech when he says: “God gave them over to a reprobate mind” (Rom. 1).

Thus there are three persons and one Creator: one God, who made this mass of the universe without movement, labour, or assumption of matter, altogether impassible and altogether unchangeable. Therefore, in His own work which He made, He had no need of instruments. The same Creator implanted a certain example of this in the human soul. For the motions of our soul are accomplished without labour, are formed without substances from things, and occur almost without time.

But if we cannot inspect the substance and actions of the soul, much less those of angels, how shall we perfectly know the properties of the divine persons? We must certainly believe the holy men who confess that the Spirit proceeds from the Son. This is also manifestly apparent to those wishing to understand it by many necessary arguments. For since Son and Spirit alone have being from the Father—the one immediately, the other mediately—the Son must be from the Spirit, or the Spirit from the Son. But the Son is not from the Spirit. [Col. 0292A] It remains, therefore, that the Spirit has being from the Son as from an immediate cause.

## Chapter VII

For, as Basil the Great says in his Letter to a Canon: “There is nothing between the Father and the Son.” But if the Spirit is not from God through Christ, neither is He at all.

> [Note: [Col. 0291D] Read cautiously, for theologians do not admit the expression “the Holy Spirit is the image of the Son,” although Greeks use it commonly; Etherianus wished here to indulge them. [Col. 0292D]]

Therefore, any emptying of His existence with respect to order entails rejection and is altogether a denial of the faith. Accordingly, the Spirit is the image of the Son and rests in Him, just as the Son is the image of the Father and rests in Him, each being from an immediate cause—although according to the Greeks the Spirit does not proceed from the Son.

For if the Son has being from the Father because He is the Father’s image, it is clear that the Spirit, being the image of the Son, has being from Him. He makes us sanctified sons, and through Him we cry, “Abba, Father.” If the Spirit does not have being from the Son, whose image He is, it must be said that image and that of which it is made are equivocally related. If this were so, the image and that whose image it is would not have the same account of substance. In what respect, then, shall we call the Spirit image of the Son, if He has no personal community with Him by reason of the Son?

Every image receives likeness, type, and figure from its archetypal idea. Behold, the Son, being the image of the invisible God, the brightness of glory, and the figure of the Father’s substance, has being from Him. But the Spirit is image of the Son, as the saints testify: not from external marks, as a king from purple, cloak, and diadem, but from what He has and emits inwardly, just as does the Father.

> [Note: [Col. 0292D] See St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, Part I, question 35, article 2.]

From this there is some likeness, not according to shape and colour, as in material images, since there is nothing of that sort in them. Rather, the comparison is in being eternal, incorporeal, and immovable according to substance—features from which the Spirit does not seem greatly to be the image of the Son, nor the Son the image of the Father. For according to what is common to the three persons, no difference of persons appears and no property of person is discerned. For it is not according to these things that one is counted Father, another Son, and another Spirit. If image were said according to substance, the Son would not be called image of the Father any more than the Father would be called image of the Son. Therefore the Spirit is called image of the Son according to property, not according to substance, such as eternity, uncircumscribedness, and the like.

[Col. 0292D] Hence Basil the Great says in the third discourse against Eunomius: “The Spirit is the true and natural image of the Son—not an image of the divine image, as we are.” Indeed, because He is image, He does not have an image; and because He is anointing, He does not have an anointing. Gregory, surnamed *Thaumaturgus* (“Wonder-worker”), says by revelation: “One Holy Spirit, who has existence from God: the perfect image of the perfect Son.” John Damascene likewise, following in the footsteps of the Fathers, writes: “The Son is image of the Father, and the Spirit image of the Son.” Gregory the Theologian also, speaking of the Son, declares: “He is image because He is consubstantial, and because He is so from Him, not He from Him; for this is the nature of an image: to be an imitation of the archetype and of that of which it is said to be the image.”

Whence it is clear that if the Spirit is image of the Son, He has being from Him. But whoever says that the Spirit has no relation to the Son abolishes the character of image. For with relation removed, an image cannot be understood. Therefore, if the Spirit is image of the Son, it is clear that He has a relation to Him. For what else is an image than to be from the cause—namely, from Him whose image it is? Substance, however, insofar as it is substance, is not called image, cause, causative, greater, or less; nor is “substance” a name signifying image. [Col. 0293B] For the persons are consubstantial, but they are not substances.

## Chapter VIII
But Nicetas, as it seems to me, does not press what has been said to a futile conclusion; for he says:

> “If all who wish to think rightly must confess that the Son and the Holy Spirit proceed from God the Father—this one by generation, that one by procession—sprung forth from the Father’s substance according to nature, timelessly and eternally together, like shoots from God; and if neither is prior nor the other later, lest perhaps one anticipate the other in time: for wherever there is prior and later, there is altogether an interval of time. But if this is admitted concerning the Trinity, then one of the life-originating persons [Col. 0293C] will be under time, and therefore a creature, as receiving existence in time and not consubstantial with its cause. This is the activity and shadow of the Arian, Eunomian, and Macedonian heresy. If, then, it is true—or rather, since it is supremely true—that the Son and the Spirit shine forth from the Father’s substance timelessly and eternally together, one must ask whether the Spirit is himself simultaneously timelessly and eternally from God the Father, and naturally shines forth from him as does the Son, while proceeding from the Son in the same manner as from the Father, or later. If later, the Spirit will be prior and later than himself, before time and under time, eternal and non-eternal, because he has an existence concurrent with his procession—which [Col. 0293D] is wholly full of impiety. But if, in order to avoid saying this because of the impossible and profane consequence, they say the alternative, namely that he proceeds timelessly from God the Father and eternally from the Son, how is it possible for him simultaneously, timelessly, and eternally to have existence from two causes, unless both are first and principal causes? Or by what reasoning can one cause have existence from two causes, when one of the causes, together with that which it emits from itself, has existence from the other cause? This is more irrational than every prodigy and demonic fiction. If those who maintain this position should insist that everything which pleases God and the Father is possible to him, it must be answered that he cannot [Col. 0294A] deny himself, nor, while he is the principle and cause of the Son and the Spirit, fail to be what he is.”

Therefore, if many absurdities follow from that abominable opinion which says that the Spirit proceeds from the Son, it is clear that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, as the word of truth has plainly proclaimed from antiquity until the present day. I forbear to return a response fully commensurate with the insult to this impious babble.

Certainly nowhere in Sacred Scripture is it found that the Father alone is the cause and principle of the Spirit, or that the Spirit proceeds from him alone; whereas Scripture bears witness in many places that the Father alone begets and that he alone is the cause and principle of the Son. For he alone has the Son; but he alone does not have the Holy Spirit [Col. 0294B], since he neither sends alone nor gives alone, because the Son gives and sends the Spirit just as the Father does. Since, then, the Spirit is possessed, sent, and given equally by the Father and the Son, there are two causes possessing, sending, and giving the Holy Spirit.

It has been said above that the Father and the Son are not simply called “two.” When they are called two, the sense is this, as some suppose: the Father is not alone, nor is the Son alone, but there are the Father and the Son. For another reason, however, dual number must not be admitted in them, for the reasons stated above. For two, like all the other numbers, is properly predicated not of divine persons but of things having discrete or continuous quantity.

[Col. 0294C] Continuous quantity, which is predicated only of magnitudes, is, as philosophers state, that whose parts are joined at a common boundary. But to understand parts in the Father or the Son which a common boundary joins is a fiction that admits not even of imagination. The three dimensions, although continuous in their parts, are nevertheless said to be determinate—not because they are cut off from one another, but because each possesses its own definition. Such things do not apply to the divine persons in any way.

Discrete quantity is that whose parts are considered separately, so that they are not joined together. But although the Father and the Son have distinct definitions, they are in no way understood to possess parts. Thus the Father and the Son are called two persons, or two hypostases, only with respect to their properties [Col. 0294D]. Therefore it is plain that those who confess that the Spirit proceeds from the Son introduce no prodigy, bring forward no monster, and fashion no satanic fiction. For every impiety and every impossibility flee from one who declares such things.

For the Father and the Son have one and the same hand, as he testifies when he says: “My Father, who gave them to me, is greater than all; and no one can snatch the sheep from the hand of my Father”; and a little later again he says: “No one snatches them from my hand” (John 10). Behold one hand, not two, of Father and Son, because each is one cause and one principle of the Spirit. From this hand proceeds the finger, namely the Holy Spirit, as the Evangelists testify. Matthew writes: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” [Col. 0295A] (Matt. 12); but Luke: “If by the finger of God” (Luke 11), unmistakably calling the Spirit “finger,” in order to make plain that, just as a finger is consubstantial with the hand and proceeds from it, receiving substance and existence from it, so the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with the Father and the Son, proceeding mediately indeed from the Father but immediately from the Son.

For radiance is understood together with substance, an image with its archetype, and the Son altogether with the Father; but the Spirit is neither the image nor the Son of the Father, nor indeed does the Father seem to have much of a relation to him in that respect. From this it is clear that neither from the mode of understanding, nor from the order of procession, nor from Scripture is it possible to infer that the Spirit comes immediately from the Father and not through the Son. For if, because the Son is born immediately from the Father, he is given to us without a mediator, and the Spirit likewise proceeds from the Father without a mediator and is given to us immediately: yet he is not given to us without a mediator; therefore he does not proceed immediately from the Father [Col. 0295B].

## Chapter IX

Moreover, the bishop of Nicomedia strongly attacks both those who maintain that the Spirit is from the Son and those who profess that he proceeds from the Father through the Son, as through a mediator:

> “Consider,” he says, “the consequences that follow for anyone who asserts that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. But if we hear some objecting that the Latins do not assert procession from the Father and the Son, but from the Father through the Son—then, if the Spirit proceeds altogether from the Father through the mediation of the Son, whereas the Son is from him without mediation, the Spirit is less than the Son. For what participates through some intermediary is less than that which participates immediately. Thus the doctrine of Macedonius again finds a place, diminishing the Spirit and abolishing equality of dignity and power.

> “But how shall we grant that he proceeds from the Father through the Son? For if the Father is emitter and the Holy Spirit emitted, these are names of relation and at the same time of nature: the emitter is emitter of the emitted, and the emitted is emitted by the emitter. But none of the things said relatively is said through some intermediary. How, then, can we say that the Holy Spirit proceeds through the mediation of the Son? This is plainly contrary to syllogistic reasoning [Col. 0295D] and true demonstrations.”

These arguments are directed against those who are inconsistent in their discourse and think to overthrow by plausible inferences the doctrine that shines brightly among us. But if anyone asks us how the Son and the Holy Spirit alike are from the Father, we answer: as from the sun come ray and brightness, heat and light—although even these comparisons involve much interchange and deficiency of likeness. For in what way can the divine nature be likened to any of the things below when compared for resemblance?

The Latin agrees with him who asserts that the Spirit has existence from the Son as from the Father; but he rejects one who says “from the Father through the Son” without understanding “from the Son.” Why he does this has been shown above, and the discussion will remain on the same point. But now, before proceeding, we must examine this question: does the Spirit proceed immediately from the Son, or not? The following syllogism can establish that he proceeds immediately.

If the order and relation of names are capable of truth and firmness, then the order and relation of the persons are true and firm. For written characters are signs of spoken words; words are signs of concepts; and concepts attain their end in the apprehension of things. Concepts are truly concepts when they are, as it were, fitted to the things themselves. For concepts are images in the soul of things, and words indicate concepts; therefore words were bestowed by nature so that through them we might signify to one another the soul’s conceptions according to the arrangement of things [Col. 0296B].

Now the invariable order and relation of the three names of the divine persons, capable of truth, joins the name of the Paraclete to the name of the Son of God without a mediator, just as it joins it to the great name of the Word of God. Indeed, when the Lord Jesus Christ, in instituting saving baptism, commanded his disciples to baptize all nations “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” he established this order (Matt. 28). In it he joins the Spirit to himself and to the Father, undoubtedly because of some commonality and equality. For it is not right to suppose that such an order relates to the divine nature but to no property of the hypostases; for nature, being one, is assigned neither order [Col. 0296C] nor number.

That which never exceeds unity is wholly innumerable. For one God, one substance, and one nature are understood in three persons. These are ordered; these are numbered; these possess commonality and connection with one another. What is common by nature requires no order: whether we say “the Son and the Spirit and the Father are God,” or “the Spirit and the Father and the Son,” we remain on the straight path of faith. But the commonality which belongs to properties is not so constituted. In this case the order must be preserved which the Lord delivered to the disciples when he commanded them to baptize all nations “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” and not in the name of the Spirit and Son and Father, or of the Son and Father and Spirit. For the Father is cause and principle of the Son, and the Son in turn is cause of the Holy Spirit.

Since the Spirit is joined to the Son according to the dignity of baptism, I judge it unfitting to declare that the stated order of the divine personal names is pronounced in vain. The order and arrangement of the names correspond to the relation and order of the persons. Yet perhaps the order found in the Apostle may seem contrary to this, when he says: “There are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit; there are diversities of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are diversities of operations, but the same God who works all things in all” (1 Cor. 12). Behold: he mentions the Spirit first, the Son second, and God and Father third [Col. 0297A].

But we must not suppose that the Apostle overturned the order, since, as the great Basil testifies, he began from our relation to them:

> “For,” he says, “when receiving gifts, we first call upon the distributor, then upon the sender, and finally raise our thought to the source and cause of all good things”—an order which the Apostle employed.

Likewise when he says, “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God and Father, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Cor. 13), and in all similar cases, the same answer applies. For the glory and order expressed by us in this way are not according to the order or glory which they receive among themselves. There the relation of the persons is considered; here our relation to them. This neither lays down a law nor contradicts that order or conflicts with glory, since it takes its beginning, as it were, from the remembrance of a benefit received.

It is therefore evident from what has been said that, if the order and relation of names are capable of firmness and truth, then, as the name of the Paraclete is joined without a mediator to the name of the Word of God in the order of names, so the person who is the Spirit is joined to the Son without a mediator, but to the Father through that same Son [Col. 0297B].

Therefore he proceeds immediately from one, but mediately from the other. For what is called a mediator has, on either side, things that differ from one another; and where three persons are named in order, how can none of them be intermediate?

As for the objection advanced—namely, “therefore the Spirit is less than the Son, since what participates in something through a mediator is less than what participates without a mediator”—it is inconsequential and need not be feared. The Spirit is not therefore less than the Son because he comes from the Unbegotten through the Son’s mediation, as is most evident in sensible things. For the Atlantic shares in the Pontic Sea through the Propontis; yet the named sea is greater than the Propontis. Likewise the Nile and rivers like it share in a spring through a channel, though they are much larger than the spring itself. And the most general genus, substance, is participated in by rational and irrational beings through a middle term, though it is greater than both. But the Word of God participates in the human race through a rational soul [Col. 0297D]; yet who would dare to declare him less than the rational soul or than the Virgin Mother? Therefore the doctrine of Macedonius will not find a place for this reason.

But now we must proceed to the second objection, which says: “How shall we grant that he proceeds from the Father at all?” The answer is that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have very many common and proper names, which Sacred Scripture makes manifest. Therefore some of them must be briefly recalled here, as the matter itself seems to require.

Thus the Father is called unbegotten, cause, principle, and emitter. Likewise the Son is called begotten, Word, principle, cause, and emitter—namely, immediate emitter. But the Paraclete, the Spirit, is called caused and emitted [Col. 0298A]. Although under this designation he is called the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, nevertheless the Father and the Son are by no means reciprocally related to him according to these appellative names. For the Father is not called unbegotten Spirit, nor is the Spirit called the Son, that is, the Word, Wisdom of God.

Accordingly, if someone calls the Father the mediate cause and the Son the immediate cause, because no person mediates between the Son and the Spirit whom he emits, he does not depart from truth. Again, since Father and Son are one principle and one emitter of the emitted Spirit, whoever calls them wholly one and the same cause commits no error.

A cause is cause of what is caused, and what is caused is referred to its cause; an emitter is emitter of what is emitted. But perhaps someone may object: “How can the Father be the mediate cause of the Spirit according to the stated reasoning, and the Son immediate because no person stands as a mediator between him and the Spirit—unless there are two causes of the Spirit, one mediate and the other immediate, namely the Father and the Son?” This conclusion does not follow, just as it does not follow that there are two gods or two lords because there is a God who has a Son and a God who does not have one [Col. 0298B].

It should be known that some say that Father and Spirit, or Son and Spirit, are not relatives, because a relation is not discerned from a word indicating a relation to a word which does not possess a corresponding relation. For one is not known from the other; nor is everything said “of another” immediately relative, as disposition and virtue are said to be of the soul. These and similar things require only that they belong to something, as occurs in Father and Spirit, and Son and Spirit. Some therefore say that in this and similar cases, because there is no reciprocal conversion through such names, it is required only that they belong to something. Yet these persons establish the Father as the immediate cause of the Spirit and the Son likewise as immediate, while making them the same cause.

Nor is this contrary to Aristotle or other philosophers, who employ divisions concerning human rather than divine matters. Of causes, some are per se and others accidental; again, some are remote and others proximate; some potential and others actual. A per se cause is, for example, the *andriantopoios* (ἀνδριαντοποιός), “maker of a statue,” with respect to a statue; accidentally, he is a human being and simply an animal. A remote cause is, for example, a physician with respect to health [Col. 0298D], but a proximate cause is material. Again, in a musical interval spanning all four strings (*diapasōn*, διά πασῶν), the double is the proximate cause and number the remote cause. But the case is not the same with the divine persons. For the Father, insofar as he is emitter, is called the mediate cause of the emitted Spirit; whereas the Son, being the same cause, is called immediate.

It should be noted here that some place the Father as a middle between the Son and the Holy Spirit. Likewise, they make the Spirit a middle between the Father and the Son. I do not think this should be pressed as a consequence. For insofar as the Father bestows existence on both, he is considered the middle and bond of the two; while the Spirit, because he is properly called neither begotten nor unbegotten, is placed between Father and Son. It remains that the Son alone is properly intermediate [Col. 0299A], as may in some way be observed from the most general genus. Although it gives existence to subordinate and most specific genera, none of them calls the most general genus itself intermediate, just as no one makes a river intermediate between a channel and a spring.

Therefore, since the Son stands immediately related both to the Father and to the Spirit, he alone is simply and absolutely intermediate between Father and Spirit. But it is very fearful to treat extensively of the divine, as Socrates too feared when he said: “I undertake discourse about the gods with difficulty, lest someone readily say that I err.”

Thus Father and Son, emitter and emitted, cause and caused, are said relatively. For in these, existence is present through relation [Col. 0299B]. Yet from the benefits by which God benefits us we have learned to call God beneficent and Father; and we believe in one God and one beneficent Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, though neither mind can imagine nor reason describe the mode of their existence. Nor is their unity known in another way than through the activity which is wholly one and the same in all three: that unity is one God and one substance. Though the Father is called one thing in one respect, the Son another, and the Spirit another, this does not abandon the principle of simplicity.

They are altogether inseparable, although these three persons are distinguished by properties. Unless the Son is intermediate between them, as is said in “the name of the Father and of the Son,” it could equally be said “in the name of the Father and of the Spirit”—which ecclesiastical tradition does not admit [Col. 0299C]. From this it is evident that neither the Spirit nor the Father should be understood as intermediate in the enumeration of the three. The same thing is affirmed by the outflow of procession from the Father and the Son.

For the attribution of principles passes through proximate relations. A begotten offspring is proximate to its begetter and equal to him; if it fell short of equality, it would cease to be God, falling from the highest excellence, which has infinite power, since it is equal and coeternal with the Father who begets it. The Father, by subsistence in being alone—that is, by begetting [Note: [Col. 0299D] These statements do not cohere.]—therefore begets alone; but he does not emit the Spirit alone, because he is cause and principle not insofar as he is Father, but as emitter, through the Son as mediator.

This should surprise no one, since many things in nature are found to be related to one another through a mediator. Tantalus is called the great-grandfather of Agamemnon through Pelops and Atreus; likewise Pelops is called the grandfather of Agamemnon because Agamemnon is called his grandson. For this reason they are considered both Pelopids and Tantalids. But uncle and nephew are among those things which are said relatively and through a mediator; they cannot be understood without a mediator. The same holds for son-in-law, father-in-law, and all similar terms.

Were this not so, the line of kinship would not be extended very far; nor in logic would the most general genus be called the genus of the species contained under it, nor would the most specific species be called the species of the things above it, since the intermediate and most general is called the genus of these [Col. 0300A], and the most specific the species of those. Therefore there is nothing improper in saying that the Spirit proceeds through the Son and from the Son.

## Chapter X

But Nicetas, in an excessively lengthy discourse, again launches a most sweeping attack against these points, as follows:

> “If it is plainly established among all who wish to offer reverent worship concerning the divine that it is uncaused, unchangeable, and admits no variation or shadow of change; further, that it is omnipotent, infinite, and whatever designations worthy of God anyone may draw from Sacred Scripture and common conceptions of God—whatever he declares concerning God in respect of existence—then it is plain [Col. 0300B] that he speaks these things substantially, because the divine is incapable of accident. Since the principle of divine piety instructs us to think and speak in this way, it must be considered whether the divine admits the predication of things called opposites or not.

> “Those who treat these matters divide them fourfold. For opposites, they say, are either in speech or in reality. Those in speech are opposition as affirmation and negation; those in reality are understood either in relation or without relation. Those in relation mutually imply and are implied, and are opposed as relatives. Of those without relation, some are capable of being changed into one another, while others are not: the former are contraries, the latter opposites as privation and possession.

> “[Col. 0300C] It is plain why the divine does not admit as predicates those oppositions which are according to contrariety, privation, and possession: its nature is altogether unchangeable, while such oppositions have their existence in things capable of alteration and change. Nor does it admit the opposition found as contradiction, because the things considered concerning the divine always exist in the same manner and alike. Since, therefore, the divine nature is common to the three persons and is the universal creator, it in no way permits relatives opposed according to the same species of relation to be predicated of itself, lest perhaps the uniform and single character of relation should seem to be destroyed.”

From these common conceptions of God, and from natural and demonstrative arguments proclaimed by the investigations of philosophers, attention must be directed to those who confess that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as from the Father. For if this is so, the emission will be common to Father and Son, and the Son will be cause of the Spirit’s existence just as the Father is, insofar as he is emitter. But the Son is begotten from God the Father and describes that cause as begetter, according to the word of truth. It follows, therefore, that the Son receives an opposition of relative terms: he is both cause of the Spirit and from God the Father as cause. But it has been shown to us by universal reasoning that it is impossible for opposites to be predicated of the divine nature [Col. 0301A], or of any of the three hypostases. Therefore the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son, as some impiously and profanely imagine.

But how frivolous this is is sufficiently clear, since it follows neither from common conceptions, as he claims, nor from philosophical principles. This is true only of hypostatic properties: the Father is never Son, nor the Son Father, nor either Spirit. But regarding other things, nothing prevents one and the same person from receiving one relative opposition in one respect and another in another respect; though in one and the same respect it cannot. For it is impossible for the same thing to be cause and caused of itself.

That the conclusion advanced concerning hypostatic properties is true is manifest from preserving the order of those persons. Behold, the holy and blessed Trinity has many names because it bestows many benefits upon humankind. Some of these show substance, others do not; among them no necessary order exists. But in the three names, as expounded above—Father, Son, and Spirit—and in any similar names found in Sacred Scripture, order is preserved. If that order does not imitate the persons, the glorification is false, indecent, and like a dream: it is something, yet possesses none of the things whose appearance it presents. So such an order would be an image of an order that does not exist [Col. 0301B].

Therefore the order of names imitates the persons themselves: the Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son. The Son is from a cause, namely the Father, from whom he is begotten; and he is likewise cause of the Spirit, as its emitter [Col. 0301C].

The Savior intended to show this when, commanding the disciples to baptize, he delivered the aforesaid order of the three names; we must in no way suppose that he did so in vain. The Savior affirms the same when he says to the Father: “All mine are yours” (John 16). For he refers to the Father, as principle, both the emission of the Spirit and the creation of the universe; and “yours are mine” (ibid.), because, although I have the Spirit from you, I emit him as you do, and likewise create all things, needing no assistance. For assistance belongs to servants and is far removed from the dignity of the Son.

Therefore there is no absurdity in saying that the same person is cause and caused, as one is called sender and sent, glorifier and glorified, preached and preacher, when these are taken in one respect and another. For on Mount Tabor the Father preached, the Son was preached, and the cloud—the Holy Spirit—overshadowed, so that there was no need of a tabernacle made by hands [Col. 0301D].

From what has been said, then, there is plainly refuted what some advance as an irrefutable argument. “One cause of existence,” they say, “is seen to have many effects in natural, artificial, voluntary, and almost all things. Thus Adam, though one man, was cause, as father, of many effects proceeding from him. Likewise Bezalel, though one craftsman, was cause of very many and different things. The same is found in voluntary actions: Peter and Paul, by the teaching of evangelical preaching, drew very many to faith; and each one, being a single person, became an agent of reconciliation for the salvation of many and voluntarily begot many in faith.

“But the reverse is the case with effects. When there is one effect, there must be one proximate cause, unless that cause, because of its deficiency and weakness, takes another cause with it.” This is plainly evident from things themselves. If this is so, the Spirit’s procession from the Father and the Son indicates defect and weakness in the Father—which does not follow at all. For if we wish to follow this reasoning, since the world is caused, it has neither Son nor Spirit as proximate cause unless this is due to weakness and impotence in the Father [Col. 0302B]. But each of the three is equally maker and creator of the world; for, as was said above, the Father alone begets, but he does not alone create and fashion.

## Chapter XI

But the bishop of Methone still objects to this:

> “If the Son has received from the Father everything that he has, then undoubtedly he has also received from the Father the emission of the Spirit. Thus this very unequal generosity follows: the Son received from the Father that he too might be cause of the Spirit, while the Spirit, although he has equal honor and proceeds from a cause of the same substance, is deprived of equal honor because he does not receive from the Father the power to be cause of the Son, or of another like himself—unless one dare to impute to the Father the charge of injustice.”

But this man can be pressed by the same difficulty. For if the Son received from the Father all that he has, and received from him the sending of the Spirit—for the Son sends the Spirit: “Unless I go away,” he says, “the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you” (John 16); and again, “I did not say these things to you from the beginning, because I was with you; but now I go to him who sent me” (ibid.)—then it is evident that the Son sends the Holy Spirit, and that the same Spirit is sent by the Father [Col. 0302C].

How, then, when the Son receives from the Father the emission of the Spirit, is he sender and sent, whereas the Spirit has not received a sending, either of the Son or of another like himself? Thus this generosity deprives him of equal honor. Yet such an objection can easily be resolved, since it may suitably be answered that the Spirit did not receive the ability to be cause of the Son because the Son is his cause; whereas the Spirit is nowhere found to be the Son’s cause, nor the cause of another like himself, lest a fourth person be introduced into the Trinity [Col. 0302D].

Further: how does the Son receive all judgment from the Father, while the Spirit is not granted it? For it is written: “He gave all judgment to the Son, that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father” (John 5). I suppose—indeed, I firmly believe—that if the emission of the Spirit pertains to the honor of the Father, it pertains also to the honor of the Son, who, just as he has life from the Father, has judgment; so likewise he has the emission of the Spirit. And just as being begotten does not prevent the Son from having the nature of the Father—indeed, he is proved to have it from this—so the procession of the Spirit from Father and Son does not prevent the Spirit from having the nature of Father and Son. Otherwise the Spirit and the Son would not be of the same nature as the Father, since the Father alone begets and, as the Greek thinks, alone emits the Spirit. But the Spirit and Son do so in no way [Col. 0303A].

Yet this same man further insists, saying that the Spirit is not one and simple because he is not from one but from two. Of these, one, though cause, proceeds from no cause; while the other, proceeding from a cause, is itself cause.

But if the Spirit is divisible because he proceeds from two, someone may say that the Father is likewise divisible, since from himself he begets the Son and emits the Spirit. For how do two things, as if different—the Son by generation and the Spirit by procession—proceed from the indivisible? There is surely a fallacy in thinking that composition arises from relative terms. For things said relatively show nothing beyond their underlying substances. Hence it often happens that, without any change in the underlying substance, a relation is changed: for example, one who was formerly on the right, though in no way altered, becomes on the left when another moves to the other side, the relation being changed.

Therefore the category “relative” is called by philosophers an offshoot among the nine categories. In them it is regarded as a slight accident, because it is often present or absent in many cases without any change, or even alteration, in the underlying substance [Col. 0303B]. From this it is clear that it by no means follows that, if the Son is cause and proceeds from a cause, he is neither wholly cause nor wholly from a cause, but is composed out of one part and another imperfect part. On the contrary, he is undoubtedly wholly cause and wholly from a cause, since he is indivisible and incorporeal.

But if cause and caused introduce composition, consider: the Son and the Spirit, together with the Father, are principle and cause of the creation of all things. The Father is cause of the Son and the Holy Spirit according to one species of relation and another—where composition would appear more than in anything else. For each is called cause of creatures as efficient creator; yet it is not according to this species of relation that either Spirit or Son proceeds from the Father [Col. 0303D], for each of them is Creator, not creature.

And it should be noted that here Nicetas’s objection concerning opposites is plainly resolved. Therefore, if cause and caused—terms applicable to the Spirit and the Son according to differing relations—produce no composition in them, it is evident that neither does the Son acquire composition from the fact that, in like manner, the Father is called the cause of the Spirit.

Moreover, the same bishop argues as follows: If the Son is immediately begotten from the Father, while the Spirit proceeds from the same Father through the mediation of the Son, then the same Father must be regarded as both a proximate and a remote cause. But this, as already said, may perhaps apply among things in which there is prior and posterior: thus the same man, insofar as he is an *andriantopoios* [statue-maker], is per se the cause of the statue; but insofar as he is an artisan, he is so accidentally, and is accordingly called both proximate and remote cause. [Col. 0304A]

In the divine persons, however, “mediate,” “immediate,” and “proximate” may indeed be said; but “remote,” I think, ought not to be said. For the divine is not subject to nature; whence it is clear that the sending forth of the Spirit is not a personal property of the Father, nor is the Father distinguished from the Son by this. For if it were a personal property of the Father, the Father’s sending forth of the Spirit would never be a mediate cause of the Spirit, but always an immediate one, as is said of the Son. Yet the Father is the cause of the Spirit through the Son. Therefore being sender is not a personal property, either of the Father or of the Son.

But since the Spirit proceeds through the mediating Son and from the Son—it being always the case that the Son is joined to his Father without mediation—and since the Father begets not through anyone but sends through the Son, and therefore has the Spirit as Father, as the Son himself testifies: “The Father has not left me alone”: if, moreover, the Spirit belongs equally and similarly to the Son as to the Father, and the Father sends him while the Son does not send him, it follows that the Father leaves the Son alone in this respect. To think this surpasses every impiety. [Col. 0304B]

But perhaps someone may say: If the Son is not from himself, neither does he have the Spirit through himself; and if he does not have him through himself, neither does he send or emit him similarly and equally with the Father. But the Son is not from himself, as he himself declares: “I have not come from myself” (John VIII). This has been sufficiently resolved above. For if this is granted, the Son would by no means have life equally and similarly with the Father—a confession no intelligent person makes. And it should be observed that he said such things not by diminishing his own power, but by destroying what is alien and contrary.

For if man naturally possesses free choice, and is lord over all that the earth nourishes, much more does the only-begotten Son of God—who emptied himself and gave himself for us—have the Spirit and life, as is clear; as he himself declares: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John V). And how could he fail to give the Son, similarly, both to have the Spirit and to send him, just as he himself has and sends the Spirit? [Col. 0304C]

The Son does not have the Spirit by participation—he who is life through himself, light through himself, and truth through himself. Nor does he receive some small portion of the Spirit from another, so that he should be incapable of sending him while the Father can do this fully. How could what he always had have been received from another? And what more would the Apostle possess if, by entreating the Father, he sent the Spirit, without having him through himself or proceeding from himself?

Therefore the Son sends and emits the Spirit just as the Father does. Moreover, the Spirit suffers no loss in being sent and proceeding; for although he is sent, he is present everywhere, distributing to each one as he wills.

God is he whose proper characteristic is not merely to foreknow future things, but to do whatever he wills. “To each,” as the Apostle says, “is given the manifestation of the Spirit for usefulness” (1 Cor. XII). Furthermore, believers are led by the Spirit and made sons of God; they are also sanctified “in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God,” as the same Apostle says. [Col. 0305A]

This is the Spirit who knows the deep things of God, who fills the whole world, who leads into all truth, who is present everywhere and lacks nothing; nor has he anything added or adventitious. From this it is evident that when the Son says, “I have not come from myself” (John VII), and concerning the Spirit, “I will send [him], and he will receive from what is mine and glorify me” (John VIII), and whatever expressions of this kind occur, they show only the distinction of persons, which had been wholly unknown to humankind.

This is the Spirit who spoke in the apostles, for the apostles spoke as the Spirit gave them utterance; and again: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who is in heaven speaks in you” (Matt. X). This same Spirit also spoke in the prophets. Moses says: “Would that all this people might prophesy, when the Lord gives his Spirit upon them!” (Num. XI). And Agabus, the prophet of the New Testament, cried out: “Thus says the Holy Spirit” (Acts XI).

Therefore one and the same Holy Spirit spoke in the prophets, in the apostles, and in Christ; yet the same Spirit was possessed differently by them and by Christ. For Christ had the Spirit through himself, whereas they had him through Christ. Since, therefore, the Word of the Most High has the Spirit through himself and gives the Spirit through himself, it is clear that he sends him through himself and that the Spirit proceeds from him. [Col. 0305B]

Furthermore, the signs performed through the apostles were not their own, but belonged to God working through them. But the signs performed through the Son of God belonged to the Son himself, who can have nothing added in respect of his being God. For the divine being, simply good, is self-sufficient and comprehensive of itself, although certain persons admit that what is simply self-sufficient is inferior to the good. “For,” they say, “what else is self-sufficient but that which possesses the good from itself and in itself?” But this, they say, is already full of the good, insofar as it participates in it.

Yet in this they unknowingly divide, by participation, that which admits no division. The Son therefore sends the Spirit, but not without the Father, just as the Father is not without the Son. For as the Spirit belongs to the Father, so also he belongs to the Son. Therefore the Son is the Word of God, and the Spirit of the Son is the Paraclete. [Col. 0305C]

Hence he says: “The Father will send [him] in my name” (John XIV), which signifies nothing other than “in my power and in my authority.” For I am sender, just as the Father is, because the Spirit proceeds from me. For I am joined to the Father without mediation. “I am the life and the truth and the way to him” (ibid.). No one comes to him unless I am the mediator; and elsewhere he says that the Father draws people to him: “No one,” he says, “can come to me unless my Father draws him” (John VI).

It is therefore clear that the Son presents to the Father and the Father draws to the Son—the Son who is immediately joined to the Father and is in every respect equal to him. Hence: “He who sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV); and, “The Father abiding in me, he does the works” (ibid.). I have nothing peculiar to myself or separate from the Father, [Col. 0305D] just as the Father has nothing separated from me; rather, all things are common. Therefore, if the Son is in the whole Father, the Father does not send the Spirit alone. For if he alone sends the Spirit, the Son is not in the whole Father without mediation.

## Chapter XII

Yet the bishop of Methone maintains that the Spirit is not equal to the Son if he proceeds from him, employing the following syllogism: What is from two is never equal to what is from one only; but the Spirit is from two, while the Son has his birth from the Father alone; therefore the Spirit is not equal to the Son, but is either greater or lesser.

What answer should be given to this except to draw an absurdity by a similar argument, as follows: What is from one is never equal to what is from none. But the Son has existence from one only, namely the Father, whereas the Father has existence from none. Therefore the Father and the Son are unequal.

These things do not belong to the category of quantity, since neither measure nor quantity is in the divine. [Col. 0306A] Therefore the Father and Son are not properly two, from whom, as from two different things, the Spirit should derive existence; for God the Father alone is as great as the Father together with the Son.

But this man again attempts deception, arguing thus: If the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, the Father will no longer be Father alone, nor the Godhead wholly unity. And how, indeed, when the Son shares the paternal causality, is the Son any longer Son alone? How, when the Father is in some respect the Spirit’s [cause], is the Spirit thereafter one alone? How, indeed, when he is not from one alone?

This man weaves together this and many other such arguments in order to appear to be arguing; for, as Aristotle says, they especially wish to appear to be arguing. Yet because he mingles falsehood with truth, he concludes nothing. What force of consequence can there be: if the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, the Father is not Father, nor the Son Son, nor the Godhead unity? [Col. 0306B]

By the same kind of reasoning one might conclude: The Spirit is possessed by the Father according to nature; therefore the Father is Son to the Son, and the Son is Father. Or: if the Son and Spirit derive existence from the Father in a divided manner, the Father will no longer be one and simple God. This perhaps would follow if the Spirit and Son were said to be two by nature and not only by their properties. But unity according to nature is not three persons taken together separately, but undividedly. Therefore neither Father and Son are two unities, nor Father, Son, and Holy Spirit three unities.

Rather, the three persons are one unity, as they are one God and the whole unity; and the whole Trinity is Godhead. Yet just as there is no trinity of the persons [considered separately], so none of them, as shown above, can properly be reckoned a unity. Certainly the Father alone and only is Father; the Son alone and only is Son; and the Holy Spirit alone and only is Holy Spirit. The whole Trinity is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; unity is Trinity and Trinity unity; for this three is one God, and God is this three, and God alone. [Col. 0306C]

For this reason a duality or trinity of unities is not understood. The Father is indeed the source of the two persons who are from him, and from him proceed not unities but persons. Therefore not two fathers, not two sons, not two spirits are believed; nor are there three gods, but one alone and whole God, who exists before all things, above all things, and as the cause of all things.

It is therefore plain that the inference brought forward is invalid. For every inference from nature to properties, or from properties to nature, is invalid, as this example shows: “One God is three persons. Therefore the three persons are either unbegotten God, or begotten God, or proceeding God.” The syllogism has not been established, because “one” is said according to nature, whereas “unbegotten,” “begotten,” and “proceeding” are not. Consequently nothing can be inferred from these things. [Col. 0306D]

Furthermore, unity, insofar as it is unity, is immovable, since it has no cause of its existence. For whatever was not previously something else is rightly held immovable. But no cause can be thought prior to God. Great Dionysius bears witness to this:

“In nearly every inquiry of theology, we behold the most sacred Thearchy: unity indeed, because of the simplicity of supernatural indivisibility, from which, as from a unifying power, we understand the harmony worthy of God; Trinity, however, because of the manifestation of the superessential fruitfulness of the three persons.”

Accordingly, unity belongs to nature, while Trinity belongs to persons. Therefore, when the holy Fathers speak of unity as moving, the motion is not to be attributed to unity itself but to our mind, which is moved while contemplating God as one in three persons possessing exactly the same nature. [Col. 0307A]

And this is what Dionysius says again: “The fountainhead Godhead is the Father; the Son and Spirit are, if it is appropriate to speak thus, shoots planted by God from the fruitful Godhead.” By “fountainhead Godhead” he means the Father as the fountain in the Godhead. He calls him so solely because the Father is without beginning and alone gives being to the two; but he calls the Son and Spirit shoots planted by God because each has being from the Father. Yet because the Father is called Godhead improperly, he adds: “if it is appropriate to speak thus.”

By these words Dionysius seems not to deny that the Spirit is from the Son, but rather to affirm that he is from the Son, since he says “the Son and the Spirit,” not “the Spirit and the Son”—as though the Spirit comes from the Father through the Son. But the manner of this coming forth can neither be expressed nor understood, since it is wholly ineffable.

It is thus clear from what has been said that neither the Son nor the Spirit is called unity. The Father, however, seems to some persons occasionally to be signified by the term “unity,” as in Gregory the Theologian, who argues thus: “Unity, moved from the beginning into duality, came to rest in Trinity.” [Col. 0307B]

This holy man, however, seems in that place to use “unity” abusively for the Father, “duality” figuratively for the Son, and “Trinity” for the Holy Spirit. For “unity” is a name signifying nature, not person; and the Word of God is by no means called Son of unity, since his Father is in no way called unity.

The meaning of the saying is as follows: The Father, rejecting barrenness, moved into duality—that is, he begot the Son—and came to rest in Trinity, that is, in the Spirit: he sent forth the Spirit, and did not proceed further by either begetting or sending. Others, however, wish to interpret this chapter differently, saying that unity moves into duality and Trinity without a mediator. They suppose that, just as the Father moves without mediation to the generation of the Son, so also to the sending forth of the Holy Spirit.

If this were true, the Father would move from the beginning not into duality but into Trinity, immediately begetting the Son from himself and immediately sending forth the Spirit. For this is surely contrary to the order given by Christ to the disciples concerning baptism; and likewise to the glorification already mentioned, since he begets truth not through anyone, but sends forth through the Son. [Col. 0307C]

Furthermore, it is impossible to pass to Trinity except through duality. For if two are prior to three in learning and rank, it is impossible to conceive that one has come to rest in Trinity without advancing through duality. Yet duality is prior to Trinity in learning and rank. Unity is prior to duality, because the implication is not reversible in the order of subsistence. For when there are two, as Aristotle says, it immediately follows that there is one; but if there is one, it does not follow necessarily that there are two.

Similarly, if there is Trinity, it immediately follows that there is duality; but if there is duality, Trinity does not necessarily follow, because the third is related to the second, but the second not to the third, rather to the first. From this it appears most clearly that Father and Son equally give being to the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Son too is called a principle in the Holy Trinity, as was argued above. The Father alone, then, exists for the others as beginning and without cause; but he is not alone as cause and principle.

He is said to move as knowledge moves the ignorant by instructing them, while itself remaining immovable; or as Aristotle says that the sun sets in the day and the fixed stars move—things which move not in themselves but because our sight is absent from them. [Col. 0307D] “Our vision,” he says, “weakened by distance, wavers because of its infirmity; this perhaps causes the fixed stars to seem to tremble, whereas the planets do not tremble, since sight can reach them.” That the sun’s setting seems to occur by its progress from east to west belongs not to the sun itself but to our vision.

Thus the divine, though wholly immovable in nature and substance, is said to move because it moves our understanding to contemplate it and to make distinct investigations concerning Trinity, unity, and the properties of the persons. Again, unity is said to move into duality and to Trinity, but no farther, because this number possesses permanence and identity: it has the same beginning, the same middle, and the same end—something no other number has attained. [Col. 0308A]

For unity is beginning, unity middle, and unity end. “All things are one, and three are all things,” as Aristotle affirms. “Body alone,” he says, “is perfect among magnitudes, for it alone is defined by three; and it is said to be all because it has beginning, middle, and end, and because no magnitude has more than three dimensions.”

Therefore, just as the divine has perfection in three persons, so every body has perfection in three distances, as Ptolemy teaches: “It is necessary,” he says, “that three distances be defined, and that they be taken as perpendicular straight lines. For only three mutually related straight lines can be taken: two by which a surface is defined, and a third which measures depth.” [Col. 0308B]

But the conjunction of the three persons surpasses every sequence of thought, every power of reasoning, and is set above all nature, because the three divine persons possess one beginning without time. For although the Son is from the Father and the Holy Spirit from the Father and Son, the Son did not begin after the Father, nor did the Spirit begin after those two. No instant or point whatever may be assigned in which the Father preceded the Son or the Spirit, just as the sun did not exist before its light, nor light precede its rays. Therefore the Father is not simply cause, since a cause appears older than what proceeds from it.

But the bishop of Methone says: “We must examine what those think who confess that the Spirit proceeds from the Son, whether because he is called the Son’s, or because universally everything said to belong to someone appears to proceed from that very one. If this is so, since God is said to be Abraham’s, Isaac’s, and Jacob’s, he will also proceed from them, as will the whole world. And, to use more familiar examples,” he says, “since he himself is called both Father and God, and Father of Christ, [the Spirit] will proceed from him, so that blasphemy may pass from the Son to the Father and to the whole Godhead.” [Col. 0308C]

## Chapter XIII

Theophylact, archbishop of Bulgaria, likewise argues on the same chapter as follows:

“It is not untimely to speak here, since the subject itself presents the occasion, about how the Son has the Spirit and how the Spirit is the Son’s. For the Apostle says: ‘He sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying: Abba, Father’ (Gal. IV); and elsewhere: ‘If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, this person is not his’ (Rom. VIII). But the Latins, seizing upon this and reasoning foolishly, affirm that the Spirit proceeds from the Son.

“But we first say to them that to be from someone is one thing, and to belong to someone another. That the Spirit belongs to the Son is indeed unquestionable and confirmed by the witness of Scripture; but no Scripture testifies that he is from the Son, lest we introduce two causes of the Spirit, namely Father and Son. [Col. 0308D]

“But he breathed on the disciples and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John XX). O folly! Did he give the Holy Spirit to the disciples three times when he breathed? How then did he say: ‘You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, not many days hence’ (Acts I)? Or how are we to believe that the Spirit came at Pentecost, if he had already given him on the day of resurrection and had breathed on them three times?”

These are indeed laughable matters. It is clear that he did not give them the Holy Spirit three times, but one of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, namely the remission of sins.

And again: “The Son has the Spirit substantially, as consubstantial with himself, not as one possessed by the Spirit. For the prophets are moved [by the Spirit]. And the Spirit is also said to be the Son’s because the Son is unity, power, and wisdom; while the Holy Spirit is described in Isaiah as the Spirit of unity, strength, and wisdom. But he is called the Spirit of the Son because he is given to human beings through the Son.” [Col. 0309A]

To tell the truth, each of these men draws water at ground level and does not reach the creature of God; each entangles himself in very many absurdities. But because arguments not supported by demonstration are incredible and uncertain, since these reasonings are illuminated neither by common conceptions nor by the authorities of the saints, I shall attempt, as the Lord grants, to disclose and uncover the truth, lest falsehood be received as truth and the lamp of truth appear extinguished amid the assault of such storms.

First, then, it must be said that, just as the Holy Spirit is specially called Spirit, so the Son is called wisdom, power, and unity. Nevertheless, the Father and the Holy Spirit too are so called when these same designations are used. For the wise cannot be understood without wisdom, nor the powerful without power, any more than the loving can be understood without love. The Father is wise, the Son wise, and the Holy Spirit wise; likewise each is true and powerful. [Col. 0309B]

The Father gives being to the Spirit, and the Son gives it with him. For the Spirit is the love of Father and Son, equally, substantially, and according to nature.

Perhaps, however, the men previously named denied that the Spirit is from the Son because the Spirit is not from the Son according to any of the modes which philosophers customarily use when they speak of one thing being from another. These customary modes are as follows. A thing is said to be from another when it consists of matter and form: things made of matter are said to be from matter, and things formed in them from form. According to this mode the Spirit is not said to be from the Son.

Again, something is said to be from another as from an efficient cause, and the perfect from the imperfect, as we customarily say that a youth becomes from a child. Likewise, the whole comes from parts, contraries from contraries, and what is later comes to be—for example, Greek from Hebrew and Latin from Greek. [Col. 0309C]

But according to none of these stated modes is the Spirit from the Son, nor indeed from the Father. For the Father is neither matter nor form of the Holy Spirit, neither a part nor a contrary from which something comes to be through the alteration of a contrary while the same subject remains, which occurs by passion and the destruction of another. But every corruption and every change is absent from the Holy Spirit; nor does he vary through times, as though he were first a little child and then, like a boy becoming a man, came to growth through moments of time.

There is another mode of existence according to which the Spirit is held to belong to both, Father and Son: ineffable and unsearchable, though the Spirit is said to promise to speak to every creature.

Nevertheless, among the Latins it is manifestly held by faith that the Spirit belongs to Father and Son substantially, according to nature, and equally. For he is no less the Son’s than he is shown to be the Father’s; that is, he belongs equally in every respect to both. [Col. 0309D] For this reason neither has superiority or deficiency over the other, because in however many ways he belongs to the Father, in the same ways he belongs to the Son—according to nature, substantially, according to cause, and according to sending, that is, procession.

Moreover, the things set forth above as opposites—namely, that being from someone and belonging to someone are different—are found together in many instances. A part belongs to the whole and is from the whole; the fruit belongs to the tree and is from the tree; foam belongs to the sea and is from the sea. And just as it is impossible for water to belong to a fountain and not be from the fountain, so it is impossible for the Spirit to belong to the Son and not be from the Son, or for the Son and Spirit to belong to the Father and not be from the Father.

The Father, however, is not someone’s in the sense of being from someone; rather, in that he begets the Son, he is called the Son’s. Therefore the comparison between Abraham and the Spirit is unsuitable. For God is called Abraham’s as Abraham’s creator and lord, perhaps also as his friend. [Col. 0310A] He is called the God of understanding, strength, and similar things as their efficient cause. But the Spirit is called the Spirit of the Son and Father as one who is from God and himself God—not as something adventitious which comes from outside (for who would dare to assert this?), but as their fullness.

Certainly this cannot be grasped by sound understanding otherwise than by considering that, as he is called third from the Father, as stated before, he has his substance from the Son. This Spirit is, according to the Lord’s true word, the Spirit of truth, because he is called the Spirit of truth. And insofar as he is of truth, he is so far the Son’s and derives his existence from him. This may perhaps be made clearer as follows. If the Spirit is of truth but does not have being from truth, then the Spirit himself is “true” accidentally, as something is called hot accidentally because it makes hot. But he is not true accidentally; therefore he has being from truth.

A multitude of examples lends support to this syllogism. The human soul, because it is not from unity, is called truly [or is true] accidentally, just as it is known to possess the other virtues. For virtue and vice are not naturally present in it, as is evident from their easy changeability. Although it has existence from reason, it is not rational accidentally. A body, because it does not have being from color, is colored accidentally. [Col. 0310B]

Thus, if the Holy Spirit does not have being from unity, his truth is an added and adventitious quality, although he is called the Spirit of truth and is said to belong to truth. Therefore, just as he is of truth, so he has being and subsistence in that truth and from it—that is, he proceeds from the Son—according to the order of the persons. For there is no order among the true [persons], nor is one the cause of another. If that is established, neither principle nor cause can be found in the Trinity.

Again, philosophers recognize three orders of existing things. Some are wholly separable, namely subsistence and intelligence, like divine things. Others are inseparable in every respect, both in reality and in thought, like natural things. Others are separable in one respect and inseparable in another, like mathematical things; these occupy an intermediate position between the foregoing, sharing with divine things separability, and with natural things non-separability. [Col. 0310C]

Likewise, in the terms of syllogisms having the proper order of a perfect figure, the middle always communicates with the extremes and, according to its relation, always looks to one or the other: now predicate, now subject.

Furthermore, philosophers divide the rational soul into three parts, proposing that it has the irascible, rational, and concupiscible faculties. They say that the rational faculty rules, the concupiscible is subjected, and the irascible sometimes performs a divine function and sometimes adheres to subjection.

It is therefore clear, I think, that in the solitary unity of nature and the ineffable threefold order of persons, just as the Son is begotten from him who has no beginning, so the Spirit proceeds from the Son. But since this is now plainly evident, we must proceed to the other part of the objection: namely, whether Christ, by breathing upon the faces of the disciples, gave them the Holy Spirit; or whether the disciples received a gift without the Spirit—that is, the power of working miracles. [Col. 0310D]

Perhaps speech would not fail even in resolving this point; but since Gregory surnamed the Theologian has argued concerning it, we ought for a little while to serve silence. He thus discusses the Spirit given to the disciples:

“The Holy Spirit worked in Christ’s disciples in three ways, and at three times: before Christ was glorified by his passion, after the glorification in the resurrection, and after the ascension into heaven. At first gently, then more powerfully, and thirdly more completely—not merely being present in operation as before, but substantially, as one might say, by association and abiding with them.”

Christ breathed upon them in order to show that he was the one who had created our nature from the beginning. For Moses says somewhere: “God formed man, taking mud from the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life” (Gen. II). Because humanity was led into death through disobedience and had fallen from its ancient honor, Christ renewed it again by the death of his flesh, destroying death and restoring it to its former honor; and by his breathing he restored to us the Spirit who had flown away and withdrawn from us. [Col. 0311A]

Apollinaris likewise declares: “He breathed into Adam’s face the breath of life; and after he returned from the dead, he breathed into the faces of the disciples, so that, re-formed according to the ancient image, they might appear conformed to their Creator through participation in the Spirit.”

The renowned bishop of Rome, Gregory, likewise affirms in his *Dialogues* that by that breathing Christ gave the Holy Spirit to the disciples: “On earth the Spirit is given so that one may love one’s neighbor; from heaven he is given so that one may love God.”

## Chapter XV

Yet John Chrysostom alone seems to assert the contrary opinion:

“How then did he say, ‘Unless I go away, he will not come,’ if he gave the Spirit? For he did not then give the Spirit, but through the breathing made them fit to receive him.”

And shortly afterward he says: “No one would be at fault in saying that they then received some spiritual authority and grace.” Not, however, the power of raising the dead and performing miracles, but that of remitting sins. For the gifts of the Holy Spirit differ; therefore he adds: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose you retain are retained” (John XX), showing what kind of operation he grants. [Col. 0311B]

But after forty days they received the efficacy of signs; hence he says: “You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you” (Acts I). Chrysostom therefore interprets himself correctly: when he said that the Spirit was not then given, he meant that Christ did not then fully bestow every kind of operation of the Spirit—agreeing with Gregory the Theologian, who said: “At first gently, then more instructively, and thirdly more completely.”

Jesus himself testifies that the disciples received the Spirit through the breathing, when he says: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX). For no one who gives nothing, unless he is a deceiver, says, “Receive.” But Jesus said to them, “Receive.” It is therefore evident that he granted them something. If he gave them something, either it was what his words signified, or something not signified by the words. But no one handing over a stone, intending to deceive, would deliberately say afterward, “Receive bread.” Therefore he gave what the words signified, namely the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0311C]

If anyone, still wishing to bring the dispute to an end, says that he did not then give the Spirit but one of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, namely remission of sins, let him consider whether such a power is separable. Clearly it is not separable, since nothing accidental belongs to the divine hypostases. Therefore, when he gives the Spirit, he grants the whole Spirit, not a part; for we know that the Holy Spirit is not divided. In him there are no parts to receive, since he is wholly indivisible. Therefore he gave the whole Spirit to the disciples at once.

But some ask: If he gave the Spirit then, why did he say, “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you” (John XVI)? They also say: If he gave the Holy Spirit by breathing then, how did he give him again on the day of Pentecost?
