To this one must answer that on the day of resurrection he did give the Spirit, but not according to every mode of operation; on the day of Pentecost, however, he gave them the Spirit according to every mode of operation in them. [Col. 0311D]

Moreover, let them also be asked: “Is the Holy Spirit God?” “Surely he is God; therefore the Holy Spirit surely exists?” But if so, it is evident that he was then present in the apostles. How then, on the fiftieth day, did he send the Holy Spirit to the disciples, with whom that same Spirit was present? Such distinctions are certainly made with respect to the distinction of persons and the efficacy of their operations in the apostles. To this end Christ, as sender, is believed to have breathed upon the faces of the disciples as God: both that by this we might understand that the Spirit truly proceeds from him—as that breath visibly issued from the depth of [Col. 0314B] his body—and that he might give them the Spirit to have and, as it were, possess. But on the day of Pentecost he is said to have sent him to those same disciples for strength, operation, and the manifestation of signs from heaven.

This is clearly apparent from the following: while Christ was present, his disciples rarely performed signs; but when he departed into heaven and sent the Spirit, signs were performed through the hands of the apostles. Hence he is said to have been sent in the form of fire, so that he might strengthen and confirm those who were still, as it were, soft clay. Had not Peter, the first of the disciples, previously been frightened by the voice of a maidservant? Yet afterwards, strengthened at that time, he despised the tyranny of the rulers of the world. From these things it can therefore be evident [Col. 0314C] that it is neither folly nor ignorance if someone says that Christ then gave the Spirit to the disciples, when after the resurrection he said to them: “Receive the Holy Spirit”; since the most learned and holiest of the Greeks have confirmed this, as has been shown. Yet men of our own time count this an error and madness solely because they strive to abolish the procession of the Spirit from the Son—a procession which has testimony from the Savior himself, when he said to the woman suffering from an issue of blood and touching the hem of his garment: “Who touched me? For I know that power has gone out from me” (Mark 5). For I am God, and I have the Spirit, by whom I cast out demons, a giver of healings equal to me.

For power to go forth from within, and from one’s own nature, belongs to God alone; and it is proper to him alone who is rightly believed by faith to be above every creature. The prophets, indeed, did not possess powers issuing from themselves; they shone with miracles only by God’s grace, were illustrious in their teachings, and disclosed God’s counsels. But Christ, the source of every good and of all power, has the Spirit issuing from himself—not migrating locally, to be sure—just as learning, abiding with teachers, is imparted to pupils. “I know,” he says, “that power has gone out from me,” inasmuch as I am God; for inasmuch as he is man, he does not have the Holy Spirit consubstantial with himself and proceeding from himself, but resting upon him. Therefore, since he showed that power goes out from himself, he taught most clearly that the Spirit proceeds from himself.

But when [Col. 0315A] he raised the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, and did not wish to show anything of this sort, he took the girl’s hand and cried out, saying, “Girl, arise” (Luke 8). This does not signify any weakness of the Holy Spirit, nor that the Spirit was insufficient to restore the woman to life; rather, it shows only that his flesh, which was the same flesh through which the Spirit worked, was destructive of death and corruption, because all things became proper to the life-giving Word. Yet one must not believe that he did this apart from the Spirit, by whom he renewed humanity, restored lost grace by breathing upon the faces of the disciples, and accomplished every such dispensation through faith. Hence John the Theologian declares in a certain epistle:

> “But these things I have written concerning those who deceive you, [Col. 0315B] and may the anointing which you received from him remain in you; and you have no need that anyone should teach you. But as that same anointing teaches you concerning all things, it is true and is not a lie.”

Behold, he calls the Holy Spirit the anointing which they received from Christ; those who steadfastly retain him within themselves have no need that anyone should teach them.

Luke also, speaking of Christ, says: “In that same hour Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said: ‘I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent’” (Luke 1). “He rejoiced in the Holy Spirit,” that is, he gave proof that the Spirit proceeds from himself as from the Father—the Spirit who reveals such mysteries to the little ones and the pure in [Col. 0315C] heart. The apostles were filled with the Holy Spirit, but not in the same manner as Christ. For they did not have him from themselves, but received him from without. Jesus, however, as Son of God has and has had the fullness of the Spirit not by advent, addition, or external reception, but from himself.

The great Cyril states this plainly in the new chapter against Nestorius and his accomplices:

> “If anyone says that the one Lord Jesus Christ was glorified by the Father as though using an alien power through him and receiving from him the ability to act against unclean spirits and accomplish divine miracles among human beings, and does not rather call the Spirit his own, through whom he wrought heavenly miracles: let him be anathema.”

The same saint explains this as follows: The only-begotten Word of God, made man, remained such, and thus, being God in all things whatsoever the Father is—except only that he is Father—and having from himself, properly and substantially by nature, the Holy Spirit, wrought divine miracles. Therefore, having become man, he nevertheless remained God, so that by his own power, through the Spirit, he fulfilled miracles. But those who say that he was one man like ourselves, that is, glorified like the saints, and that he acted through the operation of the Spirit, not as his own but as an alien power unworthy of God, and as though he had received from the Spirit, as one possessing a share in grace, that by which he ascended into heaven, shall justly lie under the force of anathema.

## CHAPTER XV

Yet Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, in the eleventh chapter, with foolish confidence unlawfully undermines these points, making light of things worthy of great regard and holding impious things in high esteem. Concerning these words of Cyril, namely, “the Spirit is proper to the Son,” he wrote as follows:

> “If he asserts that the Spirit is similar and proceeds from the Father, we shall agree and receive the statement as pious. But if he asserts that the Spirit has existence from the Son or through the Son, we shall reject it as blasphemous and impious. For we believe the Lord when he says: ‘The Spirit who proceeds from the Father’ (John 15); and likewise the most blessed Paul when he declares: ‘We have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God’ (1 Cor. 2).”

But when this same Theodoret was fully assured from the writings of great Cyril that he taught with the Latins concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, he uttered the following abuse:

> “He blasphemes against the Holy Spirit, in asserting not that he proceeds from the Father alone, according to the Lord’s saying, but that he has existence from the Son. These are Egyptian offspring—shoots worse than their evil father.”

This reviler deserved an answer; but since that great and righteous man himself answers and makes a response to his reviler on his own behalf, I shall be silent while he answers thus:

> “We know,” says the saint, “that Christ crushed evil and unclean powers by the operation of the Holy Spirit. But we do not say that he used the Spirit as an alien power, as any one of the saints does. For the Spirit was [Col. 0316C] and is his, just as he is also the Father’s. And Saint Paul makes this plainly evident to us, when he wrote: ‘Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you; but if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his’ (Rom. 8). The Holy Spirit indeed proceeds from the Father, according to the Savior’s saying, but he is not alien to the Son; for he has all things in common with the Father. And he himself taught this, saying of the Holy Spirit: ‘All things whatsoever the Father has are mine; therefore I told you that he will receive of mine and declare it to you’ (John 16). Therefore the Holy Spirit glorified Jesus, performing extraordinary works; but as his Spirit, not as an alien power and one superior to him, insofar as he is understood to be God. We have therefore not blasphemed the holy angels or the prophets, as one who knows only how to revile dared to say. For his and his associates’ purpose is to divide Christ into two: one who is glorified and acted upon, and another who glorifies and acts. They foolishly disparage every pious word that restrains them from such perverse opinion.”

And again, in an epistle against impious Nestorius:

> “For even if the Spirit is proper in person and is understood as existing by himself, insofar as he is Spirit and not Son, nevertheless he is not alien from him. For he is called the Spirit of truth, and Christ is the truth, from whom he flows forth, just as he does from God the Father.”

[Col. 0317A] Hence it is clear here that Theodoret interpreted “the Spirit has existence from the Son” as “the Spirit proceeds from the Son,” which is true; and that he opposed great Cyril because Cyril affirmed that the Spirit has existence from the Son. Even a Greek must confess that Cyril is especially to be believed—unless perhaps he follows in the footsteps of Photius, patriarch of Constantinople. Since the course of the discussion requires it, the snares of his sophisms and his grievous, cruel insults against the Latins must here be briefly set forth.

For this is he who, after Theodoret, dug in the sand a well beside the sea, burying not seeds but Cienian poisons, and became the cause of a most dreadful sickness in the faith of Christians. Isaiah indeed laments him and his accomplices, saying: “Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and prudent in their own sight” (Isa. 5). But now the haughty contradiction and foul speech of this patriarch who loves falsehood must be set out. “There is,” he says, “a sharp and irresistible weapon against the Latins, and before all else the Lord’s saying, which, striking dumb, destroys and demolishes every wild beast and every fox. What is this? ‘The Spirit who proceeds from the Father.’ Yet the Son maintains that the Spirit proceeds from the Father. And do you seek an author through whom you may commit—indeed, complete—your impiety, while you invent that the Spirit proceeds from the Son? If you have not feared to attack the doctrines of the common Savior, Creator, and Lawgiver, so that they may be overthrown by your folly, what else can anyone seek by which utterly to refute your impious enterprise? If you despise the Lord’s laws, what religious person would not abhor your opinion? What else can raise you from your ruin? What skill of remedy can heal a wound which has occupied the whole body? Not the remedy furnished by the saving word, but that which voluntary sickness has introduced—sickness which, through unbelieving contention, changes the medicine of the Lord’s teaching into something unable to help, something deadly. Rather, while snatching away the sword that conquers enemies, he seeks to be numbered among their party. Therefore, although you lie on the ground beneath the two-edged sword of the Spirit, nevertheless we too, out of love for the common Lord and with willing zeal, shall bring forward whatever the reckonings of our sacred warfare, arming us for battle, move us to produce. Nor shall we leave you without care to flee the wounds thereby inflicted. For if the Son and Spirit proceed from one cause, the Father—though the one by generation and the other by procession—and if, again, the Son is producer of the Spirit, as blasphemy cries out—

How can any reasoning consistent with the consequence maintain that the Spirit is not producer of the Son? For since both proceed equally from one cause, if one supplies to the other the function of cause, while the other does not do the same to the first, does not the observance of an immutable order require, for an equal return of favor, that the Spirit be a cause? Behold, after this first babbling and these seductive arguments, how great a blasphemy this leader and author of the whole schism, with shameless tongue and corrupted conscience, conceived and brought forth—daring to write what no one else has written, and to construct utterly arrogant and superfluous syllogisms.

A similar question presses upon him: for if the Son and Spirit proceed from the one cause, the Father, and if the Son in turn sends the Spirit, as he himself asserts, how can any reasoning consistent with the consequence maintain that the Son is not begotten or sent by the Spirit? For since both proceed equally from one cause, the Spirit ought to receive as much as the Son receives from the Father. Therefore, if the Son sends the Spirit, the Spirit must beget the Son from the Father in return for favor, so that, as the Son sends the Spirit from the Father, so the Spirit may beget the Son from the Father in reciprocal return.

Moreover, the Son receives from the Father that the Paraclete may be his; why should not the Spirit similarly receive that the Word may be called his? Thus the reciprocity and equality would consist in this: as the Son receives from the Father to be the cause of the Spirit, so likewise the Spirit receives from the same Father to be the cause of the Son. In this account the rationale of faith would not be corrupted, since their properties would remain mutually intact, alike and equal.

And again this same heresiarch and fabricator of a new philosophy does not blush to attribute a shameless opening to the discourse:

> “O mind drunken with intemperance and impiety! O tongue made bold by impiety! Which of our priests or Fathers has said that the Spirit proceeds from the Son? What synod, established and adorned with universal attestations—or rather, what divinely assembled college of bishops—has not condemned this opinion, even before it appeared, by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit? Through them it is evident, according to the Lord’s institution, that the Holy Spirit belongs to the Father, from whom they proclaimed in loud voices that he proceeds. Those who did not think thus they subjected to anathema as despisers of the universal and apostolic Church. For from ancient times, with the foreseeing eyes of providence, they condemned in writing, word, and judgment this newly arisen impiety, together with its manifold anticipated deviation.

> The second of the universal and sacred synods at once defined that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father; the third accepted it, the fourth confirmed it, the fifth consented, the sixth adjudged it, and the seventh sealed it by splendid contests. In each of them one may plainly see that piety acted confidently, and that the Spirit was divinely proclaimed to proceed from the Father but not from the Son. But what impious flock taught you? Who, setting laws contrary to the Lord’s laws, led you into impious sects?”

By this insinuation and appearance of plausibility, this heresiarch tries to lead into trackless error not merely the unlearned but even the learned. Since he speaks from his own inventions, he makes his discourse an instrument of falsehood: he scatters words, searches out his own notions, while asking what synod decreed that the Spirit proceeds from the Son. Thus I may now without complaint employ the same abusive words against him and exclaim: “O mind drunk with incontinence and impiety!” I omit the rest, which scarcely has a determinate number, and come to the great articles of faith.

What synod decreed that leavened bread be offered and that it be pierced with a lance? Yet the bread which the Lord took and said, “This is my body” (Luke 22), was unleavened; for he first completed the legal Passover, then performed that mystical supper at the same table. Chrysostom relates, when discussing Judas’s betrayal and the Passover: “Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” (Matt. 26)—not our Passover, but the Jewish one; for the disciples prepared that, while he himself prepared ours. And again, at the same table, both Passovers took place: that of the figure and that of the truth.

Great Cyril too, in the sixth discourse *On Worship in Spirit and Truth*, speaks thus: “The saving and desirable day of this sacrifice was the fourteenth according to the moon. Thus the law clearly foretold the time of the sacrifice of our Savior, since we say that he endured it for the life of the world: ‘On the tenth,’ it says, ‘of the first month, let every man take a lamb for his household according to the number of souls; and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month, and the whole assembly of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it at evening.’ Do you hear how it was taken on the tenth and kept [Col. 0319C] until the fourteenth, formerly a victim, so that you may understand the fifth time, in which, having become man for us, he endured death, when the moon, which is devoted to the beginning of night, had already begun to wane?”

## CHAPTER XVI

But Epiphanius, archbishop of Cyprus, in the book called the *Panarion*, against the Ebionites who prohibit the eating of meat, says:

> “How is their madness not immediately refuted, first by the Lord’s eating the Passover of the Jews? Now the Jews’ Passover was a lamb and unleavened bread, the lamb’s flesh roasted with fire; and these were eaten, as the disciples say to him: ‘Where do you wish us to prepare,’ etc. And again: ‘With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you’ (Luke 22). He did not say merely ‘Passover,’ but ‘this Passover.’ But the Passover, as I have said, was flesh roasted with fire and the rest; and again the same saint spoke truly when he said: ‘With desire I have desired to eat this Passover,’ that is, the flesh, with you. He plainly showed that he both completed the Passover and ate flesh, as stated.”

And the Law also says: “You shall have this day as a memorial, and you shall celebrate it as a solemn feast to the Lord, with perpetual worship. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread; on the first day there shall be no leaven in your houses. Whoever eats leavened bread, that soul shall perish from Israel, from the first day until the seventh. In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month at evening, you shall eat unleavened bread, until the twenty-first day of the same month at evening. For seven days leaven shall not be found in your houses; every one who eats leavened bread, his soul shall perish from the assembly of Israel, both among the resident aliens and among the natives of the land” (Exod. 12).

But Christ was in no way a transgressor of the Law; otherwise they would justly have killed him. Therefore, blessing unleavened bread, he broke it, gave it to the disciples, and said: “Take, eat; this is my body” (Matt. 26). Thus the holy Church of the Latins perpetually offers and sacrifices unleavened bread, not Judaizing in this—for the Jews do so once in the year and not with a like intention, whereas the Church does so perpetually according to Christ’s institution. Indeed, if this were Judaizing, then those who use a temple, altar, oil, water, lights, incense-burners, images of angels, and who do not shave their beards, would certainly agree with the Jews. That the Jews had images of angels is evident from the Lord’s words to Moses: “You shall make for me two Cherubim of beaten gold and set them on either side of the mercy-seat, stretching out their wings over the mercy-seat and facing one another” (Exod. 37). It is therefore clear that the Jews possessed the use of images.

Moreover, what assembly of bishops handed down that those to be baptized should first be anointed with oil, when the Lord taught that baptism should be in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, adding nothing further? Moreover, what synod decreed that hot water should be mixed with the Lord’s blood? This seems rather to make more apparent the Son’s assumption of a body that is animal and endowed with the grace of healing than his assumption of a rational, living, or spiritual body. For it is never written that the Lord put hot water into the cup when, at supper, he said to the disciples: “Drink all of this; this is my blood” (Matt. 26). Nor should the teacher of sobriety and every restraint be thought to have given wine without water when he handed over the sacrament of the mystery to those same disciples.

And again, what synod established that in the services of the churches one should chant only *Kyrie eleison*—“Lord, have mercy”—and not join to it *Christe eleison*—“Christ, have mercy”? The Lord said: “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father” (John 15). The holy synods confirmed this, and the whole body of the Latins has not only not denied it, but with all diligence and from the whole heart believes, says, and confesses that he also proceeds from the Son. For although the Father alone is named, the Son is altogether understood as well, because the Spirit does not proceed from the Father without the Son as mediator. Nowhere is the Father found to have said, “I alone send forth the Spirit”; nor has any prophet or other Father ever uttered, “The Father alone sends the Spirit.” Nor does this stand contrary to the decrees of the holy Fathers who assembled at Nicaea, Constantinople, Chalcedon, or elsewhere to establish the faith. For it says the same thing differently, by explaining and interpreting how it ought piously to be understood: that the Spirit proceeds from the Father, with the Son understood—both because it is most true that the Spirit proceeds from the Son and because many separated him from the Son.

For just as the Son is understood when the Spirit is said to belong to the Father, so the Spirit is to be understood to proceed from the Son when he is said to proceed from God the Father. For if the Spirit, by being possessed, does not indicate the Father’s distinctive property, neither does he indicate it by proceeding; but he does not indicate it by being possessed. For the Spirit is proper to the Son, though this does not rest upon the fact that the Father possesses the Spirit, because the Spirit is not possessed as offspring. Yet this good shepherd removes what is sound and well-founded through his false opinions, condemns the holy Church of the Latins by his own authority without a synod, and lies against the holy synods and the men of apostolic holiness, asserting that they decreed that the Spirit proceeds from the Father but not from the Son. He plainly slanders the holy Fathers as having declared what they did not declare, and as having taught a meaning which their wording does not signify.

The Savior indeed said, “Who proceeds from the Father.” The holy councils and venerable Fathers confessed the same. But this reviler asserts that they taught what he supposes the expression indicates, namely, “who proceeds from the Father alone.” Therefore, applauding as though decreed what they did not declare, he charges the Savior, the holy synods, and the venerable Fathers with teaching that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone. For these two expressions do not signify the same thing: “who proceeds from the Father,” and “who proceeds from the Father alone”—neither among Greeks nor Latins, neither among rhetoricians nor philosophers. Certainly one must examine not merely the wording but [Col. 0321C] the intention of the wording.

Indeed, doubtful matters are at times made clear through other matters and through what has been written elsewhere. “From the Father alone” appears known to the Latins, while “from the Father and the Son” appears known to the Greeks, because neither is found written in the Gospels. Yet they are so opposed that one of the two must necessarily be true and the other false. But that he proceeds from the Son accords and agrees with the Scriptures, and nothing contrary or incompatible with it is found, even though it has not been expressly stated by synods. For every Roman pontiff who sanctified and confirmed the synods always said and taught this. Athanasius, Basil, Cyril, and the rest of the saints plainly followed them. Therefore it is right to hold and say that he proceeds from the Son.

In all matters in which it is not common to understand the Spirit together with the Son, the Father alone is understood, as when he is called unbegotten, without cause, without beginning, and in anything similar. But in all matters in which it is common to understand him with both, or with one of them alone, even though only one is named, that one is not understood alone. Now the Father has the Spirit in common with the Son. Therefore, when it is said that he proceeds from the Father, that he proceeds from the Son must also be understood.

But many inconveniences follow one who says “from the Father alone,” of which I mention very few here. For if the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, he is not the image of the Son but of the Father, since he shines forth immediately from him. But this is not so, since the Spirit is the image of the Son and shines forth immediately from him. Therefore, if the Son proceeds from the Father because he is his image, the Spirit has existence from the Son because he is his image.

Moreover, he will be nearer to the Father than to the Son, and more the Father’s than the Son’s. Moreover, if he proceeds from the Father alone, the Father gives the Spirit to the Son by measure, since he attributes to the Son merely mission and not sending-forth. Thus the Son does not seem to possess the Father’s excellence in equal measure, nor to have the Spirit wholly, with all that is considered in relation to him, as the Father has him.

For great Cyril says: “The Son does not give the Spirit by measure, according to John’s saying, but himself sends him forth from himself, just as the Father does.” Therefore whoever transforms the statement “who proceeds from the Father” into “from the Father alone” weakens the saying of the Savior, the perennial source of truth. But “a lying mouth shall not go unpunished,” as Solomon says. The good shepherd has vomited forth something dark and black, like the fish called *sepia* [cuttlefish]. For neither any synod nor any holy Father said that the Spirit does not proceed from the Son, or that he proceeds from the Father alone. It remains, therefore, that after Theodoret the heresiarch Photius was the herald of this doctrine, which he labored to demonstrate by muddy and superfluous arguments. One of these is the following:

If all things belonging to the Father, Son, and Spirit are common—such as God, king, creator, almighty, simple, incorporeal, and absolutely all other such things—and if the procession of the Spirit from them is common to the Father and Son, then the Spirit will proceed from himself and will be his own principle, cause, and productive cause at once. Not even the fables of the pagans invented this.

## CHAPTER XVII

The argument of this sharp sophist and skilled craftsman, it seems, does not preserve the faith inviolate. By employing words in deceit and cunning, he has made himself liable to accusations concerning the poison of heretical impiety. Though unwilling, he does so because he does not have divine Scripture as his advocate. He mixes things that ought not be mixed, compares things that ought not be compared, and, because he does not distinguish natural qualities from properties, falls into the Acherusian marsh. For property is not the same as a natural quality, nor substance as equality.

> **[Note: [Col. 0321D] When Hugh distinguishes in some places the divine essence from personal properties, he does not mean a real distinction, nor an actual formal distinction, but a reasoned distinction of reason—formal, virtual, and [Col. 0322D] eminent, as theologians speak. See St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, I, question 28, article 2, and question 39, article 1, and his commentators at the same places.]**

For whatever natural qualities the Father and Son have, the Spirit also has. But whatever properties two have, the third does not have, as was shown above. Therefore the sophist contradicts himself when he says that it is common to the Spirit and the Son, from one indivisible cause, to have procession. This certainly cannot belong to the Father, who has no cause. Nor does Gregory the Theologian agree with this opinion, in a certain discourse addressed to Irenaeus the philosopher:

> “Not being made is common to Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; but being from the Father is common to the Son and Holy Spirit.”

Accordingly, just as the procession of the Spirit from the Father and the Son is a property, no reasoning compels it to be a property of three because it is a property of two. Incorporeality, superessentiality, and similar qualities that pertain to nature are, as has often been determined, equally common to all three.

Yet again, full of hostility toward the divine, he says: “But the Spirit proceeds from the Son, receiving something that he did not have when proceeding from the Father. For if receiving something means that one who receives was imperfect without the addition, how is he not imperfect? But if he received nothing, other consequences are likewise overthrown: namely, that he is twofold and composite, violating the simplicity of a nature that admits no composition. That reasoning can establish nothing concerning procession.”

But the property does not follow from the terms, nor does the conclusion follow from what is inferred. Falsehood, as they say, is an illness more of the speaker than of the hearer whom it deceives. The Father acts through the Son, receiving something without which he was unable to create—he who works all things in all. Is the operation of the Father, Son, or Spirit imperfect? The Father, being perfect and self-sufficient, needs no one. Nevertheless, he creates all things through the Son, receiving nothing that he did not possess. So also the Spirit proceeds from the Son and through the Son, receiving nothing from him except what he receives from the Father. The Father, being perfect God and in need of nothing, nevertheless begets from his substance the Son, through whom he creates all things, a Son equally powerful with himself.

Nor does the procession of the Spirit from both in any way imply excess, since it neither indicates an imperfect Spirit, nor shows the Father or Son powerless, nor introduces any composition. If cause and productive cause were parts of the substance, the argument for composition would indeed have a place. But now the Son is called begotten, and the Spirit sent forth—not insofar as they are substance, but insofar as the former is begotten and the latter proceeds. Yet this does not pertain to the nature of the Godhead.

Further: Since the Word of God is perfect and lacks nothing, what did he receive from the Holy Spirit when he assumed flesh, with flesh attending upon flesh, and when that anointing of his took place, as it is written: “Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Acts 10)? The Son, therefore, is not an emitter of the Spirit as one supplying some need or deficiency in himself. Rather, God emits [the Spirit] together with the Father, lacking nothing: both because the Spirit belongs equally to both, and because the Son proceeds immediately from the Father [Col. 0324A]. Therefore the Spirit is not from the Father alone, but also from the Son, who alone is the fruit of the Father, according to the same relation by which he proceeds from the Father.

Further, the same abusive opponent says: “If the Father is the cause of those who are from him, not by reason of nature but by reason of person; but the rationale of the paternal person has hitherto not included the person of the Son, this has been spoken impiously. Therefore the Son must in no way be the cause of any of those who are in the Trinity.” Yet it must not be passed over here that this impiety either divides the very person of the Father into two, or asserts that the person of the Son is received as a part of the paternal person. And indeed, a great multitude of other tares has sprung up from that evil sowing which was cast in at the beginning. The enemy of the race comes upon the wretched souls of those who, as it seems, are not asleep [Col. 0324B] but wakeful in soul, madly seeking death, and sows tares among them so as to make the noble and health-giving seed degenerate. To which should an answer be given—to blasphemies or to fallacies?

This lover of contention reproaches the holy Church of God, inflicting a thorny insult without blushing. The dispute is twisted by his malicious arrangement of the utterances of the prophets. It is said: “He who lacks self-control has no virtue; he who has no virtue lies under disgrace.” This reviler seeks victory by insults and dishonour, after the manner of a robber. But the argument is empty and ineffectual which, on account of “cause” and “causing,” as is clear from what precedes, divides the person of the Father [Col. 0324C], or makes the Father the Father of the person of the Son. For cause and that which causes do not know how to divide a person—not even among lower things. Therefore the Spirit’s being cause together with the Father does not divide the paternal person.

[Col. 0324C] Accordingly, that sophism is altogether superfluous, as is this one also: “If the Father sends the Son and the Spirit, not by reason of nature but by reason of person; yet the rationale of the Father’s person does not include the person of the Son; therefore the Son must not send any of those who are in the Trinity.” Again, this excellent shepherd says: “Yet the Saviour, instructing his disciples, said: ‘For he will receive from what is mine and declare it to you’” (John 16). And you are surely unaware that you have resorted to the Saviour’s utterance not in order [Col. 0324D] to take it as your advocate, but in order to reproach him through discordance. For your tongue is so bold and shameless that it invents and insinuates occasions for objection in matters that are incomprehensible.

Why have you not restrained your discordance with the law—a discordance that destroys immutable and unchangeable truth—when you deserve punishment? Indeed, rashness has deprived you of understanding, so that, like a child, you attempt impossibilities without recognizing them. But come now: even if you ought not previously to have understood that nothing so plainly stands against your insolence as this saving utterance of the Lord. For if he had said, “He will receive from me,” even thus your invention would not have found its limit; nevertheless error would have had some plausible occasion. Therefore the Saviour, foreseeing so great a magnitude of impiety [Col. 0325A], did not utter such a phrase, lest perhaps the devil’s cunning should devour many through you.

And shortly afterward, the Saviour did not say “from me,” but “from what is mine.” Though the alteration is brief, there is a great and considerable difference between “from me” and “from what is mine.” For “from me” introduces the very person uttering the words, whereas “from what is mine” introduces a person wholly other than the speaker. And a little later: who is this from whom the Spirit receives, if not the Father? For those who fight against the Lord will invent nothing else: not from another Son, nor from the Spirit who receives. When he said, “he will receive,” he clearly declares also for what purpose he receives—not in order to proceed or subsist.

Attend to the Lord’s words, O man: but why will he receive? “In order that he may declare to you the things that are to come” [Col. 0325B]. Then, explaining more plainly what he means by “He will receive from what is mine,” he immediately adds: “All things that the Father has are mine” (ibid.). Therefore, since they are mine, he receives from my portion; and for this reason he said, “He will receive from what is mine,” because they are mine in respect of participation. But the Spirit receives from the Father. For the things that are the Father’s are mine. Therefore, when he says “from what is mine,” the mind must be directed to the Father and not diverted elsewhere.

## Chapter XVIII

The insults of this man, like abyss or Tartarus, have no bottom, since rivers of Avernus flow from his mouth. Their names, as Socrates thought, are these: Acheron, Pyriphlegethon, Cocytus, [Col. 0325C] from which the Stygian marsh arises, and the unloved water called Acherusian. Would that he had drunk the water of forgetfulness and lost all memory of his insults!

The prince of the apostles himself commanded us to be ready to give an account to everyone who asks us concerning the faith that is in us, but with gentleness and fear, having a good conscience. But this man does not seek with gentleness and fear, according to the apostolic instruction; therefore truth has not revealed itself to him, since he does not seek rightly. Truth must indeed be sought as though God were present. Had he regarded God as present here, he would never have poured out so many insults upon God’s Church. For no prudent servant behaves shamelessly in his master’s presence [Col. 0325D], despising the honour of his own lord.

But it should be observed that the aforementioned words of Peter concern both teaching and the investigation of Christ. Where, however, he commanded: “When you stand before kings and governors, do not consider how or what you shall speak and answer them” (Mark 13), this concerns the glory of testimony and the presence of the Holy Spirit. For someone may often possess this wisdom and boldness in disputations; yet, because he is easily disturbed in tumults, he will be confounded in speaking. But the apostles received grace in both respects; hence the governors marvelled, and they themselves were assured that the Spirit’s presence was with them.

[Col. 0326A] This man makes great efforts, according to the rule of grammarians, to show that *me* and *meum* (“of me” and “what is mine”) differ very greatly in meaning. For *meum*, like every possessive pronoun, signifies two persons: one inwardly, namely the possessor, and another outwardly, namely the possession. Therefore, when Christ is understood as possessor in saying, “He will receive from what is mine,” and the Spirit is the receiver, the Father is doubtless the person called the possession. Yet truth seems not at all compelled by this, as is evident.

For the same Saviour says: “I cannot do anything of myself; as I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just, because I do not seek my own will” (John 5). And again: “Everything that the Father gives me shall come to me; and him who comes to me [Col. 0326B] I will not cast out, because I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me” (John 6). And again: “My teaching is not mine” (John 7). But if, according to the position of Photius the patriarch, the pronoun *meum* everywhere signifies two persons, the will of the Son would be another person from the Son. Thus not four or five persons, but a hundred or more, could be understood to exist in the Trinity.

Therefore it is not necessary that the pronoun *meum* should everywhere signify two persons, since it is also used figuratively of the same person, as Persius says: “Vengeance, after I departed from my praetor”; and Euripides: “But I am my own.” This man ought to have observed that “person” is understood differently among grammarians and among theologians [Col. 0326C]. For in grammar any thing whatsoever may be called a person [Note: [Col. 0325] Grammarians and theologians differ in their understanding of persons.], whether it subsists through itself or through another, whether it is substance or accident.

Therefore, according to this discipline, when the Son says, “My will,” “my judgment,” “my teaching,” “my generation,” and whatever similar expression occurs in individual clauses, one person and another is understood after the likeness of possessions. But in theology, setting aside properties, only three persons are distinguished among all things said according to substance. None of these appears to be expressly understood where the Saviour says: “He will receive from what is mine and declare it to you.” And he proves this to be so by saying: “All things that the Father has are mine; therefore I said that he will receive from what is mine [Col. 0326D] and declare it to you.”

If the Spirit receives from those things which are the Son’s and which the Son has, he receives from those things which are the Father’s and which the Father has. Likewise, if he receives from those things which are the Father’s and which the Father has, he receives from those things which are the Son’s and which the Son has. For all things which the Father has are the Son’s, and those which the Son has are the Father’s. But the Spirit receives from those things which are the Father’s and which the Father has; therefore he receives from those things which are the Son’s and which the Son has. If, in receiving from those things which are the Father’s and which the Father has, he receives from the Father, then in receiving from those things which are the Son’s and which the Son has, he receives from the Son. It is therefore manifest that the Spirit does not receive from the Father alone, as Photius asserts.

[Col. 0327A] Further: in the things which are the Father’s and which the Father has, the Father himself does not appear at all to be communicated; nor, in the things which are the Son’s and which the Son has, is the Son himself communicated. For the Father is not the Father’s, nor does he have the Father; nor is the Son the Son’s, nor does he have the Son. Nevertheless, in receiving from those things which are the Father’s and which the Father has, and from those things which are the Son’s and which the Son has, the Spirit is unquestionably said to receive from both, because the cause of his emission and procession, according to which the Spirit receives being, belongs to the treasury of the Father and the Son. Although both emit him, they do not do so inasmuch as Father or Son gives him being and brings him forth.

Therefore I judge that “He will receive from what is mine” should be understood thus: from my treasury, namely that of the Father and of the Son, he receives essence, and he will declare to you the things to come [Col. 0327B]; that is, you will recognize through what he teaches you that he himself is God as we are. For he has the same knowledge as we do substantially and according to nature. Things that share a nature are known from one another. For through one human being the whole human race may be seen, and through one ox the whole race of oxen; but not sheep through an ox, nor angels through human beings. For things of differing nature cannot be known from one another.

Further: if the Father is emitter of the Spirit not inasmuch as he generates according to nature, while the Son is not [an emitter], how will the Saviour speak truly when he says: “Therefore I said that he will receive from what is mine, because all things that the Father has are mine”? Either the Father will have according to [Col. 0327C] nature what makes him emitter, though not as begetter; or, if this is not so, those things which belong to the Father are indeed the Son’s, but those which are the Father’s do not pertain to the Son. Therefore, if the Son has all that is the Father’s except what belongs to the Father as begetter, while emitting the Spirit belongs to the Father not as begetter, this cannot be absent from the Son. For in saying, “All things that are the Father’s,” he leaves out nothing belonging to the Son except the Father’s being begetter. Therefore emitting the Spirit, which is the Father’s not as begetter, cannot be excluded [from the Son].

Further: the great Athanasius writes in one of his letters to Serapion as follows:

> “As the Only-begotten Son is one offspring, so also the Spirit, who is given and sent by the Son, is himself one and not many—not one made from many, but the Spirit alone. For since the Son of God is one living Word, it is necessary that there be one full sanctifying and enlightening Life, which is his operation and gift; it is said to proceed from the Father because it plainly shines forth [Col. 0327D], is sent, and is given from the Son, who is from the Father. Thus the Son is sent by the Father: ‘For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son.’ But the Son sends the Spirit: ‘If I go, I will send him to you.’ And the Son glorifies the Father, saying: ‘Father, I have glorified you.’ The Spirit likewise glorifies the Son: ‘He will glorify me.’ And the Son says: ‘The things which I heard from my Father, these I speak in the world’ (John 17). But the Spirit receives from the Son: ‘He will receive from the Son,’ he says, ‘and will declare it to you.’”

Likewise [Col. 0328A] the great Basil, in his third discourse on the Spirit, affirms: “In dignity he is second to the Son, having his being from him; receiving from him, he declares to us; and the discourse of piety hands down that he proceeds altogether from that cause.”

But the great Cyril too, in his sixth discourse to Hermias, says similar things:

> “How then, they ask, do they say that he is sanctified through the Spirit, when he himself plainly says concerning the Spirit: ‘Because he will receive from what is mine and declare it to you’? And this they do not mean as though he possessed something through participation in the Holy Spirit, since he is altogether perfect and without need according to his own nature and existence. Rather, they signify that the Spirit exists from the substance of God the Father and of the Word; according to his own [Col. 0328B] nature, the Spirit is from the Word and appears in him.”

Nor does Chrysostom, in his exposition of John’s Gospel, seem to refer “He will receive from what is mine” to the Father:

> “‘He will receive from what is mine,’ that is, he too will say the things I have said; or, ‘from what is mine,’ from those things which I know and from my knowledge. Again, ‘from what is mine,’ that is, he will declare things consonant with mine. ‘All things that the Father has are mine.’ For he will speak from the things that are the Father’s, and he will speak from mine; he will declare to you the things to come. It is most proper to God to declare things to come. If he learns from another, he has nothing more than the prophets possess.”

But in this passage that holy man also demonstrates the most exact knowledge in God. What, then, could more fittingly be called most exact knowledge than the wisdom of the Father, which is Christ [Col. 0328C], and from which the Spirit receives? This is clear from the fact that he did not say it as though the Spirit were unworthy or merely said “from another,” but to show that the Son, like the Father, is his cause.

## Chapter XIX

You have heard, Photius, these glorious men—I mean Athanasius, Basil, and Cyril. They refute your insistence. You heard them affirming: “The Spirit will receive from the Son and declare it to you,” and yet you did not immediately fall silent in obedience to their divinely manifested teachings, with which every wise person agrees and which all ratify by the highest choice. You render no good return to your fathers, whom you proscribe so that they may appear witnesses of falsehood.

How much better and more fitting it would have been for you to think and say [Col. 0328D] what those celibate men thought and wrote, rather than dishonour and insult the Church of God while asserting that it has attempted, by adulterous and deceitfully inclined reasonings, in excessive confidence to discredit the holy Creed. Therefore you cry out—O contrivances of malice—that it professes in vain that the Holy Spirit proceeds not from the Father alone but also from the Son. Who has ever heard such a voice break forth, even from the most impious? What crooked serpent instilled such things into their hearts?

Yet you confess, indeed solemnly confess, that the Spirit is of the Father and of the Son; but you apply “consubstantial” to the two merely in words, saying in this fashion: “We know that the Spirit is consubstantial with the Father because he proceeds from him; but he is consubstantial with the Son not because he proceeds from him—far be it!—not because the former proceeds from the latter by generation, but because there is an equal procession before the ages from one undivided cause.”

But it seems to me incorrect to say that “consubstantial” is predicated equivocally of the three persons. For many incongruous and impossible consequences follow [Col. 0329A]. If the Spirit is consubstantial with the Father because proceeding from him is substantial to the Spirit—for if Socrates is consubstantial with Plato because he is rational, rationality belongs substantially to both—yet proceeding is substantial neither to the Father nor to the Son, then the Son and the Spirit are not of the same nature as the Father.

[Col. 0329B] But if that were true, they would not be one God, since “consubstantial” would not be predicated equally and univocally of the three persons. This is also what appears to Photius, when he says that we apply “consubstantial” to both merely in words and not in meaning. Yet this is not well said. For substantial things belong to the same substance and nature. Things of the same substance and nature receive the same account of substance. All things consubstantial receive the same account of substance. Hence “consubstantial” is predicated similarly and in the same manner of all consubstantial things.

Indeed, just as the most specific species is predicated of its individuals, so God and substance are predicated of the three persons. And just as all things participating in a species are judged to be of the same nature and consubstantial, so surely Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are equally said to be of the same nature and consubstantial, according to the name of substance and not equivocally. Therefore, in the manner in which the Spirit is said to be consubstantial with the Father, in that same manner he is consubstantial with the Son. And just as the Son is consubstantial with the Spirit, so the Spirit is consubstantial with the Son and the Father [Col. 0329C].

For they possess no difference insofar as they are consubstantial. Therefore the Spirit is not consubstantial with the Father because he proceeds. Further: because the Spirit is consubstantial with the Father, he does not differ from the Father; but because he proceeds, he differs from the Father [Col. 0329D]. Therefore, because he proceeds, he is not consubstantial with him.

Further: “consubstantial” gathers a plurality into one; for, as the philosopher says, by participation in a species many human beings are one. Socrates and Alcibiades, though two, are reduced to “human being,” narrowed into one, and become one in species. But what is common is collective and unifying; therefore all human beings are consubstantial with one another, yet no human being is said to be another’s inasmuch as he is human.

Further: what is said substantially is incomparable and incommunicable with “to proceed,” or with any of those things called properties. For nature is not cut off, since there is no diversity among the persons according to substance; rather, only the nature of properties displays alternation within identity of substance. [Col. 0330A] Accordingly, there is no interchange between “consubstantial” and “substantial,” whether in expression or in meaning.

Further: if procession is the substance of the Spirit, the nature of the Spirit is processible. If the Spirit proceeds by nature while the Father does not, the Father and the Spirit are not of the same substance. Therefore the Spirit is not consubstantial with the Father because he proceeds from him.

Further: neither does this appear true: that the Spirit is the Son’s because both proceed equally before the ages from one indivisible cause. For incongruous consequences follow from stating this. Namely, according as both are from one invisible cause, they are united. They are not shown to be so many, but such, because number does not intervene according to union. For it is impossible for things to be numbered insofar as they do not differ at all, since they acquire number only through distinction. But insofar as the Spirit is the Son’s, he differs from him and is shown to be, as it were, another person. For nothing can be its own. Therefore he is not the Son’s, nor consubstantial with him, because both proceed equally before the ages from one indivisible cause.

Further: the Spirit is not called the Son’s merely as consubstantial and as sent through him, as Photius’s account declares. For either he is eternally the Son’s and is eternally sent through him, or he was the Son’s before he was sent through him. But if the Spirit was the Son’s before he was sent through him, he is the Son’s because he is sent through him.

[Col. 0330C] Again, if the Spirit is eternally sent through the Son, either he is sent by the Son together with the Father who sends him, or he is sent through the Son as through an instrument, as an arrow is sent through a bow. But this is impossible, because the nature of the cause is one thing and that of the instrument another; the Son would surely be alien from the Father as an instrument is from its craftsman. Therefore the Son sends and possesses the Spirit in every respect as does the Father. The Spirit, of course, is not consubstantial merely inasmuch as he is sent anywhere. Things which do not belong substantially cannot be substantial.

For I consider it incorrect to transfer an argument from properties to substantial qualities—that is, substantial differences. A property is not the same as a substantial quality [Col. 0330D]; therefore “consubstantial” cannot be reduced to a community of properties. Thus the Son of God is giver and sender of the Spirit out of his own fullness, for the Holy Spirit is his fullness, as John says: “Of his fullness we have all received,” namely, of his Spirit (John 1). But if the Spirit, inasmuch as he is a person, does not communicate to the Son, the fullness of the Son does not communicate to the Son [Col. 0331B].

Likewise, if the Spirit is not from the Son, the fullness of the Son is not from the Son. This is incongruous; therefore, since it is from the Son, it also proceeds from him. Those who deny this seem to assert that Christ did not work miracles through his own power by the Spirit. Since they know that the Son has all the things that the Father has, as additions and gifts, except that he is not the Father [Col. 0331A], they must acknowledge that he is cause and sender of the Spirit, as is the Father himself from whom the Spirit goes forth and proceeds.

Thus Luke testifies, saying: “All the people sought to touch him, because power went out from him and healed them all” (Luke 6). What is this power except that of which I spoke: “You shall receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you” (Acts 1)? Christ is the cause and fountain of this power as is the Father, because he heals, strengthens, makes wise, and bestows benefits without number.

Christ also speaks through Matthew: “When they hand you over, do not be anxious how or what you shall speak. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking in you” (Matthew 6 [probably 10]). And again, through Luke, he says: “Settle it in your hearts not to prepare beforehand how you shall answer; for I will give you a mouth and wisdom” (Luke 21). Mark likewise affirms the same: “When they lead you away and hand you over, do not premeditate what you are to say; for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit” (Mark 13).

We know without doubt and firmly maintain that Christ’s words are full of truth, and that he himself gave what spoke in the apostles, and that it was the Holy Spirit. From these things the following true conclusion is gathered: Christ gives and sends the Spirit in this way. Christ gives that which spoke in the apostles; this proposition is true by the Saviour’s own testimony: “For I,” he says, “will give you a mouth and wisdom” (Luke 21). But that which spoke in the apostles was the Holy Spirit, as the same Saviour bears witness.

[Col. 0331C] Therefore Christ himself gives the Spirit as does the Father. For he does not say, “The Father will give through me,” but, “As the Father [gives], I will give.” Thus it is clear from what has been said that, just as the Son gives the Spirit, so he also sends the Spirit who is the Son’s and proceeds from the Son.

Why then do you not understand the Spirit to be called the Son’s in the same way as he is called the Spirit of counsel, might, fear, wisdom, adoption, and, simply, of every benefit, gift, and grace? The Spirit is by no means called the Son’s in this manner. He is truly the Spirit of the Son where he is equally and without distinction regarded as the Spirit of the Father. But he is called the Spirit of graces and gifts as their giver and effective cause [Col. 0331C].

Just as he is called the Spirit of God, so he is also named the Spirit of the Lord; yet the relation is not reversible. For although God the Father is Spirit, according to the Lord’s utterance, and the Spirit is God, and the Spirit is also the Son of God according to the saying, “Christ the Lord is Spirit before your face,” nevertheless neither the Father nor the Son is called the Spirit of God [Col. 0331D]. Therefore, just as it is common to the Father and Son not to be anyone’s Spirit, so it is proper to the Spirit to be the Spirit of both.

Further: as among those born from God only the Word of God is declared to have been begotten from his womb, so among the Spirits of God only the Holy Spirit is believed to proceed from the mouth of the Son. “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth” (Psalm 32), namely, by the Word—according to the Apostle—all their power. By this Spirit that lawless Antichrist will be destroyed: “The Lord Jesus will slay him with the Spirit [Col. 0332A] of his mouth and destroy him by the brightness of his coming” (2 Thessalonians 2).

As Paul says, no one should presume to understand this of Christ’s soul. For insofar as it is a soul, it neither slays nor destroys anything. It remains, then, to attribute this solely to the Holy Spirit. From this it is manifest that, as the Son exists from the Father by birth, so the Spirit exists from the Father and the Son by procession. This may be shown again thus: the Spirit of Christ’s mouth proceeds from Christ, a sign of which is the breathing upon the faces of the disciples. That is, the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of Christ’s mouth; for as the Son of God he has one Spirit consubstantially, not many [Col. 0332B].

Therefore the Holy Spirit proceeds from Christ, the Son of God. But perhaps the opponent will say that the breathing, giving, procession, or sending of the Spirit to the apostles or prophets, performed by Christ, is undoubtedly temporal. But that [procession] by which the Spirit’s existence is considered in itself is not understood in relation to something, but in relation to the one from whom he is. The Greek understands this when he asserts that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone. But the things previously mentioned, being temporal and directed toward human beings, are not eternal; they neither create ambiguity in doctrine nor greatly concern the schism that has been spread abroad. Therefore the solution of this objection does not, it seems, constrain one who disputes from the opposite side by the arguments set above, although it is made evident from the previously cited chapter of the great Cyril against Nestorius, and from the fact that the relation of such things belongs more to creatures than to the Creator.

[Col. 0332C] Yet this will be explained more conveniently in what follows, because the course of the present volume demands an end. For now, as I judge, nearly all the objections of the Greeks have been resolved. It has been shown in every way that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, yet does not proceed from two principles or two causes. It has appeared how cause, principle, and unbegottenness are not personal properties, since the begetter does not emit the Spirit insofar as he is Father, nor does he do so alone [Col. 0332D].

It has also been shown that no property belongs to the persons in such a manner as to belong to only one person, since it is one thing to possess a property and another to be distinguished by a property. Likewise it has been made clear that, according to none of the causes spoken of by philosophers, is the Father or the Son cause of the Spirit, just as the Spirit is not the cause of either, according to the stated line of reasoning, since he is the love of both.

It has also been explained that no inequality among the persons arises from properties, since the Spirit belongs equally to two. It has also been made plain that the Spirit and the Son, and the Father together with the Spirit, possess certain things reciprocally in a singular way; and that the Father is likewise cause of the Son, not insofar as he is Father together with the Son. It has been elucidated that the Father’s emission of the Spirit is perfect, and the Son’s emission is perfect, and that neither exceeds the other, since they are one and the same.

Likewise, the Son, being principle in the Trinity, emits the Spirit immediately—not by reason of nature [Col. 0333A] or person, but by reason of cause and principle. The Spirit proceeds from both, yet is not double or composite by proceeding from two; nor is the Son made composite because he is cause and causing. The discourse has also made clear that the first human being was not like God the Father in unbegottenness, and in how many ways “unbegotten” is understood.

Further, it has shown that the Spirit is the image of the Son, the Father being an intermediary [the syntax is uncertain], and the Spirit being so according to order; that unity is referred in some respect to nature, not to person; and that the Spirit is the Son’s not as the spirit of understanding, counsel, fear, adoption of sons, or anything similar. It has also shown that Christ, by breathing upon the faces of the disciples, gave them the Spirit.

Further, necessary arguments have made it evident [Col. 0334A] that Photius’s assertions are invalid, and that the Spirit is the fullness of the Son, proceeding from him, according to the testimony of the Evangelists. This Spirit is called the Spirit of Christ’s mouth on the authority of Paul.

Therefore, henceforth, by your favour and encouragement—my dearest brother Leo, and Caciareda, eminent above many and skilled in definition—we must pass on to a kind of demonstration suited to the sublimity of this matter. So that, with prolonged nocturnal studies beneath crackling lamps, and after consulting as many volumes as possible of the holy and philosophical writers, Latin and Greek, I may discover what the third book may first offer for the reading of your diligence and that of others.

## Preface to the Third Book

[Col. 0333]

You urge me, my brother Leo, powerful in intellect, and you, Caciareda, most eminent in learning in the best arts, to renew the style of my discourse and, through variety in the argument, to relieve the weariness of readers. You seem to think that such a renewal, proceeding by this method, is particularly suitable for the exposition of questions concerning the solitary nature and for the elucidation of that purity which must not be defiled by any contagion of falsehood. Yet we must again proceed against the oil-cellars of the Pelasgians; malign opinions must be refuted—not in a hostile spirit—and a connected sequence of demonstrations together with authorities must be begun, setting forth the procession of the Spirit from the Father and the Son as surpassing all other emanations. By this means, the concern for seeking truth, more perfectly recognizing the disease now worsening—the forest that destroys the crops—disperses the darkness and more readily pursues truth's rightful claim.

Moreover, truthful understanding judges that from such diversity there arises an exceedingly abundant harmony of judgments. For it is clear that from these things the brightness of knowledge is increased; the ruggedness of ambiguities is smoothed; the points of those lying in wait are blunted by daily watchfulness; and the inextricable difficulty of a reflection supervening upon reflection is, as it were, opened by the eastern revolutions of the seasons of the year. This investigation certainly has a sure guide: namely reason, nobly elevated in keenness. Since it is always the same, it is most certain and invincible concerning that which it is able to grasp. At times, however, strengthened by the authorities of the saints, it tramples down winter springs, raises its gaze to things on high, and, while it attains the highest and loftiest things, is not wholly exhausted by the losses incurred in proof. For although the surpassing brightness of divine fruitfulness, apprehended with excessive subtlety, is not wholly subject to human investigations, nevertheless, because the same arguments apply to the greatest and smallest causes, it does not entirely withdraw itself from our demonstrations.

The mind must therefore be carefully cultivated: it is one and the same intelligence that knows the likeness, difference, identity, and diversity of the categories, and wonderfully contemplates both the lowest things and the highest. From these, certainly not without reason, fallen hope is raised and enlarged. This is all the more so because, now that the two preceding volumes have undergone the judgment of your most vigilant breast, the most exact file of your intellect, and your most approved test, they need no longer fear shipwreck from Charybdis or Scylla.

And since, as I think, you now embrace the Mareotic ebony, which drives away decay and, as they say, has the customary effect that its black appearance should not inspire fear, the cylinder of your unchangeable perseverance is unquestionably excellent: it levels the ground by daily smoothing, replenishing what is abundant and supplying what is deficient, and cauterizing errors. While this judgment approves what has been said, it gives great confidence to the work in its exercise: it has faith joined with soundness of understanding, and admiration with glory. By it you sharply discern wherever woven trifles are ignobly joined to the most eminent wisdom, or reeds to the masses of immense columns. Yet none of this is at all necessary to the subject; for, as is known from a report not without warrant, bulls float unharmed with camels in the Asphaltic lake of the province of Judaea. Whoever plunges to the bottom in seeking the pure stream of the divine words is not prevented by the thinness of the water.

Nor may one delay the day longer, since to do so has become execrable and liable to the severest reproof. It is therefore fearful to publish anything on this subject. For in these matters not only weak ability in reasoning and discourse, but even the strongest, scarcely restrains itself from falsehood and unconsidered errors. Moreover, the mirror of absolute purity is hidden from those who do not depart from the depths: it is accessible to everything, and nothing can be devised that can cast even the slightest cloud before its eyes. Therefore, for one desiring to write of such matters, the sweetness of heavenly music must be greatly enticed to sink into the lowest regions of the southern pole and to be exiled there, so as to restrain the tumultuous freedom of speech, which cannot stand still amid the perpetual agitation of excess and repetition.

For when that freedom luxuriates, it does so not only in sweet but also in bitter flowers; and where there is often no water but mud settles, it imitates the rays of Phoebus, not Phoebus himself—impatient of delays, yet never exceeding the boundaries of the Zodiac. Thus, if those skilled in the sea fear struggling winds at the farthest shore, frequent storms, and hostile rain, what can a passing spark, late soil, and violent torrent accomplish in writing—things which are causes of barrenness rather than sources of fertility?

But I, with the Spirit of truth dropping into my conscience and fostering the proposition, further illuminated by the support of the good faith of you both, and also by the intimate friendship of you, Calciareda—by your chrism, or rather oracle, as I prophesy about these matters—I do not at all fear to write, so that I may clear away the ambiguity of the question defended by us. For things that are cut back, even though they sprout again in many branches, rise again only more feebly. But lest the reputation of license to wander should protest, my pen must be turned so that the discourse may produce what it promises.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0335]

# CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0335A]

Although the human mind, setting out as a stranger, can scarcely investigate invisible things, and especially those that belong to the three divine persons, nevertheless it labours in inquiry and endeavours, by such arguments as it can, to show that God is one: from whom, through whom, and in whom are all things.

There certainly cannot be several first principles, since there must be one that is the source of all things, both similar and dissimilar. If, when another thing is set alongside it, the supreme unity and the truly One would no longer exist. For if God is not one through himself, but has within himself something by whose name he may rightly be designated, he will not be the sole cause, if he himself proceeds from another cause and the reasoning advances to infinity, with no point found at which it is possible to stop—like the divisions of continuous quantity.

[Col. 0335B]

Since every portion produced by such a division can again be divided, division proceeds to infinity. Therefore there must be a cause without a cause, and a principle without a principle: that which, sharing in nothing, is simply one, the first cause and the first principle of all things that exist. This becomes clearer as follows. If every multitude is posterior to the one and in some manner participates in the one, a simple and unitary principle is prior to every multitude. But every multitude is posterior to the one and participates in it in some manner; for if multitude preceded the one, it would not derive its being from the one, since it would itself have existed before the one. For there is nothing in what does not exist that can participate.

[Col. 0335C]

Therefore, since no multitude and no division precedes the supreme principle, the supreme principle is one and simple.

Further: everything divisible seems capable of division either according to multitude, or magnitude, or actions that take place in time. But God, being wholly immovable and eternal, and preceding every multitude, cannot be divided in any of the ways mentioned. It is therefore clear that before the supreme principle there is no other principle without principle, equal or better; nor is there a God before God, nor another after him that is God. For this reason one must seek in the divine persons neither a most general genus, nor a subordinate genus, nor a particular or species.

[Col. 0335D]

For where there is genus, there are also what is prior, species and difference, property and accident. But, as has been shown, nothing is prior to God; nor is he constituted from any differences, since he exists as a nature above every nature and has nothing by participation. The divine is simple and uniform, beyond every duality and composition.

Indeed, what is composite is composed either from diverse pre-existing things—as electrum from gold and silver—or from things considered together, as a head from bones, flesh, and other things of this sort.

[Col. 0336A]

For these things and others like them simultaneously acquire their constitution, even though they differ, because no one of these things precedes the head constituted from them. Therefore, since the divine is without principle and without cause, there is properly neither instruction, nor demonstration, nor definition of it. For instruction comes through demonstration, and demonstration through first principles and definition; but nothing is prior to God. A definition has a beginning and an end: its beginning is the most general genus, sometimes also what falls under the most general genus; its end is the differences. Hence no definition can be assigned to the divine, nor can any such demonstration, woven solely from affirmations, concern God, because he is infinite and without principle.

For these reasons, by removals and negations, I shall now undertake, so far as ability itself permits and with God as guide, to show that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, now in the following manner.

# CHAPTER II

Dearest friend, that which separates and cuts one thing off from another is understood either as substance, quality, quantity, relation, or one of the other categories. Apart from these, nothing of this sort can either exist or be understood. But that which separates and cuts off the Holy Spirit from the Son with respect to cause cannot be understood as substance, quality, or anything else of the kind.

[Col. 0336C]

For it is not substance that cuts them off, since Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of the same substance and nature. Nor is the Spirit separated from the Son, in respect of principle, by quantity. For it is evident that neither discrete nor continuous quantity can accomplish this. Discrete quantity, considered according to division and collection, presents its parts to the mind actually, not merely potentially; otherwise what is discrete will be thought continuous. It is conceived in the understanding, and one may think how great it is. But we are not capable of understanding how great God is, whose majesty is defined as indivisible, undivided, without composition, and without quantity or quality.

[Col. 0336D]

The same must be thought concerning continuous quantity. To consider it according to joining and succession is to consider a divisible thing as divided into things always divisible, since its parts are to be taken not actually but potentially. Let us not make the continuous discrete, nor heavenly things, which are impassible, corruptible.

Further: everything that can be measured either is quantity or participates in quantity.

[Col. 0337A]

For among measurable things, some are measured in their own right, such as a line or a surface; others by participation, such as a human being or wood. Socrates is measured not insofar as he is a human being, but insofar as he participates in magnitude; he is measurable only accidentally. But no person among the three divine substances is measurable. Therefore none of them is quantity, nor does any one of them participate in quantity.

Nor can any quality be conceived that distinguishes the Spirit from the Son on the ground that the Son is his cause; for no difference accomplishes this. Difference is spoken of in three ways: commonly, properly, and most properly. Only that which is called most proper makes one thing other than another by cutting it off from the other. But the Son of God and the Holy Spirit are substantial and have acquired no separable property.

[Col. 0337B]

From this it is clear that the Spirit differs from neither the Son nor the Father most properly or commonly. For what is said commonly does not comprehend anything of the being of a thing, nor does it show that anything belongs specially to a particular thing. It remains, then, that the Spirit differs from the Son only properly. The Spirit differs from the Son by an inseparable property, which in no way completes substance and does not show that contrary states can at any time be participated in under the same subject.

For an Ethiopian’s blackness is not changed into whiteness through the succession of time. Nor does one who is bald become hairy again. Nor do grey-blue eyes naturally at any time receive black colour.

[Col. 0337C]

So also, in the Holy Trinity, the Father does not become the Son, nor the Son the Father or the Holy Spirit, nor the Spirit the Father or the Son. Therefore these persons, because they admit no change, differ properly; and in things of this kind reciprocal change is impossible. Not only do inseparable properties remain together with the three persons, but they are also unchangeable—like, indeed much more than, privations themselves.

Hence the divine persons seem to differ from one another by the difference that is called proper, which produces merely an alteration and not another thing. They do not differ by common difference, which can be separated, nor by the most proper difference, which makes another thing. In the Holy Trinity there is nothing separable, nor one thing and another thing, but one person and another person.

[Col. 0337D]

It is therefore evident that the three persons differ from one another neither commonly nor most properly, but only by proper difference.

Further: every privation called a proper difference, while it is present in its suitable subject, excludes from it only the opposite—for example, baldness excludes being hairy, blindness having sight—and of itself determines nothing else. But not every common and most proper difference has this character. The Holy Spirit, however, differs from the Father and the Son as privation differs from possession. Similarly, the Son, in the same manner, is marked off by difference from the Spirit and the Father. Likewise, the Father differs from the Son and the Spirit,

[Col. 0338A]

as is plainly evident from the personal, distinctive properties: fatherhood, birth, and procession. Each one of these, belonging to its own person, excludes only two things as one opposite. Thus procession equally distinguishes both begetter and begotten from the person of the Spirit: for the Spirit is neither begetting nor begotten. In the same way, begetting and being begotten each exclude two things: unbegottenness excludes procession and birth; birth excludes procession and unbegottenness.

From this it clearly appears that procession does not cut off the Spirit from the Son more than from the Father, since it excludes two things only—namely, unbegottenness and begottenness—as one opposite, as is clear from what has preceded.

Further: if fatherhood does not exclude the Spirit from the Father in respect of cause or principle, neither does begottenness exclude that same Spirit from the Son according to the same relation.

[Col. 0338B]
