For the Spirit is equally and similarly other than each of the two; and concerning similar things the same judgment holds. Therefore no difference distinguishes the Spirit from the Son on the ground that the Son is not his cause. Hence the Holy Spirit, proceeding from both, is properly of the Son just as he is of the Father.

That the properties in the three persons are considered after the manner of privations is clear from their common features with privation. For privations and the properties just mentioned have this in common: they are present inseparably, but not substantially; they make merely an altered thing and not another thing; and they make change into one another impossible.

[Col. 0338C]

But one must observe that “privation” is said in many senses. The absence of a form in that which is fitted to have it is called privation. In this sense Aristotle says: “Everything that comes to be in some manner comes to be from contraries, that is, from opposites, and is corrupted into contraries, that is, opposites.” By contraries he means privation and form as two principles.

For everything that comes to be in some manner, when it casts off its former condition, acquires the state according to which it is said to come to be. When that former state is absent, the absence of form obtains a substantial subject; for example, if something unjust becomes just, or something foolish becomes wise, or an ignorant person becomes learned. Unless it casts off its former state, privation of form has no place.

[Col. 0338D]

For it is impossible that a privation of this kind should exist simultaneously with its form in the same substantial subject. Yet according to ordinary usage, nakedness is called a privation, from which there is a return to possession. Likewise, what is weak or unarmed, though privations, readily return to possession. Again, loss of money is considered a privation of possessions and honour, and a return can be made from all such things.

But the present discussion is not concerned with privations of this kind. It concerns only those which, in composite things, arise through an unnatural disposition and from which there is no return, as Aristotle teaches, saying: “Change takes place from possession to privation, but from privation to possession it is impossible. For one who has become blind did not see again; nor, when bald, did he again recover his hair; nor, when toothless, did teeth grow for him again.”

[Col. 0339A]

Therefore one of two things must be said: either the three persons do not differ according to any difference, or they differ according to what is called proper difference. But reason does not permit them to differ according to no difference. For individual things differ from one another by difference; and where there is no difference, no property is perceived, because things have a difference by some property through which they differ reciprocally.

But no one should suppose that I assert the divine persons have fallen into privation because I have declared their properties similar to these privations. Nothing in them is violent or contrary to nature, because each is ineffable simplicity, having nothing extrinsic. Indeed, knowledge of things is often achieved from features not present in them.

[Col. 0339B]

For one who defines a point, which has no part, makes it known by what is not present in it and establishes the rationale of the definition. Similarly, one who declares that difference in the three persons is to be considered after the manner of privation does not place privation in God. Rather, he shows that the hypostases called persons have inseparable, non-substantial properties and that these properties exclude only their opposites, as privations do.

For this reason, I think, Plotinus said: “One must bring many tongues—that is, turns or revolutions—into one, and thus understand God and comprehend him with closed eyes.”

[Col. 0339C]

For he surpasses every understanding; and though simple, the universe nevertheless flows forth from him, since he is superior to all things that he created. For one who excels is better than those who receive from him; and supremely so is God himself, who alone is good, to whom envy comes from nothing, because he needs nothing, while all other things have need of him.

Therefore these three persons, although they have an inborn concord with one another according to nature, nevertheless differ also according to quality, as appears from their properties, which do not inhere substantially. For from properties a figure or character seems to arise. Every figure or character, as the philosophers have thought, is referred to quality and exists according to the account and participation of quality. Therefore, in the individual categories, general or specific names seem to signify quality, because they determine a quality around substance.

[Col. 0339D]

Quality alone has obtained, as it were, a special and chief place among the other categories, so that under such an account the figure of every existing thing is referred to it in itself. For that which participates in quantity, according to which it is called quantitative, is thereby marked with a figure of difference in which quality is considered. The same must be said of each of the other categories.

Yet it is not fitting to discover or investigate a quality of quality, or a difference of difference. But it is necessary to seek the differences of the three persons, by which each is distinguished from the others.

[Col. 0340A]

Their difference is considered only in reason. For differences of this kind differ by themselves, and there is no difference of them, because they themselves are differences. Just as there is no motion of motion, no generation of generation, nor change of change, so neither is difference found to differ. This must be accepted concerning almost all properties. For nothing is rightly said to participate in itself: goodness is not made good by goodness, nor is equality equalized, but it equalizes.

From this it is evident that the three persons are distinguished from one another by differences, while the differences themselves differ by themselves. Someone may perhaps raise the following doubt. Of that which truly exists, and of those things which are carried through generation and corruption, substance, quality, or relation cannot be one genus, although it is proper to these to subsist under another category: for example, Father under substance, greater under quantity, educated under quality, and likewise in the rest.

[Col. 0340B]

But the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, being one God, possess true existence. Therefore they are not contained under the genus of things carried through generation and corruption. Nor are they under any genus of eternal things that simultaneously contains both eternal and corruptible things.

Since this is so, how can it be true that the three divine persons have properties, common features, and differences? For wherever a difference is present, a genus immediately follows. To this one must answer without hesitation that the divine is not a genus, since it is neither most general nor subordinate; nor is it contained in a genus, since nothing is prior to the divine either potentially or actually.

[Col. 0340C]

Nor is anything prior to it by order, as dialectic is prior to grammar among disciplines; nor by reason, as universals are prior by reason to particulars, while particulars are prior by sense to universals. It is therefore evident that the divine is neither in a genus, since nothing is prior to it actually or potentially, nor itself a genus, since it is not predicated of things differing in species.

For it must be known, as is clear from what has been said, that properties are considered in the divine persons differently from their consideration in rational and mortal creatures. The demonstration of those properties that belong to the divine persons is most suitably made from what is not present in them. But the demonstration concerning rational and mortal creatures is customarily made in the reverse direction.

[Col. 0340D]

For absence is judged from what exists, and things not yet present are known from things that are present. Thus Adam knew death, which he did not have and had never seen, through life. For he had not yet beheld anyone dying; but from the contrary, namely life, he understood death, which is the privation of life. Likewise a rich man recognizes poverty, and a healthy person sickness: non-existent things from existent things.

Further: either we ought to investigate the substance, identity, and difference of the three divine persons, or we ought not. If we ought not, how shall we know that God the Father is not the Son, and conversely? How shall we assign their properties?

[Col. 0341A]

How shall we perceive that God the Father lives, hears, sees, and has a Son, unless these things are referred through whatever demonstrations may be made from the things and words that are among us? It is clear that we understand what exists concerning God from the things and expressions among us. For we have never seen him; yet we describe him by those things that have greater honour among us, removing from what we say about him incursions and passions, lest the human race remain wholly in the darkness of ignorance.

Thus, since life and death occur among us, and life is superior to death, we believe and confess that God lives. Again, because the life that is here has a beginning and an end and needs food and drink and very many other things, we name God from that which is more honourable among us, asserting that he needs none of these things and has a life ignorant of beginning and end.

[Col. 0341B]

In the same way, we confess that he sees, hears, and begets, because sight is superior to blindness, hearing to deafness, and fertility to barrenness. Since, therefore, it is necessary and fitting to inquire what the personal properties of the three persons are and what they are not, and since it is altogether useful to dispute about these matters through the things and words among us, the objection of those who suppress all discourse concerning the divine is undoubtedly resolved.

Nevertheless, it is fitting to grant to the nature of the ineffable reality that one should not labour further to discover the properties of these persons than the matter under investigation permits, since it is evident that each person is denoted by its own proper character.

[Col. 0341C]

Some think that it is common to the three persons to be marked by a proper character, their constitution supporting this view; and that a common idiom of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is, as it were, a collection of non-substantial properties. Perhaps this is like its being common to the multitude of the human race to perceive day, night, hours, and every determinate period of time.

For irrational animals, though they seem to have a perception of time—for example, of winter, summer, heat, and cold—do not perceive time itself but the things occurring in time. For time is an incorporeal thing and is not perceived by the senses. Irrational animals do not know what escapes sense.

[Col. 0341D]

It appears, therefore, from what has been said that it is common to the three persons to be marked by an immutable, non-substantial property and to have one character. But it is evident that these common features are not substantial, since they are not spoken according to substance, do not inhere substantially, and are not singular. For the persons do not all include the same distinctive properties, whereas an individual has the complete fulfilment of its own character and an account differing from all others.

Therefore the three divine persons have some distinguishing features and other features by which they are not distinguished, as may be seen in Adam, Eve, and Cain.

[Col. 0342A]

For Adam had as his own property that he was a plasma, that is, a formed being—an immutable idiom existing in him. Eve’s property was to have come from the cutting of a rib. Cain’s was to be the first offspring of all, which did not happen to any other human being. Yet none of these things was distinctive of the persons mentioned, since that collection of properties was never in another in the same way. That is, the property arising from such a collection of their properties and of any similar properties is considered a distinctive property; no two or more individuals can be marked by it. Yet each element of this collection may, according to species or genus, belong to others besides those mentioned—for example, being a philosopher, an Athenian, bald, and the like.

The three distinctive properties of the three persons, however, are fatherhood, begottenness, and procession.

[Col. 0342B]

Therefore, since each marks only one person, each is considered with respect to only one. It should be observed, however, that in the three persons quality is considered in two ways: substantially and according to the properties by which they are distinguished. This pertains to quality and is proper to quality, as has been explained.

Therefore I do not think it should be granted that the distinctive property is the person which it distinguishes and around which it exists, as a character exists around a substance according to which the person has constitution. Nevertheless, such a property is always conjoined with the person, having with it an immutable subsistence.

Thus the individual persons have singular properties and certain others common to one or two persons.

[Col. 0342C]

From these considerations, as the foregoing makes clear, no quality distinguishes the Spirit from the Son more than from the Father.

> **[Note: [Col. 0341D] Read cautiously, for true theology teaches that personal properties are in reality identical with the persons, [Col. 0342D] but are distinguished only in reason; and perhaps this is what Etherianus intended to suggest.]**

# CHAPTER III
Moreover, relation does not divide and distinguish the Spirit from communion with the Son any more than from communion with the Father. For relation is also the communion of things differing from one another, as harmony of sounds, proportion of minds, and the union of soul and body. And it is characteristic of relation to gather difference into communion. But “relative” looks toward another and does not subsist in itself. Its form indeed is to be said in reference to another; and that to which it is said likewise adds what is said of itself—the consequence of those things which are relative [Col. 0342D]. But things that subsist are not said relative to one another; thus light is of the sun, but is not said to be “toward” the sun. For it is one thing to be someone’s measure, action, passion, possession, or property, and another to be, or to be said, relative to something. For the former, although they are of another, seem to possess a proper nature. But what is relative has its being in looking toward another, because it undergoes a certain reciprocal conversion toward its correlate. Certain persons do not think this should be admitted concerning the Holy Spirit: although he is of the Father and of the Son, nevertheless the Father or Son is not reciprocally referred to the Spirit. For neither is the Father or the Son the Father or Son of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0343A], who is called the gift of both; and he is adorned with the equal honors belonging to each donor. For he is heavenly, fills the world, and, being the gift of life and power, through this gift the Son reconciled all things to God and the Father. By this gift, the soul that has not been salted decays and is defiled by foul thoughts; strengthened by this gift, the apostles traversed the whole world, preaching the commands of their Teacher, sanctified by the Father and the Son, as the Savior says: “For their sakes I sanctify myself, that they also may be holy in truth” (John 17). Although he asks the Father to sanctify them, Christ himself sanctified himself for the apostles and the other faithful when he was offered as a sacrifice for the world, and when all humanity, as first-fruits, was sanctified in him through the cross. The Father also [Col. 0343B], receiving the sacrifice, sanctified the world, through whom, having been renewed, we are called sons of God.

But the Holy Spirit too is true sanctification, by which the faithful through him become one—he who has received, as it were, the proper designation and distinctive character, namely “holy.” Yet, as the nature of the Spirit is holy, so by nature the Father is holy, and by nature the Son is holy. Therefore Isaiah describes the Seraphim as crying “Holy” three times, because in the three persons the signification is considered according to nature (Isa. 6). Nor does he share with the Father and Son only this name of sanctification; he also shares the very designation “Spirit,” whose plurality of senses must briefly be distinguished here.

“Spirit” is certainly said in many ways. For God is Spirit, and “those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4); and the prophet says: “Christ the Lord, a spirit before your face.” “Spirit,” and “Holy Spirit,” occur as in: “Go, baptizing in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). Angels are called spirits, as it is written: “He makes his angels spirits” (Heb. 1). The gifts of the Spirit and of the Holy Spirit are also so called; these the prophet called operations. [Note: [Col. 0343D] Didymus says the same concerning the Holy Spirit.]

Again, his grace is sometimes called fire and sometimes water: water, indeed, as in: “Whoever drinks of this water which I shall give him, there shall come to be in him a fountain of living water unto eternal life” (John 4); and again: “From his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (John 7). It is called fire, however, as in [Col. 0343D]: “He himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Mark 1). “Spirit” is again used for living spiritually and conducting oneself according to God. “For whoever,” he says, “lives in the Spirit of God”—that is, spiritually. Scripture also knows how to call wind “spirit,” and likewise that which distinguishes the letter, as in: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3). Again, “spirit” is said by which the adoption of sons is distinguished, as in: “For you have not received the spirit of slavery” (Rom. 8). “Spirit” also means a notable disposition, as Isaiah says (Isa. 29): “Those who err in spirit shall be known.” “Spirit” is also called vital power, according to Ecclesiasticus (3): “Who knows the spirit of the sons of men, whether it goes upward, and the spirit of beasts, whether it goes down to the earth?” “Spirit” also denotes the human soul: “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Ps. 30).

It is therefore clear from what has been said that not only the Father and the Son, and the Spirit, who is the gift of both, are called “Spirit”; many other things are designated by the same name. Thus, wherever “Spirit” is said, God is not thereby shown; nor, conversely, wherever “Paraclete” occurs is the Spirit necessarily understood—although this too is his name, by which he is especially known. For, to omit other instances, Christ, who is the wisdom of God, is called Paraclete, yet he is not that third person who is called the Holy Spirit. But perhaps someone will ask: since the Father is called Spirit, the Son Spirit, and the Holy Spirit Spirit [Col. 0344B], how can a difference from the Father and the Son be marked according to this designation? The answer is that, although the Father is Spirit and holy, he neither is nor is called anyone’s spirit. Likewise, although the Son is Spirit and holy, he is by no means called anyone’s spirit, because this designation, so received, signifies the nature of divinity itself. But the Holy Spirit both is and is called someone’s Spirit: for he is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son. The Apostle testifies when he says: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts” (Gal. 4). Indeed, he is the gift of the Father and the Son, in which name relation seems to be signified.

For things which are relative are assigned this sort of property and relation, since to be relative is to have a relation toward another, from which relative things have the capacity of existing no less in things external than in themselves [Col. 0344C]. Certainly, when external things change, those things come to be and perish; but that which is said to be in itself is not relative, as a man three cubits high. [Note: [Col. 0344D] Something is missing here.] Although these are said of another, they nevertheless are what they are in themselves. For although “man” is said of another, it is said not only in respect of what he is—a man—but also in respect of his being a son or father, or something of that kind. Relatives are sometimes expressed through the accusative case, and otherwise, as “great in relation to small”; and sometimes by “from someone,” as a gift from a giver. This seems suitable to the Holy Spirit: that he is said to be another’s and, according to such a relation [Col. 0344D], is relative. For he is the gift of the Father and the Son, and riches knowing no lack because they have no limit; he distributes the gifts of both, which, as some think, both give from eternity—the receptacle of all good gifts.

For they say that, although before every creature there were no persons to be enriched by such gifts and to render service in response to these bestowals, the Spirit was nevertheless a perfect gift, with no one sharing in him; otherwise something added and accidental would have accrued to the divine. In the same way, the Lord was Lord before he was served, and Creator before he created anything. If this does not stand, it follows that creating and ruling came to him accidentally and not by nature [Col. 0345A], that they were recently added and superinduced rather than coeternal. Again, they say, if before creatures he was not Lord, Creator, and gift, then creatures were made in vain to provide him with a reason for ruling and giving, promoting him into being for themselves Lord, Creator, and gift. Therefore, if creation should withdraw its foot backward, the Spirit will be stripped of gift and lordship. It is therefore plain that from eternity he possesses the principles of such relations. From this it is evident that the Holy Spirit has some relation to the Son.

Indeed, relation seems to run through all the categories, even through opposites: through substance, as in Father and Son; through quantity, as in double and half; through quality, as in instruction and the instructed; place, as in [Col. 0345B] above and below; time, as in earlier and later; action, cutting; passion, being cut; position, lying, being placed before, being placed beneath; possession, as in footwear. If these did not adhere to things, all things would be torn apart from one another. Through relations, then, difference and number appeared in the divine hypostases. How this is so must briefly be recalled, since it concerns the discussion.

## Chapter IV

The faith of Christians holds as indubitable and firm that God is born from God, light from light; and that God proceeds from God: one is he from whom another is born, another he who is born from someone, and another he who proceeds from someone. The Father indicates God from whom another is born; the Son [Col. 0345C] signifies God who is born from someone; and the Holy Spirit, because he is not stated absolutely but as the Spirit of the Father and the Son, is shown to proceed from persons. Therefore the three are distinct from one another. For the Father is neither Son nor Spirit; nor is the Son Father or Spirit; nor can the Spirit be those whose Spirit he is. For it is impossible that what exists from another should be that from which it exists, or that that from which something exists should be what proceeds from itself. These are indeed relations from which plural number arises and the holy Trinity is shown; yet, because Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, unity is understood. Therefore unity is in the Trinity, and Trinity in unity. But unity [Col. 0345D] is attributed to nature, while Trinity belongs to persons, not to nature. Natural unity does not arise because there is a hypostatic Trinity, nor again does hypostatic Trinity arise because there is natural unity.

Accordingly, some object: “If the unity of nature is one thing and the Trinity of persons another, four realities are found in the Godhead: namely, Trinity and Unity.” [Note: [Col. 0345D] Ambrose said similarly in the *Hexaemeron*: “Things are counted together which are not compared, because neither things eternal, consubstantial, coequal, nor anything of this kind falls under comparison with respect to its parts.” [Col. 0346D]] The answer is sufficiently clear: no person forms a number with the nature which that person possesses. Thus we do not count Christ and his human nature as two things, professing that he himself and the human nature which he has are two realities. Moreover [Col. 0346A], nothing which completes another—whether genus, difference, nature, substance, or something determining and constituting a person—forms a number with the thing constituted. Therefore, since the Godhead is the nature of the three persons, it is not counted together with them so that four realities may be declared: the unity of nature, namely, and the Trinity of persons. Nevertheless it is truly believed and said that the nature of the Father is not the Father, since no person is a nature, neither that person’s own nor another’s.

In this matter they use the following analogy. They say: “Someone who says, ‘I weighed a coin,’ indicates that he weighed gold by the pound. And someone who says, ‘I weighed gold,’ affirms that he weighed a gold coin. For the coin’s stamp [Col. 0346B], once it has expressed the weight, is not itself weighed.” Thus, they say, when we state that the Son is born from the substance of the Father, we are not compelled to confess that he arises from two things, but from one and the same begetter. That the Son is born from the Father’s substance is manifest: either he is born from the Father’s substance, or from something external. If he is born externally, the Son is not of the same nature as the Father, but is sanctified by participation in another—which it is profane even to think. But if the Son flows forth from the whole substance of the Father, and the Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and Son, then either division, partition, or passion must occur in the Father’s substance, or else the Spirit must be of the substance of the Father and Son impassibly and indivisibly. For the substance of the Father is indivisible [Col. 0346C], and the Son, whose Spirit he is, fills it wholly. It is therefore clear that only relations prevent the Son from being the Father and the Spirit from being the Son. For no understanding can conceive that what flows from something is that from which it flows, lest it perhaps be found prior to itself. Yet the consequence of the unity of the divine nature seems to require the Father to be the Son and the Son the Father, since these three are one God; but, as has been set forth, the intervention of relations prevents this. For the Father, being from none, cannot be the one who flows from him. The Father is without beginning and unbegotten; but the Son and the Holy Spirit exist from the Father’s substance in different ways. For the Son is from God, who is his Father. But the Holy Spirit [Col. 0346D] is not from God as his Father, but from God who is Father. Therefore the Son, insofar as he is from God, is deemed the Son of God; and he from whom he is, is called his Father. But the Spirit is not from someone as from a father, but as from a cause.

Certainly, it is proper to the Son alone to be from someone, namely, from his Father. It is clear that in the holy and most blessed Trinity the Father is Father of only one Son, just as the Son is Son of only one Father, and the Spirit—so that the Trinity may be preserved—is Spirit of only one Father and one Son. For as there is one God alone, so there is one Father alone, one Son alone, and one Holy Spirit [Col. 0347A], who is equally and without distinction the Spirit of the Father and the Son. Since these things are so, if the Son is from eternity the giver and sender of the Holy Spirit, and the Spirit is eternally the gift and image of the Son, it is clear that relation does not divide him from communion with the Son any more than from communion with the Father. As the preceding discussion shows, relation is the communion of things in some manner differing from one another. Where there is no difference, there is no relation; and where there is relation, there must necessarily be some kind of difference. Hence nothing can proceed from another unless a relation in some manner relative intervenes. For this is what joins, making the agent connected with the patient through some affinity, so that one can act upon the other and the other suffer from it. Therefore there are many kinds [Col. 0347B] of human relations, as of other things: for example, that of father to son immediately, but of a son’s son mediately, and so onward to the seventh degree. Some of these relations perish along with their subjects; others disappear while their subjects remain without any change at all. From this it is sufficiently evident that things which are relative are not according to participation. For, as some think, relatives neither participate in one another nor are predicated of one another. Hence “what is placed” and “position,” “standing” and “station,” “sitting” and “session,” and all such things are not relatives. For what lies participates in position, and one sitting participates in sitting; but relatives do not participate in one another, because they are opposites. Nor does God the Father [Col. 0347C] participate in his Son, nor is he predicated of him. For the Father is always Father and not Son; while the Son is always Son and not Father.

But when the Father is called the Father of God’s Son, this must not be understood absolutely, but as Father of the ages and of creatures. For since he is our Creator, he is called our Father through creation, not by nature as God is the Father of his Son. Nevertheless, he inseparably possesses the fact that he is our Father, just as the Spirit possesses being a gift and being given to us, as was discussed above. For nothing foreign can happen to him which has not always been about him. Certainly before the ages he was the almighty Creator and Lord, possessing without relation all the principles of those things which are seen as pertaining to him.

Since these relations are about the substance [Col. 0347D], they are by no means substance itself, yet they do not arise from external things. Likewise, those things which complete the divine substance derive nothing from things intrinsic, but are understood to be present through themselves, apart from every such relation. From this some argue as follows: if the divine is perfectly complete in itself without any defect, it has no relation to things external to it. For if it had acquired relation from things made and created, its power would have been needy, and it would seem to have received the power of creating through an external relation. But the divine is self-sufficient and complete in itself without anything external. For it is impious to attribute to God something added, as belongs to those who in turn acquire abundance from deficiency [Col. 0348A]. God does not come to know things only after they exist, because before the origin of the world he foreknew what would occur in the final times. Therefore, before he made the earth and the ages, he had in himself, as he has now and not otherwise after things had been made and created, the principles of those things concerning us. Paul indicates this to Timothy when he says: “Share in the sufferings of the Gospel according to the power of God, who saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given to us before eternal times, but has now been manifested through the illumination of our Savior Jesus Christ” (2 Tim. 1). If before the ages, when we did not yet exist, he called us according to the purpose of God who foreknows all things, it is certain that before anyone was called God existed as caller, before there was creation he existed as Creator, and before the Spirit was given he was the gift of Father and Son, having no relation to those who would receive him [Col. 0348B].

The prophet David, speaking to God, says: “Be for me a protecting God” (Ps. 30), and again: “The Lord became a refuge for the poor” (Ps. 9). Yet he was always protector and refuge. Therefore what he was, he also became to the one asking and entreating. From eternity he was king because he was God; he became Lord of the creature, receiving no relation and no alteration when creation came forth into actuality. For if humanity is not changed when its individual members continually perish and others succeed them, but remains unchangeable and unaltered, preserving its proper account, much more must the relations concerning divine persons, though considered in many distinct and distant instances [Col. 0348C], remain unalterable beyond comparison. It is therefore unfitting and impious to say that anything happens to the divine persons, who are immutable, on account of things which come to be; and likewise to destroy the eternal grounds of the mutual relation between the Spirit and the Son, who differ from one another. It is therefore manifest that the relation which the Spirit has to the Father, he has to the Son; and nothing belonging to relatives prevents him from being the Son’s Spirit and the same Spirit from the Son.

## Chapter V

But the sending forth of the Spirit from the Father cannot prevent the Spirit’s proceeding from the Son, since the Father sends forth the Spirit through the same Son, not as through an instrument, with no intervening medium understood. Therefore both the Father and the Son are cause of the Spirit. For the Holy Spirit is in the Son as in a cause—what is from a cause—not as in a place or a subject. For a place differs substantially from what is in a place, and likewise a subject from what is in a subject. But the Spirit, subsisting in the Son by the account of cause, as also in the Father, is the same in each. Therefore, as what is from a cause is in its cause, it is established that the Spirit is inseparably in and of both—the Father, namely, and the Son [Col. 0349A].

Moreover, whenever two things are understood as indivisible according to nature and without any intermediate, whoever bestows existence on one bestows it also on the other. This may be seen in vein and fountain, trunk and root, unity and the number two, and perhaps many other instances. But Father and Son are two persons, and according to nature are understood entirely without a medium; therefore each gives existence to the Spirit. Thus, as it is true that he is the Spirit of the Son, so it is manifest that he proceeds from the Son and has him as cause. But since it is now clear that sending forth does not prevent the Son from sending the Spirit together with the Father, it seems likewise necessary to show that neither acting nor being acted upon divides the Father’s causality from communion with the Son. This will become much clearer if we briefly recall what philosophers have established “to act,” “to be acted upon,” and “action” to be. This may perhaps be useful for clarifying what follows.

To act, then, as they say, is according to nature to bring something into passion; or to act is to assimilate to oneself what undergoes action, while to suffer is to be assimilated to the agent. They clarify this by examples. The agent, they say, assimilates the patient to itself, as fire acting upon water assimilates it to itself in heat. Behold: although water is potentially hot, it is actually cold; fire, by approaching and touching what is potentially hot and capable of suffering, changes it from what it was potentially into what is called actual. For what is changed from potency into what it was capable of becomes actual, whether it be form, passion, or rest; as bronze, proceeding from potency to actuality, becomes a statue, perfected by form [Col. 0349C]. For the active must touch the passive either immediately or through a medium, as a person is warmed in baths through a medium: fire heats the air, and air heats the person.

But, they say, it must be noted that contact is properly said to occur only among things moved and moving in relation to one another. For neither an image nor abuse principally touches the soul, since they suffer nothing in return from it; they are wholly dissimilar and different, and are not fit to act reciprocally upon one another or to suffer reciprocally. Thus sweetness does nothing to blackness, nor heaviness to sweetness. Therefore they say: if acting is changing something according to quality, while God is the creator of every substance, it is clear that he should not properly be called an agent [Col. 0349D], but Creator and producer of the universe. For agents are found only among natural and artificial things; but God, since he is beyond all invisible and visible things, ought not to be called an agent. For an agent brings about what is to be done through a certain process and generation; but God does nothing in time. Therefore, they say, he ought to be considered not an agent but Creator.

Moreover, if acting is assimilating to oneself what suffers according to some quality, God is not properly the maker of the world, since he has no relation whatsoever to the world or to any creature. Yet, as it seems to certain sectarians, it must not simply be granted that an agent is accompanied by something acted upon. For acting includes roaring, running, walking, writing, and other things of this sort, none of which assimilates a patient to itself. Therefore, since the Father is without cause and without beginning, and cannot be more perfect or more powerful than the one he begets—for equal is the power of two which can produce both lesser and greater things equally—therefore the Father is not the exhibitor of more things than the Son. But whatever the one who is without cause displays, the one who is from a cause also displays, immediately; and since the one without cause does not produce before the one who is from a cause, but Father and Son are simultaneous, it is evident that there is no separation between Father and Son in the causality of the Spirit on account of acting and being acted upon [Col. 0350A]. For whichever one of the two should individually send forth the Spirit would undoubtedly be more powerful than the other, as a cause more comprehensive, greater, and containing more.

Therefore, since the Father sends forth the Spirit, and the Son is the image of the Father, not **παρακεχαραγμένα** (“counterfeit” or “altered”), preserving the whole circumference intact, it follows that whatever belongs to the Father necessarily belongs to the Son. For every image that is not **παρακεχαραγμένα** always has its whole circumference in conformity with its archetype. This would be proved false if the Spirit proceeded from the Father without the Son sharing in that procession. Yet nothing of the Father is prior to the Son, nor does the Father produce anything without the Son, because the Son of God is not the Father’s Son by adoption but is truly begotten from his substance; he himself is maker and creator of those who are sons by participation in God and in the Son.

[Col. 0350C] Hence it is evident that, since the Son is the most perfect seal, preserving every correspondence with the Father, he sends forth the Spirit from himself as the Father does. Whoever opposes this doctrine seems to fear an argument devised by heresiarchs and inventors of profane novelties, who construct arguments in this manner—or rather, ignorances of refutations: if the Spirit is from the Son, who possesses authority over all things heavenly and earthly, then those who ask anything from the Father or Spirit in worship act wrongly and contrary to the Father’s will. For all things belonging to the Son were given by the Father, whose gifts are without repentance and unchangeable. Thus [the argument] excludes the Father and the Spirit from authority over all that the Father delivered, including judgment and the sending of the Spirit. Therefore [Col. 0350D] those who ask anything from the Father or Spirit in prayer sin, since the Son possesses the Spirit himself and authority over all things. But there is nothing to fear in this, because nothing is taken away from the Father by what is attributed to the Son. For all things of the Son are the Father’s. As light is inseparable from the sun, so one is inseparable from the other; yet the three persons equally preside over all creatures, each of which is irradiated by their presence according to its own order and capacity: this eternally, that temporally; this incorporeally, that bodily—each bearing a property from its proximate and kindred cause, according to which it receives existence from it.

## Chapter VI

[Col. 0351A]

Further, it must be known that wherever a given substance is present, its action is also present, but not wherever an action is present is its substance present. For the illuminating action of the sun is diffused in air and in other transparent things without the solar substance being present in them. But in the case of the supreme and divine substance, the converse is true. For where the divine substance is, there is also its action; and where its action is, there is the substance itself, which is everywhere at once and nowhere. It is not in part everywhere and in part nowhere, for thus it would be divided and separated from itself: if one part of it were everywhere and in all things, and another nowhere and before all things. Rather, it is wholly everywhere and wholly nowhere. Therefore where God’s action is, God is also present, offering himself only as much as each can receive [Col. 0351B]—not as having parts, but as existing before all things. For, though God is one, the three persons are the unchangeable and unimpeded cause of all things, before all things filled by him, governing the world by their most abundant bestowals and actions.

But when discourse is undertaken concerning action, it must not escape memory that, just as the divine substance, fatherhood, sonship, sending, and the other things in God and about God are understood as above substance, fatherhood, sonship, and sending, so God’s action must be understood as above action. For although the things considered in the three persons and about the three persons are named by the terms of the categories, no divine reality belongs to the categories. Yet some, wishing to show that acting separates the Son from the causality of the Spirit, employ arguments of this kind. If acting in the divine, as in certain creatures, is twofold—one kind according to will, as creating, writing, and the other acts belonging to artisans; the other according to nature, as begetting, and fire’s burning—then the Father, in acting according to will, is inseparable from the Son and Spirit. But in acting according to the consequence of nature he is separable: he alone, in the very being by which he is distinguished from the Son, sends forth the Spirit [Col. 0351C]. Thus the Son does not send him forth; and concerning the Spirit, it is obvious that he cannot send himself forth, because nothing can proceed or come to be from itself.

But they maintain that being acted upon in no way prevents procession from the Son, though it is said in two ways: as being cut or burned, and in a perfective sense, as learning or reading. For God suffers nothing either through corruption or through perfection, since he is incorruptible and sufficient for himself and for all creatures. Therefore these persons say that God the Father alone begets and sends forth, just as matter alone suffers; through matter, other things too participate in passion. They think that the elements act and suffer as participating in form and matter, as do almost all composite things. Thus lead, by acting upon silver, suffers and is corrupted while it purifies it. It acts when it purifies; it suffers when it is consumed by fire. Therefore, they say, the Father acts by nature and by will: by nature, in acting he begets the Son and sends forth [Col. 0352A] the Spirit; by will, in acting he creates the world and preserves it once created. Therefore he begets and sends forth one equal and coeternal with himself, because he begets being and sends forth being; but he neither creates nor preserves being. For neither does an artisan, by his own being, accomplish the things on account of which he is called an artisan: he often contemplates in himself what he does not produce in a work, from which the work that he makes is far removed, just as all corruptible things are far from the divine nature.

Again, they say: if God produced being, all things would have emerged together with him, and both past and future things would have met together—which nature in no way allows. But God’s generation is one thing, and the production of things that are not is another; they cannot coexist, because God produced them from non-being, but by will. For if he had produced being, as many things would have emerged as he could have brought forth; since he would make with his whole being, he would make with his whole power. And since that power is infinite, he could have made not only this world but infinitely many worlds like the present one. But if he could not, by what great weakness would he be oppressed, when any art of an artisan can make very many similar things? Therefore, they say, just as God the Father alone by his being begets, so he alone by his being sends forth; but he neither begets nor sends forth by will. They demonstrate this as follows: if God had begotten the Son by will and not by nature, then either, once he had willed it, he would thereafter have remained unwilling; or he would have willed again and begotten again. And if he is not of one will but of differing wills, he has not only one [Col. 0352C] Son, but several sons.

Moreover: If God does whatever he wills, then, if he does not beget, he refrains altogether either because he cannot or because he will not. If he cannot, his nature is inferior to that of a corruptible thing, which is capable of incapacity. But if, though able, he did not will what he possessed by nature, he restrained it by his will. Therefore, if he has not yet begotten, he will at some time beget because he wills it. Again: if he begot by will, the will is prior to the generation, as in creatures, according to the words, “Let us make man” (Gen. I), and, “He did whatsoever he willed”; or else the Son is the power, wisdom, and counsel of the Father, in whom he abides and through whom he works all things. For this reason he was not begotten by will; nor yet by necessity, as though the Father begot unwillingly and under compulsion, there being no one able to compel him. [Col. 0352D]

The same, they say, must be thought concerning the Spirit. Hence it is clear that, just as the Father alone begets by his very being, so he alone sends forth by his very being—by nature, not by will—which is evident also from the fact that he sends forth the Spirit coeternal and coequal with himself. Yet this question, as it seems to me, has the light of its solution from what precedes, where it has been shown that the Father sends forth the Spirit not insofar as he is Father. Such an inference indeed holds true only in those properties which distinguish the persons; for in these it is proper to speak of antecedence and consequence, as: if he alone begets by his very being, he alone begets; and if he alone is begotten, he is begotten by his very being. But not so in other matters, as may be observed from many instances. The Father knows his Spirit—not by will, that is, the same Spirit insofar as he is a person. Therefore the Father alone knows the Spirit. [Col. 0353A]

Likewise, the Father has the Spirit by his very being, not by will. Therefore the Father alone has the Spirit. But the Apostle has clearly taught that this is false. For there is one cause and one principle, Father and Son, whose Spirit is the Holy Spirit; and therefore he proceeds not from the being of one alone but from both, being equal and coequal with each. For the Father is not more magnificent than the Son or the Spirit, as a man is among living creatures, because he can produce things greater than they. Thus he does not send forth the Spirit without the Son.

Nevertheless, one must not suppose that the Spirit derives some principle from the Father or the Son as though posterior to them; for the Spirit is younger or more recent than neither. Although in many cases what proceeds from certain things seems to be posterior to them, in a few cases it is understood to be simultaneous—as the radiance proceeding from the sun is not posterior to the sun itself. In the same way are Father and Son: the Father did not precede the Son either by much or by little, nor did the Son precede the Spirit. For the Prophet says, “Before me no God was formed, and after me there shall be none.” But God is neither made nor has anything more ancient than himself. “I,” he says, “am the first, and I am the last” (Rev. I). This must be confessed of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Of these three persons Jeremiah says, “May the gods that did not make heaven and earth perish” (Jer. X); yet elsewhere it is written, “I stretched out heaven with my hand” (Prov. XXIV), in which the three persons are to be understood. For David says, “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their host” (Ps. XXXII). [Col. 0353B]

Behold: he shows the Spirit and the Son to be creators—not calling the Son a bare word, nor the Spirit a vapor diffused through the air—when he says that heaven was established by the Word and its host sanctified by the power of the Holy Spirit. For, as the holy Fathers testify, the Word bestowed being, while the Spirit bestowed holiness. From this it is plainly apparent that the Spirit has no principle before himself, although he proceeds from the Father and the Son. For what is infinite must in either case be infinite, as Paul testifies in saying, “He has neither beginning of days nor end of life.” Therefore, because the divine, superessential being, existing before all things, knows neither beginning nor end, it is impossible to say what it is according to substance. For we can scarcely and faintly apprehend anything of those things which concern [Col. 0353D] it, because its wisdom is exalted above our understanding—which, though it concerns divisible and changeable things, is itself divided. For the indivisible unity is not altered, because it is immutable; nor is it multiplied by relation, because it remains unmixed.

## CHAPTER VII

It remains, therefore, that God is made manifest to human beings only through actions. According to the opinion of some, these actions do not have what is called potentiality, since they assert that at each moment of time they arise suddenly, and that God makes all things by the concurrence of will, not by motion. For motion is not a sudden issuing forth from a state; rather, one advance toward form takes place before another. It exists only potentially, in the making of a thing, considered according to its material and unformed property through transition in divisible continuity. But God’s action is especially complete in itself, with an unfailing consummation of itself and its end. What has been completely consummated has nothing in common with what is going to be consummated by one who hastens.

Accordingly, they maintain that God works without motion and suddenly—that is, apart from temporal extension. As illustrations of this operation, they propose mind, sense perception, and the emission of light. For when light appears, it suddenly illuminates the circuit of the earth; the motion of time does not accompany the action of light, which diffuses itself equally in every direction. The action or operation of the senses appears almost to be of this kind. At the same instant in seeing, without an interval of time, sight equally comprehends visible things, whether present [Col. 0354B] or absent.

Hence some say that action is a sudden emission from a state, which the motion of time does not follow: for example, the extension of heavenly bodies—the sun and other things shining without end—or natural actions such as heating and cooling. Artificial operations, however, such as healing and constructing, are followed by time. Yet although mind and sense know and perceive without temporal extension, they do not attain consummation without temporal extension. God, however, without temporal extension accomplishes and completes whatever work of his he wills. This is plainly evident from the miracles performed by Christ: “Take up your pallet and walk” (John V). “He spoke the word, and the boy was healed” (Matt. VIII). Again: “Stretch out your hand,” and, “Your sins are forgiven you”; “Let it be done to you as you will” (Matt. XII).

The Savior performed these and similar things in the twinkling of an eye; his power and authority accomplish all things without any distinction or delay of time. This the Father does through himself; this the Son does, as the Father possesses it; and this the Holy Spirit possesses substantially. For just as a stone released is not moved downward by the one releasing it—he merely released it—but the natural impetus which it possesses carries the stone downward; and just as fire cast downward is carried back upward by the nature it possesses within, so the three persons possess equally the capacity to make or work, not from external things but from the intrinsic power which they naturally encompass. [Col. 0354D]

For although they act according to nature and will, their power is not like that of lower things, in which one power is natural and another added. Natural power is always present: as burning belongs to fire and shining to the sun. Likewise, when the external force ceases, a released stone naturally moves downward. Added power, however, comes from outside and may be absent; the effect of such power is reckoned an action. This power is sometimes called a cause and sometimes causative. It is the effect of the substance from which it proceeds, but the cause of the action which it sends forth. Yet the Father’s power is itself a cause and is from a cause: for it is begotten and sends forth, and has acquired nothing adventitious.

Nor does the statement written, “The Son can do nothing of himself” (John V), conflict with this teaching. For if whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does, and the Son cannot do anything from himself, it follows that neither can the Father do anything from himself. Therefore, if the Son cannot do anything from himself, neither can the Father; for the Father does not do one thing and the Son imitate it by contemplating it. Since he who worked through himself, having the Spirit in the midst of the earth, is the best and greatest of all good things, it follows that he can do all things as does the Father. Yet he cannot do anything from himself, in that he displays no power contrary or alien to the Father.

He makes his authority clear when he says: “I have power to lay down my life, and to take it up again. No one shall take it from me” (John X). “I have power over life and death, as does the Father. Therefore whom I will, I make alive and enlighten, giving them the spirit of life; and whom I will, I put to death and leave in darkness, taking away that same spirit.” Thus there is no contradiction between being unable to do anything from oneself and being one who does whatever he wills: “wills” signifies power, whereas inability to act from oneself would signify subjection.

For the Son possesses the immutability of power, equality of authority, communion of the Spirit, and everything which the Father has except the individual property. Indeed, he is giver of the Spirit as is the Father. Yet the converse does not hold: the Paraclete is not giver to the Son. He brings about remission of sins through the Spirit—which would not occur unless the Spirit were sent by the Son; and his shining forth from the Son, as from the Father, belongs to procession. Since God is everywhere present, this is said in order that we may understand and believe the Son to be a cause of the Holy Spirit. Their identity is divided by a few distinctions: namely, that one is Son and the other Spirit. This alone introduces division; everything else is equal and immutable. Therefore it is clear that neither doing, nor suffering, nor action divides the Son from the Father in the sending forth of the Spirit. [Col. 0355C]

## CHAPTER VIII

As for “where” and “when,” it is plain that they do not divide the Son from the Father in sending forth the Spirit. For “where” and “when” indicate place and time. But neither where nor when applies, because place is naturally prior to that which is in a place; similarly, time is naturally prior to that which is in time, since place and time preexist by nature. Then, when something else comes to be in them, that which is in a place is said to be “where,” and that which is in time is said to be “when.” But before God there is nothing: for he made all ages and every expanse. Therefore God is above times, ages, numbers, and all things. Indeed, if an age had been more ancient than he, God would not have made the ages.

In the simple name “God,” the three persons are understood: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The Seraphim testify to this by glorifying him with three sanctities, while converging upon one dominion and Godhead. Certainly God exists before not only time and place, but also angels, archangels, cherubim, seraphim, and every power; and he is so far beyond them that they cannot know God’s substance. [Col. 0356A] Hence they render God nothing but glory and peace to people of good will, while they sing only his holiness and that heaven and earth are full of his glory. The work of all the higher powers is also the praise of God: “Praise him,” he says, “all his powers” (Ps. CXLVIII).

For this reason he alone sees himself, no creature being able to see him; and man even less than the heavenly rational substances, as Paul declares: “No human being has seen him, nor can see him.” For not even the visible powers fully contemplate him as he is, although the Savior himself says, “Amen, I say to you: their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (I Tim. VI). Yet he has no local position and is not circumscribed in heaven. Thus the saying found elsewhere in the Gospel must be understood in this sense: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V)—that is, with the eye of understanding, insofar as they are able. This is how angels are believed to see him: having a pure and ever-watchful nature, they conceive the divine insofar as it is possible for them. But no one has ever seen the divine substance as the creator of all things and as existing before all ages. It is therefore clear that neither “where” nor “when” prevents the Son from sending forth the Spirit with the Father. [Col. 0356B]

## CHAPTER IX

That being situated belongs to bodies—since it pertains to the limits of magnitudes, surfaces, lines, and the like—is plainly in no way fitting for the divine persons. For as relation to place produces “where,” and relation to time produces “when,” so relation to position produces being situated. Things established in life, powers, and primary causes are said improperly to be situated. To be situated and to have position, according to place, are accidents of the things previously mentioned and similar things, except for the body which contains the universe wholly without motion (*aplanknōs*, ἀπλκνεῶς; reading uncertain). But being situated does not belong to incorporeal substances except metaphorically; one may say that all things are situated in God, as in a cause and principle. Since this is so, we must now proceed in the established order to examine whether the asserted community of cause divides or impedes them.

## CHAPTER X

“Having” has many meanings, as Aristotle has taught in the *Categories*. It is predicated of body and of incorporeal things. Of body, it is said because of things particularly situated around a body, such as a ring around a finger; and of things surrounding the whole body, such as clothing and household implements, for example weapons. Some of these, such as a breastplate, we have voluntarily; others against our will, such as our chains. For bodies, being divisible, encompass things adhering externally. Heaven, however, because it leaves nothing outside itself, encloses and surrounds within itself what adheres to it on every side.

“Having” is also said of incorporeal things, as of the soul, on account of prudence, wisdom, and similar qualities. It is also said of that which consists of soul and body because of certain incorporeal features: quantity, as being two cubits or three cubits; and quality, as being white, black, and the like. Indeed, in its own manner “having” is said of two divine persons in relation to the third. For it is truly said that both Father and Son have the Holy Spirit. If the Son did not have the Father’s Spirit, the person having him would be more worthy, while the person of the Son did not contain him. For every essence with the Spirit is more worthy and more powerful than that which does not have the Spirit; certainly animals are more worthy and greater than plants, seeds, and herbs, because, having spirit, they can act. But the person of the Father undoubtedly has the Spirit, while the person of the Son does not have him. Therefore the person of the Father is more worthy than that of the Son. Christian profession rejects this as profane. [Col. 0357B]

Therefore it must without ambiguity be granted that the Son has the Spirit as the Father does. Although John testifies that he saw the Spirit descending and remaining upon him (Mark I), Christ as God must not be believed to have the Spirit as something newly added. He has him as man, as some show by arguing thus: if the Holy Spirit promises to dwell in the souls of people living piously and religiously, though not wholly free from stain, much more did the same Spirit dwell in Christ’s soul, which was inviolate and immaculate, always existing without stain and having no trace whatever of sin. The Prophet foretold this when he said: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV). We are Christ’s brothers and companions according to humanity; the oil signifies the Spirit. Christ was anointed not as God but as man. For he is not anointed as Son of God, but Christ’s flesh was anointed with true anointing—namely, by the coming of the Holy Spirit at the very conception of the Son of Man. And he was anointed above his companions because to them a certain partial outflow of the Holy Spirit was granted insofar as they were able to receive it.

For the grace of the Holy Spirit seems to be distributed among human beings after the likeness of the human spirit, just as that spirit, descending from the brain through the sensory nerves, is distributed not to all limbs alike but in proportion to each one’s capacity to receive. [Col. 0357D] To one more capable of receiving, it pours in more; to one less capable, less. Thus the distribution of gifts is made according to the proportion of each soul.

But the Son of God has not according to proportion; the Father has the whole Spirit, and the Son has the whole Spirit—the same Spirit. For the Spirit of the Father is not one and that of the Son another; he is the same, and is possessed by both in the same manner. “For in Christ the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily” (Col. II), that is, perfectly. From this it is again shown that the Son of God has always had the Spirit. For if God the Word, in uniting animated flesh—possessing a rational, intelligible soul—to himself according to person, received the Spirit at the incarnation, he had the firstfruits of the Spirit from the incarnation, and at the same time something capable of perfection. But if he advanced, though formerly equal to God, he became greater than the Father. Yet the Son of God did not advance, because he was never in need of anything, always having the fullness of the Spirit. David proclaimed this to the Savior in prophetic voice: “Send forth your Spirit” (Ps. CIII).

But the chief of the apostles most clearly asserts that the Son had the Spirit before the incarnation, speaking thus in his first epistle: “Christ died once for our sins, the just for the unjust, that he might offer us to God; put to death indeed in the flesh, but made alive in the Spirit” (Rom. VI). In that Spirit, namely, he came and preached also to the spirits who were in prison, who had once been unbelieving, when God’s patience waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being built. Therefore the life of the Son must not be without the Spirit, whom the Word of God possessed not only before the incarnation but before the creation of the world and of all ages. [Col. 0358B]

The great Gregory, theologian and witness to the faith of the Latin Church, must also be heard and believed in these matters, saying as follows:

> “The Holy Spirit always was, is, and will be; he neither began nor will cease, but is always coordinated and numbered together with the Father and the Son. For it was not fitting that the Son should at any time be lacking to the Father, or the Spirit to the Son.”

Behold, the holy man shows that the Spirit is proper to the Son. For if the Father alone possessed the Spirit, the *symphōnia* and *symphnia* (συμφονία and συμφνία; the second form is textually uncertain) of the two would by no means be called the same. Therefore the Son has the Spirit, but not through any advance, as a human being does. Every human being has the Spirit as one introduced from without, being in need of his gifts and benefits; so too the apostles and other saints had the Spirit as light, as grace-gift, as anointing, as a gift. But the Word of God, being altogether perfect, needs no benefit or gifts of the Spirit. For he has the Spirit not merely as man, but as the Father has him.

Therefore, since he is incomparably superior to human beings, he must have the Spirit incomparably more perfectly. The apostles, needy, imperfect, and mortal, were filled with the Holy Spirit by grace; nor did they at every time possess all the Spirit’s gifts or all his operations. For only one man—Christ, namely—was embraced by the seven women, that is, by the sevenfold grace of the Spirit. It is impossible for any creature perfectly to apprehend the Spirit. But he whom the world cannot receive is possessed inherently, from himself and by the consequence of nature, by the Father and by the Son. [Col. 0358D]

From the Son’s having the Spirit, therefore, learn not that the Spirit’s procession is from the Son. Accordingly, since there is nothing that distinguishes the procession of the Spirit from the Son—neither understanding as substance, nor quantity, nor quality, nor any other such thing—it has, I think, been made manifest and evident by the argument presented that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as from the Father. Let what has been said on these matters suffice.

## CHAPTER XI

I would now gladly make known more broadly to all ears the testimonies of the holy pastors of the Church, which proclaim that the Spirit’s existence is from the Son, were I not prevented from doing this together with the rest by a certain common opinion of all the Greeks, which must be refuted. The Greeks maintain, then, that the Spirit is called the Spirit of the Son and of the Father equivocally. Gathering this from plausible arguments, they think that many absurdities follow for those who deny it, as is evident from the conclusions they offer.

They say that many expressions in divine Scripture are uttered alike but understood differently. Thus Luke the Evangelist says: “Jesus advanced in wisdom and age, and grace with God and men” (Luke II). Certainly, if anyone says that he advanced in wisdom, it follows that he did not possess perfection of knowledge. Again, if he denies that he advanced in wisdom, neither ought he to have advanced in age. Therefore the word “advance” must be understood equivocally. For “to advance” signifies becoming great from small, and coming from imperfection to perfection; in this sense he was truly said to advance in age. Since he was little, he received bodily growth. But his advance in wisdom and grace was unlike this. For he did not become learned from ignorant, or gracious from ungracious, by advancing; rather, he is said to advance in grace and wisdom with God because day by day he appeared more gracious and wiser to people, as the action of the Holy Spirit was revealed and manifested in him each day. Therefore, although “the Word advanced” appears to be said univocally, it is pronounced equivocally. [Col. 0359C]

Likewise the name “Father” is received equivocally, as the Savior himself said after the resurrection to Mary: “I ascend to my Father and your Father” (John XX). He named his own Father and that of the disciples in the same way, but did not understand them in the same way. For Christ’s Father is Father by nature, but the disciples’ Father by adoption.

The prophet David likewise, inviting creation to glorify, says: “Praise him, all his angels, powers, dragons, and abysses” (Ps. CXLVIII). The three youths also sang: “Bless the Lord, angels of the Lord, rain, dew, and everything growing on the earth: children of men, priests, servants of the Lord” (Dan. III). Behold: he exhorts all alike to bless God in the utterance of the word, though they are understood differently. Rational creatures bless the Lord through knowledge and learning; irrational things, because they do not share in such things, bless not through themselves but through us, who, being rational, understand our own Maker while contemplating them. For the Apostle says: “His invisible things are clearly seen from the creation of the world, being understood through the things which have been made” (Rom. I). For from the wonderful ordering of created things the Creator of all creatures is declared.

Matthew also indicates that Christ was conceived of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, saying: “What is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Luke I). Yet the Holy Spirit is not Christ’s Father, because Christ is not from him as from a father, but from him who prepared the womb to be fruitful for the consubstantial Word and formed flesh without the law of intercourse, in a wholly divine and ineffable manner. Hence Christ is and is called the Son not of the Holy Spirit but of the most holy Virgin, according to nature. Such a work is attributed to the Spirit on account of holiness, and because he is causative with the Father and the Son; and many other similar points may be joined to these. [Col. 0360A]

In the same way, they say equivocally that the Spirit is the Son’s and proceeds from the Father and the Son. The bishop of Nicomedia distinguishes it thus:

> “What then shall we say? Since every expression has different meanings, and some indeed are almost infinite and known to all, they ought, in my judgment, to be passed over. But concerning the one alone that confronts us and is proposed for our inquiry, a distinction must now be made—namely, ‘to proceed.’ For this term ‘to proceed’ may signify that something moves from place to place; it may signify being sent and given; and it may signify what we profess: proceeding from a cause according to the mode of existence.”

Therefore, when Athanasius, Ambrose, or any other Father says that the Spirit proceeds from the Son or through the Son, he does not mean according to the mode of existence—far be it—but wholly according to one of the other two meanings. For just as we confess that the Spirit is manifested through the Son, so we confess that he is sent and given by him.

Another says: “Thus the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, but by no means from the Son.” Nicholas, bishop of Methone, says in this manner:

> “Although he is the Spirit of the Son, he is not from the Son. For it is one thing to be the Son’s, another to be said to be from the Son. The former, whether ‘Spirit’ or ‘proceeding,’ signifies union and affinity according to nature; the latter—that is, being from the Son—signifies production from a cause. But this is not so. Whatever is related to something according to nature thereby acquires that it is from it. For brothers are related to one another according to nature; each is called the other’s, but one is never said to be from the other, because neither is the cause of the other, but the father is the cause of both; and therefore both are from the Father alone. Thus these *kesotomoi* (κεσοτόμοι; perhaps “cutters,” reading uncertain) of dogma, whom they think to evade by refutations, are caught establishing vain speech beyond measure of malice.”

The philosopher Nicetas pours forth no less bitterness:

> “Following the perverse counsel of the devil who hates the good, *hypakolouthountes* (υπακολουθοῦντες), that is, wandering or seduced, and standing very far from the truth, they miserably attempt to decree that the most holy divine Creator, the Spirit, proceeds from the Son in the same way as from a part, not perceiving the pit that opens from this and the many profane consequences that follow.” [Col. 0360D]

## CHAPTER XII

These and other objections, whose recital is not presently necessary, are brought against the Latins by Greeks highly skilled in argument. They may perhaps contain some plausibility, but they rest upon no foundation of solidity. Anyone who sees sharply and reproves the errors of others ought certainly to introduce arguments appropriate to the matters for which he seeks credence. But the statements just given are accompanied by no demonstration: they are neither confirmed by testimonies of divinely inspired Scripture nor receive any support from the holy pastors of the Church. For this reason they are useless propositions rather than demonstrations.

All admit equivocations in divine Scripture; but that the Spirit, while equally the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, should proceed differently from each, I do not think should be granted. Yet I am led to this conclusion only with the aid of demonstration, testimonies from divinely inspired Scripture, and the ordinances of the holy Fathers. I judge that faith should be given to the side to which these most fully accord. Therefore, with the Holy Spirit’s aid, let a complete refutation in truth come forth into the open. First, the comparison taken from brothers must be rejected. [Col. 0361B]

For it is very dissimilar and altogether unfit to establish faith, for two reasons. First, the Son is not called the Spirit of the Holy Spirit, as either brother is called the other’s. Second, brothers proceed alike from the Father by generation without mediation—unless someone should perhaps say that they come forth into light through the mediation of a mother. Nevertheless, with respect to the begetter, they are rightly said to be immediate. But Son and Spirit proceed differently from God the Father and are not reciprocally converted, as has been shown above. Moreover, this is not rightly said: that the Spirit is the Son’s because he is related to him by nature and united with him.

By the same reasoning, anyone might profess the Father to be the Spirit’s because he is consubstantial with him and one in nature. Therefore the Spirit must not be asserted to be the Son’s either because he is of the same nature or because he is given through the Son—which is no different from saying that the Son himself gives, as will appear below. Since they are unable to overthrow the doctrine of the Latins, we must also examine whether the equivocation of the word “to proceed,” according to the opinion of the bishop cited, conflicts with Latin faith or not.

That it does not conflict is shown as follows. If the phrase “the Holy Spirit is not the Son’s” does not admit multiple senses, then neither, when it is affirmed that the Spirit is the Son’s, ought it to be understood in multiple senses. The truth of this proposition is drawn from Aristotelian inquiry, which says:

> “If something is opposed to something else by contradiction, it is not said in many ways; neither is its opposite. Thus ‘not seeing’ is opposed, but ‘not seeing’ is said in many ways: in one way, not having sight; in another, not using sight. Therefore ‘seeing’ must necessarily also be said in many ways. For each of the two who does not see is opposed in a different way: one who lacks sight to having sight, and one who does not use sight to using sight. Therefore ‘the Spirit is not the Son’s’ is understood in one way, and ‘is’ is uttered uniformly. But ‘the Spirit is not the Son’s’ always bears the one false sense: namely, that he is not of the Son’s substance. For neither quantity, quality, possession, action, nor anything else of this sort is denied to be the Son’s; thus nowhere in sacred Scripture is the Holy Spirit found not to be the Son’s in any true sense. Yet it would undoubtedly be found if ‘the Spirit is not the Son’s’ indicated any of the aforementioned meanings.” [Col. 0362A]

Likewise:

> “Equivocal terms are not comparable: as ‘white’ in ‘white voice’ and ‘white garment’; ‘sharp’ in ‘sharp liquid’ and ‘sharp voice.’ For neither is white or sharp in the same way, nor is one more so than the other. But proceeding from the Father and proceeding from the Son are comparable, because in proceeding the one being which the Spirit possesses personally, he receives from both similarly and equally. Therefore the term ‘to proceed,’ spoken of both, is not said equivocally.”

Again:

> “Each of the three persons either gives being to one of the other two or receives it from that person. This proposition admits proof by induction. The Father is a person other than the Son because he gives him being through generation. For in this he differs from the Son: that he gives him existence by birth. Again, the Son differs from his begetter in that by being born he receives existence from him.”

Likewise:

> “The Father differs from the Holy Spirit in addition to this because he gives him being by sending him forth. The Holy Spirit, on the other hand, is not another person than the Father for any other reason than because, by proceeding from him, he receives being. Therefore, since the Spirit is another person than the Son, he either gives being to the Son or receives it from him. He does not give it, as is plain; therefore he receives it. For concerning the one simple substance of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one who holds the right faith will scarcely assign any cause of their mutual difference other than those which have been stated. Therefore, if the Spirit is a person other than the Son, he has one of the stated relations to him. But if not, he is not another person from him.
