Therefore, by the properties mentioned, the three persons differ equally from one another, and not by any accidents. For in the supreme Trinity there is nothing that can be removed or absent. But wherever anything of this sort is understood, an accident is present. Therefore there is no accident in the superessential Trinity.” [Col. 0362C]

Moreover: Wherever the understanding of an accident does not exclude its being posterior, that accident must altogether have its being in another; and whatever altogether has its being in another, and cannot exist through itself, is reckoned as, in a sense, posterior to that in which it is. Therefore the common understanding concerning God does not permit an accident to be conceived in Him, lest anything be considered in the divine nature as posterior to Him and consequently, [Col. 0362D] whether actually or potentially, as dissoluble and corruptible. For such is the existence of things supervening according to nature, that they seem capable of dissolution. It remains, therefore, that the Father differs equally from the Son and the Spirit, the Son likewise from the Begetter and the Paraclete, and the Spirit similarly from the Father and the Son. Hence, by as much as sonship makes the Son differ from the Father, by so much does fatherhood make the Father differ from the Son.

If these things are truly posited and granted, either the Father differs in no respect from the Son with respect to the emission of the Spirit, or the Father differs more from the Son than the Son from the Begetter. For if the Son is distinguished by generation alone, while the Father generates and emits, the Father differs from the Son by more distinctions than the Son differs from the Father. For to generate and to send forth are two properties by which the Father differs from the Son. [Col. 0363A] But I do not think this incongruity can otherwise be avoided except by confessing that it is common to the Father and the Son to emit the Spirit. By this, both differ from the Spirit in the same way.

According to this reasoning, it must also be believed that it is common to the Son and the Spirit to have existence from the same person; and by this their difference from the Father is understood, although the one shines forth by birth and the other by procession, as has often been recalled. But this should not be thought liable to equivocation, since among creatures things far more different are found without any equivocation. For a worm and an elephant belong to the same genus. “Animal” is the genus and cause of both, as it is of other animals. Just as it is participated in equally by them, [Col. 0363B] so it is predicated of them univocally and is called the cause of both univocally. Yet one acquires the nature of an animal without seed; and it should be known that things which come into being through generation are not made and existent simultaneously: their substance precedes their generation. Furthermore, there is something of such things while they are being made until they are completed—as with a lion and similar beings. The same may be found in trees and plants. For some arise from seeds, while others proceed from the earth without seeds, as from their cause; and no one doubts that, in this respect, they have a common causative principle.

Moreover: “Things which are altered do not undergo alteration in the same manner. For it happens that a thing is altered suddenly, and not first by one half: as water freezes, [Col. 0363C] and a silver vessel, as soon as it receives hot water, becomes hot. Sometimes, however, a neighboring part is heated or frozen by what adheres to it. Finally, genus and difference have this in common: that they are predicated of many things, but the one answers the question ‘what?’ and the other ‘of what kind?’ Yet equivocation does not therefore attach itself to alteration or predication.

“Likewise, affirmation and negation, privation and possession, contraries and relatives, have in common that they have seemed to be opposed univocally, as things that are many and especially well known. Yet affirmation and negation consist in speech, whereas privation and possession are in things; and only one of the latter, namely possession, is according to nature. For privation, precisely as privation, is always contrary to nature. And relatives, though they are predicated of one thing in relation to another and of another in relation to that same thing, [Col. 0363D] are by no means contraries, as is clear from their definition. Therefore such a mode of arising does not render the aforementioned terms equivocal.

“To this must be added that it is common to the Father and the Spirit to stand immediately in relation to the Son; from this the equality of their differing from the Son is discerned. It is undoubtedly fitting in every respect, and worthy of the divine majesty, that just as none exceeds another in substantial matters, so no excess of distinctions should find a place. Concerning the distinctive properties, it is wholly certain that they make us understand the three persons to be separated by equal distinctions. For the Trinity escapes comparison with the elements or other creatures, which differ according to more and less. Water, indeed, [Col. 0364A] does not possess as much heaviness as fire possesses lightness. Therefore fire differs from earth by lightness more than it differs from the fluid element. But the Father differs from the Son by as much as He differs from the Spirit. Likewise the Son differs from the Father by as much as from the Spirit; and the Spirit is removed from the Father by the same number of distinctions as from the Son.

“This is recognized from the fact that, with respect to each of the persons, an equal number of properties is found, whether those relations are singular or not. Thus: the Spirit alone proceeds; alone is the image of the Son; and alone is joined mediately to the Father. Yet He has in common with the Son that He has existence from the same person, and with the Father that He stands immediately in relation to the Son. The Son alone is begotten; alone is called the radiance and figure of the substance; [Col. 0364B] and alone stands immediately in relation to the Spirit and the Father. But with the Father He emits the Spirit, and with the Spirit He receives existence from the same person. The Father also, alone existing without cause, grants existence simultaneously to the two; according to this meaning He is declared univocally the cause of both, from which both are called causative in the manner stated. He alone begets and alone stands mediately in relation to the Spirit. Yet with the Son He emits the Spirit, and with the Spirit He stands immediately in relation to the Son.

“But if the Son had nothing personally in common with the Father, while He shares with the Spirit, as stated, having existence from the same person, He would differ more from the Father than from the Spirit. Again, if the Son shares something with the Spirit, and the Spirit something with the Son, as a person does with the Father, or if neither is joined by any property, then one or the other is divided from the Father by more distinctions than from the other. [Col. 0364C] These, therefore, and the matters distinguished in the preceding exposition, are the differences, or properties, or relations that can be considered regarding the three persons without danger to faith. I think that not many others can be found which should be counted in the same proportion with these.

“But in all these and similar matters one must take great care that ‘mediate’ and ‘immediate,’ ‘near,’ and whatever is similar, are not understood as signifying time, local position, space, bulk, or magnitude; rather, all must be understood in a manner worthy of the blessed Trinity. If, therefore, one reads in the saints that there is no order in the Trinity, this gives the hearer to understand that It transcends every order. Thus God is said not to be anything that exists—not because He is not, but because He is above all beings. For if order is removed, the Spirit is not third and the Son second from the Father, as Christ delivered and great Basil testifies: [Col. 0364D] ‘Then neither would the Father be cause of the Son and Spirit, nor would the Son be from the Father, nor would the Spirit be reckoned as from both. Therefore there is order in the Trinity, although it is impossible for man to know what it is. The Son proceeds immediately from the Father, but the Spirit mediately.’

“For Damascene says: ‘Through the Son the Spirit is given, and is participated in by every creature’; and Gregory of Nyssa writes to Aulalius: ‘We believe this to be cause and that to be from a cause; and again we understand another distinction in that which is from the cause: namely, this is immediately from the first, whereas that is from the first through what is immediate.’”

## Chapter XIII

Gregory, great in theology, likewise declares: “The Holy Spirit is coordinated and numbered together with the Father and the Son; therefore it is not right to separate the Son from the Father in the emission of the Spirit.” Indeed, by such a division the bond of equality among the distinctions is broken, faith in our salvation is diminished, the most magnificent order of the three persons is nullified, and “more” and “less,” “much” and “little,” are mixed into the unchangeable Trinity. To think this alone is profane and full of abomination. For each of the three persons differs equally from the other, as [Col. 0365B] has been shown; and nothing prevents its being equally fitting that the Spirit be called and truly be the Spirit of both. This may be demonstrated thus.

The Spirit is the Spirit of the Son either by reason of nature or by reason of grace. But the Word of God possesses nothing by grace, because He is God. Therefore He has nothing added, nothing newly arriving; rather, as the divine abundances subsisted from the beginning, so they subsist by reason of nature—that is, naturally. For He does not possess life and spirit as other living things do, by way of bestowed gift; rather, as the Son naturally has the Spirit from the Father. From this it is again shown that the Spirit is said univocally to be the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, equally and without distinction, sent by the Father and by the Son. John, deservedly called Chrysostom, affirms this in these words in his commentary on John: [Col. 0365C] “See,” he says, “how He introduces Him: ‘When the Paraclete whom I shall send to you comes’ (John 15), He Himself will be a faithful witness; for He is the Spirit of truth.” Therefore He called Him not simply the Holy Spirit but the Spirit of truth, who, by proceeding from the Father, knows all things exactly, just as He Himself says of Himself: “I know whence I come and whither I go” (John 8).

“See,” he says, “the Father is by no means the only sender; the Son too is sender. Who, then, would dare contradict a man of such holiness, who declares most plainly that both send the Spirit, and assert that the statement that the Spirit is sent by the Father and the Son is equivocal and not said in the same sense? But if the Spirit is sent equally by either, each is equally cause of the Spirit’s mission; Christ who says this is truthful, and the said John, bearing witness to his Master, will not be found guilty of falsehood. Therefore, if the Son is sender, cause of the one sent, and from a cause, it does not follow anything incongruous that He emits the Spirit, just as He sends Him. For if a human being, by nature and according to his own will, breathes out and inspires his bodily spirit, much more does the Son of God send and emit His Spirit, the Father equally, perfectly, and in the same manner embracing Him without diminution.” [Col. 0365D]

From this it is again clear that the Son is in some sense a natural cause of the Holy Spirit, just as the Father is. But someone may doubt: if the Father and Son send the Spirit by reason of nature, is the Spirit not exempt from His own mission? For those things which belong by reason of nature belong equally to the three persons. To this one must reply that not everything which belongs by reason of nature is nature or belongs to nature itself. For laughing is natural, yet “capable of laughter” is consequent upon the species. Likewise, being nourished, breathing, and local motion belong to an animal, yet none of these exists from animal nature itself. So living beings naturally produce offspring; the sea likewise produces plants, animals, and herbs—none of which is of the nature of earth or sea, though they produce them from an innate and natural capacity which they possess. [Col. 0366A]

In such a manner, then, the Father and Son are said naturally to send and emit: that is, not through something adjunctive or subsequently arriving from without. And this rightly, for the Father’s mission is sufficient and perfect, and is fulfilled in His one and only Son. Otherwise, if the Father had several sons, someone might say that one of them did not possess all that belongs to the Father, nor complete with the Father the emission of the Spirit. But now there is one only-begotten Son of God and true God, who, as He sends the Spirit as His own, so emits Him by granting being. Great Basil openly affirms this in the third discourse against Eunomius:

“What necessity is there that, if the Spirit is third in dignity and order, He should also be third in nature? For He is second in dignity after the Son, having His being from Him and receiving from Him, as the discourse of piety teaches us; and in every respect it delivers Him as dependent on that cause. But that He is third in nature [Col. 0366B] we are taught neither by the holy Scriptures nor can it be syllogistically inferred as a consequence from what has been said. For just as the Son is second in order after the Father, because He is from Him, and in dignity, because the Father is principle and cause and because through Him we have access to God and the Father—yet He is by no means second in nature, because the Godhead in both is one.”

Thus it is manifest that, although the Spirit is subordinate to the Son in order and dignity, it by no means follows that He is of an alien nature. Hence it is clear that all angels, as they have one designation, are altogether the same in nature with one another. And shortly afterward:

“The Holy Spirit is subordinate to the Son in dignity and order. For we have received Him as numbered third after the Father, the Lord Himself delivering the order, when He said: ‘Go, baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matthew 28). But perhaps someone will object: where there is cause, there are before and after; but in the supremely excellent Trinity there is no before and after, therefore neither is there cause. To this one may suitably reply, as the discussion above concerning the sun and its radiance has explained, that ‘before’ and ‘after’ should indeed not be said in It; but ‘first’ and ‘second,’ with respect to the ineffable order, if so said, perhaps would not be far from correctness. For in the holy Trinity there are principle, cause, and order. The Son is numbered from the Father, and the Spirit from the Son; in this order the Spirit is second from the Son. Whatever is second is second from some first, as from a cause, from which it receives such a name.” [Col. 0366D]

Knowing this to be true, Gregory of Nyssa bears witness to Basil—or rather, to the truth—in what he wrote to Aulalius:

“While confessing the immutability of the nature, we do not deny the difference of that which is according to cause and that which is from a cause. In this alone we find one distinguished from another: in that we believe the one to be cause, while the other is from a cause; and again we understand a further distinction in him who is from the cause. For this one is immediately from the first, whereas that one is from the first through what is immediate.”

And a little later: “In the holy Trinity the principle of causality distinguishes the persons, determining that this one is without cause, whereas that one is from the cause.” Behold, this man, a proclaimer of God, plainly states that the Spirit is from a cause—namely, from the Son. [Col. 0367A] Therefore, if the statement of this great man is true, the Father is cause of the Holy Spirit either immediately or through an intermediary. If the Spirit does not proceed immediately, He is from the first through what is immediate; otherwise the holy man who wrote this is found liable to falsehood. But if He proceeds through what is immediate, the Word of God the Father must be some cause of the Holy Spirit and have some relation to Him.

Consequently, the Son alone shines immediately from His Begetter, so that nothing can be conceived between Them; and the Spirit is unhesitatingly from the Father and the Son, because everything belonging to the Father belongs also to the Son, except that the one is not called Father and the other Son. He has nothing altered, by which He might be other than the Father, but is the same. Therefore the Holy Spirit, existing according to the stated order, is common to both; this order has appeared in the supremely excellent Trinity because of cause and that which is from a cause. [Col. 0367B]

But Eunomius barks against this, asserting that every order is posterior to that of which it is an order. Great Basil answers him in these words: “One kind of order is natural, another adventitious. Natural order is, for example, the arrangement of creatures according to their formative principles, the position of numbers, and the relation of causes to the things flowing from them; adventitious and artificial order is found in propositions, disciplines, and similar matters. Therefore, when there is some kind of order which does not rest upon our choice but arises from the consequence of nature, [Col. 0367C] such as the relation of fire to the light which comes from it.” And below: “We say that the Father is before the Son according to the relation of things from causes, but not at all according to difference of nature, nor according to priority in time.” Thus far the saint.

But the divine nature, because it is truly unity abiding in simplicity, surpasses all time and every order, and one does not stand at a greater or lesser distance from the One, whose being is never divided. For where there is division, multitude in relation to the one, and whole and parts, appear; and there must be time and a measure of division, lest things standing at a distance from the one proceed to infinity. Therefore multitude is measured by number, but distance across a surface by a limit of magnitude. [Col. 0368A] Multitude is reduced through division to the indivisible, whereas magnitude is extended through division into infinity. The reason for this, as geometers state, is that magnitude is grasped imaginatively, but multitude by opinion. Opinion is more bounded and comes to rest in one, while imagination has infinite multitudes.

Therefore magnitudes are imaginatively infinite, because imagination and their division are infinite; or because it is possible for the ultimate parts of magnitudes to become one continuous thing, whereas this is not possible with multitude, since units, being indivisible, have no extremities, and for this reason no one continuous thing is made from them. Finally, divine nature alone is in no way measured, because it contains all things; it is known to be free from accidents, and is in no way divided, because it is impassible. Nothing whatsoever can be joined to it—not time, not an age, nor order; and just as nothing that belongs to the Godhead can be arranged beneath another, so nothing can be numbered together with the Godhead or the divine persons. Although it is written, “It seemed good to the Spirit and to us,” [Col. 0368B] they do not number themselves with the Spirit’s power, but subject themselves to it, being filled by Him with prudence and knowledge—He who is God, the Trinity not divided or separated in nature. For the three persons are not three Spirits but one, just as there is one God.

## Chapter XIV

As these matters have been sufficiently discussed above, it follows that, concerning the statement that the Spirit is sent by the Son and has existence from Him, great Athanasius wrote to Serapion:

“Just as the Only-begotten Son is a *γέννημα* [that which is begotten], so the Spirit given and sent by the Son is one, and is the only Spirit who is said to proceed from the Father, because He manifestly shines forth from, is sent, and is given by the Word who is from the Father. ‘He,’ He says, ‘will glorify me’ (John 16), not as a creature, but as the Spirit of truth, having such a nature and order in relation to the Son as the Son has in relation to the Father.”

Great Basil writes similarly to Amphilochius: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that one is not His” (Romans 8). Therefore He alone worthily glorifies Christ, not as a creature but as the Spirit of truth, [Col. 0368D] manifestly displaying truth in Himself; and, as Paraclete, He marks in Himself the goodness of the Paraclete who sends Him and declares the greatness from which He proceeds.

Behold: in this passage these two holy men, full of God, plainly assert that the Spirit proceeds from the Son. It should therefore be clear to everyone willing to understand, from what has been said, that the Spirit is from the Son and glorifies Him, and not the Son the Spirit. But the Son glorifies the Father insofar as He is from Him; the Father does not glorify the Son except according to His humanity. The Evangelist declares this when he says: “Jesus, lifting up His eyes to heaven, said: ‘Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, that your Son also may glorify you’” (John 17).

Certainly, as God and the Father’s Word, He had no time; but, having become man, by saying “the hour has come,” He shows everyone that human time is measured, and that it is not accidental, as some Gentiles said, but is assigned to each as He who is the maker of times has willed. Therefore in this passage He calls glory that was externally manifested in the Passion, not only His own but also the Father’s: a glory by which not the Son alone but also the Father was glorified. [Col. 0369A]

Before the cross, the Jews did not know Him as fully as before; for “Israel did not know me, and my people did not understand me.” But after the cross the world ran after Him, because the greater the things appearing concerning the Son, the more greatly the Father was shown. The nature of the flesh was glorified by receiving incorruptibility and obtaining the throne of the kingdom. Therefore He says, “Glorify me”—that is, the human nature now subjected to reproaches and shortly to be crucified—“and bring me into the glory which I had with you: I, your Son, before the world was.”

Therefore, when He says “glorify me,” He indicates humanity; when He says “the glory which I had,” divinity. For He who is one and the same spoke both, because of the proper qualities and concord of the two natures in the one person. Thus He seeks glory according to His humanity; for according to His divinity, existing before the world was, He always possessed it. For one who does not exist is not glorified. Moreover, if He had not possessed glory, the Evangelist would have lied when he said, “And we saw His glory” (John 1); likewise the Apostle: “They would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2); and David: “The King of glory shall enter” (Psalm 23). [Col. 0369C] For this reason He sought to be glorified not according to what He is as God, but according to His humanity.

Perhaps there are two kinds of glory: intrinsic and extrinsic. There is glory within, as brightness is in the sun; and another which comes from without, such as honor, knowledge, praise, and the like. “The Holy Spirit will glorify me,” because He will perform gifts and works in my name—that is, in my power—since He receives existence from me; for this, and nothing else, is what “He will receive of mine” signifies. Did the Spirit not possess it? Far be it. But this was said in order to show the distinction of the persons, and that the Spirit has existence from the Son.

Therefore, if the Son glorifies the Father and not the Father the Son except according to humanity, as the preceding discussion has explained; and if the Spirit glorifies the Son, and not the Son the Spirit; the Spirit must proceed from the Son, as great Athanasius and Basil affirm. Moreover, the Son does not receive from the Spirit, but the Spirit receives from the Son, existing in His depths. For if, while remaining outside, He received from the Son, He might be thought to need the Son for knowledge or anything else. But He needs nothing. Therefore, if, abiding in the Son, He receives from Him while He is in the Son, He proceeds from Him. For since the Spirit has everything that the Son has, it seems altogether inconceivable that He receives from the Son for another reason than that He is and proceeds from Him. [Col. 0369D]

## Chapter XV

These matters having been established by necessary demonstrations, arguments, and also the authorities of the saints, it remains most necessary to show that the Latins are by no means guilty concerning that evangelical statement which says, “The Spirit of truth proceeds from the Father.” On account of this, every Latin is attacked by the Greeks beyond what is just and proper. Indeed, the Greeks tear apart Latin faith in this matter with excessive bitterness and, by contrived high-sounding decrees, judge them alien from the Church and Christian faith—as despisers, transgressors, and deserters of the Christian law.

I shall therefore set before readers certain of their charges, and their further attacks, lest an appropriate answer be omitted—although the abusive refutations of Photius upon this same chapter have been answered in a second volume. They say:

“Those who endeavor to assert that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as from the Father have no security of doctrine. For the Son Himself, consubstantial and coeternal with God the Father, who knows all that belongs to the Father and all that belongs to the Spirit, and has nothing less in relation to God the Father and the Spirit than to Himself—He who for us and according to us became man, so that through the unsearchable riches of His goodness He might save the human race and restore it to its former state—when He taught His disciples the more perfect mysteries of His kingdom, promised them the coming of the Holy Spirit, saying, ‘Another Paraclete’: that I, who am God by nature, true God, true light, and life, as are I and the Father, may send to you one who brings consolation to all. [Col. 0370C] Therefore He is and is called the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father. He did not say, ‘who proceeds from the Father and from me, the Son.’

“For what prevented Him from saying this, if the truth stood thus, lest He who is Truth Himself, namely the Son of God and Father, be found speaking falsely? But since it was not said thus, but only ‘who proceeds from the Father,’ and ‘from the Son Himself’ was not added in the Lord’s speech, it is manifest that those who attempt to decree this rise up against the Lord’s words, the other sacred utterances, apostolic traditions, and common conceptions concerning God; indeed, against the holy and ecumenical councils and the ever-memorable Fathers. If, as is fitting, they wish to return to the way of truth, thanks be to God, who ‘does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live’ (Luke 5). But if they refuse to embrace salvation, let whoever wishes to think rightly—and desires to believe and stand with the holy catholic Church, which rightly maintains the faith from one end of the earth to the other—cast them away as *ἀποτρόπεοι*, that is, persons to be shunned, hateful and impious, and judge them worthy of no word.”

These are the missiles, and many more like them, by which hatred grows hot, which the Greeks maliciously mutter against the Latins on the occasion of this chapter alone. To attend to the meaning is the judge’s virtue, but to speak the truth belongs to the orator, as Socrates says:

“Certainly they hurl very much of this sort, and not with insignificant epithets, in vain. The Latins are not sprung from a terebinth or an oak, nor born from stones, but from human beings. They possess some acquaintance with learning and are by no means inexperienced in sacred Scripture. They have their own idiom, as is evident to those acquainted with it. Its usage is that when it employs the name of the Father alone, it makes the Son understood together with the Father. At times even the name of Christ alone makes each of the three persons understood; this can be shown from many examples. [Col. 0371A] Yet the Father alone is understood in those predications which signify a distinctive paternal property. But ‘to emit’ is not a predication signifying a paternal property alone.

“Therefore, in the predication ‘to emit,’ the Father alone is not understood. It is written: ‘There was the true light’; yet the Father or Spirit is not therefore false light, for the three persons are one light, without distinction and without change. Nor is the Son diminished by saying, ‘All things which you have given me’; just as the Father is not diminished by the statement that, when the Son has delivered the kingdom to God and the Father, He gives it to Him not as a possession bestowed, but as to the Son and heir of all that is the Father’s—that is, to Christ, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

“Moreover, instructing the disciples concerning the consummation, the Savior says: ‘Of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, except the Father alone’ (Matthew 24). Who would suppose that the Son or the Spirit is excluded from that knowledge? Therefore some judge that the Gospel should be punctuated thus: ‘No human being knows, nor do the angels know that day and hour. But what follows in order should be read separately: nor the Son, except the Father alone knows.’ There is also another exposition of this same chapter in Saint Epiphanius, in the book called *Ancoratus* (Greek Ἀγκυρωτός, “Anchored”), as follows:

“‘The Father knows the day in two ways: by nature, for He knows when it will come; and by act, for He has already judged, when He determined that the Son should judge. The Son of God knows when it will come, and, since He Himself is to bring it about, does not fail to know it; but He has not yet accomplished it in actual knowledge. For the impious still act impiously; the unbelieving act faithlessly; those who believe wrongly blaspheme; the devil works; sins reign; iniquity prevails; and judgment waits patiently until He comes to know it in act, to execute vengeance and to save those who have overcome in truth, without blaspheming the same Godhead of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. [Col. 0371D]

“‘But from the angels this dignity and glory are absent in two ways: in knowledge and in act. For they do not know when Father, Son, and Holy Spirit will make that day known in actual knowledge. They have not yet been commanded to go out to gather the wicked like tares and bind them in bundles to burn with unquenchable fire (Matthew 3). They have not yet done this and do not know it. But the Father knows and governs: this is “except the Father alone”; “nor the angels, nor the Son” is often to be left unspoken where it follows necessarily. For where the Father is mentioned, the Son is not excluded, except in that He does not beget, as has often been said.’

“After He rose from the dead, before He ascended into heaven, the disciples asked Him: ‘Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?’ He said: ‘It is not for you to know the times or seasons which the Father has placed in his own power’ (Acts 1). These belong perfectly and without any diminution to the Son. For He Himself made all things; and how could the maker of times be ignorant of times? Therefore, just as it is false that the Lord does not possess the most perfect knowledge of those times and of that day because He says, ‘No one knows except the Father alone,’ and, ‘which the Father has placed in his own power’ (ibid.), so it must not be believed that the Son does not emit the Spirit because He said, ‘who proceeds from the Father,’ [Col. 0372B] and did not add, ‘from Himself, the Son.’

“But if, because it is not written there that the Spirit proceeds manifestly from the Son, this ought neither to be believed nor stated, then for the same reason it must neither be said nor believed that the Spirit was with God; that in the beginning He was; that He was God from God; true light; maker of earth and heaven; and that God is Trinity and the three persons one God—since the formulation of the holy Creed expressed neither the name ‘person’ nor the name ‘Trinity.’”

Moreover, the Apostle says: “All of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3). Yet sanctification is nowhere effected without the Spirit; but in the Son he signified the Father and the Spirit. And elsewhere: “No one knows the Father except the Son, or anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him” (Matthew 11). In this passage the Spirit is not named, yet is understood. For the Holy Spirit knows both the Son and the Father.

In Matthew the Savior says: “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’” and so forth. “For your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things” (Matthew 6). Again: “If you then, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask Him?” (Matthew 7). Therefore will not the Son give the same good things that the Father gives? And again: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking in you” (Matthew 10). Does He, by confessing Him to be the Father’s Spirit, deny that He is also the Son’s? [Col. 0372D] But it is written: “He sent the Spirit of His Son.”

Therefore, if in the cited passage—namely, “the Spirit who proceeds from the Father”—“Father” alone is to be understood, then “of the Father alone” must be understood, and it must be inferred by syllogistic necessity that the Spirit is the Spirit of the Father alone and not of the Father alone; and of the Son alone and not of the Son alone. How impossible this is admits of no concealment. Therefore, wherever something is said of the Father, unless the name “Father” is introduced to distinguish a personal property—as when He is called Father because He begets, where the Son is not understood to be begetting with Him—the same must be understood concerning the Son.

Thus, when it is said, “who proceeds from the Father,” He who is not named with the Father is necessarily understood. For the rule says: if what appears less likely to belong does belong, then what appears more likely will also belong. For example, Scripture declares that the Son will judge the age to come; the primacy of that judgment is especially attributed to Him, as administrator of all created things, which He Himself from the beginning brought from nothing into being. As He possesses a twofold knowledge of those to be judged, it is most fitting that at the regeneration, resurrection, and restoration He should sit as the most righteous Judge, the Lawgiver of the New Testament. [Col. 0373A] Yet the persons not named are understood. Although He Himself assumed human leaven, in which He suffered and was tempted, so that He may judge those tempted without intercession or exhortation, the Father and Spirit are nevertheless not absent; for what is attributed to the Son is not denied to the Father. Therefore it is vain to maintain that the Spirit proceeds merely because it is written: “who proceeds from the Father.”

## Chapter XVI
Finally, they by no means bring their calumny concerning the Greek words to bear appropriately; for they do the same thing as those who disparaged the fourth and universal synod which was held under the reign of Marcian, when six hundred and thirty holy Fathers had assembled at Chalcedon against Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, and Eutyches, archimandrite of Constantinople. These men blasphemed concerning the Incarnation and, while fleeing Nestorius’s division—which posited two sons—were rushing headlong into another evil of their own devising. For they impiously believed that the two natures, namely divinity and humanity, had after the union been reduced to one nature, so that on this account passions might befit the divinity. The synod anathematized them, [Col. 0373C] and likewise Nestorius, who cried out such things as: “Mary, most excellent sir, did not give birth to God, but gave birth to a man, an instrument of divinity”—although this Greek is himself without fault, when he attributes a Mother to gods and disgorges similar absurdities elsewhere.

For these reasons the holy synod, rightly understanding the mystery of the Incarnation, properly handed down to us one hypostasis made known in two natures without confusion, without change, and without division, opposing, as was fitting, the madness of Eutyches and Nestorius. By these expressions it equally refutes the error of both: Nestorius, who shamelessly divides the one Christ into God separately and man separately, is confounded by its confessing one person and the same one, God and man, our Lord Jesus Christ. Eutyches, who confesses one nature made up of divinity and humanity, is refuted when it speaks of two natures united without confusion and without change in one hypostasis, with the properties of each nature preserved.

Why, moreover, the accusers of truth censured this synod is evident from the definition of the same synod, which says:

> Our Lord and Saviour Christ, confirming knowledge of the faith in his disciples, said: “Peace I give you; my peace I leave with you” (John 14), so that no one may dissent from his neighbour in the doctrines of piety, but the preaching of truth may shine equally upon all, and every corruption of falsehood may be driven from Christ’s flock. [Col. 0374A] This indeed we have done by common decision: removing the doctrines of error, while renewing the faith of the Fathers—which contains no error—the faith of the three hundred and eighteen, and proclaiming the Creed to all; and we have set forth as our own Fathers those who received this covenant of piety. These are those who afterwards assembled in great Constantinople, one hundred and fifty holy Fathers, and sealed the same faith. We therefore approve the order of faith, preserving all its forms; also [we approve] the [text uncertain: *non ejus*] of the holy synod once celebrated at Ephesus, over which Celestine, bishop of the Romans, and Cyril, bishop of the Alexandrians, of most holy memory, presided “to shine forth” [*praeradiare*; or “that it may shine forth,” as the edition has, etc.]; indeed, [we approve] the exposition of the sound and undefiled faith of the three hundred and eighteen holy and blessed Fathers, who assembled at Nicaea under Constantine, of most pious memory; and [we approve] the things decreed at Constantinople by the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers, for the refutation of heresies which had then arisen and for the confirmation of our Catholic and apostolic faith.

This, indeed, was the fourth sacred synod’s approval of the faith of the third, second, and first [synods]. This faith was handed down by the holy apostles and was present in the holy Church of God, as blessed Epiphanius recalls, even if it was not then set down in writing. But because of Arius it was committed to writing in the city of Nicaea by all the holy bishops assembled there.

I have mentioned here the act of the holy fourth synod and whatever is quoted from it because the reproach of those who now criticize is like that of those earlier critics. For the censure of those calumniators concerned the expression and addition which says: “We renew the unerring faith of the Fathers” (*ἀπλάνιην*). The opponents dishonestly interpreted this as follows: “The faith was renewed because it had previously become antiquated and shaken.” Yet the synod renewed the faith not in its meaning or in any doctrinal direction, but solely by adding these expressions, while agreeing with the Fathers:

> We teach that the same one is perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity, truly God and truly man, consubstantial with the Father according to divinity and consubstantial with us according to humanity. [Col. 0374D]

This, surely, is the addition made by the holy Synod of Chalcedon to the synod held at Constantinople; that synod, in turn, added to the Council of Nicaea, as becomes evident from the respective formulations of faith. For the formulation of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers contains neither the things just stated nor that the Spirit is Lord and God, life-giving, proceeding from the Father, and worshipped and glorified together with him and with the Son; for it was the Synod of Constantinople that declared these things. The Fathers did this not as though supplying some deficiency in the earlier [synod], but by drawing forth written testimonies concerning the Holy Spirit against Dioscorus and his accomplices, who dogmatized that the same Spirit was a creature and not God.

[Col. 0375A] They also properly preserved, for the confirmation of orthodox doctrines, the letter of Leo, most holy pope of elder Rome, written to Flavian, holy archbishop of Constantinople, to refute the madness of Eutyches—as signifying, as it were, the confession of the great Peter and serving as a kind of common charter against evildoers.

Therefore, if the Synod of Constantinople added to the Nicene Creed: “the Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father”; and if the Synod of Chalcedon likewise added to the Synod of Constantinople: “perfect in humanity, perfect in divinity, consubstantial with the Father according to divinity, consubstantial with us according to humanity,” and certain other things where it was stated [Col. 0375B]—then the bishop of elder Rome [Note: [Col. 0375] “Elder Rome” is said on account of Constantinople, which was called New Rome.] ought not to be branded with any accusation, reproach, or calumny because, for the sake of interpretation, and with the agreement of many holy bishops and most learned cardinals, he added one expression, namely that the Spirit proceeds “from the Son.” For it was lawful for him, and always will be lawful, to strengthen the brethren, issue decrees, and frame interpretations, if something has been written obscurely; and, where evidence of the author’s intention remains, to argue from the writer’s intention and make this persuasive.

For he is the one to whom the sheep and lambs were entrusted; and consequently he ought not merely to be a reciter of what is written, but the interpreter of those holy men concerning things not written down. As shepherd and head of God’s sheep—just as the holy and universal second synod decreed in these words:

> Let the bishop [Col. 0375C] of Constantinople have the primacy of honour after the bishopric of Rome, because it is New Rome.

The most pious Emperor Justinian likewise promulgated such a law in his *Novella* (*νεάρα*):

> We decree, in accordance with the sacred constitutions of synods, that the most holy pope of elder Rome is first among all priests; while the most blessed bishop of Constantinople, New Rome, is to hold second rank after the apostolic throne of elder Rome.

And again, the same emperor writes among other things in a certain letter to Epiphanius, most holy bishop of Constantinople:

> We preserve in every respect this condition of concord among the most holy Churches and with regard to the most holy pope and patriarch of elder Rome, to whom we have written things similar to these. [Col. 0375D] For we do not allow anything concerning ecclesiastical order not to be referred to his Blessedness, since he is the head of all the holy priests of God. Whenever heretics have arisen in these regions, they have indeed been brought to destruction through the counsel and righteous judgment of that venerable see.

But why do I recall synodical or imperial decrees? The successor of Peter, the chief [of the apostles], has a testimony greater than these: namely Christ our Saviour. Just as Christ made Peter alone his equal in paying the tribute, so he set Peter alone over the whole world, as John the Theologian relates:

> When therefore they had dined, Jesus says to Simon Peter: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” He says to him: “Yes, Lord, you know that I love you.” He says to him: “Feed my sheep” (John 21).

John, deservedly surnamed Chrysostom, explains this passage as follows:

> “Why then, passing over the others, does he converse with Peter concerning this? Because Peter was preeminent among the apostles, the mouth of the disciples and leader of the choir. For this reason Paul also went up to Jerusalem specifically to see him before the others. He therefore says to him: ‘Do you love me? Take care of the brethren.’ He questions him a third time and gives him the same command a third time, showing how highly he esteems the rule of his own sheep.” And shortly afterwards: “If someone should say, ‘How then did James receive the throne in Jerusalem?’ I would reply: Peter appointed him teacher of the world.” [Col. 0376B]

And again:

> “When, therefore, he had spoken great things to him, entrusted the world to him, foretold his martyrdom, and testified to love greater than that of the others, Peter wished to take John as his companion and said: ‘Lord, and what of this man?’ But Christ joined no one to Peter as an equal partner.”

From this it is evident that the ruler of elder Rome received from Peter the authority to renew the faith, to “take care,” in the Fathers’ words, and the rule over all priests—indeed, over all Christians. Therefore those who resist the first see, the bishop over the whole world, resist Christ’s disposition; and unless they repent, they will be punished by the judgment upon obstinacy.

Accordingly, the Gospel phrase, “who proceeds from the Father,” and the saving Creed are interpreted by the Synod of Chalcedon as Chalcedon interpreted Constantinople [Col. 0376C] and Constantinople Nicaea, without in any way contradicting the decree of the fourth synod. Its wording and ordinance are as follows:

> The sacred and universal synod decrees that it is not lawful for anyone to write, compose, devise, or teach another faith. But those who dare to compose another faith, or set forth, teach, or hand over another creed to those wishing to turn to the knowledge of truth from paganism, Judaism, or any heresy—if they are bishops or clergy, it commands that they be deprived of episcopacy and clerical office; and it anathematizes monks and laypeople who presume such things.

If, because of an interpretation of the aforesaid clause declaring that the Spirit truly proceeds from the Son, and with every precaution under the testimony of the holy Fathers Athanasius, Basil, Gregory, Augustine, Ambrose, Hilary, and many others, the apostolic Church is believed to have written or taught another faith, then by the same reasoning the holy Fathers assembled at Constantinople issued a creed other than the Nicene one, and those assembled at Chalcedon another faith than that taught by the holy Fathers at Constantinople.

Thus, I think, it becomes plain from these matters that no one whatsoever may calumniate the most holy, great, and chief Roman Church as though it had written, composed, or taught another faith. For it neither introduces, teaches, nor hands down [Col. 0377A] another creed if it interprets that issued by the holy Fathers and does not allow the faith—among whom it has always shone—to be shaken. Though it holds primacy, it nevertheless humbles itself, replying as the Synod of Chalcedon once replied to its slanderers:

> “I am unjustly accused, for I renew not the faith but its remembrance. I have added nothing and removed nothing; if I have made an obscure expression in the saving Creed clear. For I have renewed the faith as the aforesaid Fathers did, and I have added to the Nicene, Constantinopolitan, and Chalcedonian synods nothing contrary to them. For, following the footsteps of those Fathers, I have merely clarified by interpretation and by the addition of a word, after the passage of time, matters not then examined and not clearly understood by all.” [Col. 0377B]

## CHAPTER XVII

It is therefore right to ratify what so great a Church decrees and what so great a pontiff declares, without whom all the vigour of the pen of ecclesiastical tradition withers, as blessed Stephen the Younger, worthy of remembrance among the saints, maintains. This great man, celebrated not only before God but among all the Greek multitude for apostolic holiness, when invited to subscribe to a certain synod, boldly uttered these words:

> “How have you who profaned sanctuaries established a holy synod? O impiety! How can a synod be called universal in which the Roman pontiff did not concur, apart from whom it is altogether impossible for ecclesiastical matters to be canonically [Col. 0377C] established? Therefore the summits of mountains and the multitude of all the faithful ought to bend the knee before him, and, instead of hostile rebukes, embrace the yoke of submission. For principalities and kingdoms of the nations are subject to the governance of Peter the chief and of his successor. His Church always sends forth splendour from itself and does not grow dark; from it law and judgment go forth; men come to it from every part of the earth—and rightly so. For Peter opened the door of faith to the Gentiles because of the vision that appeared to him of the vessel like a linen sheet, in which were all the beasts of the earth, four-footed creatures, creeping things, representations of owls, and many other animals. To him it was said: ‘Rise, Peter; kill and eat’ (Acts 10).”

But when the disciple objected, still fearing legal observance, and said, “Not at all, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common and unclean,” the voice again said to him: “What God has cleansed, do not call common” (ibid.). [Col. 0377D]

From these things it clearly appears that Christ established Peter and his successor as prince and head forever not merely of Latins, Greeks, the West, and the whole North, but also of Armenians, Arabs, Indians, Midianites, Amalekites, the entire East, and the southern region. For this reason all the limits of the setting sun have since then acknowledged Peter’s successor as their lord and are guided under that bishop; and it is fitting for everyone wandering from his mother’s womb to do so.

For Peter, the great apostle of Christ, ordained bishops in almost all the cities of Syria, Cappadocia, Phrygia, Macedonia, Greece, Epirus, Sicily, Italy, Gaul, Spain, and the farthest regions, as ecclesiastical history relates. For by his favour James held the throne of Jerusalem; then he ordained Evodius at Antioch, Urbanus at Tarsus, Epaphroditus in Lycia, Phygellus at Ephesus, Apelles at Smyrna, Philip near Olympus, Jason at Thessalonica, Silas at Corinth, Herodion at Patras, and Maximus at Tauromenium. [Col. 0378A] Moreover, at Ancyra, Nicaea, Nicomedia, in the regions of Thrace, and in western lands, he likewise carried out ordinations, and he directed that the same should be done by his successors.

Whoever therefore despises Peter’s little ship sails imprudently; and unless he casts away the leaden weights of obstinacy, the seas will pour in. It is indeed improper and inconsistent to dissolve the law of one’s mother. Solomon says: “Hear, my son, the words of your father, and do not cast away the law of your mother” (Ecclus. 6). This is that pious and holy mother which, not in some random manner but with Christ proceeding, the Paraclete instructing, and Peter dictating, affirms that the Spirit proceeds from the Son, with the multitude of saints testifying to the same thing.

For Hilary, most abundant in theology, says in the discourse he published on the blessed Trinity:

> “The Father is full God of himself; the Son is full God, begotten of the Father; but the Holy Spirit is full God, proceeding from the Father and the Son.”

Likewise the venerable Ambrose, who, upon learning at Thessalonica of a slaughter of many thousands, met the emperor as he approached Milan at the doors of the Church and denied him entrance, boldly raising his voice:

> “Do you not know, Emperor, the greatness of the slaughter you have committed? Perhaps your impious power does not permit you to know the greatness of your sin; deceived by purple, you do not know the weakness of your clothed body. But know that as you are corruptible and transitory, so your power is fragile and unstable; and in a short time you must render an account of it to the King of all kings,”

and similar words. This great man laid these things before the Emperor Theodosius, who withdrew with tears, remaining in mourning for eight months, after which time he deserved absolution from the [Col. 0378D] archbishop through many supplications.

This man, full of the Spirit of God, declares such things concerning the same Spirit in the book he composed *On the Trinity*:

> “The Spirit is not sent as though from a place, nor does he go forth from a place when he proceeds from the Son.”

And in the second book *On the Holy Spirit* he says:

> “Whatever is from someone is either from his substance or from his power. From substance: as the Son is from the Father and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; from power: as all things are from God.”

The great Augustine also, a lamp ever burning in the Church, argues thus in the fifth discourse *On the Trinity*:

> “If that which is given has a principle, it has as its principle the one from whom it is given; for he did not receive from another that which proceeds from himself. We must confess that the Father and the Son are one principle of the Holy Spirit, not two.” [Col. 0379A]

And again:

> “As he grants to the Son an essence begotten from the Father without beginning of time and without change of nature, so he grants to the Holy Spirit an essence proceeding from both without beginning of time and without any change of nature.”

Jerome also, who was so holy that wild savagery obeyed his commands—for indeed a huge lion, terrible to all, for a long time carefully and gently led the donkey of the church over which he presided at Bethlehem out to pasture and back to its manger—this truly holy man wrote, among other things, concerning the Trinity:

> “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father and the Son exists in every respect coequal and coeternal with the Father and the Son.”

Therefore, having the favour and agreement of these and very many others, as mentioned above, the aforesaid mother Church affirms without hesitation that, just as the Spirit proceeds from the Father, so he proceeds from the Son. Our Saviour Jesus Christ commands that every word stand “in the mouth of two or three witnesses” (2 Cor. 13). This doctrine has a multitude of witnesses who say the same thing and think alike about the Holy Spirit. They appeared worthy, as luminaries of the Church, of the illumination of the Holy Spirit; their minds were enlightened by God, so that with intelligible eyes they beheld the Father with the Son and the Holy Spirit dwelling within themselves.

God the Father indeed remains in those who observe the Gospel commandments, but he remains differently in the Son. In the Son he is present naturally, as the Son is in the Father; but in human beings he is present by a relation of grace. Those whom the Father loves, the Son and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0379C] also love. Thus the holy Trinity makes its dwelling and inhabits, by grace, those whose manner of life is excellent, insofar as it can be apprehended and received by a creature.

Some who wish to disclose somewhat the manner of this indwelling use the following comparison. They say that what common air is to a sensible house, divine grace is to a rational soul: the more you empty a house of furnishings, the more abundantly common air enters it; and the more things you put into it, the more fully that same air withdraws. Similarly, to the extent that a rational soul is stripped of its own furnishings, divine grace enters it. By the furnishings of a house they mean vessels, bedding, and the other articles of use; by those of the soul, vain glory, the lust of the eyes, pleasure of the flesh, and the like. By the heart’s capacity for God they mean the breadth of hope, and by its narrowness concern for the body.

Clearly, the blessed men whose testimony mother Church employs purified their consciences, cast out their inborn furnishings, and embraced with all their strength the threefold God who came to make his dwelling with them. Yet since the beginning of the world it has not been heard that those in whom the holy and blessed Trinity dwelt by grace should themselves have held evil and impious views about the holy Trinity. Therefore the following syllogistic conclusion necessarily follows: it is true that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. No men of apostolic holiness left a false judgment in their writings concerning the most excellent [Col. 0380A] procession of the Holy Spirit; but all those whose testimony mother Church uses concerning the Holy Spirit’s emanation were men of apostolic holiness; and since they wrote that the Spirit proceeds from the Son, it is beyond doubt that he proceeds from the Son.

## CHAPTER XVIII

But perhaps someone, after so many arguments, may again raise the obstacle of denial and, from what was set out at the end of the second book, claim that the matter is not to be regarded as settled by stipulation. He may construct the conclusion that men of apostolic holiness called the temporal procession to human beings “the giving” and “the sending” of the Spirit; whereas the Greek confesses the eternal procession according to which the Spirit has his subsistence and being from the Father, but wholly denies it from the Son.

There will therefore be one answer, I think sufficient for everything, which seems to establish the understanding of this objection. Although the apostles and prophets received the Spirit from Christ in time, the Son of God did not begin in time to possess the Spirit, nor did that same Spirit begin to go forth from the Son at any point in time. Rather, from the days of eternity, as the Son is begotten from the Father, so the Holy Spirit proceeds from both; he is sent eternally from both and, as has been shown, proceeds univocally from both. For with the three there is nothing past and nothing future; among the three persons there is no change, nor shadow of variation. [Col. 0380C]

Before Jacob, Timaeus taught the same, as did Aristotle and Parmenides; before them, Plato declared it not only in his teaching but also in his writings: that with God there is neither past nor future. For of these alternatives, one is no longer, another is not yet; one has changed, another is capable of change. Yet it is impossible to devise any conception under which change belongs to things that truly are, whether according to place, alteration, or any other kind of motion.

> “It is necessary,” he says, “that what is unchangeable wholly precede that which changes in some manner, so that the mutable may remain; otherwise it will not stand, but will run on to infinity.”

Therefore the sending of the Spirit which is in relation to the Son and Father cannot be absent from them. Thus such an inference is convicted of falsehood: “If the Spirit began in time to be sent or given to human beings, then the Son of God, together with the Father, began in himself to send or give the Spirit.” For, as regards themselves, they send and give before all ages. But they are said to begin sending or giving when persons worthy of gift or mission come into being—not with respect to themselves, but with respect to the recipients.

Therefore, if sending is eternal, so is mission; and conversely, if mission is eternal, so is sending. And mission is eternal. For in the case of stonecutters (*λιθοτόμων*), the plan for building a tower precedes and is distinct from the construction; but in the Son and Father the conception of the Spirit’s mission neither precedes the mission itself nor is separated from it. If the conception of the Holy Spirit’s mission is eternally in the Son, but the mission of that Spirit began to exist in the Son at some time, then the Son has before and after, something added and separable, and does not escape the multiplicity of accidents. [Col. 0381A]

When the sun illuminates a house, does it begin today to cast its rays upon some part of it? Precious stones likewise continually shine, as do the stars; yet the brilliance of the latter does not gleam in darkness, nor that of the former in daylight. This is not because their brightness is interrupted, but because of the weakness of those who see.

Further: the sending of the Holy Spirit and the knowledge of that sending are simultaneous in the Father and the Son, for neither of these two is subject to time; but knowledge is eternal. Therefore the sending of the Holy Spirit from both is eternal, and each is equally and eternally a cause of the Spirit’s sending, as is clear from what has gone before. If there is a cause, then the Son is some cause of the Holy Spirit; if neither is a cause, then the sending of the Holy Spirit has neither cause nor principle—which is the privilege of the Father alone in the Trinity.

Perhaps, then, it is not improper if the procession of the Spirit, eternally flowing from Father and Son, is more customarily called, in relation to creatures receiving it, mission, gift, or something similar: the higher terms always being referred to the divine, the lower always to the created. Thus the same thing is called doctrine in Christ but instruction in the apostles and in all of us. The sunlight too is perpetual, though, while it rises for us, we call it “day,” assigning it a brief span of time.

Finally, Jerome, a man of memorable holiness and friend of truth, supports this solution by instructing Paula and Eustochium concerning the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation in words of this kind:

> “It is established that time did not prejudice the sacrament of the union of God and man, so that he who had not yet been born of the Virgin Mary was nevertheless already in him through the unity of person from the beginning of the world. This is made clear by many indications of Scripture. Hence the Lord says to the Jews: ‘Before Abraham came to be, I am.’ ‘Came to be’ indicates the temporal limitation of humanity; ‘I am’ declares the eternity of nature.” [Col. 0381C]

In this eternity, Jerome indicates, the one speaking existed through the sacrament of his Incarnation. Hence the Apostle says: “Jesus, saving the people out of Egypt” (Jude 5); and again, “Let us not tempt Christ” (1 Cor. 10). This is not because Jesus or Christ had already been born of Mary, but because the unity of person was already signified in that one Son of God, who was hidden in the ministry; for surely whatever God did, Christ did wholly from the beginning through the unity of the mystery, because he was always with him and in his counsel, that it should be done thus. And now, when the time came, he became what he had always been in Christ.

Gregory the Theologian likewise declares such things in his first discourse *On the Son*:

> “Christ is God’s wisdom, radiance, image, seal—he who is the radiance of glory, the imprint of his substance, and the image of goodness”; and: “Him God sealed”; and: “He is Lord, king, almighty”; and: “The Lord rained fire from the Lord”; and: “The rod of righteousness is the rod of your kingdom”; and: “He who is, who was, and who is to come.”

These statements are plainly said of the Son, as are all similar statements of the same truth; none of them has been added to the Son or the Spirit later in time, just as none has been added to the Father. For what is perfect is not so through addition. And again, he refers the higher things to divinity and the better nature, beyond bodily passions; the lower things to the composite one, emptied and incarnate for your sake—yet he does not say “made human” as something worse—and subsequently exalted. [Col. 0382A]

And in the second discourse he says:

> “Let him be said to receive life, judgment, the inheritance of the nations, authority over flesh, glory, disciples, or whatever else is said; but these belong to humanity. If you give them to God, there is nothing improper, provided you give them not as additions, but as things existing from the beginning and by reason of nature, not grace.” [Col. 0382B]

The great Basil likewise confesses the same when he says: “The flesh shared in divinity and imparted to it absolutely none of its own weakness.”

Therefore when it is said that God began to be Creator or that the Lord [began to be] man, this must be referred to created things. Just as, when it is said that charity, which is God, increases in a human being, this means that the human being increases in it; so likewise when it is said that God began to be Creator, it means that the creature began to have existence, and that a servant and human flesh began to be united to God when the Word became flesh.

For if “Creator” and “Lord” are referred to the creature and the lorded-over thing, since relatives are naturally simultaneous, it cannot be objected that God acquired certain relations at a point in time, and thus something accidental. The divine page and Catholic faith do not accept this. In this sense may be understood the statement: “Had they known, they would never have crucified the King of glory.” Passion is attributed to the impassible divinity: as when someone’s garment is sprinkled with blood without the blood reaching the wearer’s body, and he declares himself defiled by blood. The stain of the garment is attributed to the person wearing it, who affirms that he has become defiled. In this way the Son of God suffered in the flesh; in this way the Creator admits things belonging to creation.

But if the unity of the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation in the Son did not have a beginning in time, much less is it credible that the sending of the Holy Spirit from Father and Son began in either of them under time. For the argument appears quite weak to everyone that this sending was temporal because earth, water, air, fire, and heaven itself with all that it contains are in time, since they exist in place as bodies do. [Col. 0382D] For every body is in place, and everything in place is moved, either wholly or partially, through itself or through another. Wherever there is motion, there is also time. Rest, as related to motion, is measured by time and is in time; for there certainly existed some time beyond which more could be taken, in which what was at rest was not moving. But what is at rest is what is capable of being moved.

Thus a human being and the other things of this kind are said to be in time because the being of a human being—that is, all the years of his life—is defined and measured by time. Here “the being of a human being” means the span of his existence, not his species itself, which perhaps is not subject to time. [Col. 0383A]

From this it is clear that the syllogism which certain people try to make is invalid:

> Time is the number of motion; but things other than motion are not motion; therefore things other than motion are not measured by time, and consequently are not in time.

The answer is that motion is said to be in time and measured by time directly and in itself; therefore time is primarily called its number. But human beings and all such things are said to be in time through the motion or rest which they possess. For they exist insofar as time, by its flow and extension, defines and measures the years of their life or the duration of their stay. [Col. 0383B]

But the Father and the Son, and whatever proceeds from their persons, exist simultaneously. They attribute being not only to time but to all creatures; therefore it cannot in any way be validly inferred that the mission of the Spirit is subject to time. This is demonstrated again by the definition of time given by Aristotle in the *Physics*:

> “Time, therefore, is the number of motion according to before and after—not of this or that motion, but of motion insofar as it is motion.”

For this reason many hold that there is one time for all things which move, not only in species but also in number. Others, making a distinction, say that time is one in its subject but many in account.

Moreover, the differences of motion considered within the same kinds, such as alteration, change of place, and the like, are not differences of time, as past and future are. For nothing prevents persons at Rome, Constantinople, and everywhere on earth from existing in the same instant. Certainly, just as individual moving things can have individual motions, so individual motions do not each have an individual time; rather, all have one [time]. Therefore time must not be thought to be motion, since it is the measure of motion. This is clear partly because several motions occur simultaneously while the present is everywhere the same, and partly because every motion is in time, whereas no time is interpreted except insofar as one [time] is contained in another.

Again, one motion is swift and another slow, but time is not. Time is called long or short, [Col. 0383D] but never swift or slow. The same judgment appears applicable to number. For number is a discrete quantity, while time is continuous. Number does not come to be or perish; time, however, comes to be and perishes. Further, all the parts of any number must exist: for unless three units exist, three cannot exist. Finally, the first and second numbers exist simultaneously, but the earlier and later of time are by no means simultaneous.

Therefore time is called “number,” as some have thought, both the number that counts things beneath the firmament and the number counted in the firmament. Just as a measure is called both measuring and measured—for example, a wooden bushel-measure and a bushel of grain, an amphora of water and a clay amphora—so there is number composed of units and number counted in countable things. Therefore time is called number, that is, the measure of motion of the first kind according to before and after—two things which are simultaneous in magnitude or multitude.

In time and motion, however, the later has no place unless the earlier is first removed. Clearly, “earlier” and “later” are so named because one moves away from the present instant. For toward the past, that is called earlier which is farther from the instant; later, what is regarded as nearer to the present. But toward the future the usage is reversed: earlier is what is nearer to the present; later, what is more remote from it. For there follows more quickly where there is later and more slowly. But if the Son of God attained nothing more slowly, neither did He attain anything later; by the same reasoning, neither more quickly nor [Col. 0384B] earlier.

Certainly, nothing that proceeds from any of the three persons acquires its being in time. For eternal things are not in time: time does not contain their being; things which are in time are within measure. But whatever has some measure has a measure greater than itself according to time; and it is subject to passion, whereas those who are in no way in time wholly escape passion and change. Again, in things which come to be in time, time is their measure by succession. But eternal things, being simultaneous, await no temporal production; hence they are above time. For if they were in time, they would also be in motion, nor would they be thought to subsist simultaneously, while awaiting some future time, whether through revolution or through some other cause.

[Col. 0384C] For we know in time those things which exist above time and before time; yet for that reason we shall not establish that they are in time. Nor, if what exists for a long time is in time, shall that which exists through all time be declared subject to time. From this arose the following question: whether heaven and the heavenly bodies are under time or not. “If,” they say, “heaven is not under time, there is no number of its motion.” Again they say: “If it is in time, it is contained under time, and there will be some time greater than it.”

[Col. 0384D] Some solve this by maintaining that heaven is in time because, since one motion and then another of it continually occurs, one time and then another will be future, just as it happens that a longer time is taken. But those things are properly said to be under time which receive their existence under time through flux and extension: for their being endures only as long as time is extended; while it comes to be, it has being. This belongs to none of the higher realities, much less to God. Hence it is clear from what has been said that the Son of God by no means sends the Spirit in time, although the disciples received Him in time. For just as the principle of sending, so also the sending itself, existed before it shone upon the disciples: it existed in the Son before all ages and before all times.

If He had not possessed from the beginning the principle of sending, then—since, insofar as He is God, He possesses nothing added and nothing received—He would in no way have sent the Spirit. Therefore the Son both sends the Spirit by possessing Him and always possesses the Spirit by sending Him [Col. 0385A]. He is the image of the Father—not inanimate, not carved by hand, not the work of an artisan or of thought, but a living image; indeed, He is Life itself. He preserves immutability not in a likeness of outward form, but in substance: that is, the greatness of dignity of the Person of the Only-begotten possesses immutability in every respect, without qualification.

If, therefore, when the Father sends the Spirit, the Son does not send Him, He does not possess immutability in the sending; and the image would in many ways be found defective, deprived of the greatest of goods. Then the Cherubim too would seem able to be considered images of the Father—each of whom is invisible and incorporeal and possesses fullness of knowledge—unless the fact that they do not possess and send the Spirit of themselves distinguishes the image of the Father from them.

[Col. 0385B] Thus the Only-begotten alone is properly and immutably the image of the Father, much more expressly than Seth was of Adam. For Seth and Adam are separable, whereas the Father and Son are inseparable; Seth and Adam possessed differing souls and diverse wills, whereas the Father and Son always have had and have one power and one will. Seth was called an image of his father with respect to externals; but the Word of God is in every respect the image of the Father—not in colour, not in form, nor in anything of that kind, for that belongs to artificial rather than natural images—but in substance, that is, in the Father’s Person, making those who participate in it images of Himself and gods.

For this reason the image of the Father and the Father are called God univocally; the image of the Son and the Son are not so called. Thus the image of Christ and Christ are named not univocally but equivocally [Col. 0385C]; but the image of the Father and the Father are called God univocally, for the Father, His image, and the Holy Spirit are one. For the nature of the Three is one and the same.

Therefore the Son is an equally efficacious seal, without any falsehood: the undiminished χαρακτήρ (*character*, exact impress) and likeness of the formed Father. For He is not the image of the Father merely on the surface, as an image is similar to Christ; rather, He is the wisdom of God’s innermost and deepest things, and power in the bosom of the Father, **ἐν αὐτῷ μένη**, that is, “remaining in Him”: He exists as the producer and expounder of all that belongs to the Father. Hence the Only-begotten is the most complete heir of God the Father, marking forth all His interior things.

[Col. 0385D] For an image ought to portray the nature of the thing. Nor does it belong to the artist to fashion otherwise the statue made in Socrates’ image: unless it displays Socrates’ baldness, snub nose, and protruding eyes, it will by no means be called his likeness. Grant, then, that immutability is said equivocally; yet it must possess, according to its own proper character, equality with that from which it derives being and of which it is a likeness.

Further: if the Son neither possesses nor sends the Spirit as the Father does, He is deprived of holiness, which is the greatest inheritance of the Son. The Holy Spirit alone embraces this in the enumeration when it is said, “Father and Son and Holy Spirit.” Therefore, if holiness proceeds from the Father but not from the Son, the two do not possess holiness equally and without distinction—an idea which it is not Catholic to entertain.

[Col. 0386A] For the Spirit is the fullness of the Son, as it is written: “Of His fullness we all received grace for grace” (Deut. XXXIII): the new law for the old; in place of verbal and shadowy adoption, the reality itself and the truth—those born of God through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, without whom no one shall see God, from whom all holiness flows. It is not without significance that the Son is said to be and remain in the Father’s bosom, but the Spirit is not. This expression certainly does not signify that there is a body; rather, it most openly and plainly indicates the Only-begotten’s fellowship in the sending of the Spirit. Scripture, however, has offered nothing comparable concerning the Spirit.

Therefore the Son is also called the χαρακτήρ of the substance, although a heretic may suppose that the χαρακτήρ is not a person but merely belongs to a person [Col. 0386B]. He fails to observe that the Son is called Son—which is a person—just as He is called the radiance that shines coeternally from the Father; likewise, “Angel of Great Counsel,” “Wonderful,” “Counsellor,” and “Prince of Peace” are uttered to distinguish the Person, and because He showed greater things to His servants the prophets by granting knowledge broader and clearer than the Mosaic dispensation.

Moses prayed very earnestly to receive knowledge of Him who truly is. “Show me,” he says to God, “Your face, that I may know You.” “No man,” He says, “shall see Me and live. Behold, there is a place by Me: you shall stand upon the rock; and when My glory passes by, I shall place you in a cleft of the rock, and I shall protect you with My right hand until I pass by. Then I shall take away My hand, and you shall see My back; but you shall not be able to see My [Col. 0386C] face” (Exod. XXXIII).

Moses is commanded to stand upon the rock and look through a narrow opening. By this God showed that the Law possessed only a brief knowledge of the Trinity, whose illumination appeared only through an opening. For the opening and the protecting hand signify nothing other than the Law’s partial and obscure knowledge; such indeed is what is presented to the eyes through an aperture.
