But Christ’s teaching and preaching showed us greater knowledge, training the eye of the mind to reach things above sense and reason.

The face, glory, and radiance of glory which Moses asks to see are the Word of God, the Only-begotten χαρακτήρ of the Father’s one substance. Man could not see Him without fire—that is, the soul—and the cloud of flesh [Col. 0386D]. Therefore he hears: “You shall stand upon the rock.” Now the rock was Christ. Moses had nothing glorious in the Law except the face alone. But Jesus was wholly glorified upon the mountain, and Moses and Elijah appeared in glory, speaking with Him; there not only Christ’s face appeared as the sun, but His garments also as snow.

There that promise which Moses received on Mount Sinai is fulfilled, when he was told: “I shall take away My hand, and you shall see My back” (ibid.). “I shall send My Son, whom you shall see when the fullness of days has come; but you shall not be able to see My face, because no man shall see Me and live” (ibid.). This is not because Life becomes a cause of death to those who see it—for the divine nature is life-giving—but because it is a proper mark of the divine nature to transcend every sense [Col. 0387A]. Since it alone is Life, if it surpasses all knowledge, what a human being comprehends is not Life.

Whoever, therefore, thinks that any of the things he knows to belong to God is God, has turned away from God and does not possess life. God is not seen from the front, because He is boundless and without beginning; but one sees His back who follows Him, for as He goes forward He shows a way to the follower. His back, therefore, was seen when, in the last days, having assumed flesh, He poured out His Holy Spirit upon all flesh, as He says through the Prophet.

Hence no one can say “Lord Jesus” except in the Holy Spirit. How, then, can one who does not say that the Spirit is from the Son say “Lord Jesus” in the Holy Spirit? Whoever teaches this curses and blasphemes Jesus [Col. 0387B], removing the Son from the Father’s bosom and making the Spirit a middle term between the Begetter and the Begotten. The procession surpasses human understanding; for first the χαρακτήρ of the substance must be understood, and then the sending forth of the Spirit. For without the χαρακτήρ, the Son, it is impossible to understand the Father alone.

Indeed, insofar as He is Father, He has the Son; but insofar as He is Father, He does not send forth the Spirit. Therefore, if the Son must first be understood as the immediate and immutable χαρακτήρ of the Father, then in this order He Himself is prior to the Spirit. Hence the Spirit is called the image of the Son, but not of the Father. It should be noted, however, that the teachers of the Church do not judge image and χαρακτήρ to be the same, but distinguish one from the other.

[Col. 0387C] They say, therefore, that a chest has the image of the chest-maker: for, on seeing a chest, I know that it was made by a carpenter. If I see a ship, I immediately understand it to be the work of the craftsman who constructed it; and this work is the image and glory of that craft. It is by no means the χαρακτήρ of the person of the maker. For neither the chest nor the ship contains the bodily form of the human artisan. In the same way, they say that man is the glory and image of God who fashioned him—not the χαρακτήρ of the Creator’s Person, but only an indication of His will or action. But they truly believe that the Son alone is the χαρακτήρ of the Father. For He says: “He who sees Me sees the Father”—not the Father Himself, but [Col. 0387D] One such as the Father is.

The Son is the perfect form of the Father, existing equal to Him in every respect; and the perfect form of the Father’s substance contains inwardly everything that belongs properly to the Father. Therefore it does not omit the very sending of the Spirit from the Father. If it lacks this, the Son is not the complete form of the Father’s substance, because there is something in the Father which He Himself does not possess.

Further, if the Person of the Father is greater than His χαρακτήρ, the Father did not beget Him from His whole being. Conversely, if the χαρακτήρ exceeds the Person, it lacks subsistence in respect of the excess. Therefore the χαρακτήρ must not exceed the Father’s substance, lest perhaps whatever exceeds it vanish as non-subsistent. Nor, again, should the Person of the Father be broader than His χαρακτήρ, lest that which the χαρακτήρ does not portray remain without form [Col. 0388A].

Further: either the Son portrays the whole Person of the Father or He does not. If He portrays the whole, it is evident that He does not leave the Father’s sending of the Spirit unportrayed; rather, the procession and sending are from the Son as from the Father. But if His χαρακτήρ does not mark the whole Person of the Father, He is not equal to His Father, whose χαρακτήρ contains greater things—namely, the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, which is the chief and greatest matter. Again, if it belonged to the Father alone to send the Spirit, the Son would by no means be His undiminished χαρακτήρ. But His image is equal to the Father, from whom the procession of the Holy Spirit truly flows.

[Col. 0388B] From this point we must now proceed to the subtle investigations of Nicetas, bishop of Thessalonica, concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, which do not rightly agree with the approved doctrine.

## Chapter XIX

“You Latins,” he says, “who believe that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son: if you say that He proceeds from the Son as from a first principle, and not as through the Son but as from the Father, you make absolutely two principles and, by destroying the generation of the Son, speak contrary to Damascene, Athanasius, Cyril, all the other Fathers, and to us, whose glory it is to follow the holy Fathers. But if you say that He is from the Son as from the Father through the Son, you agree with John Damascene, Athanasius, Cyril, and the other God-bearing Fathers; and, concerning the glory of the Spirit’s procession, you will be our friends and agree with us” [Col. 0388C].

And a little later: “Therefore cease to make this addition in expression, and no longer pronounce in the Creed, ‘Who proceeds from the Father and the Son’; but, according to the Fathers, say with us: ‘Who proceeds from the Father and is glorified together with the Father and the Son.’” Again: “If, therefore, you call ‘from the Son’ what we call ‘through the Son,’ having no other difference of meaning than the use of unlike prepositions, grant us these syllables, and we in turn will grant you more syllables, which may show, under this reminder, our common agreement and concord, removing the scandal caused by the destruction of syllables.”

[Col. 0388D] I should indeed have judged this man worthy of praise, had not, as I behold in the mouth of the strong Samson “food from the eater, and sweetness from the strong one,” a gourd burst forth whose extremities are exceedingly bitter. This bishop has exceedingly transgressed his proper bounds; and while instructing the venerable mother of an exemplary path, he has wandered far astray. He dared to say: “Cease to make this addition in expression, and no longer pronounce ‘from the Son’ in the Creed.” Whence comes to you, imperious bishop, this sustained confidence of speech?

The things you command and exhort men to do have neither coherence nor harmonious melody with what Christ taught, as is clear from what has been discussed above; what the apostles preached; what the holy Fathers confirmed by maintaining it, and, by confirming it, handed on to those desiring to come to faith—you shamelessly urge them to commit to silence, with arrogance and boastfulness [Col. 0389A]. You have meditated iniquity upon your bed, because you have not weighed your speech in an even balance. No logical necessity, no ordinance of the elders, no binding force of any decree, however discordant, compelled you to cry out such things. For your abundant inquiries overflow more richly with deceptive devices than they rest upon any support of even a plausible semblance.

By the same argument one may fashion any syllogisms whatever. “You Greeks, therefore, who say that the world comes forth from the Father and the Son: if you say that it comes forth from the Son as from a first principle, and not through the Son but as from the Father, you make absolutely two principles.” [Col. 0389B] Again: “If you maintain that the Father and Son send the Spirit, such that He is sent from the Son as from a first cause, you make absolutely two causes of the mission of the Holy Spirit.”

But because this has been discussed more fully in the first book, it does not now seem necessary to repeat it. Nevertheless, what must by no means be left unsaid must be confessed without fear: that a first principle and a second principle in the Trinity ought neither to be accepted nor believed. For although the Father is without a principle and the Son is from a principle, yet in the same sense and in the same way each is regarded as Creator of the world and as principle, and likewise as one cause of the sending of the Holy Spirit.

But why they are called two has often been stated. Just as the dimensions of a body are called three, not because they are divided or dispersed, but because each has its own proper account, so the Father and Son are not called two in substance; rather, because each possesses a distinct account, according to which two hypostases—that is, persons—are understood [Col. 0389C]. And just as depth, attributed to a body, receives its being depth from length and breadth, and the mind cannot otherwise admit it to be depth unless it proceeds equally from both; so the Paraclete receives from the Father and the Son that He is the Spirit of both. Nor can He properly be understood otherwise than by believing that He receives existence equally from both. Therefore it in no way follows that there are two principles or two causes of the Holy Spirit because He proceeds from the Father and the Son.

## Chapter XX

[Col. 0389D] Therefore, since the knot of this position has been untied, it follows that we must answer concerning the preposition *per* (“through”). The preposition *per*, placed with the name of the Son as stated, is either one of diminution, or of intensification, or of equality in relation to the preposition *ex* (“from”). But it cannot be placed in the sense of diminution or intensification. For the Son has nothing less and nothing greater than the Person of the Father, as has been shown; He possesses immutability in every respect. It remains, therefore, that *per*, joined to the Son, is a preposition of equality in relation to *ex*.

Therefore, to say that the Spirit proceeds through the Son does not remove His being from the Son. The preposition *per* is not one of diminution, as Paul shows by attributing it to the Father as well as to the Son: “God is faithful, through whom you were called into fellowship with His Son, our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. I) [Col. 0390A]. In this passage *per* is applied to the Father’s name: the Father called us, because we did not come to Him from ourselves or from our own works. Again, he maintains the same sense where he says: “Paul, through the will of God,” who by willing made him an apostle.

Here it appears that those who try to distinguish “through the Son” from “from the Son,” lest the Only-begotten Word of God be understood as without principle, are refuted because *per* is applied not only to the names of Son and Spirit, but also to the name of the Unbegotten. Again, writing to the Hebrews, he applies *per* to the Father, saying: “He said: Him for whom are all things, and through whom are all things” (Heb. II). [Col. 0390B] A little later, deriving *ex* from *per*, he adds: “For He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one” (ibid.).

In this passage it must be observed carefully that the Apostle resolves *per* into *ex*, not *ex* into *per*. But Nicetas, bishop of Thessalonica, urges the Latins to abandon the Apostle’s thought and expression, exhorting them to transfer *ex* into *per* where they say “from the Son.” While he removes *ex* from the Son, he removes *per* from the Father, as though *ex* must never be joined to the Son nor *per* to the Father, but *ex* should be prefixed only to the Father and *per* only to the Son in the distinctions of the Persons.

Therefore all things are through the Father: that is, the Father is the cause of the Son, the Spirit, and every creature. For He who sanctifies—that is, the Son—is from the substance of the Father by generation [Col. 0390C]; the Spirit proceeds from the same Father by procession; and those who are sanctified—that is, human beings—and every creature exist from the Father by creation. Since, therefore, the Son is through the Father and the Holy Spirit is through the Father, as the vessel of election declares, the Son is generated through the Father and the Spirit proceeds through the Father.

Indeed, nothing truer can be said than that the Son is through the Father—that is, generated from the Father—and that the Spirit is through the Father—that is, proceeds from the Father. But both Greek and Latin confess that the Holy Spirit proceeds through the Son. It remains, then, according to the Apostle’s authority and interpretation, since the Spirit has existence equally through the Father and through the Son, and *per*, placed with the names of both, retains the same signification, simply and absolutely to confess that the Spirit proceeds from the Son as from the Father.

Further, among the Greeks the preposition **διά** (*dia*), which sometimes means “through,” when construed with the genitive means, as grammarians state, either action, assistance, or a means among the Latins. It signifies action, as: “Signs were performed through the apostles”—that is, the apostles performed signs. It signifies assistance, as: “I was enriched through you”—that is, by your assistance and help. It signifies a means when it indicates passage through the middle of a place or time: for example, “I passed through the forum,” “I sailed through the sea,” “I was detained with a friend through the middle of the day.”

Thus, when it is said that the Spirit proceeds through the Son, *per* signifies either action, assistance, or a means [Col. 0391A]. But if it signified a means, the Son would not communicate with the Spirit, and the preposition would be not merely one of diminution but of complete alienation. Nor would Son and Spirit have any relation to one another other than that of water and channel, door and saw, or place and what is in a place. Therefore it signifies either action or assistance, indicating that the Son is, in His own manner, co-sender and helper with the Father in sending the Spirit.

Accordingly, the much-approved and much-celebrated substitution of *ex* by *per* is void. When these are prefixed to the Unbegotten and the Only-begotten, they retain the same sense of intensification, as is clear from what precedes and what follows. For the Apostle writes to the Galatians: “Paul, an apostle, not from men, nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father” (Gal. I): that is, from Jesus Christ and God the Father, who caused him to rely no longer upon the Law but upon Christ. Again: “I did not receive it from man, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ.”

Finally, the title “Paraclete” admits the preposition *per*, when the Apostle says: “That He may grant you, according to the riches of His glory, to be strengthened with power through the Spirit in the inner man” (Eph. III) [Col. 0391B]. The Spirit is He who grants strength. Hence Isaiah writes “the Spirit of strength,” through whom and from whom the word of wisdom is given.

[Col. 0391C] In this matter heretics and all others who attribute *per* to the Son as signifying diminution are mistaken. For from the foregoing it can be understood without error that *per* is applied to the Son and Father in the same sense, sometimes signifying action and sometimes assistance. It is nowhere found to signify diminution: “When God shall judge the secrets of men through Jesus Christ” (Rom. II). For this means that Christ will render to each according to his deeds. For the Father judges no one, having given all judgment to the Son (John V), by whom we were justified when we were sinners and, being far off, were brought near, cooperating to preserve us in righteousness; who suffered death for love and justified through death; through whom, as all things do, we came into being.

He is indiscriminately called God and Lord God: for example, “from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, Lord”; and, “The Lord said to my Lord” (Ps. CIX). Here the Father appointed the Lord heir of all things, through whom He also made the ages (Heb. I) [Col. 0391D]. How this ought to be understood the Prophet testifies, saying: “In the beginning, O Lord, You founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of Your hands” (Ps. CI). The theologian John confirms the same in other words: “All things were made through Him”—not as through an instrument, as the Arians bark when they say that all things were made through the Son, who was not Himself their maker but, falsely, an instrument. For all things were made through Him, who is the maker and creator of all visible and invisible things.

But if the proposition of Nicetas the bishop is true—that the Spirit proceeds through the Son while the Son does not send Him and is not a partner in such sending—it cannot be denied that, under such a formulation, the Spirit proceeds through the Son as through an instrument: the Father sends the Spirit through the Son, whether the Son sends with Him or does not send with Him. If the Son sends the Spirit together with the Father, He Himself sends the Spirit as the Father does, thereby eliminating “less” and “more.” If He does not send with Him, being ineffective, it remains that the Son is the Father’s instrument—the impiety that Arius vomited forth—like a ship moved by its rudder [Col. 0392A]. In the rudder there is neither the principle nor the cause of the ship’s motion. The helmsman alone, being in the ship, moves it externally by the instrument, namely the rudder.

[Col. 0392B] Whoever, therefore, asserts that the Father alone is the principle, excluding the Son from the ineffable procession, places the Son outside the Father, tears the Only-begotten from the bosom of the Unbegotten, and makes Him an instrument. What could be more impious? Therefore the Spirit who proceeds through the Son undoubtedly proceeds from the Son. For just as it is true to say that all things were made through the Son and that the Son made all things, in the same way this statement is true: the Spirit proceeds through the Son and proceeds from the Son.

This has been demonstrated by an abundance of arguments and examples which almost exceeds counting. The Spirit of the Son proceeds from the Son: He established apostles and prophets in the Church, in whom He placed the Holy Spirit, as Peter, chief of the apostles, affirms in his First Epistle: “The prophets who prophesied of the grace that was to be in you sought and searched concerning our salvation, searching what or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ in them was indicating, when He foretold the sufferings that belonged to Christ and the subsequent glories” [Col. 0392C].

For through Isaiah (LIII) He said: “Like a sheep He was led to slaughter”; through Jeremiah (XI): “Come, let us put wood into His bread.” Through Hosea (VI) He signified the resurrection: “You will revive us after two days, and on the third day we shall rise in His presence.”

[Col. 0392D] The Evangelist Mark indicates that the Spirit is Christ’s God: “There were certain scribes sitting there and reasoning in their hearts: ‘Why does this man speak thus? He blasphemes.’ And Jesus, immediately knowing in His Spirit that they were reasoning thus within themselves, said to them: ‘Why these things?’” and so forth (Mark II). They accused Jesus because He forgave sins, since forgiveness of sins belongs to God alone. But Jesus, knowing their thoughts by His Spirit, which searches the depths of God, gave them a sign that He is God, because He searched their hearts. For God alone knows what is in every person’s heart.

Therefore, although the Father is God and not from God, and the Son is God from God—not as from a first principle—neither is the Holy Spirit from the Father as from a first principle, because He is not from Him as from a first God; much less is He from the Son as from a first God or first principle. Just as no “first God” is said in the Trinity because there is no second, so for the same reason one must not speak of a “first principle” in the Trinity [Col. 0393A], because it has no second.

Since these matters have thus been demonstrated, it remains to show how far this same bishop departs from truth when he asserts that the Latins hold beliefs concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit contrary to the great Cyril, the great Athanasius, and the other holy Fathers. For the great Cyril, Athanasius in many divine Scriptures, and the other Fathers filled with God, by no means give assent to him; in their treatises they have left publicly written what the Latins believe and confess.

## Chapter XXI

[Col. 0393B] The great Cyril, therefore, in his first discourse, *Worship in Spirit and Truth* (**λατρεία ἐν πνεύματι καὶ ἀληθείᾳ**), bears witness to the Latins, saying: “Do you suppose that the divine Spirit has become a soul for a human being according to nature? And how is such an understanding not highly incongruous? For the soul itself would have remained altogether immutable; but it is now mutable, whereas the Spirit is in no way mutable. But if mutability is weakness, a stain would redound upon the divine nature itself, since the Spirit is the Spirit of God the Father, and indeed of the Son, who is poured forth substantially from both.”

[Col. 0393C] The same writer, in his commentary on the prophet Joel, on the chapter, “I shall pour out of My Spirit, and your sons shall prophesy” (Joel II), states as follows: “The grace given from above had indeed been delayed, but it was renewed in Christ, who is the second Adam. But how was it renewed? In that He is God and the Son of God according to nature: for He was born from God and the Father, is His own, and the Spirit is in Him and from Him, just as He is understood to be in God and the Father. But in that He became man and appeared among us, He is said to possess the Spirit as coming upon Him. For the Holy Spirit descended upon Him in the form of a dove when, as I said, He became as we are and, in the economy, was baptized as one of us.”

And a little later the same saint says: “Those numbered among the sons of God had to be enriched with the grace of the Holy Spirit; and Christ brought this about, as the holy Peter affirms, saying: ‘Therefore, exalted by the right hand of the Father, having received the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father, He poured out this which you see and hear’ (Acts II). He receives as man from the Father what belongs to Him naturally; but He pours it abundantly upon us because He is God according to nature” [Col. 0393D].

This is what the saint says. But where the understanding is the same, the account of substance is the same; and where the account of substance is the same, equivocation is excluded. Therefore, according to this great man’s understanding as well, it is clear that the Spirit is said univocally to be from the Father and the Son.

The great Athanasius likewise, in his confession of faith, plainly affirms procession from the Son. For he says: “The Spirit is from the Father and the Son, not made, nor created, nor begotten, but proceeding.” The most eminent teacher of the Church, Gregory the Great, pope among the saints, says to Peter the deacon concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, in a chapter whose Greek translation is not faithful: “Truth itself, in order to increase faith in the disciples, said: ‘Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you.’ Since it is established that the Paraclete Spirit always proceeds from the Father and the Son, why does the Son say that He will depart so that He may come—He who never departs from the Son?” [Col. 0394A]

The holy Epiphanius, archbishop of Cyprus, in the book entitled **Ἀγκυρωτόν** (*Anchored*), because it is an anchor of faith, records the following concerning orthodox faith. “Blessed Peter,” he says, “said to Ananias: ‘Why has Satan tempted your heart, for you to lie to the Holy Spirit? You have lied not to human beings but to God’ (Acts V). Therefore,” he says, “the Spirit from the Father and the Son is God, to whom those who withheld part of the price lied.” Again: “For the Spirit is God, and the Spirit of the Father, and the Spirit of Christ—not according to any composition, as soul and body are in us, but in the midst of Father and Son, from the Father and the Son.” Again: “God is wholly Life; therefore the Son is Life from Life. ‘For I am Truth and Life.’ But the Holy Spirit is from both, Spirit from Spirit, for God is Spirit.” And further: “Do we say that there are two Sons? And how then is He Only-begotten? Rather, who are you to answer God? If He calls the Son from Himself, but the Holy Spirit from both?” Again: “The Holy Spirit is Spirit, the third light from the Father and the Son” [Col. 0394B].

[Col. 0394C] John Damascene alone seems to dissent from the great Cyril and the other holy Fathers, if indeed he writes thus: “We say that the Spirit is from the Father, and we call Him the Spirit of the Father. But we do not say that the Spirit is from the Son, although we call Him the Spirit of the Son.” Yet even if Scripture stands thus, this saint does not disagree with the Latin truth, if this is referred to the custom of the Greek Church, which down to the present day confesses that the Spirit is not from the Son.

[Col. 0394D] For if we call Him the Spirit of the Father and the Son, as the holy man affirms with the Apostle, then we must confess that the Spirit belongs to both either equally and similarly or unequally and dissimilarly. If unequally, the Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, more of one and less of the other; and He will be infinite in respect of the greater, in relation to the Father, and finite in respect of the lesser, in relation to the Son. For everything that is contained and exceeded by something is bounded in the respect in which it is contained and exceeded. Therefore He will have a limit of intensification if He has a beginning of diminution.

But if whatever is perfect among us in nature, character, and reason rejects “more” and “less,” what must be understood in the divine Persons, endowed with every perfection? For what is perfect in every respect is stable and incapable of expansion. But whatever admits more and less suffers defect: it has participation, motion, addition, and imperfection. But the account of the three Persons remains always at the same limit.

## Chapter XXII
Moreover, the relaxation of anything arises from weakness; and weakness is contrary to nature. But in primary things, [Col. 0395A] whether simple or composite, and existing in their proper sphere, there is nothing contrary to nature. Therefore there is neither relaxation nor intensification. Thus the Spirit, who is the measure and limit of all things—which the world cannot contain—by what could he be intensified, or from what could he, through relaxation, receive a limit to his intensity? Therefore, when he is called the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, he is not more the Father’s and less the Son’s, since he exists as belonging first to both equally, inseparably, naturally, and in the same respect. For whatever belongs to two things equally and by nature is either their proper attribute or quasi-proper attribute. And it must be observed that “proper” is used in two ways: in itself and in relation to something else, as the philosopher maintains. Proper to a human being in itself is the naturally gentle animal, which distinguishes him from all other things. [Col. 0395B] But relatively, being two-footed, in comparison with a horse, is proper to a human being; and ruling, in relation to the body, is proper to the soul, just as serving is proper to the body in relation to the soul. A proper attribute of this kind does not distinguish from everything, but from some particular thing. In this sense the Spirit is called proper, or quasi-proper, to the Son. For he does not distinguish the Son from the Father, but universally distinguishes both the Son and the Father from creation.

From these facts follows a necessity of this kind: every proper or quasi-proper attribute according to nature is communicated equally by those to whom it is proper or quasi-proper. But the Holy Spirit is proper, or quasi-proper, to the Father and Son according to nature. Therefore, the Holy Spirit, being what the Father is and what the Son is, belongs equally and naturally to the Father and the Son. [Col. 0395C] Whatever belongs equally and naturally to the Father and Son belongs to both in the same respect and under the same consideration. Therefore the Holy Spirit, being what the Father is and what the Son is, belongs to both in the same respect and under the same consideration.

Faith also supports this conclusion, since contradiction finds no place in such matters. Certainly, when it is said without falsehood, “The Holy Spirit is of the Father and of the Son,” its contradictory is wholly rejected as entirely false: “The Holy Spirit is not of the Father and of the Son.” This occurs most frequently with equivocal terms.

Moreover, [Col. 0395D] the Holy Spirit, being what the Father is and what the Son is, belongs eternally, similarly, equally, and according to nature to the Father and Son. But whatever belongs eternally, similarly, equally, and according to nature to two persons, because it does not adhere more closely to one than to the other, does not have being more from one than from the other. For if it derived existence from one but not at all from the other, the dissimilarity would be evident; equality and equilibrium would not embrace both persons; and the law of things that follow nature, which knows no inequality, would abandon its proper bounds. Therefore the Holy Spirit, being what the Father is and what the Son is, because he does not adhere more closely [Col. 0396A] to the Father than to the Son, does not have being from the Father rather than from the Son.

From these reasonings, then, of the man recently mentioned, the interpolation set forth above is plainly exposed; and it is shown that the discourse issued by him on Holy Saturday has suffered violence and corruption through a detestable and wicked alteration. For where he dealt principally with the Trinity, rehearsing the properties of the three persons, he produced nothing of this sort. He merely transmitted to posterity the words read above, not as his own view but according to the usage of the Eastern Church. Nor had anyone orthodox in faith before him inscribed anything similar upon the page.

But in the aforesaid discourse, contrary to right and to the judgment of the Fathers, the assertion that the Spirit does not have existence from the Son [Col. 0396B] has been inserted by certain persons seeking solace in falsehood rather than investigating the paths of truth. That this is so is shown most aptly by the sequence of the words themselves, the difference of style, the irrelevant and erroneous insertion in the conclusion, and above all by the fact that it is nowhere found written among certain saints.

Certainly, if the Father alone sends forth the Spirit of the Son, the Son does not share in that sending forth. For if the Son shares in it, the Father alone does not send forth the Spirit of the Son, since his Word shares in it; and those who teach this are by no means to be charged with error. But if, as the Greeks say, the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, then the Father alone sends forth the Spirit of the Son, without the Son sharing in it. What consequences tortuous evasions connect, the sound of truth rejects, and the breathing-forth of that same Spirit overturns. For it follows that there is something profane and abominable: namely, that the Father sends forth the Spirit without the power and wisdom of the Father sharing in this; for Christ is the power and wisdom of God the Father, as the Apostle declares. Therefore, on this account, the sending forth of the Spirit will be powerless and foolish, and its cause and principle irrational.

The Spirit himself, being the Spirit of the Father and Son, will be adventitious to the Son unless he proceeds from the Son as from the Father. But if the Father is understood as sender while power and wisdom are excluded, the Father himself, insofar as he is constituted sender, is powerless and irrational. Yet that utterance is impious and execrable which declares the source and [Col. 0396D] cause of the Holy Spirit, giver of every good, to be foolish and powerless. For these reasons, I think it has been made plainly clear that the Son, who is the power and wisdom of the Father, sends forth his Spirit together with the Father himself. Every successor of great Peter, steadfastly, devoutly, and truly following the footsteps of all the holy Fathers, maintains this; and he publishes to the whole world the judgment of this decree—as impregnable through fellowship with truth, gratifying to just desires, rich in justice, supported by ancient authorities, issued by Christ the supreme shepherd, and possessing complete citations—and rightly judges that it should be embraced from ancient times.

## The Complete Works of Peter of Celle, First Abbot of Celle, Then of Saint-Remi at Rheims, and Finally Bishop of Chartres

In the year of the Lord 1183, alternatively 1187. Collected into one volume from printed and manuscript books through the care and diligence of a Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint-Maur (Dom Ambrose Janvier). (Paris: Ludovic Billaine, 1671, quarto.)

[Col. 0397]

## Dedicatory Epistle to the Most Illustrious Prince of the Church, Charles-Maurice Le Tellier, Titular Archbishop of Nazianzus, Coadjutor of Rheims, and Grand Master of the Royal Chapel

That our Peter should appear under the auspices of your name, most illustrious prelate, is demanded no less by the laws of justice than by our conscience. A treasure has been dug up again in your field—that is, in the monastery of Saint-Remi in your metropolitan see—where until now it had lain hidden for the most part. From there Jacques Sirmond brought forth the letters of our Peter, and we his sermons, so that at last we may offer you Peter restored to life, or whole: certainly a small gift in proportion to our wishes, yet, as we hope, not unworthy of your eyes.

Peter was a man as zealous as any of his age for ecclesiastical discipline and pure morals. All his little works breathe this one purpose. Who would not hope that the labours of so great an author will be received with kindly eyes by you, who are endeavouring to arrest and recall the fleeing discipline of the ancient canons? Such is the judgment formed of you, most illustrious prelate, by the most distinguished senate of the French clergy. When it wished the restoration of provincial councils to be approved by our Most Christian king, it selected you alone from that entire gathering of most eloquent men as its spokesman: so that, through the power of your keen intellect, you might lay that proposal before the royal ears with proper dignity, and through the ardour of your zeal might inspire them. The gravity and majesty of your eloquence surpassed the great expectation of all; nor was the speech less pleasing to the king than the person who delivered it.

In this undertaking you will find in our Peter a man in accord with your desires. For if you love—as indeed you do love—the ancient discipline of the Church, see how Peter teaches that “the old paths are not to be abandoned for new ones.” If you venerate the ancient canons, Peter, animated by the same devotion, says that “they are to be observed with an almost equal reverence to the Gospel.” If you judge that the teaching of the Fathers ought to be followed, Peter judges likewise; he held that “the novelty which departs from the footsteps of the Fathers—in faith, in morals, and also in novelties of expression—is always to be anathematized.” If you desire the use of councils to be restored, you have a man whom Pope Alexander III himself invited to the general Lateran council. When Peter could not travel there because of the infirmities of old age, he gave excellent counsel to Alberic, chancellor of Rome, and to the other Fathers of the council: above all, “that, armed with a two-edged sword, they should cut away the mad superstitions that occur throughout the Christian world.”

If you love men full of divine zeal, you certainly love Peter, who stirred Pope Alexander and other shepherds of the Church against “the two evils of the Church, luxury and avarice” among sacred ministers—especially against simony and the other plagues of his age. Finally, if you seek a frank confession of truth purified from dross, you have Peter moved by the same zeal. “One man,” he says, “puts forward, without the weight of reason, whatever pleases him; another rejects whatever is not seasoned with evangelical or prophetic salt. One thing is more useful, another sweeter. I set the useful before the sweet. Sweetness chiefly delights the throat; usefulness benefits all the limbs more.”

Here, most illustrious prelate, is a likeness of our Peter, such as it is: certainly rough and unpolished, yet one that will not displease your eyes, if only you consider the merits of this most excellent man and the dignity of the most holy episcopate, which you adorn in yourself and revere in others. And if it lacks any grace, the favour of your kindness, as we trust, will supply the rest—your kindness, most illustrious prelate, from experience of which the superiors of our congregation were led to judge that Peter should now for the first time be offered to you in his entirety, so that they might furnish a public memorial of their esteem for you.

[Col. 0399]

## Preface on Peter and His Writings

[Col. 0399A] **1.** Peter of Celle, first abbot of the monastery at Troyes, then abbot of Saint-Remi at Rheims, and finally bishop of Chartres, is better known through his name and writings than through the praises of others. Indeed, he portrayed himself vividly, especially in his letters, in which shine forth outstanding piety united with no ordinary learning, integrity of character, candour and sincerity of spirit, unfeigned friendship, prudent zeal, mature judgment, lively intellect, and other gifts that usually make a great man. Jacques Sirmond long ago published those letters in print; others published various other works of his besides the Sermons, which we now at last present from the manuscript codex of Saint-Remi, together with Peter’s other writings, so that we may possess Peter, if possible, in his entirety. It is therefore useful first to set down some matters concerning his life and likewise some concerning the writings he composed.

**2.** Our Peter seems to have had Gaul for his native land and Champagne for his birthplace. From Letter 74, he had a niece, Hawis, whose marriage with Peter of Tornelle he defends against the charge of incest, both before Hugh, bishop of Sens, in Letter 9, and before Alan, bishop of Auxerre, in Letter 10. In Letter 119 he calls Hugh, canon of the Church of Rheims, his kinsman and friend. And in Letter 97, writing to Bernered, abbot of Saint-Crépin at Soissons, he mentions a certain lady who was his kinswoman. Other details regarding his parents and lineage are unknown.

**3.** It is not easy to determine where our Peter learned the rudiments of monastic life. It appears probable that this occurred at Celle near Troyes, although Letter 159 shows that in his youth he spent some time at the Parisian monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs. “I myself,” he says, “as a young man at Saint-Martin-des-Champs, tasted and saw through the truest experiences what I say.” And in Letter 145 he congratulates Theobald, abbot-elect of Cluny, as follows: “For I myself am servant and son of the Church of Cluny.” At what time he devoted himself to the religious life we shall consider later.

**4.** Peter was placed over the monastery of Celle, concerning which Sirmond’s note on the first letter should be consulted, about the year 1150. Certainly, before the death of Saint Bernard, whom he praises as recently deceased in Letter 14 to John, bishop of Saint-Malo, Peter himself was then abbot of Celle. There is also another letter of his addressed to Pope Eugenius III, issued in the name of the community of Saint-Méen. No letters of his are found to have been written before he became abbot. Bernard and Eugenius, moreover, died in 1153. How greatly monastic discipline flourished at Celle under Abbot Peter is evident from Letters 9 and 99.

**5.** In 1162 Peter moved to the abbey of Saint-Remi, then situated in the suburbs of Rheims. Yet he did not entirely cast off responsibility for his Celle, but, indignant at the evil conduct of his successor, took pains either to have him corrected or removed. On this matter there survives Letter 99¹ to Abbot Bernered, containing these words:

> “That successor of ours, abbot of Celle, because he has not multiplied well—indeed, because he has not cherished the eggs I left him, but has trampled down what was unfinished and destroyed what was complete—I can no longer keep silence. Rather, I undertake to try and test whether God may deign to regard my earlier labours, either by removing him entirely from the abbey or at least by correcting him of his folly and changing him for the better.”

Letter 100 concerns the same subject. In governing the monastery of Saint-Remi he accomplished many outstanding things; among them, as Letter 166 states, he rebuilt with new work the head of his monastery—that is, the upper circuit of the church apse. It is not the place here to pursue the rest.

**6.** Finally, he succeeded his friend John of Salisbury in the see of Chartres, not in 1182 but at the end of 1180, or at the beginning of the following year. For the Necrology of the monastery of Josaphat near Chartres establishes that John died on 25 October 1180. This is supported by the Chronology of Hugh, monk of Auxerre and a contemporary, who places John’s death in the said year 1180. Certainly, a list of the bishops of that church records that our Peter presided over the Church of Chartres for seven years, died in 1187, and restored the city walls and paved streets. In the above-mentioned Necrology of Josaphat he is commended in these words:

> “On the tenth day before the Kalends of March: the death of Lord Peter, bishop of Chartres, a man supreme and incomparable in our times. For, in addition to the adornment of the virtues bestowed on him by the Lord, he is reported to have flourished also with the grace of virgin purity. He lies in our choir, where the letter is read.”

This is all concerning Peter’s life and achievements. We must now note some matters about his writings.

**7.** The first place in our edition is occupied by the letters of our Peter and of Pope Alexander III, published by Sirmond in 1613 and illustrated with notes.

> **[Note: Col. 0399C]** Concerning Sirmond’s edition of the letters of Peter of Celle, Dom Brial makes this observation in *Histoire littéraire de la France* (vol. XIV, p. 241): “It is not apparent on what ground Father Sirmond divided these letters into nine books. This division did not exist in the manuscript; and, if he wished to divide them into books, it would have been more natural to make only two: first placing those which Peter wrote while abbot of Moutier-la-Celle, then the letters in which he bears the title abbot of Saint-Remi, and lastly those which he wrote while bishop of Chartres.”
>
> We follow in this edition the new order indicated here—and certainly the preferable one—by that most learned man; yet at the beginning of each letter we place in brackets the numerical markings of the Sirmond edition. [Col. 0400C–D] To this latest recension are added six letters of Peter of Celle not previously published among his works: the first and second, to Saint Thomas of Canterbury; the third, to Pope Alexander in the cause of Saint Thomas; the fourth, to Hugh, abbot of Saint-Amand, on behalf of John of Salisbury; the fifth, to certain Grandmontines, urging them to persevere in their purpose; the sixth, to King Louis. Also inserted are letters of Nicholas of Clairvaux and various persons addressed to Peter. (*Patristic Edition.*)

**8.** The second place is occupied by the Sermons, which he either delivered himself to disciples or composed at the request of friends. Theobald, formerly prior of Saint-Martin-des-Champs and later bishop of Paris, requested from him Sermons on Advent. Peter replies in Letter 19: “I had received the command to compose for you sermons on the Advent of the Redeemer; but the present day has added even a scarcity of daylight to the anxiety of its own malice.” His sermons, moreover, were so highly valued that, as he himself says, they were scattered to the four winds of heaven, and a monk of Saint-Bertin requested a copy. He modestly writes to him in Letter 167:

> “You desire to possess our sermons, which the four winds of heaven have cast in various directions like useless and superfluous feathers. If you have read them, did you not find them bloodless in the substance of their thoughts and feeble in the thinness of their words? If you have not seen them, who so persuaded you to seek them eagerly that, once found, you should immediately reject them?”

Finally, in Letter 34 to Abbess Matilda: “I have not forgotten your request to compose certain sermons of a sententious kind; but, hindered by many things, I have not been able to fulfil it so quickly.” We now publish for the first time Peter’s sermons, hitherto unpublished, obtained from the codex of Saint-Remi. To speak candidly of them as I think: they are indeed filled with devout thoughts, strewn with the flowers of Scripture, and suited to the ordering of a holier life; nevertheless, they are sometimes thin and insufficiently attached to a single theme, roaming among various divisions of the subject matter—as was almost the custom of those times—and occasionally mutilated and incomplete. Yet they are altogether worthy to be read by those who love ancestral piety, and worthy to be brought into the light for the memory of an excellent author. Moreover, in Sermon VIII on the Lord’s Supper he uses the word *transsubstantiavit* (“transubstantiated”), [Col. 0401B] a term also used in the same century by Stephen, bishop of Autun, in Book 13 of *On the Sacrament of the Altar*.

**9.** There follows the book *On the Loaves*, dedicated to his friend John of Salisbury, already published in the *Library of the Fathers*, as are the two following treatises. Peter mentions the little work *On the Loaves* in Letter 168.

**10.** Two other little works follow: the two books *On the Tabernacle of Moses* and the book *On Conscience*, addressed to the monk Alcher. Nothing occurs to be noted concerning them except that *On Conscience* appears to be more compact and vigorous than the other work.

**11.** Next comes the book *On Cloister Discipline*, dedicated to Henry, count of Champagne. Peter composed this book in old age, being in the thirtieth year of his monastic profession, as he testifies in the Preface, where he mentions the gout with sciatica by which he was afflicted. If you compare that passage with Letter 83 to Pope Alexander, in which he excuses himself from the Roman council on account of the same ailment, as he calls it, you will plainly infer that this book was written about the time of the council held in 1179. If this is correct, Peter professed the religious life not much before 1158. Still, nothing prevents his having suffered from the same condition more than once. Certainly, if, as observed above, he lived as a young man in the monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, he joined our Order long before the stated year, since by 1180 he was already advanced in age. Read his Letters 151 and 166. Acherius was the first of us to publish this treatise, in volume III of the *Spicilegium*.

**12.** A learned man who recently translated into French the Letter to the Brethren of Mont-Dieu, falsely ascribed by many to Saint Bernard, conjectured that it should be attributed to our Peter. The minds of all were already inclining toward this view, supported by carefully devised conjectures, when the latter part of that letter’s Preface, previously cut out of printed editions, was brought forth from manuscript codices, both in volume II of Bertrand Tissier’s *Cistercian Library* [Col. 0402A] and in the new edition of Saint Bernard’s works. At the end of this Preface the author supplies a list of his own works, which have been established as genuine works of William, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Thierry. It follows that the letter is truly the offspring of Abbot William, whose name, though abbreviated, is read in the salutation prefixed to the letter, thus—so it is expressed in all the handwritten books that I have seen:

> “William [sends] a delightful Sabbath to the lords and brothers H., the prior, and H.”

That is, to Haimo the prior and to another Carthusian monk whose name began with H. The letter, therefore, is to be assigned not to our Peter but to William. This is demonstrated both by the letter’s salutation and by that list of William’s works which the author himself drew up at the end of the Preface. The author’s age also confirms it, for the letter was addressed by an author already old to Haimo, prior of the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu. In the Preface to Haimo, the author says that he is already old and failing. Yet Peter was in the prime of life under Prior Haimo, who succeeded the first prior, Geoffrey, in 1144 and held office seven years; at that time our Peter had not yet reached thirty.

Certainly, from the question of novelty raised against the author by opponents, and refuted by him at the outset, we understand that the letter was written at the beginning of the foundation of the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu. This Charterhouse was founded in 1136; its first prior was Geoffrey, its second Haimo in 1144, its third Gervase in 1151, and Simon succeeded him—Simon to whom two letters of our Peter survive. Add to these arguments the great difference in style and composition between Peter’s authentic letters and other works, on the one hand, and the Letter to the Brethren of Mont-Dieu on the other. For in that letter the style is more swelling, the thoughts richer, loftier, and stronger, and the sequence of argument more sustained than is apparent in our Peter’s works. All these features correspond equally to the other writings of Abbot William, which breathe a serious, solid, and exceptionally learned intellect. These gifts certainly appear sufficiently in the writings of our Peter, but not, in my judgment, by comparison with William.

These, then, are the arguments persuading us that the aforementioned letter should be restored not to Peter but to Abbot William: namely, the name William expressed in the salutation, the catalogue of William’s works at the end of the Preface, the author’s age, and the style, none of which can suit Peter. Nor is this refuted by the fact that the catalogue of William’s writings is absent from most manuscript copies. For it occurs in certain manuscripts of the best authority, especially in the Thouane manuscript, which once belonged to the Library of Mont-Dieu. The reason why William did not assume the abbot’s title in that Preface is that he wrote the letter after resigning his office, when he had transferred to the Cistercians and become a monk at Signy, where he was also buried. But enough on this matter and on our Peter for the present.

[Col. 0401]

## Ancient Testimonies Concerning Peter, Abbot of Celle

### I. Letter 25 of Nicholas, Monk of Clairvaux, Written in the Name of His Prior to Henry, Bishop of Troyes

[Col. 0401D]

The abbot of Celle, a religious man who fears God, [Col. 0402D] a good man and one who has a good testimony from good people, conspicuous for life and learning, is bound to us also by such close friendship that he is not one among the rest but, beyond the rest, one with us. All that is ours is his, and all that is his is ours; we in him and he in us [Col. 0403A] are one, of his own order, in which he greatly pleased our lord abbot, your friend Saint Bernard, etc.

### II. Letter 172 of John of Salisbury to Count Henry

When Alberic of Rheims, surnamed “of the Gate of Venus,” which is commonly called Valois, had put these questions to me in your name, with several learned men present, I confess, my lord, that I was astonished and could not give credit to the inquirer, until he brought forward the venerable man, most faithful and devoted to you, the abbot of Saint-Remi. He both proposed the questions themselves and, with much earnest entreaty, requested an answer to them for love of you and of himself, firmly affirming that in life nothing was more pleasing to you [Col. 0404A] than to converse with learned men and about learning.

### III. Calendar of the Church of Chartres, 9th Day before the Kalends of March

Lord Peter, bishop of Chartres, of pious memory, died. He had previously been abbot of Saint-Remi at Rheims and, with the consent of Count Theobald, reformed the ancient custom of the *ban*.

Bernard writes to Peter, abbot of Celle, in Letter 293; John of Salisbury in Letters 75, 77, 81, etc.; and Nicholas of Clairvaux in Letters 20, 24, and 28, etc.

> **[Note: Col. 0403]** We have placed Nicholas’s letters before Peter’s responsive letters to him. (*Patristic Edition.*)

The same John of Salisbury mentions him as abbot of Saint-Remi in Letter 280, and Pope Alexander III does so frequently. Stephen of Tournai mentions him as bishop of Chartres in Letter 136.

[Col. 0403]

## Letter of Jacques Sirmond to the Carthusians of Mont-Dieu

(Edition of the Works, 1728, vol. III.)

To the most devout and God-loving lords, the prior and Fathers of the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu: Jacques Sirmond of the Society of Jesus, greetings.

When, on my recent return from Lorraine, access was opened to me within the enclosure of your most celebrated house, most reverend Fathers, and I was permitted more closely to behold what I remembered had been extolled concerning it in the words and writings of many, I was immediately amazed, wherever I turned mind and eyes, that everything surpassed our report and expectation. But, to say what is true, I was not so captivated by the appearance of the place, though extraordinary and most delightful in its natural character and cultivation; nor did the adornment and brightness of the chapels and of the entire sacred building so affect my eyes as the sight and admiration of your most holy community affected my mind.

For what, I reflected to myself, could be more honourable? What more mature? What more fitted to piety? Or what other form, if this is not it, could be imagined as the complete and perfect pattern of religion to be imitated? Surely this was why Mont-Dieu had long been visited with such eagerness; this was the charm and attraction that caused great men to love your dwelling places so ardently. For that reason Saint Bernard, whose cell marked by his footsteps and whose sacred garments, memorials of your hospitality, you rightly preserve, would sometimes gladly hasten there, leaving Clairvaux. For that reason the other Bernard, formerly abbot and later bishop of Palestrina, most illustrious in the ornaments of life and death, preferred the retreat of Mont-Dieu to Roman delights and to the cardinal’s mitres offered him. And what did our Peter, abbot of Saint-Remi, hold dearer, once he had tasted the sweetness of your fellowship and manner of life, than to return to you again and again—as his letters testify—either in person when he could, or certainly in longing, mind, and thought when he could not?

If all these men should now descend from heaven and return to you, nothing, in my judgment, would give them greater joy than to find among you the same flower of discipline which they had seen in its first freshness, remaining unimpaired and whole after so many centuries. Yet why should I make this the special praise of Mont-Dieu when it is common to all Carthusians everywhere? For, most reverend Fathers, the distinctive glory of your Order and your household is to bear an age unshaken by time, to know nothing of the revolutions of years, and to feel no damage from the passage of time. Thus others labour to restore their ruins; you labour that you may suffer none. They labour to revive the ancient dignity of their origin, now half-dead; you labour to preserve forever the dignity which you have hitherto maintained without decline.

To me, indeed, although all things in your institute and life are excellent, nothing seems more admirable or more illustrious for the glory of your name. There may be those whom other ornaments of your Order more strongly move: who gaze in wonder upon its beginnings, full of marvel; upon its many houses founded not without heavenly miracles; upon episcopal thrones either courageously refused by your members, after the example of Bruno, or, when resistance was impossible, administered with great holiness by Hughs, Anthelms, and Stephens; and upon other most illustrious bishops of various churches. Nor these only: even princes of the highest power and dignity, such as William, count of Nevers and Auxerre, cast aside crowns and tiaras and either embraced or desired the harshness of your little hair-shirt. There are also innumerable companies of Fathers most devout and outstanding in piety and learning: some filled every region with the fame of their virtues and wondrous works, while others illuminated the Church by most salutary and celebrated writings.

These things are indeed great and not to be mentioned without admiration. But other orders also count most or all of them among their own praises. Yours, and without parallel, is the perpetual firmness and constancy of ancient discipline of which I have spoken—so much more glorious and illustrious than that of others because, amid the instability and flux of the world that we endure, it surpasses the human condition to stand firm and imitate the unchangeable perseverance of blessed minds.

More than one reason, therefore, has moved me to return, most reverend Fathers, the favour of your hospitality through these particular letters. First, I wished by this means also to make their author attain his desire: he who was accustomed gladly to make his way to Mont-Dieu while alive might now return there in whatever part of himself he can. Then I wished you, in the image of your forefathers which this book will place before your eyes, to recognize the present blessings of your happy state, you who walk in the same footsteps. Finally, amid the unceasing watches of divine praise which you maintain day and night—ordered by action, varied with the seasons, but never interrupted—while you bestow the benefit of your prayers on the Christian world, may you grant that I, your admirer and reverent servant, should have some share, if you please, in so great a ministry. Farewell.

[Col. 0405]

## Letters of Peter of Celle, First Abbot of Celle, Then Abbot of Saint-Remi at Rheims, and Finally Bishop of Chartres

> **[Note: Col. 0405C]** The monastery of Celle, over which Peter presided as abbot, is situated in the suburb of the city of Troyes, at a place formerly called Germanic Island. Hence the monastery also had two ancient names. It was called both the monastery of Saint Peter, from its guardian and patron, and the monastery of Germanic Island, from the old name of the place. Thus Nicholas of Clairvaux’s Letter 24 in our codex is addressed “To Peter, abbot of Germanic Island.” It was also called the monastery of Celle-Bobin, as the learned and diligent Nicolas Camuzat rightly observed in his *Antiquities*. But today the common people call it in their native language *Monstier la Celle*, that is, “the monastery of Celle.” It was also sometimes simply called the monastery of Troyes, and its abbots the abbots of Troyes, though they were abbots of Celle. Peter himself speaks thus in Letters 7 and 54, doubtless because Celle was the most ancient of all the monasteries of the city of Troyes.

## Book One

Containing the letters written while he was abbot of Celle.

### Letter One

> **[Note: Col. 0406C]** First letter. He writes this, as also the sixth letter, in another person’s name; the rest in his own.

### To Pope Alexander III

[Col. 0405A]

**[I, 1]** To his lord Alexander, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, G.

In the gravest questions, as formerly men had recourse to Moses, so now, venerable Father, the whole Church of God has recourse to blessed Peter’s see and to yours. For the common care of all the churches is laid upon you as universally as the words addressed to Peter appear to have been singular and special: “And when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren” (Luke 22). Yet, to spare you a long account of a protracted affair, our Church of Der [Note: [Col. 0406C] Our Church of Der. That is, the monastery of Der, situated in the forest of Der in the diocese of Châlons. Commonly called by the French *Monstier-en-Der*, as though “the monastery in Der.” Its name will recur often below in the letters of Alexander III; in Gerbert, letter 8, however, *Terdonensis* has been printed corruptly for *Dervensis*.] will not be delivered from the hand of the mighty G. except by the hand of almighty God—that is, by your bow and outstretched arm. Therefore it cries from [Col. 0405B] its distress and affliction to you, because its salvation lies in God’s hand and yours. For it looks to no human help: their hope is vain, their promise empty, their confidence nonexistent. But you, without doubt, possess a word powerful to deliver and strength sufficient to redeem. Thus, under your shadow it must either live, or else fail beneath the shadow of death—namely, G. Speak the word, holy Father, and your Church shall be healed. Behold, it has long been sick with a most desperate illness. Apply the healing poultice, so that she who is your daughter, sickly in herself, may through you become a most devoted handmaid and be redeemed.

We have instructed this our messenger both what to say and what to do. He himself will set out the matter more fully as it stands: how G. evaded justice in the presence of the bishop of Châlons; how he appealed before the archbishop of Reims solely to delay the case [Col. 0406A]; and how, after pledging faith to Lord Henry, count of Troyes [Note: [Col. 0406C] Henry, count of Troyes. To him letter 30.], he entered into a submission to arbitration, and afterwards attempted to withdraw from it. Seize the fox that is destroying our vineyard. This is our petition: that the case be remitted to the archbishop of Sens under such terms that G. be compelled either to abide by his arbitration agreement or to restore to us the possession or investiture which we shall be able to prove our Church once held.

## LETTER II. TO THE SAME

[I, 2] To his lord and father ALEXANDER, supreme pontiff, brother PETER, humble abbot of La Celle, his due submission and a son’s devotion.

[Col. 0406B] He who has no other refuge besides paternal bosoms seeks the same aid more urgently in necessity. Most holy Father, we rightly flee to you from the many tribulations surrounding us and from the oppressions of our princes, since Christ entrusted the governance of His Church amid the world’s storms to your zeal and care. We are already perishing unless the gracious God looks upon our shipwrecks. Justice, reason, truth, law, and equity are day by day banished from our borders, and their very memory is extinguished without measure and without mercy. Therefore, we beseech you, let your mercy look upon us, that our soul may live. Farewell.

## LETTER III. TO THE SAME

[I, 3] To his dearest lord and father ALEXANDER [Col. 0407A], supreme pontiff, brother PETER, the less worthy abbot of the brethren of La Celle, himself with devotion.

Where the preeminence of the cause itself suffices to plead its request, even the less worthy person of the petitioner is customarily received. The dignity of the petition makes up for the inadequacy of its advocate. Throughout our regions it is publicly known that the abbey of Fontevraud has been raised and secured by the privileges and benefactions of your predecessors. Yet the bishop of Poitiers, who ought to water and favor the plantation of God’s and your right hand, strives to diminish this Church’s liberty; contrary to established privilege, he compels the abbess to make a profession and promise obedience to him, though the see of Peter has reserved this to itself. [Note: [Col. 0407C] He compels the abbess to make a profession. This was an old controversy between them, as Abbot Suger’s letter to Eugenius III shows. There is indeed in the archives of Fontevraud a rescript of Adrian IV, which decrees that the abbess shall make profession and render obedience to the bishop of Poitiers on the condition that the bishop impose no burden upon the monastery. This shows either that the nuns did not immediately obey the pope’s decree, or that this letter was not written to Alexander but to Adrian before his rescript.] Do not, then, give your glory to another; but, removing every intermediary, foster both the abbess and the abbey, as is fitting, by your own blessing and protection.

## LETTER IV. TO THE SAME

[I, 4] To his dearest lord and father ALEXANDER, supreme pontiff of the universal Church, his son PETER, unworthy abbot of La Celle, with all affection, obedience, and voluntary submission.

Trusting greatly in your abundant goodness, I have sometimes written to you even concerning others’ affairs. But now, most holy Father, I am compelled to seek your merciful help in my own. The matter concerns the needs of our Church. We have a priory at Cantumerula [Note: [Col. 0407D] A priory at Cantumerula. It is dedicated to St. Serenus; see letter 72. Hence also the prior of Cantumerula in Salisbury, letter 115. This cell—for so they call it—is situated near the castle of Cantumerula in the district of Troyes. In the castle itself is a monastery of regular canons of St. Augustine, with whom the monks of La Celle have this dispute concerning the right of burial.], and in its cemetery [Col. 0407C] all those of the castle and of certain other villages have hitherto been recognized as having the right of burial. It is also established that in ancient times there was no cemetery at the castle while secular canons were there. But when regular canons succeeded them, our predecessor obtained, through the intervention of Count Theobald [Note: [Col. 0407D] Count Theobald the Great, mentioned in the following letter, to whom St. Bernard wrote several letters.] and Hato, bishop of Troyes, permission for a cemetery to be made there, solely for the burial of the canons and their lay brothers.

But the abbot and his canons, acting contrary to the agreement, buried even those who ought to have been buried in our cemetery both by right and by agreement. [Col. 0408A] When the matter had been disputed on both sides in the court of Troyes and had come to judgment, the abbot appealed. For this reason, sweetest Father, we implore your kindness, begging you both kindly to receive our messenger and effectively to grant our petitions.

## LETTER V. TO THE SAME

[I, 5] To the venerable father and lord, by God’s grace supreme pontiff of the universal Church, brother PETER, humble abbot of the cell of St. Peter at Troyes, all that he can offer.

May those who regard our humility as of some account before your exalted dignity find the fruit of their hope in the fulfillment of their prayers. For thereby your gracious condescension will appear more generous, our boasting in you will be strengthened, and our friends’ rejoicing at favors obtained will be more welcome. These men are our friends—indeed, friends of truth and honor—R., archdeacon, and Master H., who approach your piety and providence on behalf of granting the provostship of the Church of Soissons to Lord William. [Note: [Col. 0407D] Lord William. This was the fourth son of Theobald the Great, count of Champagne, distinguished both by his connection with royal blood and by the glory of his deeds; he was uncle and guardian of King Philip Augustus. The beginning of the ecclesiastical dignities—which he held in great number and of the highest rank—was not, however, the provostship of Soissons; for while his father was still alive he had already attained others, as Bernard’s letter 271 shows. Afterwards he was bishop of Chartres, then of Sens, finally of Reims, and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and legate in Gaul.]

Why should I explain how great his lineage is—indeed, how good—or whose son he was, unless I hoped that his father’s virtues and integrity in every kind of virtue still breathe in the Roman court? Certainly—and this is more desirable—the young branch itself does not degenerate from the rich sap of its paternal root. Since it is altogether expedient that such a man be raised up in the Church of God, [Col. 0408C] because many rise against her, saying, “There is no salvation for him in his God,” let neither the right hand of God and blessed Peter nor yours reject him. For he will bear fruit according to his kind, and will always obey with every service and obedience the commands of the Roman court and of the supreme pontiffs.

Moreover, he has two illustrious and mighty arms, by which he can raise up one bowed down and restrain one rebelling, and by which God’s shelter may protect him from storm and rain: Count Henry and Count Theobald, the king’s seneschal. [Note: [Col. 0408D] Count Theobald, the seneschal. Count of Blois, seneschal of Kings Louis the Younger and later Philip Augustus; he discharged this office at court after Ralph, count of Vermandois. In a charter of the same Louis for the abbey of St. Denis: “Publicly enacted at Melun in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1154, with those present in our palace whose names and marks are subscribed below: the mark of Theobald, count of Blois, our seneschal; the mark of Guy the butler; the mark of Matthew the chamberlain; the mark of Matthew the constable. Given by the hand of Hugh, chancellor.”] They are his brothers and will assist and advise him in every way. Farewell.

Master H., a man of proven integrity among us, taught Master I., our clerk and friend, and did him many kindnesses. We commend him to you with the utmost earnestness.

## LETTER VI. TO POPE EUGENIUS III

[I, 6] To his lord and father EUGENIUS, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, the humble convent of Saint Mevennus [Note: [Col. 0409D] Convent of St. Mevennus. A monastery of the Benedictine order near Saint-Malo in Armorica. Thus the Bishop John named in this letter is bishop of Saint-Malo; our author writes to him in letter 16.] sends humble greeting with all submission.

[Note: [Col. 0409D] To Pope Eugenius. Eugenius III sat not merely before Alexander III, to whom the foregoing letters are addressed, but also before Anastasius and Adrian, whom Alexander succeeded. Thus the person who arranged these letters did not preserve chronological order throughout. This will become apparent from many later examples.—The authors of the *Literary History of France*, vol. XIV, p. 243, consider the first five letters to have been addressed to Eugenius himself, with Alexander’s name inserted through a copyist’s carelessness. Patristic edition.]

One who returns with due humility to the bosom of your mercy customarily finds not only the caresses of maternal gentleness but also the sure protections of paternal concern. For after God, peace for all the Churches together, and for ours, lies in your hand. Therefore, most gracious Father, we pray that your goodwill may be present for our poor Church; and lest it be torn apart by a longer tempest, may it please you promptly to command silence to winds and sea by the authority divinely granted to you.

That your mercy toward us may be moved more powerfully and swiftly, we briefly make known our old and new dangers. The discipline of religious life and the fervor of the monastic order had formerly grown lukewarm as one in our Church, through negligence both on our part and on that of the abbot. Therefore, zealous for the house of God, your predecessor Lucius, of most holy memory, [Note: [Col. 0409D] Lucius, predecessor. Lucius II, successor of Celestine II and predecessor of Eugenius.] ordered our humility and our venerable bishop John to reform the order more diligently, renew discipline, and cut off its unprecedented disorder. Yielding to obey both his command and his welcome exhortation, we confess truly that we put the axe to the root of the tree [Col. 0409C] and wished the negligent abbot to be cut down, so that we might receive a more vigilant one.

And so it would have been, lord and venerable Father, had Satan, discoverer of every wickedness, not opposed us again, and had the archbishop of Tours not perversely altered his countenance and righteous judgment in this affair. For he first praised our election and confirmed it by your authority. Later, however, led—lest we say misled—by the intrigues of certain malicious persons, when no reasonable ground existed, he hardened his resolve against us and our pastor, wishing and advising him to abandon the flock entrusted to him. When the abbot perceived the unjust burden threatening him, he rightly appealed to your hearing.

After this appeal, certain members of the archbishop’s household and table pursued and persecuted our abbot, so that they seized one of his monks and one of his clerks, together with horses and certain goods, and shamefully mistreated them. Therefore, father and universal pastor of the Church, we urgently entreat your favor: look with an eye of mercy upon our misery, and allow—indeed, command—our case to be heard, not in the archbishop’s court, but in one where both our justice and his justice, or injustice, may be heard impartially. Let the grave bodily illness of our abbot, as well as the injury inflicted upon him, excuse his failure to appear before you.

## LETTER VII. TO ROLAND, CHANCELLOR OF THE ROMAN CHURCH

[I, 7] To his dearest lord and father ROLAND, chancellor [Col. 0410B] of the holy Roman Church, brother PETER, unworthy abbot of the monastery of Troyes, the little that he is and can offer.

[Note: [Col. 0410D] To Chancellor Roland. The very man who was afterwards elected pope and bore the name Alexander III. This letter was therefore written during the pontificate of Adrian IV, and the sequence is consequently interpolated, as we have noted.]

Supported by no aid of merits, but trusting only in your goodness, I ask your condescension to be present for our petitions. For, keeping more closely in my heart the word of your promise received through our messengers, I hold your person as bound to me by their right. Therefore, in the case concerning the church of Villamore [Note: [Col. 0410D] The church of Villamore. A second priory belonging to the monastery of La Celle, in the same district of Troyes.], stand powerfully for us against the injustice of the canons. Let not your conscience reproach you, for our cause is just. Farewell. The bishop of Paris will explain to you the circumstances of the matter.

## LETTER VIII. TO HUGH, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

[Col. 0410C]

[I, 8] To the venerable lord and dearest father HUGH [Note: [Col. 0410D] To Hugh of Sens. What a man he was, and how great, is declared by the letter of the clergy of Sens written to the bishop of Chartres concerning his election: “We have chosen as our pastor and pontiff our lord Hugh, our precentor, nobly born of Christian and God-fearing parents: a vigorous, modest, gentle man; competently trained in ecclesiastical learning; rendering to religious persons the service of love and honor,” and what follows.] archbishop of Sens, brother PETER, humble abbot of La Celle, himself with devotion.

Do the destroyers of Christ’s vineyard devour its grapes, or the ravening wolves of His fold its sheep, all day long—trampling them with their feet and tearing them with their hands—and do you, most gracious Father, neglect to oppose them by your watchfulness? Why do you not consider what, by office, by promise, and by love, you as a great shepherd owe to the sheep of the supreme Shepherd? Surely defense, instruction, and care. But what kind, and how great? Without doubt, as great as Christ’s and such as Peter’s. For Christ loves even unto death; Peter feeds according to a threefold feeding. Peter fed faithful souls by words, [Col. 0411A] examples, and miracles. It is not altogether impossible for any shepherd to set before the sheep entrusted to his care the pasture of God’s word and to provide good examples; but it is exceedingly difficult to revive the miracles of the ancients.

If working a miracle lies beyond men of this age, a faithful defense is enough for us. For to you, in Peter, it was said, “Feed my lambs” (John 21): that is, with sound doctrine. Again it was said to you, “Strengthen thy brethren” (Luke 22): namely, by good example. Moreover, you hold the keys of the kingdom of heaven, so that you may exclude kids and admit lambs. Meanwhile, in the field of the world, while lamb and kid live together, the more unjust kid exalts himself and the more innocent lamb is oppressed; for while the wicked vaunts himself, the poor man is set on fire. [Col. 0411B]

Therefore Sarah—that is, the Church’s patience—complains against Abraham, that is, her shepherds, because Ishmael according to the flesh plays with Isaac, the son of promise. To this complaint is joined the divine command: “Cast out,” it says, “the bondwoman and her son” (Genesis 21). Would that, most loving Father, you had cast out our Ishmael according to the pope’s command! Yet let not my will, but yours, be done. I shall not approach as an insolent investigator of the sanctuary of your secrets, but as a humble petitioner. Perhaps the losses of long delay will be repaired by full and perfect justice. If you wish me to bring proofs or witnesses with me on the appointed day, send word. Farewell.

## LETTER IX. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0411C]

[I, 9] To the venerable lord and father HUGH, archbishop of Sens, brother PETER, humble abbot of La Celle, himself with devotion.

If my lord patiently applied friendly strokes to his servant where punishment is deserved, and rendered reward where justice is due, I would confess fault as readily as I would safely hope for pardon. Yet before entering the sea of your formidable censure, I anxiously deliberate whether I should accuse or lament the fate through which I find that your serenity has been clouded against me—whether deservedly or undeservedly.

How can I fail to accuse, or rather curse, that mischance through which I feel so great a downfall? [Col. 0411D] Let every mischance perish from which the setting of friendship arises.
