Let that be solitary and unworthy of praise which, severing the veins of love, gathers together the poison of enmities. Or perhaps that lot is rather to be lamented which drives both parties into a precipice, so that one fleeing frost may fall into a brazen arch, according to Amos: “The day of the Lord,” he says, “is darkness and not light; as if a man flee from a lion, and a bear meet him; or enter a house and lean [Col. 0412A] his hand upon the wall, and a serpent bite him” (Amos 5).

Behold, I offend the majesty of my friend and lord if I stand for Peter of Tornella. [Note: [Col. 0411D] For Peter of Tornella. He had betrothed Hawis, Peter of La Celle’s niece. Some persons—including Archbishop Hugh—disapproved of the marriage as contracted between blood relatives. Peter, on the contrary, recognized no impediment to the marriage. See again in this book, letters 19 and 74.] Behold again, I am called the brother of one destroying his own work if I pass over in silence what I have done in good faith, under a just title, and according to ecclesiastical custom. On one side civil law complains of me; on the other, natural law. But what then? Civil laws never corrupt natural laws.

Thus it is said to me—or rather, not to me, but about me: “Is this the religion of La Celle? Is this its truth? Is this its reputation? See how it fosters adultery—indeed, incest; see how it loves its own flesh, despises the canons and the Gospel, and patronizes iniquity.” These things are said against us, dearest Father, not by you but by your people. I could return the like—by lying, indeed, and yet by speaking truth; but the authority of your most holy reverence restrains my tongue, as does the inviolable integrity of my conscience and profession. [Col. 0412B] For the adversary celebrates a most victorious triumph if he provokes me from the camp of patience and humility into the battle-line of impatience and falsehood. I judge myself overcome only when, under any provocation, I transgress the bounds of religious life.

Let my detractors, then, hear—let them hear. I do love my flesh, but after the spirit; I love my flesh, but according to the Apostle; I love my flesh, but not excessively. Scripture says, “Do not despise your own flesh” (Isaiah 58). Blessed Gregory also says: “There are some who love through the affection [Col. 0412C] of kinship and flesh, and sacred writings do not contradict them.” And the Apostle says: “No one ever hated his own flesh” (Ephesians 5).

“My rivals,” they say, “we grant that one’s flesh ought to be loved, but not against justice; and adultery or incest wholly opposes justice.” Nothing is truer. But I know of no incest; I acknowledge a marriage lawfully contracted. I summoned the elders and examined them with the utmost care, jointly and separately, publicly and privately; and from their statements I could discover no impediment to the marriage. Of the witnesses now produced, one is less fit because of manifest hostility; the other for a reason to be kept silent until its proper place. Therefore I did not undertake to patronize iniquity as a despiser of Gospel or canons, for I have not willingly passed over a single iota or stroke of the law of God for the sake of present convenience.

## LETTER X. TO ALAN, BISHOP OF AUXERRE

[I, 22] To his dearest lord and father ALAN, bishop of Auxerre [Note: [Col. 0412D] To Alan, bishop of Auxerre. Alan of Flanders, likewise of the Cistercian order. He had formerly been the first abbot of the monastery of Arrembatoire in the district of Troyes. After he had been promoted from there to the see of Auxerre, he voluntarily resigned it some years later and returned to the cloister at Clairvaux, where he was buried.], brother PETER, unworthy abbot of La Celle, greeting.

It is true that flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God. I know it, nor can I plead ignorance. Yet I doubt whether, in one and the same case, the virtue of piety accompanying affection for the flesh weighs equally with it, or outweighs it, toward merit. Affection for the flesh alone is without merit; yet when it becomes excessive, it is burdened with merit—but bad merit. When, however, it follows piety, it is honored with merit—but good merit. Where it goes before, the judgment is again rendered uncertain.

I cannot fully search out the paths of my heart because the darkness of its varieties obstructs me; still less can I comprehend them. Thus the throng of phantoms standing about my heart hears within and reports without to the senses that seek the matter as it is. Why this seeming parable—or rather, riddle? That I may satisfy those who stand outside and judge what is within: [Col. 0413B] I support the cause of our niece not by affection of the flesh alone, but in the spirit of true piety and justice.

Far from my mind—indeed, from yours—be the thought that, because of the bodily union of the above-mentioned niece, I should condemn my own soul to everlasting fires! Yet I would certainly do this if I defended an unlawful marriage. O lord and ever father, whenever you please, dearest friend: by what ascent did that spirit of unbelief enter the holy seat of a religious soul, so that you would credit two men of most dishonorable life and reputation, and hesitate concerning a truth expressly declared to you by a friend? What hope of friendship could remain for me when you did not believe me and received utterly false witnesses against me?

Plainly, against the truth which I had thought I had already persuaded you to hold in your ear, [Col. 0413C] you received the word of men who would sell the righteous for wine, and, if they had birthrights, would sell them for a morsel. Did you thus wound your friend? But you say: “He is no friend who has stood in the way of truth.” Certainly, I say; it is as you say. But where is the truth? In number? For they were more numerous. Among drunkards and shameless men? Such indeed are those hired by favor, price, and fear. Though I do not now affirm it as fact, I am at least drawn by the strongest presumption to believe it.

The uncle who perhaps conducted him on his journeys at his own expense is the worst enemy and adversary of the niece and her husband. The archbishop wrote to the abbot that he should send canons; he reconciled rebels and men disobedient to the former abbot until the iniquity should be accomplished. [Col. 0413D] Is this truth, or even the appearance of truth?

Does this account of ours weary you? Yet, to speak without prejudice to what remains of your favor, you proceeded more wearily to your judgment. Why did you deny a postponement? What law, what canon teaches that even one postponement should be refused in such a case? Do not say that I had one, for before this I neither asked nor obtained one from you. Those matters had never been brought before your court so that the marriage calculation might be made. You exceeded your authority, lord; you exceeded it.

I seem presumptuous, indeed, in daring thus minutely to rebuke a bishop as an abbot, a lord as a servant—indeed, to recount to him the injuries inflicted upon myself by him. I would not do this unless I saw the dawn of reviving friendship in the fault conceded and acknowledged in your letters. Pardon must never be denied to one who asks it; fault must never be imputed to one who repents. Enough. Put the sword back into its sheath. Farewell.

## LETTER XI. TO HUGH, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

[I, 11] To his dearest lord and father HUGH, archbishop of Sens, brother PETER, humble abbot of La Celle, the spirit of grace and prayer.

If we are instructed to repay insults with patience, what ought we to return for a favor except favor, both by the law of nature and by the command of grace itself? And if we are commanded to love enemies, what should we do for friends? I think we should receive them as our very soul. This is surely the proof of perfect love: that every consideration is postponed to a friend’s advantage.

Thus, thus Master M., not forgetful of your benefactions, lest he become for you a cause of offense and your eminence incur the king’s wrath, bore upon himself the danger of hostility; and for your sake he temporarily withdrew from office until the adversary’s iniquity should pass. Therefore let your mercy cherish one whom your experience has found to be no ungrateful foster-child, and temper the malice of his troubles, because he hopes in the protection of your wings. For he is said to be loved more tenderly—indeed, more intimately—whose benefactor’s peace was dearer to him than anything else. Make peace for him, who spared not even his own peace for yours.

## LETTER XII. TO THEOBALD, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

[Note: [Col. 0413D] Incorrectly given as Thomas in Sirmond. Patristic edition.]

[I, 12] To his dearest lord and father THEOBALD, archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0413D] Legate of the Apostolic See. He was made legate throughout all England, except the bishopric of York, on the seventh day before the Ides of October, in the year 1167. This letter must therefore have been written after that year.], brother PETER of La Celle, whatever kind of servant he may be, himself.

We have become as persons consoled by the consolation of your holiness, so affectionate, so merciful, so full of sweetness and charity. May the Paraclete Spirit repay you with His consolation, because you have mercifully deigned to look upon our desolation. The reception of your letter stirred up our hearts, which, though not dead, had nevertheless already grown weak. [Col. 0414D]

We showed this your condescension and consolation to our lords and friends; and, in living hope, at their counsel, we have sent our brother to sojourn with you. Receive him; and because he scarcely has a place in his own land where to lay his head, let him meanwhile serve under your shelter and bring back to us fitting wages. Indeed, we trust in the goodness of God and in your liberality of spirit, which we have already tasted, that although he crosses your sea with only his staff, he will return in companies bearing many blessings. [Col. 0415A]

We commit our brothers and messengers to the discretion of your holiness for such arrangements as you see fit. In every prayer and benefit of all your people, we include you as our lord and fellow brother. Farewell.

## LETTER XIII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF SAINT-MALO

[I, 15] To his dearest and heartfelt lord JOHN, bishop of Saint-Malo [Note: [Col. 0415D] To John, bishop of Saint-Malo. A monk of the Cistercian order. The people of Saint-Malo venerate him as a saint and, from the iron grating then surrounding his tomb, call him St. John of the Grating. A letter in his name to St. Bernard survives among the letters of Nicholas of Clairvaux; there it is headed, “Brother John, bishop of Alet,” that is, of Saint-Malo.] and to Master the priest, [Peter offers] what he is and can offer.

Charity, patient though it be—wonderful to say—almost drives me to impatience. I saw your messenger empty of letters. What is this? Is your love of parchment so great, or has your charity thus been shortened? What is the cause of such importunate silence? What reason for love so mute and silent? Is it, I ask, a consequence in Brittany that where there is scarcity of bread, a failure of heart follows as well? I had heard of want of bread, indeed, but did not believe that a famine of virtues followed from it.

Certainly the flour and cruse of oil with the woman of Zarephath have not failed since our Elijah, the bishop of Saint-Malo, tasted of them. Certainly our love does not ebb; rather, it flows in and overflows. The bishop may be excused by the pressure of his labors, care for the churches, compassion for the afflicted, and reconciliation of those at variance. But what prevents the clerk from writing? What hinders him from composing friendly letters? Idleness? But study excludes it. Ignorance? Yet he has great skill in letters. Ignorance that a messenger was coming? Yet he brought me an unadorned greeting. Hurry in one hastening? Yet he brought more seals to more people. [Col. 0415C] There remains, then, negligence in friends, which must be condemned.

Since you did not send oil, you receive a sting; and therefore you deserved to be pricked because you refused to anoint. Farewell. If you are well, it is well with us.

## LETTER XIV. TO THE SAME

[I, 16] To his dearest lord and father JOHN, bishop of Saint-Malo, brother PETER, unworthy abbot of La Celle, with the Apostle in labor and distress.

Even amid our bitterness my soul rejoices; how much more when it contemplates the glorious recompense! For I remember that the righteous, troubled in a few things, shall be well ordered in many; [Col. 0415D] and that God will repay the labors of His saints. Therefore expectation is not vain where such a certain, welcome, and abundant reward is hoped for: certain, because of the truthfulness of Him who promises; welcome, because of the fulfillment of the receiver’s desires; abundant, because of the overflowing heavenly goods in participation in the Godhead.

This treasure is laid up in our bosom; it dwells between our breasts; by it every insipid thing is seasoned and made most suitably agreeable to our taste. O sweetness of my soul, do you think that the Lord [Col. 0416A] does not heed the miseries of His bound ones, or weigh in the balance of eternal judgments the pains of His children? “Are not these things,” He says, “stored up with me and sealed in my treasuries?” (Deuteronomy 32).

I wonder that you wrote that you were deprived of the patronage of our most holy father Bernard [Note: [Col. 0416D] Our father Bernard. These words pertain to the year 1133, in which the death of St. Bernard occurred.], when his holy soul, freed from the bonds not of charity but of mortality, not of affliction but of corruption, not of will but of necessity, now appeals more freely to the ears of the most merciful Creator for the needs of his people. May it not befall me to distrust his grace or despair of his prayers.

With so great a desire to speak with you, I scarcely bring myself to an end. For one whom I love without end, I can never write to enough or speak to enough. Our convent is your people; our people [Col. 0416B] are yours; my soul is yours. Would that I might see you before you cross over to those mountains, where, as we have heard, there are so many dangers. Farewell.

## LETTER XV. TO THE SAME

[I, 17] To his dearest lord and father JOHN, bishop of Saint-Malo, brother PETER, humble abbot of La Celle, greeting.

He who has even once tasted the marrow of charity knows that pompous and empty words have no weight in true affection. I certainly regard it as vain and as contemptible pretense to repeat daily the rudiments of love once it has faithfully and firmly adhered to the roots of the heart. It is also the part of one who fears or distrusts to wish by words to renew loves once born, as though time’s age customarily made true affections old.

It is not of the image of God to fall away from beginnings; it is not of virtue to waver; it is not of the glory of God’s throne to turn itself in another direction. Is not the soul in God’s image? Is not charity God’s virtue? Is not a pure conscience God’s throne and the seat of divine majesty? Therefore, as the Son, who is the image of the Father, always governs and rules what He once created; as the power of the Most High confirms and perfects what it works; and as the immutable seat of the immutable God’s eternity remains; so charity, rooted and founded in a pure heart, good conscience, and unfeigned faith, knows no setting, abhors corruption, and never tastes death. [Col. 0416D]

This charity, by its inward bond, joined our affections to each other. Acting as mediator between us, it sweetly, strongly, and wisely cemented our souls together in a single love. It has poured your love abundantly into me and, by pouring all of myself no less abundantly toward you, has given me to you. Therefore I beg your holiness to come to your unique and special friend with singular hope and a single request. Let your holiness not doubt that I am yours, whose man I truly declare myself to be. But unless you come to us for a just reason, [Col. 0417A] you will greatly diminish the integrity of our love. Farewell.

## LETTER XVI. TO THE SAME

[I, 18] To his dearest lord and father JOHN, bishop of Saint-Malo, brother PETER, humble abbot of La Celle, whatever he is and can offer.

We are greatly astonished that for so long a time we have been left, as though neglected, without greeting from your fatherhood. We do not believe this has arisen from negligence, but perhaps you have been so crushed beneath the unavoidable weight of your occupations that you have kept silence. At last we cry out after you. For we wish to stir up in you compassion for our sufferings. For a misfortune that may perhaps steal upon one is not proudly to be concealed from friends; nor is necessary assistance to be requested stubbornly or [Col. 0417B] shamelessly. Both extremes must be avoided, but especially the latter. Both are faults; but the one is more grievous to the sufferer, the other more disgraceful to the petitioner. For an evil kept hidden presses more severely; when improperly disclosed, it harms more openly. One arises from nobility of nature, the other from the offspring of necessity. Nature is always content with its own bounds; necessity is restrained by no laws. Thus importunity, the firstborn offspring from the womb of necessity, though most troublesome—for its hand is against everyone, and everyone’s hand against it—ought never wearily to knock at the doors of friends, nor ever to burden their ears.

Therefore, after weighing the matter, I determine within myself rather to be pierced by whatever darts of evils than [Col. 0417C] to interrupt the tranquil silence of those dear to me with accumulated cries and tears. Yet I do not refuse to lay before those whose faith is certain and friendship unquestioned both our sorrows and our needs: that I may satisfy my own conscience through a concise disclosure, and may not offend a friend through immoderate importunity. For one who makes such a disclosure accomplishes both: he does not conceal his need, and he retains the laws of friendship. For he either has no friend, or does not believe that he has one, who hesitates to reveal whatever his condition may be, or who presses as though extorting something from an unwilling person. A friend, indeed, is said both to share the confidence of every plan and voluntarily to help in all things.

I do not therefore wish [Col. 0417D] to fill your ears with most extensive complaints, since it is foolish to try to explain in words a matter that seems to exceed belief. We have said this because the church of the noble Blessed Aigulf, with all its appurtenances, has been so completely burned that nothing except books and the relics of the saints was saved from the fire.

[Note: [Col. 0417D] Church of Blessed Aigulf. Below the town of Provins in the diocese of Sens, it was endowed with revenues by Theobald, count of Troyes, and assigned to monks summoned from the monastery of La Celle about the year of Christ 1048. Hence the prior of St Aigulf in Epistle 35. When this priory was damaged by accidental flames, the relics of St Aigulf were, according to the custom of those times, sent into various regions to collect alms for restoring the church; this is the “pilgrimage of Aigulf” which he again mentions in Epistle 68.]

Moreover, it reduced a great many houses to ashes, so that before our eyes she appears like a hen, plucked bare, having neither feathers [Col. 0418A] with which to protect her chicks nor food with which to feed them. We ask nothing else of you except compassion, prayer, and counsel. It is necessary that Aigulf, who has nowhere to lay his head, should go as a pilgrim among friends and neighbours, asking for what he used to give when asked—and even when not asked. If he comes into your region, receive him as you would receive him himself. For you know who he is and what honour is due to him. Write concerning this to the bishop of Chartres and to others whom you judge appropriate. Farewell.

## LETTER XVII. TO THE SAME MAN

[I, 19] To his dearest lord and father JOHN, by the grace of God bishop of Saint-Malo, brother PETER, [Col. 0418B] humble abbot of La Celle, whatever he is and can be.

Is my lord well? Is he alive? As I suppose, either the bishop of Saint-Malo has become another man, or another has been appointed in place of mine. If another, I cease to wonder—but not to grieve—that he has remained silent who could not speak. For “a new king arose, who did not know Joseph.” If altered, I wish the alteration had not been so great as almost to amount to alienation. It is surely foreign to friendship to be able both to conceal and to pretend. A friend does not pretend, because of truth; nor does he conceal, because of the ardour that breathes within him. He does not pretend because he is without flattery; he does not conceal because, being of a most effective nature, he considers concealment a tomb, and thinks that not to appear is not to exist. He does not pretend because he does not know how; he does not conceal because he cannot. He does not know how to do the one; [Col. 0418C] he cannot do the other.

For what does wisdom not know? What cannot charity do? Whatever exists, wisdom knows how to know; whatever can be done, charity can do. It is not knowledge to know how to flatter; it is not power to be able to forget. O dearest friend and lord! Shall I attribute to your forgetfulness or to your negligence your abstaining, beyond all time and measure, both from visiting and from greeting your friends? Is it forgetfulness? If it is, it deserves death, deserves exile: it has taken the diadem from the bishop’s head and removed the breastplate from his breast. Forgetfulness destroys both what is highest in dignity and what is strongest in power—that is, wisdom and memory. Therefore, guilty of so great a crime against majesty, let it suffer capital punishment and [Col. 0418D] be remembered no more. What of negligence? Let it not be unlike in punishment, since it came first in fault. For such offspring—forgetfulness, namely—is born of such a mother, negligence.

I grieve, Father, at the lapse of your memory, now suspended for two years; and likewise at the loss of a friendship, for four days as though buried, for a long time. At least friendship, if it lives, ought to have sent word of its welfare; for it is friendship’s nature always to hate absence and [Col. 0419A] to seek the presence of friends. Perhaps it is occupied; but that which is always occupied is not pleasing. What perpetually holds one is a dwelling—indeed, a possession—not an occupation. Who, then, has so preoccupied—rather, possessed—friendship, that it has not, using its freedom and native nobility, extended its rays to us since former years? Are mountains lying between us? Is there a sea between us? Is there “a great chasm fixed” between us and you, so that those who wish to pass from here cannot, nor can any cross over from there to us?

But charity surpasses every height; many waters cannot extinguish charity; none can hide from its heat; it reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly. In our bishop—indeed, in a holy man and servant of God—who, O love, [Col. 0419B] has weakened you? Who has overshadowed you? Who has blunted you? Who has changed you? In others, certainly, I do not fail to know that, when wickedness comes upon them, your strength is weakened; by forgetfulness your light is overshadowed; by negligence your edge is blunted; and by hatred your whole substance can be changed. But in a holy man, what wickedness is there? In a diligent man, what forgetfulness? In a strong man, what negligence? In one full of charity, what hatred?

For if charity ever grows lukewarm, ever slackens, ever becomes dull in a holy man, what is external, not what is internal, must be blamed. Obstacles placed in the way falsify the truth of superimposed light, heat, and sharpness. Set before a two-edged sword the hardest iron or stone: its otherwise irresistible force recoils. Set a thick wall before fire: it heats more slowly. Put a bushel over a lighted lamp: [Col. 0419C] it will not rejoice in its light. Therefore, one must not suppose that the lamp does not shine, the fire does not burn, or the sword does not cut; rather, this must be attributed to opposing obstacles.

So the virtues of saints do not vanish from their root, but often keep silence because of the Sabbath of the Jews. In the meantime their spices distil and renew themselves in secret, so that when the day of opportunity shines at dawn, they may break forth into the effect of the desired work. Yet burning desire in the repose of leisure is equally renewed, as is fervent work in action. For God accepts work for the sake of affection, not affection for the sake of work. This Sabbath day is great—indeed, long—for us; and we regard its holidays as not ordinary or festive, but deadly and foul-smelling. [Col. 0419D] For negligence smells badly, while diligence always gives off a good fragrance. The idle sloth of Judaizers does not love the Sabbath because it is holy, but because it is inactive. But Jesus stood on the great day of the feast and cried: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7).

Truly, the day of the feast is great. Your charity has a great cry: let it speak at last—indeed, let it come, indeed, let it run to us. My soul desires you; your friends desire you. Show your face; let your voice sound in our ears. We have many wealthy bishops; we seek a poor bishop, one who does not [Col. 0420A] have where to lay his head. We still have among us the resting-place—not golden but muddy—in which you once rested. And enough of this.

## LETTER XVIII. TO THE SAME MAN

[I, 20] To his lord and dearest father JOHN, bishop of Saint-Malo, brother PETER of La Celle, humble servant as he may be, greeting which is in Christ Jesus.

“Hope deferred afflicts the soul.” True love, in patiently enduring its desire, is sometimes commendably willing to be overcome without anger. For there is almost nothing else in human life that cannot be softened by some art. Therefore the hope of your announced arrival, by as much as it more richly delighted your friend, has by so much more deeply afflicted him until now through the delay of postponement. For the mind seethes amid the recurrence of unforeseen events, now fearing that one contrary thing, now another, has suddenly happened. What more? One thought passes and another arrives; but uncertainty about the delay does not withdraw from the mind for even a moment. “The one,” it says, “is coming presently; perhaps the other cannot.” One anxiously recounts the inconveniences of the season; another sighs over the intolerable burden of business. Behold how great the darkness, how great the tumult of suspicions! Where is truth? Which of the aforesaid thoughts has the truer judgment? Or is it perhaps error, where what is true lies hidden, rather than a judgment? But the case is still before the court. For from many uncertainties scarcely—indeed never—can anything certain be drawn without a teacher’s demonstration.

Tell your friends, therefore, of the working of divine mercy concerning you, [Col. 0420C] so that, with every bond of uncertainty altogether loosed, we may without doubt take hold either of the left-hand path of compassion or of the right-hand path of congratulation. For a noble spirit is quite shamefully disgraced if it does not prepare itself to meet reciprocal kindnesses at least with equal steps. I also consider it shameful not in every way to take care against being overcome by a benefit. Nature—or the Creator of nature—imprinted this one and singular thing upon his image as a special privilege: that, under the strict rule of equity, it might more fittingly and excellently give than receive.

Neither the rust of exile nor the moth of poverty has shaken this form out of you. From it came your splendid repayment of great things for small, of more precious things for worthless; indeed, you sent a customary gift without any preceding comparison of service. The kind of gift is certainly to be valued more dearly; but the giver’s affection should rather be repaid beyond all comparison. For whatever else is given is held cheap in comparison with a lofty spirit. Farewell.

## LETTER XIX. TO THEOBALD, BISHOP OF PARIS

[I, 21] To his dearest lord and father THEOBALD, bishop of Paris,

[Note: [Col. 0419D] To Theobald, bishop of Paris. Previously prior of Saint Martin’s, of the Cluniac order. Our Peter composed sermons for him, just as Salvian, a priest, is said by Gennadius to have written many homilies for bishops.]

brother PETER of La Celle, most humble, greeting.

[Col. 0421A] The river of pressing causes, which cannot be forded, prevents me both from carrying out your command and from fulfilling our desire. For I had received your command to compose sermons for you on the coming of the Redeemer; but the present day has added to the evil of its own anxiety even a scarcity of light. These days are short for giving light, and vast and burdensome for preoccupation; so that the day’s own evil is not enough for it. Your prudence knows that the repose of contemplation and the distraction of the mind by worldly occupations do not concur. The cloak is too narrow to cover both—indeed, it cannot serve for both labours.

Though someone has two eyes in his forehead, he cannot separate them for separate tasks, so that with one he may look at heaven and with the other at earth. [Col. 0421B] How much less, then, can he at once direct the single sharpness of reason and intellect toward things so different as to examine with the same mind the mysteries of heaven and earthly affairs? Thus, my lord, thus, dearest Father: unless at least I close—rather, unless I pluck out—the eye that causes me to stumble (for the world is a stumbling-block to those who seek the Lord), I shall not behold with unveiled face the glory of the Lord, or the radiant face of Moses.

But what sort of testimony, or how credible a testimony, is that of a man who speaks of neither what he has seen nor heard? Indeed, he must be refuted and rejected as one relating dreams: blind, groping with his hand like a mole, he asserts what he says not from contemplation of the Scriptures, but dares to set up the idols of his own thoughts and fantasies in the temple of God. “There is no idol,” says the prophet, [Col. 0421C] “in Israel” (Num. 23); because one who meditates day and night on the law of the Lord and follows the traces of the law with firm step, when he writes interprets not the divinations of his own heart but the mind of the law.

I have offered these remarks in advance to excuse not my own idleness, but my oppressed misery. You ought to believe the Master concerning the matters around me. He himself will recount the stirring of the count’s anger, which that robber—Barabbas rather than abbot—has raised against us, and other matters. I have begun for you three sermons on the Advent of the Lord and one on the Nativity. Farewell.

## LETTER XX. TO ESKIL, ARCHBISHOP OF LUND

[I, 23] To his dearest lord and father ESKIL, [Col. 0421D] archbishop of Lund,

[Note: [Col. 0421D] To Eskil, archbishop of Lund. He is called Esquilius in Epistle 110; but we also read Eskil in Bernard’s letter to the same man, no. 314. While returning from Rome to Denmark, he was captured and despoiled in Germany. Adrian IV, pope—who also held Eskil dear in a private capacity—pressed this affair more vigorously as an injury, sending envoys to Emperor Frederick. The resulting mutual exasperation provided an occasion for the schism that broke out between them, as Radevicus teaches in *De gestis Friderici*, book I, chapter 8 and following. But in Radevicus “London” is written corruptly; and even more disgracefully, in Innocent III, Letter 321, “Lyon” is written for “Lund.” Lund is the metropolitan city of Denmark.]

brother PETER, abbot of La Celle, every good thing from the Lord God.

Such superabundant grace of heavenly good things has hitherto flowed from both your countenance and your hands, that, if modesty had not withdrawn itself from human society in these times, your acquaintances and friends would be covered with the deepest blush at the lavishness of your blessings. Indeed, I should rather say that in giving you rain [Col. 0422A] rather than sow. For one who sows first sows in hope of receiving fruit; then he does not pour out seed but scatters it; finally, he entrusts his seed only to cultivated ground. Rain imitates none of these things. Rather, it loses itself, so to speak, in the bowels of the earth, that afterwards, rising again with the richest offspring of crops, it may yield thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold fruit.

Again I find another indication of charity in rain: it waters without distinction fruitful and fruitless land, fertile field and barren, chosen grain and rejected shoot. Is this prodigality of goodness and benefactions a virtue or a fault? Yet this is God’s fault, and in him no other fault is found except that he is kind to the ungrateful, generous to the avaricious, merciful to the impious. These faults of his win innumerable reproaches for the most gentle One. Once the feet of our most gentle David were shaken because the rain of the most gentle God poured forth upon the wicked and unjust, so that he said: “In vain have I justified my heart and washed my hands among the innocent” (Ps. 72). He had forgotten what is said in the Book of Wisdom: “But you, our God, are gracious and true and wise, patient, and ordering all things in mercy. For if we sin, we are yours, knowing your greatness; and if we do not sin, we know that we are counted as being with you” (Wis. 15).

[Col. 0422B] Behold whose imitator is reproached when he is criticized for goodness or liberality. Does not Ecclesiastes, in his discourse, by his own decree and judgment consider this an evil under the sun: that a man to whom God has given riches, substance, and honour does not have power over them, but a stranger seizes them? To what purpose is this heap of words addressed to you? That the perpetual fire upon the holy altar of your heart may not fail, but may grow stronger and stronger through this heap, until your rich burnt offering is received in the cloud where God dwells, and the face of that same altar is cleansed from the ashes of every superfluity.

The little doorway through which access lies open to the Holy of Holies is made of olive wood; because, without doubt, according to the tenor of the holy faith, entrance among the saints will not be denied to one who has not been estranged from works of mercy. I have urged this upon the ears of my lord, setting shame aside—not, however, through my own presumption, but at another’s persuasion. Yet I was by no means difficult to persuade, retaining with me the marks of your countenance, speech, and whole bearing, and judging that among the sons of men I had found none like you in humility. Therefore I do not fear to write to one whom I think need be feared only by the wicked and proud. And enough of this.

Moreover, a servant should not be blamed for neglecting a command when no negligence turns his mind and will aside [Col. 0423A] from fulfilling his lord’s will. Through your condescension I received a command last year to approach the Carthusian brothers and remind them about advancing your affair. The affair, as you know, was that Brother Roger should be sent to you, to seek out and prepare a place for their order in your territories. For the full and perfect outpouring of charity had resolved in your heart to plant throughout the province entrusted to you by God new nurseries from every kind of holy order, so that from them you might receive fruit remaining for eternity and carry sheaves of righteousness from their labours into eternal dwellings.

Already the Cistercian or Clairvaux order has grown there, through the multiplication of brothers, not merely into grass but into ears of grain; likewise the Premonstratensian religious order. Therefore, since your prudence has tasted and seen that this enterprise is good, you have stretched your hand toward further things, and have wished to adorn your treasuries from that order which, like cherubim or seraphim, draw near immediately to the Lamb seated upon the throne of grace, who has seven eyes and seven horns.

Behold, what you commanded has been done. The holy community of Carthusian brothers has assented to your just requests. The matter was indeed difficult to obtain; but who could deny you what perhaps the Holy Spirit suggested in his holy temple? Certainly neither they nor we doubt that you are his most faithful servant and the Lord’s friend, whose most splendid fame and works the world proclaims. What [Col. 0423C] you have begun so holily, so eagerly, and in a manner almost intemperately through the desire of your soul, bring thus to completion, so that the end of the prayer may be better than its beginning. Farewell.

## LETTER XXI. TO HENRY, BISHOP OF BEAUVAIS

[I, 24] To his dearest lord and father HENRY, by the grace of God bishop of Beauvais,

[Note: [Col. 0423D] To Henry, bishop of Beauvais. Brother of the king; he had been a monk of Clairvaux. Nicholas of Clairvaux accordingly writes to him, while still a monk and not yet a bishop, in Letters 1 and 39. He was afterwards promoted to the see of Beauvais in 1149, as the supplement to Sigebert records. There survives Henry’s own remonstrative letter to Peter of Cluny, in which he complains of him as the broker of this dignity.]

brother PETER, abbot of La Celle, greeting.

The recollection of benefits is more than sufficiently poor when its title bears no inscription, at least in words, of thanksgiving. Therefore, with an iron stylus and diamond point I have committed the sheaves of your generosity to deep memory, so that they may be shaken by no dizziness of mind, swallowed by no flood of temporal change, and finally darkened by no rust of forgetfulness. I always retain with me a received benefit, clear, new, and fresh. With the grateful spirit with which, when I received it, I was carried into devotion toward the gift and giver, so, as its ageing glory is clarified, I prepare myself more strongly [Col. 0424A] for service and melt more truly into love for my benefactor with all the balm of my soul.

To your gift was added a cheerful countenance, a gracious disposition, and an honourable manner. Your generous hand wholly extended itself in benefaction; but your will surpassed measure in the circumstances of the gift. For what was it to summon the abbots and priors of the diocese? Again, what proof of love did your so kindly recommendation of my person and business express? Who did not marvel that so despised a person should be thus honoured by the king’s brother, thus embraced by the bishop of Beauvais, thus named by so great a man—a monk so very small?

I could not endure what was being said above measure about me. Out of the shame of blushing—indeed, because of awareness of the truth, which warned me that I was not the man of whom such things were said—I fled and withdrew, [Col. 0424B] but not far, because urgent necessity compelled me to endure greater things. Truly through necessity I cast aside the cloak of blushes when I entered my friends’ doors in order to receive. Certainly I received many things from many people, but from none so great as those I received from my lord. The greatness of the gift and the manner of giving surpassed acquaintances, surpassed other friends, surpassed all neighbours.

I did not speak; but because I came, I departed most excellently provided for. For I obtained the benefit not by asking but by coming. The tongue promising went before the tongue asking. Royal nobility spared the delicacy of a brow quickly suffused with the blush of shame. All these your benefits, my lord, are sealed in my treasuries. What, then, shall I render to my Lord for all that he has bestowed upon me? (Ps. [Col. 0424C] 115.) Without doubt, myself: not by selling myself, contrary to law, from freedom into slavery, but by vindicating myself as the servant of your friendship into freedom. For I rejoice more in this freedom, if by the gift of friendship I am your servant, than in the freedom by which I am removed from the duty of serving you. Farewell.

## LETTER XXII. TO THE SAME MAN

[I, 26] To his dearest lord and father HENRY, by the grace of God bishop of Beauvais, brother PETER, abbot of La Celle, to be zealous with zeal for the house of the God of Israel.

Until now, battle in the arena did not demand outstanding strength with urgency. It was safe enough to ride without breastplate, lance, or sword. But now let him who has a sword take up likewise a breastplate. Behold the time, behold the day, behold the cause in which the bravest of Israel must gird a sword upon the thigh of the mightiest. For behold, the Philistines, who according to the flesh walk upon a staff of reed, breaking out from pits of hidden malice, have set up camps innumerable, camps strong, camps flashing with lightning. Octavian

[Note: [Col. 0423D] Octavian. The name has been added conjecturally. In the manuscript copy that we used, the space [Col. 0424D] was blank. Nor can these things be understood of anyone other than Octavian, the antipope who opposed Alexander III and was called Victor. John of Salisbury, Letter 48: “The Gallican Church received Alexander and withdrew from Octavian.” After his death four years later, the schismatics substituted Guy of Crema, whom they called Paschal. But Henry at that time was already archbishop of Reims, not bishop of Beauvais. Therefore these statements do not fit Guy.]

is the leader [Col. 0425A] of this army—rather, I should say, of this malice—who, without God, as they say, wishes to reign as God. Behold, he strives to tear again, in Christ and the Church, not the veil of the Temple but Christ’s tunic, not the sackcloth of mortality but the shoe of majesty. The unity of Catholic faith judges this more abominable than the piercing of Christ’s side, the nailing of his feet, and the fastening of his hands. For through the piercing our redemption, through the fastening our deliverance, was obtained. But what comes from rending, division, and schism, except the thunderbolt of anathema, damnation of souls, and corruption of morals?

Behold the water of contradiction, where the children of Israel contended. But you, my lord—what will you do? Stand with Joshua—indeed, with Jesus—with drawn sword, and say to every passerby: “Are you ours, or of our adversaries?” (Josh. 5.) You have Alexander—indeed, Peter—or rather Christ, who has Peter and Alexander as his servants. Who can fear with most mighty Alexander? Who can waver with Peter founded upon the rock? Who will not overcome with Christ, to whom all power in heaven and on earth has been given? I know in you royal courage; I know an inflexible neck against hardened injustice; I know the ardour of zeal. Act therefore as you ought and can, for the dignity of your office, the eminence of your native blood, the religion of your order, and the obligation of Christian profession. For you owe much; and nevertheless you can do very much. Enough has been said to the wise. May the hand at God’s right keep you safe and sound. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIII. TO BALDWIN, BISHOP OF NOYON

[Col. 0425C]

[I, 25] To his dearest lord and father BALDWIN, by the grace of God bishop of Noyon,

[Note: [Col. 0425D] To Baldwin, bishop of Noyon. Two men of this name governed the church of Noyon in succession. The earlier succeeded Bishop Simon in 1148, as the same continuator of Sigebert observes. Formerly abbot of Châtillon, he was a religious man of honourable life, as the letters of the clergy of Noyon, written to Abbot Suger concerning his election, testify. The other had as successor Rainald, who attended the Lateran synod in 1179. I think Peter writes here to the former; likewise Bernard in Letter 339.]

brother PETER, abbot of La Celle, not to remove the salt of the covenant of his God from any sacrifice.

It is written: “The king’s honour loves judgment” (Ps. 98). As God’s angels in heaven are ministers of the divine will, so that it may be done “as in heaven, so on earth,” so too they are most equitable guardians of divine honour, clothing both feet of their King—mercy, namely, and justice—with fitting honour, lest, if one is neglected, the palace be called the house of one unshod. Now justice almost complains in our land against mercy, because no one wishes to cultivate the field of justice or bear the burden of the day and heat in return for the agreed daily [Col. 0425D] denarius. But men of wealth and pleasure flock in companies to the pleasant [Col. 0426A] meadows of mercy, and not truly, hiding their hand beneath the armpit, sewing fig leaves over their shame, and taking counsel and saying: “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace (Ezek. 13). My lord and dearest Father, I have written this back to you, sweetly admonished not by Pharisaic haughtiness but by the graciousness of your letter. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIV. TO THOMAS, CHANCELLOR OF THE KING OF ENGLAND

[I, 27] To his dearest lord and friend Thomas, chancellor

[Note: [Col. 0425D] Thomas, chancellor. He was made chancellor by King Henry in 1157, as Roger of Howden writes; five years later he became archbishop of Canterbury.]

of the king of England, brother PETER, humble abbot of La Celle, himself and his possessions.

A man whom favourable fortune does not exalt is more admirable for humility than for eminence. Glory and prosperity in you, as I have heard from those [Col. 0426B] who saw and knew you, contend more ambitiously than contentiously; glory is never ashamed when overcome, nor does it ever grow insolent through victory. Glory yields to prosperity, but gloriously and prosperously. Whichever gains the upper hand, it does not cut off humility or moderation. Glory approaches, but not proudly; prosperity comes, but not extravagantly. Hence, from the cloud of so great an eminence, you sent to the refuge of our poverty because you could not come. You asked for familiarity and friendship. What you asked would undoubtedly be thought astonishing, if you admitted it, given the unequal fortunes of asker and asked.

For what proportion is there between the abbot of La Celle and the chancellor of the king of England? There is almost no comparison where there is no corresponding estimation. Who does not know you, second after the king

[Note: [Col. 0425D] “In four kingdoms.” By “kingdoms” he seems to mean the four provinces over which the kings of England then ruled: England, Normandy, Aquitaine, and Anjou, by whose titles they were customarily designated. In Thomas’s own letters in the same Roger: “To Henry, by the grace of God illustrious king of the English, duke of the Normans and Aquitanians, and count of the Angevins.” In other letters of William, king of Sicily: “To Henry, by the grace of God illustrious king of the English, duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and count of Anjou: William, by the same grace king of Sicily, of the duchy of Apulia, and of the principality of Capua.” Thus the kings of Sicily too called themselves kings of three provinces, although Sicily alone was a kingdom.]

in four kingdoms? Who does not take notice of me, first among the miseries of our brethren? I will speak briefly: by as much as I perceive and know the things about you to be more excellent, by so much do I perceive and know the things about me to be more worthless. Therefore I in no way stretch out my hand toward entering into friendship; but if I should be among the flock of incidental friends, I shall judge that your condescension has dealt well with me. I do not send those first fruits, however, because I hasten to do a greater kindness. I did not have those sermons of Master G.,

[Note: [Col. 0426D] Those sermons of Master G. Gilbert, I think, called “the Universal,” concerning whom see the note to Letter 167.]

but I am seeking them, and immediately assign a copyist, with every urgency, to this task for your use. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIV bis, XXIV ter. TO THE SAME MAN

[Col. 0426D] (See *Patrologia*, vol. 190, among the letters of St Thomas, Letters 334 and 335, col. 675.)

## LETTER XXV. TO PETER THE VENERABLE

[Col. 0427A]

[II, 1] To his dearest lord and father PETER, by the grace of God the Venerable,

[Note: [Col. 0427D] To Peter the Venerable. This became, as it were, his proper surname. For Peter the Venerable is called the eighth abbot of Cluny and is very well known from his own writings and those of others. He died on the Kalends of January, 1158.]

abbot of the Cluniacs, brother PETER, humble abbot of La Celle, himself.

The glowing spark of your spirit vigorously blows away the ashes within me and, by continual meditation, renews the Seraph’s never-to-be-extinguished coals. You touched, I confess, not the lips of my mouth but the veins of my heart. The goad of the conversation we held together pierced the inner marrow of my being and compelled every inward faculty of the soul to consider itself. Truly that discourse was effective in awakening a sluggish soul, examining this momentary life, observing the religious profession, emulating angelic purity, and readily contemplating the supreme and ineffable Trinity. It was living, because it spoke of true life; pure, because of highest purity; true, because of eternal truth. It spares evils not, but pleases the good; it reproves vices and commends virtues. It brings hidden things to light; like a very clear mirror, it reports back the faces of those who look into it. I confess that in contemplating it I examined my wrinkles, and found ugly what I had formerly judged beautiful in the inward person. By this lighted lamp I swept my house and found far less in my treasure than I had reckoned. I found decayed what I thought flourishing. And what more need I say? I can scarcely endure the stench of my little nest, for there I see creeping things beyond number. [Col. 0427C] There are there the stings of nettles, the pricks of thorns, the tangled growth of briars, and the unsparing burnings alike of the paliurus of anxieties and the thistle of passions. For what are sin and the punishment of sin except the stings of death, making the soul bleed, tearing and rending it? The wretched soul feeds upon its own wretchedness: “Death,” says the Psalmist, “shall feed upon them” (Ps. 48). Hence Isaiah says: “Hell has enlarged its appetite without any limit, because the people had no knowledge” (Isa. 5). Hell enlarges itself excessively—indeed, far too excessively—when it already tortures even some persons living in the body by hellish consciences. Yet these torments reach only to the door, as to the victim of the Cross, and no farther. For this monster, which even devours Jonah, snatches up all things and lays waste everything; in the throat and belly of its malice it encloses whatever it finds outside the ark. But how much more happily and delightfully would it be if the soul captured the one desiring it, swallowed the one devouring it, and triumphed over the one pursuing it! Thus the dragon would be mocked; thus at last death would be killed; thus the soul would be freed. Would that the soul thus took vengeance on its adversary; indeed, would that it so swallowed its present hellish miseries that it left no remnants of punishment for the tomorrow of the future judgment! Would that my soul awaited rather the remnants of salvation, which shall keep festival, [Col. 0428A] than the dregs that settle in the cup which is in the Lord’s hand, full of unmixed wine mingled with spices! I long for the remnants of your banquets, Lord Jesus. Behold, my belly, without breath, wholly expands itself and desires to be filled from your crumbs or remnants. I seek wine also; I seek clothing as well. I desire to be cleansed from the blood of sin by your blood; I desire to be clothed in your linen garments, Jesus, in which, adorned within the sacred virginal womb, you went forth to offer prayers and gifts for us. This most holy garment you put off at the holy supper’s feast, tore on the Cross, took up renewed in the Resurrection, and presented before the Father’s countenance in the Ascension for our propitiation. Wash me from filth; heal me from pains, purifier of the sons of Levi, restorer of the sons of [Col. 0428B] God. But if, because of the constant discharges of a sick man, you shrink from bending your now-glorified hand most mercifully to such ulcerous duties, you have another, lower hand—well instructed, richly gracious, and, like us, capable of suffering—which, if you give it authority, indeed if you command it, will readily administer to us the remedies of souls. I mean your Cluniac monk, to whom you have given wisdom in heart, eloquence in speech, grace in discourse, authority in countenance, power in action, and subtlety in understanding. You gave him permission too, to act according to your heart: entering the workshops of those who labour, he may faithfully distribute, according to each person’s health, the medicine prepared by your hands, and receive in return the coin of grace for the grace of this laborious dispensing.

You are burdened, certainly, dearest lord and Father, in administering so great a multitude, across courses so widely extended: now, with eager love, you strive toward the bounds of heaven in fiery chariots; now, bowed by concern for a people devoted to the cultivation of the calf that eats grass, you spring back toward earth’s lowest regions and remotest parts; now so far away, now so near; now above the clouds, now beside the Goel [uncertain reading], even below the citizens; now above the spirit, now beneath yourself—you are compelled to raise and lower yourself. You toil if you do not love; you toil if you do not see the fruit; you toil if you do not hope for the end; you toil if you do not consider the reward. And concerning the end it is written: “Behold, the end comes; the end comes” (Ezek. 7). Finally, the time of labour has been weighed in the balance and found [Col. 0428D] to have less than the denarius of reward. Labour is not prolonged through days and years, for the recompense of labours will come in a little while and swiftly. Again, one must consider the fruit: for your fruit is sublime fruit, the fruit of light, the fruit of the Lord’s blessings, fruit beyond number. Count the stars of heaven; count the sand of the sea; and you will be able to count the fruit of the Lord’s garden, namely the Church of Cluny. What shall I say of love? Do you not love, most loving Father, the Beloved from the beloved, wounded by charity upon the wood? I know it, I know it; your angel also knows [Col. 0429A] your love, burning strongly toward God and glowing warmly toward your neighbour in no small degree. Finally, Christ Jesus, the merciful and generous rewarder not only of deeds but also of affections, runs before your face girded with a full hand; comes alongside you with a bright countenance; and helps behind your back with an outstretched arm. He runs before as guide; comes alongside as companion; helps as physician. He runs before that you may imitate him; comes alongside lest you grow weary; helps lest you labour. He runs before in predestination, comes alongside in calling, and helps in justification.

Jacob had a guide before him in his mother’s womb, when it was said, “not from works but from him who calls: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’” (Rom. 9). The angelic nature likewise had cooperating grace in the confirmation of its stability. Did not grace from heaven come to Saul’s aid in the sickness of his unbelief? Following him as he runs, you shall not fail; walking with him, you shall suffice for all things; wholly relying upon this one with all your being, do not despair that you can do all things. “I can do all things,” says the Apostle, “in him who strengthens me” (Phil. 4). Indeed, this Son of God flies back and flies onward to the Father’s bosom on the wings of paternal and maternal generation; yet he slows his step, waiting for the weary. Nor is he ignorant of the harder and rougher parts of the journey; rather, in kindness he sets them apart for himself. For there is no pain like his pain, and, removing stones from the road, he offers us smoother paths. Hence he says: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14). As though to say: I have paid the perils of your warfare and penal debt, and have granted the remedies of complete [Col. 0429C] peace. He made his portion better, I say, not softer, because he taught that no one can have at once a softer and a better portion in the world where he promises tribulation. I indeed wish for the better by grace, but often choose the softer by nature’s impulse. God, however, does not read it so—no, not so. He has divided otherwise: he placed the better apart, but above. Men, however, as softer, weaker, or lower beings, still having before their eyes the clay of their formation, desire softer and sweeter things, not better and harder ones. It is left to our choice whether we receive better but harder things, or softer but worse. Yet I see my humanity frequently and for a long time wavering in this dilemma. At one moment it tries and handles the hard resolve because it is better; at another it falls back upon the soft because it is more pleasant. In the contract for the former, the purchase pleases but the condition displeases; in that for the latter, the condition is easy but the purchase cheap. O two-sided, O doubtful transaction! The superfluous pleasure of the flesh is certainly not altogether hateful to every person; rather, it is much sought, much desired, and much embraced by many. But for how long? It is brief, passing; even when it seems to exist, it does not exist. It consumes itself, destroys itself, and rages cruelly against itself. Yet the loss that harms nature is more bitter than that which destroys itself. This kind of pleasure enters, and nature flees. The mistress of all things rejects this maidservant as a pest, avoids it as death, and guards against it as hell. For they never—or rarely—remain in one dwelling; scarcely—or never—do they work together. There is always one activity of necessity, which is also nature’s activity, and another of superfluous pleasure. For example, when someone buries himself in wine, stuffs himself with food to nausea, and is enervated by lust, does not nature mourn? Does it not fall sick? Does it not labour heavily? Surely the flower of youth abandons such a person sooner, and the heralds of premature disease or death are summoned. [Col. 0430B] Yet who does not know that these are works of the flesh, or of superfluous pleasure? Nature, by contrast, rejoices to abstain from them and, as Seneca says, is content with little. Nature is governed by reason, but the other by abuse. Nature walks in truth; but the face of this monster is alluring in order to deceive, while behind it carries the scorpion’s sting in order to kill. It takes hold of the simple by the chin but strikes them in the groin. The company and tribune of the synagogue of sinners appoint this thing their chief and king, and reject the true Solomon riding upon the king’s mule. O sin! O wickedness! “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its driver” (4 Kings 13): let not the spirit of the righteous Nathan be silent, at least in your mouth; let it not permit [Col. 0430C] so great a crime to be done in the Israel of God. For when superfluous fleshly pleasure holds the sceptre of the kingdom, what peace remains over Israel? Indeed, what rights are not overturned? What laws are not effaced? What reason is not exiled? What virtue is not confounded? What appearance of goodness is not suffocated? What kind of error is not exalted above everything that is called God or worshipped? (2 Thess. 2). This is the root of sin, the moth of all honourableness, the pit of vices, the well of demons, the abyss of souls. Shut up, I beg you, shut up this most evil beast which devours our Joseph (Gen. 37)—or rather, the sons of Jacob and Joseph.

Certainly it is excessively exalted, and, having broken the barrier of purpose and religious observance, attempts to extend the boundaries of its rule even to the Holy of Holies of the Cluniac [Col. 0430D] order. For where meat is eaten without permission, is not Adam’s transgression renewed? Is not the paradise of vow and holy institution violated? Is it not written: “I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh” (Deut. 32)? It is an affront to holiness and an abomination of religious life—not, indeed, the eating of flesh, but eating it with the blood of disobedience.

> **Note: [Col. 0429D] “Meat eaten without permission.”** By ancient practice monks abstain from meat, lest, as Bernard writes of himself, by nourishing the flesh too greatly they nourish vices. Yet eating it was sometimes permitted, but only to the sick and with their superiors’ permission. Geoffrey of Vendôme, book IV, letter 42: “As the eating of meat is granted to monks because of bodily infirmity, so it is denied them for the pleasure of the flesh”; and later: “But because we recognize this virtue—namely, wholly abstaining from meat—to belong to few or none, when we grant someone permission to eat meat, reasonable necessity must be considered, not the fleshly appetite for nourishing flesh.”

[Col. 0431A] Therefore the Law commands abstinence from blood and from things strangled. A person does not abstain from things strangled if he does not fear to eat secretly. Transgressions of those entrusted to them bring danger upon superiors. The guardians of sacred vessels are punished when, through their negligence, those vessels are carried away from the Lord’s temple and debased even to the hands of the Babylonian king’s concubines. I do not presume to teach one wiser than myself, instruct one holier, stir one more fervent, or provoke one more diligent; but I disclose my fears, reveal my griefs, seek counsel, and ask the path of escape. I hear that the leaders of the people were hung on gallows and fastened facing the sun because of the people’s sins, and can I remain given over to sleep? At the climactic moment of judgment I read Jacob saying to Laban: “Your sheep and goats were not barren. I did not eat the rams of your flock, nor did I show you an animal captured by a beast: I made good every loss; whatever disappeared by theft, you exacted from me. By day and night I was scorched by heat and frost, and sleep fled from my eyes; thus I served you for twenty years in your house” (Gen. 31). [Col. 0431B] I read this, I say, and do I not mourn my own sloth inconsolably? Where are the sheep entrusted to my care? Where are the goats that are not barren? Those who have been regularly trained in cloisters from childhood and kept unstained the garment of their life and conduct are the Lord’s sheep. Those who flee the stench of worldly lust and assume the habit of penance are likewise the Lord’s goats. But where is Jacob? Where the abbot so diligent in exhorting, so fervent in reproving, so cautious in providing, so kindly in persuading; so mighty against the wolves’ rage, so wise against the pestilence of diseases, so patient against the inclemency of the weather, so prudent against thieves’ ambushes, so faithful in what is entrusted, so watchful in preventing loss, and so persevering in the service he began? I see my Lord’s losses, but do not know how to repair them. It would indeed be just recompense if I equalled number with number and restored value with equal value. But since I have only one soul, if three or four perish through my fault, what shall I do? Shall I pay a triple or fourfold penalty? And if I could somehow suffer that penalty, with what endurance could I perhaps bear a hundredfold one? Considering these things, I marvel that [Col. 0431D] I do not marvel; I am terrified that I am not terrified. Certainly this is no ordinary sleep: a stupor or lethargy holds me. I beg you, send an antidote.

## LETTER XXVI. TO HUGH, ABBOT OF CLUNY

[II, 2.] To his dearest lord and father, HUGH, by God’s grace abbot of Cluny, brother PETER, humble abbot of La Celle, offers himself with devotion.

> **Note: [Col. 0431D] “To Hugh, abbot of Cluny.”** To Hugh, Peter the Venerable’s successor and third abbot of that name. After Peter’s death, the monks of Cluny, amid an uproarious election and despite many protests, chose a certain Robert, a semi-layman but kinsman of the count of Flanders. [Col. 0432D] After he was later deposed and died, they proclaimed this Hugh—formerly prior—as abbot, as recorded in the continuation of Sigebert under the year 1158. This, then, is the great disturbance to which he refers: Hugh, son of the womb of Cluny; Robert, the man who sought to rule by force.

A brighter day succeeds the clouds; sweetness increases after preceding bitterness; ruin makes a state of stability more highly valued. Thus, when we heard of the great disturbance that occurred in the election at Cluny, our hearts were not a little shaken; but our soul rejoiced anew in concord. For from the setting of our holy father, your predecessor, Cluny had been as a woman in labour until it received another man to console her for her works. It sighed in pain, but behold, now it remembers its distress no more because of its joy: for it has received freedom and has set one of the sons of its own womb among the princes of its people. Foreign sons lied to her and limped from their paths, because they sought to rule not by the Lord’s word but by their own usurpation and the counsel of Ahithophel. A hateful presumption indeed: [Col. 0432B] to prostitute so chaste a matron as Cluny, publicize one so religious, and strip one so honourable of beauty. This rash violation of marriage laws must be restrained: the will of the most noble maiden is not sought, but violence inflicted; her undefiled bed is not reverently requested but shamelessly demanded. It would be a misery wholly unheard of if the mistress of the household were condemned by this necessity: rather than freely marrying whom she wills, only in the Lord, she must unwillingly submit to serve one whom she rejects—indeed, in the service of concubinage. Where is: “You have not chosen me, but I have chosen you”? (John 15.) Where is: “No one takes honour to himself, but he who is called by God as Aaron was”? (Heb. 5.) Is she not free, possessing free election in the liberty of the Spirit—she who is both servant and bride: servant, certainly, by devotion; bride by love? Where, I ask, is the reverence due the bridegroom and the bride’s glory, before which John the Baptist stands in awe, Moses veils himself, Rebecca covers herself with a mantle, the cherubim of glory overshadow it, and which flesh and blood, if it touches it, vanishes like smoke? “Flesh,” says the Apostle, “and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15). Therefore Moses removed the sandal from his feet lest, if he stood upon holy ground impeded by fleshly cares, he might offend against the face of God shining in the bush.

I do not judge it a slight danger to take a flaming and turning sword in one’s bare hand, or rashly leap over the furnace of wrath with blinded eyes. [Col. 0432D] The summit of this honour—or rather, burden—is as liable to a fall as it is weak under the load imposed. It burns with care, pricks with fear, and presses with unrest. If fortune is examined as it turns on both sides and in every direction, it brings more sorrow and less joy. Constant reckoning must be made both of the office received and of the debt to be discharged; on one side the judge’s equity and on the other the difficulty of the administration imposed must be weighed. Pardon must also be hoped for, if punishable negligence does not stand in the way. Time must be counted, interest repaid, [Col. 0433A] fruits calculated, and the total of the entire stewardship added up. If a deficiency is found, money must be placed on the table before the final crisis, and one’s dealings with the money-changers of virtues or faith renewed. Grace must be implored because of the gravity of the danger; judgment exercised according to one’s ability; and an embassy of excuse sent for what is impossible. For if a miserable and weak human being engages in combat on equal terms, he can in no proportion stand against the Lord. You would more easily compress the earth’s weight, heaven’s boundless spaces, the expanses of the air, and the sea’s vast outpourings within the narrowness of your fist than render an answer equal to the God of heaven. O abbot of Cluny, consider that he who is mighty has done great things for you, and holy is his name (Luke 1). God has made you a god, merciful, and good. He has exalted the humble and cast down the mighty (ibid.). Behold, then, you have become the monks’ eye, the mirror and example of this order. If your eye is single, the whole body of monks—that is, the Cluniac congregation—will be full of light; but if it is wicked, the body too will be dark. Take care, therefore, lest the light in you be darkness (Luke 11), if I may so speak. What emboldens me is that I once entered the threshold of your friendship, and your holy devotion to religious life. But enough of this.

Moreover, in obedience to our custom, I stood surety with the abbot of Arremar for the man of loving and pious memory, Lord Abbot Peter, for a large sum against Hulduin of Vendopera. We accordingly accepted four priors as secondary sureties, so that we might have recourse [Col. 0433C] to them. They are . . . .

> **Note: [Col. 0433D] “The abbot of Arremar.”** This is a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict. A letter of Leo IV to Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, in whose diocese it is situated, records its origin and its founder Adremarus. It retains its founder’s name even in the vernacular: it is called *Monstier-Ramey*, that is, “the monastery of Adremarus.”

> **Note: [Col. 0433D] “Hulduin of Vendopera.”** This is a hereditary family name derived from a castle in Champagne which they possessed. [Col. 0434D] I think this particular Hulduin of Vendopera is the man whom several charters of the monastery of Aripatorium name as a witness alongside Count Theobald, Bernard of Clairvaux, and the abbots Guy of Arremar—all of whom identify the period.

## LETTER XXVII. TO THE SAME RECIPIENT

[II, 3.] To his dearest lord and father HUGH, abbot of Cluny, brother PETER of La Celle, greetings.

Our justice ought to exceed the justice of the Scribes and Pharisees, not fall beneath it. I wonder what new lawgiver brought in this justice, or whence: that a pledge held by a debtor should not be restored to the surety by the principal debtor.

> **Note: [Col. 0434D] “Held by the debtor.”** The sense requires that one read “held by the creditor,” as is also made clear by what he writes on the same matter near the end of the following letter.

I also wonder at your novel kindness, which has not been willing to answer even once one now calling for a second time. This silence moves me more harshly than the loss. For patience helps one bear the loss more lightly when one knows it will be repaired by a friend’s good and renewed favour. But silence after a benefit represents the tomb of a dead benefit. It is to make a friend’s firstborn, as it were, an abortion—where the memory of service ought always to flourish and live among friends. [Col. 0434A] Until now I had offered both the loss and patience under the loss—but to friends, to lords, to truthful monks, who could, if they wished, even have taken me myself as a pledge. But what shall I say? Certainly I shall say too little, lest perhaps I lose my friends along with the money. Yet I shall speak—plainly I shall speak. Whoever may hear that the simplicity of La Celle has been so crushed, not to say mocked, by its dearest friends, for whom it laid down itself and all it possessed: do not proclaim it in Gath, nor publish it in the streets of Ascalon. Let this rather be said, even if it is not truer: the abbot does not know old debts. For when he hears, he will satisfy the creditors, free the sureties, and repay his friends’ favour with an equal balance. Farewell.

Behold, our pens, much wearied by their labour, ask as their reward to drink from the cup after heat and winter.

## LETTER XXVIII. TO THE SAME RECIPIENT

[II, 4.] To his dearest lord and father HUGH, venerable abbot of Cluny, PETER, humble abbot of La Celle, with every devotion.

At one and the same hour—indeed, with one mouth—I received the sweetness of flavour from the marrow of your letter and turned my hand to writing in reciprocal return. For something first undertaken at desire’s willing impulse always has, I know not what, more sweetness than it has after a period of longing. I therefore did not wish to postpone until later hours an opportunity that needed, as it were, warming anew, especially since I had been almost summoned by the condescension of so great a majesty. First, then, I remit the delay, harmful but well compensated by this satisfaction. Next, I guard against being found negligent before you in the duty of this office. Receiving paper and writing on paper composed with sufficient elegance, I do not merely look at it once; rather, with admiration I turn back upon myself the reflection that a person’s carefulness, even in the smallest matters, must not be overlooked. Outer form, when reshaped, is certainly an example of inward composition; and the goodness of wine is enhanced by the suitability of the cup. The beauty of its appearance suggested that it brought, as its reading showed, some great thing stored in its hidden depths. Your document poured forth from itself, from Paradise, Egypt, and every region of Scripture, such precious merchandise and pearls in full purses [Col. 0434D] that the ark of our understanding was cramped by it. But what wonder if the lord abbot of Cluny brings out of his treasures so many and such great things that the abbot of La Celle can scarcely carry out even what and how much he can? Do we not read that someone said thus: [Col. 0435A] “From yourself you will not be able to provide horsemen, whom I shall give you” (Isa. 36). Countless things perhaps walk with you, as monks do: so too do interpretations. Certainly it is so; it cannot be denied. The matter is evident. Who has ever been able so readily and at a nod to summon so great an army of philosophical examples so swiftly? O rich vein! Blessed is he who watches at the posts of your door: he will be able to eat bread in the morning and meat in the evening. I knocked, and you opened. I said one thing—which I do not regret having said. For with one small prick I touched you; indeed, I touched a heap of mercury, or of newly gathered grain; but in return I received, at no small valuation, a treasure of many opinions. What then? You sent back into our bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing. Therefore I rejoice at your condescension, am amazed at your eloquence, and run like a thirsty deer to the springs of histories, the depth of interpretations, and the sweetness of exhortations. Meanwhile, from the one name Peter you set forth two things: strength and knowledge. You illustrate both without stinginess. Then, in an honourable way, you teach me what I ought to be and say that I am such as you wish me to become. This is a persuasive method of instruction. For it is natural for a rational soul to respond by a voluntary movement to one who thinks well of it, and to incline its shoulders to an unquestioned affection. He also makes the mind ready to obey him who has first shown the faithfulness of friendship and persuaded it of his integrity. I would believe you, if I were not conscious within myself of the contrary; would that, as it is uttered by your charity, so it were fulfilled by you in truth. But, to confess the truth, the reality expressed by your name is rare in us. For there is one alone, and no second, to whom it is said: “According to your name, so is your praise unto the ends of the earth” (Ps. 47). What is that name? Jesus. What is that praise? “The Lord shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1).

Truly this is Jesus, in whose hand is our salvation. He has a name above every name (Phil. 2). Finally, he fulfils the power of his name in a manner not inferior to it—indeed, more excellent both in duration and in weight. I have said too little: “in duration”; I should better say, “in eternity.” This power is from eternity; this name is from time. The power is without time; the name belongs to time. Nevertheless, in weight the power of divinity accomplishes all things, including the very name of Jesus. O weight of the name Jesus! Who can weigh, count, or assess this name in its weight? Jesus must never be named without weight—the weight, namely, of the sanctuary—because “no one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12). And in the law of Moses it is said: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain” (Exod. 21). Lest he should run in vain, the Apostle Paul, as he could amid chains and bonds through his daily sufferings, always applied and grasped this name. This is what he says: “The sufferings of this …” (Rom. 8), etc.; and elsewhere, concerning the same weight: “I bear the marks of Jesus in my body” (Gal. 6). Elsewhere he says: “The Father gave him a name which is above every name,” and so forth (Phil. 2). This name outweighs every name belonging to a creature. I have said this briefly only to indicate who alone possesses both name and power.

I turn my gaze again to the letter, which is like a tower built with battlements: a thousand shields hang from it, all the armour of the mighty. For what purpose so great an array? I think you wished either to frighten my dull senses by the majesty of your thoughts, the number of your examples, and the intricacy of subtle arguments; or to provoke an idle man by rivalry in study; or to console a sad man by the beauty of your words; or to build up an unlearned man by persuasive exhortations; or to meet my need with a more abundant flood of authorities. But whichever of these you intend, I regard it as desirable and most dear that you grow indignant at your occupations and, as Rebecca lowered her water-jar from her shoulders for us in our weariness, so you have lowered it for us. For who could believe that the overflowing reversals of storms, by which one is sometimes raised to heaven and descends to the abyss, are absent even briefly from a new abbot of Cluny? Who, after a third day, would not marvel at emerging from the earth’s depths? Who would not sympathize with one groaning beneath the waters? How can he write whom continuous and never-quiet anxiety pelts with hail? Yet where the obstacle is more arduous, there an exceptional mind must necessarily free itself. It is undoubtedly the mark of a refined soul to resent the burdens of worldly care and, through the very ranks of those who interrupt, fly forth like a solitary wild ass to the most pleasant meadows of reading and to free solitude. [Col. 0436C] No interdict is issued by the praetor against this force. Such force is more commendable than lazy submission. This force, I say, is not blameworthy if the new cords, woven and linked in the bonds of business as though emerging from the sea’s depths, are broken.
