There is another counsel too: where one lacks strength to use force, one should have skill to commit a theft from which, however, no action for theft arises. For in the Gospel the woman is commended who, touching Jesus, is said to have secretly stolen power from the hem of his garment. A wholly commendable theft, if you withdraw yourself, for yourself and for your God, from the assault of those crowding together. “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread more pleasant.” Reading is especially savoury when the soul’s attention drinks it amid interruptions. Study, reading, and prayer do not love a crowd. They are commonly impeded by the arrival of a stranger, because consolation can scarcely endure not to share itself with a noble visitor. Perhaps I lay burdens heavy and impossible to bear—burdens that I cannot touch even with my fingers—upon your shoulders. For how could my lord of Cluny ever experience such things? Indeed, how could he live if he did not do them? If he is to belong to all after all, when will he belong to himself? Yet, conversely, if those who ought not live without him do not have him, how great the disaster and injustice! It is better that one man die than that the whole nation perish. But again: [Col. 0437A] “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but loses himself and suffers the loss of himself?” (Mark 8). Behold, as you see, the matter is tightly constrained. One must turn neither to the right for oneself nor to the left for others. What then? Let him choose the middle course; and if he cannot have every day, at least let him have a day between days. Let others have him, but let him himself have himself—and let others have him too. Let him not divide the living child as Solomon decreed: let either the mother or the non-mother have it—indeed, let the mother always have it. Let him live not for himself alone nor for others alone, but for himself and others, lest he perish; yet for others and himself, lest the sheep succumb without a shepherd. But enough of this.

Furthermore, let not my lord take offence if I say what I think. I shall speak, but I shall speak with permission. What is it? That something is always lacking in God’s service. Perhaps this is a proverb among you; but I shall make a saying from the proverb. By a certain intricacy of reasoning, you defer the knot of the debt, writing thus in your letter: “If it has been repaid, we need not be disturbed about it; if some question is raised concerning its repayment, it ought to be decided in judicial order and brought to an end by the parties’ allegations and the judge’s sentence.” Good lord, our master taught you well how to formulate an issue; would that he had taught you equally well how to discharge it! To discharge, I say, a debt, not a syllogism. Consider, not by extended disputation but by a concise account—and indeed by reason—between whom this question is said to arise, to whom the action belongs, and against whom it is given. The principal debtor and his creditor, certainly, have actions against one another, one direct and the other useful. But what has this to do with the surety? The surety must always be freed through a pledge-action brought by the principal debtor against the creditor, once the debt has first been paid, so that the pledge may be restored and the surety released. This the lord of Winchester did, but did not accomplish it: he proceeded against the creditor, but did not restore our pledge to us. Therefore I said that the matter remains incomplete until what is held on your behalf has been restored to us.

> **Note: [Col. 0437D] “The lord of Winchester.”** Henry, brother of Theobald the Great and of Stephen, king of England. He was bishop of Winchester in England, but at this time was staying in France, namely at Cluny, to which he eventually returned from England. For he was a monk of Cluny.

There is another point noted in your letter: you said, suspensively and indefinitely, what ought to be done, but you set no time, neither day nor hour—perhaps because it is not ours to know the times which the bishop of Winchester holds in his own power. I know, my lord, I know [Col. 0437D] that in much speaking sin is not absent. Forgive whatever has escaped our lips that may seem less than right in your eyes. Yet you gave the occasion for my daring to say this. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIX. TO HUGH, ABBOT OF CLUNY

[II, 5.] To his dearest lord and father HUGH, abbot of Cluny, [Col. 0438A] brother PETER, abbot of La Celle, greetings.

For our friends—indeed, for the friends of justice—never would we refuse to write to our friend, indeed the friend of truth. For in the differing causes of friends that friendship ought to intervene which, inclining no further than justice permits toward one party’s favor, weighs the affair by the rectitude of equity, not by the unjust distortion of favor or hatred. Therefore, although I owe you an eminent prerogative of affection and honor, I nevertheless give myself likewise to this abbot of Saint Lawrence at Liège [Note: [Col. 0437D] Abbot of Saint Lawrence at Liège. It is still today a noble Benedictine monastery in the suburb of Liège.], newly joined to him by a covenant of friendship, because of Christ whom I have received in him. Since, then, Christ is concerned on both sides, I myself, standing between, urge each of you to render the honor due.

You, indeed, I urge that, the greater you are in dignity, pre-eminence, and name, the more abundant humility you show in receiving him. Him I urge, according to the excellence of your majesty, to consider how he should receive the highest humility in so great a man, and, as the saying goes, support declining kindness with welcoming arms. You should weigh with an even balance the worthiness of his person and the justice of his claim upon you, rendering honor to the person and judgment to the cause. I have seen the man and loved him; I have heard the case and approved it. In his person I observed prudence, devotion, learning, and simplicity; in his cause I perceived the preservation of peace, the banishment of malice, the repression of hostility, and the tenor of justice.

Does not he who seeks peace from so far away love that which he seeks? What stings of affection, do you suppose, pierce him when for so long and at such a time he lives as a pilgrim away from the holy congregation of his brethren—like those cows which, their calves shut away, lowed as they went, overcoming by the holiness of their purpose the customary and familiar affection of the flesh? But thanks be to God, because the loss of those from whom he was absent, and his own resisting sorrow at being absent, have turned to gain for us among whom he has been present. Let therefore what you hear move and deeply stir your devout heart; attend to a good man, a peaceful man, an honorable man—indeed, to your monks and brethren. We firmly believe it very profitable for them if they preserve peace, dishonorable and unprofitable if they recoil from it. Farewell.

## LETTER XXX. TO HENRY, COUNT OF CHAMPAGNE

[Col. 0438D]

[II, 6.] To his lord HENRY, Count Palatine [Note: [Col. 0438D] Henry, Count Palatine. Count of Champagne, son of Theobald the Great, whom his generosity earned the name “the Generous” or “the Munificent.” Pierre Pithou has, in his usual careful and learned manner, discussed when and why the counts of Troyes began to be called palatine counts.], Brother PETER of La Celle, humble abbot, wishes him good rule.

Your associates have asked us what we would give you, and have fixed a day for taking counsel on this matter. First, therefore, I wonder what wrong I have done, that you always turn your face away from me in this manner, so that I can either come before you or make a request only never, or very rarely. Secondly, whether it has slipped from that most tenacious memory of yours that the year’s course has not yet been completed in which I have paid sixty pounds both to you and to your people. Thirdly, I grieve not a little that our poverty and debts, arising from this year’s affairs—both from the journey to Rome, from the church of Villa Mauri [Note: [Col. 0439D] The church at Villa Mauri. They were in dispute about it with the canons; see Letter 7.], from the infirmary for the brethren which we have built, and from many other matters—could not reach the ears of your compassion. Let your kindness, therefore, see our situation, and, condescending to our necessities, spare us; do not add a burden to these things, but relief. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXI. TO A., ABBOT OF MOLÈSME

[Col. 0439B]

[II, 7.] To the venerable lord and Father A., abbot of the monks of Molèsme [Note: [Col. 0439D] To A., abbot of Molèsme. In the diocese of Langres, of the Order of Saint Benedict. This is an exhortation to a new abbot, who had recently been made from prior. The superscription is false: read G. or W., that is, Guilenco or Wilenco. PATROLOGICAL EDITION.], Brother PETER, humble abbot of La Celle, greeting.

Among all possessions, the possession of friends excels. A friend may be acquired, but cannot be bought. For how can that which is beyond price be bought? And is not that beyond price which, not yet possessed, cannot be purchased, and, once lost, cannot likewise be redeemed? I often seek such a friend and do not find one, even in a flock of friends. I desire an excellent friend, not one merely of the flock among the flock. Let those rejoice in the number of their friends who do not know how to possess one friend. For, as Seneca says, let them have many lodgings but few friendships.

Some use friends no differently than lodgings. If an inn has served them well for the night, they praise it in the morning, exchange it as they depart, and, for as many days as their journey lasts, so many stopping-places of the road will be counted. An inn is encountered for a time and sought not for its own sake, but only that the weary may be refreshed. A friend who happens to be encountered must not be received so superficially, but sought with labor, admitted with deliberation, retained with care; if offended, reconciled with every vigilance; and, if he should perhaps slip away, pursued and recalled with insistence.

Do not possess a friend as though he were an estate. You reject or alienate from yourself an unproductive estate; you cultivate a profitable one more diligently, and direct a more eager mind toward possessing it. So too, one who seeks in a friend not character but gold, not fidelity but appearance, not manners but clothes, not nature but fortune, seeks a friend for the sake of private advantage, not natural goodness.

Nor is a sudden friendship to be approved without qualification, but rather that which buds in acquaintance, grows in familiarity, puts forth leaves in habitual association, becomes fruitful in the expansiveness of the heart, and bears fruit in perfect identity. Here the fig-tree must be planted and dug about, that it may produce the fruit of sweetness in the field of friends. Here the cord of love must be twisted with a threefold strand, lest it be easily broken. I shall twist this cord as I can, when it comes to be twisted toward me by service, by repayment, and perhaps by reciprocity. For, turning my thumb, I twist the thread in writing about friendship.

If the compact for forming an alliance pleases you, let limits be set beforehand to prevent the presumption of hateful transgression. Yet let one who advances beyond the limits be allowed to pass them without blame; but let one who falls short not be allowed to do so with impunity. For that is a good transgression when love, once begun, hastens to love beyond expectation. And how good is that which is not transgression but progress, when the promise of friends’ mutual faith has fulfilled its just measure! In friendship one should always promise less and perform more.

Now then I shall speak to a friend as to a friend. Dearest friend, God has added a new grace to His grace: from prior He has made you abbot, from sheep a shepherd. Recall your former state, remember your merit, consider the giver; and render back to God the gift of God which has been given, not to man. He tears a crown from God’s highest summit who acknowledges as coming from man what was given by God. It is idolatry to render to man the gratitude owed to God.

I know the flattering enticements of some; I know their false vanities and madnesses. One says thus, if the cloister has become burdensome: “Night and day I stretched out my hands to God that He might grant you this office, and with unceasing sighs I beat upon the divine ears until it was accomplished.” Another says: “I was his spokesman, I his persuader, I the adviser of others; I bent the minds of all toward you, and now do you shamelessly refuse what I want?” Another chants, “We praise thee, O God”; another improperly recalls that the nomination or concession was made by him. Thus more men are your abbots than those of whom you are abbot.

Let it not be so, lord and dearest friend, that you believe yourself to have received from many what you have received from one. It was not the monk who prayed who made you abbot, but God who granted it; not the one who named you aloud, but the One who made it known in hearts. In writing this I do not urge you toward ingratitude, that you should be forgetful of a kindness; nor do I raise you up into arrogance, that you should not regard the devotion of the congregation asking that you be set over them. For that would not be to instruct a friend but to destroy him; not truly to counsel what is good but wickedly to subject him to a most evil vice.

Why then have I prefaced these remarks? That you may restrain those who speak vainly; that you may not diminish the standing of your dignity and office through the importunity of certain persons; that you may acknowledge God alone as the author of this your elevation, and may do all things to His glory and honor. Let the congregation hold you bound by its devotion, yet with your authority intact; let the monk find you gracious because of his entreaty, yet with your integrity preserved. Be kindly, but also upright; merciful, but also discerning; compassionate toward weakness, but intolerant of evil; agreeable to the good, but sparing not the disorderly; humble, but not abased; generous, but not prodigal; provident, but not avaricious.

Be in the temple of the Lord a silver base, through patience; a marble column, through unbending justice; a capital carved with lilies, through constant contemplation. Be the ark of the covenant through abundant grace; Aaron’s rod through discipline; the table of the Lord through teaching; a lampstand of purest gold through a good reputation; the mercy-seat through mercy; the tablets of the covenant through knowledge of the old and new law; a curtain through charity; goats’-hair cloth through humility; the temple of the Lord through continence and chastity.

Let no wicked person dwell beside you; hear neither the voice of blood nor the speech of whispering. Let the strongest in Israel and the most skilled in war—that is, the most honorable and proven monks—surround your bed because of terrors in the night. Let men of evil suspicion neither live nor walk with you, unless perhaps you correct them rarely and more privately, and rebuke them more kindly. For sometimes evil people are thus amended, when they are recalled by a shepherd’s mercy. A sheep which does not return to the fold with the others, or at least after the other sheep: if this is from weakness, it must be carried; if from malice, it must be compelled.

Let those who flee to you in humility find a mother; let those who recoil from you in obstinacy experience a severe father. Be not hasty in judgment, silent in counsel, verbose at table, arrogant in public, disparaging in private, avaricious in your own affairs, prodigal in another’s, insulting in chapter, negligent in the monastery, or excessive in the refectory. Be frequent in prayer, discreet in confession, constant in reading, lavish in the shedding of tears, generous in mercy toward the poor, fervent in contemplation, and gracious in receiving guests. Let the utterances of your mouth be few and true. Let pretense be far from you; let deceit never be in your heart, nor fraud ever in your mouth. Keep the fear of God before your eyes and blessed Benedict before your hands. Do nothing apart from God; command nothing apart from Benedict. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXII. TO H., ABBOT OF PRULLY

[II, 8.] To his dearest friend H., abbot of Prully [Note: [Col. 0441D] To H., abbot of Prully. Also a new abbot, but of the Cistercian Order, in the diocese of Sens. Stephen of Tournai, Letter 172, perhaps mentions an abbot of Prully who was the same man.], Brother PETER, abbot of La Celle, wishes him to receive of the spirit of Moses.

The counsels of friends are received with greater affection in proportion as the bond of hearts is more eagerly strengthened between them. He does not know the adhesive bond of your mutual love who has not been familiarly admitted to the secrets of its very depths. Therefore, borrowing from those depths a word of friendly consolation, I ask that it likewise be admitted to the innermost recesses of your heart, that it may discharge the office of affection in my stead and make good the loss of our customary conversation.

What is this, lord—indeed, brother and friend? For you do not yet bear the scent of a lordship: what is this? Your friends have transferred you from the station of a most tranquil harbor to the perils of the sea; or rather, to speak more truly, the most gracious hand of your God has set you at the mill. What then will you do? Clearly, take up the millstone and grind flour from which you may make ashes-bread in the conversion of sinners, so that they may turn from their evil ways and live; and likewise fine flour in exhorting the good, lest they sin and fail to remember the righteous deeds they had done.

Truly, dearest friend, you have been set at the mill, where in a mighty spirit you grind down others in their evils, while you yourself are ground down in afflictions. But observe carefully that the millstone, moving in a circular course and nowhere ever passing outside its orbit, wears down the surface of the grain placed beneath it into the form of the finest flour, from which bread is made for human food. Thus indeed may all your labor and affliction—which will give you understanding—be revolved within the roundness of equity, so that you do nothing excessively: neither act more fervently than your constitution or the weakness of those entrusted to you can endure, nor more laxly than is fitting for your order and office, or than rule and regular custom permit.

Therefore proceed in a circular course in all your business, preserving moderation in what you yourself do and in what you impose on others. Weigh the customs of the times against the characters of persons, and turn this way and that, because “a cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of mixed wine.” Nature has not yet been strained, not yet cleared; the sediment of bodily heaviness has not yet been drained away. “The body which decays weighs down the soul.” Therefore the body must for the time being be spared; yet the soul must not be given license, by running out into its own desires, to cast aside the body as slow and weary upon the very road. “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. XXVI).

The soul ought to bear its yokefellow, not kill it. Let the spirit indeed always move toward better things, but let it not torment its sickly mount beyond measure with bloody spurs, lest perhaps, torn by blows, it die, and the Lord require its blood at the hand of the immoderate spirit. “No one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes it” (Eph. IV), as Christ also does the Church. Let the soul go forth and go before the flesh, but let it halt, so that the flesh which follows may at least late in the day attain the lodging-place. Yet one must delay, not remain behind, on account of the flesh. The delay will not be burdensome if it is moderate. One must stop until the flesh catches its breath, not until it expires. Let the flesh know how to use the refreshment of travellers, not the pleasures of permanent residents. If it is wearied by the journey, let it hasten to its lodging. For there will be for it a lodging both pleasant in its rest and certain in its eternity. To this point has our circular motion brought us.

## LETTER XXXIII. TO ROBERT, ABBOT OF BULLENCOURT

[II, 9.] To ROBERT, abbot of Bullencourt [Note: [Col. 0442D] To Robert, abbot of Bullencourt. Bullencourt, or Bullencuria, is likewise a Cistercian monastery in the diocese of Troyes, where there were formerly Augustinian canons, until Bishop Henry granted the place to Saint Bernard and the monks of Clairvaux. “Abbot of Vallecourt” is wrongly read for “abbot of Bullencourt” in John of Salisbury, Letter 115.], Brother PETER, abbot of La Celle, greeting.

I know that any consolations which can proceed from me fall short of the strength of your spirit. That fortitude alone is praiseworthy which rises stronger when wearied and freer when oppressed. It lifts without distress the importunate burdens of fortune, bears them without weight, and lays them down without fatigue. Perhaps the heap of weight grows, but so too does virtue. For virtue lies idle without an exercise-ground. Where struggle is absent, virtue seems as though ungirded. It is soft and tender when it is weakened in the bed of prosperity. But it assumes its proper garb—indeed, itself—when it meets something that must be overcome. It runs forth with arms bared where it finds the palm of victory. Challenged, it becomes better; provoked, fresher; suddenly surprised, both more moderate and more cautious. It is not disturbed by a sudden attack, nor broken by the amassed army of enemies. It does not grow old through weakness, but grows old together with maturity.

Virtue abandons one whom it has not converted to itself. It uses one man differently from another. Either it accommodates itself to you, or it makes itself fit for you by forming you. It is not less because it is less in one person, nor greater because it is more in another. It is said to advance when men advance through it. Its origin and its effect in human beings are different from those of bodily nature. Its origin is from the Creator, but its purpose is the benefit of the creature. For what is this virtue of which we speak except a vapor and emanation of God’s power? The soul subject to God gives off this vapor with the heat and fragrance of life, so that by its heat it may be justified and by its fragrance glorified.

O fragrance of glory! O warmth of life! No one lives well without both, just as no one lives blessedly without both. Angels are blessed in one way, good human beings in another. Yet angels are blessed precisely because they are good; for they could not have been blessed unless they had been good, just as fragrance is always found with warmth. Nothing gives fragrance without warmth; yet something may be warm without giving fragrance, just as a person may sometimes be found good who is not yet blessed. Goodness is the pledge of blessedness; and one who does not abandon it cannot be deprived of its attainment. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIV. TO MATILDA, ABBESS OF FONTEVRAULT

[II, 10.] To the venerable MATHILDA, abbess of Fontevrault [Note: [Col. 0443D] To Matilda, abbess of Fontevrault. At the end of the letter he states that she was the daughter of the count of Anjou. This, then, is Matilda, daughter of Fulk V, count and later king of Jerusalem, whom histories of both peoples report as betrothed to William, son of Henry I, king of the English; see also the notes on Geoffrey, Book V, Epistle 17. But when William, her betrothed, was swallowed up by the waves of the sea before the wedding, Matilda vowed her untouched virginity to God among the nuns of Fontevrault, and, as our Peter of La Celle says, exchanged the king of the English for the King of Angels. She was now abbess, as in the following letter.], PETER, abbot of La Celle, her friend in Christ, wishes her the grace and glory of the eternal Bridegroom.

God, the searcher and witness of consciences, knows with what depths of heart I received your graciousness; how beyond comprehension I rejoiced in the covenant of our mutual love; and how incomparably I preferred your friendship to all gold. For a single, pure grace first won me to you; then there came a manifold cause for enlarging that love. For where no beginnings of deeds and no pleasant preliminaries of services precede, from what source can I say that love proceeds except grace? Grace works by its own spontaneous movements in human hearts without regret, with great reverence, and beyond the slander of the envious. It removes suspicion, bestows affection, yields honor, and brings back modesty. With grace intervening, the whispers of the malicious are dissolved, the concord of the good is strengthened, and the devices of plotters are entirely removed. This adhesive bond of spirits and indissoluble bitumen of souls brings diversity of characters back into one harmony, and proportionately gathers the inequalities of merits into a tempering of equality.

O gracious grace! Without you all things are bitter; with you all things are good. Without you, I say, the whole creation is empty; by you both angelic and human creation is filled. You reform what is deformed, repair what has fallen, strengthen what is weak, open what is shut, gather what is scattered, and illumine what is dark. Yours is what I am, what I live, what I understand, and that I devoutly fall down before the footsteps of the saints. Yours, I say, yours it is that I have deserved to see and adore you in the temple of your holy name, in the sanctuary of your glorification.

For if you are worshipped more holy in holy souls than in stone temples made by human hands, how much more in sacred virgin wombs? Nothing is dearer to you than these, nothing more acceptable, since they shine more brightly than the ether, more delightfully than the firmament, and more sublimely than heaven. Where among human beings will you find such a thing? I believe it is in that abbess of your Fontevrault who is second to none in nobility of flesh, most renowned among many for nobility of spirit, outstanding in chastity, conspicuous in humility, lavish in generosity, and fittingly inflamed with religious fervor.

I restrain my pen lest I incur the danger of being a flatterer. We ought to praise friends more sparingly and love them more abundantly; likewise, to correct their evils more severely than to handle their unsoundness badly with caressing flattery. Yet no less is he condemned for sloth who, from vain fear, keeps silent about the glory of God, than he is for envy who is tormented by another’s good fortune. I judge it no less monstrous a crime to remove the sun from the world than to obscure by the silence of malice the endowment of nature and grace bestowed by the Creator upon a creature. For the proclamation of virtues is the glorification of God; nor is it safe for anyone not to know that he possesses what he ought to possess, since loss may thereby occur more readily.

“We have received,” says the Apostle, “not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we may know the things given to us by God” (1 Cor. XI). Among the children of this age, prudence is proved when their household estate has increased through frequent reckoning. Likewise, the merchant of heavenly rewards ought to weigh the daily gains by continual calculation and seek with all diligence what is insufficient for the treasury. Hence the Psalmist: “Make known to me, O Lord, my end, and what is the number of my days, that I may know what I lack” (Ps. XXXVII). For how can a person know what he lacks if he does not know what he has?

Let him therefore look for his little bundles, shake out his purses, weigh his money in the balance, consider his expenditure, count his drachmas, and sweep his house, that he may know what he lacks. If he lacks fields of firstfruits, namely the fertile charity of heavenly virtues; if a garden of pomegranates, that is, the fullness of good works; if a fountain of gardens, that is, a spring of holy devotions; if a golden reclining-place, which is the repose of all affections: let him hasten, travel about, and migrate through markets, sea-perils, and remote regions, because where one’s own resources are insufficient, those of others come to aid.

Moreover, let the maiden seek wool and flax, that from the one she may make a warm tunic and from the other a white one. Let Martha wear the warm garment, Mary the white. For the latter is suited to action and the former to contemplation; this one prays, that one works; this one sits, that one sweats; this one rests, that one runs; this one goes out, that one enters; this one begins, that one brings to completion. Happy is the soul whose storehouse exudes such ointments, whose cask pours forth such libations, whose shrubbery drips such balsams, and whose granary contains such like spices! I would call happy also the place where such wares are obtained, where incomparable gems are sold, where things greatly to be desired are acquired at a small price. I have seen—yes, seen—in the market a mirror fitting for none but a king’s daughter; I have seen a necklace to be hung upon the neck of none but an untouched virgin.

This mirror is chastity, virtue, and humility, which our land has hitherto not been accustomed to possess in public commerce. It is indeed a thing of inestimable price, rarely finding a seller and more rarely a buyer. In purchasing it, heavenly treasuries are exhausted; exceedingly rich and godlike merchants are required, and purchasers likewise most generous. For heavenly commerce requires a price beyond heaven. What is more heavenly than virginity? What higher than humility? One shines pre-eminently in Solomon’s diadem, the other is more precious in royal treasuries. Yet Wisdom, the maker of all things, has fashioned a necklace from them both and set it up for sale. “He who can receive it, let him receive it” (Matt. XIX).

The hands of young women fluttered about it, almost ambitiously attempting to buy it; but on hearing the price, they all immediately drew back. At last, when the transaction was almost despaired of, a certain young virgin, the daughter of the count of Anjou, arose, set her hand to brave deeds, and in a new exchange traded the king of the English for the King of Angels. “Glorious things have been said of you,” dearest lady. Forgive me, however, for detaining you longer than is fitting by this rather extended discourse, and believe that the abundance of my love has produced this abundance of speech. Pray for us, then. As to composing certain brief sentences of your discourse, I have not forgotten, but, hindered by many matters, have not been able to fulfill it so quickly. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXV. TO THE SAME WOMAN

[II, 11.] To his lady, from her servant: may you have a right spirit.

I write to one who knows that the Son of Man came not to bring peace upon the earth but a sword; that the Holy Spirit descended upon our leaders in fire; and that Isaac bore the fire of punishment and the wood of our discipline. Perhaps this also explains why Jacob crossed his hands in blessing Joseph’s sons: that regard might be had in each not to the order or privileges of birth, but to the services of merits and character. For when the virtue of discernment is preserved, mercy triumphs in its own realm and justice fittingly arranges the governing reins of the whole kingdom.

Therefore, when we enter the palace of mercy, we pluck the flowers and fruit of the olive. When we stand before the tribunal of justice, we bear away the palm and are satisfied with the fruits of moon and sun. This is the delightful variety in the garment of our queen; and, for removing the lofty pretensions of the children not only of men but also of God, unchangeable immutability and eternal eternity. John baptizes only in water and does not heal the wound of original sin. Christ Jesus, in the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning, opens heaven.

“All things,” says the Apostle, “are cleansed in blood, and without blood there is no remission” (Heb. IX). Therefore let no garment mixed with blood be destined for burning because of the transgression of sin. Christ sprinkled his own blood seven times with his own finger toward the veil of the sanctuary for the cleansing of our crimes. This our one Master, who is in heaven, taught us; this the Lawgiver admonished in figure: “You shall not remove,” He says, “the salt of the covenant of your God from every sacrifice” (Lev. II). Enough has been said for the wise.

I excuse that former prior of Saint Aigulf, because he did what he could and ought to do. Had he done otherwise, or acted differently, he would have incurred our displeasure. Farewell. Yet your prayer and that of your holy convent will benefit the sinner, provided repentance comes first. Farewell again.

## LETTER XXXVI. TO THE PRIOR OF LA CELLE

[II, 12.] To his prior [Note: [Col. 0445D] To his prior: of the monastery of La Celle.], from his abbot.

How human affairs are weighed in the divine mind is hidden from human sight amid the changeability of worldly things. Angelic purity alone is admitted, as it is granted, to these secrets, and, instructed from the depth of mysteries, suffices to reveal what it seems fitting to reveal. Meanwhile our rashness, thus darkened within itself, is so confounded that it neither apprehends in any degree what is remote from the senses nor attains even what is near through perfect knowledge. This is a fitting punishment for the presumptuous person: that he is reproved by past things and restrained from future ones.

Warned by fear of this danger, my sweetest friend, I am distressed about present matters; yet, foreseeing the darkness of things to come, I dread unknown paths. But if the grace of divine aid is present, I neither fear the depths of the sea nor despair of undertaking what has not yet been attempted. Although affection, insufficiently strengthened, may tremble, it can without doubt be fortified by the unconquerable protection of heavenly light.

O Jesus, for whom has it been vain to flee to you? For whom has it ended badly to seek you even when you are caught by the horns among thorns? Neither your mercy nor your omnipotence deserts you; and therefore you do not refuse your own the support of your mercy. Whoever is endangered perishes through his own distrust rather than through your lack of compassion. If you deign to use our service, pierce our minds with an inward touch; draw us back from the world in the cords of your love, and lead us into the wilderness. Let the tumult not cease until, like foam, it casts us out upon a peaceful shore. “Let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us” (Ps. XXXII).

Let not the bitterness of suffering be turned away until it has purged every superfluous moisture. Ambition for honor, pleasure of the flesh, conversation with friends, visiting relatives, precedence over subjects, display of greater power—what are these for? Are not the soul’s feet shackled by these things, lest it escape to the heights? Is it not entangled by them, lest it seek heavenly things on the wings of virtues? These things will indeed end, but punishment will endure without end. One of two things must happen: either to conquer these things or be conquered by them; either to overcome or be subjected; either to flee or be enclosed.

It is healthier to swim out naked than to be drowned clothed; to escape alone than to be endangered with many. Why do you, human heart, tremble? Why do you shrink back? The fruit of solitude is not soft, but it is strong; not rich, but sweet; hard in its rind, bitter on its surface; of a new taste to beginners; grinding the teeth of those unaccustomed to it. O human heart, why do you fear to be renewed? Why do you recoil from being restored? Willing or unwilling, you will be compelled to depart from here; willing or unwilling, you will depart without delay.

O senseless heart, why do you not run to the Lord of the heart? Why do you gather everything and not cultivate yourself? You excel in dignity, surpass in power, and by authority overcome whatever is created beneath heaven. Those who place you after their body do not consider how great is the lineage of your nobility because of their ignoble way of life; those who fail to see what difference there is between body and spirit do not remember the pattern of your formation. Read again your birth-record and recall from what illustrious stock you come. Do not bring the stain of slavery upon your race, because slavery is not owed to you by yourself. You are meant to sit in a high place, while others ought to stand before you. It is yours to command, theirs to come at your command and receive punishment for contempt. It is yours to impose; it is for subjects, without distinction, to devote to execution what has been imposed. If you render fitting service to God alone, your dominion will prevail over all things.

For the present I shall set aside this discussion and appoint a time and place at which I may hear more freely on both sides the narratives, arguments, and allegations. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVII. TO T., PRIOR OF MOLÈSME

[II, 13.] Brother PETER, abbot of La Celle, to T., prior of Molèsme [Note: [Col. 0447] To T., prior of Molèsme. Perhaps Theobald, who afterwards became abbot of the same monastery; Letter 113.], greeting.

The solemn holy days of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection have until now rightly claimed their days with their hours, their members with their duties. For what business have my fingers with writing by the pen on the day when the Beloved, beloved by his beloved, is stretched out upon the cross and has become for his bride a bundle of myrrh? (Song of Songs I.) The hands of the Lord, rounded, golden, and filled with hyacinths, are pierced by nails—shall my hand be occupied with anything other than distilling most choice myrrh? His heart is wounded by one of the eyes and one lock of the neck of his bride, and shall my heart meditate on empty and superfluous things?

Rather, may this day impress upon the Christian heart the feeling of Christ dying: compassion in the members, mortification of desires, cleansing from vices, and conformity in works of charity. This is why I did not answer your letter on the day after receiving it. For I received it when preparations were already being made to strip the skin from the fatted calf and roast the lamb, and when Rebecca was preparing to cover the hands and feet of the younger son with Esau’s very good garments—that is, with the sacraments of the Church.

Jesus was laying aside filthy garments, not because of contamination by sin but because of the defiled condition of mortality; and he designated the sacred washing of hands and feet not by the fleshly removal of dirt but by the appeal of a good conscience to God. Already the house was filled with the fragrance of ointment poured by the sinful yet penitent woman upon the Savior’s head or feet; already a banquet of rich foods, a banquet of marrow, was being set forth; the purest wine of the bowl was being poured.

O good friend, who could write—indeed, who could refrain from drinking? “Eat, friends, and drink; be intoxicated, beloved,” was being continued, and was I to think of blackening skins of dead animals with ink? [Col. 0448D] This is why I did not reply at once: I preferred to attend to those dishes rather than to think about answering you. What shall I say about the Sabbath? What, I say, except that it is the Sabbath? A Sabbath indeed—but delightful, holy, glorious. It is therefore not permissible to stretch out a finger or to speak what is unprofitable. Then, on the following day, when the Lord rose again and returned with abundant spoils, I ask for something from that most precious booty to come forth and meet me. Again I behold the triumph; I welcome the stars reborn; after the sun’s rising and the dawn’s birth [Col. 0449A] I store them among my treasures, so that this hope laid up in my breast may teach that a happier fate follows a mournful beginning. During these days no one else wrote, except Pilate alone—indeed, the bond written against us was destroyed. But afterwards, at last, when “man went forth to his work and to his labour until evening,” I reconsidered the sequence of dreams and statements in your letter; drawing it from darkness into light, I discovered that it was not mine.

For where is my letter—the one which at the beginning tells about me what it saw or heard from me; in the middle invents that I said or did what is untrue; and at the end compares itself with one who is not without sin? The likeness of your letter does not suit you, good brother and friend. First [Col. 0449B] you set out wine; then you serve vinegar; finally you add a mixture of myrrh and aloes. I do not wholly reject the praise offered me: I embrace the goodwill of the speaker, not the confidence that what was said is true. For that very powerful sickness by which, under the sun, all human vanity suffers has seized me along with others, so that I have not yet learned to drive away those pleasant modulations that reach the ears. This fault is natural; and, as Seneca says, the natural faults of body or mind may be softened by art, but cannot be erased. It is an itch of the soul, though it attacks in different ways. At times it invades the lower part, at times the higher, at times the whole together—both higher and lower. The higher part of the soul is that which pertains to reason; the lower, that which pertains to sense-appetite; the whole, that which pertains to [Col. 0449C] resolve or deliberation.

Thus, by deceptive insinuation, while the mind is perhaps otherwise occupied with certain greater and better matters, the love of empty glory slips in; shading its shame with fig leaves, it sits hidden in a corner, so that, when its mistress Reason is absent, it may join itself to the man—that is, to natural appetite—and from such intercourse Ammonites and Moabites are begotten, who do not enter the Church of God even to the third and fourth generation. For how can that which is defective from the beginning of conception and generation enter into the glory of innocence? Therefore the work of vain glory will never be counted among the rewards of true glory. Hence Abraham is told: “Cast out the slave-woman and her son. For [Col. 0449D] the son of the slave-woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman” (Gen. 21).

Then, what is more dangerous, this itch rises upward and touches the very holy summit of the soul, where the image and likeness of God are. It seeks its own glory rather than God’s; it misuses the will involved in both divine generation and regeneration. It does not name its son—that is, its work—John, but Zachariah. Now it no longer hides or veils, but reveals its shame; and, according to the wisest man, Adonijah asks Abishag the Shunammite against his own life, she who was accustomed to render King David [Col. 0450A] the most excellent services and the purest encouragements. Solomon says: “It is one and the same as though he were asking for the kingdom” (3 Kings 11).

Adonijah, most desirous of the kingdom, is reason infected with love of private advantage. He seeks to take Abishag for himself when the whole of reason is swallowed up by the abyss of vainglory. But he is killed, because he is separated from God. This evil exists under the sun. A still greater evil occurs when a person’s whole intention and action bends itself toward this iniquity and denial against God. Beware, friend, of this snare so twisted with a threefold cord: it is evil to take pleasure in honours offered; worse to seek honours denied; worst to burst forth in anger when they are withdrawn.

Was it mine to give that abbey to whom I wished, or take it away from whom I wished? And who am I? And [Col. 0450B] what am I? Especially in comparison with such persons: namely the Archbishop of Lyons, the Bishops of Langres and Autun, and the abbots of Molesme and of Saint John of Quinciac—what am I but dust and ashes?

> [Note: [Col. 0449D] “Saint John of Quinciac.” There are many monasteries in France bearing the name of Saint John. Here, however, I think that the abbey of Saint Benedict at Reome, in the diocese of Langres, is intended. By “Quinciac” I understand the other Cistercian monastery, situated not far from Tonnerre [Col. 0450D] in the same diocese.]

I call heaven and earth together as witnesses with these men, unless perhaps it has slipped from my awareness, that I have laid before their ears nothing dishonourable or criminal about your person. Indeed, I did not at once agree, and the discussion went into a distant region. This man was named; I did not conceal what I had heard or seen, but I kept silent about what I did not know. Peter of Vivariis was named—alas for me!—for whom, on another occasion, I had stood most strongly and steadfastly against friends, bishops, clerics, and intimates; and now too I stood for him as best I could. Because [Col. 0450C] I could not secure his becoming abbot, he and some of his followers turned their backs, not their faces, upon me. This year I have endured many things of this kind, not merely by sight but through feeling and experience. My former friends stood far off and no longer walk with me.

What then am I to do? Shall I not go? But I shall be disobedient. Shall I not go? But I shall seem proud. Shall I be silent? But I fear for my conscience. Shall I be silent? But I bury the Lord’s money. Shall I be silent? But I am judged either crafty or foolish. Shall I please both sides? But that would be pretence, and it would be impossible. What then? “Direct my way before thee, O Lord my God” (Ps. 5). What, I say? Give a right and well-sounding word into my mouth. Enough thus far. For I refrain from digging through—let alone attacking—the wall of your letter. [Col. 0450D] Walking around it, I merely indicate, and also seal up, its cracks and certain fissures. For what has been broken, if indeed anything has been broken, I prefer to mend rather than cause fresh harm. Let there be peace.

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO THE BRETHREN OF CAZIAC

[II, 14.] Brother Peter, abbot of Celle, to his beloved brethren, sons, and friends of Caziac: wisdom to write in a time of leisure.

> [Note: [Col. 0450D] “Of Caziac.” Bernard writes to Pope Eugenius on behalf of the abbot of Caziac in Letter 263. In the letters of Hatto, Bishop of Troyes, Simon, abbot of Caziac, is also named. Moreover, in Nicholas of Clairvaux there is Letter 19 to the abbot of Cazei—that is, as our manuscript has it, of Caziac—from which it is evident that the monastery was of the Cistercian [rather, Benedictine] order. It is situated in the diocese of Soissons. [Col. 0451D; Col. 0452D]]

[Col. 0451A] Contrary both to my usual manner and to my desire, I have resolved to write to you with a rod, not in a spirit of gentleness, since you did not fear mercilessly to pierce a father’s heart with the barbs of your letters. I am deeply moved and stirred by the pious old age of the Father, by the pitiable sympathy due to a brother’s rejection, and by the grave yet intemperate language running through your pages. To ignore this and not rebuke matters so manifest seems to be a share in the same guilt. For what is this onrush? What is this drunkenness? What flight of mind and senses is this: to renounce a brother, contradict a Father, and so disturb the right of monastic order? Harsh and dreadful, my brethren, is your zeal—more sorrowful than death, lower than hell, harder than stone, more bitter than wormwood, more sour than gall.

For what is happening? Piety is denied; mercy is put to death; paternal honour is reviled; brotherly love is accused; fellowship is repelled; the Rule is violated. O irreligious religion! O counterfeit holiness! O jealous charity! Is this, dearest brethren, is this how you have learned Christ? Is not our God a God of peace and not of dissension? O foolish madness of those who call it their peace if they do not receive their brother; death if they see him; prosperity if they expel their companion; devotion if they condemn a work of devotion! This plague, Joseph, rages against you; this undeserved misfortune is poured back upon your head. For your brothers wish to sell you because they do not wish to see you. They think you an obstacle to their father’s favour because they perceive that you are favoured by the Father. [Col. 0451C] Thus, yes thus, the Father’s gratitude purchases the brothers’ ingratitude. “If,” they say, “the beloved son is gone, paternal affection will return to us. While Joseph stands before his father’s eyes, the sweetness of fatherhood turns less often toward us. Let us remove our brother, and we shall have our father.”

How much more rightly and pleasantly would you act if you rooted filial devotion within yourselves. This would multiply affection, not lay it waste. Good brethren and dearest friends, you were running well: who bewitched you to write so to your father and proscribe your brother? What evil has T. done? What injury so atrocious has he committed as to deserve that, contrary to law and without law, he should not be restored by your judgment? Where is your former mercy, by which you granted pardon to criminals and forgave wicked men their committed crimes? O how many persons of far more impure and unworthy lives have you both granted a place of mercy and prolonged undeserved favour! Where are T.’s fornications? Where are his disordered meals? Where his disgraceful deeds? Where his unmentionable shames? T.’s works are works of light, not works of darkness; works of day, not of night; works to be proclaimed, not condemned.

O malice! O envy! With what boldness have you entered the sanctuary of God, the chamber of the Most High, [Col. 0452A] the throne of the eternal King? By what tyrannical presumption have you burst into, invaded—indeed torn apart—the hearts of the saints? Behold: by your weight you have pressed a groaning and loud cry out of the hearts of friends. For whence comes that burning of heart, whence the anguish of mind, unless you kindle it, unless you constrict it? You will surely be burned unto the destruction of the soul; and from this come poverty and straitness of heart.

No, brethren, let not your anger or agitation blaze out against me. I certainly ought not to keep silent from you about your folly. Yet accept my counsels, and do not delay to correct deliberately what was done rashly. As quickly as you can, cast yourselves together at the feet of the lord abbot, making satisfaction for no slight error; and do not rise until you have carried away a blessing [Col. 0452B] from the father’s mouth. And if I have offended in anything, I beg you to pardon me. For I love you—God knows it. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIX. TO THE BRETHREN OF CAZIAC

[II, 15.] To his dearest brethren, sons, and friends of Caziac, Brother Peter, humble abbot of Celle: greeting.

Neither frivolity nor a light necessity urges me to speak, as I consider the Father’s illness, the Mother’s desolation, and the brethren’s disturbance. It is true, dearest brethren, true is that saying of the Gospel: “I shall strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered” (Matt. 26). But which of these is graver—the shepherd’s being struck or the flock’s scattering? Each, when divided from the other, is undoubtedly grave enough; but both together are almost an intolerable loss. Shall I therefore linger in lamenting the Father’s suffering, or shall I pursue the recall of the brethren’s expulsion? Yet, to confess the truth, I shall mourn both, if both occur: the one more tenderly, the other more earnestly. For I shall pour out fuller tears for the Father, suffering the failure of nature; but I shall shoot more forceful arrows of rebuke at the brethren because of their excess of guilt. We owe compassion to the illnesses of nature, rebuke to the corruption of souls. One should pity, not accuse, an old man for departing the world; but one should accuse—or rather cut off—a Christian if he attempts to break the bond of love.

While the matter is still whole, dearest brethren, dangers not yet imminent are more profitably avoided when the eye of providence and the hand of watchful caution are present. The downfall of the strong ought to alarm the security of the weak. “Your own concern is at stake when the neighbouring wall is on fire.” However mighty, however wealthy kingdoms may be, they collapse in a short time when the trouble of disputes catches fire. The very structure of the world could not stand if the discord of the elements threw it into confusion. Recently, the Church of Cluny—

> [Note: [Col. 0452D] “Recently, the Church of Cluny.” At the election of Robert, mentioned in Letter 26, no abbot of this name is found among the Cluniacs at that time.]

—older in antiquity, [Col. 0453A] more fervent in religious observance, fuller in material abundance, and more numerous in population—what did it accomplish? A scandal to the little ones, sorrow to the devout, shame to the religious, a loss of honour to its friends, and a covering of reproach for the whole Church. Where secular honour is sought beneath the cover of religion, when will the cruel mind be restrained within the maturity of love? If a honeycomb thus turns sour, what will the bitterness of wormwood do, what the sharpness of vinegar? It is proverbial: “He is gently corrected who is amended by the example of others.” Therefore let unity, peace, and concord remain among you, so that you may all say the same thing and there be no schisms among you. So long as you can keep your Father—indeed ours—with you, do not contemplate another. But when unavoidable necessity compels some other arrangement, the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, must be invoked; the assembly of the holy must be convened; and a good, religious, discerning, learned, devout man, trained in holy religion and an imitator of your Father, must by every means be sought. Farewell.

## LETTER XL. TO THE CARTHUSIANS OF MONT-DE-DIEU

[III, 1.] To his lords and Fathers, the prior—

> [Note: [Col. 0453D] “The prior”: Simon, a most holy man; see Letter 46.]

—and the other brethren of Mont-de-Dieu—

> [Note: [Col. 0453D] “Mont-de-Dieu.” A most beautiful monastery of the Carthusian order, distinguished in many ways, founded by Odo, abbot of Saint-Remi, in the diocese of Reims, in the prefecture of Mouzon. Our Peter was the third abbot of Saint-Remi after Odo; this alone sufficiently explains why he embraced the brethren of Mont-de-Dieu with such zeal and affection. Yet there were other and older grounds besides, including the migration to them of Stephen, a monk of Celle, mentioned here. The index or heading of the letter made known Stephen’s name; we recall it as worded thus: “Letter of Peter, abbot of Celle, to a certain Stephen, his monk, but afterwards a monk of Mont-de-Dieu.” But it has not hitherto been possible to obtain this letter. [Col. 0454D]]

—Brother Peter, unworthy abbot of Celle: unto the mountain of God, Horeb.

The subject matter urges one thing, your reverence another. The subject, namely the transfer of our dearest son to you, warns me rather always to be silent, or more earnestly to weep, than to write. But reverence for your holiness demands what is holy and worthy. [Col. 0453C] Therefore, one who undertakes to write to you ought to take up not trivial and secular matters but strong and heavenly ones. And what is stronger than charity, which is strong as death? What is more heavenly, which even surpasses all understanding? Of this charity, insofar as it has deigned to bend down to our understanding, it is said: “No one has greater love than this, that one lay down one’s life for one’s friends” (John 15). He who carefully weighs the price that I have paid for it may judge how much your love has profited in my lowly estimation.

Certainly, I have offered in this exchange not gold, but a man after my own heart; certainly not silver, but one whom I had as though an only-begotten son; certainly not precious stones, but the stone which I had raised up for myself [Col. 0453D] as a memorial of special affection. I know, and do not at all doubt, that even if I gave all the substance of my house for your holy love, I would still have brought nothing in comparison with it. For from the Mountain of God descends not love of the world but love of heaven; not carnal love, which passes away like a morning cloud, but eternal [Col. 0454A] charity, which never fails (1 Cor. 13). What surpasses every bidding of contingent things admits of no valuation. The devout love of holy souls indeed breathes forth the sweetness of divine love. And what worthy recompense could human poverty find, in all the treasure of its abundantly rich want, not merely for heavenly love but even for any condescension of the saints?

Certainly, no counsel seems sounder to me than to repay grace for grace, in imitation of him who customarily gives for grace, not from need, but rather from abundance. Thus I too give thanks for your favour—not vain or empty thanks, but generous and rich ones beyond the sufficiency of my means. For what you receive I bring forth not from a chest, [Col. 0454B] but from conscience; not from the depth of a purse, but from the inmost heart; not from the furniture of a house, but from my deepest entrails. If it could have been otherwise, if your holiness had demanded another price, however great, if that exchange could have admitted some other compensation—oh, how willingly I would have given it! With what gratitude I would have counted it out! O God of my heart, how great and unbearable is the anguish of my soul in this labour, even unto death, unless you bear with me the continually lasting sorrow of this separation of affection!

Good Jesus, I shall henceforth not blush to confess with certainty that I have done something for you. But what else could I do? He is yours; I am yours. And would that I were yours as he is yours! With what face could I, being yours, presume to oppose you concerning what is yours? I do not stubbornly resist your will, so that you may mercifully attend to my desolation. “See my humility and my labour, and forgive all my sins” (Ps. 24). Lord, Lord, would you not more gently take my whole soul from me than its half? At least be pleased not to abandon the part that remains, since you take to yourself the chief part. I now truly experience that you came to set a man against his father. Truly this is Solomon’s sword, living and effective, sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit. Why, for your sake, has the wall of hearts been divided by the presence [Col. 0454D] of bodies? You are the mediator; you are the cornerstone; you gather scattered Israel; you are one God, making the two one, toward you and in you. Why do you do this—or, if you do not do it, why do you permit me to lack the staff of my weakness? Why allow the foundation to abandon its own pillar? Why should not Moses, but your wretched servant, without Aaron be compelled to endure the disputes and troubles of this such and [Col. 0455A] so great multitude? Merciful Jesus, let not your mercy suffer my frailty to be shattered longer without consolation, to be wearied without visitation.

What is this? I began to write and speak to you, and thus, in the midst of my discourse, I have with such delay unfolded my miseries before the sight of the most merciful God. Certainly, so that you may see, certainly so that you may understand, what pain it is to lose a son of the right hand and not even, once Joseph has been taken away, retain Benjamin. Indeed, so that you may more sweetly and earnestly entreat for me the God of all consolation, compassionating my sorrows. For he is a kind hearer of the devout and a generous rewarder of those who do something for his sake. Pray, therefore, that I may not lose this one also, whom you hold, as it were, in Christ’s bonds; and that, as you wrote in your desire, I may receive for our Samuel a prophet [Col. 0455B] no less worthy. Thus enriched with a good gift, and receiving some consolation through your prayers, I shall be able to await that true and eternal consolation, for which I accept this temporal and passing desolation. Farewell.

## LETTER XLI. TO THE CARTHUSIANS OF MONT-DE-DIEU

[III, 2.] To his lords and Fathers of Mont-de-Dieu, Brother Peter of Celle: the sweetness of grace which God has promised to those who love him.

My spirit exults in God my saviour, both because I have been granted even once to see and hear you, and because, through the generosity of heavenly grace, I have found the favour of friendship. To this happiness of mine is added the sweet mutual exchange [Col. 0455C] of letters, through which a soothing electuary is prepared for my bitterness, a calming medicine for my restlessness, and no slight remedy for my dullness. In short, whenever I look upon the form and countenance of your words, with great strength I escape the venomous bites of roaring cares, moderate the floods of pressing occupations, and repress the attacks of internal and long-standing enemies. I delight in the depth of thought, truth of statements, formation of morals, rebuke of errors, cutting away of vanities, and condemnation of ambitions. Your words contain more flour of the kernel and less bark and bran. From them it can readily be seen what a religious soul thinks concerning itself, what it marvels at above itself concerning [Col. 0455D] its Creator, and what it fears below itself concerning its pilgrimage in the world and the temptation of the flesh. Turned toward itself, it is troubled; raised toward its Maker, it is enlarged; returned to the body, it is confounded.

For what is the body but empty earth? What is the soul but an impenetrable abyss? What is God but incomprehensible light? Therefore, let barren and unfruitful flesh be made pregnant through affliction by fasting and vigils; let the foul and darkened soul be made bright by being stripped of its former vices and imaginary ignorance. Let the flesh, through abstinence, become a paradise of delights; let the soul, through prayer and contemplation, become the most serene heaven. Let reason be appointed guardian and cultivator of paradise; let the Creator himself be protector and inhabitant of the soul. Let careful discipline be applied to the body, lest, like an immature child, [Col. 0456A] it be carried away to its own destruction. Let cultivation be bestowed on it, lest, like a neglected field, it be uselessly occupied by the evil progeny of nettles. Let it be broken up with plough and hoe and filled with good seed. For such is the nature of this body: the more it is pressed down, the more abundantly it multiplies. Unless the earth of this flesh is broken up by the plough of discipline, it will be useless like a closed womb. But when, vigorously shaken or torn open, it has received the seed of the Lord of hosts, it will begin to germinate according to its kind.

Finally, when wounded a second time, as by a two-edged sword—namely by love and fear—it pours forth rich fruits of righteousness, most abundant waters of inward compunction, indeed blood and water for the redemption of its transgressions and the cleansing of original sins, springing up into eternal life. [Col. 0456B] Therefore let it be worn down by vigorous contrition, lest it grow insolent and bring forth, in place of the wheat of good works, thorns and thistles of evil desires. Let it be dug up—indeed pierced through—by the lance of the Saviour, lest it condemn the soul, buried in the tomb of vices, to eternal fires. Let David measure it with two cords, one to mortify and one to make alive, so that what belongs to nature may be preserved and what belongs to vice destroyed. Thus, thus, however stony it may be, it will become soft and tender; however full of salt marshes, it will become sweet and good. It will, I say, become fruitful through the blessings of heaven; it will become like gardens watered beside rivers, like beds planted by perfumers, like a rich and fat mountain, [Col. 0456C] like a wooded valley, or like a holy and most fertile land.

From this land alone truth springs; upon it righteousness looks down from heaven; holiness dwells and walks in it. Iron is taken away from it: the hammer of the whole earth and the axe of diabolical suggestion are not heard in it. This land is near to blessing. This, I say, receives, as milk from the divine breast, the first blessing in justification and the second in glorification. Therefore everyone, according to the Apostle, who partakes of milk, as if drawing from the breasts of maternal grace, sucks from this breast the milk of sanctification, and from that one the milk of consolation. For this is what the Apostle says: “You have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end, eternal life” (Rom. 6). Thus, thus one lives, and in such things is the life [Col. 0456D] of the spirit. Thus your little ones live, Lord God: from the breast of present visitation, and thus from the breast of future expectation. These two are like two fawns, twin gazelles; for from the abundance of divine sweetness already tasted and the sure certainty of the reward to come, we now run through the unevenness of adversities toward God like a stag; we now leap joyfully over the mountains of spices, which are pure prayers, crying out with the Apostle that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8).

But what kind of milk you brethren hunger for, I hesitate to say, because I observe that for human use God created not one simple milk, but sheep’s milk of one kind, goat’s of another, and cow’s of another. Human infancy also has its own milk, appropriate to its age, from its mother’s breasts. Yet it is not for me to discuss, on the basis of the richness and quality of each milk, which of them is suitable for which person or age. Goat’s milk is not very nourishing but is sufficiently digestible; cow’s milk is very nourishing but difficult to digest; sheep’s milk is moderately balanced between the two. Therefore servants are fed with one kind, sons with another, and lords with another. Who are the lords except those who rule over the whole Egypt of their flesh? Who are the sons except those born from the womb of grace? Who are the servants except those whose hands served at the basket of the old life? Servants customarily consume milk because of the necessity of want, sons because of the sweetness of indulgence, and lords because of the fullness of delights. Would that to me, a sinner, the milk of pardon might be granted; to you, already cleansed, the milk of grace; and at last, when cleansed, [Col. 0457B] the milk of glory!

O bright milk! O sweet milk! O delightful milk! Bright, because through pardon we are transferred from the region of darkness to the light of joys. Sweet, because through the sweetness of grace we are led from the bitterness of temptations to the sweetness of unfading delights. Delightful, because through glory we escape the sadness of the age and enter eternal and unchangeable joy. O overflowing delight! O delightful abundance! “On that day a man shall nourish a cow of oxen,” as Isaiah says, “and because of the abundance of milk he shall eat butter” (Isa. 7). What indeed is the cow of oxen but a soul sharing the nature and glory of heavenly spirits? Christ the man will nourish it—not as now, in the shadow of a sacrament whose truth is veiled, but in the disclosure of truth and the unveiling, by David’s key, [Col. 0457C] of the mystery opened from the table of the body and the wine of the precious blood, from garments of glory and the milk of Mother Grace. Because of the abundance of mercies, this milk turns into the butter of delights: when all changeableness and mortality have been removed, it will be transformed in every respect from glory to glory, and thus into God. For then he will be all in all.

What is richer than this butter? What is sweeter than this honey? This is heavenly honey, not field honey, nor finally forest honey. John in the wilderness eats forest honey of penitential satisfaction; Jonathan in the battle line eats field honey of justification; the child Jesus, in the Virgin and from the Virgin, eats heavenly honey of incorruption. It is enough for the lamp that shines and burns—that is, for John—to preach repentance in the fields of the wilderness [Col. 0457D] and teach the people how to flee the wrath to come; it is enough for the young man who faithfully and manfully fights in the contest—that is, Jonathan—to taste beforehand the coming sweetness at the end of the rod of righteousness. But for Christ Jesus, who is light enlightening yet not enlightened, Creator and not created, because of the depth of the riches of the hidden treasure of wisdom and knowledge (Col. 2), it is too little that he should be a preacher and not also a giver—not merely of pardon, but also of grace.

Finally, to draw an example from the greatest matters down to lesser ones: the heart of every religious person, in likeness of the Lord’s Baptist, quieted from the noise of the world, cleansed in the baptism of devotion, prepared in the mortification of the flesh, strengthened in love of God’s Word, established in the religion of angels—if it does not yet belch forth heavenly honey with full mouth and belly, at least tastes forest honey beforehand. For grace tastes differently in the homeland and in exile; differently when rare and when abundant; differently when continuous and intermittent; differently in a mortal body and in an immortal one; differently when invisibly given and visibly administered. Therefore grace, melted by the heat of charity, strained through the filter of discernment, and also poured into a person through the vessel of exquisite truth, eases the roughness of the throat in confession, cleanses the stomach receptive of innumerable thoughts, regulates the discriminating reason of the brain to a sure measure, and supplies the heart with the vital vein leading to true immortality.

Meanwhile, here we sigh after grace with the crowd, as though in the plains; there, as if on the [Col. 0458B] mountain of contemplation, we gaze upon the glorified face of Jesus. Here we await; there we behold. Here we ask; there we receive. Here we pray; there we dispense. Here we are needy; there wealthy. Here poor; there rich. Here with John in the wilderness; there with Jesus in the kingdom. Here in Herod’s prison; there in the palace of the eternal inheritance. Here grace is lent for restoration; there it is bestowed for refreshment. Here it is by measure; there beyond measure. Here in a skin-bottle; there in the belly. Here in the outer shell of sacrament; there in the manifestation of the supreme and uncircumscribed light.

Behold, milk—indeed butter; behold honey, or rather a honeycomb—is offered by your servant to the table of his lords. Why should I again offer you a vessel of water with an amphora of wine? O dearest lords and friends, the well is deep and a stone lies over it, which no angel has yet rolled away for me, which Jacob has not yet removed; and how can I say, “Drink, my lord, and I shall give drink to your camels”? O burning desire! You possess digging tools; you possess veins of living waters; you possess the wells dug by Abraham and his sons, Isaac and his servants; and do you still thirst for the water of the cistern that is in Bethlehem? Indeed, this water, though good for drinking, is difficult to find. The journey is long and beset; the place remote and unknown; strength scant and rare; on every side, enemy and sword; night at hand and darkness at the doors. Yet such labours must be expended to obtain an incomparable treasure. What shall I say? Even in one moment this most pure drop [Col. 0458D] surpasses every labour, because it satisfies thirst, washes away filth, tempers heat, moistens dry places, softens hard ones, and makes barren things fruitful.

From it you pour out the filled flasks of your eyes in your libations, and with it you offer acceptable vows to the most high God. It extinguishes fire that can be extinguished. It bends the Judge’s severity toward mercy. It restrains the cherubim and the flaming, turning sword from harming. It changes this water into wine; and, in its customary way, it displays greater gifts in blessing than in creation. Without doubt we have many strong men for drinking wine and mixing intoxication; but who is worthy for this cup? Our true Noah, who gave us rest from dead works, intoxicated by this wine, uncovered on the cross the shame of human weakness [Col. 0459A] and endured mockery from his middle son, who is neither hot nor cold. Therefore few proceed to buy, fewer to possess, very few to drink, and almost none to become intoxicated. A mighty drinker of this wine was the carpenter’s son. After him, those who drank the wine of libations migrated to the vineyards of Engaddi. Since therefore there is now left in Zion, and remaining in Jerusalem, no one to receive from the Lord’s hand the cup of unmixed wine, come forward, you who are of God’s house and God’s mountain, and eat and drink; be intoxicated, beloved.

## LETTER XLII. TO THE SAME RECIPIENTS

[III, 3.] To his lords and friends, the prior and the other brethren of Mont-de-Dieu, Brother Peter of Celle: may you not be defrauded of the prize [Col. 0459B] of the daily denarius.

Sweet morsels of flavour, like bread rich with oil, which I greedily tasted beforehand at the table of your letter, made me begin to pour forth the joy of the spirit and, again and again, in longing, to draw in the good Spirit. For you wrote amid the richness of a well-fed soul, in the abundance of God’s sweetness; and you have filled my throat, as with fatness and richness, with spiritual joy. Your discourse is not such as, by artificial forms laid over it, presents an appearance of godliness while denying its power. Such speech belongs to those who speak “with heart and heart,” or who smooth their words beyond oil when they themselves are darts. Your word, however, is neither tasteless nor made foolish in this way, but seasoned with salt and strengthened by the fullness of grace: it fills the inward parts of the saints, restores the strength of souls, heals the languor of the sick, and preserves the vigour of the healthy. Moreover, it satisfies the gluttony of the pampered and cures the revulsion of those who are nauseated. It feeds like bread, gladdens like wine, overflows in every sweetness like a paradise of delights, and shines in every beauty like a most splendid temple. It is plainly persuasive for admonition, right for ordering, effective for moving, powerful for strengthening, sweet for soothing, and ardent for kindling.

For when pure discourse is poured from a pure vessel, what is more suited to cleansing, clearer for instructing, or more useful for every good work? Indeed, a good word, distilled by frequent meditation from the good Word of God, ground by bodily and spiritual exercise as by lower and upper millstones, and sifted through the continual examination of thoughts that accuse or even defend, supplies marrow to the bones of humility, healing to a contrite spirit, and sound satisfaction to a hungry soul. This bread is baked either in the oven of the profound mystery of Christ’s incarnation, or in the frying-pan of the life-giving cross, or on the gridiron of death and burial: whenever your life, speech, and thought die with Christ, are made one body with him, or are buried with him in a new manner of life. Behold bread from the oven: “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, of the seed of David” (2 Tim. 2). Eat bread from the gridiron: “While we were still sinners, Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom. 5). Take hold of what is fried in the pan: “He was numbered with the wicked”; and, “Surely he himself bore our infirmities and carried our weaknesses” (Luke 22; Isa. 53), in his body upon the wood of the cross.

This threefold bread does not fail travellers through the desert on a journey of three days, because faith in the incarnation, passion, and death is a vehicle, like Jacob’s ladder, even for those seeking or penetrating the third heaven. But at the entrance of the tabernacle not made by hands—that is, not of this creation, which God, not man, established—bread is offered from two tenths of fine flour: that is, eternal consolation for the fulfilment of the Law and Gospel, and also for the perfect incorruption of the flesh and the true holiness of the soul.

Why do you seek a spear or a sword? Whom do you wish to kill? Whom to strike? Where is your adversary, or who is he? Have you not fled to the most secure places of Engaddi? Is not Christ for you the rock of refuge, the tower of strength, the whole armoury of the mighty, the impregnable fortress, the two swords, shield, bow, and arrow? O most valiant soldiers of Christ: you have the extended spear in continual prayers, the sword in mortification of the flesh, and holy bread in hope of eternal glorification. Your spear is not turned aside amid the adversities of the world, because you make straight steps toward heaven. Your sword does not turn aside in the conflict of desires and the assault of suggestions, because before the Lord is all your desire. Your bread does not grow stale through the delay of rewards, because charity grows green again through the sure hope of promised goods. The bread endures in its heat because charity does not grow lukewarm in your hearts. The edge of the sword is not blunted because the rigour of discipline and holy purpose does not cool. The spear is not broken because your prayer, piercing heaven with its point, is beaten back by no obstacle.

O great and grievous warfare—unequal in positions, unequal in strength, incomparable in weapons! O ruler and governor of all things, what a ridiculous battle it would be, unless you made it otherwise: a worm against a giant, a human against a demon, an earthly animal against an aerial one, the swiftest against the slowest, the most foolish against the most cunning, the ancient against the modern, the mortal against the immortal! The one stands on high; the other lies below. The one has wings; the other has not even feet. The one sees whom he pursues; the other feels, but does not notice, by whom he is being so cruelly beaten. The latter is burdened by the mass of flesh; the former, through the Creator’s goodness in his creation, flies freely wherever he will. The enemy uses this world to deceive; he uses man against man to kill; he uses the same man against himself to devour him. He triumphs by a man’s senses as though by weapons belonging to him, and strangles the captive when the spirit does not reduce its mortal body to servitude.

O wicked plague! O miserable lot of humankind! There is no power in you yourself; nor does the Lord save by the bow of your strength or by the spear of your free choice. Thus dashed among rocks, thus hemmed in among peoples, you nevertheless have battle with the sons of Anak, beside whom you appear like a grasshopper. You have a decisive duel with the rulers of darkness, with death and life set before the victor or the defeated.
