It is not the one who has fallen who will fail to rise again, but the one who has yielded. He who has ceased will not add further; he who has slipped will not approach again. When the first man was first defeated, because the second came from heaven, he had one to raise him from the mire. If he should again be overcome, he will not be restored, because thereafter no other Son of God will be born from a virgin. For those who sin deliberately, no sacrifice for sins remains. We must therefore act more urgently, lest we be compelled to return when, shut up in death, we shall no longer be permitted to retrieve the forgotten garment. Whoever has neglected the garment of repentance while in the body will have no opportunity after the passage from life.

Behold, my lords and dearest friends: as soon as I saw your messenger, I ran with Abraham to the herd, summoned Sarah—that is, memory—and the servant, that is, the heart, and mixed flour for you in order to make an ash-baked cake. You therefore have your hair-shirt, and you also have our ash-baked cake. These two work together to draw out the rust of sin, wipe away the itch, and cleanse the filth. Therefore a sound and holy conscience could truthfully cry out that “the vessels of the young men are clean.” O most precious and splendid jewel! Though a man should give all the substance of his house for it, it is nevertheless counted as nothing in comparison with it. I hold back holy hearts, clean eyes, and pure hands—more than I ought—from the pasture of life, from entrance into glory, and from contemplation of the face of Jesus now glorified and deified. But now I release them, and beg that you carry me, in pious remembrance, on your shoulders to the throne of glory. Farewell. I commend to you with special earnestness Brother Simon, the light of my eyes and a portion of my inward being.

## LETTER XLIII. TO THE SAME RECIPIENTS

[III, 4.] To his own at Mont-Dieu, their own Peter of Celle: may they be transformed from glory into glory.

“The children have come to birth, and there is no strength to bring forth.” My hand was ready to reply, my mind to dictate, and my place to sit down; and behold, the wind of the occupations of your messenger, catching the sails of our vessel, turned it back into the harbour of silence. What then? Is it not more pleasant and delightful gradually to taste, through time and seasons, the good wine which you have kept until now, than to swallow it at one draught, to the loss of its desirable sweetness? Though I desire to see you in passing, I do not at least wish to write in passing. “I tasted and saw that your trade is good.” Your hands do not serve in baskets; you do not build the cities of Egypt in mud and brick. Rather, you seek whatever is precious and beautiful; you take up spindle and distaff in order to spin or weave the breastplate and ephod and the remaining ornamental insignia of the high priest.

Hence it is that you do not put coarse garments made from the tow of the synagogue of sinners upon your delicate souls; nor, against the Law, do you clothe yourselves in a garment of wool and linen. Rather, renouncing the hidden things of shame, you wash your face, anoint your head, and, coming from the north, warm yourselves with the fleeces of your sheep, since examples of holy religious life are drawn even from the confession of your most unimpaired simplicity. It is so, beloved; it is so: “A man approaches the deep heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. 63). Does not the same thing happen with the moon when it approaches the light of the sun—that the closer it is made to the sun, the more it seems to diminish in its own brightness? A blind man’s house is not beautiful because he does not see its deformity; nor is it healthy because he does not consider where it forms a swelling. “Grey hairs are scattered upon Ephraim, and he himself does not know it” (Hos. 7).

You grieve over Lazarus’s stench; you marvel that a trunk already dead should grow green again; you do not permit the walls of Jericho to rise. For you do what the prophet Nahum says: “Draw water for yourself because of the siege; enter into the mud, tread it, and, kneading it, hold fast the brick” (Nah. 3). You understand the siege of the prince of this world; water from the cisterns, as also from the cells, does not fail. You enter into the mud of the flesh in order to press it more firmly and tread it more forcefully, if you remember, by kneading, to hold fast the brick. Let your sword therefore not rage unto utter destruction. “Take up your bed and walk,” says the Lord (John 5): that is, indulge the body, but do not be its slave. As sweetly as I am carried aloft in the rush of the spirit while writing to you, so painfully do I bear being compelled to stop in the middle of the journey. I refrain from answering your question, because I intend not to treat it superficially. Farewell.

Deprived of hope of going farther, I had sat down unwillingly, but because of him who was abandoning me, as it were, halfway along the road. Meanwhile the good Spirit blew; and, while it frustrated his plan, it fulfilled our desire. I undoubtedly feared delay and stubbornly avoided having the inconvenience of either time or bearer attributed to my own idleness. Therefore, that I may plainly disclose my foolishness to the eyes of my friends and lords, I shall set forth not something from the storeroom of a dry breast, but what I borrowed from Joseph’s granaries in the sacks of Jacob’s sons. Yet first I shall place upon this table your loaves of offering, so that vegetables from our cooking may be taken with them.

You write that some among you understand the Apostle’s words—“Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Eph. 4), and elsewhere, “Although the outward man is corrupted, yet the inward man is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4)—and the paradise of delights in which Adam was placed, together with the assertion that man was made in the image and likeness of God, in the same sense. They add that these delightful goods must be understood in a twofold way: namely, according to substantial good and accidental good. They refer “image” to essential gifts, but “likeness” to things which can be present or absent.

Before I place in the sanctuary of God this image of these interpretations, composed in such fine colours by learned painters, I ask about its origin, author, power, and indeed usefulness. For what is worshipped in a temple must be religious: its deities should not be new, unknown, or finally fictitious. “Israel,” says the prophet, “if you hear me, there shall be no new god in you, nor shall you worship a foreign god” (Ps. 80). An idol in the Church of the living God is no more abominable than a perverse interpretation of Holy Scripture in the soul of a Christian. Yet a distinction must be made here also. To err in matters concerning faith in the Holy Trinity, the incarnation, or the sacraments of the Church is perilous. But to think, concerning the multiple sense of the Scriptures or the judgments of God—which now appear many, as though diverse, yet are not contrary to faith—in a way that is different is not to wander from the path. For this is the sound of the wings of the living creatures in Ezekiel striking one another: holy souls receive abundantly from the treasury of God’s wisdom and knowledge, from which they fittingly compose the body of the Church, for the growth of Christ’s body, by the joining together of diverse graces.

Thus that brother may indeed have built for himself an ivory house according to his own good interpretation, and prepared a two-chambered or three-chambered ark for the flood of many waters. Yet I wonder that he has erected so great a building with so small an outlay; and that, though as a wise architect he ought to have established it upon the most solid foundations of apostles and prophets, supported it by the flowers of teachers, and surrounded it with the fruits of martyrs, he forgot to insert the bronze nails of Old-Testament authorities and the silver cords of the New Testament, and has left the wall exposed as though stripped of shields.

But, to explain briefly what bears upon the proper meaning of this name, it should be known that “image” is properly said relatively to another thing whose likeness it bears and which it was made to represent—such as an image of Caesar, which bore his likeness. Improperly, however, that to which another thing is made is called an image, as an exemplar is also properly called an exemplar, the original from which something is taken. Yet, by a customary misuse, one is sometimes put for the other. In this sense the Son is properly called the image of the Father. In another way, in which one name is used for another, man is called the image of God because the image of God is in him. Thus a panel and a painting are called an image; but it is because of the painting in it that the panel too is called an image. So, on account of the image of the Trinity, that in which this image exists is likewise called by the name of image. Therefore man is image and “according to the image”; the Son is image, not “according to the image.”

I wish, if you please, briefly to indicate by an example in what respect likeness differs from image. Let the soul be a precious stone, and let some image be impressed upon it, from which a likeness according to the image may be shown as impressed. Is not the engraved image one thing, and the likeness produced from the image another? Let, then, the goodness of God be the cause of this likeness. For when God wished, through his benevolence—which is attributed to the Holy Spirit—to make man God, or to make him after God, and this could not happen naturally (for none is naturally God except he who is God born, not made), he granted that man should at least have God’s likeness. In order that this likeness of God might have a seat or receptacle, the image or figure of God’s substance, which is the Son, was impressed upon the human soul, so that it might receive the aforesaid likeness from his Holy Spirit—as an opening is made in a precious stone through which it receives a slender rod of gold, by which it is bound and held. Thus man was created “according to the image,” according to the natural powers of the soul—memory, understanding, and love, as your expositor very well said—and “according to the likeness,” according to innocence and justice, which belong to the rational mind naturally rather than accidentally.

I am astonished that I have heard what I would not have wished even to dream: that the likeness of God is an accidental gift. Whoever understands the Apostle knows that it is not accidental but truly substantial—indeed, super-substantial. “We know,” he says, “that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3). What does “we shall be like” mean except that we shall have his likeness? The likeness which we received in creation, we shall possess again in the first resurrection and finally in the second, though in a different way. For in creation it was bestowed so that it could be lost, since man could sin—or rather, be disfigured. But in true immortality, when man can neither die nor sin, he shall eternally rejoice in the likeness of God.

What then? Will that supreme blessedness and glory of the ages be accidental, so that it can be present or absent without corruption of its subject? That, after all, is the nature of an accident. Where are you, O man? Are you not in mortality—or rather, in death? Why? Is it not because you have lost God’s likeness? For what is God? Is he not life? And what is the likeness of life except life? Or what is unlikeness except death? He has found death who has lost the likeness of God. If God’s likeness is called accidental because it could be taken away, the inference is unsound. It would follow that we live accidentally because we can die. For it belongs to an accident by nature that it can be present or absent without corruption of the subject. Who sound in brain or heart would dare affirm this of virtue, justice, goodness, and love of virtue in the soul? Indeed, as Augustine says, as the soul is the life of the body, so God is the life of the soul. True virtue, true goodness, true justice—indeed, truth itself—is God. Therefore, if the soul is without these, it dies; and do you call them accidental gifts?

Turning my eyes again and rereading your letters, I find not “an accidental gift” but “an accidental good”; and I marvel at still greater fantasies. Is not the likeness of God God? And is God’s good anything other than God? Augustine cries out: “Whatever is said of God is God, and nothing is said of God according to accident”; yet you say that the likeness of God is spoken of as an accidental good. But, you say, when I call God’s likeness an accidental gift, I look not to God who gives it but to man who receives it. Yet the foregoing, I think, sufficiently proves that neither assertion is true. Let this suffice concerning likeness.

[Col. 0465A] Let us now return to image and hear what the true Image says to us. For he speaks thus: “He who sees me sees the Father also” (John 14). In these words, presenting himself to those who desire to see the Father’s face as an altogether most similar image, differing in nothing, he wished to satisfy the desires of their hearts with his own goods. Again, wishing to renew his image in his image, the same Image says elsewhere: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Lev. 11). Like a good painter of souls, God created the first soul in the first man with every spiritual blessing, painting it according to the better and more beautiful image which he found—not among things already created, but among things uncreated; in painting, he created it, and in creating, painted it. He created, I say, his image in the soul—or rather, created the soul according to his image. Again, he painted his likeness in the soul—or rather, painted the soul according to his likeness.

But when it had been discoloured by the smoke of its iniquities and transgressions and defiled to the utmost deformity, its author and lover wished to restore it. Since no equally able painter could be found—neither an angel in heaven, nor a righteous man on earth, nor any spirit beneath the earth—the Image came to the image: the beautiful to the deformed, the just to the unjust, the noble to the ignoble, the merciful to the impious, the eternal to the transient. He came to restore what had perished; he came to repair what had failed. This Image of the invisible God is the Son of the Most High. For the Apostle says of the Son: “He is the image of the invisible God” (Col. 1).

But believe me, nothing is said more soundly than that there is one image of the entire Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Hence Bede, commenting on “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1), says that the words “Let us make” show the one operation of the three Persons, while “in our image and likeness” displays the one and equal substance of the three Persons. This is said by the Father to the Son and the Holy Spirit, not, as some suppose, to the angels, because God and angels do not possess one and the same likeness or image. Therefore the Son is properly called the image of the Father; the essence of the Trinity is called image less properly; man, improperly. Man is called God’s image because he bears God’s likeness in himself, as Caesar’s image bears Caesar’s likeness. Thus far I have spread my phylacteries sufficiently and enlarged my fringes. If, however, I have spoken anything too harshly, I beg you to forgive me. Farewell, and pray for me.

## LETTER XLIV. TO THE SAME RECIPIENTS

[III, 5.] To his lords at Mont-Dieu, their own man of Celle: may they penetrate the gate of the inner court.

Although my humility does not deserve to receive from you the written marks of greeting, may it at least deserve the gifts of your prayers. If both were possible, I should receive both most gratefully; yet I seek the latter more eagerly, if I cannot have both. Your letters would gladden me, if you wrote; but your prayers help me, if you pour them forth for me. My folly needs the instruction of good men; the weakness of my soul needs devout and continual prayer. O that you might perceive the wounds of my wretched and desolate soul amid the devastation of the enemy! Surely, if you loved it, you would mourn over it. O dearest lords and fathers, why do you not free this soul—wretched though it is, yet yours? Why do you not rescue it, already half-devoured, from the lion’s mouth? Why do you not ransom it, utterly humbled beneath the bond of captivity? Let the remembrance of former miseries, from which he who suffered for you redeemed you, suffice to stir your compassion. The heap of my sins stretches further still; and unless the Lord, moved by your most holy prayers, helps me, it is already drawing near to hell. Farewell.

## LETTER XLV. TO THE SAME RECIPIENTS

[III, 6.] To his dearest lords and brothers at Mont-Dieu—the prior together with the other holy brethren—Brother Peter of Celle, unworthy abbot, greeting.

Perhaps, as chicks that do not fly from the nest hunger for their father’s food, so you, dearest sons, who are growing feathers in your little nest in order to fly aloft when the time comes, expect me to pour out something worthy of the mouth and stomach of holiness. But what has a raven to do with chicks of hens? They are not fed on the same foods. A raven feeds on the corpses of decay; a dove feeds on the pure grains of chosen wheat. I know—I know—what foods nourished me among you for half a season. If I said that I know what now burdens me to nausea, I should say far too little; for wisdom surpasses knowledge, and it is greater to retain the tenor of a taste in the mouth than to recall past things to the mind. Therefore I am more distressed and groan over these things; and, since their taste affects me deeply, I do not wish by renewed rumination to rub raw former pains. “Sufficient for the day is its own evil” (Matt. 6); sufficient for the taste is its own most bitter bitterness.

But you, dearest brothers and sons, content with simplicity of food, as you have learned Christ, as you have tasted and seen that your trade is good, persevere in this way. Do not seek another table or other food. For you have a good table indeed, and good food, by which your soul lives. What can I myself say about my table? Certainly, ever since I descended from my holy Mount of God, I have been given a table at which to feast with my friends either very rarely or never. At once, the cares which lay in wait for my departure seized and swallowed me in a continual reflux, overflowing above my head. If my flesh and heart found any leisure or good in that rest, it has been sufficiently mercilessly avenged upon me. Such cares have burned more fiercely against me, and through them not even a breathing-space passes.

Among you, dearest and most desired ones, I complain of myself against myself. These things certainly—indeed, far worse—have I deserved: I am not corrected by punishment, but along with punishment I multiply guilt. Pray for your little servant, who longs for you every day, sighing for your shadow and thirsting to see your face. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVI. TO SIMON THE PRIOR AND THE CARTHUSIAN BRETHREN OF MONT-DIEU

[V, 11.] To his lords at Mont-Dieu—Simon, the prior [Note: [Col. 0467D] “To Simon, prior of Mont-Dieu.” John of Salisbury calls this man, once, most holy and most highly praised. The date written in the letter indicates the year 1161. Some years later Simon was chosen by Pope Alexander, together with Bernard of Grandmont, to carry papal letters to the king of England and exhort him to restore favour with Blessed Thomas. He carried out this embassy vigorously; John of Salisbury recounts its proceedings in Book IV of his historical collections concerning St Thomas], and the whole holy community—Brother Peter, abbot of Celle: a holy Easter.

The soul of each one of you does not cease to celebrate a daily Passover, while, like a dove, it stands at its windows and listens for the voice from heaven calling its bride from Lebanon. With neck fully stretched and bent back toward your Head, who is in heaven, you never cease to grow weary of this shadowy life and strive to fly upon the wings of the winds, in order there to celebrate Passover with him and in him who, Christ, has been sacrificed as our Passover—not by annual repetition, but in continual permanence. It is so. Yet one still ascends and descends by Jacob’s ladder until what is partial is abolished, which will happen when the vow is changed into possession and a hymn is offered to God in Jerusalem.

Meanwhile, brothers, dwelling in shelters and sitting beneath the shadow of him whom you desire, cook—indeed roast—the flesh of the lamb all night, each in his own cell, and in the morning you shall eat it. Certainly the flesh of the lamb must burn throughout the whole night, because throughout the whole time of mortality, when the cauldrons of conscience have been kindled and the face of the Saviour is to be desired, it must be thoroughly cooked amid the strongly boiling waves of desires, lest it be offered half-cooked on the day of judgment. Keep your vessels clean; water flows close at hand and before your eyes. But does it flow in vain? Does it flow freely to no purpose? Surely, gross and slothful negligence must be imputed to anyone whose vessels are not all clean, when an abundance of water overflows, opportunity remains, love of complete cleanness presses upon him, and the custom of the order does not forbid it. It is so: I saw it; I was there; and would that I had cleansed my heart as often and as diligently as I wet my hands and face, day and night, not with tears but with water. Yet I did this as a guest, because I remained not beyond the door but at the door. You, however, have advanced your foot within and beyond the door, becoming not strangers but members of the household of the cell and of heaven.

After you have cleansed by confession and meditation on the Scriptures vessels empty of ambition, fill them with water and put them to the fire; make them boil like precious ointments. An unguarded thought had entered my mouth and was already prompting my pen to write that the flesh of the lamb should thus be boiled. But remembering the legal command that forbids boiling it in water, I add that it is not lamb’s flesh but kid’s flesh that should be cooked in this manner. For we are commanded at Passover to take both lamb and kid together. What then? The lamb is cooked on the spit, or on the gridiron of the cross; the kid is boiled in water, so that, if you are innocent, you may be fitted for Passover by the fire of the spirit alone, but if you are burdened by a heavy stench, you may be cleansed through fire and water. The kid is also the body which decays and weighs down the soul. The lamb that feeds in broad pastures is that kindly spirit which, assailed by the attacks of the flesh, strikes not with its horn but seeks a deliverer with single-hearted eye, saying: “Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7).

By the blood of the lamb—that is, by contrition of heart and a troubled spirit—you are freed from Egypt and from Pharaoh’s hand, because God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart. Of the blood of the kid I read no mystery except that Joseph’s garment, dyed in a kid’s blood, was sent to his father. If, in confession, weeping and wailing, you send to the Father of spirits Joseph’s garment, stained with kid’s blood—that is, the clothing of simplicity and chastity, dyed and befouled by the corruption of lust and the deceit of diabolical trickery—the kid’s blood will be changed into purple, because through repentance one obtains not only pardon but grace also. But enough of these matters.

How can I, lukewarm, admonish the fervent; filthy, the cleansed; lying down, those who run; lazy, the eager? God knows that I have loosened the reins not through presumption but through impatience of love; and, although I had nothing to say, I nevertheless wished to say something, and so said what might make my affection known, even if it were not capable of producing fruit. The impulse still draws me and compels me to return to the feast of feasts, so that, as one beginning, I may indulge the spirit in running until it grows weary and of its own accord seeks a stopping-place and the boundaries of silence.

Under the image, therefore, of a certain precious wrapping, in which both the container and what it contains are wondrous, I shall pursue something concerning Passover, taking, as it were, from the divine treasuries a certain costly cloth of many colours. In that forty-day fast, when Moses came back from divine converse with a horned face, he set down the name of this Passover in his writings; and, binding the most holy relics within it, he ordained that, on its annual return, it should be unfolded publicly for us, and he fixed a definite day. For this cloth—that is, Passover—presents much brightness on its outer surface, but contains within far greater things and dearer pledges. It is red with purple colour because of the Passion; it gleams with hyacinth-blue appearance because of the Resurrection; it is somewhat dark because of the accumulated spittings, slaps, scourgings, and other injuries; it is white with a single cloud because of the wholeness of innocence and freedom from sin. Behold the colours, the colours that surround the glorious Passover, the delicate garment of the soul, with which poor people, girded only halfway, are more fittingly clothed than are the rich who wear purple and fine linen.

But who will unroll those precious pearls sealed in this golden and silver seal unless he has clean hands, dove-like eyes, and purified lips, unless the whole inner and outer person has been washed in the sacred baptism of the Jordanian river? Therefore, because your hands are skilfully turned by obedience, your eyes bright through chastity, your lips dripping with choicest myrrh through accusation of your sins, and closed forever against coarse jesting, take up the Paschal cloth and unfold the hidden treasure. From it may the captive borrow redemption, the dead resurrection, the sinner justification, the afflicted consolation, the bound person release, and the accursed person absolution. Sanctify your mouths with the holy kisses of these things; touch your eyes with these emeralds; gladden each of your senses with its corresponding blessing.

But what pledges are these—so dear in price, so efficacious for healing, so rare in number, so holy in merit, so everlasting in duration, so lovable in benefit! These pledges, my brothers, to be named and embraced with a modest mouth and due reverence, are the flesh and blood of the spotless Lamb; the bones, sinews, marrow, cartilages, skin, hide, and every member in the body of Jesus which the Virgin of virgins brought forth from her sacred womb. Shall I add the nails, the lance, the crown of thorns, the spittle, the mockeries and derision, the white garment, the purple robe, gall, vinegar, myrrh, and aloes? For the harsher and more worthless these things are in themselves, the more precious and desirable they have become in our Savior. [Col. 0469C] Which Christian today, if he found one of these, would not honor it more reverently than much gold and precious stone, guard it more eagerly, and adore it? It is fitting; it is just.

For if one who touches a corpse or something taken by a beast is unclean—that is, Adam and Eve, of whom the one was taken captive by his wife’s persuasion, while Eve became a corpse through the serpent’s suggestion—how should one not be cleansed from dead works who touches, by believing, loving, honoring, and adoring, Him who lives for ever and ever? For the offense is not like the gift. The gift is greater than the offense. But what is this gift? Holy Jesus Christ. What, I say, is this gift? The birth of Jesus, the passion of Jesus, [Col. 0469D] the resurrection of Jesus, the ascension of Jesus. How did He not also give us all things with Him? (Rom. VIII.) The Apostle cries: “All things are yours,” he says, “whether death or life” (I Cor. III), because He died for our sins and rose for our justification.

Lords and brothers, I detain you beyond what is right, while Jesus stands and knocks at your door, wishing to celebrate His Passover anew with you. From the remnants of that great table He has reserved the better portion, which He again brings forth to you from the ark of heaven, still fresh and warm. Do not fear that the flesh has grown old and decayed through excessive age, because it is now the year one thousand one hundred and sixty-one. By no means, brothers, by no means let this hesitation enter your hearts; for His flesh, [Col. 0470A] even while it was corruptible, did not see corruption, and much less does it do so now that it has become incorruptible, both in its mode of life and in its place of abiding. It is fresh, warm, sound, life-giving; it gives the kingdom of heaven because it possesses it. This is not the flesh and blood of which it is said: “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. XV).

The more diligently the flesh of animals—which corrupts and is corrupted—is kept from your teeth and stomachs, the more worthily should that flesh approach your souls to sanctify them: flesh which, as it does not die, so does not permit corruption to be present wherever it has supplied refreshment. Religion commands this; and the more religious you are, the more frequently—and, so to speak, the more adhesively—you ought to eat it. My hand and mind would not yet have rested, but both the measure of what has been said [Col. 0470B] and the time for other business restrain them. Pray for us. Greet your new angel A., and our little Robert. I greet each of you very warmly, individually and collectively.

## LETTER XLVII. TO THE SAME RECIPIENTS

[V, 13.] To his lords and fathers at Mont-Dieu, Simon the prior and the other brothers, Brother Peter, unworthy abbot of La Celle, wishes that they may ever keep their faces turned toward the mercy-seat.

The changing course of things, inseparably bound to the restless turning of the ages, proves by evident reason that it contains nothing stable, nothing eternal. Whatever worldly use can ever possess runs, flows, flees, slips away, and vanishes. Failure outruns satisfaction; attainment passes beyond desire; the smoke of glory escapes the pressing instant of longing; the image of happiness slips from its possessor; life vanishes from the living, “for while I was beginning, He cut me off” (Isa. XXXVIII). [Col. 0470C]

It is therefore the height of madness to run after what fails, to desire what cannot be grasped, to pursue smoke, to use an image in place of truth, to wish to live long in that life which, according to Gregory, compared with eternal life ought rather to be called death than life. You, dearest brothers and lords, have undoubtedly turned your course elsewhere. You live by another desire; with another urgency you seek the precious pearls in the market and fairs of the Old and New Testament; by another use, living in the flesh beyond the flesh, [Col. 0470D] you crucify with Christ your bodies which are upon the earth; by another manner of life you desire things eternal and unseen. For visible things are temporal, but invisible things eternal.

Therefore you have flown, like a sparrow, to the mountain of the Lord and nested in the clefts of the rock, in the hollows of the wall, lest the storm of aerial suggestions envelop you, lest the flood of carnal enticements swallow you up, lest the snare of worldly cares confine you, lest the breeze of human favor scatter every wind from the face of the earth. Behold, this is the place which the Lord appointed for Moses, in which he saw His back as He passed before him.

Unless I am mistaken, that good man who restored the dead child to the Shunammite woman, for whom she and her husband prepared an upper room, [Col. 0471A] a bed, a table, and a lampstand, often passes through among you. You behold Him in the upper room of glory; you find Him in the bed of a cleansed conscience; you feed and give Him drink in the sacrament of the divine Eucharist; you kindle Him through the gift of wisdom and understanding. I adjure you by the fields and the gazelles of the fields: when He has passed, cry after His back for the peace of the universal Church; for those in high places; for our count, whose heart God has touched to build for you a place in which you may bear fruit according to your kind; for me, his and your sinner; and for all entrusted to us. Pass with Him and after Him, so that you may behold Him who remains through everlasting eternities, whether in the twinkling of an eye, or for half an hour, or for a moment, until you are transformed from glory to glory. [Col. 0471B] Certainly, whoever follows One who is passing will see Him standing, or seated.

My dearest brothers, if a holy tasting and His remembrance are wine of Lebanon, what is His presence but intoxication of the breasts, forgetfulness of things past, and unending jubilation from the fullness of joys? If expectation of these things is joy, what is enjoyment but everlasting joy? Like a grain of mustard, your vision, Jesus, with the slight whisper of a gentle breeze strikes the ears of the heart; and who can reckon the hour of Your passing? If I sleep, I can dream, but I cannot see. If I am awake, held by other occupations and cares, I cannot so quickly become free of them. If I am awake and free, then perhaps I hear the vein of His whisper, but do not yet see. When, then, shall I see Him passing? [Col. 0471C]

If I keep a clean heart uplifted, pure hands, a washed face; if with my whole soul and all my strength I seek God alone in all things, and melt my whole self into Him, so that I no longer live in myself but Christ lives in me—He who was made for us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption.

As for the falsehood, I ask pardon and condemn myself before you. For I failed to fulfill what I promised: to revisit, even once a year, the nest of those holy virtues, Mont-Dieu, where souls grow their feathers through the charisms of graces. At that time the unknown face of future events deceived me, and the tangled sequence of very many contingencies. From my present affection, by which throughout that Lent my whole mind poured forth streams of honey and butter, [Col. 0471D] I had planned for the years that followed. But the caterpillar, locust, grub, and rust have devoured the loveliness of the desert, spreading the nets of daily cares at my feet, so as to render void what went out from my lips.

I have sinned: what else can I say? If I excuse myself, my own mouth will condemn me. Yet humble confession of error better deserves pardon for fault than clever minimization of a crime. Nevertheless, when an account of an action is given, the truth of the matter is not obscured, nor is the fault in the matter, if there is one, concealed. For false excuse and reasonable satisfaction are distinct. The one heaps up guilt; the other declares to what extent the person accused is blameworthy or blameless. Both sin: both the person who lies in accusing himself and the person who disdains [Col. 0472A] to dispel false accusations with a truthful account.

It is a reprobate humility to cast yourself down vainly beyond what you feel in your heart; it is detestable presumption to neglect one’s reputation and not remove the blemish of suspicion. Avoiding both the kind that departs from truth and that which smells of presumption, I confess that I did not come, and testify that I was detained by innumerable occupations. I acknowledge the deed—indeed, the non-deed. I leave to your judgment the cause of the deed, or rather of the failure to act. Decide which has greater weight, or whether either prejudices the other: the action in relation to the cause, or the cause in relation to the action. For I yield to your judgment, since I believe that you will settle the case by judging the act according to its cause, not the cause according to the character of the act. For greater attention must be paid to why something is done than to what is done.

An act without a cause for being done is formless; one with a bad cause is deformed; one with a good cause is well formed. Hence every act that has a just cause is good, and one with an unjust cause is bad. An act is called indifferent when its cause contributes little either to justification or to corruption. Augustine says of a good cause: “It is the cause, not the punishment, that makes martyrs.” Of a bad cause, the Lord says in the Gospel: “If your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark” (Matt. VI). Again, the laws say of an indifferent act: “Will and purpose distinguish wrongdoing.” Ambrose says: “Your disposition gives your work its name.” Yet, when the nature of certain actions is carefully weighed, [Col. 0472B] they cannot be done with any good intention or affection—for example, crucifying Christ, committing adultery, and the like.

To return to my purpose, and to make the conclusion cohere with the beginning by a fitting construction: I count coming to Mont-Dieu among those things which, if done in a good spirit, merit reward, but, if done in a bad spirit, merit condemnation. That thief who stole the clothes of the leprous brother while Mass was being celebrated will not receive a good reward for such a deed. But he who hastens to see God’s camp among you out of holy desire will receive a reward.

Enough—if indeed it is not more than enough. For, as is my custom, I begin slowly and also finish slowly. Count Henry, with spirit rekindled, presses on in seeking a suitable place and maintains that he did not abandon that other place except because you would not consent. [Col. 0472D] I therefore advise—if it is not burdensome—that you again send one of the brothers, with whom I may inspect, either personally or through our representatives, a place, as already said, suited to your order. Do this without delay. I greet all of you, individually and collectively, intending to come to you sometime, if God wills, perhaps when your messenger returns to you. Meanwhile pray for us. I greet our little Robert; Richard, Stephen, Roger, Nicholas; and again all together.

## LETTER XLVIII. TO BASIL, PRIOR, AND THE CARTHUSIANS OF MONT-DIEU

[V, 12.] To his dearest lords and fathers, Basil, prior of the Carthusians, with the other priors and [Col. 0473A] the holy community, Brother Peter, abbot of La Celle, wishes counsel and help in truth and peace.

That enclosed garden, that sealed fountain of God (Song IV), is watered with a richer outpouring whenever the pipes and channels of God’s gracious Spirit assemble in one—not to drain Babylonian cups, but to purge Jacob’s dregs and make barren wombs fruitful. The Spirit of God has called each of you from his own place from the four winds of heaven, that you might become one body full of grace and truth.

For you who are priors and have undertaken the care of others are like veins in the body of the Carthusian order. Therefore all of you ought to watch over your governance with such unanimity, and to require the commands and customs of the order from your subjects with such moderation, as all veins in the human body are joined together in charity and supply wholesome vitality to all members through an equal distribution of blood. [Col. 0473B] The same caution by which a vein should avoid excessive thinness and narrowness should also avoid immoderate thickness and fullness. Excessive fullness, unless quickly evacuated, produces a severe and prolonged illness. Conversely, excessive depletion takes away strength and destroys good health.

Dearest lords and fathers, I have already worn smooth the threshold of your order by my rare visits and frequent inquiries; and if you admit the counsel of another Jethro, do not altogether anathematize dispensations which proceed from the heart of charity. For as it is frivolous and inconstant to alter without reason and without the authority of wiser men the decrees and ordinances of one’s elders, [Col. 0473C] so it is obstinate, and outside the rule of moderation—the mother of virtues—to wish to deny to human times and manners what is fitting and expedient.

Forgive me for daring to utter in your holy assembly, from my hiding-place, a voice ominous in sound indeed but true in meaning. So much for these matters. Moreover, Lord Henry, Count of Troyes, greets you and urgently requests of your whole community that you consent to his petition. He charged us to send one of our own to you, through whom the will and desire of his heart might be made known. The reason why he did not write to you under his own seal was his very great preoccupation with his own [Col. 0473D] and royal affairs.

His petition is that you permit him, at his own expense and in his own land, to prepare a place for your order according to your custom, wherever those to whom you entrust this business judge fitting. He also asks that you assign this care to the prior of Mont-Dieu and the prior of the Valley of Saint Peter.

> [Note: Col. 0473D] The Prior of the Valley of Saint Peter. This too is a distinguished monastery of the Carthusian order, in the diocese of Laon; he mentions its prior elsewhere as well, and writes to him, but nowhere names him. He was Ingelbert, as we learned from the letters of [John of] Salisbury. [Col. 0474D]

For many years he has begun this very undertaking and, aided by your prayers, wishes to complete it. On our part also we humbly and devoutly request the same, because, with God’s help, [Col. 0474A] we shall supply genuine assistance and counsel for this work.

## LETTER XLIX. [Note: Col. 0474D: New.]  
### OF GIRARD OF PERONNE, A MONK OF CLAIRVAUX, TO PETER, ON UNITED LOVE

To his own—and truly his own—abbot of La Celle, Brother Girard of Péronne: may you be brought into the wine-cellar.

That I call you “mine” is not insolence but friendship. For my conscience, which knows that I am your servant, presumes to call you mine. Your graciousness made me familiar to you; familiarity made me a friend; friendship made one mind out of two. And although fortune has placed you on high from a lowly station, charity—which in the sanctuary of its majesty has made or received every person as equal—makes equal friends out of unequal persons. Whom do I so love, by whom am I equally loved? Are not you and I one? I have no one so united with me in the bowels of Jesus Christ: Christ is my witness.

And although a divided order divides us, charity binds us, because it was not the color of our garments but the love of our hearts that made this unity—indeed, this unanimity. Most loving father, to jest a little before my Lord, I turn back upon you what you turn upon me. For what is this? Have I become an object of suspicion to you, as is apparent also from your letter? This is a sign that you either do not love, or love less; neither possibility belongs, or can belong, to true friendship.

What if I had seen you and had not spoken, or had immediately departed? Would you therefore have loved me less? [Col. 0474C] Far be it from your servant; far be it from your heart that even the slightest suspicion could enter so great a love! As for my not breaking down the doors, spare my modesty, which, according to the holy man, came forth from the womb and grew with me from my infancy. Henceforth I shall shake off shame before I instill suspicion in you; I shall even shatter bronze gates and break iron bars. I ask pardon: do with what is yours as with what is yours.

Yet let that monk fare better on my account, for whom things went worse because of me. But know this: I have so placed the memory of you between my breasts that no occasion can tear it away. N., who is yours as you are yours, greets you; for he is yours.

## LETTER L. [Note: Col. 0474D: New.]  
### OF NICHOLAS OF CLAIRVAUX TO PETER, AN EXCUSE FOR WRITING OR DICTATING

[Col. 0474D]

To Peter, abbot of La Celle, the friendliest lord among friends, Brother Nicholas wishes that, living thus in black garments, he may be clothed in white in heaven.

It ought to have sufficed you if I loved you as myself, since it is evident that I have now loved you more than myself. I had committed a theft for your sake; now [Col. 0475A] I have stolen myself from myself for you. For I, who had renounced the pen, deserving concealment and every solitude, once I perceived—and fully perceived—the eagerness you have for the words and on behalf of the words of that man whose eloquence and wisdom, life and reputation, have not undeservedly spread through the whole Latin-speaking world, took up tablets and did what I could.

When I ought to have labored, wept, and prayed that the Lord might be merciful to my sin—for it is great—I poured myself into the volubility of speech and shook and stirred the secret of my heart together; and you say, “You could have done all this in silence, and more properly in silence.” It would be strange if you say this seriously. For who is more in a crowd than he who is entangled in composing literary works? For thoughts make a din as he seeks to discover adequately the truth of meanings, [Col. 0475B] variety of expression, what best serves coherence, and finally what ought to be expressed, when, where, and how. Do you call this silence and repose—especially for an unlearned man, who has no ideas at hand and no graceful, easy speech with which to clothe them?

> [Note: Col. 0475D] He seems to imitate the saying of Saint Jerome in *Apology* II against Vigilantius: “A monk has the office not of a teacher but of one who mourns, mourning either himself or the world, and awaiting in fear the coming of the Lord.”

In short, whether of a monk—which I seem to be—or of a sinner—which I am—dictation is not the office, but weeping is. Thus dictating is not readily available to the unlearned, not something a monk dares, nor suited to a penitent’s disposition. Yet I compelled myself against myself, and send you two volumes of the sermons of the man of God. In one of them I dictated a sermon beginning:

> “The Apostle Paul is usually brief in words, dense in thought.”

> [Note: Col. 0475D] This sermon survives as the second in order among Saint Bernard’s sermons on the words of the Apostle.

> [Note: Col. 0475D] The printed book reads “abundant.”

The other volume was dictated long ago, and has been gnawed and scraped; but seek [Col. 0475C] someone to copy it carefully and wisely, for it is full of many ideas. But know this: I have disregarded no small number of friends to whom I did not wish to grant these things, for my heart was hastening to you. Hurry, and write back concerning these matters promptly; return the copies to me, and thus have them copied for my work according to our agreement. But also send me what I sent you, and their copies, as stated; and see that I do not lose even one iota.

Return also the little book that begins, “There are three things with which we must be reconciled,” and our Hours which you have concerning Our Lady.

> [Note: Col. 0475D] In the little book of Saint Bernard’s *Sentences* you have the third section beginning with these words; thus it is clear that the little book was rearranged. In the book of Saint Bernard’s moral *Sentences* there is *Book II of the Book of Hourly Prayers in Memory of the Blessed Virgin*, to which the letters above numbered 20, 22, and 24 are prefixed.

Pray for me, and write to me through your own messenger concerning your wishes in all these matters.

## LETTER LI. [Note: Col. 0476D: New.]  
### OF RUALEN, PRIOR OF CLAIRVAUX, TO HENRY, BISHOP OF TROYES: A RECOMMENDATION FOR THE ABBOT OF LA CELLE

[Col. 0476A]

To Lord and Father Henry, Bishop of Troyes, Brother R. of Clairvaux wishes that he may walk from glory to glory, as from the Spirit of the Lord.

How gladly we hear those things concerning you in which God is honored, the Church is honored, and your mystery is honored, is known to Him from whom and through whom are all honor and glory.

> [Note: Col. 0476D] The reading *ministry* is more authentic: the author had in view Saint Paul writing in Romans II, “I will honor my ministry,” where in Greek he wrote **τὴν διακονίαν** (“the ministry”), not **μυστήριων** (“of mysteries”).

For this purpose God has set you on high: that you may cast down the proud and exalt the humble—you especially, to whom both good will and great power descend from authority as well as noble birth. We have said this in order to make a way for the following [Col. 0476B] letter.

The abbot of La Celle—

> [Note: Col. 0476D] This is Peter, abbot of La Celle, to whom the letters above numbered 20, 22, and 24 are addressed.

—a religious man who fears God, a good man bearing good testimony from good people, distinguished in life and learning, is bound to us by such intimacy that he is not one among the rest but, before the rest, one of us. All that is ours is his, and all that is his is ours; we are one in him and he in us, of his order,

> [Note: Col. 0476D] Peter, abbot of La Celle, was especially dear to Saint Bernard. Compiègne is a town in the diocese of Soissons, on the River Oise, very well known from the assemblies and councils of the kings of France cited in the chapters.

in which he was highly pleasing to our lord abbot, your friend. He found the abbey over which he presides both disgraced and disturbed by the wickedness of those living in it. He wishes to bring them back to the way of truth, but it is easier to form the ignorant than to reform the perverse. Among them are two exceptionally notorious and clamorous disturbers, who have continually worn away their own lives with evil deeds and the lives of others with curses. [Col. 0476C] Trusting in the line of their nobility, they foster scandals and contrive dissensions, because they have been caught in the works of their own hands.

Therefore, if we people of Clairvaux have any influence with you, do one of two things: either uproot them completely from the monastery, or establish them in the monastery in such a way that they no longer dare utter a word. Let them know that a prophet has arisen in Israel to stop the mouths of those who speak iniquity. Concerning the aforesaid abbot, our father and brother, we add this: whoever does him good does good to us; whoever listens to him listens to us; and whoever harms him harms us.

## LETTER LII. [Note: Col. 0476D: New.]  
### OF NICHOLAS OF CLAIRVAUX TO PETER: AN EXHORTATION TO UNITY AGAINST EVIL MEN AND CONCERNING CORRECTION

To Peter, abbot of La Celle, his special and almost unique friend, [Col. 0477A] Brother Nicholas offers himself and whatever more he may be able to give.

That I write to you frequently is proof not of insolence but of friendship. For I know who I am and to whom I write; otherwise, what could such extreme lowliness have to do with such greatness, unless your humble loftiness—or rather lofty humility—had condescended to me? I believe that you will patiently hear your servant, and, if you judge him worthy, your son; but your friend, whether you wish it or not. If anything comes forth too sharply or too boldly, ascribe it to love, not presumption.

You have put your hand to mighty tasks, and you need strength: the strength that may save you from faintness of spirit and the tempest. Strength holds the highest authority in the minds of prelates; when it gives way, the whole structure of virtues slips through dangers—indeed, over precipices. It is especially necessary for you if you consider and attend to where, among whom, for what purpose, and as whom you have been placed: where? In a place certainly honorable, but burdened; where there are many riches and many evils; a place rich in possessions, but richest in presumption. [Col. 0477B]

From ancient times the poison of death has been planted in that garden. Since regular discipline there grew weak, and the goods of the sanctuary were exposed to plunder and disposed to shameful acts, shameful men have rushed in. There was no one to stand in the breach for the house of Israel, to cut off the vines with the sword of the Spirit and prune the branches in that chosen vineyard; for those who watched over that flock all nodded and slept. But with whom? With persons working iniquity, [Col. 0477C] who, nourished from the breasts and beneath the breasts of the Church, attacked the very entrails of their mother with utter evisceration: outwardly infamous and performing shameful deeds; inwardly doing horrible and dreadful things. And for what purpose? Surely that you may destroy vices on the surface, uproot them at the root, destroy them in their extension, and scatter them in their fortification.

And who are you? Truly, according to the Apostle, a man of quiet and moderate spirit, possessing all that belongs to gentleness and little or nothing of harshness. You have drunk much honey; they have drunk much gall. Your manner of life is sweeter than honey and the honeycomb; their bitterness contains more than a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes. Such simplicity and such deceitfulness, such perversity and such holiness, such kindness and such wickedness do not fit well together or dwell in one seat. [Col. 0477D]

A lamp indeed had to be set upon a lampstand, so that whoever entered might see the light; but perhaps it ought not to have been set against such great whirlwinds of wind, lest it be extinguished. And these things were before you ascended. But after you heard from the Lord, “Friend, go up higher”—

> [Note: Col. 0477D] Luke, in the parable of those invited to the banquet.

—then action is required with a strong hand and outstretched arm; and—

> [Note: Col. 0477D] Read Numbers, chapter XV.

—the sword of Phinehas must be drawn very frequently and most powerfully to strike and pierce through the sons of Belial,

> [Note: Col. 0477D] In the Hebrew language the Devil is called Satan, that is, “opponent” or “adversary”; and by the Apostle, II Cor. VI, Belial, that is, “without yoke,” because he cast from his neck God’s service. So Blessed Jerome, on chapter 4 of the Epistle to the Ephesians. Nicholas therefore aptly calls lawless monks “sons of Belial,” that is, persons without the yoke of religion; or, if one may coin a new word, “un-yoked.”

who refuse, even when asked, to spare their own reputation and life. They need rebuke, not exhortation; command, not counsel; not teaching but the rod. Otherwise you will have made all your enemies glad and your friends sad—friends who, as they say, are ready with both hands to expel the pestilent sons from the sacred buildings and dwellings. Put on strength; let not your eye spare them or have pity. For although it is often a fault to pursue a whole fault, in their case it is a vice to have spared vice even to some extent.

I know that this is a stiff-necked people, whose old and inveterate rebellion wants wine, not [Col. 0478B] oil; the scourge, not kindness; blows, not words; piercing, not anointing; the serpent, not the dove; a master, not a father, according to the comic poet. Your gentleness has taught them badly, because it is a rebellious house. Have you read about those who put cushions under people’s elbows and make pillows to ensnare souls? Cushions and pillows, according to the Wise Man, are bland and gentle words in which the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul and the wicked person is blessed.

Eli used such a cushion and pillow with his delinquent sons when he said: “It is not a good report, my sons, that I hear concerning you” (I Kings II). This indeed was to rebuke and restrain, but with the gentleness and mildness of a father, not with the severity and authority of a bishop. Correction that never follows must always meet a judge mercilessly awaited. [Col. 0478C]

But who are those who aspire to tyranny and set their mouths in the heavens? Surely the two sons of iniquity: men who have no regard for reputation, no concern for themselves, no reverence in themselves; who have learned to weary God by contempt, nature by disgraceful conduct, and laws by abuse. Is not one worthy of a thousand deaths who has defiled his boyhood, disturbed his youth, and, as his age slopes downward, continually inclines it toward worse things? A man brazen against shame, senseless against fear, unyielding to pity, headlong toward anger, swift to crime, prone to injuries, is not merely always to be struck but also to be thunderstruck.

And that other one is still full of the contemptible youthfulness and contemptuous insolence of adolescence: a little wolf—

> [Note: Col. 0478D] Incorrectly in the exemplar, *lipecillus* for *lupicellus*, or *lupullus*, to use Saint Anselm of Canterbury’s word in Letter 68, book III, manuscript.

—has bared his teeth viciously against his father; foul in body, fouler in heart, most foul in deed beyond all his contemporaries. In the first flower of childhood he defiled himself with every impurity; and, having entered upon the paths of adolescence, he “went out with Dinah”—

> [Note: Col. 0478D] Concerning whom, Genesis XXXIV.

—to see the women of that land. Fearing no person and reverencing no [Col. 0479A] order, he did not indeed do whatever he wished, but he did whatever he was able. How greatly the enemy has wrought evil in the holy place! How much we have heard and learned—things our brothers have related to us! He must be bound, and his teeth broken in his own mouth, lest the young man become a wolf, running freely to wickedness and not to honorable conduct even for payment.

These two have erected one wall of impiety, and one hairy man cried to the other: “They are young; they are noble.” Therefore they must be corrected more cheerfully and more sharply, lest they become a scandal to you, a danger to themselves, and an example to others; and that they may know that a judge has come to their vices and a founder to their morals. But you, lord father, must not fear these two tails—

> [Note: Col. 0479D] Wittily he attributes to those two unbridled monks what Isaiah, chapter VII, says while Rezin and Pekah besiege Jerusalem.

—of smoking firebrands, because perhaps the hand of two hundred leads them, so that their works may come forth [Col. 0479B] into light and be exposed by the light in the light. Are not your men of Clairvaux with you, before whose face they will not dare even to stand, much less to speak? See to it that these things are not proclaimed in Gath—

> [Note: Col. 0479D] He drew this from II Kings, chapter I, where David laments Saul’s death.

—nor published in the streets of Ashkelon, and that the sons of the uncircumcised do not say: “Where is he whom they appointed keeper in the vineyards?” Therefore stretch out your hand and spend your arrows upon them.

Like a son of those cast out, I have spoken these things, lord father: not as directing, but as correcting, and with great affection. For I do not presume to teach Minerva or to set rays upon the sun, since you far surpass me both in life and knowledge. Keep this letter for your own eyes and those of your people; for this reason I wrote it in my own hand, lest it fall under the eyes of others. At its end I commend to you Master [Col. 0479C] John, who has impressed you upon his breast both deeply and closely. We love him especially for your sake, though he deserves special love for his own. Farewell.

## LETTER LIII. TO THE BRETHREN OF LA CELLE

[III, 7.] To his dearest brothers and sons—

> [Note: Col. 0479D] “To brothers and sons”: the monks of the monastery of La Celle.

—Brother Peter, their humble abbot in name, wishes the spirit of love and peace.

With what singular and unique affection and concern I am bound toward the salvation of all and each of you, that one Spirit knows who searches even the depths of God. My own soul also knows it; would that the eye [Col. 0479D] of your mind saw it as it is, and it would without doubt sympathize with its pains. I also presume that I am manifest in the consciences of some, to whom their own purity and my truthfulness give the same assurance. My dearest brothers, I do not wish to deceive you with any flatteries or entice you with any deceptive blandishments. But I write this so that your peace may be firm toward God and that you may not judge me alien from your hearts.

Moreover, if anyone thinks otherwise, he is thinking foolishly. Therefore let him come to his senses about injuring—indeed, damning—his own soul, whoever seeks to disturb your peace and mine. I single out no one and reproach no one for his folly. The accusation of one’s own conscience is sufficient, both for punishment of evil deeds and for reward of good merits. Absolutely let no one among you be disturbed by this, for repentance will never be vain, provided only that it is genuine. Prepare chaste minds for the Son of the Virgin; offer humble souls to the Son of the Most High; cleanse the dwellings of your hearts for the angel of holiness. [Col. 0480A] Farewell.

## LETTER LIV. TO THE GRANDMONTINES

[III, 8.] To his dearest fathers and lords of [Col. 0480B] Grandmont—

> [Note: Col. 0479D] Concerning Grandmont. This is the head and seat of a religious order of clerics, not obscure in France, who are called Grandmontines from it. It lies in the diocese of Limoges, not far from Muret. Hence Stephen of Tournai, in Letter 1, calls Stephen, the leader and chief of the religious community, “Stephen of Muret,” because he had established his seat there, although by birth he was Auvergnat, not Limousin.

—Brother Peter, abbot of Troyes, offers faithful prayers.

I know that the works of the Lord are great in the council of the righteous and in the great congregation. Therefore, dearest brothers, although I am far removed from you, I nevertheless convey into your present assembly the intention and supplication of my soul, so that it may bring back some small portion of whatever heavenly blessing, by which it may be consoled and strengthened for a long time. For I believe that, if those your angels who always behold the face of the Father in heaven should carry to the very Father of lights, and to the throne of grace of His Son, even one little prayer on my behalf from your mouth and heart, it will bear fruit above and put forth a shoot below. From this there will be for the needy and poor man the fruit of life and the hope of mercy [Col. 0480C]. Therefore raise those hands of yours, pure from every bloodshed and crime, and your dovelike eyes toward the windows of heaven, through which you are accustomed to enter to the mercy-seat and into the Holy of Holies; and do not lower them in any way until He who hears the desire of the poor—the Lord—has heard you. I am yours; but then I shall be so more worthily and affectionately. Farewell.

## LETTER LV. TO A., PRIEST OF ST. PETER AT PROVINS

[III, 9.] Brother PETER, abbot of La Celle, to the venerable A., priest of St. Peter at Provins: greeting.

I am not without reason bold enough to write to one whom I am not bold enough not to love. Could I with impunity fail to love one whom—would that I had received him even simply—as eminently worthy of honor [Col. 0480D]? Yet why do I praise so highly one whom I know only by the rarest sight? But I confess that I know him more by hearing than by sight, more by faith than by conversation, more by religious life than by familiar dwelling together. For I have heard of the man not the inflated pomp of the world, but the chosen pattern of learning; not drunkenness, but sobriety; not vain anxiety about money [Col. 0481A], but manifold meditation upon the Scriptures; not curiosity about appearances and a beauty tending toward the torches of hell, but the cleansing of the deformities of his own conscience according to the illumination of the divine mirror. These things, good young man, I have heard concerning you from others with longing, received with faith, and joyfully told to others. It is therefore no wonder if I write to such a man, whom I do not hesitate to describe as such on the report of persons in whom I firmly believe.

Yet I would far more eagerly and gladly see your face and hear your voice than utter dead words in lifeless letters, so that the presence of him whose love lives in the mind might sparkle in the eye. For a torch brought near applies its hidden heat to veins that sparkle at a distance. Thus they warm one another reciprocally, so that each fire, drawing the other to itself, strengthens and is strengthened [Col. 0481B]; so that the inner fire burns more ardently as the outer approaches it, and the outer shines more brightly as it shares more vehemently in the inner. By the likeness of this example, one whom you love in absence you begin to love exceedingly in presence. For love grows in the eyes; through the channel of the ears the voice of the beloved, stamped with the character of love, is carried back to the heart of the lover. Love, which previously existed without joy, or with weariness, now begins to exist with joy. For it wearies one not to possess the person whom one always strives to love. He too is without joy who does not possess Him without whom he cannot rejoice. Thus joy is added to love when a friend beholds his friend. Farewell.

## LETTER LVI. TO G., PRIEST OF HASTINGS

[Col. 0481C] [III, 10.] PETER, unworthy abbot of the monastery of La Celle, to G., priest of Hastings: the spirit of salvation.

[Note: [Col. 0481D] Priest of Hastings. In England. Hence he calls him a priest beyond the sea. A place memorable for the battle fought between William and Harold. William of Malmesbury writes *Hastingas*, and calls it the Battle of Hastings, as I have said [Col. 0482D].]

I write to you, a priest beyond the sea, not in presumption of my own spirit, but at the repeated request of R., whom you indeed begot according to the flesh, but I begot spiritually through the Gospel in Christ. For he desires to unite as brothers, with equal affection, those whom he has as fathers through unequal modes of generation. Indeed, he has already made me your brother, unless perhaps my brotherhood has become contemptible in your eyes because of my foreign dress. Yet among sensible people the diversity of garments is scarcely regarded as so great that their identity should thereby be torn apart. Accordingly, naked hearts are better joined, more affectionately united, more chastely mingled. For the heart of the righteous is clothed [Col. 0481D] not in purple and fine linen, but in wisdom and counsel; not in cloth and silk, but in virtues and in God. For, clothed in these according to the nature of creation at the beginning, he was not ashamed of angelic robes, nor did he dread the light of that uncreated brightness itself, so long as he displayed in mutual vision the uncorrupted features of the divinely implanted image.

But when, stripped of such splendors by nocturnal snares, he began, from shame at a more grievous misfortune, to cover himself with fig leaves: Christ came, that He might restore the garment of haircloth, tear the sackcloth, and appear naked, in our flesh—indeed, in His own—to the naked paternal gaze [Col. 0482A]. Therefore, as the naked sons of naked Christ, let us lay bare our hearts to one another and bind them together in a steadfast union in Christ: let them flow toward Christ, flow back toward heaven, and flow together toward the Three and One. “How good and how pleasant it is, brother, for brothers to dwell together in unity!” (Ps. 132 [133].) One thing is necessary. Why say much? The many things are not necessary. What vanity, then, belongs to the children of men, that they seek many things and do not care for the one thing? The one is prior to the many, and we attain the one more easily than the many. Since we cannot subsist without the one and fail amid the many, in great madness we nevertheless put the one behind us and desire the many. He is foolish who does not tend toward the one true Being; he is wise who strives for unchangeable blessedness. Truly [Col. 0482B], he alone is wise who knows only the One; he alone is foolish who wishes to know many things apart from the One. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not think too highly of yourselves, but think soberly” (Rom. 12:3).

The people of your land are accustomed to think toward drunkenness rather than sobriety. Drunkenness is a base vice, and baser than the other vices. For where is the judgment of the drunkard? Where is reverence in one who is drunk? Where is dignity? He forgets the past, is ignorant of the future, and unaware of the present. Discernment is confused, reason dulled, the senses bound, and the mind itself buried. As he laughs, he exposes himself all the more to the mockery of scoffers. From this viperous root rises—or rather creeps—lust, devastating the vigor of the soul’s entire religious life. Finally, as from a great whirlpool of destruction, there spring forth [Col. 0482C] frequent shoots of deadly transgression. The foot wanders, the tongue slips, the hand trembles, the lips quiver, sight grows dim, hearing becomes deaf. Add to these the furies raging within and pitilessly tearing the wretched breast.

Good man, do these not seem to you the beginnings of death, fuel for eternal fire, food for punishment, enticement to damnation? Therefore, if you would escape the serpent’s bite, drunkenness must be fled. He who is drunk even once is caught in the hunters’ snare. A drunken man is the sport of demons. He who is subjected to the tyranny of throat and belly is regarded as a brothel of vices. What is more stormy than a troubled sea? What more fearful than lightning unleashed? What deeper than the abyss? Yet none of these is more wicked than a drunken man. One must abstain from poison—indeed, from wine [Col. 0482D]—which turns a man into a log. The reading of divine books shows by precepts and examples how shamefully nature is dishonored by this, how cruelly it is condemned, how endlessly it is tormented, and how mercilessly it is excluded from the kingdom of God. “Neither drunkards,” says the Apostle, “shall possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10).

I have pressed the pen at greater length, in case I might refute—or at least restrain—the vice. Meanwhile, let us prick its foster-sister, lust, with the same sharpness rather than paint it. For that very fat thing, from the fatness of the earth, flourishes among you yet more luxuriantly [Col. 0483A]. Where the beauty of young men and girls is more becoming, their appearance more charming, food more abundant, drink richer, air healthier, land more fertile, and pleasantness more delightful, there a perverse mind is enfeebled by these things. For it prefers to enjoy vain desires rather than eternal goods. Deceived by artificial coloring, it does not heed the falseness hidden within. The lying woman deceitfully boasts of her empty appearance. Certainly that beauty is neither true nor her own. For, if it were true, it would endure forever. Thus, what is once true is always true. If it were hers, she would not buy it in the marketplace. “Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain.” The charm that deceives must be cast away; that which sets free must be sought. Shadowy beauty must be put aside; useful beauty desired.

Having set forth this common admonition, we ask that you take the greatest care of your one and singular soul [Col. 0483B]. For no one departing from this world changes his soul any further. This is the place, this the time for making the change; here one’s habits must be changed and corrected. Hereafter correction—not amendment—will be given; there will be threatening, not change, unless perhaps from punishment to punishment, from death to death, from misery to misery. Therefore change your life while you live this life, lest, if you now delay changing when you can, then, though wishing to change, you be compelled to remain as you are. R. fears for himself, my soul fears also for you. You are my father, and I your son. Since I entered through you into corruptible life, may it be that through me you come to the discipline of God. May it not happen that I rejoice without you; rather, may it happen that you and I reign with Christ [Col. 0483C]. Farewell.

## LETTER LVII. TO H., SUBPRIOR, THOMAS, AND ASCELIN OF CLAIRVAUX

[III, 11.] Brother PETER, abbot of La Celle, to his dearest friends H., subprior, THOMAS, and ASCELIN of Clairvaux: grace for grace.

We are more sweetly joined by a more gracious affection to those to whom we write better and sweeter things, and not without reason. For as the mind is worthier than the body, so the goods of the mind are more important than those of the body; and the mind is a faithful interpreter of itself. Thus we cultivate rather those things that belong to the mind than [Col. 0483D] those belonging to the body. For if you write about affection, but not according to your affection, you surely lie. Therefore, when affection speaks of itself, let it speak of itself and not of another. For it belongs to hypocrites to call another’s things their own and their own things another’s. Likewise it belongs to pretenders neither to love simply nor to speak or write truthfully to friends.

Accordingly, in Christ and in a true conscience I declare that you have, I believe, an affection toward me more sincere and pure than I myself do. For the more purified the eye of the mind in you, the more discerning it is also in loving friends; and the readier it is to see clearly, the freer and fairer it is in judging every matter. Only the mist of the body prevents my spirit and yours from seeing one another clearly when the obstacles are removed [Col. 0484A]. Yet, just as within a mortal body immortal hearts can approach one another by love and touch one another through mutual longings, so, in singular and special love, our affections daily travel from their respective regions, as far as possible, to greet and kiss one another. For whenever I remember you, I come to you on the feet of my mind.

Therefore, dearest and most desired brothers, I received your consolations thirstily, read them eagerly, and swiftly fulfilled them. Observe also in this how well our consciences adhere together, how perfectly they agree with one another. For while your finger wrote at the prompting of your mind, our mind was thinking; and what the finger had written, the mind had chosen. Clearly, before I heard I obeyed; before counsel was given I assented [Col. 0484B]. Such is the speed of love that it does not wait to hear what it ought to do. For it thinks itself injured unless it outruns the wishes of friends. It laments that much is taken away from its merit unless it watchfully anticipates even the movement of the will. Then it is joyful, then exultant, when it has come beforehand and in some fashion exceeded by doing greater things. O love that exceeds! O surpassing love! Alone among every kind of virtue, in exceeding you do not exceed the measure; in ascending you do not fall; in descending you ascend.

Humility is restrained according to its proper measure; chastity has its boundaries; we do not loosen the reins of obedience toward evil; generosity is extended to its limits and no farther; truth does not reach the limits of falsehood [Col. 0484C]. So too the other virtues ought only to run their own courses, not to run beyond them. Limits have been set for them which cannot be passed. But love climbs to heaven—indeed, above heaven—as though no law had been laid upon it; it descends to hell and sometimes even into hell itself. It embraces friends and is not shut out by enemies. When it extends itself, it is not injured; when it stretches itself beyond, it is not broken. It always grows and never grows old. Its years do not fail, but bring it to perfection. For the older—or rather, the longer-lasting, since it does not become old—it is, the brighter it is. Like the wine of Lebanon, it is ever renewed, ever strengthened, ever increased. Its powers always increase; the brightness of its face [Col. 0484D] never fades. O virtue of virtues! May you always so exceed in me that you may never depart. You do not allow him to depart in whom you deign to create righteous ecstasies.

Thus the Apostle knew how to go beyond himself in mind and penetrate the third heaven; thus the prophet, in ecstasy of mind, thought of God beyond human capacity. Peter likewise went beyond himself in amazement at the contemplation of glorified majesty when he said: “Let us make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah” (Matt. 17:4). He also went beyond himself a second and third time: either when, unable to bear that Christ should die, he said, “Far be it from you, Lord” (Matt. 16:22); or when he cut off the servant’s ear; or again, at the catching of fish, when he said: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5:8). O how often the bride runs out to meet the bridegroom—or, more truly, exceeds herself and everything created for love of the bridegroom! For whenever she speaks either about the bridegroom or to the bridegroom, she is said to fly beyond herself in ecstasy [Col. 0485A]. No one knows these leaps or ecstasies except one who has learned them by experience. Therefore I ought to speak more sparingly to you about them; it is fitting for you rather to practise them more widely and abundantly than to discuss them. Farewell. I shall come to you as soon as I can.

## LETTER LVIII. TO R. OF CLAIRVAUX

[III, 12.] His PETER of La Celle to his R. of Clairvaux.

Excessive haste is accustomed, from excessive appetite, to consume even things half-raw as though already well cooked, and sometimes to appease what is like the necessity of hunger [Col. 0485B]. You press me and do not cease to disturb your friend’s door as though by the need of a guest suddenly arriving. I believe rather that you act thus from grossness of soul, or from a poverty that is not necessary, so that neither my occupations may satisfy your importunities nor these customary holidays impose silence upon your will. What then? I am now experiencing what I had earlier read in Isaiah: “The children have come to the birth, and there is no strength to bring forth” (Isa. 37:3). I burn, indeed, to fulfil the new and first promise made to a new friend, but I can scarcely restrain the assaults of those who interrupt.

As I consider who asks, from whom, and what, reason presents the requester’s abundant wealth, the poverty of what is requested, and the difficulty of the request [Col. 0485C]. Who is asking, unless one who walks amid fiery stones, who is accustomed to taste the pith of cedars, and to bring back the splendid wages of maxims from the camps of the philosophers? From whom, unless from one who counts it a delight to sleep among thorns—not to say, among sayings—who neither divides the hoof by discernment of better sayings nor chews the cud if he happens to hear or read anything? Who asks from whom, unless the learned from the unlearned, the full from the empty, the seeing from the blind?

I confess that I endure no light or simple hindrance in entering the sanctuary of God in order to receive for you consoling coals from the hand of the cherubim. On one side stands in my way the flaming sword, whirling with cares that pierce to the marrow of the soul; on the other, a crowd of Philistines filling my wells with the earth of the dead [Col. 0485D]. Besides these, whenever I begin to write, such confusion is caused by those rushing toward me that almost every syllable is compelled to have a new beginning.
