Behold, one monk makes confession; behold, another denies it; behold, a knight dances; behold, a cleric greets me; behold, a servant troubles me; behold, a messenger caws more often than a dove coos.

My beloved, in the meantime how can the human heart gather together meditation upon the Holy Scriptures? How can it compose a spiritual memorandum? Yet perhaps these very things advise without advising, urge quiet by disturbing it, and, while tearing the true thing in different directions, admonish us to seek that very thing. Thus, hungry, I seek bread; thirsty, water; cold, fire; in darkness, light; fainting, refreshment [Col. 0486A]. But you, possessing another memorandum better and truer, beg again for another out of desire rather than need. I believe you do this after the example of the apostles, who, although they had Jesus, nevertheless desired to see the Father. “Lord,” they said, “show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (Luke 14). They did not yet know that he for whom the Son is not enough cannot have the Father either. For full knowledge of the Son is the fullest renewal of every rational creature.

O how splendid are the memoranda furnished by the men of Clairvaux! For what are this man’s tears but an incentive to compunction? What are another’s continual prayers but an aid to heavenly contemplation? This man’s humility confounds the pride of the apostate angel and of man; that man’s obedience imitates the obedience of Christ hanging upon the cross [Col. 0486B]. This one resembles Jacob in his labors; Joseph’s simplicity adorns that one; zeal for the order makes Moses present in another. O gentleness of David! O fervor of Elijah! O abstinence of Daniel! O chastity of Samuel—and, what is greater, O charity of Christ! O virginity of Mary! These are the camp of God. “What will you see in your Shulammite,” in your scarlet one, “but the companies of the camps?” (Song 6:13.)

I see one company going forth against the innumerable phalanxes of vices: while this man, seeking not what is his own, strangles the spirit of avarice; this man, trampling worldly glory, chokes the prince of pride; this man, mortifying the flesh, cuts off the head of lust. Whomever each encounters among the adversaries, each kills bravely and without mercy by the sword’s edge [Col. 0486C]. Finally, arrows rain constantly upon the enemies’ backs; they brandish spears and wield the sword, and extirpate, whether lions or unicorns, every beast of the wilderness. There is none among them who fails or labors. Again, on the right wing, I behold another company fighting on white horses, no longer for victory, but to heap up more precious spoils. One already tastes beforehand the reward of his labors; another receives grace upon his lips; another, stretched upon the tree that is in the midst of paradise, comes forth into the inner region of the veil through forgetfulness of earthly things and contemplation of heavenly things. These are they who have washed their robes white in the blood of the Lamb, resisting vices even to blood and attaining [Col. 0486D] the patience of the spotless Lamb.

These teach you the bow and arrow; they offer you the blood of the grape and of the mulberry. They do not bend a crooked bow; rather, with spiritual subtlety, they strike most swiftly even the hair of the smallest thought with the bow of self-reproach. They have indeed turned back on the day of battle, because they neither run aimlessly nor live sluggishly. For this purpose I send you this memorandum. For everything about them admonishes: their sitting, their walking, their speech, their silence, their fasting, and their meals. Behold, a thousand shields hang there, not only to admonish you but also to arm you. And after this, my son, what more shall I do for you?

You also possess another Paraclete, as another memorandum, which is near in your mouth and heart: the anointing of the Spirit, which teaches you concerning all things. You have wisdom, which is not found in the land of those living pleasantly, which the sons of Hagar do not find, of which the abyss of philosophers says, “It is not with me” [Col. 0487A]. Bind it continually in your heart by love; in the time of leisure write it out in three ways: by thinking, speaking, and acting. Roam through the most pleasant fields of the Scriptures; read like a bee, and store in the hive of memory flowers of sweetest fragrance: the lily of chastity, the olive of charity, the rose of patience, the grapes of spiritual gifts. Consider diligently what is set before you, because some things are for consolation, some for correction; some for healing, some for satisfaction, some for delight. Hope of the promised reward consoles the grieving; the threat of eternal punishment corrects; all languors are healed by the medicine of repentance; the joy of present justification satisfies one hungry for righteousness; grace when it comes removes the rod of fear and gladdens the soul by its infusion.

O Jesus! What taste is there for those who contemplate You upon the palate? What fragrance for the nostrils? What brightness before the eyes? What melody for hearing? What jubilation of heart? Joys fall short of no desire; they abound beyond all things—indeed, overflow [Col. 0487B]. The will unfolds and stretches itself out to will, even to fly, yet it is not enough. The oil runs over because the vessels fail. Here, here the hand of the giver is more generous, and that of the receiver more scanty. This alone is the indignation of the servants: that there are few to whom the heavenly dishes may be distributed. “Make your cords long; stretch out your tent-skins; do not spare,” for you shall expand to the east of divine contemplation, to the west of humanity’s restoration through Christ, to the north of the overthrow of demons, and to the south of glorious ascension. Farewell; and do not choose to receive our poverty without recompense. I greet from my whole heart, from my whole soul, and from my whole strength our most beloved subprior and our other friends.

## LETTER LIX. TO THE SAME MAN

[III, 13.] P. of La Celle to his R. of Clairvaux.

I would put forward an introduction to excuse myself, or cast a veil over my rusticity, if I were writing to a scholarly cleric rather than a monk of Clairvaux; to someone foaming amid secular things rather than sweating under the Rule; finally, to one pursuing the pleasures of the Sirens rather than following every hardship through the desert [Col. 0487D]. But now, since I do not doubt that only what is honorable is good, and that everything true is honorable, if I speak truth without departing from what is honorable, I do not fear shame.

I know that you have set your hand to mighty matters and have made a sophism sufficiently entangled in ancient sophistry. Believe me: gnashing and roaring, it seeks to dissolve what it cannot refute by reason. It is cunning, and highly skilled in the art of perverse cunning, since from the incomprehensibly remote succession of past times not a year, month, day, hour, or briefest instant [Col. 0488A] has elapsed for it without conflicts of this kind. How often has it conquered and been conquered, cast down and been cast down, overwhelmed and been overwhelmed? It has no shame; fear is far from it; hope of overthrow is always present. It thunders while afraid, touches while trembling, withdraws while hoping, approaches while doubting. O craft, enemy of simplicity; daughter of malice; sole moth of all religious life! You excluded our father from paradise, thrust him into exile, shut him up in death. You strip us of blessedness, heap miseries upon us, and separate us from God. What have you to do with us? You seized and deceived, but did not recover. For He who made us recovered us by remaking us.

Therefore, dearest one, the seducer must be guarded against, caught in his own snare, and cut down with his own sword. Thus he acted toward us; thus let us act toward him. It is evil to be a murderer, but not to be a slayer of the devil [Col. 0488B]. Therefore crush his head, seize his tail, divide his middle body; and so, at evening, morning, and noon, you will recount in confession, proclaim in satisfaction, and be heard in prayer. This sophist proposes badly, assumes more badly, and concludes most badly. By insinuating evil things he proposes; by drawing toward pleasure he assumes; by casting down into consent he concludes. Therefore, if you prudently foresee and repel the suggestion with the shield of sacred instruction, if you bravely shake off pleasure by remembrance of Christ’s Passion, if you steadfastly deny consent through fear and love of God, breaking his little snares like spiders’ threads, you shall be crowned from the head of Amana, from the summit of Senir and Hermon.

## LETTER LX [New]. FROM NICHOLAS OF CLAIRVAUX, IN THE PERSON OF BROTHER ADAM, TO PETER

[Col. 0488C]

To the singular father and lord P., abbot of La Celle, Brother A.: whatever he is, and whatever he can do in the Lord.

Nothing in human affairs is sweeter than friendship; but this is so when the person of a man, not his fortune, is loved. With this love, holy Father, you loved your son, so that whenever I remember your mercies, my heart and my flesh exult in the living God. For I was young in age, poor in resources, poorer in merits; and you, passing over those who surpassed me both in religious observance and learning, joined me to your side and preferred me to your community. “What shall I render to the Lord for all these things,” not which He has repaid but which He has given [Col. 0488D] me? (Ps. 115 [116].) I know what I shall do: as long as I live, I shall pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness.

But how long shall I make the prologue and not plainly and boldly say what must be said? I shall speak to my lord; may my speech be pleasing to him. For, according to the saying of the holy man Job (Job 4), “Who can hold back a conceived word?” I cannot keep silent; I dare not speak; yet it shall be said. It has long been, most loving Father, that I had set ascents in my heart, in order that I might ascend to the holy place—the place which the Lord chose from all places of the earth, that His name might be there. I was not tossed about by youthful frivolity, as is customary, but made firm by deliberate consideration [Col. 0489A]; I wove together my purpose lest, once exposed, it should wholly perish.

Therefore, seized by the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning, and no longer able or willing to disguise the spirit of freedom, I came to your men of Clairvaux, weeping and praying that they would receive me into the council of the righteous and the congregation. I knocked strongly, but was repelled more strongly. I persevered, obtained my request, entered; and behold, I am among them as one of them. I beg you through the bowels of the mercy of our God not to grieve as do the rest who have no hope, because I have passed from your people to your people: yours not in word or tongue, but in deed and truth. See how greatly they trust in you: without you they have retained me, knowing that they are in you and you in them, most serene lord and most loving Father [Col. 0489B]. Farewell.

## LETTER LXI. TO NICHOLAS, MONK OF CLAIRVAUX

[IV, 3.] His PETER to his NICHOLAS.

Whenever you write, you compose letters seasoned with a marvelous flavor for my eager appetite. For, to speak truthfully to a true friend, they almost have this as their special and proper quality: “Those who eat me shall still hunger, and those who drink me shall still thirst” (Sirach 24:21). Though I myself am unskilled in the craft of replying by letter, I am not unskilled in the knowledge of loving in return. I know whom I ought to love, why, how much, and how long. Whom, unless the servant of God; unless one who loves righteousness and hates iniquity; unless, finally, one who abides in God and God in him [Col. 0489C]? Why, unless because he is a fellow servant and brother, one for whom Christ suffered? How much, unless as much as the Son of God loves me, as much as myself, as a hand loves an eye? How long, unless unto death, unto age upon age, unto eternity and beyond?

In general, thus are disposed those who seek not their own interests but those of Jesus Christ, who, full of charity and love, rest and feed at noon among the chambers and gardens of spices. These are your men of Clairvaux—indeed, mine. They are those who do not, like him who was to deny Jesus, follow at a distance; nor, like others, stand nearby or, withdrawing from Him, return after Satan. Rather, having cast off the linen cloth, they walk naked after the naked One, cling to the Lamb’s footsteps, and fly upward toward heaven. Until they approach Him who sits upon the throne and speak their works to the King, they hasten to leap across the mountains of spices [Col. 0489D]. These are the stags of the mountains, the roebucks of the plains, the fawns of the forests. Indeed, they themselves are the lily of the valleys, the cedars of Lebanon, the fruitful olive trees in the house of God. Their cheeks are beautiful, apart from that which lies hidden within. Their virtue is greater than their fame, their ardor greater than their outward flame; their praise is established, and I cannot attain to it. Truly you too are one of them, for both your speech and your works make you manifest.

If, then, as I have said, we are specially disposed toward one another in mutual love, we shall firmly preserve these points: whom [we love], why, how much, and how long. I am almost like one blinded, not noticing who writes and to whom [Col. 0490A]. With what face do I not hide, cover, or conceal my foolishness, my ugliness, my slowness? And if I mock the eyes of fools, I presume that I can likewise deceive the eyes of the roebuck and lynx. But lest you be deceived, suspecting in me more understanding and talent than you hear, I lay completely open the poverty of my want. Indeed, since I cannot dig, I am not ashamed to beg. Therefore open your hand, unseal your mouth, that it may give birth to wisdom.

I ask, then, what Jerome means when, in his letter to Rufinus, explaining Solomon’s judgment in the question of the two prostitutes, he says: “On the third day after I gave birth, this woman too gave birth.” “If,” he says, “you consider Pilate washing his hands and saying, ‘I am innocent of the blood of this just man’; if the centurion confessing before the cross, ‘Truly this was the Son of God’; if those who, before the Passion, desire through Philip to see the Lord—you will not doubt that the Church gave birth first, and afterward the Jewish people was born, for whom the Lord prayed: ‘Father, forgive them,’ etc.” Regarding the centurion and those seeking to see the Lord, it does not seem so difficult to me that they are children of the Church; but regarding Pilate I consider it utterly unbelievable.

The same letter continues: “There is no doubt that all the things said apply not to dead Solomon but to the majesty of Christ. He feigns ignorance and, in accordance with the dispensation of the flesh, represents human emotions falsely,” etc. If our Lord Jesus Christ assumed everything belonging to human nature except sin, and had human emotions not falsely but truly [Col. 0490C], how then does He represent human emotions falsely?

## LETTER LXII [New]. FROM NICHOLAS OF CLAIRVAUX TO THE ABBOT OF LA CELLE: SUSPICIONS CONCERNING THE DELIVERY OF LETTERS

To his much-beloved and greatly cherished lord PETER, abbot of La Celle, Brother NICHOLAS: from the highest Lord, “Well done, good servant.”

Before I saw you, I loved you; and the beginning of my love was the testimony of your religious life, which I had heard concerning you from religious persons. But after sight joined hearing, the mystery of mutual familiarity followed, and friendship made equal minds out of unequal persons. Although rank made you exalted, condescension made you humble, when you emptied yourself by graciously receiving a lowly person [Col. 0490D]. For this reason, admitted into the sanctuary of your charity, I entrusted to you what I did not dare entrust to another; and I did so the more securely the more sincerely I loved you. Since true love banishes every suspicion or pretence from the truth of its purity, I disclose to you my slight suspicion.

I had given you letters to be given to Lecelin; but by some means they came into the hands of the abbot of Arras. It is difficult—indeed impossible—that either you gave them to him or he received them from you, since I do not doubt your truthfulness or his discretion. Still, I would more readily believe that the young man was led astray by youthful frivolity than that you, most loving Father, were induced to do this. Yet let it please your gracious dignity to write back to me how you delivered the letter to him. Send back to me our book by the bearer of this present letter. Know, moreover, that I am your servant and, if you judge me worthy, your friend [Col. 0491A]. Farewell, and pray for me.

## LETTER LXIII [New]. TO THE SAME MAN, COMPLAINING THAT HE HAD NOT WRITTEN AT GREATER LENGTH. FINE PASSAGES ON HUMAN MISERY. “MAN BORN,” ETC.

His to his.

Recently, when the fury of the north wind, blowing with greater violence, had scorched and struck our nakedness, we were all ordered to be bled. [Col. 0491B] This bleeding, however, is customary, and has been most methodically prescribed by those who founded the Order, so that we cannot complain of excess. For we are commanded to keep silence and lie still, looking upon everything in the refectory dry, as yesterday and the day before. We can neither work nor pray, nor read, nor even at least attend to those who are reading. It is altogether a most just arrangement: ancient pride is confounded and crushed with equal weight, so that we, who used to shut up the cracks of the walls, inaccessible to everyone else, and rejoiced in darkness, now expose our heads to the sun and air. For “a man, being the image and glory of God,” says the Apostle (1 Cor. 11), “ought not to cover his head”; and now by experience we have learned that this acquired delicacy [Col. 0491C] was a fault, not nature.

During this interval spiritual men investigate the most secret recesses of their consciences, not so that they may fail to find something to rebuke, but so that they may rebuke what they find. Then they divide waters from waters—that is, the purity of spiritual understanding from the sensuousness of low and feeble carnality—and they set reason as a firmament, lest the higher things bend down toward the lower and be defiled, or the lower be joined with the higher. Unhappy is he who does not divide thus, because whatever he offers does not please in such a way as to be acceptable, but, though apparently pleasing, provokes wrath.

I, among others and with others, have been summoned and assigned to this jubilee, amid these delights. Here, somewhat cooled from the flame of literal business continually conducted at Clairvaux, [Col. 0491D] I turned my eyes back toward the memory of you; and assuredly I love you, and am loved by you, as gladly as ardently. I left those subtle and useful meditations to others, who, worn down and constrained by exercises of harder and purer life, often soaring in the streets of the heavenly Zion, draw in visions of heavenly images. Thus, freed from the tumult and shifting whirlpool of affairs, I conversed with myself and said: “Behold, now the fullness of time has come for me to write to him whom my soul loves, if perhaps by the return of familiar pages I may call back, through the charms of his eloquence, its sweetness.”

In truth I have found that he possesses a most powerful style, sharpened by thought and polished by expression, blended in a happy balance of both qualities. While I was considering these things, another thought entered, saying: “Is this the part of a wise man, not yet repentant—to summon and challenge his friend, not to the marrow of meaning, but to the thorns of words?” This is surely the part of boys, or of those wise in a childish way, who attend not to the meaning of a reading but to the eloquence of its phrasing, longing for the flowers of thorns and recoiling from the roughness of harvest-fields. Speech of true purity, or of pure truth, ought to be uncorrupted and easy; it does not desire to be darkened by the artificial veil of rhetorical colours.

For, as the philosopher testifies, what is plain and simple befits goodness. What, then, shall I say or dictate for my requesting friend—something worthy of one beloved, to be seen and for [Col. 0492B] his lips and teeth to chew over? Shall I teach you? That would be madness. Shall I praise you? That would be folly. Shall I admonish you? That would be boldness. Yet my pen will move more safely in this field, since boldness is, as it were, the inseparable companion of affection.

I wish therefore to set before you two sayings at which I am accustomed to tremble, which a holy man, feeling them in himself and concerning himself, lamenting the miseries of human mortality as wonderfully as miserably, uttered: “Man born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries. He comes forth like a flower and is crushed; he flees like a shadow and never remains in the same state” (Job 14).

O abject condition of birth, harshness of life, misery of death! “Man born of woman”: what is more abject? “Living for a short [Col. 0492C] time, he is filled with many miseries”: what is harsher? “He comes forth like a flower and is crushed”: what is more miserable? You see, O man, the threefold but unhappy cord by which the whole human race is bound and girded, and which is not merely difficult but impossible to break.

Do you wish to see with the faith of your eyes that nothing is more abject than a human being at birth? Nature has certainly fortified the bodies of all animals and birds with many defences, meeting them as it were with a most spacious bosom of kindness. Thus she has granted bristles to the ox, feathers to the bird, and teeth, claws, and horns, that they may have means either to inflict force or repel it. You see the limbs of man alone abject and unprovided, toward which that most kindly nurse of things behaves like a stepmother, with a certain look of indignation.

Add that man comes, stained and wrapped in the deepest darkness of ignorance, into this place of torments, where he is born unhappily, lives more unhappily, and dies most unhappily. For the young of other animals, as soon as they are born, run; and amid so many thousands of the herd they know, with astonishing ease, how to return to their mothers’ teats. But a child’s feet are unfit even for motion, and its hands for touching; and unless the nurse’s breasts are pressed very closely upon infant lips, it may die before it can find what has been placed to its mouth. This inheritance was left us by that ancient Adam, who fled from the face of God (Gen. 2), and secured it by the irreversible privilege of death.

[Col. 0493A] “See, Lord, and consider that I was secretly carried off, and here, innocent, was cast into the pit”—innocent, plainly, in relation to him who ruined and killed me. I was reduced to nothing and did not know it, because I was not there when he devoured me with his most bitter bite. Observe how each word is weighed by its own force. “Man,” he says, “born,” not “man created,” because he would not have experienced the laws of this oppression had he not consented to the apostate spirit which deceitfully seduced him and led him into the place of affliction and the pit of death.

I think “of woman” was added because the Son of the Virgin was not subject to these sufferings; although he had them, they were his by will, not necessity. “Living,” he says, “for a short time”: truly, “every living human being is altogether vanity” (Ps. 38). [Col. 0493B] “Every living human being,” he says, not every human being is life. A body is living; a soul is alive; God is life: living from vanity, alive from simplicity, life from unity. Therefore the body, because it is composite, rises and dies; the soul, because it is simple, does not know setting. “All things,” Scripture says, “that arise set, and what increases grows old.” It says “arise,” not “are made,” because whatever was made by the hand of the Almighty in the first principles of things remains for ever; but things compounded and proceeding from those principles receive both rising and setting.

Life, however, is both one and a unity; neither the simple in a certain sense nor the composite can participate in it, because this prerogative belongs to the one and unique unity. Therefore, as far as a living thing surpasses what merely lives, so far life surpasses a living thing—except that the latter is carried above the former as much more eminently as the Creator incomparably surpasses the creature. “Living,” he says, “in time”—he who was made to preside over time, not to be subject to temporality—and this in a short time, so that he joins swiftness to swiftness, for nothing is swifter than years. Hence a child changes into an adolescent, an adolescent into a young man, a young man into an old man, and an old man into one decrepit, so that from the very source of his progress comes his decline, until he returns to the earth from which he was taken, that this may be fulfilled: “In the evening he falls, becomes hard, and dries up” (Ps. 89).

Remember that, although it is a short time, it is not a short labour; and therefore follows: “He is filled with many miseries.” Who could grasp in thought, much less recount in [Col. 0493D] words, the weight of human miseries? None is excepted; none escapes, even if that great eye of providence, which looks out upon all things from the lofty watchtower of divinity, has called and placed him upon the summit of affairs. For such persons, the higher they are, are entangled in more numerous miseries. Subjects are at least permitted to lament their own misery; prelates, amid their sufferings, must bare their very hearts while necessarily putting on faces of joy.

Thus man is always turned about in his misery because he is always pierced by a thorn: now toward bodily misery, now toward misery of heart; misery while sleeping, misery while awake, misery wherever he turns himself. Consider what judgment you ought to make concerning an evil conscience. I therefore judge even a good conscience to be miserable, though from a far different—indeed contrary—point of view. Is it not miserable, having fallen from eternity, being held in exile, and delayed from the kingdom?

“He comes forth,” he says, “and is crushed”: between coming forth and crushing no interval occurs; but as soon as he comes forth, he is crushed, because from the point at which he begins to live, he begins to die. For we die every day. [Seneca, *Epistle* 24.] Every day some portion of life is taken away. This is what overturns him, because “he flees like a shadow.” By what an elegant comparison he has marked the changing course of human life! As a shadow is now on the right, now on the left; now before, now behind, so man is now on the right through prosperity, now on the left through adversity; now before through pride, now behind through detraction; and he never remains in the same state.

How well the sluggishness [Col. 0494B] or senselessness of our souls is portrayed. The soul never stands still: now within, now without; now wandering and chattering in the street-corners, impatient of rest and unable to remain at home on its own feet. Alas, how true it is: “Jerusalem committed sin, and therefore became unstable” (Lam. 1).

These things, sweetest of friends, I have dictated to you at least by leaps, since I could not do so continuously, being drawn and drawn back by many affairs; and I have written them with my own hands.

For all who have business come to us; yet I alone can say with holy Jacob: “All these evils have fallen back upon me” (Gen. 42). Although this too is beyond your many and evil occupations—you whom the height of honour has swallowed up into the terrible sea of cares. Yet let this be a very strong argument for you of how deeply you have descended into the hidden recesses of my heart: I have given to your friendship that little space which I owed to my conscience. If my style here does not shine with a brighter light of words, know that ability, not willingness, was lacking.

“I have become foolish; you compelled me.” You, I say, who are rich in speech, abundant in knowledge, great in talent, first in rank, have desired the utterance of my rusticity—like Elijah, who hungered for the widow’s last food. But, unless I am mistaken, you too act with a similar purpose: you ask in order to give; you hunger in order to satisfy; and with entire generosity you heap up for me the granary of your thought.

Therefore attend not to the brilliance of the style but to the purity of the intention; and reckon that our little writings are not to be weighed after death, but rather our deeds, by him who will render to each according to his works. Therefore live toward one beneath you as you would wish one above you to live toward you; and when you have done something, think that you have done nothing. Then, fortunate man, you have done all things most fully, if you always love to be loved and fear to be feared. This thought removes self-exaltation, restrains arrogance, and casts down the first and last of vices.

Therefore let your tongue always be intent upon heavenly praises, your soul upon holy reflections, your right hand upon gifts, because whatever you grant to your people you keep for yourself, and whatever you scatter among the poor you gather for yourself. For that saying of the splendour of rhetoricians is true: whatever you do is yours; what you possess is another’s. I had indeed dictated and written these things well before your messenger arrived. With what celebration and sweetness of remembrance I uttered them concerning you, he who received this—mine, indeed also yours, who has placed the memory of your spirit more abundantly within his own spirit—is my witness. In him I greatly delighted, both for the purity of his conscience and for the liveliness of his disposition.

But you, who have now gone up to Jerusalem with the Lord, pray for both of us, because each of us is yours: that he may protect us beneath the shadow of his wings until iniquity passes away, so that, when he himself—our life—appears, we too may appear with him in glory. But how resolutely our whole community, small and great, young and old, cloistered brethren and officials—in a word, with one utterance, one spirit, and in one place—petitioned the lord of Troyes on behalf both of your person and of your church, you will do better to learn from another [Col. 0495B] than from me.

## LETTER LXIV. TO NICHOLAS, A MONK OF CLAIRVAUX

[IV, 2.] His own to his own.

“Any beast that touches the mountain shall be stoned.” Most beloved, the heights of your letters withdraw themselves, raised into such a density of clouds that they scarcely admit, by the most difficult efforts, the sharpness of my eyes in any degree. Now you fly and fly through the loftiness of cedars; now you build your nest in the highest hollows of ruins; now you walk upon the wings of the winds; now, finally, you run and race incomprehensibly over the mountains of spices. Whether you find a path by which a man has walked [Col. 0495C] or do not find one, you care not greatly.

Nor is this surprising. For your Seneca, more familiar to you than the rest, divided human talents into three kinds. First he places such as yours: those that open paths for themselves and penetrate by their own strength whatever lies remote. The talent of the second lot is less noble: it does not know how to lead, yet is not swollen with pride in following. He calls the third of more unhappy fortune: unless compelled, dragged by the hand, and put upon a chariot, it scarcely warms up or springs free from its inertia.

Nature, lavishly bestowing upon this third kind, while begrudging me the first and even the second, has, unless I am mistaken, bound me most tightly and confirmed me in a splendid inheritance by the cord of its measure, and sealed it. And alas! I do not at all envy you your sharp eye; nevertheless I grieve for myself, because the more brightly your lot shines beside mine, the more darkly mine itself appears.

While, therefore, you had put barriers upon your mouth, granted sleep to your eyes, and not brought your hand to the quiver, I spoke with the great speed of the ancients’ words; I did not equal them in penetration of intellect, yet I judged myself rich in knowledge of the Scriptures. But when you began to flash the thunderbolts of meanings, hurl the javelins of arguments, and rain down the counsels of sweet exhortations, I was found slower of tongue, poorer in understanding, and more rustic in style. I therefore see my poverty: admiring, not migrating into your abundance; looking up to, not receiving, your learning. “It has been strengthened, and I cannot attain to it.”

For in what depth, darkness, and obscurity, do you think, is this hidden: [Col. 0496A] “The body is living, the soul alive, God life”? Then “deep calls to deep”: “Living,” you say, “from vanity; alive from simplicity; life from unity.” Here—here are darkness; here shadow from cloud; clouded air at noon. But what fault is the sun’s if I am not illuminated because I lack eyes? “O man worthy, perhaps you say, of laughter, who takes day for night, shadow for light, darkness for sun!” I say: neither sun, nor day, nor light; but I plainly encounter palpable darkness.

For since it is irrefragably believed that the body has life from the soul, the soul from God, and God—life—from himself, would it not be said, though more rustically, yet more truly, that the body is enlivened by the soul, the soul enlivened by God and enlivening the body, and God enlivening all living things, living and alive in himself and from himself? But again, what is “a body living from vanity”? “The body,” says the Apostle, “is dead because of sin” (Rom. 8). Therefore, what the Apostle calls dead because of sin, do you call living from vanity? Is not vanity sin? Does what is understood in a simple sense produce both death and life? God hates those who observe vanity. But God’s love makes alive; hatred makes dead. Therefore nothing lives from vanity, but from truth. “What was made in him,” that is, in the Word of truth, “was life.” No earthly or supercelestial creature is life in itself and from itself, although in him all things, whether living or lacking life, have their life.

You add: “alive,” that is, the soul, from simplicity; “life,” [Col. 0496C] that is, God, from unity. I am not offended by these points with such violent spirit, but neither do I wholly assent. For the soul is believed to have been created from nothing, from an immortal and indissoluble unity, just as God is immortal and indissoluble in his own singular and different manner. For this reason God created it in his image and likeness. Also, because it is wholly present at once through every particle of the body—neither smaller in smaller parts nor greater in greater—and yet, as Augustine testifies, exercises its effects more intensely in some and more weakly in others, though it is essentially in every particle of the body, it is judged to be subject more to unity than to simplicity.

For everything simply simple is one thing and one; but what is one is not immediately simple. Hence God is called simple, as Isidore testifies, for no other reason than that he is not one thing and what is in him another. But two or more things in agreement sometimes make one thing, as a body consisting of four elements. Therefore the soul, although it does not receive a compaction of diverse parts in its constitution, nevertheless—because it itself is one thing and what is in it another—is, according to the authority cited above, more fittingly said to be from unity than from simplicity.

By this same demonstration of reason God is more properly said to be from simplicity, although almost nothing, or absolutely nothing, is said of him except improperly. For what does it mean to say that God is from unity or simplicity except “God from God”: namely, the Father from himself, the Son from the Father, the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son? Or is anyone so foolish as to think that God is simple by participation in simplicity, one by participation in unity, good by participation in goodness, just as a human being becomes wise by participation in wisdom, and similarly in other cases? Whatever is in God is God: wisdom is in God, and God is wisdom; power is in God, and God is power; goodness is in God, and God is goodness. Therefore God is no more from unity than from simplicity.

I would already have torn the pen from my fingers and commanded timely silence to my mouth, had I not resolved here to breathe out whatever about my friend gnaws at my mind. For my heart is more harshly pricked when the Son is depicted anywhere as being in the middle between the Father and the Spirit. Indeed, he would fashion an idol of abomination who carved or [Col. 0497B] painted any image thus. The consubstantiality, coeternity, and coequality of the one Trinity and triune unity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—admit neither before nor after, greater nor lesser, lower nor higher. Rather, the whole Father is in the whole Son, the whole Son in the whole Father, and the whole Holy Spirit, separately and jointly, in each one and in both together.

This holy Trinity, always to be named with trembling, is wholly everywhere through essence and power, not dispersed through grace and not extended by spatial magnitude, as visible light or another visible thing is, but as wisdom is in a human being. For you see two men, one small and the other large in body, yet equal in participation in wisdom. So the divine essence is uniform and of one mode in the greatest and the least. Finally, just as it is incomprehensible because of its immensity, so too it is indivisible because of its simplicity.

“Let us understand God,” Augustine says against Arius, “as far as we can: good without quality, great without quantity, creator without need, present without position, wholly everywhere without place, eternal without time, making mutable things without change, suffering nothing.” You swear, I believe, that you believe, or have believed, thus and no otherwise. I too declare upon my faith that, if my tongue, because it is moist, has erred, my heart has held this view.

For a simple thing avoids and rejects every addition and every partnership. Yet, lest you be troubled for long by turning over where you said this, you write in your sermon on Saint Victor: “Yet he is everywhere in the middle. For even in that essence of deity the Son is in the middle between the Father and the Spirit.” You ought now to remember that “a mediator is not mediator of one”: but God is one—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. If someone thinks that, because you did not add “holy,” a created rather than uncreated spirit is meant, he entirely fails to know Jerome’s rule concerning the meaning of this name: “Where,” he says, “Spirit is placed in Scripture without any addition, the Holy Spirit is rightly understood.” But if the interpreter just mentioned should stubbornly maintain that it was said of a created spirit, there remains an abuse no smaller than that shown above concerning the uncreated Spirit. For no one can comprehend on what basis he who encompasses all things in his fist, outside and inside, below and above, could be called middle.

You cry out that I have poured out all my spirit. Why not? When I pour myself out to you, I do not pour out but pour in.

> [Note: [Col. 0497D] This letter, which appears as no. 51 among the letters of Nicholas of Clairvaux (*Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyons, XXIII, 547), ends thus: “For no one can comprehend on what basis he who encompasses all things in his fist, outside and inside, below and above, could be called middle. Even in the assumption of flesh the Son is in no way middle between the Father and the Spirit, but is said and believed to be between man and God; whence he is also called mediator. But enough of this.” [Col. 0498D] “For I hear you crying and muttering within your throat: ‘Why this outpouring of words?’ Indeed, I have poured out my soul to you, half of my soul. Farewell. Greet by name my former lord Henry, Ascelin, William, Robert, Hugh your scribe, Thomas, and the other friends. Forgive me.” EDITION OF THE FATHERS.]

## LETTER LXV. NICHOLAS TO PETER, AFFIRMING NOTHING CONCERNING THE FOREGOING SUBJECT

His own of Clairvaux to his own of Celle, because he is his own.

[Col. 0498B] It causes me anxiety both to write and not to write to you: in the one case friendship is injured; in the other, my own conscience. The one is against my resolution, the other against affection. For it belongs to a monk not to write but to mourn; but it belongs to a friend both to speak and to converse through frequent letters, lest silent affection present the appearance of one who does not love.

Your friend, therefore, has fallen into these straits; eagerly wishing to make himself known by words, he burns to speak and fears to do so. He burns to reveal himself; he fears to presume. He fears that, if he speaks, he will be troublesome; if he keeps silent, estranged. Which, then, will prevail: monk or friend? Love. Love, which does not know how to be conquered, is accustomed to conquer; and it will easily triumph over a human being, since it triumphed over the Lord of heaven. [Col. 0498C] It triumphed over him all the more easily because he is not merely loving but is himself Love: whose height was brought low, whose singularity was joined to others, whose fullness was poured out, conquering the angels themselves in ministering. For he who was above them became among them as one of them—indeed, more than this, he was made lower than the angels, subject to men, last among men, a man of sorrows, knowing infirmities, and one who learned obedience from the things he suffered.

Others may judge as they please; I prefer to exceed in words rather than fail to satisfy you, and to be a talkative friend rather than a languid one. From where, then, shall I begin? From your letters, which have lodged with me no little while, and which, glittering with the gifts of more florid eloquence and deeper learning, struck and wounded me when I least expected it. For in the simplicity of my heart I had written to you as a simple man dwelling at home; but you, a hunter both of words and of meanings, believed me caught in nets and struck by a hunting-spear. Would that we could say, “The net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures.” For even if I could strike back, I would not wish to do so; but perhaps you either exclaim or think: “O long premeditation! O carefully wrought thoughts! O words kept awake!—which ought to be distinguished both by powers of intellect and by flowers of expression.”

I would not claim this for myself, since I truly lack both; nor have I thought about this matter until now, my conscience bearing witness for me. For I am busy, not at leisure; a man under authority, to whom it is said, “Come,” and he comes, and again, “Go,” and he goes (Matt. 8), entering at the command of one who orders. Indeed, even on this occasion, with business pressing upon me, I scarcely managed to steal myself away, sought but not found.

For I had hidden myself from the face of those seeking me in a most secluded and remote place; yet here, in brief and interrupted intervals, I have written this more as something said than [Col. 0499B] dictated.

I therefore pass over replying to your preface, which now anoints with praises, now pricks with blows, and in a sinewy composition alternates the force of discourse—except that at the end it brought to light whatever it had drawn over. For, turning over and striking against the words of our earlier letter, it says: “In what depth, darkness, and obscurity, do you think, is this hidden: ‘The body is living, the soul alive, God life’? Then ‘deep calls to deep’: ‘Living,’ you say, ‘from vanity; alive from simplicity; life from unity.’ Here—here are darkness; here shadow from cloud; clouded air at noon. Here I see neither sun, nor light, nor day, but plainly palpable darkness.”

These are your words, taken from ours not in order to defend them but to attack them. Yet it was your part, my beloved, to weigh every word by its proper force before passing judgment on the words, and diligently to inquire whether my deeper assertion was a mere invention or a teaching which could not be repelled or refuted.

I have with me a soul full of subtlety and holiness, eminent in fact, not in name alone, whom the company of both scholastic and ecclesiastical writers has raised to the citadel of authority. This is Claudianus [Note: [Col. 0499] Claudianus Mamertus, bishop of Vienne in Gaul, flourished in the year 440.], who, while still young, drank in the entire Christian, Roman, and Attic library through the most hidden disciplines, and by both the sharpness of his intellect and the bulk of his work has almost given us another Augustine.

This is he concerning whom the Roman schools and Gallican lecture-halls give testimony in these words: “When we came before him, we met whatever he said with the opposition of contradictory syllogisms; but with soaring intellect he broke all our efforts like spiders’ threads, eluding the very beginnings of words. For he was the most ingenious man among men, of his age, place, and people; and no one in our century has been so able to establish what he wished.”

Thus he says, in Book III, chapter 7, concerning the state of the soul, speaking in this way about the principles of things: “As formless matter, because it is capable of being formed, is superior to nothing, so that which has already been formed is better than that which, though capable of being formed, has not been formed. Likewise, as what has been formed precedes what has not been formed, so every formed inanimate thing yields to that which is at once formed and animate; for as the formed approaches form, so the animate approaches life. But as there are three things—formless matter, formed but lifeless matter, and the form of things—so likewise there are three: the enlivened, the enlivening, and life. The body is living, the soul alive, God life.”

Here—here consider what you have said, you who contradicted this, for I think Claudianus both supports and satisfies my case. But what follows—“living from vanity, alive from simplicity, life from unity”—is my own wording and must be defended all the more strongly because the person speaking lacks both authority and name. “Living from vanity” is the living body, which Claudianus’s authority also calls “enlivened.”

[Col. 0500B] Hear therefore: “Vanity of vanities,” says Ecclesiastes (ch. 1), “and all is vanity.” If all is vanity, and the body is either from all things or from some portion of all things, then the body is vanity. “Every living human being is altogether vanity,” says holy David (Ps. 38). What dies is what lives; what is born in order to live lives in order to die. For what dies except that which is deprived of life? What dies in man, what is extinguished from life, is precisely this: the body and bodily sense. For it is that primary animate element from which the living creature itself exists; thus, when it ceases to be sentient, sensation ceases to exist. Therefore what dies in man is what lives in man; and because it is mortality, it is vanity. Thus, “every living human being is altogether vanity”—not every human being is life, but every human being is living.

For life too is in some sense human, and a living human being is life insofar as he gives life, living insofar as he is enlivened. But flesh lives from the soul, and the soul in the flesh; both live, yet there is a great difference, because flesh has from the soul all that it has by which it lives, whereas the soul in the flesh does not have all that by which it lives. For it also lives in God—and would that it may live! What lives in flesh is vain, because it is from vanity. But the Apostle calls the body dead because of sin (Rom. 8) only because this too is most manifest vanity. He calls it “dead,” that is, destined to die, according to the rule of speech by which it was said: “On whatever day you eat, you shall die” (Gen. 1)—not because they died on that day, but because they received the irreversible [Col. 0500D] necessity of dying.

For how could both “the body is dead” and “man is living” be true—the former from the Apostle, the latter from the Psalmist—unless Augustine’s judgment joined both under a meaning as subtle as it is useful? Why, then, all that insistent constancy—or constant insistence—of words by which you strive to overthrow your friend? For you say: “What is a body living from vanity? ‘The body,’ says the Apostle, ‘is dead because of sin’ (Rom. 8). Therefore, what the Apostle calls dead because of sin, do you call living from vanity? Is not vanity sin? Does what is understood in a simple sense produce both death and life? God hates those who observe [Col. 0501A] vanity; God’s love makes alive, hatred makes dead. Therefore nothing lives from vanity?”

See yourselves what conclusion you have drawn. But whether these arguments have been somewhat attacked—indeed, I might say overthrown—I leave to your own judgment.

You add: “You say again: ‘alive,’ that is, the soul, from simplicity; ‘life,’ that is, God, from unity. I am not offended by these points with such violent spirit, but neither do I wholly assent. For the soul is judged to be subject more to unity than to simplicity. For every thing simply simple is one thing and one; but what is one is not immediately simple. For if anything is simple, it rejects and utterly avoids every mixture and partnership. But a thing that is one sometimes, by receiving two or more things agreeing together within itself, becomes one,” and then, a little later: “What does it mean, then, to say that God is from unity or simplicity, except ‘God from God’: Father from Son, Son from Father, Holy Spirit from Father and Son? Or is anyone so foolish as to think that God is simple by participation in simplicity, good by participation in goodness, one by participation in unity? Goodness is in God, and God is goodness. Therefore God is no more from unity than from simplicity.”

So far your words. I have cut out the middle of the letter, gathering and selecting the passages to which a reply had to be made.

For my proceeding at greater length, not only the force of your arguments but also the value, such as it is, of my own proof compels me. For I cannot render word for word, because it is not the same task to construct a calumny as to demolish one. Nor is it the same thing to pluck thorns as to sow grain; and in both of these much greater labor must be expended than in the other. Someone may deny in a single word that the world is a sphere, though Aristotle could not establish it in a single word. What then will you say, since you are not so offended, yet do not wholly agree, when I say “the living thing from simplicity, life from unity”? This is strange. I thank your grace, indeed, because you receive even part of your own words; yet in everything you depart from Claudianus, when I say “life from unity,” and no mind, however poor, understands this to mean that God is subject or superior to his own unity or goodness; or that unity belongs to him rather than being his essence; or that he is not himself his unity, but that unity is in him as in a subject. For God’s essence is not one thing and he himself another, because for him to be is to be a person. For that one unity is not something capable of being formed, or formed, or re-formed; rather, it is form—neither formless nor formed—an eternal and immutable substance unto itself.

But what you propose—“everything which is simply simple is both one [unum] and a unity [una]”—either I do not understand, as I rather think, or you attend less closely, which I do not believe. For no thing is simply simple except that one and supreme reality—if indeed it is a thing, and not the cause of all things; if indeed also a cause, since a name which can fittingly be applied to that singular excellence is not easily found. For a body is composite, as is obvious even to one of little understanding. The soul, in comparison with the body, is simple, but in itself by no means so. [Note: Origen, Homily 11 on the Song of Songs, writes that the soul ought to inquire whether there are spirits of the same substance as itself, while others are not different; but in Book 11 of *On First Principles* (περὶ ἀρχῶν, *On Principles*) he holds them to have extremely subtle bodies. Likewise St Augustine in many places; Lactantius, Hilary, Basil, and also St Bernard, Sermon 5 on the Song of Songs, and others cited by Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca sancta*, vol. II, annotation 8. But the general Lateran Council—leaving aside most ancient theologians—held in 1215, and reported in the chapter *Firmiter* “On the Supreme Trinity,” defined them to be incorporeal. Yet Luke 8 makes clear that in one and the same man there was a legion of demons, that is, six thousand, as Vegetius, Book II of *On Military Affairs*, chapter 11, calculates; and if they had bodies, they could not have been in the same man without interpenetration. Not to mention Christ saying to the disciples: “A spirit does not have flesh and bones.”]

For it has a variety of thoughts and changeability of affections. But nothing changeable is simple. Perhaps even the supercelestial spirits lack these; yet they are not simple, because one thing is that by which they are, another what they are, and yet another that by which, through participating in simplicity, grace has restored them to blessedness—not nature.

If, therefore, neither a bodily nor an incorporeal thing is simple—so that I may not bring arguments into collision with each other—consider what you had said: “Everything which is simply simple is both one and a unity,” when no such thing exists. But when you continue that a simple thing flees and rejects every mixture and association, whereas one thing sometimes receives and transforms within itself two or more things coming together, so that they may be one: I think this falls into the opposite error. For things called simple in a certain manner receive association or mixture; but what is one is free and exempt from all of these. Souls, indeed—would that not with so great a mixture—are joined to bodies; and angels either have natural bodies, or assume bodies from the air, or in the air when they are sent. I say this because the Fathers seem to have left the matter uncertain. Do not now set against me the incarnation of the Son of God, because its rationale is different—if it is a rationale rather than a condescension—and it belongs neither to this time nor to this work to introduce it into the discussion. For things probable according to reason are necessary from reason; things contrary to reason are incredible; things above reason are marvels, which may not be scrutinized but only wondered at.

But nothing is truly one except what is essentially and immutably one: uncreated, unchangeable, without limit; what is not cut off from “was,” nor erased from “will be”; to whom alone and invincibly remains “IS”: “with whom there is no change or shadow due to variation” (James 1), and to whom it is truly said: “There is no other besides thee” (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 2:2). I assigned unity to God particularly because of that most special likeness of numbers, which surpasses all likenesses. For although every countable thing is counted by numbers, the numbers themselves cannot be counted. Who, I do not say can express, but can even worthily conceive, how number, though it is from one, through one, and in one, can nevertheless have neither beginning nor end?

Yet we may say that one is the beginning of a unit; of the one itself—which you show to be a beginning—behold, you have the beginning of number without a beginning, so that number is from it. Now if you wish to count, you add one to one, making two; and one to two, making three; and one to three, making four. Thereafter, as often as you multiply one, so often the many individual units are named in their total: ten times, “ten”; twenty times, “twenty”; a hundred times, “a hundred”; a thousand times, “a thousand.” Thus you may recognize that every number, just as it exists through one, also proceeds from one.

This is most plainly evident concerning the end of number: no one can arrive at it at all, because beyond every number—which is from one, through one, and in one—there is always one. Yet in divine things these three—“from one,” “through one,” and “in one”—are equally eternal, equally coeternal, equally beyond place, wholly everywhere, always equal in the same infinity, because no true one is greater or lesser than another one. These are the beginnings, conductors, and limiters of numbers, themselves neither begun, nor numbered, nor ended, I believe, because “there is no number of the wisdom of God” (Psalm 146 [147]). For since number is from one, through one, and in one, and can be numbered only in a threefold way—so that by the same number we begin numbers and end them—it is itself wholly ternary, through which every number exists, and in which one Trinity and threefold Unity reign indivisibly.

Consider, therefore, whether a like likeness can be found; and if you do not find one, do not infer that God is more properly from simplicity than from unity. Yet that profoundly subtle argument of Plato, drawn from the innermost disciplines of philosophy, has not escaped me: it assigns the μονάδα (*monada*, “unity”) to the soul, and the δυάδα (*dyada*, “duality”) to the body, through the clearest numerical examples. For he says: “Multiply one by three, and there are three; multiply three by three, and there are nine. Multiply nine by three, and there are twenty-seven. Multiply twenty-seven by three, and there are eighty-one.”

Behold, in the fourth stage the original unity appears. The same will occur if you carry the multiplication to infinity: unity will always stand out in the fourth stage. Most rightly, moreover, the essence of the soul is expressed through unity, since it too is incorporeal. The ternary likewise, because of the indissoluble bond of its middle unity, is appropriately referred to the soul; just as the quaternary, because it has two middle terms and is therefore indissoluble, properly belongs to the body.

The first progression of the soul is that by which it extends itself from its simple essence, represented by the monad, into a functional ternary: there it desires one thing through desire, despises another through anger, and distinguishes between the two through reason. And it rightly flows from monad into triad, because every essence is naturally prior to its power. Again, the fact that the same thing is found three times in the multiplying ternary signifies that the soul exists not in parts but wholly in each of its powers. For we cannot call reason alone, anger alone, or desire alone a third part of the soul; since in substance reason is neither other than nor less than soul; anger is neither other than nor less than soul. Rather, one and the same substance receives different names according to its different powers.

Then, in a second progression, it descends from the functional ternary to govern the harmony of the human body, which is represented by nine, because there are nine openings in the human body through which, according to natural balance, everything flows in and out by which that body is nourished and governed. Here too there is order: for the soul naturally has its powers before it is joined to the body; but afterward, in the third progression, already poured out beyond itself through the senses, it is scattered through innumerable actions in administering visible things, represented by twenty-seven, a solid number extended in three dimensions after the likeness of the body.

In the fourth progression, however, released from the body, it returns to its own unity, which descends from that true Unity. Therefore, in the fourth multiplication, when three times twenty-seven has increased into eighty-one, the monad appears at the top, so that it may be clearly evident that, after the end of this life, signified by eighty, the soul returns to the simple unity of its own substance, from which it had first departed when it descended to govern the human body. Nor did this escape our philosopher, David, who fixed the limit of human life at eighty years. [Note: Rather, it did not escape St Moses, who, as St Jerome testifies in Letter 140 to the presbyter Cyprian, wrote, besides the Pentateuch, eleven psalms, from the eighty-ninth through the ninety-ninth. But whereas Psalm 98 bears in most manuscripts the title “A Psalm of David,” the Hebrew Psalter, lacking this superscription, proclaims that it is not his; for Scripture observes the custom that all psalms devoid of an author’s name are assigned to those whose names appeared in preceding psalms.]

“If [they are] in health: eighty years; and beyond them, their labor and pain.” He also assigns to the body its quaternary, just as the μονάς (*monas*, “unity”), he says, belongs to the soul, so the δυάς (*dyas*, “duality”) suits the body. Say two times two: four result; two times four: eight; two times eight: sixteen; two times sixteen: thirty-two. Here in the fourth place, similarly, the same number, two—the binary—from which multiplication began, will meet you. And if you proceed to infinity, it will undoubtedly happen that the binary always stands out in the fourth stage. This is the body’s quaternary, in which we are given to understand that everything receiving its composition from dissoluble elements is itself dissoluble.

I have set down these assertions of so great a philosopher in order that you may recognize that primitive, true unity which exists in the primordial rationale of things: not some derivative unity, nor even that which is called the seal of likeness, in which the first derivation of unity declines. But as for your being stung and pierced by my statement [Note: After the middle of the preceding letter.] that the Son is intermediate between the Father and the Spirit: you would not have been so vehemently disturbed if you had read the words that follow. For the meaning plainly offers itself to readers: I called him intermediate between Father and Spirit with respect to the difference of the names, not with respect to the undivided substance, in which no degrees, times, or distinctions can be conceived.

For we are accustomed to say, “Father, and Son, and Holy Spirit”; and so I adapted to this interpretation the verse of the Psalm: “May God bless us—our God; may God bless us” (Psalm 66 [67]). There, where “our” is added, it signifies the person of the Son, who is ours because, in his own proper person, he assumed the poverty of our flesh. But now, sweetest of friends, my friend wanders too far afield; and while he leaves a monk nothing subject to his own control, he himself does wrong.

Yet who am I, that I have dared to answer so great a name—or man? Surely I am his own, and especially his own; and he himself, my friend, is not merely half but the better part of my soul. For nothing is separated from the other, nothing belongs exclusively to the other. He who loves me as his own soul will rightly guide my inexperience; and with him I preferred to risk embarrassment rather than friendship. But you, my beloved, seal this letter for yourself and for your Thomas alone, and do not bring me into public, I who have professed secrecy and am worthy of hiding and of every solitude forever and unto ages of ages. For this reason I wrote these things in my own hand, though exhausted by severe dizziness of the head; nor did I admit even the closest of my intimates, lest perhaps I might turn youthful and ardent minds toward curiosity or suspicion. Far be it from me to pour out even myself thus to anyone other than you—to you, I say, alone, to whom I owe whatever I am and whatever I can do in Christ Jesus our Lord.

## LETTER LXVI. TO NICHOLAS, MONK OF CLAIRVAUX

### [IV, 1.] His own to his own.

Our shared charity urges that this letter banish envy, that most destructive weapon against the best things. For what you wrote to me was more than sufficiently sweet, useful, and honorable. What is sweeter than love? What more useful than a subtle and concise account of divine and human things? These, beyond doubt, comprise the beginnings, middle, and end of your letter. What is more honorable than salutary instruction in morals? By these you awakened our sluggish mind, gave us for a little while occasion not to be occupied with worldly matters, and unfurled the sails of untroubled leisure. Thus your writings, sweetest friend, water, intoxicate, and calm my soul. By their abundance against barrenness, their free repose against tumult, and their withdrawal to remoter places against the insolence of occupations, I declare that this is accomplished by the writing of my Nicholas.

Thus, with spirit failing, hand trembling, and intellect resisting, I undertake greater things, attempt more difficult ones, and seize things scarcely explicable. For when a vehement spirit, gathered from the four winds, presses from both sides, what tenderness of flower does not fade in the strength of that hope? What beauty does not fail? What greenness does not wither? It is perilous to confront an angry lion; no less foolish not to avoid an arrow once shot. Every armor of the mighty serves in your camp. Therefore I fear to engage. For though you could have triumphed sufficiently with your own armor, you have borrowed the arms even of the strongest men in order to conquer more completely. The mere gleam of golden shields casts me down.

Yet I cry: “Set aside what is not your own!” For it will matter greatly whether you can overthrow our camp by the irresistible majesty of philosophers’ authority or by the clarity of your own arguments and opinions. It will at once become clear whether victory should be attributed to you or to them: I willingly fall before their footsteps without testing the contest, but against you I shall bear arms—arms, however, of peace. For if the unassailable subtleties of philosophers are false, when only the power of our own intellects is in question, what does it concern us? I yield entirely to their authority. But what has proceeded from your lips will not so escape the pupil of my eye. Friendship would rightly complain that it was deprived of its due unless the affairs of friends were weighed on an even balance.

Having therefore run through and examined the words and thoughts of your blooming eloquence, repeatedly turning over yours and eagerly wishing to unfold my own, I fear to be seen in the light. What then? Shall I attempt the risk? But not in *filia* [reading uncertain: perhaps *fidelia*, “faithful things,” or *inutilia*, “useless things”]. Shall I speak? But would that it may not be emptiness! Shall I criticize? Yet only the excesses of a friend. Shall I praise? Yet it will be the talents of philosophers. Still I shall not proceed from here unless, with hands joined, we first make a pact that you will not be angry at any insult whatever.

Entering, then, I shall undertake not to overthrow the dwelling places of truth, but, if there is any, to challenge my friend’s own calumny concerning the foregoing differences of words, and to refute it with such arguments from authorities as I can. Yet I see at the threshold and opening of your letter something whose excessive beauty so draws the curiosity of my eyes that I can scarcely draw them away and detach them. There is something whose name is above every name, whose form is more beautiful than every form, whose stature and height extend from the end of the highest heaven to the end of the lowest hell. It is an image begotten, not made, in an inimitable manner. There is one who conceived and brought it forth from his heart—not its maker, but the maker of all things; yet this image’s Father.

To be conformed to it is to be re-formed. I found it speaking and expressing itself, resplendent in fitting colors, governing all things with an imperial scepter, joining heavenly beings with earthly ones in its arms; I adored it and held it fast. Its beauty is beyond estimation, its sweetness insatiable, its brightness inaccessible. It is as delightful to speak of it as it is wondrous to embrace it. Whoever approaches it scarcely, or never, departs. “The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear with hearing. Those who eat shall still hunger,” etc. (Ecclesiasticus 24). “It kissed me with the kiss of its mouth” (Song of Songs 1). Holding my soul by the finger of its hand, it spoke in its own voice lest I turn aside from it.

Drawn and delighted by such blandishments, I hesitate whether I ought to proceed further. For it is good to be here. At last, however, while it signaled and assented that I should go—not departing, but returning while remaining—I saw another vision. A burning bush appeared in the depths of the desert. Suspended in attentive thought, I said: “Is it as Moses’ bush burned and was not consumed, so this friend of mine gives a shining brightness but not burning heat?” For a friend’s rebuke is a welcome correction rather than a painful scorching. And indeed, you are a hunter both of words and of meanings, and you believed me caught in nets and struck by a hunting spear. For this bush brings blushes, but [also] the strength of perfect and solid charity to one who does not understand [the reading is uncertain]. The eye of a child would be pricked, even pierced, if a thorn of this kind were driven into it. But may this never happen to the eye of charity, whose sole work is to gather—or rather, produce—a rose from thorns. Thus Jesus brought forth the rose of redemption from the thorn of passion. Do you not also, in imitation of him, return good for evil, soft things for hard, sweet things for bitter, and true things for vain? Truly, you are simple and dwelling at home, as you say; you wrote in the simplicity of your heart.

I observe, therefore, that by the wondrous aid of wings you have flown to the throne of grace, and there, because you found it nowhere below, have learned that God is simply simple. I ask, then, whether you brought your simplicity back from that fountain, and whether in passing through you have drawn out as much as heavenly dwellers do by remaining and standing there. If this was impossible, it is evident that theirs immeasurably surpasses yours in simplicity, as also in blessedness, without injury to you. I believe and confess with undoubting faith that the human soul is naturally simple, and that the angelic nature is also simply simple. That this may be clearer, I wish briefly to collect before our eyes our view of simplicity and yours.

I said that everything simply simple is both a unity and one. But if it is a unity, it is not therefore immediately simple. For what is simple wholly rejects and flees every mixture. But two or more things coming together sometimes make one thing, as one body consisting of four elements. “These things,” you say, “either I do not understand, or you attend less closely.” I prefer to attend less closely than for you not to understand. Yet give attention for a little while; and if I have thought wrongly concerning simplicity, correct me again, since you have begun. Meanwhile, as is fitting, while displaying reverence for your sealed judgments and words, I shall fortify my own judgments—if not the words—with the more powerful rampart of common truth.

Everything that exists, then, is either simple or composite. A composite is either substantial or partial: substantial when one substance is joined to another substance; partial when the parts of one substance are joined together. This latter composite is simpler than the former. But that is said to be wholly and naturally simple which lacks both substantial and partial composition. The soul, therefore, because it receives in itself neither the joining of diverse substances nor of diverse parts of the same substance, is naturally simple. For it was not created from any pre-existing matter, so that it could be called composite in relation to its matter, as in every body that which is made is said to be simple in relation to that from which it is made. Rather, it is catholic belief that it was made from nothing.

But the angelic nature has this further excellence: being subject to no corruptions, it flies forth more freely than the soul, which is joined to the body, into the most hidden recesses of simplicity. In this too almost all philosophers agree: that the principle of things is perfect wisdom, radiant light, the substance of substances, the argument of all things. It is one and simple; its simplicity bestows rather than takes away simplicity. For it did not begrudge its creature its own simplicity, to which it did not deny its own image. Therefore, with that one located beyond place in the citadel of true and highest simplicity, the rational creature participates in it. Things become more or less simple as they participate in it more or less.

Therefore the simple one—or rather the simplicity of simple things, as God is the God of gods—commands that he be sought in simplicity, when he says that he walks with the simple. He grants that he be found and possessed if he is sought as he commands us to seek him. To those who seek otherwise he says, “You shall seek me and shall not find me” (John 7). Therefore, since he is not found except in simplicity, and since one who possesses simplicity is undoubtedly made simple, whoever finds him through simplicity is made simpler by participation in that same simplicity. Those who participate in unequal measure are found to be unequal in simplicity. Simplicity itself, however, is in itself true and supreme unity.

It must be understood that, just as the participant is one thing and what is participated another, so also the simple thing is one thing and simplicity another. Human language and reason—and I do not know whether even angelic language and reason—cannot make “simple” and “simplicity” the same, any more than “white” and “whiteness.” Do not, do not join laughter to our simplicity—or rather, to your own. For you have nothing to object concerning God, since whatever he is, he is said to transcend every understanding. Yet when he is called good, merciful, just, or simple, this is understood figuratively. For, as Plato says, to find God is difficult; once found, to speak of him worthily is impossible. No speech, nor any part of speech, can describe or define God. Let, therefore, no objection be made concerning God, who himself is the conclusion of all things and likewise their exclusion.

From his stable simplicity, as Boethius testifies, the generation of all things, the entire course of mutable natures, and everything that moves in any way derives order, causes, and forms. His nature, composed in the citadel of its simplicity, established the manifold mode of governing. Therefore he himself should more properly be called goodness, and the creature good by participation in his goodness; he himself piety, and the creature pious by sharing in piety; finally, he himself simplicity, and the creature simple by possessing simplicity. This is the same kind of expression by which God is called just and we are called the justice of God.

See also whether Boethius uses a fine comparison to express not merely that someone becomes simple, but even becomes simplicity through the closest possible union and fellowship with simplicity. Concerning providence and fate he says:

> “Providence is that divine reason itself, established in the supreme ruler of all things, which disposes all things. Fate, however, is the disposition inherent in mutable things, through which Providence binds each thing in its own orders.”

And shortly afterward:

> “It is evident that Providence is the immovable and simple form of things to be done; but fate is the moving nexus and temporal order of the things which divine simplicity has disposed to be done.”

Having introduced a comparison, he adds shortly afterward:

> “For just as, among spheres turning about the same axis, the one nearest to the middle approaches the simplicity of the center and is, as it were, itself an axis about which the outer ones turn; while the outermost, moved in a wider circuit, is spread out over ampler spaces insofar as it departs from the undivided middle point—if anything joins and associates itself with that middle, it is drawn into simplicity and ceases to be diffused and dispersed. In like manner, what departs farther from the first mind is entangled in greater bonds of fate.”

The “middle,” or “the middle indivisibility of the point,” of which he speaks is understood to be the truth and simplicity of God. Whatever is joined to this love is drawn into simplicity. Why, then, should the divine and heavenly substances, to which belong penetrating judgment, incorruptible will, and an effective power ready to accomplish what is desired, not cleave to that supreme and sole simplicity? Without doubt they cleave to it and are endowed with a fuller privilege of simplicity. Do you refuse to believe this and prepare to contradict it? “Not at all,” you say, “but I do not wish to attribute to the creature what belongs to the Creator.” Why? Because you are jealous for God—but not with a good jealousy. For just as he is greatly foolish who presumes to seize by personal usurpation gifts not bestowed by God, so he likewise falls away from piety who denies or conceals gifts that have been given. “We,” says the Apostle, “have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we may know the things given to us by God” (1 Corinthians 11).

For every body has been given, as has already been said, to be composite by composition; to the soul, to be naturally simple because it lacks parts, though, because of its association with clay, it is subject to vanity, which is manifold. To the supercelestial creature likewise it has been granted to be, beyond human understanding but below the divine, both naturally and simply simple. But you, while maintaining that the body is composite and that the soul is simple only in comparison with the body, not in itself, fly up to the supercelestial beings and grant them only an imitation of simplicity by grace, not by nature. O excessively simple man! Perhaps your angel, hearing this, is angry and indignant that you have confused the gifts of its grace and nature. For it gives no less thanks to the Creator for the gifts of nature than to the giver of grace. It knows itself created by grace, made blessed by grace, and confirmed by grace. Yet it remembers that it received one thing from that same grace in creation and another in beatification or confirmation. What it received in creation are gifts of nature; what it merited in confirmation are called gifts of grace.

Therefore the angelic nature is either composite, which belongs only to body, or simple, which belongs only to spirit. Since there is no third possibility, as I think, you must concede this.
