Since, therefore, its nature is simple, and since, as has been shown, the ray of the highest simplicity is more closely expressed and impressed upon it through proximity to that highest simplicity, it is not merely simple but, I think, simply simple. For it stands in service and cleaves to divine simplicity. Divine simplicity itself, however, is not merely naturally simple, nor merely simply simple, but uniquely and ineffably simple. I believe I have now adequately explained why I said, or could say, “everything simply simple.”

What follows, “a unity and one,” is a reiteration of words. Yet, to distinguish it however slightly: it is a unity because, as Seneca testifies, divine things have one nature, and nothing is more divine than the divine nor more heavenly than the heavenly; and, according to Boethius, their substance is the same when their effect is not different. It is one because the indissoluble nature of simple things does not admit a plurality of diverse parts for its constitution. Whatever is composed of diverse parts is naturally dissoluble. But every simple and uncompounded thing is one and lacks parts subject to dissolution.

Therefore any substance so simply one is not mixed at all, either with another simple and incorporeal substance or with a composite and corporeal one. For wherever and whenever substances are mixed, they must be changed and transformed into one another. For the conjunction of any things, unless they are poured into one another and transformed from their own form, is properly called a coupling, attachment, or something of this kind—not mixture or commingling.

Thus, because of the assumption of flesh and the inseparable union, the Word is said to have become flesh; but lest heretics should maintain that there had occurred a commingling—a transfusion of substances, namely the annihilation of flesh into divinity or a substantial emptying of divinity into flesh—it is said that he underwent no commingling. And lest, again, one Son of God and another Son of man should be believed in, and the one person divided into two persons, it immediately follows: nor division. If you think I am inventing novel and therefore empty things, you will immediately prove them true and ancient by the reasons which follow, if you please.

Boethius says: “Not every thing can be changed and transformed into every thing. For, since some substances are corporeal and others incorporeal, neither can the corporeal be changed into the incorporeal, nor the incorporeal into that which is body. Nor do incorporeal things change their proper forms into one another. For only those things can be changed and transformed into one another which have a common underlying subject of one matter. Nor all such things, but those which can act upon and be acted upon by one another.”

And this is proved as follows. Bronze cannot be changed into stone, nor can that same bronze become grass; nor can any body whatsoever be transfigured into any other body unless both the things that pass into one another have the same matter and can act upon and be acted upon by each other, as when wine and water are mixed. For both are of such a kind that they communicate action and passion to each other. A quality of water can undergo some effect from the quality of wine. Accordingly, if there is much water and very little wine, they are not said to be mixed; rather, the one is corrupted by the quality of the other. If someone pours wine into the sea, the wine is not mixed with the sea but corrupted in the sea, because the quality of the water, by reason of the vastness of its body, suffers nothing from the quality of the wine, but instead changes the quality of the wine into itself by its own abundance.

But if there are moderate and equal, or slightly unequal, natures which can act upon and be acted upon by one another, they are mixed and tempered with intermediate qualities between themselves. This, however, applies to bodies—not all bodies, but only those which, as stated, can act upon and be acted upon by one another and have one common, identical underlying matter. Every body which exists in generation and corruption seems to have common matter; but not every body can either act upon or be acted upon by every other, or in every respect.

But corporeal and incorporeal things cannot by any rationale be transformed into each other, because they share no common underlying matter by which, on receiving qualities, they may be changed into one another. For every nature of incorporeal substance rests upon no foundation of matter. But there is no body without underlying matter. Since this is so, and since not even things which naturally possess common matter pass into each other unless they have the power to act upon and be acted upon by one another, much less are things changed into one another when they not only lack common matter, but one rests on a material foundation, as body does, while the other requires no underlying matter at all, as the incorporeal does.

Therefore it cannot happen that a body is changed into an incorporeal form; nor can incorporeal things be changed into one another by any commingling. Things which have no common matter cannot be turned and transformed into one another. But incorporeal things have no matter. Therefore they cannot be mixed with or changed into one another. A simple thing, then, rightly rejects every commingling, because it admits no change into any creature.

Likewise, what we have set forth is taken from ourselves: “But one thing sometimes receives within itself two or more things coming together and transforms them so that they may be one.” In the copy which I wrote with my own hands, it reads thus: “But two or more things coming together sometimes make one thing, as one body consisting of four elements.”

I detect here no room whatsoever for any cavilling, and therefore refrain from answering. You also write that I maintained that God is more properly characterized by simplicity than by unity. I am astonished at the slander. Did I not immediately add that nothing is properly said of God? Now, since, my dearest one, sweetness of my inmost heart, light of my friends [Col. 0512B], I have defended myself, I find some propositions in your letter that need correction by a fitting rebuke and elucidation by the file of correction, while others call for reflection. What say you, love? Does what I say please you? Am I pursuing your favor? Command whatever you wish, and I shall do it. Keep the key of my mouth, lest injury to a friend burst forth. Constrict the jaws of my mouth, lest the Sirens’ jests flow out. Yet open my lips sometimes, that I may discharge my burdens. For your—indeed our—Nicholas gives superfluous thanks to what he calls my favor, because, he says, “you accept our words at least in part, but in everything depart from Claudianus.” [Note: [Col. 0511D] “From Claudianus”: Mamertus Claudianus, priest of Vienne, whose words Nicholas had brought forward from Book III of *On the State of the Soul* to refute the man of Celles.] Judge, judge my case, love, justly. For what is this? The threads, as it were, of nerves and veins are almost bursting from the stretching tension of excessive swelling. Understanding, reason, and memory protest, swear, and call to witness that false testimony has been brought against them. I can scarcely persuade myself to be patient. “He is a witty friend,” you will say, “cultivated in the graceful speech of jokes.” Allow him, then, both to weave with his arguments an inextricable labyrinth of disputation, now entering by the way through which he exits, now exiting by the way through which he enters; unravel what he has tangled, retangle what he has badly untangled. O sweetest friend! Were you asleep when you read our letter? Perhaps you were occupied, and therefore are not to blame. Yet in this you are inexcusably at fault: excessively lavish with your favors, you squander them by bestowing them badly. For where did you discover those favors of mine for which you thank me so ungratefully? But why am I surprised that, with marvellous [Col. 0512D] and unheard-of novelty, you assert that a favor which is not a favor is a favor, when you have already begun, by your former authority, to have power to alter and exchange the proper meanings of things and words? What can Nicholas not do—[Note: [Col. 0511D] Nicholas: from black, for example, made white. From a Cluniac monk he became a Cistercian. Nicholas himself, in Letter 18 to Theobald, once his companion in the same counsel: “Finally, by one consent we left everything and flew from the Old Testament and the shadow of the Cluniacs to the purity of the Cistercians.”]—who has been made white from black? I believe that, guided and instructed by this authority, you also presume sometimes to invert words and the senses of words. Yet you dreamed of your former blackness when you observed that I dissent from Claudianus [Col. 0513A]. Certainly, I assented and do assent to your words; in one point you contradicted, and I contradict. For where have I denied that the body lives, that the soul is living, that God is life? Nowhere—believe me, nowhere. I merely undertook to criticize the assignments of properties which you added: namely, “living” from vanity, “alive” from simplicity, “life” from unity. But I hear that monk who, together with his friend, was arguing and keeping silent at the beginning of your letter, now, out of weariness, uttering these words: “It would have been more useful, love, to have kept the barriers of our mouths shut than, by replying, to have encountered so many assaults of overflowing torrents. For torrents of vanity overflow, and words of superfluous babbling drip from the mouth of our friend; he flows everywhere and overflows altogether. He confounds our silence; [Col. 0513B] he disturbs and shakes the custom and order of our manner of life; through his importunity he provokes and draws us, if we yield, toward every pompous and superfluous thing. Therefore, write no more.”

## LETTER LXVII. TO JOHN OF SALISBURY

[IV, 4] His own, always his own, to his own.

A star sometimes appears to fall from heaven to the depths—but only to the eyes of the foolish. Yet, fastened by the bonds of nature and the divine nail of command, it clings so fixedly to heaven for ever that the same heaven will first be rolled up like a scroll before the star is torn from it. Thus, thus, my dearest friend: since God impressed in the firmament of our hearts the star of mutual love, although the sudden flashing of unstable fortune deceived the eye ignorant of the laws of friendship [Col. 0513C], the little fire of that star neither yielded nor departed. Thus even then, when I seemed to wound, I did not merely seem, but truly loved; and when I turned away my eye, I did not turn away my heart. Thanks be to God, because, renewed again in its full moon, as though its strength had returned, it has sent forth its former rays more brightly than usual, as if in resentment of its earlier waning, with affection enlarged. Henceforth may there be far from us alike the dark interruption of night and the cloudy gloom of day. But enough of this.

Since weapons strike less severely when foreseen, I direct and warn you to beware of wicked lips and a deceitful tongue. For among us certain things have been spread concerning you, by which, perhaps, unless you set against them the shield of prudent foresight, you may be harmed at court. Certain eminent men [Col. 0513D], as I myself heard, whispered to someone at our court that you had said dishonorable things about the court and had acted as the false legate of the lord pope in these regions. I do not know whether these things are more false than malicious, or the reverse. You are wise; be wise for yourself in these matters. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVIII. TO THE SAME

[IV, 5] His own—[Note: [Col. 0513D] “His own”: to John of Salisbury, to whom the next seven letters, and many others elsewhere, are also addressed. For he had a close and longstanding connection with Peter of Celles, by whom, when formerly exiled from his monastery, he was received and treated kindly, and afterward enriched with many favors. John professes himself indebted for these in various letters to him, especially Letter 85.]—always and uniquely his own.

[Col. 0514A] Behold: mourning and grieving in the ashes of blessed Aigulf together with blessed Job, ought I to strive after polished splendors of speech and choice torches? Rather, in keeping with the agitation of my heart, I present my afflicted mind in mournful, so to speak, and smoky language. My dearest friend, I run to and fro like a wanderer and an exile, if perhaps I may gather together ashes scattered by the four winds of heaven. This is why I wish to reap, even where I have not sown, not ashes but precious crops—namely, from England. I charge blessed Aigulf to reap the sheaves of alms of that people. What concern is it of mine to extend a sickle where I have never been able either to plough or to sow? Yet what I propose to do is not altogether absurd: for, though I did not cultivate that land, when you were with me, when I lived with you, when I loved you, when I deserved to keep you, I did for a time sow you—as a bed of spices [Col. 0514B]—with good fragrances.

O good God, how happily has this good threshing-floor flourished—or rather, this most fruitful olive tree! How it has sprouted upward and sent its root downward! How it has extended its branches! How the hungry are now, now being filled with the fruit of its shoots! I tasted and saw that its richness is good and its fruit sweet to my throat. It has not become the bitterness of a foreign vine. Now I sit in its shade, which I had desired; now its shelters suffice to defend me from heat, whirlwind, and rain. Blessed be that day; may the hour never pass away with the passing of time, in which I made John mine, in which I gained among the children of men so great and such a friend. To you, O God, guardian of my soul, I commend him. Give him life, give him a good life, give him prosperity; always preserve him in your arms and under the shadow of your wings. For what better thing can be wished for a friend? Thus I seek nothing else either for myself or for my friends, as these ashes which I now behold remind me. A little while ago there were ceilings, [Note: [Col. 0514D] “A little while ago, ceilings”: those of the church of St. Aigulf at Provins, which had burned down, as stated in Letter 16.] beams, doorposts, and stout timbers; now there is the finest dust and the cheapest ash. O world, or worldly things, what are you? Or rather, how vainly you deceive us! Certainly you are not what you seem to be. Certainly some beauty, sweetness, and usefulness appear to be in you; but when truth is sought, neither beauty nor sweetness nor usefulness is truly in you. True, true is the judgment concerning you [Col. 0514D]: since vanity is in you, you make vain the heart that you may possess. But enough of this.

To come to the matter: know, friend, that we are sending the precious martyr Aigulf, in no mean vessel, to travel abroad in his poverty. I place him from my hand into your hand. Whatever you wish, whatever you arrange concerning the messengers, I approve. In these matters I assign to your friendship general administration and care.

## LETTER LXIX. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0515A]

[IV, 6] Brother PETER to Master JOHN.

Your lips are a dripping honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue. When I saw your letter, my heart was filled with joy and my mouth with laughter. For you mingled jokes with serious matters, but with moderation and without damage to dignity and modesty. Your wit has no bite; your jokes no baseness. Your speech runs like one that at times touches the clouds with its head and at other times lowers its face to the ground. This has found favor in my eyes; it shall remain with me and stay with me all night. For your voice is sweet in my ears, and your counsels very delightful to my palate.

Yet a contrary wind often rises; companies of rainstorms shake [Col. 0515B] the house; and grub, locust, caterpillar, and rust attempt to devastate the beds of my little garden. But the Angel of Great Counsel rises from the ship and makes the winds calm, the storms clear, and the useless worms disappear. For if God is for us, who is against us? Certainly there are dangers of death; in the wilderness there are deadly poisons of serpents; there are indeed bitter waters. Yet the bronze serpent, the rod of Moses, the pillar of cloud by day and fire by night, turn bitterness into sweetness, snatch from death, and deliver from the bite. We are as having nothing and yet possessing all things, as dying—and behold, we live. This is my consolation in the place of my pilgrimage: that we brought nothing into this world, nor indeed can we take anything away, because the birds of heaven neither sow nor reap, and yet the heavenly Father feeds them. With my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I return with two companies. Finally, since the road is short and the place to which we are heading is near, why do we put so many burdens on weak shoulders? Why do we carry so much in vain? Certainly, if the Lord God is with me in this life through which I walk, bread to eat and clothing to wear will not fail me. Nature will be content with these few things.

But you, a great part of my delights—in you are my riches; you are the golden pillow for my head. Would that, through Christ, the same closeness of bodies might always exist as that of souls! I do not want you to be lazy, unable to put your hand to your mouth—that is, unable to do the good [Col. 0515D] which you teach. For a self-indulgent and wicked instructor is he who does not teach himself in that which he teaches another.

## LETTER LXX. TO THE SAME

[IV, 7] To his master J. of Salisbury, his own abbot of Celles, whatever is better in the present life or the future.

Like a thirsty man beneath the heat, wearied beyond measure by long expectation of a desired drink, I lovingly receive the little vessel of your letter, eagerly read it again, repeatedly incline myself over it, and, as though by renewed tastes of a new flavor, drink it to the dregs in an abundance of sweetness. The affection of the reader is doubled—indeed, tripled—when the subject matter, through gratitude for a beloved heart and the pleasing elegance of style, produces the desired sequence of narration [Col. 0516A]. What you write is seasoned with philosophical thoughts, clothed in rhetorical colors, adorned with the most becoming ornaments of law, supported by evangelical columns, and, as concerns friends, most fittingly sweetened with a honeyed flavor. If I seek profit of thought, instruction, pleasure, arrangement of words, truth and sweetness of affection, I find all these things abundantly in your letters. There is a ship for sailing, a garden of delights for walking, a full and prepared table for feasting, a flowery bed for resting, and a gymnasium for philosophy.

There is no idol of falsehood, no enticement of deception, no deep whirlpool of flattery; no promising word spills wantonly from a scanty vein of the heart, like those who say [Col. 0516B] and do not do. But what? Love, broad in the heart and sparing in the mouth, burns in smoke and runs without foam; it moves its wings, but silently; it seeks low things, yet as sublimely as befits nobility of mind, and as firmly as integrity requires. It approaches, but does not burn. For it produces warmth, but not ash. It knows an end, certainly, but an end of completion, not of consumption. The love of which I speak in writing is such as I contemplate—or rather recognize—in a friend. Happy is my soul that has borne, or at least found, such a friend. Lord God of my heart, John was yours, and you gave him to me. Therefore I am yours—shall I call myself a friend? Would that I were even a servant: certainly a servant, yet one bought! For you redeemed me by giving your Son for me; indeed, you also bought me by giving me your servant. These are among the chief benefits which, though I now pass over them in silence, I neither pass by, deny, nor forget. For they too are sealed up in the treasuries of memory; I lay them to rest, to feast and to die together with them. Without them I can neither live nor wish to die.

I approach my John, whom I received from the hand of grace, as grace from grace, though not in return for grace. For grace found me empty of grace—indeed full, but full of fault and punishment. It has now begun to lessen the punishment and to annul the fault, when it substituted John as my friend: one to instruct the ignorant, help the laboring, correct the erring, stir the sluggish, cherish the exiled, and relieve the grieving. To whom do these gifts look? To you, Lord God, supremely and principally; to you, dearest friend, secondarily and in many ways [Col. 0516D]. For a time you lay hidden under the bushel of our humility: now a lamp burning indeed in conscience, though not yet so brightly shining in reputation. But the Lord has set you as a light to the nations, that you may be an eye to the blind, a foot to the lame, a tongue to the foolish, a hand to the maimed, an ear to the deaf; so that grace, in accordance with your name, may supply in the aforesaid what nature was less able to provide. Therefore, although my soul grieves at your absence, it will nevertheless be consoled in these things, knowing that public rights are to be preferred to private advantages. Thus you began. Add the tail in the sacrifices of your God. I wrote this beside the chapel of St. Aigulf, unwilling ever to be deprived of the opportunity afforded by your messenger to send something of our rusticity for rusticating. Tomorrow we shall place the most sacred body of your lord, blessed Aigulf, whose head and body we possess, in a most fitting tomb—namely, a new shrine [Col. 0517A]. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXI. TO THE SAME

[IV, 8] P., by God’s grace called abbot of the monastery of Celles, to John his friend: may he be consoled by the God of all consolation.

Brother, you ask me for writings of exhortation, giving little thought to the torrents of our occupations. You ask, I say, for consolation because you feel desolation; you request help because you bear exile; you implore a remedy because you weep over separation. Who, then, am I, that I can write to you something by which you may be sustained, strengthened, or consoled? I can scarcely pray for you [Col. 0517B]; I cannot plead for you at all. But the Son of oil, who was conceived of the Holy Spirit, whom God anointed above his fellows (Heb. I), whose name, Christ Jesus, is poured forth, came, as he himself says, to console the mourners of Zion. Would that, according to the multitude of your sorrows, his consolations might gladden your soul! “In their tribulation,” he says, “they will rise early to me” (Hosea VI). And you, Jesus—what of you? How long do you turn away your face? How long do you not bring your hand out of your bosom? How long do you set a cloud before us, so that our prayer cannot pass through to you? It is time to have mercy. Turn, look upon us, and be mercifully entreated. Give help out of tribulation; rescue from oppression; protect from temptation. To whom have the sons of men to make supplication but the Son of Man? Whom are they to entreat but the mediator between God and man? Whither are they to flee but to the scaffold of the cross? Here, here the turtledove places its young; the vulture takes courage; the dove gives forth groans. Here are the cluster of henna, the flower of the field, the scent of the lily, the rivers of paradise, the gate of heaven, the salvation of the world. Behold the harbor, where there is the draught of mixed wine, where there is the food of bread baked upon the wood of the cross and sealed by the Father. Where else is there such delight for the eyes, such melody for the ears? Here one must pitch camp; neither remain below nor proceed beyond. Here compose your character, lay down your sorrows, set upon it your loves. Nowhere else is there propitiation or a propitiator, nor cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy-seat. Have you forgotten that Abraham saw angels by the oak of Mamre; that beneath the apple tree the bridegroom raised the bride; [Col. 0517D] that Moses changed all the bitterness of waters into sweetness by contact with wood? Therefore oppose the shield of the cross to every affliction of the flesh, every assault of the ancient enemy, every contrivance of universal malice. Remember that the hand of the Lord which touched you is the same hand that created you. Does the clay say to its potter, “Why have you made me thus?” (Isa. XLV). Rather speak in the bitterness of your soul and say to God:

> “Most merciful Lord and Father of mercies, grant angelic rest to one placed amid human labor; grant entrance into the heavenly homeland to one cast out from the face of the earth; let divine consolation be present to one deprived of human consolation.”

This voice will fly even to him who sits upon the throne, unless impatience of pain or folly of heart delays it. Indeed, brother, pains have seized you amid straits. What wonder? Jesus says, “There is no sorrow like my sorrow” (Lam. I). Why? Because I have not sinned and endure the penalty of sin; because I have not robbed and am required to pay. Indeed, there is no sorrow like my sorrow, because a purchased servant disdains to suffer what his lord endures. Sons of men, how long will you be heavy-hearted? Was I not, though Lord, made a servant? Though impassible, made passible? Though immortal, made mortal? Why does hay refuse what heaven—or rather, the Lord of heaven—bears? Jesus passed out of this world, and will hay remain? Heaven too and earth will pass away, and will ash and dust abide? Therefore, brother, let the overflowing—or rather, cleansing—scourge console you.

[Col. 0518B] Let this, I say, be your consolation: that the hand of God which afflicts you does not spare you. Thus let your dross be smelted utterly away, so that your soul may never [uncertain: the source text is incomplete here]; from pure gold may a heavenly vessel be fashioned with a heavenly form. The son of the craftsman sits steadfastly, refining silver; and he makes one vessel for honor, another for dishonor. Do you wish to see a vessel for honor? Paul, the vessel of election, is caught up to the third heaven (2 Cor. XII). There, intoxicated by the abundance of God’s house, he cries: “O Lord, how splendid is your intoxicating cup!” Thus intoxicated, he yields neither to beatings, nor scourges, nor wounds, nor pains, nor deaths. This is Joseph’s cup, in which, being accustomed to divine, he declares to his people things past, present, and future. Did not John the Evangelist [Col. 0518C], returning from the wine-cellar, pour out for us wine clarified of its lees? “In the beginning was the Word,” he says, etc. (John I). Behold a vessel for honor.

The implements of the foolish shepherd, too, are vessels of dishonor, in which the flavor of wine will turn into the flavor of vinegar. These are blown from the king’s table because they are puffed up by knowledge of the flesh. These, I say, are inflated through pride, dried up through envy, burst through anger, broken through sloth, scattered through avarice, corrupted through gluttony, trampled through lust, and reduced to mud.

## LETTER LXXII. TO THE SAME

[IV, 9] His own abbot to his own cleric. [Note: [Col. 0517] “To his own cleric”: to the same John of Salisbury, whom he likewise calls his cleric in Letter 105.]

[Col. 0518D] Whether I ought to attribute the infrequency of your visits to you or to your occupations, I do not clearly discern. This one thing I observe: a greeting from your letters reaches us very rarely. Perhaps the waves of the sea cause this? But which letters have they swallowed? Show me that a letter of affection has perished, and I shall not accuse you of forgetfulness. Or have you no one to send? And whence this poverty, unless perhaps from abundance? Certainly many run before you, innumerable persons after you. You say to one, “Go,” and he goes; and to another, “Come,” and he comes (Matt. VIII). Do you not know where you should seek me? Plainly, I dwell in the midst of my people, not in the retreat of woods or in the chasm of the earth. Can you excuse yourself and say [Col. 0519A], “Lord, I have not seen Babylon and do not know the pool”? But here—here—you often sat, slept, and stayed with me; not to mention that at one time you loved it above many other places and lands. Anyone else, entangled and caught in these chains of words, would, once the rationale of his excuses had ceased, humbly seek mercy and implore patience.

But you, armed with the horn of legal or dialectical arguments, disdain these things as spiders’ threads and strive to find another way out. “I have a lord,” you say, “and other friends also, to whom I am drawn, whether to obey out of necessity or to provide for out of affection.” Very well. Did I not love you first and more than all? Did I not myself give the right hands of fellowship? Indeed, you have found more fruitful gains among others, but not faithfulness, not love. They may give more, but cannot love more. For I have shared with you not only my property but also my soul. My mouth has not been hidden from you—nor my counsel, nor indeed any secret however remote. And after this, my son, what more shall I do for you? Shall I add, if anything can be added to a soul? “What,” you ask, “do you seek?” A soul for a soul, an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth (Exod. XXI)—not to be torn out, but to be devoted; not to be extracted, but preserved.

Having been summoned before the lord pope concerning the cemetery of St. Serenus at Cantumerula—which the all-too-presumptuous pride of the canons and abbot is trying to diminish or take from us, contrary to the privilege of Pope Anastasius [Note: [Col. 0519D] Pope Anastasius: Anastasius IV, who occupied the see after Eugenius III in 1153. On this dispute over the cemetery he had already written in Letter 4.] which you yourself saw and partly drafted, contrary to our most ancient right—I have shortened the time-limit of Luke the Evangelist, which they had extended to the first Sunday of the Lord’s Advent [Col. 0519C]. This cause is yours: consider it as your own, or as concerning you. I shall not go, but shall send someone according to your counsel. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIII. TO THE SAME

[IV, 10] His own abbot to his own cleric.

You have chosen a sufficiently pleasant exile, my dearest friend, where joys abound, though vain; where bread and wine are more abundant than in one’s homeland; where friends gather in plenty and the companionship of associates is not rare. Who other than you under heaven has not judged Paris to be a place of delights, a garden of plantations, a field of firstfruits? Yet you spoke the truth in jest [Col. 0519D]: where there is greater and fuller pleasure of bodies, there is the true exile of souls; and where luxury reigns, there the soul is miserably enslaved and afflicted. O Paris, how suited you are to capturing and deceiving souls! In you are the nets of vices; in you the snares of evils; in you the arrow of hell pierces the hearts of the foolish. My John perceived this, and therefore called it exile. Would that you regarded this exile truly as it is, and hastened toward your homeland not in word and tongue, but in deed and truth! There, in the book of life, you would behold not figures and letters but divinity and truth itself as it is [Col. 0520A], face to face: without the labor of reading, without the weariness of seeing, without deceit or error in understanding, without anxiety in retaining, without fear of forgetting.

O blessed school, where Christ teaches our hearts by the word of his power; where, without study and reading, we grasp how we ought to live blessedly for ever! There no book is bought, no master of writing paid for, no circumvention of disputes, no entanglement of sophisms; there is a plain resolution of all questions and full comprehension of every reason and argument. There life contributes more than reading; simplicity profits more than cavilling. There no one is logically concluded except one who is excluded. In a single word, every objection is resolved: to one who maliciously objects to an evil life, the reply is, “Depart, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels”; while to one who makes a good objection it is said, “Come, blessed ones,” etc. (Matt. XXV) [Col. 0520B]. Would that the children of men applied themselves to these better studies as they do to empty talk and vain, utterly worthless buffoonery! Certainly they would reap richer fruits, more excellent favor, and greater honors; and without doubt they would attain Christ, the end of perfection, whom they will not find in those pursuits. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIV. TO THE SAME

[IV, 11] To his own John, Peter, abbot of Celles, his own, the good that is above every good.

[Col. 0520C] In the outcome of events, things frequently happen otherwise than human foresight judges. This is a principal cause why lovers of truth sometimes speak, if not against truth, yet outside the sphere of truth. Hence, if the substance of a matter comes to light, they should not be called liars, because they do not speak against truth; nor, properly speaking, truthful, because they suppose something other than what comes to pass. Accordingly, as I desire altogether to avoid the precipice of falsehood, so, though I do not reach the bank of truth, I at least strive toward it. I am drawn back from falsehood willingly, from truth unwillingly; I hold the middle—or rather, am held sorrowfully at the boundary of one and the other—because, friend, I would always wish to say as surely as I know what is or will be. I know, indeed, that one ought not to impute to anyone the evil [Col. 0520D] that he suffers, but that which he does or deserves. Likewise, I think one must maintain concerning one who is merely deceived by fortune’s snares and never intentionally deceives that he is worthy of compassion, not condemnation.

I have said this beforehand, dearest friend, so that you may know that I have been unwillingly prevented from fulfilling the undertaking by which I ought to have sent either your messengers or the ashes of blessed Aigulf. [Note: [Col. 0520D] “Ashes”: that is, the sacred relics of blessed Aigulf which he had promised him. Salisbury, Letter 97: “You promised me pledges of blessed Aigulf.”] Very many things intervened which strongly hindered it. One of them was that your—indeed truly our—W. was supposed to return from Rome by way of us, and I deferred arranging that business in accordance with his counsel [Col. 0521A]. But he did not come by way of us. Therefore I am sending Brother W., our monk, so that we may do everything according to the directions which he brings back from your lips. For at your bidding I shall always do whatever you say, especially in England. Nor do I wish this kind of business to be a burden to you, since I do not doubt that it is troublesome to every honorable man. Whatever profits they may be going to derive, I shall regard them as the vilest dung if even slightly your good faith or the modesty of your countenance should judge otherwise. Therefore I command—indeed, I adjure—your most holy friendship not to move one foot from the position of your integrity on my account, but to send back without hesitation whatever appears just and good to you. With equal peace and patience, according to the words of your mouth, I shall accept either alternative: namely, to send or not to send preachers. Enough of this.

Moreover, my spirit exults in God my savior, both because of the most sweetly good fragrance of your reputation and because of your prosperity. You are the one among all mortals whom nearly all our friends would, not without cause, envy, if they considered with what great preeminence above them all you have placed your seat in our foremost place. Among the first three you are chief, and I do not know whether anyone can attain your rank. Master W. and Master R. have shown the friendship they bear you in the affair of Hawidis, our niece [Note: [Col. 0521] “In the affair of Hawidis, his niece”: namely, her marriage to Peter of Tornella, concerning whom see above, Letter 9.]. For they stood by her husband or her marriage, lest it be broken, as firmly at court as faithfully. Return them no small thanks. Greet the lord archbishop on our behalf, and all our friends of holy B. [uncertain: the text breaks off at the initial.]

## LETTER LXXV. TO THE SAME

[IV, 12] To his dearest friend and master John of Salisbury, P., his own friend and disciple, with Jesus and in Jesus always on earth and in heaven.

Your prudence knows that a grain of wheat falling into the earth remains alone unless it dies; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. I hope to receive from our little grain a hundredfold fruit, partly through the fruitful infusion of heavenly dew, partly through the joyful fertility of the field which the Lord has blessed [Col. 0521D]. For a numerous offspring of blessings arises from the conjunction of the best gift, or perfect gift, with the free choice of a good man. Where grace pours in leaping with the force of eternal outflow, what does the soul do but flow back life? The marriage of grace and soul is never barren, never empty. Jesus, who saves his people from their sins, is the blessed fruit of this union. The soul to which grace is joined has neither dry breasts nor a womb without children. The soul indeed labors in birth, but does not groan; grace gives birth, but does not corrupt. The soul receives seed with delight, but not with sin; [Col. 0522A] it bears offspring from the spirit of grace, but with salvation. The belly does not swell with pride, but grows in humility; the loins are not oppressed with heaviness, but impressed with chastity; the breasts do not swell with an influx of milk, but are emptied of the course of human frailty. Angelic hands act as midwives in so salutary a birth; the offspring is wrapped in the swaddling-clothes of virtues until it is caught up to God and to his throne.

But what of the mother? She flees into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, that there they may feed her for one thousand two hundred and sixty days. For the dragon stands before the woman who is about to give birth, in order to devour her child when she has borne him. It is not hidden from you, dearest master and friend, who do not ignore the wiles of the ancient serpent, what the dragon hungers for and what it thirsts for. What but the Son [Col. 0522B] of the Virgin? What but the desire of the heart? What but the offspring of virtue? Therefore let the purpose of the mind be snatched away not only from its jaws, but from its sight; and with all haste let it be sent to God not tasted but untouched. Certainly, unless haste comes to help or arrives first in the dragon’s mouth, our soul will become its morsel. As quickly as the mother seeks the solitude of the desert, so quickly will the son ascend the heights of heaven. The farther the mother withdraws, the higher and farther the Father catches up the son. Unless the mother flees, the dragon’s entrails will be filled with the entrails of her own offspring. One need not fear coming to the place where one ceases to fear. The devil fears, hates, and avoids nothing so much as the solitude of the cloister. He prefers a herd of swine to the solitude of saints. The bridegroom leads [Col. 0522C] his bride into solitude, and there speaks to her heart. Isaac had gone out to meditate in the field when, behold, his bride Rebecca came, having mounted camels and trampling the vices of her pride and impurity. In the wilderness Jesus, being tempted, walks upon the asp and basilisk and tramples the lion and dragon. Solitude earns merit for souls; solitude is the camp of the Lord of hosts; solitude is a net for catching fish; solitude is the paradise of delights; solitude is the gymnasium of heavenly philosophy. What more? Solitude is God’s walking-place. Solitude knows the vigils of Jesus; solitude receives the tears of Jesus; solitude hears the prayers of Jesus; solitude knew the time and hour of our redemption; [Col. 0522D] solitude beheld Jesus being born, preaching, feeding the crowds, and in the Transfiguration showing a face brighter than the sun; solitude beheld the Lord dying, rising, and ascending. Behold why the solitudes of the Jordan exult. Whatever harshness, bitterness, or fear there had formerly been in solitude has been softened by the pouring forth of Jesus’ blood, sweetened by the application of the wood of the cross, removed by Jesus’ dwelling there. With Jesus as companion, what do you fear? With Jesus feeding you, for what do you hunger? With Jesus washing and anointing you, what pain do you feel? Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVI. TO P., MONK OF NORWICH

[Col. 0523A]

[IV, 13] Brother PETER, unworthy abbot of the monastery of Celles, to P., monk of Norwich [Note: [Col. 0523] “Monk of Norwich”: of the church of Norwich in England, in which John was prior of Norwich, to whom Salisbury’s Letter 251 is addressed.], the spirit of salvation.

To write to one unknown from another unknown, your T.—indeed ours—obtained and requested it. For it would be unjust if, in so honorable a matter, a father should put his son to shame. Since, therefore, you are of tested, deep, and well-known life, learning, and profession, I hide my face beneath the mantle of modesty and send forth a voice scarcely trembling. Hear then, if you please, truth rather than vanity, piety rather than falsehood, admonition rather than flattery. I know that we are sons of one man, are shaped by one rule, and in one house seek one thing from the One.

[Col. 0523B] Therefore, if we are drawn, let us draw others; if we call, let us invite; if we run, let us urge others to run. “Let him who hears say, ‘Come.’” But if they refuse to follow, freed from the covenant by which we are bound, we shall wash our hands among the innocent, and thus feast at the entrance to God’s glory. I have said this because, in our country—and, I believe, in yours also—men who are not monks, if I may say so without offending them, but have multiplied beyond measure from among monks, bring reproach upon the holy Name invoked over them: they live shamefully; they abandon themselves to the desires of belly, gluttony, and lust; and they subject their own body—something which it is impious even to say, and a denial against God—to dishonor. Thus God’s name is blasphemed through them among the nations.

[Col. 0523C] Would that Phinehas might rise again! Would that Elijah, zealous with zeal for the house of Israel, might consume with heavenly fire those reclining in idolatry! Would that at least Jeremiah might teach, admonish, and bewail the captivity of the daughter of Zion with a threefold mourning—namely, prayer, preaching, and example! For the true Pharaoh, who scatters all things and does not gather with God, scatters the stones of the sanctuary through the crossroads of the streets; he carries off the vessels of the Lord’s temple into his shrines beside Dagon; he places the son of the Virgin alongside the son of Venus; and with his concubines he does not cease drinking from bowls and cups until morning. How long, Lord, will there be none to stir a pen and dare to whimper? Everything keeps a profound silence. Moses does not stretch out his hands to heaven, for they are heavy and full of blood. Therefore [Col. 0523D] Israel is defeated and Amalek prevails.

The four craftsmen scatter all Judah and Israel with their horns, while the locust devours what the caterpillar left, the grub what the locust left, and blight what the grub left. These are the third and fourth generation, in which the Lord repays the sins of the fathers in their children. The first generation, that is, is [Col. 0524A] the prompting of the flesh; the second, the first impulse of thought; the third, deliberation or commission of the deed; the fourth, glorying in the crime. Happy is the man not scattered by these horns.

If then there is in you any spark of mercy, any bowels of compassion, any dew of kindness, be pierced with compunction. These tears will undoubtedly not be useless. Either they will benefit those men and they will be converted, or they will return to you and come back into your own bosom. Therefore, that they may turn back from their evil way, go in warning from gate to gate, powerfully girded with the sword. Let it spare no one, but destroy from the earth the memory of those who have delayed to return to their heart, who have not taken away the iniquity in their hand.

I say this to you as a friend of righteousness, a zealot for God’s house, one who hates those who [Col. 0524B] contradict the words of the Holy One. But over those to whom nothing is sweet except wine and payment, nothing bitter except cloister and silence, nothing lovable except flesh and the world, nothing hateful except God’s word and Spirit—God’s clouds flash, heaven’s thunders blaze, and a violent wind and encircling fire hasten. O senseless men, which of you can dwell with devouring fire, or with everlasting burnings? Will you not there receive poison in place of wine, punishment in place of payment? The gate of hell will be barred against you with locks and iron bars, you who refused to be enclosed in the cloister; and there will also be crying and continual lamentation, you who would not be silent before the Lord’s face. The flesh which you carefully fed, diligently cherished, studiously suckled, [Col. 0524C] shall not possess God’s kingdom. The world, before whose claims you placed the Creator of the world, in which you were foully defiled, whose deceptive beauty delighted you so that you forgot your heavenly homeland, shall not rescue you from the enemy’s hand. God’s word will then scourge you, not free you; accuse you, not excuse you; condemn you, not save you. What have you to do with God’s Spirit, whose dishonor you do not spare, whose temple you violate, whom you do not fear to grieve? Unless I am mistaken, what you have sinned against him shall not be forgiven you, neither in this age nor in the age to come.

But enough of these matters. You, however, whose eyes are open, do not go in their way, do not assent to their deeds, nor acquiesce in their counsels. Your nephew compelled me to be excessively lengthy, urging me by repeated requests to take up my pen again. [Col. 0524D] Would that your virtue may be greater still than your reputation. Would that I may deserve to see and know you and to have with you the right hands of fellowship. Would that at least, if more is not granted, you may offer one prayer for my sins to the merciful Judge through the hand of a holy angel. Farewell.

## BOOK TWO

Containing the letters written by Peter after he had undertaken the abbacy of Saint Remigius of Rheims.

[Col. 0525]

## LETTER LXXVII. TO POPE ALEXANDER III

[Col. 0525A]

[V, 19.] To Pope ALEXANDER, PETER, abbot of Saint Remigius.

Things that are plainly and manifestly true speak for themselves; with no auxiliary support added, they bear witness to themselves. But things held in the depths of ignorance through remoteness of place, passage of time, or the entanglement of any obscurity, when the public good requires it, wish to be seen in the light. Hence it is, most holy Father, that the bearer of this letter—

> [Note: **Bearer of this letter.** Fulk, bishop-elect in Sweden, on whose behalf he again writes to the same Alexander in Letter 78. He had first been a monk of Celle, and then also of Saint Remigius, having, I suppose, followed Peter as abbot. Certainly, in the diptychs of Saint Remigius, Fulk the bishop is named among the members of that monastery who died during Peter’s abbacy.]

—having grown up in the bosom of our humility, received from us at the monastery of Celle the religious habit, and, for a long time there sucking breasts better than wine, by God’s cooperating grace advanced to become an episcopal man. Truly, embracing both the work and burden [Col. 0525B] of the office laid upon him, he does not make gold his strength, nor say to fine gold, “You are my confidence.” For he seeks from the Apostolic See death through death: summer threatens death on the journey he is undertaking; imperial power threatens it; and the unreliable alliance of barbarians, if he obtains what he requests, brings death. Thus he carries his life in his hands, offering it to God through the hand of the heavenly key-bearer—and yours. Receive, if you please, the holy sacrifice pleasing to God, this rational service; and, by the authority of your most blessed apostolate, expose the sheep to wolves, if perhaps, through blessed conduct, not the wolf may eat the lamb, but the lamb convert the wolf. Whichever of these happens, God will be glorified, your ministry honored, and the brother’s soul will suffer no loss.

For from what has gone before, in which I brought him up, and from many proofs which I have learned, I am confident that he will be faithful in the charge entrusted to him and will not, under any attack, stray from the path of faith; rather, he will give his blood before diminishing the faith. The Apostle says, “Do not quench the Spirit” (1 Thess. 5); and kindle more brightly, with ampler coverings, the lamp now lit beneath a bushel, because this is your glory and crown: if a grain of wheat, falling into the earth through your hand, bears much fruit.

## LETTER LXXVIII. TO POPE ALEXANDER III

[VI, 6.] To the lord and father ALEXANDER, supreme pontiff, [Col. 0525D] PETER, abbot of Saint Remigius: whatever a son owes to a father.

Good will stirred by the Holy Spirit must be restrained by no reins, delayed from its purpose by no evasions. For religion has now grown so lukewarm throughout all our Christendom that scarcely any are found in the whole flock of the Christian people who would not rather hide beneath the fig tree and olive tree of earthly honor and delight than smell war from afar and boldly go out to meet the sons of Benjamin and the half-tribe of Manasseh, unencumbered, though armed enemies of Christ confront them.

Therefore it belongs to you, most holy Father, who are the head in the body of the Church, from whom oil does not fail and who possess the southern bellows, to rouse the idle and to aid and impel those roused toward things better and nearer salvation. It should never, then, be burdensome to you when aid is requested from you for spreading the Catholic faith, because thereby the praise of God [Col. 0526B] and of our Lord Jesus Christ is increased, your merit is accumulated, and salvation is gained for an unbelieving people.

Accordingly, we commend to your holiness the requests of that poor bishop Fulk, who visited the curia this year and is now staying with us, knowing and considering that where the furnishings of faith are absent or scanty, fuller assistance is needed. Indulgence should therefore be granted him in many things, since he needs everything. Thus your Master and Lord, when he sent his disciples to preach new things, also added that they should perform wonders. You are not asked to bestow miraculous power, but that your authority, working with him and in him, may make unbelievers more readily believe him. For Moses also, when he was sent by the Lord to the children of Israel, asked that a sign be given by which he might be believed.

The privileges which he requests from you will therefore assist him both in place of Moses’ rod and in place of Christ’s disciples’ miracles. For no one, if God brings it about, will despise your authority or his person fortified by your authority. May your holiness prosper, to whom I owe whatever I am and can do. For I hear from many, and experience in many matters, your most magnificent favor.

## LETTER LXXIX. TO THE KING, ARCHBISHOP, AND MAGNATES OF THE SWEDES

[VI, 8.] To the king of the Swedes—

> [Note: **To the king of the Swedes.** Perhaps Charles, son of King Sverker. For at this time he ruled over the Swedes, or Sueones, and the Goths. Fulk, moreover, was bishop of the Estonians, who were then attached to the kingdom of Sweden.]

—and to the dukes and princes, [Col. 0526D] and to their archbishop and all his suffragans.

Since the chief and highest concern of a mind devoted to God ought to be to order everything toward God’s glory and honor, if it should sense, even slightly, that it has in some measure pleased almighty God, then, with its inward joys increased, it pours out its whole self, as though melted after the Bridegroom, crying aloud and saying: “We will exult and rejoice in you, mindful of your breasts” (Song 1).

Moved by these examples, though in many things—indeed almost all—I know that I sin daily and do not devote myself to divine pursuits as justice requires, in this one matter I do not wholly despair of God’s mercy: from our hand he has graciously received a sheaf, Lord Bishop Fulk, once our monk and brought up by us in cloistered religion, and has advanced him to the highest priesthood. We recognize [Col. 0527B] our own countenance in him and hope that his heart will not depart from our God and his commandments.

When, therefore, a welcome opportunity has offered us time still to instruct and shape him toward a fuller love of God, we receive it gratefully and devoutly, since we judge that we shall not see him again beyond this, until the throne of grace and the distribution of the eternal reward. The present difficulty of the season also cooperates with our desire. For, even if each of us wished it, he could not pass through the dangers and perils that lie before him. For, as we have heard, the flooding of the waters is so great that the road by which one reaches you is scarcely passable even in the calmest weather.

Finally, a third reason applies: our lord archbishop, leaving for Rome, entrusted us with supplying his office. Yet an abbot’s rank does not extend to the dedication of churches, the ordination of clerics, or the confirmation of Christians. Therefore, through him—who is ours in all things—we accomplish what we cannot accomplish through ourselves. He will come to you full of God’s blessing when the weather has improved. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXX. TO POPE ALEXANDER III

[VIII, 8.] To ALEXANDER, supreme pontiff, PETER, abbot of Saint Remigius.

The oracle of the Apostolic See must neither be approached without reverence nor entered without confidence. Therefore to you, venerable Father, [Col. 0527D] to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven have been given, power has not been given without mercy, nor justice without compassion. Let sober indulgence, then, intercede and incline the authority of your power toward our petition; likewise let devout mercy temper the rigor of justice.

It is unsafe, accordingly, to shake in any degree the throne of the great King, who is forever and ever; and it is no less dangerous [Col. 0528A] to rouse Solomon’s bed, because of the surrounding swords, without the consent of him who lies thereon, who sleeps like a lion’s cub. Who would dare doubt that God sits and rests in the saints? We perceive and believe, by the testimony of his holy life, that our most beloved brother, the abbot of Clairvaux—

> [Note: **The abbot of Clairvaux.** Henry. A little before this, that is, in 1178, he had been sent as legate to Toulouse with Peter, cardinal of Saint Chrysogonus, and several bishops, against the Albigensian heretics. On this matter there is an excellent letter of Henry himself in Hoveden. Now, after the death of Gocelin, bishop of Toulouse, he was being sought for that see.]

—belongs to their number and lot by hidden faith. He has perhaps been elected bishop of the city of Toulouse. But, being truly religious, measuring himself by himself and fearing his inadequacy, he prefers, after rejecting the marriage, to take off his shoe and receive upon his face with Jesus the spittle of every reproach, rather than abandon the sweetness of the vine, olive, and fig tree of his assumed profession.

Nor has he acted here with blameworthy fickleness, since he does this by the authority of the lawgiver—namely Moses, [Col. 0528B] who, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be afflicted with God’s people than to enjoy the fleeting pleasure of sin, and judging Christ’s reproach greater riches than Egypt’s treasure. For he looked to the reward. He considers too what is written in Lamentations: that the finest color was altered after the stones of the sanctuary had been scattered at the head of every street (Lam. 4). He fears that an eclipse of the sun may occur in himself if he leaves the station of the Hebrews for the camp of those whose mouth speaks vanity—

> [Note: **Whose mouth speaks vanity.** The people of Toulouse, whom this corruption had infected more than others. Henry himself writes: “Toulouse, which, just as it was a city of very great population, was also said to be the mother of heresy and the head of error.”]

—and whose feet run toward evil. For poison infects more quickly than antidote heals; and a fragile nature is restored with more difficulty because it is easily broken.

Let apostolic permission therefore grant this man to labor in the paradise of Clairvaux for food that does not perish, and to eat his bread in the sweat of his face; for he neither wishes to touch what is forbidden nor to put on the tunic of skins. He has pitched his tent of Solomon’s skins beside the well of the Living and Seeing One, beside the heap of new grain, and finally beside the mercy-seat, within the veil of the sanctuary, beneath the wings of the cherubim—Saint Benedict and Blessed Bernard. [Col. 0528C] He has also set his shoulder beneath the ark of God’s covenant, in which is the rod of the cross: it flowered in the apostles, put forth leaves in the regenerated multitudes of the faithful, and bore nuts in martyrs, confessors, and virgins; in which are the two tablets of the covenant, one containing the severity of the Law, the other conferring the gentleness and grace of the Gospel. [Col. 0528D] Finally, there is hidden manna there: God’s promised sweetness, which he has hidden for those who fear him and will give to those who love him.

He dwells among burning stones, by whose contemplation sight is sharpened, torpor shaken off, vital powers nourished, dead things cast away, and religion perpetuated. O how hard, how bitter is the separation from religious affection, to which carnal kinship gives way, beneath which pleasure is placed, [Col. 0529A] and ambition laid low! How unhappy is the exchange in which stench is received for sweet fragrance, baldness for curling hair, haircloth for a breast-band! This is by no means the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.

Let not, then, the apostolic ear hear Martha complaining against Mary seated at Jesus’ feet—Martha, anxious about much service, who has not tasted the cup of wine seasoned by holy contemplation and continual meditation on God’s law.

## LETTER LXXXI. TO POPE ALEXANDER

[VIII, 10.] To Pope ALEXANDER, PETER, abbot of Saint Remigius.

As we had received instructions from the fatherhood of our lord William of Rheims, [Col. 0529B] we came to settle the case pending between the bishop of Soissons and Count Robert—

> [Note: **Count Robert.** Count of Soissons. The bishop was named Nivelon, who subscribed to the Lateran Council. The monastery of Saint Crispin at Soissons has been mentioned above. There is also among them the monastery of Saint John “of the Vines,” of the Order of Saint Augustine. In the district of Soissons is Serene Valley, a Premonstratensian monastery.]

—and with us came the abbots of Saint Crispin, Saint John, and Serene Valley. There, after hearing the allegations of both parties, we received the written depositions of the witnesses produced by the bishop. Then, appointing another day at Rheims for both parties, we met again; and after much discussion, because the lord king had sent his letters to the bishop concerning this affair, we deferred deciding the case by their will and consent, until we should learn whether the lord king would settle that controversy between them peacefully.

Afterward, however, without any further summons having intervened, and without the bishop’s asking us to appoint him a day, the bishop, without consulting us, subjected the land of the aforesaid count to an interdict of excommunication. Therefore the countess, complaining on behalf of herself and the count of this injury, demanded that we absolve her land. Having taken counsel with wise men and received a guarantee from the count’s party that, if he should inflict a new loss or injury upon the bishop, he would make full restitution, we absolved the land. We therefore report and attest to you the truth of this affair.

## LETTER LXXXII. TO THE SAME

[VIII, 11.] To ALEXANDER, supreme pontiff—

> [Note: **To Alexander, supreme pontiff.** In 1179, when the Lateran synod was imminent, he calls it Alexander’s second general assembly because he had held the earlier one at Tours sixteen years before. It is also called a general council by William of Newburgh, Book II, chapter 14, and by others.]

—PETER, abbot of Saint Remigius.

No one who does not doubt that Christ said to the Prince of the Apostles, [Col. 0529D] “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church” (Matt. 16), is ignorant that the burden of all Christendom has been laid upon apostolic shoulders. It is necessary, therefore, that Aaron, who entered the heavens in his own blood, the priest established by God the Father forever, and Hur, who descended upon the apostles in fiery tongues, should raise and uphold both your hands and shoulders with their help, lest they fail.

For iniquity, which sits upon the talent [Col. 0530A] of lead, with doubled—or rather joined—wings utterly oppresses the Church: God’s by espousal and yours by administration; it oppresses it among subjects and prelates alike, so that now it may be said, “As the people, so the priest” (Hos. 4); as the sheep, so also the dogs. What should I say, and why say what is obvious to the bleary-eyed and barbers? Does not the cry of so great an evil—indeed, I might say its fury—rise up to heaven? And who doubts that you know these things, whose task is not only to discern diseases, but also to cut away or heal whatever is diseased?

Yet, supreme shepherd, your people commit two evils. Come down and you will find a molten calf, wantoning among the cows of the peoples and licking the grass down to the root. In the one is marked lust; in the other, avarice. Once this family of darkness occupied the valleys; now they are already taking possession of the mountains. Once they defiled Venus’ temple; now they pollute the courts of the Virgin, whom the Father betrothed to his Son and whom Paul wishes to present to Christ as a chaste virgin for one husband. Once, finally, they reigned in Babylon; now they reign in Jerusalem.

Jeremiah laments that avarice sits at the head of every crossroads, where, in conferring ecclesiastical honors, either carnal kinship or monetary greed is brought into play. To cut off and remove these things belongs to God alone. But yours is the task of laying the axe to the root and, to the extent of your ability, breaking this statue by the judgment of the Watchers and cutting down the tree with untiring diligence. How this may be done will teach you the One who revealed the uncertain and hidden things of his wisdom [Col. 0530C] to his servant David, and made known to his apostles everything that he had heard from his Father. The very faithful bearer of this letter, a man of complete integrity and good repute, will also inform you.

Lust, however, which transgresses not merely the bridal chambers of chastity but even every boundary of modesty, must be pierced with the two-edged sword, so that, if its sting is not broken, it may at least be blunted; if it is not buried, it may at least be hidden away. Let the two horns of avarice in ecclesiastical promotions be utterly anathematized; in secular plunder let its claws either be uprooted or cut off. May the Spirit of the Lord, who fills the whole world because he contains all things, always be present to your mouth and heart, and especially in this second general assembly.

## LETTER LXXXIII. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0530D]

[VIII, 12.] To the lord pope, PETER, abbot of Saint Remigius.

Summoned to the general council together with the other children of the Catholic Church, venerable Father, I offer an excuse—not some frivolous pretext drawn from the Gospel guests [Col. 0531A] who, invited to the supper, accuse themselves by making excuses—but one probable and true, proved by clear evidence. In me, indeed, devotion is ready for every obedience; but feeble execution gives way because of illness. The will is present, but infirmity hinders; “the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26).

Before your fatherly clemency, therefore, and the most equitable judgment of apostolic discernment, let advanced age, a long journey, a short life, and weary limbs be credible and necessary grounds of our excuse. A father prefers to have his son absent and alive rather than with him half-dead, or indeed dead. I have been struck down like grass already withered, which is here today and tomorrow will be put not into the oven but into the bier. How can I, like a cart loaded with hay, follow those who ride on horses and fly upon the wings of health and vigorous age? For what if I were present and could not take part? What could a smoking torch do among shining stars? Therefore spare us in this matter now, as you have always done, by graciously receiving and effectively fulfilling our prayers.

## LETTER LXXXIV. TO THE SAME

[VIII, 16.] To Pope ALEXANDER, PETER, abbot of Saint Remigius.

Since the whole Christian world, most holy Father, is governed by your direction, and the care of your concern [Col. 0531C] stretches to more matters than the number of stars or the sand of the sea, it is scarcely surprising if you are sometimes deceived. For more people hunt in your court by fraud than serve there with faithful devotion. I except the sincerity of the holy cardinals, whose fidelity is well known to God and to you. I rebuke the deceitful pretence of those who arrive, especially the Germans, whose snares both we have experienced and you, touched by the living coal, do not fail to know.

Throughout the entire time of the schism, although they afflicted us, exposed and as it were without a defender, with many calumnies and losses, they nevertheless never obtained in war what now, in the peace of yourself and the holy Roman Church, they strive to take from our church. For they frequently urged the lord emperor [Col. 0531D] to enable them to seize some of the prebends of Marsna, which we have possessed confirmed from times long past, by the concession of the bishops of Liège and by the privilege both of Innocent, your predecessor of pious memory, and of yourself. You ordered our provost of Marsna to give to a certain clerk of the emperor a prebend which does not exist. Therefore our community, prostrate at your feet, asks you to revoke the command and henceforth to receive no person’s petition on this matter. For they are your devoted sons, and will become still more devoted thereby.

## LETTER LXXXV. TO THE SAME, IN THE CASE OF SAINT THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

> [Note: **New.**]

(*Letters of Saint Thomas*, ed. Giles, Oxford, 184, octavo, vol. II, p. 172.)

[Col. 0532A]

To Pope ALEXANDER, PETER, abbot of Saint Remigius.

Contemplation of apostolic majesty could have restrained my pen, had not regard for your humanity raised my spirit and your clemency’s glorious condescension—accustomed to stoop to Christ’s little ones—encouraged my boldness. Among them I too dare, though I can scarcely be judged dust and ashes before my Lord, father of the faithful, comforter of the oppressed, and judge of oppressors, to speak a word for God’s Church to the glory and honor of your apostolate. I gladly hear that it is enlarged through the exercise of justice, which the whole world needs, and works of mercy, by which the oppressed are raised up and the needy refreshed.

By these titles, Father, your holiness has deserved that the Lord should go before you in a mighty arm and manifest power amid so many dangers, and should humble and overthrow before you and for you the glorious ones of the earth. Let your entrance and the course of the varying events be reviewed from the beginning, and it will be clearer than light that not human hands but the Lord has done all these things. He who began in you the great works of his mercy will establish the throne of your apostolate, because it is openly known to the world that you walk in the paths of him who rescues the poor from the powerful, rejects partiality [Col. 0532C] of persons, and will answer each person in judgment according to his deeds.

Your devoted son, the Most Christian king of the Franks, exults in what he hears concerning you; the Gallican Church rejoices, whose grief at the vain boasting of certain men insulting truth has lately been turned into joy. For at the arrival of your lord cardinals it learned that you support the cause of the venerable man—the archbishop of Canterbury—who is laudably contending for the Church’s liberty, and that you prove liars those who boasted that they had obtained from you the ruin of the innocent and the Church’s confusion. And the cardinals would plainly be wise if they remained within your boundaries. But the Gallican Church now laments again because they are said in this respect to have gone beyond them. Therefore, prostrate with all my heart, I implore [Col. 0532D] your fatherhood to hear the prayers offered on behalf of the lord of Canterbury by the Most Christian king and queen and by the bishops and magnates of France, and to render void whatever you discover has been presumptuously undertaken against his justice.

## LETTER LXXXVI. TO CARDINAL ALBERT

[VI, 1.] To Lord ALBERT, cardinal—

> [Note: **Cardinal Albert, legate.** Of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. Thus Roger calls him in the letters of absolution which, after King Henry had cleared himself of the murder of Blessed Thomas, he gave the king with his colleague Theodinus. This, without doubt, was the outcome of the legation about which he desires to hear here and concerning which Alexander writes in Letter 54.]

—and legate of the Roman See.

If so great a distance of places and the many hindrances of occupations did not detain us, we would by no means have postponed for so long visiting your fatherhood, most dear to us. For our heart has great concern regarding the business entrusted to you and its outcome, because the honor of God, the good of the Church, the integrity of your reputation, and the regard of the entire Roman curia will obtain praise and distinction in every conscience from it, if it attains an outcome according to the rule of equity and truth.

Therefore, do not find it tiresome that your friend should inform you how far the affair has now advanced. And, if you please, you have a suitable person through whom you can faithfully send a reply and securely communicate: namely, the prior of the Valley of Saint Peter, your most beloved son, whom you begot in Christ and whose spirit you have made obedient to you in all things. For he has gone to the place called the Valley of God—

> [Note: **Valley of God.** A Carthusian monastery in the diocese of the bishop of Chartres; for it is this bishop whom he means. There is another monastery of the Valley of God, of the Premonstratensian Order in the diocese of Rheims, which has nothing to do with the matter.]

—to install a prior there. He is not far from you; if you order him to come to you, you can pour into his trustworthy ears whatever, welcome or unwelcome, comes to your notice concerning your own situation.

It seems to me, moreover, that the said place greatly needs your help and counsel, because the bishop to whose diocese it belongs delays to lay upon it the hand of blessing and assistance. The brothers dwelling there cannot have either a cemetery or the consecration of their monastery. It is therefore your concern to assist in this matter, which you can readily do, the poor of Christ, so that in a blessed place they may bless their Creator.

At the end of this letter we venture to commend to you the prior who has been installed there. Your son has been compelled to appoint him—newly drawn from the furnace of religious and regular submission—to the care of governing souls. Therefore instruct him by your teaching and assistance, for you know how difficult a task he undertakes who receives souls to govern.

## LETTER LXXXVII. TO THE SAME

[VI, 3.] By one most comprehensive and universal rule, Christ briefly includes all the most holy ordinances of the Catholic Fathers both before and after him, saying of the love of God and neighbor: “On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22). Everything, therefore, that is done in God’s Church must be brought back to this most beautiful [Col. 0533D] rule, because whatever disagrees with it does not flow from the spirit of peace and charity.

Hence, venerable Father, dispensations from certain enactments are rightly granted for a greater and better recompense. We wish therefore to inform you how great the evils and how great the slaughter of men have been in [Col. 0534A] our land, in our own days and those of our predecessors, through the wars of certain noblemen: namely, Count Wischard of Ruzey, the count of Rency, and Hugh of Pierrepont. Countless men were killed, captured, and ransomed, and suffered the most extreme losses. Religious houses were plundered, and many other evils ensued.

At last, through the intervention of good, wise, and religious persons, they resolved to contract marriages with one another, so that, joined at least by this bond, they might maintain and possess peace among themselves. Let your discernment therefore consider whether, if some degree of consanguinity stands in the way, no dispensation which can be obtained from the lord pope should be refused for the good of peace and in recompense for so many evils. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXVIII. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0534B]

[VIII, 9.] To Lord ALBERT, chancellor—

> [Note: **To Lord Albert, chancellor.** The cardinal to whom Book VI, Letter 1 is addressed. Our author afterward addresses him more frequently as chancellor of the Roman Church; Stephen of Tournai likewise does so, as does Peter of Blois in Letter 38.]

—PETER, abbot of Saint Remigius.

We are compelled to plead for others, though we can scarcely obtain prayers for ourselves. Yet we do not hesitate in a petition commended by the justice of the request, the conscience of the petitioner, and the kindness of the one petitioned. Justice is to preserve to each person his own right; a good conscience is humbly to entreat a beloved lord on behalf of a faithful fellow-servant; paternal kindness is graciously to relax, for an anxious son, even a fixed resolve. We know, most loving lord, that apostolic power has under its command whatever it may choose to command, and can say to one: [Col. 0534C] “Go,” and he goes; and to another: “Come,” and he comes; and to its servant: “Do this,” and he does it (Matt. VIII). But let the chariot of power and mercy, exalted rank and gentleness, be joined together, so that charity may be spread between them for the daughters of Jerusalem.

Certainly, I think either the Church, which is our mother, has no daughters on earth, or she gives birth daily in the monastery of Clairvaux and nourishes with maternal breasts daughters who imitate their mother. For the men of Clairvaux follow the true footsteps of Jesus Christ—born of the Virgin, living religiously in the world, and nailed to the cross under Pontius Pilate—by living chastely, obeying their spiritual Father in all things, and daily crucifying their flesh with its vices and desires. If God is for them, who is against them? Behold these chicks beneath the wings of the hen, which sets herself against the hawks of spiritual wickedness [Col. 0534D]: they lap the blood of the Lord’s Passion and sleep beneath the shadow of the juniper, consoling their labours by love for their protector. Let the most discerning apostolic governance therefore judge how perilous it is to awaken those resting beneath this fig tree and vine—not with carnal but spiritual sweetness—and not take from them that which is desirable to their eyes [Col. 0535A].

Are there not others besides this man? Indeed, they have multiplied beyond number who say, “Here am I; send me” (Isa. VI), whereas he says, “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, I do not know how to speak, because I am a child” (Jer. I). Perhaps you say: “What concern have you with the men of Clairvaux, since Samaritans do not associate with Jews, and the dark face and garment of the Ethiopian woman differ from that garment and face which appeared to the apostles at the Lord’s Transfiguration?” To this I answer: From persons of many faces, the queen who stands at the right hand of the Son, clothed in gold and surrounded by variety, sings upon the ten-stringed psaltery before Him who sits upon the throne of grace, from whom proceed the diverse gifts of graces, although there is nevertheless one and the same Spirit, the same Lord.

## LETTER LXXXVIII bis. TO THE SAME PERSON

[Col. 0535B]

[VIII, 13.] To ALBERT, chancellor, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

The ark of the God of Israel, the ark of sanctification, the ark of the covenant—once, by command of the Lawgiver, overlaid on every side with gold, namely with the holiness and teaching of the ancient Fathers, and also covered above by the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy-seat—now, in the present time, through the abuse and negligence of the sons of Eli, stripped of the garments of her glory and covered over and abandoned amid fruitless willows, according to Isaiah (ch. I), like a hut in a cucumber field and a shelter in a vineyard, remembers the days of her youth; and weeping [Col. 0535C], and laying tears upon her cheeks, says: “I will return to my former husband, for then I was better off than now.”

Kicking oxen—that is, teachers—straying from the paths of justice through their desires, turn her aside, though they ought to glorify God and bear Him in their body. True grief therefore touches those who love her not in word and tongue, but in deed and truth. We do not fail to know that you are a singular and special friend, or son, of the holy universal Church, of which that ark bore the type and figure. We therefore summon you to mourning and compassion for your mother’s distress or desolation, that you may devote to her maternal sufferings whatever affectionate devotion requires.

For you hold, after the lord pope, the second place appointed by God for correcting these matters [Col. 0535D]; but beware lest you have received the grace of God in vain. For those who have seen and known your spirit and holy manner of life many years ago conceived the greatest hope for the improvement of the Church’s condition when they heard that you had been made chancellor [Col. 0536A].

> [Note: [Col. 0535D] “For those who have seen your spirit.” Albert the cardinal—later Pope Gregory VIII—was a man distinguished for piety and religious devotion.
