An old chronicle offers this eulogy: “Albert of Benevento, chancellor, a man of great holiness and praiseworthy frugality, was religious in all his actions. He always held dear the church of Saint Martin, in which he had assumed the religious habit; it also supplied him annually [Col. 0536D] with clothing according to the Rule.”]

If these things were not notorious everywhere and very well known to you, we would write more fully about them. Yet, lest with closed lips we sigh rather than speak, this letter declares what life does not keep silent about. Hell enlarges its appetite without any limit, while it ravages monstrously both sheep and shepherds. Those appointed as guides to heaven draw their followers into hell by a bad example. I do not say this of all; for the Lord knows who are His. But the more worthy the good are of better reward, the more the wicked need rebuke and correction.

Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel by their prophecy anticipated our times. Against shepherds and perverse rulers they hurled naked but true darts, proclaiming not in corners but in public streets their avarice, lust, gluttony, robbery, and every injustice [Col. 0536B]. Let their jealous spirit therefore enter into your bones and marrow, filling your spirit and mouth: a spirit which shatters mountains and rocks, and is effective even to the division of soul and spirit. Let your sword, made drunk in heaven, devour flesh, so that you may send back to us our shepherds corrected and stripped of every serpentine skin.

## LETTER LXXXIX. TO THE SAME PERSON

[VIII, 14.] To ALBERT, chancellor of the Roman Church, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

Behold, the great and fertile hen of apostolic authority [Col. 0536C] gathers her chicks in obedience and submission under the wings of kindly protection and prudent counsel. What is she to brood? What is she to bring forth? That it may be written for another generation, so that the people yet to be created may praise the Lord.

Behold Jacob, old and full of days, who long wrestled with the schismatic angel, awaiting God’s salvation, summons his sons for blessing. Will he be silent concerning what Reuben did, how he ascended his father’s bed and defiled its couch? Will he not foretell what Simeon and Levi, warlike instruments of iniquity, will do, or establish what future posterity ought to do?

> [Note: [Col. 0536D] “With the schismatic angel.” With the triple antipope. For after Octavian and Guido, mentioned in Letter 22, John, abbot of Struma, also stood against Alexander; he usurped the name Callistus in 1168. Others add a fourth, Lando, who was called Innocent.]

The great preparation of the Roman council portends great ensuing nuptials of the Son of the King, Jesus Christ. I do not fail to know that you, the ministers and officials of this holy council, together with the other cardinals—indeed, before all the others—were predestined by God; and that the sole bridegroom of the Church, our Lord, has already tested your faith, religious devotion, constancy, and equity in many matters.

He still has need that your service in this council may be reasonable and acceptable [Col. 0537A]: girded with a two-edged sword upon your thigh, may you most mightily cut away rotten flesh and unsound superstitions which are daily practised throughout the Christian world. For branching and forest-like wickedness sprouts daily among us; while the axe of evangelical discipline, with its smith asleep and negligent, lies blunted almost everywhere. Rare is the man who applies it, even blunted, to the root of the tree.

To express what I feel: what mockery and derision, what laborious and tearful—indeed, not to say wearisome—pilgrimage, what ruinous waste of expenses and consumption of the goods of good people, if so solemn an assembly of great men and religious persons should return empty and without the fruit of blessing! Beware lest it be said:

[Col. 0537B]

> “The mountains will labour; a ridiculous mouse will be born.” —Horace

May Jesus therefore find you friends of truth, so that, passing from gate to gate, you may spare no worshippers of the molten calf. I commend to you the bearers of this letter, our dearest friends and sons: the abbots of Saint Peter of the Mountains, All Saints of the Island, and Saint Mary of Virtu.

> [Note: [Col. 0537D] “The abbots of Saint Peter of the Mountains.” These are monasteries in the diocese of Châlons: the first two in the city itself, the third in a town of no small importance. But the monastery of All Saints, also mentioned in Letter 6 of Alexander, belongs to the Order of Regular Canons of Saint Augustine; the other two are Benedictine.]

May they find grace in your eyes through the favour which we possess in you. Send them back to us as soon as you can, with the favour of the lord pope and your own.

## LETTER XC. TO THE SAME PERSON

[Col. 0537C]

[VIII, 15.] To ALBERT, chancellor, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

As often as we suffer shipwreck, so often do we hasten to harbour. Long ago we fixed the harbour of our safest refuge upon the shore of your friendship. We frequently feel the winds of troubles blowing against us, but we do not trouble your harbour except in a more severe storm. Lesser dangers are either endured by patience or courageously overcome by virtue. But when a great cloud and encircling fire attack our little vessel, we must either be in danger at once or sail swiftly away.

This year, through your intervention, the lord pope granted his privilege to our church [Col. 0538A], in which he expressly confirmed for perpetual possession the canonries, or prebends, of Marsna, which for many past years we have already held for our own use.

> [Note: [Col. 0537D] “Canonries, or prebends, of Marsna.” They had been granted to the monastery of Saint-Remi on the condition that, as the canons died, they should pass to the use of the monks. A charter of Emperor Conrad, granted to Abbot Odo in 1145: “The lord Odo, venerable abbot of Saint Remigius the confessor and apostle of the Franks, visited our presence at Utrecht and requested that the possessions of his church situated in our realm be confirmed by our privilege: namely Marsna with all its appurtenances, Herta, Cluma, Litta, Angledura, Becca, and likewise the prebends of Marsna transferred to the use of the monks [Col. 0538D] upon the death of the canons [printed ‘monks’; read ‘canons’]. We therefore carefully complied with the petitions of so religious a man and confirmed by the seal of royal majesty both the aforesaid possessions and the prebends converted to monastic use.” Likewise a charter of Emperor Frederick, obtained by Abbot Hugh at Aachen in 1152: “Adding this also by royal munificence to that same church of Saint Remigius, we confirm that the prebend of the clerics of the church of Marsna shall henceforth, upon the death of the clerics, pass without anyone’s objection to the use of the monks.”]

For what were once prebends of canons passed, long ago, by donation of the bishops of Liège and confirmation of Pope Innocent, into the ownership and possession of our monastery. Recently, however, the lord pope, apparently unaware of this matter, has written a second time to our provost of Marsna, instructing him to give a prebend to a certain clerk of the emperor, although the provost cannot give one and there is no prebend that can be given. Inform our lord, therefore, that he should not wish to take the children’s bread and give it to dogs, which do not cease barking against us and taking away our goods [Col. 0538B]. Otherwise we are compelled to say: “Behold, in peace our bitterness is most bitter” (Isa. XXXVIII).

For during the schism they made the most strenuous efforts to bring this about through the emperor, but did not prevail at all.

> [Note: [Col. 0538D] “During the schism.” Before 1177, when the emperor was reconciled with the pontiff.]

## LETTER XCI. TO PETER, CARDINAL OF SAINT CHRYSOGONUS

[VII, 16.] To PETER, cardinal of Saint Chrysogonus, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

> [Note: [Col. 0538D] “To Peter, cardinal.” Legate of the Apostolic See, previously elected bishop of Meaux, as is stated on Letter 117. Letter 117 indicates his legation, and also discusses the same Crispin.]

I pray that the embraces of your friendship, most welcome to me, may not grow old, but may endure eternal days with the tree of life. For friendship is a familiar thing, to be refreshed by daily greetings, indeed watered by mutual conversations, and perhaps renewed by exchanges of gifts [Col. 0538C]. Your graciousness has been pleased to number me among the fellowship of your friends—not by any merit of mine, certainly, but not without your own merit. For it is the merit of equity when the highest bends to the lowest, the great to the small, the strong to the weak.

I consider myself a worm, corruption, already tending toward non-being; while I regard you as honouring the throne of justice with the senators of heaven, and do not doubt that, together with the Apostle, you will judge angels. Is what I say ridiculous rather than true? I affirm it plainly on the authority of Scripture. For “the lips of the priest preserve knowledge, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II).

This is friendly exhortation: let neither Lord nor friend forget that a fall from a height is more serious than one from below. Certainly, friendly concern often moves me to inquire about every aspect of your state, inner as well as outer; and I give thanks to my God, because nothing is reported except what is good, honourable, and fitting to your order and office [Col. 0539A]. I pray that He who began may Himself bring it to completion.

Master Crispin made me rejoice concerning you, reporting matters at which I might rejoice and give thanks to God. He is our clerk and friend; he equally desires to be yours. Behold, he is going to Paris for study, and asks that your name be invoked over him everywhere. This is indeed useful for so great a man, who is almost continually harassed by such great concern for everyone, and who, postponing what is necessary and healthful for his body, often falls into bodily indisposition. I ask on his behalf, and with him, that he may find in your eyes [Col. 0539B] not merely some grace, but good grace, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing.

By “grace” I mean not money. For this, according to the Apostle, is paid to the worker according to merit. Above all, at present he asks this one thing: that from your hand he may receive the first fruits of clerical standing, that is, the tonsure. Having received this sign, he will thereafter rightly regard himself as more bound to your service; and you will rightly provide for the good of one who is, as it were, your plant. I believe, through God’s grace, that each will rejoice in the other and, with God’s aid, will bring forth the fruit of salvation. For I laboured long and urged him by counsels to draw the yoke in the Lord’s threshing-floor and break up the clods behind him [Col. 0539C]. Farewell; and, when you can, inform us of your return.

## LETTER XCII. TO THE SAME PERSON

[VII, 18.] To PETER, cardinal of Saint Chrysogonus, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

I am seldom my own; whose then am I? Perhaps Apollo’s? Perhaps Paul’s? Perhaps Cephas’s? Would that I were! For they have a good table, gentle and fruitful discipline, and finally a singular and permanent gift. But I frequently experience the bench and unjust tyranny of various others: namely Rehoboam, who beats with scorpions; Pharaoh, who afflicts with mud and brick; Nebuchadnezzar, who makes those whom he has ensnared under the yoke of flesh, belly, and gluttony drink the urine of his beasts [Col. 0539D].

Finally, in my captivity and in all the vanity under the sun, I have as a fellow captive a maiden of most noble birth—namely chastity. The wrongful condemnation of her by those whose flesh is as the flesh of asses weighs upon me no less than my own misery. From my earliest age I wished to enter into a covenant of friendship with her, because of her beauty, her most illustrious birth, and also her most peaceful and honourable companionship.

When, therefore, a chaos—or horde—of most filthy men, like pigs, tramples underfoot this most precious pearl fallen from heaven, what peace is there for my bones [Col. 0540A]? What rest for my soul? I cry, “Do not, do not!” But there is neither voice nor understanding. Rather, they add iniquity to iniquity, so that they overwhelm religion together with chastity. Sparing her no pity, they tear out her eyes, turning them toward vain and false madnesses; cut off her nose, overthrowing the moderation of discernment; stop her ears, refusing to keep obedience; cut her lips, becoming accustomed to obscene speech and buffoonery; behead her tongue, rebuking evil and always speaking falsehood; bind her hands, giving no alms and devoting themselves to bloodshed and avarice; and put her feet in the stocks, failing to visit Christ in prison.

What more? Effeminate men strip religion of its sinews: they destroy and despise the abstinence, vigils, psalmody, silence, regular discipline, and cloistered withdrawal from secular affairs of the holy Fathers [Col. 0540B]. Perhaps you say, “What is this to me?” Certainly it concerns you; certainly it belongs to your office; certainly you are bound in duty, so far as you are able, to confront these wrongs with strict censure, lend a kindly ear to these cries, settle these disputes, and, after cutting off Dagon’s arms and head, restore the ark of God to the Bethshemites.

Are you to judge monetary cases and not divine ones? Who sent you? For what purpose did the Lord God appoint you through His vicar, the lord apostolic? For what purpose? That you should loose the ass, that is, religion bound fast, and the colt with her, that is, chastity. “Say,” He says, “that the Lord has need of them” [Col. 0540C] (Matt. XXI). For He who sits upon the cherubim sits upon both.

Do not neglect the Lord’s command; indeed, do not extinguish within yourselves the spirit of Moses, of whom it was said: “I will take of your spirit and give it to the seventy elders” (Num. XI), one of whom God by His grace has made you. But what is the spirit of Moses? A spirit that does not endure injustice; a spirit that kills the wrongdoer and vindicates the sufferer; a spirit that defends the seven maidens, daughters of Jethro, priest of Midian; a spirit that strikes the prince of Egypt with ten plagues and finally drowns him in the sea.

I detain you long, because I cannot do so in person, at least in writing. For it is sweeter to me than honey and the honeycomb to address you and converse with you. Yet the cause and subject of this letter is Master Crispin [Col. 0540D], our clerk—indeed yours as well; for “my people is your people,” dearest friend and lord. I therefore commend him to you as my own bowels, because I have seen his honourable conduct and his inclination toward better things and those nearer to salvation. I know that you have not rejected the companionship of such men. Let him therefore have you as lord; and, having received from you the sign of clerical standing, let him have you as patron and author of this order.

## LETTER XCIII. TO THE BISHOP OF PRAENESTE

[VIII, 21.] To the bishop of Praeneste, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

> [Note: [Col. 0539] “To the bishop of Praeneste.” Bernered, formerly abbot of Saints Crispin and Crispinian and made a cardinal at Rome by Alexander; see Letter 94.]

[Col. 0541A] A subject more troublesome than pleasant and agreeable presents itself whenever paper is taken up to write to an abbot who is my only and former close friend. For my grief is renewed by a sudden, pressing, and burning gnawing of the mind, while separation beyond the mountains intervenes and divides friends’ sight, though not their affection. To this is added the most severe despair of bodily reunion, since perhaps the very swift dissolution of either one of us, soul from body, is at hand.

Good lord now, once sweetest friend, whom will you appoint as your deputy to supply your place at my funeral rites, in closing my eyes, in the final farewell, and in the everlasting conclusion? From whose hands will the Saviour receive my spirit, when I had long chosen your clean hands for this dutiful service [Col. 0541B]? As I see it, another friend must be substituted to perform this office. But why do I complain? Why do I groan? Why do I cloud my face? Who resists God’s ordinance?

Or perhaps did God take Elijah so that Elisha might receive his double spirit? Was not Joseph’s removal into Egypt the salvation of his brothers and of all their descendants? Did not Jesus ascend to heaven before the apostles in order to send the Spirit and prepare dwellings? Behold, a place beside the apostles has been given you by God. What then? Knock, awaken, press on in season and out of season (II Tim. IV), until He who granted the grace of apostleship and a singular blessing for our salvation may pour upon our dryness dew and drops of grace from the holy bones—or rather, from their intercessions.

If this gift is bestowed through you, it outweighs the things lost, and one clause gathers together countless benefits. Give thanks to the lord pope, on account of his favour toward you. Greet for us the chancellor, the bishop of Tusculum [Col. 0541C], the bishop of Albano, Lord Hyacinth, the holy man of Ostia, and whatever other friends we have in the curia.

> [Note: [Col. 0541D] “The chancellor, the Tusculan.” There were five cardinals of the Roman curia. Of these, Albert the chancellor is already known. Letter 96 is addressed to Peter of Tusculum; Letters 50 and 89 are addressed to Stephen. Henry of Albano, formerly abbot of Clairvaux, is mentioned in Letter 80 of this book; Alexander had recently created him cardinal at the Lateran synod. Hyacinth later became pope, called Celestine III. Likewise the bishop of Ostia was Hubald, who succeeded Alexander upon his death and took the name Lucius III.]

## LETTER XCIV. TO THE SAME PERSON

[IX, 1.] To the bishop of PRAENESTE, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

> [Note: [Col. 0541D] “To the bishop of Praeneste.” To Bernered the cardinal. We have already noted on Letter 93 what is here recounted more fully. When the abbot of Saint Crispin had gone to Rome for the council with the bishop of Soissons, he was adorned with the insignia of the cardinalate and given the bishopric of Praeneste. Panvinio calls him Bernard; we have printed “Bernered,” following Cellensis, in whose manuscript only the initial letter was marked, and following Alexander III’s charter for the new monastery near Poitiers, whose copy we saw lists Bernered, bishop of Praeneste, among the subscribing cardinals. In any event, Bernared and Bernard are the same name, just as Medared and Medard, Gildared and Gildard. Letter 96 to the cardinal of Tusculum describes his blessed death, made illustrious by miracles.]

From great and almost inconsolable anguish of heart, and from many reports, I gather that you have broken out into a complaint expressing weariness of your life. [Col. 0541D] Know without doubt that this belongs to a man of too little constancy and prudence. The Apostle, certainly, teacher not only of the gentiles but of all Christians, knows how to abound and how to endure want [Col. 0542A], and how to be sufficient in all circumstances. Would that we shaped our wavering life after this pattern!

Yet I desire to hear the causes of your faint-heartedness—indeed, of your continual complaint—and then I may either disapprove or approve your grief. For a threefold reason or occasion for complaint occurs to me. Either one’s own rashness impels one to do something that ought not to be done; or another’s cunning does; or, to speak in common terms, the intricate necessity of divine predestination does. But one’s own rashness must always be blamed; another’s cunning must be guarded against; a just judgment coming from God must be feared. One’s own rashness needs a bridle, because it is unconsidered; another’s cunning needs counsel, because it is suspect; the heavenly judgment needs fear, because it is most powerful.

I do not excuse myself in my own rashness; I accuse myself when caught by another’s cunning [Col. 0542B]; I groan beneath the blow of God’s hand. Lest my own rashness hurl me headlong again, I consult reason; lest the snare of another’s cunning choke me, I consult a wise man; lest the sword of heavenly severity rage unto utter destruction, I humbly implore. In my own rashness I recognize my frailty; in another’s deceit I invoke the spirit of discernment; in divine scourges I commit myself wholly to God.

I ask you, then, which of these you regard as more suspect: one, two, or all three together? If one, and it is yours, be merciful to yourself. If it is another’s and mine, pardon me: for I acted more from simplicity than cunning when, in order that I might comply with your bishop, I persuaded him to go with you to the council. If that heavenly dispensation has ensnared you, why are you angry with yourself? Why with me? For who are you, or who am I, that either of us could prevent one whom no creature can turn aside or hinder from running his course?

What God thinks concerning us behind the veil of His secret counsel remains unknown to us until it comes forth openly in the event itself [Col. 0542C]. It is ours not to know for as long as it remains His to conceal. We must also wait long-sufferingly; and, when it comes, we must bear it patiently. We must not hurry if He delays; we must not murmur if He brings it forth. Jesus Christ is yesterday and today: yesterday, before He reveals the mystery of His will; today, when He has made manifest the secret of His foreknowledge.

Therefore let all your complaint, thus excluded, be put to rest, where neither rashness appears blameworthy, nor cunning is found condemnable, nor God’s judgment unbearable. For though the Father deprived you of your paternal soil, He honoured you with an exalted throne [Col. 0543A]. Wisdom mixes her wine in the cup, lest it be too hot for the drinker, or again tasteless. She brings exile upon the presumptuous; she grants consolation to the exile. Your consolation is of greater worth than your desolation.

You left a little flock; you received as friends and companions distinguished cardinals. You left a cloistered corner; you acquired the city that is mistress of the world. Who does not know that the rank of abbot is lower than that of bishop? If the bodies of the martyrs Crispin and Crispinian are buried at Soissons, who does not know that the holier relics of Peter, prince of the apostles, and Paul, teacher of the gentiles, are possessed in the city of Rome? If equal things are sought in your exchange, everything, both among what was left and among what was gained, will be found far from equal—except for the affection that torments one person from that which exalts another.

Affection measures all things by itself [Col. 0543B]. Nothing is great in its estimation unless it makes it great for itself and from itself. If affection is calmed, therefore, everything will be peaceful. The mind, from which affection is born, is indeed of wondrous nature; yet wherever its impulse carries it, it draws all things to itself and colours them no less with its own taste or hue. For one who is troubled, nothing is at rest; for one who is bitter, nothing grows sweet; for one who is greedy, nothing is enough; for one who is restless, nothing remains fixed. Conversely, for one who is steadfast no changeable things cause disturbance; for one who is peaceful even stormy things are calm; for one who is kindly even fierce things grow gentle.

Thus God brought to Adam all the animals of the earth and birds of heaven to see what he would call them. For whatever Adam called each thing, that was its name. Beyond doubt it belongs to the mind to judge all motions of heart and body [Col. 0543C], and to impose names upon them. Hence the saying: “Your affection gives your work its name.” It rules the birds of heaven by thinking about things above; it rules the beasts of earth by restraining movements of the flesh; it even rules the fish of the sea by moderating the shifting thoughts of the mind.

It must therefore be cultivated with every care, since without it no motion is good. We must labour lest it be evil, because, if it is evil, there is no evil in the city which it has not done. We must also strive that it may be good, so that, grace cooperating, it may create good things, make peace, and form light.

The letter has detained a friend occupied with his own affairs and those of the lord apostolic for a long time. I therefore ask pardon. For I address one who is very far away, whereas I used to occupy him not for a moment with letters, but for hours in most intimate conversation, sometimes adding many days and nights on either side [Col. 0543D]. Farewell.

## LETTER XCV. TO THE SAME PERSON

[IX, 2.] To the bishop of PRAENESTE, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

Barely can I find room to receive the crowd of thoughts and subjects which press themselves upon me, insisting, seasonably and unseasonably, on coming to you and saying, “Here I am; send me.” Yet among the other young maidens of marrow-filled meditations, that most famous, well-known, and most noble matron—brotherly charity—who from the shoulder upward surpasses and excels all the virtues [Col. 0544A], of whom the Apostle says, “I show you a still more excellent way” (1 Cor. 12), rightly occupies the royal seat; by her brightness she overshadows—indeed, illuminates—all the rest, and commands them to keep their order after her. All things obey her, not only earthly things but even heavenly things themselves; for from her fullness all receive name, power, glory, and honour.

Although I am too small of stature to attain to her, nevertheless I stretch my whole self toward one least fringe of her garment, and do not at all despair of salvation. I possess and recognize her with friends and among friends; and I would sooner rot with worms in the dust of the earth than, through negligence or deceit, break faith once given and friendship once promised.

This matron has two keys: one [Col. 0544B] by which she closes and opens the heart, the other by which she likewise closes and opens the chest of the outer court—that is, the coffer—in the needs of her household. The heart is the ark of the covenant, where the tablets of the testament, Aaron’s rod, and manna are stored. The tablets of the testament are there lest you be ignorant of, or transgress, God’s law. Aaron’s rod, which budded and flowered, is there that you may fear offence, because it is a rod, and preserve grace, because it is leafy and flowering. Manna is there so that, through the spirit of adoption, you may taste and foretaste the glory of hidden sweetness for those who fear God; a single drop of this, at which the sprouting seed rejoices, suffices in the present life, while its abundance is reserved for the other.

Therefore, with every malice and iniquity excluded from the heart, let charity alone walk in her orchard; let her alone feed there [Col. 0544C], and lie down at noon. Let not the evil eye that bewitched the Corinthians and the wicked presbyters see her entering and walking there. Yet when it pleases her, let her summon her maidens from the land of Israel, that they may bring her perfumes of sweetest fragrance and oil of gladness, with which she may sprinkle her bed for the coming of the bridegroom, who produces from his own offspring only heavenly and enduring fruits.

Then she goes out to the garden of nuts, to the garden of her fruits, that she may see the fruits of the valleys and observe whether the vines have flowered and the pomegranates budded: namely, to the garden of nuts, the hermits and recluses; to the garden of fruits, those who live religiously in secular dress; to the fruits of the valleys, those who have chosen to be lowly in the house of God; [Col. 0544D] to the vines, those fervent in spirit; to the pomegranates, those who crucify their flesh with its vices and desires.

For charity places her signs—works of mercy—openly, at the summit, in the outcome of deeds. She places and displays them so that, through outward signs, the truth hidden within may be perceived. Hence: “By their fruits you shall know them” (Matt. 7). Charity distributes her waters in the streets, so that people and beasts may drink, because she is debtor both to the wise and the foolish. Yet she goes out from the heart and returns to the heart, because the horns of the altar proceed from it, and no good work is worthy of reward unless it rises from the root of good will.

Charity therefore supplies both the affection [Col. 0545A] of the heart and the service of action. Affection is hidden; action is manifest. Thus charity has both her secret and her public aspect. In secret she rests; in public she works. She imitates Him who worked for six days and rested on the Sabbath.

But there is a twofold rule of duty. One is considered among friends, another among strangers. One gift is friendly, another general. The friendly gift is required from the heart and kept in the heart. The general gift is taken from the coffer and is not retained there. The stream of love is not dried up by giving what it has; but the coffer is diminished when it is emptied. More precious, therefore, is the gift which neither dries up through outpouring nor fails through generosity. Yet that which is poured out into hand or lap is often sought more eagerly than that which is stored through faith in the marrow of friendship.

For outward and visible things, because they are necessary to human use, are more greatly loved by those whose desire is more tightly entangled in temporal than in spiritual things. But those who, having trampled down the grosser muddy dregs of the flesh, have entered the chambers of the spirit and grown accustomed to refinement in spiritual things, seek in friends grace rather than money, faith rather than outward possession, inviolable truth rather than temporal advantage. For one who possesses a person’s heart—what belonging to that person, or in that person, does he not possess?

Hence it is that in Christ, whom the Father uttered from his heart, whether when he eternally begot him equal to himself or when he decreed that he should be incarnate of a virgin in time, all things are ours, according to the Apostle, who says: “Whether Cephas, or Apollo, or [Col. 0545C] death, or life, all are yours; and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s” (1 Cor. 3).

Perhaps you ask, “What is the point and purpose of all this?” Because I read in your letter that you had lost old friends and had acquired no new ones. I grant that you have lost them, if it is established either by report or in fact that they had grown old. True friendship, however, through virginal purity and enduring warmth, is neither adulterated nor cooled; rather, by daily renewal it rises always with the sun and never dies. Therefore, if you have ever had friends, you still have them—not grown old, which would be a fault, but distant, which is God’s work. For God scatters and sows people like grains. Did he not say, when sowing the apostles: “Go into the whole world and preach [Col. 0545D] the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16)? By coming, he scattered them through evangelical preaching; by scattering them throughout the whole world, he united them in the unity of faith.

Thus the bond of our friendship toward you exists neither broken nor loosened, but extended, uncorrupted and ever new, even to your episcopal seat. I do not know whether absence has bound me more strongly to you—or rather, you to me—but I know that it has bound us more tenderly than presence did. This is a probable and necessary proof of perfect love: affection burns the more intensely [Col. 0546A] the farther a place separates.

Presence comforts itself by sight and is satisfied by use; but hungry absence, through want, supports itself even on the bitter bark of juniper, and is inflamed more vividly and nourished more tenaciously toward its accustomed sweetness of sight. Desire is driven by hard goads when it always seeks and never finds. Hence the Psalmist: “Seek the Lord; seek his face always” (Ps. 104). And in the Song of Songs, the soul, melted away, rises and seeks through the streets and lanes of the city the one whom it loves. Therefore I write to you neither with an aged pen nor with an aged mind. So much on these matters.

Concerning our own condition, I inform you that I have recently felt certain drops of *rostra* [reading uncertain] falling. Our other affairs, with God’s help, are in every respect prosperous. [Col. 0546B] We have unanimously appointed Theobald as your abbot [Note: [Col. 0545D] “We have appointed Theobald in your place.” That is, as abbot of the monastery of Saints Crispin and Crispinian, over which he had previously presided.], and have made Brother John obedient to him in all things—provided that he can remain with your favour, as we strongly advise. For we are certain what he can accomplish where he is with us; what he will do among you, however, we do not know. What is certain ought to be retained rather than what is uncertain.

I am sending you our missal, and we have sent Brother Luke’s breviary. We do not approve your afflicting yourselves excessively in food and drink. If you desire to live and die with us, do not hasten toward death, for you do not know what tomorrow may bring forth. All things are possible with God, who frequently hears the desire of the poor.

## LETTER XCVI. TO THE BISHOP OF TUSCULUM

[Col. 0546C] [IX, 6.] To the bishop of Tusculum [Note: [Col. 0545D] “To the bishop of Tusculum.” Peter. Roger of Howden, discussing the absolution of William, king of Scotland, by Lucius III in 1182, calls him Peter of Pavia—that is, the bishop of Ticinum.], PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

The divine fire is no less perpetual than the holy fire used to sanctify offerings consecrated to God. Therefore upon the altar, where both burnt offerings and sacrifices are daily offered to God for the expiation of sins, it burns continually and perpetually. And what is this but what the Apostle says: “Charity never fails” (1 Cor. 13)?

For hearts pure from pretence and clean from worldly ambition are altars or temples acceptable to Christ. Therefore, with the tongs of your letter, I received in the golden censer of good words the sacred vapours of a furnace long ago kindled by our mutual sight of and conversation with one another. Thanks be to God, because I found not the thick water of diminished [Col. 0546D] affection, but fire itself—not smoking, but flaming—in the inner chamber of so great a lord and friend. I thought it had been choked by the ashes of so many cares and by the variety of succeeding occupations.

Moreover, I had a very serious cause and complaint against you, if I had possessed a just judge. For from whom did you receive the beginnings of acquaintance and affection with the abbot of Saints Crispin and Crispinian, of pious memory, if not from us? Why then did you stone us for our good work? Did you not stone the man whom you shook with so many bitter griefs and afflictions through his absence? Did you not commit against Jacob the theft of Laban concerning his daughters?

Perhaps you do not deny the theft, but call it pious. Yet if it was theft, how was it pious? If pious, how was it theft? I prove that it was theft. For theft is the handling of another’s property against its owner’s will. Certainly he would not have gone to Rome for the council unless I had sent him. Beyond my hope and against my will, you retained him and made him your brother and equal. Yet this pleased neither him nor us. As he often wrote me, he would rather inhabit the cell of Mont-Dieu than occupy an episcopal chair.

What then? God, who has enclosed all things, forestalled my complaints [Col. 0547B] by doing what he is accustomed to do piously and mercifully. He forestalled him with his blessings; and him whom we once had as friend and brother on earth, we now venerate as lord and saint in heaven. For the miracles which God performs are trustworthy testimonies to his holy manner of life. Thus I lay my finger upon my mouth.

## LETTER XCVII. TO BERNERED, ABBOT OF SAINT CRISPIN

[V, 1.] To his dearest friend BERNERED, abbot of Saint Crispin [Note: [Col. 0547D] “To Bernered, abbot of Saint Crispin.” At Soissons, as the following letter will show. There are two monasteries of Saint Crispin in that city, both of the Benedictine order. One was called Saint Crispin Major, and this is the one discussed here; the other, Saint Crispin in the Cave. On Abbot Bernered, see further Letter 94.], Brother PETER, humble abbot of Saint-Remi, wishes enduring well-being.

Perhaps the spaces of night are dearer and more useful to me than those of day. For the daytime, with crowds of abundant occupations summoned from every side and drawn against me, takes my soul from my hands and continually steals me from myself, as violently as deceitfully. But winter nights, by their length, do not produce disgust or weariness, but sometimes confer a double benefit. They grant rest to the body and renew the soul’s old age. They also give freedom to revisit heavenly things, to investigate their inner chambers, and to remember friends. They say to the soul’s thoughts and meditations: “Be still, and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 45). Through their quiet and silence they lead souls even to the third heaven, as holy desires raise them beyond the world, beyond the flesh, above the soul, to the royal seats of the almighty Word. Then, by peaceful reflection, they at once bring down the Son [Col. 0547D] of Man, humbly inclining him toward the abysses of human weakness.

Who, when turning over his own affairs, neglects a friend’s concerns? I would gladly write you more on this subject, but our scribe, Brother Hugh, having snatched away the little sheet, made an end of our writing because the paper had reached its end. Still, I wished briefly to touch upon the word which you sent through Brother John, and to answer so that you may say to that lady, our kinswoman: “The land lies before you; you can do good or evil.” [Col. 0548A] But it is better to do good than evil, because grace and glory follow doing good, whereas punishment and repentance follow doing evil.

Say to her: “A little is better for the righteous than the abundant riches of sinners” (Ps. 37). Tell her, I say, that it is nobler gratefully to receive lesser things from the devout than insolently to demand greater things from the unwilling. Farewell, and pray for us. Bohemond says that the roads are very bad. Keep this letter for us.

## LETTER XCVIII. TO BERNERED THE ABBOT AND THE BRETHREN OF THE CONVENT OF SAINTS CRISPIN AND CRISPINIAN

[V, 2.] To his singular friends and brethren, BERNERED, venerable abbot, and the holy convent of Saints Crispin and Crispinian, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Saint-Remi [Col. 0548B], wishes solemn days and splendid feasts.

It has not been granted me from above to keep the most important Kalends with you in Sabbath-rest on the birthdays of your precious martyrs. Since I do not do what I wish but do the thing I hate, I am almost angry with the cords of my detentions, difficult to loosen because twisted together—not merely by a threefold but by a manifold chain of linked occupations.

There is only one thing left to me, and scarcely that: I write down my bitterness, which I daily experience in the distraction and strain of my spirit, saying to God: “Why have you made me contrary to you, and I have become a burden to myself?” (Job 7). Behold, now the fatted calf is sacrificed at Soissons in honour of the holy martyrs Crispin and Crispinian; behold, the music [Col. 0548C] and choir; behold, there the holy gathering of friends. But where am I, and what am I? Not even a kid of compunction for my sins is granted me.

Yet, dearest friends, preserve and send us a share of your oil of exultation, of the fatness and richness of the visitation from above. For abundant grace from the table of your lords will suffice for us and for you; since, as they did not spare their own souls for Christ even unto death, so God, making the grace of rewards equal to the grace of merits, has nothing that he will refuse to those who pray for the salvation of souls. For now secure in themselves, they are still concerned for those who venerate them. Without doubt they are present with those who recite their sufferings, and especially with those who imitate them.

Pray, therefore, as for yourselves, so also for us; for prayer suffers no loss when shared with more people. Its nature is to abound in effect all the more as it is extended more broadly in affection. Farewell.

## LETTER XCIX. TO THE SAME

[V, 3.] To his lord and dearest friend BERNERED, abbot of Saint Crispin, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Saint-Remi, gives himself wholly to one who is his in all things.

Whenever a little sheet to be dedicated to you is taken in hand, the mind is filled, even if before it was empty of every good thing. For with great tumult and force an innumerable host of diverse subjects, hastening to go forth, crowds together at the gate of exit: one says, “I shall be the first to greet my friend”; another leaps over her, carrying an olive branch in her mouth, and stubbornly seizes beforehand the first embraces of friendship.

Rebecca marvels within her womb at these internal and more-than-civil wars of two brothers—indeed, of two nations. But what wonder if, where the body of perfect and consummate love is, there the eagles of competing affections and motions of the soul gather, striving not to enter but to go out through the narrow gate?

Perhaps what Laban said may occur: that in his country it is the custom that the elder daughters, though bleary-eyed, are given in marriage first. Thus Rachel, of wondrous beauty and most lovely grace, may not lead the dances of leaping—indeed, of greeting—before Leah, her firstborn sister, but may follow last with Joseph and Benjamin. For better, worthier, and more salvation-bringing things do not remain like dregs at the bottom of a cup; rather, like more delicate foods, they are served at the end to remove disgust and renew appetite, because the end of prayer is better than its beginning.

This I desire in myself and in my friend: that your desires may always be new and never grow old, and that we may always press onward toward the prize of the heavenly calling, forgetting what lies behind. For you ought not so much to consider how far you have come as where you must go, where the goal of your pilgrimage is to be set, and where the line must be drawn. I hear that you do this, and I rejoice greatly. Yet take care not to stretch and extend the line too far, lest it break. It is better to stretch than to break. There is measure in things: nothing in excess.

Do I envy you because you run swiftly and well? Not at all. I love your course, but fear failure. He does not gather virtues well who despises the mother of virtues. A virtue which does not preserve the line of moderation degenerates from the stock of virtues. So much on this subject.

Furthermore, because, as I hear, you intemperately desire our trifles, I wish to explain to you what our affairs now are and what labour I have presently undertaken. That successor of ours [Note: [Col. 0549D] “That successor of ours”: Drogo, who had been appointed abbot of La Celle when Peter moved to the administration of Saint-Remi, and who was later deposed from office because of maladministration, as Letter 100 records.] as abbot of La Celle, because he has not increased—indeed, has not brooded over—the eggs [Col. 0549D] which I left there, but has trampled down what was imperfect and destroyed what was complete, I can no longer dissemble. I therefore undertake to attempt and discover whether God may deign to look upon my former labours, either by removing him altogether from the abbacy or at least by correcting him of his folly and changing him for the better. Nearly all the priors are with me, and, I believe, thirty or more of the brethren. Pray that God may show mercy [Col. 0550A] to me and to that house.

Brother Hugh ought to have written this, and promised it for the evening; but he slept as long as Brother Henry wrote these things. For he has no eyes at all. Yet he extols to the heavens and the clouds the goodness and kindness you have shown him. Farewell, for the parchment is failing.

## LETTER C. TO THE BRETHREN OF LA CELLE

[V, 7.] To his dearest brethren [Note: [Col. 0549D] “To the brethren of La Celle”: the priors and monks [Col. 0550D] who, after Drogo’s expulsion, assembled to elect a new abbot. The archbishop whose counsel he urges them to follow is therefore the archbishop of Sens. After Drogo, Girard was elected abbot.], sons and friends of the monastery of La Celle, Brother PETER, called abbot of Saint-Remi, greeting in the Lord.

I have assigned this present letter to supply, among your holy convent, dearest brethren and sons, whatever business my presence would conduct if I were there. [Col. 0550B] For it may more safely state fully and boldly what is neither useless to those who comply nor blameworthy to the writer.

For wherever and about whatever I may wish to act, malicious eyes are not lacking: they interpret perversely and judge malignly matters whose reason they neither grasp nor purpose comprehend. But I set God himself as arbiter and judge of all things done by him: that he may truly determine what is doubtful, effectively bring into execution what has been determined by judgment, and firmly preserve what has once proceeded from his lips.

Through him, therefore, I adjure this solemn assembly of your brotherhood not to let slip from your memory that difficult conflict between wisdom and folly, justice and injustice, in [Col. 0550C] which you laboured painfully but courageously: some advancing faithfully and persevering steadfastly, others failing and turning back, whose glory is in their own shame, since they lied to God, to me, and to you.

Now Drogo has been cast out—lest I say, the dragon—who publicly threatened that with the arms of Judas the traitor, that is, money, he would not merely shake but even tear up earth and heaven. I do not know whether he still drags after himself a third part of the stars; one thing I know: with God’s help he will swallow none of the predestined.

Yet in this matter, because it belongs to God, let not the tow of our frailty arrogate anything to itself by insulting those who, being occupied with war, were not present, or who stood on the opposing side. We should indeed rejoice with trembling, [Col. 0550D] not insult contemptuously over God’s works; for God’s judgments are always to be regarded with fear, and we must never raise our heads while they are sealed in clouds. They make people anxious rather than secure, both in prosperity and adversity.

Therefore let the fear of God be in you, and take to heart what has been done concerning Drogo, lest you do similar things, because you would suffer not similar but worse things. There is a proverb: “The scalded man fears water.” Therefore entrust the whole matter to the Spirit, the Paraclete, and to the counsel of the lord archbishop and religious and wise men, while preserving the freedom of your election.

Let there be no question concerning my own will, for it will never differ from your glory, your honour, and the welfare of your Church. Meanwhile, let the holy observance of the rule blossom anew among you: the virtue of silence, cloistered reading, the strictness of chapter, the order of psalmody, the bond of unity, devout reception of guests; and whatever offspring of justice and honour had vanished into destruction, let it happily return to the proper seat of your conscience.

For Scripture delivers its lord’s command concisely, steadfastly, and faithfully, subtracting nothing from the command laid upon it and adding nothing; yielding not to seducers and believing not flatterers. It counts praise and blame alike. Since, therefore, I know that many are accustomed eagerly to lie in wait to catch me in speech, I have chosen rather to commit our words to writing than to pour them forth in unconsidered utterance. Farewell.

## LETTER CI. TO BERNERED, ABBOT OF SAINT CRISPIN

[V, 8.] To his dearest friend BERNERED, abbot of Saint Crispin, Brother PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi, greeting.

As I sought matter from which to begin a letter to you, scarcely one subject, separating itself from the innumerable flock, came forward [Col. 0551C], smiling indeed at first appearance but lowering its face when it withdrew into the privacy—or absence—of our presence. You ask what this subject may be, so gracious at its beginning and so reserved or timid at its conclusion?

It is certainly the report of your glory. With a cheerful and delighted face it runs through and about cities, castles, villages, and streets among your friends: to the king’s palace, the queen’s chamber, and the bedchamber of our countess [Note: [Col. 0551D] “Our countess,” who shortly afterward became countess of Troyes: namely Marie, daughter of King Louis and wife of Count Henry.]. It also walks through churches in religious garb and with modest countenance, winning over archbishops, bishops, abbots, clerics, and knights, and inclining them in no small degree toward reverence for itself.

But one must fear lest the sun of such great splendour and such rays decline to setting, and it be said: “Weeping will lodge at evening, and joy in the morning” (Ps. 29). For as much joy as flows into friends’ friends from a friend’s holiness and justice, so much grief and sorrow remains among those same persons at the evaporation or emptying out of those virtues.

I see, I see your thoughts tumultuously turning upon themselves and most anxiously considering why your friend writes such things to you. For your thoughts are timid. Do not be anxious, good friend: all is safe; the seals are closed. The north wind, a harsh wind, has not frozen your continence, charity, or our good opinion. As we have had you, so we have you, and so we shall always have you.

If anything in this is to be blamed, blame the bearer of this letter, who not only compelled me to write but also prescribed such a subject. For he recalled to mind those magnificent boasts which you had poured into our ears when you returned from that festival at Troyes, as empty of your own good conscience as you were inflated with vain joy. You said that, above others, you had been welcomed and received by the countess of Troyes, invited to the feast, honoured at table, heard in every request, [Col. 0552B] and returned with a long train of glory.

Beware the tail, since both every praise and every reproach end in the tail—that is, in the end. I ask: what sort of man do you make yourself out to be? If you do these things, make yourself known to the world and to us. For if you are a prophet in Israel, come to us, that by the events themselves we may test your power, prophecy, and virtue. For we shall not believe in the signs which you perform in your own country unless by your fruits we have known you to be a man “whose spirit is in his nostrils.”

Yet your glory has been curtailed because you did not make peace between the archbishop and his opponents [Note: [Col. 0551D] Between Henry, archbishop of Reims, and the canons. There were serious disputes between them; Alexander the pope also contributed his efforts to settle them. In the library of the Church of Reims the editor saw two letters on this matter, one to Archbishop Henry and one to his brother King Louis. John of Salisbury also discusses these same disturbances at Reims in Letter 214.]. Farewell.

## LETTER CI *bis*. TO THE PRIOR AND CONVENT OF SAINTS CRISPIN AND CRISPINIAN

[Col. 0552C]

[VIII, 18.] To the prior and convent of Saints Crispin and Crispinian, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

If there is in me any counsel, any comfort, or finally any consolation, I ought to share it with you without envy; and I desire, by whatever sprinkling of our exhortations, to water among you both newly planted shoots and fruitful trees. For I remember that, when your beloved and most dear abbot departed, I received in his absence, with heartfelt concern, the affections toward you that stood in for his own.

I desire to visit you in affectionate charity, but the chain of concurrent affairs, and the troublesome condition of the weather and journey, delay me. [Col. 0552D] Let the letter supply what my presence cannot accomplish. Therefore, dearest sons, I address and admonish your whole community in the Lord: let no vapour of unfavourable report break out from any of you; let not the fragrance of your most sweet reputation be lost; let not the strictness of the rule, in any degree flowing away through northern coldness, vanish.

For you can preserve more easily what you hold than recover [Col. 0553A] what you have lost or acquire what you have never possessed. But through God’s grace, which goes before and works beforehand, through the holy example and teaching of your good father, and through the cooperation of your own efforts, a heavenly ray has illuminated your congregation inwardly and outwardly with a threefold—indeed manifold—splendour: religious life, reputation, and temporal possessions.

Isaac gave this blessing to Jacob his heir: “May God give you,” he says, “of the dew of heaven and abundance from the fatness of the earth” (Gen. 27). From the dew of heaven spring cloistered religious life and a reputation fragrant with holiness and most sweet. From the fatness of the earth spring a fruitful possession overflowing with grain, wine, and oil.

May this grace make you grateful, not ungrateful, to God. Grace dwells in humble, not inflated, hearts—or else flees inflation. It makes unequal things equal; breaks down lofty things; removes what is exalted; softens rough things; strengthens what is broken; rejects what is counterfeit; gathers the scattered; preserves the gathered; raises humanity to God; and inclines God toward humanity. It flows down from the throne of grace to the throne of holy conscience and causes fruit to spring up thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold.

Although I cannot bestow this grace upon you, I can pray for it. Therefore may it always be with you and in you. Amen. Pray for your abbot and for us. I especially commend Brother John, who has charge of everything.

## LETTER CII. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT CRISPIN

[VIII, 17.] To the abbot of Saint Crispin, PETER, abbot [Col. 0553C] of Saint-Remi.

Wonderful is the nature of true love: it is fiery, yet contrary to fire’s nature it burns more keenly in distant friends than in those set before one’s eyes. You ask why? Because care, the servant of love, as it were lies still while it sees what it loves; but it runs with unceasing force, biting the mind because of the absent friend, saying: “Where is the one whom my soul loves? Is he alive? Is he safe? Is he sad or joyful? Is he afraid or secure? Is he concerned about me or intent upon himself? Is he needy or well provided for?”

With this little fork love stirs and agitates its coals, increases the flame, multiplies the heat, melts the marrow of the bones, and draws the anxious mind after the beloved with a long rope. [Col. 0553D] It draws more strongly, I say, the more distantly it withdraws. Thus Tobit, an old father, sighs and groans for his delayed son, blaming himself that he had not rather accepted the loss of money than sent—or lost—his son for its sake.

Love sleeps silently and sweetly when affectionate concern, seeking information about a friend’s condition, ranges on no wandering excursions. One must believe one who has experienced it. Your absence drives hard—indeed sharp—stings into our hearts, [Col. 0554A] whose piercing I had not experienced while I had you present and heard you often.

Above all, I have one complaint, not with you but against you: you live without moderation, not by exceeding the just measure of living but by falling below it. For the saying, “Nothing in excess,” reproves both more and less. To eat more is gluttony; to eat less is hypocrisy or avarice. The Apostle knows how to abound and how to suffer need. He is trained in all things to live according to rule who neither bends down toward low extremes nor stretches upward toward higher ones, but proceeds well in a straight course.

## LETTER CIII. TO ESKIL, ARCHBISHOP OF LUND

[V, 5.] To his lord and dearest friend ESKIL [Col. 0554B], archbishop of Lund, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Saint-Remi, greeting and the service of devotion.

The most sweet fragrance of your mercies not only refreshes those present with its delightful breath, but also draws to itself those absent and distant, through hope as sweet as it is unconfounded. For who has sought your aid and gone away unconsoled? Who has knocked at your door and found that you did not open to him? Who, seeking a blessing from your hand, has not brought back an abundant gift, as from most opulent treasures?

Among the rest, and from among the rest, is T., the bearer of this letter. Neither the many dangers of the journey nor the many difficulties of reaching you frightened or detained him; rather, the reputation of you spread everywhere throughout the world compelled and urged him to undertake so great a labour. Not, indeed, poverty of possessions, nor lowliness or contempt among his own people, has cast him out into your land, since he is both a canon of Saint Timothy [Note: [Col. 0553D] “Canon of Saint Timothy”: the basilica of Saints Timothy and Apollinaris in the city of Reims, frequently mentioned by Flodoard. As Alexander’s Letter 7 shows, the abbot of Saint-Remi conferred benefices of this church.] and brother of Hildoin, vice-dominus and canon of Saint Mary of Reims.

We therefore ask that he not be disappointed in his hope, lest at some time, repentant within himself and touched inwardly by grief of heart, he say: “My labour and expense have perished.” I, together with the whole convent of Blessed Remigius, am yours; and we pour out prayer to God for you, that your most holy soul may find at its departure the treasures which it has laid up in heaven through the hands of the poor, and, filled with the goods of God’s house, may rejoice in eternal gladness with the holy angels. [Col. 0554D] Farewell.

## LETTER CIV. TO THE SAME

[Note: [Col. 0553D] See Letter 20. Although Eskil was archbishop in Denmark, he also administered the churches of Sweden, because by a decree of Pope Adrian IV granted to Eskil himself, the archbishop of Lund was primate of the kingdom of Sweden. For this reason he had also appointed Fulco bishop for the Estonians.]

Eternal and ancient veins of His mercies and blessings, divine grace, poured out in every abundance, has not yet shut off in these times, although the charity of many has grown cold. [Col. 0555A] For although God still preserves within His Church the hidden and ebbing reservoirs of grace in the minds of many faithful people, He has especially anointed you, as a lamp set upon a lampstand, with manifold oil; from it many little plots belonging to churches, bishops, poor persons, and widows are watered both sweetly and abundantly. For many years past you have not received either God’s grace or His money in vain, binding it up in a napkin or shutting it within the walls of your household. For who, coming to you, has not felt your blessing? Who, however lukewarm, on hearing or seeing your manner of life—your hand extended to the needy, your door open to travellers, judgment and justice held in an even balance, discerning the cause rather than the person—and surveying the whole remaining field of your actions and words, [Col. 0555B] has departed without being warmed, improved, and well instructed? Thanks be to God, who according to His custom makes grace abound upon grace in you, so that the end of the prayer may be better than its beginning, and the outgoings of morning and evening may become delightful. For your hands still drip with God’s spices, which, from the censers of the saints and through the hands of angels, may be borne as a sweet-smelling incense to the nostrils of Him who sits upon the throne of grace; so that those whom, sustained on earth by your goodness and benefactions, thanksgiving has already received, or is yet to receive, in heaven, may receive you into the eternal dwellings.

This poor bishop, Lord Fulco, whom I begot in Christ as a monk through the Gospel, and whom you made a bishop, gives thanks to God with us for your most magnificent [Col. 0555C] generosity. He declares that in you he has the support of his life and pilgrimage, and trusts that he will always have it. You know, lord Father, how harsh a province he has received by lot, and that he has placed his life in his hands, expecting death at all times rather than a long life. You know also that he who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet receives a prophet’s reward. Therefore we send him back to you and commend him to God and to you. We kept him back in an evil time, but now send him back in a good and fitting one, that he may visit the harvest: whether it is ripe for reaping or unripe and needing labour. With your help and through his own work he has put his hand to the plough, [Col. 0555D] to enlarge Christendom and fill God’s granaries with a more fruitful crop. For whatever [Col. 0556A] increase results from his labour is yours—yours—because he lives from what is yours, as God’s labourer and yours; and whatever he can win for Christ contributes to your glory and crown. Therefore the mouth of the ox that treads out the grain must not be muzzled, nor must its straw be taken away.

## LETTER CV. TO THE SAME PERSON

[Note: [Col. 0555D] Concerning Eskil’s shipwreck, which he suffered while voyaging in Danish waters, he writes again in the following letter.]

[VII, 6.] Tossed between hope and resolve, true affection could no longer contain itself within the bounds of patience. Hope urged daily that my most devoted and beloved lord and friend would report his condition. Resolve pressed that no delay should be made in seeking certainty concerning the uncertainty of the adverse event said to have [Col. 0556B] overwhelmed so great a lord. Thus, while my mind laboured amid these storms to the point of weariness, and long considered what ought rather to be chosen, after taking counsel with your beloved son, the abbot of Saints Crispin and Crispinian, I hastened to send our messenger to you, that we might know how the Lord had tested and proved you, both at sea and on land. For He relaxed for a little while the reins of the roaring lion, which He holds in His hand; but He neither broke nor loosed them. Indeed, if God had loosed them, or the devil had broken them, the overwhelming waters would have swallowed you up. Therefore, to rouse any sluggishness that was in you or yours, He justly allowed it to roar; but, to show His fatherly love towards you, He mercifully shut the mouths of the lions and the savage [Col. 0556C] tumult of the sea. God’s justice did not sleep, nor did divine mercy withdraw itself. He willed that the devil should attack, but the Lord only purged sins. The prince of darkness wished to cloud pure faith and most holy devotion; but God, who is light and in whom there is no darkness at all, drew you brighter from the furnace and rendered His gold more precious.

If our beloved Crispin is still alive, we commend him to you most earnestly, together with the son of our John of Bourges and all whom you took with you. Your most beloved abbot of Saints Crispin and Crispinian sends you greeting. Of what is happening among us, I report to my lord that matters are quite prosperous. The archbishop of Sens has become archbishop of Reims.

[Note: [Col. 0555D] “The archbishop of Sens has become archbishop of Reims”: William, son of Theobald the Great. The Old Chronicle, under the year 1177: “William, archbishop of Sens, having been requested by the clergy of Reims after the death of Henry, brother of King Louis, who for thirteen years had most splendidly adorned the church of Reims with palaces, towers, and other fortifications, assumed its governance with the assent of Pope Alexander.”]

Master John [Col. 0556D] of Salisbury, formerly our clerk, has become bishop of Chartres.

[Note: [Col. 0555D] “Master John of Salisbury has become bishop of Chartres”: in the year 1177, as appears in the supplement to Sigebert. The catalogue of the bishops of Chartres must therefore be corrected, since it places William after our John and Peter, whereas he ought to come before them. For William succeeded Robert, who died in 1164. In the fourth year after this, he obtained the archbishopric of Sens. He also retained Chartres and was consecrated in 1168. Concerning his appointment, without naming Salisbury, see near the end of Letter 233; Robert, monk of Saint-Marian, also speaks of it in his Chronicle. Finally, as was said a little earlier, he was transferred to the see of Reims and left Chartres to John in this year. John’s successor was our Peter in 1182; Peter’s was Reginald in 1187. There survives Letter CXXXVI of Stephen of Tournai to the elected Reginald, confirming all this: “As your predecessors, the bishops of Chartres—especially our lord, namely William, Reginald’s uncle, then the surviving archbishop of Reims—and after him the bishops John and Peter, of blessed memory, treated us kindly, so may you likewise treat us with equal, if not greater, kindness.” Likewise the supplement to Sigebert under the year 1177.]

Our community [Col. 0557A] always prays for you. John of Bourges sends you many greetings.

## LETTER CVI. TO THE SAME PERSON

[VII, 13.] To the archbishop of Lund, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remigius.

The image of your love, impressed and engraved by an iron stylus upon the adamantine nail of our heart, flourishes there and will not cease to flourish. For it has sent its root downward, and the continual, daily recollection of your kindness toward your friend—indeed, I might say your servant—does not cease to water it. For grace and friendship wholly occupy the place, fear being excluded and driven out as though it were a hired servant. Hence it is, most reverend Father, [Col. 0557B] that when I offer the first-fruits of my service to the living and true Lord, I also daily set the memory of you, as far as I can, before His propitiation.

Master Crispin has returned to us, made not a little bitter by the draught of the sea, but somewhat restored by your kindness. Among other things, he recounted to us the grim story of your shipwreck: in it the hostile sea swelled against you with most savage pride, an immoderate wind violently dashed back the ship, and the tempest very nearly swallowed you up. I remember Peter walking upon the waves, with a mighty wind coming against him; Paul suffering shipwreck for the third time; Jonah swallowed by the beast, which nevertheless could not keep him. Lord Jesus, where were You? Why then did You withhold Your helping hand? Unless perhaps it was so that, from the remainder of Your cup, [Col. 0557C] which, having tasted in Your passion, You refused to drink, Your ministers and followers might drink their allotted share or draught of that same mixture, to recover health—or rather, their inheritance.

## LETTER CVII. TO THE SAME PERSON

[VII, 17.] To E., archbishop of Lund.

[Note: [Col. 0557D] “E., archbishop of Lund”: he had then entered the monastic [Col. 0558D] life at Clairvaux, after resigning the archbishopric after forty-one years. In the *Deeds of the Danes*: “In the year 1178 Eskil, the second archbishop of Denmark, withdrew and became a monk of Clairvaux. Absalon became archbishop. In the year 1182 Eskil, archbishop, died at Clairvaux.” He therefore lived there four years. Saxo Grammaticus also writes of this retirement in Book XIV of his *Danish History*.]

PETER, abbot of Saint-Remigius.

Of my two eyes, I keep one fixed upon myself, and the other I frequently turn back toward you, dearest Father and lord. What does the eye which remains with me see in me? Certainly many things over which it grieves, weeps, and is troubled unto an excessive suffusion [Col. 0557D] of tears. Certainly creeping things without number; certainly that wicked nation which Ezekiel saw painted upon the wall of the house that he had dug through at the Lord’s command. Finally, certain things unspeakable—not because of the profundity of mystery, but because of the enormity of a corrupted mind. But when does the eye see these things? When it bends down to turn over its own dregs; when it lights a lamp [Col. 0558A] and overturns the house, seeking the lost drachma; when it looks upon the breaches in Jerusalem’s walls and its ruins, to see whether perhaps, with Zerubbabel and Ezra, it may be permitted to repair them. There come into view the traces of caterpillar, locust, grub, and blight, which have devoured all the beauties of the wilderness; hairy creatures (*pilosi*), onocentaurs, screech-owls, apes, and a great forest of phantoms of every kind.

But whenever that same eye raises its eyelids upward and looks toward heaven, it sees the Lord leaning upon the ladder, calling and awaiting one badly sunk in sleep, and saying: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead” (Eph. V); “Lazarus, come forth” (John XI); “Young man, I say to you, arise” (Luke VII); and “Little girl, arise” (Mark V). He likewise extends His hand to Peter when shipwrecked; He meets Saul on the road as he breathes threats and slaughter [Col. 0558B] against the Lord’s disciples; to the prodigal son returning He restores robe, ring, and shoes, prepares a banquet and slaughters the fatted calf, and offers to those fleeing and rescued from iron snares a dense forest of His mercies, in which to refresh themselves.

With such eye-salve the eye troubled by itself is relieved and restored to itself. I now address that eye which, solicitously concerned for you as a friend, surveys our paths and endeavours from youth onward. Tell me, good eye, what occurs to you, what do you feel, what do you understand concerning our friend? “Not without great weariness,” it replies, “do I recall his deeds; for at one time I saw him walking above the clouds and soaring into the densest height. Who could adequately recount that glory, that power, that lordship, that wealth in all things, [Col. 0558C] those gifts and donations so generous and so innumerable? Who could tell of his sea-voyages, his maritime dangers, and the ambushes of mighty robbers? At last that Lucifer, who rose in the morning, who had held a throne of glory and an archbishopric among God’s stars, did not fall from heaven like lightning; rather, like the Son of Man, he emptied himself, took the form of a poor man, and cast aside the spoils of the prince of this world. Thus, should Laban pursue Jacob, he may not find his idols with him; and with the Lord—or at least with blessed Martin—he may say: ‘You will find nothing in me, enemy.’ Behold, thus humbled at Clairvaux, he gathers ears of grain behind the backs of the reapers, glorying not in his labour but humbling himself because of his incapacity. In will [Col. 0558D] and charity he runs with the priors and young men; but in age and weakness he shares the lot of the last, that he may be last in vocation and first in reward. For with the householder, whose every way is mercy and truth, he who was earlier in time is not greater in reward; rather, first in receiving the denarius is he who was later in labour and time.

[Col. 0559A] Is it not so? Truth itself plainly proves this, for He transferred the thief from the cross into paradise before Peter, prince of the apostles, although He had given Peter the keys of the kingdom of heaven. It belongs to mercy to receive one who presumes little upon his merits; but, if need be, to defer one who is secure, and more swiftly to shake the trembling from fear than to admit one already broken under the plough. Behold, most loving Father, I believe my eye has not deceived me. For many others besides it have told me these very things about you. Therefore may peace be with your spirit, and may your soul be with my God. May the end of the prayer be better than its beginning, because every praise is sung at the end. I am wholly yours.

## LETTER CVIII. TO THE SAME PERSON

[Col. 0559B]

[VIII, 1.] To ESKIL, formerly archbishop of Lund.

[Note: [Col. 0559D] “Eskil, formerly archbishop”: now a monk at Clairvaux. The bishop of Auxerre, whom the final part of the letter greets, is Alan; as noted above, he too had long since left his bishopric and returned to the monks of Clairvaux, in 1177, as the Chronicle of Saint-Marian records. Gaucher and Philip, monks of Clairvaux, are also mentioned in Nicholas’s letters.]

PETER, abbot of Saint-Remigius.

Frequent bodily affliction urges us to think of the homeland where there is no sorrow. For the more unhappy is the condition we endure, the happier is that which we hope for. Would that we might already reach its shore! Would that we might escape these waves! We are carried about, endangered, and experience shipwrecks—yet do we delay to depart? Who does not desire the harbour, lest he suffer shipwreck? Who does not cut the rope of a little vessel sticking fast in the shallows, lest he feel the storm? Who neglects his homeland and loves exile? Who flees his father and follows an enemy?

I rejoice that you now hold the harbour and sit [Col. 0559C] at the gate of the holy city, “whose participation is in the same.” Our little vessel still wavers, but I hope for and await your consolation; through our unbroken friendship I possess your whole heart. I adjure you: if you find the Beloved—or rather, if you come to His chamber—tell Him that I languish with love. Believe me: if I came to Solomon’s porch, not to say the Saviour’s sanctuary, I would speak for my friend, petition for my lord, and proclaim in the ears of the Lord of Hosts both what you have done for me and what you have done through me for the poor. I would call Him merciful and address Him as just, saying: “Remember Your word to Your servant” (Ps. CXVIII). For this is Your word: “What you have done to one of the least of Mine, you have done to Me” (Matt. XXV). Behold, the substance of my lord, formerly archbishop of Lund, [Col. 0559D] now a poor man of Clairvaux, is with You through the hands of Your poor. Therefore repay him in return and give him Your substance, he who gave You his own—yet that which You had given him and which he had received from You.

Most loving Father, my heart neither sleeps nor slumbers in remembrance [Col. 0560A] of you. It cries, knocks, and stands at our doors, saying: “When shall I see him whom my soul desires? When shall I come and see him?” The road is long, my feet can scarcely move, my loins are frozen: how shall a friend far away be seen? Therefore a remedy must be sought where consolation is first lacking. I cannot travel, but I can at least write. If the eye cannot see, let the pen speak. Let the letter run upon the parchment, because bodily presence is delayed in its limbs. Let the page report what the tongue cannot. Let the dead image supply what the living and true one cannot accomplish. Let syllables announce our state, since spoken words cannot: I long to see you. May Christ’s peace and God’s grace always be with you. I greet the chaplains, the prior, Lord Gaucher, [Col. 0560B] the lord bishop of Auxerre, Philip, and all our friends. Farewell.

## LETTER CIX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF LUND

[VIII, 19.] To the archbishop of Lund.

[Note: [Col. 0559D] “Archbishop of Lund”: Absalon, to whom both the following letter and many letters of Stephen of Tournai are addressed. Previously bishop of Roskilde in Denmark, he had succeeded the resigning Archbishop Eskil, as noted on Letter 107. Saxo Grammaticus calls him the greatest bishop of the Danes, stating in his preface that he undertook his Danish history at this Absalon’s urging. Like most writers even of that age, he writes *Dacia* for Denmark.]

PETER, abbot of Saint-Remigius.

The breath of virtues and their sweet fragrances are lasting. They neither grow old through long duration nor lessen their scent through distance. Behold: your Denmark lies far from our France. The lands differ in the customs of their peoples, their practices, and their situation. But virtue, whether here or there, changes neither face nor garb, neither fruit nor use. [Col. 0560C] Its form is one and the same in Denmark and in France. What is the point of this? What relevance has writing about the indissoluble and unmoving strength and beauty of virtue to the matter at hand, when it would suffice to give you thanks for the benefits bestowed on our brother and friend Bishop Fulco, and for the fact that so great a lord has extended his service, by his letters, to so unworthy a monk? Yet I count it a sin both to say what is false and to keep silent about what is true. For just as a wicked man is inflamed or puffed up if he is praised falsely, so one endowed with natural and freely bestowed goodness is humbled and more strongly kindled toward better things when he is recalled to himself and confronted with himself by an account that is true rather than flattering. For he fears that he may not be, or may be less than, what is said of him.

For many years, dearest Father, we have heard much about your nobility and energy, and that with most ardent zeal you strive to increase the things of God in yourself and others. I had learned this from a faint report, but our dearest mutual friend, Bishop Fulco, added the fullness of truth and certainty. Would that Phinehas might arise both among you and among us, [Col. 0561A] and that the sons of Mattathias might renew their ancient wars for God’s law and spare themselves not even unto death. May the Holy Spirit pour into you a drop of that burning spirit. Enough has been said to the wise. Concerning what is being done in your regions for the nephews and friends of your predecessor: would that I enjoyed with you the grace and friendship that I enjoy with him; and that, as you succeed him in honour, so you might succeed him in affection. Farewell.

## LETTER CX. TO THE SAME PERSON

[VIII, 20.] To the archbishop of Lund, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remigius.

We give thanks to divine grace for the sweet fragrance of your most welcome [Col. 0561B] reputation. Its abundance overflows so copiously that it rises to heaven and sweetly sprinkles even neighbouring lands. God’s generous hand has given into your bosom—indeed, upon your head—a good measure of oil from the heavenly storehouse, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing. By this oil the lamp of your own conscience is fittingly adorned, and the lamps of your entire province are sufficiently supplied. I know and hold for certain that, unless the foundation of a good conscience lay beneath it, the vapour of so bright and illustrious a reputation would not be so widely spread and prolonged. The ancient shoot of your predecessor did not wither in a single night like Jonah’s gourd. Elijah’s spirit rested upon Elisha—namely, Eskil’s [Col. 0561C] upon Absalon’s. He watered what he himself had planted; nor is it enough for you to water, unless you also add new planting. God, therefore, will give the increase, and neither of your labours will be in vain where the hand of the heavenly rewarder adds grace besides. For God never defrauds His labourer of a worthy reward.
