He mercifully helps the one who labours and justly rewards the worker. Therefore the work is His nonetheless, and so is the gift. The work of the olive cannot lie where the gift of grace works with it. Let the work, therefore, not cease where the reward remaining is utterly certain.

Finally, most loving Father, may not only hope for future things but also that foretaste by which your memory is already commended and entrusted to the prayers [Col. 0561D] of faithful and holy men most urgently suggest living, consoling coals to your mind. Meanwhile, do not wonder that I, unknown to you and from a distant land, am now writing to you for the second time. You have friends and acquaintances near you: Fulco, once our monk and now a bishop, who repeatedly urges and compels me by many persuasions to write to you; and the bearer of this letter, who extols you even to the angels of God.

## LETTER CXI. TO HENRY, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

[Col. 0562A]

[I, 14.] To the venerable lord and dearest Father HENRY, archbishop of Reims.

[Note: [Col. 0561D] “Henry, archbishop of Reims”: brother of the king and bishop of Beauvais; see Letter 21. He was the brother of Louis the Younger and was transferred from Beauvais to the see of Reims.]

Brother PETER, humble abbot of Saint-Remigius, most devotedly offers himself.

Since your presence is always necessary to us and to the whole province of Reims, and since the tribulations surrounding us have now increased and swelled beyond their usual measure, we earnestly and altogether beg you not to delay returning to us. For in your absence your enemies and ours raise their horns, so that there is no peace either for one entering or for one leaving. Without distinction they come in to seize, lay waste, and devour everything upon which they can lay hands. [Col. 0562B] They spare neither monk, cleric, layman, poor person, widow, nor misery of any condition. Therefore may it please your most loving fatherly care to bend your mind to the needs and distresses of your land, which cries out to you and after you.

## LETTER CXII. TO JOHN THE CHANCELLOR AND R., CHANTER OF COMPIÈGNE

[VI, 7.] To Master JOHN, chancellor, and R., chanter of Compiègne.

[Note: [Col. 0561D] “John the chancellor and R., chanter of Compiègne”: they seem to have been in the retinue of the archbishop of Reims, who [Col. 0562D] had set out for Rome.]

The memory of my most beloved lord the archbishop flourishes so diligently in my heart that, not only while awake but even sleeping, I enjoy very frequent visions of and converse [Col. 0562C] with him in his absence—what I cannot now enjoy in his presence. There is no falseness in his love and ours, for I always have him as a most kind and beloved patron. Thus for him, for you, and for all your companions, continual and unwearied prayer is made among us. Concerning our own condition and that of the land, I send you word that everything pertaining to our lord is at peace. For his affairs are well conducted on every side, and his nephews are in good health. Lord Galaran also acts vigorously, as do Lord Thomas the priest, Master Ralph, the archdeacon, and all your friends. One thing only is lacking to us: your presence and that of our lord. We ask that, with his honour preserved, you hasten to restore yourselves to us and to your homeland [Col. 0562D] as soon as possible. Greet all your companions and friends, especially the abbots of Beaulieu and Saint Peter of the Mountains.

[Note: [Col. 0562D] “The abbots of Beaulieu and Saint Peter of the Mountains”: both monasteries belong to the Order of Saint Benedict. The former is in the district of Argonne, in the diocese of Verdun; the latter is at Châlons, and is mentioned again in Letter 89.]

## LETTER CXIII. TO PHILIP, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE

[I, 13.] To his lord and dearest Father PHILIP, [Col. 0563A] archbishop of Cologne.

[Note: [Col. 0563D] “Philip, archbishop of Cologne”: this letter also ought to have been placed much lower down. For Peter was abbot of Saint-Remigius when he wrote it, and it is certain that Philip did not assume the see of Cologne before the year 1166.]

Brother PETER, humble abbot of Saint-Remigius, sends greetings with every devotion.

Together with blessed Remigius, we have often humbly offered prayers to your eminence, if in some way we might bend your mind—hitherto, as we believe, angered with us without fault of ours—toward mercy. Therefore again and again our whole congregation appeals to you with all the supplication humility can offer: if there are in you any bowels of mercy, do not let your hand, stretched out to scourge us, continue still. For by God’s clemency it has been granted you to have power to do us good or, if you wish, evil. Do not forget that the limits which the Lord has set to your dominion are fixed and [Col. 0563B] bounded in God’s predestination. Use, therefore, the power granted you always for good, never for evil; for eternal recompense unquestionably follows either course.

For the love of Jesus, then, and through Christ Jesus, we implore you to have mercy on poor men in fetters, who may neither enter nor depart except under the hand and with the leave of their shepherd. They are oxen treading out grain, beseeching the Lord night and day for their own sins and those of the whole world. Do not muzzle them by withdrawing the sustenance that their predecessors faithfully granted them for the remission of their sins. Certainly this will bring no increase to your reputation and glory, nor any accumulation of riches—only an accumulation of sins.

We answer, therefore, concerning the prebends of Marsna:

[Note: [Col. 0563D] “Prebends of Marna”: more correctly *Marsna*, as in Letter 90. For this is the form in the royal capitularies said to have been issued in 851, when the three brothers—Lothair, Louis, and Charles—met again beside the town of Maastricht, near the place called Marsna; and in the fragment of a French writer published by Pithou, concerning Gilbert: “He received Maastricht, Jupille, Herstal, Marsna, Litta, and Mont Capré, which stood vacant after being left by the dead.” From this it is clear that Marsna was a place near Maastricht, which is true: it is about three Roman miles away and is called Maerssen. The prebends of Marsna assigned to the monastery of Saint-Remigius and converted to monastic uses are discussed again in the letter cited above.]

You [Col. 0563C] commanded us to remove them from our own control and give them to certain persons; but we shall by no means do this for ever and ever. Falling also at your knees, we beg you not to demand this further from us. Farewell.

## LETTER CXIV. TO THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

[I, 10.] To the lord and dearest Father THOMAS, venerable archbishop of Canterbury.

[Note: [Col. 0564D] “Thomas of Canterbury”: while he was still an exile in France and negotiations were being conducted concerning his reconciliation with Henry, king of England.]

Brother PETER, abbot of Saint-Remigius, offers most devoted greeting from his whole heart.

[Col. 0564A] As I anxiously turn over in my mind what subject I should take up when I wish to write to you, scarcely anything comes to hand—not because there is a lack of things to say, but because reverence for the one to whom they are said restrains my hand. For I can say nothing worthy of the strength of your spirit; add nothing to your most steadfast endurance; and, finally, teach nothing to one who sees all things from afar and most fully measures the ends of things and future causes. Or why should I set a heap of chaff before the manger to which the ox clings, sated and fattened with the richest fatness and abundance? Yet I find myself not unworthily reserved for some service in your obedience, if I could drive away the flies that desire to sting your holiness with envious barking, or at least, by perverse interpretation, persist in blackening the sincerity [Col. 0564B] of your faith.

Indeed, those dead flies that abound in Egypt and surround Pharaoh, king of Egypt, as the man of flies, will not, with God’s help, destroy the sweetness of the ointment. For it shall be kept for the day of Jesus’ burial, and from generation to generation it shall be proclaimed that the archbishop of Canterbury, setting himself as a wall for the house of Israel, imitates the footsteps of the ancient saints, while he follows Christ hanging naked on the cross by being naked himself. How, then, with Abraham may I drive away the same flies which seek to defile the undefiled sacrifice of the Lord, unless with the holy winnowing-fan of the authentic Scriptures, by which they may either be struck or at least driven off?

For they say: “The archbishop ought not so insistently to reclaim his property [Col. 0564C] from the king of England, so as to abandon the peace of reconciliation for lost money.”

[Note: [Col. 0564D] “Reclaim his property from the king of England”: the king refused to restore what had been taken. Maurice, bishop of Paris, to Alexander III: “Furthermore, the lord of Canterbury demanded that part of what had been taken from him should be restored, while the other part should be left for his support until he had your counsel and that of religious men on the matter. For it would seem unfitting and greatly damaging to him, and a pernicious example to the holy Church, if he entirely remitted all that had been taken, as the king of England demanded, since during his absence the buildings of Canterbury church had been destroyed; he had scant recourse to its devastated possessions; and he himself was held bound by a most burdensome debt of borrowed money.” Yet he finally prevailed that they should be restored, as he himself attests in the letter which he wrote to Alexander concerning his return.]

They are deceived by the appearance of truth or by the flattery of falsehood. Those deceived by the appearance of truth must be instructed; those led by flattery of falsehood must be repelled. Simplicity must be recalled, and malice wholly cast aside. Yet in every transaction and action one must consider what ought to be done or left undone for the sake of what end. The times and their differing conditions must also be weighed, according to which the merits of cases change. For in the primitive Church patience alone had its place: one was to let him who took the tunic have the cloak also. For the persecutor was one person and in one place—outside [Col. 0565A] the Church—and the sufferer another person and elsewhere—within the Church. But now that the Church is grown up, what was once permitted to its enemies is not permitted to its children. For it is fitting for the mother to correct her son, just as it was fitting for a maiden to endure an adversary.

For the Bridegroom’s belly is read as set with sapphires; and just as before His passion Jesus had said, “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be My disciple” (Luke XIV), so in the passion He says to the apostles: “Let him who has no sword sell his tunic and buy one” (Luke XXII). These are indeed good and consoling words; and a cause just in God’s eyes, though doubtful and weak in the eyes of fools, would rightly demand them, unless the virtue of patience surpassed every consolation, and unless you rejoiced more in consolation than the striking hammer gained by the blow [Col. 0565B] it dealt. Iron sharpens iron, and from the wickedness of the king of England your invincible virtue is made more clearly bright. The more forcefully the press squeezes the olive, the more abundantly it yields oil. Bezalel does not make the beaten lampstand of purest gold in the Lord’s tabernacle unless the sheets have been drawn out by the grinding of file and hammer. The hammer of the whole earth is not yet broken: it is still necessary to supply what is lacking in Christ’s passion in your body.

But whom do I advise? Whom exhort? To whom do I apply spurs? Surely to one who needs a bridle—one who is prepared to travel farther than the road extends, who runs swiftly even past the goal-posts, hindered by no dangers. For he scents battle from afar, counts exile as homeland, because every land is a homeland to the brave. Without labour he labours; without [Col. 0565C] hunger he hungers; without pain he suffers; without bitterness he is fed on gall and wormwood. He is one man among thousands: while the giants groan beneath the waters, he laughs and mocks fortune as her wheel turns upside down. Farewell.

## LETTER CXV. TO R., ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

[VII, 21.] To R., archbishop of Canterbury.

[Note: [Col. 0565D] “R., archbishop of Canterbury”: Richard, successor to Saint Thomas. Saint Thomas’s predecessor [Col. 0566D] was Theobald, who was the first to receive John of Salisbury, later a bishop, into his household.]

PETER, abbot of Saint-Remigius.

Maximum proof of integrity and religious devotion is to draw to oneself and place beside oneself pupils and cultivators of good conduct. Proven virtue delights in the support of its like, daily recovering strength through growth, not only from its native stock but also from offspring sprung from the same womb. Thus it is, holy Father, that, to no small credit of your name, you have summoned Master G., and, as we have heard, compel him—bereft of worldly resources—to nestle in good hope beneath your wings. We know him not through a passing or accidental acquaintance, but through long and enduring neighbourhood and participation in our benefactions. Would that our poverty had sufficed for him, and that neither affection for his homeland nor confidence in your generosity had removed him from us! We have few like him among us, whom learning adorns as greatly as life does. He is worthy of a priest’s side, who does not defile his garments, who sets aside secular allurements for true philosophy. For, together with the grains of philosophy, he also retains its chaff: loving profound thoughts and not rejecting words, reading books and reforming morals. Receive the poor man and make him rich. Let your hand imitate the Maker of the world, who in creation made the earth—formerly empty and formless—so abundantly fruitful and so wonderfully shaped that its offspring are innumerable and its forms incomparable. Your predecessor of most holy memory, Archbishop Theobald, received from our bosom and embrace Master John, bishop of Chartres, needy and poor; but, with God’s help, by his encouragement he advanced him even [Col. 0566B] to the rank of the great men who are on earth. That archbishop has indeed died in body, yet he still lives in his offspring, and in him his most sweet memorial still endures. As you succeeded him and Saint Thomas in the episcopate, so may your most generous beneficence succeed theirs in the case of this Master G. May our prayers avail him; for although you do not know us by sight, yet, if occasion presented itself, you would find us not strangers in service, and meanwhile in good will.

## LETTER CXVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

[VI, 2.] To the Archbishop of Sens, PETER, abbot [Col. 0566C] of Saint Remigius.

Do not consign to oblivion the work of your hands, namely the place called the Valley of God; for a new plantation quickly fails or dries up unless it is aided by frequent watering and cherished with manifold encouragement. The spirit of your son, Brother R., has, as we believe, flown to its own homeland. As you sustained him in paternal embraces while he was in the flesh, so it is right that you should conduct him by your prayers and blessings to the throne of grace. Therefore, since you know that when bread has been removed from the Lord’s table, fresh bread must be put in its place on the Sabbath, we pray that the same affection and protection be bestowed upon the good and religious man whom your dearest friend and son there appointed, by the will of the brethren: the prior of the Valley of Saint [Col. 0566D] Peter. As you know, this house is called a house of prayer. It is therefore necessary that, without delay, it be consecrated with your assistance, so that the place may truly, and not falsely, be called holy. Whatever reward in heaven the servants of God may deserve there by maintaining religious observance, prayer, sanctification, mortification, and other holy practices, will return into your bosom and flow down upon your head; for he who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward. Do not then be reluctant [Col. 0567A] to begin spending some portion of your substance for the uses of the poor, because they will receive you into everlasting dwellings.

## LETTER CXVII. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS

[VII, 8.] To the one and uniquely reverend Father and lord WILLIAM, by God’s grace Archbishop of Sens—indeed, Archbishop of Rheims—Brother PETER, humble abbot of Saint Remigius, greeting and ready service with every devotion.

In the distinguished election at Chartres, God brought forth Master John, a morning star, from his treasures. The most watchful discernment of my lord was present—present at this birth of God’s predestination—and put forth its midwife’s hand, lest God’s unchangeable forechoice should suffer an abortion. God, to you be praise, to you thanksgiving; Archbishop, to you be reward, to you eternal recompense. This is a work admirable for its rarity, incomparable for its singularity, commendable for its purity, and, for its special goodness, worthy of imitation by all. When and where has anything like it been done in the kingdom of France: that, with every form of simony removed, with no influence of gifts at work, with no importunities of dependants stirring an itch in the ears, God’s honour alone and the people’s welfare should be sought in an episcopal election? Surely this shall be written in your breastpiece and shoulder-piece, most loving Father, with an iron stylus and an adamantine point: that in choosing Peter’s vicars no human favour moves you, no partiality, no carnal affection, no greed for money. You chose and consecrated as bishop of Troyes [Note: [Col. 0567D] Bishop of Troyes: Matthew, of whom there survives among the collections of [John] of Salisbury a letter to Pope Alexander on behalf of Saint Thomas, written in the fifth year of his exile, at the beginning of Matthew’s episcopate—that is, in 1169.] a man who honours his ministry. For the Church of Meaux you successively appointed three most honourable men: the lord cardinal [Note: [Col. 0567D] The lord cardinal: Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus. Roger of Howden, under the year 1177: “In the same year Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, legate of the Apostolic See, formerly elected to the Church of Meaux, came into France.” In the lists of bishops of Meaux, after Stephen—whose several letters on behalf of Saint Thomas are also found in [John] of Salisbury—appears Simon, formerly archdeacon of Sens; concerning him, before he became bishop, see Letter 280 of [John] of Salisbury. But Cellensis’s words here make clear that two other bishops-elect preceded Simon.], Master Peter, and Simon the archdeacon. But now, in a superlative act, led solely by the love of God, you have installed in the Church of Chartres a man from another nation. Wherever this Gospel is preached, it will be said that you are the bridegroom’s friend, since you are so truthful and faithful—not now in seeking a wife for Isaac, but in finding Joseph, husband of Mary. Mary is truly honoured in the Church of Chartres. Truly this man John, steeped in the precious blood of the blessed bishop and martyr Thomas [Col. 0567D], fully instructed in divine law, adorned with good morals and pious deeds, well portrayed by the apostolic catalogue of virtues addressed to Timothy, has been made a pillar in God’s Church, for God’s honour and for your perpetual praise. In you the ancient branch of apostolic ordination has put forth green again [Col. 0568A], when sons were anointed in place of fathers—indeed, when, every Sabbath, warm loaves with incense were substituted for loaves.

## LETTER CXVIII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF CHARTRES

[VII, 22.] To JOHN, bishop of Chartres, PETER, abbot of Saint Remigius.

Placed at the crossroads of uncertainty, I can scarcely determine whether I should complain of myself to a friend, or of a friend to a friend. Yet if I do both, I omit neither. For since I find both of us blameworthy, I excuse neither. Who does not know that I am an abbot and you a bishop? Who doubts that until now we have been singularly close friends? A pile of letters, unafraid of sea dangers, bears witness to this, when our friendship formerly revisited itself with most familiar recurrence and an embrace of the arm. Why then has our common pen grown numb—indeed, languished—not merely snoring for four days, but failing after a year’s lapse? Certainly, if the plea of episcopal cares excuses this negligence, it equally defends mine by the same reasoning. Let it be so. Was there no time free for coming or writing—none for loving, none for remembering? Beyond doubt, every action can have some excuse; love has none. If you sleep, love does not sleep. Hence: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song of Songs 5). Whatever occupations and necessities bind you, true love is neither hindered nor fettered. Where is true love? [Col. 0568C] Certainly, many wrap themselves in a purple cloak, like false prophets who come in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravening wolves—or ravening friends. I do not, I do not wish either myself or you to be among those who magnify the fringes of a counterfeit friendship, professing and promising unexpected and incredible things, yet not touching even the smallest matters with their finger. I have never found you, nor have you found me, to be of this kind or flock of friends. For my mouth moves more slowly in promising than my heart in loving. Yet this love of which I speak urges me with its goads to rebuke, neither arrogantly nor falsely, what I hear about my friend. For because of our old friendship, those who have a complaint against the bishop of Chartres approach the abbot of Saint Remigius and present him, as it were, as their master [Col. 0568D] and judge. “The bishop,” they say, “does this and this; he speaks thus, is moved thus; he is so changeable in his promises, so unstable in his words and counsels, so ungrateful for benefits, so quick to anger, so lacking foresight in arranging judgments, so wholly dependent on the will and counsel of one man, insufficiently prudent and excessively greedy.” These are the charges they bring against the bishop. But what, friend, do you answer to what these men bring against you? If you are such a man, you have been changed into another. I did not know you as such; I had not learned you as such; I had not proclaimed you as such. Our archbishop, a most discerning man and a most acute examiner and judge of character, had found, by the evidence of his own eyes through long cohabitation, that Saint Thomas’s disciple had been formed and trained otherwise. Far be it, far be it from me to believe these things; but I should like to have grounds by which I might refute these false vanities and follies! Write back, then, through our most beloved abbot of Saints Crispin and Crispinian, and send an answer both concerning the things which he will tell you on our behalf and concerning what I write.

## LETTER CXIX. TO THE BISHOP OF CHARTRES

[Col. 0569B]

[VIII, 4.] To the bishop of Chartres [Note: [Col. 0569D] The bishop of Chartres: John of Salisbury. The following letter is likewise addressed to him.], PETER, abbot of Saint Remigius.

Whenever the earlier wishes or intentions of a steadfast person are changed in his mind, one must consider whether this happens through fickleness, necessity, or a newly arising affection. If through fickleness, it is inconstancy; if through necessity, fortune; if through affection, the matter must be weighed by reason. For if the affection is vicious, it is depravity; if just, it is virtue and must be admitted. The cause from which affection arises divides it, as it were, between good and bad and gives it its name. A good cause excuses changeableness of purpose; a bad one condemns inconstancy. For one should not [Col. 0569C] withdraw without reason from undertakings begun with reason. Otherwise, in him there is not “yes,” but “yes and no”; and it is said of him that “the fool changes like the moon” (Ecclus. 27). But lest I burden the exceedingly busy ears of the bishop of Chartres, I shall state the business briefly and plainly. Our request to you on behalf of Hugh, our kinsman and friend, canon of Rheims, spent summer and winter before your barred doors, and, very weary and hungry, returned to our bosom. And behold, in the same petition there meets us a dearest friend and kinsman, to be received with fuller affection: G., your archdeacon, who is more ready to serve you at your side and to serve your Church. Therefore let the former yield if the latter succeeds; indeed, in order that the latter may succeed, I too yield in the first request, if I am heard in the second—or rather, let the second be done, and quickly, lest barren years perhaps announce to me a failure of the early and latter rain, and, despairing of harvest, I cease henceforth to plough or to ask anything of you. Farewell.

## LETTER CXX. TO THE SAME PERSON

[VIII, 5.] To the bishop of Chartres, PETER, abbot of Saint Remigius.

[Col. 0570A] It is easy to forgive the faults of friends that happen by chance rather than deliberation. He too easily corrects faults arising from circumstance when he errs through preoccupation rather than contempt. You received our mutual friend, the abbot of Saints Crispin and Crispinian, otherwise than was fitting. In this your circumspection went astray. But this debt shall be forgiven with satisfaction when you come to us and acknowledge your fault. Moreover, a report from Alexander, your friend, has now removed this little cloud from before our face, and has gladdened us concerning your condition. For he is accustomed to speak the truth. He has therefore declared that your condition is prosperous and happy in the affairs undertaken for you, and has driven from our heart the circling ambiguities. What I greatly desire, I believe is not difficult. Therefore I trust his words [Col. 0570B] and rejoice greatly. For I judge nothing that I may think concerning you to be alien from myself. A root long hardened by frost neither suddenly dries up nor withers. Thus far concerning these matters.

## LETTER CXXI. TO JOHN OF SALISBURY AND HIS BROTHER RICHARD

[V, 14.] To his dearest friends Master JOHN and his brother RICHARD [Note: [Col. 0569D] John and his brother Richard: three letters of John of Salisbury to his brother Richard are also extant. At this time, that is, around the year of Christ 1170, at the end of which Saint Thomas was killed, Richard had changed his habit, having assumed a regular one. Therefore Peter henceforth writes to him as a regular canon.], Brother PETER, called abbot of Saint Remigius, wishes abiding joy in peace.

On hearing of the death of the blessed martyr Thomas of Canterbury, I had almost shut up my writing stylus in his tomb, thinking that my dearest John and Richard were buried with him and would meanwhile enjoy no breath of liberty. For a deceptive and highly variable rumour brought us, or asserted to us, nothing certain about you. Therefore, as I judge should always be done in doubtful matters, I waited patiently, though not gladly, for the light of truth, lest I run into uncertainty while holding falsehood for truth—perhaps rejoicing when I ought to mourn, or mourning when I ought to rejoice. Yet, after a long debate with myself, I recovered courage from the unchangeable counsel of the Godhead; and whatever had happened to you after the glorification of the holy martyr, I interpreted in the better sense, because, whether you shared in tribulation or in consolation, I did not doubt that it should be taken as a proof and increase of your faith. For I do not know you to be so weak in faith that you fear to drink the Lord’s cup in suffering, which you frequently drink in remembrance of Christ. At last, from a truthful report of your condition, with every bond released, I offer heartfelt thanks to almighty and most gracious God, who does not take away from you his customary mercies; but, as I believe, because you have sent before you your most beloved patron in heaven, you will doubtless receive another Paraclete in his place on earth. Behold, my sweetest Richard, I burst into kisses upon your face, not without heartfelt affection, considering your changed habit—though I do not know whether your mind has thereby been made better. [Col. 0571A] For what of honour, maturity, piety, charity, or the whole religious life was lacking, when in my eyes and those of our community you were a mirror of goodness and a complete model for emulation and imitation? That over-hasty eagerness to return would never have existed; the dwelling of friendly poverty and of a fellowship dear enough, if you remember, might have sufficed for you. But, O blind human mind, ignorant of the future! Do not stretch your foot outside or beyond the course of divine governance, for to slip is not to be ruled by God, and to go by oneself is to perish. Had you remained with us, you would have been a consolation against almost every trouble, nor would I have believed myself forsaken by God while I kept with me such a pledge of his mercy. But what has been done has been done. Let the distressing bodily absence be a spur to greater desire, and where bodily sight is absent, let prayer continue. Lest I write longer, familiar interruptions follow, which never cease to interrupt the mind’s repose and prolong its labour. As for our condition, I inform both friends of it, and concerning bodily health I say that you may still find me as you left me. Peace is in our community, and we still run our customary course. We are at peace with all people, especially with the lord archbishop. We are not greatly burdened with debts. We have our revenues from the Marne. Our friends and yours are well: the abbot of La Celle, the abbot of Saints Crispin and Crispinian, the abbot of Saint Nicasius [Note: [Col. 0571D] The abbot of Saint Nicasius: this is a monastery of Rheims, close in location to Saint Remigius and of the same order. Its abbot at that time was Guy II, formerly a monk of Saint Remigius, to whom Alexander’s Letter 28 is addressed.], and the priors [Col. 0571C] of Mont-Dieu and of the Valley of Saint Peter. Concerning that question, however, which you raised, good friend, at the end of the Passion of the blessed martyr Thomas, I believe that the answer is by no means unknown to you. Yet perhaps you did not doubt that my mind had also come over to your opinion; but reflect that what God intends to do by himself requires neither human help nor human authority, whereas, where he does not disdain human ministries, he does this for the sake of our benefit or humility. For he could save humankind without any sacrament—that is, without the assistance of visible elements or works—unless he had provided exercises of humility or faith as useful for the salvation of those being saved. I therefore hold definitively that no lighted lamp in God’s hand can by any means be suppressed or extinguished; nor should human judgment be awaited where God’s judgment declares itself by manifest light.

## LETTER CXXII. TO THE SAME PERSONS

[V, 20.] To Master JOHN and his brother RICHARD, PETER, abbot of Saint Remigius.

Setting aside a preamble, I make haste to notify you of our condition. At present it presents an aspect neither sufficiently good nor very bad. I am, however, greatly concerned about the condition of your land, for we hold, as it were, beyond the sea, its keys [Col. 0572A] and pillars—namely, the legates of the Roman curia [Note: [Col. 0572D] Legates of the Roman curia: Albert and Theodinus, cardinals sent to King Henry of England to investigate the murder of Saint Thomas; both are mentioned in Alexander’s Letter 54.]. What they ought to establish, overthrow, open, or close is uncertain both to them and to us. For the whole conclusion of the affair depends upon the arrival and answers of the king of England. Yet I find their temper at present excessively restrained in carrying out their mandate, unless perhaps they are provoked by contempt to leap to a harsher judgment. As to my own condition, I report that, so far as my person is concerned, my health proceeds in its customary course; while as to the common peace and prosperity of the Church, it stands as it usually does. One man, however—Brother Hervey—no longer walks with us. He has gone his own way; may it not be after Satan! If he comes to you, take the horses, and [Col. 0572B] anything else that can honourably be taken away from him.

But concerning your question, Brother Richard, dearest friend, I do not wish to multiply useless circuits and windings of many words. You ask whether guilt which seems to concern the cellarer or provost passes, by a particular and certain derivation, to each individual of the community and ensnares the consciences of all. The prophet says: “The soul that sins shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father that of the son” (Ezekiel 18). Likewise, an authority says: “Those things are not evils which neither entangle the mind nor bind the conscience.” Likewise, the Apostle says: “Whatever is sold in the market, eat with thanksgiving, asking no questions for conscience’ sake” (1 Corinthians 10). From all these authorities it does not seem to me that the heads of individual members are struck if anything has been badly administered by the provost; and it is sufficient for cloistered religious not to know whence comes what they eat or what they wear. For such should be the simplicity of the dove that nests in the clefts of the rock and in the hollows of the wall: with every concern removed, whatever its hand finds in bed or in the refectory, it should receive simply and give thanks to God. But if anyone says, “This is idol-offering”—that is, acquired by robbery, usury, or any other wrongful means—let him abstain. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXIII. TO JOHN OF SALISBURY AND HIS BROTHER RICHARD

[VI, 11.] To Master JOHN of Salisbury and his brother [Col. 0572D] RICHARD.

Ardent desire suffers great loss if, when opportunity is given, gross and sluggish negligence refuses either to flow back from a friend or to receive from a friend even the refreshment of a letter. Let there therefore be an agreement between us which it is not lawful to violate with impunity: that no messenger may arrive or depart empty-handed or with only the briefest greeting. Yet I do not believe that the fleeting times will ever be so empty that we have nothing about which to complain to one another, at least somewhat, whether concerning [Col. 0573A] prosperity or adversity. Certainly most foolish is the excuse of some who, when urged to confession, say that they have nothing to report in confession. Truly, abundance makes such people poor, or the brightness of the sun has blinded them. Let us not, then, become like them by saying that we have no news to report, when neither France on this side of the sea has yet sworn itself to enduring peace and tranquillity, nor your England beyond and beside the middle sea maintains silence after Compline. For then fertile cups are accustomed, both among you and among us, to speak and do things new and old. But let us be silent about this, lest your countrymen become angry, since they are no less intoxicated by inferior drink than ours are by the strongest wine. The Emperor granted us [Note: [Col. 0573D] “The Emperor granted us”: Frederick Barbarossa. More than once, as often happens with distant possessions, the monks of Saint Remigius suffered violence on their estates in the Marne. For a few years ago, by the authority of our king, they were restored by postliminy to a possession of which they had been dispossessed and deprived for several years.] [Col. 0573B] our estates in the Marne. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXIV. TO JOHN OF SALISBURY

[VI, 12.] If I rightly recall the jokes of earlier days, when we were together and wove many jests with one another, among other things I remember that I complained, as it were, about the size of the chasuble of Archbishop Thomas—now a most precious martyr—and asked where it might be found. God made that word come true; indeed, he made laughter for us and for your whole province and ours. Hence it is that Englishmen and Frenchmen alike gather from every quarter at the tomb of the said saint, as for solemn feasts and most abundant rejoicings. May it be granted even to me, most wretched and unworthy as I am, to come, to see God’s wonders, and to worship God in his saint before [Col. 0573C] I die. Even if I could be swallowed up by the gulf of the intervening sea, I should not fear death while seeking life. Meanwhile, however, go in my heart and with your mouth into his presence; and with all your heart and soul pray, for our sins and miseries, to this foster-child of grace, lest, drunk with the immeasurable joy with which he is filled from the breasts of Christ and of the glorious Virgin Mary, he forget us—who once shared with sympathetic heart in his tribulation and who are still, to the extent of our power, most devoted proclaimers of his glory. Thus far on these matters. Moreover, the whole body of our brethren returns to you such thanks as it can for your offering, and embraces more abundantly, and binds more joyfully to perpetual remembrance, him whom, together with your brother Richard, it has numbered among the sharers in its good things from earlier years. We have not yet acquired revenues from it, because no opportunity has offered itself; but we shall work more earnestly to seek one, so that this may be accomplished sooner. As for our glosses, which you retained, we might have borne it somehow patiently, had we not discovered in you, concerning us, faith more minute than a grain of mustard seed. You were with us for so long, and I am amazed—indeed horrified—if, from former deeds and words, you conceived so small a confidence in us that you feared to retain freely from us a little book of the slightest value. Yet because this has thus gone forth from your lips, lest your words be made void, we demand expenditures utterly great and weighty, that it may be done to you according to your faith. The price, however, is without assessment or valuation. I greet the lord bishop of Exeter and commend myself to his most holy prayers. For your brother Richard, whom I love most tenderly and embrace most sweetly, I pray that he may be filled with an abundance of graces from Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit—indeed, from God the Father. For I do not doubt that I share in all his good things. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXV. TO THE SAME PERSON

[Col. 0574B]

[VII, 2.] PETER, abbot of Saint Remigius, to JOHN of Salisbury.

In the letters received from you I never find your pulse uneven or racing because of the fever of a sudden royal disturbance. I should wonder at such an excellent and most excellent disposition of mind, unless long acquaintance restrained my wonder and your condition, long known, had already made greater and better things known to me. Certainly I do not doubt that you are among those, and one of those, of whom it is said: “Wherever the impulse of the spirit was, there they went” (Ezekiel 1). Your choleric and heavenly temperament is made cheerful by its passions, puts forth leaves by its frosts, grows by its overthrowings, recovers strength by its illnesses, and shines forth stronger and bolder through its adverse misfortunes. What then? Shall I console you? But you are not desolate, since you count desolation consolation. Shall I raise you up? But you are not cast down, since when you are cast out, you are lifted up. Shall I prepare some plaster or electuary? But you are neither wounded nor troubled by any suffering. Yet for one struck but not wounded, pushed but not cast down, shaken but not overthrown, I think one should rejoice over his constancy, fear because the battle is not yet finished, and exhort him to perseverance. Behold the furnace, yet the gold does not fear; behold the sea, yet the leaf floats upon it; behold the hammer, yet the diamond is not broken; behold the wind, yet Mount Zion shall not be moved; [Col. 0574D] behold battle, yet the soldier holds his sword. He labours at superfluous expense [Note: [Col. 0574D] “At superfluous expense”: these are words of Ennodius of Pavia, Book II, Letter 22, whom Peter also imitates elsewhere.] who tries to assist the sun with torches. This is known both by learning and experience. Yet if any consolation can be afforded you by me, use it as you please: present or absent, I am yours, and all that is mine is yours. Of your people and their customs, I know well enough that they are accustomed to fill—indeed, overfill—their skins, or rather bellies, with both wine and mead, without reproach; and, like the Hebrews, to circumcise their flesh as a sign that they are Abraham’s seed, without the shame of disgrace.

## LETTER CXXVI. TO THE BISHOP OF AVIGNON

[VIII, 2.] To the bishop of Avignon [Note: [Col. 0575D] To the bishop of Avignon: probably Pons, successor of Geoffrey.], PETER, abbot of Saint Remigius.

The offspring of virtue, ever putting forth branches of its grace, by its benefaction waters new plantings in Christ’s Church just as it waters the ancient plantings of paradise, whenever, upon the death of a religious prelate, a man who is likewise good and honourable is appointed. Thus the fire upon the altar is perpetuated; thus the loaves of the Presence are renewed on the Sabbath; thus sons of the Church are born in place of fathers; thus finally the poles are fitted into the ark which must always be carried. Let us firmly retain, as is fitting, the favour of your predecessor, who, like a pious shepherd and father, while he lived preserved our brethren and what we possess in your episcopate, and defended them as far as he could from attack. We pray that his spirit may be doubled in you, so that neither the flour of governance nor the oil of gentleness may fail in the vessel. You have in heaven a faithful rewarder, blessed Remigius, whose sheep we are; and, if needful and fitting, you may borrow for your use from both our milk and our wool. We therefore send this young man in years, but mature in character as we have experienced, into your region. To him we have delivered and entrusted our priory, together with those things belonging to us in the province. We therefore pray and beseech you to receive and cherish him beneath your wings.

## LETTER CXXVII. TO B., BISHOP OF EXETER

[Col. 0575C]

[V, 4.] To his dearest lord and Father B., by God’s grace bishop of Exeter [Note: [Col. 0575D] Bishop of Exeter: Exeter is a city of Devon in England and became an episcopal see more or less 550 years ago. The episcopal seat was transferred there by Bishop Leofric, having previously been at Crediton. Thus the bishops of Exeter are the same as those formerly called bishops of Crediton.], Brother PETER, called abbot of Saint Remigius, most devoted greeting.

A doubtful proposition becomes clear when debated in questions; aromatic spice becomes fragrant when pounded in mortars; the Church grows under the oppression of evildoers. The virtue also of the good, assailed by the attacks of adversaries, blossoms in flower and fruit. That horse which smells battle from afar says “Aha!” at the trumpet’s sound, and burns all the more fiercely in combat as it is more sharply roused by the clamour poured out on every side. For the strength which it concealed, amassed in a time of peace, it repays with multiplied interest when necessity demands it—so that, if you look merely at the tiny appearance of the grain, you marvel at virtue as though it came from a mustard seed. Virtue then spreads itself in abundant offspring when it is challenged by resisting evils; nor is faith fully discerned unless it is stoutly assailed by the weapon of unbelief. [Col. 0576A] Finally, when does the righteous man—who, confident as a lion, is without fear—glory, except when he gains a testing of himself through some danger, so that he discovers then that he can do something, when an offered hardship has found an occasion for his virtue? Cause makes our martyrs glorious together with punishment, and punishment together with cause. For a long time the power of faith lay hidden—indeed, lay dormant—in your land, where more persons summoned one another to the cup of mixed drink than to the Gospel of apostolic preaching. Whence, then, has religious devotion in your time so blossomed and blossomed anew among you that you have drunk in apostolic spirits and, springing forth openly with complete confidence, say: “It is better to obey God than men” (Acts 5)? Surely they are full of new wine, not strong drink, who, having conceived strength, give skin for skin and all that they possess [Col. 0576B] for their souls. Thus far concerning these things. But if that great beast should vomit you out from your land, a new house is prepared for you among us, with every provision save gold and silver; there you will find, as you please, both an abundance of books and leisure for study. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXVIII. TO THE BISHOP OF EXETER

[Note: [Col. 0575D] To the bishop of Exeter: Bartholomew, as is clear from the letters of John of Salisbury and from Letter 83 of Peter of Blois. Therefore the same man must be meant in Book V, Letter 12.]

[V, 16.] Our mourning is turned into joy when our friend is lifted from earth to heaven. We had indeed conceived a good hope concerning him, had he lived long among us; but now, bishop of Exeter, we have an excellent hope laid up in heaven. You know what and of whom we speak. I do not doubt that you have fully played your part where so great a crime was committed. There remain the eaglets of this eagle, who has flown to the stars, licking his blood and daily making themselves drunk with gall and wormwood. Yet let the hope of things to come, the evidence of miracles, and patience amid present evils be their consolation. Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly away (Psalm 54), and visit the tomb of the precious martyr Saint Thomas? Believe me confidently: I would approach that place to obtain forgiveness for my sins, the place from which his most holy soul was received through his own blood into the fellowship of my saints. You therefore fulfil our part, pray for us, and kindly cherish those sweetest friends of ours and yours.

## LETTER CXXIX. TO THE BISHOP OF CHESTER

[Col. 0576D]

[VII, 10.] To the bishop of Chester [Note: [Col. 0576D] Bishop of Chester: William of Malmesbury, Book IV of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, states that Peter, bishop of Lichfield in the time of William the Elder, transferred the see to Chester, formerly called the City of the Legions because of the military colony stationed there. The priory of Lapley seems to have been situated in that district, not far from the monastery of Buildwas, to whose abbot the following letter is addressed.], PETER, abbot of Saint Remigius.

Your duty, dearest Father, is not to break the bruised reed, nor utterly to overthrow a religious house shaken, whether by true or false report [Col. 0577A], but to support and raise it up. For among people of whatever profession nothing is so holy and perfect, so long as it remains in the same condition, that no fraud or division intervenes. For, as Gregory says, true religion has compassion, not indignation. Hence Jesus, bending down, wrote upon the ground: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at the adulteress” (John VIII). At last He removed the guilt and acquitted the guilty woman—not by favoring wickedness, but by blotting out what had been done and commanding that it not be done again.

Venerable Father and lord, we do not excuse our sins, or those of men who, to the disgrace of their order, do what is unfitting. Yet I judge that those whose life ought to be a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men, if they stumble upon the stone of offence—not through their own desert, but through that of the holy order—should be rebuked more privately, though not more gently [Col. 0577B]. Since the cause distinguishes between person and rule, let the person be corrected while the rule remains intact, lest the name of Christ be blasphemed among the nations. Hitherto monks have customarily been judged in chapter, not in council; among monks, not among priests; by the abbot, not by the archdeacon; with corporal, not monetary, punishment.

You know, I believe, that if your fatherhood, or the diligence of the archdeacon, had made known to us the enormities of our monks, we would have shut neither our eyes nor our ears, but would have corrected their misdeeds according to rule, following the custom of the ancient Fathers. We therefore remove both that prior and his brother from that priory, and appoint, as we believe, good brothers in their place. We earnestly commend them to your fatherhood, so that beneath the wings of your protection they may not fear the rapacity of kites, and that, supported by God’s help and strengthened by your aid, they may repair whatever ruin there is in that house [Col. 0577C].

## LETTER CXXX. TO THE ABBOT OF BELDEWAS

[VII, 11.] To the abbot of Beldewas, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

In conducting the affairs of friends, as much good faith is required as in one’s own affairs. Nor am I unaware that your brotherly concern has devoted effort to ensuring that the business entrusted to your fidelity, begun with a good beginning [Col. 0577D], might be concluded with a better end. Yet Fortune, which is not subject to human choice, often mocks our care and frustrates our intention. For who rules the power of the sea—or rather, who commands the movements of an untamed heart? Hardly anyone can govern the household of his own inner chambers; how then can he govern another’s, which he cannot approach?

Therefore God’s forgiveness is not withheld from us if nothing is omitted in concern for what has been entrusted to us. Accordingly, in exacting what friendship requires, let no one be harsher than he would wish the Lord to be toward himself, whether in demanding what is not due or in remitting it. Having carefully considered and weighed all these matters, I forgive you for the barrenness of our house of Lapelee. You have, I believe, dug around it with your good admonitions, but you could not supply the increase which belongs to God alone [Col. 0578A]. Again I commend to you these young plantings, which, with God’s cooperation, as we hope, will yield a more pleasing fruit from a better stock.

## LETTER CXXXI. TO H., ABBOT OF SAINT HUBERT

[V, 6.] To H., venerable abbot of Saint Hubert [Note: [Col. 0577D] Abbot of Saint Hubert. In the forest of the Ardennes, in the diocese of Liège. Written while the schism was still raging, which he calls a time of wickedness and discord.], P., called abbot of Saint-Remi, greetings.

Everything done in time must carefully weigh the character of the time, together with all its circumstances [Col. 0578B], if it is to have a good end. Therefore, good Father and dearest friend, if you can bring the voyage you have undertaken to the harbor of salvation, do not abandon your abbey. Rather, in this time of wickedness and discord, by suffering and enduring until iniquity passes away, recover your strength; do not cast off, to the injury of yourself and many others, the burden long borne, but lay it down gradually from your shoulders. For if peace and unity were restored to the Church, and there were no abyss between us and you, many things could be done which now cannot be done. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXII. TO E., ABBOT OF STAVELOT

[Col. 0578C] [V, 10.] To the venerable lord and dearest friend E., abbot of the church of Stavelot [Note: [Col. 0577D] Abbot of Stavelot. In the diocese of Liège, in which [Col. 0578D] Saint-Remi held the prebends of Marne. On these, and on Emperor Frederick’s command, which he alludes to, see further Letter 90.], PETER, humble abbot of Saint-Remi, everlasting joy with Christ.

No negligence is good, yet not all negligence is equally blameworthy. For either a neglectful failure to do what ought to be done increases or lessens the fault of negligence, or an unconsidered haste in doing what ought not to be done. Nevertheless, things remote from us and carried out through agents are not punished by us with the same penalty if they are mismanaged as those things which are customarily performed by our own hand and effort.

Hence, lord abbot and dearest friend, the fact that we thought done last year what we now learn is still to be done offers some excuse for us, if our brothers of Marne caused you trouble by not paying the money they owe [Col. 0578D]. Forgive, then, a fault produced neither by pride nor defended by obstinacy. For he deserves pardon who quickly corrects his offence, or who pays his debt to the extent of his ability. The command of the lord Emperor has indeed troubled both your business and ours. We instruct our provost to pay promptly what he ought already to have paid. We thank you for your good patience [Col. 0579A], and inform you that that exchange has never been profitable to us.

## LETTER CXXXIII. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT EDMUND

[V, 15.] To his dearest lord and friend, the abbot of Saint Edmund [Note: [Col. 0579D] Abbot of Saint Edmund. Hugh, to whom the Sarisburian’s Letter 256 and others are addressed. On the monastery of Saint Edmund, in the diocese of Norwich in East Anglia, William of Malmesbury says much in Book II of *On the Deeds of the Bishops of England*.], PETER, humble abbot of Saint-Remi, greetings and devoted service.

For a long time we have been unable not only to write to you but even to send a messenger. The reason is neither hidden nor inactive. It is still in suspense, and among us more doubtful than certain, whether this present letter can reach you safely in any way. Yet whether it perishes or arrives, our love cannot die, because it fears neither man nor fire nor water nor any oppression arising from Fortune’s snares.

You have with you those mediators through whose intervention friendship arose between us; both your heart and ours depend upon their love. In them and through them behold our face, and weigh the affection we bear toward you [Col. 0579B]. We would write more, but we restrain our lips with a finger, because it is uncouth for truth to travel through your lands, where it was recently suffocated and strangled and now no longer dares to appear openly.

## LETTER CXXXIV. TO THE SAME

[VI, 10.] Let not our letter be cheap in your sight, for love commends it. It performs the embassy of a devoted friend and, at small expense, makes up for the impossibility of a most difficult journey. Perhaps, with unwashed face [Col. 0579C] and poorly adorned by the meanness of its garments, it would offend lofty eyes, if they were not friendly. Its stock, therefore, should be considered, not its adornment; for the proof of legitimate birth is worth more than the profitable appearance of adultery and fornication.

Our prayer to you is of the stock of Israel, not marked, or ever to be marked, by the stain of falsehood, as by adultery. It is a great thing to me to possess the friendship of religious men, and precious to retain it firmly. I therefore ask that the mutual offices of our prayers may often, in alternating return, offer one another dove-like kisses, and that the two wings may be joined, by whose aid, God granting it, the palaces of heaven may be penetrated. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXV. TO THE ABBOT OF LATINIAC

[Col. 0579D]

[V, 18.] To the abbot of Latiniac [Note: [Col. 0579D] Abbot of Latiniac. The monastery of Saint Peter at Latiniac, likewise of the Benedictine order, is in the diocese of Paris. Saint Bernard’s Letter 230 [Col. 0580D] on behalf of the abbot of Latiniac survives.], the abbot of Saint-Remi.

I could not, and ought not, fail either our promise or your request. For to one with whom we have once shared our soul, it would be very absurd to deny things that are beneath the soul. It is indeed a plain and evident proof that hearts are not well joined where things possible and worthy to be done are not granted by friends without any intervening reason [Col. 0580A]. Therefore, in this matter and in others, I place myself and what is mine at your disposal, not doubting your goodness, so that, should I at some time request a similar thing from you, it may readily be granted to me.

Yet let your affection know, brother, that we most confidently entrust our uncorrected work to you, urgently asking and entreating that you apply the file of correction: cutting away superfluities, supplying deficiencies, restoring ill-arranged matters to order, and doing with it whatever seems good to you, as though it were your own. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXVI. TO PETER, ABBOT OF SILVA

[Col. 0580B] [V, 17.] To Lord PETER, abbot of Silva [Note: [Col. 0580D] Peter, abbot of Silva. He is called of Silva Major in Book VI. Thus they name the Benedictine monastery in the diocese of Bordeaux, concerning which and its founder Blessed Gerard—then recently enrolled among the saints—Stephen of Tournai, Letter 331. It is distinct from the monastery of Grandis Silva of the Cistercian order in the diocese of Toulouse.], PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

The occasion on which we are compelled to write to you is very welcome to us. For since we would always embrace your presence with all our arms, if God granted it, what wonder if we desire at least once a year to address your absence with some sort of writing? Yet we do not disclose in this letter to our most loving friend what, or as much as, we wish, hindered by that importunity of accumulated business which, with its hostile stepmother’s eye, lies in ambush against nearly all our affections and often takes my soul from me more against my will than with it.

Our request to you concerns your prior of Noyon, an honorable man, of good repute and cheerful fame in our parts. Having been elected abbot [Col. 0580C], he excuses himself from so great a burden, both on account of his humility and because of the difficulty of work which, though he has not yet experienced it, he already dreads as though he had. He has impressed upon our ears that he would rather return to the world than undertake this burden.

I do not, indeed, approve such firmness in the man in this matter—lest I call it obstinacy—for the ordered charity of the Church requires that we minister to one another the grace received, and that, according to the Mosaic law, we avoid that curse which says, “Cursed is the barren woman, and she who has not produced seed in Israel.” Yet elsewhere it is said: “Why do you trouble this woman?” (Matt. XVI); and in the Song of Songs: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not rouse or awaken the beloved until she herself wills it” (Cant. II) [Col. 0580D].

Thus, holding back the foot of our petition and walking amid thorny uncertainty, I leave to your discernment which of the two ought rather to be chosen. Yet I perform the office of one making a request, in declaring to you that a discerning man must in no way be compelled beyond his strength.

## LETTER CXXXVII. TO THE ABBOT OF SILVA MAJOR

[Col. 0581A]

[VI, 17.] Because I once commended myself to your holy prayers and, in return, promised our prayers, such as they are, I rejoice in this covenant and desire with all my strength that it may endure. I received with great joy the glowing and rekindled sparks of this mutual love in your letter; and, as though I had drawn fire from the sacred altar, I filled the censer of my own conscience and offered, as I could, the incense of our devotions.

God knows, and the Lord of knowledge knows, that, presuming nothing upon my own merits, I confidently send, through the prayers of friends, intercessions that discharge an embassy to Him who is still far off, and do not at all hope that they will return empty [Col. 0581B]. According to my faith, then, approach Him who sits upon the throne of grace as one of the mediators and reconcilers of my frailty, and bring back to an unhappy and wretched sinner an abundant blessing from the fullness of graces.

Moreover, for the prior of Noyon, our very familiar friend, and your most faithful servant, I humbly beseech your fatherhood that, as you have begun, you may cherish him in your fatherly bosom, and never suspect anything adverse of him. For his apparently obstinate refusal of the burden of the abbacy did not arise from insolence, pride, or disobedience. He had, indeed, received intimations from the most sacred inner chamber of your heart that he could easily obtain your permission if he chose rather to remain under your authority and as your monk [Col. 0581C] than to seek emancipation and an abbacy. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXVIII. TO THE SAME

[VI, 19.] To the abbot of Silva Major, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

Your priors had already set foot upon the road to come to you when, bidding us farewell, they asked what our humility might send back to your fatherhood. I began to be pressed to decide whether, in so great haste, I ought to greet you with bare words or with some written message. Having obtained the briefest interval, I ran to the scribe, seeking nothing thought out, premeditated [Col. 0581D], or borrowed; but as words came running to my mouth and to the scribe’s hand, so I committed them, unpolished, to writing. For I could not search through either others’ treasuries or our own poor corners.

There was no need to seek long for that word which is near in mouth and heart: the word of love, the word of greeting. For it always stands at the doors and meets every passerby: that I love you, that I am wholly yours, and that I place great confidence in your prayers before God. I know without doubt that I am hastening toward judgment, where truth alone will have a place; but I do not wish justice alone, without mercy, to seize beforehand the gates of judgment. I would rather prepare myself for flight, if I could, than for [Col. 0582A] such a court, in which every human being would be condemned by his own evil desert and none would be saved unless mercy intervened on his behalf.

I believe you have some power with the merciful and just Judge, whether it falls to you to go before or to follow our cause. For He who made His faithful ones has granted them much power with Himself and opened to them the door of His friendship. Let it therefore be the certain hope of my confidence, not empty presumption, that I trust in God’s mercy and in your intercession. Enough on this matter.

I earnestly commend to you your priors, our friends, especially the Norvian prior, and those of Belleval and Saint-Paul; and I entreat you to send them back to us with good favor. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXIX. TO THEOBALD, ABBOT OF MOLÈSME

[Col. 0582B]

[VI, 13.] To THEOBALD, abbot of Molèsme, venerable friend—and would that he were so not in word and tongue but in deed and truth—Brother PETER, humble servant of Saint-Remi, the Spirit of truth.

Your voice is indeed the voice of Jacob; would that your hands were not the hands of Esau. Your words are wind; your letters, a clanging cymbal; your promises, clouds without water; speech without voice; flowers without fruit; fire without heat; water without moisture; body without soul; soul without life. How often, dearest lord, have you been to me a reed staff, when I trusted you and received nothing? How often have you wearied our messengers, not once [Col. 0582C], not twice, not three times, and deceived them with empty and frustrating delays?

Where, then, is that privilege of friendship of which you write? Where is that special affection, that singular fidelity? I judge your common dealings ill when I find your special ones so void and worthless. Why does a man of such authority, abbot of so great a community, monk and priest of the most truthful Christ, not weigh his words in a just balance, so that he may never depart from the rule of truth—he who has professed the Rule of Blessed Benedict, indeed the rule of the Christian religion?

I faithfully and truthfully declare that many inconveniences follow a liar, since everyone recoils from entrusting himself and his affairs to him. If you are willing to assent to my counsel, after changing to a better foundation [Col. 0582D], you will endure longer and better, with prosperity, in your abbey, and will not give your opponents an opportunity for speaking maliciously against you. I shall have what is owed to me when God wills and you are pleased. Yet I have not thereby deserved labor and loss, since, in good faith and for the benefit of your church, I borrowed one hundred pounds from Otranno of Troyes. My former troubles and previous labors, which I underwent in order not to trouble a creditor even for one day, are enough for me. Therefore I shall not come to meet you over this matter. There are people among us who know what we have received from the debt and what we have not. If you come to us, we shall receive you honorably, and especially peaceably, if you bring peace. Farewell.

## LETTER CXL. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0583A]

[VII, 15.] To THEOBALD, abbot of Molèsme [Note: [Col. 0583D] Abbot of Molèsme. From this letter we learn that Theobald had at one time lived among the Carthusians.], P., abbot of Saint-Remi, greetings.

When I think and think again upon your condition, I am almost carried away to—I do not know what to say. Oppressed by great darkness, I am ashamed to say whether I should choose this or that. If I say, “Stand firm,” I fear a fall. If I say, “Cast off the burden you have undertaken,” I fear that I offend God’s providence. Thus Scripture speaks truly: “The counsels of men are uncertain and timid” (Wisdom IX).

What then? Shall I be silent and conceal from my dearest friend what I think of him? Or shall I again, like a blind man, throw a stone and strike where I cannot see? Yet I know that in doubtful matters the more charitable interpretation must always be made, according to the Apostle, who says: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls to his own master; but he shall stand” (Rom. XIV) [Col. 0583B].

I counsel you always to keep before your eyes and to store in the safest place of your inmost heart the former and many labors which you endured in the cell of the Carthusian order for the love of God; and, if it is granted from above, to add new heaps to them every day. For yesterday’s gain never suffices a good merchant. Every day we spend much of what we have acquired; and perhaps in one loss we lose more than we gained in a year. Therefore the Apostle, forgetting what lies behind, always presses toward what lies ahead and, unless he does better and stronger things, sets little value on what he has done.

If, then, the things you do are profitable to you, do what you do. Weigh the profit of your soul; weigh the advancement of those entrusted to you; weigh what has increased for you in temporal matters and what again in spiritual matters [Col. 0583C]. The loss of former quiet must indeed be weighed, to see whether the new gain repairs it. Trust yourself, not me, concerning your good things; for you see and feel them, while I only hear and believe. Your inward matters are known to you because they are near. If your stomach hurts, I do not know unless you tell me, “My stomach hurts.” So no human being knows what belongs to a human being except the human spirit which is in him.

Therefore, with your own spirit—indeed, with the Spirit of God—discern your case and weigh it in a just balance, lest you be false in a deceitful balance, declaring yourself healthy when you are sick, or sick when you are healthy. But every human being is false [Col. 0583D], not only in matters whose hidden depths he does not penetrate, but even concerning himself, whom he fondles with private affection when what ought to be cut away should be bitten off sharply and vigorously. One must therefore apply to oneself the most illustrious mirror of Scripture, in order to know and judge oneself. The rule of truth must be applied—a rule which neither leaves unspoken even a small leaven nor conceals even the least and pardonable sin.

If you sleep among these sheepfolds, if you lie down between these boundaries, if you consult the oracle among these golden, outspread cherubim [Col. 0584A], it will make your steps straight, and you will have no need of Ahithophel’s counsel, which was once made foolish. Thrust your bars within these circles, and, always having the ark of God before your eyes, you will not fear your Philistines, whether spiritual or bodily. On the very day you left us, Brother Henry arrived. We persuaded him to return to you.

## LETTER CXLI. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT-RIQUIER

[Note: [Col. 0583D] Abbot of Saint-Riquier. Centula was once the name both of the place and of the monastery. Later it took, and still retains, the name of its founder, Saint Riquier, in the district of Ponthieu, in the diocese of Amiens [Col. 0584D].]

[VII, 1.] Among the principal concerns of a good shepherd, deliberation and moderation in all his actions hold no insignificant place. For rashness and a sudden disturbance of mind offend the rule of the supreme Judge [Col. 0584B]. He who does not order all things by measure, weight, and number administers all things badly as well. Yet it is more useful and advantageous to correct unlawful things and cut away superfluities than always stubbornly to flow downward toward what is base.

For Peter, prince of the Apostles, who is the best model for all prelates, is said to hold the reins of the kingdom, by which he restrains the impulse of the heart as an untamed colt and compels it to walk with ordered steps. To come to the point: that binding promise by which you bound your monk, that he should in no way return to the monastery over which you preside, so long as your administration endured, except with your permission—you may release it through holy penance, without any shame or guilt of perjury, since it was made somewhat inconsiderately [Col. 0584C].

If, therefore, you assent to our counsel, you will call back the cast-off sheep, and incline your discipline rather toward the right horn of mercy than toward the left of judgment. For mercy triumphs over judgment. Your monk also asks whether such an oath ought to be kept. I answer certainly: it ought not to be kept, unless an extremely urgent and compelling necessity of the case exists. Farewell.

## LETTER CXLII. TO THE ABBOT AND CONVENT OF VILLERS

[VII, 4.] To the abbot of Villers [Note: [Col. 0584D] Abbot of Villers. There is a celebrated monastery of Villers in the diocese of Metz, and another Villers in the diocese of Liège, both of the Cistercian order. It is uncertain whether he writes to the abbot of either of these, or perhaps of another monastery bearing the same name.] and the convent, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

Being guilty myself—not in one matter but in many—I ask pardon for a guilty man and on behalf of a guilty man. I plead not a cause of justice but of mercy; I implore that David’s fountain may be unsealed and opened for one who thirsts and returns from the way [Col. 0584D]. The Jews do not eat an animal taken by a beast, carrion, or pork; but Jesus, the lily among thorns, both frees what was taken captive and saves what was dead, and by His purity cleanses and corrects the uncleanness of swine—He who “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. VIII) [Col. 0585A].

Let the pit beside the altar, which ordinarily receives the remains or excess of sacrifices and burnt offerings, be kept open for us rather than blocked; for the altar itself too was commanded to be hollow and made in the manner of a net, so that it might receive ashes and warm inwardly, even to the soul, the vapors of the flame brought near. Our altar, which is not of this creation but, in the heights, of paternal generation alone, and on earth likewise of maternal conception alone—Jesus Christ—has a belly indeed of ivory, but set with sapphires, so that both by the power of God He may blot out our ignorances and sins, and by assuming human nature may know, from what He suffered, how to sympathize with our infirmities.

He did not will that those holy wounds and injuries received on the cross should be closed in such a way that the channels of pardon and forgiveness might be blocked to sinners; rather, He still has His hands stretched out upon the cross, saying: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI) [Col. 0585B]. Since, then, I write to wise men, may that same wisdom, which never lacks overflowing goodness and abundant generosity, grant me leave to borrow whatever trifles I need from the treasury of your wisdom.

It is neither burdensome to you nor tedious to me to convey these things on behalf of Brother Ansfred—or rather, on behalf of his case—who is returning to you. The cause of his departure was different from that of others who irreverently cast aside the purpose of holy religion and, like a dog returning to its vomit, return to the world (II Pet. II). For the result of a cause proves the cause itself. Having cast aside neither shame nor reverence for his holy profession, he did not mingle himself, like others, with prostitutes in brothels; nor, breaking the covenant of holiness, did he immerse himself in other enormities of secular life [Col. 0585C].

Therefore do not weigh all causes in one undifferentiated manner. Although in the divine mind the cause and reason of all things are held, nevertheless, just as the river that goes forth from paradise is divided into four heads, so from that root of divine ordering the branches of innumerable causes spread out; while it remains the same in itself, it brings forth diverse offshoots in the totality of things that have been, are, or will be. For every event or effect proceeds from its own cause.

Thus, as concerns the present case, Moses’ hand, which he first drew from his bosom leprous, he put back a second time, and it appeared like the rest of his flesh. Similarly, while Brother Ansfred was held within the cloister of your holy congregation, as in Moses’ bosom, no leprosy of criminal sin appeared in him. But when he left the cloister, he appeared as a leper [Col. 0585D]. Therefore, by God’s favoring and active command, returning to Moses’ bosom as to his former husband, he says: “It was better for me then than it is now,” never afterward to leave it except by the abbot’s command or by a heavenly call in the departure of death, when his soul, healthy and whole, such as it came forth from baptism, will return—with God’s favor—to its home [Col. 0586A].

Therefore do not regret having lost him for a time, since you receive him as a brother and monk forever. It will benefit him to have known the snares of the devil, through whose breaking by God’s help his soul has been freed. For we, our brothers, and also the clergy of our castle [Note: [Col. 0585D] The clergy of our castle: the castle of Saint-Remi, namely in the suburb of Reims, where the monastery and several other churches are situated. Even now, though enclosed by the city walls, they call that part the Bourg Saint-Remi [Col. 0586D].] bear him witness that, during the nearly seven years he lived among us, he behaved more religiously in the world than many do in the cloister.

I would add many examples of mercy, if I did not sense that Joseph’s bowels were already stirred to mercy within you, and if I did not fear exceeding the limits of a letter. Yet briefly and concisely I set before him the father of the prodigal son, meeting—indeed, running—to meet his returning son with the fatted calf, robe, ring, and shoes; and likewise Jesus, son of the Virgin Mary, still showing His side and hands to the Apostle Thomas, so that, like a rock, a refuge for hedgehogs, He may receive fleeing young into the caverns and openings of His Passion and protect them from pursuit by the most rapacious kite [Col. 0586B].

May the oil upon your head, therefore, not fail. For after the woman of Zarephath—that is, the Church—fed Elijah, that is, received Christ, the flour of divine mercy did not fail, nor was the jar of oil diminished. Therefore may your breasts not be dry, nor your womb barren. For Christ was not born of a barren woman, but of a maiden full of the grace both of virginity and fertility. Farewell.

A certain well-educated cleric, who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night, Master William, knocks at your door in order to be admitted to the Lord’s banquet or supper [Col. 0586C]. He has a wedding garment, namely one that is poor and humble, not shaggy or ostentatious. Therefore, the poorer he is in substance and spirit, the worthier he is of Christ’s fellowship. I ask you to receive him. Pray for us, because we have kept your shorn sheep well for you and have sent him back with much wool.

## LETTER CXLIII. TO THE ABBOT OF VILLERS

[VII, 5.] To the abbot of Villers, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

It is a friendly gift to take care for a friend [Col. 0586D]. For the gift of the heart is worth more than money. Care fills the heart, not the hand. Hence the concern of love is not removed from the heart as easily as any pledge of material things is quickly shaken from one’s bosom or hand.

When, therefore, I diligently inquired of Brother H. concerning your condition, I heard that you are in the travail of men and frequently drink, with those who are pressed in the winepress, the cup of our sister, which is Christ’s Passion. Bitter indeed is this drink to those who drink it, but it contains within itself the best hope of salvation. For nothing is safer for those going to heaven than to follow the path dyed with Christ’s blood, to behold the footprints impressed by the nails, and always to look before their eyes upon Christ inscribed and set forth [Col. 0587A].

This is the straightest road to the tribunal of grace: a road free of robbers and pursuing its course to Him who is the way for pilgrims, the truth for those advancing, and life for those arriving. Hard are the stones beneath Jacob’s head as he rests upon the road; rough are the flints for one seeking the mountain peaks; thorns and briars prick tender feet; arrows pierce the thigh. But will there not be an end? “You have seen the end of the Lord,” says the Apostle; “you have heard of Job’s patience” (James V).

What, then, lies after the end, what at the end? “I have seen the end of every consummation; your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. CXVIII). At the end, indeed [Col. 0587B], we shall apprehend what are the length, breadth, height, and depth of Christ’s cross. Length: length of days in His right hand. Breadth: that knowledge of God may be as great as love, love as great as blessedness, blessedness as great as God’s sweetness, and God’s sweetness as great as God Himself. Height: in the head of the Nazarite, Jesus of Nazareth, king of angels. Depth: when all things are subjected to Him, except Him who subjected all things to Himself.

These things, dearest brother and lord, your most dear son H. extorted from us by his insistence, unwilling to return from us empty-handed—not from one unwilling, but from one besieged by many cares and troubles.
