Most gladly we saw a new man made from an old, returned from the region of unlikeness to the Father of most merciful heart and most overflowing richness. We earnestly commend him to you as a pledge of our mutual love and as a brother whom I nourished for a while and love greatly [Col. 0587C].

## LETTER CXLIV. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT GILLES

[IX, 7.] To the abbot of Saint Gilles [Note: [Col. 0587D] Abbot of Saint Gilles: a noble and learned man. The monastery is in Septimania, not far from the mouths of the Rhône, and gave its name also to the town; it was first under secular jurisdiction, later transferred to Cluniac discipline and authority.], PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

We frequently send wandering letters rolling this way and that to different persons without any profit. Yet one serious matter redeems many idle ones. A firmly placed column supports even things resting upon it that totter. A diligent merchant compensates several losses with one gain. To come to our matter: “The transgression of the Jews is the riches of the world, and their diminution the riches of the Gentiles.” I have prefaced this in order that I may not write to you without fruit—not fruit that perishes, but fruit that remains. Whatever pleases God remains.

True love, pure prayer, holy compunction, and observance of God’s commandments please God. They make their possessor neither avaricious nor prodigal. They would make him avaricious if he did not bestow love and prayer upon friends [Col. 0588A]; prodigal, if he did not keep compunction and the observance of God’s commandments for himself. Thus Wisdom teaches: “Let your fountains be dispersed abroad in the streets” (Prov. V)—that is, toward others; “Let your fountain be your own, and let no stranger share in it” (ibid.)—that is, toward yourself. He offers well who divides in this way.

Let the letter proceed and, with lowered face, speak what follows. Your nobility and learning, being of flesh and blood, savor of flesh and blood unless the seasoning of religion intervenes. Yet regular observances are set against irregular ones as opposites. Cloistered discipline is reckoned in the habit and form of regulars. Carnal and secular concerns either put off or interrupt the rule. Let the veil of religion cover the shamefulness of slippery carnality; and in the monk-abbot let the windy vanity of nobility be hidden, while the banner of humility shines forth above [Col. 0588B].

Let the conscience, buried under sheep’s clothing, therefore say: “Because I have not known learning, I shall enter into the powers of the Lord” (Ps. LXX). Likewise: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI). True nobility is never proud; secular learning puffs up unless charity restrains it. Behold, a bright lamp has been set upon the lampstand in the abbey of Saint Gilles: if it burns clearly, it illuminates the many regions of those who come; if it declines into darkness or smoky vapor, it offends those who see. Therefore let your light so shine that those who see may glorify your Father who is in heaven.

## LETTER CXLIV *bis*. TO BASIL AND THE OTHER CARTHUSIAN PRIORS

[Col. 0588C]

[V, 9.] To the lords and fathers BASIL, [Note: [Col. 0587D] Basil, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, eminent in holiness of life and learning. To him again, and to the general chapter of the whole order, customarily held each year, he writes Letter 11, on a not dissimilar subject: here, indeed, concerning the establishment of a monastery in Denmark at the request of Esquil, archbishop; there concerning one at Troyes, which Count Henry was contemplating.] and the other priors of the Carthusian order, brother PETER, humble abbot of Saint-Remi, greeting with every devotion.

We know that whenever you assemble, you assemble to glorify Christ. Therefore it is surely right that the direction of your hearts should not be impeded by any secular business. Yet it is fitting to remind you that you should strive to do to the end what you are doing. For the strength of a good work proceeds from the root of good intention, is brought to completion in the perseverance of love, and every praise is sung at the end; indeed, the end of prayer is better than its beginning. I have said this beforehand [Col. 0588D] so that, since you have put your hand to mighty things, you may always strive to stretch it out toward ever greater and more forward-reaching works of charity, in imitation of him who, while he was in the world, by stretching forth his hand healed bodily leprosies, blindnesses of eyes, deafnesses of ears, and the silences of lips.

At last, indeed, stretching out his hands upon the cross, he healed with the antidote of his blood the plagues and wounds of heaven and earth universally; and against every recurrence he stored up, in the wood of the cross, the most powerful medicine in the horn of the cross for all posterity until the consummation of the age, so that whoever bears his cross after him, attaining and sharing eternal life, need not fear a contrary affliction. This brother, the bearer of the present letter, asks through us and many others that workers from among you be sent into the Lord’s harvest. For in Denmark the harvest is already plentiful and white for reaping; but the workers are few—too few even to suffice for eating the lamb. Let it therefore not seem to you tedious, difficult, or hopeless to send some of your number to bear the name of God and your holy order in that land, in hope of receiving a hundredfold fruit—or rather, a thousandfold. Your crown and [Col. 0589B] glory will be greater and more glorious in the sight of God and the holy angels, if God gains many souls through your good example, and in the kingdom of glory your reward comes from the salvation of others. Farewell.

## LETTER CXLV. TO THEOBALD, ELECT OF CLUNY

[IX, 3.] To THEOBALD, elect of Cluny, [Note: [Col. 0589D] Theobald, elect of Cluny. In the year 1180. He was abbot of Cluny for one year only. Afterwards Pope Lucius III created him cardinal-bishop of Ostia. Thus, in the privileges of Urban III and Clement III addressed to Hugh, abbot of Cluny and this Theobald’s successor, Theobald himself subscribes as bishop of Ostia and Velletri.] PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

I received from you a letter full of groaning, as though shaken by the tumultuous collision or complaint of its own inward parts, and as though struck by lightning and tempest. It plainly bore the marks of a man greatly disturbed and terrified, almost lying lifeless beneath the sudden onset of thunder. Nor is this surprising. [Col. 0589C] A new event, by its very novelty as well as its magnitude, could shake even the boldest and strongest man.

He who is led to the cross rightly groans and laments. If the cross is so called from torment, is not he tormented on the cross whose shoulders are placed under an unbearable burden? Certainly from now on you will bear as many millstones as you undertake the care of monks. What then? Will you not say with the Apostle: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11). Here is fear, here anxiety, here torment. But where is consolation? Where revelation? Where is a remedy for such pain? Without doubt, in Christ.

For he is the first to mount, mitigate, and sanctify the cross: by his own torment on the cross he released us from our torments; and from the cross he said, “Woman, behold your son” (John 19), and to the disciple, “Behold your mother” [Col. 0589D] (ibid.). But what has this to do with the matter? What has it to do with the present question? Much, in every way. For the Church of Cluny is the woman: she is the mother of us all; from the fruit of her womb she has already placed many sheaves of holy souls from East and West in the bosom of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; and she has frequently offered to her bridegroom, at the heavenly table, the new fruits of novices and the old fruits of the ancient and aged.

And who is the disciple of whom it is said, “Woman, behold your son,” I think you now perceive. For this saying touches you, because by eternal predestination and present calling the grace of God imposes upon you, by an inviolable decree, the care of this your mother. It is rash and inhuman alike to reject so divine an appointment and to deny faithful service to one’s mother. Therefore, like Issachar, a strong ass, place your neck and shoulders under this election; faithfully trust in God’s help, because the Spirit assists your weakness.

For me, your friend and faithful servant, it is joy and exultation that I have been granted to see so great a friend exalted to so eminent a place. For I too am a servant and son of the Church of Cluny. Farewell; and, I pray, make a journey through our region. [Col. 0590B]

## LETTER CXLVI. TO H., ABBOT OF CLUNY

[Note: [Col. 0590D] H., abbot of Cluny: Hugh IV, who succeeded Cardinal Theobald.]

[IX, 11.] Keeping your memory while not neglecting the watch at the Lord’s sepulchre, I undertake on Holy Saturday a work not forbidden by the Law. For the Law forbids neither reading nor writing. Meanwhile, according to his own Law, I mourn Jesus, proscribed against the Law: outside the synagogue, outside the holy city—then profane—and outside life. But Christ, though proscribed, entered a better dwelling, a dearer people, a holier city, a more pleasing bed, a sweeter table. Why say more? Rejected by the Jews, he was enrolled as King and Lord in heaven. From exile he passed to a kingdom; from those who hated him without cause to those who [Col. 0590C] always serve him freely; from the cross to heaven; from the gibbet of disgrace to the throne of grace.

O gracious patience, how long did I endure a place of reproach, an injurious people? Surely not one day, not one month, not one year, but many years, so that they might repent of what they had done and receive forgiveness. You sleep, Jesus, in the tomb, making no sound either with mouth or nostrils. All things keep the silence of midnight until you arise, until you awake, until you summon back the scattered apostles. Let the cock utter its voice, and sing more sweetly at Christ’s resurrection than at Peter’s denial. Then it sang hoarsely, saying: “My throat has become hoarse from the disturbance of men, from the storm of tempests.” For where on earth was a clear voice when the Word was being smothered—indeed, even beaten—so that truth might be suppressed?

But after a short interval an earthquake came, because the Lord rose; and the cock sang: “The Lord has risen from the tomb.” Not three times, but a thousand times the cock of Christians sings *Alleluia* each night, in every city, in every congregation of saints; it sings both Christ’s death and resurrection. Hence: “At the cock’s crow hope returns,” etc. Another, ineffable [Col. 0591A] cock thundered from heaven, saying: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” (Ps. 56).

O Son, my glory! For a wise son is his father’s glory. Arise: you have slept, you have taken sleep; it is enough. Arise, no longer to sleep, but to keep watch with me in my glory, singing psalms and playing the harp for my neighbors and friends, who gladly, not shamelessly, listen to your voice. Surely, by singing and psalmody you set the harmony of heaven to sleep. Come with your psaltery; come with your harp. Upon the ten-stringed psaltery you shall sing, because you shall be placed above the nine orders of angels together with redeemed humanity.

Strike also in my ears the harp of your Passion, because I condemned him who ought not to have been condemned; and I desire that the devil—that elder brother who killed Abel in the field—may hear my symphony and choir, not to delight in it but to be confounded, and that it may stand for him as testimony of his malice and of my kindness, I who gave my Son in order to redeem a slave.

This portion the Lord has bestowed upon me today from his Passion and resurrection, before we came to our chapter. Dip your bread in the rich broth of the fatted calf, and let your soul be filled, as with fat and richness. Enough of this.

I send brother Stephen, whom you love, with his brother B., on the condition that he may have under his brother the care of our house in Provence, so that I may have you and his brother as guarantors against loss to our goods. For he is new in this office, [Col. 0591C] and he needs good helpers and advisers until he learns to walk on his own.

## LETTER CXLVII. TO HUGH, ABBOT OF SAINT-AMAND

[Note: [Col. 0591D] New.]

*(The Works of John of Salisbury, ed. GILES, Oxford, 1848, octavo, vol. I, col. 192, Letter 136.)*

A point of necessity tests the fidelity of friends and proves the affection by which each is moved toward another. For us, who long ago devoted our whole heart to your service and, God being its author, have preserved that devotion inviolate, there presses upon us a grave and burdensome necessity. We hope and ask that it may be relieved by your favor, in which we place the greatest confidence.

For, perhaps to your surprise, we have been consigned to exile, and in it are continually troubled and tormented by distress. A certain clerk, always most dear to us, whose prosperity and adversity alike have for many years been ours, a man more approved than all others in learning and uprightness of conduct in proportion as he is better known, lives in exile from England among us; and we are exiles in our own home together with him. For he endures the anger of the king of England, not through any fault of his own, to speak according to both our conscience and his, but because he served, as he ought, his lord, the archbishop of Canterbury.

This is Master John of Salisbury, who has a good testimony in lands on this side of the sea and beyond the sea. [Col. 0592A] Therefore, that you may remove from us ourselves the distresses of a personal exile, both present and impending, we earnestly entreat your charity to reconcile him to the king of England through the intervention of the count of Flanders and of yourself; and, as you judge expedient, procure for him the king’s letters patent, by which he may return safely and enjoy his possessions in peace. Know for certain that in no matter can you earn our gratitude more, nor should you pretend otherwise, since it is evident to many that the power has been granted you, if only the will is present.

## LETTER CXLVIII. TO THE ABBOTS OF SAINT-MÉDARD AND SAINT-CRISPIN

To the abbots of Saint-Médard [Note: [Col. 0591D] Saint-Médard: at Soissons, an ancient and noble monastery of Saint Benedict, made especially illustrious by the privilege of Pope Saint Gregory. [Col. 0592D]] and Saint-Crispin, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

[V, 21.] He does not know the nature of true friendship who, in love, imitates a reed shaken by the wind. Friendship without a deep root is an accident, not a substance; an appearance, not a virtue; grass on a roof, which withers before it is plucked. It has three chief handmaids, companions and attendants, without whom it cannot live: justice, patience, and constancy. Justice preserves to each his due; patience, should an injury occur, bears it without violating friendship’s integrity; constancy does not expire through a breach of the agreement, whether in its quality or its extent.

Who then carried away, who seduced, who drove this threefold cord from the most sacred hearts of my lords and friends, the abbot of Saint-Médard and the abbot of Saints Crispin and Crispinian? May such a wicked and unspeakable scandal among God’s servants die and not live—a scandal which sprang from the root of that most ancient serpent, namely most foolish avarice. The occasion of avarice indeed disguises itself in the garments of justice, as Jacob did in Esau’s very good garments, and Jacob falsely declares himself to be Esau.

Yet the Father of all, who seems to have dim eyes when, although he judges and governs all things, injustice oppresses justice and receives no punishment, seems amazed at such human fraud: they do not fear, beneath his eyes, to lie and deceive one another. He says: “The voice indeed is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau” (Gen. 27). Each of the disputants claims to possess an authentic and regular right: “Our church,” he says, “has long possessed thus,” and “ours has thus.” Behold Jacob in the voice.

Then peace of heart is shaken, old familiarity is cast off, eyes are turned aside, the most chaste embraces are loosed, one complains of the other, and the interwoven walls of disciples divide into the fracture of a house. Behold the hands of Esau. Return, dearest friends, return to your heart. The complaint is not great, but the disgrace arising from this discord among your acquaintances and neighbors is great. In the days of your predecessors, neither among the persons nor in the affairs of your monasteries is such concord said to have been found as you have until now cultivated toward one another by a firm and fraternal covenant.

Whence, then, has so sudden and deeply hateful a hostility come? How has execrable and accursed rashness dared to penetrate sacred hearts, so that the bedchambers of peace should be disturbed and the most peaceful repose of both be troubled and assailed out of season? Let the bond of love be immediately restored, lest charity suffer among her own children the loss of even a single day’s prescription—let alone a month’s or a year’s.

For he who says, “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. 4), has laid down a rule of law which it is unsafe to violate. Severe vengeance is exacted from one who perpetually violates the laws of the Gospel. “Why,” says the Apostle, “do you not rather suffer wrong? Why do you not rather endure fraud?” (1 Cor. 6). Religion is defiled where ambition prevails; reputation is stained if property is unjustly taken or acquired; conscience is troubled if it is in any way pricked by the goad of pride. The oil by which the head of the mind is made fat is poured out abroad, if money is held more valuable than justice.

Therefore I interpose the claims of our friendship, in hopes that, recognizing the kinship of your old familiarity, these gaping hearts may again extend to one another the arms of mutual reconciliation. I ask that a day be appointed through your friends, on which concord may be discussed in friendly fashion. Farewell.

## LETTER CXLIX. TO THE PRIOR OF CANTERBURY

[VI, 9.] Both the service of love which you render to all who pass through your region from our side, and the favor you so fully enjoy with our most dear Master John, have made me your debtor. Moreover, the new martyr granted to you by God [Col. 0593C] draws and invites men to the place of his burial. The man whom I knew, beyond other mortals, to be steadfast and founded in the true faith, I believe in my heart and confess with my mouth now to be numbered among the holy angels and martyrs. [Note: [Col. 0593D] “Now numbered among the martyrs.” Pope Alexander decreed by apostolic authority, not long afterwards, that he was to be numbered among them, in 1172, on the first day of Lent, as appears in his Letter 54.]

I myself also trust in his prayers, since God judged me worthy of his blessings, his conversation, his acquaintance, and his friendship. This too adds to the sum of the whole friendship: in that whirlwind and tempest he was saved and preserved through Master John. [Note: [Col. 0593D] “Through Master John”: John of Salisbury, who had been secretary and intimate of Blessed Thomas. Thus, while he survived, Blessed Thomas did not seem wholly to have died.] God did not wish to remove all the stars from your land at once together with that great sun. Therefore a remnant was preserved. Indeed, I may rightly call stars the sons of so great a father and disciples of so great a teacher, shining in learning and life. [Col. 0593D] Would that they were able freely, without interruption from a dark night, to exercise their rays. For your land would seem better and brighter than other lands if it received their teaching.

## LETTER CL. TO THE SAME

[Note: [Col. 0593D] What he says at the beginning of the letter concerning a revelation of the death of Blessed Thomas seems to refer to what has been handed down by many and is found in the letter of William, archbishop of Sens, to Pope Alexander, in these words: “For it is said and constantly affirmed that, after his Passion, he appeared in a vision to many, to whom he declares that he is not dead but alive, and shows not his wounds but only the scars of his wounds.” Concerning the fame of miracles that immediately followed the death of the Blessed martyr, see the letter of King Louis to the same Alexander: “And behold, at the tomb of the champion, as has been revealed to us, divine grace is revealed in miracles, and it is divinely shown where he rests buried, for whose name he contended.”]

[Col. 0594A]

[VI, 18.] I do not recall that the archbishop of Lyons ever wrote to us about a revelation of the precious death of the holy and glorious martyr Thomas. I did hear it, but I have forgotten from whom. I was therefore unwilling to write uncertain things as certain. For the expenditure of a lamp is superfluous where the midday sun shines in its strength, and a small admixture of the leaven of lying and falsehood darkens the majesty of truths. I believe it is more necessary to labor that more miracles supported by sheer truth be removed, for the glory of God and the aforesaid martyr, than that any stolen or begged ones be added.

With every entreaty and petition I beseech both you and all who will hand down to posterity the memory of the wonders of your martyr and ours: let nothing be written about him or his miracles unless it has been examined, purified, and strained sevenfold by the most trustworthy truth.

Concerning a monk of Mont-Dieu named Geoffrey, I report what I heard had truly occurred, partly from himself and more fully from one of our monks, who was then writing there. It happened that a document recording the miracles of Saint Thomas came to us from England, and from us to the brothers of Mont-Dieu. The brother already mentioned was swollen and bloated throughout his body, so that, being truly dropsical, he could not leave his cell. Receiving the document with faith and an invocation of the saint’s name, he touched his feet, shins, and whole body with it, and he shrank so greatly that, after a short interval, he returned to church and to his duties—though not entirely cured.

I add a miracle more pleasant than useful. In our chapel someone, I do not know who, happened to steal the little book read in chapter concerning the feasts of saints and the commemoration of our dead. The next day, when according to custom I called for the lesson to be read from that book, the troubled chaplains could not find the book. As I rebuked those chaplains for negligence and careless custody, one of them, named Robert the Englishman, who frequently celebrated Mass at the altar in which relics of Saint Thomas are kept, burst out: “Certainly I shall never believe Thomas to be a saint unless he restores our little book.” [Col. 0594D] Almost a month later the book was returned to us. If this is a miracle, I affirm that it is true. Farewell. Greet the holy community and Master John.

## LETTER CLI. TO THE PRIOR AND BROTHERS OF CANTERBURY

[Col. 0595A]

[VII, 20.] To the prior of Canterbury and the other brothers, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

Blessed is the occasion that reminds me to write to you. I certainly judge myself wretched for the sloth that keeps my old age from visiting the one who was once a friend and is now our lord, father, and patron—Saint Thomas, God’s precious martyr. On one side conscience rebukes me; on the other it excuses me. “If Archbishop Thomas were living in the body,” conscience says, “would you not go and visit him? Would you not set aside even the dangers of the sea and shake off all lethargy, in order to visit your friend and exchange mutual conversations?”

On the other hand it replies: [Col. 0595B] “But you are a monk, an abbot, old, and weak in body. It belongs to a monk not to go forth from the Lord’s camp—indeed, from the cloisters of his monastery; it belongs to an abbot to manage with care the temporal and regular concerns entrusted to him; it belongs to an old man to lean upon his staff beneath his olive tree, fig tree, and vine, and to ponder ancient days and keep eternal years in mind. It belongs to a weak man to turn himself in his misery while his spine is broken, and daily to say: ‘Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ’” (Rom. 7).

While these thoughts, by their argument, thus accuse and excuse me, the balance of equity inserts itself between them and settles the dispute, so that neither need blush at the conclusion, but each yields to the other in good peace. For it is pious to go, and pious not to go. Good is the pilgrimage accompanied by holy devotion; yet religious also is the remaining behind, to which pious remembrance is continually present, and whose intention burns the more ardently because it is not satisfied by its desire.

Would that an angel might carry me to the saint’s tomb as Habakkuk was carried to the lions’ den—not to bring Daniel food, but to bring back remission of sins! Meanwhile, I appoint as substitute for my absence Master G., whom the lord archbishop of Canterbury has summoned to himself. I therefore commend to you this same G., our commendable friend and clerk, who feels in himself the affection, mercy, and kindness that you bear toward us—not for our merits, but through your gratuitous goodwill.

Certainly, if for our sake you open to him the first gate of your friendship, I believe that eager foretaste will be followed by hunger, and you will at once say: “We now love him no longer because of your word; for we ourselves know him and know that he is worthy of friendship and companionship among good men.” Receive him, therefore, as an honorable and well-educated clerk, so that in your midst I may possess this little branch as successor to that great tree which has been transplanted to the church of Chartres. For Master John was our foster-son; and may this man be likewise!

## LETTER CLII. TO THE PRIOR OF WORCESTER

[Note: [Col. 0595D] To the prior of Worcester: Ralph, to whom John of Salisbury writes Letter 205, and our author Letters 153, 154, and 155, dealing with the priory of Saint-Remi at Lappelee in England.]

[Col. 0596A]

[VI, 21.] The variety of affairs and times, which surrounds us everywhere and on every side, does not allow us to stand with a firm step in the same place—sometimes through our own fault, sometimes through another’s. For when we wish to remain in the same resolve and plant our foot firmly, the course and incursion of another’s instability frequently rushes in and takes possession of our purpose of stability.

Hence it is, dearest friend, that against the purpose and desire of your heart we are compelled to remove Brother P., prior of Lappelee. For as often as we receive travelers from overseas regions, we hear bad reports about that priory. Cloistered brethren and servants, roused in one outcry, declare [Col. 0596B] that the house is perishing, the priory reduced to nothing, and kept in utter poverty. What more? There is no monk there; only the prior is left, half alive and gasping.

Therefore we send from our side Brother Absalon, whose competence we have tested in many matters. By his diligence, if God’s grace attends him, we hope that those ruins may be repaired and turned to better things. We commend him to you so that, supported by your counsel and help, he may vigorously fulfill what has been entrusted to him, to the honor of God, the salvation of his own soul, and the benefit of our church. Farewell.

## LETTER CLIII. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0596C]

[VII, 9.] To the prior of Worcester, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

I am not accustomed to make major arrangements suddenly or precipitately, but only after much deliberation of mature counsel and weighing of the outcomes of causes. Hence it is, dearest friend, that I do not immediately believe every spirit, because of him who transforms himself into an angel of light and often offers the poison of deceit beneath the cloak of deliberation. Yet it is a fault both to believe everyone and to believe no one.

Following, therefore, the example of him who knows all things before they happen, and yet descended through angels to ascertain whether the outcry of Sodom which had risen to heaven was fulfilled in deed or not, I long hesitated to assent to the daily reports about our brothers of Lappelee, hoping either for better fruit from the fig tree or awaiting judgment like the noon-day. But because the smoke of ominous report grows more frequent, not rarer, I lay the axe to the root of the tree—not cutting it down, but raising its branches, bowed, indeed bent, all the way to the ground—in hope that, when raised, they may once more bear grapes rather than wild grapes.

I send from our side brothers who have thus far been of unimpaired reputation among us. If the past gives signs of the future, we believe their manner of life will be good and honorable in your land. [Col. 0597A] Let your hand and counsel be with them, so that anything lacking in them may be supplied for the good government of our house and the restoration of its worthy reputation.

## LETTER CLIV. TO ING., PRIOR OF LAPPELEE

[IX, 5.] PETER, humble abbot of Saint-Remi, to ING., prior of Lappelee. [Note: [Col. 0597] Perhaps Ingelbert or Ingelram, whom he had placed over the priory of Saint-Remi at Lappelee in England.]

In your letter you ask to receive my own pen, not another’s. But dull, blunted, and finally covered with grime and rust, how can it cross the sea with any face, when by its rusticity it is more likely to provoke laughter than to delight its guests? Our pen too, weakened by age and disuse, as well as obstructed and bound by constant worldly concerns, sounds hoarsely and no longer charms its hearers, but unpleasantly disturbs them.

Nevertheless, lest I reject or disappoint the small request of a most dear son and friend, borrowing subdued rhetorical colors and setting aside elegance of expression, while keeping before my eyes the days of the Lord’s Passion, I urge you with Jesus to share his insults, sufferings, scourges, spittings, and the whole course of his most patient dispensation, by which he descended for us even to hell.

Bring before your eyes Jesus wounded from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head; or lead your mind to the place and hearth where Peter denied him. What marrow of the heart would not melt and fill with its own sprinkling the whole altar, both brazen and golden? “I shall offer you sacrifices full of marrow,” says the Psalmist (Ps. 65). [Col. 0597C] The marrow of the soul exists only through the infusion of grace. If the soul, though lean, is hungry and thirsty and eagerly laps up the drops of grace in evening, morning, and noon—at evening, conformed to the likeness of Jesus’ death; in morning, renewed with Jesus rising; at noon, transferred with Jesus to the Father’s right hand—then certainly it will be intoxicated by the abundance of God’s house, saying: “Let my soul be filled as with fat and richness” (Ps. 62).

Why should it not be nourished by the fatted calf? Why should it not be intoxicated by the river which gladdens the city of God? You have wine pressed from the true vine in the winepress of the cross and drawn through the opened door of his side. For just as a barrel is bored through to obtain wine, so Christ’s side was opened by the soldier’s spear, that there might flow out the water of baptism and the blood of our redemption. This we receive daily at the altar under the appearance of wine.

The altar, indeed, is a place of pasture, of which it is said: “In a place of pasture the Lord placed me” (Ps. 22). And in the Song of Songs: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon” (Song 1). What is “at noon”? In light, purity, truth, and charity. Whoever lies hidden like a serpent in the grass, concealing his sins, is not at noon. Whoever lives shamelessly and violates God’s temple with some uncleanness is not at noon. Whoever is deceitful and fraudulent, having an appearance of piety while denying its power, is not at noon. Whoever grows lukewarm in brotherly love is not at noon.

Christ therefore does not feed him, nor feed with him, who says: “With the proud and insatiable of heart I did not eat” (Ps. 100). Nor does he lie down except where he feeds. But enough of this for the moment.

If you wish to know of me: I am daily weighed down, as is my accustomed way, by the burden both of years and of sins. Yet through God’s kindness and mercy I am still able to endure and somehow manage the business of my office entrusted to me. I also have good peace with our brothers, with the archbishop, and with all people. I have undertaken to restore the head of our monastery; with God’s help, the work already begun smiles upon us and promises noble beginnings for the work to follow.

It has not escaped my memory that you once said to me, rather reproachfully, that I was intent upon undertaking other works and did not care for the monastery. Though you said this word casually, I did not hear it casually. For I have spent a thousand pounds, and then another five hundred, on the work of the monastery. I greet Brother Dudo. I rejoice in the good fragrance of your manner of life.

## LETTER CLV. TO THE PRIOR OF THE VALLEY OF SAINT PETER

[VI, 14.] Concerning your question—whether a truly penitent person can, with a clear conscience, answer one who reproaches him with old crimes: “It is nothing,” or “I do not know what you are saying”—would that I had more time and freedom to write! Yet I shall answer what occurs to my mind in passing.

True confession and full satisfaction indiscriminately submerge all Egyptians like lead in mighty waters, so that only the Israelite—that is, the virtue granted by God—escapes, while the Egyptians—that is, the reproach of sin—are removed from conscience and from the mark of disgrace. For just as in baptism no remnants either of original or actual sins remain afloat, so in confession darkness is illumined and night is changed into day, so that to one truly converted and confessing it may truthfully be said: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.”

And as the same Apostle says of Christ, “Even though we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (2 Cor. 5), so let it be said of this person: even though we knew him as a sinner, liar, murderer, adulterer, unjust and impious, once all iniquities have melted in the furnace of confession, let him be refashioned in the image of holiness and called good, truthful, innocent, chaste, just, and devout. Scripture says: “Turn the wicked, and they shall not be” (Prov. 22)—that is, they shall not be wicked. For as blackness is removed when whiteness comes, so malice is removed when goodness comes.

Jesus never healed anyone only halfway; he measured his grace to no one with an unjust measure, so as not to receive in the full embraces of mercy one who offers his whole self to God. “The gifts and calling of God are without repentance,” says the Apostle (Rom. 11), because grace once granted by God is not recalled, except from the ungrateful. For in him there is “is”; there is no “is and is not,” but only “is.”

Therefore, when one truly confessing and truly repenting is endowed with these privileges, what evil eye would dare say that God’s judgments are not just and his works blameworthy? “Is your eye evil,” says the Lord in the Gospel, “because I am good?” (Matt. 21). Thus the last—that is, those occupied by the gravest sins—will become first through correction; and the first, who think themselves righteous, establishing their own righteousness, will become last—that is, empty of God’s grace.

On the authority of these passages we may properly maintain that one truly penitent may truthfully answer a person reproaching him with old abominations, exterminated—or rather, made old and erased—through confession: “I do not know that it is as you say,” or, “What you say is nothing.” For God judges each person according to his present condition, and God does not set the former scars of sins against anyone to shame him whose youth, like the eagle’s, has been renewed by a renewal of life. [Col. 0599B] Whatever the Judge forgives, an adversary cannot impute. Hence the Apostle: “If God is for us, who is against us?” (Rom. 8).

For God stands not merely with the penitent but even for the penitent. Thus, concerning the woman caught in adultery and brought to him for condemnation, he said: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her” (John 8). When she had been released by that judgment and was asked, “Woman, has no one condemned you?” and replied, “No one, Lord,” he said, “Neither do I condemn you.” Could she not rightly say with a clear conscience, “I am not what I was; I am not an adulteress”?

Yet it is more regular and modest to answer a reproachful accuser thus: “You might better say this,” or, “May God forgive you this sin,” or words of that kind. Follow the example of Jesus: when he was told, “Do we not rightly say that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” he simply denied one charge, saying, “I do not have a demon,” and was altogether silent about the other. Enough of this.

The abbot of Saint-Crispin will shortly come with us to Mont-Dieu and asks that you meet us there. If you can, therefore, do what a friend asks, because then we shall be able to discuss everything better, both with one another and with the prior. Ellandus, canon of Saint Mary at Reims, bequeathed you a mark and a half of silver for making a chalice. Pray for his soul. Farewell.

## LETTER CLVI. TO THE BROTHERS OF MOLISME

[Col. 0599D]

[VII, 14.] To the brothers of Molesme, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

Sitting shattered beside the tomb of our Order with Jeremiah’s Lamentations, I am deeply afflicted by its fourfold alphabet, because it now reeks with the stench of four days. This Order was once born of a great stock and noble lineage: a most prudent trainer even of angelic powers in moral conduct, a perfect despiser of worldly things, and a fitting lover of the divine will. This—this—extended its arms from sea to sea, bearing in its embrace men from every nation under heaven up to the throne of grace, and setting them upon the thrones [Col. 0600A] vacated and abandoned by Lucifer when, like lightning, he fell into the pit of filth and misery. O holy angels, how many shoots from this vine have you carried away to yourselves; how many have you caused to sit with you in heavenly places in Christ through the cloistered order?

Alas, alas! Catch the foxes that destroy the vineyards: the wearers of cowls who move the boundaries set by the Fathers and plunder the hedge of regular observance. These are they who break the Lord’s nets, who divide the Lord’s garments, who with the spear of their tongue pierce the side of the Order now hanging on the cross; they blow the entrails of religion out into the air, and extinguish whatever vital breath remained. Thus sons take arms against their father; thus the offspring of vipers cruelly tear at their mother’s womb; thus, by disordered living from their very birth, they open a gaping grave for the Order which they profess [Col. 0600B].

I believe that you are moved against the authors of such barrenness whenever, looking beside you upon the crown of holy spirits and blessed souls, you remember the former age and its great fruitfulness that filled your bosoms. If Phinehas were present, perhaps he would appease this wrath with his dagger. But behold: each man puts his sword into its sheath, and there is none to gird himself to avenge his father’s blood. Hence the world is full of cowled men and almost empty of monks. Hence, in the Lord’s threshing-floor, chaff is not winnowed but cherished; thorns are not uprooted but multiplied.

I, I myself, one of the cowled, see this iniquity—and what do I do? I cannot restore the dead Order to life; and with what patience shall I celebrate its funeral rites amid parricides? [Col. 0600C] I cannot restrain its headlong course toward the abyss; must I then become the companion of thieves? All indeed run—not for the prize, but toward evil—and what of me? With the Apostle, I wished to be accursed from Christ for my brethren. Who will grant that I may die for you, most holy Order? In your presence princes once ceased to speak and laid their finger upon their mouth. Young men hid themselves when you sat in the gate, and rose up; nor did they dare add to your words.

Now those younger in time mock it, because Isaac grew old and could not see clearly; David grew old and could not be warmed by garments. But when Moses was one hundred and twenty years old, he suffered neither dimness of sight nor looseness of teeth. And although those who profess the Rule, although those who have the appearance of godliness, have, like Isaac and David, grown lukewarm in spirit through old age and their eyes have grown dim, yet Moses—that is, blessed Benedict—now looks with clear gaze upon our perversities, and at the last will bite with his teeth, accusing before the Lord those who despise his decrees and regular profession [Col. 0600D].

Perhaps you say: “What has this parable to do with us? Why does the abbot of Rheims, with his pen, so bitingly attack us indirectly? What are we to him?” I answer: I know you and love you through the fellowship of Christianity, the ancient brotherhood of the Order, and the intimacy of neighborhood. Therefore I grieve that the good fragrance of Christ is so greatly diminished among you, both with those near and those far away. I grieve that strangers devour your region—indeed, your religious house—before your eyes; that the moth of usury and debt destroys your resources; that the noble maiden, hitherto clothed in double garments, is shamefully stripped.

For your Church, enriched by its founders with the dowries of religion and possessions, flourished long; but now it has withered. How many and what manner of offspring did that hen of Molesme, full of feathers and well-winged, bring forth from her womb, when the Cistercian community sprang from her as from its native root! God of mine, from that one egg what an innumerable sand of monks and lay brothers covered the face of the earth! With what bright splendor did it reform and illumine the skin of the world, darkened by the corrupting negligence of life!

> [Note: [Col. 0601D] “The Cistercian community sprang from her.” For Robert, abbot of Molesme, as Sigebert relates, first built a monastery in the wilderness of Cîteaux in the year 1098 and lived there with some of his monks. Thus Cîteaux was a colony of the monastery of Molesme.]

Look, look, O Zion, upon your children, and do not despise your withered skins; but recover the spirit of your youth, if perhaps, like Jacob waking as though from a heavy sleep, you may hear that Joseph your son reigns in Egypt and may, through his hand, relieve your famine—indeed, your disgrace [Col. 0601B]. My brothers, my brothers, gather again the feathers of your mother; replant yourselves in her members, reforming your manner of life, redeeming your property, regaining the fragrance of good repute, and restoring all things to their ancient condition. Let this letter not grieve you; and if it grieves you, may it be unto repentance! Farewell.

## LETTER CLVII. TO THE GRANDMONTINES

[VIII, 7.] To the prior and brothers of Grandmont, PETER, humble abbot of Saint-Remi: the hands and reward of prayer.

[Col. 0601C] The more fragile we are, and the less we hope in our own strength, the more ardently, if we are wise, do we beg for stronger and more ample assistance. For woe to one alone: if he falls, he has no one to lift him up! But if there are two, they will cherish one another. I count him alone who neither walks with God in simplicity and purity nor rides in the brotherly chariot through invincible fellowship and inseparable unity.

Dearest lords and brothers, I am a man who sees both my poverty and my insufficiency. Where I hear that heavenly banquets are distributed to the poor, I run, knock, and seek; and I wait for such little morsels as I can obtain from the crumbs left over. It belongs to you, it belongs to you, to take rich morsels of bread with the Apostle Peter when you gather for the supper of the Lamb [Col. 0601D], but also to send portions to those who have prepared nothing for themselves. For the day of the Lord is holy: it is the feast of Saint John the Baptist,

> [Note: [Col. 0601D] “The feast of Saint John the Baptist.” On this day the Grandmontines customarily held the annual assembly of their Order; see Letter 175.]

when the chicks return to their mother hen, and streams from each of your individual places flow back to the place from which they came, so that, their course renewed by paternal instruction and correction, they may flow forth again more copiously and vigorously. This worthy and holy custom must be maintained and preserved, because this institution has been approved not only by man and through man, but also by the Law and by God [Col. 0602A]. For three times in the Law the Lord commands the Hebrew to appear before the Lord, yet not empty-handed. Now it is never vain or empty to lap at paternal bosoms as children of one’s profession and there draw new savor for oneself.

Therefore, smelling from afar these delightful and festive gatherings of your holiness, I myself cry out, poor man that I am, “Amen,” with a ready heart and lowered countenance; and I request support from the suffrages of your prayers. Yet this petition of ours does not enter your holy assembly wholly feeble and without the staff of support, limping as it were; for we love and honor your brothers who live in our regions, and you also possess a good cell on our estate [Col. 0602B]. Secure, then, in this confidence, I ask for fellowship in your good things; and when my soul, released from the body, has set out upon unknown paths, I beg for your escort as far as my Judge. Write back, if you please, and report what mercy you intend to show. Farewell.

## LETTER CLVIII. TO THE GRANDMONTINES

[VIII, 22.] To his lords and friends of Grandmont, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi, greeting.

We commend ourselves to the religious assembly of your brotherhood and to your most holy prayers, at least on the recurrence of your annual observance. For it seems to me that the river of Paradise calls its streams back, as it were, to their original bosom, when from every region of the world your priors come together on the solemn day of blessed John the Baptist [Col. 0602C]. This reflux of an expanse of precious gems redounds to the benefit of spiritual merchants; and if anyone seeking precious pearls applies the pursuit of holy commerce to this shore, he will by no means depart empty and void.

Thus I, a man who sees his poverty but does not disregard it, seek to buy the support of your prayers at a good and small price. Our price is to ask, entreat, write, and render back our very slender prayers. If you weigh the value of the gift, what is given is little; if the desire—indeed, the devoted intention—it is much. Beyond doubt, what is read in the hand is assessable; what is in the mind is beyond price [Col. 0602D]. For, as Gregory says, God considers not how much is offered, but from how much; that is, not how much money, but from how great a devotion.

With humble supplication we urge your brotherhood to grant the benefit of your holy fellowship to the benefactors of our Church, especially to those who make their alms for the new work

> [Note: [Col. 0602D] “The new work”: the church of Saint-Remi, whose construction he had undertaken; see Letters 166 and, near its end, 154.]

which we have begun for the honor and adornment of the house of God and of blessed Remigius [Col. 0603A]. For, desiring to renew the head of our monastery, we set our hand to mighty works with God’s help. Therefore send a reply confirmed with your seal, so that, through your holy exhortation and grant of prayers, the minds of the faithful may be stirred. May your holy congregation prosper.

## LETTER CLIX. TO THE CLUNIACS

[VIII, 23.] To the Cluniacs, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi, greeting.

In so great a congregation of saints, my own person, if present, would appear cheap and lowly, my voice slight, and, I fear, even my letter uncultivated. Yet I shall speak in your midst as Abraham’s servant, as the boy Daniel [Col. 0603B], as the old man Jacob—not as Elihu, whose belly is like wine without a vent.

I read in the Scriptures of Jeremiah lamenting, and of Paul wishing himself accursed from Christ for his brethren. Intoxicated by the drops of so great a charity, ought I not to grieve unto the dividing of the joints and marrow over the ruin of the mother of the daughters of Zion, namely the monastery of Cluny? Is not this the city of our strength, from which a thousand once went forth through bishoprics, abbeys, and the courts of kings and princes, whereas now its inhabitants are very few? Did not this great luminary illuminate, in diverse regions, the darkness of religion obscured—reforming the Order, teaching uprightness, pouring in charity, and renewing the other offices of piety [Col. 0603C]? Did it not ascend by the steps of humility even to the Apostolic See?

> [Note: [Col. 0603D] “Even to the Apostolic See”: Urban II, who before becoming pope had been prior of the monastery of Cluny, was raised to it.]

O lords! O brothers! O sons of Cluny! I myself, when a young man at Saint-Martin-des-Champs, tasted by most genuine experience what I say and saw the place where gold was refined. Alas for grief! Such fervor has grown lukewarm and old. But what is becoming obsolete and growing old is near destruction—may that be far from you and from Jacob’s inheritance! It is certainly better for you to die in battle against vices and vicious men, who like foxes destroy the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts, than to see the final funeral rites of your mother and ours.

Therefore cleanse again the wells of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and root out the tares sown over them by the enemy in the night—above all that original evil from which a most evil crop springs up to suffocate monastic religion. This is the custom of feasting and drinking bouts held at Compline [Col. 0603D]. I beseech you, cut down this evil tree by the decree of the Watchers. May the grace of the Holy Spirit be with you, cooperating with you so that you may establish what is acceptable to God, useful to the Church of Cluny, salutary for those now living, and curative for posterity.

## LETTER CLX. TO MASTER G.

[Col. 0604A]

[VII, 3.] PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi, to Master G. Puella.

> [Note: [Col. 0603D] “Master G. Puella”: that is, Master Girard Puella, a man surnamed Puella, who later became bishop of Chester. The Supplement to Sigebert under the year 1182 states: “Master Girard, surnamed Puella, a man of great learning and integrity, was elected bishop of Chester.” This letter was written while Saint Thomas was still alive and in exile in France. For it laments two evils of the Church: the German schism and the English persecution.]

There is no loss to virtue when vice is drawn forth from its hiding places, so that what lay concealed may appear with unveiled face. In this age and these days of malignity, God makes manifest who belongs to the race of darkness and who to the people honored by day and light, while, with the sword drawn and every array of arms gathered together on either side, good and evil, virtue and vice, join hand in close and fierce battle in their camps.

O how the splendid phalanxes of the Philistines, trusting in their great numbers and in their own strength, brandish their spears and hurl arrows poisoned with the venom of worldly glory [Col. 0604B] against Israel, the humble people, the little flock that presumes nothing of itself! For from the beginning, since that murderer who did not stand in the truth fell like lightning from heaven, evils have been multiplied upon the earth; and as both virtue and religion became rarer, women—Egyptian women and Hebrew women, to be sure—increased beyond number. So much so that scarcely seven women seize one man, and a man is more precious than gold, a human being than refined gold.

Perhaps you ask what this proverb of ours means, and why we set this complaint at the opening of our letter. The matter itself undoubtedly, and the condition of the times, resolves the knot of the question: in the schismatic error, those who seemed to be pillars in God’s house slip away too readily for a morsel of bread and for the glory of the flesh, which vanishes like grass upon the housetops, which withers before it is plucked [Col. 0604C]. Men see and recognize that the dragon has cast down with himself from heaven a third part of the stars, yet, not terrified by so foul and cruel an example, they do not shrink from following Satan and holding the truth of God in falsehood.

This is one of the plagues of Egypt, which does not touch the children of Israel, but the children of this age, who seek the things that are seen and temporal, not those that are unseen and eternal. A second plague like it rages especially in your lands beyond the sea, where the king of England has made nearly all the dogs so tongueless that they cannot mutter, not to say bark. Yet some have swum above it, fearing that a like moth might gnaw them and their throats waste away. Among these is the man of Canterbury with his household company; from them we have one little dog, John of Salisbury, who does not hold his soul dearer than himself, but, when the Egyptian mistress takes away his tunic, did not hesitate first to surrender his cloak rather than be defiled by the fornication of falsehood; and, naked, casting aside the linen cloth, he desires to follow naked Christ [Col. 0605A].

Good friend, you too are among them, for even your speech makes you evident. Although you hide beneath a shadowy cloud and dwell bodily with those who grow cold from the sides of the north, yet with a good and excellent heart, like a disciple of true philosophy, you look toward the south and await from there the Paraclete, who may disperse these clouds by the brightness of his coming. He will do this when it pleases him. Meanwhile I offer you myself and what is mine, and ask you, if it should be opportune and some necessity requires it, to keep a place for us with the archbishop.

## LETTER CLXI. TO THE PRIEST-MASTER

[VII, 7.] PETER the abbot, to his dearest friend, the priest-master, greeting.

Remembering that time when, no less fervent in study than in youth, we lived together in the monastery of La Celle, I reflect how greatly the passing course of time has taken away from the body’s health and from the mind’s reading and meditation [Col. 0605B]. With insatiable desire, neither eye was satisfied with the sight of books nor ear with the hearing of readings. God was the middle and the first and the last of these pursuits. While proper order was maintained and the debt of divine praise paid, I read the laws and did not lose or omit the customary prayers.

But now, good friend, the cares and anxieties that have not ceased to tear at me since my youth increase daily and, as it seems to me, have established a perpetual siege against me. If my spirit has sometimes quickly, and almost stealthily, drawn from the divine storehouses any dew of grace or any richness of mercy, a sudden and untimely excessive heat immediately consumes it all. Therefore I cry to God: “My soul is to you like land without water” (Psalm 142).

This is of my inner state. As for my outward condition, I give thanks to my most gracious God because I am in every prosperity and peace—yet such as the world can give [Col. 0605C]. I would gladly see you and cherish my old age, even for a time, beneath the wings of blessed Remigius. Master John of England, formerly our clerk, has been elected bishop of Chartres. I received your little gift and give thanks. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXII. TO LORD RICHARD

> [Note: [Col. 0605] “To Lord Richard”: a regular canon and brother, as has been said, of John of Salisbury; Peter plays upon Richard’s name and his own.]

[VI, 16.] Like aromatic spices from the Lord’s tomb, with which Nicodemus and Joseph anointed the Lord’s body, I received aromatic spices in the memorial of your letter; applying them to both mouth and smell, I drew in a spirit sweeter than honey by reading it more than once. Your living discourse contains nothing foul-smelling, nothing ugly, nothing dead: it is bright and adequately sprinkled with salt. The memory of a kindness received lives; the account of love united together shines; your polished style glitters with the weight of its thoughts and the adornment of its words [Col. 0606A], like the sun upon golden shields, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit.

It draws forth into public view from the innermost and deepest veins of the heart, filled with heavenly ointment, the beauty of a most lovely maiden of the land of Israel, and presents her to the gaze of angels and men. I found her clothed in gold through the authorities of divine speech and the colors of rhetoric, resting on an ivory bed because of her true and chaste discourse, without the blemish of falsehood or the wrinkle of duplicity. The Spirit of truth is accustomed to beget such offspring in a holy mind and breathe into it the breath of life, so that a mind pregnant with divine love can bear nothing but what it has conceived.

While you were still, most beloved, in the outer court and in secular dress, that invisible lover put his hand through a hole unknown to us into the womb of your soul [Col. 0606B], and caressed the inward parts already about to be joined to him in lawful marriage, with a sweetness certainly known to him and perhaps to you. But what embraces he now gives you, what kisses he offers, what kind of offspring he grants, none knows unless, in speech or writing, the birth reveals the hidden grace. Your secret is for you; your secret is for you.

Yet those friends must be admitted without breach of silence, with whom all things are shared: those who do not envy but rejoice together in prosperous fortunes; who wish and say, “May you increase into thousands upon thousands.” I believe that I, Peter, am to be taken with John, both in the Transfiguration, in death, and in resurrection. I do not prefer myself to John, who reclined upon the breast; but after John I presume to have a place and to pitch our camp. Let Jesus have, as is fitting, the first seat in you with his Father and the Spirit; let the Virgin have the second; let the saints in their order have the third [Col. 0606C]. Among the inhabitants of earth, let Master John have the first; I, if you please, the second. I do not grudge any others the third, and thereafter. Enough on these matters.

If I were a physician and knew a remedy by which to repel your illness, I would employ every care. But because I cannot do this, I do what I can. I send you our spices, whatever they may be. Would that in the name of Jesus I could command them to produce the effect of health and healing!

## LETTER CLXII BIS. TO THE SAME

[VI, 20.] To Lord RICHARD, regular canon, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

The bearer of this letter, well known to you, will be able to report orally what is happening among us; and therefore we have wished to write sparingly. For one letter, written not in ink but by the Spirit of God upon our hearts and yours, is more than sufficient beyond a great heap of books: it is true and steadfast charity. This will not be erased in a flood of many waters, because many waters cannot quench charity. It will not be scraped away by any graving-tool of cares or occupations; it will not be consumed by any fire of tribulations and evils. For our charity never fails [Col. 0607A].

You can read this without sun by day, without lamp by night. I ask you to read it when you stand at the holy altars and in the presence of angels and all the heavenly powers. Let this reading continue without “But you, O Lord.” It will make no noise in the ears of the Lord of Hosts. Christ is not disturbed from his rest by the sound of this reading; the silence of heaven is not interrupted; nor is that bride awakened who, holding the bridegroom between her breasts, has his left hand under her head and his right in embrace. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXIII. TO RICHARD

[VII, 12.] PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi, to RICHARD.

Although I have no utterance upon my tongue because of lack of learning, yet I have in my hands signs of the fullness of friendship. The fountains that in previous years were broken open and poured forth even to a flood of many waters have in the present year dried up and withered, even to the failure of grasses and shrubs. This drought may indeed have touched tongue and throat, but it has not reached the vein of affection, nor has oil failed from the head. It will certainly flow as long as life does—indeed, without doubt, beyond it. For charity never fails (1 Corinthians 13) [Col. 0607B].

## LETTER CLXIV. TO R., CANON OF MERTON

[VIII, 3.] PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi, to R., canon of Merton.

> [Note: [Col. 0607D] “Canon of Merton”: in England. See Letter 28 of John of Salisbury: “I rightly sympathize with the vexations and injuries of the holy brothers who serve God at Merton and illumine our island with the light of good works.” They were regular canons of Saint Augustine; for that reason he commends them to Adrian IV, formerly himself a canon of the same Order. In the same John of Salisbury, Letter 139, “Mintona” is wrongly written for “Meriton.”]

I have received from you letters filled with spiritual fatness and richness; nourished and refreshed by them, without prejudice to the Lenten fast, my mouth became as though filled with sweet honey [Col. 0607C], and my marrow was filled with most abundant rejoicing. For from a good and excellent vessel your pen has poured forth good words, consoling words, which call me from a flood of many waters to Noah’s ark—Noah meaning “rest”—and urge me not only to think but also to write on cloistered discipline.

> [Note: [Col. 0608D] “On cloistered discipline.” He wrote a book under this title and on this subject for Henry, count of Troyes, whom Letter 30 also mentions. The old catalogue of the Library of Mont-Dieu: “Peter, abbot of Saint-Remi, *On Cloistered Discipline*. It begins: ‘To his lord and friend H., the illustrious count palatine of Troyes.’”]

You know me ready and willing in every obedience, but bound and occupied under a burdensome load, to which a most grievous illness of the kidneys has increased and been added by a new inundation. Do not suppose that this most urgent demand of the prince of these darknesses has diminished anything from the usual burden of mud and brick. Every day he piles up heaps of wood; in business he adds chaff, and dry stubble in trifles and vain wandering about [Col. 0607D]. Finally, harassed by the various blows of prayers, psalmody, holy meditations, and almsgiving, his heart is hardened more and more: he refuses permission to depart into the desert and offer God the sacrifice of righteousness and innocence.

How, then, held in iron shackles and emptied beyond measure by hunger for reading and leisure, can I number the beauties of the desert or measure cloistered discipline with the prophetic line? Joshua could not divide the promised land by lot among the children of Israel until the land had rest from wars. Would that the delightful Sabbath might come! Would that peace might rest in our chamber! Would that the jubilee year might be celebrated! So might the heart return to its possession, and the slave of sin—the mortal body—to its liberty.

Meanwhile, however, let cloistered discipline be composed not with ink but by practice, because one who is under a law—not that of Moses, but of Augustine or blessed Benedict—will receive rewards if he keeps the commandments. I sum up cloistered discipline briefly and concisely in that single saying which Pharaoh used to Joseph: “I,” he said, “am Pharaoh; without your command no one shall move hand or foot in all the land of Egypt” (Genesis 41) [Col. 0608B]. This is most holy and most equitable discipline in the cloister: that nothing be done, nothing said, nothing possessed except with the abbot’s permission; that neither eye go beyond its appointed bounds, nor hand move toward unlawful things, nor foot run toward forbidden things. With these sinews the body of religion stands firmly joined together and unmoving. We have a foundation other than which no religion is secure.

## LETTER CLXV. TO R., A CANON

[VIII, 6.] To his dearest friend R., a canon, PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi.

I had already completed one quire on cloister discipline and was greatly hastening to send it by the bearer of this letter. But friends dissuaded me from sending an unfinished work to a friend because of the rapacious hands and eyes of the curious [Col. 0608C]. For if they saw it, they would either reject it or retain it. If they rejected it, perhaps they would trample it underfoot. If they trampled it, not distinguishing useful from useless, they would sin. If they retained it, they would either read it, copy it, or neglect it. If they read or copied it, perhaps offended by its rough and insufficiently composed reading, they would attribute it to incompetence and presumption rather than haste, so that the proverb might rightly be applied to me: *Onos lyras*, that is, “an ass at the lyre”; or else they would copy it and perpetuate our defects. If they neglected it, then, as far as they were concerned, I would have labored in vain and both work and expense would have been lost.

Therefore, when any trustworthy messenger comes after a very few days, entrusting myself to chance events, I shall send what I have written at your request on cloister discipline. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXVI. TO THE SAME

[IX, 4.] PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi, to R., canon of Merton.

My hands begin to move to write to you at the same time as the messenger begins his journey [Col. 0609A]. I have not forgotten our ancient custom, for we used to share with one another every rough conception of our meditations. But I, an old man emptied in understanding, weary in age, entangled in occupations, now fail to bear offspring fit to be read. Consulting my natural shame, I bury my abortions within their hiding places rather than bring them forth outside in disgrace.

For what branch, beautiful in foliage and fruit, will sprout from an aged and lifeless trunk? What beds will a dry fountain and a broken cistern water, when not even a drop remains to console their own channels? Thus the old man that is corrupted ought to be renewed by newness of spirit—unless the spirit itself, made old through its own negligence, is, according to the Apostle, near destruction [Col. 0609B]. One of these kinds of old age is visible; the other is hidden. The hidden is more dangerous than the visible. For there is no danger in the bedchamber of vices—the animal body—not offering a dwelling to sins because it is unable to do so. It is certainly best not to sin; indeed, not even to wish to sin; but it is also good not to be able to sin.

The tinder of sin uses youthful age as a furnace into which the three boys are cast by the king of Babylon, and it most stubbornly cuts down youthful limbs as wood suited for flames. But when old age has drained the marrow of the body and utterly weakened the law of the members which wars against the law of the mind, the noises of vices grow quiet; and, because they have nowhere to lay their heads, they go out and wander through deserts [Col. 0609C]. Therefore one ought rather to rejoice than grieve over this oppression, which brings about life more than death, remedy more than ruin. This is the visible and slightly harmful old age.

But the hidden kind, because it is unknown, is hardly or only late cured. Hence Isaiah: “A wound and a bruise and a swollen sore have not been bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor softened with oil” (Isaiah 1). For who would apply a remedy to a disease that neither eye nor hand could reach? Therefore only the Spirit of God, who searches all things, heals, quickens, and renews our spirit.

Placed amid these two kinds of old age, I fear the spiritual and now despise the bodily. At the dregs of my life, where frugality comes late, I am now draining off muddy dregs from the remnants of the first transgression, and I foresee mud that will harden and dry at evening [Col. 0609D]. Yet I await Jesus, a potter no less wise than kind, who, after an earthen vessel has been broken even into the finest dust, can in the resurrection make another vessel unto honor; so that he may be more merciful—not to say more careful—or more powerful in remaking than in making; so that the glory of the second house may be greater than the first, and Adam, who was first made a living soul, may again become a life-giving spirit [Col. 0610A].

This hope, stored in my bosom, stirs my desires not to fear death but to love it, not to flee it but patiently await it. Meanwhile I wish neither to doze nor sleep, but, in accordance with the counsel of the Wise Man, to work diligently at whatever I can. Hence we have undertaken to build our noble church both at its front and in its body, which lacked a head of its own, and, as we hope, shall complete it with God’s aid.

## LETTER CLXVII. TO A MONK OF SAINT-BERTIN

[VII, 19.] PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi, to a monk of Saint-Bertin.

> [Note: [Col. 0609D] “A monk of Saint-Bertin”: of the monastery of Sithiu, formerly in the diocese of Thérouanne, now Saint-Omer.]

You desire to possess our discourses, which the four winds of heaven have scattered in different directions like useless and superfluous feathers [Col. 0610B]. If you have read them, did you not find them drained of the substance of thought and weak through the thinness of their words? If you have not seen them, who persuaded you so earnestly to seek things which, once found, you would immediately reject?

Is it curiosity or devotion to study that presses you to beg for the tasteless herbs and bark of a most worthless man, while you sit at the tables of wealthy Augustine, gracious Gregory, rich Jerome, glorious Ambrose, Bede, rich in every coinage, Hilary, as profound as a great sea, Origen, of most sweet eloquence, and countless others, of whose crumbs beneath the table I am not worthy even to gather? If new works please you, behold those of Master Hugh; behold Saint Bernard’s; behold the writings of Master Gilbert and Master Peter,

> [Note: [Col. 0609D] “Master Gilbert and Master Peter.” By Peter he means, I think, Peter of Troyes, called the Eater (*Comestor*). By Gilbert he perhaps means that canon of Saint Stephen of Auxerre who published glosses on both Testaments and, because of his outstanding learning, was called “the Universal,” later becoming bishop of London.]

in which neither roses nor lilies are lacking [Col. 0610C].

But our writings neither draw from the deep nor serve from on high, because our words are dry and perhaps barren. Yet for this purpose I often set my pen to tablets: that on the vigils of feasts I might occupy at least half an hour in contemplating the joys to come and withdraw myself from the tumults of worldly cares which continually oppress me.

For that reason you will find many of our discourses unfinished: because after an hour, sometimes through my negligence, sometimes through unwelcome occupation, I brought to birth the conceived offspring unformed and incomplete, nor did I afterwards, like a bear, bring it to full birth by licking it into shape. This, then, will be your sign if those writings of ours ever come into your hands: they will appear unfinished, rough, rustic, and badly clothed [Col. 0610D]. Yet grant pardon, for being shy, they do not thrust themselves forward but, compelled, scarcely endure public appearance.

## LETTER CLXVIII. TO A MONK OF READING

[VI, 22.] PETER, abbot of Saint-Remi, to a monk of Reading.

> [Note: [Col. 0610D] “A monk of Reading”: of the Cluniac Order. William of Malmesbury, Book V of *The Deeds of the Kings of the English*, records that the monastery of Reading in England, situated between the rivers Kennet and Thames, was founded by King Henry I and granted to Cluniac monks.]

[Col. 0611A] I did not have the letter of your friendship at hand when an opportunity arose and I resolved to write to you. For your brother, Master William, had carried it away with him. Nor had I committed its tenor well to memory; hence I was unable to recapitulate those things which were chief and worthy either of reply or of laudatory praise. I recall only very faintly that, as in a shady forest, a great abundance of both meanings and words lay before me in it, from which Wisdom, hewing her seven pillars, might build Solomon’s house or the Lord’s temple.

Thus, like a man who through poverty gathers grapes in autumn, I could not find what I should set before a friend arriving from a journey, or before a hungry soul—something from abundance rather than want. Yet I do not fail to know that those spacious walks lie open to you, where are all the trees of paradise; where the vine abounds upon the sides of God’s house; where storehouses pour forth from one kind into another; where are delights of delights; where are the songs of all who rejoice in the bridegroom’s presence and the bride’s magnificence. For to a pure heart what is more pleasant, richer, or more desirable? There is God; there the angel; there virtue; there an unceasing banquet; there the solemnity of solemnities; there the table of refreshment; there the sleep of most tranquil repose. The things perceived there are more intoxicating than those which are spoken. Thus such a conscience speaks in the Psalm: “There is no speech on my tongue” (Ps. 139), that is, what I feel in my heart I do not utter with my mouth.

Public report persuades me to think this of you; your holy manner of life testifies to it, as does the whole and inviolate observance of your purpose, [Col. 0611C] which you hold more firmly by making progress than you did by embracing it at the beginning. The opposite is done by those who, having begun in the Spirit, are completed in the flesh. You gladly eat our “Loaves” [Note: that is, the little work *On the Loaves*], if indeed they are ours, and receive our writings with a higher honour than is fitting. For water fit to drink never flows from so filthy a vessel, nor does clean bread come forth from so bran-filled and ash-covered an oven. Yet the love abundant in you—which eats ashes as though they were bread—accounts every worthless thing belonging to a friend precious, and adorns our lowly things with a more honourable cloak. But would that all our writings had been explained and corrected by the file of your correction!

## LETTER CLXIX. TO NICHOLAS, A MONK

[Note: To Nicholas, a monk: to an Englishman, a monk of St Albans, with whom he disputes concerning the conception of the Blessed Virgin in Letters 171 and 173.]

[Col. 0611D]

[VI, 4.] By an unjust allotment, worldly business and the love of eternal things divide our attention. The business of temporal affairs claims for itself, without any intervening contract of good faith, a share and a half or more of our soul, and leaves me scarcely any portion of myself. Indeed, to inflict upon others an injury one has suffered is no less foolish than unjust. Taking a probable and familiar example close at hand, everyone ought to beware lest he become sick through another’s misfortune.

Therefore, from whatever tiny portion of rest or stolen leisure remains to me, I divide it again and grant a friend a little out of my little. For your sake I make lawful what in fact, though not in law, is almost rendered unlawful. For those things alone are not permitted which alone ought to be permitted. But very many things intrude without permission which impede salvation more than they advance it.

Where, then, shall I begin? With what solemn, devout feast of congratulations shall I rejoice with my neighbours, when I have received a friend back, as it were, from death? Having often experienced that common people scatter more false reports than true ones, I usually condemn their falsehood by the judgment of fairness. But in this instance I give thanks to the lie’s luxuriant verbosity. For many years ago I had heard that you had yielded to the fates; and lately, as though waking from a heavy sleep, I rejoiced that this was truly false, when I heard that you still share our lot and life.

[Col. 0612B] I judged you to be among the number of our friends from the time when I read your writings. Moreover, this should weave the strongest bonds of friendship between us: feeling compassion from my whole heart, I commended to God more than once your soul, which I believed had flown from the body to the bosom of the Mother of Mercy. You therefore owe us a return, if you judge rightly concerning friendship. I earnestly demand it because I do not know at what hour that which I falsely supposed of you may certainly happen to me.

And I see that the bowels of mercy of our God have sprinkled your lands with abundant blessing. For the death of the precious martyr Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, opened for us an eastern window and illumined angelic darkness by the splendour of his faith and patience. For what land, after bringing forth so great a branch from itself, has permanently conciliated to itself the ministering citizens of heaven—that is, the angelic powers—for such fruit received into its bosom? By what reasoning, then, would they not often and frequently revisit the land from which they have brought so great a treasure into their own storehouses?

I believe that the hand of the cultivator or husbandman, of whom it is said, “My Father is the husbandman” (John 15), has not yet shut the channels and sluices of his clouds so as to cease blessing the land which he rained upon with the blood of the great priest Thomas. Not without reason, therefore, peoples coming from every quarter and venerating his tomb bless the race, people, and nation from which so great a witness of Christ sprang. Entreat his holy merits, then, for your friend; and, if you have any new writings, send them to us.

[Col. 0612D] I ask you—remembering favourably, not resentfully, the dispute once held between us—whether, corrected by your feigned death, you have erased or softened the error which arose not from hatred but from the highest, or more than highest, favour toward the Virgin of virgins. I should therefore like to see whether this counterfeit of real death has changed anything, since the vexation of hell, even if not salutarily, nevertheless punitively teaches its tenant, without headlong uncertainty, where he has erred.

Certainly to be imitated—indeed, to be imitated with accumulated zeal—is that serious, not tardy anticipation by which a cautious and provident mind forestalls the matter, daily summoning heaven and earth together with the whole surrounding host of angels, men, and demons, who bring forward each person’s deeds and allege the punishments due.
