Happy the soul which, accustomed to such preliminary exercises, cuts off in due time the deceitful and savage accusations of the evil ones, exacting and paying judicial vengeance upon itself from itself; so that, finding no winnowing-fan with which to toss it about in vexation, it may lay up only grain in the eternal granaries. Therefore, do not disdain to send in writing to your friend what you make of this image. For both your style and your spirit please me. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXX. TO ANOTHER NICHOLAS

[VI, 5.] Reciprocal greetings, which you, good man beneath a sheep’s skin, used to send me, and I—such as I am—to you, have now almost fallen into disuse. I do not know whether you are better now than then; nevertheless, you are older and blacker, and nearer to the earth. I expect you to pay these witticisms of ours back to me immediately, with interest.

Therefore, prostrate at the feet of that most hideous idol, I ask forgiveness although guilty of no offence. Yet I command you to come to our feast, so that the whole celebration may be illuminated by your most beautiful and holiest face, and that by that truthful mouth our souls may be healed of their blows and wounds. Meanwhile I entrust to you our business, which this brother and companion of yours in colour and face will tell you. Farewell, and pray for us; for your prayer penetrates the heavens.

## LETTER CLXXI. TO NICHOLAS, MONK OF ST ALBANS

[VI, 23.] PETER of St Remigius, to NICHOLAS, monk of St Albans.

[Note: To Nicholas, monk of St Albans. The ancient and noble English monastery of St Albans, founded by King Offa not far from Verulamium, where St Alban had shed his blood for Christ. Moreover, the dispute here between Abbot Peter and Nicholas concerning the feast of the Conception of the Blessed Virgin is the same dispute, and takes the same position, as that between St Bernard and the canons of Lyons in Letter 174: namely, that nothing in this matter seemed fit to be introduced before a decree of the Apostolic See. Had such a decree as later followed been issued in their age, there is no doubt that, owing to the exceptional reverence of both men for the Virgin, they would have received it with minds entirely fair and joyful.]

It would belong to a mind free and at leisure to recapitulate each point in your letter and answer it separately, word for word. Therefore, compressing the sum of my replies and confining myself to the more important statements of your letter, I first establish between us on either side a compact of peace and good patience, lest either of us be burned or inflamed by a spark of any disturbance because of any word whatever.

Let only injury to holy Bernard be spared me; gather whatever weapons you will, from whatever quarter—whether to confound my rusticity, to shake from my mind the most worthless scraps of opinions; whether to open your treasures to a poor man, to teach one who does not know, or to establish your views with the strongest barriers of assertions. I therefore attack your phantasms: seductive indeed by an appearance of beauty, but tottering for want of a firm foundation. For whatever is not supported on the scriptural bases of authorities is upheld by no firmness of strength.

[Col. 0614A] Nor should English lightness take offence if Gallic maturity is more solid. For England is an island surrounded by water, and thus its inhabitants are not undeservedly affected by the characteristic quality of that element; through excessive mobility they are frequently carried away into the thinnest and most subtle phantasies, comparing—lest I say preferring—their dreams to visions. And what fault is it of nature if the nature of the land is such? Certainly, from experience, I have found more dreamers among the English than among the French. For a moister brain is more quickly enveloped by the vapours of the stomach and paints within itself whatever images are conveyed by the animal faculty, itself in some sense spiritual; and these images, through the activity of all the natural, animal, and spiritual faculties, are fashioned below the truth of judgment, so as to be called phantasms or dreams.

France is not so cavernous or so watery, where there are rocky mountains, where iron is produced, where the earth is weighed down by its own weight. What follows? Its people are not quickly moved from their judgment, and they cling more tenaciously to the authorities of truth. “Gilead is mine,” says the Lord (Ps. 59), that is, “a heap of testimony”; and, “In the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Matt. 18). Every word, therefore, is light which is neither firm in testimony nor true in authority. Nor is anything of any weight which the ingenious furnace of human thought has devised, if it lacks the test of truth.

[Col. 0614C] The weight of the sanctuary, by which the merits and rewards of angels and men alike are weighed, is preserved in perpetual custody, by a dispensation reserved to truth, in the ark of justice. Thus one who is fastened to no foundation of authority wanders through the air in vain flights, whirled about by reed-like instability and mobility; a stranger to God’s covenants, he is held by no certain dwelling-places.

Wondrous is the power of truth, which catches its adversaries unwilling and unknowing in their own cunning. For it frequently drives its fugitives into the snares of an unavoidable conclusion, so that they are captured and entangled by their own words while, unwillingly, they speak truth and utter with their mouths what they do not feel in their hearts. Hence, Brother Nicholas, you spoke truth in jest when you wrote that I was fixed and you mobile. You called me a rock; and I accept this, if you meant constancy rather than hardness.

I am indeed, by nature, profession, and now also by age and will—as my name Peter suggests—rock-like, rooted and founded in the mountains of holy authorities and among rocks, where Mother Church nests in the clefts of the rock and in the hollows of the wall. [Col. 0615A] I do not leave this place except at the voice of the wheels, which have in themselves the spirit of life, and stand and move, wheeling with the living creatures that have six wings and eyes before and behind. I follow securely, because the face of a lion goes before, lest anything harm; the face of a man, lest anything deceive; the face of a calf, lest anything of vanity intervene; and the face of an eagle, lest anything uncertain remain or delay impede.

The rule of truth has turned these wheels within the compass and orbit of eternal truth. Proceeding from the divine mind, it is of such majesty with God that it dwells upon the highest summit of inaccessible light; of such authority that it lies subject to no dominion; of such steadfastness that it never turns away from the divine countenance; of such certainty that no change or shadow of variation can fall upon it; and of such severity that it neither leaves a place in heaven to Lucifer when he sins nor remits the cross and death to the man assumed by the Word when he asks, “If it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26).

Walking the star-bearing regions on an eternal path, this truth distilled the early and latter rain; and, by means of the virginal cloud, watered the dry sublunar region with perpetual streams flowing from his blood and teaching. Mercy, its foster-sister, without prejudice to the right of its inviolable privilege, obtained from it gentler laws and more tolerable ordinances, so that one who, in the kingdom of truth, lived with errors corrected and morals reformed might hope for forgiveness of sins and relief from exile. Yet neither of these sisters admits the seductive blandishments of flattery; rather, like spiders’ threads, it destroys them with a most violent blast, and weaves for both that sister and her mother an unseamed garment of faithful texture.

[Col. 0615C] Good friend, what place has tow where the priestly garment is woven of gold, hyacinth, purple, scarlet twice dyed, and twisted linen, and where a turban more precious and pure than heaven, sun, and moon is fitted for the high priest? Absolutely nothing more worthy and better than the virginal temple and the holocaust which the Word, coeternal and consubstantial with God the Father, drew and brought forth from it for sacrifice, has eternal Trinity produced from all its treasures for us or for the angels. Thus I believe in my heart; thus I confess with my mouth. Do you not also?

Indeed you do, more vehemently—lest I say more immoderately—than I. You spend your whole self in praising the Virgin; and what do I do? Plainly, I lay out, expend, and over-expend myself. You strive to honour her conception; I honour her predestination and all her ancestry before it. You honour the rose; I, the thorn also. You, the flower and fruit; I, bark and leaf. You, what appears; I, what lies hidden. You, flour; I, bran. You, bread; I, ashes. You, the throne; I, the footstool. You, the substance; I, the picture.

If it were lawful to distinguish her course, and in the divine mind to separate it from the company of all creatures, I would send forth my soul from the beginning of her predestination, that it might follow her footsteps in adoration and in holy, supreme veneration. You need to undertake again—indeed, to seek a new and long pilgrimage—not to Saint Thomas the Archbishop in England but to Saint Thomas the Apostle in India, because I shall always be present at gatherings where a worthy commemoration of our Lady is celebrated, whether it be called her Conception, Nativity, Assumption, or any other veneration.

[Col. 0616A] Since we travel one road, what does it matter if our path is different? You hold the left-hand path: why do you grumble if I keep the right? If your path displeases you because ours is broad and charitable, I yield and grant you a place beside me. There is a proverb: “Old ways are not to be abandoned for new.” Which saint, which ancient father, did not walk our path? I believe and truly confess that, if they had erred in this matter, God would have revealed it to them. For would he have kept this one point silent from those to whom he revealed his counsels so intimately that, to supplement the Gospels, Epistles, and Prophets, they established canons and decrees to be observed permanently with almost equal observance to the Gospel itself—if the matter were dangerous?

But perhaps you will say to me: “Do you, an abbot of whatever kind, dare to close the wells of devotion, which ought always to be continued, and of veneration, which ought daily to be dug more deeply? Do not modern people drink from the same Spirit as the ancients? Does not each person, as Jerome says, offer in God’s temple according to his humble means—one gold, another silver, another precious stones, another, to descend to lesser things, goats’ hair, and so forth? The Nativity of the Virgin was not celebrated in the Church from the beginning; but as the devotion of the faithful increased, it was added to the illustrious solemnities of the Church. Why, then, should the diligence of Christian devotion not likewise establish the day of the Conception?”

To this I reply: I would rather release than close the cataracts of heaven and the fountains of the deep in service to the Virgin; and if her son Jesus had omitted anything in the prerogative of exalting his mother, I, his servant and slave, would desire to supply it—not in effect, indeed, but at least in affection. I would certainly rather have no tongue than say anything against our Lady. I would choose rather to have no soul than wish to diminish her glory. Moreover, Christ’s bride, the Church, which is a pilgrim upon earth, has been permitted and always will be permitted, according to changes in circumstances, persons, and times, to vary the grounds of decrees, devise new medicines of remedies, and establish frequent solemnities for saints upon their attaining glory.

[Col. 0616D] Yet there is a place where gold is refined, and silver has the source of its veins: the See of Peter and the Roman Curia, which holds the keys of heaven principally. When the enclosure of God’s counsels is opened by God’s dispensation, it has the ointment of grace flowing from the head to the hem of the garment. This See of Peter—that is, the rock on which Moses sits, namely the spotless law of God that converts souls—crushes and dashes to pieces the rough gatherings of heretics, cuts away and tears up profane novelties of speech, pierces and slays superfluities, and fills and illumines gaps and eclipses.

Would that, without prejudice to the authority of truth, this lady and governor of all Christendom had weighed the Virgin’s Conception in the scales of a general council, approved it, and spread it from sea to sea! With the sun—that is, the Apostolic See—and the moon—that is, the Roman Curia—leading the way, I would set and order my steps in the light of their countenance as safely as readily, seeing thereby how to avoid what is slippery and follow what is solid and secure.

[Col. 0617A] Nothing in the Church is worse than erroneous presumption, nothing more foolish than rash presumption, nothing more hateful than harmful presumption. Pious presumption is in some manner tolerable, but not sufficiently demonstrable. I certainly wish to abstain from every presumption, though by degrees and with the foregoing distinctions observed according to greater and lesser measure.

I would already have ceased writing further on the subject before us—not condemning your error, if it ought to be called an error, since it comes from piety, nor setting myself against our most glorious Lady, whose very earth, indeed whose dust, I consider the highest riches to lick—especially since in the reckoning of your letter you assert that you can by no means be moved from what you wrote, saying, “What I have said, I have said; what I have written, I have written,” had you not cast into that same letter a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling.

You say that our Lady’s soul was pierced by a sword not only in the Passion of her Son, but also by the contradiction of her Conception. Here the good Homer nodded. Good master, is not our Lady—yours and mine—exalted above the choirs of angels, so wholly filled and surrounded by the glory of the Father, Son, Holy Spirit, and holy angels that, as regards herself, she has no need whatever of our services, is neither harmed nor troubled by our neglects, and is not improved by our benefits? Granted that our services please her, is her soul still capable of suffering? Faith supplies an unanswerable conclusion: true impassibility and immortality admit no sufferings, lest the dregs of evils which torment those below as punishment for sins should pass upward. This is the stone of offence.

The rock of stumbling, however, is that you strip most blessed Bernard of due reverence and launch verbal missiles after him, as though you could diminish his reputation or empty his glory. In the good faith with which I love you and the most faithful charity with which I praise you, I advise and beg you not to set your mouth any further against heaven; for unless you take heed, the stone with which you wish to pierce the iron sky will fall back upon your own head. Has it slipped your mind that to every saint belongs the saying, “The scourge shall not come near your tent” (Ps. 90)? Certainly, whoever is struck by this stone rashly hurled will be crushed by it.

[Col. 0617D] You smile, and perhaps, still uncorrected, bite your lips: “What,” you say, “is this Bernard’s sanctity? What his religious life? What prerogative of merits?” I am nobody to set forth the holy praises that ought to be set forth concerning him [reading uncertain: *referenda*]. His life, his reputation, works, writings, miracles, faith, hope, charity, chastity, abstinence, and finally the mortification in his members; his speech, expression, bearing, and gestures, [Col. 0618A] and the like—these themselves bear witness concerning him.

I pass over all these things, if your heart cannot yet be softened. There is one point in which, as I think, I shall seize you with nails driven deep and melt you into love of Saint Bernard. For he was a most intimate foster-child of our Lady. He dedicated to her not merely one basilica but the basilicas of the entire Cistercian Order, and composed polished and eloquent treatises for her praise. Therefore, if you can touch the apple of our Lady’s eye, write against her Bernard, to whom she herself says: “Whoever touches you is as one who touches the apple of my eye” (Zech. 2).

I do not know what trifles you attribute to the Cistercians, whom I see devoting themselves beyond other mortals to serious things that shall remain without end. These are the men who reformed the coinage of our Order, now placed in its death-agony. These are the men who restored the Rule of blessed Benedict, almost burned away, as Ezra restored the ancient Law. With the Apostle, they are not burdensome to the Corinthians—that is, to secular farmers and country people—but, labouring with their own hands, provide as far as they can for themselves and for other poor people.

Their cloisters are camps of God, where by night, in psalms and prayers, they are ready to rouse Leviathan, who sleeps in the shade among moist places; and by day, in the field of Jericho, they meet the prince of the host, who holds a two-edged sword to cut away superfluous thoughts and deeds. Therefore, with Joshua they ask: “Are you on our side or on the side of our adversaries?” (Josh. 5). It is a useful question, and its answer cannot be demanded too urgently: whether God is for us or [Col. 0618C] against us (Rom. 8). But if he is against us, who is for us? If he is for us, this provokes greater love; if against us, anxiety and fear.

Let us therefore put our soul in our hands, if he is against us; for although it is dreadful to fall into the hands of God after this age, yet it is better to fall in this age into the hands of one who can be propitiated than into the hands of demons. Let us therefore say with Job: “Even if he kills me, I shall hope in him” (Job 13). Such are the Cistercians’ “trifles.”

Your balance also seems to deceive in this matter, either through inequality of the weight or injustice of the one holding it—or perhaps through an ill-considered distinction of words rather than falsity of thought—when you say: “The singular Virgin conquered every sin, not by overcoming every sin, but by feeling none whatever.” Stop here, brother; hold your gaze fixed; direct the rays of the sun of your intention upon your friend, so that you may learn the difference between the Virgin not yet a mother and the Virgin already a mother. Consider the house of Wisdom begun and then completed; distinguish the wool white through the first grace from the purple dyed with shellfish blood through the second; divide the fleece not wetted by impregnation from the fleece moistened by the Incarnation.

[Col. 0618D] For how could the Church sing of her: “Who is she that rises like the dawn,” namely at her Nativity; “fair as the moon,” in her holy manner of life; “chosen as the sun,” in the divine Conception; “terrible as an army set in array” (Song 6), in her heavenly exaltation or Assumption—if she had made no progress or advance in virtues? If from the hour of her conception no struggle with flesh or enemy had remained as a ground for merit, she would have suffered very great loss, since it has been said of her that she is more [so] by merits than by nature, both virgin and human.

I grant and believe, indeed, that through God’s prior working she never felt the fierce incentives of lust, even in the least degree. But the other impediments of human frailty, which proceed from nature by natural origin or spring, she could feel before the divine conception, though she never consented to them. And while prevenient grace was already present and had its preliminary workings in its Virgin, the tinder of sin, gasping, was drawing its final breath; only the grave remained for it, until the Holy Spirit came and consigned that dead thing to perpetual burial, and slew the ancient serpent with his sword.

For it had been said: “I will put enmities between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed” (Gen. 3). Hence Jerome says: “Although the other virgins imitate her up to the conception of childbirth and the service of Gabriel’s new salutation, from that point onward everything that is done in her is divine, as the angel testifies, because she is overshadowed by the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High.”

[Col. 0619B] Before this, indeed, the Virgin’s womb, though clean, undefiled, free from the contagion of sin, and holy, was nevertheless still clothed, so to speak, in the lowliness of humanity—as if it were the whitest wool, whitened in its own colour. But when the Holy Spirit came to it, just as the same wool, when dyed in the blood of a shellfish or murex, is turned into purple, so she too was transformed without intercourse into a mother. Thus she was no longer altogether what she had been, but true purple, most fittingly consecrated by God for the garment and glory of the supreme King, so that thereafter no one might lawfully use her in a woman’s way except God.

After her conception, therefore, she attained crystalline solidity; before the fullness of grace, she had not put off tenderness, though she was pure, holy, and immaculate. She could never be burned by consent, even though she could in some degree be struck by an assaulting temptation—not to her injury but to prove her, not to mortify her conscience but to confirm grace and display constancy.

[Col. 0619D] For why should such great hidden power sleep? Why should such great grace lie idle, producing no fruit contrary to its own custom? Why, finally, should such great glory of the Lord’s mother not manifest itself to the whole world by subduing the flesh, overcoming the enemy, and conquering sin in every respect? Remove the struggle, and you remove the victory. Remove the victory, and you remove the crown. Remove the crown, and you remove the glory. Therefore, lest you take away glory, do not take away the struggle; for “he shall not be crowned unless he has contended lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:5). “If you offer rightly, and divide rightly.”

What, then, does it mean: “The singular Virgin conquered every sin, not by fighting down every sin, but by feeling none whatever”? Why do you call her a victor, yet fear to call her a vanquisher? Do you fear that she fought in the [Col. 0620A] battle, though you cannot say that she conquered except in a conflict—or without a conflict? A victory without conflict, if such there be, is less active; one in conflict is stronger. Therefore, for the greater glory of our Lady, I maintain that she conquered and vanquished every sin. You add: “Not by fighting down every sin, but by feeling none whatever.” Had you distinguished here, you would not have erred. For sin is felt in many ways: sometimes with sin, sometimes without sin. As the matter presently occurs to me, I feel sin sometimes as fire, sometimes as pitch, sometimes as a stone, sometimes as air. Pleasure produces fire; consent, or the act itself, produces pitch; habit or obstinacy, stone; the serpent’s hissing, air. It could knock at the doors of our Virgin, but could not enter. [Col. 0620B] For she was a garden enclosed. Or could not that same Lady tread upon serpents and scorpions, so that nothing should harm her? Thus, with her integrity intact, she could feel sin in this manner, but could not consent to sin. She could vanquish every sin without wound, without shame, without disturbance of her silence, without violation of her future childbirth.

As to the question proposed—that God, though able to do all things, cannot make an incorrupt virgin out of one who has been corrupted: he is indeed able to free her from punishment, but cannot crown one who has been corrupted—would that I understood the force of the expression and grasped Jerome’s meaning! Beyond doubt, I would neither maliciously conceal it nor miserly withhold it. The explanation must therefore be sought from him who was found worthy to open the [Col. 0620C] seven seals of the sealed book. Yet Jerome’s letter says otherwise: “I speak boldly: although God can do all things, he cannot raise up a virgin after her fall,” etc. We must therefore return to the subject of the statement and the speaker’s intention. The discussion concerned guarding virginity and avoiding corruption. Jerome therefore heard this, and, in praise of virginity, kindled his discourse, pouring the streams of his quiet utterance beneath the streams of God’s power and virginity’s glory; and, as though preferring the purity of virginity to every created thing, he says that it is easier for God to make a new heaven and a new earth and repair every defect of creation than to restore virginity, once fallen, to its former condition.

This, I say, is the one seal of his image and likeness which God impressed upon the soul from heaven, bearing witness in his commandments that this faithful deposit should be guarded with every diligence above all other things, and that its loss should be marked within one’s very marrow as irreparable damage inflicted by thieves and every mischance. Nothing is more blessed in possession, or more like God; nothing more miserable in loss, or more unlike God. Therefore, lest so excellent and singular a benefit be neglected, the harshest condition is imposed: God is, in a manner, rendered unable to repair this loss—not in power, but in dispensation. For if his power be considered simply, he can both free from punishment and crown as incorrupt one who was once corrupted. But if one looks to the dispensation and constitution fixed and unchangeable by eternal laws, he cannot, because he can do nothing [Col. 0621A] against himself—that is, he cannot, ought not, or is unable to will it.

For although God is of the simplest nature, we nevertheless speak improperly of him, according to the usages of our speech, when we say that he can or cannot do something, knows or does not know something, wills or does not will something. Thus, as though God were in travail through mercy to restore the broken seal of virginity, justice, acting as midwife—or rather as obstacle—through the decrees of his own ordinances, closes the entrance of the womb; and lest the restored virginity come forth from the womb, be received upon the knees, or suckled at the breast, brings about a miscarriage, lest an incorrupt woman be born anew from one who has been corrupted. So we read concerning baptism: “Can a man,” says the Lord, “when he is old, enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born again?” (John 3).

In a reciprocal reversal, justice likewise seems endangered in its own delivery when mercy resists it. Wishing to destroy the makers of the calf, God says to Moses: “Let me alone, that I may destroy this multitude, and I will make you into a great nation” (Exod. 32). But Moses, holding the sword of divine vengeance and sheathing it again in the scabbard of his customary gentleness, answered: “Either forgive them this offence, or blot me out of the book which you have written” (ibid.). Thus God, as though unable to do what he willed, bent himself more propitiously toward the friendship of his faithful servant than toward the most inborn guilt of the most ungrateful people.

It should be noted that corruption is threefold: of body alone, of mind alone, or of both body and mind together. Of the first Jerome says: “Imagine that, during a persecution, some virgin is prostituted: she is corrupted according to the Law, incorrupt according to the Gospel.” Of the [Col. 0621C] second, the Apostle says: “I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity of faith” (1 Cor. 11). Of the third the same Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are. If anyone defile the temple of God, God will destroy him” (1 Cor. 3). Yet no kind of corruption is cleansed unless God shows mercy.

But if human hands should wish to mend any breakage of their vessels upon the potter’s wheel, can negligence or inability accomplish more than God’s omnipotence? Far be it! Certainly, God cannot do only that which he wills himself not to be able to do. Who will detract from infinite power by denying that he can make incorrupt, through a changed will, even one corrupted in will—if he so wills—or crown her as incorrupt? Therefore it was said, not to diminish divine power but to commend most holy chastity, that God cannot—that is, does not will—to crown one corrupted after her fall.

This ear of grain from the field of Boaz has fallen to our lot, while the larger heaps of the reapers remain safe. We now set the final hand to Samson’s riddles, wrapped for us in many linen cloths and not to be unsealed at a small price. “Let the French,” you say, “have something to chew over concerning the English question, and let the English seek what they had asked from the French draught they had swallowed.” For as Dagon is England’s drink, so Baal is France’s food. Bad drink, bad food; bad drunkenness, bad belching. [Col. 0622A] Each of these produces hell for its worshippers. What punishment, then, would they inflict together?

If you are speaking of resistance to the conception, or of the impossibility of repairing the conception, then, with furnace and bellows sufficiently supplied in whatever fashion, with heads and limbs of all the idols crushed piecemeal and melted into powder, they may now be consumed by English and French alike, whether as food or drink. Will English thirst and French hunger, then, rest satisfied with such food and drink? I do not think so, for their thirst is perpetual and our hunger unceasing. Yet let us rage through discipline and melt down through abstinence whatever is superfluous in food and drink, as the idol of our father Adam, fashioned from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Adam and Eve, having eaten their fill from it, left its remnants to their little [Col. 0622B] children; when lots were cast, the English and French divided them between themselves, so that the former might be dissolved into humbler things, and the latter choked upon more solid ones. Unless I were writing the truth, I would recite my *Confiteor*. Yet because truth begets hatred, I restrain my lip with a finger and meanwhile, hidden in the ground, fear the new thunderings and lightnings of my Nicholas. Farewell, and pray for me.

## LETTER 172. NICHOLAS, MONK OF ST ALBANS, TO PETER

[IX, 9.] NICHOLAS, monk of St Albans, to PETER, abbot of St Remigius.  
[Note: [Col. 0621] Nicholas, monk of St Albans, refutes Peter of Celle’s Letter 171 and argues for the immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin.]

Sated with the reproach of your veiled invective and drunk on your ironic wine, I truly thought that I had received my dismissal and had already made a pact with silence. [Col. 0622C] I had written what I thought concerning the privilege of singular integrity in the Virgin, and there I had set an end. And behold, my Peter unexpectedly raises a new war from new material, provokes all the Virgin’s household to indignation, and provokes those learned in the Lord’s law to oppose a presumption insufficiently Catholic.

So long as the matter concerned propositions that could be understood in one way or another, with sound faith on both sides, I kept silence; and, if our mind conceived pain, it did not bring it forth. But now, when the trumpet sounds that the Virgin felt sin and conquered it by feeling it, I do not keep silence, I do not bear it patiently; I can scarcely restrain my hands from rushing upon the public enemy. Yet before I answer in defence of the common indignation of all the Virgin’s household, I consider the stone of offence and rock of scandal which he found in our letter—he who often seeks a knot in a reed—and I shall make the crooked paths of private injury straight and the rough paths smooth.

A stone, then, strikes against a stone in what I said: “A sword passed through the Virgin’s own soul, not only formerly in the passion of her Son, but also recently in the condemnation of her conception.” Mocking this in an ironic mode, he reasons in Aristotelian fashion that here “good Homer nodded”: “Granted that our devotions please her, is her soul still capable of suffering?” Faith supplies the irrefutable [Col. 0623A] conclusion: true impassibility and immortality admit no afflictions.

I am astonished and indignant that an ecclesiastical man, trained in the figures of divine Scripture, should not know these figures of speech, or should dissemble his knowledge of them. Do we not read, before God was made man, that God is jealous, angry, repentant, and inwardly touched with pain of heart? Does his divinity therefore experience the sufferings of passions because the authority of Scripture speaks of it in our manner? Are angels disturbed by anxiety because they are said to be secure concerning their own glory and anxious concerning ours? Such is the abundance of this trope in the divine page that abundance itself produces scarcity. A few examples among many should therefore suffice a wise man in so plain a matter.

But one must linger somewhat longer to remove the rock [Col. 0623B] of scandal from your heart, since the matter requires that I make public what I had intended to conceal. That holy Bernard, whom you say I treat without due reverence and then hurl verbal darts after, having long ago been enrolled in the catalogue of saints, was recently canonized in the Church.  
[Note: [Col. 0623] Recently canonized: by Alexander III at Anagni in 1174, twenty years after his death.]

He has been exempted from human judgment, I say, so that we may not doubt his glory—but not so that we may dispute his statements any less. Blessed Augustine does not doubt the glory of the blessed martyr Cyprian; nevertheless, he proves most truly that Cyprian erred concerning the giving of the Holy Spirit. He writes that the error was erased by martyrdom, and thus teaches the Church to venerate the martyr’s glory without imitating his error. I too, though with unlike learning, yet with like conscience, so venerate the blessed confessor Bernard that I praise and love his holiness, but neither love nor praise his presumption concerning the conception of the Lord’s Mother.

And lest you think I say what I say from obstinacy rather than good conscience, hear what I have received concerning Saint Bernard from Cistercians endowed with true religion and loving the Virgin in truth. I conceal their names under a bushel, lest I make them odious to their brethren’s community. At Clairvaux, a certain lay brother, devoutly religious, saw in a night vision Abbot Bernard clothed in snowy garments, but with a dark spot, as it were, upon the breast near the nipple. Saddened by wonder, he addressed him: “Father,” he said, [Col. 0623D] “why do I see a black spot upon you?” And Bernard replied: “Because I wrote what ought not to have been written about the conception of our Lady, I bear a spot upon my breast as the sign of my purification.”

The brother made the vision known to the convent, and one of the brothers committed it to writing. It was reported at the general Cistercian chapter, and by common counsel the writing perished in a fire. The whole body of abbots preferred the Virgin’s glory to be endangered rather than Saint Bernard’s opinion. Paul did not act thus—by no means. He calls himself a blasphemer and persecutor, in order to exalt the Redeemer’s glory more highly. And certainly, as I believe, the saint appeared in his own person to a simple man knowing nothing of such matters, and made his fault known, so that the discernment of the entire Cistercian chapter might perceive that he wished his error to be condemned and the glory of the Virgin’s conception proclaimed.

Therefore, if I make public what he himself, as I believe, wished made public, this is not to diminish his reputation or empty his glory, but to express his will concerning repentance for his sin. Then, after a light passage through purgatory, he entered into the joy of his Lord: he who in his days was admirable for venerable holiness, singular reputation, sweet eloquence, and the remarkable renewal and transformation of miracles. Thus much I say of the most blessed Abbot Bernard.

Now concerning my balance, which, as you write, appears to lie in this saying: “The singular Virgin conquered every sin, not by fighting down every sin, but by feeling none whatever.” That she did not fight down every sin is witnessed by homicide, adultery, theft, and many similar sins, which never bit her affection, never stained her memory, and never injured her reputation. The conscience of Peter also bears witness—although harder than whetstones, it nevertheless recoils from this hardness, as the whole world recoils from it. For a mouth that thinks otherwise ought not merely to be stopped with dung, but crushed with the hardest stone.

That the Virgin, destroyer of sin, felt no sin whatever seems to be the thought of blessed Augustine where he forbids mention of the Virgin when sin is mentioned. David also seems to have thought and foretold this by the prophetic spirit when, desiring the Word to be incarnate, he says: “Arise into thy rest, thou and the ark of thy sanctification” (Ps. 131). [Col. 0624C] For the rising of the Word was his coming forth from his hidden place into our public world, the invisible becoming visible, clothed in the form of flesh. Thus he desires the incarnate Word to arise into rest, which he pointedly calls *his* rest, to distinguish it from the common rest of human beings, which David elsewhere indicates: “Return, my soul, into thy rest” (Ps. 114).

The rest of the human soul in this life consists in the contradiction of the flesh being either conquered or lulled to sleep, so that sensuality readily obeys reason’s command. But the rest of the incarnate Word consists in feeling in the flesh no contradiction of the flesh, no law of the members resisting the mind. Therefore the incarnate Word rose into this his rest—and not the Word alone, but also the ark of his sanctification, namely his mother, from whom and in whom the Word is incarnate. For as in heaven, such as the Father is, such is the Son; so also on earth, such as the Son is, such is the Mother. I do not mean conceived by the Spirit, as the Son was, but filled and sanctified by the Spirit from her mother’s womb, as the Son was.

This too was thought and written by Abbot Bernard, the author whom you praise in the present matter. For this reason, he says, the day of the Virgin’s Nativity, not of her Conception, is customarily kept solemn: because she who was conceived in sins, like the whole human race, was born without sin, unlike most human beings. If, therefore, she was born [Col. 0625A] without sin, she consequently lived without sin. If she lived without sin, she consequently was assumed from this world to the Father without feeling sin. But you say that she felt sin without sinning. I confess that I do not know what you mean. For the examples of feeling which you offer have no authority and therefore no weight.

Moreover, all the examples you give are apprehended by the bodily senses alone. For they can be seen, heard, and touched, and perhaps perceived by smell and taste. Although there are five bodily senses, we do not say, “I feel fire because I see it,” nor “I feel air because I hear it,” nor “I feel a stone by taste.” Perhaps I feel pitch by smell; but the sense of smelling has nothing to do with the sense of sin. Accordingly, you say that you feel all the things you have put forward because you touch them.

If, therefore, the Virgin felt sin—and sin is understood threefold in sacred speech, namely, as the punishment of sin, the guilt of sin, and a sacrifice for sin—I should like to be taught by your mastership whether she felt all these, two of them, or only one. If you mean this: “She felt sin,” that is, the punishment of sin, then I understand it so too. For in our manner she hungered, thirsted, suffered cold, was tried by many tribulations, and endured our calamities; and from patience in such things for Christ there flowered a manifold prerogative of merits, apart from those by which she daily advanced inwardly: namely, a new love of virginity, singular contemplation of God, incomparable love of neighbour, and the whole beauty of every virtue, with no ugliness of even the slightest stain.

For since the sum of our merits consists in suffering for Christ and loving Christ—that is, God and our neighbour—our champion was stirred to the full in these two respects before the Word came into her womb, so that she lacked neither struggle with flesh or enemy nor the contemplation of a soul wholly at peace. Thus she did not suffer loss of opportunity for merit: exposed to so many temptations, yet full before the overshadowing with the grace by which the Lord was with her, she fought down and overcame them all. She did not, I say, suffer loss of opportunity for merit: daily advancing alike in action and love, she fulfilled Mary’s better part and, through the tenderness of her age, did not exclude Martha’s solicitude.

But if you mean: [Col. 0625D] “She felt sin,” that is, she felt the guilt of sin—felt, in our fashion, the law of the members; felt shameful motions; felt the pitch of titillation, and was defiled by it—far be it!

Ivo, the venerable bishop of Chartres, wrote in his Chronicles that the Virgin was greeted by the archangel Gabriel and overshadowed by the Holy Spirit in the twelfth year of her age. [Note: [Col. 0625D; 0626D] Ivo in his Chronicles. These Chronicles of Ivo are not extant. Indeed, the opinion of almost all, ancient and more recent alike, is that the Virgin Mary conceived Christ the Lord not in her twelfth but in her fifteenth year.] within this age nature does not permit the genitals of those approaching puberty to be stirred. Therefore the limit of shameful motion in the Virgin, anticipated by the Holy Spirit, leaves us uncertain [Col. 0626A] whether the Virgin was freed from the shameful contradiction of the flesh from the day of her conception, from the day of her birth, or certainly from the day of the Holy Spirit’s coming upon her. Hence Augustine also said doubtfully concerning Christ: “What he took from her, he either cleansed before taking it, or cleansed by taking it.” But it must be certain to us in every respect that the singular Virgin never, in the flesh in which and from which Christ was made man, felt an unlawful motion; never felt the law of the members; never did what she did not will; never felt what it was unfitting to feel.

Since, then, before her twelfth year she could not feel sin by nature’s benefit, and after her twelfth year by grace’s gift, when did the Virgin feel sin and overcome it by feeling it—she who lived on earth at no other times? If you cite Solomon and Ahaz, who begot sons in the eleventh year of their age, know that a singular privilege does not make a common law. Or certainly, because Scripture reproves them for incontinence, it may have happened that weakness excited them by obscene motions of the genitals, that they broke the barriers of modesty, and through the perversity of their minds perverted the innate laws of their nature; they did not abolish the common nature of human beings.

Rooted and grounded in the mountains of holy authorities, provide a holy authority that testifies that our Lady felt sin, and that distinguishes the feeling of sin into feeling fire, pitch, stone, and air; and I shall confess that I was wrong. If none presents itself, with what face do you dare to devise novel fabrications concerning so great a Virgin? With what madness do you malign with genital sensation her who gave birth to the Saviour under the title of modesty? What distinction of prerogative would remain between the singular Virgin and other holy virgins, if she felt sin as others did but did not consent to it, just as they too did not? By what superiority of grace did she excel, I mean before the overshadowing of divine power, if she had to cry out with the entire human race: “Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7)?

You ought to have been more sparing in coining from your own spirit novel inventions about the Virgin than God the Father was gloriously fruitful concerning her by his own Spirit. Therefore, if I write anything about the Virgin which I have not read in the canon, it nevertheless savours of praise for the Virgin and praise for the Virgin’s Son; and, on the occasion supplied by canonical Scripture, I write either true things, though hidden, or probable things, which are themselves Catholic. Much is presumed concerning the Virgin which is nowhere read; and such presumptions must stand until the contrary is proved. The singular Virgin’s privilege has no fellowship with similarity.

It was not only singular that the Virgin conceived, but also that she alone and first in Israel loved virginity. It was not only unheard of that the Virgin bore a child, but also that she quickly believed the angel and, not doubting the fact, asked about the manner of conception. And distinguish in this [Col. 0627A] way between the Virgin not yet a mother and the Virgin already a mother, so that in each state she is privileged above other virgins by a singular prerogative. For, uniquely while not yet a mother, as the angel testified, she was full of grace; and uniquely when already a mother, she became the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit. While not yet a mother, like the purest wool, she was unstained by any feeling of sin; and uniquely when already a mother, like purple dyed with the blood of a shellfish, she was so drenched and steeped with the Holy Spirit that thereafter she was devoted to no uses except divine ones.

Many kinds of such differences occur, by which the Virgin not yet a mother differs from herself as Mother of the Word, although she never felt sin, whether not yet a mother or already a mother. For wool, although it belongs to the body, as Jerome says, does not feel the body’s suffering; so too the virginity of our Virgin, although in the flesh, did not feel the vices of the flesh.

But you say: “Sin is felt in many ways, sometimes with sin, sometimes without sin. It is felt without sin, as air.” As has been said, this example has no authority; nor does it clearly convey any intelligible meaning. For air is felt sometimes more intensely and sometimes more lightly, according as its movement is more gentle or more harsh; and the sensation of harsher cold air is more severe than that of milder warm fire, or of a more distant stone or pitch. For that reason examples so remote from the matter they are introduced to explain do not move me.

Let us therefore return to the Church’s sense, and set forth, according to what [Col. 0627C] she understands by the feeling of sin, and see in what sense the Virgin could have felt sin without feeling sin. Since, therefore, in ecclesiastical usage sin is called three things, as has been said—punishment, guilt, and sacrifice—let us first join each to each, then each to all, so that we may test by what conjunction it is true that sin is felt without sin, and finally discover whether the truth of an equivocal conjunction conflicts with the wording in its univocal sense in the statement: “The Virgin conquered sin in every respect, not by fighting down every sin, but by feeling none whatever.”

Consider, I pray, whether the Virgin felt the punishment of sin without the punishment of sin, the guilt of sin without the guilt of sin, or sacrifice without sacrifice; and teach how these things can occur. If this does not occur to you, consider whether she felt guilt without punishment or without sacrifice, or sacrifice without punishment or without guilt; and teach what Scripture teaches these things and what usefulness they have in the present inquiry. Consider finally that the Virgin felt the punishment of sin without the guilt of sin; and perhaps in this sense it could be said that she felt sin without sin, since “sin” is said equivocally of the punishment and the guilt of sin.

But this sense detracts in no way from the statement that the Virgin is said to have conquered every sin, not by fighting down every sin, but by feeling none whatever, because there “sin” is everywhere understood univocally as the guilt of sin. For she conquered in every respect the guilt of sin—namely concupiscence—and all other things that are both punishment and guilt of sin, because she felt none of them at all. The serpent’s hissing was outside, as suggestion, not within, as the itching of titillation. Nor was it fitting that the flesh through which all flesh deserved to be cleansed from the condemnation of titillation should be titillated. It was not fitting that the flesh should be moved in disorder, when from its offspring the discipline of order flowed forth and, gathering the whole world under the governance of justice, restored it to eternal life.

## LETTER 173. PETER TO NICHOLAS

[IX, 10.] PETER, bishop-elect of Chartres, to NICHOLAS, monk of St Albans.  
[Note: [Col. 0627D] Peter of Chartres to Nicholas. He answers the preceding letter and discusses the praises of the Blessed Virgin in such a way as to make it sufficiently clear that, although his opinion concerning the feast of the Conception differed, his zeal in venerating her was not inferior.]

Your letter, toothed in many ways, while intending to bite me most sharply, not without justice strikes its teeth, blunted, against itself. I fear sharp teeth, but despise rotten ones. You reason subtly—or perhaps falsely reason—but conclude deceptively. You ridicule our simplicity; no wonder, for you do not possess truth. Contrary to the law of your brother, you reveal nakedness—not what exists, but what you invent. I fear to lie in human matters; how much more in divine ones?

I believe, say, assert, and swear that our most blessed Virgin was fortified in eternal predestination by a singular privilege and was violated in nothing from her conception; rather, she always remained and has remained inviolate. And as she is blessed beyond human nature and the nature of all other people, so she remains hidden and unknown beyond all knowledge. Yet although, like rams, we have tried our horns against one another and uttered from either side diverse sounds of words, the one single eye of us both has never grown dim in her service and devotion, nor, God willing, shall it grow dim.

As taste distinguishes food and one person demands more salt, another less, so human understanding sometimes avidly seeks harsher things and sometimes sweeter. One person brings forward without the weight of reason or authority whatever pleases him; another rejects whatever is not seasoned with evangelical or prophetic salt. One is more useful, another sweeter. I set usefulness above sweetness. What is sweet merely flatters the throat; what is useful benefits all the members more. You seek sweet words; I seek useful ones. You seek seductive words; I seek wholesome and strengthening ones.

Let us therefore attend to serious matters. Yet serious matters sometimes do not reject playful things, but gladly admit them; while some reject and spit them out so thoroughly that they even anathematize and hang them. The services offered to our Queen and Lady, the most blessed Virgin Mary, demand reverence, not flattery; maturity, not buffoonery; devotion of heart, not verbosity of mouth; admiration of mystery, not public [Col. 0629A] debate. Each of us runs after her—and would that it were toward her. As I believe, one intention makes our minds equal; but the variety of expressions, like the diversity of languages, varies the sense of Scripture while faith remains safe.

Are we more learned or wiser than Augustine and Jerome? Were they not united in faith, harmonious in religion, fervent in charity, lofty in knowledge of Scripture, and equal in authority, yet very different in some opinions? In the Epistle to the Galatians we read: “When Cephas came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face, because he was blameworthy. For before certain men came from James, he ate with the Gentiles; but when they came, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision,” etc. (Gal. 2).

[Col. 0629B] Jerome defends Peter, saying that he acted unwillingly and feigned this by dispensation, so as not to lose the Jews; nor did he sin in this, because he acted with a good intention. Augustine, on the contrary, says that Peter observed those legal practices not by dispensation but truly, and sinned in word—not by observing them, but by compelling others through his example to Judaize. Behold the cedars of Lebanon; behold the lofty firs. Moved by this impulse and that, they think differently in one way and another, yet never disagree in charity’s root. Each person, moreover, abounds in his own understanding.

For no error arises in the articles of faith—in those things which are the two olive trees and two lampstands shining before God—such that one may be endangered because of the other. It is therefore no wonder if wind carries us, dry straw, in different directions. If you strive to honour the Virgin, I approve this; if you strive to defend an uncircumcised discourse, I do not approve that. An uncircumcised discourse is one which, drawing the original foreskin from the womb of human judgment, is not cut away with the stony knife according to the rule of evangelical authority. If I were to relate all superfluous speeches and insert them into this writing of ours, I should plant a grove beside the altar.

Saving the name and divinity of the most sacred Virgin, I would not refuse a verbal duel, if I had leisure to read, to write, and to seek weapons in Solomon’s armouries. If our Lady closes her ears and eyes and thinks our disputation’s nursery-rhymes worth nothing, she will shut up and bind the Englishman, enclosed by the Frenchman in her caves, until the time of a thousand years. O most learned master! Sleeping or waking, did you hear a trumpet sounding that the Virgin felt sin and, by feeling it, vanquished it? How deceitful an interpreter you are in hidden matters is plain in matters open. For you call our stylus or pen a trumpet. But it is the trumpet’s office to raise the voice, while the stylus and pen write in silence. Be therefore Davus, who throws everything into confusion.

But in what sense I said that the Virgin felt sin and vanquished it—although, carried away in such fury that you can scarcely restrain your hands, you cannot hear patiently—let whoever reads our writings, putting favour and hatred aside, hear and carefully weigh it in the balance of equity. And lest I enter battle against Goliath naked of authority, I set before myself the shield of authority in the saying: “I will put enmities [Col. 0630A] between thee and the woman,” etc. “She shall crush thy head, and thou shalt lie in wait for her heel” (Gen. 3).

Who is this woman? The Virgin, who is called “woman” because of her sex, not because of corruption. What is her seed? Jesus, in whom all nations shall be blessed. What are those enmities? Read the Apocalypse of John: “After the dragon,” it says, “saw that he had been cast down to earth, he persecuted the woman” (Apoc. 13). Behold the Virgin Mary. The Gospel teaches that the malignant dragon in Herod, as formerly in the serpent, sought to kill Jesus, the son of this most holy woman. Therefore Joseph, warned by an angel, withdrew with the mother and child into Egypt, as into a desert place.

The discourse read on the Nativity of that same Virgin explains this saying with brighter-than-light clarity, where it says: “I will put enmities between thee and the woman,” etc. “What is it, brothers,” says the author in that place, “to crush the serpent’s head, except by resistance to overcome the devil’s principal suggestion—that is, concupiscence? If, therefore, it is asked what woman accomplished such a victory, certainly none is found in the line of human generation until one comes to her of whom we are now speaking, the Holy of Holies.”

You are deaf if you do not hear; blind if you do not see; mute if you do not cry out; unbelieving if you do not believe; obstinate if you still contend. Go to the pool of Siloam, wash your eyes, and see how it is true that she felt sin without sin. She felt it indeed, not unto injury but unto testing; she felt it not by yielding, but by overcoming; she felt it outwardly, not inwardly; she felt it when the enemy cast suggestion, not when the flesh took pleasure or the spirit consented. She felt it by repelling, not by receiving or admitting it.

Which of us honours the Virgin more: he who proclaims her happy without conflict, or he who proclaims her strong in conflict? “Who shall find a strong woman? Her price is from afar and from the utmost bounds” (Prov. 31). The Apostle says: “He shall not be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. 2). The Spirit says in the Apocalypse: “To him who conquers I will give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the midst of paradise” (Apoc. 11). Again: “He who conquers shall thus be clothed in white garments” (Apoc. 3). Again: “He who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God” (ibid.). Again: [Col. 0630D] “He who conquers, I will give him a seat with me upon my throne” (ibid.).

Our Virgin, seated beside her Son Jesus, who sits upon the throne of grace, proclaims all the victories which she obtained not by sleeping but by watching; not by idleness but by fighting; not by fleeing but by resisting; not by falling but by striking. Is the mother happier than the Son, or holier, or stronger, or fuller of grace? Yet Jesus was led into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil; and the Apostle says that he was tempted in every respect in our likeness, yet without sin. Does not one who is tempted feel temptation? But the manner of feeling depends upon the strength, not of the tempter, but of the tempted person; the experience of feeling is weak, weaker, or weakest according to the disposition and strength of the one who feels. For no one can judge what you feel except you who feel it. [Col. 0631A]

Let this suffice concerning the trumpet which you made and sounded. Now, however, that I may answer the individual chapters of your letter, by which you accuse my folly—which I too acknowledge—I leap over your thickets like a young stag. Yet I maintain that I am not ignorant of the figurative modes of divine speech; yours, however, I trample underfoot. Finally, I pity your insolence: you have descended—indeed, I might say fallen—from the most exalted mountains of our Virgin to the deepest valley. For although in her there is nothing shameful, since every one of her members is purer than the moon and brighter than the sun, nevertheless the foulest memory of our frailty, upon hearing the sexual organs named, will scarcely shake itself free from its mire; it will scarcely begin not to think its customary thoughts. Therefore, in the Virgin I prefer to envelop such things reverently beneath most holy veils [Col. 0631B] rather than handle them with bare names and hands. The Virgin surely delights to be addressed in virginal words and with a holy veil of consecrated speech. I spare my letter the insertion of your words, though I cannot refrain from reproving them. I had been hastening to finish; but first I wish to examine your new decree and ask by what counsel it was promulgated.

“As,” you say, “in heaven, such as is the Father, such is the Son; so on earth, such as is the son, such is the mother.” O Lady, forgive one who says what displeases you. Are you not, although the mother of your Son, nevertheless his handmaid? Are not your eyes, as the eyes of a handmaid are in the hands of her mistress, so in the hands of the Lord, your Son? Gold from Ethiopia cannot be compared with him, nor can he be matched with the dyed colours of India, [Col. 0631C] because none like him has been found upon earth: he is one and unique, and has no second. It is enough for you to stand at his right hand—not in a comparison of equality or likeness, but in a stable and eternal union of glory and blessedness.

Now that we have given right hands, let us have peace concerning our Lady: you are her helper, I her defender; you her zealous champion, I her lover. To expend one’s ability and zeal in praise of the Virgin is neither blameworthy nor unrewarded. Yet authority commands, and reason counsels, that in this, and in every action and intention of ours, we divide the hoof. To distinguish what and how one ought to praise is to divide the hoof. Whoever neglects either of these either perverts the office of praise or loses it altogether. You err in measure if you praise anyone above, below, or outside the bounds of truth; you err in person if you wish to praise one unworthy of praise.

To come to the point: you extol the praises of our Virgin; I offer them. You soar through the air; I, while still upon the earth, run on foot. You rush your words forth; I set my speech in order for judgment and weigh it in the balance. You bring an acrid, unripe vintage; I bring to the table, in the early and latter rain, ripe new and old fruits. You praise the Virgin, and so do I. You proclaim her holy, and so do I. You exalt her [Col. 0632A] above the choirs of angels, and so do I. You call her free from every sin, and so do I. You affirm her to be Mother of God; you establish her as our mediator with God, and so do I. In every phase and repetition of veneration and glorification, I go with you and think with you.

But if, outside the stamp of the established coinage, you wish to mint another coin which the See of Peter—whose office it is to approve or disapprove the order of the universal Church—has not approved, I plant my foot and do not cross the established boundaries. I believe and confess that more concerning the most holy Virgin is unknown to us than known, because she has been strengthened both by grace and glory, and we cannot attain to her. I believe concerning her according to the Gospel, not according to dreams; and if I think otherwise, God himself will reveal even this whenever and however he wills. Meanwhile, [Col. 0632B] while a voice is made above the firmament and does not descend to our foundation, I lower my wings and beseech the Father of lights, not you, to illuminate the darkness of my ignorance. If iron slipped from its handle and wounded you in any respect, forgive me; you will receive the same indulgence from me. Pray for me, dearest friend; and would that I might see face to face you whom the finely adorned character of your writings has more than once enabled me to hear.

## LETTER 174. TO THE CHAPTER OF CÎTEAUX

**[IX, 8.] Peter of Chartres** [Note: [Col. 0631D] Peter, bishop-elect of Chartres. After John of Salisbury, as was stated in Letter 105. Supplement to Sigebert, under the year 1182: “John, bishop of Chartres, died [Col. 0632D], and Peter succeeded him; he had been abbot of Saint-Remi at Rheims. Before this, however, he had been abbot of La Celle, while Saint Bernard was still living.”] **to the chapter of Cîteaux.**

I consider hindering studies most holy to be no less a fault than interrupting angelic and divine affairs. [Col. 0632C] Indeed, I fear to incur the punishment of so great an offence if I should detain you, occupied with divine things and in divine things, by vain and superfluous words. Yet pressing necessity sometimes excuses an importunity that forces itself upon one; for, even if it briefly checks haste, it does not altogether press down or suppress a necessary task.

“Would that you might bear with a little of my foolishness,” says the Apostle (2 Cor. 11). The ant is not accused of foolishness because it prepares food for itself in summer. The unjust steward is not accused of foolishness because, being unable to dig and ashamed to beg, he made friends for himself who would receive him into eternal dwellings. It is no folly in me if, not from the mammon of iniquity, [Col. 0632D] but from humble supplication and the debt of brotherly love, I appeal to my lords and dearest brothers, that they may remember me among the companions of their joy and friends of their future hope.

May your most holy fellowship therefore recall that I am one of the pupils of most blessed Bernard, through whose merit God extended the Cistercian Order as far as the sea and beyond, and magnified it unto the clouds, as those remnants which still survive testify. Among his other benefits, heavenly grace granted me, while he was alive, to be present at these assemblies of God’s host [Col. 0633A] and to be commended and received, both by benefits and by prayers. After he was transferred to the heavenly court, I also once came to my lords and dearest brothers, repeating and impressing upon them the fellowship and charity granted long ago.

Therefore, though absent, I fall at the feet of this whole holy congregation and implore its always expected, sought-after, and still-to-be-sought assistance. I was yours; I am yours; I shall always be yours. Does your charity gather strangers into its bosom and expose me, undefended, to lions, wolves, bears, and evil beasts? You nourished me at La Celle; you loved me at Rheims; will you cast me off at Chartres? Where necessity is greater, will charity there expire? Where danger is extreme, will there be no aid? Where one descending [Col. 0633B] from Jerusalem to Jericho is left half-dead, will the heart of the Samaritan, after the negligence of priest and Levite, harden itself so that oil and wine are not poured into the wounds of the wounded man? Far be it that the fountain of oil should dry up, that the flask of oil should fail in your holy order. Certainly, if holiness fails among you, the world will remain unclean. There would not be grief among God’s angels like this grief. Therefore may eternal peace and grace be with you. Amen.

## LETTER 175. TO CERTAIN GRANDMONTINES, URGING THEM TO REMAIN IN THE CISTERCIAN ORDER

**[IX, 12.]** To answer briefly the turbulent and scrupulous questions of your hearts concerning the profession you have made, both in the Order of Grandmont and in the Cistercian Order, [Col. 0633C] it seems to me that one who fulfils what he promised does not violate the faith of the promise; and one who fulfils more than he was bound by vow to fulfil adds the merit of grace besides. It is not mine to judge the orders of saints, nor to weigh their merits in my scales. They stand or fall to their own lord; but they stand.

Yet it is my opinion that there is more strictness, more justice, more severity, and even more discretion in the Cistercian Order than in that other order, which is unknown to me and concerning which, because of uncertainty, I do not dare to rush into any judgment. Leaving these matters aside, would that I might by a brief admonition cast out—or rather exterminate—the frogs and flies troubling the inner chambers of your hearts! I do not ignore Aristotle’s teaching that it is not useless to doubt every particular. But I hold with Hippocrates that great changes produce diseases. Gregory says that plants which are often transplanted do not put down roots. Paul anathematizes anyone, even an angel from heaven, who should preach a gospel other than that which he preached. Our Lord Jesus Christ says of John the Baptist: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” (Matt. 11). Likewise, in the Gospel parable, while the foolish virgins went to buy oil, the door was shut.

The meaning of these authorities is this: that we should not be unstable, should not waver, should not be carried about by every wind, and should not say, “Behold, Christ is here,” or “Behold, he is there.” See therefore to your calling, [Col. 0634A] and establish your bases and the soles of your feet upon the rock; and say with Job: “In this my nest I shall die, and like the palm tree I shall multiply my days” (Job 29). I ask your friendship and brotherhood that you spare yourselves and know for certain that one thing is sufficient and necessary for salvation: to entrust oneself to God and never dispute with God; to obey one’s superior in all things; to lay every burden upon his shoulders; to appoint him as a sufficient advocate at God’s judgment against every allegation of the adversary, whether true or false; and to seek God in simplicity, not in subtlety.

## LETTER 176 [Note: [Col. 0633D] New.]. TO THE SAME PERSONS, ON THE SAME SUBJECT

*(Spicilegium, quarto edition, vol. II, p. 447.)*

[Col. 0634B]

To his dearest brothers in Christ, WILLIAM, PETER, and GUY: PETER of Rheims, the spirit of counsel and fortitude.

First I shall speak to you, Brother William, because my inward parts have been stirred on your account and because of you. I have been troubled at the sight of your disturbance—or rather, your change. For I had heard of your resolve, praised your strength, approved your discretion; but now, agitated by I know not what spirit, you have begun to waver, though you ought to have been an immovable pillar. You had borne the yoke from your youth; and now at last, coming to the fruit of a better life, that is, to the Cistercian Order, you had raised yourself above yourself.

I fear, beloved, the wiles of him who transforms himself into an angel of light. I fear lest your excellent colour be changed, lest [Col. 0634C] silver—indeed gold—be turned into dross. For when the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it walks through waterless places seeking rest; then, taking with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, it returns to its house, and that person’s last state becomes worse than the first (Luke 2). This does not mean that an unclean spirit went out from you, for by God’s grace it was not in you; rather, what was farther removed from you is now, by a certain changeable lightness of yours and a light mutability, trying to become nearer to you. And he who, so to speak, cannot corrupt the substance of your religious life and the sincerity of your zeal by these worldly and manifest impurities strives to swallow you up through certain most evil incidental things—changes of places and of orders, and hidden delusions. For he hopes that Jordan will flow into his mouth. On the philosopher’s testimony, I consider the first proof of a well-ordered mind to be the ability to stand firm and remain with itself. To roam about and be disturbed by changes of place is the agitation of a sick mind; for a plant often transplanted neither takes root nor becomes strong. [Col. 0634D]

But your concern regarding the profession of your earlier vow involves no scruple. You have enlarged your vow, not broken it; for now you fulfil, and will fulfil more fully, that Davidic saying: “Because you shall eat the labours of your hands, blessed are you, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. 127). Why say more? I believe, confess, and solemnly testify that you have ascended from the lesser to the greater by the prompting and inspiration of the Holy Spirit; and the higher the ascent, the graver the descent—indeed, I should say, the fall. Therefore, dearest one, I beseech you—your Peter, already wounded for you even to the outpouring of my soul by report alone—not to add sorrow upon sorrow to me; not to provide matter for laughter to clergy, people, and devil; do not move yourself, nor fear in this happy ascent, where there is not violation of a vow but its fulfilment, where there is no cause for fear, that you should fear. [Col. 0635A]

To you, Brother Peter, unknown to me in face and absent in body, but present in spirit, I offer counsel with a devoted heart; and, cast down at your feet, I anxiously and earnestly beg you not to begin to unsettle yourself and others because you have not attained the former rest for which you long. For true rest is in the Cistercian Order, where Martha is joined to Mary (Luke 10), where, according to the saying of the Wise Man, one who acts must rest and one who rests must act. Indeed, what you object concerning the earlier quiet and leisure is, if I may speak with your leave, so plainly contrary to all reason that it needs no answer. For where are there more silence, more fasting, less worldly care, and consequently more contemplation and holy rest than in the Cistercian Order?

Let this disturbance of yours therefore be still—be still. While it is little, let it be dashed against the rock; while it is a little fox, let it be caught and killed in the morning, lest it demolish the Lord’s vineyard, that is, your conscience; lest, under the pretext of a certain empty quiet, you seem to long for fish—not, I say, those of Egypt—and for other things—not, I say, those of Pharaoh. Words are too feeble to express what I think of your and Brother William’s fantastical delusions; but you, together with Brother William, weigh much from a little. My counsel is—indeed, to speak somewhat more boldly, the command of Holy Scripture—that you run thus in the Cistercian Order and contend thus in the contest, so that you may happily attain the prize of the eternal calling. [Col. 0635C]

Concerning you now, Guy, I am for the present less anxious. To you, the last—not as one untimely born, but as one almost perfected—I write a few words, congratulating your maturity, which needs not milk but solid food, after the fashion of a mother [Col. 0636A] who is more troubled over a little and weak son than over one who is strong and mature. You therefore, strong in the Lord, strengthen others. Act manfully: rebuke, entreat, reprove—at a favourable time and an unfavourable time (2 Tim. 4). The Cistercian Order is indeed arduous, but virtue tends toward what is arduous; for, according to the philosopher’s saying:

> “[Lacuna:] the serpent’s thirst, the burning heat of the sand;  
> Patience rejoices in hardships sweet to virtue.”

Wake, therefore, glorious soldiers of Christ. Remember that the world, its appearance, its glory, and all its desire pass away. Farewell. My soul greets Master Arraud, a strong and prudent athlete of Christ, and through you requests from him the gift of his prayers.

## LETTER 177 [Note: [Col. 0635C] New.]. TO KING LOUIS

*(Duchesne, Writers of French Affairs, IV, p. 678.)*

[Col. 0636B]

To the most devout King of the Franks, LOUIS, beloved and illustrious lord: P., by God’s mercy the humble minister of the church of Saint-Remi, wishes that through temporal prosperity you may merit everlasting blessedness.

You commanded me to provide a palfrey suitable for your use. I have none of that kind, but I shall not delay in obtaining one as soon as I can, nor shall I conceal the matter. If perhaps I cannot find one that appears worthy of your favour, I shall be diligent until the feast of Saint Andrew in sending you this answer and in making recompense by another kind of service. For know that [Col. 0636C] my willingness to serve you has always been, and still is, greater than my means.

I wonder, however, in what spirit you received the services which I rendered you last year; for I have not yet been able to learn, nor has it yet become known to me, whether you know of them or regard as welcome the gift of four marks which I sent you, and the carriage with three horses which I lent our lord on account of and for the purpose of your service, and which I have never recovered. May Your Excellency prosper.

[Col. 0635]

## FIFTY-SIX LETTERS OF POPE ALEXANDER III TO PETER, ABBOT OF SAINT-REMI, AND OTHERS

*(The sequence of these letters, first published by Jacques Sirmond, has now been issued by us among the Registers of Alexander III, in volume 200 of the Patrologia.)*

[Col. 0637]

# SERMONS OF PETER OF LA CELLE, AFTERWARDS ABBOT OF SAINT-REMI AT RHEIMS AND FINALLY BISHOP OF CHARTRES

## SERMON I. ON THE FIRST SUNDAY OF ADVENT

[Col. 0637A]

Come, Lord, visit us in peace, that we may rejoice before you with a perfect heart.

With shod feet, in visible form, the Saviour came to sinners not only barefoot in faith but stripped of blessedness, and also wounded by desire. But that we may understand the Lord’s footwear more clearly, let us examine, as far as we can, his whole attire. Let us first run to the workshop of wisdom and ask the assembly of holy virtues, weaving there the most beautiful and holiest garment, whether they have already prepared cloth or a tunic for the Word to be incarnate.

“Bring forth, therefore, Rebecca, for us the very good garments which you have at home” (Gen. 27), so that in these the younger Son, clothed according to his humanity, may possess the blessing, or the inheritance of the firstborn of every creature. Bring forth, Moses, the holy garment prepared for your brother, for glory and beauty, in which he may minister when sanctified (Exod. 28). Open, Mary, your wardrobe, so that your Son, wrapped in a garment of fine linen, may offer the sacrifice which no one until now has dared to touch—much less offer. Hence the Apostle: “If therefore he were upon earth, he would not even be a priest, since there were those who offered gifts according to the law, who serve the copy and shadow of heavenly things” (Heb. 8:4). As Moses was answered when he was completing the tabernacle: “See,” he says, “that you make all things according to the pattern which was shown you on the mountain” (Exod. 25:40). [Col. 0637B]

Thus I find three most learned maidens of Israel weaving in every variety and beauty: first, predestination in the fruitful heaven of the highest heaven; then wisdom; and finally, in the vestibule of your womb, most prudent, most chaste, and most humble Virgin, divine grace. These three—first predestination, then wisdom, and third divine grace—cooperate jointly and alike in preparing the tunic of the Word of God. Predestination arranges; wisdom designs; grace composes. Predestination arranges by creating, as it were, the material of flesh; wisdom designs by inspiring, as it were, the form of the new man to be conceived and born in a new order; eternal grace composes, as it were, the joining of God and man in an unprecedented union. Only predestination could devise this; only grace could persuade it; only wisdom could fulfil it.

Wisdom declared this necessary for the redemption of humankind; grace prompted that it should become voluntary in the heart of the Most High; predestination rendered its service, so that salvation might come in the fullness of time. Predestination pointed out the way of deliverance; wisdom went before; grace completed it. Predestination shows the corpse of the dead man; wisdom washes it; grace raises it. Predestination commands; wisdom assists; grace completes all things. But because threads such as these of our salvation are exceedingly fine and demand the hand of the highest craftsman, let us meanwhile venerate them folded up in this sanctuary and turn our discourse, for the sake of the people standing by, to matters somewhat more substantial. [Col. 0638A]

Adam, dearest brothers, when he was created by God, was indeed made naked in flesh, just as all children are born naked from their mother’s womb; but in soul he was clothed with a most fitting variety of virtues. For you should know that, just as we conceal bodily ugliness with clothing, so we restrain the foulness of the soul which results from sins by good virtues.
