Perhaps something has arisen on your back, breast, or some other part of your body which darkens or disfigures the beauty of the whole body: what then do you do? Certainly you conceal it, veil it, cover it. Why? Without doubt, lest you be mocked; without doubt, lest you offend the eyes of a friend or husband. People do this before people and for people; but what of the angels? Indeed, what of God? You have sinned; you have borne false witness; you have stolen your neighbour’s property; you have killed a human being; you have committed adultery or fornication; you have committed some grave crime—and are you not ashamed with shame, nor filled with confusion? [Col. 0638B]

O human being! Do not the angels see? Does not God, who searches hearts and reins, behold? Do you fear people more than angels, your neighbour more than your Lord? You fear passing ridicule and do not fear eternal condemnation? Do not think of hell as temporary, for its torment will not be temporary but perpetual. Since you are to pass through fire, that you may not feel its burning, take with you one of the little swaddling-cloths of the child Jesus, or at least the fringe of his garment. Return to your heart and seek either cloths by which to cover your shame or garments to wear at the feast. If you are poor and sinful, the wrappings in which the child Jesus is swathed in the manger are of less value than the virtues which he brought from heaven; yet they suffice to cover shame, cover the corrupt discharge, and warm the dust of a corpse already nearly dead.

These cloths are fasting, humility, poverty, confession, and almsgiving. Whoever is clothed in such cloths will not fear the cold of snow. [Col. 0639A]

Why, Lord Jesus, do you wrap the covering of divinity in cloths, when later, without cloths, you unfold it upon the cross to nails and spear and stretch it out to its utmost extent? Do you fear frost, you who do not shrink from the spear? But in the one clothed in rags humility is denoted; in the one pierced by a lance patience is denoted. O you clothed in rags, give us—or at least sell us—cloths; for these cloths touch and cleanse leprosy, and by their gentlest touch free even the prostitute and the woman caught in adultery both from punishment and from guilt. Give us, therefore, Jesus, the cloths of humility through conversion; sell them through correction. “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven” (Ps. 31:1) through correction, “and whose sins are covered” through satisfaction. [Col. 0639B]

Hear, penitent, why you need a covering, and how, from where, and where you ought to cover yourself; finally, with what you ought to cover yourself. The cloud of Adam’s sins, and of the sins of his children, is of such stench and foulness that the offended sun turns into darkness and the moon into blood; the stars are not clean; the sea boils; the earth trembles; heaven blushes; the air swells; the angel flees; God turns himself away; and death and hell open their mouth and belly without end. Have you been able from these things sufficiently to understand the horror of sin? Certainly I have not yet expressed its abomination; I have not yet described its execrable [Col. 0639C] ferocity. Thus, the lion’s rage, the dragon’s fury, the serpent’s hiss, the boar’s savagery, and whatever may be more wildly expressed in anger among created things cannot be compared to the cruelty of wickedness or sin.

This most ferocious beast sometimes bites the soul, sometimes defiles it, sometimes wounds it, sometimes devours it, sometimes swallows it up. It bites through suggestion; defiles through delight; wounds through consent; devours through action; swallows up through despair.

But you, Lord Jesus, come visit the soul: heal the bite through confession; wash away the stain through compunction; cure the wound through prayer; draw it from the jaws through fitting satisfaction; call back what has already been swallowed through your almighty mercy. [Col. 0639D] For you rescued Daniel from the lions’ den; Jonah from the belly of the whale; Abraham from Ur of the Chaldeans; the three children from Babylon’s furnace; Susanna from the edge of the sword; the Hebrew people from Pharaoh’s persecution; Peter, sinking in the sea and denying you in the courtyard of the high priest; Paul from the depths of the sea; David from the lion’s mouth; and the thief from the jaws of death. And now do you not pity your people awaiting your coming? And now do you begin to harden yourself against your children?

Come—but in cloths, not in arms; come—but humble, not exalted; come—but upon a she-ass, not upon cherubim; come—but in a manger, not in the highest heaven; come—but to us, not against us; come—but saving, not judging; come—but in your mother’s bosom, not with the sceptre of majesty; come, [Col. 0640A] but visit us in peace, not rebuke us in fury. If you come in this manner, we shall flee not from you but to you; for unfamiliar things altogether inspire fear, while familiar things attract more sweetly.

Thus, in familiar clothing, with familiar food, and familiar speech, yet in an unfamiliar manner and under a dissimilar condition, God came to human beings as man: being immortal, he became mortal for mortals; having nothing of sin, he came to sinners, yet having the form and nature of a sinner without sin. He who came upon the asp and basilisk approached wearing shoes; he who came to cleanse lepers visited the sick in cloths. Observe that in the footwear the mystery of faith is signified; in the cloths, the sacraments of the Church, by which the poisons of sins are cleansed away, [Col. 0640B] the face of converts is adorned, and the shame of penitents is veiled.

Behold, you have coverings because you have shameful parts—that is, sins which must be covered. Perhaps you ask how? Rebecca teaches this (Gen. 27). When she presented her son Jacob for his father’s blessing, she first clothed him with Esau’s very good garments, which she had at home; and, because he lacked something with which to cover the exposed parts of his neck and hands, she put skins of young goats—whose flesh she had already cooked—around his hands and covered the exposed parts of his neck. This useful history supplies a sufficient model of repentance for sinners departing from sin and seeking the grace and blessing of the God of Jacob. But lest abundance produce distaste, we shall reserve it to set it forth more fully at another time. Meanwhile, we confine ourselves to drawing this one point from it: that we may learn how the soul of a penitent ought to clothe itself. For when we seek blessing, we must be clothed in Esau’s very good garments, which Rebecca kept at home when that hairy man went out hunting. [Col. 0640C]

But what is this? Rebecca, the virgin exceedingly beautiful, is that holy fellowship of angels which, espoused to Isaac—that is, to the joy of heavenly jubilation—always thinks and loves the things that are the Lord’s. Hairy Esau, occupied in hunting wild and woodland creatures after he had offended Isaac’s mind, is the devil who, after falling from heaven like lightning, sits crafty and cunning, like a hairy man, in ambush, that he may seize the poor person in secret and deceive the flying soul. He left behind at home the very good garments when, by apostasy, he lost the good endowments infused by God into his excellent angelic nature: “For he did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44).

But Rebecca claimed the good garments for herself when that holy fellowship, with Lucifer fallen, was more firmly established in love for its Creator, turned its minds toward God, and, lest it likewise fall, bound itself more strongly with the bonds of love. [Col. 0640D]

Esau’s very good garments, therefore, are those true virtues in which Lucifer, full of beauty in the paradise of his God, is said in the prophet to have shone (Ezek. 28). Clothed in these cloths—indeed, in far better ones—Jesus came down from heaven to us. For Adam, like Lucifer, when expelled from paradise, forgot the adornment of his breast and lost his hyacinth-blue tunic, receiving instead a garment of skins. He often wished afterwards to seek it again, but could not do so even once.

Jesus, Son of the Most High, therefore came and brought those very good garments: he restored the first robe, the ring, and the footwear to the prodigal son. For he restored the joy of his salvation; he restored an upright spirit, a holy spirit, a ruling spirit, a clean heart, a pure soul, and spotless flesh. These are the changing garments which the mercy of Jesus exchanged for loincloths and for the cloths of a menstruating woman, so that from guilty persons we might become innocent, from enemies friends, and from exiles fellow citizens. [Col. 0641A]

Moreover, the exposed parts of the neck and hands would remain without covering unless Rebecca had saved the skins of the young goats. The nakedness of the neck signifies manifest pride; naked hands, works of injustice; the skins of young goats, the repentance of converts. Therefore repentance, which an angel does not know—for neither a good angel standing in righteousness needs it, nor an evil angel persisting in injustice performs it—is taken from sinners and conceals from God’s vengeance the exposed neck, that is, the sin of pride, and the naked hands, that is, works of injustice. Behold how the soul ought to clothe itself. [Col. 0641B]

## SERMON II. ON THE SECOND SUNDAY OF ADVENT

Tell us whether you are he who is to reign over the people of Israel.

Jesus, we believe you alone in every matter because you are truth. We believe you because you alone are what you are; we also believe in you because we love you not in word and tongue, but in deed and truth. Therefore tell us whether [Col. 0641C] you are he who is to reign, because we desire you to reign over us: your yoke is sweet, your burden light, and to serve you is to reign.

The father of lies, the devil, opposes us and transforms himself into an angel of light. Since he fell from truth, he has woven so many and such great snares of deception in this exile, both for the first parents in paradise and for their descendants, that in this darkness what is true can scarcely be discerned, what is certain chosen amid ambiguity, and what is best obtained. Therefore, cautious and unwilling to stumble into an error damaging to our faith, we ask you, Jesus, concerning yourself: show us where you feed, where you lie down at noon, lest, beginning to wander after the flocks of your companions, we receive Antichrist in place of Christ, the worst in place of the good, and the devil in place of God. Tell us, therefore, whether you are he, and so forth. [Col. 0641D]

We do not wholly fail to know the reasons for your mission. You were sent to announce to your people their crimes and to the house of Jacob their sins; sent to manifest yourself to the world; sent to destroy the enemy and avenger; sent to loosen those in bonds, lead prisoners forth, free captives, destroy the kingdom of sin, and establish the kingdom of righteousness. Indeed, for a long time the prophets, whose testimonies have been made exceedingly credible, have filled many books concerning both your coming and our redemption.

Pressed by both our necessity and your compassion, we therefore come with every supplication, asking whether you are he [Col. 0642A] whom we await and to whose kingdom we desire that our lot may be transferred. For that tyrant, to whom we were delivered by the wrath of your indignation, lashes us with scorpions, burns us with whips, twists and tortures us with blows down to the marrow of our entrails. There is no health in our flesh, where sin dwells; none in the heart, where unbelief and ignorance reign. Every head is sick and every heart sorrowful; from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no health.

When the leaven of transgression has occupied the whole mass, nowhere remains a place immune from sin and the punishment of sin. Let us inspect the whole human being with all his parts, and carefully examine what vices possess which members.

From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no health [Col. 0642B] when feet run to evil in the counsel of the ungodly; knees and shins stand in the way of sinners; the reins sit in the seat of pestilence; the shameful members, which are the foxes’ parts, defile the temple of the Holy Spirit, the tabernacle of God’s name; the lower back is filled with delusions; the belly, swollen with food and wine, foams over into lusts; the throat, smoother than oil, supplies coals beneath the iron grate; the mouth boils over with folly; the tongue brandishes a burning torch; the lips speak proud things; the eyes behold vanity; the ears receive detraction; the hands shed blood; the neck raises itself in pride.

Let us consider further with what grievous goad he whose name is Death, maliciously concerned for our death, has wounded us. Thus the sole of the foot, clinging to earth, heavy and split like a calf’s hoof, weighs a person down upon the earth and divides him among many things. But the serpent lies in wait for the heel, which is adjacent to the sole; hence the Psalmist complains: “The iniquity,” he says, “of my heel shall compass me about” (Ps. 48:6); that is, the sin of the first suggestion, from the mother’s womb, never ceases at any time or in any part of life to trouble me until life’s end. [Col. 0642C]

The devil presumes that he can easily seize what follows if he has succeeded in infecting the beginnings with his poison. Therefore, whoever has had his intention breathed upon in the heel, his inclination in the sole, and his action in the foot—whoever’s breath makes the coal burn—who will prevent such a person from being held in the kingdom of sin and transferred to the kingdom of death [Col. 0642D], unless the grace and life which came through Jesus Christ come to his aid? The shins follow in the ascent of the limbs; concerning them the same Psalmist says: “He does not delight in the strength of a horse, nor is he pleased by the shins of a man” (Ps. 146:10). That is to say, neither the pride nor the power of the obstinate pleases God, nor the unregulated gait of the presumptuous and audacious person. Both excessive composure and lack of composure in one’s walk are faults: the former is a sign of luxury, the latter of instability. Isaiah rebukes the daughters of Zion who walked with studied gait. The Apostle James says in his Epistle: “A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways” (Jas. 1:8). The knees which follow must be bent not to Baal but to God most high [Col. 0643A], for every knee in heaven, on earth, and under the earth bends to him. Therefore do not bend your knees to a harlot, but to the Mother of God; not to an image, but to the living and true God. Gird the loins and reins which follow, like a man, lest they flow out in lust; say to God: “You possessed my reins” (Ps. 138:13), that is, my pleasures; and let not lust hold me, but self-control and chastity.

Next comes the belly and stomach, whose function, if lawfully governed, is useful and utterly necessary; but if it exceeds nature’s limits, it is wholly ruinous and harmful. For without it one cannot live; through it, if it has thrown off the yoke of moderation, one lives most wretchedly. Let it therefore serve the support of daily restoration, and not plunge itself into the destruction of malignant excess. [Col. 0643B] Then let us restrain the throat, which, like a funnel for the belly, pours into it almost everything it has swallowed. Thus we must guard the throat as the gate of the belly, lest anything enter through the gate that overturns nature. Fasting shuts this gate; abstinence guards it; moderate refreshment opens it beneficially; immoderation shakes its very hinges.

The jaws, as it were an inner vestibule, have the mouth as their outer door; if it is not guarded, there is no peace either for one entering or one leaving. For if evil thought conceives any offspring from the root of the serpent, while the closed mouth keeps the dead corpse confined within, the throat or jaws are indeed a tomb, but not yet an open one. But if, with the mouth opened, it exhales the pent-up stench, it is an open tomb; and in the corrupted air even the appearance of religion dies [Col. 0643C], which until then lived for the gain of a good reputation. Let speech therefore be sweet; let utterances be chaste; let the gate always be shut against evils and open to goods.

What then of the eyes, by whose ministry, like sun and moon, the day of wisdom and the night of ignorance are governed in a person, so that his darkness may be as his light? That is, let him humbly accuse himself of ignorance, and use wisely and soberly the wisdom and knowledge given by God. The eye that is not satisfied with seeing, if it is modest and chaste, looks rather to heaven than to earth; hence: “My eyes have grown dim, looking upward” (Isa. 38:14).

These eyes, then, seeing from afar the power of God that is coming, inquire more curiously into the signs concerning Jesus and from Jesus [Col. 0643D], and diligently investigate whether all that was said of him agrees. They do not say with the Jews, “You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true” (John 8:13), but with Peter, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters” (Matt. 14:28). Not testing but seeking, they say: “Tell us,” and so forth. If you are the King of the Jews; if you are King of kings and Lord of lords; if you are the King of Zion who, sitting upon a she-ass and a colt, the foal of a beast of burden, heard the Hebrew children cry, “Hosanna to the Son of David”; tell us. If you are he who came to sit upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, tell us. If you are he who has dominion upon his shoulder, tell us. If you are the Son of the King to whom the Father gave all judgment, so that all [Col. 0644A] may honor the Son as they honor the Father who sent him, tell us. Tell us whether dominion will cease from Damascus; whether you came to cast down death; whether you came to give redemption for your people; whether you came to save your people from their sins. Tell us whether you came to restore nature’s gifts and renew the gifts of grace; whether you will free creation, which was subjected unwillingly to vanity, from its necessities; whether you will release us from misery and sin.

Behold, we see the Virgin Mother; we see the time of favor, O God; we see the scepter departed from Judah and the ruler from between his thighs. We see swords forged into ploughshares and spears into sickles. We see signs made new; we see the way passing through the midst of the silence of night. All these things indicate that one new has come [Col. 0644B] upon the earth, from whom the New Testament began, the Old Law having been made old along with all its observances. Therefore, translated into the law of grace, faith, and righteousness, may we be translated into the kingdom of eternal salvation and glory, through your providence, Jesus, who live and reign as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON III. ON THE THIRD SUNDAY OF ADVENT

“Send forth, O Lord, the Lamb, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. 16:1).

Send an angel and send forth the Lamb—not a boar, not a unicorn, not a bull, not an ox, not a goat, not an ass, not a camel, not a lion, not a basilisk, not a scorpion, not a serpent. For the boar would bite with its tooth [Col. 0644C]; the unicorn would attack with its horn; the bull would toss in stubbornness; the ox would strike with its horn; the goat would stink; the ass would trouble by stupidity; the camel would displease by its hump; the lion would devour; the basilisk would kill by poison; the scorpion would sting with its tail; the serpent would deceive. These vices are to be avoided, not prayed for. In the boar, indeed, strife and contention are signified; in the unicorn, singularity and presumption; in the bull, wantonness and rebellion; in the ox, sloth or hardness; in the goat, lust; in the ass, dullness; in the camel, inflation and perversity; in the lion, fury and plundering; in the basilisk, evil persuasion; in the scorpion, detraction; in the serpent, deceitful deception; in the lamb, innocence.

Let us especially refrain from the aforementioned vices, lest, under sheep’s garments—whether woollen or skins—we feign an appearance of piety, and not—would that we did—its power [perhaps: “power”]. For an ass is dressed, as it were, in a lion’s skin when a vicious mind assumes the skins of Solomon or the Lamb in pretence. Hence the Apostle says of certain people: “Having an appearance of piety, but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3:5). Therefore let there by no means be deceit in the spirit while an outward habit of simplicity is displayed; rather, let a person have in the heart what is shown in the face. Then indeed he will pray profitably: “Send forth the Lamb, O Lord,” because, as he finds a person, so he will show himself to that person. For “with the holy you will be holy, and with the innocent innocent” (Ps. 17:26); that is, with the lamb he will be a lamb.

Send forth, therefore, O Lord, the Lamb who is not angry [Col. 0645A], who does not lie in wait, who does not kick back, who does not walk in things great or marvelous beyond himself; who gives us his wool, like snow, to warm what is cold in us and cover what is shameful; who gives his hide to restrain what is unbound and clothe what is bare upon the feet; who gives his flesh to be eaten, lest we fail on the way; who scatters the lowly and weak things of assumed humanity, like dung, upon our earth, so that, visited, drenched, and enriched by these, it may multiply and bring forth fruit thirtyfold, sixtyfold, or a hundredfold. By his hoof—that is, by rebuke—he also removes our scab: he restrains evil desires and itching; he opens and expounds the inward parts, saying: “Everything whatever I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15). [Col. 0645B] He offers his stomach, in which all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden, to his banqueters. He shows the back of patience, which Pilate scourged, for the instruction of correction. He sets upon the table of the altar, to be eaten, the ribs which his crucifiers counted as they were stretched upon the cross. He is caught by his horns upon the cross, as Abraham’s ram was caught among the thorns. He offers his tail when he says: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). His teeth are whiter than milk, because in his preaching there is nothing faulty, nothing obscure. His eyes are more beautiful than wine, because, as Gregory says, in comparison or contemplation of him all things become worthless: “This is the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world” [Col. 0645C] (John 1:29).

Send forth this Lamb, O Lord, bearing with him Wisdom, the attendant of your throne, light and truth. Hence: “Send forth your light and your truth” (Ps. 42:3), that is, grace and teaching. Send also the hand of which David says: “Send forth your hand from on high” (Ps. 143:7), that is, from the Father’s bosom: help against the Devil, the assailant. Send secretly, lest a tumult be heard in the crossroads of Ashkelon, where demons gather, thieves of souls and thieves of God’s counsels, should the goodness of God’s wisdom perhaps devise something against their malice. Send wisely, because you made all things in wisdom, and by your prudence struck down the proud Devil. Send mightily [Col. 0645D], because the Lord is mighty and powerful in battle. Send gently, that he may descend as rain upon the fleece and fill the little vessels of the virginal womb with the water of our humanity and the wine of divinity. Send willingly, because the only Son will acquire many adopted sons: “Who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John 1). Send by your permission, so that at last, in the fullness of time at the end of the ages, he may have leave to come—he who, from the beginning of Adam’s transgression and expulsion from Paradise, never ceased to send beforehand the heralds of his coming and the most frequent distillations of mercies. Send the gentle Lamb, who flees Herod as a young doe flees a lion, and flees the face of the Jews, when they took up stones to stone him, as a sheep flees a wolf.

[Col. 0646A] Send the Lamb to be shorn in circumcision, flayed in crucifixion, sold for thirty denarii in betrayal, and sacrificed for our redemption. Send the Lamb who is worthy to receive power and divinity, who is worthy to open the seven seals of the sealed book—that is, of the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation. Send the Lamb who does not immediately kill sinners, but calls them to repentance, saying: “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matt. 9:13).

Send—but for what purpose? That he may rule: “the ruler,” he says, “of the earth.” From where? “From the rock of the desert.” To where? “To the mountain of the daughter of Zion.” What is the rock of the desert? Ruth the Moabitess, whom Boaz took as wife and by whom he begot Obed; Obed begot Jesse; Jesse begot David; and from David’s [Col. 0646B] seed came Christ, who took his origin from the Virgin Mother. Therefore send forth the Lamb, O Lord, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion, so that by the line of descent, according to God’s deep and unknown judgment, the cornerstone who makes both one may embrace the two stocks of humankind, namely Jews and Gentiles. Let him move his steps from the rock of the desert—he who, although he began to come from Adam through many thousands of years, nevertheless did not leave clearly impressed footprints anywhere, but was moving with silence, like the waters of Siloam, toward our deliverance with long-drawn breath. Yet here, as though grace, victorious, had turned aside to a resting-place, taking breath from the ancient designs and thoughts, he began to draw near with more manifest steps, so that the Evangelist Matthew begins to count from this point—though the departure had begun from Abraham [Col. 0646C] because of God’s promise.

This also should be noted in the expression, “Send forth the Lamb from the rock of the desert.” The Father is entreated that, just as it is customary in watercourses to place a stone reservoir for the breathing-space or inspection of the leaping water, so the current of divine compassion flowing from the first man, as from the first stone, had as its mystical channel Ruth the Moabitess joined to Boaz the Jew. Therefore, received by King David in a more beautiful channel, it flowed on in a clearer vein to the mountain of the daughter of Zion, that is, the Virgin Mary, whom his right hand acquired. There the morning shower of divinity and the evening shower of humanity, like rain descending upon the fleece, filled the earthen little vessel because of the frailty of the female sex [Col. 0646D]. For this is the pool of the upper gate, in which grace washes and the flesh of sin is washed away: while, in preparation for the incarnation of the Word, the Virgin is cleansed from every sin, and Christ’s flesh is conceived without any sin. This flesh of the Lamb is not merely free from every stain of corruption, but is of such purity and power that by a mere nod or touch it heals the leprosy of every contagion. “He is the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). Therefore, that he may take away the sins of the world, send forth, O Lord, the Lamb, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV. IN THE FOURTH SEASON OF ADVENT

[Col. 0647A]

“Send forth your Lamb, O Lord, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. 16:1).

The necessity of the human complaint and the fitness of its remedy are known to no one more fully than to God, who prepared antidotes before the Devil vomited forth his worst poisons into the mouth and mind of man. Therefore, as the disease grew and grew beyond measure, the physician added remedies fashioned by his wisdom and suited to the particular conditions of each person and to human misery. Thus the record of the divine line of descent recounts, throughout the individual books of the prophets, forms of varied prayers and utterances, while one person is afflicted in one way and another differently. For a household servant is not afraid humbly to suggest to a good master [Col. 0647B] what he does not think will offend him. Nor is he offended who wishes to be asked before he is asked, and who extends his hand before anyone is found to receive it. Grace has never failed a worthy petitioner from the Giver, nor has he only once granted mercy in advance to the unworthy: everywhere, every day, he calls and urges all people toward the ark of his grace, full of every good thing. Thus each of the ancient Fathers, tempering his petition both to the eternal disposition and to our need, presents a little written petition through an angel’s hand to be read in the palace of the supreme King, so that, by the Creator’s good pleasure, the Lamb may be sent for the work of universal restoration.

At this time and for this task, a lion was not needed, since it is too fierce; nor a camel, because it is tall and hunchbacked; nor an ass, because it is sluggish and slow; nor a wolf, because it is rapacious; nor a bear, because it is stubborn; nor a kid, because it stinks; nor a horse, because [Col. 0647C] it smells battle from afar; nor a horn-striking ox, because it clings too closely to the earth; nor a bull, because it is stiff-necked. The Lamb alone suits the work to be done, because he is incorrupt, spotless, gentle, woolly, most tender, peaceful, and mild. Send forth, therefore, O Lord, the ruler of the earth. Send from the bosom of the divine mind; send from the summit of heaven; send from the highest pivot of invisible majesty; send according to your permission; send from your treasures and depths; send the Lamb, O Lord, ruler of the earth. Do not send Saul, who looks for his father’s asses like an ass-driver; nor Pharaoh [Col. 0647D], king of Egypt, who pursues God’s people with horses and chariots; nor Nebuchadnezzar, who ate grass like an ox; nor Alexander the Great, who devastated every kingdom like a lion; nor Rehoboam, who beats the subjected people with scorpions; nor Solomon, who, a lover of women, joined idolatry to lust; nor Zedekiah, who broke the covenant and, like a bear, was blinded and held in chains; nor Ahab, who seized Naboth’s vineyard like a wolf, through his wife’s fury as though through hunger, and killed him. Do not send any of the other kings, because they devour their people like bread for food; they do not save, free, or redeem. For a brother does not redeem, nor does a mere human being; rather, God made man does, the spotless Lamb, by whose blood we have been redeemed from our vain manner of life. [Col. 0648A] This is the Lamb whom the Father sealed and sent into the world.

Let us therefore consider the sign of the Lamb, because we must fortify both our doorposts with the blood of the Lamb against the destroying Angel. Nothing in the Lamb is to be neglected, because even his smallest part is very necessary for our salvation. The Lamb’s four feet are the four parts of the cross: length, breadth, height, and depth; or the four regions of the world: east, west, north, and south. Or, as is read in Hannah’s song (1 Sam. 2), “The Lord kills” because of the hoof, and “makes alive” because of the sole: this is the first foot. The second is he who leads the wicked down to hell and brings back those who have turned. The third foot: the Lord makes one poor in spirit and enriches with blessedness. The Lamb’s fourth foot humbles the proud and raises up the crushed and humble.

The Lamb’s face is the will of God, for Jesus says: “I always do the things pleasing to him” (John 8:29); and: “This is he in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17:5). [Col. 0648B] In the Apocalypse he has seven eyes, because the spirit of wisdom and understanding rested upon him; the spirit of counsel and might; the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him (Isa. 2). He also has seven horns because on the day of judgment he will render to each according to his works, according to what he has done in the body in four ways and in the soul in three. “For three transgressions of Damascus,” says the Lord, “and for four I will not turn him back” (Amos 1:3).

The Lamb’s belly is distinguished by sapphires because he suffered as a human being but acted divinely. His back is patience; hence David: “Sinners have built upon my back” [Col. 0648C] (Ps. 128:39). His wool is his benefits or the Gospel preaching, which the Evangelists and all the Church’s teachers spin and weave by preaching the Gospel to every creature. His flesh is food for the life of the soul; his blood, drink.

## SERMON V. IN THE FIFTH SEASON OF ADVENT

“Behold, a virgin shall conceive,” etc. (Isa. 7:14).

To say something about the weight of the letter: that “Behold” renews time, recalls faith, and restores the spirit. “A virgin shall conceive and bear a son” sustains attention, kindles devotion, and establishes Christian dignity. By the Lord’s advent times are renewed, dead faith is raised again, and the spirit, mourning through poverty and failing through the weariness of long expectation, is restored. Attention, with Job, chooses suspension in anticipation of the Savior; devotion, like Mary Magdalene upon hearing that the Lord is coming, rises quickly and offers tears to him who comes. In conception, Christian faith receives God as a life-giving spirit through divine breathing. Concerning renewal, the Lord says: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. 21:1): namely, a new advent, a new conception, a new birth, a new mother, a new son, a new manner of being born, living, preaching, dying, rising, ascending into heaven, and coming again to judge the living and the dead.

Concerning the recall of faith, he likewise says: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke 18:8). [Col. 0649A] And the Prophet: “There is no faith in the land.” The Jews inquire into days and years, says this prophet, and mockingly said: “Command upon command, wait upon wait” (Isa. 28:10, 13). Likewise: “The Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17), who said: “You believe in God; believe also in me” (John 14:1). Thus he recalled faith as it was departing and the soul as it was breathing out. Concerning the restoration of the spirit, the Prophet says: “Raise up the prophecies which the former prophets spoke in your name; give a reward to those who await you, that your prophets may be found faithful” (Ecclus. 36:17). Likewise: “This one shall comfort us from our works” (Gen. 15:29).

Concerning the suspension of attention, Job says: “My soul chose hanging” (Job 7:15); and Hezekiah: “My eyes have grown dim, looking upward” [Col. 0649B] (Isa. 38:14); and David: “I have lifted up my eyes to you,” etc. (Ps. 122:1). Nor without reason, for Moses went up the mountain and the Lord came down when he wished to give the Law. How much more rightly, then, must one ascend to the summit when God is to be received in the flesh and conceived by a virgin? The Lord descended through a space great enough and beyond when he entered the maiden’s enclosure; yet he did not touch our lower parts more than was fitting, because he admitted no male intercourse in his conception. Let our attention, therefore, attend and stretch itself out as far as faith extends the borders of its veil, so that it may believe. Let it not examine the mystery of the Incarnation, merely forming opinions about the incomprehensible union of Word and man, accomplished together in the Angel’s word, the Virgin’s faith, and the operation of the Holy Spirit, nor try to set it forth all at once or even once, until it is seen eye to eye [Col. 0649C].

Concerning the kindling of devotion, Isaiah says: “Whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem” (Isa. 31:9). The fire lay hidden in Zion while the Virgin’s conception was retained in the womb. But the furnace appeared in Jerusalem when the star led the magi to Jerusalem and revealed the King who had been born. Therefore devotion was kindled, because “the people who sat in darkness saw a great light” (Matt. 4:16), and the Sun of righteousness rose for those who fear God.

It remains to say how Christian dignity was established [Col. 0649D] in the Virgin’s conception. Whoever does not believe that Jesus was conceived and born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary will not have the foundation of faith. That foundation stands so unconquerable and immovable that the whole amassed force of aerial, worldly, and infernal powers, by assaulting it, would establish and strengthen it ever more.

## SERMON VI. IN THE SAME SEASON, VI

“Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. 7:14).

O singular and special privilege of the Virgin, surpassing angels, all saints, and all God’s gifts: that a virgin shall conceive and bear a son. This benefit was not given to angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominions, thrones, cherubim, or seraphim [Col. 0650A]. Let it suffice them to adore God, see God, love God, know God, obey God, fulfill God’s will in all things and fail in none, and fear nothing. They receive blessed gifts; and in so great a fellowship there is no one in whom there is a desire to possess more than he has received. He reserved for our Virgin the dense and concentrated height of all graces, so that she might have her own fountain, which not even an angel could share except with thanksgiving; to which all ages offer reverence with bowed head; nor could they presume to hope further for anything like it, but from this point the generations of every age should claim, with thanksgiving, the portion due to them. The inhabitants also of the region above the moon should gladly offer their services, not wondering that what God’s wisdom had so silently drawn from its unfathomable treasuries, so that it might enter the Virgin’s womb—a womb which the whole world could by no means contain—had lain hidden from eternity. It is indeed wonderful that he entered thus in order to dwell in her; but more wondrous still that he entered thus in order that the Virgin might conceive him.

One person worthily receives God as he comes, another takes him in, another welcomes him. One receives a guest, another takes in a lord, another welcomes a friend; but who contains him—or rather, who conceives him—except the Virgin, of whom it is said: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive,” etc.? Of a certain person whose feet were moved it is said: “The spirit shall pass through him and shall not remain” (Ps. 102:16). Of Moses it is said: “When I have passed by, you shall see my back” (Exod. 33:23). Job says: “In the horror of a night vision, one passed by whose face I did not recognize” [Col. 0650C] (Job 4:13, 16). It is a great thing, a very great thing, even to see God in passing; but it is more joyful and more useful to contain God and retain God, and incomparably greater to conceive God in flesh and from one’s own flesh.

For this virginal conception was made through the intervening coagulation of faith and charity; through grace incomprehensibly fervent in the observance of the Law and God’s commandments; and through the leavening of the Holy Spirit in the three measures of meal—that is, the flesh and virginal soul together with grace given from above—from which bread might be formed, with the crust of humanity and the crumb of divinity, to be baked in the furnace of the cross, received meanwhile at the table of the altar, and finally in the kingdom of God. And this is what he says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive,” etc.

[Col. 0650D] Since the Virgin is not only the full field of which it is said, “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 27:27), for producing bread—as is read in the Psalm, “That he may bring bread,” that is, Christ, “from the earth” (Ps. 103:14), that is, from the Virgin Mary—we should observe that she is also the vine from which the wine of libations is pressed, as is read in Ecclesiasticus: “I, like a vine, brought forth the sweetness of fragrance” (Ecclus. 24:23). In the unlike appearance of things, by plausible reasoning we compare the conception accomplished in the Virgin: as the earth produces its shoot and as a garden causes its seed to germinate, so the Virgin conceives God and so God is conceived in the Virgin, by the moisture of earth alone and the richness of grace.

The Father shows his colt—that is, his Son—bound to our vine, that is, our Virgin [Col. 0651A]; and the heavenly Husbandman pruned this vine when he cleansed her from every original as well as actual fault. He bound her to a stake when he betrothed her to Joseph; made her fruitful when he greeted her through the angel; she put forth branches and leaves when she answered the angel, “Let it be to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38). He filled her like a little vessel with wine, according to Isaiah, who says: “Ten acres shall yield one little vessel” (Isa. 5:10), when for ten months she cherished Christ’s flesh in her sacred womb and in his birth brought forth to the world a true and perfect man and God. For he ploughed ten acres, as it were ten furrows in Samson’s heifer, when he sent his Christ—who is the end of the Law, consisting of ten commandments—to the Virgin Mary for incarnation.

Or the ten acres are human and angelic righteousness, which was complete in Mary: angelic nature is distinguished by nine orders, while human nature was created as the tenth. Nothing of righteousness was bestowed or placed in humanity or in angels that did not flow in a full torrent to the throne of grace, so that he who rests in grace might in time abundantly fill his world by his grace. For the grace which he sent beforehand or brought with him when he was to be conceived, he carried forth, preserving the Mother’s possession, to distribute it fully, far and wide, when born.

Let us therefore bring our cups or goblets to the full little vessel, that we may be made drunk with the abundance of God’s house and drink the wine which the Virgin Vine produced [Col. 0651C], and which likewise brings forth virgins. Let us not be given over to wine in which there is lust, wine from the grape of gall, which is the gall of dragons and the incurable poison of asps. Jesus of Nazareth, because he is a Nazirite, does not drink this wine; and because he will be called Emmanuel, that is, “God with us,” let us do only what we see him doing, and let there be no schisms among us. He was certainly conceived and born from Mary, who is not divided, because she is Virgin and one in virtue, virginity, conception, offspring, dignity, profession, propitiation, and salvation. Therefore let us say, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive,” etc., “and his name shall be called Emmanuel”: with us in this pilgrimage.

I am not sufficient to conceive with what manner, speech, and language I may approach that shining cloud [Col. 0651D] in which Jesus was not transfigured but incarnate—unless I might rightly call even that incarnation a transfiguration, since he who was in the form of God did not count equality with God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man (Phil. 2:6). This truly is the wondrous transfiguration in which he did not transform something else in himself, as the Apostle and Apollos transfer to themselves the weaknesses of certain persons, but by an ineffable dispensation transformed—or rather united—himself, God, with himself, man: the form of God not lost but held in reserve, and the form of a servant displayed.

Therefore, if it were somehow possible, having changed—or rather, borrowed—an angelic manner, I would dare to think, speak, or write about my Lady [Col. 0652A]. For what can I say in this manner, whether my own or another’s, public or private? The public manner is dissolute; the private constricted; the borrowed suspect; one’s own despised. The public does not know sobriety; the private does not know the enlargement of heart; the borrowed does not know security; one’s own fears rejection. In public is the son of Belial, free from righteousness, a wild ass in the wilderness; in private, the servant of Mammon, serving belly and throat; in borrowed dress, the daughters of the leech who say, “Bring!” (Prov. 30:15); in one’s own dress, the person placed under the Law, who says: “I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind” (Rom. 7:23). Thus suspended, I do not know what I should choose.

But in doubtful matters the more kindly interpretation must be maintained. Therefore I always cast down and fearful eyes [Col. 0652B], not upward toward the face in which are two great luminaries, splendid beyond the strength of the eyes; through which, at uncertain hours, there shone forth the light of light and fountain of light, she alone bearing things splendid beyond the strength of the eyes. But I turn them downward toward the sandals of the princely daughter, who, girded and shod, trampled the world’s glory and surpassed angelic excellence; where at the roots of Lebanon Christ, the river of Paradise, rises—the one made for us God’s power and God’s wisdom, righteousness and redemption. Therefore, with contrite and humble spirit, I shall whisper in my groaning at the door of the Mother of Mercy, in case I may receive from her something which I may worthily say or write concerning her. For human reason and talent, yielding, can more readily expire than say anything worthy, without grace, concerning her who is full of grace.

Let us therefore unfold the ark of her sanctification, salvation, and glory by her garments, so that we may reverently seek to desire those things which suffice for public benefit, while sparing to touch what was born for the Son alone [Col. 0652C]. For in her there is both that which she may spread abroad without loss on the way, and that which she may preserve with joy in the homeland; here devotion is nourished from it, there vision is enjoyed. Therefore let her conception and birth be continually commemorated, because this is the chief foretaste of the eternal kingdom; and it is sweeter than honey and the honeycomb always to have Mary and Jesus in mouth and heart.

Behold, new; behold, fresh; behold, still hanging upon the tree itself: a fruit as richly savory as it is wholly delightful. For it does not become better with time, since in every time it is older, not by age but by creation. The Word did not assume human nature as something needing to mature, because by assuming it he fully matured it. Nor did he leave anything raw or half-cooked in it. Virtue did not grow in the human being whom Divinity perfectly filled by creating him. Although the boy Jesus is said to have advanced in age and grace with God and human beings, he is nevertheless believed to have had no increase in merits over time that he did not possess from the very conception of which it is said: “Behold, a virgin,” etc. He grew in age, truly multiplying days; and in grace, not by increasing virtues but by making them known before God and human beings. But this [Col. 0653A] was all for human beings. For before God he was as great and such in his very conception as he was in the most evident manifestation of the time that followed.

But he first puts forward a sign which is both a thing and a sign. “Therefore,” he says, “the Lord himself will give you a sign: behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son.” One sign was given concerning Jesus, another was performed by Jesus; both, however, came from the same God, who existed before the man Jesus and is God made man. Since nothing was made without him, neither Jesus himself—who was made from a woman, made under the Law—could be made or signified without him. But of those signs which Jesus performed Nicodemus says: “No one can perform these signs which you do unless God is with him” (John 3:2). For it was singular, and wonderfully beyond what can be believed, that God should become human. Rightly, signs had to precede this sign; for a work of God’s thought so profound could not suddenly but only gradually be poured into human minds, nor could the soul fly up to the highest mighty works of God unless supported by wings and feathers.

The prophet had also urged King Ahaz to ask for a sign in the depths of hell [lacuna] another [lacuna] surely relating to the Lord’s descent and ascent, by which the economy of the Lord’s incarnation is fulfilled. But when that unworthy and reprobate man refused, Isaiah added, saying: “For this reason”—that is, because your sins, O Ahaz, do not deserve to foreknow the mystery of the incarnation—“for this reason he will give a sign” (O faithful peoples!). Moses did not refuse a sign, nor Gideon, nor Manoah, nor [Col. 0653C] many others, whose faith, though small, was, as it is said in the Song: “Our little sister has no breasts” (Song 8:8); yet, retaining the entire nobility of their stock and the lawful propagation of the one Lord, it ventured to set its hand to the hard tasks of obedience. Faith cuts off the darts of reason, shatters the phantoms of every contrivance, unlocks customary practice, excludes the nature of impossibilities, and subjects everything to the Lord’s willing and power. It receives a sign, not because of its own weakness but at God’s command. For just as a young man, healthy and strong, holds a staff in his hand, not to support himself but to take pleasure in it, so faith seeks, for obedience rather than distrust, how things are done which [lacuna] are commanded [printed *comitem omnium opinionem*, “accompanying all opinion”; corrected *contra communem omnium opinionem*, “contrary to the common opinion”]. Hence those words: “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?” (Luke 1:34).

David asks for this sign in the person of Christ: “Work with me a sign for good” (Ps. 85:17). “Work a sign with me,” he says, “so that Mary my mother may conceive as a virgin and give birth; and this is a sign for good, because it is from the Holy Spirit, who is God’s good gift.” The sign of Moses too, by which the waters of the Red Sea stood on either side as though a wall [printed *muro*; f. *murum*], signifies the Virgin’s conception, in which there is no violation of chastity, but the itching of concupiscence is removed from both heart and flesh. Gideon likewise asks that the fleece be moistened while the threshing-floor is dry, just as the Virgin Mary was made pregnant by the Holy Spirit without an act compromising chastity. What more need be said? Above the stars, [Col. 0654A] above heaven, above every creature, this sign stands preeminent, more exalted and more glorious: that a virgin conceived, that a virgin gave birth. “Behold, a Virgin.” It seems to me that, in saying “Behold,” the prophet fixed eye and finger upon the clock of the eternal dispensation, foreseeing and pointing out that by which an angel should marvel, humanity be redeemed, and the Lord be conceived. Behold: turn your eyes away lest they see vanity, and direct them toward what the Lord has done, what is wonderful in our eyes: virginity and fruitfulness in the same person. Behold a palace built at wondrous cost, and enriched with incomparable treasures—enriched with God’s Son, and with God’s Son alone. Behold the Virgin; behold the vine; behold the grape, not sour but ripe.

Eve was a sour grape; Mary was a ripe grape. Nor is this [Col. 0654B] surprising. At the beginning of the world Eve, yielding to gluttony, rushed with immature deliberation to the fruit made bitter by prohibition, and caused the teeth of children not yet born to be set on edge in every generation. But Mary, most modest at the end of the ages, ripened by heavenly dew and sun, was neither self-willed in presumption [printed *propria*; corrected *praeceps*, “headlong”] nor slow, like something rotten, through unbelief. The angel brought her a flower, saying, “Hail, Mary”; he brought dew, saying, “Full of grace”; he brought fruit, saying, “The Lord is with you” (Luke 1:28); he brought ripeness, saying, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (ibid., 42). Therefore, in Christian custom, we bless new fruits before tasting them, lest perhaps our teeth be set on edge by the ancient curse if they fall without blessing. Behold the Virgin: [Col. 0654C] in mouth, eyes, lips, finger, foot, hand, heart, mind, and flesh. Behold the Virgin, like dawn between night and day, between the Lord and humankind. “Fair as the moon” (Song 6:9) through fullness of days, that is, of virtues; “chosen as the sun” (ibid.) through grace and the singularity of her merits; “terrible as an army drawn up in battle” (ibid.) above all angelic and aerial powers, through the fullness of her endowment. Behold the wise Virgin, who has oil poured into her womb together with the lamp of wondrous works; who entered with the bridegroom—or rather, I say, the bridegroom entered, and her son Jesus—as from [lacuna] a palace of heaven, or rather a more beautiful garden, or a more delightful paradise. Behold the Virgin: compassionate toward the weak; holy toward the just; fullers’ herb toward the unclean; salt toward the corrupt; [Col. 0654D] a ladder to the lame; a reconciler to the guilty; mercy to the wretched; a harbor to the shipwrecked; a tower to the fearful; lady to her own; singular goodness to all. Behold the Virgin, the eastern gate through which the prince alone enters. Behold the Virgin, a chamber of spices, whose fragrant words surpass every spice, because into no virgin did the Holy Spirit breathe such inspirations of virtues, by which the Lord smells an odor of sweetness and angelic censers and our own incense-burners are filled.

## SERMON VII. ON THE VIGIL OF THE LORD’S NATIVITY

On the Gospel: “When Mary his mother was betrothed to Joseph” (Matt. 1:18).

“Strengthen me with flowers, surround me with apples” (Song 2:5). [Col. 0655A] This sweet voice belongs to her who dwells in the gardens and approaches her singular and divine childbirth, calling together the inhabitants of heaven and earth to look upon and receive the birth; to receive and preserve her grace; and to contemplate and admire the glory of the Lord and her own glory. Truly, this sacrament of great godliness is lovable on account of grace, admirable on account of glory, and ineffable on account of its splendor and inaccessible light; for splendor is around and within her, from the loins upward. This is the subject of the present Gospel reading: “When Mary his mother was betrothed to Joseph.”

What in all created things is more lovable than the Virgin singularly loving the Lord, and being loved beforehand by the Lord, of whom Solomon says, “A most beloved hind” [Col. 0655B] (Prov. 5:19)? And what is more lovable than that beloved Son of God, eternally born from the Beloved, and, at the end of the world, according to the Apostle, made from the beloved woman, of whom it is added: “And a most pleasing fawn” (ibid.)? What, finally, is more admirable than that the incomprehensible One should incomprehensibly be sealed in the womb, yet neither separated nor withdrawn from the Father’s cohabitation, confession, and equality? For he was wholly in his Mother and wholly with the Father at the same time. Though this is difficult to say, it is nevertheless altogether believable in the heart. What is more ineffable than the Word becoming flesh, than man becoming God and God becoming man?

Behold, the Trinity, the divine craftsman, in this one work fashioned all this together: the Word and the human being. There the omnipotence of the Father, accomplishing what was impossible to human beings [Col. 0655C] and therefore ineffable, carved in the virginal workshop a new vessel from new material and with new workmanship, according to his omnipotence. The Wisdom of God did likewise what he saw the Father doing; and, if it may be said, expended the powers of his intelligence in this same work more diligently and affectionately than he expended them concerning himself and through himself [*per se*; or *pro se*, “for himself”]. The Holy Spirit, like fire entering a furnace, as though melting divinity and humanity together, not only applied his endeavors to this work but also, pouring forth without confusion his very self in the diverse operation of every grace, wove them together in the same vessel. Hence it was said: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). Behold the lovable: [Col. 0655D] let us tend toward it. Behold the admirable: let us stretch ourselves toward it. Behold the ineffable: let us be carried above ourselves toward it. There let us gather flowers and apples from him by meditation, in him by seeking, concerning him by loving, and through him by contemplation, that we may bring, offer, and present them to the Son and to the mother giving birth in the manger. Let us bring them by meditating on him; present them by praising him with his mother; offer them by adoring, above the mother, the Lord who is man.

But so that we may suggest to you, dearest brethren, things possible rather than impossible, we shall briefly portray the flowers that you should bring to our Lady. It is enough that you offer flowers to her through whom our flesh flowered anew by the novelty of virginal childbirth, having been stripped of its blossom through Adam by the antiquity of original guilt. Certainly nothing of the bran-like [Col. 0656A] transgression clung to Christ in his assumption of our nature. He took from his mother, in union with the Word, not sinful flesh, but the likeness of sinful flesh, from the first fruits of human nature as it was created in the first parent. Nor do we maintain that some particle of human substance remained immune from sin in Adam and flowed down by hidden channels as far as the Virgin; for true and catholic faith holds that the little leaven of the first transgression corrupted the whole mass of our nature, in soul and body.

It also greatly concerned the cause of our restoration that almighty grace should appear all the more glorious in its operation because, from the old, aged, and rotten trunk, by more wonderful power and easier work, it produced from the Virgin without sin an unfading flower—namely, the flesh of Jesus, sanctifying angels and giving life to human beings. For Christ himself says of his humanity: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2:1). Let us therefore purify and renew our hearts and bodies, that we may be able to approach him in some degree of chastity.

The first degree of chastity, then, that we may rise from the lower (*inferioribus*) [or weaker (*infirmioribus*)] things, is *fenalis* chastity (the term is uncertain), which naturally belongs to children, the decrepit, or those cold by natural constitution. It is called *fenalis* because, as far as depends upon the person, it earns little merit. For what is acquired without labor is obtained without struggle. Yet it is good, in whatever way and on whatever occasion it occurs, not to be corrupted.

The second is temporary chastity, compared to the seed that fell upon rock and, after springing up, withered because it had no moisture (Luke 8:6). So the chastity of some does not put down roots below in order to bear fruit above, but believes for a time and withdraws at the time of temptation (Luke 8:14), retaining incorruption for a month or a year.

The third is penitential chastity. Here is labor; here is work; here Jacob and Esau wrestle in Rebekah’s womb. But it is said, “The elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. 25:23; Rom. 9:13): that is, flesh shall serve spirit, vice virtue, lust chastity. Of this the Apostle says: “I see another law in [Col. 0656D] my members warring against the law of my mind” (Rom. 7:23). And again: “He shall not be crowned unless he has contended lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:5).

The fourth is triumphant chastity. Of this the Apocalypse says: “To the one who conquers I will give to eat from the tree of life” (Rev. 2:7). And Isaiah: “Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs”—who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdoms of heaven (Matt. 19:12)—“I will give them a place within my walls and a name better than sons and daughters” (Isa. 56:5). This is the chastity of those returning from war to the gate, who beneath vine and fig tree—that is, in the sweetness of spiritual grace—complete the years of virtues in fullness of days, and possess peace of heart and flesh, which neither flesh nor the world can give.

The fifth is virginal chastity. Of it the Gospel says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. [Col. 0657A] 5:8). This is the chastity of John the Evangelist. Of it it is said: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth the fragrance of sweetness” (Song 1:12). For that unicorn, who singularly and especially loves chastity, flows into the virginal breast; he speaks in the Song: “Open to me, my bride, my dove,” and so forth (Song 5:2).

The sixth is crystalline chastity. This is so vigorous and strong, like death, that it chooses death rather than violation of the integrity of virginity. And as the liquidity of water is changed in crystal into the solidity of stone, so this chastity has been made inseparable from flesh and soul. Of it the Psalmist says: “He sends his crystal like morsels” (Ps. 147:17). For it makes sips for the child Jesus and for his mother, and sometimes [Col. 0657B] morsels also.

The seventh is singular chastity; for neither the first was seen to resemble it nor any that followed. Properly and uniquely it belongs to the blessed Virgin: not merely virginity but fruitful virginity, which did not know a man and gave birth to God as man. This Virgin speaks in the Song: “My beloved is mine and I am his” (Song 2:16); “he shall dwell between my breasts” (Song 1:12). In contemplating her, our heart is enlarged in exultation, yet almost bursts with ineffable admiration and jubilation. These are the flowers of which it is said, “Strengthen me with flowers.” Concerning apples and love, of which I languish, perhaps we shall speak another time; here we are silent in order to avoid weariness.

Above all, we take care to warn your charity [Col. 0657C] not to touch these flowers with a hand defiled in any respect, but with one well washed. There are many kinds of contamination; if the flowers are touched by them, they immediately wither and disappear. For there is no fellowship of light with darkness, or of purity with uncleanness. Therefore let there be no dust, rot, scab, sweat, blood, or poison on your hand. Dust signifies thoughts which, like flies, buzz about and, according to the purity of the soul, defile Abraham’s sacrifice; but Abraham drove away the birds. Thus we must cut away from the heart and loose from affection every superfluous thought. We must also wipe away the rot which malice has wrought in us through evil and prolonged habitation. For as rot arises in an apple from its corruption, so pollution arises in us from evil thought; it must be washed in confession. Scab arises on the hand when delight and consent follow the thought. But lest the flower of your good work and your chastity be defiled by this plague, the scab of unclean pollution must be rubbed away in confession and washed in compunction.

Though all these vices have been corrected and improved, sweat must still be guarded against. It usually proceeds from excessive subcutaneous moisture and immoderate heat. By it is denoted that kind of pollution of which the Apostle speaks when he says, “It is better to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. 7:9). Isaiah also calls it “two tails of smoking firebrands,” when he says: “Do not fear the two tails of these smoking firebrands” (Isa. 7:4). By the two tails [Col. 0658A] are signified, in both sexes, those shameful members whose execrable stench corrupts every kind of virtue in us. Remove this sweat also from your hand, if you wish to flourish in the house of the Lord like a fruitful olive.

There remain two kinds, the Canaanites and Amorites, whom the true Israelite must hamstring in the promised land. One is called bloody from blood; the other is called the poison of an asp. The bloody one is the pollution of which the Apostle says: “Whoever commits fornication sins against his own body” (1 Cor. 6:18), and it is properly called adultery or incest. Whoever of the priestly order, infected by these things, handles the Lord’s holy things, let him hear from the voice of the hinges: “I have no pleasure in [Col. 0658B] you” (Mal. 1:10), because “your hands are full of blood” (Isa. 1:15). “Incense is an abomination to me,” and so forth (ibid., 13). Of the last it is said that it is a passion of dishonor, and the Apostle asks: “Let it not even be named among you” (Eph. 5:3), because, as he himself says, “Neither the effeminate nor men who lie with males shall possess the kingdom of God” (1 Tim. 1:10). Stripped, then, of all these as of the cast-off skin of the ancient serpent, let us wash our hands among the innocent; and with pure heart, chaste body, holy mouth, sanctified spirit, and purified soul, let us prepare new flowers from the Lord’s paradise for the new birth of the new King. Let us strengthen with these flowers the Holy of Holies, the Virgin of virgins, Queen of queens, Lady of ladies, that we may deserve to have a share in her childbirth. May Jesus Christ her Son, who lives and reigns, grant this to us, etc.

## SERMON VIII. ON THE LORD’S NATIVITY I

“When the quiet silence of night was midway in its course, the almighty Word came from the royal thrones” (Wis. 18:15).

Consider, dearest brethren, what the course of silence is, and what the midpoint of the silence of night is. A midpoint, plainly, is not spoken of except between two or more things. Since we have heard of a midpoint, we must seek at least three silences.

The first silence we had in our mother’s womb, when we were not yet able to speak; the second, when, after birth, we could utter sounds but not yet [Col. 0658D] form words; the third, when we are dead or placed in death and cease to speak further. Thus the world, either before it existed or while it was still unformed, was without voice: behold, the first silence. But when creation was completed and humankind perfected in the happiness of paradise, it uttered a voice of praise. Hence in Job: “When the morning stars praised me and the sons of God rejoiced” (Job 38:7)—namely, at the beginning of creation, when all creation, obedient to the eternal dispensation, proceeded in its natural course and did nothing out of order. Then came the middle silence, when either Lucifer sinned in heaven or Adam in paradise. It continued its course until the Word assumed flesh and, by his rays, broke the night, and by his voice, interrupted silence. For he raised a question, entered a suit concerning the condition of our freedom, and interrupted the prescription of ancient possession. Finally, another silence will come in the time of Antichrist or on the day of judgment; this will be the third and last. Therefore, because Christ came between the first sin and the final punishment: “When the middle silence was midway in its course, the Word came from the royal thrones.” Certainly he did not choose to come before sin, when a physician’s descent to a healthy person was unnecessary.

He also refused to delay until judgment, since he mercifully hastened to grant an extension of mercy before the sentence. Therefore he came in the middle, both to correct sin and to mitigate judgment. He came in the middle so that he might neither become unjust by remitting sin without satisfaction nor cruel by executing judgment without the restraint of mercy. He came in the middle by applying wine and oil: wine on account of sin, oil on account of judgment—lest judgment without oil, that is, sentence without mercy, should condemn; and lest sin without wine, that is, penitence, should remain unpunished.

The middle silence also lies in the course of one still living: the first at the origin of birth, the third and last in the fall of death. He came in the middle who worked our salvation in the midst of the earth; he came in the middle who lay in a manger between two animals; he came in the middle who hung between two thieves at the center of the cross; he came in the middle who was almost in every evil between the Church and the Synagogue; he came in the middle who, in the midst of the Church, [Col. 0659C] opened his mouth, and the Lord filled him with the spirit of wisdom and understanding (Sir. 15:5). He is the fruit in the midst of paradise; he is the beloved between the bride’s breasts; he is the corner; he is the cornerstone; he is “the one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5). He cuts off the first silence, interrupts the second, and conquers the third. For he frees us not only from sin, but from the punishment of sin and from sin’s guilt. He frees from sin by not imputing it, from guilt by saving, and from punishment by delivering. “The Lord,” says the Psalmist, “has delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling” (Ps. 114:8). From death—that is, from sin; from tears—that is, from the punishment of sin; from stumbling—that is, from guilt—the almighty Word who came from the royal thrones frees us [Col. 0659D].

Think, dearest brethren, think what those royal thrones are. None sit upon them except kings, nobles, and consuls. A slave of sin does not ascend these tribunals. The soul in which the spirit of fornication sits, which the spirit of avarice bends, which the spirit of anger drives, which the spirit of vain glory restrains, which the spirit of lust defiles, which the spirit of pride exalts, and which the spirit of gluttony devours, shall not have royal thrones. But at judgment the one who tames the flesh, tramples avarice, cuts off lust, humbles the neck, despises empty glory, represses anger, and, following Christ, takes up his cross, shall sit upon royal thrones. Such persons do not reject royal thrones, for they are due to them.

The wise Architect had long ago placed thrones in heaven and, in creating angels, prepared sitters upon them. Yet some fell through abuse and pride of heart; and so the royal thrones were in part left without occupants, because one who did not stand in the truth could not remain in the heavenly seat. Therefore, to prepare worthy occupants, the merciful Lord descended from his royal thrones to our dung-heaps. He came to seek on earth the poor whom he would make rich in heaven; he came to exiles to make them consuls; to the sick to heal them; to the blind to enlighten them; to the mute to restore speech; to the unclean to cleanse them; to the ungodly [Col. 0660B] to convert them; to the cast out to bring them back; to the despairing to restore hope; to the wretched to make them blessed; to the sorrowful to make them glad.

What are you doing, O people? Why do you stand here idle all day? Why do you not run? Why do you delay? Why do you dissemble? Let the bridegroom now come forth from his chamber and the bride from her bridal room, because Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church, came forth from heaven to his garden, to the bed of spices, that he might feed in the gardens and gather lilies. His garden is the Church; the bed of spices is the Virgin Mary. This garden is enclosed because sixty mighty men from the mightiest of Israel—that is, angelic powers—surround it, standing day and night upon its walls, lest a thief enter to uproot good seed or tear up the newly planted olive shoots—that is, souls newly converted to God’s mercy. The Lord himself is also a wall around it and a forewall: a wall on account of the Word assuming, a forewall on account of the human being assumed. For he is a refuge, or tower of strength, from the face of the enemy: one Christ in both, that is, in divinity and humanity. This garden has many and varied beds, because it holds apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins in the bosom of its faith and nurture, both through suffering on earth and through glorification in heaven. For the Church is one, both in members already reigning with Christ the head and in members still journeying away from their dwelling.

[Col. 0660D] Moreover, in both arrangement and fragrance it possesses the one uniquely beloved bed, the Virgin Mary. She is called a bed not because Joseph or a male touch cultivated her, but because the Spirit, the ordainer of love, sowed her with the fullness of graces. She is called a bed not because she produced thorns—that is, the shoots of evil desire; nor thistles—that is, anxieties of every kind of malice; nor hay—that is, worldly prosperity; nor straw—that is, the failure of a holy purpose; nor willows by a torrent—that is, the fruitless pursuits of worldly occupations; nor, finally, anything common or relating to market-trade. Rather, she is so called because the flower of the field, the lily of the valleys, the raisin, aromatic spices, [Col. 0661A] reed and cinnamon, myrrh and cassia, and her outpourings are things incomparable if you consider their price, marvelous in use, unfathomable in mystery, tangible to sight, sweet to taste, and efficacious in service.

Come, dearest brethren, to this bed in holy hope, right faith, perfect love, and whole chastity; and draw forth, without silver and without any exchange, if it pleases you, wine and milk; if it pleases you, honey and honeycomb; if it pleases you, pomegranates; if it pleases you, finest myrrh. You who are perfect lovers of Christ, already absorbed in the desire for wisdom, receive wine; and, like newborn infants, whether through the regeneration of baptism or the renewal of holy conduct, receive, in an abundance of grace, rational milk without guile into your inmost parts and throats; receive honey in meditation on the Old and New Testaments; honeycomb in the perfection of love for God and hope of eternal reward; pomegranates in imitation of Christ’s passion; and finest myrrh. Recall how wise the Mother of Wisdom is; how simple, devout, diligent, full of love, delightful in the integrity of her life, patient in her Son’s passion, unfading through the incorruption of chaste body and faithful soul, pleasing through the beauty of her flower, fertile through fullness of grace, admitting a cultivator through humility, and excluding a ravisher through most watchful circumspection.

By the generation of the Word, she took away the middle silence from the midst, and, sprung from a royal line, brought us from royal thrones the Son of the Most High through her chaste conception. Let us approach and fall down before this throne of grace, and worship the footstool of the Lord’s feet, rendering to her not only glory above women but also reverence on behalf of every angelic creature. O Lady, show to your reborn servant the Son who has been born, that by imploring the mercy of the newborn one, you may blot out the fault of the reborn one.

## SERMON IX. ON THE LORD’S NATIVITY II

On these words: Moses said, “Unless you yourself go before us, do not lead us out of this place. For how shall it be known that I and your people have found grace in your sight, unless you walk with us, so that we may be glorified among all the peoples that dwell upon the earth?” The Lord said to Moses: “I will also do this thing,” etc. (Exod. 33:15–17).

The blessed mind approaches God in complete confidence and, as though pleading with him on equal terms, does not judge it impossible to incline supreme majesty toward its good pleasure. For perfect love ventures upon everything; and not without reason, since it governs and weighs itself against God in the balance of equity, reckoning itself neither less, nor more unworthy, nor inferior to him who is love. Therefore, when that sweetness from the divine mind, poured out through the Holy Spirit into the human soul, is perfectly melted together, it reclaims by original right its primary channel—for rivers return to the place from which they go forth—and it dares what ought to be dared before none other than itself. As though binding God himself, it asks unexpected things, seeks difficult things, and implores unheard-of things. Hence Moses, with most familiar boldness, from a pure heart, good conscience, and sincere faith, with that same conscience bearing witness to him in the Holy Spirit, speaks to God: “Unless you yourself go before us, do not lead us out of this place.” We can do nothing without you, he says. We have most bitter enemies behind and before us; we ourselves are insufficiently taught and restrained; the route is pathless and waterless; the wilderness horrible and dreadful; the place to which we must go unknown. How then shall we go without you? Therefore do not lead us out unless you yourself go before us. This prayer of Moses indeed concerned the event then taking place when Israel was led out of Egypt; but it also seems most fittingly to allude to this glorious solemnity which is observed concerning the Savior’s nativity.

Thus it is the voice of the whole human race in the mouths of the prophets and those righteous persons who preceded Christ’s coming. “Unless you yourself, Lord, go before us, do not lead us out of this place.” Certainly the place in which we are placed—indeed, exposed—is evil because of our evil and misery. It is a dark prison because of the absence of divine light and the lack of true goods; it is a valley of tears because of the abundance of labors, thorns, and briars. We desire to go out from here, but to better things, not worse. For it is better to endure evils already known and familiar, and in some manner endurable, than to attempt worse things that will end with no relief. For a person sold under sin is certainly drawn after this punishment to eternal punishment unless the Redeemer comes to pay the price and lead the captive out.

Bound therefore by the chains of mortality and punishment, groaning that the torments of the cross and the hanging of the gallows are prepared for him at the prison’s exit, the human being says to God, who thoughtfully consoles him through his oracles and promises deliverance: “Unless you yourself go before us, do not lead us out of this place.” Michael, who will fight the dragon and conquer him in the last time, is not enough for me, because I do not trust in his goodness or power as much as in yours: nothing resists your power, and all things are filled by your goodness. I shall not entrust my cause to Abraham with his three hundred household servants; not to Joshua, who conquered thirty-three kings; not to Gideon, who overcame the Philistines with three hundred men who lapped water, with lamps and jars; not to Samson, who struck down a thousand men with an ass’s jawbone; nor to anyone from the sinful mass, because no one at this point could protect even himself alone.
