Therefore you alone must be trusted concerning the way, because you are the way; concerning the straightness of the path, because you are truth; concerning restoration from toil and want, because you are life; concerning defense from enemies, because you are almighty; concerning refreshment, because you are the bread of angels; concerning counsel, because you are wise; concerning reconciliation, because you are peaceable; concerning the remedy of weakness, because you are medicine; concerning every [Col. 0663A] misfortune, because you are blessedness. Go before us, therefore, like the sun, like a guide, like a lord, like a patron, like a hen her chicks, like a ram his little sheep, like a pillar of light and cloud. You will be an example to those following, comfort to the sorrowful, refreshment to the failing, rebuke to evildoers, a vehicle to the weary, and exultation to those journeying: “Though I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evils, because you are with me”; “though an army encamp against me, my heart shall not fear” (Ps. 22:4; 26:3).

What can Pharaoh with his Egyptians do? What can the Red Sea do? What can the Jebusite, Perizzite, Canaanite, Amorite, Hittite, Girgashite, Hivite, or the sons of Anak do? What can the wilderness do where God is? Surely everything that threatened opposition is reduced to service. For the person whom the Lord accompanies on the way prospers in all things, and all things are turned to good. Yet the presence of such great majesty demands the worship of highest reverence: namely, an eye like a dove’s in simplicity, like a turtledove’s in chastity; a tongue taught in sacred doctrine; lips purified by a burning coal from an angel’s hand; ears circumcised lest they hear blood; hands clean of a bribe, pure from every defilement; feet straight in preaching and washed of worldly vanity; a heart chaste from the phantoms of rushing thoughts and desires. One must stand in fear and trembling before the Lord of Hosts, lest he be angry and send wrath and indignation through evil angels. If beside him you uncover your nakedness, he will roar like a lion, bend his bow, shoot fiery arrows, and his sword will rage, passing through the soul to the lowest depths of hell. Certainly one must fear to stand there irreverently with uncleanness, where even the stars are not pure, where even those ministering spirits do not approach without reverence, and where even our acts of righteousness grow foul like a menstrual cloth.

But behold: the Lord descended, enclosing and, as it were, folding up that majesty of divinity within the clay of the body assumed from the Virgin, so that, humbly stooping to the cottages of our frailty and habitation, he might graciously know our customs and disclose his own to us; that he might gradually purge our impurities by the heat of his love, and imprint his own, most purely refined, upon us by impressing them into ours. For he came to give, not to receive—unless one says that he received soul and body from us. Certainly this is so: he received body and soul from us, that is, conformable to ours; yet not as from what was ours, but as from what was his own. By a new art he fashioned a new creature from old material, where the craftsman’s skill is valued more highly than the original material lying before him. For unless the flesh of God had been made flesh from the Virgin’s flesh, what would the Virgin’s flesh have been but human flesh? But when, under the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, a little branch of flesh was cut from the tree of the human race and grafted into the divine nature, it grew into the new tree of righteousness, Jesus Christ, with its condition improved. For thereafter it was never flesh of sin, nor was it called merely [Col. 0664A] human flesh, but also the flesh of God. All this, however, comes from grace, not nature; not from the merit of the material, but from the workmanship of grace and divine power.

Therefore, in this assumed flesh: “Unless you yourself go before us, do not lead us out of this place. For how shall it be known that I and your people…” And he says, “I will do that thing.” Thanks be to you, Lord, because you have fulfilled what you promised. With you there was not “yes and no,” but with you there is “yes”; for “the gifts and calling of God are without repentance.” May you always walk and pass through our midst, in our heart; may you always go before us, that you may clear the way and lead and bring us to the eternal fatherland in the light of your countenance, Christ Jesus, who with the Father and Holy Spirit lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON X. ON THE LORD’S NATIVITY III

[Col. 0664B]

On these words: “Glory to you, Lord, who were born of the Virgin,” etc.

To our good manners, against which no one ought to act, belongs the duty of devoutly and humbly offering a greeting of peace to all who newly arrive from any place or whom we meet, whoever they may be: noble or low-born, slave or master, neighbor or friend, cleric or monk, man or woman, Christian, Gentile, or Jew—all without distinction enjoy this right. Therefore, dearest brethren, let us with earnest diligence consider together by what greeting so great a Lord, so great a guest, so great a king, so necessary a physician, so beloved a friend, so true a brother, so [Col. 0664C] long-desired a Savior and Redeemer ought to be honored—he who comes to us today, who has entered our little dwelling, who has wrapped himself in our aprons. Truly, we ought to prepare for him a cheerful countenance, pleasant speech, a most clean lodging, and most excellent service. For he has come for our sake and has made our cause his own. He who comes to save is worthy of a greeting—but what greeting? Surely one new and heavenly, neither inferior nor more lowly than that with which his Mother deserved to be greeted by the angel. Thus the angel greets her: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee” (Luke 1:28). Then, after our Lady has been greeted, she herself shortly afterwards greets her kinswoman Elizabeth. Why, then, should we not add, on our own part, among these new greetings so worthy a greeting [Col. 0664D] as may receive a fitting place among them?

Let us therefore say: “Glory to thee, Lord, because thou, the wise Son, art the glory of the Father; because thou possessest glory in thy kingdom and dost not lose it in our dung-heap; because glory is consubstantial with thee, both in being born of the Father before all ages and in taking flesh from the Virgin at the end of the ages.” For thou never appearedst without glory to thy angels in heaven; nor to the upright in heart upon earth, even when thy face was hidden; even when thou appearedst as a leper, having neither form nor beauty; even when wrapped in swaddling-clothes in a manger; even when fastened with nails between two thieves upon the gibbet of the cross; even when laid in the tomb. Always and everywhere thou art glorious and gloriously magnified. [Col. 0665A] Glory to thee, Lord, fountain of glory, seat of grace: thou hast wrought magnificent works, unheard of from the ages, in the midst of the earth.

If Moses, the giver of the Law, descending from the shadowy and thick mountain, because of thy speech which he heard in the cloud, and thy face which he saw in the darkness wherein thou dwellest, brought back to the children of Israel such glory that they could not look upon his face because of the glory of his countenance—which is passing away—how much more did thy more glorious face, which shines like the sun in its power, shine forth in thy nativity: thou who art “the brightness of [God’s] glory and the express image of [his] substance”; thou who art the radiance of eternal light; thou who art “white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands”; thou who art the glory exalted above the cherubim; thou who art the image of God’s glory, the immortal, invisible King of ages, to whom be honor and glory for ages of ages. Glory, I say, to thee from the Father, from the Mother, from all thy stock and generation; from thy name, thy work, thy birth, thy life and conduct; from thy word and preaching; from the enlightening of the blind; the restoration of hearing; the cleansing of lepers; the raising of the dead; thy passion; thy death; thy descent into hell; thy resurrection; the manifestation of that same resurrection; thy ascension; thy sitting at the right hand of God the Father; thy intercession for us; and the final examination in the future judgment of good and evil.

Glory to thee, because thou hast removed from our necks the yoke of the Mosaic Law, which our ancient fathers could not bear, because [Col. 0665C] Moses’ hands were heavy and they employed surgical treatment about the healing of their sick: while they repaid eye for eye, tooth for tooth, bruise for bruise, retaliation for retaliation, without any mercy. Thou hast placed beneath us thy sweet yoke, by which thou wouldst neither kill the sinners of the earth nor treat them with unbearable severity; but, being full of grace and truth, thou wouldst continually extend grace, promising oil and applying preliminary incantations to thy sick; then thou wouldst temperately introduce truth, then wine, then judgment.

What wonder if Moses acted more harshly and thou more gently? For who was he, and who art thou? What had he to do with us, or we with him? He neither created nor formed us; moreover, he could not redeem us: for “a brother does not redeem.” [Col. 0665D] But who does? A man? Certainly—but God-man: the man who says in the Psalm, “Mother Sion, and a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Psalm 86:5). A man—the one whom that man in the Gospel did not possess, who, waiting for the moving of the water when the angel descended into the pool, said: “I have no man” (John 5:7).

O child Jesus, thou art that man, made in the likeness of men and found in fashion as a man. O man of God—indeed, God-man! Noah, Abraham, and Moses did not know us, because they did not form our creaturely frame; nor could they know what was in man, except insofar as they saw men outwardly. Indeed, they could not prepare such a medicine for souls as would heal all our infirmities, but rather one from [Col. 0666A] which the infirmity would grow more severe. For neither Law nor circumcision brought anyone to perfection. But thou alone knowest the hearts of men, thou who hast formed each of their hearts separately. Thou fully understandest how frail our bodies are, how muddy, how clay-like, how unstable, how utterly impatient: they bloom and pass away in the morning; in the evening they fall, harden, and wither. Therefore, as a good and merciful physician, thou hast applied fitting medicines to our bruised and shattered nature. Conceived indeed by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin full of grace, Son of man and Son of God, thou hast established the sacraments [Col. 0666B] of our restoration—not in fire, not in disturbance, not in burning, not in cutting, but in the water of regeneration, in the oil of chrism, and in the confession of heart and mouth.

What is easier for the forgiveness of sins than that sins were forgiven through tears to the woman who was a sinner in the city, who had spread her legs for every passerby, and who had seven demons? Likewise, to another woman caught in adultery it is said: “Go, and now sin no more” (John 8:11). Nowhere in the Gospel will you find anything cruel in Jesus: he eats and drinks with publicans and sinners; he receives little children, sinners, and harlots. He withstands scribes, proud Pharisees, and hypocrites presuming upon their own righteousness, saying: “I desire mercy, not sacrifice” (Matthew 9:13). What more can we say concerning the goodness and mercy of the child born to us, [Col. 0666C] except that even at his own death he forgives those who crucify him? Glory to thee, Lord, who wast born, etc.

## SERMON XI. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD, IV

On these words: “The Son of Man hath not where to lay his head” (Matthew 8:20).

Once the most wealthy and rich Lord among all the Orientals, whose is “the earth and the fullness thereof,” came to the utmost remnants of poverty—not compelled by fatal chance, but acting of his own accord and mercifully setting forth infinite treasures and innumerable riches—so that he said of himself: “The Son of Man hath not where to lay his head.” Why? Perhaps because he would have nothing from the accursed thing of Jericho; perhaps because he did not [Col. 0666D] come to receive money, but to give his soul as a ransom for many. “For he came unto his own, and his own received him not” (John 1:11). O his own who were not his own: his own by creation, not his own by election; his own by slavish fear, not by filial submission; his own by the root of the patriarchs, not by participation in the fatness of the olive tree; his own by legislation, not by the adoption of grace; his own in appearance, not in reality; his own in outward habit, not in spirit; his own in word and tongue, not in deed and truth. His own, I say, did not receive him in mind, heart, will, reverence, or service.

Do you ask the cause? Because “a prophet is not without honor, except in his own country.” Was this owing to avarice, poverty, hatred, negligence, or his insolence? But what insolence belongs to the lamb who “was dumb before him that sheareth him, and opened not his mouth”? [Col. 0667A] (Isaiah 53:7). What insolence belongs to him who came not to be served but to serve? (Matthew 20:28). What insolence belongs to him who, when reviled, did not revile in return; when suffering, did not threaten, but committed himself to him who judged him unjustly? (1 Peter 2:23). If, indeed, it was their negligence, it was negligence too gross and slothful: to neglect the Lord, to neglect their Redeemer and Deliverer, to neglect an incurable disease! But if it was hatred, whence comes love’s being hateful, justice’s being rejected, mercy’s being abhorred, salvation’s being spurned? Finally, if it was because of poverty, who is so poor that he has not at least a most miserable little hut, at least a cup of cold water, at least a breast, at least a lap? And if at last it was because of avarice, did you not know how [Col. 0667B] to lend at interest? Why did you refuse to lend your money at a hundredfold interest to him from whom you could gain even heaven?

Certainly he willed that the cornerstone should thus be rejected, so that he might let out his vineyard to other husbandmen and the kingdom of God might be given to a nation producing its fruits. “Woe to the sinful nation, the people laden with iniquity, the evil seed, the criminal sons!” (Isaiah 1:4).—You cast him out as a leper, as one stricken by God and wounded. But “he bore our sorrows” (Isaiah 53:4), and he has filled his lodging with blessings, so that his guests may become children of God—indeed, heirs of God and fellow-heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17)—“fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (Ephesians 2:19).

Therefore, dearest brethren, Christ’s lodging must be emptied by faith and voluntary poverty; [Col. 0667C] cleansed by confession; enlarged by charity; adorned by religious devotion; sprinkled with sweet odors; and fortified by vigilant watchfulness, lest any stranger or profane person approach. Let worldly care and anxiety, the desire of the flesh, pride with all its household, withdraw and make room for Christ in the heart. Then let gluttony, lust, avarice, anger, discord, and the whole infernal household take flight, so that the devil may go out before his feet with his sons and daughters: the Gergesite, Hittite, Amorite, Perizzite, Hivite, Jebusite, and Philistine. For they occupy the land wrongly: they neither pay their due to the Lord, nor acknowledge that they possess it from him, nor cultivate it for fruit, but prepare it for burning. Let the true and lawful [Col. 0667D] Lord enter after the unholy nation has been driven out; let him receive this inheritance as his own and recognize his image, so that our soul may return to its ancient state, when Adam had not yet sinned. “I considered the days of old,” says the Prophet, “and I had the eternal years in mind” (Psalm 76:6). For Christ dwelling in the heart breathes upon his garden, so that such aromas may flow forth—that is, desires for heavenly and eternal things. Even though the heart, emptied of anger, hatred, enmity, worldly favor, and everything that chokes the seed of virtues, does not yet worship the head, it already worships the feet of Jesus.

But what kind of head? The head of the Son of Man, which has nowhere to recline. Hear the Bride, who perhaps once parted the hair of this head and moistened it with a fountain of tears; hear what she says: “His head,” she says, “is the finest gold” (Song of Songs 5:11). And you too, John the Evangelist, friend of the Bridegroom, say what the head of the Son of Man is like. “His head,” he says, “and his hairs were white as white wool, as snow” (Revelation 1:14). Speak more plainly: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John 1:1). And Paul: “The head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11:3). This head has with the Father a golden place of repose, because it is in his bosom, because the Son is in the Father, as he himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 10:38). Equal are this head and this pillow—or head-rest. Nothing is more equal; nothing more delightful than their mutual repose. The Father delights in the Son, and the Son in the Father. They cherish one another in mutual and ineffable love, in a manner beyond expression, and cleave to one another. Preserving this same [Col. 0668B] indissoluble unity, without loss to coeternity, by a temporal dispensation he bound this head in the Virgin’s womb with another bond of humanity; so that, as by true unity with God the Father he is one God, so by the true union of Word, soul, and flesh he might be one God-man, and God and man.

Christ therefore has three resting-places: God the Father; the Virgin Mother; and the assumed manhood. For in his mother he laid down his whole head, because, when the Holy Spirit overshadowed her, reclining and resting in her, he made, as it were, a long sleep while he patiently awaited, according to the profound counsel of his secret, the delays involved in arranging or forming the human body member by member. Meanwhile, while he was reclining there, the most unblemished Virgin caused him [Col. 0668C] no disturbance. She maintained a heavenly silence through every movement of mind and body; inwardly rapt, she heard secrets which it is not lawful for a man to utter. The Lord cast a sleep upon Adam when he fashioned Eve from his rib. But there was no need whatsoever for our Lady to fall asleep when Christ’s flesh was drawn from her flesh. For what injury is there where no corruption occurs? Indeed, what is so sweet as sensibly to feel the grace of the Holy Spirit in marrow, bones, flesh, blood, and mind, and to supply one’s own substance, to be incorporated in service to God, for the glory and grace of the only-begotten Son of God? There is no pain of severance where the bond of so adorable a union restores every loss of destruction. And this is a golden resting-place [Col. 0668D].

A fourth resting-place remains: because, when Jesus had been born and there was no place for him in the inn, his mother laid him in a manger. Perhaps it was common property, or belonged to someone else. This resting-place belonged neither to Joseph nor to Mary; therefore it is said truthfully: “The Son of Man hath not where to lay his head.” The manger was for animals, not for men. O Jesus, from the highest throne of thy glory, what an incomparable descent—or resting-place—thou hast chosen! How lofty that one, how deep this one; how worthy of God that one, how unworthy this one; how glorious and noble that one, how lowly and contemptible this one! Let our miseries meet the inmost chambers, everywhere melted by the bowels of mercy of our God, as the uncertain and hidden things of God’s wisdom drip down from the highest to the lowest [Col. 0669A] level of our condition, restrained by no recompense, from whence or whither the highest Deity has come. The Lord chose to begin the mysteries of our restoration in such a manner, that, with the head of our pride crushed, man might unlearn lofty thoughts and learn to consent to lowly things.

These are signs of the child born and given to us; the apostasies of the devil and man rise up in opposition to them. Who do you think this child will be? Behold, he begins his workshop not by establishing it “on the sides of the north,” but in a manger; not on a royal throne, but in a lowly place. From this resting-place the lamb, crying aloud, is heard upon the exalted throne; and the height of heaven, by sending a star or angels, humbly and devoutly lays itself beneath him.

[Col. 0669B] I also count as a fifth resting-place that of the cross, which might more fittingly be called a bending-back than a reclining-place. His mother laid him in a manger; his stepmother, the Jewish synagogue, suspended him on the gibbet. There his power, as though bent back, stretched itself out not in avenging itself, but, enduring all the straits of death, hung there for the guilty. Nor was this bending fruitless; for like a hind in labor, as Job says (ch. 39), he bent himself, so that through the pain of the cross he might at once bring forth all the children of predestination; that Jesus, ascending to the palm of victorious triumph, might seize the fruit of the believing people. How then does the Son of Man have nowhere on earth to lay his head? Observe that he says he is to be lifted up from the earth when he foretells his crucifixion. Understand this also in another way: [Col. 0669C] the Jews set Christ upon the cross; he did not hang himself, like Judas, who, having hanged himself, burst asunder in the midst.

Let us therefore offer him at his birth a golden resting-place—that is, a heart clean through faith, enlarged by charity, raised by heavenly contemplation, and renewed through the sanctification of the Spirit. Such a heart, not earthly but heavenly, will prepare a lodging for Christ: where there is the table of the Law and Gospel; the candlestick of the cross; the bed of divine love; the choir of jubilation; the bath of holy compunction; the furnace of charity; the windows of meditation; the lattices of reading; the private chamber of holy confession; the bread of the divine will; the wine of fervor; [Col. 0669D] the threshing-floor of a level conscience, free from the prick of pressing sin. The Child born for us, Jesus Christ our Lord, does not refuse to recline in such a resting-place—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XII. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD, V

If every soul, from whatever source, should gather the powers of its intellect as though on a cord of blessed earnestness and constrain—or collect—them into the one task of seeking the Lord, would it even thus search out the wisdom of God that goes before all things? O miserable and foolish soul, why dost thou spend thy silver not on bread, and thy labor not on that which satisfies? Why dost thou disembowel thyself in vain and false insanities, pursuing the empty gains of the world, admiring philosophical intellects, reading poetic fictions, while neglecting the Gospel of God and transgressing the Law? Say rather to the Lord: “Set before me, O Lord, the law, the way of thy justifications, and I will seek it always” (Psalm 118:33), so that thou mayest never cease to seek and never cease to love, like a most ardent drinker who, the more he drinks, returns the more vehemently to the cups. Say to Wisdom: “Show me thy ways, and teach me thy paths” (Psalm 24:4).

Seek his lodging; seek his passage; seek his house; seek his chamber; seek his walking-place; seek his throne. I believe that if faithfully, humbly, piously, and continually thou bind thyself to these studies, thou mayest at least touch the hem [Col. 0670B] of his garment. “All the glory of the king’s firstborn daughter is within, clothed round about in golden hems of varied colors” (Psalm 44:15). The girdle of Wisdom, upon which the golden hems hang, is the ordering of visible as well as invisible creatures. The golden hems are either the first works of the six days; or the ages of worldly dispensations; or the works which the Son of God performed in the flesh; or also the sacraments which he left to his Bride when he returned to the Father and left her on earth after him, until the appointed time and number, to bring forth the offspring of Christians. But what is to be done if he should change his lodging before the slow desires of the soul seeking God, [Col. 0670C] seeking wisdom, run up? Let it at least seek his passage.

But where is the lodging of God? In the Law of Moses. Where is his passage? In the prophets. Where is his house? In the Gospel. Where is his chamber? In the Epistles of Paul, or in the womb of his Mother, or on the gibbet of the cross, or in the stone tomb. Where is his walking-place? In the exposition of the Scriptures, or in the ascent of clouds. Where is his throne? At the right hand of the Father. Why is the Law called God’s lodging? Because, on account of its uselessness and weakness, it was in due time removed, as the Apostle says: “That which groweth old and waxeth aged is near unto perishing” (Hebrews 8:12). Therefore Christ was like a guest in the Law: because, as Isaac, blessing his son with dimmed eyes, did not know who he was, so Christ was figured and not recognized in the calf, ram, lamb, goat, scapegoat, [Col. 0670D] turtledove and dove, fine flour, oil, and the other ceremonies. Therefore he was a guest, because he himself had caused Scripture to be read concerning himself, and, though he was heir, concealed who he was.

Yet there were some holy fathers, like apples on the topmost bough of a fig tree, who rendered him his due service and were justified by the same faith by which we also believe and are saved. The Lord still lodges with Moses, as with the ruler of the synagogue, whose daughter—that is, the unbelieving Synagogue—although dead, will be raised by him if she believes. For when the scribes and Pharisees, sitting in Moses’ chair and holding the Law, put the Lord of the Law outside the Synagogue against the Law, they deserved to have the prophets succeed them, that he might have a passage through them. For it is said of him in the Song of Songs: [Col. 0671A] “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills” (Song of Songs 2:8). Now Isaiah sees the Lord, the King of hosts, seated upon a high and exalted throne, etc. Now Ezekiel sees the glory of the Lord beside the river Chebar. Now in a field; now in a city; now in a temple. Now Jeremiah sees a wakeful rod. Now Amos sees the Lord standing upon a plastered wall, holding a hook of fruit and a mason’s trowel in his hand. Now Zechariah sees a Man—namely, the Lord—among the myrtle trees. Thus others, in their own time and in their own manner, experienced grace leaping across through them. Hence the Psalmist: “O God, when thou wentest forth in the sight of thy people, when thou passedst through the desert, the heavens dropped before the face of the God of Sinai, before the face of the God of Israel” (Psalm 67:8). For when Jesus [Col. 0671B] passed by, heaven did not cease to rain down glory [or grace]. Where the face of God is, there is the knowledge of God; where the knowledge of God is, there is devotion; and where devotion is, there is the fruitfulness of virtues.

Under the figure of this passing-by, a certain great woman says of Elisha in the Fourth Book of Kings: “Observe that this is a holy man of God, who passes by us frequently. Let us therefore make him a small upper room and put in it a bed, a table, a chair, and a candlestick, so that when he comes to us he may remain there” (4 Kings 4:9–10). By visiting and illuminating the minds of the saints, heavenly grace makes a passage, because the weight of human frailty, raised on the most slender thread of contemplation, is quickly bent back down to the depths and scarcely remains amid God’s good things. Jesus alone employed this privilege, [Col. 0671C] that the Holy Spirit descended upon him and remained.

Let us therefore make a small upper room: small indeed because of frailty, but an upper room because of aspiration toward heavenly things. Let us make in it a bed for resting, a table for refreshment, a chair for sitting, and a candlestick for seeing. The Lord rests in a quiet mind; he is refreshed in the soul intent upon God’s commandments and knowledge of the Scriptures; he sits in one who does not judge himself in that which he approves. He lights the candlestick of the person who, with a single eye—that is, a pure intention—desires to please God alone. Thus, leaping and passing over in them, he makes those same persons pass over. Yet because the title of certain psalms is prefixed “For Idithun,” which is interpreted “the one who leaps over,” you can find in the Book of Psalms—if you distinguish them well, as also in the other prophets—the steps and leaps of him who is like a gazelle and a young hart, from his first entrance into the Virgin’s womb to his return to the right hand of God the Father. Therefore meet the guest and the one passing over both in his lodging and in his passage.

From his lodging Jesus passes to the house, that is, the Gospel, because “what was impossible for the Law, in that it was weak through the flesh, God, sending his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin in the flesh” (Romans 8:3). The Gospel speaks of the mystery of this incarnation. Thus the Lord remains in the house; thus Christ is in the Gospel, where Gabriel [Col. 0672A] the archangel, sent by God, as it were shuts and opens the door, saying: “Hail, Mary,” etc., as far as “thou shalt bear a Son” (Luke 1). Joseph watches the doors in the outer court but scarcely dares to look upon them. Thus, as the centurion at the Lord’s tomb cried out in fear, “Truly this man was the Son of God” (Mark 15:39), so Joseph, troubled by the Virgin’s pregnancy, intended secretly to dismiss her. Hence it is that upon the door of the temple palms and cherubim minister to the Son of the King as to their Lord.

Accordingly, the Gospel-house has four corners, according to the four winds of heaven. The individual Evangelists fortify individual corners: Matthew in the east, beside the cedar column bearing the face of a man, wrote the Gospel in the style of a man, saying: [Col. 0672B] “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1). In the north, Mark, beside the marble column carved with a lion’s face, wrote his Gospel with the reed of the wilderness, beginning thus: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord” (Mark 1:3). In the west, Luke, beside the column of shittim wood, which resembles the white thorn and bears the face of a calf, began thus: “There was in the days of Herod the king a priest named Zacharias” (Luke 1:5). In the south, John, beside the sapphire face of the eagle, wrote his Gospel with an evangelical [perhaps “angelic”] pen, thus breathing forth from the smoke of the altar: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John 1:1). Matthew sits in the chair of justice; Mark in the seat of fortitude; [Col. 0672C] Luke, dividing the hoof, in the council-chamber of prudence; John on the throne of temperance. All have their faces always turned toward the mercy-seat: both when he enters the Virgin, when he fasts in the wilderness, when he preaches in the temple, when he lays down his soul for his sheep, and when, returning and ascending into heaven, he visits the Father and his homeland.

From this house imperial benefits are distributed, so that one who does not belong to this house is outside the kingdom of heaven. For in it are vessels of gold and silver, wood and clay, and many dwelling places. In it is the table of the altar, at which food is daily supplied by angels to the faithful. There is baptism, in which bodies and souls are washed from every contagion of unbelief. There is an oracle, in which God, anointing the palace of the heart [Col. 0672D] with his sweetness, promises the treasures of eternal blessedness; and the soul, vomiting out the bile of its inward parts by true confession and abundant compunction, asks and receives from his hand the petition for forgiveness. There is a furnace of fire for burning sacrifices and holocausts: warming what is cold, melting what is hard, burning up what is superfluous, and enlightening what is dark. There is a secret place for leisure in contemplation, for service in meditation, for converse with the heart, for searching the utterances of the divine word. Finally, there is a porch for the sick and a pool of tears. There is a place of ashes in which the last things are remembered. “Behold, here is Christ,” or certainly there. Seek him therefore in his house, because “the son remaineth in the house for ever,” saying: [Col. 0673A] “Behold, I am with you unto the consummation” (Matthew 28:20).

Let us now proceed to the chamber; for thus the Bride says: “I will lead thee into the house of my mother, and into the chamber of her that bore me” (Song of Songs 3:4). Christ’s soul knows that the Virgin’s womb is his most chaste and most peaceful chamber; the Lord himself knows it; Gabriel the archangel knows it; John the Baptist and John the Evangelist know it; finally, both the heavenly court and the universal Church of the faithful know it. For it is Solomon’s bed, surrounded by sixty mighty men of the mightiest of Israel: a bed flourishing with every grace of God, with beauty and loveliness, namely with the Word of God, soul, and flesh. If thou approach the Mother faithfully, thou shalt without doubt find the Son with the Mother; for the Mother is not [Col. 0673B] without the Son, nor the Son without the Mother, just as the Son was never without the Father, nor the Father without the Son. He whom she once had in her womb now stands ever at her right hand. What, therefore, can the Mother say that the Son does not hear? Indeed, when does the Mother hear without the Son, she who wholly, in body and soul, depends on the Son? Come then to the Mother as to a chamber, because he who is only-begotten and uniquely born from her rests uniquely in her. When the little bell of thy petition strikes the Virgin’s ears, Jesus will be awakened from the sleep of his feigned delay in hearing.

In the Gospel we read that Jesus walked in Solomon’s porch, because the Jews did not understand that he was the temple signified by that temple; therefore he walked in the porch. In the same temple, outside, around the circuit of the wall, there was a rim where there was a very pleasant walking-place; for at its summit were fastened fruits—golden grapes with golden vine-leaves—so that those looking upwards seemed to see them move. This is the order of contemplatives, whose eyes are always fixed upon the Lord. They are so attached to him that neither tribulation, distress, death, nor life separates them from the love that is in Christ. Therefore, while they behold golden grapes hanging from the true vine with golden leaves, they say with the Apostle: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18). We inwardly taste beforehand the ways of that glory—that is, its beatitudes—and, certain of the promise, do not waver in faith. In these things he [Col. 0673D] walks, with heart raised to heaven and enlarged in charity.

Having passed through these things, what remains? The high and exalted throne, concerning which it is said in the Song of Songs: “Flee, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young hart” (Song of Songs 8:14). No one will ascend there except the eagle and the children of the eagle. For “no man hath ascended into heaven, but he that descended from heaven” (John 3:13). John the Evangelist is the great eagle of great wings; and Paul is likewise another eagle of other wings, of whom Ezekiel speaks. One flew up to the third heaven, the other beyond the heaven of heavens; they tasted what it is not lawful for man to utter from the pith of cedar, and, as they were able, belched forth in the Scriptures the fat of wheat, the dew of heaven, and the honey of Divinity.

[Col. 0674A] O Lord Jesus, “my knees are weakened” (Psalm 108:24): how shall I run? O Lord, “my feet were moved” (Psalm 72:2): how shall I go? O Lord, “who will give me wings like a dove, and I shall fly and be at rest?” (Psalm 54:7). O Lord, where is the fiery chariot and the fiery horses by which I may seek the secret region? O Lord, where is the bright cloud in which I may ascend after thee, or with thee? O Lord, send a seraph who may hold my right hand and lead me to the throne of grace, that I may examine my cause and implore thy grace before, accused or convicted, I receive the sentence of judgment on the evil day. Therefore teach me thy ways, O Lord (Psalm 24:4), because thou art the way, the truth, and the life. Amen.

## SERMON XIII. ON THE PURIFICATION OF SAINT MARY

[Col. 0674B]

“Adorn thy bridal chamber, Sion, and receive Christ the King,” etc.

How pleasant and splendid this present solemnity is, the brightness itself of the lights which you will hold in your hands at Mass with festive procession sufficiently declares. For behold, two great lights approach the Father of lights in the temple when Mary offers Jesus to the Father of spirits. Mary is the lesser light; Jesus, Mary’s Son, the greater light. God is the Father of lights, who begot the Word from the womb before the morning star and ordained that he should be incarnate of the Mother at the end of the ages. From that very sun whom the Virgin conceived and bore, she deserved also to be made a great light, [Col. 0674C] whence she is called the Star of the Sea. Therefore the divine discourse addresses her, saying: “Adorn thy bridal chamber, Sion,” etc.

But it must be carefully observed that Sion is sometimes understood as the heavenly homeland; sometimes as the unique Virgin; sometimes as the universal Church; sometimes as the faithful soul. Each of these has its own bridal chamber, in which the Bridegroom lies at evening, morning, and noon. If Sion is understood as the soul, he lies in her in the morning when he begins charity in her; in the evening, when he brings it to completion; at noon, when he inflames it unto the pouring out of the soul itself. In the universal Church, however, he lay in the morning through the faith of the patriarchs before the Law; at noon, through the faith of the prophets under the Law; in the evening, through the preaching of the apostles in the time of grace. In the unique Virgin he lay in the morning through the angelic Annunciation; at noon through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit; in the evening through the birth from that same Virgin. In the heavenly bridal chamber he lies neither in the morning nor the evening, but only at noon. Hence it is said in the Song of Songs: “Tell me, thou whom my soul loveth, where thou feedest, where thou liest down at noon” (Song of Songs 1:7). Clearly, there is noon—that is, the pure day—when the sun is at its center and yields fuller light and heat, because in that eternity no evening cloud and no darkness of departing night appears, but the full and perfect brightness of the vision of God’s glory, and the full and perfect charity of the love of God.

[Col. 0675A] How then is it said to this Sion: “Adorn thy bridal chamber”? For that heavenly chamber is never unadorned, except perhaps when Jesus suffered upon the cross. Then, as it were, he laid aside his adornment, when the sun above, sensing grief among the angelic powers, in some manner changed its countenance and appearance, hiding the rays of light in its bosom and making darkness over the whole face of the earth.

Now the heavenly adornment consists in the splendors of the saints, having diverse ornaments, namely in the knowledge of beauty and admiration: displaying silken robes in the nine orders of angels; varied and figured tapestries in the merits of patriarchs and prophets; hyacinth-blue robes in the conduct [Col. 0675B] of the apostles; purple robes in the blood of martyrs; saffron-colored robes in the purity of confessors; linen robes in the integrity and chastity of virgins. This adornment we ought to await in the future, not now expound—for we are not sufficient even to conceive it.

This bridal chamber possesses, among the things brought to it from our earth, ornaments more precious than all other precious things: the robes of those who have not defiled their garments—for they are virgins and follow the Lamb wherever he goes. For wealth also customarily comes to it from a distant land, and foreign wares exceedingly dear in heaven: namely, the souls of the saints. But from its own cultivation and native resources come the angelic powers, which the hand of the Craftsman, Wisdom alone, has wondrously woven. Paint, O soul, whatever forms you can conceive more graceful and beautiful; yet you will not, I say, borrow the truth—or even any likeness at all—of heavenly adornment. Adorn therefore your bridal chamber, O Zion, because all this is owed to the boy Jesus; it is promised to his Mother.

Let us therefore turn both our gaze and our pen toward the Mother of the Lord herself, and let her make of her adornment a feast for God, angels, and human beings: for God, a spectacle, when he beholds the Word whom the Father uttered from his own heart incarnate in the Mother’s womb—being no more able to endure her absence from his sight than to be separated from the embraces of the Son. For when will the Father and the Holy Spirit turn their eyes away from the Mother of his Son, [Col. 0675D] when the Father is wholly turned toward the Son, the Son toward the Father, and the Holy Spirit toward the Father and the Son—yet no less toward the Mother and the Son? O Virgin of virgins, what is this? Where are you? In a singular and almost inestimable manner, you approach the Trinity itself almost immediately, so that, if that Trinity could in any way admit an external quaternity, you alone would complete the quaternity. But it is a Trinity, and no quaternity either could or can arise there. Therefore you are not one person of the Trinity, which is God, since those persons who are there cannot be changed or exchanged, because eternally they are what they are. Nor are you a fourth alongside the Trinity, because a fourth equal to the Trinity is nothing. What, then, are you? One and first after Unity and Trinity: the Mother of him whose Father is God the Father; [Col. 0676A] the Mother of him from whom, as also from the Father, the Holy Spirit proceeds.

You who are so great and such as this, adorn your bridal chamber, O Zion. A most illustrious guest comes to you: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Unfold whatever you have folded; set forth whatever you have laid away; kindle whatever has been extinguished; cover whatever is human. Let all be made divine, all enlightened, all simplified [read: “simply”], and sanctified for the furnishing of our nature which is to be assumed; so that what is assumed from you by the Word may be holy before it is assumed. Adorn your bridal chamber, O Zion, so that there may be nothing the Father abhors, nothing that offends the Son, nothing the Holy Spirit rejects. The Father places his Son from his own bosom in your womb; the Holy Spirit cherishes and warms your womb, [Col. 0676B] and what do you do? Adorn your bridal chamber. Abraham did not receive such guests; neither Lot nor any of the saints received such guests in such a manner. And if at any time God entered invisibly into the souls of saints through the gift of the grace of the Holy Spirit, when and into whom did the only-begotten Son of God enter in order to be incarnate? Whose womb was made pregnant by the Holy Spirit? Whose flesh and blood were formed into the flesh of the God-man? Certainly no one’s but the Virgin of virgins; no one’s but Zion, to whom it is said: Adorn your bridal chamber, O Zion.

Surely more splendid is the adornment of the virginal womb than the stars of heaven; purer is the womb from which the shoot of human nature is cut than the star-bearing sphere; more adorned is the dwelling-place of the virginal paradise than that earthly one [Col. 0676C] in which Adam could sin. Adorn therefore your bridal chamber, O Zion, driving from yourself whatever vice there is, acquiring and possessing whatever virtue there is. Above all, spread your bridal chamber with two coverings, humility and virginity; and receive from the one and triune Guest the garland of fruitfulness—or rather from him who is plainly more its resident than a guest or stranger. Thus you will honor the Father by humility, the Holy Spirit by virginity, and the Son by fruitfulness. It is enough: you are well adorned, and neither more nor less is found in your adornment.

Let us now pass to that Zion which is the Church and say to it: Adorn your bridal chamber, O Zion, etc. The Church is made lovely by so overflowing a heap of glory and splendor that I might summon even impure eyes [Col. 0676D] to admire its beauty alone, were not the eyes of vanity and unbelief blind when brought to the light. With the devout and religious eye of faith, survey the various dwellings of the faithful who are pilgrims away from God, and withdraw your mind from Babylonian spectacles, if you wish to understand that beauty of which it is said: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house, and the place where your glory dwells” (Ps. 23:8). First consider the remains of the bodies of the saints, as venerable in honor as they are fruitful and useful in protection. The devotion of the faithful prepares golden and silver shrines for them, so that those whose life and conduct were holy and chaste may have a dwelling beautiful and precious.

See the ministries of angels; observe how the arrangements of the sacred orders emulate them, so that what is fulfilled by the angels in true manifestation and manifest reality may at least be imitated by ecclesiastical ministers in a faithful and devout shadowing. For what of exorcists? What of singers? What of readers? What of acolytes? What of subdeacons? What of deacons? What of priests? What of bishops? What of archbishops? What of the supreme and universal bishop? Do these not make choirs of armies, concerning which it is said: “What will you see in the Shulammite,” that is, in the Church, which is scarlet through faith in Christ’s Passion, “but choirs of armies?” (Song 6:12). For in accordance with the religion of the angels and their administration [printed: “admiration”], the Church orders the whole army of her ministers; hence she also prays: “Your will be done, as in heaven, so also on [Col. 0677B] earth.” Adorn therefore your bridal chamber, O Zion: do not set contemptible persons over the ministries of the Church, but those whose life shines upon the earth, whose preaching is heard throughout the whole earth, and whose teaching shines like the sun and moon.

Consider the beauty of the Church in the washing of baptism, in the anointing with chrism, in the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood, and in many other matters which it is clearer to see daily than to explain now. Adorn therefore your bridal chamber, O Zion, by handling the ecclesiastical sacraments worthily and faithfully; by prudently providing for the choosing and appointment of rulers; by living according to rule and devoutly; by keeping the faith, holding the truth, and pursuing peace. We would say more about the adornment [Col. 0677C] of the Church, were we not drawing toward the end.

Let us now turn our discourse briefly to that Zion which is called the faithful soul, and so bring it to an end. The soul ought to seek and receive on loan the beauty and adornment of its bridal chamber from God, from the Church, and from Holy Scripture. For in the Scriptures, as in a mirror, it ought to behold its own form; and when it finds any blackness or ugliness in its appearance, let it run to the priests of the Church and seek a remedy for leprosy. Then, supplicating the Lord who made heaven and earth for the final hand of absolution, let it not depart until it receives healing. Let it wash itself in confession, reform itself in satisfaction, compose itself in prayer, and adorn itself in the keeping of the commandments. O soul, adorn your bridal chamber, and receive King [Col. 0677D] Christ with love, honor, faith, and reception of the sacraments—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XIV. ON THE BEGINNING OF THE FAST, I

“Remember that you are ashes and dust, and to ashes and dust you shall return” (Gen. 3:19).

The holy Fathers, watching over the Church of God with diligent concern, labored to teach, pray [Note: [Col. 0677D] “and keep vigil” appears to be lacking here.], so that she might be instructed in speech, beautiful in conduct, and fortified in all her actions. Instructed, indeed, as the Bride of him whose wisdom is without number. Beautiful likewise, as the wife of him [Col. 0678A] who is the radiance of eternal light. Fortified altogether, like her whose foundations are in the mountains and who is the city of the most mighty King; whose strength is like that of the rhinoceros, an animal also called the monoceros, or unicorn, on account of the single horn it bears upon its snout, and which is conquered by no strength.

The ashes imposed today upon the heads of Christians pertain to this instruction, beauty, and fortification of the Church: to instruction, that we may know our own formation; to beauty, that we may wash our hearts; to fortification, that we may set against the adversary the shield of humility. But in order that the beauty of the sacrament may become known to you, let us attend not to the baseness of the ash itself, but to the power of true humility; for humility is signified through ash. [Col. 0678B] This must be demonstrated to you by an example, lest we deceive some simple people by obscure and hidden language.

Here is your example. A leafy and branching tree, or a piece of wood, perhaps comes before us; we praise and extol the height of its stature, the greenness of its leaves, and the shade of its branches. Before much time has passed, it is cut down, burned, and reduced to ashes. Where, then—where is that height, that greenness, that shade? That glory has surely been humbled down to ashes. The same is true of the strongest lion, the swiftest horse, the most rapacious hawk, and of the proudest human being himself. What are all these things while they live, except a kind of mud [Col. 0678C] that stands and walks, eats and drinks, speaks and laughs, so long as there is a soul in it? The end comes; death comes; ash returns to ash, dust to dust. Why meanwhile does earth and ash grow proud? Take away the haughtiness of your eyes, O man, for these windows will soon be shut and will not be opened until the Day of Judgment. Keep your feet from evil, for these shins will be bound until the last of days. Restrain your hands from shedding blood, from robbery and plunder, for they will be struck together and, made inflexible, laid out in the belly of the earth. Chastise all the limbs of your body, for death hastens toward you like a horse rushing violently into battle, to swallow up this mortal body. What will then happen? You will be placed in a tomb and remain without a companion until you rot away.

[Col. 0678D] O good Christian, before that time comes, remember that you are dust and ash, and that you will return to dust and ash. Put ash upon your head, that you may think humbly and never, puffed up by the spirit of your mind, be proud. Remember, not with the vain turning of a superficial thought, which passes like a morning cloud, but with the weight of dove-like meditation; for the meditation of a dove is accompanied by groaning. Hence that great penitent Hezekiah, to whom the Lord added fifteen years, says: “I will meditate like a dove” (Isa. 38:14). The Psalmist speaks of this kind of remembering: “Will dust confess you, or proclaim your truth?” (Ps. 29:10). Hear the recompense [Col. 0679A] of this remembering: “The Lord heard and had mercy on me; the Lord became my helper” (Ps. 29:11). He had mercy by forgiving the past. He became a helper by graciously providing caution concerning the future.

You too, in return, say to God: “Remember, I pray, that you have made me like clay, and will reduce me to dust” (Job 10:9). O God my Creator, behold my entering in and my going out. How base was the little vessel of my birth, when, in the womb of my mother, mud was mingled in the foul and fetid discharge of paternal and maternal intercourse! Mud so base that the sense of smell could scarcely endure it, were unclean pleasure not interposed! O how base a doorway! How despised a gate of our birth and conception! Remember, therefore, O God, our origin [Col. 0679B] when we sin.

For what wonder is it that I am unclean, who was conceived from unclean seed? I do not depart from my first origin if I perform works of the flesh or am tempted by fleshly desire. Yet I do not reproach you for having made me such; instead, I appeal to your mercy, because from such a wretched material you created so precious a creature, on account of your image. If you consider in me the nobility of the soul in which your image resides and seek holy conduct, consider again that, in respect of my body, you made me as clay. With as just an eye as you require from me works worthy of your image, look with equal mercy upon the house of clay to which you have joined it by bonds almost impossible to dissolve. Remember that it is no wonder [Col. 0679C] if mud is dirty. Remember [lacuna] that, according to its nature, dust is mobile and dissoluble.

Therefore do not punish my contaminations and dissolutions as strictly as though I were a soul without a body. Did you not milk me out like milk, through the frail joining of the elements, and curdle me like cheese (Job 10:10), through the solidity of my limbs? You clothed me with skin and flesh, as with garments of skin. You bound me together with bones and sinews (ibid., v. 11), as with foundations and columns. And do you thus suddenly cast me down? (ibid., v. 8), casting me out of paradise for one taste of forbidden fruit, and placing me opposite Eden, that is, paradise? Remember, I pray, that you made me like clay (ibid., v. 9), so that when you are angry you may remember mercy, and the frailty of my condition may temper [Col. 0679D] the severity of your justice.

As you set before me, “Remember that you are ashes and dust,” lest I be proud, so I set before you: “Remember that you have made me like clay,” that you may restrain your anger. I receive ash upon my head as a sign of recognition; do not strike a soul marked with such a seal. Perhaps I speak too boldly and confidently; I do not fear your sword where I bear the standards of the cross and ashes. With this shield and this helmet I serve as a soldier for you, not against you. Will you kill your soldier, though he is sluggish, and not defend him? Behold, I serve beneath your standards. Protect me beneath the shadow of your wings, O Christ [Col. 0680A] Jesus, who live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit through ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XV. ON THE BEGINNING OF THE FAST, II

“Remember that you are ashes and dust, and to ashes and dust you shall return” (Gen. 3:19).

This admonition is sufficient for us: to repent of the past, to grieve for the present, and to abstain in the future. These three things, dearest brothers, are very necessary if that divine propitiation—that abundant redemption which daily intercedes for us with the Father in groanings that cannot be uttered—may be propitious to us. Hence John: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, who is the propitiation for our sins” (II John II, 2). And the Apostle [Col. 0680B] Paul: “The Spirit prays for us with groanings that cannot be uttered” (Rom. 8:26). We are, moreover, God’s helpers if we repent, grieve, and abstain. Let us therefore see what belongs to repentance, what to grief, and what to abstinence. First we must see what repentance is.

Repentance is, as Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0679D] Epistle 9 and Homily 34.], to weep over sins committed and not to commit the sins which must be wept over. For one who thus bewails some sins but nevertheless commits others either does not know how to do penance or pretends to do so. Isidore [Note: [Col. 0680D] Book II of the *Sentences*, ch. 3.]: “He is a mocker who still does what he repents of; he does not seem to entreat God submissively, but to deride him proudly.” Augustine: “Repentance is empty when a subsequent fault defiles it; lamentations profit nothing if sins are repeated.” Gregory: “Whoever laments things done but nevertheless [Col. 0680C] does not cease subjects himself to a heavier punishment.” From these authorities you can sufficiently understand what repentance is, or what kind it ought to be. Whoever repents holds the second plank after shipwreck: for just as whatever guilt preceded was erased in baptism, so through repentance the liability remaining from sin is erased. Therefore, in order to do penance, remember that you are ashes and dust.

You are not stone, iron, bronze, or earthenware; you are dust and ash. If you were stone, you could not bend to repentance; if iron, you would be hard and indomitable; if bronze, how obstinate you would remain in defending error; if earthenware, you would melt in no fire. Satan is iron, Pharaoh stone, Adam bronze, Judas earthenware. [Col. 0680D] But Peter, David, and Mary Magdalene acknowledge themselves to be ash; and what do they do? In the bitterness of repentance they pour themselves out upon the earth, humbling themselves even to the dust: “Our soul,” they say, “has been humbled in the dust; our belly has clung to the earth” (Ps. 43:25). This is why Peter is named expressly in the resurrection account, where it says: “Go, tell his disciples and Peter that he will go before you into Galilee” (Mark 16:7). God excluded and cast out of the heart of the truly penitent man the goad of conscience that remained from the fault of denial. He does not count him among the others, but before the others sends him through the angel the joy of the resurrection. For already [Col. 0681A] the apostolic mind had perhaps, through shame at what he had done, scarcely chosen to feed the kids, and did not dare to return to that holy assembly.

What of you, David? What do you say of yourself? “I am a worm and not a man, a reproach of men and despised by the people” (Ps. 21:17). But you, woman—a sinner in the city—with what face will you look upon the Saviour’s face? “I shall not look upon man any longer” (Isa. 38:11), she says—not to speak of God and man. I will cast myself down beside his feet, behind the door, behind the wall, because I am dust and ash, wholly burned by the fire of toilsome desire down to spark and ash. I, who until now have been trampled like the mud of the streets, will now, at the feet of my Maker, compose another mud: not from saliva but from my [Col. 0681B] tears—remembering, indeed, that I am dust and ash, and have poured out my soul within me.

Truly, as the prodigal squandered all his substance by living extravagantly with harlots, so I have laid waste all the trees of the paradise of my God—that is, all gifts of grace and nature—burning with that fire which burns down to the depths of hell. How many sparks of unlawful love I have exhaled! How high a flame I made! How great a forest of fools I consumed! How many embers, how many coals I heaped into the bosoms of many! But now at last I have declined to ash and retained for myself dead ash. The memory of evils is ash: not ash to be scattered to the wind, lest it cause blindness of the eyes, but ash to be gathered again into the inner chamber of the heart and mixed with waters for washing [Col. 0681C] the garments of a menstruating woman. For thus the Lord commanded me: “I will no longer remember your sins” (Isa. 43:25). Behold, your sins have been forgiven, because you loved much; but you, remember. Hence it is said: “Remember that you are ashes and dust,” etc. We have now set before you, dearest brothers, the authorities of the saints concerning repentance, and brought forward examples concerning sorrow and contrition of heart. It remains for us now to say something about abstinence.

Abstinence is twofold: abstinence from food and abstinence from evil. Abstinence from evil comes first; abstinence from food, second. The former is never to be relaxed; the latter must be remitted according to the occasion. For it is like a bow, [Col. 0681D] which is neither always drawn tight, lest it fail, nor always unstrung, lest it lose its function. Thus abstinence from food must be observed with measure and reason: one should fast to diminish or mortify vices, but at a suitable time one should indulge the body for the restoration of nature. For abundance of feasts and fullness of food provide fuel for the flesh’s ticklings and incentives. Hence Jerome: “A belly swollen with food foams over into lusts.” The saying is sharp, indeed, but true; for food, as though dashed against rocks in the inner spaces and receptacles of the belly, sends out foam from excesses both upward and downward.

Therefore, when by sparing food you have reduced those accumulations of humors, you will feel lesser discomfort in their evacuation or retention. When much food is cast upon them like a heap of ashes, the mind is put to sleep, the keenness of intelligence is blunted, the watches of wakefulness decline into sleep, and the whole household of virtues suffers lethargy. Abstinence, on the contrary, does the opposite: lifting with a swifter wing whatever in the soul had been languid; making green again the whole trunk of the soul, whose branches had dried through wintry negligence and torpor. This is about abstinence from food.

What more need be said about abstinence from evil, when Scripture urges almost nothing else? “Turn aside,” says the Psalmist, “from evil and do good” (Ps. 36:27). May God—and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ—deign to grant us to do this: he who [Col. 0682B] lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVI. FIRST SUNDAY OF LENT

“Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil” (Matt. 4:1).

When the people went forth to battle, the ark went before them, because before our face Christ the Lord, like Gad girded for battle, fought when he was tempted in every way in the likeness of sinful flesh, yet without sin. We who have been regenerated from water and the Holy Spirit are members of this Head and children of this Father. The head governs the members; the father instructs his children. The members likewise follow the head, [Col. 0682C] and the children imitate the father. Of the members it is said: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (1 Cor. 12:26), on account of the bond of unity and the governance of the head. Likewise, it is said of the Son: “Whatever the Father does, these same things the Son also does in like manner” (John 5:19).

Let us therefore look upon our Head and Father as the commander in battle: how he fights with the enemy, how deliberately he receives the enemy’s darts, how patiently he endures them, and how wisely he repels them. He does not receive them unwillingly; he does not endure them against his will; he does not reject them impatiently; he does not rashly hurl them back at the thrower. He does not flee the tempter in fear, just as he does not flee the traitor or his crucifiers; nor does he insult one who dares [Col. 0682D] to tempt him, but contradicts him by reason. He does not succumb to the tempter through the persistence of temptation, but first instructs him by a measured response, saying: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4:4). Second, he rebukes one who misinterprets the Scriptures, saying: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (ibid., v. 7). Third, he confounds the insolent and shameless one, saying: “Begone, Satan” (ibid., v. 10). Thus the incarnate Wisdom of God receives the darts of malice on the shield of patience; and he gains victory over the enemy not by shouting, but by reason and the authority of the Scriptures. Thus David fought against Goliath; Samson against the lion and bear; Gideon against Amalek; Moses and Joshua against Pharaoh, Sihon, Og, and the enemies of the people, [Col. 0683A] and conquered them. All these were mighty men among the mightiest of Israel, holding swords and most highly trained for war, like the tower of Lebanon that faces Damascus—that is, the devil, who thirsts for the blood of souls.

But let us come to our own battle-lines, consider the enemy’s positions, and survey what engines they have raised with so great a massing of weapons. For we shall consider what is necessary for war if we adequately assess the enemy’s strength. Attend, therefore, dearest brothers, to the armored and helmeted princes of darkness, borne on horses and chariots, carrying weapons of war, coming and converging from every wind of heaven to make war upon the Christian people, and especially upon congregations [Col. 0683B] of religious. “These trust in chariots, and these in horses; but we shall call upon the name of the Lord our God” (Ps. 19:8).

Let us therefore station them on the left like foul-smelling goats, but also raging lions: namely, the princes of darkness, who have encamped against us with their army and most wicked people. But on the right let us occupy the defenses of the triumphant standard, for the Lord knows the ways that are on the right, and “the Lord is at my right hand, that I may not be moved” (Ps. 15:8). Let the baptismal font also be placed between camp and camp. Let the city of our strength, the tower of Zion, be near us for refuge; for theirs is the tower of confusion and the city called Babylon. They trust in their strength and [Col. 0683C] their arm; we shall perform might neither by bow nor spear, but in the name of the Lord. Judah bound his colt to the vine—that is, in the Passion he gave his body over—and he will be commander in battle. With him David struck ten thousands among his thousands, triumphing in his body upon the wood of the cross over the powers of the air; and likewise Samson, whose name means “their sun,” and who with his own hand strangled that lion which goes about seeking whom it may devour. Gideon too must be asked to come with us with the three hundred marked upon the forehead with the sign of the cross, who drank the water by lapping without bending the knee.

Finally, Abraham, the father of many nations, whose children we also are—did he not himself come to our aid with his three hundred [Col. 0683D] household-born servants? Moses, who leads the people out of Egypt, is himself very useful to us in this battle. Will not Joshua bring with him the captain of the host, that he may be a mighty warrior before the Lord? Let us enter the battle with complete confidence if we have such leaders and commanders in the Lord’s camp. But before we launch the assault, let us portray how the enemy battle-lines advance. A certain tyrant, who has seven diadems—that is, all wickedness upon his head—sits in the seat of pestilence. Having summoned his princes and satraps, he contrives deceits and frauds, distrusting his strength against our contest. Yet, having received great license from him without whose permission he would not attack us, and without whose help we could not conquer him, he abuses it, breaking the reins on his jaws by which he is restrained, so that he may not harm as much as he wishes. Let us therefore judge, as we can discern through a shadow—indeed, sometimes through experience—what those powers are, and who are the principalities of this darkness that serve under that commander, the devil.

Pride, more pestilential than any prince of princes, comes forward; its name is declined in the feminine gender, but its malice does not decline even from the masculine gender. Beneath its spear it bends the necks of the proud and lofty, and itself triumphs over kings, nobles, those wise according to the flesh, saints and religious, and every kind of human being that moves [Col. 0684B] upon the earth. It sits upon the swiftest horse, which is more mobile than every wind, so that it races ahead even upon the wings of the winds, and scarcely anyone can hide himself from its heat. This tyrant is first to appear in the battle-line of Christian warfare and last to withdraw. Before the morning star it rises for combat and does not rest even after evening. Wherever you turn, it either sits upon your back or occupies your face. At times pride puffs up one who knows and notices it; at times it stains even one who does not perceive it. This queen of Amazons has acquired for herself many kingdoms and lands by a womanly warfare—not through weakness but through softness. Young men, old men, young women, old women, clerics, canons and monks, and hermits themselves do not escape her even in ash [Col. 0684C] and haircloth; but very many of these, pretending to flee her, follow her all the more. It is astonishing that all who serve her in their hearts detest her more loudly with their mouths.

With all her strength and boldness, attempting to overthrow the battle-line of humility, she attacks Jesus himself. Having endured his concealment for a long time and not yet been struck back with just retribution, she at last perceived what was contained in that earthen or glass vessel of Jesus’ body and withdrew. For she who came on one foot could not remain; with that foot broken, she departed with none. For when she said, “All these things I will give you, if, falling down, you worship me” (Matt. 4:9), promising what was above herself and showing him—not her own things, but those of him whose they were—she was dashed against the rock of truth and shattered, with her well-deserved shame, and departed. For pride lied to itself. “Begone,” the Lord says, “Satan. It is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’” (ibid., v. 10). With this strong dagger pride was pierced even to its vitals; as though despairing of life, it betook itself to its infernal couch, henceforth to be more contemptible even among the sisters or daughters of that most wicked stock.

But that same pride had first sent ahead, as though of less strength, two sisters or daughters: gluttony and vainglory. Indeed, disdaining through its pride to go forth first, it commanded gluttony and vainglory to hurl their darts and undermine the wall of abstinence; and promised that it would come afterward if it were fitting. Gluttony, then, is one among the common people, but many among the people; for through their bellies it possesses not individuals only, but very many. Attacking the unguttonous appetite of Jesus, it thought by the pull of habit to soften and entice it to seek food—not only from the habit of one who was hungry, but also from the power of one who worked miracles. Thus gluttony tempted the Lord concerning appetite, that from his own desire for food he might, by a new miracle, make bread from stones. But appetite did not so press the bread who came down from heaven that he would make bread from a stone for the sake of bread; nor did the tempter prevail so far as to anticipate in this matter the signs of divinity and become in any degree more certain concerning the God-man.

Thus the temptation of gluttony was shattered and mocked; then vainglory follows, which is often hostile to other people both through victory and through abstinence. Vainglory therefore seeks to empty out true glory in Christ by suggesting that he cast himself down for the approval of display, although he had steps by which he could suitably descend. This would indeed have been vain, because it would have been done without cause. Having been struck and repelled by this second stone of rebuke from David’s shepherd’s pouch, that one follows which exalts itself above everything called God or worshiped, so as to show all the glory of the world from a high mountain and say: “All these things I will give you if, falling down, you worship me.” Wounded in the forehead by this third, decisive stone from the same shepherd’s pouch, it too was defeated; victory followed, and angels came and ministered to him in triumph. Let us return from the camps of God [Col. 0685C] to our own, and under the same king, the same law, and against the same enemy see how we must fight.

We have already spoken of pride, which rides horses—and indeed very spirited horses. Its breastplate is impenetrable, its spear penetrating; its saddle changeable, its horse exceedingly mobile; its shield wonderfully painted; its whole equipment highly desirable, if it were not damnable. Yet they move against us in a different order than against our Head, because they see us greater in presumption and weaker in encounter. Therefore they make their courses and attacks, not always in the same order but sometimes altered deliberately, lest we learn their paths and become more wary. [Col. 0685D] Now vainglory spurs its horse ahead of the others; now envy, now anger, now sadness, now avarice, now the belly’s greed, now lust. See that vainglory has followers and companions according to its kind—disobedience, boasting, hypocrisy, contention, stubbornness, discord, presumption, novelty—which, stirring up dust with it and after it, rush forth unexpectedly and wound us with their spears. How grievously these gnats bore into the eyes of the soul! How greedily these robbers plunder our little substance, down to the strap of the sandal! How suddenly these thieves seize and capture us while we sleep!

There is, moreover, one household and another household: [Col. 0686A] the household of vainglory apart; the household of envy apart, namely hatred, whispering, detraction, exultation in a neighbor’s adversities, and affliction at a neighbor’s prosperities. The household of anger apart: quarrelling, swelling of mind, insult, shouting, indignation, blasphemies. The household of sadness apart: malice, rancor, faint-heartedness, despair, torpor, wandering of mind. The household of avarice apart: wastefulness, fraud, deceit, perjuries, restlessness, hardening of heart against mercy. The household of the belly apart: foolish merriment, buffoonery, uncleanness, much talking, dullness of mind. The household of lust apart: blindness of mind, thoughtlessness, inconstancy, rashness, self-love, hatred of God, attachment to this present age, dread or despair of the age to come.

[Col. 0686B] Behold, these are the households of vices, in which none is lacking and whose girdle is not loosed from their loins. They wage unceasing war against those who are awake; indeed, they interrupt sleep or at times corrupt it with a filthy image. Whence do so many fantastic illusions creep upon sleepers, except because evil impulses are sent in through evil angels? But since the discourse now exceeds its proper bounds, let us set against the camps of the Philistines, if not all the households of virtues, at least their leaders—that is, the principal virtues—so that, defended beneath their wings, we may escape every captivity and danger.

Therefore let that virtue, on which the whole order of commandments depends, and which is not inferior to him whose arrogance is greater than his strength, whether in swiftness or in every goodness and strength—let that virtue, I say, ordered like an army in battle array, bring forth its household into the weapons of light and put to flight the weak nation of darkness by a sudden flashing. Let it also arrange household after household, the choirs that follow it and go forth with it to battle. This is charity.

Humility, with her household, should advance by the straight path and attack vain glory. Then love of neighbour, with her household, should fall upon the camp of envy and defeat it utterly, even to “one who urinates against a wall.” After her, peace with her household should overcome anger and leave no remnant of it. Seeing the joy of the spirit—her sisters—triumphing so nobly over their adversaries, let her come with her household and drive sorrow out from all her borders [Col. 0686D], possessing the gates of her enemies. With heart enlarged, lavish almsgiving, with her household, should cut off avarice, which is the service of idols, so that its memory may not remain beneath heaven. When so many victories have been gained, let abstinence follow—being the guardian of a person’s goods, as though holding the key in her hand—and restrain the belly’s gluttony, like Nebuzaradan, chief cook of the king of Babylon. Let chastity, this most beloved sister, come with her and complete the triumph, at which hell groans and heaven rejoices. May Jesus Christ our Lord deign to grant this to us, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XVII. FRIDAY AFTER THE FIRST SUNDAY OF LENT

[Col. 0687A]

“It was a feast-day of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. Now at Jerusalem there is a sheep-pool, called in Hebrew Bethsaida, having five porticoes” (John 5:1–2).

Sin, which arose from malice and has its origin there, extended its native wickedness into many offshoots. In its first birth it brought forth punishment for its author, humankind: it discovered toil and pain, multiplied miseries, and changed feast-days—from the happy dwelling of paradise and familiarity with its Creator—into the mourning of this pilgrimage. Hence these days are days of cloud and darkness, evil and few days, days of affliction and sorrow, uncertain days that pass like a shadow. [Col. 0687B] By their misery they make people miserable; by bitterness, bitter; by barrenness, sterile; by vanity, empty and unfruitful. How then was it a feast-day of the Jews?

The prophet Joel, saying at the beginning of his book: “Awake, you drunkards, and weep; wail, all you who drink wine in sweetness, because it has perished from your mouth” (Joel 1:5), adds the following causes why that people had days not of feasting but of sorrow:

> “For a nation, strong and innumerable, has come up upon my land; its teeth are like the teeth of a lion, and its molars like those of a lion’s cub. It has made my vineyard a wilderness and stripped the bark from my fig-tree; stripping it bare, it despoiled and cast it down; its branches have become white. Mourn like a virgin girded with sackcloth,” etc.  
> (Ibid., 6 ff.)

[Col. 0687C] This strong and innumerable nation that comes up upon the land is, literally, the caterpillar, locust, grub, and blight; morally, the passions of the flesh and vices of the soul, which come up upon the land when sin reigns in our mortal body so that we obey its desires. Then it makes the vineyard a wilderness when, by its suggestions, withdrawing the moisture of grace, it empties of God’s goodness the soul made in the image and likeness of God, intended to produce clusters and grapes of God’s commandments and contemplations; and wickedly uproots the roots of good work.
