Jesus, therefore, is the one who meets you if you find anyone marked out in this way. “Such is he,” says the Bride, or Mary the Lord’s mother, or Mary Magdalene, or Joseph: “Such is my beloved, and he is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.” But if you wish to recognize him by fewer distinguishing signs, since a wise person is known by few things, hear: “My beloved is white and ruddy” (Song 5:10): white because of innocence, ruddy because of the punishment which he endured. Behold, good lady, you have satisfied us with a sure demonstration of your Beloved, your Bridegroom. But tell us of your touch, of your feeling of him: what he is like to you in feeling, how you have felt his left hand, and how his right. For he is far from us; and if [Col. 0737B] perhaps we cannot see him, much less can we touch him, much less feel him. We have now in some fashion been assured concerning sight; add assurance concerning touch also. For Scripture somewhat terrifies and restrains us from touching, when it says that he is fire: “Those who approach me,” it says, “approach fire”; for it is hard and dreadful to cast a great thing into fire.

Tell us, therefore, whether perhaps we may find him a little gentler on either right or left side. You know his right side, since his right hand embraces you; likewise his left, since his left hand is beneath your head. Speak first, then, of the left, because, as it seems to us, he sleeps upon the left on the cross. Thus he is a bundle of myrrh: “My beloved will dwell between my breasts, while his left hand is beneath my head.” Here is that heap of stones in which he passed the noonday, on the day when his mother—that is, the Synagogue—crowned him with a crown, certainly one of thorns. Hence Nicodemus, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about one hundred pounds, came to anoint Jesus’ body. One hundred pounds: it is much; it is enough. Jesus’ entire body can be embalmed with that quantity of myrrh and aloes, so abundantly that his lips will distil the first myrrh from this outpouring.

Truly, if your compassion is of a hundredfold measure—that is, perfect and complete—it does not merely intoxicate Christ’s mute limbs, but reaches even to his lips, so that he answers and says: “I thirsted, and you gave [Col. 0737D] me drink; I hungered, and you gave me food” (Matt. 25:35); and: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations” (Luke 22:28). Behold, the contrite and humbled heart has a bundle of myrrh; behold, the greatest bitterness; behold, a grief in Jesus’ passion like the sea. Through compassion there is a bundle of myrrh, and this is the left hand. But what is the right? It is certainly that of which the Psalm says: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109:1). God’s right hand is blessedness without interruption, glory without end, pleasure without corruption, health without illness, concord without bitterness, peace without rancour, tranquillity without disturbance, eternity without change.

This is God’s right hand, because at God’s right hand there is as [Col. 0738A] complete a delight as here there is an abundance of afflicted misery. And as we do not yet possess that right hand, so we do not yet know it; nor is the wondrous delight of the right hand as familiar to us as the miserable affliction of the left. Between left and right, however, there will perhaps be what we fear: namely, fire. For our God, a consuming fire, will come in a mighty storm. Then, without doubt, he will not be as one sleeping, as one dead on cross and in tomb, nor as one glorious in heaven after death, but as one mighty and exhilarated with wine, awakened from sleep; rather, as a roaring lion, of whom it is said: “The lion will roar; who will not fear?” (Amos 3:8). Again: “The Lord will roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem he will utter his voice” (Amos 1:2).

[Col. 0738B] For he will summon judgment to fire, that it may devour the great deep and consume the portion together: that is, it may swallow up the profoundly wicked in eternal damnation, and consume the imperfect in respect of their imperfection, though not swallow them up through a sentence of eternal damnation. Then he will turn neither to the right nor to the left, so as to appear either such in gentleness as he was under Pontius Pilate, or such as he will be when judgment has been completed; for then cruelty will be in his face, to avenge the injury of his passion—not the weakness which he feigned in order to fulfil the dispensation of the Incarnation.

Therefore, brothers, let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus: feel punishment without guilt; feel innocence without injury; feel the merciful one who forgives; [Col. 0738C] feel the just one who exacts; feel the compassionate one who raises you up to the right hand of the throne of his majesty. There, brothers, the hands of the poor will bear your souls; there confessions, prayers, fasts, and other good works will carry you. May Jesus Christ our Lord deign to grant this to you, he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIV. ON THE LORD’S SUPPER, I

“The sons of Dedan are your merchants. They exchanged ivory and ebony teeth for your price. They offered balm and honey, oil and resin in your markets” (Ezek. 27:15).

[Col. 0738D] Heaven and earth hurry to the present market, unpacking and displaying their wares and little bundles, so that whoever wishes to buy whatever aid necessary for feasting with the Lord may find it and buy it at a just—indeed, cheap—price. For heavenly things are sold more cheaply today; earthly things are reckoned more dearly, because things that are sold but not seen are esteemed as without price by carnal people, while things that are sold and seen are valued beyond their worth.

To recount individually all that is displayed for purchase is neither for this occasion nor within our capacity. For there is such variety and multitude of sellers and buyers, and likewise of things being bought and sold, that neither eye is satisfied with seeing nor ear [Col. 0739A] with hearing. Let us purchase and share with your brotherhood only those things which concern the feast day, so that we may have one purse, one merchandise, one market, one profit, and one loss.

Son of man, you who have arrived at this market, laden with abundant wealth from a far country, from Babylonian captivity, display for us your market-stall and unfold your pouch, if perhaps among your wares there is something worthy of the solemnity of our supper, something that may fulfil the sacred joys of this present day. But first I marvel at your bundles: where did you bring from such beautiful and precious ivory and ebony teeth? What nation, what people, uses teeth of this kind? At last I desire to have such teeth, but distrust my ability to exchange mine for them. I fear the extraction of my own; I have no example of the insertion of others. Yet surely perhaps he who planted the ear knows how to insert a tooth. Likewise, he who took a rib from Adam’s side without bitter pain can remove a tooth already rotten without harsh affliction.

Therefore I wish to buy ivory and ebony teeth, because I have a gardener who is, as of vegetables, so also an extractor and planter of teeth. Certainly today we must dine and drink among friends, among the senators of the heavenly court, among the distinguished and noble men of the great assembly. O merchants of teeth, who are you? Whence do you come? At what price will you give ivory and ebony teeth? “We are the sons,” they say, “of Dedan; we are from Ethiopia. We will give teeth for [Col. 0739C] teeth: good for bad, new for old, healthy for diseased, white for black, clean for scabby, strong for rotten and weak, sharp for dull. For we are accustomed to exchange, not to sell; and we employ an art of renewal so that, after we have rubbed down the old things in our fashion, we make them new.”

O good craftsmen, are you as generous in the market as you are skilled in your work? “Yes,” they say, “we add neither coin nor price in the exchange of teeth, except that we receive human teeth and give those of animals or trees. We have ivory teeth from animals and ebony ones from trees.” And what animal, I ask, produces such teeth, or what kind of tree? “The animal is called the elephant; the tree is the ebony.” Behold, brothers, if it pleases you, let us exchange them; let us not delay or hesitate to exchange, because we are called to the supper of the Lamb, and it is fitting that with new teeth we eat new meats. For everything at this supper is new: new bread, new flesh, new wine, a new table, a new cup, a new dish, a new towel, a new commandment, a new word, a new washing of feet, new chrism, new oil, a new diner, new teeth, new lips, and, finally, new hands.

But because the other things are sufficiently well known in themselves, let us return to the teeth and now disclose the mystery of the matter from the name of the sellers. “The sons of Dedan are your merchants.” What is Dedan? “This judgment,” or “such judgment.” [Col. 0740A] What is “this judgment” or “such judgment”? Certainly it is what the Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” (1 Cor. 11:31). What does “if we judged ourselves” mean? If we accused ourselves. But this accusation is called confession. Therefore the sons of Dedan are sons of confession, sons of judgment—not simply judgment, but this judgment, this kind of judgment. What is “this”? What is “such”? Certainly this judgment which took place under Pontius Pilate; certainly such judgment as will occur in the future and great Judgment.

Therefore make this judgment—that is, this confession—so pure, so true, so severe; make it also such a confession as all of us will make on the day of judgment. As then nothing will be hidden of sin, so now make judgment like the noonday in [Col. 0740B] confession, so that you reserve in your heart no hiding-places and no remnants of darkness. Let hell stand before you, open-mouthed, vomiting flames and sulphurous stenches; let demons, with Ethiopian blackness and draconic ferocity, stand by holding fiery hooks and forks to carry off souls; let the judge’s tribunal be set in the cloud; let the judge, wholly as though enraged and without mercy, look on; his eyes like a flame of fire; a lofty sound from his mouth like great thunder; a sword sharp on both sides; trembling angels; human beings wavering like a leaf before a violent wind. Let all that setting of the great Judgment come before your eyes as you approach the judgment of confession.

Certainly then the sons of Dedan will exchange teeth, abandoning falsehood and holding to truth, renouncing hatred and pursuing peace; casting off impurity and preserving chastity; emptying themselves of shamefulness, foolish speech, and buffoonery, and meditating upon sacred utterances. These are ivory teeth because of the chastity of their words, and ebony teeth because of the edification and fruit of truthful lips. Behold, you have teeth: eat whatever your hand finds. Eat the scroll of Christ’s passion; eat the Gospel; eat the bread of angels; eat the fatted calf; eat the yearling lamb; eat the kid; eat your own flesh; eat the calf; eat the molten calf; eat grass like an ox; eat honey in sufficiency; eat goats’ milk; eat butter; eat the fat [Col. 0740D] of lambs and rams, sons of Bashan; eat goats with the marrow of wheat.

But to make clearer what we mean: what are teeth except virtues of the soul? Yet what kind of virtues are teeth? Certainly those which are such as teeth are. Teeth ought to be clean, white, sharp, planted with a firm root in the gums, ordered, whole, and joined together. Clean because of the purity of Christ’s body and blood; white because of his patience; sharp because of justice; firmly planted because of obedience; ordered because of moderation; whole because of perseverance; joined together because of concord. Clean in thought, white in action, sharp in confession, firmly planted in temptation, ordered in prosperity, whole in adversity, joined in communal life. Let abstinence cleanse the teeth; continence preserve them when cleansed; fear sharpen them; hope plant them firmly; justice order them; remembrance of God strengthen them; love join them.

Since we already have ivory and ebony teeth at home, if we have perfectly purified our senses and are fit to exhort others, let us look around for the flask of balm; and if this balm is genuine and unmixed, let us purchase it, that anointed with it we may be made a royal and priestly race. Today, brothers, the chrism is consecrated by which priests and kings are anointed in both the Old and New Testaments, and therefore are called christs. But take care lest your balm be mixed by simony: do not wish to reign not from God but through money. For mixed balm belongs not to Christ but to Antichrist.

He mixes the balm who confers holy orders not for merit but for payment; who confers the care of souls not for God but for gold; who hands Christ over not for the redemption of humankind but for the fulfilment of avarice for money. He mixes the balm who honours God with his lips while his heart is far from him. He mixes the balm who does not proclaim Christ sincerely. He mixes the balm who leavens the purity of religion with deceptive pretence. They mix the balm who come to us in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravening wolves. Therefore do not adulterate God’s word; do not mix the balm, because “unmixed balm is my fragrance,” [Col. 0741C] says the Lord (Ecclus. 24:21). Hence the Apostle: “From sincerity and truth, as from God, before God, we speak in Christ” (2 Cor. 2:17), so that there may be no wrinkle or spot in God’s Bride.

Let us anoint the head with chrism; let us anoint the hands, the forehead, and the shoulders. The head, because of the crown we await; the hands, because of the mystery of Christ’s body and blood which we touch; the forehead, because of the cross which we bear there; the shoulders, because of the labour of works in which we sweat for divine service. The head, that we may love God with the whole mind; the hands, that almsgiving may sweat in your hand; the forehead, that you may not have the forehead of a prostitute who refused to blush, but a forehead tender to shame, marked for protection, prepared for battle; [Col. 0741D] the shoulder, that with all your strength you may bear the burden of the day and heat in the Lord’s vineyard until evening. Give two gold coins—that is, body and soul—in exchange for balm; or good intention and good action, because you have received the spirit of adoption as sons, not again the spirit of slavery in fear. Let this suffice concerning balm.

Honey follows. As among liquids nothing is more precious than balm for anointing, so nothing is sweeter than honey for eating. But since honey has its place at the Lord’s nativity or resurrection, not in his passion, let us indeed buy it, but set it aside; for we shall eat it in its own season. For what have we now to do with honey, where there is gall, where vinegar, where the thorn, [Col. 0742A] where the spear, where the nail, where the hammer, where Judas, where Barabbas, where passion, cross, and death? Let us therefore take up another kind, namely oil; and because we are weak, let us buy the oil of the weak.

Behold, dearest brothers, the olive tree which says, “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God” (Ps. 51:10), is pressed in the winepress; and, pouring forth oil, it is conveyed to our little vessels at a good bargain and price. Thanks be to you, Jesus, because with your oil we have satisfied our Creator, and have kept back no small amount for anointing our wounds; indeed, a full cask, because “your mercy is for ever and above all your works.” Behold, with your oil we illumine our darkness; behold, we lessen pain; behold, we season food; behold, we pay our debt to the creditor. All this is from your oil, all this [Col. 0742B] from your mercy, all this from your grace, all this from the depths of your compassion—you who are the God of all consolation and Father of mercies.

Let us pay a coin for that final commodity proposed by our merchants, namely resin, and bring the discourse to an end. This is necessary for Jesus suffering in the flesh, because it soothes and heals. Let us therefore purchase it with the coin of compassion, and expend it both upon Jesus’ sufferings through compassion and upon our own through correction. For if you correct yourself, you apply resin to your wounds. If you suffer with Christ, you pour resin upon his sufferings. If you rebuke your neighbour, you spread resin over his corruption. May the Lord therefore sanctify and consecrate us in balm, satisfy us with honey, anoint us with oil, and heal us with [Col. 0742C] resin—these things which the holy merchants proposed at the market of his supper and passion. May he deign to grant this to us, who lives, etc.

## SERMON XXXV. ON THE LORD’S SUPPER II

This whole day is dedicated to God and to our salvation: as many hours, so many graces. There are seven principal hours, especially adorned by seven sacraments; we are cleansed from sins and filled with virtues. The first is absolution from sins; the second, consecration of chrism; the third, consecration of the oil of the sick; the fourth, consecration of the Lord’s body and blood; the fifth, the setting aside of the Old Testament; the sixth, institution of the New; the seventh, washing of feet.

“All these things work together for good to those who love God” [Col. 0742D], because by these, as by keys, one enters the kingdom of heaven. Do not neglect these keys; do not lose them, because without a key the entrance to a house is not opened. Yet more principal and more worthy among the others is that key of David which “shuts and no one opens, opens and no one shuts”: namely, the Eucharist, which confers eternal life upon those who receive it worthily, eternal death upon those who approach unworthily. “He who eats,” says the Lord, “my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6:55): this concerns the worthy. But of the unworthy the Psalmist says: “Let their table become a snare” (Ps. 68:23).

Who, then, is the author of this table? Who its maker? Who its steward? Who prepares it? What are its food [Col. 0743A] and drink? Who is its guest? Of what form or material is the table itself? Jesus is its author; the Holy Spirit its maker; the prelate its steward; the angel and the apostolic order its preparer or minister; Christ’s flesh its food and his blood its drink; every Christian its guest. The table is the altar, or an anointed and consecrated stone; its form is square, its material stone.

Behold Jesus; behold the Holy Spirit; behold the high priest; behold the choir of apostles; behold the ministering spirits; behold the food; behold the drink; behold the table in its form and material. Why are these things here? And for what purpose? That the Passover may be eaten; that the guest may be present and satisfied. Where are you, Adam? Where are you, guest? Do not withdraw yourself; do not excuse yourself from the supper; do not deceive yourself and cover your shameful parts with fig leaves. The supper is prepared for you; for you your Father has sacrificed [Col. 0743B] the fatted calf; for you Wisdom has sacrificed her victims; for you Joseph has prepared a noonday feast; the morning and evening sacrifice await you. Stirred and invited by these things, every Christian without distinction runs and desires the prepared supper.

But see, brothers, how carefully you walk: not as foolish persons, but as wise. Look upward and read the inscription set over this table: “Whoever eats the bread of the Lord or drinks the cup unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:27). Likewise: “Let their table become before them a snare” (Ps. 68:23). Therefore do not taste that which, wrongly tasted, brings death; do not touch with a polluted mouth and unclean hands the Christ of the Lord. For wisdom wastes away [Col. 0743C], and the Holy Spirit groans with groanings that cannot be uttered in a body subjected to sins.

Let this groaning ascend to the ears and heart of the Father, from whom it also descended to see whether this cry, crying out amid continuing sins, persists: “Do not quench the Spirit” (1 Thess. 5:19), and, “Do not trample my Son Jesus beneath your feet.” For he has in his mouth a two-edged sword, sharp on either side, saying of that guest who joined himself to the supper not clothed in a wedding garment—that is, in charity and chastity—“Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into outer darkness,” etc. (Matt. 22:13). Therefore the guest sought is not one who fills the table with vomit and filth, but one who eats the lamb, innocent in [Col. 0743D] hands and pure in heart.

Behold Satan, not among the sons of God but against the Son of God; not transforming himself into an angel of light in order to deceive by pretence, but exalting himself against Jesus, who is truly worshipped and adored as God. He raises against heaven—indeed, against God—the engines of his malice; he rolls stones and missiles against the tower of David, which was built with battlements; he hurls spears and arrows, in the dark moon, before Lucifer, and after the sun’s rising. Thus at last he appears to have burst the bladder in which, from the beginning of his creation, he had coagulated his most dreadful poison, pouring it out in some manner and infecting the whole earth as with a deadly mist. So exceedingly foul was that exhalation or discharge that even the sun could not endure it. For it was darkened, and darkness [Col. 0744A] came upon the earth. Hence Judas burst open in the middle; hence that foul eruption from the mouth of the Jews: “He is guilty of death” (Matt. 26:66); “Crucify, crucify” (Luke 23:11); and, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15).

For the little flask of the heart, full and overflowing, supplied what the malicious tongue vomits forth by repeated reflux through deceitful lips. Was anything retained or reserved today from the abyss of wickedness which was not spread abroad, which was not exposed? From the beginning of time, vessels of wrath have not been drained to such an extent as now; indeed, to speak truly, they have been swallowed up by God’s patience. For “death is swallowed up in victory”; and whatever the streamlet of hell was able to heap together in order to destroy us along with Jesus, Jesus swallowed it all without harm—indeed, to the profit of our restoration. Yet “concerning sin, he condemned sin.” For Jesus was able to swallow more than the devil was able to vomit. Wisdom, indeed, conquers malice.

The devil therefore struggles and labours in sweat until his final breath, to bring forward into the midst, from every quarter, by every means, and through every person, insulting injury, so that the weight of evils may crush Jesus, their measure overcome him, their number confound him, and universal desolation provoke him to impatience. But as Jesus is yesterday and today, himself for ages of ages, so his patience was able to bear what the devil could inflict, and what he could not. Better indeed is the patient one—that is, Jesus—than the strong man—that is, the devil—who, before the coming of him who would destroy [Col. 0744C] him, guarded his courtyard as the strong man; who held the power of death before he was summoned to single combat. He came meek and gentle, not to inflict injury, but, as far as concerned himself, to endure it; as far as concerned others, to repel it.

But since it is devout to think upon one so devout and one so impious, and faithfully weigh the cause of each, it must be understood that the devil was pursuing his own cause, one exceedingly deceitful; Jesus, ours, corrupted as regards us by the enemy’s guile, but just as regards himself. Thus on the one side were set the weapons of light—humility, patience, justice, and gentleness; on the other, instruments of war and wrath—avarice, destruction, slander, insults, scourges, blows, mockeries, spittle, [Col. 0744D] the crown of thorns, lance, gall, vinegar, cross, nails, and the other things of which the Gospel speaks. Let us recount the passion in order, and let us lay up from this garden a bundle of myrrh between our breasts—that is, in our heart—so that we may place Jesus, steeped in myrrh and aloes, upon Solomon’s bed; and, because of terrors in the night, girded with swords, surround that same bed.

For while Jesus, our friend, Father, and Lord, reclines as though in the sickness of his passion, it is by no means consistent with reason that we should wander through streets and squares with scoffers. Rather, let us be sorrowful with him who says, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Mark 14:34); let us suffer with the suffering one; let us die with the dying one, as Thomas says, “Let us go and die with him” (John 11:14), so that we may rise again with the rising one [Col. 0745A] and reign with the reigning one. For with equal lot he will distribute the spoils of merits to those who went with him into battle, so that he may indeed hold primacy above his companions because he laboured more, and the greater reward may be bestowed upon him who underwent the suffering of a single combat.

The three fingers are Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The three joints in the Father are those three things which Genesis assigns in the creation of things, saying: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and light was made; and God saw the light, that it was good” (Gen. 1:2); and similarly in the other cases. In the Son likewise there are three joints: Christ’s birth, death, and resurrection. In the Holy Spirit: the appearance of a dove, fire, and tongues; or charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and faith unfeigned.

[Col. 0745B] Yet the whole Trinity speaks together: “Let us make man in our image,” etc.—that is, the priest, by ordination, authority, and execution, “in our image and likeness” (ibid., 26): that he may imitate the Creator, regenerating the new man from water and the Holy Spirit, just as in the creation of the world the Spirit was borne over the waters; that he may imitate our Redeemer, who redeemed us by his blood, by celebrating Mass and consecrating the Eucharist; that he may imitate the Spirit, namely by loving God above himself, himself after God, and his neighbour as himself. But because a human being is born once and regenerated once, while every day he is put to death with Christ by remembering Christ’s passion, let us carefully examine how [Col. 0745C] priests should approach this sacrifice: with what heart, mouth, hand, and other senses.

For the hands with which we bear Christ upon the altar are as it were a certain anointed vehicle, solid and rounded, by which that most holy Eucharist is carried to the Father and brought back to us. The mouth is as it were a gate or door through which it enters the heart, as though into the Holy of Holies. The heart is as it were the ark containing the golden urn with manna, the tablets of the covenant, and Aaron’s rod. And these three are like the three fingers with which God weighs the mass of the earth—that is, the sacraments of the Church. For the visible elements, beneath the appearance of which invisible power lies hidden, are not improperly called the mass of the earth; unless the power of faith raised the mind above this weight, it would be crushed into the fall of unbelief [Col. 0745D], and groan like a giant beneath the waters. Therefore, O priest, wash your hands among the innocent; touch your lips with the tongs from the altar, or with the carbuncle; guard your heart with all vigilance, for life proceeds from it. Thus you will worthily weigh the mass of the earth—that is, the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament.

[Note: [Col. 0745D] A new sermon appears to begin in the manuscripts.]

A new king, a new law: one and the same mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, everywhere maintaining one and the same rule of justice soberly and temperately. In the form of God, he usurped nothing that was not his due; in the form of a servant, he endured from the Jews nothing except what was not his due. Therefore, when, in place of the honour and glory owed to him, the boldness of demons together with the malice of the Jews had offered him, on the way, from the torrent, every kind of insult and injury, [Col. 0746A] he indeed tasted, but would not drink: that is, for a time he received it through the dispensation of assumed mortality, but immediately vomited it forth through the glory of the resurrection. Thus David changed his countenance before Abimelech, so that his saliva ran down over his beard and he was judged possessed. And Jesus, with the power of his divinity hidden, concealed his beard with saliva, because, displaying weakness through the failings of human frailty, he made known that God was in the man only to his little ones—that is, the apostles. Indeed, he performed among them works which no one else had done; but the heart of that people was blinded, as Isaiah says: “Blind the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy” (Isa. 6:10).

Thus they stumbled upon the stone of stumbling and the rock [Col. 0746B] of offence, striking it with their hammers, beating and piercing it on every side with cries. But this precious stone—jasper in the passion, emerald in death, topaz in the resurrection, carbuncle in the ascension—was transferred from beneath the feet of the Jews to above the choirs of angels; and it rules not only throughout the whole earth, but throughout the entire creation of heaven and world.

The proverbial saying declares: “A new king, a new law.” The king is indeed from eternity with the Father, creating and ruling the whole creation. But when he came into a far country to receive another kingdom for himself, that he might reign over the two kingdoms of angels and human beings and make one kingdom of heaven, while he sought the second, he placed the first away in its hiding places [Col. 0746C], and was as though without a kingdom, because that one was hidden and this one did not yet obey him. Thus he was almost in every evil, in the midst of Church and Synagogue, because he brought forth the Church amid the pain of his passion, while sorrowfully losing the Synagogue, as Jonah lost the gourd or ivy.

Hence in the passion he prayed: “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:39): that is, let not a Jew crucify me, but anyone else. For iniquity is added to iniquity when it kills me, the husband of its youth and the son of its own nation. For the Synagogue is my mouth and my flesh, and the Virgin Mary is its nursling. Hence the Church is not admitted unless the Synagogue is expelled. It is said in the Psalm: [Col. 0746D] “I mingled my drink with weeping” (Ps. 101:10): the drink signifies the incorporation of the Church, the weeping the driving away of the Synagogue. For by drinking we incorporate, but by weeping we pour forth tears.

Therefore, when the wicked tenants cast the son out of his father’s vineyard and killed him, he passed from nation to nation, and from a kingdom to another people or kingdom. And when the branches of the good olive tree were broken off, the wild olive was grafted into the good olive, as the Apostle says. “Is he the God of the Jews only? Is he not also of the Gentiles? Yes, of the Gentiles also.” Therefore “the Lord has reigned; let the earth rejoice,” etc. (Ps. 96:1). Let the Jews, who said, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15), will it or not. “The Lord [Col. 0747A] has reigned; let the peoples be angry” (Ps. 18:1). Behold, the eternal king has become a new king by acquiring a new kingdom, not by receiving an eternal one. The new king says to the Father: “Glorify me with the glory which I had with you before the world was” (John 17:5). It was said to him: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again” (John 12:28).

He received the eternal kingdom freely from the Father, but acquired the new one at great labour and cost. Jacob, enriched and endowed in the house of Laban over a long time and through much labour, with the honour and substance of flocks, households, and wives, says when he returns: “With my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I return with two companies” (Gen. 32:10). It is as though he said: I return to my heavenly homeland and native land, to the Father’s bosom, from whose substance I was begotten before Lucifer, [Col. 0747B] with two companies: namely, the thief from punishment, and the flock of the ancient Fathers from hell. I who, made of a woman and made under the law, descended with a staff to the valley of tears—or passed into the staff of the cross through the humility of mortality—and descended to Laban, who transforms himself into an angel of light. I took away his substance, namely all the weapons in which he trusted, and distributed the spoils, leaving him vessels of dishonour and bringing back with me to the Father vessels unto honour. [lacuna]

[Note: [Col. 0747D] Something appears to be missing here.]

The body of Christ is a mirror, a bath, provision for the journey, a tent, a shield, a propitiatory, an oracle. As mirror it says: “Consider and see: [Col. 0747C] I have given you an example” (John 13:15). As bath it says: “Unless I wash you, you shall have no part with me” (ibid., 8); and, “Unless a man is regenerated from water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5). As provision for the journey it says: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven” (John 6:41); and, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (ibid., 54). As tent it says: “As often as you do these things, do them in remembrance of me” (Canon of the Mass); and, “How often would I have gathered your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you would not?” (Matt. 23:37). As shield it says: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John 10:11); and, “I go to be sacrificed [Col. 0747D] for you.”

Likewise, the Apostle says concerning the mirror: “Before whose eyes Christ has been set forth” (Gal. 3:1). And Moses: “Your life shall be hanging before your eyes” (Deut. 28:66). And the Psalmist: “My eyes are ever toward the Lord” (Ps. 14:15). Likewise Job concerning the bath: “The rock poured forth streams of oil” (Job 39:6). And the Bride: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Song 5:3). And: “Your teeth are like flocks of goats that have come up from the washing” (Song 4:2). Jacob says concerning provision for the journey: “If the Lord my God shall be with me on this way in which I walk and give me bread,” etc. (Gen. 28:20). Likewise the Psalmist concerning the tent: “Stretching out heaven [Col. 0748A] like a skin” (Ps. 103:2). And: “He stretched out his hand in repaying” (Ps. 54:21). And: “You stretched out your hand over the wrath of my enemies” (Ps. 137:7); and: “You stretched out my shoe over Idumea” (Ps. 59). Likewise concerning the shield, Jeremiah: “You gave them your labour as a shield” (Lam. 3:65); and: “Lord, you have crowned us as with a shield of good will” (Ps. 5:13).

## SERMON XXXVI. ON THE LORD’S SUPPER III

“It is better to be called to vegetables with charity than to the fatted calf with hatred” (Prov. 15:17).

Today the Bride of the Lamb, in the Mandatum, washes her feet; at the table she eats the flesh of the Lamb; at the altar she prepares chrism and oil. In the Mandatum feet are washed; at [Col. 0748B] the table Solomon’s dishes are set forth; at the altar both royal and priestly ointment is prepared for divine rites. Sins are cleansed in the Mandatum, merits are acquired at the feast, rewards are bestowed in the ointment.

Christ cleanses the filth of the daughters of Zion and washes away the blood of Jerusalem in the Mandatum, because in baptism he remits both venial and mortal sins. Then he calls from the Mandatum to the table, because the labourer is worthy of his food, the vinedresser of his denarius, and the hired worker of his reward; so that blessed is he who has eaten the labours of his hands in the kingdom of God. Those who are joyful and satisfied, however, Christ—now called from chrism—consecrates as his members into kings and priests, so that we may be [Col. 0748C] heirs indeed of God and fellow-heirs of Christ. Hence Peter says: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition” (1 Pet. 2:9). Yet concerning the washing of feet separately, the eating of the Lamb and of the bread that came down from heaven separately, and the preparation of chrism and oil individually, we wish to say a few things, setting aside the weariness of satiety.

First, then, something must be said about the Mandatum and briefly explained why such washing of feet is customarily called by everyone the Mandatum. John the Evangelist, who set forth for us the order of this Mandatum, also explained why it ought so to be called, when he says: “After he had washed their feet, he took his garments; and when he had reclined again, he said to them: Do you know what I have done to you? You call me Master and Lord, [Col. 0748D] and you say well, for so I am. Therefore, if I, Lord and Master, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, so you also should do” (John 13:12). Behold, it is clear why it is called the Mandatum: namely, because it is commanded to us both by word and by example. For this reason too the antiphon “A new commandment I give to you” is sung there, so that, according to that which is enacted in voice and deed, our conscience may be cleansed from dead works in order to serve the living God.

But, unfolding the matter itself, let us not handle the cleansing of this bath or washing with naked and empty speech [Col. 0749A], but apply it in deed and truth to our leprous soul and unclean body. Certainly, dearest brothers, this water is not like the rivers Abana and Pharpar of Damascus, which were never able to heal Naaman the leper. It is not like the water of Egypt, which was turned into blood because of Pharaoh’s hardened heart. It is not like the barren waters of Jericho, which before the coming of the true Elisha made that place hateful. It is not like the water of Marah, which the children of Israel could not drink.

Rather, it is the water of blessing; it is the water of Siloam, which goes with silence; it is water from the rock, which Moses opened in the wilderness by striking the stone twice, and gave drink to people and beasts. It is water over which the Spirit of the Lord is borne. It is the water of the Jordan in [Col. 0749B] which Christ is baptized by John. What more need be said? It is the water of baptism; it is water from Christ’s side. Good Jesus, was there no water with which you might wash our feet unless you caused it to flow from your sacred inward parts, from your side pierced by the lance? Good Jesus, what is there between us and you, that you should wash our feet, lay aside your garments, gird yourself with a linen cloth, bend down to the ground, and place that holy head—which angels desire to behold—beneath the feet of your disciples, indeed of your betrayer? Good Jesus, seated above the cherubim, you could by a word alone accomplish the cleansing of sins; but you would soften our stiff neck too little if, having bestowed it as though without labour or cost, you demanded in return a service of obedience.

Dearest brothers, let us not permit Jesus to lie prostrate long at [Col. 0749C] our feet; rather, quickly cleansed and consenting, let us raise him up with the reverence we owe him. What then? Do you not see Jesus seeking our feet, holding them, wetting them, washing them, rubbing them, wiping them, and anointing them? If you do not see him, at least hear him lying at your feet and saying: “I am, I am he who blots out iniquities, and I will remember your sins no more” (Isa. 43:25). Surely this voice is Christ’s voice. Do you not recognize his speech? Surely his manner of speech makes him known. To Mary Magdalene he says: “Your sins are forgiven” (Luke 7:48). To the woman caught in adultery he says: “Where are those who accused you? Has no one condemned you?” And she says: “No one, Lord.” “Neither,” he says, [Col. 0749D] “will I condemn you” (John 8:10). To the paralytic he says: “Son, your sins are forgiven” (Matt. 9:2). Brothers, today, if you hear this voice, do not harden your hearts. “I am,” he cries, “I am,” so that if you are not stirred by the first utterance, you may at least awaken at the second. I am Creator; I am Redeemer. If because I created you, you do not hear or acknowledge me, at least because I redeemed you, do not disdain to recognize me as Father; for the ox knew its owner and the ass its master’s manger, but Israel did not know me. “I am, I am,” he says, “he who blots out your iniquities” (Isa. 43:25). “Blot out, blot out my iniquity” (Ps. 4:3): will you do this? “Certainly,” he says, “I shall do it, and I shall refine your dross completely” (Isa. 1:25).

[Col. 0750A] There are certainly three kinds of cleansing: one is accomplished by washing, another by removal, the third by refining. Recent and lesser faults are washed away; older and harder ones are blotted out; stronger habits, otherwise unconquerable, are refined away. By water are washed the vices we contracted from the corruption of the guilt of the first parent, that is, the tinder of sin. By iron are blotted out the passions of sins which work in our members through the law. By fire are refined the most evil habits of abomination which have festered like scars and taken possession of us in the kingdom of death. All these are cleansed in this Mandatum if faith supplies the water, hope sets the basin beneath it, charity warms the water, and through the towel covers the multitude of sins. More would remain to be said of the Mandatum [Col. 0750B], were the supper not calling us.

But what shall I say about this supper, when astonishment seizes me as I consider what was done in it and contemplate what must be done in it? If the Queen of Sheba, when she saw all Solomon’s wisdom, the house he had built, the food of his table, the dwellings of his servants, the order of his attendants and their garments and cupbearers, and the holocausts which he offered in the house of the Lord, had no breath left in her: what am I, so small before such great things, tongue-tied before ineffable things, unlearned before eternal things, senseless before transcendent things, earthly before heavenly things, unclean in lips and whole body before the Holy of Holies, before things brighter than the sun, fairer than the moon, purer than the stars? Therefore let Paul’s tongue, in whom Christ speaks, speak to you concerning the Lord’s supper; let Isaiah’s tongue speak, whose lips the angel of the Lord cleansed by touching them with the tongs of the altar—not my tongue, which is unclean and entangled, since I have become of more impeded and slower speech from the time when I opened my mouth to treat of the things set upon the rich man’s table.

Speak, Paul; speak concerning the bread and cup of this table: what do they seem to you? “I,” he says, “received from the Lord what I also handed down to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night on which he was betrayed, took bread, and giving thanks broke it and said: ‘Take and eat; this is my body, which will be given up for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup after he had supped, saying: ‘This cup is the new covenant [Col. 0750D] in my blood,’” etc. (1 Cor. 2:23). What then, Paul, does it seem to you? For you are a good man. What, I ask, do you think of eating this bread and drinking this cup? Is it beneficial for every Christian always, everywhere, and in whatever manner to approach this table?

A manifold answer is owed to a manifold question. The food of the Lord’s table, called the Eucharist, is indeed useful and necessary for every Christian, but under a condition, in a place, at a time, and in a manner. The place is a consecrated church. The time is before every food or drink. Concerning the manner, there is a manifold subdivision. To manner belongs a fitting disposition of the soul, as in the Gospel the man who entered [Col. 0751A] without a wedding garment—that is, without love of God and neighbour—is cast out. To manner belongs the quality of the mind that approaches the Eucharist.

The condition is that one be regenerated into the freedom of the Spirit. Concerning place, Moses says: in one house, that is, in the unity of the Church. Concerning time: “Let a man first prove himself, and so eat of that bread and drink of that cup.” Whether he is penitent or impenitent; whether he has begun penitence or not; whether he approaches reverently or thrusts himself forward boldly, not discerning the body of the Lord; whether he believes that he receives the sacrament or the reality of the sacrament. To manner belongs that you approach chaste, devout, reverent, and contrite. To manner belongs that you truly believe that Christ’s true body and blood are upon the altar under the visible appearance [Col. 0751B], and that that appearance is not the body or blood of Christ which is invisibly there, but material bread and wine, which are not there substantially.

Examine, therefore, your conscience within yourself. If mortal sins either have not been in you or have been blotted out through confession and penitence, approach the supper of the Lamb, secure in mercy yet fearful because of conscience; and, made a lamb, eat the Lamb—not as a wolf, but as a lamb. For Judas devours the Lamb like a wolf, but burst open in the middle, darkness not comprehending the light but vanishing away. Peter eats the lamb, and, smearing both doorposts with its blood, drives the destroying angel away from himself. These things have been said concerning the supper, not for a full meal but as a foretaste of salutary food.

[Col. 0751C] It remains to speak of the anointing with chrism and oil. But kings, bishops, and priests are anointed with chrism. Therefore he who is anointed ought to rule his own land and his own people, so that he may command and not serve the desires of the flesh. Hence the Apostle: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. 6:12). By pontifical authority we must also anathematize whatever vices in us are not subject to the law of God. By priestly administration likewise we must test everything and hold fast that which is good, just as the priests in the Old Testament determined which persons were clean or unclean, which condition was leprosy and which was not.

But because this discernment of spirits is not given to all, nor that pontifical authority to tread upon [Col. 0751D] serpents and scorpions, nor that royal freedom of justice by which we should ever serve no one—namely, always remain free from every crime—the oil of the sick is consecrated, so that, stupefied by no infirmities of sins, we may be swallowed up by the peril of despair. For we must always hope in God’s mercy; we must always return to the oil. Jesus, Son of oil, give us sinners the oil of pardons; give the holy ones the chrism of virtues; give your feasters the Lamb of redemption; give absolution from sins to those who sit at your Mandatum—you who live and reign.

## SERMON XXXVII. ON THE LORD’S SUPPER IV

It is no wonder that he orders all things sweetly, who [Col. 0752A] in his conception descended like rain upon the fleece; who in his life without sin and his preaching without falsehood filled the vessels of mercy with the oil of grace; whose name is oil poured out; who in his passion, like a lamb, did not open his mouth; who in his resurrection sent foremost greetings to Peter his denier; and who in his ascension blessed all the apostles together. This Wisdom reaches mightily from end to end, because, like a giant rejoicing to run the course of his incarnation, he exulted, where it is said: “His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his course unto its height” (Ps. 18:7).

“O Lord, all things wait upon you,” etc. (Ps. 103:27). The Father, that Ancient of Days, awaits the holocaust and sacrifice of the body assumed by the Word, for the redemption of the human race, like the two [Col. 0752B] choicest kids of Rebekah—that is, of grace—prepared by Rebekah’s hands, as she knew the Father desired them. The angel waits to see the appeased face of Jesus, into which he desires to look; not at all begrudging the restoration of the prodigal son, but rather sustaining God’s counsel, he beholds the death of his King and Lord in hope of human salvation, and does not exact vengeance.

Thus they await that bread made from two tenths—that is, compounded of divine and human nature—brought through a three-day baking, that is, the cross, tomb, and hell; they await it for three days, namely from Adam’s sin—that is, before the law, under the law, and in the time of grace—until the Lord’s ascension. But that hungry man who could not fill his belly with the husks which the swine [Col. 0752C] ate, because vices destroy rather than restore nature, awaited the fatted calf: with its horns he might scatter enemies, with its hide shoe his feet, with its flesh satisfy hunger, with its fat and richness temper pains, with its blood redeem captivity, with its entrails procure inner cleansing, with its feet return to his homeland, and with its head raise contemplation into the interior of the veil. Therefore all things wait upon you, that you may give them food in due season.

What are “all things”? Is it the dragon? Is it the small animals with the great? Is it creeping things? Indeed, these also. For, to touch briefly upon the literal sense, God feeds every creature of his. But mystically, the devil too had confidence that Jordan would flow into his mouth, because he thought that Christ, whom he considered a mere man and wholly failed to know as God, would be held by everlasting death. From Jewish voracity the roaring lion rushed forward to devour him, when he associated Judas with himself, when he stirred up the scribes and Pharisees to envy, when among the cows of the peoples he sent forth the bellowing cry: “Crucify, crucify” (Luke 23:11).

O most savage beast! O crime of an all-too-extended belly! O hell! O devil! O death! What have you to do with our Lamb? If you had wisdom, you would not touch him. If you understood, you would refrain from him. His flesh is indeed most tender and most savoury if received worthily by the worthy; but it is bronze, fire, and stone if touched by unclean lips and a corrupt conscience, so that it shatters the molars of lions and brings upon presumptuous persons the judgment of death with a soul torn to pieces. Blindness indeed happened in part [Col. 0753A] to Israel, which did not know its Lord; but in you, devil, God placed darkness so that you might not know, and night came to be, that you might kill. O most voracious one, your poison does not overcome our antidote; rather, your rotten malice vanishes away if most powerful Wisdom unveils its rays.

Thus the monster devours Jonah, so that one greater than Jonah may draw forth with himself the riches of the saints which that most bloodstained infernal leech had enclosed, and may bring into paradise new food from the prey which Jesus, the firstborn of the dead and Prince of the kings of the earth, had taken in the hunt with bow and quiver. “All things wait upon thee,” etc. The air receives him hanging on the cross; the earth receives him laid in the tomb; hell trembles as he overturns all things and seeks his drachma [Col. 0753B] in the pit in which there is no water; heaven bends down its summit to him as he ascends, and receives him with rejoicing into the seat prepared from eternity. Thus he restores all things. “All things wait upon thee, that thou mayest give them their food in due season.”

Nothing in the faith of Christians is greater or better than this sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, to be commemorated with every veneration; today the universal Church celebrates and receives it with most earnest devotion. Therefore set apart and above all else a kitchen in which the food may be prepared; likewise set forth a most splendid table, where angelic ministries may not disdain to be present. Let the kitchen be the ordering of all our senses and actions, intent upon divine offices. Let the table be the contemplation of all affections [Col. 0753C] and desires lifted up toward God. Certainly one must sweat in the kitchen and eat from one’s labours at the table. For thus it is written: “In the sweat of thy face thou shalt eat thy bread” (Gen. III, 18). Yet bread has one kind of labour, and indeed other kinds in the field, the mill, the bakery, and the oven; meat and the other dishes have another kind and other kinds, namely in the kitchen.

Observe that, if a lamb is brought to the kitchen, it is skinned, and either boiled or roasted. If a bird, it is plucked; if a fish, it is gutted. Abel offered a lamb. Abraham a turtledove and a dove. The boy Tobias gutted a fish. But since attention directed to many things is less attentive to each individually, the Psalmist says not “foods” but “food”: “All things wait upon thee, O Lord.” For there is [Col. 0753D] one sacrifice, one food, one Lord, one faith, one bread, one body. Christ is the sacrifice; Christ the food; Christ the lamb; Christ the turtledove and dove; Christ the fish. He is a dove, conceived of the Holy Spirit; a turtledove, because he is the Church’s sole bridegroom; a Lamb, because he was innocently slain; a fish, because he was the first to rise and come up from the sea, and had in his mouth the two-drachma coin of the fourfold Gospel.

Where, my brethren, is the wood sufficient for cooking? Where is the water for washing? Where the spit for holding it up? Where are lips, teeth, palate, throat, and stomach for receiving it? Food so worthy requires worthy and clean receptacles: a worthy mind, worthy soul, worthy conscience. He does not dwell in a body subject to sins. Unless the rust of habitual sin has been removed [Col. 0754A] by confession and correction, he will not enter the kitchen. If he finds soft mud and the swamp of a defiled life, he withdraws his foot. If he encounters the thorn-bush or thorn of anger and hatred, then, just as when he tasted vinegar he would not drink it, so, leaving that kitchen, he turns his face from it and departs. If he sees beautiful leaves without fruit, he curses hypocrisy and pretence.

“I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense” (Cant. IV, 6). How pleasing myrrh and frankincense are to Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church, is shown both in his birth and in his death. For the Magi who brought gold also offered myrrh and frankincense to the child at his birth. But Joseph and Nicodemus, after the Lord’s body had been taken down from the cross, anointed it with myrrh and aloes. Coming [Col. 0754B] to us, therefore, and returning to the Father, the Bridegroom speaks of going to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense. “I will go,” he says, “to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense.” Truly, the world presented itself as a mountain of myrrh to the Lord, because he came into the world and his own received him not; rather, by words and deeds they heaped every bitterness upon him. What was not offered to him mingled with myrrh, when throughout the whole time of his dispensation, driving him from place to place, they gave him no lodging in which to remain? What could they add to myrrh’s bitterness when they crucified Jesus and, as he thirsted upon that same cross, offered him wine mingled with myrrh?

But you, Jesus, where do you go from the mountain of myrrh? Surely [Col. 0754C] to the hill of frankincense. “But I,” he says, “was praying” (Ps. CVIII, 4): “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke XXIII, 34). Thus Jesus ascends at once to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense, because he both suffers and prays for his persecutors. Indeed, the union of divinity with humanity would have been more than bitter enough, unless grace, going before, corrected its natural taste and the anointing of union softened every harshness arising from the flesh. It choked sin, indeed, but did not abolish punishment. Hence: “A cup of pure wine is in the hand of the Lord, full of mixture; and he hath poured from this into that, yet its dregs have not been emptied,” etc. (Ps. LXXIV, 8). And: “He himself bore our pains” (Isa. LIII, 4). Therefore, when the Word came to human nature, he came to the mountain of myrrh.

[Col. 0754D] Again, when he went up to Jerusalem to suffer, saying, “Behold, we go up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man shall be delivered to the chief priests,” etc. (Matt. XX, 18), he went up to the mountain of myrrh. There human and diabolical cruelty exerted itself to such a degree that it set no limits, but things proceeded according to its own judgment. For diabolical promptings, brought forth with the whole blast and force of malice from the secret abyss, inflated the hearts and mouths of the Jews even to bursting, and they poured out upon the Son of God things as shameful as they were cruel. Hence he says in the Psalm: “Thy wrath passed over me, and thy terrors troubled me” (Ps. LXXXVII, 17). Behold betrayal, sale, seizure, the raven’s kiss, scourging, buffeting, mockery, blasphemy, false accusation, receiving of spittle, [Col. 0755A] fastening to the cross, offering of vinegar, shaking of heads, and every devised invention of the worst men. They hold Jesus, besiege Jesus, press and possess Jesus as the footstool of their feet.

But you who came for this purpose to the mountain of myrrh, what are you doing? What do you accomplish? “I have gathered,” he says, “my myrrh with my spices” (Cant. V, 1). I gathered a most abundant harvest in my passion, because by it I redeemed the world and brought back to my palaces countless cultivators and imitators of my passion. Those who are of his portion follow him: namely, the holy martyrs and confessors. Visiting their solemn feast today, he speaks to himself, the Father, and the Holy Spirit, saying: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh,” [Col. 0755B] etc. For nothing is festive without Jesus; nothing memorable or excellent exists in all the assemblies of the saints without him. For as a body lies a headless trunk, so the Church, unless it cleaves to Christ, rejoices nowhere and never. Therefore, as shafts adhere to the stem in a lampstand, so the faithful of diverse ranks, offices, and orders are here by faith, there in reality, incorporated into Christ their head. Yet the saints have carried with them to heaven none of the myrrh-like bitterness which has passed away, but only the fragrance of sweetness, only the fruit of immortality.

Let each, then, seek the ascending ladder to the mountain of myrrh, because the stench and rottenness have already filled the bounds of the world; and the dove sent out from Noah’s ark, [Col. 0755C] finding no rest outside amid the besieging corruption, renounces going about the age, immediately seeks inward purity, and seeks to enter into the joy of its Lord. The solemnity of these persons, dearest brethren, is commemorated by us today; their merits and rewards are celebrated by the faithful. Let us not shrink from their myrrh-scented paths, because “the momentary and light burden of our tribulation works in us beyond measure an eternal weight of glory.”

Let us therefore take up the old and bloodstained breads of their martyrdom, and fit upon ourselves Joseph’s tunic dipped in a kid’s blood. “Christ,” says the Gospel, “had to suffer and thus enter into his glory” (Luke XXIV, 26); and the Apostle says: “Through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God” [Col. 0755D] (Acts XIV, 22). The way is indeed rocky and thorny, but by it the homeland is attained. Rest also is the more pleasant after labour; and the more weary you come to bed, the more indulgently you rest. Let us not regard present labour as a grave and great loss, because it will soon be relieved by the shortness of reaching the end. Hear the explorer of future happiness and contemplator of present punishment, how he counts present things as nothing while attending to eternal things: “For a thousand years in thy sight are as yesterday which is past” (Ps. LXXXIX, 4).

Nothing more powerfully uproots the root of a good mind from the earth than consideration of this laborious instability, and of the lot never to be changed which the sentence of the future judgment shall assign. The continuation of the two extremities—that is, of this present and the future life—is doubtful and incomparably dreadful. But the Mediator, who came to resolve the winding paths and ancient interruptions between God and man, and, with repentance intervening, to renew and perpetuate our actions against the evil one, shows in today’s Gospel by what privileges and what restorations to wholeness our forefathers recovered the unfading inheritance reserved in heaven, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,” etc. (Matt. V, 3). Therefore, avoiding the weariness of prolixity, we borrow from this, as briefly as we can, moral instruction . . . .

> [Note: Col. 0755D: Something is missing.]

[Col. 0756B] In the first horn of the Lamb, grace calls its sheep by name, writing our names in the book of life. In the second, it sends the disciples like lambs into the midst of wolves, that by their patience they may conquer hostile malice. In the third, they no longer wrestle against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers; they brandish the horn against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places. In the fourth, atonement for souls is made through Christ’s blood. In the fifth, the ploughs of the Gospel are drawn, furrowing the fields of hearers and sowing the Word of God. In the sixth, the priestly office, and in the seventh the royal office, is initiated and sanctified. Not inappropriately, the seven horns are also those seven paths of reward and blessedness: namely, poverty [Col. 0756C] of spirit, meekness, mourning, hunger and thirst for righteousness, mercy, purity of heart, and peace. The Lamb’s eyes are the cooperating gifts or promised rewards of these exercises: the kingdom of heaven, possession of the earth, consolation, satisfaction, recompense of mercy, the vision of God, and adoption as sons. These are also the teeth of which it is said: “Thy teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing” (Cant. IV, 2). For, having chewed the saints by suffering or mortification, he conveys them into the more secret parts of his stomach and makes them aware of his hidden things, because he hides them from the disturbance of men. O saints, O blessed ones, O chosen people of God to be numbered among his inmost parts, sprinkle your hungry ones with sacred exhalations and most pure emissions; for in that very measure the refluxes [Col. 0756D] of graces will be continued to you, nor will abundance fail where no avarice closes the veins of grace. Our Lazarus lies naked, beggarly, ulcerous, hungry before your doors, awaiting crumbs, expecting remnants from the fullness of the table, from the drippings of the most fruitful supper. Clothe the naked with righteousness, and do not despise your own flesh. In misery, bring aid to the beggar; apply medicine to the ulcerous; offer bread to the hungry and comfort concerning return to the exile. Your delights neither fail those who arrive nor overflow for those who depart. Your kingdom is dispensed with such regular moderation that, as nothing is diminished from predestination, so nothing is added to it. The number of your brethren [Col. 0757A] is not yet complete. Though, because our lot is uncertain, we do not presume upon kinship with them, we nevertheless humbly ask that you admit us as fellow-citizens. Therefore, lifting our eyes to your Father and our Father, we cry from our whole marrow: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water” (Luke XVI, 24), from the cisterns of Bethlehem or from the fountains of the Saviour, and cool this flame in which we are tormented. For, kindled by sufferings and temptations of the flesh, we are burned by diabolical bellows, and scarcely anyone hides himself from this conflagration. Thus, as though drawn out from the fire and as though the face of a burned pot, we Ethiopians, anticipating the hands of God, fall down before him, having hope from the Psalm in which it is truly said: “Behold foreigners, and Tyre, and the people of Ethiopia: these were there” (Ps. LXXXVI, 4), if among you there is no place for impatience or shame. Mary Magdalene, Matthew the tax collector, Paul the blasphemer, the thief on the cross—were they not at one time of this race? But this is the hope within our breast: that the mouth of the well of such great mercies and powers is not yet closed; it still swallows up many, and those whom it swallows it makes whiter than snow and joins to the mass of the whitened.

## SERMON XXXVIII. ON THE LORD’S SUPPER, V

“Son of man,” etc. (Ezek. III, 3.)

[Col. 0757C] The Lord’s table, rich and great, receives all, and, so far as it is concerned, refreshes all. For the Lord of the table cries out, saying: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI, 28). You who labour without satisfaction for earthly honours and riches, and are burdened after acquiring them: come to me, God, and to the teaching of God, and I will refresh you—not with that desirable bread of which Daniel says, “I ate no desirable bread” (Dan. X, 3), but with the living bread which came down from heaven. I will refresh you as I refreshed Elijah, lest you fail on the way. Beneath the sacramental rind, with Christ’s holy body hidden, I will refresh you on the way; with vision and revelation unveiled, I will perfect you in the homeland. For here we walk by faith in order to be refreshed; there, in order to be perfected, we shall see God face to face.

[Col. 0757D] Since the power and truth of the holy Eucharist lie hidden within, as though enclosed, both good and evil alike rush indiscriminately to this refreshment. At times the evil come more festively and more often than the good; but the good always, though more slowly, come with a fuller devotion than the evil. I behold and lament not only spiritual persons but also natural and carnal persons forcing themselves upon the Lord’s table. The spiritual person sits at the Lord’s table with the apostles, unlike them neither in faith nor in lot. Here he feeds; here he reclines at noon, possessing a state of rest beside the table of refreshment, saying with Peter: “Lord, it is good for me to be here” (Matt. XV, 4), so that thy left hand may be under my head, as I despise worldly gains as dung, and thy right hand—in which is the cup of blessing—may embrace me.

[Col. 0758A] What of the natural person? Like a dog, he barks around the table, saying: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” (John VI, 60). He receives the Lord’s body from the table but does not comprehend it. For the natural man does not comprehend the things of God. He would comprehend if he received it unto salvation; he would receive it unto salvation if he approached with faith and devotion. But he disputes how this can happen. For as many scruples as he raises for himself or resolves, so many and more things are in God’s sanctuary which shall not be understood except in the last things. The natural man is that elder brother in the field who does not enter to feast on the fatted calf which the father had killed for the returning prodigal. He disputes and murmurs that Christ’s body cannot come from bread, although the entire world could come to be from nothing: he is a dog.

[Col. 0758B] What of the carnal person? He is a fly—a dog-fly. What does a fly do at the table? It disturbs, defiles, and destroys the sweetness of the ointment. The frivolous, unstable, murmurers, and inquisitive are flies. If it should happen that a fly has entered the chalice and touched the Lord’s body in your hands, you grieve and are angry, greatly and as is fitting. Why then do you not correct yourself, lest you yourself be a fly? Examine your actions. If you murmur, in this you are a fly, because the fly itself murmurs. If you disturb others, you are a fly, because it disturbs. If you are unstable, you are a fly, because it never, or scarcely ever, stays in one place. If by your cunning you corrupt another’s simplicity, you are a fly, because what it touches it corrupts. Abraham drove away flies lest they defile the sacrifice he offered to God. Would that, just as there are now winged flies, there were not also persons who infest God’s table by unbelief or shameful conduct. The Apocalypse (XXII, 15) casts out dogs, saying: “Outside are dogs, sorcerers, the impure, murderers, idolaters, and everyone who loves and practises falsehood.”

[Col. 0758C] Having cast these out, let us return to the son of man, that is, to the spiritual man: “Son of man, thy belly shall eat, and thy inward parts shall be filled with this scroll which I give thee. And I ate it, and it became in my mouth sweet as honey” (Ezek. III, 3). As Solomon says: “One food is better than another” (Ecclus. XXXVI, 20). There is food for the appetite; there is food for the soul. There is food for the belly; there is food for the mind. There is corruptible food; there is incorruptible food. There is food which, tasted, brings death; there is [Col. 0758D] food which, eaten, confers life. In paradise the serpent urges the eating of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. In the great furnished upper room, after the flesh of the old lamb, Jesus gives the apostles the sacraments of his body and blood. Thus the Lord sets tree against tree, food against food: today, at supper, food; tomorrow, on the cross, a tree. In the food he is received; on the tree he is crucified. In the food refreshment is received; on the tree the price of redemption is paid. The food is called Eucharist; the tree, the holy cross.

A wonderful transformation occurs in the food, when the Lord’s body is made from bread and his blood from wine. A harsh suffering occurs when nails pierce the most tender and most chaste body of the Lord, and the soldier’s lance opens the side which contains the most precious treasure. O Lord, who [Col. 0759A] feedest me with what is thine and with thyself, what shall I repay except what is mine and myself? O Lord, who redeemest me not with gold and silver but with thy blood and body, what shall I render except flesh and soul? If I hang my entire self in the balance of the cross beside thy entire self, what reciprocity of repayment, what comparison is there between so little and so much? What is the most worthless little worm at the Lord’s table?

But the Lord has not only one table, but many. As many as are the diversities of moving and self-moving creatures, so many are the varieties of the Lord’s tables under heaven. For God feeds each thing in its kind and according to its kind. By his glorious and glorified majesty in heaven, he feeds the holy angels and the blessed souls of the righteous. On earth also he feeds good and evil alike—he “makes [Col. 0759B] his sun rise upon good and evil”—with material bread, as regards bodily refreshment; but with spiritual bread, only one sort, that is, the good. Of this refreshment, he who gives food to the young ravens speaks to the prophet: “Son of man, thy belly shall eat, thy inward parts shall be filled with this scroll which I give thee.” Of this scroll he says a little above: “And I saw, and behold, a hand sent to me, in which was a rolled-up book; and he spread it before me, written within and without; and lamentations and a song and woe were written in it. And he said to me: Son of man, eat whatever thou findest” (Ezek. II, 9).

The book sent by hand to the prophet is sacred and evangelical Scripture. Before the Lord’s passion it was, as it were, rolled up; at his supper it was unfolded, and on the cross, as on a table, laid out and expended. Today it is offered to us sacramentally, and tomorrow the body itself is offered to the Jews as capable of suffering. The four Evangelists stretch out and unfold this covering in their plain narrative, writing with what words he consecrated bread into his body and wine into his blood, and by what crucifiers he was hung upon the cross. The hand of God is the very work by which he wrought salvation in the midst of the earth: salvation of life in food, salvation of freedom in the price. If either were absent, it would not be a divine work. For if he refreshed but did not free the captive, he would certainly not wipe away tears after food. For what is satiety in a slave? Indeed, satiety stings the captive more: he grieves more over captivity than he rejoices in refreshment. Again, if he redeemed but did not feed [Col. 0759D] the redeemed, surely he would murmur in hunger, like Israel led out of Egypt in the wilderness. Therefore neither was lacking, where both bread from heaven and salvation from Jesus were present.

Yet lamentations and a song and woe were written in this book. Lamentations in the passion; song, that is, alleluia, in the resurrection; woe in the condemnation of the traitor. The women lamented; the angel sang a song in face and robe, saying to the women: “Do not fear. For I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here” (Mark XVI, 6). This song, this new canticle, is written in the Gospel. But where is the woe? Judas, moved by repentance, returned the money and went away and hanged himself with a noose. Woe to him: [Col. 0760A] “It would have been better for that man if he had not been born” (Matt. XXVI, 24). His inward parts were poured out. O Judas, where is the morsel which you had received from the Lord’s hand? As is read of the ungodly in Job: “God has drawn from thy belly the riches thou hadst devoured” (Job XX, 15). For your inward parts, into which Satan entered after the morsel, were unworthy and unable to retain the heavenly sacraments of the Lord’s body. But to the prophet it is said: “Thy inward parts shall be filled with this scroll which I give thee.”

The body of Christ, given to the apostles under the appearance of bread and to be consecrated on the altar until the end of the age, is a scroll, or a rolled-up book: for what it is does not appear, and what appears is not it. It is written within and without: outwardly is the visible sacrament; inwardly [Col. 0760B] are invisible power and truth. Read what is outward; believe what is inward. Lamentations are written so that the penitent may grieve; a song, so that the righteous may rejoice; woe, so that he who is in filth may become still more filthy, for he who receives unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself. But the inward parts of the person who has inward parts of compassion, chastity, and charity shall be filled. On such a couch Solomon rests.

Son of man, eat the Son of Man. This Son of Man is not slain and eaten. Rather, he is first eaten at supper and then crucified in the passion. The Eucharist is communion, not crucifixion. For the living do not commune with the dead, nor the dead with the living; rather, the living with the living and the dead with the dead: that is, “if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him.” If we have died with Christ, [Col. 0760C] we believe that we shall also live with him. Therefore, if we live Christ’s life, we rightly commune with him who, risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him (Rom. VI). The son of man communes rightly with the Son of Man if he communes with him in manner of life, in passion, and in resurrection: in manner of life wholly sober and holy; in passion most humble and most patient; in resurrection most beautiful and most steadfast. Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord has reigned; he has put on splendour; the Lord has put on strength and has girded himself with power” (Ps. XCII, 1).

“Son of man, thy belly shall eat”: this is contrary to ordinary usage, because to eat a rolled-up book or scroll is beyond the usual manner of eating. We are accustomed to read [Col. 0760D] scrolls, not eat them, and it is the mouth, not the belly, that eats. What then does “thy belly shall eat, and thy inward parts shall be filled with the scroll which I give thee” mean? Christ is received unto salvation with mind, not belly; with faith, not tooth; by works, not throat, for the book is written within. Yet, because it is also written without, we ought to wash both bodily and spiritually our hands, lips, teeth, and throat in the laver which [reading uncertain: *qui*, perhaps “which”] is at the door of the tabernacle, full of water. Jesus’ monument and tomb are clean; they are new. Christ receives every injury, but no uncleanness. If you object that they spat in his face and covered him: they defiled themselves by that spittle, not Jesus; for his flesh saw no corruption, neither in action nor in death.

[Col. 0761A] Therefore let the belly be clean, sparing in foods; let the table be pure, through abstinence from vices. Let the belly be restrained, not poured out; let it hunger for food, not serve luxury; let it dispense provisions to its servants, not inflame them excessively toward unlawful things. Such are the bellies of prophets; such are those of all saints. Hence it is said: “Thy belly shall eat, and thy inward parts shall be filled,” because they are not old wineskins which burst when new wine is put into them. Hence the Psalmist says: “Let my soul be filled as with fat and richness” (Ps. LXII, 6). It follows: “And I ate it, and it became in my mouth like sweet honey” (Ezek. III, 3). The Eucharist is sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth. The holy sacrifice, the pure sacrifice, the immaculate sacrifice, whenever received by me, makes me joyful, secure, and keener. I say to my Lord Jesus: “Though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evils, for thou art with me” (Ps. XXII, 4), through thy body and blood. Would that in this reception I might taste beforehand how sweet the Lord is in the kingdom, who is so sweet in exile—Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit, etc.

## SERMON XXXIX. ON THE LORD’S SUPPER, VI

“Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. LXXVII, 25).

It must be considered—and stated—what the bread of angels is, where it is, how it must be eaten, when and where, by whom and why; and it must be said what is the bread of angels which man eats. It shuns the lips of the deceitful, abhors an [Col. 0761C] erroneous and unclean understanding, but not a humble, quiet spirit that trembles at his words. Therefore, with a true heart, chaste body, holy hand, and purified tongue, we can both touch and eat that bread, who, made from two tenths, is God and man—from divine nature, namely, and human—conceived and born in a virgin of the Holy Spirit, and made mediator of God and men.

For that woman in the Gospel—that is, the wisdom of God itself, or the Virgin Mary—mixed leaven into three measures of meal: that is, by the bond of union she inseparably joined divinity, soul, and flesh. Wisdom did so by operation; the Virgin by conception.
