The baker of this bread is the Holy Spirit, who made the most pure bread, Jesus Christ, from the entire and undivided substance of the Trinity, as from the finest flour, and from the most pure and most holy blood of the Virgin, purified beyond cleansing—not by the sieve of human ingenuity or merit, but by the overshadowing coming of the Holy Spirit. He mixed and united it, formed it in the habit and shape of a human being, baked it, drew it from the oven with the seals of virginity intact, set it as the most delicate delight of the angelic table, and prepared it as the most efficacious medicine for human weakness.

When it is tasted, the angelic palate marvels and says: “Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. XXIII, 8). The human palate, greatly hungry, delights in its flavour and is filled with its power, healed of sickness, and incorporated through love; and thus man ate the bread of angels. But where is it? Either above, or below, or [Col. 0762A] beside you. If above, one must ascend; if below, descend; if beside but hidden, seek it out; if beside and visible, grasp and eat it.

It is at once above, below, and beside us, hidden and visible. It is above, because it is God most high; below, because it is man crucified; beside us, because, “Behold, I am with you unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20); hidden, because it does not appear on the altar in the visible form in which it sits at the Father’s right hand, but under the appearances of bread and wine. Visible, first, among men, because he often visibly appeared on the altar to some through miracles; and to all faithful people he is believed more certainly by faith than he is visibly seen with fleshly eyes. Because he is above and below—for he is the one who descended and ascended above all heavens [Col. 0762B] that he might fill all things—therefore it is said in the Gospel: “You shall see the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man” (John I, 51). Because he is beside us, the Apostle says: “The Word is near thee, in thy mouth and in thy heart” (Rom. X, 8). Because he is hidden, the Gospel likewise says: “From henceforth the Son of Man shall sit at the right hand of the Father” (Luke XXII, 69). Because he is visible, the Apostle says: “Have I not seen Jesus Christ with my own eyes?” (I Cor. IX, 1). This was certainly said after the Ascension, since previously he had lived among men and all flesh saw the salvation of God.

[Col. 0762C] He is in heaven, on the altar, and in the Christian’s heart: in heaven with his glorified body, seated at the Father’s right hand. On the altar, hidden beneath a veiled mystery and covered in most sacred wrappings: just as Joseph, taking down the same body from the cross, bound it with Nicodemus in linen cloths and spices. This signified the binding of the mystery in the linen cloths—that is, in the familiar and most pleasing appearances of bread and wine—with the spices of faith, hope, charity, and the other virtues; or with the fragrant and most fragrant virtues of Christ’s own most precious body, which are a most sweet savour to the Holy Trinity, to whom that sacrifice is offered, and to the angelic spirits, by whose diligent service it is daily borne within the veil—that is, into heaven. He is in the heart through faith working through love, through holy conduct, to which God gives righteousness in acceptance.

Behold, concerning Christ’s body: where it dwells, where it feeds, where it reclines. It dwells, certainly, in heaven, as the Psalm says: “Thou who dwellest in heaven, have mercy on us” (Ps. II, 22). [Col. 0762D] But it feeds on the altar, because it delights also in our holy desires; and he prepares for us on the way nourishment from himself, called viaticum, which will be fullness in the homeland, according to the words: “I shall be satisfied when thy glory appears” (Ps. XVI, 15). In the heart, indeed, it reclines at the noon of love, if it finds a couch soft, level, and clean—that is, if it finds you meek, righteous, and chaste. This concerning what the bread is and where it is. Next it must be said how it must be eaten; for, as it has a unique manner of being, so it has a special and unusual manner of being eaten. Hence the Apostle rebukes the Corinthians, who, using no discrimination, approached everywhere and indiscriminately to receive the Lord’s sacramental body, as though approaching any ordinary [Col. 0763A] food for bodily refreshment: “He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (I Cor. II, 28).

O natural man, descend for a little while from your asinine state and, ascending to the citadel of reason—since you are not yet able to ascend to the height of contemplation—compare with the Lord’s body whatever bodily thing or spiritual creature is accessible to your mind. With a just weighing in the balance of the sanctuary—that is, not by philosophical and worldly reason but by Catholic faith and most divine subtlety—consider what this is and what that is; how great this is and how great that; what sort this is and what sort that; what dignity this has and what dignity that; what usefulness this has and what usefulness that.

What, then, is this except the most precious gem which redeemed the whole world by its own [Col. 0763B] price, which, crushed by death, flashed forth and blinded the infernal eyes, so that in darkness it might be light and the darkness might not comprehend it—or rather, so that they might be blinded by its brightness and darkened by its light? What is this except an antidote against and above all poisons, which even raises the dead? What is this except that body which before the resurrection was made a little lower than angels because it was passible and mortal, but is now raised above every heavenly height and crowned in place, dignity, majesty, glory, and honour? What is all that other thing which is subject to vanity, always tends toward non-being, and swiftly passes away and is not?

But how great or what sort it is, only the heavenly city knows: it is filled by its greatness and [Col. 0763C] illuminated by its beauty. In dignity it is joined to God; in usefulness the number of angels is restored and the salvation of the predestined is completed. Yet every creature, if you consider its quantity in relation to God, is accounted as a small weight in the balance; if its form, as deformed; if its dignity, as worthless as a menstruous cloth; if its usefulness, as of no value, because God is not enriched by his creature, but the creature is made blessed by God. Therefore distinguish this angelic bread, O man, not only from bodily foods but from all created things: honouring, worshipping, loving, adoring, believing, and eating it above all.

This is the manner of eating: that, being chaste, you receive the chaste; being a Christian, [Col. 0763D] Christ’s body; being holy, the holy; being good, the merciful; being upright, the righteous; being devout, the crucified; being earthly, the heavenly. And this concerning the manner of eating.

When should it be eaten? In tribulation, that it may be eased; in need, that it may be driven away; in illness, that it may be relieved; in health, that it may be preserved; in prosperity, that it may be moderated; in adversity, that it may be strengthened; in death, that the soul may be directed to God; in the morning, that it may be with you throughout the day and labour with you; at the third hour, that you may retain in your heart the Jews’ cry, “Away, away, crucify him” (John XIX, 15), and that in this compunction the grace of the Holy Spirit may fill your soul; at the sixth hour, that you may crucify yourself with Christ; at the ninth hour, that you may receive the spirit sent forth from the head and worthily place it in your own [Col. 0764A] spirit. Receive Christ’s body also fasting, before every heaviness of food and drink, so that by occupying your lodging beforehand he may have the first reclining places, first seats, and first greetings; and, while he reclines there, no handmaid among your thoughts may cause disturbance, no servile movement, disorderly stirring up the enticements of the flesh, may break forth. Rather, let all things keep the midst of silence while the mouth is silent, the tongue cleaves to the throat, and all inward parts sit at Jesus’ feet, meditating only upon saving things and concerned for salvation.

There are also certain appointed times when, I think, one ought not to abstain, unless there is a reasonable cause—for example, a sentence of excommunication or consciousness of a mortal sin. After confession of sins has first been made and the seven penitential psalms recited, if possible one should receive the Lord’s body. Hence the Psalmist: “Sing to our Lord with confession; make melody to our God upon the harp, who gives their food to the beasts and to the young ravens that call upon him” (Ps. 146:7, 9). For it expels superfluities and whatever the holiness of this most holy body abhors—a body which nowhere saw corruption: neither with the Father before the ages, nor in the Mother when born at the end of the ages; neither in the tomb when it rose after the third day, nor when it lodges with a Christian soul through this most sacred mystery.

For the body and soul, purified through holy confession, raised to him through heavenly desire, enlarged through charity, and moved by compassion for one’s neighbor, are that great furnished upper room where the apostles are commanded to prepare the Passover. The Apostle teaches the same order, saying: “Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened,” etc. (1 Cor. 5:7). In brief, concerning the time of reception, the Psalmist says: “The eyes of all hope in you, Lord, and you give them their food in due season” (Ps. 144:15). For fitting time is determined by the rule of devotion, faith, ordinance, and necessity. Thus far concerning when.

But where, if not in a holy place, in the temple of God, in the Catholic Church? Thus too no one carried the flesh of the lamb outside that house whose two doorposts had been stained with the blood of that same lamb. He places blood upon both doorposts who believes Christ’s passion in his heart unto righteousness, and confesses it with his mouth unto salvation.

We must now say by whom the bread of angels ought to be eaten. The Apostle shows this, saying: “Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup” (1 Cor. 11:28). This distinguishing mark of wisdom is proper to the saints whose deeds Scripture celebrates: before acting, they always diligently sought, by every kind of examination, to weigh carefully the outcome of the act. Abraham first counted his three hundred trained household servants; then he defeated five kings and freed his nephew Lot. Gideon likewise, at the Lord’s command, selected three hundred for battle against Midian—those who had lapped water thrown up to their mouths by the hand. Moses too, the lawgiver, commands that when the children of Israel are about to go to war, before the battle begins the priests and leaders should by public proclamation determine who is fit for war, and who is timid or less suited to battle. Among such persons are the man who built a new house and has not dedicated it; who planted a vineyard and has not yet made it common; who has betrothed a wife and has not taken her; and who is fearful and fainthearted. Once all these have returned, each commander shall then prepare his ranks.

It would be too long and difficult to recount how carefully the other fifty warriors of God also made it their concern always to test those whom they chose for whatever offices. Thus the Lord commands Moses to choose seventy elders whom he himself knows to be elders. For if those who are to perform appointed duties in these temporal matters are tested with such care—though neither victory produces eternal praise nor merit true salvation, unless perhaps some intend to render service to God, not in that they conquer enemies and kill men, but because they avenge God’s wrong and fight under divine commands—how much more must everything be tested where negligence entails everlasting danger and diligence everlasting remedy. Let a man therefore examine himself as one about to enter a great battle: not against flesh and blood, that is, a mortal human being, but concerning the flesh and blood of the Lord, where war is undertaken against God if they are received unworthily.

Let him therefore be one of Abraham’s trained household servants—that is, formed in the character of the Catholic Church; let him be unencumbered by every hindrance of flesh and spirit; let him be among the three hundred who, after Christ, bear their cross in faith in the holy Trinity. Let him pursue and seize the five kings, so that he may bring back and subject his five senses, from the liberty of righteousness, to Christ’s service. Let him rescue Lot, Abraham’s nephew—that is, let him recover through diligence some virtue lost through negligence. Then let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup, because Melchizedek offered bread and wine to Abraham returning from that slaughter.

[Col. 0765D] Against Midian, which means “contradiction”—that is, against the devil or the impulses of the flesh—take those three hundred who lapped water as dogs are accustomed to lap, throwing it up to the mouth with the hand. That is, take those who do not live according to the flesh and do not fulfil its desires, but, sustained by the most sparing and slender support of food, like dogs pursuing prey, refreshed only somehow, pursue the promised glory as though it were fleeing. Let these also eat of that bread and drink of that cup, because they do not wish to drink from Babylon’s cup—that is, from the pleasure of the flesh.

In the newly built but undedicated house are those who choose a good purpose for themselves but have not yet brought it into effect; in the planted vineyard not yet made common are the beginnings of devotion through holy desire, not yet formed and brought forth through practice; in the betrothed but not yet taken wife are the vow to change one’s secular habit and the promise to embrace a new life—for so long as it is deferred, the betrothed wife is not taken. In the fearful and fainthearted person are those who fear where there is no fear, who are so alarmed at a leaf on a tree as if at a serpent’s bite, and who do not approach any vow of holy religion.

When all these have been rejected as unfit, let those remaining examine themselves, preparing their ranks against the camps of vices; and, battling manfully against all assaults that wage war against the soul, let them eat of that bread and drink of that cup. Thus far concerning by whom the bread of angels ought to be eaten.

[Col. 0766B] It remains to ask: why? Why, unless that we may have life, and have it more abundantly; unless that we may have the Lord with us; unless that he may be in us for present justification and future glorification? May that living and true bread itself deign to grant this to us: he who came down from heaven and gives life to the world, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

## Sermon XL. On the Lord’s Supper VII

“Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77:25).

To the one to whom the table and dishes of angels are granted, the offices and ministries of those who serve in the heavenly court are likewise commanded. Therefore, before a priest approaches the Mass or the table of God’s ministers, let him purify and make peaceful his mind with angels unstained in any respect, so that there may be one service for those whose banquet is not different.

But since the children of men, born and nourished with heavy hearts in an earthly and dark prison, do not rise to divine and invisible things unless through human and visible things they ascend to him “who dwells in darkness” and “makes the cloud his ascent,” let the footstool and Jacob’s ladder be sought, so that “the left hand may be under the head and the right may embrace” the one ascending. Whoever attempts to creep up from worldly words and things to invisible things is helped by their use and familiarity; and, like a reptile upon the ground—that is, like a lizard—he strives with his hands to dwell in kings’ houses. Yet although angelic nature has no need of this food-bread, it is said, in human fashion, to possess and eat bread in the kingdom of heaven.

Nor should one suppose that heaven contains any support required by fragile nature. So too in paradise, where man was placed, made “a living soul,” he was to take bodily food for the support and refreshment of his body, not yet absolutely immortal; for as he sinned by eating what was forbidden, so he would have sinned if he had not eaten what was commanded there: “From every tree of paradise eat; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat.” Hence Augustine, on Genesis: “Adam’s flesh before sin was created so immortal that, aided by nourishment, it would be free from pain and death.”

The spiritual and angelic creature is eternally nourished by the blessed vision of its Creator alone, so that it is refreshed by no external provision. For the angels who are read to have eaten when appearing to Abraham, Lot, and many others did this not by natural suffering or need, but out of compassion; and when they did such things, they displayed not spirit but an assumed body. Therefore, when you hear, “Man ate the bread of angels,” seek what bread you should understand: surely spiritual, not bodily; heavenly, not earthly; living, not dead; nourishing the mind, not the belly; not failing when it refreshes.

[Col. 0767B] The bread taken from the heavenly table is made by an exceedingly good baker: none is whiter, cleaner, warmer, fresher, healthier, more savory, or holier; it is fit for the worthy lips of the Bride to chew, able to satisfy and heal. “Lord, always give us this bread”: daily bread; supersubstantial bread; bread that comes down from heaven and gives life to this world; bread from the frying-pan, bread from the griddle, bread from the oven, bread of fine flour, kneaded bread, bread anointed with the oil of gladness above its companions; sealed bread, which the Father sealed and sent into the world.

Behold, Lord Jesus, your little ones whom the Father gave you, your children whom you purchased with your blood, ask for bread, and there is none to break it for them. Your goodness and grace will be equal whether you give it or break it. For what is giving without breaking, except to provoke someone’s hunger by displaying bread, and vainly to inflame childish desires more keenly by offering and withdrawing breasts? For if, as the Apostle says, “if he were on earth, he would not even be a priest, since there are those who offer gifts according to the law”—that is to say: even if bread, that is, a sacrifice for sins, were presented upon the table, that is, in the world, if there were no one on earth to break it, that is, unless Christ, being priest, offered himself to God the Father, no one of Adam’s entire race would celebrate our reconciliation, nor would any little child eat bread, even though there were many who offered, according to the law, the gifts Moses established—not for redemption, but for a shadowing forth.

The bread, therefore, is Christ’s body. Once upon the cross it was, as it were, broken by himself, when he who had power to lay down his life and power to take it again, bowing his head, gave up the spirit. Daily, too, he mystically breaks himself upon the altar, renewing faith in our hearts and imparting to our souls the efficacy of his passion, just as at supper he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his apostles, saying: “Take and eat: this is my body.”

Now you too, priests made partakers of Christ, receive, bless, break, and distribute to the people, together with Christ, the bread which is Christ’s body. But you do this by a ministry granted to you; he does it by authority innate to himself. For he himself both baptizes and sanctifies the Eucharist. He blesses through your blessings and curses through your curses. For “in him all nations of the earth shall be blessed.” O priest, you who put your hand into the dish, beware lest, through avarice, your hand become the leprous hand of Judas the betrayer, knowing that no fornicator, unclean person, or covetous person has inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God.

God says to the angels concerning an unworthy minister: “See lest perhaps he take from the tree of life”—that is, from Christ’s body, which is the tree of life—“and take eternal life,” he who in my sight defiled his father’s bed and, wallowing in his own filth, rotted away. For he who eats and drinks the Lord’s cup unworthily takes death from life rather than life, since he is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. Therefore, lest you perish with Dathan and Abiram, with Nadab and Abihu, wash your hands among the innocent—not with Pilate. For one washes hands with Pilate who knows yet does not abandon the sin by which he is weighed down; one washes with the innocent who has no grave sin, or…

But that the flesh of the bread of angels may be chewed by a person with toothed faith, have ivory teeth—that is, senses trained according to the chastity of Catholic teaching and angelic truth. Preach upon the housetops, first concerning the institution of this sacrament: that the Lord, after the typical lamb, handed it down to his apostles at supper, so that by wondrous love he might place for his faithful, beneath mystical forms upon the altar until the end of the age, that same body which he would raise glorified above the stars.

Second, concerning its form: in wheaten bread, with wine and water mixed in the chalice, when a Catholic priest, with the intention and order of consecration, pronounces these words of Christ: “This is my body,” etc. For by these words bread becomes Christ’s body, and wine with water becomes his blood. Everything else done and said before or afterward consists of Christ’s praises and prayers.

Third, concerning the sacrament and the reality: of these, one—the sacrament—is properly called the visible species of bread and wine, as has already been said; while the reality is either the contained and signified thing, Christ’s flesh, or the signified but not contained thing, such as the unity of the Church in those predestined, called, and justified.

Fourth, concerning the twofold mode of eating: the sacramental mode, by which both good and evil truly eat Christ’s body, but the good unto salvation and the evil unto condemnation; and the spiritual mode, by which only the good eat—namely, to believe in God and to abide in God through holiness of life and unity of faith.

Fifth, concerning the conversion of the substance of bread and wine into the substance of Christ’s body and blood: although after consecration you may see bread and wine, nevertheless believe with certainty—indeed, with the greatest certainty—that there is neither bread nor wine there, except perhaps the bread of angels, of which it is said that man ate the bread of angels. Sixth, concerning the breaking, which is mystical in the form of bread and is to be believed more by faith than debated in words. Seventh, concerning the daily immolation: whether Christ is immolated substantially or in mystery. Christ was immolated once by the death of his passion; daily he is immolated by memorial and recollection of that same immolation.

Eighth, concerning the twofold cause of its institution: because it grants an increase of virtue and medicine for daily infirmity. Ninth, concerning who and when ought to receive the Eucharist: one who is not in more serious sins or in an intention to sin, at least three times a year, and better every Sunday or daily. Tenth, concerning a sinful or heretical priest: whether they consecrate Christ’s body. However sinful a priest may be, so long as he is within the Church he consecrates the sacraments by office, not by life; because the effect comes not from the merit of the consecrator, but from the word of the Creator, and nothing greater is received from a good man, nothing less from an evil man. [Note: [Col. 0769] An old error, refuted from St Augustine by St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, III, q. 82, art. 7, and by Estius, *In IV Sententiarum*, dist. 13, §3.]

A heretic, because he is outside the Church, does not consecrate. Let these things suffice concerning the true faith in the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood; for it is not good to eat much honey, lest, when filled, you vomit it. Therefore, with sound faith, whole mind, holy flesh, pure conscience, and devout soul, approach the bread of angels; be enlightened, and your faces shall not be put to shame. May he deign to grant this to you, etc.

## Sermon XLI. On the Lord’s Supper VIII

“The fathers ate a sour grape, and the teeth of the children are set on edge” (Ezek. 18:2).

Death arising from disobedience was bitter in Adam and Eve, and more bitter in the transgression of the Mosaic law: there the sinner was overwhelmed with stones and received no mercy whatever. But Christ’s death was most shameful, and all the more exceedingly bitter because he lived wholly without original or actual sin, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of an incorrupt Virgin. But why and whence was this? Because the fathers Adam and Eve ate a sour grape.

All the trees of paradise, concerning which it is said, “From every tree of paradise eat” (Gen. 2:16), were undoubtedly, by that permission, ripe and sweet rather than sour. Only the forbidden tree was sour—not by the nature of its creation, but by the disobedience of transgression. Absolutely speaking, every creature of God is good; yet it becomes evil and bitter to the one who eats through stumbling, whether it be flesh, fish, bread, grapes, or any food. Disobedience has a sharper acidity. Therefore the transgressors of the law, crucifying Christ, offered him vinegar on the cross: they had been transformed from the wine of the holy root into the bitterness of vinegar and an alien vine.

Christ, in no respect degenerating from the Father, made, from the water of mortal nature, wine of sweetest grace and eternal immortality; obedient to the Father unto death on the cross, where, breathing as it were like new wine through his prayer and patience, he intoxicated even those who trod him, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do” (Luke 23:34). But the Jews, intoxicated by their malice and shaking their heads, said: “If you are the Son of God, save yourself.” O Jews, why do you eat the sour grape so that the teeth of your children are set on edge, saying, “His blood be upon us and upon our children”? The grape is in some way sour—not in itself or of itself, but in your teeth; he says concerning himself: “If they do these things in the green wood, what shall be done in the dry?”  

Saving the faith that the Son is equal with the Father, I say that Jesus was like a sour grape—that is, unripe—while in the world he bore our defects in his body, while alive and capable of dying, as he himself says: “I have power to lay down my life and power to take it again” (John 10:18). But he was a ripe and most sweet grape when, death swallowed up, he put on the glory of immortality and retained no remnant of mortal sufferings. For, as the Apostle says, “Christ, rising from the dead, now dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9). Peter, when the other apostles fled, ate this grape as sour by denying him. Hence one of the disciples said: “We had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21). The teeth are set on edge in those who say, “We had hoped.” But who are the children of the apostles whose teeth are set on edge? Surely the holy martyrs who gave up their bodies to sufferings for Christ’s sake. In another and different way from the unbelieving Jews, the teeth of the martyrs are set on edge in wonder and imitation of Christ’s patience and goodness; those of the Jews, under Vespasian and Titus, by exile and by bearing the imprecation of their fathers’ sin, as Cain bore the mark concerning which he himself said: “Whoever finds me will kill me” (Gen. 4:14).

But let us see how the children’s teeth are set on edge because the first parents ate a sour grape: our teeth are set on edge by sin and the punishment of sin—by original sin and actual sin; by present and future punishment; by temporal and eternal punishment. Therefore, that the teeth might be healed and restored for receiving food, Jesus supped with his disciples; and lest the flesh of the legal lamb should again make the teeth sore, he set before them bread and wine and transubstantiated them into his body and blood. At this supper he both provided for our weakness by showing a visible sacrament, and instructed faith by deifying the power beneath these species of bread and wine. Much is missing.

## Sermon XLII. On the Resurrection of the Lord

“Your God shall reign, O Zion” (Ps. 145:10).

New king, new law. This king, dearest brothers, is as new in the kingdom of men as he is everlasting in the kingdom of angels. For from eternity, through wisdom, he created that angelic kingdom, in which he is adored by them as God, feared as Lord, worshipped as Father, acknowledged as Creator, and venerated as King.

But Lucifer, who had driven a third part with himself from heaven, had from the beginning revolted from the fellowship of the fellow-soldiers of this kingdom, and had established his camp in this dark air, until in the last days he should flow down into lowest Tartarus and inherit deserved punishments.

But that wise and mighty king, intending to repair the loss to his kingdom and the number of his army, substituted the human race for the flock of angels: weaker indeed because of the weight of flesh, yet not inferior in the image and likeness in which he had created it. Yet so swift was the plundering and overthrow of that new colonist of paradise, who, as a recruit, was meanwhile to complete his period of training in that gymnasium, until fully equipped with arms he should join that same angelic army, likewise united to his king by purity and charity. So suddenly, I say, did this recruit fall, that he withered before flowering, miscarried before birth, and perished before his time. For through the coagulum of a corrupted root, the whole dense growth of branches was badly fermented; whatever that whole forest of the human race, from the tree of Adam and Eve, put forth through the generation of children, it sprinkled with fuller sourness. Those who, to the original insipidity coming from original sin, daily added the poisons of asps upon the sponge of evil desires, with accumulated interest through actual sins, never diminished the evil taste.

At last divine Wisdom, narrowing the bounds of its patience—which had borne such loss with equanimity through worldly ages—girded its loins with strength and strengthened its arm, lighting a lamp to seek the drachma it had lost. Penetrating the borders of the enemy’s camp both in his birth and in his death, it snatched the prey from the hand and mouth of the plunderer, binding the plunderer with fiery chains and strangling him in the noose of his ancient deceit, when it set before him, on the hook of divinity, the desirable bait of its flesh and by holy deceit deceived the craft of malice. Thus, having subdued the tyrant, it flew to the nest in which father Adam and mother Eve, with certain of their young, were brooding; and from the infernal nest it carried away the souls of all the faithful like a barnyard cock.

And lest the one who had carried them off should drive them away again, and by his foul heat suffocate them excessively rather than cherish them, he bound the tyrant’s arm with that cloth with which the Jews had veiled Christ’s eyes; and, opening a vein of that arm with the lancet of Divinity, he drew out all the blood of holy souls. Then, bringing a scorching wind from the virginal desert in accordance with prophecy, he dried up the tyrant’s veins. O power of God! O powerlessness of the devil! For now the devil’s arm is broken and has withered. In his supposed kingdom—that is, in the world—he engaged our king. He indeed prevailed to bind, hold, and crucify him, yet not by hostile power but by God’s patience, for he had power to lay down his life and to take it again.

Our king then concealed and husbanded his strength, for a wise man reserves for the future. The cruel tyrant raged and begged strength from every side, striving with all his power to undermine our wall and intent on removing the memory of our king from the midst. He therefore did everything he could, and attempted certain things he could not do but wished to do. At last he failed and fled to his infernal hiding-place. And you, our king—what will you do? Lord, who shall judge righteousness, will you not all the more condemn injustice? Tread hot-foot upon his tracks; seize the tail of the ancient serpent, who twists as usual and flees from your face. He still conceals with himself the bond of the decree that was against us; and perhaps, if it remains with him, he will at some time raise an accusation and, as though you had not paid with interest the debt discharged for us, present the written bond as security against you.

Therefore examine his writings and chests in the light of your countenance and with outstretched arm; disembowel that fish, so that from its heart, as from a most remote storehouse, you may bring forth those stale counsels by which he never ceases to deceive the inhabitants of the earth. Thus two things are necessary for you: one, that you unlock what is shut; the other, that you penetrate and overthrow what is fortified. For the infernal city is shut and fortified: shut, because no footsteps return from it; fortified, because unquenchable fire and intolerable water surround it. Shut, because it admits no comforter; fortified, because it mocks an assailant. Shut against good, fortified in evil. Shut by the bolts of obstinacy; shut because of those who concealed their sins; fortified because of those who never repented. What then must you bring to what is shut but a key, and to what is fortified but a club? A club strikes; a key opens. Make of the cross a club; make of the club a key. The four-sided club or cross overthrows the four infernal corners; the key or nail, reaching to the division of soul and spirit, untangles and resolves the inextricable labyrinth.

The power of God and the wisdom of God are understood in the club and key, as the Apostle teaches: “The word of the cross,” he says, “is foolishness to those who perish, but to us it is the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:18). Jesus therefore, strengthened by God’s power and God’s wisdom, burst into the shut city and overthrew the fortified one, because he broke the iron bars and made a way in the deep sea for the liberated to pass through. He said to those in darkness, “Be revealed”—this belongs to the key; he said, “Come out”—this belongs to the club. The club killed the lion; the key loosed the chains of the fettered. O Zion, your God shall reign! Behold, the mouth of those speaking wickedness has been stopped: “Do not write, ‘King of the Jews,’” they say, “but that he said, ‘I am King of the Jews’” (John 19:21); and, “We have no king but Caesar” (ibid., 15).

But he who had come into a far country to receive a kingdom for himself and return destroyed the kingdom of death, and transferred us from the kingdom of death to the kingdom of his brightness—us who were by nature children of wrath, alien children, children of darkness. He joined the kingdom of the world to the heavenly kingdom and fastened it at the earth’s center, at the crossroads of heaven and earth—that is, at the cross. There angels stand as heavenly soldiers, watching their king’s contest; and humans, like dogs, lap the blood running upon the ground, that by this drink they may be redeemed and intoxicated. Soldiers love their dogs—or rather, the dogs of their lord, their king—because whoever loves me loves my dog also. The king is strengthened by soldiers, but greatly consoled by dogs. He is delighted by the running of dogs, cheered by their applause, pleased by hunting deer and hares, and takes manifold pleasure in these things.

[Col. 0773B] O Zion, behold your king has come to a great, broad, dense forest of Gehenna to take small beasts with dogs and soldiers. There he caught the fat stags of the patriarchs, the roebucks of the prophets, the hares of the Innocents, and the fallow deer of the hermits, and brought them to his Father and homeland. Therefore let us feast, because the hunting is abundant; and the more laborious it was because of the passion, the less costly it is because of the resurrection. For the Father marvels far more at its swiftness than he grieves over his Son’s labor. “How,” he says, “were you able to find it so quickly, my son?” (Gen. 27:20). As though he said: It does not concern me at what cost you bought it, or how much labor you underwent, because it is most pleasing and acceptable that you found so great and such a catch so quickly. In a single day and night you enclosed in your net all animals clean and desirable to my taste, which the fields and valleys in the world brought forth [variant: “were brought forth”], and which the infernal forests had hidden from the age as though in their caves and pits.

Therefore give me of your hunting, my son. Do not grieve over the labor, because the fruit exceeds the labor and the thing acquired immeasurably exceeds its price. You gave one soul, but how many did you receive? You poured out drops of blood, but what an outpouring of bodies and blood of martyrs did you receive? Not to mention the rest: “They poured out the blood of your servants like water around Jerusalem” (Ps. 78:3). Certainly, for every one of your drops, a thousand thousands have been returned to you from ours.

Yet not even thus can we repay them, because we lack in value what we have in abundance in number. What I say of blood, I affirm of your whole passion: for though the sufferings of the martyrs now almost exceed number, in merit and singular value they nevertheless fall beneath your passion. In you, therefore, value must be reckoned above all number; in us it must be considered that, by as much as we fall short in value, by so much we may increase in number. Yet both number and value we ascribe to you, who redeemed us by your blood and granted that we might receive your faith, Christ Jesus, Savior of the world, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages.

## Sermon XLIII. On the Resurrection of the Lord II

[Col. 0774A]

“Your God shall reign, O Zion” (Isa. 52:7).

From the prophet—or rather, from the Holy Spirit—we have borrowed this golden vial full of balsam, so that in this Paschal solemnity we may provide you through it with a saving drink. For the outward form of this little vessel corresponds well and fully to the most pleasant flavor hidden within. Those rounded hands of the craftsman’s son, with the compass of the Holy Spirit, fashioned this vial as fittingly as sufficiently both for our drink and for its solemnity. For our drink, because to hear and understand that the Lord reigns is enough for intoxication; for the solemnity, because the whole Paschal feast and joy arises from this, that the Lord reigns.

But now, after this preliminary commendation in philosophical words, let us set the beautiful and precious vial, under this figure, eagerly to our lips; and let us faithfully drink the spirit that is in the inward parts of so joyful a solemnity. For behold, we have now waited three days, and in the cup which the Father gave the Son we have drunk nothing but myrrhed wine, nothing but gall and vinegar, nothing but a bitter drink. Enough then—indeed, more than enough—of carrying and drinking such bitter cups with such long endurance. Now, approaching the wine-cellar, we ask with the risen Lord for new wine in new wineskins, so that we may no longer reap thorns and thistles from our oldness, but may receive from the newness of our redemption the pledge of the Spirit.

We belong, indeed, to Zion, to whom it is said: “Zion, your God shall reign.” O poor Zion, tossed by the storm, without consolation, having no one among all her beloved to comfort her: behold, help comes to you from heaven; behold, the voice of your watchmen: together they have lifted up their voice, because they shall see eye to eye. What will they see? What will they cry? “Zion, your God shall reign.” But who are these watchmen? Surely, the angels. They announce the Lord’s resurrection; they say, “Zion, your God shall reign.” Behold, what had been said before the passion has been fulfilled: “Now shall the prince of this world be cast out.” Behold, the stronger one, arriving, has bound the strong man in his own house and overcome him. Behold, he has drawn out Leviathan with a hook and bound him for his maidservants. Hence the Apostle to the Colossians: “When you were dead in sins and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, he made you alive together with him, forgiving you all sins; blotting out the handwriting of the decree that was against us, which was contrary to us, he took it out of the way, fastening it to the cross; stripping principalities and powers, he made a public display of them confidently, triumphing over them in himself” (Col. 2:13).

In his customary manner, the Apostle shows why and how our God reigns. Before we unpack the apostolic words, full of profound mysteries, it should be noted what reigning is. To reign is to govern a kingdom; to govern is to act rightly. To reign also is to have subjects who obey.

It must also be considered who the king is; what the kingdom is; who belong to the kingdom; what its insignia are; when the kingdom began; how long it shall last; and how far the kingdom’s borders extend. This kingdom began at the time of the resurrection; it will endure for ever and beyond. Its boundaries reach from east to west and from north to south. The king is Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews. The kingdom is the Church: partly already dwelling in the heavenly homeland, holding as it were the towers and municipalities of the city; partly cultivating the countryside in the field of this world, sowing its seed morning and evening and gathering until the year of jubilee, the year of remission, the year in which neither ploughing nor reaping can occur. Those belonging to the kingdom are marked on their foreheads with the sign of the cross, reborn from water and Spirit, given to drink from the cup of blessing, and fed with the bread of the Lord’s body: a holy nation, children of promise, a people of acquisition. The insignia of the kingdom are the triumph over demons, resurrection of bodies, redemption of souls, despoiling of hell, opening of paradise, and destruction of death. The insignia of the kingdom are the faith of peoples, Christian sacraments, religious worship, and miracles of the saints.

This kingdom had its beginning before the foundation of the world; it received its inception with the world, its renewal at the ends of the ages, and after the world its consummation in glorification. The kingdom of angels began when God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light (Gen. 1:3). The kingdom of human beings began, but secretly, when “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” [Col. 0775C] (John 1:14). It began openly, however, when Christ rose from the dead. But let us now consider the apostolic words and recognize in them the present solemnity: “And you, when you were dead in your transgressions and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, he made alive together with him” (Col. 2:13).

Observe that the Apostle, by a certain repetition of expressions, made death twofold, whereas he expressed resurrection by a single word. “Dead,” he says, “in your transgressions”—behold one death—“and in the uncircumcision of your flesh”—behold another death. Thus we die both through transgressions and through the uncircumcision of the flesh. Yet we bring upon ourselves the death of transgressions by our hands and feet; the death of the uncircumcision of our flesh we receive with the chain of mortality rather than produce by our actions. We suffer the latter [Col. 0775D] through hereditary curse; we acquire the former through voluntary transgression. Because of the latter we are exiled here, either cleansing both by good patience or binding both together by obstinacy, with one bond of present and future condemnation.

Therefore, actual sins are understood by “transgressions,” original sins by “the uncircumcision of the flesh.” But from both actual and original sin one death—or resurrection—of Christ has freed us; this is meant by the phrase “he made us alive together with him.” He made us alive together with him because he gave life to body and soul. He made us alive together with him because he forgave both actual and original sins. He made us alive together with him because he gave us life by his resurrection. He made us alive together with him because he gave us life now through righteousness and in the future through glory.

[Col. 0776A] “With him”: what is “with him”? According to his likeness. Therefore, he made us alive together with him—that is, with the Head, or according to his likeness—because in Christ’s resurrection we have tasted beforehand the hope of our own resurrection. For if the first offering is holy, so also is the mass—that is, if Jesus, Son of the Virgin, who died on the cross, rose from the dead on the third day, then without doubt the members of his body will rise in their own time. This will happen as certainly as that event truly preceded it; and it will happen without a recurrence of mortality. Thus Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him. Therefore he made us alive together with him, forgiving us all our transgressions and blotting out the handwriting of the decree that stood against us and was contrary to us.

[Col. 0776B] Observe: “forgiving”; observe: “blotting out.” What does he forgive, and what does he blot out? He grants grace, he blots out guilt; he grants life, he blots out death; he grants a crown, he blots out punishment; he grants what is his, he blots out what is ours; he grants heaven, he blots out hell. Finally, he forgives transgressions; he blots out the handwriting.

O handwriting, how evil is your script; how final is your reading! Each of your letters is a sharp arrow, whose indignation drinks up the human spirit. Each syllable is a scorpion’s stinging tail, destroying our latter parts. Each expression is “Woe, woe,” and everlasting lamentations. Each sentence says, “We receive what is due to our deeds.” Its title: *The Book of Death*. The matter of this book: the sins and punishments [Col. 0776C] of humanity. Its method of treatment: that the measure of punishment may be extended according to the quality of guilt.

Its entire reading is crying, wrath, and indignation. Its entire reading is a continuation of pains without respite. Its entire reading is affliction and exaction. There is no *explicit*, where there is no end. When it has ended, then it begins: deficiency repairs deficiency, and from death the shoots of death sprout again. This handwriting is written with a diamond-point, because unless this writing is erased by the blood of the kid who was numbered with thieves, the curse will never be absolved.

This handwriting is that flying scroll which Zechariah saw in the Spirit. Perhaps those two women who had wings like a kite’s will lift it; they lifted [Col. 0776D] the ephah-basket between earth and heaven, in the midst of which basket sat a woman, who is Wickedness, with a mass of lead upon her mouth.

That flying scroll is the universal examination of judgment, by which the consciences of all people will be unfolded. It is lifted between earth and heaven because we shall meet Christ in the air when he comes for judgment. The two women who lift and carry it are flesh and soul, because each person shall bear judgment, to receive according to what he has done in his body, whether good or evil. They have wings like a kite’s because after the resurrection of souls and bodies they possess great powers. Wickedness sits in the midst of the basket when iniquity, which is in the tent—that is, in the middle of the heart—will be unable to hide from the heat and illumination of the sun. The accused has [Col. 0777A] a mass of lead upon his mouth, because shame prevents him from opening it. Christ blots out this handwriting in his passion and resurrection—Christ, I say, our Lord, who lives and reigns, etc.

## SERMON XLIV. ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE LORD, III

When Christ laid down his soul, exposed his body upon the cross, and placed it in the tomb, he did not set aside either his mercy or his power. By his power he rose; by his mercy he revisited the apostolic household, turning his neck back toward the fledglings. He raised minds shaken by fear and grief through glorious consolation, both in person and through angels.

O holy angels, where were you in the Passion? What were you doing? Why did you not run to him? Why did you endure your king to be so shamefully disfigured [Col. 0777B]?

“Certainly,” they reply, “he had no need of our help. His cause was clear to himself with the Father and the Holy Spirit; it was hidden from many of our number; and it is not the practice of our order to undertake what has not been commanded. The good Lord did not wish to interrupt our joys by his sufferings. He did not reckon as a loss what would immediately be compensated by such great gain: he gave one body of his own and acquired thousands upon thousands; he laid down one soul—but how many did he restore and carry back to heaven? For three days he was in the heart of the earth, yet he acquired eternity and length of days for his household.”

Who can estimate the price? Who can conceive the human race redeemed by this price? Even unto [Col. 0777C] angelic peace the value of Christ’s blood, death, and resurrection flows back and overflows. Christ left nothing unpurchased that could ever be redeemed by any price. From what was ours, O Christ, you took the price; in what was ours you paid it; and for what was ours.

Body and soul are ours; divinity alone is uniquely yours. Therefore, from our body and blood, or soul, you established the price. For what—or for whom? For the human race and all people. In what was ours, how? On the cross, in the Passion. Punishment is ours; suffering is owed to us. Thus we may presume, without presumption, that this solemnity is ours in cost and in benefit.

Is it not at our cost that in this commemoration we have kept watch, fasted, restrained our wanderings and [Col. 0777D] vanities, and in many ways been crucified with Christ? He does not disdain our expenditures, though small, who does not leave even a cup of cold water unrewarded. Finally, the benefit of this solemnity belongs especially to us. Angels need not commemorate annually with devotion what they attend with unceasing celebration. The devil does not regard as a feast his defeat, his expulsion from the world, or his despoiling of so many souls’ spoils.

Yet we do not exclude the angels, through whose service we have tasted the first fruits of the Lord’s resurrection; rather, we share it with them. They have their robes; they have white garments; they have lightning-bright faces. What are these to us who are ragged, almost naked, whose garments are worn by age, corrupted by excess, [Col. 0778A] torn apart by discord? Let us therefore quickly put off the old skin with the old man; let us wash the defiled garment in compunction and sew together in unanimity what discord has torn apart.

## SERMON XLV. ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE LORD, IV

“This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. 2:23).

Seeing her firstborn and only-begotten Son clothed in the tunic of immortality in the resurrection, the holy Mother cries out with deep affection: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.” I confound the Jew; I confound the heretic who does not believe that my Son has risen. If a mother does not know her son, who knows him? She who conceived him, bore him, [Col. 0778B] nursed him, and fed him—by what clouding obstacle could she falsely declare not to be hers the one whom she loves and knows more than herself? God the Father entrusted his Son to her; and am I to doubt that he who rose is the Virgin’s Son, who suffered and was crucified? Three days’ forgetfulness does not erase a mother’s affection.

If a year had elapsed, cavilling might have had some place. Therefore let the mother speak of the Son, Mary of Jesus Christ: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.” When my Son was crucified, I saw and recognized the flesh of my flesh, fastened by nails and pierced by a lance; and bone of my bones, which those crucifying him did not break, that Scripture might be fulfilled: “You shall not break a bone of it” (John 19:36).

[Col. 0778C] This testimony is true: that of a mother concerning her Son. Adam also speaks of the Crucified: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.” This flesh is not my flesh—the flesh of sin—but it is from my flesh, from the Virgin Mary; and although this flesh did not deserve death, nevertheless it paid death for me, according to the saying: “What I did not seize, then I paid” (Ps. 68:5).

Flesh bound by no guilt frees flesh bound and bowed beneath the bond of sin. Indeed, it placed the chain of punishment [*poenae*; printed “pene”] upon its own neck and broke it, saying, “Loose the bonds from your neck, captive daughter of Zion” (Isa. 52:2); for it rose from death. “This now is bone of my bones.” From my firstborn Cain until Jesus, who among those who were bones—that is, strong men—were, as my bones before sin were without sin? None defeated the devil. [Col. 0778D] But Jesus, stronger than Samson and mighty in battle, enduring like the jawbone of an ass—that is, like one deaf and mute, like a man having no rebukes in his mouth—destroyed him who held the power of death, that is, the devil, who deceived my Eve and through her offered the deadly fruit. But now, certainly, in Jesus’ resurrection I have found bone from my bones—not bones into which decay has entered, but bones in which are the power and strength of God—and flesh from my flesh, yet not corruptible but incorruptible.

Again, these are the words of Christ’s soul returning from hell to its body. The Father, into whose hands he had entrusted it, had indeed kept it safe; without doubt he led it safe and brought it back. Coming therefore to its helpmeet, like itself—its most holy and immaculate [Col. 0779A] body, which saw no corruption, nor did corruption enter its innermost parts in conception, conduct, or death itself—it says: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.” The bone budded like a lily, and the flesh flowered again, because that which was formerly able to die will now be unable to die.

Then mercy in the flesh and truth in the soul met one another; righteousness and peace kissed. For righteousness decreed it just that the flesh, which had suffered such horrors without fault of its own, should free those for whom it had pleaded and reign in everlasting peace, according to the Apostle: “Having obtained eternal redemption” (Heb. 9:12). The divine soul alone, with the divine flesh, knew what sweetness, joy, and jubilation they had with one another in that hour, when [Col. 0779B] both substances, soul and body, passed into divine brightness while the properties of their natures remained intact. Thus the soul says: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.” But the Word made flesh, in the reunion of both through the resurrection, says: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.”

Christ also speaks in the sacrament of the altar after that consecration of the Lord in which it is said, “This is my body,” and “This is my blood”: “This,” he says, “now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.” The bone is the difficulty and depth of the sacrament; the flesh is under the species of bread, and fittingly flesh because of your frailty, which does not rise to divine things except through human things. Do not set your teeth upon the bone, seeking to strip the bones from [Col. 0779C] the king of Edom—that is, seeking to define and investigate how this occurs. God keeps his bones hidden; they are called “the hidden things of the Son” (Ps. 9:1), concerning which the Apostle says, “O the depth of the riches of wisdom!” etc. (Rom. 11:33). They are those bones which the Psalmist calls the hidden and uncertain things of God’s wisdom, saying: “For behold, you have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom” (Ps. 50:8).

## SERMON XLVI. ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE LORD, V

“Jacob cooked a stew. When Esau came to him exhausted from the field, he said: ‘Give me some of this red cooking of yours, for I am utterly exhausted.’ Jacob said to him: ‘Sell me your birthright.’ He answered: ‘Behold, I am dying; what will my birthright profit me?’ ‘Swear to me, then.’ Esau swore and sold his birthright” (Gen. 25:29 ff.).

The austerity of fasts, by which the flesh of the saints wasted away and their skin clung to their bones, is relaxed by the Paschal solemnity and by apostolic authority, which says: “Let us feast on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth; for Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5:8). Behold fire; behold wood—indeed, behold fire among thorns. For the crackling of the thorns protests under the pressing fire of envy, crying, “Away, away; crucify, crucify!” (John 19:15), and, “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (ibid., 12). Lebanon is not sufficient for kindling, when the Jews, to Pilate’s words, “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law” (John 18:31), answered, “It is not lawful for us [Col. 0780A] to put anyone to death” (ibid.). They indeed pleaded the Law, which remains laid over their hearts to this day; but in truth they were more intent upon attaching the governor to their wicked purpose together with his people.

Therefore, with such a fire kindled in the courtyard of the chief priest and in the synagogue of the Jews by him who, throughout the entire night, with bellows and winds borrowed from every side, blew and puffed up Judas and Judea together, Jacob—the simple and good man, who had not consented to the deeds of the wicked—placed an earthen vessel upon the fire, in order to redeem for himself his brother’s birthright: to acquire good from the evil of others and condemn sin through sin. For when he passed through the field of a sluggard, entirely filled with nettles, he learned wisdom from such an example.

[Col. 0780B] He put in a lentil, insignificant in outward appearance but of incomparable worth in its hidden majesty. For the lentil is small, lowly, and reddish. Behold Jesus made small: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not deem equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” etc. (Phil. 2:6). Behold Jesus made lowly: “Christ became obedient unto death” (ibid., 8). Behold him red: “Even death on a cross” (ibid.). Behold him cooked, because “bowing his head, he gave up the spirit” (John 19:30). Behold him taken from the fire: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” (Ps. 56:9). Likewise: “I have risen, and I am still with you,” etc. (Ps. 138:18).

But lest anyone be offended by the singularity [Col. 0780C] and lowliness of this dish, the flesh of the lamb remains; the flesh of the fatted calf remains; there is still an innumerable abundance, not merely promised but offered to the one seated at supper. For unexpected things are more pleasing than those requested. Appetite will fail before the table, desire before food, the stomach before the cooking-pot, the entrails before the dishes. One soul cannot contain the whole lamb. It belongs to all, not to one alone.

Behold, an angel too hastens to the body when the soul has departed and it has been buried. Tell me, holy angel: were you sent, or did you come voluntarily? Did you fly here by will or by obedience, or by both prompting you at once, with a mingling [perhaps *mixtura*, “mixture”] of whiteness and fiery brightness, to our earthen vessel taken from the Virgin and filled with soul and divinity? [Col. 0780D] Does our stew, now cooked—indeed, cooked twice, by the disciple’s betrayal and the Passion of the cross—also please you? Until now our living flesh, and not yet dead corpses, has been accustomed to stink rather than emit fragrance. Who has purified these things sevenfold? Who has filled them with such sweetness and most fragrant scent that their odor might tempt angelic nostrils and summon them with most longing desire? Behold, our stew is from your hand.

## SERMON XLVII. ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE LORD, VI

“Daniel, servant of God, take the meal that God sends you” (Dan. 14:36).

Nothing interrupts, dissolves, or buries God’s everlasting mercy. It rejects the barriers of our sins, conquers crimes, [Col. 0781A] seizes fugitives by the back, softens the hearts of rebels, quickly forgives the faults of those who return, and, conferring the abundant gift of grace upon the undeserving, dismisses every complaint arising from the old offense. Neither the tree of human luxury has dried up this channel of grace, nor the numbness of our sloth extinguished it; for it is a well of living waters flowing violently from Lebanon. Deep and continual gulfs of evils neither restrain its course, halt its force, nor swallow up its flow.

Here the leper is cleansed; here the harlot is washed; here the tax collector is sanctified; here the murderer and adulterer are restored. Neither because of disgrace nor guilt is one expelled from the royal throne or cheated of the fatherhood promised by Christ from heaven. Here the thief is suddenly sanctified [Col. 0781B] and honored by entering Paradise second after Christ. Here, finally, the souls of saints wash their robes; here priests cleanse the head, feet, and entrails of sacrificial victims; here, once by baptism and always by confession and repentance, every stain, original as well as actual, is stripped away. Therefore let no one who has not been washed with saving water carry his stench; for through his own frailty and iniquity he always stinks.

Although David’s fountain is open at every time for the washing of the woman and the menstruant, it pours itself out with more lavish overflowing at the most holy season of Christ’s Passion, when, as though harvest and vintage filled Christians’ storehouses and winepresses, minds are fervent and devotion ripens; bodies are more zealously disciplined by fasts, the poor refreshed by alms, monasteries more frequently sought, deserts of the former life visited; and consequently thorns and nettles [Col. 0781C] are uprooted with the plough and hoe of confession and burned with the fire of satisfaction.

Daniel, then, the man of desires, whose every desire is before God, enters the lions’ den—that is, the depth of conscience, where there is the roaring of lions, namely of many crimes. Yet he is not devoured, not bitten, not touched; for as an unjust cause punishes, so a just cause defends. If you approach lions—that is, impulses of the flesh—in order to play with them by consenting to their enticements, then fear their claws, fear their teeth, fear at last the lions’ madness. There is no trust where there is madness. Cunning deceives simplicity, malice innocence; pride chokes humility and devastates every shoot of virtue—broods of vipers that spring from the belly of hell. Jacob fears Esau; Isaac, Ishmael. David’s youths must not encounter Saul’s servants indiscriminately or rashly, because one must beware of what is double-edged. Delilah was able to conquer Samson by persuasion, not strength; by deception, not by the sword; by womanly pretence, not by manly assault.

[Col. 0781D] Therefore it is perilous and dangerous for reason and sensuality to sleep in one bed. For, while reason sleeps, sensuality crushes the child—that is, the natural impulse—when it bends it toward the pleasure of sin. Then it lies that the child, whom reason produced and which consents to the law of God—that is, truly lives—is its own. To consent to the flesh, beyond doubt, is to die. Solomon, however—that is, the prelate to whom this question is referred—perfectly discerns by the sword of discretion whether each movement belongs to spirit or flesh, and adjudges the dead child to sensuality, the living one to reason.

Therefore, having repudiated the seductive partnership and declared enmity between the serpent and the woman—that is, reason—and between the seed of each, let David descend against Goliath with sling and stone: certainly with Christ’s grace and confession. Enclosed in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights, let him repent of evil thoughts, words, and deeds, in adversity as well as prosperity. Let him descend with Jesus’ soul into hell, to break the iron bars—the habitual practice of sin—[Col. 0782B] and lead his captives out of darkness; that is, once the soul’s senses have been released from error, let him bring them back to the light of truth. And let him be cast with Daniel into the lions’ den, rather to mock them than to play with them.

There are seven lions: namely spiritual wickednesses and capital crimes, to whom two bodies and two sheep are given daily. The two bodies are the will to sin and the act of sin; the two sheep are error in faith and ignorance of good. With such food the devil and his angels are fattened; indeed, he would already have perished of hunger, consumed by the fires of Gehenna, unless renewed by daily sins he had prolonged the life of his malice. For just as food feeds a human being, so wickedness feeds the devil; and the more evil the vice, the more greedily [Col. 0782C] he receives it, seasoning his libations with crime and reckoning his evils by human damnation. Therefore he sets before himself and his household at table the two bodies—that is, the will to sin and the act of sin—as principal dishes, because from the one nothing sound follows, and from the other nothing incorrupt follows. The will is the root; action is the tree. Thus the whole offspring of the heart is corrupted at the root of the will, nor does a single one escape destruction from the entire progeny of corrupt action.

The second dishes then brought forward are the two sheep: error of faith and ignorance of good, or ignorance of the Law and ignorance of God. These are served daily to the lions by the Babylonians—that is, disordered and perverse evil spirits. But when Daniel enters the den—that is, Jesus enters the world or hell—they are not supplied, because “he came into this world to save sinners” (1 Tim. 19:15, as cited). He descended into hell to free the souls of his faithful; for he broke the lions’ teeth, because with the hammer of judgment he struck down from his own both human and demonic power, saying to the sea: “Thus far shall you come, and here your waves shall be broken” [Col. 0782D] (Job 38:11). For the presence of Jesus softens adversities, lightens punishments, illumines darkness, orders what is confused, joins what is divided, and makes all things tranquil.

O Daniel, member of Christ and imitator of your Head, struck in the midst of your den by divine fear and girded with love of righteousness, weigh what you have done and [Col. 0783A] what you have deserved. Examine and consider what the den contains; patiently endure whatever the judge’s discriminating examination has decreed. For it is wiser to cast vices out of the conscience than to endure Gehenna for evil deeds. There are seven domestic lions, fatally familiar: boasting, gluttony, lust, pretence, anger, cruelty, and rapine. They devour all our substance and reduce us to that poverty in which we cannot fill our belly even with the husks which swine eat.

But Daniel, like that prodigal son and like Jonah from the belly of the whale, sighing for bread from heaven—the bread which the Father gives to those who ask him—cries to him who gives food to the young ravens. And the Lord, hearer of the desires of the poor, says to Habakkuk: “Carry [Col. 0783B] the meal you have to Daniel, who is in the lions’ den.” This is what the Apostle says: “If a person is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself lest you also be tempted” (Gal. 6:1). For one fighting against the devil is owed paternal consolation.

Therefore, having seen the lions’ den and found Daniel in their midst, besieged together with them and clinging to the oppressed man, he offers bread to the hungry: “Daniel,” he says, “servant of God, take the meal which God has sent you.” This is the great meal which Jesus desired to eat—the Passover—with his disciples; concerning it the Apostle says, “Let us feast, not with the old leaven,” etc., “but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5:8). Of this the Song of Songs says: “Eat, friends, and drink,” etc. [Col. 0783C] (Song 5:1). We receive this with the mind, not break it with the tooth; the soul is fed by it, not the belly distended. By it we are transferred into angelic glory; by it we are nourished into children of God; by it we are strengthened into vessels of mercy; by it we are lifted from the world to heaven; by it we gain eternity; by it we await the communion of saints, resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life—through Jesus Christ himself, who prepared this meal from his flesh and blood for his faithful, who lives and reigns.

## SERMON XLVIII. ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE LORD, VII

“The days of mourning for Moses were completed” (Deut. 34:8).

[Col. 0783D] The children of Adam’s transgression, possessing places and times of tears, searched through many thousands of years, the ages of individual generations and the people of individual ages, to find one who might change their places and soften their times: one who might do good, one who might turn mourning into joy. Whenever the sparkling life and shining teaching of any person arose, the crowd of exiles applauded as though a torch of proven hope had arrived and the ages of deliverance were at hand. Finally, when the temporal lamps were extinguished by the death of all the patriarchs and prophets—for “what man lives and shall not see death?”—they renewed their sobbing and wept over vain and momentary consolations. Hence Jacob, having died, is mourned with exceedingly great and strong lamentation [Col. 0784A]; hence Joseph, hence Aaron, hence Moses are mourned for many days.

The passing of the ancients was lamented for a sufficiently just and plausible reason: both because of the desolation of survivors, because death’s dominion had continued for so long, and also because of descent into hell. But where the bars of hell have been broken, death’s dominions destroyed, and the eternal, perpetual aid of consolation is in Christ, rightly there is no longer mourning or pain, because the former things have passed away. Rightly God wipes every tear from the eyes of the saints; rightly the days of mourning for Moses’ mourners have been completed.

Yet even in Jesus himself while he lived in the flesh, although he did what no other had done, the settled uncertainty [Col. 0784B] in human hearts could scarcely be interrupted by the attestation of his miracles and wondrous deeds. For even in the minds of the apostles, whose hearts the Spirit nourishing within had awakened and made fruitful for faith in Christ, faith had so languished under the snow and hail of his Passion and death, and hope was drawing its last breath, that some of them said: “But we hoped that he was the one who was to redeem Israel” (Luke 22:21, as cited).

Therefore, in order to remove everything that might thereafter be raised by diabolical insinuation, human ignorance and doubt, or heretical persuasion, he rose, appearing to them with many proofs for forty days; and today, by a glorious and manifest ascension, he has placed his body at the Father’s right hand.

[Col. 0784C] Therefore Moses, who wrote these things concerning that event, should neither mourn nor be mourned, because the days of mourning for the mourners have been completed. Moses—that is, the law of Moses—showed transgression and did not restrain guilt, but heaped it up still more, as the Apostle testifies: “I would not have known coveting unless the law had said, ‘You shall not covet’” (Rom. 7:7); and elsewhere: “When the commandment came, it worked in me every kind of coveting, and what was found to be for life proved to be for death” (ibid., 8). Who, then, would not mourn because of this? But who can take away this mourning? The Spirit of life, who has freed me from the law of sin and death. Who can give this Spirit? Christ, who says: “Behold, I shall send the promise of my Father upon [Col. 0784D] you; but remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49), that is, with the Holy Spirit.

Though the Jebusite remains with us in this place of pilgrimage; though there is a wind from the north and a fire enfolding; though we dwell with serpents and scorpions; though the law of the members resists the law of the mind; though we do not do what we will but what we do not will—nevertheless, because God the Father has exalted our Head above all our enemies; nevertheless, because the Rider of heaven helps us, as it is said in the blessing of Asher, “Rider of heaven, your helper” (Deut. 33:26); nevertheless, because the nature of our flesh has flowered again like Aaron’s rod and has been placed where the testimony of our redemption is—Jesus interceding for us—[Col. 0785A] let us lay aside every complaint and approach the throne of grace, where the Lamb sits at the Father’s right hand, unto all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLIX. ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE LORD, VIII

“Now I know that the Lord has saved his anointed” (Ps. 19:7).

Jesus, Son of the Virgin Mary, giant of two substances and fawn of the most lovely hind, free among the dead—how swift and great were the leaps he made from the cross to the tomb, from the tomb to hell, from hell to Paradise—we have heard, believed, rejoiced, and adored. We have as lawful and fitting witnesses to this angels and apostles; and there remain, finally, sufficient evangelical documents and miracles, [Col. 0785B] together with the irrefutable truth of prophetic Scripture, which Peter calls the more certain prophetic word.

Thus the Lord says to Job: “Have you entered the depth of the sea, and walked in the uttermost parts of the abyss? Have the gates of death been opened to you? Have you seen the dark doors?” (Job 38:16). God speaks to his servant of his special and unique works, setting forth the prerogative of his power: that he reaches mightily from the end of heaven to the end of hell and disposes all things sweetly. Hence the Psalmist: “Where shall I go from your Spirit?” etc. (Ps. 138:7).

This walking was neither vain, superfluous, nor curious, as though it relieved weariness. For he had walked in Paradise in the breeze after noon, either to rebuke the person confessing sin [Col. 0785C] or to punish the person denying or concealing it. He had walked about alone, encircling the circuit of heaven; he had also walked through the world, seeking the sheep that had strayed. Finally, he walked in the depth of the sea and the uttermost parts of the abyss, so that the roaring lion might retain in its belly not even the tip of the finger or ear of his sheep; rather, he might shake out all the children of the scattered from the pierced sack of death and hell into the bosom of those who gather sheaves and carry them to Abraham’s bosom, to whom it is said: “Bring to the Lord sons of rams” (Ps. 28:1), that is, imitators of the apostles.

Like one unencumbered and girded with a sword upon his thigh, he stretches forth most mightily, proceeds prosperously, and reigns—as in heaven and in the world, so also in the abyss—so that he may [Col. 0785D] do whatever he wills in heaven, on earth, in the sea, and in all abysses. He sees the dark doors through which evil angels’ emissions come forth to us, through which stolen waters flow—waters that are sweeter, that is, carnal delights—through which whisperers are introduced, and through which works of darkness are supplied.

## SERMON L. ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD, I

“Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead” (4 Kings [2 Kings] 2:23).

The history from the books of Kings is well known, dearest brothers: it is read there that, as Elisha went up from Jericho to Bethel, little boys came out of the city and mocked him, saying, “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead.” Yet within it lies a most beautiful meaning [Col. 0786A], not unsuited to the Lord’s Ascension; as the Lord grants, I desire to investigate it with you and set it forth in your midst to honor so great a solemnity.

Let us summon to this wondrous and great spectacle every inward faculty of our soul, for there has not been, nor will there be, in the ages any spectacle like it for God, angels, and human beings. Only demons and reprobate people are excluded from this spectacle, because their malice and envy have blinded them: that they may not see God’s glory, may not see the Son’s Ascension, may not see heaven’s dwelling places, may not see the Lord’s splendid solemnities.

Behold, the Father runs to meet his ascending Son: he gives him a kiss, holds a staff, raises him into heaven, places him [Col. 0786B] upon the throne of glory, puts his ring upon his finger, lays a robe upon his neck, clothes his feet with sandals, assigns a sceptre to his hand, a crown of precious stone upon his head, and surrounds him on every side with glory and honor—as his only Son, as his heir, as consubstantial, as coeternal—yet only insofar as he is the Word, insofar as he is God.

For, insofar as he is man, he is neither consubstantial nor coeternal with Him, but receives gifts among men—yet above men, indeed even above angels. For to which of the angels did He ever say: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7)? To which angel did He give authority over all flesh, to which did He give all judgment, to which finally did He grant a seat at His right hand? [Col. 0786C] To none, certainly, but to the man Jesus Christ alone was all authority in heaven and on earth given; to the man Jesus Christ alone was given not adoptive but natural sonship, because of the unity of Word and flesh in the one person of God and man. Hence Augustine: “That the Only-begotten is equal to the Father belongs not to grace but to nature. But that, in the unity of the person of the Only-begotten, man has been assumed, belongs to grace, not to nature.” Likewise, in *On Faith to Peter*: “That God, who is naturally the only-begotten Son of God the Father, was made naturally the Son of man.”

Therefore, as this man Jesus Christ returned to the Fatherland and, as it were, came back by right of restoration, the whole heavenly city of Jerusalem came forth with the Father to meet him: the entire multitude [Col. 0786D] of angels, among whom thousands upon thousands ministered to him and a million stood before him; the whole choir of heavenly powers strove in fervent service to anticipate his face in greeting and attendance.
