They worshipped the traces of his feet, as it is written: “And let all the angels of God worship him” (Heb. 1:6). They embraced his feet and knees, carrying him upon their shoulders as far as the heavenly seat—him whom the cloud had received from the Apostles’ sight and borne up to the star-bearing dwellings. Thus it is said in the Psalm: “The chariots of God are manifold: ten thousands, thousands of those rejoicing; the Lord is among them in holy Sinai” (Ps. 67:18). O joy, O solemn feast, O triumph, O jubilation, O exultation, O everlasting gladness! Some cry: “Be exalted, O Lord, in your strength” (Ps. [Col. 0787A] 20:14); others: “Arise, O Lord, into your resting-place, you and the ark of your sanctification” (Ps. 131:8); others: “Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. 23:8); others: “The Lord of hosts, the Lord mighty and powerful in battle” (ibid.); others: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah?” (Isa. 63:1); others: “This one, beautiful in his robe, advancing in the abundance of his strength” (ibid.); others: “O Lord, let your hand be lifted up, that they may not see” (Isa. 26:11); others: “That they may see and be confounded, those peoples who are zealous, and that fire may devour your enemies” (ibid.).

Finally, others, recalling the memory of the Passion and setting such glory against such great humiliation, say: “Go up, bald one; go up, bald one”; as if to say: You bald one, you Jesus, you crucified one, you who suffered, you who died, [Col. 0787B] you who hung with thieves, you bald one whose hair the razor of the malicious Jews shaved from your forehead when it turned all the disciples to flight. You bald one, in whom the prince of this world found nothing; you bald one, who had nowhere to lay your head, who at your birth found no place in the inn; you bald one, who never appropriated anything superfluous, but, living with the utmost continence, very often refused even the necessities of the body: go up to your Father and our Father, to your God and our God. Go up into Bethel, that is, the house of God; go up above the setting, go up above the mountains of spices, go up above the cherubim, go up above all the earth, go up above the lofty and exalted throne, [Col. 0787C] go up above the wings of the winds; go up not upon the sides of the north, but upon the seat of majesty; and, seated at the Father’s right hand, be like the Most High, receiving in your humanity all that, before the world was made, you possessed with the Father in your divinity—so that divinity may restore in the Ascension to humanity all that it promised in the Descent.

For when the Word united flesh to himself in the unity of person, he promised, as it were, equality with the Father—not by equating human nature with the divine, but by wholly comparing the person of the Son with the person of the Father. Today, in the Lord’s Ascension, the work of the Incarnation, the merit of the Passion, and the reward of glorification have been consummated. Now the flesh of Christ no longer remembers the pressure of the afflictions that surrounded it in [Col. 0787D] the Passion, because of the joy it found in the Ascension; for according to the multitude of its sorrows, the consolations of God made it glad.

Therefore rejoice, O flesh, O man, with your sister, your nature, which has been glorified in Christ. Now take confidence from the husband of your sister, from the bridegroom of human nature, because she has been crowned, because she has been made queen, because she has been appointed lady of angels together with her bridegroom—his bride, our sister. O good sister, remember your mercies—rather, your miseries—which have passed away, and ours, which have not yet passed away but increase more and more day by day. Remember your brothers—rather, your servants—who lack the resources to live well; who lack health to resist sin; who lack the light [Col. 0788A] of the eyes sufficiently to distinguish good from evil; who lack the wing of love to fly to God; who lack strength to go after you and attain you.

Draw us after you. Say to your bridegroom; say to yourself; say to our God; say to your Father: “Father, I will that where I am, there also may be my brother, my minister, my servant, and my captive.” We know, we know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you. What will he deny you, when he did not deny himself to you? What will he deny you, who says: “All mine are yours, and yours are mine”? What will he deny you, with whom there are one purse, one body, one soul, one divinity, one will, one obedience, one merit, one reward, one willing and one not willing, one dying and [Col. 0788B] one living, one asking and one granting?

Behold, we are as sure that you will obtain it, if you wish to ask for us, as we are willing to be delivered from this captivity and misery, when we flee to you, O flesh of our Savior, O human nature of our head, Jesus Christ. Do not abhor the Egyptian, nor despise your flesh; turn your kindly eyes toward us, and deign to pour out upon us the blessing which you left to your Apostles when, with hands raised, you were borne into heaven: Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, God, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Sermon LI. On the Ascension of the Lord II

“Does the hawk grow feathers by your wisdom, [Col. 0788C] spreading its wings toward the south? Or will the eagle be lifted up at your command, and make its nest in the heights?” (Job 39:26).

In each kind of these birds, dearest brothers, our Lord Jesus Christ is signified—indeed for different reasons, but by mysteries that are not opposed. For in the manifold and varied nature and activity of creatures, the simple purpose of our Creator and Redeemer concerning our salvation is often signified in many ways; and what is one in effect is expressed in varied speech. Why, then, the Lord’s Ascension is mystically shadowed forth in Scripture by the hawk, and why by the eagle, is worthy of investigation and useful to set forth.

[Col. 0788D] Accordingly, when the respective natures of the hawk and eagle have been considered, we can plainly understand that this comparison fits Christ, according to the Apostle’s words: “He who descended is the same also who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things” (Eph. 4:10). In the hawk, then, we understand him who descended; in the eagle, him who ascended; in hawk and eagle together, “that he might fill all things.” In his descent the hawk grows feathers through the assumption of man; in the Ascension the eagle is raised up and makes its nest on high through the glorification of the Son of man. In descent and Ascension he fills all things through the redemption of the human race and the restoration of the angelic falling-away. He descends without feathers; he ascends with feathers.

Now the feathers in Christ Jesus are soul and flesh. [Col. 0789A] The feathers are the college of the Apostles. The feathers are the gathering of the nations. The feathers are those charisms of virtues which rest upon that flower which comes forth from the rod of Jesse, the Virgin Mary. With these feathers the hawk grows feathers in the virginal womb by the wisdom of God, when, through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, the fullness of virtues was thus originally woven into Jesus’ human nature, just as original sin is perpetually implanted in Adam’s children from the propagation of sin in conception and birth. The first feather of Jesus is wisdom; the second, understanding; the third, counsel; the fourth, fortitude; the fifth, knowledge; the sixth, piety; the seventh, fear of the Lord. Thus feathered, human nature ascended to fellowship with God, to the divinity of the Son’s person, to the summit of heaven, and above every principality and power, [Col. 0789B] or dignity of the angelic order.

For no weight of corruption presses down the flesh or soul of Jesus so as to prevent its running toward merit or flying up toward a reward both singular in number and special and inimitable in example. Jesus’ conception is not imitable, nor his birth comparable, nor his life comprehensible, nor his death similar, nor his Resurrection common, nor his Ascension customary. For where has it been seen [variant: *used*] that a man visibly ascends into heaven? Where has it been heard that a man rises from the dead on the third day? Where has it been heard that a man is without sin, and dies when he wills? Where is a man’s life on earth for thirty-three years unstained by the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, the pride of life, and every [Col. 0789C] stain of sins? Where is the birth of a man while his mother’s womb remains closed? Where is the conception of a man without a man’s seed? Where, in conception, is the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit?

Thus, O Lord Jesus, these works of yours lack plurality both in number, because of the singularity of their author, and in example, because of the difficulty of their accomplishment. Yet your conception is an example to us, that from your Spirit we may conceive your fear; your birth, that we may bring forth your love; your life, that we may hold fast poverty, innocence, humility, meekness, charity, chastity, mercy, and piety; your death, that we may keep obedience and patience; your Resurrection, that we may believe in the resurrection of the flesh; your Ascension, that we may hope for the glorification of bodies and souls. [Col. 0789D] Thus we too, your young, beneath your wings and feathers, become fledged and grow feathers, when, through devotion to virtues, we provide supports for our nakedness. Hence it is said in the Song of Songs: “Strengthen me with flowers; surround me with apples” (Song 2:5). For what a feather is to the bridegroom, a flower is to the bride; and what a wing is to one flying back to the heavens, a pomegranate is to one reclining at table.

The bride seeks flowers in the bridal chamber and pomegranates at the banquet. The bridegroom loves feathers, which serve him for beauty, softness, and warmth, and wings, which give uplift; for the mysteries of faith are beautiful because of their uprightness, soft because of their ease, warm because of charity, and raise one upward because of hope. Faith indeed abhors dishonesty, moderates the difficulty of legal [Col. 0790A] commandments, warms the lukewarmness of the negligent, raises the burden of carnal people, and reclines, as it were, upon uprightness as on a clean cloth; rests its head upon ease as upon the softest pillow; stretches charity over itself as a covering; and relies upon the firmness of hope as upon wings.

But now, at the end of the sermon, let us turn our head back to the little wings—or rather, let us lift the little wings to the head—and, in the nest of cloistered custom, packed round with the feathers of holy observances, let us fly after the great hawk. He, indeed, like a giant, passes over lofty things in marvelous flights; we, because small things suit the small, according to the progress possible to human frailty, if we cannot fly, should at least humbly crawl after him; and, as God has apportioned to each a measure of faith, advance through smaller or larger [Col. 0790B] stretches of virtues. For behold, one who wished to fly after Jesus says: “Lord, I will follow you wherever you go” (Luke 9:57); but this man promised that he would fly without wings. Therefore the Lord said to him: “Foxes have dens and birds of heaven nests, but the Son of man has nowhere to lay his head” (ibid., v. 58). Another, however, seeing his own weakness and wishing to fly but unable, says: “Draw me after you” (Song 1:4), as though he said: “To will is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish it” (Rom. 7:18); “the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26:41). “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9:15), so that I do not do what I will, but do what I do not will; and because it is written: “God will set apart a voluntary rain,” that is, a good will, “for his inheritance, and it became weak, but you perfected it” (Ps. [Col. 0790C] 67:10), that it might recover strength better through humility.

Another follows and says: “We shall run after the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1:24). Behold, one who without grace, as though his wings were bound and glued down by the infection of the first transgression, could not fly, having received grace runs in the way of God’s commandments; so that it may not be of him who wills or runs, but of God who shows mercy, and so that everything—that we run, that we will the good, that we do the good—may come from the fragrance of the ointments, lest anyone glory in himself. A fourth among those who fly after eagle and hawk says: “I shall seize [Col. 0790D] you” (Song 8:8). You are no longer of the earth; you have now forgotten the body’s heaviness, you who say this. Perhaps this is he who says: “I fill up in my body what is lacking of Christ’s sufferings” (Col. 1:24).

Still another person, I know not who or what, follows, and with intense flight even passes this one and says: “I hold him.” O power that holds the Power of powers! O spirit exceedingly swift, that seizes the spirit of the gods! A more cautious woman follows, who had seen her sister seize and hold the hawk but not retain him, and says: “I have held him, and I will not let him go” (Song 3:4). Behold perseverance, which offers the tail in sacrifice. Another follows, saying: “I shall bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of my mother who bore me; there he will teach me” (Song 8:2) the commandments of the Lord. [Col. 0791A] Still another follows, who, seeing her own soul within herself, says: “My soul has clung after you; your right hand has upheld me” (Ps. 62:19). She is with God and in God, and is not without God: the one dove, the only one to her mother, chosen by her who bore her. She follows and observes the others, saying: “My beloved is mine and I am his; he shall dwell between my breasts” (Song 1:13). God is with her and in her; and toward her the grace of God is good, well-pleasing, and perfect.

These, dearest brothers, are the divisions of graces, which have divisions of dwellings in heaven and divisions of perfections in pilgrimage; so that, as there is heaven, and heaven of heaven, and heavens of heavens, so the practices of virtues may learn gradually to encamp among God’s faithful, until we all meet in the perfect man, [Col. 0791B] in the measure of the age of Christ’s fullness. Let us hasten, brothers, to enter into that rest before the door is shut so obstinately that it may no longer be opened to those now crying, “Lord, Lord, open to us” (Matt. 25:11). Behold, Jesus has divided the spoils; behold, he has led ships full, as though rowing them across this great and wide sea, to the port of heaven; he unloads them and assigns individual gifts to each of his friends.

Throughout that flock of innumerable thousands of angels, there will not be even one who is not honored by him with new gifts. From eternity there has been no festival so great among those celebrating in heaven, no joy so great conceived, no jubilation so great heard among every kind of musician, singer, and psalmist. Who has made so great a banquet? Who has seen so great an assembly? Who has entered so great a treasury? O Jesus, yours is the festival, yours the assumption, yours the glorification, yours the dedication. Grant grace to your servants, to your poor, to your bound ones, to your exiles, to your condemned; grant mercy, release, liberation, refreshment, salvation—you who live with the Father and the Holy Spirit, etc.

## Sermon LII. On the Ascension of the Lord III

“Does the hawk grow feathers by your wisdom, spreading its wings toward the south? Or will the eagle be raised at your command and make its nest in the heights?” [Col. 0791D] (Job 39:62).

Today, dearest brothers, Jesus, the supreme priest who is a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, entered the Holy of Holies in his own blood, and offered incense to the Father of spirits: the most fragrant perfumes of his merits from the censer of his glorified body. Today too the golden band returns, because Jesus has returned to where he came from; and the sun returns to its place, where, rising again, it turns through the south and bends toward the north. For from the throne of grace he illumines southern souls by his grace, sustains northern souls unto repentance, and receives them when converted.

Today that shadow of Christ Jesus, in whom we shall live [Col. 0792A] among the nations, was turned back ten degrees by the Ascension; this occurred in the sign of Hezekiah’s healing. For by ten degrees our Lord Jesus went back in his Ascension, because, one degree surpassing them, the human nature assumed in God rose above angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominations, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim, and subjected all things beneath his feet by dominion—so that he himself may be subject to him who subjected all things to him, until he puts all his enemies beneath his feet. To touch briefly upon everything that belongs to the present feast in one short sermon would be as burdensome as it would be difficult to express. Let it suffice for the present to see how that hawk, which grows feathers by the wisdom of God, spreads its wings toward the south, and how the eagle makes its nest on high.

Noble and wealthy people take great delight in the hawk, both for sport and for profit. They play with this bird against boredom; they catch birds, but for food; finally, they carry it about through pleasant places in which other birds were, as it were, enjoying freedom and solitude. There they catch birds by means of a bird. But none of this would occur unless the hawk first grew feathers in a varied and delightful arrangement, and the mildness of heaven smiled with the south wind blowing. Then it spreads its wings toward the south; then it leads captivity captive; then it gives gifts to its masters, prey to its household, and food to its maidservants.

Jesus is the hawk, whose feathers are virtues—beautiful [Col. 0792C] because of truth, light because of holiness, soft because of meekness, varied because of the multitude of graces. By these the hawk grows feathers through the wisdom of God, because human nature by no means deserved to be united to God’s Word and to have the fullness of the Godhead poured into it bodily. By wisdom hidden in mysteries from ages past, it was brought about, at the end of the ages and in the fullness of time, from a virginal womb and with the feathers of heavenly virtues, that Jesus should be born God and man, and man and God. For our hawk grows feathers in that cave, because before he was conceived of the Virgin, the flesh of which he was to be conceived was sanctified through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit; before he came forth from the womb, God was made man.

[Col. 0792D] Therefore, with the fullness of feathers—that is, of graces—our hawk came forth from the Virgin’s womb to fly throughout all lands and catch every kind of bird. Having sent a star, he immediately caught the Magi in the wings of faith and brought them to worship him. He also spread his wings toward the south, saying: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24), who, because of the fathers and the Law, worshipped one God with southern fervor. Beyond those feathers of virtue belonging to his origin and birth, which were naturally rooted in him and could not be plucked out, this hawk assumed other feathers in gathering the disciples, and in them traveled throughout the whole world, because “their sound went out into all the earth”; they were like the sound of a multitude [Col. 0793A] and of armies. But the Jewish thorns stripped him of his apostolic feathers in the Passion, as in winter, when all fled, leaving him. Yet at the scent of the Resurrection and the warmth of the summer season, the feathers returned; adhering better and more strongly, they were able sooner to die with him than to be plucked away from him.

Therefore, on the day of the Ascension, or flight, the hawk addresses his feathers thus: “Going into the whole world, preach the Gospel to every creature; he who believes and is baptized shall be saved,” etc. (Mark 15:24). Behold, our hawk that grows feathers through wisdom spreads its wings southward—not only assembling in the conception a body of virtues and a soul of graces, but also in the Resurrection recalling the college [Col. 0793B] of Apostles; for in the Ascension he summons them to fly by command and example, when he sends them into the whole world while he himself, with uplifted hands, was borne into heaven. Then the hawk became the eagle that makes its nest in the heights. So long as they could see him, they looked upon the hawk in flight; but when a cloud received him from their sight, he was raised up like an eagle and made his nest on high—that is, at the Father’s right hand—and his nest, that is, his throne. This throne is rightly called a nest, because there he cherishes, begets, and nourishes his young: he cherishes sinners through patience, begets them through mercy, and nourishes them through pardon.

But now, dearest brothers, let us consider whence our hawk or eagle flew, where he flew to, and by what way; and although we cannot grasp him fully, yet let us make an effort with halting footsteps to limp after him from afar. One very brief phrase in the Gospel defines this flight: “He came forth from God and goes to God” (John 13:3). Again, he says: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 16:28); and again: “I leave the world and go to the Father” (ibid.). Behold whence and where he flew. Do you wish to see by what way? “I am the truth, the way, and the life” (John 14:6). Behold by what way, whence, and where. He came from the Father because the Father sent him; he returned to the Father because the Father glorified him with the glory he had before the world was; through himself he came and goes, because he obeyed the Father freely unto death through a will uniform and identical with the Father’s, just as he returns freely to immortality and glorification.

Therefore let each of us say to the Father: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world”; again: “I leave the world and go to the Father.” The father from whom I came forth is Adam; the Father to whom I return is God. Thus I came from father Adam with original sin; I go to Father God with spiritual grace. I came forth badly; I entered badly. I came forth from evil and came to evil; therefore evil is evil, says everyone who has come forth from the father of flesh and come into the world of wickedness. Original evil, actual evil: from an evil root I came to an evil branch; but the root’s evil sprouted poison, by which the shoot of the branch was poisoned.

[Col. 0794A] Therefore, from the sole of my foot to the crown of my head there is no soundness in me, because my mother conceived me in sins and my conscience conceived me in evil habit. In my flesh I find no good, because my scars have become corrupt because of my foolishness; and in my soul I find evil, because evil concupiscence reigns there. For sin proceeds from sin, when the vapor of evil desire comes out from the soul as from the inward parts into the flesh; and in the flesh, as by reciprocal friction, the fuel of sin rises more forcefully, setting ablaze the tinder of our frailty and burning it away unto destruction. What then shall I do, unhappy man? Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ, who likewise left the world and goes to the Father.

O man, leave the world in manner of life, hatred, contempt, departure, and mortification, so that you may be dead to the world by affection and the world may be dead to you by rejection. Leave it as excommunicated, as leprous, as heretical, as a destroyer, as a thief, as a murderer, as a dung-heap, as a pit, as hell, as a most foul sewer. But go to the Father as to a feast, as to a wedding, as to a homeland, as to a crown, as to a robe, as to a refuge, as to a harbor, as to heaven, as to God.

But because you came from father into the world, or because again from the world you go to the Father: certainly you came forth from father [Col. 0794C] through the lust of the flesh, through the burning of desire, through disobedience to the commandment; and you came into the world, where you multiplied at interest the sin you had brought with you, when you added hay, straw, and wood of worldly words, deeds, and thoughts as fuel for sin. And as long as you lived in the world, you were carried headlong from pit to pit, from evil to worse, from iniquity to iniquity, so that blood touched blood, the locust consumed what the caterpillar had left, and one hairy creature cried to another; and you drew sin as with a rope, when you ran from brothel to robbery, from robbery to perjury, from perjury to wrongdoing, from tavern to theatre.

[Col. 0794D] Behold the way by which you came forth from the Father and came into the world, and also the way by which you traversed the world. Therefore one must again leave the world and come to the Father—but by another way, because it is to another homeland. My brothers, behold the routes by which you come from dormitory to monastery, from monastery to cloister, from cloister again to monastery or chapter-house, from chapter-house to field, from field to refectory. Without doubt these are good routes; without doubt they go to the Father—if you always behold God before your sight, if you always have your hearts above, if you always seek the things above, if you always pour out your desire before God, and do not cease to run after his back until you come to the place where Israel beholds the God of gods in Zion—he who lives, etc.

## Sermon LIII. On Pentecost I

[Col. 0795A]

The divine fire came, not burning but illumining; not consuming but shining; and it found the disciples’ hearts clean receptacles and bestowed upon them the gifts of charisms. It found them united in charity, and the overflowing divinity of brightness illumined them. Before I set tongue to speech and hand to writing concerning the Spirit of God, I implore the grace of him concerning whom I wish to speak, so that, washed in the fountain of grace, I may offer a true discourse concerning the Spirit of truth; that I may draw forth a pure channel of conscience from the Spirit of truth, so that the little boat of my tongue may neither sink in the marshes of falsehood nor stick fast in the shallows of vanity.

[Col. 0795B] Come, therefore, Holy Spirit; fill the hearts of your faithful, and kindle in them the fire of your love. Fill us from your fullness; kindle us from your fire and warmth—you who contain all things, who cherish all things. Fill those whom you contain; make fruitful those whom you cherish, that through your filling we may be satisfied, through your fire kindled, through your fruitfulness live, through your adoption ennobled, in number multiplied, in duration made everlasting: satisfied with sweetness, kindled with charity, living through brightness, ennobled by adoption, multiplied in number, made everlasting in age.

Plainly, that Spirit is noble by procession, not by birth: for he has no birth from the Father, but procession; none from a mother—who does not exist—whether birth or procession; but as he proceeds from the Father, so also he proceeds from the Son. Nothing is nobler than the Father and the Son, just as nothing is higher than God. And, to take an example from lower things to higher: what in man is nobler than the spirit of man? So in God, nothing is nobler than his Spirit. But what do I call the Spirit’s nobility except identity with the Father and the Son? Or what nobility do we seek from the Holy Spirit except that we may be one with the Father and the Son? May he grant us unity with the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

But how shall this be, O Holy Spirit—that the most abject little worm be assumed into so sublime a unity of the Trinity, and that the supreme Trinity suffer from this no injury, the supreme unity no multiplication, the supreme majesty no degeneration, the supreme identity no change, the supreme stability and immutability no mutability? [Col. 0795D] Yet this does not occur separately, so that some whole greater than that entire whole may exist; nor is that whole itself, taken together, so astonishing that you should despair of believing it, because the whole Trinity, being such a whole together in Trinity, is greater than its whole taken separately in the distinction of persons. Whatever is added to that whole—as the Incarnation of the Word—does not make that whole some greater whole, since it does not make another whole than the same whole it was before there was added to it that which was not with that whole and therefore could not itself be a whole, since it could not exist without that whole. Therefore, when we are made one in that whole which we call Trinity and unity, we indeed are made better, but it is not made greater or better.

[Col. 0796A] Let us therefore ask what happens to us when through the Holy Spirit, as through a bond and rennet, we are joined to the Father, the Son, and that same Holy Spirit. For although the rennet is consubstantial with the Father and Son, it binds us together with one another and joins us to the Holy Trinity. By the customary name this rennet is called charity; and this rennet is made from nothing other than the most tender and most tenacious marrow of the Father and Son, by which they flow toward one another in an eternal course of mutual love.

When, therefore, this rennet of charity has been poured into the hearts of believers, by its tenderness it softens its vessels, and by its tenacity it makes them firm, so that, softened and as though melted, the hearts themselves run together and mingle. It works similarly in different persons by likeness of liquid, and, binding and strengthening within itself what had first been separated from itself, makes them hold firmly and not let go what they have grasped in tenderness. Thus, from diverse hearts made one by a gathering of dispositions, he who makes those of one disposition dwell in a house recalls dispersions to unity, dissensions to peace, heresies to faith, and those at discord to charity. Thus unity arises for us from multitude, concord from diversity, peace from rancor, chastity from corruption, security from fear, tranquillity from disturbance, charity from rivalry, grace from derision.

Behold what the Spirit’s rennet does for us: gathering us together with one another, and joining us [perhaps *conjungens*] to God. Consider, if you can, how the Spirit [Col. 0796C] of God, taking up the spirit of man, introduces it into the palace of the Trinity and, with unutterable groanings, longs to draw it after himself into the familiar chambers of the Father’s and Son’s inmost being; so that there it may hear what man is not permitted to speak, see what eye has not seen, hear what ear has not heard, and understand what has not risen into the human heart. Consider what the human spirit thinks when it sees thoughts of peace and not of affliction; when, without a vessel of bodily fantasies and imaginations, it sees itself sailing upon those streams of heavenly charisms; when it sees the return-flowings of sweetness from Father to Son and from Son to Father, carried back by the rowing of the Holy Spirit. Consider what delight the human spirit drinks in when, in its ecstasy, it sees the threads of predestination tied in [Col. 0796D] the heart of God: so subtle that no one can grasp them; so strong that no one can break them; so long that they contain within themselves the bounds of the ages; so retentive that no one can escape; so intricate that no one can untie them.

Consider how greatly your spirit marvels when, according to its name, it sees itself made spiritual through close kinship and received into the fellowship of the Holy Spirit: from the Good One receiving goodness; from the Holy One innocence; from the Just One justice; from the Living One life; from the Chaste One chastity; from the Wise One wisdom; from the Meek One meekness; from the full One, and the One wholly full, a fullness of fullnesses and a fullness of graces. Consider with what mighty shock your spirit shudders at [Col. 0797A] its evils when, reflecting and reckoning upon the depth of sanctification in God’s Spirit, it sees that, if it had lacked iniquity, it would not have lacked so great and such a fellowship. Consider with what desirable progress it is borne onward, that it may drink more closely of those foretaste joys, until living waters flow from its belly and there comes to be in it a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.

Consider—and always consider—lest grief seize the end of joy; lest, having begun with the spirit, you be completed in the flesh; lest, with Lucifer, you fall from heaven to Tartarus; lest you be drawn from your holy purpose to worldly things; lest, abandoned by the Holy Spirit, you be handed over to an evil spirit; lest, having lost paradise, you be tormented in hell with the devil. To a spirit so considering the divine fire comes, not burning but illumining; not consuming but [Col. 0797B] shining. It comes freely, because it is neither preceded by merits nor compelled to come; it comes also when drawn, because it does not refuse, through a mind prepared beforehand by operative grace, to enrich it through cooperating grace with a fuller gift of charisms.

He came as lord, as guest; he came as a cultivator; finally, he came as divine fire. The lord comes to the servant, the guest to the lodging, the cultivator to the field, the fire to a forest of wood. The lord does not oppress the servant by imposing everything in a spirit of servitude; the guest does not trouble his host or lodging by demanding impossibilities or presumptuously expecting possible things without recompense. The cultivator does not neglect his field: he uproots thorns and thistles, yet carefully cultivates it by sowing good seed. [Col. 0797C] That forest of silver, gold, and precious stones the fire does not burn up, but illuminates; it does not consume, but tests, so that the silver may be purified sevenfold, the gold may be refined, and the stones may be kindled to disclose from prophetic lips the reproach of Egypt.

Therefore, when prevenient grace has thus, as it were, run ahead of itself, it finds the hearts of the disciples to be clean receptacles and bestows upon them gifts of grace. For subsequent grace finds them such as prevenient grace prepares them: “clean receptacles,” he says. However adorned those temples—that is, hearts—to which the Holy Spirit comes may be with the equipment of other virtues, the dwelling is still scarcely worthy unless the whitening of charity has further adorned the whole floor and walls. Fasts summon the Holy Spirit; prayers urge him on; vigils call him; silences move him; almsgiving restrains him; contemplation or meditation brings him; compunction introduces him; continence receives him; charity serves him; peace gives savor.

If grace finds such a household in the heart, what can it do except render grace for grace? For what else is meant by “he found the hearts of the disciples clean receptacles and repaid them with gifts of grace,” except that he gave grace for grace? O Holy Spirit, create a clean heart in us, that we may prepare clean receptacles for you; that we may empty, before your face, the bile of resentment and the poison of malice; so that you may take pleasure in our souls, and so that we may be fit, if not for kinds of tongues, yet at least for the fullness of graces. May he deign to grant this, who lives and reigns through all things, etc. [Col. 0798A]

## SERMON LIV. ON PENTECOST II

“The apostles were speaking in various tongues the mighty works of God” (Acts 2).

Drums or cymbals give forth no sound unless a certain striker hangs in their middle, commonly called a *batallum* [clapper]. Reverberating now here, now there, it sends back through the air a musical sound far and near. Thus surely the apostles, before the coming of the Holy Spirit, were without a voice: they indeed possessed faith in Christ, but did not dare to preach. That founder [or: “fury,” *furor*] of heavenly signs, while he was still with them in the flesh, had melted their hearts from the purest metal in the rounded casting of perfection [Col. 0798B] and had already prepared them as most suitable instruments; for he had made known to them all that he had heard from his Father and had handed over to them all the mysteries of the Church.

Yet those instruments or drums lay without the clapper which afterwards sent their voice through all the earth and their words to the ends of the world: “When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, there suddenly came from heaven a sound, as of a violent spirit coming; it filled the entire house where the apostles were sitting; and all were filled with the Holy Spirit, and they began to speak in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (ibid., 1). Therefore the Word who had ascended to the Father sent the apostles the clapper of preaching [Col. 0798C] in fiery tongues, by which they might strike the cymbal of faith and thunder into the ears of minds the sound of the exalted God through teaching and exhortation. Having received such a plectrum, the apostles spoke in various tongues the mighty works of God.

Because the Holy Spirit, dearest brethren, appeared in fiery tongues, let us chastise our tongues against idle, superfluous, harmful, lying, slanderous, murmuring, impure, and filthy speech. For a tongue immersed in such dregs and marshes will not speak the mighty works of God; it will not speak the powers of the Lord; it will not sing the mercies of the Lord; it will not meditate upon praise, law, or wisdom of the Lord. O tongue, if you are filled with the Holy Spirit, you will be God’s instrument; but if [Col. 0798D] infected with serpentine poison you sow discords among brethren, you will be the devil’s fan—indeed, his scourge. A good tongue is a good messenger: it neither yields to flattery nor approaches offence nor departs from truth. A wicked, deceitful tongue is indeed a small member, as the apostle James says (ch. 3:5), but it makes great boasts. “Behold,” says that same apostle (v. 5 ff.), “how great a forest so small a fire sets ablaze; and the tongue is a fire, which stains the whole body and sets ablaze the wheel of our birth, itself set ablaze by Gehenna: an unruly evil, full of deadly poison.”

Such was the tongue of the ancient serpent, which in Paradise set ablaze the whole forest of the human race: it kindled the root by suggestion and consumed the multitude of branches by the tasting of the forbidden fruit. Hence original sin spread through all the posterity of Adam’s children. Without doubt it stained the whole body of Adam and Eve, immediately offering the first beginnings of disobedience in their shameful members as soon as the human being ate the fruit. And as the human being had been disobedient to God, so that movement of the private parts would thereafter by no means consent to obey the mind—or even the human being himself. It also set ablaze the wheel of our birth, itself ablaze from Gehenna, because we are born with original sin, from which arise the tinder of sin and concupiscence, or the law of the members. Thus the wheel is always turning; thus from the day of our birth we are never shaken free from the yoke of sin—an unruly evil because of avarice, full of deadly poison because of wickedness. [Col. 0799B]

O human being, O Adam, O human race, O soul: what shall be given you, or what applied to your deceitful tongue? Surely, the sharp arrows of the Mighty One with desolating coals—indeed, fiery tongues, varied tongues, tongues of dogs, tongues of angels. Sharp arrows are against deceit; desolating coals against poison; fiery tongues against sin; varied tongues against weariness; tongues of dogs against the wound inflicted; tongues of angels against the serpent’s tongue. The arrow opens a way to the heart; the desolating coal consumes rust; the fiery tongue teaches and kindles what is frozen and foolish; the varied tongue raises up what is lukewarm and weary; the tongue of dogs heals the wounded; the tongue of angels teaches the earthly one the Canticles of the songs of Zion.

[Col. 0799C] Therefore those who received the firstfruits of the Spirit spoke in various tongues the mighty works of God. Clearly, what was within came forth, so that from the fullness with which they had been filled by the Holy Spirit they might pour forth a good word and speak in harmony, comparing spiritual things with spiritual. For the tongue sits like a doorkeeper at the door of the heart, the interpreter of thoughts and affections which lie hidden within as though in a cloister and never proceed into public unless the doorkeeper opens the gate. Accordingly, the heart fears to persuade it to speak cold malice just as a lukewarm affection of the mind cannot remain long shut within a fiery tongue. For what is within warms; what is without burns.

A fiery tongue knows no cold heart: it is a flaming and turning sword—flaming because it nourishes charity, turning because it resists the heart’s instability; flaming because of charity, turning because of variety. Charity is the movement of the mind to love God for his own sake and a friend for God’s sake. For as the nature of fire seeks upward and warms what is near, so charity, which is within us, both returns in love to God from whom it comes and gathers the neighbor who is near by embracing him. Nor is charity itself different, but its effect is different, according as we love God or neighbor; just as the Spirit who appeared in tongue and fire is not different, but we understand one thing in the tongue and another in the fire. In the tongue we have sobriety toward our neighbor; [Col. 0800A] in the fire, ecstasy of mind toward God—so that whether we are sober, it is for ourselves, or whether we are carried beyond ourselves in mind, it is for God.

In the tongue let us preach Christ crucified; in the fire, wisdom among the wise. In the tongue let us be active; in the fire contemplative. In the tongue let us receive with Moses the first tables of the Law; in the fire the second tables of the Gospel. In the tongue let us order our conduct; in the fire search out the deep mysteries of our faith. In the tongue let us receive confession; in the fire, power. The apostles, however, spoke in various tongues the mighty works of God: accusing themselves and glorifying God; recounting wisdom in the creation of things and commending goodness in the restoration of the human race; rejoicing with those who rejoice and weeping with those who weep; going wherever the Spirit went and returning in the likeness of lightning; preaching the face of a human being, setting forth the incarnation; preaching the face of a calf, the passion and death; preaching the face of a lion, the resurrection; and preaching the face of an eagle extended above, the ascension. [Col. 0800B]

Behold how the apostles speak in various tongues the mighty works of God. Why in various tongues, when it is one and the same Spirit who speaks in them? Surely because there are divisions of graces; certainly because the spirit of understanding is holy, one, manifold, subtle, eloquent, mobile, undefiled, certain, gentle, loving the good, keen, hindering nothing from doing good, humane, kind, steadfast, certain, secure, possessing all power, beholding all things, and comprehending every intelligent spirit: pure and subtle. [Col. 0800C] Why, then, should it be surprising that he makes tongues varied, when he has graces so varied? In a harp or psaltery, the stroke of one and the same finger yields one sound on this string and another on that; and the melody is varied in as many ways as the finger touches more strongly or more lightly the plectrum in which the whole assembly of strings hangs.

Yet two matters are chiefly to be considered in the various tongues: either this variety belongs to the Spirit that strikes, so variously described above, or it belongs to the differing condition of hearers, which the teacher can perceive only through the Spirit. For no teacher would know how men ought to be admonished, how women, secular persons, religious, beginners, those making progress, the perfect, the modest, the obstinate, or each person according to age, temperament, rank, and every distinction arising from all circumstances—unless he who possesses all knowledge taught him. Therefore the Spirit supplies variety of tongues: he is called by a varied description but defined by none.

He is called the Spirit of understanding, by equality with the Son; holy, both in name and reality; one, by the singularity of his procession; manifold, by the manifold distribution of graces; subtle, by the incomprehensibility of his nature and reason; eloquent, by his most ready power of discourse; mobile, by his immensity; undefiled, by his purity; [Col. 0801A] certain, by his unchangeable truth; gentle, by the long-suffering of his patience; loving the good, by the property of his nature; keen, by the liveliness of his intelligence; one who hinders nothing from doing good, by the precept or prohibition of his command; humane, by compassion; kind, by the bestowal of gifts; steadfast, by eternity; certain, by promise; secure, by protection; possessing all power, by might; beholding all things, by illumination; comprehending every intelligent spirit, by clarity; pure, by uprightness; subtle, by foreknowledge or predestination.

Nevertheless, the one and same Spirit is not varied so that at one time he is holy and not one, at another one and not manifold, at another manifold and not subtle, at another subtle and not eloquent, at another eloquent and not mobile, at another mobile and not undefiled, at another undefiled and not certain, at another certain and not gentle, or at another loving the good and keen, and so forth. Rather, all these things are embraced together and at once by the nature of the Spirit. For from whatever quarter, at whatever time, and in whatever need or want you ask for the grace of the Holy Spirit, you will receive from a full chest that whereby all your troubles may be driven away; yet the abundance of the chest is not thereby emptied. In this chest may grace preserve garments of many kinds and colors, so that, just as our folly is instructed by various tongues, so our nakedness may be clothed by the variety of garments, our ugliness adorned, and our rusticity decked about. O fountain of oil, Holy Spirit, pour forth and pour into our hearts from your streams forgiveness of sins, fullness of graces, and abundance of heavenly blessings. [Col. 0801C]

But let us portray our own spirit in a corresponding description, as best we can, so that a particular title of God’s Spirit may come to each of our needs, and he may return contrary things for contrary things—not for evil, but for good: that good Spirit who does not repay us in the present according to our merits, but according to his gratuitous goodness. My spirit, therefore, O Lord, is a spirit of folly, while yours is a spirit of understanding; mine is sinful, while yours is holy; mine, would that it were adoptive, while yours is one; mine, would that it had even one blessing, while yours is manifold in blessings; mine is crude, while yours is subtle; mine mute, while yours is eloquent; mine slow, while yours is mobile; mine defiled, while yours is undefiled; mine changeable, while yours is certain; mine impatient, while yours is gentle; mine loving iniquity, while yours loves good; mine dull, while yours is keen; mine hinders beneficence through negligence, while yours hinders nothing from doing good; mine inhumane, while yours is humane; mine cruel, while yours is kind; mine unstable, while yours is steadfast; mine fearful, while yours is secure; mine has no power, while yours [Col. 0802A] possesses all power; mine has no prudence, while yours beholds all things; mine does not comprehend even itself, while yours comprehends every intelligent spirit; mine is impure, while yours is pure; mine is dull, while yours is subtle.

Turn, therefore, gracious Spirit, and pour out from this your Spirit into this our spirit, so that your wisdom may overcome our folly; your sanctification our impiety; your single procession our descent; your manifold grace our manifold offence; your subtlety our grossness; your eloquence our impeded tongue; your mobility our sloth; your undefilement our corruption; your certainty our doubt; your gentleness our harshness; [Col. 0802B] your love of good our malice; your keenness our inertia; your humanity our hardness; your kindness our avarice; your steadfastness our inconstancy; your security our fearfulness; your certainty our uncertainty; your power our weakness; your providence our blindness; your divinity our frailty; your purity our impurity; your subtlety our dullness. We shall speak these your mighty works in various—indeed, transformed—tongues, O Lord, if you give us from your Spirit, as the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, spoke in various tongues the mighty works of God. May you deign to grant this to us, you who live and reign, God, through all ages, [Col. 0802C] etc.

## SERMON LV. ON PENTECOST III

“Create in me a clean heart, O God,” etc. (Psalm 50:12).

Today the apostles take their noon-day rest amid a heap of divine benefits: intoxicated with the new wine of grace, they have melted into divine love; surrounded on every side by the lilies of graces, they have passed from human fear into eternal security, saying: “It is better to obey God than men” (Acts 5:29). Until now God had neither given to humankind all that he possessed nor done for humankind all that he was able; but, having sent the Holy Spirit from heaven, he said all that he had heard from the Father, gave all that he had received, and did for human beings all that he could and ought.

[Col. 0802D] O human poverty, have you a repository or treasury where you can preserve riches so great and so many? They indeed rejoice in the gift by a singular prerogative, but it also demands no lesser solemnity in its reception and depositing. Woe to that person who tied up the Lord’s grace in a napkin and hid it in the earth! Nor did that prodigal escape punishment who, by living luxuriously, consumed with harlots—that is, carnal desires—the portion of divine grace given him by the Father. Therefore every corner of the house must be examined, and the whole house swept out, so that we may find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob, lest grace, offended by the unfitness or foulness of the place, fly away from us—for it does not dwell in a body subjected to sins.

[Col. 0803A] Therefore, before you offer us this great gift, this good bestowal and perfect gift, prepare, O God, in us a suitable place for yourself and for your grace. For just as we await from you alone, who are rich, the gift that is above every gift, so we ask from you alone, the wise architect, that a place be created: namely, a clean heart. For nothing in a human being is more excellent than the heart, and nothing is more acceptable to God than a clean heart. Meanwhile, dearest brethren, wait and each enter into your own heart. Open its windows, kindle its lamps, carefully investigate whatever is there or is done there. Seize whatever great or small thing whispers there, and bring it before the judgment of reason. Then at last judge rightly whether it is fitting for the grace of the Holy Spirit to enter among things not washed and not cleansed.

[Col. 0803B] But in order that I may keep the seal of your hearts intact, let me be silent about them; if I wish to judge my own heart and judge how great in it is the stickiness of past evils, how great the rottenness of evil affections, how great the filth of carnal passions, and how great the occupation of the scab of depraved desires, I believe that it cannot endure angelic purity—how much less divine purity! Therefore, because my whole heart is foul and rotten, O God of my heart, create a new one according to your heart. In this vessel I dare to place the Holy Spirit, as Moses placed manna before the Lord—as much as a *gomor*, which is three measures, could contain—in a golden vessel, to preserve it for future generations.

This is the purest place, outside the camp of the five senses, where the priest—that is, Christ—having changed his former garments, that is, having put off on the cross the assumed mortality, clothed in the tunic of immortality and the linen garments of impassibility, deposits the ashes: that is, the memorial of the Lord’s passion and the completion of all holiness through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit. Just as a defiled body was not fitting for Christ, so an unclean heart is not fitting for the Holy Spirit. Therefore the immaculate, inviolate Virgin, fitted for God alone, incorrupt in flesh, whole in faith, fair as the moon and chosen as the sun, became the workshop of the divine incarnation. And what kind of heart must be sought in which the Spirit of sanctification may rest with the Father and the Son? [Col. 0803D]

Let the unclean spirit, then—like a robber and a possessor in bad faith—depart from the heart, or rather be cast out, with all the most foul offspring of vices. Let the grace of the Holy Spirit, with the most noble gathering and bestowal of his gifts, enter—or rather possess—the heart cleansed from every defilement of flesh and spirit: grace working and cooperating with a double benefit. It gladdens and makes blessed the heart which it illumines by its outpouring. For it frees from evil and assists in good; it frees the oppressed and gives the freed person nobility and liberty; it excludes vices and implants virtues. Hence in the Song of Songs: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow” (Song 4:16). From the north every evil will be laid open, because the contrary wind extinguishes the seeds of good will as they spring up [Col. 0804A] and, lest they be renewed through repentance, cuts them off with its poisonous blast.

But the coming south wind casts out the demon, so that it may not retain what it has possessed or stretch its sickle into another’s harvest. It blows through the garden, set ablaze with charity, causing the richest aromatic species to bubble up from the heaviness of the earth: humility, chastity, gentleness, innocence, peace, concord, obedience, patience, poverty of spirit, wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, fear of the Lord, justice, sobriety, prudence, and every shrub of that field which the heavenly Father planted, the Son cultivates, and the Spirit causes to germinate.

Today, in a good, clean, and new heart, the south wind visits these little beds planted by perfumers—that is, established by preachers through urgent preaching—perfecting and strengthening the swelling figs which it has brought forth, that is, the beginnings of good work inspired by the Holy Spirit; or ripening the grapes of apostolic devotion, sweetened by the nocturnal dew of the Lord’s passion and the morning heat of the resurrection. Hence the Psalmist says: “You visited the earth and made it drunk; you multiplied to enrich it” (Psalm 64:10). [Col. 0804B] You visited the earth, that is, the primitive Church in the apostles, by calling, choosing, receiving, teaching, and dwelling with it until the Passion; you made it drunk with the wine of joy through the manifestation of the resurrection and the glorification of the ascension; you multiplied to enrich it through the most abundant sending of the Holy Spirit.

But because the Holy Spirit can never possess an unclean heart, the person who desires to receive him first asks that a clean heart be created within, saying: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 50:11). Neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem is the place where God must be worshipped, but he must be worshipped in spirit and truth—that is, with a clean heart. For what is purer than heaven? A clean heart. What is brighter than the sun? A clean heart. What is fairer than the firmament? A clean heart. What is more solid than earth? A clean heart. What is deeper than the abyss? A clean heart. What is more excellent among human creatures? A clean heart. What is more like an angel? A clean heart. What is nearer to God? [Col. 0804D] A clean heart. What is more desirable among every gift of graces? A clean heart. Therefore: “Create in me a clean heart, O God.” For who can do this except God? A clean heart, if left to itself, is empty unless it is filled with God.

Three things, therefore, come together for a heart to be clean: good will, holy thought, and right intention. If an unclean thought has not polluted the bed of the heart; if a warped and dark intention has not distorted the heart’s direction; if the turning away or overthrow of evil will has not shaken the foundation of faith, hope, and charity—then you have a clean heart; you have a fitting lodging for the Holy Spirit. But if you have a clean heart, you have nothing unclean: a clean eye, a clean hand, clean lips; inward and outward things are without doubt clean. For as sin entered the world through one human being, so malice drips from an unclean heart like water from a leaking roof, into every affection of the soul and every sense of the body, so that in the whole human being there is no cleanliness from sole of foot to crown of head. But Jesus Christ, who came to save the whole human being, sent his Holy Spirit into our hearts, crying, “Abba, Father” (Galatians 4:6), so that, when the heart is healed, the whole human being may be healed; when the heart is cleansed, the whole human being may be cleansed; and when the heart is renewed, the whole human being may be renewed—through the same our Lord Jesus Christ and through the Holy Spirit from God the Father, to whom be honor and glory. Amen. [Col. 0805A]

## SERMON LVI. ON PENTECOST IV

Today Jesus Christ, according to his promise, baked the twelve loaves of presentation in a heated oven [Col. 0805B] by his own and his Father’s heat. He drew them out well crusted and placed them with incense upon his table at the entrance of the tabernacle. Nothing burned, nothing raw, nothing unbaked or half-baked remained in them: strength was increased, not nature extinguished; the human fear that makes people raw was removed. Patience works testing and, poured into the apostolic inmost parts to the marrow, bakes away every weakness; perfect charity is thoroughly rooted.

For what would the Holy Spirit not accomplish in this furnace of his upon the apostles that that fourth one, who appeared in the Babylonian furnace like a Son of Man, accomplished for the three boys? As Scripture says: “The fire did not touch them at all, nor did it grieve them or bring them any distress” (Dan. 3:50). What are you doing, Holy Spirit? Why have you come? For what purpose did you descend upon the apostles in fiery tongues? Was it to torture them, to burn them? Rather, to cook them and make food which Isaac, old and full of days, gladly eats; indeed, to strengthen them for receiving and retaining the heavenly liquid, so that henceforth they may be like a wineskin in frost, fearing not what a human being may do, holding the word of life and fearing no disturbance.

For if those three boys were of such constancy that they said to the king urging them to worship his golden image: “We have no need,” they say, “to answer concerning [Col. 0805D] this matter. Behold, our God whom we worship is able to rescue us from the furnace of burning fire and to deliver us from your hands, O king. But if he does not will it, let it be known to you, O king, that we do not worship your gods, nor do we adore the golden statue which you have set up” (ibid., 16–18). O faith, O grace, O power, O spirit of fortitude! Few in number, because three; weak in age, because boys; miserable in condition, because captives; besieged by place and time, because the king had summoned the whole province to idolatry; threatened by torment, because the furnace was heated seven times more than usual—and what did faith do? It did what it is accustomed to do. It conquered the world, conquered age, conquered condition, conquered the pressing necessity of time and place, conquered the king, conquered the furnace, conquered every fear.

[Col. 0806A] Nebuchadnezzar, what do you put under and add to your fires? Surely naphtha, pitch, tow, and faggots. Naphtha, which among the Persians is the refuse of flax or fuel for fire, is the vanity of this world; tow is the concupiscence of the flesh; pitch, the defilements of avarice and luxury; faggots, the assaults sent through evil angels. The furnace burns fiercely where malignant spirits blow with the bellows of their temptations, stirring the incentives of the flesh, the voracity of gluttony, the rapacity of avarice, the intemperance of luxury, and the vanity of the world. But, as the Psalmist says, “If I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, because you are with me” (Psalm 22:4)—you who said to your apostles: “Do not fear, because I have conquered the world” (John 16:33).

Another furnace was kindled by the carpenter’s son, who sits refining and cleansing silver and purifies the sons of Levi. Today, from the seat of his majesty, Jesus sent fire to where the apostles were arranged as in a furnace: to teach every truth; to remove the weakness of the flesh; to speak the variety of every language; to perform the power of miracles. In this furnace the Lord tests his chosen ones, as Gideon tested the people who went with him to war, by their lapping of water; as Moses tested his people at the waters of Contradiction. [Col. 0806B]

He who is the Word forms weapons for himself—not discordant tongues, but tongues suited to the office of preaching laid upon them. For the world is converted not by spears but by tongues, so that the one who had perished through the serpent’s tongue might be restored and redeemed by tongues received from the Holy Spirit. Observe the shape of the tongue: it is broad, flat, round, long, and pointed. Broad, because God is charity; flat, because he is merciful and gentle; round, because eternal; long, because long-suffering; pointed, because the word of God is living, effectual, and more penetrating than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit. [Col. 0806C]

In the Book of Wisdom, Wisdom, the artificer of all things, who promised and sent the Holy Spirit to the apostles, is described thus: “In her,” it says (Wisdom 7:22), “is a spirit of understanding: one, manifold, subtle, eloquent, mobile, undefiled, certain, gentle, loving the good, keen, hindering nothing from doing good, humane, kind, steadfast, certain, secure.” A tongue upon which the Holy Spirit confers benefits truly comes from heaven; beyond doubt it is the minister of God’s Word, kin and sister to the Spirit. It has a spirit of understanding, that it may understand parables, riddles, and the deep mysteries of Scripture; holy, that it may not utter shameful, dishonorable, or poisonous things; one, lest it rend the tunic of the catholic and universal Church; manifold, that it may bring forth many branches from the one root of charity; subtle, that it may comprehend the mystery of the kingdom of God; eloquent, lest it be entangled by an evil conscience; mobile, that it may follow the revolving wheels of the two Testaments; undefiled, that it may speak from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith; certain, lest it be carried about by every wind of doctrine; gentle, lest it [Col. 0807A] reject or flee human frailty; loving the good, that it may say, “How sweet are your utterances to my palate”; keen, that with the eagle it may seek above the stars of God the Word who was in the beginning with God; hindering nothing from doing good, always urging toward better things; humane, because of weakness; kind, because of the abundance of mercy; steadfast, because of the desire for eternity; secure, because of the testimony of conscience and good works.

Whatever the fire of God bakes inwardly for one’s own salvation, the fiery tongue draws out entirely, like a shovel, for the neighbor’s outward edification. For the tongue is mediator between the Spirit dwelling in the mind and the neighbor waiting at the doors of wisdom. The Spirit enters without voice and commands the tongue to utter audibly what it has heard. Things silently imparted are sweetly commanded; things humbly suggested through the tongue are lovingly received. When Christ feeds the soul with his marrow, he is a shepherd; when he commands one to undertake care for one’s brethren, he is a baker. Thus he is both shepherd and baker: shepherd in the quiet and secluded refectory of contemplation; baker in the laborious and tumultuous duty of providing for the brethren and preaching truth; shepherd in the morning, ministering the verdant things of the field of most delightful reading; at noon, opening the wine-cellar of highest delight. [Col. 0807B]

Behold the baker; behold the bakehouse; behold the bread; behold the fire; behold the cook; behold the oven. The shepherd ground flour on the cross as on a mill, while Pilate’s wheel—the sentence of condemnation—turned amid the waters of Jewish accusation. Then the disciples, unable to bear the tumult and clamor of the mill and the sound of many waters, all left him and fled; and, shaken as if by a winnowing fan, they were reduced almost to the finest dust of despair. But the good baker presented his bread to the apostles in the resurrection, now so baked that he dies no more and death no longer has dominion over him. Appearing to them for forty days and speaking of the kingdom of God, he refreshed them with the strength of that food until the day of the ascension. [Col. 0807C]

Certainly throughout this whole period he as it were leavened the hearts of the disciples with the leaven of faith. On the day of the ascension, raising his hands, blessing them, and commanding them to remain in the city until they were clothed with power from on high, he covered his dough, so that at the coming of the Holy Spirit, on the day of Pentecost, they might be baked by the fire sent from heaven where they were gathered. And just as the good angels, after Lucifer’s fall, were established and confirmed by God’s grace so that they could fall no more, so these men were united to Christ by this furnace and the curdling agent of charity, so that thereafter they might not fall away from his charity. It is written that “charity never fails” (1 Cor. 13:8), and “there is perpetual fire upon the altar.”

They received crusts above, below, and around, and crumb within, from the fire. The lower crust was confidence, that they might not fear death. The upper crust was love of God, that they might love God with all their heart, all their soul, and all [Col. 0808A] their strength. The surrounding crust was chastening of the flesh, that they might resist the flesh’s concupiscences and be strong in battle. The crumb in the middle was charity, which Solomon spread in his litter, as it is said: “He spread its midst with charity because of the daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 3:10). Again, this baker makes both lay and priestly loaves: for I bring a lay loaf to the altar, but receive back a priestly one.

The Creator of all things created bread in the field among other things; but above and beyond all things, at the altar he ineffably changes this same bread into his body by his power. God chose for himself, as it were, a grain of wheat: the body conceived from the Holy Spirit in the virginal womb, in which he completed all the things said above. He chose, and chose beforehand, the Virgin from whom he would take flesh; he winnowed by assuming our nature, so that from flesh of the sinful mass he might receive it without sin, creating it, sanctifying it, and creating it by sanctifying.

In that cross he ground [the grains written above]; in the resurrection he sifted them—hence: “Even though we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him thus no longer.” He mixed the flour with water when, in a sinless body, he received baptism from John; he shaped the loaves when he chose the apostles; he had an oven and fire in the oven, because “the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily in him”; he cleansed the threshing-floor—that is, the Church—so that it should have neither spot nor wrinkle, and should shake the dust from its feet; he arranged the loaves, whether the disciples or [Col. 0808C] his own deeds; he awaited the time of the Passion, as he says: “My time has not yet come” (John 7:6); he drew out the bread when he gave up his spirit, or when he rose from the tomb; he placed it in the chest when he took his soul again; he brought it to the table when he raised the assumed nature to heaven. *(Some material is missing.)*

The baker’s work is to choose good grains, winnow them, grind them, sift them, mix the flour with water, and knead it vigorously with hands and arms, or even press it with a millstone; to leaven it, have an oven, apply fire, cleanse the threshing-floor, arrange the loaves, and guard or wait for them until they are baked; finally to draw them out, place them in a chest, and bring them to the table. The Lord chose the finest grains, as he says: “I chose you out of the world” (John 15:19); and: “Did I not choose you twelve?” (John 6:7). He winnowed them when he said: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33); and the apostle Peter: “Behold, we have left everything” (Matt. 19:27). He ground them when he said: “Behold, I send you like lambs among wolves” (Matt. 10:16); and: “As the Father sent me, so I send you” (John 20:21), certainly unto suffering.

He sifted them when, by rejecting Judas the traitor, he separated him from the apostles as chaff; he mixed the flour with water when he baptized and taught others to baptize; he pressed it with the millstone when he said: “In the world you will have tribulation; but take courage: I have conquered the world” (John 16:33). He leavened it when he said: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God” (Luke 8:10), or when he breathed upon them, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit” [Col. 0809A] (John 20:22). He shaped the loaves when he said: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14), “you are the salt of the earth” (ibid., 13); he made the oven when he preached the Gospel, in which indeed the whole Christian religion is baked.

He applied the fire when he sent the Holy Spirit upon the apostles in tongues of fire; he cleansed the threshing-floor when he said: “Carry neither purse nor bag nor sandals, and greet no one on the road” (Luke 10:4); and: “You are already clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John 15:3). He arranged the loaves when he appointed some as apostles, others as evangelists, others as teachers, others as prelates, and others as subjects, until they should be baked. He guarded them when he said: “Holy Father, I have kept those whom you gave me”; and he waited when he said: “Have I been with you so long, and you have not known [Col. 0809B] me?” (John 14:9). He drew them out when he said: “Going into the whole world, preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15); he placed them in the chest when he said: “Do not rejoice because spirits are subject to you; rather rejoice in this, that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). He brought them to the table when he said to Peter: “Feed my lambs” (John 21:16); or when he said: “I will that, where I am, there my minister also may be” (ibid., 12).

Predestination is signified in the choosing: for those whom he predestined, these he also called. The scrutiny of judgment is signified in the winnowing; persecution in the crushing of the millstones; the rejection of evil and choosing of good in the sifting; the attainment of purity and devotion in the mixing of flour and water [Col. 0809C]; the virtue of patience in the oppression of adversities; the binding agent of unity in leavening; the distinction of offices, ranks, and merits in the arrangement of loaves; cloistered or eremitic religion in the oven; love in the fire; true confession in the cleansing of the threshing-floor; regular profession in the forming of loaves; the time of baking, the growth of religion; drawing out, the separation of body and soul; being placed in the chest, the expectation of the day of judgment; being brought to the table, the resurrection of bodies and eternal recompense according to merits.

## SERMON LVII. ON THE NATIVITY OF ST JOHN THE BAPTIST, I

The highest praises of blessed John the Baptist are borne out both by the testimony of his wonderful deeds and by the proved witness of divine utterances. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “Among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen” (Matt. 2:2). We must therefore inquire whence this man, so great, is thus great; admirable indeed in his great things, but in our own affairs—whether great or very small—to be invoked as a gracious patron. For, when we are to plead on the great day before the supremely great One concerning great matters, we shall, if we are wise, seek a great advocate for our case. The judge before whom we shall stand—of things, arguments, thoughts, and deeds—is as unknown to us as he ought greatly to be feared: great in wisdom, that he may not be deceived; great in power, that he may not be resisted; great in justice, that he may not be corrupted by the promise of gifts; [Col. 0810A] great in sovereignty, that he may not be escaped by fleeing into another’s kingdom.

Our case is great, because salvation or condemnation is at issue; the day is great, because small and great are there, because earth-dwellers and heaven-dwellers come together into one place. Therefore a patron so solemn must be engaged—one who is neither ashamed by the crowd, nor finds the judge hostile, nor is overcome by legal pleas, nor proves excessively expensive in seeking his fee. John the Baptist is neither avaricious in his price, nor unskilled in advocacy, nor unknown to the judge, nor timid because of a multitude. Let us therefore place him in the court on our behalf, entrusting our whole case to him and setting forth both guilt and innocence. Let us see him armed with a golden rim, honoured with a golden crown, and moreover clothed with an aureole-crown.

The Lord said to Moses concerning the table: “You shall make for it a golden rim all around; for the rim itself, a pierced-work crown four fingers high, and above it another aureole-crown” (Exod. 15:24). The rim on the Lord’s table is not bronze, not tin, not wood, not stone; it is not hard, not iron, nor indeed silver, but gold. It is not bronze, because it is not clamorous; not tin, because it is not false; not wood, because it is not mute; not stone, because it is not hard; not iron, because it is not without covenant and is not unpeaceable; not merely silver, because it is not only melodious. Rather, in John the Baptist we have a golden rim [Col. 0810C], supremely precious and resplendent.

This rim encircles the Lord’s table, because it makes no blemish, cut, or interruption in the purpose of religion; but, always without complaint and without offence, living in the law of the Lord, it does not overturn the circuit of perfection. This rim travels all around, because the span of his life was fulfilled in the preaching of truth. It is said that he taught those who came to him to repent; it is said that he sharply rebuked their reprobate life, saying: “Generation of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matt. 3:7). It is said that he rebuked Herod because of Herodias, whom he had taken as wife from his brother Philip. From every side, then, and everywhere this rim goes round about: it is neither terrified by high rank nor softened by flattery, nor delayed by the lack imposed by necessity from speaking what belongs to truth, religion, piety, and faith.

The rim, then, is golden all around when it says: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3:2). It is a golden rim when it says: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). But what reward is there for the rim itself? A pierced-work crown. Observe that one crown is plain-work, another is not plain-work, and another is pierced-work. In the Old Testament there is a crown not made by plain work; in the New, one made by plain work; at the boundary of Old and New, one made by pierced work. The unworked crown is first spoken of in the Old Testament, because the Law brought no one to perfection. It therefore did not shave away the hairs, but multiplied them, saying: “You shall eat the good things of the earth; I shall give the early and the latter rain, if you keep my commandments.” The Law did not shave, because its iron edge was blunted by fear rather than sharpened by love. Servile fear blunts rather than sharpens, because by necessity it restrains the deeds of the flesh but grace does not cut off the desireful motions of affection. It clipped rather than shaved, because it pressed by fear and did not set aflame by love.

The ancients therefore had a crown, but not one made by plain work, because they awaited Christ’s coming but did not enter the gates of the kingdom. But once the way of the saints was made manifest through Christ’s blood, sprinkled seven times before the veil of the Temple—so that souls of the saints, having laid down the burden of the body, may return to the throne of grace as freely as a labourer may easily gather the fruit of his reward—then, with the head as it were shaved and every difficulty removed, they receive a golden crown. Therefore the razor of the Gospel, which cuts off every hair of the head in the time of truth, not through imperfection of holiness—“Sell everything that you have and give it to the poor” (Luke 18:22)—indeed imposes a plain-work crown, restoring the reward without hindrance just as it had made the course free from restraint. Finally John, reclining at the borders of oldness and newness, Law and Gospel, figure and truth, shadow and light, fear and love, holds a razor in his right hand to shave the Christian; in his left he holds shears to clip the Jew, according to the imperfection of the Law. He leaves the people a few hairs for use, according to the perfection of the Gospel; for himself he cuts off food and clothing, even what is not superfluous. Therefore he has a pierced-work crown: so that, for his intermediate preaching, he may possess a pierced-work crown; for the holiness of his way of life, a plain-work crown—that is, full and perfect blessedness. Or the pierced-work crown placed upon the rim signifies the cutting off of his head for the testimony of truth.

It follows: “You shall make for it a golden rim all around, and for the rim itself a pierced-work crown four fingers high, and above it another aureole-crown.” Not *rims* but a *rim*: and a golden rim is made upon the table of divine Scripture, because it does not admit heresies and schisms, which chatter that the Son is less than the Father, and the Holy Spirit less than the Father and the Son.
