Divine Scripture, however, affirms the unity of the Trinity and the Trinity of unity, saying: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4). Likewise: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4:5). Thus the table, uttering the fullness of its dishes and the abundance of its fare through harmonious preaching by means of a golden rim, does not employ puffed cheeks and stretched lips, speaking grand things and magnifying its own lips. For the more exalted divine utterances are in meaning, the more restrained they are in voice and subdued in delivery. The voice belongs to the Lamb, “who did not cry out, nor was his voice heard in the streets.” Whatever divine utterance speaks, then, is one through the unity of faith, and golden through the depth of its meaning: one, lest it be torn apart by schismatic error [Col. 0812A]; golden, lest it become cheap through bare and rustic speech; all around, lest it be thought to concern a transitory good. Understand “all around” as eternal; “golden” as the supreme good; and “rim” as life-giving and delightful.

Understand by the rim the life-giving thing promised; by the gold, the delightful; by “all around,” the supreme and immortal. Add to the rim a pierced-work crown, so that the crown may display what Scripture promised and, by profession, may bite the rim—paying the crown of the prize as faithfully as the promise was truthfully maintained. Hence the Psalmist says: “Uphold me according to your word, and I shall live” (Ps. 118:116), and many similar things. Yet observe the pierced-work crown, because of the distinction between merits in the present and rewards in the future. It would indeed be an encouragement to negligence and nourishment for injustice if reward made equal those whom merit had made unequal. Who would cultivate vigils if one asleep gathered the fruit of vigils? Who would twist and mortify his body with fires, fasts, austerities, and innumerable sufferings, if naked, soft skin amid pleasures made as good a sound as a drum rings clearly when stretched and continually shaved? For one star would not differ from another in glory if differences of merit did not determine the measure of their weight. Therefore the pierced-work crown is placed beneath the golden rim, because a distinction among commandments is followed by a distinction among those who fulfil them, and among the labours of fulfilment by a distinction among those rewarded.

It is four fingers high, because, while the fullness of righteousness and the consummation of glory are described in the four books of the Gospels, the crown is as it were measured by four fingers. But John the Baptist’s Passion is sanctified and exalted in Christ’s Passion, without which anyone’s suffering would be in vain. Therefore it says, “four fingers high.” The Apostle marks four fingers in the cross when he says to the Ephesians: “That you may be able,” he says, “to comprehend with all the saints what is the height, length, loftiness, and depth” (Eph. 3:18). The first finger is love, by which demons are cast out in the Gospel, and this love covers a multitude of sins. The second is long-suffering, by which he writes on the ground: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her” [Col. 0812D] (John 8:7); by this the Saviour’s patience and mercy are signified. The third is hope, by which the commandments and promises of God are written upon the stone of the Law; by it the religious observance of the divine command is indicated. The fourth is judgment, by which miracles are performed in Egypt, at which the magicians fail, saying: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. 8:19); by it fear is instilled in us, for God will subject all things to himself, and the Son will be subject to him who subjected all things to himself.

Behold how far the crown of John the Baptist extends: it is four fingers high, so that he may then appear glorified in the kingdom of the Father and of the holy angels. For he was stretched out by four fingers in the Passion, he who crucified himself with vices and concupiscences; and he will likewise be crowned by four fingers [Col. 0813A], when “what is sown in corruption shall rise in incorruption; what is sown in dishonour shall rise in glory; what is sown in weakness shall rise in power; what is sown a natural body shall rise a spiritual body.” Meanwhile, rising as the dawn, let us gradually separate ourselves from corruption and tend toward incorruption by the pursuit of chastity. Let us separate ourselves from that dishonour of which it is said: “He who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34), and hasten to that glory which will never be taken from us. Let us recover strength from the weakness that casts down the soul’s vigour, and arrive at the strength that does not fail. Let us drive away from ourselves what is natural, as Moses loosed the strap of his sandal; and in the principal Spirit [Col. 0813B] let us grasp what is spiritual—may he deign to prepare it for us, he who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LVIII. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE SAME ST JOHN THE BAPTIST, II

“It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth; for he shall sit alone and be silent, because he has lifted himself above himself” (Lam. 3:27).

If the heavenly seats, emptied of their unworthy occupants when Lucifer apostasized and exalted himself upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north, drawing a third part of the stars after him—if, I say, those blessed dwellings are to be filled from the children of Adam, it is credible that blessed John the Baptist will ascend either to the blessedness of the first of those seats, or at least to the second. For our Lady, the Queen of Virgins, has worthily been placed after her Son; and John the Baptist after her, so that, as “among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen” (Matt. 11:11), so among the order of saints none may appear before him and none sit above him.

Do you suppose that John the Baptist was diminished in heaven, where an abundance of honour and glory is reserved for God’s friends? Does Christ Jesus cast aside his friend, his kinsman, his herald, his forerunner, his baptizer, his angel, his counsellor—he who never abandons those who hope in him? Far from it. Rather, the friend of the bridegroom unquestionably stands and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice; the kinsman approaches his blood-relative in a nearness as intimate as the relationship is chaste and dear. Having completed the office of the first heralding, the herald still proclaims in his resting-place, with jubilation both new and eternal, not God’s future wonders but those already accomplished, and the wonders of the Lamb who sits in the midst of the throne. Now the forerunner runs through those heavenly courses as eagerly as he once did not cease boldly to praise the Lord’s name and preach the Saviour’s coming even to the furthest regions of hell.

Oh, in what delightful baths the Lord’s Baptizer now bathes himself: he swims not in the Jordan but in angelic joys. That angel of the Lord’s face rejoices with the angels, and is magnified by all the angels in glory and honour alike. Finally, the counsellor, having entered God’s sanctuary, now unfolds, reads, and apprehends whatever mystery laid up in the heavenly [Col. 0814A] treasuries he had not yet grasped. Amid the splendours of the saints he shines with such varied radiance of merits, graces, and glories that the region of heaven in which John the Baptist dwells shines more brightly than the others, and, from its abundance of glory, more richly illuminates, more fully gladdens, and more lavishly satisfies his neighbours.

Thus John is first, more illustrious, and nearer among God’s sons, the stars of heaven, and all the courtiers of the supreme King. By birth he precedes the Virgin’s Son; by dignity he surpasses all children of women; by blood-relationship he comes nearer to Mary’s Son. Before his birth he is named by angelic promise; in the womb he is sanctified by the spiritual anointing of the Holy Spirit; from his mother’s womb he is received by the wondrous and most humble midwifely care of the Lord’s Mother; at his birth he is celebrated by the amazement of neighbours and all who heard; in the desert he is made illustrious by a manner of life as marvellous as his preaching was exalted; in the Lord’s baptism he is distinguished by the unique singularity of name and dignity; in death he is dedicated to the blessed dwelling-places of the saints by the shedding of his head’s blood. Thus the variety of merits is born from Joseph’s multicoloured tunic and dyed by the streams of the sevenfold Spirit. Yet to investigate by what channels this torrent has flooded John’s little plot with gifts so numerous and so great is as devout as it is useful to recall.

The two principal streams in which the whole discourse of divine Scripture floats are the Law and the Gospel. The Law runs down into the Gospel and flows into that great river, so that through this mingling it may cast off both the severity of its name and the imperfection of its authority—seasoning its tastelessness with salt and sweetening its bitterness with the honey of grace. John the Baptist, therefore, reclining between the boundaries of Law and Gospel, like a middle channel joins the Law to the grace of the Gospel: he either brings the Law to its end through grace or abolishes it through righteousness. He brings it to its end—that is, fulfils it—in moral matters, as it is written: “For I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfil it” (Matt. 5:17). He abolishes it in ceremonial matters—that is, circumcision of foreskins, sacrifice of cattle, observance of foods, and other such things. John is circumcised in flesh and heart, bidding farewell to the circumcision done in only one member and beginning that of the inward [Col. 0814D] person, which cuts away the superfluous outward circumcision.

John does not offer God the blood of goats or calves, but sacrifices himself as a living, holy offering acceptable to God for the cleansing of all offences. John does not distinguish flesh from flesh or judge food from food; rather, being most abstinent, he restrains his own flesh from every luxurious drink and food. John is perfect in every humility, obedience, chastity, gentleness, faith, hope, charity, and every kind of virtue. Therefore it is said of his humility, obedience, chastity, and contemplation: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth; he shall sit alone and [Col. 0815A] be silent, because he has lifted himself above himself.” Sitting refers to humility; bearing the yoke, to obedience and gentleness; bearing it from youth, to chastity; lifting oneself above oneself, to contemplation.

But in the actions of other people we must distinguish how and how long they work with God, and when, how, and how long they work without God. When does a person work without God? When he sins. Why? Because he does evil; for sin is evil, and evil is nothing. But God made all things very good, and he did not make evil or sin, since sin is to do, say, or desire something contrary to God’s will. Behold when a human being works without God. How does one work without God? Faithlessly, negligently, stubbornly. [Col. 0815B] Faithlessly, because he does not believe; negligently, because he does not fear; stubbornly, because he does not love. Behold how he works without God. And for how long? Until, taking off the yoke of discipline, though bound by the tether of God’s commandments he drags the clods of the valleys behind God. None of this applies to John, because he never departed from God, was neither faithless, negligent, nor stubborn, and did not refuse to bear the Lord’s yoke.

But when does a human being work with God, and how and for how long? When grace breathes upon him and he humbly and faithfully subjects himself to God, until he becomes one spirit with God. This is the yoke which it is good for a man to bear from his youth. Until you take up the yoke, you are without a yoke: you are a son of Belial, an untamed calf, a wild ass accustomed to [Col. 0815C] solitude, devoid of grace and discipline. For free choice is thus hurled headlong into the abyss through the liberty of sinning, until it is curbed by the yoke of divine grace, just as a foolish, unbroken colt wanders over every pathless and perilous way before its jaws are constrained with bit and bridle.

But when prevenient grace has acted, begins to tame it and accustom it to the yoke, so that it is willing to run and cooperate with grace, then it receives the yoke; then it breaks up the clods; then it sows upon the waters; then it works its own land and is filled with bread; then it bears the fruit of birth. Therefore it is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth, because up to this point the tenderness of age excuses a weak neck from bearing the yoke of most severe discipline. For just as wax that is too soft and tender, when impressed, does not retain the image of the seal, so childhood is less suited to seek and retain regular discipline. What follows? “He shall sit alone and be silent.” We must examine more deeply what it means that “he shall sit alone and be silent,” and join what follows to what went before. It was said when, how, and how long a person works without God.

It must be said, however, that God, who made man without man, works certain things in man without him, certain things in him with him, certain things in him for him, and certain things in him against him. He makes man without man; after man has been made, he works some things in him without him. A human being, also made by God, does some things without God, some with God, some for God, and some against God. These statements must be explained briefly. God works in man without man prevenient grace, which is voluntary rain: that movement of the soul by which the soul desires to desire God’s ordinances; the movement by which, finally, it was said from the One who calls, not from the one who works: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. 1:2; Rom. 9:13). God works this in a human being without human aid, because as yet there is no aid like to himself; but our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.

But God then works in a person with that person when grace releases one who is fettered and raises one who has been cast down, so that, released, he may run with grace, and, raised up, may advance from grace to grace—with grace proceeding from prevenient grace toward subsequent grace, accompanied by grace. A person is released when his free choice is freed from sins, so that he no longer serves mortal sin by obeying its desires, but resists the devil and bears fruit for God unto eternal life. Therefore, when free choice rises to meet grace, it joins hands with grace in working well; and when grace and free choice work together, they acquire good merit for the human being. Then God, with that person, restores the human being to his own image and likeness.

Let us now come to the third member, in which God works in a human being for that human being. Sometimes a person is tested by God and does not understand that he is being tested by God for his own good. Certainly he would not wish to be tested; indeed, he asks that the angel of Satan who buffets him be removed from him. But God considers the profit and crown of the trial, and permits him to be assailed more and more, against that person’s own will. Yet he does not lead him into temptation by consent to sin, but preserves his soul as he preserved Job. Therefore God works the trial in the person for that person, though he himself is unwilling, so that, once tested, he may receive the crown of life.

In the fourth member it was said that God works something in a person against that person, and this happens only in the reprobate. When God sees a perverse and stubborn person ungrateful for his benefits, he blinds [Col. 0816D] him, so that seeing he may not see and hearing he may not understand. Such are either those who have zeal for God but not according to knowledge, like the Jews who crucified the Lord; or those who would not understand so as to act well, who said to God: “Depart from us; we do not desire knowledge of your ways” (Job 21:14). For, as Gregory says, a sin not corrected immediately draws another after itself by its own weight. Therefore everything that such a person does is against himself, even what he sometimes thinks he does for himself. For as all things work together for good to those who love God—even mishap and ruin toward evil—so all things work together for evil to the reprobate, even the performance of virtues and the pretence of progress. Thus far concerning those things which God does generally either without a person, with a person, for a person, or against a person.

But we must now briefly say, specifically, how these things apply to John the Baptist. The sending of the angel and the promise of John to parents advanced in years and barren was done by God alone, who alone “does great wonders” (Ps. 135:4). Again, while John was still in his mother’s womb, the Lord alone caused his exultation at the voice of the Lord’s Mother, who had come to serve Elizabeth; likewise, that he was filled with the Holy Spirit while still in his mother’s womb; and that he was born with the guilt of original sin and the tinder of sin very greatly diminished—although he was conceived with sin—all this belongs to God alone. In these matters God does certain things concerning John without John, so that [Col. 0817B] at his birth the neighbours might rejoice with him; and certain things to John himself.

Let us come at last to those things which God does with John, in John. The evangelist Luke reports of this John that “the child grew and was strengthened in spirit, and was in the deserts until the day of his manifestation to Israel,” that he might be filled with the Holy Spirit. And Mark says: “He was in the desert baptizing and preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins” (Mark 1:4); and shortly afterward: “John was clothed in camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his loins, and he ate locusts and wild honey” (ibid., 6). These things God worked with John, and John with God, through his grace, without which he could surely do no good thing.

We must also now see how a person sometimes works without God, sometimes with God, sometimes for God, and sometimes against God. Without God we do vain and useless things, because the Holy Spirit withdraws himself from thoughts that are without understanding. With God we do whatever good we work, because every good thing proceeds from God. For God we do whatever sufferings we endure for him. Against God we act whenever we sin grievously. John did either nothing or little without God; much with God and for God; nothing against God. For he walked with God and did not depart from the commands of his lips. Therefore it is said of him: “It is good for a man when he bears the yoke from his youth,” and so forth. But one yoke belongs to the Law [Col. 0817D], another to the Gospel; likewise, one to disobedience, another to obedience; likewise, one to unbelief, another to faith. Of these, three are good and three are evil.

## SERMON LIX. ON ST PETER, OR THE CHAIR OF ST PETER

“Let them exalt him in the assembly of the people, and praise him in the chair of the elders” (Ps. 106:32).

Setting aside a long preface, let us begin the discourse with the chair itself. There are four principal beings who have their chairs: God in heaven, the devil in hell, Moses in the desert or synagogue, and Peter in the temple or Church. Everyone who applies himself to teaching, or rests in imparting doctrine, sits in a chair. God teaches well; the devil unteaches; Moses initiates the rough manners of the stiff-necked people so that they may come [Col. 0818A] to instruction; Peter perfects his disciples in knowledge, so that they lack nothing in any grace: “Let them exalt him,” and so forth.

The prince of the apostles, called by God like Aaron, changes seats and manners—not presumptuously falling from higher to lower things, but ascending and advancing through obedience from lower things to loftier and worthier ones. For Peter’s first seat was in the little boat which he had chosen through his occupation of fishing; the second was the chair which God gave him through the office of preaching; the third was the one divine predestination had prepared for him upon the cross; the fourth was the one heavenly reward had laid up in the throne of the kingdom, where the twelve apostles sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. We must accordingly consider what is the office of one sitting in the boat; what the dignity of one presiding in the chair; what the merit of one dying on the cross; and what the glory of one reigning in eternity.

He is a fisherman in the boat, a teacher and apostle in the chair, an imitator of Christ on the cross, a confessor and fellow-heir with Christ in the regeneration; untrained and new in the boat, prudent and learned in the chair, holy and perfect on the cross, joyful and glorious in the regeneration. From the boat he teaches novices; from the chair, elders; from the cross, those departing the body; from glorification, those arriving at their homeland. The beginning of wisdom, which is the fear of the Lord, instructs from the boat, where rivers of temptations raise their voice, battering the sides of one newly converted to religion. Unless he steers the vessel of his life straight through the midst of the waves with the oars of religious observance and the rudder of equity, a rising storm and tempest of snares quickly sink it and bring about the loss of the whole gain together with the one gaining it. For it would be better not to have known the way of virtue than, after knowing it, to turn back: that is, better not to have entered the little boat of religion than to perish in a shipwreck of temptations under the garb of holiness.

Peter experienced in himself the temptations of novices, for his feet were almost moved and his steps poured out when, for the third time, he denied with oaths and curses that he knew the man. He was indeed driven and overthrown so that he might fall, but he was not struck down into condemnation, because the Lord upheld him. Thus he gave us an example: we must not yield to temptations, give place to the devil, or despair because of sin. For who would despair of the Lord’s mercy, when so great a crime found relief so swiftly? Without doubt no sin is more desperate or more monstrous than denying Christ: this Peter did. Yet people are often accustomed to weep for a slight and trifling cause. Peter too wept, and the little stream of compunction drowned Egypt—that is, a denial of gigantic magnitude. Thus we read that Peter’s offence was forgiven by tears alone, and God was not slow to pardon once Peter began to love weeping. Therefore may your mercies come to me, Lord, and I shall live: you not only received Peter as he wept, but also wept for foul-smelling [Col. 0819A] Lazarus and, through the power of tears, raised one dead four days.

Thus Peter teaches novices from the boat; thus he draws the fish tossing in the belly of the sea out of it; and, lest they fail in temptations, he protects them by his examples and advocacy. But Peter changed his state, because he who called him from the boat placed him in the chair of the elders, that he might teach the elders prudence. For when he was younger, he girded himself and walked where he wished; but when he has grown old, he must sit in the chair of the elders, teaching them by word and example to grow with age in knowledge and religion. Those who are elders in the order of a regular cloister under the profession of Christianity must not be mere beginners; for, as Jerome says, “an elderly beginner is ridiculous.” They therefore ought not again turn to the needy and weak elements of the world, wishing to live as human animals do; nor, in accordance with the weakness of novices, should they again need milk rather than the solid food of religious life. For it is written: “Wisdom is found among the aged” (Job 12:12), etc.

Peter therefore teaches the elders from the chair of the elders, that they may be wise in mystical utterance, that they may penetrate those mysteries and secrets which Paul saw in the most exalted seat of the third heaven, and which, as he himself says, it is not lawful for a human being to speak (2 Cor. 12:4). For the religious soul ought so deeply to incorporate the marrow of religion into its own marrow that it would sooner shake the marrow from its entrails than faith and religion from the marrow of its heart. It is as though those mysteries may not be spoken by man because our longings are to be entrusted only to the sight of the Godhead, lest either the favor of flatterers diminish them or the detraction of whisperers steal them away. Thus Peter teaches the elders, in the chair of the elders, concerning uprightness, knowledge, steadfastness, observance of God’s commandments, and the perfection of righteousness. But let us see what this chair is and who this craftsman is.

This chair is the Church, which has, as it were, four feet: the four regions of the whole world—that is, east, west, north, and south—as it has baptism, Eucharist, confession, and penance. It consecrates baptism in the east, as at the entrance of the tabernacle; the provision for the journey, the body and blood of the Lord, in the west, as at Israel’s departure from Egypt—that is, from this body or from this worldly pilgrimage; finally, it has confession in the north, where are the sides of the north, accusing itself of transgression rather than exalting itself in vanity and carnal glory, which, like a flower of the field, shall fall and wither. It also has penance in the south, because there the bridegroom of the soul feeds and rests with his brethren and angelic spirits, rejoicing more over one sinner who does penance than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance.

Behold, indeed, the chair of the elders; for this chair began to be fitted and hewn from Abel onward: hewn, certainly, in the martyrs; fitted together in the confessors. Suffering in passion hews well indeed, if anything swollen, misshapen, or blemished is found in our mortal body, when it blots out like a cloud all the iniquities of him who has shed his blood for Christ. But this chair is fitted together in the confessors, who, rooted and grounded in charity, maintain that joint by which head and body are united through the incarnation of the Word and the union of bridegroom and bride, so that they may comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height, and depth, and may know the surpassing love of Christ. That love, then, which according to Solomon is as strong in confessors as death is in martyrs, joins the members hewn by mortification of the flesh to those hewn by the martyrdom of suffering.

But the prince of the apostles sits in the chair not of the young, but of the elders, because our faith is not in a recently arrived God, as it is written: “Israel, if you listen to me, let a new God be known in you” (Ps. 80:9); rather, it is in the eternal, unchangeable, ancient, and Ancient of Days. And although the sacraments were changed in the Old and New Testaments, yet there is one faith and one Lord in both peoples, as the Apostle, recalling that saying of the Psalmist, “I believed, therefore I spoke” (Ps. 115:10), adds: “We also believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Cor. 4:13), thereby indicating the one and same faith of prophets and apostles. The chair of the elders, therefore, is the Church because of the bronze bases placed beneath silver columns: for the prophets and patriarchs precede the apostles, concerning whom it is written: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you” (Ps. 44:17), that is, apostles in place of prophets. For the preceding words, “Let them exalt him in the assembly of the people,” are explained when it is said, “and let them praise him in the chair of the elders,” so that the chair of the elders belongs to the faith of the ancient fathers, and the assembly of the people to the faith of Christians.

But because both the feast of the present day and this sermon concern Peter’s chair, we should take the occasion to consider how many other chairs Scripture treats. There is a chair of God, a chair of the devil, and, finally, a chair of Moses. The chair of the invisible God is that power by which he created and governs the whole world; and the four feet of this chair are, as it were, either the four primary elements from which every body subsists, or heaven itself, air, earth, sea, and all things. For “our God has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths” (Ps. 134:6). He has beneath himself, as a cushion, his mercy, upon which he rests gently, because his mercies are over all his works. Of this chair it is said: “Heaven is my seat, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66:1). Likewise: “The Lord has prepared his seat in heaven, and his kingdom shall rule over all” (Ps. 102:19). He therefore sits in the chair who reigns everywhere, as it is written: “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with splendor; the Lord has clothed himself with strength and girded himself” (Ps. 92:1). This is concerning the chair of God.

But the chair of the devil is in hell, where the power of darkness is. The devil sits there as in a chair, sending suggestions through evil angels, sending his emissaries across the sea to a deceitful nation, to a people convulsed and torn apart, whose sneezing kindles coals. For he not only sets youthful marrow aflame in his fires toward the heat of lust, but also inflames the deadened senses of certain decrepit persons toward desires, and makes the coals of longing burn when he sneezes, heaping fiery coals upon the head of a soul snoring in the sleep of negligence. The four feet of this chair are four kinds of suggestion or temptation: the first is light and hidden; the second, light and open; the third, grave and hidden; the fourth, grave and manifest. In Psalm 90 they are called respectively: the terror by night; the arrow flying by day; the business walking in darkness; and the assault and noonday demon. Upon these he sits and presses down the earth—that one who goes about roaring, seeking whom he may devour. There are also other feet of the infernal chair: heat and cold, stench and darkness. Its cushion is that of which it is said: “The maggot shall be spread beneath you” (Isa. 14:11). And this is concerning the chair of the devil. It remains to consider the chair of Moses, of which the Gospel says: “The scribes and Pharisees sat in Moses’ chair” (Matt. 23:11).

[Col. 0821C] This chair is of stone, for he sits upon a stone when Hur and Aaron supported his hands, because they were heavy. He also wrote upon stone, because those tablets upon which he wrote the ten words of the Law were stone. Nor is this surprising, for the people to whom he spoke was stiff-necked. There is nothing soft, nothing sweet in this chair, because in the law of Moses there is no remission except through fire, blood, ashes, sacrifice, and the slaughter of animals. In it too, one is forbidden to offer honey in sacrifices. The feet of this chair are circumcision of the flesh, the curse of the Law, ceremonial observance, and the severity of commandment. What circumcision is, is plain; but something must be said about the curse of the Law. When Moses had completed the commandments of the Law, he added: “Cursed is he who does not keep all that is written in the Law” (Deut. 27:26). The apostle Peter proves that all Jews were under this curse of the Law, saying in the Acts of the Apostles: “Why do you test us by placing upon us a yoke which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?” (Acts 15:10). Moses therefore imposed this curse of the Law, because no one kept the Law according to the letter, as the Gospel says: “Moses gave you the Law, and none of you keeps the Law” (John 7:19). It is plain how stony ceremonial observance is, how stony the commandments in the Law are. Let us therefore pass from the chair of Moses to the chair of Peter, because the gates of hell cannot prevail against it. For it is founded upon the rock, that is, Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LX. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT MARY MAGDALENE, I

From his prepared dwelling-place, as from royal seats, the compassionate and merciful Lord, having assumed the cloud of flesh, humbled himself according to the time of his predestination to the lower regions of our earth; and, as the maker and interpreter of laws, he took charge of the legal rights and every concern of our commonwealth. Therefore, while with his senators he inquired into the merits and cases of individuals—not in the manner of one judging, but with the mercy of one instructing, for he had come to teach the ignorant, not to judge the innocent—a woman who had offended against the laws and violated the rights of nature approached, seeking not the censure of a judge but the indulgence of a father.

After considering both her case and the remedies appropriate to it, he tempered the harshness of the Law by his kindness; and, by enacting a new decree of the Gospel senate, he established a general law of forgiveness. For under the law of the two tablets, written indeed by the finger of God but nevertheless of stone, its transgressors were punished without mercy, and sins were not removed without the shedding of blood. Thus, by his gentleness and wisdom, our jurist, having received authority from the Father, removed from the ancient Law certain burdensome or impossible matters; he softened certain cruel matters, adjusted certain less fitting ones, and altered certain ones as the time had changed, so that he might bring in, more clearly, peacefully, joyfully, and honorably, the time of the Lord rather than that of the servant, and that those oppressed by the heavy yoke of the servant might be relieved at the coming of the Lord.

Perhaps a certain Simon the leper wished to bark against this merciful dispensation of the Lord, clinging to the old Law and ignorant of the new, muttering thus with leprous mouth: “This man, if he were a prophet, would know the prophet Moses; he would also know the Law; and without doubt he would know this woman. But if he knew, he would assent to the Law rather than to the prostitute. Nor would he merely incline himself with so favorable a countenance to receive her; indeed, armed with the Law, he would judge her fit to be overwhelmed with stones. Thus he would preserve the justice of the Law and establish the work of justice. Since he acts otherwise, what justice, holiness, or prophecy is in him? Is not this woman who touches his feet a known and notorious sinner in the city? Is not he who is touched defiled by her? Surely she would not have entered my house unless I believed that he would reject and condemn her.”

After he had hissed these things for some time in the ears of the Lord of Hosts, in the silence of his mouth, the Lord proposed an aptly pointed question in the form of a parable concerning Simon’s own law, and convicted the wicked servant out of his own mouth. When Simon’s boasting had been excluded by the law of works—or rather, by the law of faith—he turned his face, desired by all nations, toward the grieving and afflicted sinner, and immediately pronounced the sentence of acquittal: “Your faith,” he said, “has saved you; go in peace” (Luke 7:50). Truly, as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so the ways of the Lord are separated from the thoughts of the leper. The leper rejects the leprous woman, but the Lord receives her; she is advantageously cast off by the leper, and therefore is received all the more by the Lord. The leper adds leprosy to his leprosy in a leprous way, because he joins stinging envy to his pride. Yet no trace of leprosy now appears in the woman, because, prostrate at the Lord’s feet, she receives the remedy of grace.

Simon, you judge according to the old Law—indeed, according to the old man. Jesus judges no one, but acquits the repentant soul.

You attend to the Law upon stones, where there is the ministry of death; Jesus attends to spiritual gifts, where the power of mercy is set above all things, for “his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 144:9). Rather, rejoice with the healer of the brokenness of the miserable, because you too need a physician if you wish to be healed from the disease of pride. This woman, although she is not free from sin, is nevertheless free from the grave offense of despair or presumption. She seeks a remedy; she does not sluggishly plead for pardon, nor does she do so in passing. She persists continually, cries out strongly, weeps abundantly, and acts before acquaintances and proud members of the household—everything as humbly as patiently.

Why, then, do you wish both to nullify the merit of conversion and to block up the fountain of mercy? If, drunk with malice, you despise our streams, why do you reproach the wild ass drinking in its thirst? Yet it is uncertain whom you rebuke more insultingly: the one who drinks or the one who needs drink. [Col. 0823C] What is this, Simon? In judging another, you condemn yourself. For if pardon is denied to penitents, the rites of ceremonies and sacrifices in your Law are observed in vain. Why then are you yourself circumcised? Why do you render your firstfruits and tithes to the Lord? Why do you offer for sin and offense, if you forbid mercy and deny pardon? But perhaps you say: “My Law condemns fornicators and adulterers; forgiving lesser offenses, it imputes and cuts off greater ones without regard for mercy.” O Pharisee, if your Law is such that in greater matters it does not—or cannot—do what it does in lesser ones, then it is either insufficient or unjust. But it is not; for the Law is indeed holy, and the commandment holy, righteous, and good. For God who gave the Law is righteous and good; Moses, who brought the Law, is righteous and gentle. Without doubt, each established in the Law only what was righteous and holy.

It remains, therefore, that it is insufficient—and this is true. For neither the Law nor Moses led to perfection; rather, Jesus brought the children of Israel into the land flowing with milk and honey. For it had its course for a time, until John: “for the Law [was] until John”; and fittingly until John, whose name is interpreted “grace.” For the Law, as you maintain, Simon, is without grace. John is therefore followed, when Jesus comes in the flesh—not one whose name is interpreted “grace,” but one who is truly full of grace, indeed grace itself in fullness. John intervenes between the Law and Christ, as though he were the dawn ending the shadow of night and, by proclamation, opening the light of the sun.

Mary Magdalene, then, fearing the Law without grace, approached the fountain of grace; and lest she be overwhelmed by stones, she clung to the feet. Simon, you bring stones of cruelty; Jesus offers Mary feet of mercy. You strive to strike according to the Law, but the stones you throw are shattered below—or rather, they roll back upon your own head. For behind Mary, who stands at the feet of grace, the Law sits and does not stretch forth its arm of threat when it sees the Savior’s feet present. It imposes silence upon itself when it hears the Word; it sees the Lord’s back and does not dare burst forth into his face. For it was enough for Moses to have seen the back of God. Therefore halt your step, Simon, with Moses behind the Lord’s back, because the disciple is not above the master. Let the Lord do his own work in receiving Mary the sinner, because it is foreign to him to condemn one who repents.

O Simon, you are blinded by the light near at hand; you die amid resurrection; you perish amid sweet fragrance; you vanish amid fullness. But at last drive malice from your heart, falsehood from your mouth, and envy from your eyes; and wonder that the guest at your table does not fill his stomach with the food of the table, but with Mary’s humility and faith. See fulfilled before your eyes what customarily occurs in holy things. In the inner rooms of your house, a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, is offered in a new manner of sacrifice upon an altar consecrated from incorrupt earth. Blood is poured out at its base; oil is scattered; incense is burned; a goat is slain for the sin of ignorance—and your soul is angry at it.

Without doubt, when Mary renounces movements of lust, she kills the goat; when she prays for pardon, she kindles incense; when she pours out devotion, she pours out oil; when she is ashamed of what she has done, she pours out blood; when she dies to sin, she offers a sacrifice. Behold the altar; behold the victim; behold the fire; behold the wood; behold the water; behold the baptizer. Such things customarily are, and ought to be, done in a holy place; but where is a holier place than where the feet of Jesus stood? “Worship,” says the Psalmist, “his footstool, for it is holy” (Ps. 98:5). Upon this footstool Mary laid her head and moistened it with most sacred weeping. For Mary, standing behind beside the feet of Jesus, began to wet them with tears, wipe them with her hair, and—[Col. 0824D]—anoint them with ointment. Mary watered the plants born in Mary’s garden. Mary—the Mother of God—planted these plants from her flesh and blood; indeed, she caused the plants she had planted to sprout—[perhaps: “which now”] Mary, though a great sinner, watered them from the fountain of her inward entrails. Another also watered them, not with water but with the oil of grace: when the Father from heaven planted in Mary’s womb—indeed, in Mary—the one whom Mary Magdalene watered with water and anointed with ointment while he reclined in Simon’s house.

Mary Magdalene’s watering or anointing is good, because it wiped away the stains of sins. Better is the anointing or watering of the Holy Spirit, because it richly endowed, in Christ Jesus, a barren and unfruitful nature with heavenly virtues and gifts. That is the higher; this the lower. For the former takes place in the oil of grace; the latter, in the water of repentance. Mary Magdalene would not have watered Jesus reclining at table with water unless the Holy Spirit had watered him with grace as he was born from the Virgin. Read Moses’ Scripture and understand the sacrament of this watering: “The Spirit of the Lord,” it says, “was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1:2). What does it mean that the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters, except that the soul is cleansed by a higher and better expiation in God’s Spirit than in water? Or again, what does it mean that the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters, except that through the Spirit the soul is cleansed, while the body is cleansed in water? Or that by the watering or overshadowing of the Spirit, nature could be conceived without fault, whereas in Mary Magdalene’s watering, fault deserved to be removed without nature? With good reason, therefore, the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters.

Mary conceived our nature in Jesus through the Spirit; the Spirit was borne over the waters without sin. Mary Magdalene received from Jesus, with the same Spirit cooperating, her soul darkened by the abyss of former offenses, cleansed of the devil. The Spirit was therefore rightly borne over the waters: because grace descended more abundantly in the mother, pardon more liberally in the sinner, and even now the Spirit is borne over this sinner’s waters when her soul is cleansed by the sprinkling of spiritual grace amid an outpouring of tears and repentance. The Spirit of the Lord is borne over the waters when God is reconciled to sinners more through the devotion of their hearts than through the barren moistening of the brain. The Spirit cleanses without water, or in water; water without the Spirit who is borne over the waters is not from the waters of paradise but from the pools of Egypt: it is a feigned moisture issuing from the eyes merely to beguile people, not to remove the filth of crimes. Behold the goat changed through water and Spirit is moved, approaches the altar, when Mary Magdalene, putting away the vices of her former life and transformed by conversion of heart, embraces the feet of mercy.

## SERMON LXI. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT MARY MAGDALENE, II

“Mary Magdalene,” says the Evangelist, “standing behind beside the feet of the Lord Jesus, began to wet his feet with tears; and she wiped and kissed them with the hair of her head, and anointed them with ointment” (Luke 7:38).

“Go to the ant, O sluggard, and learn her paths”; for in summer it gathers food for itself for the winter season. By a most fitting likeness of activity, we may without doubt compare Mary to the most prudent ant. For just as the ant most diligently carries grains of wheat in summer to its dwelling, providing lest it lack in winter, so Mary Magdalene, hearing that the grain of wheat which falls into the earth remains alone unless it dies, but if it dies bears much fruit, reclined in Simon’s house, ran to him and, as if having seized the grain of wheat, brought it to her soul by most humble conversion. For as the ant receives the marrow of the grain, so Mary received Christ’s grace.

But consider more fully the order of her conversion, and observe how she who has converted is converted. She omitted not one iota of the law of return, she who had wandered far off in the region of unlikeness. For in her turning away she had overthrown the house of her mind and had squandered by luxurious living the entire substance of her nature. As Solomon says: “A wise woman builds her house, but a foolish woman destroys what has been built” (Prov. 14:1). Thus this woman, first foolish from the highest summit down to the foundation, had daily cast down the dwelling of her mind into worse and worse ruin. And just as, in the collapse of a wall, one falling stone drives another, so she joined evil to evil in her actions. For, according to the Psalmist, “Deep calls to deep” (Ps. 41:8), when fault summons fault—or even fault summons punishment—in blinded minds. Thus the whole house had collapsed: it had cast its timbers, ceilings, columns, and floors to the ground, and absolutely nothing upright remained, even down to its firm foundation. For from the sole of her foot to the crown of her head there was no health in her, because the breasts of her youth had been broken in Egypt, and she was wholly naked and barefoot.

At last, returning to her heart and remembering the husband of her youth, she began to gather her understanding and wisely say within herself: “I will return to my former lord, for then it was better for me than now: then, namely, when I received from his hand morsels of bread soaked in oil; when, clinging to his side, I did not fear the snows for my house. For when there are two, they warm one another; but woe to the one alone, because if he falls, he has none to raise him up” (Eccl. 4:10). Then, I say, it was better for me, when I reclined in his bosom and upon his breast and walked in the innocence of my heart in the midst of my house. But now, cast far away, I am exposed to terrors by night, to wild beasts and animals, and also to frost and winter drippings, by which I am distressed and chilled both in heart and body. Therefore I shall take up strength and rise in the night, seeking him who gave me wool and flax, if perhaps I may obtain a tunic or cloak for my shame.

I hear that the Lamb is in the house of Simon the leper, who dwells near me, a leprous woman. Perhaps he who did not refuse the leper’s house for a meal will not despise me, a leprous woman, for healing. If the leper offered him food, why should not I too bring ointment, although leprous? Simon shall provide food; I shall minister ointment. Simon could have poured water with his hands, but neglected it. I, if I can in any way, shall fall down at his feet and pour over the steps of the Godhead water warmed by vital heat—not from the common well of the townspeople, but from my own fountain. Simon is leprous only in the head, because he is proud in mind; I am leprous in my whole body, because I am full of lust or a demon. For whoever commits fornication sins against his own body; but whatever sin a human being commits is outside the body. Yet I do not turn these thoughts over concerning Simon in order to set aside my own sickness, aggravate his disease, and presume to insult one better than myself; rather, I do so in order to persuade my faint-heartedness in whatever direction the stream of mercy has turned, and to come to the fountain in hope of pardon.

[Col. 0827A] I have heard two things about the Lamb’s host: he is called Simon, and surnamed leper. In that he is leprous, I approach by a certain proportion; in that he is Simon, I wholly yield. In that he is leprous, I recognize my own frailty; in that he is Simon, I am reproved for my disobedience. In that he is leprous, I recall Scripture: “God has shut up all under sin”; in that he is Simon: “He who has done the righteousness which is from the Law shall live in it.” Yet in both respects this is true: “Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners” (1 Tim. 1:15). In that he is leprous, he is by no means better than I; but in that he is Simon, he is beyond me. For the difference between an obedient and a disobedient sinner is not slight.

I will therefore go to the house of obedience, and there receive from the Lamb the wool of pardon. For he dispenses it and sends it to penitents who ask: he who gives snow like wool; who warms the poor from his fleeces; who sheared it with the scissors of the cross or Passion; and who sent it forth to all for weaving the garment of immortality, with the distaff and spindle of preaching and faith. Therefore, while the Lamb is with his fleece, he who descends like rain upon the fleece because the Word assumed flesh from the Virgin, I shall go to his feet, where he touches the earth without hooves and has greater compassion upon our humility, not to the head, which is higher and has seven horns and seven eyes.

I fear his eyes, for the light of my eyes is not with me; still more I fear and dread the horns, because I am still soft and tender. I shall therefore take hold of the Lamb for the sake of the wool, but from the side of his feet, from the soles. Though I have no clean sole myself, I shall touch the gentle and clean sole. If I were not a sinner, I would not dread the place of the hoof; I know the Lamb to be most gentle, but I recall that I have offended so grievously that I may have exasperated even the Lamb’s eye. What is more innocent, what more tender, than the sole in the innocent Lamb? Therefore I shall make the sole, tender by nature, still more tender by my tears. Abundant crops springing from a field delight the farmer’s mind; for the heavenly gift is more lavishly increased when human merit has prepared itself fitly to receive it. The hand grows more generous in reward when the mind receiving the benefit has not been ungrateful.

But what—and how great—is this benefit: that I may touch, Lord Jesus, the footstool of your feet; indeed, what and how great a grace you bestow on a sinner when you do not refuse to offer your sole! This is all beyond me: “Your mercy has been strengthened,” and I cannot attain to it. For as what is weak in God is stronger than men, so what is lowest is higher. Yet if the watered sole, with the heel close by, drives me away, I shall still hold the sole and, as though planted alongside it, shall not cease through impatience. But holding the sole, what shall I say? “My God, his mercy shall go before me” (Ps. 58:11). His mercy—that is, his sole—shall go before me: while I hold the sole, I gather wool. The Lamb will not escape me, because either he will give wool or I shall always hold the sole.

O Lamb, when you have given the wool of pardon, give also the spindle of repentance. For wool, unless apportioned by spinning upon the spindle, does not make a garment. So too mercy, or pardon granted to penitents, without the fruit of repentance, does not fittingly cover the nakedness of one confessing it. God remits the guilt of sin, but you must pay, according to the measure of the fault, the measure of punishment. For although the Lamb said, “Her many sins are forgiven,” Mary nevertheless did not therefore cease from repentance. Her fingers grasped the spindle, and they distilled the choicest myrrh by loving, following, and ministering to God beyond all things. We unravel her spindle and now weigh it out when we speak of her repentance.

Let us weave ourselves a tunic against the cold of winter, because the sluggard will not be able to plough, from the Lamb’s wool on Mary’s spindle, so that we may be converted to God as Mary was: thus affected, thus loving, thus following. And when we have received wool from the Lamb, let us obtain flax from the Word with the same insistence. Flax is finer and scarcer, but also more precious. So the Word of God is more precious than the body of the Word; so too eternal life is more precious than present pardon. For sometimes some receive the wool of pardon but do not attain to the flax—indeed, the flax of life—because they do not persevere. For those who, after receiving knowledge of the truth, return to the vomit, crucifying again the Son of God and exposing him to contempt, are excluded from the kingdom. For to those who sin deliberately, “there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins” (Heb. 10:26). These, then, had wool through pardon, but by tearing it apart and twisting it onto the spindle, they did not merit the flax of perseverance.

But Mary sought wool and flax and worked with the counsel of her hands. Thus she has a tunic of the Lamb’s flax at the sole, and a cloak of the Word’s flax at the head. In this way the wise woman rebuilt her house, completing it from the sole of Christ’s human feet up to the head of his divinity. For she anointed both the feet and the head: the feet while still a sinner, the head as a lover. The Lord’s feet are holy feet, by which the divinity of the Word walks even into our Idumea; by which our humanity returns upon the wings of the cherubim; by which he first came to his Mother in being born, and then returned to his Father in ascending. The Son of God is everywhere, filling all things, and absent nowhere, governing all things. Mary rightly took hold of Jesus’ feet, because the devil went out before his feet.

O Mary, when you held Jesus’ feet, what did you feel, what did you think, what did you desire? Would you exchange that holding for any gold or precious stone, whether estimable or beyond estimation? Could your mouth be satisfied with kisses, your hands with touch, your eyes with sight? Surely, if you could have drawn out your heart, you would not have refused to pour it out at Jesus’ feet. You poured out water, but also ointment. Yet how much water? I recall well enough the measure of the ointment: certainly a pound of precious ointment—very lavish in the value of the ointment, but more lavish in the outpouring of water. You drew priceless water without price from your own well; and therefore your head offered water without measure, because your heart did not incline to avarice.

This water covered the Lord’s feet and washed away the stains of your soul and body. The Egyptians of former evils were submerged like lead in mighty waters. By her contrition, water caused a dead trunk to live again, when it made the sinner’s soul—long dead from nakedness of good work—fruitful in worthy fruits of repentance. She poured out water and dried up lust. Perhaps Elijah’s miracle is more wondrous: for it is said that by his prayers he brought down water from heaven for three years and six months, so that the earth might bring forth, and so forth. But behold a more useful deed: she drew from her own entrails a rushing river, to reconcile Christ to herself and, like a young olive tree, to produce throughout the world the brightest and most worthy fruits of repentance. For what is brighter on earth than this most holy sinner’s faith and devotion? What in the world is more fragrant than Mary Magdalene’s renown? What in the Church is more efficacious for sinners than the prayer and aid of this beloved of Jesus?

She is certainly most powerful before the Judge, most compassionate in hearing the prayer of the miserable, most effectual in raising the poor from the dung heap. May my soul choose her above all in the company of heaven; may it not be ashamed to confess its evils to her; through her as mediatrix may it seek tears with their proper affection, and may it not doubt Christ’s love. She knows more feelingly how to receive the miseries of the miserable; reflecting on the sins of her youth, she remembers more tenaciously how fragile our earthen vessel is and how prone to falling. She has not yet ceased to touch wounds more sweetly, handle them more gently, and endure more patiently the stench of wounds.

O Mary, wash the consciences of penitents; cleanse the defilements of hearts. Him whom you transformed into your advocate by weeping, obtain by prayer as one who, for the guilty, is not an angry avenger of offenses but a gracious forgiver. You who, while still guilty, pleaded sufficiently for yourself, now, beloved, be a merciful mediatrix for the sins of those who confess. It was not by words but by tears, not by voice but by compunction, not by ornate prayer but by tearful watering, that you forced pardon forth. The inward mercies of God did not restrain themselves when the inward parts of the afflicted sinner began to pour themselves out. We beseech, Lord Jesus, the depths of your compassion, the depths both of your mother Mary and of the sinful Mary: that, with our inward parts opened, we may reject malice and receive pardon, cast away every hardness and obtain the affection of devotion.

O Mary Magdalene, when you had not yet tasted the purest wine, with most confident boldness you brought your mouth and hands to David’s open fountain. And now, when you have entered the wine-cellar and burn with the wine of heavenly abundance, do you hesitate to approach those who, poor at the door, cry out tirelessly at least because of their distress? Do you refuse to bring a little bread from the remnants of your table and a small quantity of water? Bring, I beg you, a morsel of bread and a vessel of water, for I have been sent to you in a time of famine, as Elijah was to the widow of Sidon. For, like an exile, I do not yet dare enter the city gates. May I find you and come to the gate, so that under your guidance we may enter the holy places of the sanctuary and the secret chambers of the palace, with our Lord Jesus Christ going before us, whose kingdom and dominion endure without end through ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LXII. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT MARY MAGDALENE, III

As a stag [runs] to springs of water, so Mary Magdalene, from the heat of fevers, hastens back to the fountain of Jesus. The more fiercely she thirsts, the more swiftly she runs. She does not measure out the stages of her journey, heed the hunter’s snares, or regard the hardships of travel; she seeks only to quell the heat, renew her burning veins, and restore her failing strength. See Mary acting with greater urgency, like a most welcome hind, hurrying to Simon’s house, that she may lay bare her thirst, set forth her need, and at last lay down her misery.

What is it, Mary? What business have you in the Pharisee’s house? Do you wish to anoint his head with your oil? “By no means,” she says. “I come not because of Simon the leper, but because of Jesus, the healer of souls. I approach sick with tertian and quartan fevers; for I suffer at once from a contrary fever, since I miserably succumb to vices contrary in themselves. By public report I have heard that a physician has come whose art drives away every weakness, and restores, without price yet beyond price, the health of the former age. By a single medicinal word [Col. 0830C] he employs a new manner of healing, sufficient to cure every disease of all people; as his Father created all things by one word, so likewise by one command he heals all things.

Besides this, many great and wonderful things are reported of him: that he commands winds and sea; that he immediately changes water into wine; that by the touch of the fringes of his garment he checks a woman’s flow; that by touching with his hand he draws out leprosy; that he feeds crowds with miracles. He is also said to be full of compassion, full of kindness, full of gentleness: he despises no one, rejects no one, receives everyone who comes to him. Therefore I come to Jesus, not to the Pharisee; to the Saviour, not to Simon; to the physician, not to the leper. I come, [Col. 0830D] I say, I now come to the fountain of mercy, not to the mountain of pride; to the compassionate remitter of a debt, not to the impious exacter of what is not owed.

Perhaps the contemptible leper despises me; but the Lord Jesus, who is to be adored, certainly regards me. That man imputes my sins to me, though he is weighed down by his own; he forgives the offences of my youth, whom the deadly and universal stain of our corruption did not infect. My creditor acts mercifully toward me; the superstitious and wicked accuser acts cruelly. Therefore I do not come to Simon’s house for its resident, but for its guest. For although the humble one lodges with the proud—Jesus with the Pharisee, the physician with the proud—yet he does not turn his face toward one who disparages his neighbour, but toward one [Col. 0831A] confessing her guilt. For pride disdains humility, discord unity, uncleanness chastity, vice virtue. Yet sometimes the stronger virtue enters the lodging of sin, so that, after Satan’s dominion has been destroyed, it may carry off as spoil the soul fettered by habitual evils, while vice, deserted by its dwelling, may sit in the wilderness.

Therefore she runs to the word which the Lord sent into Jacob and which fell in Israel, if perhaps I may seize the kingdom of heaven from the Pharisee’s house—a kingdom which he neglects for the sake of his fatness and abundance. I shall do what a certain woman did, my equal and like in sex and in the pride of former evils, yet nevertheless not unlike in faith and devotion. Others once pressed upon Jesus; but from the pressure of others she who suffered from an issue of blood received the juice of power. For she placed beneath it the throat of faith, and from the cluster of henna (*cyprus*) sweating and overflowing in the winepress [Col. 0831B] drew forth balsam. Thus, yes, thus I too: because the Pharisee’s pride outweighs the humility of Jesus in his own arrogance, I shall rise to the feet that are pressed but not oppressed, and shall store up the hanging jewel of grace in the vessel of my heart placed beneath it.

I shall anoint my breasts, which were broken in Egypt, with a drop of that oil which shall not fail from my head, just as the flask of oil was not diminished; so that, at last corrected through repentance, they may be better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments. Simon, trusting—indeed presuming—upon his own righteousness, presses out the wine of righteousness; but oil or balsam is fitting for me because of my sex and because of my sickness. Woe to you, Simon, who rise in the morning in order to burn with wine! For oil would be more useful in the morning, wine in the evening; because, if you had first taken the little boat of mercy, you would less fear the storms of judgment. “I will sing to you of mercy and judgment, O Lord,” says the Psalmist (Ps. 101:1): mercy in the morning, judgment in the evening. For the morning of redemption comes, and the judgment of vengeance; indeed, no one could endure the harshness of wine and the darkness of night unless he had first received the light of morning and the sweetness of oil. For who, in the night of judgment, except Simon, who glories in his own strength, [Col. 0831C] will stand to behold him when he appears like fire melting and refining silver?

“You wish to drink wine, Simon: you will begin to burn. For the severity [Col. 0831D] of judgment is an intolerable heat. Therefore let us rather in the morning be anointed only with oil than burn with wine; let us humble ourselves for pardon, not raise ourselves up to empty boasting. No,” Mary says, “I do not run to wine, because I have no garment. First a garment, then ointment, and afterward I seek wine. For I am drenched in a twofold shame: I am naked of the garments of grace, and therefore I blush; I am wounded in the gifts granted to my nature, and therefore I groan. Accordingly, for my shame I ask a covering of forgiveness, and for my wounds a medicine of restoration. For the watchmen of the walls wounded me and took away my cloak; indeed, the robbers of darkness did so. Whatever gift of grace or gifts of the Holy Spirit I had received, I lost through using them badly, keeping them negligently, and living most wickedly at the prompting of demons. [Col. 0832A] ‘For my strength has forsaken me, and the light of my eyes itself is not with me’” (Ps. 38:10).

“The spirit of fornication took from me the cloak of integrity; the spirit of anger, the tunic of charity; the spirit of gluttony or drunkenness, the linen garment of sobriety; the spirit of pride, the footwear of humility; the spirit of impatience, the shirt of mildness and gentleness; the spirit of avarice, the ornament of my head; the spirit of disobedience, the earrings from my ears. Behold how seven spirits more wicked than the others divided my garments and cast lots over my clothing. From these I suffer tertian fever; from these, quartan fever. For because of three and four crimes committed by me, my soul and my belly—that is, body and spirit—are troubled.

“Nevertheless, thus stripped, thus naked, thus full of shame, I fall at the feet of the Lamb who has seven eyes and seven horns, seeking wool and linen with which to weave a garment and cover my reproach. For this reason I approach from behind at his feet and pour out my soul in tears, watering my bed with tears every night. Henceforth I have no other bed except the feet of Jesus: here is my rest for ever and ever; here is sweet sleep; here shall be for me the tabernacle of everlasting dwelling. If those who have no clothing, according to Job (ch. 24:8), embrace stones, why should not I, who am naked, embrace the feet of the Lord Jesus?

“Jesus, who has become for me wisdom and righteousness [Col. 0832C] and sanctification and redemption; who, virgin born of a virgin, was conceived and born to restore integrity; who, like a lamb before its shearer, to restore charity, did not open his mouth except to pour forth prayers, so that the governor marvelled; who, to extinguish drunkenness, taught sobriety by deed and word; who is the beginning and head of humility, to direct our steps in the way of peace; who, when reviled, did not revile in return, to provide an example of patience; who had nowhere to lay his head, to pierce the spirit of avarice; who was obedient to the Father unto death, to complete the victory of his dispensation—he has clothed me again in the garments of his glory. For when he forgives sins, [Col. 0832D] he is as though mending garments.

“Thus delivered from cold and shame, I set about healing my wounds. The lust of the eyes wounded me; the vanity of the ears; the appetite of the belly; an excessively refined taste; touch that caressed beyond what was right; scent purchased from every quarter; and bodily pleasure exceeding nature’s necessity and changing the image of God into a beastly image. At last I open the wound, uncover the bruise, expose the swelling sore to medicinal remedies, crying: ‘My scars have become corrupt because of my folly’; and you, Lord—what will you do? Heal me, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved. Naked, I seek the Lamb; wounded, the physician; thirsty, the living fountain; trembling, the fortress; darkened, oil; ulcerated, ointment; dead, [Col. 0833A] life. May the Lamb grant me wisdom, the physician understanding, the living fountain counsel, the tower strength, the oil knowledge, the ointment compassion, and life the fear of God.

“I renounce luxury; I impose repentance upon myself; I shed tears; I wash his feet; I wipe them dry with the towel of my hair. In the midst of Church and synagogue I confess myself guilty; I disdain to live for myself any longer. I shall call to mind the time of my youth, so that, if I cannot recall its days through innocence, I may at least cut them in half through repentance. Although I cannot suffice to repay hours for hours, moments for moments, days for days, months for months, years for years, still I shall set all that remains in payment for the whole. May the right hand of God, holding the balance of guilt and punishment, mercy and justice, [Col. 0833B] incline it from the one to the other, so that what belongs to justice may be lightened, what belongs to mercy increased, what belongs to punishment pardoned, and what belongs to guilt erased.

“If Simon’s sentence is accepted, the weight of the scales presses down on the left and empties the right. According to Simon, the whole of guilt demands the whole of punishment. But let not the enemy prevail, O Lord Jesus: withdraw the sentence from wicked lips and a deceitful tongue, a sentence not pronounced according to the laws of your mercy. Finally, as Daniel, the man of desires, rejected the false testimony against chaste Susanna, so you, wholly desirable, do not approve the condemnation against Mary, whom you are to save. Let guilt be removed, so that punishment may be mitigated; let the fullness of justice be poured into the fullness of mercy, the fullness [Col. 0833C] of vengeance into the fullness of pardon. Let the weights of justice become fewer, that the sceptres of mercy may shine more brightly; for through Jesus a passage lies open from the kingdom of justice, through repentance, into the kingdom of mercy.

“Justice too has its innocent ones; mercy has its penitents. Yet those whom mercy has led by the way of repentance pass into the kingdom of innocence. Whose is the kingdom of justice, if not his whose kingdom is also that of mercy? There is no one to accuse you if you transfer someone from the kingdom of justice to the kingdom of mercy. Long ago Jacob exchanged his hands in blessing Ephraim and Manasseh: right for left, first for last, head for tail—surely inspired by prophetic mystery. Therefore Joseph wished to judge according to outward appearance and, as though the old man had forgotten, recalled to him the order of birth, saying: ‘It is not right, father, for this one is the firstborn; put your right hand upon his head.’ To him the father replied: ‘I know, my son, I know’ (Gen. 48:19).

“O depth of mystery! O unsearchable sacrament! The Ancient of Days knows what Joseph does not yet understand: the wild olive is grafted into the olive tree and becomes a sharer in the root and richness of the olive. At last the natural branch, broken off, became alien to its brothers, so that not everyone who is from Israel is an Israelite. Likewise Jacob is chosen and Esau rejected. What more? ‘The kingdom of God,’ says the Lord, ‘shall be taken from you Jews and given [Col. 0834A] to a nation producing its fruits’ (Matt. 21:43). But when and how did this happen? In the transposition of the hands, when the mystery of the cross was consecrated: promising greater and better things to the lesser, but granting in the present the left hand of an earthly kingdom to the proud and those who glory in the flesh. Simon judges himself worthy of the right hand and Mary of the left; but the Lord of knowledge is the most just assessor of merits.

## SERMON LXIII. FOR THE FEAST OF ST MARY MAGDALENE, IV

Mary Magdalene is set before all sinners as a complete and clear image of most health-giving conversion and repentance. For in her, as upon a certain most beautifully fashioned tablet, the loving-kindness of Jesus has carved, with the living works of the Lord and the most lovely colours of his mercies, [Col. 0834B] the limbs, sinews, and veins of our conversion and of his justification; so that she who had first been of the worst condition might afterward be found of the most perfect beauty. Truly, if you compare her former state and her latter, you will without doubt observe them proceeding, as it were with equal steps, in contrary directions: as she had turned away and withdrawn into the depth of wickedness, so, once converted, she returned into the depth of repentance.

But what drew her into the depth of wickedness except the depth of ignorance? And what drew her back to the depth of repentance except the depth of divine mercy? O depth between depth and depth: what will you make of the depth of iniquity, so as to open the depth of conversion? Powerfully fill up the cistern [Col. 0834C] of old corruption, and mercifully dig the way of holy change. Let the surface of the abyss of darkness and gloom be levelled; let the fountain of David’s house be opened for the washing of the most holy sinner; let the well of ancient rottenness be made level with the embankments of satisfactions; let the renewed breast, wholly sweating in tears, be diligently pierced through. Behold how the depth of God changes the depth of erring humanity into another depth: namely, that of one confessing and repenting.

The devil and a human being first dig the depth; God and a human being bring about the second. For the devil, by suggestion, opens, as it were, the pit of sin; the person, by consenting and taking delight, extends himself and the pit even to the deepest point. This pit is a pit of misery, dregs, and mud. But by adding transgression to transgression, by adding iniquity upon iniquity, he advances—indeed declines—into the infinity of error, so that what had first been a pit is no longer a pit but an abyss. Then darkness rises upon the face of the abyss, as Scripture testifies. Behold the pit; behold the abyss; behold darkness upon the face of the abyss. But whence, or why, is this? Whence except from the confusion of deeds or desires? Why, except because the earth is empty and void: empty, that is, of the seeds of good will; void of the fruits of good action?

Before Mary Magdalene was watered by the rivers of paradise, impregnated by the words of truth, made fruitful by the condescension of the most loving [Col. 0835A] Saviour, washed by her own tears already sanctified through faith, and clothed in the garment of confession and beauty, she was earth empty and void. For what was emptier than she, who, subjected to vanity, spoke vain things, pursued vain things, and was made altogether vanity, wholly immersed in the pleasures of the flesh? What was more void than she, who was emptied of the whole fullness of graces and filled with no fruit of good work? But how was she empty, from whom the Lord cast out seven demons? How void, who was full of so many demons?

Certainly she was void precisely because she was full of demons. For demons, by filling the soul, empty it rather than fill it; they produce solitude, not fullness; hunger, not satiety. The nature of vices is always vain, always empty: it consumes itself, and by breaking the vessel into which it has entered, renders it flowing away from all its integrity. It devours whatever it finds, and, lest any good enter, shuts the gates of the heart with the bolt of wickedness. It burns up greenness, scorches the flower, snatches away leaves, corrupts fruit, gnaws away the root of natural good, and consumes the beauty of branches by breaking them. What more? It overthrows the whole region of the heart as in hostile devastation. Thus a lodging that has been filled by such a guest is better level—indeed, empty.

But what happened? The Full One came to the empty woman—or rather, the Full One to one who was full: full of grace and truth, to one full of wickedness and infirmity; full of goodness, to one full of malice; full of health, to one full [Col. 0835C] of sickness; full of fullness, to one full of emptiness. At last he emptied her who was full and filled her who was empty. Whom he emptied of demons, he filled with virtues; whom he emptied of the old man, he filled with the new; whom he emptied of dead works, he filled with the gifts of charisms; whom he emptied of the spoils of lusts, he filled with the trophies of true and perfect humility; finally, whom he emptied of iniquity, he filled with love.

“O earth empty and void, God has set apart for you a voluntary rain, a latter and early rain, that you may be intoxicated with the drops of the heavenly gift. Let Simon, like a fleece, be dry because of the aridity of his proud heart. Far be it from me to rest asleep in my house while the soul of my Lord labours in the camp of the Philistines [Col. 0835D] far from his home. For he follows his prey and, now that the strong man is bound, sweeps out his house by the light of a lamp, in order to restore to the very ground—indeed to the paternal throne—the lost drachma. How then shall I go up into the bed of my couch while the ark is under skins and in tents, without the soul of my Lord? His wounds in feet, hands, and side are not yet wiped, and shall I sit? I have not anointed him, and shall I eat? I have not kissed him, and shall I rest? I have not touched him, and am I secure? I have not embraced him, and do I fear darkness? Where are you, my faith? What are you, my health? How long are you silent? How long do you hide? How long do you fear man? How, seeing impiety, did you not burst forth into a public cry? How did you not, to the best of your strength, wrest your deliverer from them?

“Certainly I feared not Pilate scourging, nor the roaring crowd, but the Lord thus willing it. For I knew his face, and therefore observed his sign. I considered the sign that indicated patience, not the raging tumult; and, troubled within myself, I poured intolerable pains into myself. Tears could scarcely come forth safely; a groan could scarcely shake the air without danger; a sob scarcely dared to tremble within the walls of the household.

“Now, indeed, now my patience, wearied beyond measure, may run to the patience of my God, wearied indeed but released and extended even unto hell. I shall not live unless I find life. I seek life—not another’s, but his who lies in the tomb. I shall keep watch at his sepulchre until I see Jesus; and if I could not die with the dying one, I shall live with the dead one, or even die for the dead one. Those who hated him killed him; those who loved him buried him. What of me, who did neither—the one because I did not wish to, the other because I could not? Not forgetful of my duty, at least I shall anoint his feet, anoint his hands, anoint his side, anoint his whole body. The ointment of my faith shall not fail, because the effect of the deed shall never deprive the reward-worthy affection of so devout a purpose.” Thus she meditated like a dove in her throat; thus she spoke in her spirit.
