And behold, the angel of the Lord, hearing the veins of her whisper and seeing the suffusions of her eyes, and observing the most frequent repetitions of her sobs, being taught by signs not unknown what her spirit asked and what her mind desired, himself first announces and supplies the fulfilment of her vows, declaring that Christ has risen. [Col. 0836C]

Now weigh the balance of this present joy against the balance of former sorrow; and as you shared in the gravest sufferings, so you will marvel at the triumphs of the coming jubilation. For now day utters a word to day, just as night had once announced knowledge to night. For while the apostles were still held in the night of ignorance of the Lord’s Resurrection, they were, as it were, night. She came to the tomb while darkness still remained; and, not finding the Lord’s body, believed that it had been taken away. Therefore she came to the apostles, saying: “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him” (John 20:13). [Col. 0836D] Thus it was night because of ignorance.

## SERMON LXIV. FOR THE FEAST OF ST MARY MAGDALENE, V

Human nature, the nature of Adam’s children, needs no example for committing transgression, no instructor for unrestrained lust, no guide to turn it aside from the path. But once it has fallen, it is scarcely helped even by remedies gathered from every side and every source; scarcely healed even when every possible care of treatment has been applied; and scarcely brought back to the way of truth even when truth itself recalls it. No effort is needed for it to be carried from a height into a precipice; but to regain the things above, strength must be gathered, virtue exercised, and help sought.

Thus, dearest brothers, thus the occasion of evil stands ready [Col. 0837A] and at the door. It presents itself spontaneously to one wishing to sin; indeed, it even draws to itself and compels into its embraces anyone unwilling. It is an insolent harlot, wounding the eyes, burning the heart, enclosing the whole person in the chains and fetters of unlawful love. In the city of this world she allows no one to go away untempted, untroubled, or free of her: she plays in towers, circles the walls, explores houses, and walks about the earth. She wanders even to the feet of Jesus, but there she fails; and she who until then had triumphed over all is herself overcome by a better triumph. For Jesus, the fountain of graces, having widened the bosom of mercy according to the multitude of his mercies, grafts the olive tree into the wild olive; repairs a vessel of dishonour into a vessel of glory; taking iron from the earth, makes silver; [Col. 0837B] from an unclean woman makes a clean one, from a sick woman a healthy one, from a stranger a member of the household.

“O how healthy is the head whose feet are so holy that they make a harlot chaste; that by their touch they stop the flow of the disordered woman; that they dry up the well of iniquity and the fountain of all wickedness! O sinful soul, in which iniquity sits, in which sin reigns: made a harlot by taking evil delight, worse by consenting, worst by acting. Hear that most loving Jesus reclines in the house of Simon the leper; do not despair, do not fear, do not flee. For he who does not disdain to eat with a leper—can he reject a weeping sinner? He received a meal from the hand of a leper: will he despise the tears of a confessing soul? He reclines beside a leper: will he not regard, or rather receive, one prostrate at his feet? Whose iniquity is greater: that of the proud leper or of the humble harlot? Surely every proud person is a leper in soul—and is not every envious person as well? Perhaps Simon is proud because he is righteous, holy, clean? But what righteousness is there where pride is? For pride is the beginning of every sin.

“Therefore, since the height of God’s mercies does not flee even the house of the proud and envious sinner, but enters it to dine, humbling even the proud soul and recalling the envious soul to gentleness, let Mary Magdalene not despair. Instead, let her wrap herself about the feet of Jesus, humbly confessing the foulness and disgrace of her former life. Let her enter the cloister of obedience; let her whole body, which is the body of vices, [Col. 0837D] be prostrated at the feet of Jesus—that is, of all virtues. Let her be baptized anew in the river of tears; let her wipe away the defilements of her former conduct with the varied adornment of renewed thoughts and works; let her pour over herself the ointment of the good and precious fragrance of spiritual contemplations. With these her head shall be made rich; the oil of the sinner—that is, of Simon—does not make it rich. By these shall he be delighted whom the transgressing house provokes; by these shall he be watered whom the torrent of iniquity does not surround.

“Let us now, brothers, call to mind the ancient paths—indeed the preceding errors—and, dried up by the barrenness of evils, with the hoes of prayers dig at the feet of Jesus the river of paradise. Thus whatever in the garden of our souls is dry may be watered; whatever is filthy cleansed; whatever is withered restored to life; whatever is sterile [Col. 0838A] made fruitful; whatever is deformed made beautiful; whatever is useless cut away; whatever is useful enlarged; whatever is stained whitened; whatever is wrinkled stretched out. For at the fragrance of this Magdalene, long dead, like Aaron’s rod, she returned to life by penetrating grace, budded, flowered anew, and bore fruits worthy of repentance.

“Truly dead, because, possessing none of the life of virtues, she lay buried in the hell of vices. Truly dead, because, full of spirits of error, bearing the standards of death in the camps of crimes, she raved unto the death of innocents. Truly dead, whose throat was an open grave, whose tongue dealt deceitfully. But the fountain which watered the whole surface of the earth rose up, preaching, working miracles, and coming into the Pharisee’s house to eat with him; [Col. 0838B] it breathed forth the word of life-giving preaching, opened the hidden and unknown sweetness of the ointment brought from the secrets of heaven, and with wondrous swiftness sprinkled the neighbouring air with the novelty and cheerfulness of its balsam. When the woman who was a sinner in the city heard—or rather drank in—this, she brought an alabaster vessel of ointment; and standing behind at the Lord’s feet, she began to water them with her tears and wipe them with her hair.

“Therefore she now lives, she who hears the Gospel. For it is said in the Gospel of John: ‘Those who hear shall live’ (John 5:25). Without doubt, the word of life enters into the bones and sinews of one receiving it; Ezekiel testifies to this (ch. 37), when he says that the Spirit came from the four winds of heaven, entered, and raised dead bones. For wherever prudence, courage, [Col. 0838C] justice, and temperance come with the Spirit of God, there life follows and death departs. ‘The woman who was a sinner in the city came,’ it says. Previously, turning away, she departed by sinning; she went away by delighting in the counsel of the wicked; she stood by consenting in the way of sinners; and she sat in the seat of pestilence through obstinate hardening. Then, converted by turning away from evil, she came by doing good; she approached in shame, stood behind in humility, and by persevering clung to the pavement.

“This should be understood thus: to think evil is to withdraw from God, for perverse thoughts separate from God; to add pleasures to wicked thoughts is to go away in the counsel of the wicked; deliberately to choose evil through consent is to stand in the way of sinners; finally, to stink in one’s sins through evil habit and offer others examples of death is to sit in the seat of sinners. But one must set back the foot of the mind by a backward-moving conversion, so that by thinking good things, delighting in good things, following better things, and persevering in holiness, we may restore the years consumed by the caterpillar, the grub, the locust, or even rust: the years of the lustful are consumed by the grub; the years of the gluttonous by the caterpillar; the years of the proud by the locust; the years of the envious by rust. Thus by self-restraint, abstinence, humble living, and innocent conduct, we repair the losses of former evils.

“Therefore she who had withdrawn approached; and she approached with as many steps of devotion toward light, to be illumined, as she had passed away through as many steps of iniquity, failing in the region of the shadow of death. [Col. 0839A] Hence Gregory says: ‘She found in herself as many holocausts as she had had pleasures of the flesh.’ She offers a victim, brings a sacrifice, carries a holocaust within the veil: a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God; a sacrifice of a contrite spirit; a rich sacrifice of most sweet fragrance. She also strips the skin of the old person from her victim and cuts its limbs into pieces. ‘She began,’ says the Evangelist (Luke 7:38), ‘to water his feet with tears and to wipe them with her hair.’

“In the house of Simon the leper I see astonishing things: Simon murmuring; Jesus showing mercy; Mary weeping bitterly. The gall of bitterness and wind of pride burst Simon’s veins; the honey of sweetness and spirit of compassion overflow upon the Son of the Virgin; contrition of heart and the impulse of compunction flow from the inward parts [Col. 0839B] of the sinner. Jesus overflows with mercy, Simon with malice, Mary with repentance: mercy comes from heaven, malice from hell, repentance from the world. Heaven alone knows mercy; hell alone produces malice; the world alone practises repentance.

“In heaven there is no seat of malice, because from it was cast out the accuser of our brothers, who dragged after himself a third part of the stars; nor is there a place of repentance, because it is the homeland of those who reign, not those who fight; of those who have been proved, not those being tested; of those crowned, not those running uncertainly. Likewise, in hell there is no place of mercy, because it is the lake of the despairing, the Gehenna of the condemned, the hammer from whose punishment there is never a rebound; nor is there a place of repentance, because as the sentence of punishments is confirmed, so their hearts are hardened in impenitence. Repentance is practised only in the world, because no inhabitant of it is [and not] a transgressor. [Col. 0839C]

“Now the inhabitant of this world receives mercy from the borderland of heaven, malice from the contamination of hell, and misery from his own dwelling. For the righteous person is not raised into the highest fullness of mercies unless the incitements of sin are broken; nor is the reprobate plunged into the abysses of miseries unless he has passed through the whirlpools of human desire. For the former shall be absorbed in glory and the latter in punishment. But while destination or predestination is pending, one must neither rush carelessly into the latter through despair nor irreverently rush into the former through presumption; for a human being does not know whether he is worthy of hatred or love.

“Therefore let him flee malice, take refuge in mercy, and so escape misery. Let him seize the feet of mercy; wash, wipe, and anoint them. Let him seize them through fear, wash them through compunction, wipe them through confession, anoint them through devotion. Nevertheless, let him seize the head of malice, cut it off, burn it, and reduce it to ashes: seize it through courage, cut it off through confession, burn it through fervour, reduce it to ashes through discernment. Such a seizure of virtue and detection—or rather suppression—of vice makes the sick woman healthy, the leprous woman clean, the sinner holy, and the harlot an apostle.

## SERMON LXV. ON THE TRANSFIGURATION OF THE LORD, I

[Col. 0840A]

“As an eagle provoking her young to fly,” etc. (Deut. 32:11).

After mentioning his Passion, Jesus forestalled sorrow with consolation, sickness with remedy, bitterness with sweetness, and finally the most shameful death of the cross with glorious transfiguration, lest the apostles’ faith, still small and tender, like a grain of mustard, should be crushed by so great and burdensome a weight and millstone. For it is a fitting compensation of profit, and every reckoning according to equity weighs in a just balance both the labour and the reward of the work, so that what is expended and what is demanded may proceed with equal steps, though by different paths meeting at a single crossroads. [Col. 0840B]

To be honoured and despised, glorified and disfigured, are indeed different things; yet Jesus bore both the cross and the glorification of transfiguration upon one shoulder. For the same face that shone like the sun in the transfiguration endured spittle and blows in the Passion. If the face of the image of God’s glory assumed the brightness of the sun, that was not a great thing. But that the most foul unbelief of the Jews poured the poisons of its own breast upon the face of God—who, hearing this, does not waste away? Who does not close his ears or rend his faithful heart? Even the garments that became white as snow are taken away and distributed by lot among the soldiers.

O patience of God! Things which scarcely could worthily be entrusted to angelic guardianship, things most mercifully designated for the Christian people as incomparable treasures, are handled by the unworthy hands of those crucifying him. But the reason for this truth and contrast lies hidden in mysteries concealed from ages. Meanwhile, until the childhood of faith grows feathers, before it is exposed to the kite, instruction in flight is set forth and explained. For after the Lord had foretold his Passion, six days later he took Peter, James, and John, led them up a high mountain, [Col. 0840C] and was transfigured before them.

The Lord’s transfiguration is an eagle-like flight. For as the eagle is borne in swiftest flight into the sun itself, so human nature, assumed by the Word and soaring most powerfully, in that hour cast away all mortal hindrances—holding solar or snowy brightness in contempt, but clothed with the brightness which it had in the Word before the world existed and into which even angels desire to look. For the Evangelist could not express it as fully as divine power could accomplish it. A human being spoke as he could by comparison; but God could do more in action than human speech could relate.

Thus the hen led her chicks up the high mountain, and, not like a hen but like an eagle, provoked them to fly. For it belongs to a hen not to fly but to nourish chicks; whereas it belongs to an eagle to fly and to provoke them to fly. Therefore Jesus was a hen on the plains, an eagle on the mountains: on the plains he instructs in moral matters, on the mountains he reveals heavenly things; on the plains [Col. 0840D] he heals illnesses, on the mountains he teaches the beatitudes. On the plains he spreads out Jacob’s stone; on the mountains he raises the ladder. He provokes by wonder, by delight, by fatherly consolation, by promise, and by compassion—because, if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him.

Why was he transfigured not merely in their presence but before them, except because he shall conform the body of our humility to the body of his glory, so that we may be changed from glory into glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord? He is before them as the head; we follow after as members. For members everywhere follow their head, whether to death or to life. Hence: “Whoever serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also my servant shall be” (John 12:26).

[Col. 0841B] There follows the manner of the Transfiguration, like the singular flight of an eagle, difficult to imitate: “And his face shone like the sun, and his garments became white as snow” (Matt. 17:2). When the eagle grows old, it is renewed. So too, when Jesus, as though wearied by the old age of the world’s troubles and stirred by a desire to finish his course, proposed, like Jacob, to revisit his father and homeland, he was first transfigured: his countenance changed into the brightness of the sun and his appearance into the likeness of snow. For the face of the old man ceases when the glory of the new approaches: “You shall cast away the old,” Moses says, “when the new things come” (Lev. 26:10). But Jesus, having taken up the winnowing-fan, began to cleanse his threshing-floor when he changed the tent of Kedar into the skin of Solomon—that is, the oldness [Col. 0841C] of mortality into the glory of transfiguration. And because there was nothing artificial in the Transfiguration, the comparison was taken from the sun, not from any earthly form; for who can reach the sun in order to practice deceptive art upon it? Therefore that was heavenly: by divine power alone the face of Jesus shone like the sun.

This familiar mystery is also concealed in the comparison: the sun always shines when it is not covered by a cloud, but withdraws its rays when it is overshadowed by a thick and dense cloud. The ignorance and malice of the Jews made a thick cloud and a dark blindness; hence it was said that “their own malice blinded them” (Wis. 2:21). Thus, blinded, they stumbled upon the stone of offense and rock of stumbling, attending to the cloud that covered it [Col. 0841D] rather than to the sun concealed within it. For Isaac had grown old and could not clearly see what was present, though he most truly prophesied what was to come. Jesus had veiled himself in the thin and bright cloud of flesh; but his persecutors, to their own harm, made it threefold, when, instilling the lethargic hatred of the devil and their own perverted understanding, they twisted together the threefold cord of their condemnation. Therefore they did not see the sun, because fire fell upon them, because their fury was according to the likeness of a serpent, etc.

Certainly the eagle had the strength to fly away, since a net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures, and to escape their snares. Yet he stooped toward the food which is the will of his Father; hence: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John 4:34). He therefore preferred to be caught [Col. 0842A] in the trap rather than remain fasting and without the food of obedience. This eagle had worn down its old beak by fasting forty days and forty nights, and would take up a new one in the kingdom of its Father, where it was to drink new wine with its disciples and share new bread.

It follows: “And his garments became white as snow” (Matt. 17:2). Distinguish between sun and snow, between face and garment. For “the disciple is not above the master”; but he will be perfect if he is like his master—not in equality but in likeness, just as snow is not compared with the sun in dignity, but in a certain participation in brightness. By the face, indeed, Christ himself is meant; by the garments, his disciples. Observe in this how the eagle summons [Col. 0842B] its young to fly. The faithful will not be made equal to the Son of God, but will be glorified with him. “There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory. So also is the resurrection of the dead.”

Therefore he summons his young to fly—not to fly away or fly together with him—so that, as those who are of his company, they may imitate him in simplicity of life, in suffering for the faith, and in hope of the glory of the children of God. Snow is light because of simplicity, cold because of suffering, bright because of resurrection. Compare the Gospel with the song: “Like an eagle summoning its young to fly and hovering over them.” “And his face shone like the sun, and his garments like snow”: what else is this but that he summons his young to fly and hovers [Col. 0842C] over them? “Look,” he says while hanging on the cross, “and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow” (Lam. 1:12). Behold how he hovers above them in suffering. “It cannot be compared with the dyed colors of India, nor can the gold of Ethiopia equal it” (Job 28:16).

Behold how he hovers above them in the splendor of wisdom and in the loftiness of virtues. The song continues: “He spread out his wings and took them up,” etc. (Deut. 32:11). In the Gospel: “Moses and Elijah appeared with him, speaking with him” (Matt. 17:3). Who brought Moses from death and Elijah from the most remote region, except the eagle that spread out the wings of its will and power and carried them on its shoulders—that is, by its unconquerable operation? For he bears all things by the word of his power. By that word, by those shoulders, he brought Moses and Elijah [Col. 0842D] so that they might attend his Transfiguration. It follows: “And behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them” (ibid., v. 5). Perhaps this is the cloud which received Jesus from the apostles’ sight as they watched, and in which he will also come for judgment, according to the saying: “He will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

It follows: “The Lord alone guided him, and no foreign god was with him” (Deut. 32:12). In the Gospel: “And a voice came from the cloud, saying: This is my Son,” etc. (Matt. 17:5). Here is what the Apostle says: “One God and Father of all, who is above all and through all and in us all, who is God blessed for ever” (Eph. 4:6). For there are not two gods, [Col. 0843A] Father and Son, but one God, one Lord, one faith, one baptism. The voice came from the cloud—namely, the voice of this Lord, the Father—saying: “This is my Son; this is he whom the Father has sealed and sent into the world; this is, distinctively, my Son.” For all others are sons by adoption; this one is Son by nature according to divinity, and by unity of person according to humanity. “This is my beloved Son”: beloved in generation, beloved in operation, beloved in death, beloved in resurrection; he lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LXVI. ON THE TRANSFIGURATION OF THE LORD, II

We cannot worthily write or say anything about Jesus unless we have received it from him—from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift—according to the measure [Col. 0843B] of his giving. For the Spirit, who speaks mysteries, proceeds both from the Father and from him; he searches out the inexpressible secrets of God, nor is he overwhelmed by the majesty in which he reigns equally, without inequality of substance. Therefore may he be present with us, teaching all truth, especially when we speak of Jesus and write about Jesus.

Lord Jesus, since according to the nature of your divinity there was in you no change nor shadow of alteration, you assumed a human condition which, subject to time and vanity, does not at all escape the lot of mutability, but runs in time and with time according to the order of nature. Hence the saying: “The boy Jesus grew in age and wisdom before God and men” (Luke 2:52). In this nature, therefore, and according [Col. 0843C] to this nature, you were the Bridegroom of the Church. Your belly, ivory, set with sapphires, distinguished—not only by preaching with words but also by acting in deeds—what and when you should say, what and when you should do, according to the lines of eternity, so that you might not only provide for human weariness, but also preserve the rationale of the Father’s everlasting ordinance and eternal decree. Thus in the Gospel you say: “As the Father commanded me, so I do” (John 14:31).

Therefore, lest the devotion of his faithful should recoil from something almost incredible, he willed to suffer the sufferings of a human being, so that he might be known as human; and he performed signs and wonders which, as Nicodemus said, no one could do unless God were with him (John 3:2). This was not only by grace for humanity’s sake, but also by nature for divinity’s sake, that he might be believed to be God. Yet the clearer and more beautiful signs of his humanity appeared even before the eyes of the foolish; the rarer signs, which would indisputably establish him as God, scarcely touched even the hearts of the disciples. Undoubtedly the unprecedented novelty of the mystery of the incarnate Word hindered belief: that the world should believe what had not been heard from ages past, what human reason could not comprehend, and what neither use nor custom could in any way approve—namely, that God should become man.

At times a ray of divinity flashing forth roused the slothful torpor of the Jews, but did not shake it off; it encouraged the disciples’ watchfulness, but the sublimity of the matter, by filling them with astonishment, sometimes for a little while [Col. 0844A] bent them back from the strength of faith. Thus they often heard: “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” Again: “Are you still without understanding?” (Matt. 15:16). Therefore, amid the mixed course of apostolic firmness and instability, until the time of the Passion drew near, he took Peter, James, and John, and went up a high mountain, where he was transfigured before them, in order to wipe away every darkness of doubt.

This is the strongest and most impregnable argument of the Christian faith: beneath the veil of flesh lay the power of divinity, and the very one who outwardly appeared to be human was God, though what lay hidden within did not appear. For not even at the very moment of the Transfiguration did the apostles see the substance of divinity; rather, by a holy foretaste, in healing fashion, they tasted beforehand the flesh that was shortly to be glorified by everlasting resurrection, [Col. 0844B] so that through the strength of this refreshment they might not fail before reaching the mountain of God, Horeb—that is, the resurrection, in which, according to the interpretation of this name, both mortality and every capacity for suffering were dried up in Christ. For “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more,” etc. (Rom. 6:9).

This holy and splendid solemnity is rightly honored by Christians. In it faith, as it were, set its foot: though it did not waver perilously, it had not yet put down deep roots. The event at John’s baptism had indeed preceded it, where the Spirit was seen in the form of a dove and the Father likewise heard in a voice: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” [Col. 0844C] (Matt. 3:17)—a certain anticipation of this most beautiful Transfiguration.

Indeed, that event was more fruitful through the obscuring of the sacrament, because the mystery of our regeneration then began; this is higher in splendor and stronger in the attestation of witnesses. For the testimony of one person is far weaker than that of five or three. John alone heard and saw the former event. Peter, James, and John, together with Moses and Elijah, were present at this one and are competent witnesses. There neither the flesh nor the face of Jesus changed its beauty; here his face shone like the sun beyond human sight. That occurred in the wilderness, this upon a high mountain; there and here alike was the glory of Jesus. There one beholds, as it were, faith’s entrance; here, as it were, its exit, [Col. 0844D] where the thing believed is clearly seen. Of the former the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror and in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13:12); of this John says: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father” (John 1:14).

Lord Jesus, just as you now, for an hour, as it were, put off our mortality, could you not—if our salvation had required it—have put on your power and beauty without the painful and groaning stripping-off, and not permitted your sack to be torn by the Jews, but more easily have made a sock from a sack than wine from water? But in order that the Passion, which was near, might plainly appear more clearly than light to be voluntary, not compelled or to be undergone by unavoidable necessity, the great mystery of godliness was disclosed in the sack opened on the road: what was in the mouth of Benjamin’s sack was revealed, namely, that the money by which the Son of the Right Hand would redeem Israel and the nations should be in the mouth of Jesus. Hence, when he said, “It is finished” (John 19:30), [Col. 0845A] and gave up the spirit, the price was paid and the bond that stood against us was erased.

Without prejudice to so great a mystery, this pertains to the Transfiguration: on the way—that is, before he arrived at the dwelling-place—Benjamin’s sack was opened, not torn. The tearing is the Passion; the opening is the Transfiguration. At the opening, the sack was not emptied or drained, because after the Transfiguration he received, or displayed again, the same form and appearance of mortality which, on entering the world from his mother, he had received and had, as it were, laid aside in a prelude to the resurrection. But in the tearing, mortality was swallowed up in victory; and Jacob did not play with Esau—that is, the devil—but mocked and supplanted him, so that, once the body of sin had been destroyed, no root might remain from which the revived deception of the human race could spring forth and make a repetition of Christ’s death necessary.

The Transfiguration, therefore, was a kind of interruption of the necessary mortality arising from sin, by which Jesus proved that he was not subject to the laws of death except when, how, and as far as he willed. For what there was momentary, could, had he willed it, have been continual. Therefore he showed himself not such as the Jews thought him, but such as the apostles believed him—not to all the people, but to witnesses foreordained by God. For the truth was neither to be suppressed so that no one should know it, nor disclosed to the rulers of the world before he should bring the beginning [Col. 0845C] of his prayer to a better end. The latter would obstruct his purpose; the former would damage the Christian faith. For who could know the mind of the Lord unless he who is in the bosom of the Father declared it, since no one knows the Son except the Father, nor knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him? Therefore in this Transfiguration both the Son commends the Father and the Father commends the Son: “This,” he says, “is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matt. 3:17).

“Sweet is the light,” Solomon says, “and pleasant to the eyes to see the sun” (Prov. 2:17). The apostle Peter proves this. When he saw Jesus clothed with light [Col. 0845D] as with a garment—for “his garments were white as snow” (Matt. 17:2)—and saw that his face had shone as the sun shines in its power, he said: “Lord, it is good for us to be here” (ibid., v. 4). For caught by the hook of such sweetness, forgetting what lay behind, he had filled the vessel of his heart with the dew that waters from the outflowings of Paradise. Drawn by these, he cried: “Draw me after you; we will run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1:3). Although the Gospel, for the brevity appropriate to its office—like a girded cock running so quickly and with such fixed purpose that it greets no one on the way—omitted to express the fragrance of the breezes brought by the south wind, yet it must be believed and understood that those garments, which became white as snow, sprinkled upon all [Col. 0846A] who stood there a sweet fragrance surpassing every perfume. For he would have rejoiced less fully in the consolation afforded to his sight if he had not shared, for his part, the blessing granted to smell; nor would full kinship have been preserved if sight were satisfied while smell remained hungry.

Therefore he poured out streams of his oil upon Peter and his companions, not uniformly but in manifold ways, so that whatever thirsty senses they had brought might, intoxicated by one such solemn feast, say: “Lord, it is good for us to be here.” It should be observed that what refreshes bodily affects one way, and what refreshes spiritually another. Because of their poverty, you will rarely find bodily things, and rarely such things, as by one condition serve different senses at the same time. Different senses or appetites have different ends of delight or satisfaction, and thus always demand either different times or different pleasures at the same time. Spiritual gifts, on the contrary, at once and together supply every variety of desire. In the true good, just as there is no falsehood that deceives, so there is no diminution of fullness that requires supplementary alternation or compensating attention.

“And behold Moses and Elijah appeared, speaking with him” (Matt. 17:3). The wandering question that often circles around the circuit of heaven sets out to ask why Moses and Elijah, rather than others, came in body or in spirit, and what they spoke with him about. But why press a question to which no certain answer can be given? Even if it contains a desirable marrow, the hard and solid bone can indeed be gnawed by the gums of puppies, [Col. 0846C] but cannot be penetrated. Desire presses to break it open, but strength fails to draw out marrow protected on every side. Yet because persistent labor conquers all things, it is pleasant to knock and to circle the city of circumstance, so that in the labor itself this honorable concern may at least provide consolation.

The investigating mind therefore considers that Moses and Elijah were mountain-dwellers and shunned human company. On mountains, through angelic assistance, they learned much about God, and, insofar as they could, dedicated their lives to solitude. Thus, as if by custom, because they had already attended many councils concerning Jesus held on mountains, when the angelic ministry announced this most solemn council concerning [Col. 0846D] the Transfiguration, they were eager to be present. Rightly, among such splendid lights and at the glorification of the assumed humanity which was to be proclaimed, there hastened Moses, whose eyes had never grown dim nor his teeth become loose; and rightly also he whose flesh did not see death’s corruption, whose mortality, by an almost unique privilege, was neither consumed by the fiery chariot nor swallowed by death, but now enjoys the realm of immortals and almost conquered death by an unusual and long delay.

Perhaps too Jesus, while spending nights in prayer upon the mountains, had made use of their presence, and this day had been appointed so that, concerning their differing states, he might ask each—according to the humanity assumed—whether the state of Moses, stripped of the body, or that of Elijah, still living [Col. 0847A] in the body, was better. For it was in the power of Jesus to choose whichever he preferred, though in his purpose he undoubtedly held to one alternative. One would indeed seem fitting for the person of the one assuming and of that assumed; the other, however, was unquestionably necessary for the office of one interceding, for the business of one pleading, and for the cause in which he strove. Yet, in his dispensation, the Mediator would borrow something from both: that he might first put off his mortal body without dying, in a glorification that was not permanent but transitional, retaining something at once from the old state and borrowing something from the new and future state, so that what was borrowed might accord with Moses and what was retained with Elijah.

There is another reason why Moses and Elijah were seen with the Lord in the Transfiguration. The assumed humanity did not refuse to have witnesses, both among human beings and among angels, that it depended on his own will either to die for humanity and thus enter into his glory, or, with the work [Col. 0847B] of our redemption left undone and without death intervening, to return to the right hand of the Father. Therefore, intending to do all things with counsel, he commanded authoritative human witnesses to be present at his Transfiguration, so that unbelieving Jews might be convicted by Moses as their own author, and Elijah, who is to come at the end of the age, might proclaim with complete assurance that Christ, not Antichrist, is to be worshiped. There are other reasons too, which have already been explained by the holy Fathers or remain to be expounded in their proper times.

“They were speaking with him,” it says. They observe discipline and do not exceed the bounds of their commission. They do not speak to the apostles but with Jesus, because they had not come here [Col. 0847C] either to hear worldly reports or to recount the holy ordinances, already written but not yet to be expounded, concerning the Lord’s Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension. They speak concerning that and to him for which and to whom they had come; and beyond this they put a finger over their mouth, lest they speak of the works—not, I say, of human beings, but not even of angels. Perhaps, according to his custom, Moses prays for the Jewish people, whose ruin he foresees as imminent, that at least a remnant may be saved. Perhaps Elijah, not having laid aside his zeal, decrees the vengeance that was to come under Titus and Vespasian. Yet let us keep their secret conversation rather than examine it, because “the glory of God is to conceal a matter.”

It follows: “And behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them” [Col. 0847D] (Matt. 17:5). We must hold closely to the Gospel reading and weave together the course of our discourse from it. For we must not construct for the God of Jacob a tabernacle from our own resources; God does not dwell in things made by hand—that is, in things devised by human ingenuity without grace, by which the knowledge or love of God is acquired. God does not make himself known through vain philosophy, foolish fables or genealogies, and endless questions. Hence a grove is forbidden to be planted—namely, sophistical quibbles and obscure arguments—beside God’s altar. Only the authentic Scriptures drawn from the prophetic and apostolic treasuries and strengthened by ecclesiastical authority are to be read and sung in the Church. These, namely [Col. 0848A] the bright cloud—that is, divine Scripture or the Catholic Church—are a bright cloud.

Scripture is a cloud for three reasons. It cools in the heat of temptation by teaching appropriate remedies; it overshadows in the distress of persecution by promising rewards, since the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory to be revealed in us; and it waters in time of drought, setting before our eyes, on the one hand, infernal exhalations and smoking encampments, and, on the other, spring-like and health-giving breezes from the region above the stars, which is wholly filled with most pure and most blessed spirits, is ineffably fragrant, and is not troubled by even one little cough. “A bright cloud,” he says, “overshadowed them.” The Psalmist seeks out and implores this overshadowing, saying: “Overshadow [Col. 0848B] my head in the day of battle” (Ps. 139:8). The day of battle is this whole life, because “the life of man upon earth is warfare,” where there is struggle against flesh and blood, against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this darkness, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places.

An iron helmet will be of little use in these things unless the bright cloud overshadows it—that is, grace which brought forth divine Scripture from its own womb, and does not allow its offspring to be violated through it. For through the breasts of the Old and New Testaments it presses forth both drops and tricklings from its womb, with which the Virgin Mary was impregnated; and through these the adopted offspring is regenerated by the bright cloud, which is the Church. For one equal measure, filled to the brim, fills both breasts alike—both the Church and Scripture—with divine grace. Therefore the nursing is twofold, but the rearing of the children is one. The Church, then, is a cloud that journeys away from the Lord; it is bright because it is always made fruitful by the Holy Spirit; it overshadows its children as a hen her chicks, lest they yield in adversity, fail in persecution, or fall into danger through delay of the reward.

## SERMON LXVII. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY, I

“And the cherubim lifted up their wings, and the wheels were with them, and the glory of God was over them” (Ezek. 11:22).

In today’s sermon the subject is effective, and the abundance of speech still more effective. Yet less labor is needed to praise her who is praiseworthy without commendation, lovable without exhortation, venerable not without recompense. For she is lovable to all: namely, Mary the Virgin, Mother of Mercy; desirable to all, because she is wholly beautiful; venerable to all, because she is full of grace. The singular Virgin draws each person to her love by the fragrance of her ointments. She alone suffices for all, like a salutary ingredient which, without the admixture of other ingredients, is most effective in preparing the ointment of human salvation. If another ingredient is mixed with this one, it seems to take something away from its fragrance but to add nothing to its power. She alone pleased God the Father so as to deserve to become the mother of his Son; she alone, without precedent, pleased Christ so that he might be born from her, and pleased the Holy Spirit so that she might become his temple and be filled by him. She alone is not without reason [Col. 0849A] sufficient for our salvation, since from her the Savior deigned to be born for us.

She is the gate through which Christ entered the world for our redemption, and she is the Virgin through whom we have found God and man. She is the handle by which we hold Christ as iron inseparably joined to it; she is the axe by which timber necessary for the eternal tabernacle is to be cut. Wisdom held this handle when it built itself a house and cut out seven pillars. By this handle iron is better held, more readily moved, and more useful in work. Whoever lacks this will accomplish little with the iron, because he will not control it. Unless Christ had been born from her, human blindness would not have been enlightened, human weakness would not have been healed, and the human race would not have been redeemed.

See how joyful, necessary, and venerable the Virgin Mary is to us, from whom true light, eternal health, and abundant redemption appeared to the world. Certainly, whoever does not have this handle will not have this iron; for once these were joined, they shall remain joined forever. Today Christ assumed her into glory so that she might no longer endure our misery. Mindful of the law which says, “Whoever abandons parents in calamity, let him be cast out unburied,” he did not leave her on earth but assumed his mother into heaven and set his tabernacle around her. What is unknown, though devoutly believed—namely, whether she was assumed bodily—must be regarded as a reason for venerating the feast, in the manner of those who bring gifts and do not uncover them until they reach those to whom they are to present the gifts.

Yet by no unfitting comparison, Ezekiel’s statement may be applied to this Assumption: the cherubim, who always stand before God, were sent for this Virgin and lifted their wings. According to Isaiah, with two they covered her head and with two her feet—that is, her conception and assumption, both of which are hidden from us. Or they covered her head with one wing placed beneath and another above, namely in subjection and veneration, unwilling to uncover that temple of God before presenting it to the divine majesty. Likewise, they covered her feet with two wings, in service [Col. 0849D] and proclamation, singing: “Arise, make haste, my beloved” (Song 11:10 [probably 2:10]); “Come from Lebanon; come, you shall be crowned” (Song 4:8).

“And the wheels were with them,” concerning which the same prophet says: “As I listened, they called them ‘whirling ones’” (Ezek. 10:14): that is, Mary’s body and soul, which in body and soul were subject to the divine will, never experiencing the law of the flesh resisting the spirit. What follows? “And I heard behind me a voice of great commotion” (Ezek. 3:12). This is the voice of the Church, journeying and laboring, which cries to God: “Do you not care that Mary has left me to minister alone? Tell her therefore to help me” (Luke 10:40). It also cries after Mary in prayer: “Holy Mary, help the wretched; aid the faint-hearted; revive those who weep; pray for the people; intercede [Col. 0850A] for the clergy; plead for the devout female sex. May all who offer you gifts of praise experience your help.”

## SERMON LXVIII. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY, II

“Virgin of Israel, return to your cities” (Jer. 31:21). To the Mother of Lights, who today is reverently received with rejoicing by all from the everlasting mountains, let us turn, dearest brothers, the light of our eyes, the speech of our lips, the clapping of our hands, the affections of our hearts, and the intention of all our movements. For behold, after Jesus, her firstborn and only-begotten, she penetrates beyond the veil that is before the oracle—not only assumed above the highest seats of cherubim and seraphim, [Col. 0850B] but also wonderfully and magnificently exalted above their wings. For it is said of her that she has been exalted above the choirs of angels to the heavenly kingdoms. Therefore, so that she may return to the land of her birth, now ripened by the gathering of every virtue, and enter the house of eternity, a voice from the royal seats thus exhorts her: “Virgin of Israel, return to your cities.” It is as though it said: “Your kingdom indeed, O Queen of Heaven, was prepared for you from the foundation of the world. It now grieves and longs for your return and arrival, so that it may offer you its acceptable service and receive within itself your most welcome rule.”

Indeed, neither is your command burdensome to your servants, nor is their obedience murmuring against your arrangements. The heavenly household is weary of your delay; heaven’s dwelling-place asks that the place so long vacant be adorned by your presence. With what reverent eagerness those heavenly powers, who never or rarely leave their ranks, repeatedly inquire of those angels who are sent in service for those who shall inherit salvation, saying: “When will our lady come—our queen, our sister, the mother of our King and Lord?” With what affection they send and return the message to her: “Virgin of Israel, return to your cities; ascend to our high places; come to our palaces; enter our storehouses; penetrate our chambers, for all these things are yours: your possession, your inheritance, your house. What is possession without a possessor, inheritance [Col. 0850D] without an heir, a house without an inhabitant, a city without a ruler? Return then, return, Shulammite; return, return, that we may gaze upon you” (Song 6:12 [probably 6:13]).

First, return from the captivity of the world, because she through whom captives were freed from their captivity ought not to be subjected to captivity. Second, return from humanity, without the corruption of flesh, because, just as you are immune from the corruption of sin, so you must pass into immortality, mortality being swallowed up through the grace of God. Third, return to the freedom of the glory of the children of God, because, just as sin never reigned in your mortal body, so you are worthy to enjoy, even in your virginal flesh, that same liberty of spirit which angels enjoy in their spiritual substance from their very creation—or rather, from their confirmation. Fourth, return [Col. 0851A] that we may gaze upon you: from the dignity of angels to the surpassing excellence of spirits now made blessed. For just as we long to behold the face of your Son, so we desire to fix our gaze upon your form and beauty, and strive in every way to be illuminated by the light of your countenance. Finally, these returns become more numerous ascents, concerning which it is said in praise of Wisdom: “I was exalted like a cedar in Lebanon, and like a cypress on Mount Zion; I was exalted like a palm in Kadesh, and like a planting of roses in Jericho,” etc. (Ecclus. 24:18).

Our Lady is exalted like a cedar in Lebanon by the merits of her holy manner of life; like a cypress on Mount Zion by the height of her most pure contemplation; like a palm in Kadesh by the rewards of eternal recompense; like a planting of roses in Jericho by mortification of the flesh and compassion for her Son hanging on the cross; like a beautiful olive in the plains by the abundance of her mercy; like a plane tree beside water in the streets by the diffusion of her fame and glory among all languages and peoples; like cinnamon by the fragrance of her good repute; like aromatic balsam by the conception and birth of Christ, from whom, as from the head, the ointment of our Christianity flows down; and like choice myrrh by the robe of immortality which she received from her Son on the day of her Assumption.

From all these, as from ivory houses—that is, the most chaste palaces of heaven—she gave forth the sweetness of fragrance. Drawn by it, let us cry out to her with all desire and all sighing: “Draw us after you; in the fragrance of your ointments we will run to the mountains of spices,” where the saints, breathed upon by the sweetness of that garden of delights, exult in glory and rejoice in their dwellings; the exultations of God, because of such fragrances, are in their throats, in the presence of the Lamb, clothed in white robes, through the gift of Christ Jesus himself, who lives and reigns through all things, etc.

## SERMON LXIX. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY, III

“What woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma of them, does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds [Col. 0851D] it?” etc. (Luke 15:8).

From the sacred palace of the supreme and eternal King, through continuous channels, God’s abundant goodness flows into our garden-beds. Every station, both of times and of persons, is enriched from the beginning of the world, not stingily, by a general and particular benefit according to the measure and order of innate goodness. Therefore, since, as the Apostle says, “Each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that” (1 Cor. 7:7), God—who not only gives but also receives gifts among human beings—has made no one’s portion inferior. For he says in the Psalm: “The measuring-lines have fallen to me in pleasant places; indeed, my inheritance is splendid to me” (Ps. 15:6). Truly the lines fell to him in splendid places, who, being the radiance [Col. 0852A] of glory, proceeded in eternal generation from the Father of lights before worldly ages, and who, taking flesh from the Virgin of virgins, appeared in the fullness of time in human nature, true God and true man, without sin.

His inheritance too is glorious to him, because he rescued the Church, formed from Jews and Gentiles, from the power of darkness through faith, and through hope and charity transferred her into the kingdom of his brightness, so that the radiance of eternal light might have as bride one without spot or wrinkle, but beautiful like the dove who is one for her mother, chosen for her who bore her—that is, for divine predestination and justification. Therefore, when from the eternal counsel the time of good pleasure was at hand, so that God the Father through his only Son might gather the dispersions of Israel into an unfading inheritance by adoption, he betrothed to himself a maiden from the land of Israel and endowed her richly from his treasures, confirming the marriage by public instruments and strengthening the marriage-gift by lawful privilege against the wiles of demons and heretics. For she alone among women is the one in whom the prince found nothing of his own; concerning her heretical deceit could not establish its lies. In this privilege are contained the birth-conditions of both Mother and Son. It also contains the dowry proceeding from the Virgin—namely chastity, innocence, and humility—and likewise the gift on account of marriage, namely the fullness of grace restored by God the Father.

[Col. 0852B] His inheritance too is glorious to him.

[Col. 0852C] This privilege, impressed and sealed with the seven seals of the Apocalypse, is open to chaste and virginal eyes, while it condemns and darkens the evil eye, lest it see the glory of God. Finally, certain more secret matters, not to be disclosed to any mortals until, at the resurrection, the veil of the temple having been torn, we enter the sanctuary of God, are concealed by definite coverings in the Holy of Holies—that is, in the depth and secrecy of God’s judgment. For then, by the law and right of the city said to be like glass, nothing will be closed to those reigning with God; nothing of the Son’s hidden things will remain unknown. The hearts of all will with equal openness desire to know and to be known; then conscience will hasten and press more eagerly to come into public view than it now seeks private and secret silence. For evil fears to be seen in the light; good disdains to be hidden. But in all the fellowship of that entire court nothing but good will be present.

Yet meanwhile let us turn over the first leaves of this privilege and, from the foretaste of the riddle, shake out a few crumbs that have fallen from the masters’ table for the little dogs. “What woman,” says the Lord, “having ten drachmas,” etc. Scripture does not customarily use this manner of expression concerning our Lady. For in the Song of Songs, where her prerogative mystically rests, as it were, in her chambers and upon her flowering bed, Solomon often sang thus of her: “Who is this that comes forth? Who is this that comes up from the wilderness? Who is this that comes up through the wilderness?” (Song III, 6). The majesty of what is said is diminished when the things said do not suit, in quality and manner of speech, the subject of which they are said. Nor does he sin least in speaking who strives to explain the inexplicable, or who labours to make difficult what is easy to say. But the fitting narrator is one who chooses words according to his capacity, and hangs in admiration before what he cannot adequately express.

Therefore the Lord says, “What woman,” etc., not as one overcome by poverty, but as one mercifully condescending to those of lesser capacity, as though he said: “Before all women this woman surpasses all comparison—in lineage, sanctification, name, integrity of life, contemplation, angelic familiarity, conception of God and man, novelty of childbirth, cohabitation with her Son, and assumption into heaven.” Who then is the woman having the ten drachmas which we have enumerated? Without doubt, she of whom the present sermon speaks and whose day of Assumption is celebrated today in heaven and on earth. If the King of glory, accustomed to heavenly delights, furnished his future chamber with finer and softer furnishings and enclosed it with a strong defence, so that it might be “a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed,” what wonder is it? You see even senseless little birds gathering soft things from every direction and carrying what is useful to a nest, so as, as it were, to make themselves a house in which to place their young.

Accordingly the Wisdom of God gathered fitting treasures for himself in the virginal dwelling-place when he granted ten drachmas to his Mother: for he who is of great lineage according to his generation from the Father caused his Mother to be born from a great and worthy lineage; and he who is the sanctifier of all sanctified from the womb her into whom he was to come; and he marked with a distinguished name her from whom he would assume the man Jesus; and in each thing that he was to do concerning her or receive from her, he sent beforehand certain unprecedented preliminaries. For if Abraham’s servant gave Rebecca golden earrings and bracelets weighing ten shekels because she was to become Isaac’s wife, what ought not the Lord of heaven and earth to have given Mary his Mother? Therefore he gave her ten drachmas, her to whom he also rightly subjected the nine orders of angels and all human beings. For the angels of God receive her voluntary obedience, her whom they receive as set above themselves at the right hand of the Son. And how should every human being not obey her, now reigning in heaven, when on earth God made man for us obeyed her?

Do not be troubled or ashamed, holy angels, because she is called a woman, to whose dominion your entire court is subjected. For “woman” is a name not of vice but of nature: it does not signify weakness but denotes capacity for conceiving. Perhaps he who has knowledge of speech would have called her by a more honourable name, had he judged that this would be more fittingly said in his eternal reasons. But the giver of names and author of the work, balancing the thing and its name, tempered both together, lest grace wholly recoil from nature and the use of antiquity from the novelty of conception: from custom he retained the name, while from novelty the work of grace excelled. She is therefore woman by nature, Mother by grace. Grace does not prejudice nature, nor does nature take away grace’s power. Rather, nature is improved through grace, and grace is not diminished because of nature. For the giver of grace is the same as the author of nature, so that, while nature as it were grows old, grace, ever vigorous and powerful, may succeed it. Peninnah reproaches Hannah, and Leah reproaches Rachel, for barrenness; but the younger in time are preferred to the older by beauty and sometimes by fruitfulness, lest priority in time derogate from the effectiveness of the virtue that follows. Nature indeed gives birth, but without merit; grace gives birth, but with merit and reward. Everywhere nature lies beneath the feet of grace, and it is raised to the good that receives reward only with grace herself as its leading guide and companion.

This woman, therefore, like a tree at the ends of the earth, shares antiquity in name without the guilt of sin; in newness she conceives him who blotted out guilt and destroyed liability. Let it therefore be said: “What woman?” There follows: “having ten drachmas.” Now “to have” is said in many ways—as to have hunger, whiteness, a cloak, body and soul, and finally virtue—and because it lies outside our present subject to treat of these, let us set forth the two senses known to Scripture, one temporal and the other perpetual. Of the one the Apostle says: “Possess the blessing by inheritance” (I Pet. III, 9); and elsewhere: “The gifts and calling of God are without repentance” (Rom. XI, 29). The Bride also says of the Bridegroom in the Song of Songs: “I held him, and I will not let him go” (Song III, 4), according to which “charity never fails” (I Cor. XIII, 8). Of the other Job says: “The Lord gave, and the Lord took away” (Job I, 21); and the Psalmist: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. L [51], 14); and in the Gospel: “I go and I come to you” (John XIV, 28).

In both senses of having, the woman had ten drachmas: for she lost one, but neither lost nor could lose the others. They are ten, just as there are ten strings of the psaltery and ten commandments of the law; whoever does not keep them endures the ten plagues of Egypt. Let us now approach to handle the drachmas with eyes and hands, so that, with Benjamin’s sack—the son of the right hand—opened, we may pour them out like merchants intending to buy, or at least to see that by which the eye is fed and the soul made joyful. For of these neither eye is satisfied by seeing nor ear by hearing, because their appearance shines ever as newly as our devotion stands attentively before the blessed Virgin.

But just as twelve precious stones are woven into the pontifical garment, so our Virgin is wrapped in a garment of gold with ten drachmas. They are distinguished by name, value, and appearance. The first, therefore, lies in lineage; the second, in sanctification; the third, in name; the fourth, in integrity of life; the fifth, in contemplation; the sixth, in angelic familiarity; the seventh, in the conception of God and man; the eighth, in the novelty of birth; the ninth, in the upbringing of and dwelling with her Son; the tenth, in assumption into heaven. O my soul! O good friends! O dearest brothers! What fragrance, what colour, what taste can one breathe around these things, gaze upon such things, and fill lips, tongue, and palate with matters of this kind?

[Col. 0855A] Do not quickly be moved away from your understanding, since understanding is perfected if you can apprehend virginal members; if not the members, at least the drachmas; if not the drachmas, at least the golden fringes; if not the fringes, at least the footprints; if not the footprints, at least the shadow; if not the shadow, at least the memory. Let us make for our Lady these golden chains, inlaid with silver, so that if I—defiled in soul and flesh—cannot grasp the members, the drachmas, the fringes, the footprints, or the shadow of an image, because they are golden, I may at least have a share in the fact that they are inlaid with silver. While I do not forbid my lips to speak of you, our Lady, in accordance with what has been set forth in the Gospel, the law, and the prophets.

I shall therefore speak, though I am dust and ashes, of the dignity of your lineage. Born from royal and priestly stock, you display an elect race and royal priesthood, so that, as you surpass all things in every virtue, you may also excel in lineage. For God’s merciful care provided oil and wine for the wounds inflicted upon humankind by robbers, so that priestly oil might reconcile us to God and royal wine might defend us against the devil. Therefore he established king and priest upon earth, so that the king might repel the enemy by strength and the priest might mitigate the Lord’s wrath by sacrifices. When the time of our redemption drew near, these two powers, joined into one structure, brought forth a virginal body from their combined composition; and, like two olive trees, two lampstands shining before God, two horns on Moses’ face, they came together to form the Virgin, from whom the giant of the twofold substance was conceived—he who by his Passion reconciled us to the Father and defeated the powers of the air. Thus the diversity of temporal dignities, having received its time, as it were flowed into one channel, and in the Virgin together gratefully acknowledged its author, placing its shoulders beneath the Lord’s body with due contribution and rejoicing. Thus, like a rose sprung from thorns, or a beautiful olive tree in the fields, his most holy body received substance from the pith of cedar and the fat of wheat.

But perhaps, if anyone does not agree that dignity of lineage ought to be reckoned among the Virgin’s dowries because God chose the ignoble things of the world, let him observe that powers and dignities both in heaven and on earth are from God, and that branches of heavenly and earthly heights spring from the stock of the one and supreme power. For collateral misuse of power, which comes from man, does not corrupt the good which comes from God. Remove arrogance, and in power bestowed on a human being you will find God’s grace, or justice. Therefore do not throw away the good grain because of the chaff; rather, remove the chaff so that you may keep the grain. The Virgin therefore does not despise her root from Jesse and Aaron, although it is in the earth, because the branch that springs anew from the goodness of the root—which is from God’s promise—grows rich from the fullness of graces. Hence the Apostle: “You do not bear the root, but the root bears you” (Rom. XI, 16). For is it not written: “The Lord swore truth, and he will not fail in it: ‘Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne’” (Ps. CXXXI [132], 11)? Likewise: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek’” (Ps. CIX [110], 4). This is concerning dignity of lineage, the first drachma.

Now let us consider the second, which is sanctification from her mother’s womb. From the leaven of the corrupted mass, from the sourness of the unripe grape, from the swelling of the first apostasy, from the rust of a corrupted origin, and from the malice of an offshoot infected in the trunk, he immediately cleansed the virginal vessel as it was formed—he who sits like fire, smelting and purifying silver—lest the holy flesh, which was to bear Jesus, who saw no corruption either in the womb or in death, should feel the itching worms of the common dungheap. The Lord did not delay, but anticipated her in blessings, because he gives twice who gives quickly; and he pays more in time who pays before the due time; and wisdom offers herself first to those seeking her. He did so also lest a vessel once steeped should long retain its odour.

[Col. 0856B] Therefore the Spirit of the Lord, who in the creation of the world was borne over the waters, in order to foreshadow what mysteries were to be produced from them through his operation, in the creation, as it were, of the new and second world which was to come through Christ—of whom it is said, “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (II Cor. V, 19)—cleansed from the Virgin Mary, by winnowing in the maternal granary, the stale refuse of the first parent, which had become fixed in and almost inseparably mixed with human nature. He so baked the vessel destined for himself and Christ, fashioned from clay, that, once every frailty and softness of original sin had been taken away, it might not again become raw under any fire or water of worldly or carnal desire, nor in any way feel the rebellious stimulus of the flesh. If John the Baptist was sanctified from the womb, how much more Mary? If such was the preparation of the herald, what justification ought there to have been for the Mother? And this is concerning the second.

The third is called the reverence due to the name: “And the Virgin’s name was Mary” (Luke I, 27). There are certain names of the unnameable God, not names in which he is expressed, but names by which something is said concerning him—even if not what he is, at least what he is not—lest, if we cannot grasp him in what he is, we mistakenly hold another in his place. It is much, if you cannot know what he is—for his knowledge is beyond our strength, and you cannot attain to it—at least to know what he is not. Thus you will never err by wandering or cling by stopping short; but, with reason, intelligence, and faith unfolded and enlarged, you will run after him as far as you can, and beyond. For the Lord says: “No human being shall see me”—much less know me—“and live” (Exod. XXXIII, 20). There is, therefore, among the other names of God a certain ineffable name which, even when spoken, should not be uttered except in utmost necessity. I grant that all the names of God are to be honoured and revered with the highest veneration, and that no name of God is to be taken in vain. Yet he gave his Son one name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. II, 9).

[Col. 0857A] After that name, exalted above all throughout all ages, comes this name Mary, always held solemn in the angelic assembly; and at its invocation the assistance of the heavenly host is at hand. On hearing this name, dangers flee, benefits return, and hells tremble; blasphemers are destroyed, those in despair are reconciled, and no one finds it difficult to recover grace who has Mary as helper of his vows. When I surrender my limbs to sleep, may Mary rest upon my lips and in my mind; when I awaken, may Mary open my lips; when I breathe my last, may Mary be present; when I come to judgment, holy Mary, meet me with your patronage. The judgment will not be perilous for one to whom Mary has given aid. Our Lady, I expect to say greater and better things of you; let these suffice concerning the third drachma.

The fourth is integrity of conduct. Divine protection and angelic guardianship so guarded our Virgin’s childhood years that she incurred absolutely no loss to her chastity or integrity, whether through her own ease or an adversary’s cunning. But when her free will had escaped the fetters of weak age, cooperating with grace she so bound herself within the circles of regular discipline and holy observance that she was wholly kindled with love of the divine commandments. As though swallowing, she committed the words of God to her soul, and in return gave herself to their inner substance. For she had three modes of mutual exchange: one by which she poured herself into the law of the Lord and the prophets; another by which she caused that same law to flow into herself; a third by which she cultivated the divine substance of the Word in both her flesh and soul, and by the coagulating power of the Spirit was conformed to God and man. Thus the divine commandments and the Virgin Mary walked with equal steps, as Ezekiel (ch. I, 21) says of the holy living creatures and wheels: “When they went, they went; and when they stood, they stood.” And, to state briefly what I think, the angelic religious life almost emulated the conduct of this one earthborn woman; it marvelled that holiness was acquired on earth by one’s own labour and cooperation with grace, whereas grace itself retained it, with no labour at all, after the greater part of its own being had departed. What the Apostle says to the Thessalonians, “May the God of peace himself sanctify us wholly, that your whole spirit and soul and body may be preserved at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (I Thess. V, 23), was fully accomplished in our Virgin. And this is concerning the fourth.

The fifth is contemplation of heavenly things derived from divine reading and meditation. Just as food is useless without digestion, so reading profits little without meditation; and sound digestion of what has been eaten is the body’s complete nourishment. Likewise, reading is effective when constant meditation follows it. For it is said of the blessed man that “he shall meditate in the law of the Lord day and night” (Ps. I, 2). The law is a river flowing out of paradise and divided into four heads: namely, the literal sense, allegory, morality, and anagogy. But our Lady flies like a beautiful dove over streams of water, that she may look upon herself and know her condition, or beware the enemy lying in wait for her offspring, or at least have nearby the bath of confession and the fountain of devotion. The daughters of our city often go down to the waters, there weave familiar conversations with those whom they find on the bank, and sweetly learn reports concerning both future and absent matters.

[Col. 0858B] Since our Lady had pitched her tent there, she frequently received from the daughters of Jerusalem an answer concerning her great undertaking. There with Jacob she placed green poplar rods, almond rods, and rods from plane trees, partly stripping their bark, so that she might conceive while looking at them: speckled, because of flesh like the flesh of sin; varied, because of the two natures of God and man; of differing colour, because of the Beloved, who is “white and ruddy.” She placed the rods in the watering-troughs where water was poured out, because in her eyes, which are like pools in Heshbon, through continual compunction she retained the greenness of chastity, which is the quality of these trees. She placed almond rods also because of bodily mortification, the soul’s passion, and the inward sweetness of conscience; and she placed plane-tree rods because of the breadth of charity. In such a gaze the Virgin conceived, the Virgin gave birth, and after giving birth the Virgin remained a Virgin. And this is concerning the fifth.

The sixth is the angelic salutation. A person’s manner of life is approved or disapproved according to the company he keeps; for the social soul scarcely avoids the vices or virtues of those with whom it is brought up or has long associated. Thus the Virgin Mary, anticipated by the Spirit of God, was instructed in the religious discipline of angels and trained by their example to please God ever more and more. For just as Moses was told, “See that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain” (Exod. XXV, 40), so Mary was commanded and enabled not to make for the Lord a tabernacle of curtains, coverings, boards, bases, and columns of wood, silver, or gold, but to prepare a place in her own flesh and soul. Likewise, when dogs suffer hunger, they eagerly return to the place where they smell bread or meat, or where they are accustomed to receive it, retaining hope from what went before. So the angels, returning from the Virgin, their memory refreshed by her sweetness, hurried back to visit her again as though hungry, and, if there was anything to report, did not withhold it.

[Col. 0858D] But because natural affection, restricting itself from plurality, contracts into a special intimacy, so as to love all the more as it gathers itself into one, it is said in the Song of Songs: “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart with one of your eyes and with one lock of your neck” (Song IV, 9), that is, by contemplation and love of me alone. Therefore Gabriel’s eye, by God’s favour, hastened to become an impressed intermediary joined with Mary’s spirit. Accordingly, by his own desire and the Lord’s command, he entered the chamber familiar to him, greeted one well known to him with words hitherto unknown in their intimacy, and, as a faithful interpreter of the divine command, added nothing and took nothing away. He explained the matter, won over the maiden with heavenly tenderness, strengthened her weak sex, reported the undertaking already begun, foretold its immediate completion, and departed, intending to return. The Virgin’s womb, filled from the channels of grace, conceived as she believed; attributing nothing to herself, she committed herself wholly to God alone, to whom belongs whatever he has decreed to do. And this is concerning the sixth.

The seventh is the Incarnation of the Word. No price for this drachma is found in heaven, on earth, or in all the abysses; for it is so great that upon it rests the valuation and redemption of the whole human creature, and the appeasement of the Father’s wrath. This is Joseph’s long-sleeved tunic, which clothes Jesus in the mystery of the Incarnation and joins threads of miracles, marked out with sapphires, in a varied fabric upon the warp of his sufferings. No insolent and persistent rashness of heretical perversity or tyrannical power could interrupt even one thread of this fabric—that is, of the Lord’s Incarnation. He says too little about it who tries to say more. It can certainly be believed; it cannot be spoken. This is concerning the seventh.

The eighth resembles this: the rejoicing and wonder of the new birth. There is no speech for this birth upon my tongue, because neither letter, syllable, nor incomplete utterance can loosen the strap of this sandal, as the voice crying in the wilderness truly declares. For how great is the power of a mother giving birth without corruption? What birth is without labour? In this birth nature yields, grace prevails; what is beyond custom, beyond the order of human nature, depends only upon the divine, not human, will. With two wings the seraphim veil this mystery, lest vain philosophy or imprudent curiosity presume to profane the Holy of Holies. And this is concerning the eighth.

[Col. 0859C] The ninth is her life on earth. He who before his Incarnation used to look down from heaven through windows and gaze through lattices, while secretly bestowing his benefits on whom he wished, at last came forth through the eastern window like the noonday sun. In the assumed habit of humanity he shared with his brothers food, drink, and other human necessities—brothers to whom he had to be made like in all things. Thus, nursed at his mother’s breasts, carried in her arms, and provided with the other aids of infancy, according to his custom—by which he considers giving more blessed than receiving—he gave the milk that he sucked, just as he sanctified the flesh which he had received; and already he sent forth certain veins of foretaste of future joy, which were both consolation for his Mother’s present labour and a most certain pledge of future reward.

What, then, did Mary lack, she with whom God the Son dwelt? Yet she feared an interruption when she heard of her Son’s Passion; at last the fear she feared came upon her. The Lord suffered, died, and was buried, and her soul was troubled within her even unto death. But he rose on the third day, and she remembered the anguish no more because of joy. Then he ascended into heaven and sat at the Father’s right hand. Thereupon she did not extinguish the lamp in grief and despair; rather, she kindled it still more and swept the house, because she raised her mind above body and world and diligently sought him whom she loved ardently, until she found him today, assumed into the ethereal chamber in which he sits upon a starry throne.

[Col. 0860A] Behold, she now sits beside the King, she who once stood beside the cross. There she saw her Son crucified; here she beholds him crowned with glory and honour. There she saw the Jews grinding their teeth in envy and cruelty; here angels fervent in service and love. There was insult; here glory. There a sword, because of the things that were done, passed through her soul; here, in eternal recompense, jubilation fills her soul. May her Son and Lord Jesus bring us to that joy through her intercession, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LXX. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE MOST BLESSED VIRGIN MARY, IV

To the Queen of heaven, to whose service I desire that the duties of my whole life may be dedicated, I offer myself to serve more devoutly than usual at her Assumption. I ask that I may take nothing from our own storehouses, but that the resources necessary for the work of so great a solemnity may be poured out from the treasures of wisdom. Therefore we must approach and adore the Lamb who sits in the midst of the throne, who will distribute from the throne of grace that by which we may set forth anew Solomon’s great ivory throne. For the glorious Lady has today been assumed and transferred from the throne of grace to the throne of glory, and has passed from the ivory throne of chastity to the starry throne of brightness: gracious on the first, judging no one; most gracious on the second, freeing the guilty; a propitiator on the first, a reconciler on the second.

Let us therefore approach both thrones, the ivory and the starry, and, with face cast down to the earth, imagine both the form of their construction and the glory of their signification. For Solomon son of David neither passed over human expense in the workmanship of his throne, nor made it empty of the weight of virtue, nor exceeded the limits of wisdom. Its appearance, therefore, is good; its wisdom better; its signification best. Appearance delights; signification incites; wisdom satisfies. Let appearance hold you by occupation, signification aid you, and wisdom be your remedy. Appearance raises the mind; signification holds it in suspense; wisdom receives it.
