The letter lies in the appearance, allegory in the signification, moral sense in the power of wisdom.

Therefore King Solomon made a great throne of ivory and covered it with exceedingly pure gold, etc. The Wisdom of God made the holy Church and also made our Lady, not as other works, but above all his works. For he will not change his bride, nor has he had or will have another mother. What is sweeter than a bride? What more venerable than a mother? Taking flesh from his Mother, he rested in her womb as upon an ivory throne; cleaving to his Bride, he shared all his possessions with her and advanced her from the marriage-bed to the throne. Nor was he forgetful of his Mother: just as, in the land of his pilgrimage, he for a time occupied without causing or suffering inconvenience the lodging of her bed and throne, together with the homage of service, so today he has placed beside his own throne of sapphire stone, because of the glory of his deity, a throne of ivory for his Mother, because of the incomparable merit of her virginity. For Solomon made a great ivory throne, archetypal of this one—that is, figurative of it. Ivory is the bone of elephants once the flesh has been removed; and our Virgin lived in flesh beyond the flesh. But flesh was separated from bone more completely when every corruption of mortality was swallowed up in this Assumption.

[Col. 0861A] Therefore from ivory he made a great throne; or, from the Virgin—her flesh purified and her heart enlarged—the Word assumed flesh; or, according to the rule of his institution and the abyss of his profound kindness, today Jesus placed his Mother, raised in angels’ arms with every reverence, in his own and his Father’s splendid dwellings. There, a throne surpassing sun and moon, suited to her maternal glory, had from eternity already been prepared amid the heavenly stars. Today every question and doubt has been removed as to whose glory this was, a glory which angelic sublimity after Jesus feared to attain and which none of the saints dared claim. Today it has been proven that divine predestination established nothing out of order or in vain, because this throne was due to Mary alone and could suit no other.

> **[Note: Col. 0861D. Some material is lacking.]**

From Solomon’s throne: equity is represented in the throne; chastity in the ivory; humility in the footstool; wisdom in the gold; ascent from lesser to greater things in the six steps; perfection in its roundness; the end of this life in its rear portion; mercy and truth in the two hands; God and the devil, or fear of death and hell, in the two lions; and, in the twelve little lions, vigilant concern amid ambiguity in every action and thought. Hence Job: “I feared all my works” (Job IX, 28).

The six steps are humility of dress, maturity of demeanour, sobriety in food and drink, usefulness of words, acuteness in reading, and constancy in prayer. By these steps the ivory throne excelled and surpassed all those dwelling on earth, whose dress is excessive, demeanour disorderly, way of life immoderate, speech vain and idle, approach to meditation and reading rare or nonexistent, and whose countenance in prayer is unknown. From this final step of holiness her Beloved summons his Mother, saying: “Come from Lebanon; come to the highest step of glory at the right hand of your Son.”

## SERMON LXXI. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY, V

“What will you see in the Shulammite but the choirs of camps?” (Song I, 7).

A venerable day, a singular Virgin, and today’s procession distinctive; a sound of fullest jubilation in heaven as well as on earth; a blessed sight, a great exaltation, the admirable kiss of justice and peace between Mother and Son, and inseparable confession. Meanwhile the Father, thus honouring not his own wife but nevertheless the most beloved Mother of his Only-begotten Son, addresses the Son as though offering congratulations, saying: “What will you see in the Shulammite but the choirs of camps?”

[Col. 0862A] Ever since the Son of that Virgin was assumed into heaven and sits at God’s right hand, the ministering spirits—the angels—burned with most ardent desire to have among themselves that woman, such as she was, the woman from whose flesh and blood they saw human nature, in their King and Lord, placed in the seat of majesty above themselves. Some frequently ran to her; others cried: “Return, return, O Shulammite; return, return, that we may gaze upon you” (Song VI, 12). She is not unworthy of heaven who brought forth from her womb such and so great a fruit; a most pure fountain from which so excellent a stream was derived; wholly incorrupt flesh, from which was taken the flesh united to the Word; a pleasing soul, from which flowed the grace that tasted death for all and swallowed it up by the resurrection. We do not deny our fellowship to her for whom we prepare perpetual service. No one shall remain in our number or fellowship who has not sworn in her honour and rendered every submission.

Therefore, the choirs being arranged, let every order of angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominations, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim come forth to meet our Queen as she comes to the Father of her Son, to that same Son, and to the Holy Spirit, whose honourable temple she is. Let the procession be extended far; let each stand in his own order. Let patriarchs and prophets come with us, that the former may marvel at their stock so honoured in the Virgin, and the latter rejoice that their prophecy has been so fulfilled. Let the apostles be present, who are already associated with you; then martyrs, confessors, and likewise virgins. Whoever does not honour the Mother does not love the Son.

O Lord Jesus, we too, together with the Father, say on our own part: “What will you see in the Shulammite but the choirs of camps?” We believe what we say and that for which we say it. All things that are in heaven are from God and are ordered. There is no disorder where there is no disturbance; there is every ordering where God’s command is kept and an unshaken vision is possessed. But we earthborn people both suffer evil disturbances and often commit disorders. For reverence toward our Lady, at least today let us suppress every evil disturbance and restrain disorders, so that in our Shulammite there may be found choirs of camps, not choirs of female drummers or actors. Elders, superiors, younger adolescents, and children: keep your eyes guarded, restrain your hands, open your mouths, incline your ears, and let not your feet move toward evil. This concerns outward matters; what of the inward?

Let every faculty of the soul gather itself into the heart; let it order all its inward parts and establish the procession, the camps of God, so that on the Virgin’s day no movement [Col. 0863A] of mind or body may overstep the bounds of chastity. The Virgin recognizes the adornment of chastity and the garment of humility. Is not one counted out of her procession who is disfigured by shamelessness and uncleanness? “What will you see in the Shulammite but choirs of camps?” God the Father speaks to the Son concerning the assumption of his Mother: “What will you see in the Shulammite,” etc. Gabriel likewise, the archangel, guardian and bridal attendant of the Virgin, speaks thus to each of his companions: “What will you see in the Shulammite,” etc. The Holy Spirit also addresses the Church, which journeys on earth or is glorified in heaven, saying: “What will you see in the Shulammite,” etc. In the Father there is congratulation; in the archangel, wonder; in the Holy Spirit, commendation or exposition of this most celebrated Assumption.

[Col. 0863B] We must therefore ask why Solomon, most wise, prefigured the Assumption of so great a Virgin under the name of the Shulammite, and what are these choirs, not of others, but of camps. There are choirs of clergy, choirs of young women, and choirs of soldiers. Choirs of clergy are choirs of those who chant psalms; choirs of young women are choirs of those who rejoice and dance; choirs of soldiers are choirs of those who fight and wage war. In a choir of clergy harmonious modulation is sought; in a choir of young women, delight; in a choir of soldiers, courage. This threefold choir serves our Lady today. Angels sing as clergy, lead dances as young women, and fight against the powers of the air, lest they dare to come in her way. They gnash their teeth and roar with shouting; they waste away with envy when they hear that the maiden, the Mother [Col. 0863C] of mercy, has ascended to the throne of grace above the choirs of angels, from which their prince fell like lightning.

## SERMON LXXII. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY, VI

“My dove is one” (Song of Songs 6:8).

With intimate familiarity and a sweetness unknown to every creature, the true Solomon delights in his dove: she who is Queen of angels, Virgin of virgins, gracious Mary. Within her womb, by his wisdom, he recalls human folly to dove-like simplicity; with the salt of heavenly wisdom he renews the corruption of our nature. “My dove is one,” he says: either the nature which I receive from my mother, or the Virgin from whom and in whom I unite the marriage of divine and human natures. “My dove, the Church, is one bride”; “my dove, the Virgin Mother Mary, is one.” I am one and unique: I do not desire a widow, a divorced woman, or one joined to another husband; I seek one dove.

I desire one, that she may not disagree with my will; a dove, that she may not be excessively cunning; one, according to the Apostle: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2); a dove, that she may not think beyond what she ought to think, but think soberly; one for friendship, a dove for grace. For who does not love his mother or his bride? Who does not bestow every grace upon mother or bride? And therefore I desire to possess both mother and bride [Col. 0864A] wholly and entirely: chaste, the chaste one; beautiful, the beautiful one; merciful, the merciful one; undefiled, the undefiled one; one, the one; simple, the dove. The mother has no other son, nor does the bride have another bridegroom. One in faith, a dove in simplicity; one in unanimity, a dove in gentleness. “My dove,” he says, “is one.”

The reason must not be passed over why Solomon, king of such wisdom, power, and riches, extolled in words his dove—whatever dove it may be—with such wondrous praises and rich prerogatives, and also commended her in the most surpassing writing of his books. We must observe, therefore, that profound words from the mouth of a man contain something most sacred in their depth, as is read in the Psalm: “They saw the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep” [Col. 0864B] (Ps. 106:24). Thus, with the light of grace leading us, although we are not sufficient to penetrate this sanctuary, nevertheless we prostrate ourselves in adoration and, as it were, touch holy relics.

When the most holy Virgin entered the world by her birth, the angelic powers—servants of heaven—examining with holy curiosity the maiden marked by the traces of divine predestination, reported to the heavenly palaces, as is customary, the new thing found in the world; and humbly inquiring from the royal seats what this might be, they hear: “My dove is one; she is one to her mother, chosen by her who bore her.” As though he said: She who was born outside and above the number of women is outside and above the merit of all women.

She is one dove in the whole human race, having no like; in angelic purity and dignity, because of the divine generation, she has no equal. “Mine”: if the Son speaks, she is his mother; if the Father, she is the future mother of my Son. “One to her mother”: chosen by a singular dignity for her who bore her, through divine predestination. She is one by the incorruption of her integrity; a dove by the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, who appeared over the Lord in the form of a dove; mine by my love, my election, my conception, my generation. Her wings, silvered, shall be whitened in Salmon. The wings are action and virginal contemplation, which shall be whitened by chastity as by snow—that is, incomparably—in Salmon, interpreted as “shadow”: that is, in the conception of the Word by the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0864D] This dove at her birth was white as milk; in her conduct and profession of chastity, as wool; in her conception, as snow; then, made heavenly, in childbirth as the moon; in her Assumption as the sun, or as an ordered army. This dove feeds at God’s table, reclines at noon in Solomon’s bed, sits in the litter, sleeps in the bridal chamber, walks in the garden, bears in the chamber, and is honored in heaven with a golden crown alongside her Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is blessed for ages. Amen.

## SERMON LXXIII. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY, VII

No virtue is nearer to God than virginity; none is more familiar to angels; none is more desirable to saints still placed in the flesh, because it is rarer than almost all other virtues. [Col. 0865A] At the predestined time it established its kingdom and dominion in the glorious Mother of the Lord. No angelic spirit in heaven was purer than the Virgin’s womb in the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit and the conception of her Son. An angel indeed cleaves to God by obeying, standing near, and ministering; but not by uniting himself with him in one and the same person. But what of the Virgin’s flesh? Was it not the material lying beforehand from which the creative Trinity fashioned human nature, which it inseparably united to the Word of God by one simultaneous operation—though not by the same assumption of the Trinity?

From this sanctified mass the Son of God took a part for himself; in taking it, he immediately deified it, and through both it and that from which it came he worked, in the whole mass of the first-created man, salvation for the entire same human race by redemption and sanctification alike. And then did he despise, abandon, and forget his bed, his chamber, his temple, his garden, his paradise, his Mother? Far be it! “Even if a mother should forget her son,” he says, “I will not forget you” (Isa. 49:15). No one hates his own flesh; nor did Jesus delay to loosen, even in his mother, the bonds of flesh, nor cease to prepare a dwelling beside himself.

Indeed, it would be unworthy to insert anyone else between himself and his Mother in heaven, in whose womb he was coagulated by an ineffable sacrament. For when the Lord’s Prayer says, “May your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth,” the mother in effect speaks thus to the Son: “May your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth”—as though: Because, Son, you chose [Col. 0865C] to have a mother, receive her also among the angels as one who stands beside you. No one has a greater right in your flesh, in your face, than your Mother. “I yield,” says the Son, “and grant it. Come, my chosen one, and I will set you upon my throne.” He spoke, and it was done—he who said, “Let there be light,” and there was light (Gen. 1:3); he who speaks once and does not repeat the same thing a second time, because his word remains for ever and ever.

But what sort of throne is yours, O God, O Lady? The Psalmist says: “His throne is like the sun before you, and like the full moon” (Ps. 88:30). Perhaps for this reason the heavenly powers, wondering, say: “Who is she that rises like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an ordered army?” [Col. 0865D] (Song of Songs 6:9). Like the dawn to those who confess; like the sun to saints who receive her; like an ordered army to evil spirits. Converts call upon her, the righteous love her, sinners entreat her, demons fear her. The camps of demons are powerless against the army of our Lady, of whom it is said in the Song: “What will you see in the Shulammite but choirs of camps?” (Song 1:7). This Shulammite pleases the king by her beauty; she preserves the aged king by chastity and cherishes him with the warmth of wisdom. Who is so beautiful as she to whom it is said: “You are altogether beautiful, my beloved” (Song 4:7); and again: “How beautiful you are, beloved, how beautiful in delights, dearest one!” (Song 7:6).

The Ancient of Days chose her beforehand and gave his Son to her. She warmed the heart of God, almost grown cold [Col. 0866A] as charity failed in the human race; and, while we were still sinners, because of his exceeding love he decreed that his Son should be incarnate from the Virgin. She, most wise, as she wished to deceive no one, so could be deceived by no one. If the Creator ever found in his creature any proportion corresponding to himself, he honored this woman alone with that privilege: “When I was undefiled, I came into an undefiled body” (Wisdom 8:20).

What, then, O most mighty one, will you see in the Shulammite? “In me,” says the Shulammite, “is every grace of the way and of truth; in me is every hope of life and virtue” (Sirach 24:25). There are two things: the way and the homeland. On the way is grace; in the homeland, truth. In me is every grace, or every grace of the way and of truth. There is no grace in any path by which one comes to the homeland except through [Col. 0866B] our Lady, whose Son is he without whom we can do nothing. Again, in her is every grace of truth, because grace and truth came through Jesus Christ; and no one will possess truth in the homeland who does not love Christ on the way.

This vision, that is, knowledge of the Son, is in the Mother; for just as he said of the Father, “No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Luke 10:22), so likewise it may be said of the Mother: No one knows the Mother except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal her. Nor is it absurd to read thus: “What will you see in the Shulammite?” so that the question concerns not things which cannot be seen within, but those which occur about the Shulammite. Hence it adds: “Except choirs of camps.”

Therefore, it is in the authoritative books, not in fanciful inventions, that we must seek the choirs of camps. We read in Numbers: “The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: The children of Israel shall encamp, each by his companies, signs, and standards, according to the houses of their families, around the tabernacle of the covenant” (Num. 2:1). Judah shall pitch his tents to the east. And, lest we extend the discourse beyond measure, let us say briefly that around the tabernacle of the covenant—which we understand as the body and soul of the Virgin—all the children of Israel encamp.

All the children of Israel are all the faithful; yet they are arranged according to the several quarters: Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun to the east; Reuben, Simeon, and Gad to the south; Ephraim, Benjamin, and [Col. 0866D] Manasseh to the west; Dan, Asher, and Naphtali to the north. Judah means “confession”; Issachar, “reward”; Zebulun, “tabernacle of strength.” These sing toward the east: “A star shall arise from Jacob” (Num. 24:17). Reuben, “seeing”; Simeon, “hearing”; Gad, “happiness.” These sing toward the south: “You are altogether beautiful, my beloved,” etc. (Song 4:7). Ephraim, “fruitful”; Benjamin, “son of the right hand”; Manasseh, “forgetfulness.” These sing toward the west: “Arise, hasten, my beloved; come, my dove” (Song 2:10). Dan, “judgment”; Asher, “blessed”; Naphtali, “conversion.” These sing toward the north: “Arise, north wind” (Song 4:16); “winter has passed, the rain has gone and departed; flowers have appeared in our land” (Song 2:11). Behold, the Shulammite has choirs of camps surrounding her like rose blossoms [Col. 0867A] and lilies of the valleys. “The queen stood at her son’s right hand, clothed in variety.” “Surround Zion,” says the Psalmist, “and embrace her” (Ps. 47:13).

## SERMON LXXIV. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY, VIII

“Rejoice with me, because I have found the drachma which I had lost” (Luke 15:9).

This is the solemnity of the present day, on which in heaven nothing is idle from praises, and in the Church of God, journeying upon earth, nothing is idle from holy prayers. The stars possess blessed praise according to their lot, because no diminution of true blessedness can befall them. But we, wandering in this exile through faith, ought to extend our supplication all the more earnestly because we are held farther and more perilously from the kingdom. Yet Christian devotion and angelic exultation turn back into themselves and revolve in a circular course: we indeed are in hope, but they in possession. And as possession bestows reward, so hope obtains merit.

Why, then, should we despair of a reward from heaven, when today we have sent there from earth and from our own race so excellent an exchange? Does ingratitude have any place where grace possesses an everlasting dwelling? We have sent her who is full of grace back to the palaces of grace; therefore let the drops of grace overflow upon our excessive barrenness. Filled and replenished with God’s good gift in the realm of grace and glory, let our Lady’s Assumption not become in us an emptying of the heavenly gift. O our Lady, what congratulation will there be for faithful souls toward you [Col. 0867C] if you are translated to heaven without recompense, taking away both what you had received from them and what you had received from us? It is fitting that so great a treasure be surrounded by such a wall, guarded by such a watchman, enclosed in such a repository.

May the Church also retain your loving remembrance, by which she casts out demons, expels vices, restrains temptations, orders disordered movements, opens channels of sweetest compunction, pours in healthful and sweet tastes of the heavenly homeland, and daily brings to our teeth and lips at the altar the fruit of your womb to be chewed over. Then indeed we shall exult and rejoice in you, O Lady, remembering your breasts. Your breasts flow with that sweetest nourishment for angelic spirits, which your Son’s hands made—hands fashioned on a lathe, [Col. 0867D] golden, filled with hyacinths. For above themselves they see the Word made flesh, crowned with glory and honor in the humanity he assumed; and from that ineffable contemplation they are suffused with so joyful a delight that neither lack lessens desire nor satiety produces disgust.

Your breasts still flow with the honey of tender affection for the righteous and good servants of God. By tasting it, the bitter things of this world become sweet and the enticements of the flesh become cheap, so that a mind filled with virginal honey becomes dull and almost insensible to carnal blandishments, and says with Barzillai: “Are my senses strong enough to distinguish sweet from bitter? Or can food and drink please me, or can I hear the voice of male and female singers?” (2 Sam. 19:35). [Col. 0868A] The mind made glad by the outflow of the words of the Virgin Mary thus forgets every earthly desire. And not only do words flow, or thus overflow; they flow through even to the sinners of the earth, because Christ Jesus, her Son, came into this world to save sinners.

Will the Mother cease to suckle those whom her Son came to save? Indeed, can the Mother of mercy refrain from nourishing with the full torrent of her milk those for whom her Son could and would breathe out his spirit? We stretch out neither mouth nor hand, O our Lady, for the angelic portion, because “the beast that touches the mountain shall be stoned.” Let the angels have their firstfruits, and thus the first drop from companionship with you, because they kept their dwelling places and did not go after Satan, who drew a third part of the stars after himself. Let the faithful and righteous succeed in second place, whose lot it is to sit upon twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel, so that from your winepress—whose soul a sword pierced—they may, bearing the marks of Jesus in their body, press out the second drop and at least console their desires by your transformation.

But we, whose mouth is full of bitterness and deceit, what share can we have with virginal chastity, purity, and gentleness? Yet surely no nurse is as attentive to her foster-child as you, most gracious one, are toward the Christian who confesses and returns to his heart. Although a little child is stained with childish, itching impurities, she who has undertaken his care does not therefore cast him away or deny him her breasts; rather, she washes him in a bath and refreshes him with her milk. O most merciful one, what will you do? Our face is filled with shame before our own eyes; even our righteous deeds are like the cloth of a menstruating woman—how much more our unrighteous deeds?

Most merciful of the merciful, turn your face away from sins until they are blotted out by your compassion, covered by your intercession, and wiped away by penitential satisfaction. Blessed are your breasts, which feed angels, refresh the righteous, and nourish sinners. Your spirit exults in the fellowship of angels; your soul rejoices in the imitation of the righteous; soul and spirit rejoice together in the repentance and conversion of sinners. We turn to you face and hands, mouth and heart, mind and soul, the inner [Col. 0868D] and outer person; crying after you with full voice: our salvation is in your hand. May your mercy look upon us; may those tender bowels of yours not restrain themselves toward us, which, watered with heaven’s dew, are accustomed to rain drops dripping upon earth and to raise those who have fallen from the deepest gulfs of sins and are almost despairing.

Do you see, our Lady, how that red dragon, with savage open mouth, tears apart, snatches away, devours, and almost drags our wretched souls into its lair? You observe how shamefully our nature is dishonored, from which you took your origin and your Son Jesus took flesh. It is now afflicted by such mockeries that no stain of demonic filth remains which [Col. 0869A] human lust has not experienced. O your flesh, O our flesh! What such chaos has been placed between us, that your purity conquers and surpasses heaven, while ours—though related and akin—has been corrupted by such uncleanness as no patience can endure?

Yet although the condition of my most wretched lot of pilgrimage does not permit me to be absent, still, sprinkling the bed of my mind with your milk and the blood of your Son, I trust that by your aid and his protection I shall be rescued and, after fitting punishments at least, admitted among the young women of your court. For that voice of yours, like that of a most chaste turtledove, has been heard in our land, saying, “Rejoice with me”; it has shaken off despair, restored hope, and raised the spirit, so that one who lay oppressed by consciousness of evils has, upon hearing that most joyful [Col. 0869B] voice, recovered breath and, as it were, awakened from a heavy sleep. For a voice that comes from heaven not only strikes the mind but helps it: it strikes, so that the mind may attend to itself; it helps, so that it may turn to God. Turned toward God, it hastens to go. Set upon the journey, even when weary it cries: “Draw me after you” (Song 1:3). Holding the hand stretched out to it, it exults: “We shall run,” it says, “in the fragrance of your perfumes” (ibid.). Arriving, “we shall exult and rejoice in you” (ibid.). Finally, speaking for those who remain, it says: “Mindful of your breasts above wine, the upright love you” (ibid.). If all, from the least who hears her voice to the one who reaches the palace, rejoice with you, O our Lady.

## SERMON LXXV. ON THE SAME MOST BLESSED VIRGIN

[Col. 0869C]

“I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices” (Song 5:1).

Christ addresses both the bosom of the universal Church and the womb of the Virgin Mary, saying to each: “I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride.” The Church is his sister, because he himself was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, while the Church is reborn from the same Spirit. As he is Son of God by the union of person, so she is daughter of God by adoption; she is also bride because of the common agreement—or indivisible cohabitation—of the two natures, divine and human. But the Virgin, though she is mother according to the flesh, is called neither sister nor bride except according to the Spirit; [Col. 0869D] hence: “Whoever does the will of my Father, that one is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. 12:49).

Lord, nothing is more difficult than finding you. I know indeed that you are everywhere, but everywhere I encounter a closed door, which denies you and conceals that you are even where you are. Though what I have said—“conceals that you are”—is much, yet it is true: it does not permit, or does not enable, us to see what you are or where you are. For you are the sun—indeed, a radiance brighter than the sun. Therefore either my blindness or your brightness prevents me from seeing. It is no wonder that blindness impedes sight, since it is a privation; but brightness, whose function is to illuminate—how can it fail to show him from whom it has the power to show? Perhaps because it is rare—indeed, because it is excessive: for God dwells in inaccessible light. [Col. 0870A] A light moderated, therefore, from the light of deity and the cloud of humanity knows how to receive the weakness of our dim sight and to narrow or adapt the immensity of divine light.

Accordingly, he places two veils between: the wall of the Virgin who gives birth, and the most pure lamp of the Lord’s body, so that human sight, gradually accustomed to these, may by penetrating eagerness endeavor to see Jesus, know what it sees, love what it knows, worship what it loves, believe in what it worships, and adore what it believes. Thus, with the inmost stirrings of his mercy moved, he himself tells the one seeking him, calling him, and knocking for admission to him both where he is and what work he has performed, saying: “I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices.” “I have descended,” he says, [Col. 0870B] “from paradise into my garden; from incomparable glory and the service of angels I came to accomplish my work. I have come into my garden; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices.”

From the beginning God planted a paradise of delight, in which he placed the man whom he had formed. Latest things and ancient things smile and return a smile to each other: “Behold, Lord, you have known all latest and ancient things; you formed me and laid your hand upon me” (Ps. 138:5), Jesus says to the Father in the Psalm.

But notice the reversed order of times: he does not say “ancient and latest,” but “latest and ancient.” For the glory of the second house is greater than that of the first; the first man was made a living soul, and the second a life-giving spirit. [Col. 0870C] The old man is Adam; the new man is Christ. Through Adam sin, and through sin death, entered into the world. Through Christ comes righteousness, and through him eternal life is restored. Therefore the latest things go before in prophetic spirit, because they are better and more important than ancient things. In the ancient things he formed man from the mud of the earth; in the latest things, by creating he sanctified and by sanctifying he created his Son Jesus from the flesh and womb of the Virgin Mary. “You formed me and laid your hand upon me.” The formation is common to latest and ancient things as regards the state of the body; but the laying on—or placing—of the hand is contained uniquely in him who was formed in the latest things, because of the Spirit with which Jesus was anointed above his companions. Hence the Father’s voice says to John the Baptist: “He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, this is he who baptizes,” etc. (John 1:33).

God placed this man in the garden, that is, in the paradise which he had planted from the beginning. For God’s foreknowledge, just as it does not err in distinguishing things to be created, so makes no delay in foreseeing all future things. At once and in one act it conceives every condition and fall, what is to be restored and what is not, and also the manner of restoration. It does not itself depend upon future events; rather, all things issue from its immovability, amid the changeableness of things, as from the womb of all. Thus, as Jacob and Esau in one womb, Eve’s rashness and Mary’s [Col. 0871A] holiness, contending with different aims, in some manner shook the bowels of foreknowledge, so that, as has been said, the latest things might precede the ancient in usefulness and dignity, and Mary’s singular conception might be celebrated more favorably than the planting of the earthly paradise, and Christ born from the Virgin more than Adam placed in paradise.

In that paradise the serpent is found with man; in the Virgin, with Jesus, only the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit is received. The devil, corrupter of all good, sent no breaths or hisses within the boundaries of our garden, because she is “a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed,” opening her bosom only to the King of the ages, who is the image of the invisible God, if she set the iron bars of most exact watchfulness against every stealthy vanity. For the glory of God, which was taken from the cherub to the threshold of the house, guarded her from her enemies and protected her from deceivers.

For I faithfully believe that the hidden deity often shone forth through the Virgin’s eyes and mouth, and that something ineffable, if anyone noticed it, streamed out. For what else? Was she not full of grace, and from this fullness bringing forth a good word and the most splendid ray of the brightness of eternal light? Hence, at the sound of her greeting, Elizabeth’s womb was moved, and John’s infant limbs were touched and, as it were, warmed into exultation. Whence came such power, except from the glory of God which was taken from the cherub—that is, from the height of heaven—to the threshold of the house, that is, to the Virgin, [Col. 0871C] who without doubt is the gate and threshold of the heavenly homeland? From her, going forth like a bridegroom from his chamber, the Dayspring from on high visited us.

Let no one place his threshold beside this threshold, because God complains of this: “They have made their threshold beside my threshold, and their doorposts beside my doorposts” (Ezek. 43:8). There is no kinship between chastity and impurity. Priest, in your uncleanness do you not fear to lie beside the altar of God and the Blessed Virgin Mary? Worse still, you do not veil your shameful parts beside God’s sanctuaries; indeed, you make the house of prayer a prostitute’s brothel. Of such persons it is said: “They have defiled your holy temple” (Ps. 78:1).

The glory of God which is at the threshold of the house therefore troubles Joseph, the Virgin’s betrothed. Hence he wishes to dismiss her secretly; but he is warned by an angel not to fear the majesty which gathers up the humble and confounds the slanderer. “What,” Joseph says to himself, “is within? Who is within?” It is, I say, the Word of God; God is in Mary’s womb. Who placed him there? Who admitted him? God, who placed the man whom he had formed in paradise; who is held back by no barriers; who enters without breaking in and departs without corruption; whose willing is the key that opens all things, whose unwilling is the bar that shuts all things. Neither hammer nor axe has need to hew or cut where the one power of God could, in the blink of an eye, both make and restore the world.

At last, Joseph, recognize that the solemn day has come, when for the Paschal feast the lamb is prepared for sacrifice. There, the high priest alone, in blood received [Col. 0872A] from the Virgin, prepared the saving victim and, as it were, gathered his myrrh when he borrowed holy and incorrupt flesh from the maternal womb together with spices—that is, fragrant virtues. Compounded of these, both soul and flesh gave forth upon the altar of the cross a most sweet fragrance to the Father’s affections for the redemption of the human race, and in the acceptable time completed the long-desired propitiation as a thing ripe. For he would not reap unripe myrrh who does all things in weight, measure, and number. Hence the Psalmist: “It is the time of favor, O God, and the time to have mercy upon her” (Ps. 68:14), that is, Zion; and: “Remember us, Lord, in the favor of your people; visit us with your salvation” (Ps. 105:4). Therefore he came, as at harvest time—that is, at the fullness [Col. 0872B] and end of the ages—into his garden, saying: “I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride.”

But who, Jesus, brought you in? Who admitted you without an entrance? Who inwardly gave permission, though no marks of entry appeared? “God,” Scripture says, “placed the man whom he had formed in paradise” (Gen. 2:8). Let the true simplicity of our faith not be swallowed by the abyss of wicked interpretation, so that you believe Jesus was first formed and afterwards conceived by the Virgin. Rather, flesh from the Virgin’s flesh and blood was simultaneously created in that virginal womb, and Word, flesh, and soul were simultaneously joined. But this wording—“he placed the man whom he had formed in paradise”—belongs to the ancient things, not the latest. “He placed”: who placed? God. Where? In paradise, that is, the garden of delight—namely, in the Virgin’s womb. Neither Mary, nor the angel, nor Joseph placed him, but God, who willed, could, and knew. God placed him by working power; Mary conceived him by supplying flesh and faith; Joseph stood outside, wondering and marveling at what had occurred within.

This Joseph rightly defended the Virgin from reproach by the name of marriage, just as another Joseph took Christ down from the cross and placed him, anointed, in a tomb, hiding him from the sight of the Jews. Now there was a garden there, and in the garden a new tomb. This young stag of the deer seems to love vegetables; he seems to seek green things, gladly to plant trees, to cultivate beds of spices, to recline at noon [Col. 0872D] and feed in gardens, and to gather lilies. The quickly fading vegetables of herbs are the defects of our humanity which Christ assumed when he willed to become man; green things are works that spring from the root of faith and chastity; trees are those that bear the flowers of conversion and fruits of religious devotion; beds of spices are the minds of saints; the lily is chastity. Christ himself has sown, watered, and brought all these things to growth both in the virginal garden and in the Church. The Queen of Sheba brought to King Solomon spices so many and of such a kind as were never again seen in Jerusalem. Likewise our Queen, from heaven and through prevenient grace, brought forth in the incarnation of God’s Word from her mind such dispositions as no creature could hope to offer to its Creator.

[Col. 0873A] No sect of Gentiles, Jews, or heretics could compare itself to the Church in spices. Each garden is well-watered, fruitful, pleasant, solitary, secure, consoling, and delightful. It is well-watered by the upper and lower watering, that is, by Christ’s divinity and humanity, or by angelic and human devotion. It is fruitful because by its fruitfulness it even feeds the young of ravens, preparing food for the peoples of Ethiopia—that is, Christ’s flesh and blood—for those who confess their sins and truly repent. It is pleasant because spring’s mildness, when the south wind blows, produces varied colors, so that you would rank a picture of heaven below it if you attentively and chastely contemplated the virginal and ecclesiastical temple. It is solitary because the One, uniquely set apart from sinners—Jesus—so occupies all that belongs to the Virgin and [Col. 0873B] the Church that he admits no companion. Hence: “Hear, Israel: your God, God is one” (Deut. 6:4). It is secure because it is a tower of strength from the enemy’s face; a thousand shields hang from it; and it is enclosed and guarded by sixty of Israel’s strongest men. It is consoling because from it is known the God of all consolation and the Angel of Great Counsel, who remains with it until the consummation of the age. It is delightful because the beautiful Virgin has been made in your delights; by royal power and dignity, nothing in the heavenly storehouses is not set at her will and service.

## SERMON LXXVI. ON SAINT BERNARD, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX, I

“Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit,” etc. (John 1:47).

[Col. 0873C] After long service, prolonged exiles, the reception from his wives of beloved pledges, and the acquisition of gains in flocks, servants, and maidservants, Jacob returns to his father’s house and to the land of his birth. But on the journey he is frightened by an encounter with Esau, his elder brother. When the soul, wearied by worldly life, reflects upon eternal years, desires the heavenly dwelling, and groans in travail, crying: “Wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24); “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged” (Ps. 119:5); “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41:3); and “My tears became my bread day and night” (ibid., 4)—then it makes provision for its household. It does not place the wages of its labors in a torn purse by hunting for human glory from them and dividing them wrongly; rather, it orders its household like an army, distinguishes its flocks by number, weighs out its gifts by weight, inserts measured spaces between flock and flock, adorns the lamps of its works with the oil of a pure conscience, and with the reed of a soul purified through confession. Behold, the prudent man measures his brother’s disposition by the gifts offered, giving money to gain favor. He causes not only people but even flocks to advance in regular order, so that the greatness of the order preserved in his mind may appear, from whose abundance even animals are ordered.

He carries across the ford of Jabbok, which is interpreted “struggle” [Col. 0874A] or “dust,” everything belonging to him. By a religious ordering, the mind that awaits angels, longs for its homeland, and desires its Father’s house, removes from itself every animal impulse; and, mourning itself, it crosses Jabbok—the ford of ashes and dust, that is, the fluctuation of the world and the movement of the flesh—through laborious conflict, resting at times in this distress as though among thorns. At last, when the mind is released from worldly cares and freely occupied, the angel of the Lord stirs the water of the pool, declares a conflict, and summons reason and sensuality to battle. Good thoughts immediately bubble up: on one side they blaze like precious ointments; on the other, the whispering stings of former incitements gnaw like thorns under a pot.

[Col. 0874B] Thus the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. Hence Jacob—that is, “the combatant”—is compelled to say: “I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but the law of sin with my flesh” (Rom. 7:25). Likewise: “I was turned in my misery while the thorn is fastened in me” (Ps. 31:4 [Vulgate]). For the thorny flesh brings forth thorns from its own thicket, as Ishmael plays with Isaac, afflicting the righteous soul and piercing it so as to draw out the blood which is the life of the spirit. Proceeding indeed from the school of the Epicureans, it establishes wicked laws in order to live according to the flesh and not according to the spirit. For the Apostle says: “If you live according to the flesh, you shall die” (Rom. 8:13). On the other hand, the angel, the mind, reason, and understanding establish their position on the other side within the mind [Col. 0874C] and, once reason has been granted the duel, gird themselves for battle.

Reason, therefore, armoured with faith, counts every pleasure of the flesh as foam upon water, and by arguments most strong and evident concludes that one ought not to seek what contains within itself immense loss and no profit. The pleasure of the flesh consumes the flesh and nourishes worms. Hence Job (17:14): “I said to corruption, ‘You are my father’; and to the worms, ‘My mother and my sister.’” And the Apostle: “He who sows in the flesh shall reap corruption from the flesh” (Gal. 6:8). The angelic hosts together with all the sacred pages strengthen the side of reason, and declare that the flesh is not to be buried entirely, but, being sick, is to be relieved by medicinal remedies. This duel or contest rises perhaps more fiercely [Col. 0874D] when, having left the world—like deceitful Laban, full of cunning—the spirit returns to God who gave it.

Then, with grace suddenly arriving like rain upon fleece, a person, pierced by the goad of divine fear through remembrance of his own frailty, finely shakes the whole flour of human substance in the sieve of a strict examination, separating the precious from the vile. He does not cease to renew the struggle until the dawn of his knowledge of himself and of God; now he lifts his spirit upward to God, now he lays down a measured care for the low and weak concerns of the flesh. But when the flesh’s insolence restrains the impulse of the spirit beyond measure and the due proportion of time, the stirred spirit strikes the sinew of the thigh—the sinew of movement—and, as it withers, the sinew makes him lame.

[Col. 0875A] Jacob’s two feet—that is, those of the flesh—are the appetite for eating and the appetite for procreation. For gluttony and lust carry and plunge a person into almost every work of the flesh. When gluttony and lust proceed with equal strides, a person’s steps are crooked rather than straight; nor does the angel bestow blessing unless, by contracting the sinew, he has withdrawn unrestrainedness from one foot. He therefore removes lustful action, though not the movement itself; for to be without every movement of lust would not be to limp, but to be angelic. Thus this foot remains, but curtailed below delight—or at least below consent—and wholly below action. But the foot of gluttony remains in both appetite and action: no longer Jacob of the former manner of life, but Israel of the religious life undertaken. “Your name,” he says, “shall by no means be called Jacob [Col. 0875B], but Israel” (Gen. 32:28), translated to Rachel’s embraces, so that you may see the Lord’s delight and visit his temple. Hence in the choirs of angels it will be said of you: “Behold, truly an Israelite” (John 1:47)—by imitation, attainment, encounter, contemplation, and blessing.

Blessed Bernard is truly an Israelite: by holy conduct, continual mortification of the body, most urgent pastoral care for the flock committed to him, the multiplication of children from both wives and likewise the begetting of them from maidservants, the stripping of rods in the exposition of Scripture, and contemplation among angels.

## SERMON LXXVII. ON THE SAME SUBJECT, II

[Col. 0875C]

“Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no guile” (John 1:47).

The Apostle says: “Not all who are of Israel are Israelites” (Rom. 9:6). Israel limps because the sinew of his thigh has been struck, when his seed is divided into chaff and grass. For those who have preserved unimpaired and unstained the faith and devotion belonging to the richness of this olive tree are counted among the seed and are called true Israelites. But those who have lied like the work of the olive tree, who have limped away from their paths by following the Baals and by failing to know God their Creator—of whom it is said, “But Israel has not known me” (Isa. 1:3)—have no share in Israel’s blessing, for they do not remain in the root. The branches indeed are broken off; they are not shoots remaining [Col. 0875D] in the vine, and therefore must be cast into the fire.

It belongs to God alone to know the merits of these people: his is the power to choose Jacob and reject Esau; his is the power to have mercy on whom he wills and reject those whom he does not know. Therefore the Spirit of God, marking the footprints by which he makes his passage in the minds of the faithful, gives honourable names to the individual lodgings on the journeys of eternity, to the individual halting-places of fruitful visitation, and to the fixed dwellings of his most health-giving indwelling grace; and he illumines them with eternal rewards. For he calls his sheep by name, and says to Moses: “I have known you by name” (Exod. 33:12); and to the Apostles: “Rejoice and exult, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20); and Isaiah says (65:15): “He shall call his servants by another name.”

Thus, kindling more brightly by his gracious favour the lamp of virtue hidden in the marrow of the soul while he himself works invisibly [Col. 0876A], he sets it not under a bushel but upon a lampstand. Bringing the offspring of grace to birth according to his purpose, he distinguishes it by proper or figurative names. Hence in both the New and Old Testaments there are not only namings but changes of names: Isaac, Jacob, Israel, Simon, the sons of Boanerges—that is, sons of thunder—and Nathanael, of whom it is said: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no guile.”

This drop, fit to be drunk and delightful to taste with excessive desire, commending the sweetness of its originating fountain and spring, sends us back to the history and compels us to investigate how deep and capacious it is. The fountain, or Jacob’s well, of which it is said that Jesus, wearied by his journey, sat thus beside the well [Col. 0876B], is the history of Genesis. There we read that, when Jacob was returning to the land of his birth and feared Esau his brother, he first sent presents ahead to appease him by gifts. But he himself stayed that night in the camp. Rising early, he took his two wives and the same number of maidservants, together with his eleven sons, and crossed the ford of Jacob. Having brought over everything belonging to him, he remained alone; and behold, a man wrestled with him until morning. When he saw that he could not overcome him, he touched the sinew of his thigh, and it immediately withered. He said to him: “Let me go, for dawn has now risen.” He replied: “I will not let you go unless you bless me.” Therefore he said: “What is your name [Col. 0876C]?” He replied: “Jacob.” But he said: “Your name shall by no means be called Jacob, but Israel,” etc. (Gen. 32:20 ff.).

O Jacob, O Israel, how blessed is the encounter in which the victor yields; in which the defeated man, by striking, makes his wrestler lame, yet by blessing makes his seed and name equal to the angels; in which, finally, strength is perfected in weakness. Blessed is the encounter in which the stronger yields to the weaker, the superior to the inferior. The superior yields and, as it were, succumbs through patience, not through powerlessness. Supreme power yields to a little worm and dust, so that human sloth may have a means by which to lay hold on the divine and, as if baited, may never recoil from divine love, saying: “I will not let you go unless you bless me.”

Jacob asks no gold or silver for his wrestling. He does not contend for an earthly kingdom; he is not ambitious for empty glory; he has forgotten the human fear through which he feared Esau; he does not ask for the head of John the Baptist. He asks for a blessing to possess as an inheritance. He had tasted beforehand his father’s blessing. Under Rebekah’s instruction, in the offering of food and drink, when Isaac’s eyes were dim with old age, he had been enriched in every way by the offspring of that most abundant blessing: in wives, children, household, flocks of sheep, goats, camels, cattle, and much other wealth besides. Drawn and enticed by the first blessing, he seeks the second with his whole intent, so that he who gave him wealth may add grace also. He values wealth at nothing unless he has grace too. Already he possessed wealth from the richness of the earth, and therefore [Col. 0877A] he presses to receive heavenly grace also from the dew of heaven.

“Let me go,” says the man who wrestled with him, “for dawn has now risen.” O, if that supremely robust and mighty one, whose strength is that of the rhinoceros, had willed it, how easily would Jacob have been consumed like a spark by a breath of wind and carried off to a foreign region! But, as though matching his opponent’s strength, he conceals his own power and magnifies his wrestler’s persistence, saying: “Let me go.” O dart of love! To kindle the burning furnace more fiercely, he casts on it water that does not extinguish but increases the flame. He says, “Let me go,” yet in order that Jacob may not let him go, he inflames and intensifies him.

Thus he also says to Moses: “Let me go, that my wrath may be kindled against your people” (Exod. 32:10). Could he not surely have become angry without permission? Who asks leave to become angry? But mercy does not yet wish to inflict the punishments which the people’s impiety deserves. Thus for God to say to a human being, “Let me go,” is for him to penetrate more peacefully into that person’s inmost parts and bind himself more tightly to him. It is an exhortation to hold fast, not an evaporating departure.

“Dawn,” he says, “has now risen.” What is dawn, and how does dawn rise? It is the mind’s going forth in the contemplation of God. Dawn rises when the eagle—namely, the soul—sets its nest above the stars, forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead.

After night, dawn rises, as the Apostle says: “The night has passed; the day has drawn near” (Rom. 13:12). Likewise: “Whether we are sober-minded, it is for you” (2 Cor. 5:13): behold, night declaring knowledge to night. “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God” (ibid.): behold dawn; behold [Col. 0877C] day uttering speech to day. Dawn is the middle silence; dawn is the half-cubit in Ezekiel’s measuring reed for the temple; dawn is the beginning of the substance of God; dawn is the boundary between earth and heaven; dawn is Mount Sinai, where Moses ascends and God descends.

What, then, does “Let me go, for dawn has now risen” mean except: “My grace is sufficient for you, for strength is perfected in weakness”? Therefore he strikes the sinew of Jacob’s thigh, lest Jacob presume as much upon his swiftness as upon his strength. It is better to limp after God and, with one foot, hope in God, while with the other not presume upon oneself, than to vanish away in empty presumption with a hard and uplifted neck. Therefore, with at least one foot fixed, Jacob clings to him, firm as a cedar, saying: “I will not let you go unless you bless me.”

This persistence is pleasing to God: “I seek the pledge of grace, the earnest of return, the substitute for your presence, the dowry of marriage, the mirror of contemplation—your blessing. Or rather: I will not let you go because you came to me, because you embraced me and allowed yourself to be embraced by me. I would not hold you unless you came to me; you would not come to me unless you loved me; you would not choose me unless you wished to save me; you would not save me unless you blessed me. Therefore I will not let you go unless you bless me.”

He says: “What is your name?” He replies: “Jacob.” But the other says: “Your name shall by no means be called Jacob, but Israel; because I have found you strong in wrestling, steadfast in petition, gentle under the blow, chaste in the disabling of your thigh, humble in limping. Your name shall by no means [Col. 0878A] be called Jacob, but Israel. My blessing changes both things and the names of things. Nature called you Jacob; grace makes you Israel; yet my predestination granted both beforehand. It was not an astrological constellation, but the divine governance that creates and rules all things, which made you grasp your brother’s heel in the womb. It was not your mother’s deceitful counsel, but the preparation of grace, which made you steal the blessing. I came for you to wrestle with me not by fatal accident but by merciful descent—not that I might conquer you, but that I might bless you. Nor do I reluctantly provide what I suggest that you ask for; but I delay granting it because I desire to preserve you more dearly.”

## SERMON LXXVIII. ON ST NICHOLAS, I

[Col. 0878B]

“Conduct business until I come” (Luke 19:13).

The merciful and just Lord, who is rich toward all who call upon him, by an inscrutable dispensation partly gives his gifts and partly sells them. Where he gives, he displays grace; where he sells, he applies justice. There is no greed where grace is concerned; rather, justice prevents grace from making people idle, and grace prevents justice from making them prodigal. If grace perhaps delays giving what is necessary, justice sets it forth in the marketplace for a price. No one has ever justly regretted buying from justice, nor has anyone been deceived by grace’s frivolous promises.

God therefore wishes us to make profit from the coinage of grace in the transactions of justice, saying: “Conduct business until I come.” Do not let free will cease from its task [variant: “relax”]; for if it did not labour, it would not dare hope for anything on the basis of merit. Therefore prevenient grace rouses it to hasten to the regular and frequent markets of justice, so that, with justice’s assistance, it may turn over its rewards and purchase food and clothing sufficient for its needs.

Certainly nothing necessary for human salvation is lacking in the market of justice. Therefore, examining and searching the books of the prophets and of the old law as though they were old purses, let a person test by touch and sight what is useful for beggary, nakedness, poverty, need, salvation, tranquillity, delight, and eternity. Let him first lay out from these what belongs to him: namely, for reason, the whole substance of intelligence, memory, will, delight, mouth, [Col. 0878D] eyes, ears, hands, feet, and all the members of the body. When he sees that his own little store is insufficient, let him return to the purse of grace; for grace will never lend less than justice can sell. The Father of justice and the fountain of grace do not exceed one another in the allotment given: for all that belongs to justice is grace, and all that belongs to grace is justice. Therefore, with grace as your companion, you can acquire all that justice offers for sale.

Justice, however, has its merchants, who wrap precious goods in very cheap cloth. They hide most holy meanings under the obscurity and lowliness of words; and the less they entice the eyes of observers by meretricious adornment, the more truly they flourish inwardly in usefulness and shine more beautifully with divine subtlety. What form of paradise, whether of human creation or restoration, is not contained in the little bundle of the Psalter? There the mysteries are complete; there is sufficient instruction in morals, an entire fabric of faith, and a recapitulation of almost all God’s works and sacraments. What does Isaiah do but plainly perfume the air with sweetest fragrances? Ezekiel scarcely unfolds his tangled cords; and no one understands him unless he unties them. Jeremiah laments the people’s sins beneath a dark covering. Each prophet, according to his own little burden, awaits a buyer.

Moses brings on his shoulder many bundles, very heavy and difficult to carry; annual cycles scarcely suffice for all these. Turn them over and read what is better—that is, read and commit them to memory, for it is great profit to know and do God’s commandments. Of this it is said: “Conduct business until I come.” Whoever reads God’s law not to become better but to appear more glorious is not a merchant of grace but a scout for empty glory. Unless you store up in your understanding a good meaning from your reading, you will return empty from the market. But if, through the reading and meditation of divine Scripture, you commit goodness, discipline, and knowledge to memory, will you return to your own household without profit? Therefore buy from Moses, the man instructed in every discipline and the meekest of all, from the first bundle, which is Genesis: whence, by what route, and in what condition you came—namely, from paradise through disobedience into [Col. 0879C] worldly exile. In that same book consider the delightful grove of trees, the river of paradise divided into four heads, the vein of precious gems, and the life-giving and healthful breezes lost through one sin. Continue at greater length, handling the text through Jacob’s blessings: each form, in its intervening connection, is most useful either for the remedy of evil or for the gain of good. After this follows . . .

> [Note: [Col. 0879D] The remainder is missing.]

## SERMON LXXIX. ON THE SAME SUBJECT, II

“Conduct business until I come” (Luke 19:13).

No disciple of Jesus can, while preserving his purpose, neglect the study of wisdom and entangle his mind in the cares of the world and the flesh. For the law of God rejects and casts away sluggish idleness: when uncultivated it withers, when neglected it rots, when transgressed it kills. Therefore it must be meditated upon, cultivated, and kept day and night, so that it may teach the one who keeps watch at its doors, enrich its cultivator, and adorn the obedient person with a royal necklace.

God loves the readers and lovers of his law. The more vigorously he finds a disciple loosening every restraint of study, the more lavishly and broadly, when invoked, he opens the inner chambers of his mystery, so that the disciple may drink in the character of the teacher through his commandments and abstain from their opposites. Therefore, amid the solemn and abundant throng of disciples hanging upon his words, he finds one above the rest, committing the master’s commands most carefully to the depths of his being [Col. 0880A] and carrying them out most diligently. This is the Lord’s confessor and outstanding bishop Nicholas, whose holiness is celebrated with such joyful renown throughout almost the whole world that, if the merits of his reputation are compared and the regular recurrence of his glory is matched, he appears, having obtained the best portion among the saints, to be a participant and co-heir in the chief privileges of all the saints.

Thus, following closely the discipline of his Master, he pitches his camp beside it and, in most exact imitation, corrects every movement both of mind and body according to its prompting and directs it according to its command. Before he heard with his bodily ear, “Conduct business until I come,” prevenient grace had led him into the paths of repentance, and he curbed the vice of gluttony. Before the thorns understood the buckthorn—that is, before sin understood punishment—he choked sin by punishment. From the cradle he practised this commerce, by which he diminished sin through a smaller penalty and increased merit. For when the vice of gluttony is subdued, lust’s weapons are taken away, and the passion of the body grows cool as the heat of the belly declines. Likewise, a child’s abstention from unlawful things lays a road for a good habit that will rule in later life, so that in greater age he may use lawful things more moderately and resist unlawful things more sharply.

How powerless is Nicholas lying at the breast! How powerful in abstaining from the breast! If a boy is known by his pursuits, what shall we say of an infant and nursing child? What will you do when you are able, you who do such great things when you are not yet able to do anything? How eager, how avaricious in heavenly [Col. 0880C] transactions you will arise as an adult, you who, scarcely born, already bring your hand against the serpent’s first suggestions in paradise and against the deception of our first parents. One who seeks profit must avoid loss. But the human race sustained enormous loss when Adam and Eve took the fruit. Yet who had taught Nicholas that death had entered the world through this? Moses indeed, at the Lord’s command, seized the serpent’s tail; Nicholas seized gluttony. He attacks the enemy more fiercely who grasps its throat than the one who grasps its tail. Great profit is gained by the person through whom so great an enemy is overcome; for he takes away all the weapons in which it trusted and distributes the spoils.

For the devil has, as it were, seized as many spoils as he has corrupted saints’ virtues; yet he does not clothe himself with the goods of others, since the utmost evil clothes him. It is enough for him to have taken what he cannot himself possess. Therefore let a person count it as gain when he has escaped the pit of destruction and the snares of most deceitful deception.

## SERMON LXXX. ON THE FEAST OF ALL SAINTS

Before the human soul sinned, emulating angelic purity, it reached in its swiftness the flights of heavenly spirits in contemplation, and by the liveliness of its intelligence contemplated nothing inferior concerning God. It was replenished in like manner by the fullness of divine gifts and strove most earnestly to equal them in emulation. But after it had been soaked in the corruption [Col. 0881A] of sin and begun to feel the heaviness of the flesh, it found its efforts at flight slower and its courses far unequal. Thus, gradually weakened by the failure of its former strength, it did not cease to languish in the bed of the body and in the prison of worldly life until it was oppressed by the weight of wrongful action and buried under the mass of a worse habit.

So that, lacking a monitor, it might not fall asleep in death as its faults increased, Moses sounds the trumpet in letter and spirit; the boy musician strikes with his fingers the psaltery of heavenly desire and the harp of mortification; Gideon breaks jars in the martyrdom of the saints; Jesus restrains the apostles from sleep on the eve of his Passion: “Watch,” he says, “lest you enter into temptation” (Mark 14:38). Whoever fears the fiery chains of temptation should abstain from sleep. But if anyone, drawn away and enticed by his own desire, has fallen through human weakness, let him immediately spring back, immediately withdraw his foot, immediately, like the most powerful Samson in the strength of the sevenfold Spirit, break the new cords of sin.

For sometimes even he whose heart is like a lion’s in Israel, while the vanity of the world caresses him, lays down his head in its lap and falls into a very dangerous sleep. Thus provident and loving concern runs to and helps one sleeping—or rather dying—when it says: “How long, sluggard, will you sleep?” (Prov. 24:30 [cf. 6:9]). O how dangerously one sleeps when one delights in the world’s pleasures without regard for the soul’s fullness! For the person enters into temptation who does not forsake evil [Col. 0881C] to the end; the person does not leave temptation who yields his soul to sin; the person approaches but does not enter temptation who thinks, but does not do, iniquity. O sluggard, O sinner, how long will you sleep in the suggestion, delight, consent, and perpetration of sin? Consult reason; consult the natural law; consult the excellence of your creation, and you will cease to love the world’s cheapness and vanity.

How long, sinner, will you sleep? Consider with how great a threat and severity Moses acts in order to call you back from idleness and awaken you from sleep. For where the divine law is received, voices and lamps are seen. Certainly one of these would drive away a light sleep; but a heavy sleep is scarcely removed even by both together: the lamp awakens the eyes, the voice the ears. Yet not even thus does the stiff-necked people awake: they shut their eyes lest they see and make their ears heavy lest they hear.

How long, sinner, will you sleep? Look and see at least him in the Gospel who opened the eyes of the man born blind, who unlocked the ears of the deaf, and who drove away the torpor of souls by his preaching as by a lion’s roar. You are excessively engulfed in drowsiness if you do not behold the blazing lamps of Christ’s miracles. Why do neither the voices of roaring lions nor the tumult of peoples raging against Christ shake you from sleep?

How long, sluggard, will you sleep? Watchmen who keep nighttime vigils, concerned for both public and private welfare, advise those oppressed by excessive sleep and deeply drowsy to rise and turn to the day’s work. But they do not merely awaken the delayed and idle; they repeat in a reproving voice: “How long, sluggard, will you sleep?” As though they said: “O sluggard, the collapse of your house is threatened, and you sleep? Thieves are breaking in, and you rest? Fire is already burning the rafters, and you do not notice? Enemies are now brandishing daggers at your head, and you do not perceive it? Your throat is about to be bound by a noose, and you do not awake? An adulterer is entering your wife, and you do not burn with jealousy? Your children are already being carried away, and you do not come to their aid?” These losses will befall you while you sleep; these misfortunes will meet you unless you come to your senses. Indeed, even if fear of evil did not shake you, at least the desire for profit would inflame you, if you were not idle.

[Col. 0882B] For solemn fairs are being held in the marketplace, and do you not run there? Most beautiful spectacles are prepared, and do you close your eyes? Glorious spoils are being distributed, and do you ask for nothing? A great and splendid banquet is set out, and are you hungry? A king, after countless triumphs, is crowned before his people, and do you not assemble? Royal treasures are laid out for all who are needy, and do you not extend your hand? A beautiful bridegroom is joined to his bride, who is wholly beautiful, and do you not look on? How long, sinner, will you sleep? O how great a good you lose! O how great an evil you incur! You lose heaven, the vision of God’s glory, the blessedness of the saints, fellowship with angels, the immortality of the body, the happiness of the soul, and the loveliness of paradise. And what exchange do you receive for these? The stench of hell, the horror of companionship with demons, fear of endless evil, pain of heart and body, despair of a better lot, subjection to the worst tyrant, and an everlasting renewal of punishment.

How long, sinner, will you sleep? Does not one who sleeps lose an inheritance? What is this sleep, what this inheritance, or who is so idle and drowsy? In Scripture, sleep sometimes means sin and sometimes death. Hence in the Gospel, “Lazarus sleeps” (John 11:11), meaning, in death; and the Apostle says to the Thessalonians: “We do not wish you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep” (1 Thess. 4:13), that is, concerning the dead. Elsewhere the same Apostle speaks thus of the sleep of sin: “Those who sleep sleep at night” (1 Thess. 5:7), that is, those who act wickedly seek darkness.

Sleep, moreover, has four watches, or four stages of sleep. The first sleep of night is the enemy’s suggestion. He adds a second to the first when he gives assent to suggestions. He does not awaken before the third who does not hesitate to perpetrate evil. He is buried in the fourth whom habit rules, etc.

## SERMON LXXXI. ON THE APOSTLES

“You are those who have remained with me in my temptations,” etc. (Luke 22:28).

These are the words of that testator to whom his Father said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and you shall possess the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:8). Drawing up the document of his final will, final disposition, and supreme distribution, he bequeathed his goods in this testament to sons, friends, and servants alike; and he appointed heirs who would be co-heirs in the table, in judgment, and in the kingdom to come. But lest some haughty person should impugn the document of the testament and criticize the heirs as instituted not by right but merely by will, without reason, Jesus set forth the cause and merit for which he had honoured his apostles with such gifts: “You,” he says, “are those who have remained with me in my temptations.”

Behold the labour, the task, the merit of faith: to follow a poor and needy man who had nowhere to lay his head; against whom the Jews, the sons of his mother, fought; whom the scribes and Pharisees envied and plotted against; whom everyone slandered; whose life they sought; whom they frequently drove out from their cities. It was a matter of great faith and great labour. Jesus calls all these his temptations, although our temptations did not touch him, because no stimulus of sin ever arose in his flesh. In it the tinder of original evil was not merely absorbed or cut off; it was utterly banished far away, from the uttermost bounds of conception and birth. For an unlawful movement of the flesh could approach or penetrate Jesus, filled as he was with the Holy Spirit, no more than Lucifer’s breath—which aspired to sit on the mount of the covenant on the sides of the north—could drive God from the throne of eternity. Yet it could pierce, rend, tear, and even strip off the garment of assumed mortality, with the permission of divine kindness and the patience of incomprehensible dispensation.

[Col. 0883C] He calls these assaults and insults of the wicked Jews his temptations. “You,” he says, “are those who have remained with me in my temptations.” “You” denotes divine election, which chose them before the foundation of the world. “Who have remained” denotes their constancy and perseverance. “With me” denotes their harmonious affection and special love. “In my temptations” denotes that there was in them no flattery, no feigned and effeminate softness, but the firmest stability and tested courage—such as Caleb and Joshua had as scouts of the land; such as those who will fight with Gideon; such as David made companions in war and leaders of the people.

It follows: “And I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom and sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Luke 22:29). God graciously accepts acts of service, yet not empty ones or ones without reward. Thus Laban said to Jacob: “Because you are my brother, will you serve me for nothing? Tell me what wages you will receive.” He had two daughters: the elder was named Leah, the younger Rachel. Leah had weak eyes, but Rachel was beautiful in face and lovely in appearance (Gen. 29:15).

If grace, through a devout and pure understanding examining the inner chambers of this text, opens it, this harp will sound a harmonious song with David’s psaltery. The Lord calls his apostles his brothers, saying: “Go, tell my brothers” (Matt. 28:10). He does not permit their service to remain unrewarded with him, though he needs no one’s service. Thus Peter, after saying, “Behold, we have left all things and followed you,” added: “What then shall there be for us?” And the Lord said: “Amen, I say to you, that you who have left all things and followed me, in the renewal when the Son of Man shall sit,” etc. (Matt. 19:27).

Elsewhere, after he had said, “But whom do you say that I am?” (Matt. 16:15), and Peter had answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid., 16), he added in almost the same order of words: “And I say to you that you are Peter,” etc. (ibid., 18). Therefore, after he had said: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations,” he adds: “And I appoint for you,” etc. I perceive in this recompense Laban’s two daughters: one at the table, the other promised in the kingdom; the elder—that is, the earlier—at the table, the younger—that is, the later—in the kingdom. Leah, weak-eyed, is at the table; Rachel, beautiful in face and lovely in appearance, is in the kingdom. Hence, opposite the table in the tabernacle, the lampstand is set, so that the table of God may never lack the aid of light. It stands on the north side, whence the storm-wind comes. For partial blindness has happened to Israel from the prince of darkness, who sits on the sides of the north, so that the glory of God may not be seen in this world except in the cloud of sacraments.

Is the altar’s table, then, Leah—though older by birth in the promise—when it is said, “That you may eat and drink at my table” (Luke 22:30)? She labours to see what is set and consecrated there, but cannot, not because the truth present in that sacrament is defective, but because light is lacking. For now we see through the mirror of the lampstand of faith and in the enigma of the covering, which is the appearance of bread and wine. Yet when seven days have passed and that which is perfect has come, then that which is partial shall be done away. Then in the kingdom of brightness we shall eat and drink not standing and labouring, but sitting and judging the twelve tribes of Israel. Then Rachel, beautiful in face and lovely in garment, shall be joined to us. But because we are still on the way and fail without provisions, let us return to the rich man’s table and see who communicates from the table, beneath the table, in the table, at the table, or above the table.

[Col. 0884D] Above the table, without doubt, is he of whom the Apostle says: “Such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens” (Heb. 7:26). This is Christ Jesus, who is a pure sacrifice, a holy sacrifice, an immaculate sacrifice: pure from original sin; holy from every actual sin; immaculate even from every venial sin. For he is the Lamb of God who does not touch, but takes away, the sin of the world. All Christian households eat from the table, those who through faith are in the body and of the body of Christ. For the food of this table is grace, which tasted death for all, so that, death having been swallowed up, all might taste life. Hence: “The eyes of all hope in you, Lord, and you give them food throughout the whole world; you open [Col. 0885A] your hand, and all living things shall be filled with blessing” (Ps. 144:15).

Every action that is not performed at the proper time suffers grave and great harm. Hence Solomon: “There is a time for all things” (Eccl. 3:1). If, polluted by fornication, adultery, or unspeakable uncleanness, you thrust yourself forward to the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, God does not give you food, because he gives it only at the proper time. If, burdened by hatred, anger, wrathfulness, or any grave sin, you approach the blood of Christ, know that your garment, mingled with such blood, will be for burning and will be fuel for fire. Therefore, at the proper time one approaches God, having washed one’s garments: cleansed by the water of confession and compunction from the greatest offence—that is, from every [Col. 0885B] grave sin—faithful, devout, hungering and thirsting for righteousness. Thus Moses said to the people: “Be ready for the third day; do not approach your wives” (Exod. 19:15). If it is unlawful to approach one’s wives, is it lawful to mingle with prostitutes? If lawful intercourse with wives must be abstained from, must the utterly abominable violation of males and beasts be permitted? Marvel at God’s patience: he is pierced more cruelly by the hands and mouths of such persons than by Pilate’s scourges, the soldier’s lance, the Jews’ thorns, and the soldiers’ nails.

Such persons are not of the Lord’s table, because they do not hope in him.
