But to those who hope in you, O Lord, you give food at the proper time: to each according to his own strength—to Peter and Andrew, bread upon the wood; to Stephen, amid a heap of stones; [Col. 0885C] to Lawrence, bread upon the gridiron; to the individual martyrs, their individual torments, as though small fragments of their own passion and cross. Hence in the Gospel: “Gather the fragments that remain, lest they perish” (John 6:12): that is, lest the martyrs pass without suffering, when I myself have broken the loaves and endured in my own body whatever belongs to temporal punishment. He therefore gives food at the proper time, not sending all his martyrs at once, but scattering and arranging them throughout the whole course of time in the Catholic Church. Yet these are not merely of the table, like an untaught flock and household; they are in the table, at the table, and above the table.

But beneath the table are tax collectors and sinners, who, like [Col. 0885D] dogs, suffer hunger and return at evening, saying with that evangelical Pharisee: “Lord, I am not worthy to raise my eyes to heaven” (Luke 18:13); and: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle” (1 Cor. 15:1); and: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” (Matt. 8:8). These neither withdraw from the table in despair, like him who said, “My iniquity is greater than that I should deserve forgiveness; behold, you drive me today from the face of the earth, and I shall be hidden from your face” (Gen. 4:14); nor do they rush upon the table with a harlot’s brow and unrestrained rage. Instead, they await the proper time, so that, when the children have been filled, the good father may shake out his lap and, as though not deliberately, cast to the dogs the crumbs which abundant plenty, rather than negligence, had allowed to fall into his bosom. Thus [Col. 0886A] the little dogs and dogs eat of the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.

The Levites approach the Lord’s table, carrying all the vessels of the sanctuary both in their hands and on their shoulders. These receive good portions from the Lord’s table; for already in faith they possess the firstfruits of the Spirit, and in hope the tenth parts of the denarius promised and given to those who labour in the vineyard.

Those who are in the table are those who always stand before God, and draw marrow from the fat of wheat, honey from the rock, and oil from the solid rock. They are the priests and sons of Aaron, who lawfully succeed the Father: having lips crimson from the blood of grape and mulberry; ivory and ebony teeth, from the chastity of the divine utterances; and the wedding garment of love for God and neighbour. From this flow the myrrh of mortification, the drop of [Col. 0886B] humility, cassia of hope, devotion, and prayer. Hence: “The fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense” (Song 4:11). From them also proceed, as it were from a throne, the lightning flashes of excommunication, the voices of exhortation, and the thunders of the warning of eternal damnation, etc.

## SERMON LXXXII. FOR THE COMMON OF CONFESSORS

On the words: “Take heed, watch, and pray” (Mark 13:33).

We ought neither to be secure in vain hope nor to grow numb in deceptive sloth. In the one case we are led astray; in the other, overwhelmed—hoping for a reward which we have never earned by our works. We are overwhelmed when, taking no anxious precaution, we are suddenly summoned by death to the tribunal of eternal judgment. Against vain security it is said: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful; but he who is hard of heart will fall into evil” (Prov. 28:14). Solomon says of the accursed body: “Because of the cold the sluggard would not plough; therefore he will beg in summer, when sudden destruction comes upon him” (Prov. 20:5). Therefore the Lord, who wills all people to be saved, removing security and shaking off torpor, says: “Take heed, watch, and pray.” Take heed against ignorance; watch against the devil’s deceitful snare; pray for divine mercy. For it is little enough to know what must be done, and little enough to set camp against the enemy, unless God’s wisdom and God’s strength provide counsel and help. God alone illumines [Col. 0886D] our darkness; he alone teaches hands for battle and fingers for war, he who is our strength, fortress, and refuge.

Therefore, if you are blind, that you may receive light, seek the Lord’s mud and spittle. If you are bleary-eyed, anoint your eyes with eye-salve. If the eye is troubled, moisten it by bathing it with the water of patience, and wipe it with the towel of a gentle reply; for a gentle reply breaks anger. The Lord’s spittle is the saliva descending from the head to the mouth: namely, wisdom, which, made flesh, descended to us from the Father of lights; and, making mud from the divine and human through the union—not confusion—of natures, it enlightened the human race, born blind through original sin. This race answered, in the Gospel, when asked, “What do you wish me to do for you?”: [Col. 0887A] “Lord, that I may see.” What eye is so blind that the brightness of eternal light, the splendour of glory, the sun of righteousness, by a ray of such mercy driving away darkness, does not illuminate it? Unbelief closed the eyes; faith opened them. The Lord anointed the blind man’s eyes when he taught him to believe: he went who obeyed; he washed who received baptism; he saw who acknowledged his Creator. “Be still,” he says, “and see that I am God” (Ps. 45:11).

Why do you distract, divide, diminish, and halve the eye of your intention toward many things and things that can be bounded? Even when multiplied a hundredfold and purified, it could not comprehend that which is unbounded. “You have wounded my heart,” says the Bridegroom, “my sister, with one of your eyes and with one hair of your neck” (Song 4:9). Do not look at me with one eye and toward another with the other, for it is better to enter life with one eye than, having two eyes, to be cast into the hell of fire. He has only one eye who loves nothing except God and for God’s sake. Such a person wounds God’s heart because, though frail and sinful, he penetrates God’s inmost being. God does not suffer from this wound, since this wound is not one of pain but of love; it is not a disease beyond cure, but one curable by the Word. O soul, what will you see when you enter through this opening, this wound, this door open to friends and shut to enemies? Certainly that which it is not permitted a human being to speak, not even in a whisper through the veins.

In the vineyard of this contemplation, it is permitted to eat grapes, but not permitted to carry them out. “Let my soul,” says the Psalmist, “be filled as with fat and richness” (Ps. 62 [Col. 0887C]:6). What then? Will you bring out and carry forth portions for us who wait with the strong man and the ass of sensuality, explaining and expressing what you have tasted? By no means. “My mouth shall praise with lips of exultation”; it shall not narrate. Therefore a veil was placed over Moses’ face when he came forth from fellowship and conversation with God. Hence the Apostle: “Now we see through a glass, in an enigma; but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12). Thus we cannot see because our eyes are bleary, through superfluous and viscous humours, both from our frailty and from evil habit. Accordingly, eye-salve must be sought. In accordance with the cause and effect of the disease, the physician prepares a plaster of eye-salve. The sinner accuses himself; the priest listens; the former laments [Col. 0887D] his illness; the latter applies compassion and adds care according to the fault. He imposes a penalty, not by pouring in the bitterness of penitence beyond what the person can bear, but by healing below that point and moderating the measure of the remedy.

He heals a wound badly who, in confession, lays wound upon wound: either aggravating or diminishing penance excessively, harsh in the one case and lax in the other. The Samaritan avoids both faults when he puts oil and wine upon the wounded man. In the oil is the gentleness of consolation; in the wine is understood the biting rebuke of satisfaction. Thus the bleary condition of sin must be wiped away, lest the pupil of the penitent’s disposition be flooded. It is better that something of the bleariness remain than that the correction of penance be removed through excessive weight. [Col. 0888A] Therefore those confessing their sins must be told: “Take heed, watch, and pray.” Take heed to the penance enjoined; watch against sin, lest the dog return to its vomit; pray for forgiveness, lest the judge hand you over to the torturers until you pay the very last farthing of evils and penalties.

Take heed to death, take heed to hell, take heed to the devil. Death is greedy, bitter, bloody, horrible, foul, and fetid: greedy, because it is one of the four insatiable things, devouring the whole human race; it neither satisfies its hunger nor fills its belly, but is made hungrier by its own taste. And as many kinds of deaths as it has in the world, so many kinds of dishes it prepares, as it were, upon its table. It is bitter: no gall is more bitter than death. It not only consumes fleshly pleasures, but even turns them [Col. 0888B] into most bitter bitterness. It is bloody, like a most savage beast that lives on blood and thirsts for nothing but blood—from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Christ. Certainly, even to the blood of Antichrist, no blood has been shed which death has not licked and swallowed. It is horrible: not only the rational animal, but every irrational creature too, recoils from death. What is more horrible than a dead human body? It is foul: in the Apocalypse, death followed the pale horse, and it blackens whatever is beautiful and gathers into itself every abomination and ugliness. It is fetid: a rotting corpse corrupts not only moisture but the air as well. Its face is corruption; its hands, which work in the mud of an animate body and in the side of an inanimate one, are abomination. [Col. 0888C] Its hinder parts are intolerable filth.

This death dissolves what God has joined; in hell it feeds upon souls, while in the grave it strips sinews and flesh from the bones above and reduces them to the most unclean dust. Is it therefore to be feared, fled from, or despised? Indeed, it is to be feared, for the fear of death troubles me; it is also to be fled, but with discernment. At times it must be desired, as Elijah says: “Take my soul” (3 Kings 19:4), and the Apostle: “I desire to be dissolved” (Phil. 12:3). At times it must be accepted, as by the apostles and martyrs in defending the faith; at times it must be fled, as the child Jesus fled into Egypt, and Paul, lowered in a basket, escaped the hands of the governor of Damascus—when [Col. 0888D] no fruit would be gained from death. Therefore it must be despised as a passage to better things; though difficult, it is beneficial, for there is no passage to life except through death. Yet one must beware of the shipwreck of death that sinks the shipwrecked person to the deepest hell.

Let us now see by what flames hell boils, by what gnashings it freezes, by what filth it is defiled, by what stenches it fills the nostrils, by what deformities it offends the senses, by what pains it torments its inhabitants, by what enormities it overflows—finally, by what calamitous tortures it abounds. In hell there is no order, but everlasting horror dwells; in hell there is outer darkness, there weeping and gnashing of teeth; in hell [Col. 0889A] the moth is bedding, and the worms that do not die are covering; in hell is the voice of the Lord dividing the flame of fire, and that flame will burn but not give light. In hell they will pass from snowy waters to excessive heat; in hell the damned, set there like sheep, are fed upon by death; in hell, “O God, who shall confess you?”

Hell is the place of lions, the lair of dragons, the dwelling of demons, the gibbet of the damned. Hell is the anvil of those who are hammered, where the heads of many are shattered; where there is torture beyond tortures, evil exceeding all limit both in duration and in the measure of punishments; where there is torment that always afflicts and never fails. Enough concerning hell. Let us see the devil as prince—may we never see him—not now after the judgment of this world, but only as prince of hell. His licence has hitherto ranged freely, but then it will be shut up; and the more briefly he exercises his power, the more fiercely he rages in severity. He is weighed in the balance and found wanting, both among a people and throughout the world. His power to deceive will be restrained, not his will to harm. Job, struck by Satan from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head, as though he had seen him under the sight of what he endured courageously, describes him under the figure of Behemoth, assigning him individual members by which his manifold wickedness is typologically shown. His description is long, but his wickedness is graver and longer: “He shall eat grass like an ox,” etc.

## SERMON LXXXIII. SYNODAL SERMON

[Col. 0889C]

“Son of man, I have set you as a watchman over the house of Israel; and you shall hear a word from my mouth and announce it to them from me. If, when I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ you do not announce it to him, nor speak so that he may turn from his evil way and live, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but I shall require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. 3:17–18).

The peril of souls is a great loss; among created things under the sun nothing is of such value that it can repair so great a loss. The Creator and Redeemer of souls knows their price best: first, because before he created them, he fixed the price of those to be created; for the price was established by him from whom they have their cause and origin. Then, by paying the price in redemption, [Col. 0889D] he learned—if not more certainly, at least more laboriously—how great was the value of those whose debt could not be discharged unless the crucifixion of the Lord of heaven and earth intervened. Therefore a serious and supreme matter is at stake where the soul is concerned. “What exchange,” says Christ, “shall a man give for his soul?” (Matt. 16:26). Again: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but loses himself and suffers the loss of himself?” (ibid.). Moses too, the lawgiver, by an equitable interpretation admits certain exchanges in many cases of the law, as here: “You shall exchange the firstborn of an ass for a sheep” (Exod. 13:13). But where mention is made of a soul struck down and killed, no remedy but an equal one is found for it: namely, that there be life for life.

Consider, therefore, O rulers of souls, what a deposit you have received; and be wise indeed, because it is safer to return it sound than to have it with you, under a simulated and deceitful guardianship, ruined and badly kept. Let not the gains of present relief entice you, for those aids are not to be desired by which eternal beggary is purchased, for which such present aids are exchanged for eternal miseries, in which there is no abiding. Hear, therefore, the Lord’s saying, explained and needing no explanation, which declares: “Son of man, I have set you as a watchman over the house of Israel … but I shall require his blood from your hand.” The throne of priestly dignity is exalted to the clouds, to the stars; but if in the end it brings about ruin, it is cast down to the dung-heap of hell, according to the saying: “Having lifted me up, you dashed me down” (Ps. 101:11). Let there be elevation in aspiration; let there be, in the mind’s consideration, the awareness of a fall so penal and damnable. Behold, the priest is another God upon earth: God remits sins, the priest remits them; God blesses, the priest blesses; God opens heaven, the priest opens it; God absolves a person, the priest absolves; God condemns, the priest condemns. God the Father ineffably begot from himself, from eternity, the Word consubstantial with himself. The priest too imitates him in this, though from far off—yet this should be spoken more simply and preached soberly—when, after the most divine words have been pronounced in the Mass, he brings about the body, personally united to that Word which is the Son of God, and with his own hand distributes it for salvation to the faithful people, just as God sent him as redemption to his people.

[Col. 0890C] What dignity is this: thus to follow in the divine footsteps, and, with justice going before, thus to set one’s steps in his way? What more, and whither beyond? The Lord left to his Church, and especially to priests, all the insignia which could and ought to be entrusted. Thus Jonathan and David entered a covenant of peace and perpetual friendship; so Christ with his Church, whom, as it is said there, he “loved as his own soul” (1 Kings 18:1), for he laid down his soul for her. It is also said there that Jonathan stripped himself of the tunic with which he was clothed and gave it to David, together with the rest of his garments, even to his sword and bow and even to his belt. “Even to” must be read inclusively, not exclusively. For Jonathan, the king’s son, compassionating from his palace and glory the young David—that is, the Church—who was still poor and exiled, wandering here and there while she sojourned on earth, gave her the tunic of his humanity which he had put on in the dispensation of the Incarnation, dying for her; and, in the Supper, gave her the sacrament of his body; and the rest of his garments, that is, everything he did and said in this body; and his sword, that is, the power of binding and loosing, or of preaching; and his bow, that is, Scripture and the Gospel; and his belt, that is, evangelical continence, concerning which it is said: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:3). But Jonathan did not impose his own name upon David.

Christ, however, did not take his own name from the bosom of his bride, but shared almost all his names without envy. Hence he says here: “Son of man, [Col. 0891A] I have set you as a watchman.” By what other name did he call himself so often in the Gospel? How often he called himself Son of Man does not come to mind. This most customary name he granted principally to bishops, and secondarily to all priests. Thus *episcopus*, “overseer,” is interpreted as “watchman”; and lesser priests, although they do not possess the fullness of power, have nevertheless been called to share in the burden of care, and receive the same responsibility of watchfulness together with the care of governing the people. But this Son of Man watches from the watchtower of heaven over the children of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God. He watches whether the consciences of all present here are good or evil, clean or unclean, devout or undevout. He watches the watchman: whether he stands at his watchtower all days and all nights, whether he cries out powerfully like a lion. For this is the office of a watchman: to keep watch, look, and cry out continually, and to stand or sit in a higher place. In vigils, diligence is denoted; in looking or beholding, reading and contemplation; in crying out, preaching; in the higher station, religious observance. Diligence excludes negligence; reading, ignorance; contemplation, concern for secular affairs; preaching arouses divine fear and love; religious observance shapes the conduct of those entrusted to it.

Consider your high priest, O son of man, great and small priest; observe how he not only always stands in his watchtower in heaven, but also on earth frequently [Col. 0891C] goes up, as though to a watchtower, onto a mountain: he ascends, teaches, prays, and spends the night. Finally, upon the mountain he is transfigured before the apostles; from the mountain he ascends into heaven. He also ascends to the watchtower when, bidding farewell to the world, he mounted and died upon the cross, so that he might teach you to defend priestly dignity even unto death, lifting the heart upward to heaven, not turning aside toward shameful gain. Son of man, attend to your frailty, and have a heart of compassion for the poor, strangers, widows, orphans, needy persons, sick persons, and those afflicted by any calamity. Son of man, have compassion upon those confessing their sins; groan with those who groan; suffer with those who suffer; weep with those who weep; labour with those who labour; fast with those who fast; lighten the penance of those contrite in heart and exceedingly ashamed of their sin.

[Col. 0891D] Son of man, recognize yourself in others. Son of man, be humble, not arrogant and proud, so that one who, trembling and afraid, dreaded the severity of the physician and the medicine for his soul before approaching, may depart from you encouraged by a good and kindly exhortation, about to return with better hope. Yet, “Son of man, I have set you as a watchman over the house of Israel,” so that you may repay compassion to nature and rectitude to vices. Thus release one who is ensnared, lest you fall into a snare; thus cleanse the pit, lest you fall into it; thus apply oil to the wounded man, that wine may bite the putrid flesh. Therefore, son of man, I have set you as a watchman. Over whom? Over the house of Israel. Over whom? Over my vineyard; for the vineyard of the Lord is the house of Israel.

[Col. 0892A] Behold the Lord’s vineyard: the Christian people, the Catholic Church. In it is that exceedingly large cluster of Cyprus-grapes which two men—two peoples—carried, suspended from the pole of the cross, out of the land of promise to show the fertility of the land: so that it may be planted, cultivated, pruned, dug, enclosed, shut in, guarded from birds, thieves, and foxes; so that it may be gathered, pressed in the winepress, and its wine preserved. “I have set you as a watchman over the house of Israel.” Therefore let it be planted through the regeneration of baptism; cultivated through instruction in holy religion; pruned through the cutting away of carnal desire; dug through confession of heart and mouth; encircled or bound through the strictness of holy resolve; shut in through withdrawal from secular intercourse; guarded through the aid [Col. 0892B] of its angel and prelate; gathered through the surrender of good works and merits by the angel on the day of judgment; meanwhile pressed in the winepresses of worldly tribulation; and stored in casks of eternal happiness. May Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns, deign to grant this to you.

## SERMON LXXXIV. SYNODAL SERMON

“Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine” (Matt. 7:6).

It is foolish and shameless for one not called to approach the Lord’s table, whether to receive it in communion or to administer it. It is rash and presumptuous for one driven away by excommunication to thrust himself forward. It is faithless [Col. 0892C] and ruinous for one called to rely irreverently upon it with an evil conscience. Presumption is condemned in the first, insolence in the second, injury in the third. Of the first it is said: “No one takes the honour to himself, except one called by God, as Aaron was” (Heb. 5:4). Of the second Adam is told: “Do not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (Gen. 2:17). Of the third: “When the king entered to see those reclining at table,” etc. (Matt. 22:11).

When his friend has come to him from the road—that is, when the mind has turned back to itself from ignorance—the first has no priestly authority with which to set something before him for his refreshment and redemption. The second, turning at evening, suffers hunger like dogs, because, ashamed of sin, when he comes to Babylon, there he shall be delivered. The third, because he eats [Col. 0892D] and drinks unworthily, eats and drinks judgment upon himself. The first is an unbeliever; the second is excommunicated from the Church; the third is a hypocrite and wicked person, whose mind and conscience are defiled. Of the first, because he is already judged, as having no standing to speak and judge; the Lord speaks concerning the second and third thus: “Do not give what is holy to dogs,” etc.

We must consider this holy thing and these pearls, and know that the term *holy* has different meanings. For “holy” is said not only of animate things, but also of inanimate things: holy ground, a holy place, holy fire, holy vessels, and the like. God is called holy; an angel is called holy; a human being is called holy; Christ’s body is holy; and the Gospel is holy. A place is called holy, [Col. 0893A] first because there things pertaining to sanctification have been done, are done, or will be done—as where the Lord was crucified, where his body is made, and where he appeared to Moses in the bush. Fire is holy either because it came from heaven or because it was used only in divine burnt offerings and sacrifices, and for lighting lamps. Holy vessels are so called because, separated from human uses, they were employed only in divine service.

God is called holy because he sanctifies all holy things. An angel is holy because, confirmed in good, he continually serves the divine will. A human being is holy because, initiated into the mysteries of sacred regeneration, he is counted among the citizens of the heavenly court. Christ’s body is [Col. 0893B] holy because, through the working of the Holy Spirit by the priestly ministry, visible matter, transformed into a visible and true substance, is believed—and held with greater certainty than certainty—to be the body of Christ taken from the Virgin. The Gospel is holy because, through the promise of heavenly things and the present sanctification of believers, it sanctifies minds. Therefore the saying, “Do not give what is holy,” etc., refers especially to the word of the Gospel and to Christ’s body.

But what can be understood by dogs except the rapacious, greedy, gluttonous, and those who have returned to vomit—that is, to sin? And what by swine except the unclean, brutish, and those never devoted to honour? O what precious and beautiful pearls Christ Jesus, king of virtues and merchant of souls, has today displayed in his market! If a man were to give all the substance of his house and purchase even one pearl, he would never regret it, because it is a desirable treasure—indeed, beyond price. The first is absolution of sins; the second, reconciliation of penitents; the third, the making of chrism; the fourth, consecration of the Lord’s body and blood; the fifth, washing of feet; the sixth, that splendid and most salutary preaching of the Lord; the seventh, the beginning of the Passion. No price can reach these, because every one of them, and all of them together, surpass not only all wealth but even all understanding.

Why, then, did our merchant bring and display them, unless perhaps because he wished not to sell but to give them? Does not Paul, carrying on his shoulders full sacks of pearls of this kind, suggest that he came to our market rather to give than to sell, saying: “The gifts and calling of God are without repentance” (Rom. 11:29); and again: “What have you that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7). Therefore one must not boast of things received as though they were one’s own. Rather, “let him who boasts boast in the Lord,” give thanks for his freely bestowed benefits, and distribute freely to the faithful what one has freely received—not to dogs or swine. Let each also beware lest he approach holy things as a dog, or devour them as a swine. Rather, let them test and examine themselves by confession and penance, so that they may deserve to be sanctified and, being holy, receive holy things.

## SERMON LXXXV. SYNODAL SERMON

[Col. 0894A]

“If I am Lord, where is my fear? And if I am Father, where is my honour?” (Mal. 1:6).

He is exceedingly proud who disdains such a Lord; exceedingly ungrateful and mad who rejects the affection of so great and kindly a Father. He has lost reason’s gift who prefers to resist God rather than serve him, when he cannot cast off the yoke of that service even if he chooses to flee. The fugitive serves a harsher power than the one who follows at heel; for obstinacy alone afflicts the reluctant more cruelly than the obedient. Certainly the finest fruit of a good servant is to have done his master’s will. Thus the faithful and prudent servant, not serving merely before the eye, having his eyes also in his master’s hands, constantly prays and says: “Teach me to do your will, for you are my God” (Ps. 142:10). And again, setting out at the Lord’s command and pitching his tent at his word, like the scapegoat (*hircus apopompeius*), ready to seek any wilderness and undergo any hardship, he says: “Lord, what do you wish me to do?” (Acts 9:3).

O priests of the Lord, servants not of any sort or of just anyone, but particular servants of Jesus Christ: your office is not to make Pharaoh’s bricks, but to build up the Church upon the rock of firm foundation for the increase of Christ’s body; not to burn upon a pile of wood, after skinning and cutting them into pieces, the flesh of bulls, or pour out the blood of goats, or wet the horns of the altar with a calf’s blood; [Col. 0894C] but, by the life-giving power of divine words, to consecrate in the sacrament of bread and wine the flesh of the uncontaminated and immaculate Lamb, Jesus Christ; to represent the blood in which Christ’s soul is signified; and, through the power of this sacrament, to incline the angelic powers to assistance. What nobility, liberty, or free-born status can be compared with this our servitude? For the priestly condition rejoices in such ineffable nobility, not merely sacramental but temporal as well, that no person born of servile stock may ever be ordained unless first manumitted, so that he may know no human being as lord who is to serve the Lord God of hosts alone.

[Col. 0894D] Hence the apostle Peter: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession” (1 Pet. 2:9). “A chosen race,” he says: truly, chosen as the tribe of Levi from the twelve tribes; as better grains from the whole field of the children of men; as David from all his brothers; as sheep from goats; as precious stones from the innumerable sand of the sea; as approved and royal coin from a heap of many coins; as the lily of the valleys from the daughters of the Canaanites, whom Isaac’s soul hates; as bright stars for everlasting ages. You, O priests of the Lord, from a people unchosen and chosen, unloved and loved, not his own and his own: a chosen race, not rejected; a chosen race, not cast away; a chosen [Col. 0895A] race, not unclean; a chosen race, not cursed; a chosen race in deed, speech, and thought; a chosen race in root, flower, and fruit; a chosen race in sanctification and honour; a chosen race for the ministry of apostles, the witness of martyrs, the fellowship of confessors, emulation of virgins, and society of angels.

Hence “a chosen race, a royal priesthood.” For a long period these two branches of Israelite dignity held their distinct boundaries; and although, through kinship, they regarded each other as of higher rank, they nevertheless did not come together in any union except very rarely, lest there be confusion among the tribes and diminution of dignities. Yet at the end of the ages and the coming of the fullness of time, at the advent of him who makes both one, the Virgin Mary, going before, united in her origin the summits of both branches; and, abolishing the plurality of christs, conceived and brought forth one Christ, since in him were the royal sceptre from Judah and the highest priesthood from Levi. Thus the Psalmist says of royal dignity: “The Lord shall send forth the rod of your power from Zion” (Ps. 109:2); and of priestly dignity: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: you are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (ibid., v. 4). Therefore Christ’s high priesthood is a royal priesthood because royal and priestly lineage are united in him.

By his gracious condescension, this sacramental mixture [Col. 0895C] flowed from the head itself down to the hem of the garment, so that from the supreme pontiff Peter, or Peter’s vicar, to the last priest, the Holy Spirit has always filled, and fills, all who are ordained in a catholic, pure, and worthy manner with the same full anointing of grace: with royal honour, signified by the crown upon the head; and with priestly dignity, shown by the stole and other insignia of priestly vesture. Therefore it is truly said that you are “a chosen race, a royal priesthood.” A royal priesthood requires morals suited to royal acts; a royal priesthood demands morals suited to priestly acts. Do not entangle yourselves in rustic sins, you who are designated by Christ’s name. Honour your ministry; fulfil the name by your works, so that the fruit of the shoot may breathe forth the sweetness and richness of the [Col. 0895D] root. For, grafted into the olive tree and cut off from the wild olive, made Christian priests from a corrupt stock—from that mass in which all we children of Adam are born children of wrath—God has taken and separated us according to the purpose of his grace; and, from vessels of dishonour, has by the workmanship of mercy fashioned vessels of gold and silver for his honour and glory. With these, as Joseph was accustomed to drink and divine from his cup, so may Christ by your ministry both fulfil his will in those entrusted to you and announce what evils are prepared for the reprobate, and what good things for the elect, in the age to come. For by diligently fulfilling this, you will be what follows: a holy nation.

“Separation of life and cause from secular persons,” O priest, understand as “a carcass,” by which one’s own [Col. 0896A] concupiscence is denoted; “taken by a beast,” by which diabolical suggestion is understood; and “every unclean thing,” by which every sin in general is made manifest. Do not touch them, holy nation. Rather, when you approach the Holy of Holies, say the psalm: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Ps. 42:1). For as God divided light from darkness, and called the light day and the darkness night, so the holy nation ought to shine amid a crooked and perverse nation. Yet let the priest’s honorable conduct and religion differ from the sons of Belial, who perform works of darkness, as far as east is from west, day from night: a holy nation by the Holy Spirit, by whom it has been regenerated and anointed; a holy nation by the holy place—for “the place in which you stand is holy ground”—a holy nation by its holy attire [Col. 0896B]. For holy are the garments in which you minister: those which Rebecca gave Jacob when he presented food and drink to his father and sought his blessing; those which Moses prepared for Aaron when he came forward to minister in holy things. A holy nation by the holy table, in which no stranger shall share; a holy nation by a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith; a holy nation with dove-like eye, rounded hand, golden and full of hyacinth-blue, calf-like foot, discriminating nose like the tower of Damascus; with truthful mouth, from which the outpourings of paradise proceed; with sealed ears, lest they hear bloodshed, like an enclosed garden, a sealed fountain; a holy nation, that it may be holy in body and spirit. There follows: “A people of possession.”

[Col. 0896C] There is a people of possession; there is a people of dissipation; there is a people of withdrawal, and also one of perdition. Hence the Apostle: “We are not children of withdrawal unto perdition, but of faith unto the gaining of the soul” (Heb. 10:39). A people of possession—at what price? at the cost of how much blood? At a great price: by whom? By Christ, who gave his life for our life; who gave his flesh for our flesh. Where? In a place of horror and desolate wilderness, in the place of the cross. How? Triumphing over the powers of the air in his body upon the wood of the cross. From where? From captivity, from death, from the power of him who held the power of death. To what end? To the kingdom: “Blessed are the poor, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” But since “a people of possession” is said in two senses, namely, acquired or acquiring, and since we have spoken of the acquired people, we must see what this acquiring people of possession acquires.

What? “I have acquired your testimonies as an inheritance,” he says (Ps. 118:111). Come now, brethren: behold the little hare which we have been pursuing since the beginning of this sermon—namely, the precepts and testimonies of God. Observe the acquisitive servant, and the acquisitive one whom the Lord found according to his heart: how he recognizes himself as a most devoted servant and the Lord as most gracious, who says: “If I am Lord, where is my fear?” “Behold,” he says, “I am your servant”—not once or in one matter only, but always and in every commandment, “I am your servant.” Therefore he repeats, “I am your servant, I am your servant.” Nor am I your servant only since yesterday or the day before yesterday [Col. 0897A], or newly; but “from the womb I am your servant, and the son of your handmaid.” O servant, by what means do you serve? “I will sing to you on the harp, O Holy One of Israel” (Ps. 70:22). Have you another instrument by which to sing? “O God, I will sing a new song to you; on a ten-stringed psaltery I will sing to you” (Ps. 143:9).

If perhaps you have not sung well, what then? “I am ready for scourges, and my sorrow is always before me” (Ps. 37:18). When scourged, will you flee from him? “Where shall I go from your Spirit?” etc. (Ps. 138:7). And yet, “we shall not depart from you; you will revive us, and we shall call upon your name” (Ps. 79:19). If he casts you down from your rank, what then? “I chose to be cast down in the house of my God” (Ps. 83:11). If he denies you bread, what then? “I shall eat ashes like bread” (Ps. 101:10). [Col. 0897B] If he throws you a stone, what then? “For your servants have been pleased with its stones” (ibid., 15). If he turns his face from you, what then? “I became troubled” (Ps. 29:8). If he commands you to be silent, what then? “I became dumb and was silent even from good things” (Ps. 38:3). If he casts you into prison, what then? “Bring my soul out of prison” (Ps. 141:8). If he appoints a day for action, what then? “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O God” (Ps. 142:2). If you do not know the customs of his court, what then? “Set before me, O Lord, the law, the way of your justifications” (Ps. 118:2).

Are his commandments burdensome and unbearable to you? “How sweet are your utterances to my palate, above honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” (ibid., 103). Will you persevere in his commandments? [Col. 0897C] “I have acquired your testimonies as an inheritance” (ibid., 111). It is little to receive, little to do, little to retain; even to acquire is little, unless he acquires as an inheritance. “I am heir,” he says, “to the commandments, and the commandments are my inheritance. I serve the testimonies of God with no less zeal than my inherited possessions.” Hence also the Apostle: “May you possess a blessing as an inheritance” (1 Pet. 3:9). And you, dearest brethren, a people of possession, may you possess as an inheritance the sanctuary of God, the testimonies of God, and the blessing of God—which God, who is blessed above all things for ever, may deign to grant us. Amen.

## SERMON LXXXVI. SYNODAL SERMON

“We do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses” [Col. 0897D] (Heb. 4:15). Therefore, lest the final day of that supreme council—which in the Scriptures is called the day of judgment—overtake, as persons inexperienced and untrained, the faithful and prudent servants of the householder, this holy assembly, lords and dearest brethren, presents itself with fitting emulation before the judging Lamb, who has seven eyes and seven horns, to perform deeds pleasing to God, hear things worthy of God, and bring back things worthy of the soul.

The instruction of God concerning sound faith must therefore be set first: faith is the foundation and support of our Christianity; then hope, which is the protection and elevation of the wondrous tabernacle even to the house of God; then charity, which is the covering of sins, the summit [Col. 0898A] of virtues, the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy-seat. If it is absent, the other things are possessed in vain; if it is present, all things are possessed. Then come reading and understanding Scripture, which is the table of the hungry; the commandments of God, which are healing instruments for souls; the promises of God, which are ointments of healing; the sacraments of the Church, which are antidotes and restorative medicines for every sickness; baptism, which is the Red Sea drowning Pharaoh with all the pursuing Egyptians—that is, original sin with all actual sins; the body and blood of Christ, by which our mortal bodies are made alive and souls refreshed as with heavenly bread; the holy anointing of chrism, in which the powers of the soul increase; confession, [Col. 0898B] which surpasses every poison; almsgiving, which extinguishes eternal fire; the unity, peace, and concord of all the faithful, which beats back the boldness of the aerial powers; and every uprightness of conduct, which gains the friendship and fellowship of angels.

But who will be able to dispense these things to you unless Joseph opens his storehouses, old and new; unless the Bridegroom introduces you into the wine-cellar, the chamber of spices, the garden of nuts; and unless God has allotted to each person a measure of faith, but a double measure to the steward, so that he may retain one portion for himself and send another to those who have not prepared a portion for themselves? Let faith, therefore, like a lamp lit in the night, illuminate [Col. 0898C] the cloud of all the sacraments which we have at hand; and, by its exceeding brightness, let it show to pure understandings even the things above the firmament, both in the orders of angels and in the banqueting chamber of the supreme and true Trinity and Unity. Let it adore the unbegotten Father, the only-begotten Son from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from both.

Here let it devote itself more to devotion than disputation. Let it not plant a grove of questions and many arguments beside this altar, because it is safer, after adoring God, to grant quiet to one’s mind with reverence than irreverently to disturb the secrets and mysteries of God [perhaps: “to investigate”]. Let it converse, if it is able, with the angelic spirits, briefly recounting the patterns of life left to us by Jesus Christ; partly considering the misery which grows from every side and overwhelms Christ’s faithful in [Col. 0898D] the world; partly imploring their aid; partly seeking out the divine counsels concerning the Church which is a pilgrim on earth. Accordingly, let it present fragrant observances to each of their orders, offering thanksgivings for their untiring care and concern for our illnesses and troubles, and entreating that, not repelled by the stench of our sins, they may not despise our needs. After this, let it turn its countenance toward the hinge of heaven; and, having adored the footstool of our Lady, let it humbly address the choirs of confessors, martyrs, apostles, and virgins, and return to itself full of tears.

Behold how faith leads the righteous by straight paths. But from the root of so great a faith there suddenly springs [Col. 0899A] the shoot of hope, causing one to hope in the Lord, in those things which God has promised to those who love him, like a great eagle of great wings, feathers, and plumage. Hope flies up to the pith of the cedar—that is, the grace of God—and, hoping in his goodness, establishes among the stars and the sons of the Most High a nest for its offspring. For it gives birth to righteousness. But lest hope, naked and alone, bring shame, let it first immerse itself, as in a most soft and delightful bath, in charity, so that the possessor of such faith and hope, inwardly intoxicated with charity and outwardly anointed with precious ointment, may through these abide in God and God in him.

Take heed, holy priests, lest when you put on the alb you set faith aside; lest when you assume the stole you lack hope; lest when you put on the chasuble, which is above [Col. 0899B] all charisms, you abandon charity. Let our meditation grow warm in these things day and night, lest the bars ever be removed from the ark, or the fish from the water—unless, perhaps, having fins and scales, they make a leap through contemplation over the waters of this mortality, just as the Spirit of God was borne over the waters of the first creation. For sound and clean is the fish of the religious mind which is caught up in an ecstasy of mind, so that its citizenship may be in heaven, and from the whisper of a gentle breeze it tastes beforehand those mysteries which it is not lawful for a human being to utter.

Read, therefore, the divine Scripture, priests whose lips preserve knowledge, because it is useful for teaching the ignorant; for refuting heresies; for [Col. 0899C] correcting those who persist in evil; and for instructing penitents. God has prepared this table before you with the bread of presentation, that is, sayings most richly filled with the grace of God, so that the desire to learn, read, and know may not feel hunger without grace; and so that the taste of knowledge may not consume the grace of satiety, but reading may desire eagerness, and eagerness reading. For in this it bears the image of the vision of glory, which is renewed by its continual fullness, so that in a reversed order abundance seems to produce want, and want abundance—though there is no want there, but full plenty, granting to desires not weariness but eternal desire.

Now, that the arrangement of the table may be understood and what is read may be known, Bezalel made a wrought candlestick of the purest gold [Col. 0899D], and Moses placed it on the north side beside the same table. Therefore such study must be applied to the holy books as may be immovable and fixed upon a threefold foot: historical, allegorical, and moral, in accordance with Solomon, who says of the law, “Write it threefold” (Prov. 22:20), and “bind it continually upon your heart” (Prov. 6:21). Let it also be wrought through the instruction of elders seated in the chair of ecclesiastical faith, in accordance with the Apostle speaking to Timothy his disciple: “But you have followed my doctrine, instruction, purpose, faith, long-suffering, love, patience,” etc. (2 Tim. 3:10). Let it also be of the purest gold, of sincere and sound understanding, according to the same Apostle: “Take diligent care to present yourself approved to God, a workman [Col. 0900A] unashamed, rightly handling the word of truth. But avoid profane and empty talk” (2 Tim. 2:15–16); and elsewhere: “For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own desires will heap up teachers for themselves,” etc. (2 Tim. 4:3).

Finally, let there be those six branches, so that good understanding may be occupied with the works of the six days: from the light made, deriving clarity of intelligence; from the firmament, discernment; from the dry land, firmness and stability; from the green herbs and fruit-bearing trees, a sense of the soul’s virtue and the production of sound judgments; from the two luminaries, illumination from the Old and New Testaments, or from divine and human literature; from the heavens, the expositions of orthodox Fathers; from creeping things, birds, and fish [Col. 0900B], thoughts either actively creeping about earthly things, contemplatively flying toward heavenly things, or deeply enfolding themselves in the hidden things of God; from cattle and beasts of the earth, the dullness of brute, carnal, and animal beings to be governed by enlightened reason; and from man made in the image and likeness of God, the prerogative and surpassing dignity of our condition.

There are further, in this candlestick, reeds of sweet and clear eloquence; cups of sober and pleasant intoxication; little spheres of rounded and perfect reasoning; lilies of good reputation and an excellent conscience. Priests of God, if you sit at the rich man’s table with such a candlestick, it will be said to you: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14); and again: “You will sit [Col. 0900C] at my table in the kingdom of my Father” (John 22:30); and this: “Passing by, he will minister to them” (Luke 12:37). Hear what is said in the Apocalypse to the angel—that is, the bishop—of the Church of Ephesus: “These things says he who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks in the midst of the seven golden candlesticks: I know your works, and your labor, and your patience, and that you could not bear evil men” (Rev. 2:1). And shortly afterward: “But I have against you that you have abandoned your first charity. Remember, therefore, from where you have fallen; repent and perform the first works. But if not, I come to you and will remove your candlestick from its place unless you repent” (ibid., 4).

May so loving and welcome an exhortation to repentance move and stir our hearts, however [Col. 0900D] hard and stony they may be. “I,” he says, “appointed you as vicar to my bride, just as I appointed John, my beloved, to my most beloved Mother. John received her as his own, and himself as hers; nor did John’s faith deceive me. For he guarded my deposit as faithfully as he truly loved me. What of you, good manager of my affairs, excellent steward of my goods, most watchful shepherd of my sheep? What of you, who undertook to feed my lambs ambitiously indeed and quite greedily, who promised care and guardianship—and Benjamin, that is, the son of the right hand, became a ravening wolf, feeding upon lambs, that is, devouring them, not feeding them, that is, providing pasture? Hence the Psalmist says: ‘They devour my people as bread is eaten’” [Col. 0901A] (Ps. 13:4). “And in Amos they are called fat cows on Mount Samaria, who calumniate the needy, crush the poor, and say to their masters, ‘Bring, and we will drink’” (Amos 4:1); “but they are lifted upon poles, and their soft remains boil in everlasting fire.”

Are you, O man, my like-minded companion, my guide and acquaintance, one of these? And have you set your portion with those who overthrow the houses of widows? Sparing you, I urge you not to walk with them; indeed, bearing with you, I urge correction; I exhort you to repentance, because I, the Lord your God, am merciful. The candlestick of your priestly honor and office indeed totters; but I do not quench the smoking flax or break the bruised reed. Repent, therefore, and offer [Col. 0901B] the fattened calf for sin, confessing truthfully and giving alms generously. Perform the first works: that is, either return to the innocence which you received from the font of baptism, or return to that love of God and neighbor and holiness of life which you promised at your ordination. If you do this, I shall command the destroyer not to shake its horns over Judah confessing and Jerusalem repenting, and I shall not remove your candlestick, just as I did not take away from Peter, prince of the apostles, even after his denial, the keys of the kingdom of heaven which I had given him, because he wept bitterly.

Who, brethren, could remain in wickedness at these bowels of mercy of our God, where mountains [Col. 0901C] melt like wax, where even stone is dissolved by so great a heat into white lime, with which the walls of God’s house are plastered and whitened? Indeed, after hearing of the enormity of so great an apostle’s sin and seeing Jesus’ swift and easy mercy, it is astonishing if every sinner does not run to repentance and melt into weeping and tears. Such is their efficacy and power that they utterly destroy sin as though it were an untimely birth, so that it may not exist, and restore the first grace—indeed, a greater grace. For tears wash the offence which true repentance has confessed. Thus Scripture is to be read, reread, and understood at God’s table and candlestick; thus what has been set forth is to be read and retained: because “we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses,” Jesus Christ our Lord [Col. 0901D], who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ever.

## SERMON LXXXVII. SYNODAL SERMON

“Do not give what is holy to dogs,” etc. (Matt. 7:6).

This is the form of a perpetual edict, for whose transgression the perpetual law provides that punishment is to be inflicted by the most grave censure of judgment. For in Leviticus we read concerning this religious ordinance, where it is shown quite clearly which persons are to abstain from holy things and for what causes. We must therefore speak concerning the eligibility: who are admitted to offer and who are rejected; likewise, who are permitted to eat of the offerings and who are not; likewise, what causes entail perpetual prohibition and what temporary prohibition. When we have carried out what we have proposed, the evangelical command will become clearer than light to us: “Do not give what is holy to dogs,” etc. And it must be carefully noted and committed to memory that Moses marks and condemns in the Law the faults of priests, for which they are deprived of heavenly things [Note: Something is missing at Col. 0901D]. But the Apostle Paul depicts the ornaments of virtues by which an evangelical priest may administer the holier sacraments more holily.

Thus the Law speaks: “Any man of your seed through your families who has a blemish shall not offer breads to his God, nor approach to minister to him” (Lev. 21:17). It immediately subdivides the blemish in many ways: if blind—that is, dark through ignorance [Col. 0902B] of the sacraments of faith; if lame, one who scarcely does even the good which he understands; if with nose small, large, or crooked, one who is less discerning and does not distinguish vices from virtues, whether from deficiency of understanding, excessive presumption, or the avarice of unjust desire; if broken in foot or hand, one who in no way rises to a good work; if hunchbacked, one bent entirely toward earthly things and not seeking those above; if bleary-eyed, one who indeed has good intelligence but, like the slothful servant, buries the talent received; if having a white spot in the eye, one lifted up by arrogance and eating much honey, so as not to be wise unto sobriety; if having continual scab, one oppressed by the wantonness of the flesh; if drunken, one inflamed by continual thought of luxury. Thus far is the catalogue of vices which render an administration impious if they possess the dispenser of divine things.

Let us see, therefore, how the priest, stripped of these serpent-like skins, may acquire Solomon’s skins from that eminent tanner, Paul the Apostle, who is said to have practised this craft. Thus, clothing the bishop of the New Testament, he says in the Epistle to Timothy: “A bishop, then, must be blameless, the husband of one wife, sober, prudent, well-ordered, chaste, hospitable, a teacher; not given to wine, not a striker, but modest; not quarrelsome, not covetous, but chaste; ruling his own house well, having his children subject with all chastity. [Col. 0902D] Not a novice. Moreover, he must have a good testimony from those who are outside” (1 Tim. 3:2). These are the very good garments which Rebecca has at home, and with which she clothes Jacob, her simple and beloved son, when setting him before his father’s blessing.

Genesis notes that those garments contributed greatly to gaining the grace of blessing: “As soon as the father perceived the fragrance of the garments, he said: ‘Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field, which the Lord has blessed. May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth abundance of grain, wine, and oil. Let peoples serve you and tribes worship you; be lord of your brothers, and let the sons of your mother bow down before you. Let him who curses you be cursed, and let him who blesses you be filled with blessings’” (Gen. 27:27–29). Behold to whom priestly blessing is given by God: certainly not to those naked of good will or badly clothed in the scaly foulness of vices, but to those well ordered in the moral character of good dispositions.

Let bishops who ordain, therefore, see what sort of priests they ought to consecrate; and let those being ordained themselves see what sort they ought to be when they approach, fearing what Jacob said to his mother: “I fear lest I bring upon myself a curse instead of a blessing” (ibid., 12). Certainly those who, when approaching holy orders, do not count the costs necessary for the journey, to see whether they have enough to complete it, ought greatly to fear, lest [Col. 0903B] their prayer or consecration become sin to them. It would be better for them not to have taken up the Lord’s name than to have taken it in vain, and not to have entered into holy things than to have defiled God’s sanctuary by offering strange fire. Therefore, bishops, do not give what is holy to dogs—that is, to robbers, the avaricious, schismatics, detractors, and those relapsed into criminal sins; nor set the pearls of holy things before swine—that is, gluttons, the lustful, the unclean, and persons most base in every manner of life.

This is enough concerning those admitted to offer and those rejected. We must now speak concerning those who are permitted to eat of the offerings and those who are not. When, according to the ability of human frailty, persons of honorable and moderate conduct have been enrolled in the lot of the saints [Col. 0903C], instruction is given them concerning the manner of ministering, so that, as faithful and prudent stewards, they may carefully distribute the Lord’s money and chastely dispense the table of the most undefiled sacraments. Thus it is said to them: “Do not give what is holy to dogs,” etc.

Let us again turn our lights toward the face of Moses; and, with the veil removed, let us draw out the marrow of sacred things from the letter of the Law, if perhaps in this matter too the Law may serve the Gospel, as Moses did the Lord glorified on the mountain. For it is unfitting that a king should proceed without his armour-bearer. Therefore Moses says in Leviticus to Aaron, his sons, and their descendants: “Every man of your stock who approaches those things which have been consecrated [Col. 0903D] and which the children of Israel have offered to the Lord, while uncleanness is in him, shall perish before the Lord. I am the Lord” (Lev. 22:3)—as though his decrees may not be violated. “The man of Aaron’s seed who is leprous”—that is, tainted by grave sin—“or who suffers a flow of seed”—that is, one who does not restrain himself from sin—“shall not eat of those things sanctified to me until he is healed” (ibid., 4). Certainly, through confession and repentance.

Here a certain grave offence occurs to me, which under that Law is frequently committed, not without divine punishment. For, while remaining the next day in the same will or sickness of sin, someone, having merely resolved verbally to make confession, returns to the holy things of the Lord, forgetting what is said: that one who approaches them while uncleanness is in him shall perish before the Lord—that is, in his soul. But he objects to me: “I have been healed through confession; why should I not receive communion?” I answer: if what you say is true, you do well. But you truly claim that you have been healed by confession, although it has not yet extinguished in your mind the perverse affection, nor in your flesh the unclean stimulation. So long, therefore, as the law of sin reigns in the heart and the law of the members in the body, you say you are healed while you are sick both in soul and flesh. Believe me: what you say is false, because bare confession does not heal the wounds of sin which still gape and stink most foully; while corruption flows, while the worms of desires boil forth, while the cancer creeps onward, while the streamlet of the bituminous well runs.

[Col. 0904B] In the laws it is said that a bare agreement produces no action. An agreement is bare when I simply promise to give or do you something; if I do not fulfil such a promise to you, you cannot sue me by any action. Thus there is no legal obligation, nor have you done something for me by which I am legally bound to you. Similarly, it seems to me concerning bare confession that God is not bound to grant forgiveness of sins, when it ought rather to be called confusion than confession, where satisfaction for the offence does not follow. Therefore one still remains in the uncleanness which one has not expiated by suitable repentance; nor ought one presume health before one has experienced, after some interval of time, that that fever has cooled. If you had suffered from a tertian or quartan fever, would you ever be secure of recovery unless its customary attack had failed to come once and again? So also with sin: do not be secure unless every movement of it has died within you. Unless the Law itself, under its covering, affirms the same things I have plainly told you, do not believe me. For shortly afterwards it adds concerning him: “He who has touched an unclean thing upon a dead body” (Lev. 22:5) . . . [lacuna: some material is missing].

## SERMON LXXXVIII. SYNODAL SERMON

“What will you see in the Shunammite, except the dances of camps?” (Song 7:1).

These are words of love taken from the Song of Songs, by which we are urged to behold a certain woman [Col. 0904D]: strong, chaste, beautiful, devout, well ordered, beloved by a friend, or even betrothed to a husband. “I,” Solomon says, “loved her from my youth, and sought to take her for my bride, and I became a lover of her beauty; for she glorifies her noble birth, having fellowship with God” (Wis. 8:2). At times, like a solitary turtledove caught up over the mountains of spices to meet Christ in the clouds, she lingered in most desirable contemplation. But he who is of the earth and speaks of the earth, not yet possessing the cherubim’s wings by which he might be lifted from the earth—a man walking by faith, not yet by hope—cries out to her: “Return, return, O Shunammite; return, return, that we may behold you” (Song 6:12). Return from the paths of eternity; return [Col. 0905A] from the heights of heaven; return from contemplation of the angels; return from ecstasy of mind, that we may behold you soberly preaching Christ crucified to us, offering us milk, not yet solid food, which neither we nor those like us could bear.

The Bridegroom, hearing the desire of those who desire, addresses them all as though they were one: “What will you see in the Shunammite, except the dances of camps?” An unusual expression summons its hearers to unusual matters. If the Shunammite is a woman, as we read in the history of Kings, how shall we see dances of camps in her? If she is something other than a woman, why does Solomon address her thus? Or perhaps she is that Shunammite Abishag, of whom it is said in Third Kings that King David had grown old and was advanced in days; and, when he was covered with garments, he was not warmed. Therefore his servants said: “Let us seek for our lord the king a young virgin, and let her stand before the king and cherish him; let her sleep in his bosom and warm our lord the king.” So they sought a maiden beautiful throughout all the borders of Israel, found Abishag the Shunammite, and brought her to the king. The girl was exceedingly beautiful; she slept with the king and ministered to him (3 Kgs. 1:1–4).

Behold, a little movement has brought us to another shore—not a whirlwind’s wind but a gentle breeze—so that, just as Laban substituted Leah for her sister Rachel before Jacob, so, through the Shunammite spoken of in Fourth Kings, the one spoken of in Third Kings may be brought forward. Yet the agreeable face of the Shunammite, pleasant because of her beauty, makes this error [Col. 0905C] or transition not unpleasant. Both, indeed, are to be embraced: this one for chastity and beauty, that one for fruitfulness and generous hospitality. This one warms the now cold and aged King David; that one receives the Prophet Elisha, passing through Shunem, with hospitality.

One sacramental reality is represented under a double sign, and the mystery of the divine Incarnation is indicated both by the warming of the king advanced in days and by the reception of the travelling prophet. Without doubt Abishag the Shunammite signifies the Church, redeemed by Christ’s blood and dyed with the blood of martyrs; her name is interpreted “roaring” or “my father is superfluous,” and “Shunammite” as “scarlet”; she who speaks in the person of penitents: “I roared from the groaning of my heart” (Ps. 37:9); and who hears in the Psalm: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; and forget the house of your father” (Ps. 44:11)—namely, the superfluous father, the old Adam.

She was sought in the Virgin Mary throughout all the borders of Israel: a virgin and young woman, that she might stand before the king in chastity and humility and cherish him through an ineffable conception by the Holy Spirit; and that the king might sleep in her bosom, or she herself rest in the king’s bosom, free from every assault of vices; that she might contain God by the consecration of her most inviolate womb and warm him by the illumination of singular charity. O Abishag the Shunammite, how beautiful you are! How gracious, wise, and diligent in the service of King David! You are beautiful [Col. 0906A], yet with chastity; young, yet with chastity preserved; warm, yet by charity; reclining and sleeping with the king, yet with every sobriety. He who, covered with garments, is kindled by no warmth is revived by the life-giving warmth of virgin service.

But what are those garments which do not give warmth, except curtains, hair-cloth coverings, ram skins dyed red, and hyacinth-blue skins, together with their sacrifices and offerings? These cannot make perfect in conscience one who serves only in foods and drinks and various baptisms. For the Law brought no one to perfection: it chilled its worshippers with fear; it did not kindle them with the spirit of adoption. But when the fullness of time came, the young Shunammite was sought throughout all the borders of Israel, and she was found scarlet through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit. She warmed the Ancient of Days, so that he sent his Son and he slept with the Virgin, until the Lamb came forth with our fleece and, by redeeming the world, saved and ruled it.

We must now sail onward, with the south wind blowing where it wills, to the Shunammite whose son Elisha, drawing himself together and bending over him, raised to life. She is interpreted “captive” and “despised”; for Isaiah speaks to her: “Loose the bonds from your neck, captive daughter of Zion” (Isa. 52:2); and it is said in the Psalm: “We have become a reproach and an object of contempt to the proud” (Ps. 122:4). But she too will be delivered from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God, when the Son hands over [Col. 0906C] the kingdom to God the Father. By what merit? Because she received the Prophet Elisha with hospitality, and “he who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward.” Thus the Shunammite said to her husband: “I perceive that this man of God who frequently passes by us is holy. Let us therefore make for him a small upper chamber, and put in it a bed, a table, a chair, and a candlestick, so that, when he comes to us, he may stay there” (4 Kgs. 4:9). Practising hospitality before the apostolic command, this woman, fulfilling the law of hospitality, was so generous and beneficent that she prepared even a special dwelling for a religious and holy man, lest he suffer any inconvenience.

But what does “he frequently passes by us” mean, except what the Apostle says: “God, who at many times and in many ways formerly spoke to the fathers in the prophets, in these last days has spoken to us in his Son” (Heb. 1:1)? He passed through Abel, through Noah, through Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; he passed through Moses and through the other ancient fathers. He truly passed through, because none there made an upper chamber except the Shunammite who assumed flesh from the Virgin. The upper chamber plainly was the Virgin’s womb, into which the Son of God descended from the Father’s bosom. Yet, though the Word became flesh, he neither remained invisible in divinity alone nor emptied himself so far as the contagion of sin. He was therefore in the upper chamber because he assumed not sinful flesh but the likeness of sinful flesh; and it was small because he was made a little lower than the angels, becoming passible and mortal.

[Col. 0907A] She set down the bed, namely the womb itself, or the tomb, or the baptismal font; for in the font, as upon a marriage-bed, the Word—as Augustine says—approaches the element, and a sacrament comes to be. “Unless a man is reborn of water and the Spirit,” says the Lord, “he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John IV, 5). Therefore, with the Holy Spirit working in this sacrament, Christian rebirth takes place, not from corruptible seed but by the power of God. Upon this bed human faith, through the power of the Holy Spirit, conceives and bears a son whom it calls Christian. Finally, she sets down the table: the holy altar, where Christ feeds his guests and gives them drink from his own flesh and blood.

O priests of God, you are fellow-diners and ministers of this table. Consider with what vestments, [Col. 0907B] with what lips, with what hands, with what inward parts and feet you approach the flesh of the Lamb, whom you must eat wholly with wild lettuces. “The head,” says the Law, “with the feet and inward parts you shall devour” (Exod. XII, 9). The head signifies divinity; the feet, humanity; the inward parts, the great mystery of godliness, which was hidden from the ages in God and revealed in the last times. Let there therefore be in you steadfast faith and a pure conscience, and let all that is yours, inward as well as outward, be clean.

She also set down the chair, in which sits he who judges the world in equity, to whom the Father gave authority also to execute judgment because he is the Son of Man. And you are assessors of the Judge, who must judge between clean and unclean, [Col. 0907C] leprosy and non-leprosy, dead and living, as Solomon judged whose the living son was. Therefore turn neither to the right nor to the left, deceitful in the balances; rather, judge the children of men rightly. She set down the lampstand both at the bed, at the table, and at the chair: a lampstand is necessary, that it may give light to all who are in the house. The lampstand is the Gospel: no sacrament in the Church would be open to view unless the Gospel disclosed it. Paul bears this lampstand when he says: “I am a prisoner in the Lord, but the word of God is not bound” (Ephes. IV, 1). And the Lord says concerning Paul: “I will show him how much he must suffer for my name, so that he may bear my name before Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel” (Acts IX, 16).

[Col. 0907D] “What will you see in the Shulammite but choirs of camps?” The choirs of camps are the orders of angels; hence their king is called the Lord Sabaoth, that is, “of hosts.” Thus also in the Apocalypse of John we read that war arose in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon; that great dragon was cast down, and his place was no longer found in heaven. As many as are the orders among the angels, so many are the choirs—nine, indeed. But those wars with the race of darkness are unknown to us, though not useless; for they fight with us and for us. Yet when our Lord Jesus, the coming King of the Jews, chose new wars, receiving the first and fiercest assaults of Satan in the days of his flesh, it was in order that he might triumph over and bind in his body upon the wood of the cross the powers of the air and him who held the dominion of death, [Col. 0908A] for his handmaids.

That mighty man in war, Gideon, likewise says to his followers: “What you see me do, do” (Judg. VII, 17). Hence in the Gospel: “He who does not carry his cross and come after me cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV, 27). After him follow the choirs of camps, holding the weapons of warfare which Paul, the most vigorous prince in the choir of martyrs, describes when he says: “Put on the armour of God, that you may be able to stand in the evil day,” etc. (Ephes. VI, 2). Therefore they follow him on red, dappled, and white horses, as is read in Zechariah. The martyrs, who did not love their lives even unto death, follow the Lamb on red horses, their blood poured out through a thousand endeavors [Col. 0908B] as far as the horses’ bridles. The confessors follow on white horses, mortifying their flesh with its vices and desires. The virgins—some of whom served God in virginity, while others also courageously endured martyrdom—have followed their King on dappled horses.

Behold the choirs of camps in the scarlet Shulammite, to whom it is said: “Your cheeks are like those of a turtledove” (Cant. I, 9); or in the captive Shulammite, while this pilgrimage is a time of war and not a time of peace, which will be in the glory to come, where there will be choirs not of camps but of singers. “For, O glorious city, the dwelling-place of all who rejoice is in you.” O priests, God has appointed you leaders in these camps: sound [Col. 0908C] the trumpet in Zion; rouse Leviathan; run from gate to gate, lest thief, robber, or adversary enter and set ablaze the camp entrusted to you; lest the devil, like a lion, seize the souls entrusted to you. To you, shepherd of the sheep, to you, bishop, it is said: “What will you see in this Shulammite—that is, in the Church entrusted to you—but choirs of camps?”

## SERMON LXXXIX. SYNODAL.

When I hold the body of Christ in my hands before my eyes, I set it like a mirror before my face, so that, by the cooperating purity and beauty of it, I may blush when the foulness and impurity of my manner of life are exposed; and, striving through the shame of blushing to cleanse evil [Col. 0908D] deeds, I may put on the new man, who was created according to God. I also keep at hand this bath, warm with the blood of the Lamb and most effective against every disease: namely, the cup of salvation. Entering into it, I lay aside my old leprosy; and, as the soul blossoms anew and the flesh is stripped of its old rust, our nature is fittingly engraved anew in its first image. Hence the Apostle says: “[He predestined us] to be conformed to the image of the Son of God, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren” (Rom. VIII, 29).

This conformity proclaims the power of its works to his people, especially to the chosen, royal, priestly, peculiar people—which you are: priests of God, ministers of God, vicars of God, made one body with God and fellow-partakers with God. This conformity is seen in the fact that Christ [Col. 0909A] was conceived and born from the womb of the Virgin under the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit; he was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions, so that his name became “oil poured out”; and he was made high priest by God the Father according to the order of Melchizedek. Having penetrated the heavens in his own blood, he entered the Holy of Holies; there, before the Father, our advocate prays and pleads for the sins of the Christian people. He will come to the great synod and judge all according to the works and merits of each, all respect of persons set aside; by a definitive sentence he will absolve the sheep and condemn the goats.

Therefore, as our Head went forth, so let us who are his members follow; and let us be made like him both in name and in offices. Hence in the Song of Songs: “We will make for you likenesses of gold” (Cant., passim). That is to say: we cannot have or retain you present in bodily and visible form; but at least we shall imitate the examples of your most upright way of life and most blessed passion. Thus, conceived in the womb of holy mother Church, we are regenerated from water and the Spirit; we are anointed with holy chrism both at the font and upon the forehead, and in ordination; like Aaron, not simoniacally, we are called by God to sacred orders. In the blood of Christ we frequent the hidden oracles of angels; contrite and cleansed in heart, we lay open our sins and those of all the faithful, and, with God working with us, obtain abundant propitiation. By accusing ourselves, we attempt to forestall and moderate the judgment to come. [Col. 0909C]

For we make of the mirror a shield, setting the body of Christ before his Father in a twofold way, lest he grow angry and, impeded by his own Son, return the sword to its sheath if perhaps our wickedness had drawn it out. We likewise set this shield against enemies, so that, terrified by so great a majesty, they may flee and utter no word. Once indeed, in the battle-line of the Passion, it was pierced by nails and a lance, while the invincible power hidden beneath it received the most savage and stubborn blows both of Jews and of demons. Yet what it suffered in the flesh was well repaired in the Resurrection; for Christ, risen from the dead, dies no more, etc. Therefore diabolical fury will not add a second assault upon the strength of this shield, [Col. 0909D] which, with the spear-point turned back upon itself, brought forth maternal entrails, and from a death of three days won for itself eternal life. Therefore, priest, hold this shield with both hands against the enemy, and you will be able to fear no plague.

Its image, or engraved work, is patterned in silver where it says: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34); it is gilded with the glory of the Resurrection where it says: “I lay down and began to sleep, and I rose” (Ps. III, 6). The body of Christ is also the Gospel of the kingdom. In it, as in a field of delights, after the mirror, after the bath, after the shield, we enter, drawing in its fragrant sweetness; contemplating the flowers of miracles, plucking the fruits of sacraments, drinking the streams of wisdom, touching the pleasantness of herbs, [Col. 0910A] and abounding more than Solomon in every glory and richness.

Behold: the bride has the mirror and the bath; the soldier, the shield; the priest, the book. Let the bride adorn herself in the mirror and wash herself in the bath; let the soldier arm himself with the shield; let the priest read in the Gospel. From the mirror let the bride depict Christ’s form for herself, and from the bath his purity. From the shield let the soldier take strength against enemies; from the book let the priest learn knowledge and teaching. By the judgment of the priest the form and purity of the bride are determined, and likewise the soldier’s warfare, as the book of righteous judgments teaches him.
