For this you have come—indeed, assembled—most beloved brothers: that you may judge what is being done in the Province contrary to the Gospel, what is presumptuously undertaken outside or contrary to the form of decrees, [Col. 0910B] etc.

## SERMON XC. SYNODAL.

“To you praise is fitting, O God, in Zion,” etc. (Ps. LXIV, 1.)

The pregnant soul, impregnated by a foretaste of future joy, it gives birth to offspring who are neither conceived in iniquities nor born in the sins of paternal transgression. Yet while the law of divine judgment remains, it bears children in pain; and they have not received forgetfulness of righteousness, because their descendants are a holy inheritance. From a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith arises this generation of those who seek the Lord: remembrance of ancient days, longing for the eternal hills, meditation on hymns from [Col. 0910C] the songs of Zion, and the rush of holy thoughts already leaping toward everlasting eternities. What are these but the children of the saints?

Yet sometimes, groaning beneath the waters of worldly occupations but scenting the return to their homeland, they run, touched and drawn by fragrance—not only by the fragrance of ointment but also by the cry of wine. They prudently approach the chamber of spices and without delay enter the wine-cellar. There they are filled with wine as though they were horns of the altar; there, in their garments from ivory palaces, they are drenched with the wondrous scent of incense and every powder of spices. What then? Psalm, hymn, and song are their custom all day long. A song indeed upon the harp, a psalm upon the ten-stringed psaltery, and a hymn upon well-sounding cymbals, [Col. 0910D] upon cymbals of jubilation: they resound before him who sits upon the throne, saying, “To you praise is fitting, O God, in Zion,” etc.

Such priests sing before the ark and propitiatory in the temple of the true Solomon; such officers minister in the Lord’s service. For in Zion and Jerusalem this most sacred and incomparable temple is read to have been built by Solomon in honor of God and for the commendation of human service. Peoples and nations from every direction came together at that temple, as at a place of sanctification, in order that they might there pay their vows and render praise to God, both for the forgiveness of sins and for the receipt of temporal blessings. Therefore it is said: “To you praise is fitting,” etc. Although God’s holy name should be honored and worshipped in every place [Col. 0911A] of his dominion, praise is especially fitting to him in Zion, because this is the place of which it is elsewhere said: “His place was made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” (Ps. LXXV, 3).

The psalm states sufficiently plainly the place of praise, the manner of praise, and the person praised; but the person who praises is unmentioned. God, certainly, is the one praised; Zion is where he is praised; a hymn is that by which he is praised. But by whom is he praised? Perhaps by Wisdom, for Wisdom shall praise her own soul. Perhaps also the waters above the heavens praise the name of the Lord. Do not you too, morning stars? Was it not said in the book of Wisdom: “When my [morning] stars praised me” (Job XXXVIII, 7)? What is the force of this addition, [Col. 0911B] “morning”? It seems to indicate that no stars but morning stars praise God. Without doubt, the stars fixed in the firmament do not change their station; but because some appear at sunset and some at the day’s rising, those which appear before dawn are properly called morning stars.

Behold: from their office the holy prudence of the Lord’s priests may perceive that they are not inappropriately called morning stars. For who says, “My eyes anticipated the watches” (Ps. LXXVI, 5), unless he is a morning star? Who says, “My prayer will come before you” (Ps. LXXXVII, 14), and, “My eyes came before you at daybreak, that I might meditate on your words” (Ps. CXVIII, 148)? Is he not a morning star? Most beloved brethren, we must rise at midnight and come to Zion before dawn—that is, to the Church—because “To you praise is fitting, O God, in Zion.” Rise from bed with the bride, and seek him whom your soul loves through the lanes and streets of the city, singing psalms and reading the prophets and apostles. “A little while,” she says, “after I had passed them by, I found him whom my soul loves” (Cant. III, 3). She had encountered the watchmen of the walls, who wounded her because they took her mantle from her, so that she might be wounded by love and stripped of temporal pride through love of poverty. [Col. 0911C]

In keeping with this likeness, when the priest approaches to perform the sacred mystery of Christ’s body and blood, let him lay aside the mantle he used in secular service and put on the most holy vestments in which he performs the ministries of angels. With his own mouth he makes the Lord of angels himself; with his hands he holds him; with his eyes he sees him; and, by reception, he faithfully unites him to his own body and soul, so that, being himself united in God, God may remain in him. Then that soul becomes Zion, or indeed the daughter of Zion, and sings a hymn to her God, directing all her inward faculties to praise and to contemplation of that face which became radiant as the sun and whose garments became white as snow. She is carried beyond—indeed above—herself, reckoning the desires of the flesh as dung; she despises as nothing all the substance of her house; she forgets, as by a holy covenant, the conflicts of flesh and spirit; she does not remember the condition of mortality. The appointed law, which no mortal has been able to evade, [Col. 0912A] she seeks to pay before the tribute is yet rendered, when she says: “It is good for us to be here; let us make three tabernacles: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah” (Matt. XVII, 4).

Let us say a little concerning these three tabernacles. Christ’s tabernacle is far larger and more perfect, “not made with hands,” that is, not of this creation. This tabernacle is Christ’s body, in which all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily. Of it also it is said: “He who created me rested in my tabernacle” (Ecclus. XXIV, 12). To this tabernacle of the Son the Father came, not repeatedly by departure and return, but once, through the work of the Incarnation; he made his dwelling and rested there, because it pleased him in it. Through it [Col. 0912B] he destroyed every sin and established all righteousness; he not only repaired the loss but increased gain from the loss. For where sin abounded, grace abounded still more.

Observe a certain wonder discovered through the Word made flesh. From the beginning of the course of things, it had not been so: that what life gave life to, death should extinguish; that what fullness filled, emptiness should empty; and likewise with all else in this manner. But now through death life is restored; through loss renewal is made new; glory is born from dishonor; abundance proceeds from want. These things, more precious than gold and silver, are received from Christ’s tabernacle, so that whoever comes to it a slave of sin may be justified in it and become free; [Col. 0912C] that he who is crooked may be converted; that he who is cruel may be led back to mercy; and that heaven, which had been closed to one through hardness of heart, may be reopened through repentance and the humility of confession.

If famine comes through unbelief, pestilence through error, corrupted air through detraction, blight through avarice, locust through boasting, rust through envy, or any other plague oppresses our land, let us raise our hands in this wonderful tabernacle and trust in help. We pay hymn and vow to God in this tabernacle if we faithfully retrace in our paths the footprints of his way of life among men. As this tabernacle is not made with hands, so neither can it ever be explained in human speech. It is above understanding; above [Col. 0912D] every thing called God or worshipped. Let our thought always stretch into it and toward it, but let us never enter irreverently.

Let us now pass to Moses’ tabernacle, because Moses built his tabernacle according to the pattern shown to him on the mountain. Survey all the furnishings of the tabernacle; count its width, length, and height; unfold the beauty of the priestly vestments; weigh out the mixtures of ointments and incense; expound the import of sacrifices and burnt offerings. Carefully consider the offerings of birds, cattle, metals, fruits of the earth, liquids, flowers, or even branches. What will you see except certain prefigurations of invisible things, expositions [Col. 0913A] of heavenly mysteries, introductions to goods not merely represented but true? If you can take all this in broadly, you have material with which to expand the phylacteries of your little intellect for not one but many days, and to extend a web of discourse to a hundred cubits. Yet, lest we impose the whole labor upon you, let us explain something of these matters briefly.

After that unbounded light of the supreme Trinity—to which, we do not doubt, the flesh of our Savior is joined—the angelic nature ever abides in stations near the sight of the Lord, bordering upon the wells of unchangeable truth and sending back streams, toward that very same object, of its intent attention. Of them, under the figure of living creatures, it is said: “Their faces and wings were stretched out above” [Col. 0913B] (Ezek. I, 11). For the face and wing of an angel are stretched out above when, in unwearied zeal, they fix both the merits of their virtues and the desires of contemplation upon their Creator in rapt courses. What pure services, what services pleasing to God, they render, we are not yet able to know, because it does not yet befall our unpurified senses to hear or see them.

Yet this much, as God pleased, could become known to the humble concerning the angels’ diligent charity: by their intercessions they seek remedies of health for our weakness; they provide the lamp of truth for ignorance, restoration for destitution, consolation for the sorrowful, and renewal for the despairing. They receive our weeping, store up our tears, write down confessions, hear prayers, labor before God for our peace, and commend their suppliants to the Mediator. They drive back enemies, extinguish temptations, introduce holy meditations; they surround souls departing from the distress of the body through the midst of enemy battle-lines, lead them to prepared dwellings, and kindly instruct the newcomers by teaching them their order and customs. They excuse when they can; they plead when they cannot excuse. They wage war for us against demons; with ever-watchful care they direct our entrance and our steps, like instructors of our infancy or guardians of orphaned childhood. [Col. 0913C]

These are represented by the cherubim which Moses carved in his tabernacle upon the panel; in the middle he had the propitiatory, and cherubim or seraphim stood on either side before it with intent countenance, six wings to one and six wings to the other. That Moses, who in familiar boldness had dared to ask to behold God’s face without the veil of any eternal image, so that he might augment in contemplation of the face the grace he had deserved in the secret place of the mind, heard from the Lord: “I will do the thing you have spoken, for you have found grace before me, and I have known you by name. I will also show you all good things; but you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII, 20). At this my soul is troubled within me: hearing every good thing promised to the Prophet, yet God’s face denied.

Surely, what good will there be where God’s face will not be? Or perhaps it may not seem unreasonable to understand this thus: that his “back parts,” which Moses standing upon the rock could see, are every good thing which he attains by faith in the present Church—namely, the sacraments of Christ’s body and blood together with his other sacraments; while his face is above every good thing, when that which is now held in hope will be possessed in the reality of things. By this distinction, not indiscreetly made, you may also distinguish Zion and Jerusalem, hymn and vow: for in Zion—that is, in present contemplation—those who fear God will lack no good thing; but in the future, enjoying God and seeing him face to face, eye to eye, as he is in the nature of divinity, they will nevertheless abound in every good thing; so that here is a well of living waters, and there a fountain of water springing into eternal life. [Col. 0914A]

For there the angels, dispensers of the rewards of future expectation, will give into our bosom a good measure, pressed together and running over, when in their fellowship they receive human nature in the elect, admit it to equality, and establish it in the glory of the countenance of ineffable brightness. There deficiency will not even be named, because the moon will be taken away, according to which we now undergo increase and decrease in her cycle. The sun itself—whose rising we cover because of our work, whose setting we await because of rest, so that, as though by its permission, we go out and come in—having received the wages of its service, will cease to make us labor any further. For, when new things come, we shall cast away the old. The eyes of the Lamb who sits in the midst of the throne will provide light sufficient [Col. 0914C] for the whole city, so that the gaze of a pure heart may penetrate, toward God, even to the innermost parts—not only of the veil but also of every womb—the ark of God’s invisible glory.

O Lord, then your children will walk in the light of your countenance; they will recline with you at noon, and will be like new olive shoots around your table. For the light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon them, so that, when the body of their weakness has been refashioned and conformed to the body of your glory, they may be made conformed to the image of your Son, that he may be the firstborn among many brethren. For they will shine like the sun in the kingdom of heaven, or like the stars unto everlasting eternities.

[Col. 0914D] Then, at last, the vow will be paid in Jerusalem; then “I will pay my vows in your midst, Jerusalem.” There all is “midst,” where there is no angel—perhaps *angle* [*angulus*]—of duplicity; all is midst, because he paved the middle with love for the daughters of Jerusalem. Truly from its midst there will appear, as it were, the appearance of electrum, in which love of God, golden, and love of neighbor, silvery, are as though fused in one affection. For, as Moses says: “The Lord will surround your heart and the heart of your seed, so that with your whole heart and whole soul you may love God and your neighbor” (Deut. XXX, 6); “God is in your midst” (Deut. VI, 15), God is around you, etc.

## SERMON XCI. SYNODAL.

“You are the seal of the likeness of God, full of wisdom, [Col. 0915A] perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God; every precious stone was your covering: sardius,” etc. (Ezek. XXVIII, 12).

That great King, who fills all things with royal majesty, fills the universe with goodness, and orders all things by his power, although he could alone arrange and administer his commonwealth, nevertheless wished to have helpers. He appointed stewards and assigned many officials in his court to diverse ministries—not that his own service or labor might be diminished, for he works all things at rest and by his word alone, nor that created things might be administered more easily and conveniently by individual overseers and caretakers, though all things are cared for, preserved, and governed by one nod of God alone—but so that he might have many to whom he could distribute his gifts and, as it were, associate with the merit of heavenly goods. Therefore he chose from among his people a chancellor, to whom he entrusted the signet, that is, the seal. But it would have been unseemly for one so wise to place beside himself a malicious and foolish man, especially one to whom he intended to communicate counsels and secrets; he therefore chose one full of wisdom.

Again, if the splendor of glory and brightness of eternal light placed beside itself an Ethiopian or an uncultivated barbarian, the face of that most orderly city would be marred: desiring to behold the King in his beauty, it would at the same sight see both light and darkness. Therefore he most fittingly chose his chancellor perfect in beauty. Again, if he suddenly put a rustic, reared beneath thickets, in charge of such riches, that man, whether greedy or ignorant, would disorderly handle the treasures of delights. He therefore appointed as chancellor one who had been delicately educated amid the delights of God’s paradise, lest he become insolent through learning or squander his lord’s goods. Let him know, then, how to keep watch carefully; let him know how to honor the King’s friends and either reconcile or destroy his enemies. This is a great matter. [Col. 0915C]

Most beloved brethren, if you were assigned to guard the Lord’s stable, the sheepfolds, the palace gate, or the bridegroom’s chamber, would this not be beyond all merit? And who would be adequate for these things? What recompense, then, will you render to him who has entrusted even the seal of his likeness to you? It was too little for him merely to entrust you with the seal, unless he also made you the seal of his countenance—you who have the care of souls, who must reform his image in those committed to you. For this is the priestly office: to reform the image of God and engrave his likeness upon souls. Nothing worthy is done either in heaven or on earth when conformity to God is not sought according to one’s power. For this alone is good, this alone fitting and necessary for a rational creature: to be reformed from perversity and conformed to God in righteousness and truth. Whatever does not actively—or at least cooperatively—advance this holy endeavor, which must never be laid down, never postponed, but always undertaken and placed before all things, is brutish, animal, irrational, and unpriestly. [Col. 0915D]

From the least to the greatest, the whole assembly, the whole host of heavenly spirits, in holy striving and peaceful rivalry, labors to be especially irradiated and distinguished by the splendor of its King, the image of its Creator, the likeness of its God. In that heavenly school nothing else is read, nothing else learned, nothing else taught. According to the measure and share of likeness and conformity to God among the angels, there is a corresponding difference and inequality of orders, ranks, and dignities—yet, through most perfect peace and love, a difference almost without dissimilarity. To recoil from this purpose is to abandon the good and will to resist God. Thus Lucifer, the beginning of God’s ways, the seal of God’s likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty, was in the delights of God’s paradise so long as, observing this law and custom, he did not, distracted and puffed up by pride, tear apart the fabric of angelic unity.

[Col. 0916B] But when, in subject humility, he refused to be conformed to God and instead presumptuously sought to be like God by transgression, he lost likeness and the seal of likeness—not into non-being, but into ill-being. Yet, just as God retained for himself the truth of being and of subsisting in the highest blessedness forever, which no one can snatch from his hand, so he granted to the abiding angels likeness and the seal of likeness according to his good pleasure. But because those things enacted in heaven, set apart by so many barriers, are closed and sealed to those who dwell on earth, God, out of inexhaustible compassion for his image exiled for its committed fault, chose through certain chinks of the eternal counsel to report again, by angelic ministry, what occurred in the angelic choir. At last, the human being began to burn with longing to return home; [Col. 0916C] rubbed by those fragrant exaltations sent through good angels, he opened his mouth and drew in the spirit, by whose revelation he learned to imitate, in the order of life, the pursuits and courses of angels. He heard: “Your God is one God; thousands upon thousands minister to him, and ten times a hundred thousand stand before him.” He heard of seraphim, cherubim, thrones, dominions, principalities, powers, virtues, archangels, and angels; and by their example learned hidden wisdom.

According to this pattern, therefore, he wished to fashion for himself a new heaven on earth with its orders and offices, establishing at the highest summit, as it were God, that supreme pontiff whom he calls pope or apostolic. Then, in a subordinate order descending from this head, he comes down through patriarchs, metropolitans, archbishops, bishops, priests, deacons, subdeacons, acolytes, readers, candle-bearers, doorkeepers, and clerics. Their offices and names have been richly infused with the balm of divine gift, and they imitate the heavenly ministers. But it may briefly be summed up: the lord pope is the vicar of Christ, and so is the bishop together with the rest named above. [Col. 0916D]

Therefore it is said to him: “You are the seal of the likeness of God,” etc. In the bishop’s face the form of the glory of the vision of God ought to shine forth, so that, just as the image of the person whose seal it is is engraved by a signet or seal in soft wax, so whoever seeks a rule for good conduct may receive from the bishop an example of life. Let the patience of Jesus, humility, poverty, chastity, charity, together with his other virtues, be not merely written superficially but engraved to the marrow upon this seal, so that it may truly be said to him: “You are the seal of the likeness of God.” In what respect? “Full of wisdom, perfect in beauty.” Behold the bishop’s teaching; behold his life. Wisdom belongs to teaching, beauty to life. Let him be full of wisdom, lest he be a blind man leading a blind man; perfect in beauty, lest in judging another he condemn himself. Full of wisdom, that he may have the rational breastpiece; perfect in beauty, that he may have the ephod.

This is the double spirit which Elisha asks for: “I pray,” he says, “that your double spirit may be in me” (IV Kings II, 9). I do not wish my whole fountain to be poured out [Col. 0917B] into the streets; rather, I wish to divide the little meal of preaching so as to make from it loaves for myself and for my son—for myself by living well and for the flock entrusted to me by preaching well. Reading belongs to wisdom, prayer to beauty: these are the wings of the dove by which, through the clouds after the ascending Christ, the bishop full of wisdom and perfect in beauty ascends to the right hand of the Father. For this is what follows: “You were in the delights of paradise.” When the bishop rises from reading or from prayer, what else should be said to him except: “You have been in the delights of paradise”? Paradise is divine Scripture; what is prayer? Heaven. What has God withheld from his delights? For with an ungrudging hand he has scattered all his delights abroad, in both the Old and the New Testament. But the person who loves only fleshly delights neither knows, possesses, nor loves these; whereas he who desires the episcopate desires a good work—that is, prayer and reading—so that he may be full of wisdom and perfect in beauty. [Col. 0917C]

## SERMON XCII. FRAGMENT OF A SERMON ON THE SAME SUBJECT.

“What will you see in the Shulammite but choirs of camps?” (Cant. VII, 1.)

> [Note: These passages are already printed above, col. 907, near the end of Sermon 88.]

The choirs of camps are the orders of angels; hence their king is called the Lord Sabaoth, that is, “of hosts.” Thus also in the Apocalypse of John we read that war arose in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon; that great dragon was cast down, and his place was no longer [Col. 0917D] found in heaven. As many as are the orders among the angels, so many are the choirs—nine, indeed. But those wars with the race of darkness are unknown to us, though not useless; for they fight with us and for us. Yet when our Lord Jesus, the coming King of the Jews, chose new wars, receiving the first and fiercest assaults of Satan in the days of his flesh, it was in order that he might triumph over the powers of the air and him who held the dominion of death in his body upon the wood of the cross, and bind him.

He also says, that mighty man in battle, Gideon, said to his followers: “What you see me do, do” (Judg. 7:17); whence in the Gospel: “Whoever does not carry his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple” [Col. 0918A] (Luke 14:27). After him follow the choirs of the camps, bearing the weapons of warfare which Paul, the most valiant prince in the choir of martyrs, describes when he says: “Put on the armour of God, that you may be able to stand in the evil day,” etc. (Eph. 6:11).

Therefore the martyrs follow him on red, dappled, and white horses, as is read in Zechariah. Those who did not love their lives unto death follow the Lamb on red horses, their blood poured out through a thousand struggles even to the horses’ bridles. The confessors are on white horses, mortifying their flesh with its vices and desires. Virgins—some of whom served God in virginity, while others bravely endured martyrdom—followed their King on dappled horses. Behold the choirs of camps in the crimson Shulamite, to whom it is said: [Col. 0918B] “Your cheeks are like those of a turtledove” (Cant. 1:9); or in the captive Shulamite, while this pilgrimage is a time of war and not the time of peace which shall be in the glory to come. There will be choirs there, not of camps but of singers; for, “The dwelling of all who rejoice, O glorious city, is in you.”

O priests, God has made you princes in these camps: sound the trumpet in Zion, rouse Leviathan, run from gate to gate, lest thief, robber, or adversary enter and set ablaze the camp entrusted to you; lest the devil, like a lion, snatch away the souls committed to you. To you, shepherd of sheep; to you, bishop, it is said: “What will you see in your Shulamite—that is, in the Church committed to you—except choirs of camps?” etc.

## SERMON XCIII

[Col. 0918C] “Let your garments be white at all times” (Eccl. 9:8).

In the Apocalypse a woman appears clothed with the sun; an angel clothed with a pure stone; and one clothed to the feet amid the seven golden lampstands. The Lord Jesus, at the Transfiguration, had garments white as snow; and at the Resurrection an angel appeared clad in a white robe. The queen stands at the king’s right hand in a garment embroidered with gold; and the bride in the Song of Songs is “like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon” (Cant. 1:4). Jacob made for his son Joseph a long tunic. The woman who possesses wool and linen, and has worked with the counsel of her hands, made fine linen and gave a girdle to the Canaanite. Fine linen and [Col. 0918D] purple are clothing. David says in the Psalm: “You tore my sackcloth and girded me with joy” (Ps. 29:12). Jeremiah took from his loins the loincloth which rotted in water. Isaiah is told: “Loose the sackcloth from your loins” (Isa. 20:2). And in Job: “The Lord loosens the belt of kings and girds their loins with a cord” (Job 12:18). The garments and sandals of the children of Israel did not wear out in the wilderness for forty years. Concerning the Hebrew servant it is commanded that he shall leave in the same kind of clothing in which he entered. The high priest, when approaching the holy things, uses eight most precious pontifical vestments. And he who entered the wedding feast without a wedding garment was bound hand and foot and cast into outer darkness.

[Col. 0919A] Therefore, whoever you are who approach the Lord’s table, whoever minister in holy things, whoever say to God, “Before the angels I will sing psalms to you” (Ps. 137:1), whoever serve in the camp of God: attend to your weapons; attend to your garments. Let not your weapons be blunted, nor your garments torn and worn out; rather, let your weapons be polished and two-edged, and your garments new—or at least mended and renewed. For they are mended by confession and renewed by repentance. Weapons are polished by reading and sharpened by disputation.

“Let your garments be white at all times.” An unclean life and a defiled conscience cannot endure divine or angelic sight. Disordered itching of the flesh makes coverings for itself, saying: “I heard your voice, Lord, and hid myself because I am naked” (Gen. 3:10). A great chasm [Col. 0919B] has been fixed between the nakedness of an infant and the nakedness of a shameless harlot: the one is utterly pure, the other utterly foul.

So long as Adam was clothed in the robe of innocence, he was not ashamed of his nakedness. But when innocence was corrupted, the goad of sin immediately invaded him, and wicked passion seized his shameful members. He was ashamed to have lost mastery over his own members, since he had been disobedient to the commands of his Lord. Thus he guarded his garments badly—not bodily but spiritual garments. He wished to hide himself, but could by no means remain hidden. For the divine eye is exceedingly penetrating, sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, etc.

O watchman standing above, [Col. 0919C] is it better for me to flee or to stand before you? Yet I cannot flee; but how shall I dare to stand naked, rotten, foul-smelling, and defiled? With your drawn bow you strike the naked man; with open mouth you spit upon the rotten one; you cast the foul-smelling one outside the camp; you throw the defiled one into the lions’ pit. Therefore the naked must be clothed. Thus Scripture says: “When you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh” (Isa. 58:7). Do not despise your flesh as though it were to return to ashes and dust and not rise again on the day of judgment. Do not despise it by defiling it with the unclean pollution of demons and with accursed luxury. Do not despise it, for it shall at last rise again and be conformed to the glorified body of Jesus.

Cover the naked person with the harshness of haircloth; with the gentleness of curtains; [Col. 0919D] with the mortification signified by red skins; with the contemplation signified by blue skins; with the fine-linen robe of chastity. Therefore let your garments be white at all times: at all times—in summer, winter, autumn, and spring; at all times, by day and by night. What is “by day and by night”? That is, in light and darkness. What are light and darkness? “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night”: the sun is the heat of lust; the moon, the lukewarmness of faithlessness. By day there is consent to pleasure; by night, blind ignorance of what ought to be done or avoided. Therefore, by day let not the sun burn you, so that you consent to the desires of the flesh; nor the moon by night, so that through ignorance or negligence you sin in grave offences. “At all times,” that is, in summer, let your garments be white, lest you be hot; in winter, lest you be [Col. 0920A] cold; in autumn, lest you be lukewarm; in spring, lest you be eager for novelty.

The sun discolours, as is said in the Song of Songs: “Do not look upon me because I am dark, because the sun has discoloured me” (Cant. 1:6). The sun discolours one who presumes upon his own righteousness, because he who thinks himself to be something when he is nothing deceives himself. Righteousness which is from God gives good colour; human righteousness, regarded as coming from man himself, discolours the face because it has no grace before God, etc.

## SERMON XCIV. TO MONKS

“These are the camps of God” (Gen. 32:2).

Neither unarmed, nor idle, nor weak, nor snoring, nor fearful men are to be admitted into the camps. They must therefore be armed against enemies; zealous to fight skilfully against crafty foes; strong and fierce against Sabaeans and Giants; watchful against nocturnal thieves and plunderers; vigilant against presumptuous and proud men who are bold. By such men the walls of Jerusalem are rebuilt; by them that great ruin is restored which the red dragon made in heaven, drawing after him a third part of the stars; by them, finally, the promised land is cleansed of most unclean nations.

Therefore let there be nothing in these camps of God that is disordered after the image of hell, where there is no order; nothing confused after the remnants of Babylon, where the speech of those building the tower was confounded; nothing luxurious from the seed of Behemoth, whose strength is in his loins and whose force is in the navel of his belly; nothing lax, as among the people who had neither prince, king, [Col. 0920C] nor priest, but each did what was good in his own eyes; nor anything superfluous by which temperance, the mother of virtues, may be disturbed. Let the battle-line therefore be ordered, like ranks of soldiers arrayed. Let the choir, with shields of gold flashing in the sun, be prepared to withstand the devil and his attendants; whence in the Song of Songs: “What will you see in the Shulamite except choirs of camps?” (Cant. 7:1).

This camp—indeed, this little fortress—to which Jesus came meekly upon an ass, that the meek might hear him and rejoice, has the tower of David, upon which hang a thousand shields, all the armour of the mighty: the examples of martyrs and the sayings of confessors—indeed, together, the life and teaching of all good persons. For a brave man, and especially one among the thirty mighty princes of David, it is not enough to defend himself unless he can also burden the enemy. He will indeed receive his pay if, by serving well, he retains his place, according to the saying: “If the spirit of one in authority rises against you, do not leave your place” (Eccl. 10:4). If he takes a prize and reduces it to captivity, he will no less receive the little golden crown if he conquers, just as Christ in his body upon the wood of the cross triumphed over him who possessed the power of death, together with death itself.

Therefore gird yourselves, sons, and be ready for battle, for it is better for us to die bodily in this war than to see the evils of our people and of the holy things. As the will is in heaven, so let it be done. Let our soldiers be armed with the armour of God, according to the Apostle: [Col. 0921A] “Put on,” he says, “the armour of God, that you may be able to resist in the evil day,” etc. (Eph. 6:13). Finally, let centurions, tribunes, and each of the princes exhort their companies to battle, teach them, and help them. Let us therefore number and name the princes, and determine which company each ought to provide for and govern in these camps.

The first company, or choir, or battle-line, is that of converts; the second, of the weak; the third, of novices not yet professed; the fourth, of those already professed; the fifth, of officials; the sixth, of cloistered monks; the seventh, of abbots. To these are assigned the seven Spirits of God, which Isaiah enumerates: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge and piety, and fear of the Lord (Isa. 11:2). Of these, the Spirit of fear of the Lord is prince of the converts; the Spirit of piety, of the weak; the Spirit of knowledge, of novices during their probation; the Spirit of fortitude, in profession; the Spirit of counsel, of officials; the Spirit of understanding, of cloistered monks; and the Spirit of wisdom, of abbots.

Then converts ought to say with the converted apostle Paul: “Lord, what do you want me to do?” (Acts 9:6). For he said this in astonishment and trembling. Such men sit at the mill, bringing back food for Jacob and his sons from Egypt when, from their labour, they provide bodily things to spiritual men. And, like Issachar, a strong ass, they bend their shoulder to carry the needs of those who remain to guard David’s baggage, [Col. 0921C] namely the works of God’s incarnation. For the entire life of Jesus in the world, together with his mortal flesh itself, was in some fashion a burden of the Word—indeed, of the assumed man. Whatever he found, saw, heard, and endured in the world was a burden. Guard these excellent burdens, my brothers, because the share of those who go forth to battle, that is, of the martyrs, is equal to that of those who remain by the baggage, that is, of all the elect who bear Christ’s sufferings in themselves.

Turning through the choirs, let us now come to the Spirit of piety, whom God, the source of all consolation, has set over your sick, so that, with his aid, the rock may pour out in infirmaries streams of oil, butter, and honey for the work of the sick, lest sweet consolation be lacking: butter, lest suitable refreshment be lacking; oil, lest lamps fail at night; for consolation is understood in honey, refreshment in butter, and night-light in oil. Even if you make yourself a rock, abbot, by maintaining an austere life, nevertheless pour out streams of oil, butter, and honey for your sick man. Unless you do this, the Spirit of piety accuses you, and you will not find God merciful when you come before him. Hezekiah the righteous was once ill in the infirmary, and Lazarus the sinner was sick. What did Isaiah the prophet do, what did Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit? Isaiah visited the sick man; the Lord goes and raises one already stinking. Let worm and dust not recoil from a stinking brother, because the Lord raises the poor from the dust and lifts him from the dunghill.

Let us now come to the novices who keep watch at the gates of knowledge. These, under the hand and protection of the [Col. 0922A] Spirit of knowledge, are placed by God’s ordinance as persons leaving the fantasies and darkness of this world, opening their eyes with the man born blind but illumined by God, at the dawning of the rising morning light, and seeking the light of knowledge. Thus they say to God in the person of the Prophet: “Teach me to do your will, because you are my God” (Ps. 142:10). Likewise with blessed Augustine: “Grant that I may know myself, know you”: myself, namely, as weak; you as physician; myself—what I am by origin, condition, corruption, and also redemption; you, one and three, almighty, wise, and kind. Likewise with the Prophet: “Teach me goodness and discipline and knowledge” (Ps. 118:6): goodness, lest I recoil from novelty; discipline, lest I run to excess through laxity; knowledge, lest through ignorance and error I wander after the flocks of my companions; goodness, lest malice remain; discipline, lest vain buffoonery remain; knowledge, lest incompetence remain. At the beginning of their way, novices are thus armed with the shield of such knowledge against the devil’s wiles.

While these fight bravely and happily, let us visit the fourth choir, that of the professed. Following the pattern of Joshua, who commanded the sun to stand still and doubled the day while fighting in the battle-line, let us carry the same novices from the first day of war on to the second day of profession. There, their habit and weapons changed, they pass to the Spirit of fortitude. For it is little to know good things unless you also add doing them. Hence the Lord says: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them” (John 13:17). Therefore they set their hand to mighty things, binding themselves by a threefold—indeed fourfold—bond: namely, by word, consent, writing, and oath. All these are observed in profession, when one says: “I promise my stability and conversion of my manners and obedience,” etc. For stability imitates eternity; conversion of manners, the confirmation of angels; obedience, the perfection of the Lord Jesus. What is stronger than this threefold cord? Good brother, unless you break your profession, confidently await eternity, the fellowship of angels, and the inheritance of Jesus.

Let us now approach the fifth prince of military warfare, the Spirit of counsel. Fortitude is of little value in war unless it is governed by counsel. Therefore the Spirit of counsel has the Spirit [Col. 0922D] of fortitude as neighbour to his house. He exercises his principate over the officials of works—not Pharaoh’s works, but Solomon’s; not works in mud and brick, but in the timber of Lebanon and marble stone. These are our obedientiaries, who ought to do everything according to the will and counsel of the abbot. Solomon says: “Do everything with counsel, and after it is done you will not repent” (Ecclus. 32:24). Their office is to keep the watches of the night over things that must be done; to guard what has already been prepared; to work upon the walls of Jerusalem with sword girded upon thigh; and, like sackcloth coverings, to cover the precious things of God’s sanctuary. Concerning the daily questions that arise, they must also consult the divine oracle and seek an answer from the law and the testimonies. Like Ezra the prophet, [Col. 0923A] by their counsel, aid, and action they must repel those who hinder the divine work.

Let us now turn the pen to the sixth choir in the Shulamite, which sits with Mary Magdalene at Jesus’ feet, or stands with the mother of that same Jesus beside his cross, looking upon her Saviour set forth upon the cross. Thus the sword or lance from the side of him who hangs there passes through her soul, even to the division of soul and spirit. These are our cloistered monks, who devote themselves night and day to divine praises and are ready to rouse Leviathan. They never leave the camps or cloisters—that is, the holy places. For our camps are cloisters, where chastity and enclosure ought to be perpetual, so that there may be “a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed, a well of living waters” flowing [Col. 0923B] with force from Lebanon. Like shining cherubim, full of knowledge, and burning seraphim, full of love, they immediately surround both sides of that great warrior who is strong and mighty in battle. They truly say with Peter: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matt. 26:35); likewise with Paul: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” etc. (Rom. 8:35); likewise with the Psalmist: “As the eyes of servants are in the hands of their masters, as the eyes of a maidservant are in the hand of her mistress,” etc. (Ps. 122:3). Servants, indeed, are in the field, maidservants in the chamber, so that, according to the Apostle, whether absent or present, they strive to please God. What is meant concerning the will of the Lord, whom they serve in simplicity and not for appearances, since the Lord is faithful to all who call upon him [Col. 0923C] in truth, is not understood [reading uncertain].

They therefore have as their prince the Spirit of understanding, who searches the depths of God and reveals them to his little ones; for he intercedes for us with unutterable groanings. These are refreshed daily at the Lord’s table with the bread of angels; these, mighty men among the mightiest of Israel, surround Solomon’s bed, all holding swords and thoroughly trained for war. In this sixth choir the Lord made man, as the horn of the battle-line, in his image and likeness, so that the conversation of cloistered monks may always be in heaven and may never descend from the rigour of religion except for the reason of compassion; for this inclined Jesus from the bosom of the Father down to us.

The highest and final battle-line contains abbots, that is, the vicars of Christ. They have above them as king and prince [Col. 0923D] the Spirit of wisdom, who proceeded from the mouth of the Most High. Rising in the morning and approaching the throne of grace, which is the altar, the abbot ought thus to offer prayers to God: “Give me, Lord, wisdom, the companion of your throne, that she may be with me and labour with me, so that I may know what is pleasing before you at all times” (Wis. 9:4). Then he ought to swallow this saliva drawn from the mouth of God and pour it out through the vessels of converts, the weak, novices, probationers, the professed, officials, and cloistered monks, so that the dew which descends from Hermon upon Mount Zion may flow from the head down to the hem of his garment. For it is the salt of the earth, the salt of the covenant, with which the sacrifices offered to God are seasoned.

Therefore [Col. 0924A] he ought to season, according to each one’s proper measure and capacity, the simplicity of converts, the weakness of the sick, the newness of novices, the advancement of the professed, the care of officials, and the solitude of cloistered monks. According to Job, when the days of feasting make their circuit, he must summon and sanctify his sons, lest perhaps they have blessed God in their hearts. For there is the vice of negligence, against which converts fight; the evil of impatience, against which the sick contend; the sin of former pleasure and former impurity, which novices resist; the vice of distrust, against which the professed rise; the evil of avarice, which officials oppose; weariness of religion, against which cloistered monks rebel; and the storm of worldly care, [Col. 0924B] against which abbots stand firm. Behold, these are the camps of God, in which the life of man upon earth is warfare; in which the kingdom of heaven suffers violence and the violent seize it; in which, “To him who conquers,” says the Lord, “I will make him a pillar in the house of my Father” (Apoc. 3:12). May he deign to grant this to us, he who with the Father, etc.

## SERMON XCV. ON THE NATURAL, WRITTEN, AND EVANGELICAL LAW

“Moses commanded us a law and an inheritance for the multitude” (Deut. 33:4).

As many transgressions as have been committed by man, so many restorations have been granted by God. For just as no disease escapes the heavenly physician, so everything pertaining to remedy and health lies under his knowledge and power. Medicine follows disease close upon its tracks and does not rest until it has enclosed it. Hence the Apostle says: “God enclosed all things under sin” (Gal. 3:22). Human nature, therefore, had to be recalled to the beginnings of its happiness. It had to be warned to turn back from the path by which it had departed and to beware of renewing its plunges into precipices, since the last error would be worse than the former.

Thus from its very cradle divine mercy attended to that same nature with maternal concern: it warned it beforehand lest it fall, and prepared a remedy if it did fall. It fixed in nature’s own inward parts the law which we call natural, so that it might be nourished with the same milk as nature, grow with the same growth, and likewise decline with its defects. Then, after the first [Col. 0924D] sin had transgressed this law—where there is no law, neither is there a transgressor—lest it perhaps be entirely extinguished, God supplied another law in aid, called Moses’ law because the law was made through him. It brought forth from the natural womb many legal observances like multiple offspring, so that what lay hidden in natural right might emerge into the light upon written tablets, and henceforth no one could be excused by the privilege of ignorance, since, looking upon unworked stones, he could learn the commandments of morals and honourable living. Concerning this, therefore, it is said: “Moses commanded us a law,” etc.

But because it is written, “Man sees the face, but God sees the heart” (1 Sam. 16:7), the whole observance of this law constrained the hand rather than the mind, reserving a place for God, who, incarnate afterwards, reaches both mind and hand. Therefore the evangelical law was given by Christ at the last, in order that he might fulfil both the natural and written law, as he himself says: “I came not to destroy the law, but to fulfil it” (Matt. 5:17). This law was given when it was said: “A new commandment I give you, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John 13:34).

Of the law of Moses and Christ it is said in the Apocalypse: “I saw angels standing upon a sea of glass, holding the harps of God and singing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb” (Apoc. 15:2). The song of Moses is the law, or praise of God, concerning the creation of the world; the song of the Lamb is the Gospel, or praise of God in the Gospel concerning the redemption of the world. But where is one who has kept the whole law, whether natural, Mosaic, [Col. 0925B] or Christ’s? According to the Psalmist, such a person is not found on earth. For he says: “I have judged all the sinners of the earth transgressors” (Ps. 118:19). There is no one who is not a transgressor, whether at least in himself or in the first parent. For where there is sin, there is transgression; but where there is no law, neither is there transgression.

Natural law is, as it were, a universal regimen; the law of Moses is, as it were, hellebore; the law of the Gospel is, as it were, medicine having neither bitterness nor sharpness. It is enough for one who has not abandoned natural law to use lawful things and abstain from unlawful things. But one who has sinned grievously or criminally ought both to abstain from lawful things and, in his cleansing, receive the purgative of most severe penance from the law of Moses, so that he may render eye for eye, tooth for tooth, bruise for [Col. 0925C] bruise; for calumniators demand a punishment proportionate to the offence. But one who through perfect love has cast fear outside ought, as Christ himself walked, to walk likewise, repelling every vice and gathering every virtue.

Thus Peter’s keys bind and thus loose. They do not accept persons; they do not judge for gifts; they do not give life to souls that die, nor kill souls that do not die. Rather, in a just balance they rightly weigh both the merit of the case and the end of the sentence.

Hear that he deserves to lose Peter’s privilege who abuses the authority granted him. In judgment one must incline neither to right nor left because of anyone’s favour. Truth needs no recommendation. Yet, clothed for human eyes in a moderated brightness, intolerable beauty sometimes offers itself, not so that it may appear more splendid with aids taken from outside, but so that it may admit the vision of the beholder. Therefore authorities must be brought forward in what we say; perhaps examples are also required, so that what is said may be more credible. Nor is authority sought unreasonably where neither the person speaking nor the matter spoken satisfies faith.

Divine authorities support our propositions. The first of them is: “Unless you are converted and become like little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:3). Turning away expelled us from paradise; conversion restores us. That turning away is the mother of guilt and punishment, which have poured innumerable streams from themselves through the whole world, and whose torrents have troubled the whole nature of Adam’s children.

Therefore let the first word of those who weep, *aversio* (“turning away”), be removed, so that there may be no turning away; and let that which is the first syllable in consolation, *conversio* (“conversion”), be put in its place, so that paradise may receive the converted person whom it had expelled as one turned away. But how, he says, “like little children”? A little child, like soft wax, is suited to every obedience; he does not resist in anything or inquire into the reason for a command. The serpent, craftier than all animals, raised a question for the woman concerning God’s commands. Because she listened to a sophist, God excluded and shut her out. Abraham’s faith, which was reckoned to him as righteousness, set aside reason, custom, affection, and impossibility; acquiescing in God, contrary to hope and already possessing the promise, it believed in hope with most certain expectation, knowing fully that God is truthful in promises and powerful in fulfilment, able to do whatever he has promised. This model is set before those who wish to enter the kingdom of heaven.

There is also another authority of the law: “You shall exchange the firstborn of an ass for a sheep” (Exod. 13:13). As Gregory says, to exchange the firstborn of an ass for a sheep is to convert the beginnings of an unclean life into innocence of life. For whoever ceases to be what he formerly was, and, having laid hold of purity of flesh, keeps innocence, exchanges the firstborn of an ass for a sheep as an offering to God.

Job too, by a most apt comparison, indicates that cloistered confinement is most salutary, so that there a person may pay for the sins which worldly vanity had contracted through pride, luxury, [Col. 0926C] rapacity, and service to belly and gluttony. “Because of pride,” he says, “you will take me like a lioness” (Job 10:16). The lioness is our flesh. It nourishes lion cubs, the enticements of carnal desires. If anyone captures one of them by denying unlawful things, it shakes the whole forest of the body in the fiercest rage and vents itself with the claws and teeth of murmuring against those present and absent. This flesh, as Gregory says, is restrained by a double pit: the first because of gluttony, the second as punishment; the first of the world, the second of the cloister; the first of desire, the second of the scourge. It would not come to the second unless it sought the first. For one who does not sin has no reason to repent.

“But sin,” says the Apostle, “that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through the commandment,” that is, through transgression of the commandment (Rom. 7:13). This is death in the pot—namely, in the cloister—which the inexperienced flee as death. Of those who have experienced it, some patiently endure it with Jesus as a cross; others abhor it as Gehenna. Paul glories, saying: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6:14). Another cries out: “Bring my soul out of prison” (Ps. 141:8). “Two women shall be grinding: one shall be taken and the other left.” Hence the grieving prophet says: “Consolation is hidden from my eyes because he himself will divide between brothers” (Hos. 13:15)—namely Esau and Jacob, etc.

# THE SHORTER WORKS OF PETER OF CELLES

[Col. 0927]

## THE LETTER OF PETER OF CELLES, ABBOT, TO MASTER JOHN OF SALISBURY, CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING WORK, BEGINS

PETER, abbot, greetings to his dearest friend.

Because the height is great, steep in ascent, and dark to behold, I turned back with measured steps to the flatness of the plain. From the Lord’s harvest I gathered such sheaves as I could, and composed new loaves, though not from new flour of meanings. For I have always judged that novelty which strays from the footsteps of the Fathers—in faith, morals, and even novel expressions or names—to be anathematized. But if I have been able, through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, to apprehend something seemingly new, provided that it looks upon the cherubim and the mercy-seat with a gaze as diligent as it is humble, I have not rejected it.

Therefore I wrote this book, *On the Loaves of Holy Scripture*, not in order to make myself a great name, after the manner of those great men who glory in secular philosophy; rather, from the table of the rich man I joined together scraps of bread gathered from every quarter, by which the minds of travellers might be refreshed through divine readings. For unless travellers find bread and wine during their passage to assist the completion of their journey, they are compelled to suffer the loss either of delay or of hunger. Therefore the welfare of the commonwealth quite reasonably requires that, within the household of the householder, work in the house of one at rest should serve the needs of one labouring in public affairs. For the commonwealth is well governed when the services of one support another.

Would that I were worthy enough for my labours to deserve acceptance, and that the poor might be comforted from the fleeces of my sheep! Would that, if I cannot compose new things, I might at least mend old ones! Would that, if not from my own resources, then at least faithfully from another’s, I might prepare fitting expenses for Solomon to build the temple! Who, then, except a presumptuous man, would call me presumptuous because I have carried loaves from the chest to the table? If the chest is the Lord’s, and the table is the Lord’s, and the guest too is the Lord’s, why is the Lord’s servant reproved for his due services?

Eat then, whoever reads this book, the loaves set before you; and do not gnaw at the very laborious sweats of the one who sets them forth. Rather, gratitude than envy is due for a service rendered. If, through poverty of books or readings, you need daily bread, take it, and give thanks for gifts granted without price. But if you abound, rejoice with the poor who do not have it; otherwise, in one respect you are proud of your own poverty, and in another you envy our compassion. In the one case you are wicked toward yourself; in the other, toward your neighbour; in the one, pitiable; in the other, condemnable.

But do you fear for yourself or for me? Perhaps you fear for yourself, lest your own writings, if you have any, not seem unique; or for me, lest my talent appear scabrous and my eloquence be published bloodless. But neither, O faithful and most dear friend, is to be feared. First, if your writing is good, there is no need for fear, for what is good and precious is never made cheap by the number and abundance of ragged wares. On the contrary, people always run to what shines more brightly, and neglect what is contemptible. Therefore do not suppose that your work is diminished by comparison with our little work, if it is good. But if it is useless, do not seek for it glory from being singular; it ought rather to be cut away as superfluous.

Nor need you fear for us. I do not wish insolently to thrust my writings upon fastidious people to increase their nausea; but I am afraid to hide or deny them to those who ask and need them. For just as it is shamelessness to force oneself upon those who do not wish or who refuse, so it is impiety to deny oneself to those who wish and need. Let the willing reader, therefore, have in one repository an abundance of every kind of loaf prepared; and let him rather help our insufficiency with goodwill than embitter our weakness with ingratitude.

In this little work I have neither raised my little vessel to the most impetuous currents of profound disputations, nor carelessly allowed it to sit upon the land of the letter that kills. With moderate sailing, however, I drew the present style a little away from land, lest, if I presumed on higher things and contrary winds perhaps blew, I should either contend with them by resisting or succumb to them by failing to answer. Again I withdrew a little from land, lest, labouring through the nearness of the banks and lack of water, I should offend through the cheapness of my speech or the rusticity of my material and be unable to swim freely.

Having therefore weighed the proper conditions of sail, vessel, and winds, I have gone beyond neither the level plain through despairing humility nor the deep through hateful presumption. To you, then, my dearest friend, I send this one little work of ours, so that by your permission it may, as is fitting, enter into privacy and come forth into public. I ask you to set your hand to it: approving what is useful, cutting away what is superfluous, supplying what is insufficiently full, making clearer what is insufficiently plain, clothing what is unseemly, stripping off what is overburdened.

I call God to witness that you would equally offend our friendship if you praised what is unworthy or censured what is worthy; for I shall endure a corrector of error more patiently than an unscrupulous flatterer. [Col. 0929] Therefore, because of the love between us, do not shrink, if it is just, from deleting either a part or even the whole discourse and sending it back to be treated differently. For I seek fruit in the fig tree, not leaves alone. Far be it that the trees of our cultivation should provide only shade and not food [variant: *parent*, “bring forth”]. Both please me: both to possess and to prepare the shade of leaves and the food of fruits. But if I am compelled to lack one of them, I shall more patiently renounce leaves than fruits. Farewell.

[Col. 0929]

# BOOK ON LOAVES

## CHAPTER ONE. On the manifold table and its furnishings.

In the tabernacle of testimony, at the Lord’s command, the table is placed [Col. 0929A] before the veil, and opposite the table the lampstand stands on the south side of the tabernacle; for the table itself stands on the north side (Exod. XXVI). It should be carefully observed that Moses—or rather, the Lord through Moses—has, in the mystical foreshadowing of the construction and arrangement of the figurative tabernacle, included both the observances by which those driven out of paradise may be restored or brought back to their homeland, to the Holy of Holies, and the foods by which they may meanwhile be consoled while wandering outside. For within the veil no food is needed, because there is never any want there: there is one satiety where the unchangeableness of everlasting glory abides. To have entered once and tasted at the same time is to remain satisfied forever. “I shall be satisfied,” says the Psalmist, “when your glory appears” (Ps. XVI [17]:15). But outside the veil there are both failing [Col. 0929B] and refreshment: failing because of sins and in sins, which miserably corrupt nature; refreshment because of the commandments and divine benefits which mercifully aid us.

Just as God set the firmament to divide the waters from the waters, so Moses placed the veil between them: outside it the people sacrificed the flesh of animals, while inside it the high priest alone—that is, the chief priest—burned incense. But Jesus penetrated heaven and ascended above the firmament. He entered in blood, because through his Passion he presented to the Father’s lips—while angelic spirits stood by—the drink, indeed the price, of our redemption, accomplishing the work which the Father gave him to do, and offering him the blood poured from his side for abundant redemption. [Col. 0929C] Finally, for the hungry, starving outside the veil, the merciful and compassionate Lord left a table and loaves upon the table—of which, after eating with them, he ascended into heaven—and “gave food to those who fear him” (Ps. CX [111]:5). Likewise, he set aside a portion of his blood for his friends and imitators to drink from sacramental cups until the end of the age; and the other portion, as the price of our liberation, he piously and justly paid both to the Father and to the enemy-creditor. For his body, which is the Church, keeping watch outside the veil until the day-star rises, he prepared a table lest it fail upon the way, and a lampstand lest it stray from the way.

But it must be noted that there is one table at which the Trinity alone delights in a singular manner; another at which it feasts amicably with angels; another at which Jesus visibly eats with mortal humanity; and another at which the faithful are sacramentally and invisibly refreshed. There is [Col. 0930A] also the devil’s table, at which nothing but the blood of souls is drunk, and nothing but human torments is consumed as food. There is likewise the table of an angel, who drinks the repentance of converts and eats salvation. There is the table of a human being, to which he sometimes invites God, sometimes a good angel, sometimes an evil angel.

Accordingly, as concisely as I can, I shall set forth a brief treatment of this abundant and profound subject, so that the wise person, taking occasion from it, may enlarge his phylacteries and make his fringes great, while the person of moderate understanding may comfort the miseries of his hunger. That table of the Trinity is one cubit in the unity of substance; it has hidden loaves, wine ever new, and everlasting, blessed dishes. The service of any other creature is not admitted, neither cherubim nor seraphim, to that table [Col. 0930B] “of which even those who serve the tabernacle have no authority to eat.” They minister to one another: the Father to the Son, the Son to the Father, the Holy Spirit to the Father and Son, and the Father and Son to the Holy Spirit; the Father gives the Son generation; the Son gives the Father birth; the Holy Spirit gives the Father and Son procession; and the Father and Son give the Holy Spirit mission or gift.

Let every creature stand far off from this ministration, for “the beast that touches the mountain shall be stoned” (Heb. XII:20). Let the seraph withdraw his hand, because such an office admits no hand other than God’s right hand alone: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son” (Matt. XI:27). The viands—indeed, the dishes—of this table are as many [Col. 0930C] as those who sit at it; they are such as those are whose table it is. Yet do not imagine that one sits above like a master of the feast in a higher place, another below, and another last; for there is one seat and one who sits, on account of concord of will, identity of substance, and equality of power; yet there are three on account of the distinction of persons. If you cannot at all grasp how the three sit thus, without distinction of rank and without variation of honor, without extension or measurement of place, do not be surprised; for not even the summit of Carmel—that is, an angel’s knowledge—comprehends this: “No one has ever seen God” (John I:15). Therefore it refrains and puts its finger upon its mouth, neither laying its hand upon the table nor opening its mouth [Col. 0931A] toward the denied divinity, wishing to swallow it. For it saw Lucifer, one sharing its own nature, once stretch out the throat of desire toward this table and taste from it not divinity but death. It saw him stretch out his hand toward the sides of the north, and immediately grow stiff with northern ice or wither in infernal flames. Perhaps that savage beast wished to devour the Father’s omnipotence, the Son’s wisdom, or the Holy Spirit’s goodness. For these are the dishes of God’s table, due to the King of the ages alone, immortal and invisible, forever and ever.

This is said concerning God’s table, in which no one alien by nature, condition, or lot has a share, but the Trinity alone gloriously partakes, singularly, eternally, and invisibly. Now let us bend the sight—or rather the pen—of Jacob’s ladder, [Col. 0931B] and from ourselves ascend to the table of angels, while from God we descend; for the two lower tables are higher than we are. Their table is the mercy-seat, upon which they always gaze with faces turned toward it and from which they long to fulfill their desires. For of this mercy-seat—that is, Jesus, or the table of angels—it is said: “into which angels desire to look” (1 Pet. I:12). At this table—compacted from two natures into one person by the workmanship of the Holy Spirit—stand ministering spirits, serving the Lord and eating with him what is set there: namely, God’s goodness, the restoration of the human race, and the replenishment of their number diminished by the apostasy of the degenerate branch from the good olive into the nature of the wild olive. From that table they are told: “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams” [Col. 0931C] (Ps. XXVIII [29]:1); that is, you angels, bring the souls of Christians to the Lord, their Creator and Redeemer, for heavenly fellowship. God has placed his benefits upon this table; the angel, his services: God, that he created the angel good; the angel, that he stood in truth and goodness and cleaved to God; God, that he added the grace of a second gift to the grace of the first; the angel, that he turned free choice to the good of obedience and reverence for his Creator. God brings forth the rays of his contemplation; the angel returns pure glances at the encounter with the dawning light. The angel opens his mouth in praise of God; God fills it, both with the rich nourishment of divinity and with the flesh and blood of the wholly sound human nature.

[Col. 0931D] This is concerning God’s table with angels. Let us now go “outside the camp” (Heb. XIII:13) of heaven and, beside the foot of the mountain—that is, the Passion of the cross—contemplate the supper of the Lamb with his rams. The table of this supper, at which God visibly renews—or rather continues—the relation of shadow to light, figure to truth, the New Testament to the Old, is prepared in a great upper room through the ministry of the apostles, so that the Lord, fed on pasture in the figurative upper room, may suffer as the spotless Lamb upon the gibbet; and so that anyone who has ascended to the upper room of prelacy may not refuse, after Jesus, to undergo the ordeal of Passion, in order that, strengthened in the upper room by life-giving foods, he may not be shaken by fear and the weight of tribulations. At this banquet the Lord sets forth blood, flesh, skin, fat, [Col. 0932A] entrails, and a head with feet, so that redemption may be supplied in the blood, refreshment in the flesh, clothing in the skin, anointing in the fat, knowledge of hidden mysteries in the entrails, the first robe in the head, and blessed consummation in the feet.

That poor friend of the rich man who reclined at the banquet cries out amid the abundance of his fullness and sweetness: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. CXV [116]:13). But he should have known what the Wise Man says: “When you sit at a rich man’s table, carefully attend to what is set before you, knowing that you must prepare such things” (Prov. XXIII:1). Therefore set flesh in return for flesh: for holy flesh, sanctified flesh; for chaste flesh, chastened and made chaste; for whole flesh, undefiled flesh. Likewise, blood for blood: namely, in return for blood poured out upon [Col. 0932B] the altar of the cross, blood shed in the redness of confession; for pure blood, impure; for good, evil; for tranquil, troubled. We must also repay skin for skin, as Job says (II:4): that is, patience and imitation of the gentleness of the spotless Lamb, Jesus Christ. For the skin of the victim belongs by perpetual right to the priest who offers the sacrifice (Lev. VII:8). Although I do not grasp, O Jesus, the knowledge of miracles and secrets, the purity of conscience, the head of righteousness, or the feet of your perfection and consummation—for “they have been strengthened, and I cannot attain to them” (Ps. CXXXVIII [139])—at least grant me hide, at least skin: dried and stretched hide, so that from it I may make myself a drum or a ten-stringed psaltery; [Col. 0932C] warm and white skin, so that I may prepare from it a garment of virtues, and my skins may be like Solomon’s skins (Song I:4). One who comes to the wedding in this skin is not cast out, but is compelled to enter and go up higher. Therefore repay, guest of Christ, skin for skin—or rather, according to the Law, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, bruise for bruise, life for life (Exod. XXI:24; Lev. XXIV:20; Deut. XIX:21; Matt. V:38). For what could God do for you except lay down his life? Go, then, and do likewise. “I have given you an example,” he says, “that you also may do thus” (Luke XIV).

See: there is flesh at the supper, since we have now stretched out the skins; but where are the loaves? “Where,” the Lord says to Philip, “shall we buy bread for these people to eat?” (John VI:5). Lord [Col. 0932D] Jesus, do not ask Philip; ask your betrayer. For he has one purse together with the scribes and Pharisees; he plots against blood, and against the innocent man he lays snares—indeed, vainly for the fulfillment of his own avarice, yet not vainly for our salvation. He, I say, has the thirty denarii with which loaves are bought to satisfy all flesh. Grain is also sold by Joseph, from which loaves are made. Joseph shows his brothers a work of generosity combined with the shrewdness of commerce: he fills their sacks in return for money; he fills their mouths and bellies by grace (Gen. XLII); he gives the provisions for the journey freely, but does not hand over without a price the means by which they themselves may nourish the family in their homeland (Gen. XLIII). What is this but: “He shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life”? [Col. 0933A] (Matt. XIX:29). See grace; see merit. Joseph prepares the feast from grace, not “as the trespass, so also is the gift,” because Christ died freely; yet he receives payment to fill the sacks, because “faith without works is dead” (Jas. II:17).

But for a little while it pleases me, at the table of the supper and Joseph’s feast, to set before our eyes light and shadow in the arrangement of the dishes and of those reclining: to receive through interpreters the speech of the Lord and his brother; to behold with the utmost reverence a face now unknown because of the glorification of majesty, though joined by blood-kinship; to weigh carefully the robes bestowed with their portions; and to drink wine even to drunkenness, without the vice of gluttony. Finally, with lavish hand Joseph, whose bellies he had filled with his good things, nevertheless fills their sacks with as much grain [Col. 0933B] as they can hold; he secretly but not deceitfully ties each man’s own money in the mouth of his sack, and places his own cup with the money in the sack of the youngest (Gen. XLIII). Joseph is gracious everywhere, but at the banquet more gracious and far more delightful. At the banquet he does not deny his sellers the brotherhood which they denied him; at the banquet he does not retain the injury but extends generosity; at the banquet, according to Scripture, by feeding his enemy he extinguishes envy and heals ill will.

But because this feast is no less religious than abundant, let us remember that we must nourish ourselves with words and nourish the belly as well; for action is more necessary than speech. We do not reduce the table of the apostles to the rule of monks, because [Col. 0933C] above the table of Saint Benedict stands the table at which the Son of the blessed God presides. At a monk’s table two dishes suffice and silence must be kept; but at the table of the Word made flesh, both the Lamb’s flesh is consumed and the words which are spirit and life, flowing most abundantly from Jesus’ tongue, are found after supper. For, as the Wise Man says, he had reserved his spirit until then: “The fool pours out all his spirit, but the wise man reserves it to the last” (Prov. XXIX:11). Therefore he retained a good word—or rather, good wine—for the disciples at the hour of departure, the hour of their final refreshment and conversation. The bells placed at the hem of the priestly garment seem to me to signify this (Exod. XXVIII), [Col. 0933D] so that, when the high priest enters, not without blood, within the veil which divides sanctuary from sanctuary and holy things from holy things, they may be heard from afar announcing that most illustrious and most health-giving discourse which Jesus delivered to his apostles at the end of the most sacred supper (John XIV and following). The bells themselves were also among the pomegranates, because this discourse admonishes us both concerning present justification and future glorification. There are pomegranates below, about the feet of the tunic, all around (Exod. XXVIII), so that your soul may possess the supper of the eternal feast. There are bells among the pomegranates, so that it may receive teaching which now illuminates by grace and afterwards makes glorious by glory. This is concerning the Lord’s table with mortal humanity, [Col. 0934A] at which visible Jesus visibly shared food with the apostles.

There is again a table of the Lord at which he now feasts, not visibly among mortals, but sacramentally and invisibly among the faithful, until the consummation of the age. This is the table of the altar, where the reality of the Lord’s body and blood is present, though hidden beneath the visible appearance of bread and wine; there the memorial of the Lord’s Passion, together with the effect of our redemption—if integrity of faith is present—is daily recalled as profitably as faithfully. For faith accomplishes there for worthy recipients all that Christ’s death accomplished for believers on the cross with most certain manifestation, except that the latter pertains in some sense to the restoration of all, while the former pertains to that of individuals; and except that this [Col. 0934B] works subsequently and cooperatively in relation to the thing of which that was not merely antecedent but is even now coeffective. There Christ’s death works the salvation of all; here the memorial of that death likewise does not cease sacramentally to work our salvation. And truly, the immaculate body taken from the Virgin—the body which on the cross, under Pontius Pilate, was hung up and sacrificed by Gentile soldiers while the Jews cried, “Crucify, crucify” (Luke XXIII:28; John XIX:6)—is handled by the priest’s hand, made by the power of Christ’s words, and given to the faithful people. By means, indeed, of the familiar and customary appearances of bread and wine, we receive the true flesh and true blood of Christ. But, through the intervening flesh and blood of the Lamb, sharing in the divinity of the Word, [Col. 0934C] we undoubtedly approach the Father of the Word as well, through the Son himself, with the Holy Spirit cooperating and assisting. And thus from him and through him and in him we live, move, and are (Acts XVII:28), not like any created thing whatsoever, but as a rational creature made new and renewed in God’s image.

At this table God sets forth power and grace; the human being, faith and obedience. Marvelous is God’s power, by which bread is changed into flesh and wine into blood! Equally marvelous is the power by which so great a thing is performed in such a way that, enclosed beneath the seal of faith, it is penetrated beyond the intervening veil only by the pure sight of faith. Grace, surpassing nature’s usage and course, just as by sanctifying it created the Virgin’s flesh into Christ’s flesh and by creating it sanctified it, conforming the likeness of sinful flesh to the Word of God but refining the nature of humanity to purity so that it might not be flesh of sin—thus, by a marvelous conversion, it makes Christ’s body from bread, concealing under the appearance of bread that which in reality, not merely in likeness, is the true bread that came down from heaven; while it is bread from the oven only in likeness, not in reality. See the grace; see the power, which adorn and also give form to this table.

## CHAPTER II. Again, concerning the threefold table—sacramental, natural, and mystical—and its faithful stewards, Moses and Paul.

[Col. 0935A]

In the tabernacle of testimony, at the Lord’s command, the table is placed outside the veil, and the lampstand opposite it on the south side of the tabernacle. This table sets forth food for souls, nourishment for spirits, and dishes of heavenly delights; this table, I say, full of the bowels of mercy and filled with the gifts of grace, marvelously filling the innermost parts of those who eat, does not satisfy the desires of those reclining so as to end them, but presses them more keenly and more sacredly.
