For the nature of this banquet and of its guests alike is that they always yield to desire, never to weariness. For what person [Col. 0935B] to whom is given the vision of glory, the blessedness of eternal life, unfailing exaltation, ever-sufficient jubilation, could become weary? Without doubt, the voracity at this table deserves commendation rather than condemnation. To refrain there is both fault and punishment; to devour is glory and crown. Surely you do not fear exhaustion where every good thing overflows in consummation? Do not dine sparingly where you find God as food. If today you have presumed to take the whole, tomorrow you will nevertheless have the whole without doubt. By loving the whole, you receive the whole but do not consume it. For just as love is not exhausted by loving, so when he who is true love is received by us through love, he is by no means brought to an end. Do you fear burdening your belly? Rather, receive abundantly if you wish to relieve both belly and mind. [Col. 0935C] For he takes away our burdens; he does not impose them. There is no swelling in the stomach, no superfluous fluid accumulating in the veins. He seeks and heals the heart; he fills and cleanses the heart; he purifies and illumines the heart. This food prepares life without distress, relief without burden, immortality without corruption. Nor are the fruits of trees lacking from the Lord’s table: neither the cluster of Cyprus-henna (Song I), nor the pipe of cinnamon, nor ointments of sweetest fragrance, nor, finally, anything delightful to the sight.

Let this suffice concerning this table and what is upon it. Whoever, then, strengthened by these blessings of the Lord’s table, wishes with the door of faith opened to approach beyond the veil of the sanctuary, with all desire, him who sits upon the throne [Col. 0935D] should turn the hand of devotion more frequently toward that same table and take from it the food of life. For no one reaches the station of the middle veil who does not receive below it spiritual strength from the Lord’s foods. Nor does the person have a fitting palate for receiving the invisible and more sacred mysteries of the Trinity who has not first tasted the visible sacraments of our faith. For this reason, the Lord of all, weighing in a just balance the ages, names, number, sex, offices, ranks, health, capacities, regions, customs, habits, and dispositions of those who come to him, sets forth loaves of diverse graces, lest any of the poor or weak have just excuses available from want. Therefore, from the field—that is, the belly—of Jesus, [Col. 0936A] in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden, like a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies, I have gathered in this little work twenty-four loaves—according to the number of the twenty-four elders standing before the Lamb (Rev. IV)—to restrain every hunger, cure every plague, and remove every languor, with such diligence as I could amid the interruption of overflowing cares. This number signifies the doubled number of twelve, both of Jacob’s sons and of Christ’s apostles. Under this number, too, are contained the books of the Old Testament. Thus complete instruction of souls is tasted beforehand from this number of books, and likewise full refreshment is apprehended from this number of loaves. Therefore, coming together from east and west, [Col. 0936B] north and south, at Abraham’s signal, lest they fail upon the way, they refresh themselves with the loaves of the Lord’s mercies and provide lasting refreshment for their failings. For besides and above the nature of our daily bread, which fails even as it refreshes, the Lord’s loaves are such that, conversely, they increase as they refresh: when received, they are not consumed; they are broken, but not diminished; they change those who receive them, but are not changed by their recipients. First, then, briefly outlining the names and virtue of each of these, I shall afterward explain them somewhat more fully, as the Lord gives.

One bread is for little children and infants; another for the perfect and advanced. Likewise, one bread is unleavened, [Col. 0936C] another leavened; likewise, some loaves are of firstfruits, others of the presentation; likewise, one is of fine flour or wheat, another of barley; likewise, one is for mourners, another for the joyful; likewise, one is for servants, another for sons, another for hired laborers; likewise, one bread is baked under ashes, which does not turn over; another, made from many ingredients, is covered instead of human dung with bovine dung; likewise, one is common and plebeian, another sanctified and suitable only for priests; one is baked in an oven, another in a frying pan, another on a griddle; likewise, one is anointed with oil, another mixed with it; one is hot, another hard and cold. See the loaves; see the table; and the elders of the house of Israel, who eat with the younger men, praising the Lord’s name. But who ministers? Certainly Moses, as a faithful steward in the house of God [Col. 0936D] (Heb. III:5), which is the Church, administers all the vessels, utensils, and lights necessary for the use of those feasting; yet he exercises his office especially in preparing waters, from which he also takes his name. For what else does he indicate, while setting forth the order of the creation of every creature, except when, by whom, from what, how, and for what end this table—or mass—of the universe exists? Thus you may observe the founded earth like a table set in place; heaven placed over and around it like a cloth spread about it, just as the ark too was overlaid all around with gold; the firmament like a lampstand, and in the lampstand the two great lights, sun and moon, with the shining stars like lamps (Gen. I); rain-bearing air like a basin [Col. 0937A] or ewer, and again clear air as providing a hand-towel; the sea as the cleanser of all filth; and the earth, through the moderation of the Spirit governing and disposing all things, supplying bread and wine, flesh and spices, and other sufficient sustenance for this life. Such is the order at the table of those feasting upon history.

Then, when these people have been satisfied with history and rise, and others succeed to be satisfied by allegory, another adornment is required. For the more refined mind, after tasting historical sense for a little while like a humbler vegetable dish, seeks subtler things and desires the more elegant mysteries of allegory. Therefore Paul, caught up to paradise or the third heaven, learned what and how he should serve; first vigorous in his office, he afterward shone without equal [Col. 0937B] in all his stewardship. He prepared delights, not as one given to luxury but as a fervent seeker, restorer, and contemplator of ineffable delights. How many labors this cook endured in preparing foods! How diligently he investigated another’s palate, and how merciless a persecutor he was of his own! This gracious steward knew how to season the words of his exhortations with the salt of grace according to his hearers’ will and benefit, and to pour over them every blessing and spiritual grace as though rich fat. Here—here—he regarded the Church as the table: the cloth on the table, faith in the Church; the great lights, the four Gospels; Solomon’s water, the sacrament of baptism; bread and wine, the mystery of the Eucharist; innumerable foods, holy virtues; servers, the distinct orders [Col. 0937C] of the Church; guests, all the faithful; the diners’ garments, believers’ conduct; fruits of trees, the examples of the saints. Wretched and miserable is the person who does not enter the place of the feast, or the wonderful tabernacle (Ps. XLI [42]:5); who remains outside like the elder brother in the field; who hears but does not heed the symphony of unity and the choir of love (Luke XV); who hears, but from outside, the organ of divine jubilation; who hears, but excluded from its share, the psaltery’s melody. For the one within rejoices, while the one outside is tormented. The one within is satisfied with good things; the one outside fails amid evils. O how good and delightful it is to sit at Paul’s table! And this is allegorical refreshment.

Therefore we must rise from this table, because it is a table of pilgrimage, [Col. 0937D] and hasten to that which is in the homeland, where the Bridegroom sups with the Bride. That true and eternal table is the blessedness of the saints. Wisdom adorns it; mercy prepares it. None are admitted to it except those whose names are found in the book of life: “Thousands of thousands minister to him, and ten times a hundred thousand stand before him” (Dan. VII:10). There no water or wine is drunk; rather, the most complete joy of God’s children is filled from abundance. A diversity of flavors is not required, because every flavor is perceived in a single flavor. What more is there to say? In the contemplation of Jesus are most exquisite refreshment, ultimate inebriation, fullest rest, most spacious movement, unshaken health, strong strength, secure possession of every good, and blessed life. You look upon Jerusalem [Col. 0938A] and receive desire; Jesus looks upon you and draws your soul into himself. O table, what are you? Can you be spoken? Can you even be thought? Certainly an unclean tongue does not grasp you; polluted lips, even if they speak about you, do not speak you, because “no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. XII:3). Would that, my heart, either you entered into it, or it entered into you! Without doubt, if you entered, you would contain the whole; indeed, you would be happy either way—whether you were contained or carried away. For if you were contained, you would contain; if you were carried away, you would carry away. But what would you contain or carry away? Perhaps you would contain food and carry away fruit? Rather, you would contain the Spirit and carry away God. Let one who thus contains or is contained not fear being accused criminally or civilly. You are indeed, O immeasurable table, wondrous even in this respect [Col. 0938B] and no less lovable, because one who enters into you does not go out from you. For he is enclosed within your circuit, yet not imprisoned: rather, happily enclosed by full blessedness and delightfully bounded.

O hateful weight of flesh, by which our leaping out toward salvation is denied! O tinder of sin, to be pierced through by every virtue, by which we are held in this necessity! O table of God, would that my soul melted within itself because of you! Would that it failed from itself into itself, so as to slay itself! O wondrous sweetness! Certainly this pen is more delightful to me now: from the time it began to write of you, it has not ceased to run more readily. I pray that there may come to you not a writing pen but a loving soul; not the pen’s inscription but the heart’s devotion. Give a morsel of bread, give a honeycomb, give a cup of wine, so that, strengthened by [Col. 0938C] your refreshment, I may distribute from your remnants to the poor and say something worthy concerning the loaves of the Scriptures. Now, now let us come to the loaves; but first let us briefly recall the ascents we have conceived in the tables. At the first table we ascended from flesh to soul; at the second, from soul to spirit; at the third, from spirit to God. At the first, we live, but not always; at the second, we do not die, and do so always; at the third, we cannot die, eternally. The first is the wine-cellar; the second, the storeroom of spices; the third, the bedchamber. At the first we are called; at the second we are justified; at the third we shall be glorified. At the first we are with the saints; at the second, with angels; at the third we shall be in God, and God in us.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning leavened bread and the old leaven, to be purged through confession (*exomologesis*).

[Col. 0938D]

“The righteous man at the beginning of his speech is his own accuser” (Prov. XVIII:10). Another passage of Scripture shows the benefit of accusing oneself: “Declare your iniquities first,” it says, “that you may be justified” (Isa. XLIII:26). See the joining; see the mixture of wine and water, leaven and flour, truth and justice. “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and justice has looked down from heaven” (Ps. LXXXIV [85]:12). The earth is the sinner; truth is confession. Justice, which knows our formation to be fragile because it is clay, and proud because it is born from the stock of Adam’s transgression, is from heaven, because it guards the heavenly host. Perhaps it was Justice itself that stationed the deputy guard, the cherub and the flaming [Col. 0939A] and turning sword, “to guard the way of the tree of life” (Gen. III): the cherub, which is fullness of knowledge, lest the sinner be deceived by lying and flattering blandishments; the sword, lest, without a cutting of the heart, trusting in his obstinacy, he might evade entrance into his homeland and return from banishment to exile; flaming, lest, clothed in garments of skin and beset by feathers, he touch and be burned by the flame of worldly vanity; and turning, because “when God is angry, he does not forget mercy” (Hab. III:2), or lest entrance be stealthily gained by the swiftness of any deceit. All these obey Justice. When sparing is decreed, they sheathe themselves; when striking is commanded, they send forth arrows and flash lightnings. They advance with raised neck against the senseless; they lower their wings at [Col. 0939B] the voice of the humble and at the confession of converts. They pursue sinners; they bend toward those who confess.

Therefore let one who hungers for the tree of life take up the sword of accusation, casting aside the shield of excuse; let him take fullness of knowledge, take the image, take truth, which is round and turning. For with these emblems and banners Justice is softened, now turning toward the confessor a face not angry but mild: “Permit,” she says, “O cherub, those who confess to come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX:14). They have cast away the weapons of iniquity and taken up the weapons of justice: “For just as they presented their members as slaves to impurity and iniquity unto iniquity, so now they present them as slaves to justice unto sanctification” [Col. 0939C] (Rom. VI:19). See truth in the mouth, love in the heart, purity in the conscience, humility in manner, abstinence in food, modesty in gait, chastity in the gaze, prayer in every place, meditation at every time, affliction in the whole body, devotion in the whole soul, longing before God, tears to God by day and night. Thus the soul is justified when it confesses well and fully: washed from former filth in the river of tears, wiped with the cloth of truth, kindled with love, cleansed by confession, adorned with humility, girded with abstinence, wrapped about with modesty, glorified with chastity, raised by prayer, supported by meditation, anointed with devotion, and received through desire into heaven; it is to be approved by us and honored by the angels.

It must be explained why I have compared leavened bread with confession of sins [Col. 0939D], and why I have placed this same bread before all the others of which I am about to treat. Leaven is sin; hence the Apostle: “Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new dough” (1 Cor. 6:7). For just as the leaven of oldness spreads through the dough into which it is mixed its flavor and corruption, so sin removes the purity of all works into which it has mingled itself. As the Apostle says: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5:6). And James: “Whoever keeps the whole law, but stumbles in one point, has become guilty of all” (Jas. 2:10). Behold how the poison—or leaven—of sin infects every channel of the veins, so that none of the righteous deeds which a man has done is remembered after he has turned away. What then? Does wickedness [Col. 0940A] overcome wisdom? Why then did the Apostle say: “The gift is not like the trespass” (Rom. 5:15)? What is this righteousness? Truly, it is like a vast abyss. Who can illuminate this depth and abyss of mysteries except God, who “commanded light to shine out of darkness” (2 Cor. 4:6)?

It is written that “wisdom overcomes wickedness” (Wis. 7:30); it is written that “the gift is not like the trespass” (Rom. 5:15), and: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (ibid., 20). Conversely it is written: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump”; “whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all” (1 Cor. 5:6). Here the teeth are stunned; here Isaac’s eyes grow dim and he cannot see clearly. Who can bring this discordance—lest I say discord—[Col. 0940B] into peace, into the light of truth, except the key of David, which opens what is shut and distinguishes what is confused?

Therefore, once the key has been applied, we easily loosen the bars of this question as follows. A little leaven corrupts the whole lump when free will submits its neck to the spurs of sin; when a small evil in the extent of the act grows through an overflowing desire to sin and overcomes the impulse of resistance through the habitual practice of evil, both by delight and by consent. Thus, “a little leaven corrupts the whole lump” when malice invades, freely and unhindered, the court of the mind and finds no barrier of righteousness or discipline. But wisdom overcomes wickedness (Wis. 7:30) when grace enters and frees [Col. 0940C] free will, held in chains, while the one who was bound has not yet risen or cooperated. For grace alone looses the chains; but once they are loosed, free will follows grace and clings to grace, so that thereafter, with grace going before and cooperating, free will pursues and overtakes the enemy, taking from him the tribute of servitude and vindicating itself in the freedom of its native liberty. Where grace was absent, a little leaven corrupted the whole lump; but when the fullness of grace comes, free will shakes its neck free from beneath the yoke and reign of sin, and so wisdom overcomes wickedness.

He therefore goes out, fettered—or rather, now freed—to the gate of confession and brings suit against sin. He recounts the injuries which wretched conscience has suffered from sin [Col. 0940D]; he sets forth the course of the case as completely as he inwardly grieves. For true sorrow touches him. Therefore he omits neither what ought to be said nor what ought to be left unsaid; for he is in bitterness. He specifies to the smallest moment the time when he sold himself to the exacter. He states the place—because it is called a holy place—in order to magnify his wickedness and misery. With tears he explains the manner of the deed, and everything that death raged within him from the first movement of sin until the entrance of grace. He puts disordered things in order. He casts the ashes outside the camp of his heart (Num. 19), lest even the memory of Amalek be found among its abortions (Exod. 17). For he desires utterly to overthrow both sin and the memory of sin.

Thus truth springs from the earth. It first desires to restore the order of the first nature and first condition, but it depends upon the path nature would have followed had it not had twisted feet. For a straight foot and a twisted foot are recognized differently by their tracks. Therefore the order of nature, now corrupted by sin, walks perversely against the order of holy nature established by God. It must consequently be pursued by its own tracks and recalled from the wandering of error to truth. Hence one must investigate whence and whither it had fallen, and likewise inquire by what way and to what place it ought to be brought back.

That we may in some measure grasp what the condition of rational nature was in the beginning, let us bring together the cause of creation, and the knowledge, power, and goodness of the Creator; and let us consider what sort of work could and ought to have been produced from the workshop of so great an artisan, when the underlying cause was not ignoble [Col. 0941B]. The cause of the human creation, indeed—as far as the testimony of Scripture has made it clear—was either the restoration of the angelic fall, or the familiar, certain, and unshaken vision of the supreme and unbounded Spirit.

Beyond these, which still lie hidden in the secrets of the divine mind, there doubtless exist causes far more excellent and also subtler. Yet, with the aid of either or both of the causes mentioned, one may adequately discern what we seek: namely, how surpassingly excellent human nature was in its creation. For Adam—even though bent beneath the hump of disobedience—can measure himself in this respect if he numbers the stars of heaven; and he perceives that he would have remained forever, not merely like the stars but above the stars, if he had not moved his foot. “Thus,” says the Lord to Abraham, “shall your seed be, like the stars of heaven” (Gen. 15:5). Through the merit of faith, there shall come from Abraham’s seed what would indeed have existed in Adam and his offspring, with no punishment or bodily death intervening, if, through cooperating grace, he had maintained obedience. At the end of the age, through the blood of Christ, the possession of the redeemed inheritance shall be restored; there shall be what would have been, certainly, when the congregation of the saints had been fulfilled without the price of blood. For without the cost of journey and labor he would have reached the place to which he will scarcely at last be able to be brought back by the ship of the cross, while Christ’s hands and arms are greatly wearied at the oars. Had he waited in the harbor, God and Father would have transferred him from servant to son in the inner chambers of the palace, without the circuit of distresses [Col. 0941D]. His foot would have been neither stained with blood nor fouled with dust. Likewise, he would have passed through mortality as easily as one who, awake, gently falls into sleep and rests. Once stripped of mortal flesh, he would have attained equality with the angels as swiftly as the rising sun is accustomed to carry with it the rays of light to the eyes of beholders. Surely not much labor would have been expended if the effect proper to the causes prepared by God for humankind had been realized through human obedience. Virgin birth would not have bowed down the heavens had Eve’s rash touch not reached the forbidden fruit. But transgression of the command and eating the fruit brought an impediment to that purpose: that man should not live immortally and be joined eternally to angelic glory.

The place was sufficiently near to the purpose, so that man might be transferred from paradise to heaven [Col. 0942A]; likewise, the person was suited to it, so that obedient man, through obedience, might receive the lot lost through disobedience. As a faithful servant he was to sail from the slippery sea of mortality to the firm harbor of immortality; and, made comparable to angels in rationality and immortality, he was to attain by recompense in the instrument of the body what he had not yet obtained by creation. He was to become a life-giving spirit, though he had been made a living soul, so that not only the necessity of dying but even the capacity for it might be removed, when the body that was animal became spiritual. Hence the Apostle: “If there is an animal body, there is also a spiritual one” (1 Cor. 15:46).

Before sin, the animal body was such that, through free will and its mortal condition, it could sin and fail if it wished, but could not do so if it did not wish; after sin, however, it sins and fails even unwillingly. Hence the Apostle: “Creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope, because creation itself also shall be set free from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 8:20). But after the full liberation to come in the common resurrection, they shall neither sin nor be able to sin, but “shall be as the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. 22:30); and this is to be spiritual rather than animal.

But since you have not yet attained the spiritual state, and are wholly unable to return to the animal state as creation established it, consider carefully how you may meanwhile renew the corrupted animal state; and how you may sustain that which is not yet reformed, but is decayed [Col. 0942C] and made like senseless beasts. Will you give it hay because it is animal? By no means. For it is a rational, mortal animal. Rational and irrational animals feed on different food: the irrational is fed with hay; the rational is refreshed with bread. Therefore let us serve our bread to the animal, because it is rational; but let it be leavened, because it is corrupt and has become abominable in its practices. Let us not first set unleavened bread before it, but leavened, and then unleavened; because “not first that which is spiritual, but that which is animal; afterward that which is spiritual” (1 Cor. 15:46). For just as it is unfitting to put new wine into old skins (Matt. 9:17), so it is perilous to set unleavened bread, which has not known corruption, before a stomach corrupted by wickedness and teeth decayed through the lies of the lips [Col. 0942D]. “Let a man first prove himself, and thus eat of that bread,” that is, of the unleavened bread (1 Cor. 11:28). Judas indeed received a morsel of unleavened bread, but burst open in the midst. For great is the power in that bread which distinguishes clean from unclean; it does not allow itself to remain with the filth of the betrayer’s greed and unbelief. It is “for the fall and rising again of many” (Luke 2:34). It is “an odor of death unto death,” and “an odor of life unto life” (2 Cor. 2:10). It either purges or kills. If you are curable, it heals you; if incurable, it increases your sickness. It is medicine. If the disease is curable, it receives the medicine fittingly: for if things which ought to be purged are purged, they benefit and bear it well. But if contrary dispositions take it unseasonably, then the person who receives the holy bread without reverence and without discernment is harmed more by his irreverence than helped by the holiness of the food.

Therefore, whoever is still submerged in his iniquities, like a sow in the mire where it wallows, should eat leavened bread in the sweat of his face, groaning and saying: “I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have deserved it” (Mic. 7:9). Let him declare himself unworthy to eat unleavened bread and say: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter beneath my roof; but only speak the word, and my servant shall be healed” (Matt. 8:8). But what is leaven? I believe that vengeance for sin is leaven. Leaven is mixed into bread or dough when “the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against every soul of man that does evil” [Col. 0943B] (Rom. 1:18). Yet God’s scourges are to be borne patiently, because they are food that restores. “Let him who began,” says Job, “himself crush me” (Job 6:9). For the potter of clay can remake a ruined vessel for the better, even if he has broken it. Thus Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, because “against hope he believed in hope” (Gal. 3:6). What is it to believe against hope in hope except, when God has scourged you, to hope in him the more? “Though he kill me, I will hope in him,” says Job (13:15). And he who believed against hope in hope did not consider his own body dead, nor Sarah’s barren womb, in which womanly functions had ceased.

So too, though the sinner’s body may already be dead through age or sickness, let him nevertheless believe that the veins of mercy still beat in God [Col. 0943C], by which he justifies the ungodly, gives life to the dead, and calls things that are not. With him, loss spoken by the mouth is not imputed, provided only that utter destitution is renewed, even at life’s end, with full groanings. Let him knock at the door, for it is not yet shut while a human being lives, confesses, groans, and has breath in his nostrils. Let him eat leavened bread and sacrifice praise from what is leavened. For he “sacrifices praise from leavened bread” (Amos 4:5) who offers true confession of sins. For as you dishonored God by sinning, so you honor him by confessing. “Give thanks therefore to the Lord, for he is good; for his mercy endures for ever” (Ps. 105:1). Amen.

## Chapter IV. On Unleavened Bread

[Col. 0943D]

Therefore the Son of God came, born of the Virgin, without the leaven of guilt; and from the mass of human nature he took only the flour of incorrupt flesh, not the leaven or foment of original sin. For with the sieve of the Holy Spirit he winnowed away the bran of wickedness from the most holy flesh conceived in and born from the Virgin’s womb. He also assumed to himself a rational soul in the unity of his person. He set his flesh before us in the most holy banquet of the Supper as the unleavened bread of restoration; and immediately afterward, instituting the new Passover on the cross, he offered it. But he sent his soul to despoil hell. His conception destroyed leaven; his birth destroyed sin. For what was impossible for the law, as the Apostle says (Rom. 8:3), because it was weakened through the flesh—namely, to justify man once sin had been destroyed—God accomplished by sending his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, that through sin he might condemn sin: that is, the new condemned the old, the unleavened the leavened [Col. 0944A].

Therefore, cleansed in mind and spirit, let us solemnly celebrate “with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5:8) the day of our redemption from Egypt (Exod. 1), that is, from sin or the devil. Let us remember with certainty how mercilessly Pharaoh’s servants burned against us, compelling us beyond our strength to the work of mud and brick. O miserable soul, to whom not even the straw of passing happiness was formerly given in Egypt, and yet, by diabolical exaction, works of defilement and stain were demanded! The body was plunged into the desires of the flesh; the soul was swallowed by evil desires [Col. 0944B]; and even so it did not satisfy the spirits of error. For the demon’s gluttony is not satisfied so long as there remains hope of amendment for the soul. He feels beyond his throat and stomach the one whom he groans not to have retained through despair. For Abraham’s bosom rejoices forever and beyond forever that many have been snatched from the midst of his teeth and jaws by the hook of conversion, the fish-spear of confession, and the trident of heavenly mercy. Yet as long as the soul, without the light of truth poured upon it, was darkened by the shadows of ignorance, it followed wherever the evil spirit led and did not complain. It was fed on the vilest food of swine; in place of a bath, it used the most foul impurities of the Egyptians. It devoured pots of meat, onions, and garlic so as to stink more abundantly in the sight of its Creator [Col. 0944C]; it did not know unleavened bread, nor recognize manna.

O miserable and pitiable soul, there is no one among all your dear ones to comfort you! But you, merciful and compassionate Lord, hear, be appeased, attend, and act. Whoever you are that possess a soul, if you rehearse its heavenly birth and the exalted dignity of its Parent, you will be moved to more abundant pity at its disgrace. For although it may not produce the documents of its birth—perhaps because they are kept stored in the chests of angels, lest they be destroyed by hostile interference or eaten away by moths—yet it is established by sufficient testimony that, made by God and reborn from God, it is called the daughter of the King.

She is a high-born maiden, tender and delicate, beautiful and fair; ignorant of deceit, unused to labor, capable of virtues, condemning vices, inventing arts, constant in love, truthful in promise, generous in giving, companionable toward citizens, gracious toward all. Yet the maiden is carried off—what a crime! High birth is enslaved—what a shame! Delicacy is torn to pieces—what a shipwreck of compassion! Beauty is blackened—what a loss of loveliness! Fairness is obscured—what an insult to glory! She who knew no deceit is deceived by fraud—what a destruction of justice! She who was unused to labor is worn down by labor—what an exile of pity! She who was capable of virtues is emptied of virtues—what an exclusion of good things! She who condemned vices is corrupted—what an exchange for demons! The inventor of arts forgets her inventions—what nourishment for sloth! She who was constant in love is found unstable—what slipperiness of nature! She who was truthful in promise lies daily [Col. 0945A]—what a pathless exile! She who was generous in giving is turned into a miser—what a drying-up of veins! She who was companionable is without covenant—what a corruption of life! She who was gracious is made rude—what devastation of the bond of love!

O mercy of the Creator: rescue her from the lion’s mouth; restore to her the state of freedom; replace her in her former delights; reform her who is deformed; renew her who is darkened; free her who is deceived; remove her labor; restore her virtues; heal her corruption; teach her who has forgotten; strengthen her who has fallen; set her upon the path of truth; destroy her avarice; establish the covenant of fellowship; make her gracious again!

Behold, O soul: by the fifteen steps through which you fell in sinning, receive in repentance the unleavened bread of sincerity. For by as many steps of virtues as the falls through which we departed from God, we fly back, on the wings of desire, to God’s own power. By these we ascend from Egypt to the land of promise; by these we proceed, clothed in priestly vesture, to the altar of incense; by these we attain the promises of the New and Old Testaments; by these, finally, when we have ascended, we feast on “the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” [Col. 0945B] (1 Cor. 5:8).

These words of Paul concerning unleavened bread do not disagree with what is written in Exodus concerning its observance: “For seven days,” Moses says, “you shall eat unleavened bread. On the first day there shall be no leaven in your houses. Whoever eats leavened bread from the first day to the seventh, that soul shall perish from the assembly of Israel” (Exod. 12:15). We must therefore explain what the first day is, what the second is, what the third is, and so through the seventh; and what mystery each contains.

The first day of the Lord’s people is the illumination of the mind through faith; the second, the very profession of faith; the third, reception of the visible sacrament; the fourth, the working of faith; the fifth, discernment of good and evil; the sixth, endurance of suffering for keeping the faith; the seventh, the desired rest from vices. Therefore, whoever eats leavened bread from the first day through the seventh shall perish from the assembly of Israel, because he shall have no share in the kingdom of Christ and God who, insulting the Spirit of grace, returns after conversion to faith to the vomit of unbelief. Hence the Apostle says: “It is impossible for those once enlightened, who have also tasted the heavenly gift and become partakers of the Holy Spirit, who have likewise tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and have fallen away, to be renewed again unto repentance, since they crucify the Son of God again for themselves and hold him up to contempt” [Col. 0945D] (Heb. 6:4).

The force of the statement plainly shows how grave it is to sin after conversion; this is to eat leaven from the first day through the seventh. In accordance with the Gospel, we must beware of the leaven of the Pharisees (Matt. 16:6), because a little leaven of vices corrupts the whole lump of virtues (Gal. 5:9). “Whoever keeps the whole law,” and so forth (Jas. 2:10). Observe that a little leaven corrupted the whole lump: in Adam’s single sin, the whole posterity of his children was infected. The leaven of perverse pleasure was certainly very small, but the torment of just condemnation was more than sufficiently great and severe. Indeed, one who even briefly delights in the leaven of worldly concupiscence is punished by harsher torment and for a longer time [Col. 0946A]. Hence Job: “Would that my sins, by which I deserved wrath, and the calamity which I suffer, were weighed in a balance! This would appear heavier than the sand of the sea” (Job 6:2). It is as if he said: if guilt and punishment are weighed on either side in the just and equal balance of moderation, punishment afflicts incomprehensibly more heavily than guilt delighted. For the pleasure of sin flowed away in an instant and in something slight, like foam upon water, or vanished like smoke from a chimney; but inward torment is prolonged in the duration and anguish of cruel penalties.

Therefore leaven must be feared and avoided from the first day through the seventh, so that, once you have been enlightened by the light of faith—which precedes all works of God and of the day—you may not return again to the confusion of ancient, and to-be-made-ancient, darkness [Col. 0946B]. For Lucifer, who looked backward in proud presumption by turning his love toward himself, leavened the first day; and therefore he perished eternally from the assembly of the sons of Israel—that is, the angels who followed and attained God through love and obedience—by exclusion both from place and from merit. Therefore do not look backward; but with holy souls, always before your face, where is “the impulse of the Spirit” (Ezek. 1:12), strive and press on without retreat. For “no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62).

This is concerning the leaven of the first day. We must examine the leaven of the second. Paul rebukes certain persons who, having professed the faith of the Gospel, were already shining like the firmament amid a crooked and perverse generation. As the firmament divides the higher waters from the lower, they wished to leaven the firmament of evangelical faith. Along with the sacrament of baptism, which is a sufficient cleansing of all leprosies, they imposed recircumcision [circumcision] as though necessary; and so they confused the newness of grace with old leaven. Thus he says: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5:2); and elsewhere: “I wish that those who trouble you would even cut themselves off; for they compel you to be circumcised in the flesh,” and so forth (ibid., 12).

See how he is to be condemned who, renewed in the spirit of his mind and established by his religious profession between the waters of heavenly virtues and the waters of carnal desires, thirsts for the former and dries up the latter, draws in the former and draws out the latter, drinks in the former and swallows up the latter [Col. 0946D], if he rebuilds what he had destroyed; if he condemns again what he had washed; if he dissolves what he had established. In the temple of your heart, do not set up the statue of Dagon with the ark of sanctification; not the son of Venus with the Son of the Virgin; not Beelzebub with Jesus. “For what fellowship has Christ with Belial?” (2 Cor. 6:15). Therefore, on the day of unleavened bread do not taste leaven, because you shall be cut off from the assembly of the sons of Israel.

This also concerns the leaven of the second day; now let us consider the leaven of the third. It is not enough to believe in the heart unto righteousness unless you confess with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. 10:10). The preceding illumination of grace and the following profession of faith require the reception of a visible sacrament. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 0947A] (John 3:5). Regeneration of the Spirit concerns the invisible faith of the heart; regeneration from water concerns the visible—that is, sacramental—regeneration.

This is why on the third day it was said: “Let the waters under heaven be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear; and let the earth bring forth green grass yielding seed, and fruit-bearing trees producing fruit according to their kind, whose seed is in itself upon the earth” (Gen. 1:9). Otherwise the dry land does not appear unless the waters are gathered into one place, because the soul is not worthy of the countenance of the Godhead unless, in one Catholic faith, it has completed all the sacraments of the Church. All waters are rightly said to gather into one place because all sacraments and charisms meet in the unity of faith and love [Col. 0947B]. Then dry land appears, free from the impurities of idols and previous sins. Then it brings forth green grass yielding seed, because what had still lain hidden in the inward parts of faith bursts forth into a shoot and bears fruit above, before God, angels, and human beings.

Those who taught that people ought to be rebaptized wished to leaven the newness and purity of this day. Baptism, once received, is not repeated, because Christ died once for our sins, rose once, and “now dies no more; death shall have no more dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9). But whoever establishes rebaptism crucifies Christ anew. Therefore whoever eats leaven on this day—that is, whoever is rebaptized—shall perish from the assembly of the sons of Israel [Col. 0947C].

This is concerning the leaven of the third day; now let us consider that of the fourth. Since, as James says, “faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2:20), the faithful soul must be saved through the begetting of children, that is, of good works (1 Tim. 2:15). For “the children of your servants shall dwell for ever and ever” (Ps. 101:29), because that faith is rewarded which is enriched with the children of good works. The fruits of faith shine in the soul and illuminate the whole sphere of human life like the great lights in the firmament of heaven, which were made on the fourth day. The soul has two great lights: “the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night” (Gen. 1:16), when it fulfils the two commandments of love, illuminating by one the day of contemplation and by the other the night of its action [Col. 0947D].

It also clothes and adorns Joseph’s many-colored tunic (Gen. 37), that is, the Church redeemed in the blood of Jesus, with an innumerable variety of stars: when it prophesies according to the measure of faith; gives in simplicity; rules with diligence; shows mercy with cheerfulness; loves without pretence; clings to what is good (Rom. 12:8); speaks truth; and loves peace. These are the stars to which Abraham’s seed is compared; these are the wings of the silvered dove (Ps. 67:14), because one flies upon wings. These are the varieties that embroider the queen’s garments. Finally, there are also a thousand shields hanging on Zion, the tower of David, against hostile powers [Col. 0948A]. Strong is the soul thus armed; beautiful, thus adorned; warm, thus clothed. Splendid is the newness of the fourth day!

But behold hypocrites, like the pale horse followed by death; behold false Christians, concerning whom it is said: “Behold, in peace my bitterness is most bitter” (Ps. 38:17): they introduce the leaven of hypocrisy, the leaven of schism. For those who say, “Let us do evil that good may come” (Rom. 3:8); who say, “It is vain to serve God”; who say, “There is no resurrection of the dead”; who say, “All things are governed by fate”; who say that events cannot happen otherwise, so that by fate they may abolish merit and exalt negligence—these and others like them eat leaven and suggest it for others to eat; and their souls shall perish from the assembly of the sons of Israel. Yet they weave spiders’ webs, and what has been warmed will break forth into a basilisk; whoever eats of their eggs will die (Isa. 59:5).

This is concerning the leaven of the fourth day; now concerning that of the fifth. The law declares every animal unclean which does not chew the cud and divide the hoof, because no work pleases the divine majesty unless the virtue of discernment commends it. Hence even one with a crooked or small nose does not minister: it is exceedingly unfitting to entrust the reins of government to one who has never grasped the bridle of discipline. One wholly without discernment has no nose; one who discerns, but insufficiently, has a nose but a small one; one who can discern sufficiently but neglects to do so has a crooked nose (Lev. 21:18). Such a person must not touch the most holy vessels of the Lord.

But the Church, which discerns all its things in number, measure, and weight (Wis. 11:21), and weighs each matter belonging to each of its members in a just balance, is said to have a nose like the tower of David (Song 4:4) [Col. 0948C]. The work of the fifth day fittingly corresponds to this discernment, when it is said: “Let the waters bring forth the creeping creature with a living soul, and birds above the earth under the firmament of heaven” (Gen. 1:20). Here the discernment of the baptized is indicated: some, preserving the faith and devotion of baptism, never depart from the bosom of the Church; others, soaring through pride—or rather vanishing into the air of presumption and vanity—fabricate blasphemous heresies. Here, here discernment is necessary for the Church, that it may know how to choose godly meanings as the dove chooses select grains, and avoid the deadly voice of heretics with its profane novelty [Col. 0948D]. “There must,” says the Apostle, “also be heresies.” Why? “That those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Cor. 11:19). And elsewhere: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1).

Therefore discernment of spirits must be sought, so that we may distinguish the spirit which dissolves Jesus from the spirit which confesses that Jesus came in the flesh. Let not the one who deceived Eve by his cunning deceive our simplicity; for he transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11:14) and strives to corrupt the goodness of our faith with the leaven of his fraud. This leaven must be avoided, not eaten. This is concerning the leaven of the fifth day. Let us now pass to the leaven of the sixth day.

Endurance of suffering for the faith is the sixth day. Of it the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess him before my Father” (Matt. 10:32). To suffer for Christ is the perfection of faith and the destruction of all unbelief. This virtue is rare, but precious; and the rarer it is, the more precious. No one attains it unless he bears the image of the Son of God. For just as above we compared the works of the individual days with these individual days of the soul by expounding them, so in this sixth day we must consider and apply the work made in it. “Let us make man,” says the Lord, “in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). Christ, who is the Son of the Father, was obedient to him unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. 2:8). You may therefore reproduce the image and likeness of God in yourself if you can die for Christ’s faith [Col. 0949B]. For then the seal is impressed, as it were, upon wax, when our death is made like Christ’s death.

The wax is first softened when the soul, aflame with divine desire in the furnace of grace, is conformed to Christ’s body; and it finally approaches the seal, or even yields itself to be sealed, when it hangs at Christ’s side in enduring insults, in the chastisement of scourges, in the stretching of limbs, and in the final breathing forth of the spirit. God has fittingly re-impressed his image upon his martyr, so that we who can no longer see that first and true image, because of its brightness and heavenly exaltation, might behold, through suffering, the image of the image conformed to us. I judge that the leaven of this day is the suffering of those false martyrs who did not refuse to die rather for vain glory than true glory [Col. 0949C]. This leaven will not be found in the tents of the righteous. For it is not punishment but the cause that makes the martyr; therefore, when the Gospel says, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution,” it adds, “for righteousness’ sake,” or “for my name’s sake” (Matt. 5:10).

Therefore let Christ alone, bearing his cross, stand before your gaze when you deliberate on enduring punishment and offer your body. Thus you will abstain from leaven on the sixth day.

But now, with the Apostle, let us hasten to enter the rest of the seventh day (Heb. 4:11), where unlawful things are wiped away from the soul and burdensome things from the body. For then it will not be hard to abstain from the leaven of sin, when death has already been swallowed up in the victory (1 Cor. 15:54) of resurrection. Of this Job says: “In six tribulations the Lord shall deliver you, and in the seventh evil shall not touch you” (Job 5:19). Thus God first frees the soul from the tribulation of error when he enlightens it through faith; secondly, from the superstition of religion, when he teaches it not only to offer rightly by good will, but also to divide rightly by discerning its works wisely; thirdly, from violating a good purpose, when with every effort and care it orders what is disordered, corrects what is erring, cleanses what is unclean, restrains what is uncontrolled, and frees the face of the heart from every superficial covering; fourthly, from the twofold ignorance, namely conquerable and unconquerable, when, by the sun of heavenly illumination, he makes known to us the hidden things of his wisdom (Ps. 50:8), according to what is known of God—that is, what can be known of God—and by the moon of his sacraments consoles our darkness in the dense night until day dawns [Col. 0950A]; fifthly, he moderates it from intemperance, so that it is neither cast down in adversity nor lifted up in prosperity, and knows both how to accommodate itself to the needs of neighbors and to spread the wings of lofty contemplation; sixthly, it is strengthened against the disturbance and storm of persecutions, when it rises stronger from its wound, passes from the instability of water into crystalline firmness, and advances from soft, earthen fragility into the glory of impassibility. Hence: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. 21:16).

Behold, in six tribulations the Lord shall deliver you. What in the seventh? “Evil shall not touch you” (Job 5:19). Why? Because “the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and the torment of death shall not touch them; they are in peace” (Wis. 3:1). Well shall it be in the uttermost parts of the earth for the soul which has not eaten leavened bread in this manner from the first day through the seventh [Col. 0950B].

Once the leaven of malice and wickedness has been driven from the house of conscience, the newness of the spirit succeeds, like unleavened bread, in the order of our deliverance. For just as it is of little use to leave Egypt unless you enter the land of promise, so likewise it is not enough to turn away from evil unless you do good. Everything is imperfect unless it be brought to completion; and in order truly to have completion, it must endure unto the end: “He who perseveres unto the end,” says the Lord, “[Col. 0950C] shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22). Therefore unleavened bread is to be eaten for seven days—that is, at all times spirit, soul, and body must be kept blameless.

Morally. He who, having abandoned secular dress and manner of life as though Egypt, enters into the wilderness of religious life under the guidance and authority of the divine law and divine love, as though in the hand of Moses and Aaron (Ps. 76:21), must fear lest he have a leavened conscience; for it is dangerous to taste religious profession while still bearing the leaven of the world. Leavened bread, however, is not forbidden to those dwelling in Egypt by so irrevocable an authority or such severity, because they are not bound by their own mouth to the religious obligation of this command. But violation of a vow is an approach to death. He who sins without a vow is like a colt that runs headlong over a precipice without a bridle; but he who acts contrary to a vow is like one who, while falling, strikes against the bridle. It is clear, therefore, that a fall unimpeded by the obligation is at last more easily recoverable than that of one who needs to be raised from both the fall itself and the obstacle. Yet Egypt is not therefore happier or safer because it is more impure. For it would be to do evil so that good might come, if religious life were not undertaken for the reason that one might later be condemned more severely for transgressing a resolution once embraced. Indeed, one is already punished for the evil of unbelief whose mind is restrained from good by such timidity. Such a person, detained by fear of this kind, is [Col. 0951A] like one among the Israelites who would not have followed Moses because he considered the Red Sea or the bitterness of the wilderness.

Let us therefore come into the wilderness of religious life and eat the unleavened bread of renewal. In Egypt unleavened bread is not even named: everything is leavened, everything corrupted. The more corrupt a person is, the better he is thought to be. “To the defiled and unbelieving,” as the Apostle says, “nothing is clean” (the citation appears as 2 Tim. 1:15); rather, their mind and conscience are polluted. Even when Egypt rests from outward activity, as Solomon says: “Hand in hand, the wicked shall not be innocent” (Prov. 11:21). While it does not take heed, it ferments. Just as dough is not fermented only when leaven is mixed into it, but much more when the person who mixed it ceases from the mixing, and the dough itself, well covered, as though resting, falls asleep. So too malice conceived in the mind, even if for some time it seems to abstain from evil action—perhaps because opportunity is lacking—nevertheless rages in the heart all the more fiercely insofar as it does not pass into action.

Thus Hosea says: “For a little while the city ceased from the mixing of leaven, until the whole was leavened” (Hos. 1:4). It is as if he said: In order to carry out more eagerly the evil it has conceived, it more cunningly withdraws its hand for a time. A fire covered over with a layer of tow does not sleep but creeps on; it is not extinguished but renewed. So an evil will, like a hidden flame, eventually devours the materials placed beneath it and sweeps away, like a torrent, the barriers of delay. What is feigned through fear is superficial; what is not done willingly is futile. Therefore, that we may eat unleavened bread for seven days, let us sacrifice willingly to God, and from the heart serve him in holiness and righteousness all the days of our life (Luke 1:75). Let this suffice concerning unleavened bread.

## CHAPTER V. On the Bread of Little Children

Jeremiah speaks thus of the bread of little children: “The little children,” he says, “asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them” (Lam. 4:4). He breaks bread who expounds the law; he gathers up the fragments who faithfully stores in memory the meanings of the Scriptures. It belongs to teachers to break bread; it likewise belongs to little children to eat the fragments. If the teacher does not break it, he is accused of negligence. If the little child neglects to receive it, he is endangered by hunger. Yet one who shares in milk should not lay claim to more solid food, because either gums not yet furnished with teeth will be hurt, or perhaps the narrow opening of the oesophagus or throat will be blocked. Of these, the one evil is bad, the other worse. In the former there is injury; in the latter, human presumption. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not think proudly, but think unto sobriety” (Rom. 12:3).

Excess is more dangerous than spareness, abundance than scarcity; and at times one is more grievously ill from superabundance than from want. Empty bodies are more easily filled than emptied. Yet neither is good: neither excessive fullness nor immoderate emptiness. What is temperate is healthy and, without doubt, praiseworthy. Therefore he says: “Do not think proudly, but think [Col. 0952A] unto sobriety.” Lest perhaps you glory in excessive presumption, remember that you are human; lest, by despairing, you sink into the depths, remember that you are the image of God. To exalt oneself above oneself is presumptuous; to cast oneself below oneself is fearful. One who bursts too far into the light of mercy is dazzled; one who plunges into the thick density of shadows is equally blinded. The seraph veils its head: do not uncover it. Its feet too are veiled; certainly, if you saw the flaming sword, you would not dare tear away that veil.

It is enough—and more than enough—for you; indeed, it is above you, to see those things which are in view and are not veiled, such as those which, in the Song of Songs, the Bride shows to the friends of the Bridegroom concerning the Bridegroom:

“His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk and sitting beside overflowing waters; his cheeks are like beds of spices planted by perfumers; his lips, distilling the finest myrrh; his hands are rounded, golden, full of hyacinths; his belly is ivory, set with sapphires; his legs are marble columns founded upon golden bases” (Song 5:12).

What more? “His appearance is like Lebanon, choice as the cedars; his throat is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable” (ibid., 15). If you are a mother and nurse your son from your own body, mix this flour from Jesus and offer him something strengthening, or gruel. If you are a father, divide it according to the members and set the best portions before your guests. But since we have in hand the care and provision of little children, let us, with grace’s help, prepare for our little ones, like mother Rebecca, the food of our womb.

[Col. 0952C] In contemplating the Bridegroom’s eyes, we apprehend simplicity and innocence. In his cheeks, which are beds of spices planted by perfumers, we apprehend piety and modesty: in the account of his miracles and works, the Apostles, as it were perfumers, planted these by faithful exposition, whether for the instruction or the delight of those who behold them. In the lips that distil the finest myrrh, we apprehend mortification and abstinence. In the hands which are rounded, golden, and full of hyacinths, we apprehend action that is excellent and perfect and most full of heavenly reward. In the ivory belly set with sapphires, we apprehend our nature: fragile indeed, yet chaste, and acting now divinely, now humanly. In the legs founded upon silver bases, [Col. 0952D] we apprehend rectitude and firmness foreknown by divine predestination and proclaimed by the holy prophets. In the appearance like Lebanon or the cedar, we apprehend the exaltation attained from God the Father in the resurrection. In the most sweet throat, the inward savor and sweetness of words. In the statement that he is altogether desirable, divinity and humanity, everywhere and always desirable.

Behold, from the incomprehensible majesty we have set before our little children a thin, light, and easily swallowed food. But those who bear palates of wider and more capacious understanding we send on to richer tables. For those who run like stags upon mountains of spices delight in a more expansive leap and are refreshed by a more eager taste. But one who, like a little beast, has not yet emerged from its den must necessarily feed, in its own lair, upon what has been gathered within the circuit of father or mother. Those, I say, who leap like young gazelles over mountains and bound over hills surely eat the marrow of the earth and refresh themselves with the fat of wheat. But for one who makes its nest in valleys, or in the holes of the rock and caverns of a wall, where it may lay its young—or rather, where its young may grow feathers—the grains of the elementary teaching of the word of God suffice.

What, finally, of those whose citizenship is in heaven and whose understanding penetrates the abyss of the Godhead? Without doubt, in the Psalmist’s words, they will fly; they will fly as far as the clouds and above the heavens, and will not fail. Beyond doubt, like a great eagle with great wings, with extended limbs, full [Col. 0953B] of feathers and of varied color, holy teachers come to Lebanon and carry away the marrow of the cedar. They also pluck off the topmost branches and carry them into the land of Canaan; they set them in the city of merchants (Ezek. 17:14).

The contemplator of the divine law is not undeservedly compared to an eagle, which gazes with undazzled vision upon the sun amid the clouds. Thus the investigator of the Scriptures directs his gaze into the solar rays when he fixes the eyes of his mind keenly upon divine meanings. This eagle has great wings: such are those who, through the subtlety of very well-exercised faculties, are borne into the depths of God’s mysteries and, by the advancement of perfected virtues, into a foretaste of Christ’s rewards. They are also of extended limbs, because they do not abandon their intended studies through any obstacles of adversity. Fullness and variety of feathers signify full knowledge of the various arts, or a conscience filled with the multiplicity of good works.

They come to Lebanon when they reach the height of some interpretation or virtue. They take the marrow of the cedar when they drink in the sweetness of a meaning penetrated, or the delight of a virtue possessed. They pluck off the topmost branches when, by expounding them, they make known something that had been uncertain and hidden. They carry them into the land of Canaan when, leaving earthly works behind, they preach heavenly blessedness. They set them in the city of merchants when they speak to those who do not receive the grace of God in vain, [Col. 0953D] but bring back multiplied profit from divine talents.

Having at last tasted these things in passing, let us return to our little children, who wait with Abraham’s ass at the foot of the mountain, and again offer them the breast of their nourishment. Nurse our little child, Moses: for you have good and full breasts. Speak to him yourself; let not the Lord speak to him, lest perhaps he die through fear of his majesty. For this reason the Lord says to Moses: “You shall set bounds round about for the people, and say: Take care not to go up on the mountain or touch its boundaries; everyone who touches the mountain shall die. A hand shall not touch him, but he shall be overwhelmed with stones or pierced with darts; whether man or beast, he shall die” (Exod. 19:19).

The gracious Lord did not begrudge us the sight [Col. 0954A] of his mysteries, he who came for this purpose, that he might be seen. Therefore he speaks, that he may be heard; therefore he commands, that one may live in his commandments. Yet he instructs us where, meanwhile, the weak may stand without danger, where the heavenly gift must be awaited, until this mortal thing is swallowed up by life, or the day dawns and the day-star rises in our hearts: namely, around the mountain. There let us set our bounds, so that we establish our minds in the camps of humility and charity. Let us not climb the mountain either—that is, let us not be proud of our good deeds. For whoever touches the mountain dies, after the example of him who on the mountain of the Covenant, on the sides of the north, presumed to fly above.

No hand touches him, but he is crushed by stones or pierced with darts, because he falls rather by the weight of his own iniquity or the sharpness of devised wickedness than by the blow of divine vengeance; for the hand of God is more ready to spare, if it were possible, than to punish. Whether he be man or beast—that is, whether he has transgressed by his own judgment or another’s counsel—he shall die. A human being is governed by his own direction; a beast needs human restraint and guidance. Therefore by “man” is meant anyone discerning and wise; by “beast,” the fool who does not grasp reason.

Let the prudent person therefore restrain himself, lest he be crushed by a stone falling upon him; let the foolish be held in check, lest, striking against the stone of stumbling, he be dashed to pieces. For once an angel wished, on this account, to kill Moses’ son, [Col. 0954C] because he was not circumcised from the foreskin of pride. Zipporah immediately took a stone, circumcised the flesh of his foreskin, touched his feet with blood, and the angel left him after she had said: “You are a bridegroom of blood to me.” Accordingly, every superfluous flesh must be cut away from Moses’ son; and whoever subjects himself to the rule or law of any religious profession, unless he guards himself from violating that same law, sees the angel against him brandishing a drawn sword. But if conscience—the mother, that is, of the child—restrains unlawful impulses and draws forth the blood of sorrow through penitence, it will mitigate the wrath of the angel of the Lord. For the conscience of a religious person has a bridegroom of blood, because in the espousal of its profession it continually remembers the slain Lamb. This conscience should now nourish [Col. 0954D] the child with milk—indeed, with the pure affection of its heart; for in the future there will be a time of weaning, when the elements of childhood or instruction are abolished.

Meanwhile, let the little child become accustomed to hang by its arms about its mother’s neck; to turn its hanging and frightened face from every evil encounter toward its parent’s face; to flee all but its nurses as enemies; against every misfortune, to fly back to the breasts and lie continually in its mother’s lap. Such a one the Lord receives; such a one he guards; indeed, of such is the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 19:14). Whoever is such a one is greater in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 11:11). For one who commits himself wholly to heavenly grace hangs his arms around his mother’s neck. One who sets nothing before his eyes but Christ rightly does not fear the snares of those hunting for death. One who knows Christ alone, as though already swallowed up into God, judges himself to know nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Cor. 2:2). One who is fixed like the bars in the ark by continual meditations upon the holy Scriptures has sure comfort against every assault of demons. One who frequents the bosom of charity continually deserves the kisses of inward consolation.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Bread of the Perfect, or the Advanced

As ages differ, so do the refreshments suited to ages. Fewer, simpler, and more liquid things refresh a little child’s age; but the stomach of the perfect desires more things, and those more sacred and solid. [Col. 0955B] For a holy soul, strong through exercise in the virtues, delights in the deeper meaning of the law; but one still new in the regeneration of faith and the rudiments of God’s words is refreshed by its plainer meaning. Hence the Lord says to Aaron: “All the choicest part of oil, wine, and wheat, and whatever the children of Israel offer to the Lord as firstfruits, I have given to you” (Num. 18:12).

The marrow of oil, wine, and wheat is the most delicate food and the richest refreshment. It is received not by just anyone of the common rank and manner of life, but by one called by God like Aaron (Heb. 5:4), anointed among his brethren, and offering incense at the altar of incense as a most sweet odor to the Lord. Who else, like Paul the imitator of Christ, offers sacrifices rich with marrow? Who so pours the juice of flesh upon the rock with his hand? Who so loves God from his whole heart, his whole soul, and all his inward parts? Such a spirit passes through fire and water to God; it also runs with God into death and prison.

When the Apostles were passing with the Lord through the grainfields, they sometimes plucked, rubbed, and ate ears of grain, in signification of their heart and of this matter. To pluck ears of grain is to call back one’s own purpose or another’s mind from earthly pursuits. He does not cease to rub the plucked ear who, exercising himself in the love of God, puts off the garment of former error. Then he eats the grains who keeps himself chaste through purity of body and cleanness of soul.

[Col. 0955D] Therefore, he who is not lazy like an ass in its dung, eating the hay of luxury, nor refreshed like a luxuriant beast by the grass of vanity, but receives his allotted portion with the high priest Aaron—the bread from the fat of wheat—and with Jesus suffering on the cross, the shell stripped and the outer husk broken, receives the kernel of the nut, the marrow of oil, wine, and wheat. O marrow, eternal, creating marrow, pouring inward things into us, enriching all things by enriching the soul! But what is the marrow of oil? The power of the Holy Spirit. What is the marrow of wine? The grace of the Son of God. What, finally, is the marrow of wheat? The goodness of the Father.

O power! O grace! O goodness! Where do you dwell? What is the dwelling-place of the Spirit? What the seat of grace? What the abode of goodness? First, without doubt, you dwell principally and originally [Col. 0956A] in the most remote region of the Trinity; second, graciously and immutably in angelic spirits; third, still temporally and changeably in holy souls. In the first station you reign, but without your own exaltation or another’s oppression. In the second you help angels, but without any labor. In the third you struggle in man, but solely through mercy toward man. You are adored in the first, glorified in the second, worshipped in the third. We await the vision, not the habitation, of the first; we implore both the vision and reception of the second; we seek possession of the third now in hope, then in reality. We are enriched in remembering this oil, made drunk in drinking the wine, and satisfied in the refreshment of wheat. Oil begins us, wine advances us, wheat perfects us.

[Col. 0956B] These are the advances of charity; these are the stages of perfection. For whenever something is called perfect, it is not immediately called perfect either in a perfect or in the highest sense. “Perfect” is said in one way of man, in another of angel, and in another of God. A human being is sometimes called perfect, yet still needs to be perfected. An angel too is called perfect: not indeed needing perfection, but made perfect. But God is called perfect neither as needing to be perfected nor as having been made perfect, but as always existing perfect.

God therefore fills the inward parts of imperfection, both angelic and human, from the marrow of his perfection. He fills the angel at once in such a way that it needs no further filling; but he continually fills man in such a way that, unless he continually fills him, man becomes empty. For the marrow of grace poured by God into man flows out through the cracks of sin in the course of mortality. But angelic nature, made firm in crystalline stability, now possesses without possibility of loss whatever grace it holds. God himself, however, is eternally altogether full and perfect as the whole God: he is never made, nor will he become, better or more perfect. Do not believe that God will be poorer if you depart, or richer if you draw near. Your approach benefits you; your withdrawal harms you. You provide nothing for the Most Excellent; you give nothing to the Most High. If he receives something from you or through you, he receives what is his; likewise, if you withdraw, he does not lose what is his but disposes it otherwise. Without God an angel becomes a demon; without God a human being is reduced to nothing. With God the angel is already eternally [Col. 0956D] beatified; with God man is justified in the present and glorified in the future. The angel is drawn into God, present through vision; man, absent, through contemplation.

The angel clings to God without interruption; man sighs without interruption. The one stands; the other fluctuates. The one rejoices; this one wails. The one sings; this one weeps. The one abounds in delights; this one in miseries. Yet both are called to the banquet, though differently: the one from near at hand, the other from far away. Both are clothed with a robe, but it already hangs from the one’s neck, while the other still trembles in expectation of things to come. Both are absorbed by glory: the former from the brightness of creation into the brightness of confirmation; the latter from forgiveness of sins into the true justification of the saints.

Both feed upon one bread; but the former upon it whole in divinity, the latter upon it divided into fragments of sacraments, in humanity. For the angel receives incorporeally the impassible divinity; man receives sacramentally the impassible humanity, and, according to the difference of their kingdoms, receives the satisfaction of his desire—as one reigning and the other exiled. For when you faithfully recall the incarnation, you set a good fragment of bread to your mouth; when the Passion, you do likewise. But when you set before yourself the resurrection or ascension, you eat, as it were, morsels rich with marrow or honey. Hence the Bride, well nourished upon the dishes of these mysteries, belching forth and exulting in praises, says: “I ate my honeycomb with my honey; I drank my wine with my milk” (Song 5:1). In the milk is understood the incarnation; in the wine, the Passion; in the honeycomb, the resurrection; in the honey, the sweetness [Col. 0957B] of the ascension.

These are our portions in you and from you, Jesus. Since we cannot receive you wholly at once, from what is indivisible we have received divided portions of grace—if indeed anyone may dare call the sacraments of your dispensation “portions.” Otherwise it would have been fitting for us to comprehend God; but it did not otherwise befit God to teach our infancy. He chose not to spare himself when he wished, O man, to feed you from himself: he is the great God, exalted above all things. But what are you? A little worm, scarcely lifting yourself from the earth; “a land without water” (Ps. 14:26), producing only dust.

He remained in the retirement of his divinity; you had fled into the hiding place of iniquity. Yet the Exalted One descended; the Distant One came to your hiding place; he entered your little hut and placed his shoulder beneath you. He was burdened, not by the weight of iniquity, but by the obstinacy of one refusing to be healed. Nevertheless, “Wisdom conquers malice” (Wisdom 7:30), and patience conquers stubbornness. Therefore your failure, restored, began to advance toward perfection.

But so long as we endure the weakness of nature, wasting away through daily decline, and groan also under the sentence of the first curse, we are in every respect held short of consummate perfection. Properly and specifically, perfection is not said to exist where some imperfection still remains. Nor is virtue perfected while remnants of vices are found still alive. Who, while the corruption of human life remains, will boast that he has a chaste heart? The Prophet? Yet he declares that he was conceived from unclean seed, and confesses that he was conceived by his mother in iniquities (the citation appears as Job 14:4). The Apostle? Yet he said that he offended in many things. A patriarch, or any soul of the human race? Yet God “shut up all under sin, that he might have mercy upon all” (Rom. 11:32). Moreover, that pipe of the Holy Spirit, crowned with every kind of virtue and already almost above humanity, deservedly placed alongside an angel in merit and virtue, cries out concerning his imperfection: “Brothers, I do not consider that I have apprehended; but one thing: forgetting what lies behind, I stretch toward what lies before” (Phil. 3:13), “and pursue the prize of the heavenly calling.”

Where now are you, O presumption of spirit, O swelling bladder of an erring heart? Why do you boast, earth and ashes? [Col. 0958A] (Ecclus. 10:9). Paul, in whose bosom the overflowing abundance of all virtues is gathered as water into the sea, says: “Perfection in good things is not with me”; and you, a well springing up with vices, dare to whine: “I am without sin.” “We have heard the pride of Moab: he is exceedingly proud; his arrogance is greater than his strength” (Isa. 16:6). For he alone, uniquely, is “free among the dead” (Ps. 87:6): Jesus Christ, who assumed nature but not guilt, conceived of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, and fulfilled all righteousness.

Finally, in his breast and soul, the King of virtues himself assembled the court of every grace; honored individually by each and jointly by all, he brought back to the Father the one palm of all. Therefore he who filled our vessels not only from his fullness but also from his self-emptying, always perfect God, was also perfect God and man from conception. At the feet of his humanity the twenty-four elders continually fall down and cast their crowns (Rev. 4:10), because all the saints humbly acknowledge that they possess from him every merit and reward. Do you wish to have righteousness? Do you wish to have wisdom? Do you wish to have grace? Jesus is righteousness; Jesus is wisdom; Jesus is grace. For, speaking of Christ, the Apostle says: “He was made for us by God wisdom and righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (the citation appears as 1 Cor. 13:30).

Behold, this bread is one and has, if one may so speak, four quarters. For one and the same Christ is wisdom; one and the same is righteousness; one and the same is sanctification; [Col. 0958C] one and the same is redemption. Therefore, because he is wisdom, he illumines the dark hearts of fools with the light of true wisdom; because he is righteousness, he justifies those weighed down by the burdens of sin and malice; because he is sanctification, he sanctifies those unstable and wandering down the slopes of vain glory; because he is redemption, he has redeemed those carried away or borne off into places of virtue and reproach. “Blessed is the man who has fulfilled his desire from these; for he shall not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate” (Ps. 126:5).

## CHAPTER VII. On the Breads of Firstfruits

As I am about to treat of the breads of firstfruits, I first invoke the firstfruits of the Spirit; for without the Spirit of God my spirit fails everywhere and in all things. Therefore, in the principal Spirit, enlightened however little, not by merit but by gratuitous gift, I shall speak also on this subject what I have been taught from the treasury of the Scriptures.

The subsistence of the creaturely universe has one principle from which it exists: God. For whatever is, does not exist from itself; and whatever is, is good. For that alone exists from itself which exists in the highest degree—that is, the Creator. But that which does not exist from itself can exist only from him who exists in the highest degree. Evil does not exist, because it neither creates itself nor was created by God; and nothing exists unless it is either Creator or creature. Therefore evil does not exist, because it is neither Creator nor creature. Accordingly, whatever has a temporal beginning must be referred to the one beginning without beginning, so that it may also have an appropriate end.
