[Col. 0959A] For then a good end follows upon any action when the creature’s beginning has not turned away from the creating Beginning. Indeed, the works of human beings are innumerable, yet, if they are good, they have one good and eternal beginning. For unless every particular beginning of some will is derived from the beginning of the divine will, it will always be evil and will end in a most evil end. Therefore one must always return, in and from all things, from a beginning to the Beginning. This Beginning “was in the beginning with God” (John 1); it was the Word of the Beginning and the beginning of every word.

Let us therefore borrow a word from the Word, but a passing word from the eternal Word; a beginning from the Beginning, but a created beginning from the uncreated. Perhaps the lawgiver gives this instruction when he says that a man should ask from his friend and a woman from her neighbor vessels of gold and silver (Exod. 3:22). For who is such a rich friend as God in the gold of good meanings, so wealthy in the silver of examined discourse, so abundant in vessels of heavenly graces? Surely he showed himself a friend to our poverty when, because of the exceeding charity with which he loved us, he decreed that his only-begotten Son should be incarnate (Eph. 2:4). And lest you complain that this friend—God, of course—remains most remote in his divinity, you have near you divine Wisdom incarnate, exceedingly rich in vessels of gold and silver.

For he brought vessels most pure and precious from heaven, and likewise took such vessels from earth, [Col. 0959C] in which he might dine and drink the food of the Father’s will. Without doubt, angels ministering and Apostles serving the incarnate Word, Wisdom hidden in the flesh—what else are they but the golden and silver vessels of our friend and neighbor? And perhaps the lawgiver prefigured this incarnation in the Lord’s dispensation, accomplished by the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin, when he said: “Two loaves of firstfruits, baked from two tenths of fine flour, for the firstfruits of the Lord” (Lev. 23:17).

For what are the two loaves of firstfruits, made from two tenths of leavened fine flour, except two pure and perfect natures inseparably united in the one person of Christ Jesus? Here leaven signifies not the coagulating agent of corruption, but the operation of inseparable union. These loaves are baked as the firstfruits of the Lord because the same person, God and man, in both his joined natures, is called and believed by the Catholic Church to be the firstborn, or firstfruits, of those who sleep.

In the nature of divinity he was born from the Father before all things; in the nature of humanity he was brought forth from the Virgin at the end of the ages. Certainly these loaves were baked in the oven of that same Virgin, because the Word and the flesh were so united to one another in the virginal womb, in one and the same unity of person, that afterward he was no longer called separately man or God, but was called one person, inseparably God and man. According to Moses, there are indeed two loaves because of the unchangeability of the natures, for they remained without confusion. The divine nature has the Father as its principle, from a principle yet without a beginning; the human nature has the Virgin as its principle, together with a beginning of existence. Nevertheless, there is one loaf because of one and the same person, according to the Apostle, who says: “One bread, [Col. 0960A] one body are we many in Christ” (1 Cor. 10:17).

But why does Moses call Christ two loaves and Paul one loaf? With faith and the authority of the Fathers preserved, it may be said, as it seems to me, that in Moses’ time the incarnation of Christ had not yet been accomplished in fact. Therefore those natures were, as it were, two loaves: one existing in its majesty and that of the Father, the other not yet appearing in its own essence; joined only by predestination, not yet by assumption or union. But in Paul’s time—that is, the time of grace, for he was called after the Lord’s ascension—after the assumption of humanity by the Word had already been accomplished, the one and same person of Christ, subsisting from two and in two natures, divine and human, was eminent in apostolic preaching. Therefore Paul, attending to the person, not undeservedly says “one”; Moses, beholding the two natures, names two loaves. The former does not divide the person; the latter does not confuse the natures.

It must also be observed and carefully explained what the lawgiver says beforehand: “When you have entered the land which I shall give you and have reaped the harvest, you shall bring sheaves of ears, the firstfruits of your harvest, to the priest, who shall raise the bundle before the Lord, that it may be acceptable for you on the day after the Sabbath” [Col. 0960C] (Lev. 23:10). The literal sense is plain. Allegorically, we enter the land that he will give us when through faith we enter the Church, communion with which we deserve only by heavenly calling; or whose possession we shall have much more worthily in the other life than now, because then we shall possess face to face the reality itself which now we perceive dimly, with veiled face, through a mirror and in an enigma (1 Cor. 13:12).

We reap the harvest when we receive the reward of good works. We carry sheaves of ears to the priest when we entrust to him who intercedes for us with the Father our collection of virtues in good action. He raises the bundle before the Lord, that it may be acceptable for us on the day after the Sabbath, because, in order that the Father may be gracious toward us and may come favorably on the day after the Sabbath—that is, in the common resurrection—he lifts up before the Father’s eyes the bundle of our merits together with his intercession.

Morally, however, we enter the land when we examine the recesses of conscience. We gather the harvest when we weigh the works of our past life in the judgment of examination. We carry sheaves of ears to the priest when, in full and clear confession, we humbly disclose to our prelates grains together with ears and straw. By the grains are also signified good thoughts or works. The priest raises this bundle before the Lord when our superior, to whom we have entrusted our soul and disclosed every burden, effectively retains in his memory and prayer the weight of our sins set forth in confession, asking God concerning them [Col. 0961A] and obtaining God’s propitiation.

But if present confession or penitence is not sufficient, because of the sudden moment of death, for the sins committed to be at once wholly erased, at least on the day after the Sabbath may our God be made gracious toward us. “On the day after the Sabbath,” he says. Therefore there are two Sabbaths, one and another. Truly, already resting from evil is one and the first Sabbath of the mind, which must without doubt be possessed necessarily in the present. For in the future, from such merit, there will be rest in good, which is Sabbath from Sabbath. Then, I say, you will find not merely Sabbath, because there is rest without disturbance from all troubles, but Sabbatism.

Accordingly, we must proceed briefly, and, with God’s help, say something about the first, second, and third Sabbath. In this body, when one ceases from evil, there is already a certain foretaste of the future Sabbath. When the soul leaves the body and departs this life, it already rejoices in the second repose. Finally, at the coming of the Judge, the Sabbath-rest is celebrated in the renewal of soul and body. Yet six days of affliction precede the coming of the seventh day of rest. For Moses says: “For six days you shall do work” (Exod. 20:10); “the seventh day, because it is the rest of the Sabbath, shall be called holy: you shall do no work on it; it is the Sabbath of the Lord in all your dwellings” (Lev. 23:3) [Col. 0961C]. The first day is conversion; the second, confession; the third, profession; the fourth, mortification; the fifth, devotion; the sixth, prayer; the seventh, calling—or contemplation. For we do not gather the harvest of contemplation unless we have first sown the fruits of righteousness; nor does one rest on the seventh day who has not laboured in the preceding six. We must therefore apply ourselves to the virtues and advance from the confusion of original darkness to the illumination, or ordering, of new creations, if we wish to continue Sabbath unto Sabbath. Thus, on the first day the one turned away should be converted; on the second, the one denying should confess; on the third, the offender should profess that sin lives in our body; on the fourth, the ungrateful person should be mortified [Col. 0961D]; on the fifth, the hard heart that sins should become devout; on the sixth, our conscience should pour itself out in prayer, away from worldly care; on the seventh, it should be lulled to rest.

First imitate Paul in conversion; second, the thief in confession; third, Stephen in profession; fourth, John the Baptist in mortification; fifth, Mary Magdalene in the outpouring of tears; sixth, the holy apostles in prayer; seventh, Christ in contemplation. In conversion possess humility; in confession, truth; in profession, steadfastness; in mortification, patience; in devotion of the body, remembrance of sins and the strictness of the future judgment; in prayer, a good conscience and unfeigned faith; in contemplation, forgetfulness of all visible things [Col. 0962A]. If, with righteousness going before and directing your steps, your soul orders the days of life in this manner, it is not fitting to labour further. For: “Does the ploughman plough all day, breaking up and harrowing his ground? Does he not, when he has levelled the surface of the earth, sow nigella and scatter cumin?” (Isa. 28:24). When sufficient labour has been expended in rooting out thorns, cutting up the ground, shaking rocks, and levelling mountains and valleys, then nigella must be sown through leisure; then cumin must be scattered through subtle contemplation. And perhaps contemplation involves a certain labour—but one better than rest, sweeter than leisure, more delightful than sleep, and more pleasing than every pleasure. It is labour, I say, yet without sweat; work, yet without vexation; occupation [Col. 0962B], yet without distraction; study, yet without affliction; progress, yet without movement; elevation, yet without ambition; rest, yet without rust.

The soul, an imitator of the works of its Lord and God, and likewise an emulator of the wisdom of the Most High, made effective amid so great a variety of virtues, works with Him who works and rests with Him who rests. It has within itself God working; it has Him resting; and it itself works in Him who works, rests in Him who rests, works in Him who rests, and rests in Him who works. For God does not fail to rest when He works: He works while resting, lest He be called idle; He rests while working, lest He be thought wearied by labour. When you labour, you do not rest; and when you rest, you do not labour, because you change in time and times change in you. But it is not so with the Almighty; it is not so with the Eternal, because, being unchangeable, He changes all things and creates all things at once by the power of His will alone [Col. 0962C]. For when God is said to labour, something is said of Him according to us, not according to Himself. Likewise, when He is said to have rested on the seventh day—although He daily works for us all and all that is ours, and one who does anything can never properly be said to rest—He is not properly said to have rested according to the manner of our rest. That activity, or that repose, of the Creator is beyond every understanding; for that activity surpasses every rest in tranquillity, and that repose shines forth in its effect as more productive than every activity. Therefore let the action or repose of our contemplation be fashioned, however in very distant outlines, after this exemplar [Col. 0962D], and let it be enticed to emulation, however with very slow steps, so that it may rest while acting and act while resting. These things do not occur in shadow or in night, but in day, in light, in the sun of righteousness; for one snoring in the night of vices knows nothing of the light of contemplation.

Why indeed would this day be called holy unless the work of righteousness were performed on it? “You shall do no work on it!” Again and again we are warned not to perform work on the Sabbath—but, of course, servile work, condemnable work, bestial work. It is only from those things by which the joy of solemn observances is defiled that one must refrain in observing the Sabbath. For luxury, drunkenness, talkativeness, and similar shameful deeds are the dung of solemnities. Thus Pharaoh, thus Herod, defiled their Sabbaths [Col. 0963A] with the blood of cruelty. He says that no such work is to be done on the Sabbath, because it is the Sabbath in all your dwellings. Let the eye withdraw from indecent spectacles; the tongue from evil-speaking words; the ear from hearing bloodshed; the smell from strange odours; the hand from deeds of cruelty; the foot from the company of a thief; the soul from perverse thoughts. Thus the Sabbath of the Lord shall be celebrated in all your dwellings. But once the Sabbath of present justification has passed, one passes to the Sabbath of future consolation, just as Mary Magdalene came from the Sabbath of the Passion to the Sabbath of the Resurrection. The souls of the blessed know their Sabbath; without doubt they know the difference between being girded for spiritual wickedness and being ungirded [Col. 0963B] from the troubles of the flesh and the assaults of demons, as is written in the Book of Kings: “Let not him who is girded boast as one ungirded” (3 Kings 10:11). For he securely rejoices in the gift to whom it has been granted that nothing can take it away in everlasting reward; but he dangerously exults in the gift to whom greater anxiety increases together with the gift. For the bestowal of graces makes you more exposed to envy; for whose envy is kindled by your poverty? When no glory of virtue adorns you, there is no reason to fear the arrows of an adversary. But if a place of honour has raised you too ambitiously, if your shining reputation has spread your name among all nations, then the edge of envy is sharpened; then the flattering face of a false friend is changed into the blackness of a scorched pot [Col. 0963C] (Nah. 2:10).

It is therefore miserable, in accordance with the condition of mortality and the place of unhappiness, either to lack envy because of a poverty of virtues, or to be envied because of an abundance of graces. The righteous fear being pierced by either dagger, or even by one alone; for if some are without virtues, they are tormented by conscience, whereas if they are full of virtues, the wrath of demons burns against them. Hence they very often feel their Sabbath attacked or mocked by enemies. Thus the prophet says: “The enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths” (Lam. 1:7). But those who have flown free of these shackles, whose hunters’ snares have been broken, and who have escaped sudden dangers, now placed beneath the altar, sound forth with a triumphant voice: “Glory to you, Lord, because you have rescued our souls [Col. 0963D] from death and our feet from falling, that we may please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 114:8–9). For now winter has passed and gone; flowers have appeared; the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land (Song 2:12). Thus, I say, freed from past things, blessed in present things, and to be made still more blessed in future things, they rejoice without anxiety, feast without weariness, and delight without sin. They savour all the more sweetly because they now taste—or rather, anticipate—the torrents of blessedness more eagerly; they love more dearly because they perceive the splendours of the saints more clearly; they are more fittingly disposed because they stand immaculate in the circumscribed lights of the Trinity more blessedly. Who but such persons keep Sabbath? Who but such persons celebrate splendid solemnities? O Sabbath from Sabbath! O reward of virtues! Let my soul enter into you; let my conscience penetrate [Col. 0964A] you. For this Sabbath truly proceeds from Sabbath, when, because the soul has ceased from evil, a good recompense is made to it. Hence the Psalmist says: “Thus will I sing a psalm to your name for ever and ever, that I may render my vows from day to day” (Ps. 60:9)—that is, from the day of merits to the day of rewards.

Much remains to be said concerning the condition of the second Sabbath; but because it is far from the knowledge of this age of ours, we can sigh for it, not explain it. Now at last, therefore, let us move our foot and advance our mind from this place to the Sabbath-rest. This advance alone is to be sought, because none better than it can be found in all creation; for worldly advancement is rather removal or destruction from God. Yet this progress does not occur except in a place set apart for it [Col. 0964B], and in a human being chosen by God. Moses desires to behold this vision in the wilderness. What he sees is beyond the ordinary, and what he hears is above the ordinary. The bush burns but is not consumed. He sees this and marvels; then he hears: “Remove the sandal from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground; I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3:5; Matt. 22:32). He hears this and hides his face. O what a difference between the bush and heaven, between the flame of the bush and the glory of heaven, between the one speaking from the bush and the one reigning upon the throne, between the solitude of the desert and the fellowship of paradise, between Moses the stranger and the new human being seated in heaven! If Moses feared its shadow [Col. 0964C], who would dare approach the very light? Moses, however, while shod, was able to see the bush; but, until unshod, he could not long hear the Lord’s voice.

Quickly, therefore, must the strap of the sandal be loosened when we stretch toward things above. Let no pleasure of sin bind us, no habit of sinning constrain us, no worldly care impede us. The mind entangled in these things will be able neither to see nor to hear what God is. Why, then, is He called the God of Abraham? Why the God of Isaac? Why the God of Jacob? Without doubt because those patriarchs, faithful, obedient, and wandering, showed forth God: obedient in commandment, believing in promise, estranged from the world in name, deed, speech, and affection. Therefore let not the dwelling of this body delight you [Col. 0964D]; let not the difficulty of the commandment delay you; let not the postponement of the promise make you slothful, if you wish to possess the God who is the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. Remove the sandal; break the bond from your feet—from the affection and desire of the mind. Thus unburdened, you will in some manner taste the surface of the other world beforehand; thus released, you will in some manner dream an image of eternity; thus free, you will attempt, as though in a prelude, to touch the beginnings of the future state. O God, what do You do there? What does an angel do? What does a soul do? What words do You speak to an angel? What conversations do You hold with a soul? What, and concerning what, do angel and soul set before You? Is there anything they may ask when You openly reveal to them all things concerning the Father? Is there anything they do not know about the future, have forgotten about the past [Col. 0965A], or cannot grasp about the present? What is closed there? What is not opened?

But why should anything be concealed there, when all friends are present and all enemies absent? Envy touches no one; pride exalts no one; anger does not disturb; luxury does not tempt; gluttony does not press; ambition does not torment. Every vice is absent; every evil wastes away and languishes by failing or fleeing. Harmony reigns everywhere; humility moves through each dwelling-place; goodwill sits in the midst; chastity stands prominent in the towers; sobriety orders all things wisely, administering to each person sufficient provision, adequately and at will; health guards the gates; charity, or goodness, illuminates all stations and tents. The soul is led into the refectory, where it is refreshed without hunger, made drunk without thirst, and says: “He has placed me in a place of pasture” (Ps. 22:2) [Col. 0965B]. Into the dormitory, that there it may sleep without sluggishness and say: “In peace, in the selfsame place, I shall sleep and rest” (Ps. 4:6). Into the oratory, that there it may pray without weariness and say: “To you will I pray, O Lord; in the morning you will hear my voice” (Ps. 5:4). Into the cloister, that there it may sit without disgust and say: “You have protected me in the shadow of your wings” (Ps. 16:8), or: “I sat in the shadow that I had desired” (Song 2:3). Into the chapter-house, that there it may observe discipline without fear and say: “Your discipline itself will teach me” (Ps. 13:31) [citation as printed]. Into the lecture-room, that there it may live without transgression. The breast of Jesus is there the refectory; the bosom of Jesus is there the dormitory; the countenance of Jesus is there the oratory; the breadth [Col. 0965C], length, height, and depth of Jesus are there the cloister; the fellowship of Jesus and of all the blessed is there the chapter-house; Jesus’ discourses concerning the unity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and concerning the unveiling of the mystery of His incarnation, are there the lecture-room.

O human heart, why do you stretch further? Why do you seek further? For to stretch further is not to stretch but to strain, or rather to tear yourself apart through overextension. O human heart, why do you linger below, if you wish not to die? Death is below and above, although there is nothing above. For death strikes the one who presumes to ascend above—not because death itself dwells above, for it is in hell, but because by divine vengeance it kills the one who exceeds the bounds set for him. The name of death, the name of sickness, the name of poverty, the name of anxiety [Col. 0965D], the name of pain, are not even named among you, citizens of heaven and members of God’s household. What then is there? Life, delight, jubilation, exultation, glorification, blessedness, eternity, immortality, and incorruption abound and overflow in paradise. In the mouths of its inhabitants are always praise, alleluia, glory, peace, blessing, honour, power, and strength. What do their eyes see except the Father of lights, light from light, the radiance of eternal light? What do their ears hear except the praises of God? What do their nostrils breathe except the fragrances of life? What do their hands touch except the Word of life? By what path do their feet walk except the way of peace? What of taste? It tastes indeed how sweet the Lord is (Ps. 33:9). Why say more? In the single clause which says [Col. 0966A] that “God will be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:39), all the gifts of that blessedness are contained. Arise, my soul; run and hasten to enter such nuptials! Turn and change your desires! You were accustomed to gaze with pleasure upon a beautiful prostitute; gaze now upon the Mother of God. Gold pleased you: let what is true please you now. You sought silver: seek now the Only-Begotten of God. You delighted in human favour: now be refreshed by the divine Spirit. Put aside pleasures of the flesh and take up pleasures of the mind. Behold how you will keep Sabbath—not merely keep Sabbath, but keep Sabbath with Sabbath-rest. Let this suffice concerning the twofold Sabbath.

## Chapter VIII. Again, concerning the loaves of firstfruits

Because, avoiding excessive length, we could not explain in one discourse what had to be said concerning firstfruits—especially because the intervening Sabbath compelled us to keep Sabbath in its own subject—we shall again attempt, with the Lord’s assent, and yet not with an unrelated sense or beginning, to add and set forth something further concerning both firstfruits and tithes [Col. 0966B]. Thus we read in Exodus: “You shall not delay to offer your tithes and your firstfruits. You shall give me the firstborn of your sons; you shall do likewise with oxen and sheep. For seven days it shall be with its mother; on the eighth day you shall render it to me” (Exod. 22:29). The two worthier and more important extremities of the human being are those called head and feet. By one part, namely the head, the human being figuratively looks toward heaven; by the other, he touches the earth. Hence, just as in this world earth and heaven embrace, as it were in their arms and lap, the extent of all creatures and the diverse distinction of innumerable things [Col. 0966C], so in the human being head and feet are the pillars and support of all human limbs. By an apt signification, drawn through likeness from visible things to invisible, the soul possesses both parts in its affection: for in every movement and willing it always principally intends something, and always finally tends toward something. The head of the human will is that at which it particularly aims; the feet are the end toward which it tends.

Therefore, so that the Lord may teach the human being what he ought to intend in willing and toward what he ought to tend in acting, He indicates this in saying: “You shall not delay to offer your tithes and firstfruits”; as though He said: Dedicate as tithes to the Lord your God the beginning and end, the initiation and completion, of your thoughts, words, and deeds [Col. 0966D]. When, therefore, one’s desire burns more ardently to fulfil its own lusts than to obey the divine commandments, that person’s firstfruits or tithes are by no means rendered to the Lord but are poured out to an idol. When earthly things rather than heavenly, temporal rather than eternal things, are sought more zealously—when what belongs to divine right is set aside and what belongs to oneself is preferred—human presumption, through a perverse order, abuses firstfruits and tithes. But if you consecrate to God your firstborn, or firstfruits, by seeking first the kingdom of God and His righteousness (Matt. 6:33), you will rejoice in the stream of blessing in all that follows. For as the Apostle says: “If the first portion is holy, so is the whole mass” (Rom. 11:16); and the Lord says in the Gospel: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light” (Matt. 6:22). And the Psalmist: “If I do not prefer Jerusalem,” etc. (Ps. 136:6) [Col. 0967A].

Let God the Father have, together with the firstborn of His wisdom, the firstborn of your devotion, so that the firstborn of the creature may be sanctified by the Creator’s Firstborn. For why did the Firstborn of the Father become the firstborn of a mother, except that He might redeem for Himself every firstborn of humankind? Blessed is the one whose firstborn God accepts. For He destroys the firstborn of Egypt and rejects the firstborn of asses; but He takes to Himself the firstborn of a human being, the firstborn of sheep and ox. Whether, then, you are wise as a human being, strong as an ox [Col. 0967B], or simple as a sheep, you must pay the firstfruits of your heart and the firstborn of your work. But if you are impious like an Egyptian, unclean like an ass, useless like a heretic, your firstborn must be changed, killed, or redeemed. Paul changed—or rather killed—the firstborn of Egypt, when from persecutor he became preacher, a lamb from a wolf, a Christian from a Jew. Did not Mary Magdalene kill the firstborn of the ass when she washed the filth of her crimes at the fountain, changed her life, and loved Christ? She changed the firstborn of the ass and received the firstborn of God. But Judas not only failed to pay God his firstborn; he even stole from God the Father His own Firstborn and Only-Begotten. Therefore he passed over into the devil’s firstborn, because [Col. 0967C] he transgressed against God’s Firstborn. Most deceitful Judas, is it too little for you to have committed fraud concerning your own soul, unless you add sacrilegious hands laid upon the very bowels of God’s mercy? Is it too little for you to have offered your own throat to the devil, unless you also cut the throat of our Lord? Is it too little, I say, for you to have lost your reward, unless you also took away the price of our ransom? You would have done far better to remain a disciple of Christ than to emerge as a master of Antichrist.

Do not delay, O religious soul, to render your firstborn, so that you may love God with all your heart and with all your soul. Yet let it remain with its mother for seven days, so that you may remember not to depart this life except with fullness of grace. For seven days it remains with its mother, who never errs in faith, never fails in hope, never grows cold in charity, never turns aside from justice, never departs from prudence, never succumbs in courage, and never exceeds measure in temperance [Col. 0967D]. For seven days it remains with its mother, who is whole in faith and conduct; for seven days it remains with its mother, who is with the Lord unto the shedding of blood; for seven days it remains with its mother, whose conscience has never been stained by crimes; for seven days it remains with its mother, who has never crossed the bounds of obedience. “But on the eighth day you shall render it to me”: that you may believe Christ rose from the dead. “On the eighth day you shall render it to me”: that you may believe in the future resurrection of all human beings on the day of judgment. “On the eighth day you shall render it to me” (Exod. [Col. 0968A] 22:30): that you may believe that after judgment both the rewards of the good and the torments of the evil will never end. “On the eighth day you shall render it to me”: that you may believe the merits of each person will be requited by the reward of the eight beatitudes. By believing and living thus, you will attain the firstfruits of eternity.

In the beheading—or rather, the gathering—of the holy Innocents, the Church has firstfruits most pleasing to God. For as is read in the Apocalypse of John: “These were purchased from among all people as firstfruits to God and to the Lamb, and no lie was found in their mouths” (Rev. 14:4). The good seed had already burst forth from the ground of the virginal womb, but had not yet grown into a great tree, because the sound of the apostles had not yet gone forth into all the earth (Rom. 10:18). Yet Bethlehem and its neighbouring places offered the firstfruits of flowers and did not delay to render little palm branches [Col. 0968B]. Truly, a field of firstfruits in which the firstfruits of martyrs were found so quickly! Christ’s Passion had not yet occurred, and already the blood of an innocent little child was shed for Christ. In a manner, our firstfruits run before Your firstfruits, O Christ. They truly run before You in dying before You, but they do not run before You in coming to the kingdom without You. They will wait for You at the gate, because the guards will not open the heavenly doors unless they see You. Thus, in the suffering of blood, not in the possession of blessedness, the little lambs precede their shepherd. But if they precede, how is it true that “they follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. 14:4)? Both are nevertheless true: they precede and they follow. They precede in death; they follow in resurrection. They began to run earlier, but stopped in the race [Col. 0968C].

## Chapter IX. On the loaves of the Presence

Because the loaves of the Presence are commanded to be made from fine flour, grace must be borrowed and the conscience of the mind cleansed. But from whom is grace to be borrowed or received, except from Him who, full of truth and grace, was born of a mother full of grace? O Jesus, You possess grace in the vein, not in the bottle; in the well, not in the pitcher; in the womb, not in the skin; in the soul, not in the cistern; in the fountain, not in the vessel! Waters indeed flow impetuously from Lebanon (Song 4:15); but graces flow forth gently and abundantly from Your Spirit [Col. 0968D]. If fine flour is lacking, where will the loaves of the Presence be? If grace is lacking, where will there be hope of salvation? There is no bran in fine flour, because the spirit of pretence is far from grace. Fine flour is shaken out from the purest grains, and grace flows from the richest marrow of God’s mercies. Let Moses receive fine flour from the children of Israel; let us implore grace from the Lord God of Israel. It is little for Moses to receive fine flour if there is no one to make the loaves of the Presence; and it is little for us to receive grace if we do not follow through with the effects of its working. Therefore let many loaves be made from the received flour; let many virtues proceed from the bestowed grace. Let a loaf be made from two tenths; let virtue arise from the root of twofold love.

But we must examine, and ponder with the utmost attention [Col. 0969A], what the Lord commands in Leviticus concerning the loaves of the Presence: “You shall take fine flour and bake from it twelve loaves, each having two tenths; six of them you shall set on each side upon the purest table before the Lord, and you shall place upon them the brightest frankincense, that the loaves may be a memorial of an offering to the Lord. On every Sabbath they shall be changed before the Lord, received from the children of Israel by an everlasting covenant; and they shall belong to Aaron and his sons, that they may eat them in a holy place, because it is the Holy of Holies, from the sacrifices of the Lord, by a perpetual right” (Lev. 24:5–9). These Mosaic mysteries demand clean ears, purified lips, a pure conscience, and an honourable rather than death-dealing voice—how much more the Christian mysteries? I hear fine flour; I hear a most pure table; I hear brightest frankincense [Col. 0969B]; I hear “in a holy place”; I hear “Holy of Holies”: all these things are expressed in the superlative of purity. Nor is this surprising, for the dignity of the material from which the loaves are made, the name of the person for whom they are made, the manner in which they are made, the number by which they are distinguished, the place in which they are set, the time when they are taken, and the arrangement in which they are ordered are filled with most sacred meaning. What is the material? Surely fine flour. Whose loaves are they? Aaron’s and his sons’. What is the method of making them? They are made and baked separately, two by two, from two tenths of fine flour. What is their number? Twelve. What is their place? Certainly a holy one. When are they set out or removed? On the Sabbath. What is the order of their placement? Six are set on each side upon the purest table before the Lord [Col. 0969C], and brightest frankincense is placed upon them.

Now the mysteries hidden within almost speak of themselves. Indeed, they shine with such great splendour even in their outward covering, and by that external shadowing they sparkle with a certain token of inward goodness and beauty. Yet with what daring could I, poor in intellect, sluggish in service, tiresome in speech, strip the veiled things bare or reveal the hidden things? Certainly this subject suffers great damage if it is treated or handled negligently by an unlearned person. It is more useful for suitable and fruitful material to be kept untouched than for it to be badly confused and emptied by the craftsman’s incompetence. Yet now, let the pen speak what the mind feels: John the Evangelist, the eagle of great wings [Col. 0969D], investigating in most exalted flight even the most remote mysteries of God, found in the divine storehouse twelve loaves of the Presence upon the purest table. For he heard the number and names of the twelve sealed sons of Israel. Perhaps these are the loaves of the Presence whose deeds and sayings are set before posterity as patterns and examples of action to be imitated; who, both in themselves and in their deeds, unquestionably marked out traits of virtue greatly to be noticed and retained; and who deliberately left for us poor people—labouring after their footsteps in the field of this life—the ears of their examples. For works of virtue sufficiently feed with inexhaustible nourishment both their author and the imitators of their author. The more tasters of virtue arrive [Col. 0970A], the richer the remaining abundance always becomes; and as guests arrive, the hand of charity becomes more lavish toward all.

Why does each tribe of the patriarchs have so great a multitude of children that it has twelve thousand sealed, except because true virtue, with barrenness removed, propagates even to a thousand generations? For Judah’s offspring of virtue grows as numerous as there are imitators of confession. Reuben begets as many as he enlightens to understand their works. As many arise from Gad as gird themselves against temptation. Asher bears as many children as he makes blessed; Naphtali propagates those whose hearts he enlarges; from Manasseh are born those who forget the world. Simeon has as heirs and survivors those whom he leaves as witnesses of past evils [Col. 0970B]. Levi recognizes as his generation that which daily adds new exercises of virtue. Issachar declares a bosom (sinus) for one to whom the reward of eternal recompense is set before him. From Zebulun’s womb has come forth the one who has chosen the dwelling-place of strength. He who grows in increase remembers that he was born from Joseph. The one who always seeks God’s right hand takes his origin from Benjamin’s stock. Behold how Joseph filled his brothers’ sacks with good and excellent grain, and even stuffed their asses with it.

Truly, Joseph, our salvation is in your hand! Give us food, that we may be able to live; give us seedbeds, by whose blessings we may water and enrich the dry and southern land. For one who has seed from you possesses the shoot of blessing. Your seed grows rich in the root, swells in the stem, puts forth leaves or blossoms at the summit [Col. 0970C]. In its shadow is life, in its taste health, in its scent medicine, in its appearance delight. All the remedies of preachers are strengthened by the richness of this root, never grow old through the greenness of its leaves, and grow green anew through the beauty of its flowers. Thus, though exhausted, faith puts forth leaves in the soul, hope blossoms, and charity is enriched. Faith, I say, puts forth leaves in the soul through discernment of what is to be understood, opined, and believed. For one thing is what is opined, another what is believed, another what is understood. Thus hope blossoms through a tasting of future rewards [Col. 0970D]; thus charity is enriched in the fullness of innumerable graces. If a human being sows these three grains in the field of his heart, they will yield fruit: one thirtyfold, another sixtyfold, another a hundredfold. And if their flour is ground by the upper and lower millstones—that is, God’s grace and human capacity—and kneaded with the dew of heaven and the richness of earth—that is, faith in the Word and in His humanity—it can supply from itself the two tenths of love for God and neighbour, from which the twelve loaves of the Presence are baked separately, two by two.

Each of them must have two tenths. For in every human purpose, unless love of God and neighbour intervenes, a loaf of the Presence made from two tenths does not exist. Therefore, if in charity, like Judah, you have confessed your sins, you make the first loaf of the Presence from two tenths of fine flour. If, girding the loins of strength, you have stoutly endured temptation through the patience of charity, you have baked the third loaf, like Gad, from two tenths of fine flour [Col. 0971A]. If, led by grace, you run with all your effort toward the promised blessedness, you have prepared the fourth loaf with Asher from two tenths of fine flour. If, forgetting what lies behind, you are drawn by the impulse of the Spirit in the cords of charity, you have made the sixth loaf with Manasseh from two tenths. If, possessing sorrow according to God for your sins, you are troubled into love of the Creator, you make the seventh loaf, like Simeon, from two tenths. If every day, going and advancing with Abraham toward the noon of divine illumination, you advance in the fragrance of charity, you make the eighth loaf with Levi from two tenths. If, thinking only of God’s reward, you have placed your shoulders beneath every danger to be endured in the endurance of charity, you make the ninth loaf with Issachar from two tenths of fine flour [Col. 0971B]. If, full of charity, you have set your nest in heaven like an eagle, as a most secure dwelling-place, you make the tenth loaf with Zebulun from two tenths of fine flour. If, embracing Christ, you love Him as much as you are able, full of increase in virtues, you make the eleventh loaf with Joseph from two tenths of fine flour. If the Bridegroom’s left hand is under your head and His right hand embraces you (Song 2:6), being established in the highest degree of charity, you have made the twelfth loaf with Benjamin from two tenths [Col. 0971C] of fine flour.

Behold, the twelve loaves of the Presence, prepared from two tenths of fine flour, await the purest table upon which they may be set before the Lord. Divine Scripture is the Lord’s purest table. For, like a table composed of the incorruptible wood of divine commandments, it overflows with every abundance of delights. The Christian soul also, wholly purified from both original and actual sin by the threefold immersion of baptism, is the Lord’s purest table. For, despising the tables of proud kings and of all the very rich, the Lord approaches this table in order to refresh and be refreshed, to minister and be ministered to. He first sets upon this [Col. 0971D] table the offerings of His body and blood, and then, in recompense, most graciously receives the imitation of His Passion. Likewise, holy altars solemnly dedicated in honour of God are the Lord’s purest table. The Lord also has other tables unknown to us, far removed indeed, yet suitable for banquet and banqueters. Thus the loaves of the Presence are arranged in Scripture because there the teaching and benefit of confession are contained. There we are also admonished concerning confession of sin and praise of God; good works; girding the loins; seeking blessedness; enlargement of heart; forgetfulness of the world; sorrow for sins; progress in virtue; divine reward; the most secure dwelling-place of heaven; perfection in good things [Col. 0972A]; and the Lord’s right hand of virtues. And these things, indeed, are on the table of the Scriptures.

The soul too, when it has traversed this whole region of divine plantings and, having woven from all these things a little crown, has brought forth its head crowned, will appear as the most pure table of the Lord. At the holy altars too, commemorations of all the saints are made daily without ceasing. And what is the commemoration of saints but a kind of setting forth of the loaves of presentation? For which bread is more useful to you: that which fills the stomach, or a saint who heals the mind? What is more desirable: the satisfaction of bread, or the intercession of a saint? Each saint is a loaf made from two tenths of fine flour: whether because of the perfection of faith and conduct, or because of love of God and neighbour, [Col. 0972B] or because of perfect examples for the instruction of others and continual intercession for us. Thus the loaves of presentation are set upon the most pure table before the Lord when the feasts of the saints are celebrated by the faithful in the Church in honour of God. Incense, moreover, is placed on top when prayers to God are raised for the people.

They belong to Aaron, because we have been saved by grace, and this is not from ourselves, for it is God’s gift (Eph. II, 8). They belong to his sons, because the apostles are God’s fellow-workers, partakers of God’s grace, and co-heirs with Christ. They belong to Aaron and his sons because lightnings, voices, and thunders proceed from the throne: namely, the miracles, exhortations, and rebukes of the saints. Or they belong to Aaron and his sons because the faithful have from [Col. 0972C] God what they are, and attain the kingdom by imitating the apostles. They are eaten in a holy place, because in faith or in the heavenly kingdom they are regarded by God. They are changed on Sabbaths, because at the consummation of virtues, as at the end of the days of the weeks, some are taken away and others are put in their place. Hence: “Sons have been born to you in place of your fathers.” They belong to an everlasting covenant and a perpetual right, because from the beginning of the world to the end of the age the generation of saints will not fail. Hence: “This shall be proclaimed from generation to generation”: from the generation of preceding fathers to the generation of succeeding sons, namely Christians, and this for ever. And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Behold, I am with you [Col. 0972D] on all the days of life, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20). Amen.

## CHAPTER X. On fine-flour bread

Having therefore, by God’s gift, prepared refreshment from the loaves of presentation for those fleeing from the north, let us now turn pen and mind in due order to fine-flour bread. For it is something most divine and beyond human understanding that, by the command of the Law, where the loaves of presentation are treated, the portion of fine flour is not customarily mixed with water but with oil; nor is it baked in a frying-pan, on a griddle, or in an oven, but is offered with oil upon the altar, as a memorial of sweetest fragrance to the Lord. [Col. 0973A] For thus one reads in Leviticus:

“The priest shall take a handful of the fine flour mixed with oil, and all the incense which has been placed upon the fine flour; and he shall burn it on the altar as a memorial of sweetest fragrance to the Lord. But Aaron with his sons shall eat the remaining portion of the fine flour, and they shall eat it in the holy place of the court of the tabernacle of the Lord. It shall not be leavened, because a portion of it is offered in the Lord as an offering burned with fire. It shall be most holy, like the sin-offering and trespass-offering. Only males of Aaron’s lineage shall eat it. It is an everlasting ordinance in your generations, from the sacrifices of the Lord; everyone who touches them shall be sanctified” (Lev. VI, 15–18).

Let us lift the veil and unveil the face of Moses, so that, entering the sanctuary of God, we may understand the sound of the wings speaking, like the sound [Col. 0973B] of the Most High God (Ezek. I, 24), and hear the spirit of life that is in the wheels (ibid., 21).

That flour, therefore, which is most pure and most white is called *simila*, “fine flour.” But what is purer, whiter, or more subtle than the divine nature or wisdom? For what is most pure among creatures is most filthy in comparison with God’s nature. What can be imagined as whitest among human things is judged most foul when set before the eternal light. Finally, whatever is found most subtle among all the inventions of human imaginings, when compared with the splendours of divine wisdom, is discovered to be most foolish. Therefore the sluggish soul does not rise to this; the impure soul does not approach it; the gross soul does not pass beyond it; [Col. 0973C] the bleary-eyed do not see it; the deaf do not hear it; the mute do not speak of it; the scabrous are not admitted to its embrace; the foul are not united to it; the stinking are not received. Therefore let the slow take wings; let the defiled cleanse itself; let the gross become thin; let the bleary-eyed be cleansed; let the deaf recover hearing; let the scabrous be purified; let the foul be adorned; let the stinking be steeped in a good fragrance. For however much you may formerly have been oppressed, O soul, by the habit of evils, you may nevertheless easily fly upward when supported by charity; however swollen or puffed up you may be, you are made thin by continual affliction; however blind, you are enlightened by measured chastisement. True obedience also restores hearing; holy continence repels scabbiness; a good conscience banishes foulness; an excellent reputation cleanses stench.

[Col. 0973D] In whatever manner these and similar things rekindle the extinguished marks of ancient nobility and lineage, one returns to the former title of the glory of God’s children. Yet in the present life a portion of that glory is given, not fullness; a handful, not a measure; a foretaste, not satiety. For God is not yet seen by sight, but by faith. “Now,” says the Apostle, “we see through a mirror and in an enigma; but then face to face” (I Cor. XIII, 12). Nevertheless, pursue with more ardent longing: grasp from God not what is unknown, but what is encountered as knowable, as though a full handful of fine flour. See, finally, Paul our priest measuring out to us a full handful from the incomprehensible mass of flour: “The invisible things of God,” he says, “are clearly seen, being understood through the things that have been made” [Col. 0974A] (Rom. I, 20). The whole fine flour, as it were, is the incomprehensible substance of divinity itself. Since it is impossible to grasp this, it is enough for the priest to take a full handful, so that he may dare to discourse only as much as is sufficient to understand. For the priest’s handful is the capacity of the devout mind; and fine flour fills the handful when one fills one’s understanding with God. Yet let him not take the fine flour without the mixing of oil, so that he may always remember God’s power together with his mercy.

The incense too is upon the fine flour, because “mercy exalts itself over judgment” (Jas. II, 13); because the intercession of the Spirit, who prays for us with unutterable groanings (Rom. VIII, 26), overcomes, as it were, what is insuperable, when it mercifully inclines the Almighty to hear us instead of applying the rigour of most just severity. Observe the Trinity: in the fine flour, the Father; in the oil, the Son; in the incense, the Holy Spirit. The oil inseparably mixed with the fine flour signifies that the Son is one in substance with the Father; the incense looking toward both signifies the Holy Spirit proceeding from both. This whole offering is always to be burned upon the altar as a memorial of sweetest fragrance to the Lord, so that in this faith and devotion our heart may always burn toward God with its whole desire. “But Aaron with his sons shall eat the remaining portion in the holy place of the court of the tabernacle” (Lev. VI, 26), so that Jesus, through the dispensation of his incarnation, with his disciples in Jerusalem, the holy city, [Col. 0974C] BY CHANGING BREAD AND WINE INTO THE SUBSTANCE OF HIS BODY AND BLOOD, may fulfil the life-giving mysteries of the altar and hand down this saving mystery to his faithful unto the end of the age. Or again: the priest’s handful is the operation of creation; the fine flour in the handful is the operation of creation in God.

The oil upon the fine flour is the good Spirit cherishing every creature; whence that saying: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (Gen. I, 2). This is to be burned upon the altar as a memorial of sweetest fragrance to the Lord; for, delighting in God’s work, we ought to glorify the Creator on account of his creature, and not become vain in empty thoughts, like those who, though they knew God, did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts (Rom. I, 21). Fine flour is flooded with oil when the knowledge received concerning God is enlightened. [Col. 0974D] Right enlightenment of knowledge is present when prayer proceeds with devotion in accordance with knowledge. For activity without devotion is fine flour without oil. Conversely, devotion without activity is oil without fine flour. The priest also fills his handful with fine flour mixed with oil when his entire activity is consecrated by the example and grace of the Saviour. It is burned on the altar when the heart, burning with heavenly longing, is borne upward with the fragrance of good work.

Aaron eats the remaining portion of the fine flour with his sons, without leaven, when the justice of God does not impute for punishment those things which we are unable to do because of natural weakness, but the mercy of the Creator forgives through the apostles’ intercession. “Only males of Aaron’s lineage shall eat it” (Lev. VI, 18): the soft and delicate soul, weakened by evil desires, does not touch the fine flour; that is, it should not suppose itself able to grasp divine wisdom, for wisdom will not dwell in a body subject to sins (Wis. XIV). But males—that is, those who subdue hostile powers, bringing under themselves whatever opposes and exalts itself against the knowledge of God (II Thess. II, 4), and who tread upon serpents and scorpions—shall eat the fine flour. A woman’s belly does not receive the food of fine flour, because a corrupted understanding is by no means suited to the divine nature or knowledge. But the solid and healthy stomach of a male seeks and understands what God is.

I do not, however, distinguish sex in the flesh, but disposition in the soul: I reject what is depraved and approve what is sound. [Col. 0975B] For the Creator’s hand in making the female sex did not create another or different image of his goodness, nor assign to woman an image inferior to that assigned to man. Scripture says of humankind: “He created him in the image of God; male and female he created them” (Gen. I, 27). Thus woman is not excluded from this eating while males are admitted because of an apparent distinction of food or sex, but because of the hidden sanctification or signification of the mystery. Let disposition, therefore, not sex, distinguish those who eat; grace, not nature; discernment of mind, not limbs of body; the habit of the soul, not hair upon the face. Virtue is sought; vice is rejected. Constancy is admitted; wantonness is cast out. Patience is recognised; anger is anathematized. If you approach [Col. 0975C] the banquet of fine-flour bread, you are immediately questioned by the angel as to your condition, age, lineage, and sex. For angels principally and properly serve in these offices: to examine the mind, purpose, and merit of those who come to God. It is certainly part of their office both to admit the worthy and cast out the unworthy; to receive those who have earned well with reverence, and to expel the undeserving with disgrace. If you unlawfully force your way in against the established rule and law, beware lest your head be cut off: for the cherub does not brandish the flaming sword without cause. It strikes the proud, defends the humble, dashes out the brains of the shameless, honours the chaste, consoles the mourning, threatens the scoffer, communicates with the believer, and condemns the unbeliever.

[Col. 0975D] Was it not in the midst of Jerusalem that the man who had a writing-case at his loins marked all its inhabitants with the pen of his examination, appointing some to death and others to life? (Ezek. IX, 2.) Yet one must firmly maintain that this angel marked for death or life not whom he himself wished, but those whom the Lord commanded—so that you may fear divine judgment more than angelic judgment. Therefore conduct must be corrected and the mind raised to obtain grace and to receive the fine flour. For “everyone who touches it shall be sanctified” (Exod. XXIX, 37). Whoever touches as did the woman of whom it was said, “Someone touched me” (Mark V, 31). There is a touch of faith and a touch of unbelief. Faith touches in order to obtain a reward; unbelief touches in order to betray. Faith touches by bringing devotion near; unbelief touches by disgorging its own wickedness. Mary touches by kissing and anointing the feet; Judas also touches, by kissing and selling. Faith touches by loving and imitating; unbelief touches by persecuting and cursing. Faith, by touching, shall be sanctified; unbelief, by touching, shall be defiled. For holiness, as it sanctifies when fittingly received, so it condemns when irreverently handled. After the morsel, the devil’s power was able to rage more fiercely in the traitor’s heart, because the injury of suffering is increased not by a defect in what is received but by a defect in the receiver. What is received would heal, unless the sick person became more severely sick through the medicine; for medicine extinguishes disease and heals the diseased person. Thereafter the soul that has died with its disease will not be without disease.

[Col. 0976B] Therefore, O soul, separate the disease from the medicine, lest you always die with punishment; and understand every vice to be a disease of the soul. Touch, then, without vice the remedy of vices; approach with faith the cleanser of our souls. For fine-flour bread is clean, white, savoury, warm, neither laborious in the mouth nor heavy in the stomach. This order of words in some way sets forth the fitness of consecrated understanding. Unless divine grace is tasted with a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith, its flavour is not known. Unless the baseness of earthly understanding is cast down, the brightness of divine meanings is not penetrated. Therefore one who is clean in thought, white through the renown of a good reputation, warm in fervent love, and savoury in holy speech receives fine-flour bread, [Col. 0976C] because that person’s hand does not disagree with the table, nor the mind with the fine flour. If you are able, contemplate the Creator in his glory: this is to take all the fine flour. If you are unable, at least behold the most powerful and most merciful works of the Redeemer: this is to fill a handful of fine flour. You will not take all the fine flour in your handful, because you will not comprehend the incomprehensible nature. Only fill the handful, that you may glorify God according to your capacity.

Do not commit robbery against God concerning God himself, by usurping for yourself a grace which you have not earned by the handful of your merits. Remember also that whatever you grasp in your handful is to be offered to God, not to yourself: “For what do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, [Col. 0976D] why do you boast as if you had not received it?” (I Cor. IV, 7). Fine flour is never without oil, because God is never deprived of his mercy. You too must never approach the table without oil for the fine flour, because one who is hard toward the merciful One, cruel toward the compassionate One, and ungrateful toward the most kind One cannot fittingly approach. Pass from flesh to spirit, and from spirit to God; for the breads before us are breads of souls, not of bodies. Therefore, with common benefit preserved, let the ambitious greed of the seller be far off and the sloth of the buyer cease. According to the distribution of their functions, the diligence of writer and reader ought to be equal: the former’s, that he may write worthily; the latter’s, that he may read graciously; the former’s, that he may compose for usefulness; the latter’s, that he may read for edification; the former’s, that he may distribute; the latter’s, [Col. 0977A] that he may ask; the former’s, that he may relinquish; the latter’s, that he may repay; the former’s, that he may be generous; the latter’s, that he may be thankful in receiving. Yet neither should deceive or be deceived, defraud or be defrauded. Let the writer decide whether he ought to write thus; let the reader judge whether he ought to accept what has been written. I suffer no injury if, in seeking to establish my own opinion, I find the reader’s assent where it is good and rejection where it is bad.

## CHAPTER XI. On barley bread

Being now about to treat of barley bread, I shall not reject a rougher style of speech, provided that the meaning of faith is preserved. For with a humble pen one must write of barley bread, because those who use it are in a servile condition. Thus barley bread is not set forth as a delicacy, [Col. 0977B] but only that a servant’s hunger may be relieved. It flays the throats of the fastidious, burdens the stomach, and irritates the windpipe; for it is covered with a hard husk and presents its bristling surface to the teeth of those who eat it. Yet in a great house this food is necessary, even if it is not for the great; it is not more delicate, indeed, but is more useful, because it would strengthen servants’ powers more. So too the more lowly offices of those who use barley bread, though mean, are necessary. The office of the dung-clearer in the house of a rich man is utterly lowly, yet it cleans what is worst in stench. The condition of maidservants is likewise very low, yet most useful in washing clothes. For how could the master go out in public unless a maidservant washed his dirty garment? A woodcutter too, or driver of an ass, has no dignity, but neither is he without usefulness. For how would the son warm himself unless a servant brought wood from the forest? The stoker or charcoal-burner, his whole face blackened by continually turning coals and ashes, can scarcely sit beside the ashes [Col. 0977C] when a crowd arrives; but unless he had prepared the hearth and coals, who would have a place at the fire? The cook too, dirtied by handling kettles and pots and by the very sweaty preparation of dishes, does not recline first or best, perhaps not even last, at the banquet; but who would dine unless he cooked the food?

Behold: in offices it is evident that, although they are lowly, they are nevertheless very necessary. Perhaps it is so with barley bread: the lower in value it is, the more useful it is for feeding the household. For why did the Lord of all feed his household in the desert with barley loaves (John VI, 9), except to give a sign to those who fear him that barley bread is altogether useful and abundant food? Observe that above I numbered five servants, and now have found in the Lord’s storehouse five barley loaves. Not only the number but also the kind of service and bread correspond. Consider, therefore, the dung-clearer eating barley bread; likewise the woodcutter, stoker, cook, and maidservant. It must therefore be expounded, both as to number and order, what these things figuratively signify; and the authority of Scripture must show, if the Lord grants it, [Col. 0978A] what a sewer is, or a dung-clearer in a sewer; what maidservants or washerwomen are; what clothes are cleansed by them; and likewise concerning the rest.

This world, then, like a sewer, is full of the stench of sins, a receptacle of every evil, as it were, of all filth. In it Adam first emptied his belly—not in order to cleanse or disclose it, but so as, by crushing all his descendants, to contaminate them. For when he excused his sin, he emptied his belly, as it were. But alas, wretch! Where, or against whom, did he cast his excrement first? Certainly beside God, who created him, and into his own soul and the posterity of his offspring. For excusing himself, and thus as it were accusing God, he says: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Gen. III, 12). Why, Adam, do you not have a peg beneath your belt, according to the precept of the Law, so that, when you go outside the camp for nature’s necessities and cover the refuse with earth (Deut. XIII, 12), you might hide the thief of your belly? Certainly, if on hearing the Lord’s voice you beat your breast and, by accusing yourself, pierced your own conscience, then by humble satisfaction and confession you would undoubtedly conceal from God’s eyes the stench of your committed iniquity, restraining the noise of pride. But God did not wish paradise to be contaminated any longer by you thus shamelessly exposing yourself—or rather, covering your hind parts in shame and giving out obscene sounds of lying. Instead, he prepared this valley as a sewer and shut the wretch into the world to swallow his own stenches, excluding him from paradise.

[Col. 0978C] Wickedness grew; the sewer was filled. The Flood came to wipe out guilt and cleanse the sewer. At the Lord’s command Noah first built the ark, in which he might save his life with his descendants. Therefore, while he laboured upon the ark and while shut up within the ark awaited the end of the Flood, what did he eat except barley bread amid a flood of many waters (Ps. XXXI, 6), as in a cleansing of unclean superfluities? Behold Noah, as the world’s sewer-cleaner, sealed every window of the ark with pitch because of the excessive stench, and prefigured the form of the second regeneration in which old filths are purged. But he lived upon wholly barley bread, because the tribulation of that time was harsh. Moses carried this bread stored away in Genesis; [Col. 0978D] but Jesus, coming to John, receiving and opening the sacrament of baptism, and providing saving cleansing, broke it for the hungry crowd in the desert of the Church. This is the one and first bread of the five barley loaves.

The second bread is made in Exodus, when the children of Israel, brought out from Egypt through the Red Sea into the desert, cleansed, as it were, the garments of their souls infected by dwelling with the Egyptians; and, celebrating a new Passover, renewed them with the blood of the Lamb. For thus it is written in Exodus:

“Moses came down from the mountain to the people and sanctified them. When they had washed their garments, he said to them: ‘Be ready for the third day, and do not approach your wives.’ Now the third day had come and the morning had grown bright; and behold, thunders began to be heard, lightnings flashed, a very dense cloud covered the mountain, and the sound of the trumpet rang out ever more loudly” (Exod. XIX, 14–16).

And shortly afterwards: “The Lord descended upon Mount Sinai, on the very summit of the mountain, and called Moses to its top” (ibid., 20). It should be observed that the garments of the children of Israel are washed first, second, and third: namely, in the Red Sea, in the blood of the lamb, and in receiving the Law. For Christ’s baptism cleanses us; Christ’s body cleanses us; God’s Law cleanses us. The maidservants are the sacraments, which whiten the garments of consciences in such a way that they enable them in some measure now to ascend to angelic purity. The Lord will not come to us unless these maidservants have first cleansed our garments, because Christ will not be in us unless we receive the Church’s sacraments. For “a garment mixed with blood shall be for burning and fuel for fire” (Isa. IX, 5). But if our sins are, according to Isaiah, like scarlet, darkened by the enormity of committed crime, when cleansed by the power of baptism they shall be made white like snow (Isa. I, 18), so that the soul may sing and say, like one shorn and washed ascending from the washing-place (Cant. IV, 2): “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. L, 9). Again: “If they are red like a little worm,” because they have become base through daily persistence, “they shall be white like wool” in true confession. All the Church’s sacraments, which are like the pools in Heshbon (Cant. VII, 4), are sufficient to erase whatever sin has stained the soul, whether small or great, old or new. By their benefit and office, therefore, the whitened soul is exhorted by the Bridegroom’s voice to come from Lebanon: “Come,” he says, “from Lebanon, come” (Cant. IV, 1).

[Col. 0979C] Behold why the infant to be baptized is immersed three times in the font and raised three times. Moses comes down to sanctify the people when any prelate, through his condescension, provokes the subject person to lamentation; and he commands that, having washed his garments with tears, he be ready for the third day. The first day is the day of birth; the second, the time of youth, when one begins to exercise one’s powers in rational understanding; the third, when bodily strength fails in the dissolution of soul and body. The regeneration of baptism prepares the first day; mortification of the flesh prepares the second, for as soon as reason of mind perceives a stirring rising against chastity of mind, it subdues and extinguishes it; meditation on death likewise prepares the third, for like a sharp razor it shaves away the flesh’s superfluous desires, which grow anew every day.

In Leviticus (ch. VI), the priests are commanded to lay a pile of wood upon the altars, so that the fire for the Lord may be perpetual and never fail. What, then, is Aaron, the chief priest appointed to this office, except a servant in the house of God preparing a fire? What does the entire book of Leviticus do except prepare fire, stir ashes, kindle coals, supply wood, sacrifice calves, slaughter rams, and roast year-old lambs? Yet the barley bread is that close-fitting labour in stripping skins, opening entrails, washing, dividing every limb, cooking and serving, shedding blood, burning things, or carrying them outside the camp. [Col. 0980A] These veils of the sacraments are in many respects coarser than ours, more laborious and lower; ours indeed are fewer but more worthy, slower but more useful. Those were copies of heavenly things; ours, however, are the heavenly things themselves. Then the old priesthood was transferred; the rite of sacrifices ceased; anointing came to an end. At last the new priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek succeeded, and the reality of Christ’s body and blood fulfilled the preceding figures.

After the sons came for whom the fire was prepared, he who had prepared it withdrew and no longer had a place once the fire had begun to burn clearly. Aaron therefore ate the third barley bread with his descendants while he prepared the fire. But we, once the fire of the Gospel has been kindled after the Lord’s resurrection, may eat the bread of glory without labour, sweat, or pain; may behold the light; may stand by the fire. For he himself bore our pains, sweats, and labours; and so that we might not again be afflicted by the same things, he nailed them to the cross and decreed that they were not to be paid again. He said, as it were: “Until now Aaron has eaten his barley bread by offering sacrifices and gifts according to the Law of Moses. But now, since it is finished, I hand over to you not the letter but my Spirit, so that henceforth you may live not according to the flesh but according to [Col. 0980C] the Spirit, and offer a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God.” Behold, the cook, worthy of his food, awaits his bread, and for all the distress of the kitchen at least asks for barley bread.

But who this cook is, or whose throat and belly he ought to satisfy, must be investigated, if perhaps the divine Law shows it. Perhaps we shall find it if we turn over the book of Numbers more carefully. For there one reads that the rabble which had come up from Egypt with the children of Israel burned with desire for Egyptian meats and said: “Who will give us meat to eat? We remember the fish which we ate freely in Egypt; cucumbers and melons come to our minds, leeks and onions and garlic. Our soul is dry; our eyes see nothing but manna” (Num. II, 4). [Col. 0980D] Here you have who ask, what they ask, and from whom: namely, the children of Israel ask Moses for meat. Thus Moses himself, as a good cook, asks how and from where he may satisfy their importunity; and says to the Lord: “Whence shall I have meat to give such a great multitude? They weep before me, saying: ‘Give us meat, that we may eat’” (ibid., 13). Moses’ labours must be weighed: he works day and night lest his people suffer hunger. Yet equally hateful is the people’s ingratitude, for which neither God’s care nor man’s care is enough. For by ten plagues he strikes the Egyptians in their punishment (Exod. VII); he makes them a way through the Red Sea (Exod. XIV); he drowns Pharaoh and his pursuing people; he brings forth water from the rock; he changes bitter water into sweetness (Exod. XVII); he rains manna from [Col. 0981A] heaven (Exod. XVI); he bestows many further benefits—yet they still seek meat with murmuring! These things God does for the people; these things the people do toward God.

Moses, however, exposes himself to every danger in order to lead them out and rescue them from Pharaoh’s hand. To receive the Law he fasted through two periods of forty days; he climbed the mountain; and then descended with urgent concern lest their camp perish through the Lord’s anger on account of the molten calf. He almost succumbs to the unbearable burden of daily disputes. But what does the people do in return? They murmur against God, prepare to lay hands on Moses, loathe manna, seek meat with desire, long for Egyptian foods, and complain that things had been better for them in Egypt than they now are in the desert. The rebellious and ungrateful people hunger, not altogether inappropriately, for tasteless cucumbers and melons, leeks, onions, and garlic—foods stimulating lust. For idleness pleases them more than labour, and luxury delights them more than continence. Yet meat is granted, more from indignation than mercy, because after their carnal desires are obtained, the extremities of the camp are destroyed. “While,” says the Psalmist, “the food was still in their mouth, the wrath of God rose against them” (Ps. LXXVII, 30). Behold how Moses sweats in the Hebrews’ kitchen, yet receives for his service not wheaten but barley loaves: “For the Law brought no one to perfection” (Heb. VII, 17). Let this suffice concerning the fourth barley bread. It remains that we borrow the fifth as well from the boy who has “five [Col. 0981C] barley loaves and two fishes” (John VI, 9), and place it before our crowd with the blessing of Christ’s hands.

First, according to the reasoning of what precedes, it must be investigated for whom and in return for what work this bread is to be paid. Yet it must first be recalled that above the woodcutter or builder was counted among the other servants. But who the builder is, and for whom he carries wood, whether to the fire or to the house, must be diligently examined. In the signification of this mystery, in Deuteronomy Moses, like one gathering wood from the boundless forest of the Lord’s benefits, enumerates all the deeds of the Lord, of himself, and of the people Israel. Therefore, like a good [Col. 0981D] builder, by recalling to their memory the good things the Lord had done for them—or rather, bestowed on them—he brings out the wood, as it were, for a second fragrance, and by extending cords and lines shows beforehand how each piece is to be fitted into the building of God’s house. In no fewer than 155 sectional divisions, in Deuteronomy, he recapitulates, like beams and ceilings, all the preceding acts of the people from the departure out of Egypt; and he composes one book like a single house. Moses also asks for bread as recompense for such work. Attend to the end of this book and understand what sort of reward it is:

“Moses went up from the plains of Moab to the summit of Nebo, to the summit of Pisgah opposite Jericho; and the Lord showed him all the land of Gilead as far as Dan, and all Naphtali, and the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, and all the land of Judah as far as the western sea, and the southern region, and the breadth of the plain of Jericho, city of palms, as far as Zoar. And the Lord said: ‘This is the land concerning which I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying: I shall give it to your seed. You have seen it with your eyes, and you shall not cross into it.’ And Moses, the servant of the Lord, died in the land of Moab at the Lord’s command, and they buried him in the valley of Moab opposite Beth-peor; and no one knew his grave” (Deut. XXXIV, 1–6).

[Col. 0982A] What is this, Lord? Is this your friendship, celebrated and preached throughout all nations, toward your friend Moses? Are your promises ended in this manner? Are those who serve worthily in your camp unto death rewarded thus? If Moses was cheated of his desire, whose hope does not hang in doubt? But grant that you did not wish to bring him into that desirable land: why did you show what you would not give? You hold out an apple to a child, as it were, and draw back your hand. Perhaps he would not grieve so intensely if he did not see it; desire, sparked by sight, grows, and the soul burns more ardently at the offering of the gift. But the more abundantly conceived hope rejoices, the more sharply it grieves when frustrated. Whom will you spare if you do not spare Moses? Who obeyed your commands so faithfully? Who for your sake so indiscriminately opposed enemies and exposed himself to dangers? Is it not written: “No prophet ever again arose in Israel whom the Lord knew face to face, in all the signs and wonders which he sent him to perform in the land of Egypt, before Pharaoh, all his servants, and all his land, and in all the mighty hand and great wonders which Moses performed before all Israel?” (Deut. XXXIV, 10).

[Col. 0982C] As it seems to me, you are indeed to be loved above all things, but nevertheless also feared. For you do not flatter the faults of those who love you, but correct them; and the sting of your fear does not pass over unpunished even the faults of one who loves you. O Moses, he who threatens is a friend, and therefore not to be feared. He who speaks is Almighty, and therefore not to be provoked. He who decrees is God, and therefore to be judged just; a friend does not transgress the law of friendship so as finally to depart from his friend. Therefore the Almighty and merciful One perhaps denies the land of the dying for this reason: that he may raise Moses’ soul to heaven. God thoroughly purges in the present what he perceives to be an impediment to attaining eternity. Let Moses therefore see the land concerning which the Lord swore to his fathers, as wheaten bread, and not eat it, since he does not enter it; but let him eat barley bread by dying in the land of Moab—perhaps because of the sin committed at the water of contradiction. Behold, we have touched five barley loaves and placed them on the table; but we have still left untouched more abundant remnants. For the more often they are touched in exposition, as though broken, the more abundantly they increase when faithfully understood.

## CHAPTER XII. On the bread of mourners
After barley bread, both in sequence and in significance comes the bread of mourners; for when Moses had died, [Col. 0983A] who would not grieve, who would not mourn? Yet blessed are those who mourn the death of Moses—that is, the failure of the Law—for they have Jesus as their ruler in place of Moses, receiving grace in place of Law. The bread of mourners, then, is an abundance of tears; for as bread restores one who is hungry, so a tear refreshes the grieving soul. The hungry person fails without bread; the wounded soul languishes without an outpouring of tears. Bread alleviates hunger; a tear softens grief.
