Yet this bread of tears is not eaten always, everywhere, or by everyone. For the angel who never sinned, and Adam before he sinned, did not eat this bread. From the spring of sins, therefore, the vein of all tears burst forth. Yet the artistry of God the craftsman is wonderful in this: that the tear which breaks forth from the veins of sins, when [Col. 0983B] humbly shed, should swallow up every sin. Clearly, in this way sin is condemned by sin; thus the water of compunction extinguishes the fire of illicit pleasure.

A tear submerges the multitude of crimes; it dissolves the hardness of the rocks of our breast; it softens the wrath of the judge; with humble boldness it bends the threats of wrath not yet unleashed; it sheaths drawn swords again; it overthrows punishments already raised; it sprinkles overflowing flames; it pours waters from the rock. It softens what is harsh, bends what is rigid, moistens what is dry, makes the barren fruitful, washes what is filthy, adorns what is ugly, revives what is dead, opens what is shut, hastens what is forbidden, moderates what is unrestrained. It breaks the gates of hell and extinguishes the coals of the iron furnace. What more? It conquers the unconquerable, binds the almighty; it is the shipwreck [Col. 0983C] of vices and the harbor of the shipwrecked. It bends the Son of God down to us and, through the Spirit’s intervention, raises us to the true Trinity. Adam ate this bread of tears in exile; Noah in the Flood; the people in the wilderness; Hezekiah in his bed; Job on the dung-heap; David in adultery and murder; Peter in denial; Mary Magdalene in the prostitution of her body; the thief in his suspension upon the cross. Why? That the soul may be renewed and the pursuing enemy submerged. For Satan endures his own flame more readily than our tear, and the tear of a contrite heart torments him more sharply than the flame of hellfire.

While the sinner sheds a tear, he shuts the adversary [Col. 0983D] up in flame; indeed, our refreshment burns the adversary. For he delights in our torments, is refreshed by our pains, and the shedding of our blood is for him a cup of honey. He swallows all rivers, but he does not drink this water; for the inward parts of his belly burst if they are sprinkled with this water. His teeth are knocked out, his throat pierced, his veins swollen, and his sinews loosened. Yet not every liquid flowing from the eyes accomplishes these things, but humility proceeding openly in the vessel of tears. O humble tear: yours is the power, yours is the kingdom. You do not fear the judge’s tribunal; you impose silence upon the accusers of your friends; at times you snatch away even the sentence from the judge’s mouth! You dare where an angel fears. There is none to disturb you [Col. 0984A] from entering the inner chambers, from pleading for the crimes of the guilty; none forbids you to approach. If you enter alone, nevertheless you never return alone or empty. You bring back pardon for guilt, restore lost innocence, recall exiles, and crown the innocent. This water irrigates paradise and washes the Church so that she may be without spot. It either makes paradise or finds it. For when the entire conscience is watered by the pouring forth of tears, trees are produced which bear the fruit of life. Virtues never come, or do not long survive, without the heart’s irrigation. For if temptations daily creep into the green tree of the heart, “what will happen in the dry?” (Luke 23:31). If even after a tear the worm of corruption gnaws the mind, what destruction belongs to that dryness where the Lord never rains? If the dew [Col. 0984B] of grace sometimes dries up through weariness, what of the place where dew never comes?

Therefore let the more zealous imitator of the patriarchs have a well in paradise, a spring in his garden, and streams in his meadow. Certainly, when you pour out deep tears in remembrance of grave sins, you draw water from the well; but when you weep over daily transgressions, drink is taken from the spring. You pour out diverse streams when you weigh all thoughts in measure and balance. Every planting of ours fails without water; every barrenness increases. Yet in some places we read even of barrenness in waters themselves—indeed, of barren waters. Jericho had barren waters until Elisha healed them by his blessing (4 [Col. 0984C] Kings 2). Coming there and receiving from the sons of the prophets their complaint about the harmfulness of the waters, he mixed water with salt in a new vessel and drove out the waters’ barrenness. Thus, indeed, human nature, lacking the verdure of faith and good works according to its own defect, was freed from its dryness by the coming of the Son of the Most High and rendered exceedingly delightful by the growth of virtues. For the earthen and new vessel is the new body of Christ taken from the Virgin. The salt poured into the water is divinity united to the body through the mediation of the soul. Thus water healed waters: water with salt, waters marked by barrenness; but the water of blessing, waters of poured-out curse; sweet water, waters of utter bitterness. Let us not drink but pour out barren waters; for the inward parts are tormented by drinking barren [Col. 0984D] waters, because the soul’s belly is disturbed by the useless acquisition of worldly things. Tears that flow through pretence confer more dryness than quickening. Every outpouring of tears not shed for the kingdom of heaven is barren. Empty are the tears which temporal loss or inconvenience wrings out.

Let not, then, the water of this world’s Jericho, but water from paradise, be your bread and refreshment. For one should weep only either for sin committed or for paradise lost. This is what Scripture says: “A river,” it says, “went forth from the place of pleasure to water paradise, and from there it is divided into four heads” (Gen. 2:10). In the place of sorrow one must attend—or at least sigh—over where and what is the place [Col. 0985A] of pleasure. The place of pleasure is in God, and is God. Therefore, when you hear that pleasure is in God or that God is pleasure, think not of carnal but of heartfelt delight. For “Jews do not associate with Samaritans” (John 4:9), since the delights of spirit and flesh have neither one origin nor the same end. Moreover, that supreme pleasure does not permit itself to dwell together with our lowest pleasure: for the former cleanses; the latter defiles; the former joins one to God; the latter separates one from God; the former is always without satiety, the latter full of weariness. But the person who can say what that pleasure is will be one who can define what eternity is. “From the place of pleasure,” it says, “a river went forth to water paradise.” A blessed place is watered by such a river! For what is watered is paradise; what waters is the Paraclete. Indeed, paradise can neither be watered [Col. 0985B] by another nor ought the Paraclete to water another. Among the things above, nothing is more excellent than that river; among earthly things, nothing is more heavenly than this place. That river is the river of pleasure; this place is the place of delights. There is one pleasure, because there is one unchanging desire by reason of eternity; here there are many delights, because there are many and various desires owing to the alternation of diverse movements. That one pleasure not only contains these delights within itself, but what it has beyond those delights is greater than the entire assemblage of those delights; for while you are making your way toward God, many delights of graces meet you on the journey before you reach the one God.

But when you reach him himself, you will have not graces but grace; not delights but one pleasure. [Col. 0985C] Each of the blessed spirits sails—rather, swims with naked intellects—in delight in that river; and the more deeply they are immersed, the more freely and sweetly they enjoy eternal happiness. When each has filled the little flask of his desire from it, he nevertheless neither constricts nor delays the rush of God’s river. By its first and chief draught, the Seraphim more richly kindle their fires, because it nourishes rather than extinguishes love. The Cherubim, intoxicated with fuller knowledge, emit sweetest belches in their vicinity, because the water of saving wisdom proceeds from the Spirit of God. The Thrones, filled with more abundant equity, judge human injustices more gently, because softened by the spirit of piety they always weigh the causes of defendants more kindly. The Dominations [Col. 0985D] receive from that same Spirit their manner of ruling, and extend their dominion neither otherwise nor beyond what they are commanded. The Principalities receive, by the inspiration of this Spirit, the care and dignity of their delegated office. The Powers borrow from this Spirit the capacity to do whatever may serve our good. The Virtues receive from God’s Spirit the power to work miracles in imitation of God. The Archangels hear, in the wine-cellar, so that they may announce the highest things. The Angels possess from him—“the one and same Spirit who works all things” (1 Cor. 12:11)—what enables them to suffice for our protection. Behold: we have explained as briefly as we could what the river which went forth from the place of pleasure to water paradise signifies.

It remains to explain what is added: “which [Col. 0986A] is divided from there into four heads.” The mind, weighed down by bodily mass, is too weak to receive those impulses of grace by which angelic nature, intoxicated in God’s higher realms, is accustomed to overflow inwardly and outwardly. Accordingly, that grace which exceeds human measure is apportioned to us according to measure—not because of any sparingness in the giver or gift, but because of the smallness of the vessel. For perhaps the soul’s skin-bag would burst if grace were poured over it beyond its capacity. Indeed, a weak soul is accustomed not only to burst under the superabundance of grace but even to melt in the furnace of love. Yet it goes well with the soul which is thus filled; for, with grace flowing into it, it begins to flow—indeed, by a now familiar return, to flow back toward the source of goodness. Thus it enters and goes forth at the king’s command: entering the house of eternity, going forth [Col. 0986B] into the court of immortality. But before grace comes upon it, there is no peace for one entering or going out. For since Adam left paradise in his transgression, peace did not come to him unless grace went before to lead him.

Therefore, because the fullness of grace gathered all at once cannot be grasped by the capacity of the human creature, it is said to be divided into four heads. Yet, by the privilege of her Son, the Mother of God, above the merit of all creation, was wholly suffused with all the grace of the Godhead by the sprinkling of the Holy Spirit. Thus there are four heads of the one and indivisible grace, though it is always one in itself and has itself as its one head. For when grace is given to each of us “according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. 4:7), grace is divided in us, [Col. 0986C] though it is never divided in itself. From the first head, you have the soul in the image and likeness of God; from the second, you have God in the image and likeness of man; from the third, you have the visible species of bread and wine to be transformed into the invisible substance of the body of Jesus, now glorified in heaven. From the fourth, you have hope of escaping from this mutable and corruptible birth into “the liberty of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 8:21). In the first, man is created; in the second, redeemed; in the third, sanctified; in the fourth, glorified. In the first is goodness; in the second, mercy; in the third, truth; in the fourth, glory. When the civil strife of spirit and flesh has been settled and every tumult of inward movements stilled, the table of the joyful is to be arranged with solemn [Col. 0986D] banquets, and vegetables of herbs are certainly no longer to be set out.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the bread of the joyful.

When Pharaoh with his horsemen had been submerged in the sea, Moses sang a song to the Lord and said: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; horse and rider he has cast into the sea,” etc. (Exod. 15:1). This song of joy is the bread of the joyful; for as bread refreshes the body, so the spirit is refreshed by exultation. Hence Solomon: “A sad spirit dries the bones; a cheerful spirit fattens the marrow” (Prov. 17:21). But the soul is never filled with true exultation unless it is delivered from this pilgrimage in which it is afflicted by great tribulation. What exultation can there be [Col. 0987A] where there is continual tribulation? For the soul suffers from the body, suffers from the world, suffers from the devil, and suffers also from itself. Where, then, it endures so many and such sufferings, from what source can it eat the breads of joy? Truly, among serpents and scorpions it has only barley breads. One must therefore cross the Red Sea in order to eat pure bread; cross through fire and water so that you may possess full joy. For this was shown in the Apocalypse by the angel to John, who, when he showed certain persons standing before the throne and asked who they were—not to learn, but to teach—added: “These are they who came out of great tribulation, and washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb; therefore they are before the throne of God and serve him day and night” (Rev. 7:14). “They came,” he says, [Col. 0987B] “out of great tribulation.”

If you recall the sufferings of the martyrs, you will indeed find that they endured great tribulations. Some, we read, were hung upon crosses; some beheaded by the sword; some flayed alive; some tortured on the rack; some plunged beneath snowy ice; some shot with arrows; some buried beneath stones; some publicly beaten. And, to speak briefly, almost everything that human malice could devise was endured by the patience of the saints. Therefore those came out of great tribulation who preserved true faith and firm patience in suffering. “They washed,” he says, “their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb”; for truly the blood of the Lamb is the blood of saints dying innocently. Those [Col. 0987C] who suffer for the Lamb imitate the Lamb in suffering, for this Lamb suffered in his innocence. Note that it was a lamb, not a goat, that suffered. For when someone suffers for his own sin, it is a goat that suffers; but when he suffers without sin, a lamb. Therefore, because Christ alone suffered without sin, he suffered as a lamb. And because Christ’s Passion is the redemption of the whole world, the saints are rightly said to have been washed and made white in the blood of the Lamb. These, then, eat the bread of joy: those whom conscience does not gnaw concerning the past, sorrow does not torment concerning the present, and no power threatens concerning the future.

Nor do these alone eat the bread of joy, but also those who, when the civil strife of spirit and flesh has been settled and every tumult of inward movements stilled, [Col. 0987D] already presume to take solemn banquets from the table of the joyful. No longer, indeed, should vegetables of herbs be taken by the weak, but olives of graces should be tasted by the healthy, and the flesh of the lamb should be received without wild lettuces. The cup is to be drunk of wine unmixed—pure wine; grains without chaff; oil without dregs; rose without thorn; kernel without shell; nature without fault. The hunter is slain; the snare broken; the sting of death crushed; the pit opened; the last enemy is destroyed as it falls with death. The chains of the neck are loosed, fetters unfastened, prison opened, the accused brought forth; the father runs to meet his returning son, rushes into his embrace, and by forgiving repairs the shame of cast-down—indeed, stolen—chastity. He removes the hair-shirt tunic, clothes him in a robe, places a ring on him, shoes his feet, sets [Col. 0988A] the table, kills the fattened calf, prepares the meal, and feeds his son most excellently. The household exults, the master rejoices, the jealous one does not enter, and none within hungers in want.

O feast of rich fare, furnished by the Father! O feast of marrowed foods and clarified vintage, of those rejoicing together in wondrous solemnity! What will be given so that one may enter you? What, I ask, shall I give that I may come to you and be refreshed? “Silver and gold I do not have; but what I have, this I give you for your sake” (Acts 3:6). What is it? An open palate, an empty stomach, hungry throat, eyes weakened by poverty, open hands, swift feet. Only feed them, and let these cattle of mine be yours. I pray that they may always attend you and never depart. For if they depart, they fail; if they attend, [Col. 0988B] they are refreshed. My eyes always toward you; my hands in service; my feet in obedience; the rest at the feast. Whatever is on this table is health-giving; the things served here are nourishment of blessedness. The virtue of love is taken here for bread; the virtue of faith for fish; the virtue of patience for meat; the virtue of piety for rich food; the virtue of humility for vegetables; the virtue of truth for wine; the virtue of contemplation for delights; the virtue of mortification for game. Each virtue displays its tentacle (tentaculum). This is the wedding feast which the king prepared for his son at his betrothal; the nobler the provision of the one inviting, the more ardently the appetite of those invited comes forth. Appetite is not sated by taste, nor the eye by sight, nor the ear by hearing.

[Col. 0988C] Concerning the place of this feast spoke the hearer of God’s words, he who beheld visions of the Almighty, who falls and thus has his eyes opened: “How beautiful are your tents, Jacob, your tabernacles, Israel: like wooded valleys, like watered gardens beside rivers, like tabernacles fixed by the Lord, like cedars near waters. Water shall flow from his bucket; his seed shall be in many waters” (Num. 24:4–7). Thus speaks one who thus hears, who thus sees; thus hears one who thus sees, thus sees one who thus hears. We must therefore take care in such a way that we may thus see; see in such a way that we may thus hear; hear in such a way that we may thus speak. But what is this “thus and thus”? A “thus” does not follow unless another “thus” goes before. It does not happen to anyone to speak thus unless hearing comes first; nor does hearing follow unless sight goes before. He who does not fall does not receive sight. In falling, humility is received; [Col. 0988D] in seeing, understanding; in hearing, obedience; in speaking, sound doctrine. Thus love is ordered; thus times are arranged. For day does not follow unless dawn comes before; dawn does not come unless night passes. Thus voice precedes word; thus the morning star, the sun; thus shadow, truth; thus virtue, virtue; thus grace, good action. Accordingly, some virtues are accustomed to go before, some to follow, some to accompany a good work.

Faith, always in the battle-line of the spiritual camp, attacks the opposing adversary’s flank; then it summons beside itself the army of good works, surrounded by whose strength it breaks through and bursts into opposing ranks. Prudence [Col. 0989A] then prepares its wedge; courage also strengthens its arm; justice throws up a rampart and overthrows walls; temperance compels the squadrons of combatants into array. The battle-lines of virtues are ordered and prepared with shields and spears against the camp of vices. From the camp of virtues, the virtue that wanders outside order is cast out; for what departs from order loses the name of virtue. Therefore virtue is not virtue if it is not ordered. For this reason the camps move at the sound of the Gospel trumpet and follow the banners of the cross. They hurl the javelins of confession and ride upon the horses of mortification. What can the crowd of vices do against these things? With order confused, it is carried headlong to battle. Indeed, the incitements of vices confuse voices and mix ranks. But again, with slow steps and measured march, [Col. 0989B] the army of virtues advances to battle; yet the more slowly it comes, the more insistently it strikes: “I will not turn back,” it says, “until they fail” (Ps. 17:38). It is indeed good for vice to be killed by virtue, but evil for the vicious person to resist virtue.

But if, when virtue is challenged in some respect, it has stood opposed, one must immediately fall down with Joshua son of Nun (Josh. 5), and reconciliation must altogether be sought. For the eyes of one who falls in this manner will be opened—not as those of the first humans were opened through transgression, but as those of the man born blind through Christ’s illumination. The serpent opens eyes for lust (Gen. 3); Christ, for knowing and glorifying God. The serpent opens them in order to seize; Christ, in order to rescue. Thus, falling at the feet of virtues, one receives the light [Col. 0989C] of the eyes (John 9). Humbled, he hears God’s words; enlightened, he sees God’s visions and speaks the vision: “How beautiful are your tabernacles, Jacob; your tents, Israel, like wooded valleys, like watered gardens beside rivers.” Jacob does not know the tabernacles of vices; he always either dwells at home or serves in the Lord’s tabernacles of virtues. This is the soul that is simple in innocence, pure in cleanness, not rough with cunning, not hairy with wickedness; pleasing in service, faithful in what is entrusted, provident in office, steadfast in what it has begun, patient under insults, wise in appeasing anger, cautious in escaping snares, discerning in ruling flocks, devout in offering gifts, upright in ordering speech, inclined to obedience, ready to reverence, generous in [Col. 0989D] liberality, strong in wrestling with the angel, humble in yielding to God, formidable to enemies, lovable to friends, full in blessings, sparing in curses. This is Jacob, who by his mother’s stratagems seized his father’s blessing and escaped his brother’s fury (Gen. 27).

Likewise, fleeing to his uncle Laban, on the journey itself, with a stone placed beneath his head, he saw a ladder set up to heaven; he saw the Lord leaning upon the ladder; he saw angels ascending and descending; and, rising from sleep, he said: “Truly the Lord is in this place,” etc. (Gen. 28:12). But what are Jacob’s tabernacles except the exercises of a soul wrestling and fighting against the base things of the flesh and the enemy’s suggestions? [Col. 0990A] For Jacob dwells in tabernacles so long as the bonds of flesh remain to be loosed. Finally, while the soul dwells in the body, it is surrounded by a multitude of enemies. Lust attacks it; anger seizes a shield; luxury a spear; envy a sword; rashness a buckler; boasting a horse; impatience spurs; pride a helmet. These are the tabernacles or camps of the Philistines, detestable like the tabernacles of Kedar. Jacob, on the contrary, has his own tabernacles, covered with skins of rams dyed red or with violet-blue skins, wholly mortifying himself and flying with his whole heart to heaven. He has goat-hair coverings: the spirit of humility; curtains: the Ten Commandments; loops: concord; golden rings: perpetual brightness. He has upright boards: souls always stretching toward the Lord through the enlarged [Col. 0990B] desire of the heart. He has bases: the prophets; and bars: the preachers. Above all these he has a veil of violet-blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted fine linen, woven in embroidery and beautiful variety: this is heaven, within which the whole Church of saints desires to be received.

O Jacob, behold how beautiful your tabernacles are—would that they were also beloved! Why indeed would they not be blessed if they were beautiful and beloved? But perhaps they are not yet beloved because they are still exceedingly laborious. When they have become tranquil and beautiful, then they will be beloved and blessed. But while they are not only tabernacles but also tents, they are beautiful indeed insofar as they are a spectacle to the world, angels, and human beings; [Col. 0990C] yet they are not beloved, because they are burdened beyond measure and beyond their strength, so that they grow weary of living. They are tabernacles, therefore, because of pilgrimage; beautiful because of love; tents because of the stretching out of mortification. “Like wooded valleys,” because of self-abasement and removal from human eyes; “like watered gardens beside rivers,” because of the pleasant beauty of faith and all good works; “like tabernacles fixed by the Lord,” because of steadfastness of purpose; “like cedars near waters,” because of the height of contemplation. “Water shall flow from his bucket,” because of the incarnation of the Son from the Virgin; “his seed in many waters,” because of the conversion of the nations.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the bread of sons.

[Col. 0990D] Once the distribution of the lower rank of household members has been made, the arrangement of the sons’ table must now be explained. For as the Son “has inherited a name more excellent than all others” (Heb. 1:4), so a richer and more generous provision ought to be set upon his table with a more glorious privilege. The first and ample grace of this table is that it is not arranged through servile duties, but managed by the most orderly actions of wisdom and grace. Certainly, no negligence intervenes where wisdom is the stewarding minister; no offenses occur where grace has been assigned the service. One of these presides over the kitchen, the other over the table. What wisdom prepares in the kitchen, grace sets on the table. Wisdom strongly [Col. 0991A] prepares what is to be cooked; grace sweetly serves what is to be eaten. Wisdom pours in salt; grace, fat or oil. Wisdom makes it boil abundantly; grace knows how to cool it in moderation. Wisdom presses the laboring; grace stands by the resting. Wisdom girds her loins with strength; grace relaxes her folds with the abundance of satiety. Wisdom weighs the labors of merits; grace repays the rewards of prizes. Whose appetite for heavenly desire wisdom judges broader in hunger, for that person grace sets a fuller dish at the banquet table as recompense. Wisdom boils the various stews of labors in its pots; grace places seven loaves of graces upon its tables. Finally, from its garden and irrigation wisdom brings forth most wholesome and delightful [Col. 0991B] vegetables; from its storehouses grace brings back most delicious breads.

Let us enter, therefore, the kitchen—not in the white garment of angelic calling, but in the filthy garments of Jesus the high priest, that is, in garments of penance to be performed. By the whitening of baptismal or penitential grace, these garments shall be taken from him among every nation and people; and through the renewal of glorified immortality a clean mitre shall be given to him. Thus let us see the pots and the stews in wisdom’s pots. There are, indeed, two pots in wisdom’s kitchen: the two tablets containing the commandments of life. The commandments are ten, written on the tablets, like stews minced in the pots, because the preparation or restoration of eternity is obtained from the commandments of the tablets. [Col. 0991C] We draw stews from the pots when we receive commandments from the tablets. In its heart, as in its garden, divine wisdom devised these remedies for human salvation; and when it wrote them with its finger upon the tablets, it was as though it minced them in the pots. The kitchen is Mount Sinai; the sons for whom these dishes are prepared are the sons of Jacob or Israel, not according to the flesh but according to the spirit. For of them the Gospel says: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs” (Matt. 15:26) of the Gentiles for eating.

The sons’ table is the mind of the good; the house is synagogue or Church; the ministers are the angel and Moses. But the stews of the legal commandments kill rather than nourish when they are tasted without grace. Thus [Col. 0991D] the sons of the prophets cry to Elisha—whose name means “the salvation of my Lord”: “There is death in the pot, man of God” (3 Kings 4:41). But he orders Gospel meal to be poured in and restrains the harmful evil. For even in the letter of the Law the precept of legal observances is deadly unless the saving remedy of grace is present. But wherever grace comes, every difficulty or evil is at once driven away. Certainly, although wisdom teaches by teaching what you ought to do, it is either little or evil unless grace intervenes. It is little because to know what ought to be done and not to be able to do it contributes less to life; it is evil because “for one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin” (Jas. 4:17). Therefore let us be taught by wisdom and helped by grace. Let us seek instruction [Col. 0992A] from wisdom and the vehicle from grace. Let wisdom cook the stew; let grace season it.

These are your two hands, these your two arms, O Jesus: with one redeeming us from evil, with the other filling us with good; with one destroying death, with the other granting life; with one conquering the enemy, with the other liberating humanity. “These your hands made me” by creating and “fashioned me” by redeeming (Ps. 118:73). Let one be under my head, lest I fail; let the other embrace me, that I may live; let one labor with me, the other place me with itself; let one rise by night and give food to its maidservants; the other, prey to its household; let one give a richly patterned garment, the other a girdle to the Canaanite. Let both together clothe with double garments; let both refresh with manifold things. For “the Lord is my strength and my grace, and he has become my salvation.” With strong hand [Col. 0992B] and outstretched arm, let us now bend back the pots and see and receive what they contain. Let us therefore see what the first commandment is, as though a stew: “You shall have no strange gods before me; you shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness that is in heaven above, or in earth below, or of those things which are in the waters beneath the earth,” etc.—behold the first commandment. “You shall not take the name of your God in vain”—behold the second. “Remember to keep holy the Sabbath day”—behold the third. “Honor your father and your mother”—behold the fourth. “You shall not kill”—the fifth. “You shall not commit adultery”—the sixth. “You shall not steal”—the seventh. “You shall not speak false testimony against your neighbor”—the eighth. “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house”—the ninth. “You shall not desire [Col. 0992C] your neighbor’s wife, his servant, his maidservant, his ox, his ass, nor anything that belongs to him”—the tenth (Exod. 20:3–17).

Each of these is a stew or dish for souls. For nothing necessary has been omitted, and nothing superfluous added, in these ten commandments of the Lord. In them the soul lives; without them it dies. Whatever is taken from them with grace is life-giving; the edifice of our faith is supported by these columns and painted in these colors. If you understand them historically, they are columns raising a house; if morally, they are colors painting a palace. Therefore, in the first commandment, understood morally, guard against stealthy insinuation; in the second, error; in the third, love of the world; in the fourth, [Col. 0992D] impiety; in the fifth, credulity; in the sixth, fornication; in the seventh, rapacity; in the eighth, falsehood; in the ninth, worldly covetousness; in the tenth, the thought of adultery. Wisdom nourishes little ones with these foods, suckles its children at these breasts, and refreshes its young men with these stews. We thus have wisdom’s stews, from the vegetables of herbs that never fall away. Let us also seek the loaves of grace, without which none of the others suffice. These loaves are figured more than once in the shadow of the Law and are also found not infrequently in the prophets.

What does the Gospel speak of except the sevenfold Spirit? Read in the Gospel the seven beatitudes, as seven loaves of grace; read in the Lord’s Prayer [Col. 0993A] seven petitions; read of the seven loaves with which the Lord fed four thousand people in the wilderness; read in the Psalm seven voices; read in Isaiah seven women; read in the same prophet seven spirits resting upon the flower; read in John’s Apocalypse seven golden lampstands, seven eyes, and seven horns of the Lamb; read in Exodus seven lamps; read in the Prophet seven eyes upon one stone; read that the Lord rested on the seventh day; read that there are seven Penitential Psalms. Read also that seven qualities meet in the constitution of a human being: four elements in the body and three powers in the soul—rationality, irascibility, and concupiscibility. If you investigate further, you will find many more besides these.

O soul, if you hunger for grace, knock at the door. If [Col. 0993B] you knock, it shall be opened; if you ask, it shall be given. Grace does not hide itself, flee by lurking, or conceal itself in pits. It is at hand, lest you tire in seeking; it meets you, lest you be wearied by tedium; it goes before you, lest you be ashamed by the embarrassment of conscience; it rouses you, lest you become sluggish; it carries you, lest you stumble; it directs your steps, lest you go astray; it feeds you, lest on the road you fail and grow sick through want. It teaches the foolish, because it is wise; gives understanding, because it is understanding; supplies counsel, because it knows the mysteries of all things; confers strength, because it is almighty; illuminates with knowledge, because it is the mother of all sciences; bestows piety, because it is the honey of all affections; applies fear, because it is the guardian of all goods. For just as a certain guardian over innumerable treasures, fear is placed last among the [Col. 0993C] gifts in order to preserve incomparable graces. Piety is a most precious jewel, yet it is easily stolen by impiety unless guarded by fear. Knowledge is above gold and topaz (Ps. 118:27), but the better it is, the more desirable it is to the envious. Strength is not found in many markets; but the rarer it is, unless it is preserved more diligently, the more desirable it is to seize. What is better than counsel? Yet unless it is hidden and preserved, what is more vain? In heaven nothing is dearer than understanding, yet if it is corrupted in a human being, what is more destructive? Nothing is more sublime than wisdom in the heart of a man, yet if it is darkened by the senses of the flesh, what is more base? “Man,” says the Psalmist, “was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:2). Better, therefore, is the good safeguarding of things acquired than [Col. 0993D] the laborious effort of acquiring them.

Keep the maidens of grace good and beautiful, but under the guardianship of a most watchful tutor—namely, fear. Surely the adorned beauty of my maiden summons a concourse of an unchaste crowd; the adulterer besieges the maiden’s door or chamber. He tells her to come out; he promises in order to draw her out; he flatters her in order to behold her beauty. Do not, daughter of Jacob, do not go out without your brothers to the women of this land, for there is a lion on the way (III Kings 13:14): Shechem son of Hamor, a young man burning with desire for you. At least let Simeon and Levi—that is, fear of present and future things—always stand beside your chastity as protectors and avengers, lest you be carried off, lest you be captured, lest, softened by flatteries, you be prostituted to the disgrace of your nobility. [Col. 0994A] Virgin Israel, if you fall, Simeon threatens present punishment and Levi future punishment; the one has a sword piercing at close quarters into the prostitute’s inward parts, because “the axe is already laid to the root of the tree” (Matt. 3:10); the other is girded with a two-edged sword, namely one striking the hind parts. Hence: “He struck them on their hind parts; he gave them everlasting reproach” (Ps. 77:66). Therefore let fear, as by the authority of a guardian, exercise vigilance over its ward, lest she be harmed in anything, suffer loss, or be contaminated by someone’s shamelessness.

## CHAPTER XV. On the bread of servants

“Whoever commits sin is the servant of sin” (John 8:[Col. 0994B]34). The misery of this age is the servant’s bread; and this bread lasts as long as the form of this world does not pass away. For, says the Apostle, “the creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope, because the creation itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 8:20). By the sentence of the just Judge, the neck of the proud sinner is bound in this world beneath the yoke of perilous vanity. For the first fruits of the wages of original and actual sin are the nets of inextricable vanity; and vanity is grievous in every way when holiness does not lighten it. For it bends the eye of reason downwards and prevents the eye of contemplation from looking upward to higher things. This servant remembers the ancient courses of freedom; he sighs for angelic food; he laments the exchanged spacious regions of most delightful air. He bears thorns fixed into his spine; he feels arrows swimming through the marrow of his entrails. He groans that his back is bent back beneath the worst constructions piled upon it, and, with his heart trembling, sees the abyss of miseries already swallowing him.

A consolation harsher than every desolation, food more austere than all fasts, clothing rougher than nakedness. He is more indignant at such servitude than at servitude itself; for it is slavery to sin, the slavery of slaveries. For the servant of sin is servant to as many masters as there are vices. The vices command him—not masters, but tyrants; not well-wishers, but enemies. They preside, but without benefit; they rule, but without pity; they command, but without discernment; they reign jointly over one [Col. 0994D], but in dissension. If any one of them is not obeyed, it makes the wretched side bleed; if it is obeyed, it kills. Under these masters life is worse, death better—if only it is not more bitter. For if the servant asks for bread, he receives a stone; if a fish, a serpent; if food, a viper; if wine, poison. They often quarrel over which of them, claiming for itself the servant’s eye, hand, foot, or any other limb, shall cut it off. Lust claims that it has reigned in the eyes; gluttony in the throat; lying in the tongue; cruelty in the hands; frivolity in the feet; vanity in the ears. Conversely, curiosity claims the eye, disobedience the throat, whispering the tongue, avarice the hands, intemperance the feet, injustice the ears.

[Col. 0995A] I would rather have no limbs than pay the taxes of so many torments! Nothing is more merciless than this exaction, where what has always been paid is demanded again, renewed in a repetition accompanied by tortures. Lust is not sated by inciting to evil; misery does not end by demanding punishment. You fill lust, and it still hungers; you endure punishment, and it still increases. Because you have not extinguished the vice, unhappy one, you have kindled for yourself an inextinguishable flame. Therefore one must fight—indeed, rebel—against the phalanxes of vices, lest you suffer without end that accursed dominion of demons over you. Seek therefore a judge; state your case; demand judgment; implore an advocate; set forth the injury; recite the sentence; acknowledge the Lord; renounce the tyrant’s sovereignty. The judge is now present, the tribunal is set, the assessors stand around; let the litigants advance, let them present their pleadings in their customary manner. Servant, speak; proceed.

**SERVANT:** Judge of equity and most just ruler: before you, the truth of cases is weighed, not the blandishments of flattery. You detest falsehood, reject calumny, and punish the rashness or lies of deceivers. Only truthful, unornamented speech reaches your ears. For the lying adversary and his father have more than once been convicted of lying; yet he still breathes and presumptuously hopes in the same artifice of deceit. But both reverence for your authority and love of truth restrain me from the presumption of deception. I ask that this speech of mine may not be reckoned arrogance, since it is produced by the unbearable endurance of one suffering evils, not by corrupt character. O [Col. 0995C] Lord, compassionate and merciful, attend to my soul; deliver it; rescue me because of my enemies. For behold, I shall relate things wonderful indeed—true, yet stern.

When I had as yet done neither good nor evil, these seducers forestalled me; “they surrounded me and wounded me” (Song 5:7). They took from me the light of my eyes, tripped up my feet, dug through my hands, and crushed my bones. The wounds are still fresh; blood is still before my hands; bruising is still before my eyes; the wound still swells; the arrows are still fixed within me. “See, O Lord, and consider whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow” (Lam. 1:12). Why then do you not avenge my blood, my Savior? [Col. 0995D] Why do you not avenge me upon my adversary? Why are such things presumed in the kingdom of your power? Why does injustice rage so unbridled in the kingdom of justice? This audacity of the adversaries, if it prospers, will surely afterward tempt another besides me. Surely, unless the authority of your judgment restrains so wicked a power, he himself will dare to assail your throne, my Lord. See, Lord, and consider how, like a lion ready for prey, he roars. Already he draws arrows from his quiver; already he hurls the darts of lies; but shut, I beseech you, the mouth that speaks iniquity. Judge my cause, Lord, defender of my life. I do not wish, Lord, I do not wish to multiply words, because your knowledge precedes my telling. At last let my judgment come forth from your countenance; let your eyes behold what is equitable. [Col. 0996A] To this let the judge say: let the adversary also speak, if he has anything.

**ADVERSARY:** I marvel that you have endured so long the foolishness of my most wicked, flattering servant. Why is one readily convicted of perjury heard in court? Indeed, he can be rejected by a twofold charge, both ingratitude and perjury. For against you, his Creator, he stands as an ungrateful transgressor; against me, his purchaser, he is faithless in withdrawing himself. For he did both: he despised you and sold himself to me. He also spent my money, adopted my customs, frequently invoked me through idolatry, and for innumerable days, months, and years lived solely for my purposes—in lying, perjury, fornication, theft, drunkenness, impurity, pride, envy, gluttony, and avarice. [Col. 0996B] Perhaps now, because I demand the debt, I am accused of calumny. Is it just that I should lose one whom I have possessed under such a title and for so long? The wicked servant is justly condemned out of his own mouth, for he testifies that he has been mine from his mother’s womb. I too, therefore, shall stand by the judgment.

**SERVANT:** The beginning of your words, most wicked Satan, is falsehood. I am not the devil’s servant but God’s; I am not a most wicked flatterer but a reporter of truth. I have spoken not my own foolishness but your cruelties. I do not deny that I was harmed both through the pliancy of youth and through the cunning of your deception; but, having fallen through both causes—namely youthful pliancy and hatred of fraud—I ask the most kind and just Judge to restore me to my former state. Since you deceived me by fraud so that I might borrow your money, contrary to a perpetual prohibition, I desire that, the contract being rescinded, I may not be bound, because fraud gave cause to the contract. Nor does prescription run in this contract, since divine law forbids it and prolongs indulgence while one lives in this world. For thus it is provided in the eternal laws: “I do not will the death of the sinner, but that he turn from his way and live” (Ezek. 33:11); and elsewhere, “in whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (ibid.). Every human being enjoys this right. Lord Jesus, you gave the law and taught thus in the law; let your judgment therefore decide the ambiguities of disputes, so that one suffering calumny may be freed and one committing injury condemned. But lest there be doubt concerning the fraud, let the contract, if it please you, be recited in order. Why, says this serpent to Eve, [Col. 0996D] mother of all, did God command you not to eat of every tree of Paradise? To him the woman answered: “We eat of the fruit of the trees that are in Paradise; but of the fruit which is in the midst of Paradise, he commanded us that we should neither eat nor touch it, lest perhaps we die.” But the serpent said to the woman: “You shall not die at all. For he knows that in whatever day you eat of it, your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be as gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3:1).

Behold the contract; behold the fraud. If it please you, these matters ought to be stronger than every proof, for Moses, the public recorder, wrote them in the public records; this therefore ought to suffice for proving the fraud. Yet, if I must also produce witnesses, I bring forward Joseph, a man of proved integrity. I also bring forward Job, [Col. 0997A] known to the judge and greatly commended by the judge himself, who says of him: “In all these things Job did not sin with his lips, nor did he speak anything foolish against God” (Job 1:22). Moreover, I summon Isaiah, most noble and most familiar to the Judge, as a witness for my cause. Speak, Joseph, testimony for me—indeed, for our race—as concerning yourself: “I was taken away by theft,” he says, “and here, though innocent, I was cast into a pit” (Gen. 41:14). What say you, Job? “I have not sinned,” he says, “and my eye remains amid bitterness; if my step has turned aside from the way, and if my eye has followed my heart, let him weigh me in a just balance,” etc. (Job 21:25). Isaiah too dares to say: “My people went down into Egypt, and Assyria oppressed him without any cause” (Isa. 32:4). Besides these witnesses, [Col. 0997B] who sufficiently suffice, since “every word shall stand in the mouth of three,” all truthful people also agree in this testimony. Judge me therefore, Lord, according to my righteousness; save me.

**JUDGE:** By the sentence of my mouth I free from the seducer’s power the child who was deceived, who had neither foreseen by personal experience nor learned from another’s example how great the punishment of sin is—especially because of the severity of the penalty suffered and the malignity of the fraud. Yet this condition remains: that meanwhile the servant shall pay for having transgressed my covenant, doing penance in ashes and dust, in sackcloth and with barley bread, until he comes who shall pay on his behalf the whole amount of the debt, with centesima interest (one per cent). The judgment having thus been confirmed, the man began to be distressed, considering [Col. 0997C] his poverty and despairing of the price, crying: “Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24). But the Judge’s Son—indeed, the Son of oil—standing by this spectacle and having compassion on the miseries of the miserable man, says: “Accept me, and repay the whole debt; for in my keeping are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. Behold, I go to be sacrificed for you. Do not at all shrink from my death, if you wish to recover your life; for your life depends upon my death.”

**SERVANT:** If it must be so, let not my will but yours be done.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the bread of hired laborers

[Col. 0997D] That Painter whose seat is heaven and whose footstool is earth; whose white and best colors are natural goodness, and whose blacker and darker colors are the rational will failing from the good beginning into a most foul end; whose palace is the heaven of heavens, whose private chamber is that which surpasses every understanding and thought—ordering his arrangement as wonderfully as wisely—first established in the Church patriarchs and prophets, then apostles and evangelists (Eph. 4:31), afterwards good teachers and shepherds, and finally did not refuse to have even servants and hired laborers for the benefit of his household. But just as no abuse appears in a painting if a somewhat dark color is laid beneath white, so likewise, if Judas the worst traitor is found among the good apostles, or if Satan [Col. 0998A] is present with the sons of God, this is accepted without astonishment when God’s patience is considered. A hired laborer is one who serves God not for God’s sake; a hired laborer is one who proclaims Christ from opportunity rather than truth. A hired laborer is one who seeks “his own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 2:21). His bread is the wisdom of the flesh, or temporal advantage. He does not eat the fine-flour bread of sons or the barley bread of servants, but the swine’s bread of bran or chaff. For the son receives the grain of grace; the servant, the straw of the letter; but the hired laborer receives the chaff of secular philosophy or glory. The son dwells among sayings, the servant among thorns, the hired laborer under thorns. Moses signifies the son; the people Israel, the servant; Heliab, Moses’ kinsman, the hired laborer. For in Numbers it is read that [Col. 0998B] Moses asked this Heliab to lead them through the desert, saying: “Come with us, that we may do you good, because the Lord has promised good things to Israel” (Num. 10:29). And when he had answered: “I will not go, but will return to my own land, from which I was born,” Moses said: “Do not leave us, for you know in what places we ought to set up camp in the wilderness, and you shall be our guide; and when you come with us, whatever of the riches the Lord is going to give us, we shall give you” (ibid., 30).

Many aspire to preeminence not in order to lead others, but in order to mislead; not in order to show the way, but to set a stumbling-block. These are full of malice. Many, indeed, point out the path, but while sitting still instruct others beforehand in what must be done, doing nothing themselves: sluggish negligence possesses these. Others desire only temporal profit in their elevation to high rank, neglecting the salvation of those committed to them: avarice draws these. Others teach good things and sometimes acquire honorable things, but not well and not chastely, because they do this not for God but for vain glory: the Lord calls these hypocrites and hired laborers. Observe the hypocrite. The hypocrite pays attention to the eye, not to God; to appearance, not faith; to money, not grace. He does not enjoy God, but uses him as though he were money; and he enjoys money as though it were God. With God he buys the world; with faith, money; with religion, the age; with tears, wine; with fasts, a banquet; with sackcloth, linen; with silence, human applause. A marvelous thing to say: he hides in order to appear, is silent in order to be heard; he does not follow in order to attain, withdraws in order to go before, flees in order to seize, weeps in order to laugh, fasts in order to be filled. Thus gangrene spreads (2 Tim. 2:17); thus the fraudulent fox proceeds by winding its crooked turns. He keeps vigil at the temple of holy vain glory and celebrates solemn vigils of most holy avarice. For thus he prays: “God, give me that honor, that money, that glory!” And these prayers are commended by a great outpouring of false tears and by emaciation of the body.

Perhaps he sometimes obtains the effect of his requests; but what then? Vigils are changed into continual sleep, abstinence into constant feasting, weeping into loud laughter, silence into much talking, mourning into mockery. Truly the eyes [Col. 0999A] of this man are upon the Lord (Ps. 14:15), not always but temporarily, until he has mercy upon him. For although, in its budding, the hypocritical vine may flower, it produces wild grapes, not grapes. Truly, a detestable image painted with the finest colors and filled with the foulest rust! For polished falsehood, by its feigned likeness, almost surpasses in the eyes of the foolish truth that is content with naked simplicity. An elaborate lie, dressed in fig leaves or garments of skins (Gen. 3), boasts with greater pomp than simple truth; but virtue, more precious in its hidden things, refuses to be obscured by borrowed glitter. It is ashamed to be burdened rather than honored by another’s splendors. Naked, it is more beautiful; open, more becoming; when seen, more lovely in flashing lights; revisited again and again, more desirable. Indeed, it is clothed for this reason alone: lest, intemperately contemplated, the weakness of the eyes be dazzled. It rejects a softer touch, is irritated by the caresses of seducers, repudiates the pretender, anathematizes the hypocrite, knows no hired laborer. It does not lay its head in a harlot’s bosom, but on a golden couch. Having been illuminated by light, it illuminates the light itself rather than being illuminated by it. Virtue is the prize of contestants, the palm of victors, the scepter of those who fight back, the crown of saints, the instrument of Deity. It never grows old, but becomes youthful as it advances with the increase of time.

## CHAPTER XVII. On ash-baked bread

[Col. 0999C] We must now treat of ash-baked bread. First it must be explained who are the ashes covering the bread, and what it means, according to the prophet (Hos. 7:8), for bread covered with ashes not to be turned; and it must also be investigated what fire is and in what material it makes ash. But, to state the substance of the matter more plainly and briefly beforehand, we say that fire is desire, the material the soul, ash mortality, bread the human being; bread that has been turned is a human being fallen into sins; bread not turned and ash-baked is a human being weighed down by mortal sin and not raised through penance. We also say that the Law of Moses is ash-baked bread, which, while carnally understood, is as though covered with ash and is not turned until the veil [Col. 0999D] of ignorance is removed from those who turn to the Lord. We say also that a soul occupied with secular affairs is ash-baked bread; for as ash blinds the bodily eyes, so curiosity clouds the sight of reason or contemplation. Let us therefore see by what blowing the fire burst into flame, what and how far it devoured—namely, as far as the ashes of mortality—and finally who placed bread beneath ash: namely God, by the sentence of the eternal curse. For until this covering of mortality, daily gnawed by moths and torn by worms, is worn away, the ash of our mortality will not be lifted and the bread will not be turned.

Therefore bread is placed under ash, though unwillingly, [Col. 1000A] when the human being is naturally subject to vanity and mortality. Yet I say that the human being is naturally subject to mortality, not through a defect in creation but through the punishment of transgression. For from creation he had the power not to die; from transgression he has the necessity of dying. This transgression spread its branches and shoots from the first man Adam to the last human being yet to exist in flesh: “It covered the mountains,” that is, the people of the former age, “with its shadow,” which is mortality, “and its branches,” which are the suffering of mortality, “the cedars of God” (Ps. 79:11), that is, Christ’s apostles. For Adam, with all the fathers who were before the Flood, although they lived longer lives and were, as it were, upon the higher summit of time, nevertheless died. The apostles also, in the fullness [Col. 1000B] of time, although redeemed by the blood of the Lamb, although raised with Christ, although made partakers of eternal life, nevertheless died. For what human being shall live and not see death? (Ps. 88:49). For even the Lord Jesus has an issue of death (Isa. 67:21); nor is it surprising that we die, who are born with sin, since by nature we are all, as the Apostle says, children of wrath (Eph. 2:3). Since the Son of grace, owing nothing to death, nevertheless by dying paid the debt assumed under the condition of debtors, by what reasoning can the son of wrath escape the bonds of death? Ought he not to pay the tribute of death for himself? This, then, is the debt: that the human being be covered with the ash of mortality until he is altogether freed from sin and the punishment of sin.

[Col. 1000C] But at the end, together, heaven shall be rolled up, earth renewed, and the human being turned. Heaven indeed shall be rolled up because, released from the service of this administration, it shall endure no further clouds, darknesses, or storms. Accordingly, in the dreadful coming, this airy heaven too, renewed, shall bloom in most serene tranquility and perpetual beauty—though meanwhile it is afflicted by many disturbances and defiled by the malice of spiritual wickednesses. The earth also, purified by fiery vapors from the salinity caused by blood and by the pollution of its inhabitants, shall thereafter be fitted for glory and delights; and anew, as it had been in ancient ages, shall be called the land of peace and life. Then the human being shall be summoned from the tomb; then he shall be turned from the left side to the right; [Col. 1000D] then what was sown in corruption shall rise in incorruption, what was sown in dishonor shall rise in glory, what was sown in weakness shall rise in power (1 Cor. 15:42). When such a change comes, then there shall be turning; then, I say, ash-baked bread shall be turned, because every human being shall rise again. But whence comes ash so hard, so vile, so hateful? Hard because of the harshness of sufferings; vile because of the abomination of vices; hateful because of aggravation. Hard in death, vile in birth, hateful in the mysteries [perhaps “ministries”] of this life. Vile because of guilt, hard because of penitence, hateful because of punishment.

[Col. 1001A] Whence, I ask, is ash except from fire, and whence is fire except from the serpent? And what is the fire that makes ash except desire giving birth to death? For when desire has conceived, it bears sin; and sin, when it has been completed, generates death (Jas. 15:15). For as consuming fire devours nearly everything down to ashes, so the fire of desire burns the soul it has touched by temptation; it burns up the soul it has drawn headlong into consent; it turns into ash-burning the soul it has shut up in the furnace of action. The viperous tongue, by insinuating this fire into Eve’s soul, kindled the forbidden thing, blew it aflame by displaying the fruit, set it ablaze by promising immortality, and finally burned it up by leading it into sin; and, when the sentence of mortality had been proclaimed, reduced it [Col. 1001B] to ash. With this ash the whole offspring of transgressors is not only covered but buried; with this ash, I say, every sinner is sprinkled, fed, and buried. He is sprinkled as one originally guilty; fed as actually wicked; buried as condemned without end. Nor after death, rescued by God’s mercy from penal flames, is one turned who before death has not been turned through the conversion of confession and penitence, under the inspiration of the most merciful Creator. Behold, that rich man clothed in purple, because he was turned in feasting and was not turned by the benefit of almsgiving, was at last buried in hell (Luke 16:22) and did not deserve to be turned even by a single drop of water. Lazarus, however, because he was turned by poverty, sores, and hunger, was lifted by angels into Abraham’s bosom.

Job indeed, ten times covered with the ashes of affliction in the furnace of his temptation, was turned, as he himself testifies while speaking to his friends: “Behold,” he says, “ten times you confound me” (Job 19:31); and again: “My harp has been turned to mourning, and my organ into the voice of those who weep” (Job 30:31). Conversely Pharaoh, though stirred ten times by the hand of the Lord on account of the heaviness of his heart, was nevertheless not turned. First God changed his waters into blood, and he was not turned from hardness; second, he multiplied frogs in their inner chambers, and not even so did he turn; third, he brought forth gnats, most savage flies which in summer are inflicted upon people’s hair with a burning bite [Col. 1001D] (Exod. 8); fourth, he brought dog-flies, offspring of decay and mothers of worms, and Pharaoh’s heart was not softened; fifth, he killed their beasts, and the insensible stone-like heart remained; sixth, Aaron and Moses taking their hands full of ash from the furnace, Moses scattered it into the air before Pharaoh, and behold, sores and swelling blisters appeared throughout all Egypt; yet he could not turn from the oppression of his pestilence. Seventh, in hail he devastated everything that was in the field, and he did not recall his hardened heart from his own devastation. Eighth, the locust came and consumed whatever remained from the hail, and he did not move his dead heart from the place of his wickedness. Ninth, horrible darkness came over all the land of Egypt, so that for three days no one saw [Col. 1002A] his brother or moved from the place where he was; nor could the heart blinded by malice be enlightened. Finally, tenth, he struck every firstborn of the Egyptians; and then, although Pharaoh was stirred and violently shaken, he nevertheless neither returned nor was turned to penitence or faith.

O how weighty, how hard to lift or uncover is the human heart! The almighty hand labors to rescue and does not free; it warns with words and presses with blows, yet cannot draw the raging beast from its pit. O how merciful is God’s hand, which strikes mercifully in order not to punish cruelly; scourges temporally in order not to burn eternally! It now rages compassionately, in order to turn the impious to piety and bend the impiety of evildoers toward the justice of the good! For who knows, as the prophet says, whether God may turn and forgive, and leave behind him a blessing? (Joel 2:14). Let us therefore turn and return, as persons turned, to the Lord our God, because he is kind and merciful, and readily relents from evil (ibid. 13). O how many saints, first turned astray and even turned away, afterwards wonderfully returned and were turned! Behold David was “violently thrust that he might fall” (Ps. 117:1), and, joining murder to adultery, he almost rolled down into hell. Thus he says: “Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell” (Ps. 93:17). But what did the strong hand do? How did it turn him? Immediately, surely, he laid his hand upon his wound and exposed his sin to be treated by the physician, humbly and faithfully confessing it [Col. 1002C] as promptly as publicly as possible. “I have sinned against the Lord,” he says (2 Kings 12:13). Behold, confession and penitence turn back, by forgiving sin, the man whom desire had turned astray by drawing him into consent.

It is indeed evil to be turned astray, but worst not to be turned back. The one turned astray is wounded; the one turned back is healed. One is turned in fleeing; one is turned back in returning. It is disgraceful to be turned astray, but a reproach not to be turned back. The devil turns me astray, but Christ turns me back. The devil turns badly, because toward death; Christ turns back well, because toward life. The devil turns toward hell; Christ turns back toward Paradise. The devil turns toward despair; Christ turns back toward living hope [Col. 1002D]. Impatience also turns astray, but patience turns back. Bread that has been turned once is not properly baked unless it is frequently turned again; one side of bread is darkened by ash laid over it, and the other, if not turned, remains raw. The ash must be removed and the bread turned, so that the heart may be lifted from the earth and illuminated by grace. For does one who falls not add to it that he may rise again? For why did Christ die except for our sins, or rise again except for our justification? (Rom. 4:25). You had slipped, O soul, from the handle of justice and were rolling, through the sin of transgression, in the mud of the deep (Ps. 68:3); but behold, Christ sent forth his soul from the handle of the body after you—not to pursue you, not to plunge you down, but to redeem you. [Col. 1003A] He came as far as the abyss of punishments, to which the abyss of vices had brought you. He put forth the wood that you might swim out; he stretched forth his hand that you might escape; from the punishments in which you were turning, he called you back to the penitence from which you were turning away.

Behold why Christ died: namely, that one dead might raise the dead. But why did he rise again? Certainly, that one living might raise the dead; certainly, that he might bring our iron back to its handle; certainly, that he might raise with himself the bodies of the saints; certainly, that he might teach the way of return and the pattern of being turned back. O sinner, if under Pilate—whose name is interpreted “mouth of a hammerer”—you suffered with the head the rending and condemnation of the soul, fastening, mockery, tasting of vinegar, hanging on the cross, the sending forth—or rather the loss—of the spirit, descent into hell; [Col. 1003B] why not also resurrection? Why not the manifestation of life? Why not the injury of the nails and lance? Why not the change into new life? Why, finally, do you not imitate the glorious ascension? But who sold the soul? Indeed, indeed, Jesus, who was the traitor? “A man of one mind with him, his leader and his acquaintance, who together with him took sweet food” (Ps. 54:14).

O my soul! Your intimate companion, sleeping in your bosom—namely, your flesh and bone, your body—sets the price of your valuation at thirty pieces of silver, when, in order to fulfill the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, it reckons the loss of the soul as the profit of its avarice, as though thirty pieces of silver. As Judas hands Jesus over to the Jews (Matt. 26); as Delilah hands Samson over to the Philistines (Judg. 16; 2 Kings 17); as Absalom hands over his father David to be afflicted—so carnal desire betrays you to malignant spirits, in order to destroy life, weaken the strongest one, and drive the king and his father from the throne of the kingdom. Finally, you are handed over to Pilate to be crucified when you are condemned with Satan to punishment. He strikes you with whips and scorpions when he afflicts you with present and future punishments; he stretches out your hands and fastens your feet with his nails when he pricks your affections and actions with the stings of unlawful desires. He pierces the inward parts of your ribs and entrails with his lance when, removing shame at your evils, he has persuaded you to glory in evils. At last he hangs you on the cross when he makes you a companion of spiritual wickednesses both in malice and in punishment. For one who despairs of penitence, like one hanging, despairs of life. Such a soul is buried in hell and reckoned among wicked demons.

Thus you had proceeded—indeed, exceeded all bounds—O soul; and unless Jesus had mercifully come to your darkness, you would always have departed miserably and never returned to the true light. Therefore he came and received your wounds in his own body, in order that by the wounds of his body he might heal the wounds of your mind. You indeed went before your Lord toward death and wounds; but follow your Redeemer toward life! If he [Col. 1004A] did not disdain to go as far as your dunghill, why do you refuse to follow him to his heaven? Follow him now as he rises, since he followed you as you died. He followed one turned astray, but must be followed by one turned back. First, therefore, rise from the dead by abandoning sins; appear to the living by confessing your evils to your superiors. Then show the places of the nails; show how the side was pierced; do penance; renew your life, that you may no longer die to sin, as Christ, risen from the dead, now dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him (Rom. 6:9). Finally ascend to heaven, that you may sit at the Father’s right hand: caught up through contemplation and fixed in heavenly things through love. Behold how evil it is to be turned astray, but how pleasant to be turned back!

## CHAPTER XVIII. On bread of many kinds, from the prophet Ezekiel

[Col. 1004B]

The Lord speaks thus to Ezekiel concerning the making of bread composed from many and diverse kinds: “And you,” he says, “take for yourself wheat, and barley, and beans, and lentils, and millet, and vetch; put them into one vessel, and make for yourself bread according to the number of the days during which you shall sleep upon your side: for three hundred and ninety days you shall eat it” (Ezek. 4:9). The more unusual this bread is, the more difficult its exposition. That breads are made of wheat and barley is not remarkable, because it is customary; but from beans and lentils, millet and vetch, people make for themselves not bread but dishes, nor do they customarily mix them even then, but separate them, so that they have beans separately, lentils separately, and likewise each of the others separately as food. What then does the mixture made at the Lord’s command from kinds so unlike indicate, unless perhaps that the people for whom the preacher did this had, by living wickedly, confused the natural sense of the human mind with the animality of irrational cattle? For this man was a transgressor both of the natural and the written law; he, I say, did not divide the hoof according to the law, because he did not divide rightly (Lev. 11:3), because he did not separate the precious from the vile (Jer. 15:19), because he did not distinguish dross from silver, because he mixed water with wine; finally, he did not remain in charity, upon which all order depends, but lived in exile in the captivity [Col. 1004D] of flesh and soul, in which there are only error and horror.

Plainly, it is a dreadful and utterly to be abolished mixture of faith and unbelief, darkness and light, life and death, good and evil. When someone worships the Creator in spirit and truth (John 4:23), he has wheat; when he serves God for temporal things, barley; when he is puffed up by his riches, glory, or secular learning, beans; when, by exchanging the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of corruptible man, he is dulled, lentils; when, in investigating subtle matters concerning God beyond what is fitting, he becomes vain, millet; when, through lack of understanding, he compares himself—made in God’s image—to senseless beasts, vetch or oats. But a soul or people of so unstable a purpose, [Col. 1005A] so diverse a counsel, so slippery an order, is fed, in proportion to the confusion moving within its mind, with an ordered meal. For, that it may notice the disorderly condition of its own heart, the preacher prepares before its eyes an unusual concoction—rather than a meal, I know not whether bread or pulse, or bread and pulse together. “You shall put them,” says the Lord, “into one vessel.” The one vessel in which the incomprehensible variety both of thoughts and of affections, whether good or evil, is stored is the human heart. And rightly are they commanded to be put into one vessel, because the one heart receives or conceives all a person’s goods and evils. For it is capable of justice and injustice, truth and falsehood, religion and superstition, hatred and love. “And you shall make for yourself breads, according to the number of the days during which you [Col. 1005B] sleep upon your side.” The prophet had been commanded to sleep upon his left side, and afterwards to sleep upon his right; we must therefore consider what each side signifies, and who sleeps upon the left and who upon the right. There are, then, two things in which the heart is enlarged either toward good or toward evil: namely, charity and desire. Charity is the right side; desire is the left side. He sleeps upon the right side whose heart is enlarged in charity. But he sleeps upon the left who stretches the reins of his desire everywhere, even to avarice. Yet whether you sleep upon the right or upon the left, you shall make for yourself breads according to the number of the days during which you sleep: so that, whether you seek the glory of eternity or present and momentary pleasure, by earning breads of virtues or of [Col. 1005C] vices you may establish for yourself, on your present journey, a day of good things or a day of evil things.

But as the glory of the righteous is eternal, so the punishments of the wicked are infinite; and as the works of each of the godly receive a reward worthy of their merits, so the reprobate endure eternal condemnation according to the number and measure of their evils. The sacrament of baptism is also understood: the one vessel in which the Son of Man gathers good and evil people alike, as crops of different ranks. For in the one vessel of regenerating baptism, divine consecration mercifully places whatever kind of human beings it has admitted, like differing species of grain and legumes. Indeed, in bodily form and in the dissimilarity both [Col. 1005D] of character and pursuits, some people are compared with wheat, others with barley, others with beans, others with lentils, others with millet, others with vetch: while some are conformed, through the imitation of charity, to the grain of wheat—that is, to the incarnate Word whom the Lord sent into Jacob and who fell in Israel. Others are fed upon the barley of the Mosaic Law through continual meditation upon divine severity; others are like beans, puffed up by the vain glory of worldly wisdom. Others are blinded by the lentil of sophistical arguments, presuming upon the powers of their own intellect; others, vanishing into the emptying-out of truth through refined reasonings, are made thin like millet; others, beastly in both life and understanding, are confounded by sinking their eyes to the earth through the lowest baseness, as though they were vetch or oats. [Col. 1006A]

Therefore the mercifulness of God, healer of every brokenness and medicine for every sickness, constructs the vessel of the Church broad, solid, wide, and round. It is broad, so that it may suffice to receive not only useful things but even useless things until the threshing-floor is cleansed; not only clean things, but unclean as well. It is solid, so that, enduring every assault both from inward and outward occurrences, it may evade them. It is wide below, so that it may not stagger even amid the surging of waters; round above, so that it may in no way fear a division of unity. Into this vessel human beings enter by believing well; beasts and cattle are gathered by living carnally. Seeds—that is, evangelical commandments—are brought in by preaching; and provisions for every soul which enters the Church through faith, namely the promises of the life that now is and of that which is to come, are supplied in sufficiently ordered fashion according to the diversity of merits. [Col. 1006B] In it bear and lamb, lion and calf (Isa. 11:7), dove and raven, believer and reprobate, are contained until the iniquity of the flood passes away (Ps. 56:2; Gen. 7). In this same signification, the apostle Peter, while praying, was shown a linen vessel let down from heaven by its four corners (Acts 10:11), in which were all four-footed animals, creeping things, animals and beasts of the earth; and it was said to him, “Slay and eat” (Acts 11:7). But while he did not yet understand the mystery of the vessel and what it contained, and said with Ezekiel, “Nothing common has entered my mouth,” he heard, “What God has made clean, do not call common” (Ezek. 4:14).

[Col. 1006C] We read that we must remove the covering of the letter with worthy reverence, as wise and faithful Ruth is recorded in the book of Judges to have done: at Boaz’s feet (Ruth 3), she uncovered the bedding, fearing, that is, to put her hand to his head and uncover the priest’s head contrary to the ordinance of the Law. Let us therefore again examine more carefully what this one vessel signifies, in which the prophet Ezekiel mixes wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and vetch (Ezek. 4).

The body of Christ, which is the Church—as was shown above—is a most precious, most spacious, most solid, wide, and round vessel. It is indeed more precious [Col. 1006D] than gold, silver, and precious stone, because the Church regards all these things as the mud of streets or as dung, in order to gain Christ. From her girdle golden tassels hang, and she herself stands in clothing embroidered with gold and surrounded by variety (Ps. 44:10). Within her also is a beautiful place for dwelling, because the upper room in which the disciples prepare the Passover is large and furnished; and, according to the prophet, “The house of God is great, and the place of his possession immense” (Baruch 3:24). Truly she extends her branches as far as the sea, and her shoots as far as the river (Ps. 79:12); indeed, she has stretched out her skins and widened her cords in glorious things, that she might reach mightily from end to end [Col. 1007A] and order all things sweetly. She also sends her ambassadors by sea in vessels of papyrus, to a nation torn apart and mangled, to a people beyond which there is none other (Isa. 18:2). Behold how broad is the Church, which cries from the ends of the earth and rules from sea to sea, and from the ends unto the bounds of the world! (Ps. 77:8.)

The vessel of the Church is also most solid, because it is the world that shall not be moved (Ps. 95), from age to age; because it is the seamless tunic (John 19:23), which could not be torn by Arius, Photinus, Nestorius, Eutyches, or countless other heretics. Like evil fish, they wished to break the net of God, but did not prevail. For certain men entered in sheep’s clothing, while inwardly they were ravenous wolves [Col. 1007B] (Matt. 7:15), in order to destroy and lay waste, like foxes, the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts; but the gates of hell did not prevail (Mark 16:18); rather, the hammers of the whole earth were broken, and the autumnal trees, twice dead, were uprooted.

Thus the vessel, so precious, so spacious, and so solid, is figuratively Noah’s ark amid the flood-waters; in reality it is the Church amid a crooked and perverse nation, or amid many afflictions. It was let down from heaven by its four corners (Acts 10:11): both because of the four Gospels by which the Church’s faith is founded, and because of the principal virtues by which it is perfected; because of the four living creatures which appeared to the prophet [Col. 1007C] by the river Chebar (Ezek. 1), or to John in the Apocalypse; and because of the four regions of the earth from which the elect are gathered, from the highest heavens to their bounds.
