It contains every kind of four-footed animal, creeping thing, and beast of the earth, because Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners (1 Tim. 1:15), not only those from Judaea, but those of every race, language, tribe, people, and nation. For he is the one who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of truth (2 Tim. 1:4). He saves the proud, but first when humbled; he saves the avaricious, but first when freed from avarice; he saves the lustful, but first made chaste; he saves the ungodly, but first made godly; he saves the unjust, but first justified. Thus it is said: [Col. 1007D] “Slay and eat” (Acts 11:7): that is, convert the ungodly from their ungodliness, and in converting them convey them into your inward parts.

For Peter’s inward parts are receptacles of divine salvation. Certainly no one is taken into Peter’s inward parts who has not been chewed by the example of conversion. He is crushed by Peter’s teeth who, having received faith, turns himself from error. But he twists Peter’s inward parts, rather than being cherished by them, who, converted to faith and having entered the Church, does not reform his conduct but repeats the errors he had renounced. Such a person must nevertheless be endured, because he can be converted to what is better, and it is not yet the time for uprooting but for planting. Whoever is baptized thus enters Peter’s vessel. Yet among the baptized, neither their endeavour is uniform, nor their dwelling the same, nor their rank of merits one and undifferentiated; rather, “one is the glory of the stars, another the flesh of birds, another of fishes” (1 Cor. 15:39). [Col. 1008A] Therefore the seeds are different and there are many breads in one vessel, because from many persons of differing faces (2 Cor. 1:11) one body is gathered and one Church built, as the Apostle says: “We, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another” (Rom. 12:5). Nor is it surprising that God’s Church is one and manifold: John writes in the Apocalypse (ch. 1) to seven Churches, and in the Song of Songs she is called one dove (Song 6). For even the Spirit himself, by whose filling she is joined to divinity in marriage and called the Bride of the Lamb, is described by Solomon not only as one but also as manifold.

The Spirit is one indeed in essence, [Col. 1008B] but manifold in gifts. “To one through the Spirit is given a word of wisdom, to another of knowledge, to another faith in the same Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:8). Again elsewhere: “There are diversities of ministries, but the same Spirit; and diversities of operations, but the same Spirit; and diversities of graces, but the same God who works all things in all” (ibid., 5). What then? Let not wheat grow proud because of the nobility of its stock; let not barley despair because of the coarseness of its lowliness; let not the bean be puffed up with the wind of arrogance; let not the lentil of earthly dullness raise its eyes so as to grope at noon; let not the millet of ingenious presumption exalt itself above itself; let not the oat of lowest extremity rot in its own body. If you are wheat from the stock of the patriarchs, do not be exalted. But if you are exalted, it is not [Col. 1008C] you that bears the root of unity and grace, but the root bears you (Rom. 11:18). If, compared to senseless beasts (Ps. 48:13), you are barley, do not cast yourself down, because the spirit of wisdom is kindly and knows how to take iron from the earth and turn it into silver, to raise the humble from dung, and set him among princes. If puffed up by renown and nobility of flesh, or by fleshly understanding, deflate yourself and remember the manger, or the cross, of Jesus. If you are a lentil, for which Esau lost his birthright (Gen. 25), losing the sight of faith because of empty philosophy, cry to Jesus: “Jesus, Master, have mercy on me, for the light of my eyes is not with me” (Luke 17:13). If you are millet, by excessive presumption in your own intellect, having refined yourself more than is just, bend down and worship the top of Joseph’s staff (Gen. 47:31), worshipping rather than disputing the sacrament of his incarnation; for he who made you was made for you, that he might restore you. [Col. 1008D] If you are vetch, oats, or spelt—black, that is, like the face of a scorched pot; light upon the surface of the waters; rough as a hedge-thorn—lay hold of goodness, discipline, and knowledge from God’s law, and you shall have a place in the vessel, or in the Ark, or in the Church.

Behold, this is a time and place not for separation but for mixture; not for winnowing but for threshing; not for being stored in the granary but for being shaken on the threshing-floor. At present there is not yet a right side on which, resting, we shall be satisfied with clean and bare bread, beholding [Col. 1009A] God’s glory face to face—not receiving a brief and slight recompense by measure and weight, as now, but seeing all without measure and drinking all that belongs to glory, to grace, to peace, and to jubilation. Meanwhile, as we rest upon the left side, let us warm ourselves with whatever consolations we can and be consoled as much as we can, until we are turned from the left side to the right. For to be freed from present tribulation and pain is to be turned from the left side to the right; to be received into future joys and blessedness is to sleep upon the right side. Meanwhile the bride’s left hand is placed under our head, lest we fail on the way; breads are set before us, and, if not such as those which shall belong to the exulting in their homeland, at least such as the want of hungry exiles deserves. [Col. 1009B] For “to a hungry soul even bitter things are sweet” (Prov. 27:7); for the hungry person desires what the sated person disdains.

## CHAPTER XIX. On common bread for the people.

Full is the hand of God, for whom it is as ready a thing to refresh the desires of his whole creation as to answer the prayers of individual persons. From his abundance he never becomes poorer; rather, through the lavish distribution of his gifts, he is ever more glorious. For he receives when he gives out; he overflows when he flows forth, because he both gives and receives in giving: what he gives is his, and the recipient to whom he gives is his; what he creates is his, and what he gives to his creature is his. When he creates anything, it is his; [Col. 1009C] when he gives created things to any creature of his, neither are the powers of the Creator weakened in creating all things nor are the riches of the Giver exhausted in distributing his gifts. Therefore he breaks for the whole household of the nations the breads of his mercies; and, after measuring out suitable portions to tribes, peoples, languages, and nations with the incomprehensible profundity of his eternal mystery, he finally sent down to the lower parts of the earth one bread in which the whole assembly of the faithful might partake. This bread both satisfied the foremost desires of all individuals and, by a single taste of his mercy, filled every hungry soul.

This bread did not come to satisfy the proud righteous, but to heal converted sinners. He eats with publicans and sinners (Matt. 10:11): either he figuratively eats those same persons, or he is eaten by them. He eats with them when he frees those who labour by the gift of his grace from their miseries. He eats them when he utterly justifies them from sins. Finally, he is eaten by them when, in their heart cleansed from dead works, he delights in the expansiveness of charity. O that my soul might be swallowed, not by Jonah’s whale, but by Jesus! O sweetness of Jesus’ merits! O warmth of Jesus’ inward parts! O secret of Jesus’ breast! Jesus’ belly sounds to me like a harp! The harmony of those strings in their modes lulls the concert of heaven to sleep. He is carried away by delightful sleep for whom Jesus plays the harp in the whisper of a gentle breeze. He beats the drum mightily upon the cross, but sings profitably in evangelical preaching; [Col. 1010A] he plays the psaltery sublimely in the resurrection, rejoices sweetly in the ascension, and pleads wisely the cause of his poor ones in his confession before the Father.

The soul of Jesus is a golden bowl full of perfumes, which are the prayers of the saints (Rev. 5:8). Because of its sweetness, if you are in Jesus’ inward parts, you do not fear the lance by which you are sweetly wounded—not through an enemy’s hatred but through Christ’s charity. From this wound she who had placed the Bridegroom between her breasts, and had her inward parts pierced by his lance, languished vitally, not mortally, and cries out: “I am wounded by charity” (Song 2:14). The charity of Jesus, in the inward parts of his mercy, spared itself neither from the pouring out, nor indeed from the piercing, of his side, so that he might admit you—once received like a dove through this opening into the very caverns of his feet, hands, and side—to all his counsel; mingle you with his joys; join you to divinity; establish you in eternity; and make you equal to angelic blessedness. [Col. 1010B] May these inward parts of God’s mercy penetrate our inward parts, the mercy in which he visited us (Luke 1:78), he who fed—or restored—us with the richness and fatness of his blessings. This mutual folding together, or reciprocity, of the inward parts of God and man—through God’s dispensation and humankind’s imitation—embraces God and man so firmly that it bends God himself down to our little huts and lifts us up to his palaces; it makes the impassible God mercifully compassionate toward us and makes the still mortal human being, through God, steadfastly invisible.

[Col. 1010C] Do not, O soul loving God and beloved by God, be opened by the short and slight needle of love, because Jesus’ side was opened by the lance like a great door in heaven, so that countless peoples streaming to the Father through the same Son might suffer no narrowness in entering life. “Rend,” says the prophet, “your hearts and not your garments” (Joel 2:13). If Jesus has expanded his bosom so that you may possess more fully and perfectly the tabernacle not made with hands—that is, not of this creation—why do you not likewise stretch out your heart like Solomon’s curtains, so that the fawn of the deer may walk and leap within it without hindrance? Stretch out your whole self, so that, enlarged with your whole soul and all your strength, you may love him whom, in order that you might possess him whole, you see stretched wholly upon the cross. By such extension do not fear rupture; for the extension of love knows how to produce increase, not loss. [Col. 1010D]

It also girds hearts; it does not tear them apart. For those who are torn from the unity of the Church by schism and heresies do not feed on this bread; rather, those who, by the coagulum of unity in conduct and Catholic faith, are converted into the same thing. For of this bread, as has already been said, the Apostle says: “We, though many, are one bread, one body” (1 Cor. 10:17). And elsewhere: “All ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink” (2 Cor. 10:3). Likewise in the Songs: “One is the dove” (Song 6:8), because the Church’s charity is one; one sister, one tunic of Christ. It admits no separation and consents to no divisions. It resists the division by which Solomon decrees that the son of the harlot be divided, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed [Col. 1011A] (1 Kgs. 3:25), renewed in the birth-pangs of a renewed sorrow through compassion for him hanging on the cross, whom one mother bore for one person, one only-begotten for one only-begotten, and whom she sees cut into parts (Luke 2:15). For she would rather lack the comfort of her son than tear unity apart, according to the saying: “If your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it from you” (Matt. 5:24). She prefers to retain the inward parts of compassion in love for unity, setting aside the comfort of her son, rather than consent to cruelty by dividing the one.

This unity of faith and religion is common bread—but it is common to the faithful; the stranger does not share in it, and the heretic does not taste it. Each prophet indeed has a prophetic bread set before him, yet not for himself alone. Likewise the apostolic table has evangelical breads, spread over the whole earth through manifest preaching. Each order of saints has, according to the merits of its virtues, bread privileged for spiritual devotion, yet not private through individual ambition. [Col. 1011B] For how could citizens of heaven, in their commonwealth, claim for themselves separately a private possession of blessedness, when that entire inheritance, according to merits, is the one patrimony of all who dwell there? The inheritance of the Lord’s servants is indeed one, but the dwellings of the saints are many, according to the diversity of merits, because “we, though many, are one bread, one body” (1 Cor. 10:17). In heaven there is one bread: eternal life; one bread: faith, or the highest Trinity. Refresh your soul with unity of faith, lest you be either unfaithful to God or intolerable to your neighbour.

When Lucifer, who rose in the morning, by pride cast off humility, he lost charity together with the unity of the good spirits. When Adam preferred his wife’s will to love for the Creator, stripped of the humility of paradise and disturbed within himself, he made within his one self a great multitude through the manifold discord of thoughts. To remove and pacify this multitude, the mediator of God and men united in himself diverse natures—that is, divine and human—and by that union joined heavenly and earthly things in covenant, so that every soul, as if clothed and renewed in Christ through faith, might share in the fellowship of angelic spirits and become one with the Spirit of God. This is the bread which worked salvation in the midst of the earth, [Col. 1011D] hanging between two living creatures; who, born in the midst of the earth, worked salvation while hanging between the Church and the Synagogue. This is he who opened his mouth in the midst of the Church, and who, as chief of priests, is always in their midst. This is the fruit placed in the midst of paradise, which heals every brokenness, relieves sicknesses, feeds conquerors, gathers the scattered, cleanses lepers, heals the lame, brings the dead to life, gives light to the blind, and strengthens the paralysed.

This is the shaft of the lampstand, which has three branches on this side and three on that: for the innocent cleave to him through innocence, the righteous through righteousness, sinners through repentance, virgins through chastity, martyrs through the shedding of blood, married persons through the generosity of almsgiving. [Col. 1012A] This is the cornerstone made the head of the corner (Ps. 117:22), so that angel on one side and human being on the other, coming together from remote regions, might have one head, and there might be one shepherd and one fold (John 10:16). Therefore let not the harlot be ashamed to be washed in the trench of the altar which the soldiers opened when they dug through the hands and feet (Ps. 21:18) of the Saviour. Let Naaman run, covered with leprosy from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head (2 Kgs. 5); and, cleansed in the waters of the Jordan by a sevenfold purification, let him give thanks to his cleanser. Let the man blind from birth come forth and, after his eyes are anointed with the mud of the Lord’s incarnation (John 9), recognize the Word of the almighty Father sent from royal thrones. Let the paralytic go up into the house; and, because he cannot enter through the door, let him enter through the roof, uncovering his sins [Col. 1012B] (Mark 2), not presuming upon his merits. For he would enter by the door if he had not defiled his garments; but he climbs up through the roof when, doing violence to the kingdom of heaven, he subjects his body to mortification and his spirit to humility.

Let the adulteress be brought forward by her accusers, but mercifully absolved by the finger that writes upon the earth the law of mercy. Let the sick Lazarus be announced (John 8), then declared asleep, and at last found stinking; but let him be enlivened by tears, recalled by a voice, and, at the command of Life, raised to life. Let the hungry crowd be fed, the raging wind calmed, and the woman flowing with menstrual blood touch the hem and be healed. Whatever infirmity may hold them, let every person who comes and believes be freed. [Col. 1012C] Let the thief, placed at the hem of the garment, touch the ointment flowing from the head down into the beard—the beard of Aaron—and let him breathe healthfully from the very jaws of death. O how common is this bread, which makes itself like, and joins itself to, those who were exiled outside the camp because of the multitude and uncleanness of their souls! Finally, he says: “Come to me, all who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28). O Jesus, whom the Father sent to feed his people, give us our bread; give us yourself, the food of life, in the innocence of your heart and the understanding of your hands! O Lord Jesus, our soul does not live except by your food; it is not satisfied except by your body. This food alone fills every living creature with blessing. It ensures that whoever has eaten it shall not lack.

## CHAPTER XX. On sanctified and priestly bread.

[Col. 1012D]

Would that one of the highest order of seraphim might cleanse my lips with tongs from the altar (Isa. 6), both for speaking and for eating priestly bread! For it is both dangerous and presumptuous through rash boldness to handle the most holy mysteries with unclean lips or unwashed hands—mysteries which, when touched only by ministries worthy of apostles, rebuke the irreverent, condemn the shameless, and deify the humble. The priest, moreover, must be clothed in new and various garments, anointed with oil, purified by manifold sanctification, and at all times received among holy things, that he may be refreshed with the breads of sanctification. For what punishment or penalty a priest incurs when he does not minister in priestly fashion is shown both by the Law itself in the vengeance, or burning, of Aaron’s sons Nadab and Abihu, who, when they kindle strange fire, are burned (Lev. 10), and by the Gospel example, when the man who is recorded to have reclined at the banquet without a wedding garment is cast into the outer darkness (Matt. 22). [Col. 1013A]

Therefore the priestly attire must first be explained, and then the food considered, because an honourable cultivation of character merits the food of angels. The Lord says, speaking in Leviticus of the pontifical garments: “The pontiff, that is, the great priest among his brethren, upon whose head the oil of anointing has been poured, and whose hands have been consecrated in the priesthood, and who has been clothed in holy garments, [Col. 1013B] shall not uncover his head, nor rend his garments; and he shall not enter at all to any dead person, nor be defiled for his father; nor shall he go forth from the holy things, lest he pollute the sanctuary of the Lord, because the oil of the holy anointing of the Lord God is upon him” (Lev. 21:10). Allegorically, Christ is the pontiff—that is, the great Priest among his apostolic brethren. By his help, we cross with dry footsteps the rivers of mortality, poured out on every side from the bank of birth to the shore of death, once the bridge of the cross has been laid upon them; and we have access to God in the vessel of his blood. But oil was poured out upon his head, either because he was conceived of the Holy Spirit or because the Spirit was given to him without measure. His hands also were consecrated to the priesthood [Col. 1013C] when, stretched out all day toward an unbelieving people and crucified upon the wood, they were consecrated and dedicated in his own blood for sprinkling the peoples. And he was clothed with holy garments: that is, with the virtues of charity, justice, patience, strength in suffering, or with glory and honour in the resurrection.

He did not uncover his head, because in his passion he concealed his divinity, or because in the nature of his divinity he was never separated from the Father. He did not rend his garments, because God the Word, once united to humanity, never departed from the flesh. He does not enter at all to any dead person, because he neither committed nor contracted sin, neither in conception nor in death. He was not defiled for his father and mother, because Joseph his father—in the office, that is, of guardianship, not through participation in generation—did not know the Virgin in the defilement of lust; and Mary his mother conceived not from a man but from the Holy Spirit, inviolate, and gave birth incorrupt. [Col. 1013D] He does not go forth from the holy things, because, even while he was with people on earth, he nevertheless always was and is with the Father in heaven. He did not pollute the sanctuary of the Lord, because his flesh did not see corruption. These things I have briefly set forth beforehand concerning the attire of the high priest, namely Christ.

In the moral sense, therefore, the holy temple of God—which is the faithful soul—has its own pontiff: namely, the mind, which is the great priest among its brethren. For as many movements as are produced by the soul, so many brethren, as it were, arise beside the mind. [Col. 1014A] The oil of anointing is poured upon its head when the mind is divinely suffused with the richness of devotion and rubbed with the sweetness of chrism through constant meditation. Its hands are consecrated in the priesthood when the works of the flesh are mortified and those things pleasing to God are performed without ceasing. It is clothed in holy garments when it is adorned with holy virtues. It does not uncover its head when it does not admit an evil thought into the mind. It does not rend its garments when, by committing grave sin, it does not transgress the sacraments of its regeneration. It does not enter to any dead person when it is not brought to consent to sin. It is not defiled for its Father when it fears to offend its Creator through erroneous belief or perverse conduct. Nor is it defiled for its mother when a good intention is corrupted by no malice of corruption. [Col. 1014B] It does not pollute God’s sanctuary when it keeps itself free from consent to illicit pleasure. These matters concerning the mystical priestly attire, not unworthy of angelic contemplation, we have surveyed briefly, in order to show with what sort of garment the priest ought to eat his bread.

Moreover, he must adorn his breast, cover his shoulders with the ephod, cover his whole body with a linen tunic—that is, a close-fitting shirt—crown his head with the turban, fasten both tunic and ephod more tightly to his body with the girdle, cover his nakedness with breeches, and place above the turban a gold plate marked with the title of the supreme Name, completing the glory and splendour of the pontifical attire. The close-fitting linen garment should also cling to the body, with sleeves so tight that it has no wrinkle, descending to the legs; in Greek it is called ποδήρης (*podērēs*), “reaching to the feet” (Wis. 18). [Col. 1014C] In these eight kinds of garments the pontiff is clothed when he wishes to sacrifice—that is, to eat his bread. Every priest, however, even if he is not a pontiff, wears at least four: the breeches of chastity, the linen tunic of charity, the girdle of continence, and the turban of highest reverence. But the pontiff is distinguished by all of them. For one who excels in rank of honour ought equally to surpass others in the merit of virtues. All these things are made of gold and precious colours, because nothing base or filthy ought to appear in a priest’s mouth, work, or thought.

[Col. 1014D] We must also consider where priests cook their flesh, or where they eat their bread. Ezekiel was shown a place facing west, and it was said to him: “This is the place where they shall cook the sacrifice, and they shall not bring it out into the outer court” (Ezek. 46:20). And shortly afterwards: “Kitchens had been constructed beneath the porticoes all around”; and he said to me: “This is the house of the kitchens, in which the ministers of the house of the Lord shall cook the Lord’s victims” (ibid., v. 24). What do these things signify? The place facing west signifies the thought of death. Here priests cook for sin and for offence when minds devoted to God boil the rawness of their evils in divine heat and consume, in the blazing evaporation of the spirit, sins both daily and grave. [Col. 1015A] He cooks for sin who anxiously groans over evils committed. Likewise, he cooks for offence who knows how sharply to rebuke himself for things negligently omitted. Sacrifices must not be carried into the outer court, because repentance ought to be performed, not feigned. For one who confesses sin without contrition carries his sacrifice outside. One who fasts in order to be seen as religious is defiled by that through which the people are sanctified.

Therefore the victim of the Lord must be washed apart and cooked apart, lest it be touched by the people’s breath or overwhelmed by the company of those who live carnally. Let priests wash, through true confession, the hearts of those who sacrifice themselves to the Most High God; let those hearts be cooked through the satisfaction imposed upon them. But where? In the inner court, where are the four [Col. 1015B] corners of the court, and again separate courts within each court. The inner court is the hidden conscience, in which there are four corners: fear, desire, joy, and sorrow. Every soul has these four corners around it, because at one time it is weighed down by fear, at another it wanders through desire, at another it is raised up by joy, and at another it is afflicted by sorrow. Beneath this circuit the whole wheel of human life is always turned; a soul living and feeling in a body is never led beyond or outside these corners. Hence Solomon says: “The spirit goes round and round, and returns in its circuits” (Eccl. 1:6). By the mobility of its nature, the human spirit is moved circularly through diverse motions: now rejoicing, now grieving, now desiring, now fearing. Surely in one court [Col. 1015C] there are four corners, because in one spirit or soul there are four passions of the mind. But the little courts arranged within each court signify that particular movements are present within these general affections.

Perhaps the Psalmist denotes the varieties of these affections of the soul when he says to the Lord: “Yours is the day and yours is the night; you fashioned the dawn and the sun” (Ps. 78:16). By day, indeed, holy desire is signified; by night, sorrow; by dawn, fear, which is the beginning of wisdom; and by sun, joy. In the soul of Jesus too these same affections existed—not falsely but truly—as the Gospel testifies when it records that he rejoiced, grieved, feared, and willed; yet he allowed human affections to approach him by his own power, not from weakness or under a necessity ruling him against his will. [Col. 1015D] Behold the place where priests shall cook for sin and for transgression: so that the divine fire may continually possess our four corners, that we may desire God, fear God, grieve in God, and rejoice with God. Having shown where the flesh is cooked, let us now inquire where it is also eaten with bread. We read in Exodus that Jethro, Moses’ kinsman, offered burnt offerings and sacrifices to the Lord; and then it is added: “Aaron and all the sons of Israel came to eat bread with him before the Lord” (Exod. 18:12). Behold the place where the priests and elders of Israel shall eat bread: “before the Lord,” it says.

It belongs to a pure and sound conscience to be able to receive the brightness [Col. 1016A] of the Lord’s countenance—the unbounded light. Satan, the first transgressor, therefore fell from heaven like lightning (Luke 10:18), because, as he was unwilling to stand in the truth, so he rightly shrank in horror from the rays of divine righteousness, as one fleeing the light, through the shame of his apostasy. Thus Adam sought a hiding-place among fig trees, because by eating the forbidden fruit he shamelessly brought the guilty stain of confusion upon his shameful parts (Gen. 3). Thus Cain fled from the face of God with all the offspring of his sins (Gen. 4). Thus “everyone who does evil hates the light” (John 9:20). Such persons eat hidden away in secret places bread polluted with dung. Hence the Psalm: “My belly has been filled from your hidden things; but I shall appear before your face in righteousness; I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” [Col. 1016B] (Ps. 16:15). This is the bread of priests: namely, the glory of God. Very fittingly, without doubt, after the habit of those who eat has been set forth, the workshop where foods are cooked shown, and the place assigned where priests eat bread, there is consequently placed before them bread spiritually prepared for their use. The glory of God, O priestly soul, is your bread. If you seek anything outside the glory of God, having forgotten to eat your bread, you feed upon the husks of swine, which it is unlawful to eat.

What, then, is meant by the statement concerning priests: “They eat the sins of the people” (Hos. 4:8)? Are the people’s sins the glory of God? Far be it! Rather, it is the glory of God to eat the people’s sins by praying that they may be erased and rebuking them that they may be healed. Is not the destruction of sin the glory of God? The priest takes up the people’s sins [Col. 1016C] in confession, but consumes them in prayer. For thus the injustice of sin is destroyed and the righteousness of God established: when the wicked person turns back from his thoughts and abandons his way, correcting error and grasping truth.

Thus Moses first reduced to fire the molten calf which the Israelite people had cast and worshipped; then he gave it to that same people for food and drink. Certainly he thereby indicates that one must burn and grind down one’s own evil inventions in the heat of a contrite spirit; then chew them by accusation and swallow them in execration; finally, punish and expel the members of sin by fitting vengeance. Behold how the calf of sin is eaten by the people! Do you wish, finally, to see how a priest [Col. 1016D] eats the people’s sins? “Either forgive them this offense,” he says, “or blot me out of the book which you have written” (Exod. 32:32).

Truly this man stands before the Lord and eats his bread! He does not diminish his own glory; and by praying thus he obtained pardon for the people. He broke the bread when he corrected their error; he ate it when he poured forth prayer. He broke the bread, I say, when he restrained the sinner; but he ate when he restrained the Judge. A morsel of priestly bread is to appease God when angry and to restrain the people most strictly from their evils. God is not to be asked for mercy before the people have bowed their neck to the discipline and correction of their teachers. First let sin be destroyed; then the sword of divine vengeance will be sheathed, or appeased. [Col. 1017A] If you eliminate the rust of sin, you will weaken the force of Gehenna’s fire. For the purifying flame of life, if it precedes death, does not follow death as an avenger. You yourself will be able to draw the thorn from yourself more gently and advantageously if you renounce sins, than to endure at judgment the hand of zeal, which pierces to the marrow, if you persist stubbornly in evil. But if you cannot do it by your own hand, employ the tongue and lips of a priest: “For the lips and tongue of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth” (Mal. 2:7).

The priest therefore has on his lips knowledge of how to midwife or draw out the pains of wounds, the blood of sores, and the itching of scars; hence the dogs of the rich man lick Lazarus’s wounds (Luke 16). “My scars,” says he who had concealed or repeated his sins, “have become corrupt because of my folly” [Col. 1017B] (Ps. 37:6). Let the priest, therefore, bend down by accommodating himself to the weaknesses of the fallen, just as Christ, bending down, wrote with his finger on the ground (John 8:6). Let him not wrap consecrated flesh in the hem of his garment (Hag. 2:13); that is, let him not sympathize with the offender and confessor merely perfunctorily or in words alone, for by such a touch whatever he touches is not sanctified. For thus we read in Haggai: “Ask the priests concerning the law, saying: If a man carries consecrated flesh in the hem of his garment, and touches with its edge bread, or cooked food, or wine, or oil, or any food, shall it be sanctified?” [Col. 1017C] And they shall answer: “No!” (ibid. 2:12–13).

Therefore consecrated flesh is not to be taken in the outer edge of the cloak, but in the depth of the heart; for it is not an appearance of piety but strength rooted in the marrow of the soul that sanctifies. The bread, cooked food, wine, oil, or any food of the confessor is not sanctified if it is touched only with the hem of the cloak; because neither humility, wisdom, devotion, nor any virtue sanctifies one who loves God not with all his heart, all his soul, and all his strength (Deut. 6:5), but only with his lips. Therefore the priest should bend down with his whole condescension to the ground of the person confessing sins, since he cannot write unless he has taken pains to humble himself.

## CHAPTER XXI. On bread baked in an oven.

[Col. 1017D]

Three matters present themselves for setting forth and explaining when we wish to discuss bread baked in an oven. First we must consider what the oven is, what the bread is, and by what fire either the oven is kindled or the bread cooked. Briefly, then, it must be said: the oven is the virginal womb; the fire is the grace of the Holy Spirit; the bread is the incarnation of the Son of God. The Virgin prepares a place in womb and heart for the Word to be incarnate; the Holy Spirit prepares a dwelling-place; the Son himself brings about the nuptial covenant of Word and flesh in a lawful union; the archangel Gabriel pleads the rights of this marriage on both sides; Joseph, acting as a porter, provides comforts, asks for wages and payments, and solicits provisions in his official capacity. We must next see what each of these accomplishes [Col. 1018A] and from what source each arises. The Virgin is from us; the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit is from the supreme Trinity; the generation of the Son is from both parties, namely from the Father and from the Virgin. For the Word is from the Father, the flesh from the Virgin. But how, where, when, and by whom this figurative bread should come to be at the end of time was decreed from the days of eternity (Mic. 5:2). This oven had necessarily first to be fashioned, not from a lowly lineage nor in an ordinary manner, so that in the fullness of time the bread descending from heaven and giving life to the world might, in accordance with his dignity, find a fitting place in which, by assuming flesh, he could suitably be cooked.

The Virgin of virgins is an oven [for receiving bread, [Col. 1018B] not for consuming or using it. For she never admitted a burning fire, since she did not experience the lust of the flesh; she did not receive a smoking fire, since she did not conceive iniquity; she did not know a consuming fire, since she received most fully in heart and womb the dew from heaven. This Virgin, I say, is not only an oven in receiving the Spirit, but also a bridal chamber in conceiving God, and a temple in living chastely. She is an oven through wholly worthy conduct; a bridal chamber through ineffable conception; a temple through offering herself as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God. An oven for preparing bread; a bridal chamber for receiving the Bridegroom; a temple for admitting the High Priest. An oven for the food of the hungry; a bridal chamber for the offspring of Christians; a temple for [Col. 1018C] cleansing offenses. The oven signifies life’s sustenance; the bridal chamber, the delight of embraces; the temple, the dedication of new life. The Holy Spirit kindles the oven, makes the bridal chamber fruitful, consecrates the temple: fire in the oven, the Bridegroom in the bridal chamber, the priest in the temple; in the oven bread is cooked, in the bridal chamber the womb is made pregnant, in the temple the Most High is appeased. New bread proceeds from the oven, new offspring from the bridal chamber, a renewed people from the temple.

The oven does not burn with the fire of lust; the bridal chamber is neither corrupted nor violated by male defilement; the temple is not profaned by the admixture of unbelief. In the oven we are warmed again; in the bridal chamber we come to maturity; in the temple we grow old in a good birth. [Col. 1018D] Bakers attend around the oven, virgins around the bridal chamber, singers keep watch at the temple. Labor is in the oven, rest in the bridal chamber, singing in the temple. We hasten from the oven to the bridal chamber, from the bridal chamber to the temple. The oven is set out in public, the bridal chamber is kept in secret, the temple is set above on high. The Virgin is an oven in her betrothal to Joseph, a bridal chamber in her impregnation by the Spirit, a temple in the birth of the Son. She is betrothed seemingly as a woman of the common people, but, as a heavenly virgin, she is made pregnant by divine power while Joseph is unaware. As a temple she is purified by the flesh of the Lamb in her maternal womb and blood. Coals of virtues are in the oven; streams of paradise in the bridal chamber; incense of prayers is offered in the temple. Joseph stands by the oven, seeing the flame of the pregnant [Col. 1019A] womb but not understanding what kind of fire it is that makes it pregnant. He is astonished at who put the bread in, when, anxiously searching, he finds the signs of virginity closed on every side and unharmed. Though the doors are shut, he perceives that the bread of angels has already begun to bake in the oven; but he wonders how, and who brought it in without opening a way. He judges it unbelievable and beyond human comprehension that he can be ignorant both how it entered without breaking the seal and how it can emerge without breaking it.

But let him cease to wonder, for thus he acts whose deeds we must not investigate but believe and venerate. He who beyond human understanding placed his Word in human entrails to be incarnate could, beyond our understanding, bring it forth incarnate. [Col. 1019B] The bread will indeed come out as easily as the fire came in without obstruction. The fire did not both cook and draw out the bread. In cooking, it inseparably united the Word with flesh; in drawing it forth, it presented to the world—the world’s Creator and Redeemer—for the instruction of humankind. This fire illuminated and strengthened the oven; it cooked and strengthened the bread. It in some sense preceded the bread, when it came before and descended upon the Virgin; yet it in no way abandoned him, for, proceeding always from him and the Father, it rested wholly and without limit in him from the very conception. From the warmth of this fire the bread received both its fragrance and taste, so that, if you experience the fire of grace, the inner parts of your soul are refreshed as though you had tasted the bread of faith; and again, if you receive the bread of humility, your inner parts grow warm as if you had touched fire. [Col. 1019C] The exceedingly sweet fragrance of both fire and bread—one and indistinguishable—similarly heals every corruption of this air infected by the malice of the prince of these darknesses.

Now we must enter the bridal chamber and contemplate on what couch the Bridegroom lies with his Bride and delights in the embraces they desire, and in some manner consider how we may be admitted. There surely mutual kisses are enjoyed; there the Bridegroom receives anew the words of the Bride, fragrant with the finest perfumes; there the delicate threads of desires are woven; there garments are begun, both linen garments of most pure action and silken garments of angelic contemplation; there, finally, Bridegroom and Bride become [Col. 1019D] one flesh, one soul, and one spirit. The Bridegroom pours into the Bride whatever sweetness, honor, and power he has in himself. Again, by a mutual exchange, he takes back into himself from her whatever poverty, bitterness, reproach, and suffering there is. By this exchange she is undoubtedly enriched, but he is not diminished; she is improved, nor is he deprived of his majesty. For he turns our bitterness into his sweetness, changes reproach into glory, gathers figs from our thorns, harvests grapes from the bramble (Luke 6:44), and purchases life from death and glory from suffering.

Moreover, the Bridegroom is a giant in magnitude, a sun in beauty, a lion in strength, an abyss in depth of knowledge, God in eternity. The Bride, however, is a girl in age, [Col. 1020A] tiny in size, an Ethiopian in the blackness of her color, a woman in weakness, foolish in every kind of prudence and skill. Therefore in the bridal chamber he contracted himself, “made a little lower than the angels” (Heb. 2:5); he stripped himself of garments of glory and girded himself with sackcloth; he laid aside strength and was surrounded with weakness; he hid wisdom so that, made like a beast, he might be a mockery all day long to all the people; he concealed eternity, made subject to the sun, so that he might seem to run temporally with time and not fail. That mouth of the Most High was joined and restricted to the smallness of the Bride’s mouth; the “turned” or “shaped” hands (Song 5:14) that stretched out the heavens were nailed and wounded together with wounded hands; feet adhered to fettered feet; belly was joined to belly. This is indeed a devout matter: that the infinite [Col. 1020B] and immeasurable is shortened to the lowly; but it is no less wondrous that the nature of Adam’s children is restored to unity with the person of the Son of God.

Let us now go out with the Bridegroom from the bedchamber, and with the Bride from the bridal chamber. Let us approach the temple, between vestibule and altar, that we may see and understand our priest completing the offices of sacrifices. This High Priest, according to the order of Melchizedek, upon whose head the oil of anointing was poured and whose hands were consecrated for sacrifice, is not defiled over his father or mother (Lev. 21:11). In the temple of the virginal womb, clothed in every pontifical ornament for offering the sacrifices of our redemption, he proceeded to the altar of the cross not without [Col. 1020C] his own blood, and made peace between things on earth and things in heaven. Here is the ark of sanctification; here the tablets of the Covenant; here Aaron’s rod, which put forth leaves, flowered, sprouted, and bore nuts. Here is propitiation, or the mercy-seat; here the holy place and the Holy of Holies. Here are bowls, a censer, much incense, an altar of earth; and sacramentally all things are found here which are depicted figuratively in Moses’ tabernacle or Solomon’s temple as a shadow of truth. For what is the oil of chrism, from the purest olives, poured upon Jesus’ head, so that he is rightly called “son of oil,” or the poured-out ointment, except the grace of the Holy Spirit by which he was anointed above his fellows from the very day of conception? What is the consecration of hands except their extension upon the cross or their fastening by nails? [Col. 1020D] What does “he shall not be defiled over his father” mean except that, begotten from the Father as equal in all things, he is in no way—as said above—deprived of equality by any diminution? “For he did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized” (Phil. 2:6). And what again does “he shall not be defiled over his mother” mean except that he was conceived not from a man but from the Holy Spirit?

Further, what else can I say concerning the ark of the covenant—or rather, of sanctification—except that the Mother too is an ark of the covenant, containing within herself everything belonging to sanctification, whether of creature or Creator; and that the Son within his Mother is likewise the ark of sanctification, existing rather as sanctification itself than merely containing the sanctification of sanctifications? He has the tablets of the Covenant because all commandments of life and peace are written in his heart. He also has [Col. 1021A] Aaron’s rod: “A rod of equity, the rod of his kingdom” (Ps. 44:7). It put forth leaves in the Nativity, flowered in the Resurrection, sprouted in the Ascension, and bore nuts in the promise or sending of the Spirit. Our rod—or Virgin—also put forth leaves in believing the angel, flowered in conceiving in her womb, sprouted in giving birth from the womb, and bore nuts in fleeing to Egypt with her Son, or in seeing him hang upon the cross. The Son is our propitiation with the Father, because he intercedes for us; the Mother with the Son, because she prays for our offenses. The Son is the Holy of Holies, because he is God of gods; and the Mother is holy among holy women, because she is Virgin of virgins. The Son has the bowl of most pure flesh, from which the cup of life is taken. Likewise the Mother, chaste and pure in all her conduct, [Col. 1021B] offers us an example of living without reproach. From the Son’s censer the Father smells the incense of propitiation; from the Mother’s censer the whole house is perfumed with angelic conduct. The Son is an altar of holy earth because he has a body without stain from his Mother, upon which burnt offerings are consumed when sins are forgiven. Our Lady is nevertheless an earthly altar because she is the refuge of the wretched.

And what greater divine gift and honor can we assign to her than that—to confess what is true—she is mother of God and of man? Whatever is offered in praise of her falls beneath this. If you call her queen of heaven, lady of angels, or anything else supremely excellent conceived by the human heart or uttered by the human mouth, it will not rise to this [Col. 1021C] unutterable honor by which she is believed and proclaimed to be Mother of God. Having said these things about the oven, insufficiently for the subject, let us nevertheless compare the Virginal womb and the enclosure of our religious life further with a material oven. For in an oven a large pile of wood is kindled and bread is baked; in a cloister the discipline of many observances is maintained, so that a secular soul may be strengthened from the rawness of its old life into the firmness of true love; in the Virgin a choir of virtues is gathered, so that the King of virtues may be received. A material fire burns in the oven; spiritual love burns fervently in the cloister; special love glows in the Virgin. Fire accomplishes everything in the oven; the virtue of charity in the cloister; the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit or sanctification of the Trinity [Col. 1021D] in the Virgin’s womb. The oven floor is cleaned by the baker of the remains of coals and ashes; the simplicity of the cloister, by its ruler, from useless superstition and worldly thought; the Virgin’s unchangeable resolve, from desire of the flesh.

The support of temporal life is prepared in the oven, the remedy of eternity in the cloister, the transaction of universal redemption in the womb. The vapor of the kindled fire is retained in the oven, religious fervor in the cloister, love of eternity in the Virgin’s womb. Soft dough comes to the oven; a weak soul to the cloister. Passible flesh, however, does not come from elsewhere, but is granted from and in that virginal womb to Christ. It is not scattered as seed but placed in the oven; in the cloister order ought to be preserved not separately but jointly; the Virgin of virgins conceives or bears not piecemeal or drop by drop, but wholly, the divinity of the Word. [Col. 1022A] Dough, not shapeless but kneaded and formed, is baked in the oven; in the cloister an order must be established not without rule but with a fixed form; the Virgin conceives and bears human nature not without receiving sevenfold grace. The oven breathes sweetly from its loaves; cloistered religion, from its virtues, provides a devout example to secular believers; the Virgin’s virtues render a pleasing fragrance even to angelic ranks. Flesh is fed from the oven’s bread, the soul from cloistered instruction, and the whole Church together from the Virgin’s fruit. Let the poor run to the oven for bread, the humble to the cloister for mercy, and all people to the Virgin’s [Col. 1022B] temple for common salvation. Thus far we have prolonged our pen in setting forth the comparison of oven, cloister, and virginal womb.

## CHAPTER XXII. On bread fried in a pan.

With our face still moist from the oven’s sweat, we continue with the frying of the pan: useful but laborious vexations. Yet, with this one chief consolation, we offer our limbs more cheerfully to undergo the pan, because we shall not fry fine flour in it without oil. For flour mixed with oil and without leaven is cooked in a pan. What does not grow soft before oil? Virtue tested—[more correctly: wearied] and already almost expiring—is restored by oil’s aid; sores [Col. 1022C] are warmed, rough things softened, bitter things sweetened, darkness thinned out [perhaps: made bright], dry things liquefied. How could the pan endure the scorching fire if it were not drenched with oil? Certainly it would not cook food if it burned, if it saw coals without oil. Therefore let the pan first be enriched with oil; then it will not consume the oil-anointed cake by punishment, but cook it profitably. But we must see what the pan is; it is understood in three ways. For the cross of Jesus is an iron pan; likewise the zeal for saving souls is a pan in rulers; and confession of sins or penitence is also an iron pan.

Would that the pan of zeal or confession were so poured over and filled with the oil of mercy and peace as the oil of Christ’s pan overflowed even upon the coals [Col. 1022D] of his persecutors! Consider, then, the ever-increasing and bubbling oil of the Lord’s cross, or pan. The fine flour of the Redeemer’s flesh was pierced, enriched, bloodied, crucified, scourged, and spat upon in the pan of the cross; and what boiled up except the word of patience, like olive oil? For the more fiercely the savage flame of the Jews, like coals, raged, the more richly the wave of bubbling oil sprinkled those standing by. Observe, finally, the wave springing back from the pan, not from the murmur of one impatient but from the desire of one who loves: “Father,” he says, “forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). This wave of oil begs for their illumination; it does not inflict blinding upon them. Before the Passion, the oil in the heart of the Son of Oil seemed indeed to languish, not through loving less, [Col. 1023A] but through displaying itself less because of the obstacle of flesh. But then, boiling in the pan, it began not only to flow out in doing good, but to be carried beyond the capacity of the world, as of a pan, in dying—or rather, redeeming.

It was stirred in the pan, inflamed by sufferings, but it was not moved away from charity, aggravated by pains. The fine flour of his immaculate body was also hung in the iron pan—that is, the harsh and contemptible cross—but it was anointed with poured-out oil so that it should not burn up, because it was comforted by the fullness of grace and did not grow angry for vengeance upon its persecutors. For as Christ dies, he is anointed all the more: the more heavily he was pressed, the more abundantly oil without dregs was squeezed out; nor did the moisture of blessing dry up while the fury of cursing blazed on every side. Hence the patriarch Jacob, recoiling from both the rage and the enormity of the crime of the scribes and Pharisees, abhorred Christ’s persecutors, saying: “Simeon and Levi are brothers, instruments of iniquity for warfare. Let not my soul enter into their counsel, nor my glory be in their assembly, because in their anger they killed a man, and in their will they undermined a wall. Cursed be their anger, because it is obstinate, and their indignation, because it is harsh” (Gen. 49:5). By these Simeon and Levi, the scribes and Pharisees are understood: from Simeon come the scribes, from Levi the priests. These are instruments of iniquity for warfare, who devised iniquities in their heart [Col. 1023C] (Ps. 139:3), saying, “Let us take him from the land of the living.” These, indeed, in their rage killed the man by delivering him up and crying to Pilate that he should crucify him; and in their unjust will the Jews undermined the wall, who stood in opposition for the house of Israel and who is for us a tower of strength against the enemy. Their rage was obstinate and their indignation harsh, because, when Pilate judged that he should be released, they cried: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend; away, away, crucify him!” (John 19:12). Behold the coals; behold the hissing forks pressing on the embers and striking the pan with the rocks of slanderous tongues.

But why do they accomplish nothing—indeed, why do they fail? The pan does not spill out in a stirring of anger; it does not give forth the ugly sound of a threat; its mouth does not dry up [Col. 1023D] through the emptying of love; it does not melt in condemnation of enemies. The flame, whether of Christ loving or the people persecuting—his through mercy, theirs through killing—is spread over the furnace for forty-nine cubits (Dan. 3:47); but inside the pan, as in the Babylonian furnace, dew descends, and burns only those raging outside—not by the assembling of boys taking vengeance, but by the just and customary retribution of evildoers. For just as a viper, at its birth, ruptures its mother’s vital organs, so malice never ceases to punish the conscience from which it arises; it destroys the place of its own birth before it infects the innocence of another’s simplicity. Let us therefore now see what the Law says about the pan: “If your offering is of fine flour mixed [Col. 1024A] with oil and without leaven, baked in a pan, you shall divide it into small pieces and pour oil over it” (Lev. 2:5–6).

We have said that the pan is the cross, in which fine flour mixed with oil is cooked when Christ, full of truth and grace, is sacrificed for us. The flour is without leaven because no stain of original or actual sin was ever found in Christ. They counted his bones while frying him in the pan, so that from the sole of his foot to his crown no part of his body might be free from punishment, in order that, being wholly leprous in punishment without guilt, he might heal all our leprosy in guilt and punishment. Divide it into small pieces: now turning over in mind the nails in his feet, now in his hands, now the crown of thorns on his head, now the covering over his eyes, now the lance in his side, now the scourges and stripping [Col. 1024B] of his whole body, now the words of reproach in his ears. And pour oil over it, that you may suffer with compassion for his sufferings—not by contributing anything to him, but by aiding your own soul or the brothers for whom he died. One must never approach the pan or the flour cooked in the pan without oil, because Christ’s Passion should never be recalled without the compunction of devotion. Oil is poured upon it when a benefit is bestowed upon Christ’s poor for Christ’s sake.

Concerning this pan the prophet Ezekiel is told (ch. 4:31): “Take for yourself an iron pan and set it as an iron wall between yourself and the city.” What iron pan, indeed, must we take for ourselves except Christ’s discipline? Though it may seem somewhat harsh to our carnality, it must nevertheless be taken up and placed between us and the city, so that fortified with this sign on our foreheads, we may not perish with the city of blood which killed the prophets; but may be saved with Rahab from the evil generation, with the scarlet thread of the lamb’s blood hung in the doorway or window of the house (Josh. 2). For the destroying angel reveres this sign and does not kill those marked with Tau—the one who bears the instrument of slaughter and a writing-case at his loins (Ezek. 9:2). Thus far concerning the pan of the cross; now we must consider the pan of zeal. Gregory says that no sacrifice is so pleasing to God as zeal for souls. Zeal is aptly called a pan because, just as meat in a pan is dried of its moisture, [Col. 1024D] so by holy zeal the soul is emptied of the excesses of its carnality. Likewise, as food in a frying-pan dries out in itself yet imparts the richness of its fat to others, so the devout soul of a ruler imposes harsher things upon itself and grants kinder and gentler things to the weaknesses of subjects. “For he seeks not his own interests, but those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 2:21).

Moses says in Leviticus (ch. 6:20) that Aaron, on the day of his anointing, is to offer a tenth of an ephah of flour mixed with oil as a perpetual sacrifice: half in the morning and half in the evening; it is to be broken up in a pan, mixed with oil, and offered by the priest succeeding his father as a most sweet-smelling odor to the Lord; and it shall be wholly burned upon the altar. This authority also applies to the pan of zeal. As applied to the cross, the day [Col. 1025A] of Aaron’s anointing is the day of the anointing of him who was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, who descended from Aaron’s line.

For Aaron was truly then anointed, then sanctified, then dedicated to the priesthood, when in Christ Jesus the power of sanctification fulfilled every mystery of both Old and New Testament. The tenth part of an ephah is not inappropriately understood as Christ’s flesh: in a manner it is a tenth part, being in some sense lower in the order of creatures than the angels, who have nine orders. In the constitution of creation, body is generally subject to spirit. What wonder, then, if flesh capable of dying was lower than the angelic spirit which can no longer decay? This follows Gregory, who [Col. 1025B] says that there are nine orders of angels and that humanity was created tenth. It has very often already been said why Christ’s flesh is called fine flour and why it is mixed with oil. It is offered as a perpetual sacrifice because “he is able to save forever those who approach God through himself, always living to intercede for us” (Heb. 7:25). Finally, what does the phrase “half of it in the morning and half of it in the evening” mean? The Gospel teaches where it is read that in the morning he was led to Caiaphas, in whose courtyard he was beaten with slaps and afflicted with many insults [read: *ludibriis*, “mockery”] from that hour until he was raised on the wood. Behold the half in the morning; the half also in the evening, because Joseph of Arimathea with Nicodemus took Jesus’ body and, when it was evening, buried it [Col. 1025C] in a new tomb (Matt. 27).

This flour mixed with oil, as explained above, is offered hot in the pan as a sweet-smelling odor to the Lord by the priest who succeeds his father: because Jesus, who preceded Aaron in dignity and succeeded him in the time of the flesh—or rather, who approached God the Father, not succeeded him, by the assumption of flesh—offered himself as a sacrifice, hottest with the fire of charity, for a sweet-smelling odor. What is sweeter than the fragrance of human redemption? And the words “It shall be wholly burned on the altar” mean that he did not descend from the cross before giving up his spirit. The passage must be repeated point by point and explained according to the meaning of zeal exercised by any ruler toward the flock [Col. 1025D] entrusted to him. Fine flour is a pure mind; the pan, zeal; oil, mercy; frying, constriction of heart; the hot sacrifice, fervent charity; the priest succeeding his father, the imitator of God’s goodness. Fine flour is fried in a pan when the mind of the righteous is burned through the zeal of holy ardor; oil is poured in when he also loves the very person whom he pursues. The pan must be iron, as the Lord says to Ezekiel: “I have made your face like adamant and flint, and your forehead harder than their foreheads” (Ezek. 3:9). It must not be earthenware, for it would quickly break; nor lead, for it would quickly melt; but the ruler’s mind must be iron or bronze, that it may be hard in endurance and resonant in teaching.

When you pass through fire, O ruler, [Col. 1026A] let not the fire of tribulations burn you; when through water, let not the water of pleasures or the enticing seductions of the flesh penetrate or engulf you. Let your bronze indeed grow hot through bodily weakness, but by no means melt through carnal dissolution. “Scrape the discharge with a potsherd” (Job 2:8), so that by the virtue of patience you may wipe away the stain of your own or another’s corruption. Through your mediation, let the faithful soul being prepared by you for the divine taste experience vapor that gently cooks; through your resistance, let it not experience fire that cruelly burns. O admirable patience of the pan: strong as death, hard as hell, conquered neither by the power of attacking fortune nor bent by the prayers or price of flatterers! “Who,” he says, “shall overcome us or separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation?” (Rom. 8:35). But this produces patience; patience [Col. 1026B] testing; testing hope (Rom. 5:4). “Distress?” But this enlarges the heart. “Persecution?” But this compels one toward God. “Nakedness?” But this frees the course. “Hunger?” But this prepares the living bread. “Danger?” But no danger remains for one who comes. “The sword?” But he is sharper than every sharp sword.

Our frying-pan despises all these things; it goes boldly to meet those who are armed, and says: “For neither death—that is, the promise of life—nor angels, whether evil ones who might wish it, or good ones if somehow they should wish it; nor any principality in heaven or on earth; nor powers—that is, miracle-workers; nor things impending—that is, neither future goods nor evils; nor strength—that is, any violence; nor height—that is, the promise of exaltation; nor depth—that is, the threat of being cast down; [Col. 1026C] nor any other creature, if there were one not yet created, will be able to separate us from the love of God” (Rom. VIII, 38). See how strong the frying-pan is. See again how ready it is to receive burning, so that the food to be cooked may suffer no injury. “I wished,” he says, “to be anathema from Christ for my brethren according to the flesh” (Rom. IX, 3). Whose voice is this but that of the frying-pan, casting itself upon the coals of every punishment so that God’s food may be prepared without being burnt? Would you hear how this frying-pan proved itself before it undertook to cook another’s rawness? “I chastise my body,” he says, “and reduce it to slavery, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (I Cor. IX, 27). But enough of these matters [Col. 1026D] for now.

In a moral sense, however, the frying-pan is compared to confession. For just as, when a great heap of wood has been laid beneath it, a frying-pan is placed over it, and water, oil, or fat poured into the pan boils so that meat or bread may be cooked; so memory, surrounded on every side by the fires of hell, makes all its possessions boil through fear and expectation of the future judgment. Thus, by the force of confession, it casts forth the foam of its sins and, as charity increases, cooks away whatever rawness was in it. It draws the fire inward and cooks whatever raw things had been put in. Foam or dross is cast out when, in true oral confession, every impurity of the heart is cleansed away.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On bread baked on a gridiron.

[Col. 1027A]

One thing is commonly called by many names and signified by many figures. The infancy of human understanding is here provided for by the wisdom of the Father: because the thing is hidden and cannot be comprehended as it is, it may at least somehow finally be reached by a wide circuit of words and meanings. For truth is sometimes covered round, as it were, with many wrappings and clothed over with many garments. It must therefore be stripped of its garments with great reverence, so that its form and beauty may appear like the morning star or like the sun in its strength. For what else is done when the figure of a thing is explained, except that the garment of wisdom is, as it were, unfolded or removed? But when something is shadowed under a proverbial [Col. 1027B] comparison, it is as though a beautiful maiden were covered with her garment. I have said this so that, when you hear of an oven, a frying-pan, or a gridiron, you may understand diverse figures concerning the same thing. For Christ is, figuratively, in the oven; Christ in the frying-pan; Christ on the gridiron. But as bread is put to one purpose in the oven, another in the frying-pan, and another on the gridiron, so Christ is interpreted differently in the oven, differently in the frying-pan, and differently on the gridiron. Bread, indeed, is baked in the oven, fried in the pan, and finally roasted on the gridiron.

The oven, then, corresponds to Christ’s birth; the frying-pan to his Passion; the gridiron to his death: purity in his birth, patience in his Passion, gentleness in his death. For there was no corruption in Christ’s birth, no [Col. 1027C] impatience in his Passion. The Lamb is silent; the Lion sleeps; Christ is not disturbed in death. Let us therefore be conformed to our Head in his birth, since we could not be so through the first birth, at least through the second birth of baptism. Let us imitate our patient brother, if not to the shedding of blood, then at least to the repression of vices, to the piercing of the side; at least to the burying of desires. Let us behold the Redeemer dying; and with the same calmness with which he gave up his spirit, let us proceed, by so peaceful an injunction, to govern the word of our own rule. Let not baptismal regeneration be violated by the sickness of grave sin; let not the garment of patience be torn by the furious onset of anger; let not the sleep of contemplation be disturbed by the disorderly [Col. 1027D] movement of ambitious agitation! Character must be formed in the oven, strengthened in the frying-pan, and brought to perfection on the gridiron. The Lord says in the Gospel: “Behold, today and tomorrow I perform cures, and on the third day I am brought to completion” (Luke XIII, 32). Today is for us in the illumination of faith; tomorrow, in the work of righteousness; the third day, in the completion of glory. Today he enlightens the blind man; tomorrow he strengthens the paralytic; on the third day he raises Lazarus.

As a type of this mystery, when the children of Israel go out of Egypt, they do not offer their God a sacrifice, an offering, and a rational, holy victim pleasing to God until a three-day interval has passed. Under this figure also, the chief festivals are rendered to God three times in the year by the entire people, both in the desert and in the land of promise: namely Passover, Pentecost, and the Feast of Tabernacles. One of these figuratively belongs to penitents, another to the righteous, and the third to those glorified. For the blood of the Lamb washes away the sins of penitents: “Even if they have been as scarlet, or red as the worm, they shall be made white as snow” (Isa. II, 18). The destroyer also passes over the doorposts of penitents, daubed—or rather fortified—through confession and penitence with the blood of the spotless Lamb, Jesus Christ. Yet this sacrifice is by no means offered in Egypt or upon its borders, but in a retreat and dwelling very far away. For first, in deed, word, and will, the house of slavery—that is, the will to sin—must be abandoned, if the offering of our victim is to become acceptable. Then the Passover of those converted is pleasing to God, [Col. 1028B] when, with all the Egyptians of long-standing offences submerged, we have utterly removed from ourselves, with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength, the assemblies of evildoers.

Here the new man of the new life, having cast off the poisonous suggestions of the ancient serpent, is bound to God and justified from sins. Then he advances like the dawn rising toward the sunrise and passes from the cold of snow to excessive heat, so that after the Passover of penitence he may celebrate the Pentecost of righteousness. For as Passover is eaten with wild lettuces, so Pentecost is made splendid by trumpets of rejoicing. Then every possession returns to its owner; slave and maidservant are freed; no one is troubled by the disturbance of any labour; the voice of the taskmaster is silenced; and the voice of bridegroom and bride, the voice of exultation and rejoicing, is heard in the tabernacles [Col. 1028C] of all the saints. This glorious festival belongs to minds that have been justified. For as it belongs to the penitent to bow his head and spread sackcloth and ashes, so it belongs to the souls of the righteous to exult, rejoice, and be glad. One freed by the Lord from the dominion [f. *dominio*] of sin exults; one entering upon a restored inheritance rejoices; one who has a covenant of peace with the stones of the fields and with the beasts of the wilderness is glad.

Look still more carefully at the difference between Passover and Pentecost. Passover is celebrated with blood, unleavened bread, flesh roasted by fire, lettuce, a staff, loins girded, and feet shod. The doorposts are indeed marked with blood; the Lamb is roasted; what remains of the Lamb’s flesh is burnt; the flesh of the Lamb is eaten with lettuces; a staff is held in the hands; the loins [Col. 1028D] are girded with royal belts; and the feet are clothed with new shoes. What, then, do these things signify? In the blood is understood contrition of heart; in fire, confession of the mouth; in unleavened bread, good works without vainglory; in the staff, the vigilance of an unbending resolve; in lettuce, the compunction of tears; in girded loins, the mortification of lustful motions; in shod feet, imitation of the saints, or continual remembrance of one’s end. These are the weapons of the penitent, the implements of one cooking in the oven, the necessities for the nourishment of one celebrating Passover. Passover takes place in the evening, namely when a person has withdrawn from the heat of concupiscence; hence: “They shall return at evening and suffer hunger like dogs” (Ps. LII, 7). For the only true and [Col. 1029A] complete conversion from sins is that by which the ardour of evil desire is excluded and which faithful confession follows, devouring the preceding evils.

This is also why anyone who leaves the camp because of some contagion of the soul returns clean to it only in the evening, after washing his garments. Passover therefore rightly begins in the evening, because then the salvation of the soul begins. Pentecost, however, bright at dawn, has thunders, lightnings, very dense clouds, the sound of a trumpet, the mountain summit smoking, Moses speaking, and the Lord answering. In morning is self-knowledge; in thunder, the sound of preaching; in lightning, rebuke of evils; in voices, exhortation to good; in lamps, the brightness of miracles; in the trumpet blast, the strong preaching [Col. 1029B] of the saints; in smoke, the contempt of the saints, or the blinding of evildoers; in the very dense cloud, humility which protects; in Moses speaking, conscience making petition; in the Lord answering, grace that helps. With these splendours the soul of the righteous is adorned; with these honours is marked the temple of the Holy Spirit, where the oil of charity boils as in a frying-pan, so that, as the penitent is cleansed from defilements by the Lamb’s blood, so the righteous person is anointed against sorrows with the oil of the Holy Spirit. Behold the Passover of the penitent; behold the Pentecost of the justified.

Then follows the Feast of Tabernacles, the festival of tents, in which one must rejoice, not wage war, on the first and on the eighth day, when the Son shall hand over the kingdom to God the Father, so that God may be all in all (I Cor. XV, 14). These are the Lord’s festivals of tents: from the fifteenth day of the seventh month for seven days. The first day is called most solemn and most holy. The eighth day also shall be most solemn and most holy. “These,” says the Lord, “are the festivals which you shall call most solemn and most holy, and in them you shall offer offerings to the Lord.” A blessed but long boundary lies between the first, seventh, and eighth days. The first day is the beginning of the substance of God, which is faith; the seventh, the perfection of righteousness; the eighth, the beginning of glory. The first day is of propitiation, the seventh of sanctification, the eighth of glorification. “Everyone who is of the race of Israel shall dwell in booths” (Lev. XXIII, 42). Good booths are the wings of the seraphim; the cherub also spreads out its wings and protects; likewise [Col. 1029D] the hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings (Matt. XXIII, 37); and the Lord says: “Like an eagle provoking her young to fly and hovering over them, he spread his wings, received them, and bore them upon his shoulders” (Deut. XXXII, 11). The overshadowing of Jesus’ wings is imitation of his virtues. For the King of virtues uses the feathers, or wings, of virtues to fly again above the stars of heaven, to the right hand of the seat of God’s majesty, so that it may be said to him: “Sit at my right hand” (Ps. CIX, 1).

Therefore, whoever is of the race of Israel should live among the nations in this shadow, until he ascends to our girded people. Meanwhile one must keep festival in tents, but abstain from dead works: on the first day through faith, on the seventh through action, so that faith may be without error and works without pretence. Let faith be an eye-salve [Col. 1030A] enlightening the eyes; let faithful works be like an antidote, restoring the dead to life. Let Christ dwell in us through faith; and through works of righteousness let the kingdom of God be within us (Luke XVII, 21). For if the kingdom, or joy, of the Lord is within you, you shall be on the eighth day. For month shall follow month, Sabbath Sabbath (Isa. LXVI, 23), when we have passed from faith to faith; when with unveiled face we are transformed from the brightness of good work into the brightness (II Cor. III, 18) of divine recompense. “This day in the courts of the Lord is better than thousands” (Ps. LXXXIII, 11), a day in which we shall exult and rejoice, no longer mindful, through the bride’s revealing of her breasts (Cant. I, 4), but beholding through present contemplation the face of bridegroom and bride, no longer through a mirror in an enigma, but face to face. For what is partial shall be done away, what is perfect shall be brought to completion: where the oven burns, but with love; where there is a frying-pan, but of praise; where there is a gridiron, but of consummation; where there is Passover, but in the life of the Lamb; where there is Pentecost, but in the tranquillity and manifestation of God’s counsels; where there is the feast of tents, but in the eternal possession of the highest heaven; where there are booths, but of God; where there is not a first day but one day, not a seventh but an everlasting day; where there is not an eighth but eternity.

Yet something must still be said specifically concerning the gridiron; for above we have continued—or rather joined together—the oven, the frying-pan, and the gridiron. The distinctive property of the gridiron must therefore be assigned, and the mystery it contains explained. Zechariah [Col. 1030C] the prophet saw among the myrtle trees a man riding upon a red horse, and behind him followed red, dappled, and white horses (Zech. I, 8). Mystically, therefore, the man riding upon the horse is Christ, who assumed a human body. The Lord sat upon his body as upon a horse, because God would not visibly visit or traverse our valley unless he had assumed a body. The Father fitted to the Word a body not of just any colour or condition, but such as befitted God, such as was necessary for completing the course, and such as our redemption required. Hence that passage in the Psalm: “You have fitted a body to me,” or “You have made ears for me” (Ps. XXXIX, 7; Heb. X, 5). He fitted, I say, the horse to the rider, so that a nobler soul might be associated with the most noble body, and divinity might sit over both. Perhaps this horse is red because it beholds the dignity of its rider not without shame, and so is suffused with blushes from reverence. Indeed, this horse is red because, “being in agony, he prayed more earnestly, and his drops became like drops of blood running down upon the earth” (Luke XXII, 44).

But perhaps this is too little. See where it is red not merely here and there, but throughout the whole body, from the sole of the foot to the crown [Col. 1030D] of the head (Deut. XXVIII, 35): in his Passion the soldiers put a scarlet cloak around him (Matt. XXVII, 28), and here he is red. Finally, he was fastened with nails and his side opened by a lance, from which blood and water came out (John XIX, 34). Behold how he has become worm-coloured; behold how red our horse is, just as David too was a ruddy youth and beautiful in appearance (I Kings XVI, 2). But John the Evangelist saw this same horse on another occasion as white, certainly under another sacramental sign: namely, because the Lamb was without the stain of sin. Thus it might be said to him in the Song: he who sat upon the horse was wholly white because of freedom from guilt, yet also red because of the affliction of punishment: “My beloved is white and ruddy” (Cant. V, 10). And in the Gospel: “Jesus came forth bearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment, and he said: Behold the man” (John XIX, 5). Behind this horse followed red, dappled, and white horses. The red are the martyrs, always enduring to the end the mortification in their bodies for Jesus’ name (II Cor. IV, 10); the white are confessors, [Col. 1031B] ever flourishing in the peace of the Church through virtues and teaching; the dappled are those who were sometimes tortured and sometimes released, neither continually suffering persecution nor enjoying unceasing peace.

Their life or Passion is rightly compared to a gridiron. A gridiron is an instrument having, as it were, certain ribs, and between them certain openings through which the heat of the fire penetrates to the interior of that which is stretched over it. For whatever is placed on it is roasted; and perhaps not bread alone, but also the flesh of the roasted lamb is roasted here. For of the lamb’s flesh it is lawful to eat nothing raw, as the Jews do, nor boiled in water, as the philosophers do, but only roasted with fire, as true Catholics do. Truly, that gentle Lamb in whom it pleased God to dwell [Col. 1031C] (Ps.
