LXVII, 17), upon whom John saw the Spirit descending and remaining (John I, 33), free from every contagion of sin, roasted his flesh upon the gridiron: for when he willed, the fire of persecution touched him; and when he willed, he prevented the lash or penal snare of hunters from approaching him. For he had power to lay down his life and to take it up again (John XVI). Why, when they wished to seize him, did no one lay hands upon him (John VII, 44)? And why, when “I am” was heard, did they fall backward (John XVIII, 6), except because at that point there was no opening in the gridiron of human power, by God’s permission, through which the penetrating force of fire could reach even to the Lamb’s flesh? But at other times they took stones [Col. 1031D] against him (John VIII, 59), seized him, and crucified him: that is, when an opening appeared in the gridiron by divine permission. Here the bread that came down from heaven (John VI, 33) is cooked, and the flesh of the Lamb—or of the fish that comes up from the sea—is roasted in the fires of harsh Passion. Therefore, those who mortify their flesh for Christ are restored by this food lest they fail. For the constant remembrance of the one hanging on the cross soothes the pains of the suffering Christian. Sweet remembrance of the prayer enriched with the fatness of grace and the strength of patience drives the dart of impatience from the heart: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34). The honeycomb dripping from lips of oil heals every bitterness of the mind; blood flowing from the veins of mercy extinguishes the poisons of malice [Col. 1032A] and wickedness. The throat is filled with delight, the belly with satiety, the bones with marrow, and the sinews with strength, when bread from the gridiron is received in entire faith.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On bread anointed with oil.

Our spirit, hitherto distressed by a threefold toil—namely, the oven of inward temptation, the frying-pan of most bitter persecution, and the gridiron of daily mortification—wholly weary, dry, and weakened, quite rightly longs with all its sighs to be refreshed, anointed, and made fat by bread anointed with oil. For it heals those broken in heart, cures every contrition of the soul, and comforts sufferings of whatever anxieties. Therefore, if we have tasted, while labouring along the way of this our pilgrimage, from the torrent of wintry floods—that is, the oven, [Col. 1032B] frying-pan, or gridiron—what do we await except the anointed bread of recompense in our homeland, from him who will give life to our mortal breasts? For he who in exile gave the evangelical law for suffering on account of faith will give in heaven the angelic blessing of reigning with Christ, so that, according to the multitude of sorrows (Ps. XCIII, 19), a just recompense of goods may be weighed out in an equal measure and just sextary upon the scales. Accordingly, the frying of the pan, where the fat of the inward parts flowed out amid sufferings, is recompensed by the anointed bread of redemption, by which our soul shall live immortally; and the gridiron, upon which it held out unto death, by bread sprinkled with eternal glorification. For passibility is changed into impassibility, mortality [Col. 1032C] into immortality. Each bread must therefore be set forth separately, because each is sufficient to fill the entrails of the hungry in its own day.

One bread is anointed, another sprinkled; yet they are not altogether different. For Christ is one, because of the conjunction of two natures in the unity of the same person; but two things are considered in him according to the mutual communication, in the same person, of their respective properties. Likewise bridegroom and bride are one flesh, but the bridegroom is one and the bride another; just as the head is one thing and the body another, yet head and body are one person. Thus Christ is one—the Word made flesh from the Virgin (John I, 14)—together with his bride, the universal Church of all the faithful. Yet we sometimes treat separately of Christ the Head, and sometimes jointly of Christ, Head and body. For we sometimes assign to the Head what ought to be attributed to the body alone; and sometimes ascribe to the body what cannot truly be understood to be attributed to it except by participation in the Head. Therefore, when it is said of Christ that he is the bread which came down from heaven, whom the Father sealed and sent into the world (John VI, 33), this is to be understood of the Head. But where, in another sense, the Church is called the Bride, or sprinkled bread, or fine-flour bread, this is said more particularly because of her union with her Bridegroom, not because of her own dignity. For it belongs rather to the Church to be refreshed by God than [Col. 1033A] to refresh herself by her own power. But now let us return to the breads, whether anointed or sprinkled.

The bread anointed with oil is Jesus, whom the Spirit of the Lord anointed and appointed Bridegroom of the Church. The sprinkled bread is the Bride, one with the Bridegroom, and possessing this very thing from the Bridegroom, at whose betrothal she was sprinkled with sacred chrism. Setting aside, then, the sprinkled bread—not in the faith of belief, but in the course of argument—and reserving it for another day, let us now, with grace assisting, consider the anointed bread. First, however, it must be considered that this anointing was wondrous beyond us in the depth of its mystery both in conception and in birth; it was also confirmed above the angels by the glorification of the Resurrection; and we cannot attain it, so long as we dwell in houses of clay and inhabit earthly understanding, before the ascension to the Father’s right hand on high. For who knows the ointment of the Lord’s goodness in his counsel determining to become incarnate? Or who was his counsellor in effecting this very assumption of our nature? Or who, in the redemption of humankind, supplied to him the spices of our salvation? From the fragrance of this ointment both the Church that journeys on earth has been filled and follows the Bridegroom in the fragrance of this ointment; and the very court of heaven as well. For at the beginning of God’s ways, when it was said, “Let there be light,” and light was made (Gen. I, 3), the heavenly creature was enriched with a more sublime nature, more excellent goodness, and a readier use and office—that is, with the angelic gift of divine knowledge—and in our restoration was restored to its full [Col. 1033C] number.

But the Son of Oil himself is anointed, or enjoys the delights of God’s paradise, in another manner; yet how, none can know except you, Lord, whose name is “poured-out oil” (Cant. I, 3), and from whose horn—that is, glorified humanity—outpourings of graces overflow with rushing abundance toward humankind. For the whole horn of oil, that is, the fullness of grace, is poured upon the head of the Son of Man, because the Lord’s blessing is poured out upon the head of the righteous one who justifies all those justified, wholly and originally, not partially. The entire ointment, I say, is poured into him to whom God does not give the Spirit by measure (Rom. XII, 3). Moreover, he dips even his foot in oil, because the infusion of grace flowing from the holy mountain overflows even to [Col. 1033D] the hem of the garment, that is, to the last believer. Thus he blesses the little with the great. For the oil flows down from the head, but is not exhausted, since it is an unfailing spring which neither the wind of demons nor human inconstancy can absorb from age to age: “For his mercy is from everlasting and unto everlasting upon those who fear him” (Ps. CII, 17). This oil is conveyed by the paths of righteousness because it is denied to no worthy person and beneficially given to no unworthy person. All the beasts of the field which the Lord has blessed shall drink this oil, but the wild asses wait in their thirst (Ps. CIII, 11). This oil wondrously both gives drink, gives food, and anoints. It gives drink to the thirsty, feeds the hungry, and anoints those struggling. It feeds the strong mightily, gives drink mercifully to the weak, and anoints the delicate and those reared amid saffron. It feeds those who work, gives drink to those who desire, and anoints those who languish from love and fail within themselves. It feeds those fighting in the frying-pan, gives drink to those sweating in the oven, and anoints those fixed upon the gridiron. Finally, it feeds martyrs with the tree of life; gives confessors drink from the fountain of knowledge; and anoints virgins with the privilege of chastity and the singularity of glory.

Thus the grace of the oil is not simple but manifold: one cause indeed, but manifold effects, as there is one Spirit but many graces. To Jesus alone all grace was present at once, and all grace flowed infinitely into Jesus in his entirety. He was wholly anointed because wholly holy; wholly anointed because wholly desirable; wholly anointed because wholly full of the Holy Spirit: “For we saw [Col. 1034B] his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John I, 14). John the Baptist dipped him in water; God the Father anointed him with the Holy Spirit. For from God, not from man, he received the oil of divinity; but from man, the water of humanity. He received the oil of miracles from the Father, the water of sufferings from humankind; the oil of sweetness from the heights of heaven, the water of pain from human nature. Jesus is also dipped with water by those below, if people believe in him, even slightly; he is anointed with oil by those above, if the saints consecrate their faith with lofty devotion. Moreover, with the Father is found a unique ointment, wondrous and incomparable, fragrant above every spice, gathered not from mountains of spices but from the first virtues of the supercelestial [Col. 1034C] dwellings. Every order of the heavenly powers perceives it above itself, yet does not presume to claim this ointment for its own anointing. For those heavenly spirits regard themselves as sufficiently blessed if they even perceive its fragrance; they acknowledge that its anointing has been prepared and is due not to themselves but to the Father’s own Son.

The devil, a thief and robber, stretched out his hand toward this ointment, but drew it back leprous, withered, and contracted. For this ointment is “for the fall and rising again of many” (Luke II, 34): the fall of the presumptuous and proud, the rising again of the humble and contrite. “Upon whom,” he says, “shall my Spirit rest, except upon the humble person and one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI, 2). The Spirit boils and bubbles like vinegar upon nitre, bursting and burning up the old wineskin, if he descends into an ill-disposed soul; but he rests and anoints if he descends into a simple and chaste one. If Lucifer had moderately sought the portion belonging to him, and had not usurped by robbery the whole substance of the ointment, like a dying fly, perhaps he would still live happily in its fragrance with the Bridegroom’s companions. The Father eternally destined this ointment for the purposes of his wisdom and ordained it so that his Son might enjoy it uniquely beyond all his companions. “You are my Son,” he says; “today I have begotten you” (Ps. II, 7). Let creation adore, not touch, this ointment of eternal and singular generation. Whoever touches it shall be overwhelmed with stones; “a hand shall not touch him” (Exod. XX, 13), because the hand of human disputation desired to touch [Col. 1035A] what it is not permitted to touch. But if one asks who anointed this anointed bread, with what he anointed it, and how he anointed it, the Psalmist teaches, Isaiah speaks, and the Apostle Peter shows. “God, your God,” says the Psalmist, “has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV, 8). Isaiah says: “The Spirit of God, the Spirit of wisdom, etc., shall rest upon him” (Isa. XI, 2). Peter likewise says in the Acts of the Apostles: “How God anointed him with the Holy Spirit” (Acts X, 38). And this is the anointing by which the Father anointed the Son.

This anointing of the Father is wondrous, because he anointed his only-begotten Son with a unique ointment. This ointment is truly precious: no creature was capable of receiving it by creation, nor of buying it by merits. For whatever has been created, whether in heaven, on earth, or bodily, does not love the Father as the Son loves him, nor is it loved by the Father as the Son is loved. For the love of Father and Son returns uniquely and without distinction upon itself, since the Father, who is love, loves the Son with his whole self, and the Son, who is likewise love, loves the Father with his whole self. Nor does the Son love the Father less than the Father loves the Son, because the Son is in no respect less than the Father. But if you ask how the Father anoints the Son and the Son does not anoint the Father, if love itself is the anointing and the Son loves the Father as the Father loves the Son, I reply: because the Son is from the Father, but the Father is not from the Son; or because the Father begot the Son, but the Son did not beget the Father. Thus one is he who anoints and another he who is anointed, [Col. 1035C] because the Father is one and the Son another; but the anointing by which the Father is anointed and that by which the Son is anointed are the same, because the same Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and likewise from the Son. The woman who was a sinner in the city also anointed him (Luke VII, 37): for she anointed his feet and anointed his head. Anointing of the feet—that is, conversion from sins—is certainly pleasing to God; but progress toward virtues, which is the anointing of the head, is much more acceptable. “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy and wanderers into your house”: you have anointed Jesus’ feet with ointment. Give alms not out of sadness or necessity but with great cheerfulness, and you have poured ointment upon his head. Therefore the person who shows mercy with cheerfulness is refreshed by anointed bread.

## CHAPTER XXV. On sprinkled bread.

[Col. 1035D]

As the body is joined to the head, and the Bride to the Bridegroom, so sprinkled bread rightly follows anointed bread. For as Jesus is signified in anointed bread, so the Church, washed in Christ’s blood, is signified in sprinkled bread. Although we no longer receive sweet food from the very hand of the Word, nevertheless let us receive with all eagerness the Church’s charisms as morsels of sprinkled bread. And because that anointed bread, who came forth from the Father and came into the world, is not always visibly present with us—for, leaving the world again, he returned to the Father—let us at least eat sprinkled bread, as our daily bread, not with distaste because of its constancy, but with desire because of its nourishing power for our souls. For this bread is sprinkled from the fatness and richness [Col. 1036A] of the anointed bread, because, as he who tasted the morsel of oiled bread from his breast says: “We have all received from his fullness, grace for grace” (John I, 16). In exchange for the grace of anointing in the Head, grace of sprinkling in the body; in exchange for grace given without measure, grace received by measure. For as among the former people the high priest was anointed with the same oil, but with a more abundant pouring, and the lower priests with a sparser sprinkling, so in the New Testament Christians are regenerated by the same Spirit by whom their Head was conceived and born of the immaculate Virgin—although in an unequal measure and operation. For in Jesus Christ the Holy Spirit poured out the oil of grace, good measure, pressed down, and overflowing, like a fountain full of swelling streams, so that he might cause that same grace to flow back to his members—or rather to his fellow-poor—and might dispense it at will as God, though he had received it as man without preceding merit. Yet his grace is in no way diminished by his generosity, but ever increases in its outpouring.

But those who, from the name derived from him, are called Christians are otherwise situated. According to their capacity and strength, they receive little streams of grace from the fountain of blessing, through the kindness of the giver; they do not presume through the power of their own will to be sprinkled by the Anointed One, or rather dipped by the Only-Begotten. Hence Isaiah: “He shall sprinkle many nations; kings shall shut their mouths before him” (Isa. LII, 15). Here the prophet seems to teach that Christ sprinkled the Church drawn from the nations. [Col. 1036C] But since sprinkling is manifold, he did not state by which sprinkling. For there is one sprinkling of water, another of blood, another of ashes, another of hyssop, and finally another sprinkling of oil. Sprinkling with water is celebrated in baptism; sprinkling with blood in the Passion; sprinkling with oil in confirmation by chrism. The diverse sprinklings work one salvation; but from the differing merits of dispositions they prepare different dwelling-places for the faithful through everlasting eternity. Behold, the Ninevites are sprinkled, but with ashes, so that, as though by an opposing shield, the vengeance of God’s wrath may either be restrained when appeased or mitigated in its more merciful exercise. Behold, too, the veil of the Temple is sprinkled with blood so that the Father’s emotion may be moved more to spare than to punish when he sees the garment of his Son’s flesh reddened by the sprinkling of his own blood, or by the cruelty of the Jewish people, whose cry was: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII, 25). Behold: priests at their consecration, the altar at its dedication, and certain breads at their offering are sprinkled with oil, so that priests may be sanctified by imitation of Christ and exalted by participation in authority; so that the altar, although insensible, may be fitted, through visible consecration, for the most divine sacraments; and finally so that the breads may be divinely set forth as figures of those breads which are converted into the true body and blood of Christ.

Behold, the Christian people have received the sprinkling of water sanctified through priestly invocation and adjuration by the highest Name, so that, drawing the power of that water which flowed out from His temple on the right side (Ezek. LXVII, 2), it may drown both original sin, as Pharaoh, and every offense, as the pursuing Egyptian. Moreover, the temple or even the altar is figuratively sprinkled with hyssop at its dedication, so that whoever wishes, by living chastely, to dedicate the members of his body as a holy temple of God may, by having in himself the same mind which was in Christ Jesus, repair through humility the damage of pride and let the swelling of guilt subside through the correction of justice.

But to what end is all this? That the Bride may wash herself wholly by these sprinklings: clean through water, holy through blood, pleasing through ashes, healed through hyssop, devout through oil.

[Col. 1037B] For when the soul, still sinful and blackened by the sun of temptations and spiritual wickedness, has been stirred by dread of its sins, it sprinkles its head with the ashes of mortification, eating ashes as bread (Ps. CI, 10), so that, being penitent at the end, it may delight in affliction as once, by living wickedly, it had poured itself out in the desire of the flesh and the pride of life. Thus it has received ashes in its mouth against the desire of the flesh; ashes in its belly against the desire of the eyes; ashes on its head against the pride of life: in its mouth, that it may openly confess sin; in its belly, that it may be converted vehemently in heart; on its head, that it may be humbled altogether.

This will be an effective remedy when some sinner, [Col. 1037C] shaken like a locust, or like the trees of the forest moved by the wind, has conceived from the fear of the Lord and brought forth the Spirit of salvation (Isa. XXVI, 18). For it is said to him: “Do not fear because of these two tails of smoking firebrands” (Isa. VII, 4), since one who thus repents and consumes his sins will be condemned neither presently by anathema nor eternally by Gehenna. And this concerning the sprinkling of ashes.

But if the leprosy of lust has defiled the soul through temptation or the flesh through delight, Elisha the prophet commands that the place of leprosy be washed with water from the springs of the Savior, so that the leprosy may be driven away by the Lord’s mercy and compassions; and not only may the flesh, renewed like the flesh of a little child whose name is Emmanuel, [Col. 1037D] be restored, but also that the soul of Christ, returning from the lower regions, may be illuminated. And this concerning the sprinkling of water.

But if the sword of temptation has passed through the soul and, its foot having slipped, it has already been buried in the hell of evil habit, it will not be freed except by sprinkling with the blood from the side of Him who slept upon the cross. The rich man clad in purple, burning amid the punishments of Gehenna, asked for a drop of water when he said: “Father Abraham, send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue” (Luke XVI, 24). But he asked little, and perhaps therefore did not obtain it. He asked little, I say, because the infernal flame is extinguished not by water but by blood. For a grievous fault is not cleansed by a light and momentary compunction; rather, the force [Col. 1038A] of grief must penetrate as far as iniquity had gone.

Therefore let the conscience of one confessing grave sins demand a full hand of the Redeemer’s blood, not the tip of a finger dipped in water. Yet let him seek to move and remove the punishment not by another’s finger but by his own—the same finger by which, by moving his mind wickedly, he brought it upon himself. Let him wash his hands not in the blood of a sinner but in the death of the Redeemer. Let him dip his finger in the place of the nails and put his hand into the Savior’s side, so that, as the Lord Himself laid down His soul for us by dying and redeemed us from death, so this man may expose his own conscience for himself by confession and repentance.

If, however, you plead that there is a lack of blood and that therefore you cannot dip your finger, attend with the eyes of faith: [Col. 1038B] behold, the yearling Lamb; behold, the fatted calf is slaughtered and killed. Abundant redemption has been poured forth; blood runs down the base of the cross and over all the horns of the altar. Dip, then, dip your finger, and sprinkle seven times toward the veil of the sanctuary (Lev. IV, 17), so that the blood of the Lord’s Passion may be for you the key that opens heaven. Heaven’s gates will not bar themselves when they see blood lifted toward them from the inward parts of Christ. At last the gates of paradise are opened, that it may be sanctified for Him with a better and purer sanctification than at the creation of the world, lest it thereafter admit a transgressor as it endured Satan’s transgression. “Lift up your gates, O princes” (Ps. XXIII, 7), for with us we bear keys [Col. 1038C] not made by hand.

Let the veil be rolled back; let the mercy-seat appear; let the seraphim lower their wings; let all things that move in the stars stand still and lower their wings, because the voice of Christ’s blood speaks better than Abel’s (Gen. VIII) and is “the voice of thunder in the wheel” (Ps. LXXVI, 19). Behold, the kite in heaven recognizes its time, and the stork and swallow know it in order to prepare a nest; and do the angels not recognize their Lord, our price, so as to make room? Oh, with what reverence the veil of the angelic powers reverences—or rather yields—to the finger of the Lamb moistened with blood! Indeed, falling down, it trembles at the approach of the blood from the inward parts of its God and Creator. They hasten to open what was shut, to grant what is asked, to heap up what has not yet been understood. They lick the finger, kiss it, and mark it as full of every blessing [Col. 1038D] and worthy of the Father’s gaze.

Therefore, O soul, dip not only your finger but, with Peter, your foot and head also, so that the foot of affection, the finger of action, and the head of intention, dipped in this blood of Christ’s Passion, may act thus: the finger may work righteousness, the foot run toward glory, and the head behold glorious majesty. For if your foot and your finger are dipped—indeed immersed—in blood by loving and working righteousness unto the shedding of blood, you will not see eternal corruption. For whatever is sprinkled with the blood of the Lamb or calf is consecrated to God. Blood confers life and sanctification, because every soul—that is, life—is in Christ’s blood. Take away the blood, and the soul departs. If you deny Christ’s death, the Christian’s life is slain.

[Col. 1039A] Those who planned to reject our price condemned this blood (Ps. LXI, 5). This concerning the sprinkling of blood. But if the blood of the Lamb is too much for you and beyond your soul’s powers, seek at least hyssop, a lowly herb and not difficult to find: “Come down; sit in the dust, daughter of Babylon, for there is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans” (Isa. XLVII, 1). God had taken you from the dungheap of human corruption, washed you, clothed you, and you had advanced into a kingdom; but you uncovered your bed, brought an adulterer over your husband, despised the husband of your youth, and sold wool and flax to strangers. Yet after all these abominations, marital mercy and indulgence remain behind you, so that you may return to your former husband.

[Col. 1039B] He wishes you to be sprinkled with hyssop on account of the innumerable fornications of idols or phantoms of your heart, and thus, whitened above snow, to be received into the marital bed [the text reads *thronum*, perhaps for *torum*]: “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Ps. I, 19). Outwardly you are sprinkled with hyssop; inwardly you are made drunk with wine. This concerning the sprinkling of hyssop.

The sprinkling of oil follows; the rarer it is, the dearer it is. For above all other substances, oil is sweeter, more penetrating, and softer. It should be understood that this sprinkled bread of which we are now speaking is sprinkled not with blood, ashes, hyssop, or water, but only with oil, because it describes the life not of beginners but of the perfect. Therefore a soul advancing well from lesser things to greater, from lower things [Col. 1039C] to higher, begins with ashes and completes its justification in oil. It begins with ashes when it laments that through the transgression of sin it has been reduced to ashes and dust from the unfading state of eternity. Then it proceeds to tears, if perhaps it may be re-formed from the dust of mortality, or at least into mud possessing some tenacity.

In this respect mud is better than dust, because it is not carried about by every wind in vain lightness and dissolution (Eph. IV, 14), as dust is, but is glued together and gathered into unity by the weight of moisture. Thus it has weight, whereas it had been weightless; it has unanimity, whereas it lacked unity; it is also soft, whereas it was dry and without moisture. Something can now be formed from it, [Col. 1039D] whereas formerly from dust nothing else could happen except that an eye might be blinded. Thus it now accepts discipline, receives precepts, and through progress in union knows how to submit to every obedience under the yoke. Then, through practice and habit, this water is changed into blood—not the blood of Egypt, but of Christ—so that a person is now ready, if need be, to lay down not a tear but the soul, not a wave but life, for Christ or the brethren.

But lest one leap toward martyrdom from presumption rather than humility, hyssop follows, representing a most steadfast humility founded upon the rock; so that one may rightly attain not merely unto death but unto death upon a cross. Finally comes the oil of gladness, so that Christ’s victim may no longer merely be humbly or courageously, [Col. 1040A] but willingly and joyfully, not burnt up but cooked through in the fatness and richness upon the coals of sufferings; that it may not mourn but laugh, not suffer torment but gain the kingdom. The apostles and martyrs, sprinkled with this oil, run as though to a feast. And this concerning the sprinkling of oil.

## Chapter XXVI. Concerning cold bread

Not all taste uniformly, in one day, the one sweetness of grace; rather, according to the capacity of their merits and the fitness of their dispositions, each receives from the invisible Word of God a portion suitable to himself. Thus manna descending from heaven is varied in the mouths of those who eat it according to the diversity of their desires. It tastes one way in the mouths of beginners, another [Col. 1040B] in those of the perfect; one way in the mouths of the hungry, another in those already full; one way in mourners, another in the joyful; one way in servants, another in sons; one way in hired laborers. Finally, leavened bread tastes one way, unleavened another; first-fruit loaves one way, loaves of presentation another; fine-wheat bread one way, barley bread another; common bread one way, consecrated another; bread baked in an oven one way, in a pan another, on a griddle another; bread anointed with oil one way, sprinkled another, hard another, hot another.

As best we could, though stammering, we have explained what flavor all these breads possess, except cold and hot bread, of which we have not yet treated. Not without reason we reserve these for the end of the banquet [Col. 1040C] and place them after bread sprinkled with oil, because hard struggles always remain for us even though grace has suffused our minds. Thus Moses, when blessing Asher, said: “Let him dip his foot in oil,” and added, “His sandal shall be iron and bronze” (Deut. XXXIII, 25). Observe that the foot moistened by dipping becomes softer and more tender.

It would therefore wear softer footwear more conveniently than iron footwear, unless a spiritual mystery were understood under the sacrament. What, then, does the foot dipped in oil signify except a mind inspired by the Holy Spirit? And what do iron and bronze footwear signify except the laborious journey through this present age to heaven? Plainly, as if by a sandal, [Col. 1040D] the foot of one traversing the road of this age is worn down daily; and unless it were relieved by the pouring of oil, it would be utterly crushed by the harshness of the sandal.

Therefore, that present things may be despised in a swifter course and future things sought with greater eagerness, bitterness from this exile is meanwhile mixed with the sweetness of graces, so that heavenly watering may incite and earthly affliction compel our soul toward God. For the desire to return to one’s homeland is kindled by two fires: longing for the fatherly dwelling and weariness of this exile. The former urges one to return; the latter compels one to depart. Desire softens the soul, so that, made free, it may flow toward God; weariness roughens it, so that, embittered, it may flee from here. Thus God’s animals are led out and led back, that they may go out and find pasture, not only touched by the whistle but also [Col. 1041A] struck by the lash.

At one time the sighing for eternal delight prevails; at another, the misery of present calamity moves more ardently. With this consideration, they now eat hard and cold bread, now bread anointed or sprinkled, lest, if anointed bread were always served, we become secure, or, if cold bread were always served, despairing and lukewarm.

This alternation sometimes happens to correct us, but always for our benefit. For when the soul is illumined by spiritual blessing so as to love God, it uses bread anointed or sprinkled; but when it is pricked by its own goads so as to flee the world, it uses cold and hard bread. Both occur: the one through a heavenly gift, the other through human merit. For, just as grace sometimes [Col. 1041B] anticipates a person’s mind through works and anoints it with joy in the future reward, so God in His goodness at times mercifully rouses an undeserving person both toward merit and toward reward.

But what sort of thing, or to what end, is our merit? Without doubt, our merit in itself is so evil that we are deservedly abandoned by God, so utterly evil that we are not undeservedly condemned. Yet through God’s gift it becomes good by prevenient grace, and better by cooperating grace. Thus bread anointed is set upon the table from God, hard bread from man, so that you may ascribe to God the anointing of illumination, and to yourself, a sinner, the hardness of blindness. From His heaven God pours light upon you, and from your abyss you serve yourself immense confusion. Your good comes from God; your evil comes from yourself. From God comes the ointment of health; from yourself [Col. 1041C] the poison of death.

The former, therefore, must in every way be received by you; the latter must not altogether be rejected. For God’s gift must everywhere, always, and indiscriminately be received by all; but our evil, insofar as it is punishment and not malice, inflicted by God’s justice, must be endured patiently. Indeed, in Jesus our Head, the entire sequence of the Gospel interweaves, in wholly truthful narratives, this alternation of miracles and sufferings. Thus the evangelical lyre-players sometimes produce a fuller and darker sound upon the lyre of Jesus’ body by relating the insults of tribulations, and sometimes a finer and sharper sound by presenting the flashes of divine deeds and words.

Hence too some Psalms are titled “A Psalm of a Song,” others “A Song of a Psalm.” Hence again, Jesus’ sufferings sometimes precede His glorification and sometimes follow it. They precede, as the Lord Himself said to the apostles after the resurrection: “It was necessary for Christ to suffer and so enter into His glory” (Luke XXIV, 20). And the Apostle says: “Christ became obedient unto death, even death on a cross; therefore God also exalted Him,” etc. (Phil. II, 8). Thus too the apostle Peter calls the resurrection and ascension—the glories which follow suffering and the cross—later glories.

But glorifications follow His sufferings when, for example, an angel [Col. 1042A] or a star appears for the glory of the Child, and afterward He flees into Egypt from Herod’s cruelty. Many similar cases are found in which works of divinity come first and sufferings of humanity follow. Hence the saying, “After glory He sent me to the nations,” as though He said: First I work miracles, so that the nations may know that I am the Word who was in the beginning with God (John I, 1); afterward I am consumed by suffering, so that the Christians’ faith—that believes the Word became flesh—may nevertheless be firm and true.

For in miracles one may discern whence I came; in sufferings, for what end I came. Yet Christ is one and the same: He who suffers because He is passible man, and He who does not suffer because He is impassible God. But when God is called passible, this is not said according to [Col. 1042B] the nature of the assuming Word, but according to the passibility of the assumed flesh.

You may, without injury to God, take up what is yours—namely, the penalty of sin; but what belongs to God, namely the glory of the kingdom, must not be presumptuously claimed without God. Therefore, if you enter into God’s labors, do not glory as if this had come about through your own labor; rather, humbly receive the sufficiency for your present need, entrusting your salvation to Him. Bring forth nothing beyond this through presumptuous confidence in free will. For the foot of free will, without the foot of God’s grace, never has been and never will be able either to stand or to walk. When, outside this grace, the foot of pride or free will attempted to raise itself, it was struck down and could scarcely afterward be healed even by many remedies.

Observe the Bridegroom’s belly [Col. 1042C] everywhere set with sapphires (Song V, 14), so that He now performs heavenly things and now suffers human things. Do not wonder if, having first tasted the oil of glory, you receive for His sake the wormwood of reproach: from the little gardens of your nature both myrrh and wormwood are gathered in bundles; in the divine beds are found only oil and balm. Bitter and hard are the things you sow; sweet and soft are God’s. And what wonder if a person reaps what he sowed by eating what was forbidden (Gal. VI, 8), when he goes to destruction?

Thus surely Christ’s killers, abandoned by grace, sowed—indeed, scattered—His blood over their own heads, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” Behold how these worst of sowers do not produce the fruit of begetting (Ps. CVI, 37) by obedience, [Col. 1042D] but the fruit of destruction and captivity by killing. Therefore they were fed upon and strangled by Vespasian and Titus from this harvest and from bread gathered in flour: bread at once cold through slaughter and hard through everlasting devastation.

There is another manner in which Christ’s members are fed with cold and hard bread. Whether they are buffeted by Satan through the goads of the flesh or afflicted in the winepress of worldly pressures by various tribulations, they are nourished with hard and cold bread. Thus Jacob, worn out by a long journey, placed a stone under his head when he was about to rest; and rising in the morning and understanding the mysteries of his vision, he anointed the same stone.

For a stone often confronts us when we wish to rest on this road by which we walk toward the house of eternity: in [Col. 1043A] our very rest, a conscience full of troubles and anxieties receives the soul’s fatigue according to its hardness. But in the morning we anoint the same stone when we raise our hope toward the rewards of the saints that will recompense the labors of this night; for hope of arrival lightens the losses of the journey. Love also of the rest that is always near bears, on light wings, every misfortune of a pilgrimage soon to end.

With this ointment Paul anointed his wounds when stoned; with it the lacerations from scourges; with it he had placed beneath himself his manifold sufferings as a stone, for he had exposed his whole self to death. Yet in this hardness of his sufferings he was refreshed more than afflicted, so that his spirit was strengthened all the more as it was pressed more harshly. For, as he himself testifies, “Power is made perfect [Col. 1043B] in weakness” (II Cor. XII, 9).

Therefore he does not reject bread however hard who fears no labor, however harsh. He has teeth trained to break not only hard bread but bread of stone and iron; for he knows how to subdue not only the assaults of flesh and blood, but also the principalities and powers of this air. He despises death and does not dread the devil. He willingly receives, if there is someone to inflict them, both things that human frailty can endure and things that it cannot endure at all, saying: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18).

Therefore let us also, made imitators of him as beloved children, not yield to temptations of the flesh [Col. 1043C] nor be cast down by the adversities of the world. Let harshness be softened into gentleness of spirit. By the anointing of the sweetest oil—that is, the Lord’s compassions—let us make the stony heart soft again; as sons of oil, let us be sprinkled with heartfelt mercies, that we may more peacefully avoid the swellings of the sea.

For this anointing wonderfully makes firm rather than weak; it raises us to labor rather than dissolving us into softness; it makes us fit rather than feeble for every good work. Finally, having received the anointing of the Spirit, the apostles burst forth into contests and bear the marks of Jesus’ name among all nations. Then, fed with hard and cold bread by the persecutors of the Church, they endured the harsh and severe mortifications of the body. Then they endured “in labors more abundant, in prisons more abundant, in deaths often.” [Col. 1043D] Then they endured dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from their own people, dangers from Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brethren, and so forth.

Therefore we rightly set bread sprinkled with oil first, then cold and hard bread, because after receiving grace we ought to expect not pleasures of the flesh but the world’s bitterness. Hence the Bridegroom’s belly is said to be set with sapphires (Song V, 14), because now we are raised by consolation from God, now instructed by temptation. Under the same mystical meaning, the Bridegroom’s companions promise the Bride “golden ornaments studded with silver” (Song I, 11). By the ornaments and golden adornment are understood the divine commandments themselves, which are studded [Col. 1044A] with silver because one must distinguish where there is a precept that exercises and where a promise that refreshes. Promise soothes, but precept terrifies.

Thus John observed both together in the appearance of Him seated upon the throne: “He who sat,” he says, “was like the appearance of a jasper stone and a sardius” (Rev. IV, 3). Jasper is green and watery in color and signifies promised immortality. Sardius is red and signifies the labor of the commandment; hence the Psalmist: “You who fashion labor in the commandment” (Ps. XCIII, 21).

Therefore let us not lose confidence because of labor if we are striving for rest, since “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Judith VIII, 23). Thus after Passover, after manna, after the manifold visitation of His consolations, the Lord did not immediately lead His people into the land flowing with milk and honey. Instead, He led them around for forty years through the losses of the desert and admitted only a few with difficulty of journey.

[Col. 1044B] Hence Scripture says: “When Pharaoh had sent the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt, God did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines, judging lest perhaps they should repent if they saw wars arise against them and return to Egypt; but He led them around by the way of the wilderness which is beside the Red Sea” (Exod. XIII, 17). We are sufficiently taught by this example that bread sprinkled or anointed is first served, and that afterward bread is set before those converted to obedience to the Lord. For by the sweetness of the Spirit, which is first tasted by those newly coming to true teaching, their powers are gradually nourished, so that when a grievous war arises [Col. 1044C] with a gathered host of vices, their small faith, not yet strengthened by the food of spiritual gifts, may not fail.

Therefore the Lord does not immediately lead those departing Egypt by the way of the Philistines, because He does not allow the intolerable contest of temptations to arise before He has taught our hands to fight. For if a Philistine skilled in battle catches the Lord’s people unprepared, while they have not yet attained the rudiments of spiritual warfare, he will overcome them and lead them back to Egypt. But if they have learned and become practiced in arms, they can neither easily be captured nor deceived by enemies.

## Chapter XXVII. Concerning hot bread

[Col. 1044D] At last, with God cooperating, we have now put our hand to the final and highest bread, which is neither cold nor lukewarm but hot, so that both the weariness of the work and the desired refreshment may happily be brought to completion through it. This bread is for the heart, not the belly; it is not cast out into the privy, but is taken at the entrance of the tabernacle not made by hands, but from the midst of the wheels, in the burning spirit of the Cherubim. The turning sword or blade does not touch anyone whom it finds holding this bread either in the mouth or in the belly. For when will charity attack itself, since it spares even enemies? When will it oppose friends?

But is charity bread? Rather, what is better than bread? For if bread is the beginning of human life, much more is the bread of love the beginning and completion of the soul. Bread refreshes the hungry, [Col. 1045A] and charity perfects the failing. Bread strengthens a person’s body, but charity gives life to the heart. With bread other things are profitably eaten; with charity all things are healthfully received. Bread is the special food of human beings; charity the singular strength of souls. Without bread, a table is poor; without charity, a soul is contemptible. Bread is brought from the earth by labor; charity is gained by much earnest effort. Bread grows stale, and when neglected becomes hard and cold; charity, if it ceases from action, is either extinguished or diminished as iniquity increases.

Therefore let us now grow warm; and if we do not have hot bread, let us urgently seek it again from our mother, the Jerusalem above. For if Rebecca, who is the Church, sets before Isaac hot bread—that is, charity—which she cooked in the midday heat of her faith, it is not, of course, Isaac the son of Abraham according to the flesh, now made most ancient by the aged revolution of time, but the only-begotten Son of the most high Father, eternal and immortal Jesus Christ, who enables Jacob, the younger son, to gain both paternal blessing and inheritance.

[Col. 1045B] For unless He receives food from us, He does not give greater grace. It is fitting, indeed, that we who desire the Father’s blessing should anticipate the Lord’s mercy by desire, so that, glorifying God for what has already been received, we may receive better things and things nearer to salvation. Therefore, while seeking greater things, let us not refuse to offer lesser ones, so that we who seek rewarding grace may not reject cooperating grace. To possess the inheritance, let us offer bread.

Let us also offer the kids of confession and repentance, that we may receive the fatness of the earth—that is, remission of sins. Let us likewise offer the wine of devotion, that we may harvest the dew of heavenly grace. Otherwise Jacob would have been set before his father for a curse rather than a blessing, unless the aged father had been abundantly refreshed with very hot loaves, wine, and the flesh of kids; and, filled with these, had bestowed the remembrance of his own abundant sweetness and become more disposed to pour forth blessings. Thus the son, instructed by his mother, prepares this meal and gains by his father’s blessing the birthright which nature had denied him.

Jacob therefore serves his father hot bread [Col. 1045D] when the humble and simple soul, set aflame by desolating coals, offers its Creator faithful and fervent service. For the more devout the spirit is, the hotter it is; and the hotter it is, the more suited it is to divine works. Perhaps seraphic services are more pleasing to God because they are more fervent. For those who draw near to Him draw near to the fire who “makes His angels spirits and His ministers a flame of fire” (Heb. I, 7).

[Col. 1046A] But near fire nothing cold remains, nothing lukewarm. If you place any solid body before the face of fire, it is either burned or set aflame. If it is liquid, either the fire’s entering force heats it quickly or, by drying it, makes it vanish. Of these alternatives one is for profit and the other for harm. For what does burning produce but consumption? What does being set aflame produce but illumination? It is hard, then, to approach in such a way as to be burned; but it is best and pleasant to cling in such a way as to be illumined. “Draw near to Him,” says the Psalmist, “and be illumined” (Ps. XXXIII, 6). Thus does a cleansed and simple conscience approach: not to experience the curse of eternal burning, but to obtain the inheritance of everlasting blessedness. These are the birthrights of every creature, granted to the last laborers in the vineyard as to the first, that the first may be last and the last first (Matt. XX, 16).

Therefore the birthright will be given if hot loaves and a fervent spirit are offered to Isaac; if the flesh of kids is served with the loaves, so that the disordered movements of heart and flesh, extinguished by spiritual slaughter, may be made fit for the divine mouth through exquisite flavors. Finally wine must be added to all these things, so that we may serve the Creator of all not through a spirit of bondage but through the Spirit of adoption as sons.

[Col. 1046B] If by this Spirit the soul grows hot and in its meditation the fire blazes which, through priestly care, is kept perpetual upon the altar, then, obeying the divine commandments from love and not from compulsion, it will offer hot and most sweet bread to God the Father and receive a blessing. O soul melted at the Bridegroom’s voice, this is your food! O heart burning in Jesus, this is your refreshment! For him whose garments, according to Job, and whose spices, according to Solomon, are blown upon by the south wind, such dishes are prepared. He knows nothing cold, abhors lukewarmness, and seeks what is hot, keen, and intensely fervent.

For by faith it grows warm—or grows together; by hope it is sharpened—or rises—to true sublimity; by charity it grows beyond measure into the fullness of virtues. This dares to fill the hand of faith, which works through love, with the coals of fire in the midst of the cherubim. This is not ashamed to set the censer of conscience before angelic nostrils. With lips impatient and mouth eager, it snatches the bread of sweetness from the furnace of glory. In the impatience [Col. 1046D] of its impatient desire, it leaps among the coals themselves and feels vapors not burning but shining, not afflicting but refreshing, not consuming but illuminating. Returning from contemplation, it bears back its countenance stamped by the gladness of God’s face; and, wholly fragrant from the Bridegroom’s embraces, breasts fragrant above all spices. ***

[Col. 1047]

# Peter of Celle, Abbot: Mystical and Moral Exposition of the Mosaic Tabernacle

## Book I

[Col. 1047A] Having invoked the aid of the Holy Spirit, I undertake, at your urging, to write something concerning Moses’ tabernacle for the edification of conduct, entrusting all the sails of my intelligence to the south wind of divine illumination and, at its prompting, both moving and setting down the camp of my discourse—would that I always did so. One who is illumined by the pillar of heavenly light safely measures the stages of the journey: observing in his soul the risings and settings of the several virtues, he awaits grace’s return and rises at its coming. For, when grace is absent, to remain seated in fear and expectation is beneficial; when it comes and helps, to rise and cooperate is fruitful [the text has *fluctuosum*, perhaps for *fructuosum*].

But where should one treat of the tabernacle except in the tabernacle? The tabernacle, however, of which we have proposed to treat is [Col. 1047B] not made by hands—that is, not of this creation—but wondrous, heavenly, spiritual, angelic, and everlasting. Nevertheless, let us set before our eyes that earthly tabernacle of Moses, fashioned by earthly workmanship; and, transferring our attention from visible things to invisible, let us not stop hesitating between earth and heaven through lukewarmness or the distrust of unbelief—for there Judas burst asunder in the middle (Acts I, 18)—but with an undivided heart let us ascend above the heavens of heavens toward the East, singing: “Blessed are those who dwell in Your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise You” (Ps. LXXXIII, 5).

I propose to employ a plain and pedestrian style in the construction of the tabernacle, called the worldly sanctuary, lest, carried aloft by lofty speech, I should weave rather Daedalus’ house than God’s temple, and there should be produced an inextricable winding rather than a devout disposition.

[Col. 1047C] Let whoever wishes have in Plato’s *Timaeus*, concerning the creation of the world, the palace of this visible creation hung with invisible cords [the text reads *gunfis*, evidently for *funibus*], where the reader labors more over the subtlety of the narrator than is enriched by admiration or delight in the Creator. O soul too delicate and excessively pleasure-loving: if you desire to behold the house of Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, or the painted and insatiably elaborate dwellings of the princes of this world, gather wood from the forests of poets so that from their reading you may build luxurious Gentile brothels, not the religious temples of Christians!

For the books of secular authors seek theaters, love publicity, and summon crowds with frequent applause; they do not aspire to conscience but to popular glory. Moses, however, in the wilderness of solitude portrays the morals of the deserted soul by emulation of the wondrous tabernacle—namely, angelic conduct—setting forth in a grosser letter or figure the subtlety of the gloss, that is, of angelic glory, for a stiff-necked people.

[Col. 1048A] And first he explains to the wise and spiritual, in the construction of his tabernacle, “that which is natural, then that which is spiritual” (I Cor. XV, 46), arranging what is material beneath the eyes of the body and what is spiritual beneath the understanding of the mind.

Its material, form, length, breadth, height; curtains, coverings, priestly vestments, ark, tablets of the covenant, Aaron’s rod, the golden urn containing [Col. 1048B] manna, cherubim, mercy-seat, veil of blue, scarlet, purple, and twisted fine linen; blue skins, table, lampstand, loaves of presentation, seven lamps, snuffers, boards, bases, poles, five gilded columns. The altar of Sethim wood; pans for receiving ashes; tongs, forks, fire-pan, bronze vessels, a bronze grating in the form of a net, and so forth—if you understand what these signify morally and mystically, you will be able to construct a throne of conscience such as no king has built in all kingdoms.

For the dwelling of this tabernacle, devised through such divine meditations, is compared with heavenly tabernacles or dwelling-places; to add to its glory is superfluous, to add to its grace difficult, and to add to its sacramental mystery impossible. [Col. 1048C] For the individual joints of its several constructions are fruitful in mysteries, so that nowhere in its entire fabric is there a barren meaning in the Law, when spiritual things are compared with spiritual things; and the mind, made pregnant by continual attention to the holy Scriptures, rejoices together in the sacred birth of good understanding.

Therefore now, as though having tested an axe for hewing each component of the future structure, let us set the very words of the Law before our eyes and, according to our measure, construct the mystical or moral house. The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel, that they may take for me first-fruits from every person who offers them willingly; and these are the things which you must receive: gold and silver, bronze and blue, fine linen, [Col. 1049A] goats’ hair and dyed red rams’ skins, and blue skins, Sethim wood, oil for preparing lamps, spices, ointment and sweet-smelling incense, onyx stones and gems for adorning the ephod and breastpiece” (Exod. 25:2).

We do nothing out of the ordinary if, when approaching the treatment of the tabernacle or sanctuary, we first specify by enumeration what things, and how many, are to be offered—at the Lord’s command—from the people’s offerings to the Levites or priests of the tabernacle. For it is useful and reveals the expositor’s intention to set separately before us the outward outline of the work to come; moreover, things treated separately are understood better.

Finally, we must observe that the good and rich Lord, although he does not need our goods through any necessity of want, [Col. 1049B] nevertheless does not refuse our gifts, because of the goodness of his mercy. It is indeed a great gift which he bestows upon me from the depth of his riches if he accepts the tiny service of a sinner—he for whom even what is heavenly and angelic is scarcely judged worthy, since he is eternal and unchangeable. Moreover, supreme Majesty stoops more graciously toward its creature if it does not refuse that creature’s services than if, exceeding in its own benefits, it grants what human vows request. For by practice and habit God has already learned to serve us freely; but rarely, and never without the privilege of grace, has he required service back from anyone.

He therefore says: “From every person who offers willingly you shall receive them.” Whoever unwillingly and reluctantly [Col. 1049C] bestows a benefit upon another is like one uprooting nettles and thorns with a bare hand and rubbing the recipient’s face with them. But grace, sufficient in itself, refuses the ungrateful mind of one who serves. “God loves a cheerful giver,” so that the face of the service rendered may not be darkened “from sadness or necessity” (2 Cor. 9:7), but that the head of the burnt offering may exude richness from the fat of overflowing generosity.

Thus one offers willingly whose desire exceeds his ability, and who judges that he has done little unless, by a fuller will, he has surpassed his ability. One offers willingly who hastens to fulfil divine commands, not in the spirit of slavery in fear, but in the spirit of adoption. But what does one offer willingly? “You shall receive,” he says, “first-fruits from every person who offers them willingly.” Both every movement of good will [Col. 1049D] and the beginning of every righteous action must be dedicated to divine grace. For “what have you that you did not receive?” Do not therefore boast as though you had not received it (1 Cor. 4:7); rather, “honour your God with your first-fruits,” from whom comes “every good gift and every perfect gift, descending from the Father of lights” (James 1:17).

The Pelagian, who judges that he possesses some good independently of God, does not offer first-fruits willingly. But you, servant—indeed, son of grace, for you were originally sold for nothing and mercifully redeemed without silver, namely by the blood of the spotless Lamb, Jesus Christ—give glory to God and render your first-fruits to the Most High, saying: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. 113:1). It follows: “These are the things which you must receive: gold, silver,” and so forth.

[Col. 1050A] Having thus first tasted the mystical sense of the signification, as though having kissed the tabernacle, let us swiftly fly on to what follows. In peace from these matters, where a more laborious task awaits us, let us hasten to move on while our spirit is not yet wearied. Then, when the occasion arises, each of the things here separately apportioned may be received without distaste; and what was offered them with less solemnity in the first greeting may be supplied by a full recapitulation. For the discussion which follows will frequently repeat both the names and functions of gold, silver, bronze, blue, purple, and the rest.

In a brief exposition, then, gold signifies the brightness of true wisdom; silver, the splendour of sacred eloquence; bronze, confession of the mouth unto salvation; blue, heavenly conduct; purple, the body’s suffering; [Col. 1050B] twice-dyed scarlet, love of God and neighbour; fine linen, chastity of the flesh; goats’ hair, the garb of penitence; dyed red rams’ skins, teachers of the Lord’s flock baptized in their own blood; blue skins, spiritual bodies in the resurrection; Sethim wood, the steadfastness of the saints, whom no fault corrupts; oil for lamps; spices, the shining fruits of charity and mercy; ointment and sweet-smelling incense, the reputation of good work as an example of good living; onyx stones and gems for adorning the ephod and breastpiece, the miracles of the saints and works of virtue by which thoughts and actions are adorned.

Behold, we have run briefly through the individual types of offerings, whose significance is repeated as often [Col. 1050C] as their use is enumerated in the description of the priestly vestments or in certain other matters. Let us now proceed to the sanctuary: “Let them make me a sanctuary, and I shall dwell in their midst, according to every likeness which I shall show you, and according to all the vessels for its service” (Exod. 25:8).

In human contracts, of which there are many and various kinds, just as the intentions of the contracting parties are diverse, something is proposed by which both parties, consenting, assent to the contract. For example, in buying a horse, an agreed price pleases each party in exchange for delivery of the horse; or, if you are to build me a house, it is agreed that I shall pay you a stated price. In both these contracts, one called named and the other unnamed, [Col. 1050D] one thing is given and another received. Contracts in which the benefit of only one party is considered are indeed rare: a loan for use benefits the borrower, and a deposit benefits the depositor.

I have inserted these remarks about our human transactions not without purpose, since something must here be said about the divine contracts made with human beings. For through Moses God commands the children of Israel to make him a sanctuary. But is it without payment, or at what price? Certainly not without payment. At what price, then—expressly stated or unstated? I truly hesitate to say, “unstated,” because he says, “I shall dwell in their midst.” Yet I am no less prevented from asserting that it is expressly stated, because God’s dwelling among human beings cannot be expressed. I say: expressed in promise, unexpressed in enjoyment. For it pleased God to express his promise by the word [Col. 1051A] of his power; but humanity could glorify in complete exultation the gift of God, blessed and glorified above all things, yet could not explain it in words.

Children of Israel, understand that God is not prompted by any need to ask you for a sanctuary, as though he had nowhere to place his holy things. Is heaven not spacious enough? Or is not “the heaven of heavens” the Lord’s? (Ps. 113:16). Are there holy things which the vastness of the heavens cannot contain?

Truly, the heavens are full of God’s glory; they are the sanctuary which the hands of God established. But the earth, cursed in Adam’s sin, is empty and void (Gen. 1:2). Yet it pleased the depth of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge to stoop from above to below, watering lower things from higher ones, so that at least through the likeness [Col. 1051B] of God’s glory, in the mirror and enigma of the visible structure of Moses’ tabernacle, the eye of illuminated reason might anticipate the majesty of the true inward goods; might in some measure judge truth from likeness; and, enticed by the visible appearance, might be drawn toward an apprehension of the invisible glorious substance.

Unusual figures are displayed before human eyes, so that thought, recalled from familiar things, may ponder by subtle reflection that there are other things more unfamiliar still. Pregnant with their eternal brightness and invisible fellowship, these temporal holy things shine for their measure only as an alluring likeness, not as truth that satisfies. Therefore, Jew, do not with greedy haste swallow the pen of history which has been placed in your mouth—not so that [Col. 1051C] you may gulp it down, but so that through it you may drink sweetly and temperately the wine stored, as in casks, in the cloisters of heavenly wisdom. You indeed grip the pen of the Law far too sharply when, in the books of Moses, you attend only to the letter without the Spirit. Whenever you close the pen in your mouth thoughtlessly and without moderation, blocking the channel of spiritual understanding, you chew the bark and do not drink the wine.

Attend carefully, then, to what is said: “Let them make me a sanctuary according to every likeness of the tabernacle which I shall show you.” Angels possess the truth; you possess the likeness. If you believe that you possess likeness and not yet truth, you will come from likeness to truth.

Likeness therefore leads into truth. But if, [Col. 1051D] being under the Law without grace, you presume that you possess truth rather than likeness, you will lack truth and be deprived of likeness as well. Seek, therefore, the end of the Law, which is Christ, full of grace and truth; for its end is in truth, not in likeness. He says, “According to every likeness of the tabernacle which I shall show you.”

In such great abstinence from food and such prolonged withdrawal from secular concerns, Moses is believed to have nourished the eyes of his mind and his spirit upon divine revelations. I believe, moreover, that with his bodily eye he saw certain wonderful and unfamiliar visions. But however he saw that heavenly and angelic manner of life, whether in the flesh or in the spirit, he is commanded to make it known to his people by whatever representation, so that those who, through the dimness of bodily life, could not receive the rays of truth itself [Col. 1052A] might, by contemplating visible forms beneath a mystical shadow, become somewhat accustomed, through the invisible meanings of the tabernacle’s visible forms, to transfer their minds from visible things to invisible.

This whole mystical likeness pertains to the fullness of the gifts of the universal Church, from the fountain of grace; and love, with Jesus supplying it, drinks that fullness even on the way of pilgrimage because of its abundance. Finally, the fullness of the sacraments imitates the likeness of the angels.

Examine the deep mysteries of our faith, and no reward of future hope will emerge which invisible faith—“the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. 11:1)—has not first tasted through the visible administration of the sacraments. I speak of the faith of the Church, [Col. 1052B] not of the faith of one believing person, although whoever belongs to the Church believes the whole which the entire Church itself believes. Yet “the queen stood in gilded clothing, clothed round with variety” (Ps. 44:10): variety of persons and merits. She has as many chambers of faith as there are hearts of the faithful, and as many likenesses of angels as there are distinctions of graces.

But when, at the consummation of the age, every likeness of the angels has been fulfilled in the Church both in merit and in number, so that it passes from likeness to truth and “the measure of a human being” is that “of an angel,” then there will be “one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:16), of human beings and angels, so that God may be “all in all” (1 Cor. 15:39). Then teachers will no longer make for the Church “likenesses of gold,” as it is said in the Song of Songs, but equalities; for human beings will no longer imitate [Col. 1052C] the conduct of heavenly beings, but will be changed into fellowship with blessed spirits, that they may be “like the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. 22:30), not in the labour of merits but in the reception of rewards.

Then the one who has merited more in likeness will be crowned more abundantly in truth; and the more similar one was in virtue, the more conformed that person will be in majesty. For the heavenly court is distinguished among angels by office, rank, and order; and likewise the Church of God among its ministers. The individual orders fulfil their assigned offices in heaven, and likewise in the Church; nor does anyone, through rash presumption, presume to take hold of what he has not received in the assignment of his office.

These, then, are “vessels unto honour” (2 Tim. 2:21) [Col. 1052D] and usefulness in the great house, of which it follows: “and all the vessels for its service.” Mystically speaking, it is as though God, the uncircumscribed Spirit, drinks from one vessel, eats from another, sits upon another, washes his hands with another and his feet with another, receives incense in another, lights a lamp with another, stores manna in another, encloses treasures in another, and performs in another whatever other services are fitting to divinity.

With carnal understanding restrained, and the mind set above the imagination of every phantom, understand customary actions in an uncustomary manner. Cherubim and seraphim, inflamed with charity, as it were bring food and drink to the divine mouth when, by their rank and the dignity of friendship, they stand nearer than all other spirits. Thrones, standing in truth, provide a tranquil and pleasing seat. Principalities and powers, as it were, [Col. 1053A] provide water and a hand-towel when, defending us against enemies, they grant the grace of security and boldness in resistance. Dominions wash the feet when, by their intercessions, they lessen our sins and enable us to obtain dominion over sins. Virtues kindle sweet-smelling incense when they return thanks to incomprehensible Majesty for the virtues of the saints. Archangels light the lamp when, by revelation, they explain the deep mysteries of heavenly secrets. Angels store manna when they hide divine counsels from us; and they enclose treasures when they defend our good works against evil spirits and bring them into the sight of the Lamb.

In the same order the Church also advances, “ordered as an army in battle array” [Col. 1053B] (Song 6:3), and in each rank of its ministers receives the corresponding virtue of the angels. See the golden and silver vessels in the great house which is the Church, for its service. There are there a chalice with paten, a vessel of oil and chrism, a wine flask and a vessel for water, basins, a censer, lampstands, a pool, lamps, and certain other things.

The holy soul that is inflamed with the charity of seraphim is assigned to the chalice and paten; the soul filled with the fullness of cherubic knowledge is assigned to the wine flask; and the soul calmed by the tranquillity of thrones is appointed to the vessel of chrism. The soul able, by grace, to heal those broken in heart and cure the ailments of the spirit also bears the vessel of oil. The soul that, sharing in human afflictions through the sufferings of Jesus, is crucified and dies with him, both in remembrance of his death and in the sacrament of the life-giving communion of the Lord’s body and blood, bears [Col. 1053C] the vessel of water.

The one who, as the sweet fragrance of Christ, spreads a good reputation everywhere and makes known by holy conduct the holy name invoked over him, both to those outside and those within, ministers the censer. The one who, considering Pilate’s cruelty and Christ’s innocence, washes his hands not only in the blood of the Lamb but also in that of the kid, bears basins or trumpets, receiving “the upper irrigation” (Judg. 1:15) from the Lamb and the lower irrigation from the kid. For when I receive the Lamb at his birth, I am admonished concerning kindness and innocence; when I see him dying for sinners in the likeness of sinful flesh and among thieves, I conceive hope of forgiveness in such great patience of Jesus.

The one who, with the Lord working together and confirming the word, offers the Gospel without charge, proclaiming the kingdom of God for heaven and not for money, bears lampstands. The one who, enlightening the consciences of the simple, fixes love of God in the reed of their memory, lights lamps. The one who, pierced by continual lamentations, has eyes “like the pools in Heshbon,” presides over the pool.

It follows: “And thus you shall make it: Construct an ark of Sethim wood, whose length shall be two and a half cubits; its breadth a cubit and a half; likewise its height a cubit and a half; and you shall overlay it inside and outside with the purest gold, and shall make above it a golden crown round about” (Exod. 25:10).

[Col. 1054A] In an order not unfitting, the heavenly command proceeds to arrange how the tabernacle ought to be made according to the mystical sense. It first sets forth the ark, which signifies Christ, and defines it by the limits of its own construction, assigning the measure of its length, breadth, and height. For we believe as firmly as we live faithfully that the entire mystery of Christ’s Incarnation was disposed from eternity in the divine mind; that, borrowing all from the hidden things of God’s wisdom, it was allegorically signified by fitting figures in patriarchs and prophets; and that it was humbly fulfilled in Christ himself in the last times.

Christ is not undeservedly called an ark, because just as an ark is very necessary in a house, in order that not only bread but also clothing, money, and any other things that must be sealed and kept under lock may be placed there, so in Christ is stored the work of our salvation. There is stored the bread of refreshment; there is stored the garment of whitening, as is written: “All of you who have been baptized have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27); there is likewise stored the money of redemption, as it is written: “The Lord sent redemption to his people” (Ps. 110:9); and there are stored the treasures of the whole divinity, because “in Christ dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Col. 2:9).

[Col. 1054B] The ark, then, is neither always open, lest the zeal of seeking be removed, nor cruelly closed, lest the persistence of those seeking be frustrated. Its key is unsealed in the Father’s hands because of the mystery hidden from the ages, lest thieves dig through into God’s counsel and steal the purpose of Christ’s Incarnation. The Father “shuts and no one opens,” because he hid the divine birth in his own secret; he “opens and no one shuts” (Rev. 3:7), because he made the human birth known to the world. “No one,” he says, “knows the Son except the Father,” and so forth (Matt. 11:2).

The ark was opened to the prince of the apostles when he said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16). Hence he was told: “Blessed are you, Simon Barjona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (ibid., 17). Likewise, the eyes of those two walking on the road “were kept from recognizing him” (Luke 24:16); they were not opened until the bread was broken.

To this ark the little ones who hunger and thirst for righteousness (Matt. 5:6) approach and ask for bread, saying: “Give us this day [Col. 1054D] our daily bread” (Luke 11:3). To it dogs and little dogs return at evening (Ps. 58:7) when they suffer hunger; for sinners, finally, and those newly converted to God are sharply reproved in conscience for their evils, anxiously seek the fragments or morsels of God’s mercies, and desire penitence not delicately but indiscriminately: whatever is brought or imposed upon them, they seize and swallow with eager mouth. For as charity “believes all things” and “endures all things” (1 Cor. 13:7), so hunger eats all things and swallows all things. It does not examine what delights, but what satisfies; it consults not taste, but the stomach. It grants no delays to the palate, but quickly sends what it receives to the stomach.

Likewise, beyond doubt, one hungry for righteousness and hungry for patience, setting aside deliberation of counsel, does what must be done before deliberating; as quickly as such a one receives a command, so quickly does he fulfil the good. There is no difficulty in doing where will always abounds in goodness.

These things concern the name “ark.” Let us now look at its construction. “Construct an ark of Sethim wood,” he says. That body of the Lord, conceived and born from the sacred womb of the Virgin under the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, is suitably compared with Sethim wood, because this wood is incorruptible and light; when exposed to fire it suffers no harm from burning but becomes hardened into more robust solidity. It also resembles the white thorn. For Christ’s body is incorruptible: it neither ever decayed in the dung of human life through the corruption of sin, nor in the tomb [Col. 1055B] through the dust of death. Hence: “You will not allow your Holy One to see corruption” (Acts 2:27).

It is light because it was in no way weighed down by original or actual sin: “upon the wings of the winds” (2 Sam. 22:11), still in the flesh, it walked and trod the waves with solid step; and after death and resurrection, lifting up its hands, it ascended bodily to the right hand of the Father. Finally, the Lord’s body, exposed to the fire of the Passion, like Sethim wood did not vanish into ashes of burning but grew strong in the impassibility of the resurrection. For the Jews’ envy against Jesus blazed, as the Psalmist says, “like fire among thorns” (Ps. 117:12); but Moses’ bush, burning in the flame, was not consumed. In its punishment it annulled our punishment and, through punishment, freed nature from guilt.

All this is because this wood resembles the white thorn—not in identity of nature, of course, but in similarity of condition. For the reality of flesh in him is not leavened by the corruption of old age, but is conformed to the likeness of sinful flesh, so that by his appearance he might entice the adversary while by his reality he might procure protection for us. He presented an appearance to the dragon in order to deceive him; he retained reality in order truly, not deceptively, to separate human nature from misery. He was a true human being because of the true human nature in him; like a human being because of punishment, not guilt.

This ark has two and a half cubits in length because he was patient and long-suffering both in his teaching and in his action—these are the two cubits—and endured the disciples’ slowness with equanimity, which is the half-cubit. [Col. 1055D] It has a cubit and a half in breadth, so that the one cubit signifies that perfect charity by which he willed to unite us to himself, saying to the Father: “That they may be one in us, as we also are one” (John 17:20). The half-cubit likewise teaches that “we love in part, as we know in part” (1 Cor. 13:9); and the Lord embraces this imperfection of our capacity.

It also has a cubit and a half in height, because even in this corruptible flesh he fully knew how great was the glory prepared in heaven both for himself and for us—that is the one cubit. He further willingly bore in himself the devotion of our flesh, because with devout intention we love the country to come, yet do not as yet comprehend what its happiness is: that is the half. It is a great thing, with all the saints, to comprehend what is this breadth which the Apostle divides into height and depth. Having at last expressed the measurers’ cord by which the length, breadth, height, and depth of the heart are measured, let us consider what is the measure of Christ’s body and compare with it the measure of our own heart and body.

[Col. 1056A] Behold: with the evangelical cord, from Christ’s conception, count his patience—shaken by no interruption of impatience—until the giving up of his spirit on the cross; and you will find it surpassing every calculation. For the patience of his humanity was strengthened by the comfort of his divinity.
