I, whose impatience is sharpened by the weakness of nature and inflamed by the perverse habit of keeping silent, cannot attain to it.

Christ’s patience is higher than heaven, because he who dwells in heaven is not shaken from his tranquillity even by the disturbance of heaven against the senseless. It is deeper than hell, because he does not grow angry even with those condemned in hell as much as they deserve. It is broader than the earth, because although the earth was cursed in Adam’s deed, nevertheless “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. 118:54), whether in saving those converted or punishing the impious more mildly. What more need be said? There is no number to his patience—indeed, neither to his wisdom, charity, nor any of the virtues which are in Christ; for the Spirit was not given to him by measure, and certainly neither were the gifts of that same Spirit.

It follows: “And you shall overlay it with the purest gold, [Col. 1056C] inside and outside.” So great was Jesus’ purity of soul and so great the magnificence of his deeds that angelic nature cannot attain his purity, nor Scripture comprehend the majesty of his miracles. Within is purity of conscience; without, brightness of reputation. “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18:2), which was hidden in his soul; and the evangelical firmament “proclaims the works of his hands” (ibid.), namely all the miracles of divinity.

Jesus’ ark was overlaid with the purest gold within, because neither passion nor the preliminary stirring of passion knocked at the doors of his soul. It was overlaid with the purest gold because, united to divinity, it was deprived neither of God’s wisdom nor of glory; because it thought thoughts of peace and not of affliction. It was overlaid with the purest gold without, because for it to be able to do good was as easy as to will it; it was overlaid with the purest gold without because it redeemed outwardly what it created inwardly. For inwardly, by invisible majesty, it created the human being; outwardly, in humble form and condition, it redeemed the human being. It was overlaid with the purest gold without, it which says: “Which of you will convict me of sin?” (John 8:46). It was overlaid with the purest gold without in the Transfiguration—indeed, in the resurrection and ascension—since, “although we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16).

It follows: “And you shall make above it a golden crown round about.” “We see Jesus,” says the Apostle, “who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honour” (Heb. 2:9). The golden crown is the glory of Jesus’ resurrection and ascension; “round about,” because [Col. 1057A] from that time now and forever Christ Jesus sits at the right hand of Majesty on high, made “so much better than the angels” (Heb. 1:4) as he has inherited a name more excellent than theirs. “Round about,” because “the Lord shall reign for ever and beyond” (Ps. 9:36). “Above,” because in his humanity he merited what he never lost in his divinity; above, because, begotten of the Father of lights according to divinity, he was deified according to humanity. Hence: “Father, glorify me with the glory which I had with you before the world was” (John 17:5).

It is called a crown because of eternity; golden because of brightness. A crown, because it is rendered to merits; golden, because merits are crowned through grace—for God rewards his own gifts in us. A crown, because it will not be taken away eternally; golden, because it will not grow cheap through satiety. “Therefore you shall make above it a golden crown round about.”

It follows: “And four golden rings which you shall place at the four corners of the ark” (Exod. 25:12). There were four golden rings in the ark of Jesus because the four principal virtues—prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance—were pre-eminently in him, as in the King of virtues. Or there were four golden rings in him because the books of the Gospels received their titles from the wisdom which went forth from his mouth and spread from end to end of the whole world.

Both the virtues and the Gospel books are fittingly called golden rings, because in them there is no crookedness of falsehood, no interruption of vanity, no excess of superfluity, no constriction of imperfection. They are wholly round through truth, [Col. 1057C] wholly equal through equity, wholly complete through the restoration of nature, wholly perfect through the consummation of glory. Every effort of preachers returns to this same point: that wherever, whenever, and however far their discourse may proceed from its beginning, the life of the soul may be sought, salvation considered, God loved, and remembrance of the heavenly homeland celebrated.

There is one mutual turning-back of each and all the virtues, while their interwoven arms alternately impede mutual gaze and embrace: prudence enters with fraternal love into the bosom of justice, fortitude, and temperance; likewise justice enters into prudence, fortitude, and temperance, each of them in turn and reciprocally doing the same. But the rings are golden where nothing is done from necessity, but virtue is cultivated by natural goodness and freely performed service, good is done, and goodness is maintained through love of the good. For Christ’s virtues existed without avarice, and the preaching of the Gospel without deceit. Thus they are golden rings.

It follows: “Which you shall place at the four corners of the ark.” The four corners of the ark are understood either as the four regions of the world or as the four passions of the soul. Four golden rings are placed at the four corners of the ark when either the Gospel is preached throughout the entire world or the entire soul is renewed by fourfold virtue. It follows: “Two rings are on one side, and two on the other” (ibid.). The two Evangelists John and Matthew are placed on one side because they lived with Christ in the flesh; and the other two—Luke, that is, and [Col. 1058A] Mark—on the other because they were taken up into the ministry of the Gospel after the resurrection.

Plainly also, those who preached the Incarnation and Passion are on one side, while those who preached the resurrection and ascension are on the other. Prudence and justice likewise fortify, as it were, one side of Christ, since the work of the Incarnation was begun so prudently that it was concealed from the devil, and so justly that all righteousness might be fulfilled through it. Fortitude and temperance hold the other side, because fortitude wrought the resurrection and temperance the ascension. For it was supreme temperance when God, equating our nature united to himself with the Word, glorified it most highly, and raised to the summit of rewards through the second Adam that nature which through the first Adam he had humbled to the extremity of punishments.

Fortitude pertains to the resurrection because, as the Psalmist says: “Through the multitude of your power your enemies shall lie to you” (Ps. 65:3)—those who had said: “There is no salvation for him in his God” (Ps. 3:3). For in the resurrection “iniquity lied to itself” (Ps. 16:12). The Apostle also places four golden rings at the sides of the ark when he says of Christ: “Who was made for us by God wisdom, justice, sanctification, and redemption” (1 Cor. 1:30). Our ark is borne about by these rings, because in these virtues lies the cause and effect of our salvation. On one side are placed wisdom, which teaches, and justice, which fulfils; on the other, sanctification, which heals, and redemption, which frees. Wisdom removes folly, justice injustice, sanctification uncleanness, and redemption punishment.

[Col. 1058C] The two rings on one side may also signify the Saviour’s earnestness by which he removed guilt; the two on the other, the equal earnestness by which he drove away punishment.

It follows: “You shall also make poles of shittim wood, and overlay them with gold, and shall put them through the rings which are at the sides of the ark, that it may be carried by them” (Exod. XXV, 13). He indicates what the teaching and life of doctors ought to be, when he says from what the poles must be made and for what purpose. Why, indeed, are the poles made of shittim wood, unless that the life of doctors should be incorruptible through chastity; their reputation pleasing through holy conduct; their bearing humble through their own self-abasement; their speech modest through seriousness; their mind learned [Col. 1058D] through continual meditation upon the Scriptures? For what sort of men ought the poles—that is, the preachers—to be, who are to bear the ark of the covenant, except men of shittim wood, that is, chaste and humble men? For such as the master of the household is, such are his household servants. As the words are related to the matters of which we speak, so the morals ought to accord with the words by which we speak. Let your conduct be chosen, that your preaching may be upright; indeed, strive more diligently to live well than to speak eloquently. For the poles must be overlaid with gold, so that they may speak wisdom among the perfect; that they may shine by good example among the wicked; that they may have good conduct among the Gentiles, and so forth (I Pet. II, 12).

They must be overlaid with gold because the ark is covered with gold on every side. It is certainly incongruous if you bring your bare wood into God’s gold [Col. 1059A], examining the depths of mysteries by human understanding and opening the golden door of venerable treasures with a wooden key. Surely the things of God must be explained by divine utterances; nor should an Aristotelian grove be planted beside the altar, so that we overshadow the sacraments of faith with endless and superfluous inquiries, which “are not useful except for the subversion of the hearers” (II Tim. II, 14). The poles must be put through the rings which are at the sides of the ark, lest, as has been said, the reed of the tongue be dipped in prophetic inks, but only in evangelical ones. Let not the preacher teach doctrine in the Church according to the errors of heretics or the seductions of philosophers, whose “stolen waters are sweet, and hidden bread more pleasant” (Prov. IX, 17). In the Gospel, let him use an evangelical understanding [Col. 1059B]: not wrenching and drawing the rings out of the sides of the ark, but putting the poles through the rings which are at the sides of the ark, so that he may not bend God’s word to his own meaning, but may bend both word and understanding to the Gospel. “That it may be carried by them”: “Glorify,” says the Apostle, “and bear God in your body” (I Cor. VI, 20); bear the ark, that you may obey the Gospel; bear the ark, that you may proclaim the kingdom of God.

It follows: “They shall always remain in the rings, and shall never be withdrawn from them” (Exod. XXV, 15); whence: “The meditation of my heart is always before you” (Ps. XLVIII, 4). To be always, and never to be, in the rings are very contrary things. Those doctors are seldom or never in the rings who have the forum instead of the monastery, [Col. 1059C] clamour instead of the Gospel, hawks instead of a sheaf, a purple cloak instead of a stole, dogs for hare-hunting instead of the reading of books. These “exchanged the truth of God for a lie” (Rom. I, 25), so that when the Lord has said, “They shall always remain in the rings and shall never be withdrawn from them,” they themselves are never put in; but let the good doctor always be in the rings, because “blessed is the man who meditates in the law of the Lord day and night” (Ps. I, 2). Likewise: “The mouth of the righteous shall meditate on justice” (Ps. XXXVI, 28). He is always in the rings who neither violates the precepts of the Gospel in living nor offends against the rules of truth in teaching; he is always in the rings who, as if shackled by evangelical bonds, never acts according to the whim of his own will, restraining his eyes, hands, feet, ear, tongue, and other members by the evangelical fetter [Col. 1059D] so that he never draws them out at the impulse of any disturbance, but contains them under the eternal law of sanctification.

“And you shall put in the ark the sanctification which I shall give you” (Exod. XXV, 16). In the same order and likewise for the same reason, the ark is first constructed and then the testimony is decreed to be placed in it: just as, after the worldly dwelling had first been made and adorned, man, as its inhabitant and lord, is said to have been created last. Certainly nowhere is the testimony of divinity to be placed bodily except in the body of Jesus, except in the ark of sanctification, except in a soul uniquely worthy of God: a soul so thoroughly refined in the furnace of the Holy Spirit, from its creation onward, from its original coagulations, that it was as far removed from sin [Col. 1060A] as it was united to God. Nor was it preoccupied by sin, since God preceded it in His blessings, as though He laboured in its purifications whom He was preparing for divine espousals; but He was as holy in its creation as He was gracious in its union with the Word.

With no interval of time intervening, the ark is constructed and then the testimony placed in it; rather, the ark of Jesus’ soul and body is joined at the same instant with the imposition of divinity, so that by assuming He created, and by creating He assumed; and by sanctifying He assumed or created, and by assuming He created or sanctified. Nor should you object that the ark is first constructed and the testimony afterwards placed in it, as though concluding from this that Christ’s flesh was first conceived and afterwards assumed by the Word; [Col. 1060B] but believe that, in the conception, soul and flesh were assumed together, and that in the assumption they were received and conceived. Hence Augustine: “Hold most firmly and doubt in no way that Christ’s flesh was not conceived without divinity in the Virgin’s womb before it was assumed by the Word in the womb; but that the very Word, God, was conceived from the conception of His own flesh.”

Therefore put in the ark the testimony which I shall give you, so that you may believe concerning Christ on the testimonies of God, because the Father has borne testimony concerning His Son; so that you may assent to the oracles and testimonies of prophets and apostles concerning Christ, because they are God’s witnesses, as it is written: “You are my witnesses” (Matt. XLIV, 8); and in the Acts of the Apostles: “And you shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem,” and so forth (Acts I, 8).

There is also a testimony placed in [Col. 1060C] the ark: the law, or the ten commandments of the law, written on two tablets. But according to the Apostle: “In the ark were the two tablets of the covenant; there was a golden jar containing manna; and also Aaron’s rod, which had budded” (Heb. IX, 4). The tablets of the covenant signify all knowledge of the Father’s secrets in Christ and all power of judgments; for upon them were inscribed both faith in divinity, the commandments by which God must be served, and the discrimination of judgment by which He condemns those who hate Him and rewards those who love Him. The golden jar is Christ’s soul, containing manna—that is, all the fullness of divinity. Aaron’s rod is the righteous power of the priesthood, which budded on the second day of the resurrection, without awaiting the general resurrection. All these things were in the ark—that is, in Christ [Col. 1060D]—and this is the testimony which the Lord gave. For God did all these things as a testimony to His goodness and to our rebellion, as Job says (X, 17): “You renew your witnesses against me.”

It follows: “You shall make also a mercy-seat of the purest gold” (Exod. XXV, 17). The ark of shittim wood is first overlaid with gold; then the testimony is placed in it; thirdly, it is covered above by the mercy-seat—that is, the board called the mercy-seat. What would your incarnation, what would your testimony, profit us, Lord, if propitiation were lacking? The accumulation of your benefits would increase our guilt, unless, together with the benefits granted, the benefit of propitiation were added over and above. For ingratitude alone would condemn us, unless the forgiveness of propitiation also received [Col. 1061A] our ingratitude. The more numerous the Creator’s benefits, the more tirelessly ought our grateful service to repay them.

But, above all the others, He bound more closely the bond of His benefits by one benefit of His goodness: that, when despised, He might not disdain; when cast out, might not reject; when offended, might not injure; but might make satisfaction to Himself for us from our injury, might seek us, and might bring us back. Who was raised to this summit of compassion except Jesus? Who attained this height of graces except the Son of oil? Who poured forth from His own breast such torrents of mercies except the mercy-seat? Truly, if there is anything in Jesus better than Jesus Himself, that for me is the mercy-seat, that is, the reconciliation-seat. Yet Jesus is wholly desirable; He is wholly lovable. Thus He is lovable in the ark, but more lovable [Col. 1061B] in the mercy-seat; desirable by reason of goodness, but more desirable by reason of propitiation, which is the richness of goodness, because “mercy triumphs over judgment” (Jas. II, 13).

Hence, in the Mass of the most saving offering, the priest, before that supplication in which he asks that the offering be carried to the holy altar before the sight of the divine majesty, first introduces the mercy-seat, saying: “Upon which do Thou deign to look with a propitious and serene countenance, and to accept them, as Thou didst deign to accept the gifts of Thy righteous servant Abel,” and so forth. For unless this veil, as it were, of human shame and dread were first set before him, the sinner would not presume to approach the inaccessible brightness of that countenance. But with this little board of the mercy-seat set before him, he neither fears the rays of the sun for their burning heat nor blushes [Col. 1061C] for their brilliance. Therefore God would not look with a propitious and serene countenance unless man had a mercy-seat to set before the angry God, to show Him when moved, to oppose to Him when striking.

But of what material shall this mercy-seat be made? Of shittim wood? Far from it! For such wood resembles the white thorn, and, though it does not prick in truth, it is nevertheless feared because of its appearance. Thus incarnate Wisdom, when the man rebuked men and the innocence of the Lamb condemned no one, nevertheless the evil conscience of the Jews, because of its own bleared vision, recoiled from seeing Him, fearing Him as the judge of its evils and not as the Saviour of souls. Therefore the faint-hearted [Col. 1061D] nature of mortals still seeks a gentler mercy-seat: that is, a kindly Jesus, who wholly in the truth of His nature, in the appearance of His likeness, and in the designation of His name echoes propitiation, offers pardon, exudes grace; who receives the fallen, strengthens the weakened, restores the lost, overcomes evil with good. The mercy-seat does not attend to judgment: it does not find merits, but makes them; it does not count former errors, but cuts them away. The mercy-seat commands accusing truth to stand far off; it hastens to preserve the innocent. The mercy-seat floats in the blood of Jesus as a ship upon a river; the mercy-seat receives the harlot from the brothel and swiftly washes away all her abominations; receives the fugitive and restores him to his country; receives the sick and heals him; the blind [Col. 1062A] and enlightens him; the leper and cures him; the dead and raises him.

But whence comes this mercy-seat? From the purest gold. The mercy-seat upon which that thief fixed his gaze from the cross was of the purest gold: to him, who deserved most ill, the true and abundant propitiation of God not only granted release from punishment by grace but also bestowed paradise on that same day. Our Redeemer’s mercy-seat was of the purest gold, because in Him not preceding merits of human nature but prevenient grace united that very nature to the Word and completed the reconciliation, or propitiation, of God and man. He was of the purest gold who was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the most undefiled Virgin; He is of the purest gold who bestows His grace upon good and evil alike [Col. 1062B]. He is of the purest gold who brings it about that “where sin abounded, grace might abound still more” (Rom. V, 20). He was of the purest gold who shines in fire, is improved by the hammer, is made sweet by suffering, grows strong through death, is made gentle by insult, abounds in poverty, and shines forth more precious than every price among all things of price.

It follows: “Its length shall be two cubits and a half” (Exod. XXV, 17). The ark and the mercy-seat have the same measure in length and breadth. This measure of length is five palms, since two cubits and a half make five palms, saving the authority of our elders. I think that the five palms in the length of our mercy-seat may not unfittingly be understood as the five wounds of His body. For He extended the long-suffering of His patience so far that, marked by these five most familiar and renowned wounds, He delivered us from five chief miseries: first, the cruel oppression of the devil’s slavery; second, the strong bond of sin; third, the mournful exclusion from paradise; fourth, the continual exile of the world and temporal punishment; fifth, the miserable eternal punishment of hell. Human nature lay sick in these five porticoes; and unless it had a man—indeed, a propitiator—who paid for it the penalties of the toll in each portico, and brought it through the sacrament of baptism into the water poured from His side, it would not escape.

In the first palm, or wound, of the mercy-seat, we are delivered from the power [Col. 1062D] of the devil, of whom the Apostle says: “Death”—that is, the devil—“reigned from Adam unto Moses, even over those who had not sinned after the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Rom. V, 14). But the Apostle says: “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (I Cor. XV, 22); for He “destroyed him who had the power of death” (Heb. II, 14), and thus delivered us from the devil.

In the second palm and wound we are mightily delivered from sin, which is most evil, when we are justified in Christ’s blood—that is, released from sin—and thereby freed from the bonds of the devil. In the third palm and wound of the mercy-seat, we are healed from the third wound, the exclusion from paradise, when that first judicial decree of God, pronounced by the sentence of truth [Col. 1063A] concerning man’s expulsion from paradise for sin, is changed through the bettering compassion of our propitiator. The mercy-seat itself fulfils the decree which it had formerly promulgated, paying what it had not taken, so that by its most perfect humility it might overcome the guilt which the human race had contracted through the pride of the first man. Thus it opened paradise and called back the wanderer. In the fourth palm and wound, we are healed from the fourth, which is temporal affliction and exile from the world; but meanwhile in hope, not yet in actuality. In the fifth palm and wound of the mercy-seat, we are delivered from that incurable wound, eternal punishment, when, death having been wholly overcome in victory, we triumph over death, saying: “Where is thy victory, O death? Where is thy sting, O death?” (I Cor. XV, 59). Thus much concerning the mercy-seat’s length.

[Col. 1063B] In breadth, however, it is one cubit and a half, that is, three palms. For we have been reconciled to the Trinity in the mercy-seat, so that we now have peace through Christ with God, stripped in the blood of the Lamb of the stain of past sins, the spring of present sins, and the darkness of future sins. In the breadth of the love with which He loved us, the mercy-seat conceals our preceding sins, mitigates our present ones, and cuts off future ones. For “love covers a multitude of sins” (I Pet. IV, 8), through which God is propitiated for all our iniquities (Ps. CII, 3), not by approving them but by blotting them out.

It follows: “You shall also make two golden cherubim, hammered work, at each end of the oracle” (Exod. [Col. 1063C] XXV, 18). Christ, who is the ark in the incarnation and the mercy-seat in the passion, was “made a little lower than the angels,” as the Apostle says, according to the passibility of the flesh (Heb. II, 9). Therefore the Lord commands that two golden cherubim—that is, angels—be made at each end of the oracle, so that you may plainly understand that ministering spirits were never absent from the ministry and mystery of the Lord’s incarnation; as it is written in the Gospel: “They came and ministered to Him” (Matt. IV, 11). Their love and perfect harmony with one another is signified when two are commanded to be made: “Woe to him who is alone, for if he falls, he has none to raise him up; but if there are two, they shall warm one another” (Ecclus. XIV, 10). Surely singularity of presumption fell in Lucifer when, having broken the covenant of angelic fellowship [Col. 1063D], he stretched himself upward and ruptured within himself the veins of grace. For he had no one to raise him, because he was unworthy of restoration; because, empty of twofold love, he did not deserve to be restored. But those angels who kept their own dwelling-place, preserving due subjection to their Creator and mutual love, warm one another in their own little nest and are prepared for the birth of obedience.

“Golden and hammered.” Among inquirers, various and ambiguous debate is reported concerning the condition of angelic creation. Some maintain that there was no interval between the creation and the fall of the evil angels, according to the saying: “He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth” (John VIII, 44). Hence Augustine: “It must not without reason be thought that from the very beginning of time [Col. 1064A], or of his own creation, the devil fell and never stood in the truth.” Others, contrariwise, prove that all were created good—that is, without vice—and righteous—that is, innocent—but not righteous in the sense of possessing the exercise of virtues.

Some also say that there was an interval between creation and the fall, and that during that brief time all were good, not through the use of free will but through the benefit of creation. This is the truer opinion, because God made the nature of angels good; and we must believe that it was not nature but an evil will that was to be punished—unless indeed a good nature is sometimes punished on account of an evil will. Therefore God made the cherubim golden because He made them free in will, simple in essence, and immaterial; because through reason He implanted intelligence, memory, and will; because He distinguished each individually both in number and in merit. The cherubim were also made “hammered,” not because they were created willing to turn away or turn back, but because they were capable of willing either this or that. After creation, however, because they were made capable of progress by free will, some chose good and others evil; and, by preserving the operative grace which they had received in creation, the former deserved co-operating grace: not grace by which the ungodly person is justified from being an operative cause, but grace by whose co-operation the godly person is helped to will well and to persevere. Thus they were made capable of progress, able to advance from good to better.

“One cherub shall be on one side, and the other on the other side” (Exod. XXV, 19). By this is indicated either the separation made through the conversion of the good to God and the turning-away of the evil from God, as between light and darkness; or the distribution of those who remain and those who minister: some always stand before the invisible God, while others go forth obediently to exterior ministries. One cherub was on one side, namely the right, and obeyed; another was on the other, but on the left, and grew proud. Or one cherub is on one side of heaven; the other, on the side of hell.

It follows: “Let them cover both sides of the mercy-seat, spreading their wings and covering the oracle” (Exod. XXV, 20). When the Lord comes for judgment, the cherubim cover both His sides, because, with angels standing around, the wicked shall see Him whom they pierced (Apoc. I, 7), yet shall not see the glory of the saving God. But the good, with unveiled [Col. 1064D] face, shall see and rejoice in that which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (I Cor. I, 9). They cover both sides because “they shall separate the wicked from among the righteous” (Matt. XIII, 49), and because they shall gather the children of God from the four winds of heaven, from the highest heavens to their ends.

Where were you, cherub, who ought to cover the Saviour’s right side, when the lance was driven in, when His side was opened? Or were you present but forbidden to defend Him, like him to whom it was said: “Put your sword into its sheath” (John XVIII, 11)? The blindness of the Jews did not see you in the passion, whom the ass of the mad prophet Balaam saw on the road. The ass turned aside and, seeing you, was afraid; the Jew did not understand you, covering both sides of the mercy-seat [Col. 1065A] in the tabernacle, and therefore struck irreverently against innocent blood! But he who had come to suffer plainly uncovered both sides of the mercy-seat, that He might enter into the solitary combat and turn away the help of His sword (Ps. LXXXVIII, 44): “I have trodden the winepress alone,” He says, “and of the peoples there was no man with me” (Isa. LXIII, 3). Perhaps something would have been diminished from the mercy-seat’s propitiation had everything that the malice of the adversary could do not been received without mitigation upon the right side of the mercy-seat, by powers untried in suffering. Therefore humanity also cries upon the cross, not in complaint but for instruction, saying to Divinity: “Why hast thou forsaken me?” (Matt. XXVII, 46). As though saying: You forsook me for this purpose, not by personal separation but by withholding assistance [Col. 1065B], in order to prove whether such great patience would persevere in me as the grace united with me is great, lest wisdom united to that humanity should without cause be spoken of, if such great patience in suffering were not proved. Therefore the cherubim did not cease to cover both sides of the mercy-seat even in the passion, but did so with compassion, not with defence.

They also cover both sides of the mercy-seat because they protect martyrs in persecution, lest they fail in faith; and confessors in peace, lest they grow lukewarm in love. “Spreading their wings and covering the oracle!” The oracle is nothing other than the mercy-seat, but it is called an oracle because divine answers were given there, as will be shown below, where it says: “From thence I will command and speak to thee above the mercy-seat” (Exod. [Col. 1065C] XXV, 22). Thus the cherubim spread their wings and cover the oracle because they conceal the mysteries of God’s secrets from malignant spirits and profane people, because “it is good to conceal the king’s counsel,” and “the glory of God [is] to investigate a matter” (Tob. XII, 7; Prov. XXV, 2). They spread their wings that they may carry our concerns to God; they cover the oracle that they may bring divine help back to us.

“And let them look one upon another, with their faces turned toward the mercy-seat by which the ark of the Lord is to be covered” (Exod. XXV, 20). In a brief clause he concludes how the angelic powers love one another in God, saying, “Let them look one upon another,” and how they magnify God in themselves, adding, “with their faces turned toward the mercy-seat.” For those do not turn their faces toward the mercy-seat who do not look upon one another, because “he who does not love the neighbour whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (Rom. XIII, 8). In their mutual regard, brotherly love is understood; in their faces turned toward the mercy-seat, humble reverence toward our Creator.

“From thence I will command and speak to thee”: namely, from above the mercy-seat and from between the two cherubim, which shall be above the ark of testimony: all things which I shall command through thee to the children of Israel (Exod. XXV, 22). Behold the place where God speaks! There is no place like this place, which is a place of counsel, refuge, and aid. Do you doubt concerning some question? Go to the oracle, to the mercy-seat, to the midst of the cherubim, because there is the Lord, the God of knowledges! (I Kings II, 3). Are you oppressed by tribulation? [Col. 1066A] Run to the mercy-seat, because there is the God of help. Are you shipwrecked by temptation? Seize the oracle and the mercy-seat, because there is God our refuge (Ps. XLV, 2). Behold, from the midst of the cherubim the consolations of God gladden your soul, because “He has commanded His angels concerning thee, that they may guard thee in all thy ways” (Ps. XC, 11). Behold, from above the mercy-seat the sentence of our indictment is removed and our names are written in the Book of Life. Behold, from the oracle the “voice of the turtledove is heard in our land” (Cant. II, 11): “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. IV, 17).

Observe that ark, mercy-seat, oracle, and cherubim come together to pronounce the divine judgment upon human affairs. The ark brings forward the question of our earthly sojourn; [Col. 1066B] the mercy-seat pleads the case; the oracle gives the definitive sentence; the cherubim execute whatever has come forth, whether good or evil, from the lips of the oracle. For the oracle which absolves is good because it is pleasing; but the oracle which condemns is, as it were, evil because it is grievous and bitter.

Let us devote the solemn worship of service to the honour of the saints, that the memory of the ark may be refreshed amid our calamities. Let us unload our burdens before the mercy-seat, so that it may be made propitious not by its own burnt offerings but by our miseries. Let us offer to the oracle “the voluntary utterances of our mouth” (Ps. CXVIII, 108), both in our accusation of ourselves and in thanksgiving. Let us honour the cherubim as brothers and friends [Col. 1066C], so that, aided by their patronage, we may avoid the snare of stumbling, and, lifted by their conveyance, may return to our homeland.

We are not unaware that there survives another exposition by Bede concerning the ark and the cherubim. In it the ark is understood as the Church, built of incorruptible woods—that is, holy souls—and, extended through the four parts of the world in the faith of the Gospel, awaiting from God the crown of life. It has within itself the tablets of the covenant, in continual meditation upon the law; the golden jar with manna, in faith in the Lord’s incarnation; the golden rod which budded, in participation in the Lord’s kingdom and priesthood; the mercy-seat above, so that it may acknowledge that it has received all good things from God; the cherubim, angelic safeguards or the testaments by which we are instructed [Col. 1066D] how to live.

They are above the mercy-seat, being sustained, of course, by its support, so that angelic ministries and divine utterances may help the Church more truly because she herself is founded upon the foundation of the highest truth. Gregory’s exposition of the ark likewise differs little from the matters set forth above. “The ark,” he says, “is the Church; the four golden rings, the four books of the Gospels; the four corners, the four parts of the world; the poles of shittim wood, strong and persevering doctors. They bear the ark when they preach to others; they always adhere to the rings through the unity of the Church; they are overlaid with the gold of knowledge; they are always in the rings through reading, for it is shameful then to seek when one ought to resolve a question.”

I have gathered these points in summary from the sayings of the saints [Col. 1067A], so that, if our little work displeases in itself, it may at least not be wholly rejected on account of the saints’ holy relics. For although I do not receive a wooden casket for its own sake, nevertheless, because it contains the bodies and bones of saints, I receive it with due veneration; holding the wood with the tips of my fingers and with washed hands, I honour it otherwise than as wood.

In the moral sense, the human heart is an ark either of God or of the devil. But that it may be God’s ark, let it preserve both the ark’s measure and its material. Let its material be incorruptible, like the wood of life; its measure equal, like the virtue of temperance. Therefore let the virtues which alone do not wither or decay beneath the sun construct the ark of our heart, so that God’s deposit in it may not be corrupted because of the ark’s incorruption, and so that the purpose of religion once undertaken may not be abandoned through the virtue of constancy. Let a human being provide one thing for God and another for himself. Let him offer God the custody of His deposit, which is grace; let him retain for his own dignity the firm support of faith, because the image of God ought not to be altered by the trifling tossings of this world [Col. 1067B].

Let the ark be neither broken nor empty. If the ark were full but broken, you would fear loss; if whole but empty, you would vainly hope for help from it. Finally, when the ark is sound and full, let it be shut and sealed: shut lest mice enter; sealed lest thieves open it. Let it be locked and unlocked with a key: locked against demons, unlocked for friends and the hungry. Take heed, O soul, that your ark may be sound through faith, full through love, shut through humility, sealed through steadfastness, unlocked through confession [Col. 1067C] and thanksgiving. Finally, let it obey the key of obedience in both closing and opening.

Let it be fashioned from shittim wood by the squared joining of many virtues. Let it be extended to the length of two cubits and a half: namely, from the beginning of a good work, through the patience of pilgrimage, to perseverance in completing the labour. Let the ark be broadened in width to one cubit and a half, so that it may love God with all its heart, all its soul, and all its strength, more than itself—this is the full cubit—and its neighbour as itself—this is the half-cubit: not because its affection is imperfect, but because its performance in action is imperfect. For we ought to love our neighbour with full affection, but with scarcely half-full affection can we relieve or meet his needs. For no one loves his neighbour who does not divide his cloak in the cold, as Martin did. Certainly Martin’s love extended almost beyond half a cubit when, stripping and disfiguring himself by half his cloak, he exposed himself to cold and mockery. You can possess the half in the breadth of love through affection, though not through effect, when you are constrained in resources but enlarged in compassion. Toward your neighbour have a half-full measure in performance, where necessity prevents you from having a full measure, and your ark has a cubit and a half in breadth: full with respect to yourself, half-full beyond yourself. Therefore have toward God a full cubit of love in affection, because He does not need our half-full measure for the supplying of His needs. Toward your neighbour have a half-full measure, because no one before [Col. 1068A] his end is secure concerning the perseverance of his work.

Right intention at the beginning is one cubit; patience in tribulation, the other cubit; the half-cubit lies in fear and uncertainty concerning perseverance. In height the ark has a cubit and a half when, by the prompting of virtues and confidence in grace, it rises above the common hope of the faithful to the future reward which exceeds your merits. You have one cubit of height in Christ’s death, in which hope of salvation and redemption was given commonly to all the faithful. You also have a half-cubit through receiving holy baptism, in which you are indeed already justified but not yet glorified. This cubit is therefore halved in justification and will be made full in glorification. You complete one cubit of hope when through the sacraments of faith you are in Christ’s body; nevertheless, you begin the other when you taste the pledges of the glory to come by a hidden and particular foretaste of the Spirit. If faith is lacking, the cubit is not completed; if the mind is endowed with the pledge of the Spirit’s adoption, the other cubit is not halved. Thus much concerning the ark’s height.

It follows: “And you shall overlay it with the purest gold within and without” (Exod. XXV, 24). The ark is most purely overlaid with gold within if the mind is cleansed of impurity; it is overlaid within when it is made fruitful with a new offspring of virtues; it is overlaid within when no defilements remain in the mind. It is overlaid without when speech is sparing and true, when the eye is single and [Col. 1068C] modest, when the hand is devout and generous, when hearing is pure and chaste, when the gait is upright and good, and when, over the whole body and its senses, great caution and watchfulness are poured before and behind.

See the ark overlaid within: “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I, 12); and elsewhere: “I am conscious of nothing against myself” (I Cor. IV, 4); likewise: “My heart does not reproach me throughout all my life” (Job XXVII, 6). See it overlaid without: “It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you or by a human day” (I Cor. IV, 3). Zachariah and Elizabeth were overlaid with gold within, because they were righteous before God; without, because they walked in all the ordinances of the Lord without blame (Luke I, 6). The ark is well overlaid with gold within and without when its soul and good conscience are united to God and angels [Col. 1068D], and when its reputation is magnified among believers and unbelievers. The ark is overlaid with the purest gold when, for God’s cause alone, thoughts are disciplined in the mind and good works are performed.

It follows: “And you shall make above it a golden crown round about” (Exod. XXV, 24). We make a golden crown round about above the ark when, with the heavenly reward set before us, we seek nothing beyond it, wander nowhere from it, and never let it fall from our mind. We always wear a golden crown above the ark when we set God as the end and intention of all our works and desires; and this “round about,” so that no part of the soul admits an interruption of good endeavours, and no part of life makes an excursion away from God. The golden crown is round about when eternal life is always set before your sight, and you compel all the windings of temporal life to remain within the bounds of eternal glory [Col. 1069A]. Enclose life within life: the meritorious within the rewarding, the miserable within the blessed, the transitory within the eternal, the shadowy within the true.

Then follows: “And four golden rings, which you shall place at the four corners of the ark” (ibid., 26). A corner is where the ends of two walls meet. Four walls in a house, where the ends of each are joined, make four corners; and every quadrangular form produces four corners. Thus in our soul there are four passions, or natural virtues, which make corners: fear, hope, sorrow, and joy [Col. 1069B]. Where fear fixes its beam to hope, and hope to fear, they make a corner. Where sorrow approaches joy, or joy sorrow, they again make another corner. If you join fear to sorrow by desire, you will have made a third corner; if you add joy to hope, a fourth. Behold: when separately you fear punishment, hope for reward, grieve over exile, or rejoice in the promise, you do not yet have a corner. But mingle the ends of each, so that you fear with hope, hope with fear, desire with joy, rejoice with desire, fear with joy, and hope with desire—or desire with hope—and you have made corners. Hold fast the corners and sit in the corner, for “it is better to sit in the corner of a roof than with a contentious woman in a common house” (Prov. 25:24).

For if fear seizes you and oppresses you too greatly through remembrance of preceding sins, let hope offer its head, so that the abyss of God’s mercy may break forth before you and soften the sharp point of your miseries, which accusing fear had brought into memory. Therefore, “lying down between the boundaries” (Gen. 49:14), weep on the one side for your sins; on the other look toward the mercies of God, and restrain the weight of terror by the security of divine goodness.

Again, if you are affected and afflicted by an excessive desire for the glory and face of God, beyond what can be borne, let hope embrace your desire, persuading it that you must await with patience, because “he who is coming will come and will not delay” (Hab. 2:2). It promises the most sweet fruit of the sacraments [Col. 1069D] that is to come, while meanwhile displaying no unbeautiful flower in visible form. Lying also between these boundaries, wait “until the day breathes and the shadows of the things to come decline” (Song 2:17), which are present in the sacraments of faith, until “the morning star arises” (2 Pet. 1:19), so that the truth of things may be disclosed in the face of manifestation, which now lies hidden beneath the shadow of faith.

Likewise, if joy over the beauty of the present Church, retained too strongly, begins to move the foot of the mind more slowly toward future things—as though it persuaded you that, by a longer labor against wickedness, fuller rewards might be deserved—let desire run to it and awaken joy that has fallen into an evil sleep. Let it suggest that a station near the camp of the foreigners, or Philistines, is unsafe, and that men have often lost what they had gained while pursuing superfluous things. Nor should “he who girds himself boast as much as he who ungirds himself” [Col. 1070A] (3 Kings 20:11), because to rejoice in the kingdom while outside the kingdom is uncertain, but to glory in the kingdom while in the kingdom is safe and certain. O joy, which, because of premature ripeness, already eats the early grapes in the morning! Why was it said to the apostles, “It is expedient for you that I go” (John 16:7), except that they might never stay their step until they reached him? But perhaps the gain of others pleases you. Yet while gain is sometimes sought, loss results. And for the Apostle, “to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21).

Thus joy is stimulated by desire; and, with its course renewed, joy runs together with desire. Likewise, if hope, vainly casting aside fear, has raised its head into the clouds beyond what is just, let fear bring a just balance and weigh how great are the things for which, and the degree to which, it has deserved to hope [Col. 1070B]. Let it enumerate what it has done for God and what it has committed against God, and it will understand how much it ought, or ought not, to hope. “For at your side,” says the Psalmist, “a thousand shall fall”—that is, those who presumed that they would stand with you in judgment without works—“and ten thousand at your right hand” (Ps. 90:7), those who boasted of merits without merit. Therefore let fear oppose weight to the lightness of hope, so that hope may entrust itself not to wind but to truth.

It would take long to explain what ought to be said or considered in each individual corner. But, sitting in the corners, turn over your corners in mind, and add to these things more and better things. Therefore, “you shall place four golden rings at the four corners of the ark; according to the corners you shall place the rings.” The first ring is continual meditation on death; the second, constant mortification of the body; the third, voluntary confession of sin; the fourth, voluntary submission to a superior. Meditation on death belongs in the corner of fear and hope; mortification of the body, in the corner of hope and fear; confession of sin, in the corner of desire and fear; submission to a superior, in the corner of joy and hope.

Certainly the corner of fear fittingly receives the ring of meditation on death, because one who meditates upon death fears to commit that for which he may be condemned. Hence: “My son, remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Ecclus. 7:40).

Likewise, the corner of hope suitably receives mortification of the body, because “he who ploughs ought to plough in hope, and he who threshes in hope” (1 Cor. 9:1) of receiving fruit. For this reason bodies must be mortified: because “our life is hidden with Christ in God; when Christ, your life, appears, then you too shall appear with righteousness in glory” [Col. 1070D] (Col. 3:4). Likewise, the corner of desire rightly receives confession of sin, because confession must be made not unwillingly but willingly, not with weariness but with desire. From a thief or criminal, an acknowledgment of theft is extorted as from one unwilling and caught; from the penitent sinner, confession is received as a welcome sacrifice: “Willingly,” says the Psalmist, “I will sacrifice and confess your name, because it is good” (Ps. 53:8).

Likewise, the corner of joy and hope receives voluntary submission, because when creation “shall be delivered from the slavery of subjection into the liberty of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 8:2), those too shall be freed who, not “serving before the eye” [Col. 1071A] (Col. 3:21), submit to their superiors; who have freely offered their souls to the Lord; who, as Christ was obedient to the Father even unto death, say: “My Father, not what I will, but what you will” (Mark 14:36). Thus they place their souls in their own hands, obedient with joy and hope to their superiors.

These rings are golden, so that they may be fashioned in charity, brightness, wisdom, and chastity: in charity, that compulsion may be excluded; in brightness, that dark duplicity may be removed; in wisdom, that rashness may be taken away; in chastity, that superfluity may be cut off. Charity is in submission, brightness in confession, wisdom in meditation, chastity in mortification.

Then follows: “Let there be two rings on one side, and two on the other” (Exod. 25:12). Meditation on death and mortification of the body are on one side, guarding the soul lest it sin; confession and submission are on the other, correcting the soul if it has sinned [Col. 1071B]. For unless a person sinned, he would need neither confession nor rebuke. Again, unless he could sin or feared that he might, he would mortify himself or think of death to no purpose.

Then follows: “You shall also make bars of setim wood, overlay them with gold, and bring them through the rings which are on the sides of the ark, that it may be carried by them” (ibid., 13). Judgment and justice are bars of setim wood. The Psalmist made them so that the ark might be carried, saying: “I have done judgment and justice” (Ps. 118:121), and: “Blessed are they who keep judgment and do justice at all times” (Ps. 105:3), because setim wood is incorruptible. Thus the soul that ought to do judgment and justice at all times must not be corrupted by love, hatred, deceit [Col. 1071C], favor, or money.

“You shall overlay them with gold,” lest you do your justice before people in order to be seen by them (Matt. 6:1), but in secret (Rom. 2:29), before God, so that your Father who is in heaven may be glorified. Overlay them with gold, so that you may do what is good with a good intention. Those bars were not overlaid with gold which belonged to those who “have received their reward” (Matt. 6:2), who regarded piety as gain, so that all their labor was in their own mouth. But those whose sins are covered (Rom. 14:7) through repentance are covered with gold. Hence it is said to one: “Repent; otherwise I shall remove your lampstand from its place” (Rev. 2:5).

“And you shall bring them through the rings which are on the sides of the ark, that it may be carried by them.” He brings the bars through the rings on the sides of the ark who, through every corner of the heart and through the rings of all his actions, continually ponders the strictness of the future examination and the equity of the righteous Judge, groaning in expectation of him like a dove and running like a stag to springs of water, toward the living God [Col. 1071D]. The bars must never be withdrawn, but must always remain in the rings, so that the entire mass of our actions and thoughts may be conveyed by these vehicles.

Perhaps I am invited to an unlawful banquet: I will not go, because I fear judgment. I am invited to intercourse: I do not do it, because “there is a lion in the road,” and a fire that devours unto utter destruction. Whatever other services of corruption may be suggested, I restrain my members; I do not present them as “weapons of iniquity to sin” [Col. 1072A] (Rom. 6:13). I do not withdraw the bars from the golden rings, because I do not use for evil but for good the virtues bestowed upon me by God, so that the ark of the soul may be carried by them—by natural support, not by the seductive enticement of concupiscence.

Then follows: “And you shall put in the ark the testimony which I shall give you” (Exod. 25:16). What ought to be laid up in the soul, which is the temple of the Holy Spirit, except God’s testimony? The Apostle had placed God’s testimony in his ark when he said: “The Spirit of God himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God” (Rom. 8:16), that is, God’s ark. God’s testimony is in heaven—that is, in the ark—for “there are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit” (1 John 5:7); and they are not testimonies [Col. 1072B], but one testimony, because “these three are one” (ibid.).

If the Father is in your mind, the Word in your understanding, and the Holy Spirit in your love or will, God’s testimony is in your ark. Likewise, Spirit, water, and blood are one testimony of God when you preserve unstained the sacrament of regeneration. The testimony is in the tablets of the law, so that, by meditating upon them, you may order your conduct and instruct your tongue. The testimony is Aaron’s rod that budded, so that by it you may recognize yourself to be of royal and priestly stock: acting royally in governing your movements and limbs, and priestly by living chastely and devoutly. The testimony is the golden urn containing manna, so that a good conscience may be fragrant with grace before God and preserved as a memorial of righteousness for the day of judgment.

[Col. 1072C] This whole testimony does not fear the tribunal of the Judge, but cries confidently: “Who shall bring an accusation against God’s elect? God is the one who justifies; who is the one who condemns?” (Rom. 8:33). Yet there follows the mercy-seat, so that propitiation may supply whatever the testimony was unable to provide. Then follows: “You shall make a mercy-seat of purest gold,” etc. (Exod. 25:17). However richly the soul may be endowed with the treasure of a good conscience, it always remains below the rule of justice; and, if human righteousness were compared point for point with divine righteousness, Scripture testifying, it would be reckoned “like the cloth of a menstruous woman” (Isa. 64:6).

Therefore let human effort labor together with grace, so that it may not be accused of sloth [Col. 1072D]; but let it not presume upon its own harvest, lest, condemned for folly, it be shut out with the foolish virgins. Let it place the ark beneath the mercy-seat, saying with the Psalmist: “For your mercy is better than lives” (Ps. 62:4). For no kind of life is sufficient for salvation by itself, since without grace it could not even be called life or a good work: “Without me,” he says, “you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

Therefore the mercy-seat must be made of purest gold, so that you may say: “Hear me, O Lord, not because I have deserved it, but because your mercy is gracious” (Ps. 68:17). One must always set before God not our own merit, which is evil, but the privilege of his nature and goodness, which the wicked sometimes employ almost more boldly than the good. For because the Pharisee gave thanks without the authority of this privilege [Col. 1073A], he was rejected as a lying preacher. But the publican, rereading the tenor of the privilege and possessing nothing of his own except guilt, set before the Judge the sum of his prayers from the commonality of this privilege: “God,” he said, “be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 10:31).

O mercy-seat! O privilege of the mercy-seat! Neither the enormity nor the long-standing corruption of the mind causes you horror; indeed, you receive all the detestable crimes of human beings. You pardon what should be pardoned; I dare say, according to the atrocity of crimes, you almost pardon even what ought not to be pardoned, unless you were the mercy-seat. Yet plainly you can and must pardon everything that you do pardon, so that “as your name is, so is your praise unto the ends of the earth” (Ps. 47:11).

You have two cubits in length [Col. 1073B], so that you may forgive sins of thought and action; you have a half-cubit, so that you may forgive ambiguous sins arising from the collision of flesh and spirit, when the thought that excuses and accuses labors in darkness, not discerning whether it belongs to flesh or spirit—whether it is a living or a dead son, and of what nature it is. Hence the Psalmist says: “Cleanse me from my hidden sins” (Ps. 18:13). O mercy-seat, you have not only two cubits but also a half, because you save by hope, not yet in reality.

The mercy-seat also joins to itself two golden and outspread cherubim—not for help or ornament, but for our aid and service. For it chose to have ministers who might run on a faithful embassy to those bound, see whether all was well with the flocks and herds, and report what was being done [Col. 1073C]. Thus the mercy-seat has angels, “a helper like itself” (Ecclus. 17:5), not in the effect of power but in the reason of compassion: angels to whom it might more safely entrust its secrets, more faithfully commit our ministries, and more quickly hear our petitions.

They are on either side of the oracle, so that one cherub is on one side and the other on the other. The two sides of the oracle are the removal of evils and the attainment of goods [Col. 1074A]. For one cherub of the mercy-seat is on one side, driving evils away from us; the other is on the other side, procuring goods for us. The entire angelic office, so far as we are concerned, is to defend us from evil and preserve us in good.

They cover both sides of the mercy-seat when they delay or at times hide the assistance of the mercy-seat in order to exercise us by temptations, and when they conceal the love of the mercy-seat in order to stir us to seek more ardently. When Mary believed the Lord to be the gardener, did not one cherub cover one side of it, so that the flame of love might increase more strongly through seeking? Likewise, when Peter denied the Lord, did not the other cherub cover the other side of the mercy-seat [Col. 1074B], so that afterward he might weep more abundantly in remembering his denial and the Prince of the Apostles might recognize what remained of human frailty in him?

Therefore, spreading their wings, they cover the oracle, because, obedient to divine commands, they keep under seal, until “a time and times and half a time,” what the divine counsels concerning us are. For they would make us less vigilant if they made known that we were predestined; and they would stir those who despair to greater recklessness if they revealed that we were already condemned. They also look upon one another, their faces turned toward the mercy-seat with which the ark of the Lord is to be covered, because they always agree in their counsel, drawing from the mercy-seat what they ought to do for themselves and for us.

From there he commands and speaks—namely, above the mercy-seat and in the midst of the two cherubim [Col. 1074C]—all that he commands the children of Israel. From the mercy-seat, or oracle, the decree of judgments is principally established, so that in every question concerning the children of Israel it may be decided what must be concealed among God’s secrets, how long each thing must be withheld from public disclosure, and when it is to be brought forth. But now let the eagle lower its flights to food and table, so that it may pass from the vision of angels to the refreshment of food.

## BOOK II

[Col. 1073]

[Col. 1073D] “You shall make also a table of setim wood, two cubits long, one cubit broad, and one cubit and a half high” (Exod. 25:23). The table of setim wood is never empty of refreshment, because Holy Scripture is not devoid either of the feasts of its sayings or of dishes of examples. It is of setim wood because “heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Mark 13:31). The servants of this table are the writers and practitioners of divine Scripture. The Lord of the table is the Holy Spirit, who both enlightened the hearts and instructed the tongues of those who handled the word of life, opening their understanding so that they might understand and write miracles in the law of the Lord; the guests meditate on the law of the Lord [Col. 1074D] day and night.

The dishes of the guests are the instructions of readers, by which the soul is filled as with fatness and richness. Beef is the recital of those who bore the yoke of the law while acting under the law, serving in foods and drinks and diverse baptisms until the time appointed by the Father, pondering the grain of grace only in the cultivation of the law. Fattened birds, flying near heaven, bring a dish different from oxen to the table, because the lives and examples of contemplatives show how we ought to seek the things above. She places upon the table for the beloved all fruits, new and old, beloved by the beloved, because Scripture, preserving individually from the beginning of the world the names, works, sayings, and examples of the faithful, sprinkles the entire table with the memory of the old and new fathers [Col. 1075A]. It is as impossible to explain the delights of this table as to swallow up the entire sea of the abyss.

It has two cubits in length, one cubit in breadth, and one cubit and a half in height. The length of the table signifies action, the breadth love, and the height hope or contemplation. Action has two cubits: purity and innocence. Hence: “Pure and undefiled religion before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their tribulation and to keep oneself undefiled from this world” (Jas. 1:27). Likewise: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke 12:35). Breadth has one cubit, because charity is one and perfect; height has one and a half, because of the unity of heavenly hope and the beginning of contemplation [Col. 1075B].

Then follows: “And you shall overlay it with purest gold” (Exod. 25:24). Scripture, like some grave and venerable matron, although she refuses to adorn her cheeks—which are sufficiently ruddy with natural vigor and beauty—with antimony, purple, and red pigment, is nevertheless by no means inferior to those philosophical pursuits and teachings which glory only in the outward appearance of words. For her majesty of sense is more beautiful, the ordered construction of her sentences stronger, her meaning more useful, her fruit more abundant, her reading more modest. She rejects both the dress and vice of harlots, so that the kernel beneath the bark may please more than false paint upon the surface. Therefore she is overlaid with gold, because she is beautiful in appearance and good in meaning.

Then follows: “You shall make for it a golden rim round about, and for the rim itself an openwork crown, four fingers high, and above it another little golden crown” [Col. 1075C] (ibid.). He who has unclean lips and does not have the lips of a priest, which preserve knowledge, does not belong to the table until one of the seraphim touches his lips with tongs from the altar. Not *lips*, but a single *lip* and rim of gold is made upon the table of divine Scripture, because it admits neither heresies nor schisms, which chatter that the Father is [greater than] the Son and that the Son is less than the Holy Spirit. Rather, divine Scripture asserts the unity of the Trinity and the Trinity of unity, saying: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one” (Deut. 6:3). Likewise: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4:5).

Therefore the table, with its golden rim, proclaims the fullness of its courses and the sum of its dishes by harmonious preaching; it does not use puffed cheeks and stretched lips, speaking lofty things and magnifying its own lips [Col. 1075D]. For the loftier divine utterances are in meaning, the more modest they are in voice and restrained in delivery. For they are the voices of lambs: “He cried out, and his voice was not heard in the streets.” Whatever, therefore, divine speech utters is one through the unity of faith and golden through the depth of meaning: one, lest it be torn apart by schismatic error; golden, lest it become cheap through bare and rustic speech; “round about,” lest it be thought to concern a transitory good.

Understand through the rim what is eternal and pleasant; through the rim, what is life-giving; through “round about,” the highest good; through “golden,” what is promised, life-giving, and pleasant; through “golden,” the supreme good; through “round about,” what is immortal. Add [Col. 1076A] to the rim an openwork crown, so that the crown may display what Scripture promised and may bite into profession: the rim is the crown of the prize, as faithfully paying what is owed as it truly continues the promise. Hence the Psalmist says: “Receive me according to your word, and I shall live” (Ps. 118:116), and many such things.

Yet observe the openwork crown because of the distinction between merits in the present and rewards in the future. For it would be an encouragement to negligence and nourishment for injustice if reward made equal those whom merit had made unequal [the printed reading is corrupt: *meritum disparasset*]. Who would keep vigils if one asleep plucked the fruit of vigils? Who would torment and wear down his body with fires, fasts, mortifications, and countless sufferings, if moist and soft hide sounded as well amid its pleasures as a drum resounds clearly under continual stretching and scraping? One star would not differ from another in brightness if merits did not differ in weight.

Therefore the crown placed upon the golden rim is openwork, because distinction of performers follows upon distinction of commandments, and distinction of rewards [or: of acts of rewarding] follows as well. It is four fingers high, because, when the fullness of righteousness and the consummation of glory are described in the four books of the Gospels, the crown is measured, as it were, by four fingers [Col. 1076B].

Then follows: “You shall make an altar,” etc. (Exod. 27:1). That great King, “of whose greatness there is no number,” gradually draws inward the mind that wanders outward. After he had completed the structure of the tabernacle, he assigned within it a place especially to himself, where acceptable victims might be burned and, by mystical sacrifice, the wrath of heaven might be appeased and human errors forgiven. He calls this place an *altar*, demonstrating by the name itself the height of the mystery, because an altar ought ever to be consecrated to God alone and only for divine uses.

Thus, more sacredly forming those who approach his altar by the steps of virtues, he first placed them at the ark of testimony, then at the mercy-seat. He also seated them at the table of refreshment, illuminating it with the fashioned lampstand and its seven lamps. Then he spread curtains, coverings, dyed ram skins, violet skins, upon boards standing upon bases [Col. 1076D]; he set columns before them and hung a veil of violet, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted fine linen, placing it between the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies. By this progress, as though in paradise, the Lord leads the righteous person before he approaches the altar, so that with the Psalmist he may say: “I went around and sacrificed in his tabernacle a sacrifice of rejoicing” (Ps. 26:6).

“Therefore you shall make for me an altar of setim wood, five cubits in length and as many in breadth”—that is, square—“and three cubits in height” (Exod. 27:1). The altar is the hearts of the elect, consecrated by the Lord for offering the works of works. They ought to be pure and incorruptible; they should exercise the five bodily senses in the length of patience and breadth of charity, in the service of faith; and, in faith, hope, and charity, they should tend toward heavenly things.

But there is a literal question about the altar’s height: how could anyone minister, since the height of a man is scarcely as great as the height of the altar, and no step could be made according to the law lest nakedness be exposed? The solution is this. Steps are forbidden on an altar of stones or even of earth, because, being as it were built together with the altar, they seem to belong to the altar itself. But on this altar of wood, a small bench could be placed beneath it during the time of ministry and, when the service was completed, removed [the printed reading is corrupt: *tolli*]; this was not contrary to the commandments of the law [Col. 1077A].

Then follows: “The horns shall be from it at its four corners, and you shall overlay it with bronze” (ibid., 2). The Church is extended through the four regions of the world in the unity of the Catholic faith; or the hearts of the elect are fortified by four virtues—sobriety, prudence, justice, and fortitude—than which nothing is more useful in human life. The horns proceed from the altar itself when they are not produced for outward appearance but arise from the root of the heart. “You shall overlay it with bronze,” that is, with perseverance.

Then follows: “You shall make for its uses pots to receive the ashes” (ibid., 3). These different vessels signify different persons among the faithful in their actions, offices, and thoughts. Ash signifies the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion, or the perfection of the virtues of the righteous. Something beyond the material must be said concerning the significance of ash. Moses says of the burnt offering: “It shall be burned upon the altar all night,” etc. (Lev. 6:9): that is, throughout the whole time of this life, until the morning of the age to come, good work in the heart devoted to God must burn with the fire of charity [Col. 1077C].

“The fire shall be from the altar itself” (ibid.), because we ought to burn from that charity which the Lord gave to the Church. But one offers strange fire who does heavenly works not for reward but for temporal profit; and he is consumed by heavenly fire, that is, by the sentence of God’s wrath. “The priest shall be clothed with a linen tunic and linen drawers” (ibid.): that is, Christ sets forth the purity of his incarnation and death.

> [Note: Col. 1077D. The passage is corrupt.]

“He removes the ashes which the fire has consumed and puts them beside the altar” (ibid.), when the Lord puts an end to laborious works and commands that the crown be received in eternal life. “He is stripped of his former garments” (Lev. 10:11), when, recalling for the righteous the good things they have done, he shows that they need labor no longer but must devote themselves to rest of heart and divine contemplation. “Clothed in other garments, he shall carry the ashes outside the camp” (ibid.), when he causes the labor of his saints to appear, in that life, worthy of reward [Col. 1077D].

In the most clean place, which is the mind of the righteous taken from this life, the ash of the burnt offering is consumed even to the last spark, when there the reward for good works is so rendered that all labor is entirely consumed. “But the fire shall always burn on the altar” (ibid., 12), because, once every kind of laboring has been exhausted, charity shall blaze and never be extinguished. In order that you might understand more clearly of what usefulness the pots are which are made to receive the ashes, we have explained these matters more fully.

“And tongs,” he says, “and forks, and fire-pans” [Col. 1078A] (Exod. 27:3). The tongs are preachers, who use, as it were, a double tooth in order to kindle in us the fire of charity when they instruct us from the pages of both Testaments, or when they instill the virtue of twofold charity and thereby make us burn and shine. The forks also are those by which victims, cooked for food, are brought to those who are to be refreshed. Their use is fitting for preachers, because it belongs to teachers to assign each person a ministry with discernment: they may bring out some things for all to eat, but leave other things to be consumed by the fires of the altar, things which transcend our capacity.

The fire-pans are censers, by which fire and coals were carried from the altar of burnt offerings to the altar of incense, for incense to be placed there morning and evening [Col. 1078B]. This occurs when they advance their hearers from virtue to virtue. Those who imitate the fervor of holy hearts are themselves also fire-pans. “You shall make all the vessels of bronze” (ibid.), that is, the hearts of the saints shall possess perseverance and shall instruct others with a clear voice.

“And a bronze grating in the form of a net,” etc. (ibid., 4). Literally, the altar is wholly hollow and has in its middle a grating arranged in the form of a net, upon which the flesh of victims to be burned was placed. Beneath it was a small hearth, where, after wood had been arranged, a fire burned, ready to devour the burnt offerings. Opposite the hearth, on the eastern side of the altar, was an opening through which wood could be thrown in to feed the fire and coals or ashes could be removed. The grating was made in the form of a net so that the fire might freely pass through its many openings to devour the victim [Col. 1078C].

Mystically, the grating signifies the place prepared in the innermost heart for the Lord, where holy persons place devout thoughts. “At its four corners there shall be four golden rings, which you shall place before the altar’s hearth” (Exod. 4:5). Literally, it seems remarkable that an altar made of wood was not burned by such a nearby fire. But Jeremiah says that the altar’s wood was from the wood of paradise and therefore is not burned by fire but made purer. And lest this seem incredible, there is a certain kind of wood called *anthitau* which, the more it has burned, is found the cleaner.

Mystically, the books of the Gospels, which promise the crown of eternal life to their hearers, strengthen by the word of faith and truth the Church spread through the four regions of the world [Col. 1078D], and raise the minds of the humble by the defense of their consolation.

“And the grating shall reach to the middle of the altar” (ibid.). It is necessary for us to open our hearts to God’s grace and, as though with very many doors opened, to pray diligently that, through each good work which we undertake—like each separate piece of the victim—he may deign, by his mercy, to enlighten us and kindle us in his love. But the Pelagians set not a grating in the form of a net, but a solid wall in the altar of the heart between themselves and the fire of the Holy Spirit, lest they be warmed by charity.

The altar is not solid but hollow and empty [Col. 1079A], providing within itself ample space for fire, burnt offerings, and wood to be consumed. You too, if you wish to be God’s altar, empty yourself of every contamination of earthly things, so that understanding of heavenly words and sacrifices of virtues may have spacious room, and so that you may receive the flame of the Holy Spirit, by which the Church’s sacrifices are consecrated to the Lord and brought to the end of perfection.

“You shall also make two bars for the altar of setim wood, which you shall overlay with bronze plates, and bring them through the rings; they shall be on both sides of the altar for carrying it” (Exod. 4:6). What was understood mystically of the bars of the ark must be understood of the bars of the altar, except that these are overlaid with bronze plates and those with gold. The plates signify the urgency of preaching and the sound heard throughout all the earth.

“You shall make also a table of setim wood, two cubits in length and a cubit and a half in breadth” [Col. 1079B]. What meditation stores in the ark, memory sets forth on the table. Meditation reaps and gathers at the appropriate time what memory demands when some circumstance of necessity presses and urges. The table is enriched from the ark when prayer is nourished from a good conscience and unfeigned faith, and preaching is formed by them. At times a veil of silence is hung between ark and table, when—with lips described in the corrupt text as *tantis*—the mind is filled with God and not with understanding; when, from the fatness and richness of a good conscience, holy preachers refresh their hearers with most welcome utterances.

This table has neither cheap nor stale loaves. For just as it knows nothing of the hardened oldness of loaves, lest they rot through error, so it rejects the usefulness of material things, lest it be defiled by secular vanity [Col. 1079C]. Nor do the loaves remain on the table beyond the sevenfold number of grace, lest you speak without grace; nor are they made except from fine flour, lest you adulterate truth by an admixture of falsehoods. By rule they are placed on the Sabbath and removed on the Sabbath. For when should the word of God be preached except when both hearers are free to listen and preachers to teach?

He does not place loaves on the Sabbath who evangelizes those who do not receive God’s word, who speaks into the ear of those who do not hear. He does not place loaves upon the table on the Sabbath who gives what is holy to dogs and puts pearls before swine (Matt. 6). He does not place loaves on the Sabbath who does not consider what he says according to the subject matter, to whom he says it according to the person, when he says it according to time and cause, or how much he says according to the adequacy of the business.

But just as one sins by indiscretion in confession when he does not distinguish these things, so likewise one sins by rashness who removes the loaves before the Sabbath: who speaks before the cooking of meditation, before inquiry into appetite, before deliberation about hunger, before the emptying of the stomach [Col. 1079D]. He removes the loaves on the Sabbath who gives food to the young ravens at the fitting time; who weighs meaning, intention, and the benefit of hearers, fitting the matter of speech to the meaning, moderating its measure to the intention, and supplying to usefulness an appropriate end and beginning.
