Place loaves on the table on the Sabbath, so that, grace giving light, you may begin your sermons; remove the loaves on the Sabbath, so that, with that same grace cooperating [Col. 1080A], you may return the fruit of the sermon to grace itself. Finally, place incense upon the loaves, so that you seek devotion rather than favor, and so that you spread the good fragrance of sound doctrine both in moral teaching and in mystical matters. When your speech lifts to God, by the exhalations of chaste desires in groans and sighs, as though by some rowing of wings, you will have placed incense upon the loaves of presentation. Thus the table smells sweetly in hope of future things and feeds well in the reality of present things, when, by the merit of faith, righteousness, and charity, it fattens humbled bones with the richness of present justification and draws holy sighs by the sweet fragrance of future reward.

All these things are set forth upon the table of memory, if it is made of shittim wood, so that it may not decay through forgetfulness; if it endures in continual vitality, losing nothing of its perception and [Col. 1080B] never spilling itself abroad. Let memory have two cubits in length, that it may hold fast its evils in order to mourn them, and its goods in order to render thanks to God. Let it have a cubit and a half in breadth, so that in the one cubit of breadth it may understand God’s perfect love toward itself, and in the half-cubit recollect its own imperfection and transgression. In one cubit, the benefit of creation; in the half, the abyss of its fall; in one, the price of redemption; in the half, the gulf of the distrust of certain persons, who, though redeemed, do not love the Redeemer, and though set free, do not wish to depart.

Let it likewise have a cubit and a half in height, so that in one cubit memory may recognize our Head as already perfectly glorified, and in the half-cubit may observe that division among the members [Col. 1080C] of Christ by which one part reigns with its Head, while another part still serves as a soldier in this pilgrimage. In one it retains that the Church has already been freed, in the saints who have put off the flesh, from necessity, misery, and sin; in the half, that among pilgrims it is freed only from necessity, and not from misery or sin. These things have been said concerning the length, breadth, and height of the table which is our memory.

It follows: “And you shall overlay it with the purest gold” (Exod. 25:24). When the dark mists of errors and the foulest marshes of enticements have been cleansed away from the face of memory, then you will overlay it with gold if you bind it to the sacred Scriptures and to pure understandings of them, so that it may discern soundly, understand truly, and see clearly. Let the empty seductions of thoughts, the novel illusions of phantasms, and the fabricated recollections of imaginings be excluded, [Col. 1080D] lest memory be occupied in mud; rather let it be honored in gold; lest it become cheap in filth, but shine in a heaven gilded with the purest gold of the Old and New Law. Behold the table of memory overlaid with gold: “The memory of the righteous is with praises” (Prov. 10:7); likewise: “The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance” (Ps. 111:6). Therefore, that memory which is accompanied by praise and is eternal is overlaid with gold. But their memory is not overlaid with gold, concerning whom it is said: “Their memory has perished with a sound” (Ps. 33:17).

It follows: “You shall make for it a golden rim round about” (Exod. 25:24). The word of the heart and the word of the mouth ought to be one, so that the pure milk of thought [Col. 1081A] may be drawn from the breast of speech, not degenerating in excellent color, good taste, or true liquid. Let your word be colored by truth, flavored by goodness, and made fluid by charity. Let all this be present both in all speech and in each individual word, so that every word may be truthful [the text reads *mendax*, “false,” probably for *verax*, “truthful”] through simplicity, good through usefulness, and charitable through affection. This is the golden rim round about the table: when the memory of the heart supplies the mouth with such things that both the hidden face of our secrets may come forth publicly in the light, and may declare the purpose of the office of speech, which was established for usefulness.

It would indeed be destructive if the innumerable, untamable revolutions of the heart lay open to everyone, both because of shame and because they would be a seedbed of discord. Who could patiently admit human sight into so incomprehensibly defiled a bosom of the heart? Surely a person would either succumb beneath excessive blushing, or grow contemptuous of evils through their continual presence, or infect those who saw him by their seductive foulness. For this reason, therefore, the counsels and secrets of the heart had to be concealed. Again, if a person’s will were shut and hidden in perpetual obstinacy, the bond of human society would perish, and eternal silence would be the nourishment of malice. How could you love a friend whom you could in no way recognize as a friend and faithful? It was therefore for our benefit that the word should lie hidden in the heart and be manifest in the mouth. But lest you be double, let it be a rim; lest deceitful, golden; lest faithless and unstable, it must be made round about. The rim [Col. 1081C] signifies simplicity in confession; the gold, purity of intention; the circuit, integrity in action.

It follows: “And for the rim itself, a chased crown, four fingers high” (ibid., 25). In the Gospel the Lord makes a crown for the golden rim when he says: “Whoever confesses me before the Lord,” etc. (Matt. 10:32). The golden rim is the confession of martyrs, because, as gold shines more brightly than other metals, so faith and confession, tested in the fire of assault, are more precious through patience, stronger through constancy, brighter through punishment, and loftier through reproach. Increased punishment increases brightness; constancy proves strength; patience weighs the amount of the price; reproach multiplies honor. In punishment is the persecutor’s cruelty; [Col. 1081D] in constancy, the martyr’s long-suffering; in patience, kindness; in reproach, humility.

Perhaps this is why the crown is called four fingers high: because the reward of prizes rises according to the height of merits, so that the crown grows, as it were, by as many fingers as the flesh was twisted by torments in punishment. Likewise, upon the golden rim in the confession of sins he places a chased crown four fingers high, when by the first finger he corrects an evil will; by the second he accuses one’s sins; by the third he washes them; by the fourth he exchanges them for virtues. By the first finger Jesus cast out demons; by the second he wrote on the earth; by the third, on stone; by the fourth, in the heart. Of the first: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke 11:20). Of the second: “Jesus bent down and wrote on the earth” (John 8:6). Of the third: “He wrote on tablets of stone [Col. 1082A] the ten commandments of the Law” (Deut. 5:12). Of the fourth: “I will write my laws in their hearts” (Jer. 31:33). In the first is prevenient and operative grace; in the second, assisting and cooperating grace; in the third, the command that gives orders; in the fourth, free choice following grace. In the first, God acts without assistance; in the second, free choice acts with God; in the third is God’s admonition; in the fourth, fulfillment of the command. In the first he frees those in chains; in the second he assists those freed; in the third he enlightens the blind; in the fourth he strengthens the paralyzed.

These are the four fingers to whose measure the chased crown is extended, which is placed upon the golden rim, because whatever Scripture promises and memory can retain from the Scriptures has neither less nor more, whether in hope or in possession, of the eternal prize. [Col. 1082B] For it is little to have operative and cooperating grace, or a commanding precept, where our free choice or will does not feel it; and it is sufficient where, by obeying, it gives consent and, by not willing otherwise, effectively fulfills the law. But he makes the crown chased because no merit exists without grace, and because merit can never [perhaps: “be”] exist without free choice. For merit is principally from grace and secondarily from free choice. The crown is chased: if you consider free choice, it is cut away and sparse, yet full and whole. Grace alone could give the crown, but it preferred to prepare merit together with free choice and to render the crown for merits. That it is a crown belongs to God; that it is chased belongs to us. Had man not sinned, the crown would not be chased. For the angelic crown [Col. 1082C] is not chased: it fell from their head through no offense. But the human crown is chased: it fell through sin and returned through grace.

It follows: “And above it another little golden crown” (Exod. 27:27). To the evangelical innkeeper, to whom the half-dead man had been entrusted for healing, it was said: “Whatever you spend beyond this, I will repay you when I return” (Luke 10:35). The impulse of the spirit, overstepping the common law of merits and always digging new channels in the heart from the unsearchable depth of promises, never says, “Enough.” For there is a new savor in God for one who, with renewed desire in the purpose of religious life, neither grows old nor lukewarm. Therefore, when, surpassing the glory of his own powers, he presses on not with his own strength but [Col. 1082D] with God’s power—not now with his foot but with wings—he hastens toward the little crown, so that one who has anticipated may dare to do what was not commanded and receive what was not hoped for; for God gives us more than we ask or understand. Of the little crown it was said: “Let him who can receive it, receive it” (Matt. 19:12), so that, because the Apostle has no command concerning virgins, he suggests that when counsel without a command has been fulfilled, a little crown remains above the general promise; and one may excel in reward who excels in merit. Those who conquered the world by faith, insofar as they surpassed others in age, sex, profession, chastity, charity, and the course of the other virtues, flew higher toward the little crown.

It follows: “You shall also prepare four golden rings [Col. 1083A] and place them at the four corners of the same table, by its four feet” (Exod. 25:26). Memory has four golden rings, four corners, and four feet. With one foot memory deals with things that have indeed passed, but still stand at the doors and have not gone far away; with another, with remote things that have withdrawn farther from present knowledge; with a third, with more remote things, which can be recalled only with great effort; with a fourth, with the most remote things, which can be discovered only by the reading of books and the testimony of the ancients. Or with one foot it treads the earth; with another it walks upon waters; with another it flies in the air; with the fourth it ascends upon the wings of the winds in heaven. In the first it is humbled; in the second it is pierced with compunction; in the third it is kindled; in the fourth it is exalted. In the first it is born with sin; [perhaps: in the second it is judged; Col. 1083B] in the third it is raised and judged; in the fourth it is glorified. In the first it remembers Jesus’ birth; in the second, his baptism; in the third, his transfiguration; in the fourth, his ascension. In the first it recalls the guilt of original sin; in the second, absolution; in the third, justification; in the fourth, glorification. Or with one foot it encompasses the inanimate body; with the third, the created spirit; with the fourth, the uncircumscribed Spirit. With one foot it proceeds prudently; with another courageously; with the third justly; with the fourth temperately and soberly. With one foot it seeks history; with another allegory; with the third morality; with the fourth anagogy. These things concern the four feet of the table.

Let it also have four golden rings, so that it may humbly hear teachers, faithfully and firmly retain [Col. 1083C] understanding, vigorously exercise its intelligence, and draw forth from [Col. 1084A] the old things new things with profit. Of the first, Solomon says: “Hear, my son, the commands of your father, and do not abandon the law of your mother” (Prov. 6:20). Of the second: “Bind it continually upon your heart” (ibid.). Of the third, the Psalmist: “I meditated at night with my heart; I was exercised and searched my spirit” (Ps. 76:7). Of the fourth, the Lord in the Gospel rebukes the lazy servant: “Why,” he says, “did you not put my money to the table, so that when I came I might certainly have exacted it with interest?” (Luke 19:23). Let these rings be golden, lest secular learning occupy you, which will be reckoned as mud in comparison with true wisdom. For every doctrine which neither forms character, nor instructs faith, nor kindles charity, is vain: it does not enrich like gold but soils like mud.

Finally, the moral rings are obedience unto death, charity unto blood, chastity unto the mortification of fleshly desires, and humility unto utter abasement. [Col. 1084B] In the ring of obedience we are recalled; in the ring of chastity we are re-formed; in the ring of humility we are exalted. Let disobedience not break the ring of obedience; envy not divide the ring of charity; uncleanness not contaminate the ring of chastity; pride not rupture the ring of humility. Therefore let these rings be golden, so that you may obey, love, chastise, and humble your soul for true rather than vain glory. This concerning the rings. Concerning the corners of memory, I think enough has been said where we treated the corners of the ark.

[Col. 1083]

# PETER OF CELLES, *BOOK ON CONSCIENCE*, TO ALCHER, MONK OF CLAIRVAUX

[Col. 1083D] Brother PETER of Celles to his dearest brother ALCHER, monk of Clairvaux: greeting, and a good conscience.

A religious mind, with religious curiosity, inquires about the religion of conscience, that it may know—or rather, possess—a good conscience. I embrace your question, more indeed in order to learn than to teach. For recalled by your question from wandering through the circuit of the world, I make a question for myself out of your question. I therefore undertake, blind and poor, to dig deeply like a mole seeking to come to the light of conscience, though I lack the light of knowledge. For in a marvelous way that little creature uses hands and feet—indeed, hands and [Col. 1084D] feet—to throw off the weight pressing upon it, seeking, despite the darkness, the freedom of the air and perhaps even light without the light of its eyes.

Thus I too, caught until now in the hiding-place of shadowy negligence, gave little thought to how pleasant it is to break forth into the light and freedom of conscience. But when the scalpel of an inquirer’s insistence—asking what conscience is—cut the vein of my heart, I summoned from every side the living blood of the veins of all my meditation, so that from the blood of clarified contemplation the heart might, through the pen, entrust—or lend—what would suffice for the writer and retain for itself that from which it might live. For writing is useful when one is corrected both by one’s own treatment of the subject and one’s own life, and when another’s conscience is likewise instructed. Nor should one believe that the vein of the heart is always emptied harmfully when it is cut piously; rather, from the outpouring of charity it flows more usefully and freely.

Having therefore divided the labor of the work which I received as an assignment from you, here I began rather to blush at my own conscience, rotten in dead works. From the holy books I then investigated more carefully what yours and other saints’ conscience is, or ought to be. Because of the slowness of my mind, I could not dispatch so difficult and great a matter in one brief discourse, and therefore I ran to length. Another consideration also drew me into a long discourse: that conscience might at least be enclosed within itself for as long as one read or discussed conscience. For it is highly beneficial for conscience, by slow and prolonged meditations of rubbing, to cherish itself in itself: so that it may rest joyfully, grow fruitfully warm, and, illuminated and made bright by the sun, recognize itself in itself. Do you think that, if she recognized herself as fair among women, she would thereafter leave herself to follow the tracks of the flocks upon muddy paths and pasture the kids of wanton flesh? Do you think she would come among the trees of the forests, having with difficulty abandoned her own sweetness and richness, if she knew how great a good a devout conscience pleasing to God is? Do you think she would patiently bear even for a moment to refrain from the Bridegroom’s embrace, if she had held fast his words? But she is wretched, blind, and foolish because she embraces dung, loves darkness, and, what is more wretched, seeks misery even with misery. For the higher a thing is in the world, the more wretched and miserable it is.

[Col. 1085C] But from this misery of ambition, hardship—that misery which obstructs her on the road—does not draw her back, because it is not counted misery. The deceitful grace and vain beauty of the great harlot drinking from a golden cup are called happiness. Yet truly that misery by which the soul is killed—the prosperity of fools—is more unhappy than that misery by which the body is afflicted, the punishment of evils. A good conscience feels the sting of neither misery. It does not feel the misery of the journey, because it does not go out onto that evil way which leads to hell. It also escapes the misery of remaining, because it has shut the door by which death enters into our souls. For just as it refuses to go out because there is a lion on the road, so it avoids opening the door because there is a raven at the window. It equally abhors the raven’s blackness and the lion’s ferocity: the blackness, lest it be dishonored; the ferocity, lest it be devoured. Perhaps, it says, the raven’s stain would have swallowed our beauty, or the lion’s appetite our tenderness, unless the Lord had helped us, lest the flood submerge one left exposed, and lest the evil beast, removed from the road, devour Joseph as he came to his brothers.

In the Gospel the Lord teaches how conscience ought to shut itself within itself, saying: “Enter,” he says, “into your chamber” (Matt. 6:6). What is your chamber except the secret place of conscience? What is the door except your mouth? Therefore, when you pray, enter the chamber of the tranquil and quiet mind, where the Lord is [Col. 1086A] who dwells in Zion, and whose place is made in peace; and there he speaks to the heart of Jerusalem.

It enters, I say, into the chamber, so that by its own voice the heart may be shut toward the Lord, the door of the outward senses being closed. For that wife who does not trouble all the air through the passages of the throat, but by the secret path of spirit, in spirit and truth, knocks upon the Holy Spirit, is more effective in her petitions; and as soon as she is heard, she is answered. She is heard without the striking of sound as soon as the affection of the heart is moved. For if affection agrees with God and itself, it delights the harmony of heaven by its own consonance. God also sings, plays the psaltery—indeed, exults.

Conversely, certain persons who pray and sing daily in other tongues and with their lips, and are therefore not heard, say indignantly to the angels: “We sang to you, and you did not dance; we lamented, and you did not weep” (Luke 7:32). That is: You did not join us in rejoicing over our prosperities, though we sang daily in the oratory; nor did you sympathize with our troubles, though we were pierced even to tears. For concerning tears of this sort, shed in pretence or with impurity, it is written in the prophet: “You have polluted my altar with your tears.” Rather, conscience is polluted by its own tears than washed by them when, delighting in sin, it sheds pretended tears, unwilling to abandon sin but wishing by such weeping to redeem it and sin again. Thus it was also said of Judas’s prayer: “Let his prayer become sin” (Ps. 108:7). Therefore a pure conscience causes an angel both to dance—that is, to rejoice with it—when it has sung, [Col. 1086C] and to weep—that is, to sympathize—when it has lamented. “For there is joy among the angels in heaven over one sinner doing penance” (Luke 15:7). Again elsewhere it is written that “the angels of peace shall weep bitterly” (Isa. 33:7), namely, they shall sympathize over penitents.

Behold how great a thing a good conscience is. It is the sister of angels; yet certainly, while it still hangs small at the breasts of the Church, it has not yet the breasts of angelic perfection. Once it has them, it will come even to companionship with God. A good conscience is the title of religion; a good conscience is a garden of delights; a good conscience is the ark of the covenant; a good conscience is Joseph’s cup, in which it is accustomed to divine—or rather, become intoxicated; a good conscience is a royal treasury; a good conscience [Col. 1086D] is God’s hall; a good conscience is a sealed and closed book; a good conscience is whatever can be called or conceived more delightful, more beautiful, more honorable, more useful, more pleasant, better, or more wholesome. For devout minds, a good conscience is the unique and singular bond of the pledge of future blessedness. It does not know how to be carried about by the instability of a wandering *muteronis* [so printed; uncertain]. It reckons beneath itself whatever obscure or flattering thing presents itself to sensuality. The conscience that will never wither is also bright: it is not overshadowed by black clouds, scorched by the blazing sun, infected by pestilence, or made to relapse by the wandering revolution of the stars. Let the world weep or laugh, be whirled about in every instability, burn, perish, pass away: conscience will never wither.

[Col. 1087A] Therefore let the body be subdued by punishment, wasted by fasts, torn by beatings, stretched on the rack, slain by the sword, afflicted by the punishment of the cross: what is that to conscience? These things are written, rather, upon mortal skin as merit for a crown than inflicted as punishment for the fault of guilt. And what, then, is any affliction to conscience?

“Wherefore,” conscience says, “malicious torturer, the more sharply you pierce me, the more beautifully you paint the skin of my flesh, which is one of Solomon’s skins. Your piercing is a painting to me. Yield then to the skin, that you may paint as you pierce; for by piercing you both pierce and paint. Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his conscience.” You stretch the skin in torture, but then the painted figure appears more clearly. I glory in my variegated garment.

Finally, when I behold embroidered wounds, shining lilies, the rose from the thorn, when the practices of the individual virtues depict the individual dwellings of the heavenly chambers—what glory, what grace then overflows beyond measure in the joy of conscience? Would that that hour might spread itself beneath that conscience like a pavement. What refreshment then, O God, would the fasting soul receive from the sacred mouth; what utterances would the enriched and enlarged conscience return? Willing or unwilling, it could not restrain itself from the flashing splendor of the wonders God works in it, just as Joseph, full of the new wine of piety and compassion, could not contain himself.

Does she envy others this grace of hers in every conscience? But with envy wasting away, she has it no longer. Is she difficult, such that even devout solicitude cannot approach her? But she is easily seen by those who seek her. Does she delay opening, so that, overcome by weariness, you might draw back? But she anticipates those who desire her, that she may show herself to them first [variant: “shows herself”]. Are you too sluggish [variant: “Is she sluggish?”] to go to her? But she will come to you. Whoever keeps watch from dawn for her will not labor, for he will find her standing at his doors. What more may I say about conscience? I say one thing: to think upon it is consummate understanding; and whoever keeps watch for it will always be secure. With due reverence for wisdom, it is more useful to run to conscience than to wisdom—unless it is wisdom that builds conscience.

But wisdom [Col. 1087D] and conscience come to the mind with equal steps, so that wisdom may never come without conscience, nor conscience without wisdom. Let us see from the Book of Wisdom, from which we have already received much, to what end each of them—wisdom, that is, and conscience—leads the soul, as its own vehicle, with proportionate progress. We join each to the other in such a way that what is said of one may be transferred to the other. In the Book of Wisdom, then, concerning the beginning and end of wisdom, it is said: “Its beginning is the truest desire for instruction. Care for instruction, therefore, is love; and love is the keeping of its laws. But keeping the laws is the perfection of incorruption. And incorruption makes one near to God. Therefore desire for wisdom leads to an everlasting kingdom.” [Col. 1088A] Behold the fiery chariot and fiery horses, and God as charioteer: they carry not an amphora but a soul, certainly to an everlasting kingdom. You desire a kingdom, and especially an everlasting one. Attend, then, and ascend—not with a headlong and disorderly course like Satan, who fell like lightning from heaven into hell, but like the dawn of the sun rising and growing unto perfect day.

Therefore take hold of instruction, where cedar beams are cut and shaped. “For if you are without instruction,” says the Apostle, “then you are bastards and not sons” (Heb. 12:8). Shaped and fitted by the cutting of instruction for the construction of the city that is set foursquare, and brought into the breadth, length, depth, and height of charity, lay hold on and keep love itself. “For he who loves has fulfilled the law” [Col. 1088B] (Rom. 15:8).

Love, therefore, is the keeping of laws. What wages, then, does one earn who keeps the commandments? “If anyone loves me,” says the Lord, “he will keep my words, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23). But when the Lord comes, spread out before him the little cloak of incorruption, so that you may wrap, in such a shroud, not now Jesus’ body but the very grace of the Trinity coming to you and abiding in you. And what then will you do for the immortal, invisible King of ages—or rather, what will you receive from him? Surely a kingdom and the diadem of a kingdom upon your head. There will also be a necklace upon your neck. Reign, then, in the kingdom of conscience and likewise of wisdom.

[Col. 1088C] So much for these things. I wish this letter to be hung at the threshold of the book on conscience, so that, having tasted this foretaste, the reader may either reject it if what is said tastes bad, or more eagerly penetrate the inner things of the veil, beneath which are contained several matters—not only concerning conscience, but also concerning the purification of the heart—not altogether useless. For certain brief notes are set down below concerning the heart’s emission, retention, outpouring, loosening, loss, restoration, and recovery.

To calculate the provisions for a year and for a household is as much the mark of an excellent and prudent man as to live not by chance but by a certain and just rule. For it is base to a good reputation and burdensome to depend either on another’s hand or another’s table. Therefore, having calculated and laid aside for himself the expenditure of the time to come, the prudent man already begins to taste in advance the consolations of future rest, intending to live not by random chance but in cheerful and tested security. He accordingly compares fitting resources of times and seasons with one another, lest, if a time of the coming year should follow empty of its provision for the journey, want rebuke the idleness of the lazy man, and when he ought to find leisure for resting, he incur the torment of hunger. Finally, he hastens to extinguish the troubles of the collector who, by the daily roar of the entrails, plunders his substance, while a superabundant plenty of every kind universally excludes the straits of table and harvest; so that month may follow month through the continuity of frugality, and Sabbath follow Sabbath through the unbroken succession of joy and leisure.

Therefore, once the inner chambers have been searched and the recesses of the mind explored, we must, with no dissimilar example and no less concern, examine what is expended in the storehouses of conscience for the sustenance of our soul from generation to generation, [Col. 1089A] so that we may know what is sufficient and what falls short of the full and perfect measure of sufficiency.

Accordingly, I observe that you, good friend and holy monk Alcher, are diligently occupied with the household affairs of your soul. For you do not cease not only to gather daily food—indeed, spiritual provisions—from the most fertile fields of the holy doctors, but you also stretch out your hand to the very slender storehouse of our poverty, asking from a poor man not a poor gift: namely, conscience. And how shall I give what I do not have? Certainly I have no conscience but a ragged and marshy one: if you touch it, your hand will be defiled; if you look at it, your eye will be ashamed. It would therefore be safer for it to hide in its own lurking-place, lest, sending forth from its tomb poisonous and foul exhalations, it set ablaze the incentives of pestilence and not merely fail to awaken to life those torpid in the death of an evil conscience, but extinguish even good consciences, still faintly throbbing with however little life, by infecting them.

Nevertheless, I will rise and go to a friend whose door is now shut and whose children are with him in bed, and I will say to him: “Friend, lend me three loaves” (Luke 11:5), so that I may know what a good conscience is and what an evil one is. For my friend, Brother Alcher, has come to me from the road of inquiry, seeking what a good conscience is, and I have nothing to set before [Col. 1089C] him.

Therefore, having received these things from my friend, I now lay them up and begin to treat of conscience. Teaching about everything to be discussed becomes clearer for apprehension and easier for retention if, by a concise connection, the whole matter to be treated—or its parts severally—is placed at once before the eyes, with distinction as manifest as it is definite in definition. This method of proceeding in the composition of treatises, handed down by teachers, some employ more nobly according to the capacity of their fine intellect; others, more obscurely, because of slowness of understanding and little exercise in writing, have committed their subject matter to the understanding of later generations through interpretation in their own style. Since I have attained neither of these alternatives, [Col. 1089D] I myself marvel at my presumption—indeed, my rashness—in undertaking to arrange letters without learning, and in now assuming the office of a treatise-writer when I am not equal even to the service of a reader. Yet this is the one thing by which I excuse myself before myself and answer others’ rebuke: I devoted myself to this work not from my own importunity but at the prompting of brotherly charity; and I do not know whether usefully, but I do know that humbly, I accepted the burden imposed by a good and holy man most dear to me.

## What conscience is, and whence it is named

I have been asked, therefore, to treat of conscience, and to say not what kind I have but what kind I ought to have. For not every conscience is of one kind, so that all who have conscience should believe themselves to possess the same [Col. 1090A] innocence. We must therefore explain what conscience is and whence it is named; then, insofar as it is granted to recall from hidden things or understand from the Scriptures, I shall set forth, as it were, certain parts—or rather species—of consciences, and, as grace grants, bring the matter to completion.

But first let our reader be warned not to seek learning in these pages, but conscience. Let him have elsewhere an abundance of reading, whether divine learning among our own writers or prophetic learning among domestic investigators of nature, for the cultivation of knowledge; let him have this little parchment for investigating and forming consciences. What, then, conscience is, let us consider not by a definition but by a certain description. Conscience is knowledge of oneself, either drawing from good or dissenting from evil. What is meant by “knowledge of oneself” becomes clearer if we inquire into the etymology of the name.

The etymology of this name is as follows: *conscientia* is knowledge of the heart. Perhaps, according to this etymology, conscience appears to be nothing other than knowledge. For knowledge of the heart is either that which is in the heart for grasping the external prophetic discipline, or that which remains better in the heart by understanding the heart and is more profitably consecrated there. In both senses it is called knowledge of the heart, but in only one sense conscience. For knowledge of the heart is understood in two ways: either that by which it knows itself in itself and through itself, or that by which it knows, from itself, other things besides itself. The heart knows both itself by its own knowledge and many other things. [Col. 1090C] When it knows itself, it is called conscience; when it knows things besides itself, it is called knowledge.

Thus, of that wisdom which is in the heart, it is said: “God gave wisdom in the heart of Bezalel for doing every work, whether in gold or silver,” etc. Likewise it is said of one person that he is “wise in heart and mighty in strength” (Job 9:4). Again, of that knowledge which is possessed in relation to oneself, not to other things, it is written: “Would that God would grant me to speak these things according to sound judgment” (Wis. 7:15). Likewise: “The mouth of the righteous will meditate wisdom, and his tongue will speak judgment” (Ps. 36:28). Many, then, seek knowledge; few seek conscience. And if conscience were perhaps sought with as much labor and concern as vain and secular knowledge undoubtedly is, it would be both more truly attained and more fruitfully retained. For if a person penetrated not far from himself, investigating himself within himself under himself as teacher, with grace, what wonder if he found it? Indeed, it would be a wonder if he could find in himself anything other than himself—unless, perhaps, the image of God, inclined toward its own soul by operative grace, occupied him. And if this were so, what would it be? For what is the creating image in the created image, except wisdom in the soul, glory in conscience, sanctification in the ark? Then the soul understands itself; then conscience is illumined; then the heart’s knowledge is fulfilled; then the created image receives itself in God and God in itself by a mutual turning.

For this restoration of our soul and the Word of God, grace performs the part of a certain minister of God, so that God may be willing to be poured into us. Purity [Col. 1091A] prepares the soul for receiving him, lest the majesty of the Word reject the bosom of the heart. Grace leads God to our lodging; purity busies itself with faithful service. Grace pours cups for the guest already received; purity welcomes him as he comes. These are what gladden the righteous soul; these are what present a conscience pleasing to God, venerable to angels and human beings, peaceful and quiet to itself.

These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands shining before the Lord. There are, indeed, two olive trees: one by which that sublime eye of majesty is bent in compassion toward the pitiable sickness of our dunghill; the other by which the festering scars of our inward parts are sprinkled and the troubled eye of our face is anointed for healing. There are likewise two lampstands: one by which the will of the divine good pleasure is suggested to our minds; the other by which the majesty of recompense is already offered to the gaze of our hope. A conscience made bright in this way by two olive trees and two lampstands is good, rich, and bright before God and human beings: good in simplicity, rich in brightness, bright in chastity.

## A description of conscience under the image of a certain woman
Of whose bearing, that I may give you an example—not under the error of idolatry, but under the form of a clearer teaching—imagine in your mind something that may pierce the understanding toward the devotion of piety, and from a visible example kindle the soul to invisible contemplation. Set, therefore, a table laden with the variety and abundance of diverse dishes [Col. 1091C]. Place the King, crowned in his diadem and distinguished by every triumphal exaltation, seated at the head and in the foremost place; let the hands of those standing by and serving be most assiduous, both for food and drink. Let there be vessels of gold and silver for every use; let there also be cups seasoned with honey; and let whatever is set forth be obedient at a nod to palate and throat. Let harp, lyre, and psaltery refresh the hearing of the guests with their melodies. Let there be royal garments, measured movements of young men and maidens, honourable manners, and in the whole household the strictest rule of equity, ordering everything exactly, down to the slightest movement. Here and there, tapestries or hangings woven in embroidered or figured work. A flowered bed [Col. 1091D], ceilings of cypress. What more need be said? Let everything be arranged in the most orderly disposition, so that nothing is lacking for splendour or superfluous unto weariness.

Yet meanwhile let a place, more spacious and beautiful than the rest, stand vacant, prepared especially for the queen and mistress of the household. Perhaps, detained by business at an inn, that Queen delays her coming to the King’s solemn feast. Meanwhile let the faces and sighs of all desire the filling of that seat. At last let the woman come, whose beauty sun and moon admire; and, being seated, let her close the doors, and let the wedding-feast of those reclining be fulfilled. Finally, let the mystical chests be sought out and opened, let them proclaim her name in the hall, and let this lady be called Conscience. But when Conscience asks for the seat prepared from of old [Col. 1092A] and takes her place, the Bridegroom’s voice is heard, satisfying the whole court concerning the bride: “My dove is one,” he says, “she is one to her mother, chosen for her who bore her” (Song of Songs 6:8). Certainly Conscience is one because of the unity of faith and the unchangeableness of purpose; she is a dove because of the gentleness of simplicity; she is one to her mother because of the perfection of charity; she is chosen for her mother because of the grace and beauty of charity.

## On the Form of Conscience

Reading figuratively the character of this beauty in her very appearance, I again gird her qualities with such a description, distinguishing all her members by the variety of colours of the virtues. She is of tall stature because of the long-suffering of perseverance; she has emerald eyes because of the perpetual freshness of chastity; a nose like the tower of Lebanon that looks toward Damascus, because of prudent discernment of attacking temptations; cheeks somewhat ruddy because of compassion for a brother’s oppression; lips overflowing with honeycomb and honey, because of the sweetness of mystical speech; rounded hands, because of the perfect practice of obedience; a strong breast, because of watchful resistance to the assaults of demons; shoes of bronze and iron, for crushing the heads of dragons; a golden crown about the loins, for restraining the incentives of lust. She is clothed in garments whose scent and fragrance breathe myrrh of mortification, a drop of humility, and cassia of good repute.

But, to return [Col. 1092C] to the little wings of divine fear and the final judgment, let us see how securely such a conscience comes to judgment in her own form and beauty: neither fearing want because of her abundant sufficiency of virtues, nor sentence because of the bond of marriage, nor shame or confusion because of the adornment or fragrance of her garments.

## On the Security of Conscience

When winter, the cruel necessity that prematurely seizes the doors, comes—a winter in which it will be impossible either to plough for merit or to reap for reward not yet obtained, and which will endure through a long, indeed an eternal, course—it will refuse the begging of aid from any intercession. For the door of mercy, now open [Col. 1092D] and even widening itself until the final time of judgment, will be shut; the opportunity of escape and every possibility of self-defence will also be shut. Conscience alone will comfort the misery of the poor, if it has something with which to fill its hand; it alone will be able to afford refuge; it alone will offer a barrier against trembling fear and the face of majesty.

Therefore, when the fire of God’s vengeance and wrath burns up heaven and earth and wholly carries them from this state into another form and appearance, a human being caught up in the clouds, if he brings with him a pure and whole conscience, will not fear the crashing of thunders, be stupefied by flashes of lightning, be driven to flight by angelic trumpets, or be struck by the radiance of the life-giving Cross that stands there, or by the majesty [Col. 1093A] of the horned and many-eyed Lamb seated in judgment. “The lion has roared: who will not fear?” Surely, the one who has entered the enclosed cave of conscience. Leviathan, or Satan, will be loosed: who can escape? Beyond doubt, the one who has sufficiently armed the tower of conscience. “Woe, woe” will be heard on every side: and who will glory in security? Indeed, the one who thought of war while at peace, and who wept while others laughed.

Everyone who drank the luxury of the world from the Babylonian or golden cup down to the dregs of death will be like a drunken man vomiting. And who will drink the wine of sobriety and gladness with sound head and stomach? Certainly, the one who, repressing the motions of impurity, made his soul and conscience chaste. “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity” (Luke 13:27) will be cried aloud with a mighty shout [Col. 1093B]: and who will ascend to God, so that his face may be enlightened? Surely, the one who has not defiled his garments, or who at least has washed them in the blood of the Lamb through true confession and complete contrition of heart.

There will be no bread and water: and who will live without bread and water? Without doubt, the one whose life is a clean and pure conscience. For a good conscience has full storehouses, as it is written: “Nothing is lacking to those who fear God.” For conscience that fears God keeps within itself every instrument of blessedness.

It has a walk of truth; it has a meadow or garden of delight; it has a well of the deep heart; it has a place where it may sleep and rest in unity; it has the table of the altar; it has the temple of chastity; it has the hearth or furnace of charity; it has the bath [Col. 1093C] of confession; it has the garments of satisfaction; it has the robe of immortality; it has the shoes of imitation of God; it has the ring of eternity. What more shall I say? It has the crescent ornament, necklace, head-bands, anklets, turbans, chains, and many things like these, whose interpretations are the best instructions in good conduct. Their perfection is fullness: so that, just as a revolving wheel in a chariot is swiftly and forcefully borne wherever the gaze of the presiding charioteer directs it by four horses, so may the Lord, presiding and governing in justice, direct the wheel of the soul according to his will by the four horses of the principal virtues—prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance.

Certainly, conscience [Col. 1093D], whose reins are drawn at the front by prudence, on the right by justice, on the left by fortitude, and behind by temperance, is lifted to heaven in harmonious rather than discordant motion, crying and saying: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Finally, it is too little for a good conscience merely to be in heaven unless it itself becomes heaven.

## How Conscience Is Made Heaven by the Lord’s Word and the Spirit of His Mouth

For it is made heaven by the indwelling Spirit of him who made heaven and earth and dwells in the heavens: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made, and by the spirit of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 32:6). Truly these [Col. 1094A] three—namely, the Word, the Lord, and the Spirit of his mouth—create, form, and adorn the heaven of conscience: the Lord creates, the Word forms, the Spirit adorns. Yet the Trinity works these things together; but, according to our different merits, they are individually distinguished by us within us. “For whatever the Father does …”

> [Note: Something is missing at Col. 1093D.]

But behold: having marked the mystery of the Trinity, let us direct our attention to the trinity, or threefold disposition, of conscience. The Lord creates conscience by his fear; the Word of the Lord strengthens it by wisdom’s instruction; the Spirit of his mouth adorns it by the variety of gifts. Notice here, as it were, three persons distinguished by their modes of regard: the servant who fears, the master who teaches, and the friend who loves and communicates everything to his friend. The lord employs the servant [Col. 1094B], the master employs speech, the friend employs honour and gift; the servant goes before the lord, wisdom sends forth the word, the friend sends a gift beforehand. Without a servant there is no lord; without speech, no master; without a gift, no friend. In accordance with the majesty of the lord is the authority of the servant; in accordance with the wisdom of the master is the teaching of the word; in accordance with the love of the friend is the worth of the gift. If the lord is great, let the servant be faithful; if the master wise, let the words of his mouth be good; if the friend loving, let his gifts be beautiful, good, and useful. Let the servant gain all his profit for his lord; let “not yet” [nondum, sic] of teaching secure honour for the master and benefit for the disciple; let the gift bestowed render a return to the friend.

## That Fear Orders Conscience

Conscience begins from fear, is led onward and guided by subjection, and is perfected and completed in love. Unless conscience fears, it attempts or commits every crime; unless it is subjected to the words of truth, it evaporates into the wind of pride and falsehood; unless it loves what ought to be loved, it is always spurred on and halted around its purpose. Fear lays the foundation; humble subjection builds the walls; sublime love adds the roof. Or rather, fear constructs the framework of this building, subjection plasters it, and love paints it. This construction pertains to the hewing, smoothing, and shaping of the material of thoughts according to the measure and form of justice. For from the forest of our impulses and imaginings there must be selected, as good material, timbers fit and suitable for the structure [Col. 1094D] of Solomon’s temple—timbers whose nature receives the plane of discipline through the knowledge of rebukes.

Fear approaches all these things as a good carpenter, so that, receiving from the heart, as from a forest, the material of thoughts, it may arrange it: now cutting off what is superfluous, now straightening what is crooked, now gathering unequal things into the measured condition of equity, and making beams, columns, ceilings, and the rest of the structure level and joined together. Finally, with the nails or spikes of divine fear the Prophet desires the construction of his edifice to be fastened, when he says: “Pierce my flesh with your fear, for I have feared your judgments” (Ps. 118:120). So much concerning the construction wrought by fear, which is, as was said above, a kind of creation of conscience.

## On the Plastering of Conscience through Observance of the Commandments

Now concerning the plastering, or tempering, of God’s commandments, of which the Psalm says: “From your commandments I have gained understanding” (ibid., 104). For when we run from fear to the commandments, we lay plaster over the underlying construction. The fulfilment of the commandments both softens the harshness of fear that exasperates the soul, brings the little valleys of imperfection, through the completion of hope, to the level of unity and unanimity, and places between them stronger bonds, drawing stones together without the striking of a hammer. Hence, as is written, neither hammer nor axe was heard [Col. 1095B] in Solomon’s temple. Finally, it strengthens things that were about to collapse—or rather, which, according to the Apocalypse, were about to die. For whatever fear has proposed without love and the observance of the commandments is unstable. Therefore Scripture says: “Fear God and keep his commandments” (Eccl. 12:13).

Behold: perhaps someone, shaken by fear of his evils, returns to his heart, sets before himself the guilt and punishment of his offences, counts the stones of torments, and begins from these to build walls of penitence and conversion, so that he may at least place between himself and the infernal city an iron pan, or a wall of bronze or brick.

For from baked bricks—that is, corrected conduct—or from stones—that is, former evils—a person builds a wall [Col. 1095C] who, turned back to himself, reforms old offences into the bettering of a new life. He places an iron pan between himself and the city who opposes firm, stable, and hard penitence to the consuming coals of eternal torments. But who is sufficient for these things? Whose strength is the strength of stones, whose flesh is bronze? In labour and trouble, in many vigils, in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness, in the prison of the cloister, in the struggle of flesh and spirit—who does not fall, who does not fail, unless the Spirit helps our weakness, unless strength puts its hand beneath us?

Therefore the Lord says: “While you are on the way with your adversary, make peace, lest perhaps he hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over [Col. 1095D] to the torturer” (Luke 12:58). On the way of labour and pilgrimage, the word or fear of the Lord opposes our desires. We make peace with it if we fulfil the law of the commandments. For there is no reason to fear the judge if you fear the law. According to the law, the judge punishes transgressors of laws, not observers of them. For keeping the law is a soothing of the judge. Thus whoever keeps the commandments diminishes—indeed, softens—fears, and strengthens the powers of loving and restraining oneself. This is enough concerning the plastering of the word through the tempering of subjection. What follows is the painting of love.

## On the Painting of Charity in Conscience

The living and true colours of charity do not depict, under the seal of the image of God, images of birds, quadrupeds, or sacred—indeed, fanatical—figures [Col. 1096A]. Rather, by the renewing kind of painting they fashion in the soul, through the sinews and veins of the principal virtues, the conformity of adoption as children and of grace. For love paints not with the iron stylus of fear upon the adamantine nail of the stubborn heart, but with a flying brush, toward the charity of Christ surpassing knowledge. How beautiful and lovely are the forms that love knows how to paint!

In its statue, charity paints a spherical and rounded head, yet of gold, because it makes the intention pure and perfect. It adds dove-like looks through innocence; rounded hands through almsgiving; an open and curved nose through the moderation of discernment; full breasts through abundance of grace; straight feet through the walk [Col. 1096B] of mercy; the whole body full of eyes through vigilant carefulness.

It paints the triune and one God in the head; it paints suffering Jesus in the eyes; it paints the book of the Gospel in the ears; it paints scourges on the back; a lance in the side; the whole body stretched out so that the bones could be numbered; it paints vinegar in the drink and gall in the taste; it paints the crown of thorns on the head; it paints the face veiled; it paints him struck with slaps; it paints him dead; it paints him appearing and conversing with Mary Magdalene in the garden; it paints him eating with the apostles; it paints him ascending to heaven; it paints him seated and reigning at the right hand of the Father; it paints him openly coming to judgment with great power and majesty—terrible to those on the left, lovable to those on the right.

[Col. 1096C] Behold the carving; behold the painting of charity. But what are, and whence come, the colours by which the immaterial image of the soul is painted so sublimely? Consider whence the colours come and how great they are, and you will receive the conformed images more affectionately.

It has vermilion or red in the blood; black in the Passion or death; green in the resurrection and ascension; earth-colour in mortal life; purple in the vexation of continual struggle, whether with human beings or with evil spirits. These are the colours. But where are the little vessels—or rather, where are the horns—in which these colours are kept? What horns of justice contain the colours, except the horns of the righteous, except just hearts? Yet the true horn in which these things are best stored is that little horn of humility of which Daniel speaks, which became great toward the south, toward the east, and toward strength. Truly humble is the conscience which, like a horn, proceeds indeed from flesh, but surpasses flesh in strength, hardness, and a certain prominence of length [Col. 1096D]. It becomes great toward the south when it conquers the harmful heat of lust; toward the east, when it conquers empty glory; toward strength, when it conquers every diabolical temptation.

The power of conscience appeared so greatly in the face of Moses that he was said to be horned, because the overflowing holiness of the lawgiver dazzled the eyes of the foolish. Yet it must be understood that the surge of burning grace, like new wine, is held within the holy breasts by the weight of flesh, if the law with grace ascends the mountain of the mind and fills all the tablets with the inscription of the commandments. For just as an unstable letter or picture is entrusted for the instruction of minds or the delight [Col. 1097A] of eyes, so in the heart the memory of heavenly goods is retained, either for the merit of glory or for the defence of conscience itself. “The merit of glory repents,” etc. [The reading appears corrupt or incomplete.]

[Col. 1097]

# PETER OF CELLE’S TREATISE ON CLOISTRAL DISCIPLINE, ADDRESSED TO HENRY I, COUNT OF CHAMPAGNE

## Letter

To his lord and friend HENRY, illustrious man: Brother PETER, humble abbot of Saint-Remi, greeting and every prosperity.

Unless liberty of mind had been made foolish through its own choice and its associated partnership with the muddy body, it would by no means have needed the penal discipline that bends, levels, and binds. It bends what is upright, levels what is rough, and binds what is wanton. It bends what is untamed, levels inequalities, and binds what is unrestrained. It bends the mind, levels the body, and binds both. It bends by humility, levels by equity, and binds by religion. It bends by conversion, levels by confession, and binds by profession. It bends the branch into the vine, levels the tablets of the heart to receive the commandments of life, and binds its colt to the vineyard—that is, the mind to grace. Finally, it bends the stiff-necked bull of the world, levels the hunchbacked camel, and binds the buffalo or wild ass.

But after both mind and body had been deprived, each in its natural kind, of their natural goodness, the Creator’s mercy began to furnish ways by which it might repair the damage of such great rashness. And because the cause of so great a sickness was found to be the privilege of inborn freedom, by a healing art it bound together, through regular discipline, the wings of corrupted freedom and humbled the neck of rash presumption. What God ordained by a general judgment for the whole human race, I have experienced as done to myself by his most gracious mercy. For I was wandering about here and there, setting aside the maturity proper to our order; and I was neglecting the secular business and earthly occupations that, like thieves and robbers, were carrying away from me almost every furnishing of religious life. But behold: the hand of God sent the daughters of his quiver into my reins, and a most severe gout froze my kidneys and compelled me to remain at home.

Feeling discipline, therefore, I began to think about discipline, and to write down my thoughts. As patiently as I endured discipline, so willingly and diligently—and, if not elegantly—I wrote about discipline. Saint Augustine wrote as Augustine and as a bishop concerning Christian discipline; I have written as an abbot and monk concerning cloistral discipline. He, a most learned giant, bears the mountains of stags and the minds of the humble upon his shoulders; I, a very slight ant, drag not whole grains but broken ones to the contemptible little hut of my treatise, and prepare some small provision for the coming famine and winter.

Let our little work, then, *On Cloistral Discipline*, unadorned either in style or title, not enter the splendid palaces of ingenious philosophy, but appear with a humble countenance. With what face, therefore, most noble prince—indeed, most keen in the liveliness of your intellectual subtlety—do I send you for reading a shabby and ragged treatise? Yet, snared by the words of my own mouth, I would rather be accused of ignorant speech than of lying speech. Let a pious and intelligent mind therefore read it, attending not to the form of the words but to the strength of the meanings. For as the soul is greater than bodily beauty, so in writing one should seek rather the spirit that gives life than the letter that puffs up; fruit pleases more in a tree than leaves. Both, however, are good if both are present; but beautiful leaves without fruit are more an enticement for the eyes than a support for the stomach.

The Apostle condemns the appearance of piety where the power of charity is absent (1 Cor. 13). Likewise the Lord, coming to the fig tree that had no fruit but nevertheless had leaves, cursed it and condemned it for ever. I entreat your nobility that in this reading you attend not to what we are, but to what we ought to be; nor let it escape your wisdom that the lamp of our order in Israel is utterly extinguished, but that Isaac’s eyes have grown dim because he has become old. When Elijah complained against Ahab and Jezebel, saying, “Lord, they have dug down your altars, killed your prophets, and I alone remain; and they seek my life” (3 Kings 19:10), he was answered: “I have reserved for myself seven thousand men who have not bent their knees before Baal” (ibid., 18).

Thus certainly, thus, dearest lord and friend: even though the great regular virtue of the ancient Fathers has grown weak in our times, it has not breathed its last; though it has departed, it has not died; though it has grown cold, it has not perished. Those who are as nothing among men, often like a lamp held in contempt, are of greater worth before the Lord than those who seem to be something. I do not excuse the wicked, but proclaim the good. I set aside prejudice because I await God’s judgment. It is ours to honour the name of God not only in the holy but also in the perverse. For whatever person, even the meanest, bears [Col. 1099] your seal, must be received and honoured on the authority of your name—not because that person is worthy, but because you are worthy. Thus one who is worthy often makes the unworthy worthy: unworthy properly speaking, worthy improperly speaking; unworthy in himself, worthy through the performance of an office.

I do not want you to spare me in anything in which I have erred. I ask also that you not read with distaste; but, as soon as it begins to burden your mind, cast it from your hand; if it pleases you, take it up again later; if it displeases you, condemn it, shut up in everlasting darkness. Poor yet glorious people, truly enduring poverty while vainly desiring glory, are accustomed, in order to conceal poverty and obtain glory, to cover the edges of their cloaks with either costly or beautiful furs—not for usefulness, but to answer the curiosity of beholders. So I myself, because our poverty left this work lacking in the value of thought and the beauty of words, have set your name as a title before it and most becomingly adorned its entrance, so that a reader, expecting only the best to be offered by you, may run to read it through—not because of the flavour of a seasoned cup, but because of the splendour of the title of so great a prince.

## Preface

[Col. 1099]

[Col. 1099A] It belongs either to the skilled or to the experienced to judge a known matter; for the unskilled and inexperienced to treat an unknown matter is rather to presume than to define. If I confess myself skilled or experienced in cloistral discipline, I lie. I do not deny that I have seen regular and religious men; though I have at times been in their company, I did not retain their virtue. How, then, do you ask to hear from me about cloistral discipline, when for nearly thirty years I have scarcely tasted it with the tip of my lip? Nevertheless, because “charity believes all things” (1 Cor. 13:7), and I know that you ask this from devotion, not from testing, setting aside the difficulty of refusal I dare to write what I cannot practise. Nor am I greatly ashamed if in this little work you recognize me as the sort of person you have known from your childhood—unless perhaps because our age, now drawing toward evening [Col. 1099B], has little of noon and more of evening.

Your often-repeated request, and the sciatic gout which for a very long time held my kidneys under harsh discipline, have made me prolix in this treatise *On Cloistral Discipline*. In this little work, like a preparation made from customary and familiar herbs growing in our own gardens rather than from precious spices of distant lands, I have added more honey of the flock than Jerome’s scammony, fearing that the discovery might be rejected if the scammony bit, and that the usefulness of the work might be despised as much because of the technique as because of its maker. As recompense for this labour I ask this reward from you: read it carefully, boldly remove whatever displeases you in it, [Col. 1099C] and correct what needs correction.

I render with interest a debt not promised by me to you, but often demanded by you from me. The ground of obligation is enough for me where a friend’s desire to ask has come first; I add interest because a long delay intervened in payment. Give thanks to God, who gave the opportunity without which I would not yet have been released from that debt. What opportunity? Pain in my kidneys, which long bound me under harsh discipline and denied me the power of wandering here and there. Therefore I too rejoice in my infirmity and say: Let us suffer evils, that we may do good; indeed, let us suffer evils, lest we do evil. This belongs to our cloistral discipline: to suffer and not to do evil, but rather to return good for evil.

He taught this who discovered every way of discipline and taught it to Jacob his servant and Israel his beloved. He suffered evils from evil men and on account of evils, but rendered good for evils and made good persons out of evil ones. Do not be surprised, dearest friend, if you find my style limping, because along with the whole body the hand also limps. A wavering hand does not keep straight lines; and what wonder if a lame man produces something lame? It would be more wonderful if what is crooked produced what is straight. But you, since you think rightly and walk rightly, excuse lame-footed Ishbosheth before David, and correct or cut away every halting expression [Col. 1100B]: “It is better to enter into life with one foot than, having two feet, to be cast into Gehenna” (Matt. 18:9).

Now the Gehenna of readers is envy. Envy rightly collapses where the subject matter escapes the lips of its biters through succinct truth, clear construction, and armed reasoning; or where it is so extinguished by dullness, so contemptible in form, so thin in the substance of its words, so bloodless in the slenderness of its meaning, that envy’s tooth has nowhere to bite. I do not regard my little works as worthy of public view; “my secret is mine, my secret is mine” (Isa. 24:16). Let simple devotion, not ornate eloquence, read my writings—not for applause but for lamentation. For my dove mourns in her clefts; [Col. 1100C] the raven croaks among corpses and carrion. The raven cries “tomorrow, tomorrow,” either claiming for itself what is fat, as certain people are read to have said at the Lord’s Passion, “Behold, this man calls Elijah” (Mark 15:35), when the Lord said, “Eli, Eli” (Matt. 27:47); or promising itself long days and years; or pledging a futile repentance, “tomorrow, tomorrow”—that is, never. As the saying goes: today with payment, tomorrow without payment. I too ask today and tomorrow for the price of prayers and intercessions for this work.

## Second Preface

[Col. 1101]

[Col. 1101A] Richard, dearest friend of discipline, as though I had experienced it, you repeatedly trouble an old beginner, asking me to gather for you from it in some writing what I think. If not for friendship, then at least because of the importunity of the friend in the Gospel, I cannot fail to rise from the bed in which, with the door shut, I was lying down with the children of my other senses, and give—not as much as your affection demands, but as much as my fist can hold. I fear that a hungry person may come and, finding not fruit but only leaves on the fig tree, [Col. 1102A] curse the false hope or promise. Again, if a nauseated person comes who curiously picks apart every detail and scornfully despises it, I expect vomiting rather than tasting. But because “charity believes all things” (1 Cor. 13:7), and no one is compelled to accept my gift, I shall gather for you alone—who, from great love even for the marrow, gnaw our tasteless bark—whatever may occur by God’s will, and hand it to mother Rebecca for preparing food from it.

# On Cloistral Discipline

[Col. 1101]

## Chapter I. On the Authors of Disciplines

[Col. 1101B]

Accordingly, turning over in the repositories of authoritative Scripture the authors of this discipline, I find as the chief and greatest: Moses in the wilderness, Jesus in the world, and Paul in the office entrusted to him of teaching the Gentile people. Two streams issuing from them likewise enclosed monks and regular canons in the cloister, as deer and gazelles in an enclosed park, so to speak: Benedict and Augustine.

In Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy, retain the cloistral discipline of the Lord’s chosen people in the law and in the commandments which, under a bare meaning, shape conduct. But tear away the ceremonial matters as things clothed in Esau’s very good garments, and eat the spiritual kernel hidden within. Certainly that discipline was most severe; if ours is compared with it, ours is found more tolerable. So unbearable indeed was it that not merely any weak or common person, but not even every righteous and holy person, could fulfil the commandments of the law. Hence Peter says: “Why do you try to impose upon us a yoke which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear?” (Acts 15:10).

But our discipline is sufficiently tolerable, as it is said in the Epistle of John: “This is charity: that we keep his commandments; and his commandments are not burdensome” (1 John 5:3). What is our discipline, then, except to live according to God’s commandments? Jesus, the great and good teacher, whose chair is in heaven and whose school is in the world, described in the Gospel, as though in a book of antidotes, the things that he did and taught [Col. 1101D]; and he taught cloistral discipline to his twelve cloistered apostles together with the seventy-two disciples. No one left that evangelical cloister except the one who was the son of perdition, or those who said, “This saying is hard,” and went back and no longer walked with him (John 6:61).

## Chapter II. On Apostolic Discipline

Observe apostolic discipline, worthy of reverence everywhere and in all things [Col. 1102B], especially as Peter indicated to John, who reclined at supper upon the Lord’s breast, that he should ask who would betray him. So great was their reverence toward the teacher, so great their obedience, so great their subjection, so great their brotherly love for one another, that not even the breath of a whisper passed among them—except perhaps when contention arose among them as to which of them seemed the greater, or when they were indignant at the two who sought to sit at the right and left.

Yet whatever human frailty committed in earthen vessels, not yet sufficiently fired by the fire of the Holy Spirit, the hand of the potter immediately repaired and made firm. At one time he rebuked them, saying: “Men of little faith, why are you troubled?” (Matt. 8:26). At another he comforted them: “Take courage,” he said, “I have overcome [Col. 1102C] the world” (John 16:33); and, “Behold, I am with you until the end of the age” (Matt. 27:20). At one time he spoke in parables, at another without parables; at one time he withdrew, spending the night in prayer; at another he concealed himself while walking upon the sea, and they thought him a phantom; at another he returned to his community and conversed with them in all familiarity. At one time, because of excessive hunger, they plucked ears of grain after him and ate; at another they gathered twelve baskets of fragments left over from the five loaves. They possessed nothing as their own, who said: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. 19:27). They never wished to be separated from him when he said, “I am going into Judaea”; and Thomas said to the disciples: “Let us also go, and die [Col. 1102D] with him” (John 11:14).

What shall I say of these monks, namely the Apostles? I compare them with angelic spirits—except that, still not stripped of mortality, they ministered to Him who was made a little lower than the angels (Heb. 2:9). But when He, crowned by the Father with glory and honour above every principality and power, shall sit upon the throne of His majesty, upon the throne of greatness, these too shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel [Col. 1103A] (Matt. 19), perhaps angels also, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Do we not judge angels also?” (1 Cor. 6:3). This hope is laid up in the bosom of cloistered religious, because the reward has been promised for a similar discipline—not by Paul, but by that same Jesus Christ.

Peter succeeded to the apostleship of the circumcision, and Paul among the Gentiles, as Paul himself says: “He who worked through Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision worked through me also among the Gentiles” (Gal. 2:8). The Apostle teaches in the rule—that is, in his Epistle: “Those who use in this manner [should be] as though they did not use” (1 Cor. 7:31). And: “Having nothing, and possessing all things” (2 Cor. 6:10). And: “Obey your superiors and be subject to them” (Heb. 13:17). And: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. 6:2). And: “Let no one seek what is useful to himself, but what is useful to another” (1 Cor. 10:[Col. 1103B] 24). And: “Outdoing one another in honour” (Rom. 12:10). And: “Let no shameful speech proceed from your mouth; nor let obscenity or foolish talk even be named among you” (Eph. 4:29).

The entire apostolic book blossoms with flowers of this kind; it governs a vast and spacious cloister, extending its rod in hand, as it were, from Jerusalem to Illyricum, as he writes to some: “What do you desire? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in a spirit of gentleness?” (1 Cor. 4:21). He also delivers certain persons to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme. Here he rejoices with those who rejoice in the guest-house; here he weeps with those who weep in the oratory; here he is weak with the weak in the infirmary; here he burns with those who are scandalized in the chapter-house; here, in the novices’ cell, he speaks to his novices: “My little children, whom I begot through the Gospel, and [Col. 1103C] for whom I am again in labour until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4:19). Here, in the refectory, he chastises his body, lest, after preaching to others, he himself should become rejected (1 Cor. 9:27). Here, finally, always and everywhere, he is found “in watchings and fastings, in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness; in blows beyond measure, in deaths often” (2 Cor. 6:5; 11:27).

Here he says to those responsible for hospitality: “Be hospitable to one another without murmuring” (1 Pet. 4:9). To those who are in the oratory: “I will sing with the spirit among the brethren; I will sing also with the mind; I will pray with the spirit; I will pray with the mind” (1 Cor. 14:15). To those in the infirmary: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. 6:2); “Receive the weak in faith” (Rom. 14:1). But to one sitting in chapter: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke” (2 Tim. 4:2). To those in the refectory: “Do not be drunk with wine, in which is excess” [Col. 1103D] (Eph. 5:18). To the almoners: “He who sows sparingly shall also reap sparingly; and he who sows in blessings shall also reap eternal life” (2 Cor. 9:6). Finally, he cries out to all cloistered religious: “Watch; stand firm in the faith; act manfully, and be strengthened” (1 Cor. 16:13). In this manner, whatever belongs to rule, whatever can be formed by uprightness and faith, whatever in the footsteps of Jesus is fit for imitation, is not foreign to Paul. Yet one clause sums up the whole cloistered discipline: “Let all your things,” he says, “be done in charity” (ibid.).

Now let us turn our pen to our particular teachers, blessed Benedict and Saint Augustine: the one an abbot and monk, the other a bishop and canon; each holy, each an outstanding teacher and guide of the Lord’s flock [Col. 1104A]. In some respects our cloistered discipline and yours agree; in some they differ. For some things are, as it were, the substance of religion, while others are accidental.

That without which religion is not religion is substantial to religion. An accident is what is present or absent according to place, time, cause, person, and other circumstances, without corruption of religion. These matters are left to the discretion of the administrator, so far as, peace and unity being preserved, they may be strengthened or relaxed. Yet they should not be strengthened too much, lest frailty be broken; nor relaxed too much, lest the rule be injured.

The substantive elements of religion are silence, concerning which it is said: “Let every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak and slow to anger” (Jas. 1:19); likewise reading, concerning which it is said: “Until I come, attend to reading” (1 Tim. 4:13); likewise confession of sin, concerning which it is said: “Confess to the Lord, for He is good” (Ps. 117:1); and all things are washed in confession, whence: “I said, ‘I will confess,’ and You forgave the impiety of my sin” (Ps. 31:5); likewise prayer, concerning which it is said: “If you ask the Father anything in my name, He will give it to you” (John 16:23); likewise meditation on death, concerning which it is said: “My son, remember your last things, and you shall never sin” (Ecclus. 7:40). But we shall deal with these more fully below.

## Chapter III. A Comparison between Jewish and Our Cloistered Discipline

[Col. 1104C] Just as the legal commandments written upon two tablets contain Jewish discipline, so every regular religious, whether monk or canon, ought to live “between the lots” (Ps. 67:14): that is, between the rule of the institution and the good custom handed down by the elders. In the one, dispensation is permitted; in the other, one is bound. For a judge does not judge the law, but judges according to the law. Custom and usage, moreover, as they are introduced by the will of those who use them, so they are changed by a contrary will. If in these matters anything needs to be altered, corrected, or supplemented by necessity, a dispensational alteration is not altogether forbidden. Thus, by these as by most powerful bonds, cloistered life is so constrained that neither hands nor feet may move beyond what is permitted.

[Col. 1104D] Profession, therefore, according to the rule and the custom of the place, restrains the bound person in its fetters; laying the sweet yoke and light burden of Jesus Christ upon the shoulders of one renouncing the world, it binds the she-ass and colt before the manger and at the cradle of Emmanuel, upon which Jesus sits and follows the hour of glorification. Yet, as in the head so also in the members, sufferings come first and glories afterward. Jesus is led away because He stood bound before the governor; and because the disciple is not above the master, the true religious should willingly and gladly desire to be bound, as with swaddling-bands, by regular discipline against the desire of the flesh.

The bonds of religion are the ordinances of the rule: for example, silence, fasting, enclosure within the cloister, a gait notable in no respect, brotherly compassion and love, paternal [Col. 1105A] reverence, constant reading and prayer, recollection of past evils; fear of death, of purgatorial fire, and of eternal fire. Hardly can any thought be so wandering or so wanton that it is not restrained by so strong and manifold a cord. Silence buries an idle, superfluous, or disorderly word. Continual fasting puts to sleep the ticklings and incitements kindled among the thorns of evil desires. Cloistered enclosure checks wandering and vain excursions through the streets and lanes of the city of blood. A gait at once modest and measured crushes movements tending to evil suspicion and the glances of those who gaze.

Compassion shuts out inhumanity, love discord; paternal reverence, obstinacy; reading, ignorance; prayer, impurity and malice; meditation, sluggishness and drowsiness. Recollection of past evils brings caution concerning the future, sorrow for the past, and concern for what is to come. Fear of death, like myrrh, kills the dying flies and the worms that do not die, devouring the wretched soul. Purgatorial fire recalls one from venial sins; eternal fire, from grave sins.
