None of these observances is barren in Israel—that Israel who, wrestling with the angel, is called not Jacob but Israel.

Yet all the glory of the king’s daughter lies, not in things outwardly visible, but within, in golden fringes (Ps. 44:14), which, with faces turned inward beyond the veil of the Holy of Holies, look with the cherubim only toward the mercy-seat. The cardinal virtues are golden fringes, because “the hinges of the earth belong to the Lord” (Prov. 8:26). They are also silver columns upon golden bases: saving virtues proceeding from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith. Of these it is said: “I have established its pillars” (Ps. 74:4). These bear Solomon’s temple, when true religion, founded in a good mind, is not ashamed of the Gospel of God amid regular disciplines, but sustains the evangelical commandments as a superimposed structure upon the shoulders of voluntary observance—as Mary kept all these words (Luke 2:19). Let us therefore keep our pen to cloistered discipline, and define, as it were, in one body the form of a beautiful maiden, not of Amalek’s race, but of Abraham’s seed.

## Chapter IV. On the Observances of Cloistered Discipline

[Col. 1105D]

Cloistered discipline is a spectacle to God, angels, and human beings: to God in the marrow of intention; to angels in groanings and sighs; to humans in deeds and words. “Man sees what is before the face, but God sees the heart” (1 Sam. 16:7); an angel sees the intermediate ends of thought and action. Toward God looks charity from a pure heart, good conscience, and unfeigned faith; toward angels, holy simplicity with a good appearance, concerning which it is said: “In your splendour and your beauty, aim prosperously, proceed, and reign” (Ps. 44:5).

“For,” as Augustine says, “a consecrated and pious signification is pleasing to the holy angels. Hence, too, in Exodus [ch. 12:23], while striking the Egyptians, the Lord does not permit the destroyer to enter houses upon whose lintel and both doorposts [Col. 1106A] He sees the blood of the lamb.”

Toward human beings there is love without pretence and conduct without complaint. Thus clothed with such spiritual ornaments, cloistered discipline by no means lifts its neck and walks with outstretched neck; rather, with Rebecca, it covers its face before God’s sight with the veil of modesty and humility.

When it walks, it says: “At every one of my steps I shall declare the Lord” (Job 31:37). Likewise: “I went around and sacrificed in His tabernacle a sacrifice of rejoicing” (Ps. 26:6). For it does not walk about like the impious in a circuit of vanity and curiosity, but with angels ascends Jacob’s ladder in an ecstasy of mind, and descends in contemplation of its own frailty.

When it sits, it considers what it shall say or do before the face of God’s power, on the day of wrath and revelation of God’s just judgment, concerning the throne of majesty and the throne of eternity [Col. 1106B]. If it stands, let it say: “The Lord lives, in whose presence I stand” (2 Kgs. 3:14). And: “In the morning I shall stand before You” (Ps. 5:5). And: “Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem” (Ps. 121:2). And: “The place upon which you stand is holy ground” (Acts 7:33).

If it lifts its head, let it say: “To You I lifted my eyes, You who dwell in the heavens” (Ps. 122:1). And: “I lifted my eyes to the mountains, from which help shall come to me” (Ps. 120:1). And: “As the eyes of servants are upon the hands of their masters, and as the eyes of the maidservant are upon the hands of her mistress” (Ps. 122:2). If it opens mouth and lips, let it say: “My mouth shall speak wisdom” (Ps. 48:4). And: “Set, O Lord, [Col. 1106C] a guard upon my mouth, and a door of restraint about my lips” (Ps. 140:3). And: “Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit” (Ps. 33:14). And: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth” (Eph. 4:29).

If it lends its ears to one speaking, let it not listen to blood; let it not receive reproach against its neighbours (Ps. 14:5). If it eats, before eating let it sigh with Job over necessity inflicted for an apple, and because the stomach importunately hears the voice of the taskmaster, making a confusable and deceptive mixture of necessity and pleasure. For that person is prudent who always interposes the wall of discernment between necessary and superfluous appetite. If it drinks wine, let it not take poison. Hence the Apostle: “Do not be drunk with wine, wherein is excess” (Eph. [Col. 1106D] 5:18); and: “Use a little wine because of your stomach and your frequent infirmities” (1 Tim. 5:23).

If it sleeps, let it say: “I sleep, but my heart watches” (Song 5:2). And: “In peace, in the selfsame place, I shall sleep and rest” (Ps. 4:9); and: “My flesh shall rest in hope” (Ps. 15:9). Rising, therefore, for the vigils, if it prays, let it pray with spirit and mind. Let it enter its chamber and, the door shut, pray to its Father more with heart than with voice, more with faith than with melody.

If it comes to confession, carrying a flask of water beneath the belt of contrition, let it carry the stake of self-reproof with which it may cover the earth of its heart and lay down the burdens of its mind. Blotting out the remnants of Amalek, let it put to death within itself all who work iniquity. Let it pour the blood of the sacrifice of confession beside the base of the altar, so that with the pure blood [Col. 1107A] from Christ’s side its mind may be cleansed; and let it hide the idols of its sins beneath the terebinth of the cross. Let it not flatter itself; let it not turn to the right by praising its good deeds, nor to the left by concealing what is true or inventing an evil that does not exist.

If it accuses a brother’s fault, let it beware lest the iron fall from the handle: that is, lest it rage beyond what is just, lest Joab, holding Amasa’s chin in a flattering gesture, strike him deceptively in the groin. If it rebukes an open fault, let it retain the words of gentleness of the gentle Lamb: “Judas,” says the Lord, “do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22:48). If an hidden fault, let it employ private correction, not public betrayal. If it concerns a powerful person or a prelate, let it observe Nathan before David and Noah’s two sons. Nathan cautiously, indirectly, surrounding the lion with the lamb, placed even a most powerful king in his bonds more by skill than severity. Noah’s sons refused to see their father’s shameful nakedness. “If they covered [him] with their backs turned” [perhaps: “but they covered him with their backs turned”].

If it reads, let it bring a simplicity friendly to the divine law; and while eating grapes in the vineyard, let it not carry them outside, by interpreting otherwise and adding perverse meanings. Let it not sweat over questions tending not to edification but to contention and the overthrow of hearers. Let it read in order to understand; understand in order to do God’s commandments. Let it seek compunction there, not superfluous occupation. Let it entrust the marrow of the law to the marrow of its heart, so that, thus enriched, it may offer marrowy burnt offerings with incense of rams—that is, the sincere truth and true charity of apostles and prophets.

And: “Because [Col. 1107C] a cup is in the hand of the Lord” (Ps. 74:9), namely Holy Scripture; and: “He inclines it from this to that” (ibid.). At one time divine commandments are to be read; at another, the examples of saints, because the word of God lives in the sufferings of martyrs and in the holy conduct of confessors. For what lies as though dead, deformed into the letter upon a dead skin, lives with life when what is read is done.

If necessity brings it out into public, let it return quickly, as from a prison, from a snare, from a furnace, from the lowest hell. David saw iniquity in the city. Dinah saw the women of the land, and Hamor, son of Shechem, perished from it with his father and his people. Thus the belly of cloistered discipline is ivory through chastity, set with sapphires in this most beautiful variety.

[Col. 1107D] I judge that cloistered discipline was instituted for this purpose: that, as is read in Esther (ch. 2), maidens might be selected from every kingdom for the king’s service, delivered into custody, carefully trained, anointed with oil of myrtle and other most precious ointments, and, after prolonged and most exact testing and adornment with a most beautiful countenance, that one who pleased the king might spend the night with the king and enter and leave at his command. So the great King, King of kings, King of ages, calls His predestined ones from all nations, tribes, tongues, peoples, and every nation under heaven—from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and the sea—and gathers them to cloistered discipline. He smooths unformed manners with the file of the rule, drives out the stench of vices with the ointment of pious conduct [Col. 1108A], prepares minds and bodies worthy of royal embraces, and on the day eternally appointed calls them to the bed and bridal chamber of glory and blessed life.

## Chapter V. That the First Transgression Is Repaired through Cloistered Discipline

Human nature, or freedom of choice, exceedingly weakened in its powers and natural goodness by the original transgression, needs, from the moment a human being comes forth from the mother’s womb, to be restored little by little by discipline, as by remedial aids. For by breaking the most firm gates of the first and new commandment, it put the nobility of free choice, bestowed in the beginning, in fetters, and weakened the strength of bodily health. The cause of so great an evil was that it did not keep heavenly discipline [Col. 1108B]; and that discipline was no more difficult to keep than to command.

Pleasure did not draw the appetite; necessity did not press; hunger did not bite; the flavour of the forbidden tree did not surpass the permitted fruits in sweetness, although it is written: “The woman saw that the tree was beautiful to look upon and sweet to taste” (Gen. 3:6). Certainly this “beautiful” and this “sweet” do not exclude the beauty and sweetness of all the trees of paradise; rather, the woman’s mind is shown to have been pierced by the serpent’s suggestion. For a soul assailed—or absorbed—by temptation weighs the desired thing not by judgment but by delight.

Therefore human nature, wholly fashioned by God’s hand all around, might have been preserved in its sweetness through a very easy discipline, burdened by no weight at all; but, grievously wounded, it could not be fully freed by any remedies until the blood of the Lamb [Col. 1108C].

How many remedies of medicines did the great physician attempt to apply to human wounds? Abraham in circumcision is a witness; Moses in the immolation of victims and the offering of other kinds of sacrifices is a witness; all the prophets in rebuke and continual preaching are witnesses. The disease had hardened through excessive age and inadequate treatment; nor did fraternal treatment free the sick person, who awaited the Lord the Saviour, so that the Lord might free the servant and the Saviour the sick. This Saviour sent discipline beforehand as Moses’ rod, but reserved to Himself the rod of His power in the cross; upon it, by shedding His blood, He extinguished the fiery darts [Col. 1108D] of the most wicked devil and healed His infirm one from every fever.

## Chapter VI. That the Cloister Is the Vicar of the Cross

He therefore established the cloister as the vicar of His cross, so that, just as the discipline of our peace was upon the wood of the cross in His body, so we, going outside the camp of worldly things, may bear His reproach to the cloister and, as children, according to the counsel of most wise Solomon, lay hold of His discipline. Solomon says: “My son, lay hold of your father’s discipline, and do not abandon the law of your mother” (Prov. 6:20). And the Psalmist: “Lay hold of discipline, lest the Lord be angry at any time” (Ps. 2:12). And the Apostle: “If you are without discipline, then you are bastards and not sons” [Col. 1109A] (Heb. 12:8). And elsewhere: “All discipline indeed for the present seems not to be joy but sorrow; yet afterward it yields to those exercised by it the most peaceful fruit of righteousness” (ibid., 11).

The cloister stands on the boundary between angelic purity and worldly pollution. If a Hebrew, passing over from the world as from Egypt, brings into the cloister any grains of uprightness borrowed from neighbouring arts called liberal, he may use them once the appearance of theft has been removed. For “all wisdom is from the Lord God” (Ecclus. 1:1). Cloistered discipline does not love carnal wisdom, which is hostile to God, because it tends rather to overthrow simplicity—God’s only one, the daughter of the cloister—than to edification.

Therefore, once the eyebrows of pompous vanity have been shaved away—as the Apostle says, “Let no one deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit” (Col. 2:8)—and the nails of greedy rapacity have been cut off, [Note: [Col. 1109] This alludes to Deuteronomy 21:11–12.] the inhabitant of the cloister may safely contract marriage with every branch of learning that is not against faith. For whatever is of another flavour outside the cloister, even if it is a wild olive or a branch grafted into the good olive-tree, is sweetened by the richness of the root and, cherished in the bosom of divine wisdom, is changed from instability.

Thus grammar, dialectic, geometry, and astronomy, seasoned with the most savoury salt of divine Scripture—subjects which, when tasted, used to bring death, as the sons of the prophets cry to Elisha the prophet, “There is death in the pot, man of God!” (2 Kgs. [Col. 1109C] 4:40)—through the admixture of flour, that is, grace, provide wholesome refreshment. Like the Gibeonites, they carry wood and water for cloistered discipline. The Israelites rightly bring these into their cloister as spoils of war from the Philistines’ camp, so that, instructed in secular letters, they may read divine writings more diligently, understand them more acutely, detect the deceptions of heretics more cautiously, and defend the simplicity and truth of faith more strongly and firmly.

Occupied with these, our cloistered religious is not idle; intent upon them, he drives away the idle, vain, and superfluous phantasms of the heart; buried with them, he watches while sleeping. These are the changes of garments which Naaman the leper brought with him to the king of Israel.

But if we draw such minds out of the world, what [shall we draw] from heaven? What from God, from whom is every good gift [Col. 1109D] and every perfect gift? (Jas. 1:17). He waters the mountains from His heights, and waters paradise with the river which goes forth from the place of delight and then divides into four heads, so that the fourfold cloister may have distinct streams of irrigation. It is said in the Gospel: “Whoever drinks the water that I shall give him shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:14). But He said this concerning the Spirit, whom those believing in Him were to receive (John 7:39).

The four rivers of paradise are known to those who, with the Apostle Paul, are caught up into the third heaven—or into paradise itself—and are made drunk with the abundance of God’s house and with the torrent of delight. The waters from the fountains of the Saviour are likewise known, waters which gladden the city of God with a sevenfold force. Of them it is said: “Let your fountains flow abroad in the streets” (Prov. 5:16), from which no stranger drinks. Job calls these fountains streams of oil, saying: “When the rock poured out streams of oil for me” (Job 29:6).

Isaiah (ch. 29), who saw the Lord seated upon a high and exalted throne, enumerates and names the fountains of the Saviour, or streams of oil: fountains, because He Himself promised and sent the sevenfold Spirit to the Apostles; streams of oil, because, although He is in all things equal to the Father and the Son, yet He is not from Himself but from the Father and the Son. For this reason the gifts of grace are called streams of oil. According to His humanity, the Son was anointed with this oil of gladness above His companions (Ps. 44:8). Hence Isaiah says: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon Him: the spirit [Col. 1110B] of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill Him” (Isa. 11:2).

The evangelical lamp, thus poured upon and poured into, is not merely a lamp but “the true light which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:1). And we receive from His fullness; and in that outpouring, when the soldier opened His side and blood and water came forth, the olive in the press sent forth the Spirit as oil.

But what has this to do with cloistered discipline? Plainly, the whole form of cloistered discipline flowed forth from the cross. For Christ, raised from the earth, was suspended on the cross, stripped of His garments, and stretched out [Col. 1110C] so that all His bones could be counted; so fixed to the wood that He moved no limb except His tongue, which He retained for prayer and for commending His mother to the beloved disciple.

So the cloistered religious—if he is truly cloistered—ought wholly to crucify himself with his vices and desires. He ought to raise himself from the earth, as it is written: “I shall raise you upon the heights of the earth” (Isa. 58:14); and: “I shall feed you with the inheritance of Jacob your father” (ibid.). He ought to strip himself, as it is said in the Song: “I have stripped off my tunic” (Song 5:1), that is, fleshly desire. He ought to stretch himself toward what lies before, without pretence, even unto the dividing of joints and marrow, so that the soul may melt after the Beloved. He ought to be fixed to the wood, so that this mortal body, with all its members, may through divine fear be powerless for every evil [Col. 1110D] but powerful for every good. Let him retain only his tongue for confession and prayer.

What more? With a deaf ear, let him pass mockers and deceivers by, like the Prophet, as a deaf man. Let him not hear the suggestions and temptations that croak of leaving the cloister as of descending from the cross. At last, let him yield back his spirit to God who gave it, saying: “Into Your hands I commend my spirit” (Ps. 30:6), until the resurrection, lest the torment of malice touch it; for “the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and the torment of malice shall not touch them” (Wis. 3:1).

## Chapter VII. How the Cloister Was Instituted

[Col. 1111A]

From the time when Lucifer, or Satan, fell like lightning from heaven and did not return to it, because he did not keep cloistered discipline—for cloistered discipline is to mourn one’s own sins and those of others; to submit to one’s prelate; to obey in all things; to beware of plots while plotting against no one (for, according to Jerome, there is not much difference in fault between deceiving and being capable of being deceived); to fulfil the first and second commandment of the law, concerning love of God and neighbour; to preserve innocence and holiness; always to cleave to God; and with all desire to long for the heavenly homeland.

Once he had broken the covenant of due submission, the devil fell downward, and then, gnashing and grinding his teeth [Col. 1111B], overturned rather than kept all discipline. Therefore he did not obtain mercy, because he neither sought pardon nor confessed his fault. But humankind, formed from mud, expelled from the cloister of paradise because of sin, weeping at the eastern region over its wounds and saying to God, “Remove Your blows from me” (Ps. 38:11), at the acceptable time and at the end of the ages eternally predestined, the way of the saints having been opened out in Jesus and with Jesus, returned to the cloister. Subjected to regular discipline, it received not only pardon but also the first robe—indeed, a greater glory.

The subsequent children of men, having their eyes in their head, learned wisdom from the things which had happened: by it they might avoid the irreparable fall of the devil [Col. 1111C] and, living according to rule with their predecessors, might gain entrance, through the indulgence of God’s mercy, into their fatherly inheritance.

I judge this to be the principal reason why human beings leave the world and enter the cloister. Those who are in a flood of many waters—of vices and riches—will approach neither the cloister nor the Lord unless the rain has dried up. He who is in the cloister is with Noah—whose name means “rest”—in the ark; but whoever is outside the discipline is outside the ark. Yet few—that is, eight souls—are saved in the ark, because “Many are called, few chosen” (Matt. 24:14), those who shall rise in the eighth age in the resurrection of life.

In the cloister Jacob dwells with Rebecca, who is the homeland. In the cloister Benjamin is with his father, lest any harm happen to him on the way of sinners, where there is the lion, where the wild beast of lust, which devours Joseph—often in reputation, sometimes in actual fact. In the cloister Jonah is in the whale’s belly: “For as Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so the Son of Man [shall be] in the heart of the earth” (Matt. 12:40). Thus the cloistered religious, buried with Christ, dies to sin in thought and action and lives to God.

In the cloister is Jeremiah, sanctified in the womb, who sits alone and is silent, and raises himself above himself—not through pride but contemplation; who takes up the sweet yoke and light burden in order to be meek in heart. In the cloister is John the Baptist:

> While still in tender years,  
> He sought the caverns of the wilderness,  
> Fleeing the crowds of citizens,  
> Lest even the slightest breath  
> Stain his life.  
> —Paul the Deacon

[Col. 1112A] In the cloister is Mary, when the angel entered to her and said: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you” (Luke 1:28). In the cloister is Jesus when, at twelve years old, sitting in the temple, He answered His mother who said, “Your father and I were seeking you”: “Did you not know,” He said, “that I must be occupied in the things of my Father?” (Luke 2:48). In the cloister are the Apostles: “When it was evening on that first day of the week, and the doors were shut where the disciples had gathered, Jesus came, though the doors were shut, and stood in their midst and said: ‘Peace to you’” (John 20:19). And: “When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, all the disciples were together in the same place,” etc. [Col. 1112B] (Acts 2:1).

See what forerunners the cloistered life possesses. How devout, then, how good, how pleasant, and how safe it is to dwell in the cloister! For “a brother helping a brother is a fortified city” (Prov. 18:19), concerning which it is said: “Who will lead me into the fortified city?” (Ps. 59:10). The cloister is a city because cloistered religious gather there to live well; it is fortified because they live under the protection of the God of heaven. The discipline of the cloister is the iron gate leading to the city, the way of which those who wander in the wilderness do not find and whose hearts always wander.

The discipline of the cloister is a rock of scandal and a stone of stumbling to those who do not believe the word in which they also have been set. The discipline of the cloister is the rock which, struck twice by renunciation of the world and profession of religion, gives water for humans and beasts to drink: the prudent and the simple, to whom it is said, “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10:15). Cloistered discipline is Christ’s cross, from which one is not taken down except dead. For the cloistered religious is obedient to the Father unto death, even death on the cross. The feet of the one hanging are so fixed that his steps cannot move from the cloister. His hands, fashioned on the lathe, are for obedience; golden for purity; full of hyacinths for almsgiving; dripping choicest myrrh for mortifying the flesh and for not receiving money.

His eyes are toward the Father, the disciple, and the mother: that is, always toward God, and toward the Virgin Mary [Col. 1112D] and John the Evangelist. God possesses heaven; the Mother entreats her Son; John holds the Gospel. It is good to shift one’s gaze among these and in these: now to invoke the Lord, now to entreat the Mother of the Lord Jesus, now to read John’s Gospel with head bowed; for “He bowed His head and gave up the spirit” (John 19:30).

Whenever the cloistered religious comes into public, he keeps his head fixed toward the ground; but when, with the door shut, he enters his chamber, then let him raise his eyes to heaven and his head upward. Let his back be beaten with scourges, whether for sin, for fault, in thanksgiving, or in recompense for Christ’s passion; his side pierced or opened, from which he may bring forth and offer marrowy burnt offerings with incense of rams, and from which blood may flow beside the base of the altar [Col. 1113A], as he confesses his sins to his prelate; and water of compunction may also come forth, to wash away the stains of crime.

Let his belly be stretched, not with superfluous refreshment of food and drink, but with the continual emptiness of fasts, so that he may say: “My bone has clung to my skin, my flesh being consumed” (Job 19:20). And: “All my bones have been counted” (Ps. 21:15). Let his belly also be set with sapphires, so that in mortification his skin may appear not scarlet with blood but hyacinth-blue; nor may a storehouse for worms be built there, but, like a wineskin in frost, may it be continually hardened by afflictions.

Let Joseph and Nicodemus—the angel and the prelate—take down this crucified person and embalm him with a mixture of myrrh and aloes, so that, as he has not loved corruption in the cloister, he may not feel the worms that do not die in hell. Without doubt, he shall have angels at his head and feet, guarding his entrance and departure, receiving the soul as it leaves the body and leading it to rest.

## Chapter VIII. A Comparison between the Discipline of the Philosopher, the Jew, the Christian, and Every Religious Person
The natural spark of good which remained in humanity, when the original seed-plot planted by God’s hand had been extinguished, running by God’s grace through the reed-bed of all the arts, discovered many disciplines, by living according to which, even if the first creation were not wholly restored, it would at least not be extinguished by failing altogether, down to ashes. Therefore every nation and region under the sun fashioned for itself a discipline according to its capacity of reason, [Col. 1113C] by which the excesses of fools and the equity of the wise might be regulated in their manner of life. Thus the philosophers established their own discipline; the Jews received theirs; the Christians theirs; and finally hermits and cloistered persons theirs.

A different intention distinguishes one discipline from another. The philosopher aims to gain human glory and favour for himself; the Jew, earthly goods; the Christian, hope of pardon and grace; and the cloistered person, an abundance of grace and glory. The philosopher searches out nature’s secrets; the Jew, the earth’s gross abundance; the Christian, the promise of the life which now is and which is to come; the cloistered person, partly the fruit of the active life and partly that of the contemplative. The philosopher casts off fleshly impediments and worldly burdens; the Jew applies himself to sacrifices and offerings [Col. 1113D] for cleansing of the flesh; the Christian is cleansed from dead works by the Church’s sacraments; the cloistered person abstains not only from unlawful things but even from lawful ones. The philosopher sows in a spirit not God’s but his own and vain; the Jew in the flesh; the Christian in faith, hope, and charity; the cloistered person in filial adoption. Presumption assists the philosopher; temporality the Jew; faith lifts up the Christian; a foretaste of future hope strengthens the religious cloistered person. The philosopher sharpens his intellect; the Jew seeks gain; the Christian implores the good; the religious person hopes for a golden crown. The philosopher delights in novelty of words and opinions; the Jew in the letter and carnality; the Christian in spiritual understanding; the religious person in austerity of life. The philosopher eats flour from the mill of [Col. 1114A] intellect; the Jew an insipid husk from the Law; the Christian fine flour from the Gospel; the religious person marrow from a good purpose. The philosopher scatters; the Jew gathers; the Christian distributes; the religious person renounces all. The philosopher teaches in schools, the Jew in the Synagogue, the Christian in church, the religious person in the cloister. The philosopher loves applause, the Jew money, the Christian God, the religious person lamentation. The philosopher is as a stag in the woods; the Jew as a bull in the fields; the Christian as a dove in the clefts of the rock; the religious person as an eagle in contemplation. The philosopher lives by art; the Jew by flesh; the Christian by faith; the religious person by mortification of the flesh. The philosopher disputes; the Jew dreams; the Christian reads and understands; the religious person prays. The philosopher catches gnats, [Col. 1114B] the Jew dying flies, the Christian birds, the religious person bees. The philosopher weaves spider-webs out of sand; the Jew tends his eggs; the Christian mends Peter’s nets; the religious person weaves the breastpiece and ephod.

If the bond of faith intervened, cloistered and philosophical discipline would embrace one another in mutual arms and kiss one another in their withdrawal from crowds. For worldly occupation impedes the powers of the intellect and delays the senses of the soul, as does idle conversation. Therefore, in order to claim the whole mind for itself, philosophy sought quiet and secluded places, where it might raise the mind on high and, with the understanding purified, bring forth a faithful understanding leavened with the leaven of the Gospel. Yet if Jacob, among the peeled rods [Col. 1114C] of the arts, had passed from an invented plausible truth of not one but varied colour, from the sense of the flesh to the senses of the soul, and then had crossed over to the sense of God and faith, he would be saved; but “whoever stumbles in one point has become guilty of all” (James 2:10).

Would that with as much severity and constancy, together with faith and regular observance, we afflicted our flesh and loved poverty as very many philosophers have uprooted from themselves the vices of the flesh. But because faith cleanses hearts and true repentance through confession destroys every sin, whatever the outward civic order lacks is wholly repaired by the inward form of the new creation. For “all the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44:14); nor is any religion or discipline deserving of reward which grace together with a good conscience does not commend. Let our discipline, therefore, maintain fruitful silence; with the Jew, continual sacrifice; with the Christian, the shared solace of charity; and, in accordance with its own profession, a singular obedience to the divine will. Let it exclude concern for worldly anxieties together with the philosopher; observe the worship of one God with the Jew; commend itself to grace with the Christian; and surpass itself through inward desire for God. Let it fulfil what is first in the vow with the philosopher, what is intermediate with the Jew, what is final with the Christian, and what is highest through grace together with free will. Let it reap what is green with the philosopher, what is fertile with the Jew, what is ripe with the Christian, and what is fruitful according to its own vow.

## CHAPTER IX. On angelic discipline.

[Col. 1115A]

There remains angelic discipline, which is wholly voluntary, has everything from love, and nothing from difficulty or labour. When it ministers to God, it is refreshed; when it stands before him, it is satisfied; when it is sent, it runs with exultation; when it returns, it is received with jubilation. It always runs beneath God, never outside him. Nothing in that discipline is confused, nothing burdensome, nothing irregular. It binds together all those spirits, melted into love of God and of one another; and, gathered into one spirit, they are joined in so great a unity that it is as though there were only one spirit in that entire multitude.

In that order are nine orders of angels, to which a tenth order, that of human beings, is added, so that the Psalmist may [Col. 1115B] sing in the midst of the cloister, upon the ten-stringed psaltery with song, upon the harp of the cross and the Crucified. Of this harmony the Apostle speaks: “Though I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels,” that is, upon the ten-stringed psaltery, “but have not charity,” that is, the harp of the cross and unity, “I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13:1). For there is participation in that one reality until Christ is formed in you—by that formation through which all members, joined to their head, will become faithful partakers of the divine nature.

Shut within the cloister-cell as though in a womb, we acquire the features by which, mortality dissolved, we shall be made like the angels: “When we shall be like God,” as the Apostle says, “because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). What, then, are these features? Angelic purity, cleanliness, chastity, [Col. 1115C] charity, peace, truth, and all those virtues of which it is said: “Bless the Lord, all his virtues” (Ps. 102:20). We must pray that he who created them in heaven may impress them upon us in the cloister, lest dissimilar faces divide our dwellings. For if an angel sees his own face in you, he will love you as himself.

## CHAPTER X. On the form of cloistered discipline.

The form of cloistered discipline bears the appearance of the angel announcing the Lord’s resurrection: “His appearance was like lightning, and his garment like snow” (Matt. 28:3). For the timid hearts of carnal people, who do not go forth to battle [Col. 1115D] and disdain to come to the wedding feast, are frightened at the first sight of religious life; and, imagining through fantastic illusions that they cannot do without their accustomed pleasures, they make excuses. For they are occupied with the five yokes of oxen in the Gospel, with the purchased estate, and with the wife taken in marriage; they claim that they lack the resources necessary for patience, austerity in food and drink, cheapness of clothing, continual silence, the yoke of obedience, constant enclosure, perpetual continence, and similar things. They call themselves men, but by their conduct place themselves among the effeminate. Of such people Gregory says: “What are we bearded men to say amid these things, when we see girls going through iron to the kingdom?”

We do not deny the harshness of this discipline of ours; but with the Psalmist we say: “Because of the words [Col. 1116A] of your lips”—that is, “Whoever does not hate his father and mother” (Luke 14:26), and “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (ibid., 33)—“I have kept hard ways” (Ps. 16:4). “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels” (Ecclus. 27:6); and “he shall not be crowned unless he has contended lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:5). They flee at the sound of a leaf when no one pursues them. Touch and taste are truer in judgment than sight alone. The discipline of the cloister ought to be touched and tasted, and thus judged whether it is good or bad.

Its garments are like snow: the garments of cloistered discipline are regular observances. Why snow? Because they extinguish desires and incentives of the flesh; because they chastise by affliction but whiten by reward. Isaiah says: “If [Col. 1116B] your sins are as scarlet, they shall be whitened like snow” (Isa. 1:18). When? When God judges kings: good cloistered persons will be whitened with snow, becoming “as the angels of God in heaven,” shining as the sun unto everlasting eternities.

Nor is it inappropriate that the cloister should be regarded by some as a race-course, by others as an inner court, by others as a treasury, by others as a worldly holy place, by others as a royal bedchamber, by others as a gallows, and by others as a marketplace.

## CHAPTER XI. It is shown that the cloister is a race-course.

A race-course (*stadium*) is so called from standing, because one who is in the cloister must stand in virtue with every care, rather than fall into vices. Hence the Apostle: “Let him who stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10:12). A race-course, however, is that in [Col. 1116C] which all run, but one receives the prize. Although a *stadium* is named from standing, one nevertheless runs through the race-course in order to reach the prize; and there the race is completed, as the Apostle says: “I have fought the good fight, I have completed the race, I have kept the faith,” etc. (2 Tim. 4:7).

Therefore all who have laid aside the hair of their head for Christ and received the habit of religion are running while they press toward the end; but one receives the prize: the one who is not changed like the moon, who does not depart from the unity of faith and the religion he has professed. “He shall receive blessing from the Lord and mercy from God his saviour” (Ps. 23:5). The law of this race-course is that one hastening toward the prize abstain from all things. Our law binds less harshly: [Col. 1116D] it removes few things and permits more. It removes fornication, adultery, every impurity, and marriage itself, because “he who is without a wife is concerned for the things that are the Lord’s” (1 Cor. 7:23). It removes drunken excess, removes money, removes superfluities, and grants necessities.

Thus Moses commands Sihon, king of the Amorites: “We shall go by the king’s highway; we shall not drink your water or take anything of yours, but we shall buy necessities at a price” (Num. 21:22). The pilgrim and stranger, who daily passes from this world to the Father, takes nothing of the substance of the prince of this world, even to the thread of a woven web, so that when his soul is departing and that prince claims what is his, he may confidently say: “You will find nothing deadly in me.” Behold, this is the light runner, making straight his ways and running swiftly in the fragrance of the bridegroom’s ointments.

[Col. 1117A] Of this race-course the Lord says to the children of Israel: “Every place which the sole of your foot shall tread shall be yours: from the wilderness, and Lebanon, and the great river Euphrates, unto the western sea shall your borders extend” [Vulgate: “shall be”] (Deut. 11:24). One who abandons the world and comes to the cloister already begins to tread underfoot the age and his own body. This is the wilderness: a deserted land, trackless and waterless—deserted because of its harshness, waterless because of the discipline’s severity, trackless because few travellers enter it. “But in the sanctuary,” says the Psalmist, “I have appeared before you, O God, that we may see your power” (Ps. 62:3), because of hard labour, and your glory, namely everlasting consolation.

Therefore one must begin from the wilderness of renouncing the world, and run through Lebanon of chastity and whitening, or sprinkling [Col. 1117B] with the blood of Jesus Christ, so that it may be said: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6:14), where the saints whitened their robes in the blood of the Lamb. Again, one must sail through the great river Euphrates: first through baptism, and secondly through continual compunction. Our course will end at the western sea, lest we fail on the way, until life is ended through death. Therefore every place that we have trodden we possess, like him who says: “Having nothing, and possessing all things” (2 Cor. 6:10).

## CHAPTER XII. On the inner court of the cloister.

The cloister is called the court of the mind, where the skins of sacrificial victims were stripped off, limbs were cut piece by piece, [Col. 1117C] ashes were poured out, entrails were washed, and every laborious office was performed. Thus one entering the cloister gives skin for skin and all that he possesses for his soul, when he puts off the old person and puts on the new, walking in newness of life and uncovering in confession the vices of his former way of life.

First, then, in offering sacrifice to God, he mortifies his members which are upon earth: fornication, impurity, lust, and all the rest. Then, after stripping off in confession the skin of all perversity, he cuts his limbs into pieces, concealing none of the circumstances of any sin but laying before himself, one by one, the headings of accusation and complaint. Let the fire of contrition and repentance devour all these things [Col. 1117D] until they become ashes, which he sprinkles upon his head, saying: “My sin is always before me” (Ps. 50:4); and “I said to corruption, ‘You are my father’; to worms, ‘My mother and my sister’” (Job 17:7). Let compunction be added to these, which, like water from Christ’s side, cleanses the conscience of the entrails from dead works.

Near the sanctuary’s entrance the inner court is situated; outside it lies the outer court, and within it the first tabernacle, called the holy place. Thus the novice coming to religious life, placed on the border between prayer and sensuality, is indeed no longer in the flesh, but is not yet in the spirit. Meanwhile he hears, between the boundaries, the familiar bleatings of flocks of flesh contending with one another: in mind consenting to the law of God, but in flesh to the law of sin. He hears the bleatings of heavenly flocks singing [Col. 1118A] songs of Zion, calling him toward the sleeps of contemplation, and calming the disturbances of carnal movements.

## CHAPTER XIII. The cloister as treasury.

The cloister is also a treasury, where gold, silver, and precious stones are stored; where we have our treasure in earthen vessels—that is, a good conscience in regular observances. In the cloister, religious persons who trade for themselves in eternal life are treasures; to them the nobleman departing into a far country entrusted his goods. Individual psalms, individual prayers, individual confessions, individual tears, individual fasts, individual alms, individual afflictions of unremembered labours—[Col. 1118B] do they not make a heap of graces, which is a desirable treasure in a cloistered congregation?

Over these treasures the eunuch of Queen Candace is appointed: when one who has castrated himself for the kingdom of heaven is placed in the office of prelacy. Indeed, distinguished by the title of modesty and chastity, and as one girded about the loins, he is not undeservedly appointed guardian of Christ’s bride. Such was Joseph in the house of Potiphar, priest of Heliopolis; such was John the Evangelist, to whom Christ, entrusting his mother on the cross, entrusted her; such a person the Apostle chose; such a person blessed Benedict describes. By what reasoning would the jealous Lord entrust the bride whom he redeemed by precious blood and joined to himself in indissoluble marriage, [Col. 1118C] unless that friend or vicar of the bridegroom should serve faithfully and keep her chastely in his charge?

## CHAPTER XIV. The cloister is a worldly holy place.

Let us now enter the sanctuary, called the worldly holy place, where priests continually entered while completing the offices of sacrifices. Justice, dwelling as a pilgrim upon earth, meanwhile appoints the cloistered discipline as its lodging. Therefore it knocks at the cloister door, saying: “Open to me, my sister; my head is full of dew” (Song 5:2), which I shall pour over the cloistered air, so that dew may remain upon my harvest and my locks with the drops of the nights, which a devout conscience steals in the hiddenness of God’s face and in the secrecy of silence.

One must run and hasten to meet [Col. 1118D] such kind promises with the untiring foot of holy desire, and lift the bolt of the door, which is the difficulty and slowness of human frailty in fulfilling vows. Therefore the worldly holy place is to will, and scarcely to do good things; but the heavenly holy place is to will and to accomplish. Hence the Apostle: “God is he who gives us both to will and to accomplish according to good will” (Phil. 2:13). Of the worldly holy place he says: “To will is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish” (Rom. 7:18). The cloister is therefore rightly called a worldly holy place, where neither do we do what we will, nor do we complete what we do.

## CHAPTER XV. The cloister as royal bedchamber.

The cloister is also called a royal bedchamber. Thus in the Song of Songs cloistered discipline says: “While he was [Col. 1119A] at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song 1:11). To recline is to incline oneself for rest. In Isaiah the Lord says: “I have laboured in bearing” (Isa. 1:14). In Jeremiah: “Labour in praying” (Jer. 15:6). And in the Gospel: “Jesus, wearied from the journey, sat upon the well” (John 4:6).

Not only Jacob’s crimes and our sins vex him who is himself the same and judges all things in tranquillity; even the peace-offering, incense, and songs of those priests whose hands are full of blood, avarice, and lust vex him. Therefore, provoked to weariness by profane and evil people, and desiring to keep sabbath, he seeks places of silence, peace, unity, and honour, and there establishes his bedchamber. “This,” says cloistered discipline, “is my rest; here I shall dwell, because [Col. 1119B] I have chosen it” (Ps. 131:15); and, “My delights are to be with the children of men” (Prov. 8:31), whose manner of life is not animal but rational and spiritual, in heaven.

Melted by a certain humble love of the stag that leaps over the mountains of spices, it says to him: “Tell me, whom my soul loves, where you feed, where you lie down at noon” (Song 1:6)—when the spirit is fervent, when the whole mind glows, when fire burns fiercely in the bones of one who loves and cannot endure. Clearly, amid heaps of new grain, among lilies, in the fields of the forest of minds removed from worldly arts, he feeds and lies down at noon.

Young men and young women guard the royal bedchamber, holding swords which devour flesh upon the thigh of evil desire, surrounding [Col. 1119C] King Solomon because of fears by night, lest the howling of wolves and the snarling of foxes break the silence of midnight, when Egypt’s firstborn die.

## CHAPTER XVI. It is shown that the cloister is a gallows.

The cloister is called a gallows, where Jesus is suspended with the thieves; but Jesus not because he deserved it, but because he willed it; they not because they willed it, but because they deserved it. Hence one thief says to the other: “We indeed receive things worthy of our deeds; but this man has done no evil” (Luke 23:41). Whoever enters the cloister willingly with Jesus should choose hanging with the thieves because of the merit of and satisfaction for his own evils.

The whole multitude of cloistered persons is classified in three ways. In the cloister there is one innocent and without complaint before God and human beings, with Jesus. There is one guilty but repentant, with the right-hand thief; and one guilty and unrepentant, with the left-hand thief. The innocent suffers for increase of his crown; the penitent suffers to merit pardon; the unrepentant suffers for an increase of punishment. Jesus prays on the gallows; one thief seeks pardon; the other insults Jesus. One who is good and endures the gallows has a good conscience that makes punishment light; but it makes punishment grievous for one who is evil and endures it. Yet one who does not murmur under the scourge merits pardon; one who is wickedly scourged and crackles in despair like fire among thorns is condemned.

A threefold distinction of cloistered discipline is to be noted in the gallows: [Col. 1120A] for there is the discipline of the Son, of whom “the Father did not spare his Only-begotten, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8:32). Of him Isaiah says: “The discipline of our peace was upon him” (Isa. 53:5), and: “Truly he bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows” (ibid., 4). This only and most beloved Son, in whom he was well pleased, the merciful Father and God of mercies struck with whips—indeed, with most severe scorpions—without any reservation, as though he were an enemy, for the reconciliation of enemies. Hence the Son says: “I gave my body to those striking me, and my cheeks to those plucking them; I did not turn my face away from those rebuking and spitting upon me” (Isa. 50:6).

O harsh—indeed merciful—mercy! Harsh according to human judgment; merciful according to the divine secret; harsh with respect to [Col. 1120B] the merit of the sufferer; merciful with respect to the cause and effect of the Passion. One acts the cause of all: the good one for the evil, the just one for sinners, the son for servants. Therefore the discipline of our peace was upon him, who paid our whole debt with interest—not merely at one per cent but at an infinite rate—so that the gift might weigh more heavily in the balance of the cross than the offence, and so that the superabundant grace of remission might pardon sins not only original but actual.

Great and grievous was the discipline under which the gentlest Lamb, with a gentle and meek voice, sighs, saying: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; and if it cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done” (Matt. 26:39). If you are a son in the cloister, let your heart be [Col. 1120C] thus peaceful and ready to suffer, even to rejoice with others, saying: “For I am ready for scourges” (Ps. 37:18). If Judas the wolf, perhaps once of one mind with you, raises his heel against you—“your” [perhaps *his*]—let him neither strip away the skin of your gentle face, nor swallow the flesh of patience, nor bite the entrails of intention. If manifest Satan wishes to ulcerate your reputation from the sole of your foot to the crown of your head, sit in the dunghill of humility and scrape away the pus with a potsherd, attributing it to your own fault, not another’s malice; as David did not impute Shimei’s curses to Shimei, but ascribed them to divine vengeance.

Again, one discipline is that of the disciple and another that of the servant. The disciple hears the master’s teaching. The servant, who does not remain in the house forever and awaits [Col. 1120D] the end of his work, is slow to hear, negligent in working; he does everything merely for appearance and seeks not grace but money. The holy disciple is the thief who hung at the Lord’s right hand; the servant is he who hung at the left. The disciple cries: “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom” [Col. 1120D] (Luke 23:41). In the briefest time he had already learned patience and repentance; “made perfect in a short time, he fulfilled many years, for his soul was pleasing to God.” Hence: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (ibid., 42).

And so you also, cloistered person, whether perhaps you came from the east, entangled in sins from your earliest age, or from the west, having lived in sins even to old age: having turned to religious life, hope in the Lord and do good. Say: “Lord, remember me when you come [Col. 1121A] into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42). Again: “My soul has clung after you” (Ps. 62:9), following and obeying you; “your right hand has upheld me” (Ps. 17:36), because though I have sinned, though I have deserved death, nevertheless I hope in your mercy, which is your right hand.

One who sits at the right hand, or even hangs there, is not outside discipline; rather, he embraces the discipline of the cloister with delight. He hangs there who has lowing calves, but keeps the appetites of the world shut in, and hears the impulses of the flesh without going after his lusts. Carnal suggestion is stirred, but consent or delight does not go forth. The flesh conceives pain but does not give birth. Why? Because he is not outside discipline, nor outside the right hand. For he always says: “The Lord is at my right hand, that I may not be moved” [Col. 1121B] (Ps. 15:8). The disciple does not die.

But what of the servant who is a servant of sin and sin’s punishment? “Cast out the bondwoman and her son; for the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman, Mary” (Gen. 21:10). This is the cloistered person who seeks his own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. He seeks obedience not to Jesus Christ but to his own will; he seeks money, seeks his own will, seeks to serve two masters, God and Mammon. He honours God with his lips, but his heart is far from him. He comes in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly is a ravening wolf, whose god is his belly. He has the appearance of godliness but denies its power. He is not of us, although among many he is with us. He prefers to feed the swine of unclean desire rather than remain in his father’s [Col. 1121C] possessions, living soberly. Let us now descend to the marketplace and buy necessities for ourselves.

## CHAPTER XVII. The cloister as marketplace, and its moral likeness to the city of Tyre.

The cloister is a marketplace, where every kind of merchandise is displayed for the profit of the soul, whether things pertaining to beauty or to necessity. Read of Tyre in Ezekiel (ch. 27), furnished and adorned in every thing and kind by diverse peoples and regions, according to the capacity of each and their foreign merchandise. It belongs neither to this work nor to our ability to unfold [Col. 1121D] and explain their mystical meanings from the sacks of history and purses of exposition. We leave this to the shoulders of Jerome and Gregory, and other interpreters, who have sharp sickles to reap where others have laboured. Yet, having paid the cost, I carry thence something back for our discipline and our cloister.

Just as neighbouring and distant provinces filled that most wealthy city, so the cloister of religion has been filled by those who pleased God from the beginning of the world until our own times. For they prepared all their sayings and deeds for our use. If you seek strong examples of chastity, you will find countless incorruptible cedars. If of patience, conscience, faith, truth, gentleness, religion, obedience, justice, courage, prudence, temperance—if you seek possessors [Col. 1122A] of all virtues—countless numbers will meet you, more than the sand of the sea and the stars of heaven. Hence: “But to me, O God, your friends have become honourable; I shall number them, and they shall be multiplied beyond the sand” (Ps. 138:16).

Let each person buy from God’s good and lawful merchants whatever pleases him and whatever is necessary for the feast day. For then nothing is found in the marketplace when the door has been shut and the foolish virgins are told: “Go to those who sell, and buy for yourselves” (Matt. 25:9). This will be said not as advice but in mockery. Wisdom says: “I shall mock when what you feared comes upon you” (Prov. 1:26).

Tyre, moreover, fittingly signifies cloistered discipline, for Tyre means “narrowness.” “Bad, bad,” says every buyer; but when he has come home [Col. 1122B] he rejoices. “For this present momentary and light tribulation works in us beyond measure an eternal weight of glory” (2 Cor. 4:17). Nor is the equipment of souls in the cloister less than the equipment of earthly wealth in Tyre. Tyre’s wealth is scarcely gathered; the cloister’s labours are scarcely enumerated. Whatever Tyre gathers for the world’s perishing glory, the religious community patiently endures in order to acquire blessed life.

First one must consider that it is situated in the heart of the sea, where fear is greater and labour harsher. Its neighbours are Elijah, John the Baptist, blessed Benedict, and Saint Augustine, who built cloistered religion by word and example and filled it with incomparable holiness and beauty: [Col. 1122C] fir-trees and cedars incorruptible through purity and incorruption of mind, and lofty in contemplation. From Senir—that is, “the way of the lamp,” or “the teeth of vigils”—or from Lebanon, they build (Ezek. 27) the cloister, when such persons are perfected whose life is a way for others and a lamp, or an exceedingly vigilant and biting rebuke of those who err, and a most brilliant whitening of those whom they invite.

The cloister also receives oaks of Bashan (Isa. 2), that is, dishonoured sinners, and makes them oars, as Joshua did the Gibeonites (Josh. 9), water-carriers in the Temple and wood-cutters. Hence the Apostle: “Appoint those who are contemptible in the Church to judgments” (1 Cor. 6:4). It has benches, whose feet carry peace, and little chambers (Ezek. 27:6), whose soul clings [Col. 1122D] to the pavement; of Indian ivory because of mortification; and of the islands of Italy (ibid.), or Kittim, meaning “struck and grieving under the fear of God.”

Variegated fine linen from Egypt—that is, from the world—is woven into a sail (ibid., 7), when people converted from worldly life oppose themselves like a wall for the house of Israel against the difficulties and objections of adversaries. Likewise hyacinth comes from nobility, and purple (ibid.) from an obscure and low-born stock, yet one very laborious; these become a covering for the security and shelter of the weak from storm and rain. The inhabitants of Sidon and Arvad (ibid., 8), once rhetorical hunters, laying aside their power—as Nebuchadnezzar raised up whom he wished and humbled whom he wished—are now our rowers, steering the ship and drawing it to port.

“Your wise men, O Tyre, are your pilots” [Col. 1123A] (Ezek. 27:8); when the commonwealth is governed by them, it is well governed. “The elders of Gebal and its wise men” (ibid., 9), reared in the order from childhood, “had sailors for the service of your varied equipment” (ibid.); because the custom and practice of the cloister must be sought from such persons. “All the ships of the sea and their sailors were among the people of your trade” (ibid.), because cloistered persons live by the labour of worldly people, according to the Apostle: those who sow spiritual things reap carnal things (Gal. 6).

The Persians (Ezek. 27:10), that is, those tempted by their own desire, drawn away and enticed, and begotten by the devil—for “you are of your father the devil” (John 8:44)—and the Libyans (Ezek. 27:10), whose mouth is full of cursing, have been converted into the cloistered army: [Col. 1123B] either by remaining in malice to exercise Abel, or by being changed to serve the living God. “Your warriors hung shield and helmet in your adornment” (ibid.), putting on the armour of God in time of war, resisting the devil and the vices of the flesh; and, after the malice which is human life upon earth has passed, leaving powerful examples of virtues to their followers, like Eleazar, who refused to pretend that he had eaten swine’s flesh contrary to the holy laws.

“The sons of Arvad, with your army, were upon your walls and around you” (ibid., 11). The Arvadites, putting off the old person with his deeds, are upon the walls, guards who do not cease continually, day and night, but fight against aerial powers. “And the pygmies, who were in your towers, hung their quivers upon your walls round about; [Col. 1123C] they completed your beauty” (ibid., 12). Observe that the Pygmies, who are cubit-high people, are said to complete our beauty. Indeed, one who humbles himself like the little one of the Gospel completes, in towers of peace and security, the fullness of religious life.

“Greece, Tubal, and Meshech: they were your merchants” (ibid., 13). In sum, it must be said concerning all nations now converted to religious life and those still to be converted in greater number: each, from its manners, regions, and customs, makes many dwelling-places in God’s house, so that from many persons of diverse faces the great body of Christ, which is the Church, may be built up.

Perhaps beneath these coverings the very modest face of cloistered discipline pleases you little. You prefer it naked, [Col. 1123D] stripped of the leaves of the proud and girded with worldly custom, lest the reader, delayed by the obstacle of shaded speech, lose the sense through weariness. In this matter too I may satisfy both your will and others’ profit.

The sinews and joints of cloistered discipline, then, are: the restraint of silence; a rare and reasonable permission of speech; eyes fixed upon the ground; a gait neither too slow nor too hurried; continual sitting in the cloister, interrupted by attendance in choir; standing, trembling and fearful, as though before God; food and drink keeping their camp within the bounds of sufficiency; sleep sufficient for digestion; chastity of both kinds possessing all the boundaries of the human person; fear of God laying the foundations of all actions; [Col. 1124A] love of God stretching out the heaven above; constancy and perseverance in good supporting the walls; purity and cleanliness sweeping the cloister and casting out every superfluity; humility spreading straw beneath the feet; obedience guarding entrance and exit; charity arranging the whole community in order; faith giving life; and hope restoring strength.

Where this discipline is observed and order is not broken, believe me, Jesus stands in the midst of his disciples, gives peace, and enters and goes out with them. There is peace for one entering discipline and for one departing into eternal life. Let these words be inscribed with the blood of the Lamb upon the lintels of cloistered houses for another generation.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On silence.

[Col. 1124B] Again I repeat that I would commend still further those things which I judge most lovable, or even necessary, to religious life: namely silence, reading, confession, and prayer. Cloistered silence should be neither dumb nor talkative: it should not be dumb in the ears of the Lord of hosts, but should always say: “Give ear to the voice of my prayer” (Ps. 16:2). And: “With my voice I cried to the Lord” (Ps. 141:1). For to Moses, though silent, it was said: “Why do you cry to me?” (Exod. 14:15). For that voice penetrates the depths of the mercy of our God: the voice which the spirit alone and wholly, groaning in its inmost depths, sends forth with most powerful force to the third heaven. Hence the Apostle says of the Lord: “In the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications with a loud cry and tears to him who was able to save him from death, he was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5:7).

Such silence has bells at the hem of the priestly garment together with pomegranates, because, solicitous concerning the end of this life, it prays for the refreshment and perfect fullness of eternal life. Again, it should not be talkative, for: “In much speaking sin will not be lacking” (Prov. 10:19). And the tongue, set in moisture, if it moves without the support of the fear of God, scarcely escapes slipperiness and scarcely avoids falling. Therefore let it not open the doors of the lips, except perhaps on the Sabbath or at the Calends, in recalling the future rest and the joys of the saints.

Under such silence, holy desires, peace and tranquility of heart with true purity, grow and multiply; for windy and empty talkativeness, mixed with the frost and hoarfrost of words that sow discord, quickly and repeatedly scorches the fig tree, the vine, and the tender plants by causing scandal. But the seal of silence, if it lies beneath the shadow of its sealing, nourishes good seed and brings it to fruition.

Hence in the Apocalypse the book which is in the right hand of him seated upon the throne, written within and without, is sealed with seven seals. We too, and our words, are in the hand of God, shut under seven seals until the Lamb who was slain opens our mouth. He has the key “who opens and no one shuts” (Apoc. 3:7); hence Paul, though bound, says: “But the word of God is not bound” (2 Tim. 2:9). He shuts and no one opens; whence in the same Apocalypse: “Seal up what the seven thunders spoke; do not write it” (Apoc. 10:3). And in Daniel: “The words are shut up” (Dan. 12:24).

[Col. 1125A] This book is written within and without, lest, while your lips are silent, you should meditate upon iniquity in your bed—that is, in the secret place of the heart. It is sealed with seven seals lest an idle word go forth, since we must render an account for every idle word: lest it be empty, like those of whom it is said, “Each one has spoken empty things to his neighbor” (Ps. 11:2); lest it be deceitful, because “the instruments of the deceitful are evil” (Isa. 32:7); lest it be false, because “you will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. 5:7); lest it be evil, whence: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth” (Eph. 4:29); lest it be schismatic, heretical, or murmuring, because Dathan and Abiram were swallowed alive, and the murmurers perished by the destroyer; finally, lest it be blasphemous, which will be forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come.

[Col. 1125B] There are also seven seals by which the book of cloistered silence is sealed: the principle of tranquility; the principle of one’s profession; the principle of preserving peace; the principle of ordering the affections and movements of the heart; the principle of withdrawal from secular affairs; the principle of searching the law of God; and the principle of contemplation. For where the barriers of silence are broken, tranquility is disturbed, profession is dissolved, peace is thrown into confusion, and the affections and motions of the heart are beaten about like waves in a stirred sea. Whoever becomes entangled in secular affairs is stripped of eternal and heavenly things; whoever is occupied with sophistical and rhetorical deceptions does not meditate upon the law of God; whoever is held fast by chatter and vain talk is not raised in mind to God.

Therefore let these seals remain safe until the Lamb loosens them and opens our lips. The book of silence, closed by these seals,

[Col. 1125C] is not unsealed unless the Lamb who was slain unseals it; that is, this discipline of silence is to be preserved unto death. But it will be unsealed by the Lamb, “who is worthy to receive power,” that he may be the King of powers; and divinity (Apoc. 5:12), that he may be consubstantial with the Father according to the eternal generation and the Wisdom which says: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Ecclus. 24:5); and strength, that he may be strong and mighty in battle; and glory and honor, because the Father crowned with glory and honor him who was made a little lower than the angels; and blessing (ibid.), he who “received blessing from the Lord” and is God blessed above all.

For these purposes the Lamb opens the mouths of the mute and loosens the seals, so that we may speak “wisdom hidden in mystery,” so that we may say of Christ: “He has done all things well: he has made the deaf hear and the mute speak” (Mark 7:27). Therefore let us read in the sealed book, that is, in silence; and let us examine what is shut beneath the seal—as though the stone had been removed from the mouth of the well by Jacob, or from the Lord’s tomb by the angels—and drink from these waters. Cloistered silence, therefore, is good.

## CHAPTER XIX. On reading

Reading is joined to this silence, and the rings should, as it were, be fixed into the rings of the curtains in the temple of God. Reading is a most abundant pasture, in which lesser animals together with greater ones, continually feeding, prepare rich burnt offerings for the Lord, when, inwardly

[Col. 1126A] ruminating upon the sweetest flowers of divine Scripture, they hold nothing else in heart and mouth. Indeed, continual, attentive reading with devotion cleanses our inward parts of the bones of the dead and the corpses of thoughts that must be cut away. Even if the fruit of understanding and knowledge did not follow from reading, it would still be useful always to read, so that our occupied mind might be excused from the vain and superfluous thought which intrudes upon it and stubbornly forces itself in.

“Until I come,” the Apostle says to Timothy, “attend to reading” (1 Tim. 4:13). And: “Blessed is the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night” (Ps. 1:1). And: “Let the poles of the ark always be in the rings” (Exod. 25). Let the devil always find you occupied; for the unclean spirit enters no house except one that it finds empty.

[Col. 1126B] But lest reading should be vain and chattering, rather than quiet and impressed with the seal of meditation, it is said in the Apocalypse: “When the Lamb had opened one of the seven seals, I heard one of the four living creatures, as the voice of thunder, saying: ‘Come and see’” (Apoc. 6:1); that is, read the Gospel of Matthew, who is one of the four living creatures, and which begins thus: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ.” For what is it to begin the Gospel in this way, except to say: Come and see in this book the mystery hidden from the ages, shown and revealed through Christ’s generation? Come and see the incarnate Word, who until now had lain concealed with the Father under the seal of divinity.

“And behold, a white horse” (ibid., 2): Christ, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin without sin. “And he who sat upon

[Col. 1126C] it had a bow” (ibid.), drawn from the divine and human natures against the devil. “And a crown was given to him” (ibid.), that he might be King of angels who had been King of the Jews. And he went forth to the place of Calvary, conquering by patience in order that he might conquer (ibid.) by power.

Whoever applies himself to this reading becomes a white horse, when, like a dove, he flutters over streams of water; and, like a flock of shorn sheep, he comes up from the washing, putting on the new man, created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth. The understanding, too, which sits upon the white horse and governs all the senses, has the bow of Holy Scripture, which is now bent taut, now unbent: it is bent when it threatens punishment, unbent when it promises pardon. “And a crown was given to him” (ibid., 2).

[Col. 1126D] We already wear the shaven crown upon the head, but let us seek glory and a good conscience in the mind; and continual reading with attentive devotion is a crown upon the head. Hence Solomon says: “Bind it continually upon your heart, and put it around your throat” (Prov. 6:21). And: “Let it be a necklace upon your neck” (Prov. 1:9). He who meditates on the law has a crown upon his head. He who speaks of the law has “the exaltations of God in his throat” (Ps. 149:6). He who submits to the law has a necklace around his neck.

## CHAPTER XX. On confession

One must rise from reading to confession, in which you accuse yourself of transgressing the commandments of God, whether through negligence, ignorance, or weakness. Yet the confession of cloistered persons should not be coarse and slovenly like that of secular people. Confession is water that is neither muddy, poisonous, nor bituminous, but clear, pure, and clean; it purifies, as though by a second regeneration of baptism, those who have not kept their garments white as snow from the washing of sanctification.

There is one kind of confession before a judge, another to the Lord, another to the Father. Before the judge, one is an accused person; before the Lord, a servant; before the Father, a son. Let the accused seek an advocate; the servant, a scourge; the son, a friend. Let the accused pursue reconciliation; the servant, propitiation; the son, peace. Let the accused offer gifts; the servant, service; the son, himself. Let the accused offer mortification; the servant, correction; the son, a saving offering. Let the accused prostrate himself before the gate; the servant

[Col. 1127B] before the door; the son enter the inner chamber. Let the accused confess great and monstrous crimes; the servant, sins; the son, faults.

Let the accused say: “Do not condemn me” (Job 10:2); let the servant say: “Have mercy on me, O God” (Ps. 50:1); let the son say: “Father, I have sinned” (Luke 15:18), but “spare me” (Job 7:16). He who by departing had become a servant from being a son, and an accused person from being a servant, should by returning become a servant from an accused person and a son from a servant; so that by the same steps by which he had gone into the region of unlikeness, he may return to the likeness of the Father.

And because the image and likeness of God in the soul had been deformed by sinning, through confession let him seek the seal of restoration. Therefore, in confession, let the Lamb now open the second seal: “I heard the second living creature saying: ‘Come and see’” (Apoc. 6:3). The second living creature is Mark,

[Col. 1127C] who roars like a lion in the wilderness, especially treating of the Lord’s preaching and resurrection. Confession is aptly compared to a wilderness, because it is more often deserted than frequented, not only by secular persons but even by religious people. In this wilderness that sinner roared who said: “I roared exceedingly because of the groaning of my heart” (Ps. 17:9).

“And another horse went forth, red” (Apoc. 6:4): allegorically, Christ, who is white in birth and red in passion. Morally, however, the person who confesses his monstrous crimes is put to shame with a blush, and he becomes red through a sprinkling of blood who blushes at his correction. Hence the Apostle: “What fruit, he says, did you then have in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6:21). The red horse is the one who bears

[Col. 1127D] his own shame, saying: “I, a sinner, am not worthy to lift my eyes to heaven” (Luke 18:13). And: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” (Luke 7:6). And: “I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have deserved it” (Mic. 7:9). And “to him who sat upon it”—that is, the fear of the Lord—“it was given to take peace from the earth” (Apoc. 6:4); whence the Lord says: “I came not to send peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10:34). Hence a great sword was given to this one also (Apoc. 6:4).

This great sword devours flesh, and “has been made drunk in heaven.” And: “Cursed is he who restrains his sword from blood” (Jer. 48:10), that is, he who does not cut away by confession the sins which arise from flesh and blood, of which it is said: “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15:50).

## CHAPTER XXI. On true confession and its efficacy

[Col. 1128A]

The sword of confession is “living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow; and a discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Heb. 4:12). And who could express the power of confession in this way? Who could portray its nature and form so aptly? “The word,” he says, “is living.” Where is the dead matter of confession? Where is the lifeless image which has a mouth and does not speak; hands not of Jacob but of Esau—hairy, that is, but not smooth; feet, and does not walk? As a dead man is not a man, and dead faith is not faith, so feigned confession is not confession.

Therefore let the word of confession be living,

[Col. 1128B] so that it may proceed from a living heart and truthful lips, not from the tomb of a dead corpse which rots and stinks. He adds: “And sharper than every two-edged sword.” Grammar, dialectic, and rhetoric are swords with which clerics fight among themselves, and they are deeply skilled in their doctrines and rules; but the word of God and the word of confession are sharper than every two-edged sword, seeking to avoid loss and gain profit, since they not only penetrate into the inward parts of man but also pierce the entrails of the devil’s suggestions and break the gates of hell.

And how? “Reaching even to the division of soul and spirit,” that is, of sensuality and reason. For true confession omits nothing, but accuses every excess both of sensuality and of the higher reason. For it is one thing to sin

[Col. 1128C] from sensuality, which we share with animals; another from reason, which we possess specially through humanity and perhaps share with the angel through divine dispensation. Sins from sensuality are those committed through frailty and sudden impulse; a lesser punishment and penance are owed for them. Sins from reason are committed through deliberation or ambition, and a sharper vengeance threatens them.

He continues: “Of joints also and marrow.” There is a certain joint of soul and spirit: that boundary of reason and sensuality in which it is scarcely discerned to which lot it belongs, to reason or to sensuality. Hence the Apostle says: “I do not understand what I do” (Rom. 7:15), because at that boundary the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against

[Col. 1128D] the flesh (Gal. 5:17), that is, against sensuality. The living word must also determine this boundary, and pursue and investigate sins even into the innermost marrow.

Finally he adds: “A discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” In confession thoughts must be unfolded and intentions examined, so that not even the smallest hoof of sin escapes without coming into God’s sacrifice. For in confession one distinguishes mortal sin from venial sin. But it belongs to few to distinguish night from night—that is, venial from mortal—because many things are reckoned venial which are mortal according to the sinner’s intention. In confession there must be expressed not only the deed, nor only the thought, but also the very intention which makes the entire work either bright or dark. And this is the great sword

[Col. 1129A] given to him who sits upon the red horse; its edge cuts through completely and splits the scales of the ancient Leviathan, each of which is joined to the next so that not even a breath passes between them.

## CHAPTER XXII. On prayer

Therefore, having stripped off the serpent’s skin in confession, washed with leprous Naaman in the waters of the Jordan, and anointed a second time with the boy David, let him lift hands and eyes to the Lord in prayer, that past sins may be blotted out and future ones guarded against. The house of prayer is upheld by these, as by two pillars: if God’s wrath is removed and grace granted. Prayer does both: it extinguishes wrath and implores grace.

One kind of prayer is laborious; another is devout. The laborious prayer extinguishes

[Col. 1129B] wrath; the devout prayer draws forth grace. Yet neither should come to the throne of grace without the other. Rather, let Jacob bring both and bind Leah and Rachel—laborious prayer and devout prayer—together in his household. One night he lies with Leah, another perhaps with Rachel. From each is born offspring: children from Leah, the dearer children from Rachel; both these and those are counted among the seed and number of the patriarchs.
