For according to Leah, the one who labors more will receive a greater reward; and according to Rachel: “To him who does not work, the reward is reckoned not according to merit or debt but according to grace” (Rom. 4:4).

> [Note: [Col. 1129D] Here Peter’s memory failed him; or rather, what I find easier to believe, he altered the Apostle’s words in order to make them accord more closely with his point. For the Vulgate reads: [Col. 1130D] “But to him who works, the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt.”]

When, therefore, grace precedes reward, prayer is called grateful and devout, and is the early rain. Prayer is laborious when the heart is far from the person,

[Col. 1129C] and God far from the heart. The heart is far from a person when it is occupied with superfluous cares, cooled from the fervor of religious life, or immersed in carnal desires. God likewise is far from the heart when he withdraws grace, delays his presence, or tests the patience of the petitioner.

Laborious is the prayer of which Peter says: “Master, we have labored all night and have caught nothing” (Luke 5:5); and of which Job says: “They dig for death as for treasures, and when they find it, they rejoice” (Job 3:21). Again Job says: “I cry out, and you do not hear me” (Job 30:20). And the bride in the Song of Songs: “Upon my bed, by night, I sought him whom my soul loves,” etc. (Song 3:1). And in the Psalm: “You have delayed your Christ” (Ps. 88:39).

Prayer is devout when grace swiftly comes to meet one, anticipates the mind,

[Col. 1129D] is present before being called upon, and grants more than we ask or understand. But when a person knocks at the door of grace, saying: “My prayer will come before you” (Ps. 87:14), and: “My eyes came before you at dawn” (Ps. 118:148), then it is called laborious, and the latter rain. “I will cause,” says the Lord, “the early and latter rain to descend upon you, that I may keep your entrance and your departure” (Joel 2:23).

At one time, when Jesus prayed in his Passion, “his sweat became like drops of blood”; he also frequently prayed in complete tranquility, as there: “Father, glorify your Son”; and a voice came from heaven saying: “I have glorified him, and I will glorify him again” (John 12:23). And the Lord said to the crowd: “This voice came not for my sake, but for yours” (ibid., 30). And to the Father: “For I knew from the beginning that you always hear me” (John 11:42).

Whoever conforms himself to this seal of the Lord’s prayer beholds the example of the same good Master in this as in other matters. For the Apocalypse continues concerning the same subject:

“When he had opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature saying: ‘Come and see’; and I saw. And behold, a black horse; and he who sat upon it had a balance in his hand” (Apoc. 6:5). The third living creature is Luke, physician and evangelist, who prepares draughts for the soul to heal all its infirmities. He begins with prayer thus: “In the days of Herod king of Judaea there was

[Col. 1130B] a certain priest named Zacharias,” etc. And because in Ezekiel’s vision he is represented under the figure of a calf, and a calf is sacrificed to God, he is aptly called a black horse because of the mortification of the cross, which he preached by word and fulfilled in deed.

Christ, who was white in birth and red in passion, is black in death. But he holds the balance of the cross in his hand, because he has power to lay down his soul and power to take it again. When the guilt of the human race and the punishment of the Lord’s body were weighed in this balance, his punishment was found greater than our guilt. Therefore the punishment of Christ’s Passion itself wiped away the guilt of our first parent’s transgression and that of the whole world. That Passion also—what else was it but

[Col. 1130C] his prayer and our reconciliation? Christ therefore rides upon the black horse, for lifted up from the earth he hangs upon the gibbet of the cross.

Let us, cloistered persons or priests, imitate him praying upon the cross, raising pure hands and dovelike eyes to God, confessing the blackness of our sins and, through penance, anticipating death. Hence the Psalmist says: “Ethiopia will hasten her hands to God” (Ps. 67:32). The Ethiopian woman, darkened by the sun and blackened upon coals by the affliction of the flesh and mortification of her limbs, prays, saying: “Turn your face away from my sins” (Ps. 4:11); and: “My bones have dried up like fuel” (Ps. 101:4); and: “I am struck down like grass, and my heart has withered” (ibid., 5).

To the soul thus praying, the bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots” (Song 1:8). As though God rode before the children of Israel upon a black horse, the pillar of cloud by day; and upon a red horse, the pillar of fire by night. Pharaoh’s chariots, however, are horses deceitful for salvation, which run throughout the whole world: pride, deceit, gluttony, and lust, carrying their riders into hell. But Jesus’ cavalry is salvation, of whom it is said: “The chariots of God are manifold, ten thousandfold” (Ps. 67:18). And the Psalmist says to them: “Bring to the Lord, sons of God,” that is, angels; “bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. 28:1), that is, Christians who imitate the apostles and

[Col. 1131A] prophets.

He who sits upon the black horse has a balance in his hand, in which he weighs what he ought to ask concerning temporal things and what concerning eternal things: how continually for eternal things, how moderately for transitory things. Hence what follows: “A two-pound measure of wheat for a denarius, and three two-pound measures of barley for one denarius” (Ps. 24:17). Wheat signifies eternal things, barley temporal things. A simple and single prayer—the two-pound measure of wheat—is for eternal life. Hence: “One thing I have asked of the Lord” (Ps. 26:4). Prayer that is manifold and varied—the three two-pound measures of barley—is for the needs of earthly support. Hence: “Deliver me, Lord, from my necessities” (Ps. 24:17).

“Do not harm the wine and oil” (Apoc. 6:6): that is, do not harm unto condemnation those baptized in Christ and anointed with holy chrism, which is oil, and redeemed by the blood of the Lamb, which is wine. And even if I command you, “Do not harm” the soul, as was said of Job: “But preserve his life” (Job 2:6), nevertheless in the pressure of the winepress I do not wish the treader of grapes to spare. For in this affliction God, while not sparing, spares his faithful. This is enough concerning prayer; we must speak of meditation on death.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On meditation on death

Nothing is more certain than death, nothing more uncertain; nothing more desirable to the good, nothing more hateful to the evil. Its coming is certain; its outcome uncertain. For those who are not of the world and have their citizenship in heaven, it is a welcome departure from prison to kingdom, from shame to glory.

[Col. 1131C] For when death intervenes, naked truth will manifest the glory of the supreme and undivided Trinity, the glory of the Blessed Virgin, the glory of the heavenly powers, and finally the glory of all the saints, in which all things will be new, certain, enduring, wonderful, and lovable. The veil of the present sacraments, which is of blue according to the hope of the kingdom, of purple because of the blood of the Lamb, of twice-dyed scarlet because of the love of the mediator between God and men, and of twisted fine linen because of the purity of the Catholic faith and its indissoluble truth, will then either be removed or torn.

It will be removed according to the saying: “When that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will be done away” (1 Cor. 13:10). It will be torn, as in the Lord’s Passion:

[Col. 1131D] “The veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom” (Mark 15:38), so that the judgment of the great God may be as midday, when the counsels of hearts will be made manifest. And: “There is nothing covered that will not be revealed” (Matt. 10:26).

Therefore let one who expects, once the debt has been paid, the dowry of so great a recompense not fear to pay the debt of death. Yet it is a debt owed and paid by all to all. But the time and hour of payment are not in the debtor’s power or knowledge, but in the Creator’s will. He has set bounds which cannot be passed (Job 14:5). Concerning the payment of death, neither creditor nor exactor can anticipate and seize the day, nor can the debtor defer and prolong it. No one has been granted exemption from this debt or tribute by God; not even the Son of God has been released from it because he is the Son

[Col. 1132A] of Man, although from his origin he was free through immunity from sin. For “the issues of death belong to the Lord, the Lord” (Ps. 67:21).

Therefore we must think, and always think carefully, that through death we may pass over and not remain in death; let death be the lodging of a traveler, not the dwelling place of one dying; release from a burden, not the crushing of calamity; interruption of punishment, not its continuation; a way to the Father, not a wandering away to a host; progress toward the homeland, not sinking into Gehenna; a saving draught, not an infernal potion; finally, an end not of consumption but of consummation.

Before death, mortal guilt must be avoided, or at least wiped out by confession and penance. Before death, provision must be made for living happily after death. Death does not swallow up good merits, but it brings forth even forgotten evil deeds; death heaps together all past works, assigns the eternal dwellings, and places souls not where they would wish, but where they have deserved to be.

[Col. 1132B] To be certain concerning uncertainties, hold fast to certainties and do not follow uncertainties. For the Apostle runs not uncertainly, but with certainty, because neither death nor life can separate him from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus (Rom. 8:38–39). Certain faith, certain hope, certain charity, certain obedience, certain humility, certain chastity, certain observance of the Christian religion and of your profession will make you certain.

Paint death before your eyes: how dreadful its face, how dark and grim its countenance, and what the individual offices of each of its members accomplish in the individual members of the human being. For they devour and consume like tender grass whatever strength and vigor there is in a person, both in the soul and body of the damned; hence in the Psalm: “Death will feed upon them” (Ps. 68:15).

Therefore, that the Lord may draw us from the belly of this whale, let us anticipate its face in confession, so that he who pierced its jaw with a ring may free us from eternal death. The divinity hidden in Jesus’ flesh broke the harmful molar teeth in its mouth when, in rash biting, it bit the flesh of the Word. Therefore, even if it bites us like a serpent and a horned viper, if we bear before our hands the horns of the cross and carry the blood of the Lamb upon both doorposts and upon the lintels, that entire

[Col. 1132D] dreadful armor of Leviathan which is described in Job will be destroyed, and its entrails will be pierced and searched out by this dart.

O sulphurous pit! O intolerable stench! O confinement! O darkness! O heat! O gnashing of teeth! O shame! O pain! O despair! O desolation without consolation! Evil without end; an issue without restoration! Would that I had before my sight the recompense which death repays for evil pleasures. What may lessen death’s bitterness and make bearable what is unavoidable must be obtained by long forethought and preparation.

There are remedies that mitigate death: confession of sins and penance against the aerial powers; the fortification of the holy cross; the provision of the Lord’s body and blood for the comfort of so great and so unknown

[Col. 1133A] a journey; the oil of anointing to sustain the lamp of conscience and dispel the thick darkness of death; God’s protection, the help of all the saints, and the prayers of the brethren. By these remedies the second death either succumbs or gives way; the first, indeed, may rage in its accustomed manner against mortal man, but it is weakened and does not hold the soul in its nets when it sees it defended by such great forces. It fears the power of the cross; it knows that a traveler passing on with the viaticum cannot possibly fail; it remembers that true penance and confession have powerfully drawn countless souls from its womb and infernal belly; and by experience it knows that it has never been able to resist God’s will or harm human bodies or souls if the help of the saints comes to their aid.

[Col. 1133B] It flees the prayers of the brethren as fiery arrows. From all these things let us make lumps that burst the inward parts of the devil, death, and hell, and cast them into the dragon’s mouth with Daniel. In the cloister this compound should be prepared by those who always think themselves about to die, who, like the palm tree, multiply their days while looking upward, and who mortify vices in themselves. Death has no power over these, who have power to tread upon serpents that killed the children of Israel in the wilderness, and scorpions that lie in wait for our heel.

O soul released from the body, where do you dwell? In heaven, or paradise, or purgatorial fire, or hell? If in heaven, you are blessed with the angels; if in paradise, safe from these miseries; if in purgatorial fire, anxious concerning punishments, yet awaiting

[Col. 1133C] deliverance; if in hell, in despair, you await not misery but truth and severity. O soul without a body, where is your body now? Where is your brother Abel? Behold the worms; behold the moth; behold the decay that was once in your bones. But what of you? Do you ask Abraham to send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool your tongue? Do you have the flame of punishment in part or in whole? Is there hope of escape?

O soul, if you are in hell, your eye will not return to see good things. If you are in purgatorial fire, the Babylonian furnace burns less fiercely, whose flame rose forty-nine cubits. The most cruel Ethiopians are intent upon supplying to the fire of purgatory wood, hay, stubble, and also pitch and firebrands, which they have industriously gathered and maliciously stored from the forest of our evils; and until a voice comes from the throne of grace, they do not cease to scourge the wretched soul.

[Col. 1133D] O soul, whether blessed or wretched, how useful it would be for the soul still journeying in the body to see and hear you, who have not forgotten our lot and have already experienced your own. Behold, you have a balance in your hand, weighing in it what you deserved in the body and what you received outside the body. Here, here human beings are deceitful, paying no heed in judgment to the prepared balance which with an even beam weighs punishment and guilt, inclining neither to the right nor the left.

In the present life, mercy is mingled with justice and justice with mercy: God inclines from the cup which is in his hand, from this part of mercy into that of justice, and from this part of justice into that of mercy.

[Col. 1134A] But in the future judgment there will be justice without mercy for the one who did not show mercy; for then there will be no oil to buy. Now it is said: “Do not harm the wine and oil” (Apoc. 6:6), because correction and compassion are necessary to heal the man left half-dead by robbers. At judgment correction will be severe, because it will not be a time for sowing but for reaping. Compassion also will be vain where no mercy has gone before.

The soul in the body smells these things but does not taste them, like ships bearing fruit; but the soul that has put into harbor already tastes what flavor the ages to come have.

[Col. 1134B] Of meditation on death it is also said: “In my meditation a fire will burn” (Ps. 38:4): certainly the fire of which it is said, “Their worms shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. 66:24). Yet it is remarkable how meditated death causes fire to burn, though death, being cold, takes away and extinguishes all vital heat. But when is fire kindled except in winter? Thus one contrary is repelled by another, and fire is sought when the numbness of cold prevails.

[Col. 1134B] What, then, does the burning fire accomplish in meditation on death? It burns wood, hay, stubble, and chaff, reducing worldly pleasures to ashes. For death, occupying the whole mind, makes all temporal things seem of little worth. Who, after all, when submerged in waters, loves the waters that submerge him? And do not the lust of the eyes, the lust of the flesh, and the pride of life sink their possessor into the deepest hell?

Leviathan swims in these waters and lies hidden in ambush, in order either to submerge those who carelessly approach him or to burn them by casting smoke from his nostrils like a heated and boiling pot. Hence Job says: “From his nostrils smoke proceeds as from a heated and boiling pot” (Job 41:11). His breath makes coals burn, and flame issues from his mouth. The smoke, of which it is said, “Smoke rose in his wrath” (Ps. 57:9), produces darkness of the eyes; but darkness is beneath God’s feet. The flame from the dragon’s mouth is that of which it is said: “Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun” (Ps. 57:9): namely, evil desire, which makes the coals burn,

[Col. 1134D] while it deceives the soul here or draws it at death to punishment.

> [Note: [Col. 1133D] Gregory, Homily 27 on the Gospels.]

Against these things the bride’s nose, like a tower looking toward Damascus, meditates upon death against death; for missiles foreseen strike less severely, and there is no beast so savage that it is not tamed and softened by continual training. Thus death, coming neither unknown because of meditation nor unforeseen because of expectation—not rushing upon us, but penetrating our open doors without breaking through; entering, not bursting in; awakening, not striking the side of the sleeper—is received by us quite calmly and not with horror.

For it comes as a good messenger, not as a hostile adversary; it conveys a command, it does not inflict punishment; for it does not exceed the limits of its command and can do nothing of itself.

[Col. 1135A] “With bit and bridle he will break their jaws” (Ps. 31:9), God the righteous Judge, so that, when shell and husk are broken, the kernel of glory which God has hidden for those who fear him may fill the inmost parts of the blessed.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On meditation on the death of Christ, of man, and of the devil
And when he had opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature saying: “Come and see.” And behold, a pale horse (Rev. VI, 7). Observe that in the three preceding instances he says, “one living creature,” “the second living creature,” “the third living creature”; but in the fourth he writes not that he heard the fourth living creature, but “the voice of the fourth living creature.” For John the Evangelist is the voice of the Word, who thus begins his Gospel: “In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word,” etc. The pale horse is he who, before the Passion, [Col. 1135B] began to fear and be distressed, saying: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. XXVI, 38). And his name is Death, he who is now dead because of our offences; and in Hosea he says: “I will be thy death, O death” (Hos. XIII, 14); and according to those who say: “His name shall die no more” (Jer. XI, 19). And hell followed him below, according to that saying: “They have laid me, as though condemned, in the lower pit, in darkness, and in the shadow of death” (Ps. LXXXVII, 7).

Therefore the death of Christ, the death of the devil, and the death of man belong to the meditation on death. Christ’s death killed death in the devil, so that it should no longer live; in man, so that it should not remain. In the devil, so that it might perish; in man, so that he might not perish. In the devil, so that it might not reign; in man, so that he might not be enslaved. In the devil, [Col. 1135C] so that it might not rage; in man, so that he might not fear it. In the devil, so that it might not deceive; in man, so that he might not believe it. In the devil, so that it might despair of life; in man, so that through death he might aspire to life.

Meditation on Christ’s death visits the sick; meditation on the devil’s death strengthens the weak; meditation on one’s own death humbles the proud. Meditation on Christ’s death is a saving draught; meditation on the devil’s death is a purging of pride; meditation on one’s own death is the restoration or preservation of health. Meditation on Christ’s death extinguishes poisons; meditation on the devil’s death dissolves an abscess; meditation on one’s own death applies a plaster to the disease. The pale horse is he who mortifies himself in these meditations in order to punish death, and meanwhile submits his neck to death, yet in death leaps up from beneath the yoke of the one who comes.

[Col. 1135D] Concerning the meditation on death, the Lord says to Job: “Have the gates of death been opened to thee, and hast thou seen the shadowy doors?” (Job XXXVIII, 17). To God, before whom all things are naked and open, who measures the earth with his palm and holds all things in his fist from the highest hinge of heaven to the deepest depth of hell, nothing is closed. His eternal power enters and goes out through every province of his kingdom, with none resisting, because “Whatsoever he willeth, he doeth in heaven, and on earth, and in all the deep places” (Ps. CXXXIV, 6). To him undoubtedly the gates of death stand open, so that, when he willed, he might enter and go out, bring in whom he willed, and recall whom he willed.

But to none of the saints are they opened except through Jesus, so that every human being departing this world must inevitably enter through them into the age to come, whether to punishment or to glory. [Col. 1136A] There are gates of death, gates of hell, gates of the world, gates of the cloister, and finally gates of heaven. Of the gates of death it is said in the Psalm: “Thou who liftest me up from the gates of death, that I may declare all thy praises in the gates of the daughter of Sion” (Ps. IX, 15). Of the gates of hell it is said in the Gospel: “Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI, 18). And: “I shall go to the gates of hell” (Isa. XXXVIII, 11). The gates of the world are entrance into life and departure from life. The gates of the cloister are regular profession, with observance and the hope of renunciation [perhaps: recompense]. The gates of heaven are the holy angels and ministering spirits, who are sent on account of those who receive the inheritance of salvation.

[Col. 1136B] The gates of death are penal; the gates of hell abominable; the gates of the world dangerous; the gates of the cloister religious; the gates of heaven glorious. The Lord passed through the gates of death; he broke the gates of hell; he entered and departed through the gates of the world without a bolt; by his life on earth and by his death he fashioned the gates of the cloister; in his Ascension he opened the gates of heaven. The gate of death turns upon a harassing hinge; the gate of hell upon a punishing hinge; the gate of the world upon a changing hinge; the gate of the cloister upon a meritorious hinge; the gate of heaven upon a rewarding hinge. A holy angel guards the gate of heaven; a good prelate, the gate of the cloister; daily failure, the gate of the world; the condemned devil, the gate of hell; the prince of this world, the gates of death.

The key of heaven is glory; the key of the cloister is the rule; the key of the world is vanity; the key of [Col. 1136C] hell is everlasting punishment; the key of death is the divine sentence. At the gate of heaven there is rejoicing at the end of labours; at the gate of the cloister, purification from sins; at the gate of the world, uncertain occupation; at the gate of hell, despair; at the gate of death, trembling. Noon belongs to the gate of heaven; dawn to the gate of the cloister; twilight to the gate of the world; evening or night to the gate of death; midnight to the gate of hell. At the resurrection of the dead the gates of death will be opened, because we shall all rise; but not the gates of hell, because we shall not all be changed. At departure, the gates of the cloister and of the world are opened; after judgment, [the gates of heaven].

He says, then: “Have the gates of death been opened to thee, and hast thou seen the shadowy doors?” (Job XXXVIII, 17), as if to say: [Col. 1136D] Is your conscience now pure, and is your life so secure through my grace, that you await death without fear? And when it comes like wormwood, will you swallow it, entering its gates without toil and departing without difficulty? “And hast thou seen the shadowy doors?” If you have oil in your lamp, you will not strike your foot against the shadowy doors, because you will direct your steps according to God’s word, in which there is no darkness.

## CHAPTER XXV. On participation in the body and blood of the Lord

In the discipline of the cloister, what is especially necessary must not be omitted, and must also be committed most deeply to memory. For the Eucharist holds in the body of the Church the place which the human heart holds in [Col. 1137A] a human being: with a whole and healthy heart one lives; with a corrupted and wounded heart one dies. Hence Solomon says: “Keep thy heart with all watchfulness, for from it life proceeds” (Prov. IV, 23). And the Lord says of his body in the Gospel: “He who eats me, he too shall live because of me” (John VI, 58).

It is the life of the angel, into which angels desire to look; it is the life of the Christian, through which he may advance. One who lives in the flesh and according to the flesh receives this life in one way; another who sows in the Spirit, in order to reap eternal life from the Spirit, in another; those whose “mouth is full of cursing and bitterness” (Ps. XIII, 3) in another; those who “hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. V, 6) in another; and those to whom it is said: “You are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you” (Rom. [Col. 1137B] VIII, 9), in another. Likewise, he who says: “Yet I live, now not I; but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II, 20), whom I love with all my heart, with all my soul, and with all my strength.

Such a heart thinks, loves, and desires God alone; the soul proclaims God through every spectacle and ever breathes and sighs toward God. Strength can do all things in him who strengthens himself, and can do nothing without him who says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5). Whoever is thus occupied with God and by God in the morning hours, under the urging of holy hunger, is daily refreshed by communion in the Lord’s body and blood. Yet, according to the Apostle, one must distinguish between this spiritual food and daily bodily food; for with the greatest discernment one must consider when one should approach Christ’s body, when one should give way, and when one should withdraw.

[Col. 1137C] To approach Christ is to approach the Lord, to approach the king, to approach light, fire, bread, the vine—indeed, life. Do you seek freedom? Approach the Lord. Do you seek security? Approach the king. Do you seek brightness? Approach the light. Do you seek warmth? Approach the fire. Do you seek refreshment? Approach the bread. Do you seek drink? Approach the vine. Do you seek resurrection? Approach life.

Have you offended the Lord? Give way. Have you acted against the king? Give way. Are you blind or bleary-eyed? Give way from the light. Do you bear strange fire upon your loins or in your hands? Give way, lest the fire from the altar consume you. Are you full of murmuring and sated with opposition? Give way, and do not approach the bread of angels. Are you drunk from the vineyard of Sodom and Gomorrah? [Col. 1137D] Give way, and do not approach the wine from the vineyard of Sorech. Are you dead through grave sins and buried in hell? Give way.

Yet there is a great difference between giving way and withdrawing. To give way belongs to reverence; to withdraw belongs to irreverence. He gives way who says: “Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldest enter under my roof” (Luke VII, 6); he withdraws who says: “Behold, thou drivest me from thy face” (Gen. IV, 14), and: “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve pardon” (ibid., 13–14). Jonah too, fleeing and withdrawing from the face of the Lord, was swallowed in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights. And the Psalmist says: “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity” (Ps. VI, 8). What, then, is the end of those who withdraw from God? “All who remove themselves far from thee shall perish” (Ps. LXXII, 27). Therefore, when I have sinned, I give way; I do not withdraw if I have confessed my error and amended it.

[Col. 1138A] But one must consider still more carefully when, how, and why one should approach communion. The benefit of this refreshment has a discernment of time, a determination of manner, and also an account of cause. In time three things are considered: suitability, custom, and solemnity. In manner: purification, intention, and devotion. In cause: institution, benefit, and necessity. What has here been enumerated must briefly be reviewed and explained.

Suitability escapes and drives away distraction; this service must be performed with minds at liberty and with obedience rendered to God. Custom removes lay negligence and excessive sluggishness concerning one’s own salvation. It is enough for a layperson to communicate once [Col. 1138B] a year; but devout and solicitous Mary, sitting at the Lord’s feet with our cloistered brethren, is not thus satisfied—her eye is not sated with seeing nor her ear with hearing. Thus she daily receives the angelic bread, that is, the Lord’s sacrament, and daily nonetheless hungers, according to the saying: “They that eat me shall yet hunger; and they that drink me shall yet thirst” (Ecclus. XXIV, 29). An approaching solemnity also admonishes us to approach communion. What solemnity is there where hunger and want are? Where there is not food that perishes not but remains unto eternal life, there is want and deadly poverty. Therefore let the solemnity of the saints have and provide solemn food.

This has been said of time. Let us consider the manner, which includes purification, intention, and devotion. Of a certain holy man it is said, [Col. 1138C] that Christ “purified his sins” (Ecclus. XLVII). And the Apostle says of Christ to the Hebrews: “Bearing all things by the word of his power, making purification of sins, he sits at the right hand of Majesty on high” (Heb. I, 3).

O my heart, my soul, my mouth, my lips, my throat, my tongue, my stomach! What is upon the altar? Is it not the body taken from the Virgin Mary, the body conceived of the Holy Spirit, the body that suffered on the cross and was buried in a new tomb; the body that on the third day rose from the dead, that ascended above all heavens, and that sits at the right hand of the Father on high; the body in which Jesus, judge of living and dead, shall judge the living and the dead and the world [Col. 1138D] through fire? What then are you, all my inward and outward parts? How will you receive one so chaste, so holy, so pure, when you are defiled with such impure menstrual uncleannesses, such damnable, continual, and unspeakable faults?

Therefore our stains must first be cleansed by the water of compunction, the fire of brotherly compassion, the hyssop of faith and most humble confession, and the ashes of most salutary submission and mortification. Of this purification the Apostle says to the Hebrews: “Having confidence in entering the holy places by the blood of Jesus Christ, the spotless Lamb, because he has inaugurated for us a new and living way through the veil, that is, his flesh, and a great priest over the house of God, let us approach with a true heart in the fullness of faith, our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water; let us hold fast the unbending confession of our hope” (Heb. X, 19).

[Col. 1139A] Let him enter securely to the altar of God and approach with confidence the communion of the Lord’s body who has a heart sprinkled—that is, cleansed—from an evil conscience, and a body washed both by the sanctification of baptism and by the compunction of devotion, and who holds the unbending confession of hope. Observe “unbending confession,” so that his feet may be straight feet: accusing himself concerning himself, not complaining against the Creator or the devil. For “God is not a tempter of evils” (Jas. I, 13); and the devil tempts, but not without permission nor beyond permission: “But every man is tempted, drawn away and enticed by his own concupiscence” (ibid., 14).

Let us now speak of intention, [Col. 1139B] which is threefold: one kind good, another bad, another worst. It is good if Christ’s body is received with true faith and a conscience pure from every crime, so that Christ’s blood may justify the righteous still more: this person receives in order that he may become good. It is bad when it is placed in a vessel dried by hatred, defiled by lust, and corrupted by malice—not so that one who is bad may become good, but so that one who is bad may appear good. Such a one is a hypocrite. It is worst when someone irreverently approaches the Lord’s sacrament like a rabid dog, with a most evil heart, not in order to become good, but so that Antichrist may lie concealed beneath Christ. Such a one is a ravening wolf who devours the lamb beneath a sheep’s skin, covering his shame with fig leaves—not for remission, like him “whose sins are covered and whose iniquities are forgiven,” but as Adam and Eve sewed fig leaves together in Paradise: not accusing themselves, but excusing themselves.

[Col. 1139C] Therefore let the intention in receiving the Eucharist be: for the good, sanctification; for the bad, correction; for the worst, compunction. For God sends the crystal of his most chaste body like little morsels, so that the weak may be healed, the hungry satisfied, and the healthy made rich and strengthened. The intention is expressed in the prayer which says: “Let it not be for us guilt unto punishment, but saving intercession unto pardon; let it be washing away of crimes, strength for the frail, defence against the perils of the world, and remission of all sins for faithful living and dead.” Let us speak of devotion.

[Col. 1139D] Devotion too is threefold: one kind compunctive, another sighing, another tearful. Compunctive devotion is a spring welling forth; sighing devotion is a spring leaping up; tearful devotion is a spring boiling over. Compunctive devotion pierces; sighing devotion draws forth; tearful devotion pours out and rains. Fear pierces, hope draws forth, love rains. Fear constricts the vein; hope opens it; love brings forth the moisture with the impetus of the spirit.

Thus, diminished by the blood of sin, by bonds, by iron, and by the voluntary movement of the heart, let him say to the Lord: “I will sacrifice to thee willingly” (Ps. LIII, 8)—to thee who didst stand bound before the governor, hang fastened with nails upon the wood, and, pierced by the spear, didst give blood and water; who wast offered as though not compelled, as though thou hadst not willed it, yet wast devout and voluntary because thou didst will it.

We must now speak of the cause, in which we noted three things: institution, benefit, and necessity. [Col. 1140A] In considering the institution, we must ask who instituted this sacrament, for whom, when, and how. Who? Christ. For whom? The apostles. When? At the last supper. How? “Taking bread, he blessed and broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take and eat of this, all of you: this is my body.’ Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: ‘Take and drink of this, all of you: this is the cup of my blood, which shall be poured out for you and for many. Do this in memory of me’” (Matt. XXVI, 26; Mark XIV, 23; Luke XXII, 17; 1 Cor. 2, 24).

In the agent I recognize goodness, knowledge, and power: goodness, because he willed it; knowledge, because on his departure he prepared, to comfort [Col. 1140B] his absence, an antidote sufficient for future diseases and easily obtainable; power, because he could and can do what a human being can scarcely believe and cannot in any way define. In the apostles I contemplate friendship, obedience, and reverence: friendship, then indeed still tender as grass, but after receiving the Spirit, firm as fire; obedience unto the division of soul and spirit, unto death, unto the cross, unto beheading; reverence toward him as teacher, as Lord, as father—indeed, as God. Hence: “Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God” (John II, 27).

In the time, I consider the strongest cement, [Col. 1140C] the most powerful proof, the most excellent gift, which he had hitherto kept in reserve and had from eternity predestined to give to his friends in bodily separation. The cement is Christ’s body, binding together into one the God received and the Christian who receives him, according to the Apostle, who says: “The bread which we bless, is it not a communion in the Lord’s body? And the cup which we bless, is it not a communion in the Lord’s blood?” (2 Cor. XVIII, 16). It is also a convincing and necessary proof of divine love, because he would never have given himself to us if he had not loved us especially. What, moreover, is better in heaven and on earth than Jesus, what dearer, what more precious? For this is “the best gift and the perfect gift,” descending from the Father of lights.

[Col. 1140D] The Father had indeed given his Son Jesus incarnate to humankind, but on the condition that, after fulfilling the office of his embassy, he should receive him back in the humanity assumed. Then he added grace upon grace: under another species yet in the same truth, he gave the same Son Jesus not only as companion on the journey, but as provision for the whole pilgrimage, so that he who had once redeemed us by visible suffering might always strengthen us by invisible refreshment.

How the Lord handed over his body to the apostles, the Apostle teaches the Corinthians and the Evangelists show more fully. For he took bread—he who had created bread itself—and by the same power by which he had first created it for the bodily refreshment of human beings, through thanksgiving to the Father and blessing with the Father, changed it into the substance of his body for the redemption of souls and bodies. Likewise also the cup.

Let us now consider the benefit. [Col. 1141A] The preceding commandment was set aside because of its uselessness and weakness. For the Law “brought nothing to perfection”; and if the former had been free from fault, a place for the second would certainly not have been sought. But Christ was “offered once to exhaust the sins of many” (Heb. IX, 28). And: “Offering one sacrifice for sins, he sits at the right hand of God” (Heb. X, 12). Strength must be sought against weakness, usefulness against uselessness: the Gospel succeeds the Law as strength. Hear the Apostle: “I am not ashamed,” he says, “of the Gospel, for it is the power of God unto salvation to every believer” (Rom. I, 16).

What of Christ’s body? “Sacrifices and offerings thou didst not desire, but thou hast prepared a body for me” (Ps. XXXIX, 7). Is this the body of Christ? Again the Apostle says: “What is weak in God”—that is, the assumed body—“is stronger than men” (1 Cor. I, 25). Elijah found at his head an ash-cake and walked in the strength of that food forty days. And do you doubt that in the strength of the bread which came down from heaven you can walk, not merely to Horeb, the mountain of God, but to the mountain in which God was pleased to dwell? Therefore there are strength and health in Christ’s body. Thus the power of the Eucharist, like health, excludes weakness. Hence the saying: “Health under his wings” (Mal. IV, 2).

[Col. 1141B] Under the wings of the visible species of bread and wine, as beneath the swaddling clothes of faith in the manger of the altar. Hence the angel said to the shepherds: “You shall find the infant, who is eternal in his own things, wrapped in swaddling clothes” (Luke II, 12), namely, according to Adam, in garments of skin. But what lies hidden [Col. 1141C] under these—whether garments, skins, wings, or swaddling clothes? Certainly power, for the power of God was in him. Thus, when weakness is excluded by power, uselessness is excluded by usefulness.

Grasp the apostolic sense: the blood of a heifer was sprinkled for the emulation of the flesh; it brought nothing to perfection and seated no one at God’s right hand. But the living sacrifice, the holy sacrifice, the immaculate sacrifice fulfils all these things, and by its threefold effect grants cleansing, sanctification, and fellowship not merely with angels but with God. For communion in the Lord’s body and in the sprinkled blood of Jesus Christ, the spotless Lamb, cleanses us from the greatest offence and from every sin. Hence [Col. 1141D] John the Baptist says: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I, 29). And John the Evangelist says in the Apocalypse: “Who washed us in his blood” (Rev. I, 5).

Of sanctification he also says in the Gospel: “And for them I sanctify myself, that they too may be holy” (John XVII, 19). And the Apostle says to the Hebrews: “He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all in him” (Heb. II, 11); and concerning the Passion: “I go to be sacrificed for you.” Therefore the Eucharist cleanses our conscience from dead works, and likewise sanctifies it in the Lord’s ordinances, so that one who sits at a rich man’s table may carefully consider what is set before him, knowing that he ought to prepare such things (Prov. XXIII, 1, according to the Septuagint), so as to offer chaste hospitality to the chaste, devout to the devout, just to the just, pure to the pure, holy to the holy. Hence the Apostle Peter says: “Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps,” etc. (1 Pet. II, 22). Thus cleansed, thus sanctified, we are companions in sanctification; thus we shall also be companions in glorification or consolation.

[Col. 1142A] Hence John says in his Epistle: “What we have seen and heard, we declare unto you, that you too may have fellowship with us; and your fellowship may be with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ” (1 John I, 2). O fellowship—not leonine, which devours its companion; not canine, which snarls and grumbles within its jaws, barks openly, and hunts after the soul of the righteous; not raven-like, which ever bites and croaks over corpses; but sheep-like, which covers what is foul with its fleece and warms what is cold; lamb-like, [Col. 1142B] which gives itself over to death that it may feed its friends; dove-like, which sees all things with a single eye and removes all bitterness, wrath, and indignation. O fellowship, which bears or removes our evils and bestows its own goods; which asks from us nothing except what it has given, receives nothing which it has kept for our own use, never cheats in business but always gives aid by eternal help; which lays out all that is its own and orders all that is ours.

Behold, we have said a few things concerning the benefit of the Eucharist, which sanctifies and gives fellowship with God. Let us finally consider necessity. It too is threefold. [Col. 1142C] One necessity arises from the authority of a decree; another from the obligation of a promised vow; another from impossibility or difficulty in thing, reason, and fact. From the authority of a decree, as: “On whatever day thou shalt eat, thou shalt die by death” (Gen. II, 17). From this decree every human being is mortal. Again, from the obligation of a vow: every Christian is bound by the promise made in baptism; a monk and canon by religious profession; a priest and every ordained person by consecration to holy orders. Therefore, by the necessity through which a human being dies because he tasted what was forbidden, he who has violated the covenant of his vow is condemned. Hence the prophet says: “He who breaks the covenant, shall he escape?” (Ezek. XVII, 15). He shall not escape; and: “It is better not to vow than to vow and not perform vows” (Eccles. V, 4).

[Col. 1142D] Again, one necessity arises from God’s difficulty or impossibility: for example, what is white necessarily is not black, because nothing white is simultaneously black. From the impossibility of reason: a stone is not a human being, because a stone is insensible and a human being sensible. From the impossibility of fact: a human being does not touch heaven with his finger.

But let us return to the matter at hand. Every Christian must receive the Eucharist by the authority of the decree: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you” (John VI, 54). By obligation of vow we are bound to renounce the devil and his pomps, and thus to communicate. But if we break the vow and communicate, what does the Apostle say? “He who receives unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself” (1 Cor. XI, 29). Therefore we must communicate—and worthily.

The reality, with the visible sacrament and the invisible power, shows one thing and stores up another. The visible sacrament presents itself outwardly; it contains and offers inwardly, to pure hearts, its invisible power. If you approach it wholly, you will have it wholly; if only partially, then only half—namely, the sacrament, not the reality of the sacrament. You will be a branch in the vine which bears no fruit, but is cut off and cast into the fire. Therefore approach worthily a reality so worthy; and he who never fails anyone worthy will not be lacking. If he has failed anyone, that person was not worthy. He approaches worthily who yields to no mortal sin and humbly makes daily satisfaction for venial sins.

[Col. 1143A] Next, our reason sees little in so great a ray of the sun—or is blind. It sees little because of the bleary weakness of natural ignorance; or it is blind because of the unbearable brilliance of the divine work. If it walks in its own customary tracks, it will not grasp the wisdom of this [Col. 1143B] mystery, which is hidden from the eyes of all living things. But if it leans upon its beloved, who illumines the darkness of that same reason with the true light, now by faith and afterwards by reality, then, sated from his breasts, which are above all spices, it will say: “I hold him by faith and love, and I shall not let him go until he bring me into the house of his mother Mary and into the chamber of his mother, grace, from whom Jesus was conceived and born, the creator and illuminator of all reason.”

[Col. 1143C] Come then, reason, to the altar, not with proud eye and outstretched neck, but with knee bent and face lowered to the earth, worshipping the footstool of the Eucharist, not disputing or judging why or how this happens. For the Lord says to Peter: “What thou knowest not now, thou shalt know hereafter” (John XIII, 7). Are you better than Peter? Are you more familiar with God? Peter, the most beloved disciple, to whom the Father had revealed that Christ was the Son of the living God, had not yet learned; and do you, by disputing, examining, and defining, wish to strip to ashes the king’s bones, which are hidden until “a time and times”? Wait in prayer until *Sela* grows, which is interpreted “his shadow”; until the morning star rises in our hearts, who will tell us all things that he has heard from his Father and make all of us teachable by God.

[Col. 1144A] It remains to speak of fact. This is a wonderful fact, a delightful fact; hence the Psalmist says: “Thou hast delighted me, O Lord, in thy making” (Ps. XCI, 4). This fact is impossible among human beings: that God should die, that the Lord of glory should be crucified, that bread should become Christ’s flesh and wine his blood. But with God all things are possible. In God there is no labour in doing great, difficult, and impossible things: it is as easy for him to make all things as it is ready for him to will them. Indeed, for every human being it is one thing to will, another to suffer, another to do; but there is no delay and no difference between God’s willing and God’s doing.

Yet this is according to what is ours, not according to what is his—unless perhaps you say that what is ours is his because it was assumed by him, and that what was ours only by the property of nature has now become his by condescension and assumption. Therefore, in that which is ours and his, he willed something according to us and something according to himself; but he subjected what he willed according to us to what he willed according to himself, saying to the Father: “Not my will, but thine be done” (Luke XXII, 42). He did something according to us, and something according to himself. He was conceived, born, wearied, suffered, and died according to us. He was worshipped, gave sight to the blind, cleansed lepers, raised the dead, and did such things according to himself. Yet he is one and the same, both according to us and according to himself, God and man, and man and God.

Finally, he suffered not according to himself but only according to us, because it was in that which is ours and his, not in that which is his and his. Therefore, what he suffered on the cross and what he does in the cup seem impossible if we look to ourselves; if we look to him, they are easy and possible. This deed, more necessary for our redemption than can be spoken, more than any merit can attain, is merciful and holy. And let these remarks on necessity suffice.

## EPILOGUE

[Col. 1143]

[Col. 1143C] It is a great labour to put one’s hand to these mighty tasks and, with Joshua, to continue the battle against enemies; but great rewards are not attained except through many labours. By right, merit and reward would advance with equal steps; but by grace the reward exceeds. It is no wonder to be enclosed for a short time in the narrow cave of the cloister and afterwards to possess the infinite spaces of heaven with eternity; to dry out muddy flesh by abstinence and receive in the resurrection a spiritual body, without any burden, with the angels; to exchange worldly tumults for angelic harmonies, consolation for desolation, riches for poverty, glory for subjection, God the Father for one’s father, God the Son for one’s children, and God the Holy Spirit for every kinship and carnal affection. No seller has ever sold thus; no buyer has ever bought thus; no merchant has ever made such an exchange.

Yet “thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and so to enter into his glory” (Luke XXIV, 26). Thus [Col. 1144C] he who restored all things in heaven and on earth both made the exchange and taught others to make it. He who “learned obedience from the things which he suffered,” that is, the virtue and glory of obedience. This hope is laid up in the bosom of cloistered persons: it neither grows lukewarm in winter cold nor dries up in summer heat; it does not contemplate things that pass away in time, but those that endure eternally. It understands that laborious discipline has an end and perpetual glory follows.

Now that the pledge has been tasted beforehand, patience—which without hope would be bitter—grows sweet. Weariness will be changed into desire, vexation into delight, delay into welcome sustenance, just as, for love of Rachel, the days seemed few to Jacob. Conversely, let the one who is in the cloister and murmurs, grating like the wheel of a cart loaded with hay; who says, “This saying is hard” (John VI, 61); who, like Jordan, turns backward; who murmurs for meat; who is in the rebellion of Korah against Moses—that is, the abbot; who in Gideon’s army [Col. 1145A] drinks water with bent knee and does not lap like a dog, seeking not nature’s necessities but its desires—hear this: “It would have been better not to have known the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn backward” (John [Col. 1146A] VI, 61). Those who break Peter’s net, darken the moon, and call sweet bitter and bitter sweet must be rebuked, corrected, and wept over. Yet “they are multiplied beyond number” (Ps. XXVIX, 6).

## EXHORTATION TO THOSE IN THE CLOISTER

[Col. 1145]

[Col. 1145A] “Put on the armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and to stand perfect in all things” (Eph. 6:11). Hence: “You are beautiful and comely, terrible as an ordered army in battle array” (Song 6:3). Be an army; be terrible. Every army that is not ordered is not terrible; and if it is not terrible, it cannot be the Lord’s army. For the things that are from God are ordered. You know that those concerned with military affairs station slingers and archers in their proper places, standard-bearers where they belong, the strength of the battle in reserve, [Col. 1145B] and weaker men in safer positions, because they cannot bear the attack of their opponents. Thus the battle line itself, being ordered, will be terrible to its enemies, because it leaves them no opening by which to enter it.

So the army of God’s camp must proceed in ordered fashion through the plains and rough places of this world, lest it leave any opening whatsoever to an enemy eager to attack; if it leaves one, it will offer its hand captive to the victor. This care of arranging the battle line belongs to prelates, who ought, by the impulse of fatherly affection—not under the pretext of proud domination—to know kindly the capacities of all and place each person in his suitable position. Those whom they see to be strong and tested by good conduct they should send out on external business: not the inexperienced, not the greedy, not the restless, not the irascible, but [Col. 1146A] the gentle and humble. They should cherish in the bosom of the cloister all who are weak and inflamed by the heat of secular life. If anyone has been wounded by the dart of temptations, they should heal him with wholesome counsels. Thus arranged, it will be terrible to him who goes about seeking whom he may devour.

Yet each one of us must also order himself, so that he may be beautiful within, so that his glory may be from within: comely and ordered in conduct, devout, chaste, patient, humble, gracious, compassionate, and loving. For when the devil sees persons compacted and united by charity, [Col. 1146B] he greatly abhors them; but those who lack it he attacks without fear. Hence Gregory says:

> Whatever good things may be in us, if charity is lacking through the evil of discord, a place is found in the battle line where the enemy may enter. He does not fear chastity without charity, because he is not tempted by the flesh; he does not fear abstinence, because he does not use food; he does not fear the distribution of goods, because he has no need of riches. But if he finds in us the true unity of charity, he fears it and exceedingly envies concord, because he sees it held on earth which he himself lost in heaven.

Therefore it is rightly said, “Terrible as an ordered army in battle array,” because wicked spirits dread the number of the elect, whom they see fortified by concord.

## In the Year of the Lord 1187: Gilbert Foliot, Bishop of London

[Col. 1145]

## Historical Notice

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, I, 174; II, 56.)

Gilbert Foliot, an Englishman, formerly abbot of Leicester and archdeacon of Middlesex, became bishop of Hereford in 1149, and bishop of London from 1161 until 1187. He wrote Homilies, still unpublished, manuscript copies of which occur in the British Museum and elsewhere; and an Exposition of the Song of Songs, addressed to Robert of Melun, his successor in the bishopric of Hereford, which Patrick Young published in London in 1638, quarto, together with Alcuin’s work on the same book. Gilbert’s letters were published among the letters of St Thomas of Canterbury by Christian Wolf at Brussels in 1682, quarto. [Most recently these were again put into print by J.-A. Giles (Oxford, 1845, octavo), much enlarged beyond the earlier edition; from them we have extracted Gilbert’s preface to his collection of Homilies. Editors.]

[Col. 1145]

## Letters of Gilbert Foliot and of Various Persons to Him

(Because Gilbert’s letters are especially commended by their close connection with the letters of St Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, King Henry II, Pope Alexander III, and distinguished men of his own time, we have presented them together with the others, while preserving the integrity of the collection. See *Patrologia*, vol. 190, col. 747 onward.)

[Col. 1147]

# Exposition of the Song of Songs by Gilbert Foliot, Bishop of London

Edited by Patrick Young, Royal Librarian. (London, Royal Press, 1638, quarto.)

## Dedicatory Epistle

To the most reverend and most eminent prelate, Lord WILLIAM JUXON, bishop of London and Lord High Treasurer of England, PATRICK YOUNG sends greetings.

Most eminent and reverend prelate, deserted walls and ruins long neglected, which, laying aside their age, assume a new face and more august form, do not alone furnish proof and abundant testimony that oblivion has often afforded an occasion for more celebrated renown, and that many things have fallen only to rise again later in greater splendor. The monuments of intellect do so as well: they are corrected day by day, published in a more accurate form, and first brought by the diligent care of scholars from decay and dust into the light of day.

Among these is this devout and elegant work by your predecessor. Perhaps it has until now lain buried in oblivion so that, in this learned age, it might emerge from darkness with greater brilliance and, under the auspices of your most celebrated name, once more behold the light which it first drew within your walls. If, in accordance with your exceptional kindness, Your Most Eminent Lordship should be willing to cover the infirmities of its old age—or rather of the age in which it lived—which occur rather rarely in diction or subject matter, with but the hem of your garment; and to deem it worthy of your patronage together with its acolyte—for it was neither fitting that it should go forth publicly alone and unattended, nor did the condition of so great a man permit it—and kindly to receive this slight undertaking of ours in publishing both works, it will make a step toward greater works which may later be dedicated to your name, and will bind me, most devoted to Your Eminence, in a closer bond of reverence hereafter. Given on the day before the Nones of November, 1638.

## Gilbert’s Preface

[Col. 1147A] To his dearest lord and friend Robert, by the grace of God bishop of Hereford, brother Gilbert, humble minister of the Church of London: may you be occupied in those things which are God’s, and in them be brought to fulfillment in a most blessed end.

Lest the authority of your command, my lord, should seem to me vain or insignificant, I immediately sent you the book you requested: namely, the book which, with the Lord’s help, I recently composed on the Song of Songs, and which I had entrusted to no one before you either to be copied [Note: [Col. 1147A] Perhaps “to be copied out.”] or inspected. For I wrote it not for praise or the sake of commendation, but so that I might retain in memory what I had learned under the Lord’s teaching, and might show that these things should not be contemptuously scorned, as the Jews do, but humbly read with inward understanding and understood in the same spirit in which [Col. 1148A] they were spoken.

When you had read it with very great attention from beginning to end, you received it with much gladness of heart and, as I hear, greatly praised my application to this study. So that nothing might be lacking to its completeness, you asked me to add a prologue, that the completion of the work might thus be worthy of an offering of thanks; for it is written, “Love is strong as death” (Song 8:6). For as nothing mortal can undo the bond of death, so there is nothing impossible for the persistence of love to obtain. Love emptied the Lord, bound him in human bonds, and, after the cross and the tomb, led him to the lowest regions, that from there he might rescue those who had believed that he would come [Col. 1149A] and had diligently awaited him. Love reforms into the freedom of grace those whom justice had made children of wrath, mercy tempering judgment.

This changes my purpose, so that I append a prologue to a work which I undertook to expound without a prologue. For Solomon was the author of the work, and he imitated ancient writers, who do not make their readers attentive by prefacing a prologue, but stir their attention by setting forth the matter itself of which they will speak, and direct their eagerness toward understanding what has been said. Hence those words of Moses: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth; but the earth was without form,” and so on (Gen. 1:1). And those words of Exodus: “These are the names of the sons of Israel who entered Egypt with Jacob” (Exod. 1:1). Thus, running through the entire Pentateuch, the books of Judges and Kings, and other books, you will find them written without a prologue; and if prologues have been added to them, you will recognize that they were added long afterward, after the coming of the Savior.

Imitating these writers, Solomon begins at once with the matter about which he will speak, knowing that the matter itself possesses a manifest usefulness by which it may attract; or an evident reason by which it may despise desirable things; or theological insights by which [Col. 1150A] the mind may reject these things and cleave to him alone who is their maker and creator. Therefore he produced three books, which he neither adorns nor extends with prologues: one, *Proverbs*; another, *Ecclesiastes*; and this third, *Sirasirim* [Hebrew *Shir ha-Shirim*, “Song of Songs”].

In *Proverbs* he attracts us to possess those things by which the present life is secured: that one may provide for one’s own need, assist one’s neighbor where necessary, and give to the needy as necessity requires. But in *Ecclesiastes* he warns that the mind should not be entangled in such things, nor love incline toward things that are transitory; rather, it should judge them as vain, and determine [Note: [Col. 1149B] Perhaps “discern.”] and desire things higher than these. Therefore, subsequently adding *Sirasirim*, which is called the “Song of Songs,” a work in which the soul passes beyond all things and stands before the divine majesty, [Col. 1150B] embracing him as bridegroom and representing to him from affection all that love can be, he introduces the soul—or the Church—set ablaze by love, seeking not visible things but sighing for invisible things with the whole affection of its heart and the whole intention of its mind, as though seeking God but not yet having grasped him, and saying these words in order to hold him once grasped.

# Exposition of the Song of Songs

[Col. 1149]

## Chapter One

[Col. 1149C]

### 1. “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

Who is this woman, so illustrious, of such elegant beauty and grace, that she boldly desires the kiss of the supreme King and says, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth”? Does this soul act in dreams, imagining for herself what she wants, carrying herself away into a hope without reality, inwardly fashioning empty visions, and already hoping to grasp what she could not attain even by laborious efforts?

To what height has this spirit ascended, so forgetful of gold and heedless of silver, reckoning no precious stone of account, rejecting so utterly all that the world possesses and offers for possession, that, thrusting them away with the hand of holy perfection, it says: “Away from me! My love, withdrawn from you, [Col. 1149D] has passed to things above, desiring him alone who alone truly is, and who equally supplies to all things both the cause and the effect of their being.” Sighing for him and impatient with holy longing, this soul speaks within itself and says, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” A soul inspired in this way does not speak vain things, but the highest things.

For a long time it has drunk the streams of Solomon’s wisdom, and it has heard him disputing in *Ecclesiastes*. Formerly delicate and tender, when it had not yet passed from external forms to inward things, when it had not yet ascended from creature to Creator, it clung to the world with all its embraces and bound itself with all its affections to visible things. But having entered the school of spiritual teaching, it deserved to hear not some common teacher, but Solomon, that supreme master in wisdom, establishing a kind of introductory lesson for holy Church, by which he might call every chosen soul away from the world and unite the soul thus called and withdrawn with him who is above the world by an indissoluble bond of charity.

For that supreme Solomon, seeing in the Spirit almost every soul on earth as though digging, entangling itself in secular affairs, and no longer lifting its love upward but bending it downward, descended from the height of his contemplation to the lowliness of human life, in order to raise the bent and miserable soul. He recalled the erring soul, [Col. 1150D] instructed and reformed it with saving precepts, and finally led it, by certain steps as it were of ascent, to the heights of holy contemplation and love.

First, therefore, he promises great things to tender age, saying: “The Proverbs of Solomon: to know wisdom and discipline, to understand words of prudence, and to receive the instruction of teaching” (Prov. 1:1 ff.). He offers gentle inducements, adding: “The wise hearer will become wiser, and the intelligent will possess guidance.” Thus he does not immediately preach contempt for the world and the things which are in the world, nor recount the arduous and lofty demands of a stricter life; “for first comes that which is animal, then that which is spiritual” (1 Cor. 15:46).

Therefore the best teacher, lest by immediately urging difficult things he crush at the very beginning the soul whose instruction he had undertaken, permits it to pass, as it were, through the years of its infancy, freely using and taking pleasure in the world and the things of the world. Yet he establishes for it a law: that it should not dissolve into sin or turn to the service of wickedness and lust that which it has received as a great gift from a great Author. He therefore lays before the now attentive hearer the *Proverbs*, and by as many proverbial sayings as he teaches, he forms and binds the soul under as many laws for living well and honorably. If the prudent reader examines these Proverbs more attentively with the eye of the mind, [Col. 1151B] he will understand that in them a complete pattern of life is set forth for honest conduct among possessors of this world and those living in common life.

For since “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6), faith and the worship of the supreme Divinity are impressed at the very beginning of the treatise, where it is said: “Hear, my son, the discipline of your father, and do not forsake the law of your mother” (Prov. 1:8). For the discipline of the supreme Father, which the Church learned most fully from him, is this: “To believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him” (Heb. 11:6); and that at the end of the ages he sent his Son into the flesh and fulfilled his promises through him.

But the law of Mother Church is, first, that natural law inscribed by the finger of God upon human hearts; second, the law written upon [Col. 1151C] tablets of stone; third, the law of the Gospel administered in the Holy Spirit and grace. Therefore not to forsake the law of our mother is not to depart from the unity of the Church and from the worship of the supreme Divinity which one has received inwardly through the inspiration of grace.

Moreover, the remaining commandments of the Decalogue shine forth in distinct places throughout the entire volume of Proverbs. By these and by very many other precepts, a kind of holy secular life is proposed, and the life of secular persons is established by a fitting moderation of reason, so that one may use the world without turning away from God; may possess lawful things placed beneath one’s authority, yet continually abstain from forbidden things.

When, in the first instruction, human desires have been satisfied and the human being permitted to use temporal things soberly, according to what was said by the divine voice to the first human being: “Increase and multiply, fill the earth, subdue it, and have dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, and all things that move upon the earth” (Gen. 1:28), there is now room for the second instruction: that a person may hear what judgment should be made about things long possessed—whether love ought to cling to them, or whether love ought to be raised from them to something higher and far better.

Thus Solomon, running through by the pen of truth every individual thing under the sun, says in the second volume: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccles. 1:2). Forcefully showing that this vanity belongs to every transitory thing, he separates from vanity the soul whose instruction he had undertaken, lest the mind be enwrapped in vain things or love entangled in vanities; and he directs it apart to truth when, at the end of the work itself, he adds: “Youth and pleasure are vain” (ch. 11:10). And shortly afterward: “Remember the Lord your Creator in the days of your youth, before the time of affliction comes and the years of which you say, ‘They do not please me’” (ch. 12:1). And shortly afterward, at the very end of the discourse: “Fear God and keep his commandments: this is the whole human being” (ibid., 13).

By this concise conclusion of words, what else does he impress on human minds but fear of the supreme Divinity itself and the reverence of worship due to him? For this is the way; this is the approach to life: if the soul, seized by holy fear, always turns away from unlawful things, and the mind, kindled inwardly with the fire of love, continually arms itself for good works. For the human being is placed midway in the order of rational creation, having the good angel above him and the evil angel below; after leaving this life he is to be brought, according to the merits of his life, to equality with one or the other.

Therefore, just as he is midway between these, so he has something in common with each: love with him who is above, fear with him who is below. Evil angels indeed fear and tremble; good angels love perfectly. As the evil angel does not rise to love, so good angels do not descend to fear, according to the saying: “Perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). Therefore, while love alone wholly carries the good angel into itself and fear alone presses the evil angel downward, there is, apart from the human being, nothing in the entire order of creation in which fear joins with love, in which these two are fittingly conjoined.

Thus it is said to the human being: “Fear God and keep his commandments: this is the whole human being.” It is as though he said: All this—that is, this whole matter, namely “to fear” and, by loving, “to keep the commandments”—belongs to the human being, so that by fearing he may avoid wrath and by loving attain grace. Or if it is said, “This is the whole human being,” that is, through fear and love the human being becomes perfect. Or, “This is the whole human being,” that is, every human being was created for this. The sense does not differ, since this is the manner and purpose of human creation: to avoid wrath in this way and merit grace.

This soul, therefore, receiving counsels of salvation not now derived from afar but from the fountain itself—from Solomon, that is, the supreme one—has already learned in Proverbs how to possess worldly things, and in Ecclesiastes on what grounds it should now abandon and despise things already possessed in its mind. Now in the Songs it hears how to pass from visible to invisible things and cleave to the Author of all with all the power of its mind and fullness of affection.

Thus, having entered that holy and supreme *theoria*—contemplation—by way of moral discipline, through which it shares its possessions in holiness, and rational discipline, through which it rightly judges worldly things, it utterly forgets the things behind. Ascending that holy mountain and summit of its mind, it follows holy Moses through the midst of cloud and darkness to the heights of contemplation. [Col. 1153A] There, remaining in the hidden dwelling-place (Exod. 19:20; 20:21), it desires neither high coffered ceilings, nor painted walls of attendants, nor acres of fields stretching without limit. Rather, that it may abound in all things, it desires him alone who is all things: the light and rest of souls, the fountain of good things and source of virtues; him whom to grasp is supreme, and whom to enjoy is most delightful.

Impelled inwardly by desire for him, it expresses what it feels. No longer restraining itself within the barriers of silence, it speaks, in a lover’s manner, either to itself or to some heavenly Virtue akin to itself, saying: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” Love indeed often errs in judgment, and while it is carried headlong by its own desire, wherever it turns, it thinks that it contemplates what it desires and that any other person experiences in himself what it feels. Thus, as though it were evident to others who draws love itself and absorbs it, as it were, into himself, when it expresses outwardly what it does inwardly, it names no one but says with a certain discriminating lack of discrimination: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

This is indeed the secret of a perfect mind and the soliloquy of a soul already clarified with its heavenly Bridegroom. Come now: turn the gaze of your mind somewhat aside, and descend for a little while from the heights to lower things. Consider a soul still bound by unbelief, which has not yet received the illuminating rays of faith, has not yet touched the threshold of the Church, and utterly does not know the Bridegroom. Would you judge the Song rightly applicable to such a soul, that it should speak to the Bridegroom of holy souls and say, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth”? Would not this saying be unfitting in its mouth?

But if you consider a soul enlightened indeed by faith but dead in works, grievously oppressed and overwhelmed by sins, making for itself a long rope of sin and not having recourse to the remedy of repentance for good: can the Song rightly be applied to it, so that, though ugly of mouth, terrible in face, and foul in its whole body, it may nevertheless say to the Father of all, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth”?

And if you consider a soul strengthened by faith and imbued with the sacraments, at one moment raising itself to the good of virtue by the law of the mind, at another encountering, in a fall into sin, the law which resists in its members; mourning under this alternation and crying out in mourning, “O who will deliver me from this body of death?” [Col. 1153D] (Rom. 7:24)—would it fittingly sing the Song, so that, covered with tears of sorrow and drawing sighs of repentance, it might say, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth”?

But if, advancing a little, you consider a soul on a somewhat higher level, moderating itself with a certain equal middle measure, so that it no longer admits sins deserving condemnation, yet has not risen to the heights of virtue—dwelling, as it were, with Lot in Zoar and not yet reaching the mountains—then, inasmuch as it has not yet touched the summit of virtue, it delights the more in external things and burns less strongly with desire for the heavenly kiss. Thus the saying, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth,” does not rightly apply even to it.

Now enter the secret place of the spiritual soul. Consider the soul already established by grace, which the Spirit has drawn into the mountains, which has resolved to dwell in the heights, which, the world now conquered, has trampled down sin, and which, running after the Lord with Peter, has already said, “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. 19:27). Although it is far removed from the darkness of unbelief, from the kingdom of sin and death, from the assault of temptation, and from the torpor of mind, it nevertheless does not presume to dare, while it awaits the kiss of the supreme King—which perhaps it has not yet tasted—to say, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” Rather, satisfied with the kiss of the saints’ feet, it sits with Mary; or, with John, “it stands with the friends of the Bridegroom and rejoices with joy at his voice” (John 3:29), [Col. 1154B] a voice which it has deserved already to hear inwardly in fullest sweetness, and in that very form [Note: [Col. 1153D] Perhaps “hope.”] and promise of future things to delight and rest.

From here, if you can, ascend the sixth degree of perfection, where love consecrated to the heights of contemplation enters. There the Lord is transfigured for the soul upon the mountain; and that most holy Moses, hidden from human eyes and now privy to heavenly mysteries, rests most sweetly in the very secret of divinity. Here the most blessed soul, contemplating in its heart the King whom it loves and stretched forth toward God—as far as is permitted in this life—is refreshed by the sweetness of eternal vision. Turning the eye of contemplation back upon all created things, and marveling not so much at them as at the wisdom [Col. 1154C] and inexpressible power of their supreme Maker within them, it disdains all created things, gathers itself wholly into God himself, and is bound to him by the bond of charity and the light of contemplation.

And while it sees that all beauty in creation is not comparable in the least to his beauty, it burns and is inflamed by that invisible fire. Experiencing the wound of charity inflicted upon its mind by the sweet sting of divinity, it asks that certain pledges, as it were, may be given it beforehand: pledges of future blessedness and of that most sacred union in which the created spirit will without end be joined to the uncreated by an indissoluble bond of charity. Then, with an inward cry audible only to holy and heavenly powers, it says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

For love kindled toward God is charity; and the concentrated examination of the one who is loved by an attentive mind is contemplation. These accompany each other in such a way that contemplation gives rise to love, and love always advances contemplation further. Wherever contemplation penetrates by a ray of heavenly light, it draws love after it; thus, for the soul making progress, the Lord is illumination through contemplation and true salvation through charity, as it is said: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Ps. 26:1).
