Therefore, the soul turned away from the world and wholly converted in mind to Christ, forgetting the things behind (Phil. 3:13) and vigorously stretching itself toward those before, now seeing the world far below it, rapt wholly into eternity, contemplating the supreme and eternal things of the Lord Jesus and eagerly desiring them in love, languishes with spiritual desire because it wholly yields to love. Yet, not presuming upon the Bridegroom’s full embrace, it asks for a kiss, that in some degree its love may be satisfied. Speaking in mind either to itself or perhaps to a familiar angel, communicating spiritual things to the spiritual, it reveals its love; and, loving from love, begins thus: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

Since these things have been said by way of a brief preface, we shall expound the rest in the following volume, with the Lord’s inspiration—he who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

### “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

By unceasing labor and continual exercise in virtue, this faithful [Col. 1155B] soul has been brought so far as to aspire to the kiss of the supreme King, saying, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” Hence we do not proceed with a rapidly flowing pen, but stand as though fixed upon the heights, wishing intently to examine and imitate the hidden and perfect state of this holy soul.

In this matter, the first thought which occurs is that the soul seems most confidently to glory with the Apostle, saying: “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12). For a soul which seeks the kiss of supreme Divinity undoubtedly knows that it has a clean heart, clean lips, an honorable face, and one not unworthy of the kiss of so great a King. Thus it seems rightly to fit the saying: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present a chaste virgin to Christ” [the printed text reads *casto*, “to a chaste man”] (2 Cor. 11:2); and elsewhere: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, without spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5:27).

For it has no “spot” from uncleanness, no “wrinkle” from duplicity, no conscience corrupted by hatred of neighbor. Murders, adulteries, and the other things which oppress conscience and commonly defile a person do not proceed from its heart. For it guards its heart with every vigilance, attentively hearing through Solomon: “For from it proceeds life” (Prov. 4:23).

Prudent and watchful fear of God stands at the doors of this heart, lest a passage to its secrets should lie open on every side to vices. Stern companies of virtues stand at the fortifications of this heart; they no longer fight against sins as once they did, [Col. 1155D] but glory in the Lord Jesus, now that victory over them has been won. The more bitterly they have experienced the battle for so long, the more joyful is the glory in which they now triumph.

Above stands chaste chastity, girded for action, rejoicing that it has crushed the uncleanness of the flesh with the stone of abstinence. Humility stands beside chastity with a gentle countenance, thinking nothing lofty; yet by the Lord’s power it continually restrains the exaltation of mind which seeks high things, and boldly and wisely dashes against the Rock, which is Christ, the foul madness of that exaltation’s own head.

Thus faith despises unbelief, hope desperate misery, charity envy, simplicity deceit, innocence malice, truth falsehood, and each several virtue despises its opposing vice as a monstrous corpse, now violently dashed against the rock of truth. [Col. 1156A] Here you may see that ancient lust of the flesh lamenting at the funerals of its extinguished offspring, carrying about diverse pleasures and everything that can be contrived by the most refined art of temptation in Babylon’s golden cup, employing all its strength and all its art to see whether the chilled may be warmed and the extinguished restored to their former spirit of life.

That holy chorus of virtues mocks its darts, knowing that the Egyptians struck by the hand of the Lord cannot be recalled to life again. Therefore, exulting spiritually, it takes up psalm and timbrel and chants with full delight in the Lord that song of Moses: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; horse and rider he has cast into [Col. 1156B] the sea” (Exod. 15:1).

The evil rider is every malignant spirit; the evil horses are the most wicked vices. It is evident toward what destruction the evil angels riding them are borne, since they drag miserably tempted souls into the depths of hell and subject them, through the operation of divine justice, to eternal torments.

This soul glories that these have been destroyed for it. Sitting in the midst of virtues, it now entrusts itself wholly to them and commits itself entirely to their service; and every virtue humbly serves it, each rendering what is its own. Who could now run through with the pen, or follow in speech, what outstanding beauty each virtue confers upon this perfect soul, what admirable grace each supplies? Who could fully express its beauty—how continence makes it chaste, innocence simple, gentleness mild, mercy devout, circumspection provident, temperance sober, prudence discerning, patience strong, and charity, now made perfect, directs it along the sacred paths of justice with great reverence? [Col. 1156C]

For from the very beginning of holy fear, immediately fixing its steps in humility, it passes from there through the camp of unchastity and then ascends through the remaining virtues as they are arranged in the mind by the Spirit of God. No longer looking back upon empty and false insanities, from a now higher place it entrusts itself wholly to love and commits itself to its surpassing fullness. Dwelling apart here, it cannot fail to meditate upon what it loves; it cannot fail to contemplate what it desires. Sent from above with thirst, it burns for that living fountain and is daily refreshed with the sweet bread of tears, grieving that its desires are prolonged and making its complaint with tear-filled eyes.

Here it frequently repeats and ponders within itself: “For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain. I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:21, 23). And: “Alas for me, that my sojourn has been prolonged” (Ps. 119:5). It is indeed compelled to feel and experience in itself what it lacks from the Supreme One, how far it is from eternity. The spirit released from the flesh sees plainly him whom it loves, enjoys the good which it desires, is not tormented by the postponement of its longing, and is touched by no sorrow at all. There love is wholly in light and wholly rests in joy. [Col. 1157A] But love’s weariness in the present life is beautifully described where it is said: “Laughter will be mingled with sorrow, and grief occupies the end of joy” (Prov. 14:13).

In this life, indeed, the faithful soul’s laughter consists in this: that, with a clean conscience, a perfect heart, and a most complete integrity of love, it knows itself to pursue the Lord Jesus in the heights, and to extend the kiss of its mind toward him in both his human and divine nature. Yet this laughter is still mingled with pain, and grief overtakes this joy, because it knows that it has not yet laid hold of him whom it follows in heart, and sees that what it desires above all things is deferred from it. Hence comes the pain of the loving soul; hence the tears with which it washes itself by night and waters the couch of its mind, so that, already cleansed, it may be cleansed yet more, and, having been beautiful, may shine forth far more beautifully. Trusting in these virtues, conscious of this beauty in itself, after vices have long since been overcome, after the gifts of virtues have been attained, after desires have been prolonged for a long time, languishing with love and raising itself upward in contemplation, passing through heaven in its mind for the solace of its pain and as a certain foretaste of the joy it desires, it seeks a kiss and begins in this manner the Song which is called the Song of Songs: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

Perhaps you may see an Angel indignant and saying: What has happened? What is this change in affairs, so great and so unprecedented? Why are the lowest things mingled with the highest? Is heaven stretched out above in vain? Is humanity’s seat established on dung in vain? Does the human mind penetrate heaven [Col. 1157C]? And does it range not only through the regions of heaven, but even through the innermost parts of the heavens, no longer content with its own limits? But if this has in some fashion been permitted to it, what is this—that the human mind should raise itself to this height and seek the kiss of the creative power, of the wisdom which accomplishes all things by a word, of goodness subject to no necessity, that is, of the supreme and inaccessible Godhead, saying, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth”? Has any Angel or Archangel, or any spirit among the Powers, Cherubim, or Seraphim, ever silently spoken or thought thus within himself, so as ever either to seek or to hope for the kiss [Col. 1157D] of him before whom we stand trembling, and in whose embassies we have served obediently for so many ages?

When the Word was incarnate and the Lord Jesus passed through the earth in his humanity, we have called it great [Note: [Col. 1157D] Perhaps: “we have judged it great.”], and have regarded it as marvelous in our eyes, that a woman should be admitted to his feet and should press kisses upon them—feet which she had first wiped with her hair and washed with the stream of her tears (Luke 7:38). When the Lord was transfigured on the mountain, revealing to human eyes that divinity which he had always possessed, did that loving Peter, or most beloved John, presume to seek the kiss of his majesty? Unable to bear the voice descending from the magnificent glory, they fell face-down upon the earth [Col. 1158A] (Matt. 17:2). Likewise the Apostle caught up into heaven (2 Cor. 12:4), to whom the secrets of heaven were entrusted and those holy words of silence revealed—did he, though wise in lofty matters among us, so set his mouth toward heaven as to aspire to the kiss of the supreme Godhead, without measuring himself or considering his human condition?

Moses also, ascending the mountain (Exod. 19), hidden within the cloud and trembling at the sound of the trumpet—did he offer himself for the delights of this kiss, he who requested that merely carnal law, soon to be abolished, be inscribed not on human hearts but only on tablets of stone? Since, according to Truth, “among those born of women none is greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11:11), and since, according to that same Truth, “he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is far greater than he” [Col. 1158B] (ibid.), it might have been enough for the human soul had even the least Angel received it with a kiss.

Perhaps some heavenly power moderates this zeal—which proceeds not from anger or malice—replying to its severe judgment: Mortals ought not to be begrudged if they desire to escape the snares of death and strive with the whole effort of their minds to grasp the liberty of the glory of the children of God. For the condition of mortals is exceedingly miserable. Placed in the midst of the world, they behold hell below and heaven above; and for a human being not only is descent easy, but it is exceedingly difficult not to fall. To this end the flesh, by its own weight, inclines downward; temptations press hard; malicious spirits drag people along with cords of sins, envying human salvation always, just as they have long envied our glory.

But as descent [Col. 1158C] is easy, so ascent to the things above is difficult. In this consists the life of human beings; in this is the battle of souls; in this the endeavors of those who live holily in the world burn fervently: that, escaping the snares of sins, they may pass into our liberty, conform themselves to us by purity of life, and be joined to the love of the supreme Godhead. Souls that have come forth from the pit of misery and the mire of filth, abandoning—or rather trampling underfoot in mind—the vanities of the world: how devoutly ought they to be received, with how great a love ought they to be cherished by us, lest by degenerating they ever look back, but may continually kindle their love toward the Father of lights until they receive the promises granted to the blessed!

Therefore, while the soul is established in holy desires, rejecting earthly things and not yet attaining heavenly ones [Col. 1158D], let it be permitted, as a kind of incentive to its love, to employ the forms of its own words; especially since, in naming a kiss, an embrace, a bed, or anything of that kind, it thinks nothing carnal, presumes nothing unworthy, meditates upon nothing whatever except what is holy. For all that the wretched soul sins in a kiss, and every carnal affection, is as far from its mind as it has itself withdrawn from vice, purified by virtue. For there is also a holy kiss, as the Apostle recalls: “Greet one another with a holy kiss” (Rom. 16:16). And, according to Truth, the father meeting his returning son “was moved with compassion, ran, fell upon [Col. 1159A] his neck, and kissed him” (Luke 15:20). Since, then, these matters which zeal had stirred up among the heavenly beings have been quieted by modest restraint, we shall defer to the following discussion the things which, by the Lord’s inspiration, must be said.

“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

As was said in the preceding volume, there is a kiss of foul pleasure, which the mind already raised to heavenly things disdains even to recall. But there is a holy kiss, of which the Apostle speaks, saying, “Greet one another with a holy kiss”; and Truth in the Gospel says: “Moved with compassion, the Father fell upon his son’s neck and kissed him.” A kiss, therefore, may be one of reconciliation, one of congratulation, one of joy, and of a certain permitted and sanctified delight.

A kiss is one of reconciliation when minds formerly at discord are brought back into peace and the favor of friendship through some mediator; and the kiss outwardly bestowed is a sign of the covenant and union of minds which takes place inwardly. But a kiss of congratulation occurs when we receive with rejoicing kinsfolk and friends, absent for a long time and returned to us from travel or elsewhere, and by the kiss which we give outwardly demonstrate the certainty of our inward joy. The bridegroom’s kiss to the bride, however, is one of a certain sanctified delight.

There are, then, three kisses for which the Church sighs and which every faithful soul desires to receive. For the holy Church desires reconciliation; it desires congratulation [Col. 1159C]; and it desires that holy joy which is to be without end. For before the Word was incarnate, the Church had no peace with God; after departing this life, it was wholly drawn down into hell.

For humanity made itself wholly liable to eternal death, in both its root and its offspring, when it disdained to obey its Creator—he from whom it had so recently received so many and such great gifts—although he not merely willed and commanded this, but even uttered threats, and this in a matter of the least importance. For though it is not a great proof of love if one obeys in a small matter, yet it is a great sign of an irreverent mind and evidence of the highest contempt if anyone disdains to obey in a small matter. For, according to Truth, “He who is not faithful in a little thing, how will he be faithful in a great?” (Luke 16:10). Therefore, the less important the matter in which humanity disdained obedience, the greater the sin it incurred and the greater the punishment it deserved. For whoever offended against the eternal Judge undoubtedly deserved what was eternal; for that judicial power which has no end inflicts punishment without end. And so humanity deserved good without end from the hand of the Lord when it departed from truth.

For as the good Angel was first light and afterwards a firmament, when he did not consent to him who desired to set his throne toward the North (Isa. 14:13), so too, if humanity had resisted temptation, it would by that very act have deserved to be strengthened against temptation and sin, so that thereafter it could neither sin nor be tempted. But, having innocently completed here its allotted number of days [Col. 1160A], having tasted of the tree of life, it would have attained equality with the Angels, through the powerful working in this matter of him who had created it. Therefore, just as the reward of obedience would have been eternal, so by the equal balance of justice the punishment of disobedience was owed eternally. After sin, the whole human race being liable to it, the whole fell into hell.

Thus the prophet says: “Mercy and truth have met one another” (Ps. 84:11); which is the same as saying that mercy and justice began to come against one another. For those who meet one another come from opposite directions and tend, as it were, toward opposing ends. Thus, immediately after sin, mercy and truth began to tend in different directions: truth demanded punishments for humanity, while mercy was devising something better for its restoration [Col. 1160B]. And this was a marvelous meeting: justice drawing humanity down to hell, mercy desiring to bring humanity back to what had been lost.

But justice prevailing, humanity was delivered over to punishments: tasting miseries, afflictions, and death in this world; corruption in the grave; and, after all these, darkness in hell. And when justice had now been satisfied in great measure, guilt having long been punished, after the passing of many years, at last a very great place was given in the heights to mercy, ever knocking and urgently pleading—in the hidden and secret depths of the holy and supreme Trinity. There it was ordained, as wonderfully as mercifully, that he through whom the Father had created all things should restore in himself the things that had perished.

This counsel is that ancient counsel of which the prophet says: “May your ancient, true counsel, O Lord, come to pass.” This is the “mystery hidden from the ages” (Col. 1:26), as Paul calls it. The Son therefore obeyed the Father, and did so all the more wonderfully and holily because it was not a younger obeying an elder, nor a lesser obeying a greater, but the great obeying the Almighty; the immense obeying the Almighty; one equal in all things obeying—as it is said in the prophet: “At the head of the book it is written of me, that I should do your will” (Ps. 39:9).

For great is the book of God’s knowledge and wisdom: though you read in it always, you never encounter its end. Its inward pages have been inspected only by its Author. In it both human beings and Angels advance without end; and that treasury of God can never be exhausted by however many continually draw from it. Wisdom alone, supreme Wisdom, reaches from its end to its end. In this book all human beings are written; their days are formed; the merits of each are comprehended; and the blessedness due to each is explicitly contained.

At the head of this book, as in its chief part, this mystery of the Incarnation is written, because among all the wonders that God has done—creating each thing, preserving created things, and arranging by a marvelous law the things he preserves—nothing is so astonishing or marvelous as that, by his own self-emptying, he appears to have endured an affront at the command of mercy. But “the works of the Lord are great, sought out according to all his wills [Col. 1161A]” (Ps. 110:2), “and his judgments are true, justified in themselves” (Ps. 18:10).

Therefore God, ascending the cross and stretching out his innocent hands to the nails, consecrated the place of death unto life, and thus recalled to life those who were held in death. For when his blood dripped from the cross, the rocks were split open, so that a bodily passage might be opened through which that most holy price, received by angelic hands, might be carried to hell; so that, sharing the fruit of the tree of life, those held in hell under the faith and expectation of this grace might return to the liberty of life.

What, then, remains for justice to complain of? In Paradise a tree was set, “good for food, beautiful to the eyes, and delightful to behold; and the woman took of its fruit and ate, and gave to her husband, who ate” (Gen. 3:6). Thus disobedience was consummated and the way to death prepared. In the Church likewise the tree of the cross was raised, terrible in appearance and most bitter in taste. Its fruit was that temporal death by which criminals condemned for various offenses were punished upon the cross. To this tree eternal Wisdom stretched out his hands and tasted this fruit, not because a serpent prompted him or a woman persuaded him.

Formerly the serpent had acted so that the woman, desiring what she ought not, might take delight as flesh does; and the man, as the rational sense, might consent to the same thing. Thus it had prepared for itself a way by which it might enter the hearts of immortals [Note: [Col. 1161D] Perhaps: “mortals.”] and draw all things to itself. But at the cross all that belongs to it is undone [Col. 1161C]. The serpent suggests nothing to Christ; here the flesh takes no delight; rational sense itself, in the spirit, draws the flesh after it to endure the hardships of the cross and taste the bitterness of death. Therefore power resides in the cross; and when he who is God’s power and wisdom ascends it, both power and wisdom are placed in it. This opens the way of virtue, which, although narrow, leads to life.

The tree of Paradise therefore produced fruit by which suggestion might be received and desire stirred up by certain enticements. But the cross, now placed within the bosom of the Church, presents a fruit such that, if you taste it in mind, you do not succumb either to the enemy’s inward prompting or to the flesh’s enticement. Rather, the enemy is conquered at his first encounter; the flesh is immediately recalled to serve the spirit [Col. 1161D]; and the whole human being is brought back to the love of perfected virtue.

This, therefore, is the place where mercy, which is true peace, kisses justice. For here both are satisfied together: humanity is redeemed through mercy’s action, and far more than was owed is paid to justice. And, according to the Apostle, “the bond written against us is powerfully nailed to Christ’s cross and erased” (Col. 2:14). For a bond is so written that, after it has been cut and divided into parts, a full record of the transaction remains in both its portions.

Such is our arrangement with the evil enemy. When we sin [Col. 1162A], our fault is with us, deeply inscribed by the very pen of the perverse deed; and the memory of the ancient enemy immediately receives it and firmly retains its impression, so that, if there is no one to redeem or save, he always has at hand something to bring as an accusation. This bond, however, has been erased by Christ’s death; through it our guilt is forgiven and his accusation against us is no longer feared.

But what is this? When humanity was bound to eternal punishment, the Son of God endured only a temporal death of forty hours. How was satisfaction made to divine justice, which required eternal punishments from humanity, by his death? Yet without doubt satisfaction was made. Put in the balance, if you please, the death itself of the Son of God, even if only momentary, and the eternal death owed by all human beings, however great that debt may be. Who can doubt that the death of the Only-begotten, though temporal, outweighs the death, though eternal, of any number whatever of mortal persons? For it is rightly greater, and more marvelous by nature, that God—subject to neither sin nor death—should die, than that however great a multitude of mortal and sinful people should die.

Hence blessed Job says: “Would that my sins, by which I have deserved wrath, and the calamity which I suffer, were weighed in the balance” (Job 6:2). That Job means “suffering one,” and signifies the Lord Jesus, no one now doubts. Pleading our cause before the Father, as if set upon the cross, he says: “Would that my sins be weighed”—calling our sins, by which we have deserved wrath, his own in the unity and mystery [Col. 1162C] of body and head—and saying: Would that you consider, Father, the sins by which humanity has deserved wrath, and the calamity—that is, the punishment—which I suffer upon the cross, having become human in obedience to you. For if you consider both, as you truly do, my punishment will appear heavier than the sand of the sea: that is, my punishment together with obedience will far outweigh the sins of humanity, and will suffice for you as the expiation of its guilt and the payment of the punishment owed by it.

Therefore the holy Church, understanding through the Spirit by whom it was enlightened that this reconciliation was to be given through the hand of the Mediator, the Lord Jesus, amid the inward communings by which the Spirit cherished it and kindled holy love, during the long delay of continuing hope, repeatedly uttered with frequent sighs in the hearts of the elect this Song of love, saying: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” In the kisser it understood the Father, by whom the Son was sent for this grace; in the mouth itself, customarily extended for a kiss, it signified the Son who was sent, who is the Father’s mouth and wisdom; and in the kiss itself, which is the pleasing sweetness of those who kiss, it expressed the Holy Spirit, who is the love of both. Thus it professed, as truly as devoutly, faith in the holy and supreme Trinity; the future Incarnation of the Word; and, through the mysteries of the incarnate Word, the full reconciliation of humanity with God.

For what could be more devout than this holy petition? What could be purer than this prayer [Col. 1163A]? In its very beginning it teaches how one ought to pray and make supplication to the Most High. For “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6), and a prayer without faith cannot be heard. Hence James says: “Let each ask in faith, wavering in nothing” (Jas. 1:6). For faith first opens the entrance to the inner sanctuary of lofty majesty for prayer. Therefore prayer which desires to be heard begins with the mysteries of faith and says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth”; as though it said: In this faith I stand to make the petition which I desire to be heard. I confess unity in the very substance of the Godhead; I confess and adore the Trinity in the persons themselves.

The confession of unity lies in the words “Let him kiss”; the confession of the Trinity lies in the fact that kisser, mouth, and kiss [Col. 1163B] are named. The kisser is the Father; the mouth which is extended for the kiss is the Son; and the kiss effected by the mouth of the one who kisses is the Holy Spirit. Yet this truth does not dissipate or divide the substance of the Trinity’s unity. The kisser is neither his own mouth with which he kisses nor the kiss itself which is conveyed by his mouth. Likewise the mouth itself is neither the kisser nor the kiss which is given. The kiss itself is neither the kisser nor the mouth from which it comes. Yet far be it from us, when we see a kiss given by someone, therefore to understand three substances. For the substance of the kisser is one, and both the mouth itself and the kiss exist not in another substance but in the one substance of the kisser alone.

So the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, though they are most truly three Persons, none of whom is another, do not, by this truth of the Trinity, take anything away from the unity or simplicity of God’s substance; nor does that simplicity add anything to or diminish anything from the Trinity of Persons. Since it is not enough to believe what is divine concerning God unless his humble things also are believed most truly, the text uses the most apt word, “kiss,” thereby most fully signifying both the Word who was to be incarnate and the mystery of human reconciliation that was to come. Since these things have thus been said, with the Lord’s help let us renew both our breath and our pen for the following discussion.

“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

[Col. 1163D] We understand that not merely one righteous person from Adam to Christ, but all persons throughout the world, far and wide, upon whom the grace of the Holy Spirit had poured itself, understood that one would someday be born from Adam’s seed who would someday destroy it [the referent of *ipsam* is unclear in the supplied text], concerning the offense committed by one for all his members, and, having handed over the kingdom to the Father, would make human beings equal to Angels. This faith and revelation in the Spirit kindled the desires of the Saints and drew their minds out toward future ages, so that they considered the delay of this life long, because so great an expectation was deferred, and considered it brief, as though it were to be ended before they should behold this with bodily eyes.

All these, therefore, whom one faith governed and one hope summoned—the whole multitude, that is, of those who believed devoutly—Solomon, in whom Wisdom had made its dwelling [Col. 1164A], beholding them in the very light by which he was enlightened, introduces as a Bride placed in longing for her Bridegroom, long promised to her, uttering the words of her desire in this way: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” By the threefold repetition in “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth,” he indicates the threefold kiss which she shows herself to desire: first, the kiss of reconciliation, as has been said; second, that of congratulation; third, that of eternal joy.

The Church desired reconciliation because it knew that it had sinned wholly in Adam; and this it knew could occur through no other than the Father’s Only-begotten, namely its own Bridegroom. It desires that the Father should kiss it—that is, should remit his wrath toward it by the kiss of his mouth, namely by the Incarnation [Col. 1164B] of his Only-begotten, who is both the Father’s mouth and Word. Hence it was explicitly said that the Father is the kisser, but that the kiss is the Son’s; because, although the Father saves those whom he saves through not his own but his Son’s Incarnation, nevertheless, since the Father truly brings about that Incarnation—as the operation of the entire Trinity is indivisible—the Father is rightly said to “kiss” by the kiss of the mouth: that is, to effect in the Son the assumption of flesh, which he does not possess in himself.

Having said these things concerning the kiss of reconciliation, let us proceed, with the Lord’s help, to investigate what is called the kiss of congratulation. For both ordinary usage and Scripture frequently mention it. Isaac says to his son: “Come near to me and give me a kiss, my son; and he came near and kissed him” (Gen. 27:26–27). We also read concerning Jacob that, when he saw Leah and learned that she was his cousin, “he moved the stone with which the well was closed, and, having watered the flock, kissed her and wept aloud” (Gen. 29:10–11). Laban also, “when he heard that Jacob had come, ran to meet him, embraced him, fell upon him with kisses, and brought him into his house” (ibid., 13). Again, after Jacob’s return from Syrian Mesopotamia following that long journey, we read that “Esau ran to meet his brother, embraced him, clasped his neck, kissed him, and wept” (Gen. 33:4). Joseph likewise, “when he had fallen in embrace upon the neck [Col. 1164D] of his brother Benjamin, wept; and he kissed all his brothers and wept over each one” (Gen. 45:14–15). And concerning the prodigal son: “While he was still far away, his father saw him, was moved with compassion, ran, fell upon his neck, and kissed him” (Luke 15:20).

In all these instances, undoubtedly, a kiss of congratulation is understood: a kiss by which parents and relatives rejoiced in the good fortune of their own people and inwardly exulted, showing outwardly by a kiss the joy which they cherished inwardly. The Church hopes and awaits that this kiss of congratulation will be given to it. It will be given on that last day, when the merits of lives are set forth and the Lord Jesus renders to each according to what he or she has done in life, whether good or evil.

For when the lost sheep has then been carried back upon the shoulders of the good Shepherd to the folds [Col. 1165A], his friends and neighbors will be summoned: namely, the holy Angels, who keep his will among themselves with constant steadfastness and are therefore his friends, and who continually enjoy his vision and are therefore rightly called neighbors. To them he will say: “Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep which was lost” (Luke 15:6). He will say the same thing similarly concerning the lost drachma.

This will be the supreme congratulation, when not only that heavenly Church of blessed spirits applauds the good Shepherd, but also the Church which has been carried back upon the shoulders of his humanity will congratulate the Bridegroom who rejoices at its restoration, and will congratulate the rejoicing multitude of heavenly powers. On that day there will be fulfilled what the history relates: Joseph, revealing himself to his brothers, “ordered all to go out, that no stranger should be present at their mutual recognition. Then he raised his voice in weeping and said to his brothers, ‘I am Joseph’; and he kissed them” (Gen. 45:1).

On that day strangers will be those to whom the Lord will say: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire, prepared for the devil and his Angels” (Matt. 25:41). When these have been separated on that day, the Lord Jesus will reveal himself to his brothers, saying: “I am Joseph”; as though he said openly: Recall how I was sold and placed in the prison of death, and how I came forth from it in resurrection; and now see plainly that I possess both the scepters of the kingdom and the summit of judicial authority, granted by the Father over every creature [Col. 1165C].

Here Bridegroom and Bride will congratulate one another, and the indivisible union of their minds will be made firm by an everlasting covenant. The Bride will congratulate the Bridegroom because, after the frailties of flesh, after prison, after scourges, after blows, after spitting, after nails, after death, after the tomb, after the great stone laid against it, he has been so exalted that in his assumed flesh he judges all flesh and bends to himself every knee of things heavenly, earthly, and infernal unto glory. The Bridegroom’s congratulation to the Bride will be this: that he did not run uncertainly or fight in vain; that, having triumphed over death and trodden Satan under his feet, he acquired the Church for himself, and acquired it all the more gloriously because he did so with such labor; and that he has now endowed the acquired Church with unspeakable glory. On that day its good will bring him applause both from all collectively and from each individually.

For what is that thanksgiving of the Lord, by which he will say on that day, “I was hungry and you gave me to eat” (Matt. 25:35), and the rest in the same manner, except a certain congratulation by the Judge himself and the Bridegroom over the inward goods of his Bride? For the perfection of the number six, distinguished by six clauses, signifies the whole fullness of all goods by which every faithful soul pleases the Lord in this present life and by which the whole Church conforms itself to its Bridegroom. For works of mercy consist in feeding the poor, giving drink, clothing the naked, receiving the stranger beneath one’s roof, visiting the sick, and visiting [Col. 1166A] the imprisoned.

But is God pleased only by these things? Does not every virtue please him? What of holy virginity? What of honorable chastity? What of the Saints’ frugality? What of silence? What of holy preaching? What of justice, fortitude, temperance, and prudence? What of the countless virtues praised in the holy Scriptures, in acquiring which the continual and unremitting labor of the Saints sweats? If the Lord is pleased by these, why is it that, when he congratulates the Church on its goods at the judgment, he will mention only those things which were outwardly rendered in bodily form? They are indeed goods, but not the only ones.

It is evident, then, that the clause of words already mentioned comprehends all the endowments of the soul, and in general all the goods of the Church [Col. 1166B]. For the Lord hungers and thirsts. Yet in saying this, we do not subject the holy Godhead to any suffering; for the life of the supreme Godhead itself is impassible. And insofar as temporal life is subject and liable to suffering, so far is that eternal and uncreated life wholly distant from and untouched by every suffering. Nevertheless, according to the customary language of Scripture, he is said to hunger and thirst—and not in one way only, but in several.

For the Lord hungers in his members; he hungers in himself. He hungers in his members when one of his own is brought into need of bodily or spiritual nourishment. Charity, assuredly, comes to the aid of this suffering by diverse works of mercy: refreshing one worn down with food and drink; instructing and building up spiritually one who desires spiritual things [Col. 1166C]. For as it is pious to relieve bodily hunger and thirst, so it is most pious to relieve the need for spiritual nourishment. For as the soul surpasses the body by the judgment of truth, so it is far better and far holier to assist the soul than the body. Yet both are good; both are pleasing to the Lord, even as an occasion for thanksgiving.

The same consideration applies to nakedness. The Lord is cold in body, and cold in spirit: in body, when the severity of cold is not repelled by any covering of clothing; in spirit, when someone inwardly is clothed with no garment of virtue. This cold comes from the North, by which the hearts of many are not merely chilled but hardened (Job 37:9; Ecclesiasticus 43:22); concerning which the prophet says: “Who can endure before his cold?” (Ps. 147:17 [Vulgate]; [Col. 1166D]). He covers this nakedness of Christ in Christ’s members who forms and instructs one deprived of virtue by examples of virtues. To such a person the Lord will say in congratulation at the end: “I was naked, and you clothed me.”

In what manner the Lord is a stranger and guest in his members is plain. But in himself he is a stranger and guest among those who have not yet received the faith which is in him. To such people he himself says: “Foxes have dens, and birds of heaven nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 8:30). For unclean and deceitful spirits dwell in and possess the dark hearts of sinners; “but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” Christ is the head of the Church, and God is the head of Christ; and the Son of Man lays his head among those who confess him equal to the Father, coeternal and consubstantial with him [Col. 1167A]. To these, the Son is neither a newly arisen God nor a foreign one. For he is newly arisen to those who maintain that he at some time began and was not begotten eternally from the Father; and he is foreign to those who strive to affirm that he is not of the same substance as the Father.

Among such people he is a guest and stranger—of all whom it is said through the prophet: “Let lying lips be silenced, which speak iniquity against the righteous with pride and contempt” (Ps. 30:19 [Vulgate]). Among these he is a guest and stranger, knocking through the prophets, through the apostles, through all the Scriptures, that they may open to him. To them the Lord will say on that day: “I was a stranger, and you did not take me in” (Matt. 25:43 [Col. 1167B]), because you did not admit the faith which is in me, which I preach, and for which I was sent.

From this it is understood who they are who receive the Saviour as a guest: namely, those who receive the doctrine of sound faith with fitting reverence, utterly abhorring heresy, and, simple as doves, gathering only the clean grains of faith. For it is not enough for them merely to receive the Saviour under their roof through faith, unless they also receive him with every charity and virtue. For he himself says: “Behold, I stand at the door, knocking; if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter in to him, and dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. 3:20). The Lord enters us when we ourselves open the door of the heart in order to believe; we are refreshed by a shared meal when, having received love from above, we are stretched forth to every good work by the gift of spiritual grace [Col. 1167C].

> [Note: Col. 1167D: Perhaps: “we are kindled.”]

Both fraternal charity and divine authority command us to visit the sick. For what better accords with humanity than that one human being should aid another—brother a brother, the strong the weak—both with the consolation of speech and the help of action, with pious affection and full compassion of mind? This must be rendered not only to one bodily ill,

> [Note: Col. 1167D: Perhaps: “who is ill.”]

but also to one spiritually sick. For the languor of the spirit grows so strong in many

> [Note: Col. 1168D: Perhaps: “grows stronger” (*invalescit*).]

that there is now in them neither a voice of confession nor the feeling of penitence. Of these the Apostle says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11:29). These must be visited frequently and admonished with the word of life [Col. 1167D], until, yawning seven times, they open their mouth in confession by the gift of the sevenfold Spirit, and conform themselves to the teachers of life—not only by being inwardly warmed, but also by the complete ordering of their outward person.

For this reason, when Elijah raised the dead man (3 Kings [1 Kings] 17:21), he stretched himself over him; and Elisha, when raising the dead, “placed his mouth upon his mouth, his eyes upon his eyes, and his hands upon his hands” (4 Kings [2 Kings] 4:34). Thus, as the Apostle says, all the members of their body which formerly “were instruments of iniquity unto iniquity” may, through those who are raised from death, be compelled, by imitating holy teachers, now to serve virtue. Of such persons Truth itself says: “Those who are healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are ill” (Matt. 9:12) [Col. 1168A].

Some of these are afflicted by lighter diseases, others by graver and longstanding ones. Thus those whom the age-long persistence of sin oppresses are enclosed as though in a certain prison of souls. Taking their person upon himself, the prophet says: “Bring my soul out of prison” (Ps. 141:8 [Vulgate]); and, “I am sunk in the mire of the deep” (Ps. 68:13 [Vulgate]); and again, “The cords of sinners have encompassed me” (Ps. 118:61 [Vulgate]). To visit these in a spirit of gentleness, pierce them with the word of life, and restore to virtue those drawn away by vices, is a mercy far greater than to bring out those bodily imprisoned after piously loosening their chains.

Since, therefore, there are two commandments—one concerning love of God [Col. 1168B], the other concerning love of neighbour—on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend, and in which the perfection of human life consists, the clause already mentioned comprehends within itself everything by which both commandments are fulfilled. For through those things that are bestowed upon neighbours with God in view must be understood everything by which we relieve any need of theirs, whether spiritual or bodily. For among sufferings there is nothing more bitter than hunger, thirst, nakedness, lack of shelter, sickness, and imprisonment. Therefore, through these things which most severely trouble and afflict any brother, absolutely all the things must be understood by which, through the action of mercy and with God in view, we provide help for any bodily or spiritual need that demands it.

For in his members, as has been said, the Lord hungers, thirsts, and is cold in two ways, now desiring a bodily remedy, now a spiritual one; but in himself in one way only. For he does not require from us merely that we provide necessities for our brethren; he wills that our faith and charity be directed principally toward himself, and derived from him secondarily toward our neighbour. Therefore, those things which concern the neighbour are what the Lord hungers for, thirsts for, and demands in his members. But those which do not concern the neighbour, but are observed out of reverence for Christ, are those which the Lord is said to hunger and thirst for in himself—which for him is the same as willing.

“When the Lord came to the fig tree, he hungered” (Matt. 21:18); and hanging on the cross, he said: “I thirst” (John 19:28). What did he hunger or thirst for? Undoubtedly for our salvation, our faith, and charity toward himself; for long-suffering, continence, and the other virtues which, although not directed toward our neighbour, are practiced for God’s sake [Col. 1168D]. For the virtues directed toward one’s neighbour he hungers for both in himself and in his members; but those directed toward himself, in himself alone.

It is evident, then, that the clause of words already mentioned comprehends all the endowments of the soul, and in general all the goods of the Church. This is the kiss of congratulation for which the Church sighs, which every soul asks in the Spirit, saying: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” Thus she speaks to the Father, naming his mouth, in this sense, as the Son [Col. 1169A], and understanding the kiss of both Father and Son as the Holy Spirit. For she says: “Let him kiss me”—that is, let the Father who created me make me worthy of the kiss; and “with the kiss of his mouth”—that is, through the Holy Spirit of his Son, who is his mouth.

For that Spirit is the kiss given by the Father, the kiss given by the Son, because he is the breath and sweetness proceeding from both. And as he proceeds from both, so both Father and Son pour him into the hearts of the blessed. Of him the Lord says: “I will send you the Spirit” (John 15:26); and elsewhere: “the Spirit whom the Father sends in my name” (John 14:26). Therefore she asks that the Spirit be given to her from the Father through the Son, so that, receiving from him the gifts of grace, she may pass into a certain new beauty [Col. 1169B], and on that day hear from the Father through the Son the voice of congratulation and receive the kiss of congratulation.

For the voice of congratulation is that by which the Lord will say on that day: “Well done, good servant” (Matt. 15:6 [as printed]); and that which he says to the heavenly Powers: “Rejoice with me over the lost sheep. Rejoice over the drachma that has been found” (Luke 15:6). It is as if he said: Consider what the beauty of the Church is, and how great it is; understand with how many gifts of grace and with what glory of virtues she shines; rejoice with me that I have laboured for one so great and such as this.

What peace, I ask, will then belong to the whole Church at this voice? What tranquillity will there be in the minds of holy souls, when, secure now concerning her own glory at this congratulation of the Bridegroom, she will no longer have anything to fear or dread hereafter? This peace, indeed, is that security for which the Church sighs: that on the day when angels tremble and archangels are afraid, she may have the Bridegroom favourable to her; and, sanctified by his Spirit, may please him in the beauty of her virtues; and through the kiss of the Son, who is the Holy Spirit, may receive from the Bridegroom peace, congratulation, and the promised gifts [Col. 1169C]. May the Lord Jesus, who is for ever, make us participants in these things. Amen.

“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

The kiss of reconciliation and congratulation has therefore been shown; it remains, with the Lord’s help, to pursue the kiss of delight. And lest delicate ears perhaps be offended because in treating spiritual matters we recall a certain bodily delight [Col. 1169D], let them keep before their eyes that what is being treated is the epithalamium of Bridegroom and Bride, a bridal song concerning the flesh. Nor is it surprising that in a wedding, in the sacrament of spiritual realities, mention should be made of this kiss, since even the carnal union of Bridegroom and Bride sets forth no small sacrament of spiritual things in the Holy Scriptures.

For this carnal union is a sacrament of that union which is in the Lord Jesus—namely, of flesh and Word. So also this kiss of Bridegroom and Bride is a plain manifestation of the delight which will endure eternally after that dreadful judgment and the heavenly Bridegroom’s congratulation over the Bride’s good deeds [Col. 1170A].

For one kind of delight is foul, while another is most holy. The holy delight is that of which the prophet speaks: “They shall be made drunk from the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. 35:9 [Vulgate]). This delight is called a “torrent,” not because it quickly passes away, but because it pours forth abundantly. Of this Isaiah also says: “No eye has seen, apart from you, O God, the things that you have prepared for those who love you” (Isa. 54:4 [as printed]). In accordance with this Paul says: “Eye has not seen, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9).

Therefore the prophet fittingly says: “They shall be made drunk from the abundance of your house” [Col. 1170B]. For drunkenness changes the condition of the mind and in some fashion makes it alien to itself; so in that glory there will be no small transformation of the mind. In this life, a certain affection of the flesh draws us toward parents, relatives, acquaintances, and loved ones; in that life all this will be absorbed. All love will be extended toward God; the whole mind will gather itself into him. It will not know its father; it will be ignorant of its mother; it will be touched by affection toward no one except one whom it knows to be conformed to Christ, whom it perceives to be joined and united to his body. For “the Lord Jesus will hand over the kingdom to God the Father,” and he himself will be “all in all” (1 Cor. 15:24, 28).

In this life we are transmitted through father and mother by a certain propagation of the flesh, and thus many are joined to one another among ourselves by a certain blood relationship and affection [Col. 1170C]. But in the regeneration nothing is owed to flesh or blood. For what father will raise you from the dust? What mother will bring you from death to life? The order of things will be restored to its own beginning. The first man was created from the earth, and woman was formed from his bone; and all were propagated from them through a certain flowing forth of blood.

The first creation of human beings, therefore, was from earth; the second, from man; the third, from man and woman; the fourth, in the Lord Jesus, not from man but from woman. But in the regeneration there will be only that which preceded in Adam. There will then be nothing which we owe either to woman or to man. He who formed Adam from the earth will on that day raise all from the dust, so that we may owe everything now to creation—

> [Note: Col. 1169D: Perhaps: “to the Creator.”]

—and nothing to flesh [Col. 1170D]. And as Adam owed and was bound to the Lord alone in all affection and love, and in every good thing both bodily and spiritual, so on that day we shall owe anything whatever to none but the Lord. He himself will be our father, mother, brother, and sister; and in the true vigour of resurrected flesh, the spirit will possess all things. Everywhere—

> [Note: Col. 1170D: Perhaps: “there also.”]

—there will no longer be a father or mother according to the flesh, nor can there be any degrees whatever of kinship according to the flesh.

When all these things have been changed in a blessed exchange, so that in place of what we had in the flesh we may now have God as our Father even according to the flesh; when he himself may be sufficient delight to us and “all in all” [Col. 1171A]. But if you turn the eye of the mind toward spiritual things, you will find the same truth more abundantly. Here a person delights in gold, in silver, and in precious stones; in affection for loved pledges; in abundance of grain and fruit; in the subjection of birds, beasts of burden, and fish; and in the broad world that lies open and subject beneath him. This is a great delight—but for senses still imperfect and only slightly illumined.

The brightness of gold strikes the eye, but an eye not yet illumined. If you offer gold to a glorified human being, you do not affect or delight him by it. The glorified eye, looking inwardly upon the creature, sees and contemplates him who presides over the creature. To me while I look, the body which is outside is set before me, and that which is within is hidden; this is not the vision of the glorified person. To such a one the creature does not hide the Creator; rather, through the body it discloses the soul; in the soul, the mind; in the mind, memory, understanding, and reason; and also all the virtues which mother grace forms within [Col. 1171B]. Nor does such a one see only the effect of the work, but also beholds the hand which wondrously forms all things.

He sees that heavenly wisdom working wondrously in bodies, and far more wondrously in spirits; and while he marvels at the work, he marvels much more at the craftsman who powerfully sustains all things. He marvels at that highest and superessential Spirit, poured into every creature, immense and simple: granting being to some, but not life; to others life, but without sensation; to others sensation, but without reason; to others reason, but impeded by mixture with a body; to others a substance not enveloped in any mixture with a body [Col. 1171C].

Considering in all these things a venerable beauty and indescribable loveliness, he nevertheless marvels more at the art itself in the artisan than at all that he observes in the order of creation. Fixing the eye of the mind upon him, he flies forth, as it were, into the depth of the sea, contemplating in the Godhead itself things so great that neither tongue can utter nor even a holy mind in the present life conceive them.

The heaven moves; the stars are carried in their courses; the planets move in their circles; the air allotted to them is stirred by the breath of spirits; the sea, encircling the earth, leaves it unmoved. In these, animals move about in diverse shapes and forms; kinds of metals gleam; the pleasant sweetness of fruits smiles upon us; and the colour, scent, and taste of innumerable things strike the senses of mortals with their great variety. In all these there is a most beautiful order, rightly praiseworthy because Wisdom itself has so arranged all things [Col. 1171D].

But the glorified spirit, surveying with the mind every form in matter and all the beauty of creation, enters that holy mystery of the supreme Godhead. There it sees far more fully the causes of all things—in short, every creature—as it exists and ever lives in the divine mind, than it saw it while it passed under time. Entering, therefore, the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, it finds in abundance everything that can adorn and make the mind blessed, so that no grace is now lacking to it, but it can confidently say to the Lord Jesus: “Your grace is sufficient for me” (2 Cor. 12:9) [Col. 1172A].

For a human being gathered within the flood of the Godhead, his mortality absorbed by that magnificent glory, abounds in peace, tranquillity, and the abundance of every desirable thing. Thus, as that superessential and uncreated Spirit pours himself into each of the elect, he himself is all things in all, because he is in himself and from himself the unfailing sufficiency of every object of desire, for every individual and for all together. This is the hope of the saints; this their expectation; this is the end at which, when every soul arrives, it will rejoice that it has most blessedly completed its course.

This is the kiss of delight which holy Church and every faithful soul desire to be given them from the place of delight which the Lord planted in the beginning, saying: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” [Col. 1172B]. Thus, in a wonderful manner, at the very beginning of the work she immediately recalls the end, saying: “Let him kiss me,” so that she may testify that he for whom she burns with desire—he who is the beginning and end of all things—is also for her beginning and end. May the Lord Jesus bring us to him, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory, honour, and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.

“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

These are the words by which the Bride addressed the Bridegroom above. The words that follow are the Bridegroom’s, which he immediately joins to them, saying:

> “Because your breasts are better than wine.  
> 2. Fragrant with the finest ointments.”

Let us see how these cohere with what has been said [Col. 1172C]. The Bridegroom immediately notices her who asks for the kiss and burns in this zeal of the spirit. And because hope deferred afflicts the soul, lest he afflict her likewise by postponing and protracting her hope, he answers her desire thus: What you ask will come to pass, “because your breasts are better than wine.”

This is as though the Bridegroom said within himself: You indeed, my beloved, joined to me in heavenly marriage, are not useless nor barren, but are one able to bear children and nourish them until they attain perfection, because you have breasts made fruitful by heavenly dew. These matters are thus joined together so that the reading concerning the Holy Spirit may not seem insufficiently coherent or, as it were, unstitched. Let us now see what the words mean. First, however [Col. 1172D], we must ask why the Bride’s praise begins with her breasts. Why does the Bridegroom himself pass over the praise of the other features which stand out as worthy of praise? For why is not the face adorned with hair praised, nor the cheeks, lips, or eyes—which he subsequently calls dove-like? And why is the Bride’s whole praise initially contained in her breasts?

This is because, although, as has been said, many things please the Bridegroom in the Bride, there is nothing in which he delights more than that she should become a mother, nourish peoples, and, made fruitful by heavenly dew, administer holy teachings as nourishment of milk to innumerable children from breasts full of the Holy Spirit. This, therefore, is that in which the Bride is more pleasing, which is more dear to the Bridegroom’s heart, for which she is more praised and exalted by him, as though by a herald.

Shall we turn aside to the breasts and consider what the Church’s breasts are? Breasts are so called from abundance (*ubertate*), because a great quantity of milk flows into them, milk which we suck, by which we are nourished, and by which we are sustained while we pass through the years of infancy [Col. 1173A]. As they are set in the breast, so the two Testaments are set before the mind of the Church, which is the Bride, that she may meditate in them day and night and gather from them an abundance of milk by which she may feed, nourish, and bring innumerable peoples to perfection.

For some milk is sweet and some sour; yet both are good and pleasant. What is sweeter than to believe in one God and love him with all the heart, all the soul, and all the mind; not to injure one’s neighbour; and to abstain from murder, adultery, theft, false testimony, and everything prohibited by the Law? But for those who sin willingly and maliciously, the Law itself offers sour milk, adding: “Let one render life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burning for burning, wound for wound, bruise for bruise” (Exod. 21:23–25). This milk indeed seems sour to the sufferer, but to a good king and a ruler established in the fear of God it is gentle milk and most sweet to the taste; because “when the pestilent man is scourged, the fool will become wiser” (Prov. 19:25).

And this is the Lord’s will: that one person within the people should restrain many, and punish malicious sinners in such a way that the Church of God rejoices in great peace and abhors that any of her children should be grieved by the sour taste of milk [Col. 1173B].

The substance of this milk under discussion is separated into butter, curd, cheese, and whey. These signify the stages of virtues through which one must ascend from the least to the perfect. Whey, which is gathered late from milk, is the fear of the Lord, of which it is said: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10 [Vulgate]). From this one ascends to repentance of heart, confession of mouth, and satisfaction in deed; so that by the support of prayers, many fasts, broadly distributed alms, and all things by which sins are cleansed, one may come to the firmness of cheese, as it were a certain consolidation of virtues. Then, when a certain curdling of peace has been produced toward all, one may ascend to the broad realms of charity, which are signified by butter [Col. 1173C].

The page of the New Testament also overflows abundantly with the sweetness of this milk. It shows that the floodgates of heaven have been opened to us, and that what was held sweetest among God’s delights has been sent down from heaven for our salvation. It declares that the Word was made flesh—that is, that God was made man—and that God mercifully came to the assistance of humanity in the manhood he assumed. Setting forth his sayings and deeds, which Christ wonderfully performed in this life, it also promises his kingdom and the life which will lack an end, together with every good thing. It cheers every person coming into this world with the sweetness of this milk.

Yet to others it gives sour milk, saying: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, because you shut the kingdom of heaven before men” (Matt. 23:13) [Col. 1173D]. In that passage, uttering “Woe” seven times, it indicates that milk which at the end will truly be given to all the reprobate as sourness that numbs the teeth, when he says: “Depart, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 15:41 [as printed]).

Having thus sampled these matters concerning the Bride’s breasts by way of a small preface, we must add that just as breasts are fixed in the human body, so that one occupies the right side and the other the left, so all divinely inspired Scripture is distinguished in its admonitions and words: some things are assigned to the Church’s left side, others to her right. For the Church has a left hand and also a right. Her left is this life; her right is the life to come, which is eternal.

Therefore all the Scriptures, whether contained in the first Testament or the New [Col. 1174B], which have been issued so as to instruct this present life—teaching how a human being ought to use this world and the things of this world, so as to pass through this life without offence against God, avoiding the vices which he forbids and attaining the virtues which he commands—all these are assigned to the Church’s left breast. But to the right breast are assigned those which persuade one to despise the world and the things of the world, abhor its delights, love God alone, desire him, depart hence, and be with Christ.

Thus: “Behold, God’s elect subdue the flesh, strengthen the spirit, command demons, shine with miracles, proclaim the heavenly homeland by their conduct and life, and hasten to attain it even through torments; they may be killed, but cannot be bent.” These and such things rightly belong to the right breast [Col. 1174C]. Enriched with these breasts, therefore, the Bride feeds peoples and leads those nourished in the first virtues to the heights and to perfection. Rightly the Bridegroom applauds her, saying: “Your breasts are better than wine.”

What then does wine, with which the Bride’s breasts are compared and pronounced better, signify except the innumerable branches of learning in which the human mind entangles and involves itself, so that it neglects the things of God and disdains to seek and investigate them? Who could enumerate these? Who could contain them in a number?

There are seven arts, called “liberal” because free men devoted their studies to them. First they learn the elements of speech, expressing them by their written characters and names; joining these together, they construct syllables, then words from syllables, and sentences from words. Such labour entangles a person, extending the mind into infinity, and, unless it is first greeted at the threshold, cruelly torments him by its own exertions [Col. 1174D].

Let logic be left to its own sweats: the more it advances within itself, the more it turns those who devote themselves to it away from God. The ornamented labour of rhetoricians serves falsehood no less than truth; they judge as excellently said, whether true or false, whatever is pronounced ornamentally and, as they would put it, fittingly. To the extent that this gives service to falsehood, it is far from him who is simple truth, offering the holy and unadorned learning of the Gospel.

Why should I enumerate the numbers of arithmetic, the harmonies and discords of music, or the figures of geometry? In these “there is labour and affliction of spirit” (Eccles. 1:17), as Wisdom says: “God created man upright, and he has involved himself in endless questions” (Eccles. 7:30) [Col. 1175A].

Astronomy, moreover, divides the heavens with colures and parallels, gives names to planets and stars, assigns the motions of each within their appointed circles, marking now their stations, now their progressions, now their retrogressions. In short, by its rules it measures all their equalizations in one philosophical year, which contains no fewer than fifteen thousand years. Observing the risings, settings, and middle stations of the sun in one hundred and eighty-two circles and of the other planets in their appointed circles, it distinguishes floods, excessive heat, abundance and want, and intermediate seasons; and it presumes, in some manner, to foretell what God ordained before the ages to come in a fixed order.

This intoxicates minds with much wine; and while it diligently considers God’s works, it departs from God and either entirely fails to know his humility or loves it too little [Col. 1175B].

There are also arts called “mechanical.” They are indeed necessary for the uses of the wise in this world, but are not considered so worthy: agriculture, architecture, wool-working and weaving, shoemaking, tailoring, metal-casting, and innumerable others which necessity, pleasure, or indeed delight has invented. This is the wine with which the world drinks, or rather becomes intoxicated: while it seeks what necessity, pleasure, delight, or curiosity suggests, it neglects the things of God. It either wholly fails to know, or perhaps scorns though it knows, whether God was incarnate, suffered, rose again, ascended, and promised eternal things to mortals.

But what does the Bridegroom say to the Bride concerning these things? “Your breasts are better than wine,” declaring that it is far better to be simply nourished by the milk of the Church than proudly and uselessly intoxicated by the matters mentioned [Col. 1175C]. Hence Isaiah says: “Why do you weigh out your silver for what is not bread, and your labour for what does not satisfy?” (Isa. 55:2). To spend silver not on bread is to consume eloquence and labour on things which do not grant knowledge and vision of God. Of this David says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16:15 [Vulgate]).

He adds the reason why they should be judged better, saying that they are “fragrant with the finest ointments.” Ointments well prepared by the art of physicians undoubtedly smell good. Some are pungent, some soothing, some preserving. Some sting in order to heal; some soothe what is painful; some preserve so that things remain untouched by decay. This is the effect of spiritual virtues. For penitence grieves that a person has committed what he mourns; after lamentation, confession, and works of satisfaction, hope now soothes what grieved him; thereafter charity preserves unto eternal life the things that have been made firm.

Therefore the Church’s “breasts are better”—that is, those simple teachings drawn from the Church’s breasts are more powerful and more effective for the salvation of the soul than “wine,” that is, all the fictions and inventions which secular wisdom devises in order to make those who follow and devote themselves to it drink and become intoxicated. Therefore they are “fragrant with the finest ointments” [Col. 1176A], that is, fragrant in the manner in which the very finest ointments are fragrant.

> “Your name is poured-out oil.”

This is the Bride’s friendly and honourable answer to the Bridegroom. The Bridegroom had just gratified her with his praise, saying: “Your breasts are better than wine; fragrant with the finest ointments.” As though giving him thanks, she answers him with this praise, saying: “Your name is poured-out oil.” It is as though she said: If my breasts are praiseworthy, this has come to them through your commendation; for what is brought forth from my breasts is from you, whose name is poured-out oil [Col. 1176B].

By this answer she indicates that the faith which is in Christ’s name surpasses every faith. And just as oil, with whatever liquids it is mixed, undoubtedly surpasses and floats above them all, so the faith marked and founded by Christ’s name and declared by the teachings of the apostles surpasses and prevails over all the inventions already mentioned which are opposed to it, or which perhaps can be invented. Hence it is said: “Your name is as oil”—that is, the faith which is in your name is like oil. To express this more fully, “poured out” is added.

For throughout the time when the Word had not become flesh, this oil had not been poured out. Then, when sin prevailed and mercy did not obtain, the whole human race was consigned to the darkness of hell and held beneath the dominion of the evil one. But after satisfaction had been made to wrath and the time of fullness and grace had come, that fruitful olive tree—God the Father, namely, from whom is the source of every good—sent forth the dove as though carrying an olive branch, and decreed that his Son should be incarnate through her. The oil pressed from this branch he poured out through the world as widely as this incarnation became known throughout the entire world in many and various ways [Col. 1176C].

By its anointing this oil benefited innumerable persons. “For power went out from him and healed all” (Luke 6:19). By illuminating them it converted innumerable persons from the darkness of blindness to faith. It gave sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, speech to the mute; drove away fever, restored paralysed limbs, and raised the dead by restoring to them the vital spirit. By it he made the waves of the sea firm beneath his steps. By it he multiplied twelve loaves to satisfy nine thousand people [Col. 1176D].

What need is there for me to linger over recounting these things? Let us hear John saying: “There are also many other things that Jesus did; if every one of them were written down individually, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would have to be written” (John 21:25)—that is, could not credit the multitude of signs which would have to be committed to books. For this outpouring of oil illumines the world. It cheers the countenance of the Church; it seasons and prepares foods, so that without its admixture the spirit can scarcely be made savoury by its own food. [Col. 1177A] For, as Paul says, “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6). For if, without charity, I offer all the things that belong to the world, even giving myself up to be burned, I am nothing (1 Cor. 13). If I am nothing while offering this without charity, then, doing it without faith, I am found to be altogether nothing. In Mark, the widow offering two small coins is said to have offered more than others who offered great things (Mark 12:44); here, by the two coins he understands love of God and of neighbour. In offering these, the Church offers more than those who, giving their goods without them, offer much and squander it. Therefore the faith of Christ—without which neither charity nor any good whatsoever can be possessed—is that which seasons, makes fit, and prepares the food of the soul, so that things offered in faith may be pleasing; and however small they may be, they are nevertheless great [Col. 1177B] and obtain from God the great kingdom, namely that of heaven. Rightly, then, has the “name” of Christ—that is, faith in him, in which we must be saved—been called “oil poured out”: that is, communicated to the world and approved by mighty works. Hence follows:

Therefore the young maidens loved you.

For from this the love of the young maidens was awakened; from this sprang the source of their affection. They saw signs; they also saw wonders that obeyed his nod. They saw a man subject to weakness, possessing everything belonging to humanity except sin and ignorance, yet doing things beyond human power. They were moved to believe him more than human: him whom they saw enduring fasts of forty days and nights, afterward changing water into wine, then transfiguring himself upon the mountain, his face shining like the sun, his garments displaying the whiteness of snow, conversing with the dead, and the Father testifying from the cloud: “This is my beloved Son, who pleases me in all things; listen to him” (Luke 9:35). Finally, seeing him openly accept death and triumph over it by immortality, and thus return to the heavens from which he had come—what could they do but believe him to be God, venerate and worship him, and love him above all things? Thus “the young maidens loved him”: that is, souls newly converted to faith. I judge Peter’s soul to have been such in the first instance when he said, [Col. 1177D] “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord” (Luke 5:8). Peter had fished all night and caught absolutely nothing; at Christ’s word he cast the net and caught an abundant multitude. Peter had been a youth and gladly listened to the Lord; but strengthened by this deed, he grew into an adolescent, then into a most steadfast young man, and so became a perfect man.

What shall I say also of Paul the persecutor? He who had been a persecutor became an adolescent when the Lord illumined him and said: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you persecute” (Acts 9:45). At once, truly converted by this voice, he said, [Col. 1178A] “Lord, what do you want me to do?” (ibid., 6). Having become an adolescent, he heard from Ananias words by which he grew, by which he became a great man—the wall, defender, and propagator of the whole Church. So an innumerable multitude of believers, first approaching and hearing from him the word of life, initially attracted in a small measure and then drawn more fully by the word, once they understood the signs and wonders—which they could neither withstand nor deny—testified in word and deed that this name alone ought to be worshipped and loved above all things under heaven. Thus it is added: “Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young maidens loved you.”

It follows:

### 3. Draw me after you.

[Col. 1178B] Accordingly, the Bride, considering the glory of the young maidens, into which they have been received through love—and by virtue of which those who had been young maidens are now reckoned queens—and seeing that they could not have been raised to this glory unless they were drawn by the Father, opens her bosom and enlarges her prayer. She prays for herself, that she too may be drawn in her least members to the Father, desiring that all of us together with her may attain “to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4:13). Hence she adds what follows: “Draw me after you.”

For it must be understood that all of us who run are drawn in two directions: one called the right, the other the left. He is drawn to the left who, always entangled in evil works, spends his life in them. But he is drawn to the right over whom a good angel presides, showing him the good things he should do and directing him always to apply himself to accomplishing them. Therefore, speaking to God, she says, “After you”: that is, keep me in those things that please you, in which I may have you as my guide; do not allow me to wander or turn aside elsewhere. For it is written: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). Therefore, if we are to come to God, the Father must draw us: he must first go before us, thus [Note: [Col. 1177D] Perhaps: “himself.”] offer himself as guide, and when he has led us, himself receive us.

Likewise we read: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32). Christ was indeed lifted up from the earth when he was raised from the ground upon the cross; [Col. 1178D] likewise, he was lifted up when, leaving the earth, he was placed in heaven at the right hand of the Father. By contemplation of himself, whether placed upon the cross or raised to the Father’s right hand, he draws every elect person to himself, while they crucify themselves to vices and, taking no thought for earthly things, hang their hopes on him who sits above in the heights. For he who is drawn seeks the heights and strives wholly to raise himself above himself; he beholds before him the mountain of virtues, and while striving to grasp its steep places, sometimes sees himself in the depths and marvels. Therefore he cries: “Draw me after you,” because I do not ascend from this valley except through you.

But if you perceive the hand of God stretched out to you, and recognize that you have been drawn from the valley of miseries and from [Col. 1179A] the mire of filth, grasp that hand, hold it, kiss it, and say: “I will not let you go unless you bless me” (Gen. 32:26). Give thanks to him who will truly lead you so that you may run in the fragrance of his ointments—an expression you will understand by analogy. Dogs run by the keenness of their nostrils in order to seize wild beasts; while these flee, they taint the thickness of the air with their scent, and so show those following the path by which they may be caught.

This comparison is an image of demons: for those who are tempted flee, while malignant spirits or evil men pursue them, in order to drag the fugitives into evil, kill them, glory in their deaths, and sate themselves. Thus this hateful hunt is carried out in the world. In it the spirit that is the author of malice [Col. 1179B] gives the signal with his horn, warns with his voice, and admits evil men and perverse spirits in order to suggest what he wishes; and he kills innumerable persons who do not resist temptation.
