But the Spirit of God works altogether contrariwise: he gives the will for good; he gives the power actually to perform what is good; he gives delight in the things above and an unceasing sprinkling with the fragrance of the things above.

Marvelous indeed is the anointing of the divine Spirit: it makes the skin which it anoints supple and fit for sewing, and makes it suitable for the adornment of the highest King. He is suffused with the fragrance of this ointment who continually meditates on the law of the Lord, preparing himself to resist every harmful thing, to devote himself to no sins, to conform himself to the conduct of the saints, to sanctify himself by imitating them, and, suffused with the fragrance of spiritual ointments, [Col. 1179C] always to rejoice, delight securely, and rest in these things.

Accordingly she prays in this manner: “Draw me after you”—that is, You, to whom no one comes except through you, bind about me the cord of your love, by which I may be drawn to you and which will not allow me to turn elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1179D] qui alio: “who [turns] elsewhere.”]. For Solomon says that “a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Eccl. 4:12). If you allow the evil one to bind such a cord upon my members, so that it draws my heart to itself by thinking evil things, wholly inflames my tongue from itself by speaking them, and bends and turns my whole body toward itself by doing them—what remains for me except to say the apostle’s words: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24). You, Lord, answer me: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (ibid., 25).

May this your grace, Lord, free me, because you are strong and mighty. In this battle, being stronger, snatch its cord from his powerful hand; break it; fasten your own threefold cord wholly upon my members, so that inwardly I may know you in my heart, proclaim you and your things with my tongue, and in devoted action fulfil only what pleases you. Powerfully rescue me, though willing to follow you, from the evil one; make me walk after you, so that when I have walked after you I may not begin to run uncertainly, but, drawn here through you, may attain the crown you promised to those who love you. This is what follows:

Run we shall in the fragrance of your ointments.

That is: rescued from the evil one through you, stirred by you toward good, and led to the highest end as you draw us, “we shall run”—that is, we shall advance throughout our whole life—“in the fragrance of your ointments”: that is, in the scent of spiritual virtues, with which you touch and anoint your own. Therefore, desiring good [Note: [Col. 1180D] Perhaps: “good things.”] gifts for them and wishing them to be drawn toward better things, she says: “Draw me after you,” so that you may help me—willing, running, and desiring you with my whole heart—to attain you at last in a blessed end, and, when my good course is completed, to rest securely and delight in you.

But since some neither run nor wish to undertake the course after you, may your visitation deign to visit them, opening to them the light of truth; and, having illumined them, draw them to yourself and, giving them the cord of charity, lead them to yourself. That great Paul signifies such persons: before his calling he ran wholly after Satan; but afterward, struck down by the Lord, prostrated and illumined, he became a marvelous preacher. Bound by this threefold cord, he ran after God and was brought to completion by the sword. Whether, then, you draw after yourself one who is willing and able to run, so that he may run more and reach where he could not reach except through you; or convert one unwilling and unable to run, and so illumine him by grace given, that he too may attain you: in the sweet fragrance “of your ointments”—that is, of the virtues breathing forth from you—we shall run, rendering you thanks [Col. 1180C] because you have laid hold of us, and offering praises in the glory to which you have led us by your gift. It follows:

The King has brought me into his storehouses; we shall exult and rejoice in you.

Above, the prayer was set forth in which it was said: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments.” Lest it seem to have been uttered uselessly and without fruit, there follows: “The King has brought me into his storehouses.” Behold, she has now been drawn—drawn indeed and brought into the King’s very storehouses. Who can more worthily be called King than he who holds the rights of all kingdoms and distributes them to whom he wills, when he wills, and for as long as he wills; and, considering human conduct within them, either crowns people according to their merits or, observing their insolence, fittingly afflicts them for their offences? [Col. 1180D]

This is truly God: he who governs all things by one command, who contains the things above and those below, granting to each creature its being, so that it may exist and exist well, while he himself reigns as God over all things. This is he whom this Bride—that is, the soul or the Church—desires. Entirely cleansed of sins, she has long sought his kiss, seeking to apprehend him whose desire she already feels within herself. Yet because this is close to the highest blessedness, it is still deferred, and the kiss is not given until the soul or Church understands from created things whether she has chosen one worthy of it. Hence this Bride is introduced, either through an angel or through some virtue, into the King’s storehouses, that she may know his riches and, from those riches, recognize who, what sort of being, and how great is he whom she desires.

Perceiving this and giving thanks, the Bride says: “The King has brought me into his storehouses; we shall exult and rejoice in you.” Behold: she who is in the storehouses exults in the storehouses. The storehouses are, indeed, a part of the divine palace, containing the King’s riches and secrets. The King’s palace is that of which the prophet speaks: “O Israel, how great is the house of God, how vast! Great is the place of his possession, and it has no end; it is high and immeasurable” (Bar. 3:24–25). Let us consider from this his palace, which is as extensive as the creaturely realm extends. Its length, breadth, and height measure every dimension of creation.

But if in thought you proceed further, hear Scripture: it says, “It has no end; it is high and immeasurable.” For God is in every creature. But is God thereby bounded by creation, so that where creation comes to an end, God too receives his limit? Far be this thought; let it be utterly rejected from human understanding. For as God is immeasurable, so he is infinite and eternal; and if he is infinite, he cannot have an end. Rather, where he establishes the boundary of creation, there in his simplicity and purity he receives himself, according to the testimony of Truth in the Gospel: “Father, glorify me in yourself with the glory that I had before the world was made” (John 17:5). For then the Father was in the Son and the Holy Spirit; the Son was in the Father and the Holy Spirit; and the Holy Spirit was in the Father and the Son—completing the blessed Trinity and sanctifying a single unity in substance. [Col. 1181C]

This, then, is the King’s palace; and its storehouses are certain heavenly dwelling places, of which the Lord speaks: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14:2). These dwelling places are the different abodes and different glories of the heavenly powers. In his secret manner, known to himself, the Lord arranges and orders them so as to establish in them a place of glory and of his holy dwelling. Who distinguishes and separates these? [Col. 1181D] Who divides and judges their fellowships? That habitation of all powers and angels is high, unknown to our understanding, and incomprehensible. These angels, invisible to us, were found standing and steadfast in temptation; when those who had been exalted in mind against the Lord fell, they were established by the merit of their constancy and united to God in everlasting charity.

As their names are known to us, so their powers are unknown: they encompass heaven and earth, order all things done within them, govern the life of the just, and do not fail to know the punishments due to the wicked. Their number is known only to God their Creator, who made them from the beginning and delights in their everlasting service. The Holy Trinity knows their nature; the second Person in the Trinity, our Lord Jesus Christ, knows their number. When he was being led to his Passion, he said: [Col. 1182A] “Return your sword to its place. Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will furnish me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matt. 26:52–53). These twelve legions are found to make seventy-nine thousand, nine hundred and ninety-two—that is, eight short of eighty thousand. But the number of the others is unknown to us. They resound with inestimable praises to God; occupied in those praises, they neither grow weary nor fail, but rather find ever greater delight in the frequent offering of such praise, so that either they continually advance in love and knowledge of the majesty which they behold, or, having been brought to perfection, persevere without end, steadfast in what they have long attained. [Col. 1182B]

These dwellings, then, are the storehouses into which this Bride says she has been brought. She shows that, by an angel or some virtue, she is instructed by their examples, so that in contemplating God she may love him with all her strength, cherish his praise without interruption, and show that her delight lies not in an abundance of temporary and passing things but rather in the continual fellowship of these dwellings, saying: “The King has brought me into his storehouses; we shall exult and rejoice in you.” For to exult is to rejoice in the mind; to rejoice is to show by an outward sign the joy that is within. Therefore, that she may attribute wholly to God the joy she declares herself to have conceived, she adds: [Col. 1182C] “In you.” For both exultation and joy are vain unless founded in the Lord. Hence the Psalmist says: “Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous, and glory, all you upright in heart” (Ps. 31:11). Again he begins a psalm, saying: “Exult in the Lord, you righteous; praise befits the upright” (Ps. 32:1). Behold the joy and exultation which praise and glory follow: all indeed come from God when God is embraced with all one’s heart, all one’s soul, and all one’s mind; when your heart is opened to love your neighbour as yourself. The reward for all these things is not sought in this life, but is most patiently awaited in the life to come. Hence it is added:

Mindful of your breasts above wine.

Here it must be observed that this exultation and joy proceed wholly from remembrance of the breasts, which the Bride confesses to be the Bridegroom’s breasts. In what sense this is true must be considered. In his first answer above, the Bridegroom replied to the Bride: Your prayer is not to be rejected, because “your breasts are better than wine.” Thus, since here the Bridegroom says that the breasts belong to the Bride, while in what follows the Bride declares them to be the Bridegroom’s, it is necessary either that they be the same breasts or that different ones be assigned. But lest delays create obstacles, we affirm that the Bridegroom’s and Bride’s breasts are the same. These breasts, we affirm, are the divine utterances, which belong to God because they are divinely inspired by him; they also belong to the Church because they have been granted to her by God’s grace for nourishing and instructing peoples. Therefore this Bride says: [Col. 1183A] “We shall exult and rejoice in you, mindful of your breasts”—that is, of the divine utterances inspired by you and granted to me through your giving—“above wine”: that is, above the understanding of all utterances which, just as wine turns minds aside, turn the soul away from you and hold it busied by earthly concerns. It follows:

The upright love you.

This addition is plainly a commendation of the preceding words. For no one loves unless upright, nor can anyone be upright without loving. The upright person raises his head toward that for which he was created, and stretches his whole body toward that from which he recognizes that being, life, wisdom, and understanding have been granted to him. And from whom does anyone have these things except God? For the Psalm says: [Col. 1183B] “Know that the Lord himself is God; he made us, and not we ourselves” (Ps. 99:3). Therefore he who raises himself toward God is upright, because he surely tends toward that from which he recognizes that these things are present to him. But he who bends downward, inclines toward the world, fixes his head below and raises his feet above, resembles a monster and is crooked. Of him the prophet says: “I am made miserable and bowed down utterly” (Ps. 37:7), undoubtedly lamenting the misery of one who, departing from good, ends his life in death.

Since the Lord does not wish us to be bent over in this way, he healed and raised upright the woman in the Gospel who had been bent over for eighteen years and could not look upward, making the weak sound and the crooked straight. He showed himself to be the one whose love heals, raises up, makes upright, and receives. It follows:

### 4. I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem.

Up to this point the Bride has addressed her Bridegroom. She is either the Church of God or every perfect soul, now disgusted with the world and contemplating God with a pure heart. Seeking the kiss, she says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” Since it is not yet given, it is deferred until that time when, after the resurrection of all, souls reunited with the very bodies in which they rendered service pleasing to God will enjoy everlasting joy and at the same time be endowed with immortality. But the Bridegroom answered her: The kiss you seek I do not give now; but when God will be all in all and the number of your brothers has been fulfilled, then I promise to give it. I consider you suited to help fulfil that number of brethren, and this because “your breasts are better than wine.”

Cheered by this answer, she again addresses him, saying: “Your name is oil poured out”; and again: “Draw me after you,” so that, aided by the power of your breasts, I may finally come to you with the multitude that befits you. Now taught what must be done, and that peoples must be nourished from his breasts so that she may come enlarged with them into salvation, she keeps before her eyes: “Obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen than to offer the fat of rams” (1 Sam. 15:22). She obeys and, [Col. 1184A] humbling herself, turns to the peoples, saying: “I am black, daughters of Jerusalem.”

Who does not know Jerusalem to be the city which the Lord chose before all others, that in it he might teach, utter words of life, and perform in it and its borders miracles at which the world might marvel? There the work wondrously begun by an angel in Nazareth, afterward brought forth in Bethlehem, was finally completed by his Passion, the glory of his resurrection, his ascension, and the sending of the Holy Spirit. Addressing this city, she says: “I am black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem.” She calls its daughters all souls converted to the Lord Jesus through his preaching: those worthy to hear him either bodily, or previously through the prophets and other righteous people, or afterward through the apostles and those who gave them credence. She calls them daughters, as suppliants, as parents, doing nothing against the command of their Father, preserving the faith entrusted to them and persevering most steadfastly in keeping it to life’s end, despising every death.

But, as Solomon says, “The righteous person is the first accuser of himself,” she begins with herself, saying: “I am black.” Such testimony about herself—though contemptible—is more worthy of attention than anything deserving commendation. For what is the Bride’s beauty if she is black, dusky, and horrible in the Bridegroom’s sight? If she presents for embraces what love flees, and is found utterly lacking those things that love pursues and joyfully receives? We must therefore observe that this blackness possesses more beauty, more loveliness, more honour, and more dignity than all that attracts sight or ravishes and distracts mortal affections. Hence she adds: “I am black, but beautiful.”

Spiritual affections produce this blackness. The Holy Spirit brings on this blackness: he pours God’s love into hearts, grants contempt for the world, grants scorn for transient things and love for eternal things. He stirs the affections toward these things; he labours to acquire them; he prays and fasts for them; for them he continually mortifies the body and renders the world contemptible to himself and himself contemptible to the world. Our Lord Jesus Christ declares this blackness to be awaiting him, saying: “I must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things from the elders, [Col. 1184D] scribes, and chief priests, and be killed” (Matt. 16:21). The text of the Gospels proclaims his blackness by narrating what he endured and what he chose to suffer for the redemption of humankind. Finally, by rising wonderfully, ascending into heaven, and sending the Holy Spirit, he changed it into a wondrous beauty of form.

This blackness also overtook Peter, his apostle, when Herod handed him over to four squads of soldiers, held him captive, and firmly bound him in prison with two chains. When he was to be brought out to the sword in the morning, that very night, instructed by an angel, he passed through all the guards and, led by the angel, escaped through the iron gate, which opened of itself for him. “Coming to himself, he said: [Col. 1185A] Now I know truly that the Lord has sent his angel and delivered me,” etc. (Acts 12:11). Paul too, affirming that he shared in this blackness, says: “In labours more abundant, in imprisonments more abundant, in blows beyond measure, in deaths often” (2 Cor. 11:23).

We have thus attributed this blackness to Christ, the head of the whole Church, and to his chief members, Peter and Paul, in order that it may be evident from this that all who wish to live piously in Christ must endure either bodily persecution, such as these men endured or such as martyrs everywhere throughout the world suffered invincibly for Christ; or certainly spiritual persecution, such as the apostle laments when he says: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24). For blackness envelops everyone [Note: [Col. 1185D] Perhaps: “wraps around,” as below.], whether it be the kind arising from bodily persecution or that arising from the onslaught of a resisting mind.

Therefore this Bride says to the daughters of Jerusalem, whom she has undertaken to instruct: Daughters of Jerusalem, observe that “I am black”—ready to undergo every danger and every kind of death, prepared to face every temptation—so that “neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers” (Rom. 8:38–39), nor the other things which follow and which the apostle enumerates, “may be able to separate her from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus.” You also, if you desire to be called a daughter of Jerusalem, look to me and set me before yourself as an example: stand firm when you enter the service of God, lest [Col. 1185C] you be easily moved. For from this blackness an unspeakable beauty of form will come to you. Thus it is written: “I am black, but beautiful.”

This beauty is first of all due to the fact that man was created in God’s image and likeness: “in the image,” by reason; “in the likeness,” by imitation of virtue. For if someone possesses reason but ceases to imitate virtue, he indeed retains the image, but lacks the likeness by which he can be pleasing. Of such people it is written: “God, seeing that human wickedness was great on earth and that every thought of the heart was intent upon evil at all times, repented” (Gen. 6:5–6), and destroyed them, not recognizing the disfigured image and admitting no likeness into beauty. [Col. 1185D]

Yet among the great multitude of people destroyed by the waters, how many faces were said to be most beautiful by human standards, owing to God’s fitting composition! How many lofty heads of hair! How deep their chests! How broad their shoulders, well fitted for work! How many bodies made for good purposes, had they been willing! How many legs, hands, and arms! If nothing had been sought in them but outward beauty, they certainly would not have been engulfed by the waters or consigned to the depths. But all of them, wrapped in the blackness of sin, were plunged into the black house—namely hell—assigned to the ruler of this kind of blackness. There they experience what difference there is between those blackened by sin and [Col. 1186A] those who are bound for Christ by sufferings and the things that accompany suffering. The former gnash their teeth in darkness; the latter’s glory is in light. Hence it is said here: “I am black, but beautiful.” For the Church of God is black, either through bodily suffering or through the mortification of the flesh and contrition of the spirit, because she follows Christ until she reaches him. It follows:

Like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon.

Two things having been stated first, two also are then placed beneath them. To what was said, “I am black,” is joined what was said, “like the tents of Kedar”; while to what was added, “but beautiful,” is appended what was said, “like the skins of Solomon.” Let us understand these phrases as they are set down. Kedar is understood to have been a son of Ishmael (Gen. 25:13). When he grew up, he disdained to dwell among his brothers and chose a wilderness for his habitation. There he set up tents able to receive every harshness of weather and to escape neither excessive heat nor cold. In them he endured Cancer’s burning heat; in them he did not fear Capricorn stiff with cold; in them he withstood the attacks of anyone who came against him, breaking the weapons of those fighting him and resisting them both by bodily strength and by the solidity of his tents.

Therefore the Church, or every perfect soul, says that she is black like the tents of Kedar, because, just as these could not be overcome by any assaults, so neither could these be turned from the love of God and the worship of his righteousness [Col. 1186C] by any threats, terrors of opponents, or scourges—according to blessed Paul’s saying: “I know that absolutely no creature will separate me from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8:39). There follows what has already been said: “like the skins of Solomon.” This skin must not be understood as that of sheep, goats, or any animals whatsoever, but as Solomon’s own skin, of which elsewhere it is said: “You clothed me with skin and flesh; you knit me together with bones and sinews” (Job 10:11).

This is the skin covering his face, protecting his neck and throat, covering his breast and arms and even the vital organs, and enclosing within itself all the rest of the body, [Col. 1186D] so far as it extends. And who does not know that Solomon was a most wealthy king, to whom the Lord gave a wise and understanding heart, so that none before him had been like him, and who held all kingdoms from the river of the land of the Philistines to the boundary of Egypt, bringing him gifts and serving him all the days of his life? What could have been lacking to such a man that did not obey him in the matter of food and adornment of dress? For the highest elegance and supreme beauty belonged to him; anyone of sound mind understands that he lacked nothing by which human life can be adorned.

Therefore the holy Church, or every perfect soul, rightly compares itself to this skin, [Col. 1187A] saying: “I am beautiful like the skin of Solomon,” because, as among human things nothing is understood to be more beautiful or more worthy than this skin, so among things belonging to God nothing is found more adorned or more exquisitely ordered than the holy Church or a perfect soul. But if someone raises contemplation higher, by this Solomon may be understood that great Solomon, our Lord Jesus Christ, who made peace with all things in his blood, who made both one, reconciling heavenly and earthly things, so that in heaven there may be glory to God and on earth peace to people of good will. The Church and every faithful soul conform themselves to his skin, hoping with sure hope to be with him in blessed immortality, themselves to become immortal and be granted eternal blessedness in incorruption. Hence follows:

### 5. Do not look upon me because I am dark, because the sun has discoloured me.

As though she were saying: I am indeed black, discoloured by innumerable sufferings and afflicted by horrible torments. But you who wish to be daughters of Jerusalem, do not dwell on this; do not set my sufferings before your eyes and reckon them unbearable. Do not consider what I suffered in Rome through Peter on the cross, through Paul by the sword, through John in the cauldron, through Andrew in Achaia, through each of the apostles in different regions of the world; finally, through Stephen, through James in Judaea, through Polycarp, Dionysius, Lawrence, Vincent, the Theban Legion, [Col. 1187C] and all martyrs throughout the world. Do not consider how I was discoloured in them. Instead, consider why I suffered these things, what fruit I shall gain by them, and what blessed glory I hold in most certain hope will be granted to me. Consider this: the very Sun of righteousness caused this discolouration in me. I suffered these things for him who is the Sun of righteousness, who will refashion our body, conforming it to the body of his glory, so that I may live with him in everlasting glory and enjoy eternal blessedness. It follows:

The sons of my mother fought against me; they made me keeper of the vineyards.

The Church says that she was black; and then she shows in what way this blackness first befell her, saying: “The sons of my mother fought against me.” [Col. 1187D] By the sons of her mother she means those descended from the stock of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. While all the children of men throughout the whole world turned aside to the left, to worship idols and sacrifice to them, these refused to do so; instead, steadfast and immovable in faith in the one God who had created all things and through whom all things subsist, they remained firm. She declares that these were sons of her mother—that is, of divine grace—whom, while the world was perversely going astray, she recalled from its errors and preserved for herself in this faith as sons.

Although the time of grace had been revealed to them in many ways through the prophets, and afterward the Lord, born from heaven among them, had plainly manifested himself by signs and powers, they nevertheless refused to receive him, to believe in him, or to give credence to his preaching, though it had been demonstrated by countless miracles. Determining to remain steadfast in the Law given through Moses, after his signs, powers, and miracles they chose to accuse before an innocent judge the one betrayed through the hands of his disciple, to receive him as delivered over to them, and to fasten to the cross the one who endured all things innocently. Rejecting this life, they were given over to a reprobate mind; and those who received it were granted power to become children of God, as it is said in the prophet: “I will call that which was not my people, my people; and her who was not beloved, beloved; and her who had not obtained mercy, one who has obtained mercy. And it shall be, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called children of the living God” (Hos. 1:10; Rom. 9:25–26).

These, formerly sons of the mother of grace, while that former state still endured, while the prophecies still remained in suspense, and while signs and powers had not yet been manifested—these she now says, no longer sons but most bitter enemies and impure murderers, fought against her, so that, once the head had been broken, the members too might be shattered; and, Christ being removed from her midst as they hoped, the Church might be utterly taken away.

This is plainly shown in the Acts of the Apostles, where “the high priest rose up, and all those who were with him (which is the sect of the Sadducees), and they were filled with zeal; and they laid hands upon the apostles and put them in the public prison” (Acts 5:17–18). [Col. 1188C] After these had been powerfully delivered through an angel, they afterward blindly charged them not to speak at all in the name of the Lord Jesus. Those who had formerly been sons of divine grace, now utterly reprobate by the grace offered to them, made war against me.

But those who received the faith of the new people and the Word of God—confessing God as true God and made man, submitting themselves to him in heart—set me, who have existed from the first Abel, who deserved with Enoch to have God, and who received within myself all the righteous to whom this grace was revealed, as their keeper in the vineyards which they established far and wide throughout the world. By these vineyards the Church means the holy churches which they planted in their own blood—those who had received the faith of Christ—and consecrated to his glory. This Bride says that, set over them, she was appointed keeper of the vineyards; and although she exercised over them such protection as she could, she nevertheless confesses that she did not preserve them.

We understand this to have been said in accordance with human opinion. For those who were finished by the sword, consumed by fire, and destroyed by whatever punishments the world could devise—who would judge these to have been adequately protected? In this sense the Bride says:

> I did not keep my vineyard.

That is: I did not prevent them from undertaking torments for Christ. Yet I have already sent them ahead into eternal life, where there are no dangers but only everlasting joys. There follows:

[Col. 1189A]

> 6. Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you feed, where you lie down at noon, lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.

This Bride confessed to her Bridegroom that, though she had been appointed keeper in the vineyards, she “did not keep” them—or it—for the single love of faith and charity; that is, she did not restrain them from the ardor of undergoing suffering. Rather, by exhorting and encouraging them, she sent them on with most certain hope to the promised joys of heaven. Therefore, that she may be made more certain, and that no one may entertain doubt concerning that hope, she offers this prayer, saying: “Tell me where you feed, where you lie down,” while first adding, “You whom my soul loves.”

For it is customary for suppliants, when they ask that something be given or done for them, to present or offer something by which they may understand that the countenance of the one petitioned will be favorably inclined to them. Therefore, since among heavenly gifts nothing excels charity and nothing that can be given is found more precious than love, she presents the love with which she makes her request, saying: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves,” so that what she asks may not be refused to one who both asks and loves. For what is dearer to God? What is more acceptable than the love of our soul? Search through all things in the world: nothing comparable to this, nothing so acceptable to God when offered, will meet you.

God created the world and all that is in the world; but for what purpose? That it might indeed be a dwelling-place for humanity. And for what purpose did he place humanity here? That humanity might obey him and, from love of soul, submit to him. The end and purpose of the creation of things, therefore, is this: that we may love God with the whole soul, please him in all things, and cling to him indivisibly, as it is said: “He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17).

This Bride, then, joined to God and possessing all souls, present and future, joined to God in that unity taught us by the Apostle Paul—what can she ask from the Bridegroom that he will refuse? On what matter can she appeal to him and not be heard? Therefore she says: “You whom my soul loves, tell me where you feed.” We understand how widely this brief expression may extend if we rightly acknowledge the Lord as shepherd of all that are fed far and wide.

For he himself says, “I am the good shepherd; the shepherd,” indeed, “good” (John 10:11), through whom no bird goes hungry and through whom nothing that is sustained by food goes hungry. But what concern is it of ours to inquire into the feeding of creatures which, though fed by his gift, neither give thanks to the giver nor have received the grace by which they might know how to give thanks? It is human beings, then, whom God feeds, subjecting to them everything in the world: sheep and oxen, all the cattle of the field, the birds of heaven, and the fish of the sea. Some receive these gifts of God with worthy thanksgiving; others, paying no attention to what they are, whence they come, or for what reason they are given, seize all these things as though by accidental possession, and by no reasoning recognize who is their author or giver. [Col. 1190A]

Since God feeds them all, it belongs to him either to reward those worthy for their thanksgiving, or to reject the unworthy from his table unto eternal condemnation. But why discuss such matters, since these are bodily things while this Bride of God seeks spiritual things more earnestly, saying: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you feed.”

We must therefore seek the spiritual food by which it is fitting that the Bridegroom should feed, and by which those who are fed may become spiritual. There is a bodily bread by which the body is nourished, and there is bread by which the spirit is nourished. Bread by which the body is fed is procured by plough and hoe; bread by which the spirit is nourished is supplied from heaven above. There is bread of life: holy Scripture, divinely inspired by the Father of lights. There is bread of life: every perfect virtue. There is bread of life: the body of Christ, granted to us as sacrament and sanctification.

These are the breads of which the prophet speaks when he says to the daughters of the Bride: “Blessing I will bless her widow, and I will satisfy her poor with breads” (Ps. 131:15). For Zion, “watchtower,” is the holy Church, constantly contemplating the Lord Jesus from the lofty watchtower of virtues and fearfully and anxiously awaiting his coming. One part of her, already glorified with the Lord, rejoices in heaven; another, still enduring exile, is away from the Lord upon earth. In respect of this latter part she is a widow, as though separated from her husband, namely the Lord Jesus, who went into a far country when, in the reality of his assumed body, he penetrated the heavens and will return at the day of the full moon—that is, of the coming glorification.

The Lord blesses this widow with a blessing, namely a twofold blessing [Note: [Col. 1189D] f. “and.”]: granting her grace on the way lest she fail, and finally granting her glory in the homeland that she may rest from her labors. He refreshes her poor with breads: those who are poor in spirit, who, although they possess certain temporal things for consolation in their pilgrimage, do not bend their hearts toward them, but lift upward their love and affection to the giver of all things. He refreshes these with the breads already named: the bread of the Scriptures, the bread of virtues, the bread of sacraments, and the purest bread, the bread of angels, of which it is said: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77:25).

These are the breads mentioned in the Gospel discourse: “Which of you will have a friend and go to him at midnight, saying: ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, because a friend of mine has come to me and I have nothing to set before him’?” (Luke 11:4–5).

One receives a friend well who intends to refresh and honor him with this threefold bread. The bread of the Scriptures, therefore, comes first among these breads, because in spiritual progress the first thing is to know in whom you believe and whom you love; the second is to be conformed to the one you love; the third is to be confirmed in this very conformity, so that you neither look back nor withdraw. Thus we know through the Scriptures, are conformed through virtue, and are confirmed through sacrament. By the bread of the Scriptures we are enlightened unto faith, so that afterward we may be strengthened unto virtue. Hence it is written: “The unfolding of your words gives light and gives understanding to the little ones” (Ps. 118:130).

There is a spoken word which is heard, and there is a Word who remains, begotten eternally. From the exposition of the spoken word which is heard there arises understanding and knowledge of the Word who remains eternally begotten. This is Christ Jesus our Lord, whose faith is surely conceived when the Word of God, holy Scripture, is soberly and faithfully opened and explained. For it is written that “they knew him in the breaking of bread” (Luke 24:35). The Gospel narrative is plain: the Lord was walking with the disciples, and was not recognized; he was received by them as a guest, and at last was known in the breaking of bread. O blessed breaking, by which Christ is known, by which Christ is conceived in the hearts of his own!

The bread of the Scriptures, then, is first. The Lord also reveals this when, performing miracles, he deigned to feed five thousand people with five loaves, and four thousand with seven loaves. For it is written: “When he had taken the five loaves, looking up to heaven, he blessed and broke them, and gave the loaves to his disciples, and the disciples to the crowds” (Matt. 14:19). O wondrous blessing! When it breaks the loaves, it does not diminish them; it increases them by distributing them; it multiplies them by spending them in the refreshment of many. What is unnatural to bodily bread, it makes natural to this bread.

He entrusted the Pentateuch to the apostles, commanding that they break it and distribute it to all, so that all might be satisfied from it and many remnants of interpreters might remain. Likewise he blessed the Heptateuch and commanded it to be broken for the peoples, so that very many baskets of interpreters might be filled from it. For it is the nature of this bread that, when it is broken, distributed, and shared in the correction of many, it is always increased; and from that source whence it seems to be diminished, it rather receives expansion and growth.

By the Pentateuch, that is, the five books of Moses; and by the Heptateuch, the four Gospels, the epistles of the apostles, and their Acts written by Luke, “and also Paul the apostle” [Note: [Col. 1191D] “and also the Apocalypse of John.”] are meant. These the Lord sets before his own, that they may be like seeds and that many crops may arise from them, by which the whole multitude adhering to God may be fed and fully refreshed.

The bread of virtues is present when from the word heard we conceive virtue in the mind and remain firm and steadfast in it; when, repelling the disgrace of vices, we mortify them in deed, avoid them in speech, and fear to touch them in thought. Thus a place is made for virtue in the mind: what ambition embraces broadly is despised for Christ; what incontinence suggests is “destroyed by chastity” [Note: [Col. 1192D] f. “let it be destroyed by chastity”]; what exalts itself through pride is broken by humility; and every far-reaching vice is driven away by the mighty command of charity. [Col. 1192A]

The Psalmist mentions this, saying: “My tears became my bread day and night” (Ps. 41:4). For when he declared that the love of God ought to be preferred to the world, he was answered—so that this might be openly made known by a miracle—for they said: “Where is your God?” (ibid.). On hearing this hardness of heart, the prophet turns to tears, praying for them that they may be softened and at last converted; he regards these tears as breads and considers them a refreshment to himself.

He mentions the same thing, saying: “I was struck like grass, and my heart dried up, because I forgot to eat my bread” (Ps. 101:5). For unless this bread of virtues is continually eaten, so that a person may be strengthened by it, that person is struck by the sickle of sin; his greenness falls away and at once his flower withers. The same prophet repeats: “All day long my enemies reproached me” (ibid., vv. 9–10). And why? “Because I ate ashes like bread”; that is, I delighted in sin as though it were virtue.

These are the breads which Habakkuk had crushed in his bowl (Dan. 14:32), to carry them to the reapers. The angel of the Lord carried him by the hair of his head and, in the rush of his spirit, placed him in Babylon so that he might bring them to Daniel. For Daniel had crushed these breads of virtues in the bowl of his heart, and there he experienced what virtue could do, of what kind it was, and how great it was.

This is that bread which was placed at the head of Elijah when he fled from the face of Jezebel, and concerning which it was said to him: “Arise, eat, for a great journey remains for you.” Therefore he rose and ate, and walked in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights, as far as Horeb, the mountain of God (3 Kings 19:7–8). This, then, is the bread for which we ask daily when we say: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Luke 11:3), because without this bread of virtue and grace it is unjust for anyone to approach, or to attain, the bread of the sacrament.

This is the third bread, the bread of sacrament, which the Lord wondrously makes from himself and grants to his Church to be shared unto life. Whoever does not share in it both by believing and by eating will undoubtedly not possess eternal life.

Let these things said about the feeding of the Bridegroom suffice. Whether we understand him as providing food or as himself receiving it makes no difference: when he distributes these breads to them by preaching, or when they receive the same breads by believing and loving, he is one and the same who feeds and is fed, and who delights and rests in them as in his faithful members. [Col. 1192D] Therefore it is added: “Where you feed, and where you lie down,” because he has the bed of his rest in those whom he feeds with these breads, or who are refreshed by the same breads while a faithful teacher ministers the word.

This is further qualified: “At noon.” Noon is so called because it is the middle of the day, when the sun shines more fiercely and the day dawns more serenely than usual. Each person has his own noon when, forgetting temporal things, the mind now ranges through spiritual things; and, unmindful of bodily things, sets before the eyes of the mind the things of the spirit [Note: [Col. 1193D] f. “of the mind.”]. Hence came the doctrines of the Stoics, Epicureans, and Peripatetics, and hence many inventions of learned people: since the way had not yet been disclosed to them, one defining the highest good in one way, another in another, and not having Christ as guide, each went astray in his own noon.

But the Lord appeared to Abraham as he sat in the valley of Mamre (Gen. 18:1), at the entrance of his tent, in the heat of the day, as Scripture says. Showing him clearly both the unity of substance in which he truly is and the Trinity of persons, he displayed him as a confessor of the true faith. Of him the Lord says in the Gospel: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8:56). For then he clearly beheld the day of the Trinity, when he understood the third person in the Trinity itself and one God in that Trinity.

For Scripture says that “the Lord appeared to him as he sat in the tent” (Gen. 18:1), in which the unity of substance is shown. Then, when he opened his eyes, “three men appeared” (ibid., v. 2): behold the mystery of the Trinity. When afterward it is said to them, “Lord, if I have found favor in your eyes, do not pass by your servant” (ibid., v. 3 ff.), behold the mystery of Unity. “But I will bring a little water, and wash your feet; and I will set a morsel of bread, and strengthen your heart; afterward you shall pass on, for this is why you have turned aside to your servant.” And they said: “Do as you have said.” Behold the mystery of the Trinity. After this, all things are comprehended under the mystery of the Trinity as far as the words: “Returning, I will come to you at this time, life accompanying” (ibid., v. 10).

This is that noble noon in which the Lord lies down and rests; as also was that of Moses (Exod. 12), in which he understood that the people of God were to be led out of Egypt by the blood of the lamb; and, finally, this noon in which the Lord, prefiguring himself to the apostles, showed his face like the sun and his garments bright as snow, while a voice also sounded from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17:5).

Of this the Bride says: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you lie down at noon”; that is, what that noon is “where you lie down”—where you rest and prepare for yourself a place of inward rest and repose—“lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.” A person is said to wander who is not held by one settled judgment of mind, now approving one thing and now holding another opinion concerning the same matter, determining nothing certain for himself in which he may remain and establish the foundations of his belief.

Lest this happen to her, the Bride asks the Bridegroom to make her certain what contemplation should please her, what she should think concerning him or preach to others, so that, persevering in these things, she may not run after the flocks of his companions or add to the number of those who build themselves up as the Lord’s companions by thinking some good things about him, but contradict other things by speaking falsely and most wickedly. There follows:

[Col. 1194A]

> 7. If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful among women, go out.

Instructed by the Spirit of wisdom, this Bride prayed to the Lord that he might teach her by his Spirit where he feeds and where he chooses for himself a resting-place at noon. But afterward, somewhat lifted up in spirit, she adds what was said: “Lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.” Thus she seems to utter a threat: unless what she asks is done, she will mingle herself with the flock of strangers.

Observing this, the Lord, at once somewhat angry with her for being lifted up, speaks [Note: [Col. 1194D] f. “is carried/speaks.”] in accordance with the saying: “With the holy you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent; with the chosen you will be chosen, and with the perverse you will be perverse” (Ps. 17:26–27). For the Lord is holy to the holy, innocent to the innocent, chosen to the chosen; and thus he is most justly found perverse toward the perverse.

Therefore, to her who says, “Lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions,” the Lord replies: “If you do not know yourself, O beautiful among women, go out.” We should observe what is said: “O beautiful among women!” The Lord chose her for himself as Bride, that she might be with him, remain with him, keep with him the fellowship of good faith, and never depart from him through the perversity of anyone. She is beautiful, therefore, because she has been so exalted and so loved that, while others remain in the condition of women, she herself has been chosen for the throne of the Queen and appointed to have preeminence over all.

These women among whom she was chosen—and in comparison with whom she seems beautiful, indeed admirable—are all the souls of the Gentiles, tax collectors, Jews who do not follow the Law and do not confess Christ, and also Christians who confess in words that they know God but deny him by their deeds. Therefore, that she may recall this to mind, it is said: “O beautiful among women, if you do not know yourself.”

It is indeed a great danger for a perfect soul, or an elect Bride, not to know herself: not to know that she was created from nothing by God, the supreme Father of all, and yet formed in his image and likeness. “Image,” as we said above, consists in reason: knowing what is just, what is unjust, what ought to be done, what ought to be avoided, that what one does not wish done to oneself ought not to be inflicted upon one’s neighbor, and many things of that kind. By observing all these things, the soul fully expresses and preserves the image of him by whom it was created.

“Likeness” exists when, after receiving faith, the soul proceeds further, choosing virtues to love and cherish, virtues by which it may rightly please him by whom it was created; and when, gathering all these things in mind and action, it perfects them in charity and gives and offers them. Moreover, the soul is said to be created in the image and likeness of God because it was created never to cease to exist, but to endure in perpetual eternity, forever retaining either the good which it deserved through virtue from the hand of the Lord, or indeed evil, if its merits have required it.

There is another matter in which it is unfitting for the Bride not to know herself, but right for her to retain everlasting knowledge: he who before the ages is always God and not man, in order to redeem and restore her and fit her to himself in the dignity of Bride, became man for her sake—mortal from immortal, passible from impassible, corruptible from incorruptible—and suffered and endured all those things which the long sequence of the Gospels recounts, in order to bring her back to the Father and glorify her with himself in glory.

Who can recount this glory, which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the human heart, which God has prepared for those who love him? If the soul or beloved Bride does not know these things, what remains except that it be said to her: “Go out,” as though, Depart from my fellowship, “and go after the tracks of the flocks”—proclaim and announce everywhere their sufferings, that is, the sayings and judgments of those whom you call flocks—“and feed your kids”? [Col. 1195B]

See what fruit will come to her if she goes out from the fellowship of the good, if she listens to those who walk badly, and if she announces what they preach and teach. What fruit is this? That she will feed “her kids,” that is, carnal, wanton, and foul impulses. She will feed them by loosening the reins of lust and of every vice (Matt. 25:41), so that they grow into those kids whom the Lord will send on the last day, placed at his left hand, into eternal punishment. There follows:

> Beside the tents of the shepherds.

Some shepherds are good: they train their sheep for life and, if necessity demands it, do not shrink from dying for them. Our Lord Jesus Christ is their highest example. Others drag the flocks entrusted to them into death through evil teaching. For this purpose they set up tents for themselves, as though certain lecture-halls in which they may be heard publicly.

Thus the Bridegroom, offended, gives counsel to the presumptuous Bride: if weary of good counsel she attempts to escape, let her try to pitch her tent beside the tents of these shepherds and teach there, so that those whom equal guilt binds together in sin may equally be tortured by punishment. There follows:

> 8. I have likened you, my friend, to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots.

Here the Bridegroom acts as one who loves. He commended in words the one whom he had chosen as his Bride, soothed her with attentions, and enlarged her with promises. Receiving these promises, while carried away by eager desire, she went a little too far in speech, saying: “Lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.” This was a word she ought not even to have thought; and, even if it had been rashly conceived in thought, it was not permissible to disclose it in speech.

Somewhat moved by this word, the Bridegroom indicated that threats were being directed against him from the very source whence thanks should have been given for grace. He answered moderately with a word of anger: “If you do not know yourself, O beautiful one, go out,” and follow the tracks of those whom you call your shepherds. Since I have no fellowship with them, you must withdraw from my fellowship.

But the Bride, understanding that her word had been taken seriously by the Bridegroom, groans and grieves; and because she had offended in speech, she trembles even to utter anything at all. When this became known to the Bridegroom—whether through an intervening angel or by that manner in which he knows all things—he forgot his severity and put on the Bridegroom’s character. He shared the grief of the grieving woman and at once forgave the penitent woman her offenses, mindful of what is said: “I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (Ps. 31:5).

Therefore, with hatred wiped away and anger removed, so that the things just said may be put from memory and this Bride restored to her former state, he addresses her with the friendly term which she had not yet deserved to hear: “My friend.” Thus he indicates that all which had been diminished from grace is now pleasing to him in her. [Col. 1196B] He says: “My friend, I have likened you to my cavalry.”

What cavalry of the Bridegroom is meant here, if not those who fight bravely everywhere for the Bridegroom and extend his victories through heaven and air, land and sea? This is that multitude of angels which, when the first battles were fought and the proud host said, “I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:14), clung harmoniously to its own prince, giving honor and glory to him who had created it and resisting the expeller, to his utter confusion and disgrace.

Accordingly, this host casts into hell the one cast down from heaven, irrevocably deprived of the glory he had once been able to hope for; it assigns him regions of horror and vast solitude to inhabit, so that no way out may be open to them except such as divine dispensation allows: either that by coming out they may test the elect, or that by suitable temptation they may hurl those foreknown for condemnation into ruin.

Thus the Lord Jesus and his chief members—Peter, Paul, all the apostles, and countless thousands throughout the world—were, at his instigation and through his suggestions cast into the hearts of evil people, delivered over to cross, sword, and countless other sufferings, so that they might be tested by these temptations and, unconquered even by death itself, might be received into eternal glory. For John says: “When the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, to betray him” (John 13:2). And the Lord says in Job: “Behold, he is in your hand; only preserve his life” (Job 2:6).

See that power was given to him over the head and also over its chief members. For the power given to him over Job was the same power granted to him over Peter, Paul, and all the elect throughout the world: that he might test them either by death or oppress them by the flesh, while God himself preserved their souls unharmed.

Thus the cavalry of God, gaining victory in them, also exercised that victory over humankind: first drowning in the waters of the Flood those stained by its deceit; afterward destroying with sulfur and fire the cities given over to sin [Note: [Col. 1195D] f. “devoted [to sin].”]; then, against the children of Abraham, the Lord dealt grievous plagues upon raging Pharaoh. When he still did not come to his senses and entered the sea with chariots and horsemen, intending to overtake the children of Israel as they walked on dry ground in the midst of the sea, the heavenly cavalry was sent in; it wrought vengeance for the Lord and, by restoring the waters to their former place through its agency, engulfed both the king himself and the princes, chariots, charioteers, and horsemen. Thus it delivered his people by a glorious victory.

This, then, is what the Bridegroom says: “My friend, I have likened you to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots.” That is, while the angelic company was occupied in overthrowing Pharaoh’s chariots, I made you like that company of mine: so acting for you, so fighting for you, so delivering you, as though I desired always to have you share in my cavalry. In accordance with what the Lord said to the Jews: “You err, knowing neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. 22:29–30).

How great a thing it is to be likened to those whose power and might were shown at Lachish in the army of Sennacherib (4 Kings 19:39), when he threatened Jerusalem and it came about that in that night the angel of the Lord came and struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand men in the camp of the Assyrians, in order to deliver Jerusalem. If so many thousands of people were laid low by one striking angel, what would happen if the whole cavalry of God rose up upon the earth? Not even one of the reprobate would remain.

For when the profane crowd seized him and Peter, defending him, struck the servant of the high priest with a sword, the Lord said: “Put your sword into its sheath. Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matt. 26:52–53). This number contains eighty thousand, less eight. Likewise, many thousands were sent for Elisha’s defense; when Elisha prayed that the Lord would open the boy’s eyes, they were shown to the boy. For it is said: “Behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha” (4 Kings 6:17).

This, then, is the cavalry of God: those in whom he fights and through whom he performs his mysteries [Note: [Col. 1197D] “ministries”], to whom he likens the Bride whom he has chosen from humankind, conforming her to himself in beauty, power, and strength. Therefore he says: “My friend, I have likened you”—that is, in my predestination I have already made you like—“my cavalry,” that is, my angels, whom I send to carry out my acts of vengeance, my wars, and things that seem very grievous to human beings, as was lately shown in Pharaoh’s chariots. There follows:

[Col. 1197D]

> 9. Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove; your neck like necklaces.

The Bridegroom says to the Bride, in order to soothe her, make her entirely reconciled to himself, and prevent her from turning back in any way to feed her kids: “I have likened you, my friend, to my cavalry”; that is, in predestination I have made you in all respects like my fellowship. But because what has been predestined must necessarily be fulfilled in act, in order that you may become worthy of the heavenly fellowship, those who occupy in your body the place of cheeks must be like the cheeks of a turtledove and display in themselves, as it were, the likeness of this bird.

For this is the nature of that bird: it joins itself to one mate and, when that mate has been killed, it associates with no other. It sits upon branches of trees already dead, devoid of leaves and fruit; there it mourns and gives forth mourning instead of song. Therefore those whom this Bride is understood to have in her body as cheeks are commanded to have them like the cheeks of a turtledove.

Cheeks chew, masticate, and break food down, making it fit to pass into the body. These are the holy writers who, taught by God’s word, conceive the holy Scriptures in their minds and are refreshed by them; and, by sharing them for the use of the holy Church, make her fit for marriage, dear to God, and worthy of eternal union. They understand themselves to be joined to their mate, our Lord Jesus Christ, “who, though he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as robbery, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2:6–7).

They join themselves to him as to a mate, cling to him, and love him; and, though he has now been taken up from them into heaven, they affirm and establish that “there is no other name under heaven in which human beings must be saved” (Acts 4:12). They sit upon dead branches because they delight and rest in those whom they regard as dead to the world but alive to God: those whom the leaves of worldly wisdom do not clothe and whom worldly fruits—quickly withering and perishing—do not delight. They give forth mourning instead of song, grieving because they lack what they desire and do not attain the Lord Jesus for whom they long.

Of them gathered together into one it is said: “Blessed is the one whose will is in the law of the Lord, and who will meditate on his law day and night. He shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which will give its fruit in its season. Its leaf shall not fall, and whatever he does shall prosper” (Ps. 1:1–3). These things are assigned to the writers of the divine law; as the following things are attributed to its teachers and preachers.

[Col. 1198D]

> Your neck like necklaces.

For the neck is so called from binding, because it binds the body to the head and joins these two into one. By this name preachers and holy teachers are aptly designated: receiving what has been given by the Holy Spirit, and expounding it through his own gift, they set it before the whole Church and make her cleave to her head. They must assuredly be like necklaces fastened upon the breast, admonishing for good those to whom they are attached. For a necklace fastened upon the breast thus speaks and says: “You whom I have undertaken to guard, be chaste; be modest; be a lover of all honour. Let no adulterous hand know you, nor let anything touch you [Col. 1199A] by which the fidelity owed to your Bridegroom may be injured or love in any respect diminished.” Such a voice is indeed fitting for a preacher and teacher: that he be chaste and honourable, and, like a rounded necklace, be everywhere perfect by his roundness and circumspect. Let him preserve these things in himself and teach them everywhere to be observed. Thus that golden necklace rightly resounds when it says: The loins of the faithful are girded when evil desire is restrained; when wicked thought is checked; when the mind resists lust; when effect is denied to wantonness; when luxury is trampled down; when greed and robbery are despised; when injury to one’s neighbour is avoided; when pride is conquered; when envy is overcome. And that these necklaces may hang fittingly from the neck and remain firmly fixed upon the breast, the Bridegroom says:

[Col. 1199B] 10. We will make for you golden chains.

A *murena* is a fish, beautiful for its length and speckled with diversity of colour. Hence *murenulae* are called chains fashioned from gold, which, encircling the neck, extend lengthwise and, joined to the necklace, bind it immovably to the breast-band. These, therefore, he declares that he will make for his bride the Church. For just as the understanding of those who give the Law, or who set forth the first principles of the writings from which either the Old or the New Testament arises, comes from divine wisdom; so also the understanding, ability, and entire invention of those who expound these same Scriptures come from him. And the means by which they enlarge, magnify, or strengthen the Church proceed from the abundance of the divine gift. The Bridegroom says [Col. 1199C] that he himself will make these interpretations, but “worked with silver,” that is, adorned with divine speech. He thereby indicates that he gives expositors not only the sense which they utter, but also the grace of expression by which they please and are welcomed to minister to the company of their hearers. [Note: [Col. 1199] reads: “they are thought to provide things fitting for the hearers.”] Therefore he says, “We will make for you golden chains,” that is, we shall confer on you divine interpretations, “worked,” that is, adorned in the manner of little worms, and “with silver,” that is, embellished with divine speech, which rings more sweetly than all metals.

The change in wording itself should be noted. Although until now the Bridegroom has used singular speech, he now speaks to the same Bride in the plural: “We will make for you golden chains,” thus displaying the mystery of the Trinity, which established the whole of both Laws and supplied grace to the expositors of each, enabling them to do this work and to be pleasing. From this she may hope for the restoration of her highest salvation: she whom above he calls “friend,” lest she should ever turn her attention to feeding her goats, and to whom here, in promising his gifts, he now reveals the mystery of the supreme and adorable Trinity.

11. While the King was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance.

When the Bride has heard what the Bridegroom has set before her—namely, that she has been likened to the heavenly cavalry; that those who hold the place of cheeks in her body [Col. 1200A] ought to bear the likeness of the turtledove; that those who are in the place of the neck should be likened to necklaces; and, moreover, the promise that chains made by the hand of the supreme Trinity are to be given to her—she opens her mouth and draws breath. Yet she has nothing to offer, nothing worthy to render in return, except that love alone with which she was endowed both from the beginning, before Christ’s incarnation, and after his coming and ascension into heaven, when she was drawn to him by a wondrous gift. Hoping that this love is precious, though judging it unworthy of acceptance, she recalls it and promises that it will remain with her in eternal steadfastness, saying: “While the King was at his table.”

By the King’s table she means that purpose of the divine mind by which the Father resolved to send his Son into the world, to take flesh from the gracious Virgin Mary, to be born from her and teach the world, to be crucified and die at the hands of those who would not endure holy teaching, to rise after death by his own power, and then mightily ascend into heaven—love working these things wonderfully, the Son obeying in this, and the Holy Spirit consenting in it. Although this was ordained by an eternal law, it was nevertheless delayed: from Eve until Adam, and, because of Adam’s offence, until this fullness of time. But now through Christ grace and truth have been given (John 1:17), and what had been ordained by the Father has been completed through grace at work.

Therefore she says, “While he was at his table”: that is, while he who is King over all by judgment—the Son, [Col. 1200C] namely, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit rules the universe—while he “was at his table,” that is, rested without labour in this purpose of mind, “my nard gave forth its fragrance.” Nard is a low-growing and fragrant plant. By it the Bride denotes those to whom, before his coming, God himself granted knowledge of the mystery and sacrament which he was to accomplish. They proclaimed and loved him who was to come, and burned with an inward desire that, since they beheld him in the Spirit, they might be worthy also to behold him with bodily sight. This ardour is love, and the fragrance of pious desire with which the holy Fathers mutually kindled themselves toward him. This is the fragrance which the Bride declares that her nard gave forth while the King was at his table.

[Col. 1200D] This fragrance first went forth from the Father into the world and into the hearts of mortals, when, angered with the serpent because it had deceived the woman, he said: “Because you have done this, you are cursed among all animals and beasts of the earth. Upon your breast you shall go, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Gen. 3:14). As has been said, this divine sentence has thus been fulfilled in him. For what goes upon its breast is never lifted from the earth. This is true of the serpent himself, because, while he rules in the hearts of those whom he inhabits, he himself never willingly allows them to be raised from earthly pleasures and thoughts, or to rise into the light of virtues which comes from heaven. Rather, all their days he compels them to “eat earth,” that is, to delight in earthly pleasures, to sleep and rest in them, by persuasion as false as he himself is.

But at last mercy looked down from heaven. For God says: “I will set enmities between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed” (Gen. 3:15). It is as though he said: “This woman escaped you by believing you; I shall create one woman who will crush your whole head, who will crush by the counterforce of virtue the beginnings of all your suggestions which you implant in mortals, and will in no way allow them to attain the effect to which you urge them.”

This was the blessed Mary, sanctified from the womb, so immediately surrounded by the Holy Spirit that the serpent had no opportunity to tempt her or suggest anything sinister. Whatever is accustomed to move the hearts of mortals, if it were offered or presented to her, was immediately crushed beneath the heel of virtue. Therefore enmities were placed and confirmed between her and the serpent, so that what pleases one displeases the other; what one side urges the other utterly abhors; and wills so wholly opposed can agree in no particular. She possesses the glory of heaven and rejoices to have eternally with her all who entrust themselves to her devotion. Those dwelling here below whose heart is directed toward her she protects by her prayers, and does not permit them to be led astray or altogether subjected to his [Note: [Col. 1201D] reads: “does not permit.”] suggestions. The serpent, however, prowls through the hiding places of hell and prepares places there for his own; here he prepares immeasurable punishments [Col. 1201C] and deadly griefs for those who depart from the faith and do not fear to carry out in deed what he suggests in a thousand ways.

These, then, are the enmities established between this woman and the serpent; and they are likewise firmly established between the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent. For the seed of this woman is Jesus Christ himself; the seed of the serpent is all who are not Christ’s. The first of his seed was Abel, who bore witness to the Son of the Virgin by faith, sacrifice, and death. His seed was Enoch, who bore witness to the same Son by true faith and by his ascension. His seed was Noah, who, in the likeness of that same Son, saved the Church amid the flood of many waters in wood. His seed were Shem and Japheth, who did not look upon their father’s nakedness, but, turning away their faces, covered it by veiling their own faces.

For God the Father is said, in the likeness of Noah, to have fallen asleep when he consented that his Son should be seized, [Col. 1201D] shamefully fastened to the cross, and displayed in reproach. Ham, the accursed people of the Jews, saw and mocked him. But the two brothers, with faces turned away, neither saw nor mocked these things: that is, the two peoples, one composed solely of Jews who repent and are converted, the other of Gentiles. Revering what was done upon the cross, they regard nothing as shameful; but, covering all these things with the mantle of the Scriptures, they venerate and adore them all.

Abraham is fittingly reckoned to this seed. While he sat at the entrance of his tent in the heat of the day, the Lord is read to have appeared to him and disclosed the outstanding mystery alike of the supreme Trinity and Unity. Later, in his son Isaac, the mystery of the Lord’s passion was revealed to him, when Isaac was bound for suffering, the father’s sword was withdrawn from his neck at the angel’s command, and the ram caught by its horns was offered. In this instance the will truly counts as the deed, a deed which the angel alone prevented, to which the father, with sword already raised, and the son, with neck extended, consented.

To these two patriarchs the third, Jacob, is worthily added. We know that, while he slept upon the rock which is Christ and saw the ladder raised to heaven—by which some angels descended to visit the elect, while others carried upward those already elect and long deserving well—he was worn down by the long squalor of toil, and received Laban’s two daughters, that is, the two Churches, one devoted to action and the other to contemplation. Though their father Laban was unwilling, he returned with them to his own country. And as he lay at the point of death, we do not doubt that, by a prophetic spirit, truly prophesying of Christ in his son Judah, he said: [Col. 1202B] “Judah, your brothers shall praise you” (Gen. 49:8). Having foretold much in this passage concerning Christ’s passion and resurrection, he also adds: “The sceptre shall not be taken from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the Gentiles” (ibid., 10).

This is true of Christ. From David, their first king, they successively had kings of the tribe of Judah, or at least rulers, until, having seized Christ, they said: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15). “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” [Col. 1202C] (ibid., 12). They added also: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25). Consequently they were overwhelmed by that blood; and when the Roman army came, they were so destroyed by sword, hunger, and pestilence that countless thousands of their people died, while all the survivors were handed over to exile and scattered under various kings, serving foreign rulers and preserving their lives by doing what they were commanded.

This was the consequence they suffered from the death of Christ, of whom it is said: “And he shall be the expectation of the Gentiles, who shall wash his garment” (Gen. 49:11)—that is, his inner clothing—“in wine,” namely white wine, pure, clarified, and brilliant: that is, he shall purify it by a certain interior and spiritual [Col. 1202D] understanding. “And his cloak,” namely his outer garment, he shall cleanse “in the blood of the grape,” that is, in Christ’s passion. For those who serve Christ inwardly, examining his mysteries in their minds and scrutinizing more closely every teaching concerning his Trinity and Unity, his divinity and assumed humanity, and each of the Church’s sacraments, must excel in a higher and more eminent understanding. For the rest it is enough to confess and believe his death and blood and their own deliverance. Of them the preceding statement says: “Binding his cloak to the vine, and, O my son, his she-ass to the vine-stock” (ibid.).

For Christ is the vine, to whom the she-ass is bound: that is, the primitive Church of the Jews, which established both Laws, was converted by his preaching. But to his “vine,” that is, the apostles, both the Church of the Jews and that of the Gentiles were bound when, resting upon their words and admonitions, they believed in and adored Christ, the power and wisdom of God, who bears our weaknesses and redeems by his death the death to which it was subject. Who can doubt that Moses belonged to this seed? He was the first to write: “I will set enmities between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed.” And who could enumerate David, Job, Isaiah, and all the prophets? Whoever undertook to write all their testimonies concerning Christ’s coming would take upon himself the labour of composing a great volume. All these are remembered as the seed of the blessed Virgin; [Col. 1203B] she bore them as they bore witness in word, desired in heart, and earnestly ministered to one another and to others the good fragrance and desire of him.

These, then, are the things this holy Bride recalls to her Beloved: that these holy Fathers believed in Christ before he came in the flesh, foretold him, and desired him with wondrous expectation. She now proceeds further, showing how, after he came among us and, having completed in our flesh the mystery [Note: [Col. 1203D] reads: “ministry.”] for which he came, ascended into heaven, the Church follows him there. She counts herself among that Church, saying:

12. My Beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me; he shall dwell between my breasts.

[Col. 1203C] This is as though she said: “My Beloved has been removed from me in body, but he has not departed from me in spirit. For he will make his dwelling with me.” But what dwelling? That of which the Lord says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him; and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23). Behold: this dwelling is the dwelling of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit with the Bride, in whom she knows the Father. For she has power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and to resist every evil spirit that draws her toward evil—indeed, that urges the worst things. She also has wisdom by which she knows how to do what she can do; and in the Holy Spirit she has the will always to do what is good. Thus, because she can always act, always knows, [Col. 1203D] and always wills what is honourable and virtuous, you may recognize in her the dwelling of the supreme Trinity.

John also says in the Apocalypse: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I shall enter in to him, and dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. 3:20). Who can doubt that this Bride heard the voice of her Beloved? Who can question that she opened the door to him? Who would fail to understand that she rejoices with him at supper? Who would not judge that at this supper the Father and Holy Spirit sit with the Son? It is a rich supper, at which the heavenly spirits undoubtedly minister, and over which he presides who is their Lord. What foods, dishes, [Col. 1204A] and gifts are set at this banquet, understand from the Apostle’s words: “Comparing spiritual things with spiritual things” (1 Cor. 2:13). For the things which the Church sets before her Bridegroom together with those fellow-guests are spiritual.

First is set before God the humility pleasing to him, together with the virtues accompanying it: fear of God, repentance, confession pleasing to God, and holy satisfaction in deed. In a second order are set orderly chastity, moderate sobriety, commendable abstinence, and the things pertaining to these. The third place is occupied by peace, patience, brotherly love, love for God—which surpasses all things—and holy contemplation. The Lord calls this a “supper” in John because, as no other meal follows supper, so he desires the end of our life to be completed in these things: that by fearing, repenting, making satisfaction, living chastely, loving all people, and loving God above all, we may attain this end and enjoy him without end.
