Therefore the Bride says, “My Beloved shall dwell with me,” as if to say, “He will make his dwelling.” And to indicate the place where he will dwell, she adds: “Between my breasts.” The breasts contain within themselves the chest, the principal part of our body, in which the heart, the liver, and very many other parts are contained, from which virtues arise and by which the human body is in great measure ruled and nourished. Therefore, to designate by name the place in which the Beloved dwells with her, she says: “Between my breasts,” that is, in the midst of my breast, so that [Col. 1204C] he may possess my heart, kindle it with love of himself, and weaken and turn away whatever might seek to turn me elsewhere.

For with the heart we love God; with the heart we retain love. If we retain love, we certainly have justice, prudence, fortitude, and temperance, for love contains in itself the effects of all these. Justice renders to each what is his: it renders to God what is his—every honour, every glory, and the humble, holy devotion of every creature. It renders to one’s neighbour by loving him as much as oneself, by caring for his advantages as for one’s own, and by grieving and sorrowing at his disadvantages as at one’s own. In resisting lust and other unrighteous impulses of the mind, what does it perform but an act of fortitude and strive to fulfil it in itself? It fulfils temperance when, in all these matters, it considers and provides that there be nothing excessive and nothing deficient from what is right. Let us heed what Paul asserts of it: “Love is patient, is kind; love is not jealous, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own,” and so forth (1 Cor. 13:4–5).

Whoever carefully undertakes to pursue these matters will discover this more excellent way: the way lacking no effect of virtue and deprived of nothing by which one may draw near to God. Hence the Apostle says: “You were bought at a great price. Glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:20). Therefore [Col. 1205A] the Bride says that her Beloved will dwell with her and will be to her like a bundle of myrrh.

Myrrh is an ointment which flows from the tree also called myrrh. They bear the same name because they have the same quality: myrrh is both a tree and the bitter ointment which flows from it. Therefore corpses are sprinkled with this ointment, lest decay corrupt them or worms come to consume them. Thus the Lord’s body is read to have been anointed with myrrh and aloes. Therefore this Bride says, “My Beloved shall dwell with me between my breasts” (John 19:39), and he shall be to me like a bundle of myrrh. If you refer this to the ointment, it is as though she said: “He shall be to me like a small supply of myrrh, protecting me from decay, lest I be corrupted, and from the bite of worms, lest I be consumed.” If it refers to the tree, it is clear that a bundle is made from a tree and kept between the breasts for the same protection.

For this “bundle of myrrh” is the manifold remembrance of Christ’s passion. By it each person sees himself to be continually bound to every neighbour, and understands how great a debtor he is to God, who suffered such things for him. If you hold this remembrance—if, wherever you turn, you behold God suffering upon the cross—you shall free yourself by this very contemplation from the decay of vices and from the bite of worms, that is, the temptation of unclean spirits. It follows:

13. My Beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus.

Because this Bride, speaking of the Bridegroom, says: “My Beloved shall dwell with me [Col. 1205C] between my breasts, and shall be to me like a bundle of myrrh,” which offers bitterness alone, one might infer that Christ’s passion affords only a cause of pain and no joy to the mind. Therefore, after the bitterness which is rightly due to Christ truly suffering, she adds the delight bestowed by his death upon all who venerate it. For just as pain and compassion are rightly shown to one in pain, so joy and exultation are truly due to him who liberates and redeems the world. Thus this Bride says: “My Beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus.”

Cyprus is an island abounding in vines, bearing clusters unequalled by others in size, and producing wine which gladdens those who taste it by its native sweetness and softens and mitigates whatever pain may arise from the passion. For Christ is the bread that strengthens; he is the wine that gladdens; and he is the oil which makes the human face joyful. Therefore the Bride says that her Beloved has become a cluster of Cyprus, because, just as a cluster is nothing other than a collection of many similar grapes firmly joined into one, which, when pressed, yields wine abundantly and delights those who taste it in every way, so Christ has become one, joining many to himself by his death and reconciling them to himself in faith in his passion. When they are pressed—that is, questioned by trials and other most wickedly devised methods—they pour forth the wine of pious confession, confessing and glorifying the Lord Jesus and, if necessary, undergoing death; [Col. 1206A] they confess and know him alone to be the living and true God. If they survive, as confessors they exult in joy; if they are consumed, they rejoice gladly in death as victors with Christ who conquers.

Paul expresses both, saying: “Christ became obedient for us unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:8). Behold the myrrh, to which we owe myrrh, bitterness, and every kind of compassion. “For this reason God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth; and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (ibid., 9–11). Rejoicing in this joy, the Bride says: “My Beloved is to me a cluster [Col. 1206B] of Cyprus.” For, hanging on the wood, he shook the earth and darkened heaven; crucified, he crucified the world. Thus he drew all things to himself, and the victor, flooding me with joy, gladdened me as I suffer with his death. It follows:

In the vineyards of En-gedi.

This is as though she said: “I suffered with the Lord Jesus as he suffered, and I rejoice gladly with him as he conquers.” For the world resounds far and wide with his victory, proclaims it, and in proclaiming echoes it, as is manifest in the vineyards of En-gedi. En-gedi is a plain near Jericho, where trees planted like a vineyard grow; when wounded, balsam flows from them, useful and precious indeed. [Col. 1206C] This plain signifies the breadth of the Church, which is known to have extended itself now into the four parts of the world.

It is called “En-gedi,” meaning “spring of the kid.” As it signifies the Church, so the spring within it signifies baptism, the spring given to the Church, in which, when kids are cleansed, they are made into lambs. Christ’s power is apparent in them where balsam flows from the wounded tree, just as the oil of blessing flowed from wounded Christ when he said: “Father, forgive them; they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). This balsam is mixed with oil to make the most holy chrism. By this chrism the spring of En-gedi, that is, the font of baptism, is consecrated; with it the kids are anointed, and thus pass over into the people of God; with it they are confirmed anew, lest Satan tempt them and they turn from the truth; with it churches and altars are consecrated to God; with it the chalice is anointed, by which God, giving himself wholly to humanity, is made propitious; with it kings are consecrated anew, pontiffs are anointed, and priests are ordained, offering their own gifts to Christ for the people and rendering what is theirs to him. This, then, is what the Bride says: “My Beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus,” as is manifest in the “vineyards of En-gedi,” that is, in the Churches spread throughout the whole world, all of which proclaim his glory and announce his victory with great praise. It follows:

14. Behold, you are beautiful, my friend; behold, you are beautiful. Your eyes are those of doves.

At this point it should be observed that the Bridegroom has now magnified his Bride by a threefold praise, saying: [Col. 1207A] “I have likened you to my cavalry”; then, “Your cheeks are like those of a turtledove”; and, adding a third, “Your neck is like necklaces.” The Bride likewise answers with threefold praise, saying: “While the King was at his table”; then, “My Beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh”; and what follows, “My Beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus, in the vineyards of En-gedi.” Since words of peace have now been exchanged between them, the Bridegroom, applauding the integrity of the Bride—whom he knows that he loved, now loves, and will always love in the future, and that all this increases her beauty—confidently commends her, saying: “Behold, you are beautiful, my friend; behold, you are beautiful.”

But when we hear this beauty commended, let us not attend to that by which little women are accustomed to entice their lovers and lead those who have trusted them from the camp of chastity to the camp of uncleanness. We know that God detests this beauty, through the prophet who says: “The day of the Lord of hosts shall be upon everyone proud and lofty, and upon everything beautiful to look upon” (Isa. 2:12, 16). Pursuing it also, he says: “On that day the Lord will take away the adornment of shoes, crescents, necklaces, chains, bracelets, and mitres” (Isa. 3:18–19), and the rest that follows. All these things minister to this corruptible beauty, which leads to corruption, and turn the mind away from what is honourable and pleasing to God.

Rather, the beauty to be regarded is that which true humility, fear of God, holy repentance, humble confession, satisfaction for sins, peace with all, true concord, moderate chastity, and, above all, holy love for God produce in the mind. The prophet recalls it when he says: “All the glory of the King’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44:14). That is, all the glory of the faithful soul, which is God’s daughter, comes from the beauty that is within; and her glory lies “in golden fringes,” that is, in the consummation of virtues. For a fringe is the completion of a garment, and it is appropriately remembered as “clothed round about with variety,” that is, adorned with the diverse variety of all virtues.

This beauty is indeed to be considered; in it God is well pleased. Scripture recalls it, saying: “I shall call to mind [Col. 1207D] all my years in the bitterness of my soul” (Isa. 38:15). For it omits no time without recalling both that time itself and the sins committed in it. It laments what was committed in infancy, childhood, and youth; it most bitterly accuses the excesses of adolescence; it strongly rebukes the weakening of mature strength; and it is gravely ashamed of whatever wrong it committed in the sloth of old age. This shame confounds demons, puts hell to flight, opens heaven, reconciles angels, and makes God propitious. When, fallen down, it says, “Father, I am not worthy to be called your son; make me as one of your hired servants” (Luke 15:21), it deserves the first robe, the ring, and shoes [Col. 1208A] of glory placed upon its feet, and glories in them.

Thus, yes, thus he calls her beautiful, saying, “Behold, you are beautiful,” and repeats that she is beautiful, adding, “Behold, you are beautiful.” This repetition indicates that another beauty awaits the soul or Bride, as he makes clear to the understanding in this way. For however perfect the soul or Bride may be, and however much she rejoices here in beauty, she experiences a threefold misfortune: one from the flesh, which the Apostle laments when he says, “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24); a second from her neighbour; a third from any unclean spirit. This is manifested in Job, whom the flesh troubles, whose wife gives him bad counsel, and whom friends, at the prompting of a malign spirit, compel to go astray.

But the prophet gives her counsel, saying: “His truth shall surround you with a shield; you shall not fear the terror by night, the arrow flying by day, the thing that walks in darkness, the attack and the demon at noon” (Ps. 90:5–6). Here one temptation is shown to be manifest, another hidden; one grave, another light. For the “arrow flying by day” is manifest and light; the “noonday demon” manifest and grave; the “thing walking in darkness” hidden and grave; while the “attack” is hidden and light. But none of these temptations will be present in the life to come. For glorified flesh cannot be tempted, nor will there be in it anything resisting the spirit. Then no spirit will be harmed by its neighbour, because love will then be complete, so that each loves his neighbour as himself. What affliction could come from the malign spirit? It will neither be present nor retain any licence to tempt the good, even for their testing. From then on its dwelling will be in hell, where it will be tormented by the very fire in which burn the wretched whom God has cast away, who, by yielding to temptations, have been sold under sin. It follows:

Your eyes are those of doves.

Having shown the Bride’s beauty, he now adds what causes this beauty: its cause is that “her eyes are those of doves,” that is, her whole gaze is dove-like. For a dove, walking while feeding, gathers only clean grains, feeds upon them, and nourishes itself by them. So too this soul, or Bride of God: while refusing no one as a source of nourishment, but listening to many, she considers everything individually, retains in her mind whatever is said purely, holily, and truly, and rejects and abhors the rest.

The dove also has no gall; it harms no other bird either with beak or claw. This denotes the simplicity of this Bride, who does not become angry without reason and harms no one either by word or by deed [Note: [Col. 1207D] reads: “harms.”] but, however greatly offended, keeps herself within the camp of her innocence. She has groaning instead of song because, longing to be present with her Lord, and grieving that this is denied her, she laments that all things are absent from her. Taking this groaning for song, she says in her groaning: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41:3). She flies in flocks because, in all that she flies toward, in all that she desires to be above, she does not wish to be separated from the Lord’s flock, but desires to be received, glorified, and blessed together with them.

This dove-like eye would have been necessary for Eve when “she saw that the tree was good for food, beautiful to the eyes, and delightful in appearance; and she took of its fruit and ate, and gave to her husband, and the eyes of them both were opened” (Gen. 3:6–7). Then they knew that they were stripped of obedience, entangled in disobedience, and surrounded and made subject to every evil. From her there proceeded in Cain an eye far from dove-like; from there it wandered wickedly throughout the world and was opened to the desire [Col. 1209B] of women. Thus few now remain who can say: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. I was a father to the poor, and the cause which I did not know I investigated most diligently” (Job 29:15–16). It follows:

15. Behold, you are beautiful, my Beloved, and comely.

Thus the lover answers the beloved with equal praise: she who has called him beautiful declares that he too is beautiful, saying, “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved.” Hearing this, let us not attend to the beauty found in creatures, whether bodily or incorporeal. For these bodily things possess a certain beauty arising from the fitting arrangement of their parts, when part is suitably joined to part and one graceful form is produced from their apt conjunction. [Col. 1209C] Greatest among creeping things is the dragon; among swimming creatures, the whale; among flying creatures, the griffin; among four-footed creatures, the elephant; among human beings, the giant. In all these, if one considers the disposition of the parts themselves and the fitting conjunction of part with part, an unquestionably most beautiful form and the supreme wisdom of the Creator are found. Thus some are understood to be of middle size, others very small; unless they have contracted sin, or divine power has reserved them to be healed, they are recognized as displaying wondrous beauty in themselves.

If, therefore, you consider that great Adam, from whom the whole human race is begotten—consider what and of what sort he was created, what he was before sin, and what he was when the Lord brought to him [Col. 1209D] every living creature of the earth and taught him what he should call them—it will be clear that he shone with a certain marvelous beauty. Abraham, knowing that Adam would later obtain mercy through Christ’s incarnation and death, passed through all places and chose, for his own burial, only that place in which Adam was buried: that double cave which he bought from Ephron the Hittite (Gen. XXIII, 19), where Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and great Adam rest with their wives. But is the Beloved called beautiful with this beauty? Far from it; for what follows is, “And comely.” We are thereby given to understand that he is beautiful with that beauty to which nothing is fitting, nothing is joined, nor can anything be joined, except what is comely [Col. 1210A]. Adam did not possess this beauty: even if sin was absent from him for a time, it nevertheless could be present, and therefore he sinned.

But if you consider the heavenly bodies—the sun, moon, and stars—they are indeed beautiful, illuminating the world’s darkness by their light, so that things lacking their own light may shine when illuminated by them. Yet it is written of them: “They shall perish, but you remain; and they shall grow old like a garment” (Ps. CI, 27). If, however, you behold the angels and the orders up to Cherubim and Seraphim, and direct your gaze higher still, the Holy Trinity alone meets you: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Their beauty is that which eye has not seen (I Cor. II, 9), nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, and which God will reveal [Col. 1210B] to those who love him. Of it Moses was told: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII, 20). For the living are not granted to see it; but the glorified human being, taken up already into true life, is promised that sight, as the Lord says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII, 3).

This is the form, this the appearance, this the beauty into which even angels desire to look (I Pet. I, 12). This is the beauty of which David says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. XVI, 15). When it appears to us and visibly reveals itself, there is nothing further for us to seek, nothing further by which we might wish to be refreshed. [Note: [Col. 1209D] f. “Of.”] Thus it was said of this beauty: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved” [Col. 1210C]. And because nothing can adhere to or be mingled with this beauty except what is honorable and believed worthy of every glory, “And comely” is rightly added. Whoever seeks to stand before this beauty should always maintain himself at the summit and adornment of virtue.

It follows:

**Our little bed is flowering.**

Behold, she who praises beauty in the Bridegroom, apparently pierced by love for him, calls him to the bed, that she may enjoy his presence and delight in his companionship. She seems to attract him both by the pleasantness of the bed and by the charm of the place, saying: “Our little bed is flowering. The beams of our houses are cedar; our ceilings are cypress.” For it is pleasant [Col. 1210D] to rest in a flowering bed, and safe to lie beneath cedar beams and cypress ceilings. These things are indeed true; but let us consider them more deeply, if we endeavor to understand them spiritually.

For this bed is not a place of softness or obscene buffoonery. Rather, it is to be understood as the bed of delightful rest in the Lord and of perfect contemplation in him. Contemplation occurs when a person first considers himself: who he is, whence he came, and for what he came. He discovers that God created him with a rational soul and placed it in his body; he knows that, having thus been born, he received the grace of baptism and thus grew in faith. Taught by faith, he does not doubt that the Son of God came into flesh, accepted death in that flesh [Col. 1211A], rose on the third day for humanity’s redemption, ascended into heaven so that humanity might ascend to life, and thus drew all things to himself—the truth of faith teaching this.

Considering these things, he does not know where to turn. He despises all that he has done hitherto; he laments in tears the sins committed in childhood, youth, or later age; he humbles himself; he intends to transform himself into another person. Thus he himself prepares a bed for God by the hand of devout and diligent contemplation. Yet this “little bed” is still understood to be “flowering.” For these are the beginnings of contemplation, which give hope of good progress and of ripe fruit that will then be present when the world has been abandoned and wholly trampled beneath the foot of the mind; when all passing things have come to be despised [Col. 1211B], and those alone loved which remain always and stand unchanging.

Therefore, this soul or Bride, knowing that this flower of good imitation has come through God’s gift and has preceded the first beginnings of his advent, calls him to the flowering bed, that he may rest in it and bring this flower to the ripeness of holy perfection. She also declares this bed to be common to Bridegroom and Bride, since she receives this contemplation within herself and knows it to arise from God’s gift and his presence.

It follows:

**16. The beams of our houses are cedar; our ceilings are cypress.**

This is an assurance of security. For, as it is pleasant to rest in a flowering bed, so it is safe and secure to rest beneath a roof [Col. 1211C] covered with cedar beams. Cedar and cypress are by nature incorruptible: they do not know decay, but preserve both their greenness and fragrance. By their scent they also drive away and kill serpents, and thus provide security for those resting beneath them. Thus is this house covered, into which the Bridegroom is invited by the Bride.

No rain descends here from which the shade of cedars and cypresses must protect it. These cedars are, indeed, the angels to whom the guardianship of this house has been entrusted. Of them it is said: “Do not cause these little ones to stumble; for I tell you that their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII, 10). The “ceilings,” however, [Col. 1211D] which provide the beams with defense and strength, which preserve their greenness and retain their excellent scent, and by which serpents are killed, are the holy archangels. They furnish strength to the angels, ever green with the very greenness in which they were created and with which they were endowed when they resisted him who said, “I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 14). The fragrance of their virtues kills malignant spirits, lest they disturb good hearts and prevent them from rising from good beginnings to greater things.

It should be noted that, when the Bride says, “The beams of our houses are cedar; our ceilings cypress,” she employs that manner of speech in which the whole is understood through a part. For in the “bed,” to which the principal part is assigned, the foundation and walls of the house itself are understood; while in the “beams” [Col. 1212A] and “ceilings,” the principal parts of the roof, all that belongs to the roof is included.

It follows:

## CHAPTER II

**1. I am the flower of the field, and the lily of the valleys.**

The Bridegroom, called to rest, answers thus: “You call me to rest, my friend, my Bride; and, to attract me more strongly, you add that ‘our little bed is flowering.’ But I give you this answer: ‘I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.’”

Here it should be noted that there are two fields: one heavenly and the other earthly. The heavenly field extends as far as heaven itself extends; because it has no end, it is great and immeasurable. [Col. 1212B] This field has flowers: angels, archangels, virtues, dominions, thrones, principalities and powers, cherubim and seraphim. There are many thousands of each of these orders; heaven is filled with these flowers. Every saint desires to share in these flowers; they pant with groans and sighs to share the companionship of their hosts. “I am the flower of them all.” From me they receive what they are; from me they possess the fragrance by which they are good. All these unceasingly stand before my majesty and sing me the hymn of glory: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty” (Rev. IV, 8).

Why then do you ask me, who refresh all these with a good fragrance and provide sufficient fragrance for their sustenance, to be present at your flowering bed, and repeat your invitation as though it might add something to my glory? This is said not because the Bridegroom disdains to be present at the good beginnings of believers, but so that, hearing it, the Bride may be more inflamed in her desire and more earnestly desire the presence, according to her wish, of him who is the flower, beauty, and illumination of the whole world. The Bridegroom also indicates this when he says, “I am the flower of the heavenly field,” yet “I am also the lily of the valleys.” The earthly field, therefore, is this world. When that higher flower visited it, he showed himself as a lily to the faithful and gave and manifested himself humble to the humble.

In the lily there is a flower sweetest in fragrance and most pleasing in appearance; there is also [Col. 1212D] a branch thick with leaves. Though it does not nourish by its fragrance nor have sweetness of taste, it nevertheless has great efficacy in medicines. These things suit Christ, who, sent by the Father, truly appeared on earth as a lily of sweetest fragrance. Paul says of him: “Thanks be to God, who always triumphs us in Christ Jesus and manifests through us in every place the fragrance of his knowledge. For we are to God the good fragrance of Christ among those being saved and among those perishing” (II Cor. II, 14–15). He was most pleasing in appearance to those who received him. Hence Peter says: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life. And we have believed and known that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (John VI, 71–72).

The branch thick with leaves is his humanity, which displeased many through the words by which he rebuked the world, though he sought to offer them the help of saving medicine. He is the “lily of the valleys” because “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. IV, 6). It has also been said above: “Let the proud be confounded, because they have unjustly committed iniquity against me” (Ps. CXVIII, 78). But of the humble it is said: “The valleys shall abound in grain; they shall cry out; indeed, they shall sing a hymn” (Ps. LXIV, 14).

**2. As a lily among thorns, so is my friend among the daughters.**

He who spoke of himself as the flower of the world, saying, “I am the flower of the field,” and who declared that he was true God and a man who would benefit the humble in the world, saying [Col. 1213B], “And the lily of the valleys,” now continues concerning the Bride joined to him by love of heart: “As I lived in the world as a lily among thorns, so my friend will dwell in the world among the same thorns.”

He calls “thorns” the reproaches, rebukes, and mockeries with which the world contemptuously derided him. He also calls “thorns” their deeds and assaults: seizing him with swords and clubs, they brought him like a robber and murderer before the rulers, Annas and Caiaphas; then, before the judge, they demanded that he be spat upon, dishonored with blows of the fist and slaps, crowned with thorns, condemned, and nailed to the cross. He calls the Bride to these thorns, to this thorny bed—the Bride who had prepared for herself a flowering bed under cedar beams and cypress ceilings. Humbled, she did not refuse this bed, but joyfully accepted one like it in Peter, Paul, the other apostles, Stephen, and many thousands of martyrs throughout the world.

He adds from whom she accepted it, saying, “Among the daughters”—that is, among crooked and perverse generations, to whom the Lord presented himself. Yet they did not know him. For thus it is written: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John I, 11). He calls them “his own,” not by affection but by creation alone, since, laying hands upon their own, they afflicted them with torments and sufferings. He calls them transgressing daughters, sometimes on account of their original creation, sometimes indicating that he has a filial affection for his own.

It follows:

**3. As an apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons.**

Bridegroom and Bride answer one another with reciprocal praise; refreshed by their mutual praises, the more they praise, the more they desire to praise. For the Bride says: “As an apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons.” The apple tree is a tree spreading its branches widely, producing leaves, putting forth blossom, and from its blossoms bringing the fruit of apples to ripeness. Whether this fruit is called *pomum* or *malum*, it is of outstanding color, pleasant taste, and fragrance surpassingly excellent, beyond what can be said. Laden with this fruit, the tree called the apple tree not only receives beauty in itself [Col. 1214A], but clothes the surrounding woods with beauty, makes the whole place around it most pleasant, and most worthy of holy dwelling.

Therefore the Bride says, “As an apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons,” intending by the tree of excellent fruit to signify the only-begotten Son of God, her beloved. He so clothed and adorned with glory and honor the flesh which he assumed that it is deservedly considered worthy of honor and reverence above all saints and is preeminently exalted. Hence it is said: “The Lord has reigned; he is clothed with splendor; the Lord is clothed with strength and has girded himself” (Ps. XCII, 1).

She adds also, “Among the trees of the woods.” For as Christ is a heavenly tree, so every saint is a heavenly tree, living in the flesh yet yielding fruits pleasing to Christ. Among them are numbered the apostles, holy martyrs, and all the saints together, who, knowing nothing but Christ, followed him in glorious death, bore witness to the truth, and long ago received glorious seats in heaven. Of these the Psalms say: “Then all the trees of the woods shall rejoice before the Lord, because he comes; because he comes to judge the earth” (Ps. XCV, 13). For the Lord will judge this world. In the body once condemned and now marvelously glorified, he will visibly reveal himself to all the saints in their resurrected bodies. Then the heavenly trees of the woods will rejoice, when they know with certain apprehension and glorification not only of spirit but also of body [Col. 1214C] that they have not run uncertainly or labored in vain.

But the trees of the wood through which beasts and lion cubs pass to snatch prey for themselves will then be assigned to their night and to everlasting darkness. This, then, is what the Church says: “As the apple tree,” laden with its fruits, “shines with marvelous beauty among the trees of the woods, so my beloved,” the only-begotten Son of God, upon whom all my love has been bestowed, “stands incomparably higher in ineffable glory among all the saints,” whom he adopted as sons not by creation alone but also by grace.

It follows:

**Under his shadow, whom I had desired, I sat.**

Here we must consider how a shadow comes about. Shadow occurs for these bodies through a luminous body, a shadow-casting body, and the place into which the shadow is cast; if any of these is absent, there is no shadow. Therefore, when this apple tree stands among the trees of the woods, spreads its branches, and abounds in leaves, it must cast a shadow in the sunlight. Under this shadow the Bride consequently sits and rests.

This “shadow” is the frequent meditation upon the divine incarnation and passion, as also upon his resurrection, ascension, deeds, and sayings. She declares that she has yearned for it with her whole heart’s desire, so that what had been promised by the Father and foretold in the prophetic promise of the holy Fathers might be accomplished in fact. Hence Isaiah says: “May your ancient counsel, O Lord, be made true” (Isa. XXV, 1). Jeremiah too, desiring this, says in the Lamentations: “Christ the Lord, the breath of our nostrils, was taken in our sins; of whom we said: ‘In your shadow we shall live among the nations’” (Lam. IV, 20). There are also other oracles of the holy Fathers which the diligent reader can readily find.

This, therefore, is the shadow in which the present Bride testifies that she has sat. For there are four positions of the body: standing, sitting, reclining, and lying down. Sitting is particularly suitable for arranging and ordering matters, giving counsel, and forming judgments. Hence Sacred Scripture often mentions it. David says: “The Lord shall sit as king for ever” (Ps. XXVIII, 10); and, “Your throne, O Lord, is for ever and ever” (Ps. XLIV, 7); and what follows: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. CIX, 1). In the Book of Kings, the prophet Micaiah says: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high throne, and all the host of heaven standing at his right and at his left” (III Kings XXII, 19). Isaiah also says: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne; and those things that were beneath him filled the temple” (Isa. VI, 1). And finally the Lord himself says: “When the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, then all nations shall be gathered before him” (Matt. XXV, 31–32).

Armed also with these authorities, the Church says of herself: “Under his shadow, whom I had desired, I sat”—that he might come; or, “the shadow which I had desired, I sat,” deliberating and desiring that what was promised to me as Bride might be fulfilled, wholly bent in this desire, and that he might not defer my wishes without limit. “I sat” in his shadow because I applied my whole mind to this: devoutly to receive him, whether he was yet to be incarnate or perhaps already incarnate; faithfully to adore him when born; to behold him teaching the fullness of faith; not to despair when he died, but to rise with him as he rose, in great certainty of faith; to follow, with the whole attention of my mind, him ascending to the place whence he had come; and to cling to those who rendered him service.

It follows:

**And his fruit was sweet to my throat.**

As the shadow differs from its body, so the fruit of this apple tree differs from its image. For this apple tree is the heavenly [Col. 1215D] tree, heavenly wisdom, and is in heaven because it is rooted in the Father’s heart. It is rooted not only in heaven but, when it pleased the Father, also took root on earth: on earth, indeed, when the whole flood of divinity poured itself into the heart of the immaculate Virgin, and the heavenly rain, descending gently, drenched the virgin fleece completely. Being rooted in heaven and on earth, it bears fruit and supplies sweetness to those in heaven and those on earth.

But what is this fruit? It is the flesh which, from pure bread, has been made upon the holy altar through the ministry of the minister and the power of the word, and granted for the Church’s nourishment, lest perhaps it fail on the way, to be received with the most sacred taste. Of this the Church, to which this too has been granted, says: “And his fruit was sweet to my throat.” [Col. 1216A] O blessed throat to which this sweetness has been granted: remaining in the human being, it carries itself above humanity; existing on earth, it joins itself to him who presides in heaven, and from this sweetness mingles itself with that which belongs to eternal life. Because this has been granted only to the good and holy, the Church says in her elect: “And his fruit was sweet to my throat.”

For nothing in this life is sweeter than to pass from this taste into that life which has no end and no evil, and from this image of fruit to attain that fruit which will always satisfy us and make us joyful in eternity.

It follows:

**4. The king brought me into the wine cellar; he set love in order within me.**

For a long time Bridegroom and Bride have had mutual conversations: she addressed him, he answered; she commended him with many praises, and she in turn was highly commended by his praise. Therefore, since words have been joined to words and similar sayings answered by similar sayings, lest sameness produce weariness, the Bride moderates this manner of speaking. She no longer speaks to the Bridegroom, but directs her words to her friends and says: “The king brought me into the wine cellar.”

At this point it must be observed that in Sacred Scripture some wine is commendable and some is reprehensible. Reprehensible wine is that mentioned by Moses: “Their vineyard is of the vineyard of Sodom, and from the suburbs of Gomorrah; their grape is a grape of gall, and their clusters most bitter. Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable poison of asps” (Deut. XXXII, 32–33). [Col. 1216C] The wine pressed from this vineyard, these clusters, or these grapes is most bitter. Its meaning is this: the reprobate, by understanding the Holy Scriptures perversely, introduce an alien interpretation; fixing their eyes indiscreetly upon the sun, they are themselves darkened by the light and draw others with them into condemned error.

There are also those who, even if they do not raise their friends to the Holy Scriptures, nevertheless corrupt simpler people by their daily deeds and words, and compel them, bound with a threefold chain in hell, to have themselves as leaders in their dwellings there. Of these the Prophet says: “There is none who does good, not even one. Their throat is an open tomb; they dealt deceitfully with their tongues; judge them, O God; the poison [Col. 1216D] of asps is beneath their lips” (Ps. V, 11; Ps. XIII, 3).

Commendable wine is that of which Solomon says: “Wisdom has built herself a house; she has hewn out seven pillars. She has sacrificed her victims, mixed her wine, and set forth her table. She has sent her maidservants to call to the citadel and to the walls of the city” (Prov. IX, 1–3). For heavenly Wisdom “built herself a house” when God appeared wholly in a human being. She “hewed out seven pillars” in it because the sevenfold Spirit administered grace to the world in it. She “sacrificed her victims” because by both his own passion and that of his people he prepared the same house. She “mixed her wine” because, for those unable to grasp the mysteries of divinity, he opened the sacraments of assumed humanity. She “set forth her table” because, by opening the nourishment of Scripture, he prepared it for us. She “sent her maidservants to call to the citadel and to the walls of the city,” because, as the Apostle says: “Not many are wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; and the ignoble and contemptible things of the world he chose, and the things that are not, that he might destroy the things that are” (I Cor. I, 26–28).

These are maidservants because of their humility and lowliness. Through them the Lord exhorted people toward “the citadel,” that is, the height of eternal life, and toward possession of the walls of the heavenly Jerusalem. This is the wine pressed from that vine and its branches, he who says: “I am the vine; you are the branches” (John XV, 5). The heavenly Father presses these, and they yield the finest wine—the wine of which David says: “They shall be made drunk with the abundance of your house” (Ps. XXXV, 9). Peter and Paul were drunk with this wine when one by the cross, the other by the sword, bore witness to God at Rome. All the apostles and martyrs were made drunk by this wine when, despising all the things of the world and reckoning them as dung, they rejected them, followed Christ in pure confession, and resolved that death with him and for him was more to be chosen than life with those things.

Therefore the Church says: “The king brought me into the wine cellar,” that is, into a certain storehouse of the divine Scriptures, by which he drew me away from the world and by which he now permits me to have my dwelling in the things above. Hence follows: “He set love in order within me.” Behold how God establishes love in order in the Church: without it one does not ascend into heaven, and without it one cannot in any way reach God. For “God is love” (I John IV, 8), undoubtedly loving every creature; unless he loved it, it would not exist at all, nor would any cause or manner of its existence among creatures appear.

He bestowed heavenly glory upon the good angels and upon all the heavenly powers that persist in the goodness in which they were created, yielding in no respect to the spirit of deceit who said, “I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 14), but firmly adhering to the highest goodness from which they were created. Thus, though they could have sinned, they did not sin; now they lack every possibility of sinning, and, truly called the “firmament,” [Col. 1217D] they adhere to him firmly and indissolubly, love him, and obey him. Since he has love toward them, he is in turn loved by them; and here the first stage of love is found.

He also loves malignant spirits—not approving their malignity, by which they turned away from him, but approving what is from himself: that they are knowing, trembling, strong, continually possessed of their own existence, and continually obedient to the command of the highest King. This he approves, finds acceptable to himself, and retains as his own; he confirms them in everything that he himself wills. Hence Job is not tempted (Job II, 8) except by permission granted from the highest Father; and when, sitting on the dung heap, he scraped his discharge with a potsherd, Satan was forbidden to test him in his soul. Satan fulfilled these commands: Job was fully tested in body, but not struck in soul.

Likewise, when Ahab was to be tested, the Lord is read as saying to the adversary: “Who will deceive Ahab king of Israel, so that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?” Then a spirit went out, stood before the Lord, and said: “I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.” And the Lord said: “You shall deceive him and prevail” (III Kings XXII, 20–22). Thus, having received permission, Ahab was tested by the malignant one and perished. So too God loves evil human beings, entirely rejecting their wickedness but approving and loving that they exist, that they are human beings, capable of receiving instruction and capable of reason. For these things are from him. But that they use all these things for evil, that they decline from the purpose for which they were made—this he neither approves nor loves, because it is not from him. Hence there is no inconsistency in the Scriptures. Thus it is said to God: “You hate none of the things that you have made” (Wis. XI, 25). And thus the Lord also says: “I will be an enemy to your enemies and oppose your adversaries” (Exod. XXIII, 22).

Thus in the Scriptures you will find many things that seem contrary to one another. But once it is understood that God loves some things in the same creature and hates other things in that same creature, you will find nothing contrary. Did God persecute Judas the betrayer (John XIII, 2) with hatred, when the devil had already put it into his heart to betray him? [Col. 1218C] Surely he gave him the dipped morsel, saying: “What you are doing, do quickly”; and many other words by which he could have been reproved and corrected, unless of his own will he had wholly delivered himself to Satan.

Likewise Saul (Acts IX, 1), breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went with letters to Damascus to persecute Jesus with the utmost hatred. Yet the Lord saw him: heavenly light shone around him, and, falling to the ground, he could see none of the things he had formerly been accustomed to see. Counsel was given him from heaven to enter the city, be baptized, and obey the things Ananias would say to him. He obeyed, was baptized, and preached Jesus all the more exaltedly because he had become not earthly from the earth, but wholly heavenly, taught from heaven. Had it happened that he died before he was called, God would have found for him a ground upon which he might justly be saved.

Therefore God loves all good and evil persons: the good, because they persist and advance in goodness; the evil, because, falling away from good, they furnish a ground for God’s justice, and, making themselves worthy to be tormented eternally against their will, demonstrate and prove that God brings all things to their just end. Thus he fulfilled what he commanded to be done: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. V, 44). No one can easily comprehend how many good things God bestows upon his enemies and those who hate him.

Thus God establishes love in order [Col. 1219A] in himself, teaching the Church how it ought to possess love ordered within itself (I John IV, 19). Since God loved us first, this is the order: that we should love him first and above all. Let us love “with all the heart, with all the soul, and with all the mind” (Matt. XXII, 37). We love with the whole heart if we desire nothing in the heart and turn over nothing in the mind that we believe displeases him. We love with the “whole soul” if we apply the soul which moves the body to accomplish in action nothing that displeases him. We love with the whole mind when, in doing some good, there is nothing in our devotion which [Note: [Col. 1219D] f. “which.”] draws us toward anything other than God.

This is the first order of love (ibid., V, 39). The second is that a person should love his neighbor as himself. But whom do we judge to be our neighbor? This is an ancient question, put to the Lord himself and answered by the parable concerning the man who fell among robbers. For the Lord says: “It happened that a certain priest went up the same way, and, seeing him, passed by. Likewise a Levite, when he was near the place and saw him, passed by. But a certain Samaritan, traveling, came near him, and, seeing him, was moved with compassion. Drawing near, he bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine. Setting him upon his own beast, he led him to an inn and took care of him. On the next day he brought out two denarii, gave them to the innkeeper, and said: ‘Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, when I return I will repay you’” (Luke X, 31–36).

This good Samaritan is said to have been the neighbor of the man whom, seeing him, he was moved with compassion and cared for. [Col. 1219C] O how many of us are priests! O how many Levites! Passing by, we see the afflicted, we see the wretched, yet do not bind up their wounds by pouring in the oil of mercy and the wine of justice! O how many of us, who possess not merely two denarii but many weights of silver and gold, contribute not even a single small coin to the innkeeper, that he may undertake his care and that the Lord himself, when he returns, may answer for us!

Therefore, whoever you see moved with compassion for one who is afflicted, whoever you see taking care of him and grieving and suffering with his pain as though it were his own—regard him as your neighbor, you who have entrusted your whole self to God in heart, soul, and mind; and love him as yourself. This is what is meant by “and love yourself” in the command, “love your neighbor as yourself.”

For this Scripture, which says, “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart,” agrees with what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8); and again: “From the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies: these are what defile a person” (Matt. 15:19–20). Hence Solomon also says: “Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it life proceeds” (Prov. 4:23). Likewise he adds in Proverbs: “There are six things God hates, and a seventh his soul detests: [Col. 1220A] haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands shedding innocent blood, a heart devising most wicked thoughts, feet swift to run to evil, a deceitful witness uttering lies, and one who sows discords among brothers” (Prov. 6:16–20).

Whom, then, do you love as yourself? The person to whom you wish to happen what you wish for yourself; whom you assist in this matter; whom you call back from evil, which is always evil; and whom you turn away and separate from it as far as you can. What need I say to you about father or mother? They are indeed to be loved in that in which they are loved by God; but in other respects they are to be rejected.

The Lord loved the Egyptians, sharing with them those good things which he made common to good and evil, showing signs and wonders by which they could have been converted, if they had possessed minds capable of turning to good. When he made no progress among them, he gave them over to destruction, that they might go to the punishment which they themselves had deserved. Thus God teaches in what respect a father or mother, or parents and other relatives, ought to be loved: namely, in that respect in which they too are loved by God. In other things, in which they turn away from God, they are certainly not to be loved, yet they are to be honored, according to the saying, “Honor your father and your mother, that you may be long-lived upon the earth” (Exod. 20:12). For honor is rendered to many, while love is directed by them far elsewhere. It follows:

### 5. Support me with flowers; surround me with apples, for I languish with love.

This Bride of Christ—that is, the Church, or any perfected soul—having been led into the wine-cellar of the King [Col. 1220C] and made to drink of the Lord’s wine, manifests within herself love rightly ordered, saying to the angels, or heavenly Powers, or the very governors of the Church: “Support me with flowers; surround me with apples; for I languish with love.”

This languor is good; this languor is desirable. It seeks no remedy to be administered to it except one from flowers, or at least from apples. This languor arises from the order of love when someone loves God with the whole heart, the whole soul, and all strength, and embraces him with the whole mind (1 John 2:15–16). Here there is no lust of the flesh or lust of the eyes; here there is no pride of life, which comes from the world. That [worldly desire] has truly died to this love, and in it lives the Spirit who truly gives life; nor does the flesh rule, which truly profits nothing. Such a soul seeks help for itself: to be supported with flowers and surrounded with apples.

What flowers shall we give? What apples must be sought, that we may assist one who languishes? Fragrant flowers indeed, refreshing by their scent, nourishing and strengthening souls, so that the soul may remain and advance in that very state in which it stands, and may not grow lukewarm until it attains that goal. [Note: [Col. 1220D] f. “Huic” (“to this one”).] If you bring here the flower of the violet, the whiteness of the lily, red roses, flowers of every herb that do not wither, and flowers of every fruit-bearing tree, you will be welcome; and you will cooperate in supporting this soul, lest perhaps it slip to the other side.

These are the words of the saints: when questioned concerning the Lord, [Col. 1221A] they answered most readily. In them you can find faith, humility, patience, constancy and courage, peace and hope, and the love of which we speak. If you begin with Abel and rightly trace the line of the righteous to Abraham; if you proceed from Abraham’s sacrifice as far as Moses; if, led by the Spirit, you reach from Moses to Christ Jesus God; if from the Lord Jesus you direct the eye of your mind aright toward those whom he himself sent throughout the world—you will find in their words nothing except what teaches faith, strengthens hope, and spreads love far and wide.

But because fruits arise from flowers, it is rightly added: “Surround me with apples,” that is, strengthen me by their fruits. For their fruits are their works, by which they put into practice the faith they proclaimed in words; by which they were not ashamed to give their sufferings to Christ; indeed, by which they consecrated with most courageous death the truth that they preached. Here you will rightly give a cross to blessed Peter, chief of the apostles; a sword to Paul; a cask of boiling oil to John; a beam to Andrew; Herod’s sword to one James; and a fuller’s club to the other. As you pass through the remaining apostles and show all the holy martyrs crowned for Christ by most courageous death, you will most firmly surround this soul, remaining in its languor, with these fruits, lest it waver or doubt, but may pass from this life, which must end, to the life that is everlasting and without end. It follows:

### 6. His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me.

[Col. 1221C] Having addressed her friends, this Bride included in her prayer the request that through them she might be supported with flowers and surrounded with apples, lest her attention should ever be turned away from the love of the Godhead, for which she had already begun to languish. Rejoicing in them, then, as though they had been heard for her, she says: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me”; as if to say: I understand that your prayers for me have been heard because his left hand is now beneath my head, and I now certainly conceive that his right hand will embrace me.

Here it must be observed that the Lord has both a left hand and a right, in accordance with what Solomon says of wisdom in Proverbs: “Length of life is in her right hand, but in her left are riches and glory” (Prov. 3:16). Now no one doubts that the head [Col. 1221D] of the Church is Jesus Christ. For just as all members depend upon the head, and a member that does not serve it is useless, so all the faithful have from Christ what they are, that they are faithful, that in faith they work well, and that in good works they conceive hope of eternal life, to which they are already joined by love.

These are God’s gifts: temporal blessedness, and that blessedness which is now the angels’ and which will be eternal for us. Hence the Lord says: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:18–19).

The bodily senses, by which all the members of the body are governed—namely sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch—are also most vigorous in the head; and these are acknowledged to flourish in Christ above all mortals. For he sees every work that we do; he hears what we say and what we think; he smells, indeed, the good which we conceive in the mind; and he tastes what we accomplish in deed. What shall I say of touch? It is wondrous indeed: whomever he touches, he immediately changes into himself; he changes him into another man, so that he becomes estranged from himself.

Therefore, the person understands the left hand to be under the head who knows that all riches and this entire temporal glory come from him (1 Sam. 2:7). [Col. 1222A] For the Lord makes poor and makes rich; he humbles and lifts up, that one may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory. Of himself the Lord says: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go therefore [Col. 1222B] and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.”

If, then, all power has been given to him not only in heaven but even on earth, it is clear that all riches, all glory, and all temporal blessedness—which is known to have an end—come from him; and likewise that blessedness which has long been granted in heaven to angels and is promised without end to all his own. Hence God’s left hand is rightly said to be beneath the head of the Bride, because it is certain that no one obtains this temporal prosperity and glory except by his gift. For in Wisdom’s figure it is said: “By me kings reign, and lawgivers decree what is just; by me princes rule, and the mighty decree justice” (Prov. 8:15–16).

[Col. 1222C] Therefore, since kings of the age are now for the most part subject to Christ—for to him every knee of kings, prelates, mighty men, and rulers is bent—the Church rightly says that God’s left hand stands beneath “her,” that is, the Church’s, head: Christ, who plainly dispenses all these things to his members as he wills. Yet he gives them to certain people who receive his benefits ungratefully, exalt themselves in the gifts bestowed, and, failing to give thanks to God, heap up wrath for themselves in those very gifts for the day of eternal recompense.

But God gives these things to his faithful so that they may distribute every good thing well, lest, behaving shamefully on the way, they fail; that they may show themselves children of love and regard this grace as given to them not for merit, but seek rather that grace [Col. 1222D] which is to be bestowed upon his own hereafter. Hence it is added: “And his right hand shall embrace me.” For what is God’s right hand except God’s own eternity? It embraces the whole Church: first glorifying her in the patriarchs and prophets, crowning her in the apostles and martyrs, and worthily rewarding all her other members, so that there may be no part of the Church able to complain that it is exempt from his grace. It follows:

### 7. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and the stags of the field: do not rouse or awaken the beloved until she herself wills it.

Up to this point the Bride has continued at length, speaking about the Bridegroom, though not to him—indeed a sign of exceptional love. For love stirs the mind so that, even if shame or fear does not allow it at times to speak to the Bridegroom, nevertheless, inflamed by the goads of love, it does not refrain from speaking of him, either to itself or to anyone else. Observing this, the Beloved himself gives an equal indication of love, now speaking not to her but of her to others: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and the stags of the field, do not rouse her.”

[Col. 1223A] He sees her, now in great part languishing with love for him, desiring to rest in his bosom away from the disturbances of the world, weary even of necessary conversations, cheerful only in the Bridegroom’s delight. He also considers another part of her, ignorant of this languor and greatly bound to the age, which regards her as though dead and wishes her to yield to its own need and undertake a share of its labor. Taking pity on the one who languishes, he says: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not rouse her,” that is, do not call her away from tranquil rest.

But the adjuration by which he says, “by the gazelles and the stags of the field,” must be considered. This adjuration is not without cause. These animals are removed from the world and set apart from human society, refreshing themselves with herbs; they are clean animals, which chew the cud and divide the hoof. All this befits the saints, who, set apart in mind from carnal things, feed on green grass—that is, the unfading teaching of the saints—which they chew again, namely, often recall to memory after once understanding it; and they divide the hoof because, having understood these things, they separate eternal things from temporal.

It also belongs particularly to little goats that they seek the heights and, when wounded, touch dittany; and this is fittingly applied to the saints: namely, to seek heavenly things and, if there is any injury from sin, to heal it through Christ’s healing. The stag also has this nature: when it is a hundred years old, or perhaps of a greater age, it is already [Col. 1223C] declining into old age; wherever it may be, it marks the serpent’s dwelling, and, as nature teaches it, immediately draws the serpent out by its breath, devours and consumes it. Then, after drinking this meal down with a draught from a fountain of purer water, it immediately sheds its antlers, changes its hide and hair, recovers its sight, and, wholly renewing itself, becomes young again and passes into another life, now destined to live long. [Note: [Col. 1223D] f. “jamque” (“and now”).] [Note: [Col. 1223D] f. add. after “post” (“after”).]

This is applied to the saints in the following manner. The saints, having lived long and preserved virtue, and now having brought it to maturity, when they are declining into old age, mark wherever they may be the dwelling-place of the dreadful serpent: where it rules, where it dwells, where with much craftiness it scatters the hearts of those who inhabit there and separates them from love. Hoping, therefore, that the consummation of their virtues will be good if they crush these movements, restore peace, and teach that restored peace to be preserved, they go to the serpent’s place. Instructed by the breath of the Holy Spirit, they draw out this ancient serpent, scatter what it has sown, and as though crushing it with their teeth, devour and consume it; [Col. 1224A] they bring its deeds to nothing. Then, instructed by a draught from the clear fountain—that is, by the gifts and teachings of our Lord Jesus Christ—they pass over into eternal life. There, changed into the new human being, they live a blessed life, lacking nothing, nor able to lack anything that it desires.

The adjuration, then, is this: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and the stags of the field, do not rouse her”; that is, may it be granted to you to attain the virtues signified by the gazelles and stags, in such a way that you do not rouse the beloved until she herself wills it.

[Note: [Col. 1224D] f. “Designantur” (“are signified”).] Here the times for action and contemplation are defined. The times of contemplation are pleasing and acceptable, so that those to whom this grace has been given can scarcely be torn away from it. For they love, and by loving understand how much they lack of what they behold in contemplation; they strive to attain these things and consider burdensome those through whom this calling is hindered. But the voice of the Beloved is what is added: “Until she herself wills it.”

From this it is understood that there are times when the Bride may wish to be drawn away from this calling and conformed to lower things: for example, when faith is weakened, when heresy is spread abroad, and when it has itself already clung like a cancer, so that, unless remedies are applied, it takes possession of the whole body and hopes to possess it altogether. Thus Arius said, “There was a time when the Son was not,” supposing that the whole Trinity was not coeternal with itself; but imagining that divine generation—of which it is said, “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8)—was like our human generation, in which the one who is father comes first, and from him then follows the one who is son.

[Col. 1224C] This heresy certainly spread throughout the whole world, so that scarcely four bishops could be found in the Church who held right views concerning faith in the eternal Trinity. For, to say nothing of other parts of the world, I shall disclose how great were the evils that arose from it in Africa alone. Huneric, son of Genseric, who succeeded to the kingdom upon his father’s death, stirred by Arian perfidy, drove 334 Catholic bishops into exile, closed their churches, and afflicted the people with various punishments. Thrasamund, who succeeded him in the kingdom, likewise closed the Catholic churches and banished 220 bishops into exile in Sardinia; Pope Symmachus supplied them with daily assistance.

This heresy also spread so widely through other parts of the world that it was necessary to summon the whole Church and assemble it in one place, entreating God with poured-out prayers that, once this pest had been removed, he might declare the truth of the matter under discussion. Inclined by the pious prayers of his Beloved and of the other faithful, God compelled Arius—when he had come to Constantinople to defend his heresy and had, by necessity, gone aside to the public privies—to die by the pouring out of his inner vital organs; nor afterward did any defender of his heresy appear.

[Col. 1225A] Likewise, when contemplation penetrates the secret things of heaven and occupies itself with them insofar as it can, but, as teaching has ceased, either heresy or perhaps other sins reign among those subject to it, or help is desired for neighbors in distress, it is the time when contemplatives should wish to descend and aid those who await assistance from them. The order of the passage, then, is this: This is the voice of my Beloved: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and the stags of the field, do not rouse or awaken the beloved until she herself wills it.” It follows:

### 8. Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills.

This is the Bride’s assertion. For she had said that the voice declaring, “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem,” [Col. 1225B] and so forth, was the voice of her Beloved; she now affirms this. Seeing her Beloved coming and not contradicting those for whom the Bride had testified that he was their author, she announces his coming beforehand in these words: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills.”

A broad exposition opens here wherever Sacred Scripture speaks of mountains and hills. Scripture considers some mountains evil and declares others worthy of praise. It considers evil mountains such as the mountains of Gilboa, where those who seemed strong in Israel fell; David abhorred them, saying: “Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain descend upon you” (2 Sam. 1:21). For Gilboa is interpreted “descent,” signifying mountains of pride and boasting, upon which, the more one climbs, the more one falls and descends. Hence it is said: “Every mountain and hill shall be humbled” (Luke 3:5).

On these mountains fought Saul and Jonathan, sons of Israel already rejected by God; puffed up and rejected by God, they led the people who followed them out against the enemy and fell together with those who were falling. Thus David says: “Mountains of Gilboa,” that is, mountains of vices, on which the more one ascends, the more one descends; “let neither dew nor rain”—that is, heavenly teaching—“descend upon you,” where those fell who, hoping that they were strong in Israel, fell because they were conscious of their own weakness. These are evil mountains. David himself recalls that they must be avoided, saying: “The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord” (Ps. 96:5).

[Col. 1225D] Those who are powerful and exalted in the world, prefer themselves to others, and despise others as though inferior to them, do not behold the Lord coming in wrath and fire; but as wax before fire, so they melt away and fail. But the good mountain is that of which David says: “Mount Selmon, mountain of God, rich mountain” (Ps. 67:15). For Selmon is interpreted “shadow,” signifying the Lord Jesus Christ, whom divinity wholly overshadowed. Hence it continues: “Mountain of God, rich mountain; curdled mountain, rich mountain.” For among the children of men there is none upon whom the flood of divinity has so entirely poured itself, none in whom the whole fullness of divinity has dwelt bodily. Hence it adds: “Why do you look with suspicion upon the curdled mountains?” (Ps. 5:17 [citation apparently corrupt]).

[Col. 1226A] For there is none among the children of men in whom holy divinity has been so united with humanity that one and the same person is both true God and true man. This is the mountain in which it pleased God to dwell; for in him the Lord shall dwell unto the end, which is understood as without end. Surely divinity is not to be separated from humanity—to whom has been given all power in heaven and on earth to judge, to take away, and to remove. As “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev. 19:16), he may indeed be called mountain of mountains. Hence Isaiah also says: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared” (Isa. 2:2).

For the house of the Lord, which God inhabits bodily, is the Lord Jesus Christ; and the mountain of this house is the very height of divinity. Upon it the Lord Jesus himself is raised above the summit of all mountains, to whom all nations and all peoples shall flow. Hence all the saints are understood as mountains. Thus it is said: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains” (Ps. 120:1); and elsewhere: “You shine wondrously from the eternal mountains” (Ps. 75:5). By his own fullness he illuminates the mountains, establishes them in eternity, and grants them to others throughout the world that they may be enlightened by their light.

Therefore, seeing her Bridegroom coming, the Bride says: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains.” From what mountain does he leap? From the heart of the Father. Upon what mountain does he leap? Into the heart of the holy Virgin, in whom he put on humanity, fitting to himself a body and soul and taking upon himself this mortal life. From there he makes a leap to the cross, by which he redeemed us. [Col. 1226C] From there his next leap is into the tomb, in which, remaining forty hours, he makes a leap by rising thence into immortal life. In it he remains forty days with the apostles and his other followers, then ascends to the place from which he came forth, teaching us to ascend there through virtues and to regard this as the end of our course.

The Lord is also said, in coming, to leap upon the mountains. For the mountains are the teachers of the Church, illuminated by the eternal mountains; because of the eminence of their knowledge and understanding they are rightly called mountains. He leaps upon them when he illumines them with the fire of his splendor. He made a leap upon the apostle Peter when the Lord asked: “But who do you say that I am?” (Matt. 16:15). While the others were silent, Peter answered: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God.” Hence he received the keys of the Church, the power also of binding and loosing, and, after Christ, obtained the primacy of the whole Church.

That he made leaps in Peter and the others is left beyond doubt: he assured them of his resurrection; on the day of Pentecost he glorified them with the Holy Spirit; he made them steadfast and courageous in every examination; Peter and John healed with a word alone at the Beautiful Gate a man lame from his mother’s womb; and through his preaching Peter converted and baptized now three thousand, at another time five thousand, to the Lord Jesus. For it is certain that these deeds came to pass not through the power of a human being alone but through the true presence of God.

[Col. 1227A] Since it is certain that Peter knew Ananias and Sapphira’s deceit with no one but God revealing it, and that they themselves expired at his rebuke, who would not understand that God leapt into him, and that he performed these things at the command of the one who willed them? And when Peter was praying at Joppa in an upper room at the sixth hour and fell into an ecstasy of mind, so that, with heaven opened, he saw a great vessel like a sheet lowered to him from heaven by its four corners, containing every kind of four-footed creature, creeping thing of the earth, and bird of heaven, and heard a voice saying to him: “Peter, kill and eat” (Acts 11:6); and he said: “Far be it from me, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common and unclean”; and the Lord said to him: “What God has cleansed, do not call common”—who would not say that the Lord leapt into him, when, after hearing Cornelius’s messengers, he came to Caesarea and, discovering that God is no respecter of persons, baptized Cornelius himself and all his household, upon which the Holy Spirit had descended?

Since it is established, therefore, that the Lord made leaps in Peter, first of the apostles, in these ways and in very many others, it remains that we should understand the same in the same ways concerning all the others whom, sent into the world, he himself both preached through and converted the nations to himself by the wondrous demonstration of their works.

[Col. 1227B] He made a leap into Paul, the last of the apostles, when, after a light had been sent from heaven, Paul was thrown to the ground and saw nothing, and he called him thus: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts 9:4–15). Sent to Ananias, he received sight and was baptized; and, as the Lord leapt into him, he openly confessed before all that he was his disciple. How many leaps God made in him, how wonderfully he raised him, how wonderfully he made him eloquent in doctrine and conspicuous to all—his letters teach, and those writings called the “Acts of the Apostles” clearly declare.

The Bride therefore says of him: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains.” She also joins what follows: “Bounding over the hills.” Let us see why it is thus. What we have said about mountains must also be said about hills. Some hills are good; thus it is said: “Bless the Lord, mountains and hills” [Col. 1227D] (Dan. 3:75); and Isaiah says: “The Lord shall be raised above the hills” (Isa. 2:2). But some are evil. Hence in this place it is said that the Lord leaps upon mountains but bounds over hills: for where he leaps, there he is; but those over whom he bounds, he does not remain with them but leaves and abandons them.

Who, then, are these? Those who make themselves great by inventing heresies; they exalt themselves in these, desire to make themselves equal to the height of mountains, turn and draw peoples after themselves, and make themselves great when they are nothing, boasting that they have God while they are far from him. Among them are Arius, Eutyches, and all heresiarchs, whom holy Church identifies, escapes, and condemns. These the Lord passes over. [Col. 1228A] He also passes over hypocrites, who confess in words that they know the Lord but deny him by their deeds. Thus he passes over all whom neither faith fortifies nor holiness of life makes honorable. The reason for this is that:

### 9. The Beloved is like a gazelle and a young stag.

The Bridegroom is rightly compared, as he comes, with these animals: both because God sees all things clearly, and because he dwells upon the lofty summit of virtues, feeds there, measures out his leaps there, and sees also those in whom the ancient serpent lies coiled in rest or uncoiled stretches out its coils. These he avoids, as Christ has no fellowship with Belial. [Note: [Col. 1227D] f. “hos” (“these”).] It follows:

[Col. 1228B] Behold, he stands behind our wall.

This is indeed declared of the Beloved because he is like a gazelle. For he is keen of sight, as one who sees the Father and, living in the Father, beholds all things in the Father—not only the acts of deeds but also the dispositions of thoughts. Therefore he now admonishes everyone that we should all fortify ourselves for his gaze, thinking what is good, useful, and worthy to appear before God’s sight, and then fulfill these same things in the ensuing deed. For he says: “Behold, he stands behind our wall.”

He also said that he is like a young stag, that is, the son of the ancient fathers, having a body taken from them through the Virgin, yet subject to no sin nor weighed down by the burden of sin. For the power of his paternal nature has grown within him, so that hidden things do not escape him, serpents flee from him, and poisons do not harm him. Therefore let us fit ourselves to him—to whom our hidden things must be disclosed, to whom the whole serpent is hateful, who rejects everything infected with its poison—so that he may see what is worthy of God and see in us nothing infected with the serpent’s poison that might please him to turn away from us.

“For behold, he stands behind our wall, looking down through the windows.” He is said to stand, that is, to possess himself immovably in the best disposition of his state for beholding all that he sees before him. Neither do the good things we do add anything to him, nor do evils perpetrated by us diminish anything from his glory; rather, all things are subjected to the eternal recompense they have deserved.

[Col. 1228D] He “stands behind the wall.” For the wall is that outward part of our created condition—by which we are clothed, by which we are covered, and to which innumerable temptations are addressed—namely, our body. As a wall is built of stones and mortar, so the body is fitted together for us by the suitable arrangement of its parts. Since the Bride sees that her Beloved will assume, or perhaps has already assumed, this body, she calls it “our” wall, showing him to be a participant in our condition.

But this Beloved “stands behind the wall,” so that he may behold it freely, as though placed before him, and freely observe through the windows and lattices what happens within. The windows of our body are the five bodily senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. Some use these for good and make themselves good; others, drawing them by utterly corrupt habits toward evil, consequently make themselves utterly wicked. Of these Jeremiah says: “Death has climbed up through our windows” (Jer. 9:21). This occurs when a sinner’s eyes see a woman in order to desire her; for he has already committed adultery with her in his heart. Thus death has entered the soul through the windows of the eyes.

[Col. 1229A] And when someone admits vain hearing, especially the false teachings of perverse doctrines, then death enters the soul through the windows of the ears. So also with the remaining senses: smell, taste, speech, and touch. When a soul abuses these and applies itself to evil, death enters through these windows and assumes dominion.

But if a soul looks upon the adornment of the world and, from the beauty of created things, understands God to be the Creator of all, marvels at his works, and praises the Creator of works, life enters that soul through the windows of the eyes. Likewise, when it inclines its hearing to the word of God and delights in the reasoning of his knowledge and wisdom, the light of wisdom enters that soul through the windows of the ears. Of these Isaiah says: “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. 60:8). For, seeing in the Spirit the height of the apostles and marveling at their swift course through the world, he says, “Who are these?” and so forth.
