Marveling at their simplicity and innocence, he adds: “And like doves to their windows”: that is, simple and innocent, imitating in every use of sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch the dove that appeared above the Lord on the day when he was baptized.

[Col. 1229C] Thus the Beloved, standing behind the wall, looks through the windows to see by which gate each person seeks to enter, as the Lord says: “For broad is the gate and spacious the way that leads to death, and many enter through it; but narrow is the gate and strait the way that leads to life, and few find it” (Matt. 7:13–14). He looks down upon these, as though they labor below; he looks upon them in order to help them in their beginnings and, as they labor in their straitness, by grace now freely given to lead them further, so that, having begun the narrow way and finally established in the breadth of love, he may bring them to blessed glory.

But those entering the broad gate and following the spacious way that leads to destruction he exhorts, warns, and calls back: first through the natural law, then through Scripture, then through the patriarchs and prophets, afterward through himself, then through the apostles and through all teachers. He calls them back so that they may return and abandon the way they have begun, lest, glorying in the breadth of the way and finally entering through the spacious gate, they enter darkness and the dreadful places of destruction, which are now truly appointed for those running on this way.

The Beloved observes these things through the windows, contemplating plainly [Col. 1230A] the plainly good and the plainly evil. Nor is he content with them alone: he looks through the lattices, for he says: “Looking down through the windows, looking through the lattices” (1 Tim. 1:15). The lattices are narrow openings, not open in the manner of windows, but drawn out narrowly in length beneath the archwork of masons; through them the observer sees whom he wishes, though he cannot be seen by them, because he does not wish it.

Who, then, are those whom he thus beholds? Those who either do evil not evilly, or perform good deeds not well. They do evil not evilly, as Saul did, and those like him. For they dragged men of this sect, bound, to synagogues and courts of judgment. This was indeed evil, but it was not done evilly. For they judged that by this they were [Col. 1230B] rendering service to the Creator, serving the Law, and repressing transgression; and, zealous indeed with a good zeal, though not according to knowledge, they burned with indignation and believed that they were worthily avenging an injury done to the supreme Divinity. Hence Paul himself says: “I persecuted the Church of God; yet I obtained mercy, because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (1 Tim. 1:13). For he did not know that God the Father had a Son, and that He had sent this very Son into the world as a remedy; he did not know that this was Christ Jesus. He knew that Abraham’s circumcision and Moses’ Law had been given by the Lord, but he did not know that this Law had remained in its integrity until the time of John the Baptist, and that then the promises contained within it had expired in their fulfilment. Therefore these things were revealed to him, and the deeds done in ignorance were pardoned.

[Col. 1230C] Thus the Lord looked upon him through the lattice, seeing him and having mercy on him, although he expected nothing of mercy but wholly “breathed threats and slaughter” toward evil. [Note: [Col. 1229D] end: “threats and slaughter.”] There are also those who perform good deeds not well: namely, those who possess faith and practise works of faith, who pray much in the streets, distribute their goods to the poor and needy; yet while doing these things they lack charity, which is the virtue of works, and do not seek to attain God through these works. Rather, because the whole world is subject to God, they desire themselves to be honoured and set over positions of honour. Thus they lose all that they do; and that which has been distributed without charity, they forfeit. For Paul says: “If I distribute all my goods to the poor, and even give up myself so that I burn, but have not charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3).

[Col. 1230D] He also says: “The word of God is living and effective, and more penetrating than any two-edged sword; reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart; nor is any creature invisible in His sight” (Heb. 4:12). Therefore, whatever they do, they are before God and do not escape His eyes. Not only what they do, but also what they intend by it, He does not fail to perceive in their minds: He sees the openly good and evil through the window; but those who conceal themselves He beholds through the lattice. It follows:

[Col. 1231A] **10. Behold, my Beloved speaks to me.**

The Bride has warned all these to beware of her Beloved, who comes leaping over the mountains and skipping over the hills; who comes like a roe or a young hart; who stands behind the wall, looking through windows and lattices to see what is done within, what pleases Him, or what displeases Him. Now, however, she indicates that the Bridegroom speaks to her, saying: “Behold, my Beloved speaks to me: Arise, make haste, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one.” He had seen her sitting, as though in a lofty place by the window in the house, fostering her love for the Bridegroom by holy contemplation and meditating upon ways by which her love for the Beloved might burn without ceasing. Therefore, in order to raise her up as though languid—and by that very languor as though dead to the world—and, [Col. 1231B] once raised, to inflame her anew with the fires of fresh love, He says:

> Arise, make haste, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one, and come.

With three words He exhorts her, saying, “Arise, make haste, come”; with three names He designates her, saying, “My friend, my dove, my beautiful one,” so that the gracious placing of the names may soften all that the threefold command of the words urgently requires. For He says, “My friend,” because I have known from this that you love Me: you left father and mother, brothers and sisters, house and fields, and followed Me. I also heard you speaking in Paul: “Who shall separate us from the charity of God which is in Christ Jesus? For I know that neither death nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, [Col. 1231C] nor powers, nor any other creature shall be able to separate us from the charity of God” (Rom. 8:38–39). I also heard you declaring in Peter: “Lord, You know all things; You know that I love You” (John 21:17).

He adds also, “My dove”: like that most innocent bird, intent upon rearing its young, fed on the purity of grains, having a moan instead of song, flying in flocks, counting no good as good except what is held in common, and neither tearing with beak nor claw a bird unlike itself. You conform yourself, so far as you can, to the dove which bore witness to Christ in baptism, and you please Me in such a form. You whom I rightly approve as beautiful for these reasons—arise. But when He says, “Arise,” [Col. 1231D] He does not utter it in the way in which it is said to a sinner. To the sinner it is said: “Arise, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14). This is said to a person entangled in grievous sins, in which he is said to sleep—that is, to rest in grave delight. By a holy voice he is told to arise, that is, to cease resting in sins; and to rise from the dead, that is, not to appoint for himself a place of abiding among the dead in hell. When you have ceased to sin and have begun to abhor those things which formerly pleased you, then “Christ shall enlighten you,” that is, He shall show you the way in which He wishes you to go.

[Col. 1232A] Yet it is not in this sense that the Bride is here told to arise, she who long ago had left father and mother, house and brothers, and the other things possessed in the world, and who, following Christ, had said: “Draw me after You; we shall run in the fragrance of Your ointments.”

What, then, is it to tell the Bride to arise? He had recognized that her whole concern was continually to meditate upon the love which had drawn Him from the Father into the holy Virgin, and that He, born of her, had passed through the evils of the world, had risen again crucified with death despised, [Note: [Col. 1231D] end: “overcome.”] and had thereafter ascended to heaven, promising heavenly good things to those who followed Him. She embraced this with her whole desire, longed for it in prayer, and delighted in it in solitary meditation. Therefore the Beloved says to her, “Arise,” that is: Awake from this [Col. 1232B] rest of yours, from this peace of yours. I am indeed He who, adjuring the daughters of Jerusalem, said: “Do not arouse or awaken the Beloved until she herself wills it.” Now you are one spirit with Me; I do not doubt that you will what I will. Do not ask to die while you are able to benefit many; let not this delay draw danger upon itself. Make haste; by hastening, come to Me. I am He whom you love; you now have outside yourself Him whom you desire. Therefore I tell you to come, that with Me you may see and understand your works and, if they are good, rejoice with Me in them.

**11. For now winter has passed.**

Winter is that part of the year in which daylight is shorter for us and the darkness of night is deeper; in which all things are bound fast by frost, [Note: [Col. 1231D] end: “are constricted.”] in which everything is stiff with winter ice, and moisture rules over bodies. All these things signify the harshness of the season, which He testifies has now passed, and therefore that the time of His coming is fitting. Such a season was present when unbelief oppressed the world on every side, when the light of faith illuminated the hearts of only a few, when evil came from the north and held all hearts chilled by the frost of malice, and when hardened impiety did not permit the ice of hearts to be melted by any warmth of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1232C] Moisture ruled in bodies in which no restraints of chastity or love of honourable conduct curbed lust; rather, luxury and the wantonness which accompanies luxury commanded that everything be mingled in foul intercourse. The disobedience of Adam, the first father, bears witness to this; Cain’s wickedness bears witness; Lamech the “murderer” bears witness; [Note: [Col. 1232D] end: “murder.”] and likewise the impurity of the ages bears witness, destroyed first by water and afterward by fire, except for eight persons. It follows:

> The rain has gone and departed.

“Rain” does not mean any sort of shower, but winter rain alone: rain continuing almost day and night, which even roofs cannot contain; [Note: [Col. 1232D] end: “restrain.”] by which rivers are swollen, bridges collapse, overflowing fords deny passage to travellers, and all things, swept along by its force, are carried down into the deep. This fittingly describes the time of unbelief. Wherever faith was lacking, all spiritual goods were also lacking. [Col. 1233A] There was no hope, no charity, no fear of God, no obedience to God, no reverence; and nearly all that humanity owed to God, it paid over to Satan.

This was the unceasing rain: the impious teaching of its masters, magnifying Jupiter and offering sacrifices to him; revering Apollo, Mercury, and Bacchus; worshipping Juno, Diana, Venus, and Pallas, and the rest—things which shame blushes to name even in a sacred exposition and modesty refuses to utter. Yet necessity alone, the necessity of expounding sacred Scripture, sets them forth. For this rain overthrew the foundation of faith, the walls of hope, and the roofs of charity. For when rain descended upon this house, the rivers also came. Once this unbelief had been received, the swollen minds of men overflowed the channels assigned to them. [Col. 1233B] Those to whom faith, worship, and reverence for the one God had been granted by God the Father and by the fathers who themselves believed in Him, assigned these things to many gods and confessed many gods to exist. They left the channel and banks appointed to them, and drew innumerable thousands of human beings down with themselves into the depth of hell.

For the winds blew, because the blast of the evil spirit was not lacking to them. The bridges were overthrown because Holy Scripture, which makes for us a bridge to God, was held cheap. Passage was not open to the traveller because, for one departing from this life, there was no access to God. Thus, as the Lord says, “the ruin of that house was great”; and truly great, since it has no return to life and no future communion with the good in eternity.

[Col. 1233C] Therefore you, whom I perceive to be My friend because you will what I will; you, whom I understand to excel in dovelike conduct, whom I judge conformed to Me and therefore beautiful—I call you, saying, “Arise,” that is: Leave this contemplation of peace and rest in which you are detained. Make haste, so that the command of My precept may be followed immediately [Note: [Col. 1233D] end: “immediately,” or “at the word.”] by the service of your obedience; “and come,” that, made a partaker with Me of one spirit, you may rejoice with Me, who aided you by My Spirit to do these things and to remove these scandals of the world. For winter having been removed, and the rain which disturbed all things having gone, a gentler breath now blows over the face of the earth; and the breath of the Holy Spirit, sent from above, has adorned it—once faith has been received—with the flower of its own beauty. This is what is said:

**12. Flowers have appeared in our land.**

[Col. 1233D]

Where unbelief ruled, faith now reigns; where misery was hopeless, there good hope now hopes and rejoices to attain eternal things; where the mind, cold and unstirred by any fire of charity, lay numb, charity now disposes all things by its own authority, raising what was below upward and presenting everything to the good Creator through good works. He also adds:

> The time of pruning has come.

This pruning, indeed, signifies the time of sacred confession. Trees are pruned, and useless branches that bear no fruit are removed; and useful shoots, if they grow excessively, are hindered from bearing. Thus vines, [Col. 1234A] and likewise other trees, are cut of useless branches so that those which are useful may become more useful and bring their cultivator more abundant fruit.

This fittingly applies to the time of fullness and grace. Some trees are dry and dead, producing neither leaves nor fruit; some have leaves indeed, but no fruit; others have fruit, but bad fruit; still others have both leaves that provide beauty and fruits of the highest excellence. The whole human race is comprised in these. Three kinds of them await the axe and fire: those whom neither the leaves of words nor the fruits of works clothe, and those who produce some fruit indeed, but bad fruit. These the judicial axe of the Lord, making proper distinction, cuts off and assigns, by a just judgment, to the fire appointed for them.

But those to whom leaves give beauty and excellent fruits give worth are trees of Paradise, in which God dwells and among which He walks; to these He calls His Bride, and He cleanses them with the pruning-hook, so that they may bear fruits enduring in them unto eternal life. This pruning-hook is sacred confession, by which a person considers himself, recalls all that he has done in life, lays himself open to himself and condemns himself; and, confessing by mouth to Him to whom he is accountable, repenting in heart, washing and cleansing himself with tears, undertaking and performing the fitting burden of penance, becomes a fruitful tree planted beside streams of water. Bearing the fruit of grace, it is received most joyfully by the Lord.

[Col. 1234C] There is also a most welcome time of pruning for the Lord, when He sees the glory of the apostles and the constancy of martyrs throughout the world. They were cut off by the grievous pruning-hook of martyrdom and cast down as though useless; but now, as members of Christ’s most exalted body, they have been gloriously received by Him in heaven, already judging nations and reigning forever. It follows:

> The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.

That is: throughout the world, the voice of the preacher has been heard in the land that is now ours. For every preacher, seeking neither the wisdom that is of the earth nor utterly empty fables, announces in his song the departure of winter and the arrival of spring. He mourns, loves chastity, dwells in high places, shuns human company, remaining in body in the world but in mind in heaven. Thus John the Baptist says: “Offspring of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore bear fruits worthy of repentance; and do not begin to say, ‘We have Abraham for our father’” (Luke 3:7–8). [Col. 1234D] But Peter says: “Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins; and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:38). Paul likewise says: “Not in revelries and drunkenness, not in beds and impurities, not in strife and envy. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 13:13–14).

Who could enumerate these voices of the turtledove? He alone knows them—God, who forms the voice and the hearts. It follows:

**13. The fig tree has put forth its early figs.**

[Col. 1235A] The fig tree is a very familiar tree, abundant in leaves and filling with fruit the one who cultivates and possesses it. It produces fruit in different ways. For at the beginning of spring, and when spring has advanced, it produces its first fruits for a little while, which are called *grossi* (“early figs”); they are bitter and, because of their bitter taste, are rejected and cast aside among bitter and worthless things. But after some further progress of the season, it bears fruit again, giving fruit that is most sweet and most delightful to the taste by its natural sweetness. This is the fruit for which it is cultivated, for which the soil around it is dug, and for whose cultivation much labour is expended.

[Col. 1235B] When its first fruit grows abundantly, because then nearly all the bitterness in the fig is released, this is a good hope of what follows: the more bitter this fruit is, the sweeter the next is produced. Therefore it is said of this fig tree: “The fig tree has put forth its early figs.” This is the fig tree of which the Gospel says: A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard; and when for three years its master came and found no fruit on it, he said to the cultivator: “Cut it down.” But the cultivator said: “Lord, leave it this year also, until I dig around it and put manure upon it” (Luke 13:7–8).

This fig tree is called the Church. The Lord came to it for three years—one year, namely, the time before the Law; another, the time under the Law; and the third, the time which began under grace—[Col. 1235C] and found no fruit. Therefore, angered, He uttered these words: “Cut it down.” For although the Church has existed from the very beginning of creation, during all that period it existed in so few persons that, when its smallness was compared with the abundant multitude, it was regarded as nothing and reckoned as nonexistent. For throughout this period, if you find any righteous persons and compare them with the remaining multitude, the comparison will be as though you compared some tiny thing with an infinite multitude. Thus our Lord and Saviour says: “Foxes have dens and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head” (Matt. 8:20).

But now, having been dug around and strengthened by the holy admonitions of the apostles, instructed by the holy examples of the martyrs, and having despised the bitterness of martyrdom, [Col. 1235D] this Church bears sweet fruits throughout the world. It now fills with sweetness the fig trees of its own planting, whose bitterness it lamented in their passion. Hence it is added:

> The flowering vines have given forth their fragrance.

The Lord’s vines are both one and many. The Church is one, and yet many. The one Church is the assembly of all believers who have loved God from the beginning, who love Him now, and who shall love Him. It is one, remaining in the unity of faith, hope, and charity. It shall appear when the Lord judges the world, when those who receive the kingdom from the Lord shall hear Him say: “Come, blessed of My Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34). [Col. 1236A] They will then be free from “the snare of hunters and the harsh word” (Ps. 90:3).

The snare of hunters is the temptation of evil spirits, which they spread for wretched mortals, in order to ensnare them in sins and lead them, once ensnared, to death. The harsh word—than which nothing in the world can be harsher—is that which they will hear: “Depart from Me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). The good will indeed hear this word, but, protected by the Lord’s hand, they will not fear; for He who delivered them from the snare of hunters also delivered them from the harsh word, so that they do not dread it but rest secure in the glory already received.

[Col. 1236B] This one Church will exist there, but here it is divided into many parts. There is a Church of Jerusalem, a Church of Antioch, a Church of Rome, and countless others throughout the world. Every congregation of faithful people, in the places chosen for it by the Lord, establishes there a solemn house of prayer, in which they pray, lament, and render thanks for blessings received. These are the vines which, flowering, have given forth their fragrance. For all the good done here is still in flower, emitting from itself a good reputation; but it will bear fruit when it receives an everlasting reward for the good rendered in time. [Col. 1236C] It follows:

> Arise, my friend, my beautiful one, and come,  
> **14.** my dove in the clefts of the rock, in the hollows of the wall.

The Beloved has already called the Bride to come to Him. He also invited her by setting forth these seven matters: “Winter has passed; the rain has gone and departed; flowers have appeared in our land; the time of pruning has come; the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land; the fig tree has put forth its early figs; the flowering vines have given forth their fragrance.” By all these things the fitting time for her coming has been shown. Still continuing in the same summons to Himself, He repeats: “Arise, my friend, my bride, and come, my dove.” He adds: “In the clefts [Col. 1236D] of the rock, in the hollows of the wall.”

These words recall the Lord’s Passion. For who does not know that the Apostle said of Christ: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4)? And who, not doubting that Christ was fastened to the cross with nails, does not know that this rock has clefts? Who, likewise, does not know that this wall has a hollow, if he does not doubt the truth of what he reads? For it is written: “One of the soldiers opened His side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came forth” (John 19:34).

That side is rightly called a wall, for a wall is a joining of stones without cement; and this side was joined without the cement of human seed and [Col. 1237A] composed and formed by the hand of the Holy Spirit. Therefore let the Beloved come to her Bridegroom who calls her: secure in the protection of His Passion, fortified by the defence of faith. Let her come from the world to Him who conquered the world; from the place of pain and suffering to the place where there is no pain or suffering, but everlasting peace and unceasing exultation. It follows:

> Show me your face.

The Bride obeys her Beloved; when called, she knows no delay. For she was told: “Arise, make haste, come to Me.” Thus called, she rises at once, comes hastening, and stands before Him without intervening delay. Yet she comes with her head covered, lest the sun burn her face, lest her brightness degenerate before the brightness of the sun. But to the Bride standing before Him and covering herself, the Beloved says: “Show [Col. 1237B] me your face.” It is right that the Bride be presented to her Beloved with unveiled face.

For if Rebekah, at the well whose name is “of the Living One” and “of the Seeing One” (Gen. 24:65), when she saw Isaac, descended from the camel and covered herself with a veil—this was done because she was not yet his bride and he had not yet received her, but brought her, who was destined for him, into his mother’s house and took her as his wife, loving her so greatly that she assuaged the grief caused by his mother’s death—then this woman, long beloved by her Beloved, long betrothed to her Bridegroom, and already known through spiritual love and divine colloquies, need not appear covered before the Bridegroom. Rather, with unveiled face she should behold and love Him.

“For the word of God is living and effective, and more penetrating than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. No creature is invisible in His sight; rather, all things are naked and open to His eyes” (Heb. 4:12–13). [Col. 1237C] What need, therefore, has He of a covering, since neither flowers, leaves, trees, clothing, nor any veil can obstruct Him from observing and considering a thing from the beginning of its origin to the end of its outcome, and from rightly discerning for Himself all matters of thought, speech, ancient habit, and action?

Thus David himself says three times in the psalm: “O God, restore us” (Ps. 79:4); again, “O God of hosts, restore [Col. 1237D] us” (ibid., 15); and a third time he adds: “Lord God of hosts, restore us” (ibid., 20). For a person needs to be turned away from the sins committed in thought, from the sins committed in speech, and from the sins committed in deed and habit. Therefore after this threefold invocation he adds: “And show Your face, and we shall be saved” (ibid.). For we shall be able safely to see God’s face when God has shaken these sins away from us and, when duly invoked, has—as His mercy brings it about—wiped them, as it were, from His own memory.

So too God desires us to be seen by Him with unveiled face: that nothing unworthy of Him may appear in us in thought, nothing at all offensive in speech, and nothing displeasing in act and deed. Therefore He says: “Show me your face,” which you have made worthy [Col. 1238A] to appear before Me, now after long labours in virtues and long desires for My kiss, so that I may see whether you have done anything worthy of My kiss, anything worthy to be rewarded with the prize of My kiss. It follows:

> Let your voice sound in my ears.

Where the face is now pleasing and nothing blameworthy intervenes, permission is given to advance further. As the sight delights in the Beloved’s face, so hearing may delight in the sound of that same voice. Hence it is said: “Let your voice sound in my ears.” Ask what you will; for you will ask nothing except what is fair and just, and worthy to be heard.

Here it should be observed that our voices sound in the Lord’s ear in different ways. Sometimes we sound with a voice audible to God alone, when we speak to Him solely by the devotion of the heart. Thus it is written of Hannah that “she spoke only in her heart, and only her lips moved, while her voice was not heard at all” (1 Sam. 1:13). [Col. 1238B] For her whole devotion was directed toward God; hence she deserved to be heard and congratulated, and was found worthy to bring forth the great prophet Samuel into the world.

God also attends to voices uttered with an audible sound, provided that the intention of the heart is present and the devotion which makes those voices audible accompanies them; so that His hearing may not merely be pleased, after the manner of birds, but rather, in a human manner, may hear the groans of the inward heart. Hence psalms resound in the Church; hence hymns; hence the sweet melody of Alleluia resounds; hence other diverse and innumerable voices, which human invention brings forth in God’s praise. [Col. 1238C] If fitting devotion accompanies them, there is no doubt that they sound in God’s ears and that the petitions made are received.

Thus the prophet also says: “Make a joyful noise to God, all the earth; sing a psalm to His name; give glory to His praise” (Ps. 65:1). And at the close of his work he concludes with the final psalm: “Praise the Lord in His saints; praise Him in the firmament of His power; praise Him in His mighty acts; praise Him according to the multitude of His greatness; praise Him with the sound of the trumpet; praise Him with psaltery and harp; praise Him with timbrel and dance; praise Him with strings and organ; praise Him with well-sounding cymbals; praise Him with cymbals of jubilation” (Ps. 150). [Col. 1238D] There, exhorting to praise ten times, he invites to praise the nine orders of heaven and the human being joined to them and made equal to them by grace, saying: “Let every spirit praise the Lord.” It follows:

> For your voice is sweet, and your face beautiful.

“Your voice is sweet,” because it confesses and prays to Me alone, magnifies and glorifies Me, judges that supplication must be made to Me for sins committed, and, after forgiveness has been granted, longs for grace and glory to be given to it. “And your face is beautiful”: a face without blemish, a face without wrinkle, a face unacquainted with rejection and most worthy to be received and numbered among friends.

**15. Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vines; for our vineyard has blossomed.**
This Bride knew no delay: summoned by her Beloved to come to him, she at once rose and stood before his majesty. And because he came veiled, lest she be overwhelmed by glory, she deserved to hear what was said: “Show me your face,” that is, contemplate me with your face unveiled; “and let your voice sound in my ears,” that is, ask for what you wish, since I know that you will ask for nothing but what is just. Received by the Bridegroom, she merits to understand and see what was promised: namely, that “winter has passed, the rain has gone and departed; flowers have appeared on the earth; the time of pruning has come; the voice of the turtledove has been heard in the land; the fig tree has put forth its young figs; the flowering vines have given their fragrance.” Over these things the Bride gives thanks to the Bridegroom, knowing that all this is his work; and she herself receives praise and grace from the Bridegroom, because [Col. 1239B] his grace in her was not empty, but she worked outstandingly together with the grace bestowed upon her.

Now, however, it is time for him to instruct her concerning heavenly things, to teach her about matters above herself, so that, called from common activity to contemplation, she may understand what she contemplated, lest, when she possesses it, she prove altogether inexperienced. Since this is what he must do, and since in a sense he must devote himself to the honour of his Beloved, he admonishes his companions meanwhile to guard the vineyards that have already blossomed and “given fragrance while flowering,” lest foxes ruin them and the labour expended upon them be reduced to nothing. He therefore exhorts them thus: “Catch for us the little foxes.” He speaks to his companions, that is, to the ministering spirits, of whom Paul says: “Are they not all ministering [Col. 1239C] spirits, sent to minister for those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation?” (Heb. 1:14).

These are the angels to whom the guarding of human life is entrusted; Jacob saw them while sleeping on a stone. He saw a ladder standing upon the earth, its top reaching heaven; and angels of God ascending and descending by it, and the Lord leaning upon the ladder (Gen. 28:12–13). To them God speaks here, commanding them to seize the foxes who desire to injure this flowering vineyard, to lay it waste, and to destroy its fruits. These are the opposing powers: made reprobate by God, hardened for the evil of the Church. In this they consist, in this they remain, and they count it as their success if they can in any respect hinder or disturb [Col. 1239D] the Church as it tends toward God, desires him, and already sends forth from itself the holy fragrance of a good reputation.

This is evident in Job; it is evident in Joseph; it was made manifest in Tobit. Though those powers drew all of them downward through adversities, they were prevented by good angels from completing what they had begun. Seeing that all these things worked together for their good, they perceived that their power was nothing except insofar as God permitted it. Therefore the Lord commands the good angels in the words: “Catch for us the little foxes”; that is: Seize and restrain those whom you see wandering like foxes and disturbing all things by deceit; make them accomplish nothing except what pleases my will.

The Lord mentions these foxes in the Gospel, saying: “Foxes have dens, and birds of heaven have nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 8:20). For to the man who said to him, “Master, I will follow you wherever you go,” the Saviour replied, “Foxes have dens,” as though saying: I do not receive you; I understand that you are not predestined for me, but given to foxes, so that foxes may tear you apart and the birds of heaven—that is, evil spirits—may plunder you. He likewise says of Herod, who threatened him: “Go and tell that fox: behold, I cast out demons and accomplish healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am consummated” (Luke 13:32); as though saying: Tell this to him who is given over as food to the fox: He will not kill me. Rather, today and for the time which is to remain until my death [Note: [Col. 1239D] perhaps: “quod usque” (“that/until”).], I bring healing to all who are burdened by sickness; and then on the third day I shall be consummated—that is, I shall die, and everything that the enemy-man can do against me will have been completed.

David also mentions these foxes, saying to the Lord: “But they sought my life in vain” (Ps. 62:10). Those who killed the Lord sought to destroy his life, but in vain, because he lives: behold, the Lord is King for ever. “They shall enter into the lower parts of the earth” (Ps. 28:10); for they shall be swallowed up by love of an earthly kingdom and blinded, so that they shall seem to have entered the lower regions of the earth. Grieving [Note: [Col. 1239D] read: “Unwilling.”] to submit to the Romans, they were broken by the edge [Col. 1240C] of the sword; and the greater part of them was given to foxes—that is, they were handed over to evil spirits, that these might feed upon them and that whatever they do might please their will.

We also read that Samson caught three hundred foxes among the Philistines, tied their tails together, placed the fire of torches between their tails, and thus sent them into the crops, grain-fields, vineyards, and olive groves of the Philistines, consuming everything (Judg. 15). This occurs whenever some Catholic teacher of the Church gathers together all the heresies of heretics and places in their midst the lamp of heavenly fire—that is, the fire of eternal condemnation. Sending it thus into their labours, he consumes and brings to nothing what belongs to them.

Here it must be observed [Col. 1240D] that these foxes are commanded to be caught while they are little. They are little at the very beginnings of temptations; they become great when, as temptation grows, they crush human minds and lead them into wickedly persuaded deeds. Thus chastity is destroyed. First, a woman is seen; through repeated sight she is desired; after desire, the mind is shaken by conversation; after sight, desire, and conversation, as evil stimulation increases, the wickedly desired act is carried out, and chastity, long assailed, is cast down.

So too greed is fed and nourished by seeing, when a person does not consider what he ought, what he does [Note: [Col. 1240D] read: “what he ought to do.”], or what ought justly to be done, but stretches himself to do things beyond his means or unjustly. Possessing one unit, he seeks a second, that it may be multiplied tenfold; then, seeking a third, he acts and seeks in order that it may be multiplied a hundredfold. Unless a thousand is added, he considers that nothing has been accomplished, although he knows that something is lacking to him. Thus this infinite disgrace of wickedness strives after the multiplication of number, never setting itself a limit whenever it finds a larger number into which it can grow.

Hence the Saviour says: “A rich person shall enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty.” And again: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19:23–24). A *camelus* is the great rope used on ships, by which, when a storm rises, ships are compelled to remain fast after their anchors have been cast. It is easier for this to pass through the eye of a needle—that is, to depart, having despised all things, through the hard suffering of death—than to enter the kingdom of heaven while avoiding this. Yet, if this is difficult for a human being, it is easy and possible for God. For we have known many rich people to leave everything for this and enter to him through the eye of the needle. This is the power and ineffable mercy of God alone, who snatches them from Satan’s mouth and deepest jaws and brings them to the heavenly kingdoms.

Thus the other virtues are softened and perish; thus vice takes possession of what it has captured by the craft of the evil one. Hence it is rightly said: “Catch for us the little foxes,” meaning: Resist these foxes while they are [Col. 1241C] little; strike down their first movements, lest they grow; dash them against me, who am the firmest rock. “For our vineyard has blossomed,” that is, it has given forth from itself the hope of good work; and, if defended by you, it will fulfil this hope of yours by the fruit of good work. It follows:

16. **My Beloved is mine, and I am his.**

This is the voice of the Bride, who, called to the Bridegroom, has now come. With her the Lord mingles conversations and, so to speak, soliloquies; for these things that are said and revealed to this Bride are known only to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Therefore she says, “My Beloved is mine,” as though I address him; “and I am his,” as though I answer his words. But I do not reveal to you what these secrets are. God keeps certain things secret, lest we try to enter into them or presume to disclose what he reveals to the Bride alone. We pass over these things; we entrust them to him alone to whom they were committed, since he has not willed them to be disclosed to us. It follows:

**Who feeds among the lilies. 17. Until the day breathes, and the shadows incline.**

Having omitted these matters and committed them to silence—the things God speaks to the Bride alone—the Bride adds what the Bridegroom does in the heights, what delights and refreshes him, what food is most pleasing to him, saying: “Who feeds among the lilies.” These lilies, sprung up in heavenly gardens and fields, possess beauty, fragrance, and sweetness all the more abundantly because he who planted them delights to be among them and to be refreshed by their appearance and scent [Col. 1242A].

These are the heavenly virtues; their beauty and heavenly fragrance are wonderful. He alone is said to feed on them who alone creates, alone orders, alone feeds all that he creates and sustains. The Beloved is said to feed among them so that those who live on earth and already desire heavenly things may strive to become conformed to them: that by guarding integrity they may raise the palm of chastity to the manner of life of angels; that they may remain otherwise free from vices, claiming none of this world for themselves, so that lust may not inflame them, greed sting them, wantonness enervate them, ambition overthrow them, envy consume them, or worldly concern for business trouble them—“until the day breathes and the shadows incline.”

It has been said that the Beloved feeds among lilies. Now it must be said how long he will remain feeding among them, with others not yet joined to him in this feeding. This is what is said: “He feeds among lilies”; and he shall feed among these alone, with others not joined to him, until that day of judgment breathes forth, when God will openly show himself, rendering to each according to his works: endless good to the good, and evil likewise enduring without end to the evil.

Two days are rightly called days of the Lord. One is that on which he was judged, concerning which it was said: “Not this man, but Barabbas” (John 18:40); and likewise: “Let him be crucified; his blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:23, 25). The other is that on which, having raised the whole world from death, he will judge it: “He shall judge all in equity, and peoples in his truth”; the day on which “the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, as the light of seven days” (Isa. 30:26). This too is rightly called the Lord’s day, when he will show himself to be the true Lord and render to all what they have deserved.

When, therefore, this day has breathed forth—that is, begun to appear—then he will join the lilies gathered from the earth to those sprung up in heavenly gardens. Then one Church of human beings and angels will come into being, when people will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but will be like the angels of God (Matt. 22:30). Then he will feed at once among the heavenly lilies and those taken from the earth, made equal to heavenly things, and, through virtue working by grace, made conformed to their glory [Col. 1242D]. Then the shadows shall incline.

The time we spend here passes wholly under a certain alternation: now we measure the day and its hours, now we count the night and its equal number of hours. This night is produced by the shadows cast by the earth and the bodies upon it. For when the sun travels beneath, the upper regions of the world and the earth are darkened; and because the multitude of bodies upon the earth casts its shadow upward, the covering of night is spread over the earth. But when this day has breathed forth, the sun abiding perpetually there will illuminate it; the saints will shine with clear light in the sight of the Most High and will not experience this alternation of approaching night. Rather, all these shadows that make this night will slope downward into the lower regions of the world and produce that dark night, now to remain for ever, fitting indeed for the condemned and wretched [Col. 1243A]. It follows:

**Return; be like a gazelle, my Beloved, or a young stag upon the mountains of Bether.**

The Bride, long ago called, has stood before the Bridegroom who calls her; she has seen him feeding among the heavenly lilies. She has merited to hear, for herself and her own, that she should await “until the day breathes and the shadows incline.” Then the lilies sprung from the earth shall be gathered, joined and made like the heavenly lilies; and they shall receive this gift: that the Bridegroom may feed among them and delight in them for ever, while they sing what the Apostle sang: “I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course; I have kept the faith” (2 Tim. 4:7). “There is laid up for us [Col. 1243B] this crown of righteousness, which, behold, the just Judge will repay to us.”

Therefore she humbly prays that the Bridegroom may return and visit and cherish the Church labouring on earth; that he himself may take up its labours, advance them, and bring them through to perfection, saying: “Return, my Beloved.” It follows: “Be like a gazelle,” that is, make present to her your incarnation, by which you are like a gazelle—that is, one who sees all things clearly—and by which you are likened to a young stag, that is, you are regarded as one wondrously born into the world from the ancient fathers, as a fawn. Recall this to her memory, so that she may praise, adore, and glorify you above all the mountains of Bether, reckoning no one equal to you in the Church, but understanding you to be far higher and far holier than all the mountains in Bether, meaning “House of God,” or “Rising House,” or “House [Col. 1243C] of Watchfulness”—all of which is the Church.

## CHAPTER III

1. **Upon my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him.**

This Bride—or any faithful soul—has prayed that her Beloved, though not leaving heaven, might nevertheless look upon the Church labouring on earth and, moved with pity for its labour, stoop down to it. Now, in order that mercy may more readily move him and incline him to the requested things, there are added the words with which she entreats him: “Upon my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves.”

Here it should be noted that Solomon, a king given to festivity, abounding in all things, and devoted to pleasures—as is the custom of most kings—makes his own wealth known to the world, writing: “There are sixty queens, and eighty concubines, and young women without number” (ch. 6:7). Where there are so many queens, so many royal concubines, and an unknown number of young women nourished for the Bridegroom, there luxury abounds in perfection: there are means to cheer one who eats delicately and disdains common fare; there are expenditures, so that the adornment of these women may not displease the coming King; and all else that may draw and entice him, when he comes, to love.

Whoever you are who hear this, it is not good that you should be broken in spirit, relax your mind toward softness, delight in shameful things, or fix your thoughts upon the things described. Rather, through these bodily statements understand spiritual realities, as is the custom of the Scriptures, and raise and kindle your love toward spiritual things. For this festive King Solomon is that great King who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who, while the ages run their course, joins to himself one Church in three orders. He designates its part which is first and principal [Note: [Col. 1243D] read: “which is first and principal.”] by the title of queens; its second part by that of concubines; and its third by that of young women.

The title of queens designates those who have long since run together, who have ascended after the One who draws them, and have deserved to lay hold of this One who draws them, so that with the Apostle they can say: “For we know that neither death nor life nor any other creature shall be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8:38). In this order consider Elijah, and consider Elisha. One was taken up to God in a fiery chariot with fiery horses; the other, ascending from Jericho to Bethel, received the mockery of the boys of that place, who said, “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead.” He cursed them in the name of the Lord; and immediately two bears came out of the forest and tore forty-two of them. He then went up from there to Mount Carmel (4 Kgs. 2:23–24; the preceding citation is printed as 3 Kgs. 2:11).

These two, therefore, and many others of the Old Testament, you will rightly assign to this order: knowing nothing but God, foreknowing that he would be born from a virgin, they truly ran after him, laid hold of him, became heirs of his kingdom, and glory with him for ever. But what are we to think of those whom the Gospel page remembers—those who saw God present in the flesh, recognized him from his words and deeds, and, following him alone, said: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you; what then shall we have?” (Matt. 19:27)?

What of Peter, who, when the Lord asked, “But who do you say that I am?” (Matt. 16:15–16), confidently answered: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”? The Lord declares him blessed, because he answered that this had been revealed to him not by flesh and blood but by the Father who is in heaven. The Lord distinguishes him as blessed by six clauses, saying: “You are Peter” (ibid., 18), that is, you are firm in faith in me as in a rock, and thus are called Peter from me, the rock. “And upon this rock,” which I understand to be myself and establish to be in you, “I will build my Church”; that is, I shall give strength to the Church and build it so firmly that “the gates of hell shall not prevail against it,” that is, evil spirits and the rich wicked men who follow them shall not harm it. “And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (ibid., 19), so that none may enter the kingdom of heaven except through the faith and sacraments [Col. 1245A] entrusted to you by me. And the one whom you curse shall be cursed—that is, the faith or sacraments he has received shall not benefit him—just as they shall be saving to the one whom you bless.

What is to be said of John the Evangelist, who says: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us; and we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14)? It must indeed be said that these men, all the apostles, and all who resemble them—not in rank, indeed, but in love and works—are those whose souls have been received into heaven and honoured. They possess such dignity that they deserve to be called queens by the King himself, in whom he so glories that he says, “There are sixty queens.” All of them, however many they are, he includes under the number sixty, calling them sixty.

The number sixty consists of two perfect numbers multiplied into one another. Whether you say six times ten or ten times six, you produce one number, namely sixty; and you will assign the two numbers on both sides: the ten of the Law and the six of the Gospel. Therefore those who are perfect in both, fulfilling the Law and the Gospel, are rightly applied to the number sixty.

These souls, then, are rightly called queens: joined to Christ by the lawful bond of marriage, they clung to him with an inward affection of love and bore children after their own example, rightful heirs of the eternal kingdom. Of them it was said: “A chosen race, a holy nation, a people for possession” (1 Pet. 2:9). Truly blessed are those who have deserved to become companions of the heavenly powers and to enjoy that glory of love which knows no failure.

In the second place are numbered those souls called concubines. For, as the Apostle says, “God has set some in the Church: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, kinds of tongues, interpretations of speeches” (1 Cor. 12:28). Among these perhaps you will find a place for the concubines. These are souls which, although joined to God in some fellowship, have not clung to him with all their heart, all their mind, and all their strength, nor become equal to the apostles; for, as the Apostle says, not all are appointed apostles and not all prophets.

For to some perfect grace is given, whom the Lord knows; to others imperfect grace, or grace perfect in one respect but not perfect in others. These indeed bring forth children of themselves, not as though born of marriage or heirs of the kingdom; but the Lord helps them through his mercy, so that they may be received, nourished, instructed, and saved in his kingdom. “But young women are without number.” Young women are souls recently converted to faith, or indeed converted after the commission of many sins. It is unknown what their final consummation will be; yet he looks upon them and, as gifts of his mercy, draws them to himself in the manner he determines.

These, therefore, are the distinctions within the Church which Solomon distinguishes in what follows, saying, “There are sixty queens,” and so forth. We have touched upon them here in order to show that this Bride, called by the Bridegroom, addressed with heavenly words, and instructed by soliloquies, is the one whom Solomon honoured by the title of queen when he said, “There are sixty queens.” But she who remains on earth and is designated by the title of concubines and young women is the one for whom the higher Church prays, saying, “Return, my Beloved” (ch. 2:17).

That the majesty of the Beloved may more easily be inclined by her prayer and hear her voice, the words which she pours forth weeping are added: “Upon my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves.” Our bed is our conscience, in which we rest if we set good things before ourselves; but if evil and most wicked things confront us, we are distressed and afflicted. For the person reproved by his own heart, who confesses that he has sinned wickedly against the Lord and behaved badly toward his neighbours, has no rest, but labour, affliction of spirit, and the wide confusion of sorrow. Hence the Prophet says: “I have laboured in my groaning; every night I shall wash my bed” (Ps. 6:7).

He means the labour of conscience, which he shows as groaning and labouring and washing its bed every night. It washes the bed when, repenting, it grieves and groans that it has offended God. It washes it every night when it weeps that through each individual sin it has incurred God’s wrath. He repeats that he has drenched himself with tears when he says that he has drenched with tears his body, in which he had laid himself down by sinning: “I have watered my couch with my tears.” For the eye of my mind has been troubled by anger—that is, the manifest wrath of the Lord—at the presence of my enemies, namely sins, among which I have grown old and become aged from the very first beginning of sinning, and have been almost rejected from the very grace of the Lord. For Isaiah says: “The bed is too narrow, so that one must fall; and the covering is too short to cover both” (Isa. 28:20).

The human mind is narrow and confined: if an evil spirit occupies it, the Spirit of God departs; and when the Spirit of God occupies it—through the action and better judgment of free will—that evil spirit will justly and altogether depart. For the “covering,” that is, the measure and narrowness of our created nature, cannot “cover both,” that is, comprehend both God’s Spirit and the evil one.

Therefore, although this soul seeks God every night, and although the Lord has said to it, “Ask, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. 7:7), why does it say: “I sought and did not find him”? This is what we have said: she has not yet ascended to higher things or attained that dignity granted to queens, whose petition is refused nothing, whose seeking finds nothing shut, and whose knocking is met with a readier opening. She still acts in the lower regions; therefore she says:

2. **I shall rise and go about the city; through the lanes and streets [Col. 1247A] I shall seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him and did not find him.**

“I shall rise,” that is, I shall shake off at once this burden of my sin and my filth. “And I shall go about the city,” that great Church which is now shared by good and evil, intending to carry out whatever counsel and help useful to me I may find in it. And to show more narrowly what she will do, she adds: “Through the lanes and streets,” that is, through those bound to an order, those married, and those remaining free without marriage: through these “I shall seek him whom my soul loves.” But although she is plaintive and eager in seeking, she nevertheless adds: “I sought him and did not find him.” What then?

3. **The watchmen who guard the city found me.**

[Col. 1247B] Who are these watchmen? They are the angels, guardians of the Church, to whom this guardianship is entrusted, so that they may know and understand what good or evil each person has done and what recompense each has deserved. Of them the Lord says in the Gospel: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones; for I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 10:18). She addresses them, saying:

**Have you seen him whom my soul loves?**

She addresses these, from whom she does not openly receive an answer. For after she has twice surveyed the whole Church and said in each case that she has not found her Beloved, she is to hear secretly from the watchmen why she has not found him. She said: “Upon my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him.” This means that in her conscience she recalled the “nights,” that is, the dark actions by which she had offended God, but said no more and did nothing further. Yet it is not sufficient with God, for the remission of sin, merely to review in one’s conscience what one has done, unless one strives humbly to correct in heart, speech, and deed what one has done.

You make correction in heart when you repent; in speech when you confess to the one appointed for you; and in deed when, by fasting, discipline, prayer, almsgiving, vigils, and instruction, you desire to make good what was wrongly done. For blessed James says: “Therefore confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (Jas. 5:16). The blessed watchmen teach her this law of confession. She obeys them and accepts the stated law of confession, repenting in heart, confessing in speech, and desiring to fulfil in deed what is enjoined. It follows:

4. **When I had passed them by a little, I found him whom my soul loves; I held him and shall not let him go, until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me.**

See how greatly this threefold confession advances her. Having confessed her transgressions in heart, speech, and deed, and having now passed beyond the “watchmen,” that is, the angels guarding the Church, in the Spirit, she finds him whom her soul loves—God, namely, whom she recognizes as propitiatory [Col. 1248A], and from whom she understands that her sins have been forgiven and all cast away from eternal remembrance.

Therefore she says: “I held him,” that is, I have clung to him by the firm root of love, and I shall not let him go “until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me”; that is, until I convert to him the Synagogue, which is my mother, and the Gentile world, which is she who bore me. For this holy Church, gathered from the whole world, had Judaea as mother in faith: from her it first received the worship of the one God, rejected idols, offered sacrifices and victims of burnt-offering to God alone, and obtained very many legal precepts. But it had the Gentile world as its mother because, when Judaea rejected it, the Gentile world became the one that brought it forth to faith in Christ; taught by it, the Church received his faith fully and all his sacraments.

Therefore she will not let him go, because she will not be silent and will not cease from preaching and bearing witness to what Christ taught, until both the Gentile world and all Judaea receive him; and, through the activity of both them and the Church called upward and honoured alike by the name and dignity of queen, the truth of Christ may become fully known to the world. It follows:

5. **I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and stags of the fields: do not rouse or awaken the Beloved until she herself wills.**

Where a statement is repeated, one rightly recalls what was said. Above, the Bride said: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (ch. 2:6). This was pleasing to the Bridegroom, for he approves the faith by which she subjects every temporal good to the power of the Lord Jesus Christ; and he approves the hope by which she expects to be embraced by God’s right hand in eternity. Here too, her declaration that she will not let him go until he has been perfectly brought into the world through the preaching of both peoples is gratefully received by him. Therefore, under the same adjuration, the children of Jerusalem are commanded not to presume to hinder it: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not rouse or awaken the Beloved until she herself wills.” Since this was said because the Lord gave it, we pass on to the rest.

6. **Who is this who comes up through the wilderness?**

This Bride, exalted by God’s presence, binds herself by promises that she will not rest—that is, will not cease preaching Christ—until the whole world acknowledges him [Col. 1248D] and is made subject to him. Seeing her fixed in fulfilling this promise, and seeing her now converting some, now others, to faith and ascending with them to things above, the daughters of Zion admire her foresight and perseverance and say: “Who is this?” That is, what kind of woman, how great a woman, is this! How wholly worthy of admiration, “who thus comes up through the wilderness”?

A wilderness is a place which all judge worthy to be deserted and therefore inhabit no one; they shrink from and fear the brambles and thorns it produces and vigorously flee the poisonous things it brings forth. By this name is understood this world, which brings forth the thorns of sins, receives the poisons of unclean spirits, and sends those who receive these things into the caverns of hell.

“Who,” then, “is this?” That is, what kind of woman, how great, and how worthy of admiration, who through this world, subject to infinite temptations and subjecting to countless temptations those who devote themselves to it and turn back to it, sets for herself steps of ascent and seeks to ascend where we know that so many thousands have hitherto gone down; and seeks there to win rewards for herself where we have seen so many thousands of people incur the punishments of hell. “Who,” then, “is this,” who tramples the glory of kings, does not fear the threats of judges, does not dread reproaches, despises flattery, laughs if tortures are inflicted, joyfully receives the penalty of death, and joyfully transcends this world attended by virtues?

Great indeed is this woman [Col. 1249B] who, if pressed by adversities, is not broken; if she receives prosperity, is not exalted; but shows herself the same in either condition and intends, through this wilderness, to flee, ascend, and draw near to God. Hence it follows:

**Like a little rod of smoke from spices of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer.**

At one and the same time smoke partly rises, and partly that which had risen before tends to disappear in the higher regions. So the Church is always newly born in some of its members, while in others who were born earlier it is always gathered up to heavenly things. For smoke, born from fire and rising high, gradually withdraws itself from human sight. So the Church, kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit into the love of God, does not cease to ascend until, withdrawn from earthly things, it is caught up to the invisible things of heaven.

It is rightly called not a “rod” (*virga*) but a “little rod” (*virgula*), because this manner of ascent is such that the ardour of compunction is sometimes so subtle that even the person who has received it cannot comprehend or discern it. Therefore it is rightly called not a “rod” (*virga*) but a “little rod” (*virgula*), because it signifies a compunction of heart that is upright, slender, and swift, known to arise from spices of myrrh and frankincense.

Myrrh preserves bodies from decay; frankincense, when burned, gives forth fragrance. Thus myrrh signifies the mortification of the flesh, and frankincense the purity of prayer. The Church mortifies the flesh when it renounces pleasures; and, when it sends forth to God the fervour of prayer, it draws out, as it were, smoke of spices from its censer—that is, from its heart—so that it may smell sweetly to God and inflame its neighbour.

And lest it should display only mortification and prayer and approach while deprived of other virtues, there is added: “and every powder of the perfumer,” meaning: She is a little rod of smoke arising not only from myrrh and frankincense, but also taking her substance from the powder which the perfumer crushes and mixes to make good perfumes, and being offered to God for glory. In mentioning these spices, he sets myrrh first, then frankincense, and afterwards every powder of the perfumer, because one must first mortify the desire of the flesh, then offer to God the pleasing vows of the heart, [Col. 1250A] and then grow in humility in every kind of virtue by which one may please God. It follows:

7. **Behold Solomon’s bed: sixty mighty men surround it, of the mightiest of Israel.**
The daughters of Jerusalem have already foretold this Church, wondrous in beauty and in the marvelous exaltation of her work; now they continue their account, showing and magnifying the blessedness toward which she tends, to which she ascends, by which she is drawn, and into which—reduced to powder—she will presently appear worthy to be placed as a *pigmentarium* (“perfumed preparation”? reading and syntax uncertain), raised up, and exalted. They indicate this blessedness, namely, by setting forth Solomon’s bed, his litter, and the diadem of glory in which, on the day of his espousal, he was judged worthy to be exalted above all. Concerning the bed, indeed, it is said thus: “Behold, sixty mighty men surround Solomon’s bed.”

Now it is certain that Solomon, whose name is interpreted “peaceful,” signifies Christ, who made all things peaceful by his blood and brought into one commonwealth those things which are in heaven and those which he redeemed from the earth. His bed is the blessedness in which the King rests with the saints, and to which the Church daily ascends through the wilderness. How great are the adornments spread upon it, with what ornament it shines, how it abounds in stores of delights, and with what abundance of love it overflows, is known to those whom that same bed now receives, to whom the Lord has already granted that same blessedness. Indeed, “sixty mighty men surround it”; for, that the chastity of this bed may be kept inviolate, sixty mighty men “surround” it—that is, guard it.

By the number sixty are denoted the preachers of the word, instructed in the Law and the Gospel, who train the good by knowledge and lead them even to perfection. For the number six belongs to the Gospel: by this number the Lord measures the good deeds of the good and the evil deeds of the evil, saying: “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you took me in; naked, and you covered me; sick, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you came to me” (Matt. XXV, 35–36). Thus this number is rightly assigned to the Gospel; when ten is multiplied six times, sixty results. Therefore those guardians of the bed are rightly counted as sixty, who, wherever they are carried in their preaching, do not depart from the Gospel or withdraw from the Law.

They are called “mighty”; for strength is the virtue which alone defends the virtues, preserves judgments, remains unconquered in labors, is strong in battles, despises money, flees greed—which makes virtue effeminate (for nothing is so contrary to courage as being conquered by gain)—is not tempted by covetousness, and is not broken by fear. For virtue is consistent with itself when it pursues vices as the poisons of virtue. And, lest he express this merely moderately, he adds: “From the mightiest of Israel.” For they are the mightiest who contemplate eternal things without the weakness of desire; who conquer the flesh, resist pleasures, endure the harsh things of the world, despise its enticements for the sake of eternal things, overcome adversities, behold their end, labor outside in order that they may rejoice within. It follows:

### 8. All holding swords.

It has been said who guard the bed; now it must be said how, armed as they are, they guard it—namely, “holding swords.” Here is expressed the armor of teachers, which the Apostle displays more fully. Blessed Paul says: “Stand therefore, having your loins girded with truth, and clothed with the breastplate of righteousness, and having your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace; in all things taking up the shield of faith . . . and take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI, 14–17). This is indeed the armor of teachers, which is denoted here by the sword, the chief part of that same armor.

For the sword cutting on both sides is the word of God, dividing bodily from spiritual things, separating shadow from truth: “For the word of God is living and more penetrating than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” The mighty hold this sword in their hands, putting into practice what they perceive in meditation. For they do not reckon knowledge and understanding sufficient unless they fulfill in action what they have understood. For we see many who admonish well but live badly, who do not fear to do what they condemn in word, and who are understood to practice with their hands what they “weave together” in speech. [Note: Col. 1251D: Perhaps, “despise.”] Thus the scribes and Pharisees taught, whose words the Lord commands us to accept but whose works to avoid; and he commands his own to teach otherwise, saying: “So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16). Thus swords are held in the hands of those who confirm their teaching by devout actions and confidently teach what they themselves fulfill in deed. It follows:

### And most skilled for wars.

For he is trained for war who resists sin in action; more trained for war, who resists it both in action and by the word of teaching; but most skilled for war is he who resists it in word and deed, applying also the zeal of discipline. For he delivers the innocent to destruction who frees from punishment one in whom the desire to commit robbery still breathes; and he plans the destruction of many who spares the wicked through indulgent pardon. For readiness to pardon is an incentive to sin. It follows:

### Each man’s sword upon his thigh.

Many are restrained from fighting by the very inability to fight: though they have a sword and hold it in their hands, they cannot draw it, or can do so only with difficulty. Therefore the enemy is not killed, and he who deserved punishment escapes unpunished. Thus it is added: “Each man’s sword upon his thigh,” so that both ease of drawing it and the opportunity quickly to strike the enemy may assist him. The sword is upon the thigh when, by preaching, one’s own flesh is subdued, lest, after preaching to others, one should himself become reprobate. It follows:

### [Col. 1252A] Because of the terrors of the night.

The life lived here is spent through days and nights. Some works done here are assigned to the day, others to the night: to the day, those belonging to light; to the night, those belonging to darkness. But the life for which we wait will be wholly day, wholly light. Then there will be no fellowship of righteousness with iniquity, no partnership of light with darkness, no agreement of Christ with Belial. Belial with his own will shudder wholly in darkness, and thenceforth no exit will be open to him by which he may in any way tempt the faithful. Since he is not yet bound by this strict judgment, he now goes forth; now, while there is time, he strives and works by every means to bring in the works of night and darkness.

But these mighty men repel him, lest perhaps the snares of the tempter overthrow them when secure and unarmed, and wickedly carry anything away from the guardianship entrusted to them. It follows:

### 9. King Solomon made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon.  
### 10. Its pillars he made of silver, its resting-place of gold, its ascent purple; its middle he paved with love for the daughters of Jerusalem.

After the description of the bed, the description of the litter is rightly placed. For, rising from the bed, the King takes his place in the litter, to be carried from place to place according to the business which he sees each person desires. He says, therefore: “King Solomon made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon.”

Lebanon is interpreted “whiteness”; and the woods of Lebanon are cedars and cypresses, which are straight and upright, sending their foliage aloft, unfading, incorruptible, and giving forth from themselves an excellent fragrance. From these the King made for himself a litter in which he might be carried wherever the matter required that he should be carried. These woods signify the companies of saints, who are upright, tending straight toward God in meditation and action; and incorruptible, because, once received into eternity, no corruption touches them, nor does any suffering of death, pain, or distress affect them. Among them count the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and the others raised to apostolic dignity, who bear the Lord through the world and bear witness and proclamation to the world concerning his deeds, words, and promises.

He also regards as silver pillars those whom God gives as preachers to the Church, strengthened by the uprightness of righteousness, so that they support the Church by their examples and adorn her with the brightness of their speech, as with the splendor of silver. In it he also made a resting-place of gold, namely the illustrious minds of faithful hearers, in whom, while he displays beforehand heavenly joy, he has made, as it were, a resting-place from the gold of wisdom. For Wisdom “is more precious than all riches, and all things that are desired cannot be compared with her” (Prov. III, 15).

And because one arrives there through much tribulation and ascends by the shedding of blood, it is added: “He made an ascent of purple.” For each person is carried there through martyrdom, which purple signifies; or, certainly, through Christ’s Passion, more precious than purple, through which one enters the Church and heaven. Entrance into glory is opened by the sacrament of the Passion. The litter having been shown, its pillars revealed, together with its resting-place and purple ascent, it remains for the floor of the litter to be shown. He shows it thus: “Its middle”—that is, the floor in the middle of the litter—“he paved with love.”

The preeminence of love shines forth fittingly. For if you are an apostle, you belong to the litter; if a martyr, you belong to the same; if a virgin, you shine in it through the merit of virginity. But if you do not equal these in merits and yet love, you are rightly received in this litter; for its middle is paved with love, so that whoever believes and loves may sit in its midst. What is added, “for the daughters of Jerusalem,” means for those who are younger in time and inferior in merit; even if they are not equal to the highest, they are nevertheless not strangers to this litter, since they are preserved in love. It follows:

### Go forth and behold, daughters of Zion, King Solomon.

The bed and its guard have been discussed; the litter and its adornment have been discussed. It remains to speak of his kingdom and glory, which he continues, saying: “Go forth and behold, daughters of Zion, King Solomon, in the diadem with which his mother crowned him.” By King Solomon, as has already been said, Christ is understood: he bore the cross upon his shoulders and through it has now subjected to himself all the kingdoms of the earth.

Therefore the present Scripture urges all who desire to be “daughters of Zion”—that is, daughters of the heavenly watchtower, who long with full devotion of heart that a place may be prepared for them in heaven—to go forth, and, after going forth, to behold King Solomon in the diadem with which he was crowned (Gen. IV, 8). Yet it does not urge them to go forth as Cain went forth, who rose against his brother and plotted against him. O wretched Cain—and one not to be pitied—who crossed the boundary of innocence, forgot brotherly affection, opened to the world the broad way of parricide, and, by killing the innocent man, declared himself guilty before the world (Gen. XXXIV, 1). Nor does it urge them to go forth as Dinah went out from her father’s tent to see the women of that land. Acting from curiosity and lifting her eyes to things which she was not permitted to imitate, she was seen by Shechem son of Hamor, who loved her and lay with her, violating the virgin by force. Her vengeance is attested by the death of Shechem himself, of his father Hamor, of all the males found in the city, and by the plundering of the city itself.

For these departures are evil. They are not written so that it might be lawful to imitate them, but so that, being written, they may be avoided and rejected alike in thought and action. There are many good departures, such as that of which the Lord spoke to Abraham: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and come into the land which I shall show you. And I shall make you into a great nation, and bless you, and magnify your name, and you shall be blessed. I shall bless those who bless you and curse those who curse you; and in you all the kindreds of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. XII, 1–3). This was fulfilled by Abraham in obeying, and is now fulfilled by the Lord in truly accomplishing what was promised.

It is likewise said of Jacob that, departing from Beersheba, he went toward Haran (Gen. XXVIII, 10), and there, placing a great stone beneath his head, he saw a vision and heard the Lord saying to him: “In you and in your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed.” The result of the work that follows demonstrates that this departure was good.

It is also read of blessed Peter that, when he had gone out of the courtyard in which Christ was being judged, the cock crowed and he wept bitterly. This departure signifies that he had now been separated from the denial by which he had denied the Lord three times, and that his tears poured out from the bitterness of his heart, forgiveness having been granted from above, had already been received in heaven. Since, therefore, one departure is wretched and withdraws far from God, while another is blessed and approaches God, as far as possible, by the steps of repentance and love, which of these departures [the text reads “Aaron”; perhaps *earum*, “of these”] are the daughters of Zion advised to make, that they may be able to contemplate and behold the King of glory in his diadem?

Certainly not that by which Cain went forth, killed his brother, and deserved to be killed himself; nor that by which Dinah, following curiosity, wished to see foreigners and grieved that she had joined herself to a foreigner and suffered the loss of her virginity; nor that by which the spirit departing from the presence of the Lord said: “I shall go forth and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets” (III Kings XXII, 22), and shall kill Ahab. Rather, it is the departure followed by Abraham and Jacob, Peter and Paul, who became familiar with God and his friends.
