Therefore one must go forth from the camps of unbelief and disgrace, from the camps of vain fear and impenitence, from the camps of envy and malice, from the camps of unchastity and every impurity, so that, having gone out from these, we may enter the camps of all virtues, in which we may merit to behold the supreme King and please him. It follows:

### In the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his espousal and on the day of the joy of his heart.

The holy mother of this supreme King is that blessed Virgin Mary whom the angel greeted, whom the Lord chose above all, whom the Holy Spirit overshadowed, whose praise surpasses every utterance. Whatever may be said of her is less than the praise which is due her; words fail before her, and however worthy the praises offered, they ask pardon, confessing that nothing can be said by which her merits may be increased or equaled.

She crowned this King with a diadem, because this King took flesh in her and from her, and in that flesh gloriously triumphed over the devil and death, by which the world was oppressed. For it is her flesh with which the woman encompassed him—him whom, born from her, the most holy Virgin wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger. He is the one whom the star showed from heaven, drawing the kings from the East to worship and honor him with gifts; he is the one who advanced in wisdom, age, and grace before God and men; he is the one who cleansed our crimes in baptism; he is the one who shone forth to the world through miracles; he is the one whom the holy cross bore in its arms; he rose from the tomb and, on the fortieth day, ascended into heaven before the watching peoples; and on the last day he will openly judge all.

Those, therefore, who desire to be daughters of Zion are invited to behold him, so that, having departed from the camps of vices and entered into the camps of virtues, they may say with the apostle Thomas: “My Lord and my God” (John XX, 28); and may see and contemplate him on the last day, because “this is eternal life: that they may see thee, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent” (John XVII, 3).

With this diadem his mother crowned him on the day of his espousal. For the blessed Virgin was truly espoused to this God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—when, acknowledging her as the Mother of the Son of God, they joined themselves to her in true love and espoused her to themselves in all the fullness of love. Hence joy enters the Virgin’s heart; hence she declared herself blessed, saying: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior” (Luke I, 46–47).

This Bride, summoned to life’s end, is warned lest she become entangled and ensnared by these passing things; she is admonished now to hope for what is said to be coming, so that the Bridegroom may now be seen and touched bodily. The Bridegroom repeats what was said above, declaring:

## CHAPTER IV

### 1. How beautiful you are, my beloved, how beautiful you are! Your eyes are those of doves.

Concerning this, since by the Lord’s gift we have already said what occurred to us, we are now silent, wishing to undertake what has been added:

### Apart from that which is hidden within.

He called his beloved like a dove in her eyes; and lest this be understood too perversely, he added: “Apart from that which is hidden within.” For if the dove feeds on clean things, is without gall, does not tear with beak or claw, has a groan instead of song, and flies in flocks, it is led to these things by a certain natural impulse. It is bound to them by no fear of God, but is confined within them by an innate law of nature. But if the soul beloved by God makes itself like the dove in these respects, it has within its mind that by which it is found unlike the dove.

For if the dove feeds on clean things, it seeks food, not God; if the soul feeds on clean things, it seeks God, not food. If the dove lacks gall, this is nature; if the soul governs itself without anger, this is grace. If the dove has groaning instead of song, it does not grieve but modulates the song given to it. If the soul groans, it prays that God’s very presence may be with it and that it may glory in him. “Great indeed,” as blessed Gregory attests, “is the glory of an open mouth; but incomparably greater is the glory of hidden recompense.” Beautiful is that which is seen outwardly, but far and incomparably more beautiful is that to which one comes invisibly. Beautiful is outward conduct, but more beautiful is the unblemished desire of the heart by which blessedness is sought and conscience is cleansed. This, therefore, lies hidden in the soul beloved by God and is altogether unknown in the dove. It follows:

### Your hair is like flocks of goats,

It should be observed that this commendation is contained in the number seven, so that you may understand that the things said of her are said spiritually and must be understood spiritually. For as was said concerning the eyes, so must be understood concerning the hair.

Hair belongs to the body and lends beauty to the face. It is sometimes cut, and the cutting itself adds beauty; should it be absent, the face would appear deformed. Thus the hair represents the faithful peoples, by whose multitude the Church is adorned. Recalling and ruminating upon the heavenly things that they have heard, they seek food on high and contemplate eternal things in the purity of faith. They are, indeed, cut when they confess that they have sinned in some way, whether in action or contemplation; and this cutting adds beauty to the face, because true confession is renewal and restoration of the spirit.

Or, if the subtlety of meditations is understood by the hair, it is rightly compared to goats, since it both tends toward the heights and, if bound by temporal necessity, nevertheless does not depart from the intention of eternal things. It follows:

### Which have ascended from Mount Gilead.

Gilead is interpreted “heap of testimony,” namely the multitude of martyrs who died for the faith of Christ and are witnesses of the truth. Or “Gilead” is Christ himself, in whom the multitude of martyrs is one. The goats ascended from this mountain because the saints, imitating his death, ascended to the things above. It follows:

### 2. Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing, all bearing twins, and none among them is barren.

“Teeth” are the teachers and interpreters of the divine word. They grind and incorporate food for those whom they teach; faithfully understanding and teaching the Lord’s words, they convey them into the substance of their souls and preserve and break down the life already received by faith. Compared to a flock of shorn sheep, they are said to come up from the washing, because in baptism, laying aside the fleece of sin, they take up the way of virtue, draw peoples after them, and establish from Gentiles and Jews one Christian people. Or they render them perfect on this side by faith and on that by works, enriching and adorning them with twin fruits. Hence none is found barren among those in whom the received preaching of the word is diligently fulfilled in action. It follows:

### 3. Your lips are like a scarlet cord, and your speech is sweet.

The lips cover the teeth, utter words, and make audible outside what is formed within by the tongue and teeth. Therefore those who are teeth are also lips: they form things within and bring them forth into the light outside. And so that all they say may be heard more attentively, they color these things with the Lord’s Passion and cooperate with the sweetness of honeyed humility, in order to make them savory to the taste of spirits. Hence it follows here: “Your speech is sweet.” It follows:

### Like a fragment of pomegranate are your cheeks, apart from that which is hidden within.

The pomegranate is the Church, which contains as many grains under one rind as it contains faithful persons. Its cheeks are the Churches established in different places by the devotion of the faithful. For some delight in his holy humanity, and the Church is consecrated to him by them; the Holy Trinity is dear to the hearts of others, and a place is sanctified by the most devoted to it.

These, then, are cheeks converging upon one head, namely the Lord Jesus Christ, who is God, three in persons, and one in humanity: the head and beginning of all things that are, were, and will be. Yet these cheeks are “like a fragment of pomegranate.” For as the grains in one fragment of a pomegranate differ from the grains in another part, so in these places there are diverse devotions among the faithful: in one place, one worships and follows the majesty of God; in another, another most devoutly follows his humanity and humility. Yet none fully comprehends the hidden things of God which still remain unknown. Hence it is added here: “Apart from that which is hidden within.” For that which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and has not entered into the heart of man, God keeps with himself, to reveal it when he wills. It follows:

### 4. Your neck is like the tower of David, built with battlements; a thousand shields hang from it, all the armor of the mighty.

These parts having been shown—the eyes and hair, teeth, lips, and cheeks—the structure of the neck follows, its continuous composition being formed from the things already mentioned. He says, therefore, that this neck is like the tower of David. For the tower was built by David in Jerusalem, repelling the missiles of enemies and fearing none of the engines of foes. This is the lofty and impregnable preaching of teachers: while it proclaims truth, no falsehood of opponents repels it; while it shines with miracles, it is proved true by the demonstration of the thing itself.

These are therefore the battlements with which this tower is built: the Holy Scriptures, by which it truly establishes its truth; and “a thousand shields,” that is, a thousand defenses, by which it repels and restrains the perversity of those who argue against it. These defenses hang from holy preaching, because everything holy in the patriarchs, noble [Note: Col. 1257D: Perhaps, “notable.”] in the prophets, and outstanding in miracles bears witness to the Gospel and confirms its truth, together with the remaining armor of the mighty.

Who can express this armor of the mighty? Who can worthily comprehend in words that which transcends all speech? For who could adequately declare Peter’s constancy, Paul’s courage, John’s love, or the virtue of all the saints? This armor proceeds [Note: Col. 1257D: Perhaps, “precedes.”] through them and affirms that the things proclaimed are true. It follows:

### 5. Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a doe, which feed among lilies.  
### 6. Until the day breathes and the shadows incline.

These are the breasts which we suck, from which we receive growth, that we may please Christ the King: the two Testaments, one preparatory and the other completing. The preparatory Testament is that given through Moses, in which it promises concerning Christ the things that we now see fulfilled concerning him in the New Testament. For the first prophecy was this, in which the Lord said to the serpent: “I shall put enmities between you and the woman, and your seed and her seed: she shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel” (Gen. III, 15).

It depicts the blessed Virgin, at whose heel—that is, at her lowest part, by which she trod the earth [Note: Col. 1258D: Perhaps, “trod.”]—the serpent lay in wait; but lest he prevail in his bite, he was crushed by that very heel. In her seed, as Adam taught, righteous Abel first appeared: offering a lamb, he foreshadowed Christ’s Passion; confessing it, he fell innocent and a martyr in it. In this seed we count Seth, “countable” [Note: Col. 1258D: Perhaps, “we shall count.”], and Enoch, Noah also saving the world by wood, Abraham not sparing his son, and Moses himself saying: “God shall raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren, like me, and shall put his words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all things which he commands him. But whoever shall refuse to hear his words which he shall speak in the name of God, he himself shall be the avenger” (Deut. XXVIII, 18–19).

Isaiah too bears witness and says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a Son” (Isa. VII, 14). Jeremiah says concerning this: “The Lord shall make a new thing upon the earth, and a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. XXXI, 22). Ezekiel confirms it, saying: “This gate shall be shut and shall not be opened, and a man shall not pass through it; and it shall be shut for the Prince” (Ezek. XLIV, 2). Daniel says: “When the Holy of Holies comes, anointing shall cease among you” (Dan. IX, 24).

Thus, surveying the whole Old Testament, you may find it to be in some manner preparatory to the New Testament in promises, burnt offerings, and sacrifices. The New Testament is that which we hear, read, and attest with Christ as its author. Now that it stands established, the old has passed away, except that it bore faithful witness to this truth.

These are breasts “like two fawns of a doe”: when you wish to comprehend them, they immediately flee from you, and you see them climb into the heights. For human understanding does not grasp the lofty mysteries of the righteous, nor does faith have merit when human reason supplies proof by experience. Therefore faith must be followed in these matters; and human reason must be wholly silent in confessing the truth of Trinity and Unity, the mystery of the Incarnation and sacrament of the Passion, and the gift which we offer at the altar. It must revere and love what faith proclaims. For these “feed among lilies”—that is, they receive faith from those assemblies of saints which, like lilies, stand before God and receive from him the splendor of everlasting glory—until we stand with them, when the day of judgment breathes forth and these shadows of ignorance which presently hinder us are wholly removed. It follows:

### I will go to the mountain of myrrh, to the hill of frankincense.

Having completed this present sevenfold course in praise of the Church, lest he delay by carrying it through in the remaining members, he does what belongs to a lover: he desires to see what he loves and to be present with her whom he magnifies with so great praise. Therefore he says: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense”—that is, I myself shall be present and visit the Church, which is the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense.

The mountain of myrrh is the height of mortification, of which the Apostle says: “Mortify your members which are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols” (Col. III, 5). The Church mortifies these things by considering the things above, where none of these things is or can be. The hill of frankincense is the humility of prayer, by which the Church raises itself to the heights, and from the censer of the heart, as it were, rises like the smoke of frankincense.

By these virtues the Church, or every faithful soul, is cleansed: in mortifying vice, struggling in prayer, and washing itself with tears, so that when its filth has been washed away, it may appear beautiful to the Bridegroom. He assists her effort; and, praising his work in her, he says:

### 7. You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you.

This, indeed, is why I shall go: because you are “wholly beautiful, and there is no blemish in you.” He fully describes her fullness [Note: Col. 1259D: Perhaps, “beauty.”], placing last what is first. For the first requirement of this spiritual beauty is that blemishes be erased in the washing of baptism or the shedding of blood; then the spiritual virtues which please God must be assumed, so that the Bridegroom, piously desiring her adorned in head and members, may approach and delight in making in her a holy dwelling for himself. Hence he says:

### 8. Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon, come. You shall be crowned from the summit of Amana, from the peak of Sanir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.

Lebanon is interpreted “whiteness.” Therefore she too, suffused with the light of virtues, is called to come to God. She is told three times, “Come,” so that, approaching him with perfected faith and enlivened hope, she may rejoice with him, refreshed by the eternal fullness of brightness. This joy is marked when it is said: “You shall be crowned from the summit of Amana.” This crown is shown to be made from the summit of Amana, the peak of Sanir, and Hermon.

Amana is a mountain of Cilicia, called “Restless” or “Turbulent,” signifying people of the world, who are always found restless and disturbed through greed and desire for passing things. Sanir is a mountain in Judea, interpreted “Stench,” signifying those whose bodies are driven and defiled by the fires of lust. Hermon is a mountain of Judea, interpreted also “Anathema,” signifying those so lifted up by pride that they have no fellowship with the Lord, who says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV, 6).

What, then, does it mean for the crown of his beloved to be made from these summits, except that those who had been disturbed and overthrown by the filthy desire for possessions are fully converted to Christ; that those whose bodies were distracted by countless lusts embrace and love Christ alone; and that those who preferred themselves above all others humble themselves for Christ even unto death and say: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. I, 21)?

With these, therefore, the Church is crowned and exalted. Gathering them in one expression, he adds and says: “From the dens of lions and the mountains of leopards.” These mountains are dens, that is, places in which lions rest. The evil spirits are called “lions,” for they lie down in those in whom the aforesaid vices already reign. The mountains of leopards are those in whom virtue is mixed with vice, and what is called hypocrisy delights to be honored by all, vice being covered with the cloak of virtue.

Therefore, when those who had been mountains of leopards and dens of lions are converted to God with pure minds—embracing purity in place of leopards, and loving simplicity and humility in place of lions—the Bride’s crown is prepared. It now shows itself to be her sign of victory, because she has conquered the world. It follows:

### 9. You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart.

The Church, which is rightly called the bride of this supreme King, purchased by his blood, consists in a division of two parts: one already perfect, the other not yet perfect. The former is perfect: it has long since entered upon the ways of life [Col. 1260D]; long ago it went in the counsel of the good, stood in their way, and established its seat for itself in the chair of wisdom. Long ago it left behind Egypt’s darkness, escaped Pharaoh’s persecution, and saw him, pursuing it, destroyed amid the waves, because it recognized that his power had been nullified by the waters of baptism. It followed Moses in the wilderness, beheld God’s mighty works, and deserved to hear from his mouth the words of the Law uttered by him. It held to these until it heard the Lord saying to Moses and to the people: “I will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren, like you; and I will put my words in his mouth, [Col. 1261A] and he shall speak to them all that I command him. But whoever will not hear his words, which he shall speak in my name, I shall exact vengeance” (Deut. XXVIII, 18–19).

In this part I would rightly number all the fathers of the Old Testament—the patriarchs and prophets—and, in the New Testament, the apostles, martyrs, and confessors. All these are joined and made one with God, so as to be one spirit with him—that is, of one spirit with him. For they will what he wills, and do not will what he does not will; so that there is no discord in those whom he has taken to himself in glory. To these I would rightly add God’s elect who live in the flesh, yet, as far as is lawful, are unaware of the flesh, and long ago “fortified [Note: [Col. 1261D] F. united.]” by God’s Spirit with God; for them “to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” They say continually to God: [Col. 1261B] “Draw us after you, that in the fragrance of your ointments we may come to you.” This part, indeed, is perfect.

But the other is imperfect: it has recently received the faith, but has not yet fulfilled God’s works. It has recognized that the Lord is good, but, not yet having attained the works of his goodness, says with the Prophet: “For what have I in heaven? And what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Ps. LXXII, 25). It has not yet left house, father, or mother; this poor woman has not yet followed the poor Christ. Others, having left father and mother, parents and children, houses and fields, do indeed follow Christ, yet do not deserve fully to attain him. For the flesh presses upon them, urging and inviting one who remains in the flesh toward the flesh’s enticements and its innumerable works [Col. 1261C]; and the adversary presses upon them as well, aiding this persuasion of the flesh by promising long periods for repentance and suggesting that, after vows have been fulfilled, God—if offended—can easily be recalled by tears to pardon as a merciful and appeasable Judge.

Therefore she laments, saying: “Oh! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. VII, 24). Thus she has recourse to the times that have elapsed, considering infancy, childhood, and adolescence; reviewing youth, mature age, and old age; condemning every occasion on which she offended God; cleansing and purifying herself by repentance of heart, confession of mouth, and satisfaction in works—through abstinence and discipline, prayer and almsgiving, vigils and instruction—and calling down heavenly mercy upon herself. Her sins having been forgiven, the more deeply she sinned, the more ardently she now burns, saying: “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride.” As though she said: O you rightly betrothed to God through your works, who are justly called God’s bride—yet you are my sister, since we have one Father, God, through creation, and one mother, the Church, through regeneration—you have great influence with the Bridegroom: show for your sister what you are able. I beg you, enlarge the wound of love which I have endured by imitating you; expand charity within me; and by your holy intercession bring me to that perfection in which you rejoice. It follows:

In one of your eyes.

The Church has two eyes: one of action, the other [Col. 1262A] of contemplation; one by which it looks upon its neighbor, the other by which it sees God; one by which it attends to its neighbor’s needs, the other by which it searches into God and heavenly mysteries. Therefore, with the eye directed toward its neighbor and that neighbor’s needs, it does not seek its own advantage; but with the eye by which it sees God, it contemplates eternity [Note: [Col. 1262D] F. eternity.], and understands secrets hidden from a person living in the flesh: what is the breadth, what the length, what the height, and what the depth.

For since God is charity, and the length of charity is the same as God’s own length: as God is from eternity, so charity has existed from eternity; and as God is forever, so charity will forever remain in his creatures. This is God’s length. Since there is no greater love than that [Col. 1262B] someone should lay down his life for his friends, his breadth appeared in this: that he laid down his life for his friends, in order to convert into the unity of faith, charity, and peace those whom he had had as enemies.

God’s height, moreover, is this: everything that is, is from God. Bodily things exist because God joins together the parts from which they consist; spiritual things because God gives them the life by which they live, understand, and comprehend the existence of all things through the wondrous opening of the mind. Yet these things are finite; beyond them you understand nothing except God. This is God’s height: he descended from it into the Virgin; he descended from it to the cross, so that even thus, through the man himself, he might restore by the power of his death all who confessed and believed him to be man. [Col. 1262C]

The depth is that of hell, into which he descended in order to rescue from it those in whom he recognized the seed of his mother. Thus in the principal and first prophecy the Lord said: “I will put enmities between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed.” He understands all to be her seed who believed that one would be born, or had been born, from her seed who, free from sin, would rescue the world from sin. It follows:

And in one lock of your neck.

That is: in the unity of the locks of your neck, locks which are as one lock. For the locks are those which descend from the head onto the body, adorning the face and covering the neck; all of them are joined together so closely in unity that they seem to be a single lock. These are the individual persons of the saints [Col. 1262D], who, though all are from God, are so intent upon him in charity and contemplation that they all appear as one; according to the saying: “Now the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV, 32). Therefore, desiring to belong to this multitude, this part says: “You have wounded my heart”—not with the wound of death, which is said to be fatal, but with the wound by which life in God is conceived, nourished, and perfected.

Desiring to be wounded still more by this wound, and to be illuminated more fully by this light through which God is seen, it says twice: “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart,” desiring that a third wound [Col. 1263A] be inflicted upon it, in which it may no longer depend upon hope, but rejoice in the apprehension of the reality for which it longs. It follows:

10. How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride! Your breasts are more beautiful than wine, and the fragrance of your ointments than all spices.

This is a fitting commendation of a sister by a sister. For she says: O you who have deserved to be worthily called God’s bride, yet have not denied that you are my sister, “how beautiful are your breasts!” That is: how beautiful is the teaching of your breasts for the consolation of the weak and the nourishment of little children! She makes the praise of these breasts clear by repeating it: “Your breasts are more beautiful than wine, and the fragrance of your ointments than all spices.” Since we have shown above what the Lord has given concerning these, we refrain for the present from repeating it. It follows:

11. Your lips, bride, are a dripping honeycomb.

The sister continues in praise of the bride, saying: “Your lips, bride of Christ, are a dripping honeycomb.” Nothing is sweeter than a honeycomb; and of the divine utterances it is said: “How sweet are your words to my throat—more than honey to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII, 103). For the honeycomb is honey in wax—that is, the spiritual meaning of utterances in the letter. From the wax, which is as the letter, it drips forth the spiritual understanding, whether allegorical, moral, or anagogical. Or, because all divine utterances proclaim the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in which diverse natures are joined: as honey is concealed in wax, which is visible, so [Note: [Col. 1263D] F. thus.] divinity is concealed in flesh. [Col. 1263C] Therefore the lips of this bride are compared to a dripping honeycomb, since they are shown not to keep silent about the testimonies of the divine incarnation.

Honey and milk are under your tongue.

For those who preach his incarnation have honey and milk under their tongue: they declare God in the sweetness of honey, and bear witness to the innocent man in milk, which is gathered from the earth. Honey, indeed, is from heaven, because the virgin bee receives it from heavenly dew and gathers what it has conceived in wax. So too the virgin mother conceived God’s Son from heaven, clothed the conceived one in flesh, refreshed him when clothed with the nourishment of milk, and thus brought forth life to the world from herself. Rightly, then, those who meditate upon these things in heart and bear witness to them with their tongue are said to have them under their tongue; they retain them in memory and proclaim them in preaching. [Col. 1263D]

And the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense.

Garments cover the body, protect it from cold, and, if they are more splendid, provide adornment and confer grace upon their wearer. The virtues provide this for souls; without them souls are naked and exposed to the cold winds that come from the north, where the one who has sought to chill everything has established his seat. But souls which have already left the world and followed Christ more closely are safe from this cold; they have deserved to hear: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI, 28). [Col. 1264A] He refreshes them well indeed, when he commands them to despise the world, seek God, and cling to these things with their whole mind.

A soul clothed in right faith, clothed in humility and repentance, clothed in confession and every kind of satisfaction, when it now has good hope of pardon, clothes itself in perfect charity; and, exercising itself as much as possible in this care, it now uses garments in which God is well pleased, garments whose scent is excellent and whose fragrance sweet, “like the fragrance of frankincense.” Frankincense, placed upon fire, gives forth a most sweet scent; so virtues mingled with the fire of charity offer the people here a good example, render an acceptable honor to the Lord, and give forth the sweetest fragrance. It follows:

[Col. 1264B] 12. A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain.

With beautiful praise he has extolled his sister: he has praised her eyes and the unity of the locks of her neck; he has commended the beauty of her breasts, the fragrance of her ointments, her lips and tongue, together with the fragrance of her garments. Now he identifies the place in which such things are stored. They are stored in an enclosed garden—not merely enclosed, but enclosed again. This garden, enclosed twice, is understood to be she to whom it is thus said: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride.”

A garden is called a pleasant place, where flowers give fragrance, beds of various kinds bloom, perfumes and incense answer to balsam, and the shaded places of every sort of fruit-bearing tree offer a pleasant seat and dwelling to one desiring rest. Such a garden [Col. 1264C] is the Church, which has already been received by God or is prepared to be received shortly; it does not delay to present to God the strength of good works, the beauty of holiness—signified by balsam or other spices—and the shade in which the Lord may show himself, rest, and delight himself. This, indeed, is an enclosed garden.

By what enclosure? By the enclosure of faith. True faith closes and fortifies it on every side, so that the enemy finds in no part of it a door or opening by which, through temptation or any assault, he may gain access to it. It is again called “a garden enclosed”; but by what further enclosure? He shows this in saying: “A sealed fountain.” It is as though he said: You are closed by faith, and not by faith alone, but also [Col. 1264D] by baptism. For the Church has received baptism, which is the fountain sealed in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Wherever the enemy finds this worthily preserved, he flees, vanishes, and melts away as wax before fire. It follows:

13. Your outpourings are a paradise of pomegranates, with the fruits of apples.

“Outpourings” are good words and works, through which the Church begets and nourishes martyrs and sends them to heaven; it sets forth others who live holy lives as examples to their neighbors, and thus sends forth the fruits of pomegranates. The pomegranate encloses a multitude of seeds beneath its red rind; its fruit refreshes sweetly. [Col. 1265A] So those who shed their blood for Christ gather for themselves a multitude of virtues. Others who live in peace do good works, instruct and refresh their neighbors; and both send forth the fragrance of virtues, like a paradise of sweetness. For “paradise” in Greek is called in Latin “garden” or “irrigation.”

Paradise is within us when the soul is animated and made alive by virtues and by the infusion of the Holy Spirit, bearing fruit in plantations of virtues. In it God principally established the tree of life, that is, the root of devotion; for this is the substance of our life, if we render to God the worship owed to him. Therefore let the righteous person remain in paradise, so that against the heat of the body and the burning of the flesh he may be refreshed by the shade of virtues and guarded by their aids. This is what is meant by “with the fruits of apples.” Pomegranates are those who depart from here crowned by their own blood; but the fruits that are called simply apples are those who, though not called martyrs, nevertheless follow God through uprightness of life and confession of the true faith. [Col. 1265B] It follows:

Henna with nard. 14. Nard and crocus, cassia and cinnamon, with every tree of Lebanon, myrrh and aloes, with all the finest ointments.

This returns to what was said: “Your outpourings are a paradise of pomegranates.” Not only pomegranates are sent forth by you; rather, “henna with nard,” and the other things that follow, are your outpourings. Henna is an aromatic tree, with white seed [Col. 1265C] and a pleasant fragrance; it is boiled in oil, and from it is made an ointment called henna. Princes too are anointed with it, so that they may raise themselves above others in virtues; and it is with nard [Note: [Col. 1265D] F. together with nard.], which is lowly, fragrant, and warming, and signifies charity. This indicates that a prince, however greatly he surpasses others in virtue, should always cleave to them in charity, which is signified by nard.

“Nard and crocus.” Crocus is golden in color, signifying divine wisdom, which a prince must observe, keeping before his eyes: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Sirach III, 20); and: “He who humbles himself shall be exalted, and he who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke XIV, 31).—“Cassia and cinnamon.” Cassia, also called *fistula*, is an aromatic [Col. 1265D] tree, small but with a strong purple bark. It is effective in curing disorders of the internal organs and, because of its small size, is counted by some among fragrant herbs. It signifies those who are humble in spirit and, mindful of the Lord’s passion, are prepared to suffer for the Lord.

Cinnamon, however, is a short tree, fragrant and sweet, ash-colored, useful for medicine, and twice as excellent as cassia. It signifies those who consider themselves weak, whose humility possesses praise and sweetness before God. Cinnamon, ash-colored, is rightly placed after purple cassia, because through remembrance of the Lord’s passion there arises in us contempt for our own virtue. [Col. 1266A] “With every tree of Lebanon.” As cassia and cinnamon signify the humble thoughts of the saints, so the trees of Lebanon, which are tall and strong, show forth the lofty actions and prayers of the saints.

“Myrrh and aloes, with every tree of Lebanon.” Myrrh and aloes are continence of the flesh and chastity, which mortify the decay of lust. Myrrh makes the body incorruptible; so bitterness and patience fortify souls against fleshly desires and defend them. The varieties of spices are the honor and advancement of the various virtues found in the saints. From these spices are made the first and choicest ointments, which heal bodies. Thus they fittingly signify the virtues of souls: when these have been gathered and compounded, a good fragrance comes forth and health is restored. [Col. 1266B] It follows:

15. A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters that flow in a rush from Lebanon.

The sister’s praise of the sister is repeated thus: “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters.” For she herself is the one in whom is the fountain of all gardens, that is, the Holy Spirit, who is God; he waters the gardens and causes them to produce shoots, flowers, fruits, and seeds, by which they please him and for which they are cultivated.

From him comes Scripture, which produces the water of wisdom, refreshes, and does not cease to flow. It is rightly called “of gardens,” because it belongs especially to those in whom virtues spring up. On the surface it is a fountain; in its depth, a well. For Scripture is open in some [Col. 1266C] places and easily grasped by the understanding; in others it is obscure and cannot be understood unless expounded. Yet the waters that flow are living waters—that is, the people for whose sake they have been given, if they are understood, are certainly led to life. Hence it is said: “The rushing of the river makes glad the city of God; the Most High has sanctified his tabernacle. They flow in a rush from Lebanon” (Ps. XLV, 5): they flow from heavenly Lebanon, that is, from the brightness of spiritual and heavenly virtues; “in a rush,” that is, impetuously.

For they run with great force into Moses, who described the origins of the world and spoke with God at a time when no human being had resisted [him] [Note: [Col. 1266D] F. had stood before him.]; with great force into the prophets, who foretold that God would become man when he [Col. 1266D] was not yet man; with great force into David, who traversed all mysteries so that nothing in them is left untouched; and with great force into the apostles, who, renewing the world anew, preach and foretell eternal life to us. It follows:

16. Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; breathe upon my garden, and let its spices flow.

Thus far the Bridegroom has heard the praise of his Bride, divided into six clauses; now he declares his approval of it, saying: “Arise, north wind.” For God commands every heavenly power: both that one which was created in heaven and made reprobate by pride of mind, and those which stood with him [Col. 1267A] and are united to him by the firm root of charity.

Therefore, as the Lord is about to come into his garden, so that nothing sad may meet him and nothing may be found to offend him, he powerfully commands the north wind to arise, to remove itself far from that place, to go to foreign nations, chill them, and make them like itself. But he commands the south wind to come to his garden and breathe upon it with its gentle breath, so that its spices may flow and a holy dwelling pleasing to God may come into being.

Therefore he says, “Arise, north wind,” that is, Depart; I have no fellowship with you, no sharing of light with darkness. Let that Spirit of mine come, who softens the necks of my people, who turns rock into water; who makes the innocent youth Samuel judge of the whole people; who makes David, the boy harp-player, king, singing psalms in the spirit [Col. 1267B] of prophecy; who makes Daniel, a young man, the judge of elders and deliverer of an innocent woman; who equips Amos, too, a rustic separating bramble-berries, with that same spirit of prophecy. Let him come who—to return to more recent times—made Peter the fisherman and Paul the persecutor teachers of the whole Church, who chose to have Matthew the tax collector as an evangelist and Mary Magdalene as herald of grace and resurrection; who—to mention her from whom all these things began—consecrated Mary, a virgin pure, holy, and untouched, as *theotokos* (θεοτόκον), that is, Mother of God.

When this one breathes upon my garden, “let its spices flow”: that is, the spices—God’s virtues and gifts—that had been constrained by the blowing north wind will flow [Col. 1267C], drip, and become manifest to all, though until now they had lain hidden. It follows:

Let my beloved come into his garden and eat the fruit of his apples.

Upon hearing the word by which all things were made, to which it is not lawful to contradict, the north wind immediately departs. The Holy Spirit is present; at his coming its spices flow and emit the sweetest fragrance. Hoping that this fragrance will please God, the Bride says: “Let my beloved come into his garden.” There is now nothing in the garden that can harm, or that can displease by sight, smell, or taste. Therefore let him come into his garden, “that he may eat the fruit of his apples”: that is, that he may “eat” the apples—which are his fruits—by incorporating them into himself and transferring them into his body.

This, then, is the general prayer of the whole Church: that the Bridegroom may come into his garden, that is, into the Church itself, with a certain spiritual grace; visit its trees, herbs, and fragrant beds; pluck them; and taste fruits of different kinds. These are as numerous as the various observances, ordinances, and customs in God’s Church. This diversity of apples signifies the virtues of the various Churches throughout the world: differing from one another in some respect, yet undoubtedly converging in service to the Bridegroom. Apples are all fruits that possess a tender skin; the Bride desires that her Bridegroom be fed by them—that is, delighted by every kind of virtue through which the Churches stand and minister. [Col. 1268A] As this is the Church’s general prayer, so it can be the particular prayer of every faithful soul: that he may come into that soul, which is known to be his garden, and refresh himself with the variety of virtues found in it. It follows:

## CHAPTER V

1. I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices.

The Bridegroom answers her longing and testifies that he has already done what she asked, saying: “I have come into my garden.” Since the sister, addressing her sister, long used the name “sister,” he conforms himself to her and answers her with the same term: “My sister, my bride,” as if joined and united to me by my own blood. “Sister,” because we have one [Col. 1268B] Father, God, and one mother, the Church, which nourishes us with her sacraments.

Thus he says: “My sister, my bride, I have long since come into my garden, and I have given this sign of my coming: ‘I have gathered my myrrh.’” That is: by a certain sickle of death, I have cut down in this life and brought into the storehouses of eternal blessedness martyrs who suffered bitter things for me, and also all others who crucified the flesh with its vices and desires, “with my spices,” that is, with all those distinguished by the renown of good works and therefore worthy of much reverence and fame.

He gathered this myrrh when he received Abel, the first martyr, from Cain’s hand. He also gathered it when he rescued Noah, Abraham, and all whom he recognized as his mother’s seed from the curse. [Col. 1268C] It follows:

I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk.

The honeycomb contains honey in wax; when it is taken, it fills the one taking it with great sweetness. So when a preacher of the obscure word expresses the sweetness contained within it, he pleases God; and insofar as God delights in him, he is received and incorporated into him. “I have drunk my wine with my milk.” The preacher of an obscure word pleases God when he has expressed its sweetness; so also the preacher of a word that is not obscure pleases him by its cheerfulness and mingled sweetness, and is received into his body. It follows:

Eat, friends; drink, and be inebriated, dearly beloved.

[Col. 1268D] Invited into the garden of delights, the Bridegroom has enjoyed its delights—the honey by which he was fed and the wine which he drank. Now, lest he seem to possess his feast alone or to enjoy it alone, he performs the work of charity and, inviting his friends, namely the heavenly virtues, to the same feast, says: “Eat, friends,” that is, be refreshed by the same delights by which I am refreshed, you whom I have known as friends from of old; and “be inebriated, dearly beloved,” you whom I held dear when I created you, and most dear when I confirmed you in the grace of my charity. “Be inebriated,” that is, forgetting every care, be made joyful by the wine of gladness. It follows:

2. I sleep, but my heart watches.

[Col. 1269A] The Lord came when invited into his garden; he was fed with honey and drank wine. Such refreshment indeed prompts sleep. Therefore, to show that this same place is one of rest, not laborious action, the Bridegroom says: “I sleep.”

This sleep was fulfilled in Abraham, to whom, while he slept after the sacrifice, the Lord said: “Know beforehand that your seed will be a stranger in a land not its own; they will reduce them to slavery and afflict them for four hundred years. Yet I shall judge the nation whom they will serve; and afterward they shall go forth with great substance. But you shall go to your fathers in peace, buried in a good old age. In the fourth generation they shall return here, for the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet complete [Col. 1269B] up to the present time” (Gen. XV, 13–16). Behold how the Lord spoke to the old man sleeping, yet with a watchful heart, and plainly foretold to him things that would occur four hundred years later (Gen. XXVIII, 12).

The Lord also slept in Jacob. With a stone placed beneath his head, Jacob saw a ladder standing upon earth, its top reaching heaven, and angels of God ascending and descending by it. Behold how the Lord spoke to him with a watchful heart, showing him ascending angels, who presented to the Lord, standing upon the top of the ladder, the good who had served virtue and had devoted themselves to him by grace; and other angels descending, who might by grace rescue and raise up those entangled in sins, so that, presented to the Lord, they might form one body with the others.

The Bridegroom also slept in Joseph and kept fully awake in heart—that is, in the soul, wherein is the seat of the heart (Gen. XXXVII, 7). For he saw himself and his brothers binding sheaves in a field, his own sheaf standing upright, and the sheaves of his brothers standing around and worshipping his sheaf. Likewise he saw the sun, moon, and eleven stars worshipping him (ibid., 11). The Bridegroom disclosed the meaning of these visions to his father and brothers. For his brothers said: “Will you be our king, or shall we be subject to your dominion?” (ibid., 8). Similarly his father said: “Will I, your mother, and your brothers worship you upon the earth?” (ibid., 10).

The Lord also sleeps in some and watches in heart in others: he preserves the memory of the vision for some [Col. 1269D], and grants others its interpretation (Gen. XL). For Pharaoh’s servants saw dreams, and when they related them to Joseph, each received the interpretation of his dream. One was restored to his position (Gen. XLI); the other perished by hanging.

The Bridegroom also slept in Pharaoh, and, awake in heart, Pharaoh beheld seven fat cows feeding in a marsh, and seven others, ugly and wasted by leanness, devouring them; their appearance and bodily form were remarkable. He also testified that he had seen thin ears of grain, scorched by blight, devour the beauty of seven other ears. The one who watched in his heart gave him the interpretation, declaring to him seven coming years of abundance and seven years of famine. [Col. 1270A]

The Bridegroom also slept in Nebuchadnezzar. Although the latter saw the vision, it was revealed to him neither for memory nor for understanding; but it was plainly disclosed to Daniel through a watchful heart, when he said: “You, O king, saw, and behold, as it were a great statue. Its head was of the finest gold, but its breast and arms of silver” (Dan. II, 31–32). Thus he revealed the dream to him and then showed him its mystery and interpretation.

Such, then, is the meaning of the saying: “I sleep”—that is, I cause those whom I will to sleep. But when the outward sense is lulled, the inward mind freely contemplates those things which God, watching in the heart, provides. If you refer it to the Passion, the saying means this: “I sleep,” that is, enduring the toil of death upon the cross, I thereafter rest from [Col. 1270B] death. Yet “my heart,” that is, God’s wisdom, for which my heart is a seat, itself “watches”: that is, it keeps, orders, and disposes all things watchfully. It follows:

The voice of my beloved knocking: Open, my sister, my friend, my dove, my undefiled one.

While the Bridegroom sleeps in the garden, after a long delay the Bride, lest she seem improperly to pry into his secrets, leaves the Bridegroom in the same place under the guard of his friends and withdraws to her own dwelling. Yet she meditates upon him in her heart, seeks him, and prepares herself so that she may meet him worthily when he comes and prepare what is pleasing for his coming.

But the Bridegroom, awakened from sleep after a delay, knows that she has departed and is concerned for him. He does what belongs to a lover: he follows her, finds the door closed, and knocks upon it, saying: “Open to me, my sister.” It is as if he said: Receive me as I come to you; do not reject me as I seek a dwelling in you. Rather, strive to open to me in yourself the door of your mouth, the dwelling-place of your heart—I who, seeking you alone, desire to find you, who are “my sister, my friend, my undefiled one, my dove.” There is no need to linger in explaining these names, since they can easily be understood from what has already been said. Yet we should observe how greatly he desires to be heard, since he chose to summon her to himself by so many affectionate names. [Col. 1270C] It follows:

For my head is full of dew, and my curls of the drops of the night.

[Col. 1270D] The Bridegroom explains in these words why he asks to be admitted, saying: “For my head is full of dew.” Thus he shows that he had lain down and slept not beneath a roof but in the garden. For, as stated, a garden has no roof; it admits nothing beneath a roof, but, for one resting in it, the shade of holy trees affords a holy remedy. Thus he says: Here, sleeping by night, I bear back a head full of dew and curls full of the drops of night:

> For dew comes by night; by night it enters  
> The plants, and as that period stretches on,  
> It follows it, and, resting on its highest point, makes a drop,  
> And thus produces a kind of shadow of rain.  
> [Note: [Col. 1270D] Perhaps:  
> “And thus creates a certain shower of rain.”]

[Col. 1271A] This is the dew by which herbs grow green again, plantings put forth shoots, the fertility of the earth is opened, and abundant delight is generously spread in common to all. Therefore the Bridegroom, wishing his Bride to be sprinkled with this dew and filled with these drops which are formed by night—that is, apart from human awareness—asks her to open to him, saying: “Open to me.” Giving the reason, he says: “For my head is full of dew.” For the head of Christ is God, in whom all fullness of wisdom and knowledge is known to dwell. Those who receive Christ are known to have him and his gifts within themselves, and to have “the drops of the nights”—that is, heavenly virtues—which were bestowed upon them by night, that is, when humanity did not yet exist or was not yet conscious of them. [Col. 1271B] It follows:

3. I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?

Hearing the voice of the Bridegroom knocking and desiring to enter her, but not yet understanding the dew which the Bridegroom wishes to bring, nor the drops of the nights, the Bride is alarmed. Without answering the Bridegroom, she speaks to herself, saying: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on?” Thinking that she is being recalled to her former and old manner of life, fearing and lamenting that she will be entangled in worldly business on account of her neighbor’s need, yet not answering the Bridegroom, she says to herself: “I have taken off my tunic”—that is, I have been stripped of my former way of life, converted to Christ in baptism, and joined to him through the preaching of good things. How shall I now put that former life on? How shall I embrace what I do not know?

Therefore she says: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” Her feet are her affections, which she washed by believing, by complying with the exhortations of the saints, by listening to Paul, who says: “Not in reveling and drunkenness, not in beds and indecencies, not in strife and jealousy. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. XIII, 13–14). [Col. 1271C] How shall I defile these? How, by departing from them, shall I incline myself again toward the customs of the age which I had rejected? It is indeed to be feared to return to worldly action, which cannot long be administered without sin. It follows:

[Col. 1271D] 4. My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my inward parts trembled at his touch.

With a reverent excuse first offered within herself, yet without giving the Bridegroom an answer, she next shows what her Beloved did to her, saying: “My Beloved put his hand through the opening, and my inward parts trembled at his touch.” Hence blessed Gregory says: “Abundant is the mercy of God, which opens the gate of life equally to all who return after sins, so that they may know the mysteries of the heavenly homeland; knowing, they may thirst; thirsting, they may run; running, they may arrive.”

He had felt these secrets of the heavenly visitation [Col. 1272A] who said, “My soul thirsted for the living God” (Ps. 41:3); and likewise blessed Paul when he said, “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23). Blessed Ambrose also says here that our opening—that is, that by which we see the works of Christ—is the eye of the mind, through which Christ enters, and by which we truly recognize him to be God; through it we most joyfully sing with the Prophet: “Your testimonies, O Lord, are wonderful; therefore my soul has searched them out” (Ps. 118:119). And likewise: “Your testimonies have become exceedingly trustworthy” (Ps. 92:5). These testimonies are his wondrous works, which he performed in the flesh, to the amazement of all. Thus he restored paralytics, cleansed lepers, raised the dead, and finally cured every disease [Col. 1272B] by the word alone, by which all things were created and remain for ever.

Seeing these things and marveling at the testimonies, the world declared them true; for if they were false, they could produce no effect of power from falsehood. Therefore she says, “My inward parts”—that is, I became wholly inward parts—I trembled and was afraid. For the belly lacks bone and shares no firmness: it receives what is put into it and returns it when digested. So too our humanity, not resisting divine works, trembles throughout and fears God made man; yet it recognizes with its mouth what is given from above, loves it with its heart, and, touched by the gifts of the Holy Spirit, says tremblingly: “My inward parts trembled at his touch.” Then, having been touched, she shows what she did, saying:

[Col. 1272C] **5. I arose to open to my Beloved; my hands dripped with myrrh.**

“I arose”: that is, I shook off from myself the burden of sins by which I was weighed down. Hence it is said: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14). Rising, I also admonished others to rise. In this I displayed to them in myself an example of good work; opening the door through which they might enter to the Beloved, I first caused my hands to drip myrrh for them, and my fingers with the choicest myrrh.

Myrrh, by which the bodies of the dead are anointed and protected from decay and corruption, signifies the mortification of the flesh. By it the spirit is fittingly anointed when, through salutary continence—practised [Col. 1272D] through fasts, abstinence, vigils, and other such things—the flesh is recalled from the allurements of lust and adorned with the blessed end of continence. She declares that she caused this myrrh to drip from her hands—that is, that she displayed it in all her works—saying: “My hands dripped with myrrh.” She therefore adds “first,” because that which first flows from the tree preserves bodies more effectively from corruption. She shows that she caused this to drip in order to show that she had devoted the greatest vigilance to practices of frugality. It follows:

**And my fingers were full of choicest myrrh.**

In this place she discloses the virtue of “discernment.”  
[Note: [Col. 1271D] F. *discretionis*, “discernment,” for *discerptionis*, “separation/division.”]

For by fingers discernment is signified, [Col. 1273A] because  
[Note: [Col. 1273D] F. *quod*, “that,” for *quia*, “because.”]  
what is touched by the touch of a finger is understood by a certain rational operation of the mind. Therefore, lest measure be exceeded in this observance of chastity, it is added: “My fingers were full of choicest myrrh.” Myrrh is good when found in a wife, better in a continent widow, best in a virgin who remains holy. It follows:

**6. I opened the bolt of my door to my Beloved.**

Lest access to the Beloved be shown only in the continence of chastity, this is added: “I opened the bolt of my door”; that is, I removed the silence of my mouth by which I had hitherto been restrained, opened my mouth, and drew in the spirit. And because I desired your commandments, I disclosed those things which you commanded me to keep, and which you willed to be commanded and observed by all your people. [Col. 1273B] I disclosed these things and admonished them to observe them, so that they might thus approach the Bridegroom and please my Beloved. It follows:

**But he had turned aside and passed on.**

It has been said that she arose to open, and prepared her hands—that is, her works—to preach; that she admonished all to continence, so that they might thus approach the Bridegroom; and that she removed the bolt of the door, so that all might cleave to Christ and thus possess him. “But he had turned aside,” lest he be held when apprehended; “and passed on,” that is, surpassing far whatever can be said or promised concerning him, he had withdrawn into that delight which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, which he himself prepares for those who love him. This happens so that [Col. 1273C] the sluggish soul may not cease to seek him, nor the laboring soul suppose that it has fully comprehended him. It follows:

**My soul melted when he spoke.**

This Beloved had passed on; but behold, according to his custom, he now returns. He had knocked and asked to be opened to him; and when the Bride arose to open to him, he passed by and did not allow himself to be found even by one seeking him. This is the activity of the inward person: for such a person sometimes seeks God and does not find him. He is also found when one who is sluggish has already ceased seeking him.

For behold, this Bride had now arisen and had taken hold of the bolt in order to open it; not finding him who knocked, she stood astonished within herself. But God, seeing her astonished and marveling, [Col. 1273D] returns, lest he afflict her long by his absence, in order to console her and gladden her with his speech. These, then, are signs of his coming. As wax melts at fire, and white snow at the sun, so this Bride melted at the coming of her Bridegroom and was changed from the sluggishness and hardness which she had already gathered in herself.

Thus she says: “My soul melted”; that is, from hard and impenitent I become repentant; from impatient, compassionate; from merciless, merciful; passing from every state of vice which I had already begun to experience in myself into the contrary state of virtue, I melt and now rejoice in union with God. Thus, when she laments her own sins; when she grieves for the misfortunes or sins of others; when she laments the condition of this misery to which she is necessarily subject; and when she laments the delay of the future glory to which she is not admitted according to her desire—then she melts, saying: “My soul melted.” These are the four rivers of Paradise [Col. 1274A] in which faithful souls wash themselves, by which they are purified, wash away sins, nourish virtues, and stand worthily and purely, without spot or wrinkle, before the sight of the divine majesty.

By “my soul” she means all who, from Adam to the end, have believed or will believe that Christ, the Son of God, would be born or has been born from the Virgin and would redeem the world by his death. Naming all these as one soul because of the unity of faith, she says: “My soul melted.” She adds: “When he spoke.”

To consider this more carefully, one must attend to what blessed Paul says: “God, who long ago spoke to the Fathers in the prophets in many portions and in many ways, has in these last days spoken to us in the Son” (Heb. 1:1–2). He spoke “in many portions” through the prophets—that is, through many words; for the great multiplicity of meanings which the Lord spoke through them could not be explained in few words. Compressed brevity produces obscurity, and such obscurity does not admit understanding. He spoke “in many ways” through them, now mixing words historically, now allegorically, now tropologically, now anagogically.

“But in these last days he spoke to us in the Son” [Col. 1274C] (Matt. 4:17), whom, sent forth from the Father’s bosom and brought forth through his mother’s womb, the world heard teaching and saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 5:3). Likewise: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Blessed are the meek; blessed are those who mourn; blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness; blessed are the merciful; blessed are the pure in heart; blessed are the peacemakers; blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

They also saw works marvelous to speak of: a leper came to him, to whom Jesus said, “Be cleansed” (Matt. 8:3), and immediately his leprosy was cleansed (ibid., 13); he likewise said to the centurion, “Go, and as you have believed, so be it done to you” [Col. 1274D] (ibid., 14), and his servant was healed in that hour; he touched Simon’s mother-in-law when she had a fever, and she was immediately healed. They saw him cast out all evil spirits by a word, and heal every blind, mute, deaf, and lame person, and all who were sick. Speaking thus, confirming his words by accompanying signs, and raising the dead so that he might be believed to be Lord of death and life, they saw him give himself over to death, be placed in the tomb, rise again, and promise this resurrection in eternal life to those who believe in him.  
[Note: [Col. 1274D] F. adds *credentibus*, “to those believing.”]  
What could they do but marvel, be astonished, believe, and worship?

Hearing from him that on the last day he would bring all things to judgment [Col. 1275A] and say to the righteous, “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34)—for I was hungry and thirsty, naked and a stranger, sick and in prison, and in all these things you helped me—what could they do but melt, so that they might sell their possessions, distribute everything to the poor, give and subject themselves to them, and thus fulfil the Gospel? Rightly, therefore, this whole soul melted when the Beloved spoke.

For there is nothing which the Father loves more than the Son, to whom he bears witness by his voice at the Baptism, saying: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3:17), whom I love above all who are in the world, because I find him wholly righteous in every thought, word, and deed. [Col. 1275B] It follows:

**I sought him and did not find him.**

This soul, or Bride of God, testified that she melted at the voice of her Beloved; from this one might understand that she had comprehended him and found the end of her labors in this friendly speech. Lest anyone conceive this in the heart, she adds: “I sought him and did not find him.” For all chosen souls seek him; they desire to stand in his presence  
[Note: [Col. 1275D] F. adds *una cum*, “together with.”]  
when their bodies have been raised. Since this has not yet happened, though it is most certainly promised for the future, she says: “I sought”; that is, I asked for the resurrection of all of them, and desired assurance to be given concerning the end of all the labors by which we seek God and long for him. I desired him indeed, yet did not find him, [Col. 1275C] because there will be waiting until the day fixed by his Father, and then the certain recompense of all.

Yet it is written: “Everyone who asks receives; and whoever seeks finds; and to the one knocking, it shall be opened” (Matt. 7:8). This means: every time in which we live, in which we run, is present to God; for eternity is the ever-present state of all things which have been, are, or will be. Since the Lord, sitting at the centre of the circle, beholds in one gaze what has been, what is, and what will be, all these things are judged present to him, by whose single gaze they are clearly seen. Therefore he says: “Everyone who asks receives”; that is, everyone who truly asks that eternal life be given to him, who seeks the incorruption granted to the saints, and who knocks with multiplied prayers that the glory of the saints may be granted him—when that day comes, he will receive this, find this, and truly be led into that glory of which it was said: “Father, I will that where I am, there also my servant may be” (John 17:24). It follows:

**I called, and he did not answer me.**

Every chosen soul certainly cries to God, saying: “O God, attend to my help” (Ps. 69:2), so that whenever the evil one tempts us, your grace may oppose him, lest he bring to the effect of sin what has been conceived at his instigation. It also adds [Col. 1276A]: “Lord, hasten to help me” (ibid.), as if saying: You, O God, who protect us by helping us when we are tempted, hasten to bring us to that state in which neither his suggestion can move us nor any temptation of his incline us to evil. This will happen when the whole multitude of the elect is joined to the angels of God; then they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but will be as the angels of God. It follows:

**7. The watchmen who go about the city found me; they struck me and wounded me; the watchmen of the walls took my cloak from me.  
8. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my Beloved, tell him that I am sick with love.**

She said that the one whom she sought was not found, nor did he whom she called answer her. Hence it might rightly have been said and thought [Col. 1276B] that the Bridegroom had abandoned her to her own counsel and rightly permitted her to be occupied by those passing by. She removes this thought, saying: “The watchmen of the city found me.”

The city of God is the holy Church. He who reigns in it and orders all its ordinances appoints for it watchmen, who forbid it both to sin and to enter by the broad way which leads many to death, and who diligently teach it to take up the narrow way of virtues, known by few, and to enter by the strait gate until it reaches eternal life. These are the watchmen of the Church, whom the Lord instructs by his Spirit and fills more abundantly with the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of fear. He commands this Spirit to be poured out through the Church, so that they may securely apprehend God, whose Spirit this is.

Those to whom this guardianship of souls is entrusted, observing this soul—or this multitude of souls—seeking God and laboring precisely in order to find him, receive it mercifully and devoutly. They preach to it words of life; they mortify in it whatever sins remain; and in the one whom they receive they kindle ever more fully and keenly the love of divinity. This, then, is what is meant by: “The watchmen of the city found me; they struck me and wounded me.” For those words strike well which kill sins, and those wound well which cause the love of God already conceived to burn more ardently and grow. “The watchmen of the walls took [Col. 1276D] my cloak from me.”

We have already said that the watchmen of the churches are their prelates. We must now say who the watchmen of its walls are. For it has been said: “Surround us, O Lord, with your impregnable wall, and always protect us with the arms of your power.” This city is surrounded by a wall which needs guarding lest it be undermined somewhere; otherwise, if an entrance should be opened somewhere to the enemy, the inhabitant within will sleep less securely. This wall of the Church, then, is faith; if it should lie open anywhere by being broken, there will be less rest for every citizen dwelling within.

But the heavenly citizens—the angels of God—guard this wall, striving to prevent Satan from piercing it, and refusing to permit the Church to be scandalized or disturbed in any part of the faith. These are the watchmen of the Church: the angels of God, going about and surrounding it, striving that faith may not be broken in any part, hope diminished in any respect, or the charity of God, the highest virtue, corrupted by growing cold. These watchmen take away the cloak of the Church: they establish faith in it, strengthen hope, and root charity within it, so that there may now be nothing [Col. 1277A] but contempt for all earthly things, while it may cleave to Christ alone. This, then, is what she says: “The watchmen of the walls took my cloak from me.”

The cloak is the outward covering—that is, this whole earthly substance which was created for the Church. By it the Church covers and protects herself. But she wholly abandons and despises it when she sees herself being given to God and drawing near to him. Therefore she prays, saying: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem”—that is, heavenly powers, who share in none of this misery, who owe to heavenly Jerusalem alone all that you are, all that you know, and your protection of us—“if you find my Beloved” (and it is certain that you will find him), “tell him that I am sick with love”; that is, in his love I rest from all earthly things. It follows:

**9. What is your Beloved more than another beloved, O most beautiful of women? What is your Beloved more than another beloved, that you have thus adjured us?  
10. My Beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands.**

The daughters of Jerusalem, adjured to report to the Beloved the love-sickness of this woman, inquire by what sign they may recognize her Beloved, lest they err and perhaps bring to one person the love given to another, or carry the message of love uncertainly. Thus they say: “O most beautiful of women!” They call her most beautiful because there is no spiritual beauty by which a soul may please God in this life which the Church does not possess in herself and represent from herself. She does not care for the beauty of which Solomon says: “Grace is deceitful, and beauty is vain” (Prov. 31:30); rather, she receives and does not hesitate to offer to the Lord the beauty which follows: “A woman fearing the Lord, she shall be praised” (ibid.).

Countless virtues arise from fear, [Col. 1277D] and many from love. If you count all these, you will find in the Church a noble gift worthy to be presented to God. She is therefore rightly named thus: “O most beautiful of women! What is your Beloved?” By what sign do you make him clear to us, so that we may recognize the one whom you love, and recognize his Father, by whom he was sent, whom you also love? Since this is highly divine and most fully comprehends both natures in Christ, she repeats her question, saying again: “What is your Beloved more than another beloved, that you have thus adjured us? My Beloved is white and ruddy.”

This description of the Beloved is comprised under the number twelve  
[Note: [Col. 1277D] F. *binario*, “twofold,” for *duodenario*, “twelvefold.”]  
[Col. 1278A] when she says: “My Beloved is white and ruddy.” In this she comprehends the twofold nature in Christ Jesus our Lord: one divine, the other human. She comprehends the divine nature when she says, “He is white”; but the human when she adds, “and ruddy.” In his divine nature he is white, retaining nothing mixed with himself—not anything black, red, or colored with an intermediate hue—but white himself, indeed whiteness itself, diffusing himself into all his creatures. Though he shines in all things, he diminishes himself in nothing, but remains wholly intact in himself.

Thus he is white because he is truly God, truly light, truly the simple good, diffused through all things that are his and yet remaining in himself the one simple good. Having long pitied human nature, he descended into the Virgin after many thousands of years; taking flesh from her and creating a soul for himself, he came into the world as man. From the world he chose certain people for himself, to whom he said: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16). First by himself, then through them, he afterwards taught the world, performing virtues. Since the world could not oppose these, it plotted his death on the cross, placed his body in the tomb, from which he rose when he willed; afterward, for forty days, he remained on earth to console the disciples, and then, while all present watched, he ascended powerfully into heaven.

Placed upon the cross, because he redeemed the world by his blood, whose colour is red, he was rightly called ruddy. Thus, in his memory and praise, the Bride says: “My Beloved is white and ruddy,” and adds: “Chosen from among thousands.” For he alone, among all the thousands of human beings, ought and was able to be chosen to wipe away human sins, since he had no human sins, but was as the innocent lamb who takes away the sins of the world and by his innocence destroys the offenses of all who believe in him. Of him David says: “You are fairer in form than the children of men; grace has been poured out upon your lips” (Ps. 44:3); and Isaiah: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah?” (Isa. 63:1). It follows:

**11. His head is the finest gold; his locks are like the elevated branches of palms, black as a raven.**

His praise begins with his head, which is compared to gold. For just as the finest gold is more precious than all desirable things, so God is found more precious than all things that can be desired or longed for. “His locks are like the elevated branches of palms.” The elevated parts of palm trees are called the upper parts of the palm; these bore the sign of victory, for victors carrying them declared that in battle they had obtained the highest part—that is, victory.

His locks, therefore, adhering to his head and giving ornament to the head, are the faithful: obedient to God in all things, keeping his commandments, and fulfilling in deed what they preach in speech. Thus, in the battle of this life, they rejoice that they have won the victory of the palm. It follows: “Black as a raven,” because, although they advance in virtue, they profess themselves to be black as ravens. It follows:

**12. His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk, and sitting beside brimming waters.**

That is, spiritual men, keen and penetrating for the sight of his mysteries, are “like doves washed with milk.” The milk by which they ought to be washed is rational, guileless understanding; hence it is said: “As newborn infants, desire rational milk without guile” (1 Pet. 2:2). “And sitting beside brimming streams” [Col. 1279B]: that is, beside the most abundant writings of the ancient Fathers, by which nothing but truth is taught and simplicity is everywhere commended. It follows:

**13. His cheeks are like beds of spices planted by perfumers.**

The cheeks have many uses: they receive food, grind it, and transfer it into the body. They are also the seat of modesty, to which blood rises when someone is ashamed to have said or done something less than justly. By them words are formed which teach Christ and show that we ought to believe in him, follow him in heart, and follow him in deed.

The “beds” which are “planted by perfumers”—that is, by those who know the powers of spices—are the writings of prophets and teachers. When we receive them, transfer them to our hearts, and proclaim them to eager hearers, we become the cheeks of Christ’s body, taking every precaution that we say or do nothing at which modesty may blush, and fulfilling these things in faith and deed, so that our hearers’ concern for Christ and their understanding may grow. It follows:

**His lips are lilies, dripping first myrrh.**

That is: those are rightly called his lips who are like lilies dripping first myrrh. The heavenly lips, rightly dripping to God the sweetness of fragrance, are the companies of angels. Created among the first companies by the supreme Power, which is God, when others sinned and wished to reign with power equal to God, they expressed this,  
[Note: [Col. 1279D] F. *spr*—reading uncertain.]  
and, devoting themselves in all humility and obedience to God by whom they were created, they trampled beneath the feet of their minds pride and disobedience, which were the first sins.

This was indeed the first myrrh, because it was the first mortification of sin. All who similarly urge the mortification of sins are rightly called the lips of God, persuading what is dear to his heart. It follows:

**14. His hands are golden, rounded by the lathe, full of hyacinths.**

[Col. 1280A] It is clear that his hands should properly be understood as his works. Since nothing is understood to be more precious or more dear than gold, his hands are rightly called golden—that is, more precious than every work. What works can be compared with these? He made the deaf hear, the mute speak, restored sight to the blind, cured paralytics, cleansed lepers, raised the dead, commanded the sea and winds, put demons to flight, raised himself when already dead, showed himself to his followers after death, and thus ascended manifestly victorious into heaven. Nothing is dearer or more precious than these works; and they are rightly called shaped by the lathe.

Nothing is more easily turned on a lathe in workmanship. The one who works with a lathe sits and so shapes and unfolds whatever unformed material there may be that what was rough and unformed becomes smoothed and takes the most suitable shape. A leper was brought to him and healed by one word; a dead person was brought and, healed by one word, went away alive. His hands are therefore rightly understood as “rounded by the lathe,” that is, healing easily, since by a word alone they work all things so that they are seen to be better now than they were before. Therefore it is added: “full of hyacinths.” Hyacinth is a stone whose colour is that of the sky when it is clear. So that you may understand all these works to be from heaven and not doubt the power of heaven on earth, it is added: “full of hyacinths,” that is, full of heavenly good works. What follows agrees with this:

**His belly is ivory, adorned with sapphires.**
