The belly is the part of our body most readily injured; thus it here signifies that nature of the Lord which was human, by which he could be injured, weakened, and afflicted even by the cross. As it is said of him: “Truly he bore our weaknesses and carried our sorrows” (Isa. 53:4). Yet this belly is called “ivory,” in order that his firmness, acquired through the passion he endured, might be shown. Ivory is exceedingly solid and white, and in time becomes ruddy from white.

All these things belong to Christ. His whiteness of chastity was incomparable; none among the children of men could equal it, as the Psalmist testifies: “Fairer in form than the children of men” (Ps. 44:3). In it, too, was firmness which could not be corrupted. Therefore, when his soul descended to hell, it could not be detained, because there was no sin in it by which it could be held. His flesh likewise suffered nothing in the tomb after death, because sin was absent on both sides, by which corruption and accusation against the soul might be added. Hence the Psalmist says: “You will not abandon my soul in hell, nor give your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 15:10).

That ivory becomes ruddy after a long time [Note: [Col. 1280D] probably denotes the sufferings of martyrs.] signifies martyrdom of suffering: those imitating him gave their bodies over to punishment long afterward and deserved now to live with him eternally. It is adorned with sapphires—that is, adorned by their heavenly martyrdoms.  
[Note: [Col. 1281D] F. *adornatur*, “is adorned.”]  
It follows:

**15. His legs are marble columns, founded upon bases of gold.**

This fittingly applies to preachers, who run through the world and exalt Christ’s name, standing upright and firm, and in all their preaching confirmed upon golden bases—that is, prophetic sayings. As it begins with gold, so it ends in gold, so that, discerning reader, you may understand that it truly concerns Christ. It follows:

**His appearance is like Lebanon, chosen like the cedars.**

Lebanon is a great forest, beginning near the Jordan and stretching high and far even to the Eastern Ocean. Its chief trees are cypress and cedar, whose whitish leaves give the forest its name, so that it is called Lebanon; for *Libanus* means “whitening.” In it are beautiful and delightful dwellings, so that, if anyone reaches them, there is no concern to return or delight in dwelling with human beings.

This appearance is attributed to God, who is the brightness of souls and the delight of all virtues. Whoever reaches him has no will to return to human things, no recollection in the soul of what has gone before. Why? Because he is “chosen like the cedars.” Cedars are trees of Lebanon, rising long and high, wonderfully and nobly crowned with foliage, incorruptible, fragrant, and unafraid of the gnawing of worms. Whoever reaches this glory finds it enough to be honored by that glory itself. It follows:

**16. His throat is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable. Such is my Beloved, and he is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.**

What is signified by this throat except the utterance of the New Testament? The Old preceded it, in which it was said: “A man shall render life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth” (Exod. 21:24), and the other things which follow. But what is said in the New? “If anyone strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other also; and to one who wishes to contend with you in judgment and take your tunic, surrender your cloak as well. And whoever compels you for a thousand paces, go with him another two. Give to the one who asks of you” (Matt. 5:39–41). What could be sweeter? What could be more pleasant?

If you consider the whole New Testament, you will find absolutely nothing except what is sweet and desirable. Having said these things, she continues: “Such is my Beloved, and he is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.” It follows:

**17. Where has your Beloved gone, O most beautiful of women? Where has your Beloved turned aside, that we may seek him with you?**

Having heard the praise of this Beloved, by which his Bride commends him member by member, the daughters of Jerusalem also judge him worthy of commendation and consider themselves worthy to bring him a message of love. [Col. 1282A] Therefore, lest they run aimlessly, they ask the Bride in this way: “Where has your Beloved gone?” Since “to go away” can mean to depart far off—which would seem strange in one who belongs to this most beautiful of women—they correct and repeat the question: “Where has your Beloved turned aside?” That is, where has he withdrawn for a time? Perhaps it is your business that he may convert some people and join them to you, making you grow and become known where you are not yet present. When we know this, we shall seek him with you and endeavor to offer him the gift of your love. It follows:

## CHAPTER VI

**1. My Beloved went down into his garden, to the bed of spices, to feed in the gardens and gather lilies.**

[Col. 1282B] This garden of the Beloved is the blessed multitude of the faithful, opening to him the whole bosom of its mind, loving and contemplating him with all its strength, embracing him with the fuller affection of the heart, so that it considers even death for his sake a gain and does not disdain to endure his sufferings. In this number you will count Abel, who first received the Lord in his death, being both virgin and martyr: priest and sacrifice in himself, he confessed as both priest and sacrifice, virgin and martyr, and died as sacrifice and priest. You will count also Enoch, whom God took from the world; and because he walked with God, he deserved to possess life in himself. Noah likewise, whom God saved in wood when the world perished. Abraham also and his noble offspring.

You will count Moses himself, who openly confessed the Lord, saying: “I will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like you; I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all the words which I command him. But whoever will not hear his words, which he shall speak in my name, I shall be the avenger” (Deut. 18:18–19). In the midst of these you will observe the blessed Mary, highest among virgins and hope of the ages, in the bed of spices, trusting with her holy guardian John; at the right hand of this fragrant bed stand Peter and Paul, Andrew and James, and all the rest who, bearing witness to him by their own blood, gave forth a most sweet fragrance to the world and by their death brought the dead back to life.

This [Col. 1282D] is the bed of spices, which you understand more by the mind than you can teach by speech, and which deserved to confess Christ by its own blood and by punishments which cannot be told. Here balsams give fragrance, spices exhale perfume, and every kind of incense scatters the sweetest scent. Here the Beloved sometimes turns aside, to feed in these gardens—that is, to be refreshed by the glorious testimony of them all—and to gather these true lilies, truly worthy of his companionship; that is, to establish them in supreme peace and blessedness.

The Lord is sometimes said to visit this Church separately, so that it may be understood that the palm of martyrdom, granted to persons of both sexes, has obtained something from him far beyond the rest;  
[Note: [Col. 1282D] F.: “the palm of martyrdom granted to persons of both sexes, [so that it may be understood that they] have merited something far beyond the rest.”]  
while the remaining universal Church, dispersed throughout the world far and wide, is seen to be much greater in number but lesser in merit. It follows:

**2. I am for my Beloved, and my Beloved is for me, who feeds among the lilies.**

This is the voice of the Bride, who says that she and her Beloved exchange private speech. Since these things are secret, we leave them so and do not communicate them to others in any way. It follows:

**3. You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and comely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army arrayed in battle order.**
Some of these matters have indeed already been discussed: for what occurs concerning the beauty of this Bride has been mentioned [Col. 1283B]. It remains for us also to say, as the Lord shall teach us, what concerns her sweetness. This is not a bodily sweetness, delighting and alluring some by touch, but rather that of the spirit; hence it is said also of the Lord: “You, O Lord, are gracious and gentle” (Ps. 85:5). So too she is gracious: when injured, she does not murmur; she patiently bears what is inflicted upon her. Thus she obtains the beauty of patience, like that heavenly Jerusalem to which no peace was granted on earth, but which, now taken up into heaven, rests in an abundance of peace; for “she is terrible as an army drawn up in battle array.” For an army drawn up in battle array is present when those about to fight, gathering all their strength, stand armed in a suitable place; and they have on right and left compact ranks of fighters [Col. 1283C] that resist those who approach and, before battle is joined, shatter their rushing assaults by the force of arms. This inspires fear in enemies; and therefore she rests in the utmost peace. It follows:

**4. Turn your eyes away from me, because they have made me fly away.**

Behold, the Bridegroom has declared his Bride to be beautiful, gracious, and fair, as one pleasing to the Bridegroom; he has also called her terrible, so that she fears no encounter with an opposing enemy but stands secure. As she gazes upon him so intently and desires now to enter into the secret places of the Godhead, hoping already to possess the fullness of glory which the Lord promises to his own, he fittingly reproves her, [Col. 1283D] saying: “Turn your eyes away from me,” that is, do not seek to grasp the beauty of my sublime glory; “because they have made me fly away,” that is, to rise beyond human understanding and to show myself as still incomprehensible to humankind. For before the common resurrection of humankind and their reunion with their spirits, he is unwilling to show this to anyone: “what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart.”

It follows:

**Your hair is like a flock of goats that have appeared from Gilead.  
5. Your teeth are like a flock of sheep that have come up from the washing, all bearing twins, and none among them is barren.  
6. Like the rind of a pomegranate are your cheeks, apart from what is hidden within you.**

These same things have been said and explained above; to repeat them [Col. 1284A] would be superfluous and burdensome. It follows:

**There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number.**

Since, under the Lord’s instruction, we have also explained this above, we refrain from explaining it again and turn our attention to what follows. It follows:

**8. My dove is one, my perfect one; she is the one of her mother, chosen for her who bore her.**

This is reciprocal praise. For the Bridegroom commends his Bride, who praises him, with worthy praise, saying: “My dove is one.” From what has been said above you may understand how she is called a dove and in what sense she is understood to be perfect. But she is here called one because, just as one heap is made from many grains, one cluster [Col. 1284B] from many bunches, and one flock is aptly spoken of from a multitude of animals, so this one Church, the one Bride of God, is understood from the multitude of all souls which have been or will be called to God in unity of faith, strengthened in unity of hope, and established or to be established in unfeigned charity toward God.

Though she is one, she is nevertheless “one of her mother,” that is, one in likeness to her mother—namely, the heavenly Jerusalem, which the Bridegroom declares to be her mother. For just as that Jerusalem consists of a multitude of heavenly spirits and is one through charity united to God, so he understands this Church, gathered from an infinite multitude of souls, to be one, and in this to be like and conformed to her mother: she in no way separates herself from God [Col. 1284C] but binds herself by steadfast charity to him whom she loves. Hence follows: “Chosen for her who bore her,” that is, chosen in the manner of her mother.

This mother is the same as she who bore her; yet the difference of words denotes different matters. He calls her mother because she consists of a diversity of spirits and is one, while this Church, collected from a diversity of souls, likewise exists in unity. He calls her begetter because God, having condemned the reprobate portion of spirits, established and confirmed her as chosen for himself; and similarly, having condemned the reprobate multitude of human beings, he chose this Church for himself and determined that she should share his glory. It follows:

**The daughters saw her and proclaimed her most blessed; the queens and concubines also praised her.**

[Col. 1284D] It has been said that the heavenly Jerusalem—that is, the Church consisting of blessed spirits—is the mother of the Church consisting of souls and existing on earth, and that this latter has been chosen by God for glory in likeness to the former. If, then, it is asked by what testimony this is true or by what reasoning it is proved, this answer is added: because the daughters of Zion saw her, namely, that heavenly Jerusalem which is mother of this earthly Church and which has been assumed and chosen by God for glory. The queens saw her, and the concubines saw her; and contemplating her with the eyes of the heart, they proclaimed her most blessed: some of the blessed spirits stand in attendance, privy to the divine mysteries; others minister with utmost diligence; others laboriously range through the regions of the world, [Col. 1285A] announcing and bringing to effect in all things and through all things the will of God.

The “queens,” understood as the highest order in the Church, and the “concubines,” the order nearest after them, together with the daughters of Zion, looking upon her, proclaimed her truly most blessed and commended her as worthy of every praise. This is the testimony of the whole Church on earth; there is no one who can deny its truth or rightly contradict it. It follows:

**9. Who is she that comes forth like the rising dawn, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army drawn up in battle array?**

Whatever love draws one toward, to that one swiftly turns and recalls it in the mind. Therefore the Bridegroom, conscious of his love and not unaware how worthy of admiration is the Bride whom he has chosen, turns toward her in order to show her admirable to all, and says: “Who is she that comes forth like the rising dawn?” Dawn is called, as it were, the golden hour: preceding the sun, it announces that the sun will come, and, glowing like gold, foretells that an end of darkness is at hand. Who does not know that this existed in the primitive Church, if he knows from Scripture’s revelation that those first fathers preceded the rising of Christ, the true Sun of righteousness, and preceded him with their testimony? For who doubts that righteous Abel fell by his brother’s sword and displayed Christ’s passion by his own suffering; that Enoch was taken up by the Lord; that Noah was saved by wood when the flood overwhelmed the world; and that Abraham [Col. 1285C] foreshadowed the Lord in many ways? These, certainly, and all the fathers of that covenant, were a dawn in which the rising Church foreshadowed that the true Sun, Christ, would be born and would more fully illumine her.

But when the Lord was born, what is written came about: “He came unto his own, and his own received him not. But as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God” (John 1:11–12). Made children of God and illumined by his light, they shone as the moon, not by their own light but by another’s light; hence is added: “Fair as the moon.” For the moon receives from the sun the light by which it shines and floods the world with a fuller light than dawn. Thus the rising Church, [Col. 1285D] first as dawn, then as moon, and thirdly as the chosen sun, supplied the world with full light.

After the wondrous things which occurred at Christ’s birth had passed, after the miracles that bore witness to Christ preaching had been performed, and after the signs which appeared at his death and after his death had been seen, the Church rose powerfully: in the first fathers, as dawn; in the second, as the moon; and now, refreshed with full light, she appeared as the chosen sun, shining with full radiance and providing light to all by her splendor. This is the meaning of “Chosen as the sun.” Among all bodily creatures created by God, none was chosen to be the eye of the world and to provide light and illumination to the world on every side, except the substance of the sun alone, which alone circles us, warms us, and increases and protects us by its benefits. In this manner too this Bride was chosen, to provide the world with spiritual light and, after the darkness enveloping the world had been removed, to bestow and impart to it the light of faith through the apostles, holy martyrs, and all teachers of the faith. When she shall be gathered whole after the resurrection, she will appear terrible as an army drawn up in battle array. For when the Lord sits on that day and pronounces the sentence of judgment, “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34), she will appear so terrible and admirable that she gives no opening to an enemy approaching her; but, like an army ordered by the hand of the Lord, she will contain her own and repel all outsiders by the power of her Lord.

[Col. 1286B] Blessed Gregory, however, says of this: “Dawn announces that night has passed, yet does not display the brightness of day; but while it drives away the one, it receives the other, holding light mingled with darkness.” Therefore one who follows truth in this life is dawn, because he does certain things belonging to the light, yet does not lack remnants of darkness. Thus, while the law of sin contends with the law of the mind, it is still dawn, because the light that has shone has not yet utterly overcome the darkness; and because the law of the flesh strikes against the law of the mind, and conversely light and shadow contend with one another in turn. It will be day when the shadow of sin remains no more, when inward light shines perfectly. The Church, therefore, whom the Bridegroom admires, is rightly compared to dawn, because, leaving the darkness [Col. 1286C] of sin, she breaks forth into the light of eternity and is transformed through the knowledge of faith into the light of righteousness, just as dawn is turned from darkness into light. Faith is light; unbelief is night. Therefore, longing for eternal things, the Church shines with heavenly brightness and the light of righteousness, and rises like dawn, because, abandoning the perversity of the world, she turns herself toward the brilliance of new light. It follows:

**10. I went down into the garden of nut trees, to see the fruits of the valleys, and to observe whether the vine had flowered and the pomegranates had budded.**

Having above addressed the whole Church, the Bridegroom now turns to that part which is here below and subject to temptation. When rain falls, rivers come, winds blow and rush against her house, [Col. 1286D] she needs aid all the stronger as she is shaken by more frequent storms. Coming down to her, therefore, he says: “I went down into the garden of nut trees,” and so forth.

A garden, as has been said, is a place set apart, planted with health-giving herbs and wholesome trees, which it is pleasant to visit after labors and there refresh the spirit. This place signifies the Church set here below. Isaiah shows how she is set apart, saying: “As the heavens are exalted above the earth, so are my ways exalted above your ways, and my thoughts above your thoughts” (Isa. 55:9). By these ways and thoughts he signifies the thoughts and works of the Church, which are as far removed from every wicked purpose as heaven is distant from earth.

This garden is planted with nut trees [Col. 1287A], which are various: some are hazelnuts, some filberts, some chestnuts, some almonds, some pine nuts, some Libyan nuts called nutmeg, and some Gallic nuts, which alone are customarily called *nux* (“nut”) in common speech. What do these nuts signify? Surely the hearts of the saints, which inwardly present the sweetness of the kernel—that is, the usefulness of the spirit—but outwardly display the usefulness of the flesh, which is so hard that it is said of it: “We have this treasure hidden in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7). Again it is said of it: “I know that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor any other creature, will be able to separate us from the charity of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8:38).

He descends, therefore, into this garden of nuts, to strengthen their kernels inwardly and subject their bodies outwardly to suffering, reserving for them the rewards of life, which will fail none who die for him. He descends also to see the fruits of the valleys. This garden is not planted with nut trees alone, but also with trees that bear fruit. Fruits are all produce covered with soft rind; they signify confessors, who, burning inwardly with love of God and confessing him outwardly, receive from God a reward in eternal blessedness, even though they are not equal to martyrs. To these, therefore, he descends: both to those who follow him in the sublimity of martyrdom and to those who remain in the valley of humility and likewise do not delay to follow him in death. Yet the Lord spares the latter, [Col. 1287C] wishing them to receive eternal blessedness by will alone and not also through death actually undergone.

He also descends to vines recently planted, to see whether they flower, whether they give hope of fruit from themselves, whether they persevere in faith, and whether, by providing others an example of approaching, believing, and persevering, they magnify his name. He desires the same of the pomegranates: namely, that they may bud and, by budding, courageously offer others examples of the suffering to be undergone for Christ, and may pledge the rewards of the recompense for which they wait. It follows:

**11. I did not know; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Amminadab.**

In the preceding words the Lord admonished his Bride, made known to her what he sought, and set himself before her as the goal of her course. For we run in vain if we do not attain, if we do not find him whom we seek. Hard things were proposed to her, which the flesh fears and at which it trembles; but for these the spirit is strengthened and armed by God’s gift, accounting everything it suffers light as it glories in the gift of its recompense.

Hearing this, the Synagogue stands, marvels, and trembles; at last returning to herself, she says: “I did not know,” that is, I did not know that so great a grace and gifts of the Spirit had been bestowed upon you; and therefore “my soul troubled me,” because I wandered in darkness, “because of the chariots of Amminadab.” This Amminadab is read to have been Judah’s great-grandson (1 Chron. 2:10), and by interpretation of his name signifies Christ. For Amminadab means “the willing one of my people.” He was made the head of the whole people, at whose birth the angel said to the shepherds: “Do not fear; for behold, I announce to you great joy, which shall be for all the people: for today a Savior has been born to you, who is Christ the Lord” (Luke 2:10–11). He was indeed their willing one: willingly born, willingly manifested through angels and mighty works, willingly adorned with miracles, willingly handed over, willingly given to death. Since he endured all these things willingly, he is rightly called both the willing one of the people and their willing one.

His chariots are the four Gospels, which are drawn through the world while they are preached to peoples, believed, and received with every reverence. Beholding this, [Col. 1288B] the Synagogue is troubled, despairing that what is received in the heart by all, splendidly honored, and crushed neither by carefully devised tortures nor by any kind of death can be false.

Saint Ambrose, however, identifies two chariots. He makes anger, desire, pleasure, and fear the wheels of one chariot; to the other he assigns prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. The spirit of life is in these wheels when a good driver directs them—restraining some, warning others, recalling others, and urging still others on. These are horses subjected to the yoke of faith, bound by the bond of charity, with the reins of justice and the bridles of sobriety. It follows:

**12. Return, return, O Shulammite; return, return, that we may look upon you.**

[Col. 1288C] As the Synagogue confesses her slowness, the Church replies in consolation: “Return,” and so forth. She is called Shulammite and told to return because, at the end of the world, faith will be offered by the Church to the Synagogue, which was held captive under unbelief. She is urged four times to return because the Jews, dispersed through the four quarters of the world, will be gathered at the end. Thus she is told: “Return, return, O Shulammite, who were held captive or despised under the prophets; return, return, that we may look upon you in the freedom in which we are.” It follows:

## CHAPTER VII

**1. What will you see in the Shulammite, except the dances of the camps?**

This is the Bridegroom’s voice. Behold, as the Church exhorts the Synagogue, the rejoicing Bridegroom promises to bring it about, saying: “What will you see in the Shulammite, except the dances of the camps?” The dances of the camps are those who, stationed as in camps in the battle-array of virtues, fight against the devil and, God protecting them and bringing aid by his power, overcome. Then the camps of soldiers will be seen in the Shulammite, when she shall fight for the faith which she now opposes and, as Enoch and Elijah preach it, shall affirm it to be true and the faith in which salvation is necessary, and shall attest this by her death. It follows:

**2. How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of the Prince!**

Behold, the Bridegroom praises the Bride, beginning with her steps. In commending her, he says: “How [Col. 1289A] beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of the Prince!” He commends with twelvefold praise her who, in her first fathers, was “daughter of the Prince,” that is, of God who rules over all. Beginning with her steps, proceeding through the middle parts, and completing her praise with the fruitfulness of her breasts, he says: O you who now in your manner of life are worthy to be called daughter of the Prince, and who even in your first fathers deserved worthily to be called his daughter, how beautiful now are your steps! For you now approach God by those same steps by which the apostles approached: confessing that God’s Son was sent by the Father in flesh; that in that same flesh he underwent death for the salvation of all; and that after three days he rose again and so, having won victory, ascended into heaven. You stand for him, bear witness to him, and do not refuse to die for him. Very beautiful, therefore, are your steps by which you walk toward God—and this, “in sandals.”

Sandals are made from the skins of dead animals; hence they signify the examples of the saints: namely, the fathers, apostles, and all martyrs, because in confessing Christ they suffered their skins to be stripped from them and their bodies to be taken away from their souls. You are therefore made equal to them, who, having received a sure faith, fight for it and labor in striving to be crowned with the glory of the apostles. It follows:

**The joints of your thighs are like necklaces, fashioned by the hand of an artisan.**

[Col. 1289C] The thighs—or, according to another reading, the “steps” [Note: [Col. 1289D] F. *gressus*]—by which we walk and direct our progress are the two Testaments, the Old and the New. Their joint is the harmony of the Testaments, concerning which he says: “The joints of your thighs are like necklaces.” Necklaces (*monilia*) are so called from *monendo*, “warning,” because when they are suspended from the neck and lie upon the breast, they warn the wearer not to admit another’s hand to her bosom but to preserve unsullied fidelity to the one to whom she is betrothed. They also warn anyone not to be drawn in love to where he sees these ornaments suspended, nor to be carried there by love under any circumstance, lest, perhaps, being caught in this, he be judged guilty of adultery.

Therefore the two Testaments are rightly called necklaces, for they warn us to fear and venerate God, to love him with all [Col. 1289D] our heart, soul, and strength, and to meditate upon him with steadfast mind. They also warn us to love our neighbors and neither devise nor do anything to them that ought rightly to displease them. In these matters the two Testaments agree; they also strengthen faith as it truly is and confirm that things are as we believe them. These necklaces too “were fashioned by the hand of an artisan,” that is, they were proclaimed and written for humankind through the Son, who is the Father’s hand and the supreme artificer of all. It follows:

**3. Your navel is a rounded bowl, never lacking cups.**

The navel is in the middle of the belly, having one part of it below and another above. This navel is the weakness of our mortality, one part of which is below and the other above. The lower part is that of which it is said: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. The grass has withered, and the flower has fallen” (Isa. 40:6–7). David says of it: “In the morning let it pass away like grass; in the morning let it flower and pass away; in the evening let it fall, grow hard, and wither” (Ps. 89:6). The morning of our infancy, childhood, and youth passes away; the flower of our young adulthood also passes, and the evening [Note: [Col. 1290D] F. *vespere*, “in the evening”] of our old age passes. In this, a human being falls in death, grows hard in the corpse, and withers into dust.

The upper part is that of which blessed Paul speaks: “It is sown in corruption; it shall rise in incorruption. It is sown in dishonor; it shall rise in glory. It is sown in weakness; it shall rise in power. It is sown an animal body; it shall rise a spiritual body” (1 Cor. 15:42–43). [Col. 1290B] This navel, therefore, is like a rounded bowl. For the operation performed by a lathe is exceedingly easy, and equally easy is God’s work that will occur in the resurrection of all. For just as the angel lifted Habakkuk with the greatest ease, set him in Babylon, brought food to Daniel, and restored him to Judea (Dan. 14:35), so it will be at the resurrection: at the angel’s voice and the sound of the sounding trumpet, the dead will rise at once incorruptible, though they had been liable to corruption. This, therefore, is the part of our weakness that will be effortlessly brought about by the lathe-like operation of God; it is called a rounded bowl, which neither here lacks cups nor will lack them in any way in the future. Thus great glory is said to await them, a glory then to be seen and manifested bodily. It follows:

**Your belly is like a heap of wheat, surrounded by lilies.**

The belly is the part of the body that receives what is put into it; it retains whatever can contribute to its substance, thereby nourishes, enlarges, and advances the body, and rejects and expels the rest. Therefore it signifies the holy memory of this Synagogue, which comprehends all things yet loves, preserves, and advances only those things that are holy, cooperate toward eternal life, and direct one’s steps thither; the rest it rejects and ejects as vain and useless. Hence it is said: “Your belly is like a heap of wheat.” For in a heap of wheat some things cooperate toward life and some are otherwise disposed; but concerning those things that cooperate toward life, it is added that this heap is “surrounded by lilies,” that is, instructed by the examples of the Fathers and taught by the precepts of heavenly spirits, who are truly lilies. It follows:

**4. Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle.  
5. Your neck is like an ivory tower.**

This is understood of the breasts of the converted Synagogue, as was said above concerning the breasts of the Church; likewise of what follows concerning the neck: “Your neck is like an ivory tower.” Yet here “ivory” is added, [Col. 1291A] so that both the brightness of preaching and the firmness by which they preach Christ truly and confirm this by their death may be shown. It follows:

**Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon, which are at the gate of the daughter of the multitude.**

After the neck has been described, one comes to the eyes, concerning which it is said here that they are “like pools in Heshbon.” Heshbon means “girdle of sorrow.” The “eyes”—that is, those who contemplate the mysteries of faith and show to the now-converted Synagogue the things that are to be seen and believed—are “like pools in Heshbon.” For Heshbon, whether a fortress or a city, had pools at its very entrance, in which the bodies of those entering could be washed and cleansed, so that those entering might thus be trusted to devise nothing evil against or in any way harmful to the place.

So too those who prepare and show the paths of life to this converted Synagogue foresee and show the way of life for others who are to be converted to her; and they ensure that people do not enter under false pretenses, receive baptism in vain, or deceitfully devise opposition against those among whom Christ already reigns and now holds his dominion. This is what is meant by “which are at the gate of the daughter of the multitude”: that is, at the entrance of the fortress or city, where there is a multitude of nations to whom the word of God is now preached and who receive it for ever and ever.

Simon Magus did precisely this falsely: he falsely received baptism and falsely came to know the sacraments of faith; after all this, he fiercely assailed Peter, the teacher of the Church established by Christ. Therefore, lest a similar attack trouble this Synagogue in her conversion when it is granted to her, it is said that she will have eyes which foresee for her, just as provision was made for the city at Heshbon’s gates. This multitude is rightly called a “girdle of sorrow,” because it is surrounded on every side by sorrow. On one side it grieves that it has sinned against God; on another it has again the tears of fear lest it sin. On one side it fears that the one it loves may be lacking to it, and that the rewards it seeks and desires may be lacking to it. Surrounded by this sorrow, therefore, it is rightly called Heshbon; surrounded by these and other tears bestowed by compunction, it rightly laments. It follows:

**Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus.**

[Col. 1291D] Those who sense nearby in the Church the fragrance of virtues and discern from afar the stench of vices in her are assigned as the Church’s nose. In Lebanon, which signifies the Church’s whiteness, they stand like a tower: they receive in God’s Church above others the name and office of prelates, and they look toward Damascus. Damascus is the capital of Syria, where Cain is said to have killed Abel. There many evils were inflicted upon Israel; there unbelief reigns and sin is very widespread. The Church of God looks attentively toward it, considering whether there may be anyone whom she can snatch away from it and, having rescued that person from the devil, turn to Christ. It follows:

**5. Your head is like Carmel; and the locks of your head are like royal purple bound in channels.**

[Col. 1292A] Carmel is the mountain upon which Elijah ascended and obtained from God an abundant rain, shut up for seven years. It surely signifies Christ: confessing him and affirming as true what is said concerning him, we pray to the Father that he may send us gifts of his graces, by which he may make us pleasing to his will. Carmel means “mountain” or “knowledge of circumcision,” which fittingly applies to Christ, for he was the beginning and end of circumcision.

He imposed it upon Abraham—who saw his day and rejoiced—and upon Abraham’s household; by the severe cutting away of this member, he forbade intercourse that was forbidden to it, along with all other shameful and superfluous acts of every member. He also received circumcision in himself and foretold that it had been fulfilled in himself. For the shedding of his blood, both on the cross and in this circumcision, is correction sufficient for the people of grace, so that they may refrain from vices and correct and amend evil impulses not by that severe sacramental observance, but solely through faith and reception of holy baptism.

The locks of this head are those mentioned next: “The locks of your head are like royal purple bound in channels.” The locks of the head adorn the head, beautify the face, and, always clinging to the head, render it honorable in many ways to every person who meets it and most worthy of all reverence. By them we understand those who, clinging with their whole heart to Christ the supreme King by an indissoluble bond of love, could never be separated from him—not by any principality nor by any power acting to that end. Rather, through every torment that could be devised, they deserved truly to cling to him and to be called inseparable locks.

The locks of the head are like royal purple bound in channels. The channels are outpourings of God’s graces, which he sends forth in many ways into those whom he chooses, makes worthy of the grace of martyrdom, and receives. In these channels, therefore, are these locks; joined to them, they do not know how to be separated from them. Rather, receiving some heavenly liquid in them, they become ruddy like royal purple bound in channels, conformed to Christ suffering on the cross and now conformed to him in glory. It follows:

**6. How beautiful you are, and how fair, most dear one, in delights!**

[Col. 1292D] After commending the matters already mentioned, he adds praise of the Synagogue which has now become the Church, saying: Since the things just stated are so, you are very “beautiful” in the work of virtue and “fair” in its contemplation; dear to us through conversion, dearer through the practice of virtue, and to God “most dear” in your arrival. Hence he adds, “in delights,” that is, in the things mentioned, which God declares to be delights and in which he delights as in pleasures. It follows:

**7. Your stature is likened to a palm tree, and your breasts to clusters.**

Her commendation began with her steps; the joints of her thighs, her navel, and belly were also praised; her breasts and neck, nose and eyes, together with head and locks, have been described. So that this may not seem discordant and excessively contracted within itself in relation to her stature, he adds concerning her stature that it is like a palm tree: stretched upward, narrow and rough at the base, spreading and opening its branches toward heaven, producing most sweet fruit. Joined to clusters, the fruit of the vine, this makes a rich banquet, delightful through the vine’s own fruit. It follows:

**8. I said: I will climb the palm tree and seize its fruits; and your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine, and the fragrance of your mouth like apples.**

The Bridegroom says that he himself will climb the palm tree. We believe this was fulfilled [Col. 1293B] when he ascended the wood of the cross. It was granted to that wood that, just as he himself became victor over all things by ascending it, so it too justly attained preeminence over all the trees of the forest and rightly deserved to be called a palm tree. Thus it is sung to it: “Above all the trees of the forest, you alone were worthy to bear the King and Lord of the ages.”

“And I will seize its fruits.” The fruit of this palm tree was immortality, impassibility, and eternal joy. Christ received these fruits upon the cross. For because he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father upon the cross even unto death, indeed the death of the cross, the Father exalted him, so that at his name every knee should bend—of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings—and every tongue confess that he is in the glory of the Father, to which no one comes except through him.

“And your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine.” Breasts are those by which the infancy of little children is fed and nourished. They are the utterances of the prophets, by which Christ’s passion was prophesied long beforehand and proclaimed by many of their declarations. These breasts have now become clusters of the vine, now showing the very fruit that they foretold, when Christ at last suffered on the cross, manifesting the fulfillment which they had proclaimed.

“And the fragrance of your mouth like apples.” Before Christ ascended it, the smell of the cross was dreadful; but after Christ, the giver of life, ascended it, all its odors became most sweet and, like the odors of apples, most delightful. Hence Paul says: “We are the good odor of Christ to God among those who are saved and among those who perish” (2 Cor. 2:15). It follows:

**9. Your throat is like the finest wine, worthy for my Beloved to drink, and for his lips and teeth to chew over. I am for my Beloved, and his turning is toward me.**
The Bridegroom has long commended her as worthy of praise, beginning from the lowest point and proceeding to the highest. Gratefully receiving this, the Bride replies: “Your throat is like the finest wine, worthy for my Beloved to drink, and for his lips and teeth to chew over.” She therefore shows that the praise which the Bridegroom himself has uttered concerning her is such as it is fitting that he should drink, and, having taken it into his body, retain it in memory [Col. 1294A]; and this is what is meant by “to be chewed over by his lips and teeth.” For in the Law (Lev. 11:3), an animal which does not chew the cud is considered unclean, whereas that which does chew the cud is undoubtedly reckoned clean. For one who recalls to memory the good things he hears or reads, and declares them by chewing them with his teeth or pronouncing them with his lips, is declared to be a clean animal. Thus, affirming that this cleanness belongs to the Bridegroom, she urges him to recall this praise to memory and judge her worthy of it. And she declares that this will indeed occur, saying, “I am for my Beloved, and his turning is toward me”; as though she said: I am worthy of my Beloved’s remembrance, and he is most worthy to be held by me in remembrance. For I love the Father; I venerate and adore his only-begotten Son; and I judge the Holy Spirit equal to them in all things. I understand the works of the Father, which he performed to redeem me; in them I recognize the obedience of the Son, and, through his Spirit coming into me, I receive him as turned toward me, together with his gifts. She says therefore: I am worthy and dear to my Beloved, for he emptied himself for me, making himself a child and an infant. Of him the Church sings that saying of Isaiah: “A little child is born to us, and a Son is given to us” (Isa. 9:6). He also emptied himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death. And what death? The death of the cross, which was deemed most shameful: by it heaven was denied to a man, the earth was withdrawn from him, water afforded no relief, [Col. 1294C] and, when dead, he was exposed in the air to be torn by birds:

> By these merits deservedly dear,  
> By these merits to be held dear.

“His turning,” moreover, “is toward me.” For what kind of death should I dread, when I understand that the Son of God suffered such things for me? Certainly none. For in Stephen I endured stones; in James, the sword; at Rome, the cross in blessed Peter; and in his companion, blessed Paul, the torments of the sword. I bore boiling oil in John, and the bitterness of the cross in Andrew; and in the apostles, and in all martyrs throughout the wide world, I displayed every torment that could be devised. It follows:

**10. Come, my Beloved, let us go out into the field.**

Having shown the love by which the Church is united with Christ, [Col. 1294D] she confidently calls upon him, desiring that he too may come to her who loves him, behold her love, and perceive whether the things said concerning him are true. She says therefore: “Come, my Beloved,” whom I love unto death; you who, when departing from the Church, promised, saying: “Behold, I am with you always, unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). “Come, let us go out into the field.” A plain is a broad open place, containing woods and places without woods, and showing here ground beset with thorns, there places not thorny but nevertheless uncultivated. It signifies this world as it was when Adam was cast into it after sin, and when this sentence was pronounced upon him: “Because you have eaten from the tree from which I commanded you not to eat, cursed is the earth in your work; in toil you shall eat from it all [Col. 1295A] the days of your life. Thorns and thistles shall it bring forth for you, and you shall eat the herb of the earth” (Gen. 3:17).

But it was called a field after the ploughshare and hoe had attacked the face of the earth, stripped it of its dreadful appearance, made it responsive to cultivation, and delighted its cultivators with good fruits. It is called a field because it began to be worked by the ploughshare and broken up by the hoe and, as is customary with cultivators, overturned in the same place so as to be fitted to receive seed and become fruitful in propagating it. Therefore the Bride invites her Bridegroom into this field, saying, “Come,” that is, consent that I may have access to you. “Let us go out”: come forth from the hiddenness of your ineffable majesty in assumed flesh—that is, appear openly. And I, wholly departing with you from my hidden things, my uncleannesses, and my unbelief, believing in you with my heart, confessing you, humbly adoring you, inseparably cleaving to you, am prepared to come with you into this field, [Col. 1295B] that we may see whether it has been well cultivated, whether seeds of the word ought to be entrusted to it, and whether any hope of good is to be expected from it. It follows:

**Let us remain in the villages.**

Dwellings are indeed made in fields, as was said of the plain of Shinar, in which the city of Babylon was built by Noah’s sons (Gen. 11:2); towns are made, and villages too. The rich dwell in a city, the powerful in towns; but the dwelling of the lesser and humble is in villages. It is so much more pleasing to God as it is humbler, and so much more acceptable as it is receptive of virtue and teaching. Here she desires the Bridegroom to make a stay, [Col. 1295C] and herself to remain with the Bridegroom: where his holy body and blood are consecrated; where cleansing from sins takes place in baptism; where sins are confessed daily; where the faithful people frequently offer themselves to the Lord; where tithes and other gifts are often bestowed; and where, at their departure, there is recognition of the Lord’s sacred things and their own passage into eternal blessedness. It follows:

**11. Let us rise early for the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has blossomed, whether the blossoms bear fruit.**

Blessed is he whose vineyard is visited by the Lord in the morning. For each person’s vineyard is this present life, and morning for each is the beginning of this present life. There are some whom God visits, directs, and glorifies in the morning—that is, from life’s very [Col. 1295D] beginning—and even demonstrates by the display of miracles that great fruits will come from them: “Let us see whether the vine has blossomed.” The Bride invites the Beloved to these, that he may remain with them, cause them to blossom, and himself guard their fruit-bearing blossoms.

These are indeed our advances in God. For as a vine first produces leaves, then a flower, and afterward fruit, so in matters belonging to God, for those anxious to see and possess him, the first stage is a turning away from evil; for a happy conversion to the things of God is great progress. But the highest point in these matters is a love for the things of God that pleases God, and blessed fulfillment in them by action. Hence it continues:

**If the pomegranates have blossomed.**

[Col. 1296A] In the pomegranates, love of martyrdom is indicated. For no one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends. Though she urges him to observe all her own, she nevertheless particularly urges him, by a special visitation, to attend to those who burn with love of martyrdom, who desire to lay down their lives for Christ and to ascend upward through death. Hence she says:

**There I shall give you my breasts.**

What are these breasts which the Bride will give the Bridegroom when he has thus come and visited the Church in this way? Breasts are that part of the body by which the Church feeds her children, sustains their infancy, and brings them into youthful strength. And when they have grown into this strength, she leaves them to themselves, to the martyrdom they desire, [Col. 1296B] and to him for whom they desire it. She says therefore: “There I shall give you my breasts,” that is, I shall open all the recesses of my mind, that I may understand from you what must be said to each order, and how each order is to be admonished so that it may come to you and possess you eternally. It follows:

**The mandrakes have given forth their fragrance. At our gates are all fruits, new and old; my Beloved, I have kept them for you.**

Having called her Beloved to come to the Church, visit her, and attend to those who desire to see him, she adds this, saying: I do not doubt that you will be hard to find for that which I seek, because I understand that the mandrakes have already given forth your fragrance at our gates. By mandrakes she means the Prophets, which retain the form of the human body and cure, with powder scraped from the corresponding limb, whatever member of the human body disease has seized. They also make a barren woman fruitful and are useful in many ways to those suffering from ailments. Thus they signify the Prophets, who set forth Christ’s humanity and the things he did as a man; and they do not cease to proclaim and prophesy this at our gates, that is, in the Scriptures which have now become ours. All these are the fruits which the new and recent prophets foretold; “and old” means the ancient things, namely, those spoken from Adam until now. I have kept them for you, because they must be fulfilled in you and displayed by the very accomplishment of the work. It follows:

## CHAPTER VIII

**1. Who will grant me that you may be my brother, sucking the breasts [Col. 1296D] of my mother, so that I may find you outside and kiss you, and no one may now despise me? 2. I shall take hold of you and lead you into the house of my mother; there you will teach me, and I shall give you a cup of spiced wine and new wine from my pomegranates.**

The Bride, concerned about the coming of her Bridegroom, had long prayed and desired it, saying, “Come, my Beloved; let us go out into the field.” And she foretold that what she prayed for would certainly come, because the mandrakes had foretold it, because all the Prophets had foretold it. Therefore, regarding that which is certainly to come, she asks already, saying: “Who will grant me that you may be my brother?” That is, who will be worthy to show you visibly to me as my brother, to reveal you to me as my brother in bodily form?

For it is ancient knowledge, known by hearing, that God the Father created me among other things, became my Father among other things, and that I among creatures have always invoked him as Father. But that he should be my brother is new and unheard of through the ages, though it must nevertheless be proclaimed to the world. For the angel Gabriel was sent to Mary, saying: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you. The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you. Therefore the holy thing that shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:28, 35). Behold: the Son of God, born of the holy Virgin, reborn through holy baptism, became a son of the true Church and began to be brother to us all, though before all things he had been our Father. Hence after the resurrection [Col. 1297B] he said: “Go, tell my brothers that they are to go into Galilee; there they shall see me” (Matt. 28:10).

Thus he whom I had hitherto called God the Father, I now call my brother; and brother because he sucked the breasts of my mother, namely Mary. Because she became his mother, she is worthily mother of all who invoke him and implore his aid in any necessity. Through her indeed the Son of God was found outside, that is, in this bodily form which he newly assumed; in it he appeared to the world, and in it he received from it, as has been said, the kiss of reconciliation. Hence she says: “And no one may now despise me.” For before God had offered the kiss of reconciliation to humanity, man was regarded as contemptible by angels, demons, and even by himself, since he was wholly dragged down to be possessed by Hell. But after he was reconciled through the death of the only-begotten Son, abandoning Hell, he began to possess the region of Paradise and heaven; and thereafter he was held in contempt neither by the possessors of heaven nor by those of Hell.

She says: “I shall take hold of you,” that is, I shall hold you in the firmest embrace. Neither threats nor blows nor any kind of death shall remove or tear me away from you. And so I shall lead you “into the house of my mother,” namely, heavenly Jerusalem, which instructs me and shows me an example of the love by which I may always cleave to you and never be removed from you. And I shall lead you into “the chamber of her who bore me,” that is, into that ancient dwelling-place of love in which my mother has always held you: the most ancient assembly sprung from patriarchs, prophets, and other faithful persons, the sacred congregation which could never be torn away from you. “There you will teach me,” because then we shall all be taught by God. And what shall we give you? “A cup of spiced wine,” namely eternal love, formed in as many ways as wines are flavored with different spices; “and new wine from my pomegranates,” that is, the passion of my martyrs, united to themselves in the sweetness of love as the seeds are joined within pomegranates, and unable to be turned from you by any evils. It follows:

**3. His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me. 4. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not arouse [Col. 1298A] or awaken the Beloved until she herself wills.**

Since these matters have already been spoken, we do not repeat them, but entrust diligent readers to read where they were stated. It follows:

**5. Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights, leaning upon her Beloved?**

One who loves readily looks upon one who loves him, and easily imparts to her words shaped by love. Therefore, since the affection of the Bride who loves him is readily made known by what has just been said, the Bridegroom suddenly gives her an answer of love, asking and inquiring who she is—not because he does not know her, but so that he may permit no one to be ignorant of her. What kind of woman is she, and how great, how supremely worthy of admiration, who thus comes up from the wilderness?

He calls this world a wilderness, a place which many try to inhabit as their homeland, but, disappointed in their attempt, descend from it into the lower regions and thus learn what homeland has been appointed for them. This wilderness is the place which the Lord left by ascending, when, before the eyes of many, he was lifted up and ascended into heaven. It follows therefore that she is “mighty in delights,” abounding in those delights which she understands to be most pleasing to the Lord; by right faith, firm hope, and ardent love she seeks to stand beside him and offer him these gifts, knowing that they were given her by him. This, then, is what he says: Who is she, and of what great merit, who, forsaking this world as a wilderness—which God left by ascending from it, and which has customarily been a place of descent for others—makes it for herself a place of ascent, springs to the heights, [Col. 1298C] and offers God the delights of virtues which she recognizes have been bestowed upon her by him?

But blessed Gregory, considering these things more deeply, says: “The Church, abounding in the delights of God’s words, ascends from the present wilderness to higher things. To abound in delights is to be satisfied, in the love of God, with the feasts of the Scriptures. Therefore she ascends abounding in delights, because she daily raises us, fed with mystical understandings, to heavenly things. In her words there are as many delights as there are varieties of spiritual understanding. At one time history feeds us; moral allegory refreshes us; at another time contemplation suspends us toward higher things. The soul abounding in these delights is refreshed by mystical understanding, in which present obscurity is illumined by the splendor of the coming day, so that even amid this corruption it may break forth into an understanding of that true light, and, fed upon the delights of words, may learn by foretaste what nourishment of truth it should hunger for.” It follows:

**Under the apple tree I awakened you; there your mother was corrupted; there she who bore you was violated.**

It has been said that she who abounds in delights leaned upon her Beloved. It is now accordingly shown why she could and ought to lean upon him. For he says: “Under the apple tree I awakened you,” that is, I recalled you from death, you who were under the apple tree, that is, subject to sin, which was contracted through the apple tree.

For they say that the forbidden tree from which man was commanded to abstain in Paradise was an apple tree; and that this wood, which was good for food, beautiful to the eyes, and pleasing in appearance, became an object of desire to the woman. She took from it and offered it to her husband, making herself guilty of disobedience and rendering her descendants guilty as well. By bearing the cross, this Bridegroom delivered all from the evil of that disobedience; therefore he confesses that he awakened and redeemed her who was placed under the apple tree, that is, under sin contracted through the apple.

Lest this be thought a small matter, he adds: “There your mother was corrupted; there she who bore you was violated.” By mother he means the whole generation extending from Adam to Abraham; by her who bore you, that generation extending from Abraham to Christ, bound under a stricter law of commandments. By these he teaches that all who have been begotten by human generation are subject to this sin, unless the Spirit sanctified them before they were born—as the holy Virgin, made God’s dwelling-place, John the Baptist, and Jeremiah, whom we know to have been sanctified from the womb—or unless God aided them through his sacrament. If anyone wishes to examine this more deeply, let him reread the treatise in which, above, we discussed the kiss of reconciliation and expounded the things granted to us by the Lord’s dictation. It follows:

**6. Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm.**

Because I delivered you from the death which you deserved through the death of my cross, I therefore command you in consequence to set me—that is, my love, by which [Col. 1299C] I became man for you, by which I was crucified for you, by which I humbled myself to rescue you from the death you had deserved—always as a seal, that is, as a memorial, upon your heart, that is, within your heart. Thus, in everything that you resolve to do, always consider this love, lest you presume to accomplish anything unless you see that it coheres with this love.

He adds the same concerning the arm: “As a seal upon your arm.” These are indeed corresponding things: the heart deliberating, and the arm carrying out what the heart has deliberated. If both retain the memorial of this love, they will restrain themselves from every work that does not accord with that love. Thus, fortifying heart and arms, he urges what was elsewhere said: “There are six things that the Lord hates, and a seventh his soul detests: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a heart devising wicked thoughts, feet swift to run toward evil, a false witness uttering lies, and one who sows discord among brothers” (Prov. 6:16–19). All these things, if you possess the love of God and fasten it as a memorial in your heart and arm, will be far from you; nor is there anything that can impede you even slightly.

**For love is strong as death.**

Death is strong because it destroys kings, casts down tyrants, despoils the rich, and finally draws to itself everything living in the world, ending all things in one common end and enclosing everything. So too Christ’s true love is strong: rejecting everything opposed to Christ; not shrinking from the sword; not fearing prison; not dreading chains; willingly taking upon itself every kind of punishment that can be imagined [Note: [Col. 1299D] F. adds: *genus*, “kind”]; and regarding such things not as torments but revering and adoring them as aids to its salvation. The world devised beasts, burning plates, wheels, and racks; yet love dwelling in the hearts of those whom wickedness attacked overcame and conquered them all. Therefore this love is not merely strong as death, but stronger than death itself: when death rushes upon it, it remains whole and merits through death the attainment of eternal rewards. It follows:

[Col. 1300B] **And jealousy is hard as hell.**

As love is commended, so jealousy is condemned; for jealousy is called the envious imitation of love. Some, seeing martyrs honored and holy confessors revered by all, envied these honors and desired them for themselves. They put themselves forward as though they were followers and imitators of the martyrs, and so considered themselves martyrs, or as good as martyrs. The Bridegroom condemns their endeavors in this way, saying: “Jealousy is hard as hell.” For as Hell drags away those whom it seizes and permits none of them to be pulled out of itself, so their condition is hard: by evil deceit they join themselves to Hell while merely pretending to be good. It follows:

[Col. 1300C] **Its lamps are lamps of fire and flame. 7. Many waters could not quench love, nor shall rivers overwhelm it.**

This is praise of love, which is the true love of God. Its lamps, namely, are the hearts of the saints, formed after the likeness of lamps: narrow below, widened above, and prepared as a dwelling-place for spiritual fire. This fire is always fire, always warming and always setting the heart ablaze in the love of God. At times it is fire with flame, when it not only burns and kindles but also shines in action and manifests outwardly what it accomplishes inwardly. Thus many waters cannot quench this love: no tribulations, no contrivances of persecutions can extinguish this love; because, as evils multiply, it is evident that it thereby increases toward God. For “rivers shall not overwhelm it,” that is, evils heaped upon evils shall in no way prevail against God’s grace. It follows:

**If a man should give all the substance of his house for love, he would despise it as though it were nothing.**

This is its complete praise. For if a person gave everything acquired in time in order to obtain this love, he would despise all that substance as though it were nothing and would think that he had given nothing, because what he obtains is dear and lovable. It follows:

[Col. 1301A] **8. Our sister is little, and she has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed?**

The Bridegroom has commended the Bride, reminded her that she has been redeemed by him from death, and taught her to retain this memorial in her heart; he has also taught her that love conquers all things. She receives all these things gratefully, and now, reminded of love, adds a question, saying: “Our sister is little, and she has no breasts.” The Apostle’s saying comes to her mind: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel shall be saved” (Rom. 11:25–26). Thus she remembers this synagogue, which at present walks in darkness, denies Christ, and blasphemes the things said and believed concerning him.

Knowing that the holy Apostle foretold that it would be converted at the end, and that Elijah and Enoch have been reserved by Christ to convert them, she calls it sister because of its future conversion and says with love: “Our sister is little, and she has no breasts”: little in faith, very small in hope, and now possessing no love at all. She has no breasts: she contains in herself no supports of teaching; she denies and suppresses the things done for her sake. Therefore, knowing that she will come to faith at the end, she asks the Bridegroom: “What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed?” What shall we say? How shall we admonish her? What words of salvation shall we give her? To these questions the Bridegroom answers:

[Col. 1301C] **9. If she is a wall, let us build upon it silver battlements; if she is a door, let us fasten it with cedar boards.**

Among those who are to be converted, some are like a wall: they possess great learning and knowledge of letters, and, precisely because they are walls, hardness against those assailing them. To these the Bridegroom says that silver battlements are to be built upon them—that is, that they are to be given testimonies of the divine Scriptures and authorities by which we are fortified. Let them be granted those insignia by which, now fortified, they may become defenders and protectors of the true Church.

“But if she is a door, let us fasten it with cedar boards.” Those are doors through whom some enter and others depart. They are lesser in learning [Col. 1301D] and less instructed in Scripture; to them the highest and difficult matters of understanding should not be proposed, but cedar boards should be fastened—that is, easy Scriptures should be set before them. Such is the tablet drawn by the Lord when he said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth. Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5:3 ff.). This tablet is cedar: incorruptible, setting forth undefiled, true, and unbreakable statements. So too other tablets like these, which, set before them, can aid and strengthen them in the truth they have received. It follows:

[Col. 1302A] **10. I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower; since then I have become before him as one finding peace.**

Having heard the Beloved’s answer, by which he instructs the Bride to offer silver battlements also to the converted synagogue and to send suitable champions for the Church’s defense, she says joyfully: “I am a wall”; I too shall set myself against the blows. And my breasts—that is, the prelates of the churches, whom I call my breasts because I nourish them with my milk—will be with me a firm and impregnable defense of the Church, and with me an unassailable attainment of eternal life. For, when my sister who had perished has been restored to me, “I have become before him as one finding peace.” For then peace will truly have been found, when none of those foreknown for life is still lacking, [Col. 1302B] but the Church, now containing all her own within herself, enjoys the highest prosperity. It follows:

**11. A vineyard belonged to the Peaceful One in her who has peoples; he entrusted it to keepers.**

Now that the praise of this song is complete, and the fullness of this Bride complete, when the synagogue, which she calls her sister, has been converted to the faith and the fullness of the Gentiles has entered the faith, the Bride speaks wholly concerning herself, saying: “A vineyard belonged to the Peaceful One.” I, with the fullness of the Gentiles now called and the synagogue now converted to faith, have become a vineyard for the Peaceful One—that is, our Lord Jesus Christ, who made peace between all things on earth and in heaven—“in her who has peoples,” that is, among the multitude of the Gentiles. It was all created by God, but not all predestined to life, for “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16). But together with the multitude of all the chosen, Jews and Gentiles, I have been a vineyard for the Peaceful One, producing choice fruits for him, worthy to be received by him and presented to God the Father.

This vineyard, he says, the Peaceful One entrusted to keepers. For the portion of the Church that existed from Adam to Christ was committed to the keeping of patriarchs, prophets, and teachers of the holy Law. But that portion which is to exist from Christ to the end of the age was granted to be instructed by the holy apostles, martyrs, and others distinguished in honor. It follows:

[Col. 1302D] **A man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit. 12. My vineyard is before me. A thousand are yours, O Peaceful One, and two hundred for those who keep its fruit.**

The Peaceful One cultivated, planted, pruned, and brought this vineyard to flower and fruit. It did not turn to bitterness or produce wild grapes, but elegant grapes, altogether worthy to be presented to God the Father. Thus it is said: “A man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit.” Who is this man? That good man of whom David speaks, saying: “The man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence; but his delight is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night” (Ps. 1:1–2). He alone, most worthy to be called a man, receives the fruits of the Church [Col. 1303A] and offers them to God the Father. From him, in order to reward the Church, he receives a thousand silver pieces, which he brings so that the Church may be enriched and rejoice that it has borne fruit well.

By the thousand silver pieces he signifies eternal life and its infinite blessedness, by which the Lord will reward his own when he presents them to the Father and places them in heavenly seats. He indicates that this blessedness is comprehended by the number one thousand, which is the fourth unity: the first unity is unity itself; the second, ten; the third, a hundred; the fourth, a thousand. After this the number extends to infinity, always having a thousand as its root and unit. Thus infinity is rightly shown by this number, and the excellence of blessedness by silver. For it is said of this: “The words [Col. 1303B] of the Lord are chaste words: silver tested by fire, proved in the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. 11:7). For the words that proclaim the Lord contain chastity in themselves, admitting no heresy and no impurity whatever. They are like silver tested by the fire of the Holy Spirit: nothing rings more sweetly in speech, nothing is more savory to the soul, nothing is proved more fully in the earth, and nothing is found more purified by the fire of the sevenfold Spirit.

Concerning this, he receives this answer from the Father: “My vineyard is before me,” that is, this whole multitude of the elect is pleasing to me and is with me in every thought and work—the multitude which you signify to me by the Peaceful One’s thousand and by the two hundred who keep its fruit. These indeed are those perfect persons who, from Adam to Christ, instructed this whole body by words, guarded it by examples, and adorned it by merits. The remaining hundred are those who presided over that chosen multitude from Christ to the end of the age. They are presented to God the Father and are crowned in eternal blessedness together with those over whom they presided. It follows:

**13. You who dwell in the gardens, friends are listening; make me hear your voice.**

This is the Bridegroom’s final admonition, by which he reminds the Bride of her praise, saying: “You who dwell in the gardens, make me hear your voice.” Since she now holds primacy in Judea, retains it now converted to faith, instructs it with the precepts of life, [Col. 1303D] fully possesses the multitude of the Gentiles as well, and plainly abides in the gardens of virtues, containing within herself all virtues that breathe sweet fragrance to the Lord, she is rightly said to dwell in the gardens of the churches. By heavenly admonitions she is called upon to offer praise to the Lord, when it is said: You who dwell in the gardens of the churches, [Col. 1304A] make me hear your voice, so that my praise may resound from all the churches and rise from all with thanksgiving.

For “friends are listening”: the angels and all the angelic powers united with Christ from the beginning through the power of faithful friendship await and listen for the glory of my reward, which they already hope for in the glory of your praise. It follows:

**14. Flee, my Beloved, and become like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of spices.**

This is the Church’s final answer, by which the Bride replies to her Beloved, saying: “Flee, my Beloved.” The Bridegroom reminds her of praise and urges her to sound forth praise, not because he wishes her to begin songs of praise now, but when the resurrection awaited by all has come; [Col. 1304B] when the Bridegroom comes in a cloud; when the angel proclaims his coming in a clear voice, saying, “Behold, the Bridegroom comes; go out to meet him” (Matt. 25:6); when the mournful trumpet sounds for all to rise [Note: [Col. 1303D] F. adds: *resuscitandum*, “for raising up”]; when the Judge, surrounded by angels, sits on the throne of his majesty; when the world, no one excepted, comes before him; when he pronounces the dreadful sentence upon the reprobate and speaks to all his elect the sentence he will utter: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

Then the Church, with all the saints, will sound forth praise and thanksgiving such as has not been heard from the beginning of time, and all sharers in that praise will be blessed by the Lord forever. Since this has been shown beforehand to the Bride who loves him, she answers thus not in indignation but patiently bearing this delay: “Flee, my Beloved,” that is, withdraw yourself for the present from our sight, standing in this like a gazelle or a young stag—clean animals that keep themselves on mountain ridges away from human sight. To distinguish the mountains where this young stag dwells from other mountains, he adds, “of spices.” The mountains of spices are the holy companies of angels and the dwelling places of every heavenly power, from which breathe all fragrant graces that certainly please the Lord. The Lord pours out upon them the balm of life from himself, so that, anointed with it, they may live eternally. Desiring to share in this anointing, and always longing for it in the matters stated above, [Col. 1304D] the Church asked that the kiss of most holy sweetness be given her; and now, made certain by the sure promise of her Bridegroom that she will shortly receive it with all her fullness, she rests content.

[Col. 1305]

## GILBERT’S PREFACE TO HIS COLLECTION OF HOMILIES

*(D. Giles, Letters of Gilbert Foliot, epistle 329.)*
[Col. 1305A] You have, brother, what you asked for, what charity could no longer deny one who had been knocking for so long. For while I was within, withdrawing my senses from the things outside lest they perhaps be distracted by certain enticements, and peacefully cherishing them within the chamber of my mind, the door indeed shut, I suddenly noticed you knocking outside and asking for something.

You were asking that some bread from Holy Scripture be lent to you, so that you might fittingly set it before a friend who had come to you from the road—that is, before your mind, withdrawn from outward things—for his refreshment, with the grace of hospitality. If in this matter you were truly acting with the disposition of a supplicant, you ought rather to have considered what I might offer than to have prescribed terms for my generosity toward you. But now, without considering what my powers are, you have chosen according to your own judgment what you wished to be given to you.

For you requested that some discourse be expounded for your benefit, and in praise of the blessed apostles, on the passage sung at the Octaves of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul: “These are the two olive trees and the shining lampstands before the Lord.” You assigned the subject as you pleased and prescribed the form of the exposition. For you also included in your request that I should not compress your proposition, after the manner of schoolmen, into brevity, but that, as though wisdom had entered my house, in accordance with the saying, “A wise man extends himself in words” (Ecclus. 20), and, “The lips of the wise adorn knowledge” (Prov. 15), I should surround what you had proposed with authorities and, enlarging it in words and arguments, extend it not merely into an exposition but into a treatise.

In this, one might rightly rebuke the presumption of your mind, if charity did not excuse all things [Col. 1306A]. But I take it without doubt as a proof of love that you confidently disclose your desire to me. And let it be an indication of charity toward you that, although hunger for the word prevails in the land of my mind, I nevertheless do not fail to share with you the little bread that I have. Perhaps it would have been better for me to obtain peace by silence than, by writing something, to submit myself to the judgment of many. But show yourself a monk toward me, and by prayer remove the danger into which the urgency of your long-continued request has drawn me.

### Homily 1

“These are the two olive trees and lampstands,” etc.

### Homily 2

After the vine of paradise, the olive tree next presents itself for consideration [Col. 1306B], etc.

### Homily 3

That the olive tree planted in paradise is the wisdom of God, etc.

### Homily 4

In the paradise of God nothing at all is beautiful or, etc.

### Homily 5

“These are the two olive trees and lampstands,” etc.

### Homily 6

It follows: “shining before the Lord,” etc.

### Homily 7

It follows: “before the Lord certain things shine,” etc.

### Homily 8

“They have power to close heaven with clouds,” etc.

### Homily 9

There are two keys of heaven, which, so that they may be for us, etc.

## In the Year of the Lord 1186, Robert of Torigni, Abbot of St Michael in Peril of the Sea

[Col. 1305]

## Notice

(D. Ludwig Conrad Bethmann, *Prolegomena to Sigebert*. See *Patrology*, vol. 160, at the beginning.)
