Robert, a Norman by birth from the village of Torigni, professed the Rule of St Benedict at Bec in 1128; in 1149 he was elected prior there; on 27 May 1154 he was summoned to the abbacy of Mont-Saint-Michel in Peril of the Sea, which he administered with the highest distinction until his death on 25 May 1186. A man outstanding for nobility of birth [Col. 1307], as active in public affairs as in letters, and highly esteemed by the king and queen [Note: [Col. 1307] So much so that he held their daughter Eleanor at the font in 1161 and was granted the custody of Pontorson in 1162. Earlier, King Henry II himself had come to him at the Mount in 1156, and again two years later with Louis VII. Pope Alexander likewise summoned him to Tours for the council of 1163; after it ended Robert travelled to Rome and, on returning thence, visited England.—For Robert’s life, see himself throughout the *Chronicle*, from 1154 onward; Labbé, *Bibliotheca manuscripta*, I, 348; *Gallia Christiana*, XI, 520; from which drew *Histoire littéraire*, XIV, 363; Bouquet, XIII, preface, 30; Hirsch, p. 387. Almost everything that Fabricius says is false.], he was a most diligent seeker and collector of books [Note: [Col. 1308] As Henry of Huntingdon calls him. Among other things, he was the first to bring Pliny into Normandy], and the foremost Norman of his age in the renown of learning.

He both urged others to write history and cultivated it himself in writings, among which the first place belongs to the *Chronicle* added to Sigebert. For, wishing especially to recount the history of his own country, he joined it to universal history in the medieval manner: borrowing a manuscript from the bishop of Beauvais, he copied Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper from it without alteration; he changed and omitted nothing in Sigebert, but inserted the archbishops of Rouen and the history of the English and Normans, drawing everything from the Annals of Rouen, Bec, and Mont-Saint-Michel, from William of Poitiers, William of Jumièges, and Henry of Huntingdon.

These are Robert’s writings: *The History of Henry I*, or the eighth book of William of Jumièges, between 1135 and 1150.—*Continuation of Sigebert*, begun in 1150.—Letter to Gervase, between 1150 and 1154, published by d’Achery after Guibert’s works, p. 715.—*On the Change in the Order of Monks in Normandy*, 1154, in d’Achery, p. 811.—The Annals of Mont-Saint-Michel from 1154 to 1159, inserted in his own hand into the monastery cartulary, now in the public library at Avranches, no. 80.—Prologue to Augustine’s *Flowers*, in d’Achery, p. 716.—Prologue to Pliny, corrected by Robert himself; this book, sent to Saint-Germain two centuries ago, is now presumably in the Royal Library at Paris.—Letter to the abbot of Bec, 1182, in Bouquet, XVIII, 333.—What is attributed to him besides these lacks supporting testimony. The catalogue of abbots compiled in 1643, in d’Achery’s works of Lanfranc, p. 351, says that Robert produced 154 volumes and that the *History of St Michael* reports that they decayed beneath the ruins and rainwater of a tower. There is evidently an error in this: those 154 books were not written by him, but collected by him.

[Col. 1307]

## Robert of Torigni’s Book on the Deeds of Henry I, King of England

(It is the eighth book of William of Jumièges’ *History*. See *Patrology*, vol. 149, col. 879.)

[Col. 1307]

## Robert of Torigni’s Continuation of Sigebert

(See *Patrology*, vol. 160, col. 423.)

[Col. 1307]

## Robert’s Letter to Gervase, Prior of Saint-Cénery

(*Works of Guibert of Nogent*, p. 713.)

[Col. 1307A] To his dearest brother in Christ, GERVASE, prior of Saint-Cénery, brother ROBERT, least of the monks of Bec: greeting and service.

Since I hear that you have been freed from secular business and are occupied in religious leisure, I beg your affection to undertake an account of those things that occurred in the province of Normandy after the death of Henry, the most noble king of the English and duke of the Normans [Col. 1308A], down to the death of Geoffrey, the illustrious duke of the Normans and count of the Angevins. For this will contribute to the increase of your reputation, make me pleasing to you and indebted to you for recompense, and, what is greater than all these things, may perhaps acquire in no small measure the favour of the new duke. But if you put your hand to this work, I wish you to carry it out in the following order.

[Col. 1309A] First of all, briefly and as though by recapitulation, enumerate the names, genealogies, successions, and the number of years during which each of all the counts of Anjou—from Ingelger to Geoffrey himself—held the county; also the distinguished deeds worthy of annalistic remembrance which each performed, whether in spiritual or secular matters; and under which king of the Franks the Angevins first had Ingelger as count. When you come to Fulk, Geoffrey’s father, since his wife was the daughter of Elias, count of Maine, I wish you, for this reason, to make an epitome of all the counts of Maine just as you have made one of all the counts of Anjou; and to observe in their case everything which I have set out above as requiring observation in the latter.

I would more gladly accomplish all this myself somehow or other [Col. 1310A], if leisure, resources, and an abundance of chronicles pertaining to those two counties were supplied to me as fully as to you.

And since among us there are separate books concerning each of the dukes of Normandy from Rollo down to Henry, the most noble king of the English and duke of the Normans, I judged it fitting to add, by briefly describing his deeds, an account of that man to the histories of the preceding dukes, lest the greatness of one who greatly benefited many by his actions in his lifetime, and will benefit them by his example after death if they deign to imitate him, should be buried in silence. Because of the continuity of time, I wish the work which I ask from you to be joined to this, so that we may transmit by writing to the knowledge of those to come what was done in our own times in our province. Farewell.

[Col. 1309]

## The Same Author’s Letter to Roger, Abbot of Bec

(See *Patrology*, vol. 160, col. 34, note 132.)

[Col. 1309]

## Robert of Torigni’s Treatise on the Change in the Order of Monks

(*Works of Guibert of Nogent*, p. 811.)

### Chapter I. On the Origin of the Cistercians

[Col. 1309B]

1. I wish at present to show how, and by whom, the ancient custom of monks’ food and clothing was changed.

In Burgundy there is a place called Molesme [Note: [Col. 1309C] Molesme.]. There, in the time of Philip, king of the Franks, Abbot Robert founded a monastery and gathered disciples of great religious devotion. After some years, having investigated the Rule of St Benedict according to the letter, he wished to persuade his disciples to live by the labour of their hands, to leave tithes and offerings to the clerics serving the diocese, and to abstain from breeches, woollen undershirts, and furs. But they, on the contrary, clinging to the customs observed in the monasteries of the western world—customs known to have been instituted by St Maurus [Col. 1309C], disciple of St Benedict, and by St Columbanus, and, to come to more recent times, by St Odo, abbot of Cluny—said that they would not depart from them.

[Col. 1310B] Hearing this, Robert persisted in his opinion and withdrew from them with twenty-one who agreed with him. For a long time he sought a suitable place for himself and his companions, who had resolved to observe the Rule of St Benedict completely according to the letter, as the Jews observe the Law of Moses.

2. At last Odo, son of Henry, duke of Burgundy, took pity on them and granted them an estate at a place called Cîteaux [Note: [Col. 1310C] Cîteaux.], in the diocese of Chalon. There Abbot Robert lived for some time with the chosen brethren and, by God’s gift, soon deserved to have very many emulators both of the strict religious life which he had embraced in that wilderness and of his own holiness.

When the monks of Molesme had for some time lacked a shepherd [Col. 1310C], and, because the man of God renowned for virtues had left them, had become more contemptible in the eyes of neighbours and acquaintances, they humbly approached Pope Urban. Having set before him in full detail the sequence of events which I have recounted above, they sought counsel [Col. 1311A] and assistance from him. With paternal affection he provided for both parties. By apostolic authority he commanded the abbot to return to his former monastery and govern it, lest regular observance should fail; and in the other monastery, which he had subsequently begun, to appoint any suitable one of his own brethren in his place.

Accordingly, when Abbot Robert returned to the monastery of Molesme by Pope Urban’s command, Alberic became the first abbot of Cîteaux after him; Stephen the Englishman succeeded Alberic. Both were men of great religious devotion.

During Stephen’s life and by his command, Guy was elected abbot of Trois-Fontaines; after governing that monastery for two years, he eventually abandoned it, foolishly enough. Then Renaud, son of Milo, count of Bar-sur-Seine, succeeded him. After Renaud’s death, in the year from the Incarnation 1151, Gotswin—formerly abbot of a monastery in the province of Vienne, a Lotharingian by birth—became the fifth abbot of Cîteaux, excluding Robert, abbot of Molesme, who had begun that order but, as stated above, had been compelled by the complaint of the monks of Molesme and Pope Urban’s command to return to his former monastery.

It is now almost fifty-five years since Abbot Robert, as has been said, inhabited Cîteaux; and such a multitude of men flocked there that nearly five hundred abbeys arose from it, from the year 1098 of the Lord’s Incarnation to the year 1152 of that same divine Incarnation. For this reason [Col. 1311C], at the general chapter, where every year in the middle of September the abbots, and even bishops chosen from that order, assemble at Cîteaux, the negligences which cannot altogether be avoided in so many and such great communities are corrected. For this reason, I say, because the abbeys of the same order were multiplying so greatly, it was decreed that they should establish no more new abbeys in desert and wooded places.

They founded monasteries by their own labour and, with diligent foresight, gave them sacred names: House of God, Clairvaux, Alms, Court of God, and many other such names, by whose sweetness of name hearers are invited to hasten to experience how great the blessedness is there which is denoted by so distinctive a title. Many nobles and wealthy people, and subtle sophists, flocked to them because of the novelty of their distinctiveness [Col. 1311D], and voluntarily embraced an unfamiliar strictness.

### Chapter II. On the Origin of the Carthusians

At almost the same time as the Cistercian order arose in the diocese of Chalon, the Carthusian order was also devised in the diocese of Grenoble. This kind of hermit lives under a prior; their community does not exceed the number thirteen. Each, on ordinary days, is separated from the others in his own cell, where he prays, sleeps, and eats; yet the cells are adjoining and joined together in one place. On feast days they gather in church and at table and confer with one another on spiritual matters [Col. 1312A]. They perform the ordinances of both the night and day offices according to the Rule of St Benedict.

### Chapter III. The Monastery of Chezal-Benoît

Some time after the Cistercian order had begun, Andrew, an Italian by birth from the Valley of the Bruttians, flourished as a monk and built in the district of Bourges the monastery called Chezal-Benoît [Note: [Col. 1311D] Chezal-Benoît.].

### Chapter IV. The Monastery of Fontevraud

[Note: [Col. 1311D] Fontevraud.]

At the same time there were three companions in religious life: Bernard, formerly abbot of Quincy in the region of Poitou; Robert of Arbrissel; and Vitalis the hermit, formerly chaplain to the count of Mortain. Each built a separate monastery.

[Col. 1312B] Bernard, unwilling that the monastery of Quincy, hitherto free, should be subjected to the monks of Cluny, was induced, when Pope Paschal brought pressure upon him in this matter, by the venerable Ivo, bishop of Chartres, and Rotrou, count of Mortain, to leave it. In a wooded place called Tiron he built a monastery in honour of the holy Saviour. He received all who came to him and directed them to practise within the monastery the lawful crafts that they knew. William of Poitiers, a learned man and exceedingly devout, succeeded him.

Robert of Arbrissel, a man fitted to gain souls and preach the word of God, built the monastery called Fontevraud on the border of Anjou [Col. 1312C] and Poitou. Gathering religious women there, he set Petronilla over them as abbess; upon her death Matilda, sister of the count of Anjou, succeeded to the governance of the same monastery.

Vitalis the hermit, a most excellent sower of the word, built a monastery at Savigny [Note: [Col. 1312D] Savigny.], on the border of Normandy and Lesser Brittany, and imposed upon his monks observances in some respects similar to the more recent Cistercian institutions. Geoffrey of Bayeux, a monk of Cerisy, a man exceedingly learned and fervent in religious life, succeeded him. He built many monasteries and imposed stricter customs upon the Savigniac monks than their former ones.

After Evand the Englishman, who presided over the same monastery for a short time [Col. 1312D], there succeeded the venerable Serlo of Valbadon near Bayeux. He had been Geoffrey’s disciple in the world and had first taken monastic vows with him at Cerisy; but, leaving that monastery in pursuit of a more exact religious life, he had sought Savigny. Because the monasteries subject to him did not obey him as he wished, by the authority of Pope Eugenius of Rome he subjected himself and all his monasteries to the Cistercian order. A few years later, in order that he might devote himself more freely to God, he relinquished responsibility for the monasteries and hid himself away at Clairvaux, occupied with God and with himself. Richard of Courcy, prior of the same place, succeeded him in the governance of Savigny.

### Chapter V. On the Monastery of Saint-Victor at Paris

[Col. 1313A]

At the same time Master William of Champeaux, formerly archdeacon of Paris, a man exceedingly learned and devout, assumed the habit of a regular canon along with some of his disciples. Outside the city of Paris, at a place where there was a chapel of St Victor the martyr, he began to build a monastery for clerics. When he was raised from there to the bishopric of Châlons, his venerable disciple Gilduin became the first abbot there. Under his government many noble clerics, educated in secular and sacred letters, assembled to live in that place; among them Master Hugh of Lotharingia flourished especially in literary learning and humble religious devotion. He published many books [Col. 1313B], which need not be enumerated because they are widely known.

### Chapter VI. On the Regular Canons of Arrouaise and Prémontré

At the same time new regular canons were gathered at Tronc-Bérenger and at Prémontré. They lived by the labour of their hands, wearing woollen garments, rough and inexpensive ones.

### Chapter VII. On the Reform of Certain Monasteries

Thus, seeing that monks of the new orders—the Cistercians and Carthusians, as well as the canons mentioned above [Col. 1313C]—lived their lives in strict religious discipline, the abbots of very famous monasteries built upon their estates by kings of the Franks and other men of consular rank and powerful men, but excessively lax because of abundant wealth, were covered with shame. Either voluntarily or unwillingly, compelled by kings and bishops, they summoned to themselves monks from the most orderly monasteries—Cluny, Marmoutier, Bec, and others striving equally to live in religious discipline—and endeavoured to shape the lives of their subjects after their example.

Very many abbots from monasteries which appeared to excel others in religious discipline were also appointed to govern less devout abbeys.

### Chapter VIII. On the Restoration and Foundation of the Ancient Monasteries of Normandy

Since we have said something about newly founded monasteries, it is pleasing to recall at least briefly some of the pious works of the dukes of Normandy in building or rebuilding monasteries [Col. 1313D]. Rollo, therefore, also called Robert, being overtaken by the shortness of time after baptism, neither founded nor restored any monastery; but, as we have already said above, he bestowed many possessions upon several churches and monasteries.

### Chapter IX. On the Monastery of Jumièges

[Note: [Col. 1313D] Jumièges.]

William Longsword, his son, restored the monastery of Jumièges, which St Philibert had built but the pagan Hasting had destroyed. From St Philibert down to [Col. 1314A] the destruction of that monastery there had been twenty abbots. From its restoration under Abbot Martin—whom Countess Gerloc of Poitiers sent with twelve monks from the monastery of St Cyprian at Poitiers to William, duke of Normandy, her brother—to the year 1154 of the Lord’s Incarnation, when we made this Catalogue of Norman Abbeys, there had been fourteen abbots, the last of whom was Eustace, monk of that place.

### Chapter X. On the Monasteries of Fécamp, Saint-Ouen, and Saint Michael on Mont-Tombe

[Note: [Col. 1313D] Fécamp, Saint-Ouen, and Mont-Saint-Michel.]

Richard I, son of Duke William, restored three monasteries by restoring to them many possessions that had been taken away by pagans: one at Fécamp, in honour of the most holy Trinity; another on Mont-Tombe, in honour of St Michael; and a third at Rouen, in veneration of [Col. 1314B] St Peter and St Ouen. Yet Richard, his son, completed the work by adding very many estates and establishing monastic order in them.

The first abbot over the monastery of Fécamp was William, a monk of Cluny. Under his government he had the monasteries of St Benignus at Dijon, Holy Trinity at Fécamp, St Germanus at Paris, St Faron at Meaux, St Michael on Mont-Tombe, and nearly thirty other monasteries. The second abbot of Fécamp was John the Lombard; the third, William, monk of St Stephen at Caen; the fourth, Roger, monk of the same place; the fifth, Henry, a monk of Cluny.

[Col. 1314C] There have now been nearly fourteen abbots at the monastery of St Michael, ten of whom came from other monasteries.

Hildebert was made the first abbot of the monastery of Saint-Ouen after its restoration; Herfast was second; Nicholas, son of Richard III, duke of the Normans, third; Hisgot, prior of Caen, fourth—he reformed the order; William and Reinfrid, monks of the same place, fifth and sixth; Freher, a monk of Cluny, seventh.

### Chapter XI. On the Monastery of Saint-Wandrille, Otherwise Called Fontenelle

[Note: [Col. 1314D] Saint-Wandrille.]

Richard II, duke of Normandy, rebuilt in its entirety the abbey of St Wandrille, anciently called Fontenelle [Col. 1314D]. From St Wandrille to Mainard, who in the time of Richard I had begun, to the extent of his power, to restore the same place, there had been twenty-four abbots; from Mainard to the present time, twelve, the last of whom was Roger, a monk of that place, who is still living.

### Chapter XII. The Monastery of Bernay

[Note: [Col. 1314D] Bernay.]

Countess Judith, wife of Richard II, founded the monastery of Bernay. Its custodians were Ralph, abbot of St Michael, and after him Theodoric [Col. 1315A] of Jumièges. The former gave Ouche and Beaumontel to Humphrey of Vieilles; the latter gave half the borough of Bernay to the father of Roger of Montgomery, his kinsman, that he might maintain himself from it whenever he came to Bernay.

The first abbot there was Vitalis, a monk of Fécamp. After William, king of the English, later gave him the abbey of St Peter at Westminster, his brother Osbern, a monk of Tiron, became the second head of the monastery of Bernay; Nicholas, monk of Fécamp, was third; Richard, monk of the same place, fourth.

### Chapter XIII. The Monasteries of Saint-Taurin and Villiers

[Note: [Col. 1315D] Saint-Taurin and Villiers.]

The aforesaid Richard II, duke of Normandy, partly restored the monastery of St Taurin at Évreux [Col. 1315B]. In our times its abbots were Ralph, William, Paul, and Philip, monks of Fécamp.

Likewise, the monastery of Villiers, which St Philibert had once built, was repaired for the use of religious women by Judith, wife of the aforesaid prince.

### Chapter XIV. On the Monastery of Bec

[Note: [Col. 1315D] Le Bec.]

The venerable Herluin built the monastery of Bec on his own land and was its first head. He was succeeded by Anselm, William, Boso, Theobald, Letard, and Roger, monks of the same monastery.

### Chapter XV. The Monastery of Cerisy

[Note: [Col. 1315D] Cerisy.]

Robert, duke of the Normans, son of Richard II, built the monastery of Cerisy [Col. 1315C]. The first abbot there was Durand, monk of Saint-Ouen; the second, Almod, former abbot of Mont-Saint-Michel; the third, Garin, monk of St Michael; the fourth, Hugh, monk of Toarn; the fifth, Hugh, monk of the same place.

### Chapter XVI. The Two Monasteries at Caen

[Note: [Col. 1315D] Saint-Étienne and the Trinity of Caen.]

Duke William, son of the aforesaid Robert, built two monasteries at Caen, one for men and the other for women. The first abbot of the monastery of monks was Lanfranc, prior of Bec; the second William; the third Gilbert; the fourth Robert; the fifth Eudo; the sixth Alan; the seventh Peter, all monks of the same place.

### Chapter XVII. On the Monastery of Ouche, or Saint-Évroult

[Note: [Col. 1316D] Saint-Évroult.]

[Col. 1315D]

William, son of Herou, a monk of Bec, and his nephews Robert and Hugh of Grandmesnil, restored the monastery of St Évroult at Ouche. But because this same William, when he had taken the monastic habit at Bec, had given the same place to the monastery of Bec, Lanfranc—who later became abbot of Caen—was sent there with three monks to live. Therefore he gave the village of Rousserie to the church of Bec in exchange [Col. 1316A] for the church of St Évroult.

The first abbot of this monastery was Theodoric of Jumièges; the second, Robert, prior of the same place; the third, Osbern, monk of Holy Trinity at Rouen; the fourth, Manerius; the fifth, Roger; the sixth, Garin; the seventh, Richard; the eighth, Ranulf [lacuna]; the eleventh, Bernard, monks of the same place.

### Chapter XVIII. The Monasteries of Holy Trinity, or Saint Catherine, and Saint Amand at Rouen

Goscelin, viscount of Arques, godfather of Geoffrey, father of Matilda, wife of William the chamberlain, founded the monastery of Holy Trinity on the hill at Rouen; and he established the monastery of St Amand within the walls of the same city for the use of religious women. The first head of the monastery of Holy Trinity on the Hill was Isembert the German [Col. 1316B], a devout man and monk of Saint-Ouen; the second, Rainer; the third, Walter; the fourth, Elias; the fifth, Walter, monks of the same place.

### Chapter XIX. On the Monastery of Saint-Leufroy

[Note: [Col. 1316D] La Croix-Saint-Leufroy.]

At the same time, namely under Duke William, the monastery of Holy Cross and St Leufroy was restored from land which had belonged to Helton of La Croix. The first abbot of this monastery after its restoration was Alberic; the second, Henry; the third, William, monks of Saint-Ouen; the fourth and fifth, Garnerius and Roderic, monks of the same place.

### Chapter XX. On the Monastery of Conches

[Note: [Col. 1316D] Conches.]

Roger of Tosny built the monastery of Châtillon [Col. 1316C]. Its first and second abbots were Giles and William, monks of Fécamp; the third and fourth, William and Lotard, monks of Blois; the fifth, Gilbert, monk of Bec; the sixth and seventh, Simplicius and Vincent, monks of La Colombe; the eighth, Bernerius, monk of the same place; the ninth, again the aforesaid Vincent; the tenth, Silvester, monk of Lyre.

### Chapter XXI. The Monastery of Lyre and That of Cormeilles

[Note: [Col. 1316D] Lyre and Cormeilles.]

William, son of Osbern, seneschal of Normandy and kinsman of Duke William, built two monasteries in honour of Mary, blessed Mother of God: one at Lyre, where he subsequently buried his wife Aelisa, daughter of Roger of Tosny; the other [Col. 1316D] at Cormeilles, where he himself was buried after death.

The first abbot of Lyre was Robert, monk of the same place; the second, Erfast; the third, Barno; the fourth, Ernald; the fifth, Hildebert; the sixth, Gilbert, monks of St Évroult; the seventh, William, monk of the same place; the eighth, Ralph, monk of Bec—he restored the order; the ninth, Hilderic, monk of St Évroult; the tenth, William, monk of the same place.

The first head of Cormeilles was Robert, monk of Holy Trinity at Rouen [Col. 1317A], who perished in a shipwreck; Geoffrey, monk of the same place, succeeded him; then William of Bec; then Benedict, monk of the same place.

### Chapter XXII. The Monasteries of Préaux and Saint-Vigor of Bayeux

[Note: [Col. 1317D] Préaux and Saint-Vigor.]

Humphrey of Vieilles built two monasteries at Préaux, one for monks and the other for religious women.

The first abbot of the monks was Aufrid, monk of Saint-Wandrille; Geoffrey, monk of the same place, succeeded him; then Richard of Dammartin, a devout and very learned man, who had been a monk of Saint-Vigor at Bayeux under Robert of Tombelaine, the first and last abbot of that place [Col. 1317B]. Richard was succeeded by another Richard; then by Renaud, monk of the same place; then by Michael, monk of Bec.

### Chapter XXIII. The Monastery of Sées and That of Toarn

[Note: [Col. 1317D] Sées and Tiron.]

Roger of Montgomery, son of Roger, viscount of the Hiémois, built two monasteries in honour of St Martin, one in the suburb of the city of Sées, the other in his own village of Toarn on the Dives.

The first head of the monastery of Sées was Robert, monk of St Martin at Toarn; the second, Ralph, monk of the same place; he was succeeded by Hugh, and Hugh by Gilbert. Likewise Gilbert and John, monks of the same place.

But the first head of the monastery of Tiron was Durand [Col. 1317C], monk of Fécamp; Arnulf, prior of Fécamp, succeeded him; then Andrew, monk of the same place; then Richard, monk of Cluny; then Gilbert, monk of that place itself.

### Chapter XXIII bis. The Monastery of Almeniscariae, or Almonachae

[Note: [Col. 1317D] Almenêches.]

The aforesaid Count Roger also founded—or rather restored—the monastery of women at Almenêches, where St Opportuna had formerly been abbess, before the Normans came into the kingdom of the Franks.

### Chapter XXIV. On the Monasteries of Saint Peter, or Saint Mary of the Dives, and Saint Peter of Lisieux

[Note: [Col. 1317D] Saint-Pierre-sur-Dives and Saint-Pierre de Lisieux.]

Lesceline, countess of Eu, widow of Count William, who had been the natural brother of Richard II [Col. 1317D], duke of the Normans, assisted by her sons Robert, count of Eu, and Hugh, bishop of Lisieux, courageously built the men’s monastery of St Peter on the Dives and the women’s monastery before the city of Lisieux.

The first abbot of the monastery of St Mary of the Dives was Ainard, monk of Holy Trinity on the hill at Rouen; Fulk of St Évroult succeeded him; Benedict, prior of Saint-Ouen, succeeded Fulk; Walter, monk of Jumièges, was fourth [Col. 1318A]; Robert, monk of St Denis, fifth; Ralph, Richard, and Haimo, monks of the same place, sixth, seventh, and eighth; Warin, monk of Cluny, ninth.

### Chapter XXV. The Monastery of Le Tréport

[Note: [Col. 1318D] Le Tréport.]

Robert, count of Eu, son of the aforesaid Lesceline, built the monastery of St Michael of Le Tréport. Its first abbot was Herberius, monk of Holy Trinity on the hill at Rouen; the second, Alvered; the third, Osbern, monk of the same place; the fourth, Fulcher, monk of Cluny.

### Chapter XXVI. On Saint-Victor in Caux and Saint-Sauveur at Évreux

[Note: [Col. 1318D] Saint-Victor-en-Caux and Saint-Sauveur d’Évreux.]

Roger of Mortemer, son of Walter of [Col. 1318B] Saint-Martin and brother of the first William de Warenne, founded the monastery of St Victor on his own land. Its abbots were Richard, Robert, Mainard, and Hugh, monks of Saint-Ouen.

Richard, count of Évreux, built in the same city the monastery of St Saviour for the use of religious women.

### Chapter XXVII. The Monastery of Grestain

[Note: [Col. 1318D] Grestain.]

Herluin of Conteville founded the monastery of St Mary at Grestain; there he and his wife Helena rest in body. Their sons were Robert, count of Mortain, who enlarged that same monastery, and Odo, bishop of Bayeux. The first abbot of this monastery was Geoffrey, monk of St Sergius at Angers [Col. 1318C]; the second, Fulcher, monk of Sées; the third, Herbert, monk of the same place. At the beginning they received customs and monks partly from Saint-Wandrille and partly from Préaux.

### Chapter XXVIII. The Monastery of Saint-Sever in the Diocese of Coutances

Hugh, viscount of Avranches and later count of Chester, founded the abbey of St Sever in the diocese of Coutances. Its first abbot was Anselm, monk of Jumièges; the second, Arnulf of Évreux; the third, Peter, monk of St Benedict at Fleury; the fourth, Robert, monk of the same place; the fifth, Guy of Chester.

### Chapter XXIX. Holy Trinity of Lessay

[Note: [Col. 1318D] Lessay.]

Eudo with Capella founded the monastery of Holy Trinity at Lessay [Col. 1318D]. Its first abbot was Roger, monk of Bec; the second and third, Geoffrey and Garin, monks of the same place; the fourth, Robert, monk of Caen; the fifth and sixth, Ralph and Roger, monks of the same place.

### Chapter XXX. Saint-Sauveur of Coutances

Nigel, viscount of Coutances, built the monastery of Saint-Sauveur. Its first abbot was Benignus, monk of Fécamp; the second, Hamelin [Col. 1319A]; the third, Anfrid; the fourth, William; the fifth, Hugh, monk of Mont-Saint-Michel.

### Chapter XXXI. The Monastery of Fontenay
The monastery of Saint Stephen of Fontenay was founded by the first Ralph Taison, who was the grandfather of the third Ralph, that is, the father of Jordan Taison, aided by his brother Herneis. The first abbot appointed there was Geoffrey, a monk of Saint-Wandrille; the second, Hugh, a monk of Tournai; the third, Herbert, a monk of Caen; the fourth, William, a monk of the same place; the fifth, Robert, a monk of Caen.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the monastery of Montebourg.  
[Note: [Col. 1319B] Montebourg.]

The monastery of Montebourg was built by Roger, a monk of Holy Cross, on the demesne of the duke of Normandy. [Col. 1319B] Its first abbot was the same Roger, a religious man and companion of Wymond, who later became bishop of Aversa. To this Roger the aforesaid Wymond addressed a book *On the Body of the Lord*. The second abbot was Ursus, subprior of Jumièges; by rule and buildings he ennobled the same place. The third was Peter, the fourth Walter, monks of the same house.

King Henry of England gave this abbey to Richard [Col. 1320A] de Reviers, to guard and enlarge it as his own; and Richard took care to do so.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. The monastery of Ivry.  
[Note: [Col. 1319B] Yury.]

Roger of Ivry founded the monastery of Ivry. Its first abbot was Peter, monk of Coulombs; the second Durand, monk of Bec; the third Osbern, monk of Fécamp; the fourth Hubert, monk of Coulombs; the fifth Norman, monk of Bec; the sixth Hubert, monk of Saint Peter of Chartres. Yet none of them has thus far been able to find burial there.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the monastery of Lonlay.  
[Note: [Col. 1320B] Lonlay.]

The monastery of Saint Mary of Lonlay was built by the first William Talevas, who raised the castle of Lord Fronton upon the mountain after felling the forest. Although that place [Col. 1320B] lies in the diocese of Le Mans, it nevertheless belongs to the duchy of Normandy. Its first abbot was William, monk of Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire; the second Hugh, monk of that monastery itself; the third Garin, monk of Évron; the fourth Ranulf, monk of Caen; the fifth Lamfred, monk of the same monastery; the sixth John, monk of Saint-Laumer of Blois. After he was deposed, Bermo, monk of Saint-Martin of Tours, succeeded as the seventh.

[Col. 1319]

# ROBERT OF TORIGNY’S PROLOGUE TO THE ABRIDGMENT OF AUGUSTINE’S EXPOSITION OF THE APOSTLE’S EPISTLES

[Col. 1319C] There is a certain book of immense size, containing what Blessed Augustine expounded in his books or letters from passages taken from the Apostle. This work is called by some *Florus*, because it has been excerpted and, as it were, gathered as flowers from the various little works of blessed Augustine. Yet many doubt by whom that work was collected and arranged.

Some attribute it to the priest Bede, for this reason: at the end of his *History of the English*, when enumerating his own little works, he set down among others these exact words: “Whatever sayings in the Apostle I found in the little works of Saint Augustine, I took care to transcribe in order.” Hence some persons take the aforesaid words, together with certain other words connected with them in the same history, and place them as the prologue to the said collection of sayings of Saint Augustine, intending thereby [Col. 1319D] to prove that Bede was the author of this work.

I, however, agree more with Cassiodorus, senator and monk, a man most learned in every respect. By the antiquity of his time—indeed, not to mention his manifold knowledge of affairs—as consul and *apocrisiarius* (envoy) of Theodoric, king of the Goths, he must beyond doubt be considered earlier than Bede; especially since Bede’s own annotations on the Apostle, drawn from the books of Saint Augustine, are commonly available. That book is not in its entirety equal in size to half of the exposition on the Epistle to the Romans alone contained in this work.

Cassiodorus thus states in one of his books who arranged the aforesaid collection: “Peter, abbot of the province of Tripoli, is said to have annotated the Epistles of Saint Paul from chapters of the works of Blessed Augustine, so that through another’s mouth he might disclose the secret of his own heart. He fitted these passages so suitably to their respective places that I believe this work to have been perfected rather by the diligence of blessed Augustine. It is remarkable that he has so elucidated one writer by another that, without any admixture of his own added words, he seems to have fulfilled the desire [Col. 1320D] of his own heart. From this work we have made the following excerpts out of the greater part of the remaining books of Blessed Augustine, and have added to them flowers of sententiae.”

# APPENDIX TO ROBERT OF TORIGNY

[Col. 1321]

# CHRONICLE OF SAINT MICHAEL AT THE PERIL OF THE SEA: Containing much that concerns Lesser Brittany and the province of Anjou

(LABBE, *Nova Bibliotheca librorum mss.*, vol. I, p. 347.)

[Col. 1321A] In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 506 [Note: [Col. 1321C] I think that the year should be read as 494, or one of the nearby years.], the revelation of Blessed Michael took place on Mount Gargano, under the emperor Zeno (correct: Anastasius) and Pope Gelasius.

708. The revelation of Blessed Michael took place on Mount Tumba, under Childebert, king of the Franks, and Aubert, bishop of Avranches.

851. Hasting came into the kingdom of the Franks.

876. Rollo came into Normandy on 27 November.

917. Rollo died, and his son William succeeded him.

942. William, son of Rollo, was killed; his son Richard succeeded him. He was the first to place monks in the church of Saint Michael at the Peril of the Sea.

966. Namely, Mainard, the first abbot, who had been abbot of Saint-Wandrille for five years, [Col. 1321B] and another Mainard, his nephew, with other monks.

991 (perhaps 996). Richard I, duke of the Normans, died, and his son Richard II succeeded him. This Richard married Judith, sister of Geoffrey, count of Brittany, and by her begot two sons, Richard and Robert, who succeeded him. Geoffrey, count of Brittany, married Havoise, sister of the aforesaid Richard, and by her begot two sons, Alan and Eudes.

1009. By the counsel of Duke Richard, the second Mainard, now burdened with old age, chose as his successor Lord Hildebert, a monk of the same place.

1023. The new church of Blessed Michael was begun by Count Richard II and Hildebert, the second abbot. That abbot died in the same year, and Almodus succeeded him.

1026. Richard II, duke of the Normans, died; [Col. 1321C] his son Richard III succeeded him, who died in the same year, and his brother Robert succeeded him.

1033. Suppo was ordained abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael.

1035. Robert, duke of the Normans, died while returning from Jerusalem. His illegitimate son William, still a boy of seven, succeeded him.

[Col. 1322A] 1048. A battle was fought at Val-ès-Dunes by William, duke of the Normans, against his kinsman Count Guy. In the same year Suppo resigned the abbacy of the Mount, and Ralph, monk of Fécamp, succeeded him.

1053. A battle was fought at Mortemer. In the same year Ranulf, monk of the same place, succeeded Abbot Ralph.

1063. Le Mans was subdued by William, count of the Normans.

1066. William, duke of the Normans, crossed the sea, defeated Harold, and subdued the kingdom of England.

1087. William, king of England, died, and his sons succeeded him: William Rufus in England and Robert, the firstborn, as duke in Normandy.

1090. This Mount was besieged by William, king of England, and Duke Robert, their brother Henry being shut up in this Mount.

1095. Pope Urban held a council at Clermont.

1096. The Christians set out for Jerusalem.

1100. William Rufus, king of England, was killed, and his brother Henry succeeded him.

1102. Blessed Michael the Archangel was seen by some both near at hand and far off, as we believe, in the form of a fiery pillar, entering the church of this Mount on the night of his feast.

1106. A battle was fought at Tinchebray between Henry, king of England, and his brother Robert, duke of the Normans. In it that duke, William count of Mortain, and many others were captured. In the same year Abbot Roger resigned the abbacy of Saint Michael, and King Henry made him abbot of Cerne. Roger, prior of Jumièges, succeeded him.

[Col. 1322C] 1112. The church of Saint Michael was burned by lightning, together with all the monks’ workshops; the town, though it lay below the monastery, remained unharmed—a remarkable thing.

1117. A violent wind arose on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord.

1119. A battle was fought between Henry, king [Col. 1323A] of England, and Louis, king of France; in that battle many leading men of France were captured.

1120. William, son of Henry king of England, was shipwrecked at sea before Barfleur, along with many others.

1123. Abbot Roger resigned the abbacy of the Mount.

1124. Richard de Méré, a Cluniac monk, was made abbot of the Mount, which he held for three years.

1128. William, count of Flanders and son of Robert, duke of the Normans, was killed. In the same year Robert of Torigni, later abbot of the Mount, assumed the religious habit at Bec.

1131. Bernard, monk of Bec, became abbot of the Mount.

1135. Henry, king of England and duke of Normandy, died; [Col. 1323B] Count Stephen succeeded him.

1138. In August, through the furious ravaging of the men of Avranches, the castle of the Mount was burned, except for the church and the monks’ buildings.

1141. Stephen, king of England, was captured in battle at Lincoln by Count Robert.

1144. The tower of Rouen was surrendered to Geoffrey, count of Anjou, who from that point became count of Normandy.

[Col. 1324A] 1145. Men and women began humbly and with great devotion to draw upon their shoulders carts laden with stones and other material for the work of the church; and many miracles occurred there.

1147. Conrad, emperor of the Germans, Louis, king of France, and their companions went to Jerusalem, where they achieved little or nothing.

1149. Bernard, abbot of the Mount, died, and Geoffrey, monk of the same place, succeeded him; he died the following year. Of the dispute over the abbacy of the Mount between Richard de la Mouche and Robert Hardi, there is no need to say anything except that they, together with Richard, bishop of Avranches, died while on the journey to Rome.

1151. Geoffrey, duke of Normandy and count of Anjou, died. His son Henry, [Col. 1324B] born of the Empress Matilda, daughter of Henry I, king of England, succeeded him.

1153. Stephen, king of England, and his kinsman Henry, duke of Normandy, came to an agreement.

1154. In May, on 27 May, Thursday within the octave of Pentecost, Robert of Torigni, cloister-prior of Bec, was elected by the whole community to govern the church of Saint Michael. In the same year Stephen, king of England, died. Henry II, duke of Normandy, succeeded him.

[Col. 1323]

# ANOTHER CHRONICLE OF THE SAME MOUNT, WHICH MAY PROPERLY BE CALLED ARMORICAN OR ANGEVIN

[Col. 1323C] 421. Saint Gildas was born. In these days Arthur, a strong and witty king of the Britons, lived.

513. Britons from overseas came into Armorica, that is, Lesser Brittany.

534. Cavallonus, the most mighty king of Greater Brittany, was killed.

580. Saints Samson, Malo, Magloire, and Paul were bishops.

643. Dagobert, king of the Franks, and Saint Judicael made peace.

823. The monastery of Redon was built in Lesser Brittany under the pious Emperor Louis, on royal demesne land, with Conwoion as its first abbot.

843. The city of Nantes was captured by the Northmen under Duke Lambert; they killed Gohard, bishop of that city, while he was saying in the Mass, “Lift up your hearts.”

847. Pope Sergius died and Leo succeeded him. The latter [Col. 1323D] sent the body of Saint Marcellinus, pope and martyr, to Prince Nominoë; it was placed in the monastery of Redon.

851. Nominoë, under-king of the Bretons, died; his son Erispoë succeeded him.

857. Erispoë, king of the Bretons, was slain by Salomon. During Salomon’s time, the body of Blessed Matthew the Apostle was brought into Lesser Brittany.

869. King Salomon sent to Pope Adrian at Rome a golden statue together with many other gifts.

874. Salomon, king of the Bretons, was killed.

920. The Northmen devastated all Lesser Brittany, killing or expelling all the Bretons. Then the bodies of the saints who had been in Brittany were carried away into various lands.

[Col. 1324C] 931. The Bretons who remained killed all the Northmen on the feast of Saint Michael, first slaying their leader Feletan.

944. The Northmen killed the Bretons and scattered them from their land, in the time of Berengar and Alan.

966. Monks were sent into the church of Saint Albinus of Anjou, after the clerics had been expelled by Fulk the Good, count of Anjou, and Countess Adela.

970. Fulk, count of Anjou, surnamed “the Jerusalemite,” son of Geoffrey Greymantle, count of Anjou, gave his daughter Ermengard to Conan, duke of Lesser Brittany. By her Conan begot Geoffrey, who succeeded him, and Judith, wife of Richard II, duke of Normandy.

972. The second battle was fought at Conquereuil. Count Fulk of Anjou emerged victorious, and Conan the Breton was killed, on 27 June, by the sons of Juhel Berengar.

[Col. 1324D] 981. Conan the Curved fought very well against the men of Anjou at Conquereuil. At the same time, under Geoffrey, Conan’s son, Abbot Mainard governed excellently both the monastery of Redon and the abbey of Saint Michael at the Peril of the Sea, but willingly—or perhaps “as a young man” [*juvens*: reading uncertain]—resigned Redon.

997. Geoffrey, count of Anjou and father of Fulk, died.

1000. The city of Angers was burned after the burning of Countess Elizabeth.

1008. Geoffrey, duke of Brittany, son of Conan, son of Juhel Berengar, died while going to Rome for prayer. Richard II, duke of Normandy, married his sister Judith; and Geoffrey himself married Hamdis, sister of the aforesaid Richard, [Col. 1325A] by whom he begot two sons, Alan and Eudes, who succeeded him when the duchy of Brittany was divided.

1026. Sarmul was captured by Fulk, count of Anjou.

1032. Geoffrey Martel, count of Anjou, married Agnes, countess of Poitou, in an incestuous marriage. He built the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Vendôme.

1033. Geoffrey Martel captured William, count of Poitou, whose wife he had previously married.

[Col. 1326A] 1040. Alan, duke of Brittany, son of Geoffrey, died on 1 October, and his son Conan succeeded him, whom he had begotten by Bertha, sister of Theobald, count of Tours.

1044. Geoffrey Martel captured Count Theobald of Tours and extorted from him the city of Tours.

1056. Conan, duke of Brittany, captured his paternal uncle Eudes. This Eudes had many sons.

[Col. 1325]

# ON THE ABBOTS OF MOUNT SAINT MICHAEL AT THE PERIL OF THE SEA

[Col. 1325B] In the time of King Lothair and Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, in the year 965, Richard, duke of Normandy, acting under the commission of Pope John XIII, expelled the canons who had served in the church of Saint Michael on Mount Tumba at the Peril of the Sea for 258 years from the foundation of that place. He installed religious of the Order of Saint Benedict there, enriched and adorned it with many estates and with vessels of gold and silver. In the same year all these things were confirmed at Rome in a synod, with Maynard as abbot. After Richard’s death, Richard his son confirmed everything at Fécamp by charters and procured that they be signed by Richard and Robert, his sons, and others, among them Maugis, bishop of Avranches. Since disputes frequently arose between the bishop of Avranches and the abbot over the jurisdiction which the duke had formerly granted the abbot on the Mount, a settlement was finally made between William de Ostillon, bishop, and Abbot Rodulf in 1236.

On Mount Tumba, the revelation of Blessed Michael occurred [Col. 1325C] in the year 708, under Emperor Justinian, Pope John, Childebert king of the Franks, and Aubert bishop of Avranches. In that place many miracles took place during the 258 years in which canons ministered in the church.

966. Duke Richard replaced the canons with monks and appointed Maynard, from the monastery of Fontenelle, now called Saint-Wandrille, as their first abbot. Maynard had governed that monastery for five years before he came to the Mount.

991. Mainard I was succeeded by Mainard, his nephew and prior. In his time the monastery, with all its buildings, was burned.

1009. Mainard, burdened by old age, chose Hildebert as his successor. During Hildebert’s time the body of Saint Aubert was discovered; it had been hidden by the canons.

Hildebert was succeeded by Hildebert II, his nephew. In his time a woman gave birth upon the sands. The new church was begun by Duke Richard II and Hildebert himself in 1023; he died in the same year. In the same year Suppo, abbot of Fruttuaria, accepted the grant of the abbey [Col. 1325D] of Saint Michael. While he was occupied in resigning the monastery of Fruttuaria and in obtaining full possession of the Mount, two abbots governed the abbey of Saint Michael: Almodus, abbot of Césaire, and Theoderic, abbot of Jumièges. These two rest in their own abbeys.

1033. Suppo was ordained abbot. He conferred many benefits upon the abbey, but departed because of hatred from the monks and returned to his own home.

[Col. 1326B] 1048. Ralph, monk of Fécamp, a nobleman, was guardian of the monastery. Ber[lacuna]. He died while on the journey to Jerusalem in 1058. He rests in the church portico.

1060. After an interval of two years, Ranulf, a monk from childhood, became abbot. He sent to Duke William, who had subdued the kingdom of England, four monks: namely, Rual, prior, afterwards abbot of Hyde at Winchester; Scolland, treasurer, afterwards abbot of Saint Augustine’s at Canterbury; Serlo, a young man of distinguished nobility and religious life, afterwards founder and abbot of Saint Peter’s, Gloucester; and William of Agon, abbot of Tewkesbury. He presided for twenty-three years and bestowed many lands of the church on his kinsmen. He rests in the church portico.

1085. Roger, monk of Caen, began to rule. He had formerly been chaplain to the king of England.

1102. Blessed Michael was seen by some both near and far off, as we believe, in the form of a fiery pillar entering the basilica of this Mount on the night of his last feast; and the like occurred in the time of Saint Abbot Mainard and Norgod, bishop of Avranches.

1103. The *ciborium* of the nave of the church, which Roger had built, fell down and crushed part of the dormitory, though the monks were unharmed.

1106. Roger resigned the monastery of Saint Michael and was made abbot of Cerne in England by King Henry of England. In the same year Roger II, prior of Jumièges, a religious and wise man, succeeded Roger I.

1112. The church of Saint Michael was burned by lightning; the monks and the town remained unharmed.

1123. Roger placed the pastoral staff upon the altar of Blessed Michael and returned to Jumièges, receiving by the king’s order twenty-five marks annually from the revenues of the church of Saint Michael. He died in the following year. This happened because of a certain injury that he had suffered from one of his own men, who claimed a certain fief in the abbot’s chamber which the abbot [Col. 1326D] refused to restore to him.

1124. Richard, a Cluniac monk and almost a layman, yet noble in lineage and worldly manners, was made abbot. After three and a half years, by the counsel of King Henry and of Matthew, bishop of Albano and legate, he resigned the care of the abbey and returned to Saint Pancras, where he had taken monastic vows. The abbey remained in the king’s hand without an abbot for almost three years; through his officials the king caused the debts contracted by Richard de Méré to be paid. Their amount was 700 pounds of Le Mans, without interest, the payment of which the king forbade.

1131. At Rouen, on the feast of Saint Agatha, King Henry gave the abbey to Bernard, prior of Cernon and monk of Bec. He did many good things for the monastery: a vessel of gold and silver in which he placed the head of Blessed Aubert; and also two excellent medium-sized bells, imitating Abbot Ralph, who made the bell called “Rollo” to ward off the Bretons from the borders of Normandy. In England, at Saint Michael of Cermeria, he provided a church and sustenance for thirteen monks under a prior. Before Bernard had even been buried, Geoffrey, monk of the same church, succeeded him through a hasty election in 1149. He died the following year amid the greatest distress, leaving the church in debt because of his own peace with the count. He was buried in the church portico.

1152. When Abbot Geoffrey had died, Richard de la Mouche, a monk of this place, was elected abbot at the urging of his kinsman Richard, bishop of Avranches. Because the election had been held without the knowledge and assent of Prince Henry, that Richard was banished not only from the abbey but from all Duke Henry’s land. For two and a half years all administration of the monastery was carried out by three laymen who succeeded one another. At length the monks annulled the said election and, at the instigation of Rainald of Saint-Valery and with Duke Henry’s consent, elected Robert Hardi, cellarer of Fécamp, neither cleric nor layman.

Accordingly Richard de la Mouche went to Pope Eugenius. At his command Richard, bishop of Avranches, blessed the aforesaid Richard as abbot in the church of Saint Andrew. No monk of the Mount attended that blessing except one, who had left the community and accompanied him. Finally, monks were sent to Rome by both parties. Richard de la Mouche and Robert Hardi, and also Richard, bishop of Avranches, followed them, and within a short time all died abroad, namely in 1153. I do not count these two in the catalogue, because they never exercised the office of abbot either in the church or in the refectory.

1154. In May, on 27 May, Thursday within the Octave of Pentecost, Robert of Torigni, [Col. 1328A] cloister-prior of Bec, was elected. He performed very many good works and was keeper of the castle of Pontorson. He died in 1186.

1187. Abbot Martin, duly elected, governed honorably, wasting nothing but gathering back what had previously been scattered.

1191. Abbot Jordan. In his time the church was burned by the Bretons. He died in 1212.

Ralph of the Isles.  
Thomas of Champeaux.  
Ralph of Villedieu.  
These men governed for twenty-four years.

1236. Richard Justini. He died in 1264.

Nicholas Alexander.  
Nicholas Favigot.  
These men governed for thirty-four years.

1298. Abbot John le Fac died, and William de Castro succeeded him. He died in 1314.

John de la Porte succeeded William. He withdrew this monastery with all its appurtenances [Col. 1328B] from under the king of Navarre. He had its charters confirmed by Lord Philip of Valois, king of France. He resisted vigorously those who wanted the monastery to pay the wages of the men whom the king stationed to guard the Mount. He died in 1334. He was buried in the new chapel of Saint John, which he himself endowed and in which he established two chaplains.

Nicholas le Vitrier, prior of this place and a native of this Mount, governed honorably for twenty-seven years and six months. He caused the fortress of the Mount to be held in obedience to the king of France by the religious and servants of the monastery, repulsing all assailants. He died while the wars still raged, on 30 October 1362.

Geoffrey de Seraone, prior of this place and native of the city of Avranches, governed for twenty-three years and three months. He acquired many fiefs. The church of Saint Michael was burned by lightning; the bells melted almost like lead. The English who occupied the rock of Tombelaine, built by them, were captured by force of arms and wholly expelled from it. He died in 1386.

1386. Peter Regis, abbot of Exmes, governed for twenty-five years.

1411. Robert Jolivet, monk of this place, governed for thirty-four years.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1187: URBAN III, ROMAN PONTIFF

[Col. 1329]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE

(MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, col. 495.)

Urban III, a native of Milan and formerly called Lambert, of the Crivelli family, was elected pope by the remarkable unanimous consent of all in 1185, immediately after Lucius had died on 25 November. He had been archbishop of Milan. In the time of Emperor Frederick, he would have excommunicated him again for his repeated encroachment upon the Church’s honors and rights, had death not overtaken him first.

He directed all his efforts toward reconciling the minds of the Christians who were embroiled in wars in Syria. But while he labored in such undertakings to no effect, and the Christian princes remained entangled in hatreds and dissensions, the Sultan, after gaining possession of many places, also added Jerusalem to his dominion on 28 September, in the eighty-fourth year after it had been recovered by Godfrey. On hearing that the Lord’s Cross had been subjected to mockery, that the king of Jerusalem had been captured, and that the enemy forces were marching toward Antioch, he was struck with grief and fell ill. He died at Ferrara on 20 October 1187, after sitting one year, nine months, and twenty-five days.

Thus Roger writes concerning the death of that excellent pope, judging more truthfully and rightly than Urspergensis, supporter of schismatics. After recording the death of Pope Lucius, Urspergensis writes, in his customary manner:

> “Then the cardinals who were with him were greatly distressed about their return, for they feared that the emperor might inflict some violence upon them concerning the election of the Roman pontiff. Yet the archbishop of Milan conducted them safely as far as Ravenna, and they elected him pope; he was called Urban III. Many called him *Turbanus*, because, being Milanese by nation, he wished in hatred of the emperor to disturb the Church, which had already obtained a little peace. But, struck down by God’s will, he perished. He sat one year, ten months, and twenty-five days.”

So writes Urspergensis.

In his time, namely in 1186, the daughter of Roger, king of Sicily—whom Baronius proves was not a nun, the contrary being a fable [Note: [Col. 1329] The fiction that she had been a nun was perhaps devised because she was kept in a monastery, so that, should the kings lack male offspring, she might marry with the kingdom as her dowry.]—was joined in marriage to Henry IV, king of Germany. VITERBO.

[Col. 1329]

# LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES OF POPE URBAN III  
(For the books used, see *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXIX, beginning.)

## YEAR 1185

[Col. 1331A]

## I. He receives the church of Saint Evasio of Casale under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges.  
(Verona, 9 December.)

[DE CONTI, *Notizie Storiche*, I, 360.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the provost of the church of Saint Evasio of Casale and his brethren, present and future, who profess the regular life: in perpetuity.

The authority of the Apostolic See, over which, though unworthy, we preside, admonishes us to labor with provident vigilance for the welfare of all Churches, and to strengthen them by the safeguard of apostolic protection, lest they be exposed to the plundering or harassment of the wicked. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously consent to your just requests. Following the example of the Roman pontiffs Calixtus, Paschal, Innocent, and Lucius, of happy memory, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid church of Saint Evasio, in which you are dedicated to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. First, therefore, establishing, etc. At Fraschineto, one and a half *mansus* holdings. We also forbid you to grant ecclesiastical estates in fief to any secular persons. Further, concerning your newly cultivated lands, etc. You may also receive clerics, etc. Furthermore, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in [Col. 1331C] your house, to leave the cloister, except under the pretext of a stricter religious observance. But if one departs, etc., as in the bull of Lucius III for the same monastery.

I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina, subscribed. [Col. 1332A] I, Henry, bishop of Albano, subscribed. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri, subscribed. I, John, cardinal-priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber, title of Calixtus, subscribed. I, Pandulf, by God’s permission alone cardinal-priest of the Twelve Apostles, subscribed. I, Adelard, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, subscribed. I, Audisio, cardinal-deacon of Saint Theodore, have subscribed. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, subscribed. I, Geoffrey, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, subscribed. [Col. 1332B] I, Ralph, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Verona through the hand of Transmund, notary of the Holy Roman Church, on 9 December, in the year 1185 of the Incarnation of the Lord; in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban III.

## II. To the clergy and people of Split.—He states that he has deferred judgment because the archbishopric of Zadar is vacant.  
(Verona, 12 December.)

[FARLATI, *Illyricum sacrum*, IV, 245.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy, the nobleman Count M., and the people of Split: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When the beloved sons B., canon and judge of your church, had come into the presence of Pope Lucius, our predecessor of happy memory, our venerable brother P., your archbishop, subsequently arrived. They reported to him the injury which you appear to suffer in regard to the bishopric of Hvar. Although he wished to provide for your church’s immunity and to hear you, as beloved sons of the Church, in your petitions and to comply with the wish of your envoys, nevertheless, because the Church of Zadar is vacant, he could neither confirm, as they requested, that bishopric to your church, nor, before that Church should be provided for, wished to take up the settlement of the matter. He therefore permitted it to remain without dispute in the condition in which it now stands.

In [lacuna], we command your discretion by apostolic writings that, when that church of Zadar has been provided for, you shall come into our presence with the envoys of the opposing party, to receive through us, with God’s help, your justice. For we are prepared, both in this and in other matters, to provide, so far as we can in the Lord, for the honor and advantage of your church. We do not, however, wish any rescript obtained from the Apostolic See by suppression of the truth to prejudice your right.

Given at Verona, 12 December.

## III. To Peter, Archbishop of Split.—He confirms his right to have the cross borne before him throughout the kingdom of Hungary.  
(Verona, 12 December.)

[FARLATI, *Illyricum sacrum*, III, 221.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother PETER, archbishop of Split: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1333C] We ought to love our brethren and bishops with sincere charity, to give more earnest care to the advantage of their honor, and, so far as lies in us, to preserve their rights unimpaired. Therefore, giving favorable assent to your just requests, we confirm by apostolic authority, and fortify by the protection of this present writing, the custom reasonably granted to your church and hitherto observed, of bearing the cross—that is to say, the Lord’s banner—throughout the whole kingdom of Hungary. We decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to act contrary to it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty [Col. 1333D] God and of His apostles, the blessed Peter and Paul.

Given at Verona, on the second day before the Ides of December, in the first year of our pontificate.

### IV. Privilege by which he confirms all the goods, rights, and possessions of the priory of St. Peter of Consiac, in the diocese of Soissons, under the obedience and subjection of the monastery of Cluny. (Verona, Dec. 16.)

*[Bullarium Cluniacense, 85.]*

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JOHN, prior of Consiac, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

[Col. 1334A] Whenever something is requested of us which is recognized as befitting uprightness and religion, it is fitting that we grant it with a willing spirit and provide appropriate support for the petitioners’ wishes. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the church of St. Peter of Consiac, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present document.

First, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in that place according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall there be observed inviolably for all time. Accordingly, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have judged it proper to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances. The altar of the village of Duroman. The altar of Robert’s court. The altar of Gentovillari. The altar of Sarmasia. The altar of Besona. The four altars given you by Hugh, bishop of Soissons, of blessed memory: namely, Saponiac, Runcheries, Berniac, and Espargo. And the four altars given you by Lisiard, bishop of Soissons, of blessed memory: namely, Cresenci, [Col. 1334C] Condez, Vulcenis, and Calte. The church of St. Peter of Calte, with its appurtenances. The lesser tithe from the parish of St. Leodegar of Soissons. The church of Bruilio, with its dependencies. The church of St. Mary of Fonce, with its dependencies and the persons belonging to the altar of that church, wherever they may be. The altar of Despalx. The altar of Ascerpiniac, with its dependencies and every tithe, from which the priest serving those altars receives each year two modii of winter grain and one modius of oats. The greater and lesser tithe of Luy. The tithe of St. Remigius of Ivery; and whatever John of Brumes and Hugh surnamed Punarque possessed in the altar and tithe of [Col. 1334D] Uveseli. The tithe of Maisiac. The altar of Raoulcourt. The altar of Carcobio. The tithe of Armenteria and Cursabro. In the tithe of Cugny, one modius of winter grain, from the alms of Hugh of Magny. Half a modius of wheat from the *terragia* of Ton, from the alms of John Christion. One modius of winter grain at Asunliz, from the alms of Guy of Conce. Whatever John of Ulchei, surnamed the Viscount, possessed in the *terragia* of Ulanzi and in the woodland. The greater and lesser tithe of Sarmasia and Ciriac. The entire greater tithe of the districts, and a third part of the lesser tithe. The tithe of Berciac of St. Basolus. The tithe of Bernerda and the entire tract. The tithe of Grisoltis and Raoulcourt. One modius of wheat [Col. 1335A] in the tithe of Aucensvilla, from the alms of Lisiard Teuvagia of Lasteli; and every rent from all the holdings which are in the churchyard; and, in the altar of Duro Magno, what you possess every day: three parts of all offerings, while the fourth belongs to the priest; together with the offering of coin and candle on Sunday for blessed bread; the offering of those being married after the celebration of Mass; also the offerings and blessing of pilgrims; and whatever a woman to be purified offers with her own hand. Of the lesser tithes—namely wine, beans, peas, wool, flax, hay, livestock, and poultry—you have three parts and the priest the fourth; but of the greater tithe you have seven parts and the whole tract, while the priest has the eighth, excepting the tithes of the Count of Caltararum, [Col. 1335B] from which the priest receives nothing; three parts of all candles offered throughout the year, excepting the Sunday candle, which belongs to the priest. If incense or a candle is lacking, or should fail, in the church, it shall be purchased from the common offering. Likewise, whatever Peter of Noroy possessed at Vismolin, and one modius of wine at Palie, twenty solidi at Bac. At Pontuert, one modius of grain—half wheat and the rest oats—from the alms of Ailard the Armiger. Whatever he held from Brenna at Berniac and at Crucem: namely, the altar with its dependencies, and the persons belonging to the altar with all the customary dues which they owed him. At Longavilla, whatever he held, except the heads of persons. At Cresanciac, [Col. 1335C] whatever he held in the district of Brienne. His freehold at Robert’s court; the freehold of Werdon; and everything belonging to those freeholds in men, women, lands, meadows, waters, mills, and woods; and the firm hand of Janvillari—that is, the village with all its dependencies. At Roncheries, two parts of the greater and lesser tithes; in the village, a third part of all rents and revenues, however they arise; and in the woods and pastures belonging to the village, wherever they may be, a third part, except the holdings, whose rent belongs exclusively to you, and one holding with full jurisdiction.

That portion of your own village which begins at the houses situated below the road lying beneath your house, and extends to the little street that turns toward Hubert’s spring; on the other side it runs along the public embankment leading toward Châtillon, as far as the wood of Campo-vicini; thence by the ditch called Brunhild’s ditch it extends to the spring of Boel; then it returns to the corner of the old wood, which lies at the exit of the village toward Châtillon; and the church of St. Fidolus with all its appurtenances, as you reasonably possess it by the gift of Philip, formerly bishop of Troyes, of blessed memory. Likewise, at St. Fidolus, that which Count Theobald, of blessed memory, and his son Hugh, formerly count of Troyes, gave by pious grant to you and your church as alms, as is contained in their authentic document, [Col. 1336A] together with what you possess in the altar of Sticourt and Toncourt. The liberty of your village in which your church is founded, as Count Theobald the elder formerly gave it to you by pious grant, and afterwards his son Count Stephen. Also the altar of Misiac with the greater and lesser tithe. The liberty of the village of Ulcenis granted to you by Hugh, count of Troyes. The altar and *personatus* of Glivoliis, with all their appurtenances. At Roncheries, your *terragia* of Carturagium, without a share for the knight; and the viscounty of the same village—its *terragia*, rents, and complete jurisdiction—without claim or advocacy by the knight.

Moreover, no one shall presume to demand or exact tithes from you upon your newly cleared lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or upon the produce of your animals.

You may receive clerics or laymen fleeing the world, free and released, into conversion, and retain them without any objection. When a general interdict is imposed upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. In the parish churches which you hold, you may choose priests and present them to the diocesan bishop; if they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust the care of souls to them, and they shall answer to him in spiritual matters but to you in temporal matters.

Furthermore, we hold valid the ancient liberties and immunities, and the reasonable customs granted to your monastery and observed hitherto, and decree that they shall remain unimpaired in times to come. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and ordinations of clerics or monks to be promoted to sacred orders, from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to furnish these things freely and without any improper exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested.

Moreover, we decree that the burial place of that location shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wishes of those who choose burial there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken shall be preserved. Since tithes have been assigned to ministers of churches by both the Old and New Law, we forbid by apostolic authority any layperson to presume to demand or extort tithes from you. We also forbid anyone to construct a new church or oratory within the boundaries of your parishes without the consent of the diocesan bishop and of the abbot and chapter of Cluny, while preserving the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. We further prohibit any church, land, or other benefice of your church from being personally granted to anyone or otherwise alienated without consent of the entire chapter, [Col. 1337A] or of its greater and sounder part. If any gifts have been made otherwise than stated, we judge them void.

Desiring also, with paternal solicitude, to provide for your peace and tranquility, we forbid by apostolic authority anyone within the enclosures of your sites or granges to presume rashly to commit violence, robbery, or theft; to set fire; or to seize or kill a person. The place itself, with all its appurtenances, shall remain forever, as it is known hitherto to have remained, under the obedience and subjection of the monastery of Cluny.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may unlawfully disturb the aforesaid place, or take away, withhold, diminish, or harass its possessions by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the use and benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to act contrary to this page of our enactment, and, after a second or third warning, does not amend his offense by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 1337C] our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. Amen. Amen.

I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theodinus, bishop of the see of Porto and St. Bartinus. I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, John, cardinal priest of St. Mary in Trastevere, of the title of Calixtus. I, Pandulf, of the title of the Twelve Apostles. I, Albinus, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Melior, cardinal priest of SS. John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of St. Theodore. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of SS. Cosmas and Damian. I, Sofredus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Via Lata. I, Roland, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Portico. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. [Col. 1338A] I, Radulf, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Verona by the hand of Transmundus, notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, in the fourth indiction, in the year 1185 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban.

### V. Privilege by which he confirms all the goods and rights of the priory of Blessed Mary of Mont-desir, of the Cluniac order, in the diocese of Amiens. (Verona, Dec. 16.)

*[Bullarium Cluniacense, 87.]*

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BERENGAR, prior of the church of St. Mary of Mont-desir, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

[Col. 1338B] It is fitting that apostolic protection be present for those choosing the religious life, lest an attack of anyone’s rashness either turn them from their purpose or—God forbid—weaken the vigor of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and, following the example of our predecessor Pope Alexander of happy memory, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document.

First, we decree that the monastic order known to have been instituted there according to God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the observance of the brothers of Cluny, shall be observed there inviolably for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have judged it proper to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church stands, with all its appurtenances: namely, the church of Blessed Mary with the thirteen prebends which the secular canons used to hold, and that prebend formerly held by the masters of the school in the castle of Mont-desir who directed the schools—or, in place of that prebend, thirty Provins solidi; the direction of the schools; the oil of anointing; the church of St. Peter with its churchyard, tithe, and annual rent of seventeen solidi, which the priests of that church must pay each year.

As to the offerings of the altar of St. Peter, it has for many years been ordained that five parts of those offerings made at Masses for the living should fall to the monks and the sixth part to the priests; but of those received at Masses for the dead, one half should belong to the monks and the other to the priests. Guarinus, bishop of Amiens, of blessed memory, also forbade any alteration of this arrangement under anathema.

The church of the Holy Sepulchre, with altar, churchyard, and tithe; the church of Ficurlicurte, with altar, churchyard, and tithe; the church of Villa, with the chapel of Masnil, their altars, churchyards, and tithes; the church of Nova-Villa, with altar, churchyard, and the entire tithe; the church of Freteio, with altar, churchyard, and the entire tithe; the church of Souvillier, with the dependent chapel of Aubevillier, their altars, churchyards, and tithes; the church of Dommalich, with altar, churchyard, and tithe; the church of Domna Petra, with altar, churchyard, and tithe; the church of Brachi, with altar, churchyard, and the entire tithe; the church of Contorium, with altar, churchyard, and the entire tithe; one half of the churches of Anethi and Feneriis, and of their altars and lesser tithes; the church of Caiis, with altar, churchyard, two parts of the entire greater tithe, and the whole lesser tithe; the church of Curte Dominica, with altar, churchyard, and the entire lesser tithe.

Likewise, the village of Curcellis with its dependencies; at Mont-desir, the mill of the Bridge; and, each week, three denarii of Vermandois currency from the bread toll. At Furcemviller, the entire freehold in lands and woods given by Elizabeth Rabies; likewise, the tithe of Spateris received from you through the hand of our venerable brother Odo, bishop of Beauvais, at the request of Count Radulf of Vermandois and also Count Ivo of Soissons. Likewise, in the diocese of Amiens, the greater tithe of Septem Fortis; twelve modii of wheat at the new mill, from the alms of Robert of Tornella and of Peter his father; and the grain revenue of Corrobeiis at Contorium; one half of the upper mill and of the lower mill, and of the water and marsh belonging by right to it; at Le Plessis, of Radulf Vitulus, three parts of the *terragium* of Gay; the wood of Surella, with its ground and its tithe; at Mont-desir, half the mill called Engelran’s. Moreover, no one shall presume to demand or exact tithes from you upon your newly cleared lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or upon the produce of your animals.

You may also receive clerics or laymen fleeing the world, free and released, into conversion, and retain them without any objection.
