When a general interdict is imposed upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. In the parish churches which you possess, you may choose priests and present them to the diocesan bishop; if they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust the care of souls to them, so that they answer to him in spiritual matters but to you in temporal matters.

We hold valid the liberties and immunities, the ancient customs reasonably granted to that monastery and observed hitherto, and decree that they shall remain unimpaired in times to come. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and ordinations of clerics or monks to be promoted to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to furnish these freely and without any improper exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what you request. Moreover, we decree that the burial place of that location shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wishes of those who choose burial there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which dead bodies are taken shall be preserved.

We also forbid anyone to construct a new church or oratory within the boundaries of your churches without the consent of the diocesan bishop and the abbot and chapter of Cluny, while preserving the privileges of the Roman pontiff. Since tithes are known to have been assigned to ministers of churches by both the Old and New Law, we prohibit under threat of anathema any layperson from presuming to demand or exact tithes from you. We further prohibit any church, land, or other benefice of your church from being personally granted to anyone or otherwise alienated without consent of the entire chapter, or of its greater or sounder part. If any gifts have been made otherwise than stated, we judge them void.

Desiring also, with paternal solicitude, to provide for your peace and tranquility, we forbid by apostolic authority anyone within the enclosure of your sites or granges rashly to commit violence, robbery, or theft; to set fire; or to seize or kill a person. The place itself, with all its appurtenances, shall remain forever, as it is known hitherto to have remained, under the obedience and subjection of the monastery of Cluny.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may unlawfully disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, or diminish, withhold, or harass what has been taken by any vexations; but that all these things shall be preserved wholly unimpaired for the use and benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority [Col. 1340D] of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to act contrary to this page of our enactment, and, after a second or third warning, does not amend his offense by worthy satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

[Col. 1341A] I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theodore, bishop of the Apostolic See of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Mark. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of St. Mary in Trastevere. I, Paul, by God’s permission alone cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Twelve Apostles. I, Albinus, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Melior, of SS. John and Paul, of the title [Col. 1341B] of St. Pammachius. I, Ardelo, cardinal deacon of the title of St. Theodore. I, Gratian, cardinal of the title of SS. Cosmas and Damian. I, Goffredus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Via Lata. I, Roland, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Portico, of the title of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Radulf, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Verona by the hand of Transmundus, notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, in the fourth indiction, in the year 1185 of the Lord’s Incarnation, [Col. 1341C] and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban III.

### VI. To [Sicard], bishop-elect of Cremona, and the abbot of St. Lawrence. (Verona, Dec. 18.)

*[Tiraboschi, History of Nonantola, II, 310.]*

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the bishop-elect of Cremona [Note: [Col. 1341D] The bishop-elect of Cremona mentioned here is the celebrated Sicard, author of the Chronicle published by Muratori (*Scriptores Rerum Italicarum*, vol. VII, p. 521). He himself says, under the year 1185, that he was elected bishop in that year. This brief shows that on 18 [Col. 1342D] December he had not yet been consecrated—if indeed it should be assigned to the year 1185, since it could also belong to the following year, during which Urban III continued to reside at Verona. But it is not likely that the bishop’s consecration was deferred for so long.] and the abbot of St. Lawrence, greetings and apostolic blessing.

At the complaint of our beloved son A., archpriest of Poliniano, we have learned that our beloved son, the abbot of Nonantola, claims unjustly to withhold the chapel of St. George of Monticello, which belongs by right to the parish church of that place. [Col. 1341D] Therefore, entrusting this case to your care, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to summon the parties before you, hear and ascertain fully the arguments on both sides, and determine the case by a canonical judgment, setting aside appeal; compelling the parties to appear before us and, by our authority, to observe the judgment which you shall render.

Given at Verona, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January.

### VII. He confirms the assignment of tithes made to the Venetian church of St. Sylvester by Mark, bishop of Castello. (Verona, Dec. 18.)

*[Cornelius, Ecclesiae Venetae, III, 80.]*

[Col. 1342A]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son DOMENICO MINOTO, parish priest of St. Sylvester, greetings and apostolic blessing.

What has been inviolably ordained by our brother bishops ought likewise to remain firm and unimpaired; and, lest it be changed in the course of time by any rash action, it is fitting that it be strengthened by an apostolic document. As we have learned from the authentic instrument of our venerable brother M., bishop of Castello, that bishop, having regard to your devotion and the advantage of the church entrusted to your care, granted to you and your successors a fourth part of the tithes of your parish, so that you might receive it without anyone’s opposition and distribute it among the clerics of that church according to each one’s merit, while reserving entire for himself and his successors the fourth part belonging to them.

But of the share for the poor, he left one half to be divided, with the counsel of your brethren, among the poor of your parish; the remaining half he ordered to be bestowed upon the bishop and his successors—with your and your clerics’ consent—because of the multitude of poor persons, especially nobles, coming to his church. Yet, from the fourth part assigned for the repair of the church, he reserved forever a fourth for himself and his successors for the benefit of the mother church. He directed that the other shares of that same fourth should be given to you and your successors for restoring the fabric of your church, its books, and its other needs.

We therefore strengthen by this present document that grant, as it was made by the same bishop and confirmed by authentic instrument both by him and by our venerable brother H., patriarch of Grado. Let no person whatsoever therefore infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Verona, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the first year of our pontificate.

## Year 1185–1186

[Col. 1342D]

### VIII. He commands R[adulf], bishop of Angers, M[aurice], bishop-elect of Nantes, and the abbot of Foarcia, to expel the abbot of St. Melaine of Rennes, appointed by the count contrary to the privilege of the brethren of Saumur. (Verona, Dec. 10.)

*[Morice, Memoirs for the History of Brittany, I, 703.]*

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother R., bishop of Angers, and to his beloved sons M., bishop-elect of Nantes, and the abbot of Foarcia: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of St. Florentius of Saumur, having sent us a complaint, showed that it has been ordained and observed from ancient times that, when the abbot of St. Melaine of Rennes dies, the monks of that place, if no suitable person is found in their own community, shall choose an abbot for themselves from the cloister of St. Florentius. When the abbot of the said monastery of St. Melaine died, they canonically elected one from their own community. The count, however, grievously displacing him and wishing to usurp that election according to his own will, inflicted so many troubles and injuries upon the aforesaid chapter that the said elect preferred to relinquish the election rather than have the monastery suffer those burdens on his account.

When the monks wished to elect an abbot from their own house or from the monastery of St. Florentius, the count, not at all content with his first act of oppression, violently intruded into that church, against the objections of the brethren, a monk of another monastery, contrary to ancient custom and to the dignity of both churches. Consequently, several monks of that church, lest they appear to acquiesce in the aforesaid imposition, fled from that monastery to the house at Saumur.

Desiring therefore to provide for the said monastery with pastoral care, we command and enjoin your discretion to go to that monastery and investigate the truth concerning all these matters. If the aforesaid intrusion is established before you, then, setting aside all favor and fear, remove that intruder from the same church without hindrance from appeal; and arrange for the said monastery to be provided, through canonical election, with another suitable person according to the ancient and reasonable custom hitherto observed. Thus, if the brethren of that place cannot agree, you shall appoint by apostolic authority as abbot the person whom you find more approved in both manner of life and learning, and upon whom the votes of the greater and sounder part concur, etc. If not all of you can be present to carry this out, you, brother bishop, together with the other, shall nonetheless carry it out.

[Col. 1343D] Given at Verona, on the fourth Ides of December.

### IX. Bull by which he confirms the judgment rendered by Robert, archbishop of Vienne, and Hugh, abbot of Bonneval, concerning the disputes between Bishop Arducius and Count William. (Verona, Dec. 10.)

*[Spon, History of Geneva, II, 41.]*

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother NANTELLINUS, bishop of Geneva, greetings and apostolic blessing.

From the tenor of an authentic document, it has become known to us that, when a dispute had arisen between Arducius, your predecessor of blessed memory, and William, count of Geneva, concerning the *banna* and jurisdictions of your church, and persons newly come or others belonging to the city, our venerable brother Robert, archbishop of Vienne, and our beloved son Hugh, abbot of Bonneval, had undertaken, with the parties’ consent, to settle it. The count promised under oath, and the bishop upon his word of truth, to observe their arbitration inviolably. Many hostages also swore to accept and preserve the arbitration.

After diligently investigating the truth, they decreed that the arrangements formerly made by the men of the church and of the count, and confirmed by their oath, should be observed forever and inviolably. Therefore, since you request that this arbitration be strengthened by our document in order that it may possess greater force, we assent to your just requests and, as it is contained in the authentic instrument, confirm it by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the protection of this present document. Its text is as follows:

> “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. I, Robert, Archbishop of the Church of Vienne, and I, Hugh, Abbot of Bonnevaux, appointed, by the choice of both parties, as examiners of the cause which was pending between Arducius, Bishop of Geneva, and Count William, having also received an oath from the count and a firm promise upon his word of truth from the bishop, and having received many hostages from either side, judicially [Col. 1344C] settled the same controversy concerning the bans and jurisdictions of the Church of Geneva, and concerning all appurtenances or other things belonging to that city, in the following manner:
>
> “After the bishop had produced before us written instruments—first, that of our glorious lord Emperor Frederick, concerning the regalian rights of the same city, rights restored and confirmed to the bishop by a judgment delivered in a solemn court and authenticated by the seal of that same lord and the subscriptions of many very eminent witnesses; then other instruments concerning agreements made between Humbert, Bishop of Geneva, and Count Aymon, and between Arducius, the bishop now in possession, and Count Amadeus—the first document authenticated by the seals of the aforesaid Humbert and Count Aymon, and the second likewise authenticated by the seals of the venerable archbishops Heraclius of Lyons and Stephen of Vienne; and after many suitable witnesses [Col. 1344D] concerning the authenticity of those documents and the form of the agreements, likewise concerning the agreement subsequently made through the venerable Archbishop Peter, had been carefully examined and lawfully received; and after the allegations of both parties had been heard and discussed with every care, while there sat with us the venerable bishops John of Grenoble, J. of Aosta, of Saint-Jean-de-Maurienne, G. of Avenches, W. of Sion, J. of Intermont, Brother, formerly Abbot of Saint-Maurice, together with the priors of the Carthusian Order, of Repausatorium, Vallon, and Pomerium: with their counsel and assent, justice intervening, we decreed that the authority of these charters should remain inviolate and that full credit should in every respect be given to them.
>
> “Accordingly, we adjudged and by firm authority ordered that the settlements formerly made by the men of the bishop should stand. And the count ought to seize no persons in Geneva. He ought, as lord, to possess lodging-right, the general court, the wine dues, the whole Rippale, Coroada, and the succession of houses if the lord has died; likewise, the market of the whole town and jurisdiction over the market. Nor ought the count, either personally or through any of his men, to make any mounted levies in the pastures of Geneva. Coinage is to remain in the hand of the bishop alone; and if, God forbid, the moneyers make false coin, the count is not to administer justice except by command of the bishop. If any robber is captured, the bishop is to have him and all his goods; but if the bishop decides to condemn that robber, he shall surrender him to the count, so that the count may administer justice. [Col. 1345B] The count’s residence at Geneva shall be subject to the bishop’s cognizance, provided that the count and his household do no injury to the church, the citizens, or ecclesiastical property, and do not impose their *radinconia* upon anyone by force; and when he departs, he shall not leave unless he has made peace with his creditor.
>
> “Moreover, concerning the new wall which Count William had built outside the castle, it was established before us with the utmost certainty through lawful witnesses that the aforesaid most reverend Archbishop P. of Tarentaise had, in the settlement made by him between Arducius, Bishop of Geneva, and Count Amadeus, determined and forbidden under excommunication that no wall whatsoever should be built anywhere beyond the old wall of the castle, and that any wall built outside the old one should be demolished. Therefore [Col. 1345C] it was also stated and determined in the judgment we delivered that the same wall be demolished, and that henceforth no structure be built outside the old castle wall contrary to the aforesaid settlement and the excommunication of so great a pontiff.
>
> “Count William indeed alleged that he and his father had exercised and held, for a long time, jurisdiction over robbers and adulterers. This the bishop and the Church of Geneva did not acknowledge. Since, however, by the settlement first made between Bishop Humbert and Count Aymon before the Archbishop of Vienne, and subsequently by the second settlement made between Count Amadeus and Arducius, Bishop of Geneva, before the venerable archbishops [Col. 1345D] of Lyons and Vienne, and thirdly before the Archbishop of Tarentaise—in which, following the excommunication concerning the wall as stated above, it was expressly provided that the earlier settlements should be inviolably maintained—that long-standing possession, even if it had existed, had been interrupted so often that we judged it could not benefit him. In all matters, therefore, as stated above, the aforesaid fathers adjudged to the Church of Geneva the ban of the whole of Geneva and the other matters written above; and Count William himself acknowledged that dominion over the entire city belongs to the Church of Geneva, and that whatever he possesses there he holds from the bishop.
>
> “It was further added to the judgment that, since Count William, entirely contrary to reason, had laid hands upon certain regular clergy and clerics on the pretext of crimes, and upon the patrimonies of churches, he shall no longer, on grounds of crime, theft, homicide, or any other matter, lay hands or cause hands to be laid upon regular clergy, church patrimonies, or movable goods; nor upon secular clerics within the county of Geneva, until the offence has been made known and proved to the bishop, and they have been deprived of office or deposed by the bishop. [Col. 1346A]
>
> “The witnesses to this judgment are all those named above; and among the clergy of the Church of Geneva: Pontius the sacristan; Nantelinus the provost; Bartholomew the dean; Pontius of Saisireu, dean; Anselm of Villonay; Peter of Dorchia; Roso of Confignon; Freuvardus; Guitbertus; Giroldus of Villeta; William Jospergue; Peter Bauconus; and other clerics. Among the laymen: Boemundus Laurentius, Maurice Jordan, [Col. 1346B] and many others.
>
> “Count William accepted this judgment as delivered by us and promised before us two, the three bishops named above, and other persons—almost all the knights, as well as Amadeus, the count’s brother, William of Nangeio, Peter of Cletis, William of Festerna, William of Graisie, William of Altavilla, Guy Bressenco, William Turumbertus, William of Ayma, and many others—to observe it. This judgment was delivered in the town of Aquiranno in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1184, while the most blessed Pope Lucius III presided over the Holy Roman Church and the glorious Frederick, ever august, ruled as emperor. This present instrument was written by the hand of Peter, notary of Vienne, at our command, carefully examined, [Col. 1346C] and secured with our seals and those of other persons.”

Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this document of our confirmation or rashly to act against it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Verona, 12 December.

X. He confirms the judgment delivered by the Bishop of Lodi and Provost Martin, that “two parts of the tithe from the lands which are in the court of Porto-Albara” are to be paid to the canons of Piacenza. (Verona, 30 December.)

[CAMPI, *History of Piacenza*, II, 368.]

[Col. 1346D]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the provost and canons of Piacenza, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since a controversy had formerly arisen between you and Vicinus, archpriest of the Church of Porto-Albara, concerning two parts of the tithe from the lands which are in the court of Porto-Albara or within its boundaries, our venerable brother, the Bishop of Lodi, and our beloved son Martin, provost of the greater church, having heard and considered the arguments on both sides, settled that cause by delegation of the Apostolic See, condemning the said archpriest by definitive judgment to pay you henceforth [Col. 1347A] the two parts of the aforesaid tithe.

Because matters reasonably decreed by apostolic authority ought to possess perpetual force, we decree that the judgment lawfully promulgated in this matter by the aforesaid judges is valid. We confirm to you and to your church by apostolic authority the two parts of that tithe, as they were adjudged to you and as you hold them peacefully, and strengthen them by the protection of this present document. Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this document of our confirmation or rashly to act against it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Given at Verona, 30 December.

## YEAR 1186

[Col. 1347B]

XI. Privilege for the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Lucerne (diocese of Avranches). (Verona, 11 January.)

[Gallia Christiana, new edition, XI, 330.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ANGOT, abbot of Holy Trinity of Lucerne, and his brethren, present and future, who are to observe the rule, for perpetual remembrance.

A pious request ought to be fulfilled with effective result, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the requested benefit may assuredly acquire strength. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid Church of the Holy Trinity at Lucerne, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it with the privilege of this present document. We first establish that the canonical order which is known to have been instituted in that church according to God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the constitutions of the Premonstratensian brethren shall be inviolably observed there for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, with the Lord’s help, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. [Col. 1347D] We have thought it proper to specify these in their own terms:

The site on which the aforesaid church stands, with all its appurtenances; the church of St John of Château-Gontier, with its appurtenances; the church of St Mary of La Rochelle, with its appurtenances; the church of Campeaux; the church of Angey; the church of Montviron; the church of Subligny; two sheaves of tithes from the land of Alan the knight in the parish of St Peter; the entire manor which you possess at Crollon, with its appurtenances; all the land which you possess at Lucerne, with mill and woodland; all the land which you possess at Avranches, with vineyards and winepresses; land which you possess at Subligny [Col. 1348A] and Noir-Palud, at Lande, and at Rosigny; the land of Osbern the steward at Marcey, with half an acre of land formerly belonging to Juclin; land formerly belonging to William, son of Emma, and the meadows which you possess there; tithes from all the mills of Alan of St Peter; the tithe of the mill of Henry of St Peter; the tithe of the mill of Carantilly; one sixth of the mill at Noir-Palud; vineyards, land, and fishing-rights which you possess at St John; land and meadows which you possess at St Lô; one third of the mill, with the land which you possess, at Cambas; the prebends of deceased canons of Avranches annually, as the charters made concerning this attest; one half of the tithes of the whole parish of Domville; two sheaves of tithes from the whole [Col. 1348B] fief of William of St John at Grimouville; in the diocese of Coutances, the church of St Mary of Tourville, with all its appurtenances; the church of St George of Raiz, with its appurtenances; the church of St Martin of Tribehou, with all its appurtenances; the church of St Peter of Mesnil-Guildouin; ten acres of land at Tsnanville, given by R. of Altavilla; at Cambas, two holdings of land, given by G. of Cantepie; at Clincamp, one holding, given by Denis; at Angey, in Geoffrey of the Wood’s fief, ten Angevin shillings, given by R., son of Ralph, and his wife Philippa; at Avranches, an acre of vineyard with a press [Col. 1348C] at Messiomore, given by William, Archdeacon of Avranches; at Monchaton, seven quarters of grain in the holding of R. of the Meadows, with one acre of land at the place called Wasme; at Grimouville, seven quarters of grain in the holding of Ralph of the Monastery, with one acre of land and five perches at the Great Cross, given by W. of St John and his wife G.; one quarter of rye in the tithe of Dominic Roger of St George, given by R. himself, at Curva Fossa; the tithe of the entire wood of that place, whether from pasture or sale of timber, together with a certain portion of woodland in the demesne, as the boundary divisions show; at Grippon, tithes of all revenues belonging to that castle, including the tithe of the fair of that village, given by Asculf of Subligny; [Col. 1348D] at Virey, one quarter of grain in the holding of Roger of the Fields outside the gate, given by Albin; on the land of Oger of Nuilley, one mina of grain, given by Geldoin Cati; at Dragey, one quarter of grain in the holding of Penerel, given by Robert of Percy; at La Rochelle, seven quarters of grain, given by Robert Heriz and his son Roger, payable to you after the first ten at Mont-Aigu; one acre of land, given by Malefont and his brothers; at Crollon, three shillings of Le Mans, given by William of Magney, which you were accustomed to receive annually; at Cancey, three quarters of grain from land customarily held by G. Mandarius in the manor of St Nicholas; in Roger’s wood, one mina of grain, given by William of Albigny, earl; [Col. 1349A] at Fornes, two quarters of grain in the holding of John, son of Arnulf of Rua, and in that of Richard Israel, given by Ralph of Fornes; at Holy Trinity of the Wood, two holdings of land; at Neuville, two fields of land—the Marine Field and the Castle Field—given by T. of St Pancras and his son H.; at Longueville, three acres of land, given by R. of St-Lô; at Noir-Palud, the whole *mouta* of the land of Pellevilain, given by R. and his son; at Grimouville, one acre of land, given by Alan; at Tourville, one holding of three acres and half a virgate, given by William of St John; at Heenvilla, the tithe from [Col. 1349B] the fair and the fisheries of that village; at Tourville, all his lordship between the two valleys; at Saint-Lô, one mina of grain, given by Jordan of Sainteville from his mill; at Mortua Femina, the whole fief of Geoffrey Maugier, given by William of Angerville and his wife B.; at Cortis, the salt tithe from the entire revenue of Ralph de Fougères, given by him; at Meurdracheria, the tithe of the mill, given by Robert Murdrac; given by Hugh of St Denis, three quarters of grain from the mill of that village; at Grimouville, two sheaves of tithes from all the land of William of St John; in the same village, given by that same man, at Tribehou, the holding of William Vassal [Col. 1349C] with two acres of land, one old fishing-right, and two sheaves of tithe from his whole fief at Tribou, given by Ambrose; at Romeia, two sheaves of tithes from the whole lordship of William and T. de Piris and his wife G.; beside Lucerne, the hill overlooking Lucerne Abbey, given by Robert, Abbot of Mont-Saint-Michel; likewise, the agreement made between you and the monks of Mont-Saint-Michel concerning the danger from the sea, concerning the church of St John and your other holdings, insofar as it was made without fraud, accepted by both sides, and contained in the public instrument made concerning it—we confirm it by apostolic authority.

Moreover, no one shall presume to exact from you tithes of your newly cultivated lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or of the fodder of your animals. You may also receive into conversion free and unencumbered clerics or laypersons fleeing the secular life, and retain them without any opposition. In the parish churches which you possess, you may install four or three of your canons, one of whom you shall present to the diocesan bishop, so that they may answer to him concerning spiritual matters, but to you concerning temporal matters and observance of the order. Furthermore, we forbid anyone to presume to build a new church or oratory within the boundaries of your parishes without the assent of the diocesan bishop and yourselves, saving nevertheless the privileges of the Roman Church. When a general interdict has been imposed upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding [Col. 1350A] excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. Further, by apostolic authority we forbid any archbishop, bishop, or their official to dare, without manifest and reasonable cause, to pronounce a sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict against you or your church, or to impose upon you or your churches new or unlawful exactions. We also decree that burial in your church shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last wishes of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while preserving the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of this place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed in charge there by any deceitful device or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine. [Col. 1350B] Wishing also to provide henceforth with paternal solicitude for your peace and tranquillity, we forbid by apostolic authority anyone to dare within the boundaries of your lands or granges to commit violence, robbery, or theft; to set fire; or to seize or kill a person. We likewise forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in the same place, to leave it without his abbot’s permission, except to enter a stricter religious order; and no one shall dare retain a departing brother without letters of the community attesting the matter. We regard as ratified the liberties, immunities, reasonable customs, and dignities hitherto observed in your church, and decree that they shall remain unimpaired for all time. We also forbid a benefice of your church, personally conferred upon anyone, to be transferred without the permission of the abbot and chapter. [Col. 1350C]

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away or retain its possessions once taken, or harass it with any vexations; rather, let all things be preserved intact and be of every benefit to the uses for which they were granted, for the governance and support of those concerned, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes fitting satisfaction for his offence, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know that he stands guilty of divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

[Col. 1351A] I, Urban, Bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Conrad, Bishop of Sabina and Archbishop of Mainz. I, Theodoric, Bishop of the See of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Henry, Bishop of Albano. I, Theobald, Bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Mark. I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the title of the Twelve Apostles. I, Albinus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Melior, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, title of Pammachius. [Col. 1351B] I, Adelard, cardinal priest of the title of St Marcellus. I, Ardino, cardinal deacon of St Theodore. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Soffredus, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Via Lata. I, Roland, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Ralph, cardinal deacon of St George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Verona by the hand of Transmundus, notary of the Holy Roman Church, 11 January, in the fourth indiction, in the year 1186 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban III. [Col. 1351C]

XII. To all bishops.—Concerning his election. (Verona, 12 January.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 496.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the archbishops and bishops, and to his beloved sons the abbots, priors, and other prelates of churches to whom these letters shall come, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The heavenly height of counsel, retaining firm authority in its ordering, founded the most holy Roman Church—which, though unworthy, we have been appointed to govern—securely upon the rock of faith. It bestowed on her that foundation in the strength of apostolic confession over which neither the storm of a whirlwind nor the blast of a tempest can prevail. Thus the universal mother Church, retaining with herself the Saviour who abides until the end of the world, embraces Him whom she loves, according to Solomon’s song (Song of Songs 3), so that no change of circumstances or times may separate her from the unity of her faith or the purpose of her devotion. Although she may often have fallen into various dangers through the frequent succession of departing shepherds, or endured countless persecutions and labours through the assaults of worldly malice, divine grace has nevertheless never deserted her, but has caused [Col. 1352A] her strength to increase in every temptation and enabled her to obtain the joy of her hope from the very source from which she received the foundation of faith.

Thus, a few days ago, when the Lord gave her a sign for good, although no small grief and sorrow troubled her at the passing of the pious Father Lucius, divine providence nevertheless preserved her condition in the unity of the Spirit and bond of peace. After evening weeping, morning joy succeeded; and she, like a most beautiful dove gladdened by her own sighs, retained the beauty of her brightness wholly without wrinkle or blemish. For when our Father and predecessor, Lord Pope Lucius of pious memory, had died and his most reverend body had been honourably buried, the brethren held deliberation concerning the election of a successor. In this [Col. 1352B] there was such unity among all and such mutual harmony in each that it must be understood that He worked in them in whose hand are the hearts of all and through whom diversity of minds is made one.

Moreover, although there were in the Church of God many venerable and prudent men upon whom their votes might, as we believe, have more wisely and worthily converged, they turned their eyes toward our insufficiency. It came about, as pleased the Lord, that they chose us—though neither strength nor merits recommend us for the summit of so great a dignity—as father and shepherd for themselves. Although we were conscious of our own weakness and believed not without reason that their decision ought to be resisted, nevertheless, lest danger arise in the Church from delay in the business [Col. 1352C] or stubborn resistance, we consented, though unwillingly, to undertake the labour of the burden laid upon us. We hope that our steps will be directed by Him who gave blessed Peter, sailing amid the waves, confidence to descend upon the sea and powerfully came to meet him lest he perish when he doubted (Matthew 14).

Now, therefore, established in that place and office in which we greatly need the assistance of the prayers of all the faithful, we turn to you with confidence and security as special sons of the Roman Church. Preceding you with the address of apostolic blessing, we admonish you by these familiar letters, earnestly entreat and exhort you in the Lord: follow the passing of the aforesaid Father and our lord Lucius with the devoted support of prayers, and show especially to us the faith and devotion which all generally owe, out of reverence for the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and the Apostolic See; so that by this you may obtain a reward from God and may always deserve greater favour in our eyes and in those of the whole Church. [Col. 1352D]

Given at Verona, 12 January.

XIII. To B[aldwin], Archbishop of Canterbury.—Of the same purport and in precisely the same words as the preceding. (Verona, January?)

[GILBERT FOLIOT, *Letters*, ed. Giles, II, 114.]

XIV. He announces to the bishops and all persons established throughout the province of Canterbury that his vicariate in their province has been entrusted to Archbishop B[aldwin]. (Verona, January.)

[TWISDEN, *Historical Writers of England*, X, I, 630.]

[Col. 1353A]

Pope URBAN to his brother bishops and to all persons established throughout the province of Canterbury.

Turning the eyes of our paternal care toward the English Church, we have decreed, with the common counsel of our brethren, that provision be made for its welfare and its spiritual advancement in Christ: our venerable brother B., Archbishop of Canterbury—whose merits, virtue, wisdom, and learning are jointly the joy of the universal Church—having received the office of legate, shall exercise our authority throughout the province subject to him, for the honour of the Church and the welfare and peace of the whole realm. [Col. 1353B]

XV. Privilege for the monastery of St Sixtus at Piacenza. (Verona, 20 January.)

[AFFO, *History of Guastalla*, I, 347.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot of the monastery of St Sixtus, situated at Piacenza, and the brethren of the same house, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

We read in the prophets that Almighty God, threatening a people who transgressed against Him and did not walk in His commandments, fulfilled His threats sufficiently by uprooting them from their territory. We read also in other books that different peoples were driven from their homes for their iniquities, and that others were placed in their stead by God’s judgment. We see this judgment of divine ordering fulfilled in the monastery of Blessed Sixtus at Piacenza. For, after holy women had lived there for many years, they subsequently abandoned the discipline of the regular order, fell into the precipices of vice, and the great abundance of possessions bestowed upon that monastery by kings and other faithful servants of God was seriously diminished and destroyed. Therefore, by the counsel of wise and religious men, and especially through the action of Countess Matilda of illustrious memory, provision was made [Col. 1353D] that men should be installed in that monastery in place of women, so that the same religious observance—the monastic order—might be maintained there, and that the possessions of the monastery, long alienated, might be restored through their industry.

This change ordained in the administration of that place, by God’s authority and following the example of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs of happy memory Paschal II, Anastasius IV, and Lucius III, we confirm by this document of privilege. We establish that a community of men who are servants of God shall remain there in perpetuity under the observance of the monastic order. We decree that the place itself and everything belonging to it shall be kept under the guardianship and protection of the Apostolic See, free from the molestation of any aggressors, as is known to have been established by our predecessors, the pontiffs of the Roman Church. [Col. 1354A] We also establish that all estates and possessions which Angelberga, empress and foundress of that monastery, is known to have bestowed upon it, and whatever villages, household dependants, cells, churches, or other possessions lawfully belong to that monastery, or may hereafter be justly and canonically acquired through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to us and to your successors.

Moreover, we likewise confirm to you by authority of the Apostolic See, following in the footsteps of Pope Adrian III of holy memory, the tithes of your newly cultivated lands and of your other lands which you hold by gift of the bishops of Piacenza, Cremona, Lodi, Reggio, Modena, and Mantua, in their parishes, just as they were confirmed to your monastery and to your parish churches and chapels in his privilege. [Col. 1354B] You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and ordinations of monks or clerics who are to be promoted to holy orders from the diocesan bishop, provided he is Catholic, has the grace and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to furnish these to you freely and without any abuse. Otherwise, you may approach whichever bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of this place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed in charge there through any fraudulent contrivance or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict, from their own community or, if necessary, from another. Whatever liberty or dignity has been granted to the aforesaid monastery by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, through authentic documents of privilege, and has hitherto been observed, we also grant by the authority of this privilege and decree to remain valid in future times. [Col. 1354C]

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may, etc. [Col. 1354D] If anyone therefore, etc. But upon all persons, etc.

I, Urban, Bishop of the Catholic Church. I, John, cardinal priest of St Mark. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of St Mary across the Tiber, title of Callistus. I, Theodinus, Bishop of the See of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Henry, Bishop of Albano. I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the title of the Twelve Apostles. I, Albinus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Melior, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, title of Pammachius. [Col. 1355A] I, Adelard, cardinal priest of the title of St Marcellus. I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of St Theodore. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Roland, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Radulf, cardinal deacon of St George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Verona by the hand of Transmundus, notary of the Holy Roman Church, 20 January, in the fourth indiction, in the year 1185 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban III.

XVI. He takes under protection the Church of St Mary of Reno and confirms its possessions and rights. (Verona, 27 January.)

[TROMBELLI, *Memoirs of Reno*, 378.]

[Col. 1355B]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HUGH, prior of the Church of St Mary of Reno, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Although, unworthy as we are, the care and solicitude of all churches have been entrusted to us, we are bound to exercise pastoral care for the condition of your church and, insofar as the Lord grants us, to devote diligent attention to your peace. Therefore, that you may be fortified by apostolic protection against the assaults of the wicked, moved by your devout prayers and just petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves your church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. We establish that the canonical order known to have been instituted in that church according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be inviolably observed there in perpetuity. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, with the Lord’s help, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. [Col. 1355D] We have thought it proper to specify these in their own terms:

The place itself on which the aforesaid church has been built, with all its appurtenances; the church of St. Andrew at Turicella; the church of St. Domninus near Bagno; the church of the Holy Saviour. The possessions which belonged to Gerard de Sala, with tithes, revenues, and all their appurtenances. The hospital of Casaiola with its appurtenances; the church of St. Praxedes, as it was granted to you by our predecessors of pious memory, Anastasius, Alexander, and Lucius, Roman pontiffs, saving the right and reverence due to the cardinal who shall for the time being be attached to that church. The church of St. James called Casadei, with its appurtenances; the bridge situated beside your church over the Reno, with its possessions. [Col. 1356A] We also hold ratified and confirmed the liberties and immunities reasonably granted by Henry and Gerard, bishops of Bologna of blessed memory, to your church and to your other churches named above: namely, that, with all their goods, movable and immovable alike, they shall be wholly free and exempt from every condition, and from the service and tribute of those holding from the bishop—whether monks, clerics, or laypeople—and from the lordship of any person, great or small, except for episcopal right. We decree that these liberties and immunities shall remain unimpaired for all time.

Moreover, you may receive clerics and laypeople fleeing the world, free and absolved, for conversion, and retain them in your church without any contradiction. [Col. 1356B] We further forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in your house, to leave that house without his prior’s permission, except for the purpose of a stricter religious life; and no one shall dare retain one who leaves without the security of your common letters. If any of those brethren should dare remain outside the cloister without the aforesaid permission, and, when warned a second or third time, should perhaps scorn to amend his ways, the prior of that house may pronounce upon him, as one professed to him, a sentence of excommunication. Further, by apostolic authority we confirm to you and to your church [Col. 1356C] the tithes which you have held without disturbance for forty years and are now known to hold peacefully. We also forbid anyone to impose upon you and your church new and undue exactions; rather, we decree that it shall enjoy the same liberty which it is known to have possessed during the forty years elapsed up to the present time. We likewise decree that the burial-ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last wishes of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; yet the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken are preserved.

Furthermore, we grant you the free power to receive the ordinations of your clerics from whichever bishop you prefer, as the bishops mentioned above are known to have granted you that power by authentic documents. We also confirm to you the tithes of your revenues coming from anywhere in the diocese of Bologna, as those same tithes were granted to your church by the prudent foresight of those bishops. [Col. 1356D] Upon the death of you, the present prior of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any trickery of stealth or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall determine ought to be chosen according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine. As a token of the protection and liberty received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay to us and our successors two solidi of Luccan coin every year.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb [Col. 1357A] the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the bishop of Bologna. Should any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter knowingly attempt rashly to act against this page of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he has remedied his fault by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus [Col. 1357B] Christ, our Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to divine vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. Amen. Amen.

*(Place of the seal.)*

I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Theodinus, bishop of the see of Porto and St. Rufina, have subscribed. I, Henry, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri, have subscribed. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Mark, have subscribed. [Col. 1357C] I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Calixtus at St. Mary across the Tiber, have subscribed. I, Pandulphus, priest-cardinal of the title of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed. I, Albinus, priest-cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed. I, Melior, priest-cardinal of the title of Pammachius, SS. John and Paul, have subscribed. I, Adelard, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Marcellus, have subscribed. I, Arditio, deacon-cardinal of St. Theodore, have subscribed. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of SS. Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Soffredus, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed. I, Rolland, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Portico, have subscribed. [Col. 1357D] I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed. I, Radulphus, deacon-cardinal of St. George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Transmundus, notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February [27 January], in the fourth indiction, in the year 1185 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban III.

## XVII. He receives the Venetian church of the Holy Saviour into protection and confirms its possessions and privileges.  
*(Verona, 5 February.)*

*[CORNELIUS, Eccles. Venet., XIV, 112.]*

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1358A] sons GREGORY, prior of the church of the Holy Saviour at Rialto, and his brethren, present and future, professing the canonical life, forever.

Those who choose the religious life ought to have apostolic protection at hand, lest perhaps an assault of any rash person either draw them back from their purpose or—God forbid!—weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, Innocent, Eugenius, Anastasius, Alexander, and Lucius, Roman pontiffs, we receive the aforesaid church of the Holy Saviour, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document.

[Col. 1358B] First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order known to have been established in that place according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have thought fit to specify among them the following in their proper names: the place itself on which the aforesaid church stands, with all its appurtenances; likewise the houses, lands, vineyards, saltworks, and whatever rights you possess at Clugia; the mill and [Col. 1358C] lands which you possess at Barbano; in the territory of Dese, the mill and holding, with vineyards, woods, and their other appurtenances, as the noble men Leonard, Philip, and Rigettus, sons of the late Gerard de Inginulfo, gave them to your church; the lands of Liguentia, the lands of Flumisello, the lands of Marsiliaco, and the lands of Sacco; and one half of the tithes paid by parishioners of your church, as our predecessor Pope Eugenius of blessed memory ordered, and as John Polanus, formerly diocesan bishop, granted you by his privilege. We confirm these to you by apostolic authority, both for the clergy and for repairing the *sartatecta*—the church roofs and structures.

And, so that a sentence of excommunication may be pronounced through the prior of your church upon parishioners who presume to defraud you of half of those tithes, [Col. 1358D] we grant him full power, as our predecessors of happy memory, Adrian, Alexander, and Lucius, Roman pontiffs, are known to have granted in their writings. We further grant you, as is known to have been granted by those aforesaid predecessors, that the prior of your house for the time being may freely furnish security for those tithes in accordance with the custom of the land. You may also receive clerics and laypeople fleeing the world, free and absolved, for conversion, and retain them in your church without anyone’s objection. Moreover, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, to leave the cloister without his prior’s permission. No one shall dare retain one who leaves without the security of common letters. Further, we confirm by apostolic authority the judgment reasonably delivered by our venerable brother Henry, patriarch of Grado, and Ildeprandus of blessed memory, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles and then legate of the Apostolic See, concerning the controversy formerly long contested between you and Dominic, parish priest of St. Bartholomew, over certain parochial houses—namely, the houses of the Justi, the Maroceni, the Gradonici, the Greeks, Leonard Fradelli, and Dominic Aureus—which each person claimed as belonging to his own right, as is known to be contained in their authentic document made on this matter. We likewise decree that the burial-ground of that [Col. 1359B] place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last wishes of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; yet the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken is preserved. We decree that no one, without your consent, may dare give or impose penance upon your parishioners when they are ill, or receive them for burial, unless the rights of your church established by the sacred canons are preserved.

[Col. 1359A] Upon the death of you, the present prior of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it through any trickery of stealth or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall canonically determine ought to be chosen according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb your church, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

Should any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter knowingly attempt rashly to act against this page of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he has remedied his fault by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity [Col. 1359D] of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to divine vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and St. Rufina, have subscribed. I, Henry, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri, have subscribed. [Col. 1360A] I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Calixtus at St. Mary across the Tiber, have subscribed. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Mark, have subscribed. I, Pandulphus, priest-cardinal of the title of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed. I, Albinus, priest-cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed. I, Meliorus, priest-cardinal of the title of SS. John and Paul, have subscribed. I, Adelard, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Marcellus, have subscribed. I, Arditio, deacon-cardinal of St. Theodore, have subscribed. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of SS. Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Soffredus, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed. I, Roland, deacon-cardinal [Col. 1360B] of St. Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed. I, Radulphus, deacon-cardinal of St. George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Transmundus, notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of February [5 February], in the fourth indiction, in the year 1186 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban III.

## XVIII. Privilege for the monastery of St. James of Pontida.  
*(Verona, 5 February.)*

*[LUPUS, cod. diplom. Bergom., II, 1359.]*

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GUIDO, prior of the lord St. James of Pontida, [Col. 1360C] and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

To those choosing the religious life, etc. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, and, following the example of Urban, Innocent, Celestine, and Lucius, Roman pontiffs of happy memory, receive the aforesaid monastery of St. James of Pontida, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in the same monastery according to God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the institution of the Cluniacs shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire through grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have thought fit to specify among them the following by their proper names.

The place itself where the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; one chapel with tithes and its other appurtenances; the church of St. Zeno at Prezate, and the chapels of St. George and St. Alexius, with tithes and their other appurtenances. [Col. 1361A] At Medolaco, the church of St. Mary, etc.; at Pompenico, the church of St. Michael with its appurtenances; at Marne, the church of St. Bartholomew with all its appurtenances; at Morengo, the chapel of St. John of Rovedo, a third part of the tithe of that place, and that which is called `[lacuna]`; also the right which Gregory, bishop of Bergamo of blessed memory, gave you in that church by a pious grant; the whole village of Morengo, its castle and court, and whatever you possess there, as you have peacefully possessed it for forty years past. The tithes and possessions which it has (sic) at Carpeneto; at Cerno, possessions and the chapel of St. Justina with its tithe and other appurtenances; at Montenusio, the chapel of St. George with all [Col. 1361B] its appurtenances, and the tithe of that estate; whatever you possess in the district of that place; and whatever you possess, whether by donation of John, bishop of Lodi of blessed memory, or by sale or the offering of many faithful persons, as is contained in that bishop’s authentic document. We likewise confirm to you by apostolic authority the settlement made between you and Guido de Cuziago and his brothers by amicable agreement, as it is contained in public instruments and has been accepted by both parties. At Paterno, the chapel of St. Andrew with its appurtenances, and the churches of St. Peter and St. John; at Clozago, the chapel of St. Mary with its appurtenances; at Glarola, the monastery of SS. Nazarius and Celsus with its appurtenances; the possessions which you have at Arcii. We also confirm all rights and possessions, whether held as fiefs or otherwise, which your monastery has possessed without interruption for forty years, by proprietary and *libellary* right, and of which it now has possession. [Col. 1361C] Further, by apostolic authority, we confirm to you and your successors the privilege concerning written *libelli* which our most illustrious son in Christ, Frederick, ever August Emperor of the Romans, granted to the aforesaid monastery.

No one shall presume to demand or extort tithes from you of your newly cultivated lands (*novalia*), which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals. You may also receive clerics or laypeople fleeing the world, free and absolved, for conversion, and retain them without any objection. When a general interdict has been imposed upon the land, you may celebrate the offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. [Col. 1361D] We further decree that the burial-ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and Christian wish of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; yet the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken are preserved.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or disturb it with any other vexations; but [Col. 1362A] that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

Should any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter knowingly attempt rashly to act against this page of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he has amended his fault by appropriate satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may the peace of [Col. 1362B] our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

*(The subscriptions of the pope and cardinals, the monogram, the year of the pontificate, etc., are missing.)*

`[lacuna]`, in the year of the Lord 1185, on the seventh day before the Kalends of March [23 February], in the fourth indiction. Given at Verona through the hand of Transcendilus, notary of the Holy Roman Church.

## XIX–XX. Privilege for the church of St. Mary of Spoleto.  
*(Verona, 27 February.)*

*[UGHELLI, Italia sacra, I, 1261.]*

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1362C] sons MATTHEW, provost of the church of St. Mary of Spoleto, and the brethren, present and future, canonically appointed, forever.

Whenever a request is made to us which is known to be fitting for religion and uprightness, it befits us willingly to grant it and to afford suitable support to the petitioners’ wishes. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, and, following the example of our predecessor Alexander II, Roman pontiff of happy memory, receive the aforesaid church of St. Mary of Spoleto, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that church now [Col. 1362D] justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire through grants of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have thought fit to specify among them the following by their proper names: the place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the parish church of St. John in Campo, and the tithe of St. Mary in Campo, with the tithe of Azzanina Fracta; the parish church of St. Gregory in Nido; the estate of St. Angel in Capite with all holdings subject to it; the parish church of Verclano; the parish church of Turino; the parish church of Bernano; the parish church of Lederano; and three parts of the tithe of the whole city of Spoleto, together with three parts of the offerings of the living and the dead.

[Col. 1363A] Furthermore, by this present decree we ordain that the liberties and immunities granted to that church by kings, princes, and other persons, ecclesiastical and secular alike, and its ancient and reasonable customs, shall remain whole and unimpaired. When a general interdict has been imposed upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. We further decree that the burial-ground of that church shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last wishes of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; yet the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken are preserved. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb [Col. 1363B] the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. Should any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter knowingly presume rashly to act against this page of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he has remedied his fault by appropriate satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred [Col. 1363C] body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Adelard, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Marcellus. I, Arditio, deacon-cardinal of St. Theodore. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of SS. Cosmas and Damian. ## XXI. He receives the monastery of St. Mary of Civitacula into protection and confirms its goods and rights.  
*(Verona, 27 February.)*

*[MORIONDI, Monumenta Aquensia, I, 84.]*

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons NICHOLAS, abbot of the monastery of St. Mary of Civitacula, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

Those who choose the religious life ought to have apostolic protection at hand, lest perhaps an assault of any rash person either draw them back from their purpose or—God forbid!—weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, [Col. 1364B] beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; we receive the aforesaid monastery of St. Mary of Civitacula, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in that place according to God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the institutes of the Cistercian brethren shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire through grants of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired [Col. 1364C] to you and your successors. We have thought fit to specify among them the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the site of the mill, which on the river Urbe `[lacuna]`; the grange of Castrum Vetus with its appurtenances; the chestnut groves of Noveleto; the chestnut groves of Gorreello; the house situated in the valley of Marchio, with its appurtenances; the house of Caxa with its appurtenances; the house of Campello with its appurtenances; the chestnut groves of Dondanina with their appurtenances; the wine-cellar of Varagine with its appurtenances. No one shall presume to extort from you tithes of the labour which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of [Col. 1364D] your animals.

You may also receive all clerics and laypeople fleeing the world, free and absolved, for conversion, and retain them without any objection. Moreover, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in your house, to leave that house without the abbot’s permission; no one shall dare retain one who leaves without the security of common letters. If anyone should perhaps presume to retain them, you may pronounce, by our authority, the regular sentence upon your monks or *conversi*. Further, desiring with paternal concern to provide for your peace and tranquillity, by apostolic authority we forbid anyone within the enclosures of your places or granges rashly to commit robbery or theft, set fire, seize a person, or kill a person. If bishops demand anything from abbots of your order beyond the obedience owed, or if princes of the land demand anything contrary to the liberty of the order granted by our predecessors and ourselves, the same abbots may, by apostolic authority, refuse what is demanded, lest on that pretext the aforesaid order, hitherto free, be bound in any way by the chain of servitude. If those bishops should for this reason pronounce any sentence against your churches or persons, [Col. 1365A] we decree that the same sentence shall be annulled as one pronounced contrary to grants of the Apostolic See.

[Col. 1365B] We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. Should any person therefore, etc.

## XXII. He receives the monastery of Cluny into protection and, at Abbot Hugh’s request, confirms certain goods and privileges.  
*(Verona, 4 March.)*

*[Bibliotheca Cluniac., 1447.]*

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HUGH, abbot of Cluny, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

The more especially your church is subject to us directly, without [Col. 1366A] intermediary, the more earnestly we are bound to provide for its rights, lest over time it be burdened by undue molestation concerning those things which it is known to possess lawfully. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, following the example of our predecessor Pope Alexander of happy memory, we receive the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in your monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods [Col. 1366B] that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire through grants of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have thought fit to specify among them the following by their proper names: the place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the priory of St. Mary of Nazara with all its appurtenances; the priory of the Holy Trinity of Lentona with all its appurtenances, as your church canonically possesses those priories, and as the donation of the aforesaid priory of St. Mary is contained in an authentic document. We confirm them to you and to that church by apostolic authority.

[Col. 1366C] No one shall presume to demand or extort tithes from you of your newly cultivated lands (*novalia*), which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals. You may also receive clerics or laypeople fleeing the world, free and absolved, for conversion, and retain them without any objection. We further forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, to depart from it without his abbot’s permission, unless for the purpose of a stricter religious life; and no one shall dare retain one who leaves without common authorization. We further decree that the burial-ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last wishes of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict [Col. 1366D]; yet the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken are preserved. Since tithes are known to have been assigned to ministers of churches under both the Old and the New Law, under threat of anathema we forbid any layperson to presume to demand or extort tithes from you. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. Should any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter [Col. 1367A] knowingly attempt rashly to act against this page of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he has remedied his fault by appropriate satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. [Col. 1367B] I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Mark, have subscribed. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of the title of Calixtus, have subscribed. I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed. I, Albinus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed. I, Melior, cardinal priest of the title of Pammachius of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed. I, Adelard, cardinal priest of the title of St. Marcellus, have subscribed. I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina and archbishop of Mainz, have subscribed.
