I, Hyacinth, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Bobo, deacon-cardinal of the title of St. Angelo, have subscribed. I, Octavian, deacon-cardinal of the title of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of the title of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed. [Col. 1394C] I, Pandulph, deacon-cardinal of the title of St. George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed.

Given at Verona through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June [22 May], in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1186, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban III.

### XXXVIII. He takes under protection the monastery of St. Mary Magdalene of Louth (in England), and confirms its possessions and rights.  
*(Verona, 28 May.)*

[Monasticon Anglicanum, I, 663.]

[Col. 1394D]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the prior and monks of the Church of St. Mary Magdalene of Louth, present and future, professing the regular life: for a memorial.

Since, though unworthy, we have been raised by the providence of the divine ordering to govern the universal Church, whenever matters concerning the protection of churches are sought from us, it is fitting that we graciously yield to the desires of those who petition and bring their wishes to effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid Church of St. Mary Magdalene of Louth, in which you are devoted to divine service, [Col. 1395A] and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. First, indeed, we establish that the monastic order known to have been instituted in your church according to God and the Rule of St. Benedict shall be observed there inviolably for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire through the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, through the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these we have thought it proper to specify the following by their own names:

The site upon which the aforesaid church stands, [Col. 1395B] with its appurtenances. By the donation of Adam, son of Swan: Bretton, with all its appurtenances; the mills of Derna; his father’s Lund; and Carleton, with its appurtenances; the church of Roriston, with its appurtenances; Neuhale, Rameberg, and Lunthewait; all that he held in Brampton; the mill of Neuhale; and everything belonging to the aforesaid lands. At Halethun, half a carucate of land; the mill of Chirmktschalyc; and twelve pence in Wdehusun. By the donation of Robert de Stapleton: the land of Chudewrda. By the donation of Adam of Flyisthil: four acres of land in the same village. By the donation of Swan of Derfeld: eight acres of land at Erdesley. By the donation of Henry, son of Swan: eight shillings from half a carucate of land in Wrangbrock. [Col. 1395C] By the donation of the nobleman W. de Nefvilla and his wife Amabilis: the mill of Langedenedale.

It shall also be lawful for you to receive for conversion clerics or laymen fleeing from the world, free and absolved, and to retain them without any opposition.

Moreover, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from departing it without the permission of his prior, except for the sake of a stricter religious life; and no one shall dare retain one who has departed without letters of the community giving assurance. Indeed, let no one presume to demand or extort from you [Col. 1395D] tithes of your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the produce of your animals. We also hold valid the liberties and immunities reasonably granted to you, your church, or your men by ecclesiastical or secular persons, and the reasonable customs observed in your church up to now; and we decree that they shall remain unimpaired in future times, etc.

Given [lacuna] through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June [28 May], in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1186, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban III.

### XXXIX. He takes the Church of Canne under protection and confirms its goods and episcopal rights, at the request of Bishop Boniface.  
*(Verona, 31 May.)*

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, VII, 793.]

[Col. 1396A]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother BONIFACE, bishop of Canne, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

By the office of apostolic authority laid upon us, we ought to love our brethren and fellow bishops [lacuna] with the affection of charity, and to preserve in their entirety the dignity and rights of the churches in which they serve. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the Church of Canne, [Col. 1396B] over which, by the Lord’s authority, you are known to preside, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. We establish that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and peacefully possesses, or may hereafter acquire through the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, through the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought it proper to specify the following by their own names: the church of St. James in the city of Canne, with its appurtenances; the church of St. Lucy; the church of St. Saviour in the Castle; the church of St. George; the church of St. Mercurius; the church of St. Mary by the Sea, with its hamlet and holdings; [Col. 1396C] the church of St. Mary in Pecto; the church of St. Mary in Campo Grasso, situated near the hamlet of St. Cassian; the church of St. Mary in the Borough of the Bridge; the church of St. Nicholas in Baldetta; the church of St. Clericus; the church of St. Peter in Ancello; the church of St. Anastasia; the church of St. Felix; the church of St. Apollinaris; the church of St. Panti; the church of St. Mary of the Saltworks; the church of St. Stephen; the church of the Holy Trinity; the church of St. Vitus; the church of St. Nicholas of Petra; likewise the men whom they have at Canne; the hamlet of St. Cassian with its holdings and possessions; and the hamlet of St. Eustace with all its possessions and appurtenances.

We prohibit anyone, within the bounds of your bishopric, from presuming to build anew a chapel or oratory without your consent, saving the privileges of Roman pontiffs. We further establish that, where any of your parishioners has chosen burial at some church of religious persons by his last will, the canonical portion due to your church from the testament shall be preserved. We forbid anyone to presume to admit those whom you have interdicted or excommunicated to the office or to ecclesiastical communion, unless perhaps danger of death is imminent, so that, when he cannot have your presence, he must be absolved by another form of the Church after satisfaction has first been rendered. We also hold valid the ancient customs, liberties, and immunities reasonably granted to that church and observed hitherto, and decree that they shall remain unimpaired in future times. [Col. 1397A]

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain possessions removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole, for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the apostolic see and the due reverence owed to the Church of Bari. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he correct his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be separated from the most sacred [Col. 1397B] body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights to that place, may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good conduct and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Mark. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Susanna. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of St. Mary across the Tiber, of the title of St. Callistus. [Col. 1397C] I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the title of the Twelve Apostles. I, Albinus, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Melior, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, James, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Bobo, deacon-cardinal of St. Angelo. I, Octavian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.

Given at Verona through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Kalends of June [31 May], in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1187, in the first year of the pontificate [Col. 1397D] of Pope Urban III.

### XL. At the request of Patriarch Henry, he takes the Church of Grado under protection and confirms its privileges.  
*(Verona, 31 May.)*

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, V, 1131.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, patriarch of Grado, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

We are shown to perform usefully the duty of apostolic dignity and the obligation of the stewardship entrusted to us when, with provident care, we safeguard the dignity conferred upon every church and strive to preserve whole and unimpaired the rights of individual churches. [Col. 1398A] For as it is not proper that anything unjustly sought should be granted to anyone, so it is fitting that we deny no one what is his by right. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, Patriarch Henry, gladly concurring with your just petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the Church of Grado, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document.

Accordingly, adhering to the precedents of our predecessors of blessed memory, Pelagius, Alexander, Urban II, Adrian, Alexander III, and Lucius—and especially maintaining the tenor of that constitution which our predecessor Pope Leo IX enacted and confirmed by synodal judgment and a charter of privilege—we grant to you and your canonically appointed successors patriarchal [Col. 1398B] dignity, and confirm the exercise of authority over the Church of Grado only within those boundaries established for that church by the aforesaid predecessors. We also grant that the cross may be borne before you, except when you are in Rome or in the presence or company of the Roman pontiff. Likewise, from the generosity of the apostolic see, we confer upon your brotherhood the pallium—that is, the fullness of pontifical office—which you shall remember to use within your church in celebrating the solemnities of Mass on the days on which your predecessors are known to have used it: namely, at the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, the Presentation (*Hypapante*), the three feasts of St. Mary, the Lord’s Supper, Holy Saturday, the Lord’s Resurrection, Ascension, Pentecost, the Nativity of St. John the Baptist, and of all [Col. 1398C] the Apostles; also on the feasts of St. Mark, St. Stephen the protomartyr, St. Lawrence, St. Martin, the solemnity of All Saints, and the principal feasts of your church; as well as at the consecration of churches, bishops, and other clerics, and on the anniversary of your consecration.

We wish you to uphold that dignity in every good respect: namely, in correcting your subjects, let reason have more power with you than authority; let the good find you a gentle corrector, and the wicked a kindly one; love persons and pursue the vices of those subject to you, lest, if you choose to act otherwise, correction pass into cruelty and you lose those whom you desire to amend. Thus you must cut away the wound [Col. 1398D] without injuring what is sound; lest, if the blade is applied more deeply than the case demands, it harm the one whom you hasten to help. Instead, let each be tempered by the other, so that the good may have, in love, something to beware of, and the wicked, in fear, something to love.

Furthermore, lest the aforesaid Church of Grado, committed to your rule and administration and enjoying the prerogative of honor through the favor of the apostolic see, should, because of the smallness of its patriarchate, be considered lower and more insignificant by the simple-minded, we grant it by apostolic authority primacy over the archbishopric of Zadar and its bishoprics. We establish you and your successors as presiding over the archbishop of Zadar and his bishops of the time in the dignity of primacy, and as conferring consecration upon that archbishop, while reserving to the Roman pontiff the grant of the pallium. [Col. 1399A]

We also establish that whatever goods and possessions the Church of Grado now justly and canonically holds, or may hereafter acquire by lawful means through God’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Moreover, we freely confirm to you and your successors the churches located within your bishopric which religious men have offered to the Church of Grado itself, so that no bishop may, without your consent, perform consecrations in them or forbid the divine offices to priests serving the Lord in them, for so long as you are in those places. We decree, therefore, that no one, etc. If anyone, etc. But upon all, [Col. 1399B] etc.

I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Henry, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri, have subscribed. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Mark, have subscribed. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Sabina, have subscribed. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of St. Mary across the Tiber, of the title of St. Callistus, have subscribed. I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the title of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed. I, Melior, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius, have subscribed. I, Adelard, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Marcellus, have subscribed. [Col. 1399C] I, James, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Octavian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Sofredus, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed. I, Roland, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed. I, Radulf, deacon-cardinal of St. George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed.

Given at Verona through the hand of Moses, acting in place of the chancellor, on the second day before the Kalends of June [31 May], in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1186, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban III. [Col. 1399D]

### XLI. He confirms the statutes and privileges of the Order of Arrouaise (Aridagamantine/Aroasian).  
*(Verona, 2 June.)*

[Würdtwein, *Subsidia diplomatica*, XII, 139.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GALTER, abbot of the church of St. Nicholas of Arrouaise, and the abbots and brethren of his society and order, present and future, regularly appointed, in perpetuity.

It belongs to ecclesiastical discipline to prohibit what is unlawful and beneficially cut away the faults of excesses; if this is neglected by a negligent master, all things fall into confusion. For if one destroys while another [Col. 1400A] builds, or if someone, following his own will, diminishes while another adds, not only is regular order dissolved, but material for perdition is thereby supplied. Therefore, beloved abbots, sons in the Lord, let it be your concern to love persons and pursue vices; let the good find you gentle and the wicked find you correctors. For it is blameworthy entirely to relax the punishment owed for wrongdoing; and let each be tempered by the other, so that the good may have in love something to beware of, and the wicked, in fear, something to love. Moreover, religion pleasing to God is then rightly directed and the vigor of ecclesiastical order is preserved indissolubly when a definite rule and proper discipline are established for its protection.

Whatever, through the working of the Holy Spirit, the zeal of the canonical order in the church of St. Nicholas of Arrouaise [Col. 1400B] acceptably observes according to the Rule of St. Augustine, we have been pleased, following the example of our predecessor Pope Innocent of blessed memory, to confirm your purpose by the authority of the apostolic see and to exhort you by pious admonitions to persist firmly in it.

We therefore establish that in your churches, in which brethren professing the canonical life dwell, no person whatsoever may alter the order established there according to the Rule of St. Augustine. Nor shall any bishop in future dare to expel brethren of that religious order from your churches against the will of, or without consultation with, their own abbots; nor shall anyone professing the canonical life dare depart from those churches [Col. 1400C] or cloisters without the permission of the community. No bishop, abbot, or monk shall receive one who has departed without letters of the community giving assurance.

Since, indeed, some who have been raised from regular observance to the government of churches are the more often corrupted by evil deeds because the envy of the ancient enemy exercises the craft of his deceit against them more destructively, we nevertheless establish by apostolic authority that, if any abbot of your order proves infamous, a transgressor against his order, or useless or harmful to the monastery entrusted to him, then, unless he takes care to correct his offense after being warned a second or third time by the father abbot, that abbot, joining to himself other more discerning and weightier abbots of the same [Col. 1400D] order, shall, by their counsel and consent, punish him with canonical and regular correction. If he proves rebellious against their correction, he shall be deposed by canonical severity through you, son Abbot Galter, and your successors, and also through the four co-abbots who are appointed as arbiters with you in the general chapter to correct the excesses of the order, unless he is willing to resign voluntarily. But if anyone is rightly deposed by your judgment because of his fault, he shall return to the church from which he had been taken, or to another church of the same order, and there lead a regular life under obedience to its abbot.

But if any canons of a church transfer themselves to your order with the consent of their bishop, in order to be formed by your institutions, we decree that they shall be subject, in regular observance, to the church of Arras and to the order, as are the other churches of your order; provided, however, that they shall, without opposition, have regard for that church as daughters do for a mother, in which they are known to have embraced your order. When an abbot of one of your churches dies, the vacant church shall remain under the care of the father abbot, lest it suffer serious loss through lack of a pastor, until another abbot is elected by the brethren upon the advice of that abbot and of two neighboring abbots—unless that church is so far removed from the father abbot that he could not summon it without great loss.

If, however, a dispute arises among the brethren of the monastery regarding the appointment of an abbot, and they cannot be restored to concord, the father abbot, with the counsel and consent of his co-abbots, shall appoint there without opposition the man whom he sees to be supported by the approval of the greater and sounder part of the chapter and by more commendable merits. [Col. 1401B] The person appointed shall then, as is customary, be presented to the diocesan bishop. If, when duly and humbly requested a second or third time, the bishop delays for any reason to confer blessing upon him, then, lest the church meanwhile suffer harm, the elected person shall have free administration until, through the intervention of your general chapter, he canonically obtains from that bishop or his metropolitan, or by the command of the supreme pontiff, what he seeks.

Once blessed, he shall humbly answer to your monastery, as to the head of the order, in the observance of the order; and he shall receive and observe its salutary statutes. Furthermore, by the authority of this present document we forbid any person of another order to be appointed to the office of abbot in any of your churches, except with the consent of the general chapter or by command of the Roman pontiff. Nor may an abbot in any church of your order presume to diminish or alter for the worse the statutes of the general chapter. [Col. 1401C] Furthermore, we confirm to you and to the same order by apostolic authority the annual visitation or summons of those churches which the abbots appointed in the general chapter are bound, according to your custom, to render to the aforesaid churches. [Col. 1401D] No ecclesiastical or secular person may demand a palfrey or anything else for the blessing or enthronement of your abbots. Nor may any of your abbots presume to give it if it is demanded, since the mark and danger of simoniacal depravity are known to threaten both the person demanding and the person giving.

[Col. 1401D] We therefore decree that no one, etc.

I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Henry, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna, have subscribed. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Callistus at Saint Mary in Trastevere, have subscribed. [Col. 1402A] I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the title of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed. I, Albinus, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed. I, Melior, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, of Pammachius, have subscribed. I, Adelard, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, have subscribed. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo, have subscribed. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Roland, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. [Col. 1402B] I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed. I, Ralph, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Albert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Nones of June, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1186, in the first year of the pontificate of lord Pope Urban III.

## XLII. He confirms the possessions and privileges assigned for the support of the canons of the church of Saint Peter, of the churches of Saints John and Paul, Saint Martin, Saint Stephen Major, and Saint Stephen Minor.  
*(Verona, 13 June.)*

*[Vatican Bullarium, I, 68.]*

[Col. 1402C]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles, and the rectors of the four monasteries of Saints John and Paul, Saint Martin, Saint Stephen Major, and Saint Stephen Minor, both those now in office and those canonically to be appointed in the future: for ever.

It is clear to all worshippers of the Christian faith that blessed Peter was established by our Lord Jesus Christ himself, the Savior, as prince of the apostles, and that the power of binding and loosing souls was granted to him by heavenly privilege. Hence it is said to him also: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church; and I shall give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; [Col. 1402D] and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.”

Therefore we, although unworthy, who are vicars of this same Keeper of the Keys of Heaven and occupy his place in the holy Church of God, ought to foster with our protection his special ministers and the patrimonies of the Apostolic See, and defend them against the assaults of wicked men. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we grant due and kindly assent to your petitions, and by the authority of this present document confirm the most holy churches of the blessed martyrs John and Paul, Saint Martin, Saint Stephen Major, and Saint Stephen Minor, assigned for your use and maintenance, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, Sergius II, Leo IV, Leo IX, Innocent II, and Adrian IV, Roman pontiffs. [Col. 1403A] We decree that whatever possessions and goods belong canonically to these venerable places, or may hereafter, by the Lord’s favor, be acquired through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The church of Saint Mary in Caterina, with its parish and all appurtenances, confirmed to you by our predecessor Pope Alexander of blessed memory.

> [Note: [Col. 1403C] This church, now called Saint Catherine della Rota, situated in the Arenula district, is listed by Adrian IV in the preceding diploma, in the year of the common era 1158, among the sacred buildings subject to the Vatican basilica. The Alexander mentioned here was Pope Alexander III of that name. Anibaldus, senator of the Holy City, sets forth his judgment pertinent to the matter at issue in an original diploma issued for the Vatican basilica of Saint Peter in 1224, in these terms:
>
> “We also decree and, by the authority of the sacred senate, ordain that the judgment delivered by lord Pope Alexander III between the canons themselves of the Vatican basilica and the clerics of Saint Lawrence in Damaso concerning the church of Saints Mary and Catherine, together with whatever has been done or written on the matter by him or by other Catholic Roman pontiffs, or others acting for them, shall remain valid and unshaken for all time, [Col. 1403D] and shall be inviolably observed.”
>
> The judgment delivered by Alexander III undoubtedly indicates a dispute that had arisen between the two aforesaid chapters over the church of Saints Mary and Catherine. But what particular controversy was this? If we are not mistaken, it was the same one litigated in the tribunal of the Sacred Roman Rota in the preceding century: namely, whether this church of Saint Catherine was a filial church of Saint Lawrence in Damaso, or rather belonged to the Vatican basilica. Whatever the former dispute may have been, Alexander certainly settled it and adjudged the cause to the canons of Saint Peter. We do not doubt that the supreme pontiff’s judgment was put into effect, since in an old catalogue of churches compiled through the agency of A. Demetrius of Lucca, preserved in a paper codex, p. 65 verso, the following is read:
>
> “Likewise, the church of Saints Mary and Catherine belongs by full right to that basilica [of Saint Peter], with its entire parish. It owes obedience, reverence, and subjection; it must come for [Col. 1404C] scrutiny, baptism, preparation of chrism, and processions. The chapter of that basilica has there the right to ordain, institute, and remove; to correct and temporarily deprive that chapter; and to confirm the archpriest elected by the clerics. On the feast of Saint Catherine, seven of the canons with seven squires or seven servants must go there; these canons, or others to whom they choose to assign the task, must sing the vigils. All of them, together with the squires, must dine after the vigils; at that supper the clerics must serve them good dishes with good wines. For those who choose to remain, they must prepare good beds. In the morning, after Mass has been sung there and preaching delivered, all shall dine there, and good foodstuffs and various good wines must be prepared for them. Afterwards the archpriest must ask that, if there has been any deficiency in the food, they should be indulgent; otherwise, they are prepared to make satisfaction within eight days. And the prior of the canons [Col. 1404D] who is there, if they were well treated at dinner and supper, shall give thanks; otherwise, he shall suspend them for a time from office and benefice.”]

The church of Saint Mary of Palazolo, with all its appurtenances; [Col. 1403B] the church of Saint Savior near Ferriones, built by the aforesaid Pope Leo IV for the burial of all persons from beyond the Alps, with all its uses and appurtenances; the church of Saint Justin, built for the burial of all Lombards and Italians, with all its uses and appurtenances; the church of Saint Peregrine; the church of Saint Mary of the Virgarii; the church of Saint Savior of Cossa Caballi.

At the castle of Bucceja: the church of Saints Marius and Martha, and the church of Saint Lawrence of the same castle. The castle of Bucceja with its estates, hamlets, and all its appurtenances; namely, the estate of Atticiano, Colle, and the estate of Paul; Olivetum with its dependences and other named places, together with the ruined church of Saints Cosmas and Damian; these estates, namely, being situated in the territory of Silva Candida. [Col. 1404A]

The castle of Luterni, with its estates, hamlets, and all appurtenances; the church of Saints John and Paul within that castle; the church of Saint Nicholas at Mesangia (otherwise Mesagna) of the same castle; the church of Saint Andrew outside the same castle, with all its appurtenances; the estate of Greater Sessani and the estate of Lesser Sessani; the small *massa* of Pretoriola, with its houses, lands, and all appurtenances—these estates being situated in the territory of Ceri, near the castle of Luterni, thirty miles from the city of Rome.

The church of Saint Anatolia in the old city of Porto, with the fishery adjoining it, and its lands and *manicae* in Trajan’s territory; the church of Saint Sylvester of Sutri, with the valley called Frictilli and its mills. [Col. 1404B]

The hospital of Ferento, with the oratory of Saint Lawrence and all its appurtenances; the hospital of Narnia, with the chapel of Saint Thomas and all its appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Benedict of Scalocia, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Martin of Spello.

> [Note: [Col. 1404D] This church of Saint Martin is situated in the diocese of Spoleto, near the castle of Spello; once a parish church, it is now a simple benefice to be conferred by the chapter, as Corradus reports, who visited it in 1599.]

The church of Saint Stephen of Runceja.

> [Note: [Col. 1404D] The church of Saint Stephen of Runceja is situated near the city of Assisi, in the place called Mollicola; and in ancient rent-rolls it is said to have been given to our basilica by the nobleman Perjurius.]

Situated in the bishopric of Assisi, with all its appurtenances. The hospital of Traversa, with the oratory of Saint Nicholas, situated in Campania in the bishopric of Assisi, with all its appurtenances. The castle of Cassi, with the church of Saint Peter and the church of Saint Mary, together with their estates, villages, and hamlets; the new chapel of Saint John within the castle of Coccorano.

> [Note: [Col. 1404D] The castle of Cocorano or Coccorano must be located between Perugia, Assisi, and Gubbio. See Ludovico Jacobilli, *Chronicle of the Monastery of Sassovivo*, ch. 27.]

The site for building a church which you possess on the hill of Mansi.

> [Note: [Col. 1404D] From the context of the diploma itself, we understand this hill called Mansi to be adjacent to the castle of Coccorano.]

With [Col. 1405A] all its appurtenances; the site which you possess in the castle of Coccorano, where stands the church of Saint Peter, which fire destroyed; the hospital with a church near the castle of Diruta in the bishopric of Perugia; the hospital with the crypt of Saint Michael, situated in the place called Sasso di Rapina, built by Lady Bethelehem Malvangiata, daughter of Malvagi, in the territory of Summati near the river called Trunto.

> [Note: [Col. 1405D] Otherwise called Truentus; it rises in the Apennines, on the very border of Umbria, then waters Picenum and, near Ascoli, receives the Castellano stream.]

The hospital of Turricella, with the church of Saint Walter, situated in the territory of the castle of Fortiliano; it was built by Maradianus and Hugh, sons of Count Conrad, and Henry and Oderisius, sons of Count Theobald, near the river called Tenna.

> [Note: [Col. 1405D] Now Tinia; it rises in the Apennines near Nocera and flows by the walls of Foligno.]

They delivered it into the hands of the priest Theodinus for your canonical church. The church of Saint Mary of Pacignano, situated in Marsia [Col. 1405B] near the castle of Celano; the hospital of Anatella, with the church of Saint Bartholomew, situated there; the church of Saint John in Orfocle, situated in the bishopric of Valva.

> [Note: [Col. 1405D] Now Sulmona, to which the church of Valva, not far from Sulmona, has long been joined.]

The hospital of Pretonico, with the church of Saint Lawrence, situated in the bishopric of Penne.

> [Note: [Col. 1405D] In the territory of the Vestini; the churches of Penne and Atri are now united.]

The church of Saint Michael of Revere Scriniolis.

> [Note: [Col. 1405D] A very ancient catalogue of churches places this church beside the Po, in the bishopric of Ferrara, in the book of sermons for Matins [Col. 1406D]; another rent-roll places it in the diocese of Adria, and a bull of Innocent III provides sufficient elucidation.]

With its hospital, chapels, and all appurtenances; the church of Saint Cataldus with the bridge of Saraballis, situated in the bishopric of Tortona. The castle of Capracorum, with its lands, estates, and hamlets, the ruined church of Saint John, its watermills, and its millstones.

The estate of Saint Cassian; the estate of Vicoli; the estate of Memorien.; the estate of Greater Taliani and Lesser Taliani; the estate of Casanilli; the estate of Casapindole; the estate of Cucumelli; the estate of Rotule; the estate of Procelaris; [Col. 1405C] the estate of Pritanella; the estate called Casa Lardaria; the estate of Cleandris, with the ruined church of Saint Agatha; the estate of Canutoli; and the estate of Cold Water—all mutually adjoining; the estate of Bravi; and the estate of Pallini with all its named dependencies.

The monastery of Saint Cornelius, situated in the territory of Veii, with all its appurtenances. Six *pedicae* of land in the estate called Vallis de Pertica; the land of Macerano, situated at Petra Pertusia; all the landed possessions which the monastery of Saint Sabbas holds from your canonry in the territory of Galeria; the possessions and rents of the houses of Saint Mary in Turri; one third of the offerings which come into the hands of the bishop of Porto [Col. 1405D] on Palm Sunday, on the Lord’s Supper, on Good Friday, on Holy Saturday, on the Resurrection of the Lord, and on Christmas Day; one sixth of the offerings made at the altar of Saint Peter on [Col. 1406A] Palm Sunday, from the ringing of the bells at night until the completion of Matins, and from their ringing for Mass until the end of Mass; likewise on the Lord’s Supper, Good Friday, and Holy Saturday, and from the ringing of the bells for the scrutiny throughout the entire day and night, until the Mass on the following Sunday of the Resurrection has been completed.

Mount Saint Peter, with its castle and the church of Saint Peter near the city of Osimo.

> [Note: [Col. 1406D] This notable church of Saint Peter is situated near Auximum, called Osimo in Italian. The Chapter Archive contains the instrument by which the Vatican chapter granted this sacred building, together with the castle of Saint Peter, in 1261 to Silvester, prior, and the brothers of the hermitage of Monte Fano, subject to a fixed rent. See the book of Demetrius, title A, fol. 108.]

The hospital of Montotto, with the church of Saint Peter, situated in the territory of the castle called Cecilia near the river Asu.

> [Note: [Col. 1406D] Or Clasius, commonly Chiascio, flowing from the Apennines.]

In the bishopric of Fermo, built by Transmundus Uberti (otherwise Iberti), and delivered into the hands of your brother Theodinus for your canonry. The church of Saint Scudera, [Col. 1406B] situated between the two rivers Farma and Farmolla, near the castle of Torgnallis.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars and churches, and ordinations of clerics serving in your churches from the diocesan bishops, provided that they are Catholic, enjoy the favor of the Apostolic See, and are willing to provide these without any improper exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, may grant what is requested. Moreover, we decree that no bishop, without the knowledge of the Roman pontiff, may forbid divine offices in your churches—except when there is a general interdict—or dare under any pretext to demand anything from them; rather, [Col. 1406C] those churches shall remain free under our protection.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but all things shall be preserved whole and undiminished, for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this text of our decree, rashly attempts to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, does not correct his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and office, [Col. 1406D] recognize himself or herself as guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and at the last judgment [Col. 1407A] be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. Amen. Amen.

I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Henry, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal priest of the church of Saint Mark, have subscribed. I, Peter de Bono, cardinal priest of the church of Saint Susanna, have subscribed. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of the church of Saint Callistus at Saint Mary in Trastevere, have subscribed. [Col. 1407B] I, Albert, cardinal priest of the church of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed. I, Melior, cardinal priest of the church of Saints John and Paul, of Pammachius, have subscribed. I, Adelard, cardinal priest of the church of Saint Marcellus, have subscribed. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo, have subscribed. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Soffredus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed. I, Roland, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. [Col. 1407C] I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed. I, Ralph, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Albert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the Ides of June, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1186, in the first year of the pontificate of lord Pope Urban III.

## XLII bis. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Peter of Eslonza.  
*(Verona, 17 June.)*

*[YEPES, General Chronicle, etc., IV, 456.]*

[Col. 1407D]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons MARTIN, abbot of Saint Peter of Eslonza, and his brothers, both present and future, professing the regular life: for ever.

Whenever a request is made of us that is recognized as fitting religion and uprightness, it is proper for us gladly to grant it and to afford appropriate support to the petitioners’ desires. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and confirm it by the privilege of this present document. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order, recognized as instituted according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, shall be inviolably observed there for all time. [Col. 1408A]

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the Lord’s favor, acquire through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the village of Saint Eulalia with its church; the village of Bermudo with its church; Barrium; Baldeferreru; the village of Revolar with its church; the village of Alvella with its church—all these villages with all [Col. 1408B] their appurtenances; the priory of Saint Mary of Algadefe, with the churches and possessions which you hold in the city of León; and the possessions which you hold in Ruydellozo, Villabent, the valley of Saint Vassei, the valley of Fontecha, and other places belonging to the aforesaid church, with all their appurtenances.

The possessions and right which you hold in the village and church of Mellancos; the possessions which you hold in the village of Retal, Brat Reond, Prat Cegat, Valleio, the castle, Macarieses, Sopenna, and Torre; the possessions and right which you hold in the village and church of Viliela; the church of Saint John of Villasachario; and the church of Saint Michael in Mansela; the church of Saint Mary in Majorica; the church of Saint Mary [Col. 1408C] in Villafesila, with the possessions which you hold in the aforesaid villages, together with all their appurtenances; the church of Saint Bartholomew in Rebelinos, and the possessions and right in another church which you hold in that same village; the possessions which you hold in Val Rodrigo and in the village of Quixada; the church of Saint Mary of Villarabines; the church of Saint Mary; the church of Saint Romanus; the church of Saint Thomas of the castle of Ferrer; and the possessions which you hold in the aforesaid villages with all their appurtenances; Villarei with its church; and the possessions which you hold in Pieros and Saint Vincent, with its church.

The possessions and right which you hold in the village and church of Moral; the possessions [Col. 1408D] which you hold in the village of Morchiel and in Villamoros; the church of Morales; the church of Malbarget; the church of Villamuderesu; the church of Cannones; the church of Valdealiso; the church of Palaseo; the church of la Debesa; and the possessions which you hold in the aforesaid villages, with all their appurtenances.

The possession and right which you hold in the village and church of Cerezales; and the possessions which you hold in Poiadiella, Willaatent, Villafanne, the village of Varsula, Quintanori, Vegas, Saint Eulalia of Lugam, Vega de Bermar, the village called Barrio in Riaño, Ria de Ponhlios, Larana, Caso with the church of Saint Savior, and Saint Mary of Velarda; the church of Saint Eulalia [Col. 1409A] of Pesquera, with the possessions which you hold in that same village; the church of Saint John of Verbio with its village and the possessions which you hold in Lazana and other places belonging to the aforesaid church, together with all their appurtenances; the church and possessions which you hold at Saint Michael of Ripamaris.

You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen fleeing from the world, free and absolved, and retain them without any opposition.

Furthermore, we prohibit any of your brothers, after making profession in that place, from departing thence without the permission of his abbot, except for the sake of a stricter religious observance; and no one shall dare retain a departing brother without letters of authorization from the community. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may, with closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice, celebrate all offices. [Col. 1409B]

We also decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted; nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken shall be preserved. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars and churches, and ordinations of clerics or monks to be promoted to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, provided he is Catholic, enjoys the favor [Col. 1409C] and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to provide these to you freely and without any improper exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, may grant what is requested.

We also hold valid the ancient customs, liberties, and immunities reasonably granted to the same monastery and observed hitherto, and decree that they shall remain inviolate in future times. We further forbid anyone to presume to pronounce a sentence of excommunication or interdict against you or your church without manifest and reasonable cause. Upon the death of you, abbot of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any cunning of usurpation or by force, except one whom the brothers, by common consent or by the sounder counsel of a part of the brothers, shall provide to be elected according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. [Col. 1409D] Therefore we decree, etc.

If, therefore, anyone in the future, etc. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, etc.

I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of Saint Mary in Trastevere. I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the title of the Twelve Apostles. I, Albinus, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. [Col. 1410A] I, Melior, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul. I, Adelard, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Saint Rufina. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. [Col. 1410B] I, Soffredus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Roland, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Prison. I, Ralph, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Verona through the hand of Albert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1186, in the first year of the pontificate of lord Pope Urban III.

## XLIII. To Emperor Frederick.—He complains of the injuries inflicted by him upon the Roman Church.  
*(Verona, 18 June.)*

*[MANSI, Councils, XXII, 504.]*

[Col. 1410C]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, F., illustrious Emperor of the Romans, ever Augustus: greeting and apostolic blessing.

If it had been granted from above and established by heavenly wisdom that there should be so great a bond of love between Church and empire for the salvation of the Christian people that neither the intrigues of whisperers and malicious persons could prevail against it, nor could either party do anything prejudicial or harmful to the other, this would be pleasing and acceptable to us and, as we believe, would be pleasing to all who fear God. For the wisdom of God ordained the jurisdiction of the two swords for this purpose: that, as the one adhered to the other, the severity of one might curb the malice of the wicked, and the power of the other restrain those who despise it. [Col. 1410D]

Considering this with the pious affection proper to us, from the very beginning of our elevation we conceived and have maintained the firm purpose of restoring perpetual peace and concord between Church and empire through your Serenity; and, to speak without offense to conscience, we neither sought nor seek any occasion to depart from this purpose. Certainly, we received the imperial letters with the kindness that was fitting; having fully understood their tenor, and so that your Highness may know our conscience more surely, we have thought fit to reply to your Serenity point by point.

We recall, and recount with much commendation, that at our elevation your Excellence, with due reverence and devotion, received the peace of the Church; therefore the hand of the Lord was unwilling to act through us because of our merits, but through his own mercy. We consider, as we believe, that just as you are by divine institution a Catholic prince, so you ought to reverence and preserve Catholic unity in the Church of God. [Col. 1411A]

We acknowledge that we received from your Magnificence, through letters and messengers, the assurance that you wished, as belonged to your office, to receive the patrimony of the Church under your protection; and that, without awaiting the good pleasure of our will, you intended to send Henry, your illustrious son, king, for that purpose. This was indeed a good and praiseworthy promise, had it been fulfilled with the proper effect. But what we cannot bear without astonishment is that matters have turned to the contrary: for this same illustrious son of yours seems to aim not at the defense of our land but rather at its oppression, and from cities and other places under our jurisdiction—namely Narnia, Viterbo, Verusio [perhaps Perugia], and certain others—he demands market dues and other unlawful services, and threatens those who refuse his demands according to the arbitrariness of his will. [Col. 1411B]

The promise pleased us, and the intention pleased us; but because its outcome is contrary, we take this grievously, and do not believe it becoming to your Excellence. As for the fact that your Serenity avoided the people of Novara, separated from the body of Christ, which is the Church, because of their fault, we commend this as was due; nor could you otherwise have suitably provided for your salvation and honor, since by the power entrusted to you, you ought to restrain all who exalt themselves against God and his Church and firmly observe ecclesiastical decrees.

But concerning what you informed us regarding Cremona, we are the more gravely astonished because we recognize that perhaps another’s suggestion has turned your disposition toward this, so that you seem to have conceived the contrary concerning those whom you ought to have pursued with thanksgiving. For when the Cremonese themselves repeatedly came into our presence, humbly asking that we receive them under the protection of the Apostolic See, although we could have granted this without offense to conscience, since we are bound to confer apostolic favor upon all who devoutly appeal to us, nevertheless, lest they become more insolent toward your Excellence because of our favor, we did not grant their petition. [Col. 1411C]

And so that your Prudence may not be unaware that we have not wished to disturb peace and concord between you and them, know that, had we perhaps wished otherwise, events would have taken a different course. We instructed our venerable brother, the bishop of Cremona, when he was attending to the negotiation of that peace, to labor with every possible diligence for the restoration of concord. If your Serenity finds in this any ground for complaint, let it consider that, upon examining our conscience, we do not see it.

Nor do we remember having forbidden the bishops or cities of Lombardy from assisting the Cremonese against your Magnificence and furnishing them due counsel and aid. Although from the beginning we could have forbidden the bishops, since it has never hitherto been customary to impose this servitude upon the Italian churches, and since it is expressly contained in imperial privileges—as your Serenity does not doubt—that your Highness ought not on that account introduce new conditions upon those churches, [Col. 1412A] we do not wish your Excellence to take it grievously or ill if, with God as author, we restrain by pastoral office those who have presumed to subject churches entrusted to them to so unlawful a condition.

> [Note: [Col. 1411D] A corrupt passage.]

Yet we certainly commanded some persons not to ravage the possessions and goods of the churches of the diocese of Cremona in the contribution of imperial aid. This was required by the duty of the office imposed upon us, since we are bound to provide for the condition of all churches. If any letters of another tenor have been issued, we willingly wish them to be presented to us; and if they proceeded from our knowledge—for just as fraudulent letters are obtained from your Serenity, so are some obtained from us—we shall by no means deny the truth. [Col. 1412B]

In all these matters and others, when we examine our conscience and dispositions by careful investigation, we find in ourselves nothing variable against your Excellence that gives you just ground for complaint, unless perhaps you seek a pretext for turning away from a friend. Yet we cannot recall, without injury to conscience, how many and how great injuries we have hitherto suffered you and the ministers of your Excellence to perpetrate with impunity against divine ordinance and ecclesiastical liberty; and we do not believe that imperial Prudence is unaware of them.

For, to omit the rest, you are said recently to have established your ministeriales in the dioceses of Turin and Ivrea [the text prints “Hippo,” but read “Eporedia”], so that, grievously burdening ecclesiastical persons with unlawful exactions and vexations, they may drag them before secular courts and compel them to obey their commands. Your aforesaid son and Berthold, with the mass of their assembled army, devastate the churches of Tuscany and impose assessments upon them at their will. [Col. 1412C]

The Duke of Spoleto is known to have so taken away [the text prints *attulisse*, “brought,” but read *abstulisse*, “taken away”] the spiritual and temporal condition of the churches among which he remains by command of your Highness, granting and taking them from ecclesiastical men as he pleases, seizing clerics and forcing them to ransom themselves. Ecclesiastical men living in the territory committed to his authority are compelled to abandon their own homes and, to the disgrace of the ecclesiastical order, to beg the means of life. Walter, the ministerialis in the March of Tuscany, and others in other regions do not cease to perpetrate the same things. [Col. 1412D]

## XLIV. He receives the Vallombrosan monastery under protection and confirms its rights.  
*(Verona, 26 June.)*

*[LAMI, Ecclesiastical Monuments of Florence, I, 550.]*

[Col. 1413A]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons TERTIUS, abbot of Vallombrosa, and his brothers, both present and future, regularly to be appointed: for ever.

Religious desires deserve that we readily grant them assent, so that faithful devotion may attain a swift result. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously accede to your just requests, and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Vallombrosa, in which you are devoted to the service of God, together with all the monasteries subject to it [Col. 1413B]; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that every immunity and every liberty granted to the aforesaid monastery by our predecessors of blessed memory, Victor, Gregory VII, Urban, Paschal, Innocent, and Adrian, Roman pontiffs, shall remain forever firm and unimpaired for you, your successors, and the whole Vallombrosan congregation.

We further decree that whatever possessions and goods the aforesaid monastery and the entire Vallombrosan congregation now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter, by the grant of pontiffs, the bounty of kings or princes [Col. 1413C], the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favor, acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these, we have judged the following to be specified by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances. The monastery of St. Salvi; the monastery of the Holy Trinity of Florence; the monastery of Struma; the monastery of Osella and of St. James of Castello. The monastery of Passignano, and those of St. Michael of Senis and Alphiano. The monastery of Coltibuono, of Monte Pisis; the monastery of Montescalari and that of Nerano; the monastery of Ficiclo and that of Capiano; the monastery of St. Paul of Pisa; the monastery of Plajano and that of St. Venerius [Col. 1413D] in Sardinia. The monastery of St. Angelo of Pistoia, those of Pacciano and St. Mary of Prato; the monastery of Vaiano, those of Oppleto and Monte Piano; the monastery of Fonte Thaonis; the monasteries of Musceto, Monte Armato, and St. Cecilia; the monastery of St. Reparata; the monasteries of Forlì, Trecento, Crispino, Razzuolo, Rivo Cesare, Cuneo, and Turri. The monastery of Caprilia; the monasteries of Piacenza, Pavia, and Cremona; the monasteries of Capanna, Novara, Vercelli, Genoa, Tortona, and Turin. The monasteries of Brescia, Verona, and St. Vigilius; the monasteries of Bergamo, Milan, St. Carpophorus, and Asti.

Certainly, let no person whatever dare presumptuously to seize or detain those whom they have seized—converts [lay brothers] [Col. 1414A] or monks of the aforesaid monastery or of the entire congregation—or harass them by any vexations.

Moreover, we decree that no one shall presume to demand or extort from you tithes of the fruits which you gather anywhere through your own expenditure and labor, or from the sustenance of your animals.

You may also receive, without anyone’s prohibition, free and unbound clerics and laymen for conversion, and may grant Christian burial to those who have vowed to be buried among you; and you may receive the offerings both of these persons and of other faithful people, without prejudice to other churches. By the authority of this present decree we also decree that, if [Col. 1414B] at any time a general or particular interdict is imposed by the diocesan bishop owing to urgent necessity, you may celebrate the divine offices in your monasteries, with closed doors, without ringing bells, and with excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, in a subdued voice, for yourselves and your brethren alone.

And because the Apostolic See ought not to furnish an occasion or favor to any delinquent, we further decree that the abbot of Vallombrosa shall have full canonical liberty to correct abbots or brethren of your congregation who, under pretext of the protection of the Apostolic See, wish to live less regularly than the monastic order or the custom of the Vallombrosan congregation requires. Nor may any brethren of the same congregation [Col. 1414C] establish an abbot for themselves without his consent, as is known to have been observed from the time of John, the first abbot of that congregation, of blessed memory.

Therefore we decree that no person whatever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things be preserved entire for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he correct his offense by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment [Col. 1414D]. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. Amen. Amen.

I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, Henry, bishop of Albano, have subscribed.  
I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.  
I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Mark, have subscribed.  
I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Susanna, have subscribed. [Col. 1415A]  
I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of St. Mary in Trastevere, of the title of St. Callistus, have subscribed.  
I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the title of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed.  
I, Albinus, priest-cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed.  
I, Melior, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius, have subscribed.  
I, Adelard, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Marcellus, have subscribed.  
I, James, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed.  
I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. [Col. 1415B]  
I, Bobo, deacon-cardinal of St. Angelo, have subscribed.  
I, Octavian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.  
I, Sifred, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed.  
I, Roland, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Portico, have subscribed.  
I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Albert, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July [26 June], in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1186, in the first year of the pontificate [Col. 1415C] of Lord Pope Urban III.

### XLV. He grants the brethren of Grandmont permission, during a general interdict of the land, to ring one bell.  
*(Verona, 14 July.)*

*[Gallia Christiana nova, “Instituta,” p. 191.]*

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the prior and brethren of Grandmont: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The greater and more pleasing the service rendered to God by religious men, the more willingly ought we to attend to their advantage and hear their earnest prayers. [Col. 1415D] Therefore, since your place is situated far from human habitation, we have judged that the kindness of the Apostolic See should grant you this indulgence: whenever there is a general interdict of the land, you may, by the ringing of one bell at suitable hours, summon your brethren from their labors to church. We also command that this be observed in your places, after the example of our predecessor Pope Alexander of blessed memory, where they are so far removed from cities, castles, and villages that the sound of your bell cannot be heard in those places.

Given at Verona, on the second day before the Ides of July [14 July], in the first year of our pontificate.

### XLVI. To William, prior of Grandmont.—He establishes various provisions for the peace and quiet of the monks of Grandmont.  
*(Verona, 15 July.)*

*[MARTÈNE, Thesaurus Anecdotorum, I, 627.]*

[Col. 1416A]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WILLIAM, prior of Grandmont, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Inasmuch as, through the infusion of the Holy Spirit, while subject to the instruction of heavenly discipline, you have hitherto spread more widely in your order the fragrance of the religious life observed there, so that, according to the Apostle, your conduct may be “from life unto life” [Phil. III], so much the more does our office require [Col. 1416B] us diligently to ensure that the enemy of humankind, who always prowls about seeking whom he may devour [I Pet. V], may not, in envy of the devout endeavors of the perfect, prevail against you by the craftiness of his guile, God resisting him; and that he may not by poisonous suggestion in any degree alter or disturb the purpose of religion and of the order in which you serve so praiseworthily, by violating among you the grace of fraternal peace.

Accordingly, when a seedbed of scandal had arisen among you, by the permission of him who does not allow his faithful to be tempted beyond what they can bear [I Cor. X], and could hitherto not be quieted despite the care exerted by very many persons, certain brethren from each party in the dispute came before us and our brethren, setting forth many matters [Col. 1416C] concerning the institution of your order and the injuries mutually inflicted. Having carefully heard all that they judged should be presented in our hearing, we, so that hereafter an avenue for harm might be closed to the enemy of all virtues and his craftiness might not so easily disturb the concord of fraternal peace in your order, have judged, on the counsel of our brethren, that the hand of apostolic correction should be applied to those matters which seemed to generate material for disputes.

First, we decree that those who, having left the world, take refuge in your order shall promise unconditional obedience and reverence to the prior then in office and to his Catholic successors, or to the chapter if there is no prior. Let each brother render to the others, in matters concerning the advantage and honor [Col. 1416D] of the house, the office of fraternal charity and the aid of due support. Let them esteem one another greater than themselves, according to the Apostle [Phil. II], so that, in accordance with apostolic and evangelical teaching, they may outdo one another in showing honor; and let one who is perhaps greater in merits not be ashamed, for the love of the Lord, to become the servant of those lesser than himself [Luke XXII].

Furthermore, providing for your peace, we decree that no one may compel you against your will to receive a person of another religious order, lest, while one who has fled to you seeks to reproduce the observances of the order he has abandoned, he turn the minds of the simpler brethren away from observance of your discipline; and lest you become injurious and troublesome to others if you wish to retain those professed in their orders.

To the prior, moreover, in spiritual [Col. 1417A] as well as temporal matters, we grant full authority by apostolic power, so that he may entrust to one of the converts [lay brothers], who is most suitable, the administration of temporal matters in your cells. By command of that prior, this person shall receive alms and deposits and, with provident judgment, apply them to pious uses and to the needs of the house. The care of spiritual matters, however, shall freely rest, by the prior’s command, with the clerics themselves; thus no lay brother may arrogate to himself any authority in confessions, penances, the celebration of divine offices, or the correction of the offenses of clerics. Rather, all these things shall be performed through the aforesaid prior or, by his command, through clerics.

Moreover, following the example of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Alexander and Lucius of blessed memory [Col. 1417B], we impose upon all who observe your rule, as it is wholesomely set forth in your order and in the foregoing articles of our correction, the labor which they undergo in that observance as a penance and for the remission of their sins. We also confirm by apostolic authority, and decree to remain valid for all time, the institution which you wholesomely added for your correction after the confirmation of our predecessor Pope Adrian of blessed memory. We decree that you shall be free, according to your rule and the institutions of your order, to serve the Lord without anyone’s burdens or molestations, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See.

Furthermore [Col. 1417C], we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves your house and places, together with all that you now justly and peacefully possess, or may hereafter, by grant of pontiffs, bounty of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by God’s favor, acquire; and we strengthen them by the privilege of this present writing, decreeing that they shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors.

Therefore we decree that no person whatever may rashly disturb the aforesaid house, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things be kept intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance [Col. 1417D] and support they were granted. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he correct his offense by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

[Col. 1418A]

I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.

I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of St. Mary in Trastevere, of the title of St. Callistus, have subscribed.  
I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the title of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed.  
I, Albinus, priest-cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed.  
I, Melior, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius, have subscribed. [Col. 1418B]  
I, Adelard, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Marcellus, have subscribed.

I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Moses, canon of the Lateran [Col. 1418C], acting in place of the chancellor, on the Ides of July [15 July], in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1186, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban III.

### XLVII. Privilege for the church of St. John the Baptist at Regensburg.  
*(Verona, 20 July.)*

*[RIED, Codex diplomaticus Ratisbonensis, I, 268.]*

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons EKKOLF, provost of St. John the Baptist in the city of Regensburg, and his brethren dwelling there, present and future, canonically [Col. 1418D] appointed: in perpetuity.

Whenever a request is made to us which is recognized as consistent with right and propriety, it is fitting that we willingly grant it and give suitable support to the desires of those who ask. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously accede to your just requests, and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church of St. John the Baptist, in which you are devoted to the service of God; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the grant of pontiffs, the bounty of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favor, acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your [Col. 1419A] successors. Among these, we have judged the following to be specified by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; what you possess in the church of Winkelsaezze and in the church of Ascholzhusen; the estates belonging to your prebend, namely: Windeheim with all its appurtenances; mills at Ahdorf; and tithes both of grain and vineyards, from vineyards planted and to be planted—namely, between Wisent and Teufental; Werd; Hungersdorf; Teufental; and Owe, with grain tithes; an estate at Erling (now Langenerling) and one third of the tithes throughout the village; the estate of Metzing and one third of the tithes in the same village [Col. 1419B]; and tithes at Harthusen; the estate of Schaessendorf; a mill at Vihta and tithes throughout the whole parish; tithes throughout the parish of Haybach; tithes at Ratenberg; an estate at Anger with tithes and all its appurtenances; tithes from the parish of Chunzell; tithes from the monks’ cloister called Upper Altach; tithes from Chritzenkirchen; tithes from Pfoeling; tithes at Tegernbach; one mature pig from the estate of Geisling, which belongs to the bishop; tithes at Truchtlving, which Bishop Chuno gave to the altar of St. Mary; the estates belonging to the offerings of the brethren at Gutzelhusen; a mill and estate with their appurtenances at Nisse; an estate at Windeheim; the estate of Chruchenberg [Col. 1419C]; one holding at Menzenbach; the estate of Berhartshusen; one holding at Gependorf; a mill and a holding at Susenbach; the estate of Paldwinsdorf; three estates at Prizzat; one holding and tithes throughout the whole parish of Rattiszell; an estate at Charein; a vineyard at Muln; a vineyard at Willifs; two vineyards with the fields belonging to them at Schwaeblwis; the vineyard called Chobel; three estates belonging to the clothing allowance of the brethren at Podlungsvelden; and an estate in the parish of Adratshusen.

Upon the death of you who are now provost of this place, no one may be placed over it through any cunning of usurpation or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the greater and sounder part of the brethren, in the fear of God, shall provide to be elected from the choir of St. Peter at Regensburg [Col. 1419D], as has been maintained in that church from its first foundation (1127). Nor may he give or alienate any estates, tithes, or holdings to anyone without the common consent of the brethren. Nor may the provost presume to claim anything from the brethren’s offerings for himself; rather, a camerarius appointed by the brethren shall administer the offerings with due provision. Nor shall the provost have any power to grant the brethren’s churches to anyone without their assent; but, as has hitherto been done, their canonical administration shall proceed under the oversight of the brethren.

Therefore we decree that no person whatever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them [Col. 1420A], or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole and unimpaired for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he correct his offense by due satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that [Col. 1420B] church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August [20 July], in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1186, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban III.

Lead seal. Urban, Pope III.

### XLVIII. Privilege for the church of St. John at Liège.  
*(Verona, 26 July.)*

*[MARTÈNE, Amplissima Collectio, I, 972.]*

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of the church of blessed John the Evangelist [Col. 1420C] situated on the island of Liège, present and future, canonically appointed: in perpetuity.

The authority of the Apostolic See entrusted to us urges us to provide the protection of guardianship to places and persons which duly invoke its aid in devotion. For, just as no effect is to be granted to those who ask unjustly, so the petition of those who seek what is lawful and just should not be delayed.
