Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously accede to your just requests and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to the service of God; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same church now [Col. 1420D] justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by grant of pontiffs, bounty of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favor, acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these, we have judged the following to be specified by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the village of Emurch with its fishery; Robert’s Mount; the village of Eymalam with its church and appurtenances; the church of St. Adalbert on the island of Liège, with the tithes of the same island and its appurtenances; the village of Gestele with its dependent household and appurtenances; the church of Engle; the church of Heudecusa; the church of Hosden; the estate of Comaphia [Col. 1421A] with its church; in the village of Jupelella, an allod paying annually thirty solidi; one fourth part of the village of Hoydre; the right which you possess in the village of Ferires; the village of Fleniz; Romercurt; Bushone; one half of the village of Bovingestir; the estate of Goe with its church and appurtenances; one fourth part of the tithe; and the allod which you possess in the village of Holong; Masnil; the church of Genglehey; and whatever you possess in the allod of the same village and at Waleove; the village of Tillires and Rosires; the village of Meredorp; Jusanam; the village of Raulcurt; whatever right you possess in the church of Monte Thyenes, with its endowment and in the full gift of that church; the church of Atteroda; the right which you possess at Sleduwez; and a holding of allodial land in the same village, in the place called ad Montem; the estate of Nerhenes with its church [Col. 1421B] and appurtenances, and the adjacent wood of Miradal; Holdrin; Fennache; the village of Hulgrehes, with its fishery in the Meuse; in the town of Huy, three pounds from the toll; the village of Sarto Colnois; the church of Corbion; the village of Ferires; and the right which you possess at Morelmeis; Ronredines; an allod at Halembail, and at Here, Rokelenges, Hers, and Formala; half the tithe of Bubaz; the village of Samerey with its appurtenances; Desdorp with its appurtenances; Allekenrode; vineyards at Noweroit; a holding at Bubenhen; a holding at Sescay; an allod at Falla; ten solidi at Falmin and ten at Rumines; six holdings at Rongese and ten at Brida; the toll of the market of Visé; at Liège, a mill and the allod of Parvitorrentis; an estate on Robert’s [Col. 1421C] Mount; at Vingiz, land paying five solidi annually; at Taynires and Seraing, meadow and land paying five solidi and six denarii; at Londos, five solidi; the allod of Hastaples; the church of Hares Wistrewich; likewise, at Huy, a possession paying twelve solidi and six denarii.

We further prohibit the provost, or any person whatsoever, from having any license in any manner to alienate the goods of that church without the common consent of the brethren, or of their sounder part. The aforesaid church may freely elect its dean and provost, whether from its own church or from another church anywhere in the whole bishopric of Liège. And because we have learned that the goods belonging in common to the maintenance of the brethren are deficient in one part and abundant in another, we decree that the deficiency of one village shall be supplied from the abundance of another [Col. 1421D].

Therefore we decree that no person whatever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the bishop of Liège. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he correct his offense by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment [Col. 1422A] for the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, Henry, bishop of Albano, have subscribed.  
I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.  
I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Mark, have subscribed.  
I, Peter of Bologna, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Susanna, have subscribed.  
I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of St. Mary [Col. 1422B] across the Tiber, of the title of St. Callistus, have subscribed.  
I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the title of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed.  
I, Albinus, priest-cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed.  
I, Melior, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius, have subscribed.  
I, Adelard, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Marcellus, have subscribed.  
I, Hyacinth, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed.  
I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed.  
I, Bobo, deacon-cardinal of St. Angelo, have subscribed. [Col. 1422C]  
I, Octavian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.  
I, Soffredus, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed.  
I, Roland, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Portico, have subscribed.  
I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed.  
I, Radulf, deacon-cardinal of St. George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Kalends of August [26 July], in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1186, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban III.

### XLIX. To William, king of Scotland.—Concerning the case of Hugh, bishop of St. Andrews, and John, bishop of Dunkeld.  
*(Verona, 31 July.)*

*[MANSI, Concilia, XXII, 497.]*

[Col. 1422D]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to WILLIAM, illustrious king of the Scots: greeting and apostolic blessing.

In the office of administration entrusted to us by God, we are bound to extend the gaze of our care to all churches, both near and distant, and, if we learn that anything unreasonable has been undertaken in them or against their ministers, to bring it back to a fitting course. Therefore secular rulers ought not [Col. 1423A] to be disturbed if we occasionally judge that our hands should be extended to correct things done wrongly, since they themselves ought, according to the power entrusted to them, to assist us in such matters and, when necessary because of the obstinacy of certain persons, to oppose more vigorously the wickedness of the contumacious.

For your royal excellence does not fail to know how serious a dissension has arisen between our venerable brethren John, bishop of Dunkeld, and Hugh, bishop of St. Andrews. And although both parties have endured great labors and expenses, and in the time of our predecessor Pope Lucius of blessed memory litigated for a long time before the Apostolic See, the case could nevertheless not be brought to an end. Accordingly, when those bishops recently came into our presence and argued the matter for some time in our hearing, we granted, on the counsel of our brethren, to the aforesaid bishop of Dunkeld leave to proceed against the bishop of St. Andrews concerning the bishopric of St. Andrews; and we ordered the bishop of St. Andrews to return home, sufficiently instructed, and to return to our presence at a date appointed for him [Col. 1423B]. If he does not then come, our venerable brother Jocelin, bishop of Glasgow, and our beloved sons the abbots of Melrose, Newbattle, and Dunfermline, shall from that point suspend him from episcopal office; and if he is afterward contumacious, they shall bind him by the bond of excommunication and shall not relax the sentence until he presents himself before us.

For we do not wish the aforesaid church of St. Andrews to suffer grave loss to its affairs while the case remains any longer unresolved; rather, once the truth has been established, we wish it, with the Lord’s help, to attain through us a fitting conclusion. We also command the aforesaid bishop of Glasgow and his colleagues, relying upon our authority, to defend our beloved sons Ajulf, dean of Lodonejo, Odo the seneschal, Roger of Fedic, and other clerics and friends of the aforesaid bishop of Dunkeld from every molestation; and not to permit their possessions or other goods, or the revenues of the bishop himself, to be attacked by anyone [Col. 1423C]. If any persons presume to act against their prohibition in these matters, let them restrain such persons by canonical censure, notwithstanding any appeal.

That, therefore, what we command may be carried out without any difficulty [Col. 1423D], we admonish your royal excellence, exhort you in the Lord, and enjoin this upon you for the remission of sins: for the love of justice and reverence for blessed Peter and for ourselves, permit proceedings in that case according to the tenor of our mandate. Defend by royal protection the aforesaid dean, seneschal, Roger of Fedic, and the other kinsmen and friends of the aforesaid bishop of Dunkeld, together with his bishopric and his other revenues; neither burden them yourself in any matter nor permit others to burden them. Thus may the case itself be concluded without impediment, and may royal magnificence obtain from the work of justice an unfailing reward with God and a good name among men.

Moreover, know that we have enjoined upon the said bishops, by virtue of obedience [Col. 1424A], that they shall accept nothing from churches or clerics subject to them toward the expenses which they will incur in prosecuting the aforesaid case, but shall procure what is necessary from their own revenues alone. For we do not wish churches or other persons in your realm to incur loss through their actions. We also do not wish your royal excellence to be unaware that the aforesaid bishop of Dunkeld has prosecuted his case so honorably and has shown such deference to royal honor that he has proposed absolutely nothing capable of redounding to the detriment of the royal name, or such as should move your serenity against him. Therefore, if anything to the contrary has been suggested to your highness by his enemies, do not lend a royal ear to such words.

[Col. 1424B]

Given at Verona, on the second day before the Kalends of August [31 July].

### L. To Jocelin, bishop of Glasgow, and to the abbots of Melrose, Newbattle, and Dunfermline: he gives the instructions indicated in the preceding letter.  
*(Verona, 31 July.)*

*[MANRIQUE, Annals of the Cistercians, III, 165, from the Annals of Roger of Hoveden.]*

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother JOCELIN, bishop of Glasgow, and to his beloved sons, the abbots of Melrose, Newbattle, and Dunfermline: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, by virtue of the office of administration laid upon us by God, etc.—for, when setting out the matter, he writes to them almost the same words as to the king; but presently he adds to them:

[Col. 1424C] “Therefore, lest the aforesaid business remain longer unresolved, and the church of St Andrews thereby suffer loss in its property, we command your discretion by apostolic letters, and enjoin you by virtue of obedience, to commit to writing whatever you may learn, either through yourselves or through others, concerning the tenor of that business, and to take care to communicate it to us under the protection of your seals; so that, instructed by your report and having taken counsel with our brethren, we may proceed in the matter as ought to be done.

“But if anyone, with rash presumption, should lay hands upon the aforesaid dean, Odo, the seneschal Robert de Fedic, or other friends of the bishop of Dunkeld, or upon their possessions or other goods, or upon the revenues of the bishopric or other revenues of that bishop, [Col. 1424D] restrain them by canonical censure, strengthened by our authority, without impediment from an appeal.

“Furthermore, on our behalf forbid the aforesaid bishops—as we have ourselves done orally—to take from churches or clerics subject to them anything on account of the expenses they are to incur in pursuing the said business; rather, let them provide what is necessary solely from their own revenues. For we do not wish churches or other persons of that kingdom to suffer loss through their action.

“Moreover, by our authority strictly enjoin the aforesaid bishop of St Andrews, adequately prepared, to come into our presence within the term which we have fixed for both parties. If he does not [Col. 1425A] come, then suspend him from episcopal office, setting aside any appeal. If he does not comply even then, bind him with the bond of excommunication; nor relax the sentence until he has caused himself to be brought before our presence.

“Further, inform the royal excellency that the aforesaid bishop of Dunkeld has pursued his cause so honourably, and has shown such regard for royal honour, that he has proposed absolutely nothing which could redound to the derogation of the royal name or on account of which the king ought to be stirred against him. Therefore take care, by urgent exhortation, to induce the king not to lend a royal ear to the words of his enemies if anything to the contrary has been suggested by them.”

Given at Verona, on the second day before the Kalends of August.

[Note: [Col. 1425D] Thus far the pope. Roger then adds, writing these very words: “Joscelin and his colleagues notified the aforesaid bishops of the apostolic letters. John departed in obedience; but the bishop of St Andrews, having exceeded the term given him, delayed going, and the aforesaid delegated judges suspended him from episcopal office and then, because of his contumacy, excommunicated him, according to the form of the apostolic mandate.”]

LI. He writes to Henry, king of England, that he has ordered Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to “cause the revenues of Archdeacon Savaric to be collected and keep them intact in his own custody.” (Verona, July.)

[BENEDICT OF PETERBOROUGH, *On the Life and Deeds of Henry II and Richard I*, p. 1186.]

[Col. 1425B]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son HENRY, illustrious king of England: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although we embrace your person, as that of a most beloved king and magnificent prince, whose devotion toward the Roman Church has shone forth in manifest evidences, especially [Col. 1425C] and pre-eminently with the arms of charity, and desire in all things to grant your requests according to God, nevertheless, as you know, it is neither our will nor our intention to do anything by which royal majesty may appear to be burdened.

From the letters of your highness and the careful report of your messengers, we have learned that it is most grievous to your sublimity that we ordered the revenues of Archdeacon Savaric to be collected and assigned to him, through our venerable brother Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, for payment of the debts with which he is bound. Wishing in this matter to defer to your magnificence, at your request and at the insistence of your messengers we have given orders to that archbishop that he cause those revenues to be collected [Col. 1425D] and keep them intact in his own custody. For we believe and hope in the Lord that, because of the moderation of our command, royal majesty will be the more readily inclined to open to him the bowels of compassion; since nothing is more glorious in a king or prince than to spare his subjects and restore them to his favour solely for the sake of divine recompense.

LII. He informs the provosts, aldermen, sworn officials, mayors, and people of the castle-town of Valenciennes that he has ordered Roger, bishop of Cambrai, to divide the parish of the church of St Salvius into three parts. (Verona, 2 August.)

[MIRAEUS, *Diplomatic Works*, II, 834.]

[Col. 1426A]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the provosts, aldermen, sworn officials, mayors, and people of the castle-town of Valenciennes: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although our beloved sons, the prior of St Salvius of Valenciennes and John, priest of the church of St Gaugericus, had come before us to litigate concerning the prior’s attempt to divide the parish of that church into three parts against the will of that priest, [Col. 1426B] nevertheless the priest later acknowledged that it could not remain undivided without grave danger to our parishioners. He therefore freely withdrew from the dispute of his own accord and agreed that the division of that parish into three parts should be made.

We duly receive with gratitude, and not without reason commend, your devotion in this respect: having recognized the dangers which the people of that parish endured because of the shortage of priests, you have, as the aforesaid prior maintains, worked faithfully toward the division and have applied diligent care to the welfare of the church to which you are subject by parochial right.

Therefore we have entrusted the aforesaid parish to our venerable brother the bishop of Cambrai [Col. 1426C] to be divided. We admonish your whole community and exhort you in the Lord, and enjoin this upon you for the remission of sins: when the parish has been divided into three parts by that bishop, each of you is to render due reverence and subjection to the parish to which he is assigned. You are also to pay in full, at fixed times, to the church of St Salvius its rights—which some of you are said to withhold at peril of your salvation—and, restoring what has been unjustly taken away, to show the aforesaid prior and his church the devotion that is fitting. Thus you may obtain from almighty God an unfailing reward, and, when we hear of your good works, we may commend your prudent conduct more fully.

[Col. 1426D] Given at Verona, on the fourth day before the Nones of August, in the year 1186.

LIII. He receives the monastery of St Mary of Salina-Vallis under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Verona, 9 August.)

[HUGH, *Premonstratensian Annals*, preface, p. 461.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons CONON, abbot of the church of St Mary of Salina-Vallis, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetual remembrance.

Both the force of equity and the order of reason require that just requests be granted their effect, especially when piety supports the petitioners’ wish and truth does not oppose it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and receive the aforesaid church of the blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, following the example of our predecessor Pope Alexander of happy memory; and we strengthen it by the authority of this present document.

First, we decree that the canonical order known to have been established in that church according to God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the institution of the Premonstratensian brethren shall be observed there inviolably for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s help, by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to state expressly:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated; and, after the full enumeration of its other goods, the constitution proceeds as follows in the bull of Alexander III for the same monastery.

No one shall presume to demand tithes from you on your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands [Col. 1427C] or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals.

You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen fleeing from the world, provided they are free and absolved, and retain them without any contradiction. We further forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, to depart from it without the leave of his abbot, except for the sake of embracing a stricter religious life; and no one may dare retain a departing brother without letters testimonial from the community.

Wishing also, with paternal solicitude, to provide for your peace and tranquillity, we forbid by apostolic authority anyone within the enclosures [Col. 1427D] of your places or granges to commit violence, robbery, or theft; to set fire; or to seize or kill a person. When a general interdict of the land is in force, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. In the parish churches which you possess, you may station four, or at least three, of your brethren. One of them is to be presented to the diocesan bishop in order to receive from him the care of souls, and is to answer to him in spiritual matters, while rendering to you due subjection in temporal affairs.

We also strictly prohibit by apostolic authority [Col. 1428A] anyone, under pretext of custom or in any manner whatever, from presuming to demand anything from you for the blessing of an abbot, chrism, or other ecclesiastical sacraments. On the death of you, the present abbot of the place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any artifice of deceit or by violence, except the person whom the brethren, by common consent or by the sounder counsel of the greater part of the brethren, judge ought to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine.

We likewise decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final will of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; the rights of the churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken remaining intact.

[Col. 1428B] Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they have been granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third admonition, unless he has corrected his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the power and dignity of his office; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred [Col. 1428C] body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to divine vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. Amen.

I, John, cardinal priest of the church of St Mark, with flourish. I, Peter de Bon, cardinal priest. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of the church of St Mary across the Tiber, of St Callistus. I, Pandulph, cardinal priest of the church of the Twelve Apostles. [Col. 1428D] I, Albinus, cardinal of the church of Holy Cross in Gerbin [probably “Jerusalem”]. I, Melchior, cardinal priest of the church of Saints John and Paul, of St Pammachius. I, Adelard, cardinal priest of the church of St Marcellus.

And in the middle of the parchment:

I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Henry, bishop of the church of Albano. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of the church of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of St Angelo. [Col. 1429A] I, Siffrid, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Via Lata. I, Peter in Erne, cardinal deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. All with flourishes.

Given at Verona, by the hand of Albert, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the fifth day before the Ides of August, in the fourth indiction, in the year 1186 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban III.

LIV. He receives the church of St Vincent of Bergamo under protection and confirms its goods and rights. (Verona, 11 August.)

[LUPI, *Bergamo Diplomatic Codex*, II, 1363.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1429B] sons ADELARD, archdeacon, and his brethren, present and future, living canonically in the mother church of Bergamo: in perpetual remembrance.

The petition of a pious will ought to be fulfilled in effect, so that both the sincerity of devotion may shine forth praiseworthily and the requested benefit may undoubtedly gain force. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and receive under the guardianship and protection of the Apostolic See the church of the blessed martyr Vincent, in which you are devoted to divine service, together with the body of your congregation and all things belonging to that church, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, the Roman pontiffs Innocent, Lucius, Adrian, and Alexander; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s help, by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to state expressly:

The church of St Mary in the castle of Calcinate; the church of St Martin in the village of the same place; the church of St Michael of Carpeneto; the church of St Mary of Gorlo; the church of St [lacuna] of Spalanico; the church of St Christina of Albigno; and the church of St Cassian in the city of Bergamo.

We also decree that, in all places of the diocese of Bergamo where that church has customarily held a right to tithes, tithes on lands newly cleared within the last forty years and on other matters from which tithes have hitherto not been rendered shall henceforth be conferred upon you, just as the same church is accustomed to receive other ancient tithes. We further will that you possess in perpetuity the tithes of Artola and Broseta, and of all newly cleared lands and lands situated in your parish district; likewise, tithes of newly cleared lands at Serengo and Belbiaco and in all the places of Calcinate. Saving in all respects the privileges of the Apostolic See, [Col. 1430A] we confirm these to you and your church by the authority of this present document, following the example of our predecessor Pope Lucius of happy memory.

Therefore we decree that, so long as you remain in the observance of canonical discipline, no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be kept whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they have been granted.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third admonition, unless he has corrected his offence by worthy satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

In the circle: **To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul.**

I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Henry, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. [Col. 1430C] I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Mark, have subscribed. I, Peter de Bono, cardinal priest of the title of St Susanna, have subscribed. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of St Mary across the Tiber, title of St Callistus, have subscribed. I, Pandulph, cardinal priest of the title of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed. I, Albinus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed. I, Melchior, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, title of St Pammachius, have subscribed. I, Adelard, of the title of St Marcellus, have subscribed. I, James, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin, [Col. 1430D] have subscribed. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of St Angelo, have subscribed. I, Soffredus, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed. I, Roland, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Radulph, cardinal deacon of St George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed.

Given at Verona, by the hand of Albert, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the third day before the Ides of August, in the fourth indiction, in the year [Col. 1431A] 1186 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban III.

LV. He receives the monastery of St Mary of Seitenstetten under patronage and confirms its possessions and rights. (Verona, 30 August.)

[*Monumenta Boica*, XXIX, II, 34.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons CHUNRAD, abbot of the monastery of St Mary of Sitanstetin, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Although we recognize ourselves to be debtors to all churches and ecclesiastical persons by virtue of the office entrusted to us by God [the text reads *appellatus*, perhaps *appellatis*], it is especially fitting that we cherish with paternal affection those [Col. 1431B] who, setting aside secular affairs, have bound themselves more closely to the service of almighty God. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your reasonable requests and receive the aforesaid monastery of Sitanstetin, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document.

We decree that whatever possessions or goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s help, by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to state expressly:

[Col. 1431C] By the gift of the nobleman Ulschalc, founder of the same monastery: the estate of the church of St Mary with all its appurtenances, and the properties which that founder conveyed to you near the river Urla and at Grunpach, Stille, and Hefte.

By the gift of the noblewoman Helena, her son Hertivic, and her daughter Richarda: estates near Frevinich and at Lanzendorf, Zelkingen, and Aheim.

By the gift of the nobles Eginon of Urle: a manor and mill in the vicinity of the cloister; and of Udalric of Ohsenbach: a manor at Frevinich.

By the gift of the noble Reinbert: an estate at Elsarn and a chapel with all its rights, as Bishop Dipold of Passau commended it to you by privilege.

The estate which the lady Heilwig of Pirboum gave you, with the permission and by the hand of her lord Henry, duke of Austria, through the hand of the delegate Count Conrad of Pilstein.

The serfs whom the noble Alrammus of Urle and Benedicta of Adelhartsperge conveyed to the church of St Mary.

By the gift of Udalric, bishop of Passau, of blessed memory: the parish of Aspach with all its dependent churches, namely Adelhartsperge, Piperbach, and Chrebstetn, and other chapels built and to be built therein; together with priestly right and all the tithes belonging to them, except certain tithes bound to a benefice; and tithes of newly cleared lands which have been or shall hereafter be cultivated, on both sides of the river Yps as far as Karintsgescheide, as his privilege contains.

The chapels at Clusam and Waidhoven, with their tithes and all their appurtenances. [Col. 1432A] By the gift of Reinbert, bishop of Passau: the parish of Wolfspach with its dependent churches, namely at Sitanstetin and on Mount St Michael; and the tithes at Sunnilburch with the manor itself, which you received from him by exchange for the estate of Pfafenstetn.

We therefore decree that, as you have in the privilege of the aforementioned bishop, the elected abbot of the aforesaid monastery shall always receive the altars together with the abbey from the bishop’s hand, and shall thereafter freely provide priests for those churches at his own discretion and according to their advantage; provided, however, that they answer to the bishop in his chapter for offences.

By the gift of Conrad, bishop of Passau: tithes at Rubnih. By the gift of Count Gero of Glueze: an estate at Urle; by the gift of his son Count Ekkebert: an estate at Dahspach. By the gift of Wichmann, archbishop of Magdeburg: an estate at Ibsize with the church which you built. By the gift of Liutkard, advocate of Regensburg: an estate at Flatze and Huenen with serfs. By the gift of Albert of Livprameschirchen and his son: an estate at Bretingen near Vilse. By offerings of the faithful: estates at Piperbach, Risenberge, Tulbingen, Chaetzlinsdorf, and Ydungestorf.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we decree that, according to the tenor and law of the foundation, the abbot and brethren of that monastery shall have forever the free power to elect an advocate for themselves from the founder’s kindred. If that advocate should be unsuitable and oppress the monastery by any violence, the abbot and brethren shall nevertheless [Col. 1432C] have the power to remove the same advocate and appoint another useful and good advocate from the aforesaid kindred, who is to protect the monastery not by claim of inheritance, right of benefice, or desire for any temporal gain, but for the sake of divine recompense.

If at any time the bishop of Passau should oppress the aforesaid monastery by force and unjust lordship, the founder’s kinsmen shall place gold upon the altar of St Stephen according to the law of the foundation and the privilege of Udalric, bishop of Passau; and thereafter they shall have free power to transfer that monastery to another church wherever they please. Neither the bishop, nor the abbot himself, nor any person shall have power to grant the goods of that monastery to anyone in fief or benefice without the consent of the more worthy and prudent brethren, or to alienate them in any other way.

We judge that burial in that place is free, so that no one may oppose the final wish of those who resolve to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, saving the rights of the mother church. No contradiction by any bishop or provost shall prevent you from receiving secular laymen or clerics into conversion. We also forbid any brother, after having made profession, to depart from that cloister without the permission of the abbot and the whole community, except to enter a stricter order; and no one may dare retain a departing brother without letters testimonial from the community.

[Col. 1433A] No one shall presume to demand tithes from you on your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals. Nor may anyone impose upon the monastery forced labour services or other exactions contrary to monastic peace and religious observance. You shall receive chrism, oil for the dedication of churches, and ordinations of monks from the bishop of Passau, provided that he is Catholic and enjoys the favour of the Apostolic See; otherwise you may seek them from any other Catholic bishop.

On the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any artifice of deceit or violence, except the person whom the brethren, by common consent or by the sounder part of the counsel, judge ought to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be kept unimpaired and whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they have been granted, saving the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Passau. Yet he shall in no way be permitted to impose upon it any harassment or custom harmful to the peace of regulars.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act concerning [read: against] it, after a second or third admonition, unless he has corrected his presumption by suitable satisfaction, [Col. 1433C] let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Verona, by the hand of Albert, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the third day before the Kalends of September, in the fourth indiction, in the year 1186 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban III.

[Col. 1433D] I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Mark. I, Peter de Bono, cardinal priest of the title of St Siclarin [read: St Susanna]. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of St Mary across the Tiber, title of St Callistus. I, Pandulph, cardinal priest of the title of the Twelve Apostles. I, Albinus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Melchior, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, title of St Pammachius. [Col. 1434A] I, Adelard, cardinal priest of the title of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of the title of St Marcellus. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of St Angelo. I, Octavius, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Soffredus, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Via Lata. I, Roland, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Radulph, cardinal deacon of St George at the Golden Veil.

LVI. At the request of Bishop Volscalc, he receives the church of Augsburg under protection and confirms its possessions. (Verona, 4 September.)

[*Monumenta Boica*, XXXIII, I, 44.]

[Col. 1434B]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother VOLSCALC, bishop of Augsburg, and to his successors canonically appointed: in perpetual remembrance.

Set by the Lord’s ordering upon the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, we ought to love our brothers and fellow bishops, whether near at hand or far away, with brotherly charity, and preserve for the churches in which they are known to serve the Lord their dignity and rights. Therefore, venerable brother in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and receive the aforesaid church of Augsburg, over which by God’s authority you are known to preside, under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, [Col. 1434C] and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document.

We decree that whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s help, by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to state expressly: the estate-administration at Bozan, with all its appurtenances; Staphense, Denchelingen, Mantechingen, Waringen, Maizelstein, the Greater Estate-administration, and Westendorf; Gunzeburc, Taigenhusen, Nawen, and Offingen; also the right which you possess in granting, and in electing or confirming, provostships, archdeaconries, and other dignities.

We likewise decree by apostolic authority that you shall hold the monastery of St Udalric, with the full rights and services which your predecessors reasonably possessed until your time. We forbid anyone to presume, without the consent of you or your successors, to alienate that monastery or other things belonging to episcopal right from the subjection and authority of your church. Should this be attempted, it shall have no validity.

We also forbid anyone to admit persons whom you have interdicted or excommunicated to ecclesiastical office or communion without your consent, except where danger of death is imminent; in that case, when they cannot obtain your presence, a person who is bound must be absolved by another according to the Church’s form, after satisfaction has first been made, while the canonical authority of your metropolitan is preserved.

[Col. 1435A] Nor may the possessions or any goods of the church of Augsburg, or goods held from it in fief or in another manner, be conferred upon or given to any person or church, or alienated under any other title, without the assent of you or your successors.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they have been granted, saving in all respects the authority of the Apostolic See.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third admonition, unless he has corrected his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here [Col. 1435C] they may receive the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Henry, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Mark, have subscribed. I, Peter de Bono, cardinal priest of the title of St Susanna, have subscribed. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of St Mary across the Tiber, title of St Callistus, have subscribed. I, Pandulph, cardinal priest of the title of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed. I, Albinus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed. [Col. 1435D] I, Melchior, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, title of St Pammachius, have subscribed. I, Adelard, cardinal priest of the title of St Marcellus, have subscribed. I, James, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Soffredus, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed. I, Roland, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico, have subscribed. [Col. 1436A] I, Peter, cardinal deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed. I, Radulph, cardinal deacon of St George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed.

Given at Verona, by the hand of Albert, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the second day before the Nones of September, in the fourth indiction, in the year 1186 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban III.

LVII. He receives the monastery of St Mary of Tongerloo under protection and confirms its discipline, possessions, and privileges. (Verona, 6 September.)

[MIRAEUS, *Diplomatic Works*, I, 550.]

[Col. 1436B]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HERMANN, abbot of the church of Blessed Mary of [Note: [Col. 1435D] Tongerloo, an illustrious abbey of the Premonstratensian order in the plain of Brabant and the diocese of ’s-Hertogenbosch, [Col. 1436D] not far from the town of Herentals. See the *Codex of Pious Donations*, chapter 87.] Tongerloo, and his brethren, present and future, professing the religious life: in perpetuity.

Since we have been raised, though unworthy, by the providence of the heavenly dispensation to the care and governance of the universal Church, whenever requests are made of us concerning the protection of churches, it is fitting that we graciously accede to the petitioners’ desires and bring their wishes to completion with effective result. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests; and, following the example of Pope Eugene, our predecessor of blessed memory, we receive the aforesaid Church of Blessed Mary of Tongerloo, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document.

First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order which is known to have been established in that place according to God, the Rule of Blessed Augustine, and the institution of the Premonstratensian brethren, shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s assistance, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The whole tithe of the parish of Tongerloo and the demesne, namely forty bonaria with one mill; all the land of Giselbert, founder of that church, which he possessed both in Tongerloo and in Wimple, Lanchem, and whatsoever other places; land in Ovete; land which you received from Engelbert of Casterloo, namely the co-heir of the aforesaid Giselbert, founder of the church; all Hubert’s property in Ewen, granted to you both in freehold and inheritance; the same estate, namely Ewen, with all its appurtenances; Calmpthout, by Arnold’s gift, and whatever you possess there; land granted you by Conrad both in Lifterde and in Schoonenbroeck; all Arnold’s freehold in Nile; land in Hille; land in Werbeche; land in Holenchem, by the gift of Berner Escheden, with a mill and with the marsh and wood of Eschendonck; whatever right you canonically hold in the church of Endeschit; the land of Arnold and Albert his brother, and of Arnold their kinsman, in Budincrode; all the freehold of Arnold of Ranst in Nile, and one third of the tithe of the entire village; your land in Furnhout; land in Loon, with half the tithe of the entire village and half the founder’s right; land in Beverlo; land in Donresto, granted you by Arnold of Velpa; land of Ravensloo and in Hele; land in Bosenchem and Martensele, by the gift of Henry of Hosterhoven and Walter of Villa; land of Herentholt; land in Vorsla; land in Gersecha; the church of Bruchem with its appurtenances, namely Olenchem, [Note: Aldire, now Alliere, a village.] Aldire, and Winenchem, with one third of the tithe and the ninth sheaf both in Bruchem and Olenchem, and the entire tithe in Winenchem; the church of Nispe and the church of Sundere, with the whole tithe of each church; the church of [Note: Alphen, formerly Alpheim, in the district of Taxandria, as appears in the testament of St Willibrord, chapter 8, in the *Codex of Pious Donations*.] Alphen, which you hold from the monastery of St Willibrord at Echternach, saving the right of that monastery in [Note: Diest, a town on the River Demer.] Diest; the church of Diest also, with all tithes, three holdings of land, five small enclosures, and the remaining things in that village belonging to the church of Tongerloo. [Col. 1437C] Furthermore, of your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, and of the produce of your animals, let no one presume to exact tithes from you. [lacuna]

Given at Verona, on the eighth Ides of September, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1186, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban III.

LVIII. Privilege for the monastery of St Cornelius of Ninove. (Verona, September 6.)

[DE SMET, *Corpus chronicorum Flandriae*, II, Appendix, p. 792.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ARNOLD, abbot of the monastery of the Church of St Cornelius of Ninove, and the brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Both the force of equity and the order of reason require that we grant effect to just petitioners, especially when piety supports their wish and truth does not oppose it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests; and, following the example of our predecessors of blessed memory, Innocent, Eugene, and Alexander, Roman pontiffs, we receive the aforesaid monastery of St Cornelius, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order which is known to have been established in that place according to God, the Rule of Blessed Augustine, and the institution of the Premonstratensian brethren, shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s assistance, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The whole tithe of the same church with its appurtenances; Herlinchoven with the entire tithe; the church of Lidekerke with its entire tithe and its appurtenances, namely Lumbeca and Strithem, free from every special right and exaction; two thirds of the tithe of the entire parish of Menz; fishing in the waters of Lidekerke everywhere except in the advocate’s fishpond, and use of the woodland for all necessary purposes; the estate of Nederwic with meadow; fishing in the Tenera, together with the advocate; a mill with holdings beside the church of Ninove; the land with mill and wood which William of Merbena gave you; the land which Gerard of Curia gave above Gidenghem and Guavestrata; the estate of Rubroc with its surrounding lands, meadows, and woods; the land of Hugh Cautis and his brother Giselbert; the wood of Mentogh, bought from Gerard the advocate; the inheritance of Henry, lay brother of Herlinchoven; the freehold which Herbrand of Merbena gave you, and land with woodland which Walter of Curia sold and Theodoric of Inferno gave; two thirds of the tithe of Florsenghem and the *attractum*; land given you by Gerard the advocate and Henry Warlans near Scoram, from which the church of Ninove is to receive the tithe; land given by Clarebald near Scoram; land given by Walter and Baldwin of Poleka near Okenghem; part of Quercetum, and land given by Amelric of Stenhusen; land given by the same Amelric and Hugh Rampart; in the parish of Idrenghem, a mill; meadow with pastures and all its appurtenances, which Henry and William, free men of Valran, gave to the church as freehold; the rent and the fifth sheaf of the field which lies in the parish of Herlinchoven, as Gerald and his brother Arnulf gave them to you for the soul of their mother Mathilda; the hospital of Polensele with all its possessions; land and wood given by Henry de le Roes and his wife near Lidekerke; land and grove given by Simon of Ledeberga; the altar of Pamella, with its tithe, rent, and due appurtenances; one third of the tithe of all Ockenghem and the *attractum*; the estate of Roslar with its surrounding lands, groves, and woods, given by Gosuin, Hegeric, and Alix of Scindelbena, and that given by Syger of Bosca and Gisel; likewise the land and wood given by the brothers Lambert and Syger of Horenbecca, and by Rozo of Gavera; Abon’s land near Lidekerke; land which the castellan of Brussels gave, with the consent of his lords Guy and Walter of Horden, near Senefia; there, land given by Macarius with the consent of Arnold of Fellu, and that which the same Arnold of Fellu gave; land given by Hugh Pauper, with the consent of his brother Girald, near Archen; and land with wood given by Alberic in the same parish, with the consent of his lords; wood and land given by Henry of Rut; full use of the wood of Carbonirs, and pastureland as far as the parish of Senefia extends; in the parish of Merbecca, land, grove, and meadow held by you at rent from the church of Nivelles, together with a mill and weir; beside and around the estate of Cathem, all the land and woodland with its precinct which you hold at an annual payment from the church of Haspera, and other land which you there acquired as alms from Rolino; the whole half of the entire village of Strithem, given you by William through the hands of his lords, at a rent and with the fifth sheaf of all fruits cultivated in field and dwelling-plots. In the parish of Sanctis, the estate of Hartbecca with its lands, meadows, woods, and appurtenances, as John gave it in alms with his son Walter, whom he delivered for conversion.

Furthermore, let no one dare to exact tithes from your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the produce of your animals. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen fleeing the world, free and absolved, and retain them without any opposition. We further forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, to depart from it without the permission of his abbot; and let no one dare to retain one who departs without letters of the community guaranteeing him. When a general interdict has been imposed upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. For chrism, holy oil, consecrations of churches, ordinations of clerics to be promoted to sacred orders, the blessing or restoration of an abbot to his seat, or any other sacraments, let no one dare to demand anything from you, whether under pretext of custom or in any other manner. We also absolutely forbid archbishops, bishops, or other ecclesiastical or secular persons to impose new or unlawful exactions in your churches. Moreover, by apostolic authority we prohibit anyone from usurping the advocacy of that place, from burdening the things which belong to it, or from harassing it with any unlawful exactions; rather, let him be content with what was formerly granted to that monastery and belongs to his lawful right. If any layman, without prejudice to another church and with the bishop’s consent, sees fit out of piety to grant you tithes which he holds, we grant you full liberty to receive and retain them. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, let no one be put in charge there by any artifice of fraud or violence, save the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be preserved whole and intact, to benefit in every way those uses for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he correct his presumption by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the eighth Ides of October, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1186, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban III.

LIX. He receives the convent of St Grata at Bergamo into protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Verona, September 20.)

[LUPI, *Codex diplomaticus Bergomensis*, II, 1367.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, EUGENIA, abbess of St Grata, and her sisters, present and future, to be regularly installed, for perpetual remembrance.

To prudent virgins who, beneath the habit of religion, with lamps kept alight through works of holiness, continually prepare themselves to go forth to meet the Bridegroom, the Apostolic See ought to afford protection, lest perhaps an assault of any rashness either turn them from their purpose or—God forbid—weaken the strength of holy religion. Therefore, beloved daughters in Christ, we graciously grant your just requests; and, following the example of Pope Leo, our predecessor of blessed memory, we receive the aforesaid monastery of St Grata, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in that monastery according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s assistance, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names.

The site itself upon which the aforesaid monastery stands, with all its appurtenances; the church of Calvenzano with all its possessions and appurtenances; likewise the estate and castle of Saranica with everything belonging to the same estate and castle. You may also receive free and absolved persons for conversion and retain them without any opposition. We further forbid any of your sisters, after making profession in your monastery, to depart from it without her abbess’s permission, unless for the sake of a stricter religious life; and let no one dare to retain one who departs without letters of the community guaranteeing her. When a general interdict has been imposed upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, without ringing bells, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, and in a subdued voice. Furthermore, let no one presume to demand or exact tithes from your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the produce of your animals. We ratify the ancient and reasonable customs and liberties hitherto observed in your church, and decree that they shall remain unimpaired for all time. Likewise, by apostolic authority we strictly prohibit anyone from pronouncing against you or your monastery a sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict without a manifest and reasonable cause, or from presuming to impose new or unlawful exactions. Upon the death of you, the abbess of that place, or of any woman who succeeds you, let no one be put in charge there by any artifice of fraud or violence, save the woman whom the sisters by common consent, or the sounder part of the sisters’ counsel, shall provide to be elected according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict. Furthermore, we decree that burial in that monastery shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final wishes of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while preserving the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

Also, wishing with fatherly solicitude to provide hereafter for your peace and tranquillity, by apostolic authority we prohibit anyone from presuming rashly, within the precinct of their houses, to commit theft or robbery, to set fire, [lacuna] to capture or kill, or to perpetrate any violence.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let everything be kept whole, for the full benefit of those uses for whose governance or support it was granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the bishop of Bergamo.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he correct his offence by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

In the circle: “To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul.”

I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Henry, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of St Mark, have subscribed. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of St Susanna, have subscribed. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of the title of St Mary across the Tiber, have subscribed. I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the title of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed. I, Albinus, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed. I, Melchior, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius, have subscribed. I, Hyacinth, deacon-cardinal of St Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Boso, deacon-cardinal of St Angel, title of Calixtus, have subscribed. I, Soffredus, deacon-cardinal of St Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed. I, Rolland, deacon-cardinal of St Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed. I, Radulf, deacon-cardinal of St George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, in the fifth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1186, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban III.

LX. To Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury—concerning the building of a church in honour of Saints Stephen and Thomas. (Verona, October 1.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXII, 498.]

By the authority of these presents we command you that you may build a church in honour of the blessed martyrs Stephen and Thomas, furnish it with suitable persons, and canonically assign to them the benefices which you establish for their support. Likewise, we command your fraternity that, one fourth of the offerings made to the relics of the blessed martyr Thomas having been granted for the monks’ use, one fourth assigned to the fabric of the church, and one fourth distributed to the poor, you may expend the fourth portion for other good purposes according to the discretion of your will.

LXI. He confirms the constitution that the revenues of deceased canons’ prebends are to be assigned for one year to the restoration of the church. (Verona, October 9.)

[*Works of Peter of Blois*, ed. Gussanville, p. 770.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the chapter of Bayeux: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to effective completion the wishes which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously concurring with your just requests, we confirm by apostolic authority, and protect by this present document, the constitution which you have made concerning the revenues of the prebends of canons dying in your church, to be assigned for one year to the repair of your church, as it is known to have been established by you and our venerable brother Henry, your bishop, and confirmed by an authentic document; likewise the election of the dean, as belongs to you by right. Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to violate this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Verona, on the seventh Ides of October.

LXII. He commands the bishop of Castello (Venice) to protect the parochial rights of the chapel of St Severus. (Verona, October 17.)

[CORNELIUS, *Ecclesiae Venetae*, vol. II, p. 145.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable bishop of Castello [Note: Marcus Nicolai, bishop of Castello.] and his beloved son JOHN, parish priest of St Bartholomew: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The beloved daughter in Christ, the abbess of St Lawrence, has informed us that although the houses of George Lawrence, Bon John of Morzano, and certain others stand in the parish of St Severus, which is a chapel of the aforesaid abbess, nevertheless the inhabitants of those houses do not render parochial dues to that chapel. Since it is therefore part of our solicitude and office to preserve to each church its own right, we command your discretion by apostolic letters, after full inquiry into the truth, that, if the matter is found to stand as stated, you compel the inhabitants of those houses, setting aside contradiction and appeal, by ecclesiastical censure to attend the aforesaid chapel for hearing the daily offices; to show it due reverence both in the services for the dead and in other matters; and to pay parochial dues. But should any question arise concerning this matter, we wish it to be diligently heard by you and, justice being applied, settled without evasion through appeal.

Given at Verona, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November.

LXIII. To Ubaldo, archbishop of Pisa, he affirms the primacy of Sardinia, in the year 1186, fifth indiction, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November (October 20), dated: “At Verona, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church.”

[UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, III, 408.]

LXIV. To Absalon, archbishop of Lund, he confirms the castle of Hafn, which after Absalon’s death is to devolve upon the Church of Roskilde. (Verona? October 21.)

[THORKELIN, *Diplomata Arna-Magnaeana*, I, 57.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother ABSALON, archbishop of Lund and legate of the Apostolic See: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We are bound to love our brethren and fellow bishops, both near and far, with sincere charity, and willingly and effectively to hear them in matters which they justly request. Therefore, assenting favourably to your just requests, we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen with the protection of this present document, the castle of Hafn, which Waldemar, formerly king of Denmark, of illustrious memory granted to your brotherhood, and which you gave in pious consideration to the Church of Roskilde upon the condition that you should hold it during your lifetime and that after your death it should freely devolve upon that church under the terms of the aforesaid condition, as you justly and without controversy possess it with all its appurtenances.

Namely, the village of Hafn itself; Oterslef with all its appurtenances, namely Saereslef, Solbiergh, Wanlosae, Wigheslef, one holding at Walby, Brunshöw, Ymbrethorp, the dwelling of Gefnetofte with all its appurtenances, Myrthigae with all its appurtenances, Baksuerthe, Wigherom, Husfrucöp, Awerthe, Burgheby, Mertherom with all its appurtenances; and, further, the entire share of those things acquired by your castellan Nicholas, according to the terms of the agreement made between you.

Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to violate this page of our constitution or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Witerbi [Note: Either the bull is false, or “Verona” should be read instead of “Witerbi.”], on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November.

LXV. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the canons of the Church of Pisa. (Verona, November 7.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, III, 413.]

In the year 1186, when Ubaldo governed the Church of Pisa, Villanus was archpriest, and the canons of the metropolitan see prevailed upon Pope Urban III to support by his authority the privileges and immunities which they had hitherto enjoyed. By an issued diploma, in nearly the same terms as that of the earlier Anastasius cited above [Note: See volume CLXXXVIII of the *Patrologia*, under Anastasius IV.], he graciously granted their requests.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Moses, canon of the Lateran, acting in place of the chancellor, on the seventh Ides of November, fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1186, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban III.

I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Henry, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of St Sylvester, have subscribed. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of the title of St Mary across the Tiber, have subscribed. I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the title of the Twelve Holy Apostles, have subscribed. I, Melchior, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius, have subscribed. I, Adelard, priest-cardinal of the title of St Marcellus, have subscribed. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Lofredus, deacon-cardinal of the title of St Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed. I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of the title of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed. I, Rodulf, deacon-cardinal of the title of St George in Velabrum, have subscribed.

LXVI. He amends and confirms the decrees of the council held by Peter, archbishop of Split, and his suffragans. (Verona, November 11.)

[FARLATUS, *Illyricum Sacrum*, III, 219.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother PETER, archbishop of Split: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Those matters which are reasonably transacted by our brethren and fellow bishops ought to remain firm and inviolate; and, lest in the course of time they be altered through anyone’s malice, they ought to be fortified by apostolic protection. Therefore, granting favourable assent to your just requests, we confirm by apostolic authority the divisions of parishes which you are known to have made with the assent of your suffragans and caused to be reduced to writing, because difficult disputes often arose from their confusion, inasmuch as they were made with the informed concurrence of those suffragans and are contained in an authentic written instrument; likewise, we confirm the other constitutions which, for the correction of certain excesses and for other honourable causes, you established by prudent deliberation in a council that had been assembled, together with the additions and determinations appended below to the individual chapters.

That the Office of Blessed Mary be celebrated jointly by all. Furthermore, let the canons who possess canonical revenues assemble for the celebration of the divine offices in black copes [Note: By “cope” is meant the great or long cope with a hood, lined with furs or silk according to the requirements of the season. In antiquity the canons’ cope was black, after the fashion of religious, open at the front and joined only at the bottom, as Nicholas III records in certain constitutions in a manuscript of the Vatican Church in these words: “From the vigil of All Saints until Holy Saturday, let them wear linen surplices and plain black woollen copes, or, if they wish, lined copes, fastened below at the front from the girdle downward and open.” Dominic Macer, *Hierolexicon*.], or white surplices [Note: Here the particle *vel* (“or”) has not a disjunctive but a conjunctive force [Col. 1446D], and has the same value as the conjunction “and.”] [Note: A surplice is an ecclesiastical garment, called in Italian *cotta*, either from the Greek word χιτών (*chitōn*), meaning “tunic,” or from the Arabic *Kiltan*, that is, “linen,” the material from which the surplice is made. Dominic Macer, *Hierolexicon*. Durandus, however, Book III, chapter 1: “It is called a surplice because in ancient times it was worn over fur tunics made from animal skins; this is still observed in some churches, representing that after the Fall Adam was clothed in such skins.”], and sleep in one dormitory [Note: In former times there was among canons a community of dwelling, life, and sustenance. The building in which they lived together was called the *canonica*.]. If any canon of your church, by order of the archbishop then in office or of the chapter, goes elsewhere, he shall, for so long as necessity requires him to remain away, receive in full the fruits of his prebend or his other revenues.

You also forbade the holding of gatherings [Note: Associations of pious persons, joined to one another by certain bonds of special rules, who meet on regular and feast days to perform certain duties of religion and charity, are called pious fraternities. They were customary in former times and now flourish everywhere and are highly approved. Whether the gatherings which Archbishop Peter forbade were of this kind is not clear to me. But whatever they were, and of whatever kind, he judged them rightly and deservedly to be forbidden and dissolved, because they had departed from their original institution and he had found in them more evil than good.] called fraternities [Col. 1447A]; and that no count [Note: This prohibition may perhaps have been occasioned by Count Minoslav, who misappropriated the money of Archbishop and martyr Raynerius.], or any other layman, when it happens that your church is vacant of a ruler, presume in any way to meddle with its house or other ecclesiastical property, or to appoint any person . . . [Note: Although some words are missing, the sense of this canon can nevertheless be understood clearly enough from what survives. If anything further is desired, it is expressed in the manuscript of Spalato in these words: “Let the archbishop promote no one to an order unless he has been presented through the archdeacon or through the canons of St Domnius.” In certain manuscripts of Donius of Gaudentia, copied from a canon of Spalato, I find it written somewhat differently, or explained more fully: “Likewise concerning the clerics of the parish who wish to receive orders: the archpriest of Clissa must present all the clerics of Cetina and Massaro with the knowledge of the archdeacon of the city; and so concerning the rest of the entire parish.”] whom a cleric shall judge ought to be ordained by the common counsel, or by that of the greater and sounder part, of the suffragans.

You also enacted that no one in priestly orders should take a wife, nor be admitted to the priestly order unless he promises to live continently; and we will that this also be observed in the order of deaconship [Note: The vow of continence was not yet attached to the order of subdeacon by a universal and everywhere received law. Innocent III decreed that it should be reckoned among the sacred orders. Thereafter subdeacons throughout the universal Church began, like deacons, to be bound by the law of celibacy.].
