Moreover, you enacted that no bishop should presume to receive or ordain a priest or cleric of another diocese [Note: This canon is entirely in accordance with the norm of the primitive ecclesiastical discipline [Col. 1447D], and was frequently renewed in ancient and more recent councils.] without letters from his own bishop; and that no cleric should seek to obtain a church through laymen [Note: This was to restrain the rashness and audacity of laymen, who in those times arrogated to themselves the right of conferring benefices.], or to receive from anyone investiture of a church that is not vacant. If he does so, let him be deprived, as a penalty, of his office and benefice. In an ecclesiastical cause, unless it is minor, no one’s testimony is to be admitted without an oath [Col. 1448A]; and we judge that this ought to be observed in every ecclesiastical cause [Note: The pope extends the force of this prohibition more broadly and forbids witnesses to be admitted without oath not only in more serious but in every ecclesiastical cause.].

You decreed concerning nuns that after a year of probation they should receive the veil or leave the cloister. We will this to be observed only on the condition that those expelled keep their vow in some place [Note: The word *observent* (“keep”) is missing. The pope therefore intends that those virgins who, after a year or after their probationary period, are unwilling to bind themselves to God by solemn and irrevocable profession, and who must be sent forth from the cloisters and separated from the company of consecrated virgins, should live in dwellings apart from men and from the enticements and dangers of the world, so that there they might keep the simple vow of chastity by which they had, in a tacit and implicit manner, bound themselves at their first, private reception or imposition of the veil and monastic habit [Col. 1448B]. For, as Thomassin aptly teaches in Part I, Book III of *The Ancient and New Discipline of the Church*: “The profession of virgins was twofold: one solemn, by which a virgin was veiled and consecrated by the bishop on a solemn day during the solemnities of the Mass, before the assembled people; the other non-solemn, which in the earlier centuries took place by a change of clothing alone and without assuming the veil, but later this non-solemn profession too was made with a veil, and this practice was already current in the eighth century. That non-solemn veil was imposed by the virgins themselves, whether in their paternal homes or in cloisters, or by the superior, or by a priest; it could also be imposed in the paternal home by their parents. Thus the same virgins received two veils: first, the common veil without ceremony, in their common profession; secondly, the solemn veil, also called the veil of consecration, when, having attained the year appointed for that consecration, they wished thereafter to be consecrated by the bishop.” Thomassin says this under the heading “Profession of Virgins” in his index of principal subjects, where he confirms it by the authority of the Fathers and the canons. More pertinent to our subject is what he adds there: “Moreover, however their profession was made, whether solemn or not, it equally entailed upon them the obligation of preserving chastity. For the very first reception of the veil and monastic habit, although it did not dissolve a marriage later contracted, nevertheless forbade its contraction, as Alexander III decreed: ‘Just as a simple vow prevents marriage from being contracted but does not dissolve a marriage already contracted, so the reception of the habit without profession—that is, solemn profession—and without renunciation of personal property prevents marriage from being contracted [Col. 1448D], but does not in any way dissolve a consummated marriage.’” In the Appendix to the Lateran Council, part 45, chapter 6. Thus the monastic habit voluntarily assumed without any solemn consecration had the force of a simple vow. Urban wished that this vow be devoutly kept, in dwellings separated from human society, by those virgins who, though they had assumed the religious habit, withdrew from the purpose of monastic life and profession.], lest they seem liable to rebuke for transgression.

An abbess, moreover, shall receive the blessing within a month of her election, or else be removed and another substituted. Nor shall they use linen clothing [Note: This must be referred to all nuns; the word is lacking here. They are commanded, according to the norm of the primitive Benedictine institution, to abstain both from meat and from linen garments.] or meat, unless they are hindered by illness. And because many people everywhere, having dismissed their lawful wives, take other wives, you enacted that if anyone, having dismissed his own wife, takes another, then, unless he reforms himself, neither in life nor in death shall burial or any other ecclesiastical sacraments be bestowed upon him.

What you decreed concerning the imposition of tithes [Note: Urban did not specify what the Synod of Spalato had prescribed concerning the imposition and collection of tithes, but approved what had been prescribed.] we decree is to be observed. But that which you enacted concerning usurers [Note: Neither this papal letter nor the copies of the Council of Spalato explains what penalty was established for usurers. Yet the council’s decree seems to have been milder or more indulgent than the gravity of the matter required [Col. 1449D], perhaps allowing lending at interest on grounds of necessity or for some moderate gain. The pope, on the contrary, orders that no kind of usury be excepted and that all usurers be punished with ecclesiastical censures.], and concerning the contracting of marriage before the fifth degree of consanguinity or affinity [Note: Under ancient ecclesiastical discipline, the impediment which dissolved marriage extended beyond the fifth degree of affinity and consanguinity. The pope therefore did not wish to ratify that decree by which such impediments were restricted within narrower limits [Col. 1450D].], so that indulgence might not appear to be granted in other degrees, we do not decree to be confirmed; nor do we allow usury in any case.

Furthermore, you bound by the bond of anathema anyone who removes the privileges of a church [Note: A person binds himself by a graver crime who takes away or maliciously corrupts a church’s own privileges than one who usurps something from ecclesiastical goods. For whoever despoils churches of their privileges, so far as lies in him, despoils them of all their goods and estates, possession of which rests upon the authority of those privileges. It therefore does not seem equitable that the two crimes should be punished by the same penalty.], or through his wickedness erases any useful provision from them; and this we command to be observed. But we do not decree to be confirmed the remainder of the chapter—namely, that whoever removes movable or immovable property from a church, and especially from the church of St Bartholomew, should be punished by the same penalty—because this seems excessively severe; yet we do not thereby wish in any respect to derogate from your authority.

Therefore let no person at all be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Verona, on the third Ides of November [11 November].

LXVII. In the church of St George of Brinata, “founded on his paternal allod,” he establishes a body of canons of Crescentia and endows it with possessions and privileges. He reserves the right of patronage to his brothers and their heirs. (Verona, 25 November.)

[From the Lateran Bullarium, p. 55.]

LXVIII. He takes the monastery of St Mary *de Carcere* under protection and confirms its goods and rights. (Verona, 25 November.)

[Mittarelli, *Annales Camaldulenses*, IV, 153.]

[Col. 1449C]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons LIVALDUS, prior of the church of St Mary *de Carcere*, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Both the force of equity and the order of reason require that effect be given to just petitioners, especially when piety supports the petitioners’ wish and truth is not abandoned. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just requests and following in the footsteps of our predecessors of blessed memory, Alexander and Lucius, Roman pontiffs, we take under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church of St Mary *de Carcere*, in which you are devoted to the divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, we establish that the canonical order known to have been instituted in that place according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by God’s favour, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and inviolate to you and your successors. Among these we have judged it proper to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the church of St Andrew of Curtarodulo with its appurtenances; and the tithes of all newly cultivated lands throughout the place called Caracetulum, as the privilege of our predecessor Alexander more fully contains; likewise at Agueiano; and of newly cultivated lands throughout Scudachia, Prata, Montaniana [Col. 1450B], and Vigezolis.

Whatever you possess at Cavallili, Craterolo, Carpo, Portu, Minervio, Bonadico, Urbana, Casali, Altadura, Merlaria, the town of Placentia, Montaniana, Miliarino, Palso, Vigezolo, Este, the parish church of Villa, Montesilicis, and Bavono; and whatever Gerard, Bishop of Padua, has reasonably granted you. Whatever you possess at Spaxano, Cona, Tribano, the valley of Pantena, Montagnana, and Albertone. Whatever was canonically given to you by Bellinus and Senebaldus, former bishops of Padua of good memory, we likewise confirm.

The church of St Saviour, with all possessions, appurtenances, and other things known to belong to the church—cultivated and uncultivated lands, with woods and without woods—as you justly and peacefully possess them. The land [Col. 1450C] which you possess in the village of Tinioso and at Gazolo; the church of St John at Vighizolo, with all possessions, adjacent lands, and other things known to belong to the same church, namely lands, marshes, fisheries, and tithes. Also the tithes of the whole marsh of Baone, as reasonably granted to you by the Bishop of Padua and as more fully contained in his instrument. Likewise, the tithe from the territory of the village called Cavallile.

We hold valid and confirm by apostolic authority that judgment which the aforesaid Bellinus lawfully pronounced concerning the dispute between you and the clerics of St Thecla of Este, regarding the person of Hugh Ballistarius, his son, and his property. Moreover, we decree to remain inviolate the sale which the archpriest of Runcho, together with his brethren, reasonably made to you of a certain piece of land at Minervio, which belongs to you by title of ownership.

We establish that no layman shall presume to exact tithes from possessions now held or hereafter to be held by your church; and that no one shall presume to extort from you tithes of your newly cultivated lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or for the nourishment of your livestock. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen fleeing from the world, free and absolved, and retain them without any opposition.

Moreover, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from leaving it without his prior’s permission, except for the sake of a stricter religious life; and no one shall dare retain one who has departed without letters of authorization. In the parish churches which you possess, you may choose priests and present them to the diocesan bishop. If they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust to them the care of souls, so that they must answer to him in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters.

We also confirm to you by apostolic authority the ancient and reasonable customs granted to your church and observed until these times, and the tithes which you have peacefully possessed for the past forty years until now. When a general interdict has been laid upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, with excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, bells not rung, and voices lowered. Furthermore, we decree that the burial-ground of the place itself shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted; saving, however, the rights [Col. 1451C] of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

Therefore let no person at all, etc.

I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Kalends of December [25 November], in the fifth indiction, in the year 1186 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Urban III.

LXIX. Bull for the Abbey of Exaqui. (Verona, 30 November.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, XI, *Instruments*, 245.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons THOMAS, abbot of the monastery of the Most Holy Trinity [Col. 1451D] of Exaqui, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: for the perpetual remembrance of posterity.

The authority of the Apostolic See, over which, though unworthy, we preside, admonishes us to labour with prudent solicitude for the welfare of all churches, and, lest they be exposed to the plundering or harassment of evil men, to afford them apostolic protection. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests, take under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of the Most Holy Trinity of Exaqui, in which you are devoted to the divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing.

First, we establish that the monastic order known to have been instituted in that monastery according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict shall be observed there for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by God’s favour, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and inviolate to you and your successors. Among these we have judged it proper to specify the following by their proper names.

Namely, the place itself where the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances, by the gift of Turstin Haldup and his son Eudo, and by the grant and confirmation of Robert de Haia, his wife Murieldis, and their sons Richard and Ralph; in the village of St Opportuna, where the aforesaid church is situated, all the share which the aforesaid Turstin and his son Eudo possessed there in lands, woods, waters, mills, fisheries, and salt-works; and in the village of Favilleriis, the entire share formerly held by Adelais de Balta, and the wood called Cavilleium, with all lands and the mill, with the water and mill-dues of the manor of Crienciis, excepting only their servants, and everything belonging to that aforesaid wood, as they held it; and whatever they possessed in Oreville, Awarville, and all the hamlets belonging to Orville.

At Longafames, land for one ploughland; at Coesnerios, land for one ploughland, and one vavassor with what he holds in that village; and whatever they possessed in Boseville [Col. 1452C] on the plain, Appaville, Oso-villa, and the hamlets belonging to Appaville, in lands, woods, and all other appurtenances; and two half-fisheries in the watercourse beside Hulm. Outside the park of Plesseium, pasture and grazing for all the monks’ beasts and swine, and for the animals of the servants or keepers; and, if swine are put to pasture within the park, you shall have one hundred swine free of charge in the same park from the feast of St Martin until Lent; but if no outside swine are put there for pannage, you shall have only fifty free of charge until the aforesaid term, with the same customs in the wood of Foilleia. Outside the park, timber for the church and their houses, and everything necessary to be made from that forest; likewise for the men tending their animals. In the same forest, a certain portion according to the places and boundaries which you have specified in charters, with the remaining lands and appurtenances as the aforesaid donors held and granted them to you.

The land of three servants at Balteis—namely, Ravenot, Wimund the swineherd, and Saracen—which they held from them; at Criencias, one vavassor with his land, and in the same village land for two ploughlands, three salt-works, one sea-fishery, the land of two sheepfolds, six suburban tenants with their allods, and sixty shillings from the toll of that village; in the marsh of Cressoneres, six acres of land; at Montem-catonis, land for one ploughland, free and quit of all service, aid, and rent, and the salmon caught there on Saturday nights throughout the year; at Argenceium, land for two ploughlands with the household of Rovreium and its appurtenances; also the things which Hugh de Valseio held from them at Valseium, and whatever the same Hugh held from them at Martringneium.

By the gift of Robert de Haia: Pippin’s land, free and quit of all service and aid, and one bovate of land at Brottebecum. By the gift of Renald de Aurea-valle: the enclosure called “the vineyard,” the whole share of heath beside Torkenville, free pannage for your swine in his wood, timber for your buildings at Aurea-valle, common pasture there for your animals, and *sagrimentum* [meaning uncertain]; at Guereville [Col. 1453B], two acres of land; at Lutearia, one acre of land; three acres of land from Roger de Monasteriis’s fief; the land beside the enclosure, the land of Hersendis and Annotus, and Lecelina’s enclosure with her house.

By the gift of his son Hugh de Rikevros: the land which Robert Baumer gave you. By the gift of his son Robert: land at Asambvilla; and at Baltesium, one acre of land; and everything which the same Renard gave to your church; and everything which he remitted of his claims within the borough of Exaqui, throughout the whole neighbourhood, and in other places and villages belonging thereto, free and quit.

By the gift of William de Aurea-valle: the mill of St Opportuna, with all customs, mill-dues, and everything else belonging to the same mill. By the gift of William de Abrincis [Col. 1453C], at St Saviour’s: twenty-six acres of land, and for the men of that alms-gift, common pasture and firewood on the same terms as his own men. At Vivefosse, by the gift of Geoffrey Outremer: three acres of land, free and quit of all service and aid, and one household and the land belonging to it.

By the gift of William and Richard de Pirou, and by the grant and confirmation of their heirs Ralph de Pirou and his brothers Geoffrey, Roger, and Stephen: forty-four acres of land; the brushwood beside Landa; one sea-fishery; the land on which you have built houses and gardens; the meadow of Broc; the meadow of Mela; one acre of land beside the cross; the acre which Robert son of Osmund gave you; and the virgate of land which Girold de Pirou gave you. Also by the grant and confirmation made to you by Ralph, son and heir of Richard de Pirou, and his brothers: namely, that it shall be at your discretion to bring and expend your tithes and other benefices for your abbey, to have whatever steward you wish at Pirou for your affairs, and to have such exemption from mill-dues as the charter defines.

By the gift of Roger de Albingneio and his father William: all the land which Osmund the cleric held in Kereavilla and Francavilla; sixty-four acres of land in Livervilla; whatever the sons of Ralph Espec held in Alno and Astella; in the marsh, one gardener with his land; and whatever Anicia, wife of the aforesaid Roger, gave you [Col. 1454A] at Montfamelic and the hamlet of Ogis.

By the gift of William de Brikevilla: half the mill of Matun. By the gift of his son Thomas: one acre of land in Alno, another in Verleium, and the share which he held in the fishery of Matun. By the gift of Robert de Monasteriis and his sons William and Herbert: twelve acres of land at Glatigneium; and whatever Jordan de Barneville, by the gift of his father and mother, granted and confirmed to you, namely the whole fief of one vavassor at Breteville, certain land in Jersey, and Robert Bertran’s confirmation of the liberty and exemption which he granted to you concerning your alms-gift of Sotowast, which he has granted perpetually to warrant free of claim.

By the gift of William de Asneville: a certain house beside the cemetery, and the whole marsh from the cemetery to the water. By the gift of Richard Avenel: three acres of land at Freville and another piece of land. By the gift of William de Mercato: the messuage of Pontof at Criencias. By the gift of Richard de Haia: one ploughland of land in and around Ansgoville; thirty acres of land around Haia; all the land and revenue, together with the share of the mill, which you have at Turville and beside Roger’s wood; all the land and revenue, together with the mill, which you have at Sotowast; and the fair at Exaqui on the feast of the Holy Cross.

By the gift of Alexander de Lieville: three hundred eels at Flamnigeart; the priory of Boxgrava with all its appurtenances; the three marks of silver which alone you have; the church of Felingham; the church of Rison; and the church [Col. 1454C] of St Opportuna, with its tithes and appurtenances; the chapel of St Mary of Landa; the church of Criencias with its tithes and all its appurtenances; the church of Pirou with its tithes and other appurtenances; and whatever you possess in the church of Ginefossa; the church of Torville with its appurtenances; the church of Heugeville with its appurtenances; the church of Aurea-valle with all its appurtenances; the church of Rocca with its tithes and appurtenances; the church of Felgerii with its tithes and appurtenances; whatever you possess in the church of St Saviour, with its tithes and other appurtenances; the church of Folleia with its tithes and other appurtenances; the church of Cleis with its tithes and appurtenances; the church of Plesseium with [Col. 1454D] its tithes and appurtenances; the hermitage of St Hemeland; the church of Peretot with its tithes and all its appurtenances; the church of St George of Balteis with its tithes and all its appurtenances; the church of St Susanna with its tithes and other appurtenances; whatever you possess in the church of Appeville, with its tithes and the other things you have there; the church of Cogneis with its tithes and other appurtenances; the church of Warengebech with its tithes and other appurtenances; the church of St Michael of the Wood with its tithes and all its appurtenances; the church of Haia at the Well with its tithes and appurtenances; the church of Gereville with its tithes and other things belonging to it; the church [Col. 1455A] of Alno with its tithes and all its appendages; the church of Verleium with its tithes and other appurtenances; the church of Ansgoville with its tithes and other appurtenances; the church of Breteville with its tithes and other appurtenances; the church of Sureville; the church of Glattegneium; the church of Baudreville; the church of Osmunville; the church of Orville; and the church of Merbec; and the church of Porbail; the church of St George of Rivaria; the church of Torgisville; the church of Maisnillo; the church of Aumeville; the hermitage of St Jovinus; the church of Sotowast; the church of Wisel; the church of Asneville; the church of Reville; and the church of Geroville, with their tithes and all things belonging to them; the church of Agenceium [Col. 1455B]; the church of Coesnerios; and whatever you possess in the church of Valseium and the church of Martringneium, with their tithes and all things belonging to them.

Furthermore, the church of Suavetona; the church of Bisvigetona; the church of Karletum; the church of Berlinges; the church of Cambringham; the church of Brotebi; and the church of Subroc, with their tithes and all things belonging to them; the church of St Symphorian of Haia with its tithes and appurtenances; the obedience of Aurea-valle with its appurtenances; the tithe which you have at Longafames and Vivefosse; the tithe from the wood of Plesseium and the park, from sales, pannage, hunting, livestock, birds, mills, fisheries, other petty tithes, and all [Col. 1455C] profits arising there; and the tithe from all the revenues of that manor.

Likewise, the tithes which you possess in the wood of Fulleia; the whole tithe of Criencias; the tithe of Tangue and of the mill; the tithe of the mill of Fulleia; the tithe from the grain-revenue of the lord of that village of Criencias; the tithe of salt, fairs, rams, swine, and geese; and the tithe of all revenues from that manor; the tithe of the mills of Montem-catonis, of the fisheries, and of all revenues from that manor; and the tithe which you possess at Awarville and Osoville; the tithe of the mills of Monteacuto, Bertaville, and Eudonisville; the tithe of the toll at Haia; the tithe of the park; the tithe of the mills on the water of Bo, Hardi, Ceminium, Baril, Pelemusca, and Surtran; and the tithe of the mill of Vadum.

The tithe of the money which you possess at Brotebium, Felingham, Rison, Suavetona, Lutona, and Scortona; and half the tithe of a certain mill at St Saviour, together with other petty tithes. The tithe of grain and oats which you possess at Bretteville; the tithe which you possess at Pirou, from sheaves and mills, eels, and all things liable to tithe; the tithe of the fairs of Albigney and of the market of that village; the tithe which you possess at Millerias; the tithe of the mills of Anscheterville; two-thirds of the tithes of your fief of Torville; twenty-four quarters of barley which you have from the church of Groeville [Col. 1456A]; the tithe of the mill of Rocca; and the tithe which you possess at St Sebastian.

Certainly, no one shall presume to demand or extort from you tithes from your newly cultivated lands, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the sustenance of your animals. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen fleeing from the world, free and absolved, and retain them without any opposition. Moreover, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from leaving that place without his abbot’s permission, except for the sake of a stricter religious life; and no one shall dare retain one who has departed without the guarantee of letters from the community.

When a general interdict has been laid upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, with excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, bells not rung, and voices lowered. In the parish churches which you possess, you may choose clerics or priests and present them to the diocesan bishop. If they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust to them the care of souls, so that they must answer to him in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters. We also forbid anyone to presume to impose upon you or your churches new and undue exactions, or to pronounce a sentence of excommunication or interdict without a manifest and reasonable cause.

[Col. 1456C] Moreover, we decree that the burial-place of the monastery itself shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who have determined to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; saving nevertheless the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. We also hold confirmed the liberties, immunities, and reasonable customs hitherto observed in your church, and decree that they shall remain inviolate in future times. But when you, the present abbot of that place, or any of your successors, die, no one shall be set over it by any craft of usurpation or by force, save him whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall determine is to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may [Col. 1456D] rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, or take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the benefit in every respect of those uses for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in the future, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall presume rashly to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, shall not amend the offence by due satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, and know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; let that person be cut off from the most sacred [Col. 1457A] body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But to all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Henry, . . . bishop. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of Saint Susanna. I, . . . cardinal-priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber, chancellor. I, Pandulf, cardinal-priest of the Holy Twelve Apostles. [Col. 1457B] I, . . . cardinal-priest of Saints John and Paul. I, Adelard, cardinal-priest of Saint Marcellus. I, . . . cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, . . . cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, . . . cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo. I, Gaufredus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, . . . cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in . . . I, . . . cardinal-deacon of Saint George . . . . . . .

[Col. 1457C] Given at Verona, through the hand of Albert . . . cardinal and chancellor, on the day before the Kalends of December, in the fifth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1186, in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Urban III . . . . .

### LXX. Privilege for the church of Saint Castor of Cardon

*(Verona.)*

[GUNTHER, *Codex diplomaticus Rheno-Mosellanus*, I, 449.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the dean of the church of Saint Castor of Cardon and his brethren, both present and future, canonically appointed, forever.

. . . Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their own terms. [Col. 1457D] The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the whole place for the use of the brethren; the tithes of Tris, of which two parts belong to the canons and the third to the provost; the tithes from the villages around the place called Vostra, of which villages two belong to the provost and the others to the canons; and the court of that place with its appurtenances, from which court the provost ought annually to receive half a mark and one lodging.

The place called Massenpret; the church of Afflone, with its court and appurtenances, from which the provost annually receives ten shillings; the church of Bucha with its appurtenances; the place called Rode; the place called Savirtshusen; Mathena; Limene; the church of Beltena, in which the provost possesses [Col. 1458A] as much as the canons; the church of Kirricha with its appurtenances, which belongs by right to the provost; the tithes of Elenze, of which two parts belong to the scholasticus and the third to the priest who serves in the church; the village of Bittellesdorf with its appurtenances, in which the provost has half a mark annually; the possessions which you have in Dicheset, Pumera, and Cumdeda, together with the right and liberty which the provost or dean, scholasticus, or chapter possesses therein by the ancient and reasonable constitution of the church hitherto observed.

Furthermore, we absolutely forbid the imposition of new and undue exactions by archbishops, bishops, archdeacons, deans, or any other ecclesiastical or secular persons. We confirm the liberties and immunities justly conferred upon [Col. 1458B] your church, as they have hitherto been observed, and decree that they shall remain inviolate for all time. Moreover, we prohibit anyone within the bounds of your parish from daring, without the consent of the diocesan bishop and of yourselves, to build a new chapel or oratory, saving the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. By apostolic authority we also forbid anyone to presume to pronounce against you or your church a sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict without manifest and reasonable cause. When, however, there is a general interdict upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding those excommunicated or under interdict, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice.

[Col. 1458C] I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Laborans, cardinal-priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Calixtus. I, Pandulf, cardinal-priest of the title of the Twelve Apostles. I, Melior, cardinal-priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Adelard, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. [Col. 1458D] I, Bobo, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo. I, Soffredus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Rolland, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Radulf, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Albert, cardinal-priest of the Holy Roman Church and . . . . . . . . 1186, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban III.

### LXXI. He receives the monastery of Saint Peter of Ghent, or Blandinium, under protection, and confirms its goods and privileges

*(Verona, December 3.)*

[MIRAEUS, *Opera diplomatica*, III, 63.]

[Col. 1459A]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GERARD, abbot, and the brethren of the monastery of Saint Peter of Ghent, or Blandinium, etc.

We receive the aforesaid monastery of Saint Peter under our protection and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, decreeing that the monastic order, known to have been established in that place according to God and the Rule of Saint Benedict, shall be observed there inviolably for all time. Furthermore, [Col. 1459B] whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s help, shall remain firm and inviolate to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their own terms:

This place in which the said monastery is situated, with its appurtenances.

In the diocese of Tournai: the altar of Saint Mary, established in the court of Saint Peter, with its appurtenances; the chapel of Saint John the Baptist in the borough; the chapel of Saint James; the chapel of Saint Nicholas; the chapel of Swynaerde; [Col. 1459C] the altar of Bostburch with its appurtenances; the altar of Eka; the altar of Ondeghem; the altar of Olzene; the altar of Wettrem; the altar of Lovendighem; the altar of Bergina; the altar of Themseca; the altar of Kemseca; the altar of Coesfoorde; the altar of Calloo; the altar of Wracene; the altar of Beverna; the altar of Byghem; the altar of Desselghem; the altar of Anseghem; the altar of Autrive; the altar of Avelghem; the altar of Coteghem; the altar of Bossuyt; the altar of Hollain; the altar of Baugille; the altar of Annetiennes; the altar of Werpes; the altar of Camphinio; and the altar of Carvin: these shall be free from persons and from every personal succession, as they have been canonically granted to you and confirmed by their writings by the bishops of Tournai.

In the diocese of Cambrai: the altar of Meerlebeke [Col. 1459D] [Note: [Col. 1459] The appurtenances of Meerlebeke are Bottelaere, Schelderode, and Munte.] with its appurtenances; the altar of Little Houthem; the altar of Materna; the altar of Bost with its appurtenances; the altar of Hilleghem; the altar of Woubrechteghem; the altar of Dulciaco with its appurtenance; the altar of Elinghen; the altar of Fleursighem; the altar of Ydeghem; the altar of Steenhuyse; the altar of Smeerebbe; the altar of Lecuwerghem; the altar of Dickele. In the diocese of Thérouanne: the altar of Boesinghen; the altar of Terdighem. In the diocese of Arras: the altar of Harnes with its appurtenances. In the diocese of Rochester [Note: [Col. 1459D] Commonly Rochester in England.]: the altar of Gevisham; the altar of Greenwich.

[Col. 1460A] No one may presume to demand or extort from you tithes either from your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the nourishment of your animals. You may also receive clerics and laypeople fleeing the world, if free and absolved, into the religious life, and retain them without any opposition. When a general interdict has been imposed, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we forbid anyone to presume, without manifest and reasonable cause, to pronounce against you or your monastery a sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict, or to impose new and undue exactions. No one may [Col. 1460B] presume within the enclosure of your houses to commit plunder or robbery, set fire, seize or kill a person, or perpetrate any violence whatsoever through any rashness. But when you, the present abbot of that place, or any of your successors, die, no one shall be set over it by any craft of usurpation or by force, save him whom the brethren by common consent, or the greater part of the brethren of sounder counsel, shall determine is to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. We likewise decree that the burial-place of the same place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who have determined to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, saving nevertheless the rights of those [Col. 1460C] churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

We forbid public Masses to be celebrated by the diocesan bishop in that monastery, lest any occasion for popular gatherings be afforded in the seclusion of God’s servants, or an unaccustomed access of women occur, unless he has been invited by the abbot and brethren. We further prohibit anyone within the bounds of your parish from daring, without the consent of the diocesan bishop and of yourselves, to build a new chapel or oratory, saving the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. We also prohibit your parishioners, contrary to the prohibition of Pope Innocent, our predecessor of happy memory, and to the custom hitherto observed, from receiving burial at other churches to your prejudice.

[Col. 1460D] We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, or take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the benefit of the uses for whose governance, support, and service they were granted, etc.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Albert, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Nones of December, in the fifth indiction, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Urban III, in the year of the Lord 1187.

### LXXII. He receives the monastery of Saint Mary of Sorø under protection, and confirms its goods and privileges

*(Verona, December 10.)*

[THORKELIN, *Diplomatarium Arna-Magnæanum*, I, 273.]

[Col. 1461A]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary of Sorø and the brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life, for perpetual remembrance.

It is fitting that apostolic protection should assist those who choose the religious life, lest perhaps an assault of rashness recall them from their purpose or, God forbid, weaken the strength of sound religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, [Col. 1461B] receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the monastery of Saint Mary of Sorø, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the patronage of this present writing. First, indeed, decreeing that the monastic order known to have been established in that place according to God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brethren, shall be observed there inviolably for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire by just means, with the Lord’s help, shall remain firm and inviolate to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their own terms:

[Col. 1461C] The place in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with its adjacent lands and appurtenances; the grange of Liunghe with all its appurtenances; the grange of Slaglose with all its appurtenances; Othinstorp with all its appurtenances; the grange of Aswarthabothae with all its appurtenances; the grange of Wanpose with all its appurtenances; the village called Biarbii, which you obtained by the gift of Lord Esbern, brother of Lord Absalon, archbishop of Lund, with its woods, meadows, mill, fisheries, and other appurtenances; the grange of Guthem with all its appurtenances. Assuredly, no one may presume to demand or extort from you tithes from the produce of your labour, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the nourishment of your [Col. 1461D] animals. You may also receive into conversion persons fleeing the world who are free and absolved, and retain them without any opposition. We further prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from leaving it without the permission of his abbot; and no one may retain one who leaves without letters of authorization from the community.

Furthermore, desiring with paternal solicitude to provide for your peace and tranquillity, we forbid by apostolic authority anyone within the bounds of the enclosures of your houses or granges from committing robbery or theft, setting fire, seizing or killing a person, or exercising any violence. We furthermore [Col. 1462A] decree by apostolic authority that, as has been established by our predecessors, no bishop or other person may compel you against your will to attend synods or secular assemblies. Nor may anyone presume, against your will, to enter your houses in order to celebrate ordinations, prepare chrism, hear cases, or convene any public gatherings. We further decree that, if the bishop in whose parish your house is founded, when humbly and devoutly requested three times at intervals as is fitting, should perhaps refuse to bless the abbot who has been appointed, the same abbot, if he is a priest, may bless his own novices and perform the other acts belonging to his office, until the bishop reconsiders his harshness and does not refuse to bless the abbot who is to be blessed. Assuredly, if bishops demand anything from the abbots of your order beyond due obedience, or the princes of the land demand anything contrary to the liberty of the order granted by our predecessors and by us, [Col. 1462B] those abbots shall be free by apostolic authority to refuse what is demanded, lest on this pretext the aforesaid order, hitherto free, be bound in the snare of human servitude. We add that no bishop may impede the regular election of your abbot, or in any way interfere, contrary to the statutes of the Cistercian order and the authority of your privileges, in appointing, deposing, or removing the person who is abbot for the time being. If the bishops themselves pronounce any sentence on this account against your churches or persons, we decree that such sentence is to be annulled as pronounced contrary to the grants of the Apostolic See. When, however, you cannot have the services of your own bishops, if a bishop whom you fully know happens to pass through your region, you may receive from him—and from neighbouring bishops when the diocesan see is vacant—the blessings of vessels and vestments, the ordinations of monks, and the consecrations of altars; provided that no prejudice thereby be created in future against your own bishops. By apostolic authority we likewise forbid anyone to place your neighbours or hired labourers under interdict because they have assisted you in labour on days [Col. 1462D] when you work and others observe a holiday, or on any pretext concerning the things granted you by apostolic favour; likewise, no one may dare bind your benefactors with the bond of anathema because in charity they have rendered you any benefit or service. If anyone pronounces a sentence of excommunication or interdict upon any member of your household, so long as that person remains in your service, because of the withholding of tithes or any other concession made by the Apostolic See to your order, you may absolve them in danger of death; and, if their priests, when humbly requested, refuse to administer ecclesiastical sacraments to them or maliciously delay doing so, you may also pronounce, by our authority, a regular sentence upon your monks or lay brothers who have left your cloister without their abbot’s permission, should anyone presume to retain them against your will. [Col. 1463A]

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved inviolate and whole for the benefit in every respect of the uses for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. But if anyone, knowing this page of our constitution, shall presume rashly to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, shall not amend that presumption by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, and know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; [Col. 1463B] let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, and be subject at the last judgment to divine vengeance. But to all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Peter de Bon, cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna, have subscribed. I, Laborans, cardinal-priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Calixtus, have subscribed. I, Pandulf, cardinal-priest of the title of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed. I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. [Col. 1463C] I, Henry, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Bobo, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo, have subscribed. I, Rolland, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed. I, Radulf, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Albert, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, [Col. 1463D] on the fourth day before the Ides of December, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1187; in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban III.

### LXXIII. Privilege concerning the full liberty of the monks of the island of Cara

[LANGEBEK, *Scriptores rerum Danicarum*, V, 253.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brothers ABSALON, archbishop of Lund, legate of the Apostolic See, and his suffragans; and to his beloved sons, the abbots, priors, archdeacons, and priests established in those same dioceses: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the integrity of truth is often corrupted by men’s inadequate understanding or malice, [Col. 1464A] it does not seem unfitting that even matters which appear to have been plainly stated should be explained more explicitly, so as to remove every scruple of ambiguity and take from disturbers of truth every occasion for contradiction by which they might obscure, under some shadow, matters rightly stated. We have learned that, although it has been granted to the brethren of the island of Cara, like all brethren of the Cistercian order, by our fathers and predecessors, and afterwards allowed and confirmed by ourselves, that they are not bound to pay tithes to anyone from the produce of labour which they cultivate by their own hands or at their own expense, certain persons nevertheless presume, contrary to the indulgence of the Apostolic See, to demand and extort tithes from them. By a perverse and sinister interpretation of apostolic privileges, [Col. 1464B] twisting the clause, they assert that it must be understood as referring to newly cleared lands, where it is known to be written “from labour.”

Since it is manifest to all right-thinking persons that such an interpretation is perverse and contrary to sound understanding—since, according to that clause, they are wholly free and exempt from the payment of tithes both on lands which they have brought or bring into cultivation and on cultivated lands which they farm by their own hands or at their own expense—and since no one should have material for maligning them or in any way troubling them contrary to justice, we command and strictly enjoin you by apostolic letters to take care to forbid, by our authority, all subject to your jurisdiction from presuming in any way to demand or extort tithes from the aforementioned brethren of the island of Cara [Col. 1464C] or from brethren of other monasteries of the Cistercian order situated in your dioceses, whether from newly cleared lands or other lands which they cultivate by their own hands or at their own expense. For if we had intended the word “labours” to mean newly cleared lands only, we would have written “from newly cleared lands,” just as we include that phrase in the privileges of certain others. But since it is neither fitting nor honourable that there should be action contrary to the ordinances of the Apostolic See, which ought to possess inviolable force, we command and firmly enjoin you that, if any monks, canons, clerics, or laymen burden the aforesaid persons concerning the exaction of tithes contrary to the privileges of the Apostolic See, you shall strike the laymen with a sentence of excommunication; and, laying aside contradiction, delay, and appeal, you shall suspend monks, canons, and clerics from office, and shall cause both the sentence of excommunication and that of suspension to be observed inviolably until due satisfaction has been made. Nor shall any letters obtained from anyone contrary to the tenor of this writing have force.

Furthermore, we command and enjoin you by the authority of this present document that, if anyone lays violent hands upon the monks or lay brothers of the aforesaid monastery of the island of Cara, or of other monasteries of the Cistercian order, you shall publicly declare that person excommunicated with lighted candles, and cause all to avoid that person more carefully as excommunicated, until he makes fitting satisfaction to the aforesaid abbots and brethren and presents himself before the Apostolic See with letters from the diocesan bishop setting forth the truth of the matter. [Note: [Col. 1465] According to Bartholin, in the *Annals*, this diploma was issued in 1186.]

### IN THE YEAR 1185–1187.

### LXXIV. He confirms “the customs which the Church of Chartres has used without interruption for forty years”

[Theodore’s *Penitential*, II, 434.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons . . . . . dean and chapter of Chartres: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Raised, though unworthy, by the providence of heavenly dispensation to the governance of the universal Church, [Col. 1465B] we are bound by pastoral concern to labour for the condition of all Churches and, prompted by the ministry of service which we have undertaken, to attend to their peace, so far as the Lord has granted us, yielding to their just petitions. Therefore we confirm the liberty and reasonable customs which your church has used without interruption for forty years and is known still to use without controversy, as they have been confirmed to us by the authentic writings of our predecessors; and we decree that they shall remain inviolate in future times. Therefore no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly act against it. But if anyone [Col. 1465C] presumes to attempt this, let that person know that he or she will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

### LXXV. He receives the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre of Piacenza under protection and confirms its goods and privileges

[CAMPI, *History of Piacenza*, II, 370.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot of the Holy Sepulchre of Piacenza and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

. . . . . Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive the aforesaid monastery of the Holy Sepulchre, in which you are devoted to divine service, following the example of our predecessors [Col. 1465D] the Roman pontiffs, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves; and we fortify it with the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, decreeing that the monastic order established in the said monastery shall be observed there inviolably for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may acquire in future, shall remain firm and inviolate to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their own terms: the place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Nicholas; the church [Col. 1466A] of Saint Nazarius, situated beside the monastery itself; the church of Saints Cosmas and Damian and Saint Vitalis, situated at Cremona, with its appurtenances, etc.

Furthermore, we establish and decree by this present enactment that the liberty which Denis, once bishop of Piacenza, of happy memory, granted your monastery with the assent of his canons and confirmed in his own writing—namely, that you should be free from every episcopal yoke and burden of servitude—shall, just as you have possessed that liberty down to our time, henceforth be possessed by you without anyone’s opposition, etc. We forbid anyone within the bounds of your parish to dare, without the assent of the diocesan bishop and of yourselves, to construct a new church or oratory. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, etc.

### IN THE YEAR 1186–1187.

### LXXVI. He exhorts all the faithful throughout the archdiocese of Ravenna and the diocese of Ferrara to give money to the brethren of Saint Mary of Reno for the construction of a bridge over the Reno

*(Verona, January 22.)*

[TROMBELLI, *Memorie di Reno*, 434.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, all Christ’s faithful established throughout the archdiocese of Ravenna and the diocese of Ferrara: [Col. 1466C] greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, as the Apostle says, we shall all stand before Christ’s judgment seat to receive according to what we have done in the body, whether good or evil, we ought to anticipate the day of the final harvest by works of mercy and, with eternal things in view, sow upon earth what, when the Lord gives the return, we ought to reap in heaven with multiplied fruit. We hold firm hope and confidence that whoever sows sparingly shall also reap sparingly, and whoever sows in blessings shall also reap eternal life from blessings. Therefore, since our beloved sons Hu., prior, and the brethren of Saint Mary of Reno have begun to build a bell-tower in their church and to repair a bridge across the river Reno, greatly necessary for travellers, [Col. 1466D] it is highly expedient for your salvation that you extend to them a helping hand for completing such works, so that, aided by your assistance and with the Lord’s help, they may accomplish what they cannot complete from their own resources.

We therefore admonish and exhort you all in the Lord, and enjoin remission of sins, that, with an eye to God and for the sake of your salvation, you mercifully bestow charitable aid from the goods granted you by God upon the aforesaid prior and brethren. Thus, aided by your support, they may bring what they have begun to a worthy completion, and you, through these and other good works which, by the Lord’s inspiration, [Col. 1467A] you perform, may deserve to attain the joys of eternal blessedness.

Given at Verona, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February.

### LXXVII. He informs all bishops of this privilege of the brethren of Saint Mary of Reno: “that they may be ordained by whichever Catholic bishop they prefer”

*(Verona, January 22.)*

[Ibid., p. 435.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brothers, all bishops to whom these letters shall come: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since it was long ago granted to our beloved sons . . . . . the prior and convent [Col. 1467B] of Saint Mary of Reno by the bishops of Bologna, and confirmed to them by apostolic privilege, that they may be ordained by whichever Catholic bishop they prefer, we wish and ought to provide that this liberty be preserved unimpaired to them in future times. Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, when any one of them comes to you for ordination, you shall ordain him by apostolic authority according to the tenor of our privilege, notwithstanding any objection or appeal. We do not, however, wish their opportunity to approach another bishop or bishops to be denied in any way because they have received orders once or more often from someone.

Given at Verona, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February.

### LXXVIII. He commands the archbishop of Tarragona and the bishop of Barcelona not to demand obedience from the abbot and brethren of Holy Cross until their dispute concerning the monastery has been resolved

*(Verona, January 28.)*

[MARCA, *Marca Hispanica*, 1380.]

[Col. 1467C]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brothers, the archbishop of Tarragona and the bishop of Barcelona: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The beloved sons, the abbot and convent of Holy Cross, have informed us that, since their monastery was founded on the boundary of your parishes, and a question has arisen between you as to which of you it ought by right to belong, each of you demands obedience from the abbot while the dispute is pending. Since, therefore, it is not equitable that the aforesaid abbot, until it is settled by agreement or judgment to whom the aforesaid monastery belongs, should be obliged to render either of you any obedience under parochial right, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, until this matter has been adjudicated between you or amicably settled, you shall wholly refrain from demanding obedience or otherwise troubling the abbot, and shall not attempt in any respect to burden that monastery.

Given at Verona, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February.

### LXXIX. He confirms for the sisters of Saint Nicholas of Furnes the annual fifty shillings given by Gertrude, formerly countess of Maurienne

*(Verona, February 5.)*

[MIRAEUS, *Opera diplomatica*, III, 59.]

[Col. 1468A]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, CHRISTIANA, prioress, and the sisters of Saint Nicholas of Furnes: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we should readily give assent to the just desires of petitioners, and by a resulting effect fulfil requests that do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved daughters in the Lord, graciously concurring with your just petitions, [Col. 1468B] we confirm to you and, through you, to your church, by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, fifty shillings in Flemish currency, which accrue to you annually by the pious grant of the noblewoman Gertrude, formerly countess of Maurienne, confirmed by apostolic authority, as is more fully contained in the authentic document of the nobleman Philip, count of Flanders, her brother, and in her own document.

Therefore no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our constitution or rashly act against it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let that person know that he or she will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 1468C] Given at Verona, on the Nones of February [5 February].

LXXX. He commands the monks and brothers of the military orders of the Temple and of the Hospital of Jerusalem residing in the city or suburb of Acqui not to infringe the rights of the Church of Acqui. (Verona, 12 February.)

[MORIONDI, *Monumenta Aquensia*, I, 84.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the monks and brothers of the military orders of the Temple and of the Hospital of Jerusalem residing in the city or suburb of Acqui: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1468D] The greater the benefits that accrue to us from ecclesiastical favour, the more carefully must we provide that you do not rashly disturb the rights of churches. Therefore, by the authority of these present letters, we command and strictly enjoin you in no way to infringe the boundaries of the parish of the city and suburb of Acqui, which are known to have been adjudged to the Church of Acqui by the judgment of the lord of pious memory, formerly archbishop of Milan; nor are you to admit anyone from that parish to public penances, funeral rites for the dead, or other parochial offices. For this would be grievous and burdensome to us, and we could not endure it with equanimity.

Given at Verona, the second day before the Ides of February [12 February].

LXXXI. To Reginald, bishop, and the chapter of Chartres.—That houses in the cloister are not to be given or leased by canons to laypeople. (Verona, 18 February.)

[D’ACHERY, *Spicilegium*, III, 550.]

[Col. 1469A]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother R., bishop, and to his beloved sons the dean and chapter of Chartres: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have heard—and, having heard, have been unable not to wonder—that certain laypeople, holding houses in your cloister by hereditary right, commonly admit such persons through whom the peace of the clergy is often disturbed by disgraceful noise, and the devotion of the people is hindered from attending to the divine offices. Indeed, these said houses are customarily, through a corrupt practice, let to minstrels, gamblers, tavern-keepers, and disreputable women. Wishing therefore to provide for the common decorum of the Church, by apostolic authority we forbid canonical houses henceforth to be given gratis to laypeople through whom ecclesiastical propriety is impaired, or to be leased under any pretext whatever.

We also decree concerning the houses which laypeople hold in the cloister by hereditary right: if they do not wish to inhabit them personally with a respectable household, excluding disreputable women, they are to grant them only to clerics or persons professing the regular life, either freely or for payment, should such persons wish to offer them a suitable price. Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted [Col. 1469C] to infringe this page of our constitution or, with rash presumption, to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Verona, the twelfth day before the Kalends of March [18 February].

LXXXII. Privilege for the monastery of St Mary of the Campus Martius at Rome. (Verona, 26 February.)

[MONTFAUCON, *Diarium Italicum*, 243.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ Agnes, abbess, and the sisters of St Mary of the Campus Martius: greeting and apostolic [Col. 1469D] blessing.

Matters settled by agreement or judgment under the authority of an apostolic mandate ought to remain firm and inviolate; and, lest in the course of time they again be brought into the difficulty of dispute, they should be committed to the record of letters and secured by an apostolic document. Now, whereas a dispute had long been conducted between your monastery and the churches of St Tryphon, St Saviour of Serra, St Nicholas of the Prefect, and St Blaise of Monte Acceptabile, concerning the parochial right over the people known to be contained from the house of Paul John of Mitia inward to the house of Bucacanum, and inward to the principal road which runs beside the tower of Aimeldrig of Scorza Santo, and inward on both sides of the road from the house of Monachus, and inward from the house of Benencasa of Romanello, and further inward: at length Pope Lucius, our predecessor of happy memory, entrusted the same case to the beloved sons, the rectors of the Roman fraternity, for its proper final settlement.

Having heard that your monastery had continuously held the aforesaid people as parishioners for forty years up to that time, and [lacuna], and having considered the arguments advanced on either side, they absolved you and your monastery from the adverse party’s claim concerning those people, adjudging to you and that monastery the people themselves, as you had previously been known to hold them. Therefore, that the same judgment may possess perpetual force, we confirm it by apostolic authority as reasonably rendered and as fully contained in the document drawn up concerning it, and strengthen it by the protection of this writing. We decree that no person whatsoever may [Col. 1470B] infringe this page of our confirmation or, with rash presumption, oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Verona, the fourth day before the Kalends of March [26 February].

LXXXIII. Privilege for the Church of Concordia. (Verona, 12 March.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, V, 332.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Jonathan, bishop of Concordia: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The order of reason requires, and concern for ecclesiastical advantage invites us, to love our brothers and fellow bishops with more abundant charity and to protect more generously, through the patronage of the Apostolic See, the churches entrusted to their governance, so that in carrying out the office they have undertaken they may always be the more vigilant, the more securely they see themselves preserved from the assaults of evil men. Induced therefore by this reasonable consideration, and likewise moved by your prayers, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves your person and the church entrusted to your care, with all that you now rightfully possess or may hereafter acquire by lawful means.

In particular: the city of Concordia, where the bishopric is founded, with the village of Fratta [Col. 1470D] and the chapel of St Leonard; the monastery of Summaga with all its appurtenances; the harbour of Gruaro, with its mills and everything belonging to it; the estate of Lugugnana with its village; the village of Prato; the village of Cesardo; the village of Mortulo; ten holdings in the village of Latisana; the village of Rivago; the village of Cumirago; the estate of Fossalta; the village of Gurgo; the village of Cicolino; the village of Tileo; the village of Cintello; the village of Corderado; the village of Saccudello; the village of Saleto; and all these villages, with small fields, pastures, woods, marshes, fisheries, hunting rights, waters and watercourses, cultivated and uncultivated lands—everything, in every respect, temporal and belonging to royal authority, down to the water; the estate of St John with everything belonging to it, namely [Col. 1471A] the village of Versia as far as Caxarsam, and the tithes of St Vito with one holding; the estate of Mircho with all its appurtenances; the estate of Turri with all its appurtenances; the estate and village of Arba with all their appurtenances; one third of the *muta* levied from the wood of Curto; the castle of Meduno with its village, male and female serfs, fields, meadows, vineyards, pastures, mountains, woods, hunting rights, marshes, fisheries, waters, and watercourses—everything, in every respect, including temporal rights; the village of Sequals with fifty holdings and more, and one castle-site, where the church of St Daniel stands, together with mountains and plains; the village of Ciliaco; the village of Pino; the village of Summonte; the village of Porto Vecchio; and whatever you possess in the village of Toppo and in the village [Col. 1471B] of Trevegias; the village of Stepaso; what you possess at Almutium; the castle of Maglano with its appurtenances; one castle-site and sixty holdings and more in the parish district of Fana; about thirty holdings in the parish district of Barcis; and what you possess at Calaresium, Tefam, Vivarium, and Pnicum; what you possess in the village of Gallis and in the village of Durdago; what you possess in the village of Pausis; the village of Paseglano; the village of St Andrew; what you possess in the village of Laurenciaco; two parts of the village of St Stenus; the village of Sauledo; the village of Grumelio; the village of St Lawrence; the estate of Cusano with all its appurtenances; the village of Frassenedo, and thence as far as the sea; the estate of Belgrado and its village with all [Col. 1471C] their appurtenances; ten holdings in the village of Madrisio; and the village of Arenvoluto in its entirety.

Furthermore: the parish district of the episcopal see; the parish district of the harbour of Gruaro; the parish district of Porto Vecchio; the parish district of Tileo; the parish district of Fossalta; the parish district of Jussago; the parish district of Ligugniana; the parish district of Latisana; the parish district of Corderado; the parish district of Gruaro with its chapels; the parish district of Bagnarolis with its chapels; the parish district of Azzano; of Curto; of Castellonio; of St George; of Barbana; of Gajo; of Valeriano; of Isonia; of Grovero; of Lestans; of Socole; of Meduno; of Tramontio; of Fana; of Maniaco; of Barcis; of Cavassio; of Gallis; of Poncinico; [Col. 1471D] of Riconovo; of Pausis; of Turri; of Naono; of Zaupolis; of Paseleano; of Laurentiaco; of St Stenus; and of Grumelio. On the other side of the Tagliamento, the parish district of Ripis. All these parish districts, with their chapels and all their tithes, just as you possess all these things rightfully and peacefully, we confirm to you by apostolic authority and strengthen by the protection of this writing.

Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our protection and confirmation or, with rash presumption, oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt anything against these provisions, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 1472A] Given at Verona, the fourth day before the Ides of March [12 March].

LXXXIV. He confirms the privileges of the abbots of the Cistercian Order. (Verona, 14 March.)

[MANRIQUE, *Annales Cistercienses*, III, 111.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot of Cîteaux and all his fellow abbots serving God under the same order: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, through the infusion of divine grace, your order is far and wide to Christ’s faithful “the fragrance of life unto life,” we grant our assent the more readily in those matters which you justly request, because more people, through your example, advance in the Church of God toward salvation. Therefore, [Col. 1472B] beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just requests and wishing carefully to provide that you cannot be compelled through the malice of others to do what would dishonour your religious observance, we follow in the footsteps of Pope Lucius, our predecessor of happy memory. By the authority of these present letters we grant you that, if the archbishops or bishops in whose dioceses your houses are founded, when humbly and dutifully requested, should happen to refuse to bless installed abbots and to perform the other acts belonging to episcopal office, those abbots may, provided that they are priests, bless their own novices and carry out the other functions belonging to their office; and may receive from another bishop what has been improperly denied them by their own.

We add that, in receiving professions rendered by abbots who have been blessed or are to be blessed, bishops are to be content with the form and wording known to have been instituted from the origin of the order: namely, that the abbots themselves must profess, without prejudice to their order, and must not be compelled to make any profession contrary to the statutes of the order. Should the see of the diocesan bishop happen to be vacant, you may freely receive all these things from neighbouring bishops without opposition; provided, however, that no prejudice is thereby created for your own bishops in the future. Since at times you cannot have access to your own bishops, if any bishop should happen to pass through your area, you may meanwhile receive from him the ordination of monks [Col. 1472D] and the blessing of vessels and vestments.

Moreover, wishing to provide for your peace and tranquillity, we strictly forbid anyone to summon you before secular courts. Rather, if anyone thinks that he has a legal claim against you, he shall have the opportunity to pursue it before an ecclesiastical judge. Nor may anyone compel you or your brothers to attend councils, synods, or any external assemblies, or to be subject to secular judgment concerning your own property or possessions; nor may anyone come to your houses to celebrate ordinations, prepare chrism, hear cases, or convene public assemblies. We further provide that no one may build new buildings or dwellings within one mile of your abbeys or granges. If this should be attempted by a diocesan bishop or his officials, it shall be restrained by a sentence of excommunication.

In your own cases, whether they involve a civil or criminal question, you may use the testimony of those of your brothers who are shown to be suitable for this, so that your right may not fail through lack of witnesses. By apostolic authority we also prohibit anyone from placing under interdict or daring to bind with the bond of anathema your neighbours or hired workers because they have assisted you in labour on days when you work while others keep holiday; or, on the basis of any of the concessions granted you by apostolic benevolence, from placing under interdict or anathema your benefactors because they have charitably provided you with some benefit or service. If anyone pronounces a sentence of excommunication or interdict against a member of [Col. 1473B] your household, so long as he remains in your service, on account of the withholding of tithes or anything else granted to your order by the Apostolic See, you may absolve them and, if necessary, confer the ecclesiastical sacraments together with burial.

Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our constitution and confirmation or, with rash presumption, oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Verona, on the second day before the Ides of March [14 March].

LXXXIV *bis*. Bull to the citizens of Metz. (Verona, 22 March.)

[*Histoire de Metz*, III, Preface, p. 144.]

[Col. 1473C]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the citizens of Metz: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since we hear that, in devotion to us and to the Roman Church, our mother, you remain firm and immovable according to God, we willingly attend both to your common and private interests and effectively grant your just petitions. Therefore, assenting to your requests, we confirm by apostolic authority the *Scabinat* [the body or office of aldermen], just as you possess it rightfully and without dispute and as is contained in the authenticated document of Peter of happy memory, formerly bishop of Tusculum and then legate of the Apostolic See, [Col. 1473D] and of our venerable brother, the bishop of Metz; and we strengthen it by the protection of this writing. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of the letter of confirmation or, with rash presumption, oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Verona, the eleventh day before the Kalends of April [22 March].

LXXXV. He confirms the possessions of the canons of Verona. (Verona, 23 March.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, V, 806.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1474A] sons, the canons of Verona: greeting and apostolic blessing.
