You shall regard and hold that place as accursed and profane; and you shall regard and hold as suspended from office and benefice those who celebrated in that chapel after our prohibition, until they present themselves before us, all the works which they presumed to make there having been demolished.

You shall hold restored the ministers of the convent whom you removed after the appeal lodged with us and whom we restored. Likewise, you shall hold absolved those whom, after the appeal, you presumed to excommunicate or suspend; and, the appeal being set aside, you shall restore to their former condition everything undertaken after that appeal to their detriment—namely, the seizure of their villages and possessions, their revenues [Col. 1528B] and other things which they possessed before the appeal, and likewise the taking away of other property. Unless they make satisfaction, you shall bind the unlawful invaders of the possessions of those brethren with the bond of excommunication and cause them to remain bound until due amends have been made.

You shall publicly announce that the sentences of excommunication and interdict which you rashly promulgated against certain of those brethren have no force; and henceforth, while the suit concerning the status of the monastery is pending, you shall alter nothing. Know that, if on this occasion you are disobedient and rebellious toward God and us, and delay more than thirty days after receipt of the present letters in fulfilling our command, we shall cause all the things aforesaid to be carried out by others; and we shall strictly [Col. 1528C] command your suffragans that, just as you withdraw from us the obedience due to us, so they, absolved by us, shall deny you every obedience, reverence, and honour.

Given at Ferrara, on the fifth day before the Nones of October [3 October].

CXLIII. To the bishops of (Reginald of) Bath and (Seffrid of) Chichester, and to the abbots of Battle and Faversham, he commands the following: “If the Archbishop of Canterbury delays more than thirty days in fulfilling our command, you shall carry out all these matters.” (Ferrara, 3 October.)

[Ibid., 1508.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers, the bishops of Bath and Chichester, [Col. 1528D] and to his beloved sons, the abbots of Battle and Faversham: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although we are bound to love with special charity our brethren and fellow bishops, especially those who hold a more worthy place in the Church of God, and, so far as we can with God, to honour them, nevertheless, when any grave offence is committed by them, we ought to devote ourselves to their correction with more earnest care in proportion as, through the eminence of ecclesiastical dignity, the purity of honour is more deeply blackened by their faults. We have long received the complaints of our beloved sons, the prior and brethren of the Church of Canterbury, concerning the burdens which they suffer from the Archbishop of Canterbury. Although we willingly wish, so far as we can [Col. 1529A] with reason, to show deference to that archbishop, yet, because, setting aside reverence for our commands, he seems too obstinately to persist in his purpose of oppression once begun, we neither can nor ought any longer to endure this without providing, as the duty of our office requires, for the tranquillity of the aforesaid brethren.

Since, therefore, a certain chapel, begun by the said archbishop to the grave detriment of that Church, was, as we believe, completed in evasion of our prohibition after an appeal had been made to us and after our order that the work should proceed no further; and since certain canons are said to have built dwellings around it and likewise to have celebrated divine offices in it, we commanded that same archbishop, by virtue of obedience, that, [Col. 1529B] even if he should be absent from his Church, he should without delay demolish at his own expense whatever had been done after the appeal made to us or after our prohibition in the construction of the chapel, revoking and rendering altogether void whatever had been done and unlawfully innovated concerning the establishment of canons and other matters around the chapel. He is to regard that place as accursed and profane, and regard those who celebrated in the chapel itself after our prohibition as suspended from office and benefice, and hold them so suspended until they present themselves before us, once all the works which they presumed to make there have been demolished. He is to regard as restored the ministers of the convent whom he removed after the appeal made to us and whom we restored; and [Col. 1529C] likewise to regard as absolved those whom after the appeal he presumed to suspend or excommunicate. He is to restore, the appeal being set aside, to their former condition all things undertaken after that appeal to their detriment—namely, the seizure of their villages and possessions, their revenues and other things which they had before the appeal, and likewise the taking away of other property. He is also publicly to announce that the sentences of excommunication and interdict which he rashly promulgated against certain of those brethren have no force, and henceforth, while the suit concerning the status of the monastery is pending, he is to alter nothing.

Therefore, by the authority of these present letters we command your discretion and, by virtue of obedience, order [Col. 1529D] that, if the said archbishop delays more than thirty days after receiving the letters which we sent him in fulfilling our command, you shall, setting aside every appeal, delay, and excuse, carry out by our authority all the matters aforesaid. Unless they make satisfaction, bind the unlawful invaders of the possessions of those brethren with the bond of anathema, and cause them to remain bound until worthy amends have been made. Take care, moreover, to execute the apostolic command in all these matters in such a way that you may seem to give heed rather to God than to man, and lest the transgression of anyone make you transgressors, not without the grave indignation of the Apostolic See. If all of you cannot be present for carrying these matters out, nevertheless three of you [Col. 1530A] or two shall carry them out.

Given at Ferrara, on the fifth day before the Nones of October [3 October].

CLXIV. To the prior and convent of Canterbury he grants that, “while the suit between them and Archbishop B[aldwin] is pending, he shall not dare to promulgate any sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict against their church or persons.” (Ferrara, 3 October.)

[Ibid., 1319.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the prior and convent of Canterbury: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since your venerable brother B., your archbishop, as we have learned from your repeated complaint, disturbs your tranquillity by frequent harassment [Col. 1530B] and troubles the condition of your monastery in many ways, it is fitting and consonant with reason that we, who by the office laid upon us are bound to repel injury from the oppressed, should extend to you the favour of apostolic protection against his undue burdens.

Accordingly, by the authority of these present letters we grant you that, while the suit which is known to exist between you and the same archbishop is pending, that archbishop shall not dare to promulgate against your church or persons any sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict, nor inflict any burden upon your Church, your people, or your possessions. If the said archbishop should presume to promulgate against you or your Church any of the aforesaid [Col. 1530C] sentences, we decree that the sentence itself, as promulgated contrary to apostolic indulgence, shall have no force and shall in no respect whatever be observed.

Let no person whatsoever, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our grant and enactment, or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Ferrara, on the fifth day before the Nones of October [3 October].

CLXV. He asks Henry, King of the English, not to permit injuries to be inflicted upon the Church of Canterbury by Archbishop Baldwin, and to order the observance of whatever the judges appointed by himself [the pope] have decided. (Ferrara, 2 October.)

[Ibid., 1509.]

[Col. 1530D]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the illustrious King of the English: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although we willingly desire to summon all princes and lesser persons to the paths of uprightness and, as the duty of our office requires, to lead them into the way of salvation, yet we wish and ought to do this for your excellency with more earnestness, inasmuch as we embrace the person and kingdom of your highness with greater charity and rejoice more abundantly in your spiritual as well as temporal progress. For royal wisdom is not unaware that, among other things by which you may merit grace, the preservation of the condition [Col. 1531A] of the churches of your kingdom, especially those adorned with the title of religion and order, contributes no little to increasing your glory and salvation.

Since, then, the Church of Canterbury, by the privilege of its ancient dignity and by the merits of its glorious new martyr, is renowned not only in the kingdom of your highness but almost throughout the entire world, the prudence of your discretion is not unaware how fitting it is for royal goodness always to regard it with unchanging devotion, to support it, and likewise to increase it. It is also greatly expedient for your kingdom that you should have this glorious martyr as a continual intercessor before God; and, without doubt, if, so far as lies in you, you permit reverence for him to be diminished, you will by no means be able to obtain his aid in heaven.

And indeed, just as your highness could not be ignorant of the many burdens and oppressions [Col. 1531B] which that Church has suffered from its archbishop, so it ought not to have concealed them, but should have devoted every effort to recalling that archbishop from his purpose of oppression once undertaken. But because the matter of this complaint has grown and risen excessively, although we wish, so far as we can with reason, to show deference to the oft-mentioned archbishop, we cannot pass with closed eyes over the ruin of that Church. We have therefore judged that the correction of certain matters unlawfully attempted should be entrusted to certain persons of your kingdom.

Wherefore, in the Lord we exhort your serenity, earnestly entreat you, and enjoin this upon you for the remission of your sins: as a pious and Catholic [Col. 1531C] prince, attend to the tranquillity of that Church; do not permit it, so far as lies in you, to be unduly troubled; cause what the judges delegated by us have determined to be observed; and neither obstruct it nor permit it to be obstructed by your subjects. Thus may your serenity be commended for zeal for righteousness and obtain grace from almighty God.

CXLVI. He confirms the judgment issued by the appointed judges between the Church of St. Michael of Nonantola and that of St. Martin of Causino. (Ferrara, 8 October.)

[TIRABOSCHI, *Storia di Nonantola*, II, 314.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1531D] son HENRY, archpriest of Nonantola: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When disputes entrusted by the Apostolic See are settled by judicial decision or agreement, their judgments ought to be reduced to an authenticated written record and strengthened by the protection of the Apostolic See, so that they may not in the future be brought again into contention. A controversy had arisen between the people of St. Michael entrusted to your care and the Church of St. Martin of Caucino concerning the entire tithe held by those people between Bisentulum and the river Pontilonga, the boundary of the Musone and the old Panaro and Cenosa; and concerning twenty modii of grain from a certain tract of land situated in [Col. 1532A] the village of St. Theodore, on the eastern side of which certain captains possess their estates, while on the southern side lies the aforesaid Church of St. Martin. At length our beloved sons, the abbot of St. Peter of Modena and Master Roland, canon of Brescia, received from your delegation the task of settling the matter; and the parties unanimously agreed to submit to their arbitration under a stipulated penalty. Accordingly, after hearing the arguments advanced on both sides, those judges decreed that your people should henceforth possess peacefully the entire tithe, grain, and land, imposing perpetual silence concerning these matters upon the procurator of the Church of St. Martin in the name of that Church.

Therefore, in order that this judgment may obtain inviolable force, we confirm it by apostolic authority, since it was reasonably issued and has not been suspended by a lawful appeal, [Col. 1532B] and we strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. Let no person whatsoever, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Ferrara, on the eighth day before the Ides of October [8 October].

CXLVII. Privilege for the monastery of St. Zeno of Verona. (Ferrara, 13 October.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, V, 810.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1532C] sons HUGH, abbot of the monastery of St. Zeno of Verona, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

The vigour of equity and the order of reason especially require that just requests be granted their effect, etc. Accordingly, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of blessed memory, Innocent and Lucius, Alexander and Lucius, Roman pontiffs, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the monastery of Blessed Zeno of Verona, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. First of all. For indeed, etc., the Church of St. Proculus with [Col. 1532D] all honour and jurisdiction, as canonically granted to your monastery by Bruno, bishop of Verona, of good memory, and confirmed to your monastery by the successors of that bishop, and by Peregrine, of good memory, and our venerable brother Godfrey, patriarchs of the see of Aquileia, and as contained in their authenticated documents, etc. (Thereafter all the estates and churches are described, with the subscription of the same pontiff and twelve cardinals.)

Given at Ferrara, through the hand of Albert, cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Ides of October [13 October], in the fifth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1187, the second year of the pontificate of Pope Urban III.

LETTER OF BALDWIN, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, TO POPE URBAN.—He congratulates him upon having been elevated to the pontificate after Lucius III by the unanimous consent of the electors, and gives him thanks for the pallium received. (Year 1185.)

[Letter of Peter of Blois, ed. GILES, I, 309.]

[Col. 1533]

[Col. 1533A] To the most holy Father URBAN, by the grace of God supreme pontiff, BALDWIN, humble minister of the Church of Canterbury: greeting and the service of due devotion.

The house of God, established on the stone of help upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, has always received from Peter and his successors both the pattern of instruction and the condition of safety. For what branches are to the trunk, limbs to the head, rays to the sun, and streams to the fountain, that all Churches which Christian religion has founded throughout the world owe to the eminence of the Apostolic See.

Thus it was that, when Pope Lucius III, of blessed memory, entered upon the way of all flesh—for we are all tributaries of death, have the answer of death within ourselves, and have made a covenant with it—there were among us sons who wept without a bridegroom. And while they paid funeral honours to the deceased and offered pious affections, news of your election came, removing the cloud of public mourning and making all hearts bright with more festive joy. For common report is that the Lord who, according to the word of Amos, raises up prophets from among sons and Nazirites from among young men, has by His grace now deigned to place upon the watchtower of apostolic eminence such a man for His sons as desires to benefit them and knows how to govern them, one who excels in wisdom and character and is sufficient by his merits to fill the chair of the saints. Therefore, it is recounted publicly, as a matter of common longing, in widespread speech and with thankful praise, how the wisdom of God, sweetly [Col. 1533C] ordering all things, has advanced you from rank to rank, from strength to strength, and from honour to honour.

Nor does this fail to complete the fullness of joy: so great was the unanimity of those choosing you, and Peter’s net suffered no loss through tearing or rupture. But, according to the word of Isaiah, “What the Lord of hosts has decreed, who can frustrate it?” Nor does the chance course of events alter what the height of heavenly counsel has ordained. Since, therefore, you have been taken from among men by the Lord as pontiff and appointed on behalf of men in things pertaining to God, with much thanksgiving we offer earnest prayers to Him who chose you, that He who set you apart and called you to give His people knowledge of salvation may prolong your days in prosperity and look upon the face of His covenant, or of His Anointed One; that He may, under your governance, bring tranquillity to the Church purified from every error.

Moreover, offering you not as many thanksgivings as I wish but as many as I am able, [Col. 1534B] I profess myself inferior to all your mercies. For you have many times forestalled the scantiness of my merits by the greatness of your benefits. I am unable to respond worthily to such great grace. May He deign to answer for me who, according to the riches of His goodness, supplies the insufficiency of His own. For I, a man who sees my poverty in comparison with the generosity and magnificence of the grace which you have granted me, confess that I owe myself wholly to you—whatever a servant can owe to his lord, a disciple to his master, or a son to his father.

I pray, therefore, that your eyes may see my imperfection and that, in the fullness of authority granted you from heaven, you may be willing to sustain my insufficiency. Help [Col. 1534C] me, Father, by your prayers, so that what our ability cannot attain may be supplied in this administration by the aid of your prayer and instruction. Farewell.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1187: GREGORY VIII, ROMAN PONTIFF

[Col. 1535]

HISTORICAL NOTICE

(MANSI, *Concil.*, XXII, 526)

Gregory VIII, a native of Benevento, whose name had been Albert, cardinal priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina, was elected by the common consent of all on the day after Urban’s death, in the year of the Lord 1187, in the time of Emperor Frederick. At the beginning of his pontificate he urged the Christian princes, by legations and letters sent to various places, to provide aid for the Holy Land and to undertake penance, so that, having assembled an army by land and sea, they might gather themselves to recover Jerusalem. In order more easily to achieve what he urged, he went to Pisa, to bind the peoples of that place and the Genoese by the bond of a new alliance, so that, joining forces in which they were especially strong at sea, they might be encouraged to undertake this most holy expedition. But his unexpected death put an end at Pisa to the holy expedition and to his purpose. For he died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January [16 December], on the fifty-seventh day of his pontificate.

“Gregory VIII,” says the Ursperg Chronicle, “a Beneventan by nation, succeeded Urban in the Apostolic See. He sat for two months. He was the first to send letters throughout the world for the liberation of the Holy Land, making many provisions for the correction of morals both among clergy and people, such as the avoidance of excessive dress, dances, and other vanities.” Thus Urspergensis.

[Col. 1535]

DIPLOMATIC NOTICE

(Philipp JAFFÉ, *Regesta pontificum Romanorum*, p. 866.)

Gregory VIII appended the indiction to every letter. In his bulls one finds this sentence: “DIRECT ME, O LORD, IN THY TRUTH.”

The witnesses subscribed:

Henry, bishop of Albano, from 31 October to 2 November 1187.  
Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri, from 31 October to 11 December 1187.  
Paul, bishop of Palestrina, from 31 October to 11 December 1187.  
Laborans, cardinal priest of St. Mary across the Tiber, of the title of St. Callistus, from 31 October to 11 December 1187.  
Melior, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius, from 31 October to 11 December 1187.  
Adelard, cardinal priest of the title of St. Marcellus, from 31 October to 2 November 1187.  
Peter of Bono, cardinal priest of the title of St. Susanna, from 31 October to 2 November 1187.  
Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, from 31 October to 11 December 1187.  
Radulf, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil, from 31 October to 11 December 1187.  
Jacinthus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin, from 31 October to 11 December 1187.  
Peter, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, from 31 October to 11 December 1187.  
Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, from 31 October to 11 December 1187.

The bulls were issued through the hand of Moses, canon of the Lateran and acting vice-chancellor, from 31 October to 11 December 1187.

[Col. 1537]

LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES OF POPE GREGORY VIII.

I. He announces his election to the German clergy and exhorts them to devote themselves to an expedition for the recovery of Palestine. (Ferrara, 27 October.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 531.]

[Col. 1537A]

GREGORY, to the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and prelates of the Churches in Germany.

Among the mysteries of divine providence which God works among men, there is for us great cause for amazement and wonder: He so orders the pre-eminences and subordinations of men that he who ought to be set in a low place seems to be placed on high, and conversely. Solomon himself also wondered at this, saying: “I saw servants upon horses, and princes walking upon the ground like servants” (Eccles. X [10]). Would that it had been granted to us merely to wonder at and see this, and not also to experience it! For although the Lord had called us to a lesser place and we had never acted there faithfully as we ought, we were suddenly raised to the exaltation of a more eminent office; and so great a burden has been laid upon our weak shoulders that, as far as heaven is from earth, so far do our powers appear to be from the burden.

For after our predecessor Urban had, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November [20 October], passed in good confession along the way of all flesh and had been solemnly committed to burial, we assembled on the following day. After Mass had been celebrated in honour of the Holy Spirit, as is customary, we withdrew, bishops, priests, and deacons, according to the canons [perhaps: *canonice*], to one place. Setting aside the various ecclesiastical affairs, and especially the calamity of the Eastern Church which had been reported in those days, it seemed proper to proceed to the election of a pope, lest, should it perhaps be delayed, loss through tardiness should come to the Christian people in various regions.

When the wishes of the citizens had been sought, it pleased all to lay the burden of ecclesiastical governance upon our mediocrity and to press the matter so insistently that not one excuse of mine, although I had many at hand, was heard. I did not sufficiently know what I should do, since neither resistance nor consent offered a safe freedom: on the one hand I was deterred by my great lack of virtue and knowledge, and on the other urged by the united will and insistence [Col. 1537D] of the brethren. At last, considering that the ways of man are not his own, nor is it in him who walks to direct his steps; and that Christ died and rose again for us, we committed ourselves to divine mercy and assented to the will of the brethren, [Col. 1538A] not because we believed ourselves suitable ministers or capable of bearing so great a burden well, but lest we should seem to abound too greatly in our own judgment and not to trust sufficiently in the mercy of the Lord our God.

Since, therefore, it is fitting that we remain in reverence for the Roman Church, we believe that your whole body should be admonished by this notification to persist in devotion to that Church, as is just and conducive to your salvation. Concerning the cause and affliction of the Eastern Church, moreover, by apostolic letters we make you watchful and attentive, asking, warning, and exhorting you in the Lord to exert yourselves, as you know to be expedient, for the liberation of that land. Carefully exhort our most beloved son in Christ Frederick, illustrious Emperor of the Romans, ever Augustus, together with the magnates and the entire people of the German kingdom, to perform such devoted service to the Almighty that thereby the reward of eternal life may be increased for you and for them by the Giver of all good things to those who hope in Him.

For this purpose we commend especially to your charity our beloved sons B., our subdeacon, and the prior of Pontida, bearers of these letters, learned, prudent, and honourable men, whom we are sending to announce our election.

Given [read: at Ferrara], on the sixth day before the Kalends of November [27 October], in the sixth indiction.

II. To all prelates of Churches.—Concerning the administration of justice and the settlement of lawsuits. (Ferrara, 27 October.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 1538C]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all prelates of Churches to whom these letters shall come: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since it pertains especially to the office of bishops to aid the afflicted and burdened, and God has willed that we should be one of their number, despite the deficiency of our merits, we are bound and willing to take care that no one, as a result of unforeseen circumstances arising from a visitation of the Roman Church, should be frustrated of the due effect of his labour which he has borne in coming to it. Therefore, wishing to spare many their expenses [Col. 1538D] and alleviate their labours, we have judged it proper, in accordance with the customary mercy of the Apostolic See, to decree that letters of our predecessor Lord Urban, sent during the three months before his death for the administration of justice and the settlement of lawsuits, provided that they contain no manifest prejudice against anyone [Col. 1539A] or perversion of equity, shall have during our administration the same effect which they ought to have had had he still been living.

Therefore, setting aside the exception based on the death of the mandator, carry out what he commanded to be done, so that no one who received through him the assurance of obtaining justice may be compelled, on account of such an excuse, to wander away empty-handed.

Given at Ferrara, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November [27 October].

III. To all the faithful.—Concerning the fast to be observed in order to appease God, who has been offended. (Ferrara, 29 October.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 1539B] GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all Christ’s faithful to whom these letters shall come: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Never is the wrath of the heavenly Judge more fittingly appeased than when, at His command, the carnal desires within us are extinguished. Accordingly, because we do not doubt that the peril recently suffered by the land of Jerusalem at the hands of the invading Saracens befell chiefly because of the sins of the inhabitants of that land and of the entire Christian people, we have, by the common counsel of our brethren and with the approval of many bishops, decreed that for five years all persons shall fast, at least on every Friday, with Lenten food; and that, wherever Mass is to be sung, it shall be sung at None [about 3 p.m.]. We decree that this shall be observed from Advent until Christmas. [Col. 1539C] On Wednesday and Saturday, moreover, all without distinction who are in good health shall abstain from meat.

We, however, and our brethren also prohibit for ourselves and our households the eating of meat on Monday, unless perhaps illness, a major feast, or some other evident reason is seen to prevent it, hoping that thus the Lord will forgive us and leave behind Him a blessing. We decree that this be observed so strictly that whoever proves a transgressor shall be treated as a violator of the Lenten fast.

Given at Ferrara, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November [29 October].

IV. To all Christ’s faithful.—Concerning the disaster at Jerusalem. He exhorts all to undertake penance and grants full indulgence to those setting out for war against the unbelievers. (Ferrara, 29 October.)

[Ibid., col. 527.]

[Col. 1539D]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all Christ’s faithful to whom these letters shall come: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having heard of the dreadful severity of the judgment which the divine hand has exercised over the land of Jerusalem, we and our brethren are so struck with horror and afflicted by such grief that it did not readily occur to us what we ought to do or undertake, except what the Psalmist laments and says: “O God, the nations have come into Thy inheritance; they have defiled [Col. 1540A] Thy holy temple; they have made Jerusalem a watch-place for fruit. They have given the flesh of Thy saints to the beasts of the earth, and their food to the birds of heaven,” etc. (Psalm LXXVIII [79]).

For on the occasion of the dissension which the malice of men, at the suggestion of the devil, recently caused in that land, Saladin came with a multitude of armed men into those regions. The king, bishops, Templars, Hospitallers, barons, and knights, together with the people of the land and the Lord’s Cross—through which, by remembrance and faith in the Passion of Christ, who hung upon it and redeemed humankind, there was customarily a sure protection and a desired defence against the assaults of pagans—met them. A battle was joined; our side was defeated; the Lord’s Cross was captured; the bishops were slaughtered; [Col. 1540B] the king was taken; and almost all were either killed by the sword or captured by hostile hands, so that very few are said to have escaped by flight. The Templars and Hospitallers themselves were beheaded before his eyes.

After the army had been defeated, we do not think it necessary to set forth in our letters how they subsequently invaded and plundered everything, so that only a few places are said to have remained which did not come into their power. Yet, although with the prophet we may say, “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep night and day for the slain of my people?” (Jer. IX [9]), we nevertheless ought not to cast ourselves down so far as to fall into despair and believe that God is so angry with His people that He will not soon, through mercy and appeased by repentance, relieve what in anger He permitted to occur because of the multitude of common sins, [Col. 1540C] and bring rejoicing after tears and weeping.

Whoever, indeed, in so great a cause for mourning does not mourn, if not in body then at least in heart, has forgotten not only the Christian faith, which teaches that one must mourn with all who mourn, but even our common humanity. For from the very magnitude of the danger and the barbarous ferocity thirsting for Christian blood, and putting forth all its strength in this cause so that it may profane holy things and remove God’s name from the earth, every discerning person can judge what we leave unspoken. Indeed, when the prophets first laboured with all zeal, and afterward the apostles and their followers, so that divine worship might exist in that land and flow from it to every region of the world—indeed, what is greatest and ineffable, when God, who willed to be incarnate, through whom all things were made, by His ineffable wisdom and incomprehensible mercy, through the weakness of flesh, hunger, thirst, the cross, death, and resurrection, willed there to accomplish our salvation, according to the saying, “He wrought salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 73 [Vulgate 74])—when He Himself deigned to labour for this, neither tongue can express nor mind conceive how greatly we and the whole Christian people ought to mourn that that land has now suffered what, under the ancient people, it is recorded to have endured.

Yet we must not believe that these things have happened through injustice in the Judge who strikes, [Col. 1541A] but rather through the iniquity of the offending people. For we read that, when the people turned to the Lord, one pursued a thousand and two put ten thousand to flight; indeed, while the people themselves rested, Sennacherib’s army was consumed by an angelic hand. That land too devoured its inhabitants; nor could it long possess a tranquil condition, nor retain transgressors of the divine law. Thus it offered instruction and example to those who direct their course toward the heavenly Jerusalem: they cannot reach it except through the exercise of good works and through many trials. These things could, moreover, have been feared long ago, when Arroasia [Note: [Col. 1541D] That is, Rohes, or Edessa. H.] and other land passed into the power of the pagans; and suitable provision would have been made if the people who remained had returned to penitence [Col. 1541B] and by conversion had appeased God, whom they had offended by transgression. For His wrath does not come suddenly: He delays vengeance and grants time to the penitent. But at last He who does not lose judgment in mercy exercises His vengeance, both for the punishment of transgressors and for the warning of those to be saved.

Accordingly, in so great a desolation of that land, we ought to consider and fear not only the sin of its inhabitants, but also our own sin and that of the whole Christian people, lest what remains of that land perish and their power rage cruelly also in other regions. For on every side we hear of dissensions and scandals between kings and princes, cities and cities, [Col. 1541C] so that we can mourn with the prophet and say: “There is no truth, no knowledge of God in the land; falsehood, murder, and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood” (Hos. 4). Hence all must consider—and indeed act—so that, correcting our sins by voluntary chastisement, we may turn to the Lord our God through penitence and works of piety, first amending in ourselves what we have done wrongly; then let us consider the ferocity and malice of the enemy, and, since they do not fear to attempt things against God, let us in no way hesitate to act for God.

Consider therefore, sons, how you came into this world, how you will depart from it, how all things pass away and you pass away with them. Receive with thanksgiving the time for repentance and good works, insofar as it concerns you; and give what is yours—give yourselves after yourselves—for you are not from yourselves, nor do you possess anything from yourselves, since you cannot make even a single gnat upon the earth. Nor do we say, “Give up,” but rather, “Send beforehand into the heavenly storehouse what you possess, and deposit it with Him with whom rust does not destroy it, nor moth, and where thieves do not dig through and steal.” Labour for the recovery of that land in which, for our salvation, Truth sprang from the earth and did not disdain to endure for us the scaffold of the cross. Do not look to temporal gain or glory, but to the will of God, who taught that souls are to be laid down for brethren in Himself; [Col. 1542A] and entrust to Him your riches, which, whether willing or unwilling, you do not know to what heirs you will at last leave.

It is surely not new that that land is struck by divine judgment; nor is it unusual that, once scourged and chastened, it receives mercy. The Lord can indeed save it by His will alone, but we have no right to tell Him why He acted thus. Perhaps He wished to test and make known to others whether anyone is understanding or seeks God—someone who gladly embraces the time of repentance offered to him, and, laying down his life for his brethren, is perfected in a short time and fulfils many years. Consider how the Maccabees, inflamed with zeal for the divine law, endured every extreme danger to liberate their brethren, and taught that not only possessions [Col. 1542B] but also persons must be laid down for the salvation of brethren, exhorting one another and saying: “Gird yourselves and be mighty sons, for it is better for us to die in battle than to see the evils of our nation and of the holy things” (1 Macc. 3).

They indeed were established under one law; but you have been brought through the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ into the light of truth and instructed by many examples of the saints. Therefore act without any trembling, and do not fear to give things earthly, few, and of brief duration—you for whom those promised and stored-up goods await, which neither eye has seen nor ear heard, nor have entered into the human heart. Of these the Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future [Col. 1542C] glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8).

But to those who, with contrite heart and humbled spirit, undertake the labour of this journey and die in penitence for their sins and in right faith, we promise full remission of their crimes and eternal life. Whether they survive or die, they shall know that, through the mercy of almighty God and by the authority of the apostles Peter and Paul and our own, they will have remission of the imposed satisfaction for all sins of which they have made a proper confession. Moreover, from the time when they take the cross, their goods, together with their households, shall remain under the protection of the holy Roman Church and likewise of archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of God’s Church. Concerning the things which they peacefully possessed when taking the cross, they shall suffer no claim [Col. 1542D] until their return or death is known with certainty; meanwhile, their goods shall remain whole and undisturbed. Nor, if they are indebted to anyone, shall they be compelled to pay interest. Let them not go in costly clothing, or with dogs, birds, or other things which appear to serve display and luxury rather than necessary uses; but in modest equipment and dress, in which they appear to be doing penance rather than seeking vain glory.

Given at Ferrara, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November [29 October], in the sixth indiction.

## V. He receives the monastery of Lucelle under protection and confirms its possessions and rights.  
*(Ferrara, 31 October.)*

[Schoepflin, *Alsatian Diplomatic Records*, I, 286.]

[Col. 1543A]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WIZELO, abbot of the monastery of Lucelle, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

It is fitting that those who choose the religious life should receive apostolic protection, lest the assault of any rash person either recall them from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of their holy religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1543B] of Lucelle, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document.

First, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in that monastery according to God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brethren shall there be observed inviolably for all time. Further, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with its tithes and all appurtenances. The grange of Alnofontaine, with its lands, tithes, first-fruits, pastures, meadows, watercourses, woods, groves, rights of use, and all its holdings. The grange of Liboveler, with its lands, tithes, pastures, watercourses, meadows, woods, groves, rights of use, and all its appurtenances. The grange of Courtmatrut, with its lands, tithes, pastures, watercourses, meadows, woods, groves, rights of use, and all its holdings. The grange of Chesas, with its lands, tithes, first-fruits, pastures, watercourses, meadows, woods, groves, rights of use, and all its appurtenances. [Col. 1543D] The grange of Plaigne, with its lands, tithes, first-fruits, pastures, watercourses, meadows, woods, groves, rights of use, and all its holdings. The grange of Wenckeles, with its lands, tithes, first-fruits, pastures, watercourses, meadows, woods, groves, rights of use, and all its appurtenances. The grange of Mosa, with its lands, tithes, first-fruits, pastures, watercourses, meadows, woods, groves, rights of use, and all its holdings. The grange of Annevirre, with its lands, tithes, first-fruits, pastures, watercourses, meadows, woods, groves, rights of use, and all its appurtenances. The grange of Herbeim, with its lands, tithes, first-fruits, pastures, watercourses, meadows, woods, groves, rights of use, and all its holdings. The grange of Wigehim, with [Col. 1544A] its lands, tithes, first-fruits, pastures, watercourses, meadows, woods, groves, rights of use, and all its appurtenances. The cellar or wine-estate of Steinbach, with its lands, vineyards, tithes, pastures, watercourses, meadows, groves, rights of use, and all its appurtenances. The cellar or wine-estate of Hastath, with its lands, vineyards, tithes, pastures, watercourses, meadows, groves, rights of use, and all its appurtenances. The grange of Hircewelde, with its lands, tithes, first-fruits, pastures, watercourses, meadows, woods, groves, rights of use, and all its appurtenances. The grange of Mutrisseim, with its lands, tithes, first-fruits, pastures, watercourses, meadows, woods, groves, rights of use, and all its appurtenances. The grange of Hadmanswiler, with its lands, tithes, first-fruits, pastures, watercourses, [Col. 1544B] meadows, woods, groves, rights of use, and all its appurtenances. The grange of Bures, with its lands, tithes, pastures, groves, rights of use, and all its appurtenances. The church of Wincheles with its appurtenances; the church of Hadmanswiler with its appurtenances.

No one shall presume to extort from you tithes from the produce of your labours, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen fleeing the world, who are free and absolved, and retain them without any objection.

Furthermore, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from leaving it without his abbot’s permission; and no one shall dare to retain one who leaves without letters of assurance from the community. If anyone should presume to retain them, you may, by our authority, pronounce the regular sentence against your monks or lay brothers.

We also prohibit the lands or any benefice granted to your church from being given to anyone personally or alienated in any manner without the assent of the entire chapter, or of its greater and sounder part. If any gifts or alienations are made otherwise than stated, we decree them void. Furthermore, no monk or lay brother bound by profession in your house may, without the consent and permission of the abbot [Col. 1544D] and the greater part of your chapter, stand surety for anyone or borrow money from anyone beyond the amount fixed by the prudent judgment of your chapter, unless for a manifest benefit to your house. If anyone should presume to do so, the convent shall not be bound to answer in any respect for such matters. Moreover, in your own cases, whether they involve a civil or criminal question, you may produce brethren qualified to testify, and through their testimony, as justice requires, repel violence and vindicate right.

Further, by apostolic authority we decree, as it has been granted to your order by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, that no bishop or other person may compel you to attend synods [Col. 1545A] or secular assemblies, or to be subject to secular judgment concerning your own property or possessions. We add that no one may impede the regular election of your abbot, or in any way interfere, contrary to the statutes of the Cistercian Order and the authority of your privileges, in appointing, deposing, or removing the person who is abbot at the time.

If the bishop in whose diocese your house is founded, after being requested three times with fitting humility and devotion, should refuse to bless the appointed abbot, that abbot, if he is a priest, may bless his own novices and exercise the other duties belonging to his office until the bishop reconsiders his obstinacy and blesses the abbot without any improper exaction. When your abbot to be blessed comes to the bishop, the bishop shall be content with the profession customarily made in your order and shall demand no new one. If a bishop demands anything from you or your monastery beyond the obedience due, or if temporal princes demand anything contrary to the liberty of the Order granted by our predecessors and by ourselves, you may, by apostolic authority, refuse what is demanded, lest by this pretext the aforesaid Order, hitherto free, be bound in the snare of human servitude. If bishops on this account pronounce any sentence against your persons or church, we decree that sentence void, as pronounced contrary to the grants of the Apostolic See.

Desiring also, with paternal solicitude, henceforth to provide for your peace and tranquillity, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone from daring within the enclosures of your houses or granges to commit theft or robbery, set fire, seize or kill a person, or rashly perpetrate any violence. [Col. 1545C]

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all shall be preserved whole for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical [Col. 1545D] or secular person, etc.

I, Gregory, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Peter of Bono, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Laborans, cardinal-priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Callistus. I, Melior, cardinal-priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Adelard, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. [Col. 1546A] I, Octavian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Radulf, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Ferrara, through the hand of Moses, canon of the Lateran, acting in place of the chancellor, on the second day before the Kalends of November [31 October], in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1187, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Gregory VIII.

## VI. Privilege for the monastery of Charité-Foulie.  
*(Ferrara, 31 October.)*

[*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, XIII, Documents, 158.]

[Col. 1546B]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot of the monastery of Charité-Foulie and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life.

It is fitting that those who choose the religious life should receive apostolic protection, lest the assault of any rash person either recall them from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of their holy religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Charité-Foulie, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. [Col. 1546C] First, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established there according to God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the institutions of the Cistercian brethren shall be observed there inviolably for all time. Further, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. First, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place in which the aforesaid abbey is situated, [Col. 1546D] granted by Bernard, count of Comminges, with the assent of his son Bernard and of all his heirs: everything that you possess there, with tithes, first-fruits, rights of use, pastures, and all holdings of that place; the grange of Lenerents with all its appurtenances; the grange of Montursis with all its appurtenances; the territory of Aiguas; the territory of Saint Lupus; the territory commonly called “At the Four Brothers”; and the land of Fita Hieronymi, with all its appurtenances, tithes, first-fruits, rights of use, pastures, waters, woods, and all its holdings, as is contained in the charters of that church; the mill of Tog, granted by Fortinerius and all his heirs; and the mill of Loge, situated in the territory of Ravidan, with all its waters and [Col. 1547A] the roads leading to the aforesaid mills; from the grant of Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles, toll throughout all his land; houses at Toulouse.

No one shall presume to extort from you tithes or first-fruits from the produce of your labours, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals. You may also receive into conversion clerics and laymen fleeing the world, who are free and absolved, and retain them without any objection.

Furthermore, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in your monastery, from leaving it without his abbot’s permission; and no one shall dare to retain one who leaves without letters of assurance from the convent. Desiring also, with paternal solicitude, henceforth to provide for your peace and tranquillity, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone from daring within the enclosure of your houses or granges to commit theft or robbery, set fire, seize or kill a person, or perpetrate any violence. [Col. 1547B] We also prohibit lands or any benefice granted to your church from being given to anyone personally or alienated in any way without the assent of the entire chapter, or its greater or sounder part. If any gifts or alienations are made otherwise than stated, we decree them void.

Moreover, in your own cases, whether involving a civil or criminal question, you may produce brethren qualified to testify and, through their testimony, as justice requires, repel violence and vindicate right. Further, by apostolic authority we decree, as it has been granted to your order by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, that no bishop or other person may compel you yourselves to attend synods or secular assemblies, or to be subject to secular judgment concerning your own property or possessions. We add that no one may impede the regular election of your abbot or interfere in any way, contrary to the statutes of the Cistercian Order and the authority of your privileges, [Col. 1547D] in appointing, deposing, or removing the person who is abbot at the time. If the bishop in whose diocese your house is founded, after being requested three times with fitting humility and devotion, should refuse to bless the appointed abbot, that abbot, if he is a priest, may bless his own novices and exercise the other duties belonging to his office until the bishop reconsiders his obstinacy and blesses the abbot without any improper exaction. When your abbot to be blessed comes to the bishop, the bishop shall be content with the profession customarily made in your order and shall demand no new one. If bishops demand anything from you or your monastery beyond the obedience due, or if temporal princes demand anything contrary to the liberty of the Order granted by our predecessors and by ourselves, [Col. 1548A] you may, by apostolic authority, refuse what is demanded, lest by this pretext the aforesaid Order, hitherto free, be bound in the snare of human servitude. If those bishops on this account pronounce any sentence against your persons or churches, we decree that sentence void, as pronounced contrary to the grants of the Apostolic See.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all shall be preserved whole for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. [Col. 1548B] If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

“DIRECT ME, O LORD, IN THY TRUTH. SAINT PETER; SAINT PAUL. GREGORY THE EIGHTH, POPE.”

I, Gregory, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Peter of Bono, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Laborans, cardinal-priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Cablon [perhaps an OCR error for *Calixti*, “Callistus”]. I, Melior, cardinal-priest of Saints John [Col. 1548C] and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Adelard, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, James, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Confond. [Cosmedin]. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Octavian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Julian Prison. I, Radulf, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Ferrara, through the hand of Moses, canon of the Lateran [Col. 1548D] acting in place of the chancellor, on the second day before the Kalends of November [31 October], in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation one thousand one hundred and eighty-seven, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Gregory VIII.

## VII. He confirms the Order of Calatrava and its possessions.  
*(Ferrara, 4 November.)*

[*Statutes of Calatrava*, year 1652, p. 39, as cited by Samper, *Montesa Illustrated*, Valencia, 1669, fol. I, 151.]

## VIII. He forbids the ancient rights of the Savigniac monasteries to be diminished “on account of the Cistercian monks established there.”  
*(Ferrara, 5 November.)*

[*Neustria pia*, 685.]

[Col. 1549A]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the archbishops and bishops in whose dioceses Savigniac monasteries or churches are situated, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the monastery of Savigny was formerly of another order, we do not wish it to be deprived of its rights in the monasteries or churches which it possesses on account of the monks of the Cistercian Order who have been established there. Rather, in consideration of them, we wish, as we ought, to give that monastery special and diligent assistance in maintaining its rights, etc. [Col. 1549B]

Given at Ferrara, on the Nones of December [5 December; read November], in the sixth indiction, in the year 1187.

## IX. He appoints the first Sunday of the coming Lent (6 March 1188) for the canons of the churches of Saint Vincent and Saint Alexander at Bergamo, so that their controversy may be settled.  
*(Ferrara, 10 November.)*

[Lupi, *Diplomatic Code of Bergamo*, II, 1381.]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the canons of Saint Vincent and Saint Alexander of Bergamo, and P., priest of Saint Agatha, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the case known to be pursued between you concerning various questions [Col. 1549C] could not, though long discussed in the court of our predecessor, be concluded with its proper settlement, and since at present we cannot attend to its determination, we have thought fit to appoint for you a date from the first Sunday of the approaching Lent. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command that you then present yourselves before us without excuse, or send competent representatives. Know that if either party is absent, we shall nevertheless, with God’s help, proceed in the case as far as the law permits.

Given at Ferrara, on the fourth day before the Ides of November [10 November], in the sixth indiction.

## X. To the clergy, governing authority, and people of Bergamo—he commends Lanfranc, bishop-elect.  
*(Ferrara, 10 November.)*

[Ibid., 1383.]

[Col. 1549D]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the clergy, governing authority, and people of Bergamo, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although there appears to be no reason at all to doubt your devotion, we nevertheless thought it not superfluous to commend to you by apostolic letters our beloved son Lanfranc, bishop-elect of your Church, believing that these letters will increase your devotion. We therefore earnestly admonish your whole community and likewise command by apostolic letters that you receive him with the devotion fitting to him [Col. 1550A] and humbly render him reverence and obedience.

Let none of you take it ill that, being occupied these days with many affairs, we could not conveniently decide the dispute that has arisen between our beloved sons of Saint Vincent and Saint Alexander concerning the election and the right of the cathedra. Although we defer the matter for a time, it is not our intention to deny either party its justice. Yet because the church of Saint Vincent is unquestionably regarded as the cathedral, we wish it and its canons to enjoy the prerogative of the mother church, provided that no prejudice to the case is thereby created, so that the clerics of Saint Alexander may, when the occasion is suitable, pursue their right and obtain what is just. Furthermore, if any persons should meanwhile decide to act tumultuously, we have granted the said bishop-elect authority to restrain them by a sentence of excommunication, without appeal.

Given at Ferrara, on the fourth day before the Ides of November [10 November], in the sixth indiction.

## XI. To the canons of the church of Saint Vincent at Bergamo.  
*(Ferrara, 11 November.)*

[Ibid., 1385.]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the canons of Saint Vincent at Bergamo, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since a convenient opportunity for examining the case between you and our beloved sons, the canons of Saint Alexander, [Col. 1550C] has not occurred to us in these days, as you know, we have thought fit to defer it for a time. But because we do not wish your great labour to be fruitless, we wish you to supply in full those things which pertain to the service of the bishop-elect and all the other things lawfully due to the canons of cathedral churches. If laypeople of your city should, by sedition, seek to disturb what we have ordered in these letters or tumultuously plot anything to the injury of the bishop-elect or your church, know that we have granted that bishop-elect authority to restrain them by a sentence of excommunication, without appeal.

Given at Ferrara, on the third day before the Ides of November [11 November], in the sixth indiction.

## XII. He orders two Brescian canons that one or the other of them accompany Lanfranc, bishop-elect, to his see.  
*(Ferrara, 11 November.)*

[Ibid., 1385.]

[Col. 1550D]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons J., vice-lord of Brescia, and Al. de Palatio, our subdeacons, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although efforts were made in the time of our predecessor, Pope Urban, to settle by friendly agreement the dispute between our beloved sons, the canons of the churches of Saint Vincent and Saint Alexander of Bergamo, the matter could not attain its desired result. Likewise, at the beginning of our own promotion, being hindered by many affairs, we were unable to devote ourselves properly to examining this litigation and thought fit to defer it for a time. Since it is neither fitting nor safe that, because of the dissensions of the aforesaid clerics, the welfare of the church and bishopric of Bergamo should be exposed to danger, we wish our beloved son L., bishop-elect of that city, to return to the place of his cathedra, namely the church of Saint Vincent. Furthermore, since we do not wish anything to be altered, until the case is concluded, to the prejudice of either party, and since we also provide lest any sedition arise when the said bishop-elect comes to his church, we command by apostolic letters [Col. 1551B] that one of you, whom the bishop-elect shall choose to request, attend him as he enters the church, accompanying him at his left side.

But because a dispute is raised over this matter, the clerics of Saint Alexander claiming that they ought to occupy his left side, while others maintain the contrary, we have arranged to regulate the matter thus: someone in our name shall occupy the place contested, and so the malice of indignation shall be removed from both parties. There is no dispute regarding the place of the clerics of Saint Vincent, because without any contradiction they ought to occupy the right side.

Given at Ferrara, on the third day before the Ides of November [11 November], in the sixth indiction.

## XIII. He urges the bishop of Castello (Venice) to grant the church of Saint Bartholomew to the canons of Saint Saviour.  
*(Ferrara, 11 November [Note: [Col. 1551D] Although no chronological indication of the year is read in the copy of the document, it is certain that it was issued in 1187; for Gregory VIII, elected on 21 October of that year, died on 16 December, before two months of his pontificate had elapsed.].)*

[Cornelius, *The Church of Venice*, XIV, 114.]

[Col. 1551C]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Castello [Note: [Col. 1552D] Mark Nicola.], greeting and apostolic blessing.

The duty of the government entrusted to us, and the obligation of charity, require that we provide peace and tranquillity for religious places and preserve their rights unimpaired. Therefore, since dissension has at times arisen between the beloved sons . . . . . the prior and canons of Saint Saviour at Rialto, and the parish priest of Saint [Col. 1551D] Bartholomew, because neighbours of the aforesaid church of Saint Bartholomew pay parochial dues, the said canons long ago obtained letters from you or your predecessor in order that, by episcopal generosity, they might acquire that church while preserving all the rights of the church of Castello.

Since this has not yet been carried out, and since we have hope from your devotion that you would willingly, even without our speaking, carry out what is advantageous to those brethren, we exhort your brotherhood in the Lord and command [Col. 1552A] that, out of regard for God and reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, you generously grant the aforesaid church of Saint Bartholomew to the said canons, to be peacefully possessed after the death of the parish priest of that church, saving to you and your successors episcopal right and the other dues which you have customarily received from it. Thus those canons may be more devoted to you on this account, may intercede for you with the Lord in continual prayers, and may enable us to deserve thanks for divine works.

Given at Ferrara, on the third day before the Ides of November [11 November], in the sixth indiction.

## XIV. He frees the canons of the Venetian church of Saint Saviour from payment of tithes.  
*(Ferrara, 16 November.)*

[Ibid.]

[Col. 1552B]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons . . . . . the prior and canons of Saint Saviour of Venice, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, by the inspiration of the Lord, you have professed a regular order, we desire—and are bound by a common and special obligation—to support you and to grant effectively the apostolic favor in those matters which you justly request. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, by these present letters we grant you that no layman shall have the power to demand or extort from you tithes from the produce of your labors. Let no person whatsoever, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our concession [Col. 1552C] or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Ferrara, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the sixth indiction.

XV. To all bishops, etc., and archdeacons. (Bologna, November.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXIII, 418.]

GREGORY VIII, to all brother bishops and archdeacons to whom these letters shall come.

Whether through the deceit or malice of litigants, or through our own inadequacy, we believe it comes about that we are pressed day after day by so great a multitude of business [Col. 1552D] that, burdened by the weakness of our own body and hindered also by diminished attentiveness, we cannot conveniently attend to everything or endure on every side the cries and murmurs of those who object. Thus it also happens that, occupied with lesser affairs, we cannot give attention to greater ones as ecclesiastical necessity would require; and matters which might have been decided or arranged by us in a short time are prolonged, through excessive delay, beyond what is proper, while many matters assail us at once.

Accordingly, by this general letter [Col. 1553A] we have judged that a remedy must be provided for this situation, lest we be impeded by attacks of every kind or justice perish for those suffering wrong. Therefore, by apostolic decree, we command all of you through these present letters that, if a case concerning a small matter, involving a sum below twenty marks, is being heard in your courts and one of the litigants deceitfully thinks that he ought to appeal, you shall disregard his appeal and compel them to choose, within the bounds of your bishoprics, judges free from suspicion—provided suitable persons are found there before whom the dispute may be settled. If either party believes that an appeal should be made from them, let that party lodge an appeal with the archbishop or primate.

But if such a case [Col. 1553B] involves a somewhat larger sum, they are not to be compelled against their will to choose judges within the boundaries of your dioceses if they do not choose to do so voluntarily; nevertheless, they shall be compelled to choose certain adjudicators from neighboring bishoprics, in accordance with the form set out above, to handle the case, while preserving, in greater cases and more obscure issues, the opportunity of appeal to the Apostolic See. For it does not seem free from suspicion of malice that many compel their adversaries to make the arduous journey to our presence.

Moreover, if, from the coming feast of the Purification onward, any litigants in cases concerning which the bishop to whose jurisdiction at least the person summoned is subject has not been approached, or in which clerical judges have not been chosen in the aforesaid manner, obtain letters from us [Col. 1553C] by which the examination or determination of disputes is committed to judges who are not the ordinary judges, they shall derive no benefit from the letters so obtained, and their cases shall return in due order to the hearing of their own judges. For we wish to prevent evasions in litigation in such a way that, while we oppose their cunning, we open for them another path to justice. But when some have a just cause for approaching our presence, do not refuse them letters dimissory, containing the course of the case. In making these provisions concerning appeals made to us, however, we do not alter the order of the ancient canons concerning those made to archbishops or primates.

XVI. He takes the Venetian church of St. Saviour under protection and confirms its privileges. (Modena, November 22.)

[CORNELII, *Ecclesiae Venetae*, XIV, 115.]

[Col. 1553D]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GREGORY, prior of the church of St. Saviour at Rialto, and his brethren, present and future, who profess the canonical life: in perpetuity.

Those who choose the religious life ought to receive the protection of the Apostolic See, lest an assault of any rashness either recall them from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, and, following the example of our predecessors of blessed memory, Innocent, Eugenius, Anastasius, Alexander, Lucius, and Urban, Roman pontiffs, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church of St. Saviour, in which you are devoted to divine service, [Col. 1554A] and fortify it by the privilege of this present document. First, we decree that the canonical order known to have been established in that church according to the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the grant of pontiffs, the gifts of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favor, [Col. 1554B] acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself where the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; also the houses, lands, vineyards, saltworks, and whatever rights you have at Clugia; the mill and lands which you have at Barleana in the territory of Dese; the mill, the holding with vineyards, woods, and its other appurtenances, as the noble men Leonard, Philip, and Rigetus, sons of the late Girard of Inginulfo, gave them to your church; lands at Liguentia, lands at Flumizello, lands at Marsiliaco, and lands at Sacco. We also apostolically confirm to you one half of the tithes paid by the parishioners of your church, [Col. 1554C] as our predecessor of blessed memory Pope Eugenius ordered and John Polanus, formerly diocesan bishop, of blessed memory, granted you by his privilege, both for the clergy and for repairing roofs. And we grant full power to the prior of your church to pronounce a sentence of excommunication against your parishioners who presume to defraud you of half of those tithes, just as our predecessors of happy memory Adrian, Alexander, Lucius, and Urban, Roman pontiffs, are known to have granted in their writings. We also grant you, as is known to have been granted by those aforesaid predecessors of ours, that the prior of your place for the time being may freely provide security for those tithes according to the custom of the land. You may also receive clerics and laypeople, free and released from secular ties, who flee from the world for conversion, and retain them in your church without anyone’s opposition.

Furthermore, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession, to leave the cloister without permission of his prior; and no one shall dare retain one who departs without a guarantee in letters from the community. Moreover, we apostolically confirm the sentence reasonably rendered by our venerable brother Henry, patriarch of Grado, and Ildebrand, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles, of good memory and then legate of the Apostolic See, concerning the controversy, formerly long disputed, between you and Dominic, parish priest [Col. 1555A] of St. Bartholomew, regarding certain parish houses—namely, the houses of the Justi, the Maurocenii, the Gradonici, the Greeks, Leonard Fradelli, and Dominic Aureus—which each party claimed as belonging to his own right, as is known to be contained in their authentic instrument made on that matter.

We also decree that the burial ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; provided, nevertheless, that the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken are preserved. We therefore decree that no one, without your consent, shall dare give penance to your parishioners lying ill, [Col. 1555B] anoint them, or receive them for burial, unless the rights of your church, established by the sacred canons, are preserved.

On the death of you, the present prior of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over the community there by any trick of surreptitious procurement or by force, except the person whom the brethren, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall canonically provide to be elected according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb your church, take away its possessions, retain property taken away, diminish it, or harass it by any vexations; but let all things be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those uses for whose governance and support they were granted, [Col. 1555C] saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If therefore in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Gregory, bishop of the Catholic Church, subscribe. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina, subscribe. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri, subscribe. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of St. Mary across the Tiber, of the title of St. Callistus, subscribe. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian, subscribe. I, Radulf, deacon-cardinal of St. George at the Golden Veil, subscribe.

Given at Modena, through the hand of Moses, canon of the Lateran, acting as chancellor, on the tenth day before the Kalends of December, [Col. 1555D] in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1186, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gregory VIII.

XVII. Privilege for the church of St. Apollinaris. (Parma, November 28.)

[TIRABOSCHI, *Memorie Modenesi*, III, 104.]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JEROME, prior of St. Apollinaris, and his brethren, present and future, who profess the regular life: in perpetuity.

Whenever something is requested of us which seems fitting to religion and integrity, it befits us readily to grant it willingly and to bestow apostolic support upon the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, [Col. 1556A] we graciously assent to your just petitions, and, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of happy memory Alexander, Lucius, and Urban, Roman pontiffs, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the church of St. Apollinaris, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document. First, we decree that the canonical order known to have been instituted in the same place according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grants of pontiffs or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the favor of [the Lord—missing at Col. 1556B], shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself where the said church is situated, with the parishioners and all possessions belonging to that church; what you have in the estate of Stagnani and Ciliani; whatever you have at Gauzano and in the estate of Montisolongii, at Marano, Parviliano, Badiano, St. Mark’s, Crispiliano, and Pragatuto, with all their adjacent lands and appurtenances that belong to you by right; the church of St. Michael of Sclavo with everything belonging to that church; the church of St. James of Reggio, with its entire parish, the land at Gaio, and the tithe which Reginus, archdeacon, gave to that church [Col. 1556C] in the same Gaio; the land which it has at Gavascio; the land which it has in the meadow of Fontana, around the city of Reggio, and all other things belonging to that church; the church of St. John the Baptist of Burano, situated in the Ferrarese parish, with all its adjacent lands and appurtenances; and, moreover, the possessions lawfully restored to your church by Ildebrand, deacon-cardinal of St. Eustace, of good memory, as contained in his authentic instrument. We apostolically confirm these to you, that you may possess them lawfully.

Moreover, no one shall dare extort from you tithes from your newly cultivated lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the nourishment of your animals. [Col. 1556D] We also forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in the same place, to leave your cloister without permission of his prior; and no one shall dare retain one who departs without a guarantee in letters from the community. When a general interdict is imposed upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, without ringing bells, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, and in a subdued voice. You may receive clerics and laypeople, free and released from secular ties, who flee from the world for conversion, and retain them without any opposition.

Furthermore, by apostolic authority we establish that no one may impose new or undue exactions upon you or your churches, or pronounce against you or your churches a sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict without manifest and reasonable cause.
