We direct that chrism, holy oil, church dedications, and ordinations of clerics shall be supplied to you and your successors by the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic and has the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, freely and without any improper charge. [Col. 1557A] We also apostolically confirm the liberties and immunities, and the ancient and reasonable customs of your church which have been peacefully maintained from forty years ago until these times.

Moreover, we decree that the burial ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wishes of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated [Col. 1557B] or under interdict; provided, nevertheless, that the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken are preserved. On the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over the community there through any trick of surreptitious procurement or by force, except the person whom the brethren, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to God and blessed Augustine.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain property taken away, diminish it, or harass it by any vexations; but let all things be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those uses for whose governance and support they were granted, [Col. 1557C] saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. As a token of the protection received from the Apostolic See for your church and of obedience to St. James, you shall pay two imperial solidi every year to us and our successors. If therefore in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

Fare well.

I, Gregory, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri, have subscribed. [Col. 1557D] I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of St. Mary across the Tiber, of the title of St. Callistus, have subscribed. I, Melior, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius, have subscribed. I, Jac., deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Rad., deacon-cardinal of St. George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed.

Given at Parma, through the hand of Moses, canon of the Lateran, acting as chancellor, on the fourth day before the Kalends of December, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1187, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gregory VIII.

XVIII. To Emperor Frederick.—He signifies counsels of peace, his own disposition to favor Frederick, and his approval that Frederick himself cherishes the same. (Parma, November 29.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXII, 533.]

[Col. 1558A]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, FREDERICK, illustrious king of the Romans, emperor ever august: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The envoys of the imperial magnificence, our venerable brother O., bishop of Brandenburg, and S., abbot of Hersfeld, who had been sent to our predecessor Urban, came to us, honored us by their bodily presence, [Col. 1558B] showed due reverence, and set forth what the imperial excellency had instructed them to convey to our aforesaid predecessor. We indeed found it most welcome to learn that the imperial mind was firmly fixed upon that saying: “Pursue peace and lay hold of it.” We think, however, that there is no need for much urging of this matter with us, since we have always desired its good and now desire it all the more, inasmuch as both the need of this cause and of the office which we hold, and the common good of Christendom, require it more urgently.

Nevertheless, it did not seem appropriate to us that, before the imperial letters concerning our election had reached the Church, we should engage in any negotiations [Col. 1558C] by which we might appear improperly, and contrary to the dignity of the priestly office, to seek imperial favor. For we hope, according to the disposition which the Lord has already bestowed upon us, that He will direct us in His truth and make us always seek the things that make for peace, so that neither the greatness of the Empire nor other Christian kings and princes may find in us a just occasion for appearing less devoted to God or less reverent toward the Church.

Indeed, we recognize our own insufficiency and know that we cannot usefully bear the burden imposed upon us, or meet those evils which have befallen the Christian people in this time, except through the help of great persons. God has therefore inspired your Imperial Highness to carry out in deeds what you have shown your envoys and in letters, [Col. 1558D] and to form your judgment concerning our excommunication not so much from report as from action; for, by God’s aid, we have so disposed ourselves that the Church of God ought not to remain in scandal through any fault of ours.

Given at Parma, on the third day before the Kalends of December, in the sixth indiction.

XIX. To Henry, emperor-elect of the Romans.—Of similar tenor. (Parma, November 29.)

[Ibid.]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, HENRY, illustrious king, emperor-elect of the Romans: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1559A] As we labor upon this great and wide sea and are tossed by diverse waves of thought, consolation came to us from the royal letters, when we learned that the royal mind is so inclined toward reverence for the Church that, with God’s help, we judge that we shall not labor without fruit for the salvation of the Christian people if we receive the favor of your greatness, as we confidently hope. We therefore admonish and exhort you in the Lord to persevere toward your mother, the Church, in the good purpose which you have begun, and to strive to show yourself acceptable to God and His ministers by words and deeds.

For we hope that, during our administration, the Church will conduct herself toward the royal eminence of the Romans, by the Lord’s favor, in such a way that the royal eminence may rejoice that its honor [Col. 1559B] has been preserved for it, and that the Christian people may not be deprived of the benefit for which they hope through the conflicting wills of those chiefly entrusted with their governance. We certainly are not accustomed to use, nor do we desire to use, many lofty words; rather, we ask the Lord God to make us walk in truth and uprightness, and to adorn our modest estate not so much with the leaves of words as with the fruits of deeds. Let the royal magnificence know, moreover, that the envoys whom you sent have conducted themselves in such a way that the royal magnificence ought well to be pleased with them.

Given at Parma, on the third day before the Kalends of December, in the sixth indiction.

XX. To F[olmar], archbishop of Trier.—On the calamity of the Eastern Church. He rejects harsh policies and reproves the archbishop of Trier for censures against princes and prelates, because he had been more severe than was just. (At Foro Novo, November 30.)

[LUDEWIG, *Reliquiae manuscriptorum diplomatum*, vol. II, p. 428.]

[Col. 1559C]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother F., archbishop of Trier: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Purpose overcomes inclination, and circumstances that arise often compel one to alter what had been firmly determined by the will. Nor does this leave room for blame, [Col. 1559D] since Solomon says: “There is a time for everything, and a time for speaking and a time for silence.” Accordingly, the Church of God sometimes changes her institutions because of the needs of her children, and often restrains or postpones the punishment which she had determined to inflict in a calm and peaceful time, in accordance with Solomon’s saying: “The wise man, seeing evil, turns aside; the fool passes on boldly.”

Even if this prudence can be set aside at another time, it must be observed all the more circumspectly at this time, because the Christian people seem to be in greater turmoil as a result of the calamity of the Eastern Church. Nor is the outcome easily apparent to human weakness unless the hearts of great princes are moved toward it by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. For this reason, [Col. 1560A] and for many others, wishing through the humility of the Church to draw the hearts of the exalted princes and defenders of the Church—namely, the emperor and his son—toward the good, we consider that we must proceed with them in gracious mildness, and seek help not so much against them as from God, should they determine, as we do not believe they will, to withdraw the reverence due to the Church.

Therefore, since your brotherhood, after departing from our predecessor Lord Urban and entering the province of Trier, began to proceed against bishops and other persons more harshly than seemed expedient, and, though you caused scandal to many, brought few into favor with yourself, we, wishing according to the customary moderation of the Apostolic See to provide that, through your harshness, you do not alienate from yourself the minds of many [Col. 1560B] and eventually render ecclesiastical censure itself contemptible if it is not observed, forbid you by these present letters to proceed to the excommunication or deposition of persons in the province of Trier without our knowledge and permission. Rather, maintain moderation in all things, so that, through some animosity or past indignation, you do [not] make the Church’s cause—and your own—more grievous. Since you are by no means wholly unaware of what has seemed good to us from the beginning concerning your affair, you will, as we believe, take good care for yourself if you strive in all things to show yourself such that we need have no unfavorable opinion of you.

Given at Foro Novo, on the second day before the Kalends of December, [Col. 1560C] in the sixth indiction.

XXI. He confirms the privilege granted to the abbot of Tegernsee by Otto, bishop of Freising. (At Fornovo, November 30.)

[Monumenta Boica, VI, 192.]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the abbot of Tegernsee: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to effective completion the requests which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we apostolically confirm to you and to your church, and fortify with the protection of this present document, the privilege [Col. 1560D] which our venerable brother, the bishop of Freising, moved by pious consideration, granted to your monastery concerning a certain monastery established on the estate of your church and in his diocese, insofar as it was canonically made and has been peacefully observed until these times. Let no person whatsoever, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Fornovo, on the second day before the Kalends of December, in the sixth indiction.

XXII. To all the faithful of Christ. (October–December.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXII, 535.]

[Col. 1561A]

“From the administration,” etc. (“Since creditors bind debtors by oath to pay them interest, to the manifest peril of their souls, we, wishing in accordance with the duty of our office to provide for their salvation, to remove this wicked burden from debtors, and especially from those who have pledged themselves or given assistance toward preparing relief for the land of Jerusalem for one man [reading uncertain]), command that you compel those creditors, by the severity of ecclesiastical discipline and with every contrary apostolic impediment removed, to release the oaths given concerning the payment of interest.

XXIII. To all bishops. (October–December.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 1561B]

We decree that clerics shall wear closed garments; they shall not use red or green copes or mantles, nor shall they add silk fabric or any other silken cloth to them. They shall not wear rings on their hands unless they are bishops entitled to do so by virtue of their office. They shall have a suitable crown and tonsure; they shall entirely avoid games of dice and gaming-tables, and the pursuit of hunting; and they shall apply themselves suitably to ecclesiastical offices and other human [perhaps “humane”] studies. If anyone should presume to violate this, let him be corrected by his bishop, with every apostolic impediment removed; and meanwhile let him be deprived of the immunity known to have been instituted for the protection of clerics and the restraint of lay violence.

Men likewise shall not wear garments cut open from below; and henceforth women shall not wear costly garments exceeding the length of their own bodies, [Col. 1561C] but shall go about in decent and moderate dress, which neither indicates wantonness nor displays the boastfulness of vanity. Whoever, man or woman, shall henceforth make use of such garments shall be excluded from communion of the Lord’s body until he or she reforms, and shall not be permitted to attend ecclesiastical services; moreover, such a person shall undergo a heavier punishment through the ministry of the priest if even thus he or she does not take care to correct this frivolity.

XXIV. Privilege for the monastery of St. Paul at Parma. (October–December.)

[AFF., *Storia di Parma*, II, 396.]

[Col. 1561D]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, ROMANA, abbess of the monastery of St. Paul at Parma, and her sisters, present and future, who profess the regular life: in perpetuity.

The Apostolic See ought to grant protection to prudent virgins, who, under the habit of religion, with lamps kindled through works of holiness, continually prepare themselves to go forth to meet the Bridegroom, lest an assault of any rashness either recall them from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of sacred religion. [Col. 1562A] Therefore, beloved daughters in Christ, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery of St. Paul at Parma, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document. First, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in that monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure [Col. 1562B] and unimpaired to you. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself where the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its houses, vineyards, gardens, mills, watercourses, and all appurtenances; whatever you have in the city of Parma and its district; the church of St. Barnabas near Parma, on the bank of the city ditch; the church of St. Nicomedes of Glarola; the church of St. Lawrence of Verlatica; the church of St. Paul of Rivola, with all their appurtenances; the church of St. Blaise of Turrile; the church of Sinzanese; in the diocese of Mantua, the church of St. Mary of Bosco with all its appurtenances; the church of St. Mary [Col. 1562C] of the Castle of Old Godi, with the castle, mills, watercourses on the Mincio, and all their appurtenances; whatever you have at Campitello; at Sabloneta; at Bajolis; at St. Nazarius and Flexo; in the three hamlets; in the village of St. Paul of Rivola; at Gainago and Puteolisi, with their appurtenances; in the village of Ferraria, in lands and mills; in the village of Scola; at Paradigni; at Monterone; at Rivarolo; at Vigopolo; at Massera and Vicopolo, with their appurtenances; at Sparmatico and Minganzola; at Meletulo; in the enclosures [Col. 1562D] of St. Leonard; and in all their appurtenances; in the hamlet of Barunculus; in the castle of Walterolus; and in the new castle beyond the Lenza; at Povillo, Coleredo, and Bosseto; at Casadego, Molandriano, and Albari; and on the island by the bank of the Po; at Fugnano, Runculo, Elli, and Fabrore; at Guandalese, Valeri, Vigoferdili, Madrogulo, Curia Collecti, and Tavernula; the castle of Glarola with all its lands, cultivated and uncultivated, mills, watercourses, meadows, woods, pastures, plains, mountains, valleys, hills, and everything belonging to that castle; whatever you have in the village of Opplani and its appurtenances; whatever you have at Fisano, [Col. 1563A] Coladula, Azano, Gallano, and Segalaria; whatever you have at St. Andrew’s, on the plain of Charles, at Verozano, Mataledo, Laterado, Tefaga, Puvilano, and on the island, with all their appurtenances. You may receive persons free and released from secular ties who flee from the world for conversion, and retain them without any opposition.

Furthermore, we forbid any of your sisters, after making profession in that place, to depart from it without her abbess’s permission, except for the sake of a stricter religious life; and no one shall dare retain one who departs without a guarantee in letters from the community. Moreover, since tithes are assigned by canonical institution to churches and ecclesiastical persons, [Col. 1563B] we forbid under threat of anathema that any layman presume to extort tithes from you. When a general interdict is imposed upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, and in a subdued voice. We also prohibit by apostolic authority anyone from pronouncing against you or your monastery a sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict without manifest and reasonable cause, or from imposing upon you, your churches, or your people new or undue exactions.

On the death of you, the present abbess of that place, or of any one of your sisters succeeding you there, no woman shall be set over the community by any trick of surreptitious procurement or by force, [Col. 1563C] except the one whom the sisters, by common consent or the sounder part of the sisters, shall provide to be elected according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. We also forbid anyone to presume to build anew a church or oratory within the bounds of your parishes without your consent and that of the diocesan bishop, while preserving the privileges of the Roman Church. Moreover, wishing henceforth to provide with paternal concern for your peace and tranquility, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone from committing theft or robbery within the precinct of your houses or places, setting a fire, seizing or killing a person, or rashly exercising any violence.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its [Col. 1563D] possessions, retain property taken away, diminish it, or harass it by any vexations; but let all things be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those uses for whose governance and support they were granted. If therefore in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

XXV. To the abbot and archbishop of Nonantola. (About December.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXII, 535.]

We remember that we formerly commanded you by apostolic letters, concerning your cleric Pagano, to restore the prebend which you had taken from him on account of a marriage which he was said to have contracted with a certain woman. You paid no heed to carry this out in accordance with our letters [Col. 1564A], asserting that it gave rise to scandal among others. Therefore, lest the aforesaid cleric, deprived of the assistance of an ecclesiastical benefice, be forced to return to pursuing shameful and secular gains—when many concubinarians and adulterers are maintained from the goods of the Church—and since he is established in such orders that the sacred canons exclude a man lawfully married from an ecclesiastical benefice, we earnestly request your discretion and command you through the Apostolic See to confer upon him, outside the communities of brethren, a benefice from which he may receive support.

### XXVI. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the canons of the Church of Genoa (fragment).  
*(Pisa, December 11.)*

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, IV, 875.]

[Col. 1564B]

Given at Pisa, through the hand of Moses of the Lateran, acting in place of the chancellor, on the third Ides of December, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1187, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gregory VIII.

I, Gregory, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri, have subscribed. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Callistus at St. Mary across the Tiber, have subscribed. I, Melior, priest-cardinal of the title of Pamachius of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed. I, James, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. [Col. 1564C] I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Octavian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed. I, Rodulphus, deacon-cardinal of St. Gregory at the Golden Veil, have subscribed.

### XXVII. He confirms for the monastery of St. Mary of Agnano the church of St. Christina of Clano.  
*(Pisa, December 16.)*

[MITTARELLI, *Annales Camaldulenses*, IV, 158.]

GREGORY, servant of the servants of God, to SAXO, abbot, and to the convent of St. Mary of Agnano: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1564D] It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners, and, by bringing them to effect, fulfill requests which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, concurring with favorable assent in your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the church of St. Christina of Clano, with all its appurtenances, granted to you and to your monastery by Hel, formerly bishop of Arezzo, of good memory, just as you reasonably and peaceably possess it and as that grant was lawfully made. Let no person whatsoever, therefore, be permitted to violate this page of our confirmation, etc.

Given at Pisa, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, in the sixth indiction.

[Col. 1565]

## LETTER OF GUIDO, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS, TO POPE GREGORY.  
The bishop of Laon is cleared of the crimes imputed to him.

(*Letters of Peter of Blois*, ed. GILES, Oxford, 1847, letter 165.)

[Col. 1565A] To the most holy Father and lord G., by the grace of God supreme pontiff: G., by divine permission humble minister of the Church of Sens, and his suffragans, whose seals are appended to these letters, offer the most devoted kisses to your blessed feet.

Since it cannot escape the prudence of your fatherhood that the prelates of Churches, according to the differing deserts of their subjects, are under obligations to them, so that they must honor some with worthy rewards but restrain others, without respect of persons, by deserved punishment, it is evident that those who necessarily offend many cannot please everyone, nor can or ought they to satisfy every person’s will. And therefore, in the midst of this wicked and perverse nation, even those who are like luminaries set [Col. 1565B] in the firmament, holding fast the word of life, are nevertheless today, because of the malice of the envious and slanderers, like a mark set up for an arrow. Of them the prophet rightly said: “Their tongue is a wounding arrow; it has spoken deceit” (Jer. 9). And again: “They have bent their tongue like a bow of falsehood, and not of truth” (ibid.).

And it is indeed fitting that the arrows of little children become their wounds, that their tongues be weakened against them, that iniquity lie against itself, closing its own mouth, and that those who have strengthened for themselves an evil word fail while searching with searching. Their endeavor and labor are to disturb the peace of their prelates, to the ruin of the head of the whole body—that is, to shake the members of the Church—and, in order to cloak their malice under the pretext of a false zeal which they falsely claim to have [Col. 1566A] toward their Churches, by wicked and deceitful allegations to obtain from the Apostolic See an examination by inquiry. They do not heed what the Wise Man says: “Do not lie in wait for nor seek wickedness against the house of the righteous man; do not lay waste his resting-place” (Prov. 24).

Since, then, the venerable Father, the bishop of Laon, has shone among the prelates of the Gallican Church with the prerogative of so many and such great merits, we are confounded and ashamed at the things disseminated against him by wicked men. Since we have known his integrity for a long time past, we unquestionably believe these allegations to be fabricated; and, for that reason, we believe that they ought in no way to be believed by your holiness, but rather to be wholly rejected as unworthy. This is especially so since we unanimously bear witness that [Col. 1566B] among us, with whom he has lived, no unfavorable word concerning him has hitherto been heard; rather, the fame of his serenity and integrity has spread everywhere throughout both provinces like the fragrance of cedar. Thus we may truly say of him what is read concerning Susanna: “The servants were greatly ashamed, because no such report had ever been made concerning Susanna” (Dan. 13).

What is more, not only clerics are ashamed, but priests and laymen, cloistered persons and religious, princes and bishops. Therefore our confidence in conscience concerning his integrity is so great that, before God and before you, most holy Father, we are prepared, should it be necessary, to disperse, by the light of your vindication, the cloud of this fabricated calumny.

**URBAN III, ROMAN PONTIFF**

Historical notice. 1329. Diplomatic notice. 1329.

**LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES**

I.—He takes the church of Saint Evasius at Casale under his protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. 1331.

II.—To the clergy and people of Spoleto.—He announces that he has deferred judgment concerning the vacant archbishopric of Zadar. 1332.

III.—To Peter, archbishop of Spoleto.—He upholds for him the right to have the cross borne before him throughout the whole kingdom of Hungary. 1333.

IV.—A privilege by which he confirms all goods, rights, and possessions of the priory of Saint Peter of Coucy, in the diocese of Soissons, under the obedience and subjection of the monastery of Cluny. 1333.

V.—A privilege by which he confirms all goods and rights of the priory of Blessed Mary of Mont-Desir, of the Cluniac order, in the diocese of Amiens. 1338.

VI.—To Sicard, bishop-elect of Cremona, and the abbot of Saint Lawrence. 1341.

VII.—He confirms the assignment of tithes made to the Venetian church of Saint Sylvester by Mark, bishop of Castello. 1342.

VIII.—He instructs Ralph, bishop of Angers, Maurice, bishop-elect of Nantes, and the abbot of Foucarmont to expel the abbot of Saint Melaine at Rennes, appointed by the count contrary to the privilege of the brethren of Saumur. 1342.

IX.—A bull confirming the judgment rendered by Robert, archbishop of Vienne, and Hugh, abbot of Bonnevaux, concerning controversies between Arducius, bishop, and Count William. 1343.

X.—He confirms the judgment rendered by the bishop of Laon and Martin, provost, that two-thirds of the tithe from lands in the estate of Port-Albare should be paid to the canons of Piacenza. 1346.

XI.—A privilege for the monastery of the Holy Trinity at La Lucerne, in the diocese of Avranches. 1347.

XII.—To all bishops.—On his election. 1351.

XIII.—To Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury.—Of the same subject, and word for word the same as the preceding letter. 1352.

XIV.—He announces to the bishops and all persons established throughout the province of Canterbury that he has entrusted his authority in their province to Archbishop Baldwin. 1353.

XV.—A privilege for the monastery of Saint Sixtus at Piacenza. 1353.

XVI.—He takes the church of Saint Mary of Reno under protection and confirms its possessions and rights. 1355.

XVII.—He takes the Venetian church of Saint Saviour under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. 1357.

XVIII–XIX.—A privilege for the monastery of Saint James at Pontida. 1360.

[Col. 1576] XX.—A privilege for the church of Saint Mary at Spoleto. 1362.

XXI.—He takes the monastery of Saint Mary of Civitacuculla under protection and confirms its goods and rights. 1364.

XXII.—At the request of Abbot Hugh, he takes the monastery of Cluny under protection and confirms certain goods and privileges. 1365.

XXIII.—He confirms the agreement made between the bishop of Saintes and the monks of Aizenay concerning the church of La Rochelle and certain other matters in the bishopric of Saintes. 1367.

XXIV.—He takes the nunnery of Saint Peter of Le Luc under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. 1370.

XXV.—He takes the monastery of Saint Apollinaris of Classe under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. 1371.

XXVI.—He takes the monastery of Saint Saviour of Berardinga under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. 1375.

XXVII.—He declares to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, that the chaplaincy of the church of Saint Vivian at Brollet had been granted by Adhemar, bishop of Saintes, to Theobald, now bishop of Ostia and then abbot of Cluny. 1377.

XXVIII.—He affirms to Gerard, archbishop of Ravenna, the procurations payable by the monasteries of Bologna. 1377.

XXIX.—He decrees that no prelates may presume to exact procurations from the priories of the monastery of Cluny outside those priories. 1379.

XXX.—At the request of Abbot Hugh, he confirms the goods and privileges of the monastery of Cluny. 1379.

XXXI.—He takes the monastery of Tegernsee under protection and confirms its goods. 1383.

XXXII.—He forbids archbishops and bishops henceforth to require any procurations from the priories of the Cluniac brethren, except when they come there for the purpose of visitation. 1385.

XXXIII.—He takes the monastery of Rupes under protection and confirms its goods. 1385.

XXXIV.—Fragment of a privilege for the church of Ravenna. 1387.

XXXV.—A privilege for the hospitaller house of the Brethren of the Cross of Saint Peter at Boice. 1387.

XXXVI.—He takes the monastery of Vallombrosa under protection and confirms its possessions and rights. 1389.

XXXVII.—A privilege for the monastery of Saint Saviour at Pavia. 1391.

XXXVIII.—He takes the monastery of Saint Mary Magdalene of Lund, in England, under protection and confirms its possessions and rights. 1393.

XXXIX.—At the request of Bishop Boniface, he takes the church of Caen under protection and confirms its episcopal goods and rights. 1396.

XL.—At the request of Patriarch Henry, he takes the church of Grado under protection and confirms its privileges. 1397.

XLI.—He confirms the institutions and privileges of the Order of Aridaquamant (Aroasiensian). 1399.

XLII.—He confirms the possessions and privileges of the churches of Saints John and Paul, Saint Martin, Saint Stephen Major, and Saint Stephen Minor, assigned for the support of the canons of the church of Saint Peter at Rome. 1402.

XLII *bis*.—A privilege for the monastery of Saint Peter at Exlon. 1407.

XLIII.—To Emperor Frederick.—He complains of the injuries inflicted by him upon the Roman Church. 1410.

XLIV.—He takes the monastery of Vallombrosa under protection and confirms its rights. 1413.

XLV.—He grants the brethren of Grandmont permission, during a general interdict upon the land, to ring one bell. 1415.

XLVI.—To William, prior of Grandmont.—He establishes various provisions for the peace and tranquillity of the monks of Grandmont. 1416.

XLVII.—A privilege for the church of Saint John the Baptist at Regensburg. 1418.

XLVIII.—A privilege for the church of Saint John at Liège. 1420.

XLIX.—To William, king of Scotland.—In the case of Hugh, bishop of Saint Andrews, and John, bishop of Dunkeld. 1422.

L.—He issues to Jocelin, bishop of Glasgow, and to the abbots of Melrose, Newbattle, and Dunfermline the instructions indicated in the preceding letter. 1424.

LI.—He writes to Henry, king of England, that he has ordered Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to have the revenues of Archdeacon Savaric collected and reserved intact in his custody. 1425.

LII.—He informs the provosts, aldermen, sworn burgesses, mayors, and people of the castle of Valenciennes that he has ordered Roger, bishop of Cambrai, to divide the parish of the church of Saint Sauve into three parts. 1426.

LIII.—He takes the monastery of Saint Mary of Saline Valley under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. 1426.

LIV.—He takes the church of Saint Vincent at Bergamo under protection and confirms its goods and rights. 1429.

LV.—He takes the monastery of Saint Mary of Schäftlarn under patronage and confirms its possessions and rights. 1431.

LVI.—At the request of Bishop Volscalc, he takes the church of Augsburg under protection and confirms its possessions. 1434.

LVII.—He takes the monastery of Saint Mary at Tongerlo under protection and confirms its discipline, possessions, and privileges. 1436.

LVIII.—A privilege for the monastery of Saint Cornelius at Ninove. 1437.

LIX.—He takes the nunnery of Saint Grata at Bergamo under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. 1440.

LX.—To Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury.—Concerning a church to be built in honour of Saints Stephen and Thomas. 1443.

LXI.—He confirms a constitution concerning the revenues of prebends of deceased canons, to be assigned to the restoration of the church for a year. 1443.

LXII.—He commands the bishop of Castello, Venice, to protect the parochial rights of the chapel of Saint Severus. 1444.

LXIII.—He affirms for Ubald, archbishop of Pisa, the primacy of Sardinia. 1444.

LXIV.—He affirms to Absalon, archbishop of Lund, that the castle of Copenhagen will fall to the church of Roskilde after his death. 1444.

LXV.—He confirms the possessions and privileges of the canons of the church of Pisa. 1445.

LXVI.—He emends and confirms the decrees of the council held by Peter, archbishop of Spalato, and his suffragans. 1446.

LXVII.—In the church of Saint George at Brignate, “founded upon his paternal allod,” he establishes a portion of the canons of Crescenzago and endows it with possessions and privileges. He reserves, however, the right of patronage to his brothers and their heirs. 1449.

LXVIII.—He takes the monastery of Saint Mary of the Prison under protection and confirms its goods and rights. 1449.

LXIX.—A bull for the abbey of Exmes. 1451.

LXX.—A privilege for the church of Saint Castor at Cardona. 1457.

LXXI.—He takes the monastery of Saint Peter at Ghent, or Blandinium, under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. 1459.

LXXII.—He takes the monastery of Saint Mary at Sorø under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. 1461.

LXXIII.—A privilege concerning the full liberty of the monks of the island of Cara. 1463.

LXXIV.—He confirms the customs which the church of Chartres has uninterruptedly observed for the preceding forty years. 1465.

LXXV.—He takes the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre at Piacenza under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. 1465.

LXXVI.—He exhorts all the faithful throughout the archbishopric of Ravenna and the bishopric of Ferrara to give money to the brethren of Saint Mary of Reno for the construction of a bridge over the Reno. 1466.

LXXVII.—He informs all bishops of this privilege of the brethren of Saint Mary of Reno: that they may be ordained by whichever Catholic bishop they prefer. 1467.

LXXVIII.—He commands the archbishop of Tarragona and the bishop of Barcelona not to demand obedience from the abbot and brethren of Holy Cross until their dispute concerning the monastery has been settled. 1467.

LXXIX.—He affirms for the sisters of Saint Nicholas at Veurne the annual grant of fifty solidi made by Gertrude, former countess of Maurienne. 1468.

LXXX.—He commands the monks and brethren of the military orders of the Temple and of the Hospital of Jerusalem residing in the city or suburb of Aix not to infringe the rights of the church of Aix. 1468.

LXXXI.—To Reginald, bishop, and the chapter of Chartres.—That houses in the cloister are not to be given or leased by the canons to laypeople. 1469.

LXXXII.—A privilege for the monastery of Saint Mary of the Field of Mars at Rome. 1469.

LXXXIII.—A privilege for the church of Concordia. 1470.

LXXXIV.—He confirms the privileges of the abbots of the Cistercian Order. 1472.

LXXXIV *bis*.—A bull to the citizens of Metz. 1473.

[Col. 1578] LXXXV.—He confirms the goods of the canons of Verona. 1473.

LXXXVI.—A bull for the canons of Modena. 1474.

LXXXVII.—He confirms the possessions of P., provost of Reggio. 1474.

LXXXVIII.—He appoints Henry, archbishop of Bourges, his legate throughout the entire province of Bourges, excepting the monastery of Dol. 1475.

LXXXIX.—He affirms for the Carthusian brethren their free right to elect a prior and procurator. 1476.

XC.—He grants Michael, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter at Modena, and his successors the use of the mitre, sandals, stockings, and gloves. 1476.

XCI.—A privilege for the church of Saint Salvi at Florence. 1476.

XCII.—He appoints Hugh, dean of Paris, and the abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés as judges between the canons of Beauvais and the monks of Saint-Lucian. 1477.

XCIII.—He affirms for the canons of Saint Ursus a vineyard granted by the bishop of Augsburg. 1177.

XCIV.—He confirms the judgment rendered by arbitrators between the monks of Saint-Savin and the canons of the greater church of Piacenza. 1478.

XCV.—To the abbot and convent of Fécamp.—That sons are not to be instituted in their fathers’ churches, but rather are to be removed. 1479.

XCVI.—He affirms for the Parisian canons of Saint Opportuna the church of the Holy Innocents. 1479.

XCVII.—To the abbot and convent of Fécamp.—That no one may pronounce a sentence of excommunication or interdict against their church or persons. 1479.

XCVIII.—He exhorts all the faithful established throughout the province of Ravenna and all who cross the bridge of Saint Mary of Reno to contribute toward completing the bridge. 1480.

XCIX.—A privilege for the monastery of Saint Paul at Parma. 1480.

C.—He affirms for the monastery of Cluny the monastery of Saint Germanus at Auxerre. 1483.

CI.—He affirms for the abbot of Vézelay and his successors the use of the mitre, gloves, and ring. 1484.

CII.—He commands Hubert, bishop of Aix, not to allow the rights of the canons to be violated by the monks of Saint Peter. 1484.

CIII.—He confirms the constitution of the canons of the church of Piacenza: “that, so long as the canons remain honourably at the schools and diligently at their studies, they ought to have for their maintenance one-third of all revenues which they would receive if present in that church; and, one third being left to the brethren, the other part is to be applied to common use.” 1485.

CIV.—He forbids the archpriest and canons of Bologna to inflict injuries upon the brethren of Saint Mary of Reno. 1485.

CV.—He grants G., dean, and the chapter of Chartres “that, if anyone has seized the property of their church and his offence is manifest, the robber may not evade ecclesiastical discipline by the refuge of an appeal.” 1486.

CVI.—He affirms certain possessions for Hugh, abbot, and the canons of the church of Prémontré. 1486.

CVII.—He affirms certain possessions, granted by Count Robert, for the house of Saint Thomas at Paris. 1487.

CVIII.—To Walter, archbishop of Rouen.—That, after an appeal, nothing is to be altered. 1488.

CIX.—He orders all abbots of the Premonstratensian Order established in Germany and Saxony to attend the general chapter of Prémontré annually. 1488.

CX.—To the archbishop of Tours.—At the request of Philip, king of the French, he grants him a truce, so that he may reach an amicable settlement with the church of Dol. 1489.

CXI.—A privilege for the nunnery of Saint Peter at Cremella. 1490.

CXII.—He grants the abbot and convent of Saint-Denis “that no archbishop or bishop may dare to pronounce against them or any of their monks, in head or members, a sentence of excommunication or interdict without the authority of the Roman pontiff, or of a legate sent from his side or having a special mandate in this matter, or even without the command of the abbot.” 1491.

CXIII.—He confirms the parochial boundaries of the Veronese churches of Saint Paul and Saint Vitalis, established by two cardinals. 1491.

CXIV.—He permits Sueno, bishop of Aarhus, after resigning his bishopric, to enter a monastery. 1492.

CXV.—He confirms the goods and rights of the monastery of Saint Nicholas on the Venetian shore. 1492.

[Col. 1579] CXVI.—He confirms the privileges of the monastery of Morimond. 1494.

CXVII.—A privilege for the monastery of Hautecombe. 1494.

CXVIII.—He confirms the possessions and privileges of the Venetian nunnery of Saint Zacharias. (Fragment.) 1496.

CXIX.—To Wichmann, archbishop of Magdeburg.—Concerning injuries inflicted on the Roman Church by Emperor Frederick, and requesting him to intervene as mediator of peace. 1497.

CXX.—He rebukes B[aldwin], archbishop of Canterbury, because he has afflicted the prior and brethren of the church of Canterbury with various injuries and has disregarded their appeal to the Apostolic See. He commands him publicly to declare within ten days “that the sentences of suspension pronounced both against the prior and against the other brethren are not valid; and that he restore to its former state whatever he has attempted after the first appeal to the prejudice of their rights.” He refers to this matter in the following letter. 1498.

CXXI.—He informs the abbots of Battle, Faversham, and Saint Augustine what he has commanded the archbishop of Canterbury in the preceding letter. He commands them: “If the aforesaid archbishop delays beyond the prescribed term to carry out what we command, you shall carry it into execution.” 1499.

CXXII.—He takes the church of Saint Peter at Bologna under protection and confirms its goods and rights. 1500.

CXXIII.—A privilege for the abbey of Saint Ghislain. 1502.

CXXIV.—He takes the monastery of Saint Saviour of Trebbia under protection and confirms its goods and rights. 1505.

CXXV.—To the master and brethren of the Cross-bearing Hospital of Bologna.—He approves their order. 1507.

CXXVI.—He commands Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to abandon the construction of the new church, which the monks of Canterbury had complained to him would be detrimental to them. 1509.

CXXVII.—He informs bishops, abbots, and other prelates of churches throughout England concerning the preceding letter to the archbishop of Canterbury. 1510.

CXXVIII.—He reproaches Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury, because he has not carried out his commands, given on 1 March. 1510.

CXXIX.—He rebukes the abbots of Battle, Faversham, and Saint Augustine because they have neglected his commands. 1511.

CXXX.—A privilege for the church of Pistoia. 1512.

CXXXI.—A bull for the monastery of Blessed Mary of the Vow. 1512.

CXXXII.—He decrees that alienations made by the bishops of Bologna to the detriment of the Church are void. 1515.

CXXXIII.—He decrees that the Order of Saint Benedict shall be preserved in perpetuity in the monastery of Admont; he also confirms all its goods and safeguards the immunity of the place. 1515.

CXXXIV.—He takes the nunnery of Saint Grata at Bergamo under protection and confirms its goods. 1517.

CXXXV.—He takes the nunnery of Saint Euphemia at Modena under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. 1518.

CXXXVI.—He confirms certain privileges of the Premonstratensian Order. 1520.

CXXXVII.—He confirms the laws of the Premonstratensian Order. 1521.

CXXXVIII.—At the request of Bishop Gerard, he confirms the goods of the church of Bologna. 1522.

CXXXIX.—A privilege for the canons of the church of Treviso. (Fragment.) 1524.

CXL.—He prescribes to Peter, bishop-elect of Reggio, that without a special apostolic mandate he is to swear an oath to no mortal person, except to the archbishop of Ravenna when receiving consecration. 1524.

CXLI.—A privilege for the church of Cervia. 1524.

CXLII.—He rebukes most sharply Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, because he persists both in inflicting injuries upon the monks of Canterbury and in neglecting his commands. 1527.

CXLIII.—He commands Reginald, bishop of Bath, Seffrid, bishop of Chichester, and the abbots of Battle and Faversham: “If the archbishop of Canterbury delays more than thirty days in fulfilling our command, you shall put everything into execution.” 1528.

CXLIV.—He grants the prior and convent of Canterbury “that, while the suit between them and B[aldwin], archbishop, is pending, he may dare to pronounce no sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict upon their church or persons.” 1530.

CXLV.—He asks Henry, king of the English, not to allow Archbishop Baldwin to inflict injuries upon the church of Canterbury, and to order the execution of what the judges appointed by himself shall determine. 1530.

CXLVI.—He confirms the judgment rendered by appointed judges between the church of Saint Michael at Nonantola and that of Saint Martin at Causino. 1531.

CXLVII.—A privilege for the monastery of Saint Zeno at Verona. 1532.

Letter of Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury, to Pope Urban.—He rejoices that Urban was raised to the pontificate by unanimous consent after Lucius III, and gives him thanks for the pallium received. 1533.

**GREGORY VIII, ROMAN PONTIFF**

Historical notice. 1535. Diplomatic notice. 1535.

**LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES**

I.—He announces his election to the German clergy and exhorts them to devote themselves to an expedition for the recovery of Palestine. 1537.

II.—To all prelates of churches.—For the administration of justice and the settlement of lawsuits. 1538.

III.—To all the faithful.—Concerning the observance of a fast to appease God whom they have offended. 1339.

IV.—To all Christ’s faithful.—Concerning the disaster at Jerusalem. He admonishes all to do penance and grants full indulgence to those departing for war against the unbelievers. 1539.

V.—He takes the monastery of Lucelle under protection and confirms its possessions and rights. 1543.

VI.—A privilege for the monastery of La Charité at Fougères. 1546.

VII.—He confirms the Order of Calatrava and its possessions. 1548.

VIII.—He forbids the ancient rights of the Savigniac monasteries to be diminished “on account of the Cistercian monks who have been established there.” 1548.

IX.—He appoints the first Sunday of the coming Lent, 6 March 1188, for the canons of the churches of Saint Vincent and Saint Alexander at Bergamo, on which their controversy is to be decided by him. 1549.

X.—To the clergy, magistrates, and people of Bergamo.—He commends Lanfranc, bishop-elect. 1549.

XI.—To the canons of the church of Saint Vincent at Bergamo. 1550.

XII.—He commands two canons of Brescia that one or the other accompany Lanfranc, the bishop-elect, to his see. 1550.

XIII.—He exhorts the bishop of Castello, Venice, to grant the church of Saint Bartholomew to the canons of Saint Saviour. 1551.

XIV.—He exempts the canons of the Venetian church of Saint Saviour from paying tithes. 1552.

XV.—To all bishops, etc., and archdeacons. 1552.

XVI.—He takes the Venetian church of Saint Saviour under protection and confirms its privileges. 1553.

XVII.—A privilege for the church of Saint Apollinaris. 1555.

XVIII.—To Emperor Frederick.—He declares his counsels of peace, that he cherishes goodwill toward him, and that he approves the emperor’s cherishing the same. 1558.

XIX.—To Henry, Roman emperor-elect.—Of similar subject matter. 1558.

XX.—To Folmar, archbishop of Trier.—Concerning the calamity of the Eastern Church. He rejects harsh measures and censures against princes and prelates, and for that reason rebukes the bishop of Trier for having been more severe than justice allowed. 1559.

XXI.—He confirms the privilege of the abbot of Tegernsee established by Otto, bishop of Freising. 1560.

XXII.—To all Christ’s faithful. 1561.

XXIII.—To all bishops. 1561.

XXIV.—A privilege for the monastery of Saint Paul at Parma. 1561.

XXV.—To the abbot and archbishop of Nonantola. 1563.

XXVI.—He confirms the possessions and privileges of the canons of the church of Genoa. (Fragment.) 1564.

XXVII.—He affirms for the monastery of Saint Mary at Agnano the church of Saint Christina of Clano. 1564.

Letter of Guido, archbishop of Sens, to Pope Gregory.—The bishop of Laon clears himself of the crimes imputed to him. 1565.

[Col. 1579] **END OF THE TWO HUNDRED AND SECOND VOLUME.**
